## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or a Universal Library, entire, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, carefully corrected in accordance with the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, and with titles at the upper margin of each page marking the subject treated; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched by two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father wrote on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other, of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon each scriptural text, and in what places in their works.**

**A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if one considers: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the completeness of correction, both the variety and number of reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the whole course of the work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but for the first time assembled in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.** Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Clerical Library, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. The Patrology has been issued in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. — The two hundred and sixty volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand three hundred francs; the one hundred and sixty volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for one thousand eight hundred francs. — The wholly Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied there only in Latin translation.

# [The Complete Works of Adam the Scot]

[Col. 0009]

## Dedicatory Epistle

To the most illustrious and most reverend Father and Lord in Christ, Lord Charles Fernandez de Velasco, bishop of the Church of Grimbergen; likewise most deserving father abbot of St. Nicholas at the town of Veurne, of the Premonstratensian Order; and counsellor to the Catholic King in the most illustrious and excellent Council of the States of Brabant; etc. Peter Bellerus, printer.

Not by an arbitrary choice, most illustrious prelate, but by a certain spontaneous descent—not through a sought-for pretext, but through the weight of kindred affection—Adam, called the Premonstratensian, the most renowned master and writer of the Norbertine family, comes before your eyes, seeks your episcopal dignity, and commends himself to your familiar consideration. Upon whose name, if he were still living, would he rather have wished the literary offspring of his genius to be inscribed? By whose patronage could it be more securely supported? By whose more gracious address would it be received and cherished in its bosom? Indeed, long ago he himself dedicated and commended the most refined offspring of his intellect to be handled and worn by the minds and hands of the most reverend prelates. For he, the most vigorous commander of the white confraternity, knew no more willing resting-place than the bosom of a pure heart, nor a more honorable one than beside the foremost men and bishops of the same institute. Why say more? The argument and the entire subject matter of his writing lead to the same point. He illumines the order of Premonstratensian canons with the splendor of manifold learning; through its antiquity he wins it reverence; through the eminent rank of its dignity he secures its authority; and he perfumes it with the fragrant odor of the virtues it promises. For while he forms the conduct of all by most salutary counsels, lays beneath the life of each individual a kind of foundation of precepts, and fortifies unwary minds against the precipices of vices as with hedges, he especially sets forth every part of religious discipline, private and public, and the ascent to perfection in unfeigned charity and the unity of the Spirit. Shall I mention that at other times, like one of the mystic clouds, he soars aloft through the heavenly spaces of contemplation and, pouring out a channel swollen with the dew of celestial speech, waters the lower minds of his readers? Or that, like a dove, taking wings in an exalted and elevated region of the mind, he spreads abroad amid the rains and breezes of the heights the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures? Yet he requires a reader in whom he may prove this: that the reader’s purpose be the same as the teacher’s—namely, that the former should desire to advance no less than the latter desires to be useful. The combined dignity of the person and of the subject possesses great weight, toward which every mind readily and willingly inclines. Just as a silver or ivory vessel, carved by a skillful hand and polished by ingenious art, is commonly esteemed more highly, and as it matters greatly from whose right hand a weapon is hurled, so, in order that memorials of doctrine may penetrate, the weight of concentrated authority is above all helpful—as occurs here.

I trust that no other gift could have been more welcome to Your Reverence, not merely because he is a member of your household and fellow initiate, nor even chiefly because of what we have already said, but especially because of the likeness of life and the uprightness of your conduct, which the author sets forth and refines in his writings. What each person loves and possesses, he wishes others also to love; and he hates those who disagree. That the ancient Fathers are your delight and your love may be inferred from this: all who know you venerate your striving to follow closely in their footprints and to emulate the greatness of their deeds. I often recall hearing you quote the maxim of the Doctor of Stridon:

> “My purpose is to read the ancients, to test each matter, to retain what is good, and not to depart from the faith of the Catholic Church.”

[Note: [Col. 0009] St Jerome, vol. I, letter to Minervius and Alexander.]

I do not enter upon particular actions, lest I should seem importunately and vexatiously to disturb your modesty—which looks to God alone as witness and rewarder—and thus incur rebuff rather than gratitude.

Receive, therefore, most illustrious prelate, this outstanding herald of the regular discipline which you so zealously desire to preserve; receive this teacher and master of spiritual life, while you daily form your subjects, cultivated in virtue and learning, by exhorting them and setting their steps before them. Alphonsus, that most celebrated of kings, is reported to have replied that sounder counsels and more reliable answers could nowhere be drawn than from men long dead. The pagans assert that Apollo’s oracle gave Zeno, who asked how he might attain the path of virtue, this answer: he should put on the complexion of a dead man—that is, he should read the deeds of the ancients and the writings of forefathers who had ceased in body. Nor did Sirach appear to refer the pursuit of true wisdom to anything else when he declares: “The wise man will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients” (Ecclus. 39). Hugh explains these words concerning the purple-clad Fathers: “Of all the ancients,” that is, he will seek the savor and knowledge of heavenly things, which the ancients possessed more fully; “he will seek,” that is, he will seek it apart from other things; “the wise man,” that is, the ecclesiastical man. And Jeremiah the prophet says: “Ask concerning the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jer. 6:16).

May the renowned preachers of the Word of God in your celebrated monastery, stirred by the guidance of the star going before them, also receive this master, almost the equal of the holy Fathers. Called from this spring to their chairs, may they draw the health-giving water whose irrigation multiplies the young growth, makes the beautiful places of the wilderness rich, fills the valleys with grain, and girds the hills with rejoicing (Ps. 64:11–13). Let them drink the clear water which they may afterward lead outside and distribute in the streets: the water from their own cistern and the stream from their own well (Prov. 5:15–16); for those whose house possesses an abundant store and rich resources need not live by begging.

Allow it, then, most illustrious prelate, to go forth into the world adorned by your splendor, and to illuminate the firmament of the Church. I rejoice greatly that this work has been entrusted to my press: partly because, although unequal to repaying thanks for the benefits conferred on me by Your Excellency, I was at least given the opportunity publicly to acknowledge myself your debtor, so that I might not appear altogether ungrateful; and partly because, by this new favor, a kind of hereditary right remained and was confirmed to me. Not to mention the very many other writers of the order printed by our house, Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, a most eloquent author and well known to the Beller press, first saw the light some thirty years ago. May God grant that, following the example of such prelates, men most learned in every respect and most thoroughly versed in every branch of knowledge—men with whom the whole White Order throughout Belgium abounds—may take up their pens and make known to the world that Premonstratensians not only act nobly but also, though some have seemed to deny it, have known how to write both formerly and now. It has always been, and still is, a delight to me for the writings of such men to sweat beneath our press; my presses desire to overflow with no nobler vintage. For publishing their works I gladly and joyfully devote, offer, and consecrate to the most white-clad order my types, cares, labor—in short, my whole self. I conclude by humbly kissing the hands of Your Excellency. May God, the Father of all, preserve you safe in the blessed and lasting governance of His Church.

This is the prayer of

Your Most Illustrious Paternity’s servant,  
**Peter Bellerus.**

[Col. 0011]

## Introduction to the Reader

We bring into the light and common use Master Adam the Premonstratensian, distinguished by eminent learning, exalted by rank, and very famous by ancestral descent, clothed in more fitting dress. Ancient records declare that he was the first among our own men of the White House in Scotland—whose inhabitants call it Whithorn—to ascend to an episcopal chair joined to the governance of a religious community. Of the rest, I would almost venture to declare him alone an evangelical preacher and most praiseworthy writer, equal to his dignity, whom that flourishing first age of our fathers produced; indeed, I would say that it preserved him among the best men, though mutilated, through the darkness of declining times, so that clear testimony may declare how great a good the intervening centuries have denied us. Would that some kinder genius might bring to our notice from the shipwrecked abyss of oblivion his remaining written works, which we suspect lie hidden somewhere in libraries! Whoever you are who read this, breathe upon the matter, and do not conceal from lovers the desired hem of this most beautiful garment.

“The soul of a holy man sometimes speaks truth, more than seven watchmen sitting on high to keep watch” (Ecclus. 37:18), according to the maxim of the Wise Man. Mariners certainly have their watchers stationed at the top of the mast to announce approaching dangers and to scout rocks, shallows, lands, and harbors. So we seem to hear that this man, set by the divine hand as a watchman and scout—such as he professes himself elsewhere to be—keeps vigil and thunders from a lofty lookout of the mind above the walls of Jerusalem.

Here begin the course of a better life; proceed and persist here. Thus you will attain the prize in an unhindered race. These are the weapons for pursuing enemies; take that shield for warding off blows. Turn away from that path which leads to precipices. Let this be the discipline for monasteries, that the rule for individuals. Put on this complete armor of moral conduct for all; by that way you will climb the summit of contemplation, to which no one comes unless he receives it. Do you have authority? Exercise it faithfully, wisely, and profitably. Are you under authority? Then act humbly and patiently. Do you live together with others, and, as I may say, dwell with them? Then do so gently and cheerfully. Who speaks truer words for us than he in the poet:

> These precepts the father gave. Like that aged helmsman  
> Of a ship, whom many a stormy winter has tested,  
> Now weary of sea and warfare, he entrusts to his son  
> The ocean reins of the alder-built vessel;  
> He teaches its hazards and arts—by what star  
> The hand may be guided, and by what control the waves may be mastered.

So faithfully and successfully did he conduct the business of posterity, if I may apply a few borrowed words of the philosopher [Note: [Col. 0011] Seneca, *Letters*, 8.]: he wrote for them certain things that could benefit them. He committed salutary admonitions to writing, like compositions of useful medicines, having found them effective upon his own wounds; although these were not wholly healed, they had ceased to spread. “I point out to others,” he says, “the straight path which I learned too late and only after being wearied by wandering.”

Indeed, as our author says [Note: [Col. 0013] In the Preface to Part I], while the life-giving and most sweet delights of the orthodox Fathers so greatly abound, “I blushed, and not without cause, to set before those who sit down to them not merely often but continually the tasteless vegetable of my poverty, and, amid the clearest torrents, to offer my muddy marsh.” Yet, as he subsequently admits, drawn by the prayers of his contemporaries and compelled by the command of his superiors, he applied his mind to study and his hand to the pen. Both the material which this outstanding speaker had delivered in preaching and what he had absorbed from the anointing of the Spirit teaching concerning all things, he dedicated in this literary offspring to his fellow initiates. Elsewhere he openly affirms that, from the most fruitful field of the Fathers, taking the seeds of arguments and the sources of reasons, and with permission, as it were, granted by the Bethlehemite Boaz, he shook out and gathered the remaining ears that had escaped the hands of the reapers. Hence, he says [Note: [Col. 0013] Letter to Abbot John], it is plain that those who rebuke me as Ruth gathering ears agree neither with you nor with your reapers: you permit her to reap, while they censure her for gathering. Therefore, standing with the earlier Fathers, let him say with the humble mind of the ecclesiastical sage:

> “And I, the last, awoke, like one gathering grapes after the grape-gatherers” (Ecclus. 33:16).

But more confident in hope of divine generosity:

> “In the blessing of God I too have hoped; and, like one gathering grapes, I filled the winepress” (ibid., v. 17).

Now, turning back toward posterity:

> “Consider that I have not labored for myself alone, but for all who seek instruction. Hear me, great men, and all peoples; rulers of the Church, receive with your ears” (ibid., vv. 18–19).

Thus our author teaches what he learned, not from himself—that is, not from presumption, the worst of teachers, as St Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0013] In the *Epitaph of Paula*, near the end]—but from the illustrious men of the Church. For no other reason does Hesychius, St Augustine’s intimate correspondent in Letter 79 [Note: [Col. 0013] Letter 79 in St Augustine], praise St Jerome for following the sense of the ancients; nor for a different reason does St Bernard commend Ambrose and Augustine in his letter to Hugh [Note: [Col. 0013] Letter 77] of St Victor. Finally, Thomas Aquinas, the distinguished glory of theologians in the *Summa Scholastica*, praises Gregory Nazianzen for having submitted his learned sickle to the preceding age of the Fathers. Before them, men thought that they ought to rise, as before a gray head (Lev. 19:32), no otherwise than by the oracle of the Holy Spirit.

A farmer, wishing to make a tasteless and barren tree useful to humankind, grafts onto it shoots borrowed from the branches of a fruitful olive, so that the wild olive may abound in sweet fruitfulness. In the same way, one who desires to rise into the wished-for fruits must be grafted onto and take cuttings from those sound and venerable Fathers, whom the hand of the evangelical gardener planted like olive trees in the field of His Church. Nor is it wholly empty that the common saying declares that the best is what first flows from a vessel. It is not difficult to observe that, from the beginning of many religious orders, those writers nearest the first age—boiling, as it were, with the new wine of the original spirit—quickly surpassed later authors, breathed something more vigorous, and bore away the palm. Just as sea water is said to be sweeter at the bottom than at the surface, so we find that the studies of an older and better age penetrated more deeply and display a certain sweetness tempered by paternal authority. Such is our author, whom we possess and commend: a companion of the first age, the first fervor, and the firstfruits of the Spirit from the founding of the Premonstratensian institute.

Concerning him I especially approve the practice of religious men, namely that of the convent of the Reverend Fathers the Celestines at Paris: during bodily refreshment, when food is required by the mouth and the Word of God hungered for by the ears, they customarily have this master of spiritual life read aloud from manuscript, particularly on solemn days, as the elders of their community have reported. Elsewhere, namely in the Prolegomena, I have assigned him his share of praise, particularly to the end—using St Jerome’s expression [Note: [Col. 0014] To Fabiola, *On the Priestly Garment*: “an examination of doctrine and truth.”]—that the authority of doctrine may not be destroyed by worthless works. For it becomes disgraceful to fit the sound of one’s tongue and one’s pen to a style, and yet to shape one’s mind according to the conduct of others; because, as St Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0014] *City of God*, book II, ch. 7], from old contagion people are more accustomed to consider what Jupiter did than what Plato taught or Cato judged. But our author replies [Note: [Col. 0014] In the Preface to the Second Sermon]:

> “Granted that he may be unskilled, yet he is not devoid of love. Provided that he sees the presence of that which builds up, the wise man will not rashly pronounce judgment upon the absence of that which puffs up.”

As you know, Paul calls the former charity and the latter knowledge. People say that the pyrites gemstone does not reveal its hidden fires unless someone rubs or strikes it; so the power of expression itself and the grace hidden in its veins will smile more sweetly upon one who looks within.

> By delighting and at the same time moving the reader,  
> This book earns its bronze among the Sosii; it crosses the sea,  
> And extends a long age for its renowned author.

But who can see, in these ulcerated latter times, the many who profess a higher degree of holiness in the clergy of the Church—whether they live in monasteries or mixed among the world—and not grieve that, through a certain languor of sloth, idleness, hostile to the soul according to the thundering words of Sacred Scripture, is so welcome to them, while letters are hateful and virtue neglected? Yet, unless they wish to dissemble, they cannot be ignorant of how great is the necessity of uprightness laid upon them, since, raised more highly into the Lord’s portion by the clothing bestowed upon them of holiness and by their professed purpose of life, enrolled in the sanctuary of the Church, they act before the eyes of the Judge who sees all things and dispenses rewards to the good and punishments to the evil.

> Why do they weary a spirit smaller than eternal counsels?

Our Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance, aptly says [Note: [Col. 0015] Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance in Hainaut, *On the Silence of Clerics*, ch. 49]:

> “This seems to me to be the office of a cleric; this is especially assigned to the cleric above others: since he loves God, separated from the occupations in which the life of secular persons is entangled, his chief effort should be devoted to reading and writing.”

And again [Note: [Col. 0015] Letter 17 to Count Henry]:

> “It is not idle leisure, but useful employment, to serve literature and to discover frequently in it what rightly delights or benefits; for I think that God wished such writings to be cultivated in the Church so that, through their cultivation, He whom they proclaim might be known and loved more.”

Noble indeed are the sentiments of the speaker [Note: [Col. 0015] Seneca, *Letters*, 8]:

> “All things that superfluous labor sets up as ornament and glory should be despised. One must consider that nothing is wonderful except the mind, for nothing is great to a great mind.”

[Note: [Col. 0016] See St Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, ch. 5.]

That our blessedness is within—that is, in the mind—is the settled consensus of the orthodox Fathers.

> “The strength of men lies within,” says that Roman-clad and Christian philosopher,  
> “hidden in the innermost citadel.”

[Note: [Col. 0016] Boethius, *Consolation*, book IV, metrical poem 3.]

As for what belongs to this small work of mine—or rather, to the grace of divine assistance supporting my weakness—let the kindly and candid reader not immediately attribute it to rashness, nor, I beg, at once accuse it of presumption. I do not deny that it is more necessary for one who has entered the inner chambers of my house to recognize what I lack and to confine himself within the barriers of silence and quiet than to go abroad or “walk in great matters, as in things too wonderful for me,” as the poet sings:

> Consider what you are not; let the cobbler display his own wares.  
> Keep within yourself, that you may know how scant your furniture is.

And, to speak almost in the words of our author: just as unequal in strength as a contest between a tortoise rolled up within its shell and a most swift tiger, or between a burrowing mole and an eagle concerning keenness of sight, or between an ant and a lion concerning its gait, would it be for my powers to equal those older and sounder Fathers in writing—indeed, even to penetrate their sublime meanings by reading.

> It is right that each person measure himself by his own rule and standard.

Yet it was not the purpose of this most wise master Adam of ours, nor of our foremost Fathers, that I should tread steps commensurate with theirs. Rather, to the best of my ability, I intended to rescue from darkness, and offer for the benefit and use of many, one whom the anointing of the heavenly Spirit is manifestly shown to have attended, so that his little flask, kindled by the sevenfold lamp, might by sharing itself—without diminution—heal and inflame many. Therefore, when some years ago, by chance or by the guidance of a favorable genius, as often happens, I came upon a copy from an old and corrupt edition, and a nearer inspection of the author of our profession inflamed my mind—an author contemporary with the Fathers who gave beginnings to the Premonstratensian Order and extended its bounds—I discovered that he treats matters of regular life worthy of being weighed in a balance, rises with all the force of his expression, and leads the reader where the state of the world, above the moon,

> Is disturbed by no cloud in everlasting serenity.

Finally, he seems to portray upon a tablet:

> The ordered law and sacred right of the mind, the holy recesses  
> Of thought, and a heart steeped in noble honor.

Accordingly I gave my study and mind to whether he might be read by more people in a cleaner and more corrected form. Nor did I grieve without inward complaint that so great a light had until then lain dormant beneath a silent shadow. Therefore either my own inclination, or God, impelled me to investigate his life and writings.

I reckon two consolations from the favor granted me by heaven. The first is that I have spent not a few hours—not idly and, I hope, not wholly without use—in cleansing and polishing works otherwise most refined, as though licking the cubs of a bear or, as they say, sweeping out the Augean stable. Those who have experienced it will be better able to judge what labor and weariness it is to wrestle, with uncertain success and like blindfolded gladiators, both with an old and stained edition and with a manuscript whose words are for the most part abbreviated, broken off, or decayed; especially where there are no variant copies against which the transcription may be compared, nor even the autograph itself by which the rest may be tested as by a plumb line. Thus one must frequently act as an interpreter, or even as a prophet. So many things are suspended, disconnected, or diminished.

My other consolation is the fine saying of Salvian, that prelate most renowned for learning and holiness [Note: [Col. 0016] *On Providence*, preface to book IV]:

> “The intention of a good undertaking and pious vow, even if it does not attain the effect of the work begun, nevertheless has the reward of the will. For before God the effort of one who strives to benefit many is neither futile nor empty.”

And this saying of our most blessed patron Augustine encourages me [Note: [Col. 0016] *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 11]:

> “The outstanding characteristic of good minds is to love truth in words, not the words themselves.”

[Col. 0017] For what use is a golden key if it cannot open what we want? Or what harm is a wooden one if it can, when we seek nothing but that what is shut may be opened? Yet because eating and learning have some likeness to one another, even the very foods without which one cannot live must, because of the distaste of many, be seasoned. Such being the case, St Jerome concludes [Note: [Col. 0017] Preface to the Books of Kings]:

> “I beg you, reader, do not regard labor as a rebuke of the ancients.”

And I add: of the elders as well. In the temple of God each person offers what he can. While others offer gold, silver, and precious stones, as he goes on to say, it is well with us if we offer skins and goats’ hair.

At first I wavered whether it would be more in my own interest or in the public interest to shorten somewhat, or substitute other words for, certain expressions which might seem not wholly to conform to the rules of our grammar and to be difficult in reading or syntax because of obsolete usage and form—such as *degui*, a past tense form, *innotesco* in an active sense, and a few similar examples. But when I discovered through the course of time itself that not only his manner of expression but even his thoughts and inflections of words were native, familiar, and consonant with those ancient Fathers—Augustine, Gregory, Maximus, Bernard, Anselm, Hugh and Richard of St Victor, and the rest—I at once withdrew from that intention and followed the author’s footsteps more closely. If here or elsewhere, because of gaps and scribal confusions, necessity advised an insertion, transposition, deletion, or insufficient correction of a word, it crept in unawares; in the copied text a hasty pen slightly altered it without my effort or attention. No malice or obstinacy was involved.

> For the string does not give the sound the hand and mind intend;  
> Often, when asked for a low note, it gives a high one.  
> Nor will the bow always strike whatever it threatens.

Nor shall I wholly conceal that, in order to cut off an easy harvest of criticism and fault-finding, I returned the books of the unseemly edition to the file and anvil with religious and learned men appointed for this work by the reverend general superior of our order. With the prior of the Celestine convent—whom I have mentioned elsewhere—I often compared every intricate passage; I repeatedly reread them with others; and I willingly admitted others to share my judgment and examination, and, if errors appear, my responsibility for them. Yet I do not deny that certain mistakes remain; nor do I wish therefore to be called fraudulent. If a vintager gathers the larger and obvious grapes but passes over a few hidden and smaller ones, he is not charged with deceit; so neither should I be blamed if some minor points have escaped inattentive eyes or hands, since I wished to preserve and uphold complete and unaltered fidelity to the author.

> Yet there are faults which we should wish to have forgiven.

It is easy to observe that the summaries of sermons and chapters, divisions of words, punctuation of meanings, references to Holy Scripture, and syllables added so that the reader might grasp the whole context at a glance are editorial additions. In the Prolegomena I may seem to some to have been too expansive and to others not expansive enough. The former do not fail to know that everyone is inclined to praise what he possesses; nor do the latter fail to know that a novice archer easily shoots beyond or short of the intended circle. Without prior authority and writing by others, I have wished to assert very little. I have left more matters especially for debate, both to avoid the judgments of this harsh age, in which, as the Christian poet says [Note: [Col. 0017] St Prosper, *On Ingratitude*, ch. 33]:

> Error harms so much  
> That it is thought helpful to err; and the contagions of an old disease  
> Steal upon us so pleasantly that we love the very thing by which we are sick;

and because no greater certainty concerning the author has shone upon us. Such matters include whether he earned the antonomastic title “Doctor of Contemplation”; his lineage and genealogy; the place of his birth, religious profession, and manner of life; his degree of rank, length of life, death; and similar matters. In these I have proceeded either by holding back my step or by setting it down tremblingly and without certainty.

> Such is the path through woods beneath an uncertain moon,  
> Under an unfriendly light.

Elsewhere I have wandered off the road. Do not then lash or scourge me insolently; rather bring me back, if you hear and love me. Have you discovered something distorted or wrong? Correct it, I say; instruct me, and you may guide me through yourself.

> By wisdom I shall learn to look behind me into the unknown.

As St Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0018] Letter to Jerome, vol. II of Jerome’s works], it is much more praiseworthy gladly to accept one who corrects than boldly to correct one who strays. Let abuse, envy, and serpent-like contention be absent.

> The mind is clouded and bound by reins  
> Wherever these reign.

Just as the harshness of the sky, or a field rough with brambles and burrs, does not produce an abundance of good crops, but rather well-cultivated soil and calm weather do so, in the same way the disposition to mock or tear apart does not extract fruit for the soul from the writings or deeds of the orthodox. Rather, it is produced by serenity of mind, eagerness to improve, and above all Christian charity, which is known not to be wrongly jealous but patient and kind. My desire and aim will be fulfilled if many are warmed and brought forth from this source by a better fire. It belongs to the older age, as they say:

[Col. 0019]

> No one person was born to know all things;  
> But God has assigned one reward to one person, another to another.

Yet, as Justus Lipsius relates [Note: [Col. 0019] *Against the Dialogists*, beginning, from Varro], we very often seem to ourselves witty, charming, and flavorful, when in fact we are brazen. And again: “It is easy to direct a blow to a fighter from the wall.”

Finally, let pardon be granted me on account of my condition and confession. Why should I scorn this mortal nature, prone to falling, lowly—taken, I say, from the earth and soon to return to it? Among its disadvantages is the darkness of the mind. “There is not only a necessity of erring,” says that philosopher of morals [Note: [Col. 0019] Seneca, *On Anger*, book II, ch. 9], “but even a love of errors.” Behold, this is now the twenty-third year in which the most powerful kings of the Roman and Catholic communion have met in hostile armies as adversaries. By sieges of our town—and by all that commonly accompanies them—after armies have been mustered four times in as many years and struck by alternating fortune, they have reduced us, shaken by continual terror. Nor has even yet the dawn of returning security or calm shone forth; indeed, graver threats of storms loom. “For Assur also has come with them.” O you who rule the power of the sea, calm the movement of its waves! (Ps. 88:9–10). These considerations call for compassion and readier indulgence if any things have drawn the human mind into digressions or inconsistency.

But whatever appears right and pleasing is the gift of God and the grace of His light. “It awakens free will,” says Bernard, sweeter than honey [Note: [Col. 0020] St Bernard, *On Grace and Free Will*], “when it sows a thought; it heals when it changes the affection; it strengthens so as to bring it to action; it preserves it so that it does not suffer failure.”

[Col. 0019]

# Prolegomena on the Life of the Author

## Chapter One. The Useful Knowledge of the Deeds and Writings of Illustrious Men

[Col. 0019A]

It is an ancient and praiseworthy institution to transmit to the memory of posterity the lives of those who excelled in illustrious deeds and the monuments of genius by which they flourished. And it is certainly helpful to know and repeatedly contemplate those whom accomplished virtue has raised up as an incentive to equal glory.

Did such ardour inflame Themistocles, had he not received from his forefathers Miltiades’ trophies as examples to imitate? [Note: [Col. 0019D] Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book III, ch. 28.] Julius Caesar had looked upon Alexander’s statue at Gades—what burning words he drew forth from the heat of his breast! For this reason ancient images, and the smoke-darkened wax portraits of ancestors, preserved with cedar, were displayed to descendants in the halls; and the family names, arranged in a long succession [Col. 0019B] and bound together by many twists of genealogical lines.

Thus Quintus Maximus and Publius Scipio, illustrious men of the Roman commonwealth, Sallust relates, were often accustomed to say [Note: [Col. 0019D] *The Jugurthine War*, after the beginning]: when they looked upon the images of their ancestors, their minds were most vehemently kindled toward virtue. Clearly, it was not that wax or those likenesses possessed such power in themselves, but that the memory of deeds done caused a flame to grow in the breasts of noble men; nor was it calmed until their own virtue had matched their ancestors’ fame and glory. Thus posterity would readily contend, in emulous rivalry, with the character, diligence, and courage of their forebears, and strive toward praise not unequal to theirs.

[Col. 0019C] Nor, we find, did many followers and leaders of Christian warfare act much otherwise. Their hearts, kindled by holier flames conceived on a like occasion, they fastened upon heaven through reading or hearing accounts of earlier deeds, in which a certain participation in divine power shone forth and secretly struck their wounded affections. From this they derived their pursuit of supreme and heavenly wisdom: to despise every summit of earthly happiness and to devote themselves to seeking virtues—virtues whose mere pursuit ought already to be preferred even to discovered treasures, kingdoms of nations, and bodily pleasures flowing round one at will. [Note: [Col. 0020D] See St Augustine, *Confessions*, Book VIII, ch. 7.]

Augustine, destined to become a most strenuous athlete in a better contest, heard Pontitianus recounting the notable deeds of Antony, the celebrated father of monks in Egypt. Turbulent with the travail of a new life, he uttered not so much words as flames. “Can it be,” he cries among other things, [Col. 0020B] “that because they have gone before, we are ashamed to follow, yet are not ashamed even not to follow?” [Note: [Col. 0020D] St Augustine, *Confessions*, Book VIII, chs. 6, 8.]

At Trier, one of the emperor’s court officials had examined the same book of deeds. Kindled by holy love and filled with sober shame, he turned his eyes upon his companion; laying bare the tides of his heart, he chose and resolved upon better things, and repaid words no longer with words but rather with deeds. And the other likewise declared that he would cleave to his companion in a reward and warfare so great. The holy doctor relates these events more fully in the books of his *Confessions*. This is what the Wise Man affirmed when he said: “The path of the just is like a shining light” (Prov. 4:18). And this saying of our Saviour is wholly true: “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world” (John 11:9). [Col. 0020C]

[Col. 0021A] Closely related to this, and greatly conducive to it, is committing to writing the more illustrious deeds of one’s own people, which no passage of time will cause to perish; likewise bringing into the light the writings and accounts of renowned men, so that they may thereby live splendidly in the knowledge of later ages (Ecclus. 39:2). To this one may fittingly apply the poet’s words: [Note: [Col. 0021D] Claudian, *On the Fourth Consulship of Honorius*.]

> Virtue that lies hidden is worthless: for what profit  
> can it bring, buried in darkness? Like a ship  
> beneath an unknown rower, a lyre that is silent,  
> or a bow that is not drawn.

And the saying of Sirach agrees: “Wisdom hidden and treasure unseen: what benefit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20:32; 41:18.) Therefore, just as Zeuxis, famous among painters, when intending to portray his Juno with the greatest beauty, assembled the loveliest maidens of the region [Col. 0021B] and took from each whatever was most excellent in her, so must those devoted to ancestral virtue themselves do likewise. From the examples and sayings of their Fathers—in which a living likeness of their souls still breathes and, entrusted to writing, endures—they must shape the plan of their own life and discipline.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] Livy, beginning of his history.] From these they may derive for themselves and their commonwealth what to imitate; from these they may foresee what is foul in its beginning and foul in its end, in order to avoid it:

[Note: [Col. 0021D] Claudian, passage cited above.]

> Read what you may soon imitate; and never let  
> Greek antiquity cease to speak with you, nor Roman antiquity.  
> Unfold the ancient commanders; accustom yourself to warfare to come;  
> carry yourself back into the age of Latium.

## CHAPTER II. The plan of what will be said concerning the author’s life, and the sources from which it is drawn

[Col. 0021C]

I judged that, in accordance with the purpose of my intended undertaking, when I was to issue in a more cleansed printing and for the use of many the offspring of learning which the purified mind of a most wise teacher had once produced, but which the succeeding age had partly covered with the darkness of envy and partly, through a confused sequence and crude printing, corrupted beyond measure—with the aid of divine grace, which gently gives every good willing and powerfully brings it to completion—it would be fitting first to set forth those matters which concern and surround the author’s condition of life, rank, and age. These would provide an indication of fuller knowledge, insofar as it has been granted to attain it in our time, and of a clearer reputation. [Col. 0021D] For it matters greatly to a reader and lover to know beforehand into what age each writer fell; what country and birth befell him; what community he joined, what rule of life he professed, and to what degree of dignity he was raised.

I acknowledge that, from the ancient religious communities, monuments immense both in number and worth have perished through the general decline of things and the devouring power of time. The Fathers themselves, moreover, feared that, since they had it at heart to do much and say little about themselves, if writers’ talents should exalt them too highly, their virtue might be said to have been handed down in words rather than proved by works. Yet every best man preferred doing rather than speaking, and doing good to others with a view to eternal recompense rather than seeking the pursuit of human praise—as Aubertus Miraeus says, in substance, of the most spotless order of Premonstratensian canons. [Col. 0022A] [Note: [Col. 0022D] Aubertus Miraeus, at the beginning of the *Chronicle of the Premonstratensian Order*.] But it is true: not without repeated sighs of the heart do we seek what has been lost, desire what is whole, and love what is untouched. For from no small number of the surviving pledges of most distinguished men, mutilated, I think, by the fault of ignorant or idle copying—for the world, polished by typographical labours, was not then fashioned with such elegance and finish—and disfigured by their scars and wounds, like Scaeva’s shield in Caesar, there have come into our hands.

It will occur later to record with sorrow that this stepmotherly lot of the dear age grievously bit into the salutary fruits of our author. But what has slipped away and flowed off through whatever accident—can we recall it at pleasure? In this matter someone will make no more progress than the man of whom the poet says:

> The rustic waits while the river flows away; but it  
> flows, and will flow on, rolling through all time.

Accordingly, I have collected partly what I was able to gather from manuscripts, especially the annals which Maurice of Prato, a canon at Amiens in the monastery of St John, was preparing concerning his order—a man certainly devoted to antiquarian study, but taken from us by untimely death while engaged upon the work—and partly what could be observed here and there from the author’s own remaining works. I then arranged these materials in a certain order of narrative. [Col. 0022C]

For he himself, as Tertullian writes of one in a similar case, [Note: [Col. 0022D] *On Idolatry*, ch. 23.] “speaks in his pen, is heard in wax; his hand is clearer than every sound, his letter more vocal than every mouth.” And could anyone, by familiarity with the household customs of such ancient Fathers, have known them more completely in person than a diligent reader and examiner, who frequently conversed with their writings, the remains of a pure and clarified mind? I think scarcely so. Indeed, perhaps you listen more effectively to, or enter more deeply into, interpreters of this kind, who are free from mortal breath, than into their living companions—into the dead rather than the living. Thus they converse as friends, teach faithfully, warn powerfully, advise wisely, console gently, caress without flattery, and instruct truthfully. Finally, what you might suppose they concealed while living, they proclaim with greater weight of words after they have ceased to live. [Col. 0022D]

Further, I see it affirmed by all that we turn more willingly through the writings and admit more deeply into our minds the doctrinal admonitions of one whose conduct, ordered toward every holiness, leads receptive souls to learn more securely; for the teacher’s known excellence kindles us more strongly, and his authority confirms us more robustly. [Col. 0023A] For I do not know what greater hidden energy speech possesses when it sounds through the pliant pipes of deeds. As St Gregory says, [Note: [Col. 0023D] *Pastoral Care*, Part II, ch. 3.] “That voice penetrates the hearts of hearers more willingly which the speaker’s life commends.” Hence a writer contemporary with St Fulgentius judges two things necessary in teachers of the Church: good life and sound doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0023D] *Life of St Fulgentius*, ch. 1.] “A good life commends one who teaches wisely; sound doctrine adorns one who lives well. A good life makes him lovable; sound doctrine makes him praiseworthy. A good life is always believed worthy of imitation; sound doctrine is never to be rejected. A good life removes occasions from detractors; sound doctrine withstands opponents.”

And Bernard, nearly contemporary with our author and honeyed in speech, says: [Note: [Col. 0023D] *Sermons on the Song of Songs*, sermon 85.] “Nothing is brighter than this light; [Col. 0023B] nothing more glorious than this testimony: when truth shines in the mind, and the mind sees itself in truth.” I do not wish to delay longer over a proposition established by all antiquity and by the abundance of holy Fathers and every kind of writer.

## CHAPTER III. The time at which our Adam lived. Errors corrected

Knowledge of the fixed time in which our author flourished must first be laid down as a kind of foundation upon which the remaining border of the narrative may rest. And lest any occasion be afforded anyone to depart from the truth at will, it seemed good to transcribe the author’s own words, which furnish clear testimony on this matter. In his books *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, while recounting the six ages of the world, he says as follows: [Col. 0023C] [Note: [Col. 0023D] *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, Part II, ch. 6.]

> The first age, from Adam to Noah, contains one thousand six hundred and fifty-six years; the second, from Noah to Abraham, contains two hundred and ninety-two years; the third, from Abraham to David, contains nine hundred and forty-two years; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity, contains eight hundred and seventy-three years; the fifth, from the Babylonian captivity to Christ, contains five hundred and eighty-five years; but the sixth age extends from Christ’s first coming to his second, and of this age one thousand one hundred and eighty years have already passed.

Again, in chapters twelve and thirteen of the same treatise, while setting forth the sequence and rank of ecclesiastical [Col. 0023D] and civil dignity, he follows the Roman pontiffs in uninterrupted succession from the blessed Apostle Peter and stops at Alexander, Adrian’s successor, whom it is certain that Alexander III of that name occupied the see in these times. In his catalogue he identifies Frederick as the last monarch of the Roman Empire; no one will deny that he ruled in the same age as Alexander. In weaving the succession of French kings, beginning with Clovis—sixth king of the Franks and the first king of that people to receive Christ’s name in baptism from St Remigius—he brings them down to Louis, son of Lothair, [Col. 0024A] who became king from being a cleric, was captured by the Franks, and died at Laon; with him the line of Charlemagne failed among the kings of the Franks. “After this Louis,” he says, “we set down the kings of the Franks who were of the family of Hugh Capet, and we bring them down to the present Philip, son of Louis. After this Philip we set down the kings of the English, bringing them from Alfred, the most Christian king, down to the present Henry III, son of Henry II.” Thereafter he sets down the kings of the Scots from Malcolm—or, if you prefer, from Adam himself, source of the human race—bringing them down to “this present William, king of the Scots.” William’s father Henry, earl of Northumbria and Huntingdon, descended from the most devout King David and resembling him in all piety [Col. 0024B] and countenance, preceded him in death in the very flower of life. He was buried at the abbey of Kelso in 1152, as Reusner relates in his *Genealogy of the Kings of Scotland*. [Note: [Col. 0024D] See Reusner, *Genealogy of the Kings of Scotland*.]

It is therefore manifest that our author flourished in the twelfth century of our salvation, under Alexander III, Supreme Pontiff; Frederick Barbarossa, emperor of the Romans; Philip the Fair, king of the Franks; Henry III, king of the English; and William, king of the Scots. In 1180 he dedicated the books *On the Threefold Tabernacle* to the distinguished and learned Abbot John of Kelso—called by others Calco or Kelzo—whose elegant letter to Adam concerning the arrangement of this work survives. Before this he had composed a volume of one hundred homilies for the Premonstratensian canons of his profession [Col. 0024C], and another concerning the sweetness of God (which we shall report more precisely elsewhere). [Note: [Col. 0024D] Part II, Prologue, ch. 2.] His books *On Contemplation* were later efforts.

From these facts you may firmly conclude that, in the seventies and eighties of the twelfth century, he excelled greatly in piety and learning, and in the renown and eloquence of preaching the word of God: fifty years after the establishment of the Premonstratensian Order; thirty-six after the death of St Norbert, its founder; and about seventeen after the departure of St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, whom our author elsewhere cites under the unstated name of “a holy and wise man.” [Note: [Col. 0024D] Part II, sermon in the preface.]

The error of Antonio Possevino in his *Sacred Apparatus* must therefore be removed. He writes as follows: “Adam, of the Premonstratensian Order, professor at Paris, published in 1518 a book entitled *Of the Blessed Mother of God*, in which he treats of the order, habit, and profession of Premonstratensian religious; likewise, of the threefold tabernacle of Moses, Christ, and the Holy Spirit; and of the threefold kind of contemplation.” But how corrupt and remote from truth this sequence of statements is will become clearer when its spell is removed in what follows. Nor does Aubertus Miraeus err less in his brief Premonstratensian chronicle, [Note: [Col. 0024D] Aubertus Miraeus, *Premonstratensian Chronicle*, year 1518.] where, under the year 1518, he records two writers of the same name, though wrongly. And what may perhaps surprise you more: Martin Mertz, otherwise a most learned man, was here caught in the same error in his treatise on the institution of Premonstratensian canons. But these men, and any others, merely wandering with a light and roving eye over a few pages of the author, confused the date of the printing of some of his works with the age in which he flourished, without further investigation. [Col. 0025A]

## CHAPTER IV. His name as distinguished from others, his surname, and his homeland

We read that the ancients adapted names to many people on account of some event, now for private merit and now for public distinction. Thus among the Romans Titus Manlius was called Torquatus because he stripped a golden torque from Brennus, leader of the Senonian Gauls; Marcus Valerius was called Corvinus because of the help of a raven. Quintus Servilius, after capturing Fidenae, was called Fidenas; one was later called Asiaticus, another Africanus, and many likewise. Among the Greeks, Dion of Prusa was commonly called Chrysostom because of the golden eloquence of his mouth; Ptolemy Evergetes because of beneficence; Phocion Orestes because of uprightness; Damippus Ceraunus because of boldness. [Col. 0025B] Who does not know that the Hebrews at first were called by most meaningful names derived in no other way than from the things themselves? Nor did Christians altogether depart from similar naming: to the name by which they were distinguished when washed in the sacred waters, they added another from their place of origin, profession or station, or lineage’s rank.

More nearly relevant to our subject, and formerly more usual, was the practice by which those who, having set aside worldly cares, had devoted themselves more strictly to a more perfect life and to regular cloisters, put off the name of their ancestral rank, if they had one, and took a name from the adopted purpose of a holier life or from their native soil. For this reason our Adam, concealing the distinguished name of his ancestors, is surnamed in manuscript books by the common designation “Premonstratensian,” now “English,” now “Scottish,” and at other times “Anglo-Scottish,” from his profession of the religious life. [Col. 0025C]

And lest Adam’s very name lead anyone astray, three other men of that name, besides our author now before us, are found celebrated in an age nearer to this one. The first was a disciple of St Norbert, a native of Metz. By remarkable holiness of life he nobly exalted the smoke-darkened ancestral portraits of an illustrious lineage. While still a youth, he was entrusted at Laon in France to the instruction of a certain Rudolph, for cultivation in letters; with great difficulty he overcame the muddy springs and enticements of slippery puberty. But one day, having heard Norbert, as was his custom, thundering gravely from the pulpit on the dignity of the soul and the baseness of sins, on the transience of this world and the eternity that ever remains, he was immediately seized by such a vehement contempt for earthly things and kindled with such desire for heavenly things that of his own accord he at once pressed upon the footsteps of the speaker and best of fathers; casting away all fleeting things, he consecrated himself to God. [Col. 0025D]

Thereafter he began, with such strength of soul, to tame “that beast of lust,” as St Jerome calls it, [Col. 0026A] and to devote himself to inward worship, that angelic spirits, familiar with him, supplied him with burning torches as he sang praises and hymns to the Virgin Mother, for whom he wholly pined with singular affection. Ecstasies so frequent bore him away from the body that, almost free already from the weight of bodily mass, he seemed to have passed into their lot. Finally, when Blessed Milo was raised to the episcopal see of the Morini, Adam was appointed in his place to govern the church of St Judoc in the Wood—otherwise called Dom-Martin—and there fulfilled the virtues and duties of a true shepherd, dying in 1165.

[Note: [Col. 0025D] Pagius, *Bibliotheca*, Book II, fol. 470, chapter “Mihi,” and Book V, fol. 939.] The second was Adam, abbot of the chief monastery of Prémontré and general superior of the order. Distinguished for manifold learning, he attended the Council of Vienne under Clement V; afterwards he won many favours from leading men and, after completing a rule of twenty-two years, departed this life in 1327. His office was assumed by Adam II, general provost of that name, heir no less to his predecessor’s praise and holy manner of life than to his name. Having completed six years in that rank of honour, he laid aside the remains of his mortal body before the high altar at Prémontré and died in 1333. [Col. 0026B] Nor have I been able to encounter other namesakes who transmitted to posterity distinguished renown through governmental office or illustrious monuments of genius. From this it is clear that Aubertus Miraeus must be rejected when he says: [Col. 0026C] [Note: [Col. 0026D] Miraeus, *Premonstratensian Chronicle*, year 1518.] “Adam of Prémontré, general superior of the entire order, a very learned man, wrote three books”—thus reckoning our author and his works among them.

Our writer, then, who plainly belongs to an earlier age, is distinct from the offices held by these men. He seems to me to bear the surname “Premonstratensian” either from that noble chief monastery, situated in the territory of Laon, which communicated its name to the entire order’s profession, or from his state of religious life; in the way that names are often borrowed from Chartreuse and Cîteaux, and from similar mother churches, by communities derived from or subject to them. But what homeland should we ascribe to our writer, and what seat where he began the holier life? We shall recount this in what follows. [Col. 0026D]

I assign no homeland to our author other than the kingdom of the English. An ancient manuscript among the Célestins at Paris places this on its title: “Sermons of Master Adam the Englishman, of the Premonstratensian Order.” Yet I incline rather to regard him as native to the province of Bernicia, once part of Northumbria, subject with Galloway to its ruler. We know that the southern Picts inhabited it in ancient times and that it lay within the limits of the kingdom of Scotland; but also that in the age of the Venerable Bede, as he mentions elsewhere, [Note: [Col. 0026D] Book III of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, ch. 4.] and long afterwards, it was subject to the king of the English. Thus some have been pleased to apply to our writer now the designation of his native region—Bernicia, which we identify, and which more closely touches the Scots—now that of the kingdom within whose boundaries it lay, and now that of the whole island, which, especially among foreigners, takes the name England from its more renowned part. [Col. 0027A]

I am led decisively to this by the author of the *Premonstratensian Library*: [Note: [Col. 0027D] *Premonstratensian Library*, Book I, ch. 17.] “Adam,” he says, “a Scot by nation and profession of the Premonstratensian Order, a man of much piety and learning, wrote many works, and those outstanding.” Maurice of Prato, whose manuscript annals I carefully inspected at Amiens, writes: [Note: [Col. 0027D] Maurice of Prato, in the manuscript annals, year 1180.] “In the same year, namely 1180, Adam, a canon of the Premonstratensian Order in Scotland—whom I think to be none other than Adam, or Edan, first prior or abbot of Whithorn, for the age and name agree—wrote very many works. So far as may be gathered from his writings, he was a man most distinguished in the world.” Under the year 1177 he says: [Note: [Col. 0027D] The same, under the year 1177.] “About this time Christian, bishop of Whithorn in the Scottish region of Galloway, converted the canons of his cathedral church, already regular canons, into Premonstratensians. For this reason he is named as founder of that church in the Premonstratensian obituary on the Nones of April. The first canons were called from Green Lake (*viridi stagno*); and Adam, or Edan, so named in the obituaries, was given them as their first superior or abbot.” Demster’s *On the Writers of Scotland*, which I have not been able to examine, supports this conclusion.

Then there is the synopsis of his Life preserved at Antwerp among the canons of the notable church of St Michael, arranged in nine sections, which I myself copied in 1629, as follows: [Col. 0027C] “1. Adam, in Anglo-Scotland; 2. born of noble parents; 3. having left behind the smoke-emitting images of his lineage and forefathers; 4. of Whithorn and a canon of St Norbert; 5. in a certain church of Scotland; 6. he attached himself to the community; 7. where the first Fathers of the Premonstratensian Order; 8. with whom he lived almost as a contemporary, well instructed in spirit, and shone before the companions of his own age in word and deed, leaving written by hand that by which posterity might be formed.” There was still a Prior Henry there in 1508. Finally, in the epitome of the chronicle printed at Amiens which the said Maurice published in 1655: “Christian, bishop of Whithorn, with the favour of Fergus, prince of Galloway, introduced the Premonstratensians into his cathedral, and Adam, most illustrious for his writings, was their first superior.” [Col. 0027D]

In agreement with this are the words which the author himself writes to the canons of the Premonstratensian church, among whom he represents himself as having stayed as a visitor rather than permanently: “We are astonished whenever it occurs to us how your exaltedness deigned to treat our littleness: both to receive us when we came to you, to deal with us while we stayed among you, and to dismiss us when we departed from you.” And shortly afterwards: “When we were bodily present among you—though even now, placed in the kingdom of the Scots, we are not spiritually absent from you—your humility was pleased to request what your authority was able to command: that we should send you the book which, concerning the tabernacle of Moses together with its illustration, we composed two years ago at the request of certain brothers of ours, and especially of a distinguished man, a certain Abbot John, who is in our land.” [Col. 0028A] From what has been openly suggested, anyone may readily infer which land he shared with Abbot John, and what brethren he had found.

And if anyone perhaps is not satisfied, let those examining this diagram know, as he says elsewhere, [Note: [Col. 0027D] *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, Part II, ch. 13.] “that, just as we, because we are in the land of the English and in the kingdom of the Scots, have set down in it kings of the English and the Scots, so they too, if perhaps they wish to make another according to the form of this one, may set down in it the most Christian kings of their own realms.” Here, then, he was received upon the knee; here he was taught the liberal arts, which he afterwards enlarged with extraordinary progress. From a barbarous region he derived nothing—no more, to speak in a similar manner with St Bernard, [Note: [Col. 0028D] *Life of St Malachy*.] than fish of the sea derive salt from their mother. Rather, as rays of sunlight cast upon dark and muddy places illuminate them by their brightness without being defiled, so he shone in his once rustic homeland by the splendour of virtue and the light of his manifold learning, calling wisdom his sister and prudence his friend (Prov. 7:4). But let us first examine him after he had laid aside the toga of boyhood. [Col. 0028B]

## CHAPTER V. His youth spent in the world, and his embrace of the religious state

How true is the ancient verse:

> Whom has unbridled youth not corrupted, and freedom  
> granted too early with the toga?

Who does not know this, if he considers the conduct of young people—especially those whom happier birth and richer fortune have raised above others? The course of that age is wholly steep and downward unless it is restrained by certain checks, as by health-giving reins. Otherwise, later it must wash away with lamentations and many tears what it has sinned through so heedlessly and easily. Further, by the dispensation of the secret divine counsel—as the judgments and examples of holy Fathers concerning this are not lacking—souls capable and fruitful in virtue, as St Augustine says, [Note: [Col. 0028D] St Augustine, *Against Faustus*, Book XXII, ch. 70.] often first display [Col. 0028D] vices, thereby indicating for what virtue they are especially suited, if cultivated by precepts. For divine Providence transfers to better things the vigorous impulse of nature that was previously carried toward worse; so that the soul, always like itself and accustomed to difficult things, whether it obey error or virtue, may not think that it has cast off its former exertion but that it has exchanged it for a better one.

Fixed upon these considerations and taught by his own experience, our author cries: [Note: [Col. 0028D] Sermon 4 on Advent.] “It has not [Col. 0029A] escaped your minds how formerly you walked in ways that were not good, following your own impulse and going after your own desires, running against God with uplifted neck; how, in the streets of Babylon under Pharaoh, foul with the mud of pleasure in Egypt and light as the chaff of vanity, you wandered utterly like straying sheep. But your Saviour himself, who is rich in mercy, the shepherd and bishop of your souls, because of the love with which he loved you even while you were still such, had compassion on you: he snatched you from the power of darkness and transferred you into this very good land in which you now dwell. For he sent forth his hand from on high, snatching and freeing you from the hand of foreign sons; likewise bringing you out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth, [Col. 0029B] he set your feet upon a rock and put into your mouth a new song, a hymn to your God. O change wrought by the right hand of the Most High! O good hand of God with you! O good, perfect will and gratuitous grace, through which mercy has dealt with you, so that you now rule manfully over those vices by which you were once cast down in weakness: mortifying the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, driving out those foreign nations and possessing their lands!”

And immediately showing that this applies more particularly to himself, he says: “But because I see many here who, nourished from childhood with Samuel in the tabernacle, did not come from far off as we did, we exhort them more earnestly to recognize themselves no less indebted to their Saviour. For it is the same one who kept them and who raised us: justifying both us and them in a good but different way—us, namely, by recalling us; them, by preserving them.” Thus he had gone far away from himself, carried off by a certain licence of youth—not separated in countries but in morals, not divided in lands but in pursuits—and, as though the tide of worldly vanity had flowed between, he stood apart from the saints:

[Note: [Col. 0029D] St Prosper, Epigram 80.]

> As a dark thing, unlike him, withdraws into deserts,  
> so in life he is rightly near who is like him.

[Note: [Col. 0029D] See the author, *On the Threefold Contemplation*, Part III, §10; and Sermon 9, Part I.] “For one who withdraws from the word of life hungers; one who withdraws from the fountain thirsts; one who withdraws from the treasure is in need; one who withdraws from wisdom is dulled; one alien from virtue is dissolved.” Therefore he began to be in want, since he still did not know the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge, or the depth of his riches. [Col. 0029D]

But just as a kindly father, seeing his son erring amid the precipices of vices, announces through the mother his paternal indignation unless he return as a suppliant, but grace and gifts if he obeys, so the Father of mercies sends to him the favour of divine grace, as though the mother of a better beginning, arousing the will that he may will and granting the ability that he may be able. Alarmed and shaken, he says: “Alas, what have I done? Where have I been? I have departed from my God, my Creator and Redeemer, almost dwelling in hell; and, alas beyond measure, sleeping securely in the shadow of death! I will go [Col. 0030A] to my father, in case he may have mercy and be gracious to my sins.”

As he turns these things over within the recesses of his mind, the most merciful Father sees him: illuminating the fibres of his heart, he comes to aid him, embraces him by imparting free gifts. Then, with a father’s affection, he falls upon his neck: to raise him as he lies fallen; to turn upward one burdened with sins and bent toward earthly things; to prepare a neck freed from the yoke of wrongful servitude for the sweeter burden of his commandments. Finally, the one whom he wishes to make a partner in his friendship he also makes a sharer in his gifts. He does not desire him empty, but adorned. He brings forth a robe, to clothe his former weakness anew with the strength of spiritual wisdom; a ring, to unite him to himself as betrothed by the firm covenant of charity and faith; and the shoes of preaching the Gospel, so that the hearer may say, “Come” (Rev. 22:17). Finally, the fatted calf is slain when, having attained fellowship in the holy mysteries, he himself dispenses them to the faithful; filled as with marrow and fatness, he consecrates to almighty God the enclosure of his mouth with lips of exultation. [Col. 0030B]

But it is pleasing to attend to the word of his own confession and, as it were, furtively to receive with bowed ear the veins of its whisper (Job 4:12). [Note: [Col. 0030D] Sermon 13 for Advent.] “O soul, how can you worthily comprehend in your understanding that he bore you so patiently in the world, such as you remember yourself to have been there, and called you so mercifully? There he was long-suffering; here, merciful. Having called you, he adorned you with so great and such an adornment of righteousness, granting that throughout the time of your life [Col. 0030C] you should refrain from things from which you had scarcely been able to abstain for a single day. And what had been most laborious to endure even for a brief hour may now be sweetest for you to bear all your days.

“Thanks to you, Lord, good and sweet, kind and gracious. You created me when I did not exist; you redeemed me when I was lost; you justified me when called, forgiving my sins and bestowing gifts: constancy in reading, devotion in prayer, zeal in meditation, sweetness in reflection, purity in contemplation; granting health in the body, insofar as you know it expedient for me, that you may render me fit and strong for good work; and sometimes infirmity, that you may draw me back from evil action and make me fearful. Always and in all things you are zealous for my salvation: exhausting me in the warfare of temptation, then consoling me again in the repose of peace—there, lest I exalt myself; here, lest I become too faint-hearted. Everywhere and always assisting me, and causing all my things, not only good but also evil, to work together for my good. Add after these things, add also to them, that you bestowed all this upon one who deserved nothing. For what did I do beforehand that you should judge me worthy of so many gifts, of such gifts, and of such great gifts? I did nothing good; I did nothing that was not evil; and you yourself bestowed every good thing.”

And, turning to his own brethren, he says in a discourse [Note: [Col. 0030D] See Sermon 14 on Advent]:

“Now, wherever the impulse of the Spirit leads, you advance thither, making the whole course of life an exercise undertaken as though for play. These things are lofty indeed, and no less hard than new. I call them lofty because they are in some sense above [Col. 0031A] nature; new in relation to your former custom; and hard because of the weakness of your flesh. Your frequent fasts, which you practise, rightly bear witness to these things, and we know that their testimony is true; the continual vigils which you keep; the plainness of the clothing which you wear; the austerity of the food which you endure; the restraint of speech which you practise; exposing, so to speak, every member of your body to a daily martyrdom, and not even holding your own will in your power.”

He concludes: “Therefore by the grace of our Saviour we have been saved—both we who were far off and those who were found near. For it is God’s gift, lest anyone, whether from among us or among them, should glory in this.”

[Note: [Col. 0031D] St Prosper, *On Ingratitude*, final chapter.]

For if we do anything right, O Lord, we do it with your help:

[Col. 0031B] You move our hearts; you grant the prayers  
Which you desire to give; preserving what you have bestowed, and creating  
Merits from merits, and crowning your gifts by heaping further gifts upon them.

## CHAPTER VI. The church in which, having professed the religious life, he first devoted himself to God; an outstanding herald of cloistered repose.

The rivalry and competition recorded concerning very illustrious men—when several towns and kingdoms claim their birth for themselves, while others in a pious contest reclaim them as their own citizens—also produced diverse opinions concerning our Adam. Thus the French determined that he was theirs; the English registered him as theirs; the Scots called him theirs; and the Northumbrians claimed him as an inhabitant of their country. Concerning his native land, which shared in the origin of his mortal [Col. 0031C] life, I have already stated the opinion which I was then able to attain. But I assign the cradle of his spiritual life and the exercises of his holier discipline nowhere other than to the noble mother-monastery of Prémontré. According to the testimony of Paul Morige [Note: [Col. 0031D] *On the Origin of Religious Orders*, ch. 57; and *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, bk. I, ch. 18.], this house, in his history *On the Origin of Religious Orders*, grew with such fruitfulness from the very beginnings of its foundation that, before the year 1209, it numbered above eighteen hundred monasteries, both of men and of nuns—besides very many other lesser churches, which they call priories, granges, and parishes.

Here, I say, he bound the first fruits of his spirit; this he chose as the post of his heavenly warfare; here he confirmed by vows consecrated to God his perpetual [Col. 0031D] service. Grafted into this rich and fruitful olive tree, he overflowed with mystical oil.

Nor should anyone be disturbed by the foreign country in which we place him, namely the kingdom of the English. For, besides the fact that the English at that period occupied a considerable part of France, divine love for Christ and zeal for attaining virtue summoned and inflamed many novices from remote regions of the Christian world—once they had cast aside worldly hopes and the most noble titles of their ancestors—both in the house of Prémontré and in other communities of that order fragrant with the fresh scent of holiness. Thus, about this [Col. 0032A] time, the monastery of Bucilly in the diocese of Laon produced Royard, of blessed memory, son of the king of the Scots: under a lay and humble profession, truly noble in many virtues. Thus the island of Blessed Mary, of the Premonstratensian Order in Guelders, received blessed Robert as its first abbot; his agnate was a blood-relative of Henry I, king of the English, and the widespread fragrance of his holy way of life gently inclined the king to bestow very many gifts upon that church. Nor should we forget Richard the Englishman, outstanding in innocence of life and eminence of learning, illustrious among the Premonstratensians at the monastery of Arnsberg in Westphalia in the year of the Lord 1190. His right hand, retaining its pristine wholeness four lustra after his death, claims for itself among the relics of the saints an undying memory of labour and [Col. 0032B] merit.

Heaven had promised as much when, in a marvellous vision, it marked out the first structure, truly, of the Order of Prémontré [Note: [Col. 0032D] *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, bk. II, ch. 19.]. For while the minds of the new community were in suspense, our Saviour Jesus, hanging upon the cross and visible to Blessed Hugh, the first head of the order appointed by St Norbert, displayed seven rays flashing toward him and an immense multitude of pilgrims streaming together from the four quarters of the world. With suppliant gesture, having given a kiss and adored the Redeemer, they went back in every direction as though leave had been granted them. St Norbert interpreted these as novices who would come to enter this new knighthood and carry it throughout all regions of the world to its end.

“And indeed it was true,” says the contemporary author of his *Life* (ch. 27), “as the ensuing [Col. 0032C] action daily demonstrates in those who, having left all things, come as pilgrims and, after making profession—as though giving a kiss—withdraw to different nations in order to win the battle-lines. From sea even unto sea the trumpet sounded, and their voice was heard; in it the works of God are manifest, and exquisitely ordered according to all his wills.”

But, to return more closely to our subject and give some room to probable conjecture: about thirty years after the order’s establishment, under the vigorous and fortunate government of Blessed Hugh, around the year of salvation 1150, in the solitude of Prémontré, he pitched his tent with Abraham, father of a multitude and also called “the exalted” (Gen. 12:8)—the dwelling of those who journey or serve as soldiers [Note: [Col. 0032D] See the author, Sermon 36.]. In bringing forth good action from himself, as though begetting holy offspring, the fervour of good desire made him fruitful, and the uprightness of an intention pleasing God alone made him exalted.

Clement Reyner, in his *Benedictine Apostolate*, reports that in the year 1146, the tenth of King Stephen—though Mauritius assigns it to the preceding year—the Premonstratensians first extended their shoots across the sea into England from the then-famous Liskensian monastery. The common people, he says, called them White Canons; and Peter de Saulia established in Lincolnshire the monastery dedicated to St Martial, called Newhouse—that is, “new house.” But we find that colonies came to the northern parts of England, [Col. 0033A] adjoining Northumbria and Scotland, from no source other than the illustrious mother-monastery of Prémontré, men fervent in spirit, and especially from the community of Sanlefiette, bordering the diocese of Glasgow. Thus Mauritius expressly records in his manuscript annals that Feoguz, earl of Galloway, is entered in the Necrology of Prémontré on the fourth Ides of May as founder of the abbeys of Sanlefiette—also called Green Lake and Seat of Souls—and of Whithorn; of the latter there will again be occasion to speak. The catalogues which I have been permitted to inspect while reviewing monasteries agree unanimously that a direct offshoot, flourishing with clusters of many virtues, was transplanted to the environs of that Green Lake from no mother church other than Prémontré.

[Col. 0033B] Among these first companions and new colonists I place our Adam. First at Green Lake, then elevated to the government of Whithorn, he distinguished his well-ordered character by conspicuous holiness and kindness.

Nor will it otherwise seem difficult to anyone to reconcile, in fair harmony, the differing opinions of those who think differently: so that neither the honour of his birth in the English kingdom, which old memory has assigned him in manuscripts, need be torn away from him; nor should he be subjected to the church of Prémontré, whom another claim does not with equal right claim as its own. He is altogether drawn there willingly by a decree of the general chapter, of which this copy gives the wording:

“Likewise it was ordained that a certain book compiled by Brother Adam, a religious of the monastery of Prémontré, shall be delivered for printing, and every abbot of our order shall be bound to buy it.”

This decree, enacted in 1517, brought part of his works to light. It further supports this conclusion that he repeatedly calls himself a special son of the womb of that church, from whose spiritual bosom he had plainly proceeded [Note: [Col. 0033D] See Letters I and II, to Prémontré.]. One should consult the letter which he addressed to the canons of the church of Prémontré.
