“In this solitude,” he says [Note: [Col. 0033D] *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, pt. III, ch. 2.], “he who set us free, who loosed our bonds, also gave us a house, that in it we might build for the God of Jacob a tabernacle—that is, that in this inward quiet of the mind we might build our secret place with God. O freedom! O release! O solitude!”

And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0033D] See Sermon 37]:

“What state in this life is freer, or quieter, than the state of those who live sincerely in the cloister? [Col. 0033D] The state of kings, pontiffs, any princes, or indeed any exalted conditions whatsoever in this life cannot—I will not say exceed theirs—but cannot even in any respect be compared with it. Such a condition may perhaps be higher in power, but not freer in repose. O free and quiet condition of cloistered persons! Since they neither hope for anything nor fear anything, they are content with such moderation that, made poor by a certain abundant poverty and enriched by a needy abundance, they can lose nothing old, since they are known to have as though possessing nothing; nor can they acquire anything new, since they are known to possess all things.”

He develops this subject more fully there and elsewhere. Let me conclude with the Christian poet:

[Col. 0034A] [Note: [Col. 0034D] St Prosper, Epigram 8.]

No freedom is better, nor any power greater,  
Than serving God, whom love serves well.  
The will that is strong in affection, not groaning under command,  
Is set free from the yoke and loves rule.

## CHAPTER VII. The character and discipline of the Premonstratensian order; approval by the Apostolic See; hostile attack born of envy.

That exalted mind of Norbert, strengthened by heavenly protections and furnished with aids, in the place not without reason called Prémontré, about thirty years before our Adam was to descend into that valley—spiritually fertile in wheat and destined to spring up like a lily—had so skilfully tempered his order, long established by the most blessed and great Augustine of Hippo, through a blending of elements that it might rightly seem to have omitted nothing of the former [Col. 0034B] dignity of clerics and nothing of the observance of the ancient monks [Note: [Col. 0034D] *On Clerical Continence*, ch. 126.].

No testimony occurs more clearly than that of the venerable prelates Guibert of Nogent; Henry, first monk and then abbot of St Martin among the Nervii; and Philip of Bonne-Espérance among the Hainaut people. They inspected with their own eyes and, so to speak, handled with their own hands what they transmitted in their books. I shall now weigh a few words of the latter:

“Christ gathered together in the place called Prémontré certain men fervent in spirit, through whom he stirred many others far and wide toward the religion proper to them. There the holiness of clerics indeed boiled over so abundantly that the apostolic life itself seemed truly to be restored in them—a life which had been oppressed almost unto extinction by the burden of long-standing weakness. There, [Col. 0034C] I say, having cast aside the world’s pecuniary resources, detesting the deadly allurements of self-will, abandoning the ecclesiastical offices which they either possessed or sought, and accounting dignities soon to pass away as nothing, they bestowed such zeal upon labour, silence, and poverty—indeed, such diligence upon holiness—that among them could be found both the laborious affliction of monks and the holy, devout religious observance of clerics.

“God plainly willed this to be done in a valley, so that the form of the site itself might accord with the work of salvation and openly show that, for clerics whose high dignity and freedom to govern had become occasions of ruin, voluntary abasement and the humility of repentance were fitting.”

And shortly afterward [Note: [Col. 0034D] See below, second part, Prologue, ch. 3, no. 5.]:

“For the same valley spreads out, in the manner of a cross, into four arms, and its plain is bounded by four corners; its length extends from east to west, [Col. 0034D] while its breadth runs from north to south. What does this aspect of the place, on which so great a likeness of the cross is impressed—this valley, crucified, as it were, not by human engineering but by a natural work—admonish or foreshadow, except that those flocking to it should no longer care to live for the world, but should conform themselves to it—indeed, to Christ—by a fitting crucifixion?”

And he adds, as it were, this epiphonema: “Truly blessed is this life of clerics, who while still situated on earth live according to the manner of angels: being conformed not only to angels by the whiteness of their outward clothing, but rather to the King of angels by the brightness of their minds.” Anyone who wishes may see more in that author.

Our author is a weighty and ample interpreter of a regular discipline already then fervent and rigorous; to me his discourse is the face of his mind and the image of his deeds [Note: [Col. 0035D] *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, pt. IV, ch. 6; and Sermons 46, 21.]. For he establishes the supports of outward holiness, measured by the number eight: strictness of fasts, constancy in vigils, labour of the hands, chastity of the flesh, gravity of expression, restraint in speech, plainness of dress, deliberateness of gait; and of inward holiness: purity of meditation, desire for forgiveness of sins, grace of merits, glory of rewards, the virtue of humility, steadfastness of perseverance, and similar ascetic matters. He treats these with such familiar and frequent exercise [Col. 0035B] [Note: [Col. 0035D] Sermon 14 on Advent.] that he not undeservedly compares them with daily martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0035D] For external and internal religious ordering, one should read the fourteen Sermons to religious persons.].

But as regards the austerity of food and clothing, the practice of prudent household management, the duties of superiors and subjects, and the whole dignity of the religious state—how a religious community is to be founded and established upon the rock of piety, tempered with the cement of charity, now sprinkled with the attraction of kindness, now struck by punitive terror—he explains these matters, as the outstanding master of spiritual life that he is, especially in his fourteen sermons to religious persons. Nor can I readily keep pace with him in a curtailed course of words.

He repeatedly and diligently recommended three exercises, through which, he declared, religious men should be occupied in alternating succession: reading, work, and prayer. In a sermon on the Epiphany of the Lord he says:

[Col. 0035C] “All who have professed the common life ought always, as opportunity offers, to be found either in reading, prayer, or manual work. The study of reading enlightens through instruction; the devotion of prayer sanctifies through purity; and the labour of good action produces fruit through usefulness.”

And on the Advent of the Lord:

“Let us have the first exercise, that of good action, for the relief of need, for our neighbour’s sake; the second, which is reading, for the nourishment of the soul, for our own sake; the third, which is prayer, for inward affection, for God’s sake.”

“These are the three things,” says our Adam [Note: [Col. 0035D] *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, pt. II, ch. 19.], “which the priests of ours ought continually to have in this house. For whenever they are free from the necessary care of the body, they ought always to be engaged either in work, reading, or prayer.” He praises each of these at greater length. In particular, in his fourteenth sermon to religious persons, and in *The Tabernacle of the Holy Spirit* [Note: [Col. 0035D] Pt. III, chs. 7 and 8.], he calls this the table of life-giving food for refreshment, the candlestick of unfailing light for illumination, and the altar of most fragrant incense for sweetness of odour. He says more elsewhere.

From this it is clear to one who considers the matter that the extremely strict manner of life which Polydore [Col. 0036A] Vergil attributes to the Premonstratensians [Note: [Col. 0035D] Bk. VII, ch. 3, *On Inventions*] is reinforced and increased by our author—especially in those first fathers, from whom nothing of the primitive rigour had yet fallen away through any indulgent dispensation. Even now there are those who laudably endeavour to rise to it.

This manner of life prescribed by St Norbert was honoured and confirmed by a distinguished testimonial and charter from Peter Leo, priest-cardinal, and Gregory of St Angelo, deacon-cardinal—later the supreme pontiff—legates of the Roman Church in Gaul at that time; and afterwards by Innocent II at Noyon in 1124. Perhaps it will be useful to set before the reader a few lines:

“We give thanks to almighty God, whose mercy is over lives, because you are those who renew the approved life of the holy Fathers and, by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, revive the institutions of apostolic teaching, implanted in the beginnings of the holy Church but almost erased as the Church increased.”

And after some interval:

“Pope and martyr Urban instituted this life; Augustine arranged it by his rules; Jerome reformed it by his letters. It is therefore no less meritorious to revive this life of the primitive Church, with the Spirit of the Lord inspiring and carrying it forward, than to preserve by the perseverance of that same Spirit the flourishing religious life of monks. We therefore confirm your purpose by the authority of the Apostolic See, whose legation we exercise; exhort you to stand firm in him; and command you as though God exhorted through us. We decree that no one whatsoever may alter this state of your order, whose fruit overflows in so many parts of the earth [Col. 0036C] that many are seasoned by the sweetness of your savour.”

In 1126 Honorius II [Note: [Col. 0036D] *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, bk. II, ch. 28; and beginning of the Statutes of the Order . . . . Second confirmation by Honorius II, 1126.], when Norbert sought firmer support and was graciously received in the city, ratified these concessions:

“Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Norbert, brother in Christ, and the canons of the church of St Mary at Prémontré, and their successors who profess the regular life in perpetuity. Since, therefore, by divine grace inspiring you, you have resolved to live religiously and to lead the canonical life according to the institution of Blessed Augustine, we confirm your purpose by the favour of the Apostolic See.”

Elsewhere you have the full text of those documents, which we have offered as select extracts, as it were.

This above all deserves remembrance, for I do not recall others having related it [Note: [Col. 0036D] St Gregory, *Dialogues*, bk. II, ch. 8.]: just as a certain priest, Florentius, came against St Benedict, so Hugh Metellus—otherwise very distinguished in the world by birth and learning—envied Norbert the whiteness of his garments and of his mind with hostile eyes, and attacked him in an embittered spirit. He addressed a sharp-witted writing to the princes of the Church whom we have seen above in France [Note: [Col. 0036D] I excerpted this from the Library of St Geneviève on the Mount of the Regular Canons at Paris.], entitled: “To the hinges of the earth upon whom God has set the world.”

After first praising their prudence, knowledge, [Col. 0037A] and foresight, he adds:

“Since, therefore, you are of such prudence and such power, we wonder—if, with your leave, we may wonder—why you tolerate so great a diversity of orders in garments, or rather of garments in orders. Behold, some wear surplices, others tunics—as though the kingdom of heaven were gained by clothes rather than character. . . . The tunic-wearers took their beginning from Norbert; the surplice-wearers from Blessed Augustine. The tunic-wearers emerged only yesterday and the day before, while the surplice-wearers have flourished for two hundred years and more. But, as Blessed Gregory says, we judge that custom ought to remain unaltered. . . .

“Yet this novelty might be tolerable, if the enormity of scandal did not arise from it. For many—or indeed all—who are not of that sect take offence at that dress. . . . But hear how the divine page abhors [Col. 0037B] novelty: Blessed Jerome, writing to Nepotian, says: ‘Let your clothing be neither too clean nor dirty, distinguished by no novelty.’ . . . Likewise: ‘It is praiseworthy not to go about without a linen garment, but not to possess the costly price of linen clothing.’ And Blessed Augustine, the legislator of our rule, says: ‘Let not your dress be remarkable,’ etc.

“But if the Norbertines, like centaurs, neither horses nor men, bring forward John the Baptist in his rough garment in defence of their own clothes, let them leave the midst of men and remove scandal from among the brethren; and woe to the man through whom scandal comes. We wish you to know—and perhaps you know it better than we—that Pope and martyr Urban instituted the rule of canons; that Blessed Augustine, our lawgiver, arranged it by his rules; [Col. 0037C] and that Jerome instructed it by his sayings and letters. We read that Urban II assented and subscribed to the sayings and writings of these men, and wrote to the canons of St Rufus: ‘Your purpose,’ he says, etc. These great doctors, planters of our rule, handed down to us this state of the order, by which the holy Church flourished for three hundred years. Let him fear anathema who opposes the writings of the holy Fathers.”

These matters are treated at greater length in the manuscript history of the monastery of Érival, of the regular canons in the diocese of Paris, among whose number Hugh Metellus himself was counted, vainly striving to overthrow the counsel of the Most High. “But the Lord weighs hearts” (Prov. 21:2).

From what has been said it is therefore clear on what appearance of truth Jerome Platus, in his *On the Good of the Religious State* [Note: [Col. 0037D] Bk. I, *On the Good of the Religious State*, ch. 2, vol. IV, disputation 7, section 3, no. 77.], and Francis Amicus in his Scholastic Theology, commit to their books the statement that they have read of no order before the religious orders of the blessed Dominic and Francis being approved by the Apostolic See. Nor does Bellarmine, whom the latter cites, appear openly to hold that opinion. He does indeed confess that he has not read that the ancients—Antony, Basil, Augustine, Benedict—sought approval, and that the occasion for the subsequently established precept arose from the Poor of Lyons, whose rule of life had been stained by superstitions and various heresies. [Col. 0038A] But he either does not clearly explain the rest, or must be charged with the same error. Baronius’s *Annals* for the year 1126 should be consulted on this matter. Nor do those err much less who gladly consign all others to the benches of monks so that they may raise their own chairs without companions.

As discordant music amid welcome feasts,  
And rancid ointment, and poppy mixed with Sardinian honey,  
Give offence.

## CHAPTER VIII. The studies of the contemplative and active life, in which he excelled.

“The active life,” says our author [Note: [Col. 0037D] *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, pt. III, ch. 14.], “is twofold, because it consists both in preaching truth and in practising virtue: in preaching for the instruction of the heart, [Col. 0038B] and in action for the support of the body; in preaching, that we may instruct a neighbour who has gone astray; in action, that we may assist his need. This preaching wipes away ignorance of truth; the work of virtue cuts off the excess of vain desire. Preaching sets forth law and discipline; virtue requires practice and teaching. Discipline removes the harms of concupiscence; teaching takes away the clouds of ignorance.”

Our author calls these two bonds of Satan [Note: [Col. 0037D] Sermon 27.], namely ignorance and concupiscence. The upright and elect strive to free both themselves and others from them by truth and by divine power and wisdom, and they put desire to death. To this belongs the practice, frequent from the Church’s beginning, of delivering public addresses. Our author repeatedly mentions this among his own brethren [Note: [Col. 0038D] Sermon 15, on Advent]:

“For just as iron, without care and use, is covered with the roughness of rust, so our mind, if not exercised in better discourses, is clothed with numbness. Therefore it is kindled by exercise, and nothing strikes the affections with a like power as a living voice proceeding from a heart that is not cold.”

For, the author says [Note: [Col. 0038D] Sermon 43 on the Epiphany], “we worthily perform this holy and salutary work of the tongue when we apply ourselves both in pure prayer to the praises of God and in sound preaching to labour for the exhortation of our neighbour. It is fitting for the holy tongue to persist in this twofold duty.” He says more there.

How fervent and inflamed he himself was, how eloquent and tireless an ecclesiastical preacher of the divine word, shines out to some extent in the mirror in which his mind’s countenance is reflected [Col. 0038D]—would that it had been possible to see him in person and hear the thunders of his living voice! “The north gave, and the south did not forbid” (Isa. 43:6). Drawn by social affection toward his equals, as he modestly confesses [Note: [Col. 0038D] See the author’s preface to the first part.], and compelled by the reverential command of his superiors, he weighed the matter in the Lord and was forced to apply his mind to study and his hand to the pen; adding certain matters in writing to what he had said publicly, he set it forth.

That this was familiar and customary to him he indicates quite plainly [Note: [Col. 0038D] Sermon 37]:

“In Ezekiel there is found a certain evil sword, and this is sin, of which it is written: ‘If he sees the sword and does not sound the trumpet’ (Ezek. 36).”

He was speaking of the watchman. What follows is: “May God turn this away from us, who seem to be his watchmen.” For the preacher should know himself worthy of condemnation if, seeing sin reign, he ceases from instruction. Whether he later presided over another church by authority of an ecclesiastical dignity, the following discussion will examine.

How greatly he excelled in this office of preaching, in grace and fame of name, is shown by his writings, swelling with living, lofty, fiery spirit. I append for consideration these few words from the letter to the canons of the church of Prémontré [Note: [Col. 0039D] Letter 1, to the Canons of Prémontré]:

“We are silent concerning how celebrated our name is among you, since it is plainly unworthy even to be named. Nor only that: we refrain from saying how often you have declared [Col. 0039B] that you desire our return, so that our voice may sound in your ears, though neither is our voice sweet nor our countenance fair” [Note: [Col. 0039D] In the first preface.].

“For what are we? Who are we? What sort of persons are we, or how great, that you should bring us so far?”

The things he relates in his dedicatory preface furnish evidence of this. From them one may reasonably infer that he frequently journeyed from Northumbria into France to his Premonstratensian brethren; that he was loaded with many titles of favour and honour; that he achieved great renown for eloquence; that he was reluctantly dismissed amid great longing for him; and that those accompanying him even to the harbour were torn away only by the cruelty of the sea and deprived of the sweet attraction of his words.

But, I ask you, how humbly does he forestall the celebrated opinion of himself? “The voice,” he says, “is the voice of Jacob, [Col. 0039C] but the hands are the hands of Esau. The hearing ear admires us, but the seeing eye judges us unworthy, because in deed when present we are far other than in speech when absent. For we often paint a handsome man, while we painters ourselves are ugly. We discourse on the swiftest course of tigers; yet we are pale little frogs scarcely creeping beneath our muddy pool, and soft tortoises wrapped and twisted within a distorted shell. Like lions we display strength, though with no agile swiftness; beneath our own dust we move more as ants than as living beings. We teach the eagle to fix its clearest gaze upon the orb of the sun, while we are moles burrowing underground, unable to bear the light and knowing not the sun.”

O words of an eloquent breast, a humble heart! In an orator—and singularly in our author—I perceive that which, according to Demosthenes’ judgment, is first, second, and third in a declaimer: namely delivery. Flowing from the fitting modulation of voice and of the whole body, it gives life to speech, kindles hearers, charms minds, and makes them fruitful. “The gracious tongue abounds in a good man” (Ecclus. 6:5).

It was a distinguished part and inheritance of our most holy founder Norbert that he was called by the Catholic Church, with singular praise, an outstanding preacher of the word of God. He proved himself a glorious conqueror over Tanchelin, author of a most foul and sacramentarian heresy, among the people of Antwerp and the other Belgians. Into this inheritance, as their rightful succession from so great a father, many illustrious sons came with happy and rich increase.

I call as witnesses the most blessed Isfrid and Evermod, bishops of Ratzeburg and apostles of the Wends; Cain and several bishops of Olomouc. Their voice, as their deeds testify, was sounding like a trumpet, indeed almost angelic. Nor should we forget Walter of Laon among the people of Douai; Helinus of Floreffe, preacher of Christ’s cross even to the Syrians; Waltmann of Antwerp among his own people; Henry of Tongerlo; Matthew of Ninove; and, among the people of Liège, Luke of Mont-Cornillon—most celebrated abbots. Of many, it has been possible to name only a few. They kindled in the hearts of very many the fire of the heavenly homeland with which they themselves wholly burned; they shone before those in error, and gave a helping hand and a harbour [Col. 0040B] to the shipwrecked. The harvest of their glory must be raised higher by others.

But let us return briefly to our subject. Passing alternately from burdens to the sweetness of rest, he mingles the fruitful embraces of Leah with those of beautiful Rachel. He goes out to the people to bring them heavenly answers; at other times, entering with Moses the secrets within the veil, he tramples all earthly things beneath a noble contempt, hides bodily things, reveals heavenly things, and, carried above himself, feeds upon a certain lovable sweetness and contemplates the glory of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0040D] See the book *On Contemplation*, pt. III.].

Here he finds God above all things, yet not elevated; beneath all things, yet not underlying them; within all things, yet not enclosed; outside all things, yet not diffused. Indeed, in these things he finds nothing except that he cannot find him at all. Here he confessed that he knew what he did not know; and not merely that he knew what he did not know, but that he knew also what he could not know and what he could not fail to know.

From a certain ecstasy of mind, illuminated by the light of grace, he discerned that in God there is that which is from no one, that which is from another, and that which is from both: namely, essence from itself, wisdom from essence, and love from both. He describes God as begetting, begotten, and proceeding: begetting the begotten; begotten from the begetter; proceeding not from the begotten alone, but from the begetter and the begotten together. He confesses God in himself to be incomprehensible, terrible to the reprobate, and sweet to the elect.

Then, going out again for a little while, amazed at the great magnitude of God’s works and their great [Col. 0040D] multitude, he investigates the Creator through a careful examination of the natures of each thing, as they present and convey themselves in their own kind to our five bodily senses. All things proclaim in a loud cry that God exists, but they do not determine what sort of being he is or how great.

Turning inward, however, he investigates what the life of the saints is like, and with the mouth of his heart thirsts after the streams above, from the fountain of life. Finally, looking back, he is indignant at the sins of the wicked; sighing on one side because of human frailty, breathing again on the other because of divine mercy. Like one chewing over these matters with the lower and upper millstones of his thoughts, shaken with fear and surrounded by darkness, he ventures, so far as he dares, by lamenting and questioning to investigate [Col. 0041A] why the Creator of the universe, who can do all that he wills and wills nothing except what is good, permits his rational creature to fall into sin, whereby it afterwards becomes deserving to rush headlong into sin [Note: [Col. 0041D] In the preface to the book *On Contemplation*.]. For it is truly established that, just as it cannot do good unless he first inspires and assists it as he carries it forward, so neither—at least in the state in which it now is—can it omit evil unless he restrains it, nor admit evil unless he permits it.

But unable to grind these matters with the blunt teeth of his thought, he reserves them rather for the divine fire and cries with the Apostle: “O the depth!” (Rom. 11:33).

[Note: [Col. 0041D] St Prosper, *On Ingratitude*, 3.36.]

With Paul it is fitting to tremble, and modestly  
To suspend the dull mind upon the unconquered will of Christ’s throne;  
His judgment we call so unsearchable and deep  
That we nonetheless confess it wholly true and just.

[Col. 0041B] Likewise for us:

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Virgil, *Eclogues*, 3, line 112.]

“Shut now the streams, boys: the meadows have drunk enough.”

O mind pure and worthy of heaven! How gently you remove us from these low things and graft us into the heights! We read you, and our mind is raised—if indeed we understand, or at least do not read negligently, but read attentively. And who could do otherwise? Such vigour and warmth are everywhere present. Everything is so breathing and alive that I seem to read not writings but hear words; not to take in his likeness in print, but repeatedly to apprehend the man himself by my eyes and senses. Just as someone applies a torch in vain to kindle something unless it is itself lit, so one applies discourse in vain to stir another unless it is vigorous and warm.

In our author, unless I am mistaken, his mind burned when he wrote: “From the mind comes the pen; from the pen, would that we might come!” I must confess that, when I read him, I seem again and again to stand upon the summit of Mount Olympus, as they say—above winds and stormy blasts, above the mutability of human affairs.

I conclude with the encomium which I find prefixed to an edition already one hundred and forty years old [Note: [Col. 0041D] In the dedicatory letter, 1518.]:

“In driving the four-horse chariot of virtues and keeping the royal road, Adam, the most valiant champion of our religious order, once laboured with earnest care; his writings abundantly bear witness to his life and noble character. For by these he seems, while still existing in fleshly dregs, to have seen God, whom no one has ever seen. He speaks of him so clearly and teaches so plainly the path by which he may be reached that he seems plainly to have been in heaven.”

## CHAPTER IX. Humility of spirit, singular devotion in regard to the dread mysteries of the Mass, and charity

His writings, pledges of a mind most richly adorned, abundantly testify that he possessed the highest humility. This deservedly holds the first place, being the foundation of the rest and, like a queen, leading the choir of virtues. [Note: [Col. 0042D] See Sermon 41.] For it is humility itself, he says, which destroys and annihilates vices, establishes virtues, and preserves them once established. It is the safeguard and defence of all holiness [Col. 0042A] in our soul. To remove humility from this was, in his view, nothing else than to take a wall from a city, a boundary-wall from a vineyard, or a hedge from a garden.

In his forty-fourth sermon, where he labours wholly upon the archetype of humility, speaking from his own experience, he exclaims: “O holy humility, which, among the other virtues, truly sanctifies the soul: by which we are enabled both to acquire virtues when they are lacking, to preserve them when they are present, and, when perhaps they have been withdrawn, to restore them! For we continually perceive, even by our own experience, that this is the proper office of humility.” And immediately afterwards: “I will go to her and take her as my inseparable companion, so that through her all good things may come to me when I feel grace absent; she will guard it, lest I lose it when present; and, if it has perhaps been withdrawn, she herself will restore it, so that it may be given back to me.”

He then wonderfully sets forth the ascetic steps by which this virtue is to be ascended, and through examples implants in religious hearts the practice of planting this wholly fruitful tree: its root fixed in the heart, its leaves in the mouth, and the fruit of works proving its cultivator truly humble. And lest the author himself seem like a foolish tree, rustling with green leaves but barren of fruit, the things which he publicly professes characterize him more closely. [Note: [Col. 0042D] Preface I.] “For I do not speak with a double heart, but before God in Christ, with my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit: I see myself in truth as I confess myself with my mouth; such as I behold myself in my heart, making myself lowly and nevertheless being humble in my own eyes.”

Nor should we at all pass over what he openly reveals of the secret of his heart. [Note: [Col. 0042D] Sermon 38, and elsewhere frequently, Sermons 39 and 41.] “I tell you, my friends—believe one who has experienced it: nothing can be so effective for a man in acquiring spiritual grace, not only before it has been given, but also in retaining and increasing it after it has been given to him, as always to be humble in his own eyes; always fearful and watchful; always timid and anxious; always conscious that he should not think highly, but fear; always and in all things accusing himself. For the greater the humility held in the mind, the more grace is increased in him; and to him that hath shall be given, and he shall abound.”

It is indeed a great and rare virtue that, though doing great things, you do not know yourself to be great; and that your holiness, manifest to all, remains hidden from you alone; that you appear admirable, yet reckon yourself contemptible. I judge this more wonderful than the virtues themselves. This too I especially extol in our author above others. [Col. 0042D]

But with what reverence of spirit, with what ardour of mind and outpouring of his whole self, did he minister at the sacred altars in the divine, daily, and uninterrupted sacrifice? “Wholly shaken and melted,” he says. [Note: [Col. 0042D] *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, Part II, ch. 10.] “That offering without blemish, figured by the legal rite, and which we likewise offer daily when we faithfully receive the most holy body of our Lord . . . we indeed make divisions in the sacrament, but we do not divide him from himself . . . where the part is, there also is the whole, because, as he is one in different places, so in each individual part he can be whole . . . the appearance [Col. 0043A] is seen of that whose substance is not present, and the substance is hidden whose form does not appear.” And much else with him that is true and Catholic.

Here, with sighs piercing the heavens and eyes overflowing with tears, he first offered himself as a victim to God before performing the sacrifice. Here he contemplated the human body in the Word, divinity in flesh, man in God. Here he drank abundantly from the fountains of the Saviour. Here was laid up the entire ground of his healing and confidence, and the whole life of his soul.

It is pleasant to hear him speak more fervently himself. [Note: [Col. 0043D] Sermon 40.] “I tell you, my friends: my hope is solid and my confidence firm that I shall obtain forgiveness for the sins which I committed in the body and contracted through the body, through the immolation of the spotless body of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. This hope and confidence [Col. 0043B] is surely afforded me by that saying of blessed John: ‘We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins’ (1 John 2).

“And then, what if the body which I bear is unclean and defiled? Yet that which I possess in Christ is altogether holy and pure. In everything in myself in which I find either too little good or too much evil, I flee back to the life-giving body of my Jesus, making his holiness a shield between the justice of the Father and my own iniquity. What if curiosity has defiled sight in my body, emptiness hearing, pleasure smell, gluttony taste, and impurity touch? I shall not be too troubled, nor too faint-hearted. For I know what I shall do. I will go to the most pure body of my Lord, in which none of these evils [Col. 0043C] exists, holding it as a shield in his judgment: washing away through it what is evil in mine, and claiming for myself what is good in his. Thus I shall no longer fear him as judge, but love him as brother; for he is my brother and my flesh.”

O words drawn from the purest storehouse of wisdom! O words sweeter to me than honey and the honeycomb! I confess, I broke off reluctantly. Drawn by such sweetness, I taste again a few words.

“Thus, therefore, I run to the body which committed no sin, that the sin which I committed through the body may also be forgiven me. But if flesh in me lusts against spirit; if the vices of the flesh tempt me; if its enticing stings assail me: must I not then all the more flee to my one sure refuge, the body of my Jesus, [Col. 0043D] so that the lust of my body may be extinguished, temptations overcome, and the stings blunted? For what aid is so effective for gaining such a triumph as meditation [variant: eating] of his body? For he is the one who knows how to have compassion on our infirmities.”

Thus he himself speaks; and whoever loves will dwell more fully upon these things. They celebrate the painter Timanthes because in his pictures there was always understood something more than was painted; so too, in those brief sayings which I gather from the author—“kernels,” as it were, or aphorisms—there is more contained and signified than their separate sounds express. [Note: [Col. 0043D] Augustine, *Confessions*, Book IX, ch. 13.]

In return, it should be remembered that, just as for the most devout mother and her son Augustine—her son in flesh and spirit—nothing was more urgent or more constant than to keep an unceasing remembrance at God’s altar after her death, knowing that there is administered the holy victim by which the handwriting opposed to us was erased; so our author beseeches the Premonstratensian brethren, servants of Christ, whom he served in voice, heart, and letters, his mind’s knees bent and himself prostrate at their feet, to remember him in [Note: [Col. 0043D] Letter I, to Prémontré.] their evening sacrifices, offering him to be healed before their merciful sight: before our Advocate, gentle and meek Jesus, who paid for us what he owed not for himself, who became priest and victim for us, purchaser and price, sacrificer and sacrifice, physician of our wounds and medicine—washing us unclean people and reconciling us who were guilty by the abundant outpouring of his merciful blood. [Col. 0044B]

And he concludes: “Remember, therefore, Adam the sinner who loves you, when, from the deepest interior of the golden altar, you fill the Holy of Holies with fragrant smoke sent forth from spices. And above all there, where the Son is sacrificed to the Father, whose blood cries from the earth more eloquently than Abel’s” (Hebrews 12:24). “And we would add this also to our petitions, unless perhaps it should be charged to rash presumption: namely, that after death you would command my name to be inscribed in the book of your holy congregation together with the names of those of yours who have already departed, because we too are yours.”

He obtained the request, made both fittingly and humbly; and his name is found entered in the Premonstratensian necrology on 9 December.

I have finished, if charity closes the procession of virtues—the charity which [Col. 0044C] never fails. This, as the substance of the whole work, appears and overflows everywhere. [Note: [Col. 0043D] See St Bernard, Sermon 79 on the Song of Songs.] This speaks everywhere; and whoever wishes to gain knowledge of the things being read must love. For the language of love is barbarous to one who does not love, like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal; nor can a cold breast receive an inflamed utterance. And our author says: “Granted that I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not empty of love.”

He had fixed before himself this as the motive for writing and acting, this as his touchstone: the celebrated maxim of St Augustine [Note: [Col. 0044D] Preface to Sermon 3, to Religious.] which he repeated both by mouth and pen: “Have charity, and do what you will”; and another not unlike it: [Note: [Col. 0044D] Sermon 8 to Religious, and Sermon 12 to the same.] “Have charity, and clothe yourself in whatever garment you will.”

This, he teaches, is the ladder whose lower part rests upon earth and whose summit touches heaven. This is the oil poured upon the upright stone set up as a sign; this is the unity of the cubit at the completion and summit of Noah’s ark; this is the tree of paradise—indeed, paradise itself. This makes cenobitic life holy, peaceful, and pleasant. Finally, it is so great and such a thing that it holds primacy over all other virtues; without it the other virtues may indeed be called virtues, but falsely; they cannot in any way truly be virtues. All other precepts serve the acquisition, possession, and fostering of charity alone.

And in his letter to his own brethren: [Note: [Col. 0044D] Letter I, to Prémontré.] “To this end [Col. 0045A] our Order directs its whole purpose: that it may serve charity. Whether therefore it spares or strikes, binds or relaxes, acts dispensationally in some matter because a reasonable cause has intervened, or indeed changes one thing into another, let it refer everything to the integrity of charity and in no respect exceed its measure, so that it may show that it possesses the tree of life in its midst. For if charity spares, it is not slack indulgence; if charity corrects, the discipline is not rigid.” And there is more, which one meditating on an ending must necessarily cut short.

From this fervour of charity which he breathed wholly, and by which, in an intimate embrace, he clung to his God, there arose in him a confidence so firm and steadfast—almost forgetful of mortal condition—that he seemed, after laying aside the spoils of earthly flesh, to have gone into the lot of the saints and among the household of God. Thus he rejoices in a certain rapture of mind and gives forth the voice of one feasting: [Note: [Col. 0045D] *On Contemplation*, Part III, §7.] “I consider these things, O Lord my God; I consider them, I say, and am made joyful. I see these things, and exult. I behold these things, and conceive such great hope even concerning myself that I dare hope that I too am one of them. For while attentively contemplating these things, I firmly hope that I shall be admitted into the fellowship of your elect—not through any merits of mine intervening, but through your grace alone, freely bestowed—so that I even dare now apply to myself that saying of the holy man which he spoke concerning himself and his fellow-elect; I say it of myself: ‘Now I am a son of God, and it has not yet appeared what I shall be’ (1 John 3:2).

“And whence, Lord, comes this hope to me, that I should dare hope that one so small and such as I shall become like you? Doubtless from the incomprehensible sweetness of the love by which you deign to embrace us so freely and so steadfastly. Therefore I incite my soul, through manifold contemplation of the benefits bestowed upon me by you, to praise you; and I say: ‘Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name’ (Psalm 103:1).” And what follows.

But as one entering the enclosures of a flourishing garden does not immediately set to ravaging with greedy nail every flower upon which his eager eyes range, but gathers some here and there to make from them a little bouquet whereby he may celebrate among friends the garden’s renown through its variegated garland, so I judged that I should act: from the abundance of virtues I plucked, as it were, a florilegium, so that a clearer knowledge might grow together with praise. Behold how great are the delights in the heliotrope of gratitude, the violet of humility, the many-coloured tulips of mixed life, the hyacinth of heavenly longing, the walnut-tree of temperance, the lilies of devotion and pure prayer, the amaranth of fervent spirit, and the white and purple roses of ardent affection toward the spotless Lamb, who washed us in his blood and is daily sacrificed for us! [Col. 0045D]

How great, finally, is the beauty in pomegranates sweetly fragrant because of love for one’s neighbour, and crimson-red because of charity toward God! Or do you perhaps doubt? Enter, I pray, these pleasant enclosures yourself; look within the mystical cushions; pass through the flower-beds in which there are as many blooming shoots as one encounters everywhere weighty sayings. [Col. 0046A]

Thus, out of the very many virtues remaining, we have lightly touched a few thyrsi, or flower-staffs, of virtue. We have investigated the author from his own writings; and who can know an author more rightly than he knows himself? It is a common and accepted principle that each person is more clearly known to another from his own good things. What good things could you receive, other than these writings, in which a living image of him shines forth? Aptly said someone: “Let him himself sound forth his own praise, and let his spirit, crowned with laurel, be crowned in his writings.”

## CHAPTER X. A complaint concerning lost books of the ancients, and a catalogue of Adam’s works

Famous is the saying of the Hussite prophet: “With the ancients is wisdom, and in length of days prudence” (Job 12:12); and that of another who, in the comic poet, judges those wise who use old wine—that is, the writings of the ancients. These alone among human things ought to have been works which no storm could overwhelm and no age consume. “All other things which stand by the construction of stones and marble masses raised to great height will not prolong a long day,” says Seneca. [Note: [Col. 0045D] *Consolation to Polybius*, ch. 37.] “For they too perish. The remembrance of genius is immortal.”

Therefore, when I seek and repeatedly search for older writers commended for venerable faith and sound expression, I encounter what is said to have been said long ago of Caesar: that he ought either not to have been born in the republic or not to have died. So too, illustrious men ought either not to have laboured in setting down their writings [Col. 0046C] or those writings ought not to have perished. For just as parents bear more lightly children who were never born to them than children who died prematurely, so perhaps we would not suffer such grief over the writings of many men if we did not know of them. But now, seeing fragments and titles of lost works, we are distressed with longing and tortured:

> [Note: [Col. 0046D] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book II, metre 7.]
>
> But because we know their splendid names,  
> are we thereby enabled to know those consumed?  
> Therefore you lie wholly unknown,  
> nor does fame make you known.

I confess that this repeatedly happens to me when I call to mind our most wise and renowned Adam: famed for the holiness of his life, an illustrious writer, splendid in ancestral lineage, exalted in rank, most outstanding not only as a master of scholastic theology but of mystical theology and ascetic life, and a kind of Epictetus of holier philosophy—yet lying so neglected, hidden in obscurity, or appearing only mutilated. What other thing would it have meant to us for his work to survive entire, make itself readily available and useful to all, and be transmitted chaste and unblemished to the memory of posterity? Who, once one has moved a little away from the holy Fathers, can stand on equal ground with him in grace of expression, abundance of learning, liveliness of heart, and the whole method of discourse? No other, or only a rare one, comes before my eyes who explains so copiously the compendia of holier life, raises so sublimely a spirit weighed down by mortal concreteness, sets forth more maturely the symbols of religious life, and weighs more fairly the considerations of ecclesiastical dignity. [Col. 0046D]

Cicero has his richness of expression, Laelius his charm, Fronto his gravity. Ambrose has his elegance, Jerome his sharpness, Augustine his acuteness, Gregory his emphasis, Bernard his honeyed eloquence; and so one may run through the others. Nor is diversity greater in human faces than in the styles of writers. Our author resembles a river rather than a torrent: proceeding gently from its source, it increases as it runs and enlarges in its own channel, drawing the reader along with it. [Col. 0047A]

He acknowledges that he held and followed Holy Scripture as an unfailing thread in every matter of the right way and blessed life. [Note: [Col. 0047D] The Author’s Letter to Abbot John.] He applied himself to this study day and night; there he found that the strong man ate, the infant sucked, the tender lamb walked, and the immense elephant could scarcely swim. Here beginners would be fed with the milk of history, those advancing with the bread of allegory, those doing good works with the food of tropology, and the perfect, advanced to the heights, with the wine of anagogy and theoretical contemplation. From this source he clothed himself with spirit and life; from it he scattered in his books hidden sparks of virtue, to inflame the careless souls of those who would read them.

“The man who comes into the sun,” says that philosopher, [Note: [Col. 0047D] Seneca, Letter 108.] “though he has not come for this purpose, will acquire colour; those who have sat in a perfumer’s shop and remained there a little longer carry away with them the scent of the place.” And those who have read these venerable Fathers must necessarily draw from them something [Col. 0047C] which benefits even the negligent.

Finally, this is to be observed in our author and in other writers of the Catholic Church: they often concealed and avoided a certain majesty of eloquence which they possessed, so that they might speak not to the idle schools of grammarians or philosophers, as St Jerome says, [Note: [Col. 0047D] Letter to Pammachius; see Sermons 11 and 15 of Part I [Col. 0048D].] but to the entire human race. Our author more than once confesses that he desired this, holding the instruction of hearts more important than the arrangement of words. If you please, we shall give a catalogue of his books.

[Note: [Col. 0048D] See the Author, Preface I.] Beginning from Advent of the Lord and proceeding through the more festive days of the whole year, he gathered, as he confesses, one hundred homilies or sermons, dedicated to his canons of the Church of Prémontré, both from things which he, an outstanding preacher, had said in preaching and from certain additions. [Col. 0047D] Of these, the first class proceeds in the following order, through two volumes.

**First volume.**

From the First Sunday in Advent until the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord: eighteen sermons. On the Vigil itself: four. On the day of the Nativity: six. On the day of St Stephen, the first martyr: four. On the day of St John, Apostle and Evangelist: one. On the day of the Holy Innocents: three. On the Sunday within the Octave of the Nativity: four. On the day of the Circumcision: two. On the Epiphany of the Lord: two. On the Second Sunday after [Col. 0048A] the Epiphany of the Lord: three.

The religious congregation of the Celestine Fathers at Paris kindly shared with me, from a manuscript, these forty-seven homilies arranged in one volume. At that time the Reverend Father Francis Liegault, called Prior because he held the authority of provost, was worthy of imperishable remembrance by me for his singular learning and humanity.

**Second volume.**

On Ash Wednesday: one sermon; on Palm Sunday: one; on Maundy Thursday: one; at the festival of Easter: four; in the third week of Easter, on Monday at the synod: one; on the following Tuesday at the same synod: one; on Ascension Day: one; at the feast of Pentecost: six; in its octave: one; at the dedication of a church: one; at the election of any prelate: one. There are, moreover, twenty sermons which, as he says, he delivered on the more festive birthdays of saints.

Alas, we mourn the loss of the second volume—or rather seek it elsewhere, hidden away. O whoever perhaps knows, reveal to us this concealed treasure. Grant as much to the sincerity of one who asks, and to the love of one who implores.

The second class consists of works which were ordered to be printed by James de Bachimont, president of the general chapter, doctor and professor of sacred letters, and general head of the Premonstratensian Order. Amatus a Fonte, Abbot of Camera-Fontis, set his hand to the task in the year, as we noted above, 1518, under the following titles:

[Col. 0048C] *Fourteen Sermons on the Order, Habit, and Profession of the Canons of the Premonstratensian Order.*

*On the Threefold Tabernacle*: that of Moses, which formerly existed in outward reality; that of Christ, which exists in the common faith of the Church; and that of the Holy Spirit, which consists in the hidden purity of the human soul. This treatise is completed in three parts, discussing the tabernacle in its literal, allegorical, and tropological sense. Having undertaken it at the prompting—indeed command—of John, Abbot of St Mary of Kelchou in Scotland, most distinguished in that century, as their exchanged letters make clear, he followed the prescribed order and dedicated it to him.

*On the Threefold Kind of Contemplation*: that God is incomprehensible in himself, terrible to the reprobate, and sweet to the elect. Divided likewise into three parts, he issued it dedicated to the sacred community of the Church of Prémontré. [Col. 0048D]

The third class consists again of works that have been lost to us. Specifically, there is that book which the author admits he wrote *On the Sweetness of God*. “In it,” he says, “there was sufficient instruction on divine benefits and the hymn-like praises which the elect will sing eternally to their Creator.” Let us give a kind of epitome, if it is useful: our creation, redemption, liberation, protection, and beneficence. For he created us, redeemed us, liberated us, protects us, and benefits us. He created those who did not exist, redeemed the lost, protects the weak, and benefits the unworthy. [Col. 0049A] He created us, I say, in divinity; redeemed us in humanity; freed us from captivity; protects us in present weakness; and benefits us in eternal blessedness. For he is our Creator, Redeemer, Liberator, Protector, and Benefactor. “These are the mercies of God which we shall sing for ever,” says the author, “declaring his truth with our mouth.”

The book particularly pursued these five heads of benefits. Yet I fully think that he also composed certain other little works, and he indicates this not obscurely in several places; but I have nothing more definite to assert about them, except that Pagius affirms in his *Library* [Note: [Col. 0049D] Book I of the *Library*, ch. 17. A manuscript exists among us.] that he composed a volume of letters. I recall reading the same in the manuscript treatise of Michael Ghierius, Abbot of Dom-Martin in the district of Artois, which he compiled *On the Writers [Col. 0049B] of the Premonstratensian Order*. Aubertus Miraeus also appears to incline to this view in his brief chronicle. [Note: [Col. 0049D] Under the year 1518.]

## CHAPTER XI. The writers by whom our author was celebrated; why the title “Book of the Most Blessed Mother of God Mary and of St John the Baptist” was prefixed to the old edition

The works enumerated in the second class, published at Paris about one hundred and forty years ago, which ought to have been edited carefully and correctly in view of their usefulness and dignity, reached later generations so corrupted that scarcely anyone dared touch them, much less wear them out by reading them through—deterred without doubt both by that perplexing typeface [Col. 0049C] and by monstrous errors and lacunae. Whether this occurred through the defect of that age, when printing arts were not yet so polished, or rather through the carelessness and neglect of those directing the printing, I cannot readily decide. For this reason it spread only a slight reputation among most people. Knowledge of his writings became still slighter. How few altogether do you see seeking authority and salutary instruction from him in their writings? How few do you hear in their halls, dining rooms, or studies turning over this master of mystical discourse? Rarer still is one who has pursued and grasped his sublime thoughts. Yet the chief writers who come to my attention are these.

First, John Molanus, a most distinguished theologian of Louvain, both lists the works of our author in his *Library of Preachers* [Col. 0049D] and, in the book which he entitled *On Canons*, [Note: [Col. 0049D] *On Canons*, Book I, ch. 4.] reminds his canons of their dignity and obligation through the weight of authority taken from our author.

Antonio Possevino, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, counts him among the authors in these words: [Note: [Col. 0049D] Antonio Possevino, *Apparatus*, letter 4.] “Adam of the Premonstratensian Order, a professor at Paris, in the year 1518 published a book entitled *Of the Most Blessed Mother of God*, in which is ‘On the Order, Habit, and Profession of Premonstratensian Religious.’ And the remaining works which we have published.”

Who would take this amiss in a learned man [Col. 0050A] unless candour of mind effaces the blemish—that, omitting the name “canons,” he substituted another term, not indeed inferior or less worthy, if no fault has settled on his mind or eye? What the supreme pontiffs judged the Premonstratensian institute to be, we have read above, and the author explains it clearly.

Next I see our Adam placed in the choir of the Fathers by Aloysius Novarinus, [Note: [Col. 0050D] Aloysius Novarinus, *On the Elect*, Book I, ch. 13, no. 722.] a man distinguished in this age by learning and writings. Aubertus Miraeus, in his brief *Premonstratensian Chronicle*, lists him in the same order in which we have said the works were published: [Note: [Col. 0050D] Aubertus Miraeus, under the year 1518.] “Adam, Abbot of Prémontré and general head of the entire Order, a very learned man, wrote three books, printed in Paris in folio in 1518 through the study and diligence of Amatus a Fonte, Abbot of Camera-Fontis.” Then he adds the repeated titles. The words we have previously cited must be brought into conformity with the standard and rule of truth established by this statement.

No less is there attached to this the statement which Crespetius, doctor of theology of Paris, joins in his *Ecclesiastical Summary*: [Note: [Col. 0050D] Crespetius, under “Maria.”] “We also have a chant and office issued by Adam, most devout cardinal of Prémontré, conforming in every respect in its musical setting to the office of an ecclesiastical solemnity.” Nor does Molanus object, judging that “Eucharistic” should be substituted in place of “ecclesiastical”; its solemnities are known to have been instituted almost a hundred years after the age of our Adam.

But reasoned investigation forbids us, however favourably inclined, to assign the rank of cardinal in the Roman Church to this or any other man of that name among ours. The error seems to me to have entered Crespetius from the fact that Ciaconius, in his catalogue of cardinals, includes a certain Adam, an Englishman, but one of another age and institute from our Adam. [Col. 0050C]

I am more inclined to suppose that our Adam was distinguished by the laurel and degree of most eminent theologian in the schools, or even doctor, as they call it. Old manuscripts much used among the Celestine Fathers at Paris convict us of this truth, for they contain the title “Master Adam” equally at beginning and end. That people of that ancient age bestowed such a title only upon professors laureated in the theological faculty—men highly celebrated for manifold learning and renown—can readily be proved in many instances.

In his division of the Rule [Col. 0050D] of St Augustine, flowing out into twelve chapters and still adopted for the use and constitutions of the Premonstratensians, the Fathers of the Order judged that he should be called by no other designation than “Venerable,” as we are accustomed to call Bede and eminent men in Britain by that title. A provost of the Cell of All Saints in Swabia, of the Premonstratensian Order, composed certain commentaries on those sermons of the author which more particularly concern religious observance, Servatius Lairvelz attesting this in his *Optics*. [Note: [Col. 0050D] Lairvelz, *Optical Mirror*, III.] No further information about them has been given to us, nor do I think they ever emerged into the public domain. I am aware that many of our own members mention him in their writings: Martinus Merzius in his treatise *On the Institute of Premonstratensian Canons*, Landtmeter in his commentary on the Rule of St Augustine, Moerbecius in the *Purple Ladder*, Pagius in his *Library*, Mauritius a Prato in the *Annals*, and many others. [Col. 0051A]

And lest anyone lightly wonder why the old edition bears at the entrance of its title-page the heading, “Book of the Mother of God and of St John the Baptist,” it is not difficult to make the matter plain by recalling the old custom, before printing was invented, accepted in very many religious houses: manuscripts had the name of the community to which they belonged prefixed to them, lest, when moved from their place—rightly or wrongly—they might easily become exiles elsewhere. [Col. 0051B] Therefore, since our author, as he explains more than once, had intended the offspring of his mind to be dedicated to the canonical brethren of the Church of Prémontré and servants of Christ, the part of his works subsequently sent to the press retained the inscription which it had originally borne at its head.

So that it may be more fully apparent to all from the special affection discovered in him for this Holy Lady, we must briefly recall that Norbert was first kindly and familiarly received by Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon, son of a certain prince Falcon of Burgundy, and was repeatedly conducted through the boundaries of his dominion. The bishop feared lest the proved virtue of so great a man should turn elsewhere, and wished that, if any land or church pleased him, he might choose it at his own discretion and mark it as perpetually favoured by his hospitality.

[Col. 0051C] But let us hear the bishop himself set this forth in his diploma:

> “The rulers of the Holy Church, insofar as they appear to excel others in dignity and honour, ought all the more clearly and firmly to determine what they establish and dispose. We therefore wish it to be known to present and future alike that, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1120, a man of notable religious life, named Norbert, happened to pass through our bishopric. Recognizing his holiness, integrity, learning, and eloquence, we constrained him by many prayers to spend the winter with us. The more we heard him speak and bound him to ourselves in familiarity, the more were we refreshed by the fragrance of his good odour.
>
> “Then, when winter had almost passed and that holy man wished to depart from us, we were asked by persons of our Church and by very many nobles of our bishopric—though we ourselves greatly desired it also—to establish him somewhere in our diocese for the service of God. At last, with divine grace cooperating, we obtained this from him with difficulty. Thus, while surveying the bounds of our possessions, we came to a very deserted place called Prémontré, uninhabitable at that time. Considering it, the man of God said: ‘I see a place according to my heart, prepared for me by the Lord before all ages.’ Hearing this, we rejoiced with joy and established him there [Col. 0052A] to remain with a few poor people of Christ, having assigned the boundaries of the place.”

These are his words, with much more besides. [Note: [Col. 0051D] See the Premonstratensian *Library*, Book II, ch. 12; *Lives of St Norbert.*]

Therefore Norbert, an admirable discerner of spirits and indeed of places, was not deterred from his purpose by the unfruitful soil, lack of population, roughness of immense solitude, harshness of rocks, or the gaping marsh, arousing horror like an abyssal chasm. He chose the valley of Prémontré: unattractive in its situation, unworkable in cultivation, terrifying in appearance, yet wholly venerable because of St John the Baptist, to whom the ancient piety of the Fathers had built a humble chapel in that wilderness.

There, in a night made wakeful by prayers, he was taught the secret of the divine counsel. There the most sacred Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, brighter than light and whiter than the sun, showed him the foundations to be laid for the new house, presented the habit in which he and his companions were to clothe themselves, and announced that strength must be sought for the new flock from the Roman pontiff. There, finally, through prophetic and manifold vision of divine things and of the blessed destination of God’s servants to their homeland, he actually secured for the valley what it had long borne only in name. [Col. 0052B]

They celebrate Plato because, though wealthy—as shown when Diogenes trampled Plato’s Phrygian rugs with muddy feet—he chose the country estate of the Academy, remote from urban clamour and adverse to bodily health, for the study of philosophy. He did so with the wise purpose that the conflict of illness might moderate the assaults of harmful desire, and that they might feel no pleasure except from the subjects which they themselves were learning. Thus, according to St Jerome, [Note: [Col. 0052D] Book II, *Against Jovinianus.*] he deserved to be called divine even on this account: that he chose places inimical to bodily health for pursuing philosophical studies, so that, when the flesh was weakened and its fires—which weigh down the mind—were diminished, the spirit might rise more freely to contemplation of the loftiest things. [Col. 0052C]

I understand St Norbert’s design more sublimely: inspired, certainly, by heaven, he prepared for his followers a Lyceum of eternal wisdom, all other choices rejected, in a place of horror and vast solitude.

From this origin the Virgin Mother of God and John the Baptist were appointed the patron saints by decree, and gave their titles to the greater church built by St. Norbert; their worship was thereafter transmitted throughout the whole Order and maintained with singular veneration. Here indeed, besides the solemn feasts, they receive, among the daily prayers of the canonical hours [Col. 0052D], a morning and evening commemoration in the capacity of patrons. But to his most gracious Mother and most excellent advocate with God—under whose auspices he had been formed, by whose benefits he had grown to maturity, and beneath whose protecting patronage he had flourished—he consecrated all his churches and convents, devoted to the name and honour of Mary, in order to render some testimony of a grateful heart. Each day he publicly pays her the appointed office of the sacred hours through the choirs; he observes her feast-days, prepared by fasting on the preceding day, with more solemn rite and, as they call them, with octaves.

Augustinus Wichmans, in his *Marian Brabant*, Aubertus Miraeus in his *Chronicle* [Note: [Col. 0053D] Book III, chapter 29, in the preface to the *Premonstratensian Chronicle*], Chrysostomus a Stella in the *Life of St. Norbert*, and many others celebrate her as the special protectress and patroness of the White Order [Col. 0053A]. Memorable is the testimony of the kings of France, Louis XI and his son Charles VIII, in these words:

> While we more earnestly consider in the secret recesses of our minds the sincerity, integrity, long duration, and divine—indeed miraculous—foundation of the Premonstratensian Order: which, after the passage of long courses of time, is known to have been instituted through the mystical inspiration revealed by the most blessed and most glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of Christ our Redeemer, through the pious Father and first founder of that Order, Blessed Norbert, a man resplendent in sanctity of life and illustrious through many miracles; and while the white habit of the said Order, together with the place in the district of Laon where the Premonstratensian monastery, the head and foundation of the aforesaid Order, ought to be built, was shown beforehand by the same most blessed and glorious Virgin Mary—whence it is established by many authentic documents and most trustworthy histories that the Premonstratensian Order took its name for itself—we are moved towards that same Premonstratensian Order with so much the greater and more ardent desire, etc.

Given in the palace at Paris, in the year of the Lord 1491. [Note: [Col. 0053D] See the *Premonstratensian Library*, Book III, folio 762 in my copy.]

To confirm this matter, there is the formula of profession received from our author and master, by which St. Norbert and his first companions, at the cradle of the infant Jesus on the Nativity of the Lord, and at the bosom of the Virgin Mother, enrolled themselves by solemn pronouncement of vows for that city of blessed eternity [Col. 0053C]:

> I, offering myself, give myself to the Church of holy Mary, Mother of God, and to that holy one, and promise the conversion of my manner of life.

And elsewhere you have the same formula [Note: [Col. 0053D] Sermon 5 to religious; see *Marian Brabant*, Book III, chapter 29.]. Do you see that every member, by the unchanging tenor of these words, wherever the Order extends, declared his church dedicated to the memory and worship of the holy Mother of God? This surely could not have been done universally unless this Lady had been patroness of all the churches. Nor is this contradicted by the fact that I remember many houses commonly called by the title of saints other than the Mother of God. Either they bore those names before being taken over by the Premonstratensians, or, because of sacred relics or an ancient commemoration of saints celebrated there, and for similar reasons, it was expedient that they should commonly be known under the names of one heavenly saint or another. Yet she, the more illustrious assisting Lady, presides over them by equal right and equal bond.

These matters would be treated more clearly by one whose purpose it was systematically to pursue the benefits of the Mother of God and the services rendered by the White Order to so great a devoted patroness. One of our own recently did this [Note: [Col. 0053D] Herdegom, a canon], who entitled his book *The White Premonstratensian Virgin*, except that its title may seem more restrictive than the designation “White Order” permits [Col. 0054A].

## CHAPTER XII. On the Church of Whithorn, or Witherne, over which Adam presided; and on cathedral churches occupied by Premonstratensians by ordinary and extraordinary right.

The see of Whithorn, in Galloway, beside the shore of the Irish Sea—for the inhabitants call it Witherne—is said to have been consecrated long ago by St. Ninian to God in memory of St. Martin. Others, supported by the testimony of the Venerable Bede in his English history, hold that St. Plechelm first occupied it as bishop. And what greater weight can be attached to one account than to the other? See also Miraeus in the Belgian fasti, 15 July; Usuard in his *Martyrology*; and the Life of St. Switbert in Surius, at the Kalends of March [Col. 0054B].

From these sources one may discern that Plechelm flourished in the year of our salvation 690; that Ninian shone in episcopal dignity under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius; and that, according to the Roman tables of martyrs, he died on 16 September, A.D. 432 [Note: [Col. 0054D] *Roman Martyrology*, 16 September.]. Nor would I venture to charge these statements, drawn from English annals, with error. But, in order to offer a bond reconciling the truth, I judge that St. Ninian, bishop and founder, presided without an established succession of successors; and that finally, under blessed Plechelm, the mitre was assigned to that church in a solemn assembly of the inhabitants and with the consent of the other bishops, and remained securely in force.

The lengthy and complicated question that arose over many years between the kings and bishops of England and Scotland concerning primacy, metropolitan right, exemption, and related matters, I refer for fuller discussion to Polydore Vergil [Note: [Col. 0054D] *English History*, Book IX, folio 153 in my copy; and Book XIII; Pennottus, Book II, chapter 36.], Harpsfield [Note: [Col. 0054D] Harpsfield, *English History*, Book XXII.], Baronius [Note: [Col. 0054D] Baronius, year 1191.], and Gabriel Pennottus; we too have touched upon it above. In my leisure I add only this concerning the matter, which no one can rightly dispute: after this, there were two metropolitans in the kingdom of Scotland. The first, in the church of St. Andrew, had subject to him the bishops of Dunkeld, Aberdeen, Moray, Dunblane, Brechin, Ross, Caithness, and Orkney. The other was the hierarch of Glasgow, whom the bishops of Whithorn, Lismore, and Sodor acknowledge as their superior in sacred affairs [Col. 0054C].

Turning to Adam, the first head of a religious community of our Order at Whithorn: Mauritius of Prato states openly and explicitly in his *Annals*, under the year 1177, that Adam was the first in that church to be raised to episcopal dignity [Col. 0054D]. It may not be unwelcome to reread a few lines [Note: [Col. 0054D] See Prologue, chapter IV.]:

> Christian, bishop of Whithorn in Galloway, a region of Scotland, converted the canons of his cathedral church, already regular, into Premonstratensians. For this reason he is called the founder of that church in the Premonstratensian obituary on the Nones of April. The first canons were summoned from Dryburgh, and from among them Adam, or Edan, was given as first superior or abbot; under that name he is recorded in the obituaries of the Order on the ninth or tenth day before the Kalends of December.

Dempster’s judgment in his work *On the Writers of Scotland* agrees with that of the older monuments.

An old manuscript of Averbode states distinctly and briefly: “Whithorn, daughter of Dryburgh. It is an episcopal see and a priory; and the election of the bishop belongs to the convent of this place.” The author of the *Premonstratensian Library* and Servatius Lairvelz in his *Optics of Regulars*, whom I shall cite immediately, say the same; and, I think, no one will deny a truth so well established. Aubertus Miraeus is an eminent additional witness in his account of bishops [Note: [Col. 0055D] Book V, chapter 1.]:

> Whithorn, the bishopric of Witherne, under the archbishopric of Glasgow, in the Scottish province of Galloway [Col. 0055B]. It was formerly an abbey of regular canons, in which was the bishop’s seat; nor did he have any canons in his cathedral basilica other than regular canons.

And concerning the granted liberty [Note: [Col. 0055D] Book II, following the *Notitia*.]:

> In Scotland, says he, the bishoprics exempted by Celestine II in the year 1192, according to Baronius, are St. Andrews, Glasgow, and Whithorn,

together with those he enumerates. In the catalogue of Premonstratensian monasteries appended to the *Optics of Regulars* [Note: [Col. 0055D] Servatius Lairvelz, index of monasteries; Miraeus, *Premonstratensian Chronicle*, under the year 1480.]:

> Whithorn, says Abbot Servatius, daughter of Dryburgh, a cathedral church in which there formerly presided an abbot of our Order, who was also bishop, elected by his college of Premonstratensian canons occupying that cathedral church.

Yet let no one be reluctant to travel from this shore beyond the sea [Col. 0055C], as if by leaps, through various regions of the world, in order to inspect the lofty sees occupied by bishops supplied by the Premonstratensians [Note: [Col. 0055D] See *Premonstratensian Library*, Book I, chapter 17.]. First come those which the Premonstratensians ascended by ordinary right, elected by the votes of their own religious alone, with no other body or authority giving support. Nor, perhaps to your surprise, were persons generally chosen for the offices of provosts, deans, archdeacons, precentors, and offices greater and lesser of that kind, except from the regular profession.

St. Norbert himself had first pressed this path when he was raised to the archiepiscopal see of Naples. Believing that nowhere could he rest more safely and holily, away from the pomps of the clamorous world, than among his own, he transferred twenty canons, chosen according to his judgment, from the collegiate church of Blessed Mary, almost adjoining his archiepiscopal palace, and replaced them with his own regular clerics. Thus, after placing his brethren there, he might sometimes refresh his spirit a little from the turmoil demanded by his imposed office, as the contemporary author of his Life says [Note: [Col. 0056D] Chapters 45 and 49 of the *Life.*], just as painters whose eyes have been dulled by prolonged attention restore them by looking upon mirrors or greenery.

Besides this church, and another there dedicated to St. Maurice, which was higher than the rest in dignity and primacy [Col. 0056A], he obtained from Innocent II, at the Council of Reims in 1131, an archiepiscopal church, into which he could suitably introduce canons of his own institute. As Albert Krantz relates [Note: [Col. 0056D] Book VI, chapter 12 of the *Metropolis.*], the canons of that mother church willingly endured this, being reduced into the Premonstratensian Order and called Norbertines. The churches which our brethren later held in head and members by full right, and in an uninterrupted succession for very many years, were these: the cathedral churches of Havelberg, Brandenburg, and Ratzeburg in Saxon Germany; concerning them see Krantz [Note: [Col. 0056D] Book XII, chapter 8 above; and Book VII, chapter 50.]. Płock, a cathedral in Poland; and Belbuk, a cathedral in Slavonia. We have already mentioned Whithorn in Scotland, also called by some Holy Trinity [Col. 0056B]. Riga, the metropolitan see in Livonia, had ten suffragans subject to it, all, as they say, of Premonstratensian institute: Ösel, Dorpat, Topat, Gerland, Chur, Culm, Sambian, Warmian, Pomesanian on the island of Blessed Mary, and Ruthenian.

Servatius adds in his index of monasteries: Zagreb, a cathedral in Slavonia—or rather Pomerania—the cathedral church of Holy Trinity in Denmark, and five others in Saxony; likewise the cathedrals of Rilzmadum, Lucich, Linoma, Imbria, and Aldeberch. In these, he says, there formerly presided abbots of our Order, elected by their college of Premonstratensian canons occupying those cathedral churches. To confirm these matters, Bishop Dubravius of Olomouc in his *Bohemian History*, and Augustinus of Olomouc in his catalogue of the bishops of Olomouc, make the following assertion [Col. 0056C]: that very many men from the Premonstratensians, outstanding in virtue and exalted in merit, exercised the highest authority in the Church.

Chrysostomus a Stella relates in the *Life of St. Norbert* that Cardinal Stephen of the Holy Roman Church, of the title of Saints John and Paul, in a diploma issued at Avignon in the tenth year of Clement VI, attests, on the authority of papal instruments and in express and considered words, that sixteen episcopal sees were subject and incorporated in their entirety and by ordinary right to the Premonstratensians. See Aubertus Miraeus in his short *Chronicle*. A splendid inheritance indeed, if no one had assailed it.

From Albert Krantz [Note: [Col. 0056D] Krantz, Book VI, 12, *Metropolis.*] I would add that our Order held many of these sees for two hundred, three hundred, and more years. He states this particularly of Ratzeburg: first occupied by Blessed Evermod, the disciple whom Norbert loved, then provost of Blessed Mary at Magdeburg, it continued to be occupied without interruption by our brethren until the year 1480. In the printed abridgment of the Chronicle of Mauritius, under the year 1181, it is said:

> Eskil, formerly bishop of Lund in Denmark, dies. He had subjected his cathedral to the Premonstratensian Order [Col. 0057A] and endowed two other monasteries of the same institute. In Denmark Bishop Tucho of Børglum followed his example: he too desired, and accomplished, that his canons should observe the Premonstratensian rule.

It is preserved by ancient and trustworthy authority [Note: [Col. 0057D] See Servatius Lairvelz, *Optics of Regulars*, speculum 111 and the index of monasteries; Miraeus at the end.]: “The total number of cloisters or monasteries of the Premonstratensian Order: one thousand abbeys, three hundred provostships, and five hundred convents of religious women. Moreover, in the said Order there are sixteen bishoprics: among these are seven archbishops and nine diocesan bishops.” The sees we have reviewed amount to a larger number. Let a more inquisitive reader examine more closely those which are to be approved or rejected.

Our second survey may be passed over at a very cursory glance: I mean churches not held by succession or, as it were, inheritance as before [Col. 0057B], but sees for which bishops were selected from the Premonstratensian community at the request and through the favour of Christian rulers or of the clergy themselves. From the bosom of Premonstrat, besides the most blessed Norbert and Evermod, whom I have mentioned, came forth as from a rich store: Blessed Walter, bishop of Laon [Note: [Col. 0057D] Guibert, abbot of Nogent, should be consulted in the catalogue of the abbots of the Church of Laon.]; Blessed Milo of Thérouanne; another Walter, bishop of Chalon; Navarre, bishop of Couserans; and Gervasius, bishop of Séez.

The Church of St. Martin at Laon boasts, as its monuments attest, of Pope Gregory VIII, of Blessed Godescalc, bishop of Arras, of Concordatus, bishop of Autun, and of Arnold, bishop of Courland. The Church of Strahov displayed this glory more conspicuously and splendidly [Note: [Col. 0057D] Miraeus, *Chronicle*, under 1126.].
