For in uninterrupted succession it produced and saw elevated from the pupils of its own household seven archbishops to the metropolitan see of Bohemia [Col. 0057C], to whom was added an eighth, Blessed John Lohelius. It also produced Blessed Adalbert, bishop of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 0057D] *Premonstratensian Library*, folio 317 in my copy.], and brought forth ten bishops of Olomouc in fruitful birth.

I shall not here catalogue their deeds and names in brief speech. Aubertus Miraeus and Pagius in his *Library* provide samples of them. The Premonstratensians performed this lofty office with such moderation and distinction, in an unbroken succession of one hundred and five years, that Vratislaus, duke of Bohemia, decreed in a public diploma that no canons except those of Strahov should be taken for that rank of honour. Consequently that monastery was called a seminary of bishops, from which bishops mounted their sees throughout Moravia.

I shall not mention Almaric [Col. 0057D] from the monastery of Floreffe, bishop of Sidon in Palestine [Note: [Col. 0058D] See Miraeus in the *Chronicle*, under 1548.]; Andrew of Noyon from the church of St. Judocus in the Wood, commonly called Dommartin; Nicholas Psaume, supreme bishop among the people of Verdun and present at the Council of Trent, from the monastery of St. Paul at Verdun; Blessed Alberon, formerly bishop of Verdun and thereafter a follower of Premonstratensian discipline in the same monastery; Nicholas Lagrené, bishop of Ebron and suffragan of Amiens, from St. John’s at Amiens [Col. 0058A]; Daniel Taispelius, bishop of Gibelet and suffragan of Thérouanne, from St. Augustine’s among the Morini; and Floger of Séez in Poland. We have marked the more notable churches encountered; it would be tedious to run through them all. On these matters see the *Premonstratensian Annals*.

Here I shall employ the saying of the lyric poet:

> Even faithful silence has its sure reward.

(Horace, *Odes*, Book II, ode 2, verses 25–26.) This I venture to assert: Premonstratensian clerics laboured greatly and zealously in hierarchical functions, and deservedly competed with others for the palm.

## CHAPTER XIII. That it is not alien to the regular institute of the Premonstratensians to administer churches, greater or lesser.

[Col. 0058B]

Lest anyone should at once frown or scorn, finding fault with those higher sees and reproaching the Premonstratensians for the lower parishes which they administer even now, I have thought it better to cite supporting authorities than to retain advocates. The first assistance comes from our most trustworthy author [Note: [Col. 0058D] Sermon 7, to regulars.]:

> For all of us who are in the unity of baptism and faith are members of the great body which is the Church spread throughout the whole world, under one head, namely the Mediator of God and men, God and man, our Lord Jesus Christ. In the diversity of languages, professions, and merits, in the difference of offices and ranks, we owe to our one Catholic mother, for the honour of the aforesaid head and the benefit of the members, whatever we live, are, can do, and know [Col. 0058C]. Nor should anyone in any way resist those who belong to her when the authority of the whole requires the service of a part. Therefore, when holy mother Church has recognized you as fit to serve her needs, has assumed you to her governance through a canonical election, and has judged you worthy of this, you may, I think, change the place of your profession and, with the consent of those among whom you live, move elsewhere, where you may perform that to which she has called you.

Possidius, an eminent witness, asserts that this was plainly the institute of St. Augustine: that, from it, some were placed over more eminent churches and others over lower ones, in order that they might perform the functions of the priesthood which they had undertaken [Note: [Col. 0058D] In the *Life of St. Augustine*, chapter 11; *On the Preservation of Celibacy*, volume II; and in Landtmeter, *On the Ancient Cleric*, Part III, chapter 1.]. The Premonstratensians did not depart from this. Indeed Robert of Arbrissel, bishop, rightly said that they were appointed by God: so that the fallen canonical order of St. Augustine might cleanse away its stains and, by the example of his followers, put on a better form.

The agreement of all ages proves that this came opportunely about in the Church by the design of divine counsel: that restorers of the trampled hedge [Col. 0059A], new trumpeters of the declining host, new encouragers of languishing souls—men, I say, of apostolic spirit, possessing the first-fruits of resurrection—should come forth, taught by the Lord what they should maintain through love of truth and what they should spend through the duty of charity [Note: [Col. 0059D] St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book XIX, chapter 19.]. John Molanus excellently explains, in the books he entitled *On Canons*, how this was brought about in the canonical order after it had fallen away from common life [Note: [Col. 0059D] Book II, *On Canons*, chapter 23.].

Indeed, he calls those canons blessed and truly worthy of every praise who, not content with a good life and the canonical office of the Church [Note: [Col. 0059D] Above, chapters 24 and 27: the duties of the mixed life.], desire, according to the measure of their gift, to be helpers in the Church of God, knowing this to be their calling. There is therefore no reason why anyone should criticize what he ought rather to embrace. Aubertus Miraeus speaks of the Premonstratensians [Note: [Col. 0059D] At the beginning of the *Premonstratensian Chronicle.*], whose life he had described as founded neither in contemplation alone nor in action alone, but in both. Almost every monastery of this institute has many parishes annexed to it, and superiors or pastors are customarily supplied from the number of religious. As this is almost distinctive of this Order, so it is especially advantageous to the afflicted Church of God amid so great a scarcity of good pastors.

Philippus ab Eleemosyna, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, admirably teaches that this is the proper office of clerics, among whose number he was counted [Note: [Col. 0059D] *On Clerical Continence*, chapter 97.], lest, as he says, he should appear to hate what he was and to love what he was not. And James of Vitry says of the Premonstratensian canons [Note: [Col. 0059D] *Western History*, chapter 22.]:

> They undertake in their own persons parish churches [Col. 0059C] and the care of secular souls.

Martin Mertz, canon and prior of the Church of Roth in Swabia, should be consulted in his separate treatise on the institute of Premonstratensian canons [Note: [Col. 0059D] Notes, 12 and following.]. There he removes the stains cast upon the Premonstratensians by Francisco Suárez, or by some posthumous writer of his, in a treatise on the state and virtue of religion, through decisions of the holy pontiffs drawn from every age. The arguments which Moerbecius, canon of Averbode, judges admirable in his *Purple Ladder* agree with him [Note: [Col. 0059D] In the *Basilica*, *Purple Ladder*, §10, no. 3; and *Ladder of Degrees*, 3, collation 2, §1, Book III, chapters 29 and 30.]; he removes the mote thought to lodge in certain persons’ eyes.

Augustinus Wichmannus should also be consulted in his *Marian Brabant*. There, in various scattered places [Col. 0059D], he discusses many matters which support them, and maintains that St. Norbert first and constantly bound this seasoning of the spiritual life—the contemplative and mixed life—to his Order [Col. 0060A]. Nor should Laurentius Landtmeter, of celebrated Tongerloo, be omitted: both in his books *On the Ancient Cleric* and in his commentaries on the Rule of St. Augustine [Note: [Col. 0059D] On the Rule of St. Augustine, chapter 1, no. 8, and chapter 4, no. 10.], as well as many others to be cited shortly.

For neither the grants and privileges of so many supreme pontiffs nor the determinations of so many bishops would have permitted—or rather voluntarily offered—to the Premonstratensians countless pastorates in different provinces, several archbishoprics, and bishoprics, not merely to administer but to unite to themselves by ordinary right, if this were a violation or transgression of ecclesiastical or common-law boundaries, or were discordant with and contrary to their institute.

This Order indeed enjoys very extensive and numerous favours and privileges granted by the Apostolic See [Col. 0060B]. To linger over their detailed exposition would be nothing other than to traverse anew the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*. By way of conclusion, I add and note a few matters from which many more may be inferred. First, by the concession of Boniface IX, it is fortified with complete authority not merely to seek benefices united to it or belonging to it by any title or right, but also any benefices involving cure of souls, and to serve those benefices through its own members. See Landtmeter [Note: [Col. 0059D] On the Rule, chapter 4, no. 10.] on the Rule of St. Augustine, where he extends this faculty to secular cures and simple benefices; Gabriel Pennottus [Note: [Col. 0059D] *On Regular Canons*, Book I, chapter 72.]; Pagius [Note: [Col. 0060D] Book I, section 18.] in his *Library*; and Zypaeus [Note: [Col. 0060D] Book III, *On Regulars*, no. 46; Book V, *On Apostates*, no. 10; *On Privileges*, no. 4; and *Canonical Consultations*, Book III, chapter 1.] in his *Analytics*.

Moreover, as everyone knows, this Order is directly subject to the Apostolic See and exempt from episcopal jurisdiction [Col. 0060C]. Regular parish priests enjoy this exemption likewise: they are answerable to bishops or their officials only concerning the administration of the sacraments; concerning administration and morals, they answer to their regular superiors [Note: [Col. 0060D] See Fr. Marchant, *Practical Resolutions on Regulars*, cases 2 and 3, pages 49 and 52 in my copy; Lairvelz, *Optics of Regulars*, speculum 44, instruction 19; see Chassaing, *On the Privileges of Regulars*, throughout; *Premonstratensian Library*, Book III, privileges 74 and 127 following.]. Should it happen that secular priests are substituted for their parishes as circumstances require, they retain the power to return, at their discretion, to their former right, as to an honourable but precarious possession, without loss through prescription.

Thus testify many diplomas of the holy pontiffs, both published in the *Premonstratensian Library* and preserved in monastic archives. Besides the authors already cited, see Augustinus Barbosa, Book II of *Ecclesiastical Law*, chapter 12; *On the Power of the Bishop*, Part III; and allegation 105 of *Apostolic Decisions*; and Tamburini, *On the Right of Abbots* [Note: [Col. 0060D] Volume II, disputation 5, question 11, no. 23.]. Finally, the Order is honoured by the communication and extension to it of the privileges of mendicant and non-mendicant orders. See the bulls of Clement VIII and Gregory XIII in Roderiques [Note: [Col. 0060D] Volume II, *Questions on Regulars*, bull 21; and Gregory, bull 15.]: the former issued in 1593 [Col. 0061A], the latter in 1572. They were first extended to the Spanish province; then, at the request of John Lohelius, vicar-general throughout Germany, the former, and, at the request of John Despruetis, general superior, the latter, were expressly extended to the whole Order. Paul V and Urban VIII subsequently confirmed them for Peter Gosset, then general superior [Note: [Col. 0061D] *Premonstratensian Library*, Book III, privileges 150, 152, 145, etc.].

The curious reader will find these points asserted more fully in Georgius Kiene, in his treatise on reserved cases published at Constance [Note: [Col. 0061D] Part 3, chapter 8, no. 11.]; Hieronymus Roderiques, in his compendium [Note: [Col. 0061D] Resolution 116, under *communicated privilege*, no. 44.]; John de la Cruz, *On the State of Religion* [Note: [Col. 0061D] Book II, chapter 4, doubt 1, conclusion 3.]; Ascanio Tamburini, *On the Right of Abbots* [Note: [Col. 0061D] Volume I, disputation 17, nos. 16 and 20.]; Simon Pourraeus, in his compendium of indulgences printed in the Flemish Islands in 1650 [Note: [Col. 0061D] In the preface, folio 14 in my copy.]; and others. A distinguished witness is Servatius Lairvelz in his *Optics* [Note: [Col. 0061D] Speculum 111, instruction 5; and *Premonstratensian Library*, [Col. 0062D] Book I, chapter 13.], who testifies that the Premonstratensian Order is classed in the registers of the Roman curia among the privileged Carthusians, Cistercians, and Camaldolese:

> But I myself, shut out by narrow limits of space,  
> Pass these things over and leave them to others after me to record.

## CHAPTER XIV. The blessed death of an English Premonstratensian bishop, probably Adam, distinguished by miracles. From Caesarius of Heisterbach, Book III, chapters 21 and 22.

Let whoever finds it pleasing cast a vote for taking him to be that very man whom I am intent on bringing to light. My conjecture, which seems most probable to me, is open to everyone’s judgment. The attendant circumstances of place, time, person, and character altogether lead to it and closely agree with it.

The indications of place need not be repeated [Col. 0061C]. We have heard that he acknowledged the kingdom of England as his seat. The agreement of time is weighed against the narrator, Caesarius, renowned for religion and learning in the Cistercian monastery of Heisterbach in the year 1199. Who will deny that our man flourished in those times, remembering that he was at length advanced to the mitre about 1186 and, on the more likely opinion, held it for several lustres? When one looks into the person himself, there appears most noble birth, blood related to kings and princes, episcopal dignity, and eminence in learning, which caused leading men, who loved and revered him above others, to admit him with ready counsel to the conduct of the kingdom’s affairs.

Accordingly, the clerics about him, eagerly desiring his salvation, sounded this exhortation in his ears as he lay at the point of death [Col. 0061D]:

> You were accustomed to take part in the counsels of the king.

[Note: [Col. 0062D] *English History*, Book XIII, no. 20.]

Whether this Adam is again identical with our Adam—whom Polydore Vergil notes at this period as a minister of the more private council—I leave to the investigation and judgment of one more skilled in English affairs. I proceed as though the evidence had openly urged it upon us. The stains which had clung to him from slippery association with great men’s affairs were to be washed away with tears and cleansed by salutary confession [Col. 0062A]. To them the bishop himself replied:

> I was no otherwise before the king than Christ before Pilate.

That holy bishop both said and did this as an example, knowing the text: “Before death, make confession” (Ecclesiasticus 1:16). Thus his contemporary himself writes. See how no place and no time is empty of the praise of virtue for a wise man. But just as rivers are said to pass through the midst of the sea’s tides, retaining their native waters, so he contracts no briny taint of mind from the surrounding noise of courtly business.

Let others proclaim the old proverb: “Fraud rules supreme in the lofty court, and no one stands securely upon the slippery height.” Let them say that the harmful birds of resentment and envy gnaw the liver of everyone bound to this Caucasus [Col. 0062B], and that fawning sirens prepare traps and weave snares for unwary minds. I neither deny nor disavow these things and many more. Nor do I deny Plato’s saying concerning the philosopher [Note: [Col. 0062D] Plato, in the *Theaetetus*, in Liss., 2, *Manual*, dissertation 2.]:

> In reality, only his body lives—or rather sojourns—in the city; but his mind and thought regard all these things as of little or no value. Wherever he goes with Pindar, he passes through and measures the things below the earth and above the heavens, investigating everywhere the whole of nature with curiosity.

Hence in St. Jerome: “Among philosophers, Pythagoras was the first to extol continual meditation on death” [Note: [Col. 0062D] *Against Rufinus.*]: to lead forth daily from the prison of the body the freedom of the soul, absent from it. The wise man does not abandon this meditation even amid the crowd of the court, if he is ever obliged to attend it. He knows that death awaits each person in an uncertain place [Col. 0062C] [Note: [Col. 0062D] See Seneca, Letter 26.]; therefore he himself awaits it in every place. He calls this meditation freedom. For one who has learned to die has learned to be a slave: he is above every power, certainly outside every power.

Our bishop had received this part of philosophy from heaven. Of him we have this: “Each day he was accustomed to cleanse his conscience and not defer his confession from day to day” (Luke 12:37). O blessed servant, whom the Lord, knocking at his door, finds watchful.

The holy prelate, following the established examples of the Fathers, counselled for the benefit of many among the assemblies of Christian kings at the prompting of charity; he knew nothing of the enticements of the court or its attendant vices. Indeed, just as asbestos cloth endures fire in order to shine more brightly, so he endured palaces for communion in and kindling of virtue [Col. 0062D].

The saying of St. Norbert is apt; a good son had imbibed it from the best of fathers. Princes regarded him as an instrument of a better age, bringing forth wholly sound and mature counsels. Lothair himself, first king of the Saxons and then Augustus, emperor of the Romans, as the records relate, especially loved the man of God Norbert [Note: [Col. 0062D] *Life of St. Norbert*, chapter 52.], because he constantly made use of his counsels [Col. 0063A], which were powerful in vigour and foresight; and because from him he drew the draught of heavenly sweetness and was daily refreshed by the bread of divine nourishment.

When consulting Norbert [Note: [Col. 0063D] *Life of St. Norbert.*], he dealt with the gravest affairs of the kingdom and also received from him many predictions made in the spirit of prophecy. Lothair himself, according to his contemporary teacher, was a vigorous commander in war, pre-eminent in arms, prudent in counsel, terrible to the enemies of God and holy Church, a friend of truth, an ally of justice, and an enemy of injustice. Do you see how, with an even tenor, the counsels of saints—whom one may truly call wise—water, cherish, and strengthen the mind? “Their multitude is the health of the world” (Wisdom 6:16).

From the bishop’s example I should like, incidentally, to affirm that *exomologesis*—that is, the confession of sins made to men acting in God’s stead—is numbered among the necessities for those who have fallen, and has been firmly established and preserved in the Catholic Church among the most sacred signs of reconciliation. By a power derived from Christ its institutor, it works secretly and mightily in the soul what it outwardly performs: so that a person may bring before this voluntary tribunal, for expiation, whatever he has committed with a repentant and humble heart, and “not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.” Christ’s faithful know this divine provision in the way of this mortal life, and this saving restraint upon many falls. They have always cherished it as a most ready amulet of cleansing, a training-ground for many virtues needed in the present life. Let those who wish marvel—these are the words I borrow from that greatest and most holy pontiff—at chastity’s continence in any righteous person; let them marvel at the integrity of justice; let them marvel at the tender bowels of mercy: I no less admire the most humble confession of sins than so many sublime works of virtue. [Col. 0063B–C; Note: Col. 0063D, St Gregory, *Morals*, book XII, ch. 14.]

The orthodox Church practises it as necessary for washing away crimes and commendable for daily and venial failings, not without an immense gain in piety. There the guilty person, through the embarrassment of a certain human shame and the accompanying submission of a contrite heart, easily washes away the damage of sins and obtains fellowship in divine friendship. By this sounding-lead the highest reason, gathered back into itself, like a commanding helmsman, tests the otherwise unsearchable shallows of its own self-confidence, the depths of incontinence, and the precipices of avarice; so that, should it strike upon any danger of shipwreck through a fleeting thought, a slipping word, or a wicked deed, it may draw in its sails and hold a straight course for the harbour of salvation. Nor is any other shortcut expedient for the mystery of Christian philosophy, by which one is commanded to know oneself—that is, the mind and what is done by it—so as to discern what one can accomplish by the divine gift and wherein one fails through one’s own weakness. [Col. 0063C–D.]

Our bishop was abundant in commending this teaching of *exomologesis* throughout his writings, but holier and more zealous in practising this good himself. In him, certainly, piety was stronger in the heart than upon the lips: he judged it better to exercise it in good deeds than proclaim it in laboured words. He was far removed from those whom the Apostle rebukes: “Those who teach others and do not teach themselves” (Rom. 2:22). [Col. 0064A.]

“He also shone in miracles after his death,” says Caesarius. I confess that darkness conceals the detailed investigation of these deeds and necessity prevents me from examining them. I leave it to the author’s authority to believe that the bishop was made illustrious by miracles after his death. What may more certainly and safely be affirmed is this: “Wonders do not confer righteousness upon a person, but knowledge of that person. Whoever is known to men, unless he is righteous, will reach eternal punishments under condemnation. But the person justified by the works of heavenly mercy, who has lived righteously in the sight of God alone, will receive, crowned, the blessed joys of the saints, even if little known to men.” [Col. 0064A–B; Note: Col. 0063D, *Life of St Fulgentius*, ch. 3.]

For extraordinary deeds are known to have been performed by God’s holy people, beyond the laws given to nature and above its ordinary order, not for their own commendation but to relieve another’s need and admonish others; yet they will extend among posterity the splendour of their reputation far into the future, as a jewel does gold and fragrance does balsam.

[Note: [Col. 0064D] The order of the narrative is taken from Caesarius of Heisterbach, *Memorable Deeds*, book III, chs. 21 and 22.]

Hear the good word, the holy word, the word worthy of remembrance, of a certain bishop. As I learned from an abbot, a bishop of the Premonstratensian Order, a good man of great religious devotion, died recently in England. When he was at the point of death and did not ask for confession, his clerics said to him: “Lord, you are very weak; why do you not make your confession?” The bishop replied: “I shall not.” When they repeated their exhortation, he added: “Do you fools suppose that I have deferred my confession until this hour?” They said again: “You were accustomed to attend the king’s councils.” To this he again replied: “I was before the king no otherwise than Christ before Pilate.” [Col. 0064B–C.]

That holy bishop both said and did this as an example, knowing what is written: “Before death, make confession. From the dead, as from one who is nothing, confession perishes. While living, you shall confess; while living and in health, you shall confess, and you shall praise God and be glorified in his mercies” (Sirach 17:26). He was accustomed daily to cleanse his conscience and not defer confession from day to day, as many do. He also shone in miracles after death. [Col. 0064C–D.]

## CHAPTER XV. Praises of the Rule of St Augustine: prayer and reading for its observance

Because the Premonstratensians professedly live under the Rule of St Augustine, it is pleasing to note some things concerning it with our Adam. Among the many rules received from the Latin Fathers which religious communities embrace as guides to follow, that which blessed Augustine is known to have handed down to his clerics is first in time and held supreme in dignity; easiest in observance, especially distinguished for discretion, highest in authority, most orderly in its commands, outstanding in substance: a mirror of life, a law of ecclesiastical discipline, a perfect norm of conduct, the dawn of the future blessed life, the bright pole-star of clerics, and an express form of the apostolic spirit. St Norbert beheld and praised it as compactly composed in few matters, yet ordered in many. [Col. 0065A.]

If the word *rule* derives its origin from speaking rightly, or because it is straight, leads straight, governs, or makes straight, what could be considered more upright or more orderly than the discipline here proposed? What could render us more worthy of reverence among men, more peaceful in mind, more acceptable to God, and more upright in heart? These are the words of the most holy lawgiver to blessed Norbert: “Behold, you have the Rule which I have written. If your brethren, my sons, serve well under it, they shall stand secure before Christ amid the terror of the last judgment.” Therefore, says St Norbert—as the writer of his Life reports it, whom I take to be none other, if not in pen then by command, than Blessed Hugh, his disciple and successor in government—since this Rule clearly determines concerning love, labour, abstinence from food and fasting, clothing, silence, obedience, mutual precedence in showing honour, and honouring their father, what further provision for attaining salvation can any religious require? [Col. 0065A–B; Note: Col. 0065D, Appendix of Cappenberg, ch. 5 of the *Life of St Godfrey*; ch. 24 of his Life.]

And pray, why does the very opening of this Rule so graciously and tenderly present the commandment of love? Is it because it wishes its followers immediately to enter upon the more excellent way it shows? “For,” he says, “these commandments have been given to us principally.” [Note: Col. 0065D, our Adam, Sermon 8 to religious.]

Principally, because on them hang the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22:40); principally, because whatever is commanded is established in love alone, which, being proposed to all, binds the remaining commandments. [Note: Col. 0065D, Gregory, Homily 27 on the Gospels, aptly applied.] Principally, because you should know that whatever you do is salutary if you have charity. Principally, because, as St Augustine says elsewhere, “Have charity, and do what you will.” [Note: Col. 0066D, Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Teaching*.] Principally, because love ought to be both the cause and origin of every spiritual exercise, whether we seek to please God or assist our neighbour. [Col. 0065C–D.] Principally, because love of God and neighbour, as it holds a higher rank than all other virtues, ought likewise to hold the first place in us before all else. Principally, because God is to be loved not only first but more: in our love he must not merely precede our neighbour in order, but exceed him in the measure of quantity. Finally, as our master Adam says, these commandments have been given us principally because, just as that virtue whose commandments they are holds primacy among the other virtues, so these commandments of its own hold primacy over other commandments. [Col. 0065D–0066A; Note: Col. 0066D, Sermon 8 to religious.]

Our blessed Father and advocate Augustine likewise fittingly mentions love of God and neighbour in the first chapter and very beginning of his Rule, since he knew it to be, for the whole religious exercise which we must pursue, both the cause and origin by which it begins; the form and rectitude by which it is ordered; the increase by which it grows; the constancy by which it remains; and the end by which it is consummated without being exhausted.

Thus the spiritual Father, like an eagle stirring up its young and hovering over them, now living no longer in the flesh but in the spirit, makes the spiritual path smooth for his followers. “The fruits of the Spirit,” according to the Apostle, “are charity, joy, peace” (Gal. 5:22). Accordingly, having first set before all else the commandment of love of God, as the beginning, cause, and end of all goods; and love of neighbour, so that we may rejoice not in the neighbour himself but with him in God; he then, by a wholly excellent method, lays down another commandment: sincere unity of concord in mind, the renunciation of property in the use of temporal things, and perfect self-denial. [Col. 0066A–B.]

For, I ask you, how long will love of God and neighbour remain inviolate where many indeed dwell in one house, but unity of mind is absent? How long will the serene unity of peace endure where those cold words, “mine” and “yours,” grate; where the abuse of private property rules, fellowship in goods is banished, distribution of necessities is neglected, and favouritism disturbs order? It will not stand, I say; nor can anyone establish it. Therefore the wisest Lawgiver, wishing us to be holy, joyful, and tranquil, first lays the foundation of twofold charity; then builds the firmest cement of minds through concord in unity: not in the flesh through the softness of concupiscence; not in the world through curiosity for worldly delight; not in the devil through the swelling of arrogance; but in God through the law of charity. Charity itself makes us holy; concord of minds itself makes us joyful; equal community of goods itself makes us tranquil. [Col. 0066B–C.]

“And, O holy, joyful, tranquil life!” says the author. “For we are holy when we love God from the depths of our being and love our neighbour. We likewise attain good joy and joyful goodness when we dwell together as one, all say the same thing, and there are no schisms among us. We also rest sweetly when, removing from our midst the two words ‘mine’ and ‘yours,’ we exchange the love of money born of private possession for the generosity of communal fellowship.” [Col. 0066C–D; Note: Col. 0066D, as above.]

> Fair is the concord of peace among holy dispositions,  
> When the many agree as one and are well pleased.  
>
> Yet the bonds of love must be restrained in this manner:  
> This peace is to be granted to the good alone.  
>
> [Col. 0067A; Note: St Prosper, Epigram 29.]

I might be an abundant—indeed, excessive—investigator of allegorical meanings throughout the whole texture of the Rule; for commentators, that would be a worthwhile task. But the present point is rather this: many rules exist which superiors of monasteries wisely wrote for their disciples, although they themselves were not outstanding in public renown for holiness. Other lawgivers are commended by holiness of life, but not likewise by sublimity of wisdom. Still others, finally, are celebrated for both holiness and wisdom, yet lack a certain eminent authority, being adorned by no greatness of office. [Col. 0067A; Note: Col. 0067D, see Humbert, *Commentary on the Rule of St Augustine*, at the beginning.]

Although each has a distinct measure of praise, unquestionably most excellent is the one who possesses the accumulated titles of every commendation: whose doctrines, seasoned with the salt of wisdom, are sprinkled with the proven virtue of their author; whom the eminence of an exalted person recommends; and whose weight is confirmed by received authority. Such, certainly, is the Rule of the most blessed Father Augustine, most experienced in knowledge of divine and human things, most celebrated for holiness of life, and a foremost doctor and bishop in the Catholic Church. [Col. 0067A–B.]

I admit that many doctors of the Church knew the sinews of learning with distinction: some spread the sails of allegories; others lowered their rigging to unravel the coverings of Scripture; some stopped the breaches made by hostile pagans or demolished the stubborn structures of heretics. Others, again, mounted the pulpit against evildoers and by homilies looked to the salvation of believers; or went about the public places, building up every sex, age, and rank in chaste manners; or drained the bilge-water of vices and purified the hearts of peoples from corrupt affections. [Col. 0067B–C.]

Aurelius Augustine, seated at the helm in the stern of the Church, performs every office, bears every labour, wipes away everyone’s sweat, strengthens, protects, and regulates everyone’s steps, arms, and works: gentlest of all and most laborious; at leisure in this business and busied in leisure. [Note: Col. 0067D, ch. 27 of his Life.] For after the Apostles—so his venerable father, Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, graciously says—whose doctrine shines in the Church, he shone foremost through the grace of dispensing the word of God: truly an apostolic imitator, a learned scribe, a Catholic doctor. While still a layman he dictated many books; after becoming a priest, many; and as bishop, very many, which before the day of his death he carefully reviewed and corrected. [Col. 0067C–D.]

For throughout his life he exercised himself untiringly in this study; in this wrestling-school he sweated and grew cold; in this gymnasium he contended; and in this—if I may say it without offence to the saints who then were and who came after—he laboured more than all. [Note: Col. 0068D, ch. 31 of the Life.] Elsewhere: “In my view, anyone who professes himself a cleric is not lightly to be charged with fault unless he loves to acknowledge Augustine as his teacher, recalls him devoutly, and venerates him diligently. For he is the glory and pattern of this our profession; he is the mirror and rule of our religious life.” [Col. 0067D–0068A.]

St Gregory, in the *Dialogues*, recounting the illustrious deeds of blessed Benedict, who acquired the title Father of Monks, says: “If anyone wishes to know more subtly this man’s character and life, he may discover all the acts of his teaching in the same institution of the Rule, because the holy man could not teach otherwise than he lived.” [Note: Col. 0068D, book II, ch. 36.] This is a remarkable testimony to life and teaching.

Of St Augustine, the venerable abbot Philip, called “of the Alms,” writes in his Life: “He trained the servants of God whom he had gathered to live according to rule with such habits that their continence, poverty, and obedience inflamed many far and wide to abandon private possessions and hasten together into one community, where all things might be common to all. And so that this religious life might continue without failure not only among those then present but also among those far in the future, he took care to write for them a rule of holy institution. In it he elegantly set forth what a subject ought to do, what a superior ought to do, what suits all generally, and what suits individuals particularly. [Col. 0068A–B.]

“So that none of these things might be neglected through forgetfulness, he ordered the same Rule to be read once each week, so that prelates and subjects alike might have a faithful reminder and none might offer any excuse. He also presented himself as the complete pattern of religious life to those whom he taught. He was, as it is written, among them as one of them, alike in observance and habit, differing only in episcopal dignity, not in brotherly and inward humility.” [Col. 0068B–C; Note: Col. 0068D, *Life of St Augustine*, ch. 26.]

I admit that the Rule of Blessed Benedict transferred many anchorites and hermits within the walls of monasteries, drew more persons from the world to examples of common life, confirmed very many cenobites in their holy purpose, and multiplied them exceedingly like Abraham’s seed or the stars of heaven. Yet the Rule of St Augustine is in no respect inferior. Augustine too is called the great Father of clerics; he restored the nearly obliterated traces of common life, long before formed by the Apostles and set forth in their Acts. He marvellously exalted the institutions of the primitive Church, recalled the law of holier life and evangelical discipline, and wonderfully propagated it throughout all regions of the world. [Col. 0068C–D.]

Gabriel Pennotto discusses and demonstrates these matters more fully in his *Tripartite History of Regular Canons*, and John Pagius draws from him in the *Premonstratensian Library*; so too Landtmeter, *On the Ancient Cleric*. If you wish, consult them.

This, I say, is the saving manner of life which the Apostles, drunk with the abundant new wine of that Spirit and ardent, drew from the divine Master and offered to their first disciples. This is the well-trodden path of evangelical perfection, which they afterward made smooth for their followers, and which the Catholic Church has preserved and commended from the beginning, practised throughout the Christian world even to this day. [Col. 0068D–0069A.]

The supreme bishops of the Roman Church have in a wonderful manner proclaimed and consecrated this exalted institution by the pronouncements of their oracles. [Note: Col. 0069D, see Mauburnus, *The Canonical Hunter*; Landtmeter, *On the Ancient Cleric*, book I, part III, ch. 2 and following; decrees of holy pontiffs and councils; *Commentary on the Rule of St Augustine*.] Urban I called it “the life of the primitive Church, instituted by apostolic doctrines.” Benedict XII called it “arisen in the primitive Church and established by St Augustine through sacred institutions.” Sixtus IV called it “the norm of the earliest clerics of the Christian religion, founded upon traditions.” Others say more; I have made one statement from the mouths of three.

“And who,” says Humbert, “would doubt that the apostolic life is to be preferred to the life of all who live? Antiquity too contributes much to the praise of writings, because the more ancient a work is, and the more it has passed through the scrutiny of many readers without suffering reproach, the more it is approved by the judgment of many. Since, therefore, it preceded the Rule of Blessed Benedict by many years and has passed through the judgments of so many illustrious men and councils, who would now dare to disparage it?” [Col. 0069A–B.]

“But,” someone says, “the Rule of Blessed Augustine has appeared to some more restrictive and scanty because of its brevity.” Let it be so; but must not a law be brief which, according to the philosopher, commands rather than debates? “He who teaches another to shoot,” says Justus Lipsius, “has only to direct the hand and eyes toward certain targets; thereafter the pupil uses that skill in any place or at any distance. Thus a mind which has once firmly absorbed these principles easily applies them to other cases and does not require an instructor in each particular.” [Col. 0069B; Note: Col. 0070D, see Justus Lipsius, preface to the *Politics*.]

A seed, however small, sown in good soil readily takes root; likewise a brief instruction in a good mind. Other rules prescribe bodily exercises and are largely occupied with external works; this one commends a single piety, profitable for all things. Without any exception, as Master Adam reports, everything written in this little book treats of the spiritual beauty of the soul and shows how our inner person may acquire and preserve the adornment of spiritual virtues by which it is beautified. [Col. 0069B–C; Note: Col. 0070D, Sermon 12, part II.] And the most holy doctor himself says: “May God grant that you observe all these things as lovers of spiritual beauty.”

“It is the prayer of our Father,” says the commentator, “at the very end of his Rule, praying for us and wishing good things for us.” [Note: Col. 0070D, ibid.] Behold prayer, the first aid for observing the Rule and rendering to God the fulfilment of one’s profession. But what does he pray for, what, I ask, does he wish? That, fragrant with the good odour of Christ through good conduct, we may be constituted not as slaves under the law but as free persons under grace. [Col. 0069C–D.]

And indeed the order is right: through the Father’s loving disposition we are first rendered pure; then secure inwardly by the testimony of conscience; commended outwardly by good reputation; and after this holy conduct makes us righteous. Or rather, he principally wishes this one thing: that, as a chasuble is placed over the other holy vestments in the adornment of a priest, we may run by the more excellent way, seeing the end of all perfection, that the Lord’s commandment is exceedingly broad; ready for his every will, no longer as servants fearing the face of their lord, but as children longing for the presence of their Father. [Col. 0069D–0070A.]

Therefore connect the end of this Rule with its beginning, and its last things with its first: one charity founds all, binds together what lies between, and perfects what comes last. It is the whole Law and the Prophets. And, I ask, what but flames of charity could that heart, wholly boiling over, breathe forth by speech or pen—a heart wounded by the charity of Christ, bearing his words in its inmost parts and the examples of the servants of God whom it had made alive from the dead, like consuming coals?

And since, as Humbert very fittingly observes concerning the foregoing words of our lawgiver, it belongs to a good teacher not merely to study wisdom so as to know what to teach, nor merely to teach by speech or writing, but also to labour that what he says may be observed and bear fruit—and since it belongs neither to the sower nor to the sown earth to produce the fruit, but to God alone—the good teacher therefore has recourse to prayer on this matter. [Col. 0070A–B.]

He has recourse to it himself and goes before us by example, so that we may know that all help is from God and may dispose in our hearts the ascents to him in the valley of tears. As Hugh of St Victor says concerning the words of the Rule just cited: “Those who sow, if they neglect to cover the seed, are visited by birds, which carry away everything that seemed to have been sown. So too those who have scattered the seeds of God’s word in the field of their heart through chanting, reading, and preaching: unless they afterward enclose and, as it were, bury them in the heart by prayer, birds will come—that is, the fleeting, empty, and vain thoughts of this world—and snatch away what had been sown in the flesh.” [Col. 0070B–C.]

The most prudent Lawgiver establishes for us a second aid in the study of reading. “So that,” he says, “you may be able to look upon yourselves in this little book as in a mirror, lest through forgetfulness you neglect anything, let it be read to you once a week.” Behold, you have a mirror by which to order your conduct, in which by frequent inspection you may look within upon your face and review whatever you discover ugly or beautiful, with deserved correction or approval.

For what else is inspection of the mirror than attentive reading of the Rule? Through it, our Adam says, two notable gifts among others are bestowed upon us: it instils in us knowledge of what we had previously not known, and makes our memory retentive. [Col. 0070C–D; Note: Col. 0070D, Sermon 12 to religious.] This regular reading of which we speak gives us the clarity of instruction and also removes from us the negligence of forgetfulness. Add that, just as our outward sight receives light from the air around it, so the inward eye of the mind receives it from habitual frequent reading. And by this one knows more rightly the greatness of sin, reverence for the Deity, and the value of virtue. [Col. 0070D.]

Accordingly, the Premonstratensians, intending to set before the eyes of their minds a continual remembrance of the Rule, as though a constant inspection of a mirror, are accustomed, after the divine offices—namely Prime, one of the canonical hours—and after the Martyrology has been read as customary, at the point where the Roman rite of the office is followed by a short reading, to read aloud a portion of the Rule of St Augustine. On Sunday, they read concerning love of God and neighbour; on Monday, concerning concord and the distribution of necessities; on Tuesday, concerning prayer and attention; on Wednesday, concerning temperance in food and reading at mealtime; on Thursday, concerning modesty in outward dress; on Friday, concerning avoidance of litigation; and on Saturday, concerning obedience and the governance of prelates. [Col. 0071A.]

That this custom is neither foreign nor alien to canonical observance is splendidly attested by John Molanus of Louvain, distinguished professor, in the books which he entitled *On Canons*. [Col. 0071A–B; Note: Col. 0071D, book I, ch. 11.] We give a few words taken from him:

“Our ancient and venerable forefathers reflected far more fully than we do that the Christian life ought to be a continual penance, as the Council of Trent declares. Therefore every day, at the end of the canonical hour of Prime, they were accustomed to go to the chapter assembly. There first the Martyrology was read; secondly, the commemoration of the departed; thirdly, one chapter of the Rule. When these had been completed, any matters requiring correction were handled in the chapter assembly. There is brief mention of this practice in the ninth statute of the Council of Mainz, where, among other things, it is read that canonical clerics should come every morning at first light for the reading and hear what is commanded them.” [Col. 0071B.]

No one can readily deny that all these particulars remain an uncorrupted custom and observance among the Premonstratensians and most regulars. Those who know and have examined it more closely explain that this was the cord of distribution for St Norbert and the first fathers at Prémontré: namely, to restore among clerics especially, and among persons of canonical profession, the pursuits of spiritual and ascetical life—languid, not to say dead—for that great and select part of those labouring beneath the sweet yoke of Christ the Lord and bound by the threefold cord to his cross. [Col. 0071B–C.]

There comes to mind the venerable Guibert, abbot of Nogent, his equal in time, territory, and rank, who inscribed his commentaries on the prophets to Norbert with these opening lines:

“To the most loving Father and venerable Lord, to be honoured with every affection of charity; to NORBERT, wholehearted cultivator of holy inwardness and master of true discretion: Brother GUIBERT, a monk in name, a sinner in deeds, wishes that he may rejoice in the prosperous success of himself and his own.” [Col. 0071C–D; Note: Col. 0071D, published in Paris, 1651.]

The matters related in the Appendix to the same work by the monk Herman, afterward abbot of St Martin among the people of Tournai—an eyewitness and eloquent witness of St Norbert, first serving worldly pomp and then a holier life at Prémontré—are likewise to be considered. [Note: Col. 0072D, *On the Miracles of St Mary of Laon*, book III, ch. 7.] To relieve your satiety, read these few words: “I do not know what others think; to me it seems true what very many assert: that from the time of the Apostles there has been no one who, in so brief a span of time, acquired for Christ by his institution so many imitators of the perfect life.” [Col. 0071D–0072A.]

There Norbert, compared with Bernard of Clairvaux, is preferred in several respects; but I should say more gladly that the deeds and merits of the holy Fathers are not to be equated or debated, but celebrated and imitated.

## CHAPTER XVI. Celebrated commentators on the Rule of St Augustine, and how it was handed down to St Norbert

Among the highly celebrated commentators on the Rule of the holy Father Augustine are Hugh of St Victor and Humbert, fifth Master General of the Order of Preachers. These most illustrious writers are in the hands and before the eyes of many, not without immense profit to spiritual men and a certain inward appetite. [Col. 0072A–B.]

Hugh was so learned in the divine Scriptures and so much a rival of the ancient Fathers in every branch of learning that he deserved to be called another Augustine of his age. “He was,” says Trithemius, “of a mind so subtle, adorned with eloquence and no less venerable for his way of life than for his learning.” [Note: Col. 0072D, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*.] Humbert, having held in the fifth place the mastership and highest office of his Order, had nothing sweeter than to meditate upon the sacred Scriptures and to make smooth for others with himself the path to the summit of religious perfection, toward which he himself eagerly strove. “An outstanding speaker,” says the same Trithemius, “evangelical in life, pure in conscience, eminent in action, sweet in speech, and fitted for persuasion.” [Col. 0072B.]

The former flourished about the year of Christ 1130; the latter about 1250. The former, as is evident to a reader of his commentaries, is polished in style, pleasing in the acuteness of his thoughts, at times compressed and somewhat minute. The latter is more copious and more familiar in diction, though somewhat inferior in style and, it seems, elsewhere more relaxed; nevertheless, he is a diligent observer of religious morals through the practice and experience of many. [Col. 0072B–C.]

Between these stands our Adam—or rather, he was close to Hugh of St Victor in date—who about the years 1170 and 1180 composed his commentaries on the Rule of the most blessed Augustine, and easily equalled the praises for which both are celebrated. He enters so completely into the reader’s mind, so diligently corrects what is distorted, so solidly confirms what is right, and carries the entire conduct of religious men to the citadel of perfect virtue. Thus he reveals his meanings; thus he opens the mystical recesses of Scripture and scatters throughout certain savoury and salutary admonitions which you never leave without desire and never without profit—which do what they do not appear to do and say more than they sound, so deeply do they insinuate themselves into the affections. [Col. 0072C–D.]

Moreover, throughout his entire expression he is weighty, sound in judgment, dense in thought, gentle in style, and comparable to the orthodox Fathers. Walking in their footsteps and adorned in their manner, he leaves Humbert many parasangs behind and seems to surpass Hugh in this: Hugh acts wholly as a concise and summary interpreter, whereas our author is an orator fully accomplished in every respect. He wished his sentences to be divided into sermons so that, as though continually assuming the role of bodily presence from the pulpit, he might address his own people face to face, and thus lend sharper weight to his words and to his voice a voice of power. [Col. 0072D–0073A.]

For the living voice possesses, I know not what, of energy: carried from the teacher’s mouth into the ears of disciples, it sounds more forcefully and kindles more vehemently. Thus, approximately, our author says: “For this reason I divided the work into sermons, so that their reading, as though it were a present address, may both enlighten the understanding and inflame the affection; and also so that their fitting division may remove weariness from the sluggish and confer desire upon the diligent.” [Col. 0073A–B; Notes: Col. 0073D, Preface to part II; commentary on the Rule, ch. 5.]

There were other diligent expositors, I admit: Gilbert, abbot of St Rufus, whom Humbert cites; Augustine of Pavia; John Trullus; Ricciardinus in Pennotto; and others. [Notes: Col. 0073D, book I, ch. 18, no. 2.] They may not have been inferior in age, nor perhaps in worth; but since only bare knowledge of their names has reached me, I have thought it right to make no judgment concerning them.

[Note: [Col. 0074D] See Andrew Valerius in his *Bibliotheca Belgica.*] Among our own, Eustachius Lensius, doctor of theology, canon of the Church of Vicogne, and later abbot of Val-Serain and of Chrétien in France, has deserved no ordinary praise here. Believing, as he himself says, that the canonical rule ought to be explained by the rules of the canons, he dedicated his commentaries to Gervasius, primate of the Premonstratensian Order (who flourished in the time of Honorius III, whose penitentiary he was, and was bishop of Séez). It will not be useless to append his prologue from old parchments now in hand.

“To the Reverend Father and lord worthy of honour on earth, the venerable abbot, Lord GERVASIUS, primate of the whole Premonstratensian Order: E. EUSTACHIUS of Vicogne offers this present fruit of his leisure.

“Since wisdom must be written in leisure, the wise man regards his leisure as business; and the busier he finds himself, the more completely does he judge himself to be at leisure. But amid frequent illnesses and my daily cares, I had one consolation: the love and study of letters, because of that saying of blessed Jerome: ‘Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.’

[Col. 0073D] From his prologue we give the following:

“But, setting before the eyes of my mind the mirror of our profession, the Rule of blessed Father Augustine, I observed that it is read by almost everyone, according to what is read there: ‘Let it be read to you once each week’; and I grieved that it is neglected by very many, although the same Rule says: ‘If anything has not been observed, let it not be passed over carelessly.’ Thus there are almost as many interpretations as there are dispositions among readers. For, as in the other divine Scriptures, there are many words which can be drawn toward whatever meaning each person spontaneously presumes for himself—but this ought not to be done. For just as one Testament is explained through the other, [Col. 0074A] according to the saying, ‘Deep calls to deep,’ so one canon is elucidated through another. Hence Jerome says: ‘Let us not bring a false balance, by which we weigh whatever we please according to our own judgment; rather, let us bring the divine balance from the Holy Scriptures, as from divine treasures.’

“Therefore, that my little work may serve regular clergy, I wished in this present work to devote effort to explaining the canonical Rule through the rules of the canons. For, says blessed Clement, the meaning of truth must be derived from the Scriptures themselves. But lest the reading of simpler persons be delayed by the numbers inserted, and lest the movement of their affections run unhindered over level ground, I placed the canons themselves, with their proper locations, outside the sequence of the text, that is, plainly in the margin. Thus waters of exposition will flow out from among the canons, so that both the beasts of the field [Col. 0074B] and the birds of heaven—that is, the active and the contemplative—may have something to drink.

“That I judged the present little work should be dedicated to your fatherhood was urged first by the dignity you have obtained through your prelacy; then by the keenness of understanding with which you are endowed by innate discernment; and also by the charity of your noble conscience, which showed itself so kind toward me in illness through compassion, after the example of the Apostle, who says: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak?’ Therefore, Reverend Father, may your gracious fatherhood receive this offered gift, laboured over for public benefit but dedicated to your glory; and, if it judges it worthy, may it impose upon it the weight of your authority. If it finds anything insufficiently learned, let your eyes behold my imperfection and apply the hand of perfection. But if anything from my [Col. 0074C] purgatory has emerged insufficiently polished and purified, let the file of your wisdom rub it and cleanse it.”

Thus far he speaks. He himself died in 1225, worn out with age, the father of many books which learned men ask to be given to light and public benefit rather than to moths or darkness.

I do not wish to set forth the many modern writers who perhaps have devoted no contemptible labour to commenting on the Rule, lest I seem to mix the bran of our own times with the most approved fine wheat of an earlier age. Yet I shall not pass over in the same silence two of our own whom recent times commend: Servatius Lairvelzius and Laurentius Landtmetterus. From the latter’s commentaries on the Rule, [Col. 0074D] in which he is himself concise and substantial, and especially from his three books *On the Ancient Clerk and Monk*, one may readily discern the whole ordering of religious life, both ancient and recent. The former, a doctor of theology and an abbot distinguished among a few at Pont-à-Mousson, is highly commendable not only for learning, but for his example of holier life and zeal for stricter discipline. He set these before the eyes of readers in an excellent work bearing the title *Catechism for Novices*, and in another work, namely his commentaries on Augustine’s Rule; indeed, he was raised almost to equality with the ancients. In this one matter, however, our Becardus [Col. 0075A] and others found cause for wonder: contrary to the received custom of the Order—as is evident from our Adam—and consequently while dwelling upon the spurious offspring of the Rule, he expends no small portion of his labour. Let Landtmetter be consulted on the same Rule, in his preliminary question.

Very successfully indeed, and not without divine auspices, the man of God Norbert had hastened to enlist new reinforcements for the white soldiery, to hold new levies, and to distribute new standards. At the place which not without reason found the name Prémontré, about forty clerics and several laymen had settled: certainly the beginnings, as it were, and seed of that multitude which afterwards followed. But because the narrowness of that valley was unequal to receiving those men whom heaven promised to scatter throughout the Christian world in remarkable increase, they first had to be brought into a fixed and stable manner of life, as it were under the appointed watchword of their commander, before they prepared for departure abroad; and all the companions had to maintain with inviolable constancy a state bound together by life and morals.

Until that day the recruits had lived content with the common offices of piety, eager followers of the Gospel and apostolic institutions. Father Norbert himself had often exhorted them in weighty words concerning the choice of a rule to be undertaken, the unshaken resolve of religious life, and the other marks of holy profession. Meanwhile he called into counsel various bishops, men conspicuous for their pattern of holiness, and leaders of the Church on this question. Yet he leaned more toward the canonical manner of life [Col. 0075C] which he himself, with most of his companions, had embraced from tender age, being steadier and more expectant in hope that a light from heaven would cleanse his mind, still clouded.

Then one adviser, considering the harsh solitude into which he had withdrawn, recommended the anchoritic life; another, observing the severity of penance by which he wore himself down—and many agreed with this party—recommended the eremitical life. Another, again, considering the glory of the Cistercian Order, then already flourishing anew through a fresh offshoot, which charmed by the honeyed allurement of its words and which Saint Bernard, abbot at Clairvaux, wonderfully enlarged by examples of holy life and conduct [Note: [Col. 0075D] His *Life*, chapter 24.], urged that the monastic life should be embraced altogether.

But Norbert, as an ancient writer of his Life relates—a man whose work and counsel [Col. 0075D] depended upon things above, who entrusted his undertaking not to himself, not to men, but to Him who is the beginning of all things—pondered everything in his heart, as the Wise Man says; swift to hear (Prov. 29:20; Jas. 1:19), one who defers and reserves matters for the future. In the fervour of many prayers, seeking heavenly help, he was drawn in different directions and turned over everything in his mind, as one in some measure bereft of counsel.

And—O favour!—from the inmost sanctuary of heaven there appeared to praying Norbert the most longed-for messenger, the arbiter of his twofold deliberation, the strengthener of his wavering mind: Augustine, Father and most renowned organizer of clerics, about to receive this new flock into his [Col. 0076A] own household. From his right side he drew forth and handed to Norbert a golden Rule; and he made himself known in clear speech, saying [Note: [Col. 0075D] In the Appendix to his *Life* in Cappenberg, chapter 5.]:

“I am Augustine, bishop of Hippo, whom you see. Behold, you have the Rule which I wrote. If your brethren, my sons, serve well under it, they will stand secure before Christ amid the terror of the last judgment.”

O favour, I say; O love! The favour of one who protects, the love of one who adopts: protecting and promising security amid the terror of the last judgment; adopting them as sons and desiring, through the law of life and discipline thus shown, to have them in the communion of saints—he who rejoiced therein, solicitous for our pilgrimage and provident for the salvation of his sons.

Not a few lawgivers among barbarian peoples—such as Seleucus, Zoroaster, Minos, and, most recently, Mohammed—so that they might give weight and authority to the enactments of their laws, claimed that these had been received from heaven alone, proceeding from the deity itself and uttered by a divine mouth. The Egyptians revered Mercury as their lawgiver, considering him a certain theologian and divine being, and spoke of him by no name other than Trismegistus, or “thrice-greatest.” Lycurgus, intending to give laws to the Spartans, went to Delphi and consulted the oracle. The Pythia answered that he was beloved of the gods and more a god than a man; and, when he asked concerning good legislation, she said that the gods promised his commonwealth a constitution of the highest excellence. Therefore Lycurgus called his laws, as it were, decrees of the gods.

Well known are the familiar meetings and conversations which Numa Pompilius, the second king of the Romans, pretended to have with the goddess Egeria. From these meetings, [Col. 0076C] Plutarch says, he is believed to have become a fortunate man and most skilled in divine things. They relate that Pythagoras used to stop and lead an eagle, made tame by his voice, as though through it he might obtain the doctrines of his laws ready-made from Jupiter’s throne.

But away with these inventions of fabulous antiquity, as ingenious for fabrication as they are presumptuous for deception. Let the Israelites retain the glory of a law received through the ordering of angels; among Christians, let certain religious communities retain beginnings received through divine inspirations and visions, laws confirmed, and promises ratified of the life which now is and which is to come. I would have nothing diminished or taken away from them. Nor, conversely, should anyone rail against or accuse one who asserts that the Premonstratensian family received very great prerogatives from heaven. I do not linger over each of them, being moved here only by a single narrative.

Thus the most holy bishop Aurelius Augustine,

> From whose mouth  
> Rivers of books flowed over all the world;  
> Which the gentle and humble drink, and strive  
> To send streams of life-giving teaching into the fields of minds.

[Note: [Col. 0076D] Saint Prosper, poem *On the Ungrateful*, chapter 3.]

After that most blessed man, I say, had departed this mortal life about seven hundred and ten years earlier, being now a dweller in heavenly glory, certain indeed of his own victory, yet not forgetful of our struggle and attentive to his flock as a true shepherd, he appeared to Norbert as he deliberated on a manner of life. He appeared as a heavenly envoy, an unfailing counsellor, and a most desirable patron.

No longer needing another’s counsel, rich in heavenly help, and knowing that this most blessed man, after the Apostles, had organized the institution of clerics with the greatest wisdom of all and renewed the apostolic life [Note: [Col. 0077D] Chapter 24 of his *Life*.], Norbert carefully examined the Rule brought to him. It was concise in expression, yet well ordered in many respects. Immediately, on the approaching feast of the Nativity of the Lord, as the *Deeds* relate, in likeness of the Lord’s enrolment, each one enrolled himself under it for both stability in the place and profession, unto that city of blessed eternity. [Col. 0077B]

Yet first—as an ancient manuscript codex of *Histories* [Note: [Col. 0077D] Under the year 1119.] of Rievaulx Abbey, which I examined in Paris in the monastery of the Regular Canons of Saint Geneviève, records—he taught them to make profession according to the apostolic and canonical institution and the Rule of blessed Augustine; and he carefully instructed them in voluntary poverty and ready obedience.

The considered form of words by which the first Fathers bound themselves more tightly to the manger and service of Christ crying as an infant, putting off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness, was, unless I am mistaken, of this sort:

> “I, Brother N., offering myself, give myself to the Church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, and to Saint N.; and I promise conversion of my manners and stability in this place according to the Gospel of Christ, according to the apostolic institution, and according to the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine. I also promise obedience until death in Christ to Lord N., Father of the aforesaid Church, and to his successors, whom the sounder part of the congregation shall canonically elect.”

For, as the writer of his *Life* says [Note: [Col. 0078D] Chapter 25, in the *Life*.], that spiritual Father also considered that those who wished to remain with him could never go astray if they made and fulfilled their profession according to the Gospels, the sayings of the Apostles, and the purpose of Saint Augustine. This he perceived; and he judged that these professions should be made in the manner set forth above.

And lest varying expositions and diverse interpretations of that holy Rule should bend their initial strength and youthful strictness of mind—the Rule which most regular clerics observed more mildly and under linen garments, while his own observed it more strictly and under woollen dress—he strengthened and stirred the minds of the recruits with the weight of grave words:

“Why do you wonder,” said the man of God, [Note: [Col. 0078D] Chapter 24 of his *Life*.] “or hesitate, when all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth? And if they are diverse, are they therefore contrary? If custom and institution change, ought the bond of charity, which is love, therefore to change? The Rule indeed says: first let God be loved; then one’s neighbour. The kingdom of God is not produced by institution alone, but by truth [Col. 0078A] and the observance of God’s commandments. Therefore, because this Rule expressly determines matters of love, labour, abstinence from food and fasting, clothing and silence, obedience, mutual precedence in honour, and honouring their father, what more is necessary for any regular cleric to obtain salvation?

“But if there should arise among some spiritual persons a controversy about the colour, thickness, or fineness of garments, let those who take from this an occasion for disparagement say—let them say, I repeat—where in this Rule, in the Gospel, or in the institution of the Apostles, whiteness, blackness, fineness, or coarseness is prescribed by command; then they will be believed. Yet one fact remains: the angels who were witnesses of the resurrection are read to have appeared in white; but by the authority and custom of the Church penitents wear woollen garments. Likewise, in the Old Testament, they went forth to the people in woollen garments, but in the Sanctuary, by command, they customarily used linen. Since the exposition of the holy Fathers and our predecessors teaches that holy preachers and those who follow the canonical profession perform, in the figure of these angels, their office, let them not create a scandal concerning white garments. If they are penitents, and their office compels them to go out to the people, let them not shrink from woollens. But if they are about to enter the sanctuary of God, let them not omit linens.”

These words of that excellent Father are plainly full of the Spirit of the wisdom and knowledge of God; his tongue was like a conduit of living water and the pen of a scribe writing swiftly. They are altogether worthy of being separately weighed, each by close investigation, being pregnant with a loftier meaning. But I ask you: what other counsel was there in our master Adam, what other aim did he set before himself in these fourteen sermons, than to illuminate by an elegant paraphrase the most weighty exhortation which we have heard set forth above; to demand in his successors a manner of life corresponding to the illustrious deeds of the first Fathers; and continually to place before the inward sight of the mind the significance of that holy purpose, the dignity of a profession strengthened by vow, and its consequences?

## CHAPTER XVII. The Premonstratensians’ singular devotion toward Saint Augustine. His canonical Rule. Nor are the Premonstratensians under any other Rule.

No one will think it useless to inquire separately, for a little while, why our first Fathers—men alike most wise and most holy—so distinctly and so early required the sacrament of religious profession according to the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine. Many points from what has preceded bear upon this question; and above all, Saint Augustine appeared visibly to our patriarch Saint Norbert, full of the spirit of all the righteous, while he hung in uncertainty and, as we have said, was drawn in different directions by conflicting pronouncements of ecclesiastical leaders.

Norbert himself, the defender of orthodox truth, recounted the outcome of this event to the brethren of the Church of Cappenberg, gathered in the common hall or chapter-house, humbly as though it concerned another, as the *Deeds* state. [Col. 0079A] [Note: [Col. 0079D] In the Cappenberg Appendix, chapter 5.] Yet we undoubtedly perceive that he himself was the recipient of this revelation. What then? Rejoicing marvellously in this heavenly vision, both because of the singular prerogative received from above and because he might seem to be doing injury [Note: [Col. 0079D] Chapter 24 of his *Life*.] to the canonical profession to which he himself, and all who wished to live with him, had been assigned from infancy, on the approaching Nativity of our Saviour God in the year 1121 he solemnly and by a stable vow dedicated his loves and manner of life, together with a few companions, to the infant Jesus.

Norbert passed at once from the Rule he had seen to the side of the clerics—or rather, he stood more firmly and certainly where he had stood before. He wished his brethren to seek Saint Augustine’s patronage, to invoke him reverently by the beloved name of Father, and to honour him continually in both public and private offices of piety; for Norbert had committed himself and his progress to Augustine’s protection and institution. [Note: [Col. 0080D] See Pagius, *Bibliotheca*, book II, chapter 16.] The members of the Premonstratensian family, wishing not to return equal thanks to their great Father but at least to bear witness, embrace this holy one as their protector and special patron with undying affection. In ecclesiastical offices they festively appoint, with octaves as they call them, the solemn days both of his blessed passage to eternal life and of the translation of his sacred body. In the daily and public prayers of the Church they include his commemoration and invocation. Finally, in the general confession which they customarily make at Prime, at Compline, and before the dread mysteries of the Mass, they require the invocation of the aid and intercession of holy Father Augustine; and the decrees enacted in their chapters require it often elsewhere as well. [Col. 0079C]

But could Norbert, merely upon seeing that lawgiver, have been so inflamed for canonical profession? Could Saint Augustine himself be Father to Premonstratensian clerics and they be adopted as sons by name? Could those first Fathers, I say, have sworn thus freely and solemnly to the canonical Rule if it had been doubtful what kind of life Augustine established, uncertain what sons he had from his spiritual womb, or disputed what that Rule was, or to whom it had been delivered—a Rule which the Church had then received and preserved for six hundred years and more? Certainly no rumour of a contrary opinion had touched these Fathers, whom the common and unquestioned understanding of ecclesiastical tradition had instructed.

Norbert, as the contemporary writer of his *Life* says, ordered the Rule which blessed Augustine instituted for his own followers to be brought; for he now desired to live the apostolic life which he had taken up in preaching, a life which he had heard was ordered and renewed by that blessed man after the Apostles. Do you hear Augustine, the outstanding imitator of the Apostles, who renewed in himself and his own followers their norm of life? And do you see Norbert corresponding to him, who had long before been inflamed, with apostolic ardour, toward that pattern of life? [Col. 0080A]

“This life,” that is, the life of canons, they say, “Pope Urban instituted for Saint Norbert at that time in Gaul; Augustine ordered it for his own by his rules; Jerome shaped it by his letters.” [Note: [Col. 0080D] See above, Prologue, part II, chapter 7.] Pope Honorius, moreover, wrote to the Premonstratensians:

“Since, by divine grace inspiring you, you have resolved to live religiously and to lead the canonical life according to the institution of blessed Augustine, we confirm your purpose by the authority of the Apostolic See, and exhort you to persevere firmly in it for the remission of your sins. We therefore decree that in your churches, in which brethren professing the canonical life dwell, no person whatsoever may alter the order established there according to the Rule of blessed Augustine.”

We cited these charters at greater length above, received in the years of salvation 1126 and 1124. Who, having read of the commendable life of the Fathers and the institutions of apostolic teaching renewed by Saint Norbert, seeing the canonical life derived from Saint Augustine’s institution, and considering every Rule as suited to its own vocation and, like an artisan’s tools, fitted to its own task—who would wish to veil a truth so evident with the painted cloak of dissimulation? [Col. 0080B]

If anyone should wish to see some additional light from the pronouncements of holy pontiffs, here is the charter of Innocent II to blessed Hugh, disciple and successor of Saint Norbert, issued the year after the happy death of his Father, namely 1135:

“We decree and sanction by the authority of the Apostolic See that the canonical Order, which is known to have been established in that Church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the observance of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall be observed inviolably for all time in all churches now and hereafter belonging to your Order.”

Adrian IV repeated the same in a charter dated 1154. Alexander III, in 1177, has it in slightly altered words:

“The canonical Order which is known to have been established in the Church of Prémontré according to the Rule of blessed Augustine and the arrangement of Norbert, of revered memory, formerly founder of the Premonstratensian Order, and of his successors, in the white habit, shall be observed inviolably for all time throughout [Col. 0080D] all churches of the same Order.”

The following is of one tenor in the documents of many supreme pontiffs—namely Honorius II, Lucius III, Urban III, Clement III, Innocent III, Honorius III, Gregory IX, Innocent IV, Urban IV, Gregory X, Clement VI, and many others:

“Since, by the Lord’s inspiration, you have resolved to live religiously and lead the canonical life according to the institution of blessed Augustine, we confirm your purpose by the authority of the Apostolic See and exhort you to persevere firmly in it for the remission of your sins. We decree, therefore, that in the churches in which brethren lead the canonical life, no person may alter the order there established according to the Rule of blessed Augustine,” etc.

These texts may be considered in their order in John Pagius’s *Bibliotheca*, book III [Note: [Col. 0081D] *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, book III, Privilege 19, and book I, section 1 and following.], together with his discussion of the canonical Rule in book I.

I shall finish if we listen briefly to master Adam speaking. [Note: [Col. 0081D] Sermon 9, part II.] “Our Father and advocate, blessed Augustine, most dear brethren, with great earnestness prohibits in the very beginnings of the Rule of regular clerics the sin of private ownership.” And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0082D] Sermons 10 and 12.]:

“The clerical prerogative requires that clerics apply themselves to acquiring honourableness diligently among the other virtues, practising it manfully, retaining it perseveringly, and giving attention to comeliness. For it is fitting that, just as they possess a special dignity in their Order, so they should likewise possess a special honourableness in their conduct. Otherwise—may it never be—the height of their dignity ought not rightly to be honoured, when the example of their conduct deserves justly to be reproved. Hence the great Father Augustine, founder of their regular discipline, after showing how they ought to conduct themselves in food, gives them instruction also concerning their dress.”

And finally, near the end of the Rule: “In these words, blessed Augustine placed an end to his regular discipline which he wrote concerning the institution of clerics.” There was more at hand, but it was fitting to be content with this threefold testimony.

Cardinal James of Vitry, almost contemporary with those times and eminent in learning and holiness, writes on Isaiah, “The Lord shall strike the river of Egypt into seven streams” (Isa. 11):

“From the place of delight,” that is, he says, “the primitive Church proceeded—that is, from the first believers, whose heart and soul were one in God,” etc. “From this place of delight the river was channelled as far as blessed Augustine, and he himself began to live according to the Rule established under the holy Apostles. This river produced seven streams from itself, namely seven canonical congregations—that is, distinct foundations or institutions. One stream is the Premonstratensian canons; another, Grandmont; a third, the Order of Saint Victor; a fourth, the Order of Arrouaise; a fifth, the Order of Val-des-Écoliers; a sixth, the Order of Val-des-Choux; the seventh, the Order of Friars Preachers. ‘These are the Kenites who came from the warmth of the father of the house of Rechab,’ as is said at the end of Chronicles (1 Chron. 2). *Kenite* means ‘mourning’: possession [Col. 0081D] and inheritance.”
