It should further be noted that the author, just as he constantly calls Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. 0082D] See Sermon 10, etc.] the Father of clerics and Saint Benedict the leader of monks, correspondingly and rightly styles Augustine’s Rule canonical and Benedict’s monastic, or the Rule of monks. Along the same line run the matters expanded in many treatises by Philip of alms, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, a man of great name, whose familiar letters to Saint Bernard survive, and who is believed to have been the first to compose Saint Augustine’s Life after Possidius—a work surely free of every party bias, since such parties did not yet exist. Laurentius Landtmetter, canon of the Church of Tongerlo, supports this writer among the moderns in his books *On the Ancient Clerk*, in a brief and calm style. I produce no evidence gathered elsewhere, lest I myself seem to revive a Tuscan quarrel or provoke some Pythagoras, as they say, glorying in his Euphorbus. [Col. 0082A]

Moreover, there is here a gross and intolerable error, disseminated by many writers otherwise very distinguished: they have maintained that the Premonstratensians serve under the Rule of Saint Benedict and, more surprisingly still, that Saint Norbert was a professed Benedictine monk. Others, again, while admitting that the Premonstratensians now follow the direction of Augustine’s Rule, suppose that our first Fathers originally obeyed the older Benedictine Rule. Yet they do not state at what time or for what reason this change was introduced; indeed, they confess themselves ignorant of it. Thus even today one hears certain learned men of the Benedictine family speak in such a way as to boast that this offspring came forth from the bosom of their Order. To them I say: the greatness of the Order of Saint Benedict is dear to me, and its members are dear; but truth is much dearer. Why say more? To recount the matter will itself refute it, and will more closely expose and erase the false colouring.

But, to open whatever apparent doorway there may have been to this fiction, we should briefly recall that Saint Norbert, after his remarkable conversion and the rejection of the seductive charms of the world, gradually increased from that time the fire of divine love conceived within him, as the *Deeds* state. [Note: [Col. 0083D] Book II, chapter 70, no. 1.] He did not immediately change his habit, nor at once leave the world; rather, beneath soft clothing he subdued his limbs by the harshness of haircloth, and strove to raise himself against himself. . . . Therefore, while the man of God meanwhile gathered strength, returned inwardly to himself, strengthened his spirit, and pondered higher counsels, he utterly changed and transformed all the pursuits of his life toward paths altogether different and entirely opposed to the former. Now taught to fight against the enemy, he at once withdrew his foot from the court; and, remaining at home or dwelling in the Abbey of Siegburg with Abbot Cono of good memory—who then praiseworthily governed that monastery, a man of wonderful holiness—he committed the divine Scriptures to memory and waited, as Solomon says, “the wise man until the time” (Ecclus. 20). Exercising certain novitiates of his future conversion, he smoothed by untiring meditation whatever poverty he planned for himself and whatever sufferings and struggles might befall him. [Col. 0082D]

From chapter 2 of the *Life of Saint Norbert*, you have Norbert as a novice, having changed the pursuits of his life for the better, departing to a monastery of the Benedictine Order for counsel and instruction. But was he shaved there in monastic tonsure or clothed in the cowl? Not at all. By precisely the same reasoning the hermits might claim Norbert for themselves, because in his desire to learn a more perfect life he frequented the cell of a certain hermit, Ludolph; and the Regular Canons might reclaim him as their own—and Gabriel Pennottus seems inclined to this—because impelled by the same incentive he repeatedly returned to their monastery at Rödingen. [Col. 0083A]

Hence Aubertus Miraeus, in the preface to the *Premonstratensian Chronicle*, says [Note: [Col. 0083D] Book II, chapter 70, no. 1.]:

“There is no need to speak of Saint Augustine’s patronage, since it is known to all that the Premonstratensians order their life according to the prescription of Saint Augustine’s Rule. With what judgment blessed Norbert prescribed this for his followers may be seen in chapter 24 of the history of his Life. I am therefore astonished that Lord Antoninus in his *History*, and Philip of Bergamo in the *Supplement to the Chronicles*, assign the Norbertines to the Rule of Saint Benedict—especially when Saint Augustine himself appeared and gave the Rule to blessed Norbert, as is read in the Life of blessed Godfrey, Count of Cappenberg.”

I am indeed astonished, as Miraeus is, at Lord Antoninus in his history. And who would not be equally astonished with Miraeus if he carefully examines here the books of histories of blessed Antoninus? For this is what he writes in part II of the histories, title 15, chapter 14:

“After Benedict all monks of the West serve under the Rule of blessed Benedict and have him as their Father, except the Carthusians, who have their own special constitutions.”

And after a few intervening words:

“From it come the Order of Cluniacs, the Order of Premonstratensians, Cistercians, Camaldolese,” etc.

Yet in chapter 15, §7, of the same title, he says:

“About the year of the Lord 1080 the Order of Regular Canons began to flourish anew in the Church of Saint Quentin of Beauvais, an Order regularly instituted first by the Apostles and afterwards by blessed Augustine, bishop and outstanding doctor, under the venerable master Ivo, provost of that same church and afterwards bishop of Chartres.”

Then, little mindful of himself, he adds:

“To this Order of Regular Canons [Note: [Col. 0083D] Book XV, chapter 15.] the Order of Prémontré also seems to belong, of which more will be said below.”

What, then, does he say? “In the year of the Lord 1120 the Order of Premonstratensians began, of which the man of God Norbert was founder both of the place and of the Order. . . . At last, inspired by God, he settled in the place of Prémontré and there began to lead a solitary and religious life. During Lent he went out alone to gather companions; before Easter he returned with thirteen companions, and with them in the place of Prémontré [Col. 0083D] he began to serve God according to the norm of canonical institution and the tenor of the Rule of blessed Augustine.”

Finally, near the end of the same chapter:

“Norbert, returning to Prémontré and now having forty clerics with him together with many laymen, taught them to make profession according to the apostolic institution and the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine, and carefully instructed them in voluntary poverty and the other instruments of spiritual warfare.”

These things Antoninus, in his customary fashion, followed from Vincent of Beauvais, to whom in most matters he adheres syllable by syllable. Yet everyone knows how discordantly the same author sometimes describes the Premonstratensians as subject to the monastic Rule or mingled with families of monks, and at other times as followers of apostolic institution and disciples of the canonical Rule. Thus even good Homer sometimes nods.

After this, the Benedictine writer Arnold Wion, somewhat more eagerly, [Note: [Col. 0084D] Book I, ch. 71. This author was born at Douai in 1554; concerning him see Andreas Valerius, *Bibliotheca*.] relying on the authority of several persons, enrolls the Premonstratensians among his own in the book called *The Tree of Life*, in these words:

“It is reported that three other orders follow, or at least formerly followed, the Rule of our holy father Benedict. The first is the Order of Premonstratensians, instituted by Norbert, a native of Cologne and a monk of Siegburg of the Order of St. Benedict, about the year of the Lord 1119. Thus James Philip states in Book XII of the supplement to the *Chronicle*: ‘In the year of the Lord 1119, the Premonstratensian Order, under the Rule of the divine Benedict, [Col. 0084B] began in the diocese of Laon, under a certain Norbert by name, a native of Cologne.’ Marcus Guazzo likewise states this in his history written in the vernacular. Moreover, two Spaniards agree: namely, Brother John de Pineda of the Order of St. Francis, in Book XXII, chapter 22, section 6, of his *Ecclesiastical Monarchy*; and Lord Gonzalo de Illescas, abbot of San Fromán, at the end of Book V, chapter 20, of his *Pontifical History*. From these testimonies, therefore,” he says, “it is evident that the fathers of this religious order were first established under the Rule of St. Benedict, although they do not observe it today, but rather that of St. Augustine, which they afterwards adopted. But at what time this change was made I have not yet discovered. St. Norbert was afterwards the fifteenth Archbishop of Magdeburg, created in 1126; he exercised that office for eight years and, renowned for miracles, died [Col. 0084C] in 1134, on 6 June.”

Thus far he. Again, in the martyrology of his own order, under 6 June, he says: “On the same day, St. Norbert, bishop of Magdeburg and founder of the Premonstratensian Order, who, having obtained from Gelasius II, Roman pontiff, authority to preach, led many back to the way of truth.” In his notes on that passage he adds:

“Concerning him, see the Roman Martyrology with Baronius; Molanus in his additions to Usuard; Galesinius and Felinus on this day. Surius provides his Life in volume III. Norbert was a native of Cologne, and first gave himself to Christ in the monastery of Siegburg under the Rule of our holy father Benedict. He was afterwards made bishop of Magdeburg, as Krantz notes in *Metropolis*, Book IX, chapter 12; and Demochares [Col. 0084D] in *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*, volume II, chapter 41. But before his episcopate, having obtained from Pope Gelasius II permission to preach the Gospel, he had begun the new order of Premonstratensians in the diocese of Laon, first under the Rule of St. Benedict, as Philip of Bergamo relates in Book XI of his *Supplement to the Chronicles*; as also Brother de Pineda of the Order of St. Francis, in Book XXII, chapter 22, section 6, of his *Ecclesiastical Monarchy*; and Marcus Guazzo in his history, and others. But in the course of time the fathers of the said order adopted for themselves the Rule of St. Augustine, under which they serve even to the present day. Norbert lived eight years in the episcopate and departed this world in the year from the Virgin Birth 1134.”

[Col. 0085A] Moreover, it could not have escaped him that Trithemius of Sponheim long ago stated this openly and explicitly in his *Hirsau Chronicles*. We give a few of his words on the matter; [Note: [Col. 0085D] He was alive in 1500.] the reader who consults him will encounter more:

“In 1126 the Premonstratensian Order began in the diocese of Laon, under Bishop Bartholomew, while Louis reigned as king of the Franks. Father Norbert, a man of venerable holiness, established it, together with the Rule of St. Augustine, with thirteen companions, around the feast of Easter; Pope Calixtus confirmed it. This order, afterwards growing marvellously in a short time, was enlarged.”

Here the beginnings of the order which was then commenced are declared; further origins are vainly sought.

There is also another Benedictine writer, somewhat older in age and no less weighty in authority, John Iperius, abbot, who [Col. 0085B] in his *Chronicle of Saint-Bertin* begins much more moderately and truthfully concerning St. Norbert, founder of the Premonstratensian Order:

“In the place of Prémontré, shown to him by God, he began to lead a solitary life, always going barefoot. Afterwards, in the same place, he gathered disciples and a community, for whom he established as their principal observance the Rule of blessed Augustine, with certain additions from the Rule of St. Benedict. For according to the Rule of blessed Augustine they observe the Hours with nine lessons. They wear white tunics and surplices in the services of the church; elsewhere they wear white cloaks and a scapular as their regular habit. They undertake the care of souls and call themselves not monks but Premonstratensian canons. According to the Rule of St. Benedict, however, they eat flesh only in the refectory, and nowhere else except in illness; [Col. 0085C] they are content with two dishes in the refectory; they sleep clothed and shod; they do not use shirts, nor skins except sheepskins.”

And he continues there with several similar matters. Nor do I deny that the Premonstratensians added certain observances of stricter and monastic discipline to their canonical rule and profession. [Note: [Col. 0085D] See Baronius, under the year 1124, near the end.] Indeed, this is what we maintain as a singular glory of our Father: that St. Norbert—whom afterwards most founders of religious orders emulated—was before the rest in associating, by a most well-balanced combination, clerical dignity with monastic observance, and the active life with the pursuits of contemplation. But must he therefore be assigned to the party of monasticism and, by a rash venture, [Col. 0085D] subjected to the canon of monks? I think no more than any other of the religious communities which glory in their common and clerical fellowship of life. John Iperius died, according to Andreas Valerius in the *Belgian Library*, in 1383, in the seventeenth year of his governance of the monastery of Saint-Bertin among the people of Saint-Omer.

Again, Ascanius Tamburini, more recent than all those mentioned above, a monk of Vallombrosa, following the same shadows of opinion, reported the following in volume II, disputation 24:

“The congregation of Premonstratensian regular canons, first established [Col. 0086A] under the Rule of St. Benedict by St. Norbert, is so described by James Philip in Book XII of the *Supplement to the Chronicles*; Guazzo in his history; Illescas; and others cited by Arnold Wion in Part I of *The Tree of Life*, Book I, chapter 71. Then, for some reason unknown to me, in 1120 he transferred it to the Rule of St. Augustine, under which it lives to this day. The canons of this congregation were called Premonstratensians from Mount Prémontré in the diocese of Laon, a suffragan see of Reims, where St. Norbert had already built a church. This family flourishes especially in France, Germany, Flanders, and Spain; in Italy there are almost no monasteries. Most recently Premonstratensian canons have come to Rome and, having bought houses on the Via Felice near St. Mary Major, are building their college. This congregation was confirmed in the year of the Lord 1126, on the Kalends of March [1 March], [Col. 0086B] by Pope Honorius II,” etc.

There likewise, in the fifth question of the said volume, while treating of the Rule of St. Benedict and congregations serving under it, he writes as follows:

“Likewise the Premonstratensian congregation was instituted in 1120 under the Rule of St. Benedict by St. Norbert of Cologne, a monk of Siegburg of the Order of St. Benedict. James Philip expressly attests this in Book XII of the *Supplement to the Chronicle*; Guazzo in his history written in Italian; and Lord Gonzalo Illescas, abbot of San Fromán, in chapter 20 of Book V of his *Pontifical History*. See Wion, Part I of *The Tree of Life*, Book I, chapter 71.”

These, I think, are the principal authors who, through an excessive affection for St. Benedict and his followers, or perhaps because one followed another as wiser, strayed from the line of truth. Of many writers one might fittingly repeat what Cato [Note: [Col. 0086D] Plutarch, *Life of Cato*.] once said of the Roman people: that they resemble a flock of sheep, which neither deliberate nor distinguish individually, but all follow some leader; thus the Romans, privately, consulted no one, but when forced into an assembly and gathering easily allowed themselves to be led by others. Nor did I think these things worthy of a more extended refutation. Away, then, with Iberian trifles—indeed, empty absurdities rather than things to be digested with a heated stomach. If you prefer, compare the beginnings of the Premonstratensian Order and the progress of its later age, and the earliest pursuits of Norbert’s life, transformed for the better, with the things occurring here and there throughout this work; [Col. 0086D] not even the faintest colour for disguising the truth will appear. And indeed, remembering the old proverb, “Do not walk along the public road”—that is, do not follow the errors of the many.

With far better right and clearer reason than the writers just named have vainly tried to transfer the Premonstratensian Order to the institute or Rule of St. Benedict, that same Benedictine order ought to glory—not in itself but in its God—in the Premonstratensian Order, among the many religious families which came forth like adorned brides from the bridal chamber of Premonstratensian canons. Nor shall I seem foolish if I say this openly. First, it calls to mind what, according to the testimony of the most serious writers of that institute, befell St. Dominic, the illustrious founder of the Order of Preachers. [Note: [Col. 0087D] Among our writers, Chrysostom Vander Sterre, *Life of St. Norbert*, Book II, chapter 5; Pagius, *Library*, Book I, chapter 17. From the Order of St. Dominic: Ferdinand of Castile, Book I, chapter 17; Fulk of Toulouse; Theodoric of Apolda; Blessed Humbert; and these are treated at length by Ribadeneira [Col. 0088D] in his *Life of St. Dominic*, 4 August, etc.]

When he was in Rome with Innocent III, supreme hierarch of the Church, seeking confirmation for the new order which the man of God, full of apostolic spirit, was then bringing forth, the affair—whether chance or God so ordained, I do not know—was prolonged to the great weariness of the petitioner. Entangled in the more delays because of its longer postponements, it had no result, until at length the pontiff, instructed by a nocturnal vision of the Lateran Church threatening to collapse, beneath which that man seemed to place his shoulders as it fell, changed his mind and hastened his decision. Therefore, summoning him at once, he graciously consented and granted him authority to establish the new congregation, [Col. 0087B] but with this condition: that he should not be permitted to forge a new rule or statutes of life for himself or his companions, but, after making a choice, should bind himself more willingly to one of the earlier orders of religious men sanctioned by the authority of the papal see, and conform the pattern of his life to it.

On these terms Dominic departed joyfully from Rome and went to Gaul to his companions dwelling at Prouille. Having taken counsel together, and calling upon the help of the divine Majesty, they long and earnestly prayed for a good inspiration, so that a choice most conducive to salvation might be made. At last the unanimous agreement and single voice of the fathers was that they should embrace the Rule of the most blessed Augustine, under the governance of those constitutions in which it had been introduced into practice by the Premonstratensian religious; that nothing else seemed more expedient for their proposed manner of life, nothing more fitting to bring their followers to the desired end, and nothing more able to advance the public good of the Church. They therefore matched deeds to words and, setting out soon afterwards for Spain, happily laid at Toulouse the foundations of the first monastery in the year of our salvation 1216, almost the first century after the beginning of the Premonstratensian Order had passed.

There is no testimony more weighty or illustrious than that of Blessed Humbert, fifth master general of the Order of Preachers, who affirms the following: [Note: [Col. 0088D] On Chapter I of the statutes of the Friars Preachers.]

“It should be noted that the statutes of the Premonstratensians begin in the same manner. From this it is inferred that our constitutions [Col. 0087D] were drawn from theirs, because they preceded us. And this was indeed just. For the Premonstratensians reformed and enlarged the Rule of St. Augustine, just as the Cistercians did the Rule of St. Benedict; and they surpass in austerity of life all who profess that Rule, as also in the splendour of ceremonies, the beauty and discretion of observances, and the governance of a very great multitude through general and annual chapters. Therefore, when blessed Dominic and the brothers of his time, according to the fervour they had conceived, could not obtain from the Lord Pope a new [Col. 0088A] and sufficiently strict rule or manner of life, and were thus turned back from their purpose, they chose the Rule of St. Augustine—not without reason—taking from it those constitutions which they judged more suitable to their profession.”

Thus the family of blessed Dominic is, as it were, another offspring of holy Father Norbert; or, if you prefer, the twin child of the most blessed and great parent Augustine. Thus, indeed—if you look especially at the beginnings—one order reproduced the other: not only in its Rule and constitutions, but in the ceremonies of divine worship, the outward habit of the body, and the equal purpose of its way of life. And just as St. Norbert, formerly a canon of the renowned church of Xanten in Cleves, took up, at heaven’s direction, a woollen habit, white in colour, with scapular and hood—yet no one except an unjust person would say that he departed [Col. 0088B] from the clerical order, which it is clear that he reformed and adorned—so blessed Dominic, laying aside the linen tunic which he had worn as a regular canon in the church at Osma, adopted the Premonstratensian form of dress, [Note: [Col. 0088D] Chapter 12.] differing only in the colour of the mantle or cloak, which was black for him, while for us it is white with the rest of the garment. He lost none of his former dignity, nothing of the apostolic life; rather, he increased it by a notable addition.

Concerning the Premonstratensian habit, Matthew Galenus, formerly provost of St. Amatus and chancellor of the faculty at Douai, argues in his book *On Monastic Origins* that it comes nearer than the rest to the custom of the primitive Church. He says:

“From the things which apostolic tradition has just supplied to us, anyone may readily perceive that in this matter also the Premonstratensians have returned to their origin. They have no ornament or garment that does not remind them of inward brightness, simplicity, and purity; except that the German cold, from which they first proceeded, did not permit the use of linen alone, and persuaded St. Norbert to exchange it for wool. For the fact that some put linen garments on over woollen underclothes seems more affected than genuine. That the outer cloaks or robes, and the exomides themselves, were woollen, and that in those eastern heats they sometimes served in summer in place of these, is plainly shown by the words of Philo appended in the last place.”

Thus he speaks. Yet he does not altogether please in this: that he judges the reason for adopting woollen clothing too low and measured by an inferior consideration. St. Norbert’s purpose was far loftier and purer: namely, that a woollen habit is more appropriate to penitence, of which religious men ought to be preachers both by deed and word. Further, linen clothing seemed more fittingly reserved for the services of the divine rite, because, as Master Adam says, [Note: [Col. 0088D] Sermon 3, Part II.] “what can at times be more pleasantly and gratefully resumed is that which happens to be set aside for a time.” The prophet Ezekiel describes the sons of Zadok and the priests of the old law as acting thus (chapter XLIV); so also does the received usage of the Church, the best and most approved teacher of all. [Col. 0089A]

Nor would I have all the inventions of Polydore Vergil approved, where he says concerning the Premonstratensians: [Note: [Col. 0089D] Book VII, *On Inventions*, chapter 3.] “They are clothed in a white tunic, with a linen robe beneath a white cloak, by which they differ especially from canons.” More nearly relevant is what, on the testimony of Clement Reyner, we read in his account of the apostolate of his Benedictines in England: [Note: [Col. 0089D] *On the Benedictine Apostolate in England*, Book I, §20.] that St. Gilbert in 1148 founded the Order of Sempringham under the double Rule of St. Benedict and St. Augustine, joining nuns and canons in the same church but separating them by suitable buildings. The arrangement was that the nuns, in the Cistercian manner, should devote themselves to divine praises under the Rule of St. Benedict; while the white canons, in the Premonstratensian manner, serving God under the Rule of St. Augustine, [Col. 0089B] should especially undertake the spiritual care of the nuns and the administration of temporal matters.

But, to return from the slight digression we have made, it must further be known that from the beginning a bond of perpetual association existed between the Premonstratensians and the Dominicans. This the German Preachers asked to be renewed, when they were admitted by the Premonstratensians to a communion of prayers and good works in a public and general chapter held at Prémontré in the year 1233. Miraeus in his *Premonstratensian Chronicle* and John Pagius in his *Library* attest the document of this agreement.

Hence what St. Thomas, [Note: [Col. 0089D] II–II, question 286, article 9.] prince of the scholastics, commends concerning the caution of profession among certain religious—who propose to establish their life not so much by a vow to observe the Rule as by following it, as it were, as a model, thereby cutting off the snare of graver sins—will readily appear, with little effort, to apply equally to Premonstratensian canons. “In some religious order,” he says, “namely that of the Friars Preachers, such transgression or omission, by its own nature, does not oblige one to sin, either mortally or venially, but only to undergo the prescribed punishment, because they are bound to observe such things in this manner.” What the holy doctor commends in his own brethren, both there and elsewhere, applies equally to Premonstratensian canons, as anyone who cares to consider will easily find.

This is the wording of the older Premonstratensian statutes:

“We understand that the institutions which we have written in the present book bind transgressors [Col. 0089D] not to guilt but to punishment, unless some should presume to transgress them out of contempt.”

And shortly afterwards:

“Moreover, those matters concerning privileges and statutes of the Roman pontiffs which we have inserted in this book we regard not as our institutions, but as privileges and statutes of the Apostolic See.”

The fathers of the Dominican Order also placed at the head of their constitutions that preface—which, not wishing to range through the entire codex, I may say is borrowed almost word for word from this source—and did not reject either the same preface that we have or that caution concerning obligation.

Indeed, as our Becard attests, [Note: [Col. 0089D] *Annals*, under the year 1120, no. 74.] the hermits of St. Augustine, commonly called Augustinians, likewise begin their constitutions with the same words. In agreement with this, John Pagius wrote in his *Library*: [Note: [Col. 0090D] Book I, chapter 17.]

“There are also very many other religious families and congregations: the brethren [Col. 0090B] of the Cross of Mercy; the Hermits of St. Augustine; the canons of the Holy Saviour near Florence; and most others. In all things, except clothing, they imitate and observe the customs, constitutions, statutes, and ordinances of our Premonstratensians.”

Thus he. Certainly, to add an appendix to these statements, Peter Crespet, doctor of Paris, left the following written concerning his own Celestines: [Note: [Col. 0090D] In the *Summa* under the word “Mary,” in Miraeus, *Premonstratensian Chronicle*, under the year 1518.]

“We also possess the chant and office most devoutly composed by Adam, the Premonstratensian cardinal, completely corresponding in its musical setting to the ecclesiastical solemnity aforesaid.”

These might not improperly be called certain branches of the palm of Prémontré, raised heavenward at Kadesh, planted beside the streams of saving waters, yielding its fruit in season: a palm which honour exalts, holiness confirms, wisdom adorns, and the beauty of its verdant branches makes fruitful. Blessed Humbert regarded our constitutions in this light: [Note: [Col. 0090D] Treatise 4, Conference 11, Sermon.]

“The Premonstratensians added most beautiful observances, as certain ceremonies tending to the greater worship of God. These observances serve for greater merit in relation to God: they are voluntary services added to obligatory ones. They serve for greater strength against enemies: they are an outer rampart added to the wall. They serve for greater beauty in relation to one’s neighbours: they are a variety of painting added over whiteness. Likewise, they promote a greater warming of charity, as clothing does; a better preservation of the Rule, as a hedge around a vineyard; and a firmer binding together in the good, just as doubled girths [Col. 0090D] bind a saddle more securely.”

Thus that master general of the Order and eminent ascetic.

[Col. 0091]

[SERMONS.]

PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING HOMILIES OR SERMONS OF MASTER ADAM, CALLED THE ENGLISHMAN, OF THE PREMONSTRATENSIAN ORDER.

1. SUMMARY.—1. The invention of letters aids memory.—2. Their useful and necessary employment.—3. Commanded to commit to writing what he had proclaimed from the pulpit.—4. Long deterred by regard for his own insignificance and others’ envy.—5. His own abasement and the exaltation of the Fathers and Doctors of the Church.—6. He yields to the affection of his brethren and the authority of his superiors.—7. He dedicates his labours to the canons of the Premonstratensian Church.—8. He loves them without pretence, remembering their benefits without flattery.—9. The possible rendering of repayment.—10. One hundred homilies distributed through the year.—11. Analogy between the spiritual and bodily physician.—12. He submits his writings for correction.

[Col. 0091A] I. Among other things, O man of venerable life, most beloved to me in Christ, in which there consists both the material and the means of knowing things done or said in former times and, most especially, of retaining what is known, this is surely first and chief: that in the diversity of languages under the sun, signs of letters were long ago invented. For since it is unquestionably evident that, as syllables are formed from letters, so words are formed from syllables and sentences are woven from words, the fuller and clearer our knowledge of letters appears, the more consequently does knowledge shine clearly within us against ignorance and memory remain strong against forgetfulness. Hence Isidore says in the first book of the *Etymologies*: “Letters are indicators of things, signs of words; and they have such power that they speak to us without a voice the words of absent persons.” And he adds: “The use of letters was invented for the remembrance of various things; for, lest these should flee through forgetfulness, they are bound fast by letters.” He adds the reason: “For amid such a great variety of things, not all could be learned by hearing or retained in memory.”

[Col. 0091B] II. The necessity of letters. Since, then, letters indicate things and likewise signify words, and since their power is such that they even speak to us without a voice the words of those absent, it is beyond doubt that their use is necessary. Through them, what we wish to know but do not wish to retain [alternative reading: “are unable to retain”] is bound fast for us—things which instruction by hearing alone can neither teach nor memory sufficiently retain.

[Col. 0091C] III. The reason for writing sermons. Thus the devotion of some of our brethren, both those of my own age pleading with me and my superiors commanding me, has often deigned to trouble my insignificance by its importunity: that I should commit to writing for both the former and the latter some of the things which I had previously said for the edification of those present. This, indeed, is the reason [alternative reading: “for this reason”] why whatever has been written has been committed to letters: [Col. 0092A] so that those who could not have the speaker present with his voice might yet have him speaking though absent and voiceless; and so that, through frequent reading, they might easily entrust to memory what, spoken once, they could scarcely retain by hearing.

IV. Two obstacles: first, regard for his own insufficiency; second, for the envy of others. Yet when I had often been urged both by request and command, I was on the one hand covered with shame and on the other shaken by fear: ashamed, I say, by reason of my own ignorance, and fearing also the biting tongues of detractors. Therefore I resolved neither to yield at all to those entreating me nor to obey those commanding me; but, resisting the former long as well as the latter, I allowed myself neither to be bent by their requests nor compelled by their commands. For at that time I judged it a lighter offence to disappoint kindly disposed men—companions as well as prelates—than to provoke malicious men against my faintheartedness. When the speaker displeases them [alternative reading: “the things he says displease them”], then, in consequence, what he says does not please them either. Nor can words received by the ears be held in honour when the person seen by the eyes is despised. And while they cut down with the sharp sword of their tongue what they hear spoken before them, they often rage much more cruelly against what they find written upon parchment. For while the inward malice of envy torments them, they seek rather where an occasion for blame than for edification may lie open to them—though by means of that edification they may be taught, although [alternative readings: “what” or “in what way”], how salutary is that which restrains the impetuous from evil and rouses the sluggish to good.

[Col. 0092C] V. His own submission before the orthodox Fathers. Not only this, but consciousness of my own ignorance also for some time dissuaded me from taking up the pen. For when the life-giving and most sweet delights of the orthodox Fathers abound so greatly, I blushed—and not without reason—to set before those who sit at them not merely frequently but continually the tasteless vegetable of my poverty, and to offer them my muddy pool among clearest torrents. Who would not, and justly, judge this worthy of every mockery? It would be one and the same thing as if a burrowing mole, blind rather than merely blinded, intruded upon an eagle in flight, so as to bring its gaze to the sun with the eagle, though unable to behold the sun’s rays. What sharpness have I in understanding, what brilliance in expression, or what perfection in conduct, that I should presume to add anything from my sackcloth bag to their refined and abundant delights? Such things properly belong to those unlike me: men whom gold makes exceedingly rich in keenness of intellect, silver illustrious in brilliance of speech, and precious stones adorned in praiseworthy life. But I am not such a one. I am poor, obscure, and unadorned, lacking depth of wisdom, radiance of eloquence, and merit of life. In these and similar considerations lies my excuse: it neither admits requests to be granted [alternative reading: “admits”] nor embraces commands to be fulfilled [alternative reading: “embraces”].

[Col. 0093B] VI. The authority of the commander and the charity of the petitioner prevail. Yet, although perhaps it was once fitting for me to excuse myself, it was certainly never permissible for me always to refuse; for this would no less be blameworthy obstinacy than the former was a sign of commendable humility. The humility of one entreated and commanded made the former tolerable; but the charity of the petitioner and the authority of the commander drove the latter far away. Thus it happened in every respect. I judged it better to admit the bloody hands of detractors against myself than, by resisting their wishes, to fail in fraternal affection toward my equals or filial affection toward my superiors. Drawn and overcome, therefore, casting my thought upon the Lord, I began to apply my mind to study and my hand to the pen (Psalm 44:2). Whatever, meanwhile, could occur suitably for the occasion and opportunity of time and place, I wrote down: repeating both what I had previously said in public and adding what I had not yet said before others. What I had written I sent especially to the sincerity of your charity.

[Col. 0093D] VII. Dedication of the work and of himself. To you indeed—to you, I say, O reverend men to be embraced in Christ by the arms of sincere affection—I judged this little work especially worthy to be sent. Among all servants of Christ I embrace you, as is fitting and right, in his own bowels; and I desire to hold you bound to me indissolubly, whom the one and same God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, uniter of holy minds, has granted to be joined to my spirit in himself by the unfailing bond of true love. I desire to be wholly yours, if I have any power in the word of God; indeed, if anything has been given me in any spiritual exercise that may serve for edification. Let therefore the sweetness of your sincerity receive this gift, altogether small indeed, yet sent with no small love. Let it in no way suppose [Col. 0094A] that I deem it greatly necessary for you; rather, from the sending of it let it infer and consider what sort of affection I bear toward you in the Lord. For I am always, everywhere, and in all things, insofar as knowledge has enabled us to know and ability to act, yours in Christ—if indeed I am anything. Yours, indeed; yours, I say: your servant in service, indebted in benefits received, disciple in instruction, son in adoption, companion in Catholic peace, friend in love, and finally fellow-servant in him who is Lord of lords. Would anyone call it a great thing that I declare myself wholly yours? I should not deny it, if I myself were great. But now, not thinking myself to be something when I am nothing, lest I deceive myself (Galatians 6:3), but rather knowing what I lack, I do not consider myself to be doing anything great even when I gather myself wholly to love you. For I know that I, so small and such as I am, am loved so greatly and in such a manner by men so great and of such quality.

[Col. 0094B] VIII. Love without pretence, and acknowledgement of benefits without flattery. For when I consider and reconsider, turn over and turn over again within myself how great and what kind of affection you show me in the Lord—seeing on the one hand that I am so unworthy, and on the other that I am so highly regarded among you—I blush, I confess, and am astonished at your inestimable love; and I am astonished while blushing. For I speak not with heart and heart, but before God in Christ: “my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 9:1). As I see myself in truth, and as I confess myself with my mouth, so I behold myself in my heart, making little of myself and judging myself humble in my own eyes. Yet neither do I assume a dog-like tongue of licking in remembering and confessing the benefits so abundantly bestowed on me by you, while giving thanks and uttering a voice of praise. Nor do I anoint your head with oil, admitting the unction of flattery. For who am I, or what am I, or what is my father’s house in Israel, as one says (2 Samuel 7:18), that your whole community in your house should bestow upon me so abundantly such affection of sincere love, accompanied by such fruitful dispositions? Who has found greater favour than I in the eyes of all [Col. 0094D] of you? And, to add something more, who has found even so great favour? That this is indeed so the devotion of your whole community ceases not to proclaim, in that it receives my insignificance so cheerfully when I come to it, treats me so kindly while I remain with it, and lets me go from it so reluctantly when I depart. For when has it not lamented my absence, become cheerful at my presence, rejoiced at my arrival, and grieved at my departure?

IX. What repayment can be worthy of benefits. May the Lord repay you this return [alternative reading: “recompense”], in whose sight even the hairs of his elect are numbered for reward. For to render you a recompense worthy of your benefits far exceeds my poverty, unless perhaps, in repaying some return, however very small, I may be aided in some degree by the full knowledge in my heart and confession with my mouth of the charity which I know has not been lacking in me. For I know and confess that I am your debtor; I also know and confess that I cannot be a worthy repayer. I do not fail to know that what I have received is in every respect great, but also that what might be repaid is nothing with me. This is assuredly no loss to you, because the giver and rewarder of all good things will restore to you all the more abundantly, the more you have bestowed in his name upon one who has nothing with which to repay you. Hence his exhortation in the Gospel to a certain man is in this form:

“When you make a dinner or supper, do not invite your friends, [Col. 0095B] nor your brothers, nor your relatives, nor rich neighbours, lest perhaps they also invite you in return, and repayment be made to you. But when you make a feast, invite the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame; and you shall be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. But you shall be repaid at the resurrection of the dead” (Luke 14:13–14).

Your recompense too will be at that same resurrection, because you have done good also to one who has nothing with which to repay you: one whom spiritual need makes poor, concupiscence of the flesh weak, the darkness of ignorance blind, and sluggishness in good work lame. But let us be silent about these matters thus far.

X. A Book of Homilies, containing one hundred sermons, and their arrangement. I send you this book of sermons or homilies as a token of the devoted love [Col. 0095C] with which I embrace the love of your whole community in the Lord. I ask you to receive it with the gracious devotion with which I know it is sent to you by me. And, with the knees of my mind bent in prayer before the sincerity of your charity, I add this further request: whatever your discernment finds in it conducive to edification, let it approve; yet whatever it detects that is unsuitable or otherwise defective, let it by no means leave uncorrected. For this is my wish: that whatever is right in any little works or studies of my insignificance may be approved by the sincerity of your charity, and that whatever is crooked may be corrected according to your judgment.

Beginning with the Advent of the Lord and proceeding through the more festive days [Col. 0095D], I have selected some things from what I had already spoken in public. I have also added some things which I had not yet spoken publicly; and, as best I could, I composed one hundred sermons. There are eighteen sermons from the first Sunday in the Advent of the Lord up to the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. On the vigil itself, four; on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, six; on the day of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, four; on the day of Saint John, apostle and evangelist, one; on the day of the holy Innocents, three; on the Sunday within the octave of the Lord’s Nativity, four; on the day of the Circumcision, two; on the day of the Lord’s Epiphany, two; on the second Sunday after the Lord’s Epiphany, three; on the Wednesday which begins the fast, one; on Palm Sunday, one; on the Lord’s Supper, one; at the Paschal feast, four; in the third week of Easter, on Monday at the synod, one; on the following Tuesday at the same synod, one; on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, one; at the feast of Pentecost, six; on its octave, one; at the dedication of a church, one; at the election of any prelate, one. After these sermons are fourteen others specifically concerning religious men, followed by twenty for the more solemn feasts of saints.

XI. The preacher is like a physician seeking wholesome herbs. But if there are any readers who dislike the fact that some of these sermons have been extended to such great length—which indeed greatly displeases me as well—I ask them to recall [Col. 0096B] that one who sets forth many things for the edification of his hearers cannot always suitably and gracefully bring what he has proposed to an end whenever he wishes. For a discourse once under way cannot be held back.

It often happens that a physician, seeking wholesome herbs by whose powers he may assist sick persons entrusted to his care, wanders far and wide through forests. He is delayed there for a long while, and sometimes emerges very late from them into open plains with his basket. This happens especially when the density of those forests stretches farther onward and offers him a plentiful supply of the herbs he is carefully seeking; the physician spends a longer time gathering them in proportion as he desires the health of his sick people with more ardent love [Col. 0096C].

Is not he fittingly likened to a physician who, having undertaken the preaching of the divine word by the merit of his life, seeks to heal the illnesses of souls? And what are wholesome herbs amid the density of forests but spiritual meanings in the depths of the Scriptures? In searching them out, the preacher sometimes applies himself rather slowly, because, through the Spirit’s imparted inspiration and the keenness of his understanding, he finds deeper the sacred Scriptures on which he is commenting; and because with pious purpose he seeks more diligently the edification of his hearers, whom he desires to win for Christ.

XII. Submission to correction. I have not said this because I wish to maintain that the wearisome length of these sermons is undeserving of criticism. Rather, I wish it also to be corrected at your judgment—justly criticized along with any other things in them that deserve criticism [Col. 0096D]—so that those which you judge excessively long you may reduce to a fitting and appropriate brevity. In short: just as I am most justly worthy of rebuke for having rashly committed to writing things that ought not to have been written, so you too, if I may say so with your leave, will not deserve praise in this matter if you neglect to amend what needs correction in them, since I offer them to your diligence for examination and to your skill for correction. In every respect I shall regard as settled in them only what the just decision of your judgment has accepted.

When this preface is concluded, I set forth the titles and subjects of the individual sermons, so that anyone wishing to know the subject treated in each may immediately find it without turning through them one by one [Col. 0097A]. May our Redeemer and redemption, priest and victim, purchaser and price, the Lord Jesus, by his grace and mercy protect your religious community, which prays for us, from every evil; may he always and everywhere keep it sound and unharmed; and may he happily bring it to his blessed and beatifying vision in the life to come. Amen.

# Sermons of Adam of Prémontré

[Col. 0097]

## Sermon I. The First Sunday in the Advent of the Lord

On the names of Christ, and how we ought to go to meet him when he comes.

[Col. 0097A]

**Synopsis of the sermon.**—1. The coming Savior must be met, according to the Invitatory of the divine office customarily sung at this season. — 2. Whom we must meet, by whom, and in what manner. — 3. Fervor of spirit is commended; lukewarmness is reproved even more than a certain coldness. — 4. Every weariness and instability of mind or body must be kept away from the divine offices. — 5. The danger of falling away arises when the desire to advance is abandoned. — 6. On six names attributed to God. — 7. “Wonderful,” especially considered in the creation of man. — 8. A beastly likeness must not be introduced into the image of God. — 9. Why he is called “Counselor.” — 10. Likewise “God” [Col. 0097B] and “Mighty.” — 11. Friend and Father of the age to come. — 12. Prince of peace and Savior. — 13. Called the Son of God. — 14. God and man, Emmanuel.

I. The health-giving season is now at hand, beloved, in which it is fitting that each of us perform the office of a runner. For this seems to be contained in that exhorting utterance by which tonight, at the very beginning of the vigil, you roused one another, when not only by speaking words to one another, but also by singing in harmony, to express the inward eagerness and concord of the mind, you said: “Let us go to meet him.” This is indeed a most salutary admonition, as you yourselves do not deny if you attend carefully, concerning whom it is spoken. For whom but our Savior, of whom you immediately added: “Behold, the King comes”? You also gave the reason beforehand when you said this. “Behold” is a word not only of pointing out, but of wonder, and sometimes of exultation. This King ought to be received with joy mingled with wonder, and joyful wonder; and whoever wishes fruitfully to meet this Savior must possess both. Let us therefore go to meet him who is coming.

II. For the Creator and Teacher comes; the Lord and King comes; the Friend and Bridegroom comes; the Savior and Son comes; God and man also comes. If this is so—or rather, because it is so—let the creature meet its Creator; disciples, their Teacher; servants, their Lord; soldiers, their King; companions, their Friend; the bridegroom’s attendants, their Bridegroom; captives, their Savior; co-heirs, the Son [Col. 0098A]. Finally, let human beings meet the man who is God, so that through the God-man they may be deified. Let them meet him, I say, but with devotion of mind and fervor of spirit. Perhaps this is why you exhorted one another not merely to go, but to run. Even a lazy person can sometimes go; but running always belongs to one who hastens. It is surely fitting and right that we run, because he whom we say must be met ran rather than went. Let us meet him, therefore, because he first ran for us. “He who saw bore witness” that “he rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:7). O joyful one, O strong one, O fervent one! For in one who rejoices the breadth of heart is marked; in a giant, strength of work; in one who runs, fervor of spirit.

III. Let us meet him in the manner in which he ran for us: namely, that we may be cheerful givers, since God loves such persons. Let us be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in every work of the Lord, because the labor of such persons is not vain before the Lord (1 Cor. 15:58). Let us be fervent in spirit, because one who is lukewarm will begin to be vomited from his mouth (Rev. 3:15): “Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation” (Rev. 19:11). I say these things, beloved, because lukewarmness of spirit in any religious person greatly displeases God. For while some are cold through fault, some hot through righteousness, and others lukewarm through negligence, yet in the angel of Laodicea [Col. 0098C] coldness is borne by the Lord more patiently than lukewarmness. Although those who seem lukewarm while remaining in good may appear less bad than those who lie cold in evil, yet when that fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth blows up (Luke 12:49), the cold are indeed kindled; but the lukewarm, unwilling to be kindled, are vomited from the Lord’s mouth. Likewise, cast out from grace, they are shut out; and, shut out, they are expelled.

IV. Therefore let those fear who perform spiritual work with a dry and weary heart—especially those who perform the divine office in the Church. For the prophet threatens no slight punishment to those who do the work of the Lord deceitfully (Jer. 48:10), and negligently. Every work you do is spiritual, and for every work a spiritual recompense must be awaited and desired [Col. 0099A]. Therefore, whether you are engaged in manual labor, ecclesiastical offices, or any business pertaining to God, cast aside harmful lukewarmness; renounce entirely all frivolity of body and, as far as possible, instability of mind. In bearing and gesture, in standing and walking, indeed in all your movements, outward as well as inward, let nothing be done that offends the divine, angelic, or human gaze—but rather that befits your holiness, as your blessed Father Augustine admonishes you [Note: [Col. 0099D] In the Rule, chapter 6.]—so that, showing yourselves faithful and prudent, diligent and devout in all things, you may have as your rewarder in the future him whom you now have as the observer of your struggle. Even now may you have before him as helpers those whom you have as witnesses.

V. Therefore let your mind grow warm again, let your spirit burn; and, not merely leaving but even forgetting what lies behind, stretch yourselves toward what lies before (Phil. 3:13). In spiritual conduct, not to advance is in a certain sense to fall away. And, as one of the saints says: “The danger of falling away is incurred where the desire for progress is laid aside.” Know that the Lord does not admit into the embrace of his grace one whom he finds undevout in his work. He vomits from his mouth the one whom he finds lukewarm; he excludes from the increase of his gift the one whom he sees applying himself to his service more from habit than from affection. For to everyone who possesses a good desire he gives, that such a one may abound; but from one who does not possess it, even what he seems to have is taken away (Luke 8:18) [Col. 0099C]. Therefore, let us not merely go, but run to meet our Savior; and let us run in such a way that we may take hold. For the two feet, as it were, of one walking on the spiritual path are fervor of good desire and steadfastness of perseverance, so that one wishing to run not uncertainly and to receive the prize may lack neither ardent perseverance nor persevering ardor.

VI. He who comes to us and whom we must meet is called Creator and Teacher, Lord and King, Friend and Bridegroom, Savior and Son of God; and he is the same God and man. See whether perhaps these names are also assigned to him in sacred Scripture. Isaiah says: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of peace” (Isa. 9:6) [Col. 0099D]. The first name seems to belong to the Creator; the second to the Teacher; the third to the Lord; the fourth to the King; the fifth to the Friend; the sixth to the Bridegroom.

VII. Although he is wonderful in all things without any exception, he appears especially wonderful in our creation. Creation itself plainly shows this, so wonderfully fashioned by the Wonderful One that it too is not undeservedly wonderful. For who can sufficiently wonder that, in forming the human being, he joined spirit and clay together? He formed the body from matter already at hand, that is, from earth; but he made the soul from nothing, nevertheless in his own image and likeness [Col. 0100A]. O wonderful forming of the human body! How wonderful, too, the breathing-in of that life-giving and indwelling spirit, namely the rational spirit! He marked the spirit with a twofold gift, enlightening it and moving its affections: in the one, making it bright for the knowledge of truth through understanding; in the other, anointing it for the love of virtue through affection. O understanding, by whose radiance the choice of truth shines bright; and affection, by whose anointing the love of good is made sweet!

He likewise enriched the body with a twofold gift, adorning it with senses and, through the arrangement of its limbs, preparing instruction for the spirit: one gift for the practice of good action, the other for the fruit of inward instruction. The one is that eyes are given to see, ears to hear, nostrils to smell, the throat to taste, and the other limbs—and especially hands—to touch; so that the invisible indweller may take in from without and absorb inwardly whatever is given form through sight, sounds through hearing, odors through smell, flavors through taste, and tangible things through touch [Col. 0100B]. The arrangement of the limbs itself also affords no slight instruction to that same spirit. Above all, although only the soles of his feet touch the earth, man is raised upright above the other living creatures. Hence a pagan poet says:

> And whereas the other animals look downward upon the earth,  
> he gave humankind an uplifted countenance,  
> and commanded it to look upon heaven  
> and raise its erect face toward the stars.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I

[Col. 0100C]

VIII. Consider, then, O spirit enlightened by the light of reason; consider, I say, in your beast of burden, over which you preside as a rider and go before as a charioteer, what manner of person you ought to show yourself. Raise it toward things above; abandon earthly things. Be ashamed, O human being, to introduce a beastly likeness into that part of yourself in which you were created in the likeness of God. To attend sluggishly to earthly things after casting away heavenly things, to seek what lies below, to relish what is upon the earth—this is to put on a beastly likeness [variant: “introduce”].

On the contrary, to give earthly things their useful due, yet not to wish to enjoy them; to wish rather to use them with strict restraint; to seek what is above in effect and to savor what is above in affection; possessing lower things only for use while desiring higher things in purpose [Col. 0100D]—this is, as though only the soles of the feet touched the earth while the whole body was raised up, to lift one’s head toward the highest things. Therefore, since rational soul and flesh constitute one human being, in the former the knowledge of truth shines and the love of virtue burns; in the latter the senses are present for outward necessity in such a way that the varied arrangement of the limbs also supplies inward instruction.

IX. See how the wonderful creation of man proclaims the wonderful Creator of man. He who is Teacher is Counselor; and he who is uniquely the God of all is especially the Lord of all. Does not Isaiah testify that the name of the child born for us is called Counselor and God? And in the Gospel he himself says: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for I am” (John 13:13) [Col. 0101A]. For he who undertook to give us words of life fulfilled the office of a teacher as counselor, or the teaching of a counselor; and he who alone orders all things sweetly also alone exercises the lordship of God.

X. He is likewise our King, and our Mighty One: “Reaching mightily from end to end” (Wis. 8:1). He is King, reaching from end to end as the great King and exercising full authority in his kingdom without any contradiction; mighty, because he reaches mightily. Do we not, as we have heard, also see that, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy, “He reigns as King and is wise, doing judgment and justice on the earth” (Jer. 23:5)? And that he conquers the armed strong man, daily takes away his weapons, and distributes his spoils? (Luke 11:21) [Col. 0101B].

XI. Whose friend, I ask, is he more truly than of the one whom he begets through predestination for the age to come? This was well understood by the one who said: “Everyone born of God does not sin, because heavenly generation preserves him, and the evil one will not touch him” (1 John 5:18). The one born of God does not sin at all, because whatever sins he may seem to have committed in time do not appear in eternity, since the charity of his Father covers the multitude of his sins (1 Pet. 4:8). Thus he is both Friend—preserving him from sins lest they be committed, or wholly forgiving those already committed—and Father, predestining him for the age to come.

[Col. 0101C]

XII. And who else is the Prince of peace except “our peace, making both one” (Eph. 2:14)? The time is now at hand when he comes to proclaim peace to those who were near and to those who were far off. He joined the two peoples into one Church for himself, justifying circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith (Rom. 3:30), and made Mount Zion and the sides of the north one city, of which he himself is the great King (Ps. 47:3).

That his name is Savior is attested by Gabriel, the herald of his birth, who, speaking to his mother, says: “You shall call his name Jesus” (Matt. 2:21). He also gives the reason: “For he shall save his people from their sins” (ibid.). He bears a name that truly derives from the reality, because he does what he is called. He who is called Savior works salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. 74:12) [Col. 0101D]. He is our true David, in whose hand God the Father saves us from the hand of the Philistines, slaying in his hand Goliath of Gath (1 Sam. 17:22). Burdened—not empty, but full of grace and truth—having entrusted the flock to its keeper, he came to his brothers, who were fighting against him (ibid., v. 20). That is, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, he went to seek the one which had perished (Matt. 18:12); and, having found it, he carried it home on his shoulders, bearing the head of the Gittite to Jerusalem.

XIII. And that he is called Son of God—what is clearer than the angel’s saying: “The holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35)? It is well said not “sanctified,” as though in the past, nor “to be sanctified,” as though in the future, but already “holy” [Col. 0102A]. For he who came to us through the Virgin was neither stained by any sin contracted by conception nor to be stained by any sin throughout all the time afterward when he lived among human beings.

XIV. He is God and man. Thus he is called, as the prophet testifies, saying that the son of the Virgin shall be called Emmanuel; and the Evangelist explains: “which is interpreted, God with us” (Isa. 7:14; Matt. 1:23). If Emmanuel is “God with us,” with whom is he God except with human beings—that is, with those of whom the one saying this was one, since he too was a human being? God with us—and where is he with us? With us in birth; with us in the very corruption of the flesh, without pollution of the flesh; with us in death itself. In short, he is with us in what we are by nature. What you hear as “God” is, in eternity, from the Father without a mother; what you hear as “with us” is, in time, from a mother without a father [Col. 0102B].

Therefore the Creator comes, Wonderful; the Teacher, Counselor: let his creature and his disciples meet him. The Lord God and mighty King comes: let servants and soldiers meet him. The Father, Friend, and peace-bringing Bridegroom comes: let companions and bridegroom’s attendants meet him. The Savior, Son of God, the same God and man, comes: let captives, to be redeemed by him, meet him; let human beings, to be deified through the one assumed by the Assumer, meet him—he who is God above all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Sermon II. Likewise for the First Sunday in the Advent of the Lord

[Col. 0102C]

**Synopsis of the sermon.**—1. Let the creature meet the Creator. — 2. Let disciples meet the Teacher. — 3. And servants the Lord: for he is Lord and we are servants. — 4. Fear of the Lord precedes love. — 5. Let soldiers meet the King, and what the spiritual battle is. — 6. Let friends meet their Friend, and how he proved himself a true friend. — 7. The ardor of love in Christ is considered. — 8. The name “friend” is the origin and end of the others. — 9. Reciprocal love must be shown, and how. — 10. God is faithful and merciful in tribulation.

I. The Creator comes, beloved; let his creature meet him. Let it give him devout thanks for the first gift he bestowed, crying from the deepest marrow of its heart [variant: “let it cry”]: “He made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 100:3). I thank you, eternal Creator of things, because you made me; for you would never have made me unless you loved me. Why indeed did you make me, except because you preferred that I should be rather than not be? What less could you give, or I receive? Yet unless this had first been given, nothing could afterward have been added; nor could a roof be set upon a house unless the intervening wall were in place.

II. Let disciples meet their Teacher, offering their ears, hearing, and striving to fulfill in deed what we learn. Behold, from the teaching place of our Teacher there thunders in our ears that salutary voice which says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). And this also thunders: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34). These and other precepts of this kind are the law of life and discipline. When these counsels of salvation are eagerly heard [Col. 0103A], understood when heard, held faithfully in memory when understood, and put into effect when retained, then indeed disciples meet their Teacher.

III. Servants also meet their Lord if, fearing his presence, they fulfill his commands and avoid what he forbids, lest they incur the most severe effects of his threats. For it belongs to servants to be afraid and to tremble beneath their Lord’s rod: “He gave a sign to those who fear him, that they might flee from before the bow” (Ps. 60:6). You have heard what was said to the ancients: “I am the Lord” (Lev. 16:19). As you know, when commands were promulgated, the promulgator was accustomed frequently to thunder terribly: “I am the Lord.” What do you suppose is meant by this immediate declaration, after the ordinances of the holy Rule have been laid down, “I am the Lord,” except the plain implication that he who is the promulgator of instruction to hearers will be the inflicter of punishment upon transgressors [Col. 0103B]?

IV. Yes, it is altogether expedient that, for the time being, fear restrain them and dread shake them, until they can run into the freedom of love. Jeremiah spoke for such persons when, beholding the terror of the Lord and addressing him, he said: “I sat alone because of your hand, for you filled me with threats” (Jer. 15:17). Jeremiah saw the future blow, unless he avoided transgression. Another, likewise filled with the same spirit of the fear of the Lord, said: “Your wrath passed over me, and your terrors troubled me” (Ps. 88:17). This is to say: “I feel your present scourges, indeed very heavy ones, and I fear still heavier ones in the future” [Col. 0103C]. Holy Job also says: “I was troubled at his presence; when I considered him, I was anxious with fear” (Job 23:15). And again: “I have always feared God as waves swelling over me, and I could not bear his weight” (Job 31:23). These saints, therefore, and others like them, perceiving his terror, fear him as Lord; and, fleeing to contrition of heart and humility of spirit, mistrusting the quality of their own merits, they send an embassy to ask for terms of peace.

V. Christ our Lord is also King, whom the Virgin Mother crowned with the diadem of humility (Song 3:11). The daughters of Zion are commanded to go forth to look upon him with the eye of imitation, passing from the thought and affection of the flesh to the contemplation and love of the spirit [Col. 0103D]. He fought against the world, battled against the devil, and conquered both: the former he defeated; the latter he cast out. Therefore let his soldiers meet their King, who fights for them in this way, so that he need not say to them: “You take flight, and I go to be sacrificed for you” (John 16:32); or: “Each of you is scattered to his own home, and you leave me alone” (ibid.).

And what is it for each of us to be scattered to what is our own and to leave him alone, except for each of us to be separated into our own sins, which are ours precisely because we committed them? We refuse to imitate the Lord in holiness when we allow him to be alone. But let courageous soldiers imitate their King in this battle, resisting the enticing world through temperance; the hostile world through patience; and that crafty enemy who secretly suggests evil, through prudence, while resisting him when he openly rages through justice [Col. 0104A]. Let the flattering and frightening world neither allure nor break you, and it is conquered. Let the adversary who secretly counsels and openly attacks neither deceive nor corrupt you, and he is cast down.

“Let your eyes, O wise soldiers, be in your head” (Eccl. 2:14). If you have tribulation in the world, take courage, for he has conquered the world (John 16:33); and if the world hates you, know that it hated him first (John 15:16). Unless perhaps you are greater than he, why do you fear before the face of the prince of this world? Hope in him, in whom that prince has nothing (John 14:30), and you will overcome. Fight lawfully, that you may be crowned (Rom. 8:17). Labor as good soldiers of Christ Jesus; for if you suffer with him, you will also reign with him (2 Tim. 2:3) [Col. 0104B]. That is, if you show yourselves good soldiers with him and for him, he himself will establish you as blessed kings with him.

VI. I do not doubt that many of you have been granted to feel through experience that the Lord Jesus is your friend. For “charity has been poured out into your hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to you” (Rom. 5:5). “The Father himself loves you,” he says, “because you have loved me” (John 16:27). This is the voice of the Son. But who would dare say that the Father loves those who love his Son, while the Son himself does not love those who love him? And where is that truthful promise of the Son, which he gave for the consolation of those who love him: “He who loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I will love him” (John 14:21)? How otherwise would what he says elsewhere be true: “I love those who love me” (Prov. 8:17) [Col. 0104C]?

Consider that he is your friend from the love which he bestows on you. If no one can be called a friend except because he loves, who is a better friend to us than he? Who is as good as he, who loved us so greatly? And if you too love, what is this compared with his love, since in love you are necessarily surpassed by him because he loves first and more than you? If, as people commonly say, the proof of love is the performance of a deed, what is more sublime than this? He showed by deed the love he had. It is written of him: “He loved us and washed us” (Rev. 1:5). Because he loved, therefore he washed; for unless he had loved, he would never have washed. Thus the cause of the washing which followed was the greatness of the love which came first: he performed the office of one who washes because he had assumed the role of one who loves [Col. 0104D]. And from what filth did he wash us? From our sins. And in what washing? In his own blood.

VII. Open, I beseech you, the eyes of your spirit; discern the height of this grace; and consider, if you can, how greatly love burned in this Friend toward you. While you were still sinners, so that you might not remain sinners for long, he poured out for you so abundant a quantity of innocent blood. Consider how great was the love in him which brought it about that, to wash away your sins, so great an outpouring of such great blood was given. Now indeed he loves because you are friends; but he loved first so that you might be friends. For unless he had first loved enemies, he would have had no friends to love afterward. Therefore he loved, he washed from sins, and he washed in his own blood.

For with him there is both great and “abundant redemption” (Ps. 130:7) [Col. 0105A]. And truly it is abundant, because not a drop but a wave flowed out to wash away our sins. See, then, how greatly he loved you, who judged your redemption worthy of so lavish an outpouring of his own blood. But what benefit comes to us from his thus washing us? He adds: “And he made us a kingdom and priests to our God” (Rev. 1:6). The gentle Jesus, our priest and sacrifice, did this so that we might share with him the name of dignity, we who offer his most holy body and blood upon the altar.

VIII. Certainly, we assigned four names to him whom we proclaimed must be met, and before four others we placed, as if in the middle, this name of which we are now speaking, because it is the cause of both the preceding and the following names [Col. 0105B]. Why did he show himself to you as Creator, instructor, ruler, governor, except because he is your friend? Surely the reason he granted you such profound knowledge, such fruitful fear, and such strong warfare was that he loved you. And whence comes this—that he made himself your Bridegroom, your Savior; your brother among you, a man for you? Does it not come from his being a friend? For he who loved first granted that you might be joined to him, redeemed by him, adopted through him, and deified in him. Therefore meet such a great and such a friend.

IX. How, you ask, shall we meet him? How except by loving? Since it is certain that he who comes is a lover and has come in order to be loved, I find no manner of meeting him more fitting than meeting him by loving, so that, although he has no need of our goods (Ps. 16:2), we may return love to him for love. Love him, therefore, and cleave to him with an indissoluble affection, that you may be one spirit with him: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6:17) [Col. 0105C]. And, as is commonly said [Note: [Col. 0105D] Sallust, *Catiline*.], “To will the same thing and not to will the same thing is firm friendship.” This saying is true; but if “according to God” were added, it would be firmer, and firmer in proportion as it was more sincere and fruitful.

Take care, therefore, that your willing and not willing may accord with his willing and not willing; do not dare either rashly to anticipate his will in anything, or cunningly to pass it by, or proudly to resist it [Col. 0105D]. Thus prove yourselves true friends, wholly renouncing yourselves, retaining nothing of yourselves in yourselves, and giving yourselves entirely to his hidden impulses [variant: “nods”].

“Give me, Lord, the wisdom that sits beside your throne, that it may be with me and labor with me, that I may know what is acceptable before you at all times” (Wis. 9:4, 10). Grant that I may commit myself wholly to you, rely upon you alone, and securely follow you wherever you go before me. From my Friend may I receive the good will by which you graciously desire to do good in your good pleasure to Zion (Ps. 51:20); and from the Almighty, the strength by which you are also able effectively to accomplish what you graciously desire. Why should I fear to commit myself wholly to you, who will nothing except what is good for me, and who are therefore my friend? And why fear when you are able to grant well every good thing that you will, because you are almighty?

Hold, therefore, Lord, my right hand, and lead me according to your will (Ps. 73:24) [Col. 0106A]. Therefore make known to me the way in which I should walk (Ps. 143:8), and lead me wherever you will—provided only that you lead me to yourself. For where can I fare ill with you, or fare well without you? “Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, if you are with me” (Ps. 23:4). And if I ascend to heaven and my head touches the clouds, in the end I shall perish like a dung heap unless you are with me (Job 20:6). Therefore, whether I am a sinner or righteous, I shall not be without you. For if I sin, I am yours, knowing your greatness; and if I do not sin, I know that I am counted with you (Wis. 15:2) [Col. 0106B].

X. O how zealously you everywhere pursue my salvation! With what concern you attend to me! O how often, when I am tempted, you are at hand lest I consent; when I waver, lest I fall; when I fight, lest I be overcome! O how often you offer a refuge, so that, if I fall, I may rise again from my fall! For what better refuge do I find from you to you, than you yourself? Distrusting myself altogether, and not a little fearing you, I flee from you to you. I flee from you as just, and take refuge in you as merciful, because I need mercy and cannot bear justice. Thus I come to meet you, O unfailing friend, answering love with your love, though at a rank far inferior and according to my measure; and always and everywhere giving myself to your will, and in all things [Col. 0106C].

And in this way, brethren, you ought to meet your friend, the Lord Jesus: crying aloud to him as is fitting, and committing yourselves wholly to his nods. But since much has already been said, let us defer to another sermon what remains to be said on this subject, lest it be treated with less than due dignity if, because of your weariness, we run through it too quickly; or be heard less eagerly if, because of its depth, we linger over it long [variant: longer]. Therefore retain in memory what has been said; put it fruitfully into practice; meeting your Creator by giving him thanks for your very condition. Meet your Teacher by eagerly hearing what he says and diligently striving to fulfil it; your Lord by answering his worthy threats with fear; your King by imitating him in fighting against the world and its prince [Col. 0106D]; your Friend by loving him again with all the marrow of your heart and obeying his will in all things—to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON III. ALSO FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY IN ADVENT OF THE LORD.

On how Christ, the Bridegroom who comes, ought to be met.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. By the Holy Scriptures and by all creatures, humankind is stirred to love its Creator.—2. Mutual love must be recognized and repaid.—3. The Bridegroom, namely Christ the Lord, must be met by the Church’s paranymphs.—4. Why prelates and heads of communities are called paranymphs [Col. 0107A].—5. What their office is.—6. How many turn aside from it.—7. The lamentable license of life and hardness of heart of very many.—8. One ought not to be unprepared for the Lord’s coming.—9. The Paraclete does not come unless Christ departs.—10. Why God withdraws the abundance of inward anointing.—11. Spiritual feasts and their preparation.—12. Diverse dishes and sweetly sounding instruments.—13. How providently God deals with his own, departing and returning.

I. You know, my most beloved brethren, that the whole of Holy Scripture directs its purpose to this end: to stir humankind to love of its Creator. All Scripture proclaims this in words and examples; all creation too cries it aloud in a mighty voice of instruction. All things that spring from the earth say this; all that swim in the waters; all that fly in the air [Col. 0107B]. Everything that exists, from an angel down to a little worm, from the highest hinge, so to speak, of created things down to their lowest base—namely heaven, earth, sea, and all that is in them—never ceases to say it.
