The voice of each is this: “If you love me, O human being, because you see me to be, in some respect and in some measure, good, sweet, or precious, love far more the one who made me, because he is far better and more precious than I.” But the sons of Adam, who with proud eye and insatiable heart (Ps. 100:5), having abandoned the Creator, cling with their whole affection to the creature, do not perceive this health-giving voice for their hearing. God will indeed destroy them, because they commit fornication away from him (Ps. 71:26).

[Col. 0107C] II. But you, beloved, whom the Lord has chosen and received as those near to him, consider how great is he who comes, and meet him with love. He is your Bridegroom; he is your Saviour. There honour his condescension; here embrace your deliverance. He is the Son of God, and he comes to make you heirs of his Father and his own co-heirs. And, in order to do this in some incomprehensible manner, though existing in the form of God and not considering equality with God a thing to be grasped, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being (Phil. 2:6). Who is so blind, who so alien to the light, as not to see that the coming of the Son of God is an act of inestimable love, and that God’s becoming human is likewise an act of incomprehensible humility?

[Col. 0107D] III. But let us now proceed through these four points in careful consideration, and meet him in them with the obedience due to him. We call the Lord Jesus the Bridegroom of the Church; and when they hear that he is coming, the paranymphs ought to hurry to meet him. Why the paranymphs, rather than the Bride herself? Certainly the Bride is not forbidden to meet him, although we exhort the paranymphs to meet him. Let the paranymphs therefore meet the coming Bridegroom, and let the Bride meet him also: they, by applying themselves ever more earnestly to the Bride’s adornment as they hear that the Bridegroom is nearer; she, by showing herself already adorned. Thus, wounding the Bridegroom himself with one of her eyes and with one lock [Col. 0108A] of her neck (Song 4:9), she may deserve to hear: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved; you are altogether beautiful, and there is no spot in you” (ibid., v. 7).

IV. But who are the Bride’s paranymphs? They are the prelates of the holy Church and the guardians of this holy community. Because they diligently attend to the adornment of the Bride of the Lord entrusted to them, they are said to meet the Bridegroom. Yet the Bride herself, insofar as, instructed and admonished by them, she strives always to appear lovely to her Bridegroom, is not unfittingly said to meet him too. For we read of Martha that, when she heard Jesus was coming, she went to meet him. But of Mary it is recorded that she remained sitting at home (John 11:20). Yet she too met him, invited by Martha at his own summons, as is said in what follows [Col. 0108B]: “Martha came and secretly called her sister, saying, ‘The Master is here and calls you’” (ibid., v. 28). And what follows there? “When she heard it, she rose quickly and came to him” (ibid., v. 29).

V. Hear and understand, O paranymphs! Listen, O friends of the Bridegroom—provided that you hear him while standing, and rejoice with joy because of his voice (John 3:29). Hear, I say, what your office ought to be. Run about anxiously as intermediaries between Bridegroom and Bride, asking what he wills and making known what she ought to do. Learn his commands from him and announce to the Bride the works she must fulfil. Labouring in all things, do the work of an evangelist; fulfil your ministry (2 Tim. 4:5). Watch for the Bridegroom’s coming [Col. 0108C] with concern. Meet him as he comes with devotion; proclaim to the Bride that he is approaching, declare that she is called, and urge her to meet her Bridegroom. This work, this diligence, this care belongs to the Bride’s paranymphs.

VI. But alas! Very many who are paranymphs in these days act quite otherwise. In these days perilous times do not merely threaten; they are already present. For those last days of which the Apostle prophesied are here, in which, he said, people would be lovers of themselves, covetous, puffed up, proud (2 Tim. 3:1). Many of our paranymphs are now such as he describes in what follows, seeking their own glory in the Bride rather than the Bridegroom’s. They neither meet the approaching Bridegroom themselves [Col. 0108D], nor invite the Bride to meet him. Adorned and arrayed, but bodily so, they parade in the Bride’s wealth, yet do not care at all how foul and squalid she herself is. When you see them dressed, must you not suppose them soldiers—or rather, what is worse, and worse in proportion as it is more shameful, actors?

They violently exact ecclesiastical estates and possessions, tithes and offerings from the subject peoples; greedily receive what has been exacted; and unlawfully spend what they have received. Yet they rarely speak with them about sins to be avoided or cast away, virtues to be acquired or retained, amendment of conduct, or anything pertaining to the Bride’s adornment. Thus the Bride is made squalid; thus the mud of the streets disfigures her, while her paranymphs neither show by their words [Col. 0109A] how beauty is to be acquired nor demonstrate by their examples how ugliness is to be avoided.

VII. “Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. 9:1). That day and night I may lament not only in words but weep with tears, and bitterly mourn the Bride of the Lord entrusted to such persons: not friends but enemies; not chaste paranymphs but shameless suitors; not vigilant guardians, finally, but unclean prostitutors. But for the moment let us be silent about them. For the word has no place in them (John 8:37). Indeed, as vinegar upon nitre, so it is when we sing songs to them (Prov. 25:20). For they rage against us when we say these things, and truth produces hatred. Thus we are obliged, by keeping silent, to provide for our peace and quiet: both because they do not amend themselves, and because, excusing themselves and chattering malicious words against us, they become worse [Col. 0109B]. For they neither dance when we sing, nor mourn when we lament to them (Matt. 11:17). Add that custom somehow grants them permission to do what they do, their numbers furnish boldness, and shamelessness removes shame. Therefore, hanging up our instruments not upon the cedars of Mount Lebanon but upon the willows of the river of Babylon (Ps. 136:2), let us speak to our own people.

VIII. Therefore, brethren, watch for the coming of your Bridegroom and meet him as he comes. Watch anxiously, lest, before he comes, you be unworthy to have him long [variant: while he comes]; lest, when he comes to be received, you be unprepared. You are unprepared if you do not know when he comes. Has it escaped your mind that blessed is that servant whom his lord, when he comes, finds watching? (Luke 2:36.) To watch is to watch for the Bridegroom’s coming. The Bridegroom also comes, and comes secretly; yet he does not come silently. Am I speaking to those who do not know? Do you not frequently read in the book of your own experience: “At midnight a cry was made: behold, the Bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him” (Matt. 25:6)?

He comes at night, therefore, because he comes secretly; yet he does not come silently, because he comes with a cry. Does he not likewise come to you, while you do not know the time in which he wills to come, yet while your ears are not deaf to his hidden word, whose whispering veins the understanding of the heart furtively searches out (Job 4:12)? Therefore your Bridegroom goes and returns, because in wisdom there is a spirit both stable [Col. 0109D] and mobile: that is, a spirit going and returning. Does he abandon you because he goes? Far from it. “I will not leave you orphans,” he says (John 14:18). And he added: “I go.” But what did he add next? “And I come to you” (ibid.). Indeed, just as he comes for your benefit, so he also goes. “It is expedient for you,” he says, “that I go” (John 16:7). And why is it expedient? He added: “For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you” (ibid.). Therefore he comes that our heart may rejoice, and he goes that he may send us the Paraclete.

IX. But what does he mean when he says: “For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you”? Therefore he comes that our heart may rejoice, and he goes that he may send us the Paraclete. But what does he mean [Col. 0110A] when he says: “For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you”? The Paraclete does not come unless Christ departs, because consolation from the soul’s renewal is not poured in unless the anointing is withdrawn for a time. As you know, *Paraclete* means “Comforter,” while Christ is called “Anointed One.” For the Lord takes away their spirit when he thus plays with them, with whom he is accustomed to alternate these changes; and they fail and return to their dust (Ps. 103:29). But, that that sweetest promise may be fulfilled—“I go and come to you, and your heart shall rejoice”—he sends forth his Spirit, and they are created; and he renews the face of the earth (ibid., v. 30). Therefore it is expedient for us that he too should go.

X. For if he were always present, unable continuously to bear the sublimity of his glorious presence [Col. 0110B], you would succumb. While you supposed that what comes from him came from yourselves, deprived of his gift you would sink downward under your own weight. For in his good will he deals graciously with you, giving strength to your beauty; but he turns his face away from you, and you are troubled (Ps. 29:8).

Your Bridegroom who comes to you is like a certain exceedingly rich and great king. He has with him princes and soldiers and a very large household: namely, right intention, devout will, and that inward Church of holy thoughts which you are accustomed frequently to have within yourselves. But this king comes to lodge, not to remain; to visit you, not to dwell with you. For your poverty cannot suffice long to provide a banquet for so great and such a king [Col. 0110C], especially one who has so great a court with him. Therefore, sparing your poverty and knowing that it is altogether expedient for you that he go, he withdraws himself for a time, lest, if present, he be in any way wearied of, and, if absent, be more eagerly desired. Thus, when his sweet presence is granted again, you may honour it more gloriously in proportion as, when withdrawn, it has been more ardently desired.

If he sees you so disposed, he will come to you again and your heart will rejoice; and, when you have thus gone out to meet him, you will enter with him into the wedding feast. And when he enters to you, he will dine with you, and you with him (Rev. 3:20).

XI. At these inward nuptials, at this mutual supper, at this festive banquet, the bull of stiff-neckedness is sacrificed, and the fatted creatures of sensual pleasure are slaughtered (Matt. [Col. 0110D] 22:4). For likewise in the mind, he who presides over these nuptials, the author of humility, calms swelling pride; and in the flesh, the lover of purity kills wantonness. For “the King sits upon the throne of his judgment and scatters every evil by his gaze” (Prov. 20:8). This is nothing other than the spirit of the Bridegroom resting in a rightly ordered mind and, by his inspiration, emptying it of every sin.

There are also set forth the bread of strength and the wine of contemplation, of which, according to the Psalmist, the former strengthens the human heart (Ps. 103:6), while the latter gladdens it. Honey is sucked from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone (ibid., v. 15), when upon the palate of the mind that wonderful sweetness, flowing from Christ’s miracles before his Passion, is savoured; and when the richness of the Spirit is savoured, who was given when Jesus had been glorified (John 7:39). [Col. 0111A] Nor is butter from the herd lacking there, nor milk from the sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams (Deut. 32:13): that is, the teaching of the exalted and the sobriety of the simple, together with the charity of humble subjects and leading prelates.

Goats likewise are eaten there with the marrow of wheat, and the blood of the grape is drunk most unmixed (ibid., v. 14). For, that we may imitate them, sinners indeed, but repentant ones, are set before us as examples, together with the fair intention of a good resolve and with the suffering of our grape pressed out in the winepress of the cross. This grape has upon its table both the marrow of wheat and the goat, because, eating ashes like bread (Ps. 101:10), it incorporates repentant sinners into itself just as it incorporates the righteous who refrain from sins.

XII. And, to speak briefly and comprise much in a brief discourse [Col. 0111B], however many kinds of contemplation are poured into us in this inward refreshment of the mind through the Spirit’s revelation, so many most savoury dishes are set before you at this great table at which you customarily sit, served by the Bridegroom. There are as many flavours as devotions; and as many sounding instruments as there are marks of virtues. For there first, lest anything that belongs to festive gladness be lacking, resounds the sound of the trumpet: namely, the dread of divine fear, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10).

The psaltery of good action sounds also, and the harp of bodily mortification; the drum of abstinence and the chorus of concord sound. The strings of mutual exhortation are not silent, nor the organs of religious manner of life. Far be it that the sweetly [Col. 0111C] sounding cymbals (Ps. 150) should be silent there: the companies of saints, each esteeming the others above itself and therefore outdoing one another in honour.

XIII. Behold what festive joy, and what joyful festivity, comes to us from the advent of your Bridegroom. For the great multitude which gathers for this feast day—I mean the Church of inward thoughts, since “the remnant of thought shall keep feast for the Lord” (Ps. 75:11)—therefore rejoices with great joy and exults with shouting. Nevertheless, do not rejoice with a private joy in this, that you feast thus and rejoice thus; nor say in your abundance that you shall never be moved (Ps. 29:7). For the Bridegroom will suddenly be taken from you [Col. 0111D], and then you will fast; and you who had no need to mourn while he was present will weep when he is withdrawn (Matt. 9:15).

For suddenly, while you hold him, he will vanish from your eyes; and while you embrace him, he will leap from your hands. Thus he will turn aside and pass on. Yet you ought so to sigh in the absence of him who departs that you may breathe again in hope of his return; for he who departs to remove weariness and self-exaltation will certainly return to bring eager longing and consolation. To him be honour and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ALSO FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY IN ADVENT OF THE LORD.

On humanity’s great misery and the Saviour’s benefit.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The Saviour comes to redeem, the Deliverer to release, the Protector to defend [Col. 0112A].—2. Through the Fall, humankind is subject to punishment, guilt, and temptation.—3. The threefold happiness of unfallen and fallen nature.—4. God came, assuming what he was not and remaining what he was.—5. He drew near and bore the infirmities of our flesh.—6. The sick man, his wounds bound and oil poured in, is placed on the Samaritan’s beast.—7. The Saviour’s threefold benefit.—8. The first is in faith in the Redemption, which we bear in heart, mouth, and forehead.—9. The second is liberation from slavery to sin.—10. The liberty and dignity of the religious state.—11. Both those who had come from afar and those found near owe their condition to the Saviour’s benefit.—12. The third is protection of our weakness in battle.—13. By the benefit of adoption, what Christ is by nature, the human being receives by grace.—14. The likeness of God through imitation in holy conduct.—15. The unjust aspiration of the apostate angel and the just aspiration of one consenting [Col. 0112B] to God’s will.—16. Where the merit of righteousness consists.—17. Christ, insofar as he is human, is to be imitated; insofar as he is God, desired.

Beloved brethren, as I perceive, you patiently endure the lengthy discourse on the coming of the Bridegroom, the delights of the Spirit, and the inward joy of the mind—the joy which the infusion of holy anointing produces in the devout soul. You endure it patiently, I say, because you inwardly feel what you hear outwardly. In you, not only does the ear judge words, but the palate also tastes their flavour.

Yet we must also speak something of the Saviour’s coming and show how we ought to meet him. Your Saviour therefore comes: rejoice in the Lord and exult, you captives, and glory, all you who cry to the Lord in the presence [Col. 0112C] of the oppressor; for he is now sending you a saviour and champion to deliver you (Isa. 19:20). Just as he does not come empty, because he comes full of grace and truth (John 1:14), through whom grace and truth came to be, so neither does he come to be idle. For he comes to redeem, to release, and to defend: to redeem captives, release the bound, and defend the weak. He is a sweet Saviour, a gracious Deliverer, a strong Protector.

The prophet did not pass over these three things (Isa. 19:20), when he declared that a Saviour would be sent by the Lord—not only a Saviour, but also a champion, and for the purpose of delivering. Therefore note redemption in “Saviour,” release in “Deliverer,” and protection in “Champion.” Let the one overtaken in captivity breathe again: the Saviour comes to redeem from the miseries of punishments. Let the one bound in captivity hope: the Deliverer comes to release from the bonds of sins. Let the one who wavers in weakness have confidence: the Protector comes to defend against the enslavements [variant: slavery] of temptations.

II. Behold how mercifully you are dealt with, O human being. Great is the mercy of your God upon you—great, I say, because your misery too is great. Punishments oppressed you: he redeemed you. Guilt had bound you: he released you. Temptations weary you daily, and he protects you without ceasing. These great evils afflict you; these three good gifts of your Lord assist you. So long as you stood in humble peace with God [Col. 0113A], you did not experience these things at all. But abandoning the stability of inward peace, you descended into the uncertainty of mutability, and immediately came into this danger. For who, as holy Job says (Job 9:4), has resisted him and had peace? Therefore, leaving peace, you rushed into failure; and thus you descended from Jerusalem to Jericho.

III. “In peace was his place,” where you possessed the vision of your God, fellowship with angels, and possession of yourself. In the first was blessedness, in the second exaltation, in the third strength. But descending from Jerusalem into Jericho, you exchanged the stability of peace for the failure of mutability: falling from happiness into the misery of punishments; immersed from exaltation into the dregs of guilt; and, falling from strength, broken, shattered, dissolved, and crushed into many fragments of weakness [Col. 0113B].

For you fell among robbers, because demons exercised their dominion over you. And what did they do to you? First they stripped you, second they wounded you, third they left you half-dead (Luke 10:30). First they took away the garment of happiness, clothing you in the shamefulness of captivity; second they removed the height of health, inflicting on you wounds of wickedness; third, leaving you weak, and although they did not annihilate you altogether, they nevertheless greatly weakened the vigour of your strength. For one who is half-dead, although not entirely killed, is nevertheless left wholly weak.

Behold your threefold danger, O human being: the harshness of calamity, the crookedness of wickedness, the frailty of weakness. Into it you fell from the threefold gift of your Creator [Col. 0113C]: from the blessedness of the divine vision, the exaltation of angelic fellowship, and the strength of possessing yourself.

IV. But that Guardian came—for this is the meaning of the name “Samaritan”—he came, I say, and made his journey. For unless he made a journey, he would not come. He came not to where he had not previously been, but became manifest though previously hidden. For he was in the world, and yet was coming into the world. He undertook a journey in order to come, assuming what he was not so that the eternal might become temporal, and so that he who always remains in himself might pass from place to place in the nature he assumed.

Therefore he made his journey and made it beside you, because he assumed the nature of mutability, which he did not possess, and assumed it for your sake [Col. 0113D]. “And seeing him,” it says, “he was moved with compassion; and drawing near” (Luke 10:33). What is the force of this sequence of words? He saw, he had compassion, he drew near. He saw because he chose you for life; he had compassion because he bestowed mercy; he drew near because he conformed himself to your misery, wounded one.

V. Did he not draw near—he who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being? (Phil. 2:7). Add that he even humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, indeed the death of the cross (ibid., v. 8). Read what is in Isaiah: “He himself bore our sicknesses and carried our infirmities. He himself was wounded for our iniquities, bruised for our crimes” (Isa. 53:4). And see whether he did not draw near [Col. 0114A].

How could he have been nearer to you than by delivering you from what you endured? Had he not drawn near, he would not have healed you. For that prophet, powerful in deed and word, who, overcome by the prayers of a miserable mother, descended from the high mountain of heaven and came to the dead man, would neither have raised up the one lying down nor restored the deceased to life unless, bending over him, he conformed himself to him so that his flesh became warm (4 Kings 4:34).

VI. Perhaps one of you says: “You speak well, but only if you discuss matters relevant to your subject.” I shall do so; wait a little. Is it not part of our purpose to show what the Saviour brought with him when he came to us? Whether these things suitably belong to that subject, though you do not now know it, you shall know afterward [Col. 0114B].

Therefore, after drawing near in this way, what did he do? What is written in the Gospel? How do you read it? “He bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine; and placing him upon his own beast, he led him to an inn” (Luke 10:34). Above you had that he was stripped, wounded, and left half-dead. But here the merciful Samaritan bound the stripped man’s wounds, placed him upon a beast, and led him to an inn.

This is nothing other than what the Apostle says: “As through a human being came death, so through a human being comes the resurrection of the dead; and as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:31 [verse citation as printed]). For what is the Samaritan’s beast but Christ’s body? “I saw,” he says, “heaven opened, and behold a white horse” (Rev. 19:11). And shortly afterward: “His name was called [Col. 0114C] the Word of God” (ibid., v. 13).

John here was, as he himself says (ch. 1:9), our brother, a fellow participant in tribulation, kingdom, and patience in Christ Jesus.—“And heaven opened”: I understood that a hidden mystery had been revealed to me. “And behold a white horse”: Christ’s body, free from the blackness of sin; its rider is called the Word of God, that which was in the beginning and was with God. For divinity presides over humanity. This horse belongs to that beast upon which the Samaritan placed the wounded man.

VII. What was then done belongs to that time when the Lord Jesus redeemed humanity through the Passion of his flesh from the calamity of punishments which it had incurred by sinning. He bound the wounds after pouring in oil and wine when, biting through correction and soothing through consolation, he wiped away sins. He led him to the inn when, after strengthening weakness, he bestowed their former strength upon some (*eis nonnullis*) [variant: some former strength upon them (*nonnullam*)], so that, caring for him, he would not permit him to fall into his former lapses [Col. 0114D].

Recognize, O human being, how, falling from the threefold good and rushing into the threefold danger, you now receive, in certain firstfruits, through the threefold benefit of your Saviour, that good from which you had fallen. For though stripped, you are dishonoured; when placed upon the beast, you are honoured. Though you groan at wounds inflicted upon you, you rejoice that your wounds are now bound up. Though left half-dead, you are made weak; when led to the inn, you are honoured. Thus, yes thus, through your Saviour who now comes, you are redeemed from calamity, freed from [Col. 0115A] wickedness, and defended in your weakness. Each of you can recognize these things in himself.

VIII. First, that he redeemed you by the abundant outpouring of his holy blood is not allowed to escape you by the loud voice of that innocent blood itself, crying from the earth more eloquently than Abel’s (Heb. 12:24). For you are inhabitants of that earth which does not cover the blood of our suffering one, and in which its cry finds no place of concealment. This earth too is holy: it does not fail constantly to believe with firm faith the mysteries of its Redeemer’s humanity and especially the marks of his most holy Passion, nor blushes to proclaim them in joyful confession.

You therefore clearly know that he assumed the humility of flesh for our sake [Col. 0115B], endured the ignominy of the cross, and bore the harshness of death. For your faith, which you firmly hold concerning his incarnation, continually presents this to you; so too does the saving banner of the life-giving cross that you bear upon your forehead, and that unique and most effective medicine for our wounds which you daily prepare at the altar, where for our salvation the Son is offered sacramentally to the Father. There, spiritually, God in Christ reconciles the world to himself. It is more than enough to remind you of this.

IX. Nor does the second gift, which pertains to your liberation and by which you received forgiveness of sins, escape you. For it has not slipped from your mind how you once walked in ways that were not good but followed your own impulse [Col. 0115C], went after your lusts, ran against God with neck held high, wandered through the streets of Babylon, were under Pharaoh, were made filthy with mud in the Egypt of sensual pleasure, and were light as the straw of vanity—altogether like wandering sheep (1 Pet. 2:25).

But your Saviour, who is rich in mercy, the shepherd and bishop of your souls, because of the exceeding love with which he loved you (Eph. 2:4), while you were still such persons, had mercy on you. He snatched you from the power of darkness and transferred you into this very good land in which you now dwell. For he sent forth his hand from on high, snatching and delivering you from many waters and from the hand of foreign sons (Ps. 143:7). He also brought you out [Col. 0115D] from the pit of misery and the mire of filth; set your feet upon a rock; and put into your mouth a new song, a hymn to our God (Ps. 39:3).

X. O change wrought by the right hand of the Most High! O God’s hand, beneficent toward you! O his good, pleasing, and perfect will, and the gratuitous grace by which you have been mercifully dealt with: so that you now rule manfully over those vices by which you were once weakly cast down, mortifying by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh, driving out those alien nations and possessing their lands. What it was once hard to forego for even a single day, you now count as nothing to be without for a period of time.

Indeed, to add something more, you would, I think, formerly have chosen death rather than return to certain things in which you once were engaged [Col. 0116A]. Likewise, what you once shuddered to endure for even a very brief hour, you now, where the Spirit’s impulse is, advancing toward it, regard as sport to practise manfully throughout your whole life. These things are exalted, and no less hard than they are new: exalted, I say, because in some manner above nature; new in relation to your old habit; and hard because of the weakness of your flesh.

Your frequent fasts, the continual vigils that you keep, this lowliness in dress which you wear, this harshness in food which you endure, this restraint in speech which you practise, bear witness to this; and we know that their witness is true. You expose, so to speak, all the members of your body to daily martyrdom, not even possessing your own will in your own power [Col. 0116B]. In what have you thus been washed, sanctified, and justified, except in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ? (1 Cor. 6:11). I say these things not to shame you, but to admonish, together with myself, my dearest brethren, so that, considering from how great dangers we have been delivered, we may recognize how great thanks we ought to give our Deliverer.

XI. But because I see here many who, nourished with Samuel in the tabernacle from boyhood (*a puero*) [variant: from childhood (*a pueris*)], did not, as we did, come from afar, we exhort them all the more attentively also to acknowledge themselves no less indebted to their Saviour. For he who preserved them is the same as he who raised us up, justifying us and them in a good but different manner: namely, by recalling us and preserving them.

For unless the Lord had helped them [Col. 0116C], their soul would almost have dwelt in hell. Although it has not crossed the torrent insofar as that future liberty is concerned, their soul has nevertheless crossed it in some respect. But how could their soul have crossed the unbearable water if the Lord had given them as prey to its teeth? Our soul, indeed, has been partly snatched from the snare of hunters; but they did not even encounter the same snare (Ps. 123:7). Yet in all these things their help no less than ours is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth (Col. 1:10 [citation as printed]).

He is that great physician of all: preserving health in some, healing sickness in others. He is our true Saviour, gentle and gracious Jesus, whose innocent blood is of such great worth that through it not only the things on earth but also those in heaven are reconciled. And how are the things in heaven reconciled through that blood, unless it is because he who by his gratuitous grace recalled fallen humanity to its lost peace (Eph. 2:17), by the same gratuitous grace gave the standing angel not to lose it? Therefore, through the grace of our Saviour, both we who were far off and those who were found near have been saved. For it is God’s gift, so that no one, either among us or among them, may glory in this.

XII. The third gift, however, is the grace of protection, by which he guards us in all our weakness. You have it the more clearly before your eyes because you feel it daily—indeed continuously—for you cannot remain standing even for an hour without it [Col. 0117A]. Now, under his care, you have recovered strength from weakness; and, strengthened by him, you have become strong in battle (Heb. 11:34). But this battle, in which you fight so manfully—now against the flesh, now against the world, now against your hidden adversary, who never ceases his raging but goes about without interruption seeking whom he may devour—which of you could endure for even one moment unless he had Christ himself as protector? Behold, that storm-wind comes from the north, bringing with it a great cloud (Ezek. 1:4). How, I ask, could dust, so utterly cast down, stand or hold its ground before even one breath of it [variant: “stand, or hold its ground”], unless he defended it—that one to whom the prince of this world came, yet found nothing of his own in him? (John 14:30.) [Col. 0117B] Therefore you now stand—but in the Lord. And you who, in yourselves, are altogether weak and powerless, can now do all things in him who strengthens you.

XIII. Therefore, O redeemed ones, go out to meet your Redeemer; you who have been freed, your Liberator; you who have been defended, your Protector. Go out, I say, to meet him who comes, giving him devout thanks for redemption from calamity, liberation from perversity, and protection in this your weakness. Go out to meet the Son of God. For he comes to you, and he comes for this purpose: to adopt you as brothers and to receive you as co-heirs. Being from eternity the Father’s only Son, he did not wish to remain alone; he has granted that we should be honored with him by grace with that name by which he is honored by nature. For he is our brother and our flesh (Gen. [Col. 0117C] 37:27). Thus, appearing to Mary in his risen body, he says: “Go, tell my brothers: I ascend to my Father and to your Father” (John 20:17). And holy David, speaking in his person, says: “I will declare your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23). What great dignity it is that God should be our Father and his only Son our brother! And what dignity, do you suppose, shall we receive in the future, who already hold so great and such a pledge in the present? What dignity, except that in the inheritance of our brother—which is also ours—we shall always behold the face of our Father who is in heaven?

He seems to me to have understood nothing other than this who said: “Now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3:2). This he says concerning the pledge which we have received in the present. He adds also concerning the gift which we hope to receive in the future [Col. 0117D]: “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (ibid.). O incorporeal blessedness: to see God—what is especially promised to pure hearts—and to be like him.

XIV. Yet this likeness cannot at all be attained in the future through the divine vision unless a certain likeness to him is first practiced in the present through holy conduct. If you are children of the highest Father, if you are brothers of Christ, strive to be like him. For how can you glory that you are his children or his brothers if you are not like them? As you yourselves know, these three persons—father, son, and brothers—ordinarily possess some mutual likeness, not only in body but also in character [Col. 0118A]. Thus it is written of the good son of a good father: “His father is dead, and yet he is as though not dead, for he has left a son like himself after him” (Ecclus. 30). In a wonderful manner the person even of a dead father lives in his surviving son when the father’s likeness appears in him.

Likewise, the natural heavenly Son is so like his Father that whoever sees him sees his Father also. For he himself is in the Father, and the Father in him (John 14:9). I do not say this because we can be like them in the way that they are like one another; for they are not merely one, but one thing, because one and the same nature and substance belongs to them.

XV. Certainly, one sinned who said: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:15). “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit” (Ps. 35:4), because he had first devised iniquity upon his bed [Col. 0118B]. For he wished to make himself equal, not humbly to imitate. Yet Christ not only makes us like them but even unites us to them—that is, in the agreement of the will—according to the saying: “He who is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Let us be of one will with those with whom we are not consubstantial; then no one will henceforth deny that we are like them. But to dissent from them in will is to be very far from possessing any likeness to them.

Come out, I pray you, from this region of unlikeness, and lay hold of the likeness of your Father, who willingly begot you by the word of his truth (James 1:18). Lay hold also of the likeness of your Brother: be like your Brother. For how are you his brothers if you are not like him? “We shall be like him,” he says, “when he appears” (1 John 3:2). This concerns the likeness that will be in the reward. But, as was said above, if you wish to be like him in reward, be like him in merit. “How,” you ask, “will this happen?” The Son himself says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). Therefore be meek and humble, and in this respect you are like him.

XVI. It is plainly true that we await as Savior our Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, making it conformed to the body of his glory (Phil. 3:20), if first our heart has been made conformed to the heart of his humility and meekness. If you ask what likeness to God is, “turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:15), and you have put on his likeness [Col. 0118D]. For the Psalmist says: “The Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. 91:16). Be upright yourself, that you may do good; and let there be no iniquity in you, that you may avoid evil, and you are like God.

Again the prophet David says: “The Lord is just and loves righteous deeds; his face beholds equity” (Ps. 10:8). Be just in yourself; love justice in your neighbor; let your face behold equity, so that you may strive to be present only for this end and to benefit your neighbor: namely, that you may desire to please God alone. That is, desire both to perform good works and to have your neighbor imitate your conduct, while desiring no one but God alone as the one who praises and rewards your labor. Thus, while you practice holiness in yourself, show concern for your neighbor, and offer God a right intention, you live soberly, justly, and godly in this world (Titus 2:12) [Col. 0119A]. Thereafter, secure in hope, await the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God—being thus restrained toward yourself, ready toward your neighbor, and devoted to God.

XVII. If you do these things diligently, you go out to meet the Son of God—your brother—as he comes. But consider further that he who comes is God and man. Although he is God and man in one person, in that he is man he intercedes for us; in that he is God, he helps us. In that he is man, because in compassion for our misery he is near to us, he in some way feels our danger together with us. But in that he is God, because through the union of our nature assumed in him he is not far from us, he also grants us an effective remedy [Col. 0119B]. In his humanity is what we should imitate; in his divinity, what we should desire.

Nevertheless, he of whom we speak is not one person and another, but one and the same mediator between God and human beings: God and man, our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Tim. 2:5). But because we have already said much, we are compelled to end the sermon now at hand. We cannot linger longer on these points at present, although other matters occur which do not seem fit to be omitted. Therefore you also go out to meet this coming one if you strive to run according to the example set below, so as to endeavor to attain that which is set above, ascending and descending upon the Son of Man. In these ways, then, you ought to go out to meet your coming Bridegroom and Savior, the Son of God, the same God and man, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. ALSO FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD. On the five kinds of visions.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. In the vision of God is the fullness of every good.  
2. Where the good things of the Lord are, and the land of the living.  
3. In the present life we neither truly live nor see what we shall finally obtain in the state of blessedness.  
4. God is seen here differently by those pure of heart and by those impure of heart.  
5. How understanding accompanies vision, and discernment accompanies affection.  
6. The fruitful vision merited by holiness, as Jacob set forth in a type.  
7. What was foreshadowed by God’s appearance to Moses in the bush.  
8. After King Uzziah’s death Isaiah sees the Lord; the conditions for meritorious vision are demonstrated.  
9. Five kinds of vision, the last of which is the sun of the future homeland.  
10. The cloud to be avoided in connection with each vision.  
11. The first is contemplation of creatures, and its cloud.  
12. The second is through divine visitations or images, and its cloud.  
13. The third is that of faith, and its cloud.  
14. The fourth is through spiritual anointing and manifold operation.  
15. The cloud of sluggish affections to be avoided.  
16. The necessity of discernment.

“I look from afar; behold, I see the power of God coming, and a cloud covering the whole earth.” How happy are those who carry a pure heart everywhere! Happy, I say, because they have received from Truth itself the true promise that they shall see God. “Blessed,” he says, “are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” [Col. 0120A] (Matt. 5:8).

O that we might be granted at least faintly—not indeed to taste, but at least to smell—how sweet is that sweetness and how delightful that delightfulness in the vision of God! What short of it can suffice the devout soul? What beyond it ought it to seek? There might perhaps be some sufficiency if something praiseworthy existed apart from it. Nevertheless, something beyond it ought to be sought if anything beyond it either existed or could exist. But now, since those who do not see it possess nothing, while those who see it lack nothing, the soul, impatient before attaining it, does not rest; beyond it, as already at peace, it does not stretch itself forth. What is more desired than life? The vision of God is the life of the soul.

II. “I believe,” says holy David, “that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13). What are we to understand as the good things of the Lord, if not the Lord himself? For the Lord’s good things are not one thing and he himself another, because what he has is what he is [Col. 0120B]. They are expressed in the plural, although number does not apply to him, because of his abundant greatness, which no measure confines, and because of his great multitude, which no number includes. The Prophet declares that “there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. 144:3); that “there is no number to his wisdom” (Ps. 146:5); and that he has “a great multitude of his sweetness, which he has hidden for those who fear him, but revealed to those who hope in him” (Ps. 30:20).

They are called good things rather than pleasant things; sweet rather than precious or beautiful things; rather than fitting or useful things, or anything of that sort. For whatever else may be worthy of approval is included in this word. Therefore the Prophet believed that he would see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, where seeing and living are the same. Why did he not see them here, except because this is the land of the dying? Who can see here, when he does not even possess the means of living? “I live,” he says, “and you shall live” (John 14:29). Therefore it is yet to come that we shall live—and so perfectly that we shall see also. “We shall live,” says holy Hosea, “in the sight of the Lord, and we shall know” (Hos. 6:3). Behold life; behold vision also. But both are future, not present.

III. “We all die,” says a certain woman, “and are poured out upon the earth like waters which do not return” (2 Sam. 14:14) [Col. 0120D]. The descent of waters upon the earth is an image of the human condition, which never remains fixed. For one who in a sense does not even possess being—how can that one possess vision, when by nature being precedes seeing? Of these waters it is plainly said that they do not return. Therefore we die because we flow away upon the earth like waters which do not return. “He remembered,” says the Prophet, “that they are flesh: a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77:39).

Rightly does the holy patriarch dwell by the well whose name is “of the Seeing and Living One” (Gen. 17:14), so that meanwhile the perfect person may abide at the innermost depth of this life-giving vision and seeing life of which we speak—like an eagle raised at the Lord’s command, which places its nest on high (Job 39:27). Is it not, as we said already in the preceding sermon, a great blessedness to be like God in the kingdom? And to see him is to be like him. “We shall be like him,” he says [Col. 0121A], “because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). This, then, is the reason why we shall be like him: because we shall see him as he is. Is not God light, immutability, and eternity? By seeing light, we too shall be luminous; by seeing immutability, we too shall become immutable; by seeing the eternal One, we too shall be enduring. The same must be understood also of other things of this kind. But this is the greatest, most precious, sweetest, and most delightful thing: to see God, which those who are pure in heart have in promise.

IV. There is another vision also, in which God is seen even in the present, though not in himself; yet he who is seen is himself. He is seen by those whom he judges worthy of this grace, and these too must be pure in heart [Col. 0121B]. For not even this vision can be attained except by pure hearts. It is that vision which is bestowed on the faithful soul through images displayed to the eyes, whether of the mind or of the body, or also through the anointing which “teaches concerning all things” (1 John 2:27); through it the soul sees either swiftly by understanding or with secure certainty by faith.

“Blessed,” he says, “are the eyes which see what you see” (Luke 10:23). For they saw the man with the eyes of flesh in such a way that, in that same man, they did not fail to see God with the eyes of faith, which works through love. Yet a damnable blindness oppressed others, even though they had eyes: encountering darkness in daylight and groping at noon as though in night, they struck against the very light. Of them it is said: “Now they have seen and hated” (John 15:24). They saw the weakness at which they might mock, not the power which they should honor, for they were ungodly. “Let the ungodly person be taken away,” Scripture says, “lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 35:3). They saw the disgrace of the assumed nature, not the grace of the one assuming it. Finally, they saw him “in whom there was no appearance for them”; his face was, as it were, rejected and despised [Col. 0121C]. Therefore he was not reckoned anything by them. But they did not see him as holy David saw him: “beautiful in form beyond the children of men” (Ps. 44:3); much less did they see that which angels desire to look into (1 Pet. 1:12).

V. This is the vision of faith, by which God is seen as absent and present: present indeed through faith, absent through direct sight. When it is honored by some visitation and sweetened by inward anointing, it possesses a full and perfect brightness—provided, that is, that right understanding accompanies the vision and discerning affection accompanies the anointing [variants: “but when,” or “indeed”]. For in the person to whom this vision is granted, visitation awakens wonder and anointing kindles affection.

Anointing is never without affection; but visitation is often without understanding. For to anoint is to move the affections; to visit is not similarly to enlighten—just as it is not the same thing to show an object to be seen and to provide the eye by which it is seen. Pharaoh was once visited in a dream, and Nebuchadnezzar also was visited. But what dreams were in these visitations for those two kings, prophecy was for the holy Joseph and Daniel. For the vision, not understood, made the former merely dreamers; understanding made the latter prophets [Col. 0122A]. This vision of divine visitation is sometimes given to the reprobate without understanding, but to the elect with abundant understanding. Yet it is bestowed fruitfully only when preceding holiness has merited it.

VI. Jacob saw a certain ladder (Gen. 28:11). But first, as you read, he left his own land; after sunset he came to a certain place; he took one of the stones lying there, placed it beneath his head, and slept in that place. In the same way, leave your own land, in which you have been nourished by vices and sins. When the heat of temptation by which you were burned has subsided, go to the place of holy conduct: among the many saints, who, if you count them, will be multiplied beyond the sand , choose one from among the many—namely, the Holy of holies—place him beneath your mind through imitation, and in that same conduct, by persevering repose and tranquil perseverance, devote yourself to the complete mortification of all visible things [Col. 0122B]. If the Lord so guides you by straight paths, he will show you the kingdom of God, giving you the knowledge of holy things, so that you may both see sublime realities and understand what you see.

VII. Moses too saw a vision (Exod. 3:3): in one and the same thing, fire but no burning—a truly great vision, as he himself confesses. But we read that he first fed sheep, led them into the interior of the desert, and came to the mountain of God. So you also: nourish within yourself innocent and simple thoughts; by despising visible things, lead them into the inmost recesses of secrecy through the purity of a clarified mind, insofar as this is divinely granted you; and by the flight of good desire bring them to the very height of God [Col. 0122C].

Then you will be worthy to see fire burning in the bush but not consuming the bush, so that you may know that in the one and same person of Christ, the assumption of the lower nature did not diminish the higher nature, nor did the glorification of the higher consume the lower nature. Believe that it is so; but do not presume at all to investigate why or for what advantage it is so. Lest, if you say with Moses, “I will go and see this great vision, why the bush is not burned” (ibid.), the Lord, seeing that you are proceeding to see, should say to you: “Do not come near here,” lest, as an investigator of majesty, you be overwhelmed by glory.

VIII. We read of Isaiah that he saw the Lord seated upon a throne high and lifted up; but this was not until after the death [variant: “before the death”] of King Uzziah. For thus you read: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated upon a throne high and lifted up” (Isa. 6:1) [Col. 0122D]. Let the presumption of pride die in you, and let the leprosy of lust also die; then the presumptuous and leprous king is dead. Then, pure in body and humble in mind, you will be worthy to behold the Lord present in the understanding of rational and angelic creatures preserved from falling, and of human nature raised from its fall by the mercy of the Redeemer.

Therefore Jacob did not see the ladder in his own land; Moses did not see in Egypt the fire burning but not consuming in the bush; nor did Isaiah see the Lord seated upon a throne high and lifted up except after King Uzziah had died [Col. 0123A]. Let holiness merit the vision of divine manifestation, so that it may exist; let understanding attain it, so that it may be fruitful; let faith govern it, so that it may not be rash; let anointing sweeten it, so that it may be savory. For the future face-to-face vision will provide the recompense, so that each of these visions may be rewarded.

IX. There is still another vision, which ought to be first in order and which is offered generally to everyone: namely, the contemplation of visible creatures. For it is readily available to everyone who uses reason to perceive “the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20). Yet without the preceding visions which we have briefly mentioned, this vision is altogether unfruitful.

Behold, we have set before you a fivefold vision [Col. 0123B]. Understand its mystery—or rather, experience its fruit. The first is in contemplating creatures; the second, in mystical visitation; the third, in knowledge by faith; the fourth, in inward anointing; the fifth, in the vision of God himself as he is. The first invites to knowledge; the second clarifies; the third guides; the fourth kindles; the fifth fully blesses. The first four are like luminous stars in the night of this present life; the fifth, shining with eternal light and without any defect, is the sun of the future homeland.

For who there will need to perceive the invisible things of God by understanding them through things made, when things now invisible will be visible? Who there will need to see God through dreams or night visions, “in a mirror, in an enigma,” when we shall all see face to face? (1 Cor. 13:12.) Who there will walk by faith, when all see by direct sight? Nor then shall we have the Spirit’s anointing as now; there we shall possess him and not let him go, because that eternal charity will so pour itself into us that no satiety will ever turn us away from it.

X. But since they are stars, I warn you to avoid diligently every cloud that can in any way darken them. Let the cloud which is the frivolity of pleasure-seeking sensuality be diligently driven from the light of the first star. From the light of the second, let the cloud which is the deception of a diabolical phantom be driven away. From the light of the third, the cloud which is the presumption of rash investigation [Col. 0123D]. From the light of the fourth, the cloud which is the excess of deceptive indiscretion. This is the fourfold light in which we see both light and cloud—not a cloud covering merely some part of the earth, but one covering the whole earth in many people.

The power of God is light. In this fourfold light we see the light of power as day, but the darkness of cloud as night. You, therefore, who apply your mind to the purity of contemplation, looking from afar, see the power of God coming. Look and see: that is, contemplate and understand. But look from afar; contemplate deeply. For what is deep and inward is far away. Do not those things seem far away which were at the beginning of the world and which will be at its end—those already done, these still to be done?

XI. Therefore, if with reverent inquiry you investigate the admirable and astonishing works of God; if, in the contemplation of your mind, you direct your eye from the heights of heaven to the depths of earth, from the highest summit of all creatures down to, so to speak, their lowest base; if with a pure eye you discern the things that merely are [variant: “if not only the things that are”], and those which are and live, feel, and discern, and marvel at God as the creator, disposer, and provident ruler of things so great and so excellent—does not the power of God come to you, when in his visible works, so admirable, you stand astonished before his invisible power? [Col. 0124A]

But beware in this consideration of the cloud that is accustomed to cover the whole earth. For the natural person, who cannot at all receive the things of God because they are foolishness to him and he cannot understand them (1 Cor. 2:14), nevertheless has the created things continually before his eyes. He looks at God’s works, but with the pleasure-seeking eye of the flesh, not with the contemplative gaze of the mind. He uses creatures proudly and lustfully to the injury of the Creator and therefore to the increase of his own condemnation. Is not the earth covered with cloud in such a person, since the frivolity of pleasure-seeking sensuality wholly darkens his mind inwardly through unlawful desire and defiles his flesh outwardly through wicked action? [Col. 0124B]

Since this is so, consider that where the righteous person is raised up into divine wonder, there the ungodly person is cast down into his own lust; and where the power of God comes to the one, there a cloud covers the whole earth in the other. For the righteous person, perceiving the invisible things of God through things made (Rom. 1:20), reverently and praisefully marvels at his eternal power and divinity. But the other sees what has been made only to seek in it the fulfillment of his own greed, endeavoring through it either to fulfill the exaltation of his mind or the corruption of his flesh [Col. 0124C].

XII. After this, look from afar in the second kind of contemplation, which we briefly touched on above, and see the power of God coming. You do this, surely, when you soundly understand and rightly interpret what comes to you, whether secretly through divine visitations or openly through certain images of things, so that you marvel at God’s power in them as well.

Did not the power of God come to Jacob through the ladder that he saw, when in fear he said: “Truly, the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it. How terrible is this place! This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:17)? Did not God’s power come to Joseph’s father and brothers through the dreams which Joseph himself saw, when his brothers said: “Will you be our king, and shall we be subject to your rule?” (Gen. 37:8), and his father said: “What does this dream which you have seen mean? Shall I, your mother, and your brothers bow down to you upon the earth?” (ibid., 10) [Col. 0124D]?

Did not God’s power come to that same Joseph in Pharaoh’s dreams (Gen. 41:1), since in those dream-visions he fully understood what God would afterward accomplish mightily? What shall we say about Daniel? When he heard the king’s dreams, did he not see the power of God coming in the statue fashioned from diverse metals (Dan. 2:45), in the stone cut from the mountain without hands, and in the tree that filled the whole earth? For in these dreams he saw the works of God’s power that would afterward be mightily fulfilled [Col. 0125A].

The chief of the apostles also saw new things, heard commands to be carried out, spoke true things, and in all these saw the power of God. He saw a certain vessel, like a great sheet, descending from heaven to earth by its four corners, containing every kind of creeping thing and four-footed animal. Invited to kill and eat, he refused, saying that he had never eaten anything common or unclean; but he heard: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts 10:15). Later, discerning in the Spirit that those earthly animals—by which I mean Cornelius and his close friends—were to be admitted into the vessel of faith, he said concerning the vision he had seen: “Truly I have found that God is no respecter of persons. But in every nation, the one who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (ibid., 34). And below: “God has shown me that I should call no human being common or unclean” (ibid., 28).

But here every prudent person must keep careful watch, because here Satan especially transforms himself into an angel of light, lest the cloud cover the whole of his earth and he suppose that he sees the power of God coming [Col. 0125B]. For many have been deceived by the seduction of diabolical phantoms and have thought themselves honored by divine visitation. Thus cloud covered their whole earth, because the gloom of delusive fantasy darkened their minds. Therefore, beloved, do not attend to the deceits of dreams, lest you be deceived. For, as Scripture says, “dreams and vain illusions have caused many to err, and those hoping in them have fallen away” (Ecclus. 34:7). And another Scripture says: “You shall not practice divination, nor observe dreams” (Lev. 19:26). Do not receive, in place of the brightness of God’s power, the darkness of cloud.

XIII. But the coming power of God is especially accustomed to be seen with the eyes of faith. For what other eye sees the Son descend through an ignominious death [variant: “descend into the pit”], and the Son of resurrection ascend? By what eye other than that of faith is the reality of Christ’s body and blood seen under the appearance of bread and wine? Likewise in the other sacraments: when the outward veil that is seen is one thing, while the reality of the thing believed to be there is another, undoubtedly it is God’s power which is seen as coming there [Col. 0125D].

But here too it is no less necessary to investigate, expose once investigated, and avoid once exposed the murky brightness of the dark enemy—which is a true cloud—lest, presuming to be wiser than we ought to be, we attempt to examine by human reason things which can be apprehended by faith alone. For if a beast touches the mountain, Exodus commands that it be stoned (Exod. 19:12); and what we are unable to eat of the most holy flesh of the lamb, we are commanded to reserve for fire (Exod. 12:10). Some, acting otherwise, investigated the majesty of God’s power with too great irreverence; overwhelmed by glory, they rushed from the cloud into darkness. For, refusing humbly to reverence the secrets of faith, they were blinded by God’s just judgment and fell into the darkness of error [Col. 0126A].

XIV. Next, we must see that the anointing which teaches concerning all things gives us especially to see the power of God coming. For the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father sends in the Son’s name, teaches us and brings to our remembrance whatever that same Son says to us (John 14:26). He teaches us all truth; he also announces to us things to come. He not only enlightens us toward knowledge, but kindles us toward affection.

In diverse ways he forms diverse affections within us. At one time he sets before the eyes of our mind the sins we have already committed; stirring our hearts to repentance, he wounds us with the deepest sorrow. At another time he shows us how much weakness we bear about us both in body and mind; destroying all pride within us, he humbles us in his sight [Col. 0126B]. At times he shows how insignificant all temporal things are, and, despising before our mind’s eyes all that passes here, he raises us vigorously to contempt for them. Sometimes he teaches us how terrible the Lord is over the children of men, declaring that his hidden judgments are greatly to be feared (Ps. 65:5), and shakes us with most powerful fear. Often he presents before the eyes of our consideration the dreadful punishments of hell; depicting their enormity in the mind through varied and horrible forms, he deters us with intense terror.

At times he also impresses upon our minds the festivals of the heavenly homeland and the joys of inward brightness through the breathing of his love; painting in the heart, with most choice forms, both their eternal blessedness and their blessed eternity, he kindles us strongly to longing and desire for them [Col. 0126C]. Sometimes too he stirs us with all our desires to ascend through devout conduct to the summit of perfection and to look upon the examples of the saints who have gone before. Thus not only cords but also old rags may draw Jeremiah up from the pit (Jer. 28:6); and, as Ezekiel is commanded, measuring the structure of the temple shown to us (Ezek. 45:10), we may be confounded and ashamed of all that we have done.

XV. Do you not see the power of God coming in all these things? Yet here too you must beware of the cloud covering the earth: indiscretion, which deceives the soul. For we have very often seen many people gravely deceived in the affections which we have now briefly mentioned. Because they did not know the mean of discernment, they limped away from their paths and later discovered that what they had thought a virtue was a grave sin. In that through which they thought they could reach the ascent of holiness, they were, by a reversal, cast down into a great ruin of perversity [Col. 0126D]. Thus, while they supposed themselves to see the power of God coming, they lamented—even if only late—that their whole earth had been covered with cloud, grieving that they had walked in a way which seemed right to them, “but its end leads to death” (Prov. 14:12).

From these words it is therefore clear that in every spiritual undertaking to which we apply ourselves, we should so practice virtues that we strive with all our strength to avoid the vices contrary to them, lest, if we proceed carelessly along the path of virtues and turn aside from it, we fall into the pit of vices [Col. 0127A].

XVI. Therefore, whether anything is suggested to us in contemplating creatures, in divine visitation, in the belief of faith, or in inward anointing, however plausible it may seem, it must first be examined by our careful investigation and only then, after thorough examination, be admitted. Hence afterward [variant: “after this”], in exhortation, we say [Note: [Col. 0127D] In the ecclesiastical Office.]: “All you earthborn, and sons of men, both rich and poor together, go out to meet him” (Ps. 48:3); and we add in prayer as follows: “You who rule Israel, give heed; you who lead Joseph like a sheep; you who sit above the cherubim, tell us whether you yourself are he” (Ps. 79:2) [Col. 0127B].

After this follows the petitionary utterance by which we pray: “Stir up, Lord, your power, and come, that you may save us—you who are to reign over the people Israel.” Since the prayer concerns the two verses that follow: in the first we pray that he may tell us whether he himself is the one; in the second, that he may come to save us, he who is to reign over his people through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. ALSO FOR THE FIRST SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD. On the caution to be exercised in spiritual visions, and on the mystery of Christ’s advent.

[Col. 0127C]

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. Earth-born men pertain to the first kind of contemplation.  
2. Sons of men pertain to the second, of which there are three degrees.  
3. The rich pertain to the third.  
4. The poor pertain to the fourth.  
5. A notable encomium of charity.  
6. What it is for Israel to be ruled, Joseph to be led like a sheep, and God to sit above the cherubim.  
7. The active and contemplative alike must be trained in the school of love.  
8. It is fitting that the coming Saviour should first be recognized.  
9. What remedy God immediately provided for humanity after the Fall.  
10. Punishment had made humanity weak; guilt had made it blind.  
11. The Saviour who arrived only at the end nevertheless came to its aid at once.  
12. His coming in the words and deeds of the prophets and in diverse sacraments.  
13. Knowledge of the Redeemer was less complete under the law of nature than under the written law or among the prophets.  
14. A fitting superscription for the three periods. [Col. 0127D]  
15. God is lovable in the saints, gracious in the elect, and incomprehensible in himself.  
16. How the prophets knew the mysteries of redemption.  
17. Humanity, conquered through a tree, became victorious through a tree.

I. In the preceding sermon we said that there are four kinds of spiritual contemplation: the first is the consideration of created things; the second, divine visitation; the third, knowledge through faith; the fourth, inward anointing. These are the four who are instructed to go forth to meet him who comes: “Earth-born men, sons of men, rich and poor” (Ps. 48:3). [Note: [Col. 0128D] From the First Responsory of the First Nocturn, First Sunday of Advent.]

The earth-born seem to belong to the first kind of contemplation. Their particular task is to meditate upon the knowledge of the invisible things of God through the consideration of visible things. This kind of contemplation is, as it were, the first step for those wishing to ascend to contemplation. Yet only earth-born men need it, who are not inappropriately called born of earth in this respect: they behold nothing except the visible works of God. The dwellers in heaven do not need it, for they behold God face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).

But let these earth-born men go out to meet him and say: “Make known to us whether you are he himself” (Ps. 79:1). For these observers especially need instruction, so that they may know how the purity of clarified consideration raises one to wonder. But since the foulness of pleasure-loving sensuality flows over into lust, let them beware lest, while supposing that they receive the King of Israel, they receive the king of Babylon instead. Thus, while wishing to attain the divine praise in pure [Col. 0128B] vision, they may be drawn away from that good and enticed toward evil by their own pleasure [variant: will] (Jas. 1:14), rush into the confusion of vices, and, leaving off being nourished in saffron garments, embrace dung (Lam. 4:5).

II. Sons of men pertain to the second kind of contemplation. Here we understand “sons of men” as imitators of the perfect. For there are men who are blameworthy, men who are frail, and men who are rational.

Of the first the Apostle says: “When there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not men?” (1 Cor. 3:3). That is: while through envy you are jealous of one another and through anger offend one another, you rightly show yourselves blameworthy.

Of the second the Psalmist says: “Let the nations know that they are men” (Ps. 9:21). That is: let them understand how weak and frail they are.

Of the third the same Psalmist says: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 35:7). That is: you will call to spiritual salvation not only those endowed with the highest rationality, but also those formed by humble simplicity.

It is likewise written of such people in the book of Job: “He will look upon men and say: ‘I have sinned’” (Job 33:27). When he sees others persevering by the reasoning power of their minds against the pleasures of sin, he too laments that he has weakly lain subject to the dominion of sin.

Such sons of men, namely imitators of the perfect, whom the Lord judges not unworthy of his visitation, should likewise go out to meet him and say, “Make known to us whether you are he himself,” lest, being in some way deceived, they judge the illusion of a diabolical phantom to be the honour of divine visitation.

III. By “rich” we mean those abundant in faith. For the Lord chose those who are rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which God promised to those who love him (Jas. 2:5). They too must go out to meet him and say, “Make known to us,” so that he may grant them the rule by which they should rightly proceed. Otherwise, those who can stand at the height of belief by holding a simple faith may, through rash inquiry, fall into the blasphemy of error.

IV. The poor are the humble. It is upon them that the Spirit of truth gladly pours the grace of his anointing, so that “the valleys may abound in grain” (Isa. 64:14), and, as Solomon says, he may give [Col. 0129A] grace to the meek (Prov. 3:34). “For upon whom shall the Spirit of the Lord rest, unless upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at his words?” (Isa. 66:1).

Yet these too should not omit to go out to meet him and ask him to make himself known to them, so that, adorned with discernment of spirits, they may clearly recognize what the Spirit of truth pours in for salvation and, likewise, what the seducing spirit suggests for deception. But we shall attain the knowledge of these hidden and secret matters not only by inquiry but also by prayer. Often the devout knocker finds what the rash investigator does not deserve to discover.

Therefore we must not merely go out to meet him, but must also break forth into this cry and say: “Give heed, you who rule Israel; you who lead Joseph like a sheep; you who sit above the cherubim: make known to us whether you are he himself” (Ps. 79:2). [Note: [Col. 0129D] From the ecclesiastical Office, First Sunday of Advent.]

V. You know, brethren, that charity holds the primacy among all virtues. If charity spares, its gentleness is not lax; and if charity corrects, its strictness is not harsh. If, while it raises you up, you are exalted in contemplation, you will not go astray, because you are beside yourself for God (2 Cor. 5:13). If, while it moderates you, you descend to action, you will not be thrown headlong, because you are sober-minded for us.

For this charity of which we speak is a ladder: its lower part rests upon earth, but its summit touches heaven. The Lord himself is supported upon it (Gen. 28:12 ff.), ready to reward not only those ascending [Col. 0129C] but also those descending—provided only that they take care to ascend and descend upon the Son of Man (John 1:51).

Thus Israel signifies the vision of divine contemplation; Joseph, the increase of good action; and cherubim, the perfection of love, because *cherubim* is said to mean “fullness of knowledge.” And, according to Paul’s testimony, “love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13:10).

Israel is ruled because, especially in contemplation, we need to be guided by the Lord lest we wander. Many have been illumined by the vision of divine contemplation; but because, owing to their sins, they did not have God as guide and disposer in that vision, they were struck back by the immensity of the light shining above them, upon which they rashly fixed their gaze without a guide [variant: guide], and so fell into the darkness of misty error.

Joseph is led like a sheep because he goes from strength to strength: simple in active life, like a sheep going from pasture to pasture. As a sheep grows fat upon many pastures, so the excellent worker does not cease to apply himself to holy actions. But because it belongs to motherly charity to order how holy men should be beside themselves for God in contemplation and sober-minded in good works, after Israel is ruled and Joseph led, the Lord is also said to sit above the cherubim. Thus, in the repose of twofold love, they may fully learn both when they should set action aside for a time and devote themselves to contemplation because of the sweetness of God, and when they should withdraw from contemplation and apply themselves to action because of their neighbour’s need.

VII. Therefore, “You who rule Israel, give heed”: that is, you order contemplatives lest they wander. “You who lead Joseph like a sheep”: that is, you advance simple active persons from one action to another lest they grow lukewarm. “You who sit above the cherubim”: that is, you train both active and contemplative persons in the school of love, lest the former fall into error by rash inquiry or the latter into lukewarmness through slothful neglect.

“Make known to us whether you are he himself,” so that, illumined by the light of clarity, we may know how we ought to contemplate and how we ought to act. And, inflamed by the ardour of that same clarity, may we know how we should long for you through the desire of love and may deserve to attain you through the exercise [Col. 0130B] of labour.

What is said afterward in the following verse—“Show yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh” [Note: [Col. 0130D] From the ecclesiastical Office, as above]—signifies a complete forgetting of all visible things, which can be acquired only through perfect love. Therefore, after going out to meet him and asking about himself; after praying that he would tell us whether he is the one; now, made certain concerning him, let us pray that he may come to save us, saying: “Stir up your power, O Lord, and come, that you may save us.”

VIII. Did not holy Joshua observe this order? Seeing the angel, he asked, “Are you ours or our adversaries’?” (Josh. 5:13 ff.). Once he recognized who he was, he showed himself ready and prepared to obey: “What does my Lord say to his servant?”

Likewise, the first of the Apostles wished to come to the Lord upon the sea; but first he desired to be taught whether it was he: “Lord,” he said, “if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters” (Matt. 14:28).

He stirs up his power when he determines to save us; for if he has determined to save us, we shall immediately be delivered. He comes when he bestows upon us the grace of salvation. He saves when, granting perseverance in salvation, he wholly and perfectly removes from us the disease of captivity itself.

IX. There is another meaning in these words, less subtle indeed but more common, which we shall now briefly run through, since the length of this discourse demands its end.

You know that, when humanity had fallen into guilt and thus been cast down into punishment, the cunning devil—that changeable enemy who first held humanity by fraud and afterward by force—was not satisfied with having overthrown it while it stood, unless he also exercised the dominion of his tyranny over it when fallen. Thus, so miserably deceived and so grievously bound in the chains both of guilt and punishment, humanity could in no way escape the yoke of eternal condemnation unless he who alone was able came to its aid by his free grace.

God, therefore, foreseeing the grace of humanity’s salvation, also provided the manner of redemption. He appointed human salvation in the man Christ, so that, as the Apostle says, “Since death came through one man, the resurrection of the dead should also come through a man” (1 Cor. 15:21). And, to designate by their names both our captor and our liberator, he says: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive” (ibid., v. 22).

But because, immediately after humanity had sinned, it began, from the very beginning of the world, to suffer in its body the punishment of mortality and in its soul the sickness of guilty iniquity, a physician was sent at once, even then, to heal it. Sent, I say—not in his own person, but in his remedies: namely, in diverse kinds of sacraments appointed for humanity’s spiritual healing. Through every age of the world he went about doing good and healing all oppressed by the devil, because God was with him (Acts 10:38); and he placed within the bosom of saving grace all who had been ordained to eternal life (Acts 13:48).

X. To wretched and pitiable humanity, made weak by the punishment of infirmity and blind by the guilt of ignorance, came the mighty wisdom and wise power of God, so that, being wise, he might illumine its ignorance and, being mighty, strengthen its weakness.

He came, I say—and he came from the beginning, though he arrived at the end—“leaping upon the mountains” of the patriarchs and “bounding over the hills” of the prophets, as the Bride says, until, clothing himself with mercy and truth, he became like a gazelle and a young stag. He stood indeed behind our wall, concealing under the veil of our weakness the strength of his righteousness; yet he looked through the windows of the divine works which he performed as man, and gazed through the lattices of the saving words which he spoke (Song 2:8 ff.).

Thus, seeing the works which the Father gave him to accomplish, works which bear witness concerning him (John 5:36), we may say to him: “We know that you have come from God as a teacher. For no one can perform these signs which you do unless God is with him” (John 3:2). And, likewise hearing his words, which are spirit and life, may we too break forth in this cry: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks” (John 7:46), because “he whom God has sent speaks the words of God.”
