Therefore, we affirm that he came from the time when we know that he came to our aid. We say also that he arrived at the end when he appeared visibly in that form in which he especially accomplished our salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. 73:12).

XI. Since he assisted sick humanity from the beginning of its sickness through sacramental remedies, offerings and sacrifices, and diverse commands and precepts—both in the figures of the patriarchs and in the sayings of the prophets—we do not improperly say that from that time he himself came.

For just as people commonly say of a king that he has come when his coming is announced by his soldiers who go before him, even though he himself may perhaps come a long time afterward, so also our great King, the Lord Christ, in the patriarchs and prophets who went before him and announced his coming to the world, in some manner came himself.

Do we not read in the Apocalypse that it is said of the Lamb: “The Lamb slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. 13:8)? How was he slain from the foundation of the world? Because from the foundation of the world there were those for whom he was slain at the end of the world. So too, in some manner he came from the foundation of the world, because at no time were those lacking for whom he came at the end of the world; and his coming benefited them before it was present, though it could in no way have benefited them unless it would at some time be present.

By that same coming of his—still future in itself—they were saved at the beginning of the world; by it we, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, are saved now that it has passed (1 Cor. 10:11). For both those who went before and those who followed after him cried, “Hosanna” (John 12:13), so that one and the same person might be the Saviour of those who preceded him, though he was yet to come, and of those who followed him.

XII. Therefore look from afar and see the power of God coming: that is, contemplate deeply and understand Christ our Lord, the power of the Father, approaching for the redemption of humankind in the oracles of the patriarchs and sayings of the prophets, and in the sacraments of both the natural and the written law.

See also the cloud covering the whole earth: that dark enemy, I mean the devil, ever more and more darkening the reprobate, who, forsaking heavenly things and loving earthly things without order, themselves become earth through ignorance [variant: “and the rest”; variant: “having been darkened”]. For as the power of God came in his elect from the world’s beginning in the manner mentioned above, so the devil’s cloud covered the entire earth among the reprobate. As we clearly recognize the coming of the Son of God in holy people, so we see the darkness of the crafty enemy in the ungodly.

Let us therefore look from afar and contemplate Abel’s innocence, Noah’s obedience, the good modesty of Shem and Japheth, Abraham’s faith, Isaac’s purity, Jacob’s endurance, Joseph’s chastity, Moses’ gentleness, Aaron’s holiness, the zeal exercised by Phinehas, Joshua’s courage, Samuel’s simplicity, and David’s humility.

Let us also admire the diverse kinds of sacraments instituted partly under the law of nature and partly under the written law. Let us likewise admire the deeds of the patriarchs and the sayings of the prophets. Let us read all the things written concerning Christ in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms. Then no one will be able to say that we do not see the power of God coming.

Let us look upon it from afar; and let us see the many nations under heaven, from the beginning of the world wrapped in diabolical darkness, existing without God in this world, led away to mute idols, and perishing—having abandoned, indeed wholly failed to know, heavenly things and embracing earthly things with their whole affections. Let us behold the cloud covering the whole earth.

XIII. But the power of our God, which they saw coming from afar, was less known the farther away it was. Under the law of nature it was known only to very few what redemption was to be granted to humankind. Under the law, however, humanity came to know sin through the law; but because “the law brought no one to perfection” (Heb. 7:6), perceiving that no law had been given which could justify, humanity began anxiously to seek its redemption.

Although many at that time knew that the Saviour would come to deliver humanity, only a few knew what person was to come for this saving work—whether a human being or an angel. But later, in the times of the prophets, when God spoke to the fathers in many portions and in many ways through the prophets (Heb. 1:1), both the person of the Redeemer and the manner of redemption became known to many: namely, that the Son of God would come in the flesh and in that same flesh would die for humanity.

Those who in that time were illumined by the light of this radiance so as to know such a great and such a Redeemer were not merely longing inwardly for his swift coming; they sought it with frequent and devout prayers, as you read everywhere in the books of the prophets. Thus one says: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come” (Isa. 64:17). The Bride likewise says in the Song of Songs: “Who will give you to me as my brother, nursing at my mother’s breasts, so that I may find you outside?” (Song 8:1). She wished to find him outside, so that he who lay hidden within in divinity might appear visibly outside in humanity. Nor, I suppose, is it hidden from your diligence how the Psalmist likewise calls for the coming of this Redeemer.

XIV. These, then, are the three periods: the law of nature, the time of Scripture, and the time of the prophets. In them the power of God sent beforehand sacraments, commands, precepts, and many oracles for humanity’s deliverance; and the power of God itself in some manner came in those periods.

The following three verses seem properly to refer to these times. Those who, in the time of the natural law, were content with natural knowledge were like earth-born men. Those endowed with human reason were like sons of men. Those raised by subtle perception were like the rich; those formed by simplicity were like the poor. By observing and performing the sacraments then instituted, they went out to meet the coming power of God and received it.

But those who lived under the law, knew beforehand that the Redeemer would come, yet did not know his person—whether he would be a human being or an angel—claimed this utterance for themselves, as it were, and said: “Give heed, you who rule Israel; you who lead Joseph like a sheep; you who sit above the cherubim: make known to us whether you are he himself” (Ps. 79:2). That is to say: You who show yourself to us through the law as one who is to come, tell us also through the prophets whether you are the one who is to come, or whether we should await another (Matt. 11:3).

You who rule the angels seeing you face to face; who also advance holy people, through whom you daily increase the number of the elect whom you purpose to save, from strength to strength, as a good shepherd leads sheep from pasture to pasture, so that they too may someday, with the true Israelites, see you, the God of gods, in Zion (Ps. 83:8). You who, being wholly incomprehensible in yourself, surpass the knowledge of angels and of human beings; who, “ascending above the cherubim and flying upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 103:3), exceed both the perception of those blessed spirits and the understanding of faithful souls.

XV. These words suggest what God is in the elect angels, what he is in holy human beings, and what he is in himself. By his inward governance, preserving angels from falling and always keeping them in the blessed and beatifying vision of himself, he is lovable in them.

As for human beings whom, according to his purpose, he calls saints, whom he foreknows and predestines to be conformed to the image of his Son, making all things work together for their good (Rom. 8:28), whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world so that they might be holy and blameless before him in love (Eph. 1:4): while he cleanses them through pardon and adorns them through righteousness, ordering them in a wonderful and merciful way, recalling them from evils to goods and advancing them from goods to better things, he is in every respect sweet and gracious in them, and abundant in mercy.

But in himself, because that peace surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4:7), because there is no number to his wisdom, and because there is no end to his greatness, he is incomprehensible and beyond estimation.

XVI. Those, however, who lived in the times of the prophets and understood from the sayings of the evangelizing prophets both the person of the Redeemer and the manner of redemption, prayed with all their desires that the Redeemer might come. Taking this utterance for themselves, they said: “Stir up your power, O Lord, and come, that you may save us, you who are to reign among the people of Israel” (Ps. 79:3).

Stir up your power by showing mercy; come by assuming flesh; save by dying on the cross. “Stir up your power, O Lord,” so that you may “rejoice like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6), showing yourself eager and strong in the work of our redemption. Come, so that you may appear visibly in the form of a human being, yet without losing the form of God, but retaining it; laying your hand upon both, and reproving both, since a mediator is not mediator of one alone (Job 9:33). Thus, as man, you may make satisfaction for humanity; and, as God, unite humanity to God, reconciling the guilty and appeasing the offended.

XVII. Finally, in order that these things may be so, die upon the tree, so that your innocent blood may atone for the sin committed upon a tree. Thus, as all die in Adam, so all may be made alive in Christ (1 Cor. 15:22).

Yes, yes, O Lord: you who are to reign in Israel—whether in that people which now believes in you absent through faith, or in that people which contemplates you present by sight—stir up your power by rising up and by having mercy on Zion, for “the time to have mercy upon her has now come” (Ps. 101:14). And come, emptying yourself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in outward appearance as a man (Phil. 2:7); save us, so that, with you dying for our sins, now justified in your blood, we may be saved from wrath through you, who, with the Father and the Spirit, are God, blessed for ever. Amen.

## Sermon VII. Second Sunday in Advent

On the faith of the holy Church and the calling of the Synagogue to faith.

[Col. 0135A]

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. Christ revealed himself to the Church from among the Gentiles.  
2. Christ and the Church are prefigured by Isaac and Rebekah.  
3. Christ’s love for the Church is greater than his love for the Synagogue.  
4. This is foreshadowed in the queen of Sheba and the city of the righteous, that is, Jerusalem.  
5. The adverse sense of the vineyard signifies the Synagogue, sloth, and hypocrisy.  
6. The proper sense of the vineyard signifies Holy Scripture, right faith, and imitation of Christ.  
7. The mountains of Babylon are unbelieving Jews, evil spirits, and proud people.  
8. The mountains of Jerusalem signify the loftiness of holiness, teaching, and contemplation.  
9. The various conditions of the Church are expressed through hills, valleys, and plains.  
10. The Church’s joy over Gentiles converted to faith. [Col. 0135B]  
11. The rejection and great envy of the Jews.  
12. They will be converted near the end.  
13. An apostrophe to the Jews to be converted.  
14. Their conversion prefigured in Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0135] From the First Responsory of the Third Nocturn, Second Sunday of Advent.]

“Jerusalem, you shall plant a vineyard upon your mountains, and you shall rejoice, because the day of the Lord will come. Arise, Zion; turn to your God. Rejoice and be glad, Jacob, because your Saviour will come from among the Gentiles.”

These prophetic words are deep and pregnant, and they require an attentive hearer. Therefore that gracious Spirit of wisdom must be invoked, so that he who inspired their first utterance may grant now that they be rightly understood, both by us who are to preach and by you who are to hear.

It is prophesied that Jerusalem will plant a vineyard upon its mountains and rejoice because the day of the Lord will come. Zion is instructed to rise and turn to its God. Jacob is told to rejoice and be glad; and the cause of its joy is not left unstated: “Your Saviour,” it says, “will come from among the Gentiles.”

Each of these points invites us to investigate the depth of this great mystery; and we shall not be deprived of the fruit of discovery if we are diligent in seeking. Therefore, if at present something deeper is not clear to you, I think that, in its allegorical sense, these sacred words concern the faith of the Church and the knowledge of truth by which its first and greatest leaders were illumined. For the Son of God, appearing in the flesh—who truly, according to Paul’s statement, is our peace, making both one and reconciling by his blood the things in heaven and the things on earth (Col. 1:20)—revealed himself to the Church from among the Gentiles, in order that, having been revealed, he might be seen, and, having been seen, loved.

II. He is our true Isaac, bringing us a joy which no one takes from us. When he went out into the field to meditate, the day having already declined (Gen. 24:63)—that is, at the end of the ages—he came forth from the Father and came into the world, in order to work the works and do the will of him who sent him (John 4:34); his law was his meditation.

Thus Rebekah came, representing the Church from among the Gentiles. Taught through the servant of our Father—that is, through the order of preachers—who the son of her Lord was who had appeared, and seeing him who is our peace, she descended from the height of pride to the depths of humility and from the strength of unbelief to the rule of faith. Thus Jerusalem, whose name means “vision of peace,” received its name from the reality. Taking up the veil of good work, she covered herself, knowing that blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered (Ps. 31:1).

This, then, is that spiritual Rebekah who, once she saw Isaac, descended and covered herself with a cloak (Gen. 24:66). For once the Church from among the Gentiles recognized Christ by faith, she humbled herself and adorned herself with the covering of good works. Bringing her into the tent of his mother, he took her as his bride, so that many might come from East and West and recline with the faithful fathers in the kingdom of God, while the children of the kingdom themselves, because Sarah has died, are cast into outer darkness (Matt. 8:11).

III. He loved her so greatly that he tempered the grief arising from his mother’s death. Even if Isaiah grieves that the stones have fallen, he has this consolation: that he builds with squared stones and replaces the cut-down sycamores with cedars. This was surely done when carnal Jews had fallen into unbelief, and steadfast and perfect men from among the Gentiles were called to build this Jerusalem of which we speak; and contemplative persons arose in place of the foolish persons who had been in the Synagogue.

IV. She is that queen who, hearing the fame of our Peaceful One—for that, they say, is the meaning of the name Solomon—did not fail to hasten to him from the farthest ends of the earth (1 Kgs. 10:1). She now stands at his right hand in golden raiment, clothed about with variety (Ps. 44:10), while diverse orders of faithful people serve one Lord in the unity and adornment of one faith and baptism [variant: the adornment of unity].

This is the holy Church: both Isaac’s wife and the queen coming to Solomon. This also is the city of the righteous, the faithful city, which, seeing its peace, received it into its people in order to be called and to be Jerusalem. She did not fail to plant a vineyard: first upon her mountains, then upon the hills, in the plains, and finally in the valleys. Thus the ointment upon the head might descend not merely upon the beard but flow even to the hem of the garment (Ps. 132:2), so that none might hide himself from its heat (Ps. 18:7).

This means nothing other than that the holy Church first bestowed the grace of faith upon its highest-ranking people and then transmitted it through them to those below.

V. But it should be known that there is a vineyard which Jerusalem does not at all plant upon her mountains. There is, as it were, the vineyard of the Synagogue, of which it is said in the Song of Songs: “I have not kept my vineyard” (Song 1:5), because the Lord rejected the Synagogue because of unbelief. There is also the vineyard which is the life of any negligent person, as Solomon says in Proverbs: “I passed by the vineyard of a foolish man” (Prov. 24:30). That is: I considered the life of a negligent person. There is also the vineyard of hypocrisy, of which it is said in Job: “His cluster shall be injured like a vineyard in its first flowering” (Job 15:33), because the hypocrite’s action is corrupted in its first appearance through the favour of human praise.

But holy Church plants none of these vineyards upon her mountains, because she entrusts neither the bitterness of the Synagogue, nor the lukewarmness of negligence, nor the duplicity of hypocrisy to her eminent persons.

VI. But there is a vineyard which Jerusalem diligently plants: namely, the vineyard which is Christ. Of it the Song of Songs says: “Let us see whether the vineyard has blossomed” (Song 6:12); that is, let churchly men examine whether Christ has blossomed in people through faith.

She also plants the vineyard of faith, concerning which you read in Genesis that it was said of Judah that he would bind his colt to the vine (Gen. 49:11), because Christ would bind to himself the people of the Gentiles with the bonds of faith.

She also plants the vineyard of Holy Scripture, of which you have it written in Job that he gathered the vintage of the vineyard of the man whom they had violently oppressed (Job 24:6), because heretics claim for themselves the Scripture of the Catholic man whom they have afflicted.

This, then, is the threefold vineyard which Jerusalem plants upon her mountains: a kind of threefold emblem of grace, which the holy Church entrusts to her eminent people—Holy Scripture, right faith, and imitation of Christ—so that preachers may hear Holy Scripture for instruction, receive faith for strengthening, and imitate Christ for perfection.

VII. It is therefore prophesied of this Jerusalem of ours that it will plant a vineyard upon its mountains. And fittingly “upon its mountains,” for there are certain mountains to which the prophet speaks in the book of Kings: “Mountains of Gilboa,” he says, “let neither dew nor rain come upon you” (2 Sam. 1:21), because the proud minds of unbelieving Jews, who killed Christ, do not receive the preaching of truth.

There are mountains which are proud people, concerning whom you have in Job that Behemoth brings forth grass (Job 40:15), because all proud people feed the devil through self-exaltation. There are also mountains which are evil spirits, as you read in Habakkuk: “The mountains of the age were broken” (Hab. 3:6), because through Christ the evil spirits who are the rulers of the world were destroyed.

Thus unbelieving Jews, evil spirits, and proud people are indeed mountains, but mountains of Babylon, not mountains of Jerusalem.

VIII. There are other mountains: namely, holy angels. Of these the Psalmist says: “Before the mountains were made”—that is, before the angels were created—“you are God” (Ps. 89:2). The holy prophets too are mountains, as you read: “Its foundations”—undoubtedly those of the Church—“are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1), because the holy Church itself is founded upon the prophets.

Are not the Apostles also mountains, toward whom the Psalmist says that he lifted up his eyes (Ps. 120:1), because he raised his inward gaze to the teaching of the Apostles? The lofty commandments are likewise mountains, as David says: “The high mountains are for the deer” (Ps. 103:18), because sublime commandments belong to the perfect.

The two Testaments also are mountains, as the Psalmist says: “Waters shall pass between the midst of the mountains” (ibid., v. 3), because streams of teaching run in the agreement of the two Testaments. Preachers likewise are mountains because, according to the Psalmist’s statement, “the mountains receive peace for the people” (Ps. 71:3). This means only that preachers announce repentance to those subject to them.

If we also understand inward contemplations by mountains, no one may justly rebuke us, because we read in Job concerning the wild ass that “it surveys the mountains of its pasture” (Job 39:8). For every perfect person considers the heights of inward contemplations, in which the devout soul finds pasture and refreshment.

The Gentile peoples called to faith are also mountains, as we read in the book of Maccabees: “The sun shone upon the golden shields, and the mountains gleamed from them” (1 Macc. 6:9). For knowledge shone and the Spirit’s love burned in the holy Apostles; and through them the chosen peoples from among the Gentiles were made radiant.

IX. Those whom we have just briefly mentioned are the mountains of Jerusalem, upon which she plants a vineyard: when the apostles themselves are granted the complete imitation of Christ, to whom He says, “You who have followed me shall sit upon twelve thrones” (Matt. 19:28); when preachers are given the grace of teaching, to whom “the Lord gives the word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power” (Ps. 67:12); when the foremost men from among the Gentiles are given [Col. 0138C] the strength of faith—a kind of firm stability such as belongs to the squared stones mentioned above, which were taken up for building when the bricks fell (Isa. 9:10). From these mountains the merit of holiness has flowed down to those below. For when the people received this threefold peace, they received through these intermediaries the gift of grace: not only those who ascend the slope of counsels through righteousness and are hills, but also those who rise from the depths of sins through repentance and are valleys, and those who walk upon the plain of commandments and are fields.

See how these mountains, in the strength of faith, are temperate toward themselves; in the teaching of the word, just toward their neighbors; and in the imitation of Christ, devout toward God—so that they may confidently await likewise “the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God” (Titus 2:13). Thus may be fulfilled what is afterward prophesied of our Jerusalem: namely, that the trees will rejoice, for the day of the Lord will come. And I think this is what the Psalmist says: “All the trees of the forest shall rejoice before the Lord, because He comes” (Ps. 25:12). The trees of the forest are the Gentiles, who, while they had not yet been cultivated by faith, were altogether wild.

X. But if you wish to know how these trees of the forest rejoiced before the Lord because He came, and thus to know in turn how your mother Jerusalem rejoiced because the day of the Lord came, read the book of the Acts of the Apostles. There, because the Jews rejected the word of God, judging themselves unworthy of eternal life, the apostles turned [Col. 0139A] to the Gentiles (Acts 15:40). What is written there? “When the Gentiles heard this,” it says, “they rejoiced and glorified the word of God; and all who had been appointed to life believed” (ibid., 48).

This, therefore, is the rejoicing of our mother Jerusalem. After she planted a vineyard on her mountains, she saw the day of the Lord approaching: that is, she saw the radiance of divine brightness flash over her children, so that, when the Lord had risen over her and His glory was seen in her, the Gentiles might walk in this light and kings in this splendor. Nor is it surprising that Jerusalem rejoices when she sees the day of the Lord coming; for, seeing her sons come from afar and her daughters rise at her side, she overflowed, wondered, and her heart was enlarged, because the multitude of the sea was turned to her and the might of the Gentiles [Col. 0139B] came to her (Isa. 60:4).

XI. But when such and so great joy is taking place in the Church, why do you, O Synagogue, waste away in envy? Why do you, O elder son, who have remained so long in the field, when you hear that your younger brother—after squandering all his substance—has been received by his father, clothed in the robe of his first innocence, adorned on his hand with the ring of faith and with good works, instructed in good examples as though protected by shoes upon his feet, and that the fattened calf has also been slain and the whole household of angels is feasting (Luke 15:23 ff.)—why do you refuse to enter? For they have joy over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons—namely, Jews who do not attain the perfection of the number one hundred [Col. 0139C] and do not need repentance (ibid., 7). You have always been with your father until your brother’s return and have never transgressed His command.

Why, I say, when you hear the harmony of one faith and the chorus of love through which faith works, do you disdain to enter at the end? Do you not know that you ought to feast and rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found? Do you suppose, O Esau, that your father has only one blessing (Gen. 27:38), so that, because he has already blessed Jacob, he cannot bless you also?

XII. Read in Paul that “a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel may be saved” (Rom. 11:25). This means nothing else than that you remain outside for so long, [Col. 0139D] until, at the prompting of mother grace, your younger brother obtains the paternal blessing; so that you too, coming late and weeping with a loud cry, must hear—your father so ordaining—that you are to serve your brother, until the time comes when you shall shake his yoke from your neck. Thus may be fulfilled what Isaiah prophesied: “Though the number of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of it shall be saved” (Isa. 10:22).

Nor need there be any fear concerning the twelve-year-old daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, that the Lord Jesus will not raise her up (Mark 5:41), for a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years had prepared salvation for herself when, among the pressing crowd, she alone touched Him (Matt. 9:20). And therefore Jerusalem has now planted a vineyard on her mountains, and has rejoiced because the day has come.

[Col. 0140A]

XIII. Arise, O Zion, and turn to your God. First arise, and afterward turn. Arise, you who until now lay prostrate; turn, you who were turned away. You lay through negligence; you were turned away through blasphemy. Arise, therefore, O Zion, who signifies the Synagogue. Arise and turn, so that you may love Him whom you neglected and believe in Him whom you denied.

Likewise rejoice and be glad, O Jacob, because from among the Gentiles your Savior will come. Who is this Savior, except the Lord Jesus, who saves His people from their sins? (Matt. 1:21). And where is He now? Is He not among the Gentiles? For Pharaoh’s daughter took Moses from the little basket: that is, Jesus, leaving the harshness of the Jews, came to the Church from among the Gentiles. In her faith and manner of life He now remains [Col. 0140B] even when grown great—He who, as a little child, was brought up among His own parents, that is, the Jews.

But the time will come when the Jews too “will cry to the Lord because of the oppressor” (Isa. 19:20); and He will send them this Moses of whom we speak, a Savior and defender, to deliver them. Then your Savior also will come to you, O Jacob, from among the Gentiles. For the Lord called His Son out of Egypt (Matt. 2:15), and Jesus will return from Egypt with His parents to the land of Israel, so that our grieving naked one, who came naked from his mother’s womb, may return there naked.

XIV. And when will this be? When you begin, O Jacob, to hunger for the bread that came down from heaven, [Col. 0140C] which you now ruinously despise. Hearing that grain is being sold in Egypt, you will send your sons there; and the true Joseph will reveal himself to them (Gen. 42:1 ff.), whom in our language we call the Savior of the world. He will lay upon them an embassy to you and say: “Go and bring him to me, that he may live.”

It is wholly true, O Jacob—true indeed—that you can by no means live unless you come to Joseph. Then ambassadors will come to you from Egypt and say: “Joseph your son is alive, and he himself rules over the whole land of Egypt” (Gen. 45:26 ff.), and they will recount to you all his glory. When you hear this, your spirit will revive, so that, once you have ears to hear, you may receive spiritual life in faith; awakening from the heavy sleep of unbelief, [Col. 0140D] you will at last break forth in these words and say: “I will go and see him before I die” (ibid., 28).

Thanks be to God that you now understand your life to lie in the vision of Joseph. For you agree with him, when he commands that you be brought to this end, that you may live; while you say that you wish to see him before you die. Therefore, brothers, we have expounded to the praise of God these prophetic words concerning the holy and spiritual joy that the Church from among the Gentiles now has in her children, and also concerning the return of the Jews to faith that will occur at the end. He is blessed unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN ADVENT OF THE LORD

### On the Threefold State of Holy Church

[Col. 0141A]

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The threefold state of the Church, explained through Zion, Jacob, and Jerusalem.  
2. Why she was rightly called Zion at her beginning.  
3. Why in her progress she was called Jacob because of persecutions.  
4. Her persecutors became her defenders, and her enemies citizens.  
5. As Jacob took Esau’s birthright, so she subjected the princes of the Gentiles to the obedience of faith.  
6. In the third state the Church is called Jerusalem because peace was given her.  
7. Exercises to be practiced in peace.  
8. A fourth state in the day of the Lord and the rejoicing of His brightness.  
9. This same diversity of states is signified by Arcturus, the Orions, the Hyades, and the inner regions of the south.  
10. From the sending of the Holy Spirit, martyrs and then teachers flourished.  
11. There remain the inner regions of the south: that is, the bosom of the heavenly homeland.

I. If any of you, dearly beloved, wishes to understand the words set above as referring only to the Church called from among the Gentiles to faith, he may say that she is called by these different names—Zion, Jacob, and Jerusalem—according to her different states, although she herself is one throughout the whole world. For the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “My dove, my perfect one, is one” (Song 6:8), though the Psalmist declares her “surrounded with variety” (Ps. 44:12).

There seem to me to be three states of the Church corresponding to these three names. The first is that in which, turned to her God, she contemplates the person of her Redeemer and the manner of her redemption [alternative reading: Latin *speculatur*, “contemplates,” for *speculans*, “contemplating”]. For this also seems to be the meaning of the name Zion. The second is that in which, exercised and afflicted by many storms of anxieties, she at last supplants and conquers her adversaries in Him who conquers the world. Thus, on account of this state, the name Jacob, interpreted “supplanter,” may fittingly be applied to her. The third is that in which, having been pacified and with past disturbances laid to rest, she is restored to tranquillity and can freely devote herself to planting spiritual vineyards and rejoice at this day of the Lord, which has shone upon her with so great a brightness. For, as you know, Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.”

II. At first, then, our mother Zion, seeing through a glass darkly, saw that the one and same person in Christ was God and man; she saw the Son and thereby also her Father; she likewise saw the works which the Father gave Him to complete, which also bear witness to Him (John 5:36). At once she was ashamed of her prostration, ashamed of her turning away; and, rising from the pit of negligence and turning herself also from the blasphemy of unbelief, she began to believe in Him whom she had formerly not known. She began to love Him whom she had first despised, so that in her might be that faith of which the Apostle speaks, “faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6).

Thus, rising and turning to her God by these two ways, she arrived at Zion: namely, by rightly believing in Him and ardently loving Him, lest, if she traveled by one without the other, she should be unable fully to reach Him. For Paul rightly understood: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 12:6). And, as his fellow apostle James perceived: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:26). This offering was devoutly made by that little flock to whom it pleased the Father to give the kingdom, who left all things and followed Christ (Luke 12:32). It was also what the primitive Church in Jerusalem diligently sought to offer devoutly; of them you read that “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32). And again: “All who believed were together and had all things in common” (Acts 2:49).

III. But this faith and love were immediately disturbed by many afflictions and harassed by many persecutions. For the time came of which that great Prophet, mighty in deed and word, prophesied that they would have tribulation in the world (John 16:33); and He described it in words of this sort: “They will lay hands upon you and persecute you; they will deliver you over in their councils, scourge you in their synagogues, lead you before kings and governors for my sake, and you will be hated by all men because of my name” (Matt. 10:17).

Yet they endured all these things with joy. Such great tribulations could neither bend them from the straight path of faith nor cool them from the ardor of love. Do you not read of the apostles that “they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41)? Again, you know that when the Jews assembled to make them put the name of Jesus beneath the bushel of silence, they steadfastly answered: “We cannot but speak of what we have heard and seen” (Acts 4:20).

You also have concerning the primitive Church that “a great persecution arose against the Church which was at Jerusalem, and they were scattered through the regions of Samaria” (Acts 8:1). And what do you read next? “Therefore those who had been scattered went about preaching the word” (ibid., 4). How worthily shall we admire that vessel of election? You know of whom I speak: the Lord showed him how much he had to suffer for His name (Acts 9:16). Behold, he is beaten with rods, crushed by stones, submerged in the sea; he suffers dangers from robbers, dangers from his own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, and, what was more grievous to him, dangers from false brethren [Col. 0142D] (2 Cor. 2:26). He was burdened beyond measure and beyond his strength, so that he even grew weary of life (2 Cor. 1:8). Yet amid all these things the word of God is not bound; nor does he cease to fill up what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings in his flesh, for His body, which is the Church (Col. 1:24).

IV. Thus amid all these stormy tempests that fire which the Lord sent from on high into their bones (Lam. 1:13) could not grow cold, nor could the faith by which He instructed them fail. Rather, love increased and faith was continually strengthened more and more. Does not that strong athlete, of whom we have spoken above, say that he has not only fought the contest and finished the course, but also kept the faith? (2 Tim. 4:7). And what does he say concerning love? “Who,” he says, [Col. 0143A] “shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword?” (Rom. 8:35).

But, in a negative answer to these things, he adds [alternative reading: “what follows,” or “namely: But among,” etc.]: “We know that in all these things we overcome through Him who loved us” (ibid., 37). And he adds: “For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers nor virtues, neither things present nor things to come, neither height nor depth, nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God” (ibid., 38).

Therefore the friends of God could be killed in that time, but could not be bent; they could be slain, but not conquered. Indeed, they conquered by dying; by falling, they triumphed. And not only this: they converted unbelievers themselves to faith; [Col. 0143B] they changed their adversaries into companions, enemies into fellow citizens, persecutors into preachers, so that “the tongue of the dogs might belong to their master from among enemies” (Ps. 67:24). Those who had at first opposed and attacked the faith now, converted, barked for the faith, joyfully dying for Christ, whom they had previously persecuted everywhere to the extent of their power.

In this time of persecution, holy Church truly supplanted her enemies. She supplanted enemies, I say, not so that they might remain enemies longer, but so that, ceasing to be enemies, they might henceforth be partners, in order that the name Jacob might be fittingly applied to her from the fact itself. And since the Church was shrewd, she captured them by guile—as a deceiver, indeed, yet truthful.

V. Her name was rightly called Jacob in this state because she took Esau’s birthright (Gen. [Col. 0143C] 27:36): while she not only overcame through patience the very first and highest rulers of affairs—I mean the Roman emperors—but also converted them to faith through miracles. Thus the rhinoceros serves the Lord, through her strength and skill, and remains at His manger, bound with a strap for ploughing; breaking up the clods of the valleys behind Him (Job 39:9–10), it yields Him seed and gathers His threshing-floor, so that the Lord Himself may have confidence in its great strength and entrust His labors to it.

Thus the Gentiles, who did not pursue—indeed, who persecuted—righteousness, attained righteousness, namely the righteousness that is from faith (Rom. 9:30). Christ now enters among them, goes out among them, and speaks about [Col. 0143D] the kingdom of God. And the whole world has been enrolled (Luke 2:1), while the Gospel is preached to every creature, and all go to make their profession, each to his own city (ibid., 3).

How, do you suppose, does mother Church now rejoice and exult? In her first state she was called Zion; now, claiming from the fact itself the name Jacob, she sees her Savior dwelling among the Gentiles and coming from among the Gentiles. For, when the highest princes of the world have been subjected beneath the yoke of faith and their necks bowed to the reproach of the cross and the reproach of the Crucified, throughout the lands of the world swords are beaten into ploughshares and spears into pruning-hooks; nation no longer raises sword against nation, nor are they trained any longer for war (Isa. 2:4), all running together into the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God (Eph. [Col. 0144A] 4:13).

What remains now except that, since the tranquillity of peace has been granted her, she should ascend from the name Jacob, in which her laborious struggle was expressed, to that name bearing the badge of peace—Jerusalem?

VI. Therefore, she who is Zion in conversion and Jacob in tribulation is now Jerusalem in possession of peace: contemplating the person of her Redeemer and the manner of her redemption, and fully turning herself to God in the election of the apostles; toiling in laborious struggle and winning to faith those who struggled against her; seeing and acquiring peace amid persecution through the faith of many Christians; and especially because a multitude of earthly kings and princes has been converted to her.

But because peace has been given you, O Church, will you indulge in idleness? Surely he is unworthy of peace who, in time of peace, ceases from the work of righteousness. Especially since these two—peace and righteousness—are joined together by so close a covenant that the Psalmist says: “Righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84:11). He had first said: “Mercy and truth have met one another”; and all this was well said. For mercy without truth is an excessively soft remission, and truth without mercy an excessively harsh severity. Likewise, see that peace without righteousness is an idle condition, while righteousness without peace is a frenzied movement.

VII. Therefore you may not languish in idleness, O purified Church—especially since Scripture says that idleness is an enemy of the soul. What, then, will you do? You will plant [Col. 0144C] a vineyard on your mountains. For you can more freely plant the vineyard, cultivate what has been planted, manure what has been cultivated, prune what has been manured—that is, instruct the assembly of believers in lofty teachings, correct it once instructed, humble it once corrected, cleanse it once humbled—in proportion as the storms of persecution have been calmed, as though certain tempests of rain and wind and cloudy cold had been driven away, and a serene and altogether pleasant day has dawned.

It is the day of the Lord: a day of rejoicing, not pain; of peace, not disturbance. Thus the cultivators and laborers of Jerusalem plant a vineyard on the mountains because the preachers and teachers of the Church unfold Holy Scripture into profound meanings and expound it in lofty discourses.

[Col. 0144D]

VIII. And after this, what remains for Jerusalem except to rejoice in the day of the Lord, so that she may go from peace to peace? From the peace which the Lord leaves to the peace which He gives (John 14:27), so that for her there may be “month after month and Sabbath after Sabbath” (Isa. 66:23). Thus she who now, while planting a vineyard on the mountains, sees through a glass darkly, may then, when the day of the Lord’s brightness has shone forth, see face to face (1 Cor. 13:12). She who now knows in part may then know as she herself has been known; and after planting the vineyard on the mountains may come rejoicing on the day of the Lord.

Behold the fourfold emblem of holy Church. First, seeing her Redeemer and her redemption with spiritual eyes, she rises and turns herself to her God. Second, by gaining her adversaries, she beneficially supplants them into faith. Third, now freed from laborious struggle and restored to peace, she plants a vineyard on the mountains, while expounding Holy Scripture in lofty words. Fourth, she rejoices in the day of the Lord, while delighting in the brightness of the blessed and beatifying vision.

IX. See whether blessed Job does not proceed in this same order when speaking of the different state of the Church, where he says that God made first Arcturus, second the Orions, third the Hyades, and fourth the inner regions of the south (Job 9:9). For on these words blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0145D] Book IX of the *Morals*, chapter 9] said no less elegantly than profoundly:

> The Lord made Arcturus when He founded the Church, radiant with the light of the sevenfold Spirit, in heavenly conduct. Having made Arcturus, He made the Orions [Col. 0145B] when, with the Church’s faith strengthened against the storm of the world, He sent forth the martyrs. When these had been sent forth, He also brought forth the Hyades, because, once the martyrs had grown strong against adversities and had themselves already been taken away, with the winter of unbelief also restrained and the tempest of persecution removed, and with the tranquillity of peace appearing like the gentle climate of a smiling spring, He bestowed the teaching of spiritual masters to water the dryness of human hearts. After all these things He made the inner regions of the south, because He opened to us those most secret bosoms of the heavenly homeland, which are filled by the heat of the Holy Spirit.

X. Thus, when Arcturus was made, Zion was illumined as it were with the light of the sevenfold Spirit, so that, ardently loving God, [Col. 0145C] she might rise; and, rightly believing in Him, might turn herself to Him. When the Orions were made, the martyrs went before in the Church; and when, through both their patience and the working of their miracles, the enemies of the faith had been beneficially supplanted and faith made known, the Savior Himself might come from among the Gentiles against the house that raged—just as Gideon’s enemies fled not only at the sound of the trumpets, but also because of the breaking of the jars and the flashing of the lamps (Judg. 7:19).

Likewise, when the Hyades were made, the Church, now pacified—and thus rightly given the name Jerusalem—might plant a vineyard on the mountains: that is, expound Holy Scripture in the profound discourses of teachers.

XI. It remains now for the inner regions of the south to be made, so that [Col. 0145D] Jerusalem may rejoice because the day of the Lord comes. It is very fitting that, as Zion rises and turns herself to her God, holy Church ardently loves the Lord and rightly believes in Him; that Jacob rejoices and exults because, while she beneficially supplants her adversaries through the holy martyrs, winning them to faith, her Savior comes from among the Gentiles; and that Jerusalem plants a vineyard on her mountains because holy teachers profoundly expound Holy Scripture within her. But this is all the more beautiful in her because it is happier: she rejoices and dances in the brightness of the heavenly homeland because the day of the Lord is now at hand.

Likewise it is very remarkable, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0146D] Book IX of the *Morals*, chapter 9], “that the Lord established Arcturus when the Church was made firm; that He sent the Orions when the martyrs were strengthened against adversities; that He supplied the Hyades when the teachers were filled in tranquillity. But after these things it is most wonderful that He prepared for us the bosom of the heavenly homeland, as it were the inner regions of the south.”

Let these allegorical remarks suffice for you. Whatever may occur according to the moral sense, we shall show you in another sermon; nor shall we shrink from graciously making known to you whatever that Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect donation (Jas. 1:17), may deign to send you through us. By His gift it is that we can either perceive anything acutely or express it elegantly, for our benefit, for your edification, and for the praise and glory of His name—He who is God blessed above all things for ever. [Col. 0146B] Amen.

## SERMON IX. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN ADVENT OF THE LORD

### On the Three Things Pertaining to the Fear of God and the Three Pertaining to His Love

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. Sin turns one away from the highest good and casts one down into the depths.  
2. God sets before the sinner mercy and judgment: that is, promises and threats.  
3. The threefold distinction of sin, which is the death of the soul, to be treated by the spiritual physician.  
4. Heavenly delights have no flavor for a palate corrupted by earthly pleasures.  
5. First, the sinner must be given knowledge of himself, of the evil of sin, of the brevity of life, and of the world’s transience.  
6. Next, the horror of hell must be set before him.  
7. Finally, he must be soothed with promises.  
8. Fear must be moderated by love.  
9. The fountain of divine mercy is abundant and inexhaustible.  
10. [Col. 0146C] Once converted, a person must subject flesh to spirit and not turn aside because of the mouths of those who speak wickedly.  
11. The remedy for a clamorous tongue is the examples of the saints.  
12. Hope of reward must be impressed.

I. Because the allegorical sense detained us for some time in the preceding sermon, we have until now postponed what was to be said morally, so that you might come together with greater eagerness to hear, refreshed as you have been by an interval of rest. It is therefore incumbent upon us, with the help of the Holy Spirit, without whom we can do nothing, to show what it means, according to the tropological sense and for the amendment of morals, for Zion to rise and turn herself to her God; then what it means for Jacob to rejoice and exult because her Savior comes to her from among the Gentiles; and finally what it means for Jerusalem to plant a vineyard upon her mountains, and why she is told that she shall rejoice because the day of the Lord will come.

Without prejudice, therefore, to the better and deeper understanding which may have been revealed to anyone concerning these matters, it seems to me that every soul which admits what is evil into its affection and fails to practice in deed what is good lies cast down in the depths and turned away from God. For, as you know, to embrace some grave sin in one’s mind through love is surely to be cast down into the depths. And will you not likewise judge a person to be departing from Him who is supremely good if he shrinks from practicing in deed what is good? But let Zion rise; let her rise, I say, and turn [Col. 0146D] to her God. Let her rise though cast down, and turn though turned away.

II. “By what means?” you ask. By fearing and loving. For through fear one withdraws from evil, so that Zion may rise; through love one draws near to good, so that she may turn herself to her God. Therefore, you who lie cast down in the depths, fear the harsh things threatened and arise; you who are turned away from your God, love the sweetness of what is promised and turn to Him. Consider, therefore, both those harsh things and these sweet things, so that you may love these and fear those.

God, indeed, when He wishes to correct a human soul and turn it to Himself, is accustomed sometimes first to soothe it with promises and then frighten it with threats. For thus you read of that compassionate Samaritan, who first poured oil and afterward wine into the wounds of the man left half-dead by robbers (Luke 10:34). And the scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven brings forth from his treasure not old and new things, but new and old things (Matt. 13:32). Does not Isaiah likewise first introduce the Lord promising and afterward threatening? For he says of Him somewhere: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the earth” (Isa. 1:19). These words breathe the sweetness of one who promises. Immediately afterward he introduces things that express no less the bitterness of one who threatens: “But if you refuse and provoke me to anger, the sword shall devour you” (ibid., 20).

And surely, unless I am mistaken, our Lord is called “sweet and upright” (Ps. 24:8), not “upright and sweet,” because He first offers us mercy to sing and afterward judgment (Ps. 110:1), in order to show Himself always ready to spare but slow to strike. And when He does strike, perhaps He is compelled to it more by our incorrigible stubbornness than moved by any cruel wrath of His own. Yet although He Himself, so far as lies in Him, like a bee pours out honey at the front and brings forth a sting behind, it is nevertheless sometimes advantageous for us that He frighten us before soothing us, because love would sometimes have no taste for us unless fear first bit us. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10).

III. Therefore fear this devouring sword, mentioned above, so that you may rise when cast down; and love also the good things of the earth, so that you may turn when turned away. But perhaps these matters ought to be set out more fully than profoundly for the simpler persons among you. Someone has sinned a great sin and lies in his sin, and therefore also in death. For I would say that a person who persists in grave sin is in death. Otherwise Paul would not say: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14).

Therefore someone is dead not only secretly in conscience, through consent with the ruler’s daughter, who lies dead in the chamber (Matt. 9:35), but also openly through the deed, borne outside the gate with the widow’s son (Luke 7:14). Perhaps he has been buried with Lazarus through a perverse habit and even stinks because of infamy (John 2:39). Not only so: he is pressed down in the cave of wicked conduct by the stone of obstinacy laid upon him; and according to his hardness and impenitent heart he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and revelation of the just [Col. 0148A] judgment of God (Rom. 2:5).

When you approach such a person in expounding the word whose dispensation has been entrusted to you [alternative reading: “when you pass through the word, whose”], what manner of person will you show yourself to him at the beginning of your preaching? Will you immediately promise him the joys of heavenly blessedness? You would indeed do well, but he will not hear you. For how can he hear you with ears capable of hearing when you sing to him a hymn from the songs of Zion (Ps. 136:3), he who, raised up, as holy Job says, and strengthened by riches, holds tambourine and lyre and rejoices at the sound of the instrument (Job 21:7), living according to the flesh, obeying himself, not preventing his heart from enjoying every pleasure, and denying his eyes none of the things they desire?

IV. How will he follow you, who come to invite him to the great supper, when it is clear that he has bought the farm of vanity, married the wife of pleasure, and attends through the curiosity of the five senses to testing the five yoke of oxen which he bought? (Luke 14:18 ff.) The delights you offer him are indeed exceedingly savory, but he does not know them. Rather, as soon as he sees the bread you set before him, he will cry out and say: “*Manhu*—that is, ‘What is this?’” (Exod. 16:15); for he does not know what it is.

You wish him to feed on saffron-colored delicacies, but he embraces dung (Lam. 4:5); he desires to fill his belly with the husks of swine, to feed which that citizen to whom he clings sent him to his farm. Nor does he know how to desire anything else in that severe famine which came upon that far country, where he squandered all his substance with harlots, living prodigally (Luke 15:13), “feeding the barren woman and doing no good to the widow” (Job 24:21). For how will he reject what he finds so sweet in exchange for what he wholly does not know, especially when what he loves so ardently is before his eyes? Yet you prophesy to him for a distant time (Ezek. 12:27).

V. Therefore, do not deal with him in this way at the outset; rather, heed what I say, and do what I tell you, and you will save his soul from death. Above all, strive by every means to show him to himself, so that, according to that saying of the Greeks, “Let him know himself.” And, with the Psalmist, let him know what he lacks (Ps. 38:5). Let him know what he lacks, and also what he possesses: what evil he possesses and what good he lacks. Accordingly, declare to him his sins and crimes, that perhaps he may appear to himself as he truly is. Let him encounter himself as he really is: “wretched and pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3:17). And, to say it briefly, let him see how swift he is toward evil and how sluggish toward good; how nothing is present in him for good, and nothing lacking for evil. Thus his own understanding will strike the proud man, humble the exalted, shake the bold, and terrify the self-secure. And this disclosure will be for him, as it were, a kind of transgression [variant: preparation] for health: when, abhorring himself and unable to endure himself as he is, he seeks to become other than he is.

After this, set before him that life is short, that the praise of the wicked is short, that the hypocrite’s joy lasts but a moment; and what follows: namely, “Though his pride rise up to heaven and his head touch the clouds, in the end he shall perish like dung; and those who saw him shall say, ‘Where is he?’ Like a dream flying away he shall not be found; he shall pass like a vision of the night” (Job 20:5 ff.). Make him hear also that voice—indeed far too late, but nevertheless very true—which the wicked will take upon themselves at the end, when, troubled by dreadful fear and groaning in anguish of spirit, they say: “What did pride profit us? What did the boasting of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow, like a messenger running ahead, like a ship passing over rolling water: when it has passed, no trace of it can be found, nor the track of its keel in the waves; or like a bird flying through the air, after which no evidence of its passage is found” (Wis. 5:8–9); and what follows there.

I think these matters bear upon what is read in the book of Kings: that the mule on which Absalom sat passed on (2 Sam. 18:9). This is nothing other than the world, to which the proud man clings in affection: it passes away and tends toward nothingness, according to the saying, “The world passes away, and its desire” (1 John 2:17). Therefore the mule passes on and its rider dies: because the world passes away, and the lover of the world is punished.

VI. By this twofold knowledge you will pour into the sinner of whom we speak a contrite and humbled heart, which God does not despise (Ps. 50:19). Thus he may be humbled in consideration of himself, lest he exalt himself any longer; and, recognizing the brevity of this life, may be crushed, lest he rejoice any longer.

After this lead him into that dark land of which holy Job speaks, covered with the gloom of death, which he also calls “a land of misery and darkness” (Job 10:22), declaring that there are “the shadow of death and no order, but everlasting horror dwelling there.” Recall to his mind also that saying of Isaiah: that the worm of those men—without doubt, those who have transgressed against the Lord—“shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24). Likewise, what Truth itself says: “The angels shall go out and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and shall cast them into the furnace of fire; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 13:50). What does he see in all these things that he should not fear? What does he behold that he should not shudder at?

These, then, are the three things which you must set before him in order to bring him fully to fear. The foulness of his wicked conduct produces humility in him; and humility, once produced, destroys within him the empty swelling of pride. Consideration of the brevity of the present life brings him sorrow; and that sorrow removes worldly gladness from him. Contemplation of infernal punishment introduces fear; and fear, once introduced, disturbs harmful security.

VII. I think that now he will gladly heed your promises and yield to your counsels. For, the Lord enlightening him through you, he sees that the wicked life he practices will not last long and that, if he ends in it, he cannot escape eternal punishment. Emptied and terrified, as one who has lost every hope he now has of retaining what he possesses, and having also full certainty [variant: a certain fullness] that he will incur the things with which you threaten him unless he amend himself, he will obediently submit himself to you both as commanding and as promising: commanding hardships in conduct, promising delights in reward.

And perhaps he will do so more fruitfully insofar as he is more humble, more effectively insofar as he is more ardent. Nor is it surprising if he obeys you when you promise the greatest things, since he sees that he cannot retain even the least. Thus [variant: and if] he assents to your imposing a pleasant harshness which rewards, while he sees a harsh pleasantness which damns vanish more swiftly than the wind.

VIII. Therefore, after you have thus instilled fear in him, persist also in instilling love. Let each hold the middle course, so that neither fear may generate despair nor love laxity. Let the warmth of love temper the coldness of fear, lest he be too greatly frightened by cold; likewise, let the coldness of fear temper the warmth of love, lest he grow insolent. You will rightly do this if you set against the three things which we have said concern fear three others which concern love: so that, while in the former he sees what terrifies, and in the latter what soothes, the earth may be shaken and troubled in him there, and his contrition healed here. Thus, while he is so treated, both his disturbance may be sound and his soundness disturbed; and he may receive a drink in tears, but by measure (Ps. 79:6).

We said that the first of those three things which, when seen, instil fear is consideration of one’s own iniquity. In it, what is not ugly and foul, and therefore what is not a cause of horror and shame? But lest this be excessive, let the contemplation of God’s mercy soften it; for he cannot despair because of his own iniquity while he hopes in the divine compassion. Let him see that the works of the Lord are indeed great and wonderful; yet “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9).

IX. Let him behold that open fountain flowing for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman (Zech. 13:1), so that he may see how David washed in it the stains of adultery and murder (2 Sam. 12:13); how in Mary Magdalene as many defilements are washed away as sins are forgiven her (Luke 7:37); how Peter is cleansed from the filth of denial (Matt. 26); how the woman caught in adultery is not condemned; how the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High makes a martyr out of the thief and grants him Paradise after the cross (John 8:3).

When he has considered these and other things of this kind, let him breathe again in hope of divine mercy who sighs in consideration of his own wickedness, knowing that God can forgive more than he himself can sin.

X. Encouraged and strengthened by these things, let him “put his hand to strong things” (Prov. 31:19). After this, “iron must be taken from the water” (Job 28:2), and flint given in place of earth, and golden streams in place of flint (Job 22:24). Thus he who, while unbridled, lay feebly in softness, subject to the flesh, may henceforth stretch himself out toward good action, stand erect even against the flesh, rise above the flesh, and now “present his members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:19), he who formerly presented them to serve iniquity unto iniquity.

But immediately wicked lips will chatter and a deceitful tongue will make a din. His own frailty will be set forth, so that the new beginning once undertaken may be annulled; they will point to the wind, lest he sow, and show the clouds, lest he ever reap (Ecclus. 2:4).

XI. Against all these things, and things of this sort, I do not know what could be given or applied more powerfully than what the Psalmist, speaking under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, gave and applied to himself as he climbed this step and endured such things: namely, “the sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” (Ps. 119:4).

Let innocent Abel, holy Enoch, obedient Noah, modest Shem and Japheth, faithful Abraham, chaste Isaac, patient Jacob, provident Joseph, gentle Moses, devout Aaron, Phinehas the zealot for the Law, simple Joshua, gracious Samuel, humble David, and the rest of such coals be brought before him—coals which once the fire of the Lord kindled in Zion, but whose furnace now burns in Jerusalem (Isa. 31:9). Thus, when kindled, they may devastate the deceit of the tongue and the iniquity of the lips. So that he may not consider burdensome to accomplish what he sees accomplished courageously by others, perhaps as weak as himself both in sex and age. Meanwhile let him warm his wounded inward parts with such spices. Let him rejoice in this holy newness, he who first groaned over the brevity of the present life.

XII. It remains now, in order to lighten his burden in labour, that you make known to him how great his happiness will be in recompense. Thus, as a hired labourer awaits the end of his work, let him know without any doubt that he who now goes “from strength to strength” shall hereafter, holy and blessed, see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83:8). And “if he suffers with him, he shall also reign with him” (Rom. 8:17).

Behold: through these three things you will pour full love into him. For he undoubtedly loves him in whose mercy he trusts, for whose name he persists in a devout manner of life, and whose blessed and beatifying vision he thirsts to contemplate eternally. Thus, through the preceding three things our Zion comes to fear; terrified by it, she withdraws from evil in order to rise. Through these three that follow, however, she ascends to love; soothed by it, she draws near to good in order to turn herself toward her God, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON X. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD. On Conflict and Peace, and Their Contemplation

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. In the spiritual way, conflict in battle is not absent.
2. Behind press the phantasms of vices; ahead lies the distress of temptations.
3. They serve for spiritual struggle and the preservation of humility.
4. Peace with vices is seldom safe; the peace that remains is through trust in and help from God.
5. The state and beauty of a peaceful mind are figured.
6. The conduct of the saints is set forth as an example, and the joys of the blessed draw us on.
7. On the Lord’s day there is exultation for the righteous, horror and darkness for the wicked.
8. How greatly the state of the eternal homeland is to be desired, where God is seen with unveiled face.
9. From participation in the most holy Trinity there is a threefold gift of blessedness in the saints.
10. As evils are banished there, so goods abound in body and soul.

I. While every devout person walks the royal way of fear and love, he encounters adversities on either side. For he has Leviathan ready to stir himself up (Job 3:8), and that same Leviathan rages against him with all the fiercer envy insofar as he resists him more manfully, both by fear in abandoning evil and by love in embracing good.

Now Jacob returns with these two companies to the house of his father, not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (Gen. 32:22); but Laban runs up behind, and Esau meets him in front. For the world tempts him through those things which he has already left behind, while the enemy troubles him through those which he has not yet experienced. But conscious that he has wholly despised the world and the things in the world, he says to one searching all the furnishings of his house, wishing but unable to find anything of his own either in his mind or in his body: “Search, and whatever of yours you find with me, take away” (Gen. 31:32). That is to say: “I have cast you off in complete contempt, swollen world; you will find nothing in me belonging to you.”

Jacob does not wish himself and Esau to travel together, nor Esau to be his companion on that journey, knowing that no one can carry fire in his bosom without his clothes being burned (Prov. 6:27).

II. The people of the Lord, abandoning Egypt, the darkness of worldly things, and tending toward the desert of the religious life, have the pursuing Egyptians behind them and find the sea before them. Thus every faithful person may know that he must endure the phantasms of the vices he has already left behind, and must suffer the violent distress of temptations from those things which are yet to come.

The great people Amalek (Exod. 17:11)—that is, the assembly of the reprobate clinging to earthly things in affection—is by no means overcome unless every devout person who has been saved from the flux of this age (and thus bears the name Moses, “drawn out,” from the event itself) so rises upon the mountain of contemplation [variant: prayer], so rests upon the rock of steadfastness, that he raises the hands of his works in the evening sacrifice. Such is the strong loftiness and lofty strength of humility represented by Aaron, the mountain of strength; and such is the fire of charity, which the name Ur is said to signify. Thus neither may the left hand stretch itself out toward evil if pride swells up, nor the right withdraw from good if it grows numb through negligence.

III. There are also very many other nations which we can neither utterly destroy nor yet ought to consent to. Especially since the Lord commands us to make no covenant with them and enter into no friendships with them (Exod. 34:12). It remains, therefore, that we endure them in such a way as to make them tributary to us. For they have also been left behind so that the Lord may test us through them. Although they themselves are not good and do not wish us good, they nevertheless serve us for good.

Thus Jacob ought not to groan and sorrow, but rather rejoice and be glad, because from among these nations his Saviour will come. Does not the Saviour come when salvation comes? And true salvation, as you know, is humility. These nations press hard; and by pressing they harass, and thus make Jacob afraid. Fearing, he is humbled; humbled, he is saved; saved, he rejoices and is glad, because in this manner his Saviour comes to him from among these nations.

Trusting in this Saviour, our Jacob holds beneath him those nations which we have briefly recalled, not as masters but as subjects; he cries out to that same Saviour, sometimes alluding to this, and saying: “You girded me with strength for battle, and cast beneath me those who rose up against me” (Ps. 17:33). Therefore holy men do not yield feebly to the suggestions of vices; rather, with the Lord fighting in them and for them, they destroy them beneath the heel of virtue. They do not trust in themselves, but in the Lord, who has delivered and rescues them from such great dangers, and in whom they hope because he will still deliver them—as long as it is necessary. Giving him thanks for this, attributing everything to him, they say: “He has subjected peoples to us, and nations beneath our feet” (Ps. 46:4).

IV. Happy indeed is the man whose protector is the Lord in whom he hopes, who subjects his people beneath him, who rejoices that the Lord has delivered him from the contradictions of the people and made him head of the nations (Ps. 17:44). Thus, having received peace from the Lord—as is read figuratively in the book of Joshua (21:42), among all the nations round about, so that none of his enemies dared resist him—he may rise from the laborious name Jacob to the vision and name of peace, Jerusalem.

“Who is this? And we will praise him; for he has done wonders in his life” (Ecclus. 31:9). Not indeed in himself, but in him who strengthens him, in whom also he can do all things. Of him it is written, “Who alone does great wonders” (Ps. 135:4); and “alone” is added lest man think that he can do wonders without him, apart from whom he can do nothing, and from whom he has his sufficiency, since he is not sufficient even to think anything from himself as though from himself (2 Cor. 3:5).

Yet such a person does wonders in his life, but through him who alone does great wonders. For he is one in whom the sharp goads of the flesh have, insofar as possible, been blunted, and the tumultuous movements of the mind have also been calmed, as far as this corruptible body which weighs down the soul permits (Wis. 9:15). Peaceful in himself and peace-making toward others, he sees nothing but peace. Therefore he is rightly called Jerusalem, which, as everyone knows, is said to mean “vision of peace.” All things in him are peaceable and tranquil, quiet and calmed. He loves nothing twisted or cruel. He entertains within himself nothing but what belongs to peace, displays nothing else in his face, and performs nothing else in deed.

Now “elders sit in the streets” within him (1 Macc. 14:9), while his inward senses, endowed with spiritual maturity, humble themselves in the broad expanse of this peace. For he has not delivered them into the hand of the enemy, but has set their feet “in a spacious place” (Ps. 30:9). And they meditate upon the good things of the land, because he knows that nothing moves within him inwardly which does not concern those good things which holy David believes that he will see in the land of the living (Ps. 26:13).

“Youths also put on glory and garments of war” (1 Macc. 14:9), because his vigorous thoughts everywhere carry with them the testimony of their conscience: that they conduct themselves in the world in simplicity and sincerity, not in fleshly wisdom but in the grace of God. And in the Lord, by whose strengthening they have conquered, they rejoice, being well aware of their past victories over vices. Thus, since no suggestion remains in the mind which terrifies by securing consent, and since the unlawful deed which attacked him upon the ground of his flesh has ceased, every thought in him “sits under its own vine and its own fig tree” (1 Kings 4:25). His mind is so calmed and tempered in the mean that, in the wine of fervour, it is softened by sweetness lest it be too rigid, and, in the fig of sweetness, it bites through fervour lest it be too lax.

Now it is time, since all things are quiet from wars, for Solomon to build a house for the Lord (1 Chron. 28:13), a house which David, a man of blood and war, could not build. And, now that the land rests from battles, let Jerusalem plant a vineyard on its mountains. Our Jacob had no leisure for this work, for he had to attend without interruption to the laborious struggle against adversaries and the overthrow of resisting enemies.

VI. Therefore let Jerusalem plant a vineyard on its mountains: that is, let every person who is deeply at peace within himself and peace-making toward others graft his mind into the manner of life of holy men who are exiles upon earth, and into the joys of blessed citizens reigning in their homeland. Let him admire the holiness of the former so as to imitate them, and desire to attain the happiness of the latter so as to enjoy it with them.

These are the ancient mountains, the eternal mountains, in which the vineyard of this our holy Jerusalem sends its roots downward and bears fruit upward (Isa. 37:31), while the mind of the tranquil and quiet person investigates with such subtlety both the lives of the saints and the joys of the blessed citizens. There it bears fruit for the example of living according to the saints; here it bears fruit for the desire to reign with them without end.

I think this is what I read in holy Job, with the Lord himself declaring that “the eagle is lifted up in the rocks in the morning, and dwells in steep crags and inaccessible cliffs” (Job 39:28). I think this was said because, as a holy man—subtle in understanding and lofty in contemplation—directs his thought and desire toward the good works of those steadfast in holiness [variant: lofty ones] and toward the everlasting joys of the blessed, who are fully confirmed after the fall of the apostate angels, he sets the former before himself as examples and takes the latter up as objects of desire.

How pleasant for this Jerusalem to plant a vineyard on its mountains! How sweet for this lifted-up eagle to remain among these rocks, to dwell in steep crags and inaccessible cliffs: so that the devout soul may strive to dwell there in thought where it cannot yet dwell in vision, and, as one of the saints says, may fix its desire where it cannot establish its lodging.

VII. This, then, is Jerusalem’s work: labour here without labour. Let it meanwhile leap upon these mountains, continually and frequently traverse them, and plant a vineyard upon them (Matt. 26:22), so that one day it may drink new wine with those same mountains in the kingdom of the Father and God. This will indeed be fulfilled when this same Jerusalem exults because the day of the Lord has come.

O day of the Lord! O exultation of Jerusalem! Nor is it surprising that Jerusalem should exult at the coming of the Lord’s day, since it is certain that such great exultation will be present for her on that day. But just as the elect will exult, so the wicked will groan on it, because the Lord will remember the children of Edom “in the day of Jerusalem” (Ps. 136:7). Jerusalem’s day is the Lord’s day, both because it gives exultation to Jerusalem and because Jerusalem will receive the exultation given. It is the Lord’s because it will make Jerusalem glad, and, because Jerusalem will be made glad in it, it will be hers as well.

On that day the saints “shall exult in glory” (Ps. 149:5), but the unjust will grieve in punishment. “These,” he says—the unjust, namely—“shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46). Addressing these same unjust persons, the prophet says: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you desire it? For the day of the Lord is darkness and not light” (Amos 5:19). But for whom will it be darkness? Certainly for the unjust, who, with hands and feet bound, will be cast into the outer darkness (Matt. 22:13). For the elect, however, it will be light—indeed, great light—and exultation also.

How can it not be light, when the streets of that Jerusalem of which we speak will be paved with pure gold (Tob. 13:22): that is, its citizens, enlarged by true charity, will be glorified with the eternal splendour of heavenly wisdom? How can it not be exultation, when alleluia will be sung through all its streets (ibid.), while each person rejoices in the incorruption of the body and the perfect blessedness of the soul?

VIII. Brothers, it is good for us to be here. For already in heart and speech we are in unfailing light, incomprehensible light, and ineffable exultation. I call the light unfailing and incomprehensible because that day will dawn to which no night succeeds. It knows no evening, because eternity together with stability will drive from it both decline and the threatening sunset. I call its exultation likewise ineffable because there “shall be the voice of exultation and salvation in the dwellings of the saints” (Ps. 117:15), and in the voice of exultation and praise there shall be the sound of one feasting.

And he feasts well, because the Lord will make them recline (Luke 12:37), so that they may eat and drink at his table in his kingdom; and he, girded, will pass among them and serve them.
