O love of God, full of exultation: when the righteous “shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43); when that hour shall come—and indeed it will not be without eternal duration—in which the Son will no longer speak to us in proverbs, but will openly declare the Father to us (John 16:25), showing us not merely himself, but his very self; when the Spirit of truth himself will teach us not some truth but all truth (ibid. 13); when the Father, who works until now, has ceased, and, resting from every work that he had accomplished (Gen. 2:1), heaven and earth and all their adornment will be perfected. Then no corruption will remain in the earth of our body, nor will any perfection be lacking in the heaven of our soul.

IX. Brothers, it is good for us to be here. For in thought and word we are in the day of supreme power belonging to the Father, by which he will strengthen us; in the day of eternal wisdom pertaining to the Son, which will glorify us; in the day of most gracious sweetness, which belongs to the Holy Spirit, by which he will inflame us. Thus, when we are gracious toward one another, powerful in ourselves, and wise in God, God himself may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28).

We are also on the mountain with our Lord Jesus, where we see him transfigured (Matt. 17:2). Do we not see him transfigured when we behold him beautiful in his robe, “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44:3), he who was seen in this valley of tears as mean and despised in countenance? Hence he was not esteemed, but thought to be “stricken and humbled by God” (Isa. 53:4). His face has the brightness of the sun and his garments the whiteness of snow, while, at his appearing, his elect will be like him. He is now clothed with them, as it were with garments, because they shall see him as he is. And, as the Evangelist says, no fuller can make garments so white on earth (Mark 9:2). For that spiritual fuller, who sprinkles his garments—that is, his elect—with hyssop that they may be cleansed, does not bestow upon them in exile the beauty with which he will adorn them in the kingdom. For one is the purity which they possess on the way as the merit of holiness, and another that which they possess in their homeland as the reward of blessedness.

X. We know also that on that day God “shall wipe away every tear from the eyes” of his saints (Rev. 21:4). Therefore it is good for us to be here: there shall be no more mourning, crying, or pain, but everlasting joy upon their heads, since they possess a double portion in their land (Isa. 61:8). Let Jerusalem therefore exult, because the day of the Lord has come. Let it exult in body and exult in soul: there through full incorruption, here through the eternal possession of eternal blessedness.

But although it is good for us to be here, certain matters call us back from here; though we do not wish to attend to them, we nevertheless must, because this too is fitting. For Leah calls Jacob away from Rachel’s sweetest embraces, because of her son’s mandrakes, to her own people [variant: to herself] (Gen. 30:16). Thus, for the fruit of good work, every devout person is sometimes called away from the taste of the clearest contemplation to the exercise of good action.

“Rise, let us go hence.” Let these things suffice for the present: that Zion is admonished in these words to arise and turn herself toward her God; that Jacob is told to rejoice and be glad because his Saviour will come from among the nations; that the city Jerusalem is prophesied to plant a vineyard upon its mountains and to exult because the day of the Lord will come. Therefore receive in understanding and retain in memory whatever has been said allegorically concerning these words in the preceding sermon, or tropologically in this subsequent one, glorifying and praising God and our Lord, to whom be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD. On Good and Bad Hearers; on What the Responsory “The Lord Shall Go Forth,” etc. Signifies; and on the Wisdom of God

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. Eager reception of the word of God is a prognostic sign of the children of God.
2. Some hear from vanity, curiosity, or self-exaltation; others for profit.
3. The judgment of the several kinds of hearers.
4. The responsory after the reading is obedience to what is said in preaching.
5. Fruitful hearing of the word is accompanied by action.
6. The mysteries of the Scriptures are hidden from us, and why.
7. The Samaritan woman is a type of the Church of the Gentiles.
8. The Lord’s going forth from Samaria means that wisdom is revealed to us in time.
9. By the good pleasure of the Father and the Son, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both, all things were created in order.
10. Through his wisdom God condemned evil angels and confirmed good angels in holiness.
11. Through God’s wisdom the hierarchy of the Churches is ordered and defended.

I. Beloved, you eagerly desire and expect, as it seems to me that I understand from you, to hear something from me as though something in the word of God were open to me that is hidden from you. Certainly, like those little children whom Jeremiah says asked for bread (Lam. 4:4), you too ask for bread. And you ask it from me, as though either I knew better than you how to break it, or possessed a different bread to break from that which you have.

But because you are of God—and this itself is why you so gladly hear his words (John 8:47)—you will not, I think, be weary if familiar things are said, or if I bring forward matters which you recognize more by my repetition than learn from my instruction. Yet, since it is certain that those who do not hear God’s words are not of God, you hear because you are of God.

II. See, I beg you, how you hear. Among even the most eager hearers of the word, we know some who hear only in order to know what, or in what manner, the person whom they hear will speak. And this is, as you know, an unworthy curiosity. They attend to the speaker not so much because of what he says as because of the person who says it; not so much in order that they may be instructed [variant: may seek] by what they hear, as in order to know what they ought to think of the discourse of the man whom they hear.

There are others who hear only in order that they may know what has been heard; and this is blameworthy vanity. They are proud and covetous, and desire to know much so that, being exceedingly knowing [variant: self-opinionated], they may puff themselves up with pride.

But there are some whom we rightly prefer to all these, whose purpose in hearing the word is to fulfil in deed what they receive through the ear; and this is of great benefit. For they carefully attend to what they hear in God’s word that may serve for the building up of character, the rebuke of vices, and exhortation to virtues; what concerns contempt for present things or desire for future things; what pertains to promises of joys or threats of punishments; then, what must be avoided because it is evil, and what sought because it is good. All these things, and matters of this kind, they receive with joy after the manner of good soil and bear fruit in patience (Luke 8:15).

III. Therefore, those whom I placed first are hardened by damnable obstinacy; those second, are stirred by blameworthy superstition; those third, are raised up by empty pride; those fourth, are saved by salutary edification.

To those in the first class I think belong those who, having heard the words of Truth itself, hardened almost by the horror of their wickedness, said: “He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to him?” (John 10:20); and also those who said: “He is not good, but deceives the crowds” (John 7:12).

To those in the second class belong those who, hearing that Jesus was in Bethany, came “not only because of the Lord, but also that they might see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead” (John 12:9); and that wicked man of whom we read that he had long desired to see him, because he hoped to see some sign done by him (Luke 23:8).

He appears to have been among those in the third class who, having seen the signs which the Lord performed, said to him: “Master, I will follow you wherever you go” (Luke 9:59). To him that strict examiner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart replied: “Foxes have dens, and birds of the air nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (ibid., v. 58). As though he said: “You wish to follow me with a primary intention; but arrogance and deceit also have a place in you, and therefore you are utterly unable to follow the majesty of my divinity.”

But to those in the fourth class belong those to whom the Lord himself says: “You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). You too follow these: not stirred by some curiosity, not raised up by vanity, but desiring to hear the word of God for the sake of spiritual profit alone. Thus it delights us to set spiritual food before you because you hunger for it with a pure and clean eagerness.

IV. You ask about the responsory which you recently sang, that I may explain its words to you. They read as follows: “The Lord shall go forth from Samaria to the gate which faces east, and shall come to Bethlehem, walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption. Then every person shall be saved, because behold, he shall come.”

You ask that these words be expounded to you. What you ask is just, but you ask it from one unworthy, when you ought to ask it from one who abounds. Receive, therefore, what one poor in understanding but rich in affection sets before you. And when you have accepted the tasteless vegetable of his poverty, seek sweeter delicacies from richer persons.

You ask how the words of this responsory should be understood. But first ask what a responsory is. Since through the preceding reading we receive the teaching of preachers, what should we receive through the responsory that follows except the obedience of hearers? First the reading is heard, then the responsory is sung, because first preaching is received through the ears and then a good work is obediently performed. And because “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7), it is as though, after the reading has been read, the responsory is sung: as the preceding preaching has instructed, so good work follows with cheerfulness.

For, as you know, *responsorium* is so called from responding; and in a manner you say a responsory after hearing the reading when, by doing good, you respond to the teacher addressing you through his preaching. Hence, concerning the responsory said at Mass after the reading from the Apostle or some prophet, someone sang no less elegantly than truly in the following manner:

> The reading that follows signifies the teaching of those  
> Who went before, the seventy-two;  
> While the choir sings the responsories at their admonitions,  
> It teaches that it has given its assent.

[Note: Col. 0159. Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours, in his verses *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*. See *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, vol. XII.]

V. Therefore first the reading, afterward the responsory. For by preaching you will believe; believing, you do good works, as the same writer whom we mentioned above says:

> You hear in order that you may believe; because you believe, you become an offering.

[Note: Col. 0159D. The author cited above.]

Thus we begin to be, and are, God’s.

And as the Apostle says: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10:17). That is to say, the responsory of good action proceeds from the reading of sound preaching. He likewise says: “How are they to believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how are they to hear without a preacher?” (ibid. 10:14). As though alluding to these things which we have in hand, he might add: How is it fitting [Col. 0159C] that they should sing the responsory before the reading? And how will they hear the reading without someone reading it? Yet some of the moderns act thus, being indeed ready to hear but slow to act. They wish the reading to be read to them, but refuse to sing the responsory. They imitate the man of whom Solomon says that he understands what you say, yet despises to answer (Prov. 29:19). But you, brothers, must not be so. Do you wish to hear a holy man thinking rightly on these matters? “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears” (1 Sam. 3:10).

Samuel here was a holy boy; he was holy also when he grew old and grey. No one could accuse him from childhood to old age. Certainly praiseworthy—as people commonly say—throughout all his days, one whose brightness does not fail from morning until evening [Col. 0159D]. The words you hear, “Speak,” belong to the reading; but what is immediately added, “for your servant hears,” belongs to the responsory, because, once the reading has been read, I shall immediately sing the responsory. And enough of these matters for the present, briefly indeed; perhaps what has been said has not been without fruit.

VI. But concerning what you hear said here of the Lord—that he is to go out from Samaria to the gate facing east, and to come to Bethlehem, walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption—if you knock devoutly, the key of David will be present, as is its wont: he “opens and no one shuts; shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3:7). Nor will you suffer any rejection from him who opens to those who knock [Col. 0160A] “hidden treasures and the secrets of mysteries” (Isa. 45:3).

It seems to me that something profound and mystical is contained in these things. For just as, when we take some closed chest in our hands, we perceive from its bulk and weight that much lies hidden within it—although, because everything placed inside is shut up, we do not know at all what is in it—so often, in the most holy utterances of the divine page, we infer from its weighty words that profound and mystical sacraments lie hidden there, although the eyes of our mind have not yet been unveiled by the Spirit, so that we may see its interior.

What then must we do, except knock until it is opened to us? For he who says, “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke 11:9), neither knows how to deceive nor was ever able to be deceived. And shortly afterward: “To the one who knocks,” he says, “it will be opened” (ibid. 11:10). Therefore he does not shut without eventually opening; rather, he does so in order to make us eager to knock—not only that we may praise the grace which opens, but also that we may love the inward secret opened to us. Open to us, therefore, Lord.

What does it mean to go out from Samaria? Go out, I pray, to us from this Samaria, so that this going out from Samaria of yours, of which I am now speaking, may show us what it means for you to go out from Samaria. For, brothers, can anything good come from Samaria? Much indeed, in every way. For how could much good not come from Samaria, when the Lord himself is said to go out from Samaria?

VII. And indeed, as you know, the Samaritans were once held contemptible among the people [Col. 0160C] of the Lord, and they did not deem it worthy to have any fellowship with them, according to the saying: “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans” (John 4:9). Hence, when that true Jew—namely, he who confesses the Lord, Father of heaven and earth, who hides from the wise and prudent what he reveals to little ones (Matt. 11:25)—came to the sixth hour of the world’s age, and, wearied by the journey (John 4:6) of assumed mortality, sat upon the well, humbling himself in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3), and sought drink from the faith of the Church drawn from the Gentiles: the woman, ignorant of the mystery and not knowing the gift of God nor who it was that said to her, “Give me a drink,” unable to come to him unless she brought a faithful understanding—that is, unless she called her husband—she who had formerly been joined to the five husbands of bodily senses, but now held error as faith and adultery as her husband, answered: “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask a drink of me, a Samaritan woman?” (John 4:9).

But now let the disciples marvel as much as they wish that Jesus speaks with a woman. The brothers also rebuke Peter because he enters men who have the foreskin and eats with them (Acts 11:3). It is time for gold to come from the north, and for fearful praise from God (Job 37:22); for the north must give, and the south must not forbid (Isa. 43:6). For he who “went about doing good” (Acts 10:38) and healing all oppressed by the devil had to pass through Samaria, so that, to pour into the Samaritans coming to him by faith a twofold love, he might remain with them two days [Col. 0161A], in order that they might both believe in their hearts unto righteousness and confess with their mouths unto salvation (Rom. 10:10), saying: “We ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Savior of the world” (John 4:42). Therefore no good thing is absent from Samaria, nor is the Samaritan to be abhorred, since mercy was found in him which could find no place in the priest and Levite (Luke 10:33).

VIII. But although these words can fittingly be understood of the calling of the Gentiles, let us first seek in them something higher and deeper; and then afterward we shall suitably descend from the mountains of loftier meanings to the plains of the lower understanding. Saving to each person that subtler understanding which the Spirit of truth reveals to him as he wills, when he wills, how he wills, and in whatever measure he wills [Col. 0161B], it seems to me that the Lord’s going out is the knowledge of him granted to a human being.

From the deep and lofty secrecy of his Father—where, as though in a certain keeping, for this is what *Samaria* signifies, he has been hidden from eternity—he proceeds when and how he wills, yet without departing from there. He goes forth, not away: for the Father who sent him did not lose him, but dispatched and retained him. He comes to the human heart and announces to it the Father, from the Father. For, as that theologian says: “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he himself has declared him” (John 1:18).

He is indeed our Lord, to whom it was said: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 110:1), which was said to none of the angels [Col. 0161C]. Yet he whose words were iniquity and deceit presumptuously seized it for himself, saying: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). He, I say, went out from that hidden keeping so that he might be seen. So long as he was in that Samaria, he could not be seen; nor could he be seen in any way unless he went out.

IX. Was he not in hidden keeping who was in the mouth, in the heart, in the womb? But he was in the mouth whose heart “uttered a good word” (Ps. 45:1); he was in the heart who said, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7); and, “In the splendors of the saints, from the womb before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 110:3). He was also in him “from whose mouth wisdom came forth, the firstborn before every creature” (Sir. 24:5).

What he eternally conceives in that same Wisdom, what he possesses in that same Word of his, what he deliberates with that same Son of his—while the unchangeable good pleasure of both stands present, namely the Holy Spirit, coequal with them and coeternal, proceeding from both—he brought his own creature into being. He distinguished each thing into its own form in rational order, through its own places and times [Col. 0161D]. At times he divided them by a different lot, yet one wholly fitting. He saw all things which he had made, and which he saw even before they were made; and they were good—not merely good, but, with the addition, very good (Gen. 1:31). Therefore Wisdom was always present with the wise God, Wisdom which he possessed “at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning” (Prov. 8:22).

X. For how could he know along what paths of action he ought to proceed in working, unless he saw them in Wisdom? Or how could he make anything, unless in her he recognized what ought to be made [Col. 0162A]? “The deeps did not yet exist,” and Wisdom was already conceived (ibid. 8:24); when he prepared the heavens, she was present. Nor is this surprising. How could he condemn those dark and deep spirits—I mean the apostate angels—or confirm in holiness those who remained, unless through his coeternal Wisdom he knew both the evil which he would reject in the former and the good which he would choose (Isa. 7:15) and reward in the latter? Thus, before the deeps existed, he conceived her, exercising in her a judgment of condemnation concerning those same deeps. When he prepared the heavens, he had her present; by her ordering, he bestowed upon those heavens the grace of confirmation.

XI. The “fountains of waters” had not yet burst forth (Prov. 8:24): that is, the gifts of graces had not yet proceeded. The mountains had not yet stood in their heavy mass: that is, the proud had not yet fallen through damnable peril [alternative reading: perversity]; and she, understand, was conceived, holding within himself a certain determination concerning them. Behold, he had not yet made rivers and the hinges of the earth’s circle: that is, the faithful peoples and the prelates of the Catholic Church.

When he enclosed the deeps with a fixed law and boundary, he established an order for the reprobate and a measure defining how and how long they should advance in their iniquity. When he made the upper air firm and weighed the fountains of waters, he strengthened the elect in their desire for eternal things, conferring on them the gifts of his graces. When he set its limit around the sea—that is, raging Gentiledom—lest it rage further in persecution; and set a law for the waters, lest they pass their bounds: he established an ordering for persecutions, lest they transgress the limits divinely appointed [Col. 0162C]. When he suspended the foundations of the earth, adorning the foremost men of the Church, “I was with him, ordering all things.” For he arranged all things with him. To him be honor and glory for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XII. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

### By what means knowledge of the invisible God comes to us

### Synopsis of the sermon

1. The unchangeable Wisdom of God, eternal from the beginning, made manifest through creation.  
2. How hidden it is in the reprobation and election of rational creatures.  
3. In Jacob the elect, and in Esau the reprobate, are figured.  
4. What it is for the Lord to go out to the gate [Col. 0162D] of the East.  
5. The gate of the East is threefold: first, natural reason; second, the contemplation of creatures.  
6. The third is divine manifestation.  
7. The fitting order of the threefold gate, drawn from the Apostle.  
8. A damnable knowledge of truth not accompanied by true righteousness and love.  
9. For the ungodly, both evils and goods cooperate unto evil.  
10. From vanity of thought they fall into folly of action.  
11. By what stages and advances the road to perdition is laid out.

How, brothers, shall we speak [alternative reading: were we speaking] with our passing word of that Word which was in the beginning with God and was God; through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1:1)—in whom was also that which was made in him? But the Son does nothing except what he sees the Father doing, because “whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” [Col. 0163A] (John 5:19). The Father loves him and, in that eternal and incomprehensible generation, shows him whatever he does.

Behold Wisdom proceeding from the mouth (Sir. 24:5). Behold the Word uttered from the heart (Ps. 45:1). Behold the Son begotten from the womb (Ps. 2:7). O mouth, O heart, O womb! A mouth breathing forth nothing transient; a heart casting out nothing that was inward; a womb taking on nothing new in conceiving, losing nothing old in bearing. O Wisdom unchangeable in itself, incomprehensible to us! O Providence incapable of deception in its ordering! O Samaria long and broad, deep and high! There, in that secret, all things which appear here in this public realm in time were from eternity hidden in a hidden keeping with God; and through their creation they appear and are revealed in themselves [Col. 0163B].

II. There the rational reprobate creature has a judgment which is just indeed, but hidden; incomprehensible, yet beyond reproach—terrible precisely because unchangeable. There also the rational elect creature has standing by it, and ministering for it, the fixed and immovable sentence of peace: “the mercies of the Lord from eternity unto eternity,” so that they have neither beginning, because they are from eternity, nor end, because they are unto eternity.

For there is that foreordained people, “foolish and unwise” (Deut. 32:6), a crooked and provoking generation, adulterous and perverse. There is the predestined people, that praiseworthy people whom, according to Isaiah, the Lord has blessed (Isa. 19:25); that nation which, according to the Psalmist, is blessed, “whose God is the Lord” [Col. 0163C], the people “whom he chose for his inheritance” (Ps. 33:12). Nor can the thing formed say to him who formed it: “Why have you made me thus?” (Rom. 9:20), since the potter has power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel unto honor and another unto dishonor (ibid. 9:21).

Therefore that most excellent and immeasurable, exceedingly terrible and great, hidden and just, most dread and fearsome Lord God, wishing to show his eternal grace and make known his power, “endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction,” in order also to show “the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy,” which he prepared for eternal glory (ibid. 9:23).

III. [Col. 0163D] O womb of Rebecca! O secret of divine foreknowledge! For from the same womb these two nations, different from one another, and two peoples, different from one another, are divided (Gen. 25:23). Such as they are there in eternity, such they come forth here in time. Esau, indeed, is red because of cruelty; and because of the pleasure by which he is covered and wrapped on every side, he is altogether hairy like a skin. Jacob, however, is mild, as though free from these evils—not only before they have done anything, but even before they are born through creation—so that God’s purpose according to election may remain, not from works, since they have not yet done anything in themselves, but from the calling word of the Lord, true and unchangeable: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9:13).

Esau is hated, who is enclosed in that very womb red and wholly hairy like a skin [Col. 0164A]. Having gone out through creation and grown up through free choice, he becomes a skillful hunter and a man of the field. Jacob, on the contrary, is loved, who is borne mild in the same womb with him; and, as the one whom the Lord predestined, he also called. Mild in the womb, on coming forth he grasps his brother’s heel with his hand; and, as the one whom he called, he also justified, he is a simple man dwelling in tents. And, as the one whom he justified, he also glorified, he afterward reaches the paternal blessing (Rom. 8:30). There, therefore, are hidden all things which emerge here created and visible, from the highest to the lowest: “one opposite another; and he made nothing lacking” (Sir. 42:25).

IV. [Col. 0164B] This is that Samaria from which the Lord is in a sense said to go out: namely, that he himself is known through those things which lie hidden there but emerge here visibly. Of him it is said in these profound words, as though of the future, that he will go out—he who cannot go out by departing from himself, just as he cannot enter by approaching. For, as the Apostle James testifies, with him “there is no change or shadow of turning” (Jas. 1:17).

But he is, as it were, still inside his Samaria so long as he is not made known to us through the things which come forth from that Samaria and appear here. He has gone out, but for those to whom he has already revealed himself. He will go out, but for those to whom he will reveal himself. But by what way will he go out? From Samaria. This is the entrance by which the Lord enters when he goes out from Samaria: namely, the gate facing east [Col. 0164C], which is contemplation leading to the knowledge of truth. For in the east the brightness of light rises and breaks forth, while in the west it in some manner fails and sets. The east is the brightness of knowledge; the west, the blindness of ignorance.

V. There is a certain gate in the east through which the Lord goes out from Samaria: namely, the natural reason of the human being, by which one instructed contemplates one’s God. For by the prompting of one’s own reason, naturally implanted within, a human being is stirred and invited to the knowledge of God. The ministry of the five bodily senses is also supplied from without, by which one apprehends created things—but only visible and bodily things: seeing forms, hearing sounds, smelling odors, tasting flavors, or touching tangible things.

There is also another gate facing east through which the Lord goes out. If, as we said above, the Lord’s going out is his becoming known, he goes out to this gate because the Creator is known through creation. Here the book written within and without is spread open before the human being (Ezek. 2:9): so that, entering inwardly, one may read in reason itself; going outwardly, one may read in created nature; and may know him in one’s own soul, made in his image. One may know him also in the creature created by him so beautiful, so immense, and so useful [Col. 0164D]. Thus creatures, wonderful in so many ways, are certain wonderful ways of him who made them wonderful. As is written of Wisdom: “In her ways she shows herself to them cheerfully, and [Col. 0165A] in every providence she meets them” (Wis. 6:17).

In this twofold statement you have that twofold gate which we constructed for you above: for she shows herself to us in her ways when knowledge of her comes to us through the contemplation of her creatures; and she likewise meets us in every prudence when she becomes known to us through the inquiry of your reason.

VI. There is also a divine manifestation, placing itself between the human reason which investigates inwardly and the contemplation of created nature which looks upon external things. It is, as it were, a beautiful and strong gate facing east: adorning by its beauty the gate of reason, and strengthening by its power the gate of outward contemplation. It adorns the gate of reason, lest an invading phantom disfigure it; likewise it strengthens the gate of inward contemplation, lest wanton sensuality weaken it [Col. 0165B].

Therefore, if you enter through the Lord—that is, through the manifestation of the Lord—in order to contemplate, you will be saved. You will enter into inward reason, go out into outward contemplation, and find pasture in the sweet knowledge of truth itself (John 10:9).

VII. Behold three gates from the east: the gate of inward reason, the gate of outward contemplation, and the gate of divine contemplation. See whether the Apostle does not declare that the Lord goes out from Samaria to this threefold gate facing east, when he says: “What may be known of God is manifest in them” (Rom. 1:19), and the rest which follows there.

What may be known of God is manifest in them because it is naturally implanted in them that, instructed by their own reason, they may know God. This is the gate of inward reason, to which the Lord goes out when he is known through it. He next speaks of the gate of outward contemplation: “His invisible things,” he says, “from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (ibid. 1:20). For if we are creatures of the world, through the things that have been made we know his invisible things, and also his eternal power and divinity.

But between these three gates he inserts the gate of divine manifestation when he says that God manifested it to them. For inward reason and outward contemplation would be wholly insufficient for comprehending the knowledge of God [Col. 0165D] unless divine manifestation were also present. What reason asks by searching, what outward contemplation considers, divine manifestation reveals within.

Therefore this is for the Lord to go out from Samaria to the gate facing east: that he be known by human beings through those things which break forth from his secret and lofty keeping, so as to exist and appear in themselves—through reason searching them, contemplation considering them, and divine manifestation making them known. This knowledge of which I speak indeed begins a certain holiness; but if affection is lacking, it never completes what it has begun.

VIII. For we know very many who knew much; but because they did not love, it profited them nothing. For these also, of whom the Apostle says: “What may be known of God is manifest [Col. 0166A] in them” (Rom. 1:19); “God manifested it to them” (ibid.); and “his invisible things, through the things that have been made, are clearly seen, together with his eternal power and divinity” (ibid. 1:20)—hear how he approves them; indeed, how he rejects them. “The wrath of God,” he says, “is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men” (ibid. 1:18). He reproves them of ungodliness and unrighteousness, showing that they sinned both in faith through unbelief and in action through perversity.

“Those,” he says, “who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness” (ibid. 1:19). Therefore they possessed the truth of God, but held it in unrighteousness, because though learned in knowledge, they were unrighteous in action: they “were wise to do evil, but did not know how to do good” (Jer. 4:22) [Col. 0166B]. What profit was it to them to have possessed the truth of God, when they evidently held it in unrighteousness? For what were they illuminated with the light of so great a knowledge? Hear why: “that they may be without excuse” (Rom. 1:20).

For what is of God is indeed manifest in them, because “the light shines in darkness,” yet they are darkness (John 1:5). It shines in them, and they do not cease to be darkness. Knowledge shines even in the reprobate; but it shines in such a way that it does not shine forth for them. They are flooded with the brightness of this divine knowledge of which we speak, yet, remaining blind, they do not behold it with the eye of love.

Thus, though what may be known of God is manifest in them, though God has manifested it to them, though they have perceived his invisible things through the things that are made, all these things are nevertheless for this end [alternative reading: these things]: that they may be without excuse [Col. 0166C], because when light shone in darkness, “the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). For if they comprehended it, they would not only be enlightened through understanding but also kindled through affection, and thus would already be so through affection. For now they comprehend, according to the saying: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints” (Eph. 3:18).

IX. But now light shines in darkness, and yet darkness does not comprehend the light, because the ungodly, whom ignorance makes blind, and the wicked, whom malice makes cold, are flooded with divine light; yet though flooded, they do not look upon it. They are seen, indeed, hardened in their perversity through pride, so that they may not escape the punishment of penalty; but they do not see it, softened through compunction, so that they might run to the refuge of repentance [Col. 0166D].

Therefore they are distinguished by this threefold knowledge, as though admitted within this threefold gate, in order that they may be without excuse. Since they cannot have recourse to the covering of excuse, they incur the fullness of condemnation. Thus, in a wondrous and pitiable fashion, not only the evils which they do, but even sometimes the good things bestowed upon them cooperate for their evil.

And why can they not be excusable? Because “though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God” (Rom. 1:21). See: they knew him, yet did not glorify him whom they knew. And indeed, if they did not glorify him, they dishonored him. For what follows? “But they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise [Col. 0167A], they became fools” (ibid. 1:21–22). What he first said, “they became vain in their thoughts,” he afterward stated more fully: “claiming to be wise.” And what he first said, “their foolish heart was darkened,” he expressed more plainly: “they became fools.” For from vanity of thought they came to arrogance of speech, so that from the abundance of the heart the mouth might speak. From darkness of heart they came to folly of action, so that they were first blinded through ignorance and then defiled through lust.

X. For this often happens—indeed, almost always. When the root is corrupted, the branch cannot remain whole; and when what is below, under the ground, is spoiled, the fruit above cannot remain unharmed. And in proportion as their foolish heart was darkened through vanity of thought, so, while they called themselves wise, they became fools. Hear how greatly. “They exchanged,” he says, “the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents” (ibid. 1:23) [Col. 0167B].

What greater darkness of a foolish heart can there be? What greater folly of action than that the incorruptible Creator should be changed into a corruptible creature—and not so much into a creature as into the image of a creature? And what is the reward of such blasphemy? “Therefore God gave them up,” he says, “to a reprobate mind and to the desires of their heart” (ibid. 1:24). And shortly afterward: “Therefore God gave them up to dishonorable passions” (ibid. 1:26). And again: “Since they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them up to a reprobate mind, to do things that are unfitting, filled with every unrighteousness” (ibid. 1:28).

XI. [Col. 0167C] Consider, I pray, the stages of perdition. Because they refused humbly to honor the light that shone above them, they fell into pride of mind. From pride of mind they came to arrogance of speech, because “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Luke 6:45). From arrogance they fell into blindness of mind, because when you exalt yourself in speech, by a just judgment [alternative reading: by God’s just judgment] you incur darkness even in your mind. From blindness of mind they came to the blasphemy of error, because, while they did not know where they were going, they went so far as to worship what they did not know. Finally, from the blasphemy of error [Col. 0167D], they were submerged in a horrible and detestable corruption of the flesh.

This is what I say, my most dear and beloved brothers: it is of little profit that truth is apprehended through knowledge unless virtue is also exercised through love, so that the truth which goes before may enlighten the mind through understanding, and the love which follows may kindle it through affection. Hence, after it is said here of the Lord that he will go out from Samaria to the gate facing east, it is immediately added that he will also come to Bethlehem. What this means we shall show in another sermon, with the Lord’s help, casting our thought upon him, without whom we can do nothing. To him be honor and glory for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

### On confession of sins and divine praise, and the manner of each

[Col. 0168A]

### Synopsis of the sermon

1. Let what is true delight the understanding; let what is good delight the affection.  
2. God’s gifts must be confessed to God; opposed to this confession is damnable denial.  
3. What the confession of sins ought to be like.  
4. The sinner must examine the enormity of his own fault.  
5. The severity of punishments deserved by sins removes the shame of confession.  
6. A method for confronting oneself and banishing that nocturnal terror.  
7. The sinner must be raised by hope in divine mercy.  
8. A practice for awakening confidence in divine goodness.  
9. Three ways and modes leading to confession of sins.  
10. Another confession is that of praise and of divine benefits.  
11. Consideration of particular benefits, especially those relating by name [Col. 0168B] to the religious state.  
12. An affection of gratitude and thanksgiving to God.  
13. Three ways of enumerating what must be confessed to God, with a recapitulation.

I. The Lord who is said to go out from Samaria to the gate facing east is also declared to be coming to Bethlehem. To state briefly what comes to mind concerning these things: what do we think it means for the Lord to come to Bethlehem, except that we also—who can come and go, approach and withdraw—may, under his guidance, arrive at the dwelling-place of inward refreshment?

For, as you have been taught by the frequent exposition of the Fathers, *Bethlehem* is called “house of bread.” And what else, in a moral sense, is the house of bread but the refreshment of a secure and kindly mind, which Solomon also compares with a continual feast? (Prov. 15:15). The Lord comes to this, as it were, Bethlehem, after going out from Samaria to the gate leading east, so that after our mind knows by understanding what is true, it may also relish by affection what is good [Col. 0168C].

And this is for the Lord to come to Bethlehem: by the inward taste of delight, to dwell in the habitation of our mind. For if we ardently love what is manifest in us through our reason; what God has manifested to us through his manifestation; and what, of his invisible things, is understood through the things that are made by outward contemplation (Rom. 1:20), then he himself, in a sense, after going out from Samaria, comes to the gate facing east, when after true knowledge of the things pertaining to him we taste upon the palate of the mind a sweet love toward him and in him.

II. [Col. 0168D] But by the added words, “walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption,” we understand the modes and ways by which we ascend to the love of our God. If *Judah* means “confession,” from what is Judah redeemed except from what is contrary to it, namely denial? For whoever denies does not confess, and whoever confesses does not deny. Who is one who confesses except one who acknowledges that he is indebted to God on account of what has been given and received? The waters of Judah’s redemption are gifts of grace, by which every devout person is invited to confess the giver of those graces. Thus, as though walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption, the Lord comes into Bethlehem [Col. 0169A], manifesting to us the ways by which, having cast off the damnable sin of denial, we may exercise the virtue of confession, while also infusing into our minds an inward sweetness of savor.

But now let us speak somewhat of Judah and the waters of his redemption: first, seeing in what ways we ought to exercise this confession of which we speak; then by what means we may acquire it; and finally showing that confessions are many, and assigning to each the particular means by which it must be acquired.

III. It seems to me that confession, as it is within us, ought first to be also concerning us, according to the saying: “The just man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17). Thus you may show yourself outwardly [Col. 0169B] in speech such as you are hidden inwardly to yourself in mind. And what are you in your own mind except unjust and sinful—provided you do not dissemble and turn open eyes upon yourself from every side?

If you cast away from yourself those fig leaves which, in the reading *consutis*, had been sewn together—[alternative reading: *consuti*, “having sewn them together”]—by those first-created human beings after recognizing that they were naked, and from which they made themselves coverings (Gen. 3:7), you will see that “from the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in you” (Isa. 1:6). Therefore you who already stink in the cave of conscience, four days dead, come forth in confession (John 11:39). Confess yourself a sinner as you truly are. Uncover your sin, so that Isaiah’s prophecy may be fulfilled in you: “The earth shall reveal her blood, and shall no longer cover her slain” (Isa. 26:21) [Col. 0169C].

The earth revealing its blood is the soul uncovering its sin through confession. Nor does it any longer cover its slain, when it does not conceal its inward thoughts, deprived of spiritual life through consent to sin. This confession, as you know, is exceedingly salutary, since without it we cannot attain true salvation. Did not he perceive this who said: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5:16)? The usefulness [alternative reading: truth] of this saying is made clear to us by the loss which is its contrary, namely: unless you confess to one another and pray for one another, you are not saved.

The saying of Solomon also seems to support this meaning: “He who conceals his crimes shall not prosper; but whoever confesses and forsakes them shall obtain mercy” (Prov. 28:13). Entirely true—this is true: one who reveals his sins will advance, but eternal condemnation will overtake one who conceals and cherishes them [Col. 0169D].

IV. You have heard what this first confession ought to be. See now by what paths you ought to approach it. Let your first discipline be to look fully upon the enormity of your crime. For you will by no means confess yourself a sinner if you do not understand that you are a sinner; nor will you show your wounds to the physician if you do not recognize that you are wounded. Therefore, taking yourself from behind your own back, where you had cast yourself, rebuking yourself, “set yourself before your own face” (Ps. 49:21), and see how foul and fetid you are, how wasted and ulcerous, [Col. 0170A] so that, displeasing even to yourself, you may become a horror to yourself. And, raising a voice of great agitation, address yourself in these words, and say to yourself somewhat as follows:

“Alas, alas! Why have I wounded my soul with so many and such great blows, running against God with uplifted neck through the streets of Babylon; sowing in the flesh, rolling myself in the mire of mud, fast embedded in the deep slime? Why, abandoning the waters of Judah which cleanse, have I plunged myself into the rivers Abana and Pharpar of Damascus (4 Kings 5:12), sucked the head of asps, and been killed by the tongue of the viper—that is, by admitting into my heart, at the very beginning of temptation, its flattering suggestion, and then losing the spiritual life within me through the assent that followed? Behold, I have my sins sealed up in a sack (Job 14:17); and now, made miserably an object of horror and disgust to myself, [Col. 0170B] I am compelled to look upon myself as I am, yet cannot endure what I see.”

Why, when you see yourself so sick, should you not disclose your sickness to the physician with all speed? Otherwise the wound, when neglected, and especially when concealed, turns to corruption; and corruption is followed by death. It remains, therefore, that you who are leprous should hear with ears that hear what the true physician commanded those lepers who cried to him: “Go,” he says, “show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17:14).

V. But if knowledge of guilt cannot draw you to confession, let consideration of punishment at least draw you, so that you who keep silence, confounded even by the horror of sin, may speak when shaken by fear of punishment. And why are you unwilling to confess? Perhaps because of shame. But why [Col. 0170C] are you ashamed to call yourself a sinner, when you ought rather to be ashamed to be one? Let shame, I pray, cast out shame; let modesty drive out modesty, so that, as blessed Gregory says of that holy penitent woman [Note: [Col. 0169D] St. Gregory, Homily 33.], you may blush inwardly at yourself so intensely that you count nothing worthy of external embarrassment.

Certainly you ought to be more ashamed of yourself when, having dug through the wall, you behold the abomination of animals and creeping things (Ezek. 8:10), than when, opening that same wall in order that they may be destroyed, you expose those abominations. Perhaps you do not confess out of fear, lest some severe penance be imposed upon you when you confess; terrified, you therefore choose to cover yourself by silence. But you may fear more the dreadful reproach of the Enemy after death and the horrible condemnation of hell. Address [Col. 0170D] your soul, therefore, concerning these things, if perhaps you can drive out one fear by another. And, that the fear which hinders confession may depart and that which brings it about may succeed, speak to it in these words:

VI. “Woe to me, who in the sight of the omnipotent and living God himself—into whose hands, as the Apostle says, it is fearful to fall (Heb. 10:31)—must be put to shame also in the presence of so many thousands, both of avenging human beings and spirits: then made a terrible spectacle indeed, not only to myself but also to angels, to God, and to men (1 Cor. 4:9). Woe, I say, to me, who, bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness (Matt. 22:13), must pay in the pit of hell so many and such great torments, burned alike by unquenchable fire [Col. 0171A] and gnawed by the immortal worm.

“Is it not gentler for me, by bodily suffering and a momentary grief of mind, to escape that eternal pain and torment—the fire which will be in that furnace and does not know how to be extinguished? For what can anyone endure in fastings, vigils, or, to speak briefly, in any afflictions of soul or body, that is comparable to that infernal punishment, where ‘the shadow of death’ is found, ‘and no order, but everlasting horror dwelling’ (Job 10:22): where the body, destined for burning and to be food for fire, is afflicted with eternal torment; while the soul, sustained by a life that dies, is slain by a death that lives? And he will deserve to be tormented by this punishment of Gehenna who here scorns to confess his crimes in order that they may be blotted out.”

52 This fear, therefore, proceeding from consideration of punishment, is like another path leading a person to confession, so that one who confesses may not shrink from enduring certain severe things here, since one recognizes that far more grievous things threaten one who does not confess.

VII. There is yet another path, made smooth by the sure hope of divine mercy, which likewise brings a person to the practice of confession. It is sweeter for you to travel than the two paths of which we have spoken thus far. For, whereas you perceive everything in them to be harsh, in this path you find nothing at all except level ground. What can a person, mourning former wickedness, think sweeter, more delightful, or more joyful than the ineffable goodness of divine mercy? [Col. 0171C] For as, in the medical art, hot things are cured by cold and conversely cold things by hot, so our true physician, the merciful and kindly Jesus, by his sweetness in the confession of our sin soothes us when embittered, softens us when hardened, heals us when broken, and cheers us when sorrowful.

VIII. Securely, and with every certainty of firm hope, I confess to you the wounds of my soul, O unique and efficacious medicine for my wounds, you who were wounded for my iniquities and bruised for my crimes, good Jesus! (Isa. 53:5.) For you are good, for your mercy endures for ever. You came into this world to save sinners, and not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (Luke 5:31). I see you daily gathering innumerable [Col. 0171D] sinners, giving snow like wool, and eating ashes like bread (Ps. 147:16; 102:10). For those who had long been cold in their iniquity clothe you, as it were, with your own garments; and thus through repentance and confession you unite sinners to yourself, as you unite the righteous through continence and good action.

Behold, you do not despise David when he repents, but admit him to pardon when he confesses (2 Kings 12:13). You hear the Canaanite woman crying out (Matt. 15:22); you cleanse Mary as she weeps (Luke 7:38); you embrace Peter as he weeps (Matt. 26:75); you lead the thief into paradise when he prays (Luke 23:42). Finally, transforming into a vessel of election Paul—I mean Paul, who persecuted your Church, and therefore you yourself—you make him a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth [Col. 0172A] (Acts 9:51 [sic]). This is the good and level path, brothers: walk in it, because when you confess your injustices against yourselves to the Lord, he himself will forgive the ungodliness of your sin (Ps. 32:5).

IX. Behold, I have set before you three paths by which one comes to confession of sin. The first is consideration of your wickedness; the second, contemplation of Gehenna’s punishment; the third, hope in divine mercy. Consider, then, the enormity of your perversity, and shudder. Look upon the depth of Gehenna’s misery, and be greatly afraid. Contemplate the immensity of divine goodness, and trust. The first path will lead you to confession, confounded by horror; the second, shaken by terror; the third, comforted by certainty of hope.

Receive these first three waters of Judah’s redemption, [Col. 0172B] over which the Lord walked when he came to Bethlehem: namely, the methods by which he makes known to us how the first confession is acquired, so that the savor of inward refreshment may be poured into us. What then does this accomplish, or what is its benefit? Much in every way: it grants you forgiveness of your sins. For when you approach as their devout confessor, he who remits them is immediately present to you in fullness; and, having thereafter received pardon for your sins and grace likewise bestowed, you may live henceforth more rightly.

X. This confession is followed by another, in which you must confess to God his own gifts: there you accuse your evils; here you attribute his goods to him. This confession too is good, indeed very good, [Col. 0172C] because it not only preserves for you the gifts you have already received, but also makes you worthy to receive still greater gifts. For thus our good and just Lord God is accustomed to act: he heaps the gifts of his grace more abundantly upon those who have not yet received them, when he perceives them to be devout, diligent, and grateful for what they have already received.

The right paths by which you ought to approach this confession are these. First, consider carefully how beneficent, generous, and abundant in gifts he is. Is he not abundant and generous, who withholds gifts of grace not even from his enemies, causing the sun of his grace to rise upon evil and good, and raining upon righteous and unrighteous alike? (Matt. 5:45.) How is he not abundant, who, to embrace much in a few words, opens his hand and fills, not merely some, but every [Col. 0172D] living thing with blessing? (Ps. 145:16.) Thus there is none that can hide itself from his heat (Ps. 19:7). Who is so untamed in heart that he is not softened by considering this immense generosity? Who is so hard that he does not become tender? Who so lukewarm that he does not blaze and kindle to confess him?

53 XI. The second path is contemplation of the excellence of his gifts. For as the giver is abundant and generous, so the things he gives are neither few nor slight, but great and numerous. Which of us knows how to encompass their multitude by number, or can measure their greatness? Certainly each of you, if willing carefully to examine, can clearly weigh the gifts bestowed upon you, and see how devoutly and joyfully one ought to run by this path to his [Col. 0173A] confession.

For, to pass over for the moment in silence those gifts of your creation which you received in your first coming-to-be, and likewise to say nothing of the most excellent work of your redemption, which God—God made man, and God suffering in human nature a hard, dreadful, and unworthy death—accomplished so wonderfully and altogether incomprehensibly, beyond all understanding, not only human but angelic: how can you worthily comprehend in thought that he bore with you so patiently in the world as you remember yourself to have been there, called you so mercifully, was long-suffering there, and here most merciful; and, having called you, adorned you with such and so great an array of righteousness? He gave you to refrain throughout your life from things from which you had hardly been willing to abstain even for a single day; and what had been most laborious to endure even for a short hour is now most delightful for you to bear all your days.

XII. Thanks to you, Lord, good and sweet, kindly and gracious. You created me when I did not exist; you redeemed me when lost; you justified me when called, forgiving my sins and bestowing your gifts: constancy in reading, devotion in prayer, zeal in meditation, sweetness in speculation, purity in contemplation; granting health in my body, as you know expedient for me, so that you may make me robust and strong for good work. At times you give infirmity, to draw me back from evil action and make me fearful, always and in all things zealous for my salvation. You weary me in the warfare of temptation, then again comfort me with the peace [Col. 0173C] of rest: there, lest I become exalted; here, lest I become too faint-hearted. Everywhere and always assisting me, and making all things—my evil things as well as my good—work together for my good.

Add after this; add also to these things, that [variant: because] you bestowed all this upon one who deserved nothing. For what had I first done, that you should judge me worthy of so many, such, and so great gifts? I did nothing good, nothing that was not evil; yet you bestowed every good thing. You are indeed to be praised because you gave so much; but because you gave it to one unworthy, you are surely to be greatly admired. This, then, is also the path of which we speak that leads to confession: so that, if he seems worthy to be devoutly praised because he gave such great and such gifts, he may seem to you worthy of being praised much more devoutly because he chose to give them to one so small and such as you.

[Col. 0173D] XIII. You therefore have three paths leading also to this confession. The first is consideration of divine generosity; the second, contemplation of the excellence of his gift; the third, awareness that no preceding merit made you worthy to receive anything. The first stirs you to admiration, so that you may rightly marvel at the abundance of such generosity. The second invites you to love, so that you may be inflamed with love for him whom you recognize to have given you such and so great things. The third pours into you salutary humility, so that, when you consider both that you have received much and that you have deserved absolutely nothing, attributing none of the good things you see in yourself to yourself but ascribing all to him by whose gift they exist, you may profitably humble yourself in the sight of the most generous giver.

Behold, we have shown you a twofold confession: one by which we uncover our hidden evils; the other by which we praise God for his gift. To each we have assigned three methods, by which they may be acquired when absent and exercised when present. When, by these methods, you both impute to yourself the evils which you remember having committed and ascribe to God the goods which you perceive to be present in you, the Lord breathes into you the anointing of his grace; as though walking over the waters, namely the waters of Judah’s redemption, the Lord walks. For the waters, as we said above, by which Judah is redeemed are the methods and paths by which confession is delivered from wrongful denial. Judah is, as it were, held captive when confession is not practiced because the obstinacy of denial stands in its way. There are [Col. 0174B] still other confessions belonging to Judah, which likewise have their own methods and paths—their, as it were, waters of redemption—over which the Lord walks while by these same paths and methods he stirs us to acquire and practice them. But since the hour now prevents us from speaking of these matters at present, with the Lord’s help we shall treat of them another time, to the praise and glory of him who is God blessed above all for ever. Amen.

54 SERMON XIV. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD. On the fourfold confession, the four breads, and the four kinds of human sickness.

SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON.—1. Analogy between the bodily and spiritual physician in the curing of diseases.—2. One confession concerns one’s own sin, another divine [Col. 0174C] praise; in both, steadfastness of faith is necessary.—3. The first path to steadfast confession of faith is the Passion of our Redeemer.—4. The second is the strength of your Helper.—5. The third is the greatness of the reward.—6. The confession of the blessed in their homeland, which is a voice of joy and praise, has a threefold basis.—7. The fourfold confession and the three paths of each are recapitulated.—8. Bethlehem, that is, the house of bread, in which the Lord is fed in four ways.—9. First, bread baked under ashes, that is, repentance; second, bread from the frying-pan, that is, labor; third, bread from the griddle, that is, tribulation; fourth, bread from the burning oven, which belongs to the angels.—10. The soul’s sickness is fourfold: first, hardness of heart.—11. Second, sloth in work; third, blasphemy in faith.—12. Fourth, ignorance of blessed eternity.—13. Every good must be attributed to God.

I. Whoever undertakes the medical art ought to apply such great and such careful attention to preparing remedies that, in a sick person requiring only purgation, he may purge the things which need purging, so that, according to the assertion of Hippocrates, that most skillful of physicians, he may “help and do no harm.” The spiritual physician of souls, the preacher of the word of life, ought certainly to show like care toward every sinful patient in the spiritual treatment of holy preaching. For just as one who is physically sick cannot readily attain full health unless the harmful humors which feed and cause the disease are first expelled, so it is beyond doubt that no sinner can attain true salvation if the hidden sins [Col. 0175A] are not first vomited out by the draught of confession—especially a person who, by rooting the mind deeply in an affection for criminal sin, is not merely sick but, what is worse, even dead.

For what are the corruptions of vices, especially sins committed secretly and hidden in the conscience, but certain pernicious humors lying concealed in the body and destroying it? As these, if not expelled, produce death, so those sins, if not disclosed through confession, lead to condemnation. Again, what is preaching that exhorts confession but the prescription of a potion, pointing out an antidote? Hence, in the sermon we recently delivered concerning the power of confession, we composed so lengthy a discourse because we know it to be most necessary.

II. The first confession is that by which we uncover our hidden evils. But because in this confession, which proceeds from fear, our conscience is burdened, another confession follows, by which your burdened conscience is relieved [variant: consoled]. This is practiced when God is blessed and praised in his gifts. This confession is like an electuary, soothing and strengthening the stomach of the mind; in it the soul finds the repose of consolation after it has borne the toil of distress in the draught of the preceding confession. In that confession by which you reveal your sins, receiving pardon, you are cleansed of pernicious humors. But in this confession, by which you bless God in his gifts, receiving grace, you are adorned with an inward visitation. [Col. 0175C]

Yet after being thus cleansed and adorned—cleansed, I say, through the mercy of pardon, adorned through the generosity of grace—you must possess the virtue of steadfastness. For he who visits you at dawn tests you suddenly (Job 7:18), so that, in order to preserve the devotion of holiness, you must fight against the hidden tempter and, when necessary, contend against the open persecutor in defense of the virtue of faith. Therefore, in this contest for defense of the faith, confess not only to God but confess God; for if you confess him before human beings, he too will confess you before his Father (Luke 12:8). But if you deny him, he too will deny you.

III. If you ask what path can lead you to this confession, let the first—and indeed a very straight—path be the Passion of our Redeemer. Therefore run with patience the contest set before you, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of life, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame (Heb. 12:1–2). These are Paul’s words, with which Peter, his companion and colleague in martyrdom and fellow apostle, agrees: “Christ,” he says, “suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:2 [sic]). Nor is it strange that you suffer for him who suffered for you—indeed, the Lord for the servant.

55 Remember that the servant is not greater than his master: if they persecuted him, they will persecute you also (John 15:20). Therefore, if the world hates you, know that it hated him before you (ibid., v. 18). And if they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household? (Matt. 18:25 [sic].)

IV. Let the second path be the strength of your Helper, because he for whom you fight will surely and manfully stand by you so that you may conquer. Was not blessed Stephen, surrounded by a rain of stones, granted to see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God? (Acts 7:55.) In hearing that he was standing, understand that he was fighting; in hearing that he was at the right hand of God’s power, recognize that he was overcoming. Standing, he wages war and fights; powerful, he conquers and triumphs, because standing belongs to battle and triumph belongs to strength.

Therefore, when those delivering you up lead you away, put it in your heart not to premeditate how you will answer, because he himself will give you, in that same hour, a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or gainsay [Col. 0176B] (Luke 21:14–15).

V. Let the third path be that eternal reward, because you will reign also with him for whom you suffer. Therefore, you who suffer for righteousness’ sake, know yourself blessed, because the kingdom of heaven will be the reward of your labors. Hence you may rejoice and exult in that day when people hate you, reproach you, cast out your name as evil, and falsely say every evil thing against you, because your reward is great in heaven (Luke 26:22 [sic]).

By these three paths access to this confession is granted. Let the first be the Passion of the Redeemer; the second, the strength of the Helper; the third, the greatness of the Reward. Let the Passion of the Redeemer serve you as an example, the strength of the Helper as assistance, and the greatness of the reward as consolation: the Passion as an example, that we may imitate; the strength as assistance, that we may be rewarded; the reward as consolation, that we may rejoice.

VI. This is followed by a certain confession, joyful indeed and joy-giving, blessed and beatifying; but it will be in the future, not in the present; in the homeland, not on the way; in the kingdom, not in exile. This is that of which holy David says: “With the voice,” he says, “of exultation and confession, the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 42:5). In that heavenly Jerusalem is this confession, whither the tribes ascend daily—the tribes, I say, of the Lord—to confess the name of the Lord (Ps. 122:4). The blessed citizens who dwell in the Lord’s house, not made with hands, eternal in heaven, devote themselves to it, praising him unto ages of ages [Col. 0176D] (Ps. 84:5), singing his mercies for ever; in their mouth resounds a song of joy and a voice of praise.

They practice this confession for three reasons, as though approaching it by as many paths: because they have been delivered from eternal perdition; because they have attained heavenly joys; and because they know these joys will endure without any loss. These three causes invite them to confess their God: escape from captivity, exultation in blessedness, and security concerning eternity.

VII. You therefore have set before you four kinds of confession. The saints practice three in the present exile, while the blessed practice the fourth in the heavenly kingdom. The first is confession of sin and belongs to penitents; the second, confession of merit, belongs to those living well; the third, confession of faith, is practiced by holy martyrs; the fourth, confession of reward, is practiced without any failure by the happy citizens of the heavenly homeland. The joyfulness of pardon rewards the first; an abundance of grace increases the second; the strength of steadfastness fortifies the third; the splendor of unfailing glory adorns the fourth.

Each of these four confessions has three paths leading to it. The paths of the first confession are: consideration of the enormity of guilt, of the punishment of Gehenna, and of the kindness of mercy. The enormity of guilt produces horror in the one considering it, so that one is ashamed to be such a person. The calamity of punishment instills terror, so that one fears; the kindness of mercy instills confidence, so that one does not despair.

The paths to the second confession are the abundance of divine generosity, the excellence of his gift, and awareness that no prior merit exists. As you proceed by the first path, generosity recognized stirs you to astonishment, so that you marvel. Through the second, the excellence of his gifts seen invites you to love, so that you are inflamed. Through the third, your own fragility kept before your eyes enlightens you, so that you may be enlightened [variant: humbled]. [Col. 0177B]

The paths of the third confession are the Passion of the Redeemer, the strength of the Helper, and the exaltedness of the Rewarder. The first is offered to martyrs as an example, that they may imitate it; the second as help, that they may be strengthened; the third as consolation, that they may be gladdened. The following three things invite one to the fourth confession: that they have been freed from captivity; that they have attained blessedness; and that they are tranquil in full and perfect security.

These things we have said concerning the fourfold Judah [that is, confession] and the waters of its redemption, assigning, as you know, three waters to each Judah. Over these waters of Judah’s redemption the Lord walked and came to Bethlehem. For when the soul practices these four kinds of confession within itself, 56 and approaches each by its own paths, it receives within itself as an abiding guest the almighty God, who celebrates within it and with it an inward and spiritual refreshment.

VIII. For if Bethlehem is the house of bread, how is the mind of the devout penitent who practices confession of sin not a house of bread? How is the mind of one living continently, who practices confession of merit, not such a house? Or the mind of the holy martyr who fights for confession of the Catholic faith? Or, finally, the mind of the blessed citizen who celebrates confession of eternal joy?

Is not the Lord fed at the mind of the penitent, when in the Psalms he says that he eats ashes like bread (Ps. 102:10), thus incorporating the sinner into himself through repentance just as he incorporates the saint through righteousness? As you know, although he once reclined with the Pharisee, he took delight in the feasts of the mind of the sinful—yet penitent—woman, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0177D] St. Gregory, Homily 36.] (Luke 7:36). Who can deny that he also feasts with those who live continently and act well, when he himself says that his food is to fulfill the will of his Father? (John 4:34.)

He hints at this elsewhere also, where he declares that, if one has heard with full obedience the voice of his exhortation and opened to him the door of faith and confession, he will enter that person and dine with that person, and that person with him (Rev. 3:20). Thus [Col. 0178A] the mind becomes a kind of Bethlehem, when, having attained true security through so great and such a guest, it rejoices to celebrate within itself a savory refreshment, according to Solomon’s saying that a secure mind is a continual feast (Prov. 15:15).

If anyone were to call the zeal of faith in the spiritual athlete his bread, I think no sound-minded person would contradict this. For what else did he hunger for when, coming to the fig tree, he found nothing in it except leaves, although, as the Evangelist says, it was not the season for figs? (Mark 2:13 [sic].) What else, I say, did he hunger for except the faith of the Jews? They had in themselves nothing but the leaves of legal words. And it was not the time for them to bear the fruit of faith, because the fullness of the Gentiles had first to enter, and so all Israel would be saved [Col. 0178B] (Rom. 2:25 [sic]).

That he feasts daily—indeed, continually and splendidly—with those happy persons in the heavenly homeland is beyond doubt, for he has appointed for them, as his Father appointed for him, a kingdom, that they may eat and drink at his table in his kingdom (Luke 21:29 [sic]). There he satisfies them with the fat of wheat; there David will be satisfied because the glory of his Lord will be manifested (Ps. 147:14). Behold, as we expounded Judah to you in four ways, so likewise we have shown you Bethlehem as fourfold, assigning its own bread to each.

IX. In the first house, the bread is baked under ashes, because, inasmuch as it pertains to humility, it is the ash-baked bread of repentance, and it is the bread of sorrow. Holy David seems to speak of this when he commands us to rise after we have sat down, we who eat the bread of sorrow (Ps. 127:2). This means nothing else than that we can then be raised into hope of pardon when, having first been fed in the groaning of repentance with the bread of tears (Ps. 80:6), we have perfectly fulfilled the work of complete humility belonging to true repentance.

The bread of the second house, because of the practice of laborious action, seems to me capable of being referred to the frying-pan; it is the bread of labor. The same Psalmist mentions it when he says that you shall eat the labors of your hands, and therefore you are blessed, and it shall go well with you (Ps. 128:2).

There is also bread from the griddle in the third house, because it is fried by the fire of great struggle—one who endeavors to stand and contend, even unto blood and even unto death itself, in defense of the faith—and it is the bread of tribulation. Such bread wrathful Ahab, carried away into fury because the holy prophet had spoken words of truth to him, once commanded to be set before him, saying: “Put this man into prison, and sustain him with bread of tribulation and water of affliction” (2 Kings 22:27).

But the bread of the fourth house is baked in an oven kindled by that great fire of unfailing charity—the furnace of the Lord, which is in Jerusalem—and it is the bread of angels, of which whoever eats shall hunger no more (John 6:35).

X. You therefore have the fourfold Judah and a spiritual bread assigned to each house. You also have the three waters of Judah’s redemption, over which [Col. 0179A] the Lord walks in order to come to Bethlehem: the methods and paths shown above, leading us to true confession and pouring into us the taste of spiritual refreshment, its savory sweetness, so to speak, in those four houses we have mentioned, assigned to each Judah.

There is very great benefit in this coming of his into Bethlehem, and altogether great salvation. Therefore at the end it is said here that then every person will be saved, because, behold, he will come. If you understand, according to the sense which we have had in hand until now, what it is for the Lord to come to Bethlehem, you consequently know that the salvation of every person who desires to be saved spiritually consists in that coming of his. 57 Nor can any inward person be healed at all unless one celebrates with him this sweet and savory refreshment of which we have already said something.

But consider what is the sickness of this person of whom we speak, and see whether it is not so. There is someone who has cast himself behind his own back and lies incorrigible in sin, harder than diamond; having no regard for divine fear, but with forehead outwardly worn smooth and an unconquerable heart, becoming in every respect a rebellious house (Ezek. 12:3). Is he not sick—indeed, almost unto death—who, according to his hardness and impenitent heart, stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God? (Rom. 2:5.)

XI. There is another, perhaps not burdened by any great weight of sin, yet clothed in no adornment of good work: lying languid and negligent. As not cold in crime, so neither hot in virtue, but lukewarm in torpor and therefore to be vomited from the Lord’s mouth (Rev. 3:16). Who but a madman would call this person healthy? From the sole of the foot, which walks in thought, to the head, which ought to rise high in action, [Col. 0179C] there is no health in him (Isa. 1:6).

Certainly, if in some sense the soul’s being healthy is also its being beautiful—for one who is sound in health consequently shines also in appearance—I do not know how you could admit this person to be healthy. Not watching but sleeping, he does not keep the garments of his works (Rev. 16:15). Indeed, he possesses none, but walks naked, and all see his shame. And what will you judge concerning one weakened in mind by a sluggish infirmity, who fails in faith because he does not defend it? He retains faith in his heart, by which he may believe unto righteousness, but does not dare to open his mouth to confess unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). Will you say salvation is present in one whom you see not standing manfully in defense of the faith? For while he sins against faith, which saves, salvation is surely absent from him; and therefore he is not healthy. For if he were strong and healthy in heart, he would undoubtedly fight manfully for the faith. As the Apostle says concerning the saints: “Who through faith conquered kingdoms, because they recovered from weakness, became strong in battle” (Heb. 11:34). Intending to say, “they became strong in battle,” he first said, “they recovered from weakness,” in order to make known to us that no one can [Col. 0180A] ascend against the enemy and stand in the breach for the house of Israel, so as to stand in battle on the day of the Lord (Ezek. 13:5), unless that person has first recovered from weakness through the strength of the Spirit.

XII. I think you would not affirm true health to be in that person in whose land—the land of those who live pleasantly (Job 28:13)—wisdom cannot be found.
