Since such a person is deep through concupiscence and bitter through malice, “the deep says, ‘Wisdom is not in me’” (ibid., v. 12), and the sea says that it is not with it. How can such a person be said to possess health, when one neither tastes beforehand, by the taste of contemplation, the sweetness of supreme delight nor knows how to seek it with the palate of desiring affection?

These, then, are the four kinds of human sickness: hardness, sloth, blasphemy, [Col. 0180B] and ignorance—utterly opposed to the fourfold Judah and the Lord’s four corresponding breads. The spiritual person of whom we speak will by no means be saved from them unless, in the manner described above, the Lord walks over the waters of Judah’s redemption in order to come to Bethlehem. Hardness is in the heart; sloth in action; blasphemy in faith; and ignorance concerns that eternal and blessed sweetness, that blessed and sweet eternity.

XIII. But the Lord walks upon the waters of Judah’s redemption and comes to Bethlehem. That is, He shows this infirm man the ways by which he can approach the true confession which, as we indicated above, is fourfold; and He pours into him the most delicious sweetness of inward refreshment, which, we said, consists in the fourfold house of bread [Col. 0180C]. Then indeed, to show how man is saved, hardness, which is the first kind of sickness, is softened. And, his hardness softened, the penitent first eats, in the first house, which is the austerity of penitence, the bread that is the bread of sorrow. And in the first Judah he makes confession of sin.

Next, sloth, belonging to the second kind of infirmity, is driven away; and, it having been driven away, the devout person eats in the second house, which is persistence in good action, the second bread, which is the bread of labor. And in the second Judah he makes confession of merit. After this, blasphemy, which claims for itself the third kind of infirmity, is destroyed. And, it having been destroyed, the faithful person eats in the third house, which is the strength of right belief, the third bread, which is the bread of tribulation [Col. 0180D]. And in the third Judah he makes confession of faith.

Finally, ignorance, which is the fourth kind of sickness, is cast out. Once it has been cast out, in the fourth house, which is the eternity of heavenly blessedness, he eats the fourth bread—though not yet in reality and effect, yet in vision and desire—which is the bread of angels. And in the fourth Judah, through thought and longing, he celebrates the confession of joy, “with the voice of confession and exultation,” sending forth the sound of one exulting (Ps. 41:5). Rightly, therefore, man is said to be saved when the Lord comes to Bethlehem, walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption. But what and how many these waters are, or what it is for Judah to be redeemed through them, and from what, has, I think, been shown in part above, partly in this discourse and partly in that which immediately preceded it [Col. 0181A].

Behold, brethren, we have prolonged our words upon the words of this responsory into more sermons than we had supposed. For when we began to speak, we did not have all these matters together in our meditation; rather, we searched them out afterward, as the Spirit of truth went before us by His gratuitous grace and revealed them to us. For we thought that we could encompass in one sermon what we scarcely find that we have completed in four [alternative reading: invenimur, “we are found to have completed”]. Since this is so, what else ought to be understood here except what is plainly given to be understood: that, since in expounding there afterward became clear what had previously lain hidden in reflection, we should believe that what did not at first become clear while we were thinking in secret was given on your behalf.

[Col. 0181B] Thus, indeed, we shall destroy pride within ourselves, humbly recognizing that the good which is in us is neither from us nor for us alone. But since some further matters concerning these words still occur to us for discussion, let us defer them to another sermon: both because much has already been said, and because what remains to be said cannot be completed in few words. For they are so great and so profound that we do not think they can be encompassed in one discourse. May that Holy Spirit in whom we hope, who has brought us thus far, deign to open your eyes to contemplate the wonders of His law. May He bestow upon us His grace both in understanding and in speaking, to His praise and to your edification. [Col. 0181C] To Him, with the Father and the Son, from whom He proceeds eternally, be honor and glory for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XV. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

On the ways in which the minds of preachers are disposed and moved in teaching, and on fastidious hearers.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. How we should think little of ourselves and greatly of others.  
2. Just as Blessed Augustine’s tongue sometimes moved beyond his intention, so too does that of preachers.  
3. At one time they have an abundance of words, at another a scarcity.  
4. The many snares of vainglory, and the character of this vice.  
5. Two things to be avoided by hearers: fastidiousness and curiosity.  
6. The writings of the holy Fathers commended to the preacher.  
7. In preaching, not affected arrangement of words but instruction of hearts is to be considered above all [Col. 0181D].  
8. What preachers ought to be as guardians of God’s Bride, that is, the Church.  
9. The Lord’s going forth from Samaria—that is, from hidden custody—to us.  
10. How greatly the Lord’s coming was desired by the world.

### I

“The Lord shall go forth from Samaria to the gate that faces the East, and shall come to Bethlehem, walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption; then every man shall be saved, because He shall come.”

> [Note: [Col. 0181] From the Office of the Church; see above, Second Sunday of Advent, third nocturn.]

Beloved, we acknowledge ourselves to be your debtors, and it is time that we should strive, according to our powers, to fulfill what we promised. But before we approach the investigation of the depths contained in these words, it pleases us briefly to recall how wonderfully almighty God has ordered us in His word. For very often, as we said at the end of the preceding sermon, many things occur to us while we are speaking before you which did not become clear while we were meditating in secret and perhaps seeking them with much effort. Thus we may not attribute the gift of understanding to our own subtlety, but may believe that it is bestowed for the sake of those before whom it is given.

[Col. 0182A] And thus it comes about that we think humbly and little of ourselves, but greatly of others, “not walking in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for us” (Ps. 130:1). Otherwise, we turn over in meditation many more things in ourselves in order to speak of them later than we actually bring forth in the subsequent speech, because they do not occur to us; at that time He disposes our mind and tongue and draws them to other things, in whose hand are we and our words. For although what we intend to say has been treated in thought [Col. 0182B], still the good things which, at the time of speaking, the Lord supplies to the mind and the mind to its minister are perhaps more necessary, and therefore better so far as they are concerned, for those hearers who are then present.

### II

We read that this happened on one occasion to our eminent father and teacher, Blessed Augustine. While, as was his custom, he was addressing the people, his tongue suddenly turned, in the course of speaking, to something other than either his purpose or the subject he was treating. At a suitable time afterward, a certain man humbly approached him; and that anointing which teaches concerning all things (1 John 2:27) disclosed through those unpremeditated words what the man had been carrying in his mind [Col. 0182C].

Sometimes, however, when the Spirit visits the mind, we grasp many things in meditation; and afterward, when the same Spirit moves the tongue, we pour forth those same many things in speech. In this He provides some good both for ourselves and for our hearers: He Himself feeds us inwardly. Thus it happens that, since every good in us comes not from ourselves but from Him, He provides merit both for us through our hearers and for them through us; preserving with Himself for recompense both the preaching which we expend in speaking to them and the humility which they show to us in hearing.

### III

Yet often neither are many things clear to us in meditation for us to bring forth, nor afterward, even if we wish, are we able to bring them forth. Thus, by temporarily withholding from our minds the gift of understanding, and consequently withholding from your ears a word through us, He healthfully humbles us, showing us that “we are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as of ourselves, but our sufficiency is from Him” (2 Cor. 3:5) [Col. 0182D]. And likewise He makes you diligent and devout in prayer, when you know that He has “commanded the clouds that they should not rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6), so that He may first pour into us what we are to pour out to you.

And thus, while you cry to God with one accord, both our humility and your prayer cause the gift of understanding—which we are to dispense, as He sends it—to return to us more abundantly and, in a manner, more joyfully than if it had never been withdrawn [Col. 0183A]. But while saying these things about ourselves who speak and about you who hear, we add this also: in one and the same word of God, the danger touches our tongue more than it touches your ear.

### IV

For you hear more safely in proportion as you hear more humbly; but we walk more perilously in the Lord’s discourse in proportion as the pride which, among other vices, is most hostile to grace attacks us more grievously. Sometimes we strive to say something well in order to please you who hear; or [alternative reading: qui, “who,” for vel, “or”], even if perhaps we do not greatly desire to please, we nevertheless fear to displease. Sometimes we disgracefully delight [alternative reading: delectari, “to delight”] in the praise which you offer us, though we have sought it neither in heart nor in speech. Now, to wish to please and not to wish to displease is not always evil; but blessed is he who seeks in both to please that One alone, whom it is best to please and worst to displease [Col. 0183B]. But we cannot deny that the third thing I mentioned—namely, delighting in praise not sought but offered by hearers—is evil.

Indeed, if we who speak happen to be overtaken by it, we must turn before the eyes of Him to whom alone honor and glory are due, return to our heart, and wipe it clean with frequent lamentations. For the weak mind gladly and joyfully receives sweet words of praise. It often even reviews inwardly words which it has spoken well when perhaps it hears nothing outwardly pertaining to praise; and, considering that others know these things through it, and reporting to itself that they please them greatly, it rejoices vainly in a kind of private inward gladness [Col. 0183C].

And since the mind cannot entertain even these things without serious guilt, what shall we say of the person whose mouth, “speaking from the abundance of the heart” (Luke 6:45), openly boasts, repeatedly rehearsing what he has deeply conceived and already uttered, and who, puffed up by the foulest and emptiest wind of arrogance, confidently affirms what he has said? How should that man also be laughed at and mocked, who seeks praise in his heart but appears to avoid it with his mouth, complaining that nothing at all which he has said is of any value, and declaring that he would rather have been silent than have spoken so? His whole purpose in this outward self-accusation is to incite others to praise him, so that, when they hear him complain so anxiously with his mouth and do not see the shameful appetite for empty glory which he waits for so impatiently in his heart and seeks so ardently, they may, as though consoling him, declare that he has spoken well and affirm that he is rightly to be praised for words uttered so praiseworthily [Col. 0183D]. A detestable kind of boasting indeed: humbling oneself in order to be exalted, and seeking praise by fleeing from it.

### V

These evils, brethren, and others of this kind, lie in wait for those who speak; from them you who hear are free. For the beauty of your devotion, kept hidden within you, is neither seen nor known by outward hearing, and so is not darkened by the dust of human praise. But as we must beware this destructive pest of pride, so you also must beware the most wretched vice of fastidiousness and curiosity.

For there are very many whom we have often experienced receiving with the greatest distaste the word in the sermons customarily recited on feast days. They make themselves present more from habit than from affection, waiting for and desiring the end more than desiring or gathering for themselves any spiritual edification [Col. 0184A]. Not only so; when, because of the discipline of the order, they cannot be absent bodily, burdened by the ruinous weight of fastidiousness, they draw their faces down into their hoods, restrain the wandering of their eyes as if with the bridle of gravity, and give themselves over to idle sleep.

There are others who willingly hear what is said, but approve absolutely nothing unless something new and unheard is said. Indeed, when the sermon is over, even if at that time they cannot do so with spoken words, they customarily exchange remarks with one another through gestures of the fingers—something we ourselves have often observed and frequently heard them discuss in this fashion [Col. 0184B]: “Do not Augustine, Gregory, and the other doctors say these same things? He has memorized things stolen here and there from the books of the doctors, and recited them to us as a sermon, as though we too could not see, as he did, and gather these matters.”

### VI

This is the voice of those unwilling to pay attention. For, as the comic poet says: “Nothing is said which has not been said before.” This, I say, is their voice—as though we either could or ought to say anything which the holy doctors who preceded us have not said and left in their writings for our instruction. Especially since the Psalmist commands us to “bless the Lord in the churches, from the fountains of Israel” (Ps. 67:27) [Col. 0184C]. And the sons of Aaron were struck down by God in Leviticus (Lev. 10:1), because they offered strange fire which had not been commanded them.

To whom should I say that these people are like, if not to those carnal Israelites who, loathing manna, desired Egyptian foods, as you know (Num. 21:5)? But if these people paid careful attention to what their punishment was, they would not, I think, say such things.

### VII

But with what mockery and ridicule will you judge those worthy of being censured who, having absolutely no understanding of Scripture, or very little, wholly reject a sermon addressed to them unless it is entirely delivered in Latin words—and, what is still more laughable, unless it is expressed in certain pompous and unusual words [Col. 0184D]? “He thought well and acutely,” they say, “but whatever he said is less credible and less acceptable because he used this vulgar manner of speech in his delivery”—though they themselves understand nothing whatever of all that is said unless it is explained to them in ordinary language.

But you, brethren, must not be so. Let your minds hunger for the word of God with such eagerness that you hunger for it again. But in that same word avoid every manner of speaking which does not edify. And be more intent [alternative reading: magis quoque, “moreover/more also”] that your hearts be formed than that words be artfully arranged for you. Therefore, cleansing yourselves from these dregs, have compassion upon our many miseries. With faithful minds raised up, sigh to Him for us, who is our sole hope and singular refuge in all these matters which we have explained above to you, and in the other evils which are renewed in us [Col. 0185A]. May He who washed the feet of those who clung to His teaching also make beautiful for you the feet of those who preach the Gospel (Rom. 10), so that we may not be like the many who adulterate the word of God, but may speak in Christ before God sincerely, as from God.

### VIII

And may we who have been appointed for this purpose, to serve as guardians of His bride, the holy Church—which you are—by His conveying His words through us, ensure [alternative reading: proferamus, “bring forth”] that she loves Him and praises Him, and not, by adulterating Him, seek within her anything of our own which belongs to God alone. Thus, as faithful attendants and friends of the Bridegroom, standing sincerely in the uprightness of inward intention and hearing Him with the ears of the heart, may we rejoice with joy—not because of our own voice, but because of His voice (John 3:29) [Col. 0185B].

For, as He Himself says, “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but he who seeks the glory of Him who sent him is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him” (John 7:18). He speaks from himself who judges that what he says comes from himself; likewise he speaks from himself who speaks for his own sake alone, whether for the gain of some temporal advantage or for the favor of human praise. But assist our weakness with your prayers, that, walking wisely between Him and you, we may seek in you the glory of Him who sent us.

### IX

Hear what He Himself has graciously revealed to us in these most holy and profound words, so that we in turn may reveal it to you for His praise and your benefit: “The Lord shall go forth from Samaria to the gate that faces the East.” By this going forth of the Lord from Samaria, we understand His saving coming to humankind from that lofty and secret custody in which the Father kept Him in His bosom [Col. 0185C]. For, as He Himself says, “I went forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:28). And according to the Psalmist’s saying: “His going forth is from the height of heaven” (Ps. 18:7).

Was He not in custody who, invisible, was hidden in the invisible Father? For as long as He possessed in Himself no nature other than the divine, which is also invisible, He was, as it were, within. But when “the Word was made flesh”—that is, when God became man—and dwelt among us (John 1:14), and, as Jeremiah says, “was seen upon earth and conversed with men” (Baruch 3:38) [Col. 0185D], then indeed He went forth from the Samaria of which we speak.

### X

It was this going forth that she of old ardently longed to see in the Song of Songs, she who, stirred by great desire, said: “Who will give You to me as my brother, that I may find You outside?” (Song 8:1). She had already found Him within, because she believed in Him whom she knew to be invisible in His divinity. But she desires to see Him outside, that He might appear in that nature which could be seen by bodily eyes.

But for Him to appear in such a nature, He had to assume it into the unity of His person and not hide Himself beneath some phantom form; rather, that in which He appeared had to be true. Thus He would be a brother because He would be man [Col. 0186A]. Therefore she first wished Him to become her brother, so that she might afterward find Him outside. For after He became our brother and our flesh, being made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man, He went forth from the secrecy of the Father’s Samaria into the public realm of our nature. Thus He was found outside in our nature, who had been within in His own. He is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

On Christ’s coming to the Church through the Virgin Mary.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The varied meaning of “gate” in Scripture.  
2. The eastern gate is the Virgin Mary, addressed in a notable apostrophe [Col. 0186B].  
3. Before Mary, no one consecrated to God a purpose of virginity.  
4. Through Mary, the fullness of grace flows to believers.  
5. The Church of the Gentiles received Christ born of the Virgin, as Pharaoh’s daughter received Moses from the wicker basket.  
6. Bethlehem, that is, the house of bread: three kinds of bread which it rejects.  
7. Ten approved breads of the Church enumerated.  
8. The fruit of each within the Church.

### I

Where did God, going forth from Samaria, first appear? Certainly at the gate which faces the East. For He assumed from the Virgin Mary the appearance in which He was seen. Christ is one kind of gate; concerning Him you have the statement in Job regarding the ungodly: “His friends shall be far from salvation, and they shall be crushed in the gate” (Job 5:4). For the people of the synagogue, withdrawing themselves from true salvation, were corrupted by unbelief at Christ’s coming [Col. 0186C].

There is another gate pertaining to faith, of which holy David says: “He shall not be confounded when he speaks with his enemies in the gate” (Ps. 126:5), that is, when he disputes with heretics in defense of the faith [variant: “for the protection of the faith”]. The good work we perform is also a kind of gate, because through it we go out from the good will we inwardly possess before God to the outward eyes of our neighbors. Of this holy Job says: “When I went forth to the gate of the city” (Job 29:7)—that is, when I went outwardly to perform good work before others.

And departure from this life is a gate for us. Thus we read in Ezekiel (ch. 40:3) that the prophet, standing within, had his eyes directed outward toward the gate [Col. 0186D]. This means that every elect person who lives in the faith of the Church ought to extend his desire toward his departure from this life, so that he may be with Christ.

### II

The holy and everlasting gate is also the Virgin, as we find said in the same Ezekiel: “This gate shall be shut, and it shall not be opened” (Ezek. 44:2). For she remained uncorrupted before childbirth and unharmed after childbirth. The Lord, going forth from Samaria, came to this gate; for she was open in mind through faith and closed in body through chastity, and without defilement conceived Him in purity and without injury gave birth to Him intact.

Truly, O blessed Virgin, you are the eastern gate in Ezekiel. You are also the gate of which we are now speaking, facing the East; for in you Christ had both His entrance and His exit without any violation, and through you we too have entrance to the kingdom [Col. 0187A]. And you never fail to practice holiness, being full of grace. You strive to please Christ alone, since none like you is seen before you, nor shall any follow you.

For let our youth be the east, from which the sun of our age first rises. Of it the Gospel says that “many shall come from the East” (Matt. 8:11), because many come to Christ from their very youth. And in a certain sense the Jewish people are the east, as is found in the Apocalypse: “Three gates from the East” (Rev. 21:13), because the faith of the Holy Trinity was announced to them also. There is likewise [alternative reading: quidam, “a certain”] the true East, the Lord Christ, toward whom you look, that you may please Him alone in inward intention. There is also the work of holiness, toward which you likewise look, that you may practice it in your manner of life for His name.

### III

Nearly the whole world still inclined toward the west of the flesh, working in it and bringing forth from it the fruit of death, when you, raising your eyes toward the east of virginity, bore within yourself the glory of future incorruption [Col. 0187B]. What a most beautiful and blessed state of the holy Church will shine forth, in which her faithful “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22:30)!

For what woman at that time was able or willing to utter this saying: “I know not a man” (Luke 1:34)? Certainly you will maintain that there was none then, if you fully recognize the force of those words. For what is “I know not a man” except “I do not intend to know a man”? Not merely ignorant of man in the present, but holding a firm purpose to remain so throughout all my life.

Indeed, a barren woman was then considered cursed, so much so that Jephthah’s daughter (Judg. 11:34) thought it more an occasion for lament and grief that she carried virginal flesh to the grave than that she was slain by her father’s sword [Col. 0187C]. But you looked to Christ in inward intention; in chaste conduct you looked toward the east, the virginity of the flesh. You looked, I say, beyond all women, and therefore are proclaimed blessed among all throughout the ages. Yet Him whom you alone then received, you did not wish to possess alone; rather, He who came from the bosom of the Father to you also came through you as far as us.

### IV

Thus the dew which was first upon the fleece alone afterward moistened the whole threshing-floor (Judg. 6:40), so that she alone first received Him, in order then to bring Him to all nations. This is what holy David says: “He shall first descend like rain upon the fleece, and then like drops falling upon the earth” (Ps. 71:6). He first descends upon the fleece, then upon the earth. But upon the fleece He descends as rain, upon the earth as drops. For Christ first came to the Virgin with the fullness of grace, then called His faithful and elect to share in it.

Therefore, as dew was first in the fleece and then on the threshing-floor, so the Lord, going forth from Samaria, first came to the gate facing the East and then to Bethlehem [Col. 0188A]. This is what we sing of her in the Mass:

> [Note: [Col. 0187D] In the Preface of the Mass, an encomium of Mary.]

First she conceived her only-begotten Son through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit; and afterward, while the glory of virginity remained, she poured forth upon this world the eternal light, Jesus Christ our Lord.

For Bethlehem is called the Church from among the Gentiles, that it may be the house of Him who says: “I am the living bread” (John 6:52). The Lord came to this house of bread after going forth from Samaria to the gate facing the East. For from the bosom of the Father He came to the Virgin through assumption of flesh, and through her mediation He came by faith to the Church.

### V

As I say this, I recall to mind that outstanding ancient history in Exodus (ch. 2:3) [Col. 0188B]. There it is written concerning Moses that, newly born, he was hidden by his mother for three months. And when he could no longer be concealed, she took a wicker basket, coated it inside and outside with bitumen and pitch, and put the infant within it. Afterwards, as you know—for it would take too long to go through each point—Pharaoh’s daughter took him up.

Who is this Moses, hidden for three months in his paternal house, but our lawgiving Lord, who received living words to give us, remaining hidden in that Samaria of which we have already spoken much through the three periods: under nature, under the law, and under the prophets? But lifted from His paternal house, He was placed in a wicker basket coated with bitumen and pitch. That is, going forth from Samaria, He came to the gate facing the East [Col. 0188C]. Pharaoh’s daughter received Him when He had been drawn from the basket; and the elect Church from among the Gentiles received by faith Christ born of the Virgin Mary. This is the Lord’s coming from the gate facing the East to Bethlehem.

The basket was, as it were, coated with bitumen and pitch when our Virgin was adorned with purity and humility. For in declaring that she knew not a man—which no one doubts to be perfect chastity—and calling herself the handmaid of the Lord (Luke 1:38), which is a mark of great and profound humility, she offered to almighty God both the pitch of humility in her mind and the bitumen of chastity in her flesh.

Therefore, what in Psalm 71 is said to descend first upon the fleece and finally upon the earth, and what in Exodus is said first of Moses, unable to remain hidden, being made manifest, then placed in the basket, and finally received by Pharaoh’s daughter—this is here the Lord’s first going forth from Samaria, then approaching the gate facing the East, and finally coming to Bethlehem [Col. 0188D]. That is: Christ goes forth from the Father’s secret place, though not departing from it; He approaches the Virgin, assuming flesh from her and in her; He approaches the Church from among the Gentiles and refreshes her with the nourishment of faith.

### VI

But since the Church is Bethlehem, and Bethlehem means “house of bread,” it should be known that there is a bread of which she is not the house, since she does not permit it to lodge within herself. For one such bread is heretical teaching, as we read in Proverbs: “Stolen bread is sweeter” (Prov. 9:17), because heretical teaching is sometimes more pleasing to the reprobate than sound teaching [Col. 0189A].

Carnal pleasure is also bread, upon which the sinful soul feeds, as you have the saying in Job concerning the ungodly: “When he moves himself to seek bread” (Job 15:23), that is, when he gives himself up to seek carnal pleasure. And every hardened person who persists in sin is bread, as is found in Hosea: “Ephraim has become a cake baked under ashes which is not turned” (Hos. 7:8), because the hardened sinner lies in his impurities and does not repent of them.

The Church is not the house of this threefold bread, because it has no dwelling in her either through affection or through effect. The first bread leads the eater to blasphemy in faith; the second to consent in depravity; the third to eternity in the punishment of Gehenna [Col. 0189B]. For heretical teaching deceives through error; the pleasure of sin brings one to consent; persistence in iniquity plunges one into eternal perdition, so that by God’s just judgment, as the sinner here never wished to end guilt, so there he may never end punishment.

### VII

But there is another bread belonging to the Church, of which she is also the house. The first is He who says of Himself: “I am the living bread” (John 6:52), because in Him is the life-giving refreshment of the soul. The second of her breads is that which she daily receives at the most holy altar. Of this Proverbs says that “she does not eat the bread of idleness” (Prov. 31:27), because she does not receive the body of her Redeemer without the fruit of good work.

The third is spiritual grace, as Isaiah says: “Bread is given to him; his waters are faithful” (Isa. 33:16), that is, spiritual grace is bestowed upon the ecclesiastical man, and his contemplations are not erroneous [Col. 0189C]. The fourth is sacred teaching, as Jeremiah says: “The little ones asked for bread” (Lam. 4:4): that is, the humble and simple desired to hear teaching.

The fifth bread of the Church is good action, as that utterance of the Holy Spirit in Isaiah declares: “We shall eat our own bread” (Isa. 4:1), because the sevenfold Spirit delights in the good work which He inspires us to do. The sixth bread is the strength of charity. Of it the Lord says in the Gospel: “Which of you asks for bread?”—that is, charity (Luke 11:11). The seventh is the virtue of humility, as we read in the Book of Kings: “Behold, at his head was a cake baked under ashes” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19:6), because humility is in the mind of the holy man through consideration of his own weakness [Col. 0189D].

The eighth is also a holy man [variant: “sanctified man”], as the Psalm says of the Lord that He “eats ashes like bread” (Ps. 101:10). For He incorporates into Himself not only the holy man through righteousness but also the sinner through penitence. The ninth is consolation, as Jeremiah says: “The people groaning and seeking bread” (Lam. 1:11), that is, grieving and desiring consolation. The tenth of her breads is the support of the present life. Of it holy Jacob says in Genesis: “If You give me bread to eat” (Gen. 28:20), that is, if You grant me support for strengthening.

### VIII

[Col. 0190A] Therefore the Church is the house of this bread divided twice into five, so that it is rightly called and is Bethlehem. She has the first, fed by faith; the second, nourished sacramentally; the third, visited inwardly; the fourth, instructed by hearing; the fifth, occupied in good work; the sixth, enriched by love; the seventh, humbled in herself; the eighth, sanctified through exercise; the ninth, strengthened through consolation; the tenth, fortified through support.

To this Bethlehem the Lord comes, going forth from Samaria to the gate facing the East; for, going forth from the Father’s secret place and assuming the public condition of our nature from the Virgin Mary, He manifests Himself to the Church through faith. May He grant us that, having already known Him through faith, we may be brought even to contemplate the vision of His exalted majesty [Col. 0190B]. To Him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

On the Lord’s coming to the Church in the sacraments of the Old Testament.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The word of God, the bread of the soul.  
2. The Church is signified by Judah or Bethlehem; the sacraments by the waters of redemption.  
3. Sacraments differ according to the time.  
4. The medicine of the sacrament began from the wound of sin.  
5. A sevenfold unfavorable meaning of waters: the waters of Damascus, which are waters of destruction.  
6. Their favorable meaning: the waters of Judah’s redemption.  
7. Jesus performs what His name signifies.  
8. To evangelists and those who knock, the Lord gives the word with great and hidden power.  
9. The tongue of preachers is often disposed according to the merits of their hearers [Col. 0190C].

### I

Thanks be to God for His unspeakable gift. Thanks be to Him who deigns daily to refresh us more and more with spiritual banquets, admitting us into His inner chambers, showing us His hidden treasures and the mysteries of His secrets, and also opening our eyes and face, so that we may search out the wonders of His law and behold His glory.

Behold how many deep, great, and hidden things He has revealed to us in the words of this responsory. And certainly, when I first began to ponder them within myself, I thought that I could expound them in one sermon, or at most two; whereas we have now completed six, have one presently in hand, and still have some things to say about them. I confess that this is a wonderful kind of food [Col. 0190D], which not only, because of the supreme savor within it, is hungered for all the more as it is eaten more, but also increases the more it is eaten. We have experienced this here: we have already eaten it frequently, yet the food grows in the mouths beneath the teeth of those who eat it [variant: “may grow”]. Let us now undertake to expound what remains concerning these words.

## II. Walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption

Here we must begin, because the preceding sermon ended here. Therefore the Lord comes into Bethlehem, showing himself through faith to the Church gathered from the Gentiles; but he comes walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption, establishing in that same Church from the beginning the sacraments of human salvation.

For by Judah we understand one and the same Church which we also understand by Bethlehem, because she who is nourished through the knowledge of truth is likewise exalted through the power of confession: there believing with the heart unto righteousness, here confessing with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). Judah possesses waters of her redemption, upon which the Lord walks when he comes into Bethlehem, because in her the sacraments are instituted—partly under the law of nature, partly under the written law, partly in the time of grace—in which she confesses that her salvation consists, until the true Savior himself appeared in his first coming. There, offering himself upon the altar of the cross, he ministered his flesh to us as food and his blood as drink.

And he will appear in the second coming, when the end shall be, when he delivers the kingdom to God and the Father; and God shall be all in all (1 Cor. 15:24). Then, when he himself grants us everlasting blessedness, those things will cease and altogether come to an end—not only those which existed before his first coming and promised the Savior, but also those which now promise salvation after the second [coming; variant: “promise”]. Then he will not speak to us in Proverbs, but will openly declare the Father to us (John 16:25). Nor will he approach us beneath the veil of sacraments, because we shall see him face to face; and we shall see him as he is (1 Cor. 13:12; 1 John 3:2).

## III.

But since walking belongs not to rest but to motion, the Lord walks upon the waters of Judah’s redemption in order that he may come into Bethlehem. For until the Son of God manifested himself in the flesh, he changed, one after another as reason required, the sacraments that prefigured the Church’s redemption; and he caused some to succeed others according to the courses of times and the succession of generations.

Lift up your eyes and see how the Lord, until he came into Bethlehem in the time of grace, walked upon the waters of Judah’s redemption during the time of nature and of the written law. Instituting few sacraments under nature and multiplying them under the written law, he continued until, coming through the gate that looks toward the East, he entered Bethlehem—that is, appearing in the flesh through the Virgin, he dwelt in the Church through faith; and now figures and signs ceased, while the reality itself and manifest truth reigned.

Thus, before he came into Bethlehem, he walked upon the waters of Judah’s redemption; but after he came into Bethlehem, as into his own house, he rests there, now filled with every refreshment of sweetness.

## IV. [Col. 0191D]

This, I think, is what the Lord is read to have said to Nathan in the Book of Kings: “I have not dwelt in a house,” he says, “from the day when I brought the children of Israel out of the midst of Egypt; but I have walked in a tabernacle and a tent through all the places through which I passed, with all the children of Israel” (2 Sam. 7:6).

The day on which he brought the children of Israel out of Egypt is the brightness [variant: “of brightness”] of grace, by which he visits his elect—whom he predestined to bless forever by the vision of himself—and draws them out from those darknesses which they contracted through the sin of the first parent, through mortality in the body, and through iniquity in the mind.

For immediately after sin, from which calamity began, he himself began to visit them with this grace, preparing medicine for weak humanity in diverse sacraments of the mind [perhaps: “diverse saving sacraments”], as reason required: some under nature, others under the law—diverse indeed in kind, yet tending toward one healing. But in those times he had not yet dwelt in a house; that is, he had not yet come to Bethlehem, the holy Church which now exists. Rather, he walked in tabernacle and tent through all the places through which he passed: that is, he drew near to humankind in sacraments, some of which ceased in their own time and others succeeded in their place.

For a tabernacle and tent are not permanent dwellings, but are moved from place to place and are ordinarily found only where houses cannot be built. And in this way he passed through, doing good and healing all those oppressed by the devil (Acts 10:38), whom, walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption, he chose for this healing.

## V.

But besides these, there are still other waters in the Scriptures, which the wicked drink; yet they are not waters of Judah’s redemption, but of Damascus’s destruction. For the elect are not washed in them so as to be saved; rather, the reprobate are plunged into them so as to be condemned.

Our sins too are, as it were, certain waters, which the Lord remits to us through repentance. Thus we read in Genesis that “the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters” (Gen. 1:2), because his mercy is greater than our iniquity. And his charity covers the multitude of our sins (1 Pet. 4:8).

The teachings of heretics are also waters, as it is said in the Proverbs: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9:17). For to the reprobate the secret teachings of heretics seem sweeter than orthodox instruction.

Moreover, the persecutions of the wicked are waters, as the Psalmist says, “He founded the earth upon the waters” (Ps. 103:5): that is, he strengthened the Church upon persecutions. Waters are also unstable thoughts; hence the same Psalmist asks that he be delivered “from many waters” (Ps. 143:7), that is, from many unstable thoughts.

By waters we understand the enticements of temptations, as holy Job says, “Waters hollow out stones” (Job 14:17), because the enticements of temptation sometimes soften even strong men. Waters likewise signify the pleasures of the reprobate, as holy David says: “He turned their waters into blood” (Ps. 104:29), because the Lord sometimes turns the evil pleasures of the reprobate into bitterness.

The punishments of hell are also signified by waters, as is read concerning the Egyptians: “They sank like lead in mighty waters” (Exod. 15:10); that is, sinners, heavy with sin, fell into infernal punishments. These waters, and whatever waters are of this kind, belong to the rivers Abana and Pharpar of Damascus (2 Kings 5:12), not to the waters of Judah’s redemption.

## VI.

But there are other waters which I should not wrongly call related to Judah’s redemption, such as those of which the Psalmist says: “And you waters that are above the heavens” (Ps. 148:4)—that is, the holy angels who dwell in the heights—“praise the name of the Lord.” These are waters of Judah’s redemption, because angels continually labour for the deliverance and defense of the holy Church.

So too do souls released from the flesh, praying without ceasing for the holy Church. They also are waters, of which holy David says: “You cover its upper chambers with waters” (Ps. 103:3). For we understand Holy Scripture in certain respects; but blessed souls fully comprehend its depths.

The saints who are now in the Church also labour for it, as the same Psalmist says: “The river of God is full of waters” (Ps. 64:10), because daily in the holy Church the people serving God increase both in merit and in number.

The laments of humility are likewise waters, which frequently redeem this Judah. Of these holy Job says: “If I should be washed as with snow-water” (Job 8:30), that is, if I should be drenched with the laments of humility. The devotions of the saints also belong among waters of this kind, concerning which blessed Job likewise says that God “weighs the waters by measure” (Job 28:25). For in a wonderful manner God regulates the devotions of his elect, so that they are sometimes unable to fulfil in act as much as they can grasp in desire.

The peoples who are daily delivered from evil into the Church are also waters of Judah’s redemption. Addressing the Lord, the Psalmist says of them: “The waters saw you and feared” (Ps. 76:17): that is, the peoples beheld you through faith and feared through repentance.

## VII. [Col. 0193C]

How redemption of Judah consists in these and such waters, your own understanding sufficiently suggests to you. Upon these waters of Judah’s redemption the Lord walks daily, coming into his Bethlehem and continually visiting his Church through them.

But what benefit is there in the Lord’s going out from Samaria through the gate that looks toward the East, coming into Bethlehem, and walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption? There is much benefit, and very great benefit. For it follows: “Then every human being shall be saved, because behold, he shall come.”

And rightly so. For his name is Jesus. Because he performs what he is called: namely, salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. 73:12), saving his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21). For God the Father did not send him into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). Thus is fulfilled what is said here: “Then every human being shall be saved, because behold, he shall come.”

But having heard these things according to the allegorical sense, you eagerly desire, as it seems to me, and not without hope await, that we should say something concerning this going forth of the Lord according to the moral sense. Indeed, I do not dare fail you even when you ask something perhaps beyond my capacity.

## VIII.

For I have often perceived and experienced that, when I have been knocked upon and thereby compelled to knock, I have seen something opened to me which had previously been hidden. Certainly it would not have opened unless I had knocked; nor would I have knocked unless I had first been knocked upon. This indeed [variant: “certainly”] often happens to those who are devoted and diligent in the ministry of the word.

For those who listen attentively make their teachers attentive to that to which they themselves attend; and while they knock at their teachers, the Lord opens to them what had previously been hidden from them. Thus, as he says to holy Job, he prepares food for the raven when its young cry to God, wandering because they have no food (Job 38:41).

And perhaps he often prepares that food for the raven more for the crying young than for the raven itself, granting to the faithful and wise stewards whom he has set over his household—when their little ones ask for bread—not only what they may break for them (Lam. 4:4), but also how they may break it, lest they suffer refusal in so just a request.

Therefore the eagerness which you have in hearing the word brings us great advantage; your lukewarmness brings no less loss. For when you desire not a few things, the shepherd of us all gives us not only that with which we may feed you, but that with which we may ourselves be fed together with you. But when you disdain that bread of life, we do not deserve to receive it, your disdain standing in the way.

## IX.

And this is why, when we ought to speak to you, we often become weak and poor in speech: because you have become infirm and weak in hearing. Then we can neither perceive anything sharply nor utter it readily, except in a small measure, because your lukewarmness hinders us.

Conversely, when, as we speak to you, we perceive from signs or certain manners that you are alert and eager to hear—yet with true humility and with a purpose of spiritual advancement—then in the very act of speaking there are supplied to us certain things previously unknown to us, to set before you. Thus, as your desire is suddenly recognized, a new grace is suddenly administered to us.

But now, ending this sermon, let us defer to another discourse what pertains to the moral sense, praising him who is blessed for ever. Amen.

# SERMON XVIII. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY IN ADVENT OF THE LORD

## On the threefold order of cenobites

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. Among cenobites, some are obedientiaries, some cloistered monks, and some novices.  
2. They are signified by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and by those called to the householder’s vineyard at different hours.  
3. By David going out, coming in, and proceeding at the king’s command.  
4. How much prudence and fidelity are required in obedientiaries.  
5. Novices should have contempt for the world and affection for religion; they should have a persevering love of humility and repentance.  
6. Cloistered monks need rest of soul and body.  
7. The obedientiary should avoid sloth, the novice the oldness of the world, the cloistered monk restless curiosity.  
8. They should frequent holy action, sacred reading, and pure prayer.  
9. The monastery is a voluntary prison; what its spiritual fetters are.  
10. God supplies strength to those who endure hardships from love of him, and lifts them up by hope of reward.  
11. In that rest of blessedness, not even the smallest good thought will be without recompense.  
12. The suffering of tribulation is followed by the consolation of eternal reward.

## I.

It seems to me that in these words, concerning which much has already been said, three orders of those who belong to a holy congregation may be observed.

First are those who, because of the care of external matters entrusted to them, may be called obedientiaries. Then there are admitted and called among you novices. And there is the order of those who, abandoning every external occupation and care, devote themselves only to inward things and are called cloistered monks.

For the Lord is said to go out, to come, and to walk. And in order that the proper character of each of these three may be preserved, he goes out through the gate that looks toward the East; he comes into Bethlehem; he walks upon the waters of Judah’s redemption. Yet Samaria is the origin and cause of all these, because he is declared to go out, come, and walk from there.

Therefore, to speak briefly, he goes out in the obedientiaries, who, because of the care and provision of external matters entrusted to them, often must go out—not merely in body, but sometimes even from the spiritual quiet of the mind itself.

## II.

He comes in the novices, who come either from childhood itself, as though from the very east of beginning age, or in old age, as though from the west, that they may recline with the faithful and obedient, whom Abraham signifies; with those who, conscious within themselves of good, rejoice in a firm hope of future things, to whom Isaac belongs; with those who, bravely fighting against vices, strive to supplant them in all their forms, whom Jacob represents.

They come in order that with these obedient, hopeful, and fighting persons they may recline in this kingdom of heaven (Matt. 8:11): that is, they may feast spiritually in this holy congregation of the righteous which I see before me, eating the bread of life in this holy Bethlehem.

These are those who come at different hours to the vineyard of that supreme Householder (Matt. 20:1): some in the morning of childhood, some at the third hour of adolescence, some at the sixth of youth, some at the ninth of old age, and some even at the eleventh of final and decrepit age. Although they do not all have one and the same time of coming, yet one denarius rewards each of them, because one is our Lord and mediator, who feeds his novices in Bethlehem from himself and consoles those labouring in the vineyard.

He who comes in the novices walks in the cloistered monks. Receiving aid from him, they arrange ascents in their hearts and, in this valley of tears, go from strength to strength, that they may see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83:7). They go the more easily, and arrive the more swiftly, in proportion as they are wholly free from external care and attend only to inward things.

## III.

I think this is the meaning of the praise spoken of holy David: “For who among all is like David, faithful, going out and coming in, and proceeding at the king’s command?” (1 Sam. 22:14). Coming in is for novices, going out for obedientiaries, and proceeding for cloistered monks.

But our departing ones must go out through the gate that looks toward the East; our coming ones must come into Bethlehem; and those who walk must walk upon the waters of Judah’s redemption. For David neither goes out nor comes in nor proceeds except at the king’s command.

And that you may know how they can act thus, see that Samaria too is the place from which they have to go out, come, and walk. Fidelity likewise is the reason why holy David comes in, goes out, and proceeds at the king’s command.

You perceive, unless I am mistaken, that something closed is contained in these statements; you must accordingly knock, so that it may be opened. They say that Samaria means “guarding.” Let guarding therefore be present to us as we go out, so that we may go out through the gate that looks toward the East. Let this guarding, I say, be twofold: first prudence, and second fidelity.

## IV.

For the Lord describes in such a way the steward who ought to be appointed over his household: he must be faithful, lest injustice corrupt him; and prudent, lest ignorance deceive him (Matt. 24:45). Let him be prudent in acting and faithful in dispensing, so that he may carefully acquire what is lacking and justly distribute what is at hand.

Finally, let him be prudent, so that he may know how to do whatever is to be done according to reason; and let him be faithful, willing to do nothing contrary to reason. With this double guarding our departing ones may safely go out through the gate that looks toward the East, so that they may perform external work in such a way as to deserve eternal reward.

For insofar as they are prudent, they guard against evils, that they may be free from punishment; and insofar as they are faithful, they perform good things, that they may be worthy of reward. This, then, is the gate that looks toward the East: namely, holy action, as far removed from evil as it is adorned with good, and destined to possess in reward that eternal East of which the prophet says: “Behold, the man whose name is East” (Zech. 6:12).

Thus, for those to whom Christ’s love is sweet in action, his vision may also be a radiant reward in recompense.

## V.

Let a twofold guarding also be present to our novices, so that they too may come from Samaria into Bethlehem: a complete contempt toward the world and a perfect affection toward religion.

For since there are two plagues by which they were afflicted in the world—namely, the swelling of pride, which lifted them up in mind, and the stench of corruption, which dishonoured them in the flesh—they find in holy Bethlehem a twofold antidote against these two evils: the lowliness of humility, which destroys vanity in their heart; and the rigour of austerity, which destroys pleasure in their body.

But in order that they may bear with equanimity the hardships of their new life, they must utterly despise the pleasures of their old life and perfectly hate the vanity which they loved in the world, so that they may fruitfully love the lowliness of the holy religion which they have begun. This is the twofold bread which must be set before them in the house to which they have come: contempt for this world and affection for sacred religion.

If perseverance is added, so that they remain steadfast in the goodness of both, then without doubt they have a third bread, so that your friend who has come to you from a journey—from a distant country, where he squandered all his substance in riotous living, fed swine, endured the long loss of want, and faced the danger of famine—may be refreshed by these three loaves (Luke 11:5; 15:3).

The first is ash-bread, because of the lowliness of humility; the second is barley bread, because of the rigour of austerity; the third is wheat bread, because perseverance is greater in virtue and strength, as well as in the sweetness and vigour it provides.

## VI.

A double guarding is also necessary if cloistered monks are to proceed fortified: namely, they must desire inward quiet above all things. Whatever they perceive to be opposed to it, they must, so far as they can, put away from themselves in mind, speech, and deed.

For many cloistered monks are enclosed in body but wander abroad in mind, as Solomon says: “talkative and wandering, impatient of quiet, unable to remain at home with their feet” (Prov. 7:21). They do this bodily when at every hour they can secretly go outside; spiritually, when in the inward affections of their thoughts they remain with themselves in mind at no hour.

See why I said that cloistered monks ought above all things to desire quiet—not merely bodily quiet in the cloister, but spiritual quiet in the soul. Therefore all things that happen outwardly and are opposed to this quiet of theirs, especially matters that do not concern them, they must, if possible, regard as nothing; so that they may know how both wisely to seek it and firmly to retain it when sought and found.

For they will never rest tranquilly unless, just as they love inward quiet, so they flee in every way they can from all that they consider outwardly opposed to it, especially by judging such things as nothing.

## VII.

This is your straight way, O cloistered monks: walk in it. Then you will be able accordingly to walk upon the waters of Judah’s redemption, which are the heavenly contemplations of the soul, and which you ought to frequent in that inward quiet.

In these waters the faithful soul boils itself, devout in confession of the divinity; it also drinks them and washes itself in them. It boils itself, lest it remain raw, yielding softly to the flesh. It drinks, lest it become dry, feebly yielding to the world. It washes itself, lest it become unclean by boldly [variant: “basely”] prostituting itself to the devil.

Thus in these waters Judah is delivered from a threefold calamity. Boiled in them, it is delivered from the softness of the flesh. Given drink, it is protected from the seduction of the world. Washed, it is freed from the defilement of the devil.

“Then every human being shall be saved, because behold, he shall come.” Truly then every human being shall be saved: obedientiaries are saved from harmful sloth through the good action that they perform; novices from corrupt oldness through the holy newness that they begin; and cloistered monks from restless curiosity through the inward quiet which they cultivate.

We may also understand in these words your threefold exercise, because you ought always to be engaged either in reading, action, or prayer. If you stand in Samaria with the prophet upon your watch (Hab. 2:1), and, as Solomon commands, keep your heart with all guarding (Prov. 4:23), you go out from the holiness of hidden thought to the usefulness of external action. You bear fruit above when you have thus sent your root down below; and you meditate in the mornings upon good work in the Lord when you have first remembered him upon the bed of your mind.

## VIII.

Therefore you will go out through the gate that looks toward the East, performing holy action, which will worthily receive eternal recompense for its merits. You will also come into Bethlehem, so that, placed in a pastureland, through assiduous sacred reading you may receive, in that fourfold sense—historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical—the sweet delight and delightful sweetness of a certain fourfold bread.

You will likewise walk upon the waters of Judah’s redemption, so that, brought forth upon waters of refreshment, you may entreat those inward devotions before the sight of the Most High, exercising yourself in spiritual confession and pure prayer.

Thus you will be adorned through the exercise of good action, made rich through the food of diligent reading, and given drink through the devotion of pure prayer: the first for the aid of necessity, for your neighbour’s sake; the second for the nourishment of your soul, for your own sake; the third for inward affection, for God’s sake.

And when you have thus lived soberly, justly, and devoutly in this world, you may confidently await the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of God (Tit. 2:13), so that then every human being may be saved, because behold, he shall come.

## IX.

There is yet another sense which we propose to make known to you, briefly nevertheless, because we have lingered very long on these matters. If anything further in these words appears to you to require inquiry, then, if you consider carefully what has been said, you will be able sufficiently to discover it for yourselves.

But this is what I wish to say. I greatly sympathize with you because you are in great tribulations and many hardships. For I see you confined within a certain most strict custody. I would say that you are detained in it, if I saw that you were there unwillingly. But now, because you are in it voluntarily, you hold yourselves within it; you are not held by it.

A certain wise man once said: “My son, put your feet into the fetters of the Lord” (Ecclus. 6:25). You have already done this, placing not only the feet of your inward affections into the spiritual fetters of your Lord, but also constraining your bodies within the strictest outward custody. You wear them down with fasts and weaken them with vigils; you mortify your members which are upon the earth (Col. 3:5), and crucify your flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24), even to this hour hungering and thirsting and labouring with your hands (1 Cor. 4:11).

This is the Samaria in which you now are: a guarding not only in the heart, which you keep with all guarding, and, standing upon your watch with the prophet, are prepared daily—indeed continually—to awaken Leviathan (Job 3:8). But you also hold yourselves in the strictest bodily custody, everywhere and always restraining yourselves within prescribed bounds according to place and time, reserving nothing of yourselves for yourselves: not your tongue, so that you speak anything without the file; not your hands, so that you give or receive water without measure; finally, not your feet, so that you go anywhere except where you have been appointed.

But see that you are not saddened, that your heart is not troubled, and that you do not grow weary of being afflicted with these hardships for the attaining of the kingdom of heaven and of putting your feet into these fetters. For the Lord will hear his poor, and he will not despise his prisoners (Ps. 68:34); only endure the fetters, and he will set your feet in a spacious place (Ps. 30:9).

## X.

For he himself now suffers in you and with you. He himself will then console you with eternal joy. There he will grant you an everlasting reward by his power, he who here endures in you a temporal labour by compassion.

Then he will go out from this Samaria, making you go out from it, and will lead and bring forth, as holy David prays, your soul “out of prison”—for this is the sense of Samaria—“to confess his name” (Ps. 141:8). That is, he will go out in you through the gate that looks toward the East, so that through your departure from this life he may lead you to that bright and unfailing recompense.

And he who now walks in you upon the waters of Judah’s redemption, advancing you from strength to strength according to the holy observances and customs that you keep—customs which I should not wrongly call waters of Judah’s redemption, because they redeem the soul from the softness of the flesh, the enticements of the world, and the assaults of the devil—will then come in you into Bethlehem, satisfying you in the manifestation of his glory and appointing for you, as his Father appointed for him, a kingdom (Luke 22:29), so that you may eat and drink at his table in his kingdom.

## XI.

He will go out from Samaria through the gate that looks toward the East; he will come from the East into Bethlehem, leading you from a good life to a good death. For, as the common saying goes, one who has lived well cannot die badly.

From a good death he will lead you to the blessed rest that shall be in the soul; and so he will grant everlasting happiness to both soul and body in the house of that life-giving bread, in which he will make his own recline and, passing by, will minister to them (Luke 12:37).

“Then every human being shall be saved, because behold, he shall come,” because every movement now existing in each of us, whether in mind or body, provided it accords with reason, will attain recompense. “Not even a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke 21:18); even the smallest good thought that has been in the mind will not be without reward.

There will be your silence which you now observe; there your fasts, there your vigils, there your labours; there, to say it briefly, all the good exercises which you now practise will receive their denarii, like good moral labourers who now work strenuously in this vineyard (Matt. 20:10). Nor will anything in you then be foreign to reward which now is not empty of good work in you.

## XII.

And see whether the Lord himself does not promise that he will act in this order hereafter: “I am with him in tribulation; I will deliver him and glorify him. I will fill him with length of days, and show him my salvation” (Ps. 90:15).

“I am with him in tribulation”: remaining with you and standing beside you as an inseparable companion in this Samaria, of which much has been said. “I will deliver him”: namely, walking with you at the gate and going before you—the gate, I say, which looks toward the East. For “when he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126:3). This is the gate that leads to the city; but because of the narrowness inherent in it, it is called iron. And because there is no human being who does not see death (Ps. 88:49), it opens of itself.

At that gate, I say, he will deliver him, lest in that hour you be ensnared by the crafty accuser or seized by the violent enemy. “And I will glorify him”: granting you rest in the East, when our soul rests after death. “I will fill him with length of days”: namely, in Bethlehem, which is at his right hand, filling you with that everlasting fullness whose sweetness knows no weariness and whose eternity knows no failure. “And I will show him my salvation,” so that, in the manifestation of this salvation, every human being in you may be saved, while the Lord preserves unto the salvation of eternal reward all things in you that have been done reasonably for his name, whether placed in his will or fulfilled in the effect of work.

May the Lord himself console you now in this your Samaria, accompany you as you go out, and through the gate which leads to the East bring you into Bethlehem—where you may be saved as truly as you are saved eternally—he in whom is our singular salvation, full consolation, sole refuge, only hope, firm protection, eternal blessedness: God and our Lord Christ Jesus, who is blessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever. Amen.

# SERMON XIX. ON THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

## On the prostration performed on that day in chapter

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. Why, after the Nativity of the Son of God is proclaimed from the Martyrology, bodies are prostrated.  
2. Christ’s twofold nativity, eternal and temporal, and the distinction between them.  
3. Wonder at majesty and devotion to divine mercy are the cause of profound humiliation.  
4. The prophets fell upon their faces from astonishment at God’s majesty.  
5. What preparation is fitting for solemn festivals.  
6. What ornaments of the mind are most excellent and should be practised fruitfully.

## I. [Col. 0200D]

What is this, brothers, that you heard? What is this that you did? It was read before you that Christ, the Son of God, is born in Bethlehem of Judah. You heard this read to you, and immediately upon hearing it you fell upon your faces.

What was heard outwardly was drawn inwardly. This voice entered your ears from without by sound; but its power, entering into your minds, moved them by affection. Great indeed is the power of this voice, which, as soon as it sounded in the ears, cast bodies down upon the earth. For it moved hearts also, and not slightly, so that it was a voice of great stirring. Hearts were moved to wonder and devotion; and, to show both, bodies were prostrated in humiliation.

For who, upon hearing this uttered voice and understanding what is heard, can be raised sufficiently in wonder by astonishment at the immensity of the thing, and kindled in devotion by loving delight? Thus it seems slight indeed—altogether very small—that, on hearing it, even your bodies should be inclined in the humility of prostration.

Christ the Son of God is born. This is that voice of exultation and salvation (Ps. 117:15), truly a voice of power and magnificence.

## II.

In these words the twofold nativity of the one and same Christ Jesus is declared. One is from God the Father; the other from a human mother. Who would dare deny that Christ’s nativity is twofold? Certainly no one who is sound in the confession of the true faith.

Born from God the Father, he is God; born from a virgin mother, he is human. There, from eternity and without a mother; here, in time and without a father. There, without beginning; here, without precedent: the greatness of each nativity being everywhere attested by a singular prerogative. For the Godhead proclaims an incomprehensible Father, and virginity proclaims an admirable Mother.

Moreover, just as it is a great thing to behold God born from God, so it is most sweet to see Christ born as human from a human being. For there he is not exalted, but lofty, in the form of God and in every respect equal to him; here he is so humble that, in the humbled form of a servant, the Most High is most lowly, the eternal temporal, the great and immeasurable small and little.

That, therefore, is great, wonderful, and altogether incomprehensible to behold; but this is merciful, exceedingly sweet, and delightful.

III. Yet surely, to cast oneself down upon the earth with the whole body—who would deny that this is a sign of great humility? I therefore judge that three things are to be noted in what I have here read, heard, and seen done: wonder, devotion, and humiliation. You heard the first two in what I read; but the third [otherwise, namely] in what you yourselves did—namely, falling upon your faces, prostrate upon the ground with your whole bodies. For what ought you to wonder at more than that which is so great without quantity, such without quality, which, as it is, can neither be uttered by the mouth nor comprehended by the heart? This is that eternal equality of Father and Son, and their equal eternity: in their one Godhead, one begets though unbegotten, while the other is begotten; neither is the one who does not beget prior or greater in any respect to the one who begets, nor is the begotten one later or lesser than the begetter. [Col. 0201D] Again, to what ought you to be more devoted, and more bound in obligation, than to the humility assumed by the divine nature? For it is wholly full of sweetness and delight to behold God, the maker of man, made man for man's sake. The former belongs to the loftiness of majesty, which you should wonder at in astonishment; the latter to the sweetness of mercy, to which you should be devoted in love. For these two reasons, when you heard these words, you fell upon your faces. For what was read, “Christ, the Son of God,” proclaims the loftiness of majesty, at which, as I said, you should stand amazed; but what was immediately joined to it, “is born at Bethlehem of Juda,” displays the sweetness of mercy, which you rightly love. Rightly, when you heard these things, you lay prostrate upon the earth, [Col. 0202A] showing that you cannot—and ought not—stand when you have heard of that majesty.

IV. For whom does such loftiness, when it thunders, permit to stand? And whom does such sweetness, when it caresses, not draw down into prostration? Those eminent prophets Ezekiel, Daniel, and others at times perceived something of this majesty, whether by sight or hearing; but did they stand when they perceived it? One of them, as you may understand by reading, when he saw the likeness of the glory of the Lord, fell upon his face (Ezek. 2:1); another, to use his own words, when he saw the great vision, no strength remained in him. His appearance too was changed, and he withered away, nor had he any strength left in him. But he lay stunned upon his face, and his countenance clung to the earth (Dan. [Col. 0202B] 10:8). And a little later: “My joints were loosened, and no strength remained in me; even my breath is stopped” (ibid., 10:16). Likewise the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders in the Apocalypse fell prostrate upon the earth before the Lamb, because all the saints, in contemplating the humility of that most gentle Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, humble themselves in love, seeing him humble beneath all things and not daring in any way to be proud before him. Thus both those and these were prostrate: the former wondering at power, the latter loving mercy. So also the heard name of majesty cast you down in astonishment; that of mercy, in devotion. And indeed it is most just that, upon hearing of the humility by which your nature was assumed in him, you should prostrate yourselves upon the earth in love and give thanks to him who, for [Col. 0202C] your salvation, humbled himself from that lofty palace down to earth. Thus I understood your wonder; in your astonishment I recognized your devotion; and in your love I saw your humility, because you too displayed it in your prostration.

V. But the words, “He is born in Bethlehem of Juda,” as you know, belong not to today but to tomorrow. On the morrow you ought to be very devout; yet you ought not therefore to be idle today. For “today you shall know that the Lord will come, and in the morning you shall see his glory” (Exod. 16:7). In these very few words you have what you ought to do today and what you will be able to receive tomorrow. For you must know today, so that you may see tomorrow. [Col. 0202D] And what is it to know today that he will come, except to prepare yourself for his future coming? For it seems to me that a servant fails to prepare what is necessary for receiving his master worthily as he comes precisely insofar as he does not know that his master will come.

You surely know with how much and what sort of display worldly men busy themselves in preparation for this feast. They do not neglect carefully to prepare so many kinds of food and drink, so many ornaments of clothing, and other things pertaining to temporal elegance and joy. But, since all these things concern the body, our God is spirit. “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). This testimony is true. Therefore those who strive to please him must please him in spirit and truth. He does not [Col. 0203A] require from you temporal brightness or pleasure, but desires spiritual splendor and sweetness.

VI. Strive to possess these things within yourselves, and you will show that you know he is coming. Do the will of your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 12:50), and in your house you will abound in loaves. Strive also to drink the wine of compunction and to be inwardly filled with the grace of most savory devotion, so that the bread just mentioned, once eaten, may be directed in the stomach of the mind to its spiritual health; and no one will then be able to say that you do not abound also in drink. And if you put on the armor of light, so as to walk decently as in the day—walking decently especially toward those outside (Rom. 13:13)—who will deny that you appear in bright clothing and splendid attire? All [Col. 0203B] these are delights of the mind, not of the belly; ornaments of the heart, not of the body. They are exercised inwardly fruitfully and usefully, but displayed outwardly pompously and vainly. In these things, know today that the Lord will come, showing that you know he is to come by presenting yourselves such before him, to whom be honor and glory forever. Amen.

## SERMON XX. ALSO FOR THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

On the sanctification and purity by which we behold the majesty of God within us.

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. What purity or sanctification we ought to prepare for ourselves.
2. Why religious persons alone are said to dwell alone: because of a certain prerogative of divine familiarity.
3. Sanctification is preserved by purity [Col. 0203C] and good action, and restored by confession.
4. Bodily purity, diligence in good work, and frequent holy confession are commended.
5. How greatly the concealment of sin displeases God, especially mortal sin and private possession among religious persons.
6. Our will must be conformed and submitted to the divine will.
7. What it is to know, and what it is to be ignorant, that the Lord is coming.
8. God’s majesty is to be viewed with one eye, and the weakness by which he takes away all our sickness with another.

I. As on this night, most beloved, you have reminded one another: “Sanctify yourselves, children of Israel, and be ready” (Luke 1:35). This is indeed a most salutary admonition: sanctify yourselves and be ready. To be sanctified is to be prepared. He who will come is holy. For the angel said to the Virgin, “That which shall be born of thee shall be holy”; and those to whom he comes must be holy. Hence also in the Law: “Be holy,” he says, “for I am holy” (Lev. 11:14). Therefore those to whom he comes must be holy, as he who comes is himself holy. For the holy one does not come to the corrupt; the pure one, to the unclean; the spotless one, to the defiled. Sanctify yourselves, therefore—especially you who are children of Israel. “How,” you ask, “shall we be sanctified?” Hear it briefly: your sanctification is your purity. For, as Paul says, “This is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thess. 4:3). To show us what he meant by sanctification, he added: “Let each one of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, as do the Gentiles who do not know God” (ibid., 4:4). Far be this altogether from you—far be it from you, [Col. 0204A] who are by no means counted among the Gentiles who do not know God. Rather, you are numbered among the children of God, and your lot is among the saints (Wisdom 5:5), so that you may rightly be called, and may be, children of Israel (1 John 3:1).

II. Understand spiritually of us what you read in the book of Numbers: “The people shall dwell alone, and shall not be counted among the nations” (Num. 23:9). These are the words of the Holy Spirit, uttered through Balaam, expressing the prerogative of the spiritual Israelites—those in whom there is no guile, namely you. “The people,” he says, “shall dwell alone.” Yet, though alone, they are in a certain manner not alone. For you are alone insofar as you have been chosen by the Lord and taken by him as his own, separated from the gatherings of worldly people. But you are not wholly alone, because whenever you recall in mind the lives and examples of the saints, you are joined, as it were, with so many fellow citizens and companions. “And he shall not be counted among the nations” (Rev. 22:15). For outside are dogs and evildoers—that is, unclean persons and workers of iniquity. But you dwell in the inner chambers of his bridal room because of the great tenderness of sweetest love by which you are bound to him, and are admitted more familiarly [otherwise, “bound to him whom you have chosen, and more familiarly”] to the secret counsels of his plan. “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (1 Cor. 15:13). You will precede [otherwise, “you precede”] and far surpass [otherwise, “you surpass”] even some of those who are within the body of Christ and become his members by faith, in this familiarity toward him. For while they are members, you are his inward parts. You are loved above them; [Col. 0204C] he holds you in more ardent charity and in greater intimacy with himself.
