Consider how necessary it is that each one of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, since you are so tenderly loved by him and held in such great intimacy with him—not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God (1 Thess. 4:5).

III. Indeed, you do not greatly need to be reminded about these matters; but our present discourse, which concerns sanctification, has brought us to touch on them briefly, because it speaks of purity of the flesh. Good action also has its place in sanctification, for it is not enough for you to be pure in body unless you are also adorned with good works. You ought to possess both goods and to be strong in both according to your ability, so that you may exercise one outwardly for your neighbor’s sake, while possessing the other within yourself for your own sake. Otherwise your sanctification is not complete. Did not he who said, “Holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary” (Ps. 95:6), join both together and will that neither should be lacking to sanctification? But if you suffer some loss in either of them, as sometimes happens, I know no better counsel than to flee to the remedy of confession, since confession too belongs to sanctification. I learned this counsel from him who declares that, “When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judah became his sanctuary” (Ps. 113:2). You recognize all the more fully the interpretation of *Judah* [i.e. “confession”] because you are accustomed to practise it more devoutly in daily use. If therefore you, who are accustomed in mind to see God, are perhaps for a time darkened by the enticement of the flesh; if that barbarous people of vices, which by the Lord’s aid you formerly used to overthrow, makes you cease from good work: when you depart from Egypt, from these darknesses, and when you depart from the dominion of this barbarous people, let Judah—confession—be your sanctification, so that through humble and pure confession you may regain what you seem to have lost for an hour, whether through temptation in the flesh or through lukewarmness in action.

IV. You can indeed find many other things pertaining to sanctification scattered throughout holy Scripture. But because we are speaking of the approaching outward feast, we also treat of that sanctification which can be seen by human beings. As it occurs to us on the authority of sacred speech, it is found to be threefold: purity of the flesh, diligence in good work, and earnestness in good confession. The first will make you pure, the second adorned, and the third will restore you if anything has perhaps been lost either in purity or in adornment. Great indeed is your sanctification, confession: it repairs what good has been destroyed and recovers what has been lost; it strengthens what is broken and restores what has been shattered to wholeness. Practise it constantly, exercise it unceasingly, and especially when the principal feasts draw near, so that you may be more joyful in mind on those occasions the purer you are through confession; and also more tranquil in conscience, insofar as it brings you its full testimony and you remember that you have committed nothing which has not been disclosed by confession both to the person to whom it ought to be disclosed and in the manner in which it ought to be disclosed. [Col. 0205C] For the mind will never be at peace so long as it has any sin covered up within itself. Conscience always gnaws, having within itself a worm which it carries everywhere, consuming it, while its fire devours the inner parts. And just as you pronounce that person sick and wholly infirm whom you see swollen with harmful humors, and incapable of attaining any health unless he first vomits up every harmful humor by which he is lethally swollen, so likewise judge confidently that this person is afflicted by a severe illness and that no path of salvation is open to him unless he first vomits up the poisonous phlegm of inward corruption which he has contracted in his mind through concealing sin.

V. Know further, beloved, that nothing displeases God so much as the concealment of sin. It displeases him, indeed, that you committed the sin; but much more that you concealed what was committed and refused to uncover it through confession for your absolution. For the concealment of sin has such weight before God that he judges not only the concealer worthy of punishment, but sometimes does not allow those among whom that person lives to remain free from punishment. Nor do I differ from you in this, if there comes to mind that true history of Achan son of Carmi (Josh. 8), who alone indeed, as you know, sinned; yet as long as the sin [Col. 0206A] was concealed, it greatly harmed even the innocent people. For the people could not stand before their enemies until the sin was both exposed and punished once exposed. For what does Scripture say? “The children of Israel,” it says, “have transgressed the commandment and have taken from the accursed thing” (ibid.). Mark these words carefully, I beg you. See how the children of Israel are said to have taken from the accursed thing, although Achan alone took it. And Scripture adds: “And the Lord was angry with the children of Israel” (ibid.). Achan alone transgressed the commandment, and the Lord was angry not only with him but with the children of Israel. They are said to have taken from the accursed thing because it was taken among them; indeed, because it was taken among them even while they did not know it; so it was also concealed among them. Hence the Lord says to Joshua: “Israel has sinned and has transgressed my commandment; they have taken from the accursed thing and stolen; they have lied and hidden it among their vessels. Israel shall not be able to stand before its enemies, but shall flee from them, because it is defiled by the accursed thing. I will be with you no longer unless you destroy him who is guilty of this crime” (ibid., 11). Again: “Whoever,” he says, “is found in this deed shall be burned with fire, together with all his substance, because he has transgressed the commandment of the Lord and committed an outrage in Israel” (ibid., 15). That deed, which I now set before you as a warning, was once cited, as you read, by the leaders of the Israelite delegation to the sons of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, [Col. 0206C] when they said: “Did not Achan son of Zerah transgress the commandment of the Lord, and wrath came upon the whole people?” (Josh. 22:20). Yet he was one man. And would that he alone had perished in his sin! Far be it that anyone among you should transgress the commandment of the Lord, conveyed through Joshua, so that any one [otherwise, “any one of them”] among you may take from the accursed thing—especially so as to steal, lie, and hide it among his vessels.

VI. What is this accursed thing by which the people was defiled, if not this world? In reference to it they were told: “Let this city be accursed, and all that is in it” (Josh. 6:17). These words are explained to you by that disciple whom Jesus loved: “Do not love the world,” he says, “nor the things which are in the world” (1 John 2:15). And if you commit some mortal sin in which lovers of this world are habitually entangled, and do not reveal it through confession but conceal it in the secret places of conscience; and especially if you secretly possess as private property something forbidden to be owned privately, then certainly you have taken from the accursed thing of the city of Jericho and, what is worse, concealed it among your vessels. But have mercy on yourself, and have mercy also on those among whom you live, lest perhaps, though you alone have sinned, you should not alone be punished: lest the Lord, in his just indeed but terrible judgment, involve in your sin along with you your companions in dwelling, even though innocent—not so much because of the iniquity you committed as because, while you lived among them, going in and coming out, it was concealed by you. [Col. 0207A] Brothers, though these things have been said to you, do not suppose that they have been said on your account. Rather, while we are striving to show the usefulness of confession, these reflections have occurred—not perhaps without profit—though not on account of you who are presently here, but on account of certain persons whom you may yet have among you.

VII. Therefore sanctify yourselves today, children of Israel, with this threefold sanctification: that you may be pure in body, adorned in good conduct, and pure in confession; and in this way purified and prepared. “How,” you ask, “shall we be prepared?” See how: present yourselves ready and devoted to the will of God, so that you dare not oppose him in anything; but, renouncing yourselves entirely, entrust yourselves always and everywhere to his direction. He who said, “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8), knew himself to be thus disposed. He stood ready for every will of his God, willing what God himself willed and doing what God himself commanded him to do. Hence he added: “I will sing and make psalmody to the Lord” (ibid.). The one who declares that he sings and makes psalmody to the Lord made himself a cheerful giver in fulfilling the divine will—showing joy through song and gift through psalmody. To sing belongs to one who rejoices; to make psalmody belongs to one who works. That leader and Lord of yours set before you this pattern of preparation: he who came not to do his own will [Col. 0207C] but the will of him who sent him (John 6:38), becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:8). You see therefore that the virtue and love of obedience make you prepared, since one who is not devoted to obedience is in no way prepared.

VIII. Therefore sanctify yourselves, children of Israel, and be ready, because on the morrow you will see the majesty of God within yourselves. To be sanctified and prepared is also to know today that the Lord is coming. Conversely, to grow lukewarm in good work, to cover up sins committed, and to refuse obedience to the commands of elders is in some sense not to know that the Lord is coming. If, in this manner, you know [otherwise, “if you have known”] that the Lord is coming today, you shall see his glory in the morning; and if you are sanctified and prepared today, you shall see the majesty of God within yourselves tomorrow. It is likewise said [Note: [Col. 0207D] In the Office of the Church, Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.] that “The Lord will descend tomorrow and take away from you every sickness.” Certainly, when you see the majesty and glory of the Lord, he will console you and take every sickness away from you. For no sickness can have a place in the vision of such majesty and glory. But are his majesty and his glory different? Far be it. For majesty and glory are one and the same thing in him. Yet although his majesty is not one thing and his glory another, still, as regards us, it seems to me to be one thing simply to see [Col. 0208A] his glory and another to see his majesty within yourselves.

IX. For our holy fathers of old saw his majesty in many and various ways; yet they did not see it in themselves in the manner in which you are promised that you will see it within yourselves tomorrow, seeing it united to yourselves. When “the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14), when he was made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2:7), then that majesty was seen within you—a sight specially reserved, as you know, for tomorrow’s day. Is he not himself his majesty? Certainly he is. And if this is so—indeed, because it is so—when his people is seen, is not his majesty also seen? And shall we not see God tomorrow, when we say, [Col. 0208B] “We know God visibly”? [Note: [Col. 0208D] In the Preface for the Nativity, from the Office of the Mass.] In what then will he be visibly known, except in that visible thing which he will have—and which he will have from you? Tomorrow, therefore, we shall see the majesty of God within ourselves, when we say: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Then the shepherds will hasten to Bethlehem (Luke 2:15), that they too may see the Word which was made; for unless it had been made, it could not have been seen by them. In the morning also you will see his glory, when we say [Note: [Col. 0208D] As above.]: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father.” Tomorrow we shall see the majesty of God within ourselves, but in our weakness, just as we see glory in our shame. Thus we shall see in the morning; thus you too shall see tomorrow.

X. And then it may truly be said of you: “Blessed are the [Col. 0208C] eyes which see the things that you see” (Luke 10:23), especially in the way in which you see them. For you have one eye by which, in the one and same mediator of God and men, our Lord Jesus Christ, both God and man, you see majesty and glory; and another by which you see weakness and shame. Thus you preserve in him the property of each nature, both the assuming and the assumed, without in any way duplicating the person. He will also descend tomorrow and take away every sickness from you, because he took the sins of the world away from the world; thus he is rightly called by his Forerunner “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Sin is indeed the sickness of the soul. This is the sickness which grievously infected the world until Christ’s coming. [Col. 0208D] For, as you know, the widow’s son fell sick, and his sickness was so severe that no breath remained in him (3 Kings 17:17). But Elijah, the man of God, moved by compassion, came and raised the dead boy, rekindling his extinguished breath, so that what is promised to us concerning this one might be fulfilled: that he will descend to you tomorrow and take away every sickness from you—he who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is God, blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON XXI. ALSO FOR THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

On the spiritual coming of the Word to the soul.

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. How providentially inward grace approaches and withdraws in relation to the elect.
2. The children of Israel are to be sanctified—that is, the thoughts of the heart born from holy desires.
3. Inward sanctification through abstinence, silence, rest, vigils, study of sacred reading, meditation, and fervor of good desire.
4. The last and final sanctification is perseverance in prayer, with a recapitulation of the preceding points.
5. How great a caution is necessary in repelling error, and diligence in banishing sluggishness.
6. The manner of receiving and retaining God as a guest.
7. How one should conduct oneself in the coming and withdrawal of grace.
8. To eat flesh in the evening and be filled with bread in the morning means here to be nourished by the examples of the saints until the light and fullness of glory dawn.

I. “Sanctify yourselves today, and be ready.” [Note: [Col. 0209] As above; from the first responsory of the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.] In the preceding sermon, dearest brothers, we said certain things to you concerning this humble coming of our Savior, in which, through birth in the flesh—as this most holy feast now approaching represents—he deigned, having himself become mortal, to appear to the eyes of mortals. But now let each of you turn to himself and strive to see in his own experience what we are about to say. Inward grace frequently visits you, [Col. 0209B] coming to you and withdrawing from you, and seeking your salvation alike in each of its comings and withdrawals. For it comes in order to make you joyful, and it withdraws in order to make you eager. See to it that you glorify it when present with worthy joy, and seek it when absent with tireless desire. Even if you must go throughout the whole city, through every lane and street (Song 3:2), do not find it burdensome to seek him whom your soul loves. Let such love burn toward him whom you seek that labor in seeking may not become wearisome. Your soul will have no relief while he is absent, just as it will feel no burden while he is present; for as, when he is present by his gift, you are borne upward and lifted in all lightness, so, when he is absent through your own weight, you decline and are pressed downward.

II. You have often felt and experienced that “the children of the Bridegroom cannot mourn while the Bridegroom is with them; but when the Bridegroom is taken from them, then they shall fast” (Matt. 9:15). Nor is this surprising. For when he is taken from them, bread too is taken from them, and they must fast while they have nothing to eat. I therefore counsel that the children of Israel sanctify themselves [Col. 0209D] today and be ready. For if they do this, I assure them that tomorrow they will see the majesty of God within themselves. The children of Israel are those inward thoughts of the heart which good desires, conceived from the Holy Spirit, bring forth from themselves; they see God through faith and holy fervor. For they would not extend themselves toward him in affection unless they had first seen him in some measure through understanding. Let these children of Israel sanctify and prepare themselves, so that, sanctified and prepared, they may await tomorrow with all diligence. For then they will see the majesty of their God within themselves, and will see his glory also. He descends for this very purpose, because these are below while he is on high: he descends in order to take away all their sickness.

III. [Col. 0210A] Let their first sanctification be abstinence, so that, with that man of desires, they may abstain from what is pleasant to the belly, in order that they may touch by inward taste what is sweet to the mind (Dan. 1:8). Let the second be silence of the mouth, so that they may hear more fully the hidden word spoken to them and their ears may receive more perfectly, as if stealthily, the channels of the inward whisper (Job 4:12), in proportion as, stabilized within themselves by seriousness, they refuse to dissipate themselves through harmful words; and, while they do not attend to idle tales of speech, may perceive with that inward hearing the voice as of a gentle breeze (Job 4:16). Let the third be rest from outward [otherwise, “outward things”] occupation, because wisdom is to be written in a time of leisure, and those whose activity is diminished will receive it (Ecclus. 38:25), when the deep says, “It is not in me,” and the sea says, “It is not with me” (Job 28:14). Let the fourth be diligence in vigils, so that, after the flesh has been afflicted through abstinence, the mind made mature through the seriousness of silence, and through rest from outward occupations having attained inward tranquility, it may, through diligence in vigils, gain inward purity and fully restrain that insolent instability which is accustomed to wantonness within; and may now rejoice in a kind of Sabbath day, that is, in the brightness of inward secrecy. Let there be joined the study of sacred reading, in which, as in a mirror, seeing their own face, they may discover what beauty is present in them that pleases, and what ugliness displeases; and may strive with all their strength both to perform the one and to find the other. Let the sixth be pure meditation, so that, having kindled the lamp of ready knowledge, they may sweep the house of the mind and seek with all diligence until they find the lost drachma (Luke 15:8), in whose image they may seek and discern the image and likeness of their Lord. Let the seventh be the fervor of good desire, so that, on seeing that little light which is in the image, they may burn still more to behold the brightness which is in the sun of the reality itself; and so that desire, unable through impatience to endure this and yet unable to fail because of its greatness, may increase the more the longer it is deferred.

IV. It is time that they should no longer be cheated of their desire, but let their eighth sanctification be perseverance in prayer. Let them persist in it until he whom they seek by desiring, and desire by seeking, gently and joyfully enters their awareness, granting them their hope and the desire [otherwise, “their hope, the desire”] of their heart, and not defrauding them of the will of his lips (Ps. 20:3). Let him enter them and dine with them, recounting something favorable to them from the brightness of the dwelling from which he has recently come—not making noise with words, but caressing with affections; not sounding in ears, but entering into hearts; not bringing forth speech outwardly, but pouring in anointing inwardly.

Thus fasting, even if it does not wholly uproot, at least cuts down to ground level the thorns and briars which mother Eve planted in the garden of our body; silence destroys harmful words in the mouth. [Col. 0211A] Rest from outward occupation calms every unrest in the mind. The purity of vigils disciplines insolent instability by holy maturity, so that reading may then illuminate the understanding; the illuminated understanding may generate the affection of desire; fervent desire may send forth pure prayer; and he of whom reading speaks, whom meditation seeks, whom desire finds, may be grasped by purity of prayer [otherwise, “grasps”], retained by perseverance, and say: “I will hold him and not let him go” (Song 4:3).

V. Sanctify yourselves in these things, O inward and spiritual children of Israel—more spiritual, indeed, the more inward you are. Sanctify yourselves, I say, and be ready. Now caution and diligence will make these children of Israel ready, so that they may recognize the one who comes through caution and grasp him through diligence. Caution drives error far away, and diligence puts sluggishness to flight. Many have thought a conception of their own mind to be a visitation of inward grace, and have been deceived. Perhaps they were diligent in wishing to grasp grace when it came; but, because they were not prudent in recognizing it, while they supposed that they were receiving an infusion of the Spirit, they received an unstable thought of their own heart. Others recognize the visitation of inward grace when it comes, but do not know how to be diligent in grasping and holding it. They are cautious in recognizing it, but not diligent at all in grasping it. Thus they immediately lose it, because, just as it comes suddenly, so, since they do not know how to embrace it, it immediately flees—coming abruptly and departing without delay. These have knowledge without zeal; those indeed zeal, but no knowledge (Rom. 10:2). Therefore I said that both gifts, caution and diligence, must be present in those who wish to be ready, so that neither error may deceive them and prevent them from recognizing when it has come, nor lukewarmness make them negligent and slothful, preventing them from retaining it when it comes.

VI. This guest of whom we speak is somewhat lofty, so to speak—if indeed I dare speak thus—and disdaining every ordinary movement, he does not stay overnight unless he is much entreated. Unless he is forcibly detained, he does not remain; even while remaining, unless he is held firmly, he withdraws and suddenly slips away, vanishing while you do not know it. But those men of the Gospel instruct us what we ought to do in these circumstances. Seeing that he pretended to go farther, they did not merely ask him but, as it is written, “constrained him, saying: Stay with us, Lord, because evening is coming and the day is already declining” (Luke 24:29). Go and do likewise. When, as a diligent observer and discerner of inward movements arising within you—whether those which have come to you within you, or those which have arisen from you within you—you perceive that inward grace wishes to withdraw itself, seize him [otherwise, “it”], hold fast, clasp firmly, compel forcefully, and say: “Stay with me, Lord, because evening is coming and the day is already declining.” This means: as you hide yourself, the sun of inward brightness declines in me toward setting. Stay with me, enlightening me; draw near, lest my ignorance increase if my brightness is darkened, [Col. 0212A] and my sins multiply if my charity grows cold.

VII. Then he will enter, if indeed he has already gone outside. He will enter, I say, if you enter. And therefore he will enter with you, according to the words, “and he entered in with them.” But as soon as, in the breaking of bread—that is, in the revelation of inward understanding—you recognize him with the spiritual eyes of the mind opened, he will vanish from your eyes. Yet when, according to his custom, he has behaved thus toward you, do not grieve, nor let your heart be troubled. He goes, I say, but he will come again to you, and your heart will rejoice (John 16:22). Therefore, in the day of evils do not be forgetful of good things (Ecclus. 11:27); but when grace is absent, recall to mind the gifts which it bestowed when present, and say: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

Thus it comes about that you are neither wholly dark in the absence of light, nor hungry in the absence of bread. For in this way you will turn evening into day; and, after the manner of a ruminant animal, you will chew the cud when you are unable to eat. This evening pertains to what is said to these spiritual children of Israel: “Sanctify yourselves today, children of Israel, and be ready.” And again: “Today you shall know that the Lord will come” [Note: [Col. 0211D] From the office of the Church, as above.], so that those who are desolated by the absence of the thing itself may meanwhile often be saved.

VIII. This is the evening of which it is again said to these children of Israel: “In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread” (Exod. 16:12). What is it to eat flesh in the evening, except, when grace departs—which is luminous in that it enlightens us by the knowledge of truth, and fiery because it likewise kindles us to virtue through love—when it departs, I say, and withdraws itself for a time, to season the palate of the mind with the delightful examples of the saints, until morning rises and, in that highest dawn by which he visits us—us whom he suddenly tests for a little while (Job 7:18)—sends out its rays; and, with the flesh which we ate in the evening removed from our midst, satisfies us with bread?

I think this is what the Bride says in other words: “A little while after I had passed by them” (Song 3:4). There is no doubt that, while seeking the Bridegroom, she found him absent from the watchmen of the city: “I found him whom my soul loves” (ibid.). Thus she had, as it were, already put them behind her when she reached the embrace of her Beloved, and meanwhile ceased to eat the flesh, as it were, of the preceding saints; for in the gifts of his visitation, in the approach and arrival of inward grace, she has breads so savoury that she not only eats them but is satisfied by them.

Therefore the children of Israel eat flesh in the evening and are satisfied with bread in the morning, so that in this way they may be sanctified and ready, because on the next day they shall see God’s majesty within themselves. Of this same evening it is said in the same place: “In the evening,” he says, “you shall know that the Lord has brought you out of the hand of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord” (Exod. 16:6). Therefore the children of Israel should not grieve excessively when this evening comes upon them; rather, let them remember that the Lord brought them out of the land of Egypt. Thus this remembrance will be some consolation to them in this evening, until that morning rises for them in which they shall see the glory of the Lord, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE VIGIL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

On inward grace visiting the soul.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. That desirable morning, in which the languor of soul and body is to be removed.  
2. The harm done to the soul, subjected to diverse temptations and assaults, when God’s assisting grace is absent.  
3. When inward grace is present, rest of soul and body arises, together with their subjection to the spirit.  
4. Divine grace wonderfully orders, strengthens, and adorns the whole person.  
5. The combined effects of divine grace: calming, cleansing, and raising the mind.  
6. What spiritual languor of the soul is desirable.  
7. The state of a soul enjoying the Beloved.  
8. In this mortal life, the coming and withdrawal of abundant grace are secretly dispensed.  
9. Why this withdrawal of inward health occurs in the saints.  
10. This alternation will continue in us until the day without sunset rises.  
11. How we must prepare ourselves for that morning of eternal glory.  
12. Judaea and Jerusalem, from the etymology of their names, signify confession and peace.

I. “Today you shall know that the Lord will come; and in the evening you shall know that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0213D] From the invitatory of the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord.] (Exod. 16:6). You are to know that he will come with light, he who once called you out of darkness—for this is what the name Egypt signifies—into his marvellous light (1 Pet. 2:9); and the reward of this twofold knowledge is to be the blessed and beatifying vision of divine glory. This will occur when evening wholly departs and morning dawns.

[Col. 0213C] With how great an exultation, do you suppose, these children of Israel meanwhile await that coming day, upon which they hope to see God’s majesty within themselves, and on which they know that the Lord himself will descend in order to remove every languor from them? They also await that morning with no small joy, in which they trust that they will see God’s glory. O morning in which we shall see the glory of God! O coming day in which we shall behold God’s majesty—not simply, indeed, but within ourselves! On that day he himself will descend, not to remove some languor from us, but every languor.

On this present “today” we have been in ignominy, not glory; in weakness, not majesty; not in health, but in languor. By ignominy I mean the shameful temptation of the flesh. By weakness I mean the unstable inconstancy of the mind. By languor I mean the manifold sickness of both.

II. And see whether it is not so. For when grace is absent, as each one of you often feels and experiences, the temptation of the flesh immediately rages. The maidservant tries to seize beforehand the inheritance of her mistress. That wicked and slothful servant, sometimes delicately reared, is found to be insolent, as Solomon promises (Prov. 29:21). Eve rages and suggests unlawful eating to her husband (Gen. 3:6, 17). The thorns which she planted in the field of our body rise up, sprout, and, she herself watering and cultivating them, grow without measure. Thorns and briars prick, and their goads draw blood. “My flesh is clothed with rottenness, filth, and dust” (Job 7:5); finally, the angel of Satan does not cease to buffet it (2 Cor. 12:7).

[Col. 0214A] Will you say that these things, and others of this sort, belong to glory, or rather to ignominy? The mind likewise, when this assisting grace of which we speak is absent, is immediately weakened, becoming like “the dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4): light, namely, because the force of temptation snatches it from the strength of stable constancy; chattering because of inward loquacity; wandering because of disordered desire; unable to endure rest because of the motion of the dissipation to which it has given itself; “unable to stand upon its feet in the house” (Prov. 7:21) of its own affections; sinking to the depths under its own weight and altogether unable to carry itself.

At times it falls into such a dreadful collapse that even a mountain falling upon it crumbles away, and a rock is moved from its place; waters hollow out stones, and the earth is gradually consumed by inundation (Job 14:18). This, as you know, occurs when lofty contemplation in the mind is cast down and dissolved into low things, and inward strength is changed into feeble weakness. Even strength of thought, and a mind once fruitful and steadfast, when it despises small things, is gradually emptied, dissolved, and destroyed through the creeping suggestion of the enemy (Ecclus. 19:1). You will say, I think, that all these things pertain more to weakness than to majesty.

III. You now reckon this twofold evil also [variant: “indeed”] to be a very great sickness. This shameful weakness and weak ignominy—do you not call it a most grievous languor? Such a person is certainly sick, indeed almost unto death; and his sickness is exceedingly severe, so that scarcely a breath remains in him (3 Kings 17:17).

But when that luminous morning of which we speak breaks forth, when this bright coming day dawns—that is, when the arrival of inward grace enters the mind—these spiritual children of Israel will see the glory of God, they who first saw their own utterly dreadful ignominy, who looked upon their own weakness within themselves. And the Lord, descending, will remove from them the distresses of both forms of languor, which until then oppressed them in the flesh through the stealthy onset of pleasure and in the mind through the lightness of instability.

For when his gladdening and life-giving arrival is received, weak and infirm flesh is subjected; the strengthened and ready spirit rules—that is, the spirit powerfully puts to death the deeds of the flesh. Job acts manfully when he hears his wife giving wicked advice, rebuking her as having spoken “like one of the foolish women” (Job 2:10). The spirit restrains its beast of burden; it presses its flesh lest it become impetuous, and spurs it lest it become sluggish, so that it may neither dare to be idle when roused, nor resist when drawn back, nor, as it formerly did, dare to demand superfluities; nor yet murmur if anything—even something necessary—is denied it. Fasts are regarded as sport; vigils as the most ordinary practice; nakedness as comfort; poverty as the highest delight.

IV. Whatever is considered hard and harsh is considered gentle and light. Whatever is bitter and hard becomes sweet and soft. Is this not the grace of the Lord which you behold in this morning? Vanity does not lift the eyes; curiosity does not disturb the hearing; pleasure does not infect the sense of smell; gluttony does not gorge the taste; impurity does not defile touch; frivolity does not render the movement of any member blameworthy. All the members of the body are ordered and fitted together; each attends in proper and becoming order to its own office. What each has as its own in part, it contributes in common service to the whole.

Meanness of dress shines forth in outward apparel; gravity in countenance; purity in affection; maturity in gait; poverty in food; moderation in use; usefulness in effect. And, to comprise much in few words, in all its motions absolutely nothing occurs that offends either human, angelic, or even divine sight.

[Col. 0215B] Will you not affirm that this admirable beauty of the day is the glory which this luminous morning has brought you to see? The mind too is visited; being visited, it is cleansed; being cleansed, it is adorned; being adorned, it is filled; being filled, it is perfected; being perfected, it is gladdened; being gladdened, it awaits even its reward with full confidence.

V. Thus it sleeps and rests in peace, established uniquely in hope (Ps. 4:10). In it all crooked things become straight and rough things level ways (Isa. 40:4). Dark things are illuminated, cold things are kindled, and, lest we exceed measure, what has been kindled is tempered. Hidden things are revealed; past things are reviewed; present things are seen; future things are foreseen. Sense is awakened, understanding clarified, affection inflamed. All the delights of the world are despised; being despised, they are rejected; being rejected, they are even consigned to oblivion. Heavenly things are approved; being approved, they are loved; being loved, they are desired; and the soul labours without weariness to obtain them. All toil is accounted light.

The mind is melted by love, anxious with desire, separated from earthly things, fixed upon heavenly things; diligent in reading, pure in prayer, sweet in meditation, pleasant in spiritual observation, clarified in contemplation. It bears one thing always and everywhere in thought and affection: loving one, embracing one, striving toward one, resting in one; wounded by charity until it fully possesses for ever him whom even now it loves without ceasing. It utterly disdains all else and finds absolutely no rest in any worldly thing.

When you experience this within yourselves, what else do you see but God’s majesty within you? And while you rejoice in this twofold health, do you not sense that, as the Lord descends to you, every languor is in some measure removed from you? For in a manner of speaking, on that coming day the Lord’s descent will remove every languor from you, when, amid such splendour of truth and ardour of virtue, the arrival of inward grace both extinguishes pleasure in the flesh and calms instability in the mind.

VI. Languor may also be understood as the very torment of desire which wholly penetrates and pierces the devout soul, as it ardently sighs for the presence of its Redeemer. Hence the soul itself says in the Song: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love” (Song 5:8). It entreats and earnestly charges devout souls that, when through purity they find God in prayer, they should make known to him its good purpose, recount its longing and distress, and obtain for it mercy and compassion.

Again, in the same Song of love: “Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I am sick with love” (Song 2:5). Because it is sick with love, it asks to be strengthened with flowers and surrounded with apples. This means nothing other than that the religious and devout soul, the greater the torment it endures in the desire with which it burns for its Creator, strives all the more carefully to abound both in the flowers of good thoughts, by which it is invited to inward affection, and in the apples of pious deeds, by which it is directed to outward fruit. For it knows that the proof of love is the performance of a work.

VII. Let your soul, my brother, have this languor, so that it may endeavour to take up this utterance for itself [variant: “Your soul has this languor, my brother, if it can take up this utterance in common”]: “I am wounded by charity.” The Lord, descending, removes this languor when he grants the soul what it desires—not because it then ceases to desire, even after it has received what it desired, but because, although it desires to see him whom it has desired present, yet, now holding him, it is not anxiously tormented over one who is absent.

For having present with it the one whom it had desired in absence not without torment, it feels itself relieved; yet it loves no less, indeed perhaps more than before, and in desiring it desires. In this it already imitates the angels themselves, of whom it is said: “Into which things angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12). They look continually, lest, ceasing even for a moment to behold so great a blessedness, they endure the greatest torment. And they continually desire to look, lest, not hungering after such sweetness and delight, they fall into deadly and ruinous satiety.

O morning in which, seeing the Lord’s glory, we shall be filled with his mercy! O day on which he will command and announce his mercy to us, so that we may both see his majesty within ourselves and rejoice that languor has been taken away from us!

VIII. Thus this vision is joyful and joy-giving. With this morning and this coming day, when it dawns, the languor itself is removed [variant: “when it dawns, this languor is removed”]; and as long as the morning appears and the day shines, so long that aforesaid vision of divine glory and majesty endures and continues, and the removed languor has no place.

But alas, this morning [variant: “that morning”] too quickly disappears and the day declines, so that, just as we are able to rejoice in the possession of present brightness, we must also groan in expectation of future darkness, awaiting evening with blessed Job and being filled [variant: “I shall be filled”] with pains until darkness (Job 1:4). For the day and morning depart, and all the things mentioned above which came with them likewise depart with them. The joyful vision of majesty and glory vanishes; the sorrowful vision of weakness and ignominy enters; the languor which had been removed returns; and health retreats, because it had not been given but lent.

IX. I think this is what we read concerning our holy father: that “the Lord went up from Abraham, and he returned to his place” (Gen. 18:33). So you too will return to your place when the Lord goes up from you, gathering himself into the heights and leaving you in the depths, so that, falling back into yourself, you find the place of ignorance, weakness, and languor. For when the Lord goes up from you, he takes with him his glory and majesty, and that health which, while he was with you, he bestowed upon you.

This is what holy David laments, calling to mind the good things the Lord bestowed on him while he was with him, but withdrew when he went up from him. Groaning that he had returned to his place, he says: “Lord, in your favour, not through any merit of mine, you bestowed strength upon my beauty. You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. 29:8).

But when this happens, we must return to him, in hope that he may again allow himself to be found. For holy David, though troubled, gave himself this counsel also, uttering this humble confession by which he might call back the departing one and turn back the one who had turned away: “What profit is there in my blood, while I go down into corruption? Shall dust confess you, or declare your truth?” (ibid., 10).

And did he gain anything by this? Indeed, very much. For he who asked received, he who sought found, and to him who knocked it was opened. For “the Lord heard and had mercy on me; the Lord became my helper” (ibid., 11). In what did he have mercy on him? In what did he become his helper? In that he turned his mourning into joy, tore off his sackcloth, and clothed him with gladness (ibid., 12); making his mercy heard by him in the morning, so that, standing manfully in that morning, he might again see his glory; so that, standing firmly before him and seeing clearly in that morning, rather than lying lazily and growing dim in darkness, he might have his mercy commanded to him in the day, in order that he might see God’s majesty within himself and rejoice that, with that day descending, every languor had been taken away from him.

X. Thus the merciful Lord, wisely and most healthfully alternating these vicissitudes of his dispensation within us, when he opens his hand, fills all things belonging to us with goodness (Ps. 144:16). But when he turns away his face, we are troubled; when he takes away his spirit, we fail and return to our dust (Ps. 103:29). Yet lest we be reduced to nothing if we are abandoned by him for long, according to his custom he visits us again with his salvation, sending forth his Spirit so that we may be created and the face of our earth renewed (ibid., 30).

He causes this morning to break forth anew for us, in which we shall see his glory; he causes the coming day to dawn for us, in which we shall see his majesty within ourselves; and on that same day he also descends to us in order to remove every languor from us. Nor will he ever cease to deal thus with us until that day arrives which will not decline into evening, to which night will not succeed, and which no darkness will obscure. This is that coming day on which the iniquity of the earth will be wholly blotted out and the Saviour of the world will reign over us. He will reign within us also, abolishing every principality, authority, and power, delivering the kingdom to God the Father, so that death, the enemy, may be destroyed, and God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:24 ff.).

XI. In relation to that day, all this present life is called “today,” in which we strive to be sanctified and ready, whoever we truly are as children of Israel. We are sanctified by turning away from evil; we are made ready by doing good; so that, cleansed by uprooting and destroying, and adorned by building and planting, we may be worthy to stand before him in the morning and see his glory; to see also the majesty of God within ourselves, with every trace wholly removed and utterly annihilated of both weak ignominy and shameful weakness.

The Lord will descend on that coming day, removing every languor from us, so that he may be for us a salvation propitious not merely to some but to all our iniquities; healing, not merely some, but all our infirmities unto the complete perfection of health (Ps. 102:3); redeeming our life from destruction, crowning us with mercy and compassions, and satisfying our desire with good things (Ps. 103:3–5).

O luminous morning in which the Psalmist stands before the Lord in order to see! (Ps. 5:5). O splendid morrow, in which righteousness itself will answer holy Jacob! (Gen. 30:33). O morning in which the elect will be so filled with the Lord’s mercy that they will exult and delight [variant: “rejoice”] for ever! O morrow in which true confessors will go forth from exile to kingdom, from sorrow to joy, from death to life, seeing [variant: “they shall see”] inward peace in mind and desire!

XII. For these are the meanings conveyed by those two celebrated names, Judaea and Jerusalem. They will go forth, I say, and the Lord will be with them; and they will be steadfast in every respect, seeing his help upon them. O blessed day, on which not only shall we rest, but God too shall rest from the labour now expended in us. For he labours by enduring the reprobate. He will bless and sanctify this day, resting in it from the hard labour by which the reprobate now trouble him through perverse conduct and wicked deeds.

He will also rest in it from every work which he had accomplished (Gen. 2:2), in those who have been predestined to eternal life. When heaven, earth, and all their adornment have been perfected in them (ibid., 1)—in these elect of whom we speak—there will be no corruption, no lack of perfection, no evil present, and no good absent, as they behold the Eternal One for ever and ever. To him be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON THE DAY OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

On the sublimity of Christ’s incarnation and the spiritual progress of the elect.

[Col. 0219A]

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The sublimity of the Incarnation can neither be worthily expressed by speech nor comprehended by the mind.  
2. How astonishing is the union in one person of creature and Creator.  
3. More careful consideration is required of who was born, from whom, and when.  
4. How fittingly he was born of a Virgin, at Bethlehem, in a time of peace.  
5. Violators of peace delay or drive away Christ, who is to be born within them.  
6. What it is to turn spear and sickle into a ploughshare.  
7. How greatly that which violates brotherly charity must be avoided.  
8. The same lot of birth receives elect and reprobate alike; their modes of living differ.  
9. Saint Joseph is a type of the elect, whose merit consists in holy conduct and right faith.  
10. One ought first to believe with the heart and confess with the mouth, and then to live rightly with a right intention.  
11. The ascent from Galilee to Judaea and from Nazareth to Bethlehem signifies the exercise of the cardinal virtues.  
12. No good work possesses beauty without uprightness of intention.

I. Beloved, the excellence of this most sacred day demands it, and your devotion also demands it, that today especially our tongue should not be silent among you and our word should not be struck dumb [variant: “your heart”]. It is unworthy that human speech should cease from God’s praise on the day when God comes forth as man from virginal flesh. And it is likewise unjust that we should deny you the bread of life for which you so eagerly ask.

Yet even if perhaps something has been given to me which I may set before you, I confess that I have neither such depth of understanding nor such eloquence of expression as could enable me to comprehend in mind or express in speech the venerable magnificence of this day. For when I ponder and ponder again within myself, frequently turning over and returning in my mind to what occurred on this day—something no less wonderful than sweet, no less exalted than merciful—I understand all the more that it must be considered again. And what is no small marvel: the more I grasp of it, the less, in some fashion, I find that I have grasped.

Yet why do I say, “the more I grasp”? For this alone I grasp of it: that I cannot grasp anything of it. In this contemplation I approach inaccessible light, seeing through it only my own darkness, but being entirely unable to behold that light itself. Thus God’s knowledge is made wonderful from me and strengthened, and I cannot attain to it (Ps. 138:6). Through it he makes my ignorance known to me [variant: “becomes known to me”], so that I may know what I lack, crying out with the philosophers: “I know that I do not know.”

For who—not, I say, who can comprehend what exceeds every angelic and human faculty of perception, but who can even be suitably astonished—that God was born from a woman? Who can sufficiently marvel, seeing the Maker of all things made, the Eternal made temporal, the Word made flesh, God made man? And, since it would be far too long to go through the individual instances of this kind: who can comprehend, in this child born today, a human being receiving that incomprehensible thing which belongs to God alone, and God receiving that humble thing which belongs to man alone?

II. O God, who is likewise man! O man, who is likewise God! Our Creator, our son; our God, our brother; our maker, our flesh; our Lord, our fellow-servant; our strength, our weakness; our glory, our ignominy; our shepherd, our food; and many things of this kind.

“Jesus Christ yesterday and today: the same also for ever—Jesus Christ” (Heb. 13:8): “Jesus Christ,” so that the unity of person may not be doubled; “yesterday,” lest the assumed nature be extended into eternity; “today,” lest he who assumes it be enclosed in time; “the same also for ever,” because he lives eternally—temporal in that in which he died, living eternally. In one and the same moment of time, on account of “today,” the one person of Jesus Christ reigns gloriously in heaven by virtue of the divinity which assumes [Note: [Col. 0220D] Variant: “divinity,” or “reigning”: the passage was corrupt.]; and on account of “yesterday,” he dies shamefully upon the wood by virtue of the assumed nature. [Note: [Col. 0219D] Variant: “lives eternally, temporal unto eternity”; perhaps “unto eternity” occurs redundantly once.]

Behold, our God appears visible today, though that truthful theologian says: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4:12). And he himself says to Moses, his beloved and intimate friend: “You cannot see my face; for man shall not see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). Now we perceive God with our eyes; now we touch the Word with our hands, beholding God in man, the Word in flesh, and beholding all the fullness of divinity dwelling even bodily in this little one, our brother, our son (Col. 2:9). Thus the angel no longer permits John to worship him (Rev. 19:10), because in Christ he worships John’s nature above himself.

III. Certainly, in this most holy birth, a threefold consideration fills me with wonder: when I consider the person of him who was born, the mother from whom he was born, and the time in which he was born. And I find that he who is born is God, and that she from whom he is born is a Virgin. Which of these, brothers, do you not admire? At which of them do you not stand amazed? Is it any wonder if you marvel that God comes forth as man from a human being, or if you marvel at a virgin who is a mother? There, one and the same person is God and man; here, one and the same woman is mother and virgin. There God is made man, and the same man is God. Here there is both virginal fruitfulness and fruitful virginity.

But how can a time of such great peace and quiet not also amaze you, when you look upon the proud sons of Adam, who wished to build a tower in order to make their name famous (Gen. 11:4), provoking one another, envying one another, and desiring to surpass one another (Gal. 5:26), yet converging into such concord that, with the storms of wars stilled and all nations agreeing with one another so peacefully, one ruler came to govern the whole world, the whole world was enrolled, and finally the whole world was united under one coinage?

For, as you heard read in the Gospel on this most sacred night, an edict went forth from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled. “And all went to be registered, each to his own city” (Luke 2:1, 3). And thus, as you know, it came about—through the providence of the Wisdom of God, who appears in flesh today, who “reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)—it came about, I say, through her providence, that Bethlehem was distinguished by his birth, just as the city of Nazareth was honoured by his conception. Therefore, in order to register according to the imperial decree, Joseph had to come there with the glorious Virgin, the Evangelist giving the reason: namely, because he was of the house and family of David (Luke 2:4), whose city Bethlehem itself was called.

IV. “And it came to pass, while they were there, that her days were fulfilled” (Luke 2:6)—without doubt, the days of the blessed Virgin for giving birth. “And she brought forth her firstborn son” (ibid., 7). Therefore he who was born as man is God. And he is “our peace, making both one” (Eph. 2:14), who came “to announce peace to those who were far off, and peace to those who were near,” reconciling through his blood “the things in heaven and the things on earth” (Col. 1:20).

But just as it was fitting that God should be born only from virginal flesh, so he did not choose to be born except in a time of peace. And, not to pass over the place of his birth: he was born in the house of bread, he who himself is the living bread come down from heaven, of which whoever eats “shall live for ever” (John 6:52). Therefore it was fitting that God be born from virginal flesh; Peace chose to be born in a time of peace; and Bread ought to be born in the house of bread.

When I consider the person of the one being born, I wholly fail; but when I behold the person of the one giving birth, I am exceedingly amazed, trembling before his loftiness and unable to comprehend her prerogative. I think that you yourselves also will say this of yourselves. Yet, stunned by this twofold consideration and driven back upon yourselves, set before yourselves as an example the time of his birth. Know that, just as he did not choose to appear upon earth through birth in the flesh except in a time of peace, so neither does he choose to appear among you through the coming of his inward grace unless you have peace with one another.

V. Woe to those through whom Christ, when absent, is hindered from coming, and, when present, is driven away from remaining. Who are they, except disturbers of peace, dividers of unity, people troubled themselves and troubling others, sowing discord among brothers? (Prov. 6:19). Such people the Lord not only hates, but his soul detests. Swollen with that deadly poison, they are eager not only to offer it to others through the example of their wicked conduct, but also to pour it into them through the suggestion of destructive counsel.

But you, brothers, have not so learned Christ—if indeed you have heard him and been taught in him, as truth is in Christ Jesus (Eph. 4:20). “Peace be with you” (Luke 24:36): this is the spiritual word of our peace-making Lord. “These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you, that in me you may have peace” (John 16:33). And again: “Have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). Know that “whoever he may be, the one who troubles you shall bear judgment” (Gal. 5:10). It is the voice of the Lord speaking in the Apostle and in the Prophet: “Think the same thing, have peace, and the God of peace and love will be with you” (2 Cor. 13:11).

Let every one of you in every way refrain from harming another, making himself diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; if it is possible, so far as it depends on him, living peaceably with all people (Rom. 12:18). For, as the Lord testifies, those who are peaceable are called children of God (Matt. 5:9); so I boldly say that those who sow discord deserve to be called children of the devil.

VI. Consider that at Christ’s birth that season of peace shone forth in the world concerning which Isaiah prophesied when he said: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles” (Isa. 2:4). And he added: “Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, nor shall they any longer be trained for war” (ibid.). I beg you, bring about that season spiritually among yourselves: beat your swords into ploughshares and your spears into sickles.

The sword and spear are weapons and inflict wounds; the ploughshare and sickle, however, are instruments exceedingly necessary for human use, serving the nourishment of humankind. Yet, while sword and spear are weapons, with the sword we strike at close range, whereas with the spear we reach someone at a distance. Likewise, though ploughshare and sickle are highly necessary instruments, with the ploughshare we dig the earth in ploughing, and with the sickle we cut the crop in reaping.

And what, we may suppose, are swords and spears but the hard harshness of words and their rough severity, disturbing peace in the hearts of hearers? Did not holy David mean this when he declared the teeth of the children of men to be weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword? (Ps. [Col. 0222C] 56:5.) Thus you strike your neighbour with a sword—indeed, a very sharp one—when, swollen with the bitter pride of anger, you attack him with a reproachful word. But put your sword into its sheath; turn the blade against yourself, reproving and accusing yourself, while for the moment leaving your neighbour alone, arraigning and setting yourself before your own face. Consider rather the beam in your own eye than the speck in your brother’s eye (Matt. 7:3). For although this latter disturbs in part, the former blinds entirely.

Dig through the wall, searching your inward parts deeply; and, having entered by the door that appears to you, see the abomination of beasts and creeping things, and the idols depicted therein (Ezek. 8:10). Then whatever blameworthy thing you see in your neighbour will seem tolerable in comparison with the horrors which appear in yourself. In this way you will beat your swords into ploughshares: that is, with the very words by which you were accustomed proudly and arrogantly to irritate and provoke your neighbour, you will rebuke and humble yourself. With the sharp point of self-accusation you will dig up your inward parts, whereas you were formerly accustomed angrily to wound even the outward parts of your neighbour.

With spears, moreover, you strike those who are far away when you do not allow persons absent from your slanderous words to remain at peace, making yourself hateful to the Lord by presuming, against the law, to curse the deaf (Lev. 19:14). You also show yourself worthy of destruction when you contribute to banquets, indulge in poisonous draughts (Prov. 23:20), and likewise provide flesh for eating.

[Col. 0223A]

VII. Why does it seem so pleasant to you to disparage one who is absent, to speak against one who cannot hear? Why do you not rather embrace, in the arms of love, your neighbour’s goods as well as your own, so that you may behold with the eyes of hope and certainty the reward which awaits you in the future for this goodwill? If you strive diligently to do this, you will surely change your spears into sickles: by pursuing in every way blessings both for your neighbour and for yourself, you recognize that from blessings you will reap eternal life. And, ceasing from disparagement of your neighbour, you direct your speech to what is useful for him, and on that account may be worthy to receive in the future the reward of eternal refreshment.

Let not, I beg you, nation lift sword against nation among you. You do this when, without defending yourselves, as the Apostle instructs, you give place to wrath (Rom. 12:19). Nor be trained for battle; rather, outdoing one another in honour and, in humility of spirit, considering one another superior to yourselves (Phil. 2:3), do not become desirous of vainglory, provoking one another and envying one another (Gal. 5:26).

Thus you will bring about within yourselves a season of peace, in which that author and lover of peace will deign to appear among you—he who appeared in the world in the flesh at the time when all the kingdoms throughout the world came together in a single concord, subject to one rule. By this he showed that he would one day send forth his heralds of truth, to call the sons of God—those scattered abroad—together into one, to the citadel and the walls of the city (Prov. 9:3; John 11:52), gathering them from the four winds of the earth.

[Col. 0223C]

VIII. Therefore an edict went out from Caesar Augustus—or rather, from the Lord Jesus Christ—that the whole world should be enrolled (Luke 2:1). This edict went out from him when, sending his disciples forth to preach, he said: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:15–16). Then they went, each to make profession in his own city (Luke 2:3), because believers and baptized persons, according as each one’s condition directed, adorned the confession of faith by good conduct: each in his own order.

“Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, to Bethlehem, the city of David, because he was of the house and family of David” (ibid., 4). [Col. 0223D] In these words, according to their allegorical meaning, mention is made of the state of the elect, who daily, through progress in faith and good works, press onward from present things to future ones, from what is lowly to what is high.

You know, brethren, that without any exception the same corruption of birth according to the flesh brings forth both the elect and the reprobate. There is nothing either among those belonging to the lot of the elect or among those belonging to the mass of the reprobate to which this utterance of the Psalmist does not apply: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:7), except only him who alone is free among the dead (Ps. 87:6). Though he was God, he did not contract sin when conceived in his mother, nor did he commit it while dwelling among human beings.

But although the whole race of Adam’s children has one beginning [variant: “end”], not all have one manner of life, nor do all receive one dwelling-place through death. The elect, indeed, are established by gratuitous grace in righteousness and holiness, that they may be saved; but the reprobate, abandoned by a just yet hidden judgment, are hardened through perversity in wickedness, that they may be condemned. Thus the reprobate continually rush from evil to worse evil, until they reach eternal damnation. But the elect, as though by an inborn desire for noble dignity, never cease to stretch upward in longing, until they receive the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

For just as the son of some king, born in slavery or in some lowly condition, when afterward through another’s report he learns of his noble birth, freedom, [Col. 0224B] and inheritance, strives by every means to obtain them, so the Church of God’s holy elect, captive in the slavery of this present exile and born into servile captivity, when through the instruction of teachers and divine inspiration she learns of the heavenly homeland to which she has been predestined, immediately ceases not to labour untiringly until she obtains it.

IX. Therefore the elect, predestined to eternal life, belong to this Joseph, of whom we heard that he went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David called Bethlehem. My brethren, Joseph here represents you, so that you too may go up from province to province, from Galilee to Judaea, and from city to city, from Nazareth to Bethlehem.

As you know, the Lord Jesus often used to travel through these provinces. He is also found to have honoured these two cities with the highest honour: one by his conception, the other by his birth. There are two things in which our present merit consists: right faith and holy conduct—that we may both believe rightly and live holy lives. But faith is less perfect if confession does not bear witness to it: namely, that, just as you believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10), so too an action, though good in itself, will by no means be worthy of recompense unless, just as you have holiness in outward conduct, so you maintain rectitude in inward intention. Thus you act for the reason that what is good may please the eyes of that inward judge, seeking as the sole praiser of your work him whom you await as its rewarder.

Therefore it is necessary that what you have in your heart should advance as far as confession upon your lips, so that in a time of tribulation you may neither blush nor be afraid to confess publicly what you believe secretly concerning the truth of the one faith. It is likewise necessary that you go up from the holiness of outward action to the rectitude of inward intention, so that you may perform a good work outwardly as an example before your neighbour, yet flee the full reward of human favour, and await your reward inwardly, expecting it from God alone. For “the Lord scatters the bones of those who please men; they shall be put to shame, because God has despised them” (Ps. 52:6). And those who do their works in order to be seen by men have received their reward [Col. 0225A] (Matt. 6:5): receiving as recompense only the human favour which they sought in their work, they will receive no reward from God.

X. Since this is so, most beloved, guard yourselves in your good work from the stealthy desire for praise, which is both the destroyer of present grace and the ruin of future recompense. This twofold spiritual progress—namely, from faith to confession, and from holiness of outward action to rectitude of inward intention—is signified by the twofold ascent from Galilee to Judaea and from Nazareth to Bethlehem.

For Galilee, as you know, means “revelation,” while Judaea means “confession.” Nazareth is interpreted “flower,” and Bethlehem “house of bread.” Thus Galilee pertains to the revelation of faith, and Judaea to confession by the mouth. [Col. 0225B] Likewise Nazareth signifies the blooming beauty of holy conduct, while Bethlehem signifies the savoury refreshment in which God delights: the rectitude of inward intention.

Go up, then, from Galilee to Judaea, from Nazareth to Bethlehem, so that you may not fear to confess, even before persecutors and opponents of the faith, what you believe in your heart and by faith. Whatever good work you display outwardly before others, strive humbly to offer inwardly to the eyes of him who discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart. You perform these four things fully and perfectly if you believe rightly in secret, confess boldly in public, show outwardly a good work as an example, and inwardly, through the intention of pleasing God alone, always desire that work to remain hidden.

[Col. 0225C]

XI. Observe whether the four virtues called cardinal or principal because of their great perfection are not contained in these four things. To possess the secret of faith revealed to us belongs to prudence; to confess faith steadfastly before the enemies of faith belongs to fortitude. Likewise, to practise good works belongs to justice; and to reject every human praise and favour in that same good work belongs to temperance. For temperance concerns not only restraining the flesh from the experience of pleasure, but also holding back the mind from the desire for vanity.

Go up from prudence, which lies in knowledge of faith, to fortitude, which lies in confession by the mouth. Go up from justice, which lies in the holiness of outward action, to temperance, [Col. 0225D] which lies in rectitude of inward intention. In this way, progressing spiritually from virtue to virtue, you will receive an ever greater daily increase in holiness—for this is what the name Joseph is said to signify. You too will go up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David, which is Bethlehem.

XII. Notice that Bethlehem is spiritually called the city of David because Christ dwells and makes his abode especially in the rectitude of inward intention. For he approves only that good work which he sees to have been done purely for his own sake. He also acknowledges himself bound to reward the person in whose work he recognizes himself to be present.

Nazareth is indeed a glorious city, but Bethlehem more glorious, because there is greater glory in Christ’s birth than in his conception, and greater usefulness in bread, which tastes good and satisfies by refreshment, than in a flower, which gleams in beauty and gives fragrance by its sweetness. Every good action of ours, then, is a flower, displaying beauty and fragrance in itself, so as to attract those present and summon those absent: the former by the good example which they see, the latter by the truthful report which they hear. It also offers hope concerning itself, because from a good flower fruit is hoped for in due season; likewise, from a holy work, reward at the end.

Yet the beauty of this lovely, sweet, and good flower is changed into ugliness, and its fragrance into stench; even the hoped-for fruit does not appear, unless the rectitude of inward intention protects its tenderness from the misty, cold wind—from the windy and cold mist, [Col. 0226B] that is, the wind and misty cold of human praise. In this way Saint Joseph went up from Galilee to Judaea, from Nazareth to Bethlehem.

There is another meaning in this twofold ascent which must by no means be concealed from you, since it has been revealed to us for your sake and transmitted to you through us. But it is better to defer it to another sermon, both because at present we cannot attend to its exposition and because you must not be overburdened. Let us therefore praise from the deepest marrow of our hearts, and glorify, the one born of the Virgin, true God and true man, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, blessed through all ages. Amen.

## Sermon XXIV. Again, on the Nativity of the Lord

On the spiritual progress of the saints, and on the great abundance of God’s sweetness, which he has hidden for those who fear him but accomplished for those who hope in him.

[Col. 0226C]

## Synopsis of the Sermon

1. The harms of vainglory are to be avoided, following the example of the Lord Jesus.
2. The ascent from Galilee to Judaea and from Nazareth to Bethlehem signifies spiritual progress.
3. Present things are perishable like a flower; what remains eternally is to be desired.
4. The practice of good works is an indication of blessed predestination.
5. The order of spiritual ascent is shown by recapitulation.
6. After a fall, hastening to the remedy of repentance and frequently sighing to God are probable signs of future salvation.
7. This is confirmed by perseverance, each person in his own calling.
8. Divine grace is necessary for spiritual progress, but we are not certainly assured that it will be given finally.
9. In Abishag is expressed an image of divine grace, to be revealed at the end.
10. Mystical days in which spiritual work must be carried on.
11. What grace now accomplishes secretly will then be displayed openly.
12. The acts of virtues are to be brought to completion in the heavenly homeland.
13. Why what God’s grace disposes concerning us is not now apparent.
14. This life is the tabernacle of one engaged in warfare, where Christ works upon us like a fuller.
15. The elect are like Christ’s garments, always to be cleansed on the road to the homeland.
16. One aspect of Christ is disfigured; another is beautiful and desired.

I. You now see, I think, that it is as necessary for you to go up from Nazareth to Bethlehem as it is to go up from Galilee to Judaea. For just as the Lord will not confess before his Father one who, though believing rightly, does not now confess him before human beings, so those who do their works to be seen by men will not have a reward with their Father who is in heaven (Matt. 10:33).

Make us go up, holy David, from the city of Nazareth to your city Bethlehem, so that in every good work we may seek your praise rather than our own. O gentle and humble Jesus, who, appearing humble today in our form, sought not your own glory so long as you were in the world, but the glory of him who sent you: drive far from us that evil eye which makes the body dark (Luke 11:34 [printed: 2:34]). Drive away from us the desire for human praise, the enemy of inward grace, which often intrudes into our good work and makes even a good work alien to recompense. Grant that in everything we do we may seek to please you alone; that we may desire to be seen by you in our work, and desire also to be rewarded by you for our work.

Grant also that in us the waters may return to the place from which the rivers go forth, so that we may dwell in the savoury refreshment of your city, O beautiful and mighty David, and may not take unlawful delight there in its sweet flower, beauty, and its beautiful health [variant: “sweetness”]. Thus, Lord, we shall go up from Nazareth to Bethlehem when we utterly reject the human favour which is wont to arise from the holiness and reputation of good work, and offer whatever we do to your hidden gaze through a right intention to please you alone.

Your voice, O merciful and good Jesus, says this: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing” (John 8:54 [printed: 6:54]). And again you say: “I do not seek my own glory” (ibid., 50). Brethren, if Christ’s glory is nothing when he glorifies himself, what is, or what can our glory be, if we glorify ourselves? Let us therefore cleanse ourselves from the defilement of this dregs, which gradually seeks to flow into our inward impulses. Let us strive to appear pure and clarified in the sight of him who discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

[Col. 0227C]

II. Let us now see what meaning is contained in this twofold ascent, namely, from Galilee to Judaea, from Nazareth to Bethlehem. [The printed text reverses the first direction: “from Judaea to Galilee.”] If, whatever God reveals to you concerning himself or concerning things pertaining to him, you not only devoutly believe in your heart to proceed not from the acuteness of your subtlety or the merit of your holiness, but from his gratuitous grace, but also confess with full mouth—so that with Paul (2 Cor. 3:5) you say that you are not sufficient of yourself to think anything as from yourself, but that your sufficiency is from him—then you go up from the secret of revelation to the public act of confession, and thus from Galilee to Judaea.

And if you hunger and thirst so eagerly for righteousness that you by no means judge yourself perfect, however perfect you may be, but, when you have attained completion, reckon yourself to be beginning (Ecclus. 18:6), in view of the good still lacking; if, regarding whatever good work is present in you as a kind of tender flower [variant reading uncertain: “which you have as a certain tenderness of a flower”], you strive by every means in your power to reach from what you have already acquired to what you have not yet attained, then you undoubtedly go up from Nazareth [Col. 0228A] to Bethlehem.

It is certainly most beneficial for you to go up in this manner, because the more devoutly you confess publicly that what has already been revealed to you secretly is from him, the more abundantly you will see opened to you what you had until then perceived to be hidden from you. Nothing is more pleasing to God than the progress of spiritual fervour, than hunger and thirst for righteousness. It is fitting indeed that he should fill his hungry ones with good things, making them go up from Nazareth to Bethlehem: granting them the desire of their heart by giving them the bread of more substantial activity, since, because of their excessive eagerness to please him, they count the holiness of all the conduct they practise as a kind of tender flower.

Joseph likewise goes up in this sense from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David called Bethlehem: if you confess with full mouth that whatever is revealed in your heart is from God, and run with devout eagerness from what you have already accomplished toward what you have not yet undertaken, in order to accomplish that also in deed.

[Col. 0228B]

III. Understand also that in the present God reveals many things to you, showing you both how you ought to avoid sins lest you incur punishment, and how you ought to practise virtue so as to attain reward. But in the future, concerning what is not now revealed to you, you will be occupied eternally in his praises; you will sing his mercies forever, uttering in the voice of confession and exultation the sound of one rejoicing (Ps. 41:5).

Whatever you practise here in the present is, in comparison with the surpassing reality which you will possess in that blessedness, as a flower is to bread. Does not he mean this who says: “That which is momentary and light in our present tribulation works in us, beyond measure in exaltation, an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4:17)? What is this “momentary and light” except that he counted it as a kind of tender flower? And what is there “exalted and eternal” except that he compares it to the refreshment of most savoury bread?

Therefore, if from the misery of this present life—in which the way of living well, which concerns merit, is revealed to you—you go up by the steps of love and desire to that blessedness in which you will devote yourself eternally to the praise of God as your reward, then indeed you go up from Galilee to Judaea. For here the Lord, revealing to you the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom, makes known its thickets (Ps. 28:9), in which you may appoint a solemn day; but there, “in his temple all will speak glory.” That is in the heavenly Judaea, for that heavenly Jerusalem which God inhabits consists in the perpetual confession of divine praise.
