But if you endeavour to prepare yourself to pass from the beautiful and fragrant flower to the solid bread of eternal blessedness, having the desire “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23), and desiring one day to be joined with those whom he makes recline at table and, girding himself and passing among them, ministers to them (Luke 12:37 [printed: 12:38]), you in a manner go up from Nazareth to Bethlehem. Thus, as you remain with him in his temptations in Nazareth, so, by his appointment, you may eat and drink at his table in his kingdom [Col. 0229A] (Luke 22:29). That kingdom pertains to Bethlehem because the Evangelist spiritually calls it his city (Luke 2:4).

IV. But whence does this Joseph have the ability to go up in this way? Let the Evangelist show us why he can so ascend. “Joseph,” he says, “went up from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, to the city of David called Bethlehem” (ibid.). He adds the reason: “because he was of the house and family of David” (ibid.).

Whence comes this, my most beloved brother, that you apply yourself so zealously at every place and time to the exercises of good works, except because you belong to the lot of the elect? For those whom he predestined, these he also called; and those whom he called, these he also justified (Rom. 8:30). What, then, follows except that those whom he predestined he also justified? The house and family of David, therefore, is that blessed assembly which has been predestined to eternal life. We earnestly pray that we may belong to this house and family when we say: “Command that we be delivered from eternal damnation and numbered among the flock of your elect.” [Note: [Col. 0229D] In the Canon of the Mass.] Before this we say, concerning the twofold ascent by which we go up from Galilee to Judaea and from Nazareth to Bethlehem: “And order our days in your peace.”

V. Therefore you go up from Galilee to Judaea, from Nazareth to Bethlehem, because you are of the house and family of David: because you confess God publicly even before persecutors, whom you hold secretly through faith; because you confess with full mouth that whatever you perceive to have been inspired in you through revelation is from him; because you hasten by the course of desire from the revelation that comes to you as merit in this present life to that homeland in which you will celebrate without end confessions of divine praise.

Likewise, because you strive to proceed from the holiness of good action, which you display outwardly for your neighbours’ benefit, to the rectitude of inward intention by which you please God alone; because you desire to proceed from the conduct you have already practised to that which you have not yet undertaken; and finally because you long to go up from the beauty of present holiness, which you now practise as merit, to the most savoury refreshment of future blessedness, which you will enjoy as reward: you do these things because you are a son of the highest Father and ordained to eternal life.

For we have said that spiritual Joseph goes up from Galilee to Judaea, from Nazareth to Bethlehem, in three ways; and the reason is that he was of the house and family of David. Whence do you have this earnest striving, day by day—or rather, by continual steps of love—to go up, in the ways we have taught, from Galilee to Judaea and from Nazareth to Bethlehem, unless you are of the house and family of David?

[Col. 0229D]

VI. Whence comes it to you that with all your strength you hate what is evil and love what is good; that you incline yourselves readily and perseveringly, by every way you know and can, to the divine will; and that, if under the pressure of some temptation you happen in any degree to turn away from it, you are altogether unable to have peace until, through full repentance, pure confession, and fitting satisfaction, you are reconciled to it? The spur [variant: “spurs”] of fear and love pricks you in conscience and drives you away and draws you back to God. Does this happen for any reason other than that you are beloved and joined to him by a kind of kinship?

It is something great, truly marvellous, and divine that “the love of God has been poured out into your hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to you” (Rom. 5:5). You possess its firstfruits and pledge, while he himself cries inwardly within you, “Abba, Father,” and himself bears witness that you are children of God; and therefore, if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God and co-heirs with Christ (Rom. 8:17).

It is great, I say, truly marvellous, and altogether divine that your mind prompts you to sigh toward him so tirelessly, holding it certain within yourselves that nothing can suffice you apart from him, that you ought to seek nothing beyond him, but should tend toward him and rest in him. This is surely no deceptive sign of your salvation, no false testimony concerning your election.

VII. Hence it is, beloved, that you have not only attained the state of holiness in which you now stand, but also stand manfully within it. This is because you belong to that people whom the Lord chose as his inheritance (Ps. 32:12), he who foreknew you and predestined you to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:29), calling and justifying you, in whom you hope that, confirming his work which he has wrought in you, he will one day also magnify it. Meanwhile you go up from Galilee to Judaea, from Nazareth to Bethlehem, because you are of the house and family of David.

And for what purpose did Joseph go up? Surely, to make profession. This, I think, is what the Psalmist says: “For thither the tribes went up”—not all tribes, but “the tribes of the Lord” (Ps. 121:4), namely, those belonging to the house and family of David—and they went up “to confess the name of the Lord” (Ps. 83:5). For those who dwell in that house will praise him for ages of ages; and those who live in that Judaea devote themselves, or will devote themselves, eternally to divine praises, uttering the voice of exultation and confession.

[Col. 0230D]

VIII. But did Joseph go up alone to make profession? By no means. Rather, he went up to make profession with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant. While we attend to the kinds of progress of which we have spoken on the path of this present life, we have Mother Grace accompanying us, indeed leading us. For we cannot progress at all unless she precedes us by inspiring, follows us by helping, and accompanies us by consoling.

But though she is with us on the way, what will she do for us at the end? Although we devoutly hope, we are by no means fully certain or altogether secure. Do not those possess grace working within them who, with her ministry, receive righteousness and wisdom? Yet Solomon says: “There are righteous and wise persons, and their works are in the hand of God; and yet no one knows whether he is worthy of hatred or love” (Eccl. 9:1).

Our inward mother, Grace, smiles upon us; and we devoutly hope that she who now grants holiness on the journey, guarding and perfecting the works of mercy, will correspondingly grant us blessedness in the homeland, and will complete in us the good work which she began until the day of Jesus Christ (Phil. 1:6). Yet, looking upon our life as hidden and understanding that we are surrounded and enveloped by darkness, we are not, as I have said, fully certain.

This is Mary, Joseph’s betrothed wife. She shows herself as a star upon the sea of this present life, for amid the storms which this Joseph now endures—sometimes from the flesh, sometimes from the world, and sometimes from the devil—how could he attain salvation unless he had the guiding light of the great star, inward grace? Our Joseph has her as his betrothed, but does not know her carnally. So you must understand the helping grace of which we speak to be joined to you in such a way that you seek in her or through her nothing pertaining to the softness of your own glory and praise; nor may you, who ought to be the chaste guardian of so great a bride, become, God forbid, in a reversal of roles, her shameless corrupter.

[Col. 0231B]

IX. Hence Solomon condemned Adonijah to death (1 Kings [3 Reg.] 2:25), because he wished carnally to unite with Abishag, whom the old man had as one to warm him, but whom, as Scripture says, “he did not know.” For King David had grown old and was advanced in days (1 Kings [3 Reg.] 1:1), so that you too may strive to attain maturity in holiness and endeavour to acquire the manifold brightness of spiritual virtues. “Though he was covered with garments, he did not warm himself” (ibid.), so that you too, even when earthly goods abound for you, may find no consolation in them, according to the Psalmist’s admonition: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:10 [printed: 9:11]).

For what are all earthly things but certain garments of the body? But because these garments give him no warmth, fair and chaste Abishag comes to warm the old man; so too, when you find no delight in earthly things, seek the chaste embrace of inward grace, which may set you aflame with the heat of spiritual desire. Thus, when your soul refuses consolation, remember God and love (Ps. [Col. 0231D] 76:4), so that, going up from Galilee to Judaea and from Nazareth to Bethlehem, you may have Mary your betrothed accompanying you.

We know, indeed, that our mother Grace thinks thoughts of peace and not of affliction concerning the children of her adoption. But after she has brought them from present things to future ones, only then does she first show what she thinks concerning them. Therefore Mary, pregnant, goes up with Joseph, but does not pour forth in birth the treasure she secretly bears in her womb unless she and Joseph come together to Bethlehem. Thus you also read: “And it came to pass, when they were there” (Luke 2:7)—undoubtedly in Bethlehem—“that her days were fulfilled for her to give birth; and she bore her firstborn son” (ibid.).

[Col. 0232A]

X. We understand the days of Mary, which begin in Galilee and Nazareth but are fulfilled in Judaea and Bethlehem, as blessed desires, holy works, and whatever other exercises of spiritual virtues there are, by which it is increasingly recognized that Mary is pregnant. For the greater and more numerous the holiness which Mother Grace extends to us in conduct, the greater is the reward in blessedness which she promises to grant us in the future.

For I think that when faith shines in us, it is like a bright day. Great, I confess, is the brightness of this day; shining within us, we believe God, believe God’s word, and believe in God. We believe God to be supremely powerful, supremely wise, and supremely good. In this way we believe God as a truthful promiser. We believe in God as unfailing sweetness itself and unerring delight.

Hope likewise is a day, indeed a very bright one: by its dawning in us we see spiritually what we cannot see bodily, as the Apostle declares that we have been saved in hope (Rom. 8:24), and that we hope for what we do not see and therefore await it through patience. Sorrow also, which pricks us when we consider present evils, and fear, which shakes us when we consider future evils, will seem to you days if you weigh them rightly.

Do you not say that the brightness of knowledge and likewise the maturity of wisdom are a kind of shining sun in the heaven of the mind? Through the former sorrow arises in the mind; fear, however, is the path to the latter, Solomon saying, “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18), and holy David affirming, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10).

Sorrow, therefore, is a kind of day within you, because the more you grieve in this life over present darkness, the more you see, spiritually enlightened, the brightness of the future. Fear too is a day, because the more you fear incurring the punishments of hell’s penalty, the more you are enlightened to seek the joys of the heavenly homeland. The day of repentance succeeds the day of fear, because you then rightly see how much you ought to repent for committing sin when first you have fully seen the punishments of penalty.

Justice follows this; it too is undoubtedly a day, illumined by the sun of charity so that it may render to each person what is his due. Thus one who walks honourably in this day knows to reject evil and choose good: the former so as to harm no one, the latter so as to benefit all. After this the seventh day dawns: it is the Sabbath of rest, namely the bright repose and tranquil brightness of inward contemplation.

XI. These are the mother’s days, which she indeed has in Galilee, at Nazareth, but which she shows to be completed in Judaea, at Bethlehem, when there she bore her son. So too mother Grace exercises these virtues in us in the present life, but will complete and bring them to their end in the heavenly homeland. There she will show us the purpose which she has concerning our salvation, a purpose by which she was here beforehand enriched and thereafter made fruitful in spiritual [Col. 0233A] advancement. This purpose she possessed wholly firm and stable within herself; yet, carrying it concealed within her inward places, she wished it to remain hidden from us.

Now she has her days in us in faith, when we believe rightly; in hope, when we hope steadfastly; in sorrow, when we grieve from our inmost heart over present evils; in fear, when, seeing evils, we fear those to come. She has them also in penitence, when by repenting we punish sins already committed; in justice, when we work what is good toward all; and in inward contemplation, when, through a mirror in an enigma, insofar as this is possible for us in this mortal flesh, we behold the glory of the Lord. These, I say, are the days she has in us while she dwells with us in Galilee, Nazareth. But when, ascending with her, we shall have come from Galilee into Judaea, from Nazareth [Col. 0233B] [variant: *we shall come*] into Bethlehem, then she will present herself to us as giving birth, she who now presents herself as pregnant; for she will openly show us that good and blessed thing which she now secretly purposes concerning us.

XII. “When her days were fulfilled for her to give birth”: that is, when the virtues of which we have spoken have been completed, so that what she thinks concerning us here she may disclose there. Will not the day of faith then be fulfilled—that is, ended and completed—when, as the Apostle says, we shall no longer walk by faith but run by sight? (2 Cor. 5:7). Likewise the day of hope will then end, when we see what we now hope for and fully possess what we await through patience. The day of sorrow and fear will likewise [Col. 0233C] end, and the day of joy and security will shine eternally.

The days of penitence likewise will end, because we shall no longer feel any sting of sin in the conscience that would require repentance. “Who will seek his mercy and his truth?” as the Psalmist says (Ps. 60:8). Then those who hope will not seek the truthfulness of the promiser, since they will already hold in full whatever he promised. Nor will those who repent seek the mercy of the forgiver: they will have nothing from the past pertaining to guilt that has not been pardoned, and from that point onward will commit nothing for which they need seek mercy. The day of justice will end, and the day of glory will come to its end, in which we shall reap without failing what we now sow; for in the day [Col. 0233D] of justice we sow in the Spirit, and in the day of glory we shall reap eternal life. The day of contemplation also will end, in which we now see through a mirror in an enigma; and there will succeed it the day of unfailing brightness, in which we shall see him face to face (1 Cor. 13:12).

XIII. When these days have been fulfilled—that is, when these virtues have been relinquished—Mary will bear a son: grace will reveal the sentence of peace which it has held hidden here concerning us, and the unchangeable purpose of our election. Since it held this purpose peaceably toward us here, it will then show it fully when it rewards us with eternal joy. Hence it is also said here: “And she wrapped him in swaddling-clothes and laid him in a manger” (Luke 2:7). This will in some manner take place then, [Col. 0234A] when Mary wraps in swaddling-clothes what she carried in her womb and lays it in a manger: when mother Grace, according to what she now thinks concerning us, surrounds us with the delightful sweetnesses of eternal happiness and places us in the hidden recess of the heavenly homeland.

This seems to be the point of that true assertion and joyful promise of blessed John: “Now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). That is to say: we who belong to David’s house and family now ascend from Galilee to Judaea, from Nazareth to Bethlehem. What we shall be—that which the pregnant mother with whom we ascend carries—has not yet appeared. We know [Col. 0234B] that, when her days are fulfilled for her to give birth, she will bear a son, wrap him in swaddling-clothes, and lay him in a manger. And why does mother Grace not show here what she thinks concerning us? Certainly because here we are in exile, not in the kingdom; on the way, not in our homeland; not in rest, but in labor.

XIV. This is why he is laid in a manger: because there was no place for him in the inn. Our whole life is, as it were, an inn for us. When we come here by being born, we turn aside here; and we turn aside here in order to remain here for a time, not to abide eternally. This present life, therefore, is the tent of one on military service, not the chamber of one at rest; the stable of a traveller, not the house of an inhabitant; [Col. 0234C] the prison-house of an exile, not the dwelling of a citizen; finally, the inn of one journeying, not the hall of one who remains.

Therefore there is no place for Mary in the inn; rather, she lays her son in a manger. For it is not fitting that there should be granted to you in exile what will be bestowed in the kingdom. As the Evangelist says, “No fuller can make Jesus’ garments so white” (Mark 9:2) as they appear when he is transfigured on the mountain. And who is this fuller, if not he of whom the Psalmist says that he is to be sprinkled with hyssop in order to be cleansed, and washed in order to become whiter than snow? (Ps. 50:9). Truly, Lord Jesus, you are our fuller, who declare us clean because of the word which you have spoken to us (John 15:3). For in our present condition, pouring the water of compunction into the basin of our mind, you tread us underfoot through fear and love; and thus, performing the office of a fuller and therefore bearing the fuller’s name, you cleanse your garments with the water of washing. Are we not your garments, with which you are clothed through faith working through love?

XV. Therefore you deign daily to whiten these garments of yours, pouring over them the clean water of inward compunction, that they may be cleansed from all their defilements. But who in this life can be so cleansed as to have nothing in himself needing cleansing? For, as Solomon says, “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin’?” (Prov. IX, 20). Thus holy men—the Lord’s garments—are clean, and yet still need cleansing. The Lord himself indicates that this is so: he declared his disciples clean, and yet [Col. 0235A] washed their feet (John 13:5).

But the time will come when they have nothing in themselves to be cleansed, when they need no cleansing whatsoever and are defiled by no pollution. And when will this be, unless when “they shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43); when they appear in righteousness before the presence of Christ their mediator; when the condition of holy souls shines forth, of which John says in the Apocalypse: “They are without blemish before the throne of God” (Rev. 14:5)? This is the mountain on which you will be transfigured, Lord Jesus: on which your other face will appear, namely the loftiness of heavenly blessedness, in which, according to his promise, he will show himself to those who love him.

XVI. What then? Do we make Christ two-faced? Must he be said to have a double face, so that in the Transfiguration he may be said to have another face? [Col. 0235B] Indeed, so it is. Was not that his face in which he was seen by the one who said, “We saw him, and there was no appearance in him; therefore we did not esteem him,” and added, “We considered him as though a leper, struck by God, and humbled” (Isa. 52:3)? Yet he beheld him in a far different face who called him “fair in beauty beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3).

Both these faces of his were seen by those who beheld him beautiful in his robe and his garment red to look upon (Isa. 63:4). It is indeed read in the Gospel that “the Jews spat in his face” (Matt. 26:67); but far other was that face for which he who said, “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” sighed with all his inmost being [Col. 0235C] (Ps. 41:3). This is the face which holy Moses desired to be shown to him, who, because of the great favor he had found with God, dared to say: “Show me your face, that I may see you” (Exod. 33:13). This is that other face of his which appeared when he was transfigured on the mountain: namely, the beauty of his divinity, in which his elect see him in the loftiness of heavenly blessedness.

In that blessedness his elect, wholly full of charity, will shine with him, so that in this mountain his garments may be white (Mark 9:2). And they will be as white as no fuller can make upon earth, because far greater is the purity which the Lord will confer upon his elect in that exalted blessedness than that which he now confers on them in holiness. Therefore [Col. 0235D] the garments are not white upon earth, so that Mary may lay her son in a manger, because there is no place for him in the inn. May the manger bring us to that place—Jesus Christ our Lord, who for our sake deigned humbly to be laid in a manger, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is God, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. ALSO FOR THE DAY OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY.

### On the threefold edict of the supreme emperor.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The enrolled world is the Church of the elect, whose prelates are its pivots.
2. The first enrolment occurred in the calling of the Hebrew people.
3. Its condition was threefold: first under the patriarchs; second under the yoke of slavery; third under the law of Moses.
4. The proportion of the individual stages considered in relation to one another.
5. [Col. 0236A] The progress of Hebrew religion under the Mosaic law.
6. The old law, an image of things to come.
7. The wiser persons among the ancients knew more clearly that Christ would come.
8. The edict of the second enrolment, in the calling of the Gentiles.
9. By his humility Christ destroyed Gentile pride, and by his preaching their ignorance.
10. The prerogative of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, according to Isaiah’s prophecy.
11. The sacraments of the Christian religion as though wrapped in swaddling-clothes. The faithful Gentiles succeeded the erring Jews.
12. The third edict is that of inward inspiration; the fourth will be on the last day.
13. The correspondence of present grace and future glory.
14. The twofold inn of our flesh: the world while it lives, the tomb when it is dead. Christ is born in an inn and laid in a manger.
15. An address to Christ, maker of all things, made in time, and to his virgin mother.

I. “An edict went out from Caesar Augustus that [Col. 0236B] the whole world should be enrolled” (Luke 2:1). Blessed is that meek and innocent lamb who, being born on this day in the house of bread, chose to be laid in a manger, in order to set himself before us, his beasts of burden, as life-giving food. He also, dying on the cross, caused the veil of the Temple to be torn in the middle (Luke 23:45), so that, with our eyes unveiled, we may consider the wonders of his law.

Behold, as he promises in Isaiah, he opens to us “hidden treasures and the secrets of mysteries” (Isa. 45:5), admitting us to the inner places of his secrets and opening to us the deep and mystical meanings in his Scripture. Nor does he speak to us in his Scripture in only one way, but in many and varied ways, so that, though the bread of sacred Scripture is one, the variety [Col. 0236C] of its flavor may delight us. Let us therefore open our spiritual throats and strive to taste with the inward palate what this flavor is with which the Holy Spirit has deigned to season this bread for us today. This bread is now set before our sight for the third time; yet, though old through the repeated practice of eating it, it remains new through the variety of its flavor.

For I think that an edict went forth, not in one manner but in several, from our supreme emperor, almighty God, that the whole world should be enrolled. What is this world but the Church, or the assembly of the elect, or the gathering of those who are called saints according to his purpose, for whom all things work together for good—however else it may more suitably be expressed? These God the Father foreknew and predestined to be made conformed [Col. 0236D] to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren (Rom. 8:29).

This, therefore, is the world which the Lord declares through the Psalmist to be his: “The world of the earth is mine,” he says, “and its fullness” (Ps. 49:12); for the assembly of the elect, destined to be placed in heavenly blessedness, is his in a proper and special sense. This is the world which, as that holy woman says, God set upon its pivots: “The pivots of the earth are the Lord’s,” she says, “and he set the world upon them” (1 Sam. 2:8). For the pivots are the prelates of the Church, and he imposed upon them the Church of his elect to govern.

That this world might be enrolled, you will find that an edict did not go forth from our Lord and king only once, if you carefully consider how often the Lord, from the beginning of the world, has called some of his elect to himself through the various states of time and the diverse succession of generations. [Col. 0237A] Nor will he cease at any time to call them to himself, until he comes and hands over the kingdom to God the Father: “And God will be all in all, and death, the enemy, will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 15:28).

II. The first edict went out from him that the world might be enrolled when it was ordained that the ancient people of the Hebrews should be called to knowledge of him. This first enrolment was made in the time of our father Abraham. For the condition of that ancient people began with that faithful and blessed old man, who was the first way of believing. Although the written law was given through Moses, it had nevertheless in some manner been given beforehand in the sacrament of circumcision, which contained many sacrifices of that same law; [Col. 0237B] for Abraham, as you know, was the first to receive circumcision.

Therefore, speaking to the Jews about it and showing from whom it had taken its origin, the Lord says: “For this reason Moses gave you circumcision—not because it is from Moses, but from the fathers” (John 7:22). Moses indeed gave you circumcision, but it was not from Moses; it was from the fathers. For Moses did not newly institute it as something that had not previously existed, but confirmed it by the law afterward, so that what had first been given to that supreme patriarch and transmitted through him to his descendants might not be abandoned, but devoutly practiced.

The condition of that ancient people also appears to us as divided into three parts, distinguished by different times.

III. The first stage was that in which the great father Abraham was called [Col. 0237C] to the knowledge and worship of the one true God, together with Isaac and Jacob after him, and the sons of the same Jacob, who were called the twelve patriarchs. They were separated from the other nations and taken by the Lord as his own. The second was that in which it was freed through Moses and Aaron from the dreadful, harsh, and long-lasting slavery of the Egyptians, and led out from Egypt by a strong hand and an outstretched arm.

For that people of the Lord had for some time been held in that house of bondage after Joseph’s death, and burned in the iron furnace. As is read in Exodus (ch. 1:13), the Egyptians hated the sons of Israel and brought their lives to bitterness through the hard labor of clay and brick, and through every service by which they were oppressed in works upon the land. But when they cried to the Lord [Col. 0237D] because of the oppressor (Isa. 19:20), he remembered his mercy and took pity on their misery. He also remembered the covenant that he had made with their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and sent and freed them.

For he sent Moses his servant, Aaron whom he had chosen, placing in them the words of his signs and wonders (Exod. 2:24; Ps. 104:26). Striking the hardened king of Egypt and his people with most grievous plagues, they rescued the people from his dominion and led them, once rescued, out of Egypt. The third stage of that same people was that in which the Lord instructed it in his law through Moses and Aaron, proclaiming to it various ordinances concerning the pattern of life, and imposing upon it sacraments divided among many kinds of sacrifices [Col. 0238A] and institutions.

IV. Behold, that threefold condition of the ancient people, distinguished by different junctures of time: first, that in which, in the first and highest fathers themselves, it was called to knowledge of the one true God; second, that in which it was liberated from slavery to the Egyptians; and third, that in which it was instructed in the law through Moses and Aaron.

In the first stage an edict went out from God, the supreme emperor, that the whole world should be enrolled: namely, that the Hebrew people, in the exalted father Abraham and the patriarchs who followed him, should be called to knowledge and worship of the one true God. In the second stage it afterward advanced from good to better, freed from captivity, now increased in number and strengthened in power. [Col. 0238B] For, not counting women and little children, six hundred and three thousand five hundred strong men, equipped for battle, went out of Egypt (Exod. 12:37), like a certain Joseph who, according to the spiritual sense, ascended from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David called Bethlehem.

In the first stage they all went to be enrolled, each in his own city, worshipping the one true God and each practicing the sacrament of circumcision within his own house and family. In the second, however, the same people ascended, now increased—for this is what the very name Joseph expresses. It ascended from the revelation which it had received concerning its God, and from the rudimentary character of those few sacraments which it had undergone [Col. 0238C] in Egypt, to the full confession of that same God and to a more substantial nourishment in many and varied kinds of sacraments—like Joseph, who ascended from Galilee into Judaea and from Nazareth into Bethlehem. Moses, sent by God, came to the people in Egypt, revealing and making known to them that the Lord had looked upon them; and this revelation was like a certain Galilee.

V. Later, however, in the wilderness, after it had beheld such great and numerous signs of him in Egypt, in the Red Sea, and at the very entrance into the wilderness, it knew its same God more fully and perfectly, and confessed him devoutly and faithfully. So too in Egypt holy Moses instructed the people concerning the sacrament of the paschal lamb, through whose immolation [Col. 0238D] he freed them from Egyptian slavery. This sacrament was great and exceedingly wondrous; yet in comparison with the number and variety of the many and diverse sacraments afterward added through the law, it was in some sense related to them as a flower is to bread.

Thus the stage in which it was delivered from captivity was, according to this interpretation, like a certain Galilee and Nazareth; while that in which it was instructed in the wilderness through the law was like a certain Judaea and Bethlehem. Joseph therefore ascended from Galilee, from the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, because that people, now increased, advanced from the revelation it had received concerning its God and from the few sacraments it had received in Egypt, to the full confession of its God [Col. 0239A] and to the spiritual nourishment by which it was afterward enriched in temporal things and in the wilderness through diverse kinds of sacraments.

It deserved to attain this ascent because it was of David’s house and family (Luke 2:4). At that time the supreme David chose this people above all the nations then under heaven; it seemed then, above the other nations of the world, to belong to the lot of the elect, like a spiritual Joseph who was of David’s house and family. And Joseph ascended in order to be enrolled, because that people came to the wilderness in order to devote itself to the service of its God. Does not Moses seem to indicate this when he says, “We shall go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God”? (Exod. [Col. 0239B] 5:3). Again he says to Pharaoh: “Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: Let my people go, that it may sacrifice to me in the wilderness” (ibid., 1).

VI. But what, we think, is meant by the words, “To be enrolled with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant” (Luke 2:5), unless that, to put it briefly, that people served God in the wilderness while joined and united to the law, which contained hidden mysteries within itself? This is Mary, Joseph’s betrothed wife: that is, the law given to the ancient people as in a kind of spiritual marriage. It is rightly called pregnant because of the profound mysteries which the law held hidden in itself.

This law endured until the coming of the Son of God in the flesh; it foretold that same Son of God both in its ceremonies and in the sayings of the prophets, and at the end even presented him as present. [Col. 0239C] Hence Moses, lawgiver and leader of the people of whom we speak, says: “The Lord will raise up a prophet from among your brethren; you shall listen to him as to me” (Deut. 18:15). Thus while that people was in this condition under the time of the written law and the prophets, Christ, the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, appeared; for “while they were there, her days were fulfilled” (Rom. 10:4)—undoubtedly Mary’s days—“for her to give birth; and she bore her firstborn son” (Luke 2:7).

In some manner Mary bore a son when the law proclaimed Christ. But the law kept Christ hidden beneath the veils of burnt offerings and sacrifices, victims and ceremonies; prophecy likewise held him concealed [Col. 0239D] beneath figures and enigmas. For Mary too wraps her son in swaddling-clothes when law and prophecy hide Christ, whom they foretold, beneath hidden mysteries.

VII. This law and prophecy were imposed upon all, but were not understood by all. Only the more perfect and wiser persons recognized that Christ would come to save the human race. I think the manger in which Mary laid the son she had borne, wrapped in swaddling-clothes, belongs to these; whereas I judge that the inn, in which there was no place for him, refers to those who received the law and prophecy but did not at all understand that he would come. Law and prophecy indeed turned aside to all, but were not understood by all; Christ, announced through them, rested by understanding among the more perfect and wise. Thus not without reason did Mary, who bore the son, lay him in a manger, for whom there was no place in the inn. [Col. 0240A]

VIII. These things have been said concerning the first edict, in which that ancient people of God came to spiritual advancement. But to speak of an edict that pertains to the new people of the Church, called from Gentile life to faith: then, in some manner, as it seems to us, an edict went out from Christ, that supreme king, that the whole world should be enrolled, when he laid upon his disciples that saving task, saying: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15).

Holy [Col. 0240B] Isaiah the prophet understood this edict in a spiritual sense when, speaking in the person of our supreme emperor, he cried: “Raise the banner upon the dark mountain; lift up the voice; raise the hand, and let the leaders enter the gates” (Isa. 13:2). The dark mountain was the deep mass of the Gentiles: a mountain because of pride, dark because of ignorance. For since it raised itself haughtily through the swelling of self-exaltation, it was a mountain; and because it not only swelled with pride but, blinded by the darkness of ignorance, strayed from the light of truth, it was not merely a mountain but a dark one.

The command was already arising [variant: *then*] that a banner should be raised upon this dark mountain, for an edict had gone out that the whole world should be enrolled (Luke 2:1). This banner [Col. 0240C] is the sign of Christ’s humble manner of life and of the preaching of truth in which he was set forth: showing such humble things by his life, so as to furnish an example, and preaching such true things in instruction, so as to impart teaching. Yet it is contradicted by many: the banner of truth by heretics, and that of humility by the scribes.

IX. But how [variant: *in some manner*] was this banner raised upon the dark mountain? It was when the distinction of Christ’s humble life was made manifest to proud Gentile life, so that its exaltation might be humbled; and when the distinction of his preaching of truth was made manifest to its error, so that its blindness might be humbled. “Lift up,” he says, “the voice: preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15), so that through the intervening cry of preaching and the shining of the light of truth, the darkness [Col. 0240D] of the gloom that formerly covered the mountain may be driven away.

“Raise the hand”: by displaying wonderful things in miracles, but presenting humble things in preaching, you are to transform through the example of humility the swelling and height of the mountain into level and low ground. From that time the leaders—that is, teachers—will be able to enter the gates, namely, the hearts of subjects humbled and enlightened through obedience. But upon whom did he impose this task, that in this way a banner should be raised upon the dark mountain, the voice lifted up, and the hand raised? “I,” he says, “have commanded my sanctified ones; I have called my mighty ones in my wrath, those who exult in my glory” (Isa. 12:3). The apostles, martyrs, and holy teachers are those upon whom he imposed this office.

For his sanctified ones in the spiritual sense are those of whom and for whom, [Col. 0241A] addressing the Father in his Passion, he says: “And for them I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth” (John 17:19). The mighty in his wrath are the martyrs, strong amid the fury of persecution. “Those who exult in my glory” are the holy teachers, rejoicing in the Lord when, at last, a time of peace smiles upon them.

X. Then, as is said in what follows, “the voice of a multitude sounded on the mountains, like that of many peoples,” because, as heralds of the truth zealously devoted themselves to the word of God, the sound of faithful confession rang out among innumerable peoples. The same prophet then adds: “The sound of the voice of kings and of nations gathered together” (Isa. 13:4). This means nothing other than that the apostles went forth preaching everywhere, and that the nations, gathered into the unity of faith, received and confessed [Col. 0241B] the truth.

First, therefore, sounded the voice of kings; then that of nations gathered together. For when the edict went out from Christ that the whole world should be enrolled, the apostles went into all the world to preach the Gospel to every creature. And then all went to be enrolled, each in his own city, when, as you read in the Acts of the Apostles, “the Gentiles believed, as many as were ordained to eternal life” (Acts 13:48), all nations streaming, as Isaiah says, to that mountain, the house of the Lord (Isa. 2:2). This is what holy David says: that he desires to know the Lord’s way upon earth (Ps. 66:3), namely, his faith in the Church drawn from the Gentiles, and his Jesus among all nations.

Then that distinguished choir of apostles [Col. 0241C] came from the Jewish people, to whom Christ had been revealed through the law and prophets, to the confession of the Church drawn from the Gentiles; and it came from the Synagogue, which held the outer flower of the letter of the law, to the Gentile people. By receiving faith, and by eating the bread of sacred Scripture through exposition—breaking it with the teeth of spiritual understanding—it built within itself a dwelling-place for him whom angels desire to behold (1 Pet. 1:12) and who is “mighty and powerful in battle” (Ps. 23:8). For *David* means “desirable to behold” or “strong in hand.”

Is not this holy Joseph, namely the glorious company of apostles, of David’s house and family? He calls them no longer servants but friends; elsewhere he calls them his brothers (John [Col. 0241D] 15:13; 20:17), and also calls them sons of his Father (Matt. 5:45). And he ascended in order to be enrolled with Mary, his betrothed wife: that is, in order to preach to the Gentiles the confession of faith, having joined to himself the wisdom which Solomon calls his friend (Prov. 7:4). In her the meaning of deep mysteries lies hidden, just as a fetus lies hidden in a pregnant woman.

XI. “And it came to pass, while they were there, that her days were fulfilled for the virgin to give birth; and she bore her firstborn son.” In a spiritual sense, Mary bore Christ at Bethlehem when the catholic wisdom of sound preaching infused him into Gentile hearts through full knowledge of the right faith. He is laid in a manger, wrapped in swaddling-clothes, because he lies hidden in the sacraments of faith, in the understanding [Col. 0242A] of the meek and humble.

For what else are the sacrament of baptism in water; the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood in bread and wine; the sacrament of the laying on of hands in the anointing of chrism; and the other sacraments of holy faith, in which he is believed to be known, except swaddling-clothes in which he is wrapped at birth? And what is the manger, where tamed animals are put, except the understanding of the sacred word, where the meek and humble are spiritually nourished? Therefore he rests among the Gentiles in a sound understanding of the sacred word, he who has no rest among the Jews in any carnal understanding of the letter; for this is why he is laid in a manger—because there was no place for him in the inn.

For he who came into the world first turned aside among the Jews, but found no place there, because, as he himself says, he came [Col. 0242B] in his Father’s name and they did not receive him (John 5:34). Elsewhere John says of him: “He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). But when alien sons lied to him and limped from his paths (Ps. 17:46), “a people whom he did not know served him; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed” [variant: *served*] him.

For while the Jews proclaimed through the prophets that he would come, yet denied him when present and strayed from the way of truth, the people of the Gentiles, formerly not elect, both received the same Christ the Lord through faith and obediently submitted to his commandments. These Jews, moreover—and this should not be passed over carelessly—are called both sons, because according to election they are beloved for the fathers’ sake, and aliens, because according to the Gospel they are enemies for the sake of the Gentiles. Thus, because he could not have a place in the inn, Mary laid him in a manger: [Col. 0242C] wisdom infused him into the understanding of the Gentiles, while through faith he could not gain entrance into the hearts of the Jews.

XII. There is yet a third edict, concerning which, together with the matters pertaining to it, we have spoken before your charity, insofar as the Spirit of truth has poured it forth, in the two sermons immediately preceding this one. It is that inward inspiration through which our mighty warrior, for whose blessed vision we sigh, never ceases daily to visit his elect, causing his Joseph to ascend from Galilee into Judaea, from Nazareth into Bethlehem, because he is of David’s house and family, in order to be enrolled with Mary, his betrothed pregnant wife—in the manner which we have taken care to show you in the two sermons immediately preceding this one.

We wish still to speak of one further edict, as briefly as possible, because the due edict has not yet gone out from our emperor; but it will go out when the hour draws near in which all who are in the tombs “will hear the voice of the Son of God and will come forth” (John 5:28). Then this edict will go out, when the trumpet sounds and “the dead will rise incorruptible” (1 Cor. 15:52). Then the cry will go forth that is made at midnight: “Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matt. 25:6).

When this edict goes forth, not merely some, but all will go, because all the virgins, prudent as well as foolish, rose when the bridegroom came; they had slept and slumbered while he delayed. [Col. 0243A] And all will indeed go to be enrolled, each in his own city, because, the Evangelist says, “all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps” (Matt. 25:7). On that day each will make his own profession, because conscience will then conceal none of all the things that life has previously held within itself.

Then every elect person will ascend from the soul’s rest to the blessedness which he will possess at once in soul and body, like a spiritual Joseph who ascends from Galilee to Judaea, from Nazareth to the city of David called Bethlehem. And this will be granted him because he is of David’s house and family.

XIII. Until that decree goes forth, each of the elect rejoices only in the repose of his soul, as blessed John plainly intimates in the Apocalypse, where he says that the saints were given individual white robes. But when they arrive at that heavenly city, Bethlehem; when they ascend to their own land, which is Judaea, then in that same land, according to the prophet’s promise, they shall possess double, because they shall possess without end the fullness of blessedness in body and soul together. Then holy Joseph shall rejoice eternally “with the voice of exultation and confession” (Ps. 41:5), in that house of bread, eating and drinking at his Father’s table (Luke 12:30). In relation to the happiness of that house, the repose which the saints shall have in the soul is as a flower in relation to bread. Then that same Joseph will declare, with Mary, his betrothed wife, being pregnant, so that his heart and his flesh may rejoice in the living God.

Who can deny that flesh subject to the spirit is, as it were, a wife betrothed to the soul? Certainly it is blameworthy like an unclean prostitute when, resisting the spirit, it persists in fulfilling the works of foul desire; but it is praiseworthy as a chaste wife when, yielding to the spirit, it vigorously applies itself to good deeds. Consider, too, what fitting and harmonious order God observes in the consummation of the human being. First, a good person conceives a good purpose in the soul; then, with the soul directing it toward that good, he carries the work through by the service of the body. So also the soul first rejoices in its own repose alone; afterward body and soul together enjoy eternal happiness. In this holy Bethlehem the virgin bears a son, possessing within herself the delightful fruit of eternal incorruption; and, as he is heaped with so many gifts of blessedness, so he is, as it were, wrapped in so many swaddling-clothes. He is laid in a manger when he is placed in that heavenly hidden place, because there was no room for him in the lodging.

XIV. Our flesh, it seems to me, has a twofold lodging: this world and its own grave, which will be dug after the soul’s departure. For it takes lodging in the world through birth and in the grave through death. Yet in neither is there a place where it may be honorably laid down: for this world is a place of labor for it, not of security or rest; while the grave is a place of disgrace and stench, not of honor or incorruption.

Behold, we have expounded these evangelical words to you in four ways, leaving it to your judgment which of them seems more suitable to you. But whether you accept any one of them, or reject them all together, we hold this for certain: it is altogether an act of great humility that God, the Son of God, born of a Virgin, is wrapped in swaddling-clothes; and no less an act of great gentleness that he is laid in a manger. For is not a manger the place of an ox and an ass? This child is God; this child is the wisdom of God the Father. Do you not wonder that God’s wisdom is placed before an ass, divinity before an ox? And yet this was fitting: for unless it were so, neither would the ox know its owner nor the ass its master’s manger.

XV. O child, Creator of all, how humbly you lie in a manger (Isa. 1:3), while you rule mightily in heaven! There the heaven of heavens cannot contain you; here you are content with the narrowest manger. There, at the world’s beginning, you adorned the earth with green herbs bearing fruit, and with fruit-bearing trees producing seed; you decorated the firmament with sun, moon, and stars; you filled heaven with birds, the waters with fish, and the earth with creeping things, cattle, and beasts. Here, at the end of the world, you are wrapped in swaddling-clothes! O majesty! O lowliness! O sublimity! O humility! O immeasurable, eternal Ancient of Days! O little one, temporal and an infant, whose life upon earth has not yet lasted even one day!

Rejoice and be glad, O blessed Virgin, embracing in your lap and holding in your arms him whom the innumerable choir of heavenly spirits cannot fully contain, as he lies hidden in the Father’s bosom. Here you adore him as Creator; here you carry him as an infant; here you venerate him as Lord; here you embrace him as son. Here you prostrate yourself before him in spirit as the Most High; here you caress him with your face as a little child. Rejoice and exult most greatly today in your childbirth, O sweet Virgin—O gentle, O mild one—because him whom you conceived without corruption, you bore without burden, and gave birth to without injury. Stand beside us and excuse us, loving and merciful mother, at his dreadful judgment, so that we who now joyfully receive him as Redeemer may also behold him coming as Judge without fear. He reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI. ALSO FOR THE DAY OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

### On the threefold grace of God and the benefits of his threefold grace

[Col. 0244D]

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. God’s incarnation called, by antonomasia, the work of God. The gifts of our creation.  
2. At the beginning man possessed himself, God, and creatures; by the Fall he was stripped of gratuitous gifts and diminished in natural ones.  
3. The misery of the fallen state, moved by which God assumed the nature he wished to save.  
4. The wondrous union of the divine Word and human nature, in unity of person and communication of properties.  
5. Christ’s life is the death of sin; Christ’s death is the life of man.  
6. Against fourfold misery he set the fourfold benefit of his grace; grace that saves us is more excellent than grace that creates.  
7. Our Savior is the place of delight, from whose fullness we have all received.  
8. The river divided into four heads signifies the four corresponding marks of grace.  
9. The abundance of grace as a whole is the seed of the fruit of blessedness and glory, whose gift is threefold.  
10. The state of blessedness will render us mighty, wise, kindly, and eternal in God.  
A recapitulation of God’s grace through its effects.

I. “The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all men, instructing us, so that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God” (Titus 2:11).

Although there are many great reasons, dearest brethren, which make a human being indebted to God, this also holds an eminent place among the rest: that God was made man for us. This is a work of God—indeed, an exceedingly great work, so great that none among all his works can be compared with it. For it is far greater to make himself than to create all things other than himself. Great indeed is what John says of him: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3); but far greater is what he adds afterward: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

For what man, not only enclosed in mortal flesh, but even what angel remaining in his purity, possesses understanding so profound that he is not astonished when he beholds the Maker of all made—the God-man, the Word made flesh? Whatever good God bestows on humanity proceeds from his gratuitous grace; but what can approach this grace, much less surpass it? He created man so that he might at least exist; he created him in his own image and likeness so that he might be something exalted. But unless both were from grace, neither would have existed at all. For he gave existence, and especially existence so great and such as this, to one who was nothing; he who lacked nothing, to whom nothing new could be added and nothing old could be taken away. What is greater, or what is as ancient, as the eternal? Therefore he who is omnipotent, who cannot be increased because he is perfect, nor diminished because he is immeasurable, created humanity by grace alone. He did not need man’s goods; just as man’s evils cannot take anything from the Omnipotent, so all man’s goods can add nothing to him who possesses all things.

Thus great was the Creator’s grace displayed in the human being he created: both because the one created had been nothing, and because he was created so exaltedly, in the image and likeness of his Creator. Yet this was the grace of the Creator. It was nevertheless no small grace, by which man received not only existence and such exalted being, but also a third great gift bestowed by his Creator: namely, that he should receive service from every visible creature made for his sake, and that, ruling over all creatures in the world, he should serve in voluntary freedom and free will him alone from whom all these things had been bestowed on him.

II. The Creator’s grace granted these three things to the human being it created: essence, dignity, and devotion—namely, that he might exist; that he might be something so worthy; and that he might be able to serve the Creator who bestowed such great and such gifts. The first he held in common with the creatures subject to him; the second and third, after the first, he possessed spiritually. So long as this grace remained whole in man, man himself remained whole: possessing himself in its first good, God in its second, and the creature subject to him in its third. Placed in the middle, he descended by receiving service from the creature to relieve temporal need, and ascended by rendering service to the Creator to merit eternal happiness; and both the service he received and the service he rendered returned wholly to his own good.

This grace remained with man only as long as sin was absent from him. But as soon as, deceived by the enemy’s persuasions, he approached the fruit of the forbidden tree in order to sin, this grace of which we speak largely departed from him. For the crafty deceiver took from him what his gracious Creator had bestowed: the brightness of God’s image and likeness in him was darkened, and the power he had received over the subject creature was greatly taken away, while only his essence in some manner remained with him. Thus, delivered at once to guilt and punishment because “when he was in honor, he did not understand” (Ps. 48:13), having sought divine likeness through pride and now fallen into the depths, “he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (ibid.). Ceasing to possess even himself, he felt taken away from him the universal service of the creation that had been subject to him.

III. From that time God’s wrath descended upon wretched and pitiable man: from that time blindness of ignorance darkened him in his soul, and the calamity of mortality overwhelmed him in his body. The misery of mortality planted in human flesh the tree of concupiscence. Corrupting it both by an impulse toward evil and by contempt for good, and growing without measure, this tree continually brought it about that by the one impulse man desired what was forbidden—willing what God did not will—and by the other despised and omitted what was commanded—not willing what God did will.

But what else did this miserable human being, darkened, malicious, and slothful—darkened through the shadows of ignorance, malicious through the horror of wickedness, slothful through the lukewarmness of negligence—deserve but the punishment of Gehenna? Thus there were four evils in man: ignorance blinding through error; sloth withdrawing from virtue; malice enticing into sin; and condemnation afflicting eternally. Therefore God, having compassion on such great misery, put on the form of a Savior in order to free him from this fourfold calamity. And, so that he might fittingly undertake this saving and exalted work, he assumed in himself the same nature that he had resolved to save. Thus, that man might be saved, God himself became man, so that in the human being saved might appear the grace of God the Savior, as in man when created there had once appeared the grace of God the Creator.

IV. Appearing in man for man, he exalted in himself the whole human being whom he assumed into himself. He assumed, I say, the whole human being in himself: soul and flesh, nature but not person; yet humanity in a person. He assumed nature, because he assumed a rational soul and flesh; not person, because that flesh and soul were not united into a person before they were assumed; but in a person, so that the assumed and the assumer might be one and the same person in the Trinity.

Nor did any change occur in God because the Son assumed human nature into his own person. The Trinity which had existed from eternity remained the same: neither altered in the one assuming nor increased by the one assumed. From the point at which the assumed man began to be God and the assuming God began to be man through that ineffable union—which was directed to one person and was one—no other person began to exist than the one who assumed him. Nor did he begin to be God because he began to be man, since before he began to be this he never ceased to be God.

He assumed flesh with punishment but without fault; with mortality but without iniquity. The weakness of this punishment he retained by power, admitted into himself by will, and endured not through necessity. In Christ a rational soul governed that flesh and sanctified it for life, rejecting sin and practicing righteousness according to free will. From its union with the Word by whom it was assumed, it also had this: it did good not merely by spontaneous will, but could in no way turn toward doing evil through necessity or weakness. It was joined to flesh as to its inferior and to divinity as to its superior, itself being the life of the flesh [variant: “existing for itself”]. When it departed, the flesh died; but having divinity as its life, when it departed from the flesh it was not separated from divinity. It also endured pains and sorrows for a time in the perception of the flesh, yet possessed full and perfect joy in its spiritual union with divinity.

V. Behold, God made man for man, assuming in himself both substances of man—flesh and a clean soul—although he found neither clean in man. For, as was said above, ignorance had made the human soul dark, and concupiscence had made the flesh corrupt. Under the direction of that same concupiscence, the flesh was sluggish toward good through lukewarmness and inclined toward evil because of wickedness; and so both flesh and soul in man were liable to eternal condemnation.

But he alone, “free among the dead” (Ps. 87:6), displayed in his conduct an example of holiness, so that man, receiving a pattern from him, might first turn away from evil [variant: “depart from evil”] and, cutting off at once [variant: “in one turn”] the above-mentioned branches of concupiscence, avoid sin with all his strength; then practice virtues; and finally, by offering his utterly pure flesh upon the altar of the cross and commending his utterly innocent soul into the Father’s hands, he endured on the wood the undeserved condemnation of bodily death, and thereby took away from man the deserved ruin of eternal death, which man had merited in body and soul alike.

VI. Behold how great and what kind of grace of God our Savior appears: far more exalted and far more excellent than the grace of God our Creator which appeared in the beginning. The latter adorned man, while he stood, for a time; the former advances him into eternity. This grace is truly great and utterly immeasurable: it enlightens the blind, cleanses the defiled, adorns the cleansed, and reconciles the guilty.

Thus the fourfold distinction of this effective benefit destroys in man the fourfold evil shown above: enlightening the blind by the preaching of truth; cleansing the defiled by the rejection of perversity; adorning the cleansed by the choice of virtue; and reconciling the guilty by the passion of death. Lift up your eyes, O man; look around and see how mercifully this has been done, that you may give great thanks to him from the depths of your being, who has dealt with you in this way.

Indeed, shrouded in darkness and with the eyes within torn out, you were altogether blind and did not know where to set your foot in faith or conduct. The Angel of great counsel came to you, announcing the truth of right belief and the power of holy action, so that, holding the faith which works through love, you might know that neither one without the other suffices for salvation. For Paul says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 2:6); and James likewise declares that faith, “if it has not works, is dead in itself” (James 2:17).

You were polluted and unclean, perniciously infected everywhere with the filth of sins; perniciously, because you hated nothing less than evil itself. But the deliverer who came to you admitted no evil in his conduct and omitted no good, so that, seeing in the beauty of his spiritual way of life that nothing was absent which ought to be present and nothing present which ought to be absent, you might reject evil, rising from sin, and choose good, guarding yourself against transgression. Finally, pouring out his merciful and innocent blood upon the altar of the cross, your Lord and mediator reconciled you, though guilty; and, himself undeservedly condemned to a most shameful death though worthy of no condemnation, he freed you, who deserved condemnation, from eternal condemnation.

This is the grace of God our Savior, conferring something greater and more exalted upon us than did the grace of God our Creator. That grace gave us essence, that we might exist; created us in his image and likeness, that we might be something exalted; and placed every visible creature beneath us, that we might rule it. This grace instructed us when ignorant, freeing us from error; washed us when defiled, snatching us from filth; adorned us when washed, beautifying us with holiness; and reconciled us, guilty before judgment, saving us from condemnation. O fourfold good of saving grace: preaching of truth, rejection of perversity, practice of holiness, and suffering of a harsh death.

VII. The Savior appearing in flesh bestowed many other goods upon us; but these hold precedence among the rest and contain the primacy of the others. Because of their preeminence, I judge that the text which we read in Genesis refers to this grace: “A river went forth from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it is divided into four heads” (Gen. 2:10).

Who can deny that this is the place of which the Apostle says: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:9)? Through the Apostle he saw this place, in which he declared that all the fullness of divinity dwells. But when he saw it as so great, did he not see that it was of ineffable delight? He added: “And you are filled in him” (ibid., v. 10). Therefore he is a place, indeed a most spacious one, in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells; and he is a place of delight, in whom our fullness is contained, possessing in himself every sweetness of our fullness.

Clearly my Lord Jesus is the place of delight: whatever I see in him is lovely; whatever I hear is pleasing; whatever I smell is fragrant; whatever I taste is sweet; and, lest I omit any of the senses, whatever I touch is welcome. Truly he is the place of delight, in which, to say it briefly, there is absolutely nothing that one can reject or fail to approve. Yet, although the good in him is such without qualification and so great without quantity, he is accustomed not greedily to retain it for himself alone, but, when he determines to share it, to distribute it to us abundantly. He knows that it can be communicated by reason of his goodness but cannot be diminished by reason of his immensity.

For from that abundance of his he bestows something upon us, granting us in himself the new grace of salvation, since in our first parents we lost the ancient grace of the Creator. Hence John says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16), “and grace for grace.” From his fullness not merely some, but all, have received, as holy David says: “There is none who hides himself from his heat” (Ps. 18:7). Among the elect, certainly, there is none who hides himself from his heat; and John indicates this here when he says, “We all.” For who are “we,” except we who were foreordained to eternal life, we saints called according to purpose, we whom God the Father foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son of whom we speak (Rom. 6:28)?

This fullness, I judge, belongs to the river that goes forth from the place of delight: remaining there because of its simplicity, yet flowing down to us because of its kindness, so that it does not leave that only-begotten good and head from which it comes, yet descends to the very hem of the garment.

VIII. Therefore the river going forth in paradise from the place of delight is grace proceeding from the Savior, in whom is all fullness of sweetness, coming from heaven to bedew the Church of the holy elect. It is divided into four heads because this saving grace of which we speak chiefly confers upon us four benefits: preaching, which frees us from error; cleansing, which frees us from guilt; holiness, which adorns our conduct; and finally the passion of death, which saves from condemnation. These are, in a sense, the four heads of the river, because they are the principal gifts of grace.

One is called Phison (Gen. 2:11), which they say means “the mouth of the pupil.” No one doubts that, as speech relates to the mouth, so the pupil relates to sight. And from where comes sight of knowledge in the eye of the mind except from the brightness of holy instruction proceeding from the mouth of Christ’s preaching? Therefore the first benefit of grace is aptly called “the mouth of the pupil,” so that the word may first be heard from Christ’s mouth, and then spiritual sight in man may be cleansed; and blindness of ignorance may no longer oppress the eye of the soul while the sound of the Savior’s teaching issues from his mouth.

When this doctrine of truth has fully filled a person, it immediately stirs him to undertake the newness of holiness: so that, once what is true has perfectly shone upon him through the brightness of knowledge, he may also taste in the inward relish of affection, through maturity of conduct, what is good. Hence it is said here of Phison that it “surrounds all the land of Havilah, where gold is born” (ibid.). Havilah, according to some, means “bringing forth,” and signifies those who resolve to undertake the bringing forth of a new life. What is brighter than gold? What more precious than wisdom? Phison surrounds Havilah, where gold is born, because enlightening instruction chiefly attends that mind which strives not only to see clearly what is true, but also continually to practice what is holy through the maturity of wisdom.

“And the gold of that land is excellent” (ibid., v. 12), because a prudent person declares the wisdom of that land to be approved when he displays it in holiness of conduct. But the prophet denied that the gold of the land of those of whom he says was excellent: “They are wise to do evil, but to do good they have not known” (Jer. 4:22).

IX. By the fact that the second river is said to surround all the land of Ethiopia and the third to go against the Assyrians, you are shown how great a benefit proceeds from the second and third gifts of grace. In abandoning evil, you cast away from yourself whatever illicit blackness you have contracted; and in performing good, you resist demons fighting against you by good works.

But neither preaching, which enlightens, nor cleansing, which purifies, nor holy conduct, which adorns, is of any use unless the passion which redeems follows and bestows the fruit of eternal salvation; for “the fourth river is Euphrates” (Gen. 2:14). Another grace follows this, which will be fully present to the elect in the life to come, enriching them with everlasting blessedness. This blessedness will be threefold, granting them power, wisdom, and kindness, so that they may be strong and incorruptible in themselves, kind toward one another, and therefore wise; and each of these three things will be everlasting.

Behold the four things in which this grace will establish us: power, wisdom, kindness, eternity—power that is wise, wisdom that is kind, and kindness that is eternal [variant: “eternal wisdom”]; mighty, eternal, wise kindness; eternity that is eternal, wise, and mighty. The saints will learn, when they fully comprehend, “what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Eph. 3:18): height of power, depth of wisdom, breadth of charity, length of eternity. We assign the first to the Father, the second to the Son, the third to the Holy Spirit, and the fourth to the Trinity itself; yet we must take care to assign what we assign to each individual person to all together, so that in this way God may be all in all.

This third grace pertains to the Holy Spirit and is the grace of confirmation. For the Father created, the Son will save, and the Holy Spirit will confirm.

X. The first grace is creative and existed in the beginning; the second is saving; the third is confirming and will exist without end. The first granted that we might exist, that we might be something exalted, and that we might rule over every visible creature. The second enlightened us when blind, so that we should no longer wander in ignorance; cleansed us when unclean, so that we should not remain polluted; adorned us when cleansed, so that we might shine in holy conduct; and reconciled us when guilty, so that we should not perish in condemnation. It enlightened by preaching words of life; cleansed by utterly rejecting evils; adorned by practicing holy conduct; and reconciled by dying for us on the cross.

But the third grace will strengthen us perfectly, so that we may be mighty; illumine us, so that we may be fully wise; inflame us, so that we may love one another; and perpetuate us, so that we may be utterly unfailing. We shall be able without weakness, know without error, love without offense, and remain without failure, with God being all in all, who is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII. ALSO FOR THE DAY OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

### On the fact that the grace of God benefits only the elect, on the duty by which we are bound toward ourselves, and on the obedience to be rendered to prelates

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The first grace of the Creator; the second grace of our Savior; the third grace of our confirming God.  
2. The grace of God our Savior appears to all for imitation.  
3. It instructs only the elect for action.  
4. How God’s grace appears to all whom it does not instruct.  
5. Christ’s grace teaches us to imitate Christ and the marks of his virtue.  
6. How the reprobate respond to God’s grace appearing to them.  
7. By his preaching and way of life Christ loosed Satan’s bonds of ignorance and concupiscence.  
8. We must live soberly toward ourselves, justly toward our neighbor, and devoutly toward God; in this consists moderation of soul and body.  
9. Sobriety does not deny the body what it needs.  
10. Justice toward one’s neighbor; obedience to be rendered to superiors.  
11. Examples of disobedience drawn from the utterances of Scripture.  
12. The grave crime of those who despise superiors: forgiveness wrung out is the crime of disobedience.  
13. Obedience should be ready, willing, sincere, and persevering.  
14. Christ as the prototype of perfect obedience.

I. Beloved, in the sermon immediately preceding the one we now undertake, we spoke of the threefold grace of our God. The first was, the second now is, and the third will be at the end and without end. Although our God is one and the same, we assigned the first to the Creator, the second to the Savior, and the third to God our confirmer—while nevertheless having as Creator him who is Savior and confirmer; as Savior him who is Creator and confirmer; and finally as confirmer him who is Savior and Creator.

The first grace is in all human beings; the second is for all human beings; the third is with all human beings. The first is in all because in all human beings there is the image and likeness of God, and to all, in the first father, it was also given to rule over the subject creation. The second appeared to all because the appearing of the Son of God in human nature was set before all for salvation and example. The third is with all because, just as that first grace is eternal, so this grace, displayed to them at the end, remains with those rejoicing eternally, since it will endure without end.

II. But the grace of God our Savior, of which it was our chief purpose to speak, and whose wonderful excellence caused us to mention the other two graces, does indeed appear to all, yet does not benefit all. For Christ’s saving appearing in flesh is set before every person for imitation; but not every person is thereby shaped in holiness. Hence through the prophet he complains that the reprobate not only do not accept but even reject that magnificent work which he performed in human nature; and lamenting this, he says: “All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who do not believe, but contradict me” (Isa. 65:2).

The people who do not believe but contradict are that foolish and senseless people—the accursed company of the reprobate. Although they hear that Christ stretched out his hands to them, that is, that he set forth as an example the deeds he performed in the assumed nature, they either do not believe, blinded by the error of unbelief, or, drawn away and enticed by concupiscence, contradict him in their way of life. Hence holy Simeon prophesied that he was set “as a sign that shall be contradicted” (Luke 2:34).

What is that in which the Lord Jesus is set as a sign contradicted, except, so to speak, the sharp sword of rigorous conduct, by which holy men in the Spirit put to death the deeds of the flesh, crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24), denying themselves, taking up their cross daily, and following Christ (Luke 9:23)? The elect rejoice that they are marked by this sign; but the reprobate, who, even if they perhaps believe through faith, contradict through conduct, oppose it, “professing,” as the Apostle says, “that they know God, but denying him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16).

But what the reprobate damnably reject, the elect salutarily take up for themselves: setting Christ before themselves alike as the book of life and as a sign, so that in their one and same Redeemer they may read there the saving words which he uttered, and here imitate, according to their strength, the holy actions he performed.

III. Hence in this passage Paul, the Apostle, the vessel of election, who says that the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all men (Titus 2:11), declares that it instructs us: it sets its appearing before all human beings, but imposes its instruction upon us. “The grace of God our Savior,” he says, “has appeared to all men, instructing us” (ibid.). Who are “us”? We who are elect; we who, as was said above, are foreordained to eternal life; finally, we who are foreknown by God the Father and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:9).

Grace, which appears to all, instructs us, because the reprobate either do not recognize it when set before them, being blinded, or despise it, being hardened; whereas we recognize it, enlightened through faith, as not merely set before us but imposed upon us, and love it, anointed through action. Thus our Redeemer, seeing that he stretches out his hands to a people who do not believe but contradict him, extends them to a people who believe and agree with him—not to a foolish and senseless people, but to that praiseworthy people whom the God of hosts has blessed, whom, as holy David says, “the Lord chose for his inheritance” (Ps. 32:12).

Finally, through Jeremiah he cries: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow!” (Lam. 1:11). Those passing by the way are the elect, who despise the present life: they tread it underfoot in passing but do not embrace it as a settled condition. They make use of it for a time and from necessity, but do not remain in it through an affection of love and eternity. They walk upon it for the lawful sustenance of the body, but do not lie upon it in the deceiving sleep of the mind.

These are those who attend to the sorrow of their Savior and see his outstretched hands, toward whom the peoples named above are unbelieving and contradictory. Thus the elect, enlightened through faith, behold in faith the merciful sufferings which he endured for them in the assumed nature; and, inflamed through charity, imitate them in their conduct—while the reprobate either do not know them, blinded as they are, or do not love them, hardened as they are. Behold how the grace of God our Savior, which appears to all, instructs us.

IV. But why did this grace, which appeared to all, not instruct all human beings? Because, when preachers proclaimed it to them, they either did not believe it or, if they believed it, did not love it.
