Perhaps they received it with the hand of faith, but did not gather it with the hand of charity. For they heard, so that faith might come by hearing (Rom. 10:17), because preachers made their voices resound, so that hearing might come through the word of Christ; and, so that they might be without excuse, “their sound went out into all the earth” (Ps. 18:5).

Thus the grace of God our Savior appeared among all human beings: the preaching of the Gospel went forth among all nations, as those eminent evangelists went out into the whole world to preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark 16:15). Yet it instructs us, because “they saw and hated both me and my Father” (John 15:24). But we who are spiritually his are taught not only to hear him speaking, but also to imitate him acting, according to what he says concerning us: “My sheep hear my voice and follow me” (John 10:27).

Those who are not among his sheep, even if they may at some time hear his voice, nevertheless do not follow him. Although his words penetrate their outward hearing, they do not fulfill them with a fruitful effect; so that his grace appears to them without instructing them.

V. Since these things are so, return to yourselves, brethren, and see whether the grace of God our Savior has instructed you; for beyond doubt it appears to you not in one way but in many ways. [Col. 0254A] Behold, we announce to you his grace in his word; see whether, through what is heard outwardly, your inward mind is instructed. We can indeed touch your ear by our voice, but it belongs to him alone to move your mind within you by his impulse. Therefore, that grace may appear to you all through our tongue, he himself must instruct you through his inspiration.

Behold how great a grace of God our Savior has this day appeared to all people; and yet we plainly see how few it instructs. For, to say nothing of the other virtues of grace—for who could gather them all?—there appears today, in our Savior born, throughout the whole world, the grace of great humility, chastity, and poverty. Is it not the greatest humility that [Col. 0254B] God appears in a human being, the Word in flesh, wisdom in infancy, the Lord of all things in a crying little child, strength in weakness? And what could be clearer evidence that, among the other virtues, he especially loves chastity than that he deigned to be born of a Virgin? O great poverty: to be laid in a manger because there was no room for him in the lodging-place! Do not people know this by knowledge? Yet few grasp it by imitation, so that it may truly be said in this respect also: the grace of God our Savior appears to all people, but instructs few.

Would that it might instruct us also, so that with the Apostle we may say: “The grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us” [Col. 0254C] (Tit. 2:11). This is true if you learn from him to be meek and humble of heart (Matt. 11:29); if each of you knows how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor (1 Thess. 4:4); if your conduct is free from covetousness, content with what is present, and if you do not lift your eyes toward riches which you cannot possess, but, having food and covering, are content with these things (1 Tim. 6:8).

VI. How differently almost all those act to whom this grace appears outwardly. They celebrate the birth of the humble and little Christ, while they themselves are proud and great in their own eyes; the chaste and modest Christ, while they themselves are impure and corrupt; the poor and needy Christ, while they wish to become rich, and thereby fall into many [variant: “many desires”] useless and harmful things. They seek covetousness, the root of all evils [Col. 0254D], and thus entangle themselves in many pains—swollen, defiled, inflamed: swollen by the swelling of vanity and pride, defiled by the stench of pleasure and luxury, inflamed by the heat of covetousness and greed.

Who is proud amid honors, who is unchaste, who is covetous, to whom the grace of humility, chastity, and poverty does not today appear in God our Savior? It surely appears to them, but does not instruct them. They see fire and light, yet remain cold and dark; they behold food and a physician, yet themselves hunger and are sick. For if the grace which appears instructed them, the dark would be enlightened, the cold kindled, the hungry refreshed, and the sick healed. That is, to put it briefly: they would abandon what is evil and [Col. 0255A] practice what is good. Hence Paul here declares that the grace of God our Savior, which appeared to all people instructing us, teaches us “that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, piously, and justly in this age” (Tit. 2:11).

VII. As you may infer from what has gone before, there are two bonds of Satan by which he draws the reprobate to the eternal punishment of Gehenna: ignorance, by which they are blinded so that they do not recognize what is true; and concupiscence, by which they are drawn and enticed to practice what is evil. In the first case they do not believe rightly; in the second they do not live holy lives. Ungodliness [variant: “the evil of ungodliness”], as it seems to me, belongs to the first; worldly desires to the second. For ungodliness, as some maintain, is that which causes a person to stumble [Col. 0255B] in faith; worldly desires, however, impel one toward wicked action.

The grace of God our Savior instructs us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires. For if you approach the grace of his preaching, what do you hear there that does not destroy the ungodliness of error? If you approach the grace of his manner of life, what do you find there that does not extinguish worldly desires in the mind? “Christ,” says the Apostle, is “the power and wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). With ears capable of hearing, hear wisdom, and ungodliness will not make you depart through error from right belief. Embrace power in your mind with the embraces of love, and worldly desires will not inflame you toward iniquity.

Holy David comprehended both these goods in few words when he said: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation” (Ps. 26:1). [Col. 0255C] That is: the Lord, my light, will enlighten me, lest the darkness of ungodliness obscure me; the Lord, my salvation, will save me, lest worldly desires overthrow me. Whom shall I fear, when, as he enlightens me, ungodliness can no longer blind me by error; and, as he saves me, worldly desires cannot defile me by iniquity? Thus, “Direct me, Lord, in your truth, and teach me,” lest I wander from faith through the byways of ungodliness. Likewise take concupiscence from me, lest I be defiled in perversity through worldly desires.

In this way, enlightened by grace and made bright against ungodliness, and also cleansed by that same grace from worldly desires, we must live soberly, piously, and justly, and strive to live so in this age.

VIII. [Col. 0255D] In these words, as the frequent teachings of the Fathers testify, is contained that threefold duty by which we are held indebted and bound to ourselves, our neighbors, and God: for we owe sobriety to ourselves, justice to our neighbor, and piety to God. Moreover, holy affection and rigorous mortification confer sobriety upon you, so that you neither carry about in your mind through appetite what is unlawful, nor perform in deed through desire what is unlawful. If you sin in either of these respects, you lose sobriety: both in desiring what is evil and in doing it.

Therefore let holy meditation guard you in your mind, lest you desire anything unlawful through an impure affection; let rigorous continence mortify you in the flesh, lest you commit anything wicked by an evil action. This is the twofold bridle by which the impetuous motion both [Col. 0256A] of mind and body must be restrained: so that inwardly maturity may curb slippery wantonness, and outwardly continence may draw one back from every wicked outbreak.

Let maturity, I say, be a bridle in the mind, manfully drawing it back from everything that arises within it and seeks to drag it this way and that: such as ambition for passing honor, appetite for transitory favor, the puffing-up of pride, the swelling of envy, the rancor of anger, the rust of sloth, the restlessness of avarice, the indecency of gluttony, the foulness of lust, and impulses harmful in this manner, which never allow the unhappy soul to be happy at any hour.

Likewise, let continence be a bridle in the body, restraining each of its members from perversity and fitting them to uprightness: drawing the sight back from curiosity, [Col. 0256B] hearing from vanity, smell from pleasure, taste from voracity, touch from impurity, speech from foolish talk, and gait from frivolity. This is what makes a person blameless in walking and standing, sitting and lying down, keeping silent and speaking, working and resting, praying and reading, eating and fasting—in every place and time, in every undertaking, and toward every person.

IX. This, O human being, is the duty by which you are bound toward yourself: the bridle and restraint of every unlawful thought and action—the measure of sobriety. Since you are a rational soul and flesh, be diligent to guard and preserve them both, so that no unlawful affection may defile the former within, nor any wicked effect dishonor the latter without. You owe yourself yet a third thing: that you should not fruitlessly deny your body what it needs in food and drink, sleep and clothing, and the other things required by its just necessity. For you exceed the measure of sobriety no less when you withhold necessities from your body than when you expend superfluities upon it.

For the body is a beast of burden; and therefore its discerning rider, the spirit, must take care both to place a bridle upon it lest it kick, and to set hay before it lest it fail. For the Holy Spirit, who said through the Apostle, “Make not provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14), says elsewhere through the same Apostle: “No one has hated his own flesh, but cherishes and nourishes it” (Eph. 5:29). Although in this one saying, [Col. 0256D] “Make not provision for the flesh in its desires,” he has comprehended both kinds of sobriety. For in saying “provision for the flesh,” he permits necessities; but in adding “in its desires,” he cuts off superfluities alone. Therefore, just as you drive unlawful things from the will [variant: “necessity”], lest it desire them through impurity, so remove wicked things from the flesh, lest it commit them through iniquity—yet do not take necessities away from the body, lest it collapse through weakness. Conduct yourself thus; present yourself as such; and you live soberly in this age.

X. But because none of us lives for himself, there is another duty which your neighbor requires of you; and the Apostle calls this, in this passage, justice in a spiritual sense. For justice, as some define it, is the virtue that gives to each person what is his due. Render, [Col. 0257A] therefore, to your superior what is his due; render also to your equal, and render also to your inferior—and you live justly.

What is owed to a superior? First, obedience, according to the apostolic command: “Let your soul be subject to higher powers” (Rom. 13:1). Obey, therefore, your superior, whoever and whatever he may be, who has been set over you in God’s place. And, to say it briefly: whatever he enjoins upon you, whether in forbidding or commanding—provided that it is according to God’s law—receive it no otherwise than as if you had heard it from God.

Guard yourself against negligence, which forgetfulness produces; and above all guard yourself from contempt as from death, for “pride is the beginning of all sin” (Tob. 4:14). In commands, even those that seem least, negligence cannot be excused, since it is sin; nor should contempt be dismissed [Col. 0257B] without grave punishment, since it is a crime.

XI. As you know, Saul once rebuked Jonathan (1 Kings 14:44), because he had transgressed his prohibition; and he considered that transgression of such weight that a father judged even his son, the transgressor, worthy of death, although it is agreed that Jonathan had not heard that prohibition. Likewise, the man of God who was sent from Judah to Jeroboam (3 Kings 13:22), because he transgressed the Lord’s command—not lifted up through his own obstinacy, but deceived by another’s suggestion—was delivered to a lion to be devoured.

To tell you the truth, reflection on his fault has often caused me no small astonishment, and his punishment inspires fear. For unless it is because that supreme [Col. 0257C] equity, which can do nothing perverse or crooked, is at stake in this matter, it seems that such disobedience should not have been punished in that prophet by such a vengeance—disobedience which he incurred lest he should be disobedient. For what happened? The king wished to detain him by force, and he did not consent at all, because he knew it had been forbidden him. The old man attempted to bring him back; at first refusing, he finally agreed, because he thought that what was forbidden was not merely unauthorized and unjust, but had been changed. Thus, just as he did not consent to remain in order to obey, so also, unless I am mistaken, he consented to return in order not to disobey. In both instances he was prepared to obey the will of his God, though deceived by another’s lie; and afterward he heard from that man’s [Col. 0257D] mouth the true sentence of death, having first heard from him the deceitful counsel of ruin.

XII. Consider from these examples what punishment will be inflicted upon those who, swollen with the pride of arrogance, transgress the commands of their elders in complete contempt. Consider what punishment was to be exacted from Dathan, Abiram, and Korah (Num. 16:1), who, as you know, rose against Moses, their superior, in such great and such a kind of pride. If a devouring lion killed one who, so far as he himself was concerned, in a certain sense—if it is lawful to say so—was disobedient lest he should be disobedient: for if he sinned—indeed, since he did sin—it certainly appears that he sinned lest he should sin.

Infer from this how grievously King Saul sinned (1 Kings 15:9), who, in order to satisfy his greed, refused according to the Lord’s command to strike Amalek [Col. 0258A] unto utter destruction and to demolish all that belonged to it—although the same Saul judged even his son Jonathan guilty of death because he had transgressed Saul’s prohibition without knowing it.

Guard yourself also against extorted permission, which our fathers, to show fully how evil it is, call the sister of disobedience. Guard yourself, I say, against it, lest perhaps, through the excessive importunity of your requests, you violently compel your superior to tolerate, or even grant, what you ask; and so, with the proper order confused, make him in a sense your subject and yourself his superior.

XIII. Obey your superior, then, promptly, gratefully, cheerfully, sincerely, and perseveringly. First, let the obedience you offer be prompt, so that you do not permit even a slight murmur to dwell in your mind. Let it also be grateful, [Col. 0258B] so that you show cheerfulness in your face, and thus, as you inwardly please God through a benevolent mind, you may outwardly cheer your neighbor through a cheerful countenance. Third, let it be sincere, so that you seek not merely something of your own in it, covertly working by some crafty device so that you may be commanded to do what you enjoy doing in order to satisfy your empty craving and your craving for emptiness—aiming in this rather to fulfill the will of the flesh than attending either to the usefulness of the command or to the will of the one commanding.

Do you wish to hear of sincere obedience? “Let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). Receive also from Samuel an example of sincere obedience: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears” (1 Kings 3:10). I ask not that you speak justly, but only that you speak; for whatever you, [Col. 0258C] my Lord, may say, I, your servant, shall carry out obediently. Finally, let your obedience be persevering, so that always and everywhere, according to place and time, according to your knowledge and ability, you may be ready to obey the one commanding you.

XIV. Therefore I shall call you prompt in obedience if you obey willingly and without murmuring, with a perfect heart and a willing spirit. Grateful, if in carrying out a command you display cheerfulness even in your face. Sincere, if, renouncing yourself, you seek nothing of your own fleshly interest in what is commanded, but attend only to the will of the one commanding and to the usefulness of the command, and embrace harsh and difficult things more readily even than pleasant and easy ones. Persevering, if you follow in obedience him of whom you read: “He became obedient unto death” [Col. 0258D] (Phil. 2:8), setting before yourself as the sole limit of obedience that which is also the limit of life.

We have said this concerning the obedience which we ought to render to our superiors. But since we are now compelled to end this sermon, in the following sermon, God granting it, we shall show what things are still owed by us to superiors, equals, and inferiors alike. We also propose to entrust to your devout ears whatever occurs to us concerning this subject. Let us praise and glorify, in all his gifts and mercies, our Lord Jesus Christ, who has deigned so often, in this his most holy Nativity, to satisfy us with spiritual feasts; to him be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. ALSO FOR THE DAY OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

On the fifteen degrees of charity: namely, the three greater duties, those owed to superiors; the three owed to subjects; the three owed to equals; and the other six owed to everyone. Also on sobriety, justice, piety, perseverance, and the threefold grace—of the Creator, Savior, and confirmer.

[Col. 0259A]

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. Superiors are owed obedience, reverence, and ordered familiarity.
2. It is harder to command discerningly than to obey willingly.
3. A superior owes subjects discipline, gentleness, and discernment.
4. Superior and subject are bound by mutual obligation.
5. In the superior there should be moderated discipline; in the subject, grateful reverence.
6. In the former there should be gentleness with charity; in the latter, love with familiarity.
7. Equals are owed honor and love with the humility of service.
8. Cheerfulness in the sweetness of speech.
9. Everyone without distinction is owed compassion and consolation in adversity; congratulation and exhortation in prosperity.
10. Sobriety gives power; justice, kindness; piety, wisdom.
11. The grace of the Creator is attributed to the Father, that of the Savior to the Son, and that of the confirmer to the Holy Spirit.
12. A practical summary of the virtues to be exercised.

I. At the end of the preceding sermon, brethren, you have heard what kind of obedience you ought to show to your superiors. For whoever wishes to wear the habit of religion [Col. 0259B] must, according to the Apostle’s admonition, obey his superiors and be subject to them. For, as he adds, “they keep watch as those who will render an account for your soul” (Heb. 13:17).

First, then, offer your superior the obedience which we described in the sermon most recently delivered. [Col. 0259C] Second, offer devout and humble reverence to him who presides over you, because he presides over you in God’s place. Therefore, for the reverence and fear of him whose office he performs, let him also be an object of reverence and fear to you.

Saint Samuel was once subject to sinful Eli; David, though chosen, to reprobate Saul; and neither was ever found to have dishonored his superior, though sinful and reprobate, but each held him in great reverence. Holy David, as you know, fled Saul, who was pursuing him, as from a lord (1 Kings 24:6); and, as blessed Gregory says, when he found an opportunity to strike him, he did not recognize it, but instead struck his own heart because he had dishonored Saul even by cutting off the hem of his cloak. [Col. 0259D] Yet this obedience and reverence are not of great merit before God unless love of ordered familiarity accompanies both: so that you may also, from unfeigned love according to God, be familiar in your private and inward concerns with him to whom you obey for God’s sake and whom you venerate in God’s place.

II. This is indeed a great duty which we owe to our superiors. But there is another, perhaps no less and indeed greater in weight, by which they are held bound to us. What is their duty? The Apostle embraces it in words few but most profound: “He who presides, [let him do so] with diligence” (Rom. 12:8). If you who preside wish fully to know how manifold that diligence is, read what the holy Fathers have said on this subject, especially the *Pastoral* of blessed Gregory; then you will understand what it means for you who preside to be diligent. [Col. 0260A] Certainly it is harder for you to render to your subject the many things you owe him than for him to render what he owes you. It is harder for you to command discerningly than for him to obey willingly; to preside usefully than to be subject humbly; to govern without pride than to be governed without complaint; to engage in anxious care than to remain at rest; finally, to provide what is salutary for his soul and necessary for his body than for him to make use of your provision.

III. But although the duty by which you are bound toward him is manifold, he especially requires three things from you: discipline, gentleness, and discernment. You owe discipline: give him discipline, and a twofold discipline—namely, watchful care lest he fall, [Col. 0260B] and care, if he has fallen, that he may rise from his fall. Remember that you are a physician; remember that you are a shepherd. You are not truly skilled in your art unless you know how to preserve health when it is possessed, lest it be lost, and how to restore it when it is lost, that it may be recovered.

Nor are you a good shepherd unless, among the sheep—not yours, but Christ’s, though committed to you—you preserve what is fat and strong, bind up what is weak, and comfort what is broken (Ezek. 34:4). But lest discipline exceed its measure, let gentleness temper it. Know that, because you are the base of the temple, you ought to be not only the lion of strictness but also the ox of gentleness. Yet because you must beware lest the former be too strict and the latter too lax, let their mother, discernment, intervene; under her guidance the virtues keep to the middle way. [Col. 0260C] Interposing herself, she joins the two to one another, so that, once they have been blended together, the piety of gentleness may do nothing without strictness, and the strictness of discipline nothing without piety. Therefore, if strictness is gentle and gentleness stern within you, you who are the base of the temple have the straps hanging upon your lion and ox (3 Kings 7:29), so that, according to occasion and cause, place and time, each may be drawn back from evil and each loosed toward good.

IV. See how this threefold duty by which a superior is bound to his subject, when it is duly paid, compels and brings about the payment of that threefold duty of which we spoke above, which the subject owes to his superior. [Col. 0260D] We said that the subject owes the superior obedience, reverence, and familiarity. We also said that the superior owes the subject discipline, goodness, and gentleness, and that discernment must be exercised if these are to be used profitably.

But how will your subject be willing and ready to obey you if you are excessive and undiscerning in commanding? Do you think that you may always command everyone according to your pleasure, making whatever has been conceived in your will into reason for you by adopting that saying:

> “Thus I will, thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason.”

Certainly this is unlawful. “But,” you ask, “when these two concur—what I wish and what is permitted—must the matter not always be undertaken?” Certainly not. Are you freer or more powerful than him who says, “All things are lawful to me, but not all things are expedient; all things are lawful to me, but not all things edify” [Col. 0261A] (1 Cor. 10:22)? Can you in any respect be compared to him who, lest he should scandalize even strangers, gave what he was permitted to retain precisely because no obligation at all constrained him to give it? “Lest,” he says, “we scandalize them, give to them for me and for yourself” (Matt. 17:26).

V. But if you bring before me the counsel of blessed Benedict—that if impossible things are commanded of a brother, and the one commanding refuses to relax them, he should accept what has been imposed—I say that the admonition is holy, and the counsel holy, just, and good. For one who was full of the spirit of all the righteous could not give an unjust counsel. But because it is incumbent on him to accept the command if you impose impossible things, do you act well when you impose impossible things, especially at this time? [Col. 0261B] I speak in view of the imperfection of this age. Were those blameless of whom the Lord said that they bound heavy burdens and imposed impossible things, yet would not move them with even their finger? (Matt. 23:4.)

Thus, as it seems to me, the obedience of the one obeying often proceeds from the discernment of the one commanding: if in commanding you carefully and diligently observe place and person, cause and time, then the person whom you command will be less willing to resist by contradiction, insofar as he has less cause to do so.

Your subject ought to show you reverence; but you ought to give him discipline, for there are certain subjects in whom, unless discipline is first sown, reverence is not afterward harvested. Yet I do not say this generally of all, [Col. 0261C] but only of some, and only of those who are very imperfect and immature. When they see their superior lowering himself a little and making himself common among them, they disdain to revere him, and he is in their eyes what he is in his own. But wise and good disciples, the more humbly they see their superior, the more they revere him; and the more approachable they find him, the more humbly they honor him. Yet moderated discipline in a superior produces grateful reverence in a subject.

VI. We said that a subject owes familiarity born of love to his superior; yet he will never render it fully unless he perceives him to be gentle and lovable toward himself. For how will he show himself familiar in love with you in his private and [Col. 0261D] intimate concerns unless he knows that you love him, that you are gentle toward him, and act toward him as a friend? For, as constant experience has taught us, we seldom fully open our secrets and inward matters except to one whom we love.

Moreover, love begets love. Love, once acquired, produces confidence; confidence, once produced, reveals secrets without any suspicion and makes hidden things manifest without any external disclosure. If you see yourself loved in this way, you naturally strive to love in return; and you certainly place confidence in one to whom you return love. To one in whom you rightly trust, consequently, you securely commit yourself in the disclosure of your secrets.

Therefore, to repeat briefly what superior and subject owe each other: let there be discernment in the superior’s commanding, that there may be ready willingness [Col. 0262A] in the subject’s obeying; let there be moderated discipline in the former’s authority, that there may be grateful reverence in the latter’s maturity; finally, let there be ordered gentleness in the former’s charity, that there may be unfeigned love in the latter’s familiarity. Behold how the merits of superiors and subjects depend mutually upon one another.

VII. It is time to speak of the duty which you owe to your equal. I do not now wish to set before you something newly invented by myself; rather, consider what the Apostle says here: “Render,” he says, “to all their dues” (Rom. 13:7). And he added: “To whom tribute, tribute; to whom fear, fear; to whom honor, honor” (ibid.): fear to the Lord, tribute to the collector, honor to the Father. And he added: “Owe no one anything, except that you love one another” (ibid., v. 8). [Col. 0262B] This is the duty which you must always render to one another, and render in such a way that you owe it [variant: “as you ought”]: owe it so that you render it—that is, render it while owing it, and owe it while rendering it.

You likewise owe one another honor: each of you should honor the other, rise and bow to the other, offering him precedence in every place and time, in every word and action, insofar as he knows it to be fitting, appropriate, lawful, and expedient. This is that good and pleasant thing to which Paul invites us when he says: “Outdoing one another in honor” (Rom. 12:10). And again: “Through the charity of the Spirit serve one another” (Gal. 5:13). Elsewhere: “In humility,” he says, “of spirit, considering one another superior to yourselves” (Phil. 2:3). Likewise: “With all humility [Col. 0262C] and gentleness, with patience bearing with one another in charity”; and again: “Careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2). There are many other sayings of this kind which invite us to fraternal honor, love, and service.

VIII. Thirdly, also offer one another cheerfulness of countenance. Offer it, I say, to one another, and receive it from one another, for among yourselves you can possess nothing more pleasing, nothing more delightful. For Solomon says, “A good word is better than a gift” (Ecclus. 18:17); and: “A sweet word multiplies friends, softens enemies, and a gracious tongue abounds in a good person” (Ecclus. 6:5). Concerning cheerfulness, you have: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). As seasoning among foods, so cheerfulness is among all virtues. [Col. 0262D] For what you do seems insipid to me unless the grace of cheerfulness commends it. Let love be in the charity of the mind, honor in the humility of service, and cheerfulness in the grace of the countenance and sweetness of speech. Yet charity must be without duplicity and pretense; humility without vanity and flattery; cheerfulness without frivolity, vanity, or dissipation.

IX. There are other duties also, owed not only to superiors, nor only to equals, nor only to inferiors, but owed without distinction to all people, according to your ability and knowledge, insofar as is appropriate and lawful, expedient and fitting. For one whom you see oppressed by adversity, you owe compassion and consolation: the former in the mind, the latter in speech. But one whom prosperity favors, you owe congratulation [Col. 0263A] and exhortation: the former in the mind, the latter on the lips.

Therefore, sympathize from the depths of your heart with one to whom adversity is burdensome, and console him lest he fail. But to one whom prosperity delights, offer heartfelt congratulations, and exhort him to strive to advance more and more in goodness. To both you owe help and counsel, so that you may instruct, by consoling, both the person who is in prosperity and the one who is in adversity concerning how each ought to act; and, by helping, render each strong and vigorous for what must be done.

If you add these six to the preceding nine, you will have, as it were, fifteen steps on the ladder of the justice of charity, by which you ascend and descend upon the Son of Man. If you are diligently found to fulfill all these things which we have expounded concerning justice in a lengthy but perhaps not unfruitful discussion, [Col. 0263B] you surely live justly in this age.

You live piously, however, if you persist steadfastly in the worship of your God with sincere and inward affection. For if you perceive that you always stand before his divine gaze; if you are everywhere ready for his hidden promptings; if, saying with the Psalmist, “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. 24:15), you inquire with a vigilant mind everywhere what he wills and what he does not will, in order promptly to perform it—I think that you live piously in this age. Therefore, “denying ungodliness and worldly desires, let us live soberly, justly, and piously in this age” (Tit. 2:12), until we may enjoy that age to come. For this reason the Apostle added: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ” (ibid., v. 13). [Col. 0263C] In these words, indeed, perseverance is indicated.

X. Therefore the grace of God our Savior, instructing us in these four things—sobriety, justice, piety, and perseverance—shows us in its instruction that through these four we may attain those four gifts which, in the age to come, the grace of God our confirmer grants us. We said above, in the first sermon which we delivered on this subject, that confirming grace is to grant us four things in the future: power, wisdom, kindness, and eternity. You will certainly attain these four if you diligently practice the four things which saving grace teaches us to possess: sobriety, justice, piety, and perseverance.

For through sobriety you will attain power, being plainly worthy to possess yourself [Col. 0263D] there in freedom if you have first striven here to govern yourself, both in body and mind, with the bridle of sobriety. Through justice you will attain kindness: you who on the journey render to each person what is his own will also rejoice in your homeland with each person through love; and the charity which you here had toward your neighbor you will there bring to completion with that same neighbor without end, completing it without exhaustion.

Piety will lead you to eternal wisdom, so that you who delighted here in the continual remembrance of your God may be made eternally joyful there in his presence; and that one may savor there in eternal rest as a reward who savors you here in temporal labor as merit. If you persevere, you will attain eternity, so that, living soberly, justly, and piously in this age, while awaiting [Col. 0264A] the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, you may deserve at his glorious coming to possess eternity, if the Lord, when he comes, finds you doing so.

For the virtue of perseverance displays within itself a certain likeness of eternity, and it alone also merits eternity. Unless you possess it on this path upon which you walk, you will not advance but fail; you will indeed run, but in vain, because you will not attain.

XI. What has been said at length above may be repeated more briefly, so that it may be held more firmly in memory. “The grace of God our Saviour has appeared.” There is a threefold grace: the first is that of God our Creator, and was at the beginning, pertaining to the Father; the second, of God [Col. 0264B] our Saviour, is now at the end, looking to the Son; the third, of God our confirmer, is without end, belonging to the Holy Spirit. The first, then, is creative; the second, saving; the third, confirming.

The first bestowed so great gifts upon us: being, that we might exist; the image and likeness of God, that we might be something exalted; power, that we might preside over the creatures subject to us. But sin darkened this grace in humankind, bringing it to four evils: ignorance, sloth, malice, and condemnation. Ignorance blinded; sloth drew away from virtues; malice enticed toward sins; condemnation afflicted eternally. Thus man became darkened through the error of ignorance, slothful through the lukewarmness of negligence, malicious through the filth of wickedness, condemned [Col. 0264C] through the horror of punishment.

The Saviour came: he preached truths, reproved evils, chose good things, and endured the hardships of death. Thus saving grace enlightened the blind man through the preaching of truth, delivering him from the darkness of error; cleansed the defiled man through the rejection of depravity, washing him from the filth of malice; adorned the slothful man through the choice of virtue, raising him from the lukewarmness of negligence; reconciled the guilty man through the suffering of death, drawing him out of the condemnation of Gehenna. First, therefore, by preaching truth, the Saviour enlightened the blind; secondly, by reproving evils, he cleansed the defiled; thirdly, by practising good things, he adorned the naked; fourthly, by dying on the cross, he reconciled the guilty to the Judge.

Confirming grace, moreover, grants us these four things: power, wisdom, goodness, [Col. 0264D] and eternity—the first from the Father, the second from the Son, the third from the Holy Spirit, the fourth from the Trinity itself—so that God may be all in all. We have the first in ourselves, the second in God, the third in one another; the fourth is that penny which all alike shall receive, although they have not all alike laboured in the vineyard. We shall therefore be able without weakness, know without error, love without offence, and remain eternally without any failure whatsoever.

Saving grace instructs us that, “renouncing impiety and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this world, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God.” We live soberly in relation to ourselves, that we may attain power; justly toward our neighbour, that we may attain [Col. 0265A] goodness; piously toward God, that we may attain wisdom; and, by persevering in expectation, we attain eternity.

You live soberly if, guarding your thoughts, you restrain your mind from an impure desire; if, crucifying your members which are upon the earth together with their vices and concupiscences, you restrain the flesh from unlawful desire (Gal. 5:24); if, discreetly granting what is necessary to the body, you preserve it from want.

You live justly if you render what you owe to a superior, an inferior, an equal, and, generally, to everyone: to superiors, obedience, reverence, and familiarity. Let obedience be without murmuring, reverence without pretence, familiarity without flattery. To inferiors give discipline, gentleness, and discernment: discipline which frightens, gentleness which soothes, discernment which tempers both. To equals give love, honour, [Col. 0265B] and cheerfulness: love in the charity of the heart, without duplicity or pretence; honour in humble service, without vanity or flattery; cheerfulness in the grace of the countenance and sweetness of speech, without frivolity or dissipation. To everyone generally, when they are in adversity, give compassion, that you may pity them; consolation, that you may endeavour to raise them up; but when they are prosperous, give congratulation, that through charity you may rejoice with them. Give exhortation, that through instruction you may stir them to what is good. To both—that is, to those placed in adversity and those in prosperity—give counsel and assistance, so that by the former you may instruct them concerning what they do not know, and by the latter help them in matters for which they are not sufficient by themselves.

For the rest, brothers, praise this saving grace; long for confirmation, so that, living soberly, justly, and [Col. 0265C] piously in this world, you may securely await the blessed hope and attain to the everlasting vision of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ: through the grant of him who on this day deigned to be born of a Virgin, Christ Jesus, God and man, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. ON THE DAY OF SAINT STEPHEN, PROTOMARTYR.

On the three feasts immediately succeeding the day of the Lord’s Nativity, and on the virtue of charity and patience.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. Why the Nativity of the Lord is followed by the birth-feasts of Saints Stephen, John, and the Innocents.—2. Christ in some manner suffers and dies in his saints: true and enduring joy is not found here.—3. Worldly joy is interrupted by the bite of bitterness; the death of the saints by life-giving joy.—4. In Saint Stephen, charity was eminent in compassion, zeal in correction, and prayer in amendment.—5. Among the Jews: fury in the heart, reproach in the mouth, conspiracy unto death.—6. Correction must be received with equanimity.—7. To guard against the first movements of anger belongs to prudence; to restrain them belongs to patience.—8. An explanation of the definition of the virtue of patience.—9. Conspiracy toward evil is most wicked: the remedy for enduring correction.—10. The onset of anger furnishes every evil; it must be moderated after the example of Saint Stephen.—11. The zeal of correction, shaped by the affection of love, is good.

I. If, dearest brethren, you are willing to weigh with attentive care and careful attentiveness how greatly these saints, whose feasts we celebrate on these three days, were beloved by the common Redeemer of all, each individually, among many other indications you may also discern this: their birth-feast days, following in due order so soon after that day on which he was born, and without any interval, present themselves for our celebration. Today, indeed, we devoutly commemorate the passion of blessed Stephen. As you know, he holds a great place among the martyrs in dignity because he holds the first place in order; for, as blessed Maximus says, if anything can distinguish one martyr from another, he seems pre-eminent who is first.

Tomorrow, God willing, you will celebrate the glorious feast of the glorious apostle and evangelist John. That he was held in the closest [Col. 0266B] intimacy with Christ is beyond doubt to anyone acquainted with his Gospel. Is he not the one who, as a special token of love, deserved to recline upon Christ’s breast at supper, and who also dared, beyond all the others, to ask the Lord plainly to identify his betrayer? “Lord,” he said, “who is it?” (John 21:20). Nor should this be left unmentioned: although the Lord loved all his disciples, John did not judge it presumptuous to say of himself, “That disciple whom Jesus loved” (ibid., 7).

And concerning the holy Innocents, whose birth-feast follows that of blessed John, who can doubt that they too, newly born as Christ had newly been born, were loved by Christ? For his birth was the cause and occasion of their death: the little Jesus joined little ones to himself; the innocent one, innocents; one being born, those who were dying.

II. But why, I ask, is it that although the Nativity of Christ ought to be celebrated with the greatest joy, the days of the passion and death of his chief friends and familiars nevertheless confront us? For almost at the same time we must celebrate both his entrance into the world and their departure from the world: we celebrate the death of one of these and his birth. Indeed, Christ suffers in his chosen and beloved ones, and dies in those who die. Otherwise he would not have said to Saul concerning persecution, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 28:7); nor to Peter concerning death, “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.”

What then is this: that so soon after his own entrance into the world we celebrate his departure from the world in his beloved familiars? His saints might indeed say even this to him: “You came yesterday, and today you are compelled to depart with us” (2 Sam. 15:20). What do you think is intimated to us by this, except that our stay in this world is brief, and that all the joy we have here is nevertheless sorrowful? Yesterday we celebrated his birth in himself; today, however, we celebrate in some manner his passion in Stephen. Yesterday there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising the Lord. Today there arose the fury of the Jews stoning [Col. 0267A] Stephen. Today persecutors who stoned Stephen inflicted death upon him; yesterday great joy, which was to be for all people, was proclaimed. In all these things, as we have already said, it is shown to us that life in this world is brief and its joy sorrowful. “What is our life?” says Saint James; “it is a vapour appearing for a little while” (Jas. 4:15). These words plainly show that our life seems rather to appear than to be anything, and that even the little which seems to appear cannot long remain.

III. Suppose now that someone had lived from the very beginning of the world until today and must die today: what judgment would you make concerning the length of his time? He who was ceases to be, and devouring, consuming death swallows him. Again, what sweetness of joy in human affairs is so great that no bite of bitterness interrupts it? For the pursuit of bodily pleasures, as someone has said, is full of anxiety, while their satiety is full of repentance; and he added: “What diseases, what intolerable pains, like a certain fruit of the wickedness of those who enjoy them, do they commonly inflict upon their bodies?” For anyone who chooses to recall his own lusts will understand that the ends of pleasures are sorrowful. And again concerning the same matter:

> Every pleasure has this:  
> It drives those who enjoy it with goads;  
> And, like a flight of flying bees,  
> When it has poured forth sweet honey,  
> It flees, and, when struck,  
> Presses hearts with a bite too tenacious.  
> —Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book II, metre 7

O life, how quickly you run to death! O joy, how hastily you fall into error! I believe that by this the Lord admonishes you to hasten eagerly toward that life from which eternity drives far away all setting, and toward that joy from which totality banishes every failing. This is that joy which the saints attain through present sorrow. This is that life to which they come through bodily death. How delightful is this sorrow, how desirable this death! The former will be rewarded by a joy which, because of its immensity, can in no respect be diminished; the latter by a life which, because of eternity, can never be ended. To this life-giving joy and joyful life blessed Stephen came today, exchanging temporal pain for immeasurable joy and bodily death [Col. 0267D] for eternal life.

IV. In him, moreover, among the other marks of virtue by which he shone, you have an example of charity. He possessed true charity in himself—and true because adorned. Hence he is said to have been full of the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:55), because he both loved what he ought and did so in the manner in which he ought. That is, he loved one and the same person both by fostering nature and by pursuing guilt. Otherwise he would not fully possess the Holy Spirit if he lacked either dove or fire, especially since it is certain that the Spirit appeared in both forms. Therefore there is no fullness of the Spirit in the heart unless, as it is stirred by affection toward love, so also it is kindled by zeal toward emulation.

Blessed Stephen had both in himself [Col. 0268A]—love and emulation: the former for compassion, the latter for correction. For how did he correct the obstinate Jews? “You stiff-necked people,” he said, “uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did; and they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, of whom you have now been betrayers and murderers, because you received the law through the ordering of angels and did not keep it” (ibid., 51). Yet, having thus reproved those who resisted him, how did he pray for those same people while they stoned him? “Lord,” he said, “do not lay this sin to their account, for they do not know what they are doing” (ibid., 59).

O bitter correction in the mouth, O sweet compassion in the heart! And love was the one and same cause and root of both. For he reproved those whom he wished to correct, and prayed that they might not perish; and in both—in reproving and in praying—he sought nothing but their salvation, charity so arranging and providing, which he possessed inwardly in his mind. Let us therefore imitate these great qualities in blessed Stephen, so that we may both love one another, correct one another, and pray for one another. Let love be the cause both of correction and of prayer, carefully providing and diligently ensuring that correction be discerning and prayer unceasing.

V. But as you set before yourselves for imitation these things in this athlete of Christ, so also, with every diligence, beware of the three evils by which you may recognize the wicked Jews who persecuted him: namely anger, reproach, and malice. For what does Scripture say? “When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart.” Behold the fury of anger. “And they gnashed their teeth at him” (ibid., 54): behold reproach. And shortly afterward: “But crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears and rushed upon him with one accord” (ibid., 56). In these words we can observe that they lacked nothing pertaining to malice, since, turning their hearing from the truth, they could not perceive even with their outward ears the things that were of God.

For they showed themselves to be members of him of whom it is written that his body was “like molten shields, compacted with scales pressing upon one another; one is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them” (Job 41:6). In the fullness of their madness, having conspired together, they thirsted with their whole eagerness for his most atrocious death. Keep these things far from yourselves, I ask, lest they may truthfully be said of you. Far be it that these words should ever be fulfilled in you: “When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and gnashed their teeth at him!”

VI. Far be it, I say, that when you hear a wholesome correction, which charity dictates in a brother’s heart and expresses through a brother’s mouth, you should be cut to the heart through evil exasperation and be too rashly moved against wholesome words! You know how many sayings in Holy Scripture exhort you humbly to hear words of correction, because correction is to sin as medicine is to a wound. For just as medicine brings healing to the wound, so correction brings remission to sin. [Col. 0269A] Solomon says: “He who loves discipline loves wisdom; but he who hates rebukes is foolish” (Prov. 12:1); and again: “A fool mocks his father’s discipline; but he who keeps rebukes will become more prudent” (Prov. 15:5); and again: “For the man who despises a reprover with a stiff neck, destruction will suddenly come upon him, and healing will not follow him” (Prov. 29:1).

See how great is the benefit of correction, and how great the danger threatening one who refuses humbly to receive it. Therefore, when perhaps danger touches you, remain inwardly whole, and do not permit yourselves to be cut in your hearts by the sword of anger. But if perhaps you cannot preserve complete wholeness in your hearts, strive with all your strength that the swelling of the mind may at least not come at all to the utterance [variant: “speech” or “expression”] [Col. 0269B] of the mouth, so that each of you may be able to say with the Psalmist: “I was troubled and did not speak” (Ps. 76:5).

And if you are not of such perfection that you can restrain yourself from dissenting in your heart, at least do not be of such presumption and madness as to gnash your teeth at the one who corrected you. You do this, indeed, when, seeking revenge upon the one who corrected you, you vomit out against him words of fury and reproach. For, as Saint David says, “the teeth of the children of men are weapons and arrows” (Ps. 56:5); thus to gnash the teeth is to rage with biting words.

VII. It is certainly a matter of great strength either, through prudence, to guard against anger’s rising in the heart at all, or, after it has perhaps risen—as it often does—to suppress it at least through patience. Solomon declares that “the patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his own spirit than one who captures cities” (Prov. 14:32). We surely know how greatly bodily strength is commonly loved and praised by the sons of Adam; yet strength of mind is far more excellent and more exalted. And what is this other than patience? Be patient, and you are strong; indeed, the more patient you are, the stronger you are. No bodily strength can at all be made equal to, or even compared with, strength of heart, since, according to Solomon’s saying, the patient person is better than a strong man.

But perhaps you ask: what is this precious virtue of which you speak, and how can it be acquired, when every bodily strength yields to it? Is everyone who suffers to be said to possess patience? Certainly not. For someone may suffer unwillingly; therefore he cannot at all be called patient, the person whom Solomon declares better than a strong man. For how is he patient who, sinking downward under the weight of his own faint-heartedness, lies cast down in bitterness of heart and murmuring of mouth? For even if the mouth is perhaps closed, there is nevertheless within a clamorous silence full of all bitterness; and, though silent, a torrent of words does not cease noisily to rage with great restlessness and disturbance.

Does this man seem strong to you—the one who, setting before himself in the court of his heart the person against whom he is stirred, attacks him most bitterly in silent words, giving and receiving insults, uttering threats and hurling the darts of curses, contending as an empty litigant against one who is absent? I would by no means call such a one patient. He merely seems so, because he does not possess patience.

VIII. For patience is a voluntary and enduring bearing of adversity that must be endured, for God’s sake. I said, “of adversity that must be endured,” in order to exclude from the virtue of patience every adversity which ought not to be endured. For there is an adversity which, if endured, is against God. Therefore, whenever some adversity touches you which is against God, and consequently against the salvation of your soul, it is certainly not to be endured. I said “voluntary,” because you then possess true patience when, with the desire of a kindly disposed mind, you suffer something, and afterwards, reflecting upon it within yourself, rejoice that you have suffered it—not only stirred by no anger against the person who inflicted it upon you, but even kindled with greater love toward him.

Remember what was said of the Apostles: “They went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41). And in fact they suffered not only insult, but were also severely beaten. I added “enduring” so that, however often and however greatly adversity may assail, patience may never fail in the mind as long as life remains in the body. The Lord’s saying is to be understood of every virtue: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 24:13).

Finally, I said “for God’s sake,” because only that which is done purely for God himself is rewarded by God: so that for the one to whom love of God is the cause in labour, the vision of God may also be the reward in recompense. Therefore, whoever here suffers what he ought, and in the manner in which he ought—that is, voluntarily and perseveringly—and for the proper cause, namely for God’s sake, I would call truly patient. This patient person is better than a strong man; this person rules his own spirit and is better than one who captures cities. O how greatly would the man be exalted who could subdue even one city! Yet he who rules his own spirit cannot at all be compared with such a man, even if the latter subdued not merely a city but cities.

IX. Therefore, when you hear words of correction from anyone, do not be cut to the heart, nor gnash your teeth at the one who corrects you, raging inwardly through anger and chattering outwardly against him with biting words. But also beware lest, stopping your ears, you rush upon him with one accord. This is the most wicked and harmful crime of conspiracy, from which all clothed in the habit of religion, who have even the slightest sense of heaven, must always keep themselves far away. This unanimity by which a frenzied assault is made against one’s neighbour is plainly detestable before God and men. It is far removed from that unanimity which blessed Augustine urges you to possess when he says: “These are the things which we command you to observe when established in monasteries: that you dwell with one accord in the house, and that you have one soul and one heart in God.” [Note: [Col. 0269D] St Augustine, *Rule*, beginning.]

Therefore, when you hear charity’s correction, embrace it as the cause of your salvation, knowing that “the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who flatters” (Prov. 27:6). But if, overtaken by a movement of anger, in that drunkenness of fury you cannot possess your soul in patience, at least let your lips remain closed, and let that bony wall restrain your tongue. Nor let disturbance cloud your face, so that, while your mind does not send out what it endures within, you neither offend another’s sight by a troubled countenance nor strike another’s hearing with an angry word.

Indeed, it is praiseworthy and wholly commendable that you should comport yourself with such caution in a time of adversity that you do not indiscriminately display outwardly, either in face or word, what you endure within. Rather, presenting humility, as far as you can, in speech and countenance, know that this cloudy hour of temptation into which you have come will, by God’s ordering, newly pass into an hour of peace and tranquillity. For he who permits evening to rush upon you for weeping will also immediately make morning smile upon you for joy (Ps. 29:6).

X. How many things, as most frequent experience has taught us, does anger suggest to us, when we are angry, to say and do—things which, after the time of fury has passed, once we have become calm and tranquil, we plainly perceive ought not at all to have been said or done! Therefore that person is very wise who, restraining within himself the passion that eagerly longs to burst forth through its own violence, dissimulates, is silent, and remains still with blessed Job (Job 3:28): he dissimulates, that he may preserve an unstained cheerfulness of countenance; he is silent, that he may keep himself from harsh speech; he remains still, that he may restrain himself from an unlawful act—cheerful in countenance, gentle in words, blameless in deeds.

As for your stopping your ears and rushing upon someone with one accord, you have no need for us to forbid this to you. For though you have not yet all ascended to that height of perfection at which you are always free from the hidden movement of anger, which so often rushes down suddenly and, many times before it can be anticipated or guarded against, violently and importunately thrusts itself upon you: nevertheless, far be it from me to think that any among you are infected with such a poison of malice that they would ever lay snares for people from whom they remember having received wholesome corrections!

We observe, then, that the Jews, so wicked, practised these things in the passion of blessed Stephen: fury in the heart, reproach in the mouth, and conspiracy [Col. 0271D] for his death. Scripture bears witness: “They were cut to the heart, and gnashed their teeth at him, and rushed upon him with one accord” (Acts 7:54). Having cast him out of the city, they stoned him. But the blessed martyr practised, against their three evils, three such great goods: against fury in the heart, sincere charity; against reproach in the mouth, wholesome correction; against conspiracy for his death, devout prayer. For he prayed for those who stoned him: “Lord, do not lay this sin to their account, for they do not know what they are doing” (ibid., 59).

XI. How severe was the correction; how pure the prayer! For the sincerity of one and the same love shaped both in one and the same person. Such was holy Joseph: he both loved his brothers perfectly within and, raging harshly against them outwardly, reproved them openly, in order to remove their guilt by severity; yet he wept in secret, in order to satisfy love by tenderness. Zeal formed words of rebuke in his mouth; the inward affection of love drew tears from his eyes (Gen. 43:30). For some time, indeed, though with difficulty, he concealed this affection within himself; but afterwards its great force compelled it to burst forth.

For what does Scripture say? “Joseph could no longer restrain himself before many who stood by” (Gen. 45:1). And shortly afterward: “Raising his voice with weeping, he said to his brothers: I am Joseph” (ibid., 3). But after the holy old man Jacob had died, Joseph’s brothers feared that their father’s death might release Joseph to avenge himself upon them, since, as they thought, their father’s life had held his hand back from vengeance. They sent him this message: “Our father commanded us before he died that we should say these words to you in his name: ‘I beg you to forget the crimes of your brothers, and the sin and malice which they exercised against you; and we pray that you forgive this iniquity to the servants of God, your father’” (Gen. 50:17). When he heard this, Joseph wept.

O holy and just man, so composed in both respects: lovingly reproving sternly, bearing tender affections that led to tears, uttering harsh words that led to correction! What shall we say of holy Moses? Gentle and discerning, he resisted the Lord lest he strike the people, because of the great affection he bore toward that same people; and he struck idolaters with death, lest their guilt should go unpunished, because of the immense zeal he had for the law of his God. There he was so compassionate and burned with such love for those subject to him that he said to God: “Either forgive them this offence, or, if you do not, blot me out from the book which you have written” (Exod. 32:31). Here, however, he was so stern and so inflamed with zeal that he commanded those of the sons of Levi who had joined him, saying: “Go to and fro from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each one kill his brother, friend, and neighbour” (ibid., 27).

From these things it is evident that true charity, which the Bride in the Song of Songs asks to be ordered within her, so pours gentleness into the mind for affection (Cant. 2:4) as likewise to pour in severity for zeal. Thus whoever, with the apostles, has received the Paraclete possesses both fire for the affection of love and a tongue for the word of instruction, through the gift of the same Holy Spirit, who is blessed with the Father and the Son for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. ALSO ON THE DAY OF SAINT STEPHEN, PROTOMARTYR.

On the varieties of heavens and their lights.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. Examples from Scripture from which ministers of the word may learn not to lose heart when they are despised.—2. To direct one’s gaze toward heaven comes from the Holy Spirit, as is observed in Saint Stephen.—3. Mystical heavens: the Church, the faithful soul, Scripture, mystery, holiness of life, the assembly of the blessed, and the happiness of the heavenly homeland.—4. In the first heaven, that is, the Church: the sun is the priesthood, the moon kingship, the stars holy men. How great is the obscuring here.—5. In the second: temperance in prosperity is the sun; patience in adversity, the moon; good thoughts, the stars.—6. In the third: the mystical sense is the sun, the literal sense the moon, and examples of virtues the stars.—7. In the fourth: understanding is the sun, faith the moon, and modes of contemplation the stars.—8. In the fifth: love is the sun, fear the moon, and external actions the stars.—9. Another fivefold heaven: the first is God, whose length is eternity, breadth charity, height majesty, and depth wisdom.—10. The second is Christ, whose divine and human natures are the two lights; the stars are the words of life and works of salvation.—11. The third is angelic understanding, in which knowledge of the Word, of creatures, and of itself are the sun, moon, and stars.—12. The fourth is this world, whose sun is Christ, moon Scripture, and stars the Apostles.—13. The fifth is that of birds, or the air, whose sun, moon, and stars are evident.—14. Twelve heavens with their fitting lights.—15. Angels are never without the vision of God; this vision is the sun, compassion for us the moon.—16. The blessed are powerful in God without weakness, wise without error, and loving without offence.—17. To consider God as incomprehensible in himself, terrible to the reprobate, and lovable to the elect, is to consider in him sun, moon, and stars.—18. Recapitulation with a confirmation of the foregoing.—19. A comparison drawn from travellers unable to complete a long journey in one day.

I. “But Stephen, being full of the Holy Spirit, looking intently into heaven, saw the glory of God” (Acts 7:55). In the passion of blessed Stephen the protomartyr, brothers, we may receive an example of patience for ourselves if perhaps we are despised in some respect by our hearers when we preach to them the word of life. For he himself offered wholesome exhortation to his hearers and confronted them from charity with words of rebuke; but, as we read of them, “When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart and gnashed their teeth at him.” Behold: when they heard the herald of life, they were shaken with hidden anger, as is indicated by their being cut to the heart. They were torn by open fury, as is intimated by their gnashing their teeth at him.

Nor was this all. Hearing him report that he saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God, “crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears and rushed upon him with one accord; and, casting him out of the city, they stoned him.” O manifold malice! O madness no less perverse than diverse! In their crying out, observe madness born of impatience; in their stopping their ears, the hardness of obstinacy; in their rushing upon him with one accord, a frenzied conspiracy—or, if this is understood better, a conspiratorial fury; in their casting him out of the city, contempt; and in their stoning him, understand them to be most cruel and bloodthirsty executioners.

Do not therefore take it too harshly, so far as it concerns you, when you preach the word, if you see that you are perhaps despised, knowing that you are no better than Stephen. Nor are you better than him of whom, when he spoke words of truth, faithless hearers cried out: “Take such a man from the earth; for it is not fitting that he should live” (Acts 22:22). This was Paul, with whom the word of God was never bound; he could be killed for the Lord, but he could not be silent concerning our Lord (1 Tim. 2:6).

Take also another athlete. Holy Jeremiah once addressed the people, speaking to them what the Lord had commanded through him; but, as you know, this fearful cry thundered out at the end of his speech: “Let this man die! Why has he prophesied in the name of the Lord?” (Jer. 26:8). Micaiah son of Imlah (3 Kgs. 22:27), when he spoke in the Lord’s name what was true to an idolatrous and murderous king, received an order that, consigned to custody, he should be sustained with the bread of tribulation and water of affliction.

But why do I speak of them, when “the servant is not greater than his master, nor the apostle greater than the one who sent him” (John 13:16)? Not to mention many other things, when the Lord of eternity himself uttered these words before unbelievers—“Before Abraham came to be, I am”—did they not take up stones to throw at him? (John 8:58). Therefore, when you preach the Gospel word, make your face like diamond and flint, so that you are neither puffed up with pride when accepted nor contracted with sorrow when despised; neither consider yourself precious when heard nor worthless when scorned.

II. And enough concerning these matters. Let us now see what this means which we have heard of blessed Stephen: “Looking intently into heaven, he saw the glory of God.” I confess that these words hold my attention; and I think they do yours as well. He saw the glory of God, but he would not have seen it unless he had looked intently into heaven; nor would he have looked intently into heaven so as to be able to see God’s glory unless he had been full of the Holy Spirit. For this is the very order of the words. Saint Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Stephen, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God.” It is as though he saw God’s glory because he looked intently into heaven, having been full of the Holy Spirit. So it is.

Let us see what this heaven is, so that we may consequently also understand [the text reads “whom”; apparently “why”] the person who desires to look intently into it ought to be full of the Holy Spirit. I find Scripture speaking of heaven in many places, and I think that it has not one but various meanings.

III. It seems to me that the holy Church of the Elect, spread throughout the whole world, is as it were a certain heaven, of which we read that God said in Genesis: “Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven” (Gen. 1:14). That is: let there be spiritual men in the highest eminence and in the eminent stability of the Church. There is also the holy soul, of which I think John said in the Apocalypse that “there was silence made in heaven for about half an hour” (Apoc. 8:2), because inward repose endures in the soul for only a very brief moment. Sacred Scripture too appeared to the Psalmist to be a kind of heaven, when he says that the Lord “stretches it out like a skin” (Ps. 103:3), because He opens the sacred Scripture to mortals.

Nor does anyone seem to depart from the truth if he calls the hidden mystery of God heaven, since John affirms in the Apocalypse that he saw “a door opened in heaven” (Apoc. 4:1), that is, that he perceived an understanding of the hidden mystery to have been revealed to him. Holiness of life is likewise in some sense heaven, concerning which the Lord, speaking to blessed Job, says: “Who has begotten the frost from heaven?” (Job 38:29), because He Himself sometimes permits many, after exalted holiness, to be hardened in wickedness by a hidden yet just judgment.

Holy David understood the assembly of those heavenly spirits to be heaven when he says: “For ever, O Lord, thy word remains in heaven” (Ps. 118:59). For, when apostate spirits fall, the assembly of those that remain preserves obedience to the divine Word, without any diminution of the heavenly spirits. And no one doubts that that heavenly blessedness for which we sigh is called heaven. Isaiah seems to mention it when, addressing the devil, he says: “How hast thou fallen from heaven?” (Isa. 14:12), that is, from heavenly blessedness?

Direct your attention to this sevenfold heaven which we have set before you, to see whether you may perhaps be able to behold the glory of God in it. First is the holy Church; second, the faithful soul; third, sacred Scripture; fourth, the hidden mystery; fifth, the height of holiness; sixth, the assembly of heavenly spirits; seventh, that heavenly blessedness.

IV. Does not the holy Church seem to you to be heaven, in which the priesthood shines like the sun, kingship glows as the moon, and, in the number of holy men whom it contains, it possesses as many splendid stars? In the lights of this heaven we now see brightness not a little obscured. For those perilous times do not so much threaten as already exist, in which the Apostle foretold that men would be lovers of themselves; and we see this fulfilled in these lights (2 Tim. 3:6), concerning which that prophet mighty in deed and word foretold that it would be fulfilled when he said: “There shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars” (Luke 21:25).

What sign? Surely that which Joel more plainly foretold: “The sun,” he says, “shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood” (Joel 2:31). Do you not behold the sun turned into darkness, when, as Jeremiah laments, “gold has grown dim” and “the finest color has changed,” and the stones are scattered at the head not merely of certain streets but of all streets; when “as is the people, so is the priest” (Hos. 4:9)? And do you not see, with tear-filled eyes, the moon turned into blood, when you see kings abandon the equity of justice and practice cruelty?

The dreadful sign that appears to you in the stars is what John saw in the Apocalypse (Apoc. 12:4): he saw the dragon’s tail [variant: “indeed,” or “namely”] draw half the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. Although this will then take place spiritually, when that man shall be revealed in his own time, who is properly called “the man of sin, the son of perdition” (2 Thess. 2:3)—who belongs to the mass of the reprobate, which is the devil’s body, represented by the dragon, and who, because he will appear at the end, will be as it were the tail—he will draw those who seem to shine in the Church, whether by threats or flatteries, down from the heights to the depths, from heavenly things to earthly things.

Although, I say, the devil will then accomplish this more widely and more completely through him, he does not cease to do it even now, because the ministry of iniquity is already at work. I think this also pertains to what John says in the same book: “The sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became as blood, and the stars fell from heaven upon the earth” (Apoc. 6:12). The harshness of iniquity blackens the priesthood; the frenzy of cruelty bloodies imperial power; and other holy persons, abandoning the height of heavenly contemplation, fall down into earthly things.

Yet these two great lights in heaven are the two pre-eminent orders in the Church: the greater light, which presides over the day of contemplatives, and the lesser light, which presides over the night of active persons.

V. Does not the soul also appear to be heaven, when a lofty heavenly desire moves it? In it temperance amid prosperity is like the sun by day, and patience amid adversity like the moon by night; and in it, as many good thoughts as appear, so many splendid stars surely shine. Temperance is rightly the greater light and patience the lesser, because it is harder not to be dissolved by tranquil good fortune than not to be broken under injury.

VI. In the heaven of Scripture also, do you not see the spiritual sense, revealed by exposition, as the sun in daytime, while the historical sense, not yet examined, is as the moon in night, and therefore the former is the greater light and the latter the lesser? In it behold Abel’s innocence, Enoch’s holiness, Noah’s perfection, Shem and Japheth’s modesty, Abraham’s obedience, Isaac’s purity, Jacob’s simplicity, Melchizedek’s justice, Joseph’s chastity, Moses’ gentleness, the zeal shown by Phinehas, Joshua’s uprightness, Caleb’s fortitude, Samuel’s piety, David’s humility, and countless other examples and illustrious marks of the saints in the same manner. I do not think that you will now maintain that this heaven lacks bright stars.

VII. The fourth heaven is the hidden mystery, in which understanding shines for you as the sun and faith as the moon. And however many modes of inward contemplation appear to you in it, do not just so many bright stars gleam there? Understanding is the greater light and shines by day; faith is the lesser and shines by night. For although both the one and the other show us the truth in the heaven of hidden mystery, the former displays it openly and nakedly, while the latter shows it closed and wrapped up. Thus, as we see in the visible sun and moon, in the former there is most brilliant light; in the latter, by comparison with it, although there is light, it is nevertheless dim.

For faith contains nothing doubtful, yet neither does it contain anything naked. It shines, certainly, because it possesses certainty of truth; but it shines in the night because, retaining that same truth in an enfolding, it does not set forth a naked manifestation. Understanding, however, because the truth is not ambiguous to it, is plainly a shining sun; and because the truth is not enclosed, it shines in the day. The modes of inward contemplation which you receive in this hidden mystery are the stars shining for you in this heaven.

VIII. Holiness of life is the fifth heaven, adorned by two great lights: the greater light is love, enlightening you for understanding and inflaming you for affection, so that, walking honorably by day, you may practice the brightness of justice; the lesser light is fear, shining for you so that, in the night of an assaulting temptation, you may avoid the darkness of wickedness. It also has stars: the splendid actions performed through the limbs of the body.

But where am I going? Does the present subject require that I assign proper lights to each of the seven heavens I have put before you? Would it not be more useful to show how, by looking into heaven, you may behold the glory of God?

IX. And indeed, besides this sevenfold heaven, there is also a fivefold heaven, into which, if you look, you may, I think, behold the glory of God. First, then, there is that highest heaven, loftier than all other heavens: it is our most high and unsearchable God Himself, “who alone has immortality and inhabits inaccessible light, whom no man has ever seen, nor can see” (1 Tim. 6:16).

Of this heaven holy David says: “They have set their mouth against heaven” (Ps. 73:9), that is, they provoked God by words of blasphemy. “No one has ascended into this heaven except the Son of Man who descended from heaven, who is in heaven” (John 3:13), because “no one knows the Father except the Son” (Matt. 16:27), who proceeded from the Father, who is in the Father and the Father in Him (John 16:28). He is the one who came forth from the Father and came into the world and goes to the Father, because “his going forth is unto the height thereof” (Ps. 18:7).

Great indeed, and truly great, is this heaven, whose greatness [variant: “is great”], length, breadth, height, and depth are fourfold, yet one: fourfold in the utterance of speech, but one in the confession of faith. Eternity shows this heaven to us as long; charity makes it broad; majesty makes it high; and wisdom makes it deep.

Its length is not stretched out, yet it is without beginning and without end. Its breadth is not spread out: it hates none of the things it has made (Wis. 11:25), but has care for all. Its height is not raised upward, and yet it is above all things, attended by the almighty hand. Its depth is not sunk beneath, and yet it is beneath all things, lacking not the eye that sees all things.

Behold how great this heaven is; but who shall comprehend how great it is? “Great is our Lord, and great is his power; and of his wisdom there is no number” (Ps. 146:5); so likewise there is no end of His greatness (Ps. 144:5). O height in things exalted! O length in promises! O breadth in benefits! O depth in judgments! Look up to this heaven: its height will bring amazement upon you as you consider it, so that you may be astonished; its length, hope, so that you may endure; its breadth, love, so that you may love; its depth, fear, so that you may tremble.
