See that this heaven is loftier and worthier than all the others of which we have hitherto spoken or are speaking. Do not ask me what its lights are. I confess that I turn over certain matters in my mind which perhaps may pertain to them, but I do not yet understand whether a complete correspondence can be applied to them. Therefore I do not presume to bring them before you. The Lord Himself will instruct you about them, since He does not wish to do so through me. For if He wished them to be shown to you through me, He would first reveal them to me, so that I might convey them to you.

X. We likewise call Christ, the mediator between God and men, God and man [variant: “and a certain [thing]”], a heaven, and indeed a very lofty heaven. Holy David seems then to have lifted his eyes to it when he said: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 113:16), understanding, I believe, the God, Son of God, to be as it were the heaven of heaven, wholly and without any exception present to the Father.

What do you think are the two great lights in this heaven? Perhaps they are the two natures in Christ. Consider whether the greater light is not that unfailing sun of His divinity, shining forth in the day of eternity; while the lesser light, like a certain moon, is the mutability of our nature assumed in Him—namely, His humanity. Since this nature, though pure, is united to His person temporally, it surely shines, yet in the night of this present age.

They say that the moon receives light from the sun; and what does human nature possess in the Only-Begotten that it does not receive? Have you not read in the Gospel that, when the Lord was approaching Jericho, a blind man received sight? As you know, passing by, He heard him crying; but standing still, He gave him light (Luke 18:35). What then? Is not Jericho called “moon”? Is not the passing-by an expression of the mutability of our nature in Him, while the standing still expresses His eternity? You see, therefore, that in the passing of His moon and the standing still of His sun, this heaven wiped away the darkness of our blindness. In the former He had compassion on that blindness of mine through mercy; in the latter He aided it through mercy.

But what are the stars of this heaven? I think they are the words of eternal life which He spoke and the works which He performed on earth for our salvation. Therefore incline your ear and hear the profitable things which He uttered with His mouth; open your eyes and behold the wonders that He displayed in deed; and call all these stars—indeed, very bright stars—which Jesus began to do and to teach (Acts 1:1), and you will not be charged with falsehood.

XI. There is a third heaven [variant: “a certain heaven”], lofty indeed, though lower than this: namely, the capacity of angelic understanding. It is that heaven concerning which, using the words of one of Job’s friends, the Almighty is declared to be more excellent and more exalted, when he affirms that He cannot be found out unto perfection: “It is higher than heaven; what canst thou do?” (Job 11:8).

I believe that Zophar, who is found to have uttered these words, intended by them to convince Job that, being human, he could not by his own understanding perfectly find out [variant: “be found out”] God Almighty—that is, fully comprehend Him—who, dwelling in inaccessible light, far transcends not merely any single intelligence but every intelligence, even the understanding of angels.

In this heaven, namely in angelic understanding, a threefold light shines, by which the angels know Christ, who made them: understand Him as the sun; the mutable creature which He made for them, and this is the moon; and themselves, who, arranged individually in persons [variant: “in hierarchies”] and distinguished in orders, are stars shining for everlasting eternities. Thus angelic understanding, by purely beholding the common Creator of all, mutable nature fashioned (fictam) [variant: made (factam)] by Him, and themselves, possesses the sun, moon, and stars of this third heaven of which we speak.

The fourth heaven is this world, concerning which John says in the Apocalypse: “A great sign appeared in heaven” (Apoc. 12:1), that is, a great miracle in the world. And what sign? “A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars.” In these words the Church is described, which journeys in the world clothed with Christ through the sacrament of baptism; at whose feet sacred Scripture shines, like “a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1:19). And as Christ is the sun, so Scripture is the moon. Holy David speaks of it: “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my paths” (Ps. 118:105).

This woman is also adorned with a crown of twelve stars, while she is instructed by the teaching of the same number of apostles; for they themselves are the stars. Therefore this world is a kind of heaven. Take the moon of this heaven to mean the instability of this world; its individual visible things, created by this Maker, are as certain stars; while the beauty of the universe, considered by pure reflection and attention [variant: “and observation”], presents in the mind of the contemplator a kind of image of the sun.

XII–XIII. If you wish to see the fifth heaven, it is this air itself, which Sacred Scripture in many places calls the realm of birds, because birds are seen to fly in the air. Its lights, since it is visible, are themselves visible. These are those which God truly placed on the fourth day, at the very beginning of the world, in the firmament of heaven (Gen. 1:14), that they might be, as we all now bodily see, for signs and seasons and days and months and years; that they might divide day from night; that they might shine in that same firmament of heaven; and that they might illumine the earth.

Behold, we have set before you many heavens, not under one division but under a double division, so that they might both be grasped more clearly by the understanding and retained more firmly in memory. In the first division we showed you six; in the second, five. To each, insofar as occurred to us at present, we assigned its proper lights, except for three: namely, that most high heaven which is God, and two others, one of which we assigned to the assembly of blessed spirits and the other to heavenly blessedness.

Let us now repeat them in order and place them all under one division, because what is often repeated is more firmly retained in memory.

XIV. The first heaven is this visible air; the second, this mutable world; the third, the holy Church; the fourth, the devout soul; the fifth, divine Scripture; the sixth, the hidden mystery; the seventh, the holiness of religious conduct; the eighth, the assembly of heavenly spirits; the ninth, that heavenly blessedness; the tenth, the capacity of angelic understanding; the eleventh, that firstborn of the dead, prince of the kings of the earth, mediator between God and men, God and man, our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Tim. 2:5); the twelfth, He who “inhabits inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16), the immortal and invisible King, who alone, by His rising upon us, brings us day: the almighty and ruling God, Three and One.

In the first heaven the sun is visible: by his rising he brings us day, and by his setting he takes it away; daily he rises and sets, and, as Ecclesiastes says, “returns to his place, and there, rising anew, goes round by the south and turns to the north, surveying all things” (Eccl. 1:5–6). Those who look sufficiently closely perceive what its moon and stars are.

In the second, its mutable occurrences belong to the moon; each visible thing created in it by God belongs to the stars; and the beauty of the universe, observed through contemplation, belongs to the sun. In the third—to run briefly through them—the priesthood, kingship, and holy men are sun, moon, and stars. In the fourth, the sun is temperance, the moon patience, and the stars the shining holy thoughts. In the fifth, the sun is in the spiritual sense, the moon in the historical sense, and the stars in the revelation of the virtues which the saints formerly exercised. In the sixth, the sun gleams in understanding, the moon in faith, and the individual modes of inward contemplation are individual stars. In the seventh, the sun of love shines, the moon of fear, and the stars are bodily good actions.

In the tenth, knowledge of God shines forth as the sun, mutable creatures as the moon; and while each possesses its own light, the individual stars gleam with a beautiful brightness and a bright beauty. In the eleventh, the sun is He who assumes our nature, the moon the nature assumed; and each word heard from Him and each work seen in Him are stars.

XV. I think that you very much desire to see the lights of the three heavens concerning which we have as yet said nothing. For I know that your devout and religious curiosity cannot rest until it finds what it seeks. Will that generous Lord, as is His custom, refuse to disclose the secret? Let us knock at His door, because He cannot lie who says: “To him that knocks it shall be opened” (Luke 2:10). Let us persevere in knocking, so that importunity may compel Him to give, though friendship perhaps cannot compel Him.

Let us knock, I say, in the hope that He may grant to those who knock what He refuses to those who investigate; for this is often His way. Many times, indeed, we have been permitted by knocking to extort what we could not discover by searching. Open to us, Lord, for Your praise and our benefit, what the lights are in the heaven which is the assembly of Your blessed spirits; in that which is the heavenly blessedness that You promise us; and also in that heaven which You Yourself are.

Among these blessed spirits, who rejoice with You in Your glory, we understand some to stand continually before Your countenance and never depart from Your inner presence; while others, receiving the office of ministry, go out to us, becoming, by Your ordering, ministering spirits, sent by You in service for us who receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1:14). Your servant who said, “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10), led me to understand this concerning them.

Yet again I see that neither those who go out to us are ever absent at any hour, nor those who stand unceasingly before You are absent from us. For how could either group be perfect: the former in love, if even while standing before You they had no care for us; or the latter in blessedness, if, when they go out to us, they should not merely lose Your blessed and joy-giving vision, but interrupt their seeing of it even for the briefest moment? Therefore those who stand before You are not absent from us in compassion; and those who come to us stand before You—indeed, they are in You—by contemplation.

Is not this care, by which those dwelling with us are bound to You and those attending to You are concerned for us, a great light by which those bright stars—I mean the blessed spirits of whom we speak—shine forth? And is not their ministry, because they exercise it among us who are in the mutable darkness of this present life and in a dark mutability, the moon? For continually to attend to Your brightness is to enjoy the most splendid radiance of the unfailing sun of vision. Thus the sun shines in those who stand before You, the moon in those who minister; and since each of them is perfectly present to You in contemplation and to us in compassion, this great perfection sustaining them is a great light illuminating those individual stars.

XVI. I find that the heavenly blessedness to which we aspire is threefold, when I ask within myself what we shall be in ourselves, what in You our God, and what all together in relation to one another. And I find that we shall be powerful in ourselves, wise in You, and loving toward one another (in invicem) [variants: in suos invicem, “toward one another’s own,” or se invicem, “toward one another”]. We shall be able to do all things without any weakness, know all things without any error, and love one another fully without any offense.

O strength of unfailing power, by which we shall be powerful in ourselves! O brightness of complete knowledge, by which we shall be wise in You, our God! O sweetness of true love, by which we shall love one another! Yet You will be all these things to us, You who, while You are wholly in us, will also be all things in us: granting us power in ourselves, You, God the supreme Father; wisdom in You, our God, You, the Son, supreme Wisdom; kindness toward one another, You, the Holy Spirit, supreme Kindness—so that God may be all in all (Col. 3).

But because we in whom this power will exist are mutable by nature, and as the moon, according to some, receives light from the sun, so we receive from You whatever good we possess, it seems to us that this power will be a kind of moon in the heaven of that heavenly blessedness. And to possess wisdom in You—does that not mean to possess the brightness of the sun? What is brighter than the sun in this visible sun [variant: “heaven”]? What is more splendid in that blessedness than to know all things in You who know all things?

Moreover, the kindness which unites those individual fellow-citizens in You by the inseparable bond of unfailing charity, knowing no darkness whatsoever, is a brightness irradiating each of those stars. Therefore that heaven possesses the sun when that blessedness—for this is what heaven is—bestows wisdom in God upon those children of the heavenly kingdom through complete knowledge; the moon when it bestows power upon each in himself through most vigorous strength; and also a most clear light and most luminous brightness in the stars, when it bestows upon each sweetness of true mutual love.

XVII. It remains, Lord, that we should say something about the lights of that heaven which You are. Therefore shine upon us by Your splendor and enlighten us, so that in speaking of them we may proceed without the darkness of error.

If, being heaven, You have sun, moon, and stars, You Yourself are these things, since You have nothing in Yourself that You are not. For as You, true Being, cannot not be, so neither can there be anything in You that You are not. For You are, so to speak, Your own being, into which there enters nothing except what You are. Yet to some You show Yourself in Yourself as the sun, to others as the moon, and to others as the stars, although You are not one thing and another, but are Yourself the same, since Your being is identical with what You are.

Whoever considers what You are in Yourself, what You are in the reprobate, and what You are in the elect can, I think, see sun, moon, and stars in You. I behold You in Yourself, wholly incomprehensible, and therefore a kind of sun which no angelic or human intelligence is sufficient to penetrate. You are truly one, and therefore do not admit number in Yourself; immeasurable, and therefore admit no increase; eternal, and therefore suffer no decrease. All things pass beneath You; nothing passes You by.

You are great without quantity; simple without diminution; good without quality; always, without time; everywhere, without place; in every thing, without being circumscribed by it; in every time, without change in Yourself. You can in no way be stained on account of (pro) [variant: vel pro, “or on account of”] Your purity, divided because of Your simplicity, comprehended because of Your immensity, or changed because of Your immutability. Nor can You vary in knowledge, since You are most wise; nor in affection, since You are best. Every effect is subject to Your power; every hidden thing is manifest to Your wisdom; every event follows Your deliberation; time does not equal Your eternity, virtue does not equal Your goodness, understanding does not equal Your wisdom, and work does not equal Your power.

Who does not believe that this is so? But who comprehends how it is so? Behold the sun in this great and spacious heaven which You are. Your Paul raised himself further to contemplate another sun, but, dazzled, returned to the noise of speech, where discourse begins and ends, and cried out: “O the depth of the riches of the knowledge and wisdom of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him?” And he added: “For of him, and in him, and through him are all things: to him be glory” (Rom. 11:33).

From You, Lord, are all things: You are the beginning of all things. Through You are all things: You who are the beginning are also the maker. In You are all things—namely, in power, not as in a place. “From,” “through,” and “in” indicate the Trinity in persons; “to Him,” however, indicates the unity which is in substance. In that Trinity we do not admit multiplicity, nor in this unity solitude: we do not confuse the former, nor divide the latter. For when we say “one,” the Trinity does not disturb us, since it neither changes, multiplies, nor divides the essence. But when we say “three,” unity does not rebuke us, since it neither forces those three into confusion nor reduces them to singularity.

Because reason does not fully perceive these things, yet opinion does not doubt them and faith alone persuades us of them, I think they pertain to a certain most bright sun in You, when I consider You as wholly incomprehensible.

The moon, however, though according to some it receives its light from the sun, does not retain that light long, but immediately declines into the loss of the light it has received. And who, Lord, even among the reprobate, “hides himself from your heat?” (Ps. 18:7). Yet because You do not preserve in them, through the virtue of perseverance, the brightness of grace which You grant them, but permit it to be darkened by a just and hidden judgment, do You not in some manner show Yourself to be the moon in them, since You too are in some manner perverse with the perverse?

I behold You as terrible in those whom, though secretly, You nevertheless justly reprobate from eternity, in order to condemn them eternally. But You are lovable in the elect whom You have predestined to life, since, illuminating them in Yourself with the manifold light of Your graces, You show them to be certain splendid stars in You: lights from eternity through predestination, and unto eternity through salvation.

XVIII. Therefore in that heaven which is the assembly of heavenly spirits, the sun shines when they stand before You; the moon also shines when they go out to us. The individual stars are likewise bright, while, standing before You, they are present to us in compassion, and, going out to us, they do not fail to be before You in contemplation.

But in that heaven which is heavenly blessedness, wisdom which the elect will have in You their God will shine like the sun; power which they will have in themselves, like the moon; and kindness which they will have toward one another through love, like the brightness of stars shining together.

In the highest heaven, which You are, the sun’s brightness is Your incomprehensible immensity in Yourself. You also show Yourself mutable after the likeness of a light in the reprobate; and those predestined in You to eternal life are as certain most bright stars. In Yourself incomprehensible, terrible in the reprobate, sweet in the elect: if these things can stand thus, Lord, to You be glory and praise. But if not at all, forgive, I pray, my blindness, and reveal the truth concerning all these matters to Your servants, my fellow servants, so that knowledge of them may reach me through them.

XIX. Behold, brethren: just as travellers often set out intending to complete their whole journey on the very day on which they began it, but cannot because night falls upon them, and therefore are compelled to take lodging and postpone until the next day what remains of their journey, so it has happened to us. We thought that we should complete in one day of exposition the whole course of our chapter, which we proposed at the beginning of this sermon. And behold, we have travelled as it were the whole day, yet have not been able to reach the proposed end.

This has happened because, on this journey of spiritual meanings, we saw from afar only the surface, as it were the tops of branches; but we did not at all discern their hidden depths, which are like the hollows of intervening valleys and plains. It remains, therefore, that we take lodging now by pausing, and reserve what remains of the journey of exposition, so that we may approach what remains to be said more eagerly because, after prayer has gone before, we are more secure—praising and glorifying God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is God, blessed for ever throughout all ages. Amen.

# SERMON XXXI. ALSO ON THE DAY OF ST STEPHEN THE PROTOMARTYR: ON THE GLORY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT AND SPIRITUAL HEAVENS

## SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. That we may be able to look into heaven with blessed Stephen.

2. Who is full of the Holy Spirit and sees the glory of God.

3. The Holy Spirit appears in the form of fire, a dove, and tongues: and why.

4. Where affection is lacking, there is no vision; knowledge banishes ignorance, charity banishes concupiscence.

5. The necessity of a right intention, and who is fit to preach.

6. One full of the Holy Spirit may safely proclaim the word.

7. In Scripture, “heavens” in the plural mystically signify angels, apostles, preachers, wise persons, spiritual men, and modes of contemplation.

8. How these heavens may be seen opened; and first, concerning the modes of contemplation.

9. Spiritual men as heavens, whose names shine as stars.

10. Examples of virtues in Joseph, Moses, Phinehas, and Joshua.

11. In Samuel and David.

12. In Elijah and Elisha; Jeremiah and Isaiah; Tobias and Daniel; the three youths and Mattathias.

13. To have known the virtue of the saints of the Old and New Law is to have the heavens opened.

14. What it is for the remaining heavens to be opened.

15. The nine choirs of angels and their offices.

16. God as all in all and in each.

I. Come, let us undertake the journey which we have postponed until now. We delayed so long over these heavens and their lights that we had no leisure to show how the glory of God ought to be seen in them. Since, therefore, we have already taught what these heavens are and what their lights are, let us now show, insofar as we can, how, looking into heaven with blessed Stephen, we may behold the glory of God.

On this occasion we do not wish to enter into these heavens, lest perhaps, having entered them, delighted by their beauty and detained by the brightness of the lights that are in them, we should be compelled to remain in them for some time and thus be unable to discharge what remains to be explained concerning this chapter.

But you, retaining the number of these heavens, which you have clearly set forth in the preceding sermon, ascend to them eagerly and traverse them devoutly, so that you may make your own that saying of the Apostle: “Our conversation is in heaven” (Phil. 3:10). But so that you may briefly see what it seems to me to mean to look into heaven and, in looking, to behold the glory of God: I think that you look into heaven if you strive to examine each of these—from the first, called aerial and visible, up to the twelfth, which signifies almighty God Himself—with sober inquiry, according as inward anointing has instructed you concerning each, and with the pure eye of clarified contemplation.

II. And in looking into heaven you behold the glory of God when, thus considering, traversing, and thoroughly discerning each one, you are raised into the amazement of wonder—or, if this may better be said, into the wonder of amazement—and glorify God. Yet, if you are to look fruitfully into heaven—for then you look fruitfully when in looking you behold glory—you must necessarily be filled with the Holy Spirit. For the sequence of the words themselves is thus: “Stephen,” it says, “being full of the Holy Spirit, looked into heaven and saw the glory of God” (Acts 7:55).

Therefore the reason why he saw was that he looked; and the reason why he looked in such a way as to see was that he was full of the Holy Spirit. According to my own understanding, I judge that one is full of the Holy Spirit who, persistently practicing good action everywhere according to his ability, observing time and place, manner and person, clearly acknowledges truth, ardently loves virtue, strives that the word of Christ may dwell in him, and in all these things preserves intact the true uprightness of inward intention.

III. I say this because, as you know, the Holy Spirit appeared in a dove; he also appeared in fire and in a tongue. In these you may observe four things, if you look carefully. In fire there are two things: brightness and heat—the former to enlighten, the latter to kindle. Simplicity also is customarily understood by the dove, and a word cannot be uttered except through the tongue. I believe you are already hastening ahead and know where I wish to go, when you hear that the Holy Spirit appeared in these forms and retain in memory [Col. 0285C] what we have just said: namely, that one is full of the Holy Spirit who recognizes what is true, who vigorously bears the word of God in his mouth, and who holds uprightness in his inward intention. Behold, before you, in the fire, are those two chief gifts of the Holy Spirit: knowledge and love. For illuminating brightness signifies the former, while the heat that follows signifies the latter. Both gifts are exceedingly necessary to you, since neither can be absent without injury to your salvation. For you read both that “the ignorant person is to remain ignorant” (1 Cor. 14:38), and that one who does not love remains in death (1 John 3:14). Therefore, by the brightness of this most holy fire, which the Lord Jesus came to cast upon the earth (Luke 12:49), you are enlightened in the knowledge [Col. 0285D] of truth, lest you wander through the darkness of blindness; and by its burning you are kindled in the love of virtue, lest you grow cold through its absence.

Thus these two spiritual goods drive away the two original evils: knowledge drives away ignorance, and love concupiscence. The former evil darkened the human mind, taking from it the light of truth and pouring into it the darkness of error; the latter defiled the flesh, withdrawing it from the work of holiness and enticing it toward the fruit of death. The former causes what is good to be unknown; the latter causes what is evil to be practiced. It also comes about, miserably, that whoever is infected by this twofold plague neither chooses the true nor rejects the false, blinded by the darkness of ignorance; neither admits the good nor omits the evil, pierced through by the darts of concupiscence.

[Col. 0286A] IV. You see, then, how greatly you need, in this respect, to be filled with the Holy Spirit, you who desire to gaze into heaven, so that you may be able to see God’s glory. For how can you gaze upon that thing when you wholly do not know whether it exists, much less what it is? And if you already know it, how can you claim to know fruitfully what you do not love? An old proverb says: “Where love is, there is the eye”; and it is indeed true. Yet this is no less true, a saying like it: “Where there is no affection, there is no sight.” But when you clearly know what this heaven is, you are already gazing into it with the eye of purity. And when you ardently love not your own glory, but God’s glory—which he does not wish to give to another, because it is due to himself alone (Isa. 48:11)—then, I say, you behold him with the eye of love.

These two goods are like two eyes in the head, within the mind; they make a straight [Col. 0286B] path for our feet, lest they ever encounter a stumbling-block. For knowledge drives from the mind’s understanding the error of ignorance, making it bright with the ray of clarity.

V. Love, however, banishes the foulness of concupiscence from bodily action, adorning it with the beauty of virtue. This being so, knowledge enables you to gaze into heaven, while love enables you to see God’s glory. But it is supremely necessary that, just as you gaze while enlightened and see while kindled, so in both gazing and seeing you should also be upright in mind, so that the great good you gain—while you gaze into heaven with the eye of knowledge, while you see God’s glory with the eye of love—may be preserved whole and unspoiled for you by upright simplicity and the simple uprightness of inward intention.

This is the dove in which he appeared who also appeared in fire, to show that you are not filled with him unless, just as your understanding is enlightened by the knowledge of truth and your affection is inflamed by love of virtue, so also in both—namely, in knowledge and love—you are purified from every desire for human praise and wholly free from it, and, through the uprightness of inward intention, perfectly pure, raising the eyes of your mind through all your hidden motions to the contemplation of God alone. [Alternative readings: *qui non similiter* (“who is not similarly [enlightened]”) for *sicut* (“just as”); *sicut in utraque* (“just as in each [of the two]”) for *sicut utraque* (“just as both”).]

But whoever has thus received the Holy Spirit in fire and has also thus received him in the dove, I do not doubt can safely show that he is present to him also in the tongue. Let him display outwardly, for God’s praise [Col. 0286D] and his neighbors’ edification, those most precious treasures with which the Holy Spirit has endowed him inwardly. Let him preach the word; let him be urgent in season and out of season; let him rebuke, exhort, reprove (2 Tim. 4:2). For the ungodly man has patience, and endures ungodliness. Let him safely show that he possesses the Spirit in the tongue of speech, whom he possesses so excellently in the brightness of knowledge, the ardor of love, and the dove of simple intention. Let him open his mouth and be silent no longer. Let him proclaim whatever he sees from the fullness with which he has been made rich; let him pour forth what he has drunk in, spill out that with which he has been made drunk, offer others what he has drunk. For he is full of the Holy Spirit.

VI. Is not he full of the Holy Spirit who, through knowledge of truth, is skilled in the hidden things of wisdom; through love of virtue shines in works of righteousness; through [Col. 0287A] uprightness of intention desires to please God alone; and through the zeal of preaching instructs his ignorant neighbor? Certainly this man is full of the Holy Spirit: he knows uncertain and hidden things; clearly sees what works of righteousness must be done and diligently does them; ardently loves his neighbor; admits absolutely no desire for human favor toward himself; longs to please only the hidden gaze of God; and finally proclaims Christ everywhere sincerely, never adulterating the word of God, but speaking as from God, before God, to his neighbor.

Let him now speak who has heard in this manner; let one so taught teach; let one so instructed instruct. One so enlightened will not err; one so affected will not stumble; one so raised upright [alternative: “straight”] will not bend himself toward any crooked ways. Therefore, whatever that heaven may be into which he gazes, [Col. 0287B] whatever and however great the glory of God may be that he sees, let him confidently reveal it to us; and, with blessed Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, gazing into heaven and seeing God’s glory, let him cry out and say: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power” (Acts 7:55).

VII. Who, do you suppose, are these heavens which he sees opened? I think that “heavens” has diverse meanings in the plural, as we have already shown it to have in the singular in the preceding sermon. The holy angels are heavens, and indeed very lofty heavens. Of them holy David says: “The heavens dropped at the presence of the Lord” (Ps. 67:9), because angels convey God’s commands to us. Were not the apostles also heavens, who left everything and followed Christ? Of them holy Job seems to have said: “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job 26:13), because, according to the Savior’s promise, the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit whom the Father sent in his name, taught the apostles all truth.

Certain holy preachers of ours are likewise heavens, of whom the Psalmist says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18:7), because it is the particular office of the highest preachers to proclaim Christ’s grace. Moreover, the wiser persons in the Church are certain heavens. It seems to me that the lawgiver and leader of the people Israel addresses them at the very beginning of his song in Deuteronomy: “Hear, O heavens, the things that I speak” (Deut. 32:1). In these words, I think, he commends the profundity of what he was about [Col. 0287D] to say by inviting the heavens to hear it: “Hear, O heavens, the things that I speak.” That is to say: you who are wiser, listen to the great and subtle things that I shall say.

Likewise, I frequently find spiritual men called “heavens” in Holy Scripture. Thus it is in the Psalm where it says that the Lord made the heavens “with understanding” (Ps. 135:6), because almighty God makes spiritual men not only believe heavenly things by right faith, but also understand them through inward power. Do spiritual men not seem to you to bear the name of heavens from what they are, when you see them burning in heart with the brightness of the sun, shining in mind and body with the moon of chastity, and gleaming in action with manifold splendor according to the varied brilliance of the stars? There are yet other heavens, likewise lofty ones, which contemplative observers are accustomed to frequent: namely, modes of contemplation. I think the Psalmist mentions them where he says of certain persons that “they go up even to the heavens” (Ps. 102:26), because they attain exalted modes of contemplation.

[Col. 0288A] VIII. These are the heavens of which we now speak to you, in which dwells he to whom we are accustomed daily to say in devotion: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). Holy David likewise says: “To thee have I lifted up my eyes, thou who dwellest in the heavens” (Ps. 122:1). I should like to know whether it has been granted to any of you to see these heavens opened. And when are these heavens opened to us, except when their properties are revealed to us? For they present themselves as closed to us so long as their properties are not evident to us.

Now raise your eyes to the heavens which we briefly mentioned just above, if perhaps you can see them opened. They are the lofty modes of contemplation. Beginning with them, seek by ascent the opening of all those heavens of which you have already heard an abundant description by descent. And because there are varied and many modes of contemplation by which the Spirit customarily leads us inward, bringing us to knowledge of his inward secrets—leading us indeed as far as he wills and in the manner he wills—he often, as you know, sets before our hidden gaze the beautiful and useful immensity of creatures, their useful and immense beauty, their immense and beautiful usefulness. Through knowledge of these visible things, [Col. 0288C] he brings us to some perception of invisible things. Thus, while we read in the book of Wisdom what is written outwardly in it, we attain to reading and understanding what is written inwardly in it, as that Wisdom of which we speak shows herself to us cheerfully in her ways, “meeting us in every providence,” as Scripture says (Wis. 6:17).

Whenever, therefore, you perceive that you are being dealt with in this manner, you may address us and say: “Behold, I see the heavens opened,” beholding God’s invisible things, understood through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20). And not only by these modes, but by whatever other modes you attain through contemplation to a spiritual knowledge of inward and hidden things, know that in this respect the heavens have been opened to you and the hidden modes of inward contemplation revealed.

[Col. 0288D] IX. I likewise have no doubt that those heavens which are spiritual men are opened to you when their holiness and virtue do not escape you, and you know how lofty they are in spiritual conduct. Therefore, lifting your inward eyes to those heavens, observe how innocent Abel was: though he is read to have been slain by his brother, he is not read to have resisted (Gen. 4:8). How holy Enoch was: living holily among men, he deserved to be taken away from men (Gen. 5:22). How perfect Noah was (Gen. 6:9), who, when the whole world had been corrupted through sin, shone as a light in the world amid a crooked and perverse nation (Phil. 2:[Col. 0289A]15). Obedient to God’s voice, at his command he set aside every concern of household affairs and remained occupied for about a hundred years in building the ark.

With what honorable and holy modesty Shem and Japheth covered their father’s nakedness (Gen. 9:13). Before that fitting decree had been uttered in human speech, “You shall not uncover your father’s nakedness” (Lev. 18:7), they not only did not uncover their father’s nakedness, but covered it when it had been uncovered. And lest anything should be lacking to the gracefulness of their honor, they did not permit themselves to look upon what they judged should be covered. O men outstandingly adorned with the beauty of honor! Love of honor made them both careful to cover what was otherwise exposed and modest in looking upon it.

How can we sufficiently praise and admire our father Abraham’s obedience? It was obedience that, when commanded to depart from his land, kindred, and father’s house, he went forth not knowing where he was going. It was faith that, against hope, he believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said to him: “So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven” (Gen. 15:5). And, not weakened in faith, he did not consider his own body now dead, when he was nearly a hundred years old, nor Sarah’s dead womb (Rom. 4:19). To commend the greatness of this faith, what does the Apostle add? “He did not waver through unbelief at God’s promise, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God and knowing most certainly that whatever he had promised, he was able also to do” (ibid., 21).

How greatly, in your judgment, did he add to the virtue of obedience when he did not shrink from raising his bloody hand against even the hope of his posterity—his only-begotten son, Isaac? (Gen. 22:10). The offspring of the aged father also, while through purity of mind he always flees every sight of impurity, deserves to see things far more remote, even while confined by the eyes of the flesh. His holy son [Col. 0289C] Jacob likewise dwells at home in manly simplicity and simple virtue (Gen. 25:27); humbly yielding by flight to his brother’s anger, he acquires wealth while serving in exile, which later he possesses in his native land.

X. How we extol innocent Joseph, whose innocence is commended by his long robe (Gen. 27:23): innocent, I say, and simple, obedient, patient, modest and chaste, devout and kind. Far be it from you to think that any of these qualities was lacking in him. Read his deeds, and you will find him innocent in the conduct of life; simple in the disclosure of dreams; obedient in response to command; patient even to the point of being sold; modest even to flight; chaste even to prison; devout even to tears; kind even to forgiving injury.

Moses, the man of God, because he was humble, refused to preside over the people (Exod. 4:3); but lest he should be obstinate, he at least promptly consented. In the one instance he regarded his own weakness; in the other he feared not to obey God. O how devout and how strict, how devoutly strict and how strictly devout! Do you not call devout one whom you see offer himself even to death for a blaspheming people? (Exod. 32:32). Yet he was no less strict, who at another time, angered against that same people, in zeal fiercely proceeded even to their slaughter (Num. 25:3). What shall I say of the fact that, at one and the same time, the rebellious people proposed to stone him, and he entered the tabernacle to pray for them? (Exod. 17:4). Rightly the Holy Spirit declared that he was the meekest man above all men who dwelt upon the whole earth (Num. 12:3). Clearly he was most meek, since he strove to pray for those persecuting and slandering him.

Phinehas is angry [Col. 0290B] (Num. 25:7), lest the Lord should become angry. Stretching out his hand against those engaged in unlawful intercourse, he turned the Lord’s hand away from the people (ibid.); and thus, while zealous with the zeal of the Law, he received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because this was reckoned to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever. Joshua (Num. 27:18) does not refuse humbly to be subject, so that later he may humbly preside; for he succeeds in government the one to whom he renders obedience.

XI. Holy Samuel likewise was rendered neither proud by high office nor disturbed by being cast down (1 Sam. 3:20). His fame spread so widely that it is written of him: “All from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord” (1 Sam. 12:3). This is the same man who, while in office, kept himself free both from avarice [Col. 0290C] and from complaint—here maintaining his own holiness, there safeguarding the peace and quiet of those subject to him. Do you not affirm that he governed without avarice, when you read of him that he accepted neither money nor even footwear from any person? And so that you may know that he walked in all the Lord’s commandments and ordinances without reproach, see what follows: “And no one accused him” (Sir. 46:22).

Accordingly, with a secure conscience he addressed the people, saying: “I have conducted myself before you from my youth until this day. Behold, I am here: speak before the Lord and his Christ whether I have taken anyone’s ox or donkey, whether I have wronged anyone by accusation, whether I have oppressed anyone, whether I have accepted a gift from anyone’s hand. Reject it today, and I shall restore it to you.” And they said, “You have not falsely accused us, nor oppressed us, nor taken anything from us.” And he said to them: “The Lord is witness against you, and his Christ is witness this day, that you have found nothing whatever in my hand.” And they said, “He is witness” (1 Sam. 12:2).

Indeed, a favorable testimony is not usually suspect when it is given by those known to be adversaries. But we should also greatly reverence in him this: that he believed he would sin if he failed even his persecutors either in prayer or in instruction. “Far be it from me,” he says, “that I should sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you; and I will teach you the good and right way” (1 Sam. 12:23).

Who does not admire in holy David such wisdom, humility, and strength? Attribute to wisdom that he sits as the wisest in the chair [Col. 0291A] of wisdom (2 Sam. 23:8); to humility, that he is like a tender little worm of wood; to strength, that he killed eight hundred men in a single onslaught (ibid.). He is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord appointed over his household (Matt. 24:45), choosing him to feed Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance. He fed them in the innocence of his heart and enriched them with the understanding of his mercy. For he taught him prudence, so that he fled Saul, his persecutor, as an enemy, yet, when the occasion for vengeance was offered, spared him as his lord (1 Sam. 24:3).

XII. Those eminent men, Elijah and Elisha, I mean (4 Kgs. 4:27), were so raised by zeal and so brought low by humility that neither feared to assail even a sinning king with the rod of correction. Elijah humbly girded his loins and ran before Ahab, while Elisha did not shrink from being touched by a woman (3 Kgs. 18:46). Isaiah does not disdain, at the Lord’s command, to undergo in preaching the confession of nakedness (Isa. 20:2). Jeremiah forbids the people to go down into Egypt (ch. 43:7); but because he truly loves those whom he forbids to descend, he himself descends with them—an excellent counselor for salvation, but a faithful companion in hardship.

Who does not praise Judith’s boldness, Esther’s prudence, and Tobit’s manifold holiness? The boy Daniel and his three companions, while in a place of luxury they tame the body by the virtue of abstinence (Dan. 1:8), not only attain the lofty summit of wisdom, but also receive this marvelous gift: in their case, by a new and unheard-of miracle, fire forgot its power to harm [Col. 0291C] (Dan. 3:50), and even the most savage lions, though afflicted by hunger, did not dare attack Daniel (Dan. 6:22). Recall the zeal of holy Mattathias (1 Macc. 2:2), and stand astonished at the admirable triumphs of his sons.

XIII. But where am I going? I neither know how nor am able to recall individually every man of virtue whom holiness of life brought into prominence, whether before or after Christ’s Incarnation. But, to run quickly through the Gospel period: John the Baptist [alternative: perhaps “first in holiness” is missing: “John the Baptist,” etc.], than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women (Luke 7:28); the apostles’ extraordinary distinction; the martyrs’ constancy; the confessors’ holiness; the virgins’ purity.

Therefore run in thought and eager desire through the condition and conduct of the saints, both those who were in the Old Testament and those who are now in the New; and when you return to us you will be able to say that you have seen the heavens opened (Acts 7:55). For holy men, as was shown above, are heavens. These heavens are opened to you when the conditions and ways of life of the saints are revealed. If, moreover, it has been granted you to recognize how great was the wisdom in Moses’ breast when he gave the Law, and how great it was in holy David, Isaac, Jeremiah, and the other prophets, you will likewise see the heavens opened in this respect.

[Col. 0292A] XIV. Go also to the expositions of the orthodox Fathers. By diligently applying yourself to their treatises and teachings through constant scholarly reading, you will be able to see here too the heavens opened. The apostles likewise are heavens, indeed heavens that drop dew from above. Great is their distinction; excellent their dignity. The heavens are also opened to you in their case when, through the Spirit, what pertains to them is revealed to you.

But fly also on the wings of desire to those lofty choirs of heavenly spirits; persist and knock insistently, that perhaps they may be opened to you, for they too are heavens. Behold those blessed spirits, immortal in life, happy in the vision of God, distinct in persons, ordered in ranks, powerful in themselves, loving one another, wise in God, he himself being all in all. Their ranks bear these names: angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. They possess all these names, and do so from what they are. To survey these briefly—for we must not linger long upon matters which the holy Fathers are known to have discussed sufficiently in many places—

XV. To survey them briefly, then, consider, as far as you can, how happily the holy angels excel in knowledge of divine judgments, and the archangels in knowledge of inward counsels. In accordance with the meaning of their name, they announce these things: to whom, when, how, and how much he himself judges, on whose behalf they act as envoys. See also how the Virtues powerfully perform miracles and signs; how the Powers overthrow, repel, and render void the tyrannical malice and malicious tyranny of demons and reprobate humans, on behalf of those who shall inherit salvation [Col. 0292C] (Heb. 1:14); how the Principalities distribute the rights of kingdoms and the heights of dignities at the will of that supreme and uncreated Spirit, who raises the heaven of Dominions even above all these orders.

He also decrees his judgments upon the Thrones; for, pouring himself into them and opening his hidden mysteries to them, he communicates them through their mediation and transmission to those below, so that the angels may know what, to whom, and how much they should announce; the archangels what they should reveal; the Virtues what they should do; and the Powers what protections they should provide. Above all these are the two higher companies, the eighth and ninth—Cherubim and Seraphim. In accordance with the proper interpretation of their respective names, the former are filled with the knowledge of God, while the latter are kindled by the charity which is God.

Those are the lofty heavens in which dwells he to whom we say daily: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). The Lord our God fills them. The greatest blessedness of their dwelling is that he manifests himself as loving in the Seraphim, for he is charity; as knowing in the Cherubim, for he is truth; as sitting in the Thrones, for he is equity; as ruling in the Dominions, for he is majesty; as governing in the Principalities, for he is the beginning; as guarding in the Powers, for he is salvation; as working in the Virtues, [Col. 0293A] for he is not merely virtuous but supreme Virtue; as revealing in the Archangels, for he is the brightness of eternal light; and as present and assisting in the Angels, for he is piety. The one and same Spirit works all these things: our almighty God, creator of all spirits and bodies, distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11). Therefore, when, raised to the height of contemplation, you clearly perceive these things and other matters pertaining to them with the gaze of the mind, you may, when you come down to us, say that you have seen the heavens opened, to the praise and glory of God, who is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. ALSO FOR THE FEAST OF ST STEPHEN, THE PROTOMARTYR.

On the two natures of Christ and the spiritual heavens.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. With the heavens opened, the Son of Man is to be seen.  
2. What it is to see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power; indeed, sitting and walking.  
3. In Christ’s walking, his activity is considered; in his sitting, the manner of that activity.  
4. This one thing is most marvelous in Christ’s life: that he took upon himself our weaknesses.  
5. Jesus walks in mortality, sits in glorification, and stands in eternity.  
6. What fruit is to be drawn from the contemplation set forth.  
7. What especially is to be considered in the nine choirs of angels.  
8. Happy are those who contemplate the Son of Man walking; happier those who contemplate him sitting; happiest those who contemplate him standing.  
9. Those who fail in contemplating the Word should rest in contemplating the Son of Man.  
10. The daughters of Zion are souls still weak, detained in considering the works of Christ’s humanity.  
11. Recapitulation through the coherence of the subject matter.

[Col. 0293C] I. You now have both who these heavens are and how you ought to knock, so that they may be opened to you. But you ask: What benefit is there in the opening of these heavens? There is much benefit, and great benefit in every way. For when the heavens were opened, what did blessed Stephen see? He said indeed that he saw the heavens opened; but what did he add? “And the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power” (Acts 7:55). Certainly, brothers, happy is he who can continually see the heavens opened in the manner of which we have spoken. But far happier is he who deserves to see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power.

I do not find myself sufficiently capable of opening this mystery, nor do I fully comprehend what it is to see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power. For, having clouded eyes and almost always turned downward toward low things, I cannot behold this Son of Man’s state, so exalted and so unchangeable. But those who are accustomed frequently to enter these heavens, travel through them with devout curiosity, and dare, under the guidance of the Spirit of truth, to explore this Son of Man’s state—these know and can, if they wish, tell you what it is to see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power.

II. But if they judge it safer to keep their secret to themselves, I shall say what I have thought it is to see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power—without prejudicing in any respect those who know how to speak of this more truly and profoundly. I find this Son of Man—for it is unnecessary to say who he is, since he is our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God without a mother, Son of Man without a father—I find, I say, that this Son of Man is not only standing but also sitting at the right hand of God’s power. For I read in the Gospel that he said to the Jews: “You shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God’s power” (Matt. 26:64). Mark the Evangelist likewise says: “The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19).

Thus you have him not only standing, as with Stephen, but also sitting at the right hand of God’s power, as with the Evangelist. He also at one time stood among us, as you read: “Standing, he commanded him to be brought to him” (Mark 10:49), prefiguring that state which he has at the right hand of God’s power and by which he was able to give sight to the blind. He also sat among us, as John says: “Wearied from the journey, he was sitting thus upon the well”; and he adds: “It was about the sixth hour” (John 4:6). What else do we suppose this means but that he, the firstborn from the dead, suffering through the mutability of the nature he assumed, in the sixth age of the world humbled himself even to the depth of our humiliation? He was voluntarily subject to this for a time, yet always surpassed it in power. Thus, wearied from the journey, at the sixth hour he sat—not indeed in the fountain, but above the fountain. And I also frequently find him walking in our region. For throughout all the time in which “he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil” (Acts 10:38), he did not cease to walk among us.

III. I think that Paul, Peter’s companion, explains this saying of Peter when, in the second epistle to the Corinthians, [Col. 0294C] he says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). See him conceived in the Virgin by the Holy Spirit; coming from the conception that was without corruption to the birth that was without injury; from the womb to the manger; from birth to circumcision; from circumcision to presentation; from presentation to baptism; from baptism to fasting; from fasting to hunger; from hunger to temptation; from temptation to preaching; from preaching to the working of miracles; from the working of miracles to the Passion; from the Passion to death on the cross; from death on the cross to the tomb; from the tomb to resurrection; from resurrection [Col. 0294D] to ascension. In all these things consider him walking. For his walking among us is his working our salvation in the midst of the earth, within the mutability of the nature he assumed.

If anyone should say that his sitting and his walking are directed toward one and the same thing, he does not seem to me to depart from the truth. For if his walking was the working of our salvation, how did he work except by acting and teaching? Otherwise he would not be called “a prophet mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24:19), nor would holy Luke declare that he wrote an account of all that Jesus began to do and teach (Acts 1:1). Therefore consider in his walking the activity of your salvation, but in his sitting the manner of that same activity. In both he is beautiful in a twofold way: “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” because of the wonders he did; “grace was poured upon his lips” (Ps. 44:3) because of the healing things he said.

IV. Certainly, among all the marvelous things he did, I judge nothing more marvelous than that he endured weakness. For it seems more marvelous that bread should hunger, the fountain thirst, and life die, than that he should feed many hungry people from a few provisions, change water into wine, or raise the dead. You have both these modes of activity in his twofold sitting. He sat upon a mountain teaching the apostles, so that you might receive with your hearing the sublime things that he uttered (Matt. 15:29); and, wearied from the journey, he sat above the well (John 4:6), so that with a humble mind you might reverence the weak things he endured.

Let us therefore comprehend under one meaning his sitting and walking here. But his standing—whether he opened the eyes of the blind man who cried out (Luke 18:40), or when after the Resurrection he revealed himself to the disciples, no longer on the sea but on the shore, not walking but standing (John 21:4), whereas before the Resurrection he appeared to them laboring at the oars (Mark 6:48), not on the shore but on the sea, not standing but walking; or wherever else he is found standing, in any place or manner—belongs to that eternal and immutable state which he has at God’s right hand.

After completing his walking among us, he sat down at the Father’s right hand, in the seat of glorification—he who here was accustomed to walk in the labor of mortality. But the state which he has at God’s right hand is his majesty, coeternal and coequal with the Father; and his standing at the Father’s right hand is his being coeternal and coequal [Col. 0295C] with him.

V. This being so, lift up your eyes and see the Son of Man walking; see him sitting; see him also standing: walking in mortality, sitting in glorification, standing in eternity. Happy indeed is the one who continually beholds him walking; happier the one who beholds him sitting; but happiest the one who beholds him standing.

Ask holy Isaiah what he was like in walking, and he will tell you that he saw him and “there was no appearance”; “and we desired him,” he says, “the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness; and his face was as it were hidden and despised, whence we did not esteem him. And we considered him as a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isa. 53:3). And again: “Surely he bore our sicknesses and carried our weaknesses” (ibid., 4), with many further statements of this kind.

But the Apostle in part makes known to us what he is like when sitting: he says that God exalted him in glory and honor and gave him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal (Phil. 2:9), and other such matters which are sufficiently clear to you. But who has seen him standing at the right hand of God? I think it was he who said: “In the beginning was the Word; and the Word was with God; and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him was life” (John 1:1).

Does it not seem to you that this man fixed his eyes equally upon the Father, coeternal [Col. 0296A] and equal with himself, and upon the Son standing at his right hand, and saw that neither exceeded the other in power nor preceded the other in eternity, but that they are truly and supremely one in one divinity? Go, and do likewise.

VI. With these heavens, of which we have already said much, opened to you, behold the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power; and, through the certainty of faith, recognizing him as in every respect equal to God, know that he is the Son of God. For this is their whole usefulness, this their entire fruit: that you may frequently traverse them as a devout and humble knocker rather than a rash and presumptuous investigator, so as to see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power. For what advance do you make—briefly to touch upon these same heavens once more—[Col. 0296B] what advance, I say, if you attain the lofty modes of contemplation, if by intellectual understanding you behold God’s invisible things through the things that have been made, yet do not admire in those same visible things him through whom God the Father made all things, without whom nothing was made, and in whom what was made was life? If you stand amazed at the praiseworthy conduct of spiritual men, glorify above all in them him who works in them both willing and accomplishing according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2:13); when he strengthens them, they can do all things in him, without whom they can do nothing. Whatever depth or maturity you discern in the wise men of the Church, do not ascribe it to them, since they are not sufficient to think anything of themselves, as from themselves; but rather to him whom Paul proclaims as God’s power and wisdom (1 [Col. 0296C] Cor. 1:24), whom none of their adversaries can resist or contradict. Great indeed is the honor due to those who labor in word and doctrine; and the apostles of Christ, whom he now calls not servants but friends, are most greatly to be honored, because he made known to them all things whatsoever he heard from his Father (John 15:15). Yet not more than Christ himself, nor as much as he. For the preacher of the word is not the Word himself, nor is an apostle greater than him who sent him (John 13:16). Great, therefore, and truly great, is the delight of traversing these heavens; but it is not fruitful unless you see in them the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power.

VII. What do you say of angels and archangels? [Col. 0296D] The former indeed stand amazed at the knowledge of divine judgments, the latter at the knowledge of divine counsels; but far above either order in dignity is he to whom the Father gave all judgment (John 5:22), and who is the teacher of all angels. For he has become so much better than the angels as he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”? (Heb. 1:4.) And he is certainly the one whom the angels themselves adore. The Virtues perform miracles; the Powers possess strength to restrain all things, above all demons and proud and reprobate men: yet they received all of it from him who is the Lord of hosts, “the Lord strong and mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:8). Of him too it is written that he “alone does wonders” [Col. 0297A] (Ps. 71:18).

What if, through the governance of the Principalities, every authority on earth is changed and transferred, established and ruled? That they may do even this, he gives it to them, distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11); in his hand are all powers and the rights of kingdoms; to him has been given all power in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28:18); he rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he wills. But if you see the Dominations preeminent over all these orders, know them to be subject to him (Dan. 4:14) who has written upon his robe and upon his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19:16). Thrones sit, and sit in judgment; but unless the Son of Man sat and made discernment in them, those who judge would err in uprightness, and those who sit would have no rest. For [Col. 0297B] although it is written, “There sat thrones for judgment” (Ps. 121:5), no one can fail to know how greatly, in every way, a throne differs from the one seated on the throne.

The Cherubim pour out streams of knowledge to their fellow citizens; but how could they pour them out unless they had first been poured into them? Or how could they offer drink unless they had first drawn it? For what do they have that they did not receive? (1 Cor. 4:7.) And if they received it—indeed, because they received it—from whom did they receive it except from Christ, the wisdom of God, “who came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature”? (Ecclus. 24:5.) If the Cherubim also shine with unceasing light, let them know that the Wisdom of which we speak said of them: “I caused unfailing light to rise in the heavens” (ibid., 6). [Col. 0297C] Are the Seraphim kindled? Yet God’s fire kindles them—indeed, God is fire. And if they burn with charity, they received it from him who is charity. Do you ask who he is? Why ask me? Ask John, and you will be told that “God is charity” (1 John 4:8). You now see, I think, if you have understood all these things, what it is to see the heavens opened, and what it is to see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power.

VIII. I recall that a little while ago I called happy those who see the Son of Man walking; for “the Son of Man goes,” as it is written of him (Matt. 26:24). Nor can he walk except in that in which he is the Son of Man, because he who said, “The Word walked,” immediately added, “and went out into the fields” (John 10:23 and 40): wishing, I think, to signify [Col. 0297D] that the mobility which the Word had in walking was received from the fact that he went out into the expanse of our fields. I said, therefore, that those who see him walking are happy; happier are those who see him seated at God’s right hand; but happiest are those who see him standing at the right hand.

But you ask: Why do you construct these degrees of distinction in one and the same Son of Man? Not without reason. It is because the mortality of one born from his mother, the glorification of one reigning, and the co-eternity, co-equality, and consubstantiality of the Only-Begotten from the Father with that same Father, do not shine with equal brightness in him. For if you are willing to understand: though here the Word of God is the Son of Man, nevertheless, having become flesh, he appeared contemptible, as one appearing in the diadem with which his mother crowned him (Song 3:11). But in the flesh, [Col. 0298A] after the suffering of death and the triumph of resurrection, lifted up through the glory of the Ascension, he was no longer uncomely and weak, but beautiful and strong, “beautiful in his robe, advancing in the greatness of his strength” (Isa. 63:1). And what if his garment is red, if his clothes are dyed? He borrowed this from us, so that “the hands in Jacob might be the hands of Esau” (Gen. 27:22).

IX. But his Word, which was in the beginning, which was with God and was God, dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen, nor indeed can see (John 1:18). Therefore, let those among us who are spiritual, strengthened by purity of conscience and illumined by the brightness of inward sight, who dare by themselves to follow the Spirit wherever he goes, lift their eyes [Col. 0298B] to the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power. There they shall see great glory—indeed, inconceivable glory—and likewise hear words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:4).

Yet those who aspire to these heights must lay aside utterly every grossness of the heavy and dark humanity that is in them, and assume only the subtlety of pure and clarified spirituality; especially since the Lord says to his beloved and intimate one, not so much a servant as a friend: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). But those who cannot yet lift their eyes to that lofty radiance of the most brilliant sun should behold the assumed nature glorified at the right hand of God. Let them behold, I say, that nature exalted in Christ at the Father’s right hand, which, though it never committed sin, lived with human beings on earth, and, enduring the punishment of death, so shameful and so harsh, hung upon the gibbet of the cross.

But if there are any whom an invading phantasm burdens, or a reproaching guilt tears apart, or an active sensation distresses, so that they cannot attend to either of these, while knowledge of each is altogether wonderful to them and so strengthened that they cannot attain to it (Ps. 138:6), [Col. 0298C] they may keep before their eyes this Son of Man of whom we speak, walking and passing through and healing all who were oppressed by the devil (Acts 10:38).

X. Let, then, these daughters of Zion go forth—for they are daughters—and behold King Solomon in the diadem [Col. 0298D] with which his mother crowned him (Song 3:11), until they deserve to become sons by beholding him in the diadem with which his Father crowned him. Let them withdraw and, as far as they can, call back before their eyes and gather within themselves, according as it has been granted them, how, in the movement of our stability, from the day on which he was born, “Jesus began to do and to teach, until the day on which, after giving commandments through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up” (Acts 1:1). Let them behold him walking with his forerunner, and then cry out with him and say: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:36). Nor should they think that they receive something slight from this vision, but altogether something great, since it is certain that with their own eyes they see, with their own ears hear, and with their own hands touch, in the Word of life [variant: “concerning the [Col. 0299A] Word of life”], whatever that may be (1 John 1:1). The apostle Paul also calls it “the great mystery of godliness,” and declares that it was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed in throughout the world, and taken up in glory (1 Tim. 3:16).

XI. It is, therefore, a great thing to see him walking, since “what is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1:25). But it is far greater to see him seated at the right hand. Yet I would call that person one who ascends the highest degree: the person who, seeing the heavens opened, deserves to behold him standing at the right hand of God’s power. And perhaps these are the three heavens to whose third Paul declares that he was caught up, where he also says that he heard ineffable words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak [Col. 0299B] (2 Cor. 12:2). And indeed I think that, just as this man [variant: “just as that passage was corrupt”] and that man saw things which it is not permitted a human being to disclose.

But this discourse now approaches its due end. You have heard what, for the present, we judged sufficient concerning what it is to see the heavens opened; who and how many these heavens are; and what it is, when they are opened, to see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power. We have also said what it is to see him seated, and what it is to see him walking. Likewise, we have been told what it is to look toward heaven, and, by looking toward heaven, to see God’s glory; finally, what it is to be filled with the Holy Spirit. For each of these depends upon another: you cannot see glory unless you look upward; nor can you look upward fruitfully unless you are full [Col. 0299C] of the Holy Spirit. Therefore keep in memory what has been said about these matters at somewhat greater length; put it into practice in life, so that there the understanding may be clarified unto purity, while here the affections may be adorned unto holiness. Invoke, therefore, the Holy Spirit into yourselves, and pray that he may deign to fill you, so that you too, as is recorded of blessed Stephen, filled with the Holy Spirit, may look toward heaven and see God’s glory—he who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. ON THE FEAST DAY OF ST JOHN, APOSTLE AND EVANGELIST.

On the threefold honor with which the Lord honored the same blessed John in life and in death.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. How great and how counterfeit is the pursuit of honor [Col. 0299D] among the children of Adam.—2. What true and desirable honor is.—3. St John was honored for bodily virginity, purity of mind, and the intimacy of love. The sublimity of his Gospel above the others.—4. What it is for him to be fed with the bread of life and given to drink of the saving water of wisdom.—5. How great was the intimacy of his intercourse with Christ. How great his prerogative of love.—6. Christ’s confidant reclined upon his breast, that is, upon the treasury of his wisdom.—7. Above the others, he dares to ask about the betrayer.—8. St John, a virgin, is commended by the dying Christ to the Virgin Mother.—9. The intimacy of God, not of earthly rulers, is to be earnestly sought.—10. St John’s threefold prerogative and perspicacity of understanding.—11. He is honored threefold in death: first, the Lord visits him as he is about to die.—12. [Col. 0300A] Second, he is invited to the heavenly banquet.—13. Third, what the manna found in his tomb signifies.—14. Why we ought to fear the hour of death: because of the accusing enemy, the testifying conscience, and the striking judge.—15. Honor in death corresponds to St John’s threefold honor from the Lord in life.—16. The beatifying vision makes us like God.

I. Your devotion desires, not indeed without longing, and awaits, not without hope, to hear something from us on this splendid feast of the most glorious and blessed apostle and evangelist, something that may so instruct the conduct of those who hear it as to commend his prerogative. Yet what weight can any honor paid to him by us possess, when it is evident that he is honored so sublimely and so singularly [Col. 0300B] by the common Lord of all? For compared with divine honor, what importance can human honor have?

With what eagerness the children of Adam desire to acquire honor! Yet honor which does not come from God is deceptive and utterly nothing. I do not fully understand why it is that even the perfect are not immune and alien to the desire for honor. Even if it is perhaps not sought, it delights when offered, and is not lost without pain when possessed. It is itself a witness, therefore, that it delights when possessed, since it torments when lost. This is the thing which disguises itself under the hope of spiritual advancement—I speak not of honor, but of the desire for honor—recommending that one should preside, as though solely in order to be able to be of service. But its deceitful counsel is so hidden, and whispers in such a hidden recess, as it were, [variant: “in some manner”] [Col. 0300C] that it can scarcely be perceived by any person, however wise. For while it suggests the usefulness of labor, it strives by a kind of stealthy fraud and fraudulent theft to draw one into desiring the loftiness of honor. Even if, when circumstances so require for spiritual advancement, this must sometimes be tolerated, it must never be desired for its own sake when absent, nor loved when present.

II. But since the honor which miserable mortals, deceived, regard as something great is deceptive and plainly unstable, I would call that person truly happy who can attain the honor of which the Lord says: “My Father who is in heaven will honor him” (John 12:26). He first spoke of a certain honor which he now grants his own in the present, and which is a way toward that eternal honor: “If anyone serves me” (ibid.). Therefore, to serve the Lord is to be honored; plainly so: he alone is honored who serves him; he alone also reigns who ministers to him.

This is the honor which he abundantly bestowed upon blessed John, who, having been sublimely honored by him, ought also to be honored by us, as we sang of him tonight [Note: [Col. 0299D] From the ecclesiastical office for the day of his feast.]: “Blessed John is most worthy of honor.” Certainly this is true, true indeed: blessed John is not simply to be honored, but is most worthy of honor. Christ honored him; therefore it is fitting that all who belong to Christ should honor him, because among men all the servants [Col. 0301A] of a king are accustomed to honor the person whom the king honors. Christ honored him in life; Christ honored him in death; so that it may thereby be established among us that, after death, he honors him eternally in certain ineffable ways.

III. He honored him in life in three ways: by granting him virginity, purity, and intimacy—virginity in body, purity in mind, intimacy in sweet and sincere love toward himself. Though Jesus, the distributor of inward gifts and the rewarding Lord, bestowed on him many other gifts of grace, these are what occur to us at present. He chose him as a virgin, as we sang of him today [Note: [Col. 0301D] From the ecclesiastical office above], because “a virgin was chosen by the Lord; chosen as a virgin, he remained a virgin for ever.” How great the cleanness of his heart, how great the purity of his mind [Col. 0301B], can any of us comprehend? Surely he was a man of great purity, who, transcending all visible things and even surpassing himself by the brightness of his inward eye, saw that the Word was in the beginning and with God; that all things were made through him; that without him nothing was made; and that what was made in him was life (John 1:1).

When you hear the Gospel read, are you not compelled beyond measure to marvel and stand amazed at him, hearing him, after so great an interval of time, report so promptly and consecutively the Lord’s words to others and others’ words to him, as though he had heard these same things at that very hour? Hence, although the others are represented by the living creatures, as you know (Ezek. 1:5), he too, on account of the singular prerogative of angelic [Col. 0301C] purity, so to speak, which the Lord bestowed on him, is likened to an eagle—and not simply to an eagle, but to a flying eagle (Rev. 4:7). For John is the flying eagle, comprehending above the others, through purity of mind, the lofty secrets of inward mysteries. The wonderful profundity of his Gospel bears witness to this. So too does the Apocalypse of Jesus Christ cry aloud, which God gave him to make known to his servants, and which he sealed by sending it, as he himself writes, through his angel to his servant John, “who bore witness to the Word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, in all that he saw” (Rev. 1:1).

IV. We fittingly and appropriately sing to him and say of him: “The Lord fed him with the bread of life and understanding, and gave him the water of saving wisdom to drink” (Ecclus. 15:3). These words were indeed said concerning the person who fears God, but they can most suitably be applied to him. Do you not affirm that he was fed with the bread of life and understanding, when you see how many refreshings of heavenly secrets his clarified and most pure spirit reveals, and recognize him as filled with as many courses, as it were, of savory spiritual foods? For his spirit lives in such things and by such things, when that spiritual bread enriches it, supplying inward strength for life and savor for understanding.

And who, not to say would deny, but would even dare to doubt that he was given the water of saving wisdom to drink, when he recounts and repeats in writing, with such precision and in such order, Christ’s words spoken so many years before? Surely he could never have done this unless he had been given Christ’s Spirit to drink. For the water of wisdom is Christ’s Spirit.
