[Col. 0302A] For unless water were the Spirit, after the Lord had said, “The water that I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14), this John of whom we speak would never have added: “But he said this of the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:36). Paul calls Christ the power and wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24); therefore John was imbued with Christ’s Spirit in order to report Christ’s words so profoundly. For if, according to the apostolic statement, “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3), how could this man in his Gospel say “Jesus is Lord” so profoundly and so perfectly unless he were full of the Holy Spirit?

I would therefore say that he was fed with the bread of life and understanding in his knowledge of heavenly secrets; but was given the water of saving wisdom [Col. 0302B] to drink in his precise expression and utterance of the Lord’s words. O tabernacle of the Father! O chamber of the Son! O shelter of the Holy Spirit! O resting-place of the holy Trinity! And, lest I seem to have omitted anything: O oracle of the indivisible unity—the most pure and spotless mind of this John of whom we speak!

V. What, then, shall we say about the intimacy which the Lord deigned to have with him above the others? How can we sufficiently, with delightful sweetness and sweet delight, embrace him as more loved among the rest [Col. 0302D], and received in a certain singular intimacy beyond the rest? Is he not the one who, as we recall having said on another occasion, was accustomed, with humble truth and true humility, [Col. 0302C] to say of himself: “That disciple whom Jesus loved”? (John 13:23.) What is this? Did Jesus not love the other disciples? Indeed he loved them. For, “having loved his own who were in the world,” as this same blessed John says, “he loved them to the end” (ibid., 1), so that you may know that he did not merely love them simply, but fully and perfectly. This is what it is to love unto the end.

But I think—unless some more suitable explanation occurs to you at present—that the Holy Spirit wished it to be said of John that Jesus loved him because, although he did not exclude others from the bosom of his love, he loved this one singularly; and, beyond the others whom he loved, he embraced this one in the most sweet arms of sincere love. Jesus therefore loved him among the others, so as to love none of them more; for Jesus was loved by him, and none of them loved Jesus more. But if this is so, why, I ask, is the prerogative of this love made known to us through John’s own assertion, so that he says of himself, “that disciple whom Jesus loved,” when it ought rather to have belonged to the other evangelists to say this of him, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips” (Prov. 27:2)? Is it not because we are plainly given to understand, through this, the confidence and boldness of true love?

What does perfect love dare not confess concerning itself? What can perfect charity fear, when it casts out the fear with which whoever fears fears? (1 John 4:18.) [Col. 0303A] Presumption sometimes appears to be present in charity, but pride is never present; for in not fearing it is in no way inflated. It always and everywhere exercises boldness, but never, in any place, pride. Hence the Beloved and Loving One says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song 2:16); and so this disciple says, “whom Jesus loved”: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” That is: he has the greatest care for me, and I for him: I, loved by him, love him.

Indeed lovers have this very characteristic: they can scarcely speak of anything except what pertains to love, especially when they speak either to one another or about one another. For the saying of our Redeemer is true, that “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12:34). I think this may be understood of abundance in evil as well as in good, because whatever it is that abounds in the heart, something from it must sound forth from the mouth. Boldness, therefore, is evidence of confidence—not of vanity, not of pride, but of love. [Col. 0303B] John calls himself the disciple whom Jesus loved because, loving so ardently and being loved so intimately, he could not conceal that he was the one so loved. O highest and fullest blessedness: to love Christ, to be loved by Christ, and to have intimacy with him!

VI. But in what way was John beloved and intimate to him? Whenever anyone was present at Christ’s secrets, when was John absent? Where was he left out, to whom it was granted to be admitted? Peter and James saw him transfigured—did John not see him? [Col. 0303C] On the very night which preceded the day of his passion, when he was going to the place of prayer, did he take Peter and James with him and not take John? Did he wish Peter and James to be present at the raising of the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter and exclude John? You will nowhere find a secret communicated to another disciple that was concealed from John.

Indeed, he was admitted to certain things, and that with the greatest intimacy; and all the more intimately because altogether singularly. The fact itself openly cries out and insistently bears witness that no one was his equal, not to say his superior, in the love of charity, since no one deserved to share with him in admission to intimacy. Thus, to bring forward some instances: at supper he reclined upon Christ’s breast (John 21:20), making God’s own most sacred breast his pillow. [Col. 0303D] How beloved by Christ must have been that head which he allowed to rest upon his breast! This was indeed great intimacy; yet it was external. For there was another and much greater intimacy, inward in nature—and greater not merely because it was inward, but because this was truth while the other was figure. For outwardly John’s head rested upon Jesus’ breast; inwardly, however, he placed and reclined that same head—that is, his mind—in the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge, all of which are hidden in Jesus’ breast. The former was for honor; the latter for instruction. Having then been admitted into so great an intimacy, not in one but in a double manner, [Col. 0304A] what could he seek and not find? What could he ask and not receive?

VII. The first of the apostles, weighing this well, when Jesus declared that one of them would commit the betrayal, desired to know who would commit so monstrous a crime, yet did not at all dare to ask. He judged that the beloved disciple should be approached about this matter, so that he might ask the Lord who it was. For thus it is written: “Simon Peter made a sign to him and said: Who is it of whom he speaks?” And what follows? “Therefore, when he had reclined upon Jesus’ breast, he said to him: Lord, who is it? He answered: It is he to whom I shall give the dipped bread” (John 13:24). And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot.

Peter knew that John had [Col. 0304B] the boldness to ask, because he recognized that he had found such affectionate intimacy with the Lord. Seeing him so intimate that he reclined upon Christ’s breast, Peter did not doubt that he would dare to ask whatever he wished, nor disbelieve that he would receive an answer to what he asked. That all this was so will be found contained in the very sequence of the words, if it is carefully considered. For what else does the statement appear to indicate: “Therefore, when he had reclined upon the Lord’s breast, he said to him: Lord, who is it?” It first mentions that he reclined upon Christ’s breast, then asks who it was—as though he presumed to ask who would betray him precisely because he reclined upon Christ’s breast. And is it not so? For what would this man not dare to ask, when he saw that he had been permitted to lay his head upon Christ’s breast and recline upon [Col. 0304C] it? Or what would Christ conceal from one who asked, whom he had introduced to the inward secrets of his wisdom and knowledge?

VIII. What shall we say of this: that, on the following day, as he was dying and offering himself as a saving victim upon the altar of the cross for the salvation of the whole world, when he was near to delivering his spirit into his Father’s hands, he deigned to commend his beloved mother to his beloved disciple—the Virgin to the virgin, Mary to John? For what does John himself report in his Gospel? “When,” he says, “he saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved, he said to his mother: ‘Woman, behold your son.’ Then he said to the disciple: ‘Behold your mother’” (John 19:26).

O honor, higher than every honor that can be possessed in the present [Col. 0304D] life: in a certain sense, to be Christ’s brother and Mary’s son! And John alone is judged worthy of this sublime honor. To which human being did Christ ever say concerning his mother, “Behold your mother,” except John? Or concerning whom did he say to his mother, “Woman, behold your son,” except John? O innocent Lamb, meek and gentle Jesus, how beloved you had seen him to be—how beloved, I say, him to whom you believed could be entrusted that most precious treasure of heaven and earth, your mother!

You say to the mother: “Behold your son”; but to the disciple: “Behold your mother.” I ask, what do these words mean? Why do you not command the disciple, saying: “Serve, minister to, and attend upon [Col. 0305A] her as your mistress, my mother”? Why do you not say to your mother: “Make use of the service of my disciple as of your slave and servant”? But what you say sounds far more honorable and gracious: of the disciple to the mother, “Behold your son”; and of the mother to the disciple, “Behold your mother.”

Is this not, in a certain sense, to say: “Until now, standing by you, I have been not only your son by right, but have shown myself to be your devoted son by serving you. But now, since, as you see, I die here on this cross, and depart from you bodily and am not with you, I do not wish you to remain without a son, even though for the present you cannot have me. Have this man in my place as your son, and you in my place as his mother. Among women none is equal to you, O mother; among those of your sex no one in the [Col. 0305B] world is superior to you, O disciple. Therefore it is altogether fitting that you be joined to one another: she has no equal in the female sex in bodily incorruption, while you have no superior in the male sex, except myself. Let the virgin attend upon the Virgin: John upon Mary, Mary upon John—she with a mother’s affection, but you with filial service and care.”

IX. What do you say to this, children of Adam, avaricious and ambitious race, alien children grown old, desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another (Gal. 5:26), seeking false and fleeting honors, rejecting true honors because they are heavenly, because they endure? O, how great a thing it is thought to be when someone obtains a place of intimacy with a wealthy man, when he finds favor with a king! “How well,” they say, [Col. 0305C] “this man stands with the king! See, the king smiles and rejoices with him as an equal. How intimate he is with him, and the king with him! Whoever offends or opposes this man cannot find the king peaceable or kindly toward himself.”

But if it is so, what here is stable and sincere? And, consequently, what is commendable and desirable? Does it not often happen that those who are near today are far away tomorrow, and that those who were yesterday intimate friends and members of the household are today enemies and adversaries? Frequent examples of this are seen every day. But strive to be God’s intimates and friends; endeavor to be Christ’s disciples and members of his household. “How,” you ask, “can we be Christ’s friends and disciples?” Hear how: “If you abide in his word, you will truly be his disciples” (John 8:31); and, if the question concerns [Col. 0305D] friends, “you are his friends if you do what he commanded you” (John 15:14). These are his promises. But holy John, persevering in obedience to his commands, was both his disciple and friend, and was honored by him with an honor not impure and unstable, but sincere and enduring.

X. This, then, is the threefold way, briefly mentioned, in which he honored John in life: among the many other gifts of grace with which he enriched him, he granted him virginity in body, purity in mind, and love in sincere intimacy—or, if it is better so expressed, intimacy in sincere love. He also granted him steadfastness in purity, preserving his mind fixed in contemplation; likewise steadfastness in virginity, because [Col. 0306A] he who chose him a virgin always preserved him a virgin, defending him from every contagion that might defile him. He bestowed upon him, among his fellow disciples, the prerogative of intimacy, embracing him in love and intimacy not only with the others, as has already been said, but also above the others.

The words we read concerning him bear witness that this was so: “And he shall be strengthened in him, and shall not be moved; and he shall hold him fast, and shall not be confounded; and he shall exalt him among his neighbors” (Ecclus. 15:4). Before this it had been said of him: “The Lord shall feed him with the bread of life and understanding, and shall give him the water of saving wisdom to drink” (ibid., 3). We have taken care briefly to show above how these words apply to blessed John. For he shall feed him with the bread [Col. 0306B] of life and understanding by revealing to him, for the inward refreshment of savor, those mysteries and hidden things in the knowledge of which every holy person is illumined in understanding, so that, choosing what is true, he may shine in the light of truth; and is strengthened for life, so that, loving what is good, he may exercise himself in the work of holiness.

But he gave him the water of saving wisdom to drink, inspiring him to understand words, retain what he had understood, and write down accurately and consecutively what he had retained in memory, just as it had been spoken—words which the Son himself, the Father’s wisdom, is known to have uttered in the flesh for human salvation. He was also strengthened in him and was not moved, because, established in Christ through knowledge of truth and love of virtue, he was not torn away from contemplation and love of him. Therefore, lest the purity of his clarified mind should be corrupted in any respect, he strove to be made firm through the roots of love in him in whom nothing defiled could enter, so that, being thus strengthened in him, he might in no way be moved.

He also held him fast, and he was not confounded, because, preserving him perfect in the virginity in which he found him whole, he was not confounded by grieving that he had fallen from the good purpose which he had embraced; rather, he was conscious that he had ascended in it by advancing more and more. Moreover, he exalted him among his neighbors by embracing him, among his fellow disciples, in that intimacy and love which I have shown above.

XI. Since we have in part explained how the One who loved him honored him in life [Col. 0306D], it remains for us to show how his lover Jesus honored him also in death, in whose sight death, no less than life, is precious. As he honored him in life in three ways, so too he honored him in death in three ways. The first, as it seems to me, is that the Lord himself came to him in death. The second, that he led his most holy soul, as it is right to believe, to his everlasting glory. The third, that after his departure nothing but manna was found in his tomb. Thus, as he was about to depart, he was visited by the Lord himself; his soul was placed in the glory of eternal blessedness; and his tomb was exalted by a new and unusual honor.

For, as we read, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to his beloved John with his disciples [Col. 0307A] and said to him: “Come, my beloved, to me, for it is time for you to feast at my banquet with your brethren.” The Lord fulfilled what he had promised concerning him to his companion and fellow apostle Peter, when Peter heard by what death he was to glorify God, and asked concerning John, saying, “But, Lord, what of this man?” He answered: “Thus I wish him to remain until I come” (John 21 and following). By these words he clearly showed what love he bore toward him, when he says that he wishes him thus to remain until he comes. He wishes him to remain until he comes, not until he sends. These words, as you know, seemed to the disciples then present to grant him so great a prerogative that a report spread among them that this disciple would not die.

[Col. 0307B] XII. Great everywhere [variant: “indeed”] is the honor with which the Lord himself deigned to invite him to his banquet, where his elect feast and exult in his presence, he himself appointing them a kingdom so that they may eat and drink at his table in his kingdom (Luke 22:30). And when the Lord appeared to him and invited him to his banquet, he replied—surely stretching both his hands out to God:

“I come, giving thanks, invited to your banquet, because you, Lord Jesus Christ, have deemed me worthy to invite me to your feast, knowing that I desired you with my whole heart.” [137]

And again:

“Lord, receive me, that I may be with my brethren, with whom, when you came, you invited me. Open to me the gate of life and lead me to the banquet of your feast. For you are Christ, the Son of the living God, who at the Father’s command saved the world; to you we give thanks through endless ages.”

But which of us can comprehend with how great an honor he led him to the eternal banquet?

XIII. And how can anyone worthily marvel, reading or hearing, that nothing but manna was found in his tomb? In certain passages of Holy Scripture manna is called the bread of angels; a tomb, moreover, is usually a place of decay and stench. O holy, O blessed John! How beloved you were by Christ while living in the body is plainly shown to us by these things which occur concerning you in death. Behold, Jesus, who loves you, appears to you with his disciples, your fellow citizens, and invites you [variant: inviting you] to those most delightful [Col. 0307D] feasts of eternal refreshment. He led you there with incomprehensible honor; and, so that not only nothing belonging to honor should be lacking to you in death, but that very much should also be present contrary to the ordinary course of nature, he does not allow your tomb—utterly empty, not so much emptied of all decay as vacant—to be without angelic food.

XIV. As I contemplate your most glorious departure from this life, I leap with joyous admiration and admirable joy; but when I foresee my own most wretched departure, I am shaken alike by fear and shame. I know absolutely neither when nor where it will be; yet I do not fail to know that it will someday and somewhere occur. I do not see myself as such that I may judge that he ought to send to me any one of his peaceful attendants [variant: “that he may have”], or suppose that he himself will come to me.

The prince of this world came to him, as he himself testifies, and found nothing in him. I do not deny that this same prince will come also to me; but I do not presume to say that he has nothing of his own in me. How unhappy is that city which its enemies surround with a rampart, hem in on every side, cast to the ground, and destroy with its children who are within it, leaving in it not one stone upon another (Luke 19:43). All these things, in their moral sense, apply to the reprobate soul departing from the body—a soul which, as blessed Job says, “a scorching wind shall carry away, and a whirlwind shall snatch from its place” (Job 27:21).

As I dwell upon that hour when I shall depart—though I know not where, and know not when—I tremble with mighty fear before the face of the cunning accuser and the strict judge. I portray to myself how terrible that hour will be for me: the hour in which I shall be compelled to leave the body, and in which I shall be brought before the gaze of the fearful judge. As I consider that dreadful hour, three things greatly terrify me: my manifold injustice; the malicious, though true, accusation of the cunning accuser; and the terrible sentence of the strict judge. Woe is me, whose weak case presents to me a judge no less strict than the accuser is hostile! These three things I fear in that hour: the accusing enemy, the testifying conscience, and the smiting judge.

But be present with me in that hour, though I am unworthy, yet your suppliant calling upon you for help from the whole marrow of my heart. Come to meet me [Col. 0308C] and help me then, O most holy and most blessed brother of Christ and son of Mary. Come, I say, for consolation; help me for protection; bend the judge; drive the accuser far away, so that neither may this one convict me nor that one condemn me.

Yet it is not in considering the stench and decay of my body that I fear; nevertheless I am greatly ashamed and blush, knowing that, as is altogether fitting, the disgrace and dishonor of my most filthy and foul-smelling cave will stand far apart from the honor and glory of your most pure and most beautiful tomb. For my corpse will make my cave horrible with its dreadful stench and its swarming worms; but manna makes your tomb honorable.

[Col. 0308D] XV. And see, brethren, how the threefold honor with which the Lord Jesus honored John, his beloved and intimate friend, at the end corresponds to the threefold honor with which he honored him in life. For he himself came familiarly to him at his passing, as he had been accustomed to show himself his intimate friend in life. Having admitted him while living to his inmost secrets, he invited him at his departure to that eternal banquet.

His most holy and most blessed spirit was also transported to that happiness which will endure for ever, because here, through the Creator Spirit granting and pouring himself forth, he had attained such purity that he saw the Word in the beginning. Transferred from glory to glory, from brightness to brightness, he attained from that which is now seen in a mirror, enigmatically, to that which is face to face (1 Cor. 13:12). There he may now rejoice, blessed without end, for ever, where even here, while placed in the body, he continually held the firstfruits of his spirit bound fast and his desire rooted indissolubly.

After this it was fitting and wholly appropriate that manna should beautify the place into which a virginal body entered; for I would in some sense call manna the prerogative of virginity, so that the body honored with the heavenly gift of virginity might have a tomb adorned with a kind of manna.

XVI. We ought now to say something about that honor with which he honors him eternally, if we knew how to say anything about it. But since it is established that neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what the Lord Jesus prepared—and has now bestowed—for his lover and beloved John [Col. 0309B], how can the tongue adequately express anything concerning that honor when even the mind cannot comprehend it?

There is now fulfilled in him what he said in his Epistle not only concerning himself but also concerning his fellow citizens: “Now we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared” (1 John 3:2); and he added: “We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (ibid.). Which of us now possesses such purity as to be able to comprehend the excellence of this vision—a vision which makes the one who sees like the one whom he sees, so that to see and to be like the one seen are the same thing? O joyful and beatifying vision! O blessed and beatifying likeness! In it this blessed John, of whom we have now said much, rejoices with unutterable joy with his beloved Lord Jesus through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. ON THE DAY OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS

On the fruit of salvation which heavenly Wisdom pours into us, and on how pride persecutes humility within us.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. By Joseph is signified progress in virtue; by Mary, the bringing forth of wisdom.  
2. Joseph, of the house of David, continually dwells in the palace of heaven.  
3. The soul rising upward is signified by Joseph; enlightened by the ray of wisdom, by Mary—so that election by grace may stand firm.  
4. That the aged King David is not warmed by garments means that he does not accept earthly consolations.  
5. Abishag the Shunammite—that is, true wisdom—is sought; by what servants she is to be sought.  
6. Abishag’s ministry: standing through uprightness of intention; sleeping through tranquillity of mind; cherishing through inward sweetness; warming through the fire of love.  
7. A demonstration of gratuitous election unto glory.  
8. Signs of Jesus’ presence in the heart through profound humility, of which there are three degrees.  
9. How great is the fruit of humility, to which everything ought to be made subject.  
10. The effects, from grace present, of patience and threefold compunction.  
11. Jesus produces in us the perfection of the eight beatitudes.  
12. To persist in works of salvation is to hold the child Jesus; against him Herod—that is, pride—plots, that such works may perish.  
13. The hidden craft of pride is more clearly exposed when it secretly enters good works.  
14. The woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, is the wise soul accompanied by a good reputation.  
15. What the crown of twelve stars means, and what her travail in giving birth means.  
16. The woman’s fourfold prerogative: good conduct in the garment of the sun; contempt of reputation in the moon placed beneath her; the adornment of virtues in the crown of twelve stars; the affection of good desire in the travail of childbirth.  
17. Pride, like a dragon, sets on fire with its tail, corrupting the uprightness of intention.  
18. Discretion is the charioteer and measure of the virtues, and is greatly necessary.

I. You have heard, dearest brethren, in today’s reading from the Holy Gospel, that Herod seeks the child Jesus in order to destroy him (Matt. 2:13 and following). How quickly Jesus found enemies in this world, when his birth, still so recent, was not free from the cruelty of a monstrous persecutor. He humbly fled his persecutors, so that he might also teach us what we ought to do when Herod seeks us in order to destroy us.

For even today Herod does not cease within us from seeking the child Jesus to destroy him. But an angel of the Lord appears to Joseph in a dream, telling him to take the child and his mother and flee into Egypt. Nor does he merely say this, but tells him to remain there until he tells him otherwise; nor does he conceal from him either the cause of the flight or the delay there: “Herod,” he says, “will seek the child in order to destroy him.”

Who, do you suppose, is this Joseph? Perhaps he is the sincere and pure soul, enriched in many ways, according to the interpretation of this name Joseph, with increase in spiritual virtues. Does not the name, in this sense, seem to breathe out the prayer of one who addresses the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends from above (James 1:17), saying: “You will increase strength in my soul” (Ps. 137:3)? [139]

This is he to whom Mary, joined in marriage, bears a Son whose name is Jesus, because heavenly wisdom—for this is Mary—bestows the fruit of salvation upon the faithful and devout soul through inward inspiration. For who would deny that heavenly wisdom, ministering to a sincere soul the fruit of salvation, whether inwardly in the affection of pure love or outwardly in the effect of vigorous action, is Mary giving birth to the child Jesus for Joseph [variant: “with Joseph”]? She, according to my understanding—she, I say—is the incorrupt virgin and fruitful mother, “betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, and the virgin’s name was Mary” (Luke 1:27).

II. Does not the strong and manly soul in God seem to be a man named Joseph, while it strives through the daily increases of holy conduct to be enriched ever more and more? It also rightly shows itself to be of the house of David when, with sober inquiry and devout eagerness, it strives, insofar as this is possible in the present age, to explore and traverse that eternal house in heaven not made by hands. It passes through those bright dwelling places of blessed spirits, so that it may claim for itself Paul’s saying: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

For this Joseph continually traverses the order of angels, who care and provide for us, knowing them to be ministering spirits sent forth for the service of those who shall inherit salvation (Heb. 8:14). He traverses the assembly of archangels, who reveal inward conferences to us; of virtues, who perform miracles and wonders; and of powers, who restrain and overthrow the malice and tyranny of demons and reprobate human beings. He marvels at the royal dignity of principalities, the prerogative of dominions, the most tranquil equity in thrones, the fullness of knowledge in cherubim, and the unfailing blaze of divine love in seraphim.

[Col. 0311A] He passes through the companies of patriarchs, the choirs of prophets, the senate of apostles, the purple crowns of martyrs, the white garlands of virgins, and the golden collars of Catholic doctors.

III. Behold our Joseph frequenting that heavenly house, fastening there the firstfruits of his spirit after the manner of the eagle which, raised at the Lord’s command, makes its nest on high, dwelling among rocks and abiding in steep crags and inaccessible cliffs (Job 39:28). And as he thus sees the earth from afar, his eyes sometimes see the King in his beauty [Col. 0311B]; he fixes his clear gaze upon David himself, into whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1:12).

When you discern such a state in your soul as we have described in these words, you may not unreasonably say that you are called Joseph and are of the house of David. And who can deny that the virgin’s name is Mary, unless perhaps one does not know what her office is? For Mary, as you know, is called “star of the sea.” Is not heavenly wisdom a kind of star of the sea, poured into the soul by inward inspiration, when it illumines that same soul by the ray of its discernment in this stormy sea which often floods within it, so that it may know what to avoid and by what course it ought to proceed amid the surging waves of its thoughts?

Joseph gives birth to this child Jesus, bestowing the fruit of salvation upon the devout and faithful soul. Joseph indeed bears him; but Mary did not conceive him by Joseph. This, I think, is what a certain saint said to the Lord: “You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2). For all of us who are saved are saved through the election of grace; and if by grace, then no longer by works, otherwise grace is no longer grace. Paul likewise rightly asserts that David spoke of the blessedness of the person to whom God reckons righteousness apart from works (Rom. 4:6).

Agreeing with him, holy Isaiah, taking upon himself even the voice of all the elect, addresses the common Lord himself: “You have wrought all our works in us” (Isa. 26:12). This is lest an enemy of grace should suppose that a reward is to be reckoned to him not according to grace but according to debt, when the Joseph of whom we speak receives the child Jesus from Mary in such a way that he knows that he himself did not first pour seed into her.

IV. Did not Abishag the Shunammite once warm and cherish David when he was old and cold, though David did not know her? For what does Scripture say? “King David had grown old” (3 Kings 1:1). I think that the soul which is devout in right faith and devoted in holy conduct, when it discreetly governs all its motions [variant: “all its motions within itself”], both outward and inward, when it vigorously exercises itself in energetic good action, and, as divinely granted to it, keenly directs the vision of its mind [variant: “the vision of a penetrating mind”] toward the desire for inward contemplation, may not unreasonably be called both king and David.

It also grows old when it reaches the perfect maturity of holiness. It is rightly said of it that it was advanced in days, because the devout soul possesses many virtues in holy conduct. “For old age is an undefiled life” (Wis. 4:9); and our fathers of old were said to have died “old and full of days.” That is, they were mature in spiritual conduct and filled with an abundance of holy virtues.

And Scripture adds that, when he was covered with garments, he was not warmed, because “if riches abound, he does not set his heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11), reckoning all worldly things as loss and judging them as dung. For what else are all earthly things but certain garments for the body? Yet when King David is covered with these garments, he is not warmed, because the perfect soul receives no consolation from any earthly thing.

But when this soul thus refuses to be comforted, it must remember God, take delight, and be exercised; and David’s servants give him good counsel in this matter, saying among themselves: “Let us seek for our lord the king a young virgin, and let her stand before the king and cherish him; let her sleep in his bosom and warm our lord the king.” And after this Scripture adds: “Therefore they sought a beautiful young woman throughout all the borders of Israel. And they found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king” (3 Kings 1:3).

V. But someone among you says to me: “Why are you now speaking about David and Abishag, when a little earlier, at the very beginning of this sermon, your purpose was to treat of Mary and Joseph?” My purpose remains the same. And you will immediately see that what we now have in hand fittingly pertains to those matters; and, I suppose, you will not blame the digression when you see its cause and rationale.

Who, then, is this Abishag, whose name is interpreted “the roaring of my father,” if not inward wisdom, revealing the secrets of the highest Father to the soul into which it is poured, by a certain roaring of silent cry and crying silence? Since it bestows upon that soul both spiritual tenderness in affection and beauty in understanding, it is both a young woman and beautiful. It is also Shunammite, that is, scarlet, beautifying [variant: warming] the soul it fills with the color of love.

David’s servants seek her throughout all the borders of Israel because, among all modes of contemplation, wisdom must be sought more earnestly and, once found, retained more closely. And who are these servants? Perhaps consideration, prayer, conduct, purity, and perseverance are David’s servants. I say this because the wisdom of which we speak is searched out by the sober depth and profound sobriety of consideration; sought by the devotion of prayer; deserved by holiness of conduct; attained by the cleanness of purified purity; and embraced by the steadfastness of perseverance, which says: “I held her and will not let her go” (Song 3:4).

VI. “And she ministered to him.” What is the ministry Abishag renders to David, except that for which she was sought by his servants: namely, that she might stand before him, sleep with him, cherish him, and warm him? (3 Kings 1:4). She is said to do all these things because she enables the soul into which she is poured to do them. In some sense she stands, while persuading it to stand. She also sleeps, while enabling it to sleep; and while he is cherished and warmed, she herself cherishes and warms him.

Behold Abishag’s fourfold ministry: to stand, to sleep, to cherish, and to warm. The first pertains to uprightness; the second to tranquillity; the third to sweetness; the fourth to love. Her first ministry, therefore, is that in all our motions, outward as well as inward, we should strive to have uprightness in our inward intention: continually attending within ourselves to him who discerns hearts, thoughts, and intentions of the heart; awaiting him as the approver and judge of every good within us; and finally seeking him as rewarder.

The second is like the first: namely, the undisturbed repose of the mind. For what can now disturb, sting, or shake the conscience, when uprightness of intention preserves its integrity unharmed and wholly unshaken? Thus, in peace, the faithful and devout soul—this is David—sleeps and rests: sleeping in peace through tranquillity of heart, resting in the same one thing because through uprightness of intention it tends toward one thing alone. Why should it not receive the delightful cherishing of inward sweetness?

There remains, then, that it should be firmly bound by the bond of perfection, should walk without stumbling by that royal way which the Apostle calls more excellent, and, so far as regards God, should blaze with the fire of love; while, so far as regards brethren, its ardor should kindle its neighbors. These, therefore, are the good things that beautiful Abishag bestows upon David: inward wisdom upon the faithful soul; uprightness in inward intention; repose in the mind’s thought; cherishing in inward sweetness; and ardor in sincere love.

This fourth good seems to contain the three preceding goods within itself, because Paul declares love to be threefold (1 Tim. 1:5): from a pure heart, a pure conscience, and unfeigned love. Uprightness of intention brings purity to the heart; tranquillity of heart brings goodness to the conscience; and, lest faith be feigned, the sweetness of holiness is tasted in the inward palate of the soul.

VII. After all this, how does Scripture conclude? “King David,” it says, “did not know her” (1 Kings 1:4). This is the point which we have touched upon in the foregoing brief exposition. This is true, because David did not know Abishag; likewise Joseph did not know Mary. David receives warmth from the beautiful young woman Abishag, without feeling through her any lust. Joseph receives the child Jesus from Mary, knowing no carnal union with her, so that all who are in grace may recognize that they have been saved by grace and not from themselves, and that it is the gift of God, lest anyone should boast (Eph. 2:9).

The Lord says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16). Therefore, let those who were chosen without choosing, and who, going forth, bear fruit that remains, ascribe this to him who chose them and appointed them to go forth.

Let our Joseph also know that the child Jesus is from Mary alone, who alone bore him to him, according to that angelic promise: “You shall bear a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (Luke 1:31), as one who did not beget him. Therefore the child Jesus, whom Mary alone bears of herself for Joseph, is the fruit of salvation, which Wisdom inspires in the devout and godly soul by grace alone, freely given. And he is that chaste warmth which the beautiful young woman Abishag, not known by him, gives to the aged King David.

VIII. To begin, then, to speak of humility, which is the foundation of the other virtues: when you feel your heart urged and inflamed by devout desire toward this end—that you submit yourself to everyone greater than yourself and place yourself before no equal—who can doubt that this devout affection within you is the child Jesus? For in the assumed nature, in which he is less than the Father, he wholly and perfectly submitted himself to him, becoming “obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8).

But if you strive to ascend so far in the height of humility as to submit yourself even to every equal, preferring yourself to none, nor setting yourself above an inferior either, I declare that you have received the child Jesus from Mary. He too obeyed his own Father, to whom he is equal in divinity, when the Father made him a little less than the angels (Ps. 8:6), when, by the Father’s appointment, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”—the Word which was in the beginning, was with God, and was God (John 1:1).

But if you endeavor to storm the fortress of humility and, as a devout invader and tireless climber, resolve to ascend to its summit—so that in true humility you cast yourself down before an inferior, not merely preferring yourself to no one at all, but rather being subject to every human creature for God’s sake (1 Pet. 2:3)—I do not know who possesses, in this respect, more fully than you the child Jesus, meek and humble of heart. For he did not deign to leave even this kind of humility unfulfilled in himself: he went down with Mary and Joseph, came to Nazareth, and was subject to them (Luke 2:51); moreover, he bowed himself to John’s hands to be baptized (Matt. 3:16).

[Col. 0314D] Behold the threefold degree of humility: to be subject to a superior, which belongs to beginners; to an equal, which belongs to those advancing; to an inferior, which belongs to the perfect.

IX. Therefore, when you compel whatever is carnal in you to serve this threefold degree of humility, you plainly have the child Jesus with you, displaying and fulfilling within you what Isaiah says: “Its bars”—namely, those of Moab, without doubt—“shall reach as far as Zoar, the trampling heifer” (Isa. 15:5). What else does this mean than that, when the soul is turned toward God by the affection of holiness, the harsh carnal passions—which the original seed of our fathers placed in our flesh, because Moab sounds like “paternal water” or “from the father”—are mortified, changed for the better, and made obedient to the little one, through the abundant inward grace of this threefold humility of which we speak?

For Zoar, as you know, means “little one”; and the heifer is humility, abundant in grace as a heifer is in milk. For it is written: “He gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). And this is especially so when they have ascended all three degrees. Thus humility, showing itself little and abundant in grace, is the “heifer crushing,” to which the bars of Moab extend, because it contains the threefold degree of which we have spoken; and to it, in those who are converted, the hardness of carnal passions, altered and softened, becomes obedient.

X. But if you possess a soul made perfect in the virtue of patience, so that you bear insults calmly, endure losses, and suffer scourges—by insults I mean those of words, by losses those of possessions, and by scourges those in the body, should this happen—you undoubtedly have the child Jesus. For this is the threefold degree of patience.

And if, laboring in your groaning and washing your bed every night, watering your couch with your tears, you possess the lower watering-place (Ps. 6:7); if, too, as the deer longs for springs of water, so your soul longs for God; if your soul thirsts for God, the living fountain, saying, “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” and if your tears are bread to you day and night (Ps. 41:2), so that you may ascend also to the upper watering-place (Judg. 1:15); if, finally, you lament all the calamities of others as your own—for this is the threefold kind of spiritual compunction—know without doubt that this salutary child Jesus is the one whom that affection inspires in you, whom Mary bears for Joseph.

Behold the threefold poverty to which the kingdom of heaven is promised; the threefold meekness to which possession of the earth is owed; and likewise the threefold mourning which consolation will abolish.

XI. But if, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, you strive to live so innocently that you are found to harm no one, and, being merciful, endeavor to conduct yourself so helpfully that you appear, according to your ability, to benefit everyone, rejoice with joy that you have the child Jesus with you. For because you do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself, you shall be filled by him; and because you do to others whatever you wish people to do to you, you shall obtain mercy (Matt. 5:7), God, the just judge, measuring back to you in the same measure in which you first measured.

But if you refuse to be defiled by this threefold filth—namely, carnal desire, temporal glory, and remembrance of your former wickedness—not only by consent in the will, but also by delight in the affection, and, further, as belongs to the perfect, even slightly by recollection in thought, who would dare deny that this salutary purity which you possess pertains to the child Jesus? Surely your reward will be the vision of God; indeed, the brightness of so great a purity of heart precedes that reward. If anyone doubts this, let him hear the true promise of Truth itself: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (ibid., 8).

But if you strive to calm all turbulent motions within you in your mind; if you display so complete an outward peace that in countenance, speech, and indeed all your motions, nothing is done which offends anyone’s sight; and if, wishing to offer this great good to those who do not possess it, you endeavor both to make peaceful all whom you see disturbed and to restore them to the unity of concord, no one can doubt that this is a special work of the little Jesus, “in whom God was reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). At his recent birth angels announced peace to people of good will; he too is “our peace,” making both one, reconciling by his blood both things in heaven and things on earth (Luke 2:14). Nor is it surprising if you are called a son of God, since you are found to exercise his office.

And lest I seem to have omitted any of those eight beatitudes (Matt. 5:3) which the Lord sets forth in the Gospel: if your heart ardently desires to suffer persecutions for righteousness’ sake, rejoicing when people curse you, persecute you, and falsely say every evil thing against you, this is the child Jesus whom you hold.

XII. The same must be understood not only of virtues but also of works of virtue: you have Jesus when you perform the fruit of eternal salvation. For if, for example, you devote yourself to abstinence and vigils, to prayer and reading, to holy preaching and brotherly admonition, to almsgiving or any other exercises of holy action, the child Jesus is the one you have with you. For, as has often already been said, to perform a work of salvation is to hold the child Jesus.

But, to use the words of blessed Gregory:

> It is necessary for you to preserve the good that you do with great caution, lest human favor or approval be sought through what is rightly done by you, and lest what is outwardly displayed be inwardly emptied of its reward.

[Note: [Col. 0315D] Homily 12 on the Gospels.]

And as blessed Augustine, our eminent father and advocate, says in the Rule for Clerics: “Every other iniquity is practiced in evil works in order that they may be done; but pride lies in wait for good works so that they may perish.” Hence Herod seeks this most holy child Jesus in order to destroy him. Herod is said to mean “skin of glory”; but to glory in skin is to glory in vanity. Therefore the glory of skin is the glory of exaltation. In this sense, then, Herod is pride. As blessed Augustine says, and as we feel by daily experience, while it lies in wait for good works within us so that they may perish, it is as though Herod seeks Jesus to destroy him.

This is what sometimes desires us to persist in good actions, but only so that we may favor it through the swelling of empty pride. Thus this crafty, changeable Herod cunningly urges the magi to go, inquire diligently concerning the child, and report to him when they have found him. What else does this mean than that pride sometimes approaches us with subtle fraud for the acquisition of good works, so that, once acquired, we may refer them to its vanity?

For what is it for Herod to say to the magi, “Go and inquire diligently concerning the child, and when you find him report to me” (Matt. 2:8), unless it is that the proud desire for empty glory—this is Herod indeed—suggests to the good and devout thoughts within us—these indeed are the magi seeking the Lord—that they should devote themselves to the exercise of holiness in order to exalt themselves, through that very exercise of holiness, by gaining its favor and pleasing it? Jesus is, as it were, found and reported to Herod when a good work once attained serves pride through the desire for vanity.

Herod also added, “That I too may come and worship him” (ibid.), because pride itself sometimes cloaks itself under the appearance of humility in order to destroy that same humility. For pride to transform itself into the form of humility so that it may destroy it is for Herod to pretend that he wishes to worship the child in order to destroy him.

Therefore, when you see someone, under the lowliness of dress or any other sign of humility—whether in speech, gesture, or even action—casting himself down too arrogantly or submitting himself too improperly, recognize that in such a person Herod pretends to wish to worship the child Jesus in order to destroy him.

XIII. Understand, I beg you, dearly beloved, and consider how subtle—and how difficult to detect—is the deceit of pride. For whereas the other vices are overcome by virtues contrary to them—for example, anger by gentleness, envy by kindness, sloth by cheerfulness, avarice by generosity, gluttony by abstinence, lust by chastity—this vice, conversely, is sometimes increased by the virtue opposed to it, that is, by humility, so that what ought to suffer diminution then often receives increase. This plague is indeed exceedingly venomous and altogether deadly: it suggests to devout affections that they should exert themselves in what is good in order that they may exalt themselves because of it. This is indicated by Herod’s command that they should go and inquire concerning the child and, when they had found him, report to him. But it grows greatly in wickedness when it persuades the soul to lift itself up from its very lowliness and to be proud through humility. This is indicated by the fact that Herod pretends that he wishes to worship the child in order to destroy him.

Blessed David wonderfully detected this hidden cunning of pride, and, having detected it, took care to drive it far from himself. Addressing Michal, who reproached him for humbling himself, he says: “I will play, and become more contemptible than I have become, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 6:22). For in saying, “I will play, and become more contemptible than I have become,” he implies that he is humble; but by adding, “and I will be humble in my own eyes,” he shows that he is in no way willing to be proud even of humility itself. For one is, as it were, contemptible, yet not humble in one’s own eyes, when one outwardly displays humility but inwardly takes pride in that very humility. And this is to destroy the humble child Jesus under the appearance of worshipping him. Herod, then, is the one who seeks the child in order to destroy him: namely pride, which strives to destroy in us the fruit of salvation, whether in some open way or in this hidden way which we have now shown. [Col. 0317C–0318A]

XIV. For this is also [variant: indeed] that dragon which blessed John saw standing before the woman in the Apocalypse, so that, when she had given birth, he might devour her son (Rev. 12:4 ff.). Would you be pleased for us to enter into the secret of this mystery, so that, whatever it may be necessary for us to see in it, we may share with your charity without envy and set before you without deceit?

“A great sign,” he says, “appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon beneath her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars; and being with child, she cried out in labour and was in anguish to give birth.” To run through it briefly, while preserving the allegorical sense which pertains to the Church, and also preserving every other tropological sense which expresses her prerogative, we shall now state the meaning intended here. This woman in heaven is the wisdom in the mind, of whom we have said much above. She is described here as appearing such as she makes the soul to be into which she is poured.

She is clothed with the sun because she adorns and beautifies the soul with the bright manner of life of holiness. “And the moon under her feet”: because the holy soul presses every reputation beneath its affections. They say that the moon receives its brightness from the sun. And what is it for the sun to give light to the moon, except for a splendid manner of life to bestow reputation, that it may flourish? Yet this woman is so clothed with the sun that she has the moon beneath her feet, because, as heavenly knowledge arises—or, variant, as heavenly wisdom suggests itself to the mind—the soul into which it has been poured appears adorned and radiant with a holy manner of life, in such a way that it by no means rests softly in human reputation, but presses it under the feet of its affections by despising it. Such was he who said: “If I saw the sun when it shone, and the moon advancing brightly” (Job 31:26), showing, unless I am mistaken, by these words that he was not exalted either because of the holy life he practised or because of the reputation concerning him that circulated among men. [Col. 0318A–C]

### XV

“And on her head a crown of twelve stars.” Consider whether perhaps that crown of twelve stars is formed from the virtues of which the Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, peace, patience, joy, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5:22). Or, if you prefer another interpretation, add those four virtues which you read that wisdom teaches—namely temperance, prudence, justice, and courage (Wisdom 8:7)—to the eight which James declares belong to that same wisdom which is from above, saying that it is “first chaste, then peaceable, modest, persuadable, consenting to good things, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without pretence” (James 3:17). Compose from these a most beautiful diadem, and you will have a crown of twelve stars.

“And being with child, she cried out in labour and was in anguish to give birth” (Rev. 12:2), because wisdom causes the mind into which it is poured to conceive so greatly through intention in its desire for holiness that it cannot bring this conception to fulfilment without the anguish of great labour.

### XVI

Behold the fourfold prerogative of this woman: the splendour of good conduct in her garment of the sun; contempt for reputation in the moon beneath her feet; the adornment of spiritual virtues in the crown of twelve stars; and the affection of good desire in the crying anguish of the woman in labour. Compare, if you please, this fourfold prerogative of the woman with that fourfold mystery of Abishag which we discussed above, for we said that they signify one and the same thing. Consider whether perhaps for Abishag to rest in the bed of holy quiet is for this woman to be clothed with the sun; for Abishag to stand in rectitude of intention is for this woman to have the moon beneath her feet; for Abishag to cherish the old man is for this woman to be crowned with twelve stars; and for Abishag to warm the cold man is for this woman to be with child and to be anguished and cry out in giving birth. [Col. 0319A–B]

### XVII

“And,” Scripture says, “another sign was seen in heaven: and behold, a great red dragon” (Rev. 12:3). The great red dragon in heaven is lofty and cruel pride in the mind. It is great because it makes the mind which it rules seem great to itself. He who said, “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; neither have I walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me” (Ps. 130 [131]:1), refused to possess this greatness in himself. But the one to whom it was said, “When you were little in your own eyes, were you not made head among the tribes of Israel?” (1 Sam. 15), possessed it in himself.

It is also red because it makes cruel toward others the person in whom it exists, as was that man who was “a most mighty hunter before the Lord” (Gen. 10:9). It has seven heads, because it produces from itself those seven capital vices: vainglory, envy, anger, sloth, avarice, gluttony, and lust. And it has ten horns, while by a certain hard eminence and eminent hardness it strives to surpass all others completely. For horns are both hard and rise far above the flesh. We understand the fullness both of this hardness and of this eminence through the perfection of this number, for ten is a perfect number.

“And its tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth” (Rev. 12:4), because pride directs itself to this end: to corrupt the bright intentions of the mind by the desire for earthly favour. For the dragon’s tail is the final aim of an intention of self-exaltation. And who doubts that the stars of heaven are the bright thoughts of the mind? We divide them into three parts: one we claim for ourselves, which we call temperance; a second we assign to our neighbours, which we call justice; and the third we offer to God, and this we call piety. The dragon’s tail especially strives to draw down and cast to earth this third part of the stars, because pride directs its entire aim to this end: that we may strive to possess spiritual luminaries, by which we ought to shine before God, for the acquisition either of human praises or of any other earthly things.

Such a dragon stands before the woman who is about to give birth, so that, when she has given birth, he may devour her son. For self-exaltation raises itself up in order to destroy the fruit which wisdom enables us to bring forth. [Col. 0319B–0320A]

### XVIII

“And she gave birth to a male child” (ibid.). For Mary also gave birth to the child Jesus. There the child Jesus expresses the fruit of salvation; here the male child signifies works of virtue. What is our male child but the virtue of discernment? It is so necessary to every virtue that, without it, any virtue whatsoever, though it may be called a virtue, nevertheless cannot be a virtue. Hence it is well said of this son that “he was to rule all nations with a rod of iron” (ibid.), because discernment governs not merely some virtues but all of them with unbending justice. For while discernment regulates all virtues by the rule of measure in such a way that it permits them neither to be contracted through lukewarmness below the due measure nor to be extended beyond it through excess, does it not seem to you that this male child holds the iron rod by which he rules all nations?

But how will this great child escape being devoured by the dragon? How will the child Jesus escape being destroyed by Herod? Let the Apocalypse tell us about the escape of the male child, and let the Gospel tell us about the escape of the child Jesus. “And her son,” it says, “was caught up to God and to his throne” (Rev. 12:5): this is in the Apocalypse. What is written in the Gospel? “Behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: Arise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you” (Matt. 2:13). He withdrew into Egypt, as is related in what follows, “and was there until the death of Herod” (ibid., v. 15).

The catching up of the male child to God and to his throne is his escape from the dragon; Joseph’s flight with the child into Egypt is likewise his escape from Herod. Must we omit examining these matters because much has already been said? It is better, however, on this occasion to omit such examination and for the present to refrain, lest you become weary; and to defer what must be said about them to another sermon. Yet, because we have been where there is no end, we must retain where we have been. And because we leave the subject, as it were, hanging, let us keep our memory keen and watchful, so that, when we meet again to speak of this, we may know where we ought to begin—to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, blessed for ever and ever. Amen. [Col. 0320A–D]

## SERMON XXXV. ALSO FOR THE FEAST DAY OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS

On the threefold sleep of the spiritual Joseph, and on the angel’s three appearances to him and threefold admonition.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. Recapitulation of the preceding sermon and connection with the following one.
2. Joseph’s sleeps are the mind’s withdrawal into inward things and ascent to things above.
3. Such are the daughters of Jerusalem in the spaciousness of divine contemplation.
4. For them the Bridegroom’s left hand is a pillow, his right hand an embrace, and prudence a mattress.
5. Joseph’s first sleep is the soul’s liberation from every sensible desire.
6. The second is the shaking off of useless phantasms.
7. The third is to transcend visible and invisible things and rest at the boundary of all things.
8. This same matter is signified by a threefold silence in the soul.
9. The excellence and sublimity of the third silence and sleep.
10. The angel appeared to Joseph a third time, whence the mystery is seen.
11. A vivid description of beginners on the spiritual way.
12. How the swelling of self-exaltation is to be repressed in progress.
13. Three remedies for pride: examination of one’s own weakness; uncertainty of perseverance; ignorance of the divine judgment.
14. To these darknesses the child Jesus is rightly borne, as it were into Egypt, to be saved.

### I

We showed you, dearest brethren, in the preceding sermon, what seemed to us to be capable of being understood by Joseph and Mary, by the child and his persecutor Herod. But while treating these matters, certain other things occurred to us for your edification through that anointing which “teaches concerning all things” (1 John 2:27). We intended to speak of these and connect them with what had already been said, and we lingered over them longer than we had expected. For we dare not conceal from you anything among all that the Spirit of truth deigns unexpectedly to reveal, knowing that these things have been entrusted to us for your sake and are transmitted through our ministry to your charity.

Thus it happened that in these sermons we said nothing concerning these holy little ones, slain for the little child Jesus, whose festal solemnity we celebrate today. We deferred until now, if you remember, showing you what we think is signified for us by the counsel given to the little Jesus through Joseph’s flight with him and his mother into Egypt, lest he should be destroyed by Herod; and likewise by the male child in the Apocalypse escaping from the dragon’s devouring through being caught up to God and to his throne (Rev. 12:5). Since these seem, according to the meaning we have pursued up to this point, to signify one thing, they will be found to contain and present spiritual instruction if they are examined spiritually. [Col. 0321A–C]

### II

Receive, then, what has been granted us to think concerning this; but, having received it, do not, I beg you, wish in any way to compare it with what the same Spirit may deign to reveal to you concerning the same things. “An angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream” (Matt. 2:13). Who do you think this angel is? Do you think that it is inward inspiration? This is how I take it for the present, until you instruct me more truly concerning these matters, because of the Apostle’s saying: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man; but God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” [citation printed: John 3:8]. And because of the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice” (John 3:8).

I do not doubt that this angel has appeared in Joseph’s sleeps among some of you. What are Joseph’s sleeps? Perhaps they are the withdrawal of pure and devout minds through contemplation into inward things and their ascent to things above. For the pious and faithful mind itself is Joseph: through complete mortification it withdraws from all pleasures of the flesh; through complete contempt it withdraws from all worldly occupations and secular affairs; and, entering within itself unto itself, and driving away as far as it can with the hand of holy purity all the phantasms of passing things that rush upon it, it makes for itself a bed in that inward quiet. With the door shut—not only that fivefold door of the body through which bodily things enter, but also every door of the heart through which even the images and likenesses of bodies are accustomed to intrude—it “sleeps and rests in peace in the selfsame place” (Ps. 4:9). In this peace, in this selfsame place, in this sleep, the mind sometimes passes beyond itself to God, having sleeps no less sweet than healthful, in which the angel of the Lord appears. [Col. 0321C–0322A]

### III

The Bridegroom directs his attention to these sleeps, to this sweet repose and reposeful sweetness, when, while she rests between the arms of her Bridegroom, that same Bridegroom judged it right to adjure the daughters of Jerusalem by the roes and the harts of the fields, that they should neither awaken nor cause her to awake until she herself wished (Song 2:7). This was so that weak yet devout souls—whose weakness is denoted by the female sex and whose devotion by the place of peace—might know that, when they presume by rash importunity and importunate rashness to awaken the Bridegroom from these most sweet sleeps, they are rushing upon those heavenly spirits who, like roes and harts in the fields, penetrate the innermost things and seek the highest, within the spaciousness of that divine contemplation.

But he placed the awakening of her beloved in her own will, knowing that she had been taught to discern both when she ought in mind to pass beyond herself to God and when she ought to be sober for us (2 Cor. 5:13). O how sweet and secure are these sleeps of hers! For how can they not be sweet when she rests between the arms of her Bridegroom? How can they not be secure when she has the very one who forbids others anxiously guarding against any of the daughters presuming to awaken her? [Col. 0322B–C]

### IV

“His left hand,” she says—undoubtedly that of her beloved—“is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6; citation printed “21:6”). Is not this an exceedingly soft bed for her, in which the Bridegroom’s left hand serves as the pillow; in which the embrace of his right hand serves as the covering; and in which she has prudence itself as a mattress? This is the piety that she has in both the right hand and the left, concerning which the chosen Apostle admonishes his disciple, declaring that it is useful for all things, “having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4:8)—indeed, of the life that now is because of the left hand which is beneath the Bride’s head, and of the life to come because of his right hand which shall embrace her.

Do not angels descend and ascend upon the Son of Man? (John 1:51). Yet they could not descend upon him unless he were below, where his left hand is beneath the head of his Bride; just as they could not ascend to him unless he were above, where his right hand embraces her. The Bride now sweetly lays the left hand of her Bridegroom beneath her head, knowing that his right hand will one day embrace her. From the reception of present gifts she possesses a firm expectation of future ones, “having her fruit unto sanctification, and the end eternal life” (Rom. 6:22). In this soft bed our Joseph rests sweetly, intent upon his sweet sleeps, in which the angel of the Lord appears to him. [Col. 0322C–0323A]

### V

His first sleep, then, is, to say it briefly, to be freed from every desire for visible and sensible things. This sleep is exceedingly sweet, because while our Joseph gives himself attentively to it, he rests in a threefold quiet. Through it he is released from curious and vain pleasure, and from pleasure-seeking and vain curiosity. O sweet sleep! Would you not call it a sweet sleep not to be defiled by the pleasure of carnal desire, not to be scattered by the curiosity of secular occupation, not to be raised up by the vanity of lofty dominion?

Behold the three-pronged fork in the cauldrons of cooked flesh (1 Sam. 2:13); behold the three darts fixed in Absalom’s heart (2 Sam. 18:14); behold the wife taken, the five yoke of oxen, the estate bought, which render those invited strangers to the Lord’s supper (Luke 14:20); behold, finally, the desire of the flesh defiling the reprobate soul, the desire of the eyes scattering it, and the pride of life exalting it (1 John 2:16). From all these things our Joseph is made free while he attends to this sleep, no less sweet than healthful, in this threefold quiet.

For the first quiet keeps him clean from the filth of carnal corruption; the second makes him quiet from anxiety about secular business; the third makes him free from the arrogance of swollen dominion. In the first, bodily passion is mortified; in the second, worldly occupation is laid aside; in the third, ambition to rule is despised. [Col. 0323A–B]

### VI

The second sleep of this Joseph of whom we speak is to cast out from the bedchamber of the heart the invading images and likenesses of corporeal things, and to repel every fabricated phantasm that thrusts itself in. This sleep surpasses the preceding one in sweetness by as much as it surpasses it in purity. For in that sleep Joseph attains great sweetness, since through it he is granted not to be entangled, in the course of life, by any desires for visible or sensible things. But in this sleep he attains far greater sweetness, since through it he is granted, in contemplation, not to be entangled by any images of corporeal phantasms—or, if you prefer, by any phantasms of corporeal images.

Who, I ask, can long attend to this sleep? Who, I say, is this man? “And we shall praise him, for he has done wonders in his life” (Ecclus. 31:9). For in that first sleep he conquers the world and the things of the world, the flesh too and the things of the flesh; in this second sleep he even transcends the mind itself through a certain mighty freedom and free power. What then remains for this Joseph, except that, after he has passed beyond all corporeal things in the first sleep and all spiritual things in the second, he should take a certain third sleep in which, so far as is possible in this exile, he may attain to the divine things themselves? [Col. 0323C–D]

### VII

Let him therefore transcend all created things, visible and invisible, and rest in that boundary of all corporeal and spiritual things. I judge this to be a most sweet sleep [variant: a certain sleep]. For if the first sleep seems sweet to you because of the great virtue that belongs to it, and the second sweeter because of the refined purity which it contains, why would you not call this third one most sweet because of the angelic blessedness with which, entirely full, it overflows?

Behold, these are Joseph’s sleeps, in which he rests sweetly and in which the angel of the Lord appears to him. Although the angel appears to him in each of them, the appearance of which we are now speaking seems especially to pertain to this one: in it the angel, revealing himself to Joseph, takes care to admonish him to take the child and his mother and flee into Egypt, because the time is at hand when Herod will seek the child in order to destroy him. For the more you advance in purity of mind, the more and more hostile you will find pride in its temptations. [Col. 0324A]

### VIII

Consider whether perhaps the first sleep pertains to that quiet silence of which you read: when all things kept silence [variant: “when it kept silence”], and the middle of the night’s course had come, the almighty word of the Lord is said to have come from heaven, from the royal thrones (Wisdom 18:14–15). For when the mind is entangled in desires for visible and sensible things—when, to show this somewhat more fully, it eagerly desires to be defiled by the filth of pleasure, or is scattered by the excess of earthly care, or is carried hither and thither by the desire for swollen and vain dominion—there is within it a great, powerful, and tumultuous uproar of clamour.

But let all these things be silent: the pleasure of the flesh utterly trampled down, the unrest of earthly anxiety cast off, and even the arrogance of lofty dominion despised. Let all these things be silent in Joseph, so that now, as he rests and sleeps, all his faculties may keep the first silence. Let the phantasms of corporeal things and their likenesses likewise be silent in him. When entrance is granted to them, they too are accustomed to emit a vast roar of clamour in his inner chamber, in which that serene and quiet Lord ought to dwell—as Jeremiah complains and laments concerning this, declaring that they “gave forth their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day” (Lam. 2:7).

And now all things keep his second silence, until his third silence comes to be in heaven, which, when it is granted, lasts not a full hour but half an hour (Rev. 8:1; citation printed 7:1). Indeed, scarcely even that silence is perceived, because it is, as it were, anticipated. This silence pertains to Joseph’s third sleep, in which Joseph receives the hidden word, “the whisper of which his ear secretly receives” (Job 4:12), and is held so attentively by that word alone that, because of the sweetness of the divine voice sounding in him, he imposes silence even upon angelic utterances. [Col. 0324B–D]

### IX

The third stage of the night also seems to belong to this sleep: it is sublime contemplation, by which one reaches even to God himself. When it has run thus far that it reaches the middle, while all things then maintain the second silence in Joseph and perceive something of the third, the almighty word of the Lord comes from heaven, from the royal thrones. For inward inspiration—which without exception continually teaches concerning all things in those heavenly, blessed seats of the supreme King, that is, in those spirits above—visits the devout soul. As it strengthens that soul, it grants it, as Paul says, to “do all things in him” (Phil. 4:13); therefore this word is rightly called almighty. In this sleep the angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph to fortify him with his counsel against Herod’s cruel design.

We shall understand night as rest, for night has also been instituted for rest. Blessed Ambrose declares that God, the Creator of all things and Ruler of the heavens, clothed night for the sake of sleep, “that repose might restore relaxed limbs for the usefulness of labour.” Night has the first stage in its course when this Joseph, free and relieved from every desire for visible and sensible things, rests in the first sleep, since this stage pertains to that end. It has the middle stage when he rests in the second sleep. Something has already been said about its third stage, not because it is impossible for it to be expressed fully, but lest it be omitted altogether.

Therefore the almighty word of the Lord comes from heaven, from the royal thrones, because inward inspiration visits the devout soul. [Col. 0325A–B]

### X

And certainly, as you know, we set forth above Joseph’s threefold sleep; and if you turn over the volume of the Gospel, you will find that an angel appeared to him in dreams three times. First, he appeared, warning Joseph not to fear to take Mary as his wife when he was thinking of putting her away (Matt. 1:20), explaining the reason: “For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit.” And he added: “She shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name JESUS, for he shall save his people from their sins” (ibid.).

Second, when the time was at hand for Herod to seek the child in order to destroy him, the angel commanded Joseph to take the child and his mother, flee to Egypt, and remain there until he should tell him; nor did he conceal the reason for Joseph’s and the child’s flight or their stay there (Matt. 2:13).

But perhaps someone among you says to me: “Speak and exhort on this, for your subject requires it.” I shall do so; but after the reason for the first and the third appearance of the angel has been explained, this middle one will become more evident.

The angel appeared to him a third time when, after Herod’s death, he commanded him to go with the child and his mother into the land of Israel (Matt. 2:19–20; citation printed 19:20). And, lest we appear to have passed over any of these things, when Joseph heard that Archelaus reigned in Judaea in place of Herod his father, he feared to go there. Being warned in a dream—although no mention of an angel is made in this warning—he did not withdraw from the land of Israel, but withdrew to the regions of Galilee; and, having come, he lived in Nazareth (Matt. 2:22–23).

What do these things mean? What use is there in briefly recalling them to memory unless they are also briefly expounded for understanding? I have already told you, and you have heard, what Joseph is, what Mary is, and also what the child Jesus is. But if you wish to hear it again: Mary, betrothed to Joseph, is heavenly wisdom joined to the faithful and pious mind; and the child Jesus is the pure fruit of true salvation. [Col. 0325B–D]

### XI

How often it happens, especially at the beginning of the conversion of the soul itself, that wisdom is joined to it in some measure of knowledge, but not yet in full love: the mind, that is, already enlightened by understanding, but not yet inflamed by affection. Yet wisdom itself possesses for that soul many good things within its hidden purpose, “thinking thoughts of peace and not of affliction” concerning it (Jer. 29:11), which it will one day bestow when the soul has been fully turned toward it in love.

This is what is meant when Mary, the mother of Jesus, was betrothed to Joseph, and “before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:18). For before wisdom and the mind fully consent together in one will, wisdom preserves secretly within itself the spiritual fruit by which the mind will one day be enriched. Is not Mary found with child of the Holy Spirit before Mary and Joseph come together?

Meanwhile the mind, recognizing its own weakness, understanding the prerogative of wisdom, and being astonished at the matter in which it is tested, so that this Joseph may be a just man, giving each his due in this matter, proposes secretly to separate himself. He does not wish to cleave to wisdom in exercise through affection, though he had already approached it in natural capacity through understanding. This is Joseph’s unwillingness to expose Mary publicly, but desire to put her away secretly.

Hence it often happens that many fall back from the good which, having been enlightened, they recognized, because they understand themselves to be very and excessively weak and perceive that good to be arduous and burdensome to practise. Does not he seem to you to have represented their person when, after seeing the miracle of the fishes, he said, “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8)?
