In no dissimilar way, it seems to me, this spiritual and moral Joseph is wise—or rather unwise—when he finds Mary with child but, not knowing that what she bears is of the Holy Spirit, does not wish to expose her publicly but desires secretly to put her away (Matt. 1:20 ff.). Therefore, while he thinks upon these things, the angel must appear to him, admonishing him not to fear to take Mary as his wife, declaring that what has been born in her is of the Holy Spirit, and that she will bear him a son whose name he shall call Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:20).

All this takes place when heavenly grace visits a timid and faint-hearted mind as it is about to undertake spiritual labour and therefore proposes not to cleave to heavenly wisdom in practice but secretly to abandon it. Grace awakens it to boldness and animates it to strength, enabling it to understand how great a holiness this heavenly wisdom of which we speak will bestow upon it. For “the fruit of the Spirit is love” (Gal. 5:22); and since love “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8), Mary’s son is called Jesus from the thing itself, because he “will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). For the love of sincere charity cleanses the inward thoughts of the mind from every sin. [Col. 0326A–D]

### XII

This, then, is Joseph’s first sleep: namely, contempt for all visible and sensible things. In it, through that anointing “which teaches concerning all things” (1 John 2:27), he is taught not to shrink from practising whatever may seem laborious. But just as nocturnal fear awakens this Joseph so that, fearful of labour and ignorant of future grace, he does not wish to take Mary but to put her away secretly—until, freed from the night by the angel’s revelation, he knows in his enlightenment what she bears in her womb, and, strengthened by the angel himself, freed from sluggish fear and encouraged, recognizes that she will bear for him a son as great and such as we have described above—so he must greatly fear lest Herod seek this child once born, find him when sought, and destroy him when found.

What this means we showed in the preceding sermon. In the sermon now before us, we are explaining how provision must be made for him so that he may not be found when sought, nor destroyed when found. Therefore, appearing to Joseph, the angel admonishes him to take the child and his mother and flee into Egypt (Matt. 2:13). This occurs when, taught by the prompting of inward inspiration, the mind flees to the darkness of its own weakness—for Egypt signifies darkness—or to the hiding-place of divine judgment, or to the obscurity in which it finds itself surrounded on every side concerning the things that are to come upon it. Thus, humbled in this threefold way, it preserves the fruit of salvation which it possesses free from the plague of self-exaltation, as though it were protecting the child Jesus in Egypt from Herod’s persecution.

These are the three principal means, among others, by which the discerning mind is accustomed to keep the fruit of salvation in itself unharmed from the corruption of pride. [Col. 0327A–C]

### XIII

The first is when it fully perceives its own weakness: for example, how prone it is to vices, how feeble for virtues, and all other respects in which it sees its own corruptibility and fragility. It sets these before its eyes, so that, by considering them carefully, it may either not permit itself to be wounded by pride’s arrow or may come to this its Babylon, according to the prophet, “that it may be healed” (Jer. 51:9).

The second is when, even if it seems now to be doing something good, it utterly does not know whether it will persevere in it or not: knowing in some fashion what it is now, yet entirely not knowing what it will be shortly. It sees where it sets its foot today in its work, but cannot foresee what the day of tomorrow will bring forth for it.

The third is when, even if it does certain good things, and sees that it performed good things yesterday, with respect to the past; performs good things today, with respect to the present; and hopes that it will perform good things tomorrow, on account of its present intention regarding the future—nevertheless it does not know at all how the hidden and strict Judge examines these things or in what way he weighs them with himself. For, as Holy Scripture testifies, it knows that “the just and the wise and their works are in the hand of God,” and yet that “man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccles. 9:1; citation printed Ecclus. 9:1), but that all things are kept uncertain until the future. It also hears Paul say of himself that he is conscious of nothing against himself, but that he is not thereby justified, because the Lord is the one who judges him (1 Cor. 4:4). [Col. 0327C–D]

XIV. These are the darknesses in which he saw himself enveloped who said: “for a man whose way is hidden, and whom God has surrounded with darkness” (Job 3:24). To precisely these darknesses, the soul, instructed by inward inspiration, flees, so that it may preserve its good work unharmed from the plague of pride—like Joseph, who fled into Egypt in order to protect the child Jesus from Herod’s persecution. In a third way, that male child in the Apocalypse escaped the dragon, of whom you read that “he was caught up to God and to his throne” (Rev. 12:5). For what is it for the male child to be caught up to God and to his throne, so as to escape the dragon’s devouring, except that vigorous and strenuous action is referred to God and to his strict judgment, lest it incur the corruption of pride? Therefore let the male child be caught up to God and to his throne, so that, while he considers that “no living person shall be justified in his sight” (Ps. 142:2), you may by no means exalt yourself because of your good work, but humble yourself beneath the mighty hand of God, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVI, ALSO FOR THE FEAST DAY OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS

On the same subject as above.

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. Abraham, as a figure of the religious person, flees into Egypt to escape famine, pitching his tent between Bethel and Ai.
2. One must always tremble at the sight of one’s own iniquity, yet hope in the abundance of divine mercy.
3. Our progress in the spirit is not without failure.
4. What are the harms and remedies of pride.
5. One must withdraw from the presence of Herod and Archelaus—precursors of pride, as indicated by the etymology of their names—into Galilee, and dwell at Nazareth.
6. In Egypt Abraham does not dare call Sarai his wife, because every gift is from above.
7. It is true prudence to acknowledge a divine gift if there is any virtue in the mind.
8. Pharaoh, as a figure of those desirous of vainglory, is scourged by the Lord and humbled.
9. The iron slips from the handle for the sons of the prophets when the gift of grace is lost through a movement of pride.
10. An exhortation to imitate the little children.

I. You now see, I think, brethren, what good counsel the angel gives Joseph: that he should flee into Egypt, because Herod seeks the child in order to destroy him (Matt. 2:13). We read something bearing on this meaning in Genesis, where you have the account of that most holy man Abram—he was not yet called Abraham—when he went down into Egypt because famine had prevailed in the land (Gen. 12:10). He went down into Egypt; Joseph, however, fled into Egypt: the former to escape famine, the latter Herod. See how we pass from mysteries to mysteries, from meanings to meanings, as it pleases and insofar as it pleases the Spirit who goes before us and enlightens us. Thanks be to him.

But what then? Shall it not be necessary for us to investigate what it was not burdensome for him to set before us? Scripture says that he pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west and Ai on the east (ibid., v. 8). Who is this Abram, whose name is said to mean “exalted,” except any devout and religious person? The ardour of good desire makes such a person fruitful in bringing forth from himself a good action, as though begetting holy offspring; and rectitude of intention, in seeking to please God alone, makes him exalted.

For so long as you lack the name of Father, so long are you also among lowly things: as long as you are barren through ceasing from good works and remain below in seeking human favour. This man pitched his tent between Bethel and Ai, because every devout and religious person holds the condition of his present warfare and pilgrimage—for a tent belongs to those who are soldiers and pilgrims—between the hope conceived from contemplating divine mercy and the shame incurred by beholding his own misery. For they say that Ai means “confusion,” while Bethel is interpreted “house of God.” If this is so, what is Abraham’s pitching his tent between Bethel and Ai except that a religious man should live his life in this present warfare and pilgrimage so as now to hope in contemplation of that house not made with hands, eternal in heaven (2 Cor. 5:1), and now to tremble at the sight of his own confusion?

He also builds an altar there to the Lord, because in this condition he prepares within himself a clean heart and a right spirit in his inmost parts (Ps. 50:12), so that he may offer to almighty God those burnt offerings which the Psalmist calls “fat offerings” (Ps. 65:15).

II. But we need great discernment if we are to possess this twofold consideration fruitfully within ourselves, lest indiscriminate fear perhaps make us too timid unto despair, or hope make us too joyful unto laxity. You may know that you possess it fruitfully when you strive so to think of the Lord in his goodness that you do not neglect to be confounded within yourself by considering your own frailty; and so to tremble at the sight of your own wickedness that you strive to hope in contemplating divine mercy.

Thus, while you sing not mercy alone to the Lord, lest you become presumptuous, nor judgment alone, lest you despair, but praise him with both songs (Ps. 100:1), cast down through fear and raised up through hope, rejoicing in him with trembling and trembling before him with rejoicing, you rejoice that your wounds attain perfect healing, while you pour both wine and oil into them. Thus Abraham too pitched his tent so that Bethel lay on the west and Ai on the east. So you also, when in your inward thought you see that by your own weight you must tend toward the sunset, may nevertheless hope that you belong to the Church of the blessed. For this is Bethel: when you consider that by divine gift you are made fair by the rising of the sun of righteousness, you should fear lest, deprived of the help of grace, you plunge into the confusion of vices.

We need the great caution of discernment: when we strive to contemplate divine goodness, lest we become too disturbed when we turn the eyes of the mind toward our own wretchedness, let us immediately lift them to divine mercy; and conversely, lest we become excessively elated when we behold the serenity of divine clemency, let us at once fix the mind’s gaze upon the horror of our own confusion. Thus, with our tent fixed, it may have Bethel on the west and Ai on the east.

III. When we do this diligently, we attain great progress in holiness. For after pitching his tent in this way and likewise building an altar to the Lord, Abraham went on, journeying and advancing farther toward the south (Gen. 12:10). What is Abraham’s reaching and advancing farther south except that any devout person, whom Abram signifies, should always make greater progress in holiness and, touched by the utterance of the Holy Spirit, tend toward a religious manner of life?

Yet while one is thus preparing to rouse Leviathan (Job 3:8), spiritual progress is sometimes diminished under the pressure of temptation, and there is a falling away from holiness already attained. For while Abram thus goes on and advances southward, famine comes upon the land. Famine in the land is a lack of inward refreshment in the soul. But when Abram perceived this famine threatening him, what counsel did he find, lest he perish by that famine? What does Scripture say? “Abraham,” it says, “went down into Egypt to sojourn there” (Gen. 12:10).

Why did he go down into Egypt, when shortly before he had gone on and advanced farther south? Because famine had prevailed in the land. You need not inquire what the descent into Egypt signifies, if you remember what saving mystery Joseph’s flight into Egypt contains. The cause of Abraham’s descent was the scarcity of famine; the cause of Joseph’s flight was Herod’s cruelty. But if famine is a failure of inward grace, through what is that failure incurred except through the swelling of pride? For he who gives grace to the humble neither bestows grace on the proud when they do not have it, nor permits them to retain it when they have it (Jas. 4:6). He who said, “Every valley shall be filled,” also added, “and every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (Luke 3:17). Indeed, because Saul had ceased to be little in his own eyes, the Spirit of the Lord departed from him (1 Sam. 15:17); and to Paul was given a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet him (2 Cor. 12:7)—not because the greatness of the revelations had exalted him, but lest he should exalt himself.

IV. Therefore, when this famine is at hand, Abram goes down into Egypt, so that the inward refreshment of grace may not exalt a devout person through some swelling, but that he may humble himself by considering the threefold darkness described above; and that Joseph may flee there, lest Herod destroy the child. You see, then, how necessary Joseph is, that an angel should instruct him in sleep how to preserve the child Jesus from Herod’s persecution. For in such a perfection of purity, a person needs to be taught by inward inspiration how he may protect the fruit of salvation which he practises from the corruption of pride; since the more greatly your mind strives after purity, the heavier are the assaults it suffers from pride.

“And he was there,” it says, “until the death of Herod” (Matt. 2:15). Observe that, as long as Herod lives, Joseph does not dare leave Egypt. For I find nothing more effective either for guarding against pride or overcoming it than diligent maintenance of the aforesaid threefold consideration. But when this Herod of whom we speak has died—that is, when pride has been extinguished—an angel appears in a dream to Joseph and says: “Rise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel.” He adds the reason: “For those who sought the child’s life are dead” (ibid., v. 20).

When Herod has died, that is, when self-exaltation has been extinguished, Joseph can enter the land of Israel, so that he may see God with his mind—for that is what Israel means. He is now free to devote himself to so great a matter, because he no longer needs to fight against the movement of pride.

V. Yet he must not rashly reveal his hidden goods by an incautious confession, lest that vice of pride which is born of boasting corrupt them. This seems to me to be what is signified by the fact that Joseph, of whom we have now said much, heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judaea in place of Herod his father and was afraid to go there (ibid., v. 22). Archelaus is said to mean “recognizing lion,” and by him boasting is expressed. When boasting recognizes our secrets by hidden knowledge, it strives to devour them through the open arrogance customary to a lion.

Therefore Joseph refuses rashly to confess publicly what he sees of God in this dream, knowing that Archelaus reigns in Judaea in place of Herod his father. For, once the swelling of pride, which wishes to be feared, has been extinguished, its offspring, boasting, which wishes to be loved, holds sway in arrogant confession—which Judaea signifies. Rather, withdrawing into Galilee, he should dwell at Nazareth, saying to God: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118:18); and, not considering that he has comprehended it, even when he has finished, he should reckon himself to be beginning (Ecclus. 18:6).

For Galilee is said to mean “revelation,” and Nazareth “the tenderness of a flower.” Let him earnestly ask God to reveal what he wills, filling him with knowledge of his will; and whatever he does, let him believe that he is beginning rather than that he has ever finished, and reckon himself to have the tenderness of a flower rather than the ripeness of fruit. You see, then, that Herod’s death by no means gives Joseph full security, since he fears Archelaus, Herod’s son.

VI. Nor is the descent into Egypt, mentioned above (Gen. 12:12), without relevance: Abraham fears that, when the Egyptians see Sarai so beautiful, they will say that she is his wife and kill him. Therefore he persuaded her to say that she was his sister. And Joseph withdrew into the regions of Galilee. I beg you, do not find it burdensome if we touch briefly, at the end of this sermon, upon this exposition.

What does the truthful history say concerning these things? When he was near to entering—without doubt, Abraham into Egypt—he said to Sarai his wife: “I know that you are a beautiful woman, and that, when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘She is his wife’; and they will kill me, but preserve you. Therefore please say that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me and I may live because of your favour” (ibid.).

To pass briefly over the matter: who is this beautiful wife of Abram except prudence, whom the wise man calls his friend (Prov. 7:4), and who rules in that inward house? For Sarai is said to mean “my princess”; she also shines with spiritual beauty. The just man—for, as we have often said, he is Abram—must fear concerning her lest, seeing her beautiful and asserting that she is his wife, they kill him. This occurs when the movements of a darkened heart—these too are represented by the Egyptians—persuade us that the prudence we possess is our own, and not from the Father of lights, who willingly begot us by the word of his truth (Jas. 1:18); that prudence is not entrusted [variant: lent] and granted to us by him, and so they spiritually destroy us.

For the Egyptians’ seeing that the woman is beautiful and saying that she is Abram’s wife means that the secret movements of the heart, darkened by vanity, flatter themselves over subtle wisdom and sharpness of prudence. This is to admire beautiful Sarai and draw her toward the desire of vanity: to suppose that whatever subtlety is in the mind arises more from one’s own sharpness than from a divine gift.

VII. Yet whatever empty and frivolous thing it may be in which deceived thoughts flatter themselves, prudence herself must necessarily humble herself in all things. She knows that the person in whom she is present was spiritually begotten by him from whom she herself was infused into that person; she must not disdain to confess this. This is for Sarai, while the Egyptians praise her beauty and assert that she is Abraham’s wife, rather to affirm that she is his sister.

Brethren, this is the whole fruit of prudence implanted in a person: that in truth itself the person may see himself. In all matters wherein he is subtly discerning, let him truly humble himself and recognize that he is from God alone. Though prudence is in a person, let it deny that it is from the person, so that, the more confidently it knows itself to be from God alone, the greater an increase in discernment it may receive from him.

Does it not seem right to you that Sarai herself should be Abram’s sister? Because life is thus lived in him, and “the life of his spirit is in such things” (Isa. 38:16), his soul too lives because of this favour of hers, when she calls herself his sister in this manner. What does he mean by saying, “They will kill me and preserve you”? I think that empty movements of the heart spiritually kill a person with the sword-point of vain desire and claim wisdom for themselves. This, as you hear, is the Egyptians’ killing Abram and preserving Sarai. To prevent this, she must deny that she is Abraham’s wife and affirm that she is his sister, so that prudence, humbly beholding herself, may confess herself to be a divine gift and deny that her sharpness is human.

VIII. “The Egyptians,” it says, “saw that the woman was exceedingly beautiful; and they reported her to Pharaoh and praised her before him” (Gen. 12:14). Pharaoh means “uncovering” or “scattering,” and signifies the desire for vainglory, which vainly uncovers our hidden goods and thereby destroys them by scattering them—according to the prophet who declares that his vineyard is made a wilderness when its fig tree comes to be stripped of bark (Joel 1:7).

In a certain manner, for the Egyptians to praise the woman before Pharaoh is for dark thoughts of mind, by displaying prudence as praiseworthy, to strive to persuade the appetite that it should mingle with vainglory. When this prudence listens closely to the persistent urgings of vain thoughts, it is sometimes reduced to the power of pride through seeking human favour. Yet although vainglory thus conquers by violence, the Lord also humbles the tyranny of pride in his elect; and, once it has been humbled, he restores in them the gift of grace which had for a time been withdrawn. For “the Lord afflicted the house of Pharaoh with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram’s wife” (Gen. 12:17). And so she was restored to him.

For what is it that, once Pharaoh’s house has been afflicted, Abram’s wife who had been taken away and lost is given back to him, except that, when the dominion of pride has been humbled by the Lord, grace which the just man had lost is restored to him?

IX. We read something similar in the Fourth Book of Kings (4 Kgs. 6:5 ff.). When the sons of the prophets were cutting wood in the Jordan with Elisha, the iron of one man’s axe-head sprang from its handle and disappeared after sinking into the waters. Elisha restored the fallen iron to him by cutting off a piece of wood, after learning from the man’s cry that he had received it on loan and in what place it had fallen.

The iron accidentally springing from the handle while wood is being cut is the gift of grace vanishing from the heart, in the exercise of virtues, when a movement of pride intervenes. But when something of this sort happens to you, cry with a strong voice of the heart to him who was slain for you at the place of Calvary, declaring rather that you received it on loan than that it is from yourself or your own possession.

Then he—from whom all his disciples fled, leaving him (Matt. 26:56), and who are also his hairs (Luke 7:38), all of them likewise numbered—he, I say, that bald prophet, mighty in deed and word (Luke 24:19), when you have shown him in truthful confession the place of the loss, will, once the wood of your heart has been cut through repentance, restore the gift you had lost. All these things concern the command given to Joseph to flee into Egypt, because Herod seeks the child to destroy him. But we have drawn this out at length because it delights us to search out mystical meanings in Holy Scripture. Such length now demands its proper end.

X. Therefore retain in your memory, comparing them with your hearts, the things said to you concerning Joseph’s threefold dream and the angel’s threefold appearance. Imitate the innocence of these little children, whose memory you celebrate today with devout solemnity and solemn devotion. Be children in malice, knowing and ever recalling with a devout mind that the Lord commands that little children be allowed to come to him, declaring that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these (Mark 10:14).

Let nothing remain within you that harms, just as a little child knows no inward brooding from which to strike another through malice. Carry nothing in face or speech, have nothing in gesture or action, which gives any offence to those who behold you. And, as your father, blessed Augustine, exhorts you: “In your walking, in your standing, in all your movements, let nothing be done which offends anyone’s gaze, but only what befits your holiness.”

To possess yourselves thus and to present yourselves as such is to imitate the little children whose is the kingdom of heaven. Consider that highest Lord of majesty made himself conform to the infancy of mortals. Therefore do not be unwilling to conform yourselves to his littleness, if you desire to be conformed in heavenly glory to his exaltation. May that great and little one, high and lowly, eternal and temporal, strong and weak, Word and flesh, God and man—our Lord Jesus, who is blessed with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever—grant you to attain it. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVII, FOR THE SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

On the practice of holy religious life and the condition of our inward person.

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. Joseph and Mary are said to have marvelled at what was spoken about the child.
2. The Lord’s mother signifies the spiritual congregation, and Joseph its superior.
3. Works of virtue and exercises of perfection are like the child Jesus.
4. The special prerogative of the religious state lies in freedom and quiet, at which Mary and Joseph rightly marvel.
5. The mutual obligation of superior and subject.
6. The malicious, mocking hostility of certain secular people toward the religious state.
7. They resemble Balaam, who cursed God’s people yet wished for an end like theirs.
8. A frequent influx into the religious state from every age and rank.
9. The religious state is compared with Solomon’s kingdom.
10. It is compared with the stone cut from the mountain without hands, overthrowing the statue of worldly perversity.
11. What it is for this stone to grow into the height of a mountain.
12. What sword shall pierce Mary’s soul, and the various senses in which Scripture uses it.
13. Tribulation, God’s vengeance, the devil’s malice, and the distress of death are beneficial or harmful according to their use; they are called indifferent swords.
14. Which swords belong to the evil side and must be avoided.
15. The swords belonging to the good side and to be desired.
16. The discernment to be made among swords.

I. Blessed Luke relates to us in today’s reading of the holy Gospel that Joseph and Mary, the mother of Jesus, marvelled at the things said concerning him (Luke 2:33 ff.). And what wonder is there in this? What wonder, I say, if the hearts of Joseph and Mary were raised in admiration [variant: arose] at what they heard being said about Jesus? The angels sang glory to God in the highest and proclaimed peace on earth to people of good will. The shepherds came in haste; the Magi ran up, entered, fell down, worshipped, and offered gifts. Simeon prophesied, and Anna gave thanks. Perhaps some other occurrence of no small importance took place that could have been a cause and occasion of wonder.

Yet amid all these things blessed and blessed indeed is that mother who bore for us Jesus, about whom such great and wonderful things were spoken that she was compelled to marvel, and Joseph likewise compelled. Is this, however, anything new? Certainly not—except that what we love ardently, what we are accustomed frequently to say, affectionate habit itself and habitual affection sometimes enable us unexpectedly to utter.

II. But if you delight to hear something bearing upon morals, you know that, just as that mother is incomparably blessed and blessed indeed, so you ought to know that there is another mother, although far inferior: I mean this holy congregation which I see before me. For Mary is a certain great and radiant luminary, apparently containing in herself the mystery of this name. She too bears Jesus when she produces a saving example in good conduct.

For what is the fruit of holy religious life, practised by this holy congregation, except the child Jesus whom Mary bears? Joseph is servant, not lord, of this mother and child; he is their helper and guardian. This, I think, is what Paul, the vessel of election, says: “Not that we exercise dominion over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy” (2 Cor. 1:23). And again he says: “Your servants for Jesus’ sake” (2 Cor. 4:5).

You see, then, that Mary is the mother of Jesus, who is born from her and born in her. Do you confess that he is born from her but deny that he is born in her? Hear the angel speaking to Joseph: “That which is born in her,” he says—as though he said, “was conceived in her” (Matt. 1:20). Mary, therefore, is Jesus’ mother: mother in conception, mother in childbirth. For she conceived him incorrupt and gave birth to him unharmed.

But what of Joseph? From afar he beholds this child, who has been given him to serve and to help: to serve him as Lord, to help him as a little child. See whether this is not signified by the goats’-hair coverings which covered the curtains in the Lord’s tabernacle (Exod. 26:7) and protected them, exposed as they were to frequent winds and rains, lest the curtains should suffer any darkening of their beauty.

III. This Jesus is indeed a magnificent child, of whom such great and wonderful things are said that Joseph and Mary his mother cannot fail to marvel. This happens, dearest brethren, when your state is so ordered and so irreproachable in every respect that, as blessed Augustine admonishes you, “in walking, standing, and all your movements there is nothing which offends anyone’s gaze, but only what befits your holiness.” This happens when you walk worthily of your calling, with all humility and gentleness, with patience bearing one another in charity, carefully preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:2).

And, as the same speaker says elsewhere: “Considering one another superior to yourselves, each not regarding his own interests but those of others” (Phil. 2:3); “providing what is good not only before God, but also before all people. If possible, so far as it depends on you, keeping peace with all” (Rom. 12:17). When these and countless other things of this kind are said of your Jesus—for the state of perfection which your congregation practises fruitfully is Jesus, the child born from his mother Mary—when such a report of him is spread abroad, Joseph and Mary must marvel at it.

Nor do I regret, whatever anyone may mutter, that I have said that the fruitful state of a holy congregation is signified by the Son of Mary, when I consider its admirable prerogative.

IV. For what state in this life is freer or quieter than that of those who live sincerely in a cloister? Not the state of kings, pontiffs, princes, or indeed any persons whatever in high position can exceed this state in this life—or, I will not say exceed it, but cannot even be compared with it in any respect. It may perhaps be higher in power, but not freer in quiet. O free and quiet state of cloistered persons! They hope for nothing and fear nothing; content with so great a moderation, made poor by a certain abundant poverty and enriched by scanty abundance, they can lose no old possession, since they are known to be as having nothing, and can acquire no new possession, since they are known to possess all things (2 Cor. 6:10).

These and other things of this kind are said of Jesus, at which Joseph and Mary his mother marvel. Does not Mary marvel at what is said of Jesus when this common and holy congregation, in each one of you, is astonished at the many great goods which the Spirit whispers from above into the ear of the mind concerning humility, hearing far more and greater things concerning each companion than it sees in itself? Joseph similarly marvels when he who stands beside individuals in the care of guarding them judges the condition of each one safer than his own—the condition of the one who guards safer than that of the guardian. To state it briefly, this is nothing other than what we cited above from the Apostle: “Considering one another superior to yourselves.”

V. “And Simeon blessed them,” it says (Luke 2:34). Whom did he bless? Without doubt Mary and Joseph. Do you think that Simeon’s blessing of Mary and Joseph confirms the virtue of obedience in the community and its guardian? For Simeon signifies obedience. Yet surely he knows that the community ought to obey its guardian; perhaps he does not know that obedience should also belong to the guardian himself. If you have not known it until now, know it at least now: in a certain sense, the guardian ought to obey his community.

If you say that he need not always obey it according to its will, I do not dispute it, provided you grant that he must never fail to obey its necessity [variant: that he ought sometimes to obey]. The community and its guardian are bound together by a great and very strong bond, by which each is strongly constrained by a reciprocal obligation: the guardian, always and everywhere, insofar as prudence knows and ability shows possible, to preside without pride; the community, to be subject without misery; the guardian to govern without the swelling of self-exaltation; the community to be governed without the complaint of murmuring; the guardian to provide diligently for what is useful; the community to obey promptly in humility; finally, the guardian to go before in all holiness of deed and word, while the community follows after him as an investigator, pondering his good ways and standing in his paths (Ecclus. 14:23).

I think this is the blessing by which Simeon blessed Mary and Joseph, whose meanings—the community and its guardian—are thus joined to one another, so that to separate them would be no different from severing head and body from each other.

VI. After these words there are others which Simeon is found to have spoken not to Joseph himself but only to Mary the mother: “Behold,” he says, “this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke 2:24). Those who know languages, and who are granted interpretation of speech, say that Israel means “vision of God.” Whoever sees God sees Jesus also, for Jesus is God. I have already told you, and you have heard, who this moral Jesus of whom we speak is. If you wish to hear it again, he is the fruitful work of your salvation which, in accordance with the tenor of your profession, you practise tirelessly.

If this is so, who are the many who see Jesus, for whose fall he is set and as a sign opposed? Perhaps they are those who, though recognizing upon seeing it our fruitful state—for it is Jesus—nevertheless do not merely fail to love it but, through hatred, criticize it and thus fall. They neither attain it by imitation nor cease to persecute it by detraction. They perceive that what they see among you is a sign of salvation; but while they not only fail humbly to embrace it, but even proudly criticize it, they altogether oppose it.

Certainly there are many today in Israel, among those who see God—I mean these malicious and proud secular people—for whom this Jesus is set for falling and as a sign opposed, while they pursue by criticism or contempt the good which they behold among you. Or perhaps they at least reverence it by praise only on the surface, yet never attain it through imitation. Or, as we frequently see happen, though for a time they believe and magnify its renown, they do not cease in the time of temptation to diminish it.

VII. He seems to belong to their number who, having been led and hired to curse the people, praised that people so highly that he wished his soul to die their death and his latter end to be like theirs (Num. 23:10). Yet when the time of compunction had passed, he was not ashamed to teach Balak to place a stumbling block before them, so that they might eat and commit fornication (Rev. 2:14).

Therefore be watchful against false brethren if they secretly enter to spy out your freedom, which you have in Christ Jesus, in order to reduce you to bondage (Gal. 2:4), knowing that there are many in Israel for whom our Jesus is set for falling and as a sign opposed. But the Lord has left many for himself in Israel; and may those who remain be removed from those just mentioned, who are also indeed in Israel—that is, seeing God—but falling and opposing.

The Lord, I say, has left many for himself in Israel, for whose resurrection this Jesus is set. These are those many of whom the Lord says: “Many shall come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8:11).

VIII. We certainly see this occurring daily: people hasten to this your state—for it is a kind of kingdom of heaven in which Mary and Joseph are found—and come to be refreshed there spiritually. Many come from their first age: this is the east, like that first morning when labourers are hired and led into the vineyard. Many come in old age: this is the west, like the eleventh hour when those who stood idle all day are sent into the vineyard (Matt. 20:1 ff.).

They have leaders at this banquet, and many obedient companions, whom Abraham signifies; some who hope, whom Isaac indicates; and others who devote themselves to overthrowing vices, whom Jacob signifies. For these, Jesus seems to be set not for falling but for resurrection; not as a sign opposed, but as one obeyed. Great indeed, and truly great, is this Jesus, of whom such great and wonderful things are said that not only Mary and Joseph, who are nearer, are compelled to enter, but many are invited from east and west—like the woman who, upon hearing Solomon’s fame, left her country and her people and did not shrink from coming to him even from the ends of the earth (3 Kgs. 10:1).

IX. And behold a great mystery: after she came, that woman found Solomon great indeed and exceedingly noble. She declared that his wisdom in understanding and his works in accomplishment were greater than the report she had heard. What then? Is not your most peaceful state a certain peaceful king? For Solomon too seems to signify this. His fame is spread so widely that the aforementioned woman hastens to him. Thus, when there is great wonder at what is said of Jesus, many run to him from east and west, since he is set for the resurrection of many.

“Let the north give, and let not the south withhold” (Isa. 43:6). Let young men who fight bravely against the north come to him from every direction; let virgins, radiant in the purity of the south, come; and let old people in the west come with younger people in the east. Behold Jesus, whom Solomon signifies, inviting the aforesaid queen to himself by the fragrance of his greatness. Behold also Jesus, signified by that stone which destroys the terrible and towering statue and later grew into so great a mountain that it filled the whole earth (Dan. 2:35).

X. Is not your firm stone a strong state? For that state, being mature through true wisdom, resonant through luminous preaching, robust through vigorous action, rooted through steadfast perseverance, and humbled through knowledge of its own frailty, destroys by these five virtues the five evils of the worldly state. [Col. 0338D] For by the first it abolishes the glitter of empty and deceptive wisdom, which is foolishness with God (1 Cor. 3:19)—that is, gold. By the second, the sheen of pompous eloquence—that is, silver. By the third, the strength of exalted might—understand this as bronze. By the fourth, the stubbornness of rebellious obstinacy—that is, iron. By the fifth, the mud of lust—and this is clay. When this victory has been accomplished, this stone becomes a great mountain filling the whole earth, so that the city set upon it can no longer be hidden (Matt. 5:14); and Joseph and Mary, the mother of Jesus, are compelled greatly to marvel at the things said of him, when he has been set for the resurrection of many in Israel.

XI. But this stone, which in Daniel [Col. 0339A] becomes a great mountain and fills the whole earth, and in the Gospel sustains the city set upon it—as he who believes in him, according to Peter’s saying, shall not be put to shame (1 Pet. 2:6), because Jesus has been set for the resurrection of many in Israel—will likewise be, for those who do not believe, a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to those who stumble at the word, because that same Jesus has been set for the resurrection of many in Israel and as a sign that is opposed (Luke 2:34). “And a sword,” he says, “shall pierce your own soul also” (ibid., 35). What is this sword? Whatever it may be that is to be understood by it, I think it must here be understood in a favorable sense, because it is the sword of Jesus. For Jesus is plainly good, and therefore his sword must be good. “A sword,” he says, “shall pierce your own soul also.” [Col. 0339B] What, then, is the sword of Jesus? What, I ask, is the sword of Jesus that pierces Mary’s soul? For who Jesus is, and who Mary his mother is, has been stated above not once, nor twice, but many times; and I do not think it now needs repeating.

XII. But let us inquire what this sword of Jesus is. In Holy Scripture—to which, for the recognition of truth, we must always return, as to a fountain for water—I find that there is a good sword, and therefore one worthy to pierce Mary’s soul, because it belongs to Jesus. I also find an evil sword, which consequently does not belong to Jesus, and therefore it follows that it does not touch Mary’s soul. I find also a sword [Col. 0339C] that may be understood indifferently, because, according to the merit of those who use it, it can sometimes be an occasion of good and sometimes of evil. There is indeed a sword to be understood indifferently: namely, temporal tribulation. Of this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let him sell his cloak and buy himself a sword” (Luke 22:36). It is as though he commanded that one who desires to please God should cast off worldly garments and, in their place, should not refuse temporary tribulation, borrowed for his love.

There is another sword, the vengeance of God, concerning which the Song of Deuteronomy says: “My sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. 32:42). That is: my vengeance shall destroy the carnal. Take yet another: “He who made him,” the Lord says to Job concerning the devil, “has applied his sword” (Job 40:44). For God, who created him, restrains his malice. Thus, in this passage [Col. 0339D] the sword of Behemoth is his malice. I shall show you yet a fourth sword. The name of this sword is death, by which all without exception are struck down; for we all die (2 Sam. 14:14). It is that sword of which we read in Genesis concerning our father Abraham: that he carried fire and a sword in his hands (Gen. 22:6), because the burning ardor of Christ’s Passion and the sharpness of his death were in the Father’s power. Perhaps there are still others, but these are what occur to me for the moment.

XIII. I think we may understand each of these indifferently, because one who is struck by them sometimes advances toward goodness, but sometimes declines into evil. By the sword some fall into the frenzy of madness, while others rise to the strength of patience. So too, the sword of divine vengeance makes and chastens some, while it strikes others and does not correct them though hardened. Such, I think, were those of whom the prophet, addressing the Lord, says: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to receive correction” (Jer. 5:3). Likewise, the devil’s malice trains some for the crown of blessedness, but incites others more and more to the fault of iniquity, so that afterward, and before long, it may drag them with itself as companions into the punishment of condemnation. You have examples of both before your eyes. For it was the devil’s malice by which he moved [variant: *which moved*] the Lord against Job, that he might afflict him without cause (Job 2:3), and by which he entered into Judas’s heart that he might betray Christ (John 22:3 [citation as printed; corrupt]). What the end of each was, no one fails to know.

And what shall we say of the sword of death? [Col. 0340B] Does it not, although it strikes all, cut some down in order to plant them in life, but others in order to bury them in death? “It came to pass,” he says, “that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom; but the rich man also died and was buried in hell” (Luke 16:22)—may you never go there. Both, then, were cut down by one and the same sword, yet after being cut down they received different places. Therefore I would call these swords indifferent, and would judge none of them to be that which ought properly and spiritually to pierce the soul of this Mary of whom we speak, since each is no less an occasion of evil than of good.

XIV. But I shall show you evil swords—not merely two [Col. 0340C] or three, but several—none of which is the sword of Jesus, and therefore none worthy to pierce Mary’s soul. Saint David says of one sword—which indeed belongs to the Lord, but with which he may not strike my soul—“Unless you are converted, he will brandish his sword” (Ps. 7:13). That is, unless you cease from sins, he will show you his wrath. The same man speaks of the resistance of the wicked, which is a sword: “Sinners have drawn the sword” (Ps. 36:14); that is, sinners have exercised resistance.

See also in the same David another evil sword: namely, the speech of detractors. For he says of the sons of men that “their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5), because the speech of those who imitate carnal persons is full of biting detraction. [Col. 0340D] He also speaks of another, not inferior in this evil, which we call evil persuasion: “Deliver me from the malicious sword” (Ps. 143:10). It is as though he prayed God to rescue him from deadly persuasion.

A certain evil sword is also found in Ezekiel, and this is sin. It is read thus: “If he sees the sword and does not sound the trumpet” (Ezek. 33:6). He was speaking of the watchman. May God turn from us what follows, who appear to be his watchmen. For a preacher should know himself worthy of condemnation if, when he sees sin reigning, he ceases from teaching. The Lord, speaking to his holy servant Job, likewise calls that condemned man whom Paul calls “the man of sin” and “the son of perdition” (2 Thess. 2:3) a sword: [Col. 0341A] “When the sword takes hold of him” (Job 41:17). Without doubt he means Behemoth; for when Antichrist has received the devil into himself, there will be grievous tribulation in the world.

Moreover, the final judgment at the end of the world is a kind of sword, and indeed a very sharp one, as the Lord says in the Song of Deuteronomy: “If I sharpen my sword as lightning” (Deut. 32:41), that is, if I manifest my judgment in wrath. Eternal condemnation too is a sword, as holy Job says: “If his children are multiplied”—undoubtedly the children of an impious man—“they shall be for the sword” (Job 27:14). For however many imitators the impious man has, all shall be condemned.

XV. Which of these swords do you declare good? Certainly none; and therefore they do not belong to Jesus. [Col. 0341B] We set divine wrath first and eternal condemnation last. But one of you says to me: “How long will you keep us in suspense? Why do you bring us so many swords and admit that none of them belongs to Jesus? Give us one that belongs to Jesus and is worthy to pierce Mary’s soul.” I shall seek one in Holy Scripture, and when I find it I shall bring it forward to you.

Yet, I think, we have not set forth this diversity of swords without profit, so that you may know which swords are good, which evil, and which must be understood indifferently. But, you say, you have already shown some that are indifferent, and you have shown the evil ones; it remains for you to bring us some good ones. And this we shall do, if God permits. If you wish to have a good sword, [Col. 0341C] seek it from Paul, who says: “Take up the sword of the Spirit” (Eph. 6:17)—that is, exercise spiritual preaching. For he made known what he meant there by “sword,” adding: “which is the word of God” (ibid.). But he who said this concerning the sword of the word elsewhere also speaks of the sword of intellect, where he declares that “the word of God is more penetrating than any two-edged sword” (Heb. 4:12), that is, more discerning than any sharp intellect.

The Lord himself also seems in the Gospel to mention a good sword, which, unless I am mistaken, is separation, when he says: “I have not come to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34), that is, separation. For, to show that this was what he intended to signify, he added: “For I have come to separate a son against his father” (ibid., 35). Another sword, and a most health-giving one, is the word of rebuke, by which he strikes within in mercy. Of this Isaiah says: “The sword shall devour you” (Isa. 1:20), that is, rebuke shall reprove you. This is that sword of which we read so often in the Old Testament in the battles of the saints: that they “struck their adversaries with the edge of the sword” (Isa. 21:7), that is, touched them with the voice of rebuking speech.

XVI. Behold, we have drawn forth before you evil swords and good swords, so that you may know which you ought to avoid and by which you ought to desire to be struck. The evil swords which you had above belong to those of whom Isaiah says: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares” (Isa. 2:4): that is, they shall change their evils into fruitful advantages. But these good swords appear to me to belong to those of whom the Psalmist says: “Two-edged swords are in their hands” (Ps. 149:6), because words are fulfilled in the deeds of the saints. But how the sword of Jesus pierces Mary’s soul, we have no time at present to show, since we have already lingered some while in drawing forth these swords. I have proposed, however, to undertake this in the following sermon, as the Lord may deign to reveal it to us—he who is God above all, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVIII. ON THE SAME SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD. On the inward state of our heart.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. A threefold classification of spiritual swords, compared with one another.  
2. The sword is mystically said to have pierced Mary’s soul in four ways.  
3. The passage of these swords through the soul is exceedingly health-giving.  
4. How many thoughts are disclosed by the stroke of the sword, which is the word of God.  
5. An eightfold fruit is drawn from the preached word.  
6. The sword of intellect pierces the soul through comprehension of the length, breadth, depth, and height of God.  
7. How the sword of separation and rebuke pierces the soul.  
8. In monasteries many seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ: the distinction between insincere and upright religious persons.  
9. Mary is understood tropologically as illumination, reason; Joseph as humble conscience.  
10. The guardianship of humility is necessary for virtue’s increase.  
11. Humility of mind acquires and preserves spiritual grace.  
12. Man is raised into confidence of obtaining eternal reward.  
13. God will reward the good that he performs through a human being as though that person possessed from himself whatever good he does.  
14. The inward visitation of grace is prefigured by Simeon blessing; its power and present efficacy.  
15. There is no fruit of holiness that is not attended by the guardianship of humility.  
16. Pride is the ruin of the entire spiritual edifice; rectitude of intention is the indicator of a good work.  
17. The fervor of good desire is the two-edged sword of Jesus, avoiding harmful things and performing good ones.  
18. God’s grace perfects our understanding and will.

I. “And a sword,” holy Simeon says to Mary, “shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2:35). Beloved brothers in the Lord, in the preceding sermon we brought forward several swords before you, so that you might know which are good and which are evil, and which are to be understood indifferently. But that you may retain their distinction more firmly in memory, behold, as we presented them singly, so we now set them before you briefly.

There is a sword to be understood indifferently: first, temporal tribulation; second, worldly persecution, of which we touched on nothing when we treated the others, because it did not then occur to us. The second sword, then, that is understood indifferently is the persecutor, of whom holy David says: “Shield, sword, and war” (Ps. 75:4)—supply, “he broke”; because the Lord in his Church removes both the fault of excuse, the sharpness of persecution, and the enemy’s assault. We therefore place this sword among those understood indifferently, because it is uncertain whether persecution proves a person or slays him.

The third is God’s vengeance; the fourth, the devil’s malice; the fifth, death itself. An evil sword, however, is: first, God’s wrath; second, the resistance of rebels; [Col. 0343A] third, the bite of detractors; fourth, the persuasion of deceivers; fifth, sin; sixth, Antichrist; seventh, the final judgment; eighth, eternal condemnation. All these are evil swords. But there is a good sword: first, the word; second, sharpness of intellect; third, separation; fourth, rebuke. Every one of these swords is a sword of Jesus.

II. Therefore it does not seem unreasonable to me if you say that each of them pierces Mary’s soul. For, to draw out each one briefly: did not the sword of the word pierce her soul when she said, “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5:6)? Did not he too perceive that the sword of intellect ought to pierce the soul, who said: [Col. 0343B] “Prick the heart and bring forth understanding” (Ecclus. 22:24)? And what shall we say about the sword of separation? Does it not pierce the soul in those who “say to their father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to their brothers, ‘I do not recognize you’; and they did not acknowledge their sons” (Deut. 33:9), not even rendering the service of burial to their father, that they might hasten to proclaim the word of God?

As for the sword of rebuke, we know that it is altogether good and beneficial for it to pierce the soul. For holy David desires that “the righteous man may correct me in mercy and rebuke me,” but that “the oil of the sinner may not enrich my head” (Ps. 140:5). Let this fourfold sword of your Son, then, pierce your soul, O Mary, so that you, O holy congregation—for you are Mary—may be instructed by the word, sharpened by intellect, made perfect by separation, and humbled by rebuke. Truly these several swords belong, O Mary, to your Jesus, so that of each of them it may be said to you: “And a sword shall pierce your own soul also.” Truly, I say, they belong to Jesus, to this wholesome state of yours, from which such great benefit comes to you.

III. For that it is beneficial for the sword of the word to pierce your soul has been made certain to you by him who, being supreme Truth, cannot be deceived because he knows all things, and does not will to deceive because he loves every good thing; he declares blessed those “who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11:48). The same must be said of intellect. Think likewise concerning separation: “Man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 36:7). [Col. 0343D] “And everyone who has left house, or father, or mother, or brothers, or sisters, or wife, or lands for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29).

Rebuke also confers something great upon us, something truly great; for, as Solomon says, “whom the Lord loves, he corrects” (Prov. 3:12). Another likewise says: “Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects” (Job 5:17). Hence he adds in admonition: “Therefore do not reject the rebuke of the Lord, for he wounds and heals; he strikes, and his hands shall heal” (ibid., 18). But let it be so: let us now grant what must surely be granted—that it is beneficial for the sword of Jesus to pierce Mary’s soul. But what did Simeon add after this, and for what purpose did he say that the sword of Jesus would pierce Mary’s soul? “That thoughts may be revealed out of many hearts” (Luke 2:35). See whether this is not true. See it, I say; but you will never see it better than in your own experience.

IV. For when the sword of the word pierces the soul, who is sufficient not merely to recount, but even to comprehend, how many thoughts, or what sorts of thoughts, are revealed? Thoughts are indeed revealed in many ways when the sword of the word pierces the soul, according as that sword multiplies or varies its stroke. For it frequently pierces the soul by striking in diverse ways. First, examples of the saints are narrated in its stroke, and history pierces the soul. Second, the truth of faith is revealed, and allegory touches it. Third, morals are instructed, and tropology strikes it. Fourth, heavenly joys are revealed, and anagogy sweetly wounds it.

Consider now what thoughts are thus disclosed when the sword of the word pierces the soul. See whether, in history’s touch, thoughts are not revealed that are stirred to imitate holiness; in allegory, thoughts enlightened to recognize truth; in tropology, thoughts inflamed with love of virtue; and in anagogy, thoughts melted into longing for heavenly blessedness. If you diligently endeavor to consider how many things the word of God sets before us in its exhortation, I think you will then not doubt that thoughts are revealed when its sword has pierced the soul. And behold, eight occur to us; [Col. 0344C] but, if you wish, seek more when you have leisure. These are: prohibition, command, permission, persuasion, rebuke, consolation, threat, and promise.

V. I say that when the word of God—its sword—pierces the soul, it either prohibits, commands, permits, persuades, rebukes, consoles, threatens, or promises. It prohibits evils, commands good things, permits intermediate things, persuades toward perfection, rebukes the restless, consoles the faint-hearted, threatens the punishments of hell, and promises the joys of the kingdom. Its prohibitions are at the bottom; its commands, on the slope; its permissions, on the plain; its persuasions, at the summit: at the bottom, the sphere of vices; on the slope, that of commandments; on the plain, that of permitted things; at the summit, that of counsels.

Its rebukes pertain to wine, its consolations to oil, its threats to old things, and its promises to new things. The merciful Samaritan claims the first two for himself (Luke 10:33); the scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven claims the second two (Matt. 13:52). Does not this sword, when it pierces the soul in these and many other ways, reveal thoughts out of many hearts? For from prohibition are revealed thoughts tending toward hatred of wickedness; from command, toward the performance of uprightness; from permission, toward liberty of one’s own, yet lawful, will; from persuasion, toward desire for perfection; from rebuke, toward the virtue of humility; from consolation, toward the sweetness of rejoicing; from threat, toward the terror of fear; and from promise [Col. 0345A] toward the ardor of love.

Behold the sword of Jesus, the two-edged sword. For from the mouth of him who in the Apocalypse is called the Word of God—“he sat upon a white horse” (Rev. 19:11), because “the Word became flesh”—from his mouth, it says, “a sword sharp on both sides proceeds, that with it he may strike the nations” (ibid., 15): striking the wicked terribly because of their vices, and sweetly wounding the good because of their virtues. This two-edged sword is called in the same Apocalypse, and in Ezekiel, a book written within and without (Ezek. 2:9). There indeed, in the mouth of the one devouring it, it became sweet as honey, but made his belly bitter (Rev. 10:9); here it contains both a song for sweetness and lamentations and woes for bitterness (Ezek. 2:9). From this, I think, you can infer—and you can learn still better every day from your own experience—that, when this first sword pierces the soul, thoughts are revealed.

VI. What shall I say of the sword of intellect? Do we not often experience of it too that, the more deeply it pierces the soul, thoughts succeed one another in varied ways and the mind is carried in different directions, as someone says? For very often, when rooted and grounded in it, we comprehend with all the saints “what is the length and breadth and height and depth” (Eph. 3:18), thoughts are certainly revealed out of our hearts. Does not the comprehension of length, which is eternity, reveal in us thoughts of perseverance because of the promises? Does not the comprehension of breadth, which is charity, [Col. 0345C] reveal in us thoughts of love because of benefits? Does not the comprehension of depth, which is wisdom, reveal in us thoughts of fear because of judgments?

But because all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10); because we have heard these two things, namely power and mercy (Ps. 61:12–13); because, finally, the Psalmist declares that he sings to the Lord “mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100:1): thoughts of love, sweetly consoling, are revealed when this sword pierces the soul and comprehends the length of eternity, which never fails, and the breadth of charity, which hates none of the things it has made. Thoughts of fear are also revealed when the same sword pierces the soul and comprehends the height of majesty, which is above all things and has with it a hand almighty, and the depth of wisdom, which is beneath all things and lacks no eye that sees all things. You see, then, that thoughts come to be revealed when this sword too pierces the soul.

VII. There are very many other ways in which thoughts are revealed when this sword pierces the soul; we have no time at present to demonstrate them. But if you wish to know, while we run briefly through the matter because we have already lingered some time over it, what thoughts are revealed when the sword of separation and rebuke pierces the soul, receive this answer: perfect humility of mind and the virtue of true charity. For complete and perfect contempt in the soul for all visible things, and full separation of affection even from one’s relatives, are a great occasion and cause for acquiring and retaining the charity of inward peace.

Likewise, salutary rebuke is a trench around a tree; when manure is thrown at its root, its barrenness is immediately driven away and it becomes fruitful (Luke 13:8). Thus it escapes that shameful reproach, “Why does it occupy the ground?” and does not incur that dreadful sentence, “Cut it down” (ibid., 7). You now see, I think, why thoughts come to be revealed when the sword of Jesus pierces Mary’s soul.

VIII. “That thoughts may be revealed out of many hearts” (Luke 2:35). Why “out of many,” rather than all? Because, as the Apostle says, “faith is not for all” (2 Thess. 3:2). This is what we are accustomed to lament: that when the sword of Jesus pierces Mary’s soul, thoughts are not revealed out of every heart. For when the word of preaching, received obediently, adorns and beautifies the perfect and inward men of the cenobitic congregation; when the surpassing virtue of Christ’s charity sharpens their subtle intellect (Eph. 3:19); when contempt for all visible things and even for their own relatives is found sublimely among them; when salutary rebuke is humbly accepted—yet not all belonging to that congregation, but many, are enriched by the fruits of these goods, because not all who live in it seek only the things that are Christ’s.

And thus this, as it were, fourfold sword of Jesus, of which we have now said much, pierces Mary’s soul; but thoughts are not revealed from many hearts. For not all in monasteries receive the implanted word that is able to save their souls (Jas. 1:21). But there are many in whom it grows and bears fruit, and many in whom the word of God finds no room. Likewise, many approach the deep heart so that God may be exalted (Ps. 63:8), but many grow languid through sloth, so that, while their souls sleep from weariness, enemies seeing them mock their sabbaths (Lam. 1:7).

Likewise, there are many whom no visible thing, nor even attachment to relatives, draws back from the path of their undertaken purpose. And if at times the cows carrying the ark on a cart low among them, nevertheless they always go forward and never turn to the right through pride amid prosperity, nor to the left through impatience amid adversity, until they reach Beth-shemesh (1 Sam. 6:12) and stand in that field of Joshua the Beth-shemite, full of blessing, which the Lord does not cease to bless (ibid., 18). But many, to say it briefly, are disposed in every way contrary to this. They are those who always return as they walk, not after the manner of those heavenly living creatures which “went and returned” (Ezek. 1:14), but in the likeness of those carnal and unbelieving persons who “returned in their hearts to Egypt” (Num. 14:4). There are also many who have ears that gladly hear rebukes of life; nevertheless, not a few trouble us, of whose evil heart, when we sing songs, we recognize that it is “vinegar upon nitre” (Prov. 25:20). [Col. 0347A]

IX. See, then, and consider that Simeon did not without reason assert that thoughts are revealed not out of all hearts but out of many when the sword of Jesus pierces Mary’s soul. For the Lord himself chose twelve, and one of them was a devil (John 6:7); and seven deacons were chosen by the apostles (Acts 6:5), and one became the author and inventor of foul and fetid error. Take this as the present meaning of these words of the holy Gospel. Another interpretation may indeed be understood in them, somewhat subtler and deeper still; and I do not wish to defraud you of it. Behold, receive it.

Mary is skilled reason; Joseph, however, is humble conscience. Mary is a star, because it belongs to reason, as people sail amid the hidden movements of thoughts in the depth of our inward heart, to make provision lest, dashed upon the rocks of unlawful consent, they suffer the shipwreck of wicked defilement. [Col. 0347B] Joseph is called “increase,” because the more conscience is humbled, the more it is increased by a richer gift of inward grace, according to the saying: “Every valley shall be filled” (Luke 3:5). Holy David also says that “the valleys shall abound with grain” (Ps. 64:14). Through the prophet Isaiah likewise: “Upon whom,” says the Lord, “shall my Spirit rest, if not upon one humble and quiet and trembling at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Mary is the mother of Jesus; reason is the begetter of a good purpose. Reason conceives a purpose of holiness; it conceives and bears Jesus himself. It conceives the disposition in the will and bears it into conduct through effect. Joseph is the foster-father of this Jesus and also his guardian: so that the good and fruitful purpose of holiness—which the skilled subtlety of reason first seeks from God, the giver of all good things, then receives when the will spreads open its bosom, and finally manifests in action by presenting the members of the body as weapons of righteousness to God (Rom. 6:19)—may be nourished and advanced to perfection by the humility of a simple conscience, and guarded, protected, and defended from every harmful diminution that the vice of self-exaltation commonly brings.

X. Thus the intellect seeks the purpose of holiness, the affection receives it, and its effect brings it before the public. [Col. 0347D] But it immediately suffers the loss of failure unless the care of true humility guards it with all diligence. Do you see that it was not without reason that Jesus wished to have not only a mother from whom he might be born, but also a foster-father by whom he might be guarded? Thus you too may know that the spiritual goods you gather in yourself profit you nothing unless you preserve them by diligent and watchful circumspection.

This seems to be the point of your reading that God placed man in paradise “to work it and keep it” (Gen. 2:15). God places you in paradise when, freely bestowing upon you a delightful abundance of spiritual graces, he causes you to rest in secure tranquillity and tranquil security. But see that you both work and keep this paradise of yours. Work it through the strength of courage; keep it through the protection of circumspection. Work diligently, then; keep cautiously. Moreover, humility of conscience is the safeguard of this keeping. Work, therefore, that you may vigorously preserve spiritual virtues; beware lest you carelessly lose what you have acquired.

XI. I tell you, my friends: believe one who has experienced it. Nothing can be more effective for a person in acquiring spiritual grace before it is given, or in retaining and increasing it after it has been given, than always to be humble in his own eyes, always fearful and watchful, always timid and solicitous, always conscious that he should “not think proudly, but fear” (Rom. 11:20), and always accuse himself in all things. Humble conscience, therefore, is Joseph, who is called “increase”: [Col. 0348B] for the greater the humility possessed in the mind, the more grace increases in it; and “to him who has, shall be given, and he shall abound.”

O what an abundance of spiritual gifts is found with Mary and Joseph! What overflowing fullness of spiritual graces! She rejoices to be the undefiled mother of Jesus, and he his vigilant guardian; together they conceive and bear the fruitful purpose of holiness through a devout inquiry of reason, and nurture and preserve this prerogative of Jesus—that is, the excellence of the spiritual purpose—through true humility of conscience.

XII. Certainly, the blessed confidence of hope raises a person immeasurably in expectation of his great future reward, and promises what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,” which it declares is to be given. [Col. 0348C] In a cry of silence and a clamorous silence is heard the voice of the Spirit crying, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15). Certain things are heard to which reason scarcely dares to lend its eye, and conscience scarcely dares to grant assent; so that Joseph and Mary marvel beyond measure at the things said of him.

Is it not exceedingly wonderful that, though all nations are as though they were not before him and are reckoned by him as nothing and emptiness (Dan. 4:32), the heart should dare to affirm that a human being is to be counted among the children of God and that his lot is among the saints (Wis. 5:5)—that is, that conscience and faith, charity and hope, dare to affirm it? It is wonderful indeed, yet in a sense not wonderful. For what does the heart not dare, if it is pure; conscience, if good; faith, if unfeigned; charity, if perfect; hope, if certain? It is said, therefore, that for something so small, so much will be brought forth that it cannot even be estimated by others: something so great and so abundant in every respect in exchange for what is almost nothing—future things for present ones, heavenly things for earthly, eternal things for transitory.

XIII. These are the things said of Jesus, so that Joseph and Mary his mother cannot but marvel at them, and rightly so. A stupor of great amazement arises in reason: this is Mary. A fear of great trembling arises in conscience: this is Joseph. Reason itself is astonished at what it sees; conscience trembles at what it feels. So great are the things that this inward and true report spreads concerning Jesus that Joseph and Mary his mother marvel at them.

A human being is not sufficient to think anything from himself, as from himself (2 Cor. 3:5), much less to do anything. Yet the report spreads abroad, and hope’s certainty proclaims in the marketplace of the mind that God will so reward what he does through a human being as though the person possessed from himself whatever good he does. Hope promises and pledges that poverty shall possess the kingdom of heaven; meekness shall possess the earth; temporal mourning shall receive everlasting consolation; hunger and thirst, satisfaction; mercy shall obtain mercy; purity of heart, the vision of the Creator; peacemakers shall be honored with the name of sons of God; endurance of persecution shall inherit the kingdom of heaven. These things, and many others of this kind, are so great and such that, while hope presumes concerning them [variant: *while both hope … concerning them*], reason is dazzled and conscience trembles; Joseph and Mary, the mother of Jesus, marvel at the things said of him.

XIV. But it is altogether necessary that the frequent visitation of inward grace should bring to completion and confirmation the ineffable greatness of this blessedness with which Mary the mother of Jesus and Joseph are enriched: not only because they have that same Jesus with them, but because they marvel at the things said concerning him. For thus Almighty God is accustomed to act in his chosen ones: not only does he confer spiritual goods upon them, but he preserves the gifts bestowed by the frequent visitation of his grace. Did not he experience such treatment in himself who said, “You have granted me life and mercy, and your visitation has guarded my spirit” (Job 10:12)? And indeed in such gifts—namely, life and mercy—the life of a righteous man is spirit. But unless visitation guards the life and mercy given, neither avails, because neither remains. And this is what is meant here: “And Simeon blessed them” (Luke 2:34). Simeon is the inward visitation, who is called obedient; indeed, inward visitation is called obedient because it makes obedient those into whom it pours itself, in accordance with the statement that the Spirit intercedes for us with unutterable groanings (Rom. 8:26), since those whom he fills he consequently also makes petitioners.

For what good can a human being not merely do, but even will, if incentive is lacking? Again, what is there that his mind does not dare to conceive in affection, and that his body does not fear to undertake in effect, if he has the visitation of inward grace both urging him to will and assisting him to accomplish? If you doubt either point, ask Paul, and you will find both in him. For he is the one who declares himself not sufficient to think anything from himself, as from himself (2 Cor. 3:5), and able to do all things in him who strengthens him (Phil. 4:13). You see, then, Paul as a creeping little worm in himself, but in God a mighty athlete: when he says that he cannot, I do not say perform, but cannot even think anything from himself as from himself; and that he can do not merely certain things, but all things in him who strengthens him. Rightly, therefore, is the visitation of inward grace called Simeon, which works in the human being toward whom, and in whom, it deigns to work both to will and to accomplish according to its good pleasure (Phil. 2:13), so that, when it is present, he confidently says: “I am ready and am not disturbed, to keep your commandments” (Ps. 118:60). And again: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make psalmody” (Ps. 107:2).

This is he who confirms the bright reason and humble conscience—in the great blessedness of hope, in which the former rejoices with trembling and the latter with wonder—in a stable and firm resolve of holiness. Understand this, then, to be what is meant by Simeon’s blessing them when Joseph and Mary the mother of Jesus marvelled at the things said concerning him. For his blessing is the instruction of inward grace. And it is indeed very necessary that, when Joseph and Mary the mother of Jesus marvel at the things said concerning him, Simeon should be present with his blessing, so that inward visitation may renew and cherish the many and great goods contained in this wonder, defend them from diminution, and advance them toward spiritual increase. Nor only that, but by renewing, cherishing, and increasing them, it may perfect, confirm, and establish them.

XV. This it does, of course, when it instructs reason how cautiously it ought to conduct itself in the resolve of holiness—a resolve which it conceives in affection and brings forth in effect. For if you humbly carry out the holiness which you intend to undertake in action, you will turn it to spiritual fruit for yourself; but if arrogantly, to the service of sin. And it happens, in a lamentable manner, that from what could have raised you to the summit of virtue, you fall into the pit of guilt. Therefore it is necessary that inward grace address reason concerning this, and teach it that this happens very frequently, so that it may guard against these evils.

This seems to be the point of Simeon’s words to Mary, the mother of Jesus: that he “is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel, and for a sign that is contradicted” (Luke 2:34). For if a man who sees God is called Israel, may not the manly mind which sees God through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor. 13:12) be called Israel? And Jesus is set for many in this Israel both for rising and for falling, because the exercise of holiness provides many hidden movements of the mind with occasion both to fall through exaltation from good to worse, and to rise through humility from good to better, and from better to best—not as though from a valley to a plain, but rather as from the level of a field to the slope of a hill, and from the hill’s slope to the mountain summit.

Therefore beware, brothers, of the plague of pride and the corruption of boastfulness. How many we know for whom having virtues has harmed them more than lacking them would have done! For those whose voice is, “Our hand is exalted, and not the Lord has done all these things” (Deut. 32:27), while they think that they have not received what they possess and therefore boast as though they had not received it, it would have been better for them to lack what they have (1 Cor. 4:7); for then at least they would know what they lacked. But now, when they think themselves something while they are nothing, they deceive themselves (Gal. 6:3).

XVI. Therefore beware, you who seem especially to have Jesus with you, lest you have him unto ruin. “How,” you ask, “is Jesus had unto ruin?” Just as a good work is performed unto pride; for understand pride to be ruin, and vain exaltation to be the occasion and cause of downfall. For thus you read: “Before ruin the heart is exalted” (Prov. 16:18). Did not the man who fasted twice in the Sabbath and gave tithes of all that he possessed have Jesus? Yet he had him unto ruin, when he said that he was not like other men, or even like the tax collector standing there (Luke 18:11–13).

Wholesome, then, is that admonition of the Wise Man: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20; cited here as 3:10). In these few words he exhorts us, plainly, that Jesus be held not unto ruin but unto rising. Let holy Simeon therefore say among you to Mary the mother of Jesus that he is set for the rising of many in Israel. That is: let the visitation of inward grace teach your reason—which conceives in willing and brings forth in working the resolve of holiness within you—that, through that same holiness, when certain inward movements are exercised in the mind, some rise through humility from good to better, while others fall through pride from good to worse.

Jesus is also set as a sign contradicted; but may it be far from you. For you are not among those who do all their works in order to be seen by people (Matt. 23:5).
