The uprightness of inward intention, then, is the sign for which Jesus is set, because this is the sign we possess that makes the good we practice fruitful and salutary for us: that we act with the intention of pleasing only the eyes of the inward Inspector. For just as those who do their works to be seen by people shall have no reward from their Father in heaven, so indeed only those for whom love of God alone is the cause of action shall receive the vision of God as their recompense. But this sign is contradicted by many who seek glory and praise from people and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone.

XVII. After this Simeon adds: “And a sword shall pierce through your own soul also” (Luke 2:35). For the fervour of good desire contained in a holy resolve itself pierces the inward parts of reason. The sword of Jesus is the sharpness of holy desire found in the resolve of holiness signified by Jesus. This sword is double-edged: both in avoiding what is evil and in practicing what is good. This fervour of good desire present in the resolve of holiness arouses one to avoid evils and fulfill goods; and this is the sword of Jesus passing through Mary’s soul. When this is done with care, various inward stirrings are renewed; and this is the revealing of thoughts from many hearts.

How often, then, do we feel this occurring within ourselves! When we resolve to undertake something pertaining to holiness, and when we ardently desire to commit it to execution, the sharpness of fervent desire penetrates within us into the interior parts of reason. It belongs to reason to conceive gifts and also to bring them forth, to dispose and regulate them; and the inward movements, which commonly vary in many ways, produce from this sharpness heat and cares, anxieties and foresight, so that what is boldly desired may be devoutly accomplished, and what has been devoutly accomplished may be steadfastly maintained—especially so that it may be practiced not with a view to human favor, but for the sake of inward recompense alone.

XVIII. And what else does all this seem to you to be than the sword of Jesus passing through Mary’s soul, and, as it passes through her soul, thoughts being revealed from many hearts? That Simeon makes known to this same Mary that Jesus is set for the ruin and rising of many in Israel and for a sign contradicted, and that a sword shall pierce her own soul so that thoughts may be revealed from many hearts—that, I say, Simeon announces all these things to Mary—what do we think it means except, briefly stated, that concerning these goods the visitation of inward grace, which Simeon represents, addresses reason, instructs it when addressed, and makes it certain when instructed?

For into the mind which it judges worthy of its presence, it is accustomed to pour that action which, according to the saying of blessed John the Apostle, teaches concerning all things (1 John 2:27). It enlightens the mind into which it is poured with knowledge of truth through understanding. And because it is an anointing (ibid.), it softens that mind toward love of virtue through affection. If you wish to know something fuller and more perfect concerning it, it is the love of God poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us: he is God, blessed with the Father and the Son for ever. Amen.

165  
## SERMON XXXIX, ON THE SAME SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

On the inward purity of the mind, which is to be offered to God alone.

[Col. 0352C]

1. The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech.—2. The Lord our God alone is righteous; from him comes all our righteousness.—3. The fitting order: first to do, then to teach. The author’s self-abasement.—4. The preaching of one whose life is despised ought to be despised.—5. Anna, a type of the devout soul; her name signifies grace: she should first benefit herself, then her neighbour.—6. Analogy of the natural and mystical body: how, in the distribution of graces, one is set above and below another.—7. What one has received alone as a gift, let him render to the common good as fruit.—8. No work pleases God unless he sees it done for his own sake. Concern for received grace.—9. Let the religious soul be provident for itself, useful to its neighbour, devout toward God. Like the prophetess, let it have eyes before and behind: there seeing present weakness, here past iniquity.—10. [Col. 0352D] The dignity of our creation and the mercy of redemption must be considered.—11. The eternal punishments of hell and the rewards of the heavenly kingdom. In seven things lies the strength of the provident mind.—12. Phanuel, that is, “the face of God”: this face is understood sevenfold in Scripture.—13. The tribe of Asher signifies the lot of the elect, whose age is progress in virtues.—14. The bridal bed and widowhood of the spiritual soul.—15. The mystery of the numbers seven, ten, and two.—16. The stewardly withdrawal of inward grace.

I. “And there was Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher” (Luke 2:36). Scripture says that the righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech (Prov. 18:17). I too wished, at the beginning of this sermon, to accuse myself. For if a righteous person does this, how much more is it fitting for me to do it, since I am not righteous but a sinner? And what weight can any righteousness possess unless true humility in accusing oneself commends it?

Who among us can not merely be more righteous than, but even be compared in righteousness with, the one who said, “All our righteousnesses are like a menstruous cloth” (Isa. 64:6; cited here as 74:6)? In these most humble words, and therefore most holy words, my brothers, your prudence clearly perceives how highly he valued his own righteousness in his own eyes: he chose to compare it to an object which the eye not only recoils from seeing, but the mind recoils even from thinking of.

Receive also another who had no confidence in his own righteousness: “Not in our justifications, which we have done, do we present our prayers before your face, but in your many mercies” (Dan. 9:18). This was holy Daniel. So too that disciple whom Jesus loved: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). But let this word now stand in the mouth of these three witnesses. There are countless others—indeed, all who pleased God in holiness—who, each distrustful of the quality of his merits, fled from the face of the sword, knowing that there is judgment, and fled to mercy. Hence this is the voice of every one of them: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord; for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2).

II. He alone is righteous who alone is free among the dead (Ps. 87:5). Addressing him, holy David says: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright” (Ps. 118:137); and again: “I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. 70:16). Why his righteousness alone, unless because he alone is truly righteous? Of him holy Jeremiah says: “This is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our Righteousness” (Jer. 23:6).

Yet in his righteousness he himself justifies many, and from his fullness we all have received (John 1:16), so that the ointment upon the head descends through the middle of the beard to the hem of the garment (Ps. 132:2). For no one can make clean what is conceived from unclean seed, except he who alone is able to do so (Job 14:4). Therefore do not suppose that you have nothing to accuse in yourself if you seek to be righteous. Rather, then hope that you can be justified when you have been a diligent observer and careful examiner, painstakingly and inquisitively investigating what is to be accused in yourself; and when what you must accuse in yourself appears, do not fail to accuse it. Know, dearest one, that no righteousness of yours can be greater than your self-accusation. Rightly, then, is it said that the righteous person is his own accuser. For this very thing is to be righteous: to accuse oneself; and no one can be righteous unless he accuses himself.

III. Him too, as I have already said, I wish to imitate—not as a righteous man, but as a sinner—because the words of the Gospel which I have undertaken to expound now furnish me with some ground for self-accusation. For when the Evangelist Luke wishes later to say of this woman that, coming up, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Israel (Luke 2:36–38), he takes care earlier to show that she was worthy to give thanks to the Lord and that hearers should not disbelieve her when she spoke of him. For he says: “And there was a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel,” and the rest down to “who awaited the redemption of Israel.”

You see, therefore, that he first exalts her with great and many praises, and then introduces her as giving thanks to the Lord and speaking of him to others. First, he declares that she had married a husband while a virgin; that she had remained many years in widowhood; that she had not departed from the temple; that she had always served God in prayer and fasting; and only then that she came up to give thanks to the Lord and speak of him to all who awaited the redemption of Israel.

I think this is also the point of what is said about Jesus: that Jesus “began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1); and that he was called “mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24:19). So too the Psalmist says: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. 118:104); and likewise we read of Ezra that he prepared his heart to do and to teach in Israel the commandments and judgments (1 Esdras 7:10). I say all this in self-accusation and self-reproach: I seem indeed to teach, but I am not found to act; to utter discourse, but not to possess the work; to understand, but not from your commandments; and while others seem to feast through me, I perish from hunger.

Why should I now speak to you of individual vices and virtues, declaring that I neither avoid the former nor practice the latter? I speak, briefly: of vices to be avoided, though I myself am vicious; of virtues to be practiced, though I am devoid of virtues. And I seem, after the likeness of this holy woman, to speak to you concerning the Lord—you who await the redemption of Israel. But it can by no means be said of me that I do not depart from the temple, occupied with fasts and prayers day and night, whatever those things may be which are to be understood spiritually through them.

IV. Those who so often compel me to speak should consider this: according to the judgment of a holy man, it is fitting that the preaching of one whose life is despised should be despised. Indeed, the Lord himself is read to rebuke the sinner for this by a reproving word through the Psalmist (Ps. 49:16): why he dared to declare God’s righteousness and take his covenant upon his lips, when he is plainly entangled in the offenses of which the following verses treat.

They should not, therefore, so much revere in me the beauty of leaves—if even that were present in me—when they see that the savour of fruit is absent. For what else is a hollow and empty person, uttering words indeed but performing no deeds, than a barren tree with leaves but without fruit? (Matt. 21:19.) And we surely know that the Lord struck the fig tree with the curse of barrenness when, being hungry, he found no fruit on it, although it was not without leaves. What example, then, is more terrifying for those who speak but do not act?

They should therefore seek works from me before demanding words, according to what the Bridegroom says to the Bride in the Song of Songs: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” (Cant. 2:14; cited here as 2:4). He wished her first to show him her face and then to sound her voice in his ears, so that her speech might afterward fill the hearing more sweetly when the face of her action had first gladdened the sight. You see, therefore, that the Bridegroom first seeks from the Bride a way of life for example, so that her preaching may afterward be more welcome to him for instruction. But let us now turn to the moral exposition of those things said about this woman, and let what is said in praise of her be taken as a reproach to me, who rashly claim for myself the speech which she had about the Lord to those awaiting Israel’s redemption, while I do not possess her praiseworthy manner of life.

[Col. 0355B]

V. “And there was,” says the Evangelist, “Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel.” Without prejudice to whatever allegorical sense by which this woman undoubtedly pertains to the holy Church of the elect, it seems to me that the devout soul is Anna the prophetess: the soul which does not receive the grace of God in vain (2 Cor. 6:1), which is not empty in that grace, and which, according to Paul’s admonition, sees how carefully it must walk (Eph. 5:15), not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time because the days are evil.

These names lead me to this understanding: for Anna, as they say, signifies grace, and he who today is called a prophet was formerly called a seer (1 Sam. 9:9). Moreover, you need threefold concern if you are not to receive God’s grace in vain: namely, to take careful care of the gift of grace that you have received; to turn it to your own benefit and, when your neighbour is in need, to share it with him; and in both respects to seek the praise and glory of your Giver.

For if you have the gift of grace but do not have it for yourself, you are a lamp that shines indeed, but not for yourself. And what does it benefit darkness if light shines in it and the darkness does not comprehend it? (John 1:5.) Such indeed are those who are wise to do evil but have not known how to do good (Jer. 4:22). There are also those who sow much and bring in little; eat and are not satisfied; drink and are not filled; clothe themselves and are not warmed; gather wages and put them into a bag with holes (Hag. 1:6). Therefore the Apostle took care to admonish his beloved disciple to rekindle the grace that was in him, lest he neglect what had been given; and he says of himself that he does not wish to cast it aside (Gal. 2:21).

VI. You see, therefore, that it would be better to lack grace than to possess it uselessly. And what will you say of one who, though he seems to have received something alone, greedily tries to keep it alone—seeking what is his own, not what belongs to another? I do not know how one of this kind dares to claim fellowship for himself under Christ the head in his body, which is the Church, when the members of that body are each concerned for the others, so that if one suffers, the rest suffer with it.

In our own body, do the eyes alone, which alone see, see only for themselves? Do the ears, which alone hear, hear for themselves alone? And do the feet, which alone walk, walk for themselves alone? Certainly not, but for the whole body. Each member of our body directs its own particular possession to the common benefit; and it possesses what it has as its own in such a way that it is also common. It is particular with respect to service, but common with respect to benefit, as one and the same indissoluble love directs, by which all are mutually concerned for one another.

Are not each of you, who make up this holy assembly, individual members of Christ’s body? This is Paul’s statement: “For as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ” (Rom. 12:4–5). And he adds: “Individually, however, members one of another.”

Therefore, as you see in our body that its individual members cannot all be of one and the same service or action, so neither can each of you, who are members of this body—that is, this congregation of canons—be of one and the same exercise or perfection. For perhaps one among you is stronger than another in bodily powers; another more skilful in prudent caution; another more penetrating in keenness of perception; another stronger in force of mind; another shrewder in detecting the wiles of this world; another more expert in knowledge of outward things; another more learned in the judgments of Scripture; another more pleasing in singing; another more apt in reading; another deeper in understanding; another more polished in expression; another stricter in abstinence; another more watchful in vigils; another more devout in prayer; another purer in contemplation; another stronger in manual work.

And there is none among you whom that same Spirit, whose gifts are variously distributed, does not set above another in some respect (1 Cor. 12:11), and whom he does not likewise set below another in some respect, working all these things by one and the same Spirit and distributing to each of you as he wills. To what end, brothers, does the Giver of all good things arrange you with such reverence, enriching one of you in what he allows another to lack, filling this one in what he permits that one to be empty, except that each person, recognizing what he lacks, may know that he needs another; and, by charitably offering what he has and humbly imitating what he does not have, may “take a psalm and give the timbrel” (Ps. 80:3), while among you the wings of the living creatures strike one against another (Ezek. 3:13)?

VII. Since these things are so, let it be far—once and again far—that there should be anyone among you who tries to possess alone even what he appears to possess alone. Rather, whatever he alone receives as a gift, let him return to the common good as fruit. Let him not envy those who perhaps have it more abundantly; nor let him despise those who have less. At the prompting of love so humble and humility so loving, let him mercifully bestow on those who lack what he has; let him diligently seek from those who possess what he lacks, so that, when so great and such concern has made every one of you attentive to the others, you may walk harmoniously in one peace and happily attain one rest.

“Having gifts differing according to the grace given to you” (Rom. 12:5)—whether these or those by which one among you excels highly while another humbly lacks them—“through the love of the Spirit serve one another,” regarding others as superior to yourselves, not each considering what is his own, but what belongs to others (Phil. 2:3–4). And, as the foremost of the apostles exhorts, “As each has received grace, administer it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be glorified” (1 Pet. 4:10–11).

You do these things, however, if the love of brotherhood remains in you; if you do not forget beneficence and fellowship (Heb. 13:16); if none of you seeks what is his own but what belongs to another; if the stronger among you are ready to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not please themselves (Rom. 15:1); if, finally, each of you presents himself without offense to the whole Church of God, pleasing all in all things, seeking not what is useful to himself but what is useful to many, that they may be saved (1 Cor. 10:32–33).

All these things concern what we have said: that we ought to share with our neighbours, as need requires, what we have received, lest we happen to receive grace in vain. But it is altogether necessary that in all these things we seek the glory and honour of the Father of lights, from whom, as the apostle James testifies, “every good gift and every perfect gift proceeds” (Jas. 1:17). For he loses grace who does not employ it for the giver’s glory; and he shows himself altogether unworthy who, in carrying it out, seeks anything other than him alone who grants it.

VIII. Therefore beware, beloved: let not your left hand know what your right hand does (Matt. 6:3). For, to speak briefly and truly, God has nothing to reward except what he sees done for his own sake. O hidden robber, O lurking thief, desire for human favour! You now see how necessary it is that what you read in Ezekiel should be done: “a trench in the altar” (Ezek. 43:13). That is, humility must accompany a good work, lest perhaps the wind of pride carry away, utterly scatter, and annihilate what is offered on the altar of devotion through the practice of holiness.

Keep, therefore, a single eye within yourselves, so that the body also may be full of light (Matt. 6:22): that is, a right intention, so that the work too may be acceptable to God. Let this threefold concern therefore hold the devout soul when it receives grace: that it turn the gift it has received to its own benefit; share it with its neighbour if he is in need; and in both cases seek the praise and glory of its Giver. Let it turn it to its own benefit because “cursed is he who makes his own portion worse” (Prov. 3:7, as cited). Let it share it with its neighbour because, “If you are wise, you shall not be wise for yourself alone, but also for your neighbour.” Let it seek the giver’s glory because “God scatters the bones of those who please men; they are put to shame because God has rejected them” (Ps. 52:9).

[Col. 0358A]

IX. The name Anna, which signifies grace, can now fittingly be applied to this soul when, in dispensing the manifold grace of God that it has received, it works out its own salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. 2:12); when it cheerfully and readily meets the needs of its neighbour everywhere and effectively assists according to its ability; and when, in all its movements, both hidden and open, it has the Giver of the grace it exercises as a ready witness and awaits him as rewarder. Such a soul, I say, may be called Anna. It does not receive God’s grace in vain: it is cautious for itself, useful to its neighbour, and devout toward God—cautious for itself by the holiness of religious conduct; useful to its neighbour by works of brotherly love; devout toward God by the uprightness of inward intention.

Let this soul also be a prophetess: that is, let it see what is past and what is to come, having eyes before and behind. Let it behold its past evils, which it once committed, so that it may be pierced with sorrow; and behold the future evils that press upon it in temptation, so that it may be shaken by fear. Thus a double benefit will arise for it from this twofold vision: with all harmful security removed—the mother and nurse of vices, but the stepmother and destroyer of virtues—it will be shaken and humbled; there it will fear its strict Judge, and here reverence its watchful guardian, lest perhaps the one condemn it, wicked and sinful as it is, to death, or the other permit it, weak and feeble as it is, to fall.

Let it turn its eyes backward to that miserable state in which it once lay prostrate, and recognize it as most worthy of condemnation. Let it turn them to this state in which it appears, however imperfectly, to stand, and know clearly that a fall is near if the hand that sustains it should withdraw even for a moment. There let it see the iniquity for which it should grieve; here, the weakness for which it should fear. Thus this twofold state of our prophetess presents itself to her consideration: with the eyes that look behind, she sees the state that has passed; with those before, the state now present.

X. There are still other things which she sees behind, and other things which she sees before; but both these and those are far away. If you wish to know what those things are which are behind, they are the dignity of our redemption [alternative reading: “creation and mercy”]. The former consideration arouses wonder because of its sublimity; the latter arouses love because of its mercy. For it is full of every cause for astonishment to see man created in the image and likeness of God; and no less full of love to behold God appearing in man, appearing for man, and enduring from man such and many other things for man.

Our prophetess sees these things—to pass over for the present the ease of her creation: God incarnate for her, born, wrapped in swaddling clothes, laid in a manger, fed with human milk, circumcised, presented, subject to his parents, baptized, hungry, tempted, dishonoured by wicked people; in his deeds enduring observers, in his words opponents; sought to be stoned, led away to be cast down; speaking saving words, silent under reproaches; working wonders, enduring harsh things—and not merely harsh, but unworthy things. She sees him washing his disciples’ feet, praying at greater length in agony, shedding a bloody sweat, seized with swords and clubs, bound, judged, condemned, blindfolded, struck with fists, suffering slaps, bruised by lashes, smeared with spittle, clothed in a scarlet cloak, crowned with thorns, mockingly worshipped, crucified, given vinegar to drink, wounded with a lance, praying for his crucifiers, and yielding up his spirit.

She sees him dead, buried, rising again, ascending, seated at the right hand of God the Father, coming on the last day, judging the living and the dead, and reigning eternally in his elect. These things, and others of this kind, pertaining both to the sublimity of creation and to the mercy of redemption, our prophetess beholds with the eyes she has behind: things indeed past with regard to the act, but destined to remain eternally with regard to their fruit.

XI. But if you wish to know the things that lie before you, consider the misery of the punishment of hell and the happiness of the heavenly homeland. The one terrifies the beholder; the other soothes him. For it is dreadful to one who looks upon it to see that land of darkness, covered with the gloom of death, the land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death is, and no order, but everlasting horror dwells (Job 10:21–22). Fear and trembling also come upon you when, by knowledge, you go forth to see the corpses [Col. 0359C] of those who have transgressed against the Lord. For you see that both the worm consumes them and the fire burns them, and that both are everlasting: for the one is unquenchable and the other is called immortal (Isa. 66:24). But just as it is dreadful to behold these things, so it is exceedingly sweet to see that new city, Jerusalem, coming down from heaven from God . . . having the glory of God, whose light is like a precious stone (Rev. 21:2), whose streets are paved with pure gold, and through whose lanes alleluia is sung (Tob. 13:21–22). Both of these, therefore—namely, infernal punishment and heavenly joy—lie before us; and just as the sight of the former is a seedbed of fear, so the sight of the latter is an incentive to love.

Our prophetess therefore sees certain things behind her: the dignity of creation, the mercy of redemption, and the bitterness of the Passion. The first, when she sees it, inspires amazement; the second, love; the third, shame. She sees far before her eternal punishment and heavenly joy: consideration of the former produces terror, and of the latter desire. Join to these five that sixth thing which she has in the present within herself: consideration of her own weakness. The more fully the mind beholds this, the more it is compelled to fear. Yet together with all these there must be a certain seventh thing: namely, the confidence of holy hope. Its joyful assurance and assured joy must accompany in the mind the consideration of all these things; without it, to turn over in the mind these sad matters mentioned above is too burdensome, [Col. 0360A] while even joyful things are not joyful enough (Judg. 16:19).

And see whether perhaps these are Samson’s seven very strong locks. So long as he had them, he could not be conquered by his enemies; but as soon as he lost them, he became the sport of those to whom he had formerly been a terror. Behold our Anna, our prophetess, who is also called the daughter of Phanuel for this reason, I think: because she has as her Father him who, according to the Apostle’s testimony, “of his own will begot us by the word of his truth, that we might be, as it were, the firstfruits of his creatures” (Jas. 1:18).

XII. Those who know the interpretations of Hebrew names say that *Phanuel* means “the face of God.” And indeed, if with diligent curiosity and curious diligence you range through the breadth of Sacred Scripture, you will find that “the face of God” has various meanings there. For in the Gospel the Lord calls the Father himself the face of God, when he says that their angels—that is, without doubt, the angels of the little ones—always see the face of the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 18:10). In that passage, Father and his face are not two different things.

But you need not look much farther than the Psalmist to discover what else the face of God signifies. He calls the face of God now the Son himself, now his presence, now knowledge of him, now his favor, now his awareness. Thus he says concerning the first meaning: “How long do you turn your face away from me?” (Ps. 12:2), that is: How long do you delay sending your Christ, whom you are going to send? He says also of the second: “Do not turn your face away from me” (Ps. 27:9), that is: Do not deny me [Col. 0360C] your presence in the future. Likewise, of the third: “Seek his face always” (Ps. 105:4), that is: Desire at every time to attain knowledge of him. Of the fourth: “Do not cast me away from your face” (Ps. 51:13), that is: Do not allow me to be cast out from your favor. And also of the fifth: “He has turned away his face, lest he see to the end” (Ps. 10:11), expressing what the ungodly are accustomed to say: that God does not have knowledge by which he can know their evils.

Holy Habakkuk likewise calls God’s protection his face, where he says that death shall go before his face (Hab. 3:5): for where God protects, there the devil cannot prevail. But Job takes God’s face to mean his scrutiny, saying: “Then I shall not hide from [Col. 0360D] your face” (Job 13:20). That is to say: If I am such a person, I shall not fear God’s scrutiny. If you search diligently, therefore, you will find in Sacred Scripture these meanings, and perhaps several others of the same sort, for “the face of God.” Having carefully considered these things, I think that, even if I now keep silent, you plainly understand why the woman of whom we speak is called the daughter of the face of God—which, beyond doubt, is what *Phanuel* means.

XIII. She is also said to be of the tribe of Asher, because through the election of grace she has been saved for the lot of the elect and belongs to heavenly blessedness; and they say that the name *Asher* expresses this. For she belongs to the fellowship of those whom God chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, that they might be [Col. 0361A] holy and without blemish before God in love (Eph. 1:4), foreknowing and predestining them, calling and justifying them, and at last glorifying them. Calling, I say, through right faith; justifying through holy conduct; and glorifying through everlasting blessedness.

But since you have now heard concerning this woman’s name and office, her father and her lineage, it is time to inquire concerning her age. After this the Evangelist adds: “She had advanced in many days” (Luke 2:6). Many days are many virtues. For you have made progress through as many days as you have exercised yourself in virtues [variant: “grown,” or “exercised yourself”]. These were the days of holy David, in which he declares that he wished to pray to God, saying: “And in my days I will call upon [him]” (Ps. 115:2). For he knew that the prayer of one who turns away [Col. 0361B] his ear so as not to hear the law will be an abomination. These are the days with which our fathers of old are said to have been filled; of them we read that they died old and full of days (Prov. 28:9). You understand this rightly if you recognize that they departed this life with maturity of character and fullness of virtues (Gen. 35:29). Thus this woman advanced in many days, because in holy conduct she accumulated for herself an abundant wealth of spiritual virtues.

XIV. “And she had lived with her husband seven years from her virginity. And she was a widow until eighty-four years of age” (Luke 2:37). We pass over many things that ought to be said, because we are pressing toward other matters upon which we intend to dwell for a while. For we shall not be able to pass over hastily, when we arrive at the place [Col. 0361C] where this woman is said not to have departed from the temple, serving with fasts and prayers night and day.

But in this passage you see that the time during which she lived with her husband was very short in comparison with that during which she remained a widow. And what do we suppose this means, except that it seems a small matter to that spiritual and inward Anna—I mean the devout and pious soul—when, in the presence of her lawful husband, like a loving bride embracing her bridegroom and rejoicing in his sweetest reciprocal embraces, she exults in glad dancing; and by no means a small matter when, he having been withdrawn, she groans in his absence like a chaste and loving widow? For his presence, bringing sweetness, takes away weariness; but his absence, bringing bitterness, produces disgust. Hence it comes about that to this our Anna the time in which she lives with her husband seems short; but the time in which, widowed of his presence, she sighs and groans in his absence seems long. You who are spiritual, in this holy fellowship, often experience what I say.

XV. She is read to have lived with her husband for the space of seven years, but to have remained a widow for eighty-four (ibid.). And, unless I am mistaken, none of these details is without significance; but we do not have leisure to look deeply into them. Yet, that we may touch them more on the surface than search them to the marrow, we may infer from the number of these years that the joy of inward delight, which our Anna enjoys in the presence of her husband, grants her the virtuous stability of spiritual unity. The devout mind is accustomed to preserve this unity with all its powers, provided that the Lord possesses it wholly; as we read concerning Elkanah, Samuel’s father, that he was one man, whose name means the possession of God.

Certainly this unity cannot be held in the mind unless the sevenfold grace of the Spirit deigns to grant it, because unity is multiplied seven times. And if you accept this interpretation, understand that it pertains to the passage you read in Isaiah: “Seven women shall take hold of one man” (Isa. 4:1). For this manly unity is taken hold of by seven women, so that it may be bestowed upon our Anna by the sevenfold Spirit—the Anna who is said to have been with her husband for one year multiplied sevenfold. She likewise remains [Col. 0362B] in widowhood for eighty-four years, because the chaste and ardent desire by which she is inflamed in the absence of her husband grants her, in holy conduct, observance both of the Decalogue and of the twofold commandment of love—yet through the infusion of that same sevenfold Spirit. For if you multiply ten by seven, you reach seventy; if you add two likewise multiplied by seven, you arrive at eighty-four, the number which, as you read, contains the years of her widowhood. Therefore, as the number seven commonly expresses the sevenfold Spirit in Sacred Scripture, so ten expresses the Decalogue and two the double commandment of love.

XVI. It is therefore fitting and appropriate that this widow is said to have remained in widowhood until eighty-four years of age [Col. 0362C]: for although the Spirit may seem to withdraw itself for a time as regards consolation, it does not wholly withdraw itself as regards benefit. By its grace it holds and exercises in Anna, even when she is a widow, according to the meaning of this name, the sevenfold gift, the tenfold law, and the twofold love.

Is not Anna widowed of her husband when the faithful soul, deprived for a time of the strength upon which it relied, is left desolate? This happens more through divine dispensation, as we often learn from our own experience, than as a punishment for demerit. Hence holy David does not ask the Lord never to forsake him; rather, he says, “Do not utterly forsake me” (Ps. 119:8), knowing that strength is made perfect in weakness [Col. 0362D] (2 Cor. 12:9). Thus the Spirit remains with the soul, for its holy action in the observance of law and love, even when for a time the strength upon which it relies withdraws itself, and it no longer enjoys that strength for consolation, but only for fortitude.

For one and the same Spirit is stable and mobile, forsaking and holding, withdrawing and remaining. Truthful Scripture says of the same holy living creatures both that they went and returned, and that they did not return when they went (Ezek. 1:14, 17). You see, then, what is meant by the statement that this woman lived with her husband for seven years and remained a widow until eighty-four. What it means that from her virginity she lived with her husband for seven years, and that she did not depart from the temple, we shall explain to you in the following sermon, insofar as he may deign to inspire us—he without whom we can do nothing, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

# SERMON XL

## On the Same Sunday within the Octave of the Nativity of the Lord: On the Practice of Religious Life

## Synopsis of the Sermon

1. Order and exposition of the subject.
2. Through virginity is signified the barrenness of the mystical soul; virtues of the widow Anna in the Gospel.
3. What temple it is from which one must not depart. The eightfold sense of “temple” in the Scriptures.
4. The first temple is the body of Christ the Lord, in which one must abide by continual thought and trust. The efficacy and commendation of the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass.
5. In Christ we possess what we do not have from ourselves. The unbloody offering is salutary.
6. The body of Christ is the most immediate remedy for carnal desire; by regard for it we are heard by God the Father.
7. The second temple is the Virgin Mary, whose praise and patronage are unique.
8. The third temple is the unity of the Church, outside which there is no salvation.
9. The fourth is the assembly of living saints, from whose imitation one must not depart.
10. The fifth is our body, which must be sanctified.
11. The sixth is our soul: it is sanctified by desire for pardon, grace, and glory, and by the exercise of virtues.
12. The seventh is the capacity of created intellect; the eighth, the heavenly homeland.
13. These eight temples are to be inhabited by the devout soul.
14. A fuller treatment of confession elsewhere.
15. One confession is of divine praise; another is self-accusation.
16. The law of the Lord, in the strictest sense, is love itself.
17. In what manner Christ will manifest himself to us.

I. This holy woman, concerning whom we have already said much in the preceding sermon, is said to have lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity (Luke 2:36). What she herself signifies; what it means that she is called Anna; what it means that she is a prophetess; what it means that she lived seven years with her husband; what it means that she remained a widow until eighty-four years of age; and finally, what I had almost just omitted—why she is called the daughter of Phanuel, is of the tribe of Asher, and had advanced in many days—all this we showed you in the sermon immediately preceding, as far as it then occurred to us. But what we think should be understood by her having lived with her husband for so many years from her virginity, and by her not departing from the temple, serving through fasting and prayer night and day, we deferred to this sermon, which we now have in hand. And now it is time to begin, according to our ability, to fulfill what we then promised.

What, then, do we suppose may be intimated to us by the fact that she lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity, except what we see every day: that before the soul is joined, at the call of the sevenfold Spirit, to this inward strength in stable purity, it languishes in barren idleness and idle barrenness? For just as virginity is great cleanness and purity in this mortal flesh, so it can also signify the barrenness of the soul.

II. Might not the account in the true history be fitted to this meaning, where we find that, when Jephthah’s daughter was to be sacrificed, she bewailed her virginity? (Eph. 6:17.) What else does this mean [Col. 0364A] than that a soul which is to be mortified and offered with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, ought to repent of its former barrenness? For, in this sense, virginity suggests something not altogether implausible: in a manner of speaking, the Law itself pressed a barren woman beneath the yoke of a curse. For two dangers await the fruitless tree: the axe that cuts it down and the fire that burns it up—namely, the sentence of death that takes away life, and damnation that afflicts forever.

But she who lived with her husband for seven years from this virginity of hers, and who was a widow until eighty-four years of age, applied herself so devoutly to spiritual fruitfulness after putting aside barrenness, and so diligently pursued approved action after casting away idleness, that Scripture says of her that she “served with prayers and fastings night and day” [Col. 0364B] (Luke 2:37). In these words, few in number but profound in meaning, your diligence can perceive that she persistently applied herself to purity both of mind and body. For fasting signifies the mortification of the flesh, while prayers signify devotion of mind. And by her attention to these things both by day and by night is understood the unceasing perseverance which she exercised in good work.

She gave herself to prayers and fasts night and day, so that, my brother, neither prosperity, making you lax, may draw your Anna away from those things which concern the sanctification of your mind and body, nor adversity, disturbing you. She is drawn away from them not only when she desires evil, but also when she abandons good: when, namely, she is tempted by desire, being drawn away and enticed [Col. 0364C] (Jas. 1:14)—drawn away from good and enticed toward evil. The brightness of prosperity draws her away from the former; the darkness of adversity entices her toward the latter.

III. But what does it mean that she is said not to have departed from the temple? For the preceding sequence of words is as follows: “She did not depart,” Scripture says, “from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day.” What is this temple from which she did not depart? I think that we can understand “temple” in many ways. Let us run, as we are accustomed to do whenever we need it, to Sacred Scripture, and we shall find that it calls now the body of Christ a temple, now the Virgin Mary, now the holy Church, now also the holy men who are in it, now our body, now [Col. 0364D] our mind, now the capacity of angelic and human intellect, and finally the heavenly homeland itself for which we sigh. I think suitable examples are ready to hand.

For the first, we have the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19); that is, Kill my body, and on the third day I will raise it again. For the second, holy David says in the Psalms: “The Lord is in his holy temple” (Ps. 11:5), namely, Christ conceived in the Virgin’s womb. The same writer says of the third: “And in his temple all shall speak glory” (Ps. 29:9), because the elect confess the true faith in the Church. Concerning the fourth, the Apostle Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17); he was addressing, of course, the saints who were in [Col. 0365A] the Church. Concerning the fifth, the same Paul says: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Cor. 6:19). For the Holy Spirit dwells in clean hearts.

The same writer says also concerning the sixth: “If anyone defiles the temple of God”—the phrase “May God turn [this] away from you” follows; for it continues, “God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:17)—that is, if anyone defiles his own mind, in which God ought to dwell. You have Isaiah speaking of the seventh, where he says that the things beneath him filled the temple (Isa. 8). There is no doubt that “beneath him” refers to him whom he saw seated upon a high and exalted throne. And what are the things beneath him except all creatures, which, insofar as they are creatures, are far below him in his regard and greatly inferior to him? The prophet says [Col. 0365B] that they filled the temple because even the angelic and human mind marvels at these wonderful works of God’s creation.

Seek the eighth temple in the Psalmist, who says to God himself: “They shall be filled with the good things of your house” (Ps. 65:5). And he adds: “Your temple is holy, wonderful in righteousness.” It is as if he said: We shall be filled with the joys of heaven, where your dwelling shines with every holiness and no crookedness of any wickedness appears.

IV. Behold, I have shown you temple in eight senses. Nor do I doubt that you grant it is good for you to abide in each of them in mind and not to depart from any of them in thought and desire. For to abide in mind in that temple which we have said is Christ’s body is as devout for devotion as it is fruitful for benefit. For it is full of all piety to behold the human body in the Word, flesh in divinity, and humanity in God. Nor is it filled with less piety for this reason.

For what so greatly either prevents the sins of our body from being committed or washes them away once committed as continual and pure meditation on Christ’s body? For as flesh is guilty, so flesh also cleanses. The body born of the Virgin cleanses and sanctifies our defiled body—not as though it were now sanctified after once having been unholy, or as though it were to be sanctified because it was not yet holy; rather, it was always equally holy, so that for it to be a body and to be holy were one and the same thing.

I say to you, my friends: my hope is firm and my confidence steadfast that, through the offering of the spotless body of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, I obtain forgiveness for the sins which I committed in the body and contracted through the body. That sentence of blessed John gives me this hope and confidence: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1). So also does this similar saying of his fellow apostle Paul: “Who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34). For what does it mean that he intercedes for us except that he possesses in himself the nature he assumed from us? The Father cannot fail to have mercy on us when he sees his Only-begotten Son—although unlike us in guilt, yet like us in nature. [Col. 0366A] His blood cries from the earth more eloquently than Abel’s (Heb. 12:24), and it cries for those for whom he permitted it to be poured out. The Father hears the blood of his Son crying out, and he hears the Son interceding; he hears, I say, and answers.

V. What if the body I bear is unclean and defiled? Yet that which I possess in Christ is wholly holy and pure. Whenever I find in myself either too little good or too much evil, I flee back to the life-giving body of my Jesus, making its holiness a shield between the Father’s justice and my own injustice. What if curiosity has defiled sight in my body, triviality hearing, pleasure smell, gluttony taste, and impurity touch? I shall not be overly troubled or too faint-hearted, for I know what to do. I shall go to the utterly pure body of my Lord, in which none of these evils exists. Holding it as a shield at his judgment, I shall wash away what is evil in myself through it and claim for myself the good that is in him.

Thus I shall no longer fear him as judge, but love him as brother; for he is my brother and my flesh. I shall not stand fearful before a judge, but secure before an advocate: he is my advocate with the Father and the propitiation for my sins. And why is he called not so much “propitiator” as “propitiation,” except so that I may not despair of obtaining remission of those faults for which I behold his holy body as an offering?

For why is it that, although ecclesiastical custom does not permit baptism, the laying on of hands, or almost all the other sacraments in which our sanctification consists to be repeated, nevertheless, taught by saving precepts and instructed by divine institution, we are accustomed often to celebrate the offering of the saving victim? It is so that we who often die by sinning may be made alive through the holy death of our Redeemer, recalled in the sacrament; and that through the frequent celebration of the mystery the effect of our salvation may increase. Therefore, because we often stumble in the body, it is necessary that we should often be made alive and rise again through that body; and that the flesh which is wholly free from defilement should wash away and cleanse the defilement which our flesh so frequently contracts.

Therefore, if you see yourself stained with defilements and abhor your garments, go to Jesus the great priest, clothed in filthy garments (Zech. 3:3), and recognize him as the one of whom the Apostle says: “Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:21). He was made sin for us because he was offered, because he himself willed it, and he himself bore our sins (Isa. 53:7, 4). Yet he knew no sin, because he did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2:22).

VI. Thus I run to the body which committed no sin, so that the sin I committed through the body may also be forgiven me. But if the flesh in me desires against the Spirit (Gal. 5:17), if vices of the flesh tempt me, if its prickings and titillations assail me, should I not then all the more have recourse to the one firm and solid refuge of mine, the body of my Jesus, so that the desire of my body may be extinguished, temptations overcome, and prickings blunted? What assistance is so effective for gaining such a triumph as pure and clarified meditation upon his body? For he is the one who knows how to sympathize with our weaknesses, because he was tempted in every respect according to our likeness, yet without sin [Col. 0367A] (Heb. 4:15). He is the one who, because he himself suffered temptation, is able also to help us who are tempted.

The Apostle understood this well. When he saw another law in his members resisting the law of his mind and leading him captive in the law of sin which was in his members, he was compelled to cry: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:23). Having found the saving remedy, he immediately adds: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid. 24). He applied this grace more deeply and fully in what follows, saying: “God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh because of sin, that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us” (Rom. 8:3–4).

Therefore, if you know that no good dwells in you—that is, in your flesh—if you see that sin is in it, even though it does not reign, know that he condemns it in the flesh who appeared not in the reality, but in the likeness, of sinful flesh. Therefore, when the Father sees his Son in a human being and his Word in flesh, he does not wish, in mercy, to fail those cast down in the flesh, that they may rise again; nor can he fail, in strength, to aid those tempted in the flesh, that they may triumph. Rightly, too, an angel reveres our nature and fears to see it cast down, since in its Creator he worships it exalted above himself. Rightly also does God the almighty Father have mercy on it and come to its aid, since he sees it united with his Only-begotten Son. You see, then, beloved, how necessary it is for you not to depart in thought and hope from this temple, which Jewish impiety destroyed unto death and divine power raised to life after three days.

VII. The second temple is the Virgin Mary; and I do not doubt that anyone will wish to say how good it is not to depart from it. She is our lady and our advocate; our sweetness and our life; our hope and our mediatrix. She is the Mother of God, queen of angels, lover of humankind, conqueror of demons, refuge of the wretched, consolation of orphans, help of the sick, strength of the weak, confirmation of the righteous, raising up of the fallen, absolution of sinners, joy of the blessed. She is the Father’s tabernacle, the Son’s bridal chamber, the Holy Spirit’s overshadowing shelter, the Trinity’s resting-place, a heavenly dwelling, the abode of the incarnate Word, the temple of God.

But these are words that will surely fail before her prerogative can be fully explained, so great is the fullness of grace that overflows in her. Let us venerate this temple, beloved; let us rejoice and exult and give glory to her; let us pray in her and hope through her; and, praising, praying, and trusting, let us not depart from her. The humanity of Christ is a most holy temple and Holy of Holies, since in it all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily [Col. 0368A] (Col. 2:9). Holy also is this temple of which we speak: his blessed and glorious Mother, in whom he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and remained for nine months.

O most glorious and beautiful temple of God’s Only-begotten Son, open to us the gate of your mercy and clemency. Grant that we may enter into you; admit our prayers before you. With our voice, in you, we cry to the Lord, that from his holy temple he may hear our voice, and that our cry may enter before him into his ears. Brothers, do not depart from this temple. Pour out in it your prayer, and declare in it your tribulation. For she is Christ’s Mother, and God will hear the prayer you send through her and receive through her your petition—he who, born for us, consented to be hers.

VIII. The third temple is the holy Church of the elect, from which, to speak briefly, do not depart. For we must run quickly through these temples, because we are pressed to bring this sermon to its conclusion, and certain matters remain on this subject which you must hear. You do not depart from this temple if you do not separate yourselves from the unity of Mother Church through the scandals of sects. Woe to those who strive to tear Christ’s seamless garment (John 19:23), who sever themselves from fraternal unity by divisions and dissensions. Let those who are such know that those found outside the ark are submerged by the waters of the flood (Gen. 7:23), and that Joshua’s sword slays those whom Rahab’s house does not shelter within itself (Josh. 6:1).

And, to touch upon something from the Gospel narratives: when the water is troubled, it heals only one, though a multitude of sick persons lies in the porticoes (John 5:7). But we need not admonish you much about these matters. For by experience, and indeed continual experience, you have learned how good and pleasant it is to dwell together in unity (Ps. 124:2). You have likewise heard the Lord himself saying that, although scandals must come, woe to the one through whom scandal comes (Matt. 18:7).

IX. The harmonious assembly of men of the Church is the fourth temple. Not to depart from this temple is not to turn away, in holy conduct, from imitation of them. Run, therefore, through this temple [Col. 0368D] and behold the most beautiful paintings and carvings that are in it. The more fully you behold what is beautiful and glorious there, the more, captivated by that inward beauty, you will abhor to leave it.

See innocent Abel; Enoch walking with God; obedient Noah; modest Shem and Japheth; faithful Abraham; holy Isaac; simple Jacob; chaste Joseph; gentle Moses; zealous Phinehas; steadfast Joshua; kindly Samuel; humble David; and the countless other men of virtue who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, obtained promises, and were found approved by the testimony of faith (Heb. 11:33). Then you will know how good and pleasant it is to dwell and remain in this temple.

Elsewhere this temple is called paradise [Col. 0369A], in which the trees are said to have been beautiful to see and pleasant for food—beautiful to look upon, pleasant to taste (Gen. 2:9). This is because in this holy fellowship there are holy men, as rich in savor when experienced as they are beautiful when beheld. And when from these holy men you draw many good examples—indeed many and savory ones—you gather fruit from beautiful and pleasant trees.

X. We assigned the fifth temple to your body. Do not depart from this temple either; that is, do not neglect those things which pertain to the sanctification of your body. Take care to feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, receive the stranger, come to the prisoner, and visit the sick. Behold the six works of mercy by which, according to our means, we ought to meet our neighbors’ needs, and desire, according to our means, to be of service as well (Matt. 25:35).

There are also eight other things in which our bodily sanctity consists. So long as you carefully preserve it, you do not depart from this fifth temple. If you desire to hear them: first is strictness in fasting; second, perseverance in vigils; third, exercise in manual labor; fourth, purity in chastity of the flesh; fifth, gravity in expression; sixth, useful restraint in speech; seventh, plainness in clothing; eighth, composure in walking.

XI. But we shall not depart from the sixth temple either, which is our soul, if with all diligence we apply ourselves to those things that concern its sanctification. Let us strive for our soul to be enkindled, whole, and [Col. 0369C] perfect; and let us dwell in this temple. It is enkindled if desire inflames it—and this desire is threefold: desire for pardon, desire for grace, desire for glory. Let it therefore desire with its whole affection pardon, grace, and glory: pardon for sins, grace for merits, glory for rewards; pardon for sins, that it may be cleansed from wickedness; grace for merits, that it may be adorned in holiness; glory for rewards, that it may be consummated in blessedness. That sinful but repentant woman of whom it is said, “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47), possessed the first desire perfectly. The second was possessed by him who says: “My soul has longed to desire your justifications at all times” (Ps. 118:2). The eminent preacher likewise burned ardently with the third, “having a desire [Col. 0369D] to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

The soul is whole when its memory is pure, its reason discerning, and its will devout. Let the uprightness of constancy strengthen memory; let knowledge of truth enlighten reason; let the purity of devotion adorn the will. But to acquire these, weakness must first be driven away, for it commonly weakens the strength of memory; then ignorance, which obscures the light of reason; and finally wickedness, which defiles the purity of the will. Thus, when the soul has been made enkindled and whole, let it strive also to be perfect. Its perfection consists in those four celebrated virtues called principal or cardinal virtues. I should call perfect the soul which knows what must be known and does not grow dim in knowledge of the truth; [Col. 0370A] which can do what must be done and is not weakened in performing it; which is just, so as not to offend; and temperate, so as not to exceed. Prudence gives it the first good; fortitude the second; justice the third; temperance the fourth: prudence, to enlighten it; fortitude, to strengthen it; justice, to adorn it; temperance, to regulate it. If, therefore, we diligently practise these things and others of this kind, we certainly do not depart from the sixth temple, which we have assigned to our soul.

XII. The capacity of human and angelic understanding is the seventh temple. If, by continual consideration of the mind, you weigh how greatly each—human being as well as angel—excels in sublimity, then, to speak briefly, you remain in this temple also. Let us now hasten [Col. 0370B] to conclude our discourse on these temples. If you strive with devout curiosity to survey each of those dwelling-places of blessed spirits; if you do not withdraw your thought and longing from that heavenly homeland above, then it may truly be said of you also that you do not depart from the eighth temple, by which that same heavenly homeland is signified. Does not the person who says, “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20), seem to dwell in this temple? Here is Paul, “beside himself for God” and sober for us (2 Cor. 5:13), whom the Lord “raised up together with himself and made to sit in heavenly places” (Eph. 2:6). You have therefore heard, and, as I think, now understood how our spiritual Anna ought to remain in the temple, and how she ought to serve with fastings and supplications day and night.

[Col. 0370C] XIII. In the first temple she dwells through reverence and hope; in the second through praise and prayer; in the third through ecclesiastical unity and catholic peace; in the fourth through careful imitation and careful conduct; in the fifth through outstanding deeds; in the sixth through inward purity; in the seventh through wonder and astonishment; in the eighth through longing and love. But if you weigh closely each of the things said rather diffusely in these two sermons concerning this woman—if, that is, you diligently consider among yourselves what it means that she is called Anna and is a prophetess; what it means that she is the daughter of Phanuel and of the tribe of Asher; what it means that she had advanced in many days and had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity; [Col. 0370D] and finally, what it means that she had not departed from the temple, serving with fastings and supplications day and night—if, I say, you consider all these things earnestly, then, I think, you do not doubt that one such as she is worthy to come forward to confess the Lord and to speak of him to all who await the redemption of Israel. For after all that we have expounded concerning her up to this point, the following is added:

XIV. “And she herself, coming in at that very hour, confessed the Lord, and spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Israel” (Luke 2:38). First she confessed the Lord, and afterward she spoke of him. We do not wish now to speak at length concerning this [Col. 0371A] confession of hers: both because in the sermons which we delivered during Advent we discussed confession sufficiently extensively, as it then seemed to us; and because we must hasten to bring the sermon now in hand to its due conclusion, since we have already said much.

XV. Yet we say this briefly: if you wish to offer the Lord a fruitful and perfect confession, you must bring it to him in a twofold manner—namely, by praising him and accusing yourself: him as just and beneficent; yourself as a sinner and always ungrateful for his benefits. Both confessions are indeed acceptable to him: when you accuse yourself, who have committed sin, and when you praise him, who has no sin. Yet they differ in this: the former belongs to penitents and beginners; the latter to the righteous and [Col. 0371B] perfect. Of the former you read: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50:19). Of the latter: “The sacrifice of praise shall honour me” (Ps. 49:23). The former appeases one who has been offended; the latter honours one who has been appeased. Joy and jubilation shape the latter; sorrow and the voice of great disturbance shape the former. For the former proceeds from fear, while the latter proceeds from love. Both have water, but the former has “the lower watering-place” (Josh. 15:19), whose spring is contemplation of infernal punishment; the latter has “the upper watering-place” (ibid.), which wells up from contemplation of the heavenly kingdom. In this twofold way, therefore, our Anna confesses the Lord.

Let her now speak of him, not to some, but to all who await the redemption of Israel. And what is it to speak of the Lord to all who await [Col. 0371C] the redemption of Israel, except to announce to all those things which pertain to the Lord—to all who, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within themselves, awaiting adoption as children, the redemption of their body? (Rom. 8:23). Such are you, who have been saved in hope, who hope for what you do not see, who await it through patience; who long to be clothed over with your habitation which is from heaven (2 Cor. 5:2), and therefore strive, whether absent or present, to please him.

XVI. After this the Gospel concludes as follows: “And when they had fulfilled all things according to the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own city Nazareth. And the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom; and the grace of God was in him” (Luke 2:39–40). “And when they had fulfilled,” [Col. 0371D] it says—and who were those who fulfilled? Surely Joseph and Mary. Let this holy and canonical congregation hear these words, for it is, as we have often said, Mary. Let the authority of its guardians hear them also, for Joseph belongs to them. Let Joseph and Mary, I say, hear together, because when they have fulfilled all things according to the law of the Lord, then they shall return into Galilee, to their own city Nazareth.

What is the law of the Lord except charity? It is called by the Psalmist, “the undefiled law of the Lord, converting souls” (Ps. 18:8). By one of blessed Job’s friends the law of the Lord is called manifold (Job 2:6), I suppose because it immediately extends the mind which it fills toward countless advances in holy virtues. Paul also agrees with this [Col. 0372A] exposition of ours, saying that “he who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law” (Rom. 13:8), and that “love is the fullness of the law” (ibid. 10). Therefore you who preside with diligence (Rom. 12:8), and you who ought to be subject in common subjection: if you have not merely done, but fulfilled—not merely certain things, but all things—according to this law of the Lord, you shall without doubt return to flourishing revelation and to the flower revealed. For these two names, Galilee and Nazareth, appear to contain this also: that you may see what is beautiful—and this is the flower—and may recognize what is hidden; and this pertains to Galilee, when the Lord “will reveal the thickets” to us (Ps. 28:9).

XVII. Christ, in his glory, is indeed a most beautiful flower for his elect: such as he is when manifested as one God with the Father. [Col. 0372B] And no less glorious is that manifestation in which we shall see the Father and shall see him as he is. You have his sure promise of both blessednesses, from him who, just as he cannot be deceived, likewise does not wish to deceive, when he says that he will openly announce the Father to you (John 16:25), O Joseph and Mary, in Galilee; and will manifest himself to you in your city Nazareth. Then your child—whose identity you have heard sufficiently, when you understood that Joseph and Mary, his mother, marvelled at the things said concerning him—then, I say, your child shall grow and be strengthened, full of wisdom, and the grace of God shall be in him, namely when you “meet unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13).

[Col. 0372C] You may also understand this according to another interpretation which we assigned in preceding sermons to this Joseph and Mary: namely, that when they have fulfilled all things according to the law of the Lord, they too may return into Galilee, to their own city Nazareth, where the child Jesus shall grow and be strengthened, full of wisdom and having with him the grace of God. May he grant us here the grace of living well, and there grant us to enjoy the presence of his glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLI. ON THE DAY OF THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD

### On the spiritual knives with which circumcision must be performed

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. The unlawful harms of concupiscence which must be circumcised within us.
2. The two knives of spiritual [Col. 0372D] circumcision: compunction and discipline; the time for pruning.
3. Discipline, when possessed first, preserves; compunction, when lost, recovers.
4. The use and necessity of compunction or repentance in a fallen state.
5. A sure sign of election: the fervour of a good will and continual self-accusation.
6. The removal of the reproach of Egypt: addressed to Religious who conduct themselves disorderly.
7. How God’s name is blasphemed through disorderly Religious or priests.
8. Commendation of Religious who live rightly amid a perverse nation.
9. Compunction of the soul and discipline of the body cut away what is superfluous; the usefulness of this is extended.
10. Discipline is fourfold: first, voluntary and honourable poverty; second, bodily infirmity.
11. Third is adversity arising from reproaches, losses, and scourges, in which the examples of saints observed give strength.
12. Saint Job tested by a threefold kind of adversity.
13. Fourth is [Col. 0373A] the vexation of temptations, the nurse of humility.
14. The superfluity of which vices is cut off by fourfold discipline.
15. From this discipline comes a remedy for evil security and proud vanity.

I. Glory and praise to the Son of the Virgin, God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who in this most holy birth of his deigns to gladden us by a certain lovely variety and varied loveliness, as we worthily commemorate the mysteries of his infancy; so that in the celebrated variety of these mysteries loveliness may bring delight and variety remove weariness. Behold: he who lately deigned to be born for us deigned today to be circumcised. Know, most beloved, that this was a great humility in the dispensation [Col. 0373B] of our salvation, not a necessity. For what defilement had that supreme purity in himself which might be cleansed by circumcision? Rather, he who was born for us was circumcised for us. “A little child,” says holy Isaiah, “is born to us” (Isa. 9:6); and likewise he was circumcised for us. And for which of us was he circumcised? Surely for us who are excessive in superfluity and defiled by impiety. He was therefore circumcised for us, who have in ourselves something unclean to be cleansed and something superfluous to be cut away.

This great evil consists in two things: it disfigures the beauty of the human soul, weakens its strength, mars its honour, empties its fullness, disperses its wholeness, fades its loveliness, and finally takes away from it whatever good is in it and brings into [Col. 0373C] it whatever evil is in it. If you wish to hear the name of this horrible and detestable evil, it is unlawful concupiscence itself. For, when it abandons order by seeking that which it ought in no way to seek, it stains with the defilement of pollution the subject in which it is found, whether body, soul, or both; and when it exceeds measure, moving itself in desire otherwise than is permitted, it swells that same subject through excess of superfluity. Therefore, whatever this evil—unlawful concupiscence—makes in us either defiled through impurity or superfluous through excess, we ought to wipe away by the remedy of spiritual circumcision.

II. The knives with which this spiritual [Col. 0373D] circumcision must be performed are compunction and discipline: the former washes away what is impure; the latter cuts off what is superfluous. Perhaps these are the knives with which our Joshua still today circumcises the children of Israel (Josh. 5:2). They are of stone because of the strength, I suppose, of perseverance; and they are children of Israel, yet must be circumcised by Joshua, because even he who specially received from the Lord the keys of the kingdom of heaven heard: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me” (John 13:8); and the Father, the husbandman, “will prune every branch which bears fruit in Christ the vine, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2).

The bridegroom seems to express this also in the Song of Love. After asserting that winter has passed, the rain has gone and withdrawn, and flowers have appeared in his land and the bride’s, [Col. 0374A] he then says that the time of pruning has come. For when does winter pass (Song 2:12), except when perfect charity casts fear outside? (1 John 4:18). The heat of summer which drives out winter is therefore the love of charity, expelling fear. The rain also goes and withdraws when the south wind comes and blows through the bride’s garden, and the lower watering-place is wholly dried up: the bitter and anxious weeping formed by remembrance of sins now departs. Flowers appear [variant: “appearing”]: they are the sincere and purified affections of devout and holy desires, bursting forth in the innermost places of the heart. Therefore, when the devout and religious soul is not pressed by time because it is not driven by fear; when it is not drenched by the rain of sorrow because it is filled with the joy of security; when it does not dry up in the barrenness of faint-heartedness because it shines with the flowers of desires—let it understand that the time of pruning has also come. In this acceptable time let it devote itself to this holy and saving work; let it not omit diligently to cut away and remove in its vineyard—that is, in its flesh or its mind—whatever it sees to be barren or harmful.

Thus the bride’s time of pruning arrives: winter has passed, the cloud has gone, and the beauty of flowers has shone out. Thus the Lord washes Peter, when whatever he binds or looses on earth is ratified by heaven (Matt. 16:19); thus the husbandman prunes the branch, when it bears fruit in the vine; thus finally—and this is why I have pursued all these matters—Joshua circumcises those who are children of Israel. And he circumcises them, as we read, with stone knives (Josh. [Col. 0374C] 5:2).

III. Cut, we beseech you, and remove from us with your stone knives all that is superfluous and harmful in us, O good and gracious Jesus! You succeeded Moses and lead your people, the children of Israel, into a land flowing with milk and honey, into which Moses himself could not bring them. For what was impossible for the law—which brought no one to perfection and was weakened through the flesh—God accomplished by sending you, his Son, in the likeness of sinful flesh: concerning sin, he condemned sin in the flesh (Rom. 8:3). Make us firm through discipline; make us also shaken through compunction, so that the one may preserve in us the good things already possessed, and the other may recover those lost.

Let this be your work and your concern. O my soul, let this be your care [Col. 0374D] and vigilance: first, that you “mortify your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3:5), and crucify your flesh with its vices and concupiscences (Gal. 5:24); that by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of that same flesh, abstaining from fleshly desires that wage war against you, having good conduct among the nations (1 Pet. 2:11); and that you cleanse yourself also from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God (2 Cor. 7:1). But if, forestalled and overcome, drawn away and enticed, you have been less attentive or less zealous in these things, return, transgressor, to your heart; rebuke yourself and set yourself before your own face. Grieve and weep, groan and sigh (Job 3:24); and let your roaring over [Col. 0375A] your idleness and barrenness, your softness and negligence, be like overflowing waters. Accuse yourself, so that, raised from the pit of negligence into which you have fallen, you may apply yourself to the devout and useful labour of which we spoke a little earlier. Do you not see, my brethren, how necessary for you is the knife of discipline, which cuts away what is superfluous in you, so that you go forward with such moderation and walk with such propriety that in your gait, bearing, dress, and all movements nothing is done which might offend anyone’s sight, but only what befits your holiness?

IV. But, I think, you will bring no less necessary a knife of another kind, which we shall call compunction—especially in this perilous time, in which man, full of many miseries and born of woman, comes forth like a flower and is crushed; [Col. 0375B] and, fleeing like a shadow, never remains in the same state (Job 14:2). His sense and thought are inclined to evil (Gen. 8:21), since flesh is a spirit that goes and does not return. Practise these two things diligently, discipline, I say, in your steadfast state and compunction in your fall, and you have the stone knives of Joshua with which you must be circumcised, whoever you are that belong to Israel. Acting thus and being thus disposed, you show that you are set apart from the reprobate not merely by dress but by deed and virtue, and taken by the Lord as his own. For it belongs to them to be entangled in crimes and shameful deeds, in body as well as soul, and, bearing a hardened brow and an untamed heart, to end their lives in their wickedness, like the beasts which, as the prophet Joel declares, [Col. 0375C] have rotted in their dung (Joel 1:17).

But you are not so. Either you stand manfully in the good, mature in the gravity of wisdom; or you rise powerfully from evil, set against yourselves in the severity of repentance. The latter is accustomed to abolish sin when it has been consummated; the former to guard against its being consummated at all. The former pertains to the sharp knife of our Joshua, by which superfluities are always cut off whenever they strive to grow; the latter has within itself an exercise no less necessary, by which the unclean things that defile a human being are purified.

V. Believe me, brethren: a great and certainly unfailing sign of a person’s election is the fervour of a good will and the constancy of self-accusation. [Col. 0375D] Why should you not have the Spirit himself bearing witness to your spirit that you are a child of God (Rom. 8:16), when, with your conscience bearing witness to you in that same Holy Spirit, you see that by turning from evil and doing good you condemn vices, practise virtue, subdue the flesh, raise up the spirit, hate the world completely and purely, and love God, willing no evil and willing every good; omitting, as far as you can, whatever is harmful, and undertaking with all your strength everything necessary?

Do you not likewise have good grounds for a sure hope in him who, “eating ashes like bread” (Ps. 101:10), incorporates sinners into himself by repentance just as he incorporates the righteous by continence? You should confidently expect to be incorporated into him now through the fervour of repentance, and to be united to him in the future through the reception of glory. Whenever you see yourself departing from him, even a little, you have him pressing upon your back and crying after you; you have him uttering in your mind a voice of great commotion, so that your ears may hear the warning voice behind you.
