[Col. 0376A] You perceive that he immediately repels you whenever you withdraw even slightly from him, and shakes you, moving and troubling the earth of your conscience (Ps. 59:4); showing harsh things to that lower people of your thoughts and making it drink the wine of compunction, strongly causing those thoughts to fear and giving to those who fear a sign that they may flee from before the bow. Thus he stirs up a great conflict in the soul which produces true peace within it, while that Gospel woman lights a lamp, sweeps the house, and diligently seeks the aforesaid drachma until she finds it (Luke 15:8).

VI. Behold Joshua’s stone knives: [Col. 0376B] these two virtues bestowed upon you by Christ Jesus with strong perseverance and persevering strength—namely, strict discipline, preserving good things when they are possessed; and self-accusation, restoring good things when they are lost. When you have been circumcised by these, you shall immediately hear from the Lord: “Today I have taken away the reproach of Egypt from you” (Josh. 5:9). What does this mean? Is the reproach of Egypt not removed from the children of Israel unless they have first been circumcised by Joshua’s stone knives? Indeed this is so, as you will see once it is clear to you what Egypt is and what its reproach is. Let us run through it briefly. [Col. 0376C]

Egypt is this world, for “Egypt” signifies darkness; and, since this world lies wholly in the evil one (1 John 5:19), it does not shine with the brightness of the sun of righteousness. If Egypt, therefore, is the world, what is the reproach of Egypt except the disgrace cast upon those who imitate the world? You can in no way be free from that reproach unless you are circumcised by Joshua’s stone knives. And what great shame it is when Egyptians reproach uncircumcised children of Israel, according to that prophetic saying: “Be ashamed, O Zion, says the sea” (Isa. 23:4). Thus, when you see those clothed in secular dress justly ridicule and reproach those who walk in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves (Matt. 7:15), because they see them undisciplined in conduct and, what is worse, unconcerned for their amendment on account of the excessive obstinacy by which they have been hardened, understand this to be the reproach of Egypt by which these children of Israel are touched—if indeed [Col. 0376D] they are children of Israel, though they have not been circumcised with Joshua’s stone knives.

Woe to such children of Israel, who bear this most glorious name in vain! I should rightly call them not unlike Babylonians, since in every respect they are even worse than Egyptians. Woe, I say, to those who take away the key of knowledge, for they neither enter themselves nor permit those entering to do so (Matt. 23:13). Do you not see many people today who are thus disposed: although they have knowledge and profession of holy religion, they neither do the things of true religion [Col. 0377A] themselves nor, so far as lies in them, allow others to live religiously, because they corrupt them by their depraved counsels and examples?

VII. What, or how, is one to deal with these smoking firebrands? Would it not be better for those who scandalize the little ones who believe in Christ that a millstone be hung around their necks and that they be submerged in the depth of the sea? (Matt. 18:6). Yet these people, children of Israel in dress and name alone, rest indeed in the law, say that they glory in God, and claim to know God’s will and to approve the better things, instructed by the law (Rom. 2:18–19); confident in themselves as guides of the blind, light to those in darkness, instructors of the foolish, teachers of infants, possessing in the law the form of knowledge and truth. [Col. 0377B] Yet while teaching others, they do not teach themselves. They say that adultery must not be committed, yet commit adultery; they say that theft must not be committed, yet steal. They glory in the law and dishonour God through transgressing the law. “For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations” through these so-called children (Rom. 2:20–24).

Is blasphemy not brought upon the name of the Lord through these so-called children of Israel when it is not merely “as the people, so the priest,” but rather “as the people, not so the priest” (Hos. 4:9)? It is not merely “as the secular person, so the religious,” because “as the secular person, not so the religious”: the latter is in every respect either inferior in evil or superior in good. Now Sodom and Judaea justify themselves, because the secular person who by living badly was formerly silent in praise of the Creator judges himself either less unjust or more just than Religious [Col. 0377C] who confess Christ merely by dress and name. Do you not declare such persons worthy to be called and marked by the reproach of Egypt, when many may be found in Egypt whom circumcision of the heart in the Spirit, not in the letter, adorns (Rom. 2:29), whose praise is not from human beings but from God? Yet these are uncircumcised in mind and conduct: excessive in superfluity, polluted by impurity, outwardly undisciplined, and inwardly hardened. But enough about them.

VIII. But you, brethren, are those from whom the Lord has taken away the reproach of Egypt: you who “walk honourably toward those who are outside” (1 Thess. 4:11); [Col. 0377D] who shine as lights in the world amid a crooked and perverse nation, holding fast the word of life for the glory of Christ (Phil. 2:15); who so display your light before others that, seeing your good works, they cannot but glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16). Thus it comes about that one who is opposed—if there is such a one—may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about you (Titus 2:8). For the holiness of your conduct breaks the lions’ teeth and stops the mouths of detractors hateful to God (Rom. 12:17), while you walk blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord and provide things good not only before God but also before all people, being at peace with all people [variant: “as far as lies in you, being at peace with people”].

[Col. 0378A] But if perhaps, for the increase of your glory, your rivals—infected with the poison of envy—lie in wait for you, since, according to the proverb, “envy aims at the highest,” and Cain’s malice does not assail one who cannot be Abel: if, I say, something of this kind happens to you, do not be excessively troubled; do not become excessively faint-hearted. Remember that envy kills only the small, as a certain wise man says (Job 5:11); and unless Joseph’s father loved him more than all his sons, his brothers’ envy would not have touched him (Gen. 37:4). Take also another, and not insignificant, consolation when something of this kind occurs: those Babylonians would not have found any occasion against this Daniel except in his law and his God (Dan. 6:5). Therefore those who are such, when the Lord himself dissipates their perverse counsel, [Col. 0378B] shall encounter darkness by day among you and grope as at night in the noonday (Job 5:14), as the holy guests are brought in by Lot and the door is shut, and the enemies raging outside are struck with blindness so that they cannot find the door (Gen. 19:10). You now understand, I think, how great is the benefit that comes to spiritual Israelites from these knives of Joshua: when Joshua himself has circumcised them, the reproach of Egypt is taken away from them—from you.

IX. I have already told you, and you have heard, what these knives are: I called one discipline and the other compunction. Since the human being consists of body and soul, we assigned the former to cleansing the body and the latter to cleansing the soul. We also said that the former preserves good things already possessed: [Col. 0378C], while the latter recovers those lost: the former cuts away superfluities so that they do not grow; the latter cleanses foul things so that they do not defile. You should know, however, that discipline is not simple and single, but manifold and various; and thus it works great salvation. Everything imposed by God, whether he wills or permits it, and wherever, whenever, in whatever measure or manner it is imposed, is surely beneficial if received with willing and persevering patience [variant: “if received with patient perseverance and persevering patience”].

Hence Solomon’s admonition: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are corrected by him.” He adds the reason: “For whom the Lord loves he corrects” (Prov. 3:11–12), “and he scourges every son [Col. 0378D] whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). One of blessed Job’s friends says, “Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects” (Job 5:17). Hence he adds by way of warning: “Therefore do not reject the rebukes of the Lord, for he wounds and heals; he strikes, and his hands will heal. In six tribulations he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you” (ibid. 18–19). He plainly shows by these words that those who patiently endure temporal tribulation will escape eternal tribulation. On the other hand, “upon those who fear frost snow shall fall” (Job 6:16). Hence that saving admonition of our teacher: “Persevere in discipline” (Heb. 12:7); and shortly afterward: “For what son is there whom his father does not correct? But if you are without discipline, of which all have become partakers, then you are illegitimate children and not sons” (ibid. 8). You see that those who do not share in discipline cannot be sons. [Col. 0379A]

X. You see also that discipline is fourfold, and that we have called it the first knife by which we must be circumcised if we desire the reproach of Egypt to be removed from us. This first kind is present to us when want constrains us in the things of this world. And this knife, voluntary and honourable poverty, serves well for our spiritual circumcision. For two things must belong to poverty: willingness and honourableness. When it is voluntary, it brings cheerfulness; when honourable, it confers comeliness. On the other hand, poverty when it is not voluntary produces murmuring; and when it lacks honourableness, it is excessively uncouth and therefore not greatly to be sought by servants of God. This, then, is the first kind of discipline [Col. 0379B]: voluntary and honourable poverty, which consists in clothing, food, and the other necessities of this life.

The second resembles this: namely, the weakness of bodily illness, against which firm patience must be set. Through it almighty God both heals sins already committed and resists and prevents their future commission. You have Holy Scripture bearing witness to both. Concerning the first point I made, the Lord says to the paralytic whom he had healed in the Gospel: “Behold, you have been made whole; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). The truth of the second point he set forth was experienced in himself by the one who said: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a goad of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Cor. 12:7). Who could deny that this knife [Col. 0379C] is good? Its sharpness both cuts away whatever superfluous things may have been admitted, and resists and prevents the admission of things that have never been admitted. For when a person is touched by bodily infirmity, he is turned to a more careful examination of himself; shaken by fear and struck by pain, he not only grieves because he has been wounded, but also takes care lest he be wounded further.

XI. The third kind of discipline is the struggle of adversity, by which God permits His chosen ones to be hard pressed, yet not to their ruin. It assails them in more than one way: sometimes it hurls insults; sometimes it inflicts losses; sometimes even lays on scourges. We understand insults as the indignity of words; losses as the deprivation of possessions; and scourges as affliction of the body. Whenever these severally happen to you, you overcome them fully when you endure them with a tranquil and peaceful mind. For exercising so exalted a virtue of patience, the examples of the saints who went before will give you strength and courage: they resisted even unto blood, striving against sin and fighting for righteousness; they performed holy and righteous deeds in devout conduct, and suffered harsh and unworthy things in grievous conflict.

Thus, if insults and verbal indignities befall you, call to mind the holy David, whom on one occasion a servant reviled, raging against him with abusive words. Indeed, chattering abuse at him, he called him “a man of blood” and also “a man of Belial” (2 Kings [Col. 0380A] 16:17), although He who knows hidden things and searches what is within testified of David that He had found a man after His own heart. Yet, though he received so great an injury, the holy prophet’s mind was not stirred to anger: he looked upon the present persecution by his son, and thus made his servant’s curse bearable to himself. Nor only this: he hoped that grace would be heaped upon him by the Lord, who saw him so wronged by a servant. For he knew that He who mocks mockers also bestows grace upon the gentle and humble.

Take also another example when someone hurls insulting words at you: another, I say, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who endured such contradiction of sinners against Himself (Heb. 12:3), so that you may not grow weary and faint in your minds. For He endured those who watched Him in deeds and those who contradicted Him in words. He was sought in order to be stoned; He was brought to the brink to be thrown down (John 10:31). He was called a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matt. 2:19); He was said to have a demon, and, as a great reproach, was also called a Samaritan (John 8:48). He indeed, as the prince of the apostles says, when reviled did not revile in return; when suffering, did not threaten, but entrusted Himself to Him who judged Him unjustly, because He Himself bore our sins in His body upon the tree, that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness (1 Pet. 2:23 ff.), altogether as Isaiah had long before sung of Him: “Like a sheep He was led to slaughter, and like [Col. 0380C] a lamb before its shearer He was silent and did not open His mouth” (Isa. 53:7). For, as is read of Him in the Gospel, when He was accused of many things, He answered nothing (Matt. 27:12).

XII. But if you seek someone punished by the loss of possessions and afflicted by suffering in the body, holy Job is at hand. He was stripped of the possession of so many and such great goods, deprived of so noble an offspring, and moreover smitten in his flesh with a most grievous ulcer, from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. He was reduced to such extremity of degradation that, sitting on a dungheap, he scraped away the discharge with a potsherd (Job 2:8). But after all this, what does the true history report concerning his equanimity and the long-suffering of his patience? “In all these things,” it says, “Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak any foolish thing against God” (Job 1:22). He avoided sinning lest, through inward pain, he should be sorrowful or agitated in heart; he refrained from speaking foolishly lest, through outward disturbance, he should dispute or cry aloud with his mouth.

Nor was he free from verbal insults, since his friends reviled him. Read the words of each of them, and you will find that, as they came to console him, so they rushed into insults: devoted indeed so far as concerned their zeal for piety [alternative reading: “their offering of it”], but undiscerning so far as concerned the rashness of their rebuke. Therefore in the one man, holy Job, you have a man struck by this threefold adversity: you see him afflicted by insults and verbal indignities, distressed by losses through the deprivation of possessions, [Col. 0381A] and punished by pains in the very affliction of his body.

XIII. The fourth kind of discipline concerns temptations, which are unceasingly troublesome to us. And rightly do I call temptations unceasingly troublesome to us, because “the life of man upon earth is temptation” (Job 7:1). This persistent assault of temptations I would call a knife no less good than sharp, by which the evil and reprobate excess within us must be cut away. For this very persistence of temptations is the nurse of humility; and humility, as you know, destroys and annihilates vices, while it establishes virtues and preserves those once established. For when a strong temptation shakes our humility, it brings us back also to our own mind, to knowledge of ourselves. When the mind [Col. 0381B] understands that it cannot suffice for itself, it wholly loses confidence in itself and commits itself to the grace of its Creator alone. Thus it comes about that, while it distrusts its own strength and trusts only in help from above, this providential touch of temptation becomes for it a sharp knife, by which everything superfluous in it is cut away and every carnal indecency that strives to break forth and grow within it is severed.

XIV. You have, then, a fourfold kind of discipline: the virtue of voluntary and honorable poverty; the weakness of bodily infirmity; the struggle of adversity rushing in; the trouble of wearying temptation. This fourfold kind of discipline I would call a four-edged knife, by which we must cut away and sever whatever we discover in ourselves to be excessive and superfluous.

There is an excess and superfluity of pleasure, murmuring, and impurity; and this threefold excess is cut away by the first knife, and, once cut away, destroyed. For pleasure is slain by the knife of poverty; this poverty, when voluntary, also expels murmuring, and, when honorable, diminishes impurity. There is also a certain superfluity: the deception of evil security and the exaltation of proud vanity. The second and fourth knives cut away the first excess; the third reduces the second to nothing by destroying it. What more dangerously deceives the human soul than secure vanity and vain [Col. 0381D] security? For security instills a deceptive boldness; and when it removes from itself vigilant self-watchfulness, it miserably happens that such blindness darkens it with its gloom that it utterly fails to know where it ought to go or by what path it ought to proceed. Hence it sometimes rushes into such misery that, being absent from itself and taking no care to be present to itself in any respect, it no longer perceives even how greatly it sins.

XV. See, then, how great an evil such security works. And what shall we say of vanity? Does it not immediately raise into the swelling of pride the mind which it corrupts by its own poison? And when it empties that mind of the virtue of true humility, it at once deprives it of its own defense and protection. For humility is the guard and defense of all holiness that is in the soul; and therefore it seems to me that taking humility from the soul is nothing other than taking a wall from a city, a stone enclosure from a vineyard, or a hedge from a garden. See how great a cause of evil is this vanity of pride of which we speak. For, to put it briefly: as it destroys humility, so it annihilates all holiness which is, or can be, in the soul.

But that you may know what remedy must be set against this twofold plague—superfluous vanity and vain superfluity—patiently endure bodily weakness when infirmity comes; likewise prudently receive the trouble of assailing temptation. Then I need hardly say that you possess a very sharp, indeed a twofold, knife with which to cut away the superfluity of this dangerous security. For when you are wearied by the discomfort of sickness and struck by the onset of temptation, anxiety of fear is produced within you, and the presumption of this evil security is driven far away. Thus this superfluity is cut away by the twofold knife of discipline.

But also gladly embrace the struggle of adversity when it comes rushing in: whether someone has injured you by verbal insults, impoverished you through the taking away of possessions, or finally afflicted you through the distress of bodily punishment. Then you have in your hand a good knife with which to cut away the superfluity of vanity. For when this threefold rushing adversity is received patiently and humbly, it pours the gentleness of humility into the mind and destroys the swelling of vanity. See how great a superfluity this fourfold knife of discipline cuts away in the human soul.

We should now speak of that knife which we called compunction, were the length of this discourse not an obstacle. Therefore in the following sermon we shall speak of it, in which we also propose, insofar as He Himself grants it, to treat something concerning the names Emmanuel and Jesus of this Child, to the praise and glory of Him who is God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLII. ALSO, FOR THE DAY OF THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD

Concerning the spiritual knives by which spiritual circumcision is to be performed, and concerning the names of Christ, Jesus and Emmanuel.

[Col. 0382D] SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON.—1. The use and benefit of compunction.—2. A vivid account, drawn from experience, of the fallen sinner and his rising again.—3. The sweetness of past wickedness turns into present bitterness.—4. From the foulness of sin arises the undying worm of conscience.—5. Conscience reproaches through attentive consideration of the holy conduct of many people.—6. Through the holiness or obligation of one’s professed rank or order.—7. Then through the frequency of repeated falls.—8. Thereafter through consideration of the character of the offended person: namely God as friend.—9. Finally through consideration of God’s strictness as severe Judge.—10. Recapitulation of mystical circumcision through its combined effects.—11. The naming of Jesus was not accidental, but revealed by divine counsel.—12. David’s triumph over Goliath prefigured the Savior Jesus Christ.—13. Jesus has His name from the reality itself: jubilation in the heart, honeycomb in the mouth.—14. The synonymy of the names Jesus and Emmanuel.—15. Jesus signifies salvation; Emmanuel, the manner [Col. 0383A] of salvation: from Him, being born, living, and dying with us, flowed the remedy for our calamity.—16. Being born with us, He took away the defect of origin; living with us, that of evil action; dying with us, that of eternal condemnation.—17. The whole basis of our confidence is in the life and death of the Lord Jesus.

I. If you remember, in the sermon which we recently delivered to your charity, we brought forth two knives by which not so much that Joshua son of Nun as our Jesus, the Son of God, circumcises true and spiritual Israelites. We called one discipline and the other spiritual compunction. We discussed the knife of discipline in that sermon as much as then seemed sufficient; and now it is time, according to our promise, to speak of that other knife, of which we deferred speaking until this point.

Accordingly, we said that the other knife, by which every true Israelite ought to perform a salutary circumcision in the soul, is spiritual compunction. We ought always to have it ready, so that by its sharpness we may cut away whatever superfluity we accumulate through unlawful action. Among the other gifts with which the merciful Lord is accustomed to assist me by bestowing the gifts of His generosity, I count it a great sign of His love when, after the guilt of a wrongful deed, He deigns to visit me with the saving remedy of compunction. For when, abandoning the straightness of righteousness, I rush down into the crookedness of guilt, I am not only unworthy that He should raise me up, but even that He should permit me to fall into worse things. For, as He Himself threatens through the prophet, when the righteous commits injustice, He will place a stumbling-block before him (Ezek. 3:20). Yet the pious and merciful Father and our Lord does not act thus toward His chosen ones: by His freely given grace He enables His children both fully to know their sins and, once known, fittingly to mourn them.

II. If you would like to know briefly how He does this with them, receive what follows. I shall discuss with you, from my own experience, what I have received in this respect. I committed a great sin—not once or twice, indeed, but repeatedly. Thus that prophetic reproach may rightly be addressed even to me: “How base you have become, repeating your ways so often!” (Jer. 2:36). And behold, after a little while a certain most bitter bitterness infects my mind, yet not to my destruction. For that saving antidote is poured in by the supreme Physician, so that the poison newly drunk may be torn from the inward parts of the soul and, once torn out, cast away. Therefore a salutary bitterness afflicts the mind which lethal sweetness had previously afflicted.

For this is usually characteristic of sin: while it is budding, urging, and not yet committed, it presents through temptation a very great and immediate sweetness; but when consent has admitted it and it has been brought into effect, it brings no lesser bitterness. Hence a certain wise man says:

> [Note: [Col. 0383D] Severinus Boethius, *Prose* 7, line 3.]
>
> The craving for bodily pleasures is full of anxiety, but their satisfaction full of repentance; for the unhappy soul grieves that it has done what, before doing it, it endured great anxiety to do.

And shortly afterward he adds:

> Every pleasure has this way:
>
> It drives those who enjoy it with goads;
>
> and, like a swarm of flying bees,
>
> when it has poured forth its pleasant honey,
>
> it flees, and, having struck,
>
> presses hearts with an excessively tenacious bite.
>
> —Boethius, Book III, 7.

III. For what delighted and caressed the soul enslaved to sin passes away; what bites and gnaws the wretched conscience remains. What was formerly embraced with burning love is held in great hatred. Sweetness turns into bitterness; delight into affliction. Did this not happen to miserable and pitiable Amnon? You know how, pierced by the arrow of illicit love, with how much effort and cunning he attained the fulfillment of his desire, long coveted; and he recoiled from its fulfillment no less than he had formerly desired to fulfill it. For once his desire was fulfilled, he could not bear even to look upon the very woman—his sister, whom he had made his wife—whom, before its fulfillment, he had loved beyond measure: the greatest hatred succeeding the greatest love in him (2 Kings 13:10).

It is well written of her that she was beautiful and was called Tamar, perhaps indicating through these things that the Holy Spirit, who willed that her story be inserted into Scripture for the profit of readers, teaches that the beauty of whatever sin draws and entices the soul is subsequently followed, after the commission [Col. 0384C] of that sin, by a bitterness which punishes and afflicts it. For, as you know, *Tamar* means “bitterness.” Know, therefore, my soul, that when you behold something unlawful as beautiful with the gaze of desire, after tasting it in experience you will also find it bitter.

And alas, you are not yet as wise in uprightness as you have become cast down by falling. For although this is a good voice of one repenting, “Alas! Alas! What have I done!” this is far better, as the voice of one taking precautions: “Far be it from me to do it!” Why does vexation alone give understanding to your hearing? Why do you not take counsel against the sickness which must be fled? What then? Even if death does not always follow it, yet rare is the person who sleeps in death unless he first grows drowsy in sickness; and death does not often follow unless sickness goes before.

IV. Therefore I have committed a great sin, and committed it frequently. A great bitterness also invades my unhappy conscience: it touches and shakes it, wounds and tortures it, then moves it and anxiously unsettles it. A certain voice within it does not whisper, but rather cries aloud—a voice, I say, perhaps of salvation, but not of exultation; the voice not of one feasting but of one reproving; not of tranquil consolation, but of great agitation. It cries thus: “Adam, where are you?” And what shall I say, or what answer shall I give myself, since I myself have done this? (Gen. 3:9).

For if I wish to say that the cause of my hiding is swollen fear and fearful swelling, and that I wish by it to guard against the disgrace of my nakedness, I shall hear, unwilling though I be: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” (Gen. 3:11). Is not the forbidden eating forbidden consent? The one destroys nakedness because the other brings in shame. O how great is the boldness of a pure conscience! O how great the trembling caused by its foulness!

Therefore this rebuking voice rages within the rooms of my inner house, thundering and flashing amid a great tumult, accusing and correcting with all authority in these words: “Why is there such great iniquity in you? What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed? For their end is death. If you have sown in the flesh, what will you reap but corruption?” (Gal. 6:8). “Why has this apostolic declaration escaped your mind? And why that other: ‘If you live according to the flesh, you shall die’?” (Rom. 8:13). “If you have loved the world, what profit pertaining even remotely to eternity can its love give you, when the world itself passes away and its desire also?” (1 John 2:17). “Why did you choose adultery? For to love the world itself is to hate God. You read, though in vain: ‘If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him’” (2 John 2:15). Thus this voice reproves me and sets me before my own face, sealing up my offenses as though in a sack (Job 14:17), stoning me with my own filth and smearing my face with my own mud.

V. It also sets before me the holy conduct of others, so that from it I may understand more fully that my own foulness deserves condemnation. It renews its witnesses against me, so that they almost wage war upon me. For to this end it shows me, with the prophet, the temple, that I may measure it and be ashamed of all that I have done (Ezek. 43:10). It commands me to look back upon people, so that I may accordingly say: “I have sinned” (Job 33:27). And to heap up my shame, it sets before my eyes people who appear both weaker and less learned than I, yet are far above me: more skillful in guarding against defilements and stronger in overcoming temptations.

“You are wise, then—but wise to do evil; you do not know how to do good” (Jer. 4:22). For in what way, and to what advantage, are you wise if you are not wise for yourself? And strong, if your strength is like a spark of tow? (Isa. 1:31). For as tow in fire, so is your strength [Col. 0385D] in temptation.

VI. It also sets against me my rank and my orders: the height of my profession and the time since my conversion. “Should a deacon or priest, a canon clothed in the habit of religion, have committed such a thing? Was it fitting that a servant of God should be a servant of sin? Was it therefore becoming that a friend and intimate of the Lord, the bridegroom’s friend and herald of Christ, should admit into himself something that so gravely displeased so great and such a Lord?

“Behold how often you have violated the vows of your profession, which your lips uttered” (Ps. 65:14). “How much better it would have been for you not to have vowed than not to have performed the vow! Why should not the very loftiness of profession be a greater accumulation of condemnation for one who vows many things and not merely fails to fulfill his vow, but indeed dares many things contrary to his vow? And how greatly have you advanced since you came to conversion? In the morning you seemed to set out upon the journey, and behold, with evening already falling, you have scarcely gone out the door. How many began to travel this path long after you, and have not merely reached you but courageously run ahead of you! ‘Being made perfect in a short time, they fulfilled long years, for their souls were pleasing to God’” (Wis. 4:13).

VII. After all these things, what moves and troubles me more deeply is that it impresses upon me the frequency of my falls. For it addresses me in this way and says: “Your wound is most grievous and almost incurable. So often it has been bound up; so often healed by medicine; so often soothed with oil; so often a scar has been drawn over it” (Isa. 1:6). Countless are the occasions on which you have been healed. But know that this is said not to your praise but to your disgrace: for, often healed, you show yourself often wounded. The same I understand concerning the occasions of your amendment: often cleansed, you have also often been defiled.

“And how long will these things continue with you? How long, I say, will you be like a dog returning to its vomit, or like a washed sow in a wallow of mud?” (2 Pet. 2:22). “How long will you be so dull, so devoid of sense, that, wounded so often, you no longer shrink from being wounded? Do you suppose that at some point the physician is not wearied by his patient, seeing that the patient indeed seeks health but does not wish to retain it once obtained; and that the cleanser is not wearied by one defiled, seeing that he desires washing when it is absent but, when it is present, takes no care to preserve it?”

VIII. By these and similar means this great voice impresses upon me the enormity and frequency of my sin. It also sets before my eyes Him against whom I sinned, showing Him to me sometimes as friend and lover, sometimes as strict and severe Judge: the one before whom I was ashamed, the other before whom I trembled. It says to me concerning the former:

“Why did you wish to act so as to return evil for good? Against whom did you sin, and whom did you offend through sin? He is your friend and lover; He is also your Father and Benefactor. What did He do to you, or how was He burdensome to you, that you provoked Him to anger? When you did not exist, He created you in His image and likeness. When you were lost, He redeemed you by the lavish shedding of His compassionate and innocent [Col. 0386D] blood. When you were sold under sin, He called you out of the world. He gave you a retentive memory, a learned tongue, keenness of intellect, and brilliance of expression. And, because it would take long to go through one by one the gifts of His grace that He bestowed on you: from an outsider He made you a neighbor; from a servant He advanced you to be a son.

“How worthily you responded to these and His other gifts of generosity, you may see for yourself. See what good command from Him you did not disregard, and what forbidden evil you did not commit. In a brief statement I have shown you to yourself. What more shall I say? You, as a son against a Father—and such a Father—have acted more wickedly than another would act against his enemy.”

IX. Concerning that severe and strict Judge, this voice speaks to me thus, filling all my inward parts with a very great sorrow: “How have you, light dust, you vile ash, dared to raise yourself against so great and such a Majesty? How have you been made foolish by such great folly, hardened by such insensibility, that you presumed to provoke to anger so strict and severe a Judge? Do you not know that He ‘touches the mountains and they smoke’ (Ps. 103:32); that dominions worship Him and powers fear Him; that before His presence every conscience trembles, and no creature at all can endure His anger?

“You have transgressed against Him, and you have dared by your transgressions to provoke Him to anger. You have read in Isaiah that ‘the worm of men who have transgressed against Him shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched’ (Isa. 66:24). How will you, dry straw, be able to endure when that immeasurable and consuming fire displays the heat of its flames? When His anger burns against such persons? When, finally, a fire has been kindled in His fury and burns to the lowest depths of hell, devouring the earth with its increase and burning the foundations of the mountains?” (Deut. 32:22).

“Consider now within yourself what courage you will then be able to have, when you are compelled to give an account not only of each of your deeds, but also of your words—not indeed of words and deeds alone, but even of the most minute movements of your thoughts and the intentions of your heart. Weep, weep—not a little, but long and much over your sorrow. Weep because you go and do not return, to a land of darkness covered with the gloom of death: a land of misery and darkness, where the shadow of death dwells, and no order, but everlasting horror” (Job 10:21).

X. In these ways this voice speaks within me: first, setting before my face and showing me how great the evils are that I have committed; second, how often I have sinned; third, what kindly Father and generous Benefactor I have offended; fourth, upon what strict and severe Judge I have rushed. In the first disclosure it afflicts me with most powerful horror; in the second it shakes me with boundless grief; in the third it confounds me with the deepest shame; in the fourth it terrifies me with anxious fear. This is the fourfold effect of compunction, which we said is the second knife by which we must be circumcised.

This knife is indeed exceedingly sharp: it not only cuts away superfluities already accumulated, but also resists their accumulation. For what unlawful superfluity will the mind admit into itself when, considering the magnitude of its evils, sorrow thoroughly afflicts it; when, seeing how often it has sinned, horror strikes it; when it sees how great and what manner of lover it has offended, shame confounds it; and when, finally, it beholds what a dreadful Judge it has provoked to anger, fear disturbs it?

You have, therefore, two stone knives: one is called discipline, the other compunction. The former circumcises those who stand, lest they incur monstrous superfluity and superfluous monstrosity; the latter cleanses those who have fallen, so that they may escape what they have incurred. Both have a fourfold effect in the remedy of cleansing. The former cuts off impurity already committed: through voluntary and honorable poverty, making a person temperate; through the weakness of bodily infirmity, making him fearful; through the trouble of rushing adversity, instilling humility in him; and through the assault of pressing temptations, making him concerned for his salvation. But inward compunction of mind, in the person into whom it pours itself fully, guards him lest the superfluity of anything contract impurity: afflicting through sorrow, shaking through horror, confounding through shame, and frightening through fear.

XI. But we have now held these knives in our hands long enough. Let us now speak of the name of this Child. For as He was circumcised on this day, so on this day His name Jesus was given to Him. Nor was He called by this name accidentally, but by the angel’s foretelling. Thus holy Luke says: “His name was called Jesus, which had been called by the angel before He was conceived in the womb” (Luke 2:21).

The Holy of holies does not bear this holy name in vain, but in deed and truth. For what He is called, that He also accomplishes: namely, salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. 73:12). “She shall bear you a son,” the angel says to holy Joseph, “and you shall call His name Jesus” (Matt. 1:21). Nor did he conceal the reason: “For He,” he says, “shall save His people from their sins” (ibid.). You see, then, what is the mystery of this blessed and beatifying name Jesus: namely, that He is called Jesus because He shall save His people from their sins.

For He is the true David, in whose hand the Lord delivers His people from the hand of the Philistines (2 Kings [Col. 0388C] 19:9). To this, I think, pertains what Paul says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself” (2 Cor. 5:19); and likewise what his fellow apostle Peter says: “He went about doing good and healing all those oppressed by the devil, because God was with Him” (Acts 10:38).

O our holy David, faithful not only in all things, but above all! “For who among the clouds shall be compared to the Lord? Who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88:7). O He whom God the Father found after His own heart, according to that true testimony: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17:5). “I have found a man after My own heart,” says God concerning our David (Acts 13:22). And fittingly, the man whom seven women seized (Isa. 4:1), because God does not give the Spirit by measure; Him whose glory we have seen, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). “And of His fullness we have all received” (ibid., 16).

XII. He is indeed the man whom Ezekiel saw clothed in linen among the six men (Ezek. 9:2), who came from the gate facing north, each having in his hand a vessel of destruction. This signifies, as you know, that this strong and mighty David, the Lord of hosts, appeared among men clothed in flesh assumed from a most pure Virgin Mother. All men, throughout the six [Col. 0389A] ages of the world, proceeded from sin through corruptible birth and had in their own works something belonging to deadly sin.

Perhaps this was when, after entrusting the flock to its keeper, He was sent by the Father and went laden to His brothers (1 Kings 17:20 ff.). That is, leaving those ninety-nine in the wilderness, fearing no danger whatever for them because He had left them in a safe place, He descended, sent to the sheep that had perished, full of grace and truth, to visit and comfort all who desired Him with their whole heart (Matt. 18:2). Nor did He return to His Father before He had slain with his own sword that proud Gittite who came forth morning and evening, standing for forty days—because he had no sword of his own—and brought his head to Jerusalem.

You must take care to refer all these things to our David, this Child circumcised today, whose name was also called Jesus. For as He came forth from the Father and came into the world (John 16:28), so neither did He leave the world and go to the Father until He had triumphed over the prince of this world, who oppressed His chosen ones—for they say that this name, *Geth*, has this meaning. Throughout the whole time of this life until Christ’s coming, he was hostile and troublesome in both prosperity and adversity. All fled from his face, and no one was found who dared enter a single combat with him except the humble boy David. He alone triumphed over him, striking him down and removing reproach from Israel.

And how did He triumph over him? He who had no wicked sword of iniquity in the hand of His own action received from the very members of the devil the providential sword of death, [Col. 0389C] so that, slain, He might slay; truly dying for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also that He might gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11:51–52), joining even those who were highest and most eminent in the body of the devil to the unity and peace of the holy Church. Does this not seem to you to be that proud giant slain by David with his own sword, and his head cut off from his body and brought to Jerusalem?

XIII. O holy and saving name, Jesus, because His work too is holy and saving! This name alone, as it seems to me, is the unique and singular token of our salvation. Who can comprehend—much less express—how saving either the name or the work named is? Did not the one who said that no other name has been given to human beings in which we must be saved understand this? (Acts 4:12).

This name is most beautiful and most holy: a name of exultation and salvation, a name of gladness and sweetness, finally a name of pleasantness and delight. He understood this well who said: “But I will rejoice in the Lord and exult in God my Jesus” (Hab. 3:18). How sweet this name is to his throat—above honey and honeycomb to his mouth (Ps. 18:11)! Who will grant me that not only my mind but also my tongue may be ceaselessly occupied with this name: the mind in thinking, the tongue in speaking? For Jesus is, just as He is a joyful jubilation in the heart, so also savory food in the mouth.

Surely there is no longer anything to make sorrowful the heart in which this voice of exultation and joy resounds; nor is there anything to make bitter the palate which chews this sweetest and most savory food. “His name,” says the Evangelist, “was called Jesus, which had been called by the angel before He was conceived in the womb” (Luke 2:11): before He was conceived, He was called. What is this? The Church conceived this Jesus in her womb when, through faith working by love, she admitted Him, the author of her salvation, into her inward parts (Gal. 5:6). But before she conceived Him in her womb in this way, the angel called His name Jesus.

[Col. 0390B] If an angel called Him—if an angel is a messenger—what then were Moses and Isaiah, and indeed every patriarch and prophet who foretold, by sign or word, that our salvation would be bestowed and brought to completion in this Jesus and through this Jesus, except angels? And since each of them prophesied that He would come to save us not only before the Church believed in Him, but even long before He appeared in the flesh, surely His name was called Jesus before He was conceived in the womb.

XIV. But we must speak of the meaning of this most holy and most sweet name, Jesus. A question arises: why is he called Jesus by the angel, but Emmanuel by Isaiah? “A virgin,” he says, “shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14). [Col. 0390C] Saint Matthew also took care to recall this passage, when he introduces the angel explaining the reason for this most saving and blessed name, Jesus. For after asserting that the angel said to Joseph, “You shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21), he immediately adds: “Now all this was done that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: Behold, a virgin shall have in her womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, **GOD WITH US** (ibid., vv. 22–23).

The angel calls his name Jesus and explains what this means: “He,” he says, “shall save his people from their sins.” The prophet calls the same one Emmanuel and explains what this means: “which,” he says, “is interpreted, GOD WITH US.” If this Jesus is Emmanuel, we may understand both that he himself saves us and that God himself is with us. That this is so we shall discover most certainly if we endeavor to investigate either how he saves us or how God is with us.

For if anyone asks, “Who is this God?” he himself is our Jesus. How then is he with us? Is it in the manner in which he is “King of the ages, immortal, invisible” (1 Tim. 1:17); in which the Only-Begotten is in the bosom of the Father; in which he was begotten “from the womb before the morning star,” amid the splendors of the saints (Ps. 109:3); in which, finally, dwelling in inaccessible light, [Col. 0390D] he is equal to the Father—whom no human being has seen, nor indeed can see? (1 Tim. 6:16). Not at all: God is not with us in that manner. Rather, I think, he is with us in the manner in which he was “made lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6); in which he is “the firstborn among many brethren” (Rom. 8:29), and also “the firstborn from the dead” (Rev. 1:5); in which he had with us what he received from us for us—namely, what is common among us: to be born and to die. Behold, in this manner God is with us.

Full of every sweetness and delight in the human mouth is this utterance, Emmanuel. For how should that which belongs, beyond all other creatures, to the human being alone not be sweet for a human being to pronounce? For, in this sense, angels cannot utter it, nor, briefly speaking, can any other creature; since they have the same nature with which they are creatures. But he is with the human being in such a way that he is with him, and the human being receives into himself what he is and becomes what he is.

XV. O holy and saving name, Jesus! O pleasant and joyful name, Emmanuel! The one indicates our salvation; the other, the manner of that salvation. He made us safe because he was God with us. With which “us” was God himself? With us human beings—with us, certainly, who are born, who live, who die: we are born in uncleanness; we live in wickedness; we die in sorrow. “Behold, a human being born of woman, living for a short time, filled with many miseries” (Job 14:1). This is the voice of a righteous man lamenting the threefold calamity of humankind: defiled in birth, depraved in life, condemned in death. [Col. 0391B]

Hence he added: one born of a woman comes forth like a flower in frailty; living only a short time, he is crushed, yet remains in perversity; and, fleeing like a shadow, he runs toward death with all haste. But there is great consolation: Jesus is born, lives, and at last dies. Thus God is with us in birth, in life, and in death. Yet, being born without impurity and living without perversity, he cleansed those born unclean and justified those acting wickedly; finally, dying voluntarily and without obligation, soon to rise and to live forever, he made blessed those who die under condemnation. Moreover, shortly after his birth—namely, today—he deigned to undergo circumcision in his most holy flesh, according to the law established for cleansing the flesh. [Col. 0391C–D]

XVI.

In the thirtieth year of his age, the Lord also received baptism from a servant, instituting it for the full remission of sins (Matt. 3:13). Thus in these two sacraments he established a remedy for the disease of original sin for those who are of Abraham’s stock; and, in this time of revealed grace, he established cleansing in the washing of baptism.

Then in his manner of life he displayed every holiness: uttering truth in speech, showing purity in deed. For just as, conceived from the Virgin, he did not contract sin, so neither did he commit it during all the time in which he lived in the world. Thus his manner of life made a way for us by which we might reach our heavenly homeland: for, by showing what evil must be omitted and what good must be embraced, he taught us what we ought to flee and what we ought to seek.

Finally, since he was wholly ignorant of sin and therefore in no way liable to it, he underwent for us an undeserved death, and thereby freed us from the death that was due to us. He drove from us the eternal condemnation which we deserved in both soul and body, while he admitted into his flesh alone the suffering of temporal death, which he did not deserve. For the innocent blood of the spotless and undefiled Lamb, Jesus—merciful and meek—was poured out upon the altar of the cross. By its outpouring, crying from the earth more powerfully than Abel’s blood (Heb. 11:24), God who was offended is appeased and guilty humankind is reconciled. [Col. 0392A–B]

Thus, in a wondrous and merciful way, a human being can now die without fear of condemnation, because God made man died for him without any debt of condemnation. Thus our Emmanuel, being born with us, cleansed us from the corruption of a vitiated origin; living with us, justified us from the perversity of evil works; and dying with us and for us, freed us from the condemnation of eternal death.

XVII. What, then, do I fear, or why should I tremble? What if I have contracted original defilement from the first parent, in whom we all sinned? The sacrament of baptism, instituted by our supreme physician, will cleanse it and, by cleansing, erase it: he “who heals all our infirmities” (Ps. 102:3), both instituting this remedy of purification for us and receiving it in himself for us. He had not only nothing unclean in himself that required washing, but he alone is also able to make clean one conceived from unclean seed (Job 14:4). [Col. 0392C]

But if perhaps I do not walk rightly upon the path of righteousness, I shall go to him who was made for us by God not only sanctification but also righteousness (1 Cor. 1:30). In that book of life spread open before me I shall read not only what vices tending toward ruin I ought to avoid, but also what virtue tending toward ascent I ought to practice. When I must depart from here, I shall set death against death: the death of Christ’s body against the death of my soul. Then I shall hope in his death and in his resurrection: in the former, lest I perish in eternal death; in the latter, that I may rise to life. For he who died for me so that I should not die, he likewise rose again so that I might rise.

Therefore, thanks be to you, good and gracious Jesus, who deigned both to be born from us, to live among us, and to die for us, showing yourself in these things to bear the holy name Emmanuel, which is interpreted, “God with us.” To you—to you, I say, Lord—who, being born, cleansed us from the ancient defilement of original sin; who, living, justified us from the iniquity of wickedness; who, dying, freed us from the calamity of hell: to you, from the deepest marrow of our hearts, O Jesus, O Emmanuel—O Emmanuel and Jesus!—be honor [Col. 0392D] and glory, splendor and magnificence, majesty and praise for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIII. ON THE DAY OF THE LORD’S EPIPHANY

### On the Lord’s threefold manifestation

**SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON.**—1. To praise and proclaim God: the twofold praiseworthy office of the tongue.—2. The Church commemorates three miracles performed on one day; their order briefly examined.—3. In these three miracles our calling, justification, and glorification are expressed.—4. The fitting correspondence of calling through the Magi, justification through baptism, and glorification through the wedding at Cana of Galilee.—5. The greatness and order of these three benefits further explained by the analogy of a constructed house and Christ’s age.—6. Christ as a child is recognized in Bethlehem, that is, the house of bread; he is baptized in Jordan, that is, descent.—7. [Col. 0393A] He manifests his glory in Cana of Galilee, that is, zeal for revelation. Love surpasses every contemplation and action.—8. Herod’s kingdom now prevails: that is, the kingdom of pride and luxury.—9. Mystically, Bethlehem of Judah signifies the congregation of religious persons.—10. A religious manner of life is like a brightly shining star.—11. To neglect one’s good reputation is blameworthy, indeed cruel.—12. The sin of a religious person is marked as more grievously harmful for three reasons.

I. Great is my gladness, dearest brethren, and immense the joy in my heart. I give many thanks to God for you, seeing you come together with such eagerness in these holy days to hear the word of God. Although it is fitting for us at every time to attend to divine things, reason itself also requires that on feast days we should devote greater devotion to those things which are especially God’s. For the more external works cease on such days, the more diligently it is necessary that the tongue should apply itself to the divine work, that we should offer God the holocausts of our lips, and that in opening them we should proclaim his praise.

We worthily exercise this holy and saving work of the tongue when, in pure prayer, we give ourselves to God’s praises, and in sound preaching labor to exhort our neighbor. It is fitting that the holy tongue should devote itself to this twofold office: joyfully celebrating God in prayer with worthy proclamations, and instructing the minds of our neighbors through the holy words of devout exhortation. Since we have bestowed some care, according to our measure, upon one of these saving works—namely, the persistence of devout prayers—both in the preceding night and on the present day, it remains for us to undertake the other, which is the instruction of our neighbors, since the opportunity of the time now presents itself. Thus we show ourselves as devoted to God in the former and useful to our neighbor in the latter. [Col. 0393B–D]

Since, then, we are to speak something for the benefit of our hearers, from what source should we take matter for speaking rather than from the very day on which we speak? For as the excellence of the present day demands that we say something on it for the praise of God and your edification, so it likewise requires that we speak about it—especially since its holiness is so great and such that it can provide us with abundant and sufficient material for discourse.

II. For, as we sing: “Today we celebrate the holy day adorned with three miracles: today the star led the Magi to the manger; today wine was made from water for the wedding; today Christ willed to be baptized in the Jordan, that he might save us all.”  
[Note: [Col. 0393D] Antiphon at the *Magnificat* in second Vespers.]

Concerning these miracles, indeed, the orthodox Fathers have said much, as you know. Do not expect to hear anything new from us, who are not only altogether incapable of discovering anything new, but are neither sufficiently penetrating in intellect to understand their sayings fully nor sufficiently tenacious in memory to retain what we have understood. Yet I want your love to know that not only the depth and height of these very miracles, but also their sequence and order, make me thoughtful. I look closely not merely at the fact that the Lord did great things, but I diligently investigate what he did first and what afterward. The former, certainly, seems to me to pertain to the will of the omnipotent worker; the latter to his dispensation. Both serve a spiritual signification, and through neither is our edification lacking.

But before we treat their depth, let us first say something briefly concerning their order. The order, I think, is this: first, guided by the star, he revealed himself to the Gentiles, and, when revealed, presented himself to be devoutly and faithfully adored and honored with mystical gifts. Next, he humbly bowed himself to be baptized by the hands of blessed John; and, immersed in the waters, he bestowed sanctification upon the waters for our spiritual cleansing. Finally, he powerfully changed water into wine at the wedding and, gladdening the guests, also increased the faith of his disciples. [Col. 0394A–C]

In each of these we venerate his holy and sanctifying manifestation and embrace his admirable condescension. His first manifestation he showed to the Magi; his second he granted to the people; his third he bestowed upon his disciples. For concerning the first you read that, when he was born, Magi came from the East (Matt. 2:1): coming, they sought; seeking, they found; finding, they adored. This, as you know, is the substance of the Gospel’s account of the Magi’s coming to the child Jesus.

Concerning the second, you have that, “when all the people were baptized, and Jesus also having been baptized and praying, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove,” together with the other matters which the holy Evangelist mentions concerning him afterward (Luke 3:22 ff.). We think this is the people standing before whom blessed John, seeing the Lord hasten to his baptism, immediately burst forth in these words: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). The reality concerning the third manifestation is this: “Jesus did this as the beginning of signs” (John 2:11)—undoubtedly, this changing of water into wine—“and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him” (ibid.). [Col. 0394D]

III. Moreover, if the very places in which these manifestations were granted are thought to suggest anything, the first was Bethlehem, the second in Jordan, the third in Cana of Galilee. Perhaps it is relevant that the first was in the house of bread, the second in descent, the third in zeal of migration or of accomplished revelation. For, as you know, these are the interpretations of those names. Far be it from us to suppose devoid of significance the Lord’s willing to appear in the dwelling-place of eternal refreshment, in the power of humility, and in the ardor of spiritual knowledge. Whether these places contain some spiritual meaning in themselves will become apparent when we begin to treat their significance.

To show briefly what I understand in the order of this third manifestation of the Lord, I take the first to express our calling, the second our cleansing, and the third our glorification. For the Magi would never have come from such distant and remote regions of the earth to adore the newly born child unless they had been summoned not only by the novelty of an outward sign but also by some inward voice of instruction. Thus, in the words of blessed Pope Leo which you heard last night: “He who gave the sign gave understanding to those who looked upon it; and what he caused to be understood, he caused to be sought; and, being sought, he offered himself to be found.”  
[Note: [Col. 0395D] St. Leo, Sermon 1 on the Epiphany.]

What was this giving of a sign in such a way as to give understanding to those who beheld it, except a calling by which he invited them to himself? And who doubts that in Christ’s baptism our cleansing is not only expressed but actually effected? For he who was baptized was baptized not for himself but for us. Finally, he was baptized not in order to be cleansed, but rather in order “to cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14): having no defilement whatsoever and freely bestowing purification. At the wedding, however, as the Evangelist says, “he manifested his glory” (John 2:11). That miracle which he performed there was a great work of power and glory. [Col. 0395A–C]

IV. Certainly the order is good and most fitting: that by a threefold manifestation on this day, in the first he should show us called, in the second justified, and in the third glorified.  
[Alternative reading: *innotescens in prima*, “being made known in the first,” etc.]

This is what Paul, privy to this mystery, understood when he declared—as you can understand by reading—that God called those whom he predestined; justified those whom he called; and glorified those whom he justified (Rom. 8:30). Therefore, we are called when we are summoned to faith; we are justified when, cleansed from former sins, we are adorned with works of righteousness; and we are glorified not only when, in the future, we are rewarded through the reception of heavenly glory, but also when, in the present, we glory in the Lord through the perception of inward glory, which consists in the testimony of a true and un-deceived conscience.

First, therefore, because of ignorance we are far off in the darkness of blindness; he calls us that through faith we may be near in the knowledge of truth. Second, cleansing us from dead works, he makes us serve the living God, so that, just as we once presented our members to serve iniquity unto iniquity, so now, changed by the visitation of the right hand of the Most High, we may present those same members to serve righteousness unto righteousness (Rom. 6:19). Third, when perfect love in us casts out fear, like water changed into wine, after the old wine has first failed, water is drawn from the jars (1 John 4:18), so that the new wine may not fail. Though these jars contain nothing but water, even when filled to the brim, they pour forth nothing but wine—and good wine at that, as having been kept until now. [Col. 0395D–0396A]

Thus our Lord Jesus, in this third act changing this spiritual water into wine equally spiritual, makes those inward guests of the mind—I mean pure thoughts—fully secure because conscious of their own goodness. For, as Solomon says, “A secure mind is a continual feast” (Prov. 15:15). Those guests, I say, he renders wonderfully exhilarated with exultation in the manifestation of his glory, and he presents them as glorified through revelation. This is conferred at the wedding when the bride, the soul, is joined to the bridegroom, the Word. When we come to that place, we shall endeavor, insofar as we can, to show what these nuptials signify, together with certain things perhaps pertaining to them.

Calling therefore comes first, justification follows, and glorification comes last. Thus we who were blinded and far off may be enlightened and near; we who lacked the marks of holiness may be filled with works of righteousness; and we who, having a seared conscience through desire for impure pleasure, were once shameful, may, through a stable and persevering purpose of holiness and the unfading purity of inward contemplation, become glorious, being conscious of our good estate in every respect. He would glorify in vain those whom he had not first cleansed; nor would he have any to glorify or cleanse unless he who alone is clean first called those to be cleansed and glorified—he who is truly glorious. [Col. 0396B–C]

V. The faithful soul, then, thus both justified and glorified, is in a certain sense a house in which God its Creator deigns to dwell. In this house faith, which is the foundation in calling, is laid beneath; hope, which belongs to justification, raises the walls; and love, which belongs to glorification, both lays the roof above externally and adorns the house itself within with a beautiful arrangement of various colors. See, then, that what a roof without a wall is in a house, glorification without justification is in the soul; and what a wall without a foundation is, justification without calling is.

Understand further that, just as roof and wall cannot stand without a foundation, and a foundation cannot suffice for the completion of a house without wall and roof, so glorification and justification in a soul lacking calling entirely lack stability; and calling, unless it has both of these, lacks sufficiency for salvation. The soul itself, as we said a little earlier, cannot at all attain glorification unless it has first obtained justification; nor can it be justified unless it has first happened to be called. For justification is the cause of glorification, and calling must precede so that justification may follow.

Therefore, for an evident reason, on this holy day the child Jesus was first adored by the Magi who had been called; then, no longer a child but now a fully grown man, he was baptized by John; and finally, performing a remarkable and sublime miracle, he manifested his glory and was himself glorified. In this he indicates to us, as has already been said, that we, first childish and tender—having as yet nothing toward salvation except knowledge of the truth alone—must be summoned to him through the belief of right faith; then, having attained greater strength in spiritual vigor, must be cleansed by him from every stain of evil conduct which we have contracted by sinning; and, finally, must be glorified in him through that inward purity which a pure heart and a good conscience are accustomed to possess. [Col. 0396D–0397B]

VI. That he urged the aforesaid Magi, by calling them to the house of bread—for this is what Bethlehem means—to know him: what else ought you to understand except that [alternative: *quam quod*, “than that”] knowledge of the truth exists nowhere other than in the dwelling-place of inward refreshment? For, as you know, the true bread is the Word of God; therefore the Word is known through the word. The mind which is sweetly nourished by a sound and catholic understanding of his discourse clearly apprehends the truth, which is Christ.

Therefore the Magi are called to Bethlehem in order that they may find the child Jesus, because if you lack in your house the bread of God’s word, you do not possess within yourself that true bread which “came down from heaven and gives life to the world” (John 6:33). But he was baptized in Jordan, whose name means descent, because unless you are humbled, you are not justified. Did not holy David understand this when he said that it was good for him that God had humbled him, so that he might learn his judgments? (Ps. 118:17). “Upon whom,” he says, “does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble person and one trembling at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). In the Gospel too he says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29). [Col. 0397B–C]

Let the one who desires to be justified, then, be in descent, since John baptizes Christ in Jordan. “And whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11), because no one ascends except the one who descends (John 3:13). Descent, therefore, is humility, and one is justified only in it, just as Christ is baptized nowhere but in Jordan. We pass over the many things that ought to be said concerning this virtue of humility, because we hasten to other matters and defer them to another occasion.

VII. But in zeal of migration or revelation—for these two names, Cana and Galilee, are said to contain these meanings—is bestowed this holy glorification of which we have treated above. For if, with the zeal of good devotion, you pass in the steps of love from vices to virtues by acting well, from present things to heavenly things by devout desire; if you ardently love in affection whatever has been plainly revealed to you in understanding: you have obtained this inward glorification from Jesus, who manifested his glory in Cana of Galilee.

Accordingly, you attain this glorification if you contemplate purely, act vigorously, and finally love ardently both what you grasp in contemplation and what you accomplish in action. Revelation, migration, and love seem to express these things. These are three, but love is the greater of them. For revelation sometimes deceives through the error of falsehood, and migration exalts through the appetite for vanity. But love is always in the light: if something false is suggested in revelation, it discerns it shrewdly; and, since it is not puffed up, if any swelling pride strives to break out in migration, it powerfully casts it down.  
[Alternative reading: *et si quia*; printed reading: *si quid*, “if anything false …”.]

Therefore revelation pertains to clarity, which lies in understanding; migration to usefulness, which lies in effect; love to purity, which lies in affection. So this holy glorification is conferred by this threefold gift of grace: revelation enlightens by holy contemplation; migration adorns by good action; zeal inflames by pure love; and inward sweetness glorifies the same consent. You now see and, I think, plainly recognize that not without reason did the Lord Jesus will to manifest himself to the Magi called in Bethlehem, to be baptized in Jordan for us who must be baptized, and to be glorified in Cana of Galilee for us who must be glorified. [Col. 0397D–0398B]

VIII. But having spoken briefly of the order and places of his manifestations, let us speak somewhat more fully about them one by one, and first about the first, in which we said that our calling is expressed. You heard sacred Scripture relate that when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the East (Matt. 2:1). Brethren, what we cannot say without great sorrow is that these are now the days of King Herod.

In these evil days, in these perilous times, there reigns the “hairy one,” or “the glory of skin”—for Herod contains both interpretations. I speak of Behemoth, whom the Lord in the Gospel calls “the strong man armed” (Matt. 12:29); whose strength is in his loins and whose power is in the navel of his belly (Job 40:16); who sees every high thing and is king over all the children of pride (Job 41:34). Today that prince of this world, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, powerfully rules over the earth and exercises his tyranny: the serpent who deceives the whole world; the serpent, I say, crawling upon the breast of pride and the belly of luxury.

He bears in reality that proud and unclean name, Herod: “hairy” in those who live according to the flesh; “the glory of skin” in those who glory in the flesh, rejoicing when they have done evil and exulting in most wicked things (Prov. 2:14). For this same serpent is full of the pestilence of a twofold poison, being both rigid and slippery. Isaiah calls him Leviathan, “the twisting serpent and the bar” (Isa. 27:1): exalted by the glory of skin, he subjugates to himself those who desire the ways of empty glory; seized by the foulness of hairiness, he tramples underfoot those given over in their bodily womb to lusts of the flesh. See whether these are not especially the days of Herod, when, particularly in this time, both pride reigns in the mind and corruption in the flesh among the children of perdition. [Col. 0398C–0399A]

IX. Yet in these most evil days Jesus is born in Bethlehem of Judah. What are we to understand by Jesus’ being born in Bethlehem of Judah in the days of King Herod, except that Jesus has some persons in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, “shining as lights in the world, holding forth the word of life”? (Phil. 2:15). If you are also willing to receive it, this Bethlehem of Judah is this holy and religious community, which inward refreshment enriches in mind and holy confession adorns both in word and in work.

For confession exists not only in the tongue but also in work; otherwise Paul would not say that some deny God by deeds unless he knew that there are some who confess him by deeds also (Titus 1:16). Therefore, if Bethlehem is the house of David, how could I fail to call the holy way of life which you practice a kind of Bethlehem—the way of life of those whom the Lord governs, so that you lack nothing, setting you in a place of pasture (Ps. 22:2), so that, as you eat the marrow of a land flowing with milk and honey, your soul may delight in abundance, as though filled with fat and richness?

For he feeds you in mind from the fat of wheat and satisfies you with honey from the rock (Ps. 80:17), refreshing you through inward contemplation with the sweetest savor of divinity and most savory sweetness, and likewise enriching you through outward transformation with the most sweet examples of humanity. Thus fed and refreshed in the inmost chambers of the heart, you not only confess God in words but confess God in deeds. I do not know on what grounds anyone could blame me if I called you Bethlehem of Judah, knowing that you are fed in mind, devoted to your own salvation, that you give forth a devout confession in speech and give yourselves to divine praise, and that, confessing God in holy work, you aid your brethren’s need.

We discussed at sufficient length, I think, this house of bread and the kinds of this confession in the sermons which we gave during Advent—when we showed what it means to say that the Lord comes into Bethlehem, walking upon the waters of Judah’s redemption. There is no need for us to repeat all that. Jesus was born in this Bethlehem of Judah and in Herod’s days; he has many servants strong in spiritual power—for their dominion has been greatly strengthened—full of the sevenfold Spirit, whose works are not bent toward sins. He has left for himself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal (3 Kings 19:18). Yet in these perilous times, which now are not merely impending but present, there abound those “lovers of themselves, covetous, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents,” and other monstrous people of this kind, whom he describes more fully afterward. [Col. 0399A–D]

X. This holy city, which is by no means least among the rulers of Judah and from which comes forth the leader who governs the people Israel, can no longer be hidden; nor does this lamp, once lit, allow itself to remain under a bushel but is placed upon a lampstand (Matt. 5:15), so that those entering the house may see the light. Hence, when Jesus is born in Bethlehem of Judah (Matt. 2:5), a bright-shining star appears: a star, I say, flashing like a gleaming flame and pointing out God, the King of kings. For it shines with such and so great a light, gleams with such novelty of splendor, that the Magi, seeing it, say to one another: “This is the sign of the great King; let us go and seek him, and offer him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.”  
[Note: [Col. 0399D] From the Office of Epiphany, antiphon at *Nunc Dimittis*.]

Brethren, what do you think we can say concerning this star? It shines from the East as far as Bethlehem. It appears to the Magi in the East; by its novelty it stirs their minds; it protects them on the journey; and, showing itself as their guide, brings them to Bethlehem, where the child Jesus is.  
[Note: [Col. 0400D] Antiphon at the *Magnificat* in first Vespers.]

Let us say—if, as I advise, nothing better presents itself to you at present—that the bright star leading these persons, who were so far away, to Bethlehem in order to adore Jesus is a luminous reputation, drawing worldly persons—for “salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155)—to a religious and holy way of life, so that they may embrace and practice a saving state. It leads them all the way to Bethlehem, but first it appears to them in the East; for how could they follow the reputation which religious holiness sends forth from itself unless they had at least some knowledge of the truth? “We have seen his star in the East,” they say, “and have come to adore him” (Matt. 2:2). They would never have hurried from such remote regions to adore him unless they had first seen his star. [Col. 0400A–B]

XI. A holy man rightly said that one who neglects his reputation is cruel. For just as a neglected reputation is the ruin of hearers unto evil, so a reputation preserved whole and unimpaired in truth is material and occasion for good. I think this is why the Apostle exhorts us to provide things good not only before God but before—not merely some—but all people (Rom. 12:17); and again urges us to walk honorably toward those outside (1 Thess. 4:12).

Show yourselves irreproachable before worldly persons. Let there be nothing in your word or work, nothing in your dress or bearing, that can be a stumbling block to them. Hence the same Apostle, Paul, says: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and to the whole Church of God, just as I too please all people in all things, seeking not what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:32).

Woe to those who, under the habit of religion, behave irreligiously before those who are not religious, to their ruin: conducting themselves before them so disorderly and dishonorably that through them the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles. Certainly it would be better for them to be drowned in the depths of the sea with a millstone hung about their neck than thus to be a scandal to little ones (Matt. 18:6). What would they do beneath a secular covering? Their fault perhaps would be less, and perhaps their punishment also less. But what they do under the habit of humility merits a more severe punishment, because it is judged a graver offense. For the former evil is simple; this latter is twofold, certainly threefold. [Col. 0400C–0401A]

XII. For the first thing is that you do evil—something absolutely permitted to no one, whatever profession he may hold. The second is that, under the garb of holiness, you commit a work of iniquity, having now become like a whitewashed tomb.
