The third is that you are an occasion of ruin to those whom you ought to have helped rise up: by your perverse example prostituting to the depths those whom by a good example you ought to have raised to the heights. Why should a secular person not now commit with greater confidence and boldness the evil which he sees a religious person brazenly commit, even though he fully knows it to be evil? [Col. 0401B] For what he does takes on for him a kind of covering of excuse, when he sees it committed by one clothed in the habit of religion. Woe, therefore, to him through whom in this manner the name of the Lord comes to be blasphemed among the Gentiles (Rom. 2:24); and especially to him through whom that same name ought above all to have been honoured among them. May our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God blessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever, always keep this woe farther and farther from you. Amen.

## SERMON XLIV. ALSO FOR THE DAY OF EPIPHANY. On our spiritual calling and cleansing.

[Col. 0401C] **SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON.**—1. How God’s name is honoured and blessed by us.—2. The way to gain a good reputation.—3. The stability of reputation arises from the stable practice of a holy life.—4. In monasteries holy purity and the supports of inward grace are necessary: undisciplined monasteries are rebuked.—5. The complaint of secular people concerning the disorderly condition of certain monasteries.—6. The three gifts of the Magi commend to religious persons devotion to reading, purity in prayer, and the usefulness of good works.—7. How necessary and useful is the practice of this threefold exercise.—8. Humility acquires, preserves, and restores virtues. It regards everything as received on loan.—9. Christ’s outstanding humility shines forth in his baptism.—10. The three degrees of humility contain the whole measure of righteousness.—11. The surpassing act of humility, to be practised after Christ’s example.—12. Humility of heart differs from humility of speech, and from humility of action.—13. Humility minimizes others’ faults and accuses its own; it is like a tree beautiful in root, flower, and fruit.—14. Six forms of humility are listed and explained.—15. The purity of intention necessary for virtue seeks and awaits the reward due to virtue.

I. At the end of the sermon immediately preceding this one, we said that woe is to that person through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed (Rom. 2:24). At the beginning of this sermon we say, conversely, that peace is to that person through whom the Saviour’s name is blessed. Who is this man, that we may praise him? For in his life he has done things no less salutary than praiseworthy. For he is the one who presents himself to those who behold him as so circumspect and fitting, so devout and holy, that nothing [Col. 0402A] can be seen in him or heard about him which may offend anyone’s sight or hearing. Through the holy manner of life in which he excels, he becomes an object of fear to the wicked, of love to the good, and of reverence to both alike.

His reputation, spreading far and wide and flying abroad in every direction—what is it but a certain brilliant and shining star? Since it contains nothing except what pertains to God and what commends him as an example to others who behold him, it is rightly said of it:

> This star flashes like a flame  
> and points out God, the King of kings.  
> The Magi saw it and offered gifts  
> to the great King.

[Note: [Col. 0401D] From the Office of the Church, antiphon at the *Nunc dimittis*.]

It is said to flash like a flame because of the abundant example of holiness and holy light which it does not fail to scatter among those who behold it, drawing them to imitation; and it points out God, the King of kings.

[Col. 0402B] II. What full and sufficient testimony! Happy is the person who strives with all his strength to be such that whatever is seen in him and whatever is heard of him may, without any exception, be a manifestation of the supreme King: showing by word and deed, by conduct and all his movements, that the kingdom of God has come into him and is also within him. He displays nothing but maturity in his face, nothing but wisdom in his speech, nothing but humility in his dress, nothing but moderation in his food, nothing but blamelessness in his bearing, and, finally, nothing but gravity in his walk. He admits nothing curious through sight, nothing vain through hearing, nothing pleasurable through smell, nothing gluttonous through taste; and, lest I seem to have passed over any of the five senses, [Col. 0402C] nothing impure through touch.

When, therefore, the reputation spreading abroad concerning him is truly such, is it not itself a star flashing like a flame and pointing out God, the King of kings? Why should not the Magi hasten to bring gifts to Christ the King when they are granted to see it? For secular people run with the gifts of their devotion toward the newness of holy conduct which they hear reported of such persons. You see, then, that the star was the reason the Magi came to Jesus. In like manner it is understood that, for people living in the world, the truth of a good and genuine reputation is an occasion for approaching a salutary way of life.

III. But the goodness of a genuine reputation and the genuineness of a good reputation must endure. Let the holiness of one’s life therefore be steadfast, so that the integrity of one’s reputation may likewise be steadfast. For a very grievous shame envelops a person when evil things are made public about him, because his reprobate conduct demands it, though good things had formerly been spread abroad about him through the proclamation of his religious conduct.

The endurance of the good and genuine reputation of which we are speaking seems to be indicated by what is read concerning this star: that it went before them—undoubtedly the Magi—until, when it came, it stood over the place where the child was (Matt. 2:9). For what is it for the star to go before the Magi until it brings them to the child Jesus, except for the good and genuine reputation of holiness to persevere? This is for the star not to diminish from its integrity until it draws by the effect of good works to the salutary purity conceived in the affection of their minds—[Col. 0403A] for the child Jesus signifies that purity—those whom it invites to love the new way of life.

IV. “And entering the house,” says Saint Matthew, “they found the child with Mary his mother.” O my most beloved and cherished brothers, I do not doubt that our star will lead many who are still far away to this holy Bethlehem in which you dwell. I beg you: strive diligently that, when they enter the house, they may find the child with Mary his mother; that is, that they may find among you holy purity and inward grace. For what else is the child Jesus in the house with Mary his mother except salutary purity together with inward grace, which is the author and giver of that same purity in a monastery?

When these two good things are found in monasteries by recent converts, the child Jesus and his mother are, as it were, found in the house by the Magi as they enter. But in many places today the outcome is very different; though we may speak truthfully of these things, we fear to speak because of the reproach attaching to certain people. For when the Magi enter their house, they find neither the child nor Mary his mother. Would you claim that the child Jesus is there where there is nothing pure tending toward salvation, but rather everything impure looking toward damnation? Indeed, it is altogether there: where there are swellings of pride and envies, quarrels and angers, divisions and discords, disturbances and brawls, lawsuits and insults, slanders and blasphemies, hypocrisies [Col. 0403C] and scandals, whisperings and hatreds; where even sons devour fathers, fathers eat the flesh of sons, provoking one another and devouring one another—indeed biting and tearing one another, and thereby being consumed by one another (Gal. 5:15).

Thus Jesus is not there where both prelates and subjects are full of deceit and malice: whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, arrogant, disobedient to parents (Rom. 1:30 and following); provoking children to anger—I say the former of rebellious subjects, the latter of insolent prelates—foolish, disorderly, without natural affection, faithless, without mercy; and this I say concerning disorderly companions. Where, I say, such things are in monasteries, the child Jesus cannot be found. For what purity, what salvation, is there in these things? Nor is Mary his mother found there, since there is nothing there representing inward and spiritual grace, the source of the same salutary purity.

V. This is what certain people, anxious and eager for their own salvation, commonly complain of bitterly. Despising the world with a good intention and coming to conversion for the salvation of their souls, yet not finding the very salvation which they had hoped to find, they have sometimes been discovered bursting out in these words: “Is this the state pertaining to the salvation of the soul which we thought was hidden beneath the garb of religion and holiness? Was it for the salvation of our souls that we persuaded ourselves to come here? And behold, there is here either no salvation of the soul, or very little.” [Col. 0404A]

“So great is the abundance of iniquity, while love grows cold—not now merely in many, but in almost all. What if they wear the habit of religion? In their manner of life they are irreligious. Under the garment of humility pride lies hidden among them; beneath purity, impurity; beneath quietness, disturbance; beneath peace, dissension; beneath gentleness, arrogance; beneath charity, hatred; beneath honesty, corruption; beneath kindness, jealousy; and finally beneath the covering of great holiness, malice of no slight perversity. Almost all have departed from the height of their profession; daily they break the vows which their lips have uttered (Ps. 65:13). Hardly anyone is found who does good—so great is the number of those who have become abominable in their pursuits (Ps. 13:1). Almost everyone does whatever he pleases, and boldly commits what is unlawful. And what is more to be lamented: since all alike agree in evil, whatever unlawful thing they do goes unpunished.”

I do not recall these complaints to you as though I thought such horrible and detestable monsters reign among you. For you have not so learned Christ, if indeed you have heard him and have been taught in him, as truth is in Christ Jesus (Eph. 4:20). But just as these evils have until now been far from you, so may they always be farther and farther from you. Let these evils, I say, not be found among you; but rather whatever things are holy, good, salutary, useful, devout, honourable, religious, chaste, peaceable, edifying, lovely, and of good report (Phil. 4:8), so that whoever among those still outside wishes to enter your house may immediately find in it the child Jesus with Mary his mother.

VI. Having found him together with his mother, the Evangelist says that they fell down and worshipped him, and, opening their treasures, offered gifts (Matt. 2:11). When you hear that they fell down and worshipped, understand humility of devotion, or devotion of humility. When you hear that, opening their treasures, they offered gifts, recognize in them a good purpose formerly hidden but now displayed in devout and holy conduct. [Col. 0404D] For they fell down and worshipped in order to show, by humbling themselves in all things, that some devotion was present within them. But they offer gifts from opened treasures when they openly display the good works which they had first conceived within themselves, and attribute them to God.

If anyone asks what those gifts are and what they signify, let him receive gold, frankincense, and myrrh. While preserving the familiar allegorical and moral sense—more widely known because it has been more often repeated among orthodox believers—I think that these gifts may be understood as a threefold exercise which anyone desiring to stand fruitfully in the common life he has chosen [variant: “will have chosen”] must practise diligently. This threefold exercise is devotion to reading, purity of prayer, and the usefulness of good action.

[Col. 0405A] All who have professed the common life ought always, as opportunity permits, to be found either in reading, in prayer, or at manual work. The application to reading enlightens through instruction; devotion in prayer sanctifies through purity; and the labour of good activity yields fruit through usefulness. Understand, then, the first exercise by gold, the second by frankincense, the third by myrrh. What metal shines more brightly or is more precious than gold? What gift of the Spirit is more sublime than wisdom? And when can wisdom be attained unless sacred reading is diligently practised? Frankincense has a sweet fragrance, and devotion and pure prayer offer a sweet fragrance before God. Myrrh also, as they say, preserves a dead body from decay; and the constancy of good action and the labour of stern mortification keep both the soul from idleness, [Col. 0405B] which is its enemy, and the flesh from pleasure, which incites it to lust.

VII. Therefore these Magi, entering the house in which they find Jesus and Mary his mother, offer gold, frankincense, and myrrh to Christ, so that, dearest brothers, they may instruct us by their example. We who have now entered this place and, having entered, dwell in it—where there is both a salutary state of soul and inward grace—must diligently and carefully apply ourselves to reading, ardently devote ourselves to pure prayer, and not neglect necessary activity, mortifying the flesh with its vices and desires. Of the application to sacred reading we say that it enlightens the mind against the darkness of ignorance; of the purity of devout prayer, that it sanctifies against the unlawful pleasure of either carnal or spiritual desire; of constancy in good action, that it adorns against idleness, which is hostile to the soul (Ecclus. 33:29); and of mortification of the flesh, that it is true myrrh, because by suppressing the vices of the body it also makes the soul light and ready for spiritual things.

Thus far concerning the coming of the Magi to Christ, in which, we said, our calling is expressed and in which the first manifestation granted to the world is set forth. The second is found in his baptism: for first we are called, and, having been called, we are cleansed. First he calls us out of darkness into his marvellous light [Col. 0405D] (1 Pet. 1:9); then he cleanses our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Heb. 9:14). He himself was baptized in the Jordan, because our spiritual cleansing is in humility. Jordan means “descent,” and to descend is to be humbled.

VIII. Let us therefore descend, that we may be humbled; let us be humbled, that we may be cleansed. For only when you are humbled are you cleansed. For, according to the saying of the wise man, everyone who exalts his heart is unclean; thus, surely, whoever truly humbles himself is without doubt declared clean. O holy humility, which truly sanctifies the soul among all the other virtues! It belongs to humility to acquire virtues for us when they are absent, to preserve them when they are present, and, when they have perhaps been withdrawn, [Col. 0406A] to restore them. We continually perceive by our own experience that this is humility’s proper office. We also read that it is so in both the sayings and deeds of the saints.

For what did the blessed Mary say that the Lord had regarded in her, so that all generations should call her blessed, except humility? “He has regarded,” she says, “the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48). And what more clearly shows that humility is not merely the acquirer but also the guardian of every virtue than what the Lord says through his servant: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble?” (Isa. 66:2). To recognize that humility also restores a virtue when it has been lost, recall the remarkable miracle of Elisha, who, when a piece of wood had been cut, summoned up iron that had fallen away from the deep and restored it to the person who had lost it (4 Kings 6:7).

Every day our bald Elisha—I mean he who was crucified in the place of Calvary, whose hairs likewise fell away when his disciples abandoned him and fled (Matt. 26:56)—does not cease graciously to do this for us: he breaks the mind through humility and restores the gift of grace that perhaps was lost through hidden pride. This restoration, indeed, the humble confession of the man who had lost it deserved to obtain from him, a confession which rang out in Elisha’s cry: “Alas, alas, my lord! And it too I had received on loan” (4 Kings 6:5). For what do we have that we have not received? Yet that is too little; I should have said: What do we have that we have not received on loan? Whatever is received on loan must be returned; we ought, indeed, to return what we have received, and to return it with interest. Thus humility, concerning every grace we have received in this way, is in us both the acquirer of grace absent, the preserver of grace bestowed, and the restorer of grace withdrawn.

“I will go to her and take her as my inseparable companion, that through her all good things may come to me.” When I perceive grace to be present, humility will preserve it so that I do not lose it; when it is absent and perhaps withdrawn, humility will restore it, so that it may be restored to me.

IX. Humble Jesus taught us diligently to acquire and constantly retain this humility. Though he showed it outstandingly in all his deeds, he showed it especially in his baptism, bending himself to be baptized by John’s hands although he was altogether free from every defilement that might need washing away. Who, beloved, would not be astonished to see supreme purity come to washing; God hastening to be washed by a human being; the Lord by a servant; the innocent one by a sinner; Christ by John? For, as the Evangelist says, Jesus came to John to be baptized by him (Matt. 3:13). [Col. 0406D] John himself was greatly astonished at the reason for his coming and immediately turned humbly to protest: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (Matt. 3:14). Jesus answered him: “Allow it now,” and added, “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (ibid.).

What is this, I ask, O good, gracious, gentle, and humble Jesus? What is this that you say: that all righteousness must thus be fulfilled? You who not only fulfil all righteousness, but are yourself true and supreme righteousness, teach me why you fulfil all righteousness in this: that you come to be baptized by one who ought to be baptized by you. And I hear you, my Jesus, answering these things in the ear of my heart: “I shall fulfil all righteousness in this because in it I fulfil the highest and supreme degree of humility.”

X. The first degree of humility is shown by the person who submits to one greater than himself and does not set himself above an equal. A higher degree is when, through brotherly love, which never knows how to be proud, someone subjects himself to an equal, yet does not judge himself to be preferred to one inferior. But if you add such force to the exaltedness of this great humility that you reach its summit, bowing yourself even before one inferior to yourself, you thereby become subject to every human creature for God’s sake. Then surely I do not know what you lack for all righteousness, since you permit no one to be lower than yourself—not even the person whom you know to be far inferior to you.

This perfection of humility seems to me to be what he mentioned when he said that in this he would fulfil all righteousness [variant: “that he is,” or “has fulfilled”]: when he came to be baptized by one who ought to have been baptized by him. Go and do likewise: through humility offer and render to your inferior what it is his due to offer and render to you, and you have fulfilled all righteousness.

XI. You do this in a sublime manner when through your humility you endeavour to bring gentleness to someone known to have offended against you. This is truly a good and holy work, a great and sublime work: one in which you not only do not defend yourself, so as to give place to anger, but even accuse yourself, so as to take away occasion for anger—not overcome by evil, but overcoming evil with good (Rom. 12:21).

But perhaps some proud person will say: “Far be it; this ought not to happen, for it is unfitting. It goes beyond the Gospel and therefore against the Gospel. I have received the Gospel’s command to forgive my brother who sins against me and seeks forgiveness (Matt. 18:15); but where has it commanded me so to humble myself before one who offends against me as to draw him to gentleness?”

You have appealed to the Gospel? Go to the Gospel. Who can deny that Paul’s preaching is Gospel, he who says that he received and learned it not from man but through revelation of Jesus Christ? He himself proclaims that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (Gal. 1:12). You therefore have an example in God himself: strive through your humility also to draw to gentleness the person who has sinned against you, since you hear that God through Christ reconciled to himself a guilty world (2 Cor. 5:19).

And how did he reconcile the world to himself through Christ? Paul adds: “Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (ibid., 21). For us, who know nothing except sin, he made sin the one who knew no sin. So you too should not excuse yourself as though you had committed no sin, even in the matter in which you did not commit sin, in order that you may draw to the humility of repentance the person who, by offending you, committed sin. Is this not, in a sense, your coming to him clean, as though to be cleansed by one who ought to come to you so that, being filthy, he may be cleansed by you? And to act thus is to fulfil all righteousness.

XII. You now see, I think, that Christ’s baptism overflows wholly with humility; for our spiritual cleansing consists in humility. But if this humility of which we speak is to be complete, it must be in heart, speech, and deed; and in the heart in a twofold manner, so that you think humbly of yourself and loftily of your neighbour.

First, therefore, having hidden from your own eyes whatever good things you may possess, humble yourself; and continually place before your mind’s gaze both the evils you have and the good things you lack. Consider attentively with what and how great, how many and how weighty burdens of sins you are weighed down; how inclined and swift you are toward the depths of vices; how feeble and sluggish toward the heights of virtues. Turn your eyes to men of virtue, by whom you see yourself surpassed in every holiness; and consider how far superior they are to you in humility, kinder in charity, stronger in patience, more steadfast in long-suffering, more tranquil in tribulation, more rigorous in abstinence, more resplendent in chastity, sweeter in conduct, richer in virtues, more devout in prayer, purer in spiritual reflection, cleaner in meditation, more intent [Col. 0408C] in contemplation, more studious in reading, more mature in the gravity of their countenance, more moderate in sparing food, more honourable in the modesty of their dress, more discerning in speech, more energetic in action; and, finally, far more circumspect than you always, everywhere, and toward every person, carefully observing every time and place, person and manner.

XIII. But if perhaps you see in them something that can rightly be rebuked in anyone, think at once that perhaps either weakness, ignorance, or their great holiness, by which they excel more outstandingly in other things, makes it excusable in them; or that there is some other circumstance which, if it were in your case, would leave absolutely no excuse, and which, if it is in your case, deserves severe punishment. Having carefully examined all these matters and others like them, ascend the tribunal of your mind; and, with reason and the rectitude of its judgment proclaiming, understand how greatly you yourself lie in the depths in your own sight, while your neighbour’s deeds stand on high.

These thoughts are, as it were, the roots of that salutary tree which is humility. The more deeply they are fixed in the inner parts of the mind, the more loftily the tree can grow in the outward body. It immediately grows to immense size, displaying from itself a great and wonderful beauty in leaves and a taste in fruit: the former delights those who look upon it and makes them rejoice; the latter refreshes and nourishes those who eat it. Nor need it now fear the winds of words, however much they rage in detraction or threat, nor the floods of tribulations, however fiercely they rage in affliction. For it is a plant deeply fixed in the garden of the mind [variant: “planted, from point 52, fixed”], and rests firmly upon many great roots.

[Col. 0409A] The leaves of this tree are words of true humility. They themselves, as those roots grow from the depths of the mind, spring forth in a twofold manner: always condemning one’s own evils—“you tear your flesh with your teeth; you carry your soul in your hands”—and approving the good things of one’s neighbour, you extol them with humble praises. Yet this must be so only if both your self-accusation is wholly free from pretence and their praise wholly free from flattery. Otherwise truth is diminished in you, while your deceitful lips speak “with heart and heart” (Ps. 11:3): you utter with your mouth what is true while retaining in your heart what is false.

Far from you be this impurity, surely most shameful and detestable. For what kind of impurity is more detestable than this, in which, foully infected, you accuse yourself in order to be praised, and praise another in order to accuse him—blessing with your mouth and cursing with your heart? Always turn your sword against your own flesh; confess your injustice against yourselves; exalt your neighbours’ good qualities, so that the word continually resounding in your mouth both praises others and reproves and rebukes yourselves. After the leaves of words follows the fruit of works, which you gather sweetly when, according to the apostolic exhortation, you outdo one another in showing honour (Rom. 12:10).

[Col. 0409C] XIV. As we have spoken of heart and speech, so we must also speak of our body: in its movements we must show humility in a twofold way. First, let us always and everywhere abase ourselves; then let us defer to our neighbours. This twofold manner of humility should rest upon that humility which, we said, must be maintained both in thought and in speech.

First, therefore, endeavour always to bear in your countenance gravity with sweetness, and sweetness with gravity; in dress, lowliness with honourableness. In short, take care to display nothing but humility in your walking, standing, bearing, or any movement. Choose, so far as you can, the lowest place everywhere. And if it happens that you are called to something that seems elevated, do not insist upon it improperly, but decline it humbly; do not decline it brazenly, but excuse yourself modestly. If circumstances require it, accept what must be endured unwillingly, and never suppose that you should embrace it eagerly. Never seek it, and much less thrust yourself forward.

Then, just as in humility of spirit you judge others superior to yourself, and in humility of speech confess them superior, so it is necessary that in humility of service you likewise show them to be superior: everywhere hastening about for them, dutiful and devoted; yielding them the higher place in every conversation and undertaking; always and everywhere anticipating them in honour; ready to labour with them, refusing exaltation, swift and ready for labour, slow and reluctant for honour; sparingly allowing to yourself not only what is yours, if indeed anything is yours, but generously spending both yourself and what is yours upon them.

[Col. 0410A] Behold, we have shown you six ways in which you ought to exercise the virtue of true humility: two in the heart, thinking lowly things of ourselves and lofty things of our neighbours; two also in speech, accusing ourselves without pretence and extolling our neighbours without flattery; and two in the body, always and everywhere placing and casting ourselves behind, but placing others ahead and anticipating them in honour.

XV. There is also a seventh, which is the cause and fruit, beginning and end, of all these. It is that which confers true purity upon our intention, which the Lord in the Gospel calls the singleness of our eye; if you possess it in your body, you will not lack light (Matt. 6:22). I have said that this purity of intention is the cause and fruit of all our humble thoughts, words, and actions because it must both stir us to possess them and no less raise us up so that we may possess them fruitfully.

For it benefits you nothing that you think humbly of yourself and loftily of your neighbour; that you rebuke yourself and raise him up; that you cast yourself down and exalt him—unless you practise this with such a humble intention that, in virtue, you act and accomplish what belongs to virtue virtuously, and seek and await the reward due to virtue for virtue. You act and accomplish virtuously in virtue what belongs to virtue [Col. 0410C] if, in these exercises of humility and of the other kinds of holiness—the exercises that pertain to this same humility or to any other holiness whose exercises they are—you do not fail to act usefully and perseveringly. You seek and await the reward due to virtue if, excluding every desire for human favour or any earthly advantage of this kind, you desire by devout will to attain the heavenly recompense alone, and with sure hope trust that you shall attain it.

We must now deal with Christ’s third manifestation, belonging to the present day, in which, by changing water into wine at the wedding, he manifested his glory. But we cannot undertake it now. When, on its proper day, the Gospel concerning that manifestation has been read, then we shall make known to you what he himself deigns to make known to us about it. We shall also set before your love certain matters which we have pondered in our minds concerning this spiritual cleansing, for your edification and for the praise and glory of him who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLV. SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY. On our spiritual cleansing, which consists in humility; and on the inward nuptials of the mind, celebrated together by God the bridegroom and the soul the bride.

**SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON.**—1. Naaman the Syrian and leper prefigures the proud and lustful person. Lust is the punishment of pride.—2. The foulness of leprosy signifies lust; the command of the army, pride.—3. By the prompting of reason, after sin a person voluntarily turns to the physician of his soul.—4. The virtue of humility cleanses us from a threefold defilement.—5. The Gospel passage concerning the wedding at Cana of Galilee, at which Jesus was present with his mother and disciples.—6. Nuptials are the symbol of true love, by which God the bridegroom and the soul the bride are united.—7. The Lord accomplishes four things concerning the soul as bride. First, he washes her uncleanness through self-knowledge.—8. The voice of the repentant soul conciliating God whom it has offended.—9. Second, he repairs her when torn apart through works of righteousness, supplying the aid of his grace.—10. What are the marks of the new manner of life.—11. Third, he fits her for beauty.—12. Concern for preserving beauty in the soul.—13. Fourth, he brings her to perfection. Emblems of the perfected soul desiring the bridegroom’s embrace.

I. The discourse which we delivered to you in the preceding sermon concerning humility, in which we said our spiritual cleansing consists, held us longer than we expected. Although its forms are several, we described seven of them: the first and second to be held in the heart; the third and fourth in speech; the fifth and sixth in the body; and the seventh in inward intention.

Consider whether these may perhaps be the seven times in which Naaman washes himself in the Jordan at Elisha’s command, so that his flesh may be restored to health and cleansed (4 Kings 5:10). Naaman means “beauty,” and signifies the person who is beautiful in respect of nature, because he was created in God’s image and likeness. Yet while he practises pride—which holds command among the vices belonging to the army of that most evil king, who “beholds everything high,” because he is “king over all the children of pride” (Job 41:25)—such a person is, as it were, Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, because Syria is interpreted “lofty.”

And while he pleases the one who rules over him in sin, both by the greatness of his swelling pride and by his appetite for unlawful favour, he is, as it were, great and honoured before his master. And while he becomes proud of the spiritual strength by which he is powerful and of the abundance in which he abounds, he sometimes falls into the impurity of lust. This seems to be indicated by what is said of him: that he was a strong and rich man, but a leper (4 Kings 5:1).

For by God’s just judgment, one who raises himself up into the swelling of pride is sometimes cast into the abyss of corruption, so that, cast down by lust in the flesh, he may clearly recognize how unclean he was before God when raised up by pride in mind. Hence the Prophet prays that the foot of pride may not come upon him, nor the hand of the sinner move him (Ps. 35:12), because there those who work iniquity fall; they are cast out and cannot stand. In these words, I think, he shows that he does not greatly approve in Naaman either the strength of his might or the abundance of his riches, whom he sees disfigured by leprosy.

II. For what is the disgrace of leprosy but the sin of lust? Therefore Moses expelled lepers from the camp of the Israelites (Num. 5:2), because the Law excludes the lustful from the fellowship of the saints. Thus Naaman is a man fair by nature; through the loftiness of pride, commander of the army of the king of Syria; and through the swelling and *xenodoxia*—vain-glory—by which he pleases the worst master whom he serves, great before his lord and honoured. Moreover, inasmuch as he is puffed up by spiritual strength and abundance, yet is lustful, he is indeed a mighty and wealthy man, but leprous.

From this aforesaid loftiness there proceed secret movements of temptations against the soul and against reason, by which it was accustomed to see God. Finding it delicate but negligent, they reduce it to the captivity of sin and compel it to serve an unclean will. This is what is meant here by the statement that raiding bands had gone out from Syria and had carried captive from the land of Israel a little girl who was in the service of Naaman’s wife (4 Kings 5:2). For Naaman’s wife is the unclean will of a man fair indeed by nature, but exalted through pride and leprous through uncleanness. The captive girl from the land of Israel, carried off by raiders coming out of Syria, serves this will: that is, miserable reason, transferred from the state of luminous contemplation by secret motions proceeding from pride, serves an unclean will.

III. Yet at some point, at this girl’s prompting, the will itself is reproved concerning the cleansing of the leper; for she declares that he ought to go to that great Prophet, mighty in deed and word (Luke 24:19), who is in the keeping of His elect—for Samaria is interpreted “keeping”—so that He may cure him of the leprosy he has. For what is this girl’s saying, “Would that my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! Surely he would cure him of his leprosy” (4 Kings 5:3 ff.), except reason’s affirming that it would be most beneficial for the lustful man to approach Christ through conversion—Christ who always keeps His own—since He who alone is would make clean one conceived from unclean seed (Job 14:4)?

That even this leprosy might be cured, the wicked king of Syria also intervenes: not because the ancient enemy himself loves purity of chastity in man, but because he wishes him, at least for a time, to be cleansed from the contagions of the flesh, so that he may be more grievously and damnably defiled by the exaltations of the mind. For that wily deceiver is accustomed, with no good intention, to stir a man toward some virtue—for example, abstinence—or toward chastity, so that he may subject him to himself more ruinously when he glories in virtue.

But our true Elisha graciously receives the leper anxious about his cleansing, and restores him to health in such a way that the very grace of health may be an increase of humility. For He commands him to wash seven times in the Jordan, so that his flesh may recover health and be cleansed. Plainly, we are then fully healed of the sickness which we contracted in the flesh through the flesh, and, once healed, are cleansed, when we are washed in the descent of true humility by those seven modes which we set forth above. “He went down,” Scripture says, “and washed seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was healed” (4 Kings 5:14). He went down and washed, because unless he had descended through humility, he would never have attained spiritual washing.

IV. Consider, I beg you, what we have said in commendation of this washing of ours, and weigh from it how great is the power of humility. For when you are perfectly washed in its waters, you are cleansed from three defilements: one in the flesh and two in the mind. You are cleansed from fleshly corruption; from the impurity contracted in your inward intention; and from the exaltation entertained in your thought. Thus it may now be said of you also that, when you went down into the Jordan and washed there seven times, your flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child and you were cleansed. Flesh is restored when it is cleansed from its contaminations. In the child you may understand purity, but in the little one humility.

You therefore have your spiritual washing in Christ’s baptism; and, likewise, your calling to Christ Himself is represented in the coming of the Magi. In His first manifestation your calling is expressed; in the second, your washing. Until this day, as you know, we have deferred speaking of His third manifestation, in which He revealed His glory at the wedding before His disciples, having been invited and having changed water into wine.

V. But today, as the Gospel reading discloses to us the occasion and order in which He performed that miracle, no less profound than holy, our promise compels us to discuss it somewhat according to our ability. We shall therefore speak of this miracle as God grants; and if we say things which you recognize with us rather than learn for the first time, know that the Apostle says that to write the same things is not burdensome to him but necessary for his hearers (Phil. 3:1); and, according to the comic poet, nothing is said that has not been said before.

We say this because, as it seems to us, you have more than enough at hand from which to discern what ought to be understood here—not only in the treatises of ancient teachers, but also in the opinions of modern writers. Today, then, we heard in the great Gospel of the great John that a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee and that the mother of Jesus was there (John 2:1). We find this in his Gospel, I say, because he alone among the Evangelists is found to treat of these matters: he affirms not only that the mother of Jesus was there—Jesus whom, although she was a Virgin, she did not beget according to the law of marriage—but also that He Himself was there with His disciples.

And while he does not pass over in silence that the Virgin mother, the saving Son, and His disciples were there, he does not say that the mother was invited to the wedding; yet he does not omit that Jesus and His disciples were invited. “The mother of Jesus,” he says, “was there” (ibid.). And he adds: “But Jesus and His disciples were invited to the wedding” (ibid., 2).

Then, when the drink failed—whatever it was, he does not leave unmentioned that it was wine—when, I say, the wine failed, he introduces the mother complaining to her Son about the lack of drink, and Him replying rather more harshly than seems fitting for such a son to answer such a mother. Yet because, among those who sincerely love one another, love does not timidly shrink from asking anything pertinent to the matter, however great and difficult it may be, nor can it miserly refuse anything; because she was strengthened by certainty in the hope that she had of obtaining what she requested; and because she was not at all dismayed by the harshness of the answer she had heard—the Evangelist represents her as speaking to the servants and commanding them to obey whatever He, undoubtedly Jesus, might say. She knew, I think, that He did not wish to refuse what she had presumed to ask.

Accordingly, six stone water-jars, set there for the Jewish purifications and each holding two or three measures, were filled with water by the servants at His command. When water was drawn from them at His bidding and carried to the master of the feast, his sight declared it wine, and his taste confirmed what the eyes of the servants who filled the jars had seen and their hands had touched: namely, water. Still unaware of the miracle’s novelty, but intensely astonished at the excellence of the drink, he addressed the bridegroom about it, saying that, contrary to custom, he had kept the good wine until the end.

VI. This, as you know, is the sum of the Gospel reading, which has thus disclosed to you the greatness of the miracle. As you yourselves know from reading, many have said much about this miracle, and have left much in their writings; in these they have plainly and fully shown both keenness of intellect in understanding and no lack of eloquence in expression. Therefore, if I undertake to discuss anything about it before you, do I not presume to set cheap vegetables before those seated at costly feasts?

Hear, then, a foolish man who, though he does not know how to speak, is not allowed to be silent. And although you will hear nothing from me which you have not heard before, do not on another occasion, when hungry, begin to beg from another bread which you plainly have in sufficient abundance in your own house.

Saving, therefore, that manifold and true interpretation which we have always received from our masters and Fathers concerning the profundity of this miracle, let us here apply the service of our tongue only to its moral sense, and in these weddings seek that inward, delightful, and pure union in which God the Bridegroom and the soul the bride are joined to each other in the unity of true love. It is no small undertaking to speak of this union, because no one can speak worthily of it who has not yet experienced it in himself.

How gladly I would wish that one of you, experienced in these things, might now treat of them, dipping his pen in the ink of his own experience and setting before us a picture of what it is for the human spirit, cleansed and purified, to be united to that supreme and uncreated Spirit—the Creator of spirits and bodies alike—in the holy delight of true love and in delightful holiness, so far as that is possible in this exile. This good would then be fitted together on every side and perfectly consummated, so that neither the joy of their mutual love might be unclean nor purity in any respect disturbed.

But perhaps one of you, impatient with this, replies: “What is the point of this excuse? How long will you keep us in suspense? Tell us directly, without adding irrelevant matters, what you think concerning the things you have proposed.” So be it. We have said, then, that God is the Bridegroom and the soul the bride. O how great is the dignity of the soul: to be God’s bride! Yet not every soul can attain this dignity. For the one “who spreads her legs to every passer-by, prostituting herself after her lovers” (Ezek. 16:25), ought to be called a harlot rather than a bride.

Nevertheless, God makes His bride out of a harlot, making her who was once a harlot such that she can now be a bride. For He washes and restores her, fits and perfects her, so that she may now truly be called a bride. He washes her when unclean; restores her when torn; fits her when unsuitable; perfects her when ruined. In short, He washes for cleansing, restores for restitution, fits for beauty, and perfects for perfection.

VII. Behold the fourfold work of the Lord upon the bride whom He intends to present worthy of His wedding. He begins the first work thus: the Counsellor deigns to come to one who has gone astray, the Spirit to a human being. “The Lord sends forth His word to the earth” (Ps. 147:15), pouring His inward whisper into the soul. And because “His word runs swiftly” (ibid.), as soon as it reaches its destination it powerfully displays the effect of its strength: enlightening the soul into which it is poured, stirring the enlightened soul, opening the stirred soul, and sharpening the opened soul. For He enlightens one who is blind; stirs one who is rigid; opens one whom He sees closed; and sharpens one who is lukewarm.

First, indeed, in the soul which God deigns to visit and proposes to take as His bride, He drives away the darkness of ignorance by the light of His wisdom, illumining it with the radiance of His brightness, so that it may now clearly see what previously it either did not see or saw dimly and uncertainly. But once illuminated by this inward light, what does it need to see more necessarily and sooner than itself? I would call that light altogether too obscure—and thus, in a sense, no light at all—in which the soul sees other things in such a way that it does not see itself: like a lamp illuminating darkness far away while itself remaining dark.

Let the soul, therefore, first see itself; and for it to see itself is to know itself. For its sight is its self-knowledge. Let it know what it lacks (Ps. 38:5), observing how far it is from the purity of true cleanness, how polluted and unclean it is, and how full of innumerable filth. Let it see how, through its most shameful and dishonourable prostitutions, it has wasted and enfeebled itself, made itself foul and fetid; walking through the streets of the city of Babylon, sowing pleasure in the flesh and reaping corruption from the flesh (Gal. 6:8), casting God behind its back and unlawfully obeying itself.

What remains, then, except that, seeing itself such as it is, it should shrink in horror from being such? Let it grieve and groan over such great impurity; and, taking water for its head and a fountain of tears for its eyes, let it weep night and day (Jer. 9:1), surrounded by so many and such great impurities, flowing with such stenches, and hemmed in by such foulness. Let it labour in its groaning; every night let it wash its bed and not cease to drench its couch with tears (Ps. 6:7); and let it break out in this cry, full of sighs and sobs:

VIII. “Alas for me! For so long immersed in mire and embedded in mud, I was defiled by almost every contagion, omitting nothing impure and admitting nothing pure. I have now become a horror to myself, and I cannot bear my own stench.”

What is now necessary except that the soul, seeing itself such, should lay open its foulness to be washed and uncovered? For as long as it keeps such things hidden within itself, it cannot in any way be cleansed from them. Once disclosed and shown, however, they must be subject to vigorous scrubbing, because by gently stroking it you cannot easily remove old rust.

Therefore let great bitterness overtake the person who formerly found great sweetness in committing sin; and let no lesser affliction now prick the penitent than the pleasure which formerly soothed the sinner. Let sorrow and bitterness invade the mind, and labour and affliction the flesh. Let the person offer himself to God both inwardly and outwardly, restoring to God inwardly and outwardly whatever he was accustomed to take from Him; so that God may now receive the whole person through repentance, whom He had wholly lost through guilt.

Thus God cleanses the unclean soul: enlightening it, stirring it, opening it, and sharpening it. He enlightens the blind soul, that it may see itself; He stirs it, that it may abhor itself as such; He opens it, that it may show Him its foulness; He sharpens it, that it may seek its cleansing with all its strength. It must indeed clearly see itself, groan deeply, fully open itself, and diligently devote itself to being cleansed.

IX. Once it has been cleansed in these ways, let the Lord undertake His work, so that He who has washed the unclean soul may now deign to restore the torn one. Its restoration consists in works of holiness. For just as it is unclean when, by doing wicked deeds, it admits what is evil, so it is torn when, by neglecting useful things, it omits what is good. If, then, its restoration consists in works of righteousness, its first concern ought to be to turn away from evil, and its second to do good. First, as the prophet warns, let it cease to do perversely (Isa. 1:16); then let it learn to do good (ibid., 17): first uprooting and destroying, and then building and planting (Jer. 1:10).

But here it greatly needs the assistance of its Restorer, so that it may both restrain itself from vices and practise virtues, beginning now to hate what it formerly loved and to love what it previously hated. For the old habit stands in the way of its ascending this first step of restoration; the weakness of the flesh resists; faint-heartedness of spirit dissuades it, declaring the undertaking hard to embrace and harder still to endure, predicting much labour but no fruit, because what devotion takes up, it will never be able to carry through to the end. For we are not accustomed to abandon without great grief what we were accustomed for a long time to practise with great pleasure.

Likewise, to undertake manfully the new and arduous path of virtue seems laborious, because the newness of tender conversion recoils from what the long-established perversity of former conduct had long held in great hatred. But though both these things—turning from evil and turning to good—are very burdensome and laborious, divine grace makes both not only bearable but light, so much so that what the soul formerly would not touch becomes, through the urgency of the love whose sweet torment afflicts it, its food.

Do you not all feel these things in yourselves? Which of you does not feel within himself this change wrought by the right hand of the Most High? (Ps. 76:11). It is surely His gift alone that, not merely for one day or two but for the whole course of your life, to be utterly without that from which you now refrain is not only not very burdensome but exceedingly light to you—though formerly it was not merely hard, but impossible, to interrupt it even for a short time. To whose strength is it attributed that you adhere in such continual practice to this harsh and severe way of life, a small part of which was once dreadful even to encounter for a single day, except to Him who in the Psalms is called “the Lord, strong and mighty” (Ps. 23:8), in whom you too “do valiantly,” bringing your enemies to nothing? (Ps. 108:14).

X. In these ways, then, the Lord restores the torn soul: granting it strength of virtue to restrain itself from vices and the gladness of devotion to exercise itself in virtues. After this it must show itself well disposed toward its neighbours, extending itself toward others in the compassionate tenderness of true love. It must present itself without offence to those who are outside as well as those who are within, and be without stumbling-block to the whole Church of God. In all things, following Paul’s example, let it please all: “not seeking what is profitable for itself, but what is profitable for many, that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:33). Let it seek not what is its own but what belongs to another; becoming to itself like a vessel cast away, that it may become a vessel pleasing and useful to all.

This is indeed the good mode by which the soul is to be restored. When it receives this in its restoration, a wonderful change of the right hand of the Most High occurs in it also in this respect. It now puts itself after others in order to put others first, whereas before it loved itself unlawfully and cared nothing for others. With regard to itself it is now so moderate, and with regard to others so attentive, that in matters relating to itself it is extremely sparing and burdensome to no one at all, whereas in matters relating to others it is abundantly generous and solicitous.

What remains, then, in its restoration except that, with a good conscience, it should conceive firm confidence in pardon and, sustained by the certainty of hope, not doubt that its past errors have been completely forgiven by Him from whom it knows that so many and such great gifts have been bestowed upon it both in its washing and in its restoration? In a manner, it may now rest devoutly with the Lord from its labour in this seventh light, which we call benevolence toward neighbours; and in this seventh state, called certain confidence of pardon, rise from the tomb of sorrow.

XI. The soul thus washed and restored must be fitted; and fitted by Him by whom it was washed so as to be clean, and restored so as to be whole, so that it may be beautiful. Having conceived firm hope of pardon, let it strive and persist in acquiring grace; let it pray without ceasing, lift up pure hands without anger or disputing, and apply itself to observances day and night (1 Tim. 2:8). Such a soul need no longer fear to lift its face before the eyes of that Majesty, since the greatness of His mercy has wiped away all the stains by which it was once accustomed to bear a darkened countenance.

For He who inspires hope of pardon also moves it to prayer, declaring Himself abundant in bestowing much, having shown Himself merciful in forgiving sin. But in order to be worthy to receive what it asks, it must be devoted to works of holiness; it must heed the Lord’s command, so that He in turn may deign to heed it as it prays. Otherwise, let it know that if it turns away its ear from hearing the Law, its prayer will be abominable (Prov. 28:4).

XII. But perhaps one of you says: “What do all these things have to do with the exposition of the miracle which the Lord Jesus displayed in His third manifestation?” Indeed, they have much to do with it. Did we not begin the sermon now in hand from the wedding which took place at Cana of Galilee? We have set out all these matters in order to show how the human soul can become the bride of that Bridegroom who is God. For without these two persons—the Bridegroom and the bride—a wedding cannot possibly be celebrated.

Accordingly, after these things, He makes the soul capable of receiving what He has given—He who first makes it devoted in asking and worthy to receive. He enlarges its bosom for His abundant blessing, so that it may carry it away full. “When He gives, it will gather these; when He opens His hand, it will be filled with goodness” (Ps. 104:28). But it must retain what it has received and not rashly pour it out, lest, emptied, it become void.

They are riches of salvation, received from the lavish hand of Him who is supremely rich and stored up within itself. I advise it to place them in a safe location, not putting them into a bag with holes (Hag. 1:6), lest they be poured out and, once poured out, reduced to nothing. Let it set them before its eyes as often as possible, so that it may know whether either a thief diminishes them or moth and rust corrupt them (Matt. 6:20). The thief is excessive joy conceived through human praise; rust is excessive sadness contracted through human disparagement [variant: *detraction*]. These evils lie in wait for our treasures: unrestrained joy acts to prevent our good from being pure, and the bitterness of sadness acts to prevent it from being voluntary.

Therefore let it see how the things it has received stand within it; and, that it may prove itself a clean animal, let it bring back to its mouth the food which it sent down to its stomach. Once you see a soul thus praying, obtaining, receiving, and retaining, you will declare it sufficiently fitted.

XIII. It remains for it to be perfected; and, as it seems to me, its perfection consists in these three things: contempt for present things, desire for things above, and full love for the Creator. Let the soul regard all visible things as losses (Phil. 3:8); let it count them as dung; let their beauty wither in its sight and their sweetness turn bitter. Let whatever it sees, hears, tastes, smells, and touches in this world and from this world seem unbearable and altogether intolerable to it. Let it possess the world in such a manner [variant: “possess [by use]” seems lacking] that it does not adhere to it in affection.

Let it die with Sarah in a life-giving death, and be buried in the double cave of action and contemplation (Gen. 23:19), having its life hidden with Christ in God. In simple virtue and manly simplicity, let it remain at home with Jacob; let it by no means run with Esau through the woods of worldly cares to catch some fleshly thing (Gen. 25:27). Let it be placed, dead and embalmed with spices, with Joseph in a coffin in Egypt (Gen. 50:25), so that, wholly dead to the love of this world and filled with the various fragrances of virtues, it may be hidden in an inward secret place for as long as it is compelled to dwell in the dark state of the present life.

Then, despising these earthly and lowest things, let it desire heavenly and highest things with all its effort; and the more it is mortified to the desire of transient things, the more let it be quickened to desire eternal things. Let it “desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 3:23). Such a soul is now perfectly marriageable, and the time has come for it to think of marriage—provided, however, that it has attained the third good which we said belonged to its perfection. And if you wish to hear what that is: it is the fullness of love for God, whom such a soul loves not only among all things but above all things, so that together with Him and in Him it may rejoice through ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVI. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

On the same feast, which God the Bridegroom and the soul the bride celebrate together in their inward wedding.

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. The state of the loving soul, and recapitulation of the subject under discussion.
2. The fifteen stages of ascent to God, beginning from self-knowledge: spiritual life ends in the fervour of love.
3. How God perfects His bride in the outward and inward person.
4. Mary—that is, the devoted will; Jesus—that is, inward grace; His disciples are His charisms.
5. How Jesus is to be invited to the wedding.
6. The three servants of the body who invite Jesus: first, the rigor of fasting; second, persistence in vigils; third, the maturity of silence, which is threefold.
7. [Col. 0419D] The four servants of the mind: meditation, desire, humility, perseverance.
8. When wine fails—that is, spiritual joy—the devoted soul should sigh for inward grace.
9. The efficacy of humility for obtaining whatever is sought.
10. The desires of devout minds are often repelled or delayed by a hidden divine dispensation.
11. The office of good will and the zeal of obedience.
12. Deception to be avoided in inspirations; signs of heavenly inspiration.
13. The hour does not come before the devoted will has instructed its servants.
14. The six water-jars are as many kinds of meditation: namely, concerning one’s state before the first conversion.
15. The second concerns the state of conversion; the third, the hidden judgments of God; the remainder, the last things.
16. The fruits of meditations when the grace of God breathes upon them.

I. [Col. 0420A] Why should not such a soul as we described in the preceding sermon rest happily in the love of its Bridegroom alone? Set between His arms, why should it not delight solely in His embraces and kisses? For it completely despises all things below, finding in them neither savour nor beauty; while it holds the things above already by desire, though not yet in possession. Why should it not meanwhile exercise itself in godliness, which, according to the Apostle, “is profitable for all things, holding promise for the life that now is and for that which is to come”? (1 Tim. 4:8).

Let it therefore rejoice and dance with the Bridegroom; let them celebrate chaste weddings together. Let there be union with purity, conception in fruitfulness, and birth without injury. In the preceding sermon you have, then, the ways in which God makes the human soul His bride. First, as you heard there, He washes it; second, restores it; third, fits it; fourth, perfects it. He washes the unclean, restores the torn, fits the unsuitable, and perfects the ruined.

Its washing takes place in four ways: first it is enlightened, second stirred, third opened, fourth sharpened. It is enlightened so that it may see itself; stirred so that it may grieve through itself and over itself; opened so that it may disclose its wickedness; sharpened so that it may seek with all its efforts how it may be cleansed. Its restoration also occurs thus: first it receives strength; second, devotion; third, benevolence; fourth, confidence. Strength, to restrain itself from its former foulness; devotion, to exercise itself in holy works; benevolence, to show itself ready toward its neighbour in all things; confidence, to hope for pardon for past sins. It receives strength in self-restraint, devotion in action, benevolence in service, confidence in hope.

The modes by which it is fitted are these: first, purity is granted to it so that it may pray; second, holiness so that it may merit; third, capacity so that it may receive; fourth, watchfulness so that it may retain. It is perfected when it despises all earthly things, desires heavenly things alone, and rests in the love and sweetness of its Creator alone.

II. Consider whether perhaps these fifteen modes now set forth are the fifteen steps which those ought to sing who strive to ascend these same steps. For since the soul is below and God is above, He lays out for it these fifteen steps so that by them it may attain to Him. He raises it to the first step when He enlightens it; to the second when He stirs it; to the third when He opens it; to the fourth when He sharpens it; to the fifth when He strengthens it; to the sixth when He adorns it; [Col. 0420D] to the seventh when He forms it; to the eighth when He surrounds it; to the ninth when He awakens it; to the tenth when He justifies it; [Note: [Col. 0419D] The eleventh and twelfth steps are lacking.] to the thirteenth when He instructs it; to the fourteenth when He raises it; and to the fifteenth when He kindles it.

He enlightens for knowledge, stirs for compunction, opens for confession, and sharpens for satisfaction; and in these lies the washing of the soul. He strengthens for continence, adorns for righteousness, forms for benevolence, and surrounds for confidence; and in these lies its restoration. He awakens for asking, sanctifies for meriting, enlarges for receiving, and calls back for recompense; and in these lies its fitness. He instructs for contempt of earthly things, raises for desire of heavenly things, and kindles for love of the Creator; and in these lies its perfection.

Thus the soul begins with the light of self-knowledge and reaches the ardour of divine love, because the beginning of our salvation is that we undertake the good through self-knowledge, while its end is that we attain blessedness in divine election. Accordingly, in the first four modes the soul, which was polluted, is cleansed; in the next four, the soul which was torn is restored; in the following four, the unsuitable soul is fitted; and in the final three, the ruined soul is perfected. It is washed for cleansing, restored for restitution, fitted for beauty, and perfected for perfection.

III. I no longer doubt that, occupied in such pursuits and devoted to such exercises, the bride—the soul—can be joined to the Bridegroom, God, in those holy inward joys of marriage. For He is eager to perfect the one like Himself both in matters concerning the outward person—when, in holy conduct, it moves from vice to virtue and from virtue to virtue, as though migrating from evil to good and from good to better—and in matters concerning the inward person—when, with unveiled face, it beholds the glory of God and is transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18).

This, indeed, seems to be indicated by the interpretations of these names: Cana, they say, means “zeal,” and Galilee “migration” or “revelation.” Weddings therefore take place at Cana of Galilee when the bride exults and dances with the Bridegroom in the chaste and sober joys of spiritual delight, and does so in the zeal which it possesses in its affection for outward migration and in its understanding of inward revelation.

Such zeal is formed by the devoted will, which is the mother of Jesus, of whom it is said that she was there (John 2:1)—undoubtedly at the wedding. This is the will which conceives Jesus, that is, inward grace through whom salvation and life are given to us and, once given, preserved, by affection; but gives Him birth by effect. It conceives by affection, I say, when it secretly proposes in the mind what is salutary. It gives birth by effect when it brings its good purpose out openly into action. Therefore it is fittingly said that the mother of Jesus was there, since at these weddings the devotion of a devoted will must necessarily be present. How necessary that presence is will appear in what follows.

IV. The inward grace of which we speak also attends these weddings; and, that the feast may be full, so do the spiritual charisms of that same grace. For, as we read, Jesus and His disciples were invited to the wedding (ibid., 2). Jesus is not present without His disciples, nor grace without its gifts, because, as Paul says, “grace in me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15:10). This is what He elsewhere commands to be asked: where His refreshment is, where He may eat the Passover with His disciples (Mark 14:14), signifying, I think, that He wishes to attend the wedding not alone but with His disciples.

Then, in what follows, you have that in the evening He came with the Twelve (ibid., 17). What is this except that, when the fervour of temptation is setting within us and the gentle calm of inward peace breathes upon us, grace deigns to visit us, having spiritual charisms in its company? For who are these twelve with whom He comes, except those outstanding virtues which the Apostle calls fruits of the Spirit, and which he also numbers as twelve? They are: love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity (Gal. 5:22).

But this Jesus of ours was invited with His disciples to these weddings. I believe that some of you, led by experience, are already running ahead of my words and know what I think is meant by Jesus being said to have been invited to the wedding. How do you customarily invite Jesus to your own wedding? I suppose He is often invited in different ways by different persons, according as He who is invited may choose to inspire those inviting Him. For He Himself causes us to invite Him. What do you think is the better way in which we ought to invite Jesus to the wedding? Far be such presumption from me: that I should claim knowledge of so great a matter, which I think can be known only by the one to whom it is given to experience it.

V. Therefore I, a worthless little man, do not say that I know the best way in which he is to be called. Yet I think that whatever way it may be, that is the better way in which, when called, he comes more swiftly and gladly to meet us. But who that person may be, ask, I beg you, not me, but one who has learned over a long time—by diligently observing and cautiously discerning the inward motions that arise both toward himself and within himself from himself—to breathe freely in the presence of inward grace with Jesus, and to sigh in its absence; unable in any way to rest while he is absent, or to labour at anything while he is present.

Nevertheless, compelled here too to disclose my folly, as in certain other matters which ought to be investigated by the perfect, I have become foolish because you compel me. I shall show, insofar as I have presently been granted to perceive it, in what ways Jesus seems to me to be summoned. Who this Jesus is, you have heard not once but often. I think, however, that servants of both body and mind must be sent to call this Jesus, because, when he is present, he restores both body and mind; and when he is absent, both mind and body are sick.

VI. Let the body first send its servant: the rigour of fasting; then the persistence of vigils; lastly, the maturity of silence. For we often deserve to taste what is sweet to the mind when we abstain from what is pleasant to the belly. You have an example of this in holy Daniel: when he ate no “bread of desire” and drank no water of concupiscence, he was called, in accordance with the fact itself, “a man of desires” (Dan. 9:23), and attained to knowledge of hidden things.

We are also commanded to watch while the Lord is to come ([Col. 0423A] Matt. 13:35); and the righteous man is said to have given his heart to early watching (Ecclus. 39:6). Although this may fittingly be understood of the inward watchfulness of the mind, bodily vigils also commonly profit much toward acquiring grace. What shall I say of the gravity of silence? How can one receive through the ears the hidden word that ought to be heard, who does not shrink from letting his mouth slip and run loose in superfluous speech?

With silence we attain rest from external occupation; we also attain solitude of place. For it belongs to the perfect not only to restrain superfluous speech within themselves, but often also to restrain external occupations. And, in order to acquire more abundant fruits of the Spirit, they sometimes withdraw from human society; for wisdom is commanded to be written in a time of leisure, and “he who is diminished in activity shall receive her” (Ecclus. 38:25). Holy David likewise, in order that he might rest, chose not merely to go far away and flee, but also to remain in solitude (Ps. 55:8). Blessed Job too declares that he dissembled, kept silence, and rested (Job 3:28). God likewise commanded Arsenius, as we read, to flee, to be silent, and to rest.

These, then, are the servants whom our body ought to send to summon Jesus. There are indeed many other bodily exercises by which absent grace is to be invited to visit us; but this threefold practice occurs to me at present. Perhaps the threefold bodily exercise may not unfittingly be applied to what Leah said—whereby active exercise is undoubtedly signified—[Col. 0423B] namely, that the Lord had given her her reward because she gave her maidservant to her husband (Gen. 30:18).

Our maidservant is our flesh; for as a maidservant is subject to her mistress, so it ought to be subject to the spirit. To give her to our husband means to restrain her from vices in imitation of the Lord, who alone is the lawful husband of the soul. Let her be restrained from pleasure by fasting, from sluggishness by vigils, and from talkativeness by silence; then she has been given to our husband. Once she has been given, a reward is granted us for these servants, because Jesus draws near to us at their invitation. For through the rigour of fasting the spirit is raised; through persistence in vigils it is lightened; through the gravity of the threefold silence briefly mentioned above, it is composed for inward rest.

This threefold good of grace is conferred on us through this threefold exercise. Likewise, a threefold vice is removed: by the first, pleasure is put to death; by the second, sluggishness is shaken off; by the third, restlessness is excluded. Thus, while the maidservant is given to the husband, the reward is given; and while one ploughs with Samson’s heifer, his riddle is found (Judg. 14:18). And while the flesh is afflicted, knowledge of inward things is granted; and when Jesus is called, he does not disdain to come.

VII. The mind, however, sends first the servant of purity of meditation; second, the fervour of desire; third, the virtue of humility; fourth, the steadfastness of perseverance. For by meditation the mind is taught where and how to seek; by desire, having found him, it entreats him to come; by humility, [Col. 0424A] it becomes worthy to lay hold of him; by the virtue of perseverance it sweetly embraces him, firmly binds him to itself, and says: “I hold him, and I will not let him go” (Song 3:4).

You therefore call Jesus and his disciples to the wedding if, in order to obtain grace, to acquire spiritual gifts, and to increase and order your inward joys, you mortify pleasure within yourself, shake off sluggishness, exclude every restlessness, persist in pure meditation, apply yourself to devout prayer, cast yourself down through humility, and establish yourself in all these things by the steadfastness of perseverance.

VIII. “The mother of Jesus was there. And Jesus himself was called to the wedding” (John 2:1–2). But what is the benefit of each? When, as the Evangelist says, the wine failed, his mother—undoubtedly the mother of Jesus—said to him: “They have no wine” (ibid., 3 ff.). There is a wedding, and the wine fails there. For who in this life can possess such purity that spiritual joy never at any time fails within him? A person never remains in the same state: he is always subject to change. At one time the divine gift raises him to the heights; at another his own weight casts him down to the depths. Thus, although there is a wedding, the wine fails in it.

But when the wine fails, let his mother complain to Jesus: that is, let devout will, with a pious complaint, approach inward grace concerning the lack of the cup of inward spiritual joy. The lack of wine will not keep the wedding guests sorrowful for long if Jesus is moved by his mother’s complaint about that lack. That is, our good desires need not groan long in the absence of spiritual gladness if, for the restoration of that gladness, they do not cease to sigh before inward grace with earnest prayers.

Therefore let the mother of Jesus not cease to complain, nor suppose that she suffers rejection, even if at first she receives from him a rebuking answer. Indeed, his answer is exceedingly gentle even when he rebukes. For when he strikes, he heals; and when he kills, he makes alive (Job 5:18). His blow is our correction, and his rebuke our instruction.

IX. And indeed I do not doubt that many among you have often heard with attentive ears both that the mother of Jesus approached Jesus himself over the lack of wine, and that he gave his mother [Col. 0424D] a rebuking answer: “What is it to me and to you, woman?” (John 2:4).

Brothers, from our words you have heard what it means, according to the moral sense now in hand, for the mother to approach Jesus concerning the lack of wine; but you have learned it much better and more clearly from your own experience. Yet if you still wish to hear it briefly from us, it means this: when spiritual joy, as sometimes happens, fails in the mind, devout will sighs before inward grace with pious groans, that it may deign to restore that joy anew.

But this same will is repelled by a somewhat harsh answer, not in order that what it asks may be denied it, but in order that it may be humbled concerning its petition; and, humbled, may be made worthy to obtain what it asks. For among all virtues humility is most effective for obtaining anything, and it has a great place of familiar access in the eyes of grace itself; hence it gives boldness in asking and effect in obtaining.

What, then, is it for Jesus to say to his complaining mother, “What is it to me and to you, woman?” except for inward grace, responding to devout will that knocks, to pour into it knowledge of its own frailty, lest it be lifted up into pride because of the great devotion with which it burns? “What,” he says, “is there between me and you, woman? You have fervour in desiring, indeed, not from yourself but from me; yet I alone, without you, have the power to bestow. I can grant the sweetness of spiritual wine, because the fullness of power is in me to do this; but what is there from you that obliges me to do it?

“Therefore humble yourself under my mighty hand, lest you exalt yourself because of the good devotion in willing which you have received from me; and so that, the humbler you are, the worthier you may be [Col. 0425B] to receive what you ask—what it is possible for me, and not for you, to grant.”

This, therefore, is why inward grace teaches a fitting good will to humble itself concerning the restoration of a withdrawn gift: unless our petition is humble, it will be entirely fruitless. Therefore, whenever you appeal to grace to obtain its gift, strive to have, just as you have devotion in good will, so also true humility in your intention. For this virtue alone preserves the gifts of grace that are present, lest they be lost; and obtains their restoration when they are absent.

X. This answer, then—“What is it to me and to you, woman?”—is beneficial, so that the good will which sighs for a withdrawn gift may be worthier to receive what it asks, the more deeply it recognizes both that what it has already received does not come from itself and that it possesses in itself no merit by which it deserves to obtain what it still asks.

Thus in the Song of Songs the Bride, who asks to be admitted to certain secrets of the Bridegroom through the great boldness of intimacy she has toward him, is judged to be struck by a rather harsh answer, so that the more humbly she thinks of herself, the more worthily, fully, and perfectly she may be admitted to the mysteries for which she sighs. For, addressing her Beloved and asking with great desire that he tell her where he feeds and where he lies down at noon (Song 1:[Col. 0425D] 6), she immediately hears that, if she does not know herself, she should go out and depart (ibid., 7).

You see, then, that it is not without reason that, when the Bride asks the Bridegroom to show her his secrets, he instead confronts her with the need to guard against ignorance of herself. So you may likewise understand that it is not without reason that, whenever the prophet Ezekiel is raised to behold lofty things, he is called “son of man” (Ezek. 2:1 ff.).
