As there the Bridegroom commands the Bride, who aspires to the disclosure of secrets, to go out and depart if she does not know herself, so here grace itself—the grace for which she asks—infuses knowledge of its own frailty into the good will that sighs for restoration of a withdrawn gift.

“What is it to me and to you, woman?” means: What you ask is not granted you on account of any merit of yours; you are no less unworthy to obtain it than I am powerful to grant it. Therefore know yourself, so that you may be richer in merit in my eyes to the degree that you are poorer in your own. Moreover, “my hour has not yet come,” because it belongs to me to visit not only the person whom I judge worthy, but also at the time which I judge fitting. For “my spirit is sweeter than honey” (Ecclus. 24:27): it not only breathes where it wills, but also when it wills. “There is a time for everything: a time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces” (Ecclus. 3:1–5). What pleases you is not yet advantageous to you. Your time has already come in desiring; but my time has not yet come in granting.

XI. This, brothers, is what we often experience: many times we cry to grace with a loud cry of the mind; it delays in coming. And the grace which tells our good will that its hour has not yet come thereby makes it certain that we do not yet please it, and consequently that it is not yet beneficial for us that it visit us.

We ought indeed to understand this cause justly and piously: it delays in coming for our good, so that our desires may increase, and so that, the more joyful it is because of increased desire, the more fruitful it may come to us. This, then, is why it does not hear devout will when it cries to it; nor does it act unwisely toward itself. Or perhaps it delays so that, the longer it is desired while absent, the more tightly it may be held when present. Or there may be some other arrangement on its part, but necessity on ours: it orders all things concerning us with great reverence and always provides what is useful for us in all that it is accustomed to do within us.

But during this delay in visitation, devout will must not cease from its affection; it should take care to stir toward good the inward thoughts of the mind, which are in some manner servants at these spiritual weddings. For it is not the office of good will merely to sigh to grace for grace; it is also its office to draw the thoughts of the heart toward what is good by exhorting them. Let it therefore move between grace and these thoughts: approaching grace in prayer, but exhorting the thoughts to obey its inward commands. To grace it says in prayer, “They have no wine”; to the thoughts it says in exhortation, “Do whatever he tells you” ([Col. 0426C] John 2:5). And it fittingly says “whatever,” without any exception, because nothing that Jesus says, nothing that divine grace inspires, can fail to be salutary.

XII. Certainly you know, having been taught by very frequent experience, that grace instructs you by its commands in not one but many ways. For you are not all inflamed with devotion in one and the same manner; but this life-giving grace of which we speak is so present to all that it also attends to each individual. I think there is none among you who does not receive from it something proper to himself, so that each of you may say: “My secret is mine, my secret is mine” (Isa. 24:16).

Let it not be a matter of concern to you; but do whatever it silently says in your heart. But carefully attend to this and be cautious, that it is grace instructing that speaks in your heart, and not the enemy deceiving. For promptings are sometimes made in the heart by evil angels (Ps. 77:49). You have this in the case of the traitor Judas: the devil put it into his heart to betray the Lord (John 13:2). And sometimes there is speech of the Lord in the mind, as you read that holy David said he would hear what the Lord God spoke within him—he who is accustomed to speak peace to his people (Ps. 84:9).

Grace speaks to you when what it inspires in you is ordered. I call what is inspired ordered when what you conceive in your mind is, with regard to God, pure; with regard to your neighbours, peaceable; and [Col. 0427A] with regard to yourself, discerning. For what if what you do seems good to you, is conspicuous through a kind of singularity, and, hardened by adamantine obstinacy, disturbs the peace of those with whom you must dwell in one mind in the house of the Lord, if you wish to be saved—walking with them in agreement? (Ps. 55:15.) For “the wisdom that is from above is first chaste, then peaceable” (Jas. 3:17).

Thirdly, consider whether what you do is discerning, because everything excessive turns into vice. This testimony is true. Therefore, to sum these matters up briefly: receive as the word of inward grace whatever is inspired to you for doing and practising, provided that it pleases God as pure, is accepted by your neighbour as peaceable, and is moderate and salutary so that you may carry it through to its due end. And do whatever it tells you.

XIII. [Col. 0427C] After this Jesus does what his mother asks. And perhaps that is why he said a little earlier that his hour had not yet come: he knew that his mother had not yet instructed the servants to do whatever he told them. For as soon as he saw that devout will was ready to ask, and that the thoughts of the mind, exhorted by that same will, were likewise wholly prepared to obey, he too prepared himself to hear the petition, graciously granting what devout will asked to be granted.

For such is the sequence of the Gospel reading. When it introduced the mother of Jesus speaking to the servants and saying to them, “Do whatever he tells you,” it immediately added: “There were set there six stone water-jars.” And, to show for what purpose they were placed there, it added: “according to the purification of the Jews” ([Col. 0427D] John 2:6). Nor does it omit their capacity: “Each,” it says, “holding two or three measures.” When these had been filled with water at his command and the water itself changed into wine, Jesus granted his mother the desire of her heart and did not deprive her of the wish of her lips (Ps. 20:3).

What is signified for us by these water-jars? Let us take them, if you please, as six kinds of meditations, according to the rough understanding that I am accustomed to employ in such matters. And, when you begin to examine them one by one, you will see that the purification of the Jews consists in them.

XIV. Let the first meditation concern the state that we had before conversion, in which for some time we were held under the yoke of sin in ancient slavery. Let this meditation be the first water-jar. That criminal and shameful condition itself was also, in a certain sense, a water-jar. I think it is the water-jar that the woman cast away when she heard the words of the man who told her everything she had done (John 4:28). Of her you have written: “The woman left her water-jar.”

But he sat by the well—he who humbled himself among the dead, free (Ps. 88:6)—beside the depth of our perversity, weary from the journey of assumed mortality, which he had undertaken in the sixth age. The woman came to that well to draw water, drawing unlawful pleasure to herself. Of this, everyone who drinks, as the Lord testifies and experience itself confirms, thirsts again; for fleshly delight does not bring satiety but provokes desire. Nor did he himself have anything with which to draw, [Col. 0428B] and the well is deep (John 4:11). For “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22); and human perversity is a most profound abyss.

You subsequently hear his saving words: “The woman left her water-jar and went into the city,” urging people to come to him. “And they went out,” Scripture says, “and came to him” (John 4:50). You too have now done this: having received his words with attentive ears, you have cast away the water-jar of your former condition; and you now proclaim him to others, according to the saying: “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22:17). You have therefore already left this water-jar behind as regards your manner of life; yet you retain it, when necessary, as regards meditation.

XV. Let the second meditation concern the state in which you now stand after conversion. Though it is clean from wickedness, it is not immune from temptation. The preceding state, under the king of Egypt and of darkness, was foul with the mud of lust and light with the straw of vainglory. But this state is in the wilderness; and only those who experience it know how many, what kinds, and how great are the dangers that befall it.

The third meditation concerns the hidden and strict judgment of God, who is terrible in his counsels over the children of men (Ps. 65:6). Receive this as the third water-jar. Although that judgment cannot fail to be just, yet, as long as we live here, what God thinks concerning us is entirely hidden; therefore what is just must not be reproached.

Let the fourth meditation concern departure from this life, when, having entered the way of all flesh, we shall know in receiving our reward what manner of persons we were foreseen by God to be from eternity. Receive this as the fourth water-jar. The fifth concerns the eternity of Gehenna’s punishment, just as the sixth concerns the eternity of heavenly glory. To meditate on each of these is to possess the fifth and sixth water-jars.

XVI. The servants fill these water-jars with water at the command of the Lord Jesus when, by the inspiration of inward grace, our thoughts linger in these six degrees of meditation and are shaken by strong fear. You have heard briefly what it is for the water-jars to be filled with water by the servants. But in order to show how they should be filled, something fuller must be said. We cannot do this in the present sermon; [Col. 0429A] therefore, by the Lord’s gift, you will hear in the sermon that follows how I think those water-jars should be filled and what I think should be understood by the measures which each contained.

Accordingly, whatever may be revealed to us about these or other matters, even to the end of the miracle of which we speak, we shall set forth for your edification, to the praise and glory of almighty God, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLVII. ALSO FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EPIPHANY

How we ought carefully to examine ourselves and beneficially investigate the things that pertain to us.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The state before undertaking conversion, and its consideration within that undertaking.  
2. [Col. 0429B] How strict, hidden, and incomprehensible are God’s judgments.  
3. The hour of departure from this mortal life is to be feared.  
4. The punishment of hell, lest it be incurred; heavenly glory, lest it be lost.  
5. The first mode of meditation, composed of seven circumstances of sin.  
6. The second, from barrenness in good works; the third, from considering the person offending and the person offended.  
7. In the state of conversion: I. the instability of the mind must be attended to; II. the body’s weakness for works of virtue.  
8. III. Spiritual ruin is to be feared unless divine grace sustains us.  
9. Concerning God’s judgment: I. a mode of meditation—fear lest he has left any sins unforgiven; II. lest he accept no good works.  
10. III. Lest prosperity and adversity alike increase the heap of destruction.  
11. Concerning the hour of death: I. how sorrowful and unwilling is the separation of soul and body; II. the dissolution of the corpse into stench and worms; III. the tribunal of Christ the Lord.  
12. Concerning the punishments of hell: [Col. 0429C] fire, worm, eternity; concerning glory: blessedness possessed in oneself, in fellow-citizens, and in God.  
13. These are the servants of salutary fear, to be moderated by the steward of the feast, that is, by the virtue of discernment.  
14. The carnal person sets out good wine first.  
15. Recapitulation of the spiritual wedding with the soul.  
16. The six water-jars are so many meditations for cleansing the inner senses.  
17. The perverse custom of people of this age in setting out wine, alien from God’s approval.  
18. God keeps the good wine for us in the homeland.

I. It sometimes happens that these water-jars are filled with water also in my own case. To go through them now in order, I betake myself, when leisure permits, to the first water-jar; and, looking within, I see how foul and filthy, how ugly and unbecoming I was. Struck with great fear, I wonder how I endured myself as I now discover that I then was.

In the state in which I now am, which I embraced in order to live more uprightly, I see that I have changed only a little from my former self. In it I seem neither as cold through fault as perhaps I was in the preceding state, nor yet hot through righteousness; rather, through negligence I am lukewarm and therefore must be vomited from the Lord’s mouth (Rev. 3:16). And why should I not fear even now, when I have assumed the religious habit but do not have its religious effect? Why should the one be worn as testimony while the other is not exercised for benefit? Is this what it means to have left the world?

For what works belonging to the world have I wholly left? And if perhaps the works, what of the words? And if perhaps the words, what of the thoughts? Certainly those who wish to live justly, soberly, and piously must first renounce not only ungodliness but also worldly desires (Titus 2:12). See how this water-jar too is filled with water in my case: this sloth by which I languish in this state does not allow me to be without fear.

II. After this I raise my eyes to God’s judgment, which is indeed just but hidden, and I find them blind; for in my blindness I see nothing here. Yet it is not altogether nothing that I see, since I see that I cannot see anything here. Therefore I raise the blind gaze of my mind to the blameless and incomprehensible judgment of almighty God, and I do not at all discover what he thinks of me in it.

For even if I am holy and righteous, my works are in his hand; [Col. 0430B] and I do not know whether I am worthy of love or hatred, but all things are reserved uncertain for the future (Ecclus. 9:1). I confess that I tremble greatly in this thickest darkness. My soul is troubled within me, walking by touch and not discerning sufficiently where to place its wretched foot, because my way is hidden and God surrounds me with darkness (Job 3:23). A dreadful necessity compels me to go, yet I do not know where; indeed, I scarcely know that necessity itself. And I do not know whether he thinks thoughts of peace over me and not of affliction (Jer. 29:11); but I do know that he is terrible in his counsels over the children of men (Ps. 65:5).

But who knows how terrible he is? Yet I fear lest he stir up wrath against me, pour out his anger, and arrange nothing concerning me or around me except what is against me. For if Paul, the Apostle, a vessel of election, though conscious of nothing against himself, was not justified by this, because the Lord is the one who judges him (1 Cor. 4:4), how am I already righteous, when I am conscious of guilt? My case is vastly different, yet I have the same Judge and no other.

Therefore holy David was cautious and wise. Beholding the strictness of so great a Judge, and foreseeing that, even if he wished to contend with him, he could not answer one charge in a thousand, he despaired altogether of the quality of his inward state, resorted to the humility of prayer, and said: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord” (Ps. 143:1). Trembling, he recoiled from judgment, and prudently fled to mercy. Why did he shrink from judgment? “Because,” he says, “no living person shall be justified in your sight” (ibid.). He excepted absolutely no one—not the first patriarch, not the eminent prophet—nor did he know anyone conceived from unclean seed in this mortality who could be justified if God chose to enter into judgment with him. For Peter spoke wisely: “The righteous are scarcely saved” (1 Pet. 4:18); and what did he add? “Where shall the ungodly and sinner appear?” (ibid.)—such a person as I do not deny that I am. Such meditation is the third water-jar; and it too is certainly full of water.

III. By frequent meditation I also anticipate my own departure from this life, and make that meditation my fourth water-jar; and I find it likewise filled with water even to the brim. For I know and am certain that I must depart from here; but I do not know the time, the manner, or the place. Nor, when I leave here, do I know where I shall go.

O fearful, and therefore dreadful, hour of my dissolution! Even the man who possessed desire so great and of such a kind that, being conscious of good, he desired to be dissolved, groans under his burden, wishing not to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (2 Cor. 5:4). “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38), says the spotless and unstained Lamb, Christ Jesus, when he perceived death impending over him; and shall I not dread the hour of death? When he himself was in agony, his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground (Luke [Col. 0431B] 22:44); and shall I not tremble, knowing that my dissolution will be so terrible?

I shall lose whatever is here, not knowing what I shall find there, whither I go. I know that eternal punishment awaits if a recompense proportionate to my deserts is paid me: for “the wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23). Certainly I know my own iniquity. And I have read of my Judge: “You cannot look upon iniquity” (Hab. 1:13; Job 13:25). Rightly, therefore, do I fear—though I am a light leaf carried by the wind—your so great power; and though I am dry stubble, your so severe pursuit.

IV. The fifth water-jar, then, is meditation on the punishment of hell; the sixth is contemplation of heavenly glory. And both are full of water in my case, as I fear equally lest I lose the latter and incur the former. Since this is the palace of the supreme King and that is the prison, once we are sent into either, we do not come out again. For the one holds those enclosed in eternal condemnation, and the other holds those admitted in eternal blessedness.

See, I have shown you how those water-jars are filled in my case. From what has been said, you can now clearly perceive that they contain the purification of those who are God’s not openly but secretly, whose praise is not from human beings but from God (Rom. 2:29). For in these six kinds of purification, the person is purified who confesses to God either his sins or his gifts. But you also ask about the measures which the water-jars held, because in the Gospel you read that each held two or three measures (John 2:6). You desire to hear what the measures of these water-jars are; and you must not be deprived of this.

V. I shall say how I am accustomed to find in them not merely two but also three measures, when it happens that I measure them. Perhaps you will find them in a better way; nevertheless, it will not be altogether irrelevant to hear our method, which is this.

When I recall the perverse and wicked condition that I was accustomed to lead before conversion, setting myself before myself, I first endeavour to consider what evils I committed, of what kind, how many, and how great; and where, when, and with whom I perpetrated many deadly deeds. For one who strives fully to inspect and recognize the shameful and criminal acts he has committed must recall these seven things. But let him turn them over in his mind with stern and rigid reflection for compunction, not with soft and cold reflection for pleasure. For this reason the water-jars are called stone: such things are to be pondered in steadfast meditation, not thought upon in a wandering and weak manner.

For one who, to speak by way of example of the first—while the rest may be understood—recalls the evils he has done in such a way that, in the very remembrance, he rests softly and shamefully as though in a foul and stinking bed of delight, possesses, as it seems to me, a muddy rather than a stone water-jar. This is the person who, returning in heart to Egypt, turns over within himself the curiosity for fish that he used to gorge on; recalling the cucumbers and melons of such unlawful pleasures, and the most bitter and harsh anxieties of occupations and cares, signified by leeks, onions, and garlic. Thus they despise the sweet and savoury refreshment of the mind, signified, as you know, by manna.

Therefore, as far as I can, reflecting firmly so that I may be compuncted and not softly lest I take unlawful delight, I call my years to mind not in sweetness but in the bitterness of my soul. So that my water-jar may be stone, I recall these seven matters—namely, my evils: their measure and number, manner and place, time also and persons. Returning to myself, I am struck with great grief and powerful fear as I behold so great and such an abomination of animals and creeping things painted upon my wall (Ezek. 8:10).

VI. Then I endeavour to consider that, burdened with so many and such great evils, I performed either no good works at all, or very few and small ones: as full of evils, so empty of good works. In both respects I see myself as guilty: both in omitting commandments, being withdrawn from good things, and in admitting prohibitions, being enticed to evils (Jas. 1:14). I recall that I was such in my state before conversion: foul in unlawful acts and barren in necessary ones.

These are two kinds of thought, like two measures in my first water-jar. Then I consider who I am, the one who sinned; who he is, the one against whom I sinned; and, gathering from many considerations how greatly a human being ought to obey God with devotion, I infer how earnestly I ought to have guarded against despising him in either matter—whether by admitting what he forbids or omitting what he commands. In this way I add a third measure to this water-jar of mine: the first measure is carefully to consider the evils I have done; the second, the good things which I not only neglected but also despised to do; the third, how carefully I ought to have guarded against admitting the former or omitting the latter.

VII. Now, in this state in which I presently am, I survey myself with anxious care and frequent concern; and I find myself decidedly unstable in mind and weak in body. Yet I am not speaking of the strength of my flesh, but of the vigor of true virtue. But, to pass over in silence the evils which I commit both in the mind by thinking and in the body by acting, behold how many goods in me are obscured by this very instability of mind and frailty of body. The tongue indeed speaks the words of prayer, but the mind wanders through diverse things; what is uttered by the mouth is not occupied in the heart. Rather, while flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment within me (Ecclus. 10:2), so many birds descend upon the carcasses that Abraham cannot drive them away (Gen. 15:11); and, what is worse, sometimes he does not even care to drive them away. Likewise, when I apply myself to reading, when I shut my mouth with the lock of silence, my wretched mind, unable to endure repose, being talkative and wandering (Prov. 7:10), neither gathers itself wholly there to understanding, nor composes itself here to complete quiet.

When the wavering mind sometimes admits good things, it either does not restrain itself from self-exaltation, or scarcely does so; but when it admits evil things, it pierces itself with the sword of compunction late, and perhaps not sufficiently. But why do I attempt to go through particulars? Its diseases are innumerable. And how feeble is the body for the work of virtue! For it is quick to drowsiness, gluttony, wantonness, and sloth; but slow to vigils, abstinence, continence, and the necessary work of the hands. When in this way I investigate the twofold misery in the state in which I now am, and discover it by investigation, I plainly find two measures also in this my jar.

VIII. After this I see how great and of what kind a fall threatens me—so unstable and weak as I am—if the hand of divine mercy does not sustain me; and I add a third measure. For since I am subject to so many kinds of sickness, both in soul and body—and, even if I am perhaps not yet subject to some of them, I am nevertheless fully disposed toward them—what wonder if I foresee that I shall incur both disease, unless the care of the Physician forestalls it, and death, unless His operation postpones it?

Understand this meditation as the third measure. It is indeed a good measure, one which keeps a person well within his own measure: it does not allow him to exalt himself above himself, but humbly trains him to stand firmly within himself. For how can one now walk in things great and wonderful above himself, when, fully considering the infirmity with which he is surrounded, he is compelled to cry out with blessed Job: “Behold, there is no help for me in myself” (Job 6:13)? Hence also the Psalmist humbly flees to the help of prayer and says: “Do not turn Your face away from me” (Ps. 142:7). He adds the reason why he prays that God may not turn His face from him: “And I shall become,” he says, “like those who go down into the pit” (ibid.). That is to say: Do not withdraw Your help from me, because, if it is withdrawn, I shall in no respect differ from those who, struck by the blows of concupiscence, rush headlong into sin. “For unless You, O Lord, help me, my soul would almost dwell in hell” (Ps. 93:17).

Therefore the three measures in this jar are these three reflections upon the state in which I now am. The first is when I review within myself how greatly I waver through instability of mind; the second, how greatly I suffer through frailty of body; the third, when I know fully that, oppressed by so great a misery, I cannot stand without the sustaining hand of divine mercy.

IX. The third jar is the meditation which I keep within myself when I weigh carefully the hidden and strict judgment of God. This too contains not merely two, but three measures. The first is when, fearing the face of His severity and fearing lest I myself perhaps be reprobate, I strike myself with various suspicions from every side and anxiously fear that the purity of His mercy may be unwilling to wash away any of my evils, but may rather reserve them for His judgment. Knowing, of course, that there is an avenging sword and a judgment, I entertain diverse thoughts within myself, and my mind is carried in different directions.

I fear greatly lest my sin be written “with an iron stylus, with an adamantine point” (Jer. 17:1), while the most severe scrutiny of God’s righteous judgment watches over its reprobate; and lest He who has my crimes stored with Him and sealed in His treasuries should have the means to condemn me. The second measure is the fear that, if I seem to do any good things, He who pursues me with eternal hatred may not accept them, but may somehow—justly as regards Himself, for I dare say nothing else, but terribly and secretly as regards me—make that very good cooperate unto evil. For just as “all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to His purpose” (Rom. 8:28), so some say that all things work together for evil to those who hate God, to those whose just reprobation has been immovably fixed from eternity, who have been foreseen as destined for condemnation.

O works of God, to be feared and trembled at, in which He appears terrible over the children of men! For, as Ecclesiastes says, “No one can correct him whom He has despised” (Eccles. 7:14). And according to the saying of blessed Job: “If He destroys, there is no one who can build; if He shuts a man in, there is no one who can open” (Job 12:14). Woe is me, if, to speak further of these two measures, He intends, in reprobating me—and therefore neither cleansing my evils nor accepting my goods—to cast me out from the face of His mercy and hand me over also to eternal oblivion, as “a vessel of wrath fitted for destruction” (Rom. 9:22).

X. The third measure of this jar is when, still thinking of the same judgment, I fear lest whatever He does to me He does for my evil, arranging adversities against me both in prosperity, in which He appears to favor me, and in adversity, in which He appears to rage against me. For when prosperous things smile upon me, I fear lest, by His secret ordering, they smile for the purpose of mocking me: so that their deceitful smile, if one may so speak, may be a temporal recompense for whatever good things I have done, but eternal condemnation for the evils I have committed. But when adverse things rage, I tremble lest these be only the beginnings of sorrows; for their end is an endless, eternal, unbounded, and unfailing ruin, and a death that is life.

Therefore, as one of the blessed says: “If at any time God smiles upon me, I do not trust Him; and if at any time He strikes me, I know that, when He has fulfilled His will in me, other like things are ready before Him” (Job 23:14). Therefore, “if He comes to me, I shall not see Him; and if He departs, I shall not understand. If He suddenly questions me, who shall answer Him? Or who can say to Him: ‘Why do You do thus?’ God, whose wrath no one can resist, beneath whom those who bear the world are bowed down. How great then am I, that I should answer Him? Even if I have something just, I do not answer Him, but entreat my Judge. And when He has heard me calling upon Him, I do not believe that He has heard my voice” (Job 9:11 ff.).

Read blessed Pope Gregory’s exposition in the *Moralia* on these words.

[Note: Book IX of the *Moralia*, chapter 10 and following.]

And these will be the three measures in this third jar.

XI. To think of our departure from this life is to possess the fourth jar. It too, like those through which we have passed, has three measures. I think I have its first measure when I consider within myself how hard and harsh, how sorrowful and unwilling, is that mutual separation of the two cohabitants—I mean body and spirit. Truly, “all flesh is grass,” as Isaiah says; truly, “the people are grass” (Isa. 40:6). But our life is also a vapor and will thereafter vanish away (Jas. 4:14). This house—our earthly body, I mean—is dissolved, and, as earth hastens to earth, the spirit is compelled to depart.

I add the second measure to this jar: reflection upon the body’s decay after the soul’s departure. I consider, in the bodies of the dead, what mine will be after death: namely, that, dissolved by death, it will be reduced to dust; after putrefaction it will be a worm; after the worm, dust. In this second measure great shame appears to me, just as trembling appears in the first and terror in the third.

This third measure concerns that hour in which the soul will be presented before the sight of the strict Judge, to be manifested, as the Apostle says, “before the judgment-seat of Christ, that it may receive according to what it has done in its body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10). And these three appear fearful to me in that hour: the enemy accusing, conscience bearing witness, and the Judge examining. Wretched that I am, what shall I then do, having a weak case, when I shall then be unable to hide further [*usque*; alternatively *ultra* or *ulterius*], having become a spectacle to the accusing enemy, to myself confessing, and to God judging?

XII. Since we have lingered for some time over the measures of these jars, let us run briefly through what remains to be said. In the fifth jar, which is meditation upon the calamity of hell, the first measure is the burning of fire; the second, the gnawing of the worm; the third, the eternity of both, because the former is inextinguishable and the latter is said to be immortal.

But in the sixth jar, which is the last and is meditation upon heavenly glory, you have the first measure if you consider within yourself what blessedness you shall possess there in yourself; the second, what you shall possess in your fellow-citizens; and the third, what you shall possess in God. In yourself you shall have the strength of true power; in your fellow-citizens, the sweetness of sincere love; but in God, the fullness of supreme wisdom: fully strengthened, perfectly enkindled, and illumined for all things.

XIII. Behold, these are the three measures in each of the six jars. As has already been said, the servants filled the jars with water up to the brim when, by the inspiration of inward grace, the thoughts of the mind conceive full and perfect fear in these six kinds of meditation. But He who commanded the servants to fill the jars with water must also make them draw wine from them, because the same grace which terrifies our thoughts through fear soothes them through love. For as water is fear, so wine is love.

But first water, then wine: because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10), while “perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Let discernment, which is the mother of all the other virtues, judge this exchange; and let it approve what it has judged, for it belongs to discernment to approve with its favor that which the ordered love of the mind soothes in its thoughts unto consolation, lest fear terrify them excessively unto despair.

This is why the servants are commanded now to draw and carry to the master of the feast: namely, that from the thoughts of the mind, which, at the prompting of divine grace, had poured something into each of these kinds of meditation by reflection, whereby they might fear through grieving and grieve through fearing, something may now—that is, after prolonged anguish—be drawn through the inspiration of that same grace by piously daring to hope; so that, with the prudence of discernment approving, they may hope through loving and love through hoping.

For prudent and cautious discernment is the master of the banquet, which is what *architriclinus* means. It belongs to his governance to see that memory is stable, reason skilled, and will pure. For these three concern this banquet-hall, in which discernment exercises mastery: lest memory wander abroad from itself; lest reason, deprived of inward light, be darkened in the shadows of error; lest the will, defiled by unlawful desire, be stripped of the purity of true cleanness. But to whom should discernment ascribe the good of this spiritual exchange except to Him from whom comes all our good, without whom we can do nothing? He is our Lord, “from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends” (Jas. 1:17).

XIV. Therefore, when the bridegroom has been called—who He is, you have sufficiently heard already—let this master of the feast say to Him that He has kept the good wine until now, attributing it to Him that “after the lower watered land He gives the upper watered land” (Josh. 15:19), and after the storm makes calm (Tob. 3:22).

But not every human being acts in this way; rather, he sets out the good wine first, and, when the guests have become drunk, then that which is worse. Would you like to hear how every carnal person does this? For he is the one called “man” in this passage. “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment descend into hell” (Job 21:13). Behold, when they have become drunk, that which is worse is set out.

Hear also Solomon, whose words concern the same matter: “The lips of a harlot drip honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil” (Prov. 5:3). Is not this wine also good? Yet it is set out first. See that, for those who are drunk, that which is worse is set out: “But her end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword” (Prov. 5:4). This signifies, unless I am mistaken, that in the concupiscence of this world, with which the children of this age commit fornication, something sweet and polished in seductive words comes first; but there follows that which is bitter to swallow and sharp to feel.

But God, the Bridegroom of the soul, keeps the good wine until now, because for the one who fears Him, as Scripture says, “it shall be well with him in his latter end” (Ecclus. 1:13). And His discipline “does not at first seem to be joyful, but sorrowful; yet afterward it yields to those trained by it the most peaceable fruit of righteousness” (Heb. 12:11).

XV. We have now come to the end of the miracle which the Lord Jesus performed at His third appearing or manifestation. Do you wish the things said at length in these sermons on this miracle to be briefly recapitulated, so that they may be grasped more clearly by understanding and held more firmly in memory? Behold, I shall do so as briefly as I can.

The wedding held at Cana of Galilee is the inward delight of the mind celebrated in the soul, which progresses from good to better, from better to best, both in the transformation of outward works and in the revelation of inward mysteries. The Bridegroom and bride, God and the soul, together possess these delights of spiritual refreshment. Since the mother of Jesus is there, Jesus too is called with His disciples: because, when devout will is present—which both conceives inward grace through the affection of pure love and gives birth to it through the effect of excellent action—that same inward grace and its spiritual charisms are invited by pious groans and pious works.

But when the wine fails, for the mother of Jesus to say to Him, “They have no wine,” is, when spiritual joy has been withdrawn, for devout will to sigh in pious complaint before inward grace for its restoration. But for Him to answer that same mother, “What is it to Me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come,” is for inward grace to impart to devout will knowledge of its own frailty and to make known that it is not advantageous for it yet to receive what it asks. And for His mother to say to the servants, “Do whatever He tells you,” is for devout will to exhort the thoughts of the inward mind to obey in all things the hidden movements of inward grace.

XVI. The six stone jars set there for the purification of the Jews are the six kinds of meditation to be practiced for the cleansing of the inward senses of those who confess God in faith and truth. The first kind concerns the state we had before conversion. The second concerns the state which we now maintain as converts. The third concerns the judgment of God, to whose hidden ordering we are subject. The fourth concerns our departure from this life, which all of us assuredly await. The fifth concerns the calamity of the punishment of hell, which we shudder at. The sixth concerns the happiness of heavenly glory, for which we sigh.

Each of them contains in us not merely two but three measures, when we turn over each of these meditations within ourselves in three ways. In the first, we see to what extent we were intent upon evils, and how many evils we committed in working iniquity; how we omitted goods in committing transgression; and to what extent we ought to have avoided both. In the second, we recognize in ourselves instability of mind, weakness of body, and the fact that we are in no way able either to avoid evil or to practice good unless the hand of divine mercy both withdraws us from the former and strengthens us in the latter.

In the third, we fear lest that hidden and strict Judge neither, though appeased, accept our goods, nor, though merciful, cleanse our evils; and, being offended, moreover arrange all that occurs within us to increase our destruction. In the fourth, we contemplate beforehand the hard and harsh separation of our soul and body from one another, the foul and fetid dwelling of the body under the earth, and the soul’s dreadful and terrifying appearance before the Judge. In the fifth, we shudder within ourselves at the burning fire, the gnawing worm, and the fact that both have no end: the former being inextinguishable and the latter immortal.

In the sixth, we portray upon the parchment of the heart what that future blessedness will be, which we hope to receive threefold in the life to come, concerning which we read: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, neither has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9). To speak of it, however superficially: what will be the power which we shall have in ourselves; what the wisdom which we shall have in God; what the kindness which we shall have in our fellow-citizens—first from the Father, second from the Son, third from the Holy Spirit—so that God may be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). The servants fill these six stone jars with water up to the brim when, through these six kinds of strong and steadfast meditations, and with divine grace breathing upon them, the full thoughts of the mind conceive fear.

XVII. When these same servants carry what has been drawn from the jars, he who tastes it says that the bridegroom has kept the good wine until now. This is because, when the thoughts of the mind present their inmost revolvings to the judgment of discernment, discernment approves the fact that those which formerly sighed in fear now breathe freely in love; and, praising God for this spiritual change in them, declares that He has granted them His sweetness and delight at the last.

But we see the whole multitude of carnal people acting far otherwise. They strive first to take for themselves what is sweet according to the flesh and according to this world; and afterward, having become damnably insensible, they receive what is bitter in punishment, “struck in their hind parts and disfigured with everlasting reproach” (Ps. 77:66). Thus every human being sets the good wine first, because in the lineage of the reprobate Enoch is born first (Gen. 4:17). Those who dedicate themselves to temporal things—which appears to be what the name Enoch signifies—fix the intention of their heart upon earthly things; and, seeking to have here an abiding city, do not seek the city to come.

But God, the Bridegroom of the soul, keeps the good wine until now, because in the lineage of the elect Enoch appears seventh (Gen. 5:18): since their dedication will be not merely now but at the end (Gen. 5:24). Walking with God—that is, agreeing with Him in all things in their manner of life—they do not appear in the impurity of carnal people, because God places and establishes them in His holiness.

XVIII. And, if you are willing to receive it, He keeps the good wine until now because, “when He gives sleep to His beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126:3). They shall drink this wine and be made drunk, the dearly beloved of the Bridegroom, at the wedding-feast of the heavenly homeland (Song 5:1), when both those things which are now celebrated in the Church through faith and those things of which we have now said much, which occur in the soul through inward purity, have ceased; then shall succeed those things in which those blessed guests—I mean the elect angels and human beings—shall be made drunk “with the abundance of the house of God,” and He “shall give them drink from the torrent of His delight” (Ps. 35:9), seeing Him face to face.

“Then we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2). Then the Lord Jesus will appoint for those who have remained with Him in His trials, as His Father appointed for Him a kingdom, that they may eat and drink at these royal and most noble wedding-feasts, at His table in His kingdom (Luke 22:29). Then He will gird Himself, cause His servants whom He finds watching to recline, and, passing by, minister to them (Luke 12:37).

Then water shall be changed into wine, because the human being shall pass into God. Hence this song of the man of God is no less true than beautiful:

> The flowing wave, the passing human being:  
> united with Lyaeus [wine],  
> is joined to Christ in Christ’s blood.

Hildebert of Tours, *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*.

“For wherever the body shall be, there shall the eagles be gathered together” (Luke 17:37). And the Son’s prayer to the Father is in these terms: “Father, I desire that those whom You have given Me may be with Me where I am, that they may see My glory which You have given Me” (John 17:24).

Our water also shall be changed into wine, our mortality into immortality; for this is both contained in our faith, awaited by our hope, and merited by charity. Paul’s testimony on these matters is true: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53). Truly water shall be changed into wine, because “death shall be swallowed up in victory” (ibid., 54). Until then the Bridegroom of the Church, the Bridegroom of the soul, and the Bridegroom of that blessed and heavenly Bride keeps the good wine, “delivering the kingdom to God the Father” (ibid., 24); and death itself, the enemy, shall be destroyed (ibid., 26), and God shall be all in all (ibid., 28), reigning in His elect, blessed and exalted above all for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0439]

# BOOK ON THE ORDER, HABIT, AND PROFESSION OF THE CANONS OF THE PREMONSTRATENSIAN ORDER

## PREFACE OF MASTER ADAM

I. Addressing in this preface the most reverend lords and my fathers most dearly beloved in the bowels of Christ, men of venerable life, abbots of the Premonstratensian Order who shall read this book, I do not deny that I may justly be reproved for rashness, because I—a blind mole who burrows beneath the ground—presume to appear even for a moment before such bright rays of the sun of righteousness. Yet I proceed not without great fear, and humbly direct a petition to them, crying in these words: “Bear with a little of my foolishness, and endure me also” (1 Cor. 11:1).

The Apostle Paul, the vessel of election, declares himself a debtor not only to the wise but also to the unwise (Rom. 1:14). This debt he paid them fully and perseveringly, especially in that he kindly and patiently instructed them in catholic and faithful doctrine when they were troublesome, no less than he endured them when they were ignorant.

II. That great Doctor of the Gentiles in faith and truth, whom concern for all the Churches held bound, became not merely something to some persons, but all things to all persons, that he might save all (1 Cor. 9:22). That perfection was no less great in the weight of holiness than this intention was in merit. For as the latter shone with unfailing purity, so the former appeared in surpassing greatness. Therefore, to become all things to all persons is to climb the summit of highest perfection. And he holds an exalted place in it who preserves himself perfect even while dealing perseveringly with another’s imperfection. This is not to be moved at all from the stability which is the bond of perfection, whatever kind or degree of imperfection he may encounter in another.

Such persons, whoever they may be, untiringly support others in fulfilling the law of Christ, supported with them by that charity which endures not merely some burdens but all the burdens of others; pursuing indeed, according to place and time, person and cause, the fault, but always fostering nature in all persons. The eminence of the position in which you are placed, so that you are set over others, admonishes you to be such persons. And indeed, it belongs to my humility not to disbelieve that you are such. But whether you are such belongs only to the equity of inward judgment to weigh, just as it belongs to that same judgment to condemn you if you are not such, and to reward your devotion if you are.

III. Therefore bear with my foolishness, O wise men. Endure my weakness, O strong men. My humility ventures to send to your exaltedness what I have scratched out as best I could. I ask you to be indignant, if there is any, at my presumption in such a way that you may favor the love which unquestionably exists. Grant that I may be unskilled in speech, but not empty of love. Certainly, provided that it sees the presence of that which builds up, the Wise Man will not hastily pronounce a rash judgment because of the absence of that which puffs up (1 Cor. 8:1). As you know, Paul calls the former charity and the latter knowledge.

Love therefore invites me to undertake this work, but fear forbids me to undertake it: love, that I may especially please you, by whom it is always good for me to be forewarned and fortified lest I displease; and fear, lest conversely I displease those whom I ought by every means to attend upon and to serve so as to please. But if Paul’s saying is not false, nor your own experience deceptive, the perfection of the former is the expulsion of the latter.

IV. For no boldness can be lacking to one whose whole heart sincere affection and perfect charity have claimed. For what charity does not now dare, Christ grants; and purity of a simple heart grants the same, so that it may be one in itself; goodness bears witness to truth in the conscience, so that it may be secure concerning itself; and the firmness of faith supplies the adhesive power of steadfastness, so that it may be perpetual in itself.

But let us hear the words of a holy and wise man—

[Note: Bernard of Clairvaux, presumably, *Sermon 79 on the Song of Songs*.]

—words uttered long before our time, no less true than polished, to be approved by our silence because of their authority and adopted as testimony for our assertion because of their truth:

> O headlong, vehement, burning, impetuous love! You do not allow a person to think of anything besides yourself. You disdain other things; you despise everything except yourself; you are content with yourself. You confound ranks, disregard custom, know no measure. Whatever seems to belong to expediency, reason, modesty, counsel, or judgment, you triumph over in yourself and reduce to captivity.

This, therefore, venerable Fathers, is the reason why I have not thought it presumption even to set the vegetables of my poverty before those who are delicate, and not to be silent before you when I do not know how to speak.

V. This book contains fourteen sermons. I divided it into sermons so that their character as though of a present address to the readers might both illuminate the understanding and kindle the affection; and so that their suitable division might remove weariness from the sluggish and inspire desire in the diligent. Yet let me add this also: I did not think it should be sent to you because I judged it highly necessary for you or yours, but rather in order to demonstrate in this matter my affection toward you.

Receive, therefore, the gift sent by a spiritual son of your womb: a gift which the cheapness of its own value makes small, but which the charity of its sender makes great. And I earnestly entreat your kindness that, as devotion makes it more pleasing to me in the greatness of its intent, so estimation may make it less restricted among you by the smallness of its value; but that it may be received by you in the same intention in which it is sent by me.

I also wish this to be added to my petition: when, according to place and time, business and cause, you may perhaps be able suitably to steal leisure, have these sermons diligently read aloud before you more frequently. Thus approve whatever you find suitably said in them; but where matters stand otherwise in them, leave nothing at all uncorrected.

VI. I wish this further to be added: conceal these writings, both from your own and from others, who are wise and prudent; and reveal them to little ones, so that I may be to the latter “an odor of life unto life,” and to the former “an odor of death unto death.” For there are very many in this present age whose mouth is corrupted by the rottenness which Solomon declares to be envy; they take offense at Him who is to them a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense, although He knows neither of these things. But He is honor to those in whom envy is absent.

Therefore, while in their proud arrogance the envious incur spiritual loss by disparaging what the well-disposed gain spiritual profit by approving with humble affection, it is no wonder that, when the Lamb opens the sealed book, the latter rejoice that they have been admitted now, while the former lament, even if late, that they have been excluded.

VII. The first and second sermons treat of the order of canons; the third and fourth, of the habit of the canons of the Premonstratensian Order; and the remaining ten, of their profession. Since mention is made in that profession of the Rule of our father and advocate, blessed Augustine, it was necessary to expound the whole of that Rule. This, certainly, could not suitably be brought to completion without some prolixity of exposition.

Since the principal subject-matter of these sermons is found to consist in these three matters, and indeed in a way which appears to concern our own canons more particularly than other canons, one of our brethren judges that this title should be given to this book: *On the Order, Habit, and Profession of the Canons of the Premonstratensian Order*. But why do I express these matters separately in this way? For I too shall regard as my own, without any exception, whatever pertains to the same sermons, only insofar as it receives the approval of your examination.

But at the conclusion of this preface, my final and insistent petition is that, when these works have been read aloud before you, you may make known to me clearly by your reception and eagerness, by your rejoicing and sympathy, by your approval and favor, what hope, confidence, and boldness can and ought to arise in me for sending and revealing to you certain other little works which appear to belong to my small capacity.

May divine grace preserve your venerable fatherhood, praying for us, in health and safety, and bring it to the happiness of the heavenly homeland. Amen.

# ON THE ORDER, HABIT, AND PROFESSION OF THE CANONS OF THE PREMONSTRATENSIAN ORDER

[Col. 0443]

## FIRST SERMON

Concerning the debt by which canons are bound; concerning the dignity of their order; concerning the threefold rectitude of thought; and concerning the three stages of perverse thought: suggestion, delight, and consent.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. How great is the concern required for fulfilling a vow.

2. The quantity of the debt, which is increased by order, habit, and profession, must be assessed from the quantity received.

3. Order elevates; habit symbolizes; profession binds.

4. Conduct must not be at variance with an exalted profession.

5. The prerogative of clerics over monks.

6. A canon, by etymology, is one who is regular: his rectitude toward God and himself is considered.

7. In the canon, who ought to be regular and upright, condemned is the crookedness of which the woman in the Gospel bore the type.

8. The crooked soul is the bearer of unclean spirits; its crookedness is threefold.

9. Though created upright, the human being bends himself down.

10. Inward rectitude is threefold, first that of memory; against troubling thoughts its door must be shut.

11. The threefold shut door in the Scriptures. Whence the remedy is sought: first, against the anxious concern of earthly thoughts.

12. Then, against evil and wicked thoughts, which by poisonous suggestion entice consent in order to kill the soul.

13. Finally, against the phantasms of idle and wandering thoughts.

14. Against the threefold crookedness of thought is set a threefold rectitude: of memory, affection, and intention.

15. An exhortation to maintain that rule.

I. As you yourselves know, most beloved, those who are lovers and children of truth are often greatly troubled by anxious care when they see that they have voluntarily ensnared themselves “with the words of their mouth” (Prov. 6:2) and bound themselves by some bond of promise. For the more purely they love the uprightness of the spirit of truth, the more greatly they dread incurring the crookedness of falsehood.

Thus it happens that they either never, or at least rarely, hide from the sight of their hearts, under the covering of forgetfulness, the promises by which they have at some time bound themselves; and they nevertheless strive, as far as they are able, to fulfill them. They consider not merely in a general way, but sometimes with greater care, both who they are and how much they have promised, so that they may assess how greatly and to whom they are bound—both from the persons of those making the promises and from the magnitude of the promise itself. And the more attentively they desire in this matter to be truthful, the more diligently they hasten to render what they have promised.

[Col. 0444B] **II.** But we, brethren—we, I say—are bound by a great debt, since we have received much and must therefore know with absolute certainty that much is to be rendered by us. Thus much must be rendered, because we have received much. We know that what has been bestowed is to be required in its entirety. For Truth itself bears witness: “To whom much has been given, much shall be required of him” (Luke 12:48). Yet I see that I have said far too little in asserting that what we have received is to be demanded and repaid, because I ought to have added: with interest. For the servant who returned to his lord merely what he had received was called lazy and worthless, and was judged by his own mouth. The lord does not indeed reject what is his; yet the servant does not deserve entrance into his lord’s joy (Matt. 25:21) unless he brings back [Col. 0444C] a gift from his trading doubled.

Our order, dress, and profession never cease to declare plainly that our debt is great. These are three things; among them the order is more exalted, the dress more conspicuous, and the profession also more binding. Behold the threefold badge by which you are consecrated to God; great though it is in every respect, it also makes you more deeply indebted to more persons. If you wish to know who these are [text: *innotescere*, “to become known”; variant: *innotesci*, “to be made known”], they are God, your neighbor, and yourselves. Render, therefore, what is due to all of these: always and everywhere, according to your ability and understanding, being concerned for your own salvation, compassionate toward your neighbor, and devoted to God. Thus, living soberly, justly, and devoutly in this world (Titus 2:12), you will be able safely to await, with a pure heart, a good conscience, and [Col. 0444D] unfeigned faith, “the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God” (ibid., 13).

**III.** Consider, if you please, the considerable dignity of your order; the fitting significance of your dress; and the powerful bond, wholly indissoluble in this life, contained in your profession. For order raises up, dress signifies, and profession binds. And you will, I think, see most fittingly that all these things are as we say, once the proper character of each of the three has been fully made known to you. First we shall speak of the order, second of the dress, and last of the profession. Be present in mind as you are in body. Indeed, you must be present in a twofold manner: lifting up your hearts in prayer for us, and giving us your ears, so that that inexhaustible fountain, appeased and opened by your devout prayers, may graciously pour into the little vessel of our understanding, purified by it, what we may offer you through the ministry of our tongue for God’s praise and your edification; giving joy and gladness to your hearing; and also so that what, by his own bounty, we are about to say may be poured into you—that is, may instruct the understanding through knowledge of truth and inflame the affection through love of the good.

For then no small fruit arises from our discourse, both for you who hear and for us who speak: when you earnestly entreat from the depths of your hearts the Father of lights, from whom “every good gift and every perfect gift comes down” (James 1:7), that he may reveal to us the hidden things of wisdom for your benefit and grant you the grace of understanding; and when we, casting aside every vanity of self-exaltation and curiosity of superstition, seek in our speech the proclamation of his praise and the fruit of your edification.

**IV.** The Apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, addressing his hearers at one place with his customary sound and catholic instruction, says: “I beseech you, I who am a prisoner in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling [225] with which you were called” (Eph. 4:1). This is indeed a catholic and salutary exhortation, such as it befitted so great a teacher to utter and the faithful people of the Church to hear. He wished them to walk eagerly, not to stand idly; and to walk worthily of the calling to which they had been called, so that their manner of life might not conflict in practice with the loftiness of their profession. He showed how they could walk worthily, adding: “With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in charity; careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2). Fittingly indeed: so that, while they walk in the present from virtue to virtue, they may confidently hope with certain expectation that in the future they will see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83:8).

Receive these words, brethren, as especially addressed to yourselves. Consider your calling, I beseech you, and walk worthily in it. You have been called to the canonical order and have professed it before many witnesses. It is certainly a most exalted order, shining with a certain great dignity among all the orders by which the holy Church is exalted and adorned, sanctified and governed. The apostles consecrated it by their own manner of life and raised it to the lofty summit of a singular authority. Those promoted to this order in the Church are clerics. In some respects they are even more exalted than monks, insofar as concerns the authority of power in which they surpass them.

**V.** If anyone doubts or murmurs about this—unless it is because I, a cleric, say this concerning clerics—I might answer the doubter and murmurer: “A good monk scarcely makes a good cleric.” [Note: [Col. 0445D] See St Augustine, *Letter* 76, to Aurelius.] But let a monk also answer for us, if an answer is necessary. In Blessed Jerome’s exhortatory letter to Heliodorus [Note: [Col. 0445] St Jerome’s *Gnomologia* on the prerogative of clerics], these are the words—of one who was himself a monk:

“Far be it from us to say anything unfavorable of those who, succeeding to the rank of the apostles, receive Christ’s body with their mouth; through whom we too are Christians; who, possessing the keys of the kingdom of heaven, in some manner judge before the Day of Judgment; who preserve the Lord’s bride by sober chastity.”

And, in the same work addressed to the same man:

“Clerics feed others; I am fed. They serve the altar; for me, like an unfruitful tree, the axe is laid at the root if I do not bring an offering to the altar. I am not permitted to sit before a presbyter; they, if I sin, may hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day [Col. 0446B] of the Lord Jesus” (1 Cor. 5:5).

Yet the greater their pre-eminence in dignity, the more necessary it is that they should excel in holiness also: that they may be in merit what they are in name. Hence Jerome himself, in his letter to Nepotian:

“A cleric who serves the Church should first interpret his own title, and, having stated the definition of the name, strive to be what he is called. For if in Greek *klēros* (κλῆρος) is called in Latin *sors*, ‘lot,’ clerics are so called because they are of the Lord’s lot, and because the Lord himself is the lot of clerics. And because he is either himself the Lord’s portion or possesses the Lord as his portion, he ought to show himself such that he both possesses God and is possessed by the Lord. He who possesses the Lord and says with the prophet, ‘The Lord is my portion’ (Ps. 15:5), can have nothing outside [Col. 0446C] the Lord. But if he has anything else besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. For example, if he has gold, silver, estates, or various household goods, the Lord does not deign to become his portion along with such portions.”

**VI.** By the customary name, however, they are called canons, so that they may show themselves to be in the uprightness of life. For *kanōn* (κανών), as you know, is Greek for what Latin calls a rule. A rule leads straight; and not only does it lead straight, but what is distorted is also corrected by being measured against it. Gather from this, brethren, what three things you must practice, you who are called canons. For we understand “canons” as “regulars.” These things belong to a rule: to present oneself as upright; to lead aright; to detect by its standard what is distorted; and to correct what has been detected.

Be upright yourselves, so that your title may not vainly proclaim that you are a rule. Otherwise you do not have the love of God in yourselves, nor can you praise him fruitfully. For if you act through love of him, you read in the Song of Love: “The upright love you” (Song 1:3). But concerning praise, the Psalmist says: “Praise befits the upright” (Ps. 32:1). These two belong especially to God: the one to affection, the other to proclamation. And just as these cannot belong to you unless you are upright, so neither can the other two, which belong to yourself. Those two are effects of these, while these are their fruits. If you ask what they are, they are tranquility of conscience and the grace of divine blessing.

Uprightness must come before the quiet of conscience. It must indeed do so, for holy David affirms that joy arises for the upright: “Light has risen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart” (Ps. 96:11). His statement is true, because there is sincere exultation where there is uprightness of heart. And what else is that joy but the rest of the mind? In it the mind rests more sweetly insofar as conscience more joyfully applauds itself in good and truthful testimony, providing for itself in every truth; this conscience is not merely joy but glory as well. For Paul says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and sincerity, and not in carnal wisdom but in the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves [Col. 0447B] in this world” (2 Cor. 1:12).

Therefore joy exists where there is uprightness; and where joy exists, there also is glory. Nor can this glory itself exist without uprightness. For as the Psalmist says that joy has risen for the upright in heart (Ps. 96:11), so in triumph he also says: “Glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. 31:11). What shall we say about the grace of blessing? Is it present where uprightness is absent? Far from it! Otherwise holy David would not say that “the generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 101:2). Therefore you will not be able to love God purely, praise him fruitfully, rest sweetly within yourself, or securely await any blessing, unless you are upright.

**VII.** What is this outstanding virtue, whose absence causes so many and such great goods not to be bestowed? [Col. 0447C] Who is upright except one who is regular? And he, as we have said, is a canon. But one who is bent is not upright. Clearly, for the two do not agree well and do not dwell in one seat. Therefore, if a canon is regular, and a regular is upright, while one who is bent is by no means upright, it follows that one who is a canon is not bent—and conversely.

As I say this, that bent woman in the Gospel comes to mind, of whom we read that she was stooped and could not look upward (Luke 13:11), and whom the Lord himself declared to have been bound by Satan’s bond. Thus she was first bound, in order that she might be stooped; and because she was stooped, she could not look upward. And what does this mean? The soul is first bound by Satan’s bond; being bound, it is bent; being bent and unable to look upward, it looks only at what is below. What is this bond? Whatever it is, we ought not to doubt that it is evil. For how can that which belongs to Satan not be evil? Perhaps it is perverse and reprobate fear and love. For in either case the unrighteous person is bound: in the one, eagerly seeking to acquire; in the other, fearing to lose. In the first case he is drawn away from the good; in the second he is enticed toward evil. Contracted by cowardly fear, he abandons the good; enlarged by carnal love, he admits evil. Thus, struck by the point of the former, he turns the eyes of his mind away from things above; set aflame by the burning of the latter, he inclines them toward things below. And so, while he offers his neck to things above and his face to things below, he shows himself bent: [Col. 0448A] there turning his countenance away from heaven, here nevertheless gazing without ceasing upon earth.

**VIII.** What relates to this act of looking? Perhaps thought, affection, and intention—these three. For this bentness is in the soul. Where we mentioned above that holy David says joy rises for the upright in heart (Ps. 96:11), he likewise invites the upright in heart to glory. Accordingly, we depict a person as bent in soul when, neglecting heavenly things, he unlawfully thinks, loves, and desires what is lowest. And once the soul has become bent, malignant spirits mount upon its back, pressing and oppressing it and inclining its face more and more toward low things. Perhaps the mournful voice of those who recall the mocking command made to them looks upon these events: “They said to our soul: ‘Bow down, that we may pass over’” (Isa. 51:23).

Therefore it is bent through thought, desire, and affection. Of these three, affection is the cause of this bentness of which we speak; thought is its beginning; desire, likewise, its end. Thus, when you see yourself continually turning over in your mind perishable and carnal matters—the former belonging to worldly pleasure, the latter to bodily delight—and strongly clasping them in the embraces of your mind, cleaving to them; or when, even in the exercise of holiness itself, you do not shake your hands free of every gift, do not doubt that you are bent. You must then take up that mournful utterance and say: “I have become wretched and bent” (Ps. 37:7).

**IX.** When you discover yourself to be such, know that you were made such not by God but by yourself. For he himself is not such, and he himself created you in his image and likeness. We read in the Psalm: “The Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. 91:16). He created you upright because he himself is upright. He created you upright, I say, but you made yourself bent. Perhaps this is also relevant to what Ecclesiastes says: “This I found: God made man upright, but he involved himself in endless questions” (Eccles. 7:30). Thus God made him upright in mind as in body. Indeed, the uprightness of the one is an example and incentive for the uprightness of the other. It is most unseemly for you to be upright in body but bent in mind. To show the human being in body but an animal in mind is a kind of [Col. 0448D] monster. The body’s inclination toward low things is animal-like; its direction toward high things is human.

Hence too the saying of the pagan poet:

> While all other animals look down upon the earth,  
> he gave man an uplifted face, and commanded him  
> to behold [or: gaze upon] heaven, and to raise  
> his countenance erect toward the stars.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 1.84

See heaven with your mind and raise its countenance toward the stars, so that, while you dwell upon high things in thought and longing, you may prove yourself upright. Thus in this respect you will conform yourself to the rule, so that you may rightly be called a canon from *kanōn*, that is, a regular from a rule.

**X.** Now uprightness makes you upright, and it is, as we have briefly touched upon, threefold. The first is in thought, [Col. 0449A] whose seat in the soul is memory. Let memory therefore take its stand, establishing within itself those thoughts which are unstable. It is, as it were, the soul’s door, through which either life or death must enter it. Know that this is the door which the Lord commands you to shut when you have entered your chamber, so that you may pray to the Father in spirit and truth (Matt. 6:6). This also is the door which the Lord shut from outside when holy Noah was hidden within the ark with those whom he had shut in with him (Gen. 7:16). Finally, this is the door which the holy men, received as guests, shut after Lot had been brought in to them, and which the most depraved men, struck with blindness, could not find (Gen. 19:10–11).

And behold, my brethren, a great mystery. Through this door both good and evil enter and leave. For, as the Lord testifies, and as our own weakness testifies, evil thoughts come forth from the heart (Matt. 15:19). The devil also put it into Judas’s heart to betray the Lord, for assaults are made through evil angels (Ps. 77:49).

**XI.** Behold, we have indicated to you the door in three places in Holy Scripture, and in each case we read that it was shut. Noah is enclosed, Lot is taken inside, and the one who is to pray is said to enter. Of the first we read that he was in an ark; of the second, that he was in a house; of the third, that he was in a chamber. But why do we note these places so closely? We do not wish to take each one here under a single signification. Rather, we wish to refer each one to the secret place of the inner conscience—without prejudice to those to whom it has been granted both to think more deeply and to devote themselves more fully to such matters.

The affairs of this life often weary the mind; when they burst out in many forms and intrude upon it, they are accustomed to shatter it from every side as with tumultuous, stormy waves. “I saw all things done under the sun,” says Ecclesiastes, “and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (Eccles. 1:14). What judgment does he pronounce concerning the person occupied, held, and stretched out by these things? “All his days are filled with sorrows and hardships, nor does his mind rest even by night” (Eccles. 2:23). Hence fear shakes the scattered and torn mind; pain pricks it; care stretches it; suspicion burns it. The mind itself is a great burden to itself, scarcely able to carry itself and finding rest nowhere within itself. It has nowhere to flee from itself and no place at all where it may set itself down in repose. It is pressed and oppressed, because it is burdened above its strength. Being oppressed, it cannot rise because it is not strong enough to lay down the weight with which it is burdened.

When this impetuous and tumultuous thought—assailing it in so many ways [variant: “but when thought, with so many movements…”; variant: “the impetuous care of occupations…”]—makes its noisy intrusion upon holy Noah enclosed in the ark, he himself, and every perfect person resting in the ark, judges it no less necessary than salutary [a word is missing in the source] for the Lord to shut [Col. 0450A] the door from outside. Let him shut it, that is, against the immoderate disturbance of anxieties, which miserably ravages all carnal persons. This is the flood that consumes all flesh.

**XII.** There is another kind of thought, very harmful to the mind and exceedingly dangerous—far more harmful and dangerous than that of which we have just spoken. The former troubles through preoccupation; this one defiles through wickedness. The former afflicts the soul through care; this one pollutes it through guilt. This is the thought which that ancient serpent often forms in the soul by the poisonous whisper of his suggestion, daring even to enter paradise and deceitfully inciting the woman, by false promises, to eat what was forbidden. Nor is this surprising. For he was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth (John 8:44). He can speak nothing but lies, and speaks them from what is his own, because he is a liar and the father of lies.

That most vile seducer pours the polluted and harmful seed of suggestion into the soul; and, by means of its criminal conception—which is consent—he gives it a barren fertility. I think this relates to what Isaiah says in the oracle concerning the beasts of the south: “In a land of tribulation and distress are the lioness and lion; from them, the viper and the flying basilisk” (Isa. 30:6). What is this land of tribulation and distress but the wicked soul, the dwelling and habitation of affliction and malice? In it the devil suggests, and the sinful conscience consents to his suggestions. He is the lion; it is the lioness; and the viper comes from these, because the commission of iniquity proceeds from the enemy’s suggestion and the mind’s consent. The more delightfully this iniquity is committed, the more frequently it is repeated. Such a soul is now touched by that prophetic reproach: “How cheap you have made yourself, repeating your ways so exceedingly!” (Jer. 2:36). Repeated frequently, it turns into habit; and thus it reaches the knowledge of many people. It now stinks, “for he has been dead four days” (John 11:39). What is this stench but ill repute? This is the basilisk said to fly, as though on the swift wings of fame, because iniquity turned into habit becomes known even to those far away.

Again, in the oracle concerning the Philistines, the prophet says that from the root of the serpent a basilisk shall come forth, [Col. 0450D] and that its offspring shall swallow a bird (Isa. 14:29). The ancient serpent is the twisting snake, and its root is its pestilential suggestion. The basilisk is the movement of the mind; its offspring is an evil act; the bird is the soul, light through purity and exalted through contemplation. Therefore even today the basilisk comes forth from the serpent’s root and its offspring devours the bird, whenever the mind is disturbed by the devil’s suggestion and an unlawful act destroys the soul. For “sin, when it is complete, brings forth death” (James 1:15). Thus the breath of Behemoth makes coals burn (Job 41:12).

When he has entered the house of the mind with seven spirits, he works in it nothing but what belongs to betrayal (Matt. 12:45). Who are these seven spirits? Pride, inflating the soul; envy, tearing it apart; anger, dividing it; sloth, crushing it; avarice, scattering it; gluttony, dishonoring it; and lust, trampling it down and utterly reducing it to mire. These perhaps are those most depraved men who violently force themselves upon Lot (Gen. 19:9–10). It is therefore necessary that those whom he received as guests should put forth their hand and draw him inside to themselves. These are the inner visitations which come to console us, and which come as guests, not to remain. It is nevertheless necessary that they shut the door, lest any entrance stand open to the one whom they have entered.

**XIII.** There is yet another thought that is commonly very troublesome to the soul of a perfect man, and often the more troublesome because it cannot be wholly corrected. The thought of which we have just treated, although it is a greater occasion of condemnation, is not so continual and frequent in the mind. But this one scarcely ever ceases, because when silence comes in heaven, it is granted only for half an hour. And why do I say half, when it is said to occur “as it were” for half an hour? For thus you read: “There was silence in heaven, as it were, for half an hour” (Rev. 8:1).

Our mind is always on slippery ground, weak in maintaining its position and ready to fall.
