Now outside, now inside, it wanders, talkative and restless (Prov. 7:10); unable to rest at home with its own feet, it runs through innumerable places, alienated and removed from itself, made absent from itself. The multitude of places through which it is broken into fragments inclines it, so that it can rarely gather itself back to itself; and much more rarely, when it happens to gather itself, remain within itself. But when this emptiness of useless thoughts tries to burst into the inner chambers of the heart, like a vulgar crowd unworthily and presumptuously forcing itself into a rich man’s bedchamber, shut the door at once, so that, excluding the common crowds, you may pray to your Father (Matt. 6:6). Oh, how continual experience has taught us that these popular synagogues dull the mind’s sharpness with the hard rocks of their tumultuous noise, so that Abraham cannot drive away the birds descending upon the carcasses without great anxiety and labor (Gen. 15:11).

**XIV.** This is the threefold crookedness of memory, which you cannot bring back to true uprightness without great exertion. The first belongs to burdensome thought; the second to malicious thought; the third to idle thought. The first belongs to worldly business; the second to the devil’s bite; the third to the soul’s sickness. In the first thought there is care; in the second guilt; in the third a phantom. Care pricks through anxiety; guilt bites through iniquity; the phantom rushes in through vanity. The first troubles, the second contaminates, the third disturbs. The first is produced by the anxiety of occupation; the second by the enemy’s seed-bed; the third by the heart’s offspring.

But if you are to restore the first to uprightness, you must moderate it according to place and time; if the second, you must reject it always and everywhere; if the third, you must restrain it as far as you can. Moderate it through discernment; reject it [Col. 0452A] through holiness; restrain it through maturity. This is the first uprightness which you must acquire, the uprightness in memory; the second will be in affection, the third in inward intention. But both the shortness of time and the length of this discourse, which asks to be concluded, allow us now to speak only of its nature.

**XV.** Tomorrow also, if the Lord in his mercy grants us leisure, you shall hear what he gives us to think for his praise and your edification. Refreshed in the meantime by silence, let us meet then after prayer and meditation have first been offered, so that according to custom we may be refreshed by spiritual feasting. But at the end of this sermon, I wish you to understand with me that you cannot be regulars—as your name unquestionably signifies—unless you maintain uprightness, since a regular is so called from a rule, and a rule is so named because it is straight.

We have said that the uprightness of the mind is to be referred to thought, affection, and intention: so that thought may be firm, affection clean, and intention pure. O strength in thought, purity in affection, purity in desire! Behold the threefold badge by which your soul is made upright. The more fully and perfectly you possess it, the more truly and sincerely you will be, in the eyes of that inward examiner, what human speech calls you. But we have said something about the uprightness that must be maintained in thought. For the present we defer speaking of that which belongs to intention or affection. We have said this in order that, since the subject remains unfinished, memory may stay awake, so that where we now end, there tomorrow, God inspiring us, we may begin. [Col. 0452C] To him be honor and glory for ever. Amen.

## SERMON II. On the Threefold Uprightness of Affection and the Opposed Vices: the Lust of the Flesh, the Lust of the Eyes, and the Pride of Life. On the Threefold Uprightness of Intention and the Moderation of Our Outward Conduct.

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. A person mindful of his dignity judges these lower things unworthy of his love.

2. How a person ought to relate to God, himself, and the world.

3. The world is loved—though the Holy Spirit forbids this—when one desires what the flesh finds pleasant, the eye finds delightful, and the mind declares lofty.

4. Through the lust of the flesh the licentious are cast down; through the lust of the eyes the curious go out; through the pride of life the presumptuous are raised up.

5. This is the bentness of the soul, from which canons should keep themselves apart by a threefold proposed remedy.

6. Og, king of the Amorites of Bashan, is a type of the pleasure-seeking; the definition of lust is examined. [Col. 0452D]

7. Sihon, king of the Amorites, is interpreted as the temptation of the eyes. In subduing the two Amorite kings—that is, the twofold lust—pride must be avoided, for it lies in wait even for good works in order that they may perish; King Amaziah of Judah prefigured this when he grew strong over Edom.

8. The threefold means of acquiring right affection, and the threefold means of right intention, by which pardon, grace, and glory are obtained.

9. The office of the rule, besides being upright in itself, is to lead aright: so that a just and religious man may be upright in thought, affection, and intention, and circumspect in the outward conduct of speech and deed.

10. The sum of religion consists in the right ordering of oneself and one’s neighbor; what disposition should be maintained toward each.

11. The outward honorableness of morals commended.

12. A fitting recapitulation, assigning individual matters to their proper counterparts.

**I.** The more deeply, dearest brethren, a person considers his own dignity with the eye of his mind fully purified—as far as is possible amid the blindness of this present life—the more necessary it is that whatever he sees in this world and from this world should become worthless in his inward sight. He is greatly aided in every way by carefully contemplating and ardently desiring the blessed and beatifying vision of his Creator, whom he was made to enjoy.

Why, wretched man, do you cling with such affection to these lowest things? Why do you adhere to them so strongly? Why are you so tenaciously fastened to them? You are foolish and “wear yourself out in foolish labor” (Exod. 18:18); what you glory in should make you blush and be ashamed. You yourself are something far worthier and more exalted than these, and you have been made for something altogether better and more precious than they. It is an utter disgrace to you to subject yourself in love to things that are unworthy of you precisely because they are far below you both in nature and in value [variant: “in no way worthy of you”]. Nor is it less pernicious and harmful to admit these things into your affection—not merely in preference to him, but even together with him—who is from eternity, who gave you to receive being from him, and from whom you are to receive eternal blessed being in him [variant: “who, since he is eternal, gave you to receive being from him and to receive eternal blessedness in him”]. Add also that, although these things are worthless and wholly unworthy of you, they are so unstable and nearly nonexistent that they are nothing even when they seem something supremely lofty and excellent.

**II.** Consider then, O man, how wretched and pitiable, poor, blind, and naked you are (Rev. 3:17). Set before your eyes the world, yourself, and God—these three. Turn the gaze of your mind toward what is beneath you; raise it toward what is above you. There worldly things will be revealed; here divine things will be opened to you. Consider also yourself: higher than the world but lower than God. From consideration of yourself, therefore, and contemplation of your God, weigh what you can or ought to judge concerning all things that belong to the world.

Behold: the world is below, God above, and you are in the middle. Strive in each of these matters to work out your good with fear and trembling. Use the world; enjoy God. Comprehend the world in the divine hymn; do not yourself become comprehended by it in your sleep. Finally, rely upon the former for temporal necessity; sigh for the latter for everlasting happiness. God, therefore, is to be possessed by you, not you held by the world. The world is to be taken up by you for use, not you joined to it in affection. For it is unworthy of your love, though necessary to your temporal need.

**III.** Hence comes that salutary exhortation: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15). It seemed to him, I think, that Christ’s chosen disciples would bring great disgrace and dishonor upon themselves if they admitted into their affection what they knew to be useful to them in certain respects, but knew nevertheless to be far beneath them in both nature and value [variant: “although they knew it to be useful to them in some respects, yet they did not fail to know it to be far beneath them”]. He warned us not to love the world and added the reason: because “all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16). What he wished to insert ought not to be suppressed. It is this: “If anyone loves the world, the charity of God is not in him” (1 John 2:15).

He declares that there are three things in the world in which perhaps lies the bentness of affection, concerning whose uprightness we promised to speak today; and therefore we have offered these preliminary observations. Love, desire, and will belong to affection—these three. Love kindles, desire draws, and will impels. Yet they are commonly found together in one affection, whether something is chosen as good or rejected as evil. Your affection is bent either when you love to experience what the flesh finds pleasant, when you desire to obtain what [Col. 0454B] the eye judges delightful, or when you wish to be granted what pride deems lofty. Each of these things is low, and therefore affection does not embrace them unless it inclines toward them. But to incline is to be bent.

Consider the order of this threefold evil. Even things that are not ordered in their own way are commonly not without some order. First comes the lust of the flesh; second, the lust of the eyes; third, the pride of life. For in the first, those who are in the world—indeed, who belong to the world, whose prince is the devil—fall below themselves; in the second they go out from themselves; in the third they climb above themselves. Yet always and everywhere they do so criminally and ruinously: now defiled by guilt and consequently destined for punishment. Do not suppose that I am speaking here of the fruitful falling, going out, and ascending of the elect.

IV. Thus the reprobate are cast down, go out, and lift themselves up. The causes of these three things are pleasure, curiosity, and vanity—these three. For pleasure makes them cast down, curiosity makes them go out, and vanity makes them upright. Pleasure belongs to the lust of the flesh; curiosity, to the lust of the eyes; vanity, to the pride of life. First, following their desires and unlawfully obeying themselves, they are subjected to their own flesh; they do not restrain their heart from enjoying every pleasure: they crown themselves with roses before they wither, wishing no meadow to exist which their wantonness does not pass through (Wis. 2:8); nor do they allow the flower of time to pass them by.

Second, Dinah goes out among them, [Col. 0454D] in order to see—not to see men, but women (Gen. 34:1). They run here and there through the streets of the Babylonian city, seeking to enrich their poverty from the needy resources of this outer court—the court which John in the Apocalypse is commanded not to measure, but rather to cast outside (Rev. 11:2), although it is already outside. Yet in doing this they become poorer rather than richer: always hungry and thirsty, they find in the false and deceptive goods of this life something which both satisfies their appetite less and inflames it more.

But when these sinners have thus abounded in the world and obtained riches (Ps. 72:12), pride takes hold of them; they are covered with their own iniquity and impiety (Ps. 72:6), thinking and speaking wickedness (ibid., v. 8), setting their mouth in heaven (ibid., v. 9), and building that ruinous [Col. 0455A] city whose summit they wish to reach to heaven (Gen. 11:4). They call their lands by their own names; they love the first places at feasts, the first seats in synagogues, and to be called Rabbi by men (Matt. 23:6–7). But enough concerning them.

V. But you, brothers, who are canons, do not incline your affection toward these things. Do not abandon its uprightness and let it become crooked, lest you consequently be unable rightly to be called Regulars if you are not upright. This, then, is the disordered order of the reprobate way of life: first they are defiled; second, drawn out; third, lifted up—pleasure-loving, curious, inflated. God made known in the Gospel that by this order they proceed through a criminal manner of life toward Gehenna’s 231 condemnation. He recalled their proud excuse—the excuse of those who despised to attend [Col. 0455B] the Lord’s supper—so as to state that the first said that he had taken a wife; the second, that he had bought five yoke of oxen; and the third, that he had bought an estate.

Therefore the love of the Father is not in one who loves the world, in which all that exists is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:15–16). Nor were those of whom we have just spoken worthy to taste that great supper. But let your affection embrace with the arm of love, first, the mortification of the flesh; second, contempt for the world; third, the lowliness of humility. The man of God puts to death his members which are upon the earth (Col. 3:5). He crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24), lest he have too great an intimacy [Col. 0455C] with his body, and lest he grant his soul its desire, making it a joy to its enemies (Sir. 18:31).

After this, let him close his eyes to everything that smiles upon him in this world. Let him rise above the height of the earth and, with a certain humble pride, judge as lowly all things which earthly people count lofty; and let him regard as dung (Phil. 3:8) all that they hold to be their highest delights. Let this thereafter be his voice: “Having food and coverings, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8). Let him keep firmly in mind that those who wish to become rich fall into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction (ibid., v. 9). And likewise: “The root of all evils is covetousness; those who seek it have entangled themselves [Col. 0455D] in many sorrows” (1 Tim. 6:10).

VI. In these two exercises of holiness, he conquers those mighty kings whom the Psalmist calls great and strong kings. They are Og and Sihon, the two kings of the Amorites. “Amorites” is said to mean “those who make bitter.” Certainly, whatever the flesh suggests as pleasurable, or the world suggests as an object of curiosity, is bitter. Hear what the Wise Man says concerning this: “The lips of a harlot drip honey, and her throat is shinier than oil; but her latter end is bitter as wormwood” (Prov. 5:3–4).

This is Solomon’s judgment, teaching us toward what end that tends which delights a depraved [variant: “depraved”] soul through softness from the flesh, or which the world presents as pleasant through outward appearance. For this harlot is the lust of the flesh itself, and likewise the lust [Col. 0456A] of the eyes. If she draws any [variant: “if she is able to draw any”] soul to prostitution, she defiles it there through pleasure, but here scatters it through curiosity. Her lips flow with honey and her throat gleams like oil, because what she proposes is judged sweet and beautiful. Yet her latter end has the taste of wormwood, because Sihon and Og of Bashan are kings of the Amorites. Carnal pleasure shuts in the soul so that it cannot reach God, and, once shut in, confounds it.

For they say that the definition of desire is an appetite that transgresses natural order and exceeds due measure. In drawing the soul to desire what it may not desire, it transgresses order and confounds it; and in urging it to desire otherwise than [Col. 0456B] it ought to desire, it exceeds measure and shuts it in. Again, what more than shamefulness—whether conceived in the will or consummated in deed—both shuts in the soul, so that it is not free, and confounds it, so that it is not secure?

VII. They further maintain that Sihon is interpreted “temptation of colours.” And whence comes our temptation by the world, except because we behold it as coloured? It would by no means please us so greatly if what it is in itself lay always fully open to us. But now a certain beautiful colouring appears outwardly in it; and while we fix our foolish gaze on what outwardly shines in it, it necessarily comes about that we cannot discern what inwardly is foul in it.

Therefore mortify the flesh, despise the world, and Og of Bashan is conquered; [Col. 0456C] King Sihon is conquered. But beware of self-exaltation in this great victory of yours, lest—God forbid—the victory conquer you whom the preceding battle could not overcome. Eleazar son of Saura was a man of great courage, but he could be defeated only after he had won (1 Macc. 6:43, 46). Indeed, in the very thing which he overthrew, he too was overthrown.

Therefore, after you have subdued the flesh and cast away the world, it remains for you to suppress in yourself the swelling of pride, so that the pride of life may not exalt you whom neither luxury nor avarice could subjugate. King Joash of Israel once sent Amaziah king of Judah a message relevant to what we are now discussing, as we read in the Fourth Book of Kings, and said to him: “By striking Edom you have grown strong, and your heart has lifted you up. Be content with your glory, and remain in your house” (4 Kings 14:10). Or, as it is found in the Second Book of Chronicles: “You have said: ‘I struck Edom,’ and therefore your heart is raised into pride. Remain in your house” (2 Chron. 25:19).

Who struck Edom and grew strong by striking him, except one who conquered this earthly body by continence and trampled underfoot, with contempt of mind, whatever temporal necessity takes from the earth for use, utterly removing it from his affections? For Edom, they say, means “earthly.” But let such a person beware lest his heart be lifted up or raised into pride. Rather, let him remain in his own house and humble himself in his own mind, so that, the greater he is, the more he may humble himself in all things. These words too bear upon this matter, [Col. 0457A] spoken by someone in this manner:

> Then you will fight well, when you think all things subdued:  
> Pride remains to be conquered, which afterwards attacks.  
> Unless it is conquered, the promised crown is denied.

Let humility therefore make our good works acceptable to God and commend them, so that, knowing that it is he who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2:13), we may say to him in humble confession: “You have wrought all our works in us” (Isa. 25:12); and with the Apostle: “We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5).

VIII. This, then, is true uprightness in affection: a perfect desire and love in our will—first, to mortify the flesh; second, to despise the world; third, to think humbly of ourselves in all things. But we must consider not only what we do, but how we do it. Therefore see to it that your intention is not crooked. When your affection is upright, embrace nothing except what is good, and admit into your intention nothing except what is pure. Otherwise it is not fruitful for you.

But in order that your intention may be upright, seek God alone as the observer of all that you turn over in thought and embrace in affection, and await him as its rewarder. In these matters look to no person’s hand—not to service, not to human favour. Let him be both your cause and your end. For he [Col. 0457C] alone rewards that which he sees to be [variant: “is accustomed to reward those things which he sees to be”] done for his sake. Shake your hands free not merely from some gift, but from every gift, if you wish to be rewarded by him.

Let there be uprightness in your intention, and a threefold uprightness. First, strive to refer to this end whatever you love in thinking or think in loving: that through true repentance, pure confession, and worthy satisfaction you may be cleansed from all your defilements, bodily as well as spiritual. Second, strive to be adorned with what belongs to the exercise of religion: with sincere affections of mind before God, and devout works in your conduct before your neighbour. Third, strive that, having attained a secure end after a good life, you may deserve to enjoy without end the society [Col. 0457D] of the blessed citizens and the blessed vision of your Creator.

Thus your intention will be upright, referring all your things to these ends: that you may acquire pardon, grace, and glory—pardon for sins, grace for merits, glory for rewards. Pardon, by which you are cleansed from the sins you have committed; grace, by which you are enriched with spiritual gifts; glory, by which you are rewarded in everlasting joys on high.

IX. Consider further that a rule is not only upright but also guides uprightly because it is upright. But when you are such in thought, affection, and intention, how can you fail to make a straight path for those who come after you? “The path of the just is straight,” says one; “the just person’s track is straight for walking” (Isa. 26:7). Therefore, whoever is just has a straight track. For God says: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” (John 8:12). Why is this? Is it not because he himself is light? Hence he had said beforehand: “I am the light of the world” (ibid.).

How happy is one who does not live for himself alone, but also for others: himself upright in all things, proceeding according to his ability by upright impulses, and nevertheless guiding others uprightly. Such a person shows himself like those holy living creatures of whom we read that “their appearance was like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps” (Ezek. 1:13). Thus, like a coal, he is kindled with heat insofar as he is upright in himself; but like a lamp he gives light insofar as he guides others uprightly. Hence the Lord’s forerunner was called “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:23), because of this twofold good with which, I think, he was endowed. Fervour is in thought, [Col. 0458B] affection, and intention; light, however, is in his showing himself thus in outward conduct.

For you must show outwardly that this is within you, so that those who see the face may be unable to doubt it. “How,” you ask, “shall I do this?” Hear how it seems to me that you can do it. First take care to guard your mouth, so that you do not sin with your tongue. Set a door of restraint about your lips—a door, I say, not a wall—taking care not only to utter what ought to be kept silent, but also not to keep silent what ought to be uttered. Speak rarely in your own cause, and when you have been questioned twice, let your answer begin (Sir. 32:10–11). In short, be watchful so that your hand may be over your mouth, lest you be caught in an undisciplined word (Sir. 5:14).

But according to place and time, according to business and cause, open your lips, lest you be held guilty [Col. 0458C] of foolish silence, by which a spiritual utterance that could and should have served edification is suppressed. Thus, while diligently guarding uprightness in speech, guard it with no less diligence in deed. Guard it in this way. First, do nothing by which you defile yourself. Second, do nothing by which you harm your neighbour. In the one there is disgraceful wrongdoing; in the other, there is crime. Take every care to harm no one and to keep yourself from every harmful thing.

X. In these two exercises lies the whole sum of religion. For the Apostle James says that pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, [Col. 0458D] and to keep oneself unstained from this world (Jas. 1:27). I say that the whole sum of religion lies in these things, provided you add two further points, matching each pair to the other. One is that you take care to adorn yourself with every honourable quality, diligently avoiding everything that dishonours you. The other is that you do not seek to inflict anything harmful upon the neighbour from whom you recoil, but rather, as far as you are able, bestow everything that benefits.

Attend to these two points in yourself, and to those two in your neighbour; and you will no longer incur sin in your deed by committing what is evil, nor fault by neglecting what is good. Thus your work will be upright, when in it, toward yourself as well as toward your neighbour, you both omit what harms and admit what benefits. Yet amid these matters [Col. 0459A] strive to present yourself in body in such a way that no one may justly mark you with any fault of frivolity. As the Apostle exhorts, the wise person provides what is good not only before God but also before men (2 Cor. 8:21). He further desired all persons to be such that they could be an obstacle to no one.

Hence our Father, in the Rule which we have professed, warns us that in our walking, standing, and all our movements, nothing should be done which offends anyone’s gaze, but only what befits our holiness (Augustine, *Rule*). For a truly reserved and modest man ought to respect the eyes of those who look upon him, and restrain the movements of every member of his body with the bridle of maturity under the strictness of discipline, so that no one may rightly reproach him.

[Col. 0459B] XI. Therefore, always and everywhere, walking before himself after the likeness of the heavenly living creatures shown in Ezekiel’s vision (Ezek. 1:12), and placing before his every movement the eye of providence, let him scrupulously consider in every place and at every time what he ought to be in both the inner and outer person: speaking or silent, sitting or silent, standing or walking, praying or reading, teaching or learning, rejoicing or grieving, soothing or frightening; finally, how he ought to present himself in any movement of his body, so that from the maturity he shows outwardly it may appear that his mind inwardly possesses stability and gravity.

For, as blessed Ambrose writes in the first book [Col. 0459C] of *On Duties* (book 1): “The disposition of the mind is perceived from the posture of the body.” Hence the hidden person of our heart is judged to be either lighter, more boastful, or more shameful; or else more serious, steadfast, pure, and mature. Thus the movement of the body is a kind of voice of the soul. How often it happens that those who proudly disdain to correct this outward frivolity, lacking every foundation of inner gravity, openly and repeatedly fall into horrible shamefulness.

Solomon also speaks in his Proverbs, first sharply noting the fault that dishonours such persons, and then declaring what their punishment will be: “An apostate man, a useless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, scrapes with his foot, speaks with his finger; with a depraved heart he devises evil, and at all times sows quarrels” [Col. 0459D] (Prov. 6:12–14). This concerns his fault. Solomon then adds concerning the punishment: “His destruction shall come suddenly, and he shall be crushed at once, with no remedy thereafter” (Prov. 6:15).

Holy Ambrose likewise says: “You remember, sons, a certain friend who seemed eagerly to recommend himself; yet I did not admit him into the clergy for this one reason alone: his manner of movement was greatly unbecoming. Having found another among the clergy, I ordered that he should never walk before me, because he struck my eyes, as though by the blow of an insolent gait. When he was restored to his office after an offence, I said this, making that one matter alone an exception; nor did my judgment deceive me. For both departed from the Church, so that each might reveal by his faithless mind what he had betrayed in his gait.”

Therefore, brothers, conform yourselves to true seemliness and strive with all [Col. 0460A] your might that in every outward movement the image of gravity may shine forth, rather than the ugly shadow of frivolity appear. This is your threefold outward uprightness, which will guide aright those who see you outwardly. When those who are outside have seen it, and through it have discerned what is within, they will immediately recognize their own crookedness and thereafter apply all their strength to correcting it.

When the fame of Solomon has been heard, the noble queen hastens from the ends of the earth to hear his wisdom (Luke 11:31). When the Magi see the new star, they say to one another: “This is the sign of a great King; let us go and seek him, 234 and offer him gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh” (Matt. 2:11). Moreover, one who has until now looked upon people in darkness says: “I have sinned” (Job 33:27). When the temple is shown to them, the children of Israel examine and measure the building, and are ashamed because of what they have done (Ezek. 34:10–11).

See what and how great, how many and what kinds of things are necessary for us, if we are to be in deed and truth what we are called by name. For since from the canon we are called Canons, that is, from the rule, Regulars, we are unworthily called Canons—that is, Regulars—if we are not conformed to the rule.

XII. Therefore, to recapitulate briefly some of the matters concerning spiritual uprightness which have been discussed at length in these two sermons: a Canon is called Regular from the canon, that is, from the rule. Four things belong to a rule: that it be upright, that it guide uprightly, that by its standard what is [Col. 0460C] distorted may be detected, and that, once detected, it may be corrected.

The soul is also bent in thought, affection, and intention: in thought through instability; in affection through desire; in intention through impurity. The first weakens thought; the second defiles affection; the third bends appetite. Instability of thought arises either from anxiety, resentment, or frivolity. From the first, thought is born burdensome; from the second, malicious; from the third, idle. In the first is care that pricks; in the second, guilt that gnaws; in the third, a fantasy that rushes in.

The desire of affection arises from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. The first defiles, the second scatters, [Col. 0460D] and the third exalts the soul. It defiles through pleasure, scatters through curiosity, and exalts through vanity. Impurity of intention exists when a gift is sought and expected from the tongue, the hand, or service.

But uprightness of thought exists when thought is neither choked by care, defiled by guilt, nor estranged from itself by fantasy. Uprightness of affection exists when the flesh is subdued, the world despised, and self-exaltation humbled. Uprightness of intention exists when pardon for sins, grace for merits, and glory for rewards are desired. These things concern our inner uprightness.

Outward uprightness consists in truthful speech of the mouth, beneficial effect of work, and irreproachable bearing of the body. In the first is truth, in the second fruitfulness, in the third honourableness. Keep in memory what has been said and practise it in deed, [Col. 0461A] so that you may be what people call you in the eyes of the inward Judge, who is God, blessed above all things for ever. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the Order of Canons; on the Differing Dress of Clerics; on the Use of Linen Garments in Divine Offices, and the Moral Signification of White Clothing

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. A lofty name such as that of Canons requires holy conduct.
2. Whether secular clerics may be called canons, and how that customary mode of speech should be understood.
3. Those called secular should pursue modesty, especially in tonsure and dress; unruly men are censured by a decree of Pope Eugenius.
4. The distinctive dress of Regulars as compared with others: that of the Premonstratensians tends toward austerity and humility; nevertheless, children of the Catholic Church fight in one faith with differing customs.
5. [Col. 0461B] The reasonable customs of no religious congregation are to be despised; rather, another congregation’s customs should be judged better. Yet each should retain its own customs unless a due relaxation is made. The exceptional abstinence of the Premonstratensian Canons is an example.
6. The use of surplices by Premonstratensians, in contrast to other Regulars, is prefigured in the Levites.
7. The moral reason for wearing surplices and linen clothing in the divine offices considered.
8. The clothing most pleasing to God is charity, righteousness, and the Lord Jesus himself; without him no one is a monk or canon.
9. White clothing signifies the radiance of holy conduct through the equity of righteousness and the brightness of wisdom; without these we are deservedly empty and naked.
10. White clothing is the emblem of resurrection and of the blessed recompense that shall be given as a reward; it is likewise the emblem of victory, and of the manner in which a person is victor over himself.
11. In order to be clothed in the white garments of glory, we must then triumph over the world and the devil.

In the preceding sermon, dearest brothers, we have endeavoured, insofar as we could, to show what and how much it is necessary for us to possess, so that we may be before God in deed and truth what we are called by human speech. For a lofty name requires lofty conduct. The mirror of one’s life often lies in the name itself. Therefore one rightly bears a name when he displays in the conduct of his life what its sound signifies in his own case, so that this may be said of him: “He has his name from the reality.” 235

Accordingly, beloved brothers in the Lord, we must know that we are bound by a great obligation, since we are customarily called Canons. The very name which we bear warns and invites us to maintain holy conduct in a regular life: wholly and without any exception avoiding whatever is distorted and practising whatever is upright, both inwardly in the mind before God and outwardly in deed before our neighbour. In what ways, and how many ways, we ought to avoid the former and practise the latter—would that both your diligence and ours might henceforth accomplish in action as perfectly as we have now fully taught by speaking and you have learned by hearing.

To repeat all these matters, though perhaps profitable, is nevertheless not a little tedious. Yet we say this to you: if, according to what we have already set forth, you attend to this twofold and salutary exercise, you also trample underfoot with complete contempt of mind this world [Col. 0462A] and the things that are in this world.

II. If this is so—indeed, because it is so—it is evident that those who call certain clerics “secular Canons” do not sufficiently understand that lofty name of which we have already spoken much. For if they are canons, how are they secular? But if secular, how are they canons? What is regular and what is secular neither agree well nor dwell in the same place.

For this is the judgment of the blessed Apostle James: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world shall be constituted an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4). He also asserts that pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father belongs to one who keeps himself unstained from this world (Jas. 1:27). Paul too gives this exhortation in the Epistle to the Romans: “Do not be conformed to this world” (Rom. 12:2). He says likewise to the Ephesians that they had walked in their offences and sins according to the age of this world (Eph. 2:1–2). In the Second Epistle to Timothy he says: “Demas has deserted me, loving this world” (2 Tim. 4:9). He also tells Titus that the grace of God our Saviour teaches us to renounce impiety and worldly desires (Titus 2:12). This too is the confession of our blessed father Augustine: “Whatever I did in the world displeased me” (Augustine, *Confessions*).

Since, therefore, whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is to be made God’s enemy; since that person’s religion is not pure and undefiled who does not keep himself unstained from [Col. 0462C] this world; since the Apostle forbids us to be conformed to this world, and declares that the Ephesians had once walked in their offences and sins according to the age of this world; since Demas deserted the Apostle because he loved this world; since finally the grace of God our Saviour teaches us to renounce worldly desires, and Augustine confesses that whatever he did in the world displeased him—it is plainly evident from these and from other passages of Scripture which we presently omit that one who is known to be secular is not truly Regular.

Thus, when I hear certain persons called secular Canons, I ordinarily understand it in a certain sense as though someone were saying that what is upright is not upright. Just as I hear swans called black, so I hear secular Canons called canons. But let us for the moment understand the expression in this way and not blame the usage itself. Let it be granted that they are so called, not because, entangled with the world itself through the sins of the world, they are conformed to it, but because they do not embrace as strict a purpose of life as those who are called Regulars appear to observe. Meanwhile, it should be understood that this addition is superfluous, just as, in a certain sense, the other designation appears to many to be its opposite. For according to them, just as no secular person is a Canon, so every Regular is one.

III. But those who are called secular, although they ought not to be secular, ought in tonsure and dress to appear orderly, as it befits Canons to appear [Col. 0463A] [Note: [Col. 0463D] See St Bernard, *On Consideration*, book III, near the end.]. On this subject Pope Eugenius promulgated the following decree at the Council of Rheims:

> “We command that bishops and clerics alike shall not, through excess, dishonourable diversity of colours, slitting of garments, or tonsure, offend the sight of those whose form and example they ought to be; but rather that by their conduct they condemn errors and show by their manner of life their love of innocence, as the dignity of the clerical order requires.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0463D] Eugenius’s decree concerning clerics.]

And he added:

> “If, having been warned by their bishops, they do not obey within forty days, they shall, by the authority of those same bishops, be deprived of all ecclesiastical benefices. But if bishops neglect to impose the appointed penalty, then, since the faults of inferiors are to be attributed to none more than to idle and negligent [Col. 0463B] rulers, they shall abstain from the episcopal office until they impose upon the clerics subject to them the punishment established by us.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0464D] Eugenius’s decree concerning clerics.]

This law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good: it is a precept of life and discipline. Yet what we can often read in the book, we rarely see put into practice. In this wretched age of ours, transgressors of this precept certainly multiply, but its appointed punishment is not inflicted on them. Daily we see excess in their garments and an unbecoming variety of colours; with enormous slits, both front and back are left bare. What shall we say of the tonsure? In some, the hair hangs down to the very shoulders. What is shaved at the crown of the head occupies only a very narrow space [Col. 0463C] indeed. Does the dignity of their order require them to appear in such a manner?

Perhaps, however, the saying of blessed Augustine in his Rule on behalf of clerics works in their favour: namely, that they should seek not to please by their clothing but by their morals. Certainly this does not work in their favour, for Augustine is by no means opposed to Paul, who says: “Providing things good, not only before God but also before all men” (2 Cor. 8:12). He also commands us to give offence to neither Jews nor Gentiles nor the whole Church of God. But these people offend the sight of those before whom they ought to be an example and model.

Or perhaps, while they are Canons in all else that pertains to them, they may be thought secular only in these matters—so that what I once thought impossible, I now know [variant: “would know”] is not impossible. I certainly cannot at all suppose that they would not blush to appear disorderly in dress and tonsure if they were Regular in all other matters pertaining to them. For outward bearing often offers in itself an indication of character.

But since these things are so, I do not know whether the bishops are the negligent and idle rulers to whom the Lord Pope says that the faults of inferiors are especially to be attributed. What I do know is that clerics of this kind are not, by their authority, deprived of ecclesiastical benefices in our regions; nor are they themselves suspended from episcopal office because of this idleness and negligence. [Col. 0464A] I certainly do not know whether they even warn them to reform themselves. But let us leave them for the moment, lest we seem to set our mouth in heaven—if indeed it is heaven.

IV. Let us speak of our own dress. The common people call us Regular Canons also, so as to distinguish us from them. It is incumbent upon us to surpass them by so much the more nobly, not only in dress but also in all things demanded by religious conduct, as we have inherited a name more distinct from theirs. If we wish to speak of dress, let us know that we ought to love not soft and costly clothing, but rough and humble attire. The Lord declares in the Gospel that blessed John was not clothed in soft garments (Luke 7:25). The supreme Shepherd of the Church himself prohibited costly clothing even to women (1 Tim. 2:6).

The Lord himself likewise clearly shows that luxury in dress ought not to be found among us, when he says that those clothed in soft garments are in kings’ houses (Matt. 11:8). For we serve not any earthly king but the heavenly King. Therefore, as you know, it is our custom to use no linen garments except drawers. Nor is it praiseworthy among us for anyone to wear woollen garments next to the flesh, unless perhaps, for a reasonable cause and with the permission of superiors, this is temporarily allowed by dispensation.

Yet far be it from us to judge religious men blameworthy because they wear such garments, or to raise ourselves haughtily above them as though we were holier than they in this respect. We do not set forth our own practice for the benefit of readers in such a way as to disparage the practice of others. For although all the children of the holy Church rest upon the foundation of one faith, they do not all follow the same customs in the holiness of outward conduct. The Bride herself is also the chaste Queen whom holy David says stands at the right hand of the excellent King, who is fairer in form than the children of men (Ps. 44:3). Though that Queen’s clothing is wrought with gold, she is also surrounded with variety, because one does thus and another otherwise. Yet unity remains in her, as the Bride says in the Song of Love that her dove is one (Song 6:8), so that those who labour at different times may receive the one denarius in the vineyard, although in the Father’s house there are many dwelling places (John 14:2).

V. Far be it from us, brethren—far be it once and again, [Col. 0464D] always and everywhere—that this detestable evil should be found among us: that we should presume to criticize in any respect the established customs of any religious house. Whatever the mother of virtues, discretion, with pious intention either maintains by strictness or relaxes by dispensation as useful to souls, let us devoutly embrace and humbly approve. And not only this: let us judge all who wear the habit of religion to be better and holier than ourselves, even if we do not see them attaining the rigor which we ourselves observe in clothing, food, or some other outward manner of life.

For there is one supreme Good [Col. 0465A], from which all other goods flow, as from a sufficient and unfailing fountain. It cannot be increased, because it is boundless; nor diminished, because it is eternal: from it all other streams flow. And although they do not perform the good which we perform, they surely perform some other good, perhaps far better than ours. Or if perhaps they do what we do, they do it in another way, place, or time—perhaps more fittingly than we do—and they do it better than we do. Therefore every established custom of each particular Church is religious and good. Those who are not bound to keep it ought by no means to criticize it, but to honor it with the greatest reverence. Those likewise who have bound themselves by the bond of profession to observe it must keep it diligently and perseveringly, [Col. 0465B] unless necessity requires that, by the discretion of the one entrusted with dispensation, it be entirely set aside, exchanged for another, or at least interrupted for a time.

For example, to offer a few instances out of many: certain Canons eat meat in the refectory and when travelling outside. We, however, have no custom of eating meat in the refectory, unless, weakened by illness, we need to be restored after sickness. Although the Apostle says, “It is good for a person not to eat meat” (Rom. 14:21), far be it from us to exalt ourselves above them on that account; for neither ought they to condemn us for obstinacy or misuse. For the Apostle’s wholesome judgment on these matters is: “Let not the one who eats [Col. 0465C] despise the one who does not eat; and let not the one who does not eat judge the one who eats” (ibid., 3).

VI. Likewise, they wear surplices almost everywhere, whereas we customarily put them on only in the divine service. They do well, for this linen garment greatly befits the clerical order. Nor do we think that we do ill, in reserving, by wearing them, a certain special dignity and purity for divine offices. Therefore it has been generally ordained among us that all who minister at the altar shall never appear there without surplices or albs; nor, when the community is present, may anyone presume to ascend the higher steps of the altar unless clothed in a surplice or alb. Priests and ministers also put on surplices when administering Communion or anointing the sick. [Col. 0465D] Thus we assign surplices to divine worship.

When that service has been completed, we take them off, because what is at times interrupted may sometimes be resumed more pleasantly and gratefully. Moreover, by the novelty of the garment we indicate that, in the service of divine worship, we should possess a distinctive purity and dignity not only of body but also of soul. For of old the Levites put on linen tunics during the very solemnity of the sacrifices, and when it was over they were accustomed to take them off (Lev. 8:13). We read also in Ezekiel that the Lord said that the priests and Levites, the sons of Zadok, would draw near to him to minister to him, and would stand in his presence to offer him fat and blood (Ezek. 44:15). And shortly afterward he adds: “When they have entered the gates of the inner court, they shall put on linen garments; and no woollen thing shall come upon them when they minister at the gates of the inner court and within” [Col. 0466A] (ibid., 17). And shortly afterward: “When they go out into the outer court to the people, they shall take off their garments in which they had ministered, lay them in the treasury of the sanctuary, put on other garments, and shall not sanctify the people with their garments” (ibid., 19). And much earlier: “They shall lay aside their garments in which they minister, because they are holy; they shall put on other garments, and thus go out to the people” (Ezek. 42:14).

VII. Therefore we are outwardly clothed in linen tunics, commonly called surplices, which indeed we customarily take off when we go out to the people. By this we signify that at the time of prayer—when, that is, with the door shut, we pray to our Father in the chamber—we ought to be not only more dignified and purer in the clothing of the outward person, but also more radiant and refined in the understanding of the inward person. For what else is meant by the command concerning the priests and Levites, sons of Zadok, that when they enter the gates of the inner court they are to put on linen garments and no woollen thing is to come upon them, [Col. 0466B] except that we who have received God’s gifts through grace, who are ourselves his sacred gift, and who have been taken up for divine worship—who, finally, are by adoption sons of him who is truly just, indeed who is Justice itself supreme—ought to be encompassed by refined thoughts? [Col. 0466C] We should not meditate in the mind upon anything that, through dullness, is as it were coarse, when, raised above ourselves by a pure and clarified desire, we begin in holy contemplation to enter in some manner upon the threshold of the heavenly homeland.

We lay aside these garments when we go out to the people, because neither the tumult of the crowds nor the very frailty of our own weakness allows us to remain long in the same vigor and intensity of mind in which we are during private and secret prayer before God. Yet, as we have already said, we do not condemn those who commonly wear surplices for the sake of dignity and purity; just as neither do we think blameworthy in any respect—indeed, we affirm them to be greatly praiseworthy—those who put on black copes, though we ourselves are accustomed to wear white.

[Col. 0466D] VIII. But why do we speak thus about these outward garments, when all who practice the way of true religion are clothed in the wedding garment of charity, although they appear to people outwardly in a variety of garments? “Have charity,” says blessed Augustine, “and do whatever you wish.” Similar to this saying is what another said: “Have charity, and wear whatever garment you please.” O how precious and beautiful is the garment, the Lord Jesus, with which the saints are clothed! For they would not be saints if they were not clothed with him. The apostolic exhortation to the Romans is expressed in this way: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14).

Justice too is a very good garment, of which the Psalmist, addressing the Lord himself, says: “Let your priests [Col. 0467A] be clothed with justice” (Ps. 131:9). How good and refined, how radiant and holy, are those inward garments concerning which Paul, suitably exhorting certain persons, says: “As God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, put on bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, modesty, patience; bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another. As the Lord forgave you, so do you also. But above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Col. 3:12–14).

Perhaps these are the holy garments of our Aaron and of his sons: that is, the insignia of spiritual virtues with which that man called Jesus was clothed, who was also “predestined Son of God in power” (Rom. 1:4), [Col. 0467B] and with which his chosen ones are clothed. For he “has been made for us by God righteousness” (1 Cor. 1:30). Blessed Job likewise says: “I put on righteousness, and it clothed me like a garment” (Job 29:14). If you wish to understand the fragrance of these garments, the blind father perceived it in holy Jacob, when, delighted by its sweetness, he broke forth in these words: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that is full” (Gen. 27:27). And rightly “full,” because “from his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16).

These likewise are the garments of the new priesthood, which no one is worthy to possess unless, having put off the old man with his deeds, who is corrupted according to the desires of error, he has learned now to put on the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. 4:24). Whoever does not possess these garments is not truly [Col. 0467C] a monk or a canon.

IX. Moreover, since we remember having said that our habit signifies something, you ask and expect us to say something about the meaning of this white habit which we wear. We do not dare to disappoint your desire. And if we prove foolish here too, let our readers know that you compel us. As you yourselves have often heard, the brightness of holy conduct is commonly denoted by the whiteness of a garment; likewise, the solemnity of future blessedness. There it is merit; here, reward. In both there is exultation, which whiteness also commonly expresses in certain passages. But in the case of merit it is in hope; in the case of reward it will be in reality.

For if we are speaking of the white garments in which the saints are now clothed as merit, the faithful and true Witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation, says to the angel of the Church of Laodicea: “I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, that you may become rich” (Rev. 3:14, 18). This means nothing other than that by practicing the equity of justice we ought to acquire for ourselves the brightness of wisdom, according to the saying of the wise man: “Do you desire wisdom? Keep the commandments, and God will give it to you” (Ecclus. 1:33). This is to say: Have you desired gold? Buy it for yourself, and you will have it. And it is well said, “that you may become rich,” [Col. 0467D] because true riches are acquired only when that wisdom which is from above is possessed. But when this shines within the mind, the brightness of holiness must surely shine in one’s work as well. [Col. 0468A] Hence it is added here: “And that you may be clothed in white garments” (Rev. 3:18).

White garments are works made bright by the beauty of holiness. Unless we are clothed in them, we shall be foul with a dreadful nakedness, utterly devoid of virtues; for then the shame of our nakedness will appear, against which we are most earnestly commanded to guard (Rev. 3:18). In the same book we read a little further on that the twenty-four elders were clothed in white garments (Rev. 4:4), because all who are distinguished by the faith of the twelve patriarchs under the Old Testament, or are instructed by the teaching of the twelve apostles under the New, shine with the whiteness of good works.

X. But if you ask about those white garments with which [Col. 0468B] the elect will be adorned in the glory of future recompense, read what is said in the same Apocalypse to the angel of the Church of Sardis: “The one who conquers shall be clothed in white garments” (Rev. 3:5). The adornment of white garments will follow victory, because the latter is first in time and the former afterward. The former is the fruit, and the latter the cause: “The one who conquers,” he says. Conquers what? The one who conquers himself, the world, and the devil—these three—shall indeed be clothed in white garments.

With what white garments? Surely with the immortality and incorruption of his own self; with the good and pleasant society of fellow citizens; and finally with the blessed and beatifying vision of almighty God himself. For these are garments—and indeed white garments. You will be worthy to receive the first garments if you now conquer yourself. For then you will possess yourself fully and have nothing within you that weighs upon you or opposes you, nothing in any respect rebelling against you, provided that, breaking the rigid perversity of your stiff-necked will, you submit it without murmuring or delay to the commands of your elders in carrying out the commandments of the Most High; and, mortifying your members which are upon earth with their vices and desires (Col. 3:5), you extend them to the usefulness of good works. But when “this corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53), [Col. 0468C] you will be clothed with other garments of your glory, which pertain to fellowship with angelic spirits and blessed human beings, with whom you will be united and to whom you will cleave for eternity.

[Col. 0468D] XI. And you will then attain sublimely to this pleasant fellowship if now you trample underfoot, with complete contempt of mind, the world and what belongs to it. Thus, while in the present life, after the manner of the wild ass whom the Lord set free (Job 39:6), you despise the multitude of the city, you may be judged worthy to ascend also to that heavenly Jerusalem, “which is built as a city, whose participation is in unity” (Ps. 121:3).

What shall we now say about those white garments with which we are clothed in that enjoyment of the radiance of the divine vision, and in order to receive which we say that we need victory? I say, not inaptly, I think, that we are to be clothed in white garments because there we shall enjoy the vision of our Redeemer. [Col. 0469A] For holy John in his Apocalypse says of those blessed citizens: “Before the Lamb,” he says, “clothed in white robes” (Rev. 7:9). It is not fitting that they should appear before him otherwise than in white, when he will make them glad “with joy in his countenance” (Ps. 20:7), indeed with eternal joy, according to God’s promise: “I will see you,” he says, “and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

But if anyone asks about the victory by which these garments are attained, it is that by which the saints, courageously resisting the suggestions of the prince of this world, cast him down through the power of God. Thus, while he now wondrously causes them to triumph over the enemy of the human race, he may then graciously bring them to behold himself, the Creator and Redeemer of that same human race [Col. 0469B]: he who is God over all, blessed for ever.

## SERMON IV. On the twofold meaning of the white garment; and on the four places in which the body of the Lord Jesus rested, mystically corresponding to four degrees of perfection; on the angelic appearance at the Lord’s resurrection; and on the mystery of the Transfiguration.

**240. SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON.**—1. We should be solicitous concerning merit on the way and reward in the homeland, and concerning what each consists in.—2. Both are prefigured in the white garment: both the merit of righteousness and the reward of glory.—3. Angels appeared in white garments at the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, not without mystery.—4. The four resting places of the Lord’s body: the Virgin’s womb, the manger, the cross, and the tomb. The first two are considered especially.—5. [Col. 0469C] To whom the Lord Jesus is upon the cross, and to whom he is as it were in the tomb.—6. The four places mentioned correspond to four degrees of religious perfection.—7. The repose of the Lord’s tomb, accomplished in the soul, is represented by various images of inward and perfect rest.—8. Each place is remarkable for holiness; but in the tomb there is a singular prerogative: security, rest, delight, and enjoyment.—9. There appears an angel, a young man seated at the right and clothed in white; in him threefold contemplative vision is expressed. By the young man is signified newness of life, produced by withdrawal from outward cares.—10. To sit at the right is to rest in the blessed hope of election; to be at the left is to belong to the mass of the reprobate.—11. The two angels, one at the head and the other at the feet, teach Christ’s divinity and humanity; his feet are his life and teaching. This bears witness to his presence; and white garments symbolize inward joy.—12. In Peter, James, and John, witnesses of the Transfiguration, are expressed reason, affection, and intention as companions of contemplation. What it is for the Lord to be transfigured, and what his soiled and white garments are.—13. An exhortation to express the meaning of the outward white garment in the habit of the heart.

I. Two things, dearest brethren, while we remain in the blindness of this present exile, must be considered with the greatest diligence and continually set before the eyes of our mind. One is the merit of holiness; the other, the reward of blessedness. The first is now on the way; the second will be at the end, yet without end, in the homeland. The former must be pursued by us courageously; for the latter we must sigh with longing. Both should be present together in our thought, because [Col. 0470A] the first is the cause of the second, and the second the fruit of the first.

Now the merit which we have set in this place consists of two things: the abandonment of vices and the practice of virtues. For the Psalmist’s exhortation is wholesome: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 33:15). And God set holy Jeremiah over nations and kingdoms “to root up and to destroy, and to build and to plant” (Jer. 1:10). There forgiveness cleanses us; here grace enriches us: for the former removes from us what is evil, while the latter bestows upon us what is good. In like manner, reward also consists in two things: after the labors and sufferings of this present life, the elect will escape the punishments of penalty and receive the joys of glory. Neither the former nor the latter will ever be enclosed by any end; rather, [Col. 0470B] both will be eternal. Then they will be delivered from eternal condemnation and numbered among that blessed flock, so that the most sweet promise of our Savior may be fulfilled: “That everyone who believes in him may not perish, but may have eternal life” (John 3:16).

II. Both of these of which we speak—namely, the merit of holiness which we presently practice and the reward of blessedness for which we sigh—are denoted in the whiteness of our habit. We think that this can be established by the testimonies and authority of sacred Scripture. For if the whiteness of the garments in which we ought to be clothed as merit is concerned, Ecclesiastes admonishes us: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Ecclus. 9:8); [Col. 0470C] that is, let the members of our body be clean from carnal contaminations. Or, if this seems better or more fitting to you, let the works in which we outwardly appear clothed be radiant with the splendor of righteousness.

And the angel of the Church of Laodicea, whom we previously introduced to confirm this point, is exhorted to be clothed in white garments; that is, to be adorned with holy acts of religious life. If anyone also wishes to inquire concerning that whiteness of garments in which we hope to be clothed as reward, holy John saw those blessed citizens of the heavenly homeland standing “before the Lamb, clothed in white robes” (Rev. 7:9). And below, at the opening of the fifth seal, he declares that individual white robes were given to the souls of the saints [Col. 0470D] (Rev. 6:11). The angel of the Church of Sardis is likewise told that “those who have not defiled their garments shall walk in white” (Rev. 3:4). In this promise we are plainly taught that we shall pass from whiteness to whiteness, from merit to reward, so that we may confidently hope to be clothed hereafter in the whites of glory if in the present we have been clothed in the whites of righteousness.

III. As I say this, it comes to mind that angels appeared in white both at the Lord’s resurrection and at his ascension. It also comes to mind that when he was transfigured on the mountain, “his garments became white as snow [Col. 0471B] (Matt. 17:2). And behold, brethren, a great mystery. I ask that we knock: you by praying, and we by meditating; both you and we by devoutly and humbly seeking what these things signify.

What then does the sacred history report concerning them? Entering the tomb (Mark 16:5), the holy women undoubtedly saw “a young man seated at the right, clothed in a white robe” [Col. 0471A] (John 20:11–12). Again: Mary “bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain” (ibid., 12). This concerns the resurrection. Of the ascension you likewise read: “As they were looking into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments” (Acts 1:10). Regarding the third event that we have mentioned, you have written in Matthew that “his face shone as the sun, but his garments became white as snow” (Matt. 17:2).

Each of these is pregnant with the depth of spiritual mysteries. May the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens (Rev. 3:7), be present, as is his custom, to us as we devoutly and humbly knock; may he deign to unlock for us the closed things of this mystery. The body of Jesus was laid in the tomb, that most holy resting place, attended, as you know, by the diligent ministries of holy women and the watches of angels clothed in white.

IV. The occasion of this passage invites our diligence to inquire where else that most holy body was laid. At once there come to mind the Virgin’s womb, the narrowness of the manger, and the gibbet of the cross—these three places. The fourth, of which we are now [Col. 0471C] speaking, and on whose occasion we have touched upon the other three, is his tomb. I read that the body of Jesus was in these four places: conceived in the womb, laid in the manger, fastened to the cross, and buried in the tomb. If I must say what I think should be understood concerning these matters, even today the Lord Jesus is in the womb for some, in the manger for others, on the cross for others, and in the tomb for still others.

Although all these places are most holy because of what they contained within themselves, we read only of the tomb that angels clothed in white were seen in it. To what do all these things point, or what do they mean? The angel enters to Mary; inward inspiration enters the soul. [Col. 0471D] At his announcement she conceived Jesus; and through the infusion of this same inspiration the soul receives a saving affection. For Jesus is called Savior. There are indeed some who carry the word of God with them everywhere and do not negligently hand over to forgetfulness the things pertaining to salvation which they have learned through the teaching of the anointing that teaches all things; rather, they store them in the heart, fixed there by continual meditation. For these people Jesus is in the womb: they have the word of God continually in memory.

There are others who, under the common Master and Lord of all, have become gentle and meek, bound by the reins of discipline; they remain at the manger of holy religion and are nourished by the varied food of holy Scriptures and instructions that is set before them. For these the Lord Jesus is in the manger, for he is food and refreshment for his faithful beasts of burden. There are others, however, so steadfastly joined to the love of their Creator that, united to him by the bond of love, “neither death nor life, nor principalities nor powers, nor virtues, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature, can separate them from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” [Col. 0472A] (Rom. 8:38–39).

V. At times they are raised, not only above all things that belong to the world, but even above what they themselves are, to a certain summit of perfection within themselves. Thus they reckon as very slight whatever hardship or cruelty they suffer for God. Nor only this: extending their whole selves upon the cross of charity, they glory in tribulations and count it all joy when they endure harsh afflictions for Christ and fall into various temptations [Col. 0472B] (James 1:2). They have been made so far superior to themselves, in that very summit of divine love, that they view themselves as far away from and beneath themselves, and in no way perceive themselves as enduring what they endure for God.

For these persons the Lord Jesus is on the gibbet of the cross: raised and stretched out on the cross of charity above all that is low; made glorious without spot or wrinkle; and considering every bitter thing endured for Christ as the highest sweetness. But there are yet others, wholly deadened to every desire for visible things and with all the effort of the mind directed solely to invisible things. They desire nothing more in the present than to hide themselves inwardly from the entire tumult of the world that resounds outside. They prefer the secret place of their holy and sanctifying rest to all the riches and pleasures of this world. And not only human companionship but, because of the exceeding sweetness, even angelic conversations themselves, so to speak, they are sometimes accustomed to find wearisome. For these persons of whom we speak the Lord Jesus is, as it were, in the tomb: drawn by the sweetness of spiritual delight, they shut themselves away from the public life of human society into the hiddenness of most inward retirement [Col. 0472C].

VI. Therefore, for those whom we placed first, Jesus is carried in the womb: they continually carry in memory through assiduous meditation the word of God poured in by the anointing of inward inspiration. For those whom we placed second, he is in a manner laid by the Virgin Mary in a manger, wrapped in swaddling clothes: they have been tamed and made gentle by the exercise of religious life, formed by various instructions, and placed there by Mother Grace. For those whom we placed third, he is raised as though upon the gibbet of the cross: raised on the swift wings of sincere love above all that is under the sun, they glory in suffering every hardship for Christ’s name. He is in the tomb for those who, laying aside every disturbance, pray to the Father with the door shut in the chamber of the mind, hidden within and above themselves in the secret place of their inward rest [Col. 0472D].

VII. The secret of this tomb may be referred to the sleep of the first-created father, Adam. When God cast it upon him, he immediately perceived that there was something from himself which was to be ruled, the feminine element, [Col. 0473A] and something else which was to rule, the masculine. It may also be referred to Noah’s ark, in which one is hidden from the perils of the carnal and worldly flood, so that one may not be condemned with this world. It may likewise be referred to the dream of holy Jacob, who, sweetly giving himself to contemplation with a stone placed beneath his head, saw a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, angels ascending and descending by it, and the Lord himself leaning upon that ladder.

This occurs even today when any perfect person, fleeing the malice of the world—which is to avoid Esau’s wrath—clings in mind to Christ on the journey of this present life and, ceasing altogether from every occupation of outward cares, sleeps and rests in peace in unity. In that peace, the more quietly he rests, the more purely he beholds with the spiritual gaze the ladder of charity: compassion toward one’s neighbor lets it down to the lowest places, while devotion toward God raises it to the highest. With the purified eye of the mind he also beholds the preachers of life ascending and descending by it and upon the Son of Man; and he beholds him whom they serve both in ascending and descending, ready alike to aid and prepared to reward [Col. 0473B].

The delightful secret and secret delight of this tomb—upon which we find it sweet to linger in speech—may also be understood through the coffin in which holy Joseph was placed after death. For sacred and truthful history says that he died at one hundred and ten years of age, was embalmed with spices, and was placed in a coffin in Egypt (Gen. 50:25). The age of one hundred and ten years is the maturity of approved character, consisting in the hundredfold perfection of life and the observance of the Decalogue. To die to the desire for visible things is to be mortified through a certain life-giving extinction of the mind. To be embalmed with spices is to be composed with the fragrances of virtues. To be placed in a coffin in Egypt is, so long as the blindness of this present exile lasts, to be hidden in the inward secret of the mind.

Observe, I beg you, the order of this perfection. First, holy Joseph is described as having reached such an age; then as dead; then as embalmed with spices; and finally it is said of him that he was laid in a coffin. [Col. 0473C] This, I think, is what one of Job’s friends declares concerning the holy man: that he will enter his grave “in abundance, as a heap of wheat is brought in at its proper [Col. 0473D] time” (Job 5:26). In such age is signified the perfection of religious life; in his death, contempt for the present life; in the embalming with spices, the composition of spiritual virtues; and in the placing of the dead man in a coffin, the most sweet repose and most tranquil sweetness, in the inward secret of the mind, of one wholly dead to the world.

When holy Moses drives the flock of sheep which he tends to this inward secret of mind, he sees the great vision on the mountain. For then you attain to behold something sublime at the summit of contemplation when you lead the innocent gathering of simple thoughts, which you nourish with the word of God, into the deepest recesses of retirement. This is Moses driving his flock to the inner parts of the desert (Exod. 3:1).

[Col. 0474A] VIII. Therefore, if it is perfectly clear to you what saving mystery is contained in Moses’ desert, in Joseph’s coffin, in Jacob’s sleep, in Noah’s ark, and finally in the sleep cast upon Adam, you will consequently be able to understand what perfect repose, or tranquil perfection, is signified by the Lord’s tomb. We have said that it is the fourth place in which, sacred Gospel disclosing this to us, we read that his most holy body was laid.

The womb of the Virgin Mother is indeed a most sacred place, and no human understanding can comprehend the prerogative of its holiness. Sacred also is the place where God as an infant, wrapped in swaddling clothes, was laid. So too holy is the gibbet of the cross, upon which that supremely good Shepherd gave his life for his sheep. Yet though each of these places excels in immense holiness, we read that no angel in white visited any of them. The Evangelist says that the angel Gabriel entered to the Virgin, but does not say that he was clothed in white. We read, in what appears to concern the manger, that angels appeared to the shepherds; and although it was with the brightness of light, it was not in white. And when the great Priest, soon to become a victim, was in agony and prayed at greater length—when his sweat became like drops of blood falling upon the ground (Luke 22:43)—an angel appeared strengthening him, as you may discover by reading; yet you do not read that he was clothed in white.

An angel appeared also at the tomb, and he was in white, so that we may understand that this place differs by some prerogative from the others which we have just briefly considered. And what is received in the white garments except the prerogative of spiritual exultation? This especially suits the secret of the Lord’s tomb. It is indeed a great good to be filled with the word unto the fruitfulness of recollection; to be instructed by the word unto the holiness of religious life; and to lean upon the word also unto the strength of fortitude. But it is surpassing and exceptional to enjoy the word unto the solemnity of a quiet and tranquil mind.

O to be filled, to be instructed, to lean upon, to enjoy! To be filled unto fruitfulness; to be instructed unto holiness; to lean upon unto security; to enjoy unto delight. What I placed last is more beautiful, precious, peaceful, secure, sweet, delightful, [Col. 0474D] and pleasant than the other three.

IX. This also pertains to the tomb, in which the holy women saw an angel clothed in a white robe. Mary saw not only one angel, but two angels, clothed in white. At the Lord’s ascension the apostles too saw two men in white garments. And the Lord himself is recorded to have appeared in white clothing at his transfiguration. I think—without prejudice to a deeper and more fitting sense, open in these matters, by the ministry of that anointing which teaches concerning all things, to more sacred and subtle understandings—that in those passages which we have just touched upon briefly, where we read that white garments were seen, we may note a threefold kind of contemplative vision.

The Evangelist says: “They saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe” (John 20:11). O freshness of mind! O tranquillity! O hope! O exultation—and indeed a firm freshness, a hidden tranquillity, a certain hope, a sincere exultation! For in the young man spiritual renewal is signified; in his sitting, the serenity of repose; on the right, the confidence of hope; and in the white garments, the sincerity of exultation. For this angel is inward inspiration itself, appearing here such as it is wont to make the soul to which it grants itself by being infused.

He appears young; he appears sitting; he appears also on the right; finally, he appears in white. Holy indeed is the soul which hides and rests with itself and within itself in its purified secret place; which applies itself daily to the growth of spiritual renewal, and labours by every means in its power lest, growing old in these matters, it incur some failure of its purpose. [Col. 0475B] Repose is the more fitting and effective means for this work. For whoever allows himself to be scattered and dissipated through unlawful desires amid outward cares immediately breaks the strength of his spiritual purpose and grows old in mind most dangerously.

Thus holy Job complained that his skin had dried up and contracted (Job 7:5). And lest he turn toward this old age or incur this dryness, that wild ass whom the Lord “sent out free,” and “gave a home in the wilderness,” is said to survey the mountains of his pasture and range over every green thing (Job 39:5). Holy Gregory likewise says of certain persons who pleased their Creator in a more hidden life—those, namely, who shut themselves up in the recess of the tomb of which we are speaking—that, lest through human activities they should grow old away from renewal of mind, almighty God did not wish them to be occupied with the labours of this world. What then? Does not the angel appear to us at the tomb in these words—young and sitting?

X. But he sits on the right, where the blessed company of those is indicated and expressed whom the almighty, gentle, merciful, and just Father foreknew as saints called according to his purpose, and “predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29). For the left portion of rational creation is reprobate; its right portion is elect. The prophet saw the host of heaven standing at the right and at the left, when he foresaw Ahab’s deception through a lying spirit (3 Kings 22:19).
