In his just, though hidden, rejection—so to speak, on the left—the God who is incomprehensible, irreproachable, and terrible in his counsels over the children of men (Ps. 65:5), has that synagogue of the reprobate and mass of perdition: dry stubble prepared for eternal fires. This is that crooked and perverse generation, that provoking house: “a generation that did not direct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful to God”; a foolish and senseless people, whose God is not the Lord (Ps. 77:8–9).

But in merciful election, on the right, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation has the holy Church of those whom he ordained beforehand to eternal life; whom he “blessed with every spiritual blessing in heavenly places in Christ, as he chose them before the foundation of the world, that they should be holy and spotless before him in love” (Eph. 1:3–4). This is that blessed nation “whose God is the Lord,” the people “whom he chose for his inheritance” (Ps. 32:12), whom he also willingly begot “by the word of his truth, that they might be a kind of first-fruits of his creatures” (Jas. 1:18).

Among these on the right the angel sits, when inward inspiration is granted to the pure soul to rest in hope. In this unshaken repose the devout soul hopes that it belongs to that flock to which it pleased the Father to give the kingdom. With such and so great renewal, repose, and hope, my brethren, there cannot but be a great multitude and greatness of joy, because the young man appeared sitting on the right in white. Hear, I pray, how the Psalmist expounds these things: “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121:1)—plainly indicating that the angel in white, who sits on the right, appears to him there.

XI. And what do we understand by the two angels, who also appear in white, one at the head and one at the feet? Perhaps they signify a twofold instruction infused into us through the anointing which teaches concerning all things. One teaches us concerning the head, that is, the Godhead; the other kind of instruction concerns the feet, that is, the humanity.

And what are these feet? Life and teaching. For he himself was called “mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24:19). It is also written of him that “he began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). With these two feet he walked in our land, displaying his works to the world as an example and his words as instruction. And how great an exultation gladdens the soul when, in its inward repose, it now sets before itself the heights of Christ’s divinity, and now the lowliness of his humanity! I say this because one of these angels sits at the head and one at the feet, while both are in white.

After this, we must consider that, when the Lord was about to leave his disciples bodily, he addressed them with words of this promise: “You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judaea and Samaria” (Acts 1:8). Certainly it is a good promise; when it is fulfilled, the Holy Spirit is given and received. And this is the sign of his presence among you: testimony is borne to Christ. It is borne thus: peace reigns in the heart; confession is in the mouth; watchfulness is in action—so that the first belongs to love, the second to edification, and the third to diligence. For Jerusalem signifies the vision of peace; Judaea, confession; and Samaria, watchfulness.

And these things endure “to the uttermost part of the earth,” because “he who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22): to the uttermost part of the earth, so that holy Joseph may be clothed in a long robe (Gen. 37:23), and blessed Job may persist day after day in offering burnt offerings for his children (Job 1:5).

But because, while the Beloved speaks, that beloved one turns aside and passes on: “When he had said these things, he was lifted up” (Acts 1:9). For “he ascends above the cherubim and flies upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 17:11). “And a cloud received him out of their sight” (Acts 1:9), because “he made darkness his hiding-place” (Ps. 17:12). While he speaks, he is lifted up and received by the cloud away from their sight, because, she says, “I heard the voice of my beloved; but he had turned aside and passed on” (Song 5:6).

“And while they looked toward heaven as he went” (Acts 1:10)—that is, while with devout gazes of inward longing they followed him as he withdrew into his hidden place—“behold, two men stood beside them” (ibid.). This is the voice of the Psalmist speaking thus: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have made my soul glad” (Ps. 93:19). These consolations are the men standing beside them. “They stood,” he says, “in white garments” (Acts 1:10), because, he says, “your consolations have made my soul glad” (Ps. 93:19). For they were clothed in white garments because they gladdened the soul. As we have said more than once, spiritual joy is expressed by the whiteness of garments.

And how did they gladden them? “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?” (Acts 1:11). This question is consoling, unless I am mistaken. To know that this is so, hear what follows: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will so come as you saw him going into heaven” (ibid.). Clearly they gladden them by proclaiming that he will come. For this is his promise: “I will come to you, and your heart shall rejoice” (John 16:22).

But what is meant by their assertion that he will come in this manner in which they saw him ascend? For “while they saw, he was lifted up.” Why does sacred Scripture attentively mention not only his exaltation but also their seeing? Surely Elisha would not have merited a double spirit unless he had seen Elijah when he was taken by God. And because he saw, he was not deprived of the desire of his lips: for what he asked, he received.

You know, most beloved brethren, toward what these preliminary considerations tend. For we speak to those who have experienced these things, running quickly through them and touching them briefly, hastening toward certain matters still to be considered; and the discourse presses toward its end.

XII. You know that a clear reason, a pure affection, and a right intention are very good and exceedingly necessary for the human soul. These three attain the lofty and hidden summits of contemplation within us. For “Jesus took Peter, James, and John, and led them apart up a high mountain” (Matt. 17:1). Peter means “recognizing”; James, “supplanter”; John, “in whom is grace.”

To recognize belongs to reason; to supplant what is unlawful in the soul belongs to affection, because, when it has been rightly ordered, it is accustomed “to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7:15), just as it belongs to reason to distinguish truth from falsehood. Both are a great indication of divine grace in a human being. But then it is greatest when, in inward intention, it stretches itself toward nothing that is crooked.

“Blessed,” Scripture says, “is he who dwells in wisdom” (Ecclus. 14:22): this concerns recognition, which is referred to Peter. “And who meditates in righteousness”: this concerns supplanting, signified by James. But it is most necessary for blessedness “that he consider, in his understanding, the circumspection of God” (ibid.); this is properly the gift of grace, expressed through John.

Therefore, when, with the Lord’s help, a person reaches the lofty secret of contemplation and its hidden sublimity—his reason choosing only what is true, his affection approving only what is good, and his intention extending itself only toward what is right—then Jesus indeed takes Peter, James, and John and leads them apart up a high mountain (Matt. 17:1). It follows: “And he was transfigured before them” (ibid.).

What is Christ’s transfiguration? It is the showing, through his own revelation, that he is “the brightness and image of the Father’s substance, sustaining all things by the word of his power” (Heb. 1:3). For as often as he leads us away from contemplating the form of a servant and grants us to see, through a mirror in an enigma, the brightness of the divine nature which shines in him, so often he is transfigured to us. Hence his garments appear white.

Did he never have clothing other than white? Certainly he did. In the prophet Zechariah you read that Jesus was clothed in filthy garments (Zech. 3:3). Consider his circumcision, baptism, fasting, hunger, temptations, thirst, weariness, weeping, slaps, blows, spittle, scourges, mockeries, cross, nails, spear, wounds, death, and burial; and when you behold him in these things, you cannot deny that he is clothed in filthy garments.

“But take the filthy garments from him, and clothe him in change of raiment” (Zech. 3:4). Set before the eyes of your mind this same one, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit of both, enlightening the blind, healing the sick, raising the dead, and doing many other things which belong to his divine nature; and you will see that his garments are white. But let Moses and Elijah appear to you in this transfiguration, so that you may not rashly affirm anything concerning his incomprehensible nature except what you are able to affirm upon legal and prophetic authorities.

In this transfiguration the voice of the Father sounds, bearing testimony to the Son. But then the disciples fall upon their faces, because neither our reason suffices for that supreme truth, nor our affection for its charity, nor our intention for its equity. Yet when the Father’s voice is heard on the mountain, forty-six fall prostrate: for when Elijah hears the whisper of a gentle breeze, he covers his face with his mantle (3 Kings 19:12); and when a voice is heard above the firmament over the heads of the living creatures, they stand and lower their wings (Ezek. 1:25). All these things, brethren, aim at enabling you to know what you may understand by white garments in sacred Scripture.

XIII. We have already shown, and established by the authority of sacred speech, that white garments can signify exultation both in future blessedness and in present holiness. Your habit invites you to seek both: to possess the one already and to sigh for the other; the one in practice, the other in desire; the one by which we now merit amid labour, the other by which we are then rewarded in repose.

Therefore, as you look upon your habit, strive now to be clothed in the white garments of righteousness, so that in the future you may deserve to be covered in the white garments of glory. Clothe yourselves in the white garments of thoughts, conduct, and works—you who are clothed bodily in white raiment—so that you too may be deemed worthy to be covered in the white garments of eternal blessedness. Thus, my most beloved brethren, you shall be marked by a threefold whiteness: first in signification, secondly in conduct, and thirdly in reward; through the granting of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. On the words of the profession of the Premonstratensians: on the offering and surrender of oneself to the Church in which God is served; on the figurative offering of Saints Abel and Isaac; on hope of eternal reward and the sacrilegious appropriation of oneself.

[Col. 0479B]

### SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The customary form of religious profession among the Premonstratensians. Vows must be rendered to God; first, concerning the offering and surrender of oneself, after the example of our God the Mediator.

2. The figure of the offering of oneself, represented in Saint Abel: a pure affection desiring to please God above all, and a right intention.

3. How one should offer his beloved son Isaac as a burnt offering, with the fire of love upon the altar of the heart; which cannot rightly be done unless one has first undertaken the journey to the land of the living.

4. That homeland is now possessed in hope; it is approached by continual meditation and affectionate longing; and, lest labour discourage us, a great reward invites us.

5. The reward of labour is expressed in Issachar, lying down between the boundaries, seeing that rest was good, and therefore putting his shoulder to the burden.

6. Those not sufficiently moved by rewards should be drawn by examples; and among these none is more eminent or excellent than Christ the Lord, who himself is the mountain appointed for sacrifice, shown and given to us as an example.

7. In offering himself, a man leaves nothing remaining to himself; nor may he claim anything for himself without sacrilege.

8. The offering of oneself made to the Church—that is, to the congregation and its superiors—requires ready obedience and banishes sluggishness.

9. Uriah the Hittite is an example to religious men of preferring common labours to private concerns.

10. A second spur, from Simon Maccabaeus: one who is not his own must not spare himself.

11. Christ the Lord is the example of self-renunciation and of virtues to which one should conform oneself.

I. My dearest brethren, your eager curiosity greatly desires and expects—not without hopeful concern—that we should discuss something concerning the words of your profession. It is this profession by whose bond we said that we are bound, and constrained by the vows “which our lips have uttered” (Ps. 6:14). Its bond is indeed a strong bond, which cannot rashly be dissolved without injury to salvation.

Its words are these:

> I, Brother N., offering, surrender myself to the holy Church of Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint N.; and I promise conversion of my manners and stability in this place, according to the Gospel of Christ, according to apostolic institution, and according to the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine. I also promise obedience unto death in Christ the Lord to N., Father of the aforesaid Church, and to his successors, whom the sounder part of the congregation shall elect.

These, my brethren, are your promises; these are the vows which your lips have uttered. Your promises are great and your vows lofty. No sounder counsel can be given you than that you should strive to fulfil them with all your strength. For holy David’s judgment upon this matter is: “Make vows and render them to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75:12). Whoever has made these vows, therefore, must hasten, run, and diligently render them with all his strength. For he is bound by the words of his mouth and caught by his own utterances (Prov. 69:2).

This, then, is his promise: “I, Brother N., offering, surrender myself.” My brother, you read that among the ancient people of God there were many kinds of offerings; but none at all is comparable to this, much less to be preferred above it: the offering in which you surrender yourself. In this you have pre-eminently imitated the Son of God himself, of whom Saint Paul says: “He loved me and gave himself for me” (Gal. 2:20); and the prophet Isaiah likewise says: “He gave his soul unto death” (Isa. 55:12).

Moreover, you have imitated, not only in surrendering but also in offering, the Mediator of God and men of whom we speak. Of him you read in the same Apostle: “The blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God” (Heb. 9:14). “Offering,” you say, “I surrender myself.” O offering, O surrender! An acceptable offering, a perfect surrender. For in offering you surrendered—not, I say, something of yours, but yourself.

II. Saint Abel foreshadowed such an offerer and surrenderer at the very beginning of the world. Of him you read: “God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts” (Gen. 4:4). Abel means “mourning,” and signifies you, who mourn the exile of this present life. The Lord looks upon you because the world is despised by you. He also looks upon your gifts. What are they? The offering and indeed the surrender of yourself. These are the firstborn of Abel’s flock; these are also its fat portions.

What do we understand by this flock except the collection of simple thoughts in a holy man? And what, in this flock, do we think is born first except the affection itself which arises from thought? For intentions are the fat portions. The Lord rightly looks upon these gifts of yours, through which you strive with all your strength to please him: through the purified affection of your thought and through a right intention. He also looks upon you, who in all the inward motions of your thoughts embrace nothing impure in affection, and in this sincere love seek him alone as witness and await him alone as rewarder. Thus, offering from the firstborn of your flock and from their fat portions, you offer and surrender yourself.

III. Receive also another thing that expresses the distinction of this offering and surrender of yourself. The Lord once addressed Abraham in words of this kind: “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of vision; and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall show you” (Gen. 22:2).

You are this Abraham, because as that man is the father of many nations by name, so you are the father of thoughts in deed and truth. Your son is Isaac, because the whole fruit of the spirit consists in inward joy proceeding from the expectation of blessed hope. And because this joy of the heart holds the highest and, as it were, unique place in your inward begetting, and extracts from you a certain special affection toward itself, this Isaac is indeed both your only son and beloved by you.

But it is acceptable to God and worthy of the reward of everlasting blessedness only when it is certainly known to be from God and is exercised for God, both in outward effect and inward affection. Know, therefore, that it comes from him “from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends” (Jas. 1:17); and that it must nonetheless be exercised for him, who is bound to reward only that which he sees to have been done purely for himself.

Therefore take this only-begotten son of whom we speak, your beloved Isaac, and offer him to the Lord. Offer him as a burnt offering, so that you may offer and surrender yourself. With the fire of love laid beneath, burn the whole upon the altar of the heart. For, in this sense, to offer Isaac as a burnt offering and to offer and surrender yourself are one and the same thing.

But before you offer your son as a burnt offering, it is necessary for you to go to the land of vision. For this is the order of the words containing the Lord’s command: “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of vision; and offer him as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall show you” (Gen. 22:2). And what is this land of vision except that which the Psalmist calls the land of the living? For it is the land in which he believes that he will see the good things of the Lord (Ps. 26:3). Unless he knew it to be the land of vision, he would not believe that he would see in it.

In this land the eyes of the blessed shall see the King in his beauty, and “shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). For he will manifest to them not merely himself, but his very self. Therefore the land of the living is the land of those who see. There one lives, and there one sees. Here is the land of the dying, and therefore not of those who see; for where death is, vision cannot be. “I live,” he says, “and you shall live” (John 14:19). Therefore it shall come to pass that we shall live; and likewise it shall come to pass that we shall see. Saint John says, “We shall see him as he is.” Therefore we do not live, but shall live; nor do we see, but shall see.

IV. And why is this, except because we are not yet in that land? We are not there in reality, I say, but we are there in hope. For Paul was not only still in the body but perhaps also in chains when he said of himself and his fellow citizens: “[God] raised us up together and made us sit together in heavenly places” (Eph. 2:6). That is, in him who has already risen and in reality sits in heaven, Paul sees himself raised and seated in hope.

Thus that great Father is recorded to have dwelt by the well whose name is “of the Living and Seeing One” (Gen. 16:14). There likewise seeing is the same as living, and living as seeing. Truly, life sees and vision lives. Every perfect person dwells in hope by that place, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

Go also to this land of vision, the land which the Lord still today promises to the children of Israel. It is the land “flowing with milk and honey” (Exod. 3:17): the overflowing blessedness of body and soul. You will now go to this land by meditating and longing; for thought and desire are the feet by which one goes to it. “Our feet stood,” says holy David, “in your courts, O Jerusalem” (Ps. 121:2); and again, addressing the Lord himself: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. 30:9).

For, I think, in the breadth of that heavenly homeland—the land alike of the living and of those who see, where true and everlasting peace is beheld—every holy and perfect person dwells through thought and longing, “awaiting the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of the great God” (Tit. 2:13). Go to this land in this manner, I say. Go to it and see it; and certainly going to it and seeing it are the same. For the spiritual affection which moves, stretches, and burns itself toward it is both your eye and your step. Wherever the mind has its affection, it raises its gaze and directs its footstep there.

Go to this land of vision, and offer Isaac as a burnt offering (Gen. 22:2), binding there the first-fruits of your spirit and, so to speak, offering your whole self there. I meant to say “sacrificing,” and the meaning is the same, for to sacrifice is to offer. The devout father is rightly first commanded to go to the land of vision and then at last to offer his son, so that the reward may invite him to undertake spiritual perfection if perhaps labour would frighten him away. For who would be sluggish in offering a burnt offering when he has gone to this land of vision?

But if you had not journeyed to this land of vision, how did it come about that, in offering yourself, you surrendered yourself? Does not the Lord first declare in the Gospel that the treasure has been found, and only then that its finder went away and sold everything in order to buy it? (Matt. 13:44). For he would be foolish if he converted all his possessions into a price before he had yet seen what he wished to buy. Thus you too, I think, would neither offer nor surrender yourself unless you first recognized what reward would be given to you for this offering and surrender.

The Lord says to one man, “Come, follow me” (Mark 10:44), but first adds, “You shall have treasure in heaven” (ibid.), clearly wishing him first to go to the land of vision and then to sacrifice his son Isaac.

V. As I say these things, I am reminded of what holy Jacob says concerning his son Issachar: “Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent; and he put his shoulder to the burden” (Gen. 49:13).

Who is this strong Issachar, whom the Lord grants you when, through mortification, you refrain from what is unlawful? He is the progress of spiritual grace. For there is grace for grace; and when you manfully restrain yourself from unlawful things, you deserve, through the bounty of him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends, to be enriched also by the reward of receiving fuller grace.

For Issachar means “reward”; and at his birth his mother Leah said: “The Lord has rendered me my reward, because I gave my maidservant to my husband” (Gen. 30:18). Who is this husband except Christ, the lawful bridegroom of the soul? For her maidservant is the flesh, which, as a maidservant is subject to her mistress, ought to be subject to the spirit. This maidservant is given to the husband when the flesh is mortified from its unlawful desires at Christ’s command. When this happens, the Lord renders Leah her reward. What reward is rendered to her? Surely Issachar is born: the progress of spiritual grace arises in the mind.

Holy Jacob says of this Issachar that he is both an ass and strong: plainly, gentle and robust in his course. According to place and time, he appears humble amid prosperity and secure amid adversity. He also dwells between the boundaries: leaving behind these lowest things, he almost reaches those highest things. He scarcely touches the outermost limits of the former, but tastes the beginnings of the latter—the beginnings of the latter in certain first-fruits of his own, the extremities of the former in certain remnants of his own. Thus, dwelling between the boundaries of both, he admits these things for the use of necessity in such a way that he retains those things for the fruit of delight.

Here he saw that rest was good and the land excellent. This is the land of vision, and also of repose. Nothing is obscure there, because vision is there; nothing laborious, because repose is there. The land is excellent and the rest is good. Tranquillity is understood by rest; stability, by land. But seeing this rest and land, he put his shoulder to the burden, so that, after diligently beholding the reward of eternity, he might prepare himself voluntarily and readily, ardently and perseveringly, to bear the weight of labour.

This Issachar first saw the land and the rest, and afterwards put his shoulder to the burden, just as Abraham first went into the land of vision and only then offered Isaac. In hope of acquiring this rest and this land, you offered and surrendered yourself. Therefore you did not hesitate to offer and surrender yourself: because you hope that you may thus receive the eternal kingdom of heaven. Accordingly, Issachar considers it pleasant and light to put his shoulder to the burden when he sees that rest is good and the land excellent, just as Abraham considers it pleasant and light to offer his son Isaac as a burnt offering when he goes to the land of vision.

VI. But if rewards perhaps do not suffice to invite, let examples at least draw us. Among them none is more effective than that which that firstborn of the dead—the Mediator of God and men, God and man, our Lord Jesus Christ—showed us. He is that one mountain upon which Abraham is commanded to offer his son. For “he suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

The mountains, eminent through their holiness, are his chosen ones; among them he himself is one, existing far above them: “having been made so much better than they, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they” (Heb. 1:4). He is one of them because he is first among them. Hence one who is a very lofty mountain says: “He was made before me, because he was prior to me” (John 1:15). He is one of them because he himself is “the mountain of the house of the Lord established on the top of the mountains” (Mic. 4:1).

Upon this mountain, my brother, you offered and surrendered yourself, having him as your example in the offering and surrender of yourself. Therefore do not consider it unworthy that you should now act for him, since you see that he acted supremely for you. “Whom I shall show you”: he was shown to us by the Father, who gave him to us as an example. For he became exceedingly great and filled the whole earth, so that, as Ecclesiastes says, “the eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14), and “the likeness of a man” may be in the holy living creatures (Ezek. 1:5).

VII. Therefore, at the very beginning of your profession, you said: “Offering, I surrender myself to the Church of God.” Why did you say not simply “I,” but “myself,” with some additional expression of this kind? Should our diligence pass this by? It seems to me also—if it does not displease you—that when I hear you have offered and surrendered, not merely yourself in a simple sense but your very self, you have left nothing that you are to yourself and retained nothing of yourself for yourself. In a word expressed with such emphasis, the whole extent of your person is, so to speak, necessarily marked.

Therefore, since you know that you have offered and surrendered your very self, know consequently that you have excepted absolutely nothing of yourself for yourself. Knowing, then, that you have offered and surrendered yourself to the Church of God in everything that you are, know, and can do, acknowledge that you are indebted to that same Church for every usefulness and every fidelity, according to time and place, measure and manner, cause and business, person and deed.

For this is what it means to have offered and surrendered yourself to the aforesaid Church: henceforth you owe to devote to that Church not only whatever good you possess, but also whatever good you are, whatever good you know, and whatever you are able to do. To the extent that, after this promise, you perhaps withhold from it, for your own need or advantage, your being, knowledge, or ability, to that extent you take away yourself. But I have said far too little: I should have said that to that extent you steal what belongs to it. For it is now no longer yours, but belongs to it. What you offered and surrendered ceased to be yours and began to belong to the one to whom you offered and surrendered it.

See that you do not wish to steal or take away what has been offered and surrendered by you, lest you be judged sacrilegious. Did you not, when you spoke these words, place your head upon the altar and offer upon the altar the document in which they were written, leaving it there once offered? Is not sacrilege committed when something non-sacred is taken, whether by theft or robbery, from something sacred? How much more when something sacred is taken from something sacred? Your soul is sacred, since it was created in the image and likeness of its Creator. Your body also is sacred, provided it is not subject to sin’s dominion, according to Paul’s salutary admonition: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey its desires; nor yield your members as instruments of iniquity to sin” (Rom. 6:3).

You offered and surrendered both to the Church; from that time onward you must not unlawfully claim either for private use. But it is better that I appoint you yourself as judge in these matters. If you saw someone claim for private use, secretly or publicly, what he had already placed upon the altar by offering and surrendering it before many witnesses, what would he seem to you? Would he not be an invader and a sacrilegious person?

You are that man who has done this thing, if you have unlawfully claimed again for yourself the very self which you offered and surrendered, from which you alienated yourself by offering and surrendering, and by sacrilegious usurpation have seized it for private possession. The same judgment binds you, because an equal fault defiles you. Whatever good you know in your heart, whatever good you can do in your body, and whatever good you are in both, you offered and surrendered to the Church when, offering yourself, you surrendered yourself, and surrendering yourself, you offered yourself.

VIII. But what is this Church to which you belong, since you have offered and handed over yourself to it? It is surely the religious community [Col. 0485B] of the holy men whom I see gathered here into one, sanctified and governed by one Spirit; under the supreme head of all the elect, its head is the prelate. Under that same head you too are a sound, comely, and useful member. To this Church you have offered and handed yourself over, so that, having renounced yourself, you may henceforth belong to it in all that you are, know, and are able to do.

If, then, you have offered and handed yourself over to this Church in this manner—and not merely yourself, but your very self—why, by taking away your gift, do you now deprive it, sometimes deceitfully, sometimes negligently, and finally sometimes violently, of your knowledge and ability? What you were formerly accustomed to do in the world for the world, you now do not fear to omit altogether even when commanded; and sometimes, when asked, you are not ashamed [Col. 0485C] to refuse it, or at least you accept it only with great murmuring. Even now you are often not what formerly you always were. Can you now no longer be, nor know, what then you could be and knew? For since you put on the habit of religion, your soul commonly recoils in horror from touching what previously you were accustomed gladly to embrace.

I do not know why it is that you are now almost always ill, though previously you were never without health. You are ordered to write, and, “to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4), your eyesight grows dim, your head aches, and because it is bent, your chest is constricted. Weakness of the legs and infirmity of the feet do not permit you to stand for the psalmody. Ordered to stand for your Church in some case, you immediately do not know [Col. 0485D] how to speak. Since this matter is discussed with you, your tongue has become more impeded and slow—not only that, but you are also incapable of undertaking what is commonly performed by all. While others labor, you eat bread in idleness; and though the industry of the other bees, going in and out and working vigorously within, should summon you to common labor, you, like a drone, lie sluggish within: lazy for work, ready for rest, first at table, but last at manual labor.

IX. O excellent man and vigorous soldier, illustrious and certainly praiseworthy in every respect: I mean Uriah, who thought it shameful to indulge in rest while his companions labored. Knowing that they were occupied, he wished to resemble them, if not by laboring, at least by not resting—those whom in laboring [Col. 0486A] he could not join. Indeed, when the king ordered him to go home and wash his feet, he judged it plainly unseemly and shameful to accept the comfort offered him. Finally, when questioned by the king on this matter, he replied: “The ark of God, and Israel, and Judah dwell in tents; and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord remain upon the face of the earth; and shall I enter my house, to eat and drink and sleep with my wife?” (2 Kings 2:11). He added this emphatically in refusal: “By your life and by the life of your soul, I will not do this thing” (ibid., 12).

Hear the vigor of a man who sought not his own interests but those of others: an illustrious man, surely, ready to set common concerns before private ones, not private concerns before common ones. Yet what advantage, I ask, did the servants of his lord derive from it [Col. 0486B] that he refused to enter his own house in order to eat, drink, and sleep there? Their labor was not thereby lessened because he did not accept this rest; but it increased his praise that at least he did not rest while he was unable to labor with them.

Set before yourself, then, this illustrious Uriah of whom I speak as an example, O sluggard, that you may be ashamed to waste away in idleness while others labor. But if you ask what it is to waste away in idleness while others labor, receive the answer briefly. While others apply themselves usefully and cheerfully to manual work, you whistle over your fingers; while others keep watch, you snore; while others, finally, apply themselves to the devout exercises of holy Religion, you keep one hand clasped in the other and pretend in various ways to be undertaking work. When just necessity and evident occasion [Col. 0486C] require you, you waste away through sloth and dissolve into a kind of utterly vile nothingness of laziness.

But Uriah was not like this. He could not but be sad when he was recalled from the common labor; and he was exceedingly glad when he was sent back. To be summoned away from that labor greatly displeased him; to remain at home he judged disgraceful; but to return to the same labor he considered no small glory.

X. Consider also another man devoted to the common good. In the first book of the Law of the Maccabees, when Simon heard, after his brother Jonathan had been captured, that “Tryphon had gathered a great army to come into the land of Judah and crush it,” and when he saw that the people were [Col. 0486D] trembling and afraid, “he went up to Jerusalem, gathered the people, and, exhorting them, said: ‘You know how great the battles were that I, my brothers, and my father’s house fought for the laws and for the holy things, and what distresses we saw. For these things all my brothers have perished for Israel, and I alone remain. And now may it never befall me to spare my own life in every time of tribulation; for I am not better than my brothers.’”

This illustrious man recalled to memory his illustrious brothers; setting them before himself as an example, he summoned himself to undertake labor for the common good. In every time of tribulation he refused to spare his own life. So you likewise must not spare yourself, in order that you may provide for the common necessity, knowing that you have offered and handed yourself over to the Church of God, [Col. 0487A] so that henceforth it may freely do with that which you offered and handed over to it whatever it sees to be useful, and that you may in no respect whatsoever oppose it.

For you imposed upon yourself a full and perfect silence from the moment when, offering and handing over yourself, you entirely alienated from yourself and conferred upon it all that you are, all that you know, and all that you can do. Therefore, as I have often told you already, do not take away what belongs to another, lest you be judged, and deservedly, a robber and invader. And not merely so, but a sacrilegious person, because you are proved to remove something sacred from what is sacred.

XI. A little above we recalled to your mind that pre-eminent and exceptional example which the Son of God showed you in this matter. Of him the Apostle says that “he handed over himself” (Gal. 2:26). [Col. 0487B] Of him likewise the prophet says that “he handed over his soul unto death” (Isa. 53:12). See, therefore, that in this handing-over he retained nothing of himself for himself; he claimed nothing at all. He was seized with swords and clubs, bound, led away, judged, condemned, struck with fists, subjected to slaps, scourged with whips, defiled with spittle, clothed in a scarlet cloak, crowned with thorns, despised in a white garment, filled with reproaches, fastened to the cross, and delivered to death.

Look, I ask you, upon him stretched out on the gibbet in his most holy limbs, and recognize that, in handing over his soul unto death, he expended his whole self and exempted nothing of himself. Follow him by this path, if you desire to come to him: run through patience, looking to the contest set before you, to him who, for the joy set before him, [Col. 0487C] endured the cross, despising shame.

In like manner, you too, with that freedom set before you to which you hope to advance in the future, do not shake from your own neck the yoke of glorious servitude which you voluntarily imposed upon yourself when, by handing yourself over, you offered yourself to this Church of God, and by offering yourself, handed yourself over. You will then be happily advanced to that freedom, if now you bear this yoke perseveringly, with the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON VI

On the promise of conversion of manners and the matters pertaining to it; on complete and mutilated offering; on the beauty and unbecomingness of religious conduct; on detraction to be avoided and flattery; and on the moral significance of the Magi’s gifts.

[Col. 0487D]

# SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. A mutilated offering, lacking either the ear of obedience or the tail of perseverance, is unclean through the corruption of lust and the swelling of pride.

2. In a religious man, the offering of himself orders the inward disposition, and conversion of manners the outward disposition.

3. One who converts his manners permits nothing blameworthy about himself; toward superiors he displays ready obedience, and toward fellow members devoted service.

4. Conversion of manners further requires inward renewal of mind, figured by the outward change of clothing.

5. A digression on the perverse and distorted manners of certain persons who, beneath a religious habit, falsely claim conversion of manners.

6. Such ill-tempered and turbulent persons await the sharp sentence of punishment.

7. Elegance of manners is rightly compared with a paradise of pomegranates.

8. In the pomegranate is commended the unity of peace and love, without which nothing is shown to be pleasing to God.

9. In this spiritual paradise, pomegranates signify unity; “shoots” signify the ordered composition of manners; and the fruit of the fruits signifies right intention in works.

10. The rite and abstinence of the Nazirites foreshadowed this conversion of manners. Bad wine is detraction and flattery, expressed by leeks and cucumbers, by the gall of dragons and the poison of asps.

11. From this damnable grape are pressed an example of wicked action and the vinegar of deceit, from which the Nazirite abstains.

12. The offering of oneself—soul and body—is expounded through the mystical gifts of the Magi. To return by another way contrary to Herod’s counsel is to change the carnal garment and one’s manners for the better.

13. What oldness must be put off, and what newness of manners embraced, as contrary to the former.

I. The Mosaic law formerly showed, dearest brethren, by means of offerings [Col. 0488B] both that God can be appeased by a human being and that a human being can be reconciled to God. But in order that such offerings might possess this efficacy, the same law judged that they must be such as to lack every sort of uncleanness. Not only this, but they must be whole, so that no member in them should be broken or cut off.

Thus it is written in Leviticus: “The man who offers a victim of peace-offerings to the Lord, whether discharging vows or offering voluntarily, shall offer it without blemish, whether from cattle or sheep, that it may be acceptable. There shall be no blemish in it” (Lev. 22:2). “If it is blind, broken, scarred, or has a wen, scab, or running sore, you shall not offer these things to the Lord, nor burn any of them upon the altar of the Lord” (ibid., 22).

[Col. 0488C] If, however, you inquire concerning what I said afterward, the law that follows forbids an ox or sheep whose ear or tail has been cut off to be offered in payment of a vow (ibid., 28). For every offering of spiritual exercise in you, my brother, is rejected by that supreme and singular wholeness if imperfect, and by purity if unclean; neither is it made commendable in God’s eyes unless ready obedience and steadfast perseverance commend it. The ear pertains to the former and the tail to the latter.

Therefore all these words have this purpose: that we should know that we ought to offer to God, without any exception, whatsoever we are; yet we must take the greatest care that, by his grace, we may become such that we are worthy to be received by him in this great offering [Col. 0488D] of ourselves. For what benefit is it to you that you offer yourself to God if you are defiled either in mind or body? For that supreme purity will not receive or accept you, since nothing defiled in us can please it, whether the defilement is bodily or spiritual. In the one is contained the swelling of pride; in the other, the stench of lust.

The Lord Jesus, pure and chaste in body, yet meek and humble in heart, abhors both these evils in us, rejecting altogether and driving far from himself all whom pride renders vainly lifted up and corruption renders weakly defiled. The coeternal Wisdom of the eternal Father likewise reveals himself only to the pure and meek, detesting alike the gifts of the proud and the unclean, [Col. 0489A] as the Psalmist says: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49:13). Bulls signify the proud, goats the lustful. He neither eats the flesh of the former nor drinks the blood of the latter: that is, he signifies that he does not accept the gifts of those who either swell through the elevation of pride or are filthy through the corruption of lust.

II. I think the following belongs to this matter: after, in your profession, mention has been made of the offering and handing over of yourself by yourself, you immediately also make mention of the conversion of your manners. For the words of the same profession run thus: “Offering myself, I hand myself over to the Church of God, and I promise conversion of my manners.” Thus you offer and hand over yourself; and because you judge that this alone cannot suffice you, [Col. 0489B] you promise conversion of your manners as well.

For while the right hand of the Most High changes and renews you inwardly, you must also display outwardly that same change in conversion of manners, “providing things good not only before God but also before men” (Rom. 12:17). The Apostle, whose words these are, was careful to add “before all,” so that we may show ourselves in all things and before all persons as ministers of God. Hence he also asserts that he is debtor both to the wise and to the foolish (Rom. 1:14). His salutary admonition on this subject runs thus: “Be without offence to Jews, and Gentiles, and the whole Church of God” (1 Cor. 10:32). He also adds an example: “As I,” he says, [Col. 0489C] “please all men in all things, not seeking what is useful to myself, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved” (ibid., 33).

See therefore, my brother, that you now have your manners converted, because, in offering and handing yourself over to the Church of God, you also promised their conversion. In my view, you have them converted when, in all your outward conduct, you show yourself to the ears and eyes of all people in such a manner that no one can justly rebuke you.

[Col. 0489C] Blessed Augustine also summons you to this conversion of manners in his Rule, when he says: “In your walking, standing, dress, and all your movements, let nothing be done that offends anyone’s sight, but only what becomes your holiness.” [Col. 0489D] Therefore you must show outwardly before people a certain newness of holiness in your manners, since you have now offered and handed yourself over to the Church of God; so that all who behold you may see that you have turned them toward a new rectitude from that old crookedness in which they perhaps formerly stood before that offering and handing-over.

III. Therefore show nothing bitter in speech, nothing immodest in expression, nothing disordered in gesture, nothing blameworthy in dress, nothing frivolous in walking; indeed, permit nothing to appear, insofar as you can help it, in any movement of yours that could create offence or scandal for anyone who sees it.

Run, hasten, hurry; and before all things, through all things, above all things, in everything [Col. 0490A] which your prelates command you according to God, obey vigorously and fearlessly, without delay or murmuring. Toward your fellow members also, insofar as you may lawfully do so, be diligent in service, attentive in serving, ready in obedience, devoted in helpfulness. Show yourself humble to all; cast yourself at the feet of all; seek from all grace and love according to God.

Take careful heed lest you display anything fierce in your eyes, or lest anything bitter or harsh ever sound from your mouth, anywhere; but let there always and everywhere be a word of sweetness and gentleness, a word of piety and charity, a word of compassion and love, a word of usefulness and edification. For, as Scripture says, “A good word is above the best gift” (Ecclus. 18:17).

According to place [Col. 0490B] and time, moreover, show them a cheerful and joyful countenance, so that in this way, according to God and as far as you can, you may become all things to all and please all in God, displaying to them a serene and gracious appearance. Yet do so fittingly and with moderation in both respects, so that excessive frivolity may never or anywhere make you contemptible, nor severity make you burdensome; but always possess stern sweetness and sweet sternness. Also, according to place and time, as necessity demands or usefulness counsels, show them signs that are pleasant and agreeable. Thus you will show yourself excellently fulfilling what you promised in this matter: renouncing that old perversity of manners which formerly made you crooked, and persevering in their conversion by these means.

IV. [Col. 0490C] Let old things be past with you, and let all things be made new. Let crooked things become straight, and rough things become crooked paths (Isa. 40:4). Let perversity be changed into rectitude, harshness into gentleness. If until now you have been proud, henceforth be humble; if until now envious, henceforth kind; if until now irascible, henceforth meek; if until now restless and turbulent, henceforth quiet and peaceful; if until now presumptuous, henceforth modest. If until now you have presented your members to serve iniquity unto iniquity, henceforth strive to present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification (Rom. 6:19). If until now you have been an offence and scandal to others, henceforth, if possible, and so far as depends on you, have peace with all people (Rom. 12:18), seeking to please all in what is good, for edification.

[Col. 0490D] Present your body as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your rational service; henceforth cease to be conformed to this world, but strive to be reformed in the newness of your mind, that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God (Rom. 12:1–3). Thus you will put off the old man with his deeds (Col. 3:9), who is corrupted according to the desires of error; thus you will put on the new man, who is created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. 4:24), so that the change of clothing which you bear may represent and indicate in your manners the renewal and conversion that you possess.

V. [Col. 0491A] But certain persons act very differently. Though they appear outwardly in a religious habit, they show that in their affections they have not yet put off the secular life. To all who behold them, they present themselves by perverse manners as a scandal rather than, by converted manners, as an example.

These are disobedient to superiors, murmuring at the commands of elders, envying those better than themselves, preferring themselves to equals, disturbed and disturbing others; violators of charity, dividers of unity, disturbers of peace, corrupters of order. Indeed, in a certain manner they are sometimes worse than secular persons, insofar as they are not ashamed to be in conduct something far different from what they display in habit. One can no longer say of them, “As is the secular person, so is the religious”; for the religious person is not even as good as the secular person.

[Col. 0491B] Now the sea summons Sidon to shame (Isa. 23:5); holy Jeremiah too laments that gold is darkened and its finest color changed (Lam. 4:1). One such is that apostate man of whom Solomon writes in Proverbs, declaring: “There is a worthless man; he walks with a perverse mouth, winks with his eyes, scrapes with his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil with a depraved heart, and sows quarrels at every time” (Prov. 6:12–14).

See how he walks with neck outstretched, raises his eyebrows, wrinkles his brow, turns his eyes sideways, and extends his finger. He speaks what is useless; he looks askance at all who are before him; he turns over in his mind nothing except how he may disturb the peace of those living with him. Now he calls these people, now those, into conversation; in their ears he gnaws at the lives of the absent; with venomous teeth he tears apart the deeds and words of his prelates and brethren, and especially of the officials. He declares the ordinances of holy exercise, [Col. 0491C] imposed according to the rule of the order, to be burdensome and wholly intolerable. He pours into the minds of his hearers the deadly poison with which he himself is swollen; and, clouding all the serenity of inward, pleasant goodness and good pleasantness in them by such pestilential persuasions and detractions, he entirely empties their hearts of the peace of unity and fills them with the dreadful thunderbolts of quarrels, the turbulent winds of discord, and the stormy thunders of murmurings.

VI. [Col. 0491D] Does this seem to you to be rendering to God the conversion of manners which he promised? Is this conversion: that a man shows himself frivolous in gesture, look, and other movements in choir; rebellious and quarrelsome in chapter; slanderous in the audience chamber; indecorous in the refectory; and, in every place and at every time when and where he sees no one before him whom he reveres, whispers half-gnawed little words of malice, pierces the eyes of onlookers with mocking, reproving, and threatening signs of the fingers, and, so far as lies in him, slaughters all those who dwell with him by such swords of perverse manners?

O smoking firebrand in the fire, provoking the eyes of those seated around you to tears by your most bitter and very dark blows! O venomous serpent, overthrowing even a thousand little eels which you, though only one, bring in with you among them! Behold the goring ox (Exod. 21:28), wounding those who meet it and destroying those it has wounded. But how does the legal sentence prescribe that it be punished? Surely, that it be stoned to death [Col. 0492A] (ibid.). And this is just; indeed, it is necessary. It is just, that it may receive what it wickedly did; necessary, lest it destroy many by its pestilential contagion.

VII. But you, my brother, attend with the greatest care to that conversion of your manners which you promised God. Let whatever is seen in you shine with spiritual beauty; let whatever is heard from you be sweet and gracious, so that it may be said of you also: “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchard trees” (Song 4:13).

Let whatever you utter with your mouth or display in deed breathe spiritual delights, so that your “shoots” may be a paradise. What are your shoots except your words and actions, your gestures and walk, and also your outward movements, through which you come forth to the outward knowledge of people? [Col. 0492B] Let these your shoots be a paradise, so that in your walking, standing, and all movements nothing may be done that offends anyone’s sight, but only what becomes your holiness.

What becomes your holiness? Surely that these shoots of yours should be a paradise: that is, that your speech and deed, posture and walk, dress and gesture, and every outward movement should overflow with spiritual delights—the delights which, they say, this name *paradisus*, “paradise,” denotes. “How,” you ask, “will this happen?” Hear how. Let your word be true and sweet; your work effective and useful; your posture orderly; your walk measured; your dress humble; your gesture honorable; and your outward movement irreproachable.

But let all that is yours, openly, serve the unity of brotherly love, and secretly be pleasing to the divine gaze. [Col. 0492C] This also belongs to the statement that your shoots are said to be a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchard trees. For in a pomegranate there is one outer rind, but many seeds. The rind is outward; the seeds are inward. Thus what is contained in diversity of merits is covered by unity.

VIII. Let there therefore be in your shoots a paradise of pomegranates, so that whatever is heard from you and whatever is outwardly seen in you may aim especially at preventing the unity of brotherly love from being divided, and at preventing the good pleasantness and pleasant goodness of that unity from being scattered. For the wisdom that is from above is first chaste, then peaceable (Jas. 3:17), [Col. 0492D] so that what you do may preserve you honorably through purity, while in no way disturbing brotherly peace through discord.

The Lord’s admonition on this matter is as follows: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). By this, unless I am mistaken, he makes known that the savor of knowledge does not please him where the love of concord is absent. Thus shoots cannot deservedly be approved when the paradise of pomegranates is absent.

Woe to dividers of unity! Woe to disturbers of peace! Paul admonishes us to be diligent in preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3). O health-giving unity, without which spiritual salvation cannot be acquired or possessed! Sacred Scripture bears witness to this in many places, and we know that its testimony is true.

Therefore the leper is commanded to offer one sheep [Col. 0493A] (Lev. 14:10), because the lustful person cannot be cleansed from the scab of defilement without the unity of simplicity and the simplicity of unity. There was also one loaf from two tenths (Lev. 24:5), because spiritual refreshment pertaining to the perfection of soul and body consists in unity. The acquaintances and relatives of holy Job likewise offered him one sheep and a golden earring (Job 42:11), because whoever they may be who bear our sorrows, whether they draw near through knowledge of the faith or are joined to us by kinship of life, then please God in the offering of simplicity and spontaneous obedience when they maintain unity of concord.

There was one work in the two cherubim in Solomon’s temple [Col. 0493B], because the intention of each Testament proclaims the unity of our peace in the Church (3 Kings 6:25). The mouth of the laver was likewise one cubit (3 Kings 7:31), because without unity that which is formed by inward sorrow—the confession of spiritual compunction—cannot suffice for salvation. The Lord makes people “of one manner to dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7), because he causes his elect to dwell in the Church in the agreement of one will according to himself. One man, seeing himself healed, gives thanks, because if he lacks unity, even devout thanksgiving to almighty God is not pleasing. Finally, one person receives healing in the pool (John 5:4), because if the unity of which we have said much is lacking, not even faith in the Lord’s Passion can restore anyone to health.

IX. [Col. 0493C] Rightly, as is clear from these things, the bride’s shoots are a paradise of pomegranates. For the spiritual delights which a holy soul sends forth from itself to the sight or hearing of others then abound, when nothing whatever is practiced in them by which the good and pleasant unity of brotherly charity is divided.

But you must take care that what a human being outwardly approves in you as an example may also be accepted inwardly in you by that inspector of hidden things as merit; lest perhaps, God forbid, it should happen otherwise with you, and you “sow much but gather little” (Hag. 1:6). Sowing pertains to work, but gathering to reward. And what advantage is there in the former preceding if the latter does not follow? For then the labor is great but the fruit is none.

Therefore you must strive with all your strength that what shines outwardly before people in your life may shine inwardly before God in your conscience. [Col. 0493D] This will be accomplished by rectitude of intention in the deepest inner chambers of the heart. For ordered manners please people in us, but right intentions win the favor of God himself.

Hence the bride’s shoots are said not merely to be a paradise of pomegranates, but it is immediately added, “with the fruits of fruit-trees.” What are these fruits except our works? But the fruit of these fruits is the rectitude of inward intentions. This fruit truly belongs to such fruits when right intention is not absent from our good works. Hence it appears that those of whom the Lord says in the Gospel that “they do all their works to be seen by men” [Col. 0494A] (Matt. 23:5) possess fruits without the fruit of those fruits.

Thus the whole fruit of your fruits consists in this: that, shaking your hands free from every gift, you seek and await as witness and rewarder in them him alone from whose gift they exist. Therefore let your shoots be a paradise of pomegranates; but let the fruit of your own fruits not be lacking within you. Thus whatever your neighbor perceives outwardly from you, in the manifestation of peaceful conduct, may serve brotherly unity; and what is inwardly in you, in the rectitude of inward intention, may be pleasing to the divine sight.

X. [Col. 0494B] In these things consists the full conversion of manners which you promised: if you appear peaceful before people in outward conduct and upright before God in inward intention, exercising there all that belongs to peace and quiet, and thereby doing nothing wrongly and seeking nothing of your own, while pleasing God alone.

Appropriately, therefore, when you have offered yourself and handed yourself over to the Church of God, you also promise the conversion of your manners: so that you may transfer yourself for the better from what you were before this offering and handing-over of yourself, and may convert the manners which until now you have had harsh and perverse into peaceful and ordered manners.

I think the institution which the Lord promulgated in the book of Numbers concerning the Nazirites has a legal bearing upon this matter. It runs thus: “When a man or woman makes a vow to be sanctified and wishes to consecrate himself or herself to the Lord, they shall abstain from wine and from everything that can intoxicate” (Num. 6: [Col. 0494C] 2–3).

This man signifies anyone perfect and strong; the woman, anyone imperfect and weak. They make a vow to be sanctified and desire to consecrate themselves to the Lord when they both offer and, by offering, hand themselves over to the Church of God. But they fulfill this vow elegantly and bring this will into effect when they abstain from wine and everything that can intoxicate; for they offer and hand themselves over to the Church of God in a healthful way only when they convert their manners.

For, in this sense, perversity of manners is a kind of bad wine. This perversity of manners consists not only in the harshness of detraction, but also in the vanity of flattery. [Col. 0494D] At one time they break out through impatience into the harshness of detraction; at another they bend themselves, as if seeking favor, into the vanity of flattery.

This is the twofold Egyptian food which those who return in heart to that land assert comes to mind; their voice is this: “The cucumbers and melons come to our mind” (Num. 2:5), and in these the sweetness of flattery is indicated; “the leeks, onions, and garlic” (ibid.), and in these the bitterness of detraction is expressed. This twofold evil, and this wine of which we are now speaking, is what the law commands the Nazirites to abstain from, so that they may neither rage madly through detraction nor melt into softness through flattery. For there is a wine of detraction and a wine of flattery.

Of the first it is said: “Their wine is the gall of dragons” (Deut. 32:33)—the wine, namely, of those [Col. 0495A] whose manners are disordered and who, because of the detraction by which they rage against their neighbors, resemble dragons in the fury of their cruelty. And it adds: “the incurable poison of asps” (ibid.), because this fury kills their hearers by the venomous and deadly breath of speech.

Of the second wine Solomon says in Proverbs: “Do not look upon wine when it grows yellow, when its color shines in the glass” (Prov. 23:31). This wine, I think, is said to grow yellow because flattery is ingratiating. Its color shines in the glass because its deception glitters beneath the comely appearance of deceitfully painted speech. But do not look upon this wine even when its color thus shines in the glass [Col. 0495B], so that you may not approve the sweetness of flattery when its deceit has gleamed beneath deceptive discourse. He adds the reason why we should not look upon this wine: “For it enters smoothly, and in the end will bite like a serpent” (ibid., 31–32). This wine is indeed sweet and very pleasing, but it has a destructive bite at the end.

XI. Let your manners, then, be free from this twofold evil. Abstain from this wine: neither become drunk with it yourself nor make others drunk. The law adds: “They shall not drink vinegar from wine, or from any other drink, nor anything pressed from the grape” (Num. 6:35).

This vinegar is deceit. The Evangelist says that the sponge was filled with vinegar (John 19), because the devil filled the Jewish people with fraud and guile. And what is “that which is pressed from the grape” [Col. 0495C] except a bad example, sent forth from the bitterness of wicked action? Of this grape it is said in the Song of Deuteronomy: “Their grape is a grape of gall” (Deut. 32:32), that is, their work is a work of bitterness.

You who have offered and handed yourself over to the Lord by sanctifying and consecrating yourself, and have handed yourself over to the Church of God, must not drink this vinegar or eat that which is pressed from the grape: so that you may neither delight in the deceit of those whose manners are disordered nor imitate their wicked action.

Therefore, since you have now offered and handed yourself over to the Church of God, attend to the conversion of your manners. Convert them, so that henceforth they may be far different from what they have been until now. You have offered and handed over not merely yourself, but also—if by this something fuller and more explicit can be indicated—your very self [Col. 0495D]: that is, all that is within you and all that is outside you. Complete, then, what remains: namely, convert your manners, so that henceforth you may be other in these same manners of yours than you have been up to now.

XII. And take, if you please, an excellent example concerning these matters in those Magi who came to Christ with the star as their guide. They offered gifts to the Lord (Matt. 2:12), and returned to their own country; but they returned by another way (ibid.), because they were warned by an angel not to return to Herod. And what gifts did they offer? Gold, frankincense, and myrrh: these three perhaps also pertain to your offering. For you have offered yourself—namely, your soul and body. If you please, refer the first two to your soul and the third to your body. For a certain twofold power has been bestowed upon our soul by that Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends (James 1:17): namely, the brightness of reason and the sweetness of affection. The former belongs to knowledge, the latter to love; the latter to virtue, the former to truth. By the former we choose what is true, lest we stray through error; by the latter we also love what is good, lest we grow empty through lukewarmness. And, if you please, the brightness of gold signifies the former, and the sweetness of incense the latter. No one, however, doubts that mortification of the flesh is figured by myrrh. Thus, in offering yourself, you have also offered gold, through reason, by knowing truth; incense, through affection, by loving good; and myrrh, through mortification, by extinguishing sin. [257] But do not return to Herod; rather, return by another way into your own country: so that, hating the defiled garment which is carnal—which this name *Herod* signifies, for it means “glory of skin”—you may henceforth have other habits in your manner of life than you formerly had.

XIII. Therefore strip yourself of the contagions of ancient oldness, and put on the adornment of holy newness. Let hatred be changed into charity, discord into peace, pride into humility, envy into kindness; anger into gentleness, restlessness into tranquillity; disturbance into mildness, darkness into serenity, sloth into cheerfulness, hardness into compassion, cruelty into mercy, obstinacy into counsel, dullness into understanding, faintheartedness into fortitude, fear into boldness, stubbornness into reverence, frivolity into constancy, buffoonery into maturity; rashness into prudence, rancour into piety, negligence into carefulness, harshness into smoothness, torpor into eagerness, hypocrisy into purity, flattery into severity, shouting into gracious speech. And amid all these, let bitterness be changed into sweetness. Thus, having offered gold, incense, and myrrh, you will not return to Herod, conformed to this world; but you will return by another way into your own country, reformed in the newness of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God (Rom. 12:2). And this, unless I am mistaken, is nothing other than this: that, having offered and delivered yourself to the Church of God, you should devote yourself to the conversion of your habits in the ways which we have taught in this sermon—a conversion which, with the Church as witness, you promised to God, to whom be honour and glory for ever. Amen.

# SERMON VII

On stability of place promised in profession, and how this pledge ought to be kept. On the reward of temporal and eternal service. On preserving the stability of one’s first profession; and on the grounds on which transfer to another order may be advisable or lawful.

## SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The difference between service rendered to God and to temporal lords, and the reward repaid for it.  
2. For the sake of the eternal reward, which is God, a person gives and offers himself to God with a good intention and a purpose of perseverance.  
3. Conversion of habits promised to God, and stability in one place, are to be maintained perseveringly.  
4. Transfer to another order, even a stricter one, is ill-advised because of the suspected weakness of oneself, which subsequently reveals itself in many through instability.  
5. A second motive is to be sought beneath the cloaked desire for perfection: self-love and a turbulent mind disguise themselves under it.  
6. Finally, transfer is discouraged because of scandal to one’s companions, or harm arising from oneself, whether wisely or foolishly.  
7. Sound counsel when the habits of prelates or fellow-residents seem contrary, or unhelpful to observance of life.  
8. Among lawful reasons for departing to another order, the first is being unwillingly drawn into sin, or being hindered from fulfilling one’s vow.  
9. The second is the implacable hatred of those living together, after the example of the saints.  
10. The third is canonical election or appointment to the governance of some church.  
11. The fourth is desire for a more perfect and stricter life—provided that each person suspects the instability of his own mind, while desiring his own salvation and brotherly peace.  
12. Recapitulation with exhortation.

[Col. 0497B] I. Dearest brothers, those may be called kings and princes—and ought to be called so—who strive from the depths of their hearts to serve almighty God, the author of the universe. For to serve him devoutly is to reign sublimely; to know him is to live; and to cleave to him is supreme happiness. Pride does not inflate one who reigns in this manner; error does not darken one who knows in this manner; satiety does not tear away one who cleaves to him in this manner, nor does lukewarmness dissolve him.

And certainly we see unceasingly how diligently people serve people, the poor serve the rich, and how greatly they strive to please them by continual acts of service. No anguish of heart, no labour of body, no weariness of travel, no severity of cold, no burning heat, no anxiety of pain and sorrow, no torments of hunger and thirst, [Col. 0497C] no danger by land or sea—not even, finally, at times the fear of bodily death itself—can hinder them from expending their whole selves in the service of their masters. And in all these things many often do not know what reward, what kind of reward, how great a reward, or when they will receive it for such devotion. Yet what reward they will receive, of what kind, how great, and whenever they receive it, they know this without doubt: it will be temporal and bestowed temporally.

Yet how greatly do they serve for it? Certainly, as greatly as they can. How long do they intend to serve? Certainly, as long as they live. Thus, upon this devotion which they expend in order to please a human being, death alone, as these facts show, is accustomed to impose an end, and impossibility to bring failure. We see, therefore, that in serving their masters they expend themselves, desire with all their mind to please them, and persevere in both things even until death. O great devotion indeed! For what devotion is greater, or can be greater, than to expend for others all that they are and for as long as they are, especially for the reason just shown?

II. Therefore this great devotion contains gift, intention, and purpose: these three. The gift, indeed, is perfect; the intention good; the purpose persevering. Yet its reward is bestowed in time and ends in time. And why say this? So that you may consider, my brother, how diligently you ought to practise these same three things in your devotion toward God, since your reward will be eternal. For, bestowed at the end, it will endure [Col. 0498A] without end. You will have as your reward him to whom you now both perseveringly give your entire self and desire from the depths of your heart to please.

What is loftier than this reward? This is the Lord your God, who will give himself to you as a reward—the one for whom you labour in a merit with which nothing can be compared. For he has good and beautiful things, pleasant and sweet things, which are at once many beyond number and great beyond measure; yet nothing is better or more beautiful than himself, nothing more pleasant or sweeter. And, because even this is far too little, nothing is so good or beautiful, nothing so pleasant or sweet. This is the best good of all goods; this the most beautiful of all beautiful things; this the most pleasant of all pleasant things; this the sweetest of all sweet things: since he is his own goodness and beauty, pleasantness and sweetness.

Whatever that is for which we sigh, this, I say, you will possess excellently as the reward of happiness, if you now give your whole self to him and seek, above everything whatsoever, to please him alone. But it is altogether necessary that perseverance attend both this your gift and your work; for perseverance alone merits eternity, and without it eternity is not bestowed. And these are the three things which you promised in your profession. Whether you strive to fulfil these vows of yours, which your lips have uttered (Ps. 65:14), you must see to yourself.

For if anyone asks concerning your gift, behold these are your words: “I, Brother N., offering myself, deliver myself to the Church of God.” If he asks concerning your intention: you offered and delivered yourself in order to please God, [Col. 0498C] whom you cannot please at all unless you apply yourself to conversion of your habits. Finally, if he asks concerning your purpose: it is that of perseverance, concerning which the following was added: “and stability in place.” Therefore you offered and delivered yourself; you promised conversion of your habits. Take care that you are faithful in your gift and promise, lest you presume to take away what you have given or neglect to render what you have promised. For this reason, once you had offered and delivered yourself and promised conversion of your habits, you immediately also promised stability in place: so that perseverance in purpose may establish both the perfect gift and the good intention.

III. Holy Job, sending forth, sanctifies his sons; and, rising early in the morning, offers holocausts for each of them [Col. 0498D] (Job 1:5). But observe that he is said to do this on every day (ibid.). Consider whether the offering of the holocaust is not your own self-delivery; the sanctification of the sons, the conversion of your habits; and whether the fact that this is said to be done every day cannot fittingly be referred to stability. But perhaps one of you replies to these words in silent thought:

“I know that perseverance is necessary to every good work if it is to be worthy of eternal reward. Yet I do not think that stability is mentioned here, but stability of place. For the very order of the words is this: ‘I promise conversion of my habits and stability in place.’ Since this is so, tell me, I beg you: must stability in place be maintained by me with as much diligence as a good work?”

To this I answer: “It is a good work to remain in the place in which you promised God that you would serve him.”

And he says: “I do not break my vow if I leave it.”

“How,” I say, “do you not break it, when you presume to depart from the place in which you plainly promised your stability? If you promised that you would be stable in it, and you become unstable by departing from it, how are you not a violator of your vow?”

“What then,” he asks, “shall I be bound by this pledge until the end of my life? Can this pledge not come to an end at some limit of time, just as the pledge by which I vowed conversion of my habits does not?”

“Why,” I ask, “should any limit of time end it before your death, just as no such limit ends the pledge by which you are bound to apply yourself to conversion of your habits, since you plainly promised this one as well as that one?”

[Col. 0499B] “For, as you yourself testified shortly before, the words of your promise stand thus: ‘I, Brother N., offering myself, deliver myself to the Church of God, and promise conversion of my habits and stability in place.’ You said, ‘I promise conversion of my habits and stability in place.’ Therefore, you promised both that and this. In these words no temporal limit is mentioned in your promise any more for the one than for the other.”

“But,” he says, “I know that I must always strive for my habits to be converted from evil to good and from good to better. But may I not leave the house in which I now am before the end of my life, and move elsewhere whenever I wish?”

“You may not,” I reply.

“Why may I not?”

“Because,” I say, “you promised stability in place.”

“And yet,” he says, “I see every day innumerable persons not only in another place, but in another order from that in which they made their profession. Hence it is plainly apparent to me, whatever you may say, that the place of profession may lawfully be left and another sought. For if this could not lawfully be done, surely some of them would neither leave their place and order nor be received elsewhere [perhaps *alibi*, ‘elsewhere,’ for *alias*, ‘others’]. For I know some among them so scrupulous and concerned for their salvation that, even if they could be received elsewhere because of their great virtue, they would by no means wish to leave if in any way they might thereby offend God; indeed, they went out for this very purpose, that they might please almighty God more.”

But I answer you: because what you have vowed, you are bound to render; otherwise I should disagree with the one who says, “Make vows and fulfil them” [Ps. 76:11]. That is: if you make vows, fulfil them. What should you fulfil? What you have promised. Therefore, if you have vowed stability in place, be stable in it.
