For you who vowed stability in your house, by my counsel at least, will not leave that same house before the end of your life, so far as depends on you.

IV. “What,” you ask, “if, inflamed by the Lord’s inspiration with a desire for greater perfection and a stricter order, I should wish to amend my life and increase my conversion? Do you not advise me to move elsewhere, where I may do this?”

“Perhaps,” I reply, “I do not advise it.”

“Why?”

“First,” I say, “because I suspect your weakness: perhaps you who can bear this order cannot bear that one. For I know very many who, while sitting down, neglected to count the cost, whether they had enough to complete the new and lofty tower of perfection which they began to build. Unable to complete it after laying the foundation, they deserved to hear that word of reproach: ‘These people began to build and could not finish’ (Luke 14:30). Then they returned in shame to the order and place which they had left too rashly and with too little foresight—and therefore too rashly because with too little foresight—and were perhaps received less gladly and thereafter held in less honour.

“Others, ashamed to return to their former place and order, went to another house and order; and, perhaps neither wishing nor being able to remain in it and keep it, migrated yet again to another house and another order. Thus, becoming lighter than the wind and more unstable, they tasted, as it were, many dishes and were refreshed by none. While wishing to be religious everywhere, they were religious nowhere.

“Some neither returned to their former state nor transferred themselves to other exercises of holy religion. Rather, weighed down by their own instability and gradually declining toward the depths, they either fell into a most foul lukewarmness of spirit, utterly abandoning every purpose of making progress further in anything; or even returned to the world, despairing of themselves [variant: *in themselves*], casting aside every beauty of holy modesty. Then, when death unexpectedly overtook them shortly afterwards, they were miserably cut off. Did these proceed rightly, who arrived at such an end? For this way seemed right to them, but its latter end led [260] to death (Prov. 14:12). And this is the first reason that persuades me not to advise you to depart elsewhere, even though you are inflamed with desire for greater perfection and a stricter order.

V. The second reason resembles this. I suspect your faintheartedness. For I fear that you wish to migrate elsewhere because your carnal and foolish desires are resisted in this place. And lest others should attribute your departure to this cause—or lest it should appear blameworthy even to yourself, as it truly is—you will cloak yourself in the covering of a lie: a false intention of living better and more perfectly in the place to which you migrate than you live or can live in this place where you now are.

For I have often seen some persons whose brothers or prelates resisted their desires, and who, immediately in anger, wished to migrate elsewhere in order to live more perfectly and strictly. And behold: as soon as the time of anger and disturbance passed, their own order seemed sufficiently strict to them, and they wished to leave nowhere. It would indeed be good for them to depart—if they did not carry themselves along with themselves. But now, because they carry themselves with them everywhere, they always encounter elsewhere what they flee here, and draw near in a foreign place to the disturbance from which they withdraw in their own.

Often, moreover, when they rashly take up the way of a stricter life, they too fall into that detestable evil into which, as we have often said, those briefly discussed above fall. And this is the second reason why I do not dare advise you to leave your house, even under the pretext and with the desire of greater perfection. For an end whose beginning is corrupt cannot be good. Your opinion deceives you; you will not find there what you seek. But that common proverb is true: “Every man thinks the ravens are golden in another man’s chamber.”

VI. The third reason is this. I fear that your departure may bring either scandal or harm to those who remain behind you. Scandal, because you leave them and go to others, as though the institutions of the order which they observe were to be considered of no value or little value. For your departure seems in some way to cry out that you do not greatly approve either them or what is among them. For if you approved, perhaps you would remain with them.

Harm, moreover, may arise if, being greatly needed by the house in which you are, you inflict very great loss on it by withdrawing yourself from it. You know what Christ the Lord says in the Gospel, when he speaks of the virgins, five of whom he declares were prudent and five foolish (Matt. 25:2). But whether you are a foolish or prudent virgin, great harm will result from your departure. For if you are foolish, your departure will harm you yourself; but if prudent, it will harm your house.

Therefore, if you are foolish, I do not at all advise you to leave your house for anywhere, lest the departure of a foolish person be foolish. But if you are prudent, then I especially advise you to remain, so that your prudence, above that of all others, may assist your mother—that is, your house—which conceived and bore you, carried you, cherished you, brought you to full maturity of habits, and advanced you to the prudence you now possess. What other house of yours, if you have one, is more worthy to make use of your prudence than your mother? Whether, then, you are a prudent or a foolish virgin, I do not advise you to depart anywhere: for if you are foolish, you need your house; if prudent, your house needs you.

Thus far I. But he replies: “If the habits of my prelates and brothers are so opposed to mine that I cannot remain peacefully in my house, is it not better to migrate elsewhere, even against my prelate’s prohibition, in order to live in love and peace, than to remain amid rancour and hatred?”

“This,” I reply, “is what I said a little earlier: I fear that your impatience is perhaps more the cause and occasion of your departure than your desire for greater perfection. As for the two alternatives about which you now inquire, I do not know how I can tell you which is better, since neither is good. You ask whether you should depart through disobedience or remain with anger and hatred. It would be the same as asking me whether it would be better for you to perish by fire or by a precipice. For you are burned if you remain in hatred, and cast down if you depart without permission. Which of these is good: to be burned or cast down?” [261]

“Neither,” he says. “But since both are evil, which, I ask, is the lesser evil?”

VII. And I say: “Which of these do you desire more: that I show you how not to die indeed, but nevertheless to be ill; or how to be so fully cured that you are ill no more?”

He replies: “Just as, of two evils, I choose sickness rather than death, so of one good and another evil I choose to be cured rather than sick.”

“Then do you wish me to show you how you can reject evil and choose good? That is, how you can conduct yourself so that, in avoiding what is worst, you need not do what is less evil, but what is wholly good?”

“I wish it,” he says, “and ardently desire it.”

And I say: “If the habits of your brothers or prelates oppose you, strive to correct their bad habits by your good habits. Do not defend yourself, but give place to anger. Do not be overcome by their evil, but overcome their evil with good (Rom. 12:26–27). Overcome their pride by humility, their anger by gentleness, their jealousy by kindness, their disturbance by mildness, their hatred by charity. With blessed Job, be a brother of dragons and a companion of ostriches (Job 30:29). If necessity required it, dwell as Abel with Cain, Isaac with Ishmael, Jacob with Esau. Their malice will be able to benefit you rather than harm you, if your patience does not fail you.

“If you do not believe me when I say this, hear what counsel the venerable Anselm gave on these matters to a certain Lanzon, newly made a monk at Cluny—Anselm being at that time prior of the church of Bec, afterwards abbot of the same monastery, and in the course of time archbishop of the church of Canterbury.

[Note: [Col. 0501] This letter is found in Surius, in his *Life* of Anselm, 21 April.]

“‘You have entered, dearest one,’ he says, ‘and professed the warfare in which not only must the violence of an openly resisting enemy be repelled, but also the cunning of one who appears to offer counsel must be guarded against. For often, when an openly malevolent enemy cannot destroy Christ’s recruit with the wound of an evil will, a cunning enemy attempts to extinguish him with the poisonous draught of malign reasoning. When he seeks to overwhelm him, moreover, by hatred of the life which he has professed, he strives to undermine him through weariness with the manner of life in which he is.

“‘And although he seems, as it were, to concede that the monk’s purpose ought to be maintained, nevertheless, because he began under such persons, among such persons, or in that place, he never ceases by manifold wiles to charge him with being excessively foolish and imprudent. Thus he persuades him, after receiving God’s benefit, to persist in ingratitude, so that by a just judgment he may neither advance to better things nor retain what he has received, or may persist in it uselessly.

“‘For while he unceasingly meditates, in laborious thoughts, upon changing, or, if he cannot change, at least upon disapproving his beginning, he never strives toward the end of perfection. Since the foundation which he has laid displeases him, he has no desire whatever to build upon it the structure of a good life. Hence it comes about that, just as a small tree, if it is planted often, or if, newly planted in the same place, it is disturbed by frequent uprooting, cannot take root at all, quickly contracts dryness, and never reaches any fruitfulness; so the unhappy monk, if he is often moved from place to place at his own desire, or, while remaining in one place, is frequently shaken by hatred of it, becomes established nowhere by roots of love, languishes in every useful exercise, and is enriched by no abundance of good works.

“‘And when he perceives that he is advancing not in good but in evil, if perhaps he reflects upon this, he attributes the whole cause of his misery not to his own habits, but to the righteous habits of others; and thereby he unhappily inflames himself into greater hatred of those among whom he lives.

“‘Therefore, whoever perhaps undertakes the purpose of cenobitic life should strive, in whatever monastery he has professed—unless it be such that he is forced there unwillingly to do evil—to take root there with the whole intention of his mind, in the roots of love. He should refuse to judge the habits of others and the customs of the place, if they are not contrary to the divine commands, even if they seem useless. Let him rejoice that he has now found a place where he has resolved to remain his whole life, not unwillingly but voluntarily, having driven away every concern for moving elsewhere, so that he may also devote himself diligently to seeking the exercises of a devout life alone.

“‘But if he seems to himself, in spiritual fervour, to desire certain things greater and more useful than the institutions of the present monastery allow, let him judge either that he is deceived—whether by preferring equals to equals or lesser things to greater, or by presuming himself able to do what he cannot—or else let him believe that he has not deserved what he desires. If he is deceived, let him give thanks to divine mercy, by which he is protected from his error, lest by changing his place or manner of life, without benefit or even with loss, he vainly incur the reproach of inconstancy and instability; or, worn out by attempting things beyond his strength, fail more grievously into his former condition, or even into something worse than his former condition.

“‘But if he truly desires better things than those ready to hand, though he has not yet deserved them, let him patiently endure the divine judgment, which unjustly denies nothing to anyone, lest by exasperating the just Judge through impatience, he deserve not to receive what he does not have, and either lose what he has received or retain it uselessly because he does not love it. But whether he perceives mercy or judgment toward himself in those things which he does not have and desires, let him gladly render worthy thanks to heavenly generosity for what he has received. And because he has been able to reach some harbour amid the stormy whirlwinds of the world, let him beware of bringing the wind of instability and the tempest of impatience into the tranquillity of the harbour.’”

VIII. And he replies: “Tell me, I beg you, whether there are any reasonable grounds which, if they arise, permit me to withdraw from the place in which I am bound by the bond of profession?”

“There are,” I say. “The first is this: if those with whom you live are such as to draw you unwillingly into sin. For if they are such, then I advise you to migrate elsewhere, so that you may be able to please God. Indeed, if the customs of your house are so pernicious and pestilential that your prelate and fellow-residents do not permit you to fulfil what you promised in your profession, it will not, I think, be blameworthy for you humbly to depart elsewhere, where you may live according to what you promised.”

But he asks: “What if my prelate forbids me to depart?”

And I say: “What if he forbids you to live according to what you promised?”

“In either case,” he says, “there is danger. If I depart, I offend my prelate through disobedience; if I remain, I break daily the vow which I made.”

“Must you,” I ask, “obey in matters contrary to your salvation?”

“But what,” he asks, “if he excommunicates me because I depart?”

Then I say: “What if he deprives you of communion with God by making you neglect your vow?”

“But,” he says, “the sentence of a shepherd is to be feared, whether it is just or unjust.”

“And if it is to be feared,” I say, “must it therefore always be maintained? And if it must always be maintained, what kind of shepherd is he to you who does not permit you to possess those pastures without which you can live neither spiritually in this present life nor happily in the life to come?”

Then he says: “What, I beg you, is your conclusion in this matter?”

And I say: “If you fear condemnation because, by departing, you break a command, you ought more to fear condemnation because, by remaining, you break your vow. In all commands and prohibitions issued by prelates, it must be carefully considered whether they are issued according to God or not. If they are according to God, they must be accepted obediently with all devotion and fulfilled promptly and willingly, according to one’s ability and knowledge. But if they are contrary to God, the judgment of blessed Peter must without doubt be followed, who, when the scribes and Pharisees commanded things contrary to God, replied with great authority: ‘One must obey God rather than human beings’ (Acts 5:29).

“Certainly, disobedience cannot be counted as a fault if, because you obey God, you prove disobedient to a human being; just as obedience cannot be counted a virtue if you obey a human being more than God. Therefore, just as a place is not to be left so long as you can live in it according to God’s will, so likewise, when you are compelled to live in it contrary to God’s will, it is not to be retained.”

IX. The second reason is if they are stirred against you by such great hatred and fury that you cannot possibly soften their fury—especially if it is established that you have not deserved that such madness of envy should rage against you. For when this detestable evil has fully possessed the mind, its infection poured into the marrow, it never ceases to swell more and more as long as it has before it the person against whom it is stirred. The breast is suffused and swollen with this deadly poison; the eyes blaze, the lips tremble, the inward parts are tortured, and it is as though pierced by the lethal point of a poisonous sword as often as it sees the one against whom it is stirred.

Everything that one sees in the person whom one wholly envies displeases intensely; one interprets as evil the good that one observes in him. Therefore holy persons are accustomed to change their place when they see the envious rage against them—not because they regard that rage as important so far as they themselves are concerned, but lest, as their madness increases, the envious become worse. They prefer to yield the place rather than, while the poison of fury increases in those persons because of their presence, become even in this a cause of their greater destruction.

Thus holy Jacob declined his brother’s anger no less wisely than humbly by changing his place, knowing that the same anger would increase more and more if his bodily presence were not removed. Likewise the holy father and leader of monks, blessed Benedict, when a certain priest, tormented at times by envy against him, pursued even the souls of his disciples, so far as lay in his power enticing them into sin because of him, wisely and gently left the place and withdrew his presence. Thus, when the man did not see before him the person whom he sinfully envied, he might in some measure be less malicious in the evil of envy, thirsting as he did for souls’ blood.

So too, if you happen to see someone puffed up and suffused with pestilential poison against you without desert on your part—for you have never sinned against him in any place—and persecuting you so that you are wholly unable to correct him by any means, you do not, as it seems to me, incur a great guilt if, by the counsel and assent of your elders, you humbly change your place for a time, with this intention also: that by your absence you may at least diminish something of his fury.

X. But I think that you may also change the place in which you are bound by the bond of profession if you are canonically elected to govern some church. Neither prelate nor community ought in any way to resist this third reason, if they recognize both that your election is canonical and that you are worthy and suitable, and are able to accept your absence for the greater benefit of holy Church.

For all of us who are in the unity of baptism and faith are members, amid diversity of languages, professions, and merits, and difference of offices and ranks, of the great body which is the Church dispersed throughout the whole world, under one head—the Mediator of God and humankind, God and man, our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Tim. 2:5). To the honour of that aforesaid head and the benefit of the members, we owe to our one Catholic mother whatever we live, are, can do, and know. Nor ought anything of those who are in her to resist when the authority of the whole requires the service of a part.

Therefore, when holy mother Church recognizes that you are suitable to serve her needs, assumes you to her governance through a canonical election, and judges you worthy for this purpose, you may, I think, change the place of your profession and, with the consent of those among whom you live, move elsewhere in order to perform that for which she has called you.

XI. Moreover, you may lawfully change your place if you wish to transfer yourself to a stricter life and a higher order. But you must by every means beware lest, in this intention of yours, your own impatience deceive you, and lest, while a false spirit is at work, feigning a motive of pleasing God from the heart and of cleaving to Him alone, it be your own faint-heartedness that is truly the cause in you [Col. 0506A] for doing this. For there are many who, whenever they are angry, immediately assert—as we touched upon at some length above—that they wish to move elsewhere for the sake of a more rigorous life and better manner of living; yet their impatience is more the cause and occasion of their departure than is the desire for a loftier way of life. They themselves too bear witness against themselves that this is so, when, after they have become calm a little later, they shrink from undertaking what previously, when disturbed, they had hastened to seize upon beyond measure.

For if they had first desired this with the pure intention of cleaving to God alone and pleasing Him, then, just as prosperity alone ought not to create this desire in them, so that they should begin, adversity alone could not weaken it, so that they should cease. Nevertheless, you must take care to do this with the assent of your superiors and with the goodwill of your companions [Col. 0506B], so that your sacrifice may thus be accepted as an odour of sweetness. For the perfection of this great manner of life which you undertake is, as it were, a certain sacrifice. But when the willing consent both of your brethren and of your superiors commends it, it sends forth from itself, as it were, a great fragrance. Indeed, you set an insipid dish upon the table when you do something—sometimes even something good—without the peace of those who live with you. For flavour is to a dish what peace is to a good work.

Therefore, you must first take care that the perfection and manner of life to which you now aspire with ardour are much greater and loftier than that which you had hitherto practised, so that in changing [Col. 0506C] the place of your profession you may rejoice that an increase of holiness has likewise come to you. Otherwise, what benefit is it to you to change the place of your profession if no increase of holiness comes to you thereby? Secondly, you must consider with no less deliberation lest the new holiness which you undertake become a scandal and occasion of disturbance to others. For what you do is then good, when you seek your own salvation in it in such a way that you do not thereby take peace from others.

These, therefore, are the two things which you must pursue with the highest desire in the practice of your manner of life: namely, the attainment of your own salvation and the occasion of fraternal peace. The first, indeed, is because it concerns you; the second, because it concerns your neighbour: for you hold the first place in relation to yourself, while he holds [Col. 0506D] the second. For, as James says, “The wisdom which is from above is first indeed chaste, then peaceable” (James XXXIX, 17). Therefore do not suppose that it is enough for you, in ascending to the height of perfection, to practise the first in such a way as to neglect the second. For the Law commands you to love your neighbour as yourself (Mark XII, 31). Therefore, in every exercise of yours seek your salvation in such a manner that you do not disturb your neighbour’s peace in seeking it.

If, then, true knowledge tastes sweet upon the palate of the mind, do not neglect, according to your ability and knowledge, to practise that which, with regard to your neighbour, is peaceable, just as you do not neglect that which, with regard to yourself, is chaste. And the first, because what is honourable adorns you; the second [otherwise: the second], because it makes your neighbour peacefully tranquil. For this wisdom of which we speak, which is from above [Col. 0507A], is first indeed chaste, then peaceable. Thus, by admitting the first in your practice, you offer rightly and therefore do good in seeking your own salvation; but by omitting the second, you do not rightly apportion it, and consequently sin, neglecting fraternal peace.

XII. For all these things tend to this end: if, inspired by God, you wish to change the place of your profession for the sake of a better life and greater perfection, then you should know that it is beneficial for you to bring this intention into effect if this departure of yours takes place with the peace and goodwill of your superiors and brethren, and their gracious consent in this matter is not lacking to you. Thirdly, you must endeavour to measure your strength, in case you may be unable to carry what you propose to undertake through to its due [Col. 0507B] end. For why would you take up such a thing, only to have those who see your failure mock you and say: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke XIV, 30)?

Therefore, to gather these three points briefly at the end of this discourse: if you recognize this intention of yours, by which you propose to change the place of your profession, as pure, so that it may please God; peaceable, so that your neighbour may accept it; and moderate, so that your weakness may be able to bring its effect to its due completion—I do not think that you incur any guilt, as though you were breaking your vow, if, as has often been said, you change the place in which you bound yourself by the bond of profession, not only in those cases mentioned above, but also in other not dissimilar ways which do not now occur to mind. [Col. 0507C] For I do not see how one can rightly blame you whose purpose in your practice is your own salvation, your neighbour’s peace, and the will of God, who is blessed above all for ever. Amen.

## SERMON VIII

On what we say in our profession: “according to the Gospel of Christ, and according to the apostolic institution, and according to the canonical Rule of Blessed Augustine.” On the examples of the saints and evangelical perfection; on the excellence and ordering of the common life; on love of God and neighbour; on unity of minds and external goods, and the avoidance of private possession.

## SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The teachings of the Holy Scriptures and the examples of holy men rightly form us; they dispel ignorance and sloth.

2. [Col. 0507D] In profession, self-surrender is suitably established according to Christ’s Gospel; conversion of manners according to apostolic institution; stability in place according to the Rule.

3. The summit of evangelical perfection consists especially in three things: selling all things, giving to the poor, and following Christ.

4. How these three are to be fulfilled in religious profession.

5. Conversion of manners must be examined according to the apostolic norm and institution.

6. The perfection of the apostolic life requires for itself four principal things: first, contempt for earthly things.

7. Secondly, the common life and use of those same things; thirdly, their equitable distribution; fourthly, unity of minds.

8. The first three are observed in order that the fourth may be attained: namely, to have one heart and one soul in God, and to have converted one’s manners according to apostolic institution.

9. Promised stability is to be regulated by the Rule of St Augustine, [Col. 0508A] and how long it must be kept. Division of the Rule into twelve chapters.

10. Love of God is fittingly exalted in the first chapter [265]: for God surpasses all things in the order and measure of love, the most excellent of virtues.

11. How one ought to stand in the charity of God, oneself, and one’s neighbour; charity is the source, form, and end of the whole Law.

12. Next, unity of minds in God is commended; what is earthly, animal, and devilish is to be condemned.

13. Private possession is forbidden, not only of temporal goods but also of one’s own will; through either kind the unity of peace can scarcely stand. How greatly private possession is to be detested, and equitable distribution preserved.

14. What comes under the name of private possession, which is the seedbed of discord and the destruction of fraternal unity.

I. Beloved, it is no less fitting than beneficial for us to endeavour to form the rule of our life according to the teachings [Col. 0508B] of Holy Scripture and the examples of holy men. It is beneficial, I say, with respect to merit; fitting with respect to testimony: there with respect to conscience, here with respect to reputation. For, as you know, ropes once drew the holy Jeremiah out of the pit (Jer. XXXVIII, 12–13), but old rags were placed between. What are these ropes except the precepts of Holy Scripture? And what is this antiquity of rags except the ancientness of good examples? Thus both ropes and old rags draw Jeremiah out of the pit: that is, the precepts of Holy Scripture and the examples of earlier saints raise any chosen person from the depths of evil profundity to the heights of holy conduct.

Indeed, as he ascended from the valley of weeping and sang the first Song of Ascents, holy David, instructed by the Holy Spirit, knew that sharp arrows of the mighty man and desolating coals must be given and applied against the deceitful tongue [Col. 0508C] (Ps. CXIX, 3–4). This plainly means nothing other than that every saint striving toward the spiritual progress of holiness has known that nothing is more powerful for overcoming the deadly persuasion of deceitful speech than the effective commands of the Saviour and the examples of the saints that destroy vices.

These, therefore, are the two outstanding marks of holy edification which sacred Scripture contains within itself: the exhortations of Catholic instruction and the examples of religious conduct; so that the former may instruct our ignorance lest we go astray, and the latter may stir our sloth lest we grow dull. Therefore whatever we either now do or are still beginning to do will then be weighty with the maturity of seriousness and approved by the examination of truth—whatever has been conceived in hidden intention or brought into the light in an open deed—when it accords with both the words taught by Holy Scripture and the examples set forth by holy men. [Col. 0508D]

II. Hence, in the words of our profession—which we have already discussed at length in these three preceding sermons—we shall not omit to touch upon these matters when we mention the Gospel of Christ, apostolic institution, and the Rule of our holy father Augustine. For the order of the words themselves is as follows:

> I, brother N., offering, give myself to the Church of Mary the Mother of God and of that saint, and I promise conversion of my manners and stability in place, according to the Gospel of Christ, according to apostolic institution, and according to the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine.

You see that three things are promised; and, though they are secured by the bond of profession and promise, there follow three corresponding terms. What are promised are: the surrender of yourself, the promise of conversion of your manners, and the promise of stability in place—these three. What follows is: according to the Gospel of Christ, according to apostolic institution, and according to the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine—these three.

And note, I pray you, the order of these three preceding and three following clauses, to see whether some correspondence may perhaps be found in them. First you surrendered yourself; second, you promised conversion [Col. 0509A] of your manners; third, you promised stability in place. Likewise, you first mentioned the Gospel of Christ; secondly apostolic institution; and thirdly the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine. For you would remain stable in place vainly and fruitlessly if your manners were perverse. And since it is clear that, among all the things in which the holiness of religious life consists, the exercises of spiritual virtues alone are the anchor of firm perseverance which merits the state of eternity, it is evident, unless I am mistaken, that conversion of manners would be of little benefit if constancy of stability were lacking.

Again, what benefit for the salvation of your soul would it bring for you to shine in conversion of your manners and remain stable in place, if you had been forced into the Church of God more by another’s compulsion than delivered and offered to that Church of God through the welcome devotion of a spontaneous will—given through your own offering and offered through your own surrender? [Col. 0509B] Yet I would not judge it greatly praiseworthy if you had given and offered yourself to the said Church of God in this way, while perversity of manners at the same time rendered you reprobate and instability made you a wanderer.

Therefore, what you first promised was the offering and surrender of yourself; what you promised second was conversion of your manners; what you promised third was stability in place. In the first, spontaneous devotion is marked; in the second, upright conduct; in the third, firm constancy. That is, in the first you may appear devout; in the second upright; and in the third rooted in this upright devotion and devout uprightness. Devout, that you may please God inwardly; upright, that you may show your neighbour a good example in yourself; rooted, lest in the time of temptation you withdraw from that good which God accepts or your neighbour approves. [Col. 0509C–D]

III. What does Christ’s Gospel reveal to us other than complete perfection? You ascended to the summit of this perfection when, surrendering yourself to the Church of God, you offered yourself; offering yourself, you surrendered yourself. And where will you find the fullness of this perfection more abundantly than in Christ’s Gospel? Thus, to one who asked what he must do to possess eternal life, and who asserted that he had observed the commandments of the Law from his youth, He said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21).

Consider what He declared necessary for attaining perfection: certainly, the sale of all possessions; the expenditure of them upon the poor; and finally the imitation of Christ Himself—these three. First, He says, sell: not one thing, or two, or some things, but all that you have, so that you reserve absolutely nothing of what you possess for yourself. Secondly, give to the poor, so that you do not presume to keep for yourself even the price of the things you have sold, but spend upon the needy what you deprive yourself of. Thirdly, follow me, so that, not only preferring nothing whatsoever to me for my sake, but not even comparing anything with me in any way, you cast all things utterly out from the very affection of your mind and cleave to me alone from the heart.

First, sell all; second, give to the poor; third, follow me. Sell all, so that you may loftily despise all that belongs to the world. Give to the poor, so that you may mercifully assist your neighbours. Follow me, so that you may cling tenaciously to me. Thus, by selling all, you remove worldly vanity from yourself; by giving to the poor, you perform a work of charity toward your brethren; by following me, you possess the summit of inward purity. Does not great perfection seem to you to lie in this threefold exercise? Do you not consider it a great height of perfection to despise the world, help your neighbour according to your ability, and imitate Christ? This is the perfection proclaimed by our Lord Jesus Christ to the man who asked Him what he should do to possess eternal life. [Col. 0510A–B]

IV. Offering and surrendering yourself to the Church of God according to this Gospel of Christ, you do so in order to ascend the heights of perfection: that you may renounce all things belonging to this world, assist your neighbour’s need, and conform yourself to the likeness of Christ. You sell all these things when, in order to obtain spiritual gifts, you strip yourself of bodily things as regards affection: admitting them for use, but excluding them from affection. And you spend upon the poor, as it were, the price of the things you have sold, when through the spiritual gifts which you received by means of the complete rejection of temporal things, you aid your needy neighbours not only in bodily but also in spiritual need.

Offering yourself, you surrender yourself; and surrendering yourself, you offer yourself to the Church of God, when, cleaving to Christ from the heart and adhering to Him tenaciously, you imitate Him with devout devotion both in His commands and in His prohibitions: following Him wherever He goes, both by refusing without any exception what He does not wish to be admitted and by willing what He does not wish to be omitted. [Col. 0510C–D]

Thus you may not unjustly claim for yourself that utterance of the Psalmist:

> “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. LVI, 8).

That is to say: I am ready to undertake what You command and to avoid what You forbid. “I am ready,” I say, “and am not troubled, that I may keep thy commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 60): both those things which You command to be admitted and those which You command to be omitted. Thus, thus I shall endeavour to please You in both respects: when I strive to avoid sin, willing no evil whatsoever; and when I endeavour to turn away from transgression, now willing every good thing. And because “thou lovest a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, [Col. 0511A] 7), I am not troubled in these things. Therefore “I will sing and give praise” (Ps. LVI, 8).

What is this song? Spiritual cheerfulness in the mind. What is this psalm? A useful effect in action. “There shall indeed be in me,” he says, “both the song of cheerfulness in the heart and the psalm of usefulness in action, when I am ready to follow in prohibitions and ready also in commands.”

V. Just as we do not doubt that complete perfection is in Christ, so we recognize conversion of manners in the apostles. For we know that one of them was made a preacher from a fisherman, another changed from a tax collector into an apostle. And this change was “the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI, 11). But just as their offices were changed, so too were their manners. The outstanding teacher and chosen vessel, the preacher of truth, though not among the Twelve, was nevertheless also called in his own time to Christ’s discipleship; he was changed from Saul into Paul, from persecutor into preacher. And surely that change of name was a certain manifestation of conversion of manners? For, just as in name, so also in manners, from that time he became another person. Indeed, he himself now lives, yet not he; rather Christ lives in him (Gal. II, 20). He now endures persecutions for the Church which he had formerly inflicted upon that same Church; he dies daily for brethren whose death he had once thirsted for beyond measure, “filling up those things which are lacking of the sufferings of Christ in his flesh, for his body, which is the Church” (Col. I, 24)—that Church which not long before, “breathing out threatenings and slaughter” against the disciples of the same Christ Jesus our Lord (Acts IX, 1), he was cruelly ravaging. [Col. 0511B–C]

Thus conversion of manners is expressed in the calling of the apostles, so that you may understand that those whom you read were called by Christ from one office to another were consequently changed for the better and converted to ordered manners also. According to this institution, therefore, you promised conversion of your manners, just as before, according to Christ’s Gospel, surrendering yourself, you offered yourself, and offering yourself, you surrendered yourself to the Church of God. And their institution was holy, because they themselves were holy; for those who were holy wished to establish nothing but what was holy.

VI. And what was this institution of theirs? It seems to me—unless something better or more suitable concerning this occurs to you at present—that among other things which they proclaimed as pertaining to the salvation of their subjects, the following notable holy virtues may be observed in their institution: complete rejection of earthly things; the communal sharing of temporal goods, to be expended in relieving the need of those subject to them; their fair and suitable distribution among them according to each person’s needs; and, finally, mutual harmonious unity and a single concord of minds—these four. [Col. 0511D]

But so that you may understand these things more clearly from their opposites, they plainly aim at this: that you may know that the apostles established that those who received the faith through their preaching in the primitive Church should live without desire for worldly things, without private possession, without respect of persons, and without division of fraternal peace. We think that suitable examples can be found for each of these points.

It is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “As many as were possessors of lands or houses, selling them, brought the prices of the things which were sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet” (Acts IV, 34). What else, my brethren, can our attentive consideration observe in these words except a complete rejection of earthly goods? They sold the houses and lands they possessed, turned them into money, and cast that money at the apostles’ feet. It may be inferred, unless I am mistaken, that they did not love greatly those things from which they alienated themselves by selling them. And not only that they loved them little, but also that they regarded the proceeds of their changed possessions as exceedingly base, since they cast them before the apostles, not elsewhere but at their feet. [Col. 0512A–B]

Hence the words of Arator, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, concerning these matters are as follows:

> They prove that what they refrain from touching must be abandoned,  
> And teach that the gold which they place beneath their feet must be trampled;  
> That gold from which earthly cares come to human hearts  
> Is cast upon soil of like kind.  
> —Arator, *On the Acts of the Apostles*, book I, vv. 406–409.

Therefore they plainly show that the prices of the things sold are to be despised and, as it were, trampled underfoot, when they cast them down at their feet. And they judge that those things are not unlike soil which they lay before those members of the apostles’ bodies with which they tread upon the ground.

VII. “Neither did any one of them say that anything which he possessed was his own; but all things were common to them” (Acts IV, 32). Behold the communal sharing of earthly goods. The distinguished narrator of these events, holy Luke, made this sharing known to us with no little emphasis when he states that certain among them—undoubtedly believers, of whom he had spoken before—not only did not possess anything as their own, but did not even call anything their own: “All things,” he says, “were common to them”—not merely some things, but all things.

If we wish to consider this closely, it appears that they cast away every form of private possession, since they made common among themselves even the totality of the things which they expended upon their bodily needs. It also appears, in their complete renunciation of all private possession, [Col. 0512C–D] that they not only, as we have said, possessed nothing of their own, but did not even call anything their own—alienating from themselves in speech what they did not wish to possess.

This communal sharing of temporal goods, which must by every means be sought and practised by the whole community of religious men, sets before us a certain image of that heavenly homeland for which we now sigh, as the words of the venerable Bede on this subject declare:

> Those who live in such a way that all things are common to them in the Lord are called cenobites. This life is happier in proportion as it imitates the state of the world to come, where all things are common, because God shall be all in all. And because there is supreme peace and security there, the city in which the type of this life first appeared was called Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace.”

“But it was distributed to every one according as he had need” (Acts IV, 35). Here two points call for our attention: each person received what was necessary for his support; and in this arrangement, how carefully there was considered not what will desired, nor what covetousness craved, but what utility advised and necessity required. Whoever, then, belonged to the society of the primitive Church of which we speak received, for the support required in living, what was given by those whose office it was to provide it. But there was also this surpassing good: with all respect of persons utterly removed, each individual received separately according to need.

“The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32). Behold harmonious unity and one concord of minds. The three preceding things of which we have just spoken are the cause of this good delight and delightful goodness, which we placed fourth; this unity is their fruit. [Col. 0513A–B]

VIII. For this purpose we reject the desire for bodily goods; for this purpose we wish to possess none of them as private property; for this purpose we abhor respect of persons in the distribution of bodily support: that we may obtain this most sweet unity in God, beneficial alike to body and soul. For this purpose, I say, “they that sold brought the prices of the things sold and laid them at the apostles’ feet,” so that none of them would call anything which he possessed his own. And therefore none called anything which he possessed his own, so that distribution might be made to every individual according as each had need. Finally, distribution was made to each according to need, so that they might have one heart and one soul.

Thus those three goods are the cause of this fourth good, while this fourth good is their fruit. The three precede in order that the fourth may follow; and this follows in order that the three may be rewarded in it. Rightly, my brother, you promised conversion of your manners according to apostolic institution, since you have these four things established by the apostles as a kind of form and pattern through which, by conversion, you may shape your own manners toward good in the gracious beauty of holy uprightness: namely, complete rejection of earthly things, communal sharing of bodily goods, fair and suitable distribution of them according to the needs of individuals, harmony of unity, and unity of harmony in the mind. [Col. 0513C–D]

For is this not an exalted and outstanding conversion of manners? These goods, though four in number, contain in the first contempt for this world; in the second, the honourable ordering of a community of religious men; in the third, the justification of outward effect; and in the fourth, the purification and pacification of inward affection. It purifies, I say, that it may be clean; it pacifies, that it may be tranquil.

Therefore, when the world has been wholly and perfectly despised by you; when, in the assembly of saints, you show yourself upright in all your movements; when outwardly, before Him who sees the face, you adorn your work with righteousness; when, before Him who beholds the heart, the unity of concord inwardly cleanses [Col. 0514A] and calms your thoughts—you may undoubtedly say boldly that your manners have been converted and, as you are known to have promised in your profession, converted according to apostolic constitution.

IX. We must now touch, if only briefly, upon the Rule of blessed Augustine, according to which you promised stability in place; just as, as we have said, you promised conversion of your manners according to apostolic institution, and just as, according to Christ’s Gospel, surrendering yourself, you offered yourself, and offering yourself, surrendered yourself to the Church of God.

Therefore, according to the tenor which the Rule of blessed Augustine itself sets forth, you promised stability in place: that, so long as you can observe the commands contained in that Rule and its law of life and discipline, you will not change the place in which you promised to observe them through any frivolity or impatience. But if, God forbid, because of the undisciplined conduct of your fellow residents or because of some other contingency that arises, you are drawn unwillingly away from good and enticed toward evil, and cannot observe them, then, I think, you do not sin culpably if, for this reason alone and solely in order to fulfil your vow, you also break your vow.

“What is this,” you ask, “that you have just said?” Hear what it means. If you leave the place, do you not break your vow, having promised stability in it? Certainly, you say. But if you live there contrary to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, do you not likewise break your vow? That is so, you say. But when this occurs, break the vow lest you break [Col. 0514B–C] the vow: cease to be stable in the place, lest you live there contrary to Augustine.

Moreover, when you act thus, although I speak in this manner, you do not break the vow; for you promised stability in place, but according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine. And you will certainly understand that you must act in this way when we briefly begin to address the notable spiritual virtues treated in the said Rule. Indeed, we read that many things have been promulgated there by the aforesaid Father and advocate of ours; nevertheless, we think that we can comprise their sum under twelve chapters, omitting very many things which cannot be compressed within few words.

We set down the first chapter: “Before all things, dearest brethren, let God be loved, then one’s neighbour; for these commandments have been given to us principally.” The second is from the place, “These are the things which we command you to observe,” to, “But again, even those who seemed to be something.” The third is from “But again, even those,” to “Be instant in prayers.” The fourth likewise is from that place to “Subdue your flesh.” The fifth is from that place to “Let not your dress be conspicuous.” The sixth likewise is from that place to “But whoever has advanced in evil to such an extent.” The seventh is from there to “Keep your garments together.” The eighth likewise is from that place to “Let your clothing be washed according to the judgment of the superior.” The ninth is from this point to “Have either no quarrels.” The tenth is from there to “Let obedience be given to the superior as to a father.” The eleventh is from that place to “But that in this little book.” The twelfth is from there to the end. [Col. 0514D–0515A]

In the first chapter mention appears to be made of love of God and neighbour; in the second, of harmonious unity and the common sharing of bodily support; in the third, of the virtue of humility; in the fourth, of purity in prayer; in the fifth, of discreet abstinence; in the sixth, of the beauty of uprightness and chastity of body; in the seventh, of spontaneous confession; in the eighth, of common keepers of garments; in the ninth, of the washing of garments, care of the sick, and books to be requested daily; in the tenth, of avoiding quarrels; in the eleventh, of reverence to be shown to superiors and of their office; in the twelfth, of diligence in observing this Rule.

You now see, unless I am mistaken, and clearly understand that stability in place is fruitful only when this twelvefold discipline, which we have not merely sampled in brief, is diligently practised; but when it is omitted, stability is retained in vain. [Col. 0515B]

X. [Note: [Col. 0515D] Rule, chapter 1, “On the love of God and neighbour.”] The first chapter, therefore, concerns loving God and neighbour; the tenth concerns avoiding quarrels. For love ought to be the cause and source of all the spiritual practice to which we devote ourselves, whether in order to please God or to help our neighbour; yet we do not bring that same love to the perfection of the number ten if we do not avoid the horrible and terrifying thunderclap of quarrelling.

Thus at the beginning of his Rule Augustine exhorts us to love God before all things, and then our neighbour, adding the reason: “For these commandments,” he says, “have been given to us principally.” And he rightly declares that they were given principally, because, as the Lord Himself testifies, “on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII, 40). And as blessed Gregory says: “Whatever is commanded is established in love alone.”

Likewise, he rightly exhorts us to love God and neighbour before all things, because the love of God and neighbour, just as it holds a loftier rank than all other virtues, ought likewise to hold the first place in us before all things. The order, too, is right: although both must be loved, God must first be loved and then one’s neighbour. For He alone has Himself as the cause why He should be loved; and consequently He ought to precede, in the order of our love, one who is with us a fellow participant in the same love toward Him. [Col. 0515C–D]

God must be loved not only first but also more, so that He may precede our neighbour not only in order but surpass him in measure in our love. For it is fitting and altogether just that He who is before all things should be loved before all things, and that He who is above all things should be loved above all things. He who is the beginning of the whole universe ought not to have a prior in our love; nor indeed ought He who is the end of all things to have an equal.

This is the Lord our God; and His name is **ἀ, ὦ**—“Alpha, Omega”—worthy to be loved before one’s neighbour, because He is the height that never began; and to be loved more than one’s neighbour, because He is the greatness that admits no measure within itself. [Col. 0516A]

XI. Let us therefore love God in order that we may rejoice in him; let us love our neighbour in order that we may rejoice, not indeed in him, but with him in God. These are the two commandments of charity, although there are three whom we love: ourselves, God, and our neighbour. For when we love God, we love ourselves, because we love our good, which he alone is; and when we love our neighbour for his sake, we love both him and ourselves, possessing our good, which he is. For we love him in this, that we love our neighbour for his sake; and we would in no way love our neighbour for his sake unless we loved him.

These commandments were principally given to us [Col. 0516B], because whatever other commandments there are are renewed in these and referred to them. For whatever has been instituted by the Lord himself, whether directly by himself or through his representatives in these matters, has been instituted for charity. It has been instituted for this, I say: namely, that you may acquire it if perhaps you do not possess it; or retain it when you possess it; or possess it better and more abundantly when you possess it poorly and scantily; or recover it if perhaps you have lost it; or do something of this kind pertaining to charity’s acquisition, possession, increase, ordering, or restoration.

Whatever has therefore been instituted by the holy Fathers, we should know that we are to practise it resolutely only when it contains absolutely nothing in itself [Col. 0516C] that in any way conflicts with love of God and neighbour. Know, therefore, that whatever you do is salutary for you if you possess charity. Hence also Blessed Augustine—whose words these are—speaking of ecclesiastical discipline, says: “Have charity, and do whatever you wish.” This liberty which he grants you, that you should do, not merely one thing, but whatever you wish, seems very great indeed. But observe what he first laid down: “Have charity.” You are rightly permitted to do whatever you wish, provided you first possess charity; for what evil can you wish if you possess it?

These commandments, therefore, were principally given to us because, just as that virtue whose commandments they are holds primacy among the other virtues, so also [Col. 0516D] these commandments of charity hold primacy among the other commandments. Appropriately, too, our father and advocate, Blessed Augustine, in the first chapter, at the very opening of his Rule, makes mention of the love of God and neighbour. For he knew it to be the cause and origin of every religious exercise to which we ought to devote ourselves, so that it may begin; its form and rightness, so that it may be ordered; its increase, so that it may grow; its constancy, so that it may remain; and its end, so that it may be brought to completion without being exhausted.

XII. He then adds, in the second chapter, certain matters [Note: [Col. 0515] Rule, ch. 2, “On harmony of minds and the common ownership of material goods.”] without which this love of God and neighbour of which we speak cannot remain whole and inviolate: namely, the unity of spiritual and sincere harmony in mind, and the complete rejection of all private ownership in temporal possessions. “These,” he says, “are the things which we command you to observe when established in a monastery. First, the reason why you have been gathered into one is that you may dwell harmoniously in the house, and that you may have one soul and one heart in God.” This concerns the virtue of sincere and spiritual unity. “And do not call anything your own, but let all things be common to you.” This, however, concerns the rejection of private ownership.

“That you may dwell harmoniously in the house,” he says. See that dwelling in one house is of no benefit if unity of mind is lacking. “And let there be one soul and one heart among you,” so that, just as one house contains you, so there may also dwell within you one heart and one soul. And he adds, “in God,” so that in the present life you may be enriched [Col. 0517B] by the merit of holiness, and in the future rewarded with the recompense of blessedness.

But that unity is not in God which is in the flesh, in the world, and in the ancient enemy. Behold a threefold unity wholly opposed to the unity that is in God, unlawfully joining the reprobate together and separating them from God. “The body of Behemoth is compacted with scales pressing upon one another; each is joined to the other, and not even a breath passes through them” (Job 41:6–7). The sensual, the curious, and the proud gather together as one against the Lord, and gather as one in flesh, world, and devil: the sensual through the desire of the flesh; the curious through the desire of the eyes; the proud through the pride of life. But this unity is not in God; it is earthly, animal, and diabolical (Jas. 3:15). Earthly: it entices, deceiving through curiosity after worldly delight [Col. 0517C]. Animal: it defiles, corrupting through the pleasure of carnal luxury. Diabolical: it raises up, exalting through the pleasure of demonic pride. O foul-smelling unity, glittering unity, swollen unity! Foul through softness; glittering through outward appearance; swollen 271 through self-exaltation.

But you, be of one mind in the house, and let there be one heart and one soul among you: yet in God, not in the flesh, not in the world, not in the ancient enemy. And observe that, when Blessed Augustine was about to urge us toward this unanimity, this unity of soul and heart in God, he took care first to state: “the reason why you have been gathered into one.” Hence it is clear that this external gathering of us into one represents the form of that interior unanimity and unity of which we have just spoken [Col. 0517D], so that, as we are outwardly gathered in one place, so inwardly we may be united in one mind.

XIII. “And do not call anything your own, but let all things be common to you.” The private ownership forbidden to religious men who profess the common life ought not, I think, to be understood only of material possessions, but also, unless I am mistaken, of the very will of the mind. For if in this respect we wish to ascend to the height of perfection, it is necessary that we possess nothing private even in our own will against the rectitude of justice; but that, for another’s will, insofar as is fitting and expedient, we should endeavour to break our own.

For we shall in no way be able for long to preserve unimpaired unity in the heart if we disdainfully and arrogantly refuse to subject our will—so far as reason directs and justice requires—to the wills of others, and especially [Col. 0518A] to those of our superiors, whom we ought to obey in God’s stead. But that cenobites ought to possess nothing privately in temporal goods can by no means be doubted by anyone who knows the profession of those cenobites themselves. They ought to possess nothing privately, because it is a most grievous sin if they presume to do so. For if our Father forbids anything to be called one’s own in this passage, how much less does he allow it to be possessed?

Saint Benedict also writes thus on these matters in the Rule of his monks: “Above all, this vice must be cut out by the roots from the monastery: that no one presume to give or receive anything without the abbot’s permission, nor possess anything as his own—absolutely nothing: neither book, nor writing-tablets, nor stylus, but nothing whatever. For they are not permitted to have even their own bodies or their wills at the disposal of their own will.”

Certainly, those who pursue private possession are, in a certain sense, thieves, liars, sacrilegious persons, and even apostates. They are thieves because they secretly hide for themselves things belonging to others. They are liars because they are one thing and present themselves as another. They are also sacrilegious because, while they presume unlawfully to appropriate the monastery’s goods for themselves, they take what is sacred from what is sacred. Finally, they are apostates because, in a certain way, they have already returned to their vomit: they endeavour again to possess, for their own private use—the very manner in which they had possessed them before—the things which they had formerly renounced [Col. 0518C].

Let us therefore beware, brothers, lest we presume rashly and unlawfully to possess anything without the knowledge of our Father; lest we share in the guilt of Ananias and Sapphira, whose sin’s great gravity was made known by the punishment that followed. I say, not without our Father’s knowledge, because Blessed Benedict also writes thus on this point: “Nor is anyone permitted to have anything which the abbot has not either given or allowed.”

These too are the words of Blessed Augustine: “Let food and clothing be distributed to each of you by your superior.” Not riches are to be distributed to us by our superior, nor any superfluities, but necessities alone. And if you ask what those are, they are precisely what feed us when hungry and clothe us when naked. Let us not improperly and shamelessly ask for more than these [Col. 0518D], because they ought to suffice for us. For the Apostle’s statement on this matter is as follows: “Having food and covering, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8).

Thus our Master commands that food and clothing be distributed to each of us by our superior: the former, lest hunger consume us; the latter, lest cold harm us. “Not equally to all,” he says, “because you are not all equally strong; but rather to each according to what each needs.” On this Saint Benedict says: “We do not say—far be it—that there should be respect of persons; rather, there should be consideration of infirmities. Where one needs less, let him give thanks to God and not be distressed. But one who needs more should humble himself because of his infirmity, not exalt himself because of the mercy shown him. And thus all the members will be at peace.” You see [Col. 0519A] how these words grant us support for necessity, while forbidding the vice of private possession.

XIV. But perhaps someone sitting around us, moved by clamorous silence and silent clamour, says something like this in response: “Since you advance such terrifying judgments concerning the vice of private ownership, tell us plainly, I beg you, what private ownership is. For if private ownership is whatever I love more for my own use than for my brother’s use, then I confess that I am not free of this vice.”

To him I reply: Certainly, if you wish to consider the matter closely and distinctly, you cannot call free from private ownership anything which you do not wish to flow back for your brother’s benefit, or anything which you do not wish to serve common use. The custom of our Order also [Col. 0519B] is that whatever is possessed contrary to prohibition or without due permission is called private property.

Accordingly, as you may gather from these matters, the great teacher Aurelius Augustine earnestly seeks in this second chapter to admonish us that, casting aside division and discord, we may be harmonious in fraternal unity and strive to be of one mind in harmony; that, utterly renouncing every form of private possession in those temporal things by which our passing need is sustained, we may always attend to common sharing in bodily support. In the first chapter he likewise seeks to admonish us to love God and neighbour, so that, while we diligently strive to put into effect the twofold command he proclaims in this chapter and likewise the twofold command in that one, we may live in the charity of God and neighbour; live in unity; and finally live without private property.

And, O holy, pleasant, peaceful life! For we are holy when we love God from the marrow of our being, and love our neighbour. We likewise attain good pleasantness and pleasant goodness when we dwell together as one, all say the same thing, and there are no schisms among us (1 Cor. 1:10). We also rest sweetly when, removing these two words from our midst—“mine” and “yours”—we exchange the love of money that belongs to private possession for the generosity of common sharing [Col. 0519C].

Rightly have you promised stability of place according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, so that there also you may strive to take root through constancy of purpose: where perseverance, love of God and neighbour, may make you holy; sincere unanimity according to God may make you joyful; and common sharing in bodily support may make you peaceful [Col. 0519D]. But let us defer the matters still remaining from this chapter, together with those belonging to the following chapters, to another sermon, so that, after prayer and meditation as usual, we may gather again on another occasion, when convenient, to speak for your edification to the praise of God, to whom be honour and glory for ever. Amen.

## SERMON IX

On the Rule of Blessed Aurelius Augustine, from the passage, “Those who possessed anything in the world,” to “for it is better to need less than to possess more.” On unity of harmony and common bodily support; on the virtue of humility; on purity in prayer and discriminating abstinence.

### Synopsis of the Sermon

Those whom the enemy’s craftiness cannot wholly turn aside from the purpose of perfection, it commonly obstructs in part, as is evident in abandoning the vice of private possession. [Col. 0520A]

2. Those who were more lowly in the world are very often more difficult, more complaining, and more arrogant in cenobitic communities; Saint Augustine addresses these evils in his Rule.

3. In relieving necessities, there must be no respect of persons; nor should generous provision of necessities become an occasion for holding one’s head high, as happens more often among those of humbler condition.

4. Pride must likewise not be tolerated in those who came to the monastery from wealth; it has two kinds, carnal and spiritual.

5. The antidote to both kinds of pride; and how improper it is for religious persons to boast of worldly wealth or family lineage.

6. The fruit of humility is unanimity of wills and harmony of conduct, by which God is honoured in us as in his temples.

7. Prayer from a humble and harmonious mind is fruitful. Public prayer in the Church, named from the canonical hours, has long been practised and commended by holy men.

8. The seven canonical hours have been consecrated both by mysteries of our Saviour, prefigured in the Old Law, and observed in the New. [Col. 0520B]

9. On the time, place, and manner to be observed in prayer, and on six other companions of prayer outlined in Scripture.

10. After prescribing holiness of the inner person, he prescribes that of the outer person through abstinence, by which the lust or pride of the flesh is subdued; yet it is the appetite rather than the food that constitutes the vice.

11. Regard must be had for health, and for the canonical hour of refreshment.

12. At bodily refreshment the spirit must be fed by reading, with modesty, inward hunger, and ears of the mind opened.

13. Compassion must be shown to the sick, envy being banished. To be content with the common table is a virtue; to be in need is an infirmity.

14. It is perverse for those of humble station in the world to be delicate and seek superfluities in the monastery; nevertheless, the particular infirmity of each person must be provided for.

15. Frugality, as it were the mother of humility, is commended; superfluity, the nurse of self-exaltation, is condemned. [Col. 0520C]

Our father and advocate, Blessed Augustine, dearest brothers, with great earnestness forbids the crime of private possession among regular clerics at the very beginning of their Rule, as you have already heard at the conclusion of the sermon recently delivered to you. He would not, unless I am mistaken, forbid it with such zeal if he did not know it to be exceedingly contrary to their salvation.

But since that ancient adversary roams unceasingly, seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5:8), he is accustomed to lay especially fierce snares even for those who have newly turned to the service of almighty God. If perhaps he cannot prevent them altogether from converting, that deceitful one employs all his subtlety to ensure at least that they undertake that conversion lukewarmly [Col. 0520D] and remain in it without fruit.

Those indeed take up the new life of conversion lukewarmly who refuse to spend for common use the goods which they had formerly possessed, but presume still to retain them as private property. Their conversion, certainly, though it has the name by which it may be called such, is altogether devoid of every effective virtue. For, according to Truth itself: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be his disciple” (Luke 14:33). So long as they retain anything in this manner from their possessions, they can in no way adhere from the heart to the discipline of the supreme Master.

For the right order in converts is that they should first leave their possessions and afterwards themselves. Those themselves attest that they do not know this order when, upon entering a cenobium, they retain with them as their own something, however little, of what they had formerly possessed: they remain possessors of their former goods, and consequently violators of the new conversion upon which they have entered [Col. 0521A]. They are like Ananias and Sapphira in guilt, and therefore deserve to be their equals in punishment. You read of them that, after selling a field, they brought not the whole price but a certain part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet. Of Ananias it is said that he withheld part of the price of the field (Acts 5:2). Hence it is clear that newly converted persons, so long as they retain anything with themselves, even from things that had been their own, are not merely lukewarm but fraudulent.

They remain without fruit in the same conversion if they are excessively and importunately demanding in claims that concern themselves, or vainly pleased by the maintenance supplied and honour granted them.

II. For how often a perverse habit tends to cling to certain converts: although in the world they never possessed even necessities, once converted in the monastery they are often not ashamed to seek superfluities. An undiscerning multitude has now entered; and those who are accustomed to be stricter in cenobitic communities are those who, before taking the habit, were more lowly. They exalt themselves above others in pride, though, in view of the state of their former manner of life, they ought to be deeper than others in humility.

Already swollen with unjust murmuring over the scarcity of food [Col. 0521C], they complain about food and clothing—though, when they were outside, they counted it among their greatest delicacies to be filled with barley, and thought themselves adorned for a feast day when covered with the meanest and oldest little rags. So too, some of them now judge it a great happiness to dwell with persons with whom they could not then associate. Nor only this: they regard it as something very great and outstanding that such abundance of food and clothing now enlarges those whom such great want of both had then confined.

Blessed Augustine treats these three evils in his teaching. To destroy the first, he addresses them thus: “But those who possessed anything in the world, when they enter the monastery, should willingly wish it to become common property.” To meet the second: “But those,” he says, “who did not possess anything should not seek in the monastery what they could not possess outside.” For the third likewise: “Nevertheless,” he says, “they should not think themselves happy because they have found food and clothing such as they could not possess outside. Nor should they hold their heads high because they are associated with those whom they had not dared to approach outside; but let them set their hearts on high things and not seek earthly and vain things, lest monasteries begin to benefit the rich rather than the poor: if the rich are humbled there and the poor puffed up there.”

He says, “Let those who possessed something outside wish it to become common,” wishing them also wholly to renounce private possession from the moment they have entered the monastery. And he adds, “willingly,” knowing that “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7), so that their good deed may be voluntary, not extorted by force [Col. 0522A]. “And what they could not possess outside,” he says, “let them not seek in the monastery,” because it is exceedingly ridiculous that persons who, constrained then by the affliction of poverty, had never been anything but poor, should now, swollen with the tumour of pride, long to be rich.

III. But lest the former state of their need should in any way prejudice them, so that their necessities should not now be relieved, he carefully adds: “Nevertheless, let what is needed be given for their infirmity, even if their poverty, when they were outside, could not find even necessities.” For it is certainly unjust and wholly wicked for persons in monasteries to refuse to share equally in food and clothing with those whom they know to have come from poverty.

Far be it that there should be any respect of persons in God’s house, because whether rich or poor, we are all one in Christ (Gal. 3:28). Since, therefore, as the Apostle James says, we sin if we show partiality (Jas. 2:1), what is needed must not be denied in monasteries either to those who come from wealth or to those who come from poverty, even though necessities themselves were usually lacking to the latter in the world.

Yet how carefully they must beware lest, amid this new abundance, they consider themselves blessed and hold their heads high [Col. 0522B], because they see that they are now associated with eminent and venerable men. To hold one’s head high is to swell with pride. “But,” he says, “let them set their hearts on high things and not seek earthly and vain things.” That is, through holy desires let them hold the gaze of their minds raised toward things above, not, through unclean desires, turned downward toward things below. Otherwise monasteries will be useful not so much to the poor as to the rich, when pride makes the poor exalted in them and humility makes the rich lowly.

And who would not say that pride is less tolerable and deserving of graver punishment in the poor than in the rich? For this is the rebuking voice: “Why are earth and ashes proud?” (Ecclus. 10:9), as though mud or a stone were permitted to be proud. For what are earth and ashes but something low and lightly despised? It is intolerable for that which is lowest and lies beneath to exalt itself, for that which is weak and contemptible to lift itself up. Perhaps this might somehow be tolerable in what is lofty and strong. But if that which is high presses itself down, if that which is precious humbles itself [Col. 0522D], and earth and ashes are still not ashamed to be proud, then monasteries will indeed be useful to the rich, not to the poor: for the richer, the more deeply they take root in humility, the more highly they advance; while the poor, raised upward only to fail, vanish like smoke (Ps. 36:20).

IV. It follows: “But again, those who seemed to be something in the world should not despise their brothers who came from poverty to that holy fellowship; rather, they should strive to glory not in the rank of wealthy parents but in the fellowship of poor brothers. Nor should they be exalted if they have contributed something from their own resources to the common life; nor should they be prouder of their wealth because they distribute it to the monastery than they would be if they enjoyed it in the world.”

In this third chapter our Master, by exhortation, attacks pride in those who have come from wealth to a place of humility. He admonishes them neither to lift themselves up proudly over those who came from a lowly station, of whom we have just spoken, on account of nobility of birth, nor to exalt themselves proudly over the dispersal of their wealth. In this exhortation he marks out two kinds of pride which they must avoid: one carnal, the other spiritual.

To despise brothers and glory in nobility of lineage seems properly to belong to carnal persons, and can sometimes be found among secular people themselves. For lovers of this world, who place their whole esteem in visible things, are accustomed vainly to exalt themselves above those whom they surpass in worldly goods, thinking themselves far more valuable than those whom they see themselves to be wealthier than. They also habitually judge themselves far more exalted than those whom they surpass in nobility of blood, although nature has produced both as equals.

But concerning contempt for and rejection of temporal goods, the giving of alms, and works of mercy, that hidden adversary often presses spiritual men themselves with his poisonous suggestion that they should exalt themselves. Since he cannot draw them into corrupt action, he persuades them at least secretly to glory in their own good works. He seeks to corrupt in them, by hidden self-exaltation, what has been rightly done, since he cannot induce them openly to commit evil deeds [Col. 0523C]. Therefore he continually sets their own virtues before their inward gaze, so that when the weak mind carelessly considers them, it may see something great and lofty in itself; unlawfully pleasing itself in and with itself, approving itself in its own estimation, it may vainly rush into the desire for its own glory and proudly exalt itself over others.

V. Blessed Augustine seeks by his teaching to drive far away from clerics living the common life both plagues of pride, namely carnal and spiritual. He exhorts them: “Let those who seemed to be something in the world not despise their brothers who came from poverty to that holy fellowship; rather, let them strive to glory not in the rank of wealthy parents [Col. 0523D], but in the fellowship of poor brothers.” This concerns carnal pride.
