Its kind is twofold, most especially defiling the minds of secular and carnal people in these ways: they are accustomed to be proud of nobility of stock and abundance of wealth, and vainly to prefer themselves to those whom they see to be inferior in these respects. He then adds concerning avoidance of spiritual pride: “Nor should they be exalted if they have contributed something from their own resources to the common life; nor should they be prouder of their wealth because they distribute it to the monastery than they would be if they enjoyed it in the world.”

This is indeed a salutary exhortation and thoroughly catholic teaching. Far from us, brothers—once, twice, and utterly far from us—be this deadly plague, by which certain puffed-up persons are miserably afflicted: they are accustomed to despise brothers who came from poverty and to glory in the rank of wealthy parents. Their speech is this: “We were rich and exalted in the world; they, however, were poor and lowly. They are of the lowest birth; but noble descent and high-born blood adorn us. We have contributed from our resources to this common life many things, as precious as they are useful; but they came impoverished and almost naked. We enriched this place; they entered into our riches. Far be it that needy persons should be made equal with us rich, lowly persons with exalted, commoners with nobles.”

But you, my brothers, who seemed to be something in the world, must not think thus about yourselves and your brothers who came from poverty to this holy fellowship. Strive rather to glory in their fellowship than in the rank of your wealthy parents. For I judge it exceedingly shameful and unbecoming for religious persons to glory in distinction of lineage. It is the speech of a pagan:

> “What do pedigrees avail?”  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* VIII.1

For who does not see how empty, as a certain wise man says [Note: [Col. 0523D] Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, prose 6.], and futile is the name of nobility? And indeed, if there is anything good in nobility, I think it is only this: that a duty appears to be laid upon nobles not to decline from the virtue of their forebears. For, as he says beforehand, another’s distinction does not make you illustrious if you have none of your own. And how true is his song:

> All the race of humankind upon earth  
> arises from one same origin.  
> One Father is the source of all things;  
> one minister governs all.  
> —Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, metre 6, lines 1–4 [Col. 0524C]

And in what follows:

> Why do you make such clamour about lineage and ancestors?  
> If you look to your beginnings  
> and to God the Creator,  
> none is of degenerate stock,  
> unless, nurturing worse vices,  
> he abandons his own origin.  
> —Ibid., lines 13–18

In the loins of the first-created human being, we all received equal nobility. But do not be exalted concerning those resources of yours which you have contributed. Do not wish even silently to rehearse in your mind what or how much you have contributed. To go so far as boastful speech is, I judge, excessively shameful. Avoid both kinds of this pride, lest—God forbid—you who have sown much should reap little (Hag. 1:6). For this seems to be the meaning of the following statement: “Every other iniquity is exercised in evil works in order that they may be done; but pride lies in wait for good works, in order that they may perish.”

And what good is it to give to the poor by scattering one’s possessions and to become poor, when the wretched soul becomes prouder in despising riches than it had been in possessing them? Certainly none. Indeed, it would have been far better to possess them than to despise them in this way [Col. 0525A]. Such contempt is useless: through the intervention of humility, it ought to have yielded us a ground for righteousness and glory; but through the intervening plague of madness, that deadly force which here lies in wait for a good work in order that it may perish, gives rise for us both to guilt and punishment.

VI. Therefore, all of you live unanimously and harmoniously, and honour God in one another, whose temples you have become. He has now admonished you to avoid two kinds of pride; now he urges you to practise two goods which the virtue of humility is accustomed both to confer upon us when they are absent and to preserve in us when they are present.

“Live unanimously and harmoniously,” he says. Unanimity belongs to a devout will, and harmony to good conduct. For we live unanimously when we do not draw back from one another in will; but harmoniously when, through conflicting conduct, we are not opposed to ourselves. And it is the right order that he first urges us to live unanimously and then harmoniously, because we cannot in any way be harmonious in conduct unless we have first been unanimous in will.

“And honour God in one another,” he says. How? Certainly by living unanimously and harmoniously. For then especially do we honour God in one another: when inwardly, according to him, we are unanimous in will, and outwardly harmonious in conduct. “Whose temples you have become”: because God dwells in us, we are indeed his temples. Our bodies are temples, and our hearts too are temples: our bodies through the purity of incorruption; our hearts through the virtue of divine and fraternal love [Col. 0525C]. For when we restrain by the bridle of continence the flood of lust in our members, he dwells with us in the flesh. And when we love him purely for his own sake, and our neighbour in him, he dwells with us also in the mind.

It follows: “Be diligent in prayer at the appointed hours and times.”

VII. Beautifully does Blessed Augustine, after the third chapter [Note: [Col. 0525] St Augustine, *Rule*, ch. IV, “On purity in prayer.”], in which he admonished us concerning the virtue of humility, unanimity, and harmony, invite us in this fourth chapter to purity of prayer. For you offer prayer worthily and fruitfully only when, humbling yourselves under God’s mighty hand (1 Pet. 5:6), you are lowly in true humility; when, having one heart and one soul in the Lord [Col. 0525D], you have not turned away from one another in will; and when, dwelling together in good pleasantness and pleasant goodness (Ps. 132:1), you have not become divided from one another by conflicting conduct.

He commands us to be diligent in prayers at appointed hours and times. What are these hours and times appointed for prayer, except those customarily observed by the Church? As you can understand by reading, the holy prophet Daniel entered his house and, with the windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem, three times a day bent his knees, worshipped, and confessed before the Lord his God (Dan. 6:8). Peter also went up to the upper rooms to pray at about the sixth hour (Acts 10:9) [Col. 0526A]. Cornelius too was praying in his house at the ninth hour (ibid. 3). And Peter and John went up to the Temple at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer (Acts 3:1). The holy David likewise declares that he uttered praise to the Lord seven times a day, because of the judgments of his righteousness (Ps. 118:164).

These, I think, are the hours and times appointed for us, that we may be diligent in prayer at them. There are seven hours specially appointed, at which the holy Church is especially accustomed to render the due service of prayer. Blessed Benedict, filled with the spirit of all the righteous, mentions them in this way in the Rule of his monks:

“The prophet says: ‘Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you.’ This sacred number of seven will be fulfilled by us if, at the times of Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline, we render the offices of our service. For concerning these hours he said: ‘Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you.’ But concerning the Night Offices, the same prophet says: ‘At midnight I rose to give thanks to you’ (Ps. 118:62). Therefore at these times let us offer praise to our Creator because of the judgments of his righteousness: that is, at Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline; and let us rise at night to give thanks to him.” [Col. 0526B]

Thus Blessed Benedict concerning the hours of prayer.

VIII. These are indeed the hours which the Creator of the universe and Redeemer of humankind is found to have consecrated in the work of our salvation; and therefore they have rightly been appointed for us above the rest for prayer. For in the night-time [Col. 0526C] he was born and announced by an angel to the shepherds. By night he himself prayed; by night also he rose from the dead; by night he was sought with lanterns, torches, and weapons; by night he was taken with swords and clubs; by night he was first led to Annas, in whose presence he was struck on the cheek by one of the attendants; by night he was sent bound from him to Caiaphas the high priest; by night he was accused; by night he was assailed by false testimony; by night he was blindfolded; by night he was smeared with spittle; by night he was struck with fists; by night he endured slaps upon the face (Luke XXII; John XVIII).

In the morning, however, the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel to hand him over to death (Matt. XXVII, 1 ff.); in the morning he was brought to Caiaphas in the praetorium [Col. 0526D]; in the morning he was delivered to Pontius Pilate; in the morning he was despised by Herod; in the morning, clothed in a white garment, he was mocked. In the morning also he appeared to Mary Magdalene at the tomb; in the morning, speaking to the seven disciples who were in the boat, he stood on the shore; in the morning likewise he filled the net cast on the right-hand side—which was not torn—with the sacred number of great fishes.

At the third hour he was crucified by the tongues of the Jews; at the third hour he was scourged by Pilate; at the third hour he was crowned by the soldiers with a crown of thorns; at the third hour he was clothed in a scarlet garment and worshipped in mockery. At the sixth hour, he himself, priest and sacrifice, was raised upon the wood and fastened to it with nails. At the ninth hour he cried out in a loud voice and, bowing [Col. 0527A] his head, gave up the spirit (John XIX, 30).

When evening had come, with the night now near in which he was betrayed, he reclined with the twelve and delivered to them the sacraments of his body and blood. As the day was already drawing toward evening, on the very day of his resurrection, he was invited to lodging by the two disciples going to Emmaus; and he was recognized by them in the breaking of bread (Mark XIV; Luke XXIV). Late on that same day, when the doors were shut, he came to his disciples (John XX, 19); and when they saw him, he filled their hearts with a new joy.

The holy Daniel prayed three times a day (Dan. VI, 10), at the times when, as some say, the Jews were accustomed to pray: namely, according to the opinion of certain persons, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours. They suppose the third hour to have been chosen because at that hour they believe the Decalogue of the Law was given to that ancient people [Col. 0527B] on Mount Sinai (Exod. XX). They assign the sixth because at that hour, they judge, the bronze serpent was raised as a sign; those bitten by fiery serpents were healed by looking at it (Num. XXI, 9). And they assign the ninth because at that hour they believe the rock was struck in the wilderness, from which an abundant flow of water came forth to refresh the people’s thirst (Num. XX, 11).

But we know without doubt that at the third hour the primitive Church received the coming of the Holy Spirit into itself; that at the sixth hour he who appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh was lifted up from the earth, and that, looking upon him with the eye of faith, we are healed of our spiritual wounds; and that he was also prefigured long ago by the rock struck in the wilderness, because at the ninth hour one [Col. 0527C] of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came forth (John XIX, 34).

IX. Behold, brothers, the hours and times at which Saint Augustine commands us to persevere in prayer. In the present chapter you will also find three matters pertaining to prayer that we must note: time, place, and manner. We have already said something concerning the hours and times. He adds concerning the place of prayer as well: “Let no one do anything in the oratory except that for which it was made and from which it received its name.” This is so that the brethren may safely and freely devote themselves to prayer whenever they please and whenever it is suitable. He accordingly adds: “Thus, if perhaps any wish to pray there even outside the appointed hours, when they have leisure, they may not be hindered by those who think that something else should be done there.”

After this he adds concerning the manner of prayer: “When you pray God with psalms and hymns, let that be in your heart which is uttered by your mouth.” For in one who prays, the thought of the heart ought to agree with the words of the mouth. Hence Saint Benedict says: “We believe that the divine presence is everywhere and that the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil in every place” (Prov. XV, 3). “Yet let us believe this without any doubt especially when we stand at the divine office. Therefore let us always remember what the prophet says: ‘Serve the Lord in fear’” (Ps. II, 11). “And again: ‘Sing wisely’” (Ps. XLVI, 8). And: “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you” (Ps. CXXXVII, 1). “Therefore let us consider how we ought to be in the sight of the Divinity and [Col. 0528A] his angels; and let us so stand to sing psalms that our mind may agree with our voice.” Thus Saint Benedict.

We may observe, if we look carefully, that those holy men whom we mentioned above prayed at the appointed hours and times with this purity of prayer. For Saint Daniel, entering his house and opening the windows of the upper chamber toward Jerusalem, bent his knees, worshipped, and gave thanks to his God (Dan. VI, 10). What do we suppose these things can signify for us except inward secrecy in the soul, understanding in the mind, contemplation in the spirit, desire for the heavenly homeland, humility of heart, and praise of the mouth? His entering the house signifies inward secrecy in the soul. His windows too are opened when, through the Spirit’s revelation, the channels [Col. 0528B] of spiritual understanding are uncovered. The upper room in the house is the height of contemplation in the soul. Desire for the heavenly homeland is denoted by Jerusalem. In the bending of the knees and worship we understand humility of heart; in giving thanks before God, praise of the mouth. This sixfold pattern is a notable token of a certain perfection, very necessary for those who pray.

To it may be referred the house of Cornelius (Acts X, 3), in which he is said to have prayed; that upper room of Peter, which he ascended in order to pray (ibid., 9); and finally the temple itself, into which Peter and John went up at the ninth hour (Acts III, 1). “And do not sing except what you read as being to be sung. But what is not written to be sung must not be sung” [Col. 0528C]—clearly so that, whether singing or not singing, we may be less liable either to guilt before God or to rebuke before human beings, the more carefully in both cases we follow the authority of Holy Scripture.

X. It follows: “Tame your flesh by fasts and abstinence from food and drink, insofar as health permits.”

> [Note: [Col. 0527] Fifth chapter of the Rule of St Augustine, “On Discreet Abstinence.”]

All things, brothers, which up to this point Blessed Augustine has set forth exhortatorily in his Rule are marks of spiritual virtues. For love of God and neighbor, unity of concord, the virtue of humility, and purity of prayer belong to the holiness of our inward person. But what is said in this fifth chapter concerning abstinence belongs to the holiness of the outward person. The skilled and discerning Master rightly judged that he should first treat matters pertaining to the instruction of the mind, [Col. 0528D] and afterwards matters pertaining to the cleansing of the body. For the heart must first be adorned in a person with the marks of spiritual virtues, and afterwards the body embellished with religious exercises.

Among these exercises abstinence undoubtedly holds a great and, in a sense, first place. On this subject we have in the present passage a salutary instruction from our Father. In this chapter he addresses us, as we suppose, with a sevenfold instruction. First, he commands us carefully to observe discerning abstinence; second, an appropriate hour for taking bodily nourishment; third, that at table we attend diligently to the reading [Col. 0529A] recited; fourth, that those weakened by former habit be treated mercifully in food; fifth, that something in food and clothing be likewise allowed to the delicate beyond what is given to others; sixth, that all the others should not wish to be treated in the same way; seventh, that after those who had been ill have recovered, they should return, their strength restored, to their former condition.

He says, then: “Tame your flesh by fasts and abstinence from food and drink.” The flesh is tamed when its pride is cast down. Its pride is desire; restraint in drink and food grinds down that pride.

> [Note: [Col. 0529D] In the Roman Breviary, hymn for Sunday at Prime.]

And note that in these words he by no means fixes the number of dishes or describes kinds of food. Whether one dish or several are present, and likewise whether one kind of food or various kinds are set before us, he exhorts us to take nourishment in such a way that the flesh is tamed through the intervention of abstinence. For since it is not food but appetite that is at fault, some, even when there are many dishes and kinds of food, tame their flesh by eating sparingly; while some, when there is only one dish and one kind of food, are carried away by excessive desire into the vice of gluttony and stir up that same flesh to the shameful provocations by which it is goaded.

Elijah ate flesh without fault (III Kings XVII, 9); and Esau, unlawfully desiring lentils, even lost his birthright (Gen. XXV, 34). Nevertheless, to seek after an excessive number of dishes or kinds of food, or things excessively delicate, belongs in no way to religious men. To allow some such things, indeed, according to place and time, person and cause, may often perhaps be an arrangement not to be blamed; but to demand them without reasonable cause, inopportunely and intemperately, is unquestionably a blameworthy excess.

XI. “Insofar,” he says, “as health permits.” For everything excessive turns into vice. Therefore, “insofar as health permits,” so that there may be nothing too much.

> [Note: [Col. 0530D] From the saying of Pittacus, *Cicero, Laws* III, 1.]

The Apostle forbids provision to be made for the desires of the flesh (Rom. XIII, 14). Therefore the flesh must be tamed by abstinence from food and drink insofar as health permits, lest, if it is restrained beyond its strength, it be broken and weakened for the exercise of good work. But when anyone cannot fast, he should nevertheless take no food outside the hour of the meal unless he is ill. Religious men ought not to eat before the proper time for eating, [Col. 0529D] especially when they are well. For, as Saint Gregory says, Jonathan deserved his father’s sentence of death because in tasting honey he anticipated the appointed time for eating. He was not condemned to that sentence because he took food, but because he presumed to seize it before the hour.

Some hold that the time before the third hour is outside the proper hour. They say that until that hour it is not lawful for a religious man to eat or drink unless he is ill; for this law was not laid down for the sick. But for those who neither fast nor are ill, they maintain that, according to reason and circumstance, the canonical hour for refreshment is from the third to the sixth hour. For those who fast, it is from the ninth hour [Col. 0530A] until evening. Thus we ought not only to use food and drink temperately, but also to observe the appointed hours, so that we take nothing outside them unless we are ill.

XII. “When you come to table, until you rise from it, listen without disturbance or disputes to what is read to you according to custom.” This is indeed a salutary and suitable institution: while the body attends to refreshment, the spirit should not omit its own. For the word of sacred reading is refreshment for the soul, as this visible food is refreshment for the body; because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV, 4).

“Listen,” he says, “without disturbance and disputes to what is read to you according to custom,” so that then, especially [Col. 0530B] when we come to table, as we are composed in respect of the body’s repose, we may also attend to silence of the mouth. Disturbance belongs to those who behave disorderly in the bodily movements of religious observance; dispute belongs to those who make turbulent noises through loud voice or speech. Since, especially when we come to be refreshed, we ought to restrain in ourselves unlawful movements of the limbs with the curb of maturity, disturbance is forbidden to us. And because then above all we must practise the gravity of silence, dispute too is forbidden.

“Let not your throats alone take food, but let your ears hunger for the word of God.” Strictly speaking, it is not the ears but the throat that hungers. Yet Saint Augustine wished our ears to have as great a desire to hear the word of God as the throat usually has to take bodily food when hunger burns it; and he therefore wished the ears themselves also to hunger for the word of God. For this hunger is desire. And as this hunger is spiritual, so also are the ears. Which ears are they? I think they are understanding and affection. For when you understand through the sense of hearing the word of God of which we speak, and strive to commit that understanding to action, you plainly possess inner ears [Col. 0530C] by which you hunger for the word of God. Of these ears the Lord himself says: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Rev. III, 22). Whoever does not have them cannot hear, because, while he neither receives the word through understanding nor strives through love to bring it into action, he perhaps becomes insensibly hardened.

[Col. 0530D] XIII. It follows: “But if those who are weak because of their former habit are treated differently in food, this should not trouble others or seem unjust to those whom some habit has made stronger.” These words proclaim both the virtue of compassion that we must exercise and the vice of envy that we must abhor. For compassion means that those whom former habit makes weak are treated differently in food. Envy is shown when those whom, conversely, habit has made stronger are troubled on that account and judge it unjust.

“Let them not suppose those persons happier because they receive what the others do not receive; but rather let them rejoice for themselves because they are capable of what the others are not.” Happiness is not that the weak receive what the strong do not; it is rather weakness. Therefore they ought rather to rejoice for themselves because they can do what the others cannot than to judge the others happier. For it is a strength that, through health and vigor, they are content with the food and drink common to the rest; and it is a weakness that, through illness and frailty, others need different treatment in food.

“And if those who have come to the monastery from more delicate habits receive some food, clothing, or coverings that are not given to others who are stronger and therefore happier, those to whom such things are not given should consider how far the former have descended from their secular life to this life, even though they have not been able to attain the frugality of others who are stronger in body.” Therefore it is not the weak but the stronger who are happier. Let those strong, and therefore happy, persons to whom food, clothing, and coverings are not given—though these are given to the delicate—consider how far those delicate persons have descended to this life from the height of secular life. Thus they may infer from this reasoning that those who have been humbled more by descending should also be restored more by receiving.

“Nor should all wish to receive what they see a few receive in addition, not because they are honored, but because they are borne with.” In receiving more, deference is not shown in honor of their persons; rather, provision is made in forbearance for their infirmities. Since they are seen to receive these things for this reason, the whole community should by no means wish for them.

XIV. And why is this? He adds: “Lest the detestable perversity occur that, in a monastery, where the rich make themselves laborious as far as they can, the poor become delicate.” It is indeed a detestable perversity for a poor person to insist on luxuries in a cenobium where a rich person devotes his whole self to labors for God. We see this happen far too frequently. You may see one who, while in the world, abounded in every luxury, when he has entered the common life, restraining himself with the hard labors of spiritual combat so that he may please God and appear blameless before people. Conversely, you may see one who, in secular dress, like that prodigal later reduced after a little while to want, who wished to fill his belly with the husks that the swine ate and no one gave him (Luke XV, 16), rarely ate even barley to satiety, proudly seeking every superfluous [Col. 0531D] and delicate thing in the cenobium. But it is a detestable perversity for one who always lived laboriously in the world arrogantly to desire to live delicately in the monastery.

It follows: “Certainly, just as the sick need to receive less lest they be burdened, so after illness they should be treated in such a way that they recover more quickly, even if they came from the lowest poverty of the world—as though their recent illness had conferred upon them what former habit had conferred upon the rich.” Just as he commands that the rich be treated differently in food when their former habit has made them weak, so also the poor are in every respect to be treated after illness in such a way that they may recover more quickly. And just as the former’s habit should be borne with equanimity when they receive more, so the latter’s utter poverty should not be despised in the restoration that they need after illness.

“But when they have regained their former strength, let them return to their happier custom, which befits servants of God the more because they need less.” It is therefore permissible for the holy to relax the rigor of their custom because of the weakness of illness. But once restored, they ought to return to it more eagerly, in proportion as they have less need of the restoratives by which they were refreshed. He calls that practice happier by reason of this restoration, because it is far more blessed to endure rigor than to need restoration.

XV. “Let not the pleasure of food keep those now vigorous whom necessity had relieved while they were ill.” From this it is plainly inferred that the pleasure of richer and more delicate food must always be avoided by the healthy and admitted only occasionally for the sick because of necessity.

“Let them judge richer those who are stronger in enduring frugality.” When we endure frugality manfully, blunting the impulses of the flesh, we also mortify its desires. From the mortification of vices springs the growth of virtues, in which our true and spiritual riches consist. It follows, then, that we are truly rich when we are strong in enduring frugality.

“It is better to need less than to have more.” That is to say: it is better to endure some want for God’s sake than to abound. For want that is for God’s sake is commonly a guardian of humility in good minds, whereas abundance is often a cause of pride. And in order that a servant of God may wholly avoid excess, he should always restrain himself even short of necessity, so that, while cautiously restricting himself even from lawful things, he may not, by the Lord’s gift, fall into unlawful ones also—to whom be honor and glory forever. Amen.

## SERMON X

From the passage in the Rule of Blessed Augustine, “Let your dress not be conspicuous,” through “let those under whose care the requested things are not delay to give what is necessary to those in need.” On the beauty of seemliness; on chastity of the body; on voluntary confession; on common custodians of clothing; on washing clothing; on care of the sick; and on books to be requested daily.

## SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. The seemliness of dress commended to clerics; the vanity of seeking to please proscribed. Yet in one’s gait and remaining bodily bearing, one should be composed and irreproachable.

2. To safeguard chastity, eyes fixed especially upon women must be restrained, lest desire and death enter through the windows.

3. An immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart; three forms of immodesty are distinguished according to the legislator’s thought.

4. Guilt is often more exposed the more, in the offender’s judgment, it is hidden. The holy man is more afraid of displeasing God, from whom he knows that nothing can be hidden.

5. In this matter brotherly assistance is effective, and above all the protection of divine grace.

6. Timely correction is to be applied; it must be harsher toward the disobedient than toward the well-disposed. What must be done if amendment fails.

7. It is a grave obligation to report an offending brother: to be silent is an act of cruelty; to disclose is an act of mercy.

8. The manner of correcting secret and manifest offenses, or offenses proved by witnesses; this belongs especially to superiors, whom discipline should make fathers and piety mothers.

9. One unwilling to be corrected, or incorrigible, must be expelled from the community. The same is to be observed in like cases, with love for persons and hatred of vices.

10. Secret receipt of gifts or letters is forbidden; but spontaneous confession of guilt receives easier pardon.

11. Community of clothing, as of food, must be maintained; and it is especially shameful to stir up murmuring or disputes over these things.

12. The more commendable the communion and unity of charity, the more detestable the abuse of private ownership, which bears the mark of theft.

13. In washing clothes and bodily illness, seemliness and necessity must be provided for without obeying desire; how far the sick are to be trusted and provision made for a traveller.

14. The officer in charge of the sick and other officials should be faithful and useful; nor should persons needing anything make themselves troublesome or importunate to them.

I. The prerogative of the clerical order, dearest brothers, requires clerics diligently to acquire, courageously practise, and steadfastly retain seemliness among the other virtues, and to devote themselves to its beauty.

> [Note: [Col. 0533D] Rule, chapter VI: “On the Beauty of Seemliness and Chastity.”]

[Col. 0533B] For just as they possess a special dignity in their order, so they ought likewise to possess a special seemliness in their conduct. Otherwise—far be it—the eminence of their dignity may not rightly deserve honor when the example of their conduct rightly merits rebuke. Therefore the great Father Augustine, founder of their regular discipline, after showing how they ought to conduct themselves in food, also instructs them concerning their clothing. For he says: “Let your dress not be conspicuous.”

Conspicuous dress is that in which something may rightly be noticed—either vanity, excess, or excessive shabbiness. The first concerns finery, the second measure, the third cost. He wished this threefold evil removed from our clothing when he forbade our dress to be conspicuous. He himself also diligently strove to banish such conspicuousness far from his own dress, and what he prescribed in teaching on this matter he put into practice. For we read that his clothing, footwear, and bedding were of moderate and suitable character: neither overly fine nor excessively mean. It is also reported that he said of himself: “I confess that I blush at costly clothing: it does not suit this profession, it does not suit this admonition, it does not suit these limbs, it does not suit these gray hairs.”

Clerics who renounce the world ought to have rough and humble clothing, because, as the Lord says, “those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. XI, 8). And even the faithful are told through the first shepherd of the Church:

> [Note: [Col. 0534D] Read “Doctor of the Gentiles.” For it is Paul, not Peter, who says this.—ES. P.]

[Col. 0533D] “not in costly clothing” (I Tim. II, 9). “Do not seek to please by clothing, but by morals.” By teaching, he seeks to forbid what pertains to worldly vanity and to stir us toward what pertains to true religion. For desiring to please by clothing belongs to worldly men, but desiring to please by morals belongs to religious persons.

It follows: “Whenever you go out, walk together; when you have arrived where you are going, stand together.” This is clearly so that holy men may always and everywhere have with them both guardians of their integrity and witnesses. This never displeased the wise and righteous man, because “he who does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest” (John III, 21). On the contrary, everyone who does evil hates the light. Those walk in the light and stand in the light who have with them, wherever they are, the testimony of good.

“In your walk, standing, dress, and all your movements, let nothing be done that offends anyone’s sight, but only what befits your holiness.” He desired us to be truly irreproachable when he exhorts us not to be such as to offend even anyone’s eye. Yet it must rightly be understood that, where there is no cause for offense, carnal and imperfect persons are often offended as well. Therefore we must behave so religiously, both when walking and standing, and in all our outward movements, that no one may rightly have cause to rebuke us and no one may be offended through us. For this befits our holiness: that we should appear not only pure before God but also outwardly without offense before our neighbor, according to the Apostle’s saying: “providing what is good not only before God but also before all people” (Rom. XII, 17). “Before all people,” he says, so that in none, but in all, our movements nothing may be done that offends anyone’s sight.

II. “Even if your eyes are cast upon some woman, let them be fixed upon none.” He treats of two things: one he tolerates, the other he forbids. He does not forbid that the eyes be cast upon a woman; but he forbids their being fixed upon her. Hence he adds: “For when you go out, you are not forbidden to see women; but to desire them, or to wish to be desired by them, is criminal.”

It may also be inferred from this that the glance of the eyes which he here forbids when fixed indicates an unlawful desire of the mind as well. Perhaps he judged it necessary to forbid the former because he recognized the latter as criminal. Yet this also should be added: although we are not forbidden to see women, it is nevertheless counsel that we accustom ourselves not to look, because one who does not restrain sight often falls into desire. And desire, if Saint James understood rightly, gives birth to sin; and sin, once completed, generates death (James I, 15).

I think this is why Saint Job made a covenant with his eyes not even to think of a virgin (Job XXXI, 1). What cause or occasion could he have had not even to think of a virgin? Surely this: the mind is often accustomed, even when the woman is absent, to represent to itself and unlawfully dwell upon the appearance of beauty at which the eye has looked rashly. Saint David rashly cast his eyes upon a woman, and this became the cause that afterwards, and shortly afterwards, he became both a foul adulterer and a bloodstained murderer (II Kings XI).

Thus, if we desire perfectly to overcome this vice, we must also diligently strive to guard against its cause and occasion. Hence Lot, fleeing from Sodom, is commanded neither to look back nor to remain anywhere in all the surrounding region, but to save himself on the mountain [Col. 0535A] (Gen. XIX, 17). Whoever fully desires to escape the incentives of vices must remove himself from their sight and neighborhood, and ascend to the heights of virtue on the summit of the mind, so that he may remain freer from vices in proportion as he separates himself from them even by bodily absence.

That bodily sight, together with the desire of the mind, is an occasion of lust is plainly shown when the text adds: “The lust of women is both aroused and arouses, not only by touch and affection but also by sight.” This means: desire does not arise only silently in the inner chambers of the will; through outward sight, fuel and cause, material and occasion are also supplied to it. This is the meaning of the prophet’s lament: “Death has climbed through our windows and entered our houses” (Jer. IX, 21).

Desire is the death of the soul—indeed, the soul’s death—because it is its cause and occasion of dying. For, as the Apostle James testifies, its offspring is sin; and sin’s completion is the generation of death. Our inward house is our mind. Its windows, through which it ordinarily goes forth to touch visible things, are the bodily senses, and especially these outward glances of ours. Death, then, climbing through our windows, also enters our houses when the vice of desire, breaking in through the senses of our body and especially through our eyes, penetrates even the inner chambers of our heart.

III. “Do not say that you have chaste minds if you have immodest eyes.” He forbids us to say this because we cannot say it truthfully. For he adds: “an immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart.” Certainly, an equally immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart, because by conveying messages it commonly supplies what that heart basely desires.

“And when, even though the tongue is silent, immodest hearts disclose themselves to one another by a mutual look, and, according to the lust of the flesh, delight in each other’s ardor, chastity itself flees from their conduct, even though their bodies remain untouched by unclean violation.” The loss of chastity in one’s conduct is indeed reached even where the body is not touched by unclean violation—at least insofar as the complete commission of the wicked act is concerned—when, by a mutual look, immodest hearts disclose themselves to and from one another, and those hearts delight in reciprocal ardor as the lust of the flesh titillates them.

This point is reached, I say, whenever this occurs, even though there is no speech concerning that bodily loss of chastity. For although the tongue is silent, the immodest hearts are not silent to one another. They bring it about that the lust of the flesh tickles them together and that mutual delight in ardor strikes them. “Chastity,” he says, “flees from their conduct” when this occurs, because every gravity and maturity in our outward bearing is dissipated. For chastity is present in conduct when, in all one’s outward movements, a person is so composed as to appear in all the beauty of gravity and maturity, and does not permit his grave and venerable conduct to be prostituted by the wantonness of some frivolity.

We must especially note that Blessed Augustine indicates in these words a threefold immodesty that we must avoid. He mentions wanton looks, immodest hearts, and the flight of chastity from conduct. The first occurs when wantonness is not avoided in the look; the second, when desire rules the affection; the third, when no maturity or gravity is preserved in any outward movement of the body. Let us, my brothers, flee this threefold evil with all diligence, knowing that we cannot in any way avoid the second or third unless we strive carefully to prevent the first.

For if we always and everywhere direct a fixed and wanton look around us, we shall preserve inward chastity of affection only rarely and briefly. For when immodest hearts make themselves known to one another through a mutual look, they must consequently and immediately delight in reciprocal ardor according to the desire of the flesh. And when this twofold evil precedes, the third at once follows; indeed, it does not happen when the former has departed but while it remains [variant: *accedit*, “is added”]. Thus, even though the bodies remain untouched by unclean violation, chastity itself flees from their conduct. So, while wantonness grows insolent in the look and desire burns in the affection, although the wicked violation of unclean intercourse is not fully enacted in deed, maturity and gravity are nevertheless wholly dissipated and destroyed in the outward movement of the body.

IV. Nor should anyone who fixes his eyes upon a woman, and delights that hers are fixed upon himself, suppose that he is unseen by others when he does this. He is certainly seen—even by those by whom he does not think he is seen. We quite often observe this happening: when people imagine that they are pursuing their vices cautiously and secretly, they themselves, without knowing it, make themselves known; and their fault then comes more openly to light precisely when they think it more concealed. But this is characteristic of such persons: they think that what they are doing in this manner is hidden from everyone, although it is plain to all. For lust blinds the mind over which it rules [Col. 0536D]: unable to see itself, it does not suppose itself to be seen; and, although it is concealed from scarcely anyone, it thinks itself exposed to no one.

But even if it were concealed and seen by no human being, what will he do about that Watcher from above from whom nothing can be hidden? If nothing can be hidden from Him—indeed, precisely because nothing can be hidden from Him—then neither is hidden from Him the man who fixes his eye upon a woman and delights that hers are fixed upon himself. Or is He to be thought not to see because He sees so patiently in proportion as He sees wisely? He sees wisely, because, seeing, He cannot be seen. He also sees patiently, because, though He is displeased by what He sees, He nevertheless bears with it long-sufferingly.

Therefore, since that invisible Wisdom remains within itself, nothing escapes it; and since in its rectitude it often condemns what it has seen, that supreme gentleness cannot be provoked to disturbance [Col. 0537A]. In every offence which we commit in heart, speech, or deed, therefore, we must fear the eye of that heavenly Watcher from whom nothing can be hidden. For although our secrets may be concealed and seen by no human being, all things are naked and open to His eyes. Let the holy man, then, fear to displease Him, lest he wish wrongly to please a woman. Let that good fear forestall this perverse desire, so that it may not arise; and, should it arise, let it expel it. Let him think upon Him who sees all things, lest he wish to look wrongly upon a woman. In the same way, let that good thought drive out this evil desire. Let him fear to displease his Creator, lest he wish unlawfully to please a woman. Let him think upon the universal Watcher, lest he desire to be rashly looked upon by a woman.

For fear of Him is commended even in this matter, where it is written: “Fixing the eye is an abomination to the Lord.” From these words it is clearly inferred that, while we fix our eye upon a woman, we too are abominable to God. A fearful pronouncement, brothers, and one that ought greatly to shake our conscience. Whatever we commit in deed, utter in speech, or even entertain in heart, we must always and everywhere attend to God’s eyes over all that we do, and fear lest we displease Him.

V. Not only this; we must also exercise mutual care for one another, so that we may be able to remain unharmed amid so many storms of temptation. Hence there follows this salutary exhortation:

> “Therefore, whenever you are together in church, or wherever women are present, guard one another’s chastity.” [Col. 0537C]

We are together bodily in order that we may be spiritually concerned for one another. It is written, “Woe to him who is alone”; and the reason is added: “for when he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Ecclus. IV, 10). Therefore each person ought to keep a watchful—but charitable—eye upon another. Let each extend helping hands to the others and, as far as possible, provide mutual assistance.

Thus will be fulfilled that most wholesome exhortation of the great teacher of the Church and chief of the apostles:

> “As each has received a gift, administer it to one another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Pet. IV, 10).

O how holy an exercise this is! An exercise no less pleasant than good: good for the holiness of merit and pleasant for the sweetness of the spirit. It is indeed an exercise which, among other benefits, ordinarily helps those who have fallen to rise, those who stand to be strengthened, and those who waver to become stable. Yet, because human care is insufficient without divine protection, it is accordingly added:

> “For God, who dwells in you, will also guard you in this way through yourselves.”

For, as Scripture says, “No one can be continent unless God gives it” (Wis. VIII, 21). And if, according to the Apostle, we are “not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves” (2 Cor. III, 5), still less are we sufficient in this life of ours, which is wholly temptation, to preserve ourselves unharmed from the darts of tempting lust. God will guard us, since without Him we can do nothing. [Col. 0538A] Yet He will guard us in this way through ourselves: stirring us up that we may will, instructing us that we may know, and strengthening us that we may be able to guard one another’s chastity.

It follows:

VI. “And if you observe in any one of yourselves that wantonness of the eye of which I speak, admonish him at once, lest what has begun advance; rather, let it be corrected immediately.”

The very beginnings must therefore be corrected at once, because unless the very root of the poisonous plant is dug up, it will spread to excessive size. A vice which is not resisted at the first moment of its appearance is corrected with greater difficulty as time goes on. For the more frequently it is repeated, the more it grows; and, once increased, it often attains such strength that it cannot, or scarcely can, be opposed.

Hence St Benedict says among other things concerning the abbot in the Rule for monks:

> “He must not overlook the sins of offenders; but, as soon as they begin to appear, he must, so far as he is able, cut them off at the root. Let the abbot remember the danger of Eli, the priest of Shiloh. The more honourable and intelligent dispositions he should rebuke with words at the first or second admonition; but the wicked, hard, proud, or disobedient he should restrain at the very beginning of sin by stripes or bodily correction.” [Col. 0538B]

See how Augustine, father of clerics, and Benedict, leader of monks—though they lived at different times, instructed and inflamed by one and the same Spirit—agree in this: that those who undertake to commit sin must be carefully resisted at the very beginning of the sin, so that what has begun may not advance but may be corrected immediately. Therefore, as I think, St Benedict commands the abbot not to overlook the sins of offenders, but as soon as they begin to appear, to cut them off at the root as far as he can, and to restrain the offenders themselves at the beginning of their sin.

Likewise blessed Augustine, who preceded him by some time, commands us to admonish them lest what has begun advance, but rather be corrected immediately; for unless we apply correction to them without delay, their subsequent amendment will not easily be achieved.

“But if, after admonition, you see him doing the same thing, let whoever can discover it report him as one wounded, to be healed. Yet it must first be shown to a second or third person, so that he may be convicted by the testimony of two or three mouths [witnesses] [Col. 0538D] and restrained with appropriate severity.”

If, before admonition, he was in some measure struck by what he did wrong, then surely he has already incurred, as it were, a wound in his soul, since he has despised obedience to the admonition. He must therefore now be reported as one wounded—and reported in order that he may be healed. But lest he be able to contradict the reporter by denial, the matter must first be shown to a second or third person, so that he may be convicted by the testimony of two or three; for, according to the Lord’s declaration, “Every word stands in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII, 16).

Once convicted by the testimony of two or three, he ought to be restrained with appropriate severity, because the person who does not justly punish what has been unjustly done transgresses the very rule of justice. Hence it is written in the Law: “You shall carry out what is just, justly” (Deut. XVI, 20). [Col. 0539A] He carries out what is just who, according to his position and office, pursues a fault in order to amend it. Yet he fails to carry out this justice justly if, in correcting it, he does not observe the rule of justice.

VII. “Nor judge yourselves ill-disposed when you report this.” Why those who report it ought not to be judged ill-disposed is then added: “Rather, you are not innocent if, by keeping silence, you allow to perish brothers whom you could correct by reporting them.”

Certainly, he causes harm who does not wish to correct when he is able. For one who can remove what is harmful but does not do so inflicts something harmful, as it were. Thus, as much benefit as he would bring by correcting, so much harm does he inflict when he permits destruction. He does this by silence; but he could do the other by reporting it. Therefore, my brother, let your diligence infer from these matters how destructive your silence is in this respect, when your brother perishes through its intervention.

This silence is certainly not the “work of righteousness” of which holy Isaiah speaks (Isa. XXXII, 17), but a cause of injustice and a road to everlasting punishment. Thus, you do no small harm if you keep silent when you are able to correct your brother’s fault. For how do you not harm him when, by keeping silent, you bring it about that evils already committed are neither corrected nor evils not yet committed prevented? If you reported it, perhaps your brother would grieve over the past and guard against the future.

Accordingly, the exhortation of the Wise Man is entirely reasonable:

> “Rebuke a friend, lest perhaps he did not understand and says, ‘I did not do it’; or, if he did it, lest he do it again” (Ecclus. XIX, 13).

And he immediately adds:

> “Rebuke your neighbour, lest perhaps he did not say it; and, if he did say it, lest perhaps he repeat it” (ibid., 14). [Col. 0539C]

Therefore you sin greatly against your neighbour if you do not correct him by reporting him; and when you allow him to perish through silence, you surely incur a very grave guilt. Hence it is written in Leviticus: “If a soul sins and hears the voice of one swearing: being a witness, or having seen it, or being aware of it, if he does not report it, he shall bear his iniquity” (Lev. V, 1). See why the person who did not report another’s sin, which he saw and of which he was aware, is said to bear his own sin.

It is thus clear that those who, by keeping silence, allow their brothers—whom they could correct by reporting—to perish are greatly harmful, [Col. 0539D] because they do harm in not one but two ways. They harm, I say, in two ways: they sin both against their brothers and against themselves. They sin against their brothers because they do not fear to provide them, through this destructive silence, with a cause and occasion of perdition; against themselves, because by failing to report these things they make other people’s sins their own. For one who knows that something wicked has been done but neglects to report it for correction appears in some way to consent to and approve it.

Blessed Augustine fittingly shows by an example how far from harmless such persons are, adding:

> “For if your brother had a bodily wound which he wished to conceal because he feared being cut, would you not be cruel if you kept silence, and merciful if you reported it?”

Certainly no one can reasonably gainsay this. You are altogether merciful if you report it; but cruel if you conceal it: once reported, it is healed, and for as long as it is kept silent, healing is delayed. How much more, then, ought you to disclose it lest it rot more grievously in the heart? I think you know the passage to which this refers.

If therefore it follows from what has been said that the person who conceals a wound in his brother’s body is cruel, while the person who reports it so that it may be treated is merciful, then the more cruel is he who conceals what is festering in the heart, and the more merciful he who reveals it lest such corruption find a place in the heart. Unless someone can show that the body is worthier, higher, more precious, and nobler than the heart. Certainly he is cruel—indeed, to speak more plainly, most cruel—[Col. 0540B] who conceals the wound of sin in his brother’s soul; and he is wholly and completely guilty of that brother’s death when he allows him to perish by silence. For just as the unlawful act pronounces the former worthy of death, so this silence pronounces the latter worthy of death.

And just as he is not free from cruelty who does not disclose his brother’s fault, so he is merciful who does not conceal it. For if to have mercy is to pity the miserable, I do not know how anyone can exercise greater mercy toward a miserable person than by striving to give life to one who is perishing, after removing the occasion of his destruction.

VIII. “But before he is shown to others by whom he may be convicted if he denies it, he ought first to be shown to the superior, if, after being admonished, he neglects to be corrected, lest perhaps, having been corrected more secretly, he need not become known to the others.” [Col. 0540C]

When something unlawful is committed secretly, the person who committed it ought likewise to be corrected secretly, according to place and time, person and circumstance. He says that it should be shown to the superior, so that a sin which is still hidden may not become known to everyone when it can be corrected secretly. But if the offender presumes to deny it, witnesses must then be brought in by whom he may be convicted.

This is what follows: “But if he denies it, then others are to be brought before the denier, so that even before all he may be accused not by one witness but convicted by two or three.” Once convicted by them, he is now considered worthy of a graver punishment—not only because he committed what was unlawful, [Col. 0540D] but because, once exposed, he deceitfully denied what was true and, even after being reported, refused to confess until he was convicted by witnesses.

Hence it follows: “But once convicted, according to the judgment of the superior—or of the presbyter, to whose administration the matter belongs—he must undergo corrective punishment.” He is indeed worthy to endure sharper correction, since, gently chastised, he refuses to be corrected. Having been convicted in this manner, he must undergo punishment so that the penalty may restore the soul to health which sin had made sick. This punishment ought to be imposed according to the judgment of the superior or presbyter, so that those who have received spiritual authority in the holy Church by divine appointment may inflict punishment upon the bodies of transgressors against holy religion, in order that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Concerning this punishment, it is fittingly commanded that it be corrective, [Col. 0541A] so that it may possess such discernment as both to remove past guilt and prevent future guilt, rather than either increasing the guilt already present or supplying an occasion for guilt not yet present to arise. This is precisely what occurs when, regarding the superior and presbyter of whom we have just spoken, in accordance with the sayings of the ancient Fathers, compassion makes them mothers and discipline makes them fathers—while careful provision is made that strictness be neither harsh nor compassion lax.

Concerning this, blessed Father Benedict writes in the Rule for monks:

> “In his teaching the abbot must always preserve the apostolic form in which it is said: ‘Argue, entreat, rebuke’ (2 Tim. IV, 2). That is, blending times with times and threats with encouragements, let him show the stern affection of a master and the loving affection of a father. Thus he ought to rebuke the undisciplined and restless more severely; but he should entreat the obedient, gentle, and patient that they may advance to better things; and he should rebuke and correct the negligent and contemptuous.” [Col. 0541B]

Therefore the punishment should be corrective: that is, such as amends the offender.

IX. It should be noted that St Augustine commands three things to be observed in relation to this convicted person: namely, that the fault not be left unpunished; that the superior or presbyter not be deprived of his authority in inflicting the punishment; and that the punishment itself, when imposed, not lack discernment.

And he added: “If he refuses to bear it, even though he himself does not depart, let him be expelled from your fellowship.” [Col. 0541C] This is indeed a quite just ordinance. For why, if he were unwilling to depart, should he be allowed to remain? You do not fear to commit a fault, and you refuse to bear the punishment? But perhaps someone will say: if such a person wished to leave, that might perhaps be tolerable in some way; but to expel against his will one who wishes to remain is no small cruelty. This is not cruelty at all, but exceedingly great mercy.

For this also follows: “For it is not done cruelly but mercifully.” The reason is added: “Lest he destroy many by a pestilential contagion.” It is better that one person be expelled to avert danger to many, than that many be endangered because one is tolerated. Thus it is preferable that one be cast out than that many be contaminated; that one be removed than that many be perverted.

St Benedict also, filled with the spirit of all the righteous, writes concerning this:

> “If any brother, after frequent correction for any fault, remains uncorrected even after excommunication, let a sharper correction be applied to him; that is, let punishment by stripes be inflicted upon him. But if he does not amend even thus, or perhaps—God forbid—becomes puffed up in pride and wishes even to defend his conduct, then let the abbot do what a wise physician does. If he has applied fomentations, the ointments of exhortation, the medicines of the divine Scriptures, the final cautery of excommunication, and strokes of the rod; and if he sees that his skill prevails in nothing, let him employ also what is greater: his own prayer and that of all the brothers for him, that the Lord, who can do all things, may work healing for the sick brother. But if he is not healed even in this way, then let the abbot use the knife of excision, as the Apostle says: ‘Remove the evil from among yourselves’ (1 Cor. V, 13). And again: ‘If the unbeliever departs, let him depart’ (1 Cor. VII, 15), lest one diseased sheep contaminate the entire flock.” [Col. 0542A]

So St Benedict. The Lord Himself likewise commands us in the Gospel to pluck out our eye when it causes us to stumble, and to cut off and cast away even the right hand or foot. And He adds: “It is expedient for you that one of your members perish” (Matt. XVIII, 8–9), rather than that your whole body be cast into Gehenna.

What is this eye, right foot, or hand, except our indispensable friend? The eye, providing foresight in affairs; the hand, ministering in necessities; and the foot, walking in straight paths. Yet each of these members, when they cause you to stumble, must be cut away from the body. Thus, when one has proved incorrigible—even though he be very necessary and greatly beloved—if he does not depart, he must be expelled from our fellowship, lest he destroy many by a pestilential contagion. Hence there is no doubt that this is done not cruelly but mercifully.

And what I have said concerning the fixing of the eye must also be carefully and faithfully observed in discovering, forbidding, proving, and judging all other sins, with love for persons and hatred for vices. “Carefully,” he says, “and faithfully”: carefully, so that in all these matters observance may be earnest and watchful, without pretence; faithfully, so that it may be without respect of persons. [Col. 0542C] These two qualities are very necessary to us: present in purging sins and absent in avoiding them, so that we may neither turn to the right through respect of persons nor wander to the left from the path of uprightness.

And let all this be done with love for persons and hatred for vices. For, as our Augustine says elsewhere, people ought to be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved. We may—and must—add that their errors ought to be hated in such a way that the persons themselves are nevertheless not hated. With love for persons and hatred for vices, according to the saying of blessed Gregory: so that in the same persons we love the good which they have become and pursue the evils which they have done.

It follows:

X. “But whoever has advanced so far in evil as secretly to receive from someone a letter or any gift, if he confesses it of his own accord, let him be spared and prayer be made for him. But if he is discovered and convicted by witnesses, let him be corrected more severely according to the judgment of the superior or presbyter.” [Note: [Col. 0541D] Rule, chap. 7, “On voluntary confession.”]

From these words it may be understood that St Augustine regarded it as a serious transgression for a canon who had professed the common life secretly to receive anything. For when he was about to speak of it, he carefully prefaced the matter so explicitly: “whoever has advanced so far in evil” (4 Kings IV). For a person of his order who presumes to do this is no slight violator of his order.

Long ago Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, secretly received a gift from Naaman the Syrian; and, to show that this was a great evil, the prophet struck him, as you know, with a terrible affliction. [Col. 0543A] Concerning this blessed Benedict says:

> “It must by no means be permitted to a monk to receive or give letters, *eulogiae* [blessed gifts], or any little gifts, whether from his parents, from anyone else, or among themselves, without the abbot’s command.”

Our holy father Augustine clearly shows in the present passage that this is likewise not permitted to a canon. Let us hear what blessed Jerome thinks of such things. “Holy love,” he says, “does not have sweet letters, handkerchiefs, and frequent small gifts.” [Note: [Col. 0543D] St Jerome, Epistle to Nepotian.]

Thus a regular cleric who secretly receives from someone letters or any gift advances far into evil, because he is a violator of his vow. Yet because a fault deserves immediate forgiveness when it is humbly disclosed in a confession not extorted but voluntary, it is commanded that one who confesses of his own accord be spared and prayer made for him; but that a heavier penalty be inflicted on one who is discovered and convicted by witnesses.

It follows:

XI. “Keep your garments together under one keeper, or two, or as many as may be sufficient to shake them out lest they be harmed by moths; and as you are fed from one storeroom, so be clothed from one wardrobe.” [Note: [Col. 0543] Rule, chap. VIII, “On the common keepers of clothing.”]

He wishes us to have one wardrobe for clothing and likewise one storeroom for food, with this provision: that one or two, or even more when necessary [variant: *quamplures*, “very many”], shake out our garments lest moths damage them. [Col. 0543C] Nor is this the only reason: it is also lest a brother who has a garment think that he may possess it as his own if he is permitted to put it away for himself in a private place.

Therefore it is added: “And, if possible, let it not concern you which clothing suited to the seasons is brought out for you: whether each receives what he had put aside, or another garment which someone else had had, provided that what each needs is not denied to anyone.”

“If possible,” he says—that is, even if this seems difficult to someone—I certainly say that it should not concern you which seasonally appropriate garment is brought out for you. Whether each receives what he put aside or what another had, let this not be much considered, provided only that this be most carefully ensured: that what each needs is not denied to him.

Thus, being content with necessities and renouncing superfluities, while no one is denied what he needs according to each person’s need, let no one among you demand more than is necessary. But if disputes and quarrels arise among you on this account, and someone complains that he has received something worse than he had before, and that he does not deserve not to be clothed as another brother was clothed, then prove from this how much you lack that holy inward habit of the heart for the sake of which you contend about bodily clothing.

Far be it that complaints and murmurs should rage, or disputes and quarrels thunder, among religious men concerning this outward clothing, provided there is a moderate supply with which that weak little body may be covered. [Col. 0544A] Certainly, the more one quarrels over bodily clothing, the less there is of that holy inward habit of the heart.

What is the habit of the heart? Surely that precious and holy, comely and honourable adornment of spiritual virtues with which the inward person is clothed, and of which it is read in the Apocalypse: “Blessed is he who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Apoc. XVI, 15). This is that excellent adornment with which the preacher of truth wished the elect disciples to be clothed when he said: “Clothe yourselves, as God’s elect, holy and beloved, with bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience,” and the remaining badges of spiritual virtues which follow (Col. III, 12).

But when we begin to contend, murmur, and complain among ourselves, we immediately remain empty of these spiritual goods; and, as we appear in dreadful nakedness, our shame is seen. It is seen, I say, and mocked. For virtues cannot remain together with vices, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, will not dwell in a body subject to sins, and will be reproved by the iniquity that comes upon it.”

Nevertheless, if your weakness is tolerated so that you receive what you put aside, still keep what you put aside in one place under common keepers, [Col. 0544B] with this qualification: “Let no one make anything for himself; rather, let all your works be done together, with greater zeal and more frequent gladness than if each of you were doing his own work separately” (Wis. I, 1). It should be kept in one place under common keepers so that even what is received, as it were, for one’s own use may be regarded not as private but as common.

XII. It is contrary to every form of religious life, and contrary also to the communion of brotherly charity, that someone who has professed the common life should wish to make anything for himself as though it were his own. Rather, all the works of cenobites ought to be brought into one common whole, so that as they live in one place, so they all work in common. For charity, of which it is written that it “does not seek its own,” is understood in this way: it puts common things before private things, not private things before common things. Since it puts common things before private things, it is fitting that we too strive to put them first, not private things before common things.

The fruit of charity is greater than that of private possession. Therefore, the more you care for the common good rather than for what is privately yours, [Col. 0544D] the more you should know that you are advancing, so that in all things used by transitory necessity, charity, which endures, may excel. Transitory necessity ordinarily uses temporal things, among which charity ought always to excel in us; and it is fitting that we always and everywhere put it before private concerns. It is indeed fitting that we prefer what is everlasting to what is transitory: necessity is the latter; charity, the former. Necessity passes away, but charity remains. For “charity never fails” (1 Cor. [XIII], 8). According to Paul’s statement, it is the more excellent way; and therefore all things ought to be subject to those who walk in it. [Col. 0545A]

When we do this, we should know without doubt that we advance more, because those whose inward fruit in the observance of charity is greater have also richer progress in spiritual life. It consequently follows that if anyone gives some garment or any other thing counted among necessities to his sons or to persons belonging to him through some need who are established in the monastery, it should not be received secretly. Certainly it follows that we ought to receive nothing secretly, since whatever we receive we are commanded to regard not as private property, but rather to bring into common use.

“But let it be in the power of the superior, so that, once brought into the common stock, it may be given to the person who needs it.” This is indeed a most holy institution and very salutary for those who observe it. For in this way avarice is conquered and superfluity cut away; the holy and sanctifying communion of charity is preserved; and the abominable abuse of private possession, hateful to all religious men, is despised.

Hear how St Benedict agrees with blessed Augustine in these matters:

> “If anything is sent to a monk from his parents, he must not presume to receive it unless it has first been reported to the abbot. If the abbot commands that it be received, it shall be in the abbot’s power to decide to whom it should be given. And the brother to whom it was perhaps sent should not be saddened, lest an occasion be given to the devil. Whoever presumes otherwise shall be subject to regular discipline.” [Col. 0545B]

Certainly, when anything counted among necessities has been given to a canon, if he presumes to reserve it for his own use without the permission of his superior—permission granted freely and not extorted, since extortion is the sister of disobedience—he is a violator of the vow which his lips have uttered and, in this respect, a destroyer of the holy Rule which he promised to observe.

But if anyone conceals something given to him, let him be condemned under the judgment for theft. Hardly anyone is ignorant that theft is a criminal and mortal sin. Hence, in secular laws, a judgment of death applies to the person who commits theft. In the same way, those who commit theft are surely deprived in their souls of spiritual life. The brother who conceals something given to him imitates in this matter him of whom it is written in the Gospel that “he was a thief, and, having the money-box, carried what was put into it” (John XII, 6). [Col. 0545D] Since he did not correct the abomination of theft in himself, he proceeded even to betray his Lord and finally hanged himself with a noose (Matt. XXVII, 5). Therefore let a brother fear to conceal something given to him, lest he incur a similar end.

It follows:

XIII. “Let your garments be washed according to the judgment of the superior, whether by yourselves or by fullers, lest an excessive desire for clean clothing contract inward stains of the soul.” [Note: [Col. 0545] Rule, chap. IX, “On washing garments and care of the sick.”]

What else are the inward stains of the soul except sins and iniquities, by which it is ordinarily defiled? But lest these inward contaminations be contracted through an excessive desire for clean clothing, it is indeed permitted that outward garments be washed. [Col. 0546A]

“Nor should bathing of the body be denied when the necessity of illness requires it.” When the necessity of illness requires it, he says—not when the superfluity of desire demands it. For we ought always to assist necessity and refuse superfluity.

“Let it be done without murmuring on the advice of a physician, so that, even if he does not wish it, at the superior’s command he does what must be done for health. But if he wishes it and it is perhaps not expedient, his desire must not be obeyed.” This is what we have just said: even against the will of the sick person, his health must be considered through the advice of a physician; and even if he wishes it, his desire must not be obeyed.

Why is this so? It follows: “For sometimes, even if it harms, what gives pleasure is thought to be beneficial.” Thus a person is often deceived by his own desire, so that he thinks beneficial what harms him. But the discernment of this properly belongs to superiors: they must impose a measure upon both classes, compelling the former to do what must be done for health, while restraining the latter from doing what they crave in carnal desire, which must in no way be obeyed.

But because he has spoken of illness that is openly evident, he adds concerning pain that is hidden: “Finally, if there is a concealed bodily pain, the servant of God who says what hurts him must be believed without hesitation.” [Col. 0546B] A person who serves God ordinarily abhors incurring the sin of lying in every way. Therefore, inasmuch as he is a servant of God, he must not be disbelieved at all, because he is known with certainty to be such a person as detests offending with a lie upon his tongue.

Nevertheless, if it is uncertain whether what pleases him is expedient for healing that pain, a physician should be consulted. And although his words must be believed without hesitation because he is a servant of God, his desires must not immediately or always be complied with; for unlawful desires often tempt even servants of God. For although they always knowingly avoid offending with lies upon their tongues, yet at times, deceived in mind as human beings, they too unknowingly turn aside toward unlawful desires. But if it is not certain what can make the uncertain matter certain, someone who can do so must be sought; that is, a physician must be consulted concerning it.

“Nor should they go to the baths, or wherever it is necessary to go, fewer than two or three.” [Col. 0546C] His mention of baths seems to relate to what he said a little earlier concerning bodily washing. He forbids fewer than two or three to go to such baths, or wherever it is necessary to go, so that on the journey we may especially have with us both witnesses to our manner of life and guardians of our reputation. And the person who needs to go somewhere ought to go with those whom the superior commands—so that the superior may provide for the person’s safety, and the subject may likewise fulfil the virtue of obedience.

XIV. The care of the sick, or of those to be restored after illness, or also of those suffering from some weakness or from fevers [elsewhere: “without fevers”], ought to be entrusted to one particular person, so that he himself may request from the storehouse whatever he foresees each person needs. A brother who fears God and loves his neighbour should be chosen, one who gives the greatest care to the sick, strives to minister to them devoutly and according to his ability in whatever they need, and serves them with such affection, in a certain measure, as though he were serving Him who will say at the judgment: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25:36–40). And again: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me.”

But the sick themselves also, as Saint Benedict admonishes, should consider that they are being served for God’s honour, and should not distress by their excessiveness the brothers serving them. Yet, as he adds, they are to be borne patiently, because a more abundant reward is gained through such persons. Whether those set over the storehouse, clothing, or books, they should serve their brothers without grumbling. The officials in a monastery are servants of the other brothers. For they have undertaken, at the abbot’s command, faithfully to guard and usefully to distribute their possessions; and therefore it is folly no less than fault if the brothers serve them grumblingly in matters which are their own.

Books are to be requested at a fixed hour every day; whoever asks outside that hour is not to receive one. By commanding that books be sought every day, he urges upon us the frequency of reading: so that, just as we daily approach bodily refreshment at the prompting of nature’s irresistible habit, so too we may neglect no day of spiritual refreshment. But by ordering that they be requested at a fixed hour, and forbidding those who ask outside the hour to receive them, he takes care to distinguish time from time. For, as Ecclesiastes says, “Everything has its time” (Ecclus. 3:1): just as no evil work ought ever to be done, so even a good work is deserving of reproof if it is not done at the appropriate time.

Those in whose custody the requested garments and footwear are kept should not delay to give them when they are necessary for those in need. This belongs to what he has commanded in the preceding matters, which we have already considered: that they should serve their brothers without grumbling. For when they delay giving necessities to those in need, they give the brothers occasion for grumbling—provided, however, that they possess what ought to be given but are unwilling to give it. Hence he commands those in whose custody the requested things are kept to give them. For they cannot give what is not in their custody. Therefore, when these things are available, those responsible should not delay to give them; while those who know that they are unavailable should not presume to ask importunately. Thus, while the former do not greedily withhold what ought to be given and is already in hand, and the latter do not anxiously extort what they know to be lacking, they may deserve a fitting recompense—the former for generosity, the latter for patience—through Him who is both the Giver of all good things and the gracious Rewarder of His elect’s patience, God blessed above all things for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XI

From the words of Saint Augustine, the legislator, “Have either no quarrels among yourselves,” to “your love among yourselves ought to be spiritual.” On avoiding strife; on the reconciliation of the injured party and brotherly love.

**290. Synopsis of the Sermon.**—1. The conflict of discord: an incentive of the evil demon and a seedbed of wickedness.—2.
