[Col. 0548A] The slipperiness of the tongue, a frequent cause of strife, which scarcely anyone wholly avoids.—3. Silence, the present remedy for avoiding strife, which is like an illness and a splinter; hatred is like a beam and death.—4. The harms of the contentious disposition that sows discord among brothers.—5. Reconciliation should immediately follow the violation of peace, removing every disturbance of mind and offence against one’s neighbour.—6. Three things to be avoided in injuring brotherly charity: insult, curse, and accusation of a crime; and the duty both of the injured and of the injurer.—7. The kinds of angry persons, and their differences considered.—8. Religious practices are sacrifices of a kind, unacceptable unless discord has been driven out. Three kinds of sacrifices correspond to three stages of spiritual life.—9. Mortification of one’s flesh is of no benefit while discord prevails; pretenders and the obstinate are in the monastery in vain.—10. An exhortation to preserve brotherly concord and avoid violating it.—11. The sacred prophet exhorted that swords be changed into ploughshares and spears into sickles.—12. Wounds inflicted through the tongue must be healed by asking forgiveness; this does not extend to excess in correction before superiors.—13. From whom superiors should not ask forgiveness, though they must always seek it from God.—14. One love is carnal, another spiritual: the cause of every good and evil; among religious persons it must be spiritual.—15. No one is without love: what kind ought to be directed toward God, oneself, and one’s neighbour.—16. Self-love has now degenerated from its state of innocence. Let it be devout, just, and sober.—17. Spiritual love is like a paradise pleasing to God and useful to human beings; it springs from four rivers.—18. It is the form, beauty, and perfection of the virtues; variously shadowed forth in Scripture, gathering many into one.—19. The combined effects of charity, which more clearly elucidate its character.

### I

There are many kinds of sins, dearest brothers, by which that ancient and wily enemy of humankind is accustomed to ensnare the human soul, cast it down from the citadel of virtues, and prostrate it in the depths of vices. Various, I say, are the forms of shameful deeds and crimes by which, worn down by his destructive suggestion, shaken by pleasure, overcome by consent, cast down by action, bound by habit, miserable man is subjected to the devil; and through the sickness of fault falls away from spiritual health—which purity of conscience and integrity of holy conduct confer and preserve—into the death of punishment.

Yet among all these evils, in which lie the cause and occasion of human ruin, the horror of discord and contention holds a great, indeed almost the highest, place in wickedness. It infects the wretched mind with its deadly contagion and, briefly speaking, entirely empties it of every good and fills it with evil. It clouds all spiritual serenity in the heart, darkens its brightness, changes loveliness into horror, sweetness into bitterness, rest into disturbance, love into hatred, peace into strife, concord into self-defence, kindness into malice, and finally life into death. O evil, worst of all evils! Compared with it, even other evils are in some manner good. Blessed Augustine wished to exclude this detestable evil from among us when he said:

> **[Note: Col. 0547D. Rule, chapter II, on avoiding strife.]**

### II

“Have either no quarrels among yourselves, or end them as quickly as possible, lest anger grow into hatred, make a beam out of a splinter, and make the soul a murderer. For thus you read: ‘Whoever hates his brother is a murderer’” (1 John 3:15).

How salutary is this exhortation: “Have either no quarrels”! Yet this belongs to few people, especially in this miserable age, when, owing to its innate weakness, humanity is so prone and inclined toward the evil of discord. The human tongue is always on slippery ground and inclined to fall. It defiles our whole body and sets ablaze the wheel of our birth; no human being can tame it. But “whoever does not stumble in speech is a perfect man” (Jas. 3:2).

Why does it so often happen that people rush into quarrels? Because, while they do not restrain their tongues, they proceed as far as harm. Since Saint Augustine knew how difficult it was always wholly to avoid quarrels, he took greater care to admonish us to end them quickly than presumptuously to command us to avoid them altogether. Therefore, he did not categorically command us to have no quarrels; rather, he spoke disjunctively: “Have either no quarrels, or end them as quickly as possible.” The holy man wished, I think, to exhort us to have no quarrels at all; but because, considering human weakness, he recognized this as very arduous, he admonished us at least to end them quickly.

Thus he says: “Have either no quarrels, or end them as quickly as possible.” It is as though he said more plainly: Either have no quarrels at all among yourselves; or, because to ascend to this degree belongs not to many but to few, not to the weak but to the strong, not to beginners but to the perfect, end them as quickly as possible, so that you may at least hasten to the end of an evil which you cannot wholly avoid, lest you fall into some worse evil, or into evil in its entirety. [The Latin is defective here: “in pejorem aliam vel in totum malum deesse videtur.”] Therefore he says, “as quickly as possible, lest anger grow into hatred.” For we certainly often see that anger grows into hatred in the person who does not swiftly impose an end upon quarrels.

### III

In this connection one must consider how necessary for everyone wishing to possess peace is the virtue of silence. It both avoids disturbances and preserves peace, containing within itself the causes and occasions by which the horror of strife may be avoided, the gentleness of peace attained, and, once attained, retained. For, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “He who imposes silence upon a fool calms anger” (Prov. 26:10). Rightly did holy David set a guard upon his mouth when the sinner stood against him: “I was dumb and silent, even from good things” (Ps. 38:2–3).

Anger indeed grows into hatred when we do not swiftly end quarrels, because when we despise small things we rush into greater ones (Ecclus. 19:1), and while we neglect to prevent an illness, we often rush onward even into death itself. Anger is like a kind of illness; for its full and perfect form, hatred, is death. Hatred is anger grown old and hardened, as it were, into a certain permanence, so that it can scarcely be ended and scarcely dissolved. From this destructive mother is often born the horror of deadly despair, which belongs to that blasphemy of which the Lord says that it “will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32). This indeed is the sin unto death, because it lasts until death and ought not to be forgiven before death, since it cannot be ended before death. And if it is not ended before death, then neither after death; for if a criminal sin liable to eternal damnation is not abandoned before death, forgiveness of it is vainly sought after death.

See to what great evil a person comes when he does not swiftly end quarrels: anger grows into hatred—that is, an agitation of the mind becomes inveterate anger and has now frozen into a very enduring motion of fury. “And make a beam out of a splinter,” he says. As great as the difference between a beam and a splinter, so great is that between hatred and anger. When anger passes into hatred, the splinter is, as it were, changed into a beam. For hatred, which is anger grown old, acquires from malicious age such destructive strength that what, while it was simple anger, might have been called a splinter, can now rightly be called a beam because insensible hardness and persistence have been added. And while a splinter clouds the eye of the mind, a beam utterly blinds it.

### IV

See: when quarrels are not ended as quickly as possible, anger grows into hatred, a beam is made from a splinter, a pardonable offence passes into criminal sin, and a simple illness into death itself. “And make the soul a murderer.” For murder is in a certain manner perpetrated before God’s eyes when one’s neighbour is held in hatred. Therefore, when anger grows into hatred and the soul consequently becomes a murderer, because another’s death—whether spiritual or bodily—is desired, the person who desires it is held guilty of that desired death by the just and terrible judgment of almighty God, on account of that very malicious will.

To establish the truth of his statement, Augustine adduces the authority of Holy Scripture and says: “For thus you read: ‘Whoever hates his brother is a murderer’” (1 John 3:15). Certainly, whoever hates is a murderer, because the death you desired in your mind, you have already inflicted before God. See how many, what kinds, and how great are the evils for which quarrels are occasions and causes. They bring such great destruction not merely because they exist, but because they are not ended as swiftly as possible.

Therefore, my brothers, flee always and everywhere with all diligence these dreadful thunderclaps. When they crash upon the ears with terrifying din, they themselves undermine the very depths of minds to their roots, shatter them piecemeal, cut and wound them bloodily, scatter and dissipate them, burn them down to ashes, and utterly reduce them to nothing. Woe to those who love quarrels and contentions, and nourish them by loving them! I tell you, my brothers, I do not know what can, in a certain respect, be worse among religious men. In a special sense, it seems to me, those who delight in engaging in quarrels, creating tumult through contention, and sowing discord among brothers are children of the devil. Finally, if what Solomon said is true, God detests them (Prov. 5:12). Certainly wolves among lambs and these persons among simple brothers belong together and must be referred to the same end. As serpents among eels, so are such people in the fellowship of brothers.

[Col. 0551A] When they have been seized by this detestable frenzy, cast far from themselves and outside themselves, you may see their eyes blaze, their faces grow pale, their expressions tremble, their lips foam, their eyebrows rise, their foreheads stretch, their noses contract, their heads shake, their mouths twist, their tongues stammer, insults thunder, threats rain down, hailstorms of words fall, hands clap, and, finally, their whole bodily bearing become disordered. Struck and striking; shaken and shaking; stirred and stirring; disturbed and disturbing; embittered and embittering; inflamed and inflaming; fed on gall and feeding others on it; intoxicated with vinegar and intoxicating others; in short, lethally infected with every kind of malice and infecting others. So long as they have present someone with whom to quarrel, they neither wish nor are able to end the quarrel, like untamable horses whose course is brought to an end not by the hands of those restraining them but by exhaustion itself.

### V

But you, brothers, not so. Not so, I say, you—not so; rather, always put this abominable and detestable evil farther and farther away from yourselves. You, I say, who have learned, not so much by hearing as by experience, and indeed continually, “How good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1). As your Father admonishes you, either have no quarrels or end them as quickly as possible, lest anger grow into hatred, make a beam out of a splinter, and make the soul a murderer.

But if perhaps someone among you—as sometimes happens and as can usually be avoided only with difficulty—has in some unjust way disturbed his brother, let him grant himself absolutely no peace, no rest for an hour or a moment, until, by every means he can and ought to use according to God, he has fully calmed and reconciled him and restored him to his former serenity. Hence it follows: “Whoever has injured another by an insult, a curse, or even the accusation of a crime should remember to remedy as quickly as possible, by satisfaction, what he has done.” And rightly, “as quickly as possible,” lest we allow any delay to postpone satisfaction. He commands quarrels to be ended as quickly as possible, and commands what has been injured to be remedied by satisfaction as quickly as possible, lest here the anger of the injured person pass into hatred, just as there it was said, “lest anger grow into hatred.”

For the injured person often chews over within himself, in the bitterest recollection, after the time of the injury itself has passed, what harsh and bitter words were hurled against him. He represents to himself in a sad and horrible image the absent person who hurled them; and if present, he sees him with blazing eyes, wrinkled brow, raised eyebrows, and threatening expression. Though he is silent, much speech resounds within him in the court of his heart; he turns over and turns again what he has heard; he asks and hears—he asks without speaking and hears without hearing. No one occupied and held by these inward tumults has leisure to devote himself to spiritual practice. He cannot pray purely, read diligently, meditate cleanly, speak anything gently, do anything useful, or even fully attend to his body’s needs: he cannot eat or rest; he has no repose of mind whatever, nor bodily comfort. Everything he sees displeases him; nothing he hears pleases him; everything is horror and loathing to him. Neither the presence of any good nor the absence of any evil can avail him, until the one who injured him humbles himself and gives full satisfaction.

But when full satisfaction has been made to him, then, as shadows vanish when the sun shines, so all these evils depart when serenity returns. I do not know what sort of mind a person can have who is a cause and occasion for his brother to swallow so deep an abyss of malice. Certainly, anyone through whom so many, such great, and such kinds of evils happen must have not a good but a seared conscience. For “woe to him through whom the offence comes” (Matt. 18:6–7). Certainly, if He who cannot possibly lie has spoken truly, “it would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea” (ibid.).

### VI

See why our Father has commanded the person who has caused injury to strive as quickly as possible to remedy what he has done: namely, lest, if satisfaction is delayed, the fury of the injured person extend itself without limit. It should be noted that he expressly specified three things which he admonished us to avoid in injuring a brother: insult, cursing, and accusation of a crime. Each of these is very serious. For it is an exceedingly grave fault when someone insults his brother, because “whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22). Then there is cursing, because “the revilers will not inherit the kingdom of God.” Thus both those who insult and those who curse should know that they are liable to great guilt: of the former it is said that they will be condemned; of the latter, that they will not be saved. And who does not know that accusing a brother of a crime is a great sin?

Rightly, then, the one who has injured another is commanded to strive to remedy by satisfaction as quickly as possible what he has done—he, namely, who has injured someone by insult, curse, or accusation of a crime—so that, the more dangerous the wounds he has incurred, the more swiftly and diligently he may seek to heal them by applying the remedy of satisfaction. Let him not delay to apply medicine to the wounded person; let him not neglect effective treatment, lest delay perhaps bring putrefaction to the wounds, and negligence bring death to the wounded person—something that must be carefully guarded against.

“And the one who has been injured should forgive without dispute.” The injured person, he says, should forgive without dispute, provided the injurer promptly remedies what he has done. And it is “without dispute” because forgiveness is not complete when there is dispute in the forgiver. The injured person fully forgives what the injurer has inflicted when, after forgiveness, he does not in any respect love him less than he loved him before the injury [the printed reading has “before forgiveness”; perhaps read “before injury”]. For if he takes away anything from his former affection, he still keeps something, as it were, within himself and does not forgive it.

Therefore, let the one remedy what he has done by satisfaction as quickly as possible, and let the other likewise forgive without dispute: so that the former may repent from the depths of his heart of every injury he has done, never presuming to injure again; and that the latter may fully pardon one who repents in this manner, retaining in his heart absolutely no less love toward him on that account. But if they have injured one another, they should remit their debts to one another because of your prayers, which, certainly, ought to be the holier the more frequent you have them. This is fitting: just as neither abstained from injuring the other, so neither should fail the other in mutual forgiveness. “Because of your prayers,” he says: so that, as they mutually forgive their debts, your prayers may assist them in forgiving and in deserving to obtain forgiveness from the Lord. And it is rightly said of these prayers that the more frequent we have them, the holier we ought to have them, because their frequency itself should also confer much spiritual holiness.

### VII

It follows: “But he is better who, although he is often tempted by anger, nevertheless hastens to obtain forgiveness from the person whom he knows he has wronged, than one who becomes angry more slowly and is slower to bend himself to ask forgiveness.”

Although it is not good to fall even once, nevertheless it is less evil to fall even more often, provided that a persevering rising again follows as often as the fall that is eventually to cease comes first, than to be cast down once in such a way that one never afterward happens to rise. We can and ought to understand this of the two persons proposed here: namely, the one who, tempted by the instability of his own weakness, is quickly stirred and, humbly recognizing his fault, quickly humbles himself; and the one who more slowly assents to agitation and more slowly submits himself to humility.

It should be noted, however, that in this place blessed Augustine seems to set forth two kinds of angry persons: one, those who are indeed quickly stirred but quickly humble themselves; the other, those who, on the contrary, are slowly provoked to anger and slowly incline to humility. Of these two kinds, he declares the second worse than the first. In the fifth book of the *Moralia*, blessed Gregory also treats these two, and expressly does not omit to treat two others: one, which is quickly stirred and slowly humbled; the other, which conversely grows angry slowly and inclines more quickly to gentleness. Of these latter two, the first is far worse than the second, just as, of the former two, the second is worse than the first. He says of them:

> **[Note: Col. 0553D. St Gregory, *Moralia*, book V, chapter 32.]**
>
> “It should be known that anger kindles some people more quickly and leaves them more easily; others indeed it stirs more slowly but holds more harshly. Some are like burning reeds: while they make a noise with their voices, they give forth, as it were, certain sounds of their own burning; they indeed produce flames quickly, but immediately grow cold into ashes. Others, however, not unlike heavier and harder wood, receive kindling slowly, but, once kindled, are extinguished with greater difficulty; and because they rouse themselves to harshness more slowly, they preserve longer the fire of their fury. Others—which is worse—both receive the flames of anger more quickly and lay them aside more slowly; while some receive them slowly and lose them more quickly. In these four ways the reader plainly recognizes both that the last approaches the good of tranquillity more closely than the first, and that in evil the third exceeds the second.”

We have recalled these things to your mind so that you may not be inflexible in forgiving one who, although quickly stirred, nevertheless quickly humbles himself to repentance, knowing him to be better than one who becomes angry more slowly and is slower to incline himself to ask forgiveness.

### VIII

But whoever never wishes to ask forgiveness, or does not ask from the heart, is in the monastery without purpose, even if he is not expelled from it. We are also in the monastery for this: daily—indeed, continually, by night as well as day—to offer our sacrifices to almighty God. But what sacrifices are these, if not our holy practices? Whatever good we do—whether we persist in the obligation of silence, or loosen our tongue into speech for our neighbour’s edification; whether we attend to reading, devote ourselves to meditation, give labour to necessary work, devote ourselves to prayer, and especially stand shattered and melted before the holy altars themselves—belongs to our spiritual sacrifice, which we offer to the almighty Father through His Son Jesus Christ, our only Lord, in the Holy Spirit of them both.

Yet neither this sacrifice nor any other sacrifice of this kind is accepted unless discord has first been expelled from the heart. And you do not drive it out unless you humbly ask forgiveness from the one whom you injured. For you are told to leave your gift before the altar and, before offering it to God, to go and be reconciled to your brother (Matt. 5:24).

The Psalmist’s prayer on this matter is as follows: “Deal graciously, O Lord, in your good will with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built” (Ps. 50:20). God graciously deals with Zion in His good will when He deigns to visit with the favour of His grace the mind to which it belongs now to see Him “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12). And this is done so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built: that is, so that virtues may be constructed in our inner person, by which contemplation of true peace is guarded when fortified, and fortified when guarded. For, as you know, Jerusalem signifies the vision of peace.

Therefore, from Him who is the Giver of every good, we ought to seek from the depths of our hearts the visitation of inward grace, so that we may be able to keep peace unblemished and inviolate in our mind toward God and toward our neighbour: “Deal graciously, O Lord, in your good will with Zion, that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.” And the Psalmist added: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and whole burnt-offerings; then they will lay calves upon your altar” (Ps. 50:21).

In the ancient law, it was called a sacrifice when animals were offered; an offering when something from dry goods happened to be offered; and a whole burnt-offering when the whole thing was burned upon the altar. To speak a little more fully of their distinction: sacrifice seems to belong to those who mortify in themselves, by the Spirit, the deeds of the flesh, and kill with the yoke of continence whatever carnal thing within them unlawfully desires to live. Offering belongs to those who always stretch forth toward inward things, discern and choose better things, are strengthened from virtue to virtue by the Spirit of God in their inner person, and by increasingly spiritual conduct press onward upon the perfect path of holy newness. But whole burnt-offering especially denotes those who, having overcome unlawful motions of the flesh, trampled completely underfoot earthly desires, and been borne aloft upon the wings of heavenly desires, have already reached the summit of perfection; who, so to speak, hold themselves wholly ablaze in love for their Creator alone and are united to Him by the tenacious, indeed indissoluble, glue of true love. The first, therefore, are beginners; the second, those making progress; the third, the perfect. The first walk on level ground; the second climb upon the slope [Latin printed “olivo,” apparently for “clivo”]; the third fly at the summit.

### IX

We also lay calves upon the altar when we mortify within ourselves wanton impulses with the knife of maturity, in imitation of Christ. But when we have sacrifice, offering, and whole burnt-offerings, calves will often not be lacking which we must lay upon the altar. For when we subject within ourselves carnal motions, when we make great progress in spiritual conduct, when we think we have attained the very summit of perfection, we sometimes sense certain insolent impulses of wantonness breaking forth in the secret places of our heart, through the temptation of pleasure, curiosity, or certainly vanity. Like Abraham driving away birds descending upon the carcasses (Gen. 15:11), we must subject these impulses to the dominion of the mind by a certain spiritual command, animated by the imitation of Christ.

But what do you suppose is meant by holy David’s saying that the Lord will then accept sacrifice of righteousness, offerings, and whole burnt-offerings, and that calves will then be laid upon the altar (Ps. 50:21), when God has first graciously dealt with Zion in His good will so that Jerusalem’s walls may be built? Surely this relates to God’s command that, leaving our gift before the altar, we should first go and be reconciled to our brother, and then come and offer our gift (Matt. 5:24). Therefore, brothers, since we are in this monastery in order to offer such sacrifices to almighty God in holy conduct, and God does not accept them if we are not reconciled to our brothers, so that—as we have now explained—He may then accept sacrifice of righteousness, offerings, and whole burnt-offerings, and calves may then be laid upon the altar, when He graciously deals with Zion in His good will in order that Jerusalem’s walls may be built: what follows except what blessed Augustine says in this place? Namely, that the person who is not reconciled with his brother, even after humbly asking forgiveness, is in the monastery without purpose, even if he is not expelled from it.

“He,” he says, “is in the monastery without purpose, even if he is not expelled from it, who does not wish to ask forgiveness, or does not ask it from the heart.” In these words he leaves us to understand two evils: the hardness of obstinacy and the duplicity of pretence. “Who does not wish to ask forgiveness”: there is obstinacy. “Or does not ask from the heart”: there too is pretence. Thus it is evident from these words that both the obstinate and pretenders are in the monastery without purpose, because they accomplish no special work of salvation, being rendered hard by insensibility or false by duplicity.

What then follows? Certainly, it is necessary that we wish to ask forgiveness and ask it from the heart, lest we be in the monastery without purpose, even if we are not expelled from it, should obstinacy render us inflexible or pretence make us double-minded. See, brothers, into what kinds, how many, and how great evils we rush when we do not avoid the harsh words that provoke quarrels. Hence also follows the salutary exhortation: “Therefore refrain from harsh words.” Certainly this is good, because, as Solomon says, “A gentle answer breaks anger, and a harsh word stirs up fury” (Prov. 15:1). Avoid, brothers, harsh and bitter words; speak pleasant ones and make sweet words your practice. Remember that it is written: “A sweet word multiplies friends and softens enemies” (Ecclus. 6:5).

### X

Let there be no disturbers of peace among you, no dividers of unity, people disturbed themselves and disturbing others, “sowing discord among brothers” (Prov. 6:19). God not only hates such persons; His soul also detests them, because they eagerly seek to pour into others the deadly poison with which they themselves are swollen, not only by the example of their depraved conduct, but also through the suggestion of pernicious counsel.

But you, brothers, have not so learned Christ, if indeed you have heard Him and have been taught in Him, as truth is in Jesus (Eph. 4:20). “Peace be with you” is the special word of our Peace-maker Himself. “I have spoken these things,” He says, “so that you may have peace in me” (John 16:33). Again, He says: “Have peace among yourselves” (2 Cor. 13:11). “Whoever he may be, the one who troubles you will bear the judgment” (Gal. 5:10); and, “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2:8). This is the voice of the Lord speaking in the Apostle and the Prophet. Therefore have the same mind: have peace, and the God of peace and love will be with you (2 Cor. 13:11).

Let every one of you guard in every way against injuring another, showing himself diligent “to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3), and, if possible, so far as it depends upon him, living at peace with all people. For just as, on the Lord’s testimony, peacemakers are called children of God (Matt. 5:9), so I boldly say that those who sow discord are worthy to be called children of the devil. Therefore refrain from harsh words.

XI. May that prophecy be fulfilled in you which runs thus: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles” (Isa. 2:4). And he added: “Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they be trained any more for war” (ibid.). Sword and spear are weapons, and they inflict wounds; but ploughshare and sickle are instruments greatly necessary for human use and serve for the nourishment of humankind. Yet, although sword and spear are weapons, we strike at close quarters with a sword, while with a spear we reach one far away. Likewise, although ploughshare and sickle are very necessary implements, with the ploughshare [Col. 0557A] we dig up the earth in ploughing, while with the sickle we cut the crop in harvesting.

And what, do we suppose, are swords and spears but the harsh asperities of words and their rough hardnesses, disturbing peace in the hearts of those who hear them? Did not holy David understand this, when he declares the tongue of the children of men to be a sharp sword (Ps. 56:5)? Thus you strike your neighbour with a sword—indeed, a very sharp one—when, puffed up with the swelling of pride, you attack him with a reproachful and harsh word. But “turn your sword into its sheath” (Matt. 26:52): turn the blade upon yourself, rebuking and accusing yourself; consider rather the beam that is in your own eye than the speck that is in your brother’s eye (Matt. 7:3); and with the sharp point of self-accusation dig up your own inward parts—you who, angry with your neighbour, used even to prick his outward parts.

But with spears you touch those who are far away when you do not allow the absent to remain undisturbed by the words of your detraction. You make yourself hateful to God when, against the Law, you presume to curse one who is deaf (Lev. 19:14); and you show yourself worthy of ruin when you make contributions and occupy yourself with poisonous draughts, and even provide meat for eating (Prov. 23:21). But embrace both your neighbour’s good and your own in the arms of love, and consider the reward awaiting you in the future for this goodwill. If you strive to act diligently, you will surely change your spears into sickles: by persevering in every way in blessings both toward your neighbour and toward yourself, you recognize that from blessings you will reap eternal life (Gal. 4:8); and, ceasing from disparagement of your neighbour, you devote yourself to those useful services of speech for which you may be worthy in the future to receive the reward of eternal refreshment.

Let not, I beseech you, nation lift sword against nation among you; rather, spare one another harsh words. You do this when, as the Apostle admonishes, not defending yourselves, you give place to wrath (Rom. 12:19). Nor be trained for war: spare one another harsh words. You certainly do this when, anticipating one another in honour and, in humility, esteeming one another higher in spirit, you do not become desirous of vain glory, provoking one another and envying one another. How salutary, therefore, is this saying: “Spare one another harsh words.” And if it should happen that you utter harsh words, [Col. 0557D] hear what blessed Augustine adds.

XII. “If such words have been sent forth from your mouth, do not be reluctant to bring forth remedies from that same mouth from which the wounds were made.” That is: in humbly asking forgiveness, let those who in stirring up and heaping up have uttered harsh things utter gentle things. For what else is a sharp arrow, by whose discharge a wound is inflicted, than a harsh word, by whose utterance offence is caused? For the bow is, as it were, drawn when the mouth is opened; and the indiscriminately flying arrow strikes and wounds when the tongue, moving rashly, rebukes and grieves its neighbour. But the remedies that restore these wounds to health are sweet words, which drive offence from a brother’s heart.

Yet when the necessity of discipline compels you to speak harsh words in restraining conduct, even if you feel that you have exceeded the measure, you are not required to ask forgiveness of your subjects, lest, among those who ought to be subject, the authority of governing be broken by too great a display of humility. It seems, so far as we may infer from these words, that what was said concerning the asking of forgiveness must be understood thus: not that prelates should ask forgiveness of subjects, but that inferiors should ask it of superiors, and equals also of equals. Prelates themselves, in order to bind the conduct of subjects under the rule of uprightness, are often compelled to utter stern words of reproof; and perhaps they utter much harsher words than they ought. This must be overlooked in them because they ardently love those whom they so rebuke.

As Ecclesiastes says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep” (Eccl. 12:11). Because, as their office requires, they are solicitous for them with sincere affection, they cannot in any way calmly see in them anything by which they may either offend God or incur some danger or loss in their souls. Therefore they do not dare spare their tongue when they see them sinning, sounding the trumpet so that they may perceive that the sword which comes to take away life is near. They know that the Lord was angry with Eli because he knew that his sons acted unworthily and did not rebuke them (1 Sam. 2:22). Hence it very often happens that, while they love greatly, they sometimes prolong reproof even to excessive harshness and exceed measure in correcting.

Hence blessed Gregory also says: “It often happens to great teachers that, the more they burn with lofty charity, the more they exaggerate the measure of correction, and the tongue says something that it ought not; because love inflames the mind as much as it ought.” But when this happens to them, those who are subject ought not to require them to ask forgiveness. And this is so lest, while the meekness of humility is displayed too greatly in this matter, reverence for paternal authority should become less among them. Therefore, in order that undiminished reverence may be preserved for prelates who preside in God’s place, discipline of correction must indeed be administered to subjects when they have perhaps sinned; yet forgiveness must not be requested of them even when the prelates have exceeded the measure. [Col. 0558D] I say that discipline must be administered, because there are certain subjects in whom, unless discipline is first sown, reverence will not afterward be reaped.

XIII. Nevertheless, I say this not generally of all, but of certain persons only—and only of those who are very imperfect and immature. When they see their prelate humble himself somewhat and make himself common with them, they disdain to reverence him; and as he is in his own eyes, so he is in theirs. But wise and good disciples, the more humble they see their prelate, the more they reverence him; and the more common they find him, the more humbly they honour him. If prelates should sometimes ask forgiveness of subjects such as these, they ought not, it seems to me, be called very blameworthy; for this humility is a great cause and occasion for the authority of governing to increase more and more.

Yet they are not required to ask forgiveness of those subjects whom they know to be of such a sort that, the more humbled they perceive them to be, the more contemptible they regard them in their own eyes—lest, among those who ought to be subject, governing authority be broken by too great a preservation of humility. Nevertheless, forgiveness must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with how great a goodwill you love those whom you rebuke more than is just. It can sometimes happen that they rebuke them more than is just, but nevertheless love them with no less goodwill. Therefore forgiveness must be sought from him to whom the sincere love that burns secretly toward subjects is not unknown. [Col. 0559A] He certainly grants it all the more quickly and pardons the fault all the more readily as he recognizes more clearly that it was committed for the sake of correction and through the mediating fervour of love.

That blessed Augustine here directs prelates, when they happen to exceed measure in correction, to seek forgiveness from the Lord of all is also contained in the ordinance of the Law, which reads thus: “If anyone goes simply with his friend into the forest to cut wood, and the axe slips from his hand, and the iron, falling from the handle, strikes his friend and kills him, he shall flee to one of the aforesaid cities and live” (Deut. 19:5).

What is it for someone to go with his friend into the forest, except for a prelate, as blessed Gregory expounds it, to involve himself with his subject in examining that subject’s sins?

[Note: [Col. 0559] BLESSED GREGORY’S DISCUSSION OF EXCESS IN CORRECTION.]

What is it to cut wood simply, except to cut away the offender’s vices with a devout intention? What is it for the axe to escape the hand, except to exceed the measure of rebuke? What, indeed, is it for the iron to leap from the handle, except for a harsher word to proceed from correction? And what is it to kill the friend, except to destroy the hearer by the painful distress inflicted by the spirit of charity? Finally, what is it for him who struck to flee to one of the three cities and live, except for the prelate who exceeded measure in correcting to rely on faith, hope, and charity, and, having sought forgiveness from the Lord, obtain remission from him? Therefore, what it is in the Law for the one who struck to flee to one of the three cities and live is this in the Rule of our Father: that the person whom the necessity of discipline, in restraining conduct, compelled to speak harsh words—and who thus exceeded the measure—should seek forgiveness from the Lord of all.

XIV. For love among you ought to be not carnal but spiritual. Just as no virtue is greater than love when it is in a good person and directed toward the good, so no vice is worse than it when it is in an evil person and directed toward evil. For there is good love and evil love. As the former is the cause and occasion of every good thing, so the latter is the cause and occasion of every evil. Through the former, evil being abandoned, everything good is admitted; through the latter, good being abandoned, everything evil is admitted. The latter is carnal; the former spiritual. Carnal love suggests and fosters what is pleasing to the flesh; spiritual love teaches through understanding and fulfils through affection what is useful to the spirit.

The former belongs to carnal persons; the latter [Col. 0560A] to spiritual persons. Those who indulge the flesh in its unlawful desires also love themselves carnally; but those who, mortifying the deeds of the flesh by the spirit, seek a perfected spirit in the purpose of holiness, likewise devote a spiritual affection to themselves. Such indeed ought we to be: the sublimity of our order proclaims it, the humility of our habit invites it, and the indissoluble bond of our profession compels it. And because our Father recognized that we ought to be such, he says that love among us ought to be not carnal but spiritual.

But what, do we suppose, is meant by the fact that, after he asserted that we greatly love those whom we often rebuke more than is just, he immediately said that love among us ought to be not carnal but spiritual? For he first said: “Forgiveness must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with how great a goodwill you love even those whom you perhaps rebuke more than is just.” Then he immediately added: “For love among you ought to be not carnal but spiritual.” It is as though this commonly belongs to the spiritual love that ought to exist among us: that we love with great goodwill those whom we perhaps rebuke more than is just.

And indeed it is so; for because we love greatly, we rebuke greatly. And often, while we rebuke greatly, it happens that even in the reproof itself we pass beyond measure. Thus the spiritual love that exists among us is the cause and occasion of our exceeding measure in correction. “He knows,” he says, “with how great a goodwill you love even those whom you perhaps rebuke more than is just. For love among you ought to be not carnal but spiritual.” It is as though he said: God knows that it is not strange for you perhaps to rebuke more than is just those whom you love with great goodwill, since the love among you is not carnal, which it ought not to be, but spiritual, which it ought to be.

Carnal persons rarely rebuke more than is just those whom they love carnally, because they do not rebuke them at all. They favour and foster them in their perverse actions; and the wicked deeds that they do please them, because they see those whom they love doing them. Hence they receive them with flattering adulations, not rebuke them with harsh denunciations. The cause and occasion of this dreadful evil is the carnal love that exists among them.

XV. But among you, brethren, love ought to be spiritual. When it burns most ardently [Col. 0560D] in the heart, it is accustomed sometimes even toward those whom it especially—indeed, uniquely—embraces to exceed measure in correction. But because Sacred Scripture is accustomed to commend this eminent virtue of which we speak very highly among all other eminent virtues—indeed, above all the rest—it is pleasant to treat it somewhat more fully and to show how it is necessary for our salvation.

Without love the mind cannot in any way be human; but let it carefully attend to what it loves. Among the other things it loves—indeed, before all the things a human being can love—it ought to love God, its neighbour, and itself: these three. God, as its good, which it ought to enjoy; itself, as that which ought to enjoy; and its neighbour, as the one with whom it ought to enjoy. The Lord cries out through his Law: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:5). He says further: “You shall love your neighbour,” and adds, “as yourself” (Luke 10:27). Yet nowhere is it found written: “You shall love yourself.”

Nevertheless, a person received the command to love himself when he received the command to love his God. For he loves himself when he loves his good. And what else is his good but his God? For God is he from whom a person has that he exists, and in whom he has that he may exist well and blessedly. But it is not simply said, “You shall love yourself,” lest, if he received a special command, he should think that he ought to have a carnal affection toward himself. For there are two things in a human being: soul and body, flesh and spirit. A person would love his flesh even if he had been commanded not to love it; for the constant experience of us all tells us that what the Apostle says is true: “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:29). And because it is not much merely not to hate it, he adds: “But he nourishes and cherishes it” (ibid.).

Certainly no one can ever hate his own flesh; and, because this seems too little, no one can fail to love his own flesh. Therefore, since through the irresistible force of nature—as was said long before our time—the love of his own flesh was sufficiently present in a human being, he did not need to be bound by a command to possess it, but rather tempered by admonition lest he possess it excessively. Hence the Apostle, while leaving it implicitly understood in his preaching that care for the flesh may lawfully be given in necessary matters, openly forbade it in desires: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14). What he knew to be superfluous, he cut off; what was necessary, he allowed.

XVI. In this first respect which I set forth, a human being was accustomed, before he sinned in Paradise, to care for his flesh. But in this second condition in which he now is—if indeed it ought to be called a condition, where he has fallen through sin, rather than a ruin—he consents to care for that same flesh when, tempted by his own desire, he is drawn away and enticed. Before sin, indeed, he loved his flesh through natural affection, but only for necessity; after sin, however, through the vice of concupiscence, he is now accustomed to love it unto superfluity. Therefore in this matter he has no need of a command, where he is voluntary even if he is not moved; rather, he needs prohibition and admonition, lest he rush too headlong even if no one restrains him.

If, then, love of the flesh was not to be set in a command—since it was more evident that it would be sufficiently possessed even if not commanded, and would perhaps very often be possessed too much if it were not moderated even in the respect in which it is excessive—then love of the soul, as we have already said, is understood in the command that a person is ordered to love his God. Let a person therefore love his flesh, but love it with discernment. He loves himself and his neighbour when he loves his God. Thus this threefold love must be possessed by us: toward ourselves, toward our neighbour, and toward our God. Let us love ourselves, but as regards the flesh, temperately; our neighbour justly; God devoutly; [Col. 0562A] so that, according to the Apostle’s admonition, “we may live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age” (Tit. 2:12). Thus we may securely await the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God, if we neither love ourselves superfluously, nor our neighbour unjustly, nor God lukewarmly. O happy race of human beings, if the love by which heaven is governed governs your minds!

XVII. Let us therefore examine our love, brethren most dear to us in the Lord; let us bring our affection into agreement; let us love one another in God; let us also love one another for God’s sake. This is the way: let us walk in it and turn neither to the right nor to the left (Isa. 30:21). Let us always carry about a love that is sincere, steadfast, and universal, striving with all diligence: first, that it may exist; second, that it may grow; [Col. 0562B] third, that it may remain—that it may be acquired, that once acquired it may increase more and more, and that once increased it may be retained. For what use is the first unless the second and third are present?

For this reason God placed Adam in the Paradise of delight: that he might cultivate and keep it. And what, in a moral sense, can Paradise be understood to mean except the holy affection of sincere charity: beautiful, pleasant, and, above all the delights of this life—if indeed there are any delights without it? This is the place in which God placed “every tree beautiful to the sight and sweet for food” (Gen. 2:9), because every thought conceived in our heart by the infusion of the charity of the Holy Spirit is sweet before God in its affection and beautiful before our neighbour in its effect. There it delights God through the purity of inward affection; [Col. 0562C] here it stirs up the neighbour through the fruitfulness of excellent action.

This also is that Paradise to irrigate which a river goes forth from the place of delight, and then divides into four heads. For from God, who is the place of true and unfailing delight, proceeds for the sanctification of the affection of charity that saving command which is divided in four ways: three pertaining to the love of God and one to that of one’s neighbour. For a person is commanded to love his God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength; but his neighbour as himself. Therefore God placed Adam in Paradise also for this purpose, that he might cultivate and keep it: because we ought not only to strive that the affection of charity may be in us, but also that it may grow and remain. It grows when the one placed in Paradise cultivates it; it remains when he keeps it.

XVIII. This charity of which we speak is so great and such that it holds primacy among all other virtues. Without it, other virtues may indeed be called virtues, but falsely; they cannot in any way truly be virtues. According to Paul, this is “the bond of perfection” (Col. 3:14); this surpasses the tongues of human beings and angels; this exceeds all knowledge and all understanding of mysteries; this even surpasses faith that removes mountains. Without it, not even the distribution of all one’s possessions as food for the poor is profitable; without it, even the burning of the body may indeed have punishment, but can have no merit or reward at all (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

This is the tree of life in Paradise (Gen. 2:9); this is the unity of the cubit at the completion and summit of Noah’s ark (Gen. 6:16); this is the ladder shown to him while he slept on his journey (Gen. 28:12); this is the oil poured upon the stone which he set up as a memorial (ibid., v. 18); this, since it would take too long to go through each instance, is Christ’s special command (John 15:12); this is the fulfilment of the Law (Rom. 13:10). This is the love which ought especially to exist among us, of which our Father says that it ought to be not carnal but spiritual. For it is not carnal but spiritual. In many bodies it makes one heart and one soul. See how many bodies we behold here? Yet there must be one spirit.

Know that by “one spirit” I mean one and the same consent: willing, together and toward the same end, what is good according to God, and refusing, likewise together, what is evil according to him. To this one spirit also belongs that “one” of which holy David says: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in one” (Ps. 132:1). Indeed, the brethren are many, but they dwell in one. And how good and pleasant is this when those dwelling in one themselves become one! For when they give themselves wholly to one another from the whole of themselves, as we remember having said elsewhere; when none of them belongs to himself, but each belongs to the other; when they fully will the same concerning the same thing, and fully refuse the same concerning the same thing; when none of them prefers, or even compares with another, any present thing; when none is disgusted with another in anything, but in all things and in every respect they relate to one another with goodwill and charity, as Marcus Tullius says, [Note: [Col. 0563D] CICERO, *For Laelius*.] and with the fullest harmony—what, I ask, among these present things can be seen more beautiful by the human soul, heard more delightful, smelled more sweetly, tasted more savoury, or touched more fittingly, so that I may seem to omit none of the five senses?

XIX. O sweet loveliness! O lovely sweetness! Flowing abundantly and boiling up from the depths, springing at the surface and breathing fragrance on every side: with steadfast faith, sure hope, true simplicity, and undivided innocence; anxiously longing for the beloved while absent and joyfully receiving him when he comes; caressing him while present, neither without the reverence of maturity nor without the maturity of reverence; accompanying him with grief as he departs, awaiting him while he delays, longing for him when he will come, and weeping with inconsolable sorrow when he will not come; concealing from him no secret, so far as lies in itself, but longing to pour out all of itself; wishing to enjoy no good without him and shrinking from no adversity for his sake; desiring no prosperous condition without his participation; despising pride and envy; casting away anger and sloth; knowing neither pretence nor flattery; abhorring suspicion [Col. 0563D] and detraction; rejoicing, beyond all the prosperities of this world, in the advancement of the beloved alone; grieving, beyond all the adversities of this present life, only in and over his failure; and, to comprise much briefly, not only renouncing everything of its own, but giving its whole self to him and reserving nothing of itself for itself.

My brethren, the saying is trustworthy; and though it is good for us to be here, we must nevertheless endeavour to avoid wearying the weak and to bring so great a prolixity to an end. At the close of this discourse, I wish to recall that excellent instruction of the Prince of the Apostles: “Having purified your souls in obedience to charity, love one another earnestly with a simple heart, being born again not from corruptible seed, but through the word of the living and abiding God” (1 Pet. 1:22–23). From these words we may gather that the first of the Apostles desires love among us to be not carnal but spiritual. It therefore befits us to be spiritual and to love one another spiritually, by the grace of the Holy Spirit—without whom we cannot do this—who, with the Father and the Son, from whom he proceeds eternally in one and the same substance of the Godhead, lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XII

From the passage of blessed Augustine: “Let the superior be obeyed as a father, and still more the presbyter,” to the end of the Rule. On the reverence to be shown to prelates; on their office and their concern for this regular observance.

### Synopsis of the Sermon

1. How greatly the discord of quarrels must be avoided in communal life, and the unity of concord loved.
2. We owe purity of heart to God, concord to our companions, and obedience to our superiors.
3. Mutual dependence, assistance, and reverence are necessary among superiors; those who dishonour one another do so shamefully.
4. Dissension among superiors is the dissolution of the whole discipline of the Rule.
5. It is a grave abuse when an inferior usurps authority over a superior; each must rely on the other and be united by mutual love.
6. What perfect obedience is, shown to superiors in God’s stead; by its merit murmurers fall away.
7. Obedience is threefold: servile, mercenary, and filial. The Lawgiver commends the last.
8. More serious causes are to be referred to the chief authorities; prelates, as physicians of souls, must both preserve health whole and recover it when lost.
9. Happy is the authority of prelates when charity moderates it; unhappy when the heat of domination inflates it.
10. How necessary charity in the mind and service in action are for prelates.
11. An address to prelates concerning the charity that serves, by which they are made happy.
12. How prelates, though honoured outwardly, are inwardly laid at the feet of their subjects before God.
13. Let them first provide example in deed, then correction in speech.
14. Discipline in prelates restrains subjects; those who judge others should fear God as judge.
15. Ready obedience gives superiors confidence. On the spiritual beauty and the good fragrance of religious life.
16. Charity establishes the true freedom of God’s servants.
17. Frequent reading, especially of Holy Scripture, is a mirror of the mind and produces manifold fruits.
18. The spiritual beauty of the soul must be preserved and increased; its stains are washed away by sorrow for the past and caution for the future.
19. Like a skilled physician, the Lawgiver provides both aids for preserving health already possessed and remedies for restoring it.

I. Dearest brethren, the preceding discourse which we delivered to your charity—on avoiding the horror of contention and attaining the gentleness of concord—has detained us for some time, indeed longer than we expected. We followed not our own spirit but that of truth, to whose direction our words belong: it extends them to a necessary length as it wills and as far as it wills, and when and where it wills brings them to a fitting conclusion. For we do not fail to know that all without exception who in religious life strive with their whole heart to please almighty God ought in every possible way to detest and abhor that evil which is the worst of all evils among other evils, and to embrace in affection and practise in effect that good which is the best of all goods among other goods.

Therefore it was in our heart, as we hope by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit whom we have just mentioned, to explain to you, in words somewhat more copious than profound, both the enormity of the former and the holiness of the latter, so that you might fully understand what judgment you ought to form concerning each.

[Note: [Col. 0565] Rule, chapter 11: on the reverence to be shown to prelates and their office.]

In the present discourse it remains for us to address your love concerning those matters which remain to the end of the Rule of our blessed Father Augustine, and to conclude as best we can our exposition of the words of so great a teacher, which he wrote for the instruction of clerics.

II. “Let the superior be obeyed as a father, and still more the presbyter, who has the care of you all.” As you know, we must begin today from this passage, because this is where we stopped yesterday. After our Father had taught us what sort of persons we ought to be toward one another, he also took care to instruct us what sort of persons we ought to show ourselves to our prelates.

The Apostle Paul, the vessel of election, addressing his disciples in the Epistle to the Romans with sound, customary, and salutary instruction, says: “Render to all what is due” (Rom. 13:7). He then speaks of diverse debts, because he recognized that there are diverse persons to whom we are bound as debtors. Yet at last he comprehended all these in love alone, so that we may know that the person fully renders what he owes who possesses love truly within, in affection before God, and also fulfils it profitably without, in action before his neighbour. “Owe no one anything,” he says, “except to love one another.” And he adds: “For he who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the Law.”

And who are those to whom we are debtors? Certainly God, our companions, and our prelates. In our inward things we are especially debtors to God, and it is necessary that in these things we should also render payment. For God is spirit, as the God-man testifies. And what does he add? “Those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). We must worship in spirit him who is spirit; and to worship him is to render to him what you owe. For the spirit worships God, who is spirit, when it humbles itself in his sight. Moreover, its humility is its purity. Consider this by its opposite, if perhaps you hesitate or are in doubt. This saying of the Wise Man is true: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean.” And what is this exaltation but pride? If the person who exalts himself is unclean, how is the one who humbles himself not clean? Therefore God requires purity of heart from you; you owe it to him.

But if the matter concerns your companions and prelates, since you are held bound to them by a great and varied debt, they are accustomed to cry: “Bring, bring” (Prov. 30:15): your companions call for unity of concord; your prelates for the readiness of obedience. Thus there are three to whom we owe: God, companions, and prelate. And there are three things which we owe: purity of cleanness, unity of concord, and readiness of obedience. Concerning the unity of concord which it befits us to have toward one another, you heard in the discourse immediately preceding this one, both from the words of your Father and from our own words, how you ought either to retain it when it is still preserved or recover it if it has perhaps already slipped away.

In the present discourse, you must also be instructed concerning readiness of obedience: namely, how and to whom it befits you to render it. You ask, to whom? To the superior and the presbyter. You ask, how? To the superior indeed as to a father, but far more to the presbyter. And why far more to the presbyter? You seek the reason: hear it. Because he has the care of you all. For this is the order of the words themselves: “Let the superior be obeyed as a father; and still more the presbyter, who has the care of you all.” Therefore, as we infer from this, obedience is owed to the one as to a father but to the other far more, because the latter has received the fullness of authority, while the former has been called to share in the burden of care.

### III.

For some maintain that the one here called *praepositus* [Col. 0566C] is he whom in our time we customarily call by another name, the prior; while the presbyter is he whom, in our usual terminology, they call the abbot. If this is so, then obedience is owed to the latter much more than to the *praepositus*; for scarcely anyone is ignorant that he bears the care of all. As we have just said, the one exercises the fullness of authority, while the other also has a share in responsibility; for the former presides in all things and over all, while the latter is present to assist him in these matters.

Yet the authority of the one in the whole, and the responsibility of the other in part, depend upon one another, so much so that serious confusion cannot fail to attend the office of both unless each both humbly yields to the other and effectively assists him. For what benefit can the prior accomplish among the community of brothers for those same brothers [Col. 0566D], unless the abbot’s authority is present to him in both these goods, namely reverence and assistance? Or what can the abbot himself accomplish, if—God forbid—the prior’s faithful diligence should fail him in either? Therefore let them honour one another and come to one another’s aid: the former humbly, the latter effectively. Then the fullness of authority in the abbot will not readily be diminished in its integrity, nor will the prior’s diligence be deprived of its duty of provision.

If these things are to be done thus, let fair judges, I pray, consider what benefit is conferred by an opinion altogether contrary to this—an opinion which I wish I knew no abbot had ever uttered, as I know that one has. 302 Yet it cannot possibly be that both kinds of knowledge should be absent from me [Col. 0567A]. This is the opinion—but whose it is I shall not say:

“What concern is my prior to me? Who is he, or how great is he? No one is greater than I in my presence. He is equal to him who is least of all in the community. What more should he have than any other brother, even the least, where I am present? Let him keep to himself and remain within himself; let him not presume to extend himself further among others, to rise higher, or to spread himself more broadly. Let him confine himself to his own community, for order requires it. Let him never appear elsewhere, at any time or in any place. To this end let all time be denied him and every place be closed to him. Let him draw in his horns; let him not exalt himself on account of his title. This title comes from me; it shall endure as long as I please. I lent it; I did not give it. It is my sufficiency, not his inheritance; not his possession [Col. 0567B], but my loan. I raised him up; it will be mine also to humble him. I shall do this, and shortly. I am not lacking in good men. There are enough at hand who wish to be priors, who know how and are able. I am not needy: I have and abound in men who understand more wisely than this man and can govern more effectively; thus I do not act unjustly. I shall put him back where I took him from. Let him not lift his head while I preside; while I speak, let him not dare even to murmur.”

So speaks such a man, perhaps with other words of the same kind. But how great an injury he brings upon himself by thus dishonouring his prior—would that he might recognize it not too late. For I cannot think that he will not recognize it at least some day. When the prior perceives these things, he will withdraw his shoulders and cease to labour wholeheartedly for him further [Col. 0567C]. Nor only this: he will repent of his former labour and will thereafter support no one for his sake. Then the fervour of discipline will grow cold, and perhaps the abbot will not perceive it until the discipline of religious life has been emptied—indeed, emptied down to its foundations—and scarcely any effective remedy can be applied.

### IV.

See how greatly the abbot harms himself when he considers it a small matter to dishonour his prior. What if he does not care to assist him in his responsibility? The prior has zeal for observing discipline, and the abbot himself opposes that zeal. “Why,” he says to the prior, “do you presume so miserably to imprison the brothers? Why do you afflict them with such constant labour, such strictness in silence, such weariness in the cloister, such discipline in chapter?”

What the prior refuses to those who ask rashly, the abbot grants. What the one closes, the other opens. The latter relaxes what the former restrains. And see what the undisciplined say amid these things: “Would that the abbot were always in chapter and the prior seldom there! Let this man never, anywhere, be with us; let that man always and everywhere be with us. We care nothing for the prior. Let him confine us whenever he wishes; we shall go to the abbot, and he will open for us. If he imposes fasting upon us in chapter because we have broken silence, the abbot will relax it for us in the refectory. If he denies us permission to go somewhere, however much he wishes, we shall go to the abbot, and at the first word of our request he will hear us.”

But when the prior sees these things, what will he say? “Why do I act thus? For whom do I labour and deprive my soul of good things?” (Eccles. 4:8). “What is this great labour to me [Col. 0568A], when there is no fruit? Why do I pass by with a deaf ear those words: ‘One builds and another destroys: what profit have they except ruin?’” (Ecclus. 34:28). “Why do I sow much where I gather little? I said ‘little,’ but I ought to have said ‘nothing’; for that is truer. Foolish and senseless am I, who stir up the brothers’ fury against myself while I wish to maintain the strictness of discipline, and endure an abbot who does not assist but hinders me in this. Would it not be better and quieter for me to relax along with one who relaxes, so that I may calm their fury and appease their anger? It is better for me to have them quiet than both disorderly and disturbed. I shall therefore go away and, sitting in the marketplace of indulgence, sell them laxity in order to buy quiet for myself.”

The prior now becomes the abbot’s helper in granting laxity, because the abbot refuses to help him in maintaining strictness [Col. 0568B]. But if the prior does not dare undertake this because he fears consenting to others’ sins, then, to provide for his own peace, he withdraws from office, choosing rather to yield than to remain without fruit. See what evils arise from the abbot’s disdain to assist his prior.

### V.

What shall we say, moreover, of the prior who disdains to honour or assist his abbot? For this too is a great abuse—great, I say, and detestable: that the prior scorns to honour the one who made him prior, and does not intend to offer him assistance in the office he has undertaken, though it was that man who appointed him to it.

To address the first evil: here is his voice. “What has the abbot to do with the community? Let him concern himself with external matters together with his officials; the community has been entrusted to me [Col. 0568C]. 303 Why does he henceforth interfere with the one whom he entrusted to me once for all? It is for me to restrict and relax the community. No one from the community ought to seek any permission from the abbot, nor ought he himself to give permission to anyone.”

His iniquity lies to him, brothers: it is not so. The prior must seek the abbot’s honour in the community entrusted to him and subject to him; he must arrange absolutely nothing against him. Receive a fitting example concerning this. That Egyptian master left nothing in his house outside Joseph’s authority; nevertheless Joseph himself declares that his master’s wife was excepted (Gen. 39:9). Perhaps she too had been entrusted to him—but for care, not for power: that he might provide for her, not unite himself with her; that he might serve her needs, in short, not shamefully misuse her.

So too with the prior and the community. For what is the community but the abbot’s bride? Let the prior—who is Joseph—govern this community for the abbot’s honour and arrange it according to the abbot’s provision [Col. 0568D]. For the prior, like Joseph prostituting his master’s wife, acts when he rashly claims to possess, in every respect, the same familiarity with the community and authority over it as the abbot has. This he does although our father and advocate commands that obedience be given to the *praepositus* as to a father, but much more to the presbyter.

Again, what shall we say of that prior who not only does not support his abbot in observing discipline, but even opposes him? [Col. 0569A] If he does not dare do this openly, it is surely all the more dangerous because it is more hidden. If he openly raised his neck to rebuild the walls of Jericho (Josh. 6:26), he would be resisted. But now he is thought to be among Joshua’s companions, though he is with Joshua’s adversaries. And what plague is more effective in doing harm than a familiar enemy?

See: when the abbot is absent, he permits everyone whatever he wishes; he tolerates breaches of discipline everywhere with equanimity. He stretches out his hand with Absalom and kisses each person, in order to win men’s hearts after himself (2 Sam. 15:5). Whatever the abbot builds while present, the prior destroys during his absence. Thus he himself perishes and destroys the discipline by violating its statutes: himself a transgressor and calmly tolerating—indeed, commanding—others to transgress [Col. 0569B]. Consider what punishment he deserves who does not fear to be the destroyer of the discipline whose guardian he was chosen to be.

Why did I say that the abbot and prior—that is, the *praepositus* and presbyter—depend on one another so much that neither can profitably fulfil his assumed office unless each renders the other fitting reverence and full assistance? But if they are perfectly one according to God, they will now be able profitably to fulfil their office; and in all their affairs each will be able to rely upon the other more securely, the more firmly they are united by the bond of a sincere love according to God.

### VI.

How their subjects ought to obey them, anyone who wishes may find sufficiently set forth throughout the writings of the saints [Col. 0569C]. Saint Father Benedict also writes thus in the Rule for monks:

“The first degree of humility,” he says, “is obedience without delay. This befits those who judge nothing dearer to themselves than Christ. On account of the holy service they have professed, or through fear of hell, or for the glory of eternal life, as soon as anything is commanded by a superior, as though it were commanded by God, they know no delay in doing it. Of such persons the Lord says: ‘At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me’ (Ps. 17:45). Therefore such persons immediately leave what is their own and abandon their own will; leaving their hands free from the work in which they were occupied, and leaving unfinished what they were doing, they follow with deeds, at the swift foot of obedience, the voice of the one commanding [Col. 0569D]. As if in one moment, the master’s command just given and the disciple’s completed execution are jointly accomplished with utmost speed by those upon whom rests the love of advancing toward eternal life. Therefore they take up the narrow way, of which the Lord says: ‘Narrow is the way that leads to life’ (Matt. 5:14). Thus, not living by their own judgment or obeying their own desires and pleasures, but walking by another’s judgment and dwelling in monasteries under authority, they desire an abbot to preside over them. Such persons undoubtedly imitate that saying of the Lord which declares: ‘I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’ (John 5:30).

“But this obedience itself will then be acceptable to God and pleasing to men if what is commanded is done neither anxiously, nor slowly, nor half-heartedly, nor with murmuring [Col. 0570A], nor with the response of one unwilling; for obedience rendered to superiors is rendered to God. For he himself said: ‘He who hears you hears me’ (Luke 10:19). And disciples must render it with a good disposition, for ‘God loves a cheerful giver’ (2 Cor. 9:7). If a disciple obeys with a bad disposition and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, even if he carries out the command, it will not be acceptable to God, who looks upon the heart of the murmurer. For such an act he receives no grace; indeed, he incurs the punishment of a murmurer, unless he makes amends with satisfaction.”

Therefore obedience must be rendered to the *praepositus*, but as to a father; much more to the presbyter.

### VII.

Blessed Augustine, I think, required filial obedience, when he commanded obedience to the *praepositus* as to a father, but much more to the presbyter [Col. 0570B]. For a lord has a slave, a householder has a hired servant, and a father likewise has a son. Each of these obeys: the son, his father; the slave, his lord; and the hired servant, the one who hired him. But fear drives the slave to obedience; hope attracts the hired servant; love invites the son. The first fears, the second hopes, the third loves. Thus the first obeys because he fears punishment; the second because he desires wages; the third because he loves his father.

This obedience is far more precious and exalted than the first and second, because it does not fear the hand that strikes, nor look to the hand that gives, but loves the person himself in all things and before all things. And what other reward will this obedience have except him whom the obedient person seeks in it? Let us therefore obey the *praepositus* as a father, but much more the presbyter, so that we may prove ourselves to be neither slaves nor hired servants, but sons: obeying not under compulsion of fear, nor enticed by desire, but rather inflamed by love [Col. 0570C].

### VIII.

It follows: “But in order that all these things may be observed, if anything has been observed less fully, it must not be passed over negligently, but care must be taken to amend and correct it. It will pertain especially to the *praepositus* to refer to the presbyter, whose authority among you is greater, whatever exceeds his measure or strength.”

These regular institutions have certainly been promulgated in order that they may be diligently observed. If, through some circumstance arising, they are observed less fully, they must by no means be neglected [Col. 0570D]; rather, careful thought must be given to how they may be amended. It is generally a greater fault to neglect correction after a transgression than to incur a lapse by transgressing. For contempt makes the former blameworthy; ignorance or weakness sometimes makes the latter pardonable.

Accordingly, our Father commands that all these things which he has stated from the beginning of the Rule to this point be observed; and if anything has been observed less fully, he commands that it not be carelessly passed over, but that care be taken for its amendment and correction. He also declares that it pertains especially to the *praepositus* that all these things be observed and that failures of observance be corrected. Whatever he sees exceeds his own measure in preserving and correcting them, he should endeavour to refer to the presbyter.

Thus, when that ancient people of God was journeying through the wilderness, lesser judges appointed under Moses judged minor matters, but referred every graver case for Moses himself to examine (Exod. 18:13–27) [Col. 0571A]. So here the *praepositus* is commanded to refer to the presbyter whatever he cannot determine by himself according to the canonical Rule. Hence it is clear that what we said above is true: the *praepositus* has been called to share in responsibility, not in the fullness of authority. Thus it is also said here of the presbyter: “Whose authority among you is greater.” To this also belongs the earlier command to obey the presbyter much more. Greater obedience is plainly owed to one who has greater authority.

These two duties, then—first, that all these things be observed; second, that if anything has been observed less fully, it not be passed over carelessly, but that care be taken for its amendment and correction—must be diligently discharged by the *praepositus*, referring to the presbyter whatever exceeds his measure or strength; that is, consulting him in matters for which he himself is less sufficient [Col. 0571B]. For what else are superiors but spiritual physicians? These same two concerns belong also to bodily physicians: to preserve health when possessed, and recover it when lost. True health is, as it were, preserved when unimpaired holiness is maintained in religious life; lost health is, as it were, restored when holiness that has been less fully maintained is amended.

Let the *praepositus* and presbyter therefore strive most earnestly to fulfil their offices. They are physicians of souls, and their assumed ministry obliges them both to keep the healthy free from sickness [Col. 0571C] and to restore the sick to health. But let us now approach what follows, for it contains something that must be examined carefully. It is this:

### IX.

“He himself who presides over you should not consider himself happy through a ruling power, but through love that serves.”

He presides profitably whose humility is not lacking in the care of government. 305 His will is more to benefit than to preside; he delights in the burden, not the honour; in the office, not the title; he is inflamed by love, not lifted up by power; he delights in service rendered to others, not received from them. Such a man is happy, though still in the way of merit. Through this intermediate happiness he will one day attain that which will consist in reward.

“He should not,” Augustine says, “consider himself happy through a ruling power, but through love that serves” [Col. 0571D]. It appears that presumption in authority and the harshness of domination are forbidden, but not the affection of love nor the work of service. Here are four things: power and domination; love and service.
