Domination nearly always tends to attach itself to power; but love never lacks the humility of service in the heart as long as it burns perfectly in action.

Power, however, always comes from good; domination most often from evil. The former arises from divine ordination; the latter from our own pride. “There is no power except from God” (Rom. 13:1). This is Paul’s statement; but this too is his voice: “Not that we lord it over your faith” (2 Cor. 1:23); and likewise: “We are your servants for Jesus’ sake” (2 Cor. 4:5).

Certainly, know that a great and truly surpassing gift has been granted you by divine grace if, though you possess great authority, you do not seek to dominate; and if you forcefully restrain the proud impulses which power usually generates in the mind, rather than delight in exercising authority through lordship over subjects [Col. 0572A]. Somehow the desire for power seems naturally inborn in the human mind. Thus rare is the person who does not desire it when he lacks it, or who does not fear to lose it when he has it, or who does not grieve when he does lose it. The pain with which he is tormented at its loss clearly reveals the delight that cherished him in possessing it; for no pain is normally found in losing something whose possession gave no delight at all.

Indeed, even if you do not strongly desire to have power, you nevertheless desire that it be offered to you; for, although not sought, it delights when offered, just as, as we have said, it sometimes torments when taken away. The weak mind often sews fig leaves in this matter to cover its shameful parts (Gen. 3:7), which here are especially foul. It makes coverings, pretending that it seeks the height of honour inherent in authority solely in order, by means of it, to exercise the practical benefit of labour while serving a need; though through it and by means of it, it really desires to reach the smoke of vanity. When this smoke has risen upward, it immediately vanishes in true failure and is carried away into empty air [Col. 0572B].

### X.

Yet power does not always lack goodness, since it is itself from the Good; for “there is no power except from God” (Rom. 13:1). And, as someone says: “God does not reject the mighty, since he himself is mighty” (Job 36:5). Power, then, is a good; but within this good there is often the evil of domination in authority. This comes not from the power which is from God, but from the pride which is from us.

Let him who presides therefore strive to reject evil and choose good (Isa. 7:15), exercising authority over the brothers’ transgressions according to place and time, person and cause, manner and measure—but not exercising lordship over the brothers themselves. Blessed Augustine therefore rightly says that he who presides should not consider himself happy through ruling power but through serving love. Happiness is not, therefore, in power and domination; it is in love and service [Col. 0572C]. Love is in the mind, but service in action. The former is inward, before God; the latter outward, before one’s neighbour. The former concerns conscience; the latter, reputation.

Love is like the root of a tree; service is, indeed, like its fruit. The more vigorously the former grows strong in secret, the more abundant the latter appears openly in holy conduct: the tree sends the root of love in the mind downward and bears the fruit of service in action upward. From these things it is clear what makes superiors fruitful or barren in their offices. Insofar as they are fervent in love of mind, so far do they blaze in service of action, so that they resemble the holy living creatures whose appearance was like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps (Ezek. 1:13). But insofar as they are cold in the former, they are barren in the latter. For when there is no vital moisture to nourish the root, there is consequently no fruitfulness to refresh in the fruit [Col. 0573A].

### XI.

Therefore, you who preside—of whom your father, Blessed Augustine, says: “That you should not consider yourselves happy through ruling power but through serving love”—when evident experience itself testifies that you do not fulfil service by giving your subjects the care owed to them, whether in the example of holy conduct for imitation or in the word of sound instruction for their education, infer from this the sloth by which you languish in action: the fervour of love is lacking in your mind.

Conversely, when you see yourselves powerful in deed and word through God’s help (Luke 24:19), 306 and, for the formation of those entrusted to you, show examples in the radiance of holy conduct: prudently omitting what is evil, courageously admitting what is good; forbidding evils, commanding goods, permitting intermediate things, persuading to perfect things; bringing forth from your treasury new things in the promise of reward and old things in the threat of punishment (Matt. 13:52); pouring into the wounds of the wounded oil of consolation and wine of rebuke (Luke 10:34); and doing anything of this kind conducive to the edification of speech, labouring in word and teaching [Col. 0573C]—know that this devotion of yours, apparent in public, flows from the depths of love hidden in secret.

Thus, when you serve in love in this way, consider yourselves happy. It is surely great happiness to burn with sincere love in the heart and to exercise sincere service in action. Great happiness, I say, but one in the sphere of merit; through it you will attain that happiness which will be in reward. First, as we have said, let love burn in secret; then let service shine openly.

Therefore, when the supreme Shepherd, the Lord Jesus, invited the first shepherd of the Church to the spiritual feeding of the sheep, he first questioned him about his love, in order to show that he would be fit to feed them if he cherished inwardly a true affection for his sheep. Hence he adds: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:16). He thereby plainly shows that you ought to consider yourselves happy through serving love, and that you ought first to burn with love in affection and then shine in service through action [Col. 0573D].

### XII.

This, then, concerns Augustine our lawgiver’s statement that he who presides should consider himself happy not through ruling power but through serving love. He adds: “Let him be set above you in honour before you; let him be laid beneath your feet in fear before God.”

What do these words mean—weighty indeed to hear, and no less difficult than profitable to fulfil? They are words, it seems to me, very different from one another, containing within themselves things both lofty and humble. When the prelates of holy Church perform them with devoted action, these words make them elevated through authority and lowered through humility [Col. 0574A].

There is, I think, a great difference in the persons of whom and to whom we speak. These words declare that honour is to be rendered to prelates by men, that they themselves ought to have fear before God, and that they ought to be laid beneath the feet of those above whose heads they are known to be elevated. But these things, though they appear different to some, are not in any respect opposed: they are two outstanding virtues which must be put into effect—humble reverence in subjects and perfect fear of God in prelates.

Let us, brothers, show grateful and humble reverence to our prelates. Let us honour them in every way that we can and ought according to God, in the second place after him whose role they fulfil and in whose place they preside over us. Thus they shall be set above us in honour before us.

But you, Fathers, especially worthy of reverence in him “from whom every fatherhood in earth and heaven is named” (Eph. 3:13), ought not think it unworthy that we should admonish you also, together with those who are like us, by Christ’s word. For it is clear that, together with those over whom you have for a time been set, you are subject in one and the same service to the Lord of all [Col. 0574B]. The greater the outward honour you receive from your subjects, the more deeply you must inwardly fear that awesome Majesty. Despising yourselves before his eyes, you must in your inward thought place above yourselves those from whom this passing honour is passingly rendered to you. Thus you shall be laid before God beneath their feet.

For holy men [Col. 0574C] who rejoice more in being useful than in presiding, when they have undertaken government, lay down inwardly before themselves whatever is outwardly lofty before men; through fear before God they lie prostrate at the feet of their subjects, before whom and over whom they are set in honour. Thus Moses listens to the counsel of a Gentile man (Exod. 18:24); King David dances before the Lord and is humble in his own eyes (2 Sam. 6:14); Elijah girds his loins and runs before Ahab (1 Kgs. 18:46); Elisha does not disdain to be touched by women (2 Kgs. 4:47); and this is the voice of the holy woman Esther as she addresses the Lord himself in prayer: “Lord, you have knowledge of all things, and you know that I hate the glory of the wicked and abhor the bed of the uncircumcised and of every foreigner” (Esth. 14:14) [Col. 0574D]. She adds: “You know my necessity, and that I abhor the sign of my pride and glory, which is upon my head on the days when I appear in public; I detest it as the cloth of a menstruous woman, and do not wear it in the days of my silence” (ibid., 16).

How low within themselves were these persons whom we have just briefly touched upon, though before men they were raised very high!

### XIII.

“Let him show himself an example of good works toward all; rebuke the unruly, console 307 the faint-hearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all.”

See what a prelate ought to be in relation to himself; see also what he ought to be toward his subjects. For the command to show himself an example of good works (Titus 2:7) appears to concern himself; whereas the commands to rebuke the unruly, console the faint-hearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all concern his subjects [Col. 0575A].

It is fittingly commanded that he first show himself as an example and then rebuke the unruly (1 Thess. 5:14), so that life may go before and teaching follow. He who wishes to be a priest must first put on the ephod and then the breastpiece (Exod. 29:5); and he must imitate him who came not to teach and to do, but to do and to teach (Acts 1:1), who was called a prophet powerful not in word and deed, but in deed and word (Luke 24:19). For it is also written of holy Ezra that he prepared his heart to investigate the law of the Lord (1 Esdr. 7:10), and not to teach and to do, but to do and to teach statute and judgment in Israel (ibid.).

Thus our prelate should not first rebuke the unruly and afterwards show himself an example of good works; rather, he should first devote himself to example in action, and then to rebuke in speech. And fittingly, “toward all,” so that, as he presides over all in the chair, he may likewise go before all in life [Col. 0575B]. Therefore let him show himself an example of good works toward all; and as he goes before all in rank, so let him go before them in holiness, so that subjects may learn from his preceding example how they ought to live.

In saying that Saint Augustine declares these four things must be present in him—rebuke toward the unruly, consolation toward the faint-hearted, support toward the weak, patience toward all—words which are the Apostle Paul’s (1 Thess. 5:14), he clearly shows what the prelate ought to be in words of preaching and in the depths of compassion. For the whole sum of sound and Catholic instruction concerning morals consists in the strictness of rebuke and the balm of consolation. Thus the merciful Samaritan is read to have poured into the wounds of the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho nothing but oil and wine (Luke 10:34); nor is the scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven said to have brought forth from his treasury anything but new things and old (Matt. 13:52) [Col. 0575C]. To support the weak and be patient toward all is to possess the tender and gentle depths of true compassion.

### XIV.

“Let him gladly accept discipline, impose it in a manner that inspires fear; and although both are necessary [Col. 0575D], let him desire to be loved by you more than feared, always considering that he must render an account to God for you.”

As in the preceding verse he advised that one must first show an example of good works and only then offer rebuke and consolation, so in this verse he commands that one first possess discipline and then impose it upon others. For how can one safely restrain others who does not blush to give free scope to himself in unlawful things? “You who preach that one ought not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who say that one ought not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. 2:21–22). Therefore let your labouring soul labour for itself, for your own mouth compels you.

Thus, in the building seen by Saint Ezekiel, the lips of the tables, built of squared stones, were bent inward all around (Ezek. 40:43) [Col. 0576A]. Therefore first possess discipline and afterwards impose it, so that you too may say: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (Phil. 3:17). Hence Saint Benedict says of the abbot: “Let him judge that all things which he teaches his disciples to be contrary are not to be done in his own deeds.” Otherwise, if he acts differently, the sons of blessed Job, feasting in the house of their eldest brother, may incur death.

Accept this discipline gladly, so that you may impose it in a manner that inspires fear. For when you voluntarily bind yourself with the straps of discipline, you thereby become an object of fear to others, so that they may not dare resist you in accepting discipline. And although both are necessary—both that fear may deter the unruly by rebuke and that love may soothe the faint-hearted by consolation—“yet,” he says, “let him desire to be loved by you more than feared” [Col. 0576B]. For amid the great weakness of this age, love generally finds greater fruit in modern subjects than fear.

“Always considering,” he says, “that he must render an account to God for you.” As was said long before our time, he who is judge of souls ought always to reflect that he has God as judge over himself, so that he may exercise the care of government more diligently in proportion as he weighs more deeply that he must render an account before the strict Judge for those entrusted to him. For a man is strongly prompted to good works if in everything he does he always remembers his last things, according to the written saying: “In all your works remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40) [Col. 0576C].

Saint Benedict says of this: “Let the abbot remember his own teaching and the obedience of his disciples, because in the awesome judgment of God an examination must be made of both matters. And let the abbot know that whatever lack of profit the shepherd may find in the sheep of the householder will be imputed to the shepherd’s fault.” And afterwards: “Let him know that one who has undertaken to govern souls must prepare himself to render an account. And however great the number of brothers he knows he has under his 308 care, let him know for certain that on the day of judgment he must render an account to the Lord for all those souls, with no doubt his own soul added as well.”

XV. Therefore, by obeying more faithfully, have compassion not only on yourselves but also on him who, among you, stands in a higher place and thereby in greater danger. [Col. 0576D] Certainly, where the position is higher, there the danger is greater; for the loftier the rank, the heavier also the fall, and the more will be required of him to whom more has been entrusted. Therefore, brothers, let us have compassion not only on ourselves, but also on them, because, as Scripture says: “Mercy is granted to the lowly; but a most severe judgment shall be made for those who preside” (Wis. 6:7). And let us have compassion by obeying; because, when we obey their commands humbly and readily, effectively and perseveringly, we assuredly give them cause, occasion, and confidence to await more securely that fearful future judgment of God, trusting in the fruit which they see themselves producing among us.

It follows: “May God grant that you observe all these things as lovers of spiritual beauty, fragrant with the good odor of Christ through good conduct, not like slaves under the law, but like persons made free under grace.” This is the prayer of our Father at the very conclusion of his Rule: he prays for us and wishes good things for us. He prays, I say, that we may keep all the things written in this book of regular discipline; but he wishes that we may possess the holiness of religious conduct. “As lovers,” he says, “of spiritual beauty.” Spiritual beauty, as it seems to me, is the adornment of spiritual virtues by which that inward man—namely, our spirit—is embellished. The good odor of Christ also pertains to the witness of a good and true conscience, by which a person, instructed and formed, is accustomed to discern [Col. 0577B] what judgment he may make concerning himself in the present.

This odor sends forth a most sweet fragrance to Christ when conscience bears a person testimony, in all truth, that in all his movements he desires to please Him alone. This odor is fragrant in good conduct when a person displays openly before his neighbor in deed the very person that he is hiddenly before God in conscience. Or, certainly, good conduct pertains to the holiness of religious life, while the good odor of Christ pertains to the sweetness of a good reputation. And we are fragrant with the good odor of Christ through good conduct when we both manifest holiness in a life of pure religion and, by living holily and religiously, spread far and wide a good opinion of ourselves.

[Col. 0577C] XVI. But by indicating that he does not wish us to resemble slaves under the law, but rather persons made free under grace, he is understood to wish that we should not shun evil from fear or unwillingly, but should do good out of love and willingly. For fear belongs to slaves; and those who withdraw unwillingly from evil groan as though under the law. True freedom, moreover, is charity itself. And to be “made free under grace” means to embrace what is good in the gladness of a generous will. “Not,” he says, “like slaves under the law, but like persons made free under grace”: so that we may not abandon evil in fear or unwillingly, but, with hearts enlarged, running the way of His commandments in the practice of righteousness, may do His will with a perfect heart and willing mind.

These are therefore his words, in which he both prays for us and wishes good things for us:

> “May the Lord grant that you observe all these things as lovers of spiritual beauty, fragrant with the good odor of Christ through good conduct, not like slaves under the law, but like persons made free under grace.”

And the order of these words is indeed right. First, a devout disposition makes us pure; secondly, the testimony of conscience makes us secure and good reputation commends us; thirdly, holy conduct makes us righteous. Finally, indeed, just as in the priest’s vestment the chasuble is laid over the other sacred garments, may we run by the more excellent way, seeing the end of all perfection: “Thy commandment is exceeding broad” (Ps. 118[119]:96), [Col. 0578A] ready for all His will—not now as slaves, fearing the face of the Lord, but as children longing for the presence of the Father.

XVII. “But that you may be able to look into this little book as into a mirror, lest through forgetfulness you neglect anything, let it be read to you once a week.”

Among other goods, sacred reading bestows upon us two notable benefits: it imparts knowledge of matters hitherto unknown to us, and makes our memory tenacious. For it gives us the clarity of instruction, and the assiduity of this reading of which we speak likewise drives from us the negligence of forgetfulness. Therefore our Father commands that the things written in this little book be read once a week, lest anything be neglected through forgetfulness; for what we repeatedly rehearse by reading, we do not easily consign to oblivion.

That he compares this little book, in which the institution of this regular discipline is written, to a mirror ought by no means to be passed over carelessly. In a mirror we are accustomed to look upon our face, and, enlightened by its clarity, to recognize what in it is ugly and what is beautiful; having recognized these things, we strive to remove the ugly and allow the beautiful to remain. And what is sacred reading but a mirror? When we attend to it, we behold both our own good and evil and those of others. For in it we see the vices in us which make us unsightly, and the virtues which make us beautiful; the weaknesses which make others infirm, [Col. 0578C] and the strengths which show them robust.

For concerning this, at the very beginning of the second book of the *Morals*, these words of Blessed Gregory are as lucid as they are true:

> [Note: [Col. 0577D] St. GREGORY, Book II, ch. 1.] Sacred Scripture is set before the eyes of our mind like a sort of mirror, so that our inward face may be seen in it. There we recognize what in us is ugly; there what is beautiful. There we perceive how much progress we make; there how far we remain from progress. It relates the deeds of men and provokes the hearts of the weak to imitation. And while it commemorates their victorious deeds, it strengthens our weakness against the battles of vices. Thus it comes about through its words that the mind trembles the less amid conflicts, the more it sees set before it the triumphs of so many valiant men. Sometimes, moreover, it not only declares their virtues to us, but also makes their falls known, so that in the victories of valiant men we may see what to seize by imitation, and again in their falls what we ought to fear.

What we have just said while discussing the mirror—namely, that we strive to remove our ugliness when we detect it in the mirror and allow beauty to remain—appears to contain the words of Blessed Augustine which follow in this manner:

XVIII. “And wherever you find yourselves doing the things that are written, give thanks to the Lord, the giver of all good things. But wherever any one of you sees that he lacks something, let him grieve for the past, beware for the future, praying that his debt may be forgiven him and that he may not be led into temptation.” [Col. 0579A]

With these words Blessed Augustine concludes his regular discipline which he wrote concerning the establishment of clerics. Without any exception, all the things written in this little book treat of the spiritual beauty of the soul and show how our inward man may acquire and preserve the adornment of spiritual virtues by which he is beautified. And when he says that, wherever we find ourselves doing what is written, we should give thanks to the Lord, the giver of all good things, what else does he command us except that, wherever, enlightened by the clarity which is in the mirror, we perceive some beauty to be present in us, we should ascribe it to Him by whose gift it is, allow it to remain, and strive, as far as we can, to increase it?

But when he adds that, wherever any one of us sees himself to lack something, he should grieve for the past and beware for the future, praying both that his debt may be forgiven and that he may not be led into temptation—what else do we judge him to command except that, when in the present mirror we detect that, stained by contracted ugliness, we have something lacking in beauty, we should diligently strive both to remove that stain and prudently to provide against being defiled again? “Let him grieve,” he says, “for the past; let him beware for the future.” Behold the twofold exercise of holy religion, known to all saints all the more because it is more plainly evident that, if they do not recognize it by frequent practice, they cannot possibly be saints.

For, as we perceive more in unceasing experience than we read in Scripture, “no one is clean from defilement” (Job 25:4), and man never remains in the same state (Job 14:2). Who can in any way recover holiness once lost unless he grieves for the past? Who can retain holiness already possessed unless he beware for the future? Therefore, let one who has already fallen add [what is needed] in order to rise again, guarding against the past [the transmitted wording is uncertain]. The words which he adds—“praying that his debt may be forgiven him and that he may not be led into temptation”—taken from the Lord’s Prayer, pertain to what he had said before: “let him grieve for the past; let him beware for the future.” For grieving for the past and praying that one’s debt may be forgiven have the same end; so also do guarding against the future and praying that one may avoid being led into temptation.

XIX. Therefore we, who in our profession have promised [Col. 0579D] to live according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine, are bound by the words of our mouth and obliged to observe that Rule; nor can we depart from it without grave offense. But let one who finds that he has departed from it “grieve for the past, beware for the future, praying that his debt may be forgiven him and that he may not be led into temptation.”

Therefore our Father, Blessed Augustine, the most skilful physician of souls, instructs us in both exercises of healing in the book of his regular discipline, teaching us therein how we may both preserve spiritual health when we possess it and return to it if perhaps we have lost it. We preserve this health of which we speak when we do the things that are written; but we return to health when we grieve for the past [Col. 0580A] and beware for the future, praying that our debt may be forgiven and that we may not be led into temptation.

Since these things are so, dearest brothers, we can in no way deny that we see ourselves to lack many of the things written in this book. For we all offend in many ways; there is scarcely a day on which, in some respect, we do not omit or neglect to render to the Lord our vows, “which our lips have uttered” (Ps. 75[76]:12). Therefore, seeing that we lack not one thing but many of the things written, let us cry from the depths of our whole heart to our Father who is in heaven, and, grieving for the past, say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). And, guarding against the future, let us say: “Lead us not into temptation” (ibid., 13). Thus, cleansed from past sins and fortified against future ones, may we praise and honor Him who is God, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. On the virtue of perfect obedience and its singular prerogative; and how the vow of obedience unto death in Christ is to be understood in regular profession.

## SYNOPSIS OF THE SERMON

1. A humble apology for speaking.
2. The form of profession in the Premonstratensian Order, with a recapitulation of what preceded.
3. Obedience holds the summit of religious life: the strength, increase, and material of all virtues; more acceptable to God than any sacrifices.
4. The disobedient are classed with idolaters and diviners, and deserve an equal punishment; introduction of an objector.
5. [Col. 0580C] If certain prelates are indiscreet in commanding, do not rashly fasten your biting teeth upon them.
6. To refuse obedience is damnable. Yet in commands that are excessively burdensome or impossible, one may plead one’s own weakness.
7. Forgetfulness makes transgression venial; contempt for obedience makes it mortal. Hence the fall of the first parent was of such great weight.
8. A singular example of disobedience in the true prophet sent to the king is examined.
9. Praise of the truly obedient person, whose pattern is shown in David and Samuel.
10. The type of the obedient person is considered in the words of the Virgin Mother. Humility underlies obedience; pride, rebellion.
11. The arrogance of pride, then contempt for obedience, and finally guilt and liability follow.
12. The camp of obedience must not be deserted in any adversity or at any time, according to the example of our Savior God.
13. From the Apostle is drawn the form of such obedience, which St. Benedict places in the fourth degree.
14. Obedience unto death [Col. 0580D] requires endurance and perseverance.
15. Obedience in Christ bears before it the rule of justice and the rectitude of inward intention.
16. The spur of obedience is the desire to please Christ and to enjoy eternal reward with Him.

I. Dearest brothers, the desire to speak to your charity for your edification compels us; but our own imperfection commands silence. Some of the things we ought to say are indeed strong, in some measure; yet we ourselves are weak and infirm. Greatly unlike, and separated from one another by a long interval, are the things apparent in us and the things heard from us: so that “the voice indeed is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau” (Gen. 27:22). The hearing ear admires us, but the seeing eye judges us unworthy; for in deed when present we are far different from what we are in speech when absent.

For behold, we often paint a beautiful man, while we painters are ugly. We discourse on the swiftest course of tigers, though we are pale little frogs scarcely creeping beneath our muddy pool, and soft tortoises wrapped within their twisted shell. We bring forward the strength of lions, though without swift agility—like ants moving beneath our dust rather than living creatures. We teach the eagle to fix its most clear sight upon the body of the sun, while we are moles burrowing beneath the ground, unable to bear the light and ignorant of the sun. O what great folly this is—and no lesser madness! Why does my hand not remain upon my mouth? Why do I not restrain my lip with my finger? Yet I desire to speak, though I may not; I am scarcely permitted to excuse myself, for I am wholly forbidden to refuse.

Your will alone, rather importunate—I do not know, if I may say so with your leave, whether it is just—is the cause. And therefore, while your compulsion prevails, our excuse has no place. Indeed your voice is: “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and call her” (Isa. 40:2), unless perhaps—far be it!—you begrudge your own edification. “Do not hide grain among the peoples,” unless perhaps you make nothing of their curse (Prov. 11:26). “Little children ask for bread; break it for them” (Lam. 4:4), unless perhaps you do not love their refreshment. Drawn therefore by the hooks of such arguments from the cloisters of our silence, [Col. 0581B] we no longer dare to hide in its inner chambers, although we are ashamed to come forth publicly to speak. We therefore consent and comply with you, wholly giving ourselves to you, that we may be yours and that you may enjoy us as it pleases you in the Lord, so that we too may enjoy you in Him.

II. Near the beginning of the first sermon, of which this is the thirteenth in sequence, we briefly touched upon three matters concerning which we have addressed your charity in the twelve sermons preceding this: namely, the dignity of the Order, the significance of the habit, and the strength of our profession. The discourse which we have delivered to you on these matters progressed so far that we were compelled to examine individually, with such exposition as we could provide, the very words of the Rule of our Father Augustine. From this we took cause and occasion to mention the same Rule in our profession, in the form in which we customarily make our vow: “according to the Gospel of Christ, according to apostolic institution, and according to the canonical Rule of Blessed Augustine.”

Whatever matters pertain to the dignity of the Order, the significance of the habit, and our profession itself, insofar as they came to our attention and the subject under discussion afforded occasion—would that you have heard them as fruitfully as we have expounded them fully! The wording contained in our profession is as follows:

> “I, Brother N., offering myself, give myself to the Church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, and promise the conversion of my manner of life and stability in this place, according to the Gospel of Christ, according to apostolic institution, and according to the canonical Rule of Blessed Augustine.”

We have endeavored, in the preceding sermons, to explain to you, as we could, how each of these points, together with those concerning the dignity of the Order and the significance of our habit, ought to be understood. The words which follow these in the same profession are:

> “I also promise obedience unto death in Christ to the Father of the aforesaid Church, and to his successors whom the sounder part of the congregation shall canonically elect.”

III. Great and weighty, my brothers, are the matters which precede in the profession of which we have spoken until now. But one surpassingly powerful and sublime mark of holy religious life both commends all the rest, making them acceptable, and confirms them, making them enduring. If you ask what it is: it holds an eminent place among the other virtues and, if it is lawful so to speak, a singular summit—the precious and glorious virtue of obedience. It bestows upon all the other virtues both holiness, that they may please, and strength, that they may endure. Without it they can possess neither the splendor of holiness nor the strength of perseverance. Without it, neither the offering nor surrender of yourself can be perfect; neither conversion of life true; nor stability in a place fruitful.

Therefore beware, brothers, lest perhaps—far be it!—you who “sow much, and bring in little” (Hag. 1:6): that there be much labor and no fruit. You gather little from what has been sown abundantly if you expend much sweat in the exercises of holy religion but attain no merit thereby because you are disobedient to your spiritual Father. For all the merit of religious persons consists in the virtue of obedience alone. Behold: in offering, you surrendered yourself, and in surrendering, offered yourself to the Church of God; but in these you have undertaken nothing perfect if you are disobedient to the Father of that Church, whom you promised to obey. You promised conversion of your manner of life; but to be unwilling to obey your spiritual Father is not to convert your conduct, but to pervert it.

Or perhaps you flatter yourself concerning stability in a place? For you promised that too. But remain stable there for a thousand years and refuse to obey the Father of that same place: it profits you nothing. [Col. 0582D] For what could profit you without the virtue of obedience—either the surrender and offering of yourself or the conversion of your conduct? Indeed, neither the Gospel of Christ, nor apostolic institution, nor the canonical Rule of Blessed Augustine recognizes that there can be any conversion of your conduct or any merit bestowed upon you by stability in a place without obedience.

“What then is lacking?” you ask. Render obedience to your spiritual Father, and all these things profit you. Scorn to render it, and though they may be something in themselves, they are nothing to you. Therefore perhaps you mention obedience in your profession after all those things, so that you may know that they depend upon this and that whatever usefulness they possess is bestowed upon them by this. For what are those things except certain sacrifices? But God neither receives nor accepts them without obedience. For holy Samuel says: “Does God desire holocausts and victims, rather than that the voice of the Lord should be obeyed?” (1 Sam. 15:22). Certainly He desires holocausts and victims, but when His voice is obeyed; otherwise they are an abomination to Him. And hear what Samuel added: “For obedience is better than victims, and hearkening more than offering the fat of rams.” He desires victims, then, but from one who obeys; offerings, but from one who hearkens. He does not look upon those who sacrifice if they are disobedient, nor upon those who offer unless they are obedient.

IV. But if you doubt whether obedience contains so great a good, hear how great an evil disobedience contains. Let holy Samuel show us this: “For resistance is as the sin of divination, and refusal to submit as the crime of idolatry” (ibid., 23). Is the sin of divination a great sin? Is idolatry a crime? But there is no need to wait long for your answer to these questions; for what you think about them is not unknown. See then that the prophet does not regard it as presumptuous to compare the sin of one who resists to diviners, and the crime of one unwilling to submit to idolaters.

Who now in the holy Church would tolerate diviners? Who would calmly endure idolaters remaining even for a moment among the flock of Catholics? Why is the same judgment not made concerning those who resist in the community and those unwilling to submit? Since an equal guilt binds them, there should surely be no hesitation about the sentence. Brothers, “remove the evil one from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:13). Let the idolatry of disobedience not go unpunished among you; let those who resist not be cherished. Let your hand be upon them; let so great a crime in no way flourish among you. Let them be overwhelmed with the stones of stern correction; if they resolve to remain in their foulness, let them be cast outside the camp. For they ought not to dwell with Catholics; indeed idolaters and diviners must be expelled, uprooted—nay, struck with lightning.

But some person, inwardly resentful, I know not who, mutters in silent outcry, indignant at and opposing these things: “This saying of yours is hard” (John 6:61). Who can hear you? You are too savage in your discourse, too violent in your speech. You condemn the disobedient beyond measure. You declare that they will die; but you think death itself too light a death for them. If you knew of a graver punishment, you would say that it should be inflicted upon them. You judge them worthy of this because you do not know anything more severe; yet you consider this far too light.

And I answer: “What is that to you? I do you no wrong” (Matt. 20:13). I have not summoned you to court because I am bringing accusation against sinners. I have raised a cross: what is that to you? For you are not a thief or robber. If Phinehas is brought in piercing with a dagger (Num. 25:7), you are not thereby an adulterer. Cannot Samuel rebuke disobedient Saul without your taking offense? Elisha kills idolaters: why are you angry over this? “Is it I, Rabbi?” Judas says (Matt. 26:25), and Peter is silent. Why did he himself inquire about the one who was to betray the Lord? Is it an affront to you that Paul threatens the sexually immoral with a rod (1 Cor. 4:21), or that Elisha makes the punishment of the lying and greedy man to be Syrian leprosy? (2 Kings 5). Peter strikes down the love of money in Ananias and his wife, and do you murmur at this?

> “Is your own concern at stake when your neighbor’s wall is on fire?”  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.18.84

“No,” you say; “none of all this concerns me. But you seem to me to go too far, and, as far as I can judge, your sword rages unto utter destruction. For Simeon and Levi are called by their father brothers, weapons of violent iniquity, because ‘in their wrath they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall’ (Gen. 49:5–6). Their father’s discernment rebuked their excess, cursing their fury and indignation. Nor unjustly, since they executed even a just thing unjustly. In short, he recognized stubbornness in the one and hardness in the other; therefore he cursed both. Or, ignorant that despair is dangerous, you magnify the evils of disobedience to such a degree that you consign to oblivion the weakness of this age. Modern people are not as the ancients were. Are you an angel? And if you are now, have you always been? Peter first denied Him, and afterward the Lord entrusted His sheep to him to feed.”

V. “If the guilt of disobedience is so grave, who can be saved? Especially among modern people, among whom as many prelates are found indiscreet in commanding as subjects are sluggish in obeying.” I have said far too little in asserting that they are equal in number; for I could boldly say that those who are immoderate in commanding are by far more numerous than those who are unwilling to obey. Behold: raise your eyes, lift up your ears, and observe how those who command require what they wish rather than what they ought; they order what pleases them, not what is expedient; they give commands according to will, not according to reason. Give me even one of them who does not take up this saying:

> “Thus I will, thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason.”  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* VI.223

Not only this, but they promulgate for their subjects, as it pleases them, laws hard and exceedingly difficult, “binding heavy and unbearable burdens and laying them upon men’s shoulders; but they themselves are unwilling to move them with so much as their finger” (Matt. 23:4).

To this I answer: You touch the Lord’s anointed with excessive impudence; you malign His prophets with excessive presumption; you set your mouth proudly against heaven. Beware lest, while relying too much on your own strength, you presume to touch the ark of the Lord with a rash hand and thereby deserve to be struck by Him with a deadly blow. Do not proudly scrutinize the life of your elders; do not maliciously examine their actions; do not rebuke their conduct, even if it deserves rebuke, with haughty mind and swelling speech. Recognize that you are their hearer, not their judge; and that you ought to comply through obedience with their commands, not condemn their life and conduct through pride.

Call to mind your vow, “which your lips have uttered” (Ps. 65[66]:14), namely: “I promise obedience to the Father of the aforesaid Church.” Of which Church, except that to which you gave yourself? Do not forget, moreover, the Apostle’s saying: “Obey your leaders and submit to them” (Heb. 13:17); and this: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers” (Rom. 13:1). Do you not know that their commands are the commands of God? Do you not know that they preside over you in the office and place of the supreme prelate? Do you not know that, whatever their character, they are successors of those concerning whom it is said: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16)? Has the Apostle’s saying escaped your mind: “There is no authority except from God; and those that exist are ordained by God. Therefore he who resists authority resists God’s ordinance. But he who resists”—may God turn from you what follows (Rom. 13:1–2). Yet He will not turn away the consequence unless you first cast away from yourself the preceding act.

VI. And he says: “Who, then, can be saved? For some hold that for subjects not to obey prelates is to acquire damnation for themselves, and that to fall into the sin of disobedience is to commit a mortal sin.” Do you, I ask, disbelieve that this judgment is true? “Who, then,” he says, “can be saved?” Certainly, one who endeavors humbly, cheerfully, and steadfastly to obey his spiritual Father, who presides over him in God’s place. In such obedience is salvation; because in it is the merit of holiness, and from it comes the reward of blessedness. In it humility makes good disciples meek, cheerfulness makes them ready, and steadfastness makes them persevering.

“And who,” he says, “is able to render such obedience to every command of his elders? Who can both accept each thing commanded and omit every forbidden thing? For they command so many things and forbid so many things that they can neither be counted nor retained in memory.” We do not judge you too harshly for forgetfulness; nevertheless, you may fear that, while you forget the commands of your elders, you yourself may be consigned to oblivion by God.

And he says: “This saying is hard” (John 6:61). “What of the fact that they often command things so burdensome that we cannot carry them out by obeying? They are human beings, though they are over human beings. Very often they either do not know how to observe moderation in their commands because of ignorance, or disdain it because of pride; or, as often happens with many of them, they will not observe it because of their own obstinacy; or indeed they neglect it through forgetfulness—being unskilled, proud, obstinate, and blinded.”

Neither, I say, do we condemn you for impossibility. Yet when even things which seem impossible are commanded you by your prelate, if he persists in his decision and is unwilling to relieve you, you ought, as Blessed Benedict says in the Rule of Monks, to undertake what is commanded in trust in God, with faith and humility. For these are his words on this matter in the same Rule:

> “If perhaps some burdensome or impossible task is enjoined upon a brother, let him nevertheless receive the command of the one who orders it with all meekness and obedience. But if he sees that the weight of the burden altogether exceeds the measure of his strength, let him patiently and at a suitable time lay before the one set over him the reasons for his impossibility, not in pride, resistance, or contradiction. But if, after he has made his representation, the command of the Prior remains unchanged, let the younger brother know that this is expedient for him, and, trusting in the aid of God out of charity, let him obey.”

Behold: it is not good for you to refuse commands that are exceedingly burdensome, or even those which perhaps are impossible, when they are imposed upon you by command, although it is permitted you humbly to plead your weakness.

VII. “What you say is very hard: for according to these arguments of yours, in transgression of the commands promulgated by our elders, forgetfulness and impossibility, though they perhaps do not wholly condemn, still do not fully excuse.” “And what, I ask, do you condemn in transgression?” And I answer: complete contempt. For if through forgetfulness it happens that you disobey your elders in their commands or prohibitions, you have indeed sinned, but venially—provided that, recognizing your guilt at once, you humbly confess it, make full satisfaction for it, and strive thereafter to amend yourself. But if through contempt and pride, through arrogance and rebellion, you reject the commands of your elders—far be it!—you have surely committed a very grave sin, and, if you persist in it, one that is damnable and mortal.

“This saying is hard,” he says. “But if these things are so, I suppose they should be understood concerning the greatest commands.” To this I answer: “What commands do you consider greatest?” “The greatest command,” he says, “appears to be that by which we are commanded to love the Lord our God, and others of this kind.” Such commands and prohibitions are indeed great, I say; yet not only in such matters, but also in the remaining commands and prohibitions which appear small, provided that they are promulgated by elders according to God, both forgetfulness incurs sin and contempt incurs damnation.

And if you hesitate at all concerning this, receive a fitting example. It was forbidden in paradise to our first parent by the very Author of the universe that he should eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:17). If we attend to the outward appearance of what was forbidden, the transgression of the first man does not seem great. What then are we to say? That God was unjust in casting man, whom He had created so excellently, from the place of delight into this dark exile for something slight?

And he answers: “Far be it! He did not cast him out for something slight. For although what He prohibited does not appear great, yet He who prohibited it is great, indeed truly great—He ‘whose greatness has no end’ (Ps. 144[145]:3).” And what, I ask, does He who prohibited have to do with the transgressor himself? “Very much,” he says, “in every respect. First, he ought carefully to have considered who it was that prohibited; and secondly, to have measured the prohibition itself by Him.” “And because He Himself is great, was His prohibition consequently great?” “Because of the great will, so to speak, of the One commanding.” “How do you understand this?” “Every command and prohibition of God must be received and carried out with the same will with which it was imposed. That command or prohibition is greater or less which the one commanding and prohibiting is more or less manifestly willing. Therefore, because of the excellent and great will of the One commanding, that first man ought to have avoided the slight prohibition of God just as much as a great one, since it is clear that the Lord wished the slight prohibition to be received with as great and excellent a will as He wished a great one to be received.”

“It seems to follow from this,” I say, “that that first parent sinned greatly.” “The ensuing punishment clearly shows how horrible and enormous a sin he committed—not only in him but in us as well. Yet,” I say, “as you put it, what was damnable to him was not so much that he failed to keep what was forbidden as that in this he despised the One forbidding.”

VIII. “Yes,” he said, “that is what I say.” And I: “Why then, in the commands and prohibitions of those who now hold his place, even though they be very small, do you not likewise admit that contempt is damnable, when He himself testifies that those who despise them despise Him? And behold, I shall tell you something which you recognize more than you learn—something which, when you recall it, should so astonish you that you fear no little.

“A prophet was once sent by the Lord from Judaea into Samaria, to an idolatrous king; and among other instructions he was commanded neither to take food nor drink in that place, but, once the business for which he had been sent was done, to return fasting (III Kings 13). He was ready to do this; he confessed that this had been commanded him, and did not deny it. He went and returned—would that he had not returned from his return! But the contrary occurred: for he was deceived, and, deceived, was brought back. He transgressed the command; and from the mouth of the deceiver he understood his present guilt and heard the punishment to come. A lion tore him to pieces and, to punish the transgression, required from him only bodily death. What followed made this especially clear: the lion which had been permitted to kill him while living was not permitted to touch him when dead. Nor only this: it guarded the corpse from which it had driven out the soul, and did not even injure the donkey. Yet, if we consider superficially, the cruelty of the punishment seems to have exceeded the measure of the fault.

“If, therefore, this man of God—not rendered absent-minded by forgetfulness, but deceived by the lie of a false prophet—was handed over to a lion to be devoured because he ate in a forbidden place, though he now thought that it had been permitted him, and though he intended to obey the Lord: what do you judge concerning yourself, who transgress the commands and prohibitions of your elders, not through forgetfulness but through contempt?”

And he replied: “Above all the words you have spoken on this subject, this example frightens me most. For I think that the man would by no means have eaten in that place unless he believed that the Lord had changed both the prohibition of the place and His command concerning eating there [p. 315]. For this, unless I am mistaken, is why he ate: he believed himself to be obeying the Lord in doing so. This indeed seems to be indicated by his words in reply to the king and the prophet who invited him to dine.”

And I answered: “What, then, is indicated to you by this deed, except that you should never dare, through anyone’s later suggestions, to alter what you hear forbidden by your superior, unless you know with absolute certainty that your same elder has changed it? Gather, then, from these things how greatly you ought, with the devotion of anxious and sincere humility, to reverence the commands and prohibitions of your spiritual father—not only the great ones, but also those which seem small.”

IX. O obedience, you who alone make the other virtues worthy of the eternity of heavenly reward! The true and sincere obedient person walks safely everywhere and need not doubt his reward. But where shall such a person be found, and who is he? Surely he who wholly and entirely depends upon the nod of his superior, retaining absolutely nothing of himself by which he may fail, in any respect, to bow himself lower at that superior’s command [variant: “at the same superior”]; and who never, anywhere, causes him any prejudice. Rather, he is ready to follow him wherever he goes (Apoc. XIV, 4), conforming himself to him and being formed according to him, walking toward him, yet before him; in no way wishing either to lag behind or to go beyond. “Who is this, and we shall praise him? For he has done wonders in his life” (Ecclus. XXXI, 9). And what is his life? Certainly obedience; for thus he lives, and in obedience is the spirit of his life.

If this, then, is his life—the life which works wonders in this life—do you not judge it wondrous that a person should wholly give his own will to another’s will and no longer belong to himself? At the command of his superior is every movement of his; and as the superior moves him, so he too moves himself.

Behold, I tell you: lift up your eyes and see the soldiers of the heavenly camp; search among them for the rich marrow of the virtue of which we speak. Let holy David appear to you: appearing, going in and going out, and proceeding at the king’s command (I Kings XVIII, 5). There is an entering into the secret place of contemplation; there is likewise a going out into the public sphere of action. But perhaps each becomes a cause and occasion of eternal salvation only when it occurs at the king’s command. For he truly proceeds who makes progress in each of these healthful exercises. Yet one must proceed at the king’s command; for spiritual progress increases in one who proceeds only when he wholly bends himself to the nod of his superior.

There is also something similar to this. “David went out to everything whatsoever Saul sent him” (I Kings XVIII, 5), thereby presenting you with a model of perfect obedience. His going out was not for some things, but for everything, so that you may know that nothing among all that is laid upon you is to be excepted. And what follows? “He conducted himself prudently” (ibid.), so that you may recognize that he was eager in going out and effective in acting.

Hear another: “Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening” (I Kings III, 9). His Master taught him to make this answer to the One calling him. Indeed, when called in this way, he ought to have made no other response. “You speak,” he says, “and I shall listen.” He said, “Speak,” and stopped there; he did not specify what was to be spoken. He did not, I say, specify it; yet he did not fail to say that he held his hearing ready for God’s speech. O voice uttered from an enlarged heart! “Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.” This is to say: “I except nothing; I set before you no restriction. What you speak rests in your will; for whatever it may be, I shall listen.”

X. Hear yet another voice like this: “Let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I, 38). According to whose word? According to the angel’s word, for he was speaking to her. And who is this angel? Perhaps he is your superior, announcing to you a spiritual conception and birth. For “the lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II, 7).

And what knowledge do the lips of your priest, the angel of the Lord, preserve? “Behold, you shall conceive and bear” (Luke I, 31). “You shall conceive”: that is, you shall receive within the affection of pure thought what pertains to true salvation. “You shall bear”: that is, you shall bring this very affection of true salvation to the effect of good action. What law is sought from his mouth? “How shall this be?” And this question is indeed most necessary. For why does she say, “How shall this be?” except with reference to what had been foretold to her: “You shall conceive and bear”? Who does not know that it is most salutary to inquire into the manner of this conception and this birth?

Behold, ask the angel for the law, seeking it from his mouth, according to that saying: “Ask your father, and he will tell you” (Deut. XXXII, 7); for the angel does not fail to announce it. And what does she say to him who announced it? “Let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I, 38). She had also said first: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (ibid.). It is as though the preceding words were the reason for those which followed; and so indeed they are. For unless she had first said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord,” she would in no way have added, “Let it be done to me according to your word” [p. 316].

To what do you think all this pertains? Certainly to this: when the voice of your superior lays upon you something that concerns purity of mind and bears the usefulness of action—for this is what it means to say, “You shall conceive and bear a son”—you should receive that same voice with this answer and say: “Let it be done to me according to your word.” “According to your word,” she says, not according to my own will. “You have spoken to me: let it be done to me according to your word. It shall not return to you empty, but shall do whatsoever you will and shall prosper in me, to whom you have sent it. Let it therefore be done to me according to your word.”

This voice, then, breathes perfect obedience, but profound humility must come first. For unless you first think humbly of yourself, you will not be ready in all things to obey your superior. For whence do we see some resist the commands of their superiors? Surely from this: they are proud in the thought of their heart. Since they think exalted things of themselves beyond measure, they see those set over them as far beneath themselves; and they reckon it a great extreme of baseness to lower themselves by obeying them, as though in doing so they were debasing themselves.

Therefore profound humility must precede in you, so that perfect obedience may follow. I say “follow,” not “succeed,” so that from the gentleness of humility you may produce the eagerness of obedience and preserve the latter in yourself together with the former. Now the voice of profound humility is this: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.” But that of perfect obedience is: “Let it be done to me according to your word.” “My heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Ps. CXXX, 1); and therefore “I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 60).

XI. Gather from these things how greatly you must beware the plague of pride. For it produces the sin of disobedience, which, when it has been completed, brings forth death (James I, 15). Hence it is also written in the Law: “But whoever acts proudly, refusing to obey the command of the priest who ministers to the Lord, that man shall die by the judge’s decree, and you shall remove evil from Israel” (Deut. XVII, 12).

Consider, I pray, the sequence of the words. Before declaring the punishment, it first touched on the fault, since this is the road to that. The punishment, therefore, is death; disobedience itself is the fault. But pride is the cause of disobedience. For this is contained in the order of the words, which is: “But whoever acts proudly, refusing to obey the command of the priest.” Thus first comes the arrogance of pride, then contempt for obedience. Therefore humble yourself, that you may obey the command of the priest and the decree of the Judge. That is: answer the angel, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke I, 38), so that you may add what follows: “Let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.).

For some words relevant to this are set beforehand in the Law in this manner, in which you are told: “You shall do whatsoever those who preside in the place chosen by the Lord say, and what they teach you according to His laws. You shall follow their judgment and shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left” (Deut. XVII, 10–11). You are commanded to do whatever they say and not turn aside either to the right or to the left, so that this may be your voice: “Let it be done to me according to your word.”

XII. Attend, therefore, to your vow; and render the vow which you made. That is: “I promise obedience to the Father of the aforesaid Church.” But you added, “until death.” And this perhaps pertains to the matter. In these words I perceive two things to be noted: the greatness of hardship and the utter extremity of your end.

To speak first of the former: to obey until death is, for the love of obedience, to embrace every hardship until death. Obedience is indeed a great virtue among the other virtues, by which you subject your will to another’s will. But for it to be fully and perfectly acceptable to God, it must also be pure. It possesses great purity, fitting to its prerogative, when it rejoices more to be exercised amid adversities than amid prosperities. Let it embrace every adversity within the arms of its breadth; let it undertake death itself, however it may be inflicted, so that by it eternal life may be entered.

Therefore, having obedience as companion and guide, run by patience, looking with it toward the contest set before you, to Jesus, the Author and Perfecter of faith, of whom you read that “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. II, 8). Behold what was said a little earlier: namely, that humility must precede obedience. For Paul, intending in this place to speak of our Redeemer’s obedience, first made mention of His humility, in order to show, unless I am mistaken, that it is not only difficult but wholly impossible for the one to follow unless the other happens first. He first declares that Christ was humbled, then that He became obedient; for you also, if you do not think humbly of yourself, will not gladly obey your Father.

Now He “became obedient unto death” [p. 317]: that is, obedient even to enduring those things which inflict death. And what did the Apostle intend us to understand by adding, “even the death of the cross”? Surely that through this too he might indicate His more praiseworthy obedience: he showed Him obedient unto a death not merely harsh but also shameful, not merely dreadful but also ignominious. For harshness is marked in death; lowliness, in the cross. Thus you promised obedience until death, so that you may be rewarded more happily for it in the future and honored more highly, in proportion as you have been more harshly afflicted and made more lowly for it in the present.

XIII. What then do you think? Perhaps you judged that great merit came to you when you eagerly obey one who lays upon you pleasant and delightful things, in which you aim more at indulging your carnal pleasure than at obeying your spiritual Father’s command. It is not so. For blessed Gregory says:

> [Note: St. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXV, chapter 13, on obedience; Col. 0591.] When worldly success is commanded, when a higher position is imposed, one who obeys in order to obtain these things empties obedience of its virtue if he also longs for them by his own desire. For he does not direct himself under obedience who, in receiving the prosperities of this life, serves the desire of his own ambition.

This is not the obedience which you promised until death. For it is carnal, and is found “in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job XXVIII, 13); it makes no progress in holiness and will not render a gift acceptable to God.

But I shall show you an obedience which, if you grasp it, perfects you, and which God both accepts and rewards, because He knows it to endure until death. “The Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying that bonds and tribulations await me; but I fear none of these things, nor do I make my life more precious than myself, provided that I may complete my course and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the Gospel of God’s grace” (Acts XX, 23–24).

This is Paul, to whom “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 21), and whose only glory is in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. VI, 14). Hear another utterance of his: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts XXI, 13). This was pure obedience, ready both to be bound and to die.

Holy David also says, addressing the Lord himself: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” (Ps. XVI, 4). Therefore, while you walk a hard way for the virtue of obedience, and—even if you must endure the very punishment of bodily death—you do not depart from it, however greatly tribulations afflict you, then indeed it is obedience until death: the kind which Jesus himself likewise learned from what He suffered (Heb. V, 8) and left for you to imitate.

I think that Saint Benedict speaks of such obedience when, in the Rule for monks, he defines the fourth degree of humility thus: “The fourth degree of humility,” he says, “is that, in obedience itself, if hard and contrary things, or even any injuries, are inflicted, he embraces obedience with a silent conscience and, enduring, neither grows weary nor departs.” Behold, this seems to me one manner in which obedience must be maintained until death.

XIV. But behold another: obedience is maintained in such a way that it is not abandoned before death, which is the end of this temporal life. Therefore, as long as you live in this body, you cannot cast from your neck the yoke of obedience which you once took upon yourself. For if you act otherwise, you cannot be saved. For the Savior’s saying must be understood of every exercise of virtue: “He who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

Understand these two things, therefore, when you remember that you promised obedience until death: endurance and perseverance. Thus, if you wish to carry into effect what you are known to have promised in this respect, you should gladly and courageously endure whatever hardships may be inflicted upon you—for example, insults in words, losses in possessions, beatings upon the body, or even death itself, however harsh or shameful it may be—without abandoning the virtue of obedience, and never wishing to end it until you come to end your life.

You said, therefore, in your profession: “I promise obedience until death to the Father of the aforesaid Church.” This is to say: “I shall be so obedient to him that, in order to fulfill his commands, I shall willingly endure all hardships which may be inflicted upon me; and this alone shall be the limit of my obedience which is also the limit of my life.”

And what is it that you add: “in Christ”? For this also was inserted: “I promise obedience,” you said, “in Christ.” I think that we can understand this not in one but in several ways.

XV. [Col. 0592D] And it seems to me—unless something more fitting or subtle occurs to you at present—that among other ways we may understand this in two ways [p. 318]: namely, that to promise obedience in Christ is to promise that you will render obedience to all commands imposed upon you according to Christ, and that you will carry them out for no other reason than Christ. Thus one sense concerns the rule of righteousness; the other, the uprightness of inward intention. Let us discuss the first briefly, and then the other.

You have promised obedience to your Father, but see that you obey him according to God. For evil must never be committed for the sake of obedience, even though good may sometimes have to be omitted. If, however—God forbid—it should happen that your superior commands you to do something contrary to God, then, just as I would advise you by no means to consent, so nevertheless my counsel would be that you should not at once contradict him too boldly or proudly. Rather, out of reverence for the holy governance committed to him, you should repeatedly and with all humility and gentleness suggest to him that he ought not, by his command, compel you to commit anything that would gravely offend God.

And this must also be added: when this occurs, your remonstrance should be as secret as it is humble, so that you may resist one commanding wrongly without in any way revealing your Father’s shameful matters. By his “shameful matters” here I mean his unjust commands, which you must reject by contradicting them with a certain humble, as it were, contempt; so that if he wishes by command to impose upon you something contrary to God and foreign to your salvation, you reveal it to no one at all.

If he listens to you, you will have gained your Father (Matt. XVIII, 15): correcting him indeed, but not exposing him. In the one case you provide for his salvation; in the other, you yield to his authority. In the one, you preserve intact for him the holiness which he ought to have toward God; in the other, you keep unblemished the good opinion which others have of him. In the one, finally, you withdraw him from injustice; in the other, you defend him from disgrace.

But if—God forbid—after much exhortation for his salvation and after repeated arguments from reason have been presented, he is unwilling to yield to you, then you must take up Peter’s authority, with a humility that is free and a freedom that is humble. When the Jews commanded what was contrary to God, Peter answered freely: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V, 29). Then recognize that you did indeed promise him obedience, but obedience in Christ; and when he commands things which you know displease God, know that you owe him no obedience in those matters.

XVI. Then, with no less effort, strive to direct whatever progress you make through the virtue of obedience solely toward the desire for eternal reward. Understand that every advance in the spiritual virtue of obedience, which we have now briefly touched upon in this threefold way, is salutary to you only when, in it always and everywhere, you seek as witness and await as rewarder our one Lord Jesus Christ, from whose gift it comes.

This, therefore, is to render obedience until death in Christ: with this devout intention, in those things which are according to God, whether adverse or even bringing death itself; and, until you finish this temporal life, patiently, holily, and perseveringly to persist in the exercise of obedience—so that in all these things you may please Christ alone in the present and may deserve to enjoy Christ for all of them in the future, Christ who is God, blessed for ever with the Father and the Holy Spirit of both. Amen.

# SERMON XIV

## On the obedience we have promised to the successors of our Father; on which is the sounder part of the congregation, whose election must be held valid; and on the religious exercises of cenobites

[Col. 0594A]

## Synopsis of the Sermon

1. Analogy between remedies and bodily and spiritual illnesses.
2. The necessity of obedience among cenobites; why the earlier monks were not bound by a particular vow of obedience.
3. The reason why the vow of obedience was later introduced.
4. The vow of obedience: an indissoluble bond, protection, and shelter of spiritual life.
5. What persons are to be accounted successors, and what is the sounder part of a canonical congregation.
6. Obstacles to canonical election: violence and cunning; the voice of the envious and presumptuous.
7. Honor is slippery and often flees its pursuer; the voice of one beset by fear.
8. [Col. 0594B] What is the voice arising from softness; four kinds of persons alien from the sounder part.
9. Election must be made according to God, private affection and hatred being banished.
10. How the sounder part of the congregation is to be identified [p. 319], and how much circumspection election requires.
11. The common exercises of religious: reading, action, and prayer, prefigured by the lampstand, table, and altar of the tabernacle.
12. The Church, or the state of religious life, represented in the tabernacle; in what way reading is fruitful.
13. The outward exercise of action must not be devoid of meditation, for which the keeping of silence is helpful.
14. Prayer especially commended above the rest, and what it ought to be.
15. The ordinary places of work for religious; first, how they should conduct themselves in the oratory.
16. The discipline to be observed in the cloister, refectory, and dormitory.
17. The stricter observance of the Premonstratensians in conversation with outsiders.
18. The purpose of the chapter-house or assembly room: confession, absolution, and humility.
19. To what extent a person unjustly accused may excuse himself in chapter.
20. The observance of the hospital, commonly called the infirmary, last among the regular places, where the end of mortal life is awaited.

I. The various kinds of disease, dearest brothers, compel the discovery of various kinds of medicine. Indeed, their causes and occasions also bring medicine into being; for if there were no sickness, surely no medicine would be necessary. “If you do not know the cause,” someone says, “how do you cure?” But I say: “If you do not perceive that someone is sick, whom do you cure?”

What we say about bodily diseases, we can also say about diseases of souls: their diversity and multitude compel the discovery of a diversity and multitude of fitting remedies. And what physicians are to bodies, superiors are to souls. Bodily sickness is corruption of nature; sickness of souls is the committing of fault. But why do I say that a person becomes sick when he commits a fault? For he becomes infirm even when he delights in sin; and to bring deadly sins into effect is to die.

There is likewise much diversity and manifold multitude in these sins, so much so that they can neither be comprehended by number nor grasped by understanding. For “who understands transgressions?” (Ps. XVIII, 13). To prevent and remove them—to prevent them, I say, so as to take away the cause and occasion of spiritual sickness; to remove them, so as perhaps to restore lost health—superiors have been established in the holy Church as certain physicians. By applying suitable remedies, they either keep the healthy well or restore the sick.

The medicines fitting for their preservation of health and expulsion of sickness are their institutions and canons, suited alike to acquiring, increasing, and preserving virtues, and to avoiding, diminishing, and expelling vices, faults, and sins. These are necessarily many and various, because the spiritual sicknesses against which they must be promulgated are many and various.

II. But the one virtue of obedience adorns and strengthens all virtues; it multiplies and sanctifies, surrounds and perpetuates them. It adorns through beauty, strengthens unto fortitude, multiplies unto increase, sanctifies unto merit, surrounds unto security, and perpetuates unto immortality. You, brothers, promised this virtue—upon which the fruit of the other virtues depends—to your Father, as we recalled to your memory in the sermon immediately preceding this one.

No cenobite ought to live without this promise, because without it he can by no means be a true cenobite. Yet it was not formerly imposed by necessity upon those who had placed their necks under the light and sweet yoke of religious life, because their superiors had no need to demand from them the good of obedience. For it was certainly known of them that, even without any promise, they were prepared to practice it courageously and perseveringly.

For how many men of admirable virtue do we read that there were in that ancient age of religious life! They were bound by no bond of promise to render obedience to their superiors, yet they ardently and effectively carried out the whole breadth of charity and fervor of devout dedication, ascending each of its steps, even to the very end of their lives.

> [Note: Col. 0595. See, if you please, what is noted on this matter in John Cassian, *Institutes*, book IV, chapter 33.]

But after this outward habit had covered the multitude of humility [the transmitted wording is difficult], there appeared also no small scarcity of genuinely religious persons. For the number of cenobites was thereafter greater in the sight of men, but the perfection of cenobitic practice was smaller before that hidden Inspector, according to Isaiah: “You have multiplied the nation, but have not increased its joy” (Isa. IX, 3). Hence arose the saying that there were many wearers of caps (*cappati*) but few canons; very few living in monastic perfection, though wearers of cowls (*cucullati*) had multiplied beyond number.

The monastery also received everyone, just as it now receives them, after the likeness of that Gospel net gathering fish of every kind (Matt. XIII, 47); and, as we see constantly occurring in this wretched and pitiable age—or in a most foul time—it either retained the sluggish or vomited forth those who had fallen back into their former coldness. From this there resulted for them two dreadful evils: because they did not know that they had promised obedience to their superiors, they supposed that they were permitted either to live laxly in the vocation they had undertaken or to abandon it at their pleasure. These evils, I would say, are like two deadly wounds by which any cenobite incurs harm to his own soul, unless he is helped by the remedy of repentance.

III. To prevent these wounds when absent and heal them when present, the holy Fathers found vows of obedience to be fitting remedies, so that through them elders might have full authority both to rekindle the lukewarm, lest they freeze entirely, and to restrain the wavering, lest they fall backward. For, seeing the great lukewarmness and instability of this multitude, they judged that promises of obedience should be required from the person who was still knocking, before he was permitted fully to enter. Thus, when the cenobite saw that he had been bound by his own words through obedience promised to his superior in Christ until death, he might know that great harm threatened his soul if he did not render his vows, which his lips had declared in this matter (Ps. LXV, 14).

Moreover, superiors would know that they must preserve in fervor those whom they knew had promised obedience in Christ, lest they grow lukewarm; and establish firmly those whom they knew had promised that same obedience in Christ until death, lest they vanish away.

Therefore, my brother, lest you think that you may either remain lukewarm in the place to which, in giving yourself, you offered yourself and, in offering yourself, gave yourself; or, when you wish, abandon the new life of holiness which you have undertaken to practice: know that you have made this promise, by whose vow you are bound to obey your Father both in Christ and until death.

IV. But suppose you have kept these things from the very hour of your profession, running well in this way and not even today turning aside to the right or to the left.
