Yet behold, you think: “I promised obedience to my Father until death. Whose death? Whether mine or his, I am not greatly troubled. If he survives me, I shall not be able, as long as I live, to be released from the yoke of obedience which I promised him. But if I survive him, I shall rejoice that the yoke of obedience has been cast from my neck, because he who has died—the one to whom I promised obedience—was he alone. Henceforth I may belong to myself, because the end of the obedience I promised and the end of his life are one and the same.”

O what a thought, and what kind of thought is this! Why should it not become the occasion of a certain spiritual wound in you? For one walks in this life amid the snares of the ancient enemy, namely his fiery darts; and no one is made altogether safe from their blows unless protected by the shield of obedience. For he has no one, and therefore has no one by whom to defend himself against these darts: he has no advocate when he has no Father to obey.

You know that a traveler making his way is often asked by those he meets about his master, and they customarily say to him: “Whose servant are you?” When they hear the name of his master, the more honorable they recognize him to be, the more they also show deference to his servant. But in what will they see fit to show deference to him if he declares that he belongs to no one? Certainly, not only is no deference usually shown in any respect to such a person; much is also taken from him, and perhaps often everything that he has. And everything indeed: because he himself and his possessions are his wealth and life. Yet he would preserve everything if he had a master who inspired fear and love in those people.

And why these examples? Surely so that you may know that your own case is at stake in them and that in this mirror set before you, you ought to look upon your own face. Is not making your way the same as living your life? For while you live, your way is your life. And if in this way you have a guide and instructor, with what safety do you walk through it? Do not say that the rein of obedience has been loosened for you because you see that the man to whom you remember promising it is dead; for to say this is to wound yourself.

Against this wound the holy Fathers provided a suitable and effective remedy. “And when,” you ask, “did they provide it?” When they ordained that, in your profession, you should vow to render obedience not only to the one who perhaps is now dead, but also to his successors.

V. And you have certainly done this yourself. For these are your words on these matters in that same profession of yours: “I promise,” you said, “obedience until death in Christ to the Father of the aforesaid Church and to his successors.” Do you see that, just as you are bound to render obedience to him, so also to his successors? This too is signified by the fact that the Lord’s table in the tabernacle was never without bread; for when one was perhaps removed, another was customarily substituted in his place [Col. 0597C] (Lev. 24:5–8). Thus holy teachers are always present in the holy Church, and hearers are never lacking; for sons cannot be wanting while fathers are not wanting. Nor in a monastery can monks, who are bound by their obligation to obey, cease to owe obedience when the father to whom they vowed obedience has died, so long as his successors do not fail.

You said, therefore, “and to his successors.” And why not “to his successor”? Surely, that you may know that you ought to obey not one only, but all his successors; and that only when absolutely no one succeeds your father—the one to whom you promised obedience—in the place where you promised your stability, do you owe obedience to no one. Yet in all this you must observe that you promised obedience to those successors of your father who are elected regularly, not forcibly [Col. 0597D] intruded. For this too seems to be indicated by what follows in your oft-mentioned profession: “whom the sounder part of the canonical congregation shall elect.” It is necessary, therefore, as these words imply, that there be both a canonical congregation and a sounder part of that canonical congregation, to whom the election of your father’s successors may be entrusted. But if the congregation itself is not canonical, how can any part of it be sound? Election must by no means be entrusted to a congregation of that kind, because an irregular congregation will choose only an irregular person.

Thus Saint Father Benedict, filled with the spirit of all the righteous, removes from such a congregation the authority of election in the Rule for Monks [Note: [Col. 0597D] Saint Benedict’s ruling on this subject, chapter 64.] and entrusts it to the diocesan bishop, the abbots, and the faithful who live nearby. For he writes as follows:

> “If indeed the whole congregation, God forbid, unanimously chooses a person consenting to its vices, and those vices somehow come to the bishop’s notice—to whose diocese that place belongs—or become known to the abbots or neighboring Christians, let them prevent the counsel of the wicked from prevailing and appoint a worthy steward for the house of God. Let them know that for this they will receive a good reward, if they do it chastely and with zeal for God; but, conversely, that it is sin if they neglect it.”

The congregation, therefore, must be canonical if the election too is to be canonical. It must also be understood that, just as there are many members in one body, and although each is good, not all possess the same preeminence in dignity [Col. 0598B] (1 Cor. 12:12), so there are many parts in one canonical congregation; and although perhaps each is sound, some are sounder than others. I speak here not of bodily but of spiritual soundness. For just as the election of a superior is a great and preeminent affair, so it must be entrusted precisely to that part which is soundest in the whole canonical congregation.

VI. “And which,” you ask, “is to be regarded as that sounder part?” Whatever it may be, I venture without hesitation to say and assert that violence and cunning are very apt to obstruct a canonical election. Violence oppresses openly; [Col. 0598C] cunning aims to deceive through hidden contrivances. Envy and hope, fear and softness, both reveal the fraudulence of this cunning and confirm it in being and persistence.

These four are the cause, in this matter, of wicked little gatherings being held in corners; whispering in ears; malicious agreements being arranged; words being sown; hands being joined; sacred things being touched; letters being dispatched and messages sent; promises smiling and threats thundering; judgment being rendered; and something utterly contrary to God being irrevocably decreed. And behold: in a clamorous silence, each of these hidden deceivers gives utterance in the heart.

For envious spite says: “Far be it that he should be set over me; for that would be a great disgrace to me. One whom until now I have had as my equal, and very often as my inferior, ought not to be my superior. He is younger in age; he shall not be greater in rank. Unskilled in learning and impeded in speech, he is plainly unworthy to preside over those of keen understanding and polished utterance. The nobility of birth does not shine in him; nor does bodily bearing have fitness. Why should he not disfigure the beauty of the chair? It is altogether inglorious that one so base should sit in an exalted place.”

Hope too has its voice: “Behold, the election of a superior is under discussion. I think the lot will fall upon me. It would be strange if anyone else were even mentioned alongside me. For whom could they allow to approach me in this matter—much less to precede me? The first would in some way be superfluous; the second wholly unjust. For who is my equal, or who like me? [Col. 0599A] To seek someone greater than myself—what is it but to waste oneself in foolish labor?” (Exod. 18:18.) “Oh, that all this people were in my hand, so that all who have a case might come to me and I might judge justly!” (2 Sam. 15:4–5.) “And who would not consider me worthy to be chosen, except one who does not know me? And how happy those will be who have me as their superior! What great and noble things I shall do—so new, so many, so unheard-of! Who will do them if I am not that man? It is surely unworthy both that I should not be chosen and that these things should not be done.”

VII. Yet how often one of this kind falls from his hope and another performs the office which he expected, so that, though late, he discovers that he has seen a dream while awake. He desires it for himself, and it is given to another; what he hopes for himself another receives—perhaps the very person from whom he had hoped least and whom he loved least—as we formerly read befell Haman in the book of Esther. For he supposed that the king wished to honor no one but himself. When the king asked him, he gave, for himself, the recommendation which he groaned to see given and which, contrary to his expectation, he immediately saw fulfilled in another. And how much, do you think, was added to his pain when he saw bestowed upon the man whom he hated above all others what he had desired in hope and hoped for in desire? He was finally compelled to honor the very man whom he had chosen to hand over to an ignominious death rather than allow him a life in some manner glorious.

Thus the exalted height of rank often despises its seekers and seeks those who disdain it; it withdraws itself from those who desire it and thrusts itself upon those unwilling to receive it. And [Col. 0599C] what does fear say? When one who shrinks from the rigor of discipline perceives that mention is being made of the person who loves discipline, he is cast down by cowardly fear. That same fear, having shaken and constricted him, incites him to resistance, crying with loud voices both before him and within him:

“By no means let this happen! For he is a man of blood and a man of Belial” (2 Sam. 16:7). “He is without affection, without covenant, without mercy; he disturbs peace and overthrows tranquillity. His mind is always in dispute, and his belly prepares quarrels. His teeth are weapons and arrows, and his tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5). “Conquered by anger, he will overthrow all his household in order to crush them. He wants everyone to fear him and no one to love him. He finds it sweeter than honey to flay those entrusted to him, and he will permit no one to be at rest. This is what I say in one word: to set this man over subjects is to entrust sheep to a wolf to be fed. Do not appoint him leader of the people, lest he eat the flesh of the humble and drink the blood of souls. He will scatter, not gather; making the number of his subjects small and seeking no fruit from them.”

VIII. But what is the voice uttered by softness? Certainly these three preceding evils usually resist, lest a worthy man be admitted; but this fourth presses and persists that an unworthy man be chosen. It presses and resists in this manner:

“Behold a blameless man, a man of peace and quiet, an altogether pleasant man, who has mercy and lends, who orders his words in judgment [Col. 0600A] (Ps. 111:5). He is merciful and gentle, kind and sweet, incapable of anger. Let us choose him: he will cherish us and favor us. He will speak agreeable things to us” (Isa. 30:10); “nor shall we find him resisting our unlawful desires. He will not disagree with us, whatever it may be that we want. He will rule over us, but only as a shadow; for in reality we shall be his superiors. We shall command as we please, and he will obey without delay; for he will not dare act otherwise. He will show himself to us as Titus, not Timothy: gentle, not harsh; tranquil, not troubling. He will not correct or rebuke us; for whatever we do will please him. And, that we may all hear the conclusion of the whole matter” (Eccles. 12:13), “we shall not find a superior more suitable for ourselves—not one even among a thousand.”

Therefore, those among whom these four evils are found do not seem to me to belong to the sounder part of the canonical congregation. But you, brothers, must not be so.

IX. We beseech you in the Lord Jesus: when you gather to make an election, make it an election according to God, insofar as knowledge enables you to know and ability enables you to act. First of all, we earnestly exhort you and implore you by the dreadful name of the Lord that none of you should seek anything in it that is against God; nor should anyone attend to a private love or hatred, if perhaps—God forbid—he has one. Not love, I say, so that one known to be unworthy may be admitted; not hatred, so that one known to be worthy may be excluded.

For if, far be this from you, you should wish to elect someone on account of any kinship, for example, or carnal friendship, or any other cause contrary to God, so that you may be permitted to act more laxly under him, you will indeed incur a most grievous guilt; and what you desire in hope and hope for in desire you will never afterward obtain. For he whom you admit under such a hope will afterward be far harsher toward you [Col. 0600C] than some other man whom you exclude out of fear. He who “takes the wise in their own craftiness” and scatters the counsels of the wicked (Job 5:13) so gently orders matters that what you seek with an unrighteous intention you do not find through his righteous disposition, and what you flee contrary to his good pleasure you incur through his judgment. For how often do we see all this happen in precisely this way.

Therefore, once every coercive violence and stealthy cunning have been removed from the midst, admit the man whom either the common counsel and agreement of all decrees should be admitted; or, if in order to avoid contention it is perhaps not expedient that all be present together in deliberation, let him without hesitation be chosen whom the sounder part of the canonical congregation judges, according to God, your Rule, and your Order, to be chosen [Col. 0600D].

X. But if you ask what part of the congregation is to be considered sounder, I do not think that the more numerous part is always the sounder; rather, it is that part which, though small in number, is shown to be sound by knowledge of truth, love of virtue, and rectitude of intention [Col. 0601A]. For this is the spiritual and true soundness of the heart: to know what is true; to love what is good; and in both to will to please him alone who is supreme Truth and Goodness.

Election, therefore, must be entrusted to such persons; the election of such persons must likewise be approved, confirmed, and held valid—persons who, insofar as human examination is concerned, know who ought to be elected according to God, choose him without hesitation, and do so for God’s cause alone. But those from whom, in an election, blindness removes knowledge of truth, cupidity takes away love of virtue, and vanity deprives of rectitude of intention—although a multitude grants them numerical strength—do not seem to me to possess true soundness.

Therefore Benedict, father and leader of monks, likewise writes concerning the election of an abbot:

> “In the appointment of an abbot, let this principle always be observed: that the one be appointed whom the whole congregation, in harmony and according to the fear of God, or even a sounder part of the congregation, though small, has chosen by counsel.”

After devout prayer, decide diligently and carefully among yourselves concerning the person to be elected. You ought to examine him with all the more concern while he is still to be chosen, since you have less right to criticize him once he has been chosen. For it is foolish—and worse than any civil war—to keep criticizing the man whom you must continually have as such; just as a woman complains in vain of her husband’s deformity when the law of marriage compels her to cleave to him without ceasing [Col. 0601C]. You must deliberate before, therefore, and persevere afterward. And the perseverance which follows will be easier and stronger to endure in proportion as the caution in the preceding deliberation has been greater and more discerning.

You have, then, what is to be considered the sounder part of the canonical congregation, and how your father’s successors are to be chosen. Your profession has made you liable and indebted to obey them.

XI. Behold, brothers, how far our discourse has proceeded in these twelve sermons, he himself directing our tongue, without whom we are unable—not merely to do or speak anything good, but even to think it. We have shown you, as far as we could, what our Order is, what its habit is, and what true profession is; and how this threefold badge adorns us: how the first part raises us up, what the second forms in us, and how the third binds us.

Three other goods likewise adorn, sanctify, and strengthen us: reading, action, prayer—these three. Reading enlightens; action nourishes; prayer kindles. Our practice ought to occupy itself with one of these, succeeding another according to place and time: so that the first may grant us clarity, that we may plainly recognize what is true; the second may work usefulness within us, that we may act manfully in what is good; and the third may pour inward purity into our hearts, that we may ardently sigh after what is blessed.

[Col. 0602A] O the true, the good, the blessed! The first drives error from us; the second removes lukewarmness from us; by love we ascend within ourselves to the third. For reading clarifies study; action makes practice fruitful; prayer kindles desire. O study, practice, desire! Study of wisdom, practice of justice, desire of glory: of wisdom, for clarity within yourself; of justice, for usefulness toward your neighbor; of glory, for blessedness with God.

As I say this, I recall that there were once three things in the tabernacle of Moses, outside the veil, as precious as they were holy: the lampstand, the table, and the altar (Exod. 40:20, 22, 24). In the lampstand was light, for illumination; on the table was bread, for [Col. 0602B] refreshment; on the altar was incense, which used to emit a sweet fragrance. What illuminates the darkness in a human being except the keen study of wisdom? If you doubt whether wisdom enlightens, ask holy David, and he will tell you that “the unfolding of the words of the Lord gives light and gives understanding to the little ones” (Ps. 118:103).

And what spiritually fattens a person by driving far away his inward leanness, except the necessary practice of justice? That the vigor of good action is, in some manner, a richness of inward refreshment, let the Lord himself assure you, who says of himself: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, that I may complete his work” (John 4:34). A good work is good food for him.

And what gives forth a sweet fragrance before God in our inmost parts except the desire for eternal glory joined with pure prayer? Let the Psalmist assure us that pure prayer is a certain sweet fragrance of incense before God, when, addressing the Lord, he asks that his prayer be directed like incense in his sight (Ps. 140:2). Desire itself too is prayer, according to the words: “Your ear has heard the desire of their heart” (Ps. 9:17).

XII. Brothers, we are still in the outer tabernacle of Moses. Who is this Moses? Christ. For he is the one who “received words of life to give to us” (Acts 7:38), speaking to us what he heard from the Father. This tabernacle is holy indeed, yet it is outside the veil. For it is the holy Church, still journeying [Col. 0602D] in this world. Your state also is holy and religious, because the outer tabernacle too is called holy.

Therefore, as long as you remain in it, have a lampstand by which you may see when enlightened; have a table at which you may grow rich when refreshed; and finally have an altar upon which, with the sweetest love of inward desire, you may offer to God the incense of your prayers. But for reading to be fruitful, it is necessary that pure meditation both accompany and follow it. For to read and not understand is to neglect. Likewise, what has been illuminated in you by the preceding reading is immediately extinguished by forgetfulness if no subsequent recollection preserves it in its illumination.

Therefore let holy Isaac go out with you—indeed, within you—into the field to meditate (Gen. XIV, 63), so that, possessing sincere joy in the conscience through the Holy Spirit, you may devote yourself to sacred reading with unclouded meditation. Is not this field sacred Scripture, adorned in a wonderful unity by the variety, and in a varied unity by the innumerable senses, as though wreathed with diverse sweet-smelling flowers and shining with ineffable beauty? Nor will you deserve to be numbered among the clean animals according to the Law, if you do not bring back for rumination the food already swallowed [Col. 0603A] (Lev. 11).

When we sit in the cloister for reading, each of us is directed by the institution of the Order to read in his own book; nor are we permitted to disturb ourselves by raising questions. For, if the study of reading is to claim the whole person for itself, quiet seclusion and secluded quiet must not be lacking to it. The cloister is the place of reading and meditation, and often also of prayer. Hence it is generally instituted among us that continuous silence be observed in the cloister, lest the noise of tumultuous conversation hinder goods so great and such as these.

Likewise, the practice of good work ought to be accompanied by the quiet of silence, so that while the hand is occupied in good work, the mind too may not be released from its office. It is also the mind’s duty to apply itself to purity of meditation, so that it may be wholly free from its body, although the body applies itself to its own task [the bracketed reading in the source is uncertain].

XIII. We have known very many religious men who, while engaged in outward labor, persisted in inward meditation; and who, at the hour of labor, by turning over and over in their minds what they had, as it were, eaten at the hour of reading in the cloister from the life-giving nourishment of sacred Scripture, bound it more firmly in memory with the knots of continual rumination [Col. 0603C].

Bodily usefulness alone ought not to be our reason for going out to external manual labor; spiritual usefulness must accompany it. And what is that? Certainly that we may devote ourselves to psalms and attend to meditations. But the discipline of silence will provide the opportunity for persevering in these two practices. Hence we are commanded, when we arrive at work, not to multiply signs among ourselves; nor to presume to speak, except perhaps briefly, necessarily, and quietly with the prior, concerning the work itself and apart from the brothers.

Behold what speech is permitted us at work. But we must carefully observe what we speak about, when, how much, how, with whom, and where. If anyone asks “what?”—certainly, about the work itself. “How much?”—briefly, without doubt. “When?”—only when it is necessary. “How?”—quietly. [Col. 0603D] “With whom?”—with the one who is prior over the work. “Where?”—certainly apart from the brothers.

Why, brothers, do we mark these matters so precisely? That each of you may recognize, rather than merely know, that he acts against the statutes of his Order if he presumes to speak during work either about something else, or more than this, or at another time, or otherwise, or with someone else, or elsewhere than is here specified.

We are also forbidden to multiply signs among ourselves, lest, when the sounds of words are silent—words which often soften the inward hardness of the heart—the gestures of fingers become tumultuous. Indeed, excessive gesturing with the fingers usually cannot appear unless it is preceded or accompanied by much talk in the heart; for when their many motions make a noise, it is evident proof that no discipline of silence restrains such persons. Certainly the perfect men in the community ought to abhor superfluous signs just as they do words—understand, superfluous words—lest they consider themselves silent when, without necessity and reasonable cause, they change the hand into a tongue.

When we rest, we are forbidden to make signs to one another, so that, while the hand is not occupied in work, the mind may devote itself more freely and readily to its own work. This it cannot do when a tumult of signs intruding from outside devastates its inward quiet. We are also commanded to rest beside the prior. Why do you think this is? Perhaps so that those things which pertain to them may be close at hand: for those anxious to keep order, a safeguard; and for those inclined to neglect it, a witness [Col. 0604B].

Behold that we ought not to abandon the maturity of silence in our work, since the Apostle also commands us to work in silence (2 Thess. 3:12). Once and again, far be it from every religious community accustomed to manual work that it should neglect silence during labor. For since, according to Isaiah, “the work of justice is silence” (Isa. 32:17), there you lose the cultivation of justice where you abandon the rigor of silence.

XIV. Prayer, the third practice which we said cenobites ought to pursue, must be practiced with all the more diligence because in it we are presented more especially to Almighty God. The Apostle himself teaches us by his example how we ought to pray and sing psalms: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind. I will sing psalms with the spirit; I will sing psalms also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15).

And these are the words of Blessed Benedict on these matters:

> “We believe that the divine presence is everywhere, and that the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil in every place” (Prov. 15:3). “But without any doubt we should especially believe this when we stand at the divine office. Therefore let us always remember what the Prophet says: ‘Serve the Lord in fear’” (Ps. 2:11). “And again: ‘Sing psalms wisely’” (Ps. 46:8). “And: ‘I will sing psalms to you in the sight of angels’” (Ps. 137:1). “Therefore let us consider how we ought to be in the sight of the Godhead and of his angels, and thus stand for psalmody, so that [Col. 0604D] our mind may accord with our voice.”

And again:

> “If, when we wish to submit some request to powerful people, we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence, how much more ought we to make supplication to the Lord God of all with every humility and devotion of purity? And let us know that we are heard not for much speaking, but for purity of heart and compunction of tears. Therefore prayer ought to be brief and pure, unless perhaps it be prolonged by the movement of inspiration from divine grace.”

XV. This is the threefold practice of holy religion to which cenobites ought continually to apply themselves: in the first, providing for themselves; in the second, assisting their neighbors; in the third, offering themselves to God. Thus they live soberly in the first, justly in the second, and devoutly in the third [Col. 0605A] in this world, although they are not of this world; and consequently they await in security the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God—provided that they are enlightened within themselves in the first, ready toward their neighbors in the second, and devoted to God in the third.

To add also the places in which these three marks of holy religion are customarily practiced: the oratory and cloister, refectory and dormitory, audience-room and chapter-house are their workshops. In the oratory you also have your father’s command to do nothing except that for which it was made and from which it took its name. In it nothing in your sitting or standing, nothing in your walking or any movement, should appear among you that may offend either human, angelic, or divine sight, but only what befits your holiness.

Since you ought to be holy in every place, and this place is holier than other places, so ought you to be holier in it. Therefore, insofar as the gracious power of Almighty God grants you ability, display outwardly before those who see the face nothing unreligious in gesture or expression; and turn over inwardly before him who beholds the very depths of the heart nothing impure in thought or affection. Rather, “with the door shut,” praying in your chamber to your Father (Matt. 6:6), conduct yourselves inwardly and outwardly so that what sounds among you may please human ears, what appears among you may please human eyes, and neither of these—together with what you ponder within the innermost recesses of your mind—may displease divine eyes [Col. 0605B].

XVI. In the cloister, as we briefly touched on above, your custom by ancient institution is to maintain continuous silence, lest the noise of speech hinder those who, according to the devotion which each possesses, delight in attending either to reading, meditation, or indeed sweet psalms.

In the refectory, careful gravity of expression and bearing, and likewise a grave propriety, must be observed; sobriety in tasting must also be observed, so that nothing be present for excess and nothing lacking for necessity. Above all, the eye must be restrained at table; and every unlawful movement of each individual member must be held under the rigor of discipline, so that no one among you whose office does not require it may curiously survey what is being done by others [Col. 0605D], nor make himself too conspicuous by behaving in an unregulated manner.

The dormitory is a place of bodily rest; among you, however, it ought also to be a place of spiritual rest. In the dormitory too the brothers ought to remain with themselves. No one whose office does not require it may curiously investigate what belongs to another. He does not preserve the propriety of religious life who at any hour allows his head or face to remain uncovered in the dormitory. No tumult, no noise, ought to resound there.

XVII. Brothers are permitted to enter the audience-room, but only when necessity requires it. The rule of the audience-room among us is that it admit no more than three persons. One of them shall be the prior, or someone appointed by him, that he may be present as witness to the other two—unless, perhaps, clear and reasonable necessity advises the prior himself to summon more persons [Col. 0606A]. Such is the institution laid down by our fathers concerning these matters:

> “Let them never enter the audience-room without permission. There no more than two shall speak together, in the presence of the prior or another whom he has sent; and they shall do this standing, unless the prior judges that, for some necessity, more persons should be summoned to him. When that for which they entered has been completed, let them leave quickly, unless they are detained.”

Why are more than two forbidden to speak there? Lest perhaps the conversation of many force them to irritate or provoke one another; or lest they conspire together in malicious agreement—or, if it is more fittingly expressed, in an agreement of malice. And why in the presence of the prior or someone sent by him? Surely that by the propriety of his presence he may commend good speech and by his severity restrain bad speech; or rather, what is better, that he may strive to forestall any evil there.

Why, do you think, are they commanded to speak standing? Lest the conversation be extended into too long a delay. Thus entry into the audience-room is granted to few, and only when necessary; and their departure too is commanded to be swift. Yet continual experience assures us that the saying of Ambrose is true: “I know many who speak, though they do not know how to be silent.”

Those are indeed like such people who, though no necessity calls for it, seek entrance to the audience-room most importunately merely in order to weave tales, and are neither weary nor ashamed of lingering there [Col. 0606C]. Standing there, chatterers and babblers find it so sweet to weave tales that they think every delay they make there to be no delay at all, and, unaware or forgetful of all delay, do not know how to leave until the signal is sounded and they must enter the oratory.

I marvel that their legs are so strong and sound in the audience-room, while I see them so weak and infirm in the oratory: that they can stand tirelessly for almost the whole day in the audience-room while talking idly, though in choir they can scarcely stand in prayer until the end of a single psalm without great difficulty. Whence comes this superfluous and prolonged talk except that ignorance of silence is the cause of such speech? Such men can therefore rightly be compared with those whom Blessed Ambrose knows to speak, though they do not know how to be silent.

XVIII. Who is, or can be, so religious and diligent in the community that negligence does not sometimes steal upon him in one of these places? Therefore the sixth workshop is the chapter-house, in which, according to the tenor of the Order, what is committed amiss before others in the five preceding places is customarily corrected before others strictly but without excessive harshness, devoutly but without immoderate leniency. In this place no more terror or delay of dispute ought to be admitted than Satan can remain forever in heavenly blessedness [Col. 0606D].

For the chapter-house is a place of humility, not of exaltation; of accusation, not of excuse. Few words should be uttered there, and those reasonable words—reasonable in such a way as befits such a place. They are the words which accuse, correct, absolve, and instruct. Let the person conscious of guilt accuse himself; let the brothers accuse one another; let the one in charge correct, absolve the corrected, and instruct the ignorant. These are the words which ought to be spoken in chapter.

But when discussion of external business is admitted in chapter, the discipline of correction is generally not maintained. Once it is not maintained, an indiscriminate license of speaking is indulged; once that has been allowed, something is uttered by which the hearer is provoked to anger. Thus quarrels arise and disputes grow; and the house of confession becomes a place of confusion.

Among you, however, not everyone may speak in chapter at random, nor may anyone speak there about every matter. For your Order has an institution on this subject in the following form:

> “In chapter, let brothers never speak except for two reasons: namely, by simply stating their own faults or those of others, or by answering only such questions as their superiors put to them [Col. 0607B]. Let no one raise an accusation against anyone upon mere suspicion.”

And a little above:

> “He who accuses anyone shall not use circumlocutions in his accusation, but shall say openly: ‘That man did this.’ But the accused person, as soon as he hears his name, without replying, shall ask pardon at his seat.”

This is a holy and salutary institution both for the accuser and for the accused: that the former may accuse moderately and truthfully, and the latter may not excuse himself, remaining moderately silent. The command that the accused person, on hearing his name, say nothing but ask pardon seems especially to breathe the humility and gentleness of him of whom it is written: “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a sheep before its shearer was silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7); and likewise of whom it is recorded that, “when he was accused by many, he answered nothing” (Matt. 27:12).

And what would be the humility of chapter if every accused person were permitted to excuse himself in words? Or what benefit is there, when it is clear that a fault which is excused is doubled? Do we not come to chapter so that we may accuse ourselves and be charitably accused by others, and thus be absolved from our offenses? The former is humility; the latter, usefulness. And how shameful and dangerous it is, through the vice of excuse, both to be proud in the place of humility, deny in the place of confession, and be bound more tightly in sin in the place of absolution.

[Col. 0607D] XIX. But perhaps someone among those who will read these ordinances in writing may address me thus in reply: “What you say concerning self-excuse ought indeed to be observed by one who is accused truthfully and charitably; but if someone is accused maliciously and falsely, as sometimes happens, does he sin if he excuses himself?” Our answer to him is this: even if we say that it is not a great sin for a righteous man to excuse himself, yet we may say that it is no great merit for an unrighteous man not to excuse himself. He may indeed obtain pardon and escape punishment; but he merits neither the grace nor the glory to which righteous persons who do not excuse themselves are raised in holiness and blessedness. The former is good; the latter is better. And it is better because it leads [Col. 0608A] to what is best.

You know, certainly, that on the day of the Lord’s Passion three were suspended upon crosses: namely, the blaspheming thief, the confessing thief, and the innocent Lamb himself. And what else are we to regard the severity of chapter as but a kind of passion of the cross? Yet in this suffering some blaspheme, some confess, and some are innocent. The first are rebels; the second penitents; the third humble persons. The first merit punishment; the second pardon; the third glory. The blaspheming thief signifies the first; the other thief—and truly another, because he does not blaspheme but confesses—the second; the innocent and humble Jesus, the third.

Although all are in one and the same suffering, the first murmurs and does what he ought not; the second prays and does what he ought; the third offers himself for others and does [Col. 0608B] more than he ought. And though all are accused, the first is accused justly and, defending his wickedness through pride, falls into the hell of sin. The second is accused not unjustly; recognizing his fault through confession and converting necessity into willingness, he is reconciled by the superior’s absolution; made from a thief into a martyr, he enters the paradise of the Church. But the third is accused altogether unjustly; not excusing his innocence, through the silent testimony of a good conscience, through complete contempt for all vain glory, through an unconquerable triumph over himself, he ascends even to heaven in his mind.

You see, therefore, my brother, that as far as the suffering of the innocent Redeemer differs from that of the confessing thief, so far [Col. 0608C] does the case of one maliciously and falsely accused differ from that of one charitably and truthfully charged; and as they are unequal in merit, so they will not be equal in reward. If a person falsely charged excuses himself, then, provided the severity of chapter permits his excuse, he does not fall through sin; yet neither does he rise through merit. And while he is not innocently punished in chapter, he is indeed not condemned in hell; but neither is he sublimely crowned in heaven.

XX. There is a certain workshop, seventh in the order, in which holy men of the community, when the Lord comes and finds them watching and knocks, open to him at once (Luke 12:37): when they depart from it through death, they pass from the number six, signifying present perfection, to the number seven, signifying future rest. [Col. 0608D] It is the infirmary, in which cenobites ought so to conduct themselves that they may safely await there the dreadful hour of their dissolution. Mercy must bend and condescend through compassion to each person’s infirmities in such a manner that the order suffers no dissolution.

Let no pretenders be admitted there—those who, though healthy, commonly feign some illness. And let those who are ill return to their happier customary observance when they have recovered their former strength, an observance which befits servants of God all the more because they need it less. What follows? Let not the pleasure of food hold those now vigorous whom necessity had relieved when ill.

Let the brothers who are in the infirmary consider that in this place their souls will be loosed from their bodies and carried away to the tribunal of the Judge, there to receive according to what they have done [Col. 0609A] in their bodies, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). Whatever sins they have committed elsewhere, let them strive to amend here by fitting penitence and pure confession. And, as we have already said, let them so conduct themselves that they may both confidently await the terrible hour of their departure, now impending, and receive it securely when present.

Brothers, let these things be your meditation. Let these things be your continual exercise. “This is the way; walk in it, and turn neither to the right nor to the left” (Isa. 30:21). Hence it was that [Col. 0610A] at the beginning of the first sermon—of which this is the fourteenth in sequence—we recalled to your memory those words of the Apostle: “I beseech you, therefore, I who am bound in the Lord, that you walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called” (Eph. 4:1). Walk worthily, then, as we have taken care, with God’s help, to exhort you; so that, walking thus from strength to strength, you may be worthy to see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83:8), living and reigning, Three and One, unto infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0609]

# ON THE THREEFOLD TABERNACLE

## PREFACES

### I. Letter of Brother Adam, a canon, to the canons of the Church of Prémontré, concerning the book and picture of the threefold tabernacle; and concerning the primacy and dignity of that same Church, by which it excels the other Churches of the same order.

[Col. 0609B] To his most reverend lords and foremost friends, brothers most dearly beloved in the inward mercies of Christ, serving God in the Church of Prémontré: Brother ADAM, your humble servant and sincere friend in the Lord, wishes, in Bethany, having received a pound of costly genuine nard, to anoint the Lord’s feet and fill the house with the fragrance of the ointment.

I. To speak the truth without disguise, O men of venerable life, we are exceedingly astonished and rejoice, and even as we rejoice we are no less astonished, whenever we remember how your exaltedness deigned to receive our lowliness when we came to you, to entertain us while we remained with you, and to dismiss us when we departed. This threefold devotion of yours was itself surely witness that our arrival pleased you somewhat, [Col. 0609C] and our departure displeased you no less. And lest, as sometimes happens, satiety should produce disgust, even our delay seemed to you no delay at all.

We say nothing of how celebrated our name is among you, though it is unworthy even to be named. Nor shall we recount how often you declared that you desired our return, and that our voice sounded sweet in your ears—although neither is our voice sweet nor our face lovely (Song 2:14). Someone may say that the word of God must be honoured with equal reverence in every person, and that the greatness of what is uttered cannot be diminished by however great the insignificance of its speaker. We do not dispute this. Yet we know that wine sometimes has a better flavour in a golden vessel than in a wooden one.

And, to add this also, we know that you abound in good liquor and also in precious vessels from which you can draw, indeed abundantly, whenever you wish. [Col. 0609D] O how much joy mingled with wonder, and wonder mingled with joy, does the remembrance of your affection toward us bring us! We grind this remembrance with the pestle of our heart in its little mortar, and the sweetness of the fragrance that it sends forth refreshes our inmost being. Therefore we marvel and rejoice: we rejoice because we have merited to receive such gifts; and we marvel because you have deigned to confer them upon one so small, though you are so great.

II. For what are we? Or who are we—what kind of persons, or how important—that you should have brought us so far? If the question concerns these matters: first, our nature itself is subject to the corruption of fault and the affliction of punishment, miserably defiled by the one and punished by the other. Secondly, the person is altogether contemptible: he possesses absolutely neither merit in the third respect nor eminence in the fourth. Thus the first is foul through the weakness of a frail condition; the second, through the manifold poverty of his personhood, presents what is lowly; the third, through lack of all sanctity, renders him in no way radiant with beauty; and the fourth is not raised by the summit of any dignity.

And what is our father’s house? A question might also be raised about this; even if it were something, it would especially matter in the eyes of those who have been lifted up and exalted above the height of the earth. Yet it will be easy to judge that, as regards us, this is no great thing, from the fact that he of whom none greater was born among women strove to prevent people from loudly insisting upon lineage and ancestors: “Do not begin,” he says, “to say, ‘We have Abraham for our father’” [Col. 0610D] (Luke 3:8).

But suppose that you have bestowed many great gifts upon one unworthy, placing at the head one who scarcely belongs at the tail: in the one matter you have shown that your hand is extended to give; in the other, that you are humble in your own eyes. O humble generosity and generous humility! One of these a neighbour accepts, seeing it on the face; the other God approves, searching the reins and hearts. But because you judged us worthy of such sweet embraces, you ought to seek from him a witness to these things in yourselves, and await from him the reward for them. His all-seeing eye is present to discern the merit of each labourer, and his almighty hand is not lacking to render the fitting recompense.

III. When we were bodily present with you—from whom, even now that we dwell in the kingdom of the Scots, we are not spiritually absent—you were pleased, in humility, to request what you had authority to command: namely, that we should send you the book which, two years ago, at the request of some of our brothers, and especially of a certain illustrious abbot John who lives in our land, we composed on the tabernacle of Moses, together with its illustration. What could we refuse you when you asked, or in what ought we not obey when you commanded? We therefore granted what you requested; and what we granted we confirmed by a promise, being “snared by the words of our own mouth” [Col. 0611B] (Prov. 6:2) and bound to you. Nor can we lawfully be released until we have fulfilled the promise itself.

Now we fulfil what we then promised; and just as we showed ourselves willing in promising, so we strive also to show ourselves truthful in rendering. For if it were a fault to deny those who ask, it would surely be the crime of sacrilege not to fulfil a promise made to them. Receive, then, what you requested and what we promised: certainly a small thing, yet sent with no small devotion. We pray that you may receive it with the same love with which we know it has been sent by us.

IV. How you may understand the illustration through the book and the book through the illustration; and how you ought to bring into a single harmony both what you read in the book and what you see in the illustration—you will see this in the letter which we sent to the aforesaid abbot, at whose request we also set hand to these matters. [Col. 0611C] You will find it written at the beginning of the book.

When you have read the book and looked at the illustration, we ask that your maturity may so censure in the latter the superstition of a curious man as your kindness may also accept in the former the intention of a diligent man. And what we are accustomed to offer humbly to all who look upon anything we have written in whatever manner, we offer also to you: namely, that if you discover anything set down by us otherwise than truth itself has it, you should by no means permit it to remain without suitable correction. For far be it from us—once and again, and always and everywhere far be it from us—that, puffed up by the swelling of pride, we should excuse an error plainly shown to us, or reject an amendment charitably offered.

V. You will keep this book, entitled *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, together with its illustration, and the book divided into fourteen sermons, entitled [Col. 0612A] *On the Name, Habit, and Profession of the Canons of the Order of Prémontré*, in remembrance of us. Since you cannot continually have our bodily presence among you, you may have something from us in which to retain our spiritual presence.

We earnestly commend ourselves to your prayers; we likewise lean confidently upon your merits, possessing in you what we see lacking in ourselves. We know for certain that we cannot be poor so long as you are rich. Therefore, with the knees of our mind bent, as though prostrate at your feet, we most earnestly beseech you to remember us in your evening sacrifices, to have compassion upon our manifold weaknesses, and to offer us for healing to the merciful gaze of our righteous, gentle, and meek Advocate, Jesus. What he did not owe for himself, he paid for us; made priest and victim for us, purchaser and price, sacrificer and sacrifice, physician of our wounds and medicine, he hung upon the wood, washing us unclean persons by the abundant outpouring of his gracious blood, reconciling us who were guilty; and now, seated at the right hand of the Father, he intercedes for us.

Remember, therefore, Adam the sinner, who loves you, when from the very innermost part of the golden altar you fill the Holy of Holies with the fragrant smoke of spices; and especially there where the Son is offered to the Father, whose blood cries from the ground more powerfully than Abel’s [Col. 0612B] (Gen. 4:10). We would add this also to our petitions, unless perhaps it were reckoned rash presumption: that after our death you would order our name to be inscribed in the roll of your holy congregation together with the names of your own brethren who have already departed, because we too are yours. Yet what our modesty does not presume to request, your kindness, as we hope, will give; for, unless we are mistaken, more wells up from the depth of the fountain of your riches than we dare draw from its surface. And so much concerning these matters.

VI. For the rest, O men of venerable life, “bear with a little of my foolishness; indeed, bear with me” (2 Cor. 11:1). “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God” (2 Cor. 11:2). We would propose to address you with some admonitory discourse, if there were either no presumption in it or any necessity for it: that is, if it were fitting for us to admonish you, or if you needed our admonition.

Nevertheless, your excellence should clearly know that, if one house of our order can surpass another, the principal house seems to be that which is first. It should also remember that saying of the Lord: “To whom much has been given, much will be required” [Col. 0612D] (Luke 12:48). And to what end are these words? Plainly, so that, considering how much you have received and also what you are, you may consequently know what you ought to be.

Is not the Church of Prémontré like a fountain, while the other Churches of the same order flow from it as streams from a spring? Let the fountain, therefore, guard itself against dryness, especially when its streams flow abundantly, lest it itself lack the water in which they abound. It precedes in time; it must also precede in holiness, lest, God forbid, it become worthy of the mockery of onlookers by arriving later when it began to run earlier. Nor will it be free from the same mockery if it merely arrives along with the others, unless it also comes to preside over them, because it is acknowledged to have taken the lead in the race. For it is the mother; the others are daughters. Therefore let it labour after spiritual works in such a way that this may be said to it by those who praise it: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” [Col. 0613A] (Prov. 31:29). Let the daughters rejoice that they have proceeded from a noble mother, that consequently they may rejoice to be noble themselves.

VII. The sole nobility of spiritual descent is the holiness of religious life. The daughters must constantly return to their mother and borrow from her what they see is lacking in themselves, so that they may receive growth in holy religion from her from whom they received their beginning. Therefore let a most brilliant lamp be set upon the lampstand in her, so that those who enter even into the daughter houses may see light. Most brilliant, I say, because a lamp dark in itself, though set far off, gives no illumination at all.

Let light shine abundantly in her, so that the mother may abundantly impart light to her daughters without diminishing it in herself in any respect. Let her be for them an example and pattern, a mirror also and, as it were, a book of life, in which they may plainly read what they ought to choose and what reject. In reading this book, let them see how ready affability should be at the gate; how effective, according to ability and occasion, person and cause, cheerfulness should be in hospitality; how great should be study in the cloister during reading, accompanied by perfect silence, with no half-chewed words and no superfluous signs of the fingers; [Col. 0613C] how grave and heartfelt devotion should be in choir; how mature reverence and careful cleanliness at the altar; how speech in the hearing-room should be without any murmuring, detraction, or conspiracy, brief and quiet, concerned only with necessities, and among very few persons; how few and how reasonable should be the words in chapter; how, according to person and cause, mercy should be severe and severity merciful in those who preside; how humble and true should confession be, and how steadfast patience in those confessing.

Let them see how discerning should be the zeal of those making accusations, and how absolutely absent all excuse and murmuring in those accused; how swift should be their readiness, and how ready their swiftness, in common manual work, accompanied by silence and free from superfluity of signs; how sober should be their decency and decent their sobriety in the refectory; how mature their rest and restful their maturity in the dormitory; how compassionate and helpful, diligent and gracious, infirmarians ought to be in the infirmary; how long-suffering in endurance, devoted in thanksgiving, not importunate in seeking superfluities, but cheerfully content with what is supplied to them, and in every way attentive in preparing themselves for the hour of their dissolution, the sick ought to be; how circumspect and honourable the brothers ought to be on a journey; and finally, how they must strive with all effort to appear irreproachable inwardly and outwardly, at every time and place, in every cause and undertaking, in speech and silence, in work and rest, in gesture and walk, [Col. 0614A] in habit and food, toward every person, and in every movement of the body.

VIII. “The saying is faithful.” “Everyone will be perfected if he is like his master” (Luke 6:40). And: “It is enough for the disciple to be like his master” (Matt. 10:25). Our master is the community of the Church of Prémontré; for the individual communities of the other Churches are disciples of this master. From these words it is clear that it ought to be such that we judge resemblance to it sufficient for every holiness. For if we surpass it, it is no longer our master.

Behold, people hasten from the ends of the earth to Prémontré, in order to hear from the mother something good and new which they may announce to the daughters. By decrees even of the Roman Pontiffs, the abbots who are sons are bound to visit the mother each year, so that they may hear from her the ordinances of salvation, the commandments, and “the law of life and discipline” (Ecclus. 45:6), and carry these to the daughters. Far be it forever and beyond that their first transgression should appear in the place where their first institution is celebrated.

Neither the length of roads, nor perils at sea, nor the emptying of purses, nor fear of bodily illness—and sometimes even of death—can delay the steps of the sons from eagerly approaching the same mother. Preferring maternal reverence and love to all these things, and perhaps to others like them, they humbly submit themselves to the wholesome ordinances promulgated there; they carry them to the daughters to be held firmly and observed inviolably. Nor are the daughters universally bound by obligation to observe what is known not to have been established there. See, then, what honour, of what kind and how great, is owed by children to their mother. But she may boldly and openly demand it from them only when she preserves with watchful and steadfast perseverance the ordinances promulgated at her own house.

IX. And consider whether that passage which we now have in hand may not also suitably be referred to this subject in some sense—the passage you read in the book of Genesis: “A river went out from the place of delight to water Paradise” [Col. 0614D] (Gen. 2:10). Scripture had first stated: “The Lord God had planted a Paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed” (ibid. 2:8).

What are we to say here? Can this mean that God formed the human being whom he deigns to call to knowledge and love of himself, enlightening him with rational understanding? For what else was the man asking when he said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 50:12)? That this human being was not within him was also the complaint of the one to whom two were lacking from the number forty: that is, from the perfection of Law and Gospel, love of God and neighbour. Thus the lamenting voice of the sufferer says: “I have no man, that, when the water is troubled, he may put me into the pool” (John 5:7). He indicates that he lacked rational understanding which, through remembering and imitating the Lord’s Passion, might raise him from the bed of sickness—that is, the softness of iniquity.

This human being was formed by God, indeed “in righteousness and holiness of truth” [Col. 0615A] (Eph. 4:24). May we dare say that he then planted Paradise when he first inspired our first Father that this canonical order should be instituted? If these two points are granted, why should the third not also be admitted: that to place this human being in Paradise is to inspire the person whom God enlightens with the knowledge of himself through the shining ray of his grace, so that he may humbly submit himself to this order?

Consider, if you please, the sequence of the words themselves: he planted, he formed, he placed. Through his servant he gave commandments and the law of life and discipline; adorning with spiritual and rational understanding the one whom he predestined for eternal life, he enlightened him with the light of his grace; afterwards he inspired him to submit himself to canonical observance. What benefit is there for this person in being placed in this Paradise? Much in every way. For, with the virtue of humility—which is both the cause and guardian of the other virtues—already laid down, the Giver and Rewarder of all good things adorns him with good works. These are so bright to those who behold them for knowledge, and so sweet to those who imitate them for experience, that in this way he brings forth “from the ground every tree beautiful to see and sweet for food” (Gen. 2:9). The beauty of the tree is that of good works as regards the sight of knowledge; its sweetness is that of the affection’s taste. Thus it is beautiful to see because of the knowledge of truth, and sweet for food because of the affection of charity.

X. Behold, I say to you: lift up your eyes and behold the religious men in our order, persevering in the exercises of holy life which proceed from the virtue of humility. These shine for those who see them and grow sweet for those who experience them. And in all these things praise him who “gives strength and power to his people” [Col. 0615C] (Ps. 67:36). He works in his saints both to will and to accomplish according to his good will (Phil. 2:13), bringing forth from the ground every tree beautiful to see and sweet for food.

But the exercises of holy life flourish most when the work of charity is commanded to be undertaken and the contagion of greed is ordered to be omitted. The one is commanded; the other forbidden. Someone may perhaps refer the tree of life to that command, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil to this prohibition: the former is indeed of life, the latter of the knowledge of good and evil. For the life of our spirit consists in the exercise of charity; and one who commits in deed the evil that is forbidden is at once under guilt and punishment. He also comes to know by experience the evil which had previously become known to him by knowledge alone.

Scripture says: “The tree of life [was] in the midst of Paradise” (Gen. 2:9), because our order directs its whole intention toward being able to serve charity. Whether, then, it spares or strikes, binds or loosens, whether it does something by dispensation because some reasonable cause intervenes, or changes one thing into another, it refers everything to the integrity of charity and in no respect exceeds its measure. Thus it shows that it has the tree of life in its midst.

But Paradise must be watered, lest it dry up. How do you say this? How do you read it? “And a river went out from the place of delight [Col. 0616A] to water Paradise” (Gen. 2:10). What does this mean? Let Paradise be watered, lest it dry up; let the order be renewed, lest it grow old. When the sons visit the mother, the order is restored; wholesome ordinances are established, as the river goes out from the place of delight to water Paradise.

And what is this place of delight? Let us say for the moment, if this may indeed be said, that the Church of Prémontré is the place of will (*locus voluntatis*). Not of carnal delight, not of worldly delight, but of the delight of God, “with the torrent” of which he gives drink to those who hope beneath the covering of his wings (Ps. 35:9). The river goes out from this place of delight, watering Paradise, when wholesome ordinances are established in the Church of Prémontré, which is our mother, so that the order itself may be restored.

XI. Although its ordinances are many, they chiefly instruct penitents, governors, workers, and contemplatives, together with any others there may be: these are novices, obedientiaries, prelates, and cloistered brethren. Scripture says: “A river went out from the place of delight to water Paradise, and from there it was divided into four heads” [Col. 0616B] (Gen. 2:10), so that we may know that a fourfold stream is to be drawn from it.

And what names do these heads receive? “The name of the one is Phison; the name of the second, Gehon; the name of the third river is Tigris; and the fourth river is Euphrates.” Let one who dares speak thus say that Phison belongs to those who have newly come, who must strive with all their strength first fully to see themselves; and, considering what they are inwardly, to disclose themselves outwardly with purity, because they assert that *Phison* signifies “the mouth of the pupil.” In the mouth is confession; in the pupil, sight. Let novices look and confess: look diligently and confess humbly.

I mean, let them consider their old self. For they will never be able perfectly to attain the height of newness toward which they strive unless they recognize the oldness in which they have hitherto lived, because they cannot reach the former unless the latter is wholly abandoned. And how will it be abandoned if it is unknown? What if it is indeed recognized but concealed? Knowledge does not suffice for salvation unless confession is also present, just as a wound is not healed, although the wounded person feels it, unless it is shown to the physician. Therefore, as they uncover the pupil in order to see by knowledge, so let them open their mouths in order to reveal themselves through confession; [Col. 0616C] for *Phison* signifies not merely the pupil but also the mouth. Oldness always remains as long as confession is absent, even where knowledge is present. Did not the one who said, “Because I kept silent, my bones grew old” (Ps. 31:3), experience this in himself?

But what ought to be the intention, zeal, and care of those who see and disclose themselves? Certainly this: that, having wholly abandoned the oldness which has been recognized and exposed, they may give tireless diligence to acquiring, practising, and preserving newness. Yet there is bitter pain and hard labour. For it is exceedingly bitter and no slight labour to renounce altogether the sweetness and pleasantness to which one has become accustomed, and to subject oneself to an unfamiliar bitterness and harshness. It is as though you were compelled to change your very nature.

XII. They say that this is signified by what is said of Phison: “It is that which encompasses the whole land of Hevilath” [Col. 0617A] (Gen. 2:11). For *Hevilath*, according to them, means “suffering.” What sweetness is there where pain is? What pleasantness where there is travail? O how Phison labours as it encompasses the whole land of Hevilath, while novices are troubled and saddened in the travail of new life, according to those words: “They were troubled, they were shaken; fear seized them there, pains as of a woman in labour” (Ps. 47:6–8).

Nevertheless, from the continual experience of this severe struggle, and from the great inward anxiety and sorrow that it brings to the soul, the brightness of wisdom shines forth in the mind; for of Hevilath it is said that gold is born there. The radiance of wisdom is gold in the minds of those who suffer and travail. Thus gold is born from Hevilath, “because the valleys shall abound in grain” (Ps. 64:16). And to one who desires wisdom it is said: “Do you desire wisdom? Keep the commandments, and God will give it to you” (Ecclus. 1:33). Who is wiser than the person who grieves over the present exile which he suffers, and with his whole inward being longs for the eternal kingdom?

Someone may say this because the text adds: “And the gold of that land is excellent” [Col. 0617B] (Gen. 2:11). Of which land? Surely of Hevilath. Was the gold of the land of those people excellent, of whom it is said: “They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good” (Jer. 4:22)? But the gold of the land encircled by Phison is excellent, because our novices, grieving over the past on account of sorrow, pray that their debt may be forgiven; and, guarding against the future on account of travail, pray likewise that they may not be led into temptation (Matt. 6:12).

Yet the radiance of wisdom should belong to a spiritual way of life that the virtue of humility commends and the strength of steadfast perseverance adorns and confirms. Hence perhaps someone may say that not only is excellent gold born there, but bdellium and the onyx stone are also found there (Gen. 2:12). They say that bdellium is a black aromatic tree; and if this is so, a good way of life is aromatic because of the fragrance of prayer, and black because of low self-estimation. But constancy must strengthen these two goods, because in the land encircled by Phison, along with bdellium, an onyx stone is found which, they say, resembles a fingernail. A nail covers the flesh, so that what is soft in the flesh may be protected by its hard covering; and the strength of constancy protects our softness, lest it waste away in its own tenderness.

Behold what goods, of what kind, how great, and how numerous are contained in the state of novices: the brightness of self-knowledge; the purity of humble confession; the torment of sorrow; the anxiety of careful concern; the radiance of wisdom; lowliness in self-estimation; devotion in prayer; and—so that among them Joseph’s long-sleeved tunic may be worn (Gen. 37:25), and the tail of the victim placed upon the sacrifice (Lev. 9:19–20)—the strength of perseverance is required. So much concerning them.

XIII. After this it must be said that officials should strive to cut off whatever prosperity delights them; for they assert that this is signified by the name of the second river, [Col. 0618A] Gehon, through which their state is also expressed. Of it Scripture says: “It is that which encompasses the whole land of Ethiopia” (Gen. 2:13). This is plain enough, because their manifold occupations seem to be covered with a certain blackness. Does not the Lord himself in the Gospel declare that they traverse the earth, as it were, in a laborious circuit, when, addressing Martha in their person, he says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10:4). Anxiety is a kind of blackness; disturbance is one also, because both take serenity from the mind and bring upon it a certain obscuring.

XIV. The third river signifies our rulers, who hear from Isaiah: “Go, swift angels, to a people torn apart and rent” (Isa. 18:2). They are swift, therefore, as the name of this river—Tigris—suggests by its sense of an arrow. And Scripture says, “It goes against the Assyrians” (Gen. 2:14): so that, like a swift arrow, angels may go to a people torn apart and rent. For prelates are chiefly appointed for this: to withstand the perverse by the authority of their office, and, rising up in opposition, to set themselves as a wall for the house of Israel (Ezek. 13:5).

By this arrow a wound is inflicted; yet sickness is not thereby brought upon the wounded man. Rather, health is bestowed, and, once bestowed, is increased more and more. For concerning it our bald-headed one has this saying: “The arrow of the Lord’s deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance against Syria” (4 Kings 13:17). This is an arrow of deliverance because Tigris means “from the place of delight”; and an arrow of deliverance against Syria, because it goes against the Assyrians. Syria signifies “the exalted.” Against this Syria the Tigris goes.

The saying of a certain Tigris is: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God for the destruction of strongholds: destroying counsels, and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor. 10:4). He says, therefore, that the destruction of every height and exaltation consists in his spiritual weapons, thereby showing himself to be the arrow of the Lord’s deliverance and the arrow of deliverance against Syria. And why all this? Because the third river is named Tigris, and it goes against the Assyrians.

It is not said of it that it goes around the land of the Assyrians, as is said of Phison, which goes around the whole land of Havilah, and of Gehon, which goes around the whole land of Ethiopia; but that it goes against the Assyrians. For it especially belongs to the rulers of holy communities not to yield and consent, in womanish fashion, to the perversities of the proud; but, if they truly discharge their office, they will strive manfully to oppose and resist them. Nevertheless, while they necessarily endure a certain laborious circuit, both the novices must groaningly apply themselves to the travail of the new life, and officials, in fulfilling a fatherly command and relieving a brotherly need, must bear with equanimity the administration laid upon them.

XV. The fourth river neither goes around any land nor goes against any persons, because cloistered religious neither labor in their groaning as novices do, nor are darkened by external occupations like obedientiaries, nor, like prelates fighting against beasts and resisting the perversities of rebels, do they sweat beneath the burden of a grievous struggle.

Among them are not pains like those of a woman in labor (Ps. 47:8), but the sound of one feasting, in a voice of exultation and thanksgiving (Ps. 41:5). Among them Martha does not anxiously and troubledly busy herself with much service; rather Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, hears his word (Luke 10:39). Finally, among them eleven curtains of hair-cloth do not endure the assaults of rains and the terrors of storms rushing upon them from without (Exod. 36:14); but rather ten gleaming curtains are made beautiful within by the varied adornment of their colors (ibid., v. 8).

Its name, moreover, is Euphrates. If cloistered persons conduct themselves in all things as befits the perfect, what is there in their practice that is not fruitful?

What then? Is not the practice of novices fruitful, and that of officials and prelates? Certainly it is fruitful; but it is more truly so among novices. David does not build a house for the Lord because he is a man of blood (1 Chron. 22:8): thus Phison goes around the land of Havilah. Among officials Leah is weak-eyed (Gen. 29:17): thus Gehon goes around the land of Ethiopia. Among prelates the disciples labor at rowing, for the wind is contrary to them (Mark 6:48): thus Tigris goes against the Assyrians.

But among cloistered persons there is a most peaceful man, so that from the reality he bears that excellent name, Solomon; and, being most wise, he builds a temple for the Lord (3 Kings 6:1). Rachel, beautiful in face and comely in appearance, is joined to Jacob (Gen. 29:17). Jesus himself prays on the mountain (Matt. 14:23) and stands on the shore (John 21:4). Behold the threefold fruit of cloistered persons: the serenity of peace, the radiance of beauty, and the security of rest.

XVI. Can novices, obedientiaries, or prelates possess these things as excellently as they do? Among them the first-created man sleeps in paradise, so that he may discover within himself both what is feminine and governed, and what is masculine and governs (Gen. 2:21). Among them Enoch, the seventh in descent, walks justly with God and is not seen, because God took him (Gen. 5:24). Among them righteous Noah, lest he be overwhelmed by the waters or storm, or swallowed by the deep, enters the ark to avoid the flood’s inundations and is shut in from outside by the Lord (Gen. 7:16).

Among them the dove sent forth finds nowhere for her foot to rest and returns to the secret enclosure of the ark, bearing in her mouth an olive branch (Gen. 8:8–9). Among them also the Lord appears to Abraham, sitting in the valley of Mamre at the entrance to his tent, in the very heat of the day (Gen. 18:1 ff.); so that, when he lifts up his eyes, three men standing appear: he addresses three in one and one in three. Among them, with mortal life wholly cast aside, Sarah dies a life-giving death; and, having her life hidden with Christ in God, she is buried in the cave of both action and contemplation, and therefore in a double cave (Gen. 23:19).

Among them Isaac, the seed of an aged father, possesses blessed joy—as his name expresses in reality—in the Holy Spirit; and he does not cease digging wells until he finds living water (Gen. 26:19). He walks on the way leading to the well whose name is “of the Living and the Seeing,” and goes out to meditate in the field when day is already declining (Gen. 24:62–63).

Among them Jacob, a simple man dwelling in the house of the mind, leaves his native land. Setting one of the stones lying there beneath his head, at Bethel, after sunset, he sleeps and rests together in peace (Gen. 28:11), where he beholds the ascent and descent of angels by the ladder of charity reaching to heaven, and the Lord standing upon the ladder (ibid., vv. 12–13). The same man also, having now gained his long-desired marriage, prefers the love of the latter wife to the former; yet, hired for his son’s mandrakes, he returns to the bed of that same former wife (Gen. 30:14, 17). At last, fruitful in the abundant offspring of both, he hastens to return to his father’s house; and, lest he enter the land by two ways, he is touched in the thigh by the angel as dawn rises, and, resting all his weight upon one foot, proceeds lame (Gen. 32:25).

Among them the birth of Benjamin and the setting of Rachel occur together (Gen. 35:17–18). Among them Joseph, dead and embalmed with spices, is placed in a coffin in Egypt (Gen. 50:25), because especially among them, in the dark exile of this present life, the fruit of inward contemplation is hidden away: dead to this world, filled with the manifold fragrances of virtues, and, as it were, Rachel’s firstborn. For the fourth river is Euphrates.

XVII–XVIII. Among them Moses, having struck down the Egyptian (Exod. 2:12 ff.), escapes Pharaoh’s threats by flight. Having defended the girls from the shepherds who came upon them—that is, having cleansed the thoughts of the heart from invading fantasies—he waters their flocks, encouraging and nourishing their good fruitfulness. Then, having driven the sheep into the inner parts of the desert—that is, having led simple and harmless meditations into the inmost secrets—he takes the footwear of deadly evil examples from the feet of his mind, and passes on in order to behold the great vision in the holy land (Exod. 3:3). He also makes everything pertaining to the tabernacle according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain (Exod. 25:40).

Among them Aaron the high priest is separated, with his sons, from the other children of Israel: separated, I say, and washed; anointed and clothed; crowned and specially assigned to the ministry of the Lord (1 Chron. 23:13). Among them Joshua subdues foreign nations (Joshua, throughout), so that the land may rest from wars. Among them Gideon, at the angel’s command, places flesh and unleavened cakes upon a rock and pours the broth over them, so that fire coming forth from the rock may consume all these things when struck by the angel’s rod (Judg. 6:20–21).

Among them also is Samuel, who sleeps in the tabernacle where the ark of God is (1 Kings 3:3), hewing Agag to pieces before the Lord (1 Kings 15:33). Among them is aged David, full of days, who cannot be warmed when covered with clothes until Abishag the Shunammite sleeps with him and cherishes and warms him (3 Kings 1:1). Among them Elijah, the man of God, avoids by flight the accursed and evil-working Jezebel—that is, the lust of this world (3 Kings 19:3)—and, taking the wings of a dove, flies in all haste to the desert of rest.

Among them the same Elijah leaves his servant behind in Beersheba of Judah, when by purity of confession and sevenfold aspiration he casts childish understanding from himself; and, dwelling in the solitude of the mind, asks for death for his soul (ibid.), desiring “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). Awakened by the angel of inward inspiration from the sleep of sloth, he is refreshed with bread baked under ashes, while he grows fat through the humility of good work; so that in the strength of this food he may attain, through the fortyfold span of this present exile, to stable eternity and the eternal steadfastness of the heavenly mountain.

Among them is Elisha, possessor of Elijah’s double spirit (4 Kings 2:9), who follows Elijah and gives himself to his service in such a way that, by the renunciation of the mind, he kisses farewell to his father, the world, and his mother, concupiscence; he turns his back wholly upon them and does not intend ever to return to them.
