Among them Isaiah, at the Lord’s command and unashamed of the nakedness of the flesh, utterly puts off worldly possessions (Isa. 20:2), that, relieved of earthly burdens, he may go as an empty traveller before a thief, singing, and so more easily and securely tend toward heavenly and eternal things.

Among them is holy Ezekiel, who, in the building of the city set upon a mountain and inclining toward the south, stands through the lofty merit of his life and has his eyes fixed upon the gate (Ezek. 40:2). Upon the gate, I say, that leads to the city: walking by faith and longing to walk by sight, turning his back upon transitory things and his face toward eternal things, and finally desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

Among them is the most holy Jeremiah, sanctified in the womb, virgin and priest of God (Jer. 1:5), whom rags and old ropes raise from the muddy pit (Jer. 38:6); and in his ascent, as he strives to reach the Songs of Ascents, he has both sharp arrows and desolating coals (Ps. 119:4). Among them Daniel refuses to be defiled by the king of Babylon’s table (Dan. 1:8), and Gabriel makes him understand the vision (Dan. 8:16).

Among them father Tobias, sitting by the rivers of Babylon, weeps when he remembers Zion (Ps. 136:1), sighing for the beautiful city Jerusalem: whose gates are built of sapphire and emerald, and of precious stone.

> [Note: Col. 0621. Add., V: “The whole circuit of its walls.” And thereafter: “All its streets shall be paved with white and pure stone, and alleluia shall be sung through its lanes.” Edition.]

Its circuit of walls is of white stone; its streets are paved with pure gold; and through all its lanes is sung the song of joy, namely, Alleluia (Tob. 13:21). Among them is the noble king Hezekiah, whose eyes have grown dim while looking up on high (Isa. 38:14). Among them Josiah, who celebrates the Passover most solemnly and humbly consults the prophetess concerning the book found in the house of the Lord (2 Chron. 34). Among them are Jesus the high priest, rebuilding the temple (1 Ezra 3:10), and Ezra renewing the law (1 Ezra 7). Nehemiah—whose name means “inward comforter”—builds the walls of Jerusalem (2 Ezra 2:17). The first is present for sanctification, the second for instruction, the third for security. Among them Mordecai, scorning to worship the exceedingly proud Haman (Esther 3:2). Among them Judith, killing Holofernes (Judith 13:10). Among them Esther, whose beauty the king desires (Esther 2:17).

XIX. Among them likewise, to come to the times of grace, when Zechariah entered the temple of the Lord, Gabriel the angel appeared, standing at the right of the altar of incense (Luke 1:11). Among them the child John grows and is strengthened, and remains in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel (Luke 1:80). Among them, when Jesus sees the crowds, he goes up the mountain (Matt. 5:1). Among them Peter goes up to the upper room to pray (Acts 10:9). Among them Paul is caught up into the third heaven; he is caught up also into paradise and hears words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter (2 Cor. 12:2). Among them Jesus Christ seals and sends, through his angel to his servant John, his Apocalypse, which God gave him to make manifest (Rev. 1:1).

“Who is wise, and shall understand these things? And who understands, and shall know them?” Certainly, you are wise. You are those who have understanding, to whom the Lord has given understanding in all things, and whom the anointing itself teaches concerning all things (1 John 2:27). Therefore, since we have served you things that are your own, and have not offered new matters but recalled known things to your memory, we thought it sufficient to touch them rather briefly upon the surface, rather than to dig deeply and expound copiously. We have indeed taken hold from afar and drawn out a long thread, so that you may recognize rather than newly learn the singular, fruit-bearing prerogative of the spiritual practice of those who are truly cloistered.

XX. Does it not appear from these things that this river, which they declare pertains to cloistered persons, receives its name from the reality, since it signifies fruit? Thus it is rightly said of it: “The fourth river is Euphrates.” But if what has been said concerning these rivers is not to be rejected, it is plainly evident that the river which is divided into these four heads is precious. It is likewise evident that the place of delight from which that river goes forth receives its name from the reality.

But what is that place of delight? We said it long before; it belongs to you to ensure that we have not said it falsely. What does Scripture say after this? “Therefore the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight” (Gen. 2:15). He did this then historically, and he does so spiritually today. Who that paradise of delight is has already been stated. It has also been stated who this man is.

“Therefore the Lord God took the man.” But it does not say whence he took him. Where he placed him, however, it does not keep silent: for he placed him in paradise. The place whence he took him is not specifically named, because the crimes and shameful deeds from which he takes him are diverse and often multiplied beyond number. That place therefore has no name, because, as far as we are concerned, number often cannot contain it beneath itself. It ought not to have been named, because it was not worthy even of a name, being shameful and criminal.

XXI. But for what purpose was man placed in paradise? “To cultivate it and to guard it” (Gen. 2:15). O religious observance! O perseverance! Certainly, he labors in paradise who lives in an ordered manner within the order; and he guards it who remains in the order until he dies: there, lest he become sluggish in idleness; here, lest he fail through dissipation.

But let this man beware of the serpent, for it too is in paradise. And who is this, unless it be any disturber of peace, divider of unity, sower of evil counsel in the community, disobedient to superiors, ever harmful to companions, and altogether hateful to God? This serpent is an apostate man, a useless man, who “walks with a perverse mouth, treads with his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil with a wicked heart, and at every time sows quarrels” (Prov. 6:12, 14).

He draws a human being to forbidden food when he corrupts all whom he can by words as well as examples, sowing among brothers anger and pride, envy and detraction, malice and indignation, discord and disturbances; drawing some to hatred of their companions and others to contempt for their prelates. As often as he prevails, he pours the poison of deadly persuasion into individual hearts and urges them to do that for which they deserve to be cast out of paradise.

And certainly, whoever does this is “cursed among all the animals of the earth” (Gen. 3:14). Having lost the uprightness of mind, he is bent down toward low things, walking upon his breast; and in all his works he desires earthly things, wholly casting aside heavenly things, “eating earth all the days of his life” (ibid.). Let perpetual enmities exist between him and the devout soul: let them never agree in any matter; let the latter always refuse what the former wills. However flatteringly venomous he may be, he will certainly administer to her deadly poison in the end, even if he has not been able to do so at the beginning or in the middle, lying in wait for her heel (ibid., v. 15). Therefore, so that the woman may prudently forestall and wholly avoid these snares, let her reduce to nothing the very beginning of his malicious pride, crushing his head.

XXII. Come then, Fathers and venerable brothers beloved by us and by God: we have already said much; and, delighting in speaking with you, we have now exceeded the proper length of a letter. Let your greatness therefore receive with charity what our humility has brought forth with devotion. If anything good has been set before you in it, together with which something evil has also been introduced, we ask that your discernment may strive so to avoid the thorn that your care does not neglect to cultivate the rose. Thus bring to your sense of smell what is fragrant, while removing from touch what pricks.

For the rest, rejoice in the Lord; be made perfect; think the same thing; have peace (2 Cor. 13:11): be devoted to God, ready toward your neighbors, show yourselves obedient to prelates, love one another, redeem the time, and walk in one peace, that you may be able to arrive at one rest.

## II. Letter of the venerable and illustrious man John, abbot of the Church of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, at Kelchou, sent to Adam the canon, in which he exhorts him concerning the writing of the tabernacle of Moses and the division of the same work into three parts

I. John, abbot, wishes eternal salvation in the Lord to his most beloved son Adam the canon, worthy of honor among the members of Christ.

Considering, dearest son, how very many occupy themselves with the utmost zeal concerning that knowledge in which the understanding of the divine Scriptures is contained, I greatly admire the purpose and at the same time approve the desire by which they endeavor with all diligence to attain it, judging that it will be honorable and useful to them if they strive, so far as they can, to be made perfect in it.

Preferring this knowledge to other things which pertain to empty philosophy, they lift their mind above themselves, reflecting how delightful it is to attain it. They understand one thing when they behold it in the light of truth, and another when they desire it by their own will. For, attentively looking more keenly in the light of truth, they contemplate how good it is to understand all the Scriptures in a threefold way and to explain them all without difficulty, in a clear sense, for a more evident understanding.

For this is greatly desired: it is seen in the mind as though in a mirror, and kindles the efforts of learners, so that they may occupy themselves with it and thirst after it with every effort they devote to acquiring such a capacity, in order that through it they may deserve to obtain what they foresee in meditation. Therefore, while they burn with this excessive desire, they plainly demonstrate that they are impelled by a certain force of nature to learn, desiring to know the mysteries of all the Scriptures.

For these things are brought about in them when they give the greatest diligence to the works of the saints who conveyed Greek and Hebrew writings into understanding, admiring their steadfastness against adversaries and their endurance of labors for those who were at that time instructed by them in the Catholic faith.

II. But when the hour of necessity pressed upon them to write much against heretics who taught doctrines contrary to the Catholic faith, they went out to meet them fortified by the authority of the divine Scriptures; and, since they were often few in number, they labored for a long time in disputing against them. At last, multiplied beyond the sand by the writings of the saints concerning the sacraments, they fought against adversaries and instructed the universal Church in the Catholic faith.

Some modern writers, imitating their teaching as far as they can, repeatedly resisted to their face certain profane innovations which had first arisen in the house of the Lord through the Arian sect, and brought them into disuse. Mindful of the command by which planting a grove is forbidden in the house of the Lord (Deut. 16:21), they finally, by divine operation, made the holy Church most excellent and uncontaminated by that stain.

In building up the holy Church on such occasions, they could not have prevented the sects of the wicked beyond remedy unless, steadfastly bringing forward divine utterances against them, they had resisted them. They knew that, although divine Scripture is open to them in reading, it is wholly closed and hidden in mystery. But after the holy doctors, ascending into the height of the Scriptures as though to a lofty place through the vigor of contemplation, had spiritually reached the very majesty of the Trinity, their expositions showed sufficiently clearly—though not to everyone, but to those perfected in understanding—how holy Scripture ought to be understood mystically in both Testaments.

III. Nevertheless, men of the highest learning in many places passed over certain matters, touching them only superficially, and reserved them to be explained by the labor of later writers. As though deliberately, they omitted to gather in the field of Scripture certain less full ears of grain standing after their footsteps, so that their successors might in due time thresh them with the threefold rod and minister them to those in need; lest, occupied too foolishly with barren philosophy, they should appear wholly empty before the master of the household at the examination of good works, without fruit from their labor.

Accordingly, I offer as an example one matter by which some are troubled. Why, when they proposed to interpret and explain all the Scriptures, did they pass over the tabernacle of Moses in Exodus and write little on this subject, except Joseph and the venerable priest Bede? Since their chief intention concerned the holy Church and those things which seem to pertain to it, it is strange why they passed over this subject in such a way, when that same tabernacle most elegantly prefigured the holy Church in several respects.

Yet the venerable Bede, doctor of the English, though he disclosed a few indications of his diligence concerning this tabernacle, did not provide satisfaction in writing about it. In all his other writings he was so willing an expositor that, like a schoolmaster of children spelling out syllables, he would explain every matter for wearied readers.

IV. Therefore, dearest son, I enjoin upon your gentleness the task of explaining this work, which they almost leave untouched, as though equally open to all, because you desire the salvation of the Lord and his law is the meditation of your heart. Embracing the command with confidence, set forth, with your pen serving you, whatever the Lord shall deem worthy to minister to you through his Spirit in the explanation of this tabernacle.

Do not seek a more leisurely time, since you wholly do not know what is to come. Compose, therefore, for readers a book which contains the historical tabernacle, showing how it was actually arranged by Moses. Let it be compiled from the most trustworthy sayings of orthodox Fathers, and divide it into three parts, with chapter-headings prefixed and a proper proportion assigned to each part.

In this work insert no person’s opinion contrary to Exodus, lest you seem through error to linger somewhat too long among the differing opinions of many. Rather, for the most part weave in the text of this Exodus, so that, as the clear reasoning proceeds, the book may be well formed and testimonies gathered against the enemies of Scripture, because “the mouth of those speaking iniquity has not yet been stopped” (Ps. 62:12).

Let the first part of this book state plainly, for those seeking or wishing to know, who was the craftsman of the structure and of what materials that ancient tabernacle consisted. Let it describe most clearly the entire structure, together with everything belonging to it, both within and without; and, after the walls have been placed in their proper positions and joined by the heads of their bars, let it finally cover the structure with the extension of the curtains and the other coverings.

V. But because a question is commonly raised by some concerning the half of the sixth curtain, by whose doubling the rear of the tabernacle was covered, let a fuller discussion of it be extended in that same part of the book; and especially concerning the altar’s grating, about which there appears to be very great ambiguity among both Greeks and Latins.

Do not find it burdensome to gather, as though in testimony against the attacks of many, what differing expositors have thought on these matters, so that their teeth may be broken and they may be blunted within themselves, having nothing, as it were, with which to bark. Once the judgments of many have been brought forward against them, let them be utterly ashamed to insult holy Scripture any longer.

These matters, then, are to be set in the first part of this book because of their calumnies, so that, driven out from the first threshold and unable under the law’s command to enter the more secret places of the house of the Lord, they may withdraw far from the sanctuary because of their evil conscience, carrying with them the perils of their own rashness.

VI. In the text of the second part, depict the visible tabernacle upon a plane. Set forth for the eyes of viewers, as far as can be shown by a painted likeness, the form of that structure. Within the Holy of Holies, or simply the Holy Place, set with all diligence those things which Exodus describes as having been there, because it must be believed without doubt, although not everyone can expressly understand how the sense of its words should be received.

Extend the enclosure of the court within the camp, and the structure upon its columns, all around. In the illustration carefully mark the spaces and sites in which the children of Israel encamped around the tabernacle, so that those who desire to know how it was made in times long past may have an indication of that structure through the painted likeness.

VII. When all has thus been depicted, immediately expound that very image in the same part of the book through allegorical meanings. For sacred Scripture seems humble in its words, according to the historical sense, to minds weak in understanding. Thus may the reader’s effort and understanding be enlarged; may the mind of the observer and interpreter be taught through the visible likeness to turn away from evil; and through allegorical signification may it seem to conform itself to the manner of Scripture.

For it follows that one who abstains from vices through a good example immediately shines with virtues by exercising himself in good works. But in the third part, turning what has been said above toward morality, strive diligently through mystical interpretation to direct toward the correction of morals whatever edification the image conveys to those who behold it.

For anyone who simply recounts the words of history lays, as though beginning, the foundation of the structure; and when through the exercise of allegory he discloses the mysteries of history, he raises the fabric of the mind to the citadel of faith.

VIII. Finally, one who investigates the mystical understanding from both senses through contemplation adorns the erected building with diverse virtues through the grace of morality, as though with distinct colors. When you have vigilantly completed everything according to the ordering of the divine gift, copy this letter at the beginning of the book by way of excuse, so that the diligent reader may recognize that you began this work not from presumption but, constrained by obedience, obeyed the command of your father.

But since the discourse must now end, lest excessive length produce weariness in the reader, let what has been said suffice. May the grace of the heavenly Protector deign to preserve your holy brotherhood, which prays for us, and always strengthen it in good works. Amen.

## III. Letter of Adam the canon, sent to the distinguished man Lord John the abbot, concerning the material construction of the tabernacle of Moses

I. Brother Adam, humble servant and devoted son of your excellence, embraces in Christ Jesus, with the sweet arms of true love, the most reverend Lord and Father John; and wishes him deliverance from eternal condemnation and inclusion among the flock of God’s elect.

Since it is certain, beloved father and venerable lord, that everyone travelling bodily requires knowledge of the way by which one goes to the place one desires to reach, in order to arrive there safely: surely we, all who are led by the Spirit of God and glory in hope of the glory of his children, who desire to reach that heavenly Jerusalem, “which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same thing” (Ps. 121:3), need to be fully instructed concerning the straight way that leads there. For it is certain that without its guidance we can by no means reach the aforesaid city: that is, not only must we know where we are to arrive, but we must also recognize upon what way we must travel.

This was the chief and almost sole concern, without any exception, of all the righteous who, living by faith (Rom. 1:17), saved and kindled by hope that does not disappoint and by charity that never fails (1 Cor. 13:8), lived in the various ages from the beginning of the world: not merely that they might believe by faith that there is an eternal homeland, but also that through knowledge they might clearly recognize the way by which it is attained and, once that way was known, might not cease to run upon it tirelessly in devotion until they arrived.

II. Thus one of them prayed with great desire, saying: “Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you” (Ps. 142:8). “I have lifted up my soul to you,” he says; “therefore make known to me the way in which I should walk.” As though he said: “Because, with you showing me beforehand, I already know toward what I ought to tend, make known to me, I pray, the way in which I should walk, so that, as I already know what is good for me to attain, I may likewise not fail to know what road it is safe to undertake.”

Thus the Lord says to his disciples: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. 6:33). The kingdom of God is truth; his righteousness is goodness. In these two consists the straight way leading to the eternal homeland: in the knowledge of truth and the love of goodness, so that we may choose what is true and love what is good. Thus we become both enlightened, lest we be led astray through ignorance, and devout, lest we be corrupted through malice; obtaining indeed serpentine prudence in the knowledge of truth and dovelike simplicity in the love of goodness.

“These two,” he says: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and seek his righteousness,” in order that these may be given to you; and all other things shall not merely be given to you, but added to you.

III. Of these two, one makes the understanding bright in the human soul, while the other inflames the affection, so that the soul in consequence moves even the bodily members themselves toward good action. Thus in these three—the enlightened understanding, devout affection, and good effect—consists a human being’s merit, by which one gains the reward. In that merit one possesses the way by which one travels; and in the reward, the life to which one arrives.

But he alone is that straight way and true life who created man in his own image and likeness. For as he was the cause that one who did not exist should be created, so he is the way in his humanity, that the lost person may be redeemed; and life in his divinity, that the redeemed person may be made blessed. The same person receives a threefold benefit from his triune God: first, from the Creator, that he may exist from him; second, from the Redeemer, that he may exist through him; third, from the Glorifier, that he may blessedly exist in him. For, as the Apostle says, “From him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:36). To him be glory: from whom we have our beginning, through whom our merit, and in whom our reward.

IV. Sacred Scripture is likewise a special guide to this straight way, to this blessed and beatifying life, and it plainly instructs humankind concerning both. For its pure and continual reading instils in a person understanding concerning God, his Creator, Redeemer, and Glorifier, and concerning those things that pertain to him. Understanding then gives rise to affection; affection in turn reaches forth into action; and thus, by truly knowing, fervently loving, and profitably working, one acquires merit on the way, through which one attains the reward in life. Since this is so, reason counsels, usefulness suggests, and necessity compels us to apply ourselves all the more steadfastly to sacred Scripture, because we know with greater certainty that it is the means through which so great a good is bestowed upon us.

Its book, written within and without, has written in itself “lamentations, and a song, and woe” (Ezek. 2:9). Its revolving wheels, which go when the holy living creatures go, stand when they stand, and are lifted from the earth when they are lifted, have a stature that is high and dreadful in appearance (Ezek. 1:21). For this Scripture, to use the honeyed words of Gregory [Note: [Col. 0629D] GREGORY, *Morals*, book II, ch. 1], is set before the eyes of our mind like a kind of mirror, so that our inward face may be seen in it. There we behold both what is foul and what is beautiful in us. There we perceive how much we advance; there, how far we remain from advancement. It recounts the deeds of men and urges the hearts of the weak to imitation. And it comes about, in Gregory’s words, that the mind trembles less amid conflicts, the more it sees before itself the triumphs of so many valiant men.

At times, however, Scripture not only declares their virtues to us, but also makes known their falls, so that in the victories of the brave we may see what we ought to seize by imitation, and again, in their lapses, what we ought to fear. Thus the virtue of our elders may foster our hope, and their falls may gird us with the caution of humility; so that, while the former lift us up through joy and the latter press us down through fear, the mind of the hearer, trained on the one side by the confidence of hope and on the other by the humility of fear, may neither grow proud through rashness when it is restrained by dread, nor, oppressed by fear, despair when it is strengthened toward confidence in hope by the example of virtue.

Although its depth is great and exceedingly wonderful, although it is sometimes intricate in its words and its subtle meaning is veiled by a sacred covering, yet in the knowledge of itself it admits penetrating minds in such a way that it does not altogether repel the simple. For it displays in itself both what may refresh the former and what may feed the latter with milk, so that in it may abundantly be found both what the strong may eat and what the little child may suck. By a hidden manifestation, so to speak, and by a manifest concealment, while remaining one and ever the same in itself, it varies itself: in humility lowering its majesty, and in majesty raising its humility, so that it may be compared to the somehow profound shallowness of a river, in which a lamb, though very small, can walk most easily, while an elephant, though immense, can scarcely swim.

V. Therefore, since it is one and ever the same in itself, and never disagrees with itself through contradiction, but is one countenance of chaste utterances, it produces diverse understandings according to the capacity of its readers. At one time it gives beginners and the tender milk, as it were, of history; at another, it feeds those advancing in faith with the bread of allegory. At one time it refreshes those vigorously labouring at good works with the solid food of tropology; finally, it intoxicates in the anagogical sense, with the wine of contemplative theory, those raised from low things through contempt for earthly matters and advanced toward the heights through desire for heavenly things.

And although, among its other three senses, history is usually both easier and more open for understanding, yet the diligent reader sometimes finds more things hidden in it according to the historical sense and revealed according to the spiritual sense, so that one must sometimes see less clearly in viewing the level plain than the thickness of a forest. For, to offer one example among many: in the construction and arrangement of the tabernacle which was formerly made in the wilderness among that ancient people of God, many things are read which are readily evident to most people in their spiritual significance, yet remain hidden from them in the truth of the event itself. Thus, in a wonderful and most unusual way, they can take food by swallowing, but can take drink only by chewing.

VI. But because some modern writers do not at all understand how that same tabernacle was actually made and arranged, your venerable authority has graciously commanded my littleness that I too should write something concerning this matter, though I lack both sharpness of intellect and brilliance of expression. Accordingly, I ought deservedly both to shudder in astonishment and to be astonished in fear, when in these our days I see so plainly holy Moses—who was most faithful in all God’s house (Num. 12:7)—humbly listening to Jethro’s counsel (Exod. 18:1), and choosing Hobab, son of Raguel, as a guide for the journey, although he has no doubt that God himself speaks with him mouth to mouth, as a man ordinarily speaks with his friend (Deut. 34:10), and always goes before the people in the pillar to provide a place for the camp (Exod. 13:21).

For who among all the wise men now on earth would, in this matter, I do not say be preferable to you, but even be comparable with you, if the affairs of the government entrusted to you by God allowed you to give attention to these things? Your fatherhood has fully instructed me how I ought to write of this, so that Solomon might in some manner build the temple in me all the more easily because his father David more fully showed him how it ought to be built (1 Chron. 22:8), and undertook to prepare and supply whatever might be necessary for its construction.

Therefore, my beloved father, compelled by your command, instructed by your teaching, and encouraged by your consolation, casting my thought upon him who opens the mouths of the dumb and makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wis. 10:21), I applied my mind to study and my hand to the pen, and set down in writing those things which he deigned to minister to me concerning this through his Spirit. I have tried not only to show how that visible tabernacle of Moses was actually made and arranged, but also, according to your command, as far as I was able, to explain what both the tabernacle itself and the things belonging to it signify in the allegorical and tropological senses. For your fatherhood commanded me to endeavour to show not only what in history was worthy of wonder, but also what in allegory was to be venerated with the belief of perfect faith, and what in tropology was to be imitated through the holiness of good conduct.

VII. Moreover, as your fatherhood commanded, I made a certain drawing which represents, after some fashion, the form of that ancient tabernacle, so that those things which are to be understood by faith of the Church of the elect in common, and to be constructed by meditation in each individual elect person, may in some measure also be perceived through bodily sight. But concerning the altar’s grating, about which, as you say, there is great ambiguity among Greeks as well as Latins, I did not presume to state my own opinion. Rather, I took care to set forth what men who greatly preceded me in age, learning, and life not only said concerning it but also left in their writings, judging it superfluous to light a lamp in the sun.

But concerning the half of the sixth curtain, whose doubling was used to cover the rear of the tabernacle, I have, in accordance with your command, developed a lengthy discussion; and in its proper place I have plainly shown whether I judge the opinion of the Jews or that of the Venerable Bede to be accepted on this point. Yet I especially wish my reader to know this: although, in this material description of the tabernacle, I have not removed every doubt or all occasion for questioning by disclosing the whole truth of the historical event, I have nevertheless taken care, in asserting anything concerning it, to avoid falsehood and lying, insofar as I knew how to determine them. Thus, if I could not run in the full light of truth, I might at least not remain altogether blind in the density of darkness.

For, in order that I might treat more securely and clearly both of the tabernacle of the holy Church, which is allegory, and of the tabernacle of the human heart, which is tropology, I first showed, as far as I could infer and grasp from the statements of the book of Exodus—from which the first knowledge of this matter came down to us—and from the book of the Venerable priest Bede, which contains its allegorical exposition of the same tabernacle, how that ancient tabernacle of Moses was actually made and arranged. For the stronger, so to speak, the foundation had been laid beneath the house of our book, the more securely could its walls be raised and its roof set upon them.

Accordingly, I first set down the words of Exodus, both those in which the Lord speaks to holy Moses concerning the tabernacle still to be made, and those which the author of the same book briefly repeats after it had been built. Then, wishing to show how the Venerable priest Bede agrees with my understanding, I took care to append his own interpretation of the aforesaid words of Exodus; nor did I omit, wherever needed, to include the words of a certain honourable and learned man. Furthermore, in accordance with the command of your Fatherhood, I divided this book into three parts. The first part treats the construction and arrangement of the material and visible tabernacle of Moses. The second treats its drawing and its allegorical significance. The third treats its moral significance.

VIII. Among the other things of which sacred Scripture is accustomed to speak, these three tabernacles are especially prominent: this material and visible tabernacle; the tabernacle of the holy Church; and the tabernacle of the human soul. The first is the tabernacle of Moses and exists in historical fact; the second is Christ’s and exists in the true belief of sound faith; the third is the Holy Spirit’s and exists in the inward purity of the cleansed mind. The first was made on Mount Sinai, and history treats of it, that we may wonder; the second was made in the breadth of the world, and allegory speaks of it, that we may venerate it; the third was made in purity of soul, and tropology treats of it, that we may imitate it.

Around the first tabernacle are the twelve tribes of the children of Israel; around the second, the twelve apostles; around the third, the twelve virtues mentioned by the Apostle: charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity (Gal. 5:22). “Let us make three tabernacles,” says the Apostle (Matt. 17:4). These, therefore, are the three tabernacles. The first is the tabernacle of the covenant; the second, the holy Church; the third, the human soul. Since I speak here of these three tabernacles, I judged that the work should be entitled *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, unless perhaps something else should seem good to you.

In the first part, speaking of the construction and arrangement of the material tabernacle, I wish my reader to know without any doubt that I have followed diligently and carefully the words of the book of Exodus and of the Venerable priest Bede, and that I am conscious of having said nothing contrary to them in any respect. But when neither the text of Exodus, nor that of the Venerable Bede, nor Josephus, nor the words of the man briefly mentioned above—whose religious life and Catholic teaching I do not fail to recognize—perhaps showed me the full truth of the historical event, then at last I simply set down what seemed to me right. I took care, indeed, not to affirm as certain what I said in this way, but only to put forward my conjecture plainly and leave humbly to the judgment of those who know the full truth on these matters whether it should be regarded as sound or unsound.

In the second part, I drew the tabernacle itself and certain things belonging to it on a flat surface. Yet by this drawing I did not fully demonstrate how it was actually made and arranged, but showed in some measure what its construction and arrangement were like. I wished to mark in this displayed drawing not many things, but very few, concerning the allegorical arrangement of the tabernacle, because anyone who wishes to read may find abundantly in the sayings of the holy Fathers—and especially in the book composed by the Venerable priest Bede on the tabernacle according to the allegorical sense—how all these things are to be understood allegorically. Nevertheless, I inserted into the drawing of which I speak certain seeds of arguments and sources of explanations drawn from various sayings of orthodox Fathers, which the Author of light deigned to reveal to me. The reader’s examination will determine whether they should be accepted or rejected.

IX. But if anyone wishes to maintain that I may justly be blamed in this and for this, let him know that Boaz of Bethlehem has not merely graciously granted permission to my Ruth, but has given a firm command: that, leaving every other field aside, she should gather in his own field—which is beyond doubt most fruitful—the remaining ears that have escaped the hands of the reapers (Ruth 2:2). When these have been beaten out with the threefold rod, as your Fatherhood writes, she may feed her beautiful one all the more carefully because she returned empty and bitter from the land of Moab; so that she may be full in the house of bread and joyful in the land of confession—she whom merciful Boaz does not wish to be hungry in his house, lest she fail on the way.

Thanks be to you, good and gracious Boaz, who deign to command your reapers that, if Ruth wishes to reap with them, they should not hinder her but should rather cast down from their own sheaves, so that she may gather without shame and none may rebuke her as she gathers (Ruth 2:15). Hence it is plainly evident that those who rebuke me, Ruth, for gathering ears do not agree either with you or with your reapers: for you permit her to reap, while they rebuke her if she gathers.

Moreover, there was a great reaper in the field of that heavenly Boaz, who, when Joshua urged him to forbid Eldad and Medad to prophesy in the camp, answered: “Are you jealous on my account?” (Num. 11:27). And he added: “Who would grant me that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord might give them his Spirit?” (ibid., 29). For, as the most reverend bishop Acca once wrote to the Venerable priest Bede: “It has never been the custom of the saints to envy one another or provoke one another, but for each person, in adorning the house of the Lord, to offer according to his strength what he could.” And shortly afterward: “Indeed, as blessed Augustine says, it is necessary that many books be made by many people in different styles, yet not with a different faith, even on the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach more people: in one way to some, and in another way to others.”

Let these few lofty words be said, lest we appear to have been altogether silent before our scoffing enemies. They sometimes read in secret, even with praise, our little works, yet, prompted by envious pride and proud envy, publicly despise them by criticism.

X. In the third part of this book, I also applied myself to morality; and I marked in the drawing of the tabernacle itself the divisions of ideas belonging to that morality, just as I did those belonging to allegory, by steps, drawings, or varieties of colours. Concerning these steps, drawings, and varieties of colours, the reader should especially know that they were not at all present in that visible tabernacle of Moses. But because I have treated three tabernacles in this book, dividing the book into three parts as reason requires, I assigned its own tabernacle to each part; and in the visible drawing I placed such images and colours as might more suitably indicate the spirituality of each of the two spiritual tabernacles, namely the allegorical and the tropological.

Since I have now completed this book, if not as I ought, at least as I could, I have sent it with the drawing to you, at whose command I undertook to write it. I earnestly beg you to observe diligently both where I have walked along the royal road and where I may perhaps have turned aside from it, so that your authority may confirm what I have said well and may not leave errors uncorrected. And because the second and third parts of this book concern the drawing, you will appropriately have both parts of the aforesaid book read with the drawing spread out before you, so that, receiving what is read through hearing and what is depicted through sight, you may fit book and drawing together.

But if anyone murmurs because I set the tasteless little vegetable of my poverty beside savoury dishes for one seated at a feast, you will surely be summoned to account: you who desired it, not I who gave it; you who commanded it, not I who obeyed the one commanding. May God the almighty Father, through his only beloved Son, preserve your holy Fatherhood mindful of me in the Holy Spirit, so that, aided by the help of his mercy, it may always be free from sin and secure from every disturbance. Amen.

# On the Threefold Tabernacle

[Col. 0633]

## Part One. On the Tabernacle of Moses in the Literal Sense

**344 Chapter One. On the difficulty of treating the material construction and arrangement of the tabernacle of Moses**

[Col. 0633D]

I. Since it pleases your excellency, venerable Father, that we too should endeavour to show how that ancient tabernacle of Moses was actually made and arranged, you must certainly entreat with devout prayers that supreme and true Craftsman, that he may deign to fill even your Bezalel with the Holy Spirit, so that he may be able to set forth at least some small account of so great a matter.

For your fatherhood clearly knows that there is now no human being at all who has seen the aforesaid structure with bodily eyes; and therefore it is no wonder if we too see dimly concerning its physical construction and arrangement. If someone should say that from the statements of Exodus we can fully infer the material construction and arrangement of the aforesaid tabernacle, let him know that it is not surprising if we do not fully understand the words of that book according to the letter, since some eminent teachers, far removed from us both in holiness of life and in loftiness of learning, are found to have held differing opinions concerning the literal sense of those very words.

[Col. 0635B]

II. To mention a few examples out of many: Aurelius Augustine, our incomparable father, advocate, and doctor of the Church, in many places, as those who have read him affirm, says that the altar of incense was within the veil, whereas Josephus and nearly all interpreters of sacred Scripture affirm that it was placed outside the veil, opposite the ark of the covenant, between the lampstand and the table of presentation. The same most reverend doctor further says that two bases were not placed beneath each of the boards in the three walls of the tabernacle, but that one base was set beneath the board and the other above it, so that the upper base was like a capital. Yet Scripture plainly says that two bases were placed beneath each board at its two corners, the Lord saying to Moses: “Two bases shall be placed under each board at its two corners” (Exod. 26:16). And again: “Counting two bases for each board” (ibid., 25).

And who does not know that the Venerable priest Bede, teacher of the English, was not only a diligent investigator of the word of God but also a truthful interpreter? Yet Master Andrew differs considerably from that doctor concerning the spreading of the curtains and coverings over the roof of the tabernacle and concerning the doubling of the sixth covering at the front of the roof.

III. I have said these things to you, dearest Father, so that you may consider that it is no wonder if I sink beneath the burden you lay upon my weak neck, so heavy a burden; and if I, a mole, see dimly in the rays of that sun in which eagles so great and so eminent are found to see dimly.

Therefore, because I am compelled to reveal my folly concerning the material construction and arrangement of the tabernacle, I shall first endeavour, as far as I can understand, to show how the three walls of the tabernacle were composed of boards and how those boards were joined together. Second, I shall show how the joined and secured boards and the walls together with the entrance were erected. Third, I shall show how the aforesaid walls were covered with curtains, coverings, reddened skins, and blue skins. When the tabernacle has thus been completed, I shall attempt to discuss, as far as I can infer it, the things that were inside it and outside around it.

## Chapter Two. On the boards of the three walls of the tabernacle, their bases, and their joints

[Col. 0636A]

IV. The Lord said to Moses:

“You shall make upright boards for the tabernacle from shittim wood. Each shall be ten cubits in length and one and a half cubits in width. On the sides of each board two joints shall be made, by which one board may be joined to another board. All the boards shall be prepared in this manner. There shall be twenty of them on the south side, which faces south; and you shall cast forty silver bases for them, so that two bases may be placed under each board at its two corners. On the second side of the tabernacle, which faces north, there shall be twenty boards, having forty silver bases. Two bases shall be placed under each board. For the west side of the tabernacle you shall make six boards, and again two additional boards, which shall be erected at the corners behind the rear of the tabernacle. They shall be joined from bottom to top, and a single joining shall hold them all together. The same type of joining shall be retained for the two boards which are to be placed at the corner; and together there shall be eight boards, their sixteen silver bases being counted as two bases for each board.” (Exod. 26:15 ff.)

## Chapter Three. From the Book of Exodus concerning the same matter

V. He made the upright boards of the tabernacle from shittim wood. The length of one board was ten cubits, and its width was one and a half cubits. There were two joints in each board, so that one might be joined to another. Thus he made all the boards of the tabernacle. Of these, twenty were on the south side facing south, with forty silver bases. Two bases were placed beneath one board, on either side of the corners where the side-joints terminate at the corners.

For the side of the tabernacle facing north, he likewise made twenty boards with forty silver bases, two bases for each board. Opposite the west—that is, at that side of the tabernacle which faces the sea—he made six boards, and two more at the separate rear corners of the tabernacle. They were joined from bottom to top and brought into one joining. Thus he made them at both sides by the corners, so that there were eight boards together, with sixteen silver bases, namely two bases beneath each board. (Exod. 36:20 ff.)

## Chapter Four. Literal exposition of the preceding chapter

VI. As far as I can infer from what is written in Exodus, the tabernacle constructed in the wilderness consisted of three walls: the southern, northern, and western. On the eastern side, where the entrance was, there was no wall; but a bar extended from the southern side to the northern, upon which hung the screen suspended before five columns. This eastern side must be discussed more fully below.

The aforesaid three walls consisted of boards made from shittim wood, but gilded on both sides, as is read below. There were twenty boards in the southern wall, the same number in the northern, and eight in the western. Beneath each board were two silver bases, cast and set under the two corners of each board, four fingers high above the ground, as Josephus writes. On the sides of each board were also two joints, by which one board was joined to another. The same Josephus says that two tenons were inserted into each board through two silver bases, and that the silver bases received the tenons in their own holes. Thus each board had two corners, beneath which its two bases were set; and at those same corners the side-joints terminated, by which every board throughout the circuit of the three walls was joined to another board.

[Col. 0637B]

VII. But, as the Venerable Bede says, the form of these joints could not be seen once the arrangement of the boards had been set in regular order and the tabernacle itself erected. Nevertheless, the firm stability of the walls showed that all the walls of the tabernacle were coupled together through these joint-connections.

Scripture does not expressly state the length of either the southern or northern wall; nevertheless, we can clearly establish it from the measurements of the widths of the boards from which those walls were composed. Since each wall consisted of twenty boards, and each board was one and a half cubits wide and ten cubits long, it is evident that each of the aforesaid walls was thirty cubits long and ten cubits high. For the widths of the boards made the length of the walls, and the lengths of the boards made the height of the walls. Therefore the tabernacle was thirty cubits in length, ten in height, and ten in width.

VIII. A certain man of venerable life and a diligent investigator of the word of God writes as follows, according to the letter, concerning these joints, the length of the house, and the two bases set beneath each board:

“Each board of the tabernacle had, on both sides, a joint—that is, a small hollow and a kind of cavity—and by such cavities they received and joined one another so skilfully that all appeared to be like one continuous piece of wood. Since there were twenty boards together on either side of the house and each was one and a half cubits wide, it is evident that the tabernacle was thirty cubits long. Each board had two tenons in its lower part toward the ground, and beneath each tenon was placed a base. Augustine, however, says that the two bases were not placed beneath each board on one side, but one base was placed below the board and the other above it, taking ‘base’ for ‘capital.’ But the text appears contrary, which says: ‘Two bases shall be placed beneath each board at its two corners’ (Exod. 26:19).”

Thus he writes.

[Col. 0638A]

IX. Concerning those eight boards which made the western wall, we should know that not all of them had, within the walls, the same measurement of width as the boards of the other walls. For if each of these boards had been one and a half cubits wide within the walls, as each board of the other walls was, the tabernacle would have had not only ten cubits but twelve in width; for eight full cubits and eight half-cubits make twelve.

What then is to be said of the widths of these eight boards, except that each of the six boards was one and a half cubits wide, while the seventh and eighth—that is, the two placed at the corners of the western wall—were not a cubit and a half wide; indeed, within the walls they did not even have one full cubit, but only half a cubit? The book of Exodus neither asserts nor denies that all these boards had the same width as the boards of the other walls; but Josephus says that the corner boards of the western wall were cut from a half-cubit in the middle. For he says: “Six boards made nine cubits of the rear wall, to which were joined two other boards cut in the middle of a cubit, which they placed at the corners after the manner of the larger boards.”

X. Although the book of Exodus does not openly say, as Josephus does, that these same corner boards were cut from a half-cubit in the middle, yet because it discusses them separately, perhaps it secretly indicates to us that they did not have the same width within the walls as the other six boards. Thus the aforesaid book reads: “For the western side of the tabernacle you shall make six boards, and again two additional boards, which shall be erected at the corners behind the rear of the tabernacle” (Exod. 26:22–23). Again: “Opposite the west he made six boards, and two additional boards for each of the rear corners of the tabernacle” (Exod. 36:27–28).

It first mentions the six boards in the middle, and afterward the two at the corners, perhaps thus causing us to understand that the two and the six had different measurements, insofar as width within the walls is concerned. A certain writer seems to agree with my opinion, unless I am mistaken. Speaking of the boards of the western wall and explaining literally the phrase in Exodus, “two additional boards, which shall be erected at the corners,” he says:

“Perhaps they are called ‘additional’ because, according to Josephus, they were of another size than the rest; for each was half a cubit. But it is certain that the other boards of the same wall were of the same size as the boards on the side. The same, similar joining bound all of them together.”

## Chapter Five. Words of the Venerable priest Bede on this chapter

XI. The tabernacle was a house consecrated to the Lord, thirty cubits in length, ten in width, and likewise ten in height. Its roof was level throughout, as is customary in building houses in Palestine. Its three walls—the southern, northern, and western—were constructed from wooden boards gilded on both sides.

The shittim wood from which the tabernacle was made is by nature incorruptible, exceptionally white and light, differing little from the white thorn except in size. Therefore Jerome sometimes interpreted *setim* simply as “thorns” in the book of Hebrew names as well as in his other small works; for example: “Abel: the bright setim of thorns.” This kind of wood is not commonly found except in the deserts of Arabia, where the tabernacle was built. Therefore Greek and Latin translators were unable to give it any name other than the Hebrew one. Although some, wishing to express its natural quality, translated it as “incorruptible wood,” it was a tree unknown among them.

XII. On the eastern side there was one bar, where the entrance was, extending through the middle of the boards from corner to corner—that is, from the outermost top of one wall to the top of the other wall—so that the curtains and roof of the tabernacle might rest upon it. There the screen was suspended from five columns.

The tabernacle’s length is not stated explicitly, but it is implied by the statement that its walls consisted of twenty boards, each said to be one and a half cubits wide. For twenty cubits together with twenty half-cubits make thirty cubits; Josephus writes that this was the length of the tabernacle. All the boards of the tabernacle were joined to one another through the connection of their joints. Once the tabernacle was erected and the arrangement of boards regularly ordered, the form of the joints was not seen. Yet the unshaken firmness and stability of the wall showed by what strength they had joined the boards to one another.

Two bases were set beneath each board at its two corners, so that, with its corners well supported, the whole board might stand upright and without leaning. Josephus writes that the boards of the tabernacle were raised four fingers’ breadth above the ground. From this he seems to mean that the bases of the boards were made of that height.

## Chapter Six. On the bars of the three walls, their joining and erection; on the screen of the entrance and its five columns; on the veil before the Holy of Holies and its four columns
XIII. The Lord said to Moses: “You shall make bars of acacia wood: five to hold together the boards of one side of the tabernacle, and five others of the same number for the other side, and five for the western side. They shall be passed through the middle of the boards from end to end. You shall overlay the boards themselves with gold, and cast in them golden rings through which the bars may hold the boards together; and you shall cover the bars with plates of gold. You shall set up the tabernacle according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain. You shall also make a veil [Col. 0640A] of blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, worked with embroidery and woven in beautiful variety. You shall hang it before four columns of acacia wood, which shall themselves be overlaid with gold and shall have golden capitals, but silver bases. The veil shall be inserted through the rings; within it you shall place the ark of the covenant, and it shall divide the sanctuary from the Holy of Holies. You shall place the mercy-seat upon the ark of testimony in the Holy of Holies, and the table outside the veil, and opposite the table the lampstand on the south side of the tabernacle: the table, however, shall stand on the north side. You shall also make a screen at the entrance of the tabernacle from blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, worked with embroidery; and you shall overlay five columns of acacia wood, before which the screen shall be drawn, [Col. 0640B] whose capitals shall be gold and whose bases bronze” (Exod. 26:26 ff.).

## CHAPTER VII. Likewise, from the Book of Exodus concerning the same matter.

XIV. He also made five bars of acacia wood to hold together the boards of one side of the tabernacle, and five others to fasten the boards of the other side; and, besides these, five further bars for the western side of the tabernacle, facing the sea. He also made another bar, running through the middle of the boards from corner to corner. He overlaid the boards themselves with gold, their silver bases having been cast; and he made their rings of gold, through which the bars could be passed, and covered the bars themselves with plates of gold. He also made a veil of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twisted linen, varied and distinguished by embroidered work; [Col. 0640C] and four columns of acacia wood, which he overlaid with gold together with their capitals, their silver bases having been cast. He also made a screen at the entrance of the tabernacle from blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twisted linen, worked with embroidery; and five columns with their capitals, which he covered with gold, and he cast their bronze bases. (Exod. 36:31 ff.)

## CHAPTER VIII. Literal exposition of the preceding chapter.

XV. After that firmness of joining which the mortises contributed separately to the individual boards, the bars also gave the walls a further strength. Of these, five were in the southern wall, an equal number in the northern, and the same number also in the western wall, [Col. 0640D] inserted in the middle, around the three walls, into golden rings, and cast fittings for holding and strengthening the boards in each wall. They were made indeed of acacia wood, but covered with plates of gold. Josephus writes thus concerning those golden rings into which these bars were inserted: “Each board,” he says, “had golden rings projecting from its outer faces, fixed in them as though by certain roots, regularly facing one another.” The Book of Exodus indeed does not say that there were rings in each board; but Bede says that five rings were fixed in every board: “Each board,” he says, “had five rings”; and again: “Five golden rings were fixed in each board.”

Therefore the bars were in each wall in order that, inserted through the rings—of which there were five in every board—around its whole extent, [Col. 0641A] they might firmly hold together the boarding of those walls. Thus, just as in the lower portion those same boards had been secured in their position and uprightness because, as Josephus says, the holes of the bases placed beneath received the two tenons of each board; and on the sides by the joining of the mortises—these lateral mortises ending at the corners, where the bases were also placed beneath and underneath—so likewise the same boarding might be secured through its middle all around by the bars inserted into the rings. Strengthened in this fashion below, at the sides, and in the middle, the structure would stand firmly compacted, so that no noise might arise from any force of the winds, nor the building shake.

[Col. 0641B] The Book of Exodus neither denies nor affirms that the ends of the individual bars were joined to one another by some connection; but Josephus says that “the end of each bar entered into the end of another bar in the manner of a shell.” One writer says thus of these bars: “The bars of the front and sides were equal in number, but not in length, because those of the sides were six cubits, but those of the front two cubits. There were not five rows of bars on either side, as some suppose; rather, five on this side and on that, and the same number on the western front, inserted into rings fixed in the individual boards. And the end of each bar entered into the end of another bar in the manner of a shell.” Thus he speaks of the bars.

[Col. 0641C] XVI. Therefore, to repeat briefly what has been set out more fully above, and in some fashion to erect the very walls of which we have already spoken much: there were three walls of the tabernacle—namely, the southern, northern, and western—constructed of boards of acacia wood, overlaid with gold on both sides. Twenty of these stood on the south side of the tabernacle, as many on the north side, and eight on the west; each being ten cubits in length and a cubit and a half in width. The exception was the two corner boards in the western wall, where the southern and northern walls were joined on either side to the western wall: within the walls these had only half a cubit [Col. 0641D] in width. Each board was joined by a double mortise, and each stood on two silver, cast bases, reckoned for each board at its two corners around the three walls; at these corners the lateral mortises ended on both sides, and the said bases, as Josephus says, had holes which received the two tenons inserted into each board.

The length of the southern and northern walls was thirty cubits, and the height of each wall ten cubits; the breadth of the tabernacle—that is, the space between the walls—was likewise ten cubits. There were also five bars in each wall, made indeed of acacia wood but [Col. 0642A] covered with plates of gold, for holding and strengthening those often-mentioned boards. They were inserted, in the middle around the three walls, into golden and cast rings on each side of the tabernacle; the end of one bar entered into the end of another in the manner of a shell.

XVII. On the eastern side, where the entrance was, there was no wall. Rather, one bar was stretched at the top through the middle of the boards from one corner of the wall to the other. Beneath that bar, five columns of acacia wood, overlaid with gold and having golden capitals, were raised across the width, skillfully inserted into and secured in the bar itself. Their bases, however, were bronze. Before the four columns a screen was drawn, woven from four colours: blue, purple, [Col. 0642B] twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen. For one writer says: “On the eastern side there was a bar stretched from the southern side to the northern, upon which rested the capitals of the five columns, before which was hung the veil at the entrance of the tabernacle.”

Another screen, properly called the veil, woven from the four aforementioned colours, hung through rings before four columns of acacia wood, erected crosswise between the walls, overlaid with gold, and furnished with golden capitals and silver bases. The inner place, extending from this veil to the western wall, was the Holy of Holies; the outer place, extending from the entrance to this same veil, was simply called the Holy Place. The outer section, as Josephus says, was twenty [Col. 0642C] cubits in length, but the inner section ten. Thus the whole house was thirty cubits long. Let this suffice concerning the walls of the tabernacle and its entrance. Let us now show how the Venerable Bede bears witness to these words of ours.

## CHAPTER IX. The words of the Venerable Bede, priest, on this chapter.

XVIII. “Five bars,” he says, “held together the boards of the tabernacle, and five golden rings were fixed in each board of the tabernacle; the bars held the boards together through the golden rings. Moreover, one bar should be understood as having been stretched from the top of the first boards to the top of the other side across the ten-cubit breadth of the tabernacle. Its two ends rested firmly upon the boards, while in its middle it was skillfully inserted into the capitals of the columns; and so its position both safeguarded the stability of the walls from the eastern side [Col. 0642D] and held the columns steady, so that they could not slip or be overthrown. Thus that side of the tabernacle which consisted not of boards but of columns might remain no less fixed than the others, even when the wind drove against it. There also was the screen hung upon five columns, which had golden capitals but bronze bases, and which were commanded to be made of acacia wood and covered with gold.

“There was also a veil, variegated with embroidered work, hung upon four columns, by which the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies were divided. Josephus reports that this veil dividing the tabernacle in the middle was placed so that twenty cubits of length belonged to the first chamber and ten to the second, so that it might in every respect correspond to the measurements of the Temple afterwards built by Solomon. That Temple, being forty cubits long and twenty broad, had one third of its length—that is, ten cubits—set apart for the inner house, namely the Holy of Holies, so that the length and breadth of that inner house were equal. [Col. 0643A] Thus likewise the inner part of the tabernacle had equal length and breadth, namely ten cubits each.”

## CHAPTER X. On the curtains, the goat-hair cloths, and the coverings of the roof of the tabernacle.

XIX. The Lord said to Moses: “You shall make the tabernacle thus. You shall make ten curtains of fine twisted linen, blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, variegated with embroidered work. The length of one curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and its breadth four cubits; all the curtains shall be of one measure. Five curtains shall be joined to one another, and the other five shall likewise adhere by a similar joining. You shall make loops of blue on the sides and edges of the curtains, so that they may be joined together. A curtain shall have fifty loops on each side, so placed that loop may meet loop and one may be fitted to the other. You shall also make fifty golden rings, by which the curtains are to be joined, so that one tabernacle may result. You shall make eleven goat-hair cloths to cover the roof of the tabernacle. The length of one cloth shall be thirty cubits, and its breadth [Col. 0643C] four cubits. The measure of all the cloths shall be the same. Of these, you shall join five separately and join six together; so that you fold the sixth cloth double at the front of the roof. You shall also make fifty loops on the edge of one cloth, so that it may be joined with the other; and fifty loops on the edge of the other cloth, so that it may be joined to the other. You shall make fifty bronze clasps, by which the loops shall be joined, so that one covering may result from them all.

“But what remains of the cloths prepared for the roof—that is, the one cloth which is additional—you shall use half of it to cover the rear of the tabernacle; and one cubit shall hang on one side and another on the other side, being the excess in the size of the cloths, covering both sides of the tabernacle. You shall also make another covering for the roof from reddened rams’ skins, and over this again another covering [Col. 0643D] from violet-coloured skins” (Exod. 26:1 ff.).

## CHAPTER XI. Likewise, from the Book of Exodus concerning the same matter.

XX. Bezalel, in order to complete the work of the tabernacle, made ten curtains of fine twisted linen, blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, with varied workmanship and embroidered art. Each was twenty-eight cubits long and four broad; the measure of all the curtains was the same. He joined five curtains one to another and joined another five together. He also made blue loops on the edge of one curtain, and likewise on the edge of the other curtain, so that the loops met one another and were mutually joined; [Col. 0644A] from this he cast fifty golden rings to catch the loops of the curtains, so that one tabernacle might result.

He also made eleven goat-hair cloths from goats’ hair to cover the roof of the tabernacle. One cloth was thirty cubits long and four cubits broad; all the cloths were of one measure. Five of them he joined separately, and six others separately. He made fifty loops on the edge of one cloth and fifty loops on the edge of the other, so that they might be joined to one another; and fifty bronze clasps, by which the roof might be fastened and one covering made from all the cloths. He also made a covering for the tabernacle from reddened rams’ skins, and another covering over it from violet-coloured skins (Exod. 36:8 ff.).

## CHAPTER XII. Literal exposition of the preceding chapter.

[Col. 0644B]

XXI. Since we have now raised the walls of the tabernacle, let us now cover those same walls. The aforementioned walls were first covered by curtains, then by goat-hair cloths. There were ten curtains, woven from blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen. Each was twenty-eight cubits in length and four in breadth. They also had fifty blue loops on their sides, so that, when the curtains themselves were firmly joined to one another through these loops, a single tabernacle might result from them all.

There were likewise eleven cloths, each thirty cubits long and four cubits broad. Like the curtains, each had fifty loops on its sides, so that, as I said concerning the curtains, [Col. 0644C] when these cloths were joined to one another through the loops, a single covering might result from them. Although the individual curtains and individual cloths were joined to one another, it was nevertheless commanded concerning the curtains that five and five should be joined together, and concerning the cloths that five should be joined and six should adhere by a similar joining. [Col. 0644D] This was, I think, because it seemed excessively laborious, when the tabernacle was taken down, to separate every individual curtain and cloth, and likewise, when it was erected, to join both one by one.

For the Venerable Bede says: “All the curtains were of one colour and decorated with the same colours, but they were joined five together.” Again: “The ten curtains, which when joined completed the beauty of the tabernacle, were separated at the appropriate time in such a way that five remained together on each side; [Col. 0644D] yet at the time when the tabernacle was erected, all the curtains were joined to one another.” It is also well said that the curtains had loops on both sides, so that every curtain might, as it were, embrace its adjacent curtains on either side with arms stretched out here and there. This is what Bede says of the curtains; and concerning the cloths: “The division of the cloths into five and six may be understood according to what we explained above concerning the curtains divided into five and five.” Thus speaks that venerable man concerning the curtains and cloths.

XXII. We must understand, moreover, that five curtains were joined to the other five by fifty golden, cast rings, which caught the same number of loops located on each set of five curtains. [Col. 0645A] The five cloths were joined to the six in exactly the same manner, except that the curtains, as stated, were connected by golden rings, whereas the cloths were joined by bronze clasps.

There were also blue loops on the sides and edges of the curtains. For it is written: “You shall make blue loops on the sides and edges of the curtains” (Exod. 26:4). Some hold that these “edges” of the curtains should be understood as their ends hanging down toward the ground, and that loops should be placed at those ends, in order that the aforesaid curtains might be stretched out with ropes threaded through the loops and secured by pegs, lest the violence of an arising storm tear them away. [Col. 0645B] Since neither the authority of Scripture, as with the loops on the sides, nor the exposition of teachers specifies the number of these loops, they assert that there were as many as could keep the curtains taut without wrinkles.

[Col. 0645C] But that eloquent man does not appear to agree with those who say this. He writes thus concerning the same edges of the curtains: “Some think that the edges of the curtains should be understood as their ends across the breadth, and that loops there, as on the sides, were commanded to be made. But when they are asked what use they served there, if indeed they were there, they reply that ropes were passed through the loops and the curtains stretched out on either side with pegs; yet Scripture appears to make no mention of this.” Thus he speaks concerning the edges.

Therefore this same eloquent man calls the “edges” of the curtains not their ends hanging down toward the ground, but rather their corners and lateral surfaces. On those sides there were fifty loops along the length, as he says in the preceding passage: “It seems to us that every curtain had fifty loops on each side along its length and at the edges, that is, at the corners of the sides.” He writes thus concerning the joining of the curtains and cloths: “It must be understood that the tabernacle was shown beforehand to Moses on the mountain, after the pattern of which the one he was to make would be made. He commanded the tabernacle to be made as follows: namely, that ten curtains should be taken, of the kind and dimensions he himself describes, and many other things which he adds, so that a tabernacle might be made from them.”

[Col. 0645D] XXIII. Yet the curtains are properly called the tabernacle. Blue is wool dyed this colour; purple is the colour of blood and is dyed from the blood of shellfish; twice-dyed scarlet is wool dyed twice in scarlet colour so that it may be very red; fine linen is a kind of very soft and very white flax, worked with embroidery. *Pluma*, Augustine says, means “needle” in the Punic language. Embroidered work is made when, after the cloth has already been produced, threads of gold or silver are inserted with a needle, in order to make gold embroidery (*auriphrysium*) or various figures in the cloth itself; such work is commonly called *brustatum*.

The ten curtains of the tabernacle were arranged so that five were joined and adhered mutually to one another, and the other five likewise. “You shall make blue loops on the sides [Col. 0646A] and edges of the curtains, so that they may be joined together” (Exod. 26:4). Here he shows how the curtains are to be joined to one another. It is doubtful, however, whether he commands that the individual curtains should be coupled one to one in this manner, or five with five, so that one covering may result from all.

It seems to us that every curtain, on each side along its length and at the edges—that is, the corners of its sides—had fifty loops; and that they were firmly connected to one another either by bands or by certain other fastenings through the loops. Then only five and five were joined mutually, in order that one covering might result, being joined by fifty golden rings; and those rings themselves had a small gap, so that when the tabernacle had to be set up or taken down, they could easily be inserted into the rings and easily withdrawn from them again. This is concerning the curtains.

XXIV. He also writes thus concerning the cloths: “*Saga cilicina*: in Hebrew, goat-hair curtains. Augustine calls these curtains *vela capillatia*, ‘hairy veils,’ perhaps because this is how they are rendered in the Septuagint translation which he uses. He calls them ‘veils’ because they are square in the manner of a veil; ‘hairy’ because they are made of hairs, for the hairs of the head are hairs. They are also customarily called *saga cilicia*; but the addition of *cilicina* after *saga* is pleonastic. Moreover, a *sagum* is a military cloak invented by the Gauls, and it is called *quadrum* because it was first made square, or fourfold. [Col. 0646B] Perhaps the goat-hair fabrics prepared to cover the roof of the tabernacle were called *saga* because of their square shape.

“The joining of the cloths to one another was made in the same way as that of the curtains, except that [Col. 0646C] six were on one side and five on the other, and that the curtains were coupled with golden rings, whereas these were coupled with bronze clasps.” Thus he writes concerning the curtains and cloths.

Therefore, once one tent-covering has been made both from the curtains and from the cloths, let us hang it above the walls: first the curtains, then the cloths; and let us see how they covered them. But first, taking two measuring cords, let us measure the length of the house with one and its transverse breadth with the other. The cord by which we wish to measure the entire length of the house—that is, from the base of one of the five columns at the entrance of the tabernacle to the base of one board of the western wall—will be fifty cubits long: namely, ten in ascending the eastern wall, thirty along the length of the house, and ten in descending the western wall. The other cord, by which we wish to measure the transverse breadth of the house—that is, from the base of a board in the northern wall to the base of a board in the southern wall—will be thirty cubits long: namely, ten in ascending the northern wall, ten in descending the southern wall, and ten across the level space at the top between the walls.

XXV. [Col. 0647A] The tabernacle of which we speak was not raised to a peaked roof in the manner of our houses, but was level at the top with a flat plan, just as houses were built in that land at that time. Thus Deuteronomy commands that whoever builds a new house shall place a wall around the roof, lest innocent blood be shed if someone falls and plunges headlong (Deut. 22:8). I think this is also what the Lord says to the disciples in the Gospel: “What you have heard in the ear shall be preached upon the housetops” (Luke 12:3), because people in the province of Palestine customarily sat on roofs, which were level everywhere at their uppermost surfaces.

Let us therefore hang the curtains above the walls and the cloths above the curtains. [Col. 0647B] We must understand that both curtains and cloths covered the length of the house by their widths, and covered its transverse breadth by their lengths. When the curtains have been hung above the walls, we shall see that by their lengths they cover the entire transverse breadth of the house down to the ground, except for one cubit near the ground on either side, which remains uncovered here and there because of the insufficiency of the curtains. For the transverse breadth of the house is thirty cubits, while the curtains are only twenty-eight cubits long.
