The same curtains cover the length of the tabernacle, which is thirty cubits, by the length formed when their widths are joined together; and they cover the eastern section, where the entrance is, and the western wall, descending five cubits on each side by the length of their widths. For the widths of the ten curtains joined together make forty cubits in length. Of these forty cubits, thirty-two are allotted to the southern and northern walls, since they had that length; [Col. 0647C] and of the ten remaining, five are allotted to the eastern side and five, descending from the other side, to the western wall. This was properly and particularly called the tabernacle.

Those five cubits which reach to the ground on either side in the eastern and western sections will by no means be bare. [Col. 0647D] Rather, the five cubits of curtains remaining where the walls fall short will be brought together from the eastern and western sides and joined mutually, so that five cubits of the curtains may cover both the eastern and western walls of the house. But the goat-hair cloths, because they were thirty cubits long, hung over the tabernacle and wholly covered the one cubit on either side of the southern and northern walls which, through the insufficiency of the curtains, had been left uncovered near the ground.

XXVI. [Col. 0648A] Further, because there were eleven of them, and each was four cubits broad like the curtains, they cover the entire length of the tabernacle and descend beyond the curtains by two cubits on the eastern side and by as many on the western side. For the widths of the eleven cloths, joined together, make forty-four cubits in length. Of these forty-four cubits, thirty cover the length of the walls; of the fourteen remaining, seven were allotted to the eastern side and seven to the western. The two cubits which extend beyond the curtains on the eastern side were folded double, as Exodus also says: “You shall fold the sixth cloth double at the front of the roof” (Exod. 26:9).

[Col. 0648B] The Venerable Bede gives the reason why the sixth cloth was folded double at the front of the roof, in these words: “In the literal sense, he calls the front of the roof the entrance of the tabernacle, where, as we have said briefly above, it was commanded that columns should be placed rather than boards, together with a bar stretched from one corner of the boards to the other. Therefore, as regards the form of the work, there was greater need there for the doubled protection of the cloths, where the solid strength of a wall was absent.” Thus the one cubit uncovered here and there near the ground on either side when the curtains fell short was covered by the cloths laid over them; and the same cloths, descending by two cubits on both the eastern and western sides, cover the curtains.

XXVII. And I think this is what that subtle verse, perplexing in its wording, means: “But what remains of the cloths prepared for the roof—that is, the one cloth which is additional—you shall cover the rear of the tabernacle with half of it” (Exod. 26:12). That cloth which he says is additional and by which the rear of the tabernacle is to be covered is the eleventh cloth. [Col. 0648C] It is additional to the curtains, since there are only ten of them while there are eleven cloths. Half of it covers the rear of the tabernacle in that it extends beyond the curtains on the western side, where the rear of the tabernacle is, by two cubits, as has often been said—two cubits being half the width of a cloth.

“And one cubit,” he says, “shall hang on one side and another on the other side, being the excess in the size of the cloths, covering both sides of the tabernacle” (Exod. 26:13). This pair of cubits, which he calls the excess in the size of the cloths and says hangs on either side covering both sides of the tabernacle, plainly refers to the two cubits by which the cloths exceeded the curtains. For the latter, as stated, were only twenty-eight cubits long, whereas the former were thirty; [Col. 0648D] and they covered—that is, overlaid—both sides of the tabernacle, where one cubit near the ground on either side had been left uncovered because the curtains fell short. The two cubits in the cloths that exceeded the curtains, one on this side and one on that, covered that exposed cubit.

But the space of three cubits which reaches to the ground on the eastern and western sides where the cloths fall short will by no means remain bare. Rather, the cloths of seven cubits each which remain where the walls fall short, as we said a little earlier concerning the curtains, will be drawn together and will very securely cover both the front and rear of the house down to the ground. These cloths could not only, like the curtains—which covered the eastern and western sides of the house in descending only by five cubits—reach one another and meet in the middle of both the western and eastern walls; but, being seven cubits on each wall, [Col. 0649A] they extended two cubits beyond the middle of both the eastern and western sides in each direction. Of these four excess cubits, two at the eastern wall, where the front was, doubled the covering, so that, in the judgment of the Venerable Bede, there might be the protection of doubled cloths where the solid strength of a wall was lacking.

XXVIII. Thus the cloths covered the walls of the tabernacle on every side, as did the curtains except for one cubit on every side [Col. 0649B]. [Col. 0649B] There were also two further coverings, made not to cover the walls of the tabernacle but only its roof. The first was of reddened rams’ skins; the second of violet-coloured skins. [Col. 0649C] Since the text does not specify the number, length, breadth, arrangement, or joining of these skins, it is enough to understand that, once joined, they could cover the whole length and breadth of the tabernacle on the upper surface of the roof, and that the roof and walls in those parts were considerably larger than ours.

One writer long before us wrote thus concerning these skins: “It must be understood that both this covering of reddened skins and that of violet-coloured skins should be made only according to the shape and dimensions of the roof of the tabernacle, because nothing hung down from the sides or fronts.” We have therefore explained, as it seemed to us, how the curtains and cloths covered the walls of the tabernacle and how the reddened rams’ skins and violet-coloured skins covered its roof. Let us now hear what the Venerable Bede says on this matter.

## CHAPTER XIII. Words of the Venerable Bede, priest, concerning the same matter.

XXIX. “We have said,” he says, “that the walls of the tabernacle, composed of boards and columns, were thirty cubits long, ten broad, and likewise ten high. Therefore, if anyone wished to surround the house in breadth with a cord—for example, from the base [Col. 0649D] of one board on the southern side to the base of the board opposite it on the northern side—it is clear that this cord would have to be thirty cubits long: ten cubits for ascent along the southern wall, another ten along the level surface above between the walls, and a third ten for descent along the northern wall.

“Likewise, if you wish to stretch a cord along the length of the house—that is, from the bases of the columns upward, through the entire length of the house to the western wall, and then downward to its bases—that cord will be fifty cubits long: namely, ten cubits of ascent beside the columns, thirty of level extent along the length of the house, and ten again of descent beside the boards [Col. 0650A] of the western wall. Once these points are considered, observe also the measurements of the curtains by which the house was to be covered, and how they may correspond to the aforesaid dimensions.

“There were ten curtains, each twenty-eight cubits long and four broad; when joined together and formed into one, they made the tabernacle forty cubits in breadth. Hang, therefore, the curtains, each of which is twenty-eight cubits long, and place them upon a house whose transverse measurement is thirty cubits. You will see that the curtains have ten cubits across the level space between the walls, and nine cubits in the ascent or descent beside the walls. Thus the edge of the curtains cannot touch the ground, but remains one cubit above it.

[Col. 0650B] “You will likewise see that the curtains have thirty cubits across the level space along the length of the house, and five cubits in the ascent or descent on the eastern and western sides. Therefore the lateral edge of the curtains does not reach to the ground, but remains five cubits above it. Hence it was necessary that the five cubits of curtains remaining where the walls ceased should be drawn together from the eastern and western sides and joined to one another. Thus the curtains would cover the house on every side, except for one cubit near the ground. This is concerning the curtains.”

XXX. Moreover, the goat-hair coverings were thirty cubits long and four cubits wide. Since there were eleven of them, joined to one another along their sides, they made up forty-four cubits. Place these also upon the structure; and because the length of the coverings agrees with the measuring-line by which you measured the building across, their outer edge reaches all the way to the ground. For they had ten cubits of level span between the walls, and likewise ten cubits of ascent or descent on each side. This is what Scripture says: “A cubit shall hang over on one side, and another on the other—the surplus in the size of the coverings—protecting each side of the tabernacle” (Exod. 26:13). For “tabernacle” properly denotes the fabric or joining together of the curtains themselves, beyond which the coverings extended by one cubit on the south side of the building and by another on the north. Therefore they reached the ground, because the former had thirty cubits of length, while the latter had two fewer. Likewise, the total extent of all the coverings along the length of the building stretched to forty-four cubits: that is, thirty cubits in a level span from the front of the building to the top of the boards on the western side, with seven cubits hanging down at the front of the building and seven likewise hanging down on the western side. Thus the measure of the coverings on the western side exceeded that of the curtains by two cubits. For the curtains descending from above, as we have mentioned, covered five cubits of the wall and left five other cubits untouched. This is what is said: “What remains over of the coverings prepared for the roof—that is, the one covering which is additional—shall, from half of it, cover the rear of the tabernacle” (Exod. 26:12). Now half a covering is two cubits in width; with this half the rear parts of the tabernacle were covered—that is, two cubits of the curtains properly called the tabernacle—because the last covering, extending downward by two cubits beyond them, overran them.

XXXI. Thus the coverings descending from above covered only seven cubits of the western wall. Yet the remaining three cubits were not left bare to the injuries of the weather all the way to the ground; rather, the seven-cubit portions of the coverings which remained after the walls had ended were drawn together from each side, and with them the rear of the building was most firmly covered down to the ground. Nor could these merely reach one another and meet at the middle of the wall in the manner of the curtains; rather, because they were seven cubits long, they exceeded the middle of the wall by two cubits on either side and were joined to one another by being laid one beneath the other. We think the same should be understood in every respect of the eastern side as well; hence the earlier command that the sixth covering should be doubled at the front of the roof (Exod. 26:9). The building, then, was covered above and on every side by curtains woven in marvellous variety, which were properly called the tabernacle; it was also covered everywhere by goat-hair coverings reaching down to the ground. A further roof-covering was made of red-dyed ram skins, and over this another covering again of blue skins. Concerning this most difficult matter, we have taken care to explain briefly what we seem to have understood, ready to learn a truer account if anyone is willing to teach us.

## Chapter XIV. On the fact that Josephus and the Jews seem to differ from the Venerable Bede concerning the extension of the coverings and curtains

XXXII. This is what the Venerable Bede says concerning the curtains and coverings; and we have endeavoured, so far as we could, to follow him without stumbling, as a diligent investigator of God’s word and a truthful interpreter. Yet another writer, speaking of these same curtains and coverings, judges that Josephus’s and the Jews’ opinion should in this matter be accepted rather than Bede’s view. For this teacher writes as follows:

“In the extension of the curtains and coverings to cover the tabernacle’s roof, and in the doubling of the sixth covering at the front of the roof, let us follow the view of the Jews and Josephus rather than Bede’s opinion. Since the curtains are ten and the coverings are four cubits [wide], the former, joined together, make forty cubits, while the latter, coupled in turn, make forty-four cubits. According to the Hebrews and Josephus, they were spread out in such a way that both curtains and coverings covered thirty cubits of the tabernacle roof—for that was its length—and ten cubits of the western front of the building, since that was the tabernacle’s height. The four cubits by which the coverings exceeded the curtains were doubled at the eastern front of the building, where the entrance was; doubled, they covered the columns and the entrance veil by two cubits. They were doubled because of the force of the winds. This is what the book says: ‘the sixth covering,’ namely the four cubits which make the covering’s width, ‘shall be doubled at the front of the roof. And what remains over of the coverings prepared for the roof—that is, the one covering which is additional—shall, from half of it, cover the rear of the tabernacle’ (Exod. 26:9, 12).

“The coverings exceeded the curtains by one cubit on each side of the tabernacle and therefore reached the ground, because the former had thirty cubits of length while the latter had two fewer. Half a covering in length, moreover, is two cubits; and with this half the rear parts of the tabernacle were covered on either side—that is, the curtains which are properly called the tabernacle. This is what it says: ‘And a cubit shall hang over on one side and another on the other, which is additional in the length of the coverings, protecting both sides of the tabernacle’ (Exod. 26:13). The construction must be made in this manner: ‘From half of that which remains over in the coverings prepared for the roof, you shall cover the rear of the tabernacle’; and it inserts parenthetically what this is, namely, ‘the one covering which is additional.’ It is as if it said: ‘From half of one covering—the one covering which remains over and is additional beyond the curtains—you shall cover the rear of the tabernacle,’ that is, the ends of the boards where they meet the ground, which the curtains could not reach from either side in order to cover.”

XXXIII. Behold, this is how he speaks of the extension of the curtains and coverings, and he appears to differ from the Venerable Bede. But whatever he may say, many judge Bede’s opinion more correct than the view of Josephus and the Jews in this matter, and think they can prove it as follows. The Lord said to Moses: “What remains over of the coverings prepared for the roof—that is, the one covering which is additional—shall, from half of it, cover the rear of the tabernacle” (Exod. 26:12). They say—and it is entirely true—that the Lord calls the extension of the curtains themselves, joined together over the walls, the “tabernacle”; and they call the curtains by which the rear part of the building, the western wall, was covered, the “rear parts” of that tabernacle. These curtains were called the rear of the tabernacle in distinction from those curtains which, as they say, hung on the eastern side and which, according to them, were likewise called the front of the tabernacle.

Therefore Moses, in accordance with the Lord’s command, covered the rear of the tabernacle with half of the one additional covering. For, as they say, he made the eleventh covering—which was additional among the coverings beyond the curtains, of which there were only ten—extend beyond the curtains on the western wall by two cubits, which made up half of it. Thus, according to Bede’s view, the curtains on that wall had five cubits in their descent, while the coverings had seven. Let the Jews, then, and Josephus, who says that both curtains and coverings covered the western front of the building by ten cubits, show with what half of a covering Moses covered the rear of the tabernacle—that is, those curtains which, as many affirm, were on the western wall—if on that same western wall the curtains were as long in their descent as the coverings, that is, if both curtains and coverings covered that wall entirely down to the ground.

But if someone says that the “rear parts” of the tabernacle were not the curtains on the western wall but rather the ends of the boards of both walls, south and north, where they met the ground, which the curtains could not reach from either side because they had only nine cubits in their descent, he will be asked what that additional covering was, and from what half of it Moses covered these ends of the boards of the southern and northern walls. For it is clear that there was no covering there from half of which those ends of the boards could be covered. Indeed, these ends of the boards were covered not by half of any covering, but by the ends of the coverings, which exceeded the curtains by one cubit on either side. We know, certainly, that the coverings exceeded the curtains in their descent by two cubits—one on one side and the other on the other—and that two cubits made half a covering. But beyond the ends of the coverings, which hung down and surpassed the curtains by one cubit on both sides, there was no covering at all from half of which the rear parts of the tabernacle—that is, the ends of the boards, if the rear parts of the tabernacle were nowhere other than at those very ends—could be covered.

XXXIV. Moreover, we know that, apart from the spiritual meaning hidden within, the coverings were spread over the tabernacle in order to cover the curtains and boards fully down to the ground where the curtains themselves failed, and, by covering them, to preserve them unharmed from winds, rains, and the other impurities assailing from outside. This being so, to speak somewhat by human conjecture, what reason would suggest that the western part of the structure, where there was a very solid wall—a wall composed of most sturdy boards, joined very firmly below by tenons inserted into sockets, at the sides by interlockings, and in the middle by bars set in rings—should be covered threefold, by both curtains and coverings, all the way to the ground, while the eastern side, where there was no wall at all but only five columns with one curtain hung upon them, should be covered by no curtain or covering except one alone?

When that covering was doubled at the front of the roof according to the Lord’s command, the curtain hanging there was covered by only two cubits and lay exposed for eight cubits to wind, rain, and other external injuries. For these and perhaps other reasons left unmentioned here, some judge that the Venerable Bede should be accepted in this matter without any hesitation—unless some other authority should stand in the way, speaking more fully about these things and showing more clearly why Bede should be rejected here and Josephus, together with his Jews, accepted.

## Chapter XV. On the ark and the oracle above it; on the table of presentation; on the lampstand of light; and on the altar of incense

[Col. 0654A]

XXXV. Since we have now completed the tabernacle itself, for the most part, and in a sense set it up complete in its proper form, let us speak of the things within it and show, as far as we can, how and where they were placed within it. The Lord said to Moses:

“You shall make an ark of setim wood. Its length shall be two and a half cubits, its breadth one cubit and a half, and likewise its height one cubit and a half. You shall overlay it inside and out with the purest gold, and make above it a golden crown all around. You shall make four golden rings and place them at the ark’s four corners: two rings on one side and two on the other. You shall also make poles of setim wood and overlay them with gold; you shall put them through the rings on the ark’s sides, so that it may be carried by them. They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be withdrawn from them. You shall place in the ark the testimony which I shall give you. You shall also make a propitiatory of the purest gold. Its length shall be two and a half cubits, and its breadth one cubit and a half. You shall make two golden cherubim of beaten work, at the two ends of the oracle: one cherub at one side and the other at the other. Let them cover the two sides of the propitiatory, spreading their wings and overshadowing the oracle; let them look toward one another, their faces turned toward the propitiatory with which the ark is to be covered. In it you shall place the testimony which I shall give you. From there I shall command and speak to you, namely from above the propitiatory and from between the two cherubim which shall be above the ark of the testimony, all that I shall command through you to the children of Israel” (Exod. 25:10 ff.).

“You shall also make a table of setim wood, two cubits long, one cubit broad, and one and a half cubits high; and you shall overlay it with the purest gold. You shall make for it a golden rim all around, and on the rim itself a chased crown four fingers high, and above it another small golden crown. You shall also prepare four golden rings and set them at the table’s four corners, one at each foot. Beneath the crown shall be the golden rings, so that poles may be passed through them and the table carried. You shall make the poles themselves of setim wood and overlay them with gold, for carrying the table. You shall also prepare dishes, bowls, censers, and cups, in which libations are to be offered, of the purest gold; and you shall always place on the table before me the loaves of presentation” (Exod. 25:23 ff.).

“You shall also make a lampstand of beaten work from the purest gold: its shaft, branches, cups, knobs, and lilies proceeding from it. Six branches shall come out from its sides, three from one side and three from the other. On each branch shall be three cups shaped like nuts, together with knobs and lilies. Such shall be the work of the six branches proceeding from the shaft. On the lampstand itself shall be four cups shaped like nuts, with knobs upon each and lilies. There shall be knobs beneath two branches in three places, making six branches together, proceeding from the shaft itself. Thus both knobs and branches shall proceed from it; the whole shall be beaten work of the purest gold. You shall also make seven lamps and place them upon the lampstand, that they may shine straight ahead. The snuffers likewise, and the receptacles in which what has been snuffed is extinguished, shall be made of the purest gold. The entire weight of the lampstand with all its vessels shall be one talent of the purest gold. See to it, and make it according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 31:40).

“You shall also make an altar for burning incense, of setim wood, one cubit long and one cubit broad—that is, square—and two cubits high. Its horns shall proceed from it. You shall overlay it with the purest gold: its grating, its walls all around, and its horns. You shall make for it a small golden crown on every side, and two golden rings beneath the crown on every side, so that poles may be put into them and the altar carried. You shall make the poles themselves of setim wood and overlay them with gold. You shall place the altar opposite the veil which hangs before the ark of the testimony, before the propitiatory by which the testimony is covered, where I shall speak to you; and Aaron shall burn upon it sweet-smelling incense” (Exod. 30:1 ff.).

## Chapter XVI. From the Book of Exodus concerning the same matters

XXXVI. Bezalel also made the ark of setim wood, two and a half cubits long, one and a half cubits broad, and one cubit and a half high. He overlaid it within and without with the purest gold and made it a golden crown all around, casting four golden rings at its four corners, two rings on one side and two on the other. He also made poles of setim wood, which he overlaid with gold, and put them into the rings on the ark’s sides for carrying it. He also made the propitiatory—that is, the oracle—of the purest gold, two and a half cubits long and one and a half cubits broad; likewise two cherubim of beaten gold, which he placed at the two ends of the propitiatory, one cherub at the extremity of one end and the other cherub at the extremity of the other. The two cherubim, at the two extremities of the propitiatory, spread their wings, covering the propitiatory and looking toward one another and toward it.

He also made the table of setim wood, two cubits long, one cubit broad, and one cubit and a half high. He overlaid it with the purest gold and made for it a golden rim all around; upon the rim itself he made a chased golden crown four fingers high, and above it another golden crown. He also cast four golden rings, which he set at the four corners, one at each foot of the table opposite the crown; and he put poles into them so that the table could be carried. He made the poles themselves of setim wood and overlaid them with gold, and the vessels for the table’s various uses—dishes, bowls, cups, and censers—of pure gold, in which the libations were to be offered.

He also made the lampstand, of beaten work from the purest gold, from whose shaft proceeded branches, cups, knobs, and lilies: six on each side, three branches on one side and three on the other. On each branch were three cups shaped like nuts, with knobs and lilies. The work was alike for the six branches proceeding from the lampstand’s stem. On the shaft itself were four cups shaped like nuts, with knobs upon each and lilies. There were knobs beneath two branches in three places—the six branches together—proceeding from the one shaft. Thus knobs and branches proceeded from it; the whole was beaten work of the purest gold. He also made seven lamps with their snuffers and the vessels in which the snuffed material was extinguished, of the purest gold. The lampstand with all its vessels weighed a talent of gold.

He also made the altar of incense from setim wood, one cubit square on each side and two cubits high, from whose corners horns proceeded. He overlaid it with the purest gold—its grating, walls, and horns. He made for it a small golden crown all around, and two golden rings beneath the crown on each side, so that poles might be inserted and the altar carried. He made the poles themselves of setim wood and covered them with golden plates. He also prepared the oil for the holy anointing and incense of the purest spices, the work of a perfumer (Exod. 37).

## Chapter XVII. Literal exposition of the preceding chapter

XXXVII. Therefore, in the inner place, which was within the veil and into which the high priest entered once a year, stood the ark, made indeed of setim wood but overlaid with gold on every side. It had a golden crown round about it, which a certain teacher calls a rim running around it. Others say that this crown was a golden binding encircling the ark on every side, made for its beauty and strength, so that it could not come apart and might appear more attractive.

Upon this ark rested a certain golden plate, beaten work, having the same length and breadth as the ark, called the propitiatory. The ark’s lid—the plate by which the ark was covered—was called the propitiatory because God, appearing above it, was propitiated toward the people. At each end of it stood a cherub of beaten gold; the two cherubim, spreading their wings toward one another, covered the propitiatory and looked toward one another. Scripture does not state the height of these cherubim or the length of their wings. It seems to me, however, that, since each covered one side of the propitiatory by wings spread opposite one another from either end, each wing of either cherub could have been no more than two and a half cubits long. For some say that one cherub touched one wall with his wing and the other cherub the other wall with his wing, while with their other wings they touched one another in the middle; and these middle wings covered the propitiatory, as the two great cherubim did in Solomon’s temple.

[Col. 0657A]

XXXVIII. Within the ark, too, beneath the propitiatory, were a golden urn containing manna, the tablets of the covenant, Aaron’s rod which had budded, and, according to the book of Deuteronomy, the book of Moses’ Song. For Moses commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the Lord’s covenant, saying: “Take this book and put it at the side of the ark of the covenant of the Lord, that it may be there as a witness against you” (Deut. 31:26). These things, then, were in it according to the authority of Holy Scripture; yet in the Third Book of Kings it is written: “There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets which Moses had put into it at Horeb, when the Lord made a covenant with the children of Israel” (3 Kings 8:9). If at Solomon’s time there was nothing else in it except the tablets, it would seem that at that time neither the manna nor Aaron’s rod nor even the book of Moses’ Song was in it.

Modern teachers explain this difficulty thus: they say that the passage mentioning only the tablets concerns the mystical sense, whereas the passage asserting that the other things named above, together with the tablets, were in the ark concerns the literal sense. For they say that all these things yield one and the same meaning when regarded mystically, although literally they are distinct. On this matter one writer says:

“In the books of Kings and Chronicles it is asserted that ‘there was nothing in the ark of the Lord except the stone tablets on which the ten commandments of the Law were written.’ But in the Epistle entitled *To the Hebrews* it is read that ‘a golden urn containing manna and Aaron’s rod which had budded, as well as the tablets, were in the ark’ (Heb. 9:4). We may say that in the earlier times the tablets alone were in the ark; but later, through fear of enemies, they placed in the ark the golden urn containing manna and Aaron’s rod which had budded, lest they should be taken by enemies. Yet because they knew that the Philistines had been struck with a grievous plague because of the ark which they had taken, they trusted that it would not be taken by enemies. Perhaps the aforementioned things were not in the ark itself but at its sides, as was the book of the Law. They are therefore said to have been in the ark because they were in some attachment at its side.”

This is what he says. On the tablets, however, ten words were written, as Josephus says: on each tablet, two and a half on each page. This is enough concerning the things which were in the Holy of Holies.

XXXIX. In the outer chamber, which was simply called the Holy Place, there were these three things: the table of presentation on the north side, not far, as Josephus says, from the entrance; opposite it, the lampstand on the south side; and the altar of incense in the middle, opposite the veil. The table was made of gilded setim wood, two cubits long, one cubit broad, and one cubit and a half high. The table was not of that thickness; for it would have been a block rather than a table. Rather, it rose from below, where its feet met the ground, to this height.

The same table had a golden rim all around; upon this rim was made a chased crown four fingers high, and above it another small crown. If it is asked what sort of rim ran round the table, or what these two crowns were like, perhaps there was a golden projection fixed to every side of the table; to this projection another, four fingers high, was attached, which Scripture calls a crown; and a third was joined to this. Perhaps these three projections were made around the table in order that the twelve loaves continually placed upon it—arranged not in its middle but in two opposing rows at either side—might have a secure place in which to rest, as though in a hollow and enclosed on every side, lest, when the table was carried, they should slide together if they lay on a flat surface without an enclosure.

Another opinion says that a rim encircled the table by means of a hollow made in the table itself, and that a chased crown, drawn around it for strength and ornament, covered the breadth of this rim; a second small crown was also placed above the first, contributing both strength and beauty. There were continually twelve loaves upon it, baked from fine flour, as is read in Leviticus, each containing two tenths [of an ephah]; six were arranged on each side, with two golden cups full of most pure frankincense placed over them (Lev. 24:5–6).

A certain eloquent writer also says: “The rim around it is a kind of overhanging border running around the table and facing outward. Upon this border,” he says, “a certain rim was placed—not outward on the side, but raised upward to a height of four fingers. Above these was also placed another narrower and lower rim.” He calls the crown “chased,” because it was artistically engraved. The rings were beneath the crown. He indicates the places where the rings were to be set, through which poles were inserted for carrying the table: namely, at the top next to the rim, which he here calls the crown, and not toward the ground at the bottom. Some say that the two crowns mentioned above are here called one crown, above which he says the rings were to be placed. According to this opinion, two crowns are joined externally to the side of the aforesaid rim, though why they are joined is not readily apparent. Yet they appear necessarily to be joined on the upper surface in order to hold the items placed upon the table and to prevent them, by serving as a barrier, from falling off it.

Thus he writes about the table: “Dishes are temple vessels in which vinegar was kept. A *phiala* is a kind of glass vessel. *Phiala* is said as though *hiala*, while *hialim* means glass. These vessels, as they say, are capacious, narrow at the bottom and broad above; the Hebrews call them bowls. Cups are rather narrow vessels and hold little.” There were continually twelve loaves on the table. They were called loaves of presentation because they were always set out upon the table and ready at hand. There were twelve, each made from two tenths; every Sabbath they were removed when fresh ones had been set in their place, for the priests’ use. This is what he says about the table vessels and the loaves of presentation.

The same table had four feet at its four corners beneath the aforesaid crown, and at each corner a golden ring; so that, with two gilded poles of setim wood inserted into them from either side, the table itself could be carried.

XL. The lampstand was both golden and beaten work. Six branches came out of its shaft, three from one side and three from the other. All, it seems to me, were equal at their upper ends in height, where the seven lamps were placed: three here and three there on the tips of the six equal branches, and the seventh on the top of the shaft, whose summit was level with the tops of the other branches. It seems to me that on either side the first branch was longer than the second, and the second than the third, although none was higher than another. Thus on each side the first was longer than the second, and the second longer than the third—not as regards their ends, where they converged at the same level above, but as regards their points of emergence, since they did not all proceed from the shaft at the same point on either side. This, I think, is what Scripture says: “The work of the six branches proceeding from the lampstand’s stem was alike” (Exod. 37:19). Their work was not alike where they came out at the bottom, but where their tips came together at the top.

The threefold arrangement also occupied equal intervals along the lampstand’s length. On each branch were three cups shaped like nuts, three knobs, and three lilies. Scripture does not state the lampstand’s length or thickness, but it says that its total weight with all its vessels was one talent. One writer says that there are three kinds of talent: the smallest contains fifty pounds, the medium seventy, and the largest one hundred and twenty.

Scripture says nothing here about poles for the lampstand, or whether it had rings through which poles could be inserted for carrying it; it is entirely silent on this point. Yet in the Book of Numbers, where the movement of the camp is discussed, it is written: “They shall take a blue cloth with which they shall cover the lampstand with its lamps and tongs and all its oil vessels; over all they shall place a covering of blue skins, and they shall put in poles” (Num. 4:9–10). A certain writer says concerning the lampstand:

“He calls the middle stem of the lampstand its shaft; from it three branches emerge on this side and three on that. The branches are called the lampstand’s arms because they are round like reeds. Although some branches proceeded from the stem lower down and others higher up, all nevertheless rose to the same height, so that no lamp placed upon them was higher or lower than another. Where the branches emerged from the shaft on either side, there were upon each a knob, rounded forms, lily flowers, and certain forms shaped like nuts, which Scripture calls cups. But the Hebrew does not mean that these cups were shaped like nuts; rather, if I may say so, they were *nigellated* [ornamented with niello]. Works made of silver are customarily nigellated, but I do not recall having seen golden work so ornamented. The branches have these three aforementioned features in three places: where they emerge from the stem, at the middle, and at the top. The middle stem has them in four places. The lampstand stood obliquely, but the lamps were so placed that they shone as though directly opposite the ark. The snuffers are tongs by which the wicks were trimmed so that they might shine better.”

This is what he says about the lampstand.

XLI. The altar of incense, like the table and lampstand, was outside the veil, yet directly opposite it, although some say that it was within the veil. A highly learned teacher among others says that it stood outside the veil, in these words:

“According to the Hebrews, Josephus, and almost all interpreters, the altar of incense stood between the lampstand and the table of presentation, outside the veil and opposite the ark of the covenant. Augustine, however, says in many places that it was within the veil. On the days when Aaron and his sons entered to minister in the tabernacle, they were forbidden to drink wine or strong drink. If, therefore, as some hold, the high priest entered beyond the veil every day because of the continual burning of the incense, he could never lawfully drink wine. But according to the Hebrews, the altar was outside, and the priests ministered in turns and offered incense. Hence they were commanded to abstain from wine and strong drink during their time of ministry. The lesser priests offered incense and frankincense to the Lord, but they did not enter beyond the veil before the ark into the Holy of Holies. It is therefore evident that this altar stood outside the veil; for into the Holy of Holies the high priest entered only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, with blood. The altar on which they offered incense must therefore have been outside the veil.”

By these arguments he proves that the altar of incense was outside the veil. The altar was of gilded setim wood, with its breadth equal to its length—that is, one cubit square in both dimensions—and two cubits high. It had horns projecting from it, which, together with its walls and grating, were overlaid with the purest gold. The small golden crown around it was, as some think, a slight projection running around it. Beneath this, at each side, was a golden ring, so that with two gilded poles of setim wood inserted into them the altar could be carried. Thus I have displayed my ignorance concerning these three things that stood outside the veil. Now let us hear the wise judgment of the Venerable Bede concerning them.

## Chapter XVIII. The words of the Venerable Bede, priest, on the preceding chapter
XLII. Within the veil was placed the ark of the covenant, and opposite the ark, outside the veil, the altar of incense. Likewise, in the middle of the sanctuary itself stood the lampstand on the south side; the table, however, stood on the north. The ark was made of shittim wood. Its length was two and a half cubits; its height one and a half cubits; and its breadth one and a half cubits. Some are accustomed to ask what size the cubit should be considered to be which Moses employed [Col. 0661A] both for Noah’s ark and in the construction of the tabernacle. If we consult the words of Josephus, the question will easily be resolved. For it must not be doubted that this could in no way have escaped a Jewish man of priestly descent and most outstanding intelligence. He says, therefore: “The ark was made five spans in length and three in breadth.” Hence it is plainly clear that he means the cubit made up by two spans. Now one who measures anything by a span extends his hand with the fingers spread as widely as possible, so that he may hold the measure which he is taking clearly and without any difficulty of uncertainty.

The ark is overlaid inside and out with the purest gold, and a golden moulding is commanded to be placed around it. The ark has four corners, with two rings on one side and two on the other. The poles [Col. 0661B] by which the ark is carried are commanded always to remain in the rings. But if you wish to know what this testimony is which Moses received from the Lord to be placed in the ark, listen to the Apostle: “After the veil,” he says, “was the second tabernacle, which is called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold, in which were a golden urn containing manna, Aaron’s rod that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant” (Heb. 9:3–4). Josephus relates that the tablets of the covenant were inscribed with the Decalogue of the Law in such a way that each tablet contained five commandments.

It is commonly asked what is meant by the mercy-seat with which the ark is to be covered. But since it is commanded to be made of gold, 362 and to be of the same length and breadth as the ark which he had commanded to be made, it is beyond [Col. 0661C] doubt that he intended a slab to be made large enough to cover the ark.

XLIII. “You shall also make two golden cherubim, hammered out at the two ends of the oracle” (Exod. 25:18). In the singular, indeed, it is *cherub*; in the plural, *cherubim*, and it is a masculine noun. But Greek usage has used *cherubin* as a neuter, changing the letter *m* into *n*. Our translator, however, following Hebrew idiom, used the masculine: “two golden cherubim, hammered out,” not “two golden cherubin, hammered out”; I believe that through the carelessness of copyists his translation has here been corrupted, so that *cherubin* was written for *cherubim* according to the usage of the ancients.

The cherubim look toward one another, and turn their faces [Col. 0661D] toward the mercy-seat. Above the mercy-seat, from between the two cherubim, the Lord speaks to Moses all that he commands through him to the children of Israel.

The table was made of shittim wood. Its length was two cubits, its breadth one cubit, and its height one and a half cubits. The table of the tabernacle is overlaid with the purest gold; a golden rim is made around the table; and a golden moulding four fingers high is placed upon the golden rim of the table. The table has four feet, and beneath the moulding were rings through which poles might be passed for carrying the table.

The loaves of presentation are always placed upon the table. Of these loaves Leviticus relates more fully, in the Lord’s words [Col. 0662A] to Moses, how many were to be made, what sort they were to be, and how they were to be placed: “You shall take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it, each of which shall contain two tenths. You shall set six on one side and six on the other upon the purest table before the Lord, and you shall put the clearest frankincense upon them, so that the bread may be a memorial of the Lord’s offering. They shall be changed before the Lord on every Sabbath, having been received from the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant; and they shall belong to Aaron and his sons, that they may eat them in a holy place” (Lev. 24:2, 5, 9).

Thus it comes about that the table of the Lord is never left without bread; rather, as soon as one loaf is removed, another is put in its place. What is written in the Book of Kings—that David entered the tabernacle and received the holy loaves from the priests (1 Sam. 21:6)—occurred on a Sabbath morning. For he came to the tabernacle at the hour when the loaves [Col. 0662B] of the preceding week had been removed from the Lord’s table and new loaves, baked the day before, were to be set down; thus he received the loaves in such a way that the Lord’s table was not left without bread even for the smallest moment of time.

Moreover, as Josephus writes, the loaves were baked on the morning before the Sabbath; and on Sabbath morning they were offered and set six and six upon the holy table, arranged opposite one another, with two golden dishes full of frankincense set beneath them. They remained until the next Sabbath, and then others were brought in their place; and, after the frankincense had been burned upon the sacred fire on which all the burnt offerings were made, other frankincense was added upon the new loaves.

XLIV. The lampstand of the tabernacle, like the table, stands before the veil within which the ark of the covenant is placed. Three branches come out from one side of its shaft and four from the other. Thus the branches emerge from the shaft at different points; yet each of them, bent upward in its own place and order, arrives at a single height, so that they may maintain an equal placement of the lamps above them.

The first branch had three cups, globes, and lilies. The second branch likewise had three cups, globes, and lilies. The third branch similarly had three cups, three globes, and three lilies. Again, on the other side of the shaft, the first, second, and third branches had three cups, globes, and likewise three lilies. Thus on every branch there were three cups, globes, and lilies. On the lampstand itself four cups [Col. 0662D] were made; together with each cup globes and lilies were formed, and they are commanded to be beneath the branches, not upon them. But the fourth cup, globe, and lily were above all the branches, near the top of the lampstand; and this cup with its globe and lily rose higher than the branches.

The entire work of the lampstand—that is, both the central stem and the branches proceeding from it, with all their ornament—was of gold, and that gold was hammered. Seven lamps are placed upon the lampstand; they shone straight ahead and illuminated the tabernacle of the Lord. The snuffers and vessels for extinguishing what has been snuffed are made of the purest gold. The entire work of the lampstand, with all its vessels, is shown to contain one talent of the purest gold. A talent is a full and complete weight. [Col. 0663A] 363

The altar of incense is overlaid with the purest gold; both the grate of the altar and its sides and horns are commanded to be covered with gold. The grate was within, in the middle of the altar, prepared, that is, to receive the incense. The sides appeared on the outside, and the horns likewise appearing outside rose higher in a distinctive projection. A golden moulding is also made all around the altar, and it is encircled by rings on each side. The altar stands opposite the veil which is hung before the ark.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the altar of burnt offering and the bronze basin; on the courts of the tabernacle and the hangings of the courts; on the columns of the hangings and the bases of the columns.

XLV. The Lord said to Moses: “You shall make an altar of shittim wood, [Col. 0663B] five cubits in length, the same in breadth, and three cubits in height. Horns shall be at its four corners, and you shall cover it with bronze. You shall make for its use pots for receiving ashes, tongs, forks, and fire-pans. You shall make all the vessels of bronze. You shall also make a bronze grate in the form of a net; at its four corners shall be four bronze rings, which you shall place upon the altar’s raised rim, and the grate shall reach to the middle of the altar. You shall also make two poles of shittim wood for the altar, which you shall cover with plates of bronze; you shall pass them through the rings, and they shall be on either side of the altar for carrying it. You shall make it not solid, but hollow and empty within, as was shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. 27:1–8).

“You shall also make a bronze basin with its base for washing, and place it between the tabernacle of testimony and the altar. Having poured water into it, Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet in it when they are about to enter the tabernacle of testimony and when they are about to approach the altar, to offer incense to the Lord, lest perhaps they die” (Exod. 30:18–21).

“You shall also make the court of the tabernacle. On its south side, facing south, there shall be hangings of twisted fine linen. One side shall extend for one hundred cubits in length, with twenty columns and the same number of bronze bases; their capitals and their bands shall be of silver. Likewise, on the north side along its length there shall be hangings for one hundred cubits, twenty columns and bronze bases of the same [Col. 0663D] number, and their capitals and bands of silver. On the west side of the court, in its breadth, there shall be hangings for fifty cubits, ten columns, and the same number of bases. Likewise, in that breadth of the court which faces east, there shall be fifty cubits, of which hangings for fifteen cubits shall be assigned to one side, with three columns and the same number of bases. On the other side likewise there shall be hangings occupying fifteen cubits, three columns, and the same number of bases. At the entrance of the court there shall be a hanging of twenty cubits, of blue, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and twisted fine linen, worked in embroidery. It shall have four columns with the same number of bases. All the columns of the court around its perimeter shall be covered with silver plates, with silver capitals and bronze bases. In length the court shall occupy [Col. 0664A] one hundred cubits, in breadth fifty, and its height shall be five cubits. It shall be made of twisted fine linen and shall have bronze bases. You shall make all the vessels of the tabernacle for every use and ceremony, as well as its pegs and those of the court, of bronze” (Exod. 27:9–19).

## CHAPTER XX. Again, from the Book of Exodus concerning the same things.

XLVI. He also made the altar of burnt offering of shittim wood, five cubits square and three in height, its horns projecting from the corners; and he covered it with bronze plates. For its use he prepared various vessels: pots, tongs, forks, hooks, and fire-pans. He also made its bronze grate in the form of a net, and beneath it, in the middle of the altar, a small hearth, with four bronze rings cast at the four corresponding upper points of the net, [Col. 0664B] for inserting poles to carry it. These poles also he made of shittim wood and covered with bronze plates, and he put them through the rings which projected on the sides of the altar. The altar itself was not solid, but hollow, made of boards and empty within (Exod. 38:1–7).

He also made the bronze basin with its base from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle. And he made the court: on its south side were hangings of twisted fine linen, one hundred cubits long; twenty bronze columns with their bases, while the capitals of the columns and all the bands of the work were of silver. The hangings, columns, bases, and capitals of the columns on the north side were likewise of the same dimensions, workmanship, and metal. On the side facing west [Col. 0664C] were hangings of fifty cubits, 364 ten columns with their bronze bases, and the capitals of the columns and all the bands of the work were of silver. Facing east he prepared hangings of fifty cubits, of which one side was occupied by fifteen cubits with three columns and their bases. On the other side, because he made both sides of the entrance of the tabernacle, the hangings were equally of fifteen cubits, with three columns and the same number of bases. All the hangings of the court were woven of twisted fine linen. The bases of the columns were bronze, but their capitals with their bands were silver. He also overlaid the columns of the court themselves with silver. At its entrance he made, in embroidery, its hanging of blue, purple, scarlet, and twisted fine linen, which was [Col. 0664D] twenty cubits long. Its height was five cubits, according to the measure of all the court’s hangings. There were four columns at the entrance with bronze bases, and their capitals and bands were silver. He also made the pegs of the tabernacle and of the court all around of bronze (Exod. 38:8–20).

## CHAPTER XXI. Literal exposition of this chapter.

XLVII. Within the eastern entrance of the court stood the altar of burnt offering—not at the entrance itself, but, as a learned man wrote long before me, toward the south. It was five cubits long and as many broad, that is, square, and three cubits high. It was made of shittim wood and covered with bronze, and had a bronze grate in the form of a net [Col. 0665A] so that, as the Venerable Bede says, the fire placed beneath might freely penetrate through its numerous openings to consume every part of the victims. The aforesaid altar was hollow and empty within, having one bronze ring on each of its sides, so that by inserting into them two poles, one on each side, of shittim wood covered with bronze, it could be carried.

Various bronze vessels were made for its use: namely, pots for receiving ashes; tongs, with which burning brands were arranged under the altar in the fire; forks, called in Greek *creagrae*, by which pieces of cooked meat might be lifted; and fire-pans. Concerning these vessels and this altar, a man no less eloquent than devout writes as follows: “You shall make for its use pots for receiving ashes, tongs, [Col. 0665B] forks, and fire-pans” (Exod. 27:3). In Hebrew it reads thus: “You shall make its pots for receiving its ashes, its shovels, its basins, its hooks, and its fire-pans.” The shovels are for lifting ashes, the pots for receiving them, the basins for pouring out blood, the hooks for lifting meat from cauldrons, and the fire-pans for carrying coals.

It follows: “And you shall make for it”—that is understood—“a bronze grate in the form of a net; at its four corners shall be four bronze rings, which you shall place beneath the ledge of the altar, and it shall reach to the middle of the altar” (ibid., 4). There is great uncertainty concerning this grate, both among the Hebrews and among our own writers, especially since the Hebrew truth seems to differ somewhat from our translation. For it reads thus: “You shall make for it *Michar*, a work of bronze netting; and upon the net you shall make four bronze rings at its four extremities, or horns. And you shall put it”—namely *Michar*—“or place it”—namely the net—“beneath the foundation of the altar below; and the net shall extend to the middle of the altar.”

Accordingly, under this reading, *Michar* does not seem to mean a grate upon which meat would be placed for roasting, but a square work pierced all around because of its lightness, made in the likeness of a vessel. The altar seems, as it were, to sit in it: its wall surrounding the altar rises to the middle of the altar, and at its four upper corners four rings hang, through which, when poles are inserted, the altar resting on it might be carried. For the altar is not said to have had other rings [Col. 0665D] by which it was carried besides the rings of the net.

XLVIII. But whether this net was separate in itself from the altar, detachable, and contained its own base in the upper part of the altar, so that it enclosed the altar’s walls by means of its own walls; or whether it adhered below to the lower edge of the walls by cast work, with its base at some interval of breadth set back all around from the walls, so that it finally raised its own walls to the middle of the altar—this is not sufficiently clear. Yet the following arrangement seems probable.

Some say that this altar had neither a covering above nor a base below, but only walls set in place and filled with earth, in accordance with the words, “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. 20:24); and that fire was made upon its upper surface, where the burnt offerings placed thereon were burned. 365 Others said that a grate was set between the altar’s walls and rose to the middle of its height, and that a small hearth was formed beneath that grate; fire was kindled in it through an opening facing east in the altar wall, and flesh placed on the grate was thus burned within, while smoke escaped through the open mouth above. To prevent any concern arising that the wooden walls inside the altar might be burned by the nearby fire, they affirm that the wood was fireproof. But if this wood is to be thought such that it could not be damaged at all either by water or fire, it is not clear why there was need for it to be covered externally with bronze plates. Nor can it be sufficiently seen how the grate was suitably placed inside with its poles, how the altar was carried with poles inserted through its rings, or how the rings of the grate were placed beneath that interior ledge. [Col. 0666B]

The Jews, wherever we say “altar,” say “platform.” What we call the bronze or brazen altar because of the plates fixed to its boards, they call the walls of the platform. They say that these walls, set square, were customarily filled to the top with earth; wood was placed upon the top of the clods enclosed by the aforesaid walls, and the sacrifices were placed upon the wood. They say that the grate of either altar, whether golden or bronze, was a certain work full of holes on every side, resembling those which are in churches and which they call *Kias*. These *Kiae* extended from the bottom of the altar, where it met the ground, up to its middle. They had four rings at their four upper corners. These rings were placed above the ledge of the altar. What we call the small altar or hearth, the Jews say was a little altar (*araciuncula*) or a kind of groove in the middle of the altar’s walls, as far as which the *Kiae* of the altar reached. The rings of the grate were placed beneath this groove, because they reached to it. With poles passed through these rings, the grate and the altar’s walls were carried together. It is credible that each altar was carried separately and their grates separately. This is what he writes concerning the altar of burnt offering and its grate.

XLIX. Between this altar and the tabernacle there was also a bronze basin (Exod. 38:8). Concerning it I read both from what it was made and for what purpose: it was made from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle, and it was made so that, with water poured into it, Aaron and his sons might wash their hands and feet in it when they were about to enter the tabernacle. But it may be asked how it was made: namely, what its length, breadth, and depth were; what arrangement or shape it had; what sort of base it had and how large it was; who, finally, those women were who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle; and what sort of mirrors theirs were, how large and how many, from which the aforesaid basin was made.

Indeed, it seems that it must have been of no small size, since all the priests who served in the tabernacle had to wash themselves in it when entering the tabernacle. [Col. 0667A] Some understand the women keeping watch at the entrance of the tabernacle to have been holy widows and holy virgins who had professed a vow of chastity; from their multitude of mirrors the bronze basin was fashioned. But what kind of mirrors they were, how large they were, and how many; likewise, the form and arrangement of the basin itself, its length, breadth, and depth—the authority of sacred Scripture does not declare.

The tabernacle itself was surrounded on every side by courts enclosed with hangings of fine linen. Of these hangings, each of the south and north sides was one hundred cubits long, and they were suspended on twenty columns on each side. On the west side, likewise, were hangings of fifty cubits, suspended on ten columns. On the east side, on the right, were hangings of fifteen cubits, suspended from three columns; and on the left side there were the same number of hangings, assigned to the same number of columns. Between both sides, in the middle, was a hanging of twenty cubits, not of fine linen alone, as the other hangings were, but rather woven from the four colours so often mentioned. It hung before four columns, where the entrance was.

All these columns, sixty in number, were five cubits in height, made indeed of shittim wood but covered with silver plates, 366 and having silver capitals and bands and bronze bases. Beside each base, as Josephus says, was a peg one cubit in length, by which the lower parts of the hangings were held and stretched, while above they were attached and suspended by rings. [Col. 0667C] The lengths of these hangings—one hundred cubits on both the south and north sides—exceeded the length of the tabernacle, which was only thirty cubits, by fifty cubits on the east and twenty on the west. The breadths of the hangings, which were fifty cubits, exceeded the tabernacle’s breadth, which was only ten cubits, by twenty cubits on either side, east and west.

Thus the aforesaid hangings were so long and broad around the tabernacle, enclosing the tabernacle within themselves. The tabernacle faced west and had its entrance on the east. Before the entrance of the court, on the inside, stood the bronze altar, though not in the entrance itself but separately toward the south; and between that altar and the tabernacle entrance was the bronze basin. Let this suffice for the present, according to the literal sense, concerning the said hangings and courts, and also concerning the altar and basin.

## CHAPTER XXII. Words of the Venerable Bede, priest, on the preceding chapter.

L. The altar of burnt offering is five cubits long, as many broad, and three high; it is covered with bronze and has horns at its four corners. If anyone is troubled, according to the literal sense, by how the altar’s wooden structure could remain unburned beside so great a fire, let him receive blessed Jerome’s reply to this question: “The wood of the altar, which is from the trees of paradise, is not burned by the nearby fire but is made purer.” Nor would I find this surprising concerning the sanctuary, the inner parts of the temple, and the altar of incense, since even the type of wood called *amyton*, which has the appearance of wood, is found the cleaner the more it has burned.

Various vessels were commanded to be made for the altar: pots, tongs, and fire-pans. The pots receive the sacred ashes. The tongs must be understood to have been made for tending the altar fire. With the tongs, a double iron implement, the priests cleaned the altar fire. The forks, which are called *creagrae* in Greek, were kept for this service of the altar: to remove pieces of sacrificial flesh from the cauldrons by means of them and bring them for the food of those who were to be refreshed by them. The fire-pans, moreover, were assigned for this purpose: that the sacred fire might be carried by them from the altar of burnt offering to the altar of incense, in the morning and evening, for placing incense upon it.

All the vessels are made of bronze. The altar was commanded to be made not solid but empty and hollow, so that it might have ample room to receive the most holy fire, wood for the fire, and the burnt offerings which were to be consumed by fire. It also had in its middle a grate, throughout fashioned in the manner of a net, on which the flesh of the victims to be burned was placed; and beneath it a small hearth, in which, when wood had been arranged, fire burned, always ready to consume the burnt offerings. For there was an opening in the eastern wall of the altar opposite the ledge, through which wood might be put in to feed the fire, and coals and ashes might be removed. [Col. 0668C] The grate was fashioned in the form of a net so that the fire placed beneath might freely penetrate through its many openings and consume every part of the victims. Four bronze rings at the four corners of the altar, and two poles, are commanded to be made, so that they may carry the altar by means of the rings. The altar of burnt offering stood outside, before the entrance.

LI. The bronze basin was placed between this altar and the tabernacle, because the priests themselves, twice daily—that is, morning and evening—were commanded to wash in it when they entered to offer incense to the Lord at the altar. No one from the common people was to wash there; rather, the high priest himself and his sons, that is, priests of the lower rank, were commanded to do so.

[Col. 0668D] Around everything was the court of the tabernacle, one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits broad. The west side of the court had hangings for fifty cubits and ten columns; and the east breadth of the court was fifty cubits. As one entering the court of the tabernacle, you have on either side hangings of fifteen cubits, suspended from three columns; these hangings were of twisted fine linen. At the entrance of the court a hanging of twenty cubits is suspended on four columns, because this hanging at the entrance of the court was made not, like that in the rest of the court, from twisted fine linen, but from four colours—namely blue, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and twisted fine linen—in embroidered work.

The entire length and breadth of the court, divided by hundreds and fifties of cubits, has a height of five cubits. All the vessels of the tabernacle are commanded to be made of bronze. The pegs of the tabernacle or court were made so that, driven into the tops of the columns, they projected outward; with the cords of the curtains or hangings placed upon them, they suspended the curtains above the ground. The curtains or veils themselves, however, needed to have loops or rings at their upper parts in order to receive the cords through which those cords might be passed. The cords of the hangings are put upon the pegs of the columns so that, thus spread out and lifted on high, they may complete the beauty of the tabernacle; and, spread by cords and raised up, the veils or hangings may display far and wide to all the wondrous beauty of their workmanship, which they could not display while folded.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the twelve tribes encamped around the tabernacle, and on the Levites who carried the tabernacle.

[Col. 0669B]

LII. When the tabernacle and all things pertaining to it had thus been made and arranged, the children of Israel encamped around it. On the east these three tribes pitched camp: Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun; their number, from twenty years old and upward, was one hundred and eighty-six thousand four hundred. On the south Reuben, Simeon, and Gad pitched camp; their number was one hundred and fifty-one thousand four hundred and fifty. On the west Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin pitched their tents; their number was one hundred and eight thousand one hundred. On the north Dan, Asher, and Naphtali set their camp; their number was one hundred and fifty-seven thousand six hundred. The total of all who were counted from twenty years old and upward was six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty.

Between these twelve tribes and the tabernacle the Levites pitched their tents all around, keeping watch in the services of the tabernacle. Read the Book of Numbers (Num. 1:35). On the east were Moses, Aaron, and their sons, having charge of the sanctuary. On the south were the sons of Kohath; their number, from one month old and upward, was eight thousand six hundred; and from thirty years old upward to the fiftieth year, two thousand seven hundred [Col. 0669D] and fifty. When the camp moved, these carried upon their shoulders, on their own poles, the holy and precious things in the tabernacle: namely the ark and the mercy-seat; the table with its censers, mortars, bowls, and cups; the lampstand with its lamps, tongs, snuffers, and all vessels for oil; the golden altar with all the vessels used for service in the sanctuary; and the altar of burnt offering with its vessels—namely fire-pans, forks and tridents, hooks, and bowls. These were the burdens of the sons of Kohath (Num. 4:15). But Aaron and his sons customarily wrapped first the things that were within the sanctuary and then entrusted them to these men for carrying in their wrappings.

On the west were the sons of Gershon; their number, from one month old and upward, [Col. 0670A] was seven thousand five hundred, and from thirty years old upward to the fiftieth year, two thousand six hundred and thirty. They carried the curtains and coverings: the covering made of red-dyed rams’ skins, the other covering made of blue skins, the curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle, the hangings of the court, and the veil hanging at its entrance. For carrying these they had two covered wagons with four oxen. Read the Book of Numbers (Num. 4:3, 7).

On the north were the sons of Merari, whose number from one month old and upward was six thousand two hundred; and from thirty years to the fiftieth year, three thousand two hundred. They carried the boards of the tabernacle, their bases and poles, the columns of the court before the Holy of Holies, [Col. 0670B] and those at the entrance of the tabernacle with their bases, as well as the columns of the court, their bases, and the pegs. Because their burdens were very great, they had four covered wagons with eight oxen to carry them.

Therefore, the total number of the sons of Levi who pitched their tents around the tabernacle was twenty-two thousand from one month old and upward; and from thirty years old upward to the fiftieth year, those who entered in to stand and minister in the tabernacle numbered eight thousand five hundred and eighty.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the arrangement and erection of the tabernacle.

LIII. As we read in the Book of Numbers (Num. 9:16), a pillar always hung over the aforesaid tabernacle: a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night. So long as the pillar remained unmoving, the children of Israel remained in camp. But when the cloud moved and left the tabernacle, while the Levites stood at the entrance of the tabernacle and two silver trumpets sounded sharply, the Levites dismantled the tabernacle. Each took what belonged to him; what could only be carried on shoulders was put upon shoulders, and what could lawfully be carried in wagons was placed in wagons. The other tribes likewise took their tents and all their equipment, and all set out following the cloud.

They proceeded in fitting and orderly fashion. First, as it seems to me, came the three tribes on the east: Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun; after them, those on the south: Reuben, Simeon, and Gad; then those on the west: Manasseh, Ephraim, and Benjamin; and last, those on the north: Dan, Asher, and Naphtali. They travelled as long as the cloud went before them. But wherever the cloud rested, there, having set down their burdens, they again erected the tabernacle beneath the cloud, as I suppose, and pitched tents around it, both the Levites and the other tribes, as belonged to each.

When all had been arranged in the customary manner, they remained in the same place until the cloud again left the tabernacle. Then, after it had again been dismantled and carried with them in the manner already described, they followed the aforesaid cloud wherever it led. In this [Col. 0671A] way, during the forty years in which they were in the wilderness, they changed the places and encampments—forty-two in number from their departure out of Egypt to their entry into the land of Canaan—until they came to the land of promise, where they no longer carried the tabernacle from place to place.

## CHAPTER XXV. A recapitulation of all the foregoing, with some additions and some matters stated differently.

LIV. It pleases me to repeat these matters from their very beginning, even in another’s words, so that, while we set before our hungry reader things that are diverse and in a sense somewhat contrary, we may refresh the palate of his understanding by the very variety of the dishes. A certain eloquent man, a master among other masters, of admirable learning [Col. 0671B], writes as follows concerning the walls, boards, bases, bars, and rings:

The Lord said to Moses: Take first-fruits—that is, all manner of precious things—from the people of Israel, but only from one who offers willingly: namely gold, silver, and bronze; blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet—that is, silk of blue, purple, and scarlet colour; and byssus, a kind of Egyptian linen, soft and white; also goats’ hair; and reddened rams’ skins, which we call Parthian, because the Parthians used to colour them thus; blue skins; and shittim wood. Shittim is the name of a mountain, a region, and a tree, which resembles the white thorn in its leaves and is an exceedingly light wood, incorruptible and incombustible. Also oil for preparing the lamps [Col. 0671C]; spices for ointments and sweet-smelling incense; onyx stones and gems, that they may make for me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst, so that they need not have recourse to this mountain. You shall make it according to the pattern of the tabernacle which I shall show you.

The tabernacle was a house dedicated to God, rectangular and oblong, enclosed by three walls: north, south, and west. Its entrance stood open toward the east, so that at sunrise it might be illuminated by the sun’s rays. Its length was thirty cubits, its breadth ten, and its height ten. On the south side were twenty upright boards of shittim wood. Each board was ten cubits long, four fingers thick, and one and a half cubits broad [Col. 0671D]. They were joined together by mortises, so that there might be no crack there and no unevenness in the surface of the wall; and they were overlaid with gold on both sides. Each was set upon two perforated silver bases, into the holes of which golden pivots were inserted. At each corner of the tabernacle there were projecting boards, as is customary in the making of chests.

Augustine, however, seems to hold that one base was beneath each board and the other above, serving as an architrave. But the wording is clear: “Let two bases be placed beneath each board, for its two corners” (Exod. 26:19). Whether the boards hung above the ground upon the bases, or extended to the ground between the bases, is not stated. The north wall was made in the same arrangement. On the west [Col. 0672A] there were six boards, entirely like the others and standing upon bases in the same fashion. But since they filled only nine cubits, half a cubit lay vacant on either side. Therefore a board one cubit broad was cut in half, and two half-cubit boards were made; placed at either side, these completed the western wall with the other two boards. Each of these also was set into two bases.

To prevent the walls from being shaken or forced together by gusts of wind or any other cause, each board had golden rings fixed in sequence, as though by certain roots; bars inserted crosswise through these held the framework firmly together.

LV. The bars were of gilded shittim wood [Col. 0672B], each five cubits long. The end of one bar was fitted into the end of another in the manner of a scarf-joint, so that several thus interlocked seemed like one bar of immense length, as is customarily done in the ivory episcopal staff called the sambuca. This would plainly be so, had not the Lord added that there were five bars on the north side, as many on the south, and as many on the west—which seems less fitting. For, since each bar was five cubits long, five laid out along one side reached only twenty-five cubits; thus five cubits of that side remained untouched. On the western side, moreover, only two would suffice.

Some say that, of the three superfluous bars, one was added to the five on the north side [Col. 0672C], and another to those on the south, thus supplying what was lacking; the third was cut into two and placed at the two corners of the walls, so that, bent back, they might bind the corner-joints, as the corner-joints of chests are usually bound by a beam. But this cannot be inferred from the text.

Since, therefore, the text says that five bars were inserted through the middle of the boards from end to end, it is clear that this refers to the height of the wall. Thus, near the uppermost top of the wall, one row of bars extended the whole length of the wall; near its lowest portion another row likewise; and in the middle surface, three rows. Accordingly, the statement that there were five bars on one side is to be referred rather to the number of rows than to the number of individual bars [Col. 0672D]. Thus each board had five rings; and each of the two walls had thirty bars, because each of the five rows had six bars. On the west side there were ten bars, two in each row.

Some say that the bars were not all of the same size: every bar, except the five on the longer sides, was six cubits long, and thus five sufficed to span thirty cubits; while the five bars on the west were each two cubits long. But Josephus, speaking of these bars, says that each was five cubits in length.  
[Note: [Col. 0671D] See JOSEPHUS, *Antiquities*, book III, chapter 5.]

LVI. He also writes in this manner concerning the two veils: one at the entrance of the tabernacle, the other dividing the Holy of Holies from the holy place, and concerning the columns of each. This tabernacle was divided into two parts. The rear part, toward the west, extended ten cubits and was therefore square: ten cubits in length, breadth, and height. This part was called the court, or the Holy of the Holy, or the Sanctuary of the Sanctuary, or the Holy of Holies.
