The front part extended twenty cubits toward the east and was allotted to the priests alone; this was called the Holy Place, or the Holies, or the Sanctuary. In relation to this, the rear part was called the Holy of the Holy—that is, holier than the holy place—as “Lord of lords” and “King of kings” are said [Col. 0673A].

To separate the two parts, four gilded columns of shittim wood stood in the middle, with golden capitals and silver bases. Josephus, however, says that there were four boards fashioned like the others and equally spaced apart, between which three narrow entrances lay open. Across the tops of the columns were laid two bars, each ten cubits long, extending from wall to wall. From them, through golden rings, hung a veil stretched before the four columns, square on every side—namely, ten cubits—to prevent from every direction any view of the interior.

The veil was made of twisted byssus, an exceedingly white and soft kind of linen, and of blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet—that is, of silk threads of blue, purple, and scarlet colour—fashioned in feather-work, that is, needlework; for in one usage “feather” (*pluma*) means a needle. This sort of veil is popularly called *bustratum*, as though “doubly layered.” For first a fabric is made, upon which many images are then sewn by handwork. Some say that feather-work takes its name from birds, upon which a variety of feathers is added. The same work is also called *polymitum*, from Greek πολύ, “much,” because of the multitude of its pictures [Col. 0673C].

According to Josephus, this veil was woven with beautiful variety from all the flowers produced by the earth and with other images which painters could interweave, except animal forms. At the entrance to the tabernacle were five gilded columns of shittim wood, with golden capitals and bronze bases. Upon them two bars—or one bar—of ten cubits extended from wall to wall, each end being inserted into its own wall like a beam in a house. From this hung another veil, inserted through golden rings and worked like the former. According to Josephus, however, it hung only to the middle of the columns, covering them for five cubits; the remainder down to the ground stood open for the priests’ entrance.

He also speaks of another woollen curtain laid over it and extending to the ground, with cords running through rings to draw it out and pull it back, so that on feast days, when drawn back, it afforded a view of the tabernacle, but on other days, when drawn across, it prevented the view—especially when the weather appeared cloudy [Col. 0673D]. For its fabric was strong and readily bore the strain. He says that a similar curtain hung at the entrance to the Temple also.

[Col. 0674A] LVII. In the inner sanctuary was the ark, with the things which, as we have said, were deposited in it and those placed upon it. In the front part, however, were the lampstand on the south and the table on the north; the veil was in the middle; and not far from the entrance stood the golden altar, which Josephus calls the golden censer and of which more will be said below.

He also writes as follows concerning the curtains, the goats’-hair coverings, and the two coverings of the roof. The roof of the tabernacle was not pointed but flat, like the roofs of Palestinian houses, and was fitted with four coverings. The first covering consisted of ten curtains, also called veils, tents, or sometimes the tabernacle itself. They were made in feather-work from the four aforesaid colours. Each curtain was twenty-eight cubits long and four broad [Col. 0674B]. Five were joined to one another, and five similarly, making, as it were, two curtains, each composed of five joined together. They were joined by blue loops arranged along each edge of the curtains, one coming around the other, and two were fastened by a golden ring, as golden or silver clasps customarily fasten together the two edges of a hood as an ornament for the neck. Josephus, however, says that they were joined by golden rings and hooks.

The second covering consisted of haircloth coverings, also sometimes called hair veils. They were made of goats’ hair, which we sometimes call “hair” in distinction from sheep’s wool, and from which haircloths (*cilicia*) were also made. Hence these were called haircloth coverings, and, because of their roughness, they were called *saga*. Hence we call certain rough cloths *sagii*; or perhaps *saga* takes its name from their squareness. Thus the military cloak invented by the Gauls was called a *sagum*, because it was square. Yet, since it was made from rough cloth against the inclemency of the weather, it may have been called *sagum* for that reason [Col. 0674C].

There were eleven such coverings. Each was thirty cubits long and four broad. Five were joined to one another, so as to make, as it were, one covering; and six others were joined, as it were, into one covering. They were joined by bronze rings inserted into loops which came around one another. It is not clear whether the individual curtains or coverings were thus fastened to one another; or whether five curtains were sewn together inseparably with thread into one curtain, and the other five likewise, and whether these two large curtains alone were joined by rings and loops to cover the tabernacle [Col. 0674D]. Let us see, however, how the rear of the tabernacle was covered by these.

LVIII. According to Bede, the ten joined curtains were stretched crosswise, covering the whole tabernacle and descending along its sides, one cubit short of the ground on every side. Since, joined together, they measured forty cubits, they covered the thirty-cubit length of the tabernacle: five cubits hung down at the western side and another five descended before the opening on the east. Yet, lest they hang disorderly, the curtains extending beyond the two long sides of the tabernacle were openly drawn as far as the middle and joined to each other; the same was done on the western side. Thus on every side the tabernacle was covered with curtains, except for one cubit next to the ground, which was left uncovered all around [Col. 0675A].

The haircloth coverings were laid over it crosswise in the same way. But because they were thirty cubits long, they descended along the sides to the ground and thus covered the cubit left uncovered by the curtains. And because, joined together, the eleven coverings measured forty-four cubits across—each being four cubits wide—they covered the thirty cubits of the tabernacle’s length; of the remaining fourteen, seven descended at the east and seven at the west. The portions of the coverings remaining and hanging beside the two long sides down to the ground were brought back from each side to cover the eastern entrance. But since seven cubits came from each side while the entrance was only ten cubits wide, one covering was sewn to another; or perhaps, at the top of each, two cubits were folded back and sewn like the hems of a garment, and then the coverings coming evenly from the sides were joined in the middle of the entrance, at the same place as the curtains [Col. 0675B].

Likewise on the western side, on account of this excess or folding of the coverings, Bede says that the Lord first said to Moses: “You shall double the sixth covering at the front of the roof” (Exod. 26:9), that is, you shall fold back at the entrance the half-covering which exceeds the curtains. He then added more plainly: “What remains of the coverings”—that is, the one extra covering—“with half of it you shall cover the rear of the tabernacle,” that is, the western side. They were doubled so that they could withstand the force of the winds. According to this arrangement, the tabernacle was covered on every side by the coverings down to the ground, and none of it was visible; and the precious tent-curtain at the entrance was there, though unseen. When the priests entered the tabernacle, either they had to lift the coverings and curtains to go in beneath them, or, if they were joined in the middle, the hooks and rings had to be undone for their entrance.

Josephus gives another arrangement, with which Origen agrees, and which seems more probable. He says that the ten curtains joined together, as described, were stretched crosswise from the front of the tabernacle over the entrance [Col. 0675C], covering the whole tabernacle and descending on the west side to the ground; but that the entrance was not covered by any part of the curtains, since it had its own veil. He says the same of the haircloth coverings: that the entire tabernacle was covered except for the entrance. But because the coverings exceeded the curtains by two cubits on each side, he says that they were folded under the curtain so that wind entering between the coverings and curtains should not shake the entire roof covering. This, he thinks, is why it was said: “You shall double the sixth covering at the front of the roof.”

But even on this account the beautiful and very precious exterior part of the tabernacle was not seen, nor that portion of the curtains which fell around the tabernacle. Thus things made with so much labour seemed to have been made in vain. Perhaps, therefore, the curtains and coverings were stretched by cords all around the tabernacle and their cords fastened with bronze pegs (Exod. 28:20), since Moses says below that the tabernacle had pegs [Col. 0676A]. Raised all around in the manner of a hanging roof, they allowed the tabernacle to be seen on every side and to be walked around by those entering beneath the curtains.

However these first two coverings were arranged, there is no question about the remaining two. The third covering was of reddened rams’ skins. It covered only the top and did not descend down the sides; it was secured to the ground by cords and bronze pegs. The fourth covering, laid over it in the same manner, was of blue rams’ skins. These two were placed on top to protect against heat and the spreading of rain. Therefore, as Josephus says, those viewing it from a distance were greatly astonished [Col. 0676B], for they thought its colour differed in no respect from the sky.

LIX. He writes as follows concerning the ark, the mercy-seat, and those things that were inside the veil with them. “The ark,” he says, “was two and a half cubits long, and likewise one and a half cubits broad.” Here Josephus calls a cubit a palm. The ark is said to have had no feet and to have been overlaid within and without with the purest gold. A golden crown was made upon it, like the rim ordinarily made on tables and chessboards. On each long side were two golden rings penetrating through all the wood; through them were inserted gilded bars of shittim wood by which the ark was carried, and these were never removed.

In it was placed the testimony [Col. 0676C], that is, the tablets on which only the covenant was written, insofar as the things deposited there can be called testimonies. There was placed there a golden jar full of manna, as testimony that He had given them bread from heaven; the tablets, as testimony that He had awakened in writing the natural law which had lain dormant in their hearts; Aaron’s rod, as testimony that all authority is from the Lord God; and Deuteronomy, as testimony to the covenant, because they had said: “All that God shall say to us, we will do.” For this reason it was called the ark of the covenant or of testimony, and for the same reason the tabernacle too was called the tabernacle of testimony; and also because cases were tried before its doors.

A golden mercy-seat was also made above the ark [Col. 0676D], that is, a golden slab of the same length and breadth as the ark, so that it could cover it. Its thickness is not stated. It was called an oracle because God gave responses from that place; for a divine response is called an oracle because it is given to those who pray. It was also called a mercy-seat, because the Lord, speaking from there, was propitiated toward the people; or because on the Day of Atonement they said that the glory of the Lord always descended there.

At either side of the oracle, namely at its two front corners, were placed two golden cherubim, wrought by hammering, not cast—that is, formed by blows of hammers. According to Josephus, they are winged creatures having a form seen by no human being. Moses said that he had seen these depicted upon God’s throne [Col. 0677A]. One cherub looked toward the other, though their faces were turned toward the mercy-seat. With two outspread wings, touching one another, they covered the oracle; their other wings they extended in opposite directions.

LX. He writes as follows concerning the table and its vessels: The Lord said to Moses, “You shall make a table of shittim wood, two cubits in length, one cubit in breadth, and one and a half cubits in height.” Its thickness is not stated. “And you shall overlay it on every side with the purest gold” (Exod. 25:23). According to Josephus, this table was somewhat like a Delphic table, having four legs, which are called its height. From halfway down, the legs were rounded and turned; the upper portion of the work was square. Each leg had a golden ring, and there was a socket in the leg into which the ring was set. Gilded bars by which the table was carried passed through the rings.

It had a rim all around, as the ark did, and to the rim was attached a golden crown four fingers high [Col. 0677B], so that half of it projected above the table, lest what was placed upon it should fall off. The other half hung down below as ornament. This crown was openwork—that is, varied with carved and smooth portions. The Hebrews say that the carvings were like images of kings and prophetic images: there were as many images made there as there would be kings in Jerusalem from David to Zedekiah. Josephus, however, seems to mean that the table had no rim other than this openwork, that is, lattice-like crown.

A second, smaller crown was placed upon this one; but we do not know how large it was, how it was placed upon it, or whether it was plain or openwork. It is merely called a little crown. The Hebrews say that this too was added prophetically, to prefigure the division of the kingdom into two kingdoms. For the kingdom of Israel was more populous than the kingdom of Judah, yet less worthy; therefore the little crown was placed above, yet was smaller.

This table was placed in the tabernacle toward the north, not far from the entrance. Upon it were placed twelve unleavened loaves of very fine flour, six on each side. Each consisted of two tenths of an ephah, which Josephus calls two *assarii*. A golden plate was set over each, and upon the plate a handful of incense [Col. 0677C]. Josephus says that golden bowls, full of incense, were placed upon them. Early on the Sabbath fresh, warm loaves were set on the table, and they remained there untouched until the following Sabbath. Then, after they were removed and all the incense burned, new ones were substituted with other incense upon the altar. Only the priests ate the loaves that had been removed. Hence they were called priestly loaves; or also for this reason: Josephus says that God commanded only priests to form, bake, set upon the table, and remove those loaves—though they themselves did not observe this.

They were called loaves of presentation because they were set before the Lord as an everlasting memorial of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel; or because they were set forth, that is, set there for a long time—either for the whole week, or to be set there perpetually in succession [Col. 0677D].

God also commanded four kinds of vessels to be prepared from the purest gold for presenting libations. These were given by the offerers to the priest to be sampled (*libanda*), that is, tasted, and by the priests to the Lord to be poured out (*libanda*). They were placed upon the table: dishes, bowls, censers, and cups. In them the wine to be offered was inspected and tasted beforehand, to determine whether it was worthy to be offered. But because wine is discerned by its colour and taste, the bowls are said to have been glass. Thus they were named from *phialim*, which is said to mean “glass” in Greek: narrow at the bottom and broad at the top, so that colour and taste could be discerned; the Hebrews call them little dishes. The cups, however, were smaller, narrower, and golden; with them wine was poured upon the altar as a libation for the sacrifice [Col. 0678A].

In the censers, also called little mortars, incense was inspected beforehand and offered; similarly vinegar was inspected in the dishes. But because an offering of vinegar is never or rarely mentioned, some say the word is *acceptabula*, “receptacles,” in which the priests inspected beforehand what was to be offered, whether it was acceptable—that is, suitable—or not. Afterwards he subdivides the receptacles into three: bowls, containing wine; censers, containing incense, fine flour, grain, and salt; and cups, containing oil. For the priests first took small portions of what was to be offered and put them into vessels of this kind for prior tasting, as though sampling each of the things which Moses called libations to be offered—that is, things to be taken from what was to be offered.

[Col. 0678C] LXI. He also writes concerning the lampstand as follows. God commanded that a lampstand be made of the purest worked gold. Josephus, however, says it was cast. Its shaft was fixed in a base and was of iron, overlaid with five golden, jointed tubes like a reed; the five heads of the tubes were joined to each other. The heads had swellings and were joined together in the form of a bowl, which we call a cup, like two bowls joined in the shape of a nut. From the bottom of each bowl issued curved flowers like lilies. In that very bottom, between the bowl and the lilies, was a movable little sphere, like the movable spheres beneath the tops of chairs.

Thus, when five tubes were joined in this manner in the shaft [Col. 0678D], there were four joints; each had bowls like two joined together, little spheres as well, and lilies. This is what Moses means when he says that there were four bowls in the shaft in the shape of a nut. Yet the Hebrew does not say “bowls,” but “blackened round forms,” that is, rounded forms marked with black.

From this shaft there projected from the sides three iron branches on one side and three on the other, each overlaid with golden tubes in the form of the shaft. At the joints the heads of the tubes came together, like bowls in the shape of a nut, with little spheres and lilies. Since Moses says that there were three bowls in each, it seems that each had four tubes. Yet to some it seems that the little spheres were not at the bottom of the bowls, as stated, but placed in the middle surface of each tube as movable little spheres [Col. 0679A].

Thus the lampstand was made of iron overlaid with golden tubes, if it was cast; but if it was worked, it was simply of gold, fashioned by hammers into this form with wonderful skill. According to Josephus, it was composed of seventy parts and erected on a single base. Thus in the shaft and branches there were thirty-nine tubes, not whole ones but made from two pieces. Where the pieces joined in the middle, a little sphere was placed over them so that the joint might not be seen and the tube might seem to be one. Thus there were fifty-eight tubes with as many little spheres, and five parts in the base, the seats of the seven lamps.

However it was made, at the top it had seven equal heads, upon which seven golden lamps were set. There were also seven golden pouring-vessels with which oil was poured into the lamps. The Lord also commanded the children of Israel to offer the purest olive oil, beaten with a pestle. For this is purer than walnut, linseed, myrrh, or radish oil [Col. 0679B]. From it the lamp in the tabernacle of testimony was always to burn. Aaron and his sons lit it in the evening; the seven lamps shone upon the lampstand before the Lord until morning, but only three during the day.

The wick of the lamp was papyrus. The snuffer, which we have called a *mengum*, was golden. There were also golden forceps for trimming or extinguishing the wicks, and golden vessels for putting into water the trimmings that had been removed, lest they emit a foul odour. Its whole weight, with its vessels, was one talent of gold according to the sanctuary weight [Col. 0679C]. For they had three talents: the lesser, of fifty pounds, which was that of merchants; the middle, of seventy, which was that of citizens; and the greatest, of one hundred and twenty, which was that of the sanctuary. Josephus, however, says that it had one hundred minas, which the Hebrews call *cinthares* and which in Greek translation is called a talent. It was placed on the south opposite the table, though not directly but obliquely.

LXII. He writes likewise concerning the altar of incense. This altar was made of shittim wood, one cubit long and one cubit broad—that is, square—and two cubits high. It was overlaid with the purest gold and had horns, a golden grating [Col. 0679D], chains, rings, and golden bars like the preceding altar. Whether it had a little hearth, or whether the earth received its ashes, is uncertain. Josephus adds that it had six crowns of the purest gold at each corner—perhaps an elaboration of the singular expression in Exodus: “You shall make a golden crown around it” (Exod. 30:3).

This altar was called the altar of incense, or of *thymiama*, because every day, morning and evening, incense was burned upon that altar to accompany the perpetual sacrifice offered to the Lord. Yet some said that in the morning only incense—that is, frankincense—was laid upon it, while in the evening *thymiama* was used because of the dignity of the evening sacrifice. The holy Fathers seem, however, to have doubted whether this altar was within the Holy of Holies or in the sanctuary with the lampstand and table. Nor should it be thought that the doubt arose because it was in the sanctuary, since the Hebrews say this, Josephus says it more plainly, and the original proportions of the tabernacle made by Moses suggest it—except that Paul, in Hebrews, places the golden censer within the Holy of Holies (Heb. 9:3) [Col. 0680A].

It may indeed have been that in the Temple, where everything was enlarged and multiplied, besides the golden altar outside the veil, at which it was necessary to enter twice each day, an additional censer was placed in the inner recess, in which the high priest burned the coals and incense that he carried with him when he himself was permitted to enter the inner place.

LXIII. He writes concerning the courts as follows. Around the tabernacle was a court one hundred cubits long on the south side and one hundred on the north; on the east it was fifty, and as many on the west. Thus it was rectangular, though longer on one side. On the south side were twenty columns, five cubits high, with silver capitals bearing carved work and bronze bases. They stood five cubits apart. Each had rings upon it, and cords ran from the rings to the heads of the pegs, which were one cubit long and firmly fixed in the earth through the individual columns, so that they might keep the court immovable [Col. 0680B].

A curtain of the softest byssus, one hundred cubits long and five high, hung by the columns, spread from capital to base, so that it appeared no different from a wall. Unless perhaps, owing to weather conditions, it was drawn back five cubits by cords and pegs, so that the people might be sheltered beneath it as beneath a roof [Col. 0680C]. The north side likewise had twenty columns and a curtain spread out. On the west ten columns and a curtain fifty cubits long enclosed the court. At the eastern entrance three columns stood on this side and three on that, with curtains spread beside them, differing in no respect from the preceding ones.

In the middle of that side were four columns arranged as gates, from which was hung a veil woven in feather-work from the four precious colours, easily raised and lowered for entrance or exit. It should be noted, however, that on the longer sides there were twenty-one columns, with twenty openings between them covering one hundred cubits; on the two shorter sides there were nine. But because the corner columns were shared by two sides, they are said to be twenty in the former case and ten in the latter [Col. 0680D].

LXIV. He likewise writes concerning the altar of burnt offering and the bronze laver (Exod. 27:1). God also commanded an altar to be made of shittim wood. This altar they called that of the burnt offering, or of burnt offerings, or of holocausts; it might also be called the altar of sacrifices, but it received its name from the more dignified term. It was five cubits in length and breadth—that is, square—and three in height. Something like a tower was placed upon it above at the time of ministry, upon which the minister stood; when the ministry was completed, this was removed. For the altar was forbidden to have steps; and it was hollow, like a chest without a cover. Its walls were wooden, but were lined within with bronze, so that they could not be burned outside [Col. 0681A], just as neither amianthus nor any wood of paradise can be burned, since it becomes cleaner by burning. Its hearth, or little hearth, was like the bottom of a chest, upon which the fire was made, being laid on through a window on the eastern side. At the four upper corners there were, outside, four curved horns, into which four chains were inserted through rings; from these hung a bronze grating, made like a net. It descended to the middle of the altar, and the things to be burned as a pleasing odor to the Lord were laid upon it; the fire, rising from the little hearth through the apertures of the grating, consumed them. Around the four lower corners were four bronze rings, into which poles of shittim wood, overlaid with bronze, were placed for carrying the altar.

Yet concerning this altar and its grating there is uncertainty [Col. 0681B], not only among ourselves but also among the Hebrews, especially since the Hebrew truth appears to differ somewhat from our translation. We indeed have: “You shall make a bronze grating in the form of a net, through its four corners” (Exod. 27:4). “There shall be four bronze rings, which you shall place upon the little hearth of the altar, and the grating shall reach to the middle of the altar.” But the Hebrew has: “You shall make for it a *michar*, a work of bronze netting, and beneath the net four bronze rings; and you shall place it beneath the base of the altar, and the net shall reach to the middle of the altar.” Josephus, however, has this: “Under it was a grating made in the form of a net. For the ground received the fire that was carried from the grating, because no bases were placed beneath it.” Cassiodorus the senator, however [Col. 0681C], in the drawing which he made, and which he mentions in his exposition of the Psalms, made four feet upon each altar.

Accordingly, some think that meat to be roasted was not placed upon the grating, but that it was, as it were, a vessel in which the altar sat. The height of its walls, surrounding the altar, was raised to the middle of the altar; at its upper corners hung four rings, through which, when poles were inserted, the altar resting upon it could be carried. For the altar is not said to have had other rings. But whether this grated vessel was separate from the altar, so that the altar could be removed from it and placed upon it when desired, or whether it was so fashioned as a cast work of the altar itself that it appeared to have been added to it, is uncertain.

Upon the little hearth of the altar—which they say was placed in its middle [Col. 0681D]—God commanded a pile of wood to be placed through the eastern window, and meat to be roasted upon the wood. Or else there was no little hearth; rather, the fire was made upon the grating set beneath it, which seems to have been Josephus’s understanding in the words cited above. Others think that it had neither a covering nor a bottom, but that only its walls were filled with earth, according to what God said: “You shall make for me an altar of earth” (Exod. 20:24). On its upper surface the fire was made, and the things to be burned were placed; and they think the same concerning the grating laid upon the altar. The Hebrew calls the little hearth, beneath which the grating is said to have been placed, a small enclosure or groove, which he says was in the middle of the altar walls and was reached by the height of the grating.

The altar was placed before the tabernacle in the open air, not directly before the entrance [Col. 0682A], but somewhat toward the south, so that those sacrificing before it, standing on the north, could look into the tabernacle itself as far as the Holy of Holies. And because they stood on the north, facing south, they are sometimes said to have sacrificed toward the north and sometimes toward the south. Its implements included basins for gathering and removing ashes when they became abundant; these were deposited in a secluded and clean place; tongs for tending the altar fire; flesh-hooks, which we call in Greek *creagrai*, because cooked meat was brought out of the cauldrons by them; and fire-pans, as it were, for carrying coals from this altar to the altar of incense; besides pots and kettles for cooking meat, although the meat was not cooked beside the altar. All these were bronze.

The Hebrew has: “You shall make its pots, its shovels, its basins, its hooks, and its receptacles for fire.” The Lord spoke again to Moses: “You shall make also a bronze laver with its base” (Exod. 30:18), that is, a vessel for washing, also called a luter. It stood between the tabernacle and the altar of burnt offerings. Water having been poured into it, the priests washed their hands and feet when they were about to receive the holy garments in order to sacrifice, and likewise when entering and leaving the tabernacle. It is said to have been made [p. 376] from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle. Perhaps it was made from the bronze feet of the mirrors; or, more likely, after it had been made, mirrors were placed around the outer rim of its upper lip, in which the priest might see whether he had anywhere [Col. 0682C], either on his garment or on his face, a stain needing to be washed away.

LXXV. He also writes as follows concerning the children of Israel who kept watch around the tabernacle. The Lord likewise commanded that the tabernacle should always be placed in the middle of the camp, and that the children of Israel should keep watch around it in companies and wedges—here taken as equivalent terms. A company properly consists of thirty soldiers, and is called a wedge, as though a crowd “coming together.” “Keeping watch” is also taken broadly here, for watches properly mean the night watches. The tribes were distributed, three on each of the four sides of the tabernacle, but at such a distance that they had very broad streets in the middle; their arrangement resembled a marketplace of goods for sale [Col. 0682D], each group set in its proper order. Craftsmen too were stationed in their respective places, so that their camp appeared very much like a suitably built city.

Thus Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun pitched camp to the east; Reuben, Simeon, and Gad to the south; Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh to the west; Dan, Asher, and Naphtali to the north. Between the tabernacle and the camp the Levites kept watch in their own tents, nearer to the tabernacle than to the camp; they too were stationed on the four sides: Moses and Aaron with their household to the east; the remaining Kohathites south of them, under the charge of Eleazar son of Aaron; the Gershonites to the west; and the Merarites to the north, both latter groups being under the charge of Ithamar.

The Lord said to Moses: “Number the Levites from thirty years of age to fifty, that they may serve me in the tabernacle by carrying and setting it up” (Num. 4:3). When they had been counted, they were found to be eight thousand five hundred and eighty (ibid., v. 48) [Col. 0683A]. The Septuagint, however, says from the twenty-fifth year, and we too observe this number of years for entry into the order of priests.

They carried the tabernacle in this manner, because the things beyond the veil were not permitted to be seen uncovered. First the priests entered and wrapped the ark, the mercy-seat, and the cherubim, first in the veil that formerly hung before them, and afterward in a violet-blue cloth (Num. 4:7). Likewise, they wrapped the lampstand, the golden altar, and the table with its utensils in cloths. Then the Kohathites entered and carried all these wrapped objects upon their own shoulders. The altar with its implements, as some suppose, was carried by the Gershonites, who took down the tabernacle covering and carried the other things: namely, the curtains, goats’-hair coverings, red-dyed skins, violet-blue skins, the curtain that stood before the tabernacle, the court hangings, ropes, and the implements of ministry pertaining to the bronze altar [Col. 0683B].

The book of Leviticus is silent as to who carried the altar of burnt offering. It may be said that the Gershonites carried its implements, as is found in the book mentioned above; the Kohathites carried the altar itself upon their own shoulders. In brief, the Merarites carried all the hard parts of the tabernacle and court: boards, bases, poles, columns, pegs, and each of these items. Retired Levites, however, did not serve in such work; when the tabernacle was set up, they sat as guards.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the end of the first part; and that neither an error should be excused nor a correction rejected.

[Col. 0684A]

LXXVI. Behold, venerable Father, in this first part of our book I have described both the construction, form, and arrangement of the tabernacle, and also the things which were within it—a matter most difficult, and not physically seen by any person whatsoever of our age—as I could, groping through the text of Exodus and the words of the Venerable Bede the priest, which I have been able to gather from many places; proceeding hesitantly and feeling my way uncertainly. I have inserted the statements of others insofar as I judged necessary, leaving to the reader’s discernment whose words ought to be believed [Col. 0684B].

I have described the matters aforesaid in this manner; but I not only do not prejudge one who knows how to speak about them more fully, clearly, and truly, but I also earnestly desire and urgently beg him to speak. For I have set this forth not so much in order to prejudice anyone’s learning—especially that of one more learned than I in these matters—as in order, first, to exercise myself diligently in them and, should there perhaps be any who need it, to instruct them charitably insofar as I understand. This should also be added: if I have perhaps departed from the path of truth in anything, I shall neither arrogantly excuse my error when it is charitably shown to me, nor proudly reject a correction kindly made known.

[p. 377] **SECOND PART. CONCERNING THE TABERNACLE OF CHRIST, WHICH EXISTS IN FAITH.**

[Col. 0683]

## CHAPTER I. LXXVII. On the difficulty of depicting the tabernacle on a flat surface.

[Col. 0683C]

Now that the first portion of our book has been brought, however imperfectly, to its end—in which certain matters concerning the material construction and arrangement of the tabernacle have been discussed, as the Lord granted, in accordance with your command, holy Father—I now set my hand to depicting the often-mentioned tabernacle also upon a flat surface, as far as I know and am able. Thus it may be perceived in some measure through bodily sight; and it must be understood by faith as referring to the Church of the elect in common, and as constructed by meditation in each individual elect person. But because the extensions of the curtains and goats’-hair coverings, as also the red-dyed and violet-blue skins by which the tabernacle roof was covered [Col. 0683D], and certain other things belonging to it, cannot be depicted with complete clarity on a flat surface, they must necessarily be portrayed in such a way that, while they are seen with the bodily eye, those things too which cannot be painted may be grasped by the reasoning of the mind. I say this because everything depicted on a plane appears more to lie sunk down below than to stand raised aloft; and I ought by no means to promise what I certainly cannot accomplish.

## CHAPTER II. How the boards of the tabernacle walls are to be depicted on a flat surface, how they are to be joined and laid out, and how these three walls with their entrance are to be raised.

LXXVIII. Therefore, in the middle of the plane upon which I intend to depict the tabernacle, having applied a ruler on the four sides, I draw four straight and exact lines. Of these four lines I make two—the southern and northern—as long as the tabernacle will be wide, because the two which constitute the tabernacle’s length will be three times as long as those which constitute its width. For so Moses’ tabernacle was thirty cubits in length and ten in width: that is, three times as long as it was broad. To the east, upon the same plane, at a distance from the line that stretches transversely from south to north equal to the length of that line, I lay down a somewhat broad bar, extending from south to north and as long as the aforesaid line [Col. 0685A].

After this, along the three lines—the southern, northern, and western—I make three walls of the tabernacle from boards joined side by side, with a height equal to the length of the western line and of the bar lying to the east. I overlay these boards with gold; I place twenty of them to the south, the same number to the north, and eight to the west; and I make them all of one and the same width, except for the two corner boards on either side of the western end. These two had within the wall only a third part of the width of the others, since all the other tabernacle boards were one and a half cubits wide, while these two had internally only half a cubit. After this, in the middle of each board I fix a gold ring running around it, and through these rings I insert five gilded poles along each wall, so that the end of each pole enters into the end of the next. Concerning these rings, it should be known that, according to Bede, five ought to be placed on every board; but because the boards in this drawing are very narrow, I depict only one on each [p. 378]. And in Exodus we do not plainly read that there were five rings on each board; it says of them: “You shall overlay the boards with gold and cast golden rings in them” (Exod. 26:29); and again: “He made their rings of gold” (Exod. 36:34).

Some say that these poles were outside the tabernacle. But because it is necessary to present them also to the bodily eye in order that their meaning may be understood more clearly, I place them in this drawing not outside but inside, around the middle of the three walls. Otherwise they would not appear in it, since the walls in which they are placed do not stand upright at the top in the drawing, but lie flat below. In this I think that I do not contradict the letter of Exodus, which neither affirms nor denies that they were inside; it merely clearly shows that they were made to hold the tabernacle boards together. But it does not say whether they stood within or without, perhaps leaving this rather to our judgment—a matter not so necessary that it cannot be known without great increase of true salvation, or likewise ignored without great loss.

Moreover, the book of Exodus, from which our first knowledge of this matter came, does not expressly give each side five rows of poles. In that book we read concerning the poles: “You shall make five poles of shittim wood to hold the boards of one side of the tabernacle, and five others for the other side, and the same number for the western side, which shall pass through the middle of the boards” (Exod. 26:26–28). And again: “He made five poles of shittim wood to hold the boards of one side of the tabernacle, and five others for joining the boards of the other side, and besides these five other poles for the western side of the tabernacle” (Exod. 36:31–32) [Col. 0686A].

LXXIX. Then beneath each board, at its two lower corners, I place two silver bases underneath all around, so that, just as the boards are firmly joined together in their middle by poles inserted into rings, so too they may be indissolubly secured as one at their lower part, with two bases placed beneath each and the two tenons of each board received, as Josephus says, into the holes of those bases. The mortises by which each of the boards of the ancient tabernacle was joined to the others—which mortises were in each side of every board and ended at the corners where the two bases were placed beneath each board—cannot be seen in the sides of these boards, which lie flat in the drawing. For in that material tabernacle of old, as the Venerable Bede says, when it had been erected and the framework of boards arranged, those mortises could not be seen either.

Nor can the bodily eye behold in these boards depicted here either the two tenons which Josephus says were in the middle of each board, or the separate holes of each base which, as he says, received the aforesaid tenons of the boards. Therefore, after the three walls of the tabernacle have been raised, and the western wall firmly joined on both sides to the northern and southern walls [Col. 0686C], that bar which now lies across the plane at the east, where the entrance should be, is lifted up and extended from the top of the northern wall to the top of the southern. Beneath it five gilded columns, having golden capitals and bronze bases, are raised at equal intervals across the width. Before them, from the bar projecting aloft, there hangs toward the ground a curtain woven of violet-blue, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and fine twisted linen. The capitals of these columns are skilfully inserted into the bar stretched across above and firmly secured in it.

## CHAPTER III. On the place called the Holy Place and that called the Holy of Holies; and what should be placed in each.

[Col. 0686D]

LXXX. Once the tabernacle walls have thus been raised, I divide into two the space within them by a line drawn across the width from one wall to the other. Yet I do so in such proportion that the eastern section, called the Holy Place, occupies two thirds of the length, while the western section, which is the Holy of Holies, occupies one third. For when the tabernacle was thirty cubits long [p. 379], twenty were allotted to the place called simply the Holy Place, and ten to that called the Holy of Holies.

At this holy dividing line, which separates the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies, I raise four gilded columns, set at intervals across the width, with silver bases and golden capitals. These columns are equally spaced from one another. Before them I suspend, from top to ground, a veil woven of the four colors mentioned above and inserted through golden rings. Within this veil I place the gilded ark of the Covenant, with two gilded poles inserted through four golden rings, two on each side. Above it I place the golden mercy-seat, matching the ark in length and breadth; it has a golden cherub at either end, their faces turned toward it, their wings spread toward one another to cover it.

Outside this same veil, in the Holy Place, I place on the north a gilded table resting upon four feet and bearing twelve loaves, six on either side, with two cups full of incense. Opposite it, on the south, I set the lampstand, from each side of which three branches extend. On each branch are, at three points, a cup, a little globe, and a lily, each branch having equal intervals according to the threefold division. These branches arise from different points of the shaft, yet each bends in its proper order until all reach one height. On the shaft of the lampstand itself, at four positions equally divided from one another, I place together a cup, a little globe, and a lily; and, lighting seven lamps upon the seven equal heights of the lampstand, I place the golden altar in the middle, outside the veil [Col. 0687B].

## CHAPTER IV. How the aforesaid walls are to be covered with curtains and goats’-hair coverings; and how the roof is to be covered with red-dyed ram skins and violet-blue skins.

[Col. 0687C]

LXXXI. Thus, after the three tabernacle walls have been raised, five columns set at its entrance before the curtain hung from them, four further columns erected between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies with the veil suspended before them, and the objects that were to be put there placed within the often-mentioned walls both in the Holy Place and in the Holy of Holies, I first cast over those walls ten curtains woven of the four aforesaid colors, twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits broad, joined side to side by violet-blue loops. In this way I cover the whole width of the house across by the lengths of these curtains, except one cubit on either side, which remains uncovered because the curtains are deficient there. For the width of the house across is thirty cubits: ten at the top, level between the walls, and ten in the descent of each wall on either side; while the curtains are only twenty-eight cubits long [Col. 0687D].

The length of the tabernacle, which is thirty cubits, I cover with the breadth produced by the curtains joined together. And I cover the eastern part, where the entrance should be, and the western wall, by a descent of five cubits on each side from the length arising from the widths of the curtains. For the breadths of the ten curtains joined together make a length of forty cubits. Of these forty cubits, thirty are assigned to the southern and northern walls, since they are each thirty cubits long; and of the ten remaining cubits, five are assigned to the eastern part in its descent and five to the western. Those cubits of curtain which remain after the walls end, both in the east and in the west, I bring inward from the eastern and western sides respectively to meet in the middle of each end wall and join there to one another. Thus I cover the house on every side down to one cubit from the ground.

LXXXII. But since the goats’-hair coverings are thirty cubits long [Col. 0688B], when thrown over the curtains they cover the whole length of the tabernacle and extend beyond those curtains in their descent by two cubits on the western wall and as many on the eastern side. For the breadths of the eleven coverings joined together make a length of forty-four cubits. Since every one of these coverings was thirty cubits long, they wholly cover that one cubit which was left uncovered close to the ground on either side of the southern and northern walls because the curtains were deficient.

I do not leave uncovered the three-cubit space which, where the goats’-hair coverings fall short on the west, reaches down to the ground. Rather, as I explained shortly before concerning the curtains, I bring together from both sides the coverings of seven cubits which remain at the west after the southern and northern walls end, and I cover the rear of the house down to the ground most securely. For I do not merely make these coverings meet one another and touch in the middle of the wall, as with the curtains; but because they are seven cubits long, I make them extend beyond the middle of the wall—which is only ten cubits wide—by two cubits in the middle, where they meet, and, laid one over the other, join them upon the western wall, where the rear of the house is. Thus I completely cover the western wall of the house down to the ground with goats’-hair coverings.

Likewise, from the seven-cubit coverings that remain after the aforesaid southern and northern walls end, I bring them together from both sides and securely cover the front of the house down to the ground [Col. 0688D]. Only, at the front of the house, where the face of the roof is, I double those two cubits which constitute half a covering, so that, as Bede says, there may be the protection of a double covering where the solid strength of a wall is lacking. You see plainly, I think, how, from the seven-cubit coverings that remain after the southern and northern walls end—on each side both in the east and likewise in the west—being brought together and extending beyond one another by two cubits in the middle of the wall, I cover down to the ground both the eastern side of the house, with half a covering doubled, and its western wall, with the two cubits that overlap in the middle of that wall laid one upon another. For the curtains and coverings extend beyond the length of the two walls, southern and northern, by as many cubits on both sides, east and west, even down to the ground, as they have in their descent on the eastern and western sides: that is, five cubits for the curtains and seven for the coverings [Col. 0689A]. This is concerning the curtains and goats’-hair coverings.

LXXXIII. I also make two further coverings, not for covering the tabernacle walls, but only for covering its roof: one of red-dyed ram skins and the other of violet-blue skins. In this way I cover both the walls and the things within them with curtains, goats’-hair coverings, red-dyed skins, and violet-blue skins. But neither the curtains, nor the coverings, nor the skins of which so much has been said can be seen with the bodily eye in the drawing lying flat. For the curtains are externally covered all round by the coverings so that they do not appear, as has been sufficiently shown above; and the goats’-hair coverings are understood to be almost wholly hidden beneath the three walls lying flat on the plane and beneath the curtain lying in the drawing to the east. Nor can the roof of the walls be seen when the walls themselves lie flat in the drawing. Yet those who are willing to give unquestioning credence to the words of the Venerable Bede, which he sets down on these matters, should understand all these things by the intellect of the heart and know that they existed in this manner in Moses’ visible tabernacle [Col. 0689B–C].

## CHAPTER V. On the courts, the court hangings, and what should be placed in those courts.

LXXXIV. Therefore, once the tabernacle has been completed by erecting and covering its walls in this fashion, I take a ruler and draw far around it a large rectangle twice as long as it is wide. The length of this rectangle exceeds the tabernacle’s length by as much as the combined space occupied by twice the tabernacle’s length and by its own width. For the court was one hundred cubits long; the length of this rectangle indicates that length, whereas, as has often been said, the tabernacle was only thirty cubits long and ten wide [Col. 0689D]. From this it is plainly gathered that the rectangle which I now make exceeds the tabernacle’s length by seventy cubits.

Within this rectangle the tabernacle is erected facing west and with its entrance to the east; the spaces around the tabernacle which lie within the rectangle are the courts of the tabernacle. Along every line of this rectangle, all around, I erect columns half as high as the tabernacle, each separated from the next by a space equal to its height. Having erected twenty to the south, as many to the north, and ten each to the east and west, clad in silver, I hang about them curtains of twisted fine linen, from their silver capitals down to their bronze bases, except for the four columns placed in the middle of the eastern side. Upon these I hang a curtain woven not of fine linen alone, but of the four colors often mentioned [Col. 0690A].

LXXXV. Opposite this curtain, farther inside, I set the bronze altar, though not in the entrance itself but apart from it, toward the south. Between this altar and the entrance of the tabernacle I place a bronze laver full of water. Thus the tabernacle stands within courts surrounded on every side by hangings. These hangings are suspended around the columns and are half as low as the tabernacle walls, yet much longer than those same walls—just as, in our own time, a church may stand in its cemetery enclosed all around by a wall; that wall, though much lower than the church walls, is nevertheless far longer than them [Col. 0690B].

I carefully provide that this tabernacle is not placed in the middle of the courts, but is located so that half the length of those courts extends from their entrance to the entrance of the tabernacle, and a fifth of their length extends from the western tabernacle wall, once it is erected, to the western side of the court. For since those visible courts of old were one hundred cubits long, there were, as a certain wise man writes, fifty cubits from their entrance to the entrance of the tabernacle; and from the western wall of the tabernacle to the western side of the courts there were twenty, while the tabernacle itself measured thirty cubits in length.

For the same man writes as follows: “There were fifty cubits from the entrance of the court on the eastern side to the entrance of the tabernacle; and in this space between the two entrances, namely those of the court and of the testimony, there were two places of prayer, one for the men of Israel and the other for the women. Between these and the entrance of the tabernacle was the altar of burnt offering, not in the entrance itself but lower down, toward the south.” Thus whoever wishes fully to discern how that visible tabernacle of Moses, with the things belonging to it, was actually made and arranged may infer it in some measure from the matters stated in the preceding part and shown to the bodily eye in this drawing [Col. 0690C–D].

## CHAPTER VI. On the allegorical exposition of the bases and boards of the walls.

LXXXVI. It remains now for us to adapt some of the features that we have depicted in the material tabernacle to the spiritual tabernacle of Christ, which is the holy Church, set before us in the picture. And indeed, from this picture, though it is not very beautiful, one may infer to some extent that the visible tabernacle of Moses was exceedingly beautiful and splendid. But there is another tabernacle far more splendid, precious, and exalted than that one: more splendid in beauty, more precious in material, and more exalted in holiness—namely, the holy Church. Called by the illumination of her Redeemer out of the darkness of ignorance [Col. 0691A], she began to be built in this world, as in a kind of wilderness, from Abel the righteous at the very beginning of the world, and does not cease to be built until the last elect person who is to be born at the end of the world.

As to how all these things belong to the holy Church—what, first of all, the tabernacle itself signifies with respect to faith; what its walls and entrance signify; what the boards and bases; the rings and bars; the hanging at the entrance, the columns, and the veil; the Holy Place simply so called; the Holy of Holies; the curtains and coverings; the two roof-coverings; then what the things within the tabernacle signify; namely, within the veil, the ark and its lid; the cherubim and mercy-seat; the bars and rings; what the jar with manna in the ark signifies [Col. 0691B]; 382 what the tablets and rod signify; what the table in the Holy Place signifies, its position on the north; its lid and crowns; its feet and rims; the loaves and incense upon it; what the golden lampstand signifies, why it was of beaten work, and why it stood on the south opposite the north; what its shaft, cups, little spheres, lilies, stems, and lamps signify; what the altar of incense and its horns signify; finally, what those things outside the tabernacle signify—namely, the courts and their hangings, and their sixty columns round about; the bases of the columns, the cords, and pegs; the altar of burnt offering, its projections and grating; the basins and tongs; the fire-pans and forks; the bronze laver and the women’s mirrors from which it was made; and finally [Col. 0691C] all the other things belonging to the tabernacle of which we speak; also, lest we seem to have omitted anything, the measurements of length, breadth, and height found in the aforementioned objects—you may find all this fully and plainly in the expositions of the orthodox Fathers, and especially in the book of the Venerable Priest Bede entitled *On the Tabernacle*.

If this is so—indeed, because it is so—it is surely worthy and entirely right that we should regard the holy sayings of holy men not merely as authoritative, but even judge them sufficient for our silence, and never presume to scrutinize anew by our own exposition what they have expounded, since we are not sufficiently fitted even to understand what they have said. [Col. 0691D] Nevertheless, because your good desires have requested that we say something mystically from what is visibly depicted here, showing in the picture itself, as we are able, how certain things should be understood allegorically or received morally—drawing some things from the sayings of the holy Fathers and adding some from our own—we shall do so. Where we set down the sayings of the Fathers, we write their names above them in the margin; but it has not seemed good to us to write our own name above our own remarks, lest perhaps, even if we said something well, it should for that reason alone be rejected if it were known to have been said by us.

LXXXVII. Therefore, the tabernacle of Christ is the holy Church, because from the beginning of the world until the last elect person, who is to be born at the end of the age, it extends through [Col. 0692A] three periods and six ages.

The three periods are: the time of the natural law, from the beginning of the world until Abraham, from whom the written law in a manner begins with circumcision; the time of the written law, from Abraham until Christ’s coming, through whom grace and truth came; and the time of grace, which began at the Savior’s first coming and will endure until the second, when the Judge of the living and the dead shall appear.

The first age was from Adam to Noah, comprising 1,656 years. The second, from Noah to Abraham, comprised 292 years. The third, from Abraham to David, comprised 942 years. The fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity, comprised [Col. 0692B] 873 years. The fifth, from the Babylonian captivity to Christ, comprised 585 years. The sixth age extends from Christ’s first coming to his second; of this age 1,180 years have already elapsed. The seventh is now the rest of souls; and the eighth will be the blessedness of resurrected bodies, when the week of this life will end and the eternity of the other life will succeed.

Through these three periods and these six ages, with the sequence of deeds and the ordering of events—according to the unity of their meanings and the diversity of the sacraments, which work salvation in one faith—harmoniously proclaiming one Creator and also one and the same Savior, whether preceding or following his coming, [Col. 0692C] the holy Church runs in faith, hope, and charity from the beginning of the age to its end: from labor to rest, from darkness to light, from misery to blessedness, from exile to homeland, from sorrow to joy, and from prison to kingdom. She is like a tabernacle sanctified and inhabited by the Most High, carried through the manifold perils of a kind of wilderness by the hands of Levites toward a land good and spacious, beautiful and fruitful—a land flowing with milk and honey.

LXXXVIII. The elect of this holy Church likewise devote themselves to holy conduct, some from the beginning of the world until Christ’s coming, and some from Christ’s coming until the end of the age. Therefore the bases 383 [Col. 0692D] set beneath the boards all around the tabernacle are the saints who came into the world from the beginning of the age until the Savior’s coming, who prefigured Christ’s grace and the condition of the holy Church, in both sexes, whether in their words, deeds, or even in the interpretations of their names.

The boards placed upon and supported by the same bases signify the saints who appear in the world after Christ’s coming until the end of this life; like boards resting on certain bases, they rest upon the words and deeds of the preceding saints. These saints adorned the holy Church in one faith and by the shedding of their blood, illumined it by the light of holy preaching, and embellished it by holy examples of holy lives.

[Col. 0693A] Accordingly, beginning with the first base beneath the first board of the southern wall, I write on it the name of the first father, Adam, and after him the names of the holy fathers who lived until Solomon, one name on each base, as follows: Adam, Abel, Seth, Enos, Enoch, Noah, Shem, Japheth, Melchizedek, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin, Moses, Aaron, Eleazar, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, Job, Ehud, Shamgar, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, Elkanah, Samuel, David, Solomon. These names are beneath the bases of the southern wall.

On the bases of the northern wall, beginning with the first base of the first eastern board, I write: [Col. 0693B] Nathan, Gad, Shimei, Ahijah, Elijah, Elisha, Jehoiada, Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Hezekiah, Josiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Jesus, Tobit, Nehemiah, Jesus, Onias, Mattathias, Judas, Jonathan, Simon, John, Zechariah, Joseph. These names are beneath the bases of the northern wall.

Beneath the bases of the western wall I write the names of women who were in the Old Testament, beginning with the first base of the first corner-board of that same wall on the south: Eve, Sarah, Rebecca, Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, Zilpah, Tamar, Rahab, Deborah, Ruth, Anna, Bathsheba, Esther, Judith, Elizabeth.

[Col. 0693C] These, then, are the names of holy men and women placed here beneath the bases of these three walls: saints who lived in the world until Christ’s coming. There was none among them who did not prefigure the grace of the same Jesus Christ our Lord and the state of the holy Church, whether in words which they spoke, deeds which they performed, or at least in the interpretations of their names. Then I depict the images of these saints, beginning at the head, above their names upon the bases themselves, because, as stated above, the same bases signify those saints. Beneath their names, which are written below the bases and images, from Adam to Nathan, I write this verse:

> These are the saints coming into the world from the beginning of the age until [Col. 0693D] Christ’s coming, and prefiguring Christ’s grace and the holy Church in both sexes, whether in words, deeds, or also in the interpretations of their names.

For all these saints of the Old Testament, as I said above, prophesied, whether in the words they uttered, in the deeds they performed, or finally in the meanings of their names—which they had from the reality itself—what Christ’s grace would accomplish in those who believed in him, or what the condition of the holy Church would be through his coming.

LXXXIX. Next, on the boards set upon the bases, I place at the top of each board two names of saints who lived in the time of grace—namely apostles, martyrs, and confessors—with their images above the names. Beginning with the image of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the end of the law and the beginning of grace, I write these names: [Col. 0694A] John the Baptist, Peter, Paul, Andrew, James, John, Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon, Thaddaeus, Matthias, Barnabas, Mark, Luke, Timothy, Titus, Stephen, Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, Cornelius, Cyprian, Lawrence, Chrysogonus, John, Paul, Cosmas, Damian, Ignatius, Alexander, Marcellinus, Peter, Fabian, Sebastian, Vincent. These are on the southern side.

On the first board of the northern wall I begin to write as follows; these are the names written on that wall: [Col. 0694B] Gervasius, Protasius, Lambert, Quintinus, George, Vitalis, Dionysius, Maurice, Hippolytus, Alban, Oswald, Edmund, Ælfheah, Edward, Sylvester, Leo, Gregory, Ambrose, Augustine, Martin, Nicholas, 384 Remigius, Hilary, Vedastus, Amandus, Germanus, Cuthbert, Wilfrid, John, Chad, Dunstan, Severinus, Jerome, Eligius, Benedict, Anthony, Leonard, Giles, Guthlac, Botulph. These names are on the northern wall.

On the boards of the western wall I also write the names of holy women with their images: first, on the first board of that western wall on the south, the name of Blessed Mary; and after her the others, as follows: Mary Magdalene, Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Agnes, Cecilia, [Col. 0694C] Lucy, Anastasia, Euphemia, Margaret, Catherine, Geneviève, Æthelthryth, Bridget, Hilda.

It should be noted that I depict all the saints of both the Old and New Testaments from the head upward, so that Adam, placed beneath Christ, may seem devoutly to stretch up his hands and eyes toward Christ. Likewise Eve, placed beneath Mary, raises her hands and eyes toward her. Mary holds a rose in one hand and a lily in the other.

Then, above the images of the New Testament depicted at the tops of the boards, I write in a single line around the three walls, from the image of the Lord Jesus on the first board of the southern wall to the image of Gervasius on the first board of the northern wall, this verse:

> [Col. 0694D] These are the saints coming into the world from the Savior’s first coming until the end of the age, in both sexes, adorning and illuminating the holy Church under one Lord, in one faith and one baptism, by the shedding of their blood, by the light of holy preaching, and by examples of good works.

For from Christ’s coming onward there will not be lacking in the world those who adorn the holy Church by examples of good life, illuminate it by the brilliance of holy preaching, or embellish it by the shedding of their blood.

## CHAPTER VII. On the hanging suspended at the entrance, the bar of that entrance, and the three walls of the tabernacle, allegorically expounded

XC. I now come to the hanging suspended at the entrance, [Col. 0695A] and across it I write these words: “The glory of the primitive Church.” For the aforesaid hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle, woven with a beautiful diversity of colors, is an ornament of the primitive Church, glorious with the various flowers of virtues. Luke writes of these:

> The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and there was no division among them; nor did any one call anything that he possessed his own, but they had all things in common.  
> (Acts 4:32)

It possessed blue cloth, because it was accustomed to think on heavenly things and to lead a heavenly life on earth. It possessed purple, because it was ready to die for Christ. It possessed scarlet dyed twice, because it burned with love of God and neighbor. It also possessed twisted fine linen, because it rejoiced in continence of the flesh and chastity.

[Col. 0695B] Across the columns themselves I write: “Teachers of the primitive Church.” For those columns from which the hanging was suspended are the holy teachers of that time, of whom Luke says:

> With great power the apostles bore witness to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord.  
> (Acts 4:33)

They were rightly made five in number because of the same number of books of the Law. We have placed these books beneath the bases of the same columns. Holy teachers must fortify the words of their preaching with them, especially those who established the primitive Church, which, gathered from the people of the Hebrews, knew that it must be established solely by the authority of the Mosaic Law, while evangelical and apostolic teaching had not yet shone throughout the world.

Across the golden capitals of these columns I write: “Christ, the head of all saints.” [Col. 0695C] Nor should it seem incongruous that Christ, the one Head of the Church, should be figured by the five capitals of the columns. For there were as many capitals as columns, because Christ himself is the one Head and Lord of all saints; he always remains undivided in himself, but distributes the grace of the Holy Spirit among each of the elect according to the capacity of the recipients.

Across the bronze bases of the columns I write: “Prophets of the Old Testament.” For the bronze bases upon which the columns rest are the prophets, by whose words the apostles and apostolic men are confirmed in faith. Thus much we have said allegorically concerning the entrance of the tabernacle.

[Col. 0695D] XCI. Next, upon that bar extending from the top of one wall, I write in a single line this verse:

> The Lord Jesus justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.  
> (Romans 3:30)

For this bar is the Lord Jesus, who reaches, as it were, from corner to corner, because he extended himself from the Jewish people, whom he first called, to save the multitude of the Gentiles. Thus, as he is called the cornerstone in the prophet [Isa. 28:1, as printed], so in the Law he is also called a corner-bar.

Beside the first board of the northern wall I write: “The north gives.” Beside the first board of the southern wall: “The south does not forbid.” For the southern side of the tabernacle, facing [Col. 0696A] south, signifies that ancient people of God, which, having long received the light of legal knowledge, was accustomed to burn with love of its Creator. The other side, facing north, figures the multitude of Gentiles, which did not cease to languish in the darkness and cold of unbelief until the time of the Lord’s incarnation. But the bar extends itself to both walls when he called to faith not only the Jewish people but also the Gentiles.

Accordingly, from the first board of the southern wall to the end of the bar are written diagonally these two verses:

> The shepherds came in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the infant lying in a manger.  
> (Luke 2:16)

Likewise, [Col. 0696B] from the first board of the northern wall to the other end of the aforesaid bar, these two verses are written diagonally:

> Entering the house, the Magi found the Child; and falling down, they worshipped him. Opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.  
> (Matthew 2:11)

How all these things pertain to the calling of both peoples—the Jewish and the Gentile—plainly appears. The joining of the southern wall with the bar signifies what the coming of the shepherds to the Child signifies; and similarly the joining of the northern wall with the same bar signifies what the coming of the Magi to the same Child signifies.

Above the images of the women, along the breadth of the western wall, I write in a single line from one corner to the other:

> The completion of the universal holy Church, to be accomplished at the end of the world.

[Col. 0696C] For the western side, which receives both walls into itself and completes the structure of the tabernacle, rightly signifies the completion of the whole holy Church, which is accomplished at the end of this world. To it the upright activity of both peoples will endure, as though the double length of the walls reaches onward to it.

## CHAPTER VIII. How the pictures in the Holy Place should be understood according to the allegorical sense

[Col. 0696D] XCII. Having thus depicted the walls of the tabernacle allegorically, I turn my hand to the things within the tabernacle outside the veil. Beside the table standing in the Holy Place on the north, I make four steps—two at either end, on each side—because of the four things belonging to sacred Scripture, which that table signifies: namely, its subject matter, interpretation, dignity, and number of books. Its subject matter is that of which Scripture treats; its interpretation, the manner in which it treats it; its dignity, the loftiness with which it treats it; and its books, those in which it treats it.

Its subject matter is the works of human restoration, together with all the sacraments: both those which existed from the beginning of the world until Christ’s coming and in diverse ways proclaimed the salvation of humankind, promised from the beginning, fulfilled at the end, and to endure without end; and those which are enacted in the holy Church from the Savior’s coming until the end of the world, confirming that salvation of humankind accomplished by his coming.

Its interpretation [Col. 0697A], according to which it treats this subject matter, is fourfold: history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy. History concerns the plain narration of events and is contained on the surface of the letter; it is understood as it is read. Allegory contains something further within itself: through what it says concerning the truth of a matter, it conveys another meaning concerning purity of faith, and shows the mysteries of the holy Church, whether present or future, sometimes through words and sometimes through deeds, but always figuratively and veiled. Tropology also consists, like allegory, in figurative words or deeds; but it differs from allegory in this: allegory builds up faith, while tropology builds up moral conduct. Anagogy, whether through veiled or open utterances, treats of the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland [Col. 0697B] and shows, in sayings either open or hidden, what reward awaits right faith or holy life.

Thus history, through the examples of saints that it recounts, stirs the reader to imitate holiness; 386 allegory, through the revelation of faith, to knowledge of truth; tropology, through instruction in morals, to love of virtue; anagogy, through the manifestation of heavenly joys, to desire for heavenly blessedness. Because sacred Scripture proceeds by these four interpretations as by four feet, I place them at the four feet of this table, one at each, since those four feet signify them.

The dignity of sacred Scripture lies in this: above all secular writings, it possesses not only significant words but significant things; therefore [Col. 0697C] all the arts called liberal are subservient to it. The books of which we speak, and which belong to Scripture, pertain partly to the Old Testament and partly to the New. The Old Testament is divided into three orders: the Law, containing five books; the Prophets, containing eight books; and the Hagiographa, to which nine books belong. Together these make twenty-two, the same number as the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, so that the holy life of the righteous man may be exercised toward wisdom by as many books as a tender age is instructed toward eloquence by letters.

[Col. 0697D] These four things—the subject matter of sacred Scripture, its interpretation, dignity, and number of books—are signified by the four steps which we placed by the table representing the Scripture of which we speak, two on either side at each end. If you wish to know more fully about these matters, read the first part of Master Hugh’s book entitled *On the Sacraments*.

Upon the table I place twelve loaves, which, although they were always there historically, nevertheless allegorically represent holy men endowed with apostolic teaching and outstanding in works; and tropologically they represent the spiritual virtues mentioned by the Apostle: charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, continence, and chastity. In these lies the refreshment of our living soul. This table stands in the Holy Place of the tabernacle, on the north.

XCIII. [Col. 0698A] Next, upon the trunk of the lampstand standing opposite it on the south is written “Christ”; and upon its shaft, “the Church.” The shaft proceeds from the trunk because Christ is the strength and support of the Church. The lampstand itself, visibly depicted here, figuratively expresses him who said of himself: “I am the light of the world” (John 2:12 [probably VIII:12]). It was rightly both golden and beaten work, because our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus, was free from every sin and yet accepted in himself the persecutions of the Passion.

It also had seven lamps upon it, because our Lord himself, possessing in himself the fullness of the same Holy Spirit [Col. 0698B] displayed the seven offices of spiritual ranks which he distributed to his body, the holy Church, according to the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit: namely, the office of doorkeepers and readers, exorcists and acolytes, subdeacons and deacons, and the office of presbyters.

These seven ranks, together with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—fear, piety, knowledge, fortitude, counsel, understanding, and wisdom (Isa. 11:2)—from whose sevenfold gift they derive, are written beside the aforesaid lamps of the lampstand, by which they are signified.

The Lord assumed the office of doorkeepers in his own person when, having made a whip of cords, he drove sellers and buyers from the temple (John 2:17). He showed the office of readers in himself when, opening the book of Isaiah in the midst of the elders, he read in it: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he sent me to preach good news to the poor” [Col. 0698C] (Luke 4:18). He exercised the office of exorcists when he cast seven demons out of Mary Magdalene (Luke 4:18 [as printed]). He showed that he held the office of acolytes when he said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). He exercised the office of subdeacons when, after supper with his disciples, he girded himself, poured water into a basin, washed the disciples’ feet, and dried them with a towel (John 13:5).

But he assumed the office of deacons when, after supper, he consecrated and dispensed the sacraments with his own mouth and hands; and when he invited the sleeping apostles to prayer, saying: “Watch and pray” (Matthew 26:41). He also displayed the office of presbyters supremely in himself when, himself priest and victim, he offered himself upon the altar of the cross for the sins of humankind [Col. 0698D], and entering the eternal holy places through his own blood (Hebrews 10:12), reconciled things heavenly and earthly (Col. 20 [as printed]).

Of these seven ranks Solomon says: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn her seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1). For Wisdom built herself a house and hewed seven pillars, because Christ Jesus, the Wisdom of God, assumed a human body in which he might dwell and displayed in the assumed human being the aforesaid offices of the seven ranks. Therefore, what the seven pillars are in Solomon’s house of Wisdom, the seven 387 lamps are, according to the allegorical sense alone, in Moses’ lampstand in the tabernacle. Let this suffice as an allegorical exposition of the table and lampstand.

## CHAPTER IX. On the image depicted upon the floor of the tabernacle

XCIV. [Col. 0699A] Next, upon the floor of the tabernacle itself, I depict an image of the Savior from the head to the belly in the Holy of Holies, and projecting from the belly to the feet into the Holy Place. I clothe the part of him in the Holy of Holies in white garments, but the part in the Holy Place in red garments.

For our Lord Jesus Christ is God and man, one person existing in three essences and two natures. He is one person, because the same Son of Man is without a father, while the Son of God is from eternity without a mother. There are three essences in him: Word, flesh, and soul.
