There are two natures: divinity and humanity. Thus the part of the image in the Holy of Holies signifies [Col. 0699B] the sublimity of divinity, which reigns eternally in heaven; while the part in the Holy Place signifies the humility of humanity, which for a time endured the pains of the Passion in the world.

Across the image within the Holy of Holies I write: “White.” Outside, in the Holy Place, I likewise write across the same image: “Red.” Thus it is shown that this image signifies him of whom the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and red” (Song 5:10): white in divinity, red in humanity. The Lord Jesus is indeed white in divinity because of the blessedness which he has had from eternity, in that nature equal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He is red in humanity, because, having a red garment in the Passion of that assumed humanity, though beautiful in his robe, he nevertheless comes from Edom, bearing dyed garments from Bozrah (Isa. 63:1).

[Col. 0699C] Upon the same image, within the Holy Place, from the feet of the high priest standing at the golden altar, I write downward this verse:

> Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.  
> (Luke 9:33 [as printed])

Above the head of the image, across the width of the tabernacle in the Holy of Holies, from one wall to the other beneath the images there, I write in a single line:

> Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man, what the Lord has prepared for those who love him.  
> (1 Corinthians 2:9)

I distinguish these two verses—one written in the Holy Place, the other in the Holy of Holies—by steps. At the verse “Whoever wishes to come” [Col. 0699D], I place three steps, corresponding to the three words: “deny,” “take up,” and “follow”—one step for each word. These three steps express the three things which in this verse the Lord Jesus proposes to the human soul, made in the image of the Trinity: servitude, lowliness, and hardship. In self-denial is servitude; in bearing the cross, lowliness; in following Christ, hardship.

For it is servitude for any person to deny himself to himself and subject himself to another’s dominion. It is lowliness to carry a cross, because the cross was once accustomed to be a sign of degradation. But it is hard to follow Christ, who taught us by his example and instructed us by his command both to despise things sweet and pleasant to the flesh [Col. 0700A] and to embrace things hard or bitter.

Therefore let the faithful soul obey these three commands of its Savior, accepting in self-denial servitude, in bearing the cross lowliness, and in imitating Christ hardship, so that it, which had fallen through disobedience from the state of threefold blessedness, may rise through obedience by the humbling affliction of these three things.

XCV. For it had fallen from itself, from the fellowship of angels, and from the vision of God himself: that is, from liberty, dignity, and blessedness. For liberty consists in a person’s possessing himself and enduring no contradiction whatsoever within himself against himself. Such was man before sin, when both his body was subject to the spirit and his spirit was subject to the Creator. But after the spirit swelled in pride against its Creator [Col. 0700B], not only did the body begin to rebel against the spirit, but even the spirit itself, in a strange and miserable way, began in many respects to rebel against itself. Thus man ceased to possess himself.

It belongs to dignity to be joined in fellowship with angels. Man does not now have that dignity, because he who would not understand while he was in that honor, having lost fellowship with the angels, has now been not only joined but even compared to senseless beasts and made like them. Nothing is more blessed than to see God, for this is eternal life: that we may know God the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent. But after unwary man opened his outward eyes to desire the fruit of the forbidden tree, he damnably closed those inward eyes by which he ought to have seen his Creator.

Yet, in order that man might be restored to these three things, the Creator of man deigned 388 to become man. [Col. 0700C] In his humanity, signified by the red part of the image, he proposes to man this threefold affliction: servitude, lowliness, and hardship, so that man may receive the three goods he lost—liberty, dignity, and blessedness. For beside the three words of that verse—“seen,” “heard,” and “ascended”—three steps are placed, one for each word. Liberty will be so great as no eye has seen; dignity so great as no ear has heard; and blessedness so great as no human heart has comprehended. These are the things that the Lord has prepared for those who love him (1 Corinthians 2:9).

[Col. 0700D] Accordingly, we placed the verse “Whoever wishes to come” in his humanity, but “Eye has not seen” in his divinity: because Christ proposed those three things to us in his humanity but prepared these things in his divinity, so that we may practice the former in merit and deserve to possess the latter in reward. But in our picture the verse “Whoever wishes to come after me,” and so forth, must be read first; afterward, “Eye has not seen,” because we must first suffer with him in order afterward to reign with him (Romans 8:17; 2 Timothy 2:12).

Therefore let the faithful soul read, “Let him deny himself,” that it may acquire what eye has not seen. Let it read, “Let him take up his cross,” that it may attain what ear has not heard. Finally, let it read, “Let him follow me,” that it may be worthy to ascend to that which has not entered into the heart of man [Col. 0701A]. Thus, by denying itself—that is, its own will—it may recover, in exchange for the servitude it bears, its liberty, which will consist in possessing itself, a liberty which eye has not seen. By taking up its cross—that is, by crucifying its flesh with its vices and desires—it may recover, in exchange for the lowliness it bears, its dignity, which will consist in fellowship with angels, a dignity which ear has not heard. By following Christ—that is, by imitating his Passion—it may recover its lost blessedness, which will consist in the splendor of his vision, which has not entered into the human heart.

Still further down, on the right side of the altar of incense, on the thigh of the image, I write: “King of kings.” On the left side of the same altar, on the garment of the image: “Lord of lords,” so that it may be understood [Col. 0701B] that this image signifies him of whom it is written in the Apocalypse:

> On his garment and on his thigh he had written: King of kings and Lord of lords.  
> (Revelation 19:16)

What the garment of the Lord Jesus is, what his thigh is, and why that Son of Man, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given (Matthew 28:18), had written on the garment of his humanity, with which divinity is clothed, “King of kings,” and on the thigh of flesh that proceeded from the Virgin, “Lord of lords,” is very well known from frequent exposition.

XCVI. Moreover, in these two titles—namely, in the kingship which is over all kings and in the lordship which is over all rulers—he sets forth certain things in his humanity, which was offered to us as an example, for every faithful member of the holy Church to imitate. For the impulses of vices, waging war by temptation, are in a manner kings; and those who consent to their suggestions are assuredly their attendants and slaves, because, as the Lord says, “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). And every holy man is king over these kings and lord over these rulers when he does not succumb grossly to their temptations, but, by a certain royal power and manly lordship, suppresses their tyranny by resisting it.

Now these sins, over which we ought in this manner to be kings and lords, are seven: pride, envy, anger, sloth, avarice, gluttony, and lust. These sins are called original and capital because they are the beginnings and causes of all the rest. Through these seven we sin in three ways: in thought, speech, and deed. In thought we sin through love of the flesh and love of the world; in speech, through arrogance and disparagement; in deed, through crime and disgraceful conduct. The first two defile the mind; the second two, the tongue; the third two, the body. The first two also exclude love of God and desire for the heavenly homeland; the second two extinguish humble confession of sins and true esteem for one’s neighbours; the third two drive out continence and innocence.

But because we ought both to reign over the aforesaid seven and to exercise lordship over these three—impure thought, corrupt speech, and wicked action—which proceed from those seven, therefore, to represent those seven, we have placed seven steps beside “King of kings”; and to indicate these three, we have likewise painted three steps beside “Lord of lords” [Col. 0702A]. After this, because for anyone possessing this spiritual lordship, by which these three evils are subdued, a certain newness of reward from the presence of the Godhead in the heavenly homeland awaits, and because an ineffable greatness of recompense awaits anyone possessing this manly kingship which checks those seven criminal sins, therefore in the right hand of the image, in the Holy of Holies, opposite “Lord of lords,” one scroll is held, upon which is written: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5). And in the left hand of the same image, opposite “King of kings,” another scroll is held, upon which is written: “My great reward is with me, to render to each according to his works” (Rev. 22:12).

And because both that newness and this greatness will lack every end whatsoever, a green circle is placed beside each scroll; for the rewards of the elect shall never wither through any ending, but shall flourish without end, just as in a circle neither beginning nor end is found. In the humanity which is in the Holy Place, in the lower circle beneath the candlestick, I write between the feet of the image: “Way,” at the hem of the garments of the image. But in the divinity above, in the golden centre of the circle which is above the two cherubim, I write on the breast of the same image: “Life,” crosswise, namely beneath the beard of the image. In that circle whose one half is outside the veil, beside the altar of incense, while the other half is within the veil, beneath the ark of the covenant, I write: “Truth” [Col. 0702C]. Thus two syllables of this word are in the outer half of the circle, while the third syllable is in the inner half.

These three words are to be understood as placed in these three locations in such a way that within these three circles this verse is written: “Way, truth, life.” For the Lord himself says of himself in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Christ Jesus himself, signified by this image, is for us Way, Truth, and Life: Way, that we may go through him; Truth, that we may follow after him; Life, that we may come to him. Through him, lest we wander; after him, lest we fail; to him, lest we die.

“Lead me, Lord, in thy way, and I shall walk in thy truth: let my heart rejoice” (Ps. 85:11). We are led in the way so that we may go, and we enter into truth so that we may run; he makes our heart rejoice, so that we may live forever. Again: “Thou hast held my right hand, and in thy will thou hast led me, and with glory thou hast received me” (Ps. 72:24). Thou hast held me, O Truth, lest I fail; thou hast led me, O Way, lest I wander; thou hast received me, O Life, lest I perish.

Thus Life is in the holy manner of life which he practised among human beings; Truth is in the sound preaching by which he instructed the world; Life is in the eternal exultation by which he made his own blessed. Way is in the example, Truth in the promise, Life in the reward. Finally, Way is in humanity, Life in divinity, Truth in both. Way is in humanity because in it he afforded us an example of holy conduct. Life is in divinity because in it he bestows on us the reward of eternal blessedness [Col. 0703A]. Truth likewise is in both, because what he promises us in humanity he renders in divinity. This is the reason why I wrote “Way” below in the Holy Place, that is, in humanity itself, between his feet; “Life” above in the divinity which is in the Holy of Holies; and “Truth” both in the Holy Place and in the Holy of Holies, in humanity as well as divinity: because he himself, as has already been said above, is both Way in the examples which he showed in humanity, and Life in the rewards which he bestows in divinity, and Truth in the promises which he makes in humanity and fulfils in divinity.

XCVII. Beside the image, above in the Holy of Holies, on the right, are written the nine orders of blessed spirits who are in the heavenly homeland, with their icons; while on the left of the same image I paint a large icon of a man from the breast upward, because there is this twofold creature in heaven: namely, angelic and human. Beneath the angels, in one line directed toward the image, I write these words: “This is he into whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12); and beneath the icon of the man: “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Beside this icon I also write the fourteen blessed conditions which the saints will possess in the future, seven belonging to the soul and seven to the body. The seven which belong to the soul are written between the head of the image and the icon: namely, wisdom, friendship, concord, power, honour, security, joy. The other seven, which belong to the body, are written on the other side of the same icon: namely, beauty, swiftness, strength, freedom, health, delight, enduringness [Col. 0703C]. Between these fourteen blessed conditions, above the head of the icon, is written this title: “The human race, which is the tenth drachma.” On the side where this icon stands I also write: “The boundaries of the peoples.” On the side where the angels are I write: “According to the number of the angels of God,” because it is believed that as great a multitude of human beings will ascend there as the multitude of angels who remained there. The eyes of each icon, both of the man and of the angels, are turned toward the face of the image, because the entire blessedness both of angels and of human beings consists in the vision of the Godhead. Moreover, I overlay the field in the Holy of Holies with sapphire colour, which resembles the sky when it is clear.

XCVIII. But I make the field which is in the Holy Place purple, because the Holy Place signifies the present Church, which endures the temptations of sufferings, whereas the Holy of Holies signifies the heavenly homeland. Upon these two fields I also place these titles. On the purple field in the Holy Place, at the right of the image, I write: “The glittering Pleiades” (Job 38:31). Opposite this title, above in the Holy of Holies, on the sapphire field, likewise at the right of the image, I write: “are joined together” (ibid.). Again, in the Holy Place, at the left of the image, opposite the Pleiades and on the other side, toward the north, I write in the purple field: “The circuit of Arcturus” (Job 38:31). And in the Holy of Holies, on the left [Col. 0704A], opposite “are joined together,” I write: “has been scattered.”

These four titles, two written in the Holy Place and two on the other side in the Holy of Holies, pertain to that saying in which the Lord addresses blessed Job in these words: “Canst thou join together the glittering stars of the Pleiades, or canst thou scatter the circuit of Arcturus?” (ibid.). The glittering stars of the Pleiades, which are separated by distance but joined in location, signify the individual elect of the holy Church, who have indeed held one and the same faith in their Creator and Saviour, but have not all been in the world simultaneously at one and the same time. By the circuit of Arcturus is expressed the continual toil of the holy universal Church in the present life. This holy Church is always wearied, yet never conquered, just as Arcturus always turns but never sinks.

But the glittering Pleiades shall be joined, and the circuit of Arcturus shall be scattered, because all the elect will be present together in the heavenly homeland, and the holy Church will then universally cease from its labour. This is why I placed in the purple field which is in the Holy Place these two titles: “The glittering Pleiades” and “The circuit of Arcturus”; and in the sapphire field which is in the Holy of Holies, these two: namely, “are joined together” and “has been scattered.” For then the individual elect shall be in the same blessedness—though here they were divided in time, they were nevertheless joined in one and the same faith—and the labour of the holy Church shall be changed into rest, bitterness into sweetness, exile into kingdom, and sorrow into joy [Col. 0704C].

In the purple field the Pleiades glitter in one place, though not over one continuous stretch, and Arcturus turns; but in the sapphire field the former are joined together and the latter has been scattered. For amid the pressures of the present life, which the purple field represents, each one of the elect, although not existing at the same time as the others, nevertheless shines before the Lord in one faith; and the holy catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, always conquering, labours in many ways. But in the heavenly homeland, represented by the sapphire field painted in the Holy of Holies, the individual elect shall be united together in rest, and the holy universal Church shall cease from its labour. Let this suffice as the allegorical explanation of the image painted on the floor of the tabernacle and of matters belonging to it [Col. 0704D].

## CHAPTER X. On the Paintings Relating to the Altar of Holocaust and the Bronze Basin

XCIX. Having arranged the interior of the tabernacle in this way, I go out from it to the exterior, to the courts and to the altar of holocaust which is outside, at the entrance of the courts. There I paint a Levite sacrificing a red heifer upon it with a knife. This red heifer, visibly painted here, indicates that heifer of which the Lord says to Moses in the book of Numbers: “Command the children of Israel to bring thee a red heifer of full age, in which there is no blemish and which has not borne a yoke” (Num. 19:2).

According to the allegorical sense, this heifer signifies our Lord Jesus Christ according to the humanity received from the Virgin. He is aptly called a heifer, of the female sex, on account of the weakness of the flesh: “For he himself bore our pains and carried our infirmities” (Isa. 53:4). He is called red rather than white because he came “in the likeness of sinful flesh”; he who, as the Apostle says, “was tempted in all things in like manner, without sin” (Heb. 4:15). Yet in this heifer there was neither blemish nor did it bear a yoke, because he admitted in himself neither the stains of vices nor the burdens of any sins. It was of full age, because he not only lacked every evil but also possessed every good within himself. “And Eleazar,” he says, “shall sacrifice it” (Num. 19:3).

We too sacrifice this heifer daily when we faithfully receive the most holy body of our Redeemer. Thus, on the altar of holocaust the heifer is cut with a knife, because we do indeed make portions in the sacrament, but do not divide or separate him from himself [Col. 0705B]. Outwardly the appearance is shown, by which our understanding may be instructed; inwardly the incorruption of the body is preserved, in which his unity is not divided. Where the part is, there is also the whole, because, as one can be in different places, so the whole can be in each individual part.

Beneath the sacrifice itself I also make three steps, because although there is one sacrament upon the altar, three distinct things are set forth there: the visible species, the truth of the body, and the power of spiritual grace. The visible species is what is visibly perceived there; the truth of the body and blood is what is believed beneath the visible species; spiritual grace is what is received with the body and blood [Col. 0705C]. The species is seen by the eye of flesh; the truth is attained by the purity of faith; the power is received, on account of the merit of faith, through the mediation of bodily reception. What is seen according to the species is the sacrament and image of that which is believed according to the truth of the body; and this, in turn, is the sacrament of that which is received according to spiritual grace. Though these three are one there, in the first is found the sign of the second; in the second, the cause of the third; and in the third, the power of the second and the truth of the first. The appearance of that whose substance is absent appears; and the substance whose form does not appear lies hidden. These, then, are what the three steps which we placed beneath the heifer signify.

C. But because these three are in one sacrament and are one sacrament, I draw a line crosswise through these same three steps and join them. At the bronze basin I place two priests, one washing his hands and the other his feet. These two priests allegorically signify the priesthood of the Jews and of the holy Church. The priest who washes his hands represents the priests of the Old Testament, for whom, when they were to celebrate bodily sacrifices, it was sufficient to cleanse their outward works, which outward works are signified by the hands. But the other priest, who washes his feet, represents the priests of our own time, for whom, since they offer daily to the Father the true body and blood of Christ for the remission of sins, it ought not to suffice to cleanse themselves outwardly from shameful acts and crimes unless they also purge themselves inwardly from impure affections [Col. 0706A]. This cleansing of inner affections is denoted by the washing of the feet. For the feet of the mind are its affections; it proceeds, as it were, by as many steps as it stretches itself by desire toward things desired. For to will to do something is already to go in the mind.

Outside the tent, toward the east, Moses is placed holding in his hand the tablets of the Decalogue, and holding the prophecy which he uttered concerning Christ; he addresses these washing priests and says to them: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1:16). For the law given to us through Moses stirs us to spiritual cleansing. One of them answers him: “I will wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. 25:6). The other: “I wash my feet as I enter the house of God,” because we ought to obey the legal precepts spiritually. On the other side is Aaron, and he says: “I will enter unto the altar of God” (Ps. 42:4). For he too, removing the entrance-curtain of the tent and desiring to enter, addresses the Levite who sacrifices the heifer and says: “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49:14) [Col. 0706B]. The same Levite answers: “Willingly will I sacrifice to thee, O Lord” (Ps. 53:8). For Aaron to say this is for the holy priesthood which we venerate to stir us, both by words and by examples, to mortify the flesh. And we answer what the Levite answers here if we offer humble assent to the exhortations of holy prelates. Let this suffice for the present as an allegorical account of those things which pertain to the altar of holocaust and the bronze basin.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Hangings of the Courts and Their Pillars

[Col. 0706C]

CI. Then I turn my hand to the courts surrounding the tabernacle; beginning at the pillar beside which Aaron enters after drawing aside the veil, I write in one continuous line around the middle of these same hangings, as far as the pillar opposite Moses, this verse: “The hangings of the tabernacle, made of twisted fine linen, are the first rudiments of beginners, restraining at once the enticements of flesh and spirit.” For just as the Holy of Holies signifies that portion which is in heaven, and the Holy Place typologically declares the perfect life of believers dwelling only in this present age, so the court of the tabernacle, which was exterior, shows the first rudiments of beginners [Col. 0706D]. It was fittingly made of twisted fine linen, because the first care to be bestowed upon beginners is that they restrain the enticements alike of flesh and spirit.

And because that breadth of the court which is toward the east expresses the beginning of our good conduct, which begins through faith, therefore above the hangings on the eastern side, from the pillar beside the calf to the one beside the lion, I write in one line this verse: “The breadth of the court facing east is the beginning of good conduct, beginning from faith.” And because the other breadth of the court, which faces the setting of the sun—where, the day’s labour ended, the relief of sleep comes in the night—signifies that time when, after death has brought active life to an end, the rest and eternal reward of the saints are hoped for, therefore above those hangings on the western side, from the pillar beside the man to that beside the eagle, in one line beneath the icons of the Gershonites, I write this verse: “The breadth of the court facing west is the rest and eternal reward of the elect after death” [Col. 0707A].

CII. Again, because the pillars before which these hangings of which we speak are suspended signify holy preachers who preside over the peoples of the faithful, therefore from the pillar opposite Aaron’s arm to that opposite Moses, I write in one continuous line around the lower part beneath the hangings and pillars this verse: “The pillars holding the hangings aloft are holy Teachers, drawing the hearts of their hearers away from earthly contagions and raising them to heavenly desires; and carefully stretching these hangings, as it were the Lord’s garment, lest any doubling be found in them.”

Again, beginning from the pillar opposite Moses and continuing to that beside which Aaron draws aside the veil, I write beneath the hanging which hangs there this verse: “The entrance of the court is the entrance into the holy Church.” For this is signified by the court’s entrance. From the pillar beside the lion to that beside the man, lengthwise through the middle of the Kohathites, I place this title: “The court, having one hundred cubits in length, is the holy Church, undertaking within itself the labour of temporal patience and continence for the sake of eternal life in heaven.” On the other side, from the pillar beside the eagle, through the middle of the Merarites, to the one erected beside the calf, I write this title: “The Church has one hundred cubits in length, which raises its cubits—its arms—to good works for the sake of eternal life” [Col. 0707C].

Once the courts have thus been inscribed on every side, because the holy Church is protected and fortified against the assaults of errors by holy Scripture, which the seven arts serve, I write, along three sides of the same courts beside the tops of the pillars, all the books both of the Old and the New Testament together with the seven arts called liberal. Thus the four Evangelists are painted in the four corners: at the east, the lion, to stir us at the rising of holy conduct to the strength of good work; at the south, the man, that by the breath of the Holy Spirit he may lead us to rationality of mind; at the west, the eagle, that through contemplation he may illumine us against the setting of virtues; at the north, the calf, which may exhort us against the suggestions of the ancient enemy, signified by the north, to mortify the flesh.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Clergy of the Old and New Testament

CIII. After this, around the hangings of the court of which we have spoken, I draw a large line at some distance from them, making a great square that encloses within it all the things mentioned above. Within this square I place Moses and Aaron at the east [Col. 0708A]; above Moses, in the same square, I paint an archbishop with his archdeacon; and above Aaron I likewise paint a bishop with his archdeacon. At the south, beside the line of the tent, in the middle, I place a large icon of a man with the name “Kohath” inscribed above his head, and beside him his sons, the Kohathites—six in a row on the right and six on the left. Above them I paint, in two places on either side, a priest celebrating Mass at the altar and a deacon clothed in a dalmatic, offering him the chalice at the altar.

At the north, beside the line of the tent, I write the name “Merari” with his icon, and the icons of his sons, six in a row on the right and six on the left, separate from them. At the west I place the name “Gershon” with his icon, and the icons of his sons, four on the right and four on the left, separate from them [Col. 0708B]. Then I turn my hand again to the east and, above Moses and Aaron, between the archbishop and bishop and their archdeacons, of whom we have spoken above, I write the Jerusalem patriarch with his icon, by whom those bishops were consecrated.

At the south, above Kohath, I place the patriarch of Antioch, exhorting a Levite on one side and a priest on the other, as though newly ordained by him, to preach. He hands the priest a scroll on which is written: “Cry aloud, do not cease; lift up thy voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1); and another to the Levite, containing a Gospel text, on which is written: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4:2) [Col. 0708C]. At the north, above Merari, I place the patriarch of Aquileia with his icon, handing a maniple to a subdeacon and a candle to an acolyte at their ordination. At the west, above Gershon, I place the patriarch of Alexandria with his icon, ordaining an exorcist, reader, and doorkeeper; and handing three scrolls to these three: one to the exorcist, on which is written, “Receive and possess the power to lay hands upon the possessed, or catechumens”; another to the reader, on which is written, “Receive and be proclaimers of the word of God”; and a third to the doorkeeper, on which is written, “Act thus, as one who must render an account to God for the things enclosed by these keys” [Col. 0708D]. He also gives him a key.

CIV. Thus, with the Levites of the Old and New Testament arranged about the tabernacle, I make their inscriptions in this way. At the east, between the tent and Moses and Aaron, from one corner to the other, I write this verse: “These are Moses and Aaron, who with their sons keep watch in the guardianships of the tabernacle” (Num. 1:53), “having charge of the sanctuary.”

> [Note: Col. 0707.] Not thus in the Vulgate. This discrepancy may indeed be seen in almost all the verses used in the same manner. —?ED. P.

Above this verse, from one corner to the other, to explain this verse, I write between the bishops and archdeacons, through the patriarch, this verse: “These are they who preside over the holy Church, freely bestowing blessings and promotions through the spiritual ranks.” For archbishops and bishops, having the guardianship of the spiritual sanctuary—that is, of the holy Church—and keeping watch in its guardianships with their archdeacons, primicerii, and treasurers, consecrate basilicas, anoint altars, prepare chrism, perform laying on of hands and the common blessing over the people; they distribute ecclesiastical offices and orders and bless consecrated virgins [Col. 0709A].

At the south, through the middle of the sons of Kohath, from one corner to the other, this verse is written in one line: “These are the Kohathites, who, when the camp moved, carried on their own shoulders, upon poles, those holy things which were in the tabernacle” (Num. 4:15). A little above this verse, across the heads of these Kohathites, I place this number: “Two thousand, seven hundred and fifty” (Num. 4:36). Such was the number of the sons of Kohath from thirty years old and upward to the fiftieth year, who pitched their camp at the south of the tabernacle.

Across the heads of the priests and deacons, and through the patriarch, from east to west, I write in one line this verse: “These are they in the holy Church who consecrate Christ’s sacraments and distribute those consecrated sacraments to the people of God, baptizing and preaching the word of life.” For priests ought to consecrate the body and blood of Christ; deacons ought to distribute what has been consecrated to the Christian people; and both ought to preach, catechize, and baptize [Col. 0709B].

At the north, from one corner to the other, through the middle of the sons of Merari, I write in one line this verse: “These are the Merarites, carrying the boards of the tabernacle, its bases, pillars, and bars” (Num. 4:31). Above this verse, across the heads of these Merarites, I place this number: “Three thousand, two hundred.” Above them, across their heads: “Offering at the altar the vessels of the body and blood of Christ, reading the epistle, and showing their neighbours works of light.” For subdeacons, who in Greek are also called ὑποδιάκονοι, “subdeacons,” serve the Levites; they offer at the altar the vessels of the body and blood, and hold for the bishop the water pitcher, towel, and hand-cloth. Acolytes, while the Gospel is being read, hold candles; hence they are called in Latin *ceroferarii*, “candle-bearers,” not in order to illumine the darkness of this air, but so that, just as they carry visible light in their hands, they may show works of light to their neighbours [Col. 0709D].

CV. At the west also, from one corner to the other, through the middle of the sons of Gershon, I write in one line this verse: “These are the Gershonites, carrying the tabernacle and the hangings of the court, the coverings of the walls and roof” (Num. 4:25). Above this verse, across the heads of these Gershonites, I place this number: “Two thousand, six hundred and thirty” (ibid., v. 4). A little above this verse, from south to north, across the heads of the doorkeepers, readers, and exorcists, and through the patriarch, I write in one line this verse: “These are they who guard the doors of the Church, minister the word of God, and cast unclean spirits out of the possessed.”

For doorkeepers, who in the Old Testament were called gatekeepers, guard the keys of the Church; at proper hours they close and open the church, receive the faithful, and do not receive unbelievers and the excommunicated [Col. 0710A]. Readers proclaim the word of God and recite the prophetic readings in the Church. Exorcists perform the sacraments of opening over catechumens, having spiritual authority over unclean spirits in order to cast them out of the possessed.

I suitably paint around the hangings of the court the images of all these icons, namely of the clergy of both the Old and New Testament: the priest celebrates Mass at the altar; the deacon offers him the chalice; the subdeacon reads the epistle; the acolyte holds a lighted candle in his hands; the doorkeeper, holding a key, opens the door; the reader recites the reading; the exorcist casts an unclean spirit out of a human being [Col. 0710B]. In this way I arranged around the tabernacle the ministers of both the Old and the New Testament.

CVI. After all this, at the east above the Jerusalem patriarch, I place the name and image of the apostle Peter, prince of the other apostles. Hence he was also called Cephas by the Lord, holding in his hand the keys given him by the Lord, by which whatever he bound upon earth was bound also in heaven, and whatever he loosed upon earth would be loosed also in heaven (Matt. 16:19). After Peter, within a certain square which extends all around as far as the same image of Peter, are placed the icons of other apostolic men who, after him, were successors of his apostolic see in the Roman Church, holding the same keys in their hands [Col. 0710C], so that the names of each are placed beneath their respective icons, as follows.

Peter, Linus, Cletus, Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, Soter, Eleutherius, Victor, Zephyrinus, Calixtus, Urban, Pontian, Anterus, Fabian, Cornelius, Lucius, Stephen, Sixtus, Dionysius, Felix, Eutychian, Caius, Marcellinus, Marcellus, Eusebius, Miltiades, Sylvester, Mark, Julius, Liberius, Felix, Libertus, Damasus, Siricius, Anastasius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Sixtus, Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, Hormisdas, John, Felix, Boniface, John, Agapetus, Silverius, Vigilius, Pelagius, John, Benedict, Pelagius, Gregory, Sabinian, Boniface, Deusdedit, Boniface, Honorius, Severinus, John, Theodore, Martin, Eugene, Vitalian, Adeodatus, Domnus, Agatho, Leo, Benedict, John, Conon, Sergius, John, John, Sisinnius, Constantine, Gregory, Gregory, Zachary, Stephen, Paul, Constantine, Stephen, Adrian, Leo, Stephen, Paschal, Eugene, Valentine, Gregory, Sergius, Leo, Benedict, Paul, Stephen, Nicholas, Adrian, John, Martin, Adrian, Stephen, Formosus, Boniface, Stephen, Romanus, Theodore, John, Benedict, Leo, Sergius, Anastasius, Lando, John, Leo, Stephen, Martin, Agapetus, John, Leo, Benedict, John, Benedict, Domnus, Boniface, Benedict, John, John, Gregory, John, Sylvester, also called Gerbert, John, John, Sergius, Benedict, John, Benedict, Sylvester, Gregory, Clement, Damasus, Leo, Victor, Stephen, Benedict, Nicholas, Alexander, Gregory, Victor, Urban, Paschal, Gelasius, Calixtus, Honorius, Innocent, Celestine, Lucius, Eugene, Anastasius, Adrian, Alexander [Cols. 0710D–0711A].

We have placed these apostolic men together with Peter, whose place they hold and whose office they exercise, in so lofty a position because they are the heads of the holy universal Church and the prelates of all her prelates. Ecclesiastical custom is accustomed to call them popes—that is, fathers of fathers—and instituted that they should be so called. For they are the principal and greatest successors of the apostolic see in the Roman Church; hence the holy Church is accustomed specifically to call them “apostolic.” We have therefore placed them in our painting above all persons of the Church, in eminent and highest places, upon certain lofty thrones and exalted seats, because, while they preside in the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, every ecclesiastical order ought to obey them; and they alone, by the singular prerogative of their most exalted dignity, possess the keys to bind and loose all things upon earth [Col. 0711B].

CVII. Then, on that very yellow line which, descending from these apostolic men, encloses in its circuit everything set below, I write continuously this verse: “The total of the Levites, who from thirty years old and upward to [Col. 0711C] fifty years old were counted for serving the Lord, was eight thousand six hundred and eighty” (Num. 4:48). For that was their number. The new Levites likewise possess this number spiritually within themselves when they zealously strive perfectly to preserve in themselves the incorruption and purity of the five senses, in hope of the future resurrection. For in Sacred Scripture the number five commonly signifies the five bodily senses; one hundred, perfection; eight, resurrection; and a thousand—because it contains within itself all numbers and beyond it there is no number—the complete fulfillment of the divine promises, surpassing every desire (Luke 6:38). That is, the fulfillment which the Lord in the Gospel calls “a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” [Col. 0711D] (Isa. 64:4). Isaiah also says of it that neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man. Of it the Apostle says briefly: “And God shall be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).

Therefore the spiritual ministers of our time are also five hundred when they live holily; they are eighty when they [395] believe rightly; and they are eight thousand when they seek to possess both right faith and holy conduct, in order that they may attain the full blessedness which, after the general resurrection of the dead, the righteous Judge will give to His elect. Accordingly, at the end of this long verse, which is written in a single continuous line on this yellow line from Peter the Apostle to that same Peter, I have placed three steps: one leading to eighty, the second [Col. 0712A] to five hundred, the third to eight thousand, so that this number may be shown to pertain to the ministers of holy Church. And among the eighty I write: “Right faith”; among the five hundred: “Holy life”; and among the eight thousand: “Full blessedness.” For the ministers of holy Church both believe rightly here, live holily here, and shall possess full blessedness there.

After this, from one side of Peter’s image to the other side of the same image, all around in a single continuous line—in a certain square line extending from the aforesaid image back to that same image—I write this verse: “These are the particular fathers of the holy universal Church and the prelates of all her prelates; all the sons of holy mother Church must obey them as they preside, and as possessing by a special prerogative of dignity the keys [Col. 0712B] of binding and loosing all things upon earth.” This verse is distinguished at its beginning by two steps, through which those keys are expressed. For the keys bestowed by the Lord upon Peter and his successors are nothing other than the power of opening and shutting, and discernment between those to be admitted and those to be excluded.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the faithful laity of both periods.

CVIII. Thus, the clergy having been arranged about the tabernacle, I arrange the faithful laity about that same tabernacle, yet outside the clergy; for faithful laypeople, although they do not hold spiritual office within the tabernacle of holy Church as clerics do, nevertheless belong to it through faith [Col. 0712C] and good works.

First, then, I set the laity of the old period—that is, the tribes—around the aforesaid tabernacle and within a great square which I now make, distributing them with their names and images across its four sides, three tribes to each side and a place in the middle among them. To the east Judah is placed, with Issachar on one side and Zebulun on the other. To the south, Reuben with Simeon and Gad. To the west, Manasseh with Ephraim and Benjamin. To the north likewise, Dan with Asher and Naphtali.

This should be noted: on the central place of each side, three tribes are placed round about; and on each side, beneath the images themselves, is written [Col. 0712D] the number of men of those tribes from twenty years old and upward. To the east: one hundred eighty-six thousand four hundred. To the south: one hundred fifty-one thousand four hundred fifty. To the west: one hundred eight thousand one hundred. To the north: fifty-seven thousand six hundred. And beneath the tribes themselves I place which tribes encamped on one side of the tabernacle and which on another.

Then, to the east, where the three tribes are placed, I depict married persons celebrating marriage and lawfully using an undefiled marriage bed. To the south I also depict the same householder in two places: in one, offering food to a hungry person; in the other, drink to one who thirsts. To the west the same householder is depicted twice: here clothing the naked; there [Col. 0713A] receiving a guest, that is, taking a stranger into his house. To the north, in one place he visits the sick; in another he consoles someone imprisoned, whose hands and feet are bound.

These, indeed, are the six works of mercy which the Lord specifically enumerates in the Gospel; in them the perfection of good works is signified. By these works faithful laypeople, lawfully possessing earthly things and dwelling in the four quarters of the world, stand as though stationed by the four sides of the tabernacle; and in them they show compassion to their neighbors for God’s sake, so that they may deserve to find mercy from the Lord Himself.

After this, eastward, through the middle of the images, from one corner to the other, I write continuously this verse: “These are those who lawfully use the world in lawful marriages and an undefiled marriage bed, and who, because of the six works of mercy which they perform, belong to the tabernacle.” To the south [Col. 0713B], from east to west, I write this verse: “These are those who feed Christ, hungry in His members, and give Him drink when thirsty.” To the west, from one corner to the other, this verse is written continuously: “These are those who clothe Christ, naked in His members, and receive Him as a guest.” To the north, continuously [396] from west to east, stands this verse: “These are those who visit Christ, sick in His members, and console Him when imprisoned.”

CX. After this, to the east I depict the Roman emperor, wearing a golden diadem upon his head; holding a drawn sword in one hand, and in the other a golden sceptre; with a golden ring on his finger and likewise a golden armlet on his right arm; and I depict the emperor himself clothed in purple [Col. 0713C]. For as the lord pope is head of the clergy, so the emperor is head of the laity. And as the lord pope has beneath him patriarchs or primates, archbishops and bishops, and the other ecclesiastical prelates, who preside beneath him over the same holy Church, so the emperor has beneath him other authorities—namely dukes and counts, magistrates and judges, prefects and princes—who exercise just justice under him according to the ordinances of laws and reasonable customs.

This image, visibly depicted in this place, denotes the great and illustrious [Col. 0713D] emperor Constantine, who, first after the two emperors Philip—who were the first Christian Roman emperors, and who were deceived and killed in different places through the treachery of their successor Decius—received the faith with such devotion and obtained the grace of baptism with such ardor of mind that he turned with his whole heart to the true and living God, in true confession and holy conduct. Being most Christian and most faithful, he devoutly built churches, embraced the servants of God—the ministers of the sacred altar—with great reverence and honor, and by public edict commanded that throughout the Roman Empire the temples of idols should be closed and churches built.

Of him blessed Pope Gregory writes thus to Æthelberht, king of the English [Col. 0714A]:

> Constantine, once the most devout emperor, recalled the Roman commonwealth from the perverse worship of idols and subjected it with himself to almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ; and he turned himself wholly toward Him, together with the peoples subject to him. Hence it came about that this man surpassed the name of the ancient princes by his own praises, and exceeded his predecessors in reputation as much as he surpassed them in good works. Indeed, it is incredible to recount how swiftly, through his zeal, the holy Church grew widely throughout the whole world, and how great was his ardor for expending resources on the building of churches. For while churches were being built by public edict throughout his empire, he himself supplied money for this purpose most abundantly from the royal treasuries. Moreover, [Col. 0714B] he wrote to every city of his realm that the people should supply the bishops from the royal treasury with the means by which holy churches might be completed. For his heart burned with faith in God, and his kindly and merciful disposition was nourished by good works.

CXI. After this Constantine of whom we speak, within a square extending all around back to that same Constantine, are placed images of other emperors, adorned with the same insignia, so that the name of each is written beneath his own image.

We do not depict among these emperors Julian the Apostate, son of a certain Constantius, brother of Constantine the Great by his father Constantine, not by his mother Helena. For although some other emperors assented to heretics [Col. 0714C] and, deceived by their errors, often grievously afflicted the servants of God, nevertheless none of them, having become wholly pagan, defiled himself with the worship of idols. But this man, though he had been a cleric and became emperor, shamelessly profaned holy baptism with the blood of sacrifices and did everything by which demons are customarily propitiated. He reopened the temples of the pagans and became a more cunning persecutor than the other persecutors of Christians. For not by force or tortures, but by rewards, honors, flatteries, and persuasions, he overcame almost a greater part of the people than he would have done [Col. 0718D] had he assaulted them cruelly. For he said that the military belt, the administration of provinces, and judicial office ought not [Col. 0714D] to be entrusted to Christians, since their own law had forbidden them to use the sword. Therefore he later commanded soldiers by public edict either to sacrifice or to leave military service.

For these and many other impieties of his, we do not place him among the other emperors in our picture, since we know that he does not belong to the tabernacle of the Church. We carry these emperors down to Constantine, son of Irene, after whom the Roman Empire passed to the kings of the Franks. For, requested by Pope Adrian, the great and glorious Charles, king of the Franks, son of King Pippin and Queen Bertrada, entered Italy against Desiderius, king of the Lombards; captured Pavia; killed Desiderius [397]; and brought all Lombardy under his power. The same man afterward entered Rome and was the first there from the Frankish nation to assume the name of emperor and Augustus; and he sent into exile those who had dishonored Pope Leo, after deposing them.

Accordingly, after Constantine, son of Irene, we place the kings of the Franks, returning to earlier times and beginning with Clovis, who was the sixth king of the Franks and the first king of that people to be baptized by blessed Remigius. We carry them down to Louis, son of Lothair, who, having become king from being a cleric, was captured by the Franks and died at Laon. In him the line of Charlemagne failed among the kings of the Franks [Col. 0715A].

CXII. After this Louis we place the kings of the Franks who were of the line of Hugh Capet, and carry them down to the present Philip [Col. 0715B], son of Louis, who was son of Louis, who was son of Philip, who was son of Henry, who was son of Robert, who was son of Hugh Capet.

After this Philip we place the kings of the English, carrying them from the most Christian King Alfred down to this Henry III, son of Henry II. And after this Henry we place certain kings of the Scots, from Malcolm, who took in marriage the most Christian Queen Margaret—mother of the most excellent Queen Matilda, wife of Henry I, king of the English, and mother of the Empress Matilda, who afterward married Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and bore him Henry II, king of the English, father of this King Henry III. We carry them down to this William, king of the Scots, whose [Col. 0715C] father was Count Henry; Henry’s father was the religious King David; David’s mother was the most holy woman Margaret, most excellent queen of the Scots, who surpassed the splendor of her name by the holiness of her conduct.

Her father was Edward, who was son of the unconquered King Edmund; Edmund’s father was Edbelred; his father Edgar the Peaceful; his father Edmund; his father Edward the Elder; his father the noble Elvred, who was son of King Ebelviph, who was son of King Egbert; whose father was Elemund; whose father was Effa; whose father was Eppa; whose father was Ingles, whose brother was the most famous King Ine. Their father was Ceonred, son of Ceonwald, son of Cutha, son of Cuthwin, son of Eculin, son of Cheuric, son of Cerodae, son of Ceordaic, son of Alefa, who [Col. 0715D] was son of Elsa, who was son of Gennis.

This man was the head of his people, from whom that whole people received its name. His father was Wig; Wig’s father Frewine; Frewine’s father Fredgar; Fredgar’s father Brand; Brand’s father Beldeg; Beldeg’s father Woden, son of Frabewald, who was Frelof, son of Frebewulf, son of Fingolduf, son of Beta, son of Geatwa, son of Beu, son of Sedwa, son of Heremod, son of Itermod, son of Hatur, son of Wala, son of Peadwig, son of Sem; Shem’s father was Noah; Noah’s father Lamech; Lamech’s father Methuselah; Methuselah’s father Enoch; Enoch’s father Jared, son of Mahalaleel, son of Cainan, son of Enos, son of Seth, son of Adam, father [Col. 0716A] of all.

Seth was born in place of Abel, whom Cain killed. And just as Christ’s Passion is prefigured in Abel, so Christ’s Resurrection is prefigured in Seth. For Seth is a Hebrew name, and in Latin means “resurrection.”

CXIII. From this Seth, therefore, the genealogy is led down to Enoch, who, having been taken up alive by God, awaits the coming of Antichrist together with Saint Elijah. From there it comes to Noah, who alone, with his sons and wives, deserved to be saved when the world was perishing; his firstborn, Shem, deserved to be blessed by his father. They say that Viderhem was a priest of the Most High God and was afterward called Melchizedek, who, as a figure of our priesthood, offered bread and wine. Hence Christ is told in the Psalms: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4).

From this [Col. 0716B] Shem, therefore, the genealogy is led down to Woden, who held such authority among his people that they dedicated to his name the fourth weekday, which the pagan Romans called the day of Mercury. This custom is still observed by the English today, for they call the same day *Wodnesdei* [now “Wednesday”], that is, Woden’s day.

> [Note: Col. 0715D: *Woedensdagh*.]

From Woden, moreover, the line of descent extends down to Getham, who was also held to possess such wisdom and strength that the pagans worshipped him as a god. From there one proceeds to the most Christian kings of England, Ingild and Ine. Of these, Ine, though he was one of the most powerful kings of England, abandoned his kingdom and departed as a pilgrim to Rome; and, happily living there as a pilgrim, he finally ascended still more happily to the heavenly dwelling.

From Ingles, however, the line of descent extends to [Col. 0716C] Hecbrith, who was of such excellence that he brought under his own rule all [398] England south of the Humber, which had until then been subject to several divided kingdoms, and thus was called the first monarch of all England. His son was Ebeluph, certainly the most illustrious head of his future line and a most precious root from which most holy fruits would arise.

While in his earthly kingdom, he always meditated upon heavenly things, so that it might be clearly understood that, not conquered by greed but prompted by charity, he ruled in order to provide for another’s need, not to satisfy his own will through domination. For he was a father of orphans and judge of widows, defender of churches and promoter of monasteries. He devoted himself so diligently to almsgiving that he tithed his whole land for Christ and [Col. 0716D] distributed the tenth part through churches and monasteries.

At last he departed for Rome with a great retinue and spent a full year there, visiting holy places, devoting himself to prayers and vigils, and distributing many alms to the poor. He also bestowed many gifts, with royal generosity, upon the churches of the most blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and upon the supreme pontiff himself. Thus, furnished with the rewards of many virtues, he returned to England. After two years he wisely divided the kingdom among his sons; throughout each of his territories he assigned provision and clothing for the poor; he mercifully scattered his treasures and gave them to the poor, from which he allotted no small portion to the churches of the Apostles at Rome and to the bishop of the supreme see [Col. 0717A]. And so, in a good old age, he was gathered to his fathers—not losing his kingdom, certainly, but exchanging it: abandoning the temporal and gaining the eternal.

CXIV. His son was that glory of the English, jewel of kings, and model of virtues, Alfred—lesser in age than his other brothers, but older in virtue. Therefore he was loved by his father more than all his brothers, because of the similarity of their characters and the privilege of a certain special grace, which shone wonderfully in him even while he was still a boy. Therefore, while he was yet a little child, his father sent him to Rome with many knights and very great gifts, that he might be commended to the prayers of the holy Apostles and blessed by the supreme pontiff.

The venerable high priest Leo, who then presided over the Roman Church [Col. 0717B], looked upon the boy’s face and bearing; and, perceiving in him indications of radiant virtues which showed the presence of divine majesty, he anticipated the time and age of his reign by the sacrament of royal anointing. As holy Samuel once did with the boy David, so that most holy prelate most devoutly consecrated him king.

But afterward, returning to Rome with his father, he deserved to be his father’s fellow-worker and helper in all good things. From almost his infancy he loved reading and learning, was assiduous about churches, most frequent in prayer, obedient to his parents, humble and devoted to his companions. In his boyhood he meditated upon such things as a devout old man would fulfill. Indeed, he always carried in his bosom a small book containing a portion of the Psalter [Col. 0717C] in which he especially delighted, so that what his inward heart chewed over might not depart from the breast of his outward person.

When, after the death of his brothers, with whom he had reigned for some time, the whole kingdom had passed to him by hereditary right, he became higher than all and the servant of all, so that he could say with the Prophet: “But I have been exalted, humbled, and troubled” (Ps. 87:16). He showed himself so lovable to the good, terrible to the wicked, deferential to the ministers of the churches, pleasant to friends and companions, gentle and generous to the poor, that he seemed suitably adapted to the character of every sort of person, useful and necessary to all. And—what is now rarely found upon earth—he judged it the highest dignity of a king to possess no power in the churches of Christ [Col. 0717D].

“The true dignity of a ruler,” he said, “is that he know himself in the kingdom of Christ, which is the Church, not as king but as a citizen; that he not rule over priests by laws, but humbly submit himself to the laws of Christ promulgated by the priests.”

Moreover, he took the greatest care lest the poor should be oppressed by sheriffs and officials or burdened with unlawful exactions. Hence his name became famous throughout the world, even in the great city of Rome, because he often sent many gifts and most lavish alms to the churches of the Apostles and to the supreme pontiff himself. The supreme pontiff, gratefully embracing such devotion and yielding to his pious prayers, exempted the school of the Saxons from every tax and toll; he also sent the king many gifts, and in addition a portion of the Lord’s wood—that is, the Cross. When the patriarch of Jerusalem heard his fame, he too presented the king with precious gifts.

Indeed [Col. 0718A], he arranged [399] the annual tribute paid to him according to a most just division: one third was assigned to the pay of warriors; one third was rendered for the prince’s expenses; and one third was reserved for royal gifts, which he customarily distributed with the greatest generosity to visitors, whether rich or poor. Thus King Alfred, after reigning twenty-nine years and six months, passed from the earthly kingdom to the heavenly kingdom, leaving his son Edward heir to his kingdom and to his virtues.

CXV. Edward was inferior to his father in literary learning [Col. 0718B], but not greatly inferior in holiness; he was superior in power. For he extended the borders of his kingdom far more widely than his father had done, founded new cities, and restored ruined ones. The utterly impious Danish people, whom his father had not expelled, he either drove wholly away after crushing them in many battles when they rebelled against him, or reduced them under wretched servitude; and he restored the whole appearance of the island to its former beauty.

Thereafter he ruled with such moderation and judged his subjects with such justice between neighbor and neighbor that he appeared not merely unwilling, but unable, to do anything contrary to truth. Thus he is said, when angry with certain persons, to have declared: “I tell you, if I could, I would have repaid you in kind.” What could a king not do to subjects, a master to servants, a powerful man to the weak, a leader to soldiers? Yet [Col. 0718C] whatever equity did not dictate, whatever justice did not permit, whatever opposed truth, whatever did not befit royal gentleness, he considered impossible for himself.

He founded a new monastery, and his mother, the most holy woman Ælfflæd, built a monastery of virgins in the same city. King Edward lived twenty-four years in the kingdom and begot sons and daughters by the most noble woman Edwina: his firstborn son Ebelstan by Queen Edguina; Edwin, Edmund, Edred; and four daughters. Of these, the first, Edburga, was chosen and consecrated as God’s bride; the second was taken in marriage by Otto, emperor of the Romans; the third was intended to be married to Charles, king of the Franks; and the king of the Northumbrians obtained the fourth in marriage.

King Edward slept with his fathers, and his son Æthelstan reigned in his place. “He walked in the ways of his fathers; he did not turn aside to the right hand or to the left” (2 Chron. 34:2), retaining the same faith, favor toward his subjects, devotion toward the churches, mercy toward the poor, and reverence toward God’s priests. When he had lived sixteen years, he died, and his brother Edmund reigned in his place. He was in all things an imitator of his father Edward: “a blameless and upright man, fearing God” (Job 2:3), remaining in his innocence until the end of his life.

When raised to the kingdom, he was zealous for Christ’s faith, and grievously resenting that the remnants of pagan idol-worship should defile the beauty of his realm, he wrested from their hands five most noble cities—Lincoln, Leicester, Stafford, Nottingham, [Col. 0719A] Derby—which they had hitherto occupied. Having wiped away every unbelief, he illuminated them with the light of the Christian faith. When his kingdom had been cleansed of foreigners and made subject to him in every part, he gave greatest attention to monasteries and churches; with the counsel of most holy Dunstan he established what needed establishing and corrected what needed correction. Thus he entrusted Glastonbury to blessed Dunstan to be founded as a dwelling for monks, and, with Saint Dunstan’s assistance, made many other good arrangements.

Therefore, while England flourished in great peace under so fatherly and great a king, it suddenly withered in sorrow and fear at his untimely death, which he met through wicked treachery after completing five years and five months of his reign [Col. 0719B].

CXVI. His brother Eadred succeeded him in the kingdom, walked in his brother’s ways, obeyed blessed Dunstan’s counsels in all things, and ruled his subjects by most just laws. He was also of such excellence that he easily defeated the Northumbrians and Scots when they rebelled against him, and restored them to their former subjection without great labor. Precious death brought his praiseworthy life to its end. For when blessed Dunstan was summoned to the sick king, he heard on the journey itself the voices of angels saying: “King Eadred has now fallen asleep in the Lord.”

After him Edward, son of King Edmund, took up the kingdom of the English [Col. 0719C]; after Edward’s death his brother Edgar succeeded him. For he was the son of the most noble King Edmund, who was son of Edward the Elder, the most Christian prince, who was son of Alfred, the most victorious leader.

This Edgar, happier than all [400] his predecessors, inferior to none in holiness, surpassing all in sweetness of character, shone in his days like the morning star and like the full moon. He was no less memorable to the English than Cyrus to the Persians, Charles to the Franks, or Romulus to the Romans. For he established the English kingdom in a kind of heavenly peace and joined peoples of many languages under the law of one covenant. Hence he shared the name of Solomon, so that by the common voice of all he was called “peaceful,” which is the meaning of Solomon. Nor is this surprising: for at the very time of his birth blessed Dunstan heard angels singing: “Peace to the Church of the English in the time of this child who has been born.”

Therefore, just as dawn dispels with its rays of brightness the darkness of the departed night, so, through the accession of this most holy king, the night of unbelief was banished throughout all England and the darkness of wrath and discord driven away. For he displayed such signs of inward sweetness in his speech, face, and conduct that, with God’s help, the whole island submitted to him without bloodshed, and Scotland, Northumbria, and Wales gladly hastened to submit themselves to him [Col. 0719D]. During his reign the sun seemed brighter, the sea calmer, the earth more fruitful, and the appearance of the whole kingdom more beautiful in richer splendor.

In those days, neither judicial punishments, nor exile, nor proscription was feared; only even a slight offence against so good a prince was feared [Col. 0720A]. Therefore, as everyone throughout England was united in one spirit of love for him, the king devoted care and labor to building and ordering churches and to founding and enriching monasteries. In fact, throughout the kingdom of the English he caused forty monasteries to be built, assigning some to monks and others to virgins. He completed Glastonbury, which his father had founded. With great zeal he established and with much diligence adorned the monasteries of Abingdon, Burc, Thorney, Ramsey, and the monastery of virgins at Winchester. At Winchester he caused the church of the New Minster, which his father had begun and which he himself completed, to be dedicated with the greatest honor.

In winter and spring he was accustomed to travel through his kingdom, as far as each province [Col. 0720B], carefully examining the judgments, conduct, and actions of officials and princes, and closely investigating how the rights of the laws and the ordinances of his decrees were being observed, taking vigilant precautions that the poor, suffering injury at the hands of the powerful, should not be oppressed. He had prepared three thousand six hundred very strong ships, in which, when summer returned, he was accustomed to sail round the whole island with a very great force, both to terrify foreigners and to train his own men. Amid all this he constantly conferred with bishops and very learned men concerning God’s law and the sacred writings; and what he himself was able to learn, he strove to teach his subjects not only by word but also by example.

[Col. 0720C] CXVII. But alas! In human affairs nothing is stable; among things that perish, nothing is unmoving; in temporal things, nothing eternal; among mortal things, nothing immortal. When King Edgar was transferred to heavenly things, his son Edward succeeded to the earthly kingdom. Unjustly slain by wicked men, he obtained, by God’s gift, both the name and merit of a saint, on account both of the holiness of his life and of the cruelty of his death.

His brother Æthelred, namely Edgar’s son, succeeded him in government and kingdom, and was anointed and consecrated by Saint Dunstan the archbishop and the other bishops of the English. Saint Dunstan is said to have delivered to him this oracle:

> “Because the English have conspired in the blood of your brother, the most holy king, blood and the sword shall not fail from among them until a people of an unknown tongue comes upon them and reduces them to destruction and to utter slavery. Yet at last the Lord shall visit them.”

Accordingly, during the reign of the aforesaid king, the invading Danes devastated a great part of the land with fire and sword. Then the king sent messengers into Normandy, asked for and received in marriage Emma, daughter of Duke Richard. He had already had by the daughter of the most noble Count Horethein a son, Edmund; by Emma he afterward had two sons, Alfred and Edward, of whom we speak later. Then the king, stronger than usual, sent letters throughout England commanding that all Danes be killed on one day and at the same hour.

When the Danes overseas heard this, they were enraged. Under the leadership of Sweyn, they entered England with an innumerable army and spread [Col. 0721A] through the provinces, scattered abroad, sparing neither rank, sex, nor age, and not keeping their sacrilegious hands from the holy places and sanctuaries of churches or monasteries. Although the most vigorous King Æthelred had often [401] resisted them, he was finally overcome by the treachery of his own men. He sent the queen with her young sons into Normandy, and later, stripped of his kingdom, followed them himself.

But Sweyn the Dane, either struck down by sudden death or smitten with an invisible punishment by Saint Edmund, received the wages of his cruelty in hell. Æthelred, recalled by the English, was restored to the insignia of kingship and again rose in strength against the Danes. Against him Cnut, son of Sweyn and king of the Danes, did not cease to exercise his paternal hatred.

Æthelred, having reigned thirty-seven years with great toil but great courage, died in London [Col. 0721B], leaving his son Edmund heir to his struggle and kingdom. Whatever I might say would be too little for the glory of his marvelous strength; for because of the invincible vigor of his body, he received the name *Iserensyde* [“Ironside”], that is, “of the iron side.” “His arrow never turned backward, and his sword did not return empty” (2 Sam. 1:22). Against enemies he had the fierceness of a lion; toward his own people the simplicity of a dove. No one was stronger than he, no one more secure in adversity, no one more restrained in prosperity.

CXVIII. Moreover, the Danes, and the English who had deserted the king, chose Cnut as their king; but the most valiant King Edmund, with his army, like a roaring lion ranging over the land, recovered without resistance many regions [Col. 0721C] which Cnut had occupied and brought under submission. The most valiant King Edmund died and was buried at Glastonbury with his grandfather Edgar. Then, wishing utterly to deprive both Edmund’s brothers, who were exiles in Normandy, and his young sons, Edmund and Edward, of hope of the kingdom—[Note: [Col. 0721] Supply: Cnut; and read: “wishing utterly to deprive them of hope of the kingdom, but fearing to strike them because of shame,” etc.? ED. PATR.]—but fearing, through shame, to kill them, he sent them to the king of the Swedes to be put to death. But the king of the Swedes, pitying the distress of the noble boys, ordered them to be sent to the king of the Hungarians. He received them kindly, cherished them more kindly still, and most kindly adopted them as sons. He gave his own daughter in marriage to Edmund; and joined Edward in marriage to the daughter of his kinsman Emperor Henry. But shortly afterward [Col. 0721D] Edmund passed from temporal things to eternal ones. Edward enjoyed safety and prosperity.

Meanwhile, after the death of Cnut and of his sons who reigned after him, Edward, Edmund’s brother and son of Ethelred—who, as we have said, had been exiled in Normandy—was summoned to the kingdom of the English; for his brother Alfred had perished in England by a cruel death through the treachery, as was believed, of Godwine. Edward therefore came to England and was received by all the clergy and people with great rejoicing; at Winchester, on the holy day of Easter, he was anointed and consecrated king by the archbishops of Canterbury and York and almost all the bishops of the realm. He walked in the ways of his father [Col. 0722A] Edgar: a gentle and devout man, defending the kingdom more by peace than by arms. His spirit conquered anger, despised avarice, and knew nothing of pride.

When he had secured peace both from his own people and from foreigners, and had become welcome and beloved among neighbouring kings and princes, he sent messengers to the Roman emperor, asking him to deign to send his kinsman—the son, namely, of his brother Edmund Ironside—as the future heir of the kingdom rightly due to him. The emperor graciously received the king’s messengers and kept them for a considerable time with the highest honour. At length, ships having been prepared and supplied with everything thought necessary for voyagers, he sent Edward to England, with great glory and riches as the king had requested, together with his wife Agatha, daughter of his kinsman, and his children Edgar Ætheling, Margaret, and Christina [Col. 0722B]. Arriving in England after a favourable voyage, he gladdened both king and people by his coming. But after a few days he departed this life, turning joy into mourning and laughter into tears.

Not long after this, the king himself, having caused the noble monastery which he had founded in the western part of London in honour of blessed Peter to be dedicated with the greatest magnificence, ended a praiseworthy life by a happy death on the eve of Epiphany, after completing twenty-three years, six months, and twenty-seven days in the kingdom; and he filled the whole island with tears and grief. After he had been buried in the aforementioned monastery, as befitted so great a man, some attempted to make Edgar Ætheling king, to whom the kingdom was due by hereditary right [Col. 0722C]. But because the boy seemed unequal to so great a burden, Earl Harold, sprung from a race of traitors—whose mind was more crafty, whose purse more fruitful, and whose soldiery more numerous—seized the kingdom under an evil omen.

CXIX. When William, duke of the Normans, heard that no one of royal stock, but Harold, the cousin of his kinsman King Edward, had usurped the sovereignty which was more justly due to himself by right of blood, by an ancient agreement between himself and King Edward, and also by Harold’s sworn promise, he gathered an innumerable army from beyond the sea, came into England, and by God’s judgement deprived Harold alike of kingdom and life. [Col. 0722D]

But Edgar Ætheling, king of the English, seeing all things thrown into confusion, embarked with his mother and sisters and attempted to return to the country in which he had been born. Yet a storm arising at sea compelled him to land in Scotland. On this occasion, however, Margaret was given in marriage to King Malcolm. A book published concerning her sufficiently recounts her praiseworthy life and most precious death. Her sister Christina also was blessed as Christ’s bride. Queen Margaret bore six sons and two daughters; Edgar, Alexander, and David, the glory of their line, became kings.

Edgar was a sweet and lovable man, in every respect like his kinsman King Edward [Col. 0723A], exercising nothing tyrannical, harsh, or greedy toward his people, but ruling his subjects with the greatest charity and goodwill. Alexander, moreover, was sufficiently humble and gracious toward clerics and monks, but exceedingly formidable to his other subjects: a man of great spirit, extending himself in all things beyond his strength. He was learned and most zealous in founding churches, seeking out relics of saints, and making and arranging priestly vestments and sacred books. He was also generous beyond his means to all newcomers, and so devoted to the poor that he seemed to delight in nothing more than receiving, washing, feeding, and clothing them.

King David, however, did not live for himself but for all: caring for everyone, providing for everyone’s welfare [Col. 0723B], a guide of morals, reprover of crimes, encourager of virtues. His life was a pattern of humility, a mirror of justice, and an example of chastity: a just king, a gentle king, a chaste king, a humble king. Who could easily say what benefit he bestowed upon human life, how greatly gentleness made him lovable, justice formidable, chastity composed, and humility accessible to all?

Their sister Matilda married the most glorious King Henry of the English. Whoever wishes to write of her wonderful glory, strength of spirit, and the constancy and devotion with which she attended divine offices and sacred vigils—and how humble she was amid such great power—will show us another Esther in our own times. The sister of this most blessed woman, named Mary, was given in marriage to Eustace, count of Boulogne [Col. 0723C]. From this most excellent and most Christian queen was born Matilda, who first married the Roman emperor and afterward Geoffrey, the most noble count of Anjou. From Mary, however, sprang Matilda, who was given in marriage first to the count of Maurienne and afterward to Stephen, king of the English.

King David, moreover, at the arrangement of King Henry, took as wife Matilda, daughter of Count Waltheof and Judith, who was niece of King William I. By her he had a son, Henry: a gentle and devout man, fair in appearance and of a heart like milk, in every respect worthy to be born of such parents.

CXX. Let the viewers of this picture understand that, just as we have placed in it the kings of the English and [Col. 0723D] Scots because we are in the land of the English and the kingdom of the Scots, so they too, if they should wish to make another according to the pattern of this one, may place in it the most Christian kings of their own regions after the kings of the Franks. Only let this be carefully observed: that the great square extending from one side of the image of Constantine the Great to its other side be filled with images of Christian kings, with the name of each king inscribed above his individual image.

This too must be noted: after the kings now reigning, space must be left blank, so that it may clearly be understood that the names of those who succeed them are to be written beneath the images placed above in those same spaces. For they are the ones who will first leave the kingdoms which those now reigning hold last. Therefore [Col. 0724A], what we have said above concerning the images and names of those four apostolic men is to be observed in every respect here also in relation to emperors: namely, that from one side of Constantine to his other side, round about, images of emperors and kings are to be placed with their names beneath them and without any intervening space; but the images placed after those now reigning are not to have names written beneath them.

Therefore we write the names of these rulers—namely Roman emperors, kings of the Franks, English, and Scots—together with their individual images depicted above, in this square extending round about on every side, as follows.

CXXI.
