Constantine the Great, Constantius, Constantine, Constans, Jovian, Valentinian, [Col. 0724B] Valens, Gratian, Valentinian, Theodosius, Arcadius, Honorius, Theodosius, Marcian, Valentinian, Leo, Leo, Zeno, Anastasius, Justin, Justinian, Justin, Tiberius, Maurice, Phocas, Heraclius, Heraclius, Heradonas, Constantine, Constantine, Justinian, Leontius, Abismarus, Justinian, Philippicus, Anastasius, Theodosius, Leo, Constantine, Charlemagne, Louis, Lothair, Louis, Charles, Arnulf, Louis, Conrad, Henry, Otto, Otto, Otto, Henry, Conrad, Henry, Henry, Henry, Lothair, Conrad, Frederick, Clovis, Theodoric, Clodomir, Childebert, Clothar, Charibert, Guntram, Childeric, Sigebert, [Col. 0724C] Clothar, Dagobert, Clovis, Clothar, Theodoric, Lothair, Childebert, Dagobert, Childeric, Theodoric, Pepin, Charles, Louis, Charles, Louis, Charles, Ralph, Louis, Lothair, Louis, Hugh, Robert, Henry, Philip, Louis, Louis, Philip, Alfred, Edward, Athelstan, Edmund, Eadred, Edwin, Edgar, Edward, Ethelred, Edmund, Cnut, Edward, Harold, William, William, Henry, Stephen, Henry, Henry, Malcolm, Edgar, Alexander, David, Malcolm, William.

Accordingly, as we said above, we bring forward the kings of the English from Alfred down to Henry III, who was the son of Henry II, whose mother was Matilda, whose father was Henry I, whose father was William the Bastard (Nothus), whose father was Robert, count of Normandy, whose brother was Richard, whose father was Richard, whose father was William Longsword, whose father was Robert, also called Rollo, who himself subdued Normandy to his power. [Col. 0724D]

CXXII. Therefore we give each image of the individual emperors and kings whose representations are painted in this picture a golden ring upon its finger, also a golden bracelet upon the right arm, a golden sceptre in one hand, and an unsheathed sword in the other; likewise a golden diadem upon the head, and we clothe each image in purple. These are certain ornaments of dignity granted to kings, by which both the excellence of their rank is displayed and the sacrament of mystery is figured. For they present not only visible beauty to those who look from without, but also contain a hidden spiritual significance, since each of these emblems indicates the spiritual adornments which kings ought to exercise in holy conduct. [Col. 0725A]

For the ring expresses faith, the bracelet good works, purple reverence, the sword vengeance, the sceptre justice, and the diadem glory. They fittingly receive these two ornaments, ring and bracelet, to indicate that they ought to shine both with the rectitude of faith in knowledge of truth and with religious conduct in the practice of virtue. Fittingly, too, the bracelet is not without the ring, nor the ring without the bracelet: for without faith it is impossible to please God, and faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself. Those who believe rightly and live holily will be objects of reverence and veneration to those who behold them; for right faith and holy action make a man venerable. Thus purple ought to adorn our kings just as the ring and bracelet adorn them. [Col. 0725B]

They bear the sword for the punishment of evildoers and the sceptre for the governance of justice, so that they may punish the guilty without exceeding measure in inflicting punishment; and may so observe measure in punishing that they also remove from the wicked the boldness to rage against the saints. Therefore, neither the sword without the sceptre nor the sceptre without the sword: so that vengeance may sharpen justice, lest excessive leniency weaken it; and justice may moderate vengeance, lest excessive severity stretch it too far.

Truly beautiful and exceedingly precious ornaments these are: the rectitude of faith giving brightness, holiness of life adorning, the maturity of reverence honouring, the rigor of vengeance reproving, and vengeance moderating justice. [Col. 0725C] Beautiful and precious, I say; yet it is necessary that our kings seek the Lord as witness in these matters, and await him as their rewarder for them. Let them thus act, and let their own conscience bear them testimony that within them there is a complete testimony prudent in every severity. Therefore, adorned with these emblems, let our kings bear the diadem on their heads; for then they are truly adorned, when they glory in the Lord. For this is the saying of St Paul: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I.12). Thus the splendour of the diadem upon the head is the true testimony of a good conscience [Col. 0725D] in the mind. This brief account of the ornaments of kings is sufficient.

CXXIII. Therefore, once the images of rulers have been painted in the order of their succession, and each name has been placed beside its individual image, I write in one continuous circuit, upon the saffron-coloured line which contains the twelve tribes, from Emperor Constantine to that same Constantine, this verse:

> “The total of all those numbered, from twenty years old and upward, was six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty” (Num. II.32).

This number, as we said concerning the number of the Levites, applies to the lay faithful of the New Testament, who spiritually are indeed six hundred and three thousand: because they have both the correct faith of the Holy Trinity and good present action, which is expressed by the works of the six days; and they will receive from the Lord full reward for both in the future. They are five hundred and fifty because, while striving to possess perfect purity in sensory experience, they attain rest of mind. Therefore at the end of this verse I place five steps: the first at “six hundred,” the second at “three hundred,” the third at “thousand,” the fourth at “five hundred,” and the fifth at “fifty.” Between “six hundred,” where the first step is, I write “action”; between “three hundred,” “faith”; between “thousand,” “reward”; between “five hundred,” “purity”; and between “fifty,” “rest.” [Col. 0726A]

Thus it may be understood that the lay faithful will receive full future reward both for the good works and right faith which they now exercise; and that, because of the purity of the five senses at which they aim, they sometimes attain even in the present life to rest of mind.

After this, from one side of the image of Constantine the Great to the other side of that same image, round about in one continuous circuit, upon a certain square line extending from the aforesaid image back to that same image, I write this verse:

> “These are the supreme lords of affairs, watchful defenders of the tabernacle, which is the Church, marked by the ring of faith; adorned with the bracelet of good works; honoured by the purple of reverence; a terror to the wicked by the sword of vengeance, a love to the good by the sceptre of justice, and pleasing to God by the diadem of a good conscience.” [Col. 0726B]

CXXIV. This verse is marked at its beginning by five steps, because, as Master Hugh says, that justice which is entrusted to earthly authority over its subjects is defined in five ways: according to person, cause, manner, place, and time. For what is permitted in one manner is not thereby permitted in every manner; and justice itself, unless it is administered justly, loses the name of justice. Therefore, it must be diligently examined in what manner a thing is permitted, and the modes by which the form of justice is defined must be considered.

According to person, one thing is permitted and another forbidden: for example, a secular judge may lay hands upon a lay person if he sins, but may not do so to a cleric. Justice is defined according to cause, so that secular matters are examined by temporal authority, while spiritual and ecclesiastical matters are examined by spiritual authority. [Col. 0726C] Justice is defined according to manner or measure when each offence is punished by a suitable and proportionate penalty, so that neither private affection detracts anything from the vengeance of equity nor private hatred adds anything to the severity that is due. Justice is defined according to place and time when judgement is exercised where and when it is proper, and the sentence of truth is carried out.

Therefore justice is violated in respect of person if a secular judge lays hands upon an ecclesiastical person; in respect of cause, if he undertakes to examine ecclesiastical matters; in respect of measure, if he punishes a lie or a curse by hanging; in respect of place, if he presumes to violate sacred places and attempts disorderly violence even against those who have fled to them—even offenders who deserve condemnation for their crimes; [Col. 0727A] and in respect of time, if he does not show reverence on sacred and solemn days, when even those offences to which punishments are due must be spared.

In these ways, then, secular authority ought not to exercise justice, but should follow the institutions of the laws and approve nothing in judgement except justice and truth. Secular authority has as its head a king or emperor; from him depend subordinate authorities—dukes, counts, prefects, and other magistrates—who nevertheless all receive their authority from the first power, insofar as they are set over subjects.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the different condition of clerics and laypeople

[Col. 0727B]

CXXV. Next, I cover the space of that square in which clerics are depicted with sapphire colour, and that in which laypeople are depicted with green. For clerics devote themselves to the heavenly manner of life, which sapphire signifies by resembling the sky when it is clear; while laypeople devote themselves to the earthly manner of life, which green expresses by resembling the earth. Clerics ought to live so that they can say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III.20). But to laypeople the Lord says in the Gospel, “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI.9). To the former it is said through the Apostle, “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please him to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II.4). But concerning the latter the same Apostle says: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep, as though they did not weep; those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice; those who buy, as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not use it” (I Cor. VII.29–31). [Col. 0727C]

These are anxious and troubled about many things; those choose the best part, which shall not be taken from them (Luke X.41–42). These two colours, green and sapphire, signify these two lives: one of clerics and the other of laypeople; one earthly and the other heavenly; one carnal and the other spiritual; one by which the body lives from God [the Latin construction is defective]. Sapphire, resembling the sky, signifies the heavenly and contemplative life of clerics; green, resembling the earth, the earthly and active life of laypeople.

The lay faithful deal with earthly things and the necessities of earthly life, and they are permitted to possess earthly goods. Therefore I represent them by a colour resembling the earth. Those tribes which formerly received an inheritance in the land prefigured them. Clerics, however, are called from the Greek *klēros* (κλῆρος), which in Latin means “lot”: either because they themselves were chosen by God by lot for God’s service, or because God himself is their lot and they ought to have no lot on earth except God. They are appointed to be supported by tithes and offerings made to God, and they administer spiritual things alone. [Col. 0727D] Therefore I mark them with the sapphire colour which resembles heaven. They are signified by the tribe of Levi, which once received no share in the inheritance along with that ancient people of God, but, serving the tabernacle, was fed by tithes, offerings, and sacrificial victims. [Col. 0728A]

CXXVI. Nor must this be passed over carelessly: in this green space I overlay with red—the colour which resembles fire—those spaces in which, in two places and through three of their sections, works of mercy are performed. For what is the affection of charity other than a kind of fiery ardour? Thus laypeople are depicted in green; but the spaces in which works of mercy are painted are red, because the lay faithful devote themselves to earthly action, yet both compassionately sympathize with all who are oppressed and needy through charity, and assist them through generosity.

Hence it is written of that blessed penitent woman that she both washed the Lord’s feet and wiped them with her hair (Luke VII.38). And, as blessed Gregory says, we wash the Lord’s feet if we incline through compassionate feeling toward any of his least members; if we suffer with his saints in their tribulation; if we regard their sorrow as our own. Hair is superfluous to the body. What, then, does abundant earthly substance resemble but hair? Since it exceeds the needs of use, it is not felt even when cut off. Therefore we wipe the Lord’s feet with hair when, out of the things which are superfluous to us, we also show mercy to his saints with whom we sympathize through charity; so that the mind may grieve through compassion and the generous hand may show the feeling of grief. [Col. 0728B]

What, then, is understood in the Gospel by Mary’s both washing the Lord’s feet and wiping them with her hair is here understood by the presence of red spaces within the green colour, and by the depiction of six works of mercy in those same red spaces. Thus, in the green colour in which laypeople are contained, there are red spaces and works of mercy are painted in those same red spaces, because the lay faithful both compassionately sympathize, through the affection of charity, with all needy persons, and assist them through the effect of generosity, for the love of him who, though rich, became poor for our sake (II Cor. VIII.9).

At the four corners of that outer saffron-coloured square, which encloses all the parts arranged within it, I place an image of Christ holding six scrolls. On the one scroll held toward the east is written: “I was hungry, and you gave me [Col. 0728D] food” (Matt. XXV.35). On another: “I was in prison, and you came to me” (ibid., 36). On the scroll situated in the southern part toward the west is written: “I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (ibid., 35). On another: “I was a stranger, and you took me in” (ibid.). On the scroll held toward the north is written in his hand: “I was naked, and you clothed me” (ibid., 36). On another: “I was sick, and you came to me” (ibid.). Each scroll is offered to those images which perform the work of mercy written upon it, so that we may know that whatever we do in Christ’s name, for love of him, for one of his least ones, we do also to Christ himself (Matt. XXV.40).

CXXVII. The two spaces in one of which lawful marriages are celebrated and in the other of which the undefiled marriage-bed is depicted are covered with purple, the colour signifying the straitness of affliction. For the faithful who are married, in rendering to one another the debt of the flesh lawfully, are entirely free from blameworthy crime and mortal sin; yet, because of the various events of this present life, they are not wholly free from temporal affliction, whether from anxiety in the mind or labour in the body. [Col. 0729A]

Those bound by the law of marriage are certainly often tormented by manifold tribulations: at one time their minds are stretched by the concerns of household affairs, at another their flesh is wearied by labours. Although they acquire present possessions lawfully and possess them lawfully, nevertheless, the greater the affection with which they love what they possess while they have it, the greater the pain by which they are afflicted when they lose it. For the loss of a thing cannot occur without grave pain when its possession was accompanied by great love.

Thus persons celebrating lawful marriages and using the undefiled marriage-bed are depicted beside the tabernacle; but the spaces in which they are depicted are covered with purple, which everywhere in this picture signifies the straitness of tribulation. For married believers belong indeed to the holy Church because of the good works to which they devote themselves; but although their state is free from blameworthy crime, it is not free from temporal affliction, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If you have taken a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin has married, she has not sinned. Nevertheless, such persons will have tribulation of the flesh” (I Cor. VII.28). [Col. 0729B]

I overlay with sapphire—the colour which, as we taught above, resembles the sky—the field in which a priest is depicted consecrating marriage by prayers and blessings. For when the priests of holy Church consecrate and administer in prayer the sacraments of our faith, they ought to shine with purity of mind and to be radiant before God with heavenly desire. Let these remarks concerning the spaces of our outer square suffice for the present. [Col. 0729C]

## CHAPTER XV. On the Levites sounding trumpets at the door of the tabernacle, and on the column of fire and cloud which went before the tabernacle

CXXVIII. After all this, I return again to the tabernacle and place two Levites sounding two silver trumpets, one on one side of the door and the other on the other side. For holy preachers, possessing the two commandments of charity, by holy preaching admonish believers both to avoid evils and to perform good deeds. Therefore beside one trumpet is written: “Cease to act perversely” (Isa. I.12); beside the other: “Learn to do good” (ibid.). For the teachers of holy Church urge both that evils be abandoned and goods embraced.

These two Levites may also signify the two orders of preachers, one sent to the circumcision and the other to the uncircumcision. It was said above that the southern wall signifies the Jewish people, and the northern wall the Gentiles. The bar mentioned above extends to each wall, because God and man, Jesus Christ, united both peoples to himself through knowledge of the one true faith. [Col. 0729D] Therefore the Levite who stands opposite the southern wall signifies the order of preachers who proclaimed the words of faith to the Jewish people. The other Levite, placed opposite the northern wall, signifies the order of teachers who called the Gentile people to faith by holy preaching.

On each side of the tabernacle an image of Christ is also painted, holding a column of fire in one hand and a column of cloud in the other. For the column that continually hung over the tabernacle signified our Lord Jesus Christ, who is at once Redeemer of the human race and Judge. That column, which formerly remained continually over the tabernacle, had the appearance of cloud by day and the appearance of fire by night; and therefore it prefigured Christ in two ways. Accordingly, I have painted an image of Christ on each side of the tabernacle, and a double column of fire and cloud on either side—not because there are two Christs, but because the one and same Christ must be understood in two different ways through this column of cloud and fire. This could not at all be seen on the flat plane of the picture unless the figure both of Christ’s image and of the columns of fire and cloud had been represented twice upon the same plane. [Col. 0730A]

Since this column indicates Christ himself, it indicates him in one way because it had in itself both the appearance of fire and that of cloud, and in another because it displayed the appearance of cloud by day and that of fire by night. Fire, therefore, indicates his divinity, in which he is terrible; for, as we read, “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. XII.29). The cloud indicates his humanity, in which he appeared gentle; for Isaiah says, “The Lord rides upon a light cloud and enters Egypt” (Isa. XIX.1). He rides upon a light cloud and enters Egypt because he assumed flesh clean from every sin and came into the world. Thus the column is one—namely, having in itself the appearance of fire and cloud—because Christ is one person, though there are two natures in him, divine and human. This is the manner in which the column signifies Christ by having in itself the appearance both of fire and cloud. [Col. 0730B]

Again: the column of fire expresses the terror which our Lord Jesus Christ will show to the reprobate at the last judgement; the cloud, his gentleness which he will show to the elect at that judgement. For, as has been said, the column had the appearance of fire by night and cloud by day. By night is signified the life of the sinner; by day, the life of the righteous. Thus the one column shows fire by night and cloud by day, because the one and same Christ, merciful Saviour of the elect and just condemner of the reprobate, at the final judgement both rewards the brightness of the righteous and condemns the darkness of the unjust. This is the other manner in which the same column signifies Christ by displaying cloud by day and fire by night.

This is why I have painted a double column of fire and cloud on the flat plane of the picture, although formerly there was only one column above Moses’ tabernacle: for there is only one Christ, whom it prefigured. [Col. 0730C]

That column which is to the south signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who, in the divinity indicated by the column of fire, was terrible to the ancient people depicted there on the right, because they believed in God, punishing their sins. In the terror of his divinity he was accustomed to say to them: “If anyone does this or that, he shall surely die” (Exod. XXI.17). Therefore Moses is placed beside them, with hands heavy and weighty, holding a scourge in one hand and an unsheathed sword in the other, because the Law was prepared to strike and kill sinners.

On the left of the image, however, is depicted the Gentile people, who worshipped idols. To them Christ speaks in the cloud of humanity painted there beside them: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke V.32). Therefore Aaron and Hur there support the hands of Moses, because the loftiness of the Lord’s Incarnation, signified by Aaron, and the ardour of the Holy Spirit, signified by Hur, make the commandments light for us. Let these brief remarks concerning the southern image suffice. [Col. 0731A]

CXXIX. The image opposite it, situated to the north, likewise signifies our Lord Jesus Christ and shows him as he will appear at the last judgement. The other image, to the south, of which we have already spoken fully, signifies him as he appeared both in the rigor of divinity to the ancient people and in the gentleness of humanity to the new people.

Thus that Son of Man, Judge of the living and the dead, to whom the Father gave all judgement, is shown by this northern image. In the terror of fire—or, if the expression is better understood, in the fire of terror—he will say to the reprobate, whose resurrection is painted there on the left because they will be on the left at the judgement: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV.41). They will go into that fire, as is shown both by the circle inscribed there and by hell painted in the corner. [Col. 0731B]

This must also be fully understood concerning the depiction of hell: although it is painted in the court of the tabernacle, it does not belong at all to that court in which it is situated. But because, in order to show why the column above the tabernacle displayed the appearance of fire by night and cloud by day, it was necessary also to mention the last judgement, that hell itself, into which the judged reprobate will be thrust, had likewise to be painted there on the left.

On the right of that same northern image is painted the resurrection of the righteous, to whom the just Judge, the Lord Jesus, will say in the gentle cloud of kindness: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. XXV.34). They will go to that kingdom, as the inscription written there shows. And, as the images painted there indicate, they will go there from every order and profession: bishops, clerics, regulars and monks; priests also; men who lived devoutly in secular dress; and women. These are Noah, Daniel, and Job, who will be saved on the day of judgement, when Christ will show himself in fire and in cloud (Matt. XXV.34). [Col. 0732A]

Then they will receive the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world. That kingdom, as was said much earlier, is painted in the Holy of Holies, where angels are beside the image on one side and the tenth drachma on the other. After the judgement the elect will go there, where the drachma is, because they too are that same drachma. In these images, however, the same elect are depicted as going to the kingdom, whereas in the drachma they are depicted as possessing that same kingdom.

## CHAPTER XVI. Another allegorical exposition concerning the preceding chapter
[Col. 0732B] CXXX. We may still say certain things allegorically concerning this twofold image of Christ and the pillar of fire and cloud—whether they are to be accepted or rejected, let the reader’s judgment decide. For concerning the same two images of Christ, painted on either side of the tabernacle opposite one another, this must be weighed by us with the understanding of the mind, although it cannot be seen by bodily sight: namely, that these two pillars, although now, according to the arrangement of the plan, lie on both sides, yet when the tabernacle itself is raised up, they will hang not from some one side of it, but above the tabernacle itself in its central place, together with their pillars and all the other things belonging to those pillars; and then [Col. 0732C] there will not be two images, but one joined to the other and wholly united, and one image alone will appear.

Nor will there then be two pillars of fire and cloud, just as there will not be two images; but when the two pillars lying on one side of the tabernacle are joined above the tabernacle, at the summit, to the two lying on the other side, then of these pillars—which according to the arrangement of the plan are four at the bottom—there will be only two at the summit, with one image: one of fire on one side of the image, the other of cloud on the other side.

Then also, as the righteous go to the heavenly kingdom and the Gentiles and wicked go to hell, the Jews will be joined to them. For, to pass from the general to the particular, insofar at least as concerns the present state of the world, the calling of the Gentiles is now, in some fashion, what the salvation of the righteous will be at the end; and likewise the rejection of the Jews now is what the condemnation of the wicked will be at the end. For just as on the day of universal judgment the Lord will say generally to all the reprobate, both Jews and Gentiles: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41), so now too, by the effect of the thing itself, in His just but hidden judgment, the same Lord says, in rejecting them, to the unbelieving Jews, hardened in their unbelief: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire”—that fire, namely, of which it is read in prophecy: “And now fire consumes the adversaries”; and that fire of which the Psalmist says: “Fire came down, and they did not see the sun” (Ps. 57:9), so that the fire of sin may now torment in soul those whom [Col. 0733A] the fire of punishment will then torment in Gehenna.

This fire may rightly be called eternal, because this torment indeed begins here for all wicked persons who harden themselves in their impiety, but there it does not cease to endure, without any failure or end. Again, just as on the day of universal judgment the Lord will say generally to all the elect, both Jews and Gentiles: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34), so now too, by the effect of the thing itself, the same Lord says to the Gentiles whom He purposes to receive through the election of grace and the calling of His mercy: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom.” Thus, receiving the right faith and believing in the true author of salvation, these Gentiles may come to the kingdom of holy Church through knowledge of the truth, and possess it through love of virtue.

This kingdom was certainly prepared for them from the foundation of the world, because the Church of the Gentiles, which is called in time unto life, was predestined in eternity. But in hell, to which the wicked are condemned, Moses, who has heavy hands and holds a scourge and sword in them, is fittingly joined with them; because the Law, represented through Moses, not only punished with present death those who transgressed it, but also declares that those who harden themselves in wickedness and unbelief are to be condemned eternally by the sword and scourge of infernal punishment.

Likewise, according to this meaning, the same Moses, who is painted on the other side with Aaron and Hur supporting his heavy hands and rendering them light by supporting them, is joined with the righteous who receive the kingdom. For in order that the Gentiles may glorify the Lord for His mercy in the kingdom of the Church—which in the Gospel is sometimes called the kingdom of heaven—even now Aaron and Hur make Moses’ heavy hands light: while the loftiness of the Lord’s incarnation, represented by Aaron, and the love of the Holy Spirit, represented by Hur, make the harsh precepts of the Law light, because sinners are now mercifully saved through repentance, whereas formerly they were severely punished under the Law’s strictness.

Therefore the same Aaron—that is, the Lord appearing in the flesh, signified by Aaron—when sending His disciples out to preach, commands them to say: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” [Col. 0733D] (Matt. 3:2). It is as if He said: “Let Moses’ hands be supported, and, being supported, be made light; for now is the time for the blessed children of my Father to come and possess the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world.”

CXXXI. Nor should this too be passed over carelessly: although now, according to the arrangement of the plan, both the Jews are at the right of the image and the Gentiles at the left, yet when all these things, now appearing divided below to bodily sight, appear joined together above to the understanding of the heart, the positions will be reversed. When the southern image is joined, with all that belongs to it, to the northern image, the Jews will be at the left of the image and the Gentiles at the right. For before God became man, the Jews were in some fashion at the right, because, possessing the Law, they believed in Him who gave the Law; while the Gentiles were at the left, because, wholly ignorant of the Lord, they worshipped idols.

But after the Son of God raised the image of humanity from below and joined to it the image of His divinity; after the Word was made flesh—that is, after the southern image was joined to the northern—and the divine nature, in the unity of person, though the property of each nature remained intact, was associated with human nature, so that there might be one person in two natures, as though one image made from two images: the Jews, who were formerly at the right, are assigned to the left because of unbelief; and the Gentiles, who were formerly at the left, are called by grace to the right. For our image came in judgment over the tabernacle of the Church, “that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind” (Mark 4:12). Thus not only did the first become last and the last first (Matt. 20:16), but those at the right became those at the left, and those at the left became those at the right.

Accordingly this image, in the mercy of humanity, speaks as though in a certain mildness of cloud, saying: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:3), because the Jews, who commend themselves for righteousness, are left behind because of pride and unbelief, while the Gentiles, who place their trust in repentance, are received because of humility and faith (Luke 18:14). Therefore our image says in its cloud: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance,” [Col. 0734C] because the publican went down to his house justified rather than the Pharisee (ibid.); Mary the penitent is praised, and the proud Pharisee rebuked (Luke 7:38); Lazarus, full of sores, is saved, while the rich man, feasting splendidly every day, is condemned (Luke 16:22).

Concerning the Jews also, who, having been at the right, have now become those at the left, the same image pronounces a severe sentence in the terror of divinity, as though in a certain heat of fire, saying: “If anyone does this or that, he shall surely die” (Exod. 21:17). Let not the Jews suppose that this cloud will accuse them before the fire; rather, there is one who accuses them—Moses, in whom they themselves hope. For if they believed Moses, perhaps they would also believe Him whose image this is, “for he wrote of Him” (John 6:45).

Accordingly Moses too is painted opposite, facing the fire, holding in one hand a scourge to strike with, and in the other a sword to kill with. For the holy Law announces and judges that unbelieving Jews, because they refuse to receive the gentle consolation of the cloud—that is, to believe in Christ as man—are to be punished in the fury and wrath of that fire; and Moses the lawgiver prophesies, commands, and threatens in this manner: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers like myself; you shall hear him according to all things whatsoever he shall speak to you. And it shall be that every soul which does not hear that prophet shall be cut off from its people” (Deut. 18:15; Acts 3:22–23).

It was prophecy when a prophet to be raised from among their brothers was proclaimed to them; it was a command when they were ordered to hear that prophet in all things whatsoever he should say; it was a threat when every soul from among their people which should despise to hear him was declared to be cut off. Therefore what Moses said in words concerning the Jews—“Every soul which does not hear that prophet shall be cut off from its people” (Deut. 18:19)—the same Moses, here painted, indicates: set opposite the fire, he stretches out one hand with the sword and the other with the scourge toward those same unbelieving Jews, who have thereby become those at the left.

The support and lightening of Moses’ hands, placed opposite the cloud beside the Gentiles now made those at the right—namely, those Gentiles who receive Christ’s faith, embrace the gentleness of the aforesaid cloud, and repent of their sins—both frees them from the fury of this fire and protects them beneath the sweet covering of humanity, as under the gentle shade of a cloud. For they are protected from the terror of divinity while through right faith and good works they flee for refuge to the gentle consolation of humanity; and for them that same cloud is an advocate before the fire, and itself “is the propitiation for their sins” (John 2:2).

We have treated these matters—the two images of Christ lying on either side of the tabernacle, the double pillar of fire and cloud, and the things belonging to them—under a twofold allegorical interpretation, leaving it to the reader’s judgment which should rather be chosen.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the fivefold division of the painting

CXXXII. After this, we must consider attentively that this painting, of which we have already said much, is divided into five spaces. The first space is that in which laypersons of both periods are contained. The second is that in which the clergy of both Testaments are contained. The third is that in which Levites enter in order to sacrifice. The fourth is that in which priests enter in order to offer incense to the Lord. The fifth is that into which the high priest alone was accustomed to enter once each year.

The first space is one in which good and evil persons are mingled together; for in the estate of laypeople more evil than good persons are found, so that the better they are, the fewer they are. It is like a field in which there are both good and bad plants—not good plants alone, nor bad plants alone, but good and bad together. The second space, however, is one in which good persons are contained. Although not all clergy are good, just as not all laypeople are good—and in these dangerous times, more evil than good persons are found among them as among laypeople—I nevertheless call them good and holy, because, insofar as their office is concerned, they are bound by a certain special obligation to possess a prerogative of goodness and holiness above laypeople. The higher they are in profession and office, the holier they ought certainly to be in conduct and merit; because, as it is written, “To whom much has been given, much will be required” [Col. 0736A] (Luke 12:48).

For this reason I affirm that those in this space are good: it contains those who, above other believers, ought especially to be good, even if they are not. Thus this space is like a garden in which only good plants are cultivated. In a field, plants spring up by themselves and from themselves; but the good plants which are in a garden are selected elsewhere by the gardener’s discernment, brought from elsewhere by labour, and planted in the garden itself; once planted, they are watered, and once watered, nourished. So laypeople live content with a certain natural ordering under the common title of Christianity; but from the common estate of laypeople, those who are to be ordained clergy are selected by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, as by a gardener’s discernment, and, once selected, are raised to the height of the clerical state under the bonds of a stricter profession—like plants taken from the common field and planted in a garden with diligent care.

CXXXIII. In the third space Levites enter—not all of them, but those found fit to offer a whole burnt offering upon the bronze altar which stood outside the tabernacle. This space is like a royal court in which friends and familiars are customarily received. All Levites indeed encamped around the tabernacle, but none entered to minister to the Lord unless they were mature in age and perfect in purity. Thus the Lord says to Aaron concerning the Levites: “Any man of your seed throughout their families who has a blemish shall not offer bread to the Lord or approach His ministry” (Lev. 17:18). And concerning the age of those Levites the Lord says to Moses: “From twenty-five years and upward they shall enter to minister” (Num. 4:35).

Therefore this space, in which those Levites offer whole burnt offerings to the Lord who are both mature in age and conspicuous for purity, is like a royal court, where His friends and familiars enter in order to devote themselves to His service. Priests enter the fourth space with hands and feet washed, to offer incense to the Lord; and it is like the house of a very wealthy householder, in which his relatives and kin are received. The fifth space, which is within the veil and is called the Holy of Holies, the high priest alone was accustomed to enter; and this place is like a bridal chamber, in which, with all familiars and friends set aside, and even relatives and kin excluded, bridegroom and bride alone delight in one another with a love made sweeter by their being in an inner place.

In this space the ark of the covenant is placed, and the ark in this place is like a bed in the bridal chamber. Of all places belonging to this tabernacle of which we speak, none is more private than this; and among all its objects, nothing is, so to speak, more private than the ark and those things which were within it. Therefore I compared this place to a bridal chamber and the ark to a bed: for among all the rooms in a palace none is more private than the bridal chamber; and among all things not only within that chamber but belonging to this life, nothing is more private than the bridegroom’s and bride’s bed.

Thus the first space is in some manner a field; the second, a garden; the third, a court; the fourth, a house; the fifth, a bridal chamber. Good and evil laypeople together are in the first place, like good and bad plants together in a field; clergy, who signify good persons, are in the second, like selected plants in a garden; Levites in the third, like friends and familiars in a court; priests in the fourth, like relatives and kin in a house; the high priest alone in the fifth, where the ark containing manna is, like bridegroom and bride alone in the bridal chamber, where delight is in the bed. These are the five spaces by which the painting of which we speak is divided.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the meaning of the fivefold division

[Col. 0737B]

CXXXIV. We must now explain what meaning we think this fivefold division of our painting indicates allegorically. If anyone perhaps thinks it unworthy that what we have painted on a flat surface should be drawn into allegory, we think it fitting that the fivefold distinction—or, if that is the more fitting term, division—belonging to that ancient tabernacle of Moses may be understood allegorically. For just as it is visibly painted here, so we think it was in some fashion visible in the tabernacle of Moses: in the first space, around the tabernacle itself, were the twelve [Col. 0737C] tribes; in the second, along its four sides, the Levites. The third space was the court, containing the altar of burnt offering and the bronze laver. The fourth was the outer house of the tabernacle, which, as the Apostle says, the priests entered continually, “performing the offices of the sacrifices” (Heb. 9:6). The fifth was the inner house of the same tabernacle, open only to the high priest, and not even to him except once a year.

We read that these things were thus in that ancient tabernacle, and we too have painted them here as best we could. What, then, do these things signify? For if, as the Apostle says, “All things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10:6), and were written for our correction, they must by no means be believed empty of mystery. Let us therefore humbly set forth what we think concerning this matter, without prejudice to those who know how to speak of it more subtly, truly, and elegantly. Keeping intact, then, the better and more fitting understanding accessible to more learned minds, let us see whether perhaps the fivefold state of this world may be allegorically fitted to this fivefold division.

We distinguish these five states of the world as follows. The first state of this world was from the very beginning of the world until the flood. Since no law had yet been given to humanity, by whose commandments people could be constrained and bound, we not undeservedly compare this state to the breadth of a field. In that state, because the sons of God and the sons of men were mingled together, there were, as in a field, both good and bad plants.

The second state arose after the flood, in the times of the patriarchs and of Moses, through whom that ancient Law was given to the people. This state belongs in some manner to the good; for although in neither that time nor any time of this age were there good people only, still, when the patriarchs and lawgivers called to faith and to the worship of the one true God had been planted like good plants brought from elsewhere, in God’s garden enclosed by the hedges of legal commandments, a more numerous multitude [Col. 0738A] of saints and a greater knowledge of truth shone forth upon the world.

The third state belongs to the time of the judges and kings who presided over that ancient people of God with responsibility for government. This state was like the court of a king or ruler, where his friends and familiars attended to his service; for in that time the people had been enlarged by growth and strengthened by the building of the Temple in their own land, so that they might attend more freely to divine worship.

The fourth state belongs to the time of the prophets, who, in that they foretold in many ways and by many modes the coming of the Son of God in the flesh, the mysteries of our redemption, and the sacraments of holy Church, were joined, so to speak, to the supreme householder by a certain relation and kinship. This state was in some manner the house of a very wealthy householder, in which the relatives and kin of that householder were the holy prophets.

The fifth place, called the Holy of Holies, expresses the coming of the Son of God in the flesh because the high priest alone was accustomed to enter it. What else was this state but a bridal chamber in which Christ the bridegroom was joined to His bride, holy Church?

These, then, are the five states of this world: the first, from Adam and the times of the sons of God and sons of men until the flood; the second, in the times of the patriarchs and the lawgiver; the third, in the times of the judges and kings; the fourth, in the time of the prophets; the fifth, in the time of the Son of God and man. According to the reasons set forth above, the first is like a field, the second like a garden, the third like a court, the fourth like a house, and the fifth like a bridal chamber. Therefore, in the first space, which is outermost of all, I write “Field”; in the second, “Garden”; in the third, “Court”; in the fourth, “House”; in the fifth, “Bridal Chamber,” in order to show that, for the reasons stated above, the first space is in some way a field, the second a garden, the third a court, the fourth a house, and the fifth a bridal chamber.

## CHAPTER XIX. Another exposition of the same matter

CXXXV. We may also refer these five spaces of our painting, of which we have spoken, to the five states of holy Church, called to faith after Christ’s coming. The first state of holy Church was that in which, after the Lord’s ascension, when the primitive Church had been clothed with power from on high, all who dared to believe in Christ and all who dared to preach Him were driven by diverse forms of torture to deny Him. This was when the hour had come that all who killed the apostles would think that they were rendering service to God [Col. 0739A] (John 16:2); when persecutors laid bloody hands upon them and brought them before kings and governors; when, finally, they were hated by all people for Christ’s name (Matt. 10:22).

Behold the field in which, amid many bad plants, there were few good ones: when the nettle hindered the lily from growing, when saltwort destroyed the hyssop. But after the Lord Jesus, awakened by the long and anxious cry of His disciples labouring at the oars (Matt. 8:24), commanded the winds and sea so that they obeyed Him and there came to be a great calm (ibid., 26), peace was given to the Church. Thus Peter’s little boat might no longer be troubled: the Roman Empire was preserved for the faith, and the necks of the other kingdoms throughout the length and breadth of the earth were bowed to the reproach and disgrace of Christ’s cross. Good and chosen plants, brought from that field into the Lord’s garden, could then be planted in greater number because they could be planted more freely. “Instead of saltwort the fir tree sprang up; instead of the nettle the myrtle grew” (Isa. 55:15); above Babylon’s shadowy mountain the banner of the cross was raised. The voice of preachers was lifted up; leaders entered the gates, because those whom holy Church had as powerful men in the Lord’s wrath in her first state, she received rejoicing in His glory in this second state. Now, I say, there was “a voice of a multitude in the mountains, as of a numerous people,” because the voice of the tumult of kings and nations assembled together thundered forth.

Thus this state of holy Church was a garden in which good plants were planted. Once the Church had been given peace, she rejoiced in the increase both of the merit and the number of her members. Not only right faith increased, but holy action as well. Then, in this third state, the friends and familiars of the supreme Emperor entered His court—friends by faith and familiars by action—in order to attend to His service both through right belief and energetic action. Thus the Church was raised above the height of the earth and set as the pride of the ages.

CXXXVI. Its fourth state now came, in which the devotion of believers was kindled, their resolve strengthened, and their purpose increased in goodness far more excellently than in the third or second state. For in many of her faithful this virgin, mother Church, would not be content in this fourth state merely with the common holiness of Christianity unless she utterly despised the world and the things of the world, took up the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden (Matt. 11:30), and zealously embraced in countless persons the common life which she once possessed in few at her beginning. Thus unity of minds might be fostered through the sharing of possessions, so that in this state too the multitude might have one heart and one soul—not merely a multitude of believers, but of those living holy lives—and that none might call anything that he possessed his own, but all things might be common to them [Col. 0740A] (Acts 4:32).

What else is this state but a certain holy and awesome place, rightly called Bethel, that is, “House of God”? There the ladder of charity is raised up, and angels ascend and descend by its steps (Gen. 28:12). Into this house enters “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, and a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2:9): a race, I say, chosen from those who minister outwardly in order to offer inwardly to the Lord incense of the sweetest fragrance. It is the race of regular clerics; the race of the Limousin and Premonstratensians; the race of Arrouaise and Beauvais; likewise the race of holy monks; the race of Carthusians and Cistercians; the race of Cluniacs and Cyronians; and also the race of other diverse professions. Each of these according to its kind surrounds in variety, but does not strip of unity, the one and same queen standing at the right hand of her King “in raiment of gold” (Ps. 44:10).

Religious monks and regular clerics inhabit this house. They are joined to their common Lord not only by a kind of friendship and familiarity, but also by relationship and kinship; for while each of them strives with his whole intention, in complete contempt for present things and desire for things to come, to do His will, he is indeed, as He Himself says, His brother and sister and mother (Matt. 12:50). In this house they have, upon the table, the food of good works; in the lampstand, the light of reading; and on the altar, the sweetness of incense—that is, of prayer.

That food signifies good work we have from the Lord’s saying: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). That the lampstand indicates sacred reading, the Apostle Peter shows when he says: “We have the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to give heed, as to a shining lamp in a dark place” (2 Pet. 2:19). That incense likewise expresses the sweetness of prayer, the Psalmist demonstrates: “Let my prayer,” he says, “be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. 140:2).

These are the three things which our priests must continually have in this house: whenever they are free from the necessary care of the body, they ought to be engaged in work, reading, or prayer. Work is for bodily ministry; reading, for spiritual instruction; prayer, for contemplative purity.

This house is also inhabited by three orders: novices, obedientiaries, and cloistered religious. These are they who have the Lord Jesus with them in Bethany, that is, “the house of obedience,” as John the Evangelist says: “They made Him a supper there, and Martha was serving, but Lazarus was one of those reclining with Him; and Mary took a pound of costly pure nard and anointed His feet, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12:2–3).

Thus Martha serves the Lord, Lazarus reclines with Him, and Mary anoints Him. Martha, therefore, who attends to the Lord’s service and who, as the same Lord says elsewhere concerning her, is “anxious and troubled about many things” [Col. 0741A] (Luke 10:1), represents the obedientiaries of the monastery, who ought to be faithful and prudent: prudent in acquiring, faithful in spending; prudent lest the error of ignorance deceive them, faithful lest they seek anything of their own in God’s service.

Lazarus, who now reclines with the Lord, but was formerly dead and stank after four days in the tomb, represents novices who have come to God’s banquet in the common life. Previously, however, they had spiritually died through the delight, consent, and habit of sin, and through despair of pardon; they stank before God and people through the infamy of a wicked life. But now, raised by the Lord and loosed by His disciples, they are advanced by the Lord Himself to such dignity that they are judged worthy to recline with Him. They are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household (Eph. 2:19).

Mary also especially represents cloistered religious, who can devote themselves to the Lord Jesus alone more freely insofar as they have more completely stripped themselves of every anxiety concerning earthly things. Mary is very intimate and very close to the Lord Jesus—more intimate and closer to Him than all others abiding in Bethany. Although Martha serves Him and Lazarus reclines with Him, neither he nor she touches Him. Mary alone touches Him. Bowed down at His feet, she touches what is lowest in Him; raised toward His head, she “took a pound of costly pure nard” (John 12:3). She took it, I say, because unless she had received it, she would not have had it. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” [Col. 0741C] (James 1:17).

In the pound is understood the fullness of perfection; in the nard, the fragrance of knowledge; in the *pisticum* [pure nard], the purity of truth. From these three Mary makes and compounds a choice and excellent ointment, because from full and true knowledge of the Lord Jesus cloistered religious conceive sweet love in their hearts. They anoint the Lord’s head and feet because they ardently love His twofold nature, divine and human. For, as the Apostle says, the head of Christ is God (1 Cor. 2:3). And what do His feet signify but His incarnation, by which He touched the earth of our mortality?

That Prophet, mighty in deed and word (Luke 24:19), also walked upon our earth with two feet: teaching and action, for He both did and taught. It seems beautiful indeed to our Mary to see Him acting, and nevertheless sweet to hear Him speaking, so that she may have with her both His action for imitation and His speech for consolation and instruction.

Therefore there are three orders inhabiting this house: the order of obedientiaries, the order of novices, and the order of cloistered religious. These three orders are indicated by the three steps which we placed in the sanctuary beside this word “house.” Yet there are two other steps placed on the other side of the same word, because among the other virtues there are two especially necessary for all who live the common life: the sharing of possessions and unity of souls. These two virtues were preeminent in the primitive Church, from which the cenobitic life of which we speak took its beginning. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). Behold unity of hearts. “Nor did anyone say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (ibid.). Behold sharing of possessions.

Saint Augustine also addresses the clerics concerning these two virtues in their Rule, saying: “These are the things which we command you to observe, having been established in the monastery. First, the reason why you have been gathered into one is that you may dwell harmoniously in the house, and that you may have one soul and one heart in God; and do not call anything your own, but let all things be common to you.” Therefore, to indicate these two virtues, which among the others are very necessary to all cenobites, we have painted these two steps, so that no one who has professed the common life may wish to be separated from another through discord or presume to possess anything as his own.

CXXXVII. We have spoken at length concerning the fourth state of holy Church, perhaps not without usefulness. Its fifth state belongs to the profession of anchorites, because their profession, on account of the hidden and solitary life which they practise, is not unfittingly likened to the more interior place of the tabernacle, called the Holy of Holies. The high priest was accustomed to come from the Holy Place to the Holy of Holies, because, after the vices of the flesh had first been extinguished and the turbulent movements of the mind quieted, holy Fathers of old were accustomed to advance from the perfection of cenobitic life to the purity of the secret life of anchoritic practice.

What else can this secret and solitary life of anchorites be called but a certain bridal chamber? Beside this word, namely “bridal chamber,” three steps are placed to indicate a threefold solitude especially necessary for anchorites: solitude of place, solitude from business, and solitude of mind. The first solitude flees the crowd of people; the second avoids the preoccupation of earthly things; the third avoids the wandering of the heart. The first also drives away restless curiosity; the second removes the mind’s anxiety; the third empties out the foul vanity of invading phantasms.

These, then, are the five states of holy Church, called to faith after the Lord’s ascension, which can be designated in this manner by these five spaces of our painting. The first state was in the persecution of martyrs; the second in the conversion of rulers; the third in the multiplication of Christians; the fourth in the common life of cenobites; the fifth in the singleness of anchorites. The first was like a field, the second like a garden, the third like a court, the fourth like a house, the fifth like a bridal chamber. In the field there were good and bad plants together; in the garden, selected plants; in the court, familiars and friends; in the house, relatives and kin; in the bridal chamber [Col. 0743A], bridegroom and bride. In the field there are ploughers and sowers; in the garden, planters and waterers; in the court, sacrificers and washers; in the house, eaters and drinkers; in the bridal chamber, God and the soul, like bridegroom and bride, embracing and kissing one another together.

These, then, are the things which we have said to your charity concerning the fivefold division belonging to that ancient material tabernacle, and concerning the five spaces in our picture. These likewise are the things which, in this [Col. 0744A] second part of our book, we have shown allegorically in this picture of ours, as you commanded, concerning the condition and manifold adornment of holy Church, as briefly as we could. If you judge them sound, I beg you, do not ascribe it to the leaden pipe because it has handed you a cup of wine; but rather to him who filled it with the draught which it was to offer. Nor is it strange that he should form words for his own praise through our tongue as well, when once, in order that both human and frenzied folly might be rebuked for its foolish madness, he even changed an ass’s braying into human words.

## PART THREE. THE TABERNACLE OF THE SOUL, WHICH IS IN INNER THOUGHT

[Col. 0743]

## CHAPTER I. On the difficulty of treating the third part

[Col. 0743B]

### CXXXVIII

Since your exaltedness, venerable Father, clearly recognizes that, just as that visible tabernacle of Moses, of which much has already been said, signifies in allegorical meaning the universal Church of the elect, so likewise the same tabernacle, in its moral sense, expresses the secret place of the mind: you further lay upon my littleness the task that, just as I have shown in some measure how these things painted before the bodily eye pertain allegorically to all the children of holy Church because of the common faith, so I should also show how they pertain tropologically to each individual, according to the inward purity of the heart. This is a laborious undertaking and, I confess, not merely difficult for me [Col. 0743C] but almost impossible, since examining moral character belongs more to the taste of experience than to the scent of learning.

Nevertheless, I judge it altogether unjust that my obedience should fail in those matters concerning which your command compels me, insofar as he without whom we can do nothing supplies me strength. Your command, indeed, is so just that I ought deservedly to comply with it; so sincere that I wish to do so—provided that your prayer obtains for me the power effectively to accomplish what I ought willingly to do and willingly desire because I ought. Therefore, just as we have shown that certain things we have related about the tabernacle pertain to the common Church of the elect, so let us show, as we are able, how certain of these things pertain to each one of us; so that, [Col. 0743D] just as understanding has been enlightened in us by right faith, affection may likewise be awakened and kindled in us through devout thought.

## CHAPTER II. Why the people of Israel did not build the tabernacle in Egypt; and on the three metals belonging to that tabernacle

### CXXXIX

We said at the beginning of this book that the ancient people of God, so long as they were in Egypt, never constructed a tabernacle for God; but in order that they might at some time be able to do so, almighty God led them out of Egypt. Nor did he merely lead them out of Egypt; he also placed them in the desert, so that at last they might devote themselves to building the tabernacle of their God. They go out of Egypt who renounce the world with all worldly pomps. Having drowned the Egyptians, those enter the desert who, after extinguishing their former vices in the waters of compunction, have adopted, through the choice of a new life, a hard and austere manner of life.

But those construct the tabernacle who, having laid aside every corruption of earthly things, abandoned every care without exception, stilled every disturbance also, and finally despised and consigned to oblivion all things belonging to this world, devote themselves to their spiritual repose through the steady sameness of pure thoughts and through the clarified affection of holy desire. For formerly [Col. 0744C] they remained in Egypt, because, as the Apostle says, they were once darkness (Eph. 5:8), and “Egypt” is interpreted as “darkness.” There they were slaves; there they were bound; there too they were restless. Slaves, because, according to the voice of Truth, “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). Bound, because, as it is written: “The sinner is bound by the cords of his own sins” (Prov. 5:22). Restless, because, associated with the tumultuous gatherings of the Egyptians, they were utterly devoid of true rest: “Mixed among the nations, they learned their works, and served their carved images; and these became a snare to them” (Ps. 105:35–36).

But now, through the mercy of God, who called them out of darkness into his marvelous light (1 Pet. 2:9), they have become free from slaves, released from those bound, peaceful from restless people. [Col. 0744D] Surely in each of us the Lord “has set the wild ass free, loosing its bonds and giving it a home in solitude” (Job 39:5–6). This wild ass, which is called an ass of the wilderness, signifies those whom the Lord set free when he rescued them from Pharaoh’s slavery.

Their solitude is fourfold. The first is from sin; the second, from business; the third, from company; the fourth, from mystery. The first is the solitude of goodness; the second, of the soul; the third, of place; the fourth, of the bridegroom. In the first we are purified; in the second adorned; in the third raised on high; in the fourth made blessed. In the first [Col. 0745A] we are purified from vices; in the second adorned with virtues; in the third elevated by divine gifts; in the fourth made blessed by the sweetest and most secret embraces of the inward Bridegroom.

These are the solitudes of which Isaiah says: “Let the solitudes of Jordan exult” (Isa. 35:1). They are rightly said to exult, because all who possess them are made exultant. We ought truly to rejoice in these solitudes, because through the first restoration of nature is conferred; through the second, the beauty of righteousness is bestowed on us; through the third, the loftiness of grace is acquired; through the fourth, the joy of inward glory is granted. The first excludes natural weakness; the second breaks up the soul’s iniquity; the third, every punishment and vanity; the fourth leads onward to complete happiness.

This is the fourfold solitude in which he gave a home to those leaving Egypt, he who both set them free and loosed their bonds. And what is this freedom which he bestowed on them? Certainly, he freed them from vanity; he freed them from curiosity; he freed them from pleasure; he freed them from calamity. He freed them, I say, from the vanity of spiritual pride, from the curiosity of worldly delight, and from the pleasure of carnal desire; he will also afterward free them from the calamity of infernal punishment: from the vanity that blinded them; from the curiosity that alienated them from themselves; from the pleasure that defiled them; from the calamity that will torment the reprobate eternally. Thus he freed them so that they may be free both in this life and in the other: in this life from guilt, in the other from punishment. For everyone who commits sin, just as here he is a slave of sin (John 8:34), so also [Col. 0745C] in the future he will be a slave of punishment.

### CXL

“But he also loosed his bonds” (Job 39:5). What bonds? Just as there are four solitudes and four freedoms which he bestowed, so there are four kinds of bonds. There are certain bonds by which all of us are bound together in this life and from which we are not released even before death itself: namely, the corruptions of our mortality. The outstanding Preacher bewailed himself as bound by these bonds when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). He would not desire to be dissolved unless he saw himself as bound: “Wretched man that I am,” he says, “who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). The bond by which he was bound, therefore, was the body of death.

There are other bonds properly belonging to sinners, who are bound by as many bonds as they are burdened by the weight of sins. Of these bonds the Psalmist says: “The cords of sinners have encompassed me” (Ps. 118:61). There are, however, certain bonds which belong only to the good: namely, bonds of love and affection, concerning which the Lord says through Hosea: “I shall draw them with the cords of Adam, with the bonds of charity” (Hos. 11:4). There are yet other bonds by which the damned are bound in punishments; and he who is found by the king among those at table without a wedding garment is commanded to be bound by them: “Having bound his hands and feet, cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13).

The first bonds, then, are those of necessity; the second, of iniquity; the third, of charity; the fourth, [417; Col. 0746A] of calamity. The first belong universally to all; the second to the wicked; the third to the righteous; the fourth to the damned. The first bind all Adam’s children in the corruption of this mortal body; the second bind the children of sin in the commission of iniquity; the third bind the children of God in love for him; the fourth bind the children of perdition in the affliction of Gehenna.

The Lord will loose the first bonds in us when, death having been swallowed up in victory, our corruptible nature puts on incorruption and our mortal nature puts on immortality (1 Cor. 15:54). He has loosed the second in us when he both freed us from sin and made us his servants. But he neither permits us to be released from the third nor permits us to be bound by the fourth. Thus, through God’s mercy, we have become free from slaves, released from those bound, and peaceful from restless people.

We therefore possess rest. Where do we possess it? Certainly, true rest exists only in solitude, because one who is amid tumult cannot rest at all. “But we fled far away, and behold, we remain in solitude” (Ps. 54:8). In this fourfold solitude of ours, the Lord gave us a home. In this solitude of the heart tranquility is given, serenity of soul, purity of conscience; the brightness of inward light is seen, the sublimity of contemplation is attained, and the happiness of the Bridegroom is tasted beforehand. In this solitude, he who set us free, loosed our bonds, and gave us a home did so in order that we might construct a tabernacle for the God of Jacob: that is, that in this inward repose of the mind we might build our secret place with God. O freedom! O release! O solitude!

[Col. 0746C]

### CXLI

Therefore, your tabernacle, my dearest brother, is the tranquil and peaceful secret place of your heart, in which you ought to dwell with yourself and within yourself. But three metals belonged to that material tabernacle of Moses: gold, silver, and bronze. Likewise, in you, who ought to be a tabernacle of the Holy Spirit, let these three metals exist spiritually. Gold pertains to serenity of heart; silver, to purity of speech; bronze, to strength of action. Let there therefore be gold in you, that you may have brightness in inward thought; silver, in good speech; bronze, strength in useful action.

Hence the Psalmist compares the man “who meditates upon the law of the Lord day and night” to a tree planted beside streams of water, which “will give its fruit in its season, and its leaf will not fall, and whatever he does will prosper” (Ps. 1:3). This tree signifies any religious man. The streams of water are the instabilities of worldly people, beside which streams this tree is planted, because holy men shine in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation as lights in the world.

That tree will give fruit in its season because it preserves pure thoughts in the heart. Its leaf will not fall because, avoiding the criminal lapse of the tongue and excluding it altogether from itself by the discipline of silence, it refuses to be scattered and fall away through harmful and idle words. Whatever it does will prosper, because it walks the royal road and acts prosperously in all things, departing from the straight path of action neither lifted up by prosperity at the right hand [Col. 0747A] nor broken by adversity at the left, using either hand as the right hand, and avoiding darkness as well as light.

Thus he is pure in heart, pure in speech, fruitful in deed. Behold the three days’ journey by which the Israelites go out of Egypt into the desert (Exod. 3:18): purity of mind, purity of speech, and perfection of action. O what a tree, and how great! Blessed was Samuel, who indeed bore fruit, because “he grew, and the Lord was with him” (1 Sam. 3:19–20). His leaf did not fall, because “none of all his words fell to the ground” (ibid.). Everything that he did prospered, for the fame of his way of life spread so widely that all, from Dan to Beersheba, recognized that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord.

Therefore, what the fruit of the tree given in its season is in the Psalm, that gold signifies in the moral tabernacle; what the unfailing leaf is there, that silver is here; and what the prosperity of deeds is there, that bronze is here understood to be.

## CHAPTER III. On the boards and bases, morally expounded

### CXLII

Consider further that your tabernacle must be made from boards of shittim wood, so that you may understand that you too ought to have thoughts that are pure and strong, since shittim wood is strong and incorruptible. Let your thought, then, be incorruptible and strong: incorruptible through the cleanness of purity, strong through the power of steadfastness. Let it be incorruptible, lest anything unclean dwell in your mind; let it be strong, lest you wander in spirit through many things.

But what does it mean that the tabernacle was gilded both within [Col. 0747C] and without? Let your tabernacle be gilded within, and gilded without: within, for the purity of thought; without, for the usefulness of action. Within, that you may meditate on holy things; without, that you may perform useful deeds. Within, that you may please God in your heart; without, that you may benefit your neighbor in your work. Within, for contemplation unto sanctification; without, for action unto imitation. Within, finally, for conscience; without, for reputation. For, according to the Psalmist’s saying, “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6), even though people hold a good opinion of him; and, as a certain holy man says, “He who neglects his reputation is cruel,” even though, as far as he himself is concerned, he lives well before God. So says that author.

Accordingly, he is not perfect who, while living wickedly in secret, glories in having a falsely good report of himself proclaimed publicly; nor is he perfect who considers his reputation among people as nothing, although he lives well in secret. Therefore let your tabernacle be gilded within, so that your light may shine. Nor should it be gilded only within, but also without, so that this same light may shine not only before you but also before people, that they may see your good works and glorify, not you indeed, but your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16).

Let your boards rest upon bases. The boards of your tabernacle are the thoughts of your heart; the bases are intentions. Therefore let your boards be gilded: let your thoughts be pure. Let the bases likewise be silver: let your intentions be right. Have nothing defiled in your thought, nothing pretended in your intention. God hates both in his tabernacle, in your heart: stain and wrinkle. Your heart has a stain if it is stained; it has a wrinkle if it is wrinkled.

Therefore you have gilded boards in your tabernacle if you purpose to do some good thing in your heart. You have silver bases if, by this, you desire to please the eyes of him alone who sees all things, and do not seek human praise for it. Those who plan good deeds in their mind but seek popular favor through them have beneath such gilded boards not silver bases but leaden ones. For silver becomes brighter in fire, whereas lead melts and fails: that is, when those who desire to please God by a good purpose are rebuked, the brightness of their goodness grows; but when the wind of detraction blows from that same quarter whence the breeze of favor formerly used to come to those who desire to please people, and the falsity of their intention reveals itself through the loss of the praise they sought, then it becomes apparent that their bases were not silver but leaden.

Therefore let your boards be gilded, and your bases silver, so that you may have together both a good purpose in thought and rectitude in intention, lest you incur sin even though a right offering preceded in you, when a right division did not follow. Thus gilded boards signify pure thoughts, and silver bases signify right intentions.

### CXLIII

For this reason, on the boards themselves, around the circuit of the three walls—from the first board of the southern wall as far as the first board of the northern wall—I write this verse, one syllable being placed on each board:

> These boards of the tabernacle, made of shittim wood and gilded on every side, are the soul’s thoughts, wholly clean from evil and strong in goodness.

And at the beginning of this verse, upon the first board, I make three steps, because, in order that the thoughts of our soul may be pure and strong, we must strive to have steadiness in memory, clarity in reason, and purity in will. For our mind ought to be strengthened by the steadiness of memory, enlightened by the clarity of reason, and purified by the purity of will: strengthened lest it flow away disorderly; enlightened lest it grow dark through ignorance; purified lest any stain obscure it. Let our memory therefore beware of being scattered; let reason avoid being blind; let the will endeavor to be pure; and the thoughts of our heart will be both clean from evil and strong in goodness.

But on the silver bases, which are placed beneath the boards in the picture, around the circuit from the first base beneath the first board of the southern wall as far as the base placed beneath the first board of the northern wall, this verse is written, one letter being inscribed on each base:

> The silver bases on which the gilded boards are set are the right intentions upon which pure thoughts rest.

This verse, indeed, has no division in the picture, because our intention ought to be uniform and simple. In all our movements, both inward and outward, we ought to intend this alone: to please God alone.

## CHAPTER IV. On the bars, rings, and images placed on the boards and bases

[Col. 0749A]

### CXLIV

These matters are lofty, profound, very difficult, and possible for very few. For it belongs to the perfect to possess such thoughts and such intentions in their thoughts. Therefore, after these things, have bars and rings in your tabernacle: bars, I mean, covered with gold plates, and golden rings into which those bars are inserted. These bars, which are made of shittim wood but clothed in plates of gold, are the strong and bright examples of the Fathers who went before; and the golden rings signify the abiding brightness and bright perpetuity of the rewards of those same holy Fathers.

In the bars, therefore, you see their conduct; in the rings, their reward. In the bars, their merit; in the rings, their prize. In the bars, finally, their temporal labor; in the rings, their everlasting crowns. Therefore ends are visible in the bars, whereas no end can be seen in the rings, because the afflictions of the saints have limits, but their rewards will endure without end. Hence they regard every labor they bear as slight, while they consider how great the reward will be which they shall receive.

See how little the blessed Paul reckoned his own labors and those of his fellow citizens when he said: “This present, momentary and light weight of our tribulation” (2 Cor. 4:17). He considered his tribulation slight, calling it not merely light but momentary. [Col. 0749C] But see how great he judged the reward: “It works in us an eternal weight of glory, beyond measure in sublimity” (ibid.). He truly foresaw that what he perceived to be exceedingly sublime, eternal, glorious, and weighty would be great.

Speaking of both—the bars and rings—he says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). It is as though he said in other words: Although these bars we carry are weighty, they are nevertheless tolerable and light to us, because we constantly think of the brightness of the rings, by which we shall be adorned at the end without end.
