But what does it mean that the end of one bar entered into the end of another, so that one bar seemed to extend around the circuit of the three walls, except that a holy man joins virtues to virtues within himself, so that he may contain within himself a single, firm holiness and a holy firmness? Hence the Psalmist says: “The saints shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. 87:8). It is as though he said: In order that the tabernacle may stand firm, bars are joined to bars. He adds concerning the rings into which the same bars are inserted: “The God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (ibid.).

The apostle Peter likewise admonishes us that, in the moral tabernacle, bars should be joined to bars, saying: “Supply virtue in your faith; and in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, self-restraint; in self-restraint, piety; in piety, brotherly love; and in brotherly love, charity” (1 Pet. 1:5–7). He begins from faith and comes as far as charity, [Col. 0750A] because faith is indeed the foundation of our spiritual tabernacle, hope raises the structure, but charity completes the building.

You also place these bars upon your boards whenever, by continual consideration of the conduct of the Fathers who preceded you, you stir up, raise, kindle, and sharpen good will in yourself, so that you also regard as light to accomplish what you see accomplished by them. You fasten rings on those same boards if you consider their eternal rewards through contemplation and desire them through affection, so that you may entrust yourself to them and desire to be joined with them in reward, whose footsteps you see yourself imitating.

Therefore you place bars on your boards so that you may be strengthened in labor; rings, so that you may be encouraged in hope. Bars, that you may know how well you ought to live; rings, that you may know why you ought to live well. Thus the bars inserted into the rings are the strong ways of life of the saints, made bright by the eternity of the heavenly homeland and rewarded with eternal brightness. These bars and rings are also in your tabernacle whenever you enact their conduct in deed and desire their rewards in affection.

### CXLV

For this reason, on these same bars, around the circuit of the three walls from the first bar of the southern wall to the first of the northern, I write this verse, placing individual words upon individual bars:

> The gold-covered bars strengthening the boards are the strong and pure examples of holy men, confirming our minds.

This verse has three steps on the first board above the first letter, because there are three things to which the examples of the saints draw us. First, that we should abandon evil; second, that we should practice good; third, that we should strive to persevere even in the good which we practice: namely, that we may be cleansed, adorned, and strengthened—cleansed [420; Col. 0750C] in the abandonment of vices, adorned in the performance of virtues, strengthened when we persevere to the end in the good we do.

This is the reason why, as I said much earlier, I placed these bars not outside but within the tabernacle. For since the walls are not raised upright but lie rather stretched out at the bottom on the flat surface of the picture, they could by no means be seen merely with the bodily eye; nor could their meanings be understood so clearly unless they were depicted within.

Likewise, beneath the golden rings into which the bars are inserted, around the circuit of the three walls, from that which is on the first board of the southern wall as far as that which is on the first board of the northern wall, this verse appears, its individual syllables written on individual boards:

> These rings, made of the purest gold, into which the bars are inserted, are the bright rewards, bestowed upon the blessed for holy life and destined to remain without end.

This verse too is divided by three steps on the first board next to the first letter, because there are three things which will be given to the elect in the future life: power, wisdom, and loving-kindness. For then they will be powerful, wise, and loving: powerful in themselves, wise in God, loving toward one another. There their being will know no death, their knowing no error, and their loving no offense. They will possess the strength of power from the highest Power, the Father; the brightness of wisdom from true Wisdom, the Son; and the sweetness of love from sweet Charity, the Holy Spirit; so that in this way God may be all in all.

The images which are placed around the circuit of the three walls, both upon the bases and at the tops of the boards, seem likewise to suggest to us in a merely moral sense the same thing that the aforesaid bars inserted through the middles of the boards suggest. For since, in the tabernacle of the Church, the bases signify allegorically religious persons of both sexes who were in the world from the beginning of the world until Christ’s incarnation, and the boards signify saints of both sexes who are in the Church from Christ’s coming until the end of the age: then you raise boards and place bases beneath in your tabernacle whenever you continually survey and traverse with diligent attention the saints of both periods, constantly setting before yourself both their words for instruction and their deeds for imitation.

“Go around, therefore, and sacrifice in the tabernacle of the Lord a sacrifice of joyful shouting; sing, and make melody to the Lord” (Ps. 26:6). Sing through pure thought; make melody through good action. In mind and thought, run through all the saints who lived in the world, of both sexes, from Adam, the father of us all, to our common Lord Jesus Christ; and who now are, from the beginning of his incarnation until the end of the age. Set before yourself both what they said and what they did, so that from their words you may become more learned, and from their deeds holier. And investigate carefully especially how pure were the thoughts which, in the moral interpretation, we have said are to be understood by the gilded boards, and how right were the intentions understood by the silver bases. Thus in your inward tabernacle you will have images inscribed both beneath the bases and on the boards.

For this reason, in this picture of ours, images have been painted both in the tabernacles of the saints of the New Testament and upon the bases of those who lived in the Old Testament, of both sexes: so that, for gaining purity in the mind’s thought, which is understood by the gilded board, and rectitude in inward intention, which is understood by the silver base, you may have the ways of life and the lives of the saints of both periods known by clear consideration and repeatedly practiced through fruitful imitation.

Let what has been said morally about the bars and rings, the images on the bases and tops of the boards, and finally the three metals belonging to the tabernacle of which we speak—gold, silver, and bronze—be sufficient.

## CHAPTER V. On the three walls of the tabernacle; on the bar at its entrance; and on the five pillars raised beneath that bar

### CXLVI

After this, reason leads us to inquire what the three walls of the tabernacle may morally signify; what may be expressed by the bar at its entrance; and what likewise by the pillars placed beneath that bar. These three walls of the tabernacle can suggest to us three movements found in a human being: the movement of the mind, the movement of the body, and the movement of sensuality. The movement of the mind is in the will; the movement of the body is in action; the movement of sensuality lies between the two in pleasure.

For the mind moves itself according to its own will, and is moved from itself and through itself, because it belongs to it to move itself, whether it is moved well or badly. It is moved well when it is moved toward good—that is, toward righteousness; and badly when toward evil—that is, toward guilt. And it belongs to it to move toward either good [421; Col. 0752A] or evil, because no violence compels it either to will or not to will; rather, it proceeds from itself and through itself by the freedom of its own will.

The movement of the body promptly follows the movement of the mind and effectively carries it out; such as the former precedes in will, such does the latter follow in action. But the movement of sensuality, favoring each of these two movements, moves between them in pleasure, embracing both and taking delight in both.

Since this is so, the southern wall of the tabernacle expresses the good movement of the mind. For, as has already been said, the mind has the capacity to move itself; but in order to be good it ought not to move according to itself, but rather according to him who is understood by the South—namely, its Creator and disposer, the Holy Spirit. Thus it may move itself in will then and toward that object which it recognizes that the Holy Spirit, the infuser and governor of all good things, wills, so that it may dare neither proudly to resist his will nor craftily to anticipate it.

Never willing evil, and—even if at some time willing that something should be evil—the Holy Spirit, inspirer and promoter of all good things, always wills that we should always do good and never evil. Yet he does not will that we should always do the same good thing, because, just as evil can never be admitted except unlawfully, so good may sometimes lawfully be omitted; so much so that, although all things have their season, even something good itself sometimes loses its goodness in a particular case if it is not done at a fitting time.

Therefore this wall of the tabernacle faces south, because, in order that the movement of the mind in us, who ought to be God’s tabernacle, may be ordered, it is necessary that it imitate the Holy Spirit’s inspiration both in willing and in not willing: carefully seeking, I say, what he himself wills or does not will, and when, and striving obediently to follow him in both, so that it may dare neither fraudulently to anticipate his will nor arrogantly to resist it.

But the northern wall, which is altogether similar to the southern wall in length, height, number of boards, adornment, and connection, expresses the movement of the body, which serves the movement of the mind. For such as the latter is conceived in us in will, such is the former brought forth by us in action. The third wall, which is joined and connected to each of the other walls, signifies the movement of sensuality, which in pleasure embraces the two preceding movements.

[Col. 0753A]

### CXLVII

But in order that each of these two walls may be fully stabilized in its erection, a certain bar is stretched transversely at the entrance of the tabernacle from one to the other, firmly joining them and stabilizing and strengthening both walls, so that neither may waver either short of or beyond what it ought. For in order that each of these movements may be blameless in us, the strength of reason extends itself to both the movement of mind and the movement of body, fitting them together, lest the mind defile itself through impurity of will or the body cast itself headlong through indiscretion in action.

Therefore the strength of reason intervenes in us, lest the movement of our mind be unclean or that of our body indiscreet. Beneath the bar, moreover, five pillars are raised and firmly and skillfully fitted into the same bar lest they be compelled to fall. This is because, lest the five senses of our body collapse feebly into sin, they must be subjected to and directed by reason’s command.

A curtain hanging over these pillars covers them, lest, exposed outwardly, they be defiled by any outward filth. Thus, lest the senses in us be directed toward disordered and unlawful desire for visible things, contempt for those visible things closes them off: lest vanity defile and stain the pillar of sight, curiosity the pillar of hearing, pleasure the pillar of smell, gluttony the pillar of taste, or impurity the pillar of touch.

These pillars through which one enters the tabernacle are elsewhere called “windows” by the prophet, who laments that the curtain of which we speak was not hung upon them, saying: “Death entered through our windows” (Jer. 9:21). It is as though he said in other words: Because the curtain did not cover the pillars at the entrance of our tabernacle, that which ought not to have entered could enter through them.

The southern wall of the tabernacle signifies purity of will; the northern, vigor in action; the western, the favor of sensuality. Thus there are, as it were, three walls in the tabernacle and three movements in a human being: of mind, body, and sensuality. The bar which extends to both walls and strengthens both is the strength of reason, which fits together and fortifies in us both the movement of the mind and that of the body. The five pillars placed and fixed beneath the same bar are the five bodily senses subjected to the rule of reason. By the curtain hanging over those pillars, we understand contempt for external things.

## CHAPTER VI. On the two parts into which Moses’ tabernacle was divided, and what is to be understood morally through them
CXLVIII. We must first consider that the ancient tabernacle was divided into two parts: one outside the veil and the other within; one called the Holy Place, the other the Holy of Holies. If every chosen person who is perfect in the way of God is this tabernacle, what else does its outer part signify but the body of that chosen and perfected man? And what does its inner part signify but his soul? For priests entered the outer part; but the high priest alone was accustomed to enter the inner part. Thus, what we are in outward conduct is apparent to people outside; but what we secretly are within ourselves, in our minds, is known only to that supreme High Priest, before whom the abyss of human conscience lies bare. Therefore many entered the outer part of the tabernacle, but the high priest alone approached its inner part; for “man sees what is before his eyes, but God looks upon the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7). Again, the outer part of this tabernacle is called the Holy Place, while the inner is called the Holy of Holies. For although God’s chosen ones are exceedingly holy in their outward observances, yet through the heavenly desire with which they burn inwardly before God, they are far holier still. “Your eyes are doves’, apart from that which lies hidden within” [Col. 0754A–B] (Song 1:1). As though the Bridegroom were saying to his Bride in other words: In outward observances you indeed appear very holy to human beings; but in your inward desires you are concealed in your mind as much holier before me. For in fulfilling my will you embrace it inwardly more by affection than you are able inwardly to fulfill it in deed, so that your inward holiness may rightly be called, in comparison with the outward, the Holy of Holies.

In the outer part, moreover, the humanity of our Savior is portrayed; in the inner part, his divinity. For his humanity could indeed be seen in this world with bodily eyes; but his invisible divinity had to be believed with the spiritual eyes of faith. Hence Thomas, when touching him, is told: “Because you have seen me, you have believed” (John 20:20). He saw what he touched; but he believed what he recognized to be present in him whom he touched. In short, he saw a man and believed God. Therefore the words “you have seen” refer to the Savior’s humanity, portrayed in the outer part; while “you have believed” concerns his divinity, portrayed in the inner part [Col. 0754C].

CXLIX. The space in the outer part of the tabernacle is likewise clothed in purple, whereas that in the inner part is sapphire-colored. For we ought indeed to endure tribulations and distresses in the body, but to console ourselves through assured hope and steadfast longing for our heavenly homeland. Thus the Apostle, the vessel of election, says: “Though our outward man is decaying, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” [Col. 0754D] (2 Cor. 4:16). As though he said: Although the outer part of our tabernacle is covered in purple, yet its inner part is continually adorned with sapphire color.

According to the moral meaning, the outer part of the tabernacle expresses the body’s holiness, which consists in outward action; but the inner part indicates the heart’s holiness, which consists in inward desire. Our bodily holiness, after the six works of mercy to be performed for one’s neighbor, consists in these eight things: strict fasting, diligence in vigils, manual labor, chastity of the flesh, gravity of countenance, restraint in speech, humility of dress, and composure in walking. These eight are indicated by the eight steps portrayed in the outer space, with four steps set on each side [Col. 0755A].

The desire of our mind, in which inward holiness consists, is threefold: desire for pardon, desire for grace, and desire for glory. With our whole affection we ought to desire these three things: pardon, grace, glory—pardon for sins, grace for merits, glory for rewards. The first desire was perfectly possessed by the woman of whom it is said: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). The second desire was possessed by him who said: “My soul has longed to desire your ordinances at all times” (Ps. 118:20). The eminent Preacher was fervently aflame with the third desire when he said: “Having a desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). These three desires are expressed by the three steps placed on the right side of the image in the sapphire-colored space within the veil [Col. 0755B].

In the outer part of the tabernacle are these three things: the table, the candlestick, and the altar, so that, as was said above concerning these three, [423] we may continually exercise either useful activity, diligent reading, or pure prayer. In the ark, which is in the inner part, are likewise these three things: the rod, the tablets, and the manna. The rod is straight and flowering, and signifies the memory of our soul. In the tablets was knowledge of truth, and through them the soul’s reason is understood. Manna also, being sweet and savory food, expresses the pure sweetness and sweet purity which we ought to have in the will. Our memory, then, should be clean, our reason learned, and our will devout. These three are marked by the three steps portrayed at the northern end of the ark [Col. 0755C].

## CHAPTER VII. How the two parts of the tabernacle, together with the things in them, signify in the tropological sense the twofold state of the human being.

CL. I do not think it absurd to say that Moses’ tabernacle was divided for this reason: our state is twofold—one in the present, the other in the future; one amid the labor of exile, the other in the rest of the kingdom; one called the Holy Place, the other the Holy of Holies; one in merit, the other in reward; one in affliction, the other in consolation; finally, one on the way, the other in the homeland.

At present we dwell in the Holy Place, but we cannot yet attain the Holy of Holies. For now, as the apostle John says, “we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be” [Col. 0755D] (1 John 3:2), because, blinded by the veil of our mortality, we are unable to behold clearly the hidden joys of that lower and higher homeland. We are now, I say, in the Holy Place, because in some respects we are holy now; but when we attain the Holy of Holies, we shall be holy in every respect. Now we know some things, not all, because in many matters we are in darkness. Now we can do some things, not all, because in many matters we are weak. In some respects we are righteous now, but not in all, because in many matters we stumble. And in some respects we are temperate now, but not in all, because in many matters we exceed due measure.

Behold the four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance [Col. 0756A]. Prudence enlightens us; fortitude strengthens us; justice adorns us; temperance regulates us. Of these virtues we have some now, but we see that much is still lacking to us—things which we shall possess fully in the other life signified by the Holy of Holies. Therefore I placed these four virtues not in the Holy Place but in the Holy of Holies itself, within the veil, above the very columns erected before that veil. For now we are prudent and strong only in part, righteous and restrained only in part; but “when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 15:10). Then indeed we shall know without doubt and be able without weakness; we shall be fully righteous, because we shall offend in no respect; fully temperate, because we shall exceed due measure in no respect [Col. 0756B].

For these four virtues are exercised differently by us amid the labors and miseries of this life, and differently by angels and holy souls in heaven. There, to be subject to God reigning and visibly present is justice; to prefer or equate no good with God is prudence; to cling to God with utter steadfastness is fortitude; to take delight in no harmful deficiency is temperance. But there will not be there what justice accomplishes here in helping the wretched, prudence in avoiding snares, fortitude in enduring hardships, and temperance in restraining wicked pleasures, where there will be no evil.

CLI. Across the golden capitals of these columns I write in one line these two words: “Knowledge of God.” For in the clear understanding of their minds, which those golden capitals signify, each of the elect will fully know God in the heavenly homeland. For, as the prophet says: “No one shall teach his neighbor, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least even to the greatest, says the Lord” [Col. 0756C] (Jer. 31:18). At the beginning of the first word I place three steps, because the elect will possess a full knowledge of the Holy Trinity. For then, so far as pertains to a creature, they will fully know what it is for the Father to beget, for the Son to be begotten, and for the Holy Spirit to proceed; and, finally, what are in the one Godhead both the Trinity of persons and the unity of substance.

Below, across the silver bases of the columns, I write: “Unceasing praise of God.” For all God’s elect will then be established especially upon this, as upon a foundation: that they may sing hymnic praises to their Creator forever. By the beauty of the silver we should understand the brightness of the words which they will utter without end in praise of God. And upon the first base I place five steps, because there are five things for which we shall praise the Lord eternally: namely, our creation, redemption, liberation, protection, and the benefaction which he bestows upon us. For he created us, redeemed us, liberated us, protects us, and does us good [Col. 0756D]. [424] He created those who did not exist; he redeemed the lost; he liberated captives; he protects the weak; he benefits the unworthy. He created us in his divinity; redeemed us in his humanity; liberated us from captivity; protects us in our present weakness; and benefits us in eternal blessedness. He himself is our Creator, Redeemer, Liberator, Protector, and Benefactor [Col. 0757A]. To his creation we owe our existence; to redemption, our restoration; to liberation, our calling; to protection, our justification; to benefaction, our glorification.

These are the mercies of God which we shall sing forever, proclaiming his truth with our mouths. Concerning these five matters, I think, plain and adequate instruction is found in the book which we recently composed, entitled *On the Sweetness of God*. Upon the veil itself, which here hangs from four columns, I write across it these words: “Heaven adorned with ineffable beauty.” For, as the Venerable Bede understood, this veil signifies heaven. For he says of it: “That this veil was woven in beautiful variety from blue, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and twisted linen—who does not see that even according to the letter it accords with the beauty of the heavenly vision?” And he adds: “For if you consider,” he says, “the beauty and flames of the stars, the manifold appearance of the clouds, the rainbow itself drawing a thousand colors from the sun shining opposite—do you not seem to discern in heaven far more numerous and more beautiful paintings of colors than those woven into the veil of the tabernacle?” [Col. 0757B] Let this brief account suffice, according to the anagogical sense, concerning the four columns within the veil, their golden capitals and silver bases, and the veil hanging from these columns.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the twofold division of the tabernacle; and what the things which were in the Holy Place signify according to the moral interpretation, and what those which were in the Holy of Holies signify according to the anagogical sense.

[Col. 0757C]

CLII. It has already been said that the tabernacle’s twofold division signifies our twofold state: one in which we are at present, the other in which we shall be in the future. One is called the Holy Place, the other the Holy of Holies. That in which we now are is called the Holy Place; that for which we long is the Holy of Holies. Therefore we now remain in the Holy Place; then we shall arrive at the Holy of Holies.

Now, in the Holy Place, we have the table of reading, the candlestick of contemplation, and the altar of prayer. Reading enlightens us, contemplation purifies us, prayer kindles us. The study of sacred reading enlightens us [Col. 0757D], lest we stray from God’s way; the serenity of inward contemplation purifies us, lest we be dissipated by the instability of fluctuating thoughts; the earnestness of devout prayer kindles us, lest we grow cold in the love of God.

Therefore, if you meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night; if you keep continually in your mind Holy Scripture, which sets before us holiness in the history of examples, sound belief of faith in allegory, and the blessedness of heavenly joys in anagogy: then you surely have in your tabernacle a gilded table supported by four feet. If, moreover, you diligently consider in your mind, through the purity of contemplation, the holy life and harsh passion of our Redeemer himself; the order of preachers; the obedience of hearers; the uprightness of those who do good works; and, finally, the joy of that eternal homeland of imperishable power for which we long: you certainly have in your Holy Place a candlestick made of the purest and beaten gold, with cups, globes, and lilies placed upon it [Col. 0758A]. Finally, if you pray without ceasing, if you continually lift up pure hands without anger or dispute (1 Tim. 2:8), you have built within yourself a gilded altar of incense.

Make, therefore, this table, candlestick, and altar within yourself. You have the table if through the study of sacred reading you are enlightened in mind, and if through diligence in good action you are adorned in body; for the table signifies both Holy Scripture and good action, as was said above. You have the candlestick if you are purified through the serenity of inward contemplation. You have the altar of incense if, through earnest devout prayer, you are kindled in the love of God. Let holy reading, therefore, enlighten you against the darkness of ignorance; let good action adorn you against idleness, which is hostile to the soul; let inward contemplation purify you against the emptiness of invading phantasms; let prayer set you aflame against the torpor of northern cold [Col. 0758B]. These, then, are the things which you must continually practice in this state in which you now are—that is, in the Holy Place: the study of sacred reading, diligence in good action, the light of inward contemplation, and the devotion of pure prayer.

[425] CLIII. From this Holy Place you will come to the Holy of Holies, because through the holiness of merits you will attain the blessedness of rewards [Col. 0758C]. Once a year the high priest, clothed in sacred vestments, was accustomed to enter the Holy of Holies. And you, exercising before him a certain spiritual and invisible high-priesthood, adorned by the variety of good works as though by the beauty of splendid garments, will enter once into heavenly joys with the crown of the year of divine goodness, which the Lord has blessed (Ps. 64:12) and proclaimed propitious. For, as the Apostle says, “It is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this, judgment” (Heb. 9:27).

In the Holy of Holies you will see the ark, because the Lord Jesus will show and reveal himself to you [Col. 0758D] (John 18:21). In this ark are three things: the rod, the tablets, and manna. Above this ark hangs the mercy-seat, upon which stand two cherubim looking toward one another and turning their faces toward the mercy-seat itself. This ark is the mediator between God and human beings, God and man, Christ Jesus. The ark was made from shittim wood and covered everywhere with gold. What is more precious than gold? What is more excellent than Christ’s divinity? Shittim wood is incorruptible, and Christ’s body was formed from most pure members, wholly free from every corruption of sin. For not merely some part of holiness, but its entire fullness, is breathed forth by both his conception in the Virgin and his life among human beings; for he who was conceived without sin lived among human beings without sin. As he did not contract sin, so neither did he commit it.

Yet although he possessed no sin, he came also “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” because the shittim wood of which the ark was made, although incorruptible and strong, nevertheless resembles thorns; and in Sacred Scripture a thorn sometimes signifies the sting of sin [Col. 0759A]. But a mercy-seat was placed upon this ark, because among God’s virtues his compassion most especially commends him. Hence it is said: “God is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works.” For he came to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32), being in deed such as he is in name; for he is called Jesus because he saved his people from their sins.

Both Testaments harmoniously proclaim this most gracious and sweet compassion of his: the Old Testament through his humanity still to come, the New Testament through that same humanity now accomplished—like two cherubim turning their faces toward one and the same mercy-seat of the ark, looking both upon one another and upon the mercy-seat itself [Col. 0759B]. In this ark are manna, the tablets, and the rod, because in Christ are the sweetness of mercy, the fullness of wisdom, and the equity of justice. The tablets are in the ark because in Christ “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”; the rod is in it because “the Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22); and manna is also in it because, as was said above—and ought often to be said and never consigned to forgetfulness—“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:32). The tablets, therefore, belong to wisdom; the rod, to justice; manna, to mercy.

“Advance prosperously, proceed, and reign, because of truth, meekness, and justice” [Col. 0759C] (Ps. 44:5). Advance, O wise one; proceed, O merciful one; reign, O mighty one. “Advance,” he says, O wise one, because of the fullness of truth which is in the tablets; “proceed,” O merciful one, because of the sweetness of meekness which is in the manna; “reign,” O mighty one, because of the equity of justice which is in the rod. And do these things in your beauty and loveliness: in beauty, because of the gold; in loveliness, because of the shittim wood. You are so beautiful in the gold of divinity that angels desire to look into you; so lovely in the incorruptible wood of humanity that the prophet David declares you “more beautiful in form than the sons of men,” you whom God the Father anointed “with the oil of gladness above your companions” (ibid., v. 3).

CLIV. Two poles, inserted through four rings, carry this ark, because preachers to the circumcised and to the uncircumcised, instructed by the sayings of the four Evangelists, proclaim and manifest to the world both natures of Christ, divine and human [Col. 0759D]. These three things which are in the ark—which signifies our Lord Jesus Christ—are indicated by the three steps which we placed in the lower part of the ark itself. Thus the ark contains these three things: manna of meekness, rod of justice, tablets of truth. Justice pertains to the reprobate, meekness to the elect, and truth to both.

Meekness pertains to the elect because their being absolved belongs to the sweetness of his mercy. Justice pertains to the reprobate because the equity of his strict justice decrees that they be condemned. Truth pertains to both because, in showing justice to the former and mercy to the latter, he shows himself true to both [Col. 0760A], [426] when he renders to the former the punishment which he has threatened and to the righteous the glory which he has promised. “Those who have done good,” he says, “will come forth to the resurrection of life” (John 5:29): behold the glory which he promises to the elect. “But those who have done evil [will come forth] to the resurrection of judgment” (ibid.): behold the punishment which he threatens to the reprobate.

This is the truth which is eternally in our ark: in it those who are to be saved are immutably predestined, and those who are to be damned are foreknown. This truth, together with the manna of meekness pertaining to the elect and the rod of justice pertaining to the reprobate, both reprobate and elect will fully see to be present in the ark of which we speak, when that will be fulfilled which the same ark declares in the Gospel, both threatening and promising: “And these”—without doubt, the reprobate—“will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” [Col. 0760B] (Matt. 25:26).

Therefore the ark which shines in the Holy of Holies presents itself to us as terrible through the rod and lovable through the manna; and manna and rod alike commend truth, because from eternity and unto eternity the election of God’s children and the reprobation of the children of perdition are both true, so that the reprobate do not attain salvation and the elect do not incur damnation. Therefore these three are in the ark: the rod, the tablets, and manna; and these three are expressed by the three steps placed upon the ark itself in its lower part.

## CHAPTER IX. On the head of the worm, portrayed in the Holy Place to the north opposite the candlestick; and on the seven lamps of that candlestick, expounded morally. On the tablets, rod, and manna which were in the ark.

[Col. 0760C]

CLV. Because, on account of the different meanings, one and the same thing in Sacred Scripture can be understood in several ways, provided one does not depart from the unity of faith, we think it not unfitting that the outer house of the tabernacle—which a little earlier, for the reason then given, we said signified the body of any holy person—should now, conversely and for another reason, be referred according to another meaning to the mind of that same holy person. Your diligence ought not carelessly to overlook the fact that, just as the inner tabernacle, according to the anagogical sense, signifies the hidden mystery of the heavenly homeland, of which something has already briefly been said [Col. 0760D], so the outer tabernacle may also, according only to the tropological interpretation, signify the hidden mystery of the mind.

For here, meanwhile, we rest in merit, so that there afterwards we may rest in reward; here in holiness, there in blessedness. Here, that is, in the hidden place of the mind, we secretly receive the hidden snares of the hidden enemy; having received them, we endure them laboriously; having endured them, we detect them prudently; having detected them, we overcome them courageously. Here we are enlightened and kindled by the sevenfold light of the Holy Spirit. Here we burn sweetly before him through prayers; there, however, we shall see him face to face. Here, finally, we labor in many ways so that there we may be happily crowned.

Therefore, in the outer tabernacle [Col. 0761A], which signifies the hidden place of the mind, opposite the candlestick which is set on the south, I portray, projecting beneath the table, the unsightly head of a certain horrible worm in the north, “from which every evil is spread over all the earth.” This head sends forth from its mouth and nostrils a blackest cloud. Opposite it I light seven lamps in the candlestick, because by the light of the sevenfold Spirit, signified by the south, we detect the dark temptations of that cold north so that we may overcome them.

We must carefully observe this concerning that harmful head of the venomous enemy: it emits a threefold smoke from its mouth and nostrils, because there is a threefold ignorance by which it is accustomed to deceive the human soul—ignorance of good and evil, of true and false, of beneficial and harmful. By this threefold ignorance it darkens the reprobate so greatly that, inwardly blinded, they sometimes judge evil to be good and good to be evil; false to be true and true to be false; beneficial to be harmful and harmful to be beneficial [Col. 0761B]. Of these the prophet cries aloud: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter” (Isa. 5:20). They put light for darkness and darkness for light who think that what is true is false and what is false true. Moreover, they put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter who take what is beneficial for harmful and what is harmful for beneficial.

This is the cloud which the prophet Ezekiel saw [427] coming from the north in God’s vision: “I looked, and behold, a storm-wind came from the north, and a great cloud” [Col. 0761C] (Ezek. 1:4). The prophet Isaiah also saw the darkness of this smoke rising from the north when he said: “From the north smoke shall come, and there is none who escapes its ranks” (Isa. 14:31). For the ancient enemy first darkens the minds of the reprobate, taking from them the light of truth; afterwards he inflames them, leading them to criminal action. First he darkens them by gloom; then he inflames them by the heat of desire. Thus that tempter emits both smoke and fire from his mouth, so that he may simultaneously cloud the human soul through blindness and set it ablaze through covetousness [Col. 0761D].

CLVI. But because our purpose in this painting was rather to show how that venomous enemy tempts the elect in their minds, how he is detected while tempting them, and how, once detected, he is defeated by them, than to show how he overcomes the reprobate through their consent: we portrayed only smoke in the worm’s mouth, by which temptation is signified. We lit seven lamps in the candlestick, signifying the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, by which holy persons both detect the hidden enemy’s temptations in the tabernacle of their hearts and conquer them once detected. But we did not put fire in the mouth of the aforesaid worm, by which fire concupiscence is signified—the concupiscence that burns up the minds of the reprobate.

Furthermore, in order to denote the author and instigator of wickedness, a worm of this kind seemed to me more suitable and fitting than many others [Col. 0762A]. For although the serpent itself and certain other worms sometimes perhaps signify something good in Sacred Scripture, I do not recall ever finding this one in a good signification. Therefore, when this horrible worm coming from the north has scattered against us the threefold smoke discussed above, before we are darkened or set ablaze by that worm, let us have the seven lamps of the southern candlestick lit in the tabernacle of our hearts. For we must be both enlightened by the light and kindled by the ardor of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, in order that, being enlightened, we may prudently detect the cunning wickednesses of the often-mentioned enemy and, being kindled, may courageously overcome them [Col. 0762B].

Therefore at each lamp of the candlestick I write one gift of the Holy Spirit: Wisdom is written at the lamp which is at the top; Understanding on one side of it, and Counsel on the other. Then the other four gifts are placed on either side, because by these three gifts—namely, the gift of wisdom, understanding, and counsel—we detect the venomous wickednesses of the ancient enemy; but by the remaining four—namely, the gift of fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear—we overcome them when detected.

CLVII. In the inner tabernacle, however, is the ark; and in the ark, as has often already been said, these three things are contained: the rod, the tablets, and manna. For in heaven the eternal Godhead reigns, and in this Godhead three persons are believed to be coeternal, coequal, and consubstantial with one another: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0762C]. Since power is denoted by the rod, the Father is not unfittingly understood through the rod. Since the fullness of knowledge was in the tablets, the Son is also fittingly understood through the same tablets. Since manna is said to have been sweet and savory food, the Holy Spirit is rightly expressed through manna. For power is assigned to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit; yet these three are one in God substantially, although personally distinct. Therefore the rod, tablets, and manna were in the Holy of Holies, which signifies heaven, because “there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0762D] (1 John 5:7). These three are indicated by the three steps portrayed in the upper part of the ark beneath the mercy-seat itself.

Thus nine steps are placed in the ark of which we speak: three in its northern part, three in its lower part, and three in its upper part. To repeat briefly some matters discussed more fully above: the three steps placed in the northern part of the ark express, according to the moral sense, the three things in the human soul—memory, signified by the rod; reason, by the tablets; and will, by manna. The steps in its lower part indicate the three things which are in Christ: the equity of justice, understood in the rod; the fullness of knowledge, in the tablets; and the sweetness of mercy [Col. 0763A], in manna. Through the three steps in its upper part we also understand the three persons believed in and worshiped in the one Godhead: first, the Father, whose power we judge may be signified by the rod; the Son, whose wisdom is signified by the tablets; and the Holy Spirit, whose sweetness is signified by manna.

[428] ## CHAPTER X. On the altar of incense and the paintings relating to that altar.

CLVIII. It remains for us now also to say something tropologically about the altar of incense, so that we may seem to have omitted none of the things within the tabernacle itself, whether those in the Holy Place or those in the Holy of Holies. This altar stood outside the veil in the Holy Place; and according to the moral sense it signifies nothing other than a mind clean and kindled by the fire of divine love [Col. 0763B]. Upon it, as upon a gilded altar, we offer our prayers to God as incense of good and sweet fragrance.

Therefore, in our picture, before the altar of incense outside the veil, I portray a certain high priest clothed in high-priestly vestments and offering incense upon that altar with a golden censer, so that we, who are a royal priesthood, may strive to offer to God the sweet incense of prayer upon the altar of the mind. But we must take every care, with God’s help, to prepare ourselves before the time of prayer to be such as we desire to be found before God, whom we pray, at the very time of prayer.

For we must continually reflect that, according to the Psalmist’s saying, “If we have regarded iniquity in our heart, the Lord will not hear” [Col. 0763C] (Ps. 65:18). Therefore, because he himself had not regarded iniquity in his heart, he says: “For this reason God heard me and attended to the voice of my supplication” (ibid., v. 19). Thus it is necessary that, as far as we can by God’s gift, we cleanse our heart before the very time of our prayer from every emptiness of phantasms, so that in prayer we may be able to raise the unconstrained face of the mind. As Augustine admonishes in our Rule: “When we pray God with psalms and hymns, let us turn over in our hearts what we utter with our mouths.”

For some persons, when they ought to devote themselves to prayer, continually revolve in their minds the clamor of earthly affairs and the tumult of worldly occupations; and while they are distracted by so many and such great things, they do not themselves apprehend what they utter with their mouths [Col. 0763D]. Very many others, like myself, frequently admit into their minds, during prayer, the troublesome flies of invading phantasms; hence it happens to them that they do not know at all what they are saying. Others, made foolish by still greater madness, when they pray to God, turn over within themselves the foul images of their past iniquities: they delightfully recall in their minds the persons, places, and times with whom, when, and where they committed their wicked acts. And though they come to prayer in order to beg forgiveness for what they have done unlawfully, in prayer itself they commit those very things through delight in sordid thoughts [Col. 0764A], for which they need to pray still more earnestly.

This threefold kind of thought miserably devastates us who are weak during the very time of prayer: burdensome thought, idle thought, and affective thought. Burdensome thought is to be excessively scattered in mind through the clamor of earthly concerns and the tumult of secular occupations; idle thought concerns the vanities of invading phantasms; affective thought concerns pleasurable recollections of former sins. But if we wish our prayer to emit something sweet before God upon the altar of the mind, we must make every effort, when we apply ourselves to prayer, to cast all these things behind the back of the mind through complete forgetfulness, as far as we can with the Lord’s aid, and to direct its face, as far as possible, toward what we utter.

Therefore we have portrayed three steps behind the back of the aforesaid high priest standing at the altar [Col. 0764B], because whoever desires his prayer to be fruitful must drive this threefold thought behind the back of the mind when praying, so that, insofar as divine grace grants him the ability, during the time of prayer there may not enter into his breast either a piercing care, an invading phantasm, or a seductive sin.

CLIX. But after he has expelled these things from himself, he must nevertheless attend carefully in his mind to these four points. First, namely, who it is that prays; second, who it is whom he prays to; third, what that is for which he prays; and fourth, how he prays. [Col. 0764C] Therefore, considering himself who prays, let him see himself to be such: so inclined to vices, so weak for virtues, so sluggish toward good, so ready for evil, entangled besides in so many miseries, and finally burdened by so many and such great loads of sins, that he may know with complete certainty that by his own merits he deserves to obtain absolutely nothing from God. But let him regard Him whom he prays to as both powerful and merciful: merciful to show pity, powerful to bring aid; who both can and wills to hear His elect who worthily call upon Him, because in some sense He both feels their danger through compassion and grants help through power. Thus, earnest examination of yourself gives you sorrow, and careful consideration of divine mercy [Col. 0764D] gives you hope, so that you may firmly trust that, because of His mercy, you will obtain what, because of your frailty, you had not dared to presume upon.

It follows that you should also see what you ask. What else ought we to ask for but these three things: pardon, grace, and glory? Pardon for sins, grace for merits, glory for rewards. Through pardon for sins, by means of the grace of merits, one arrives at the glory of rewards. By the first we are cleansed; by the second adorned; by the third made blessed. Therefore all who ask in the name of Jesus are accustomed to ask for these three things with all devotion: namely, pardon, grace, and glory—that almighty and merciful God may mercifully wash away the evils that are in them, abundantly confer the goods they lack, steadfastly preserve the goods bestowed, and at the end [Col. 0765A] grant them without end the joys of His blessed vision.

Lastly, you must consider how you ask: that is, you must ask your Lord fervently and pray perseveringly, so that, applying yourself to prayer with a certain fervent perseverance and persevering fervour, you may hold in supreme desire that which you ask; and may not cease from prayer until you obtain what you ask. These, then, are the four things which, at the time of prayer, you must keep diligently before the eyes of the mind: that you may consider most attentively who you yourself are who pray, who He is whom you pray to, what that is for which you pray, and finally how you pray—so that you may pour forth a prayer pleasing to God and fruitful for yourself. Therefore, after we had depicted the three steps behind the back of the priest standing at the altar, we also placed [Col. 0765B] four others before his face, that you may know that, when you pray, you must cast those three evil thoughts behind the back of the mind and keep these four good things before the sight of the heart.

CLX. After all this, it is necessary that, as the Lord Himself admonishes in the Gospel: “When you stand to pray, forgive, if you have anything in your heart, that your Father may forgive you” (Matt. V, 24). And know, as Solomon says, that “he who turns away his ear so as not to hear the poor man shall himself cry out and shall not be heard” (Prov. XXI, 13). Therefore, if you wish your prayer to be fruitful, you must both forgive from the heart those who sin against you, and effectively incline, for God’s sake, an ear of hearing toward those who make requests of you according to God.

You pray that something may be forgiven you and given to you: forgiven, the sin you have committed; given, both merit and reward—merit, I say, of a good life; reward, of blessed glory. And you, too, forgive and give: forgive those who offend against you; give to those who ask you. Accordingly, after the steps of which we have spoken above, we also placed two beneath that verse, “Let my prayer be directed” (Ps. CXL, 2), which the priest says. Thus, if you desire to pray rightly, keep in your heart by memory and practise effectively in deed what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke VI, 37). Forgive, therefore, the injuries brought against you, and grant the benefits requested of you, so that both the sins which you have committed before God may be forgiven you, and the eternal life which you ask of Him may be given you. [Col. 0765D] Let this suffice, morally interpreted, concerning the things that were within the walls of the tabernacle, and concerning that place of the tabernacle called the Holy Place and that called the Holy of Holies.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the coverings and representations of the tabernacle that pertained to the altar of burnt offering, and how they are to be understood according to the moral sense.

CLXI. We have been detained a very long time in the exposition of the tabernacle’s walls and of the things within those same walls. It remains now for us to leave the tabernacle itself, in which we have lingered so long, and consider how the things outside it ought to be understood, solely according to the tropological sense. Yet first let us say something, as we are able, concerning the coverings of that [Col. 0766A] ancient tabernacle in their moral meaning.

We know indeed, as has been fully shown above, that the visible tabernacle of Moses was first covered with curtains extending almost to the ground, and then altogether, on every side, with coverings extending to the ground. The roof of the tabernacle itself was first covered over the coverings with rams’ skins dyed red, and then overlaid with violet-blue skins. You too must cover your tabernacle with curtains, coverings, red-dyed skins, and violet-blue skins—but spiritually. For your tabernacle is spiritual, and therefore must be covered with spiritual coverings.

The curtains were ten in number and woven from four colours: violet-blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen. These curtains touched the gilded boards of the walls more closely than the other coverings, and covered everything within them. Although they covered the aforesaid walls all around externally, they did not extend entirely down to the ground, but stood one cubit above the ground on every side all round. What, do you think, do these things signify? Let us briefly show what we think of them.

These ten curtains, which both touch the boards most closely and cover the things within them, morally represent those holy persons who have chosen to serve God in a hidden manner of life, and who are able to fulfil the commandments of the Decalogue more perfectly in action to the extent that they have more fully stripped their minds of earthly cares. These curtains are fittingly made from the four colours mentioned above and woven in beautiful variety, because such saints, serving the Lord in hidden repose, shine before God’s eyes both through the fair diversity of holiness and through the varied splendour of virtues: gleaming with desire for the heavenly homeland; resisting the tyranny of vices with a kind of royal authority; burning with the fire of twofold charity; and shining in bodily chastity’s brightness.

For the violet-blue colour, which resembles the sky when it is serene, signifies heavenly desire. Purple, which belongs to a king’s adornment, signifies spiritual dominion over the assaults of vices. Twice-dyed scarlet expresses twofold charity, namely love of God and of neighbour. Linen, which springs from the earth with a shining appearance, indicates bodily chastity. That these curtains do not reach down to the ground is not to be thought devoid of mystery; rather, by this we are taught that holy persons devoted to the quiet life do not wish to cling to earthly things or secular business either by care or by affection, but fix their hearts where they know their treasure to be.

The coverings, too, which cover the curtains and protect them against every injury of storms assailing from without, so that they may shine clean within, are the prelates of the holy Church, diligently devoted to pastoral care with wakeful concern. They protect from outward impediments those who devote themselves to the repose of secret and inward sweetness. If perhaps, as persons entangled in earthly cares and at times involved in secular disturbances, they commit some fault, they do not fail immediately to scrape it away with the sharp razors of penance; for these same coverings were eleven in number and made of hair-cloth. By the number eleven is understood transgression of the law; by hair-cloth, made from goats’ skins, which of old used to be offered under the Law for sin, is understood compunction of mind. The coverings, therefore, were eleven and of hair-cloth, because if any elevenfold transgression stains a holy prelate of holy Church, the hair-cloth of compunction washes it away.

CLXII. To speak briefly of the two coverings that were made of skins and covered not the tabernacle’s walls but only its roof: the red-dyed rams’ skins are the saints who shed their blood for Christ’s name; and the violet-blue skins likewise are saints who, through incorruption, lead on earth a heavenly manner of life in the body, as angels do. Therefore, if in the chamber of your mind you carefully store the hidden life of those who live quietly in the Church, the compunction of good prelates, the patience of martyrs, and the incorruption of virgins; if you kindle your heart’s desire toward their holiness, and resolve, according to your ability, to imitate them: then indeed you hang beautiful curtains, hair-cloth coverings, red-dyed skins, and violet-blue skins over your boards.

But, as was said in the second part of this book, neither the curtains nor the coverings nor the skins of which we have now said so much can be seen by the bodily eye in this picture of ours, which lies in a plane. For the curtains are covered all around with coverings so that they do not appear, as has been sufficiently shown above; and the coverings are understood to be almost entirely hidden beneath the three walls lying in the plane of the picture, and beneath the tent which lies toward the east in the picture; and the roof of the walls is not seen at all when the walls themselves lie in the plane of the picture. Nevertheless, so that these coverings may be reckoned as visibly present in that visible tabernacle of Moses, and in this way as spiritually required in the visible tabernacle of the mind, I write near the tabernacle itself, in the court beside the northern Levite, the word: “Curtains.” Then, a little way from this word, I write in black letters: “Coverings.” Then I write these two words, namely, “red-dyed skins,” in red letters. And likewise in violet-blue letters: “Violet-blue skins.” For, as has been said, curtains covered the boards, and coverings covered the curtains. Over these coverings, wherever the roof’s area extended, red-dyed skins were laid; and over these skins others were added, which were violet-blue.

Then, outside the tabernacle toward the east, beside the entrance of the tent, I set up the altar of burnt offering, and kindle fire upon it. Two altars belonged to that ancient tabernacle of Moses: one outside, the other within; one covered in gold, the other in bronze; finally, one on which incense was burned, the other on which animals were sacrificed. But what ought morally to be understood through that inner altar has already been shown in part. Through this altar outside, however, upon which the flesh of animals used to be offered, may figuratively be understood the minds of those who, with watchful vigilance and vigilant solicitude, devote themselves to carnal deeds: either grieving through penance for deeds they have already committed, or resisting through continence those by which they are still tempted every day.

Accordingly, at this altar in our picture I depict a Levite sacrificing upon it a red heifer with a knife, so that it may be shown that we ought to burn up on the altar of the heart, with the fire of penance, carnal deeds and those things which we have committed; and to mortify with the knife of continence those things by which we are still tempted. Above this altar I also make five steps, because the wantonness of our senses is fivefold, and we must both burn it through penance and mortify it through restraint: vanity in the sight of the eyes; curiosity in the hearing of the ears; pleasure in the smell of the nostrils; gluttony in the taste of the throat; impurity in the touch of the hands.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the bronze laver and the representations pertaining to that laver.

CLXIII. After this I make a bronze laver; and, having put water into it, I place it between the altar of burnt offering of which we have just spoken and the entrance of the tabernacle itself. This laver commends to us the washing of compunction and tears, which we always need, but especially when we approach to minister the heavenly mysteries. “Aaron and his sons,” it says, “shall wash their hands and feet when they are about to enter the tabernacle of testimony and when they approach the altar to offer incense upon it to the Lord, lest perhaps they die” (Exod. XXX, 19–20).

For spiritual and eternal death of the soul is to be feared if anyone presumes to enter the most sacred mysteries without the spiritual washing of compunction and to handle the Lord’s holy things with ordinary hands. Let them therefore wash their hands and feet in the water of the bronze laver, and thus approach the altar: that is, let them wash their deeds and movements with tears, and then extend their hands to touch Christ’s mysteries and set their feet’s steps in the courts of the Lord.

Therefore, at this laver which we have made in our picture, we have depicted two priests, one washing his hands and the other his feet, because, when we are about to offer the Lord sacrifices of prayer, we must cleanse in the waters of compunction and the laver of confession both the heart’s affections, signified through the feet, and bodily acts, signified through the hands. At this bronze laver I also make four steps, somewhat separated from one another, because whoever wishes to acquire full compunction in himself must carefully consider these four things: namely, where he was; where he is; where he does not wish to be; and where he desires to be. Where he was: in sin. Where he is: in the world. Where he does not wish to be: in hell. Where he desires to be: in heaven.

The place, therefore, in which we were is sin. This was in us in three ways: in heart, in mouth, and in body. In the heart, in two ways: through love of the world, which raised us up in the vanity of pride; through love of the flesh, which befouled us with the pleasure of corruption. Likewise in the mouth, in two ways: through arrogance, when we used proudly to exalt ourselves over our own good qualities; through detraction, when through envy we disparaged our neighbour’s good qualities. In the body also, in two ways: through shameful vice, by which we lasciviously defiled ourselves; through criminal wrongdoing, by which we perversely injured our neighbours. Behold the place in which we were.

But the place in which we now are is this world. For although we are not of the world, we are nevertheless in the world, because, though perhaps we do not cling to it by affection, we must possess it for use. And this place is hostile to us in three ways, because it rages against us through the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life. For, as the apostle John says, “All that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John II, 16). This is that three-pronged fork by which flesh is lifted from the cauldrons in the Book of Kings (1 Sam. II, 13). These same three things also delay all carnal persons from the Lord’s supper, to which they are invited in the Gospel. For taking a wife belongs to concupiscence of the flesh; buying five yokes of oxen, to concupiscence of the eyes; buying an estate, to pride of life (Luke XIV, 18 ff.). These are the three evils which rage against us from this world so long as we remain in it.

CLXIV. There is still a twofold danger, arising from ourselves, which is very hostile to us. One pertains to the body, the other to the soul. The danger pertaining to the body is fivefold. In our body there are ugliness, dryness, infirmity, servitude, and corruption. Our body is ugly, sluggish, weak, subject to harsh and dreadful servitude, and liable to manifold and miserable corruption.

But the soul’s danger in this world is threefold; for our soul is sick with a threefold disease: in memory, reason, and will. In memory, through the weakness of instability; in reason, through the darkness of ignorance; in will, through the perversity of wickedness. The weakness of memory is threefold, because it is weakened by affective, burdensome, and idle thought. Affective thought is when it is occupied with necessities, such as thoughts of eating, drinking, clothing, and the like. Burdensome thought is when it is weighed down by thinking about external matters: for example, when one considers what is to be acquired, spent, built, planted, and the like. Idle thought is that with which one is neither occupied as with necessities nor burdened as with external matters, yet by which one is hindered from thinking good thoughts: as when one thinks of a running horse, a flying bird, a swimming fish, or something of that kind. Affective thought makes the soul anxious about itself; idle thought alienates it from itself; burdensome thought casts it down beneath itself.

The ignorance of reason is likewise threefold: ignorance, namely, of good and evil, truth and falsehood, advantage and disadvantage. Therefore it has lost that threefold instrument of philosophy by which it ought to have known these things: ethics, logic, and physics. For good and evil are known through ethics; advantage and disadvantage through physics; truth and falsehood through logic.

These three things commonly devastate the will: vanity, curiosity, and pleasure—vanity of spiritual pride, curiosity of worldly delight, pleasure of carnal concupiscence. Vanity exalts and blinds the human soul’s will; curiosity disperses it and alienates it from itself; pleasure affects and befouls it. Vanity pertains to the world’s temporal power; curiosity, to the mind’s empty delight; pleasure, to the foul concupiscence of the flesh. Behold the soul’s threefold disease: weakness, which debilitates memory’s strength; ignorance, which darkens reason’s light; perversity, which stains the purity of the will.

But because its sickness is very great, divine grace rather than any human power or skill will cure it. For it belongs to the creative Trinity to reform this trinity, which It created in Its own image and likeness. Therefore God the Father must be invoked with humble and devout prayer to heal the memory; God the Son, to heal the reason; God the Holy Spirit, to heal the will. For the Father, through power, creates fear in the heart, and this orders and strengthens the memory. The Son, through wisdom, pours knowledge into the heart, and this illuminates and clarifies reason. The Holy Spirit, through loving-kindness, grants charity to the heart, and this cleanses and fits the will. This, then, concerns the three evils by which this world—the place in which we now are—is hostile to us; and this concerns the two dangers which we endure in it, one afflicting us in the body and the other in the soul.

CLXV. In the third place, however, there are three things: fire, the worm, and the eternity of both; for the former is said to be unquenchable and the latter immortal. “Their worm,” he says, “shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXVI, 24; Mark IX, 43, 45, 47). These three are in the third place, and in that place they are as it were a threefold dwelling, which the reprobate reach by an equally threefold road. Their way is threefold: delight, consent, and habit. From delight they go to consent; from consent, to habit. Through delight they are weakened; through consent they die; through habit they are buried. By this threefold road they come to that threefold dwelling: namely, to the burning of fire, the bite of the worm, and the eternity of both. Through delight they go to the fire; through consent, to the worm; through habit, to the eternity of both: so that the flesh which delighted in sin may be burned by the fire; the soul which consented to the flesh may be gnawed by the worm; and, because of the habit of sin, it may feel the eternity of both, because the former is unquenchable and the latter is called immortal. And just as it never wished to end its fault, so may it never end its punishment. This concerns the third place.

In the fourth place, three things will be given to the elect by the very Rewarder of merits and Distributor of rewards: strength of power, from the Father, supreme Power, that they may be powerful in themselves; brightness of wisdom, from the Son, true Wisdom, that they may be wise in God; sweetness of love, from the Holy Spirit, sweet Charity, that they may love one another—so that in this manner God may be all in all (1 Cor. XV, 28). But because we have spoken of these matters rather fully above, when discussing the rings of the boards, we avoid lingering longer over them.

There are, then, these four places: the first, where we remember that we were; the second, where we perceive that we are; the third, where we dread being; the fourth, from which we do not wish to be absent. The first place is called the pleasure of the flesh; the second, the calamity of the world; the third, the harshness of hell; the fourth, the happiness of heaven. These are the four places from which fourfold waters flow. From careful consideration of the first place flows in us the water of sorrow, because we grieve that we were such persons. From the second flows the water of fear, because we fear lest we should still happen to be such. From the third flows the water of horror, because we fear falling there. From the fourth flows the water of love, because we desire to attain it. In the first place there are shame and sorrow; in the second, labour and fear; in the third, terror and horror; in the fourth, savour and love.

CLXVI. From these four places, therefore, four fountains flow which water the Lord’s garden. From the first place, the place of one’s own guilt, flows weeping; and this is the water that goes around the land of Havilah, that is, those bringing forth the new life. For *Evilath* [Havilah] means “a woman in labour,” and gold is produced in that land; because “he who increases knowledge also increases sorrow” (Eccles. I, 18).

> [Note: [Col. 0771D] The Vulgate has *laborem*, “toil”; the Septuagint has ἄλγημα, that is, “sorrow”—which the Vulgate word *labor* indeed names elegantly. —ED. P.]

From the second place flows compassion for the manifold misery which we endure in the present life. This is the water that goes around the land of Ethiopia. From the third comes dread of the punishment of Gehenna. This is the water that goes toward the Assyrians. From the fourth comes an affective and longing expectation of the heavenly homeland, rich in the fruit of life. This water is called Euphrates, because Euphrates received its name from fruit.

These waters also flow to us abundantly from the most merciful and sweetest Redeemer Himself, the Lord Jesus. For in the Gospel He is read to have wept twice, whereas He is nowhere found ever to have laughed even once.

> [Note: [Col. 0772D] The same words are read in that apocryphal portrait so often celebrated under the name of Publius Lentulus. —ED. P.]

He wept at Lazarus’s tomb (John XI, 35); He wept over the city of Jerusalem (Luke XIX, 41); before the Passion He sweated when, having entered into agony, He prayed more earnestly (Luke XXII, 43); and, now dead but still fixed to the cross, He sent forth from His side not blood only but also water (John XIX, 34). Behold the four fluids that are ministered to us by the Lord Jesus Himself for our cleansing—the Lord Jesus whom Holy Scripture calls a living fountain, and whom the prophet calls “a fountain opened for the house of David” to wash the sinner and the menstruous woman (Zech. XIII, 1).

Of the first fluid it is written: “And Jesus wept” (John XI, 35). Of the second: “Seeing the city, He wept over it, saying: ‘For if you had known, you also …’” (Luke XIX, 41). Of the third: “His sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground” (Luke XXII, 43). Of the fourth: “One of the soldiers opened His side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out” (John XIX, 34).

The Lord Jesus’ weeping at Lazarus’s tomb signifies the water which we draw from consideration of the place in which we remember that we were: when we grieve that we were weighed down by the stone of obstinacy, rotted in the cave of foul concupiscence, dead through consent to sin, and buried through habit. But those tears which He shed in weeping over the city of Jerusalem indicate to us the water which we conceive from considering the place in which we now are, when we fear lest our enemies surround us with a rampart, press us in on every side, cast us down to the ground, and leave in us not one stone upon another. [Col. 0772B] All these things also happen morally in us in the present, when evil spirits besiege us with temptations, trouble us with afflictions, cause us to slip down toward earthly things, and permit no thought in us to remain stable or firm.

But the sweat which that innocent Lamb produced in His agony figuratively expresses the water produced by the dreadful sight of the third place, when we fear lest those spiritual Jews seize us and deliver us over to eternal death. But when, lifted above all visible things through contemplation, and, through complete contempt for visible things, wholly deadened to all things that are in the world, we have been stretched out upon the cross of charity, then surely we are sprinkled with that water which the crucified and dead Lord Jesus emits from His side.

CLXVII. The first water is that of a fountain and gives drink to the thirsty; the second is that of a river and waters the dry; the third is that of the sea and boils the raw; the fourth is that of snow and whitens the black. It gives drink through sorrow, waters through fear, boils through horror, whitens through love. To the first two belongs lamentation for present misery; to the third, the woe of Gehenna; to the fourth, the flesh of glory. The four steps placed in the laver signify these four waters.

But because there are two defilements from which we must be cleansed—sin, namely, and offence—we placed two steps beside the priest who washes his hands, so that we may grieve both that we have committed what ought not to be done and that we have omitted what ought to be done. Again, because we must have a threefold confession in our cleansing—humble, pure, and faithful—we placed three steps beside the other priest who washes his feet. Let our confession be pure, humble, and faithful: pure, lest we conceal anything; humble, lest we take pride in our evils; faithful, lest we despair of pardon. It must be pure against dissimulation, humble against self-exaltation, faithful against despair.

Since, moreover, neither such mortification of the flesh as we mentioned in the preceding chapter nor such cleansing of the mind as we have described here can take place without great tribulation and distress, I overlay the court’s open space, where the altar of burnt offering and the bronze laver are depicted, with purple colour. We have spoken more extensively than we expected concerning the bronze laver and the things pertaining to it.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the tents of the tabernacle, and Moses’ entrance into the tabernacle and his departure from it.

CLXVIII. After this we must carefully consider that the ancient tabernacle of Moses was surrounded on every side with tents. Similarly, if you do not neglect to guard with strong caution the good things you possess, you set up tents around your tabernacle and the things within it. For it will profit you nothing at all to have gathered spiritual goods within yourself unless you preserve them by diligent and careful circumspection. Hence we read in Sacred Scripture that God placed man in paradise “to work it and guard it” (Gen. II, 15).

God places man in paradise when, freely bestowing upon you a delightful abundance of spiritual graces, He causes you to rest sweetly in a holy and tranquil conscience. But see that you both guard and work this paradise: work it by the strength of fortitude; guard it by the protection of circumspection. Work diligently, and guard carefully; work, finally, in order spiritually to acquire spiritual virtues; guard, lest you carelessly lose what you have acquired. Therefore first construct, in the way I have instructed you, both the tabernacle and those things which ought to be in it; but diligently set up a tent around it, so that you may first build up good things in yourself through earnest exercise and then strive to preserve them through prudent circumspection of life.

After this, your diligence ought not to leave unexamined what is signified by the fact that holy Moses of old, whenever he either doubted some matter or endured any tribulations, always fled to the tabernacle: so that he might consult the Lord concerning his doubt and receive from Him defence and consolation. Moses enters the tabernacle many times and departs from it. He enters in order to consult the Lord; he departs in order to instruct the people. Within the tabernacle he receives commands from the Lord, which he delivers to the people outside; and he who sweetly hears the Lord speaking to him within carefully concerns himself outside with the people’s causes and affairs.

What do you think, my brothers, does this entrance and departure of his signify? We have often said above that, according to the tropological meaning, Moses’ tabernacle represents the secret place of the soul. We enter this tabernacle when, setting earthly cares aside for a time, we devote ourselves in love of God, in the inward secrecy of the heart, to sweet meditation, pure reflection, and clarified contemplation. But we depart from this tabernacle when, laying aside somewhat the pursuit of contemplation, we apply ourselves, out of compassion for our neighbour, to lawful occupations with earthly things.

In this way, therefore, we enter and depart. We enter, I say, and depart; and by entering and departing we find pasture, so that by entering piously, departing justly, and feeding temperately, we may live in this world: piously toward God, because of pure contemplation; justly toward our neighbour, because of fruitful action; temperately toward ourselves, because of right intention. Thus we enter in order to contemplate; we depart in order to act. We contemplate eternal and heavenly things; we work with transitory and earthly things—the former through the heart’s affection, the latter for the body’s use.

Within, we contemplate the divinity of Wisdom Himself, begotten from the Father before eternity without a mother; outside, we imitate the humanity of that same Wisdom, incarnate from a mother in time without a father. In a certain book we read both within and without: in a book, I say, written both within and without (Rev. V, 1). Within we read the things written within it; without, the things written in it without. For the mediator between God and human beings, God and man, Jesus Christ (1 Tim. II, 5), is a certain book in whom we must read, written within and without: within in divinity, without in humanity.

Therefore within the tabernacle we read the things written within in this book, when in the heart’s secrecy we behold, as it were, Christ’s divinity through purity of contemplation. But outside we read the things written without in it, when, in the public sphere of activity, we follow according to our ability His humanity through imitation in action. Within we read: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). Outside: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14).

Since, therefore, there are two lives, namely the active and the contemplative, the contemplative is indicated by entering the tabernacle, the active by departing from it. And since there are two commandments of charity, namely love of God and of neighbour: love of God leads us into contemplation; love of neighbour leads us out into action.
