We enter because of the affection of delight which proceeds from Rachel’s beauty; we depart because of the fruit of fecundity which comes from Leah’s childbearing. Moses’ entrance into the tabernacle, therefore, signifies the entrance through contemplation of any perfect person into himself; and his departure signifies the going forth into action.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the twofold image of Moses, and how the image placed outside the tent tropologically signifies Moses.

CLXIX. [Cols. 0775A–0775C] In order that this entering and going out of Moses may be visible in our picture, we have painted two images of the same Moses: one outside the tabernacle, at the entrance of the tent; the other within, to the right of the altar of incense. The image that is outside also represents the exact and proper form of Moses: there he displays to the people his horned face and appears standing in secular dress, because to be covered, as it were, with certain secular garments and common clothing is to be diligently occupied with concern for earthly affairs. But the image within, although in so far as it is clothed in pontifical vesture and offers incense to God at the altar of the incense-offering, ought properly to represent Aaron himself, the high priest, nevertheless in this place and according to this signification it must also designate Moses himself, devoted to the purity of contemplation in the inward secrecy of the heart.

Concerning this image it must indeed be carefully noted that it represents Moses’ form neither in clothing nor in face, as does that image which stands outside the tabernacle at the entrance of the tent; for he who applies himself in the innermost secrecy of the heart to the contemplation of heavenly and eternal things has a state and disposition of mind far different from that of one who, mingled with popular crowds, attends to earthly and temporal occupations. Outside, Moses both displays his horned face to the people and differs from the people in no respect in his clothing; because, however holy anyone may be, so long as he is occupied with the cares of earthly actions, it is very difficult for him not to bear in his mind a face in some measure beast-like, and in his manner of life a habit in some measure secular. But within, Moses is seen both in pontifical vestments and with an unhorned face; because when we apply ourselves from the depths of our being to the contemplation of purity, then, adorned in our manner of life with the cleanness of holiness and with unveiled face, we behold the glory of the Lord. Thus, in this place, the image of Moses that is outside signifies the active person; that which is within, the contemplative person. The former signifies the active life; the latter, the contemplative life.

The active life, moreover, is twofold, because it consists both in preaching and in action: in the preaching of truth and in the work of virtue; in preaching for the instruction of the heart, and in action for the support of the body; finally, in preaching so that we may instruct a neighbour who has gone astray, and in action so that we may relieve his need. Therefore, beside that image of Moses which is outside, both preaching and action are indicated. Preaching is indicated by the words which he speaks; action is expressed by the steps placed crosswise above his head.

CLXX. [Cols. 0775D–0776D] These steps are five in number because our good action ought to be fivefold: namely, good, voluntary, pure, discerning, and steadfast. Let it therefore be good, lest it be corrupted by any dregs of malice. Let it be voluntary, that it may be done with a willing and in no way compelled mind; for the good which you do profits you nothing if you do it unwillingly and with murmuring, because, as a certain holy man says, “No one does good unwillingly, even if what he does is good.” Thirdly, see that your action is pure, so that whatever you do, you do for this reason: that you may please the eyes of the inward Inspector alone, and seek as the sole observer of your work him whom you await as its rewarder. For if—God forbid—you act in order to be seen by people and, once seen, praised, you have already received your reward; since the reward of your work is human favour, which you sought in that very work. And therefore, if you wish God to reward your work, do what you do for God, because he will reward only that which he sees to have been done for himself alone: so that the presence of God may be the reward at recompense for those whose cause for acting was love of him.

But let your action be discerning, because discernment is the governance and, as it were, a safeguard of all virtues; and, as the common saying has it,

> Everything that is excessive turns into a vice.

Finally, endeavour that your action may be firm and stable; for it is not the one who has done and begun, but the one who has done and persevered unto the end, who will be saved (Matt. 10:22). Observe how suitably these two virtues, discernment and steadfastness, are joined together, because your work can never be firm unless it is discerning. For, as someone says:

> If you do not cease to bend the bow, it will become slack.  
> (Ovid, *Heroides*, Epistle IV, 90.)

And the same author says:

> What lacks alternating rest is not lasting;  
> this restores strength and relieves weary limbs.  
> (*Ibid.*, 87–88.)

Behold, these are the five kinds of actions which the active ought to practise: action that is good, voluntary, pure, discerning, and steadfast. The Apostle mentioned these five when he said: “I beseech you, brethren, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, your reasonable service; and do not be conformed to this age” (Rom. 12:1). “Present,” he says, “your bodies as a living sacrifice.” A sacrifice is killed in order to be offered; but a living sacrifice is a body afflicted for the Lord. Our body is a sacrifice because it has been mortified from vices. But he immediately adds, and says, “holy.” For then our work is holy, if it is done with a ready and willing mind. “Pleasing to God”: behold, pure action; for what you do pleases God when you do it for this reason alone, that you may please him. “Your reasonable service”: our service is reasonable when our work is discerning. Finally he says: “And do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the newness of your mind.” Behold steadfastness and constancy in good work. For it is customary with worldly persons sometimes to begin a good work but not to persevere long in it, because “they believe for a time, and in a time of testing fall away” (Luke 8:13). Therefore our action is fivefold: good, voluntary, pure, discerning, and steadfast—good, lest it be defiled by the filth of any malice; voluntary, lest it be done with an unwilling and compelled mind; pure, lest human favour or favouritism be sought through it; discerning, lest it be broken by the violence of excess; steadfast, lest it be abandoned before life’s end.

CLXXI. [Cols. 0777A–0777D] Those five steps, placed crosswise above Moses’ head, indicate this fivefold action. In those words, “He will raise up a prophet” (Deut. 18:15), by which he instructs laypeople, right faith is understood. In those words, “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1:16), by which he instructs clerics, holy life is expressed; for all the preaching of the saints consists in this: that we should both believe rightly and live holily.

Beside his prophecy I place first two steps, because in that Prophet there are two natures, divinity and humanity. Beside these two I place three further steps, because as there are two natures in him, so there are three essences: Word, flesh, and soul. Through the middle of these steps I draw one step which cuts across them, because our Lord Jesus Christ is only one person, who in two natures, in unity of supposit, is believed to be one Son of God and son of man, Mediator of God and humankind, God and man, Jesus Christ.

The other words, directed to priests washing themselves at the laver, in which holy life is expressed, I distinguish by steps: beneath “Wash yourselves” I place one step, and beneath “be clean” another, because if we wish to live holily and devoutly, we must earnestly, as holy preaching admonishes us, both wash ourselves and strive to be clean: that we may cleanse away former stains in ourselves and guard against future ones. Hence in the Lord’s Prayer we ask that our debts be forgiven us and that we not be led into temptation (Matt. 6:12).

On the other side of this verse are eight steps, which set before us eight things in the preaching by which holy preachers strive to stir us to a holy life: prohibition, command, permission, exhortation, rebuke, consolation, threat, and promise. For holy preachers prohibit, command, permit, exhort, rebuke, console, threaten, and promise. They prohibit evils, command goods, permit intermediate things, exhort to what is perfect, rebuke the restless, console the faint-hearted, threaten the punishments of hell, and promise the joys of the kingdom. Prohibitions are at the bottom, commands on the slope, permissions on the level, exhortations at the summit: at the bottom, matters of vice; on the slope, commandments; on the level, lawful things; at the summit, counsels. Rebukes pertain to wine, consolations to oil (Luke 10:34), threats to old things, promises to new things (Matt. 13:52). The first two pertain to the Samaritan; the second two to the scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven: to wine, which bites; to oil, which soothes; to old things, which terrify; to new things, which delight.

So much, as we were able—not as we ought—to say concerning that image of Moses placed outside the tent, through which the going out effected through action is signified.

## CHAPTER XV. On the image of Moses painted in the tabernacle, and on the two spaces in which clerics and laypeople of the Old Testament are depicted: how they ought to be understood according to the moral sense.

CLXXII. [Cols. 0778A–0778C] It is now time to discuss that image of Moses painted in the Holy Place, which, as was shown above, can be referred to Moses himself. This, then, as has been said above, signifies the secret of inward contemplation. Here Moses hears the voice of the Lord speaking to him from the midst of the two cherubim; he hears, I say, his word, but sees no form or appearance of him. For when we apply ourselves to the purity of contemplation in the secret place of the mind, we ought devoutly to raise the ear of the heart to ineffable things which are uttered to us without syllables and words, without movement of lips; but we must prudently close the imaginary eyes of a foolish mind, lest in that unbounded light we fabricate something corporeal.

Thus Elijah, when he heard the whisper of a gentle breeze, covered his face with his cloak (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19:3). We too hear the whisper of a gentle breeze when by sudden contemplation we subtly taste the savour of unbounded truth. But after the whisper of the gentle breeze we ought to cover our face with a cloak, so that in that most subtle contemplation of truth we may humbly acknowledge how great is the ignorance that veils us. For to draw the cloak over one’s face is to veil the mind, by consideration of its own weakness, so that it does not dare to seek higher things; so that it may not rashly open the eyes of understanding beyond itself, but reverently close itself to what it is unable to grasp.

Therefore the Word of God, which sounds from the midst of the two cherubim in the Holy of Holies, is heard by the contemplating Moses, who is in the Holy Place outside the veil; but no form or appearance is seen by him. God addresses Moses the contemplator, and, without a word sounding outwardly in passing, tells him, where he is enclosed above himself in the tabernacle of the heart, what he is in himself, what he is in the elect, and also what he is in the reprobate. And our contemplator hears God declaring in the ear of his mind that his Lord is in himself wholly incomprehensible, in the elect lovable, and in the reprobate terrible. He plainly shows himself to be incomprehensible in himself, because the contemplator endeavours to contemplate in him what personal distinction and consubstantial unity are.

CLXXIII. [Cols. 0778D–0780A] In the ear of contemplation, in the inward and secret tabernacle of the heart, while God himself instructs him through the anointing that teaches concerning all things (1 John 2:27), he hears that there are three in him and that these three are one; that one is these three; and that these three, and this one, are he himself. He hears a voice saying to him from the midst of the two cherubim that he is Alpha and Omega, “ὰ and ὼ” (Rev. 1:8); and that there is one who is from no one, one who is from another, and one who is from both: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He hears that each of these is what the other is, but that none of these is the one who is the other; so that neither personal property may in the least be confused nor unity of substance divided.

He also hears that he is three and one, superior to all things: governing what is below, sustaining what is within, filling what is without; encompassing all things and sweetly ordering the courses of times, the motions of bodies, and the impulses of minds; establishing for every creature law, weight, measure, and number: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). He hears further that he moves, orders, and unfolds all things; and that no time can equal his eternity, no place his immensity, no virtue his goodness, no intellect his wisdom, no work his power; and that he is everywhere, yet comprehended nowhere: knowing present being, foreknowing what is future, ordering what is to be done, predestining those to be saved, providing for those subject to him—three and one.

He hears that in the Trinity there is eternity, admitting immutability and excluding time; and immensity, corresponding to simplicity and admitting no quantity. He hears that the Trinity possesses communion of unity, equality of immensity, and coeternity of eternity. Division does not separate the first; defect does not diminish the second; succession does not order the third. Our contemplator further hears that his God is in every thing without being defined by it; in every time without changeability; and that he can neither be divided by reason of his simplicity, defiled by reason of his purity, nor comprehended by reason of his immensity. In this way he hears that his Lord is altogether incomprehensible in himself.

But in his elect, the eternity of predestination, the grace of holiness, and the glory of blessedness proclaim him lovable. For “those whom he predestined, he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30). The purpose of almighty God and his sentence of peace over his elect stand firm, so that in a wonderful manner not only good things, but even evils themselves cooperate for their good. These people in some manner have never sinned, because even if they seem perhaps to have committed offences in time, these do not appear in eternity; for the love of their Father covers a multitude of sins.

Conversely, over rational reprobate creatures keeps watch—keeps watch, I say—the immovable, most secret, and most severe scrutiny of God’s just judgment, terrible in counsel over the children of humankind. In the reprobate, contempt of whatever goodness there may be, the eternal remembrance of perversity, and the hardening of a blind heart proclaim him terrible. For he neither rewards their good deeds, nor washes away their evils, nor softens their hearts, but even hardens them. Almighty God so governs their perverse will that what it unjustly attempts against him is secretly ordered according to him; and though it displeases him in so far as it is evil, it nevertheless pleases him in so far as it is ordered. Thus God, terrible and just, hardens the hearts of the ungodly whom he rejects from eternity: terribly because immovably, indeed justly, but secretly.

Therefore, although the elect seem full of every sin, they have in some manner never sinned; but the reprobate, although they appear bound by none, have in some manner never done well, since it cannot happen either that the former are condemned or that the latter are saved. This is the threefold kind of contemplation about which God speaks with Moses, teaching in this contemplation that in himself he is wholly incomprehensible, in the elect lovable, and in the reprobate terrible. In this threefold kind of contemplation, indeed, his words are heard, because these things are believed of him in this way; but absolutely no form or appearance of him is seen by Moses, because how these things are so is not apprehended even by the contemplator himself.

CLXXIV. [Cols. 0780A–0780D] These three figures, placed in the image above the mercy-seat between the two cherubim, indicate this threefold kind of contemplation. The first figure is a circle. By this figure the first kind of divine contemplation—the incomprehensibility of God—is aptly denoted, because he neither begins nor ends, just as in a circle neither beginning nor end is seen. This circle is made in green, because God is a certain life ever green from eternity and unto eternity. And rightly is the unfading eternity of God represented by a green circle, because he neither blossoms and flourishes through a beginning nor falls and withers through an end.

The remaining two figures, in which a beginning is seen but no end whatsoever appears, designate the perpetuity both of the salvation of the elect, in whom God is lovable, and of the perdition of the reprobate, in whom he is terrible; because the salvation of the righteous and their perdition begin, but neither ever ends. The sapphire-coloured figure expresses the blessedness of the elect, because of the gentleness of divine mercy which is over them from eternity and unto eternity. But the red figure, which bears the appearance of fire, indicates the perdition of the reprobate, because God appears to the reprobate as a devouring and consuming fire: he rejects them from eternity and condemns them unto eternity.

Let this suffice concerning Moses’ entry. But so that all these lofty and holy things, of which we have already treated in extended discourse, may both be acquired, when absent, by diligent concern and earnest study, and practised, when present, with persevering devotion, we have in abundance before our eyes the examples of the saints who have either preceded us on God’s way or walk in it with us. Thus they seem lighter for us to practise, the more often we know them to have been pursued by others. Therefore, after all these things, we have painted around the tabernacle faithful and holy persons: clerics of every rank and laypeople of both sexes. For in order both to acquire and retain in ourselves the practices of holy religion, we ought to take examples from good clerics and laypeople. In the sapphire space, which has the appearance of the sky when it is clear, clerics are contained with the particular ministries to which they are devoted; likewise, in the green field that represents the earth, laypeople are depicted as engaged in works of mercy, so that we may imitate religious persons in purity of contemplation and secular persons in the usefulness of good action.

## CHAPTER XVI. What, in the moral sense, is to be understood through the two Levites sounding silver trumpets at the entrance of the tabernacle.

CLXXV. [Cols. 0781A–0782A] We must next consider what the two Levites sounding silver trumpets before the tabernacle signify according to the moral sense. Of these two Levites in our picture, one is placed on the right beside the entrance, the other on the left. Nothing is more fittingly understood through them than fear and love. The Levite who cries, “Cease to do perversely” (Isa. 1:16), signifies fear, which draws us back from evil; the one who says, “Learn to do good,” signifies love, which stirs us to good.

Fear and love are like two Levites, which more powerfully move this tabernacle of the heart—our secret affections—of which much has now been said, as if by trumpet sounds. For fear and love are like two motions of the heart by which the rational soul is impelled to do everything it does. When these two are good, they accomplish every good. By good fear, evils are avoided; by good love, good things are practised. But when they are bad, they become the cause of all evils. Through bad fear one withdraws from good; through bad love wicked deeds are committed. These, then, are like two gates through which both death and life proceed: death when they are opened toward evil; life when they are directed toward good. Therefore these two Levites, who signify good fear and good love, are placed at the entrance of the tabernacle in our picture.

But those wishing to speak of fear and love, which are morally understood through these two Levites, must consider that although love is naturally one motion of the mind, it nevertheless receives different names according to differing qualities: it is sometimes called *cupiditas*—desire or covetousness—when it is directed toward the world, but *caritas*—charity—when directed toward God. And although fear is naturally one motion of necessity, it is yet designated by different names according to the various ways in which it is held or works: it is called worldly and servile when it concerns the world and sin, but initial and filial when it is directed to good and through good.

There are, then, four fears: servile, worldly, initial, and filial. Servile fear is to abstain from evil in order to avoid punishment while retaining an evil will. Worldly fear is to abstain from good in order to avoid punishment while retaining an evil will. Initial fear is, in order to avoid punishment, to cut away not only perverse acts but also evil thoughts. Filial fear is to adhere firmly to good because one does not wish to lose it.

Servile fear dreads punishment inflicted by people and therefore considers it sufficient to refrain from an evil action; because it wishes to please people, it serves only before their eyes and does not fear the guilt of conscience. Worldly fear, however, does not seek to please people, but nevertheless fears to displease them; and it too feigns what is not, as false in denying truth as the other is deceitful in concealing falsehood. Both offend against truth: the one because he timidly denies what is; the other because he perversely pretends what is not.

Initial fear is that which, while fearing and striving to avoid the punishment God threatens, sees that it is by no means enough to refrain from unlawful action unless the very thought of the heart also appears sincere and unstained. This is called initial fear because beneath it virtue begins through a good will and vice comes to an end. Yet it is not perfection, because while one thing is done and another intended, good itself is not yet loved for its own sake. Still, charity comes to enter through this fear, which, while showing us the danger we ought to flee, in some manner commands us to seek and desire protection. Thus it turns the heart toward God, so that in a manner one may flee from him to him: that is, while taking care to have him not angry, one strives to have him propitious. Filial fear follows this; it is born when charity succeeds, so that fearing God is nothing other than no longer wishing to lose the good one has tasted in charity. You now love voluntarily out of reverence; you no longer fear unwillingly because of punishment. Those four steps placed beside the Levite through whom fear is expressed signify these four kinds of fear.

CLXXVI. [Cols. 0782B–0783B] Since of these four fears two are good—initial and filial—and two bad—worldly and servile—we ought to retain two for ourselves and cast two away from ourselves. Therefore, of these four steps which indicate the aforesaid four fears, we have placed two behind the Levite’s back and two before his face: that we may cast the two bad fears, namely servile and worldly fear, behind the back of the mind through hatred; and may keep the two good fears, namely initial and filial fear, before the face of the heart through practice.

Love also, which is understood through the other Levite, as was said above, is called *cupiditas* when it is directed toward evil, but *caritas* when it is directed toward good. Charity, moreover, as we read everywhere in Scripture, is twofold: charity toward God and toward one’s neighbour. Charity toward God means loving him so that we rejoice in him; charity toward our neighbour means loving the neighbour so that we rejoice, not in him, but with him in God. That is, we must love the Lord for his own sake, but our neighbour for the Lord’s sake. God is to be loved for his own sake because he is our good; our neighbour for God’s sake because with him our good is in God. We love God so that we may attain him and rejoice in him; we love our neighbour so that we may run with him and arrive with him. We love God as joy; our neighbour as the companion of joy.

We ought to love our neighbour whether he is good or is not good, provided that he can be good. Whoever is good, or, if not good, can become good, is our neighbour and is to be loved by us. But those who are so evil that they can no longer become good are not our neighbours and therefore are not to be loved by us. Such are demons and reprobate people condemned with demons, who are not our neighbours but alien and wholly estranged from us, because the way back to good is no longer open to them. They are therefore not to be loved by us because they have irrecoverably fallen away from that good in which everyone who is rightly loved is loved.

But we ought to love those who have either not fallen away from goodness, or, if they have perhaps fallen away, can return again through God’s grace and freedom of choice. For those who can still return are not altogether far away, even if they have gone away. These are the neighbours whom we must love: in God, if they have not departed; or for God’s sake, if they can return. This is what is commanded us: that we should love both a friend in God and an enemy for God’s sake. A friend in God, because he has God—for he would not be a friend if he did not have God. An enemy for God’s sake, that he may have God: so that one who is an enemy through not having God may become a friend through having God.

We can see all this clearly by an example. If honey is sweet, the honeycomb is sweet; and if you love honey, you also love the honeycomb, which is the container of honey. But honey is loved because it is sweetness itself. When you love the honeycomb, however, you do not love it because it is itself sweetness, but because sweetness is in it—because the honeycomb is the receptacle of sweetness. Honey, then, is loved for its own sake; the honeycomb for the sake of honey. And if you see a honeycomb without honey, you see the receptacle where honey ought to be; you grieve that it is empty; you dislike its dryness; you desire that the honey which you love should be there; and if honey comes into it, you love it more. So love your God for his own sake, because he is sweetness; but love your neighbour because he is the receptacle of this sweetness. Love that same sweetness in him, love it for him, and love him for its sake. But if you find your neighbour empty of this sweetness, grieve, because you see your receptacle empty; and desire that his good may come into him, without which he cannot be good.

CLXXVII. [Cols. 0783C–0784A] This, then, is the twofold charity of God and neighbour, and in this way God and neighbour are to be loved. But because, as we said above, love is sometimes good and sometimes evil—evil when directed toward evil, in which case it is called *cupiditas*; good when directed toward good, in which case it is called *caritas*—and because charity has two commandments, we distinguish these modes of love by steps as, a little before, we distinguished the kinds of fear by steps.

We have therefore placed one step behind the back of the Levite through whom the love of which we speak is expressed, so that through contempt and hatred we may cast behind the back of the mind that perverse love called *cupiditas*. We have placed two steps before the face of the same Levite, so that we may endeavour to hold before the face of the heart, with complete approval and continual practice, the twofold charity of God and neighbour. These steps are made red, a colour that has the appearance of fire, because charity makes the one whom it affects burn. The upper step expresses love of God, who is on high; the lower, love of neighbour, who lives with us below.

From the upper step three steps extend upward, because love of God is distinguished in three ways: he is commanded to be loved by us with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the strength. In this matter, as St Gregory says, it must be noted that when divine speech commands that the Lord be loved, it not only tells from what part of us he is to be loved but also specifies how completely, when it adds “with all”; so that whoever desires perfectly to please God may leave nothing of himself for himself.

From the lower step two steps hang downward, because love of neighbour is derived from two commandments. A certain wise person says, “What you would hate to have done to you by another, see that you do not do to another.” Truth himself says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12). By these two commandments of the two Testaments, malice is restrained by one and kindness extended by the other: so that, by not doing the evil that one does not wish to suffer, a person ceases from harmful action; and again, by bestowing the good one desires for oneself, one practises kindness toward the neighbour’s benefit. When these two things are diligently considered, the heart is directed to countless ministries of virtue: lest the mind, agitated by desires, burn to inflict what it ought not; or, dissolved in idleness, grow sluggish in rendering what it ought. Let this suffice concerning the two Levites sounding trumpets at the entrance of the tabernacle according to their moral signification.

## CHAPTER XVII. How the two columns of fire and cloud, painted on either side of the tabernacle, ought to be understood according to the tropological sense.

CLXXVIII. [Cols. 0784B–0785A] Concerning the two columns of fire and cloud, which on the plane of the picture are on either side of the tabernacle, we propose briefly to treat them according to the moral interpretation; for we have lingered for some time in the preceding section over their allegorical exposition, and we hasten to examine certain matters still remaining. We have often said that, according to the allegorical sense, Moses’ tabernacle represents Christ’s Church. Above this tabernacle rises an image holding a cloud on the right and fire on the left, because the prelates of the holy Church preside over their subjects: they display the fire of terror to those subjects who resolve to persist in a perverse life, and the cloud of gentleness to those who choose to devote themselves to holy conduct.

To the former they say: “What do you wish? Shall we come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4:21). It is as if they said: “Since the perversity of reprobate conduct has placed you on the left side, you deserve to be visited with the rod of strict severity.” But to the latter, conversely, it is said: “We do not lord it over your faith, but are helpers of your joy; for you stand by faith” (2 Cor. 1:23). It is as if he said: “Since through faith working by love you stand upon the summit of holiness, it is surely more just and fitting that we assist your good resolve through charity than dominate you through harshness.”

This cloud and this fire are signified by the pastoral staff, which is curved in its upper part and pointed in its lower part: that it may prick with the sharp point of correction those who, in their affections, cling to earthly things, and that the pastor may bend toward those attached to heavenly things with an affection of compassion. Therefore, what the curved part of the staff signifies above, the cloud of the image on the right also indicates; and what its sharp point signifies below, the fire of the image on the left also signifies.

Through Moses, who there is painted among the subjects on the left with scourge and sword, the same just severity of prelates is understood, which threatens perverse subjects with the sword of correction and the scourge of discipline. Beside those subjects who are on the right, the hands of this same Moses are upheld and, being upheld, are made light, because the strictness of prelates is moderated toward humble subjects. Aaron and Hur support those hands. Through Aaron, whose name is interpreted “mountain of strength,” according to the moral signification the virtue of humility is understood, because the more anyone sees himself as lowly and weak, the more exalted and strong he is. Through Hur, whose name is said to mean “fire,” ardour of love is expressed. Thus, morally speaking, Aaron and Hur support Moses’ hands when the lofty strength of humility and the ardour of charity temper any learned and just prelate both in rebuking and in sparing, lest through pride he be excessively rigid in rebuking or through lukewarmness excessively lax in sparing.

CLXXIX. But the icon of which we are speaking says to the subjects who are on the left, in the fire: “If anyone has done this or that, let him surely be put to death” [Col. 0785B] (Exod. 21:18); and to those on the right, in the cloud: “I came to call sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9). What, then, are we to think this means, except that the prelates of the Church threaten punishment with terror to rebellious subjects and promise pardon with gentleness to the humble?

All those things which belong to the other icon, where on the opposite side both the salvation of the elect and the destruction of the reprobate are depicted, if you consider them carefully, you will see to correspond, according to this particular meaning, with the prelates and subjects of whom we speak. Thus, as we showed a little earlier in the preceding part, all these things which now, on the flat surface of the painting, lie separately divided from one another at the bottom, on either side of the tabernacle—when they are raised above the tabernacle itself and joined together—signify, according to the allegorical sense, both the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews. So too, according to the moral interpretation, these same things, joined together above, express both the office of prelates and the manner of life of subjects.

For, to put it briefly, our icon says in the fire to the condemned on the left: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41); and the same icon says in the cloud to the saved on the right: “Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom” (ibid., v. 34). This is so [Col. 0785C] whenever any prelate of holy Church declares that disobedient subjects, because of their contempt for the divine commandments which they obstinately reject in their minds, will go terribly into eternal fire; and mercifully announces that obedient subjects, because of their fulfilment of heavenly precepts which they receive in humble hearts, will possess the kingdom of heaven. This is what we have said briefly concerning the twofold column of fire and cloud.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Another exposition of the same subject, in another way, according to the moral sense.

CLXXX. There still occur together a few matters concerning this column of fire and cloud which deserve somewhat more careful consideration, and which we have thought worthy to mention now. For, as has been said more than once above, that outward tabernacle of Moses signifies the inward secret chamber of the soul. A column continually hangs over this tabernacle, because thought either constantly defends our heart or accuses it. Hence the Apostle says: “Their thoughts accusing or even defending one another” [Col. 0786A] (Rom. 2:15).

Thought defends our heart when it is conscious of good; but it accuses it when it is conscious of evil. Thus, although the column of which we speak was always over the tabernacle, by day it had the appearance of a cloud, but by night the appearance of fire. By fire, as has been sufficiently shown above, is understood the severity of terror; by cloud, the soothingness of gentleness; by night, the life of the sinner; and by day, the life of the righteous.

Therefore above the tabernacle there is a cloud by day and a column of fire by night, because the inward thought of our heart, when we are good, comforts us through the gentleness of consolation on account of the brightness of holiness by which we are illumined; and when we are evil, terrifies us through the dread of rebuke on account of the darkness of wickedness by which we are obscured.

The rebuke of our heart is twofold. When we act wrongly, it judges us worthy not only of temporal tribulation, but, if we persist in evil, of eternal damnation. Thus a twofold rebuke harshly shakes the sinful soul even in the present: one concerning the fault which it miserably commits, the other concerning the punishment which it fearfully dreads [Col. 0786B].

Likewise, the consolation of our heart is twofold. When we ardently love the good from the heart and practise it perseveringly in our disposition, we not only rest sweetly in the chamber of the mind, but confidently hope that, “from month to month and from Sabbath to Sabbath,” we shall come to secure eternity and to the eternal security of heavenly rest. Thus a double consolation receives us: one from the merit which is present in actuality; the other from the reward which is now firmly present in hope, but will hereafter be present in actuality [Col. 0786C].

This twofold consolation and rebuke of the heart will then be fulfilled in blessedness; and, I think, it can also be understood figuratively through the pictures located on either side of the tabernacle beside the twofold column of fire and cloud. Through Moses, depicted on one side of the tabernacle near the Jews, close to the fire, holding a scourge and a sword, we understand the accusation of the heart of which we speak. This accusation of the heart sharply strikes with the wound of correction, as with a stroke of a scourge, and with the bite of rebuke, as with the point of a sword, anyone who lives hypocritically under the Law—namely, one who is a Jew outwardly, who practises only that circumcision which is in the Law through outward observances and fleshly righteousnesses, striving to please human eyes, and neglects the inward sincerity of the mind and the testimony of him who knows hidden things and discerns intentions [Col. 0786D].

This is why the Jews are there depicted under the number eleven, which signifies transgression of the Law. The Law itself, understood through Moses, convicts these Jews of transgression, as the verse proceeding from Moses and written beneath the Jews shows: namely, “Convicted by the Law, as transgressors” (Jas. 2:9). Moses is therefore depicted in the tabernacle as if threatening both to strike the Jews with the scourge and to kill them with the sword, whenever thought, conscious of transgression, both strikes a mind that transgresses the Law by correction and judges it worthy of death by rebuke [Col. 0787A].

Through hell, however, which is depicted opposite, on the other side, kindled and open in the corner to swallow up the reprobate placed beside the fire, we likewise denote the accusing conscience of the sinful soul. For it judges itself, in itself, worthy even now of eternal damnation, both in respect to its evil merit and in respect to the strict judgment of God. Hell swallowing up the reprobate is, as it were, depicted in the tabernacle whenever infernal punishment and the suffering of the damned are both attentively foreseen in thought and anxiously feared through dread [Col. 0787B].

CLXXXI. This concerns the twofold accusation of the heart. Through Moses, however, depicted on the south side of the tabernacle, to the right of the cloud, beside the Christians placed near the cloud itself, is expressed the inward consolation of a holy mind conscious of its own good. This consolation gently comforts the holy mind as it approaches its Redeemer through religious conduct; the Redeemer is signified by the cloud. Appropriately, therefore, Aaron and Hur support Moses’ hands in this place.

For through Hur, whose name means “fire,” is understood the ardour of divine love; through Aaron, whose name means “mountain of strength,” the steadfastness of heavenly contemplation. For strength signifies the firmness of stability, and a mountain the loftiness of contemplation. Thus Moses’ hands make the scourge and sword heavy for the Jews placed beside the fire; but Aaron and Hur, by supporting them, make them light for the Christians situated near the cloud. This is because the inward accusation of his evil-conscious heart both strikes with the scourge of correction and wounds with the sword of rebuke every wicked person who proudly scorns the fire of Deity by transgressing the Law; whereas a certain inward consolation, produced by the full testimony of a good conscience, gives peace and tranquillity in a kind of sweet chamber to every holy person who humbly imitates the cloud of humanity by fulfilling love—while he strives both to burn ardently with love for his Creator and perseveringly to devote himself to the loftiness of holy contemplation [Col. 0787C].

These same Christians are depicted there by the number fifteen beside the cloud, because holy persons, made peaceful by this inward consolation, await in inward rest, with blessed hope, the octave of the future resurrection. Beneath these Christians is written this verse: “But that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy” (Rom. 15:9). For Christians attribute every good which they do not to their own merits but to divine mercy [Col. 0787D].

Through the salvation of the elect, depicted opposite on the other side, where these elect are shown called to the kingdom and proceeding to that kingdom in which Christ is the drachma, we understand the consolation which gladdens the saints even now in the hope of future blessedness. They are raised and strengthened by confidence in such a great hope that they can say with the Apostle: “We know that if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” [Col. 0788A] (2 Cor. 5:1).

In a wonderful way, they already have in some fashion what they firmly hope one day to have. For Paul, the vessel of election, was still not only in this mortal body on earth, but perhaps held in prison and in chains, when he said of himself and of his fellow citizens: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in heavenly places” (Eph. 2:6). Thus he already trusted that he had in some sense been raised together and would sit in heavenly places.

And David says: “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121:1). He had not yet arrived at the house of the Lord, yet he declared that he had already rejoiced because he had heard that he would go there. This must be carefully entrusted to memory and retained continually in the mind without forgetfulness: ineffable joy will then arise from receiving that blessedness which will then be present in actuality, since so great an exultation now affects them in expectation of that same happiness which is now present in hope [Col. 0788B]. For it is not surprising if that which the taste of experience will attain fully is exceedingly sweet, provided that what the faint sense of smell perceives through report is already so sweet.

All these things which have been said concerning this twofold consolation are then depicted in the tabernacle, whenever they are thus known in the mind through understanding, loved through affection, and exercised through effect.

CLXXXII. That the columns of fire and cloud of which we are speaking, when the tabernacle itself is raised, will be joined together above with the pictures belonging to those columns, must likewise not be thought devoid of mystery according to this meaning. To show briefly, without prejudice to other views, what we think concerning this: when the tabernacle is raised, the Jews are joined to the damned and to Moses holding the heavy scourge and sword in his hands, and to hell; while the Christians are joined to the elect called to the kingdom, to Moses whose hands are supported by Aaron and Hur, and to those same elect proceeding to the kingdom. This is because, when the present order of the world has ended, the wicked will eternally experience in punishment what they now fearfully dread in conscience; and the righteous will fully and blessedly possess in actuality what they now joyfully and firmly possess in hope [Col. 0788C–D].

These are the things which, saving the more subtle interpretation open to more learned minds, we have said as seemed good to us concerning the column of fire and cloud according to the moral sense. If anyone perhaps dislikes what has been said in this manner concerning the pictures, he nevertheless cannot deny that fire expresses the severity of terror, cloud the soothingness of gentleness, night the life of the wicked, and day the life of the righteous. If this is so—indeed, because it is so—we are not, I think, departing from the truth of faith if, according to the moral sense, we understand the column which once stood over the visible tabernacle of Moses as conscience, which ought to preside over the tabernacle of our mind; the appearance of cloud in that column by day as the consolation brought to our mind by that conscience because of the brightness of holiness; and the fire which was in the aforesaid column by night as the accusation brought to our heart because of the darkness of wickedness [Col. 0789A].

## CHAPTER XIX. On the five spaces of the painting: what is to be understood by them morally.

CLXXXIII. Since we intend to speak briefly concerning the moral significance of the five spaces into which our painting is divided, we must briefly repeat some of the things said at length above, so that we may arrive more suitably at what we propose to say.

We said previously that laypeople of both periods are depicted in the first space. This space is like a field in which good and bad plants grow together. In the second space are clerics of both the Old and New Testaments. This space is not unsuitably compared to a garden, in which choice plants are cultivated [Col. 0789B]. The third space was entered by Levites conspicuous for mature age and purity, in order to offer burnt offerings on the bronze altar. It may in a certain sense be called the court of a king, in which his friends and household attendants devote themselves to his service. Priests entered the fourth space, which is a kind of house in which his relatives and kinsfolk are received. Finally, the fifth space, which is within the veil and is called the Holy of Holies, into which the high priest alone enters, is like a private bridal chamber, in which Bridegroom and bride rejoice together with the sweeter love appropriate to a more secret place.

For in this place is the ark, and in the ark manna. The ark is in that place as a bed in a bridal chamber, and the manna in the ark as sweetness in the bed. These, then, are the five spaces by which our painting is divided; and all of them may be applied to the human soul according to the moral interpretation alone.

Our mind often goes forth from itself; having gone out, it is scattered among outward things; scattered, it is dissipated. Thus scattered and dissipated, it wanders through the empty phantasms of visible and invisible things: now it thinks good things well and evil things badly; now good things badly and evil things well. Yet it does not settle upon or cling to either these thoughts or those, but runs to and fro, wandering and straying, and rests nowhere in any thought [Col. 0789C–D]. This mind therefore depicts the first space in itself. Since its thoughts are innumerable and are not merely good and bad, but good and bad together, they may rightly be compared to the wide expanse of a field in which good and bad plants are found together.

CLXXXIV. At other times our mind strives to call itself back to itself from this infinite distraction. Having called itself back, it gathers itself to itself; gathered, it draws near to itself; having drawn near, it places itself beside itself. Since it does not yet know how to think fully about matters pertaining to eternal life, it turns its thought to the necessities of the present life, excluding idle, impure, unlawful, and superfluous thoughts.

It diligently strives and anxiously investigates [Col. 0790A] what and how things lacking must be sought, and things present assessed; how harmful things are to be avoided when they threaten and expelled when they injure; how beneficial things are to be acquired and, once acquired, practised; and it considers the other things necessary for this temporal life. We compared these thoughts to a garden in which only choice plants, necessary for human use, are cultivated, because they devote themselves attentively to the necessities of this life.

But when our mind thoughtfully concerns itself with good works to be performed through the body; when it diligently considers how to resist vices and apply itself to acquiring virtues; when it investigates with every care how the eyes must be closed against vanity through contempt for the world, the ears stopped against curiosity through compunction of soul, the sense of smell guarded against pleasure through the seriousness of good desire, the taste mortified against gluttony through the rigour of fasting, the tongue restrained against talkativeness through the bridle of silence, touch checked against impurity through the virtue of self-mortification, and finally all the other movements of the limbs kept from impurity through the maturity of holy conduct—then this mind constructs within itself the court of the highest King [Col. 0790B]. In this court grave and pure thoughts, like Levites mature in age and conspicuous in purity, offer burnt offerings to the Lord. In that court, I say, these moral Levites—that is, holy thoughts—strive to kill the bull of pride with the knife of humility, the goat of lust with chastity, the calf of wantonness with maturity, and the other bestial impulses [Col. 0790C].

CLXXXV. If our mind thoughtfully concerns itself not only with the outward purity of the body, but also with the inward purity of the heart, then, to speak briefly, it constructs within itself a house in which its parents and relatives are received. Insofar as our parents and relatives are nearer to us than household members and friends, so these thoughts concerning inward purity of mind are higher than the thoughts which concern themselves with outward sanctity of body. For as spirit is worthier than body, so spiritual holiness is higher than bodily holiness.

But if our mind has ascended to such heights of perfection that it no longer needs to struggle either against the impulses of the flesh or against the phantasms that resist the heart, but strives with all its power, through steadiness of thought, purity of contemplation, and sweetness of spiritual vision, to unite its spirit with God as far as is granted in this mortal flesh—thinking of him at every hour in purity, loving him ardently, and desiring him intensely—then it has undoubtedly depicted within itself the fifth space of our painting, which we compared to a bridal chamber [Col. 0790D].

In this bridal chamber, while all the thoughts are for the time being set aside—those ploughing and sowing in the field, planting and watering in the garden, offering and sacrificing in the court, eating and drinking in the house—the human soul, which is God’s bride, is joined alone to her God and Bridegroom, alone to the Alone, firmly in the embrace of love and sweetly united in the unity of spirit [Col. 0791A].

In this way we have applied the five spaces of our painting to the human soul. In the first space I write “outside”; in the second, “beside”; in the third, “near”; in the fourth, “within”; in the fifth, “above.” For in the field of unstable thoughts our mind is outside itself; in the garden of thoughts concerning temporal life it is beside itself; in the court of care for bodily chastity it is near itself; in the house of intention toward spiritual purity it is within itself; and in the bridal chamber, where it attends to the lofty secrets of contemplation, it is above itself.

It is outside itself through the unstable wandering of fluctuating thoughts; beside itself through lawful concern for necessary and earthly occupations; near itself through outward purification of the body; within itself through inward sanctity of mind; and above itself through the sublimity of purified contemplation [Col. 0791B].

CLXXXVI. Many other things, venerable Father, occur to us to be said concerning this subject. But we ought to know that, just as provision must be made for the fervour of the diligent, so also must regard be had for the weariness of those who are easily tired. We have therefore divided this book into three parts, but have given it such a measured middle course that, through a certain proportioning—as one might say—of a great brevity of sentences and a brief greatness of substance, it may be neither excessively long for the indolent nor excessively diffuse for the diligent [Col. 0791C]. Thus it can in some degree give to the latter, by its fragrance, an appetite for daring greater things; and to the former, by its taste, satisfaction in at least understanding these matters [Col. 0792A].

But amid these matters, my most beloved lord, you ought to know why—using the Apostle’s words—“I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Cor. 12:11). For, in order to comply as I should with your will, I opened my mouth and spoke; and in speaking I revealed my foolishness, lest, if I had kept silent, wisdom which I lacked might have been thought present in me. For, as a certain wise man says, “A fool, if he keeps silent, will be accounted wise.”

By speaking, I have revealed, I say, my foolishness; yet it is not foolishness for me, since love is the cause of this speech of mine and humility its fruit. It is love that I have obediently served your will, perhaps to the benefit of many; it is humility that people may see what I lack, because I know that I do not know [Col. 0792B].

Therefore, if anyone should wish unjustly to malign me with the bite of envy because that knowledge which “puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1) was absent from me in this book, I ought surely to be excused, because that which “builds up” (ibid.) and that which humbles were not lacking to me in it. Moreover, because he who errs unknowingly ought to be corrected, while he who knowingly excuses his error deserves condemnation: although I do not fully recognize that I have departed from the truth in what I have said, yet I neither rashly deny that I may have departed from it altogether nor proudly reject a correction shown to be reasonable. Thus, like David humbly repenting of his bodily fall, I may be beneficially corrected by Nathan; and may never, like Saul proudly excusing himself in his disobedience, be miserably condemned by Samuel [Col. 0792C].

[Col. 0791]

# LETTER OF ADAM to the canons of the church of Prémontré, men of venerable life, concerning the threefold painting of the aforesaid tabernacle and the threefold kind of contemplation.

[Col. 0791C] To the most beloved and illustrious community, to be embraced in Christ, of canons serving almighty God in the church of Prémontré: Brother ADAM, the most humble servant of God and of God’s servants, offers the small thing which he is, if indeed he is anything.

[Col. 0791D] O men of venerable life, while absent we have sent to you, though you too are absent, the book composed concerning the threefold tabernacle which, while present, we promised to you when you were present. It is a small gift, indeed, but sent with no small devotion. Let your balance of fairness, therefore, weigh the gift itself according to the affection of its giver.

For it is fitting and right that the recipient should by no means consider small a gift whose donor is great in the eyes of his recipient’s thought. Where the fullness of the whole takes whatever there is into itself and absorbs it, the measure of quantity can in no way appear small. But because the matter of which we were treating was not moderately profound, very many things occurred which needed to be said [Col. 0792C].

We have therefore divided the aforesaid book into three parts and have separately appended to those parts their proper correspondences, so that, once the summary of each part has been fully understood, our readers may in that knowledge grasp the entire work perfectly and in its sequence, though it is rather lengthy [Col. 0792D].

The first part treats of that visible and ancient tabernacle of Moses; the second, of the tabernacle of Christ, which is the holy Church of the elect; and the third, of the tabernacle of the Holy Spirit, which is the devout and faithful soul. To the first tabernacle belongs history, and it consists in the truth of the event that occurred. To the second belongs allegory, and it consists in the unfalsified belief of Catholic faith. To the third belongs tropology, or moral interpretation, and it consists in the inward purity of hidden conscience.

The painting contains the first and second parts within itself. On its flat surface it shows, at the very beginning of the second part, as far as can be shown on a plane, how that ancient tabernacle of Moses and the things belonging to it were actually made and arranged. After that display, in the same part you will find how all those visible things express by signification the tabernacle of Christ, which is the Church [Col. 0793A]. In the aforesaid third part, the visible things are repeated from the beginning under moral signification, and it is shown how they pertain to the tabernacle of the Holy Spirit, which is the devout and faithful soul. Nor are the differing, non-opposed moral meanings inappropriately marked by variations of colours and distinctions of ranks.

Have the aforesaid book read before you, and likewise spread out before you the painting itself, with the fields in which Emperor Constantine and the Apostle Peter are depicted turned toward the east; with the entrance to the courts and the Holy of Holies likewise turned toward that quarter, so that the Holy of Holies faces west [Col. 0793B]. Thus you may receive by sight what is depicted and by hearing what is written—things contained in the second and third parts of the book.

Fit the painting itself appropriately to the book, showing in this manner that the things seen do not differ in any respect from the things heard, nor the things heard from the things seen, but that they agree with and cohere in every respect. Yet because to do all these things in this manner belongs not to the idle but to the occupied, not to the slothful but to the diligent—persons to whom it is especially and more perfectly granted to give leisure to such matters—you may extract from the multitude of all these things a certain concise summary, clear to the understanding. Its ease will enable it to be clearly understood, and its brevity to be tenaciously retained in memory [Col. 0793C].

For this is particularly expedient for those less acute and perceptive, and likewise for those distracted or occupied by other matters: because the understanding readily admits a few things that are clear to its comprehension, and memory readily retains them. Therefore, while you sit in the deepest silence, with your ears attentive to the book and your eyes open to the painting spread before you in the manner we have just taught, let one of you take a rod in his hand and briefly join together what is seen and what is heard. By explaining with his tongue to the understanding what is written, and by indicating with the rod to the eye what is depicted, let him make you certain that these things cohere with and depend upon one another [Col. 0793D].

Thus in the middle of the very plane on which I wish to depict the tabernacle and all the other things, as they are set forth in the book, you will find each item clearly explained from the second chapter of the second part to the end of the third part, which is also the conclusion of the book. Whenever, however, it pleases you to attend to these matters—to hear all that is set forth at length in those two parts and to see whatever is marked in the painting—you must devote yourselves more attentively to those same two parts. But when other occupations prevent you from attending to the entirety of these things, let the concise summary mentioned above suffice for you. This is briefly what may be said concerning that book, entitled *On the Threefold Tabernacle*, which we have now sent you together with the painting.

[Col. 0794A] We are now producing for you another book, entitled *On the Threefold Kind of Contemplation*. It treats of how God is incomprehensible in himself, terrible in the reprobate, and sweet and delightful in the elect. Indeed, we are astonished at the great magnitude and multitude of God’s works: how each individual thing, presenting and offering itself to our five bodily senses according to its kind, declares, through careful examination of its nature, with loud voice and mighty cry, that God is the Creator and disposer of the universe, yet does not at all determine what he is like or how great he is.

Secretly asking within ourselves what will be the life of the saints, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” [Col. 0794B] (1 Cor. 2:9), we thirst with the mouth of the heart for the heavenly streams of the fountain of life. By these sweet goads we stir up our affections and fly there upon the wings of desires.

At times also, indignant at the sins of the wicked and considering their punishments with fear, we sigh amid our frailties and breathe again in the mercies of the Creator. Thus, now fearing our reprobation and now hoping for election, we are accustomed, while singing to God of mercy and judgment, to grind with the teeth of our thoughts as with an upper and lower millstone.

But among all these depths, we are moved concerning the damnation of the reprobate no less terribly than wonderfully, shaken by the greatest fear and disturbed by the most powerful astonishment, while with the most intent eye of spiritual contemplation we consider on the one hand the enormity of their crimes and on the other the eternity of their punishments [Col. 0794C]. For when we think either of God’s own greatness or of the salvation of the righteous, we find it fitting both reverently to marvel at the former and delightfully, exceedingly sweetly, to embrace the latter with the pleasant arms of sweet thoughts.

It is no wonder that a tiny speck of dust should marvel at such great majesty. Nor does it appear to us in any way unmerciful that the supremely good Creator should both justify by merit and glorify by reward an excellent creature so excellently made by him. Therefore it is in no way unmerciful, because he appears to have created it for this purpose: that as it first received being from him, so it might receive blessed being in him [Col. 0794D].

But when we think within ourselves of the destruction of the reprobate, no small fear and trembling come upon us, and darkness covers us. Anxiously, as far as we dare, we ask one another and complain: how and why does that Creator of the universe, who can do everything that he wills and wills absolutely nothing except what is good, permit a creature made in his image and likeness to fall into sin, by which it may afterwards deserve to fall into punishment? For it is certainly true that, just as it cannot do good unless he first inspires it and then assists it, so neither, in the state in which it now exists, can it omit evil unless he restrains it, nor commit evil unless he permits it.

But after grinding these matters a little with the teeth of our thoughts, and, with our teeth blunted by that grinding, humbly reserving them to the venerable fire rather than rashly swallowing them by disputation, with all answer denied to our questioning and all discovery denied to our inquiry, we are compelled to break forth in this utterance: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” [Col. 0795A] (Rom. 11:33). “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor? Or who has first given to him, and shall be repaid?” (Rom. 11:33–34).

Therefore the matter and purpose of this book revolve around these three things: it treats of how God is incomprehensible in himself, terrible in the reprobate, and lovable in the elect. This is why we have entitled it *On the Threefold Kind of Contemplation*: so that consideration of the first contemplation may enlighten us, that of the second humble us, and that of the third soothe us. Let it enlighten us lest we be ignorant; humble us lest we be proud; soothe us lest we despair [Col. 0795B; 0796A].

And you also, O men of venerable life, whom we have specially chosen for this purpose—that whatever effort our modest ability may make should chiefly be directed to you—please read this book in such a manner that you attend not so much to the properties of the words as to the veins of meaning, and consider more what we say than how we say it. We have composed it by addressing the Lord in confession, because this mode of expression, as some think, is accustomed greatly to stir the reader’s affection. If your prudence finds in it anything said otherwise than it ought to have been said, by no means leave it uncorrected.

May almighty God protect you by his grace, my venerable lords and beloved friends in Christ, order your days in his peace, command that you be delivered from eternal damnation and numbered among the flock of his elect, and, rising early in the morning, offer a burnt offering for your son. Amen [Col. 0796B].

[Col. 0795]

# ON THE THREEFOLD KIND OF CONTEMPLATION

## PART ONE. GOD IS CONSIDERED AS INCOMPREHENSIBLE IN HIMSELF.

**450 § I. — That God is invisible, immortal, and that all things are from him, through him, and in him.**

[Col. 0795B]

[Col. 0795C] You are exalted, Lord God, yet you regard the lowly, and know the lofty from afar (Ps. 137:6). You are incomprehensible, yet you catch the wise in their own cunning. You are invisible, and no creature is invisible in your sight. Beginning without beginning, end without end. You are above all things, yet not raised up; beneath all things, yet not borne beneath them. Within and without, yet located nowhere; you are, and are the same, and in the same manner: nothing either happens to you or comes to be in you; nothing passes away or has been in you. Great is your power, and there is no number to your wisdom (Ps. 146:4). O hand almighty in all things, and no less O eye that sees all things: there is no one who can escape the former or lie hidden from the latter. You are full of yourself, and without you there is nothing; you are present to yourself and to all things, because you are not shut out by place. And what place is there without you? From you, through you, in you are all things: to you be glory. To whom—to you? To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the one God (1 Tim. 1:7). You are the God of the ages, to whom the ages themselves could never either draw near or depart; yet they are not coeternal with you. For those things which in themselves at one time did not exist, or will exist, are always in you. Indeed, as you are from eternity, so you are unto eternity. For what has been does not pass away from you as something old, nor does what will be come to you as something new; rather, both stand present to you: both that which already is and that which is not yet is in you. Certainly you are immortal, and you alone are immortal, because you alone possess immortality. And you alone do so because you have it from eternity; you did not receive it through some intervening gift of grace. Is not every change in a rational creature, in some sense, a death? But you are immortal, because with you there is [Col. 0796B] no change, nor shadow of turning (Jas. 1:17). For how can anything be changed in you, [Col. 0796C] or any alternation be overshadowed, when you possess a state which is from eternity unto eternity—one and the same, in the same manner—entirely ignorant in yourself alike of anything arriving through “will be” and departing through “has been”?

But you too are invisible: no human being has seen you, nor indeed can see you. Yet you are not far from each one of us, for in you we live, move, and are (Acts 17:28). This is indeed so; but truly blessed is the one in whom you are, who lives for you, who moves in you. You appear and remain hidden. How do you appear? Light shines in darkness. How do you remain hidden? The darkness did not comprehend it (John 1:5). You shine in them, yet do not shine for them; for though you are present to them, they are absent from you. Thus they are blind, because the beam of pride presses upon and overwhelms [Col. 0796D] their eyes; they become futile in their reasonings, and their foolish heart is darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools (Rom. 1:21). Thus you reveal and conceal yourself. You are at once light and fire: unfailing light, consuming fire. You can neither be darkened nor extinguished. You always shine; you always burn. Yet you neither illumine the darkness of the reprobate nor kindle their coldness. In them, indeed, you neither enlighten the understanding so that they know what is true, nor inflame the affection so that they love what is good. You are also supreme goodness and supreme truth. Therefore the reprobate cannot in any way see either the truth that you are—for ignorance of truth renders them blind—or the goodness that you are—for desire of evil has made them cold.

[Col. 0797A] **451.** You are invisible in yourself. Yet, since the creation of the world, your invisible things are perceived and beheld through the things made; so too are your everlasting power and divinity (Rom. 1:20). And O how wonderful you are, Lord God, in yourself, you who appear so wonderful to us, who are creatures of the world, in those things which you have made. But who knows how wonderful you are in yourself? Who, I say—not merely among human beings, but even among heavenly spirits? O Creator, wonderful in yourself, whose created works are so wonderful! And indeed they are exceedingly wonderful, and loudly proclaim you to be far more wonderful than they. For your creatures show themselves, Lord God: creatures made good by you, the good Creator. They show themselves, I say, as good, beautiful, delightful, many, and great: good for use; beautiful [Col. 0797B] for sight; delightful for taste; many in number; and great in measure. They show these things about themselves, and show them wonderfully. But in showing themselves, they show you, their Creator, to be far better, more beautiful, sweeter, and greater: you who are the best of all good things, the most beautiful of all beautiful things, the sweetest of all sweet things, and the greatest of all great things—as the true, supreme, and eternal goodness, beauty, sweetness, and greatness of yourself.

Behold: to my inward self—where I am, whoever I am, whatever I am, of whatever kind I am, however lowly I am, however great I am—to me inward, through me outward; to me invisible, through me visible; finally, to me spirit, through me body, so many and such kinds, and so great, of things wonderfully created by you, the Wonderful One, appear—from highest to lowest, from greatest to least. Each one, through the natures which you, Wonderful One, have wonderfully bestowed upon them, cries aloud; piercing my deafness, they rebuke, entreat, and admonish me with all authority and teaching [Col. 0797C] that I should believe you, believe in your promise, believe in you; that I should love you, seek you, and not cease seeking until I find you, and, having found you, not let you go. I should believe you almighty; believe your truthfulness as promisor; love you as giver of everlasting blessedness; seek you as inward, find you as eternal, and not let you go for eternity. Behold how much and how great, of what sort and what rank, of beauty they present and bring before my outward sense and sight; of sound before hearing; of fragrance before smell; of savor before taste; and of suitability before touch. All these things are good, and very good. But they are good to those who know how to take them up in your hymn and do not wish to be taken up by them in their own slumber: those who, in using the things you have made, are eager in all things to please you, their Maker.

Thus these visible things created by you stand ready for my five senses. Continually offering and presenting themselves to them, they never cease to admonish me to love, praise, and seek you. Nor do they fail to cry out—those things which merely are; those which are and live; those which are, live, and have sensation; and those which are, live, have sensation, and discern. Yet when I see you in them, you are still [Col. 0798A] invisible in yourself. For whatever I see, hear, taste, smell, or touch in this world or of this world is not you. What then are you, Lord my God? What, I pray, are you? You are not the abundant and great beauty that I behold with bodily sight; not the voice that I hear bodily; not the fragrance that I smell; not the savor that I taste; not the magnitude that I touch. Yet you are a certain multitude, a certain magnitude, a certain beauty, a certain voice, a certain fragrance, a certain savor, a certain fittingness: multitude, yet with one simplicity and simple unity, into which no number enters; magnitude, yet without quantity, which no measure comprehends; beauty, which no ugliness obscures; voice, which no time carries away; fragrance, which no breeze disperses; savor, which no eating diminishes; fittingness, which decay does not defile in any respect.

You are many, yet without number; great, yet without quantity; simple, yet without diminution of yourself; good, yet without quality; always, yet without time; everywhere, yet without place; in every thing, yet without being defined by it; in every time, yet without mutability in yourself. You can in no way be stained, because of your purity; divided, because of your simplicity; comprehended, because of your immensity; or measured, because of your immutability. You can in no way be varied in knowledge, for you are most wise; or changed in affection, for you are best: every effect is subject to your power; every hidden thing is manifest to your wisdom; every event follows your counsel. Neither time equals your eternity, nor strength your goodness, nor understanding your wisdom, nor any work your power. Therefore glory be to you, immortal and invisible King of the ages, from whom, through whom, and in whom are all things. For all things are from you, because you are [Col. 0798C] **452** the beginning and author of all things; all things are through you, through whom they are granted to subsist, just as they were granted to be. All things are in you; but we ought rather to marvel at the greatness of your power than to measure the dimensions of place.

### § II.—Oil of mercy is implored for the wounded soul

Unfading beauty of my life and unfailing sweetness, Lord God: have mercy on my soul, which is burdened with sins, entangled in vices, captured by allurements, captive in exile, imprisoned in the body; which clings [variant: *adheres*] to clay, is fixed in mire, fastened to its limbs, pierced through by cares, stretched out by business; which is constricted by fears, afflicted by griefs, wandering in errors, anxious with worries, disturbed by suspicions; which is exposed to dangers, bound in chains, defiled with stains, filled with expiatory guilt, oppressed by heaps of many evils; which is assailed by promptings, wearied by temptations, lured by pleasures, drawn away from good, enticed toward evil; which is overcome by consent, polluted by impurities, cast down from the heights, bent toward the depths, trampled in the lowest places; which is shaken by fear, affected by sorrow, trembling with terror, stripped of all beauty, made ugly by every horror; which is alienated from itself, torn apart within itself, mangled inside itself, scattered outside itself, cast beneath itself; which is puffed up by pride, dried up by envy, embittered by anger, broken by sloth, dispersed by avarice; which is blinded by ignorance, deep in malice, divided by discord, dishonored by gluttony, foul through lust; which provokes you to anger, takes no thought for its own salvation, unlawfully loves the world and the flesh, does not know itself, and burns with perverse desires; which is a stranger in the land of enemies, like those who go down into the pit (Ps. 141:8), reckoned with those who are in hell, subject to perdition, liable to condemnation.

### § III.—The unworthy soul undertakes a contemplation of created things

[Col. 0799B] Behold what my soul is like: foul and fetid, wretched and ulcerated, altogether like land without water before you. For the splendor of spiritual beauty neither clothes nor adorns it; the fragrance of life does not soothe it; love of goodness does not make it blessed; the vigor of religious conduct does not make it sound; finally, neither the moisture of holiness nor the dew of grace commends it. Behold, I walk in my own innermost chambers, digging through the wall; and having entered, I endeavor diligently to survey, search out, and see thoroughly what is within. But as I survey, search, and examine, nothing appears except abominations of creeping things and animals. Even upon the very wall which I have dug through, I see [Col. 0799C] idols painted all around, throughout the whole place (Ezek. 8:8–10). Behold, I question your creatures concerning you; and scarcely have I fully opened my mouth to ask when they already answer my question without any delay. My question is my contemplation; the quality of their nature is their answer.

### § IV.—The confession of stones and rocks concerning their Creator

I address rocks and stones and say to them: “Who are you?” They answer: “We are the creatures of him whose creature you also are.”

### § V.—Turning the eyes toward the sun and moon, and their answer

I dispatch my enemies, the rays of my eyes, and, raising my head, lift them on high, for I say to [Col. 0799D] the sun and moon: “Should I believe that you are my God?” But, disdaining that I should hear this from them at all, they snatch the half-spoken word from my mouth and answer me in a loud voice: “Far be such madness from you, O human being, that you should believe us to be your God.
