He himself made us. Behold,” says the sun, “I rise daily and in some way die daily by setting; I go forth and depart; I rise and decline; I appear and disappear; I am covered and uncovered. But your God is not so. He too is indeed a Sun, yet one to whom morning brings neither a beginning in rising nor evening an end in setting; who, remaining always one and the same and in the same manner, neither rises through progress nor declines through defect.” And the moon says: “Never remaining in the same condition, now I grow and now I diminish. But your God [Col. 0800A] is one and the same, and always in one and the same manner: **453** he can neither increase, because he is immeasurable, nor decrease, because he is eternal.”

### § VI.—The beauty and multitude of the stars proclaim their wonderful Creator

And I said to the stars: “What quality of these things shall I admire in you—your light or your beauty? For you are wonderfully numerous and bright.” They answered: “It is indeed no wonder that you admire us, provided that you do not fail to marvel, in us, at him who made us. Marvel at him in whose eyes we are not wonderful, in whose eyes we are neither bright nor numerous; who numbers our multitude and calls us all by our names (Ps. 146:4); who knows our signs, powers, courses, places, and [Col. 0800B] times.”

### § VII.—Innumerable creatures indicate the creative wisdom whose number is without number

But, Lord God, as I marvel at the multitude of the stars which you have made, I cast my eyes abroad and scatter them through this great and spacious world, in case they may perhaps show me such a multitude in another kind of thing. Behold, immediately there burst forth before me and offer themselves to my sight: the stars of heaven, the sand of the sea, the dust of the earth, drops of rain, days of ages, hours of days, moments of hours, grasses of fields, branches of trees, leaves of branches, ribs of leaves, hairs of animals, scales of fish, feathers of birds, barbs of feathers, human words, the voices of living creatures, movements of bodies, [Col. 0800C] thoughts of spirits, and many other things of this kind. They say to me: “You marvel at us because of our multitude; but rather marvel at him who made us because of his wisdom, which has no number. For though, in relation to you, we are without number, yet in relation to him we are not without number (Ps. 146:4). For even though we are many, we are not so to him; in whose sight we are not even [anything].”

### § VIII.—The magnitude of created things speaks of God, whose greatness has no end

And behold, my God, while my mind is still occupied and stretched out amid this multitude of created things, my eyes address me and say: “You are astonished at the multitude of creatures; do you not marvel also at their magnitude? Measure, if you can, masses and rocks, lumps and weights, mountain ridges, slopes of hills, hollows of valleys, reaches of rivers, the height of heaven, the breadth of earth, the depth of the abyss. Measure the giant among human beings, the elephant among animals, the griffin among birds, the whale among fish.” But as I desire to measure these things, my God, and cannot, I cry out in great wonder: “O how great they are! Who can comprehend their measure?” They answer me and say: “We are indeed great; but far greater, and great in another manner, is he who made us. Are you astonished when you see our greatness? Rather marvel at our Creator, the common Lord, who is great and exceedingly worthy of praise, [Col. 0801A] whose greatness has no end” (Ps. 144:3).

### § IX.—The beauty of all things declares their beautiful Creator

My eyes still encourage one another—O light of my inward eyes and God of my life! They encourage one another, I say, and say to each other: “Having seen both the great multitude and the exceedingly great magnitude of creatures, let us now behold their great and abundant beauty. Behold how much loveliness, splendor, comeliness, and beauty they possess. Behold how many and what kinds of gleams belong to gold, silver, and other metals, and to precious stones! Behold what a variety of many colors this is of which we speak; what diversity of splendors delights us!” I answer them: “Yes, indeed, it is as you say. But do these things **454** possess any likeness to my God because of their so great and such beauty?” Yet lest my eyes produce for me a phantom dream, those very things whose beauty I admire immediately answer me, Lord God, and say in a loud and mighty cry: “In comparison with the beauty which is in your God—or rather, which your God is—we are wholly deformed. We are certainly beautiful, but he who made us is far more beautiful.” To them I say: “What then do you say of my God? Where, I pray, is he?” They answer me in a loud voice: “Seek your Lord God above us.”

### § X.—Every noise and the sweet sound of voices teach us the euphony of that Word which is God

[Col. 0801C] After all these things, O Creator of all, Lord God—things which appear to and lie before my bodily gaze, and which my eyes perceive as wonderfully many, great, and beautiful, though they do not at all comprehend how many, how great, or how beautiful they are—my ears seize me and compel themselves to attention. Thus they address me and say: “See how many kinds of sounds we present to you.” I open my ears, my God, and voices of many kinds and diverse sounds flow into them. I hear the violent blasts of winds, the dreadful crashes of thunder, the swelling waves of the sea. I hear the varied and, within their respective kinds, similar [Col. 0801D] cries of birds and brute animals; manifold kinds of musical instruments, consonant in a certain dissonance and dissonant in consonant sound; wonderfully harmonious through their mutual discord, and discordant through their harmony. And first of all, Lord God, how welcome, pleasant, sweet, and delightful are human words, intelligible to human ears! By them, through the movement of the tongue, the sound of the lips, the mediation of hearing, and the understanding impressed upon the mind, one person discloses to another his willing and unwilling, knowing and being able—his whole self. Through them there is consolation in adversity, counsel in doubt, instruction concerning unknown things, revelation concerning secrets, disclosure of hidden things, questioning about what is unknown, answer to what is asked, prohibition of evils, command of goods, permission concerning intermediate matters, persuasion toward perfection, recollection [Col. 0802A] of things past, mention of things present, and preface concerning things to come.” And I address all these things and say: “What do you sound forth or say about my God?” They answer me, saying in a loud voice: “Nothing in us resembles that exalted and immeasurable Word which was in the beginning, was with God, and was God: the uncreated Word, creating all things; immovable, moving all things; the Word not made in time but begotten from eternity; the Word ordering times and temporal things without time, places and local things without place; the Word to whom nothing is past and nothing future, but all things are present; the Word which came forth from the mouth of the Most High (Ecclus. 24:5), which the heart of the Father uttered, which teaches knowledge to angel and human alike without movement of tongue or sound of lips; the Word not passing away, but remaining and enduring; the Word pouring sweet-sounding voices into the faithful soul, singing in its inward ear, by spiritual symphony, the tone of love of God and neighbor, of faith, hope, and charity toward God; thundering the diatessaron of prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance; the diapente of the five senses of the world—so that vanity may not corrupt sight, curiosity hearing, pleasure smell, gluttony taste, or impurity touch. Finally, so that the human being may be ordered outwardly and inwardly, this Word sings the diapason in the ear of the heart with the sweet melody of its voice, making the four principal virtues just mentioned appear in the five senses of which [Col. 0802C] we have just spoken through the effect of action, as though joining a *diatessaron* to a *diapente* and composing from them a *diapason*. Our melody, then, is sweet, and very sweet; but far sweeter is the euphony of this Word, through whom we exist, and who himself is your God. But you will not find him unless you seek above us, because he too made us.”

### § XI.—The fragrance of odors displays the sweet Spirit of God

My sense of smell says this same thing to me, Lord God: “Behold,” it says, “how many kinds and what kinds of odors I show you. See how many and what kinds of perfumes issue from herbs and trees, and breathe forth from compositions of diverse substances.” But [Col. 0802D] all say in one voice: “We are not your God. We are odors, and your God is a fragrance of great sweetness—a fragrance which no breath scatters, far sweeter than we are. If you seek him and wish to find him, seek above us.”

### § XII.—Tastes admonish us to taste their God

But my sense of taste also says within me, Lord God: “Review how many and what kinds of tastes are set before you through me.” And when I attend to them carefully, they cry out to me in a loud voice: “Your God is far more savory than we. If we taste good to you, may God, the most savory savor of all savors, taste better to you. But he will not taste sweet to you [Col. 0803A] unless you have learned to taste him. Therefore taste, and then you shall see that the Lord is sweet.”

### § XIII.—These tangible things proclaim an author other than themselves

“And I,” says my sense of touch, “distinguish rough from smooth among created things.” But all tangible things say to me: “We are not your God. Seek above us him who made us.”

### § XIV.—The treasure of divinity is sought in vain within the compass of the earth

But where shall I now seek you, Lord my God? Where, I pray, shall I seek you? Where shall I seek you, most splendid and precious treasure? Where shall I seek you, O pearl of greatest worth, so that, having found you, I may sell even all that I possess, depart, and buy [Col. 0803B] you? (Matt. 13:44.) Where, I pray, shall I seek you? Behold, I have gone out through all the gates of my body, and as a diligent explorer have searched, traversed, and walked through this whole world from the summit of heaven to the depths of earth; yet I have found none of the things going out through those gates to be you.

### § XV.—Through these visible things a path is laid to the Author of invisible things

Yet, Lord God, I say further to all things that are in the world: “What do you say about my God?” Behold, they answer me in a loud voice: “Seek him above us. For unless you transcend us, you will not apprehend him at all; unless you rise above us, you will not reach him. So long as you linger only among us, you remain far from him. Therefore, if you seek your God, seek him indeed through us, but seek him above us. For through us you have some path to him; but in us you have no arrival at him. For, as the truthful Apostle says, since the creation of the world God’s invisible things are perceived and beheld through the things that are made—his eternal power and divinity as well (Rom. 1:20). But these invisible things of his transcend all visible things by far.”

### § XVI.—The judgment of the five senses concerning external things

I say further to them: “What are you, that I should seek him through you and above you?” They answer: “If we are many, great, beautiful, or finally lovely in any respect, ask your eyes and they will tell you. But if [Col. 0803D] we are sounds or voices, inquire of your ears. If we are odors, your sense of smell knows how to speak about us. And we,” say the tastes, “are known to taste. But if we are smooth or rough, or anything of that sort, we belong to touch.”

### § XVII.—The varied change of these sublunary things attests the divine power that sustains them

And I say to them: “My senses have already informed me that this is what you are; yet I still ask: what are you?” They answer [**456**] me: “We are mutable creatures, created by the common Creator of all. For now we are of such a size, now of such a kind; now thus, now otherwise; now here, now there. We change according to the quantities of our measures, the qualities [Col. 0804A] of our forms, the varieties of places, and the movements of times. For at one time we are large, at another small; at one time larger, at another smaller; at one time long, at another short; at one time longer, at another shorter; at one time broad, at another narrow; at one time broader, at another narrower; at one time thick, at another thin; at one time thicker, at another thinner; and many things of this kind. Behold change according to quantities of measure. We are also at one time of this sort, at another of that sort; at one time thus, at another otherwise: behold change according to qualities of form. We are also at one time here, at another there: behold change according to varieties of place. We also change according to time, because we are in time, are temporal, and are changed temporally. But none at all of these changes can belong to your God, because he is neither body nor anything bodily.” These things they say to me, Lord God. And I say to them: “You are mutable, indeed, but so long as this world endures you do not cease to exist.” They answer me: “The common Creator of us all, who possesses existence in himself and from himself, one and the same, from eternity unto eternity, caused us to come forth from non-being into being. He willed mutable existence to belong to us in such a way that, so long as our service is necessary for you, this mutable existence of ours should not fail altogether into non-being.” I say to them: “Then are you carried and sustained?” “Indeed we are carried and sustained,” they say. And I: “By whom?” “By him by whom we are created,” they say, “we are carried.” And I: “Then is he beneath you?” “He is above us [Col. 0804C] and beneath us,” they say. “Beneath us through sustaining; above us through power: above, in governing; beneath, in bearing.”

### § XVIII.—God orders and fills all things in heaven and on earth by the word of his power

While I still marvel at these things, Lord God, your creatures call out to me with a mighty cry and say in a loud voice: “Not only does your God bear us; he also fills us. He fills us, we say; he is not filled by us.” The sun, moon, and stars raise their voice, my God, and say: “We shine over the earth; we divide day and night; we serve as signs, seasons, days, months, and years” (Gen. 1:14). All things flying in the air, all things moving upon the earth, and all things swimming in [Col. 0804D] the waters also say: “Each of us grows and multiplies in our own kind; we decrease and become fewer; we withdraw and are present.” “We also,” say the seas, “are restrained within boundaries appointed for us; we waters flow, we springs bubble up; all things sprouting from the earth keep the order imposed upon us. Behold, I, spring, shoot forth in the infancy of the year, like a child. I, summer, like a young man, bear flowers. I, autumn, in mature adulthood, examine the ripeness of fruits by their fragrance. I, winter, bearing the form of an old man, rest as though wearied and broken by the course of the year, and receive fruit by consuming it. Again I, spring, grow young; again I appear, renew what is old, raise what has fallen; and, in a certain likeness of the future resurrection, I restore anew all things long ago brought to nothing through a kind of life-giving renewal, and cause them to appear as what they had been.”

### § XIX.—He who is above all things presides over and is present within all things

“Your God,” they say, “is within us and outside us. He is within, without, above, and beneath: above by governing, beneath by bearing, within by filling, without by encompassing. For he governs all things, bears all things, fills all things, and encompasses all things. He governs, we say, and is not governed; he bears and is not borne; he fills and is not filled; he encompasses and is not encompassed. In governing he is above, but not elevated; in bearing he is beneath, but not placed under; in filling he is within, but not enclosed; in encompassing he is without, [Col. 0805B] but not diffused.” All your creatures say these things to me, Lord God, each in its own kind—whatever I can see, hear, smell, taste, and touch in this world. Still I, a most ardent inquirer, most diligent investigator, and most earnest searcher, address them in a loud voice and say: “**457** Tell me, I pray, something further about my God.” But these things, now vexed and wearied by my repeated questions, and as though indignant and grown tired, answer me thus: “Ask nothing further from us. We have told you many times already. If you seek your God, seek above us. For he is both before us and above us, because he himself made us. Seek him, therefore, above us.”

### § XX.—With bodily mass set aside, the divine being is sought in spirit and truth

[Col. 0805C] Therefore rebuffed, Lord God, I turn to myself. I turn, I say, to myself and say to myself: “What are you?” I answer: “A human being.” And I continue and say: “What is a human being? A conjunction of soul and body.” But I have already curiously investigated through the body all things subject to the bodily senses, and found none of them to be my God. It remains now, Lord God, that I separate myself from myself and divide my visible self from my invisible self, myself as body from myself as spirit; and that I, spirit, earnestly question myself as spirit, in case I as spirit may learn a fuller and more explicit answer concerning my God for myself as spirit. Therefore I now exclude from myself as spirit both my body [Col. 0805D] and every bodily thing; I enclose myself as spirit within myself as spirit, so that, insofar as I can, with the doors of our body shut, nothing formed through sight, nothing sounding through hearing, nothing fragrant through smell, nothing savory through taste, and nothing tangible through touch may enter into me as spirit. But you, Lord God, true light, light not illumined by anyone but enlightening every human being coming into this world (John 1:9); my God, dwelling in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen nor can see (1 Tim. 6:16)—you, I pray, my God, enlighten and glorify me; shine and beam upon me; let your countenance shine upon me, lest some mist of falsehood darken me; lest, finally, some phantom dream deceive me, whether as the offspring of a foolish heart or, what is more dangerous, as the seed of a cunning enemy.

### § XXI.—An analogy and disanalogy are examined between created and uncreated spirit, the human word and the Word of the eternal Father

I therefore address my spirit and say to it: “What are you?” It answers me: “I am a certain spiritual and invisible substance, simple and immaterial, created from nothing by the common Creator of all, and infused into the body to give it life.” I say to it: “How are you infused into the body to animate it?” “I am not infused into it part by part,” it says, “so as to be divided among its individual parts, such that the greater part of it receives a greater part of me and the lesser part a lesser part of me. Rather, I am whole in the whole body at once and [Col. 0806B] whole in each of its parts. This may clearly be understood from the fact that, when any particle of the body is injured, I, the whole spiritual self, suffer pain; and I could not suffer wholly unless I were wholly there. For so long as I am in any particle of the body, I am the life of that particle; because, so long as I inhabit it, I give it life by inhabiting it. Therefore, in relation to every part—that is, in which I am life—I am simple, immaterial, and indivisible. Indeed, because I exist, it is plain that when I am in any part, I am in it not by parts but wholly: wholly in that part, wholly in this one, wholly in every one of its parts, wholly in the entire body.”

I say: “If this is truly so in you, shall I then think this of my God: that since he too is spirit, he is wholly in all things that he has created and wholly [Col. 0806C] in each?” “You shall not think so of your God,” it answers. “For I am substantially infused into the body, because when I am substantially in the body, I am not substantially outside the body; and when I am substantially outside the body, I am not substantially in the body. For I cannot be substantially in the body and outside the body at the same time. But your Word is so in all things that he has created that he is also outside them; for although he is in all things, he is comprehended by none at all, because he is incomprehensible. For if this word, which is uttered in passing, and when uttered in passing is also heard in passing, is whole and at once in all the ears to which it comes, and whole and at once in each one—not partly [Col. 0806D] in this ear and partly **458** in that, but whole in this and whole in that, the same whole in each and the same whole in all—why should not that Word which was in the beginning and was with God, the Word which was God, which was in the beginning with God (John 1:1 and following)—the Word through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing that was made was made; the Word in whom was life; the Word not uttered so as to pass away, but permanently begotten from eternity—be, though in a far dissimilar manner, wholly in all creatures which he has made and wholly in each: not partly in this one and partly in that, but whole in this one and whole in that; the same whole in each, and whole in all?

Nor do I say that it is in the creatures which He has made in such a way as to deny that it is now also there where it was [Col. 0807A] before anything had been created by Him, and where it would be even if all that He created should cease to exist. But I speak improperly of it both as “was” and “will be.” For by saying “was” I imply past time, and by “will be” I designate future time, whereas for Him nothing passes away into “was,” nor comes to pass in “will be”; for in Him there are no things past or future, but all things are present. Therefore your God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things, is now also there where He was not indeed, but where He is, before anything had been created by Him; and where He will not be, but where He is, even though all that He made should cease to exist. For just as true unity did not multiply itself in the many things that He made, nor supreme immensity increase itself in the great things that He created, so surely immutable eternity will not diminish itself even if the same many and great things should altogether [Col. 0807B] cease to be. For what is truly one admits no number; what is immeasurable, no increase; and what is eternal, no diminution whatsoever. For if this word, uttered and heard in passing, of which it was said above, is neither greater in itself—as far as it is concerned—when it is received by all the ears to which it comes, nor less when it is uttered by a single mouth and heard by no ear, but is one and the same, as far as it is concerned, both when heard by many ears and when by none: why should not the Word of God, which is God and full of itself, likewise be neither less if all things should cease to exist, nor greater because it is in all the things He created? For just as He who is from eternity did not begin to be when He made all things, so He who is unto eternity [Col. 0807C] does not cease to be, even if He reduces all that He created from nothing to nothing. This concerning the assertion that God is in all the creatures He created.

## § XXII. No likeness of a creature suffices for investigating the Creator.

Yet this comparison drawn from human speech is neither complete nor sufficient for comparison with the Word of God, because for speaking of the Creator no likeness of a creature is altogether sufficient. For there is nothing in corporeal or spiritual creation that fully displays that uncreated Spirit, the Creator of all bodies and spirits. For although rational spirits are immortal, in a certain sense they are not immortal in comparison with Him. Of Him the truthful Apostle truly says: “Who alone has immortality” (1 Tim. 6:16). Nor only this: although many great things, corporeal and spiritual alike, exist, in a certain sense they do not exist in comparison with Him. Of Him it is said through blessed Job: “He alone is” (Job 23:13). Therefore He alone, according to Paul, possesses immortality, though rational spirits too are immortal. He alone, according to Job, is, though many other corporeal and spiritual things also are. Thus nothing in immortal spirits is fully like His immortality, and nothing in existing creatures fully like His very being. For rational spirits do not live in comparison with the life that is not vivified but vivifies; nor, in comparison with that eternal being which grants being to all things that are, are any creatures in a certain sense truly existent. Thus how He is in [Col. 0808A] all the creatures He has made cannot indeed be fully comprehended, but must be believed: for it ought not rashly to be examined; and, if examined, it cannot be discovered. Therefore, just as I, a created spirit, am wholly in my whole body and wholly in each of its parts, so your God—who indeed is Spirit, but uncreated—is wholly in all His creatures and wholly in each, though not in the same manner. For I, as I have already confessed above, when I am in the body am not outside the body, and when I am outside the body am not in the body; but your God, when He is within, is without, and when He is without, is also within. For, as has already been said, He is within all things but is not enclosed; outside, but not excluded; above, but not raised up; beneath, but not laid beneath.

## § XXIII. The mind assigns its function to each sense.

[Col. 0808B]

But transcend further within me and see that I give life to the body, as do the spirits that I have in common with brute animals, spirits which animate the bodies they inhabit. Transcend further within me, I say, and see that as I give life to the body, so I also endow it with sense. For I am the one who sees through the eyes, hears through the ears, smells through the nostrils, tastes through the throat, and touches through the other limbs. Yet brute animals too see, hear, smell, taste, and touch, because these five senses are active in them also.

## § XXIV. The alternation of affections found in man is absent from God.

[Col. 0808C]

But rise still higher within me and see that I endure many changing states of affection. At one time I rejoice, at another grieve; now I love, now desire; now I fear, now am secure. But your God undergoes no such changes at all. For although the things He does are diverse, He who acts is nevertheless one and the same, and always acts in the same manner. Just as this visible sun is in itself and in no way different from itself when, by the one and same heat of its ray, it melts wax and hardens mud, so too that Sun of righteousness is not different from Himself when, by the stable and immovable distinction of His just judgment, the sinner receives punishment for guilt and the saint receives glory for righteousness. He is said to be angry, yet there is no anger in Him; He is said to have mercy, yet there is no distress in Him [Col. 0808D]. For nothing new happens to Him, and nothing old slips away from Him, who remains one and the same, in the same manner always, both when He condemns the wicked and when He rewards the just—when, finally, a different recompense is assigned to different persons: punishment to the former, joy to the latter.

## § XXV. In God there is no forgetting or recollection, for all things are always present to Him.

But go still beyond me and see how beasts also have something in common with me, since they too now rejoice, now grieve, now desire, now fear, and undergo many such changes. Behold, I move through the vast, long, broad, and lofty hall of my memory; there I walk at length in thought, think and think again. There, surely, I turn over and ponder within myself all that I have seen through my eyes, heard through my ears [Col. 0809A], smelled through my nostrils, tasted through my throat, and felt by touch, even when the same doors of the senses are shut. At times I approach through recollection and withdraw through forgetfulness, because I forget things known and call forgotten things back to mind. I look back upon the past, behold the present, and look ahead to the future. But your God is not thus. For as He is unchangeable in affection, so He is unchangeable in thought. He does not think now this, now that; now in this way and now in that; rather, He thinks all things simultaneously and alike: simultaneously without time, alike without qualification, since with Him there is no change nor shadow of any alteration (Jas. 1:17). Yet beasts too remember and forget.

## § XXVI. There is a great difference between created and uncreated will.

[Col. 0809B]

There is indeed will in me. At one time I will, at another I will not; what I approve now, I soon disapprove; what I embrace at one moment, I presently flee; what now pleases me and I choose, soon displeases me and I reject. But do not conceive your God’s will to be like this. For His will is coequal and coeternal with Him; for Him, being and willing are the same. This will cannot be frustrated, because He is almighty; nor corrupted, because He is supremely good; it is not divided by multiplicity, because He is simple; nor changed by mutability, because He is eternal. Behold your God. These things, Lord my God, and many things of this kind, my mind says to me about You—or rather, You say them, not it. For it is not sufficient to think anything from itself, as though from [Col. 0809C] itself; rather, its sufficiency is from You (2 Cor. 3:5). And if it is not sufficient to think anything from itself as though from itself—indeed, because it is not—how is it sufficient to think anything from You as though from itself?

## § XXVII. Whatever our soul understands and knows, it receives from eternal Wisdom.

My spirit calls me, Lord my God, and says to me in a loud voice: “Behold, you have searched me out earnestly and diligently in my sixfold capacity: namely, that by which I live, give life, sense, sanctify, think, and will. But rise yet higher and enter into me. Rise, I say, above me to the me that is higher; enter more inwardly to the me that is more inward, and see that I possess wisdom and discernment. For although I am one and indivisible, I nevertheless customarily receive different names on account of my different operations [Col. 0809D]. Insofar as I animate bodily members, I am soul; insofar as I adhere to sensible things, I am sensibility; insofar as I sense, I am sense; insofar as I remember, I am memory; insofar as I understand, I am mind; insofar as I have wisdom, I am intellect; insofar as I contemplate, I am spirit; insofar as I discern, I am reason. For I possess wisdom and knowledge, reason and discernment. Through the wisdom infused into me I distinguish good from evil, true from false, advantageous from disadvantageous. Through it I distinguish also things which the bodily senses cannot attain: I distinguish humility from pride, kindness from envy, anger from gentleness, hatred from charity, and many things of this kind.”

To this I say: “Are not all these things open to bodily senses?” [Col. 0810A] “No,” it replies. “The signs and actions proceeding from them through the body can indeed be perceived by bodily senses; but the things themselves, since they are invisible dispositions of the mind, cannot at all be perceived.” Therefore I possess wisdom and rational understanding, which the spirits of brute animals do not possess in themselves. In this respect I am in some way like your God. Thus I am wisdom, and He too is wisdom; I am light, and so is He. Yet there is the greatest distance between Him and me. For I am wisdom, but created; He is wisdom, and creating. I am light, but illuminated; He is light, and illuminating. I know wisdom, but one I have received elsewhere—namely, from Him, from whom is every good gift and every perfect present (Jas. 1:17); but He knows wisdom [Col. 0810B] which He has from Himself and has received from no other. And, to state it more precisely, He knows by that wisdom which He Himself is.

## § XXVIII. In man, through the likeness of the Trinity, there is procession and a confession of unity.

Therefore you are and you know; you are knowing and know yourself to exist. You are, I say, and know that you are, and also know that you know that you are. And behold, if you consider clearly and look closely, you surely see that from these two—namely, your being and your knowing—there arises a certain third thing: love. For when you see your being to be so worthy and so exalted, you naturally love it. And when you see your wisdom to be so clear, so profound, so subtle—so clear for understanding, so profound for investigation, so subtle [Col. 0810C] for comprehension—you immediately love it, approve it, embrace it, and take pleasure in yourself through it. Thus a certain trinity arises in you, while unity remains: unity, because you are one substance and one spirit; trinity, namely your being, your knowledge, and your love. There is indeed being, and knowledge from being, since in existing you know and in knowing you exist. Love proceeds, however, neither from being alone nor knowledge alone, but from being and knowledge together, since you love that you exist and love that you know; and love belongs to both and proceeds from both. Therefore your being exists; from it wisdom is born; and from both love proceeds.

## § XXIX. In divine things there is identity of substance, distinction of persons, and differentiation of properties.

[Col. 0810D]

Enlightened through me, therefore, and awakened by me, rise above me to your God; and see first that He always is. For since He gave being to everything that is, it is plainly evident that nothing existed before Him to give Him being; rather, He always is, always is wise, and always loves His own being and wisdom. He has eternal being, and Wisdom coeternal with His eternal being; and Love coeternal with both. In your God none of these is earlier or later than another; but through the narrowness of your mouth it cannot be expressed except by saying that one thing is earlier and another later. Thus with your mouth you do indeed speak of one thing in Him as earlier and another as later; but in your heart you believe that nothing in Him is earlier and nothing later. [Col. 0811A]

There are, therefore, these three in your God: being, wisdom, and love. Being eternal from itself; wisdom coeternal, begotten from being; love coeternal, proceeding from being and wisdom. In this way you see that God is threefold. But see also that He is one: “For the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). There is in Him a distinction of Trinity, but no confusion of unity. Indeed, He is not three because He is one; nor is He not one because He is three. Rather, let unity be believed to be triune, and Trinity to be one. And if you distinguish these three, you see that being is not, in a certain sense, wisdom or love; nor wisdom, love or being; nor love, being or wisdom. Yet in God being, knowing, and loving are one and the same one. Thus reason distinguishes them, but faith does not divide them; and you see in your God [Col. 0811B] an undivided Trinity and an unconfused unity. In unity you see eternity and immensity; in eternity, immutability; and in immensity, simplicity—that is, immensity without quantity and eternity without time. In the Trinity, however, you see the communion of unity, the equality of immensity, and the coevality of eternity: communion of unity without division; equality of immensity without distinction; coevality of eternity without order or succession.

Instructed by these three, call these three persons. And because in them you see what is from no one, what is from another, and what is from both—as though something begetting, something begotten, and something proceeding—call the same persons Father, Son, and Holy [Col. 0811C] Spirit; assign being to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and love to the Holy Spirit; and confess the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

> [Note: Col. 0811C. This must be read cautiously.—Ed. P.]

Thus distinguish personally what is one substantially, because in God three are one and one is three: because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are God, and God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Father is from Himself; the Son is begotten by the Father alone; the Holy Spirit proceeds neither from the Father alone nor from the Son alone, but from both, from Father and Son together. Each of these is what the other is, and the same thing, because all three are by nature one God [Col. 0812A]. Yet none of them is the one who is the other: that is, the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit; the Son is not the Holy Spirit or the Father; and the Holy Spirit is not the Father or the Son. Thus there is unity with respect to substance and Trinity with respect to persons: identity in the former, property in the latter.

## § XXX. From the eternal God is the eternal Word; from both is the Holy Spirit, who is the eternal love of both.

Therefore You are, Lord God; You are, I say, Father, and are from Yourself, not from another, having being from Yourself—which being You Yourself are. And Your Son, God begotten from You, God the Father, is coequal, coeternal, and consubstantial with You. He is what You are, namely God, because You beget Him from Your substance, and therefore He is Son. [Col. 0812B] Nor do You beget anything other than what You are—God, namely, begetting God—but You beget someone other than Yourself: namely, the Father begets the Son. For You do not beget the one You Yourself are, lest You who beget should be begotten; rather, You beget that which You are, so that He who is begotten may be what You who beget are. For Your eternal Wisdom is born from You, coeternal Being.

The Holy Spirit belongs neither to the Father alone nor to the Son alone, but to both—to Father and Son—because He proceeds from both, Father and Son: namely, Love, loving Being and Wisdom, and flowing from both. And You, my God, gracious Spirit—though the Father is Spirit and holy, and the Son is Spirit and holy—are nevertheless in Your own person specially called the Holy Spirit, because You are the love and affection of Father and [Col. 0812C] Son; their sweetness and delight; in some sense their embrace and bond; and, as it were, a covenant of the two in the one Godhead. You are also the one poured into the hearts of Your elect for their sanctification; nor do You come without Father and Son, because You are not without Father and Son. And this is what it means that You do not come without them: You do not exist without them. You are also called God’s gift, though You Yourself are God. You are eternal, though given; but You are not received eternally, because Your proceeding from Father and Son is not temporal for You, but receiving You is temporal for human beings, who are temporal.

# PART TWO. CONSIDERATION OF HOW TERRIBLE GOD IS TOWARD THE REPROBATE.

[Col. 0811]

## § I. Woe to those who turn away from the Creator toward creatures.

[Col. 0811D]

Behold, Lord God: having already heard You with the hearing of my ear through the mighty cry of Your creatures, loudly addressing me in the examination of their natures, now, stirred by diligent consideration of myself, the eye of my mind, made clearer, sees You in some measure. I see that You are, that You know [Col. 0812D], that You love; and I am, know, and love. I am, Lord my God, but let me be in You; I know, but let me know You; I love, Lord, but let me love You.

Woe to the rational creature—angel, that is, and human being—that turns away from You! By reason of its dignity it cannot attain utter non-being; nor by reason of its perversity can it attain blessed being. It would have been better for them had they not been born rational [Col. 0813A], because they would not have been summoned to judgment and therefore would not have been plunged into punishment. Woe, then, to the unjust and impious who, leaving You, stable Being, wish to be in the things beneath themselves, either by following themselves or clinging to those things. For they cease to be, who, setting You aside, clear Wisdom, wish to know themselves or the things beneath them; they become foolish, who, casting aside You, sweet Love, love only themselves or the things beneath them. For they do not love; and if they love, they love damnably. Hence, Lord my God, in Your excellent creature—whom You made perfect, radiant, and whole for Yourself—defection diminishes fullness, darkness obscures brightness, and corruption contaminates wholeness. Thus they are not unjustly condemned to perpetual deprivation of their God, since voluntary and perpetual rejection had first held them guilty of rejecting the being, wisdom, and love of that same God [Col. 0813B].

## § II. The envious, lovers of the world, the arrogant, and the gluttonous are vividly condemned.

Woe to you, mass of the lost! Woe to you, light and dry straw, prepared for eternal fires! Woe to you, fruitless and withered tree, born for burning and fuel for the fire! Woe to you, Cain, son of perdition, who, envious of the Church of the elect—your brother’s exile, present and grieving—urge him by treacherous counsels and corrupt examples to go out into external things, so that, once gone out, you may kill him! Woe to you, because, departing from the face of the Lord, you dwell wandering and fugitive upon the earth: wandering through disordered desire, fugitive through a sinful conscience [Col. 0813C]; because the former continually burns your flesh within you, and the latter gnaws your mind without ceasing. Woe, I say, to you, who, begetting Enoch in the beginning, build a city upon the earth, because, dedicating yourself to present things alone, you fix the intention of your heart upon earthly things. Woe to you, children of this age, who, armed with fat neck, run against God with uplifted neck, depart from the shining and luminous East, and, finding a very broad plain, walk by its broad way that leads to perdition; and many are those who enter through it (Matt. 7:13).

Woe, I say, to you, proud and lofty children of Adam, exalted and lifted up! Woe to you, because having been lifted up, you must be cast down, and shall vanish like smoke. You now dwell in the land of Shinar (Gen. 2:2) [Col. 0813D], that is, in the foul conduct of your sins, for *Sennaar* is interpreted “their stench.” There you dwell; there you exhort one another and say: “Come, let us make bricks for ourselves, and bake them with fire; let us make a city and a tower whose top may reach unto heaven” (ibid., 5). And you add: “Let us make our name renowned” (ibid.). Woe to you, who call your names upon your lands, loving the chief seats in synagogues, the first places at feasts, greetings in the marketplace, and being called Rabbi by men (Matt. 23:6). But your tower will fall and the city you build will be destroyed. Now you have bricks instead of stones and bitumen instead of mortar. Bitumen is envy; mortar is concord. Stones signify the strength of good works, while bricks signify the softness of fleshly [Col. 0814A] corruption. For bitumen is produced from earth struck by lightning, because envy is born in a soul struck by the swelling of pride. Bricks are baked with fire so that they may harden, because your bodies are burned by lust so that they may become foul. Therefore, O proud and impious ones, you have bitumen instead of mortar and bricks instead of stones, because, rejecting the serenity of concord, you admit into yourselves the disturbance of envy; and, abandoning the strength of good work, you love the mud of filthy desire. From these you build the height of a tower: namely, the loftiness of pride.

Woe also to you, hairy and shaggy Edom, who hunger indeed for your own death when you set your belly above the dignity of your birthright (Gen. 25:34). Certainly you are a man skilled in hunting, sending out and stirring up your dogs through the immense [Col. 0814B] forest of this world to procure flesh for you: that is, so that your eyes may bring you vanity, your ears curiosity, your nostrils pleasure, your taste gluttony, and your other limbs impurity. You remain outside so long to your ruin (Gen. 27:22), while by your delay and because of your delay you are deprived of the inheritance of your father’s blessing. By contrast, Jacob dwells in the house of the mind with manly simplicity and simple virtue, and is enriched by his father’s blessing.

## § III. The desire of the flesh and of the eyes, and pride of life, rebuked in typological censure.

Woe to you, O Egyptian mistress, exceedingly beautiful—but foul! Beautiful in face, foul in soul: you lustfully invite the innocent and chaste Hebrew [Col. 0814C] boy to lustful union with yourself (Gen. 39:12). Yet modest Joseph, mindful of his chastity, leaves his cloak in your hands and flees naked (ibid.). For holy men choose rather to be cast off in the house of God than to dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83:11), that is, to be drawn by their corrupt examples and counsels into consenting to sin. For that disciple whom Jesus loved fled naked from his persecutors, casting off his linen garment (Mark 14:52), because it is necessary even for those whom Jesus loves through the eternity of predestination, through the love and sweetness of election, sometimes to relinquish the use of certain temporal things [Col. 0814D], lest, while they fully provide everywhere for necessity, they yield in some matter to pleasure; lest, if they do not cautiously cut away even lawful things in themselves, unlawful things also secretly grow up.

Woe to you, Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who even today resist the lawgiver in the rebellion of pride! For the earth, opening its mouth, swallows you and your accomplices (Num. 26:10): that is, desire for earthly things utterly destroys you from the life of spiritual things, so that, descending alive into the hell of sin while nevertheless covered by the soil of perverse will, you perish from the midst of the Israelite multitude through the practice of perverse conduct.

Cursed be your counsel, O Balaam, son of Beor! And cursed be your teaching, by which you teach Balak to set a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication [Col. 0815A] (Rev. 2:15). Woe to you, deceitful and fraudulent Delilah! You still deliver into the hands of his enemies, after his hair has been shorn, Samson—the sun of those among whom he was, for that is the interpretation of his name—so that, both his eyes torn out and he assigned in the prison of his mind to the mill of outward pleasures, he becomes a mockery to those to whom he had formerly been a terror (Judg. 16:19 ff.). Alas, alas, most beautiful and mighty young man! Alas, I say, that you opened all your secret to a deceitful and filthy harlot; that you did not keep the gates of your mouth against her who slept in your bosom—or rather, in whose bosom you slept. For Hezekiah too is said to have sinned because he showed the treasures of the Lord to the messengers of the king of Babylon (4 Kgs. 20:13).

[Col. 0815B]

Woe to you, sons of Eli, devoted to gluttony and lust! You send forth your servant—that is, your childish understanding—holding a three-pronged fork in his hand and displaying in act the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, that he may bring you raw flesh: you who know neither the Lord nor the priests’ duty toward the people (1 Sam. 2:12–15).

## § IV. The slight itch of sin, which delights, is followed by eternal punishment, which torments.

And woe to you, proud Saul, proud and envious persecutor of humble and kindly David. When you enter the cave to relieve your belly [Col. 0815C], the gentle, exiled, and devout man spares you and does not lay his hand upon you to kill you; indeed, he even strikes his own heart because he had dared to cut off merely the hem of your cloak (1 Sam. 24:4–6).

Woe to you, miserable Amnon—miserable, I say, and pitiable—who are bound to your sister by a love so ardent and so foul: at first sweet, but afterward bitter even in name; ardent to the point of your sickness, foul to the point of her violation. Finally, once your foul and fetid desire has been fulfilled through a deed still fouler and more fetid, you hate her more than you formerly loved her; and you who before were sick for love of her cannot bear to look upon her afterward (2 Sam. 13:1–15). For every man first sets out good wine, but when they have become drunk, then that which is worse (John 2:10). Hence someone says: “The wicked live and are exalted and strengthened by riches [Col. 0815D]. Their offspring remain before them, and the throng of grandchildren is near in their sight. Their houses are secure and peaceful, and the rod of God is not upon them. Their bull has conceived and has not failed; their cow has calved and has not been deprived of her offspring. Their little ones go forth like flocks, and their children leap in play. They take up tambourine and lyre and rejoice at the sound of the instrument; they spend their days in prosperity” (Job 21:7 ff.). Behold the good wine which you, who are men, first set out. Behold also the great love with which you love Tamar, O miserable Amnon. But what does Scripture add? “And in a moment,” it says, “they go down to hell” (ibid.). Behold, when you have become drunk, what is worse is offered [Col. 0816A] to you. Behold also the great hatred with which you hate that same Tamar, O Amnon!

Woe also to you, faithless Absalom, whom a heavy head of hair—the superfluity of temporal things—weighs down, and by which you are also suspended. Three spears are thrust into your heart: namely, the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which are in the world. And the mule upon which you sit passes on (2 Sam. 18), because the world indeed passes away, and its desire (1 John 2:17). Pleasure passes away, but guilt remains and punishment endures. What delighted passes away, I say, but what punishes remains. Therefore the world passes away and the rider of the mule dies: for the world falls, but the lover of the world is punished. You are cast, O Absalom, into a great pit [Col. 0816B], because the impious are plunged into the pit of hell. “And they gathered,” it says, “over him an exceedingly great heap of stones” (2 Sam. 18:17). “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). Behold the heap of stones, not only great but exceedingly great, because there neither their worm dies nor their fire is extinguished (Mark 9:45), so that both fire burns their flesh and the worm gnaws it; for the vengeance upon the flesh of the impious is fire and worm. Neither the burning of the one nor the gnawing of the other will ever cease, so that, just as here they never wished to end their guilt, so there, ever living mortally and dying vitally, they may never end their punishment.

## § V. God is terrible in the condemnation of the reprobate among the children of men.

[Col. 0816C]

Woe to you, wicked and adulterous generation, evil and perverse generation! Woe to you, depraved and provoking generation, a generation that has not made its heart straight (Deut. 32:5), and whose spirit is not faithful to God (Ps. 77:8)! Woe to you, children of perdition—namely, wicked angels and men—who, rejecting your God, in whom you ought to exist steadfastly, know clearly, and love sweetly, fail in your own being; become foolish in your own wisdom, if indeed it is wisdom; and become bitter in your own love.

And O how terrible You are, Lord God, in them! For the hidden judgment of Your righteous sentence [Col. 0816D] watches over each reprobate—angel and human being—casting them from Your face, excluding them from the lot of Your elect, and delivering them to eternal oblivion as vessels of wrath fitted for destruction (Rom. 9:22). For You neither wash away their evils nor approve their goods; moreover, You harden their hearts lest they turn to You and be made blessed in You. This is terrible and horrible because it is fixed in eternity, altogether immovable and unchangeable. O God, terrible in Your counsels over the children of men (Ps. 65:5)! O, I say, terrible in the reprobate! Their contempt of Your goodness, if indeed any remains to them, the absence of all forgetfulness of their wickedness, and the hardening of their blind heart proclaim You very terrible toward them.

You govern their perverse will as hidden and just, all-powerful [Col. 0817A] God, disposing all things sweetly, so that what it unjustly endeavors against You is secretly arranged according to You. And although it displeases insofar as it is evil and unjust, it nevertheless pleases insofar as it is disposed and ordered. You govern it, Lord God, in four ways: by the limit of power naturally bestowed; by a miracle of possibility temporarily imposed; by the obstacle of difficulty externally presented; or by the judgment of a disposition working inwardly.

## § VI. God governs the will of the impious fourfold, yet by a gentle and strong counsel.

The first mode is when the natural ability to act is granted; the second, when that same natural ability is restrained by Your sudden and hidden power without an external impediment; the third, when, by Your will, the wills of others opposing from without through other powers are hindered [Col. 0817B] so that they cannot come to effect; the fourth mode is when Your power, Lord God, which inwardly presides over every creature, secretly bends even those wills that have arisen against Yours toward accomplishing Your will.

Thus, Lord God, the evil will of the reprobate can indeed be corrupted within itself and dissolved through its own fault, which is not given to it from elsewhere; but it cannot hurl itself outward through willing unless a way is opened for it. And when, for that headlong perverse will, You, God, open the way it desires, You in some sense incline it—not by impelling, however, but by permitting and not restraining it. You are not the author of its falling, but the orderer of its course. Thus, by whatever methods and occasions You will, whether inwardly or outwardly [Col. 0817C], You, almighty God, both arouse the evil wills of humans and demons to will and order them to endure. In these, certainly, their being evil belongs to those wills themselves, while their being ordered belongs to You.

But this inward ordering of Yours is so hidden that even the evil wills within which it operates do not know it. They therefore suppose themselves guided by their own free choice because they feel themselves moved by their own desire without compulsion. Since they are not impelled, they do not understand that they are directed; nor do they know that they have one going before them so that they may be ordered, because they do not feel one pushing them from behind so that they may be hurled headlong. Thus, thus, You, almighty God, terrible and strict, harden the hearts of the impious whom You reprobate from eternity—terribly because immovably; justly indeed, but hiddenly. For perpetuity of condemnation must necessarily follow eternity of reprobation [Col. 0817D], so that, just as they were reprobated from eternity, so they may be condemned unto eternity.

## § VII. Why a human being does not know in this life whether he is worthy of hatred or of love.

Therefore, O Lord God, how terrible and exacting you show yourself toward the reprobate, when you so reject them from eternity that you punish them for eternity! Alas for me! What is this, my God? What, I pray, is this? I ask what this is; but I do not dare to ask why it is so. Indeed, this question cannot be resolved. Therefore I tremble in astonishment and, trembling, am struck dumb; and with fearful wonder I cry out and say: O terrible Lord God in respect of the reprobate! Behold, I fail beneath your wrath, and am violently shaken beneath your fury. And who [Col. 0818A] knows the power of your anger, or can measure out your wrath according to the fear due to you? (Ps. 89:11). Who would not fear amid these things? Who would not be terrified? For who is secure concerning his election, and who is not afraid concerning his reprobation? “The righteous and the wise, and their works, are in your hand”; and yet “a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred; but all things are kept uncertain for the future” (Eccles. 9:1). “They are kept uncertain for the future,” he says; for then they will be certain. They will be certain then, I say, when there will be neither place nor time for amendment.

Now indeed, O Lord God, there are among us wise persons and righteous persons: wise in heart, righteous in deed. Wise in regard to purity of conscience; righteous in regard to public reputation; in short, wise inwardly before God, righteous outwardly toward [Col. 0818B] the neighbour. And our works are in your hand; yet we do not know whether we are worthy of love or hatred. O Lord, I say, my God—eternal and great God, exalted and intimate; mighty and righteous God—if dust dares question your Majesty: why do we not know that we are worthy of love, if we are wise and righteous? And I hear you indeed answering these things in the inward ear of my heart: “If,” you say, “you were truly righteous, you would have no need to doubt that you are worthy of my love. But you are not truly righteous unless you are righteous in my eyes; for very often your righteousness shines before human beings and is foul in mine. And sometimes I judge worthy of eternal damnation something which human judgment considers worthy of the reward of eternal blessedness; because you often provoke me to anger by the very things through which you think you can appease me when I am angry. Therefore it is no wonder if you are uncertain of love, while you still doubt your own merit; or if you do not know whether you will reach your homeland, while you still do not know whether you are travelling by the right road.”

## § VIII.—No one should be secure concerning election, and no one should not fear his own reprobation.

Having heard these things from you, O Lord God, I too say: Woe, then, even to my praiseworthy life, if it should happen to be examined by you without mercy! O terrible and mighty Lord, who does great and unsearchable things, and wonders without number! “If you come to me, I shall not see you; and if you depart, I shall not understand. If suddenly you question, [Col. 0818D] who will answer you, or can say, ‘Why do you do thus?’ God, whose anger no one can withstand, beneath whom those who bear the world bend.” How great, then, am I, that I should answer you and speak my words before you? Even if I possessed something righteous, I would not answer you, but would entreat you as my judge. And when you have heard me calling upon you, I do not believe that you will heed my voice (Job 9:11 ff.). Whatever good I have done is judged condemnable by you, if it is examined by you without mercy.

Accordingly, the prophet, shaken by consideration of this exacting judgment of yours of which I speak, says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord” (Ps. 143:2). Why he did not wish you to enter into judgment even with himself, he made known by adding: “For no living person shall be justified in your sight.” And why “every living person”? [Col. 0819A] He excepted no one. He knew that neither the foremost prophet, nor the outstanding patriarch, nor any apostle, nor anyone at all born into this mortality, could be judged righteous in your sight if you wished to enter [Col. 0820A] into judgment with him. I see these things, O Lord my God. I see them, I say, and I fear. I consider them and tremble. I behold them and quake in your hands, O God, righteous and hidden—hidden and righteous!

# PART THREE. CONSIDERATION OF HOW LOVABLE AND SWEET THE LORD IS TOWARD THE ELECT.

[Col. 0819]

## § I.—The gracious adoption of God’s children, whose sins committed in time do not appear in eternity.

[Col. 0819B]

But how blessed are your elect, O Lord God, almighty Father! How blessed, I say, are those whose names have been written from eternity in the book of life, and who through their Redeemer—your Son Jesus—have access by faith to this grace in which they stand, rejoicing in hope of the glory of your children, in whose hearts the love of God has been poured out through the Holy Spirit whom you give them (Rom. 5). Your Spirit also bears witness to their spirit that they are your children. And if children, then heirs: heirs indeed of you, but fellow-heirs of Christ (Rom. 8:16–17).

O children of blessed predestination! O pure vessels of eternal election! O holy and [Col. 0819C] beloved ones, whom you love as a sweet fragrance, taking pleasure in them! You bless them with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as you chose them before the foundation of the world, that they might be holy and without blemish before you in love. You predestined them for adoption as children through Jesus Christ in himself, according to the purpose of your will, unto the praise of glory and grace, by which you have bestowed grace upon them in your beloved Son. In him they have redemption through his blood, for the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which has abounded in them in all knowledge and prudence (Eph. 3:4 ff.).

With what sweet, wondrous, and delightful love, O Lord, you bind yourself to them—calling, gathering, and [Col. 0819D] uniting them to yourself by the indissoluble bond of eternal love—so that no one can snatch them from your hand! In a wonderful way you make not only good things but even their very evils cooperate for their good: so that, while you live as their effective helper everywhere, zealously guarding their salvation in every event and every condition of time, being for them and with them, nothing at all can be against them; since even that which seemed to be against them is with them and for them. O covenant of serenity! O covenant of peace which you make with them, smiling upon them with a cheerful and unfailing face, looking upon them with a gracious and serene countenance, even kissing them with the kiss of your mouth, cleansing them, fitting them together, and perfecting them! Cleansing them, I say, through forgiveness of sins; fitting them through the grace of merits; perfecting them through the glory of rewards: so that at last they may eternally be in themselves what they are eternally in you.

[Col. 0820B] Although one and the same corruption of the flesh brings forth both elect and reprobate together, nevertheless a different dwelling always receives them according to both merit and reward. For fish together with birds are produced from the same waters; yet fish are submerged in the depths of their original abode, while birds obtain a place in the air. One and the same earth brings forth tares together with wheat; yet the barn receives the wheat, while fire consumes the tares. Esau and Jacob were born of the same parents, at one and the same time; yet the one is loved and the other hated (Rom. 9:13).

For just as a freeborn person, raised for some time in slavery and exile, when through another’s report he recognizes both his free birth and liberty, strives with all zeal and effort to seize his inheritance, to cast off slavery and put on freedom, to abandon exile and hasten to his hereditary kingdom: so indeed, so, I say, the holy Church of the elect, born amid the misery of this present exile and servitude, when through your inspiration, O Lord, it recognizes both the dignity of its free birth and the blessedness of its inheritance, does not cease to press on with tireless strength until it acquires both. No sins remove them from you, who, as it seems to me, in some sense do not even sin; for heavenly generation—that is, eternal predestination—preserves them, and they cannot sin (1 John 3:9), because whatever sins they may appear to have committed in time do not appear at all in eternity. Their sins [Col. 0820D] you overlook because of repentance (Wis. 2:24); and your love covers and conceals them, hiding them from your judgment.

## § II.—The singular favor of the most holy Trinity toward the elect.

Thus they rest upon you, the Lord their God, and upon eternal being, that they may be strong; they attend to radiant wisdom, that they may be wise; and they are joined to sweet love, that they may be sweet and joyful, good and blessed. They have being from you because they are created by you; they are also wise through you because they are enlightened by you; and they are blessed in you because they enjoy you as well. For, subsisting from you, they are given their due measure; contemplating you, they are illumined; cleaving to you, they rejoice. O Father! O Son! O Holy Spirit! From you indeed they have the cause of nature; through you, the form of knowledge; in you, the fullness of life.

Therefore in your eternity, O Father, [Col. 0821A] they flourish; in your truth, O Son, they shine; in your goodness, O gracious Spirit, they rejoice. Having you as Father and author of their being; you as Son and teacher of truth, that they may be wise; and you as Holy Spirit and infuser of inward sweetness, that they may grow sweet in blessedness. And this, O Lord God, is the new human being, created by you who are three, according to you who are three; whom your elect, renewed in the spirit of their mind, do not cease daily to put on. They receive righteousness from you the Father, truth from you the Son, holiness from you the Holy Spirit, so that the human being may appear created according to you in righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. 4:24).

## § III.—Peace is proclaimed to those who have walked with God, spotless from this world.

[Col. 0821B] Peace, therefore, to you, O praiseworthy people, whom the Lord of hosts blesses! Peace to you, inheritance of the Lord, O Israel, who strive, whether absent or present, to please him; not conformed to this world, but transformed through the renewal of your understanding, so that you may prove what is his good, pleasing, and perfect will (Rom. 12:2).

Peace to you, righteous man in your generation, O Noah! To avoid the floodwaters, lest either the storm of waters submerge you or the deep swallow you, you enter the ark, which the Lord closes from outside; in him your soul trusts, and in the shadow of his wings you hope until iniquity passes away (Gen. 7:16, 23).

Peace to you, faithful old man! In order that you may become a great nation, you leave Ur of the Chaldeans and depart from your land, your kindred, and your father’s [Col. 0821C] house.

Peace to you, O Sarah! So that you may not live a mortal life, you die a life-giving death; having your life hidden with Christ in God, you are buried in the twofold cave of action and contemplation together (Gen. 23:19).

Peace to you, blessed seed of a father in old age, O Isaac! Even among foreigners, you do not cease to dig wells until you find living water (Gen. 26:19).

Behold, peace to you, O Jacob, simple man dwelling in the house of the mind! Yielding to your brother’s wrath, you leave your native land to avoid his threats. With one of the stones lying there placed beneath your head, after sunset, at Bethel, you sleep and rest together in peace. There too you behold the ladder of love reaching to heaven, the ascent and descent of angels upon it, and the Lord of the ladder standing upon it (Gen. 28:5, 12). How blessed you are! For the beautiful Rachel you serve so tirelessly for seven years, years which the greatness of love makes seem few to you (Gen. 29:17, 20). At last enriched by a manifold offspring of action and contemplation together, you return to your father’s house (Gen. 30:43); and lest you enter it by two paths, touched by the angel in the thigh, you walk lame, relying wholly upon one path (Gen. 32:25).

Peace to you, innocent Joseph, whose many-colored garment commends his innocence (Gen. 37:3). Innocent Joseph, I say: innocent and simple, obedient and patient, chaste and kind—innocent in [Col. 0822A] conduct of life; simple in the revelation of dreams (ibid., 5–9); obedient to his father’s command (ibid., 14); patient even to being sold (ibid., 25–28, 36); chaste even to imprisonment (Gen. 39:7–20); kind even to the forgiveness of injury (Gen. 45:1–4). Finally, when dead, you are embalmed with spices and placed in a coffin in Egypt (Gen. 50:25), because the holy Church of the elect, in the dark exile of this present life, conceals in the secret place of inward action the fruit of contemplation, dead to this world and compounded with the manifold fragrances of virtues, like the firstborn of Rachel.

Peace also to you, Moses, man of God! Having struck the Egyptian—that is, having slain sin within yourself—you escape through flight both the evil envy of Pharaoh and envious malice (Exod. 2:12, 15). Having defended the girls against the shepherds—that is, having rescued the thoughts of the heart from attacking phantasms—you water their flock, that is, foster and nourish their good fruitfulness (Exod. 2:16, 21). And, driving the sheep into the inner parts of the wilderness—that is, bringing innocent thoughts into their deepest secret places—you remove from the course of the mind the deadly sandals of evil examples, and pass on so as to behold the great vision in the holy land (Exod. 3:1–5).

Peace to you, blessed nation of the Lord! Peace to you, O people whom he chose for his inheritance (Ps. 32:12)! Casting off the dreadful and harsh yoke of Pharaoh, abandoning the assemblies of the Egyptians, and wholly renouncing the hard labours of mortar and brick, through the manifold perils [Col. 0822C] of this wilderness you enter the promised land, the land flowing with milk and honey (Exod. 13:5)—indeed, the land of the living, in which you see the good things of the Lord (Ps. 26:13).

## § IV.—The singular kingdom and adoption of three men.

Blessed are you through all ages, our Jesus, who, as you save your people from their sins (Matt. 1:21), show that your name derives from the reality. Through you God gives us all the land which he promised our fathers that he would give; and at the end we shall possess it and dwell in it without end. Through you true peace is given to us by God the Father, and no enemy will dare resist us, [Col. 0822D] when Judah is saved, Israel dwells securely, and the land rests from wars (Jer. 23:6).

The Lord is with you, most valiant of men, Gideon. Peace be with you, and be strengthened: at the angel’s command you place flesh upon the rock and pour broth over it. The fire coming out of the rock, when struck by the angel’s staff, consumes all these things (Judg. 6:21), because by the prompting of inward inspiration the elect mortify the works of flesh within themselves and annihilate even fleshly thoughts. Then, as he who precedes them by inspiration follows up their action by helping them, through the sweet infusion of his love and desire he kindles in them the fire of holy compunction, which consumes their burnt offering in his eyes.

Peace also to you, most holy servant of God, Samuel, who grow, and the Lord is with you; and not one of all your words falls to the ground (1 Sam. 3:19). Your renown spreads so widely that all, from Dan to Beersheba, know that you are a faithful prophet of the Lord (ibid., 20).

## § V.—A catalogue of illustrious men who shone through the mystical practice of virtues.

Peace to you, David—strong, humble, and kind! Strong to kill the lion of pride and choke the bear of uncleanness (1 Sam. 17:34–35); humble to dance before the Lord (2 Sam. 6:5); kind in sparing even an enemy (2 Sam. 16:10).

Peace to you, Elijah, man of God! You display the holy perfection of the elect and their perfect holiness in yourself, as you flee from and avoid, with such zeal, the cursed and maleficent Jezebel—that is, the concupiscence [Col. 0823B] of this world—and fly in all haste to the wilderness on the wings of a dove (1 Kgs. 19:3). In Beersheba of Judah you leave your servant: through purity of confession and the inspiration of the sevenfold Spirit, you cast off childish understanding. Remaining in the solitude of the mind, you seek death for your soul, desiring to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23). Awakened by the angel of inward inspiration from the sleep of sloth, you are refreshed with bread baked under ashes, because you are nourished by the humility of good works, so that in its strength you may attain, through the forty-year span of this present exile, to enduring eternity and the eternal stability of the heavenly mountain.

Therefore peace to you, Elijah, man of God, girded at the loins with a leather belt, because you shine in chastity of body (2 Kgs. 1:8). Peace to you, I say—true peace; surely the peace of the Lord, which the Lord himself both leaves and gives (John 14:27). Peace to you, who through an ecstasy of contemplation stand at the entrance of the cave of the flesh, while a great and mighty wind passes by, shattering mountains and rocks: for in his elect the Lord melts every hardness and casts down every height. But lest you search majesty in such a way as to be crushed by glory, cover your face with the cloak of work when you hear the whisper of a gentle breeze (1 Kgs. 19:12–13).

Peace to you, most holy Elisha, possessor of Elijah’s double spirit—yes, possessor of Elijah’s double spirit (2 Kgs. 2:9). For whoever believes in our Elijah will also do the works that he does, and will do greater works than these; because he goes to his Father and leaves his cloak on earth for Elisha, because he is with all his own people every day until the end of the age (John 14:12).

Therefore peace to you, Elisha! You follow Elijah so closely and devote yourself so fully to his service (1 Kgs. 19:20) that you kiss farewell to father, the world, and mother, concupiscence—not in affection but in renunciation—turning your mind’s back wholly upon them, bidding them farewell and proposing never to return to them further.

Peace also to you, outstanding Isaiah! At the Lord’s command, you are not ashamed to display the nakedness of the flesh in preaching, laying aside worldly garments completely (Isa. 20:2), so that, unburdened of earthly things and freed from transient concerns, walking like an unencumbered traveller—and therefore singing before the robber—you may journey more easily and securely toward heavenly and eternal things.

Peace to you, noble king Hezekiah, who walk in the way of David your father (2 Kgs. 18:5). At prophetic threats, you turn your mind’s face toward the wall of your sins which you have built between yourself and your God, and before him who made you, you weep for what you have done (2 Kgs. 20:2), so that from the same sacred Scripture from which you heard the dreadful threat of death, you may receive the sweet consolation of life. This life will be given you both now in the spiritual seventh day of rest and hereafter in the eighth day of blessed resurrection, so that, freed from sin but made a servant of God, you may have your fruit unto sanctification and your end eternal life (Rom. 6:22): as though receiving at once seven and eight years of life, which together make fifteen.

Peace to you, Ezekiel the prophet! Standing through the lofty merit of life in the building of the city set upon a mountain and facing south, you have your eyes fixed upon the gate—upon the gate, that is, which leads to the city (Ezek. 40:2–6). You walk by faith and desire by hope, turning your back on transient things and your face toward eternal things; finally, you desire that the earthly house within you be dissolved, so that you may receive from God a building, a house not made with hands, eternal in heaven (2 Cor. 5:1; Phil. 1:23).

## § VI.—Continuation of the same theme, with a felicitous prayer.

Peace to you, O Jeremiah most holy, sanctified in the womb, virgin and priest [Col. 0824C] of God! Ropes and old rags lift you from the muddy pit (Jer. 38:12–13), because both the commandments of sacred Scripture and holy examples raise up the saints of God, predestined by him from eternity unto life, from the foul depth of present life; so that in them they may destroy the deceitful tongue, the sharp arrows of the mighty, and the desolator’s coals, in the ascending degrees of the songs (Ps. 119:4).

Surely peace also to you, Josiah: a boy, yet not boyish! Your memory “will be sweet as honey in every mouth, and like music at a banquet of wine” (Sir. 49:2). As soon as you hear the discovered book read before you, you diligently and humbly consult the prophetess, and do not delay to carry out in deed what you hear written in the book (2 Chr. 34:16).

Peace to you too, Daniel, “man of desires” (Dan. 9:23), who shine in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation like a light in the world: humble among the proud and abstinent among the gluttonous. Since you refuse to be defiled by the king of Babylon’s table (Dan. 1:9), you attain even to the summit of prophecy; and because you spare yourself what is sweet to the belly, you ascend to what is sweet to the mind.

Peace to you, Tobit, good father of a good son, and Tobias, good son of a good father (Tob. 1:2)! In the land of your captivity you serve the Lord so devoutly and so promptly—devoutly toward the Lord, promptly toward your neighbour. You sit weeping as you remember Zion, hanging your instruments upon the willows in its midst (Ps. 137:1–2), and sighing for the beautiful city Jerusalem, whose gates are built of sapphire, emerald, and precious stone; whose encircling walls are of white stone; whose streets are paved with pure gold; through all whose lanes is sung the song of joy, namely the song of songs which is Alleluia (Tob. 13:21–22).

But to what end are all these things? What am I undertaking, and where am I proceeding? I undertake what cannot be completed; I proceed where one cannot arrive. For, O Lord God, I lack both understanding to comprehend the manifold merit of your elect and time to enumerate it. Therefore, to put an end to these matters now: peace to you, generation of the upright, which shall be blessed (Ps. 3:2); generation which receives blessing from the Lord and mercy from God its saviour (Ps. 23:5). Peace, I say, to you, generation seeking the Lord, seeking [Col. 0825B] the face of the God of Jacob; you who leave the valley of the world and ascend the mountain of the Lord; who both devoutly believe, through the faith of belief, in the blessedness for which you were created, and do not fail to seek it diligently and perseveringly through holiness of life.

## § VII.—By wonderful sweetness and favor God so directs his elect through temporal things that they do not lose eternal things.

This generation seeks you, O Lord God, because you stir it up to seek you, consecrating it with your earnest, dedicating it with your pledge, and marking it with your gift.
