You endow her—sweetly embittered and emptied by bitter sweetness—with the ring of right faith through the division of vices and the birth of virtues, and with the bracelet of good works, [Col. 0825C] so that thereafter the display of both bracelet and ring may render her immune from the terror of your dreadful judgment (Gen. 38:18).

Your old man, O Lord God—your old man, I say, David—is warmed by Abishag (1 Kgs. 1:1–2), because contemplation kindles the holy Church of the elect. Indeed, clothing cannot impart warmth to this David, who has many days of age—that is, who possesses many works of virtue—for, as is written, “though he was covered with clothes, he was not warmed” (ibid.). And what are all earthly things, O Lord, except certain garments for the body? Yet your elect are not warmed by them at all, their soul refusing consolation; rather, they remember you and are delighted (Ps. 76:4), and meanwhile rejoice in the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness, until they can enjoy the presence of that same sweetness.

O how great is the multitude, and how manifold the greatness, of your sweetness, O Lord! You now hide it for those who fear you, and one day will perfect it for those who hope in you (Ps. 30:22). And O how pleasant and sweet you are in your elect, O Lord God! For you make not only good things but even their very evils cooperate for their good, so that, as you always and everywhere order both them and all things surrounding them for their salvation, even what at times seemed harmful comes to benefit them, and what seemed to have happened to diminish their blessedness becomes an increase of that blessedness.

You strengthen their weakness, O God of power; you enlighten their ignorance, O God of wisdom; you grant them fitness, O God of goodness. O wise and gracious power! O gracious and mighty wisdom! O wise and mighty goodness! O Trinity one and Unity threefold! O Trinity and Unity, Creator; strength, light, and sweetness of created trinity and unity: Father, Son, and gracious Spirit!

I consider these things, O Lord my God; I consider them, I say, and rejoice. I see them and exult. I behold them and conceive so great a hope even concerning myself that I dare hope that I too am one of them. For, attentively beholding these things, I firmly hope that I shall be admitted into the fellowship of your elect, not through any merits intervening on my part, but through your grace alone, freely given. Thus I dare apply to myself that saying which the most holy man spoke of himself and his fellow-elect, and say it of myself: “Now I am a child of God, and it has not yet appeared what I shall be. I know that, when he appears, I shall be like him, because I shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

And whence comes this hope to me, O Lord, that I, so small and such as I am, dare hope to become like you? Beyond doubt, it comes from the incomprehensible sweetness of love with which you deign to embrace us so freely and so steadfastly. Therefore, as I contemplate the manifold benefits which you have bestowed upon me in manifold ways, I stir my soul to praise you and say: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits: he who forgives all your iniquities; who heals [Col. 0826C] all your infirmities; who redeems your life from destruction; who crowns you with mercy and compassionate acts; who satisfies your desire with good things; your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s. The Lord performs mercies and judgment for all who suffer injury. He made known his ways to Moses, his wills to the children of Israel. God is compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and greatly merciful. He will not be angry forever, nor will he threaten for eternity. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. For as high as heaven is above the earth, he has strengthened his mercy over those who fear him. As far as east is from west, he has removed our iniquities from us. As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him” (Ps. 103).

And how fitting is the comparison! As a father is toward his children, so he is toward his elect.

## § VIII.—By an incomprehensible counsel God sometimes permits those whom he chooses as heirs in the homeland to fail on the way.

O Lord God! How not merely ineffable but incomprehensible is the manifold greatness and great multitude of the sweet and steadfast love by which you and your elect are joined together—your elect and you! In this kind of contemplation, O Lord, you seem to appear to your elect as a mighty and wealthy king is accustomed to appear when, in a private hour and in the private place of his chamber, with every disturbance stilled, [Col. 0827A] every trouble set aside, every care and anxiety laid down, he rejoices and delights, takes pleasure and plays, with the dearest children of his own body in every festivity of love and joy. There he is the more serene and tranquil, the more pleasant and sweet, because he beholds with complete joy those alone whom he loves above all things, and sees in them nothing that he does not love. Even if perhaps he sees in them something which he does not love, he nonetheless does not love them the less on that account.

Such, certainly, O Lord—such, I say—you seem to show yourself to your elect, to whom you reveal yourself so pleasant and sweet, so tranquil and lovable, so kindly and approachable, so compassionate and solicitous, so cheerful and joyful, so gentle and peaceable, so merciful and calm, so serene and tender, so clement and devout, so good and delightful. They cleave to you so steadfastly from eternity that they cannot be torn away from you in eternity. No sins separate them from you, for to possess you alone as propitious is sufficient for every righteousness, since they have sinned against you alone.

There are countless witnesses to this fact. To confirm the proposition, I shall bring forward a few from among many. We know indeed, because we often read it, that David, once pierced by the sword-point of lust, desired and took another man’s wife; and, to add to his guilt, afterward killed her husband through cruel deceit and deceitful cruelty. He who, while still in exile, had known how to spare his persecutor (2 Sam. 2:2, 3, 4), now, raised to the throne, destroyed an outstanding soldier even though his army was labouring at great cost [Col. 0827C].

But you visit him, O Lord; you visit him through your prophet, lest he perish—striking and healing, raging against him with threatening words, killing and making alive, healthfully shaking him and disturbing his harmful security, scourging him through terror. You are angry with him, yet in being angry you are glad; you threaten, yet spare; you draw the bow, yet do not release the arrow to inflict a wound—so that, confounded by the enormity of his guilt and frightened by the horror of your judgment, he may feel and disclose his wound. He may feel it through repentance and disclose it through confession, so that in repenting he may accuse himself, and confessing with his own mouth may say: “I have sinned against the Lord” (2 Sam. 12:13).

It was this voice, O Lord, that you desired to hear from him; therefore you cried out so loudly to him through your prophet, so that he himself might hear the voice of one warning behind him, and you might hear from him, behind you, this voice of great agitation: “But behold, you have rejected and destroyed him, O Lord; you have been angry and have had mercy on him. You have shaken David and troubled him; heal his fractures, for he has been shaken” (Ps. 60:3). Apply to his wound, which he has shown you so humbly, an effective remedy and sufficient medicine; and answer him through your prophet: “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Sam. 12:13).

Mary Magdalene too was full of seven demons, that is, of every vice; but, however greatly the Pharisee may recoil and reproach her, the pious and gentle Jesus is more richly nourished inwardly by her than outwardly by the Pharisee (Luke 7:44). He delights more in Mary’s kisses and tears than in any attentions of Simon. Peter the apostle also committed a great sin before you, for he denied you three times. Yet let him not fear, for he will not perish. For the gracious gaze of gracious Jesus stirred him to repentance. “Jesus looked upon Peter,” it says, “and he went out and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:61). He wept bitterly for what he had denied fearfully. Once the glory of your resurrection had been celebrated, he was called by name through the angel, lest he despair because of his denial. You make him confess you three times, so that a threefold confession may cleanse and wash away what a threefold denial had defiled.

## § IX.—The Apostle, vessel of election, is offered as an archetype.

[Col. 0828B] And what shall we say of Paul? He had already been called by you “a vessel of election” when your disciple Ananias still trembled to approach him (Acts 9:15). But you came, Lord Jesus, into this world to save sinners, of whom, in his own judgment, he is the foremost. Yet he obtained mercy so that in him you might display all patience, for the instruction of those who would believe in you unto eternal life.

Already he serves you, Lord Father, in his spirit, in the Gospel of your Son; already for him to live is Christ and to die is gain (Phil. 1:21); already he is exercised in abundant labours, more abundant imprisonments, excessive beatings, and frequent deaths (2 Cor. 11:23). Already he is beaten with rods, already overwhelmed with stones, suffers shipwreck, lives amid labour and hardship, [Col. 0828C] many vigils, hunger and thirst, many fasts, cold and nakedness. “Even to this hour we both hunger and thirst, are naked, are struck with fists, are unsettled, and labour with our own hands. We are cursed and bless; we suffer persecution and endure it; we are slandered and entreat. We have become as the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all things until now” (1 Cor. 4:11–13). Finally, for the spiritual life of those whose bodily death he had once ceaselessly thirsted for above all others, he dies not once but daily.

O change wrought by the right hand of the Most High! (Ps. 76:2). And whence, O Lord God, comes such a change—so great and so sudden—in the life of your elect, except from the steadfast eternity of blessed and beatifying predestination by which you love and choose them, choose and love them? For those whom you predestined, you also called; and those you called, you also justified; and those whom you justified, you also glorified (Rom. 8:30). If, then, you are for them—indeed, because you are—who will be or can be against them? (ibid., 31). In all that happens to them, they hold the upper hand; in all things they fully overcome because of you, and through you they love those whom you love—those whom, I say, you love as a sweet fragrance.

## § X.—Though angry with the children of his kingdom, God nevertheless remembers mercy.

For as a certain father behaves toward a son who sins, whom he casts out from himself because of the son’s pride against him: when he sees him persist in his obstinacy, he secretly sends his mother to him, so that she may seem to have come not as sent by the father [Col. 0829A], but as moved by her own maternal compassion. On coming, she first reproves him for his sin, but rebukes him still more for his rebellion, and instils in him awareness of his iniquity. She declares that his father is vehemently angry; yet she promises that, if he is willing humbly to make satisfaction for the past and fully to guard against the future, she will stand as mediatrix between him and his father, intercede for him, and reconcile him wholly to his father. Frightened by the mother’s threats and drawn by her promises, the son at last yields to her counsels: he humbly casts himself at his father’s feet, asks forgiveness for what has passed, and promises amendment for the future. At first the father shows him a sorrowful face, so that the offender’s mind may be corrected through the sadness of his countenance. But when he recognizes his complete [Col. 0829B] repentance for the past, humility in the present, and firm purpose for the future, he immediately, all sadness having been calmed, tenderly embraces him, sweetly kisses him, remits his fault, and lays aside every disturbance—or rather, to speak more truly, lays aside no disturbance at all, because there was none whatsoever, but displays the serenity which was great. Or, if he does lay aside disturbance, he lays aside the disturbance which only appeared, but was not; and displays the serenity which was indeed great, but did not appear. The father receives him back into the former intimacy of paternal love—or rather, does not receive him back, because he never cast him out of it, but shows himself as though receiving him back. Such, Lord, is the manner in which you deal with your elect.

For you, the Father, cast out from yourself the son who sins [Col. 0829C], when you show that any one of your elect—whom you freely begot by the word of truth (James 1:18)—ought rightly, on account of his guilt and insofar as the enormity of that guilt is concerned, to be expelled from you. But this son of yours, Lord, not only falls into sin through frailty; he sometimes lies in it through habit. For in ourselves and from ourselves we have the capacity to fall into sin; but from ourselves we do not have the capacity to rise again. Once, having abandoned the names of righteousness, we freely slide into the crookedness of guilt, not only do we lack in ourselves the power to return to the straightness of righteousness which we left behind; but our very perversity demands that, utterly forsaken by your aid [Col. 0829D], we be permitted to sink even into worse things. For if even a righteous man, turning away from righteousness, commits iniquity, as you threaten through your prophet, “you will set a stumbling-block before him” (Ezek. 3:20), so that he who voluntarily falls from the summit of righteousness, unless he hastens immediately to return through repentance, may, blinded by your just yet hidden judgment, find that he strikes still more grievously.

§ XI.—The singular protection of divine grace toward the elect.

But it is certain that we all fall into sin, and that no one whatever, O merciful and gracious God, can be saved, if no one were visited by you after sin. You do not disdain to send to this man of whom I speak, though he is himself unworthy [Col. 0830A], the mother of your Son—that is, your grace. Through inward inspiration she instils in him consciousness of his guilt; tells him how grave it is; displays to him your anger; describes also the strictness of your judgment; judges him most deserving of eternal damnation. Yet, lest he be able to sink into the depths of despair, if he wishes to return through full repentance, she promises that she is willing and able to intercede for him before you and obtain your mercy for him. She melts his hardness, allays his fear, humbles his pride, consoles his faint-heartedness, so that by every means—now threatening the punishments of hell, now promising the joys of the kingdom, now pouring in hope of pardon—she may finally draw him wholly to her counsel. Thus your son, O Lord, through his mother’s address [Col. 0830B], confounded by acknowledgement of his guilt, terrified by fear of his perdition, and encouraged by confidence in your mercy, may at last gather the powers of faith and hope; and, rising against himself in a kind of peaceable quarrel, may arise and go to you, his Father, and say: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15:18). Thus, when the stone of hardness has been removed, Lazarus may be made alive by that loud voice which you send into his heart; and not merely made alive, but may also “come forth” (John 11:43). Let him be made alive through repentance and come forth through confession, so that at last he may be loosed by the prelates of the holy Church—namely, your disciples—and permitted to depart upon the way of righteousness. When you behold him thus, Lord, you immediately become glad and appeased; or rather, you neither become glad [Col. 0830C] nor appeased, because you were neither angry nor disturbed with him. Instead, in his inward contemplation, you show yourself glad and appeased to him—to whom, in your eternal predestination, you are never not glad and never not appeased.

§ XII.—The book of predestination, written from eternity, preserves those inscribed in it for eternity.

Plainly, then, Lord, you keep your elect safe in yourself: you who remain always the same and in the same manner. You are not angry with them unto damnation when they depart from you through sin; nor are you appeased with them through any new joy concerning them which can exist in you or happen to you when, by repentance inspired by you, they approach you. Rather, the purpose of your eternal election stands firm and unmoved in you [Col. 0830D], so that, as it is written, “even if they sin, they are yours; and if they do not sin, they are counted with you” (Wisdom 15:2).

For their predestination is not cancelled when they fall into sin, so that it should cease wholly to be, or even cease to be what it was; nor is it renewed when they rise to righteousness, so that what had ceased to be might begin again. But it is altogether invariable and immutable: as it is from eternity, so it is also unto eternity, because it neither begins with a beginning nor ends with an end. They themselves, however, are variable and mutable in the exile of this present life: at one time they sin and deserve punishment; at another they forsake sin, run toward righteousness, and deserve glory. Nor do you, insofar as you are concerned, regard them differently when they are sinners than when they are righteous, although [Col. 0831A], insofar as they themselves are concerned, they are one thing in sin and another in righteousness.

For from eternity they have been predestined by you to be blessed and to be blessed forever. Yet they have not been predestined to be blessed from eternity, because they are not from eternity. And if they are from eternity, they are not so in themselves, but in you, who alone are from eternity in yourself. They are in you from eternity, I say—in you, in whom all things also are from eternity before they exist in themselves. For you have never thought anything, nor will think anything, which you had not already thought; nor have you known or will know anything which you did not already know, nor otherwise than before. For Wisdom coeternal with you, O Father, begotten from you, full from the Full, can neither learn anything it did not previously know nor forget anything it previously knew.

Yet I do not properly speak of “before” or “after” concerning you, in whom no time at all occurs [Col. 0831B]. This I know fully: as you are unchangeable in act, so also in thought. For nothing in you is not yours; and, to express it more precisely, nothing in you is not you. Therefore, because you are eternal, nothing in you is not eternal. Hence that good and sweet word which you once—that is, from eternity—spoke concerning your elect is true unto eternity; for as they are written from eternity in the book of blessed predestination, so they are written in it for eternity.

And though in this state of their mutability they are sometimes in themselves other than they are before you in that book, nevertheless, insofar as you are concerned, you do not see them before you as other than those whom you see in that book, because that book is yourself. Therefore, insofar as they themselves are concerned, they can indeed sin, and often do sin; yet they can by no means sin [Col. 0831C] unto death, nor do they end their life in sin, because they have been predestined by you unto life. They are children not of death or punishment, but of life and glory.

§ XIII.—The impossibility of sinning in the elect, according to the mind of the beloved Apostle, considered with joy.

Thus, as it seems to me, that saying of blessed John is fulfilled: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin and cannot sin, because the heavenly generation preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him” (1 John 3:9; 5:18). How sweet this saying is, how faithful a word, worthy of all acceptance, and greatly to be loved by the elect—if only they knew that they were elect. “Everyone,” he says, “who is born of God does not sin.” What, I ask, is this? “Everyone who is born of God [Col. 0831D] does not sin.” Were the prophet David, the apostle Peter, blessed Paul the vessel of election, and Mary who chose the better part, not born of God? (Luke 10:42.) Certainly they were born of God. And did they not sin? Did David not sin in adultery and murder? (2 Sam. 12:3.) Did not Peter deny the Lord (Luke 22:61), and did not Paul persecute the Church of God? (1 Cor. 15:9.) Did Mary not have seven demons (Matt. 17:9), that is, was she not full not merely of some vices but of every vice? How, then, did those who did such things not sin—those who were born of God and are now with God in eternal glory?

They did all these things, and yet did not sin. And if they sinned, they do not sin, because although they committed these things in time, their Father’s love, covering the multitude of sins, causes what they committed not to appear in eternity. Therefore perhaps blessed John did not say, “Everyone who is born of God has not sinned,” but “Everyone who is born of God does not sin,” in order clearly to show that the sins of the elect, although past as regards time, are not present as regards eternity. Since this is so, what does it mean that he inserted the word of impossibility, saying, “and cannot sin”? It is wholly true—indeed, very true—that everyone born of God cannot sin. For just as one who has been elected from eternity can in no way be reprobate, so in time he can in no way perform something which endures in him until the end and for which he is reprobated in eternity.

And John himself, who says these things, subsequently shows why everyone born of God cannot sin: “Because,” he says, “the heavenly generation preserves him.” This is the reason why one born of God cannot sin: because the heavenly generation preserves him. For heavenly generation is eternal predestination; and because it cannot possibly be annulled, so that what is predestined in it from eternity should not be predestined for eternity, it is certainly not inappropriate to say that this same heavenly generation—that is, eternal predestination—preserves those whom it predestined to life. It preserves them not only so that they may not sin, but so that [Col. 0832B] they cannot sin; because, as was said above, they cannot sin unto death, so as to deserve to be damned after death.

O sweet saying uttered by blessed John: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin and cannot sin, because the heavenly generation preserves him” (1 John 5:18). And, I think, the elect would sing this saying without ceasing if they knew without any ambiguity that they were elect. But it is not expedient, Lord God, for some of them to possess full certainty of their election in this life, just as it is not expedient for some of the reprobate to have certainty of their reprobation: lest the former, knowing themselves fully to be elect, become too lukewarm in good works through excessive security; and lest the latter, seeing themselves wholly reprobate, become bold and cruel in evil-doing toward the elect through despair. Therefore, Lord God, your elect can be torn away from you by no events whatsoever [Col. 0832D]. I consider these things, Lord, and am amazed with joy; I perceive them and marvel with exultation; I behold them and, with glad amazement and wondrous gladness, cry out in these words: “Who is wise, and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?” (Ps. 107:43). Your mercy, Lord, is from eternity and unto eternity upon your elect who fear you (Ps. 103:17), who in this desert and trackless land so appear before you in the sanctuary that they may behold your power and glory (Ps. 63:3).

§ XIV.—A brief harmony of the five outward senses concerning the Creator of all things.

Behold, Lord my God, behold how much, through your grace going before me by inspiration and following me by help [Col. 0833A], I have been permitted to seek and inquire after you. I have sought, I say, and inquired after you; and, in seeking and inquiring, I have now found you in some small degree. But where did I find you? Where did I find you, Lord my God, my strength and the light of my eyes (Ps. 38), the beauty of my heart and sweetness of my soul—beauty that does not fade and sweetness that does not deceive? Where did I find you?

Behold: in order briefly to recall what was said above at length in discussion, I, a most diligent investigator, ranged over all things that in this world, from this world, present themselves to the five gates of my body and, presenting themselves, enter them: all formed things which bodily sight reaches; all sounding things which hearing receives; all fragrant things which smell recognizes; all savoury things which taste perceives [Col. 0833B]; all tangible things which touch distinguishes. I traversed all these things as a diligent seeker. All these, I say, I examined as I could, with you as my guide; but I discovered that none of them was you. For all of them, each in its own kind, answered me with a loud voice and mighty cry, saying: “We are not your God; seek him above us.”

§ XV.—The sixfold endowment of the inward senses is shared in common with other animals.

Then, leaving behind all these things which I have just briefly mentioned, shutting these five doors of my flesh, excluding all these things from myself insofar as I could, and enclosing myself within myself, I stirred myself to behold [Col. 0833C] myself. And I found that I live and give life, perceive and give perception, think and will. Thus I saw this sixfold power to be in me: I live and give life; I perceive and give perception; I think and will. Yet the spirits of brute animals also possess this with me in some common manner, for they live and give life, perceive and give perception, think and will.

§ XVI.—The image of the Holy Trinity impressed upon man is brought to light.

Therefore, still pressing on, importunately and opportunely, I ascended beyond all these things and entered into myself. I ascended higher to my higher self; I entered more inwardly to my more inward self. For all these things are in me [Col. 0833D]; but I found in myself something great and splendid, both higher and more inward than all of them—higher in dignity, more inward in subtlety. What was it? Wisdom, by which I am wise. For it has been given me by you, Lord God, to be wise, whereas it has not been given by you to the other living beings you created.

Therefore I know, Lord God. And what do I know? I know that I am. For I would not know unless I existed, I who know. But I am, and I know that I am. Thus I know that I am; and not only do I know that I am, but I also know that I know that I am. Therefore, by existing I know, and by knowing I exist: for I exist knowing, and know existing. And I saw, Lord, that these things are good for me—good indeed, and very good—for it is far better for me to be and to be wise than neither to be nor to be wise [Col. 0834A]. Therefore my essence pleases me, and I approve and love my essence and my wisdom.

And I saw that these three things are in me: essence, knowledge, and love. Essence comes first; knowledge comes from essence. Love, however, comes neither from essence alone, because I do not love essence alone, nor from knowledge alone, because neither do I love that alone, but from essence and knowledge together, because I love essence and knowledge together. It is therefore equally from each, because it is equally in each. And, in a wondrous manner, as you enlightened me, O light of my heart, my God, I discovered a certain trinity in myself: namely, essence, knowledge, and love. I saw that none of these was either of the others: being is not knowing or loving; knowing does not seem to be loving or being; loving is not being or knowing. For it is one thing for me to be, another to know, and another to love, although I am but one spirit, existing, knowing, and loving [Col. 0834B]. In this way trinity remains in me, and unity does not depart: trinity—essence, knowledge, love; essence knowing and loving; knowledge loving and existing; love existing and knowing. Unity—because I am but one spirit, one spiritual substance.

Since trinity and unity exist in me in this manner, so, as you enlighten me, O Lord God, I discern trinity in unity, while I do not divide unity in trinity.

In this manner I see within myself your image, in which you made me; and in this image I see you in some measure. I do not yet see you fully in the reality itself: this is the mirror through which I see you in an enigma, not yet face to face (1 Cor. 13:12). The mirror through which I see you is my heart, if only it has been so cleansed, brightened, and purified by you that your countenance can be distinctly perceived in it. Therefore, so long as you are to me either behind me or above my head, I behold you in this mirror, insofar as you deign to grant it to me, but not yet in yourself [Col. 0834C]. For you are behind me and above my head because I am both turned away from you and unlike you. You are righteous and I am unrighteous; thus we are turned away from each other. You are blessed, whereas I am wretched; thus we are unlike. Therefore I am turned away from you by unrighteousness, and unlike you by wretchedness. There I am defiled by fault; here I am afflicted by punishment.

Thus, so long as I dwell in the foul and miserable exile of this present world, neither stand before you free from every sin by the merit of my life, nor ascend to you delivered from every misery by the reward of glory, I can indeed see you, illuminated by the light of your grace, but in my mirror. I cannot yet behold you in yourself: I see you in the image, not yet in the reality itself. Now, I say, I know you, but only in part; and when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away. Therefore I open this mirror and see you in some degree. I see you, I say, who are to me both behind me and above my head: whom the fault of the first man has placed behind me, and misery—which arose from that same fault and through that same fault—above my head [Col. 0834D].

§ XVII.—In the one substance of the Godhead, the procession and distinction of the persons are examined more deeply.

[Col. 0835A]

Therefore I see that you are, that you are wise, that you love: O stable essence! O clear wisdom! O most sweet love! O essence that is wise and loving! O wisdom that is loving and existing! O love that is existing and wise! And though I utter one of these before another with my mouth, I nevertheless believe in my heart that there is there nothing prior and nothing subsequent. Taught by the three that these three could in some sense be called something, I named them persons; but because I saw these three to be one thing, I did not fail to believe the same three persons to be one substance. Thus I distinguished what was three personally, while confessing that the same three were one substantially.

Again, because I saw in you, my God, triune and one, one and triune, both that which is from no one, that which is from another, and that which is from both: namely, essence from itself, for which to be is the same as what it is; wisdom from essence; and love from both—I discovered, Lord God, illuminated by the light of your grace, that you, my God, are begetting, begotten, and proceeding: begetting the begotten; the begotten from the begetter; the proceeding not from the begotten alone, but from begetter and begotten together [Col. 0835B].

And so that I might utter with my mouth in words this lofty and profound, splendid and great truth, which through your illumination I conceived by faith in my heart, I descended from the lofty ecstasy of the mind to the sound of speech, where a word both begins and ends. I borrowed certain words from human usage, because I am human and must form human words. I called the begetter Father, because it belongs to a father to beget; and I called the begotten Son, because it belongs to a son to be begotten. And I discovered that the Father is not prior to the Son, nor the Son subsequent to the Father, because I saw both to be eternal: the Father coeternal with the Son and the Son coeternal with the Father. For the Father could in no way be an eternal Father unless his Son were eternal, of whom he had been Father from eternity; nor could the Son be an eternal Son unless his Father were eternal, of whom he had been Son from eternity. For the Father is the Father of the Son, and the Son is the Son of the Father.

And although I knew both—the Father and the Son—to be spirit, because each is God and God is spirit, and knew both equally to be holy, I nevertheless called the third person in the Trinity, namely the proceeding one, specifically the Holy Spirit [Col. 0835D], because I discovered him to be, in the one and same substance of the Godhead, the firm bond, strong covenant, sweet connection, and tender love of both, the Father and the Son: breathing and flowing from both, eternal from both who are eternal, the Spirit of the Father and Son—the Son’s, as the Spirit of the Father of the Son; the Father’s, as the Spirit of the Son of the Father.

§ XVIII.—God is shown to be above all things, beneath all things, within all things, and outside all things.

And I saw that you are above all things, beneath all things, within all things, outside all things: above all things, yet not raised up; beneath all things, yet not laid underneath; within all things, yet not enclosed; outside all things, yet not diffused. For for you to be above all things is for all things to be governed by you, and for no creature whatsoever wholly to be able to comprehend how great you are [Col. 0836A]. Your rational creature can grasp you insofar as, through your gracious condescension, you pour into it both knowledge and love; but it can never grasp how great you are. Yet you are not thereby exalted, because however much you are grasped, you do not grow in yourself. The one who grasps you can indeed become greater, and the more one grasps you now through knowledge, the greater one becomes; but you cannot at all become greater.

And for you to be beneath all things is to give to all things their subsistence. For you who gave existence to all things that were not, also give permanence to all things that are. But you are not laid beneath them, because this does not weary, burden, or fatigue you. Just as, when you created all things, you could not increase, so also, if all the things you created were utterly to cease to be, you could not in any respect decrease. For you can neither advance nor fail, neither lose anything old nor acquire anything new.

Likewise, for you to be within all things is for every nature of created things—having been wonderfully implanted in them by you, from whom they were created—to cry out with a mighty cry and proclaim as if with a loud voice without ceasing that you are; yet you are not enclosed, because neither by them nor from them can it be defined how great you are. Finally, for you to be outside all things is for no mind whatsoever to be able to comprehend how great you are; yet you are not diffused, because you alone are wholly known in your entirety to yourself, you who are wholly and steadfastly in yourself. You are not scattered, so as to be gathered; nor excluded, so as to be admitted within [Col. 0836C].

All these things, Lord, enlightened by you, I saw; but I saw them in your mirror, not in yourself; in part, not in fullness; in shadow, not in truth; in figure, not in body; in likeness, not in face; in faith, not in sight; in image, not in the reality itself.

§ XIX.—The keenness of the human mind is blunted while searching the abyss of divinity.

And what sort of being do we find you to be, Lord God, in this mode of contemplation? Entirely incomprehensible. For what have I found here except that I cannot find you at all? This, then, is the fruit of my contemplation: I now know that I do not know; and I know not only that I do not know, but also both that I cannot know and that I cannot fail to know that I cannot know [Col. 0836D].

Indeed, Lord, I have made no small progress here, since I now fully know that I cannot here fail to fall short. Here my advance consists not only in knowing that I fall short, but also in knowing that I cannot fail to fall short, so that even if I do not know, my ignorance remains with me. For in a wondrous way, even while I do not comprehend you, here I comprehend you—not because I comprehend you, but because, in not comprehending you, I see fully that not only do I not comprehend you, but that I cannot possibly comprehend you fully. For then in some manner I see how great you are, when I fully see that I cannot see how great you are. Hence I am compelled both to marvel at and to venerate what I can neither penetrate nor search out, and to break forth in these words: “Your knowledge has become wonderful to me; it has grown strong, and I shall not attain to it” (Ps. 139:5).

Behold, Lord, with you as my guide I have arrived at recognition of your incomprehensibility. Not because I recognize incomprehensibility equal to yours, but because I fully recognize that I am unable to recognize it. And how could it happen that I should act wildly there, as though I might come away bearing something with me? And what, Lord, shall I bring away from the recognition of your incomprehensibility but the stupefaction of wonder? Thus I stand amazed and marvel at you, who are indeed most wonderful in the things you have made, but far more wonderful—and, so to speak, most wondrous—you yourself who made them [Col. 0837A].

§ XX.—Thus man received the entire universe to relieve his need, that afterward he might receive the perfection of blessedness.

[Col. 0837B]

Dazzled by the immensity of this most brilliant light, I turn indeed toward you, but in another mode of contemplation; and elsewhere I inquire what you are like—you whom I find altogether incomprehensible in yourself. And I certainly find that, among all the creatures you have made, you have the greatest care for the rational creature, into which, by a great prerogative of your freely bestowed grace, you deigned to infuse knowledge of yourself. Since you willed it to endure unto eternity, you created it in your image and likeness. Moreover, you created the world and everything in it also for its sake, and set it over all these things, so that it might clearly appear how great and what kind of favour of intimacy with you that creature has found which was made in your image and likeness, for whose sake all things were created and to whose service all are subjected.

For, to say nothing for the moment of the angelic creature, after you had made this sensible world, adorned with such beautiful variety and varied beauty, endowed with such good delight and delightful goodness, you immediately made man—whom you intended to be lord and possessor of that world—in your image and likeness, and placed him, once made, in the world [Col. 0837C]. You subjected to him for service all created things of the world, and commanded him to serve you in obedience to your commandments, so that by right of creation he might rule over all things, and might subject himself by free will and voluntary freedom to you, from whom he had been so excellently created.

For you willed, Lord, that man should be served, and that man himself should serve you. Let the service rendered to him by the world and the service he rendered to you, God, flow back altogether—not to your benefit, but to the benefit of man. For you are full of yourself, sufficient to yourself from yourself; you are yourself your own good. You, who are immeasurable, cannot be increased, nor can you, who are eternal, be diminished. As you are not corrupted by our evils, so you do not need our good things (Ps. 16:2). Human nature, however, needed another’s help. It was necessary for it both to receive service from creation, so that it might preserve the wonderful thing it had received; and to render obedience to you its Creator, so that it might gain what it did not yet possess in perfection.

Behold, Lord, man’s twofold good—twofold, I say: one taken from below for necessity in time; the other to be received from above for happiness without end [Col. 0838A]. Therefore, although you are the mighty Creator, wise disposer, and gracious restorer of all things, you nevertheless have a supreme and special care for the rational creature so excellently created by you. You willed that both the good which you made it, all that you made in the world, and you yourself who made it should flow back to its benefit, so that it might have excellence from you in creation, sustenance from creation in necessity, and from you—but in you—consummation in blessedness.

§ XXI.—Some members of the rational creation, by God’s hidden but just judgment, are so destined for punishment that their works are never accepted unto glory.

[Col. 0838B]

But you do not grant final blessedness to the whole of this rational creation of which I speak, though you bestowed dignity upon its whole community in its creation. Rather, you raise some angels and human beings to reward through grace, by means of merits; but you plunge others into punishment through justice, as their faults demand. Alas! both miserable punishment and penal misery belong to a creature so excellent and noble: created by you, O Lord of all, so great that nothing whatever but you can suffice for its blessedness; yet so constituted that it cannot attain the complete extinction of its own being. Because of the enormity of its fault, it cannot rise to blessedness; yet because of the dignity of its nature [Col. 0838C], it is not allowed to vanish or altogether not to be.

Woe, then, to them! It would indeed have been better for those angels and human beings had they not been born. For if they had been born as beasts, lacking reason, then, just as the good they did would not have been imputed to them by you, so that they might be advanced to blessedness on account of merit, so surely neither would evil have been imputed to them, so that they might be cast down into damnation on account of sin. But now, though created excellently, they are, in a hidden yet not unjust manner, left without the strong aid of your grace. In the enduring perversity of their evil will, they embrace guilt, so that afterward, justly and manifestly judged by the terrible strictness of your righteous judgment, they may undergo eternal punishment for eternity.

I consider this to be ineffably terrible [Col. 0838D], because I know that both their reprobation before you and their damnation stand immovably from eternity. Therefore I say, “Alas, miserable are they,” because I perceive the dreadful woe hanging over them. As I said, it would be no small good for them to be consumed wholly through not-being, since it does not befall them to be consummated through blessed being. Thus, O Lord God, in this mode of contemplation I see you as incomprehensibly angry with them, horribly terrible, and, so to speak, tolerably intolerable. I presume, insofar as I dare, to fix my eyes even here upon you, whom I see immutably moved against them from eternity with so horrendous an indignation of most savage offence: you neither accept any of their good deeds nor wipe away their evils; you neither admit the former before you into remembrance so that they may be saved [Col. 0839A], nor remove the latter from yourself through forgetfulness so that they may escape condemnation.

§ XXII.—From this threefold contemplation, three corresponding gifts come to the contemplative soul.

But, leaving these sorrowful and grief-causing, terrible and terror-inspiring matters, I turn myself to you, Lord, in another mode of contemplation. I turn to you as other—not that you, being in yourself, are in any way other than or wholly alien from yourself, but because in this mode of contemplation I see you as other. For I consider that in this mode of contemplation you perform things different from, and far different from, those in the preceding mode, although you yourself are not different.

Therefore in this mode of contemplation I ask what you are like in the other part of rational creation—the other part, I say, truly other [Col. 0839B]: the chosen part, the part beloved by you, your part in a spiritual sense, the lot and portion of your inheritance. And I see you, Lord of the universe, my God, appearing ineffably gentle and sweet in this mode of contemplation to your elect, whom you unite to yourself from eternity by so tenacious a bond of election ever choosing through love and loving through choice that they can be torn from you by no events whatsoever for eternity. In this mode of contemplation, I see you to be ineffably lovable, gentle, and sweet.

Therefore, in the first mode of contemplation I see you as wholly incomprehensible; in the second, terrible; in the third, lovable. The first mode of contemplation raises the contemplator into the height of spiritual vision, lest he grow dull in the depths through the wrong of neglected thought. The second terrifies one raised to lofty things, lest through proud exaltation of the eyes he lift himself up because of the granted condescension of great grace. The third gently soothes and cherishes the aforesaid contemplator with the sweet encouragement of confidence, lest he despair because of the excessive sight of terror seen in the preceding mode of contemplation.

Thus the first mode of contemplation opens the eyes of my mind by displaying hidden things; the second, by the terror of hidden judgment, brings down the swelling of pride within me; the third raises my faint-heartedness through confidence in eternal election. The first, I say, opens the eyes of my mind lest I remain in blindness; the second brings down the swelling of pride within me lest I exalt myself in pride [Col. 0839D]; the third raises faint-heartedness within me lest I despair of your mercy, Lord.

§ XXIII.—Ignorance, arrogance, and distrust are the three stumbling-blocks of the reprobate.

Three evils, then, darken, cast down, and suffocate the reprobate in this life: namely error, pride, and dread. Error belongs to negligence, pride to arrogance, dread to distrust; for error blinds their minds, pride puffs them up, and dread suffocates them. It blinds them, so that they do not see truth; it puffs them up, so that they do not embrace humility; it suffocates them, so that they do not seek mercy. The first are negligent, the second proud, the third despairing. The first say to God: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job 12:14). “Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him?” [Col. 0840A] The second run against the Lord with uplifted neck; they encourage one another and say: “Let us make a tower whose summit may reach to heaven, and let us make our name renowned” (Gen. 11:5). They love the first places at feasts, the chief seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and being called Rabbi by men (Matt. 23:4), “calling their lands by their own names” (Ps. 48:12). The third take Cain’s words upon themselves and say: “Our iniquity is greater than that we may deserve pardon” (Gen. 4:13). Thus the first evil is the darkness of ignorance, the second the vanity of pride, the third the impiety of distrust.

### § XXIV.—This contemplation, bestowing a threefold gift upon the mind, removes the poison of the threefold evil.

[Col. 0840B] By these three evils they sin against you, O true, supreme, eternal Trinity—Father, Son, gracious Spirit, almighty God! For through pride the swollen raise themselves against you, O almighty Father, and sin against your omnipotence. Through error the negligent offend against you, O wise Son, and are guilty against your wisdom. Through the despair of impenitence they think wrongly of you, O gracious Spirit, benevolent God—you who are the forgiveness of all sins—and utter words of blasphemy against your goodness: namely, that they shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come (Matt. 12:32). Therefore the swelling of their exaltation drives them far from you, O Father; the darkness of error deprives them of your wisdom, O Son; and the dread of poisonous despair does not permit them, O gracious Spirit, [Col. 0840C] to taste your sweetness.

But in the elect the aforesaid mode of contemplation wholly removes these three dreadful and deadly evils, because the first enlightens them, the second humbles them, and the third soothes them. It enlightens them, Lord, through contemplation of your incomprehensibility, lest they wander through the blindness of ignorance. It humbles them through the severity of strict judgment, lest they grow proud through the inflation of vanity. It soothes them through the sweet delight of your ineffable goodness, lest they despair of their election.

Here, Lord my God, is the fruit of this lengthy discourse of mine: that I may clearly recognize how, in the threefold [Col. 0840D] mode of this contemplation, your incomprehensibility enlightens my mind, your severity humbles it, and your mercy soothes it. The first removes from me the gloom of error and bestows the brightness of wisdom; the second cuts away in me the corruption of pride and makes me fear, for my humbling, the unchangeable judgment of your terrible and hidden justice; the third extinguishes in my heart the dread of despair and pours into me the joyful and gladdening serenity of confidence.

Thus, yes, thus you enlighten, humble, and foster your elect, O Father, O Son, O gracious Spirit, almighty God: lest either the darkness of blindness obscure them, or the swelling of vanity exalt them, or the deadly dart of despair pierce them. For you, O almighty Father, pour into their hearts, in the first mode of contemplation, knowledge of your power; [Col. 0841A] and this knowledge indeed casts down every height of pride within them. You, O wise Son, enlighten them in the second mode with the brightness of your Wisdom; enlightened by it, as the shadows of ignorance vanish, their mind perceives the true radiance of inward light. You also, O gracious Spirit, in the third mode of contemplation of which these things have now been said, [Col. 0842A] grant them full knowledge of your ineffable goodness. Strengthened most firmly within by this knowledge, gathering the powers of faith and hope, they rest upon the incomprehensible sweetness of your love—by which it covers the multitude of their sins—and consider themselves incapable of ever being torn away from you by any events whatever.

## [SOLILOQUIES ON THE INSTRUCTION OF THE SOUL]

[Col. 0841]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

(From the dissertation of the Rev. Fr. Bernard Pez in vol. I of the *Anecdota*, p. LXXI.)

How many and how great errors learned men have committed in recording matters concerning this Adam may be seen in the introduction of the learned Godfrey Ghiselbert, Premonstratensian canon at Furnes, to the works of Adam, which he collected in folio and published at Antwerp through Peter Beller in 1659. Thus we cannot sufficiently wonder at Casimir Oudin, who, in the supplement to Bellarmine’s *Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 472, even after Ghiselbert’s edition—which he praises—had been produced, writes that Adam, a Scot by nationality and a Regular Canon, flourished from the year 1172 and the following years until 1180; although Ghiselbert, chapter 14, expressly teaches that Adam was only advanced to the episcopal mitre about 1186, which mitre, he says, Adam is more likely to have held for several five-year periods.

Yet the prologue to Book I of the *Soliloquy on the Instruction of the Soul* makes it no less clearly evident that Ghiselbert himself assigns inaccurately to Adam the chief monastery of Prémontré, in which he supposedly first professed the Premonstratensian Order. There Adam asks that his reverend lords and dearest fathers, to whom he dedicated his little work, offer a holocaust for “the son of your womb,” lest perhaps he sin. But Adam addressed it to “his venerable lords and friends beloved in the bowels of Christ: the illustrious Lord Walther, prior, and all the brothers consecrated to Christ’s service in the church of St Andrew in Scotland.” The manuscripts of Petershausen, Angers, and Tegernsee—each written three hundred years ago—are mistaken in reading “St Andrew in Austria” instead of “St Andrew in Scotland.” For what has that Augustinian canonry in Austria, on the river Traisen, to do with Adam the Scot? Therefore it was the church of St Andrew in Scotland, not Prémontré, that gave Adam to God and to that most white-clad Order.

But leaving these matters aside, let us discuss the very elegant and highly useful little work of Adam, and from what source we first brought it to light. Two manuscripts supplied it to us. One is held by the Charterhouse of Gaming; the other belongs to the library of Melk, marked letter b, number 23, in duodecimo. From the latter we corrected the transcript of the Gaming manuscript, procured through the efforts of the venerable Fr. Sebastian Treger, Carthusian of Gaming, our most distinguished friend and collaborator, in many places; we also added chapter headings for the convenience of readers.

The learned Casimir Oudin, formerly a member of the same Order, attests in the place cited that Dom Hermannus a Porta, abbot of St Michael’s at Antwerp, had prepared this little work together with several of Adam’s sermons for publication. In the aforementioned Tegernsee manuscript it is attributed—wrongly—to Adam of Perseigne. Nor, perhaps, are the *Extracts on Love*, attributed to the same Adam of Perseigne in a fifteenth-century catalogue of Tegernsee manuscripts, more correctly assigned to him. We think these extracts were borrowed from the book *On the Sweetness of God* by our Adam the Premonstratensian, concerning which Ghiselbert writes in the introduction to Adam’s works, chapter 10.

In several libraries there is found a certain metrical *Summa* of ritual and canonical matters and decisions. According to Simler, it was also printed at Cologne by Henry Quentel in 1502. It begins: “At the greatest feasts, one [collect] is said at Mass,” etc. It is commonly called the *Little Summa of Raymond*, because of the following verse, found both in the Cologne edition and in manuscript codices—of which the Melk Library preserves not a few:

> This little Summa from the *Summa* of Raymond has appeared.

The question is asked who was the author of this metrical little *Summa*. In a certain commentary on that *Summula*, composed by an anonymous writer and preserved in Melk manuscript, paper, folio L. 7, written in the fourteenth century, it is said that this metrical *Summula* is attributed to Raymond; by others, to another man who did not wish to state his name in order to avoid arrogance. In a fourteenth-century manuscript from Kamp it is said to have been published by Adam of St Victor. In a four-hundred-year-old manuscript from St Hippolytus it is attributed to Master Adam of the Order of Friars Minor. In another Melk manuscript, folio parchment 29, certainly written in the fourteenth century, the following rubric is prefixed to the work:

> Here begins the *Summa* of Master Adam concerning the seven sacraments. First, how the collects are to be said at Mass. “At the greatest [feasts],” etc.

At the end:

> Here ends the *Summa* of Master Adam.
>
> Adam, with lesser right, gave these verses to the learned,  
> That through them they might learn what must be avoided or retained.

Amid so great a variety of manuscripts, we suspect that the author of this metrical *Summula* is none other than Master Adam the Premonstratensian, who, wishing to provide for the convenience of clergy, composed such a compendium of canons and rites for the sake of memory before Raymond’s *Summa* came to light. But these are minor matters.

[Col. 0843]

# TWO BOOKS OF THE SOLILOQUIES ON THE INSTRUCTION OF THE SOUL, BY ADAM THE PREMONSTRATENSIAN, ABBOT AND BISHOP OF WHITHORN IN SCOTLAND

(Extracted from the manuscript codices of the Charterhouse of Gaming and the monastery of Melk by the venerable Dom Fr. Sebastian Treger, Carthusian of Gaming in Austria. Edited by the Rev. Fr. Bernard PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, p. I, col. 395.)

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0843A]

## PROLOGUE

[Note: [Col. 0843] Melk manuscript: “Here begins the Soliloquy of Brother Adam.”]

To his venerable lords and friends beloved in the bowels of Christ: the illustrious Lord WALTHER, prior, and all the brothers consecrated to Christ’s service in the church of St Andrew in Scotland—Brother ADAM, useless and unworthy servant of God and of God’s servants—may you live sweetly in one peace and happily attain one joy.

I send to you, O venerable men, the *Soliloquy entitled On the Instruction of the Soul*, which I recently composed—not indeed as I ought, but as I was able amid so many and such great occupations. I ask that you receive it with the same devotion with which I know it has been sent by me. For I did not wish it to come to your notice because I consider it very useful to you, but in order to show in this matter the great affection I have for you in Christ. Receive, therefore, this gift—small indeed, but sent with no small love. [Gaming manuscript: “but sent with ready discernment.”] Whatever your Holiness finds in it either expressed insufficiently keenly or set forth insufficiently elegantly, may it, if it has leisure, correct for itself, or direct me what must be corrected and how it should be corrected.

Farewell always in the Lord of lords, O reverend lords and dearest fathers; and, rising at dawn, offer a holocaust for the son of your womb, lest perhaps he sin.

## CHAPTER I. The religious state is not free from temptations. This is neither greatly to be wondered at nor lamented; rather, every care should be directed toward ensuring that the soul is not overcome by temptations.

[Col. 0843C]

With secret questions I shall assail my soul and confront it concerning its hidden matters: that I may instruct it when ignorant, establish it when wavering, strengthen it when standing, raise it when fallen, and lead it back to the way of truth when wandering.

**Reason.** Tell me, O my soul, what do you think of this state in which you now are? How does it taste to you? How does it please you? [Melk manuscript: “Does it please you?”] I know indeed [Col. 0844A] that you left the world long ago, renounced the world’s pomps, entered the common life, and assumed the religious habit. [Gaming manuscript: “received.”] You have been joined to the disciplines of humility in Christ’s school, choosing to be lowly in God’s house rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners. But I want you to disclose to me without embarrassment how this manner of life pleases you.

**Soul.** Just as that former secular life, in which I once lived, displeased me in every respect, and therefore I renounced it, so this life in which I am now also no longer wholly pleases me; indeed, it displeases me in many ways. For so many temptations weary me on every side, and so many tribulations shake me from every direction, that I can scarcely remain standing.

[Col. 0844B]

**Reason.** You should not greatly wonder that temptations weary you in many ways from every side. For your whole life upon earth is temptation. But with all your strength and by every means in your power, persevere tirelessly in the battle of your king, because you will not be crowned unless you have contended lawfully.

**Soul.** You speak well; yet when I renounced the world and entered religious life, I hoped that I had come to peace and rest. But now, on the contrary, I see that I have come to great tribulations and distresses, and to greater miseries than I had when I was in the world. I fled from the depths of the sea to the firm ground of harbours precisely so that I might avoid both the violence of the winds and the savagery of the waves; yet now [Col. 0844C] I feel myself more battered by gusts and driven to and fro by waves on the shore than I did when I was swimming in the sea.

**Reason.** Religious persons have tribulation, as secular persons do; but you do not distinguish properly between the two. Certainly, when you lived carnally in the world, you were in greater tribulation than you are now. Yet you thought you were then in less tribulation because you did not feel the tribulation by which you were then miserably ravaged. Your state was then more dangerous precisely because you believed it less dangerous.

You say that you are now wearied by temptations from which you felt yourself then quiet and free. This should not seem remarkable to you, because then your enemy had little need to tempt you, since [Col. 0845A] he saw that you were almost willing, even without temptation, sometimes to consent to him. [Gaming manuscript: “because.”] He had no need to assault with great labour the city which he saw he could subdue without any assault. [Gaming manuscript: “which he saw willing to be subdued.”] But now, because you have cast his yoke from your neck and renounced his dominion, your poisonous enemy persecutes you with sharper envy than before; and he seeks new gain from you all the more cruelly because he has lost more completely his former right. You have now stirred Leviathan against yourself [Melk manuscript: “roused”]; had you obeyed him fully, you would not have him roused against you. Therefore do not wonder that you are tempted; strive rather that you may not be overcome by temptations. [Melk manuscript: “by temptation.”] But if you do not know by yourself how you can resist temptations, show me by which you are most troubled, so that my instruction may teach you how you can resist them.

## CHAPTER II. By meditation on what things, and by what means and remedies, violent temptations of the flesh must be conquered and subdued by a religious person.

From what, then, are you tempted? What do you think in your heart?

**Soul.** I think of a multitude of adorned and beautiful women.

[Col. 0845C]

**Reason.** What do you think of them? How do you portray them to yourself, and how do they appear to you in thought?

**Soul.** Very beautiful, very pleasing, and very sweet.

**Reason.** Beautiful and pleasing for what purpose, and sweet for what purpose?

**Soul.** Beautiful to look upon, pleasing to embrace, and sweet to kiss.

**Reason.** What happens within you when you think these things?

**Soul.** My mind sighs, my body is stirred, my heart desires to attain the fulfillment of pleasure, and my flesh exults.

**Reason.** Such exultation is greatly to be mourned and wept over. Why do not your heart and flesh rather exult [Col. 0845D] in the living God? You ought to be not like a raven but like a dove at your windows, lest death enter through them; so that, if perhaps by a movement of mind or body you leave the ark of your peace for the flood of this world, you may find nowhere to set the foot of your heart in love.

But now, on the contrary, outward beauty deceives you; and while it rashly invites the eye of your flesh to gaze upon it, it damnably occupies even your inward sight. Hence it happens, miserably, that the more keenly your bodily eye is alive to seeing what appears outwardly, the more dangerously your spiritual vision is darkened in discerning what lies hidden within. Therefore that which outwardly shines draws you to desire it, because you do not behold what stinks within.

Do you not know that, [Col. 0846A] when you gaze fixedly and lustfully upon a woman, you seek to possess a painted latrine? [Melk manuscript: “when, with you gazing fixedly and lustfully upon a woman, there lies hidden …”] And when what appears outwardly beautiful unlawfully pleases you, you do not see what lies inwardly foul. When you desire lustfully to embrace an adorned woman, you also desire to have in your arms a silk sack full of excrement. Although the sack is pleasant to touch, what it contains within [Melk manuscript: “is contained inside”] is foul-smelling to smell. Indeed, that which shines outwardly ought not to please, while it contains within itself [Melk manuscript: “has”] something that stinks.

For what is an unchaste woman to you, when you love her unchastely—though beautiful in body, yet full in many ways of foulnesses that ought not even to be named—except a kind of tomb full both of the foul impurities of the dead and of filthy stenches? When you desire lustfully to kiss a woman’s beauty—her small mouth, soft lips, ruddy cheeks, lovely face, laughing, coaxing, beckoning, speaking, offering, seeking, attracting, captivating eyes, and all such things—when you admire a slender [Gaming manuscript: “graceful”] body and limbs suited and attractive to impure love, you both desire to gaze upon and gaze desiringly upon a whitewashed sepulchre: outwardly white, inwardly full of the stinking bones of the dead and most savage serpents. For what is an unchaste woman to you except a kind of tomb full of filthy stenches? What are her deadly words, her seductive eyes, and her tender limbs [Col. 0846C] that entice you and are unlawfully desired by you, except creeping things that bite and, by biting, kill?

Therefore you must by every means take care that, while you love too much what you see to be outwardly bright, beautiful, and alluring, you do not damnably fall into that which inwardly defiles and kills. Finally, when you eagerly and desirously set before yourself the fulfillment of your fleshly pleasure with her, you hunger for deadly bait concealing a hook. And when you seek to taste what is sweet, the sting hidden beneath the sweetness mortally pierces your throat. Behold, such are the women of whom you think; thus they are beautiful, thus pleasing, thus sweet. What do you think? Are they not such?

[Col. 0846D]

**Soul.** Entirely such.

**Reason.** Certainly they are such—if not in themselves, yet in you who desire them unlawfully. For I do not condemn either them, if they are chaste, or the form or beauty which God created in them, even if they themselves are not chaste; rather, I condemn the disordered desire of your mind [Gaming manuscript: “complacency”], by which, for the sake of their appearance, you gaze upon them with the impure eye of unlawful desire. I do not, I say, blame in them either the beauty or sweetness of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; rather, I accuse in you Eve’s wanton gaze and greedy taste. [Melk manuscript: corrupt reading, uncertain.]

**Soul.** You speak well.

**Reason.** Therefore guard yourself against the root of the serpent, from which comes forth the basilisk, lest perhaps its seed swallow up the bird (Isa. 14:29).

[Col. 0847A]

**Soul.** I have often heard these words in Isaiah, but I do not know how they should be understood.

**Reason.** The serpent is the ancient serpent; its poisonous root is suggestion; the basilisk is the movement of the mind; the basilisk’s seed is an evil act; the bird is the soul, light both through purity and lofty in contemplation. Thus from the serpent’s root comes forth the basilisk, and its seed swallows up the bird, because the mind is shaken by the devil’s suggestion and an unlawful deed destroys the soul; for “sin, when it has been completed, generates death” (Jas. 1:19).

Therefore cleanse yourself from unclean thoughts by frequent meditation upon the Scriptures, constant rumination upon the Psalms, and pure, humble confession. Mortify your members which are upon earth, together with their vices and desires, so that, holding Babylon’s little ones, you may dash them against the rock, and that moderation in drink and food may wear down the pride of your flesh.

[Col. 0847B]

**Soul.** Your words greatly gladden me when I am sad, teach me when I do not know, and strengthen me when I am weak. You have now shown me both that, when this vice tempts me, I ought not to grieve excessively, and that by despising what shines and tastes sweet, fully considering what it is and to what destruction it draws me, I can overcome it through God’s grace—so that I may know how to scrape the discharge from my sore with a potsherd.

## CHAPTER III. The chapter in which the brothers’ faults are proclaimed is burdensome only to those deceived by pride and anger; it ought not to be called a prison or dungeon, but the gate of paradise and the door of heaven.

[Col. 0847C]

**Reason.** What still weighs upon you?

**Soul.** I gladly ought to show you every burden that I endure, since such full relief is given me by your teachings. [Melk manuscript: “unfold”; “since you give me relief so fully.”]

**Reason.** What, then, weighs upon you?

**Soul.** I am greatly burdened by chapter. [Melk manuscript: “am burdened.”]

**Reason.** What do you see in chapter?

**Soul.** Little charity and love among those sitting round, almost no mercy and compassion in the presider, but great impatience and unrest in myself.

[Col. 0847D]

**Reason.** How do you see these things in chapter? For all these things ought to be alien to chapter.

**Soul.** There is little charity and love among those sitting round, because there they accuse me from every side of every negligence they see in me, even though it be slight and almost nonexistent. Just as someone surrounded on every side by companies of his most savage enemies does not know from whom he must guard himself—while those pressing upon him from every direction, one lays snares behind him, another resists him face to face, another from the right, and another attempts to strike him even from the left—so I am in chapter. And when they have said whatever they wish about me, the presider eagerly listens to these things; and, as though he desired more to hear evil than good of me, [Col. 0848A] he listens in such a way that he seems somehow very glad to have found at least some occasion by which he can burden me.

Then he adds still more bitter things to their bitter words; and by defining and dividing the fault, he exaggerates it, makes it as though monstrous and enormous, and almost declares that he does not know what penance can be imposed upon me for such a fault. In all this neither their accusations nor his rebukes permit me to utter even one word of excuse. In my view, neither they nor he would ever rage against me in this way if they loved me. Since every day I see myself treated in this manner, it is no wonder that I endure great unrest and impatience. I am therefore compelled to love chapter as though it were a deep dungeon, or even hell itself.

[Col. 0848B]

**Reason.** I believe that you endure great impatience and unrest. But I do not at all believe either that those sitting round have little charity and love toward you, or that the presider himself has almost no mercy and compassion. For the fact that your brothers accuse you of every negligence they see in you is not at all a sign of hatred, but of great love. For those who love you spiritually in Christ cannot bear to see in you anything that spiritually harms you or offends God in you. Just as in the Rule of your father or advocate-at-law, you ought not to judge them ill-willed when they point out your sins. For they are not more innocent if, though they can correct you by bringing the matter forward, they allow you to perish through silence.

If you have a wound in your body which you wish concealed because you fear being cut, you treat it cruelly; so too when guilt is kept silent and is not mercifully disclosed. Therefore merciful are those who expose it; cruel are those who conceal it.

As for your saying that the presider eagerly hears what is said about you: he listens carefully not because, as you rashly suspect, he desires to hear more evil than good of you, but because he listens carefully to what is said in order to understand it fully. For how can he fully absolve you unless he first clearly recognizes what is the sin by which you are bound? Thus those who accuse you are your friends, who lament your wounds; [Col. 0848D] while he is the physician who ought to heal you. But he does not know what medicine suits your wounds unless he first recognizes them. Therefore, with one and the same good intention, they accuse you and he listens to their accusations against you: they speak so that you may be healed, and he listens so that he may know how you may be healed.

He does not, then, desire to hear evil of you more than good; but if there are evils in you, he who cares for you more earnestly wishes to know them than not to know them; and he wishes to know them so that you may be absolved from them. Nor is he glad to find an occasion to burden you; rather, he is altogether sad. Nevertheless, lest he incur the guilt and punishment of Eli, he chooses—though he does this unwillingly—to spare both you and himself in God’s judgment by not sparing you alone in your guilt, rather than, by sparing you alone in your sin, not spare either you or himself at the divine examination.

[Col. 0849A]

When you claim that he exaggerates your fault with bitter words, you should attribute this more to his charity than to cruelty, more to your deliverance than to your oppression. For you must know that the rust of sin is not driven out of you without great correction [Melk manuscript: “great strengthening”]; nor is a harmful humour expelled from the stomach of the mind without a bitter draught; nor is an ulcer cut away from a wound without sharp pain. For “the words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Eccl. 12:11), because holy men do not know how to stroke the faults of offenders, but to prick them.

Indeed, you can leave chapter rejoicing on the day when you hear fitting rebuke for your sin, because by the harsh word that you hear [Col. 0849B] in chapter you will be delivered from that bitter word, harsher than all others, which those will hear to whom it will be said: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

Moreover, if you grieve because you are not allowed to answer even a single word in excuse to your brothers’ accusations and your father’s rebukes, remember who he was who for you “was led as a sheep to slaughter” [Melk manuscript: “to be killed”], and “like a lamb before its shearer was silent and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). Of him you read that, when he was accused in many matters, he answered nothing. And what humility of chapter would there be if everyone accused were allowed to excuse himself in words? Or what benefit would there be in it, when a fault that is excused is doubled? Do we not come to chapter for this purpose: that we may humbly accuse ourselves and be charitably accused by others, so that at least in this way we may be absolved from our offenses? The former belongs to humility, the latter to usefulness. And how foul and dangerous it is to be proud by excusing oneself in the place of humility, to deny in the place of confession, and to be bound more tightly in sin in the place of absolution!

[Col. 0849C]

**Soul.** Everything you say is true, and there is no fault in your words. Yet the rule you state about excuse ought indeed to be observed by one who is accused truthfully and charitably. But if someone who is accused maliciously and falsely, as sometimes happens, excuses himself, does he sin in doing so?

**Reason.** Even if we say that it is no great sin for a righteous person to excuse himself, we may nevertheless say that it is no great merit for an unrighteous person not to excuse himself. For he may both receive pardon and escape punishment; but he merits neither the grace nor the glory to which those righteous persons who do not excuse themselves are happily raised. Therefore the former is good, but the latter better.

You know that three persons were suspended on crosses on the day of the Lord’s Passion: the blaspheming thief, the confessing thief, and the innocent Lamb himself. And what else should we think the severity of chapter to be but a kind of passion of the cross? In this passion some blaspheme, some confess, and some are innocent. The first are rebellious, the second penitent, the third humble. The first deserve punishment, the second pardon, the third glory. The blaspheming thief signifies the first; [Col. 0850A] another thief, but one confessing, signifies the second; and innocent and humble Jesus signifies the third.

Though they are in one and the same suffering, the first murmurs and does what he ought not; the second prays and does what he ought; the third offers himself for us and does more than he ought. And though all are accused, the first is nevertheless accused justly because, defending his wickedness through pride, he falls into the hell of sin. [Gaming manuscript: “and.”] The second is not accused unjustly: recognizing his fault through confession, changing necessity into willingness, reconciled through the absolution of his superior, and transformed from a thief into a martyr, he enters the paradise of the Church. The third, however, is accused altogether unjustly; and, without excusing his innocence, through the silent witness of a good conscience, complete contempt for worldly glory, and the strength of his own triumph, he ascends even to heaven.

[Col. 0850B]

You see, therefore, that as far as the Passion of the innocent Redeemer differs from the suffering of the confessing thief, so far differs the one maliciously and falsely accused from the one truthfully and charitably accused. And as they are unequal in merit, so neither will they be equal in reward. If one falsely accused excuses himself, he does not fall through sin—provided that the discipline of chapter allows his excuse—but neither does he rise through merit. Though he is not punished in chapter despite his innocence, he will not be crowned sublimely in heaven.

**Soul.** What you say seems reasonable; yet great harm often arises if those falsely accused do not excuse themselves. For the man who maliciously and falsely accused him will remain in his sin; and those sitting round will likewise be led into error, thinking that he spoke truthfully and charitably. And if the accused person’s silence gives him great gain, it nevertheless brings no small loss to the accuser and those sitting round, because malice destroys the former altogether, and ignorance destroys [Gaming manuscript: “burns”] the latter in large part.

[Col. 0850C]

**Reason.** Your diligence is not to be despised if, being falsely accused, you set forth your innocence—where, when, to whom, how, and to what extent it ought to be set forth—without being provoked by any madness or fury of impatience, but led solely by a desire for their salvation; wholly unwilling to harm your accuser in any respect and wholly forgiving him. In this way, as it seems to me, you neither omit your neighbour’s benefit nor lose your own.

**Soul.** What you say pleases me.

**Reason.** As for your comparing chapter, at the end of your complaint, to a dungeon and hell: you would have spoken well if you had not thought wrongly.
