But now a good expression is not approved when a bad intention corrupts it. For though it is the highest blessing to be Christ’s disciple, the Evangelist nevertheless counted it a curse when the Jews said to the blind man who had been enlightened: “You be his disciple” (John 8:28).

Is not chapter in some sense the Lord’s dungeon, where holy men put their foot in his fetters? Where they are bound with the cords of voluntary discipline? Where they rejoice that they do not belong to themselves? [Col. 0851A] Is not chapter also in some sense a kind of hell, where the righteous punish their own errors? Where they consume the rust of their sins in the fire of penance, in order that they may afterward be strangers to the fire or punishment of Gehenna? Thus chapter is both dungeon and hell: a dungeon in which thieves are not confined but martyrs are trained; a hell in which those to be damned are not plunged down, but those to be saved are purified.

**Soul.** You speak well.

**Reason.** What, then, does chapter still seem to you to be?

**Soul.** No longer the horror of a dungeon, but the beauty of a bridal chamber; not the entrance to hell, but the gateway of paradise and the door of heaven.

## CHAPTER IV. The multitude and severity of commands issued by superiors ought not to disturb a religious person, since the voice of the commanding superior is the voice of God. Finally, it is not a crime to fail in any commands whatever of superiors, but to despise them, etc.

[Col. 0851B]

**Reason.** What still weighs upon you?

**Soul.** The many kinds of commands issued by my elders.

**Reason.** What sort do they seem to you in their commands?

**Soul.** Entirely undiscerning. They command what they wish, not what they ought. They prescribe according to their own will, not according to reason. And though they themselves scarcely do even certain least things, they promulgate for us, according to their own pleasure, harsh and very difficult laws, binding, as the Lord says (Matt. 23:5, 4), [Col. 0851C] heavy and unbearable burdens and placing them upon our shoulders, while they themselves are unwilling to move them with the tip of a finger.

Ratio. You lay hands far too boldly upon the Lord’s anointed; far too presumptuously do you malign his prophets; far too proudly do you set your mouth against heaven. And because, trusting excessively in your own strength, you presume to touch the ark of the Lord with your hand [Melk MS: “to touch”], you deserve also to be struck by him with a mortal blow. Therefore do not scrutinize the life of your elders; do not examine their actions; do not rebuke their manner of life, even if it be bad. Know that you are their hearer, not their judge; and that you ought to comply with their commands in obedience, not condemn their life. Do you not know that [Col. 0851D] their commands are God’s commands? Do you not know that prelates preside over you in the place of the supreme pontiff? Do you not know that, whatever they may be like, they are successors of those to whom it was said: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16)? Do you not know that there is no authority except from God, and that those which are from God are ordained? Therefore those who resist authority resist God’s ordinance. But may almighty God avert from you what follows concerning those who resist (Romans 13:1–2).

Soul. Certainly that is what they say when we do not obey them: that we have brought condemnation upon ourselves, because they assert that we have fallen into the crime of disobedience and committed a mortal sin.

Reason. They speak truly. Have you not read that resistance is like [Col. 0852A] the sin of divination, and refusal to submit like the crime of idolatry? (1 Samuel 15:23).

Soul. Who, then, can be saved?

Reason. One who obeys humbly, readily, and perseveringly.

Soul. And who can accept all the commands of his elders and omit what is forbidden?

Reason. Who is condemned for impossibility? And when impossible things are enjoined upon you by your prelate, if he is unwilling to relieve you, you ought, as blessed Benedict says, to trust in God and undertake with humility and faith what is commanded.

Soul. Certainly they command us so many things and forbid so many things that they can neither be kept in number nor [Col. 0852B] remembered.

Reason. Nor do I judge anyone excessively cruel because of forgetfulness. Yet one may fear that, if you forget God through forgetfulness of your prelates’ commands, perhaps you may be handed over by him to oblivion.

Soul. What you say is very harsh, since neither impossibility nor forgetfulness thus wholly excuses us in transgressing commands.

Reason. And who, I ask, is condemned in transgression except for contempt alone? For if by forgetfulness you happen to disobey your elders, either in commands or in prohibitions, you have indeed sinned, but venially—provided that you acknowledge your guilt as you ought, humbly confess it, make fitting satisfaction for it, and strive thereafter to amend yourself. [Col. 0852C] But if through contempt and pride, through self-inflation and anger, swelling arrogance and rebellion, exaltation and murmuring—God forbid!—you cast aside your elders’ commands, you have surely committed an exceedingly great sin; and if you persevere in it, it will be mortal and damnable.

Soul. “This saying is hard” (John 6:61). If these things are so, I think they must be understood of the greatest commands [Gembloux MS: “this”].

## CHAPTER V. The seriousness and binding force of commands must also be inferred from the authority of the one commanding. Nothing commanded, whether small or great, is to be despised.

[Col. 0852D]

Reason. Which commands seem greatest to you?

Soul. The greatest command seems to be that by which we are commanded to love our God, and others of that kind. The greatest prohibitions, in my judgment, are those by which we are forbidden to commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, and the like.

Reason. Those commands and prohibitions are indeed the greatest. Yet not only in these, but also in the other commands and prohibitions which seem small and are promulgated by the elders according to God: forgetfulness is liable to sin, and contempt to condemnation.

Soul. It ought not to be so.

[Col. 0853A]

Reason. It is so.

Soul. Can you show me this by an example?

Reason. I can. What was forbidden to our first parent in Paradise?

Soul. That he should not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

Reason. How great was that prohibition? How can we call it great, when all the other trees had been granted to that first-formed man for food and only one was forbidden?

Soul. Then was God severe enough to cast out from the place of delight, into this dark exile, the human being whom he had created, for so slight a matter?

Reason. He did not cast him out for a slight matter.

Soul. Was not that prohibition slight [Col. 0853B] for which he cast him out?

Reason. Although what was forbidden was slight, the one who forbade it was not slight.

Soul. And what does the person who forbade it have to do with the matter?

Reason. Everything, in every way. First, he ought to have considered who it was that forbade it; second, he ought to have measured the prohibition by that person. Since, because of the forbidding person’s greatness, his prohibition also had to be great, owing to the great will of the one forbidding. For every command and prohibition of God must be received with the disposition with which it is imposed. And therefore, because of the excellent and great will of the commander, this first man ought to have avoided a small prohibition just as he would a great one.

[Col. 0853C]

Soul. Then that first man sinned greatly.

Reason. The punishment that followed shows what a horrible and immense sin he committed.

Soul. Yet, as you say, what he incurred by doing what was forbidden was not so damnable to him as his contempt for the one forbidding it.

Reason. That is what I say.

Soul. Why then do you not likewise say that contempt is damnable in the present commands and prohibitions [Gembloux MS: “prohibitions”], however slight [Melk MS: “thus lesser”], of those who hold his place, when he himself testifies that those who despise them despise him?

[Col. 0853D]

Reason. I cannot deny it. This is indeed hard, but it is true. If once a prophet was sent from Judaea to King Jeroboam in Samaria, and—neither proudly contemptuous nor ignorantly forgetful, but deceived by the lie of a false prophet—ate, even unwillingly, in a place forbidden by the Lord, though he now thought it permitted to him, and was handed over to a lion to be devoured: what do you judge concerning yourself, who transgress your elders’ rules through contempt?

Soul. Of all the words you have spoken on this matter, this example terrifies me. For the man of God would by no means have eaten in that place unless he had thought that in doing so he would obey the Lord. This is plainly shown by [Col. 0854A] his words both to the king and to the prophet when they invited him to dine.

Reason. What, then, is indicated to you in this action, except that you must never dare to do, on anyone’s subsequent suggestion, what you have heard forbidden by your prelate with your own ears—unless you have certainly learned that your elder has changed it?

Soul. I tremble greatly at your words.

Reason. What, then, do you now think concerning the commands of your elders: which are to be neglected and which despised?

Soul. Absolutely none. Your words compel me to revere my elders’ commands and prohibitions, small as well as great, as if I had heard them from the very mouth of God.

## CHAPTER VI. The law of the cloister, which weighs heavily upon some who desire to wander, is holy, useful, advantageous to the soul, and suited to bodily health.

[Col. 0854B]

Reason. Tell me whether any matter still burdens you.

Soul. I still feel burdened.

Reason. By what, then, are you burdened?

Soul. By the law of the cloister.

Reason. What sort of law does the cloister seem to you?

Soul. Very burdensome. But because I now presume in no way to judge or rebuke it until I know what your judgment of it may be [Melk MS: “may rest upon it”], although I dare not call the law of which I speak indiscreet, I feel that it is by no means moderately severe.

[Col. 0854C]

Reason. In what respect do you find it severe?

Soul. In that I may never leave the cloister, anywhere at all, without permission; never set foot outside the cloister gate; never go anywhere except perhaps to the dormitory or the oratory; scarcely at any hour, even with permission, remain outside the cloister, but must return to it at once. How blessed seem to me the brethren who frequently go out on the occasion of their obediences! For such departure greatly renews and refreshes them, because it relieves their weariness and produces pleasure [Gembloux MS: “removes”; idem: “prepares”].

Reason. You are still carnal; you still groan beneath the servitude and burden of the law. You do not yet rejoice in the freedom [Col. 0854D] and gentleness of grace, sweet and not harsh. The law of the cloister is not burdensome, at least, to one who has learned to observe it. For in the cloister you search out the depths of expositions, the narratives of examples from the Law, and chew over the sweet food of the Psalms. As for your calling blessed those who often go out, you would never pronounce them so blessed if you fully knew how many bodily labours and how many losses of soul they endure. How often they fast and hunger outside while you eat and are satisfied at home! How often they are cold while you fear no cold! How often they keep watch while you sleep sweetly! How often they are weary outside while you rest peacefully at home! How often they endure storms, snow, rain, winds, and other hardships of this kind, from which you are wholly free! And besides [Gembloux MS: “and likewise”] [Col. 0855A] all these things, how many losses do you think they endure! Oh, how often in thought, speech, and deed, in sight and hearing, and in the other movements of their limbs, do they incur sin—from which you are free in the cloister?

Soul. All these things are as you say.

Reason. What, then, do you still think of the law of the cloister?

Soul. The law is holy, useful, and good: salutary for soul and body, containing in itself the health of both.

## CHAPTER VII. Divine psalmody ought to be burdensome to no one. Rather, effort should be given so that what we utter with the mouth we may meditate upon in the heart.

[Col. 0855B]

Reason. By what do you now feel burdened?

Soul. By the manner of psalm-singing and chanting in choir.

Reason. How is the divine office celebrated by you in choir?

Soul. Far too slowly, far too tediously, and indeed in a manner that is very burdensome and wearisome to me.

Reason. Do you not know, O my soul, that among all the exercises of holy religion which you undertake, this is especially the work of God [Gembloux MS: “this special work of God”]? For here you stand before God; here you are presented to him; here you also speak with him. Oh, how holy, how devout, and how irreproachable in all your movements you ought to be when you stand before God [Gembloux MS: “before him”! How wisely, moreover, you ought both to meditate in your heart upon the words by which you address him and [Col. 0855C] utter them with your mouth [idem: “it is fitting”]. Alas, alas! How often we pray to him while the heart is absent, with the mouth alone; and though we cry out in a loud voice, are nevertheless mute to his ears. We may greatly fear lest he complain of us and it be said: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8). Remember what blessed Augustine says to you concerning diligence in prayer: “When you pray to God in psalms and hymns, let that be active in the heart which is uttered by the mouth.”

Soul. You admonish and speak well.

## CHAPTER VIII. It greatly benefits and is fitting for religious men occasionally to be exercised in bodily work, according to time and necessity.

[Col. 0855D]

Reason. What, then, still burdens you?

Soul. Manual work burdens me considerably.

Reason. What do you think of manual work?

Soul. It does not seem to me to pertain to ordained men, and especially to learned men. Are they peasants, that they ought to be employed in outdoor work, lowly and servile tasks?

Reason. You would never say this if you recognized how fitting and useful manual work is for religious men. Bodily exercise greatly consoles and renews them, greatly cherishes and refreshes them, because it both removes deficiency and brings progress—not only for the service of the body, but also for the instruction of the mind. Idleness, indeed, is the enemy [Col. 0856A] of the soul; and therefore, as time or necessity requires, you must do whatever work has been enjoined upon you, lest perhaps, if the devil finds you idle, he make you occupied in his own work. Therefore cut off from yourself, O my soul, unlawful Sabbaths, lest your enemies mock them. For this reason holy men are accustomed greatly to love manual work: because through it they acquire a twofold benefit, providing thereby both for the needs of bodily life and for spiritual purity.

Soul. I no longer have anything with which to contradict you. For I plainly see that it greatly befits and is advantageous for religious men occasionally to be employed in bodily work according to time and necessity.

## CHAPTER IX. Nothing is more shameful or more unworthy of a religious person than to indulge the body delicately, desire luxurious foods, and finally have the belly as one’s god.

[Col. 0856B]

Reason. Is there still anything that burdens you?

Soul. There certainly is.

Reason. And what is it?

Soul. I am greatly burdened because I abstain from certain foods.

Reason. Relief can immediately be given you in this burden. For, I suppose, your prelates do not wish you to waste away excessively through fasting and the rigour of abstinence.

Soul. I do not complain of excessive fasting.

Reason. Of what, then?

Soul. Because I am not permitted to take from every kind of food [Col. 0856C] which God created to be received with thanksgiving.

Reason. From what kind of food [Gembloux MS: “foods”] do you abstain?

Soul. From meat.

Reason. You are burdened by a small matter. For what purpose, I ask you, did you renounce the world and take on the habit of humility? Was it not that, alongside the exercise of the other virtues, you might also tame your flesh—as you read in your Rule—by abstinence from food and drink, insofar as health permits [idem: “life”]? Does it seem hard and burdensome to you that, so long as no illness of weakness oppresses you, the eating of meat is withheld from you, while every other kind of food is permitted? Why does it seem base [Col. 0856D] and shameful to me that those clothed in the habit of religion, and wholly untroubled by any weakness, nevertheless devote excessive concern to preparing, multiplying, varying [Melk MS: “salting and seasoning”], and seasoning dishes; and, like sick persons—or, a still greater disgrace, like pregnant women—can take nothing as food unless it is savoury? It seems strange to me that they are not ashamed, clothed in a lowly habit, to wish to eat only delicacies. For if their god—God forbid!—is the belly (Philippians 3:19), such a precious god ought not to be concealed beneath so lowly a habit [Melk MS: “to eat, because perhaps their god—God forbid!—is the belly. Yet so precious a god ought not to be concealed beneath so lowly a habit”] (Numbers 11:4–5). But, O my soul, remember that even today the chief of cooks destroys the walls of Jerusalem. Conversely, the graves of craving covered those who murmured against Moses and desired the foods of Egypt: “Why,” they say, “have you brought us out of the land of Egypt, where we sat by the loaves in abundance?” And elsewhere: “Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish which we ate in Egypt freely; cucumbers and melons come to mind, and leeks and onions and garlic. Our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing else but manna.” Oh, how many today appear religious outwardly, to whom this utterance applies even literally! Yet they may fear lest they suffer spiritually what those people suffered bodily.

[Col. 0857B]

Soul. What you say pleases me greatly.

## CHAPTER X. Vigils are to be highly valued, because they render the soul more fit for contemplating divine things. Conversely, a religious person should avoid offices that are seedbeds of cares, unless obedience commands otherwise.

Reason. If anything still burdens you, make it known.

Soul. Vigils are accustomed greatly to burden me.

Reason. You are very soft, delicate, and free from constraint, since you can bear nothing; indeed, you can [Melk MS: “could”], but do not wish to. Yet you ought by no means to dislike vigils, since they raise you to meditate upon spiritual things and make you light and capable. And certainly, if you keep the appointed hours of sleep, you will have no just cause to complain about vigils, because the appointed hours [Col. 0857C] of sleep ought to suffice for you.

Soul. That is so.

Reason. But see whether anything still remains that burdens you. What do you see?

Soul. I see our obedientiaries.

Reason. What do you think of them? Do you also desire their condition? Do you wish to become entangled in their occupations?

Soul. By occasion of their obediences they have many pleasures, many comforts, and many alleviations [Gembloux MS: “reliefs”], which I, enclosed in the cloister, cannot have.

Reason. If you consider their burdens, you will surely not desire their alleviations [ibid.: “reliefs”; ibid.: “you effect”]. Oh, how many labours and bodily afflictions, cares, anxieties, disturbances, and distresses do your abbot and priors, sacristan and cellarer, and the other officials endure in mind—things from which you are all free and separate! For they are all your servants, while you rule over them. They minister; you are ministered to. You need not be anxious about food and clothing, nor about what must be ploughed, sown, planted, gathered, built, and done; how what is available should be spent, or what is lacking acquired. For they provide all these and every other necessity for you. Consider, then, whether you ought to desire their condition, so far as concerns yourself alone: you remain in the cloister as far removed from them as [Col. 0858A] a master in his house is from servants, and a mistress in her chamber from maidservants.

Soul. All these things have been well said by you.

Reason. Although I speak well, I do not say this in such a way that you should not endure the yoke of occupation being imposed upon you when, because of the need of your house, your prelate decides to impose it upon you. For although I praise your condition, I do not thereby condemn theirs. Mary’s part is thus declared the better, yet Martha’s is not denied to be good. And although it is Mary’s proper office to sit in the house, nevertheless at her prelate’s command she sometimes goes out, if she is told: “The Master is here and calls for you” (John 11:28).

## CHAPTER XI. Religious silence is like a wall and stronghold, without which the pursuit of true piety cannot long endure.

[Col. 0858B]

Soul. One thing still burdens me greatly.

Reason. What is it? [Gembloux MS: “What is that?”]

Soul. The continual silence which I observe.

Reason. Oh, how necessary it is for all who strive to please God in religion to cultivate the discipline of silence. For, as Isaiah says: “The work of righteousness is silence [Melk MS: “guardianship”], peace, and security” (Isaiah 32:17). Silence is in some manner the key, wall, and safeguard of all religious life. Without it religion cannot be fortified; without it religious men can neither cultivate righteousness, maintain peace, nor possess security. For, as is read in the book of [Col. 0858C] Numbers, a vessel that has no cover or fastening upon it will be unclean (Numbers 19:15). How do you think this should be understood? You are that vessel. The cover placed upon this vessel is the enclosure of silence. If you lack this enclosure, you will be unclean like an open vessel into which every impurity falls. The enclosure of silence is greatly praised everywhere in Scripture. Therefore love silence, because, since an account must be rendered at the last judgment for every idle word (Matthew 12:36), the less account will then be demanded from you for speech, the more diligently and willingly you now keep silence. Therefore holy men, in order to be far from evil words, sometimes become mute and are silent even from good words. For, as blessed Ambrose says, “A flooding stream quickly gathers mud.” Hence he also said beforehand: “I have seen many sin by speaking; scarcely anyone by keeping silence.”

Soul. I confess that you have said all these things well and fittingly. By your instructions I, who was unlearned, have now been greatly educated; I, who was ignorant, have been taught; I, who was desolate, have been comforted; I, who was troubled, have been calmed; I, who was weighed down, have been relieved; I, who was sad, am joyful; I, who was faint-hearted, have been made glad and cheerful. Now I live, though formerly I was in some sense dying; now I run and desire, though formerly I could scarcely crawl or walk; what I formerly hated I now love; and what my soul previously refused to touch because of distress is now my food. I now know how, through God’s grace, [Col. 0859A] I ought to resist the temptations of my flesh. I now love the strictness of chapter. I now gladly and obediently embrace my elders’ commands. The law of the cloister is now pleasing to me. Long psalmody no longer displeases me. I now approve of manual work. I praise the pursuit of frugality [Col. 0860A]. I no longer reject vigils. I now love Jacob’s simplicity more than Esau’s hunting. I honour the enclosure of silence as the very cause of salvation and gate of life.

# HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0859]

## CHAPTER I. The end for which a religious person entered religion should be kept continually before his eyes; and he should diligently consider what he has vowed to God in profession.

[Col. 0859A]

Reason. I ask you, O my soul, to consider your calling [Col. 0859B]. Apply all your strength; press forward with every zeal; strive in every way, so that a pure intention may appear in your life and conduct: God alone as your object, and not the desire for reward. For God alone as your object you left the world and assumed the habit of humility. First, before all things and above all things, whatever your elders command or forbid you according to God [Melk MS: “Whatever the elders reasonably command or forbid, whether, etc.”], receive, embrace, and revere it as obediently, as cheerfully, and as perseveringly as if it had been commanded or forbidden from heaven by the mouth of God himself. To your brethren and companions render the affection of true brotherhood, and according to your ability and permission offer service of holy usefulness; so that always and everywhere you may please your neighbours in God, and God in [Col. 0859C] your neighbours. In this way you will fulfil your profession; in this way you will render to the Lord the vows your lips have uttered.

Soul. Since the occasion has now arisen, I should gladly like you to explain to me distinctly and clearly the order of profession, so that at last you may know what I know, what I ought to do. [Probably: “so that at last I may know what I ought to do.”]

Reason. Tell me what words are contained in your profession, so that I may explain them to you in sequence.

Soul. The words of my profession are these: “I, Brother N., offer and give myself to the Church of God, and promise the conversion of my manner of life and stability in this place [Gembloux MS: “in the place”], according to the Gospel of Christ, apostolic institution, and the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine. I also promise obedience unto death in Christ to Lord N., Father of the aforesaid Church, and to his successors, whom the sounder part of the congregation shall canonically elect.” Behold, these are the things I promised.

Reason. Truly, many are the things you owe, because many are the things you promised. In giving yourself to the Church of God—in all that you are, all that you know, and all that you can do—acknowledge yourself bound to that Church in every service and every fidelity. For this is to give yourself to the Church of God: to devote to that Church not only whatever good you possess, but also whatever good you are, whatever good you know, and whatever good you can do. For insofar as you withdraw from it your being, knowledge, or capacity for its need, [Col. 0860A] to that extent you withdraw yourself from it. Therefore run about; hasten usefully and faithfully to do promptly whatever your hand is able to accomplish, because you are bound by the words of your mouth.

[Col. 0860B]

Soul. Even if I had promised nothing else, this alone would be much.

## CHAPTER II. The formula of profession customary in the Premonstratensian Order is explained, together with what those vow who vow conversion of their manner of life and stability of place.

Reason. Let us proceed with the rest.

Soul. I am pleased that you should proceed with the rest, yet I am displeased. I am pleased to hear what I owe, but the answer displeases me, since I do not see that I render what I owe.

Reason. “And I promise,” you say, “the conversion of my manner of life.”

Soul. What is this?

[Col. 0860C]

Reason. You promised conversion of your manner of life: that, if formerly you were unclean, henceforth you should be chaste and clean; if formerly proud and envious, now humble and kindly; if formerly puffed up and angry, now gentle and meek; if, finally, you were formerly adorned by no virtues but entangled in every vice, henceforth, as far as you can, you should be burdened by no vices but filled with every virtue. This is what you vowed when you promised conversion of your manner of life.

Soul. When I hear that I promised what I see I do not fulfil, I feel more like weeping than saying anything.

Reason. “And stability,” you say, “in the place.”

Soul. I confess that I promised this too. But how long, I ask, shall I be held liable under this undertaking? [Note: The following material, down to “I know indeed,” is lacking in the Melk manuscript.] Can no limit of time be set to this undertaking? These are not like the promise concerning conversion of my manner of life. I know indeed that I can never lawfully corrupt my manner of life. But may I not leave before the end of my life the house in which I now am and move [to] another?

Reason. And why do you ask this?

Soul. For every day I see countless persons not only in another place, but even in another order than that in which they made their profession. Hence it appears that one may lawfully leave the place of one’s profession and seek another. For if this could not lawfully be done, neither would these people depart from their place and order, nor would they be received elsewhere by others.

[Col. 0861A]

Reason. You are far too hasty. You yourself ask, and you yourself answer. And since you are both pupil and teacher to yourself, your teacher knows no more than your pupil; you know no more in what you answer than in what you ask. But leave it to me, and I shall tell you whether it is permissible to leave the house in which you were established by profession, or not; and, if it is not permissible, why not; or if it is permissible, how it is permissible.

Soul. I did not state my opinion so as to do anything contrary to your judgment. For whatever I decide, only what you say shall be established.

Reason. Did you vow stability in your house? In my judgment, so far as concerns you, do not leave it before [Col. 0861B] the end of your life.

Soul. What if, fired by the desire for greater perfection and a stricter order, I should wish to improve my life and increase my religious observance? Do you not advise me to move elsewhere in order to do this?

Reason. Certainly I do not.

Soul. Why?

Reason. First, because I suspect your weakness: since you cannot bear this order, it follows that you cannot bear a stricter one either. Second, because I fear that your departure may bring some loss or scandal to those who remain after you leave.

[Col. 0861C]

Soul. And how can that be? [Gembloux MS: “And why would that be?”]

Reason. Are you not one of the ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and bride? (Matthew 25:1).

Soul. I certainly desire to be one of the five wise virgins.

Reason. Are you wise or foolish?

Soul. I am, certainly. [The answer is textually elliptical.]

Reason. But if you are foolish, I do not advise you to depart anywhere, lest your going forth be a foolish woman’s going forth. But if you are wise, I nevertheless advise you even then to remain, so that your wisdom may assist before all others the mother that conceived and bore you—namely, your own house. What other house you may have is more worthy to make use of your wisdom than the mother that gave you birth, cherished you, brought you to the maturity of your perfection, and led you to the wisdom you now have? Therefore, whether you are a foolish virgin or wise, I do not advise you to depart anywhere. For if you are foolish, you need your house; but if you are wise, your house needs you.

[Col. 0861D]

Soul. What if the dispositions of both my prelates and brethren are so contrary to me that I cannot remain peacefully in my house? Is it not therefore better for me to move elsewhere, where I may be with affection and love [Melk MS: “and may be able to move with affection and love, rather than remain with hatred, etc.”], than remain in hatred and rancour?

Reason. I do not know how I can answer and satisfy you regarding these two evils—which is better—when neither is good. You ask whether it is better for you to perish by fire or by a fall. For you are burned if you remain in hatred, and you fall headlong if you withdraw without permission. And which of these is good: to be burned or to fall headlong?

[Col. 0862A]

Soul. Neither; both are evil. But which of them, I ask, is the lesser evil?

Reason. Which do you desire more: that I show you how to be sick and not die, or how to be so completely cured that you are sick no longer?

Soul. As of two evils I choose illness rather than death, so from one evil I choose rather to be cured than [Col. 0862B] to remain ill [Gembloux MS corrupt: “from one good evil to, etc.”].

Reason. Do you wish, then, that I show you how you may reject evil and choose good? That is, how you may conduct yourself so that you need not, to avoid what is worst, do what is less evil, but instead do what is wholly [Melk MS: “what entirely is, etc.”] good?

Soul. I do; I desire it eagerly.

Reason. If the dispositions of your brethren and prelates are contrary to you, strive to amend their wicked conduct by your good conduct. Do not defend yourself, but give place to anger; and if they are against you, do not be overcome by evil but overcome evil with good. Here your wisdom will appear, if you are a wise virgin: if you conquer their arrogance by humility, their anger by gentleness, [Col. 0862C] their envy by kindness, their disturbance by mildness, and their hatred by charity. Bow humbly before them, obey them, serve them, and endeavour by every means you can to overcome their evil with good.

Soul. What if they are such—that is, so hardened toward me in their malice—that I can correct them in no way whatever?

Reason. If they are such, I still do not advise you to depart. I do not advise you to harm yourself because you cannot benefit them.

Soul. On the contrary, it is harmful to me to remain.

Reason. In what respect is it harmful to you if you remain? To what sin do they draw you against your will?

[Col. 0862D]

Soul. To none.

Reason. In what respect, then, is it harmful for you to remain with them?

Soul. In that they provoke me to anger and murmuring, and compel me to live in hatred.

Reason. Why do you hate them?

Soul. Because they hate me.

Reason. If, then, they hate you, you ought rightly to hate them. Have you not heard from the mouth of your Saviour: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you”?

Soul. Do you then wish me to remain in hatred?

Reason. By no means, but in love. For I wish you to dwell with them as Abel with Cain, Isaac with Ishmael, and Jacob with Esau. Their malice can benefit you if patience does not fail you. [Col. 0863A] But if they are such as to draw you into sin, I advise you to depart elsewhere, where you may be able to please God.

Soul. Can I not lawfully depart in any other way?

Reason. You may indeed lawfully depart if, with your prelate’s permission, you are regularly elected to some church, or if something of that kind should happen through which you can lawfully leave. Therefore, to summarize briefly all that has been said at length: whatever others may say, my advice is that you should on no occasion or ground whatsoever leave your house while your prelate objects and forbids it, except only in the cases I have enumerated.

Soul. Proceed now with the rest.

Reason. You now plainly show how you gave yourself to the Church [Col. 0863B] of God, promised conversion of manners, and promised stability in a place; and in what follows you add: “according to the Gospel of Christ, apostolic institution, and the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine.” Since you gave yourself to the Church, vowed conversion of your manner of life, and vowed stability in a place, for the perfection of holiness, unity of heart, and complete renunciation of private property—matters treated by blessed Augustine’s Rule—you did well also to make these vows according to the Gospel of Christ, apostolic institution, and the canonical Rule of blessed Augustine. For the Gospel contains every perfection of holiness; apostolic institution contains both unity of hearts and community of possessions. For, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, [Col. 0863C] “the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). Behold unity of souls! “Nor did any one of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them.” Behold community of possessions! And these are the chief matters treated by blessed Augustine’s Rule. Therefore, at its beginning it says: “These are the things which we command you, being established in the monastery, to observe” [Melk MS: “being established”]. “First, therefore [ibid.: ‘because’], you are gathered together into one so that you may dwell harmoniously in the house and have one heart and one soul in God; and do not call anything your own, but let all things be common to you, and let food and clothing be distributed to each of you by your prelate [Melk MS: ‘superior’].”

### Chapter III

The remaining matters contained in the same formula of profession are explained, and it is shown how dangerous and grave is the sin of possessing private property for religious who have professed renunciation of their own possessions. Further, the obedience owed to superiors and what constitutes the sounder part of those electing a superior are taught.

[Col. 0863D]

**Soul.** Is it a grave sin if we have some private property?

**Reason.** Why do you ask me, O my soul, whether this sin is grave? For how can it not be a grave sin to possess something as one’s own, when blessed Benedict forbids you even to call anything your own? [Note: [Col. 0863D] *Rule of St. Benedict*, ch. 33.] Is theft, lying, sacrilege, apostasy a grave sin? Certainly those who seek private possessions are thieves and liars; they are likewise sacrilegious persons and apostates. For they have already returned to their vomit [Gembloux MS.: “return”], since they strive again to possess things which they had already renounced. Therefore see to it, O my soul, that you have nothing without the knowledge [ibid.: “acknowledgment”] and permission of your Father, lest you become a partner with Ananias and Sapphira in their crime—how grave their fault was, the punishment that followed made known.

**Soul.** If your words are true, not all who wear the habit of religion are religious.

**Reason.** You speak truly. For Behemoth does not wonder that it has already swallowed up a river; moreover, it is confident that the Jordan will flow into its mouth (Job 40:18).

**Soul.** We are in great danger.

**Reason.** And because in all these matters you ought to obey your superior, [Col. 0864B] you therefore add: “I also promise obedience to the Father of the aforesaid Church.” How you ought to obey your superior has been sufficiently shown to you above. And because you owe no obedience to your superior in matters contrary to God, you add: “in Christ.” For superiors must always be obeyed when [Gembloux MS.: “but when”] they do not command things contrary to God. But if—God forbid!—they should command things contrary to God, I unhesitatingly affirm that Peter’s dictum must be followed: “We must obey God rather than men.” And because, for as long as you live, you must not be released from the yoke of obedience, nor forget the tail of the victim in your sacrifice, you say: “until death.” For among the brethren you must be clothed in a garment reaching to the ankles, and in your sacrifice you must not forget the tail of the victim: for “he who perseveres [Col. 0864C] to the end shall be saved.” Again, because the very person to whom you promised obedience may depart this life before you, lest, upon his death, you think yourself released from the bond of submission, you say at the end: “and to his successors whom the sounder part of the congregation shall canonically elect.”

**Soul.** When an election must be held, what part of the congregation is to be judged the sounder?

**Reason.** I do not judge the more numerous party always to be the sounder; rather, even if its small number makes it modest in size, that party is sound which knowledge of truth, love of virtue, and uprightness of intention render sound. For this is spiritual and true health of heart: to know the truth, choose the good, and in both to wish to please God alone. Election must be entrusted to such persons; likewise, an election made by such persons must be approved, confirmed, and held valid: persons who know who ought to be chosen according to God, choose that same person, and do this for God’s cause alone [Gembloux MS.: “is done”]. But those whose knowledge of truth is taken away by blindness in an election, whose love of virtue is removed by greed, and whose uprightness of intention is taken away by vanity, do not, in my judgment, possess true soundness, although a multitude gives them numerical strength. Hence the father of monks, blessed Benedict, writes thus concerning an election: [Note: [Col. 0864D] *Ibid.*, ch. 64.]

> “In the appointment of an abbot,” he says, “let reason always be considered, so that he may be established [Col. 0865A] whom either the entire harmonious congregation, according to the fear of God, or even a part of the congregation—though small [same MS.: “though modest”]—has chosen with sounder counsel.”

Gembloux MS.: “whom the united company of the congregation has chosen.”

**Soul.** What you say appears true.

**Reason.** Behold, O my soul, I have explained to you, one by one, the words of your profession. Behold, I have shown you what you promised. Whether you faithfully fulfil these things, you must see for yourself.

### Chapter IV

How the many transgressions of vows and of the divine law are to be expiated; to whom sins are to be confessed, etc.

**Soul.** I certainly see that daily I break [Gembloux MS.: “violate”] my vows. What do you advise me [Col. 0865B] to do?

**Reason.** Fully acknowledge your fault, humbly mourn it, sincerely confess it, make worthy satisfaction for it, and thereafter cease from it.

**Soul.** You speak well. But to whom ought I confess my sins?

**Reason.** To whom, unless to your superior?

**Soul.** If it happens that I have committed some great sin, and I fear, am ashamed before, or even do not wish to reveal it to my superior, may I not confess it to another and be absolved through him?

**Reason.** I do not think that such a confession wholly pleases God, or that such an absolution is sufficient for you.

**Soul.** What then shall I do? If I show him [Col. 0865C] my great wounds, I fear that thereafter he will hold me in greater contempt and be less familiar with me. And how can I disclose to him the enormity of my crimes, when I must see him every day, must remain with him night and day, and when I am always angry with him and he with me? Whenever he looks at me, I shall think that he is thinking of my crime. Whenever he is angry with me, I shall believe that he despises me for my crime. I shall even suspect that he will never wish to love me, never wish to trust me; and inwardly tormented and devastated by these and similar disturbances, I shall never have peace.

**Reason.** O how deep, how dark, and how malicious is the human mind! You need not suspect these things of your superior. And even if he should—far be it!—be such that you could truly think or say these things of him, my counsel is nevertheless that you disclose your guilt to him. For it is better for you to suffer all these things and be saved and released, than to conceal what you have committed from him, so that you may be bound here and damned eternally.

**Soul.** And why cannot some other superior absolve me?

**Reason.** Even if I grant that you may be absolved by another, who will absolve you of the sin that you commit in fleeing your proper superior?

**Soul.** He will absolve me of both sins, if I confess both to him. For I confess to him both that I committed [Col. 0866A] that sin and that I conceal it from my superior.

**Reason.** I ask you carefully to understand what I ask, and then to answer me accordingly.

**Soul.** Ask what you wish.

**Reason.** Do you think that anyone can be absolved from a sin so long as he persists in it?

**Soul.** I think so in no way; for as long as a sin is not cast aside, it is in no way forgiven.

**Reason.** Therefore you admit that you can in no way be absolved from your sin, even though you have confessed it, unless you leave it?

**Soul.** I plainly admit it. What good does confession do me if I do not wish to leave the sin? It seems strange to me [Col. 0866B] that you ask this, since there is no one who does not know it.

**Reason.** Know now why I ask you this: whether sins can ever [Melk MS.: “in any way”] be forgiven by confession alone while sins are retained and, being retained, practised. For perhaps, if they cannot—and you do believe this—you cannot be absolved unless you confess to your own superior.

**Soul.** Certainly they cannot in any way. The Catholic faith does not admit this at all. Even if I now confess to my own superior and do not wish to leave my sin, I am in no way absolved. Everyone who wishes to be absolved from his sin must first fully acknowledge his sin; secondly repent or [Col. 0866C] grieve; thirdly confess; fourthly make satisfaction; fifthly refrain; and only then, sixthly, may he trust in God’s mercy, and seventhly rest sweetly in conscience with the Lord.

### Chapter V

It is shown at length that the sins of religious persons are to be confessed only to their own superiors, and that no one should readily be deterred from this by fear of disclosure and disgrace.

**Reason.** Therefore, as may also be understood from your words, the casting away of sin must always not only accompany confession but precede it.

**Soul.** It certainly must. For our Saviour first restored to life Lazarus, dead four days, and made him, once restored to life, come forth; and only then commanded the disciples to unbind him. Thus, at the coming of gracious Jesus, we are restored to life through repentance. Secondly, at the great cry which he sends forth from his mind, after the rock of hardness has first been removed from the cave of the fetid conscience, we come forth through confession; and at last we are absolved by our superiors, who are his disciples, and are permitted thereafter to go on the way of righteousness. What good, then, would it have done if the disciples had unbound Lazarus while he was dead, even if he had come forth from the tomb? No more, it seems to me, does it profit today that sinners appear to be absolved by their superiors, while they do not put away from themselves, by the life-giving abandonment of sin, the death of sin in which they lie dead. And what need is there to say more on this matter? For no one fails to know [Col. 0867A] that the Lord does not forgive a sin which he sees is not abandoned by us.

**Reason.** Although I know this too, nevertheless it pleases me to hear it from you; for I had not thought you so wise.

**Soul.** There would be little wisdom in me if I were ignorant of this matter. For to think otherwise concerning it is not merely ignorance but also blasphemy.

**Reason.** Since this is so, if you seek absolution, through repentance and confession, from the sin that you confess to a foreign superior that you committed, because you abandon it, you will in no way be absolved by that foreign superior from the sin which you commit by concealing it from your own superior; for although [Col. 0867B] you confess it to him, you nevertheless do not abandon it.

**Soul.** Do I not abandon it?

**Reason.** See whether you abandon it. What is the matter of which we are speaking?

**Soul.** That which I commit by keeping silent about my sin to my superior.

**Reason.** Therefore you remain in this sin as long as you are silent about that sin to your superior.

**Soul.** It certainly is so.

**Reason.** But if you desire to be absolved from this sin, you must disclose it to your superior in confession.

**Soul.** It is necessary that I do so. But if, in confessing to my superior, I confess that I concealed my sin from him, must I also say what the sin was [Col. 0867C] that I concealed from him?

**Reason.** Therefore, if you wish to be reconciled to God, you cannot do so unless you reveal to your own superior the sin by which you concealed your sin from him. But you cannot fully disclose this to him unless you confess what the sin was which, while concealing it from him, you revealed to another. What follows, then, except that you cannot be reconciled to God while concealing from your own superior what you confessed to another?

**Soul.** According to the basis of this argument, I do not think this is true. What? Cannot I confess to my superior that I conceal one sin from him, and yet not name it?

[Col. 0867D]

**Reason.** Such confession is worthless.

**Soul.** Why?

**Reason.** Are you absolved when you say, “I have done evil,” unless you confess what evil you have done?

**Soul.** I am not absolved at all.

**Reason.** So neither are you absolved when you say to your superior, “I concealed a sin,” unless you tell him what you concealed from him.

**Soul.** This does not seem tenable to me.

**Reason.** It is certainly strange. Let us suppose that I am your superior.

**Soul.** Let us suppose it.

**Reason.** Come, then, and confess to me.

**Soul.** Gladly. Behold, I confess: I concealed from you a certain [Col. 0868A] sin, and I ask of God and of you absolution for this sin.

**Reason.** Absolution for which sin? For that which you concealed from me; or for that which you committed in concealing it from me; or for both?

**Soul.** Not for both; nor for that which I concealed from you, but solely for that which I committed by concealing it from you.

**Reason.** I wish to absolve you of both, if you will confess both to me.

**Soul.** I seek absolution from this one.

**Reason.** Gladly. You are indeed to be led astray by true falsehood; therefore confess to me.

**Soul.** I concealed a certain sin from you.

**Reason.** Do you repent of it?

[Col. 0868B]

**Soul.** I repent greatly.

**Reason.** Do you abandon your sin?

**Soul.** I abandon it.

**Reason.** See that you abandon it, for otherwise you cannot be absol—

**Soul.** I know most certainly that I cannot be absolved unless I abandon my sin. But I do abandon it.

**Reason.** Do you abandon your sin?

**Soul.** I abandon it wholly.

**Reason.** What sin do you abandon?

**Soul.** This one which I confess to you: what I did by concealing a certain sin from you.

**Reason.** Do you wish to remain any longer in this sin?

**Soul.** Have I not already told you?

[Col. 0868C]

**Reason.** Yet what is it?

**Soul.** I think I see where you are going.

**Reason.** Where am I going?

**Soul.** Proceed and speak.

**Reason.** What do you think?

**Soul.** I think that I have been caught. [Melk MS., *Soul*: “Proceed and say what you think; for I think that I have been caught.” *Reason*: “Therefore,” etc.]

**Reason.** Therefore, if the sin from which you desire absolution through my ministry is the sin of having concealed a certain sin from me, and if you cannot be absolved from this sin while you commit it, and you always commit it while you conceal from me the sin of which you speak, is it not necessary, in order that you may be absolved from this [Col. 0868D] sin, also to confess to me the thing which you concealed from me?

**Soul.** Is this indeed the case?

**Reason.** It is altogether the case. [Melk MS.: “The matter is so.”] Therefore, so long as that is concealed from me, it is plainly evident that this is not remitted unless that is disclosed to me—unless perhaps, contrary to what was denied above, your sin may be forgiven you even though it is evident that you do not abandon it.

**Soul.** I cannot resist your arguments and conclusions.

**Reason.** Since, then, it is certain that you sin as long as you conceal any sin from me, your superior, does it not follow that you are not absolved as long as you conceal any sin from me?

[Col. 0869A]

**Soul.** These conclusions do indeed seem to follow.

**Reason.** Therefore, if you desire the forgiveness of the sin which you commit by concealing a sin from me, I advise you to confess not merely that you conceal it, but what it is that you conceal.

**Soul.** That is what I must do. But what if I know with absolute certainty that my superior wishes to make my sin public? Even then [Gembloux MS.: “may I”] may I conceal it, or safely reveal it to another and be fully absolved by him?

**Reason.** If you know with absolute certainty that your superior wishes to perpetrate this most abominable, utterly diabolical, criminal, and damnable deed, and if for this reason you conceal your wound from him, you must greatly fear lest, even if you are not damned because you conceal it from publication, you may perhaps be damned [Col. 0869B] because you conceal it from your own Father.

**Soul.** And how can I endure his making my sin public?

**Reason.** Although it seems grievous to you that your sin be made public, from two evils you must choose the lesser: that it be made public here and forgiven you, rather than that, because you conceal your sin from your superior, you be made public before every person at the last judgment in the sight of the Lord and be damned with the wicked in hell. Yet whether this intention of yours excuses you before the sight of the inner Judge, I do not know. This alone I know: it is very safe for every person to disclose his guilt to his own superior.

**Soul.** I am hemmed in on every side. If I keep silent, death is mine, because I do not attain forgiveness; but if I do not keep silent, I shall not escape the hands of the slanderer and accuser, because I fear public exposure.

**Reason.** Is it not better for you, then, to fall into the hands of a human being than to forsake the law of your God, lest, if perhaps you fear frost, snow fall upon you?

### Chapter VI

Nothing in religion is more necessary than mutual love between superiors and subjects. What is to be thought concerning private works of piety?

**Soul.** It can clearly be known from what you have said that it is very necessary that the part to which the election of a superior ought to be entrusted be sound. [Both MSS.: “precede.”] I do not know what more to say now about this matter. But among all things pertaining to religious persons, you know [Col. 0869D] that it is very necessary for superior and subject to have between themselves a full and supreme love and familiarity according to God [Melk MS.: “familiar”]. I learn this from daily experience. For I must love no less, but indeed just as much, him to whom I must reveal not only my actions but also my thoughts and words [Gembloux MS.: “I must”]; by whose sole judgment I must live; whom I must heed as [God] himself in all things in which he is not opposed to God; and whom, if I do not contemptuously and stubbornly despise him in any respect, I cannot perish.

**Reason.** It is as you say: and as much as you owe him, so much does he owe you. Indeed, it is more difficult for him to render what he owes than for you to render what you owe him. For it is easier [Col. 0870A] for you humbly to be subject than for him profitably to preside over you; for you to be ruled without complaint than for him to rule without pride; for you willingly to obey than for him discreetly to command you; for you to be rebuked without mad fury than for him to rebuke without the insult of arrogance; for you to confess than for him to absolve; for you to make satisfaction than for him to impose satisfaction. And, to gather much into a brief statement, it is far more difficult for him faithfully and fully to provide for you in heart and body than for you to make use of the provision obtained. Therefore, as your Augustine commands you: have mercy not only upon yourself but also upon him, who is in greater danger the higher the position he occupies.

**Soul.** You speak well. But I should gladly like to know what you judge concerning private prayers which some persons are accustomed sometimes [Col. 0870B] to practise in these communities.

**Reason.** Not only private prayers, but all private devotions undertaken with a good intention for God, provided that through them nothing of the common good is diminished—I judge such devotions, I say, to be good private devotions, but everywhere I set common devotions above them. Therefore, whether you engage in prayers, vigils, fasts, labours, or, in short, private devotions, judge them useful to you only when they neither diminish in any respect the things which ought to be performed in common nor disturb the peace of those dwelling together. For, on account of peace and the wish of your brother, you must never set your own advantage before charity [Gembloux MS.: “put before”]. For since evil should never be committed, often even good is more beneficially [Col. 0870C] performed when, for the sake of peace and brotherly goodwill, it is temporarily set aside. For, to offer one example among many: perhaps you sing Mass more devoutly when, for that reason, you do not sing, so that you yield to your brother who wishes to sing—who perhaps could not sing if you were singing. Thus, in a wonderful manner, it comes about that, when for a time you desist from one good act for charity’s sake, you acquire a double good: first, because you think so humbly of yourself and so highly of your brother that you judge his devotion better and holier than your own; secondly, because, by yielding to him charitably [Gembloux MS.: “charity”] and serving humbly, you have been so diligent in preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. What I have said concerning this one instance [Col. 0870D] must likewise be understood of the other exercises of holy religion of this kind.

**Soul.** You exhort well and beneficially.

### Chapter VII

Conclusion of the work, in which every religious person is commanded to be fervent, steadfast in every good work, humble, and holy, etc.

**Reason.** I beg you, O my soul, amid the many things we have said, henceforth work out your own salvation carefully and diligently with fear and by every means that you know and can employ. Strive with every effort to please God in God, in your superiors, in all your brethren, and also in your neighbours—and to please God in them. Strive, I say, O my soul, to avoid harmful things and seek wholesome ones; obey superiors; serve equals; be decorous in dress, moderate [Col. 0871A] in food, assiduous in the cloister, seldom in public, attentive to psalms and silent at idle talk; confessing and humble in chapter; serene [Gembloux MS.: “serious”] and simple in choir; grave and mature at the altar; useful and discreet at work; holy and mature in the dormitory; sober and cheerful in the refectory. In your walking, standing, and every movement, as you read in your Rule, have nothing that offends anyone’s gaze; but behave as becomes your holiness, so that in every word, action, place, and time, toward every person, you may be fitting and circumspect; [Col. 0872A] so that always and everywhere you may be sparing toward yourself [Melk MS.: “pure”], ready toward your neighbours, and devoted to God.

**Soul.** I confess that you have said all things well and fittingly. Blessed would be one who lived as you exhort here.

**Reason.** Let these things, then, be said in such a way that we neither prejudice in anything one who knows how to speak more truthfully, profoundly, and elegantly on these matters, nor proudly excuse ourselves if we have said anything otherwise, nor haughtily reject correction offered us [Melk MS.: “bestowed”] as burdensome. Let all say: Amen.

## A.D. 1152–1190. Godfrey of Viterbo

[Col. 0871]

## Notice

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 69)

Godfrey of Viterbo [Note: [Col. 0871A] By no means of Wittenberg, as Baronius doubted under the year 1186, no. 22; nor a Dominican monk, as Bernard de Luxembourg was persuaded. [Col. 0872A] See Jacques Quétif, vol. I, p. 740.]—priest and chaplain and notary of Conrad III, who died in the year 1152, Frederick I, and Henry IV, who assumed the reins of empire in 1190—after long and varied journeys over forty years, having acquired abundant knowledge of languages and affairs, wrote the *Memories of the Ages* [Note: [Col. 0872A] Not *Memories of the Saints*, as one reads in Vossius.] or, as it has been called by others, the *Pantheon*, or *Universal Chronicle*, partly in prose and partly in verse, from the creation of the world down to A.D. 1186. It was divided into twenty sections and dedicated to Pope Urban III, pope from 1185 to 1187.

It was first published by Basil Johann Herold at Basel in 1569, folio; then by Johann Pistorius at the beginning of the second volume of the *Writers on German Affairs*, Frankfurt, 1584, and Hanover, 1613, folio; and most recently by the distinguished Burchard Gotthelf Struve in the revised edition of Pistorius’s collection, Regensburg, 1726, folio, to which were added variant readings from a parchment manuscript at Nuremberg. Muratori inserted the last five parts, or sections XVI–XX, of this Chronicle—in which there is much concerning Italian affairs—in volume VII of the *Treasury of Writers on Italian Affairs*, p. 346; and from an anonymous chronicle in the Este library, whose author had confessed that he had drawn upon the *Pantheon*, he supplied certain readings more correct and complete.

Another manuscript work of the same Godfrey in the Imperial Library, written some years after the *Pantheon* and dedicated to Henry VI, king of the Romans and Germans, is entitled *Mirror of Kings, on the Genealogy of All Kings and Emperors, Trojans and Germans, from the Time of the Flood to Henry VI, according to the Chronicles of the Venerable Priest Bede, Eusebius, and Ambrose*. See Lambecius, vol. II, p. 774, where part of the letter to Emperor Henry is printed. Godfrey himself, in his preface to Pope Urban III, indicates what authors he used and what peoples’ affairs he pursued in the *Pantheon*.

[Col. 0871]

## The Pantheon, or Memories of the Ages, of Godfrey of Viterbo

(Edited by the most distinguished MURATORI, *Writers on Italian Affairs*, vol. VIII, omitting those matters which concern the history of the Old Testament and the first centuries after Christ’s birth.)

## Preface of Lodovico Antonio Muratori

[Col. 0871B] Godfrey, or Gotfrey, whose Chronicle deserves an eminent place in our Collection, was born at Viterbo, a city of Italy, and therefore is distinguished by the title “of Viterbo” from others of that name. Scholars unanimously assign him this homeland, Baronius excepted, who under the year of Christ 1186 calls him Gotfrey of Viterbo—or, as common report has it, of Wittenberg. Why that most learned cardinal raised this doubt concerning Gotfrey’s homeland [Col. 0873A] is unknown to me. Certainly, in his dedicatory letter to Pope Urban III, as it appears in the printed books, he styles himself “Gotfrey, an unworthy priest”; and, unless manuscript codices provide contrary evidence, this writer ought not to be taken away from Italy and Viterbo.

Nevertheless, it should be observed that Gotfrey wrote that as a boy he was educated in the church of Bamberg, and there devoted himself to the first studies of letters. In part XVII of the Chronicle, where he treats of Henry II and of the city and church of Bamberg, he says:

> I, who learned there the first lessons of the grammatical art, have set forth the remaining matters in verse as their foster-child.

Then in the poem he adds:

> Ancient Bamberg was my teacher when I was a boy.

Moreover, Godfrey was secretary or notary of three emperors, namely Conrad III, Frederick I, and Frederick’s son Henry VI. In such an office it seems likely [Col. 0873B] that the German emperors would have employed a German rather than an Italian. Yet even these matters are insufficient to take Godfrey away from our Italy. For while German emperors ruled in Italy, besides the ordinary causes there were many others why Italians often travelled in Germany; and our Godfrey, though born in Italy, could therefore have been taken there as a boy. Being skilled in German no less than Latin, he could properly serve the German emperor. Therefore I say again: unless the evidence of the manuscripts determines otherwise, we shall leave this historian to Viterbo and Italy—especially since, in the Chronicle of the Este library, which I think was written about the year 1320 and which will have its own place in our Collection, he is most clearly called Gotfrey of Viterbo.

As I indicated above, Godfrey was notary to Conrad III, Frederick I, and Henry VI. In some diplomas of Frederick I in Ughelli, Margarini, and [Col. 0873C] others, a “Godefredus, chancellor of the imperial court in place of Philip, archbishop of Cologne, archchancellor of Italy,” subscribes. I would not venture to guess whether this Godfrey has anything to do with our historian. Viterbo’s Chronicle has only this concerning himself, in part XVII, before treating of Henry IV:

> Know that I, Gotfrey, author of this book, was chaplain and notary of King Conrad III, of Emperor Frederick, and of his son Henry VI; and during their times I have investigated all these matters on both sides of the sea for forty years, from every repository—Latin, barbarian, Greek, Jewish, and Chaldaean.

These words gave Basil Johann Herold, who first arranged for this History to be printed, an occasion to write in his preface to it that our Godfrey was versed in Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Chaldaean, and many other barbarian languages; that he had travelled over every land and all the sea for the full forty years; and that he had examined the libraries of every people [Col. 0873D] whom he visited from every region. May Herold forgive me: here he seems to me to puff out his cheeks excessively. Godfrey’s words do not at all reveal such astonishing mastery of so many languages—a miracle which, in that age of infant scholarship, would have surpassed every marvel. Nor should we believe that Godfrey of Viterbo traversed every land and all the sea throughout forty years. I think that he employed far less labour, both mental and bodily, in educating himself and leaving us his History. Certainly the matters he narrates are neither of such weight nor so exotic that he can persuade us, who are not very credulous, that he was equipped with so many languages, including barbarian ones, and had examined the libraries of every people. For a man of those times, to acquire the glory of historical learning, it was enough to discover Eusebius’s Chronicle in a corner of some library. But let us come to Godfrey’s Chronicle itself.

He himself entitled it *Pantheon*, since it treats [Col. 0874A] of all the rulers of the world. It is indeed a bombastic title, and perhaps not one to be attributed to the author himself. For, according to Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, book II, ch. 54, some cite it under the title *Memories of the Saints*, as I learned from Pignorius. But I think either that Pignorius, who supplied the information, was mistaken here, or that Vossius read incorrectly. In the preface to the *Garland of Flowers*, which I shall publish in this Collection, Galvano della Fiamma, a fourteenth-century writer, among the books that he used in composing his History, cites Gotfrey’s Chronicle, called *Memory of the Ages*. I could not doubt that these words indicated our Godfrey, since passages were repeatedly brought forward from that book; and therefore you may easily understand that this was really the title of his book, not *Memories of the Saints*.

I add Peregrino Prisciani of Ferrara, a writer of extensive learning, who was still committing the *Annals of Este* to manuscript around the year of Christ 1490. He cites Gotfrey of Viterbo in the book which he called *Memory of the Ages*. From this it is now evident that among earlier writers, even before it was printed, Gotfrey’s Chronicle was entitled rather *Memory of the Ages* than *Pantheon*, and that its author was attributed to the city of Viterbo.

Godfrey began his History, according to the custom of primitive times, with the beginning of the world, and carried it down to the pontificate of Urban III, to whom he also dedicated the work. It therefore ends in the year of Christ 1186, as Baronius had previously observed. The writer treated both sacred and secular deeds, partly in prose and partly in verse; and he especially amused himself with Leonine verses, rhythms answering one another in the middle or at the end, sometimes with tasteless play.

I would have readers warned that the Este library preserves an ancient Chronicle in a parchment manuscript codex, by an anonymous author, bearing this title:

> Here begins the Book on Times and Ages, for the perpetual remembrance of the matter: a brief compendium collected from various Chronicles and arranged in order concerning the Times in which certain Roman pontiffs and emperors sat, etc.

From it I extracted what concerns the history of the city of Reggio, also to be read in this Collection. That writer borrowed many verses from the History of our Godfrey, whom he praises simply under the bare name of *Chronicle*. But when I compared that codex with the published History, it appeared that not a few of these verses differed from the printed text; indeed, many occurred in the same manuscript which are absent from the published editions, though all seem to have had the same Godfrey as their parent. I shall give a specimen. Thus it is read there concerning Diocletian:

> Diocletian together with Maximian  
> Held the empire jointly, with no one between them.  
> One food and one flesh were theirs.  
>
> Against Christ they undertake a special war;  
> Throughout every region they bring war upon Christ’s followers;  
> As they oppress them with death, they burn all writings.  
>
> [Col. 0874D] These two were the first who wore jewels on their clothing;  
> Neither before on the feet nor upon garments had such things been worn;  
> They say that purple-clad lords had existed before.

In the printed books of Godfrey, the sequence of emperors is confused, as may be seen especially in Maximian and Diocletian, who are placed before Gordian, Philip, Decius, and so forth. Whoever wishes to compare the printed text with the verses cited above will immediately discover the difference. A second example is provided by the poem concerning Emperor Constantine, which in the Este codex reads as follows:

> Now Constantine, if we wish to tell the truth,  
> Was the first true worshipper of Christ in his age.  
> East and western shores believed this.  
>
> While holding the plough, he looked back from the furrow.  
> Eusebius afterwards immersed him in a grim baptism.  
> I pursue matters well begun, but he ends them in an evil end.  
>
> The people believed in Christ and received him;  
> [Col. 0875A] then he granted permission openly to preach Christ.  
> He built churches to his praise and favour.  
>
> Remaining an Arianist, he finally mingles in contention;  
> for the crime of Eusebius corrupted that same life.  
> Read: the *Tripartite History* relates these things thus.  
>
> Rome made this foreigner its adopted son,  
> to whom it gave the highest throne of empire for all ages,  
> and who, as if guilty of death, afterwards made her a widow.  
>
> By fraud and guile he withdrew Latin nobles from the City,  
> and soon compelled the Greeks to be, as it were, captives,  
> establishing a new Rome by resources and craft.  
>
> He transferred the empire and showed favour to the Greeks,  
> giving foreigners the honour which Rome had held,  
> abandoning Romulus’s city and fostering Greek kingdoms.  
>
> This was a bastard whom golden Rome preferred.  
> Having killed his master, he is said to have seized the crown.  
> Though formerly good, now an evil report flies abroad.  
>
> Rome, by her endeavours, etc.

These, indeed, are specimens of variant readings in Godfrey’s poems. Now I shall give an example of matters absent from the printed texts. Chapter 86 of the Este codex shows whence the Teutons came before Christ’s advent:

> I have recounted enough of the glories of Rome’s kings;  
> my Muse calls me to the labours of young Priam,  
> whose offspring brings great deeds into motion, etc.  
>
> I return to Priam, from whose noble line  
> Charles was born, whose deeds I shall also give.  
>
> We divide the offspring of Trojan stock in two:  
> one line received diadems at Rome through Italy;  
> the other fostered the blessed Teutonic kingdoms.  
>
> Charles, conceived in Bertha’s womb by Pippin’s seed,  
> joins these two through both his parents:  
> Roman through his mother and Teutonic through his father, etc.

Then there is a treatment of the younger Priam and Antenor: how, after Troy’s destruction, they came into Germany, and how Teutonic princes and kings were descended from them.

> From Priam springs Priam the younger, while his sister suffers;  
> [Col. 0875C] by lot a grandson is born, to be remembered with his father’s honour,
Of whose offspring the Muse will wish to speak, etc. Here it is related at what time the Sicambri—that is, the Trojans—invaded Germany and were then called Germans. Some of these verses have been printed in Part X of the Chronicle, but all of this is fabulous. There follows in the manuscript: “How the Germans and Romans became friends.”

“While Fortune adorns their leaders with such great courage,” etc. In the following chapter occurs: “How the Germans destroyed the Alans, on account of which they were also called Franks.”

“Meanwhile a terrible people, whose name was the Alans,  
Moves toward destruction, which my Muse sings,” etc.

The one hundred and first chapter concerns the boundaries of true Francia. The following chapters treat events after Caesar’s death: of Childebert, king of the Franks, in the city of Mainz; of Mirobeus, king of the Franks; of Lothair, Chilperic, Clothar, Dagobert, and Hilderic; and of an ancient custom of the Franks, where the following verses are read:

[Col. 0875D]

It is said that among the Franks there was then a custom  
That one man might bear the office of king.  
And that he, as mayor of the household, bore the burden of that duty.

[Col. 0876A]

The name of that office does not know how to move in metre;  
So that it may be made acceptable, my Muse seeks to earn favour.  
Thus it will be possible for me to bring forth a poem.

Thus by fitting reason let the mayor of the household be called  
He who deserves to bear the king’s office and government,  
Who holds and everywhere exercises the king’s honour.

“Duke Pippin,” etc. There follows an account of Pippin the Fat, duke of the Franks and father of Charles Martel:

The duke begot by Alpaida a son not born of a wife,  
Charles Martel, so called in popular speech, etc.

After this there is an account of Pippin the Short, duke of the Franks and son of Martel, and how he acquired the kingdom in the city of Mainz:

While Pippin the Short held the government of the fatherland,  
King Hilderic nonetheless sat empty and contemptible;  
The Short One will bring written submissions to the Apostolic See.

The remainder is found in the printed editions, though in many respects it differs from the reading of our manuscript. Why such great diversity appears among Godfrey’s verses, I can imagine no other reason than that either he himself, as time went on, brought his History, already published, back to the file and made the verses more polished—as indeed the printed ones are—or that someone else, after Godfrey had been taken from the living, undertook this work in his place.

The first, therefore, as I indicated above, to bring the Pantheon, or History of Godfrey, into public light was Basil Johann Herold, at Basel in the year of Christ 1559. Then the same work was brought out at Frankfurt in 1584, and subsequently at Hanover in 1613, by Johann Pistorius, in his Collection of German Writers. But let our good Godfrey not, I pray, persuade himself that I now wish to insert his Chronicle whole into this Collection. What he has before the Nativity of Christ I do not despise; but, both because it is not free from fables and because it can be of almost no use to scholars, I have declined to publish it again. Let those who wish have it from the preceding editions.

All that I wished to retain from that part is what occurs in Part XVI of the Chronicle, since it concerns Italy and reaches more nearly to the fifth century, in accordance with our plan. There remains another work of our Godfrey, distinct from the Chronicle praised above, which has not yet seen the light: a manuscript in the Imperial Library at Vienna, according to Lambecius, *Commentary on the Library of Vienna*, Book II, chapter 8. Its title is: *Mirror of Kings, or On the Genealogy of All Kings and Emperors from the Time of the Flood to Emperor Henry VI*. Omitting matters too remote from Godfrey’s own age, and better sought elsewhere, it would be in the interest of scholarship to rescue this little book from darkness and make it public property. For apart from the fact that no writer of histories is so inept that he sheds no light upon the century in which he wrote and even upon the two or three preceding centuries, Godfrey is certainly commendable for intelligence and learning; and, trained at the court of emperors, he could teach us much that we would vainly expect from elsewhere. But enough on Godfrey of Viterbo.

## EPISTLE AND PREFACE OF GODFREY OF VITERBO TO LORD POPE URBAN III

[Col. 0875]

To the supreme and universal pope Urban III, his most reverend lord and father, Godfrey of Viterbo, an unworthy priest, most humbly submits himself in every service and obedience.

[Col. 0877A]

When I behold the summit of our most holy mother, the Roman Church, and consider the majesty of its eminence, I perceive above all that this is necessary: that, just as she is known to preside over all rulers, so all kings and princes and all the Churches of the world should be adorned by her teaching and rule, and should be instructed by her, as from a fountain of justice, in the rules of all wisdom. For no expression of the Scriptures is known to be authoritative unless it is offered to the thirsty from the streams of her wisdom.

Therefore, if some work of history is composed through anyone’s new undertaking, reason suggests that before it comes into public view it should be presented for apostolic examination; so that, if it is judged worthy of acceptance, it may be approved by that authority’s command and judgment, and may receive strength and authority from him to whom earthly and heavenly things have been divinely entrusted.

Accordingly, most reverend Father, I have resolved to bring before your examination, and have taken care to present to your grace, this small work, assembled over a long time by the studies of my simplicity and reduced in brief compass into one volume from the Old and New Testaments and nearly all histories, for the honour of God and for the correction or approval of the holy Roman Church. Thus, if by God’s authorship it is approved through you, it may subsequently be transmitted to other Churches; and not only clergy but also kings and princes may possess this work under the authority of your holiness.

For it is impossible suitably to attain excellence in perfect government and royal power for those who do not know the course and origin of the world or the doctrines of Scripture.
