An emperor or king set above other princes in power, if ignorant of philosophy, seems more often to go astray than to reign. Since he needs wisdom in matters of state, he is compelled frequently to borrow it from others; and thus he is seen to reign more often by another’s virtue than by his own. All kings ought to know the condition of affairs and the discipline of justice, which brute animals alone do not know. They must also render an account of all these matters to the Creator, because, being exempt from laws, they appear to sin not against the law but rather against God; whence it is said: “Against you alone have I sinned.”

Since, therefore, kings sin not against laws but against God, and are reserved for the examination of God alone and of you, they ought to know the lives, deeds, and histories of ancient kings, so that the causes of earlier events may become for them a safeguard against future ones. Let these princes likewise rejoice, among the other benefits of the holy Roman Church, to receive this little book of histories from the fountain of your holiness. Instructed by its assistance, they will be able to govern the peoples subject to them more reasonably.

I have also marked this work not only in prose but in verse, so that, if its readers should at any time grow weary from reading prose, when they look upon the verses that follow they may be invited to continue reading by the harmony and delight of the metres; while those who perhaps do not understand verse may at least enjoy the reading of the prose.

Our intention in this work is to begin with the very first creation of things—indeed, before all creation, namely with the divine essence, which is before time. Concerning it people often ask: “Where then was God?” “And in what world?” “And what was he doing?” “And how is God three and one?” “And of whom was he Lord when no creature existed?” “And how was the Spirit of the Lord borne over the waters?” and other such matters. Likewise, we treat of angels, heavens, planets and elements, and the creation of man; and thereafter we survey in summary the whole Old and New Testaments and all the histories of peoples, kings, and kingdoms. We shall arrange all these matters in chapters in order.

The author’s name of the book is GOTFRIDUS, which is interpreted “Peace of God.” For in the Teutonic language *Gott* means “God,” and *frid* means “peace.” Therefore this name seems quite suitable to this work, since in this book the Old Testament and the New, Latin histories and barbarian ones, prose and verse, will come together under one volume, as though reconciling one another.

I judge, moreover, that in undertakings of this kind, as commonly happens, some rivals will be tormented by the jaundice of envy. Before they see the book, before they know its great abundance of material, they will become not equitable judges for me, but detractors of the work. Against their snares I have devised such armour for the defence of my volume: in nearly every individual chapter of the book, the individual names of authors are set down in advance as testimony. These will furnish authority to readers and defend me from the savagery of detractors.

Thus, for the Old Testament I have these authors: Moses, Isaiah, Josephus, Daniel and the other prophets, Jesus [son of Sirach], David, Solomon, Esther, Judith, Ezra, and the Maccabees.

For the New Testament we introduce these authors: all the apostles; Pope Clement; Dionysius the Areopagite; Origen; John Chrysostom; Athanasius; Jerome; Augustine; Ambrose; Gregory; and several other doctors of the Church.

For the histories of the gentiles we also have Josephus, Dio, Strabo, Orosius, Hegesippus, Suetonius, Solinus, Julius Africanus, who composed the first Chronicles under Marcus Crassus.

> [Note: [Col. 0877D] Julius Africanus lived under Antoninus Heliogabalus. Others, taking this Antoninus as Marcus Antoninus, contrary to the facts, produced the reading in [Col. 0878D]. For others, such as our text, reading “Marcus,” Marcus Crassus came to mind.]

For the Chaldaeans, too, we have Berosus, who gleaned all the writings of the Chaldaeans.

For the Egyptians we introduce Manetho, historian and chronicler of the Egyptians. We also have, from the Egyptians, Mochus, Hestiaeus, and Jerome the Egyptian, most famous historians.

> [Note: [Col. 0879B] Read “Hestiaeus,” from Josephus.]

The subject matter, therefore, of the whole book is the entire Old and New Testament and all emperors, kings, and kingdoms which have existed or do exist from the beginning of the world to our own times. Of all these we record their origin and end, names, ages, and deeds.

For greater clarity, we have thought it proper in this preface to set down merely the names of the kingdoms:

> [Note: [Col. 0880B] This order is confused.]

The kingdom of the Babylonians; of the Assyrians; Indians; Egyptians; Argives; Lacedaemonians; Thessalians; Sicyonians; Lydians; Amazons; Macedonians; Hebrews; Greeks; all the Italians; Franks; Teutons; Lombards; Huns; Goths; Visigoths; Ostrogoths; English; Britons; Pannonians; Athenians; Medes; Trojans; Romans—kings and consuls; Sicambri; Senonian Gauls; Saxons; Suebi; Sicilians; Cretans; Scythians; Avars, that is, the earlier Hungarians; Vinuli, who are on the borders of Asia and Europe, above the Maeotian Marshes; Vandals; and the kingdom of the Sardinians. Likewise, concerning the prophetic Sibyls.

Similarly, after all the kings, we have also set down the histories of the emperors; likewise the deeds, years, months, days, and names of all Roman pontiffs, from blessed Peter to the venerable Pope Urban III; and up to Lord Emperor Frederick I and his son Lord King Henry VI. Happily. Amen.

# GODFREY OF VITERBO’S *PANTHEON*

[Col. 0879]

## PART SIXTEEN. THE EMPIRE IS TRANSFERRED TO THE GREEKS

### On Emperor Maxentius, son of Maximian

[Col. 0879C]

The praetorian soldiers created as emperor and Augustus at Rome Maxentius, of whom we spoke above, son of Emperor Maximian. His father Maximian, who had already relinquished the dignity of empire, when he heard that Constantine ruled the Gauls, crossed into Gaul intending to entrap Constantine by deceit. Betrayed by his own daughter, Constantine’s wife, and driven away by Constantine, he was killed at Marseilles.

But Emperor Galerius, while cruelly persecuting Christians for ten years, was at last chastised by the Lord: his inward organs dissolved, and he vomited up worms externally. Despaired of by physicians, he therefore recognized that punishments of this kind had been inflicted upon him by God’s judgment in retribution. Hence he ordered the persecution of Christians to cease. He himself soon afterward ended his life amid the same pain.

Meanwhile Emperor Maxentius exercised excessive severity against the citizens at Rome. Among other crimes, he violently seized the wives of senators and other Roman nobles for his lust and publicly abused them. He proscribed the senators themselves, bringing false charges against them. He practised magical arts to such an extent that he ordered pregnant women disembowelled and examined the place of the child in the womb. There, after performing magical incantations, he caused future events to be foretold to him.

Therefore, against this same most wicked tyrant, Constantine—now become a friend of Christians—was secretly summoned by the Roman people, and had himself prepared an army for this purpose. He was anxious and troubled over how to defeat Maxentius without great slaughter of men. While asleep at night, he saw in a vision in the eastern sky the sign of the cross gleaming with fiery brilliance. Astonished at what it was, and seeking its cause, he heard angels speaking to him: “O Constantine, by this you shall conquer!” When morning came, he summoned the Christian soldiers to him; and, learning that this sign was the seal of the Christian faith, he rejoiced greatly at the vision, fortified his forehead with the sign of Christ’s cross, and promised that he would become a Christian if he obtained victory. He prayed that God might grant victory without slaughter of Roman citizens. In this too God heard him wondrously.

For when Maxentius had cunningly placed ships near the Milvian Bridge in the manner of a mousetrap, to deceive an unsuspecting soldier, and Constantine had already appeared in battle, Maxentius utterly despaired of victory. Soon, as though driven by a demonic spirit, he fled before the pressing enemy to the Milvian Bridge, suddenly leapt into the very ship-device he had prepared for his enemies, and there drowned in the Tiber and ended his life. No one besides him from either army is reported to have perished in that battle. When a triumph was being prepared for Constantine at Rome with immense rejoicing, he ordered the victory to be acknowledged not to himself but to the Lord Jesus Christ. He ordered a cross to be set up and adored in the triumphal chariot. Later Constantine was baptized by Sylvester. But what is read concerning his leprosy seems apocryphal, because it is found in no authentic books or chronicles.

Note that the years from the time of Peter the Apostle, Prince of the Apostles, to Pope Sylvester are two hundred and ninety-nine years and twelve days. When Pope Miltiades died, Sylvester succeeded him; Constantine was baptized by him in the Lateran basilica. Again, as we read in many different chronicles, and as the *Tripartite History* also seems to indicate, Constantine is said to have been rebaptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, at the estate called Aquilona. We also read that his three sons later went astray in the same error.

The rest concerning Maxentius is presented in verse. We write several further matters concerning Constantine, which are set below on this page.

When Constantine became a Christian, he restored peace to all the Churches. Licinius Augustus, his colleague, agreed in this action. Thus both emperors jointly made a law that Christ, who had freed the City from the tyranny of Maxentius, should be worshipped by all. The two also wrote on the same matter to Emperor Galerius Maximinus, who then held the East. Galerius had previously issued a perpetual edict on bronze tablets that Christians everywhere should be punished. But when he received the edict of the two emperors, he agreed, and by an imperial writing commanded that no one anywhere should henceforth be punished for the Christian faith. He also gave this reason: the more Christians are punished, the more they increase. He further commanded that no one should be compelled to worship the gods except of his own free will.

Soon afterwards Galerius Maximinus declared war on Licinius Augustus, breaking the treaty. On this account, after many cities and provinces had been devastated, they finally came to battle. When Galerius saw his army routed, he fled shamefully. Returning home, he killed all his priests as deceivers. Afterwards, when he perceived that the Lord was afflicting him with very severe diseases and saw death approaching, moved by belated repentance he confessed the God of the Christians, and wrote concerning him as follows:

> “Emperor Caesar Galerius Maximus, Germanicus, Sarmaticus, pious, fortunate, unconquered, Augustus. Unceasingly taking thought for our provincials, and providing for their welfare, we never cease to make provision for those matters that pertain to the common and public good. Therefore I do not doubt that it is known to all that, by decree of our August emperors Diocletian and Maximian, our fathers, many seizures and plunderings were carried out by officials of the empire.
>
> “Therefore, so that in future all fear and uncertainty may be removed from Christians, we enact by the law of this our edict that it be known to all persons that all who reverence the Christian sect as a religion may, through the generosity of our indulgence, each according to his wish and pleasure, serve the Christian religion and its observance. We also permit them to have houses of prayer—that is, churches—according to their will.
>
> “We likewise enact by this law that, if any houses, lands, or any properties from the goods of Christians have been attached to the imperial treasury by commands of earlier emperors, or have been purchased by anyone, sold off, or given as a gift, we command all these to be restored to the former right of the Christians and all of them returned to their proper owners.”

[Col. 0882D]

Consider, reader: this was the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. After this Galerius, owing to varied and prolonged diseases, was deprived of the light of his eyes and met the end of his life.

Licinius, emperor and colleague of Constantine, who had initially shown himself kind to Christians, excluded all Christians from the palace and threatened persecution against everyone. Constantine rose against him, defeated him in various battles—first in Pannonia, then repeatedly by land and sea—compelled him, once defeated, to surrender, and finally killed him.

### Here the empire is transferred from Rome to Byzantium

Thus, when Constantine held sole monarchy without a colleague, the Church, long afflicted, took breath again, having received complete peace in all things. Then Constantine issued the most general edict that the Christian religion should be maintained throughout the whole world.

Then the emperor granted royal insignia to Sylvester, Roman pontiff; and he himself, in order to give the Churches greater peace, removed himself from the turmoil of the court and transferred himself with all his splendour to Byzantium in Greek territory. From this donation it appears that Rome, together with Italy and Gaul, was bestowed upon the Roman Church by Constantine.

The supporters of the Empire, however, maintain that Constantine did not grant the kingdom in this way, but chose the Roman pontiffs as fathers, as priests of the supreme God, out of divine reverence, so that they should receive blessing from them and be aided by their prayers before God. They add in confirmation that Constantine, when he divided the world among his sons, gave the East to one, the West to another, and Ptolemais with Babylonia to the third. An honourable prince would not have done this if he had bestowed the western kingdoms, including Italy, upon the Church. They affirm also that Rome with the western kingdoms fell to the lot of Theodosius and many other religious emperors, and that they possessed them.

In addition, imperial disputants cite the Gospels: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21). Likewise: the Lord himself paid tribute for himself and Peter (Matt. 17:23–26). Paul also says: “To whom honour, honour” (Rom. 13:7), because “all authority is from God” (ibid.). In saying this, Paul had in mind not Peter, but the most impious Nero, who held the empire of the whole world. They further cite Augustine as saying: “By what right do you possess an estate? By divine right or by human? By divine right, because ‘the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.’ By human right? Then it is through kings. If you say, ‘What have I to do with the king?’ he answers, ‘What have you to do with property?’”

The defenders of the Church answer thus: Christ wished his Church to be honoured with worldly possessions, called royal estates. It is not to be believed that God permitted his Church, which he redeemed with his own blood and to which he sent from heaven the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, to be deceived by some spirit of error, so that it might possess what it ought not to possess. For many men of proven life have hitherto held royal estates, and are believed to have acquired with them the kingdom of God.

In very many other ways it could be proved that Constantine both justly bestowed royal estates upon the Church and that the Church lawfully received them. For if one asks from where kings have these things, the answer is: by God’s ordinance and the people’s election. If God did no injustice in granting them to kings, how much more justly did God act in ordaining that they should be transferred from kings, to whom he himself had given them, to an ecclesiastical person. As God disposes the people’s will into a single agreement for appointing a king, so he also stirred the prince’s will to bestow royal estates upon the Church. “The heart of the king is in the hand of God.” And “all authority is from God.” Therefore the Church’s authority on earth is also from God. Thus God justly ordained that the king should have royal estates; the prince justly gave them to the Church; and the Church lawfully and worthily received them.

But, to speak my own mind, I confess that I do not know whether the glory and exaltation of the Church as it is in this time, or the humility that it had at first, is more pleasing to God. To many, indeed, that earlier condition seems holier, this one more fortunate. Yet I assent to our mother, the Roman Church, founded upon the rock—that is, Christ. I believe what she believes; I think what she thinks; I judge that what she possesses should be possessed. For it must be believed that the Church can be deceived by no error because “the gates of hell shall not prevail against her.” And it must be believed that her faith endures forever because Christ said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32). We leave the remaining questions on these matters to be resolved by our elders. Yet we shall still say a few things concerning Constantine in verse.

### Likewise concerning the same Emperor Constantine, the thirty-fourth from Augustus

King Constantine, if we would write what is true,  
Was in his first period a true worshipper of Christ;  
The East and the western region know this as well.

For twice ten years the king sat with the diadem;  
Eusebius then held the papacy for two years,  
And moreover one month and three times five days.

Under Constantine Pope Sylvester is recorded;  
He bore the pontificate for four times six years, less one year,  
And held ten months and as many days.

Sylvester baptized him, and we acknowledge the same;  
Arius later corrupted him, and for this we grieve:  
For he defiled him by his schism.

This happened at the estate rightly called Aquilona,  
When he, rebaptizing him, had polluted the crown;  
The writings of the *Tripartite History* testify thus.

By the hands of Bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia  
The king underwent a shameful washing and embraced shameful doctrines;  
His three little sons likewise held the same views.

King Constantine led the Latin nobles away by deceit,  
Forced them to become Greeks after leaving Italy,  
And established a new Rome in wealth and fortress.

He transferred the Empire to the Greeks and bestowed favour,  
Giving foreigners the honour Rome had held,  
Abandoning Italy and cultivating the Greek kingdoms.

When the regions of the hinge of Empire had been counted,  
He granted three royal zones to his three sons,  
And ordered the three to share these three gifts.

He gave the West to the first, Greece to the second;  
The third holds Babylonia and Ptolemais by full right:  
Thus he ordered all that existed in the world.

In those same times the holy cross, having been found, was raised;  
Saint Helena was she through whose efforts it is venerated,  
So that the blessed cross may be “name, side, head” (*nomen, latus, caput*; the syntax is uncertain).

> [Note: [Col. 0883D] Perhaps, by hyperbaton: “let the side be as the name,” etc.]

Pope Mark also held office with Constantine;  
To him the Roman people rendered obedience for two years,  
[Col. 0885A] Add eight months and ten days.

Counting the days between Sylvester and Peter,  
I calculate approximately three hundred years, less one,  
If in the reckoning I add ten days and two.

### On Constantine’s three sons—Constantius, Constantine, and Constans—the thirty-fifth from Augustus

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 341, Constantine, son of Constantine, received the Empire together with his two brothers, Constantius and Constans, the thirty-fifth from Augustus. Deceived by a certain presbyter, a disciple of Arius, he fell into the Arian heresy. At the same time Arius had been expelled from the city of Alexandria by Bishop Alexander because of his error.

Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, infected with Arian poison, persuaded the younger Emperor Constantine to convene a council and grant Arius a hearing there. Thus both Arius and Alexander were summoned to a council in the imperial palace at Constantinople. There Alexander, persisting the whole night in prayer, commended the Church’s cause to the Lord. In the morning Eusebius summoned Arius to the church. While Arius was going there, he turned aside to relieve a bodily need. By God’s just judgment, his entrails, in which he bore his foul error, were disembowelled into a most foul place and discharged through the lower passage of his body; and he died.

Arius’s supporters fled in shame and confusion. Yet, concealing the event from the emperor, they rose through the emperor’s eunuchs against the teachers of the Catholic faith.

After a few days Alexander died, and Athanasius was appointed in his place. Of ardent intellect and most vigilant in ecclesiastical affairs, he was not only subtle against heretics but also a most courageous champion for the Church against the emperor. Whoever desires to know his virtues, labours, and fruits should read the *Tripartite History*.

When Constantine made war against his brother Constans, he was killed by Constans’s commanders near the river Alsa, not far from Aquileia. Constantius, after Constantine’s death, held the East alone; Constans held the West. Thus the Arian heretics, fearing that Athanasius, if he obtained an opportunity to approach the ruler, might imbue the emperor himself with Catholic faith and religion, went first to the emperor and deceived him. They falsely alleged that Athanasius was a wicked and criminal man, showing him the hand and arm of a certain Arsenius, which they said Athanasius, at the demons’ prompting, had cut from Arsenius’s body in order to practise necromancy.

In response, by Caesar’s command, a synod was assembled at Tyre. When Athanasius was brought to trial there, the aforesaid Arsenius stood present, having both hands. Once this was discovered, the heretics’ lies were exposed and they were wonderfully put to shame. Nevertheless, Emperor Constantius and the heretics did not cease persecuting Athanasius; indeed, they compelled him to cross into the dominion of his brother Constans. Received quite humanely and treated honourably by Emperor Constans, he was later powerfully restored to his own see. He then remained in the Church of Trier with Maximus, bishop of that Church. In that place he is said to have written the Catholic confession, namely, *Quicunque vult* (“Whoever wishes”).

At that time Liberius was driven into exile by Emperor Constantius, and Felix, his deacon, was substituted for him by the heretics. Between Liberius and Sylvester sat Pope Julius. In the same times Victorinus the rhetorician and Donatus the grammarian were famous at Rome. Then there flourished in the Church of God the glorious bishops Paulinus of Trier, who succeeded Maximinus; Dionysius of Milan; Eusebius of Vercelli; and Hilary of Poitiers. All of them were then sent into exile for the testimony of the Catholic faith. Hilary, among them, adorned the Gallican Church with various monuments of his writings.

Emperor Constans fought nine battles, with varying outcomes, against Sapor, king of the Persians. At last, however, when he engaged rashly, he fled; afterwards, at the town of Elenau near Spain, he was killed through the treachery of a commander named Magnentius. The same Magnentius seized the empire at Autun. In Illyricum, meanwhile, the soldiers made an old man named Vetranio emperor. Constantius, meanwhile, intended to avenge his brother; thus he first compelled old Vetranio to lay aside the purple. Afterwards he also fought fiercely against him. Magnentius, defeated at Lyons, killed himself; and his brother Decentius, whom he had made Caesar in Gaul, hanged himself with a noose.

We set down the remaining matters concerning the three sons of Constantine the Great and a few matters concerning Arius in verse.

### Likewise, the sons of Constantine are related in verse

With Constantine, his brother Constans holds everything,  
And persecutes Catholics with every cruelty;  
Eusebius the Arian is pleasing to the kings.

While Arius disputes craftily against Catholics,  
Seeking the secrets of nature, he turns aside from the citadel;  
While he makes an evil crackling sound, his compressed entrails burst.

Bishops Athanasius and Hilary, without ruin,  
Restore in Catholic order the first doctrines;  
By them the order of clergy will be made Catholic.

[Col. 0886D]

Constans sits with his brother for twice twelve years;  
Then Pope Mark sat, a great salvation to the clergy,  
Who gave rule and doctrine also to the Churches.

He completed eight months and two years;  
The venerable bishop is said to have lived twice ten days  
And to have given remarkable things to his people.

Blessed Pope Julius sits while Constans sits;  
He holds the pontificate at Rome for eleven years,  
Three times three months and ten days.

Constans was always an Arian with his brother.  
For these reasons he sent Pope Julius into exile.  
Constans perishes by death; the pope is released.

Now too Donatus is supreme in the art of grammar.  
With Jerome as his pupil, he teaches the publication of the *Parts*;  
It is fitting that we too should be his pupils.

### On Julian the Apostate, the thirty-sixth emperor from Augustus

[Col. 0887A]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 364, Julian succeeded Constantius in the Empire, the thirty-sixth from Augustus. While still alive, Constantius had made him Caesar. Julian had first been ordained by emperors as a cleric and reader, but later, seduced by soldiers, he took up the military belt.

When Julian, created Caesar by Constantius, had magnificently triumphed over the Germans and Alemanni, he was elated by his successful achievements. Entering a certain temple, a crown hanging there happened to fall upon his head. On seeing this, the soldiers proclaimed from this sign that empire had been foretold for him by the gods. Raised up by this omen and his previous prosperity, Julian usurped the imperial title and utterly despised Christ’s faith.

Meanwhile Constantius prepared an army against the Persians; but learning of Julian’s treachery, he turned back toward Rome for civil war. He did not arrive, however, because on the journey itself he ended his days, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign. Julian, therefore, having been made Augustus, at first, as though criticizing his predecessors’ actions, ordered bishops recalled from exile; then he sought to weaken the Churches by cunning rather than violence. Under pretext of religion, he said that clergy ought to be excluded from public entertainments, military service, and finally from every earthly possession, as persons to whom the Gospel law says: “Unless one renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

He ordered pagan temples to be opened. He ordered the imperial establishments—cooks, eunuchs, barbers, and the public transport of horses and mules—to be cut down, as a philosopher. He devoted himself to reading by night, staying awake, and writing; by day, to reciting his writings in the senate. Thus, wholly embracing philosophy, he alone after Julius [Caesar] was called an emperor-philosopher. In his writings he fiercely attacked emperors and Christians alike.

In these days the Church of God had religious and most distinguished bishops: Meletius of Antioch, Maris of Chalcedon, Basil of Caesarea, and Gregory of Nazianzus. Among them, the aforesaid Maris, bishop of Chalcedon, while Julian was sacrificing to Fortune, resisted him to his face. Julian, using philosophical restraint, gently rebuked the bishop in these words: “Not even your Galilaean could cure you of blindness.” Bishop Maris answered him thus: “For my blindness I give thanks to my God, because it happened to me for this reason: that I might not see you, an impious apostate.”

### Likewise concerning Julian
Julian, following Pythagoras, said that the spirit of Alexander the Great had come to rest in him. He too, after the manner of Alexander, had made ready to subject the whole world to himself. With this intent, while he was proceeding with an army to conquer Persia, and on his way was threatening Basil, bishop of Caesarea, and his Church that, after completing the Persian war, he would put them to death upon his return, he himself, while engaged in battle, was pierced by a dart sent from heaven. When he saw the missile coming down upon him from above, he did not repent in his heart, but stubbornly reproached Christ, saying: “You have conquered, Galilean; you have conquered!” For he was accustomed always to call Christ either “the Galilean” or “the Nazarene.”

It is read, moreover, in the Life of Saint Basil that God sent Saint Mercurius, whose arms at that time hung in the church at Caesarea in remembrance of him, into battle to kill Julian. For on that very day the arms, when sought in the church, were not there; but on the following day they were found in the church in their customary place, spattered with human blood and as though newly returned from battle. We have set all this forth below in verse, so that the reader might take greater delight in it. Yet because Porphyry, Callistus, and other supporters of Julian himself proclaim and commend his wisdom, piety, and philosophy, while passing over his wickednesses in silence, we, who pursue truth without flattery or hatred, recount in what follows Julian’s shameful deeds and accursed acts.

After Julian’s death, Socrates in the *Tripartite History* recounts images devised and discovered by magical art, saying this:

When Julian had died and a pious emperor had succeeded the impious one, the rulers entered a temple and saw a woman hanging by her hair, with her hands stretched out. Julian had opened her womb in order to inspect her liver and discover whether he could gain victory over the Persians. This abomination was found in a place called Carrhae. At Antioch, moreover, they say that many chests were found in the palace, full of human heads, and that in wells there were the submerged bodies of many men. Hence the aforesaid writer declares that at Antioch both Christians and pagans exulted with wondrous rejoicing in the theatres and streets at the death of the most criminal Julian.

Jovian, however, honourably buried Julian’s body at Tarsus in Cilicia. As is read in the Life of Saint Fabian, Sapor, king of Persia, ordered that body to be flayed and that from its skin, dyed scarlet, a chair should be made for him as an insult to the Romans. The remaining matters concerning Julian will be indicated in verse.

Likewise, the same Emperor Julian is described in verse.

[Col. 0888D]

An apostate cleric received imperial power at Rome,  
whose name in the order of baptism was Julian.  
In his perversity he everywhere fostered his country’s crime.

He now commands that the Temple at Jerusalem be rebuilt;  
he ordered the peoples of the Hebrews to be summoned from every quarter.  
By Moses’ Law he causes incense to be offered with blood.

Thus, from hatred of Christ, he orders the Temple to be erected in due form;  
and while the masters prepare the Temple on its ancient site,  
at once the wrath of God meets the Jews.

The temples shake, the pavements collapse, and the timbers beneath them  
perish, burned by fires and ashes from heaven;  
the stones leap forth, and the open court alone remains.

Immediately a fiery globe is sent among them,  
burning men, garments, heads, and hair;  
the men standing there are justly consumed.

Lest these evils be thought to have arisen by chance,  
they are seen to bear impressed upon themselves the signs of the cross;  
the Jews bear upon their bodies the signs of God.

The apostate Julian is killed by a divine dart.

The king goes forth against the Persians; when he prepares to fight there,  
he falls, pierced by the sword of Saint Mercurius,  
as I relate the events to you also in these verses.

Thus overtaken by death, he was unable to accomplish those things which he had already decreed against the country of holy Basil, and even against Basil himself.

He knew that a field-battle was being prepared for him;  
as he hastened to it, he is repeatedly said to have threatened  
destruction to the country and to Basil.

“I shall go,” he said, “and return; I shall strive to come back,

[Col. 0889B]

then I shall order Basil the bishop to perish,  
and likewise the people, on the day of my return.”

The terrified bishop summons the people and prays.  
The holy Mother of God asks how she may defend the country for herself,  
and hears the words of God sounding in heaven.

For Christ said: “Destroy King Julian,”  
for he strives utterly to destroy the holy Law  
and commands the peoples to deny the holy doctrines.

“Send Mercurius to fight him in single combat;  
for he had threatened, if he could prevail in war,  
then to destroy the people and Basil, who is mine.”

In the church there used to remain a sword and shield  
with which, while alive, Mercurius had nobly waged his wars.  
Now neither shield nor his sword was there.

[Col. 0889C]

Because these things were absent, the bishop could know  
that, through avenging Mercurius, the king would be wounded in body,  
as he had heard from the thundering voice of Jesus.

Meanwhile a certain man came from the battle.  
He said: “A soldier has come from the height of heaven—  
Mercurius—and has dealt the king deathly wounds.”

While the people seek the weapons of war through the church,  
they could be seen spattered with royal blood,  
though no one had seen them there among the clergy yesterday.

Thus through Mercurius God destroys Julian,  
raging like a wild beast against the saints of the Lord,  
as the earlier deeds likewise sing in writings.

Emperor Julian scatters his own blood against heaven, granting Christ the palm of victory.

A mighty stream flowed from the wound in his side,

[Col. 0889D]

which the emperor scattered far into the air with his hands;  
and, more astonished as he died, he said:

“O great Nazarene, you have conquered one lesser than yourself.  
Behold, I give back to you, as victor, my own blood.”

Thus the wretch perished, cherishing the realms of Tartarus.

Likewise concerning Julian: how the king of Persia had him flayed, as is read in the Life of Saint Fabian.

The slain body of Julian, king of the Romans,  
the king of Persia orders flayed as oxen are flayed;  
and, when the body was brought before him, he said:

“This skin shall now always be an honour to us.  
Let it be so that Rome, subdued in everlasting shame,  
may herself serve me under the law of slavery.

Let the appearance of the skin be close to scarlet in colour;  
then let a chair be made from it, fitting and comely,

[Col. 0890A]

from which Rome, grieving, may be able to die of grief.”

After two years Julian’s life departed;  
Damasus the Spaniard then sat as pope at Rome,  
and completed fourteen years for himself.

Add to these two months and ten days,  
during which he detested the Manichaean heretics;  
after him Pope Siricius also repressed them.

That same pope also sat for fifteen years,  
for eleven months he struck at Manichaean writings,  
and he himself drove their adherents from his churches.

Concerning Emperor Jovian, the thirty-seventh from Augustus.

In the year 366 from the Incarnation of the Lord, after Julian’s death and when the army had been placed in the utmost danger, Jovian, a Pannonian by nation, a most Christian man, was sought by the prayers of all for the imperial office. When he said that he was a Christian and that for this reason he could not rule over the nations, they affirmed that for love of him they too were Christians.

Jovian, therefore, was created the thirty-seventh emperor from Augustus. On account of the dangers facing the Roman army, he concluded a treaty with Sapor, king of Persia, inglorious indeed for the Romans but very beneficial for the immediate circumstances. After surrendering a certain town together with the upper part of Mesopotamia, the soldiers returned cautiously. Then the Catholic ruler recalled bishops whom Constantius had sent into exile, ordered pagan temples to be closed, and drove out their priests.

After this he requested in writing that Bishop Athanasius should instruct him in the Catholic faith. Under the seal and with the consent of all the bishops of Egypt, Athanasius wrote and sent him the faith of the Council of Nicaea: that is, “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, Creator,” and so forth. The emperor gratefully received this letter and strengthened the Catholic faith by imperial edicts. He further commanded that all who abducted or violated consecrated virgins, or who looked at them immodestly, should be punished capitally. Later Athanasius saw him at Antioch and instructed him more fully concerning the Catholic faith.

The emperor, in a house recently plastered with lime, where coals had been placed, was suffocated at night, in the thirty-third year of his age and the eighth month of his reign.

It is fitting to relate the remaining deeds in verse.

Concerning the same Emperor Jovian, the following is added in verse.

[Col. 0890D]

Jovian now becomes the glory of the Romulean throne;  
in mind he worshipped God, nor does he rule from an empty height [perhaps *inani*],  
as our pipe sings also in these verses.

When the people ask him to take up the Roman sceptre,  
he says: “I am a worshipper of Christ, wholly unfit for you;  
I believe Christ to be God; you reject him.”

The assembly says: “For your sake we desire to believe in Christ,  
whom we are ashamed to have rejected for a sinister king;  
we despise idols; under your leadership we stand ready.

Empire befits you, for we prepare the diadem for you;  
we too are now marked as worshippers of Christ under you as king.  
Receive us, as we ask you; we give ourselves to you and you to us.”

His life was beneficial for twelve years,

[Col. 0891A]

fitting for worshippers of Christ and greatly harmful to tyrants;  
then too was the time of Bishop Siricius.

Siricius is recorded to have sat three times five years;  
eleven months more are counted,  
and beyond this he gave eight days of life three times over.

Concerning Caesar Phocas, the thirty-eighth from Augustus.

Phocas happily rules for three decades,  
and with him there were three venerable popes at Rome;  
the first, pious Anastasius, presided.

He lived for two years under Caesar Phocas;  
after him Innocent went to Peter’s chair,  
and he too was bishop for three times five years,

and two months and twenty-five days.  
The third bishop under Caesar Phocas was Zosimus;  
he is assigned twenty months and as many days.

Concerning Emperor Valentinian, the thirty-ninth from Augustus.

[Col. 0891B]

In the year 367 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Valentinian, with his brother Valens, a Pannonian by nation, of modest origin but distinguished by greatness of mind and body and polished in manners, assumed the empire at Nicaea by the consent of the soldiers, the thirty-ninth from Augustus. When the Emperor Julian entered the temple to sacrifice to Fortune, Valentinian struck the sacrificial minister with his fist. Therefore Julian, to whom such conduct was displeasing, removed him from military rank. But God, the just Judge, who said, “You shall receive a hundredfold,” repaid him with empire in return for military service.

Valentinian chose his brother Valens to share the empire. In the fourth year of his reign he made his son Gratian emperor.

At the same time, among the Atrebates, true wool mixed with rain was seen to descend from the clouds. After the death of Auxentius of Milan, Valentinian convened a synod of bishops and urged that another be ordained. There Ambrose, present and still a catechumen, was requested by all. Accordingly the emperor ordered that, after first receiving the grace of baptism, he should be ordained priest. Meanwhile the Emperor Valens, though at first Catholic, through the persuasion of Eudoxius, bishop of Constantinople, and led astray by his own wife, fell into the Arian heresy. He bound himself to it by oath and was baptized again by the aforesaid Arian bishop.

[Col. 0891D]

At that time Valentinian checked by war the very powerful nation of the Saxons, which was invading the borders of the Franks. In the eleventh year of his reign he died at the town of Bricto. The remaining matters concerning Valentinian are contained in verse.

Likewise, Valentinian is related in verses.

Behold, Valens rules with his brother Valentinian;  
the Goths become allies under a vain doctrine;  
each emperor was an Arianist among his own people.

The evil law of the Goths augmented their laws;  
they inhabit Istrian fields, stain the splendid diadem,  
despoil their native land, and plunder the marketplace.

We write that Valentinian lived eleven years,  
and we note his brother’s years as about five;  
we call both heretics and evil men.

[Col. 0892A]

Now Celestine presides for three times three years;  
a month is added, with twice five days to be counted,  
from which one day is deducted in the reckoning.

Likewise in these times Pope Sixtus II stands;  
for three decades the world flourishes under his doctrine,  
and the bishop sits ten years and eight days more.

Concerning Emperor Valens, the fortieth from Augustus.

In the year 373 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Valens, the fortieth from Augustus, ruled the empire of the East. Gratian and his younger brother Valentinian reigned in the West. Valens, therefore, as we have said, being an Arian, enacted a law that monks should be compelled into military service. Consequently many monks throughout Egypt, despising the authority of an earthly king, were crowned with martyrdom.

[Col. 0892B]

Valens inquired by necromantic art who would reign after him. By demonic art these four letters were shown to him: **th. e. d. a.** From that day he commanded the killing of all whom he could find with these letters at the beginning of their names. Thus it came about that Count Theodosius, father of Theodosius who later held the empire, was ordered by him to be killed. Having first received the grace of baptism at Carthage, he willingly offered his neck to the executioner. Meanwhile the Catholic Emperor Gratian, at the Gallic town of Argentaria, defeated thirty thousand Alemanni in battle, with little loss to the Romans.

At that time a dispute arose in the kingdom of the Goths between Fridigern and Athalaric. Fridigern, being weaker, obtained assistance from the Emperor Valens and put Athalaric to flight. Hence Fridigern, out of affection for the Emperor Valens, embraced the Arian faith with his people.

Gothic letters were invented at this time.

At that time Gulfias [Ulphilas], bishop of the Goths, invented Gothic letters and by means of them translated the divine Scriptures into his own language. Not long afterward, when the time of the Goths had passed, the terrible nation of the Huns arrived—a people, according to the writings of Jordanes, their interpreter and historian, begotten from incubi and prostitutes below the Maeotian Marshes, which lie on the boundary of Asia and Europe. Guided by a hind crossing over, this people passed through those marshes which had previously been inaccessible.

[Col. 0892D]

There they so terrified the Gothic people that Hermanaric, king of the Goths, who had already conquered many nations, killed himself from fear of the Huns, in the 110th year of his age. After the death of their king Hermanaric, the Goths, broken in spirit, sought settlements from the Emperor Valens, and he granted them land in Thrace. There, invited treacherously to a banquet by a certain commander, they perceived the plot before they came. They killed all who had invited them and, having destroyed the whole region with fire and sword, spread everywhere.

Valens, preparing an expedition against them and setting out from Antioch, was moved to repentance and ordered the Catholic bishops recalled from exile. A battle was joined in Thrace between Goths and Romans.

[Col. 0893A]

When the Roman army fled, Emperor Valens, wounded by an arrow, fled into the hut of a very small village in order to preserve his life by hiding. The pursuing Goths burned him up together with the hut, in the fifteenth year of his reign and the fourth year after the death of his brother. When Valens had died, Gratian, who had reigned with him, held the empire with his younger brother Valentinian.

Concerning Emperor Gratian, the forty-first from Augustus.

The Roman Caesar Gratian holds the diadem;  
then Ambrose was renowned under Christ’s doctrine,  
and Martin of Tours was a great salvation.

Whoever desires to be sanctified by Ambrose’s teachings,  
whoever wishes Martin’s miracles to be numbered for him—  
I am not sufficient for that; let him see to it more fully.

Caesar Gratian lived twice three years;  
then we note that Pope Pontianus lived;  
it is evident that he stood five years and a month.

Concerning Emperor Theodosius, the forty-second from Augustus.

In the year 383 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Gratian—who was the forty-second from Augustus—wishing to assist the commonwealth in his own time, clothed Theodosius, a Spaniard by nation, a brave and religious man, in the purple and created him emperor of the East. Theodosius defeated the Gothic nation by both courage and prudence, and summoned Athalaric, king of the Goths, to himself at Constantinople. There Athalaric died. But the Gothic people, seeing the prince’s gentleness, voluntarily subjected themselves to the Roman empire. Theodosius chose his son Arcadius as his partner in the empire.

Gratian was killed when Maximus usurped the empire in Britain; and his brother Valentinian was driven from Italy. Coming to Theodosius, he was kindly received.

In the year 388 from the Incarnation of the Lord, after Gratian’s murder, Theodosius, the forty-first from Augustus, held the Roman empire alone.

At that time there were in the Church of God most holy men: Martin, bishop of Tours; Ambrose of Milan; Severinus, bishop of Cologne; Jerome the presbyter; and Augustine, a catechumen, then baptized by blessed Ambrose.

Theodosius, moving his army against the aforesaid tyrant Maximus, killed him in the region of Aquileia. Then, with his small son Honorius, he came to Rome and there arranged the commonwealth; he left the kingdom of the West to Valentinian. He himself returned to Constantinople.

Moreover, as Valentinian was returning into Gaul, he was hanged by a noose through the treachery of a certain Arbogast and Eugenius, as some assert. Eugenius was there made emperor by Arbogast. Some say that Valentinian, because of excessive grief, inflicted this kind of death upon himself. When Valentinian’s death became known, Theodosius prepared an army against the tyrant Eugenius.

[Col. 0894A]

He also wrote at that time into Egypt to John the monk and to Eutropius the eunuch, asking the event of the matter from the man himself, who was most holy. The most blessed man promised him complete victory. Theodosius, trusting in God, advanced and sent the Goths ahead of him against the tyrants. Ten thousand of them were killed by Arbogast. The emperor advanced, and when he met the enemy in the Alps, where Arbogast had taken up a higher position so that he seemed to possess a better opportunity for fighting, Theodosius lay prostrate in prayer throughout the night. In the morning, trusting in the Lord, he engaged and triumphed gloriously. There Eugenius was captured and killed. Arbogast killed himself. Theodosius, having arranged all matters well, ended his life at Milan in the eleventh year after Valentinian’s death and rested in the Lord. We explain the remaining matters concerning Theodosius in verse.

Likewise, the same Emperor Theodosius is related in verse.

Theodosius shines with the diadem after Gratian;  
he restores the Council of Constantinople;  
mad Arius is rejected in word and deed.

Shrines and temples now wholly fall, and idols cease;  
Arian writing perishes, suppressed by fire and force;  
the emperor’s court establishes Catholic doctrines.

Theodosius lived about twice twelve years;  
then Pope Lucius sat two years more,  
living three years and eight months for himself;  
besides this, add ten days in the reckoning.

[Col. 0894C]

At Constantinople John’s head is said to be present,  
and the writings of Jerome, which he produced through many years,  
the house at Bethlehem sent forth over all the earth.

Likewise concerning the Emperors Theodosius and Arcadius.

Arcadius shines in the diadem with Theodosius;  
the authority of the Catholic Church now rises again;  
the good order of the clergy will now be the head of the world.

Arcadius is said to have sat for four times eight years;  
Pope Cornelius is reported to have had three years;  
besides, add ten days in the reckoning.

Then the fame of John the anchorite shone forth,  
because he was said to restore life to the dead;  
his remains are laid at Constantinople.

Concerning the brothers Arcadius and Honorius, emperors reigning together, about the forty-third from Augustus.

[Col. 0894D]

In the year 390 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Honorius received the empire of the West and his brother Arcadius that of the East, after the death of their father Theodosius, in the forty-third place from Augustus. Damasus was still pope at Rome; Theophilus presided at Alexandria, John at Jerusalem, Flavian at Antioch, and Nectarius at Constantinople.

In those days a monk named Dirimachus came from the East to Rome. When he wished to put an end to the spectacle of gladiators as a madness, he was overwhelmed with stones and killed by those standing around. When this became known, Emperor Honorius judged him worthy to be counted among the blessed martyrs; and for the same reason

[Col. 0895A]

he forbade the gladiatorial spectacle, so that it should no longer persist in this way.

Concerning John Chrysostom.

At that time John Chrysostom—whose name means “golden mouth”—was ordained bishop at Constantinople. In the times of Honorius and Arcadius, the most holy men Martin and Ambrose departed from this world.

Since the Goths could not receive from the emperors the payments which they had been accustomed to receive in the time of Theodosius, they withdrew from the court on the advice of the patrician Rufinus and made a king for themselves. Rufinus was later exposed because of the treachery he had committed and beheaded before the gates of Constantinople; his head, together with his right hand and arm, was carried through every street of the city as an insult and a spectacle.

Arcadius, a mild and peaceful man, ended his life in the fourteenth year after the death of his father Theodosius. He left the Eastern empire to his eight-year-old son Theodosius, then governed as a boy by the prefect Anthemius. Anthemius himself had encircled the imperial city with a very strong wall. The verses contain the remaining matters concerning Honorius and Arcadius.

Likewise, Arcadius and Honorius are related in verse.

Caesar Honorius rules all things, and Arcadius too;  
then Bishop Donatus, the blessed likeness of the Fathers,  
is read to have performed great signs in Epirus.

For he is said to have overcome a dragon by his spittle:  
he spat in the serpent’s face, and in that instant

[Col. 0895C]

it had neither venom nor life left in it.

This serpent is said to have had such weight in its flesh  
that the yokes of eight oxen could not have drawn it.  
Then was the time of Augustine’s teaching.

Now the Huns come, the Goths and Alans also come;  
woe was to the Spaniards; oppressed Gaul falls.

Honorius then lived for fifteen years;  
Pope Simplicius likewise lived for as many years;  
add also seven days more in the reckoning.

Honorius, after the death of Arcadius, rules alone, the forty-fourth from Augustus.

In the year 412 from the Incarnation of the Lord, after Arcadius’s death, Honorius, the forty-fourth from Augustus, held the empire of the West. The Goths, under their king Alaric, while Honorius was at Ravenna, travelled through Dalmatia and Venetia and encamped on the border of Aemilia. They arrogantly demanded land from the emperors to inhabit. They added that, if they could not obtain it freely, they would take it for themselves. Having taken counsel, the emperor gave them land near the borders of Spain, which at that time was in rebellion against the empire. As the Goths proceeded to take possession of it, Stilicho the patrician, Honorius’s associate, treacherously pursued them and, engaging them in battle, lost his soldiers and fled himself.

For this reason the Goths, stirred to anger, suddenly returned to Aemilia, whence they had come. Having ravaged the entire province with fire and sword, they advanced upon the city of Rome. They broke into it while it trembled;

[Col. 0896A]

and, after issuing commands that churches should not be violated, they burned some parts of the City and carried off marvellous plunder. Meanwhile Pope Innocent, lest he should see the punishments of that City, stayed at Ravenna, removed as righteous Lot had been from Sodom.

In those days pagans reproached Christians, saying that Rome had flourished in pagan times but declined in the time of Christians, and that unprecedented dangers threatened it because of Christianity. For this reason blessed Augustine then composed the book *The City of God*. Orosius then composed his histories. Jerome translated the ecclesiastical history composed by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea.

This most terrible sack of the City was carried out by Alaric, king of the Goths, in the 1,164th year from the founding of the City, and in the year 415 from the Incarnation of the Lord. In this same plundering by the Vandals, Placidia, sister of Honorius, was captured; Ataulf later took her in marriage.

Meanwhile a certain leader, Constantine, invaded the empire of Gaul and made his son Constans, a monk, Caesar. But shortly afterward the father at Arles and the son at Vienne were deprived of both kingdom and life.

The Goths, made proud by their victory over the Romans, proposed to proceed through Campania, Apulia, and Sicily into Africa. But when, on the border of the Bruttii, they rashly committed themselves to the sea, they lost many of their companions. Their king Alaric then met his final day. The Goths mourned him so greatly that they diverted the river called Barentus from its bed near the city of Cosenza. After burying King Alaric himself there with many forces of soldiers,

[Col. 0896C]

they killed all captives who knew of this deed and then restored the river to its bed.

Because of the death of Athalaric, the Goths proposed to return. Creating Ataulf as their king, they returned to Rome and plundered what they had left there. But Ataulf, king of the Goths, because of love for his wife Placidia, who was sister to the Emperor Honorius, departed from Roman territory and settled in Gaul near the city of Narbonne, where today the estate of Saint Giles is called, in a place which is still called the Palace of the Goths, above the river Rhône. Later he was driven from that place by Count Constantius and settled with the Goths in the territories of Spain.

In these days, under Pope Innocent, the bodies of Saint Stephen the protomartyr and of other saints were revealed to the presbyter Lucian under John, bishop of Jerusalem. Not long afterward, under Boniface, who had been installed as successor to Zosimus, Innocent’s successor, Jerome the presbyter died at Bethlehem in the ninety-first year of his life. After Pope Boniface died, Celestine sat in the City. Orosius brought his *Chronicle* down to this point.

Emperor Honorius died at Rome in the thirty-first year of his reign—of which years he had ruled two with his father, thirteen with his brother, and the remainder with his brother’s son.

Concerning the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in verse.

[Col. 0897A]

Again Honorius and Theodosius rule in the court;  
the most wicked Gothic people carries all away by the river Saône;  
the Vandal oppresses the Spaniards with an evil sword.

The Gothic people occupies and violates captured Rome;  
it destroys churches, the crown languishes in the City,  
and they plunder every good thing they can.

Theodosius rules as king for thirty-three years;  
then Bishop Sisinnius did not survive a year;  
his short life amounts to ten months and two days.

Likewise concerning the younger Emperor Theodosius, the forty-fifth from Augustus.

In the year 426 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Theodosius the younger, the forty-fifth from Augustus, after the death of his uncle held the empire alone. In the *Tripartite History*, his virtues are preferred to those of all his predecessors. Among them this is also recorded: after the example of Alexander the Great, while he was weary in the army from the heat of the sun, dust, and excessive travel, and was suffering from intense thirst, a most refreshing cup of water was offered him. He refused to drink it, lest he alone should have the refreshment of drinking before the others.

In his time John Cassian the hermit flourished; he wrote the *Conferences*, that is, the *Lives of the Fathers*. Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, also flourished.

Theodoric the bishop, Socrates, and Sozomen—most eloquent men—carried their histories down to this point. These were later gathered into one volume and translated from Greek into Latin by Epiphanius Scholasticus at the direction of Cassiodorus the senator; from the three authors named, they were called the *Tripartite History*.

In the time of the younger Emperor Theodosius, the Visigoths—that is, the Southern Goths—lived in Gaul. But the Ostrogoths—that is, the Western Goths, from whom descended the Avars, that is, the Hungarians, Pannonians, and Lombards—crossed the Danube. The Ostrogoths had first dwelt in Pannonia, afterward lived in Thrace for forty-eight years, and then came to the West.

The Vandals, having allied the Germans with themselves under their leader Modigisil, occupied Spain.

At that time Boniface received the command of Africa from the emperor. Crossing into Spain, he subjected all Africa to the Vandals. Ravaging the whole land, they surrounded with siege the city of Hippo, over which blessed Augustine then presided. But blessed Augustine, lest he should see the destruction of his city, departed to the Lord in the seventy-sixth year of his life. The Romans, however, gave the Vandals a third part of Africa and made peace with them. Genseric, king of the Vandals and an Arian, oppressed Christians and sent bishops into exile. Invading Carthage, he stripped it of many riches and ecclesiastical ornaments.

In the thirtieth year of the younger Theodosius’s reign, there was a dreadful earthquake at Constantinople. Because of it, there was first sung there the chant of divine interchange:

> **Ἅγιος ὁ Θεὸς ἰσχυρὸς, ἀθάνατος, ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς**  
> “Holy God, holy and mighty, holy and immortal, have mercy upon us.”

When this chant was sung by all the people with Proclus their bishop, the earthquake immediately ceased. Therefore the emperor and his sister Pulcheria then promulgated an edict that this chant should henceforth be sung throughout the whole world.

Concerning Attila and his origin.

In these days Attila, king of the Huns, having killed his brother Bleda, began to ravage Thrace and Illyricum. Theodosius persuaded him to withdraw from his territories by giving him seven thousand pounds and promising him one thousand pounds each year. But Theodosius himself shortly afterward ended his days at Constantinople, in the forty-first year of his reign and the twenty-sixth year after the death of his uncle. The verses will relate the remaining matters concerning this Theodosius and other events contemporary with him.

Concerning the same Emperor Theodosius, in verse.

While the younger Theodosius alone retained the kingdom,  
the Vandal people, full of fury, crossed over from Spain;  
Africa is crushed and, wholly captured, mourns.

The people called African had been Catholic;  
the fierce Vandal overturned the faith of the Africans,  
so that little of Christ’s faith remained there.

How the devil appeared to the Jews in the form of Moses.

Now the demon speaks to the Hebrews in the form of Moses,  
and is devoutly received in full measure by the Pharisees;  
he promises to give them back God’s former gifts.

Crete was the island where he preached future things;  
all that he tells them, he promises shall come to pass,

[Col. 0898C]

and he promises to procure their native land for them.

“Cross over the sea; go with dry feet,” he said.  
“And return to Jerusalem, with me going before you.  
There you have all the things you desire to write.”

When he leads the Hebrews through the waves of the sea,  
the crowd follows together, and great hope sustains the Pharisees;  
the surge of the sea quickly encloses them.

The part preserved, which the wave of the sea did not overwhelm,  
quickly became pure through the Catholic baptism of Christ;  
the rest that perished became food for the fish.

Concerning the Emperors Marcian and Valentinian, the forty-sixth from Augustus.

In the year 453 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Marcian, by the counsel of Pulcheria, sister of the now deceased Theodosius, received the empire of the East as the forty-sixth from Augustus; Valentinian, the forty-fifth from Augustus, was still reigning in the West. Under the Emperors Marcian and Valentinian, Attila, king of the Huns, having subjected to himself the very powerful peoples of the Ostrogoths and Gepids and other diverse nations, roamed through all Macedonia, Moesia, Achaia, and Thrace.

Attila hated the Romans because of their ancient dignity. He also hated the Visigoths because of their courage; he intended to crush both peoples. Yet he did not wish to attack both nations at once, namely the Romans and the Visigoths, for he feared that both might join together against him. Accordingly, by his cunning, he tried to separate them from one another and stir each against the other. Thus he deceitfully wrote to Valentinian, emperor of the Romans, that he did not wish to act against the Romans but against the Visigoths. He also wrote to the Visigoths that he was doing nothing against them but against the Romans.

Then Eutius, patrician of the Romans, foreseeing Attila’s treachery, wrote to Theodoric, king of the Goths, in the name of Emperor Valentinian, carefully urging him to join the Romans against Attila, the most savage tyrant and invader of the whole world. Attila therefore declared war upon the Visigoths. The Visigoths, requesting the Romans through envoys, received Eutius the patrician as assistance. Eutius, having called to his aid Franks, Sarmatians, Burgundians, Saxons, Riparians, Briones, and many Celtic and Germanic nations, came to the aid of the Visigoths.

Attila, however, set out with Aldaric, king of the Gepids, Vialamir, king of the Ostrogoths, and innumerable nations under kings. Thus each army took position in the plains of Catalaunia. Attila sought the issue of the affair by divination from the inner entrails of cattle through Python-spirits, and understood that he would be defeated. Yet, on the other hand, in his foulest omens and auguries he foresaw that the mightiest leader of all would fall.

Attila began the battle. The Romans then held the higher ground. Thus from the ninth hour until night the bitterest battle continued. Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, as Attila had foreseen in his omens, fell in battle. Attila, put to flight, showed himself defeated, but by benefit of the night was able to hide.

When morning came, the Visigoths sought their king; but, having found him dead, they resolved with Thurismund, son of the slain king, to rush again upon the enemy.

Eutius the patrician, fearing that, should the Huns perhaps be utterly destroyed, the Goths, thenceforth exalted to excessive glory, might crush Rome, said to Thurismund, son of Theodoric: “If your brothers learn of the king’s death, they will seize the kingdom. Therefore return home swiftly, lest you be forestalled by your brothers upon the royal throne.” Thus deceived by the patrician, the young man left the enemy and hurried home. It was afterwards discovered that Attila, deprived of the strength of his own men, had prepared for himself a great fire from the seats [or wooden benches] of his people, into which, if the enemy rushed upon him, he wished to plunge himself. Jornandes, their historian, relates that in this most famous battle 165,000 fell on both sides, apart from the 152,000 who perished in the encounter of Franks and Gepids on the preceding night.

Thurismund, after the son of King Theodoric had been slain, was made king by his own people and, by the counsel of the patrician Eutius, entered his city of Toulouse.

When the Visigoths withdrew, Attila, now secure, turned his march toward Rome. On the way he surrounded with siege the city of Aquileia, the metropolis of Venetia. Having besieged it for a long time, and believing that he could not take it, he was already considering retreat. But one day, walking about the walls of the city, he saw storks carrying their little young from their nests outside the city. Calling his soldiers, he said: “These birds perceive the city’s coming ruin, and for that reason they have even carried out their young.” Saying this, he more strongly encouraged his soldiers to destroy the place. Thus, with engines and various siege-machines prepared, he suddenly overcame the city and so utterly devastated it that traces of its former buildings cannot be found.

Many maintain that he found the city empty, because its citizens carried the relics of the saints, together with all their household goods, by ship across the adjoining sea into Venetia. Living there permanently thereafter, they were called Venetians, as though newcomers. Hence even to the present day there is a dispute concerning the patriarchate between the people of Grado, the earlier inhabitants of that place, and the Aquileians.

Attila’s army there was so great that it piled up with its shields an embankment resembling a round mountain, in memory of Attila’s future fame. Others, however, say that it was raised by Julius Caesar. I, Gotfridus, saw that mountain in my own time, well fortified and inhabited.

Attila, afterwards elated by such successes, devastated all Venetia as he passed through it. Advancing into Liguria, he laid waste Milan and Pavia with cruel severity. From Liguria Attila made for Rome. Pope Leo went far out to meet him and obtained by his prayers that he should not harm the City. What especially restrained Attila from approaching the City was also the fact that Alaric, the earlier king of the Goths, died suddenly after plundering Rome. For these reasons Attila turned back and returned to his own country.

[Col. 0900C] Meanwhile Valentinian, jealous of the power of Eutius the prefect, ordered him and Boethius the senator to be killed. He himself was therefore slain by enemies shortly afterward, in the thirtieth year of his reign. After his death Maximus took his wife Eudoxia in marriage and usurped the empire. He then summoned Giseric, king of the Vandals, to the City. The Romans, terrified by the arrival of the Vandals, took vengeance on Maximus; killing him, they cut him into the smallest pieces. They themselves, fleeing in fear of the Vandals, abandoned the City.

King Giseric entered the City as though it were empty. Pope Leo met him at the gate as he entered and begged him to refrain from burning the City and killing its citizens. [Col. 0900D] The barbarian king, having entered the City, seized all its plunder and carried off Eudoxia with her two daughters. After remaining in the City for fifteen days, he refrained from burning it and killing its citizens, as the pope had requested. This was the second captivity of the Roman city after that caused by Alaric, inflicted by Vandal violence, in the 1214th year from the founding of the City. Afterwards Giseric joined the daughter of the emperor Valentinian in marriage to his son Transmund.

Attila, returning from Italy to his homeland, celebrated a marriage and, on that same night, overwhelmed by a flow of blood from his nostrils, expired. This was Attila, terror of the world, scourge of God: proud in his bearing, casting furious glances about him, a lover of war, self-controlled in his own hand, powerful in counsel, responsive to suppliants, [Col. 0901A] gracious to all received in allegiance; short in stature, broad-chested, with small eyes, a rather large head, sparse beard, hair sprinkled with gray, a flattened nose, and a dark complexion.

### The time and martyrdom of the eleven thousand virgins

The author Jornandes writes that there were five hundred thousand men in Attila’s army. Attila crowned eleven thousand Virgins with martyrdom together at Cologne. He killed Nicasius, bishop of Rheims. Emperor Marcian was soon afterwards murdered by his own men through treachery, in the seventh year of his reign.

### Likewise, concerning the same Emperor Marcian, related in verse

Now Caesar Marcian stood first in rank;

[Col. 0901B] now Theodoric, king of the Goths, gives battle,

whom the Italian land fears for his savagery.

He gains Spain and oppresses the Catalans in war;

at the evil Pharos of Sicily he pitched his tents;

he plundered all things by wound, by Mars, by his own hand.

### Concerning Pope Leo

Marcian lived six years to be counted;

Pope Leo I presided for twenty years.

Add ten months and twice two days to these.

### Concerning Pope Simplicius and Felix

Simplicius at Rome, after Pope Leo the First,

received, worthily to be remembered, the honor of the Church;

a blessed life sustained him for fifteen years.

Add seven days, in which he did not live without merit.

After Pope Felix’s years, reckon seven,

[Col. 0901C] eleven months, and eighteen days.

In Felix’s time Theodoric was king,

impious, violent, the unjust leader of the Goths;

Christian in name, wicked in deed.

### Concerning Pope Gelasius

Pope Gelasius stood in Theodoric’s time,

and under Zeno defeated the doctrines of the Goths.

He held office four years and eight months,

and departed to rest after nine days.

### Concerning Leo Bissa, emperor of the Greeks, forty-seventh from Augustus

In the year 440 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Leo Bissa received the eastern empire at Constantinople, forty-seventh from Augustus. He chose his son Leo as colleague in the empire. Mauronianus received the western empire at Ravenna; he was killed near the city of Tastona in the fourth year of his reign. After him Severus, without Augustus’s command, then seized royal power at Ravenna. He too died at Rome in the fourth year.

Emperor Leo placed his son-in-law Zeno over the East. Making peace with the Ostrogoths, Leo received as hostage Theodoric, son of Theodemar—that is, the Veronese Theodoric, of whose extraordinary courage the Germans tell very often—when he was eight years old. Emperor Leo made Leo, son of his son-in-law Zeno, who held the East, emperor. He himself died in the eleventh year of his reign. Zeno, emperor of the East, came to Rome and was graciously received by the people and senate.

### Concerning Emperor Zeno, forty-eighth from Octavian Augustus

[Col. 0902A]

Therefore, in the year 476 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Zeno, an Isaurian by nation, forty-eighth from Augustus, obtained the empire. His nephew held the western—that is, Roman—empire. When he was expelled from the throne, the patrician Orestes made his own son emperor of the West, to be called Augustus.

Meanwhile Odoacer, a Rutenian by nation, came from the furthest borders of Pannonia with the peoples of the Turcilingi, Sciri, and Heruli, and moved an army to invade the Romans. When the patrician Orestes met him on the borders of Liguria, he saw his force, was terrified, fled, and withdrew to Ticinum. Odoacer pursued him, took the city, killed him, and from there, having dispersed his soldiers throughout all Italy, usurped the royal title. This Odoacer, leaving his own land, passed through the lower parts of Noricum or upper Pannonia and visited the man of God Severinus, bishop of Ravenna, who, preaching God’s word, had built a cell at the foot of a mountain. He consulted him about the outcome of events. By the spirit of prophecy Severinus foretold him all that afterwards happened.

The aforesaid Augustus—this is his personal name—son of the patrician Orestes, after his father, that same patrician, had already been killed and his country captured and devastated, voluntarily laid aside the imperial purple in the eleventh month of his reign. Odoacer, now facing no resistance, entered the city of Rome as an enemy and governed it everywhere as subject to himself, like a king. At last all Italy was subjected to his servitude for fourteen years, and he oppressed it with harsh bondage as its master.

The verses contain the rest concerning Zeno:

### Likewise, concerning Emperor Zeno, related in verse

Zeno, father of his country, while he held his ancestral kingdoms,

had a famous son, Leo, his only heir,

mighty in war, often waging battles.

He was falsely thought to have sought his father’s death;

Zeno, whose commands are openly known, orders him to die;

his mother skillfully forestalls the hostile measures.

While her son was held in prison, the most sorrowful mother

arranged that a youth like him should be substituted for death;

the son secretly escaped, but the other fell.

The father therefore believed that his son had succumbed to death;

[Col. 0902D] his mother preserved him, under the pretence of his becoming a monk;

there he was kept shut up for fifteen years.

The son himself is called Leo by common report.

It is commanded: whoever is called Leo shall die;

the cruel decree remains in force.

While Leo was thus confined for fifteen years,

an astrologer, together with grammarians, instructed him thoroughly in learning;

the youth became a philosopher, wholly skilled in the arts.

The mother rears a bird that speaks in human fashion,

which learned to lament the youth with the grieving mother:

“Alas, Leo, my son, our glory lies fallen!”

While Zeno sits, the Paschal victim is prepared;

in the midst the parrot laments, renewing the grief:

“Alas, Leo,” says the bird, “why do you perish, Leo, my son?”

As it clearly pronounces Leo’s name,

[Col. 0903A] it moves the hearts of the nobles to pity and renews their grief;

and the seated empress weeps as she is accustomed.

Zeno wonders why the gathering of nobles weeps,

asks angrily what cause or offence it is

that now troubles either foremost side.

His mother says: “Recognize more fully, Zeno, that you are feared.

Why she weeps, why the assembly grieves, it is itself afraid to say;

if you wish to know, the bird will now tell you.”

Zeno replies: “I beg you, show me the reason:

what youth does your bird lament, and what Leo?

For this parrot moves my inmost heart.”

She says: “The decree which you issued is to be withdrawn;

the judgment harms you alone, if perhaps you so choose;

Zeno granted me leave to speak.

Know that you condemned your son on a false report;

he who is believed killed is shown to be alive:

you the father, he the son, I given as mother.

He is more beautiful than Venus, wise, most mighty in arms,

dear to the greatest princes, the sole hope of the lowly,

and now worthy to retain your empire.

Therefore, if you desire the nobles to observe the Paschal feast,

if you seek to have me happy for myself, or yourself happy for yourself,

wash away your sin; act with mercy.

Be a father free from cruelty; preserve right order.

Send, father; deign to summon your son Leo.

God himself commands this; the whole court urges it.”

When she ceased speaking, the foremost court rose,

prostrated at his feet and offered prayers, pressing the king

both by entreaties and tears to bring joy to his own people.

Moved by these things, while the whole court begged, the father said:

“I myself would not have believed that I had a son.

I am silent now: he lives; I desire to grant what has been asked.”

For twenty years Zeno’s glory sat enthroned;

then another Anastasius sat as pope at Rome.

One year alone gave him his span in the world,

eleven months, and twenty days.

Symmachus was pope with Prince Theodoric,

and Hormisdas also sat as bishop under that same wicked ruler;

now too comes the time of Emperor Anastasius.

### Concerning Emperor Anastasius, forty-ninth from Augustus

In the year 491 from the Incarnation of the Lord, after Pharamund, the first king of the Franks, Clovis was reigning over the Franks. In his time Emperor Zeno died, in the seventeenth year of his reign. Anastasius, forty-ninth from Augustus, succeeded him and took Ariadne as his wife.

[Col. 0903D] While Anastasius was reigning in the East and the Arian Theodoric was oppressing Rome, Symmachus and Laurentius contended in the City for the papacy. After this dispute had continued for three years with the shedding of much blood, both clerical and lay, Theodoric summoned a synod and imposed an end upon it. For he confirmed Symmachus in the papacy, as elected by the sounder judgment; he deposed Laurentius and made him bishop in the city of Lucerna. In these times Transmund, king of the Vandals and son of Giseric, exiled 220 bishops to the island of Sardinia because of the Catholic faith.

[Col. 0904A] In those same days in Africa, a certain Arian Olympius, sitting in a bath and proudly blaspheming Christ, was struck from heaven by a fiery sword. Another man, while being baptized by a certain Arian bishop, heard the bishop say: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit”; immediately all the water vanished from the font. Seeing this, the man who was to be baptized fled to the Catholic Church and received baptism.

Meanwhile Emperor Anastasius, by letters, offered Clovis king of the Franks the dignity of the consular rank. But the emperor did not abandon the Eutychian heresy despite Pope Hormisdas’s admonition. In the twenty-eighth year of his reign he was struck by lightning and died. Clovis, king of the Franks, died in the thirtieth year of his reign and left his son Lothar with three other sons, who divided the kingdom among themselves.

### Likewise, concerning Emperor Anastasius, related in verse

Caesar Anastasius presses war against the Goths;

the heretic Theodoric now oppresses the City,

nor could he remove the Goths by his own warfare.

Now two pontiffs were exposed to those tyrants,

Laurentius and Symmachus sit for a full three years,

during which the Gothic host fostered error.

Now the Vandal people closes Catholic churches,

and the kingdom conquered by its error obeys it;

the Arian party establishes shrines in the churches.

Transmund, their king and friend of cruelty,

a wicked transgressor, gave bishops to exile;

[Col. 0904C] Sardinia holds a hundred bishops in prison.

### Miracle concerning a blaspheming Arian

When an Arian is seen to blaspheme God,

his very tongue is soon burned by lightning from heaven;
