when that tongue paid the penalty, the rest of the crowd fled.

### Miracle in the baptism of a certain Arian

While an Arian seeks to baptize someone,

the water prepared for him suddenly vanishes;

the young man was astonished and took counsel for himself.

### Concerning Emperor Justin, fiftieth from Octavian Augustus

In the year 519 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Lothar, son of Clovis, was reigning in Francia with his three brothers, the aged Justin, an Isaurian or Illyrian by nation, fiftieth from Augustus, received the empire with the senate’s consent.

In these days King Hilderic, son of Transmund, whom his mother Eudoxia had taught to be Catholic, kindly recalled all the bishops whom his father had banished into exile.

Emperor Justin also persecuted heretics through zeal for the Catholic faith. The Arian Theodoric sent Pope John to him, declaring that, unless Justin ceased persecuting Arians, he himself would afflict Christians. Justin, moved by Pope John’s prayers, assented and dismissed the pope with honor. Theodoric had earlier ordered both him and Boethius to be killed. Because of these crimes [Col. 0905A] Theodoric was suddenly snatched from this light and disappeared in the thirtieth year of his reign. According to the dialogue of blessed Gregory, a most holy hermit saw him bodily cast into fire on Mount Etna by Pope John and Symmachus, whom he had killed.

The claim made by some that Theodoric was contemporary with Hermenric of Verona and Attila is not true. It is clear that Attila was long after Hermenric, and that Theodoric too, long after Attila’s death, was given as an eight-year-old boy to Emperor Leo as a hostage. When death threatened Theodoric, he commended to the Gothic nobles the ten-year-old boy Athalaric, son of his daughter Amalsuinda, and then left him the rule at Rome. He begged the Goths to love [Col. 0905B] the Roman senate and people; and, leaving the empire to Justinian, ruler of his sister, he departed this world in the eighth year of his reign.

### Likewise, concerning the same Emperor Justin, related in verse

The elder Justin deserved now to be raised to the throne;

he ordered the pontiffs also to be recalled from exile;

he opens churches by river, countryside, and sea.

Justin happily rules for seven years.

Now come the years to be counted for Pope John:

he lived two years in this world.

Let us add three times three months to the years,

and eight and ten days, also to be noted by calculation.

Now too the treachery of the Goths rages in the world.

### Concerning Pope Felix

[Col. 0905C] Felix the Third is pope in Justin’s time;

four years are counted as the length of his time,

and in addition three months are included in the reckoning.

### Concerning Pope Boniface

Boniface too is bishop in Justin’s time;

he scarcely has the period of two years,

and twenty days grant him a fitting rest.

### Concerning Emperor Justinian, fifty-first from Augustus

In the year 527 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Justinian, fifty-first from Augustus, assumed the empire, while the sons of Clovis were still ruling in Francia. This most Christian ruler most wisely revived the empire as though it were already dead, restored the commonwealth, magnificently triumphed over the Persians through the patrician Belisarius, and reduced laws formerly promulgated and excessively diffuse into a compendium. Among the countless other benefits he bestowed upon churches, he built at Constantinople, with marvellous workmanship and adornment, the church of Saint Sophia—that is, Divine Wisdom, who is Christ the Son of God. He converted and baptized Craten, king of the Heruli.

Then also Garda, king of the Huns, together with a certain widow from among the Hun princes and others of that people, one hundred thousand in all, received the grace of baptism. Thus King Athalaric, with his mother Eudoxia, was received under Emperor Justinian’s protection. But after Athalaric was soon killed by his own people, his mother brought Theodatus to the throne; afterwards, ungrateful and treacherous, [Col. 0906A] he strangled her in a bath.

Justinian, having completely expelled the Vandals from Africa, restored Africa as a Roman province. Theodatus, traitor and strangler of his wife, fearing Justinian’s punishment, sent Pope Agapetus to the emperor to seek pardon and peace. Having obtained it, he caused himself to be recalled to the Catholic faith by that pontiff. There too the pontiff himself died; while his bier was being carried through the gate of the imperial city, a certain blind man was given sight when he touched it.

After this, the patrician Belisarius captured Theodatus for the crime committed against his wife, and sent him to the emperor, together with Witiges, who had seized the kingdom after Theodatus. He thus ended the entire kingdom of the Goths, which their author Jordanes says had endured for more than two thousand years. In this way, under Justinian, Belisarius extirpated both the Vandals from Africa and the Goths from Italy, restoring both provinces to their former Roman subjection.

Up to this point Bishop Jordanes—Goth by nation, as he himself testifies in his Chronicle—continued the histories of the Goths.

The patrician Belisarius engaged in war with Theudebert, son of Clovis and brother of Lothar, who had invaded Italy with two hundred thousand men. At the Franks’ request he granted peace and persuaded them to leave Italy without loss to the Roman soldiery.

Meanwhile the Parthians invaded and devastated all Syria and the city of Antioch. Belisarius the patrician, conqueror of Vandals and Goths, met them, defeated them, and drove them back from Roman territory. In these days the Goths, in revolt with their king Totila, turned their march toward Italy.

### Concerning the Lombards and Priscian the grammarian; likewise concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict

In these times the people of the Lombards, who came from the island of Scantia—called Scandinavia by others, from which the Goths also had departed—were dwelling in Pannonia with their king Alboin. Not long afterwards they occupied Italy, as we shall say later. Belisarius the patrician, while remaining in Italy, unwillingly exiled Pope Silverius at the command of the Empress Theodora. He did the same to Vigilius, Silverius’s successor. Priscian of Caesarea then wrote books on the art of grammar for Julian, consul and patrician. In these days also blessed Abbot Benedict wrote the monastic Rule.

The distinguished emperor Justinian, after greatly exalting the commonwealth in his time, died in the thirty-ninth year of his reign.

Up to this point Bishop Victor of Tours carried his chronicle. Let us set forth in verse the remainder concerning Justinian and the pontiffs of his time.

### Likewise, concerning the same Emperor Justinian, related in verse

Justinian receives the empire for his time;

by his office let us seek legal rights;

[Col. 0907A] we are governed by his law, for we give his laws.

By his rule the conquered Vandal people is driven away;

all the Lord’s glory is restored by his power,

and the Church rejoices as its peace endures.

For thirty-two years he had led his life;

he also often fought with the tyrannical Goths;

Athalaric, leader of the Goths, appears.

### Concerning Popes John and Agapetus

At this time there was another Pope John,

and then Agapetus, a bishop worthy of love, held office.

While these two were, Athalaric was king.

Each bishop held office for nearly twice twelve years;

the power of Theobald, king of the Goths, arose;

he committed most evil deeds throughout Italy.

### Concerning Pope Silverius and Theobald, king of the Goths, of the Arian sect

[Col. 0907B]

Justinian, whom I have described, still lives in greatness;

under him we now commemorate Pope Silverius,

to whom we rightly assign eight months of life.

Silverius is made without Justinian’s decree;

Theobald and the Goths, now heretics,

set him in place: Caesar’s anger rises.

When Theobald dies, Justinian, stirred,

commands that the harmful band of Goths

whom he knew to be heretics withdraw from Italy.

### Concerning Pope Vigilius and another king of the Goths

Pope Vigilius lived with Justinian;

we record that he lived for six years,

and grant him twenty days, and five more besides.

Now a king of the Goths called Vigilogus is captured;

Justinian judges him sent to himself by the death of evildoers,

and he brought him before the tribunal by the sword.

### Concerning Pope Pelagius

Pelagius was pope with Justinian;

we record that he lived for four years,

and add ten months in the reckoning.

When Pope Pelagius wished to be consecrated in the City,

he called two bishops to perform the sacred rites:

these two suffice for the rite, says the canon.

Thus there were the bishop of Ferentino, the bishop of Perugia,

and Andrew the priest: these three held the triclinium [dining-hall];

there were no more, nor do I tell you fewer.

### Concerning Pope John and a certain portent

The third Pope John was with Justinian;

[Col. 0907D] he had now lived twenty years with Caesar,

eleven months, and twenty days.

Now battle-lines, as though fighting, were seen above the sky,

as though fiery; and many were visible everywhere.

What it was and whence it came cannot be recounted.

### Concerning Justin the Younger, emperor of the Greeks, fifty-second from Augustus

In the year 567 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Chilperic, son of King Clothar, was reigning in Francia with his three brothers, Justin the Younger, Justinian’s nephew, a Thracian by nation, fifty-second from Augustus, received the empire, crowned by Patriarch Eutychius. He enriched with many gifts the churches founded by his predecessor. In his days peace between Romans and Persians was broken. The emperor sent Julian to Aretas, king of the Indians, [Col. 0908A] and he found him adorned as we here describe.

The king stood almost naked, wearing only a girdle about his loins; he had linen garments interwoven with gold and garments torn about the belly, studded with precious pearls. On his arms he had five rings and gold bracelets; upon his head, cloth adorned with gems; about his neck, a gold torque. Standing upon a lofty chariot, he was supported by four elephants and four wheels. He held in his hand a very small gilded shield with two small lances. Having armed him against the Persian king named Eunuchus, Julian returned.

Likewise, Justin, having sent Narses with Lombard assistance, killed Totila, king of the Goths, [Col. 0908B] and extirpated the Goths from Italy root and branch. He killed Bucelinus, leader of the king of the Franks, sent to devastate Italy; and he put to death by hanging Sindoald, king of the Brendones, one of Odoacer’s counts who still remained in Italy. Therefore, when Narses had destroyed all the barbarians and restored Italy to its former condition, the Romans, as is customary, envying his prosperous success, accused him before Augustus and before Augustus’s wife. Consequently the emperor sent Longinus to Italy to take his place.

The Empress Sophia too, inflamed with womanly fury, threatened that Narses, as a eunuch, should be placed among her little women and serve her in women’s fashion. Narses bore all this most grievously, [Col. 0908C] withdrew to Naples, and sent an embassy inviting the Lombards into Italy. Their arrival was preceded by fiery battle-lines in the sky—as Gregory testifies—which many saw and which indicated a future shedding of blood. From then on Rome lost not only its transalpine provinces but also Italy itself, which from that time has been inhabited by the barbarians whom we call Lombards.

Moreover, Emperor Justin adopted Count Tiberius as his son and elected him Caesar. When he knew he was about to die, he summoned Patriarch Eutychius and the senate, and made Tiberius Augustus from Caesar. He himself died in the eleventh year of his reign.

### Concerning the same Justin in verse, and the pope of his time

[Col. 0908D] While the younger Justin sat upon the imperial throne,

he determined to have Hungarian nobles with him,

waging many battles against the Ligurians.

Vigilogus, king of the Goths, then waged war;

by his savagery and sword he subdued the Spaniards,

and destroyed and held many cities there.

### Concerning Pope Pelagius

Now Pelagius the Second arises as pope at Rome,

Roman by birth, discerning and eloquent in speech,

yet he sat there without Justin’s authorization.

### The Lombards oppress Rome and Italy; a great flood; and Pope Fabian

For the violent hand of the Lombard peoples

oppresses the regions of Italy with fire, famine, and sword:

the City and Romulus’s soil were besieged.

[Col. 0909A] So great a quantity of rain now falls upon the world

that the people believe a deluge is arising;

it destroyed bridges and inflicted very many losses.

Now the younger Justin presides for eleven years;

then Benedict the First was the venerable bishop,

for one year, one month, and sixteen days.

A remarkable famine and abundance of war oppressed the Ligurians,

and the first glory fell to the Lombards over them.

Their renowned name derives from their long beards.

### Concerning Tiberius Constantine, emperor of the Greeks, fifty-third from Augustus

In the year 576 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Tiberius Constantine, a Thracian by nation, was crowned by Patriarch Eutychius. He ruled as the fifty-third from Augustus. While walking in his palace he saw a cross carved on the pavement and said: “Let this sign of the cross be raised from the pavement, for we ought to adore the cross of the Lord, not tread it beneath our feet.” When it was removed, he found another cross carved in the same place; when this too was removed, he saw a third cross likewise carved there. Therefore he ordered a deep pit to be made in that spot, and in digging it they found much gold.

Likewise, after the death of the patrician Narses, a great quantity of gold was found in a certain well. The emperor distributed all this, according to his custom, to the poor. At that time, when Italy was being devastated by the Lombards under Pope Benedict, the same emperor sent many ships laden with grain from Egypt to the Romans suffering famine. Through his commander Maurice he gloriously defeated the Persians, whom afterwards [Col. 0909C] he made his son-in-law and Caesar. He also sent wonderful gifts to Chilperic, king of the Franks.

In these days Gregory, archdeacon of the Roman Church, was sent by Pope Pelagius to Constantinople. He composed the *Moralia on Job* for Leander and corrected before the emperor Eutychius, bishop of that city, who erred concerning the faith of the resurrection. Tiberius, having appointed his son-in-law Maurice as his successor in the empire, rested in peace in the sixth year of his reign. The verses contain the rest concerning Tiberius.

### Concerning the same Emperor Tiberius and the pope of his time, related in verse

Tiberius sat now with Pelagius as bishop.

At last the Gothic people destroys itself by its own wound;

[Col. 0909D] thus the wicked multitude then brought about its own end.

The Caesar rests six years, the pope eleven;

add eleven months and days to the pope,

and I seek to add one day besides for his repose.

### Concerning Emperor Maurice, fifty-fourth from Augustus, and the pope of his time

In the year 583 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Maurice, born in Cappadocia, the first of the Greek race to reign, ruled as the fifty-fourth from Augustus.

In his days blessed Gregory, with the emperor’s consent, assumed the Roman pontificate. Then Saint Columbanus the Scot, abbot of Luxeuil, driven by persecution, came to Bobbio, a city of Italy, and died there. Then Romericus established on his mountain, Romericus, [Col. 0910A] a noble convent of nuns—that is, in the kingdom of Lotharingia.

Then also in Swabia, under the diocese of Constance, the highly honorable church of Saint Gall was built, while he was living and serving as abbot, as is said, of four hundred monks. All are believed holy except one, Hebruinus, who then left the monastic order and, through Queen Brunhild—a most wicked woman—became *majordomus*, that is, first after the king in the kingdom of the Franks. At Brunhild’s instigation this Hebruinus persecuted the Church of God and made certain persons martyrs. Brunhild nevertheless bore a fitting penalty for these sins: King Clothar had her tied to the tails of unbroken horses and dragged; she met a miserable but deserving end.

While Emperor Maurice did not cease persecuting the blessed pope, in the nineteenth year of his reign he saw in a vision a monk standing before him and brandishing a sword, saying: “Behold, you shall die.” Terrified by this sight and recognizing his fault, he humbly wrote to Pope Gregory, bishops, and religious abbots, asking them to obtain from God by their prayers that God would punish him for his sins not in the future life but in the present one. He himself likewise begged this of God with many tears. Therefore, when God wished to hear the emperor because of the Church’s petition, the emperor saw in a dream that he stood before the Crucified One at the bronze gate of the palace and heard a dreadful voice: “Give up Maurice, [Col. 0910C] give up Maurice.” And again: “Where do you wish, Maurice, that I repay you for the evils you have done—here or in the future?” When he answered, “Not in the future,” the voice ordered that he be led and delivered to Phocas with his wife, children, and all his kindred.

At daybreak he summoned his son-in-law Philip, told him the dream, and said: “Do you know that Phocas?” He replied: “He is a young and rash man.” Meanwhile the messengers whom Maurice had sent to men of God returned and reported similar answers seen by them in dreams. Therefore, when the army sent by Maurice was suffering hunger because of his avarice, it revolted and made Phocas emperor. On hearing this, Maurice understood it to be the forewarning of the vision already mentioned. Phocas pursued Maurice near Chalcedon and, as Maurice acknowledged his fault, beheaded him with his wife and sons, in accordance with the foretold vision. The verses contain the rest concerning Maurice.

### Likewise, concerning the same Maurice and the pope of his time

In the time when Maurice wore the diadem at Rome,

the Gothic peoples were joined to the Catholic Church in baptism,

by the gift-granting favor of God.

Maurice’s time completes twenty years;

there will also be one additional year, rightly to be counted,

under which came blessed Gregory’s life.

For thirteen years together he governs the pontificate;

through him the honor of City and world is worthily raised up.

I add six months and ten days to the years.

### Concerning Emperor Maurice and Pope Gregory, who wrote on Job and Ezekiel

[Col. 0911A]

When Gregory is raised to the throne with Maurice,

he scorns the throne and avoids the pontificate,

but at Maurice’s command is compelled and comes.

He expounded Job and illuminated Ezekiel;

he shines in the teaching of pastors, and in Daniel;

the glory of this Church is greatly established through him.

### Concerning Emperor Phocas, fifty-fifth from Augustus

In the year 603 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Phocas, fifty-fifth from Augustus, obtained the empire, having a wife named Leontia. At first he was groom to a certain patrician, afterwards a soldier, and finally emperor. In the second year of his reign the most blessed Pope Gregory passed to the Lord. Then Pope Boniface the Third obtained from Phocas, by his authority, that the Roman Church should be called head of all churches. For the Church of Constantinople styled itself first—apparently because the seat of the empire had been transferred there. After him another Boniface, the Fourth after blessed Gregory, obtained by prayers from that same Emperor Phocas that the temple built by Emperor Domitian, called the Pantheon, should be granted to the Church of God and dedicated in honor of all saints.

In these days Chosroes, king of the Persians, ranging through the East, took many Roman provinces from the Romans; and, carrying off from Jerusalem the banner of the life-giving Cross, he placed it upon his throne, where he caused himself to be worshipped as God. [Col. 0911C] But Phocas, after committing many crimes and murders, was killed in the eighth year of his reign by Heraclius, son of Heraclius the patrician and prefect of Africa, at the summons of the patrician Priscus, his son-in-law. Let the rest be set forth in verse.

Likewise, concerning the same Phocas, it is set down in verse.

Phocas sits as Caesar and restores all that has been harmed;

Under him very many Lombard bands are slain,

And he grants his churches to dwell in peace.

Under Phocas’s rule the Lombard is driven from the City;

Tuscany and Spoleto are reclaimed by his might;

There was peace for the Italians, though all too liable to relapse.

Phocas, reigning eight years, holds the empire:

Now the illustrious Fabian is called pope,

[Col. 0911D] Whose life was only one year.

Concerning Pope Boniface, who obtained from the Emperor Phocas the primacy of all Churches.

The third pope is that kindly Boniface,

Who asks of Phocas a gift worthy through the ages:

That Peter’s see may be first; and he grants it.

Constantinople’s had formerly been first;

Now Rome’s is first, illustrious in better doctrine;

For Peter, the chief, establishes the foremost teachings.

This Boniface lived eight months,

And, counting twice ten days, pause at that measure;

Thus reckon the pope’s short span of time.

Boniface the Fourth is recorded under Phocas;

His life is allotted three years and eight months;

Add besides twenty-five days.

Concerning the Pantheon temple, given to Boniface.

[Col. 0912A]

Phocas gives Boniface the Pantheon, formerly consecrated,

Where all men had ordained their shrines to be made for their gods,

Idols to be set up and rich incense offered.

This unclean house is hallowed with sacred water;

Once belonging to the demon, it becomes Saint Mary Rotunda,

And, once the demon’s hall, now remains God’s dwelling.

Concerning Pope Deusdedit.

Pope Deusdedit sat with Caesar Phocas;

For three years the Roman people obeyed him,

And his life gave him twenty days besides.

Concerning Rome’s decline under the Emperor Phocas.

This Phocas was raised up by sedition;

With the soldiery supporting him, he reigned while the senate was unwilling;

Then a portion of the nobles lost their heads by the sword.

[Col. 0912B] Now the Persian nation, long subject to the Romans,

Having broken faith, is no longer the same people;

It mingles battles, while falling Rome is silent.

Though once mistress, the Roman people loses Persia;

Thus too the ancient wars of the Hebrews have returned,

And the Roman people loses both lands.

Concerning Heraclius the Younger, emperor of the Greeks, fifty-sixth from Augustus.

In the year 612 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Heraclius, after Phocas had been killed, was crowned by Sergius the patriarch and, fifty-sixth from Augustus, obtained the empire, while Lothair, son of Chilperic, reigned in Francia. In the second year of his reign he begot a son, Heraclius Constantine, by Eudoxia. When Eudoxia died, he incestously joined to himself Martina, his sister’s daughter, [Col. 0912C] and by her received a daughter, Heraclona.

Up to this point Bishop Isidore carried his history. In the eighth year of his reign, when Heraclius sought peace from Chosroes, king of the Persians, and did not obtain it, four years later, in the twelfth year of his reign, he moved an army into Persia. On his way, upon the bridge over the Danube, he fought a single combat with Chosroes’s son. When he and part of his army had there been killed, Heraclius then advanced as a convert to Christianity and devastated all Persia. He killed Chosroes, sitting upon a golden throne together with the Lord’s Cross, and took the holy wood from there. Returning thence to Constantinople in triumph, he afterwards carried the Cross back to Jerusalem. There [Col. 0912D] at the entrance of its gate a great miracle appeared; I have recorded that miracle in verse at the end of this chapter. From that time the Exaltation of the Holy Cross began to be celebrated by the Church.

In these days a certain Anastasius in Persia, formerly a Magus, afterwards a Christian and monk, together with seventy others, received martyrdom from the Persians under the judge Marzaban for Christ’s faith. Afterwards a demoniac, clothed in his tunic, was healed. Heraclius carried his body from Persia.

At that time Muhammad, whom the Saracens worship today, born of the stock of Ishmael, with a pagan father and a Jewish mother, preached his law.

In the same days, when Lothair, king of the Franks, had died, his son Dagobert was quite a boy; Arnulf, [Col. 0913A] who was then mayor of the palace, brought him up. This Arnulf was afterwards bishop of Metz. Dagobert alone reigned in Francia, but he had left to his brother Heribert a few cities and districts around the river Loire. For from Clovis down to this Dagobert, the kingdom of the Franks had been variously divided among different brothers and among the sons of sons, and rule had been exercised confusedly and unequally. The boundary of the Frankish kingdom now extended from Spain to Pannonia, having Aquitaine at one end and, at the other, the duchy of Bavaria, which stretches as far as Hungary. The king of the Franks possessed Aquitaine in the west and Bavaria in the east. Dagobert, therefore, sole king of the Franks, gave laws to the Bavarians. While his father Lothair was still living, he had undertaken war with the Saxons [Col. 0913B] and was grievously wounded by them. Having requested and received help from his father, he again engaged the Saxons in battle. Having gloriously defeated and put them to flight, he subjected all Saxony to his dominion; and we read that then, by his command, all males of that nation taller in stature than Dagobert’s sword were put to death. At that time Saint Cunibert was bishop of Cologne.

Meanwhile Heraclius, deceived by the patriarch Sergius, was infected by the Eutychian heresy; moreover, he became a practitioner of mathematics and astrology. Then he learned through constellations that circumcised men would lay waste his empire. Believing that men of this kind were Jews, he sent envoys to Dagobert and demanded that all [Col. 0913C] Jews be baptized by royal command. This he obtained. Heraclius himself did likewise with the Jews of his empire. Not long afterwards the Hagarenes, who are all circumcised, invaded his empire. When Heraclius thought to restrain them by dispatching an army, he lost fifty thousand men from his own army. For Heraclius opened the Caspian Gates and led out the Caspian peoples, most savage men whom Alexander the Great had formerly shut in above the Caspian Sea because of their ferocity; and with these men the emperor proposed to renew war against the Hagarenes. But the angel of the Lord, on that same night before their intended battle in the morning, killed fifty thousand men of the emperor’s army. Hence the emperor, broken in spirit, became swollen from grief and, turned to dropsy, gave up the spirit in the forty-seventh year of his reign.

O most just judgments of God! For Heraclius had triumphed most gloriously through the power and sign of the most victorious Cross; but afterwards, forgetful of God and of that Cross, he trusted more in auguries than in divine help, and deserved to be miserably defeated by the Hagarenes, who were not even to be counted among men. Let us set forth the rest concerning Heraclius, the Cross, and Chosroes in verse.

Likewise, concerning Heraclius, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, and the pope of his time.

Heraclius stands magnificent, supreme in his diadem;

Sigismund, wondrous king of the Goths, reigns.

He subjected many Jews to God.

It is now fitting to recount the deeds of Caesar Heraclius,

[Col. 0914A] Who strove to defend the places and rights of the Cross and clergy;

How great were his deeds for the Cross is a tale fit to be sung.

The good Davidic city, quiet in a modest peace,

Is said to have been sought by the ancient Persian nation;

Sought by war, and thus the Cross lay hidden.

Concerning Chosroes.

Angry Chosroes orders the city to be taken;

The city where battle is fought is taken, and its people bound;

And when the Persian nation seized the Cross, it departed.

Concerning Chosroes’s hall and his son.

Chosroes’s hall was woven with a strong vault,

Its inner walls interlaced with gems and gold,

Where stars, as though fixed in the ether, glitter.

That house could appear under the likeness of heaven;

Above, he contrived at times to set chariots in motion,

[Col. 0914B] Whence, making a crash, it produced counterfeit thunderbolts.

The impious man sits in the sought-for citadel, feigning heaven,

With the Cross he had sought; he thinks to live life there,

And fears no death while he sits thus.

The son takes after his father’s very fierceness;

Fiercely he wages battles over what was lost, mingled with blood,

And rushes with his soldiers into the holy places.

Heraclius, victor over the Persians.

Heraclius confronts and restrains the proud man by his strength,

And on the bridge over the Danube wages single combat with the king;

By the power of the Cross he tears away the leader’s arms.

Here the impious man, though thought to believe, falls slain;

The conquered people returned, relying on baptism;

And his soldier too believed in the Lord.

Chosroes is beheaded.

[Col. 0914C] Caesar orders his standards to move through Persian regions;

Chosroes, hidden beneath the covering of the heaven already described,

Perishes when surrendered; the heavenly pageant is destroyed.

Heraclius cuts off the wicked king’s head with the sword.

The venerable sign receives fitting reverence;

The standards shine on their way to David’s places with the Cross.

On the Mount of Olives, trusting in the victor’s gift,

As they joyfully think to enter the gates with Caesar,

The gate becomes like a wall, and the repulsed crowd returns.

A fair angelic utterance came to Caesar:

“I do not wish Augustus to advance weighed down with gems;

Let him remember Christ entering.”

Let him remove his adornments and advance humbly on foot;

Let the blessed Cross now be borne in Heraclius’s hands;

The gate is restored, and hope gives a broad open way.

It is enough briefly to have related Heraclius’s glories;

My Muse calls me to the remaining labours concerning kings;

Charles and the rest set great deeds in motion.

Heraclius rules for almost three times twelve years,

In whose time came the most celebrated glory of Cross and clergy;

That remembrance shall be everlasting.

Concerning Pope Severinus.

Pope Severinus succeeds in Heraclius’s time.

Instructed by three, the father is first in doctrine,

And he lives two years and two days.

Concerning Pope Honorius and John.

Bishop Honorius is great in the time of that Caesar;

He completes twelve years of life,

With eleven months and likewise ten days.

[Col. 0915A] In Heraclius’s time Theodore sits in due succession;

After six years and five months he departs,

And his life gives him eighteen days besides.

Concerning Pyrrhus, patriarch of Constantinople.

At that time Pyrrhus was patriarch at Constantinople;

That Theodore constrained him by his uprightness,

Because he was a servant of the Roman see.

Pyrrhus removed the acts of his party by anathema,

And came to submit himself to the Roman pontiff.

Such a pledge shall endure through the years.

In Heraclius’s time Maurice sits in succession

At Constantinople, and Bishop Paul obeys him;

Then the pope gave him Roman doctrine.

Maurice lives six years in the order of things,

And months, with a period of twenty-five days,

[Col. 0915B] Thus the times of the pontiffs are to be reckoned.

Concerning Pope Eugenius.

Pope Eugenius sat at the same time;

Having passed two years of life, he departed from his see;

Add two months, and three times eight days.

Concerning the pontiff Dionysius.

Pope Dionysius is recorded under the same king;

He is recorded as sitting five years and five months,

And his life is given eight days besides.

Concerning Pope Agapetus.

Pope Agapetus sat at the same time;

After two years and eight months he departed,

And his life gave him twice seven days besides.

Concerning the Emperor Constantine Heraclius, son of the Great Heraclius, fifty-seventh from Augustus, and the chronicle of his time.

In the year 639 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Dagobert reigned in Africa, Constantine Heraclius, son of Heraclius, fifty-seventh from Augustus, obtained the empire; in the fourth month of his reign he was killed by poison through the treachery of his stepmother Martina and of the patriarch Pyrrhus. Martina herself, usurping the throne with her son Heraclona, held it for two years. After the noses of her son had been mutilated and her own tongue cut out, Constans Constantiniani, grandson of Heraclius’s son, was made emperor by the senate. Pyrrhus too, the author of that crime, was driven into exile, and Paul was substituted in his place. This is the Pyrrhus who, together with Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, devised the heresy that denied two wills in Christ. The rest is contained in verse.

Likewise, concerning that same Constantine the Third, and the pope of his time, it is related in verse.

The third Constantine comes as Caesar,

And Vitalian now sits as Roman pope.

Through both, great welfare comes to the Churches.

The Caesar bore eight years as his span of life;

The pope lived four times six years, to be duly reckoned,

And seven months and eight days.

Concerning Pope Deodatus.

Pope Deodatus came at the same time;

After twice two years and two months he departed,

And his life gave five days besides.

Concerning the pontiff Dionysius.

Pope Dionysius is recorded under the same ruler;

He is recorded as sitting five years and five months,

And his life is given eight days besides.

Concerning Pope Agapetus.

Pope Agapetus sat at the same time;

After two years and eight months he departed,

And his life gave him twice seven days besides.

Concerning the Emperor Constans, son of Constantine, fifty-eighth from Augustus; and the chronicle of his time.

In the year 642 from the Incarnation of the Lord, after Heraclona had been driven out with [Col. 0916A] her mother, Constans, son of Constantine, reigned, fifty-eighth from Augustus. Having fallen into the same heresy as his grandfather Heraclius, he sent Pope Martin into exile at Cherson, because Martin, after holding a synod, had excommunicated the patriarch Paul, Pyrrhus, and Cyrus. There Martin, resplendent in many signs of miracles, passed to the Lord.

Later, Constans, after convening a synod under Pope Vitalian, renounced the heresy and sent to Saint Peter Gospels of marvellous size, covered with gold and adorned with gems. Not many days afterward, wishing to wrest Italy from Lombard power, he sailed across the seas and landed at Tarentum. Coming after that to Benevento, he took nearly all the cities inhabited by [Col. 0916B] the Lombards. But he razed the city of Lucera to the ground; then, having taken as a hostage Rumald’s sister, namely the daughter of King Grimoald, he turned his way toward Naples. Proceeding thence toward the City, he found Pope Vitalian coming to meet him at the seventh mile with clergy and people. Thus he entered Rome with honour and offered Saint Peter a pallium woven with gold.

He was considering transferring the empire back to the City, because he hated the Constantinopolitans as supporters of heretics, since they had advised him in the sacrilege committed against Pope Martin.

In his days the blessed virgin Gertrude, daughter of Pippin the Fat, rested in a blessed death. When Dagobert also died, his son Clovis succeeded him. For another son, namely Sigebert, while he still lived, had left Austrasia [Col. 0916C] and entrusted him to Cunibert, bishop of the people of Cologne, and to Pippin the Elder.

The Emperor Constans Heraclius, departing from the City, entered Sicily. Having remained there for six years, he was killed through the treachery of his own men in a bath, in the eighth year of his reign. When he died, the soldiers made a certain man named Mityus emperor. Upon learning this, Constantius, son of Constantine, entered Sicily and killed Mityus with the murderers of his father; and, having settled affairs in the West, returned to Constantinople. The verses contain the rest concerning Constans Heraclius.

Likewise, concerning that same Constans, Emperor Heraclius, and the pope of his time.

[Col. 0916D] While Heraclius reigns, Pope Leo is granted his seat;

His life is reported to have lasted ten years and one month;

He is powerful in speech and brings forth blessed writings.

Concerning Pope Benedict.

In Heraclius’s time Pope Benedict now comes;

He lives three times three months, then is left to the tomb;

His life granted him eight days.

Concerning the Emperor Theodosius, son of Constans Heraclius, and the chronicle of his time.

In the year 670 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Theodosius Constantine, son of Constans Heraclius, with his two sons Heraclius and Tiberius, obtained the empire, fifty-ninth from Augustus. In these days Ansegisel, son of blessed Arnulf, bishop of Metz, [Col. 0917A] who had formerly been mayor of the palace in the Frankish kingdom, attained the dignity of mayor of the palace. Constantine Theodosius ended his life in the seventeenth year of his reign.

Concerning the Emperor Justinian, son of Theodosius, sixtieth from Augustus, and the chronicle of his time.

In the year 686 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Justinian, son of Theodosius Constantine, was sixtieth from Augustus as emperor. He made peace with the Saracens and subjected Africa, freed from them, to the Roman empire.

The descent of all the Charleses, from Ansegisel, son of Arnulf, bishop of Metz, who had formerly been duke of the Franks and mayor of the palace.

At that time Pippin, son of Ansegisel, became mayor of the palace [Col. 0917B] and administered the entire kingdom of the Franks. From this point onward the years and deeds of this Pippin the Fat are set out in the Catalogue of the Kings of the Franks. For from the time of this Pippin the Fat, who was mayor of the palace, the kings of the Franks, stripped of all affairs and honours of the kingdom, reigned in name alone; conversely, the mayors of the palace held the care and strength of the kingdom.

Justinian was mutilated in nose and lip by the patrician Leontius, whom he himself had held in chains for three years. Leontius occupied the empire for three years, while the mutilated emperor was meanwhile kept in exile. After those three years Tiberius, surnamed Apsimar, likewise [Col. 0917C] cut off Leontius’s nose, thrust him into a monastery, and himself held the usurped kingdom for seven years.

In these days, under Pope Sergius, the synod of Aquileia was assembled. Justinian, whom the patrician Leontius had earlier mutilated, recovered the captured city of Constantinople with the assistance of the king of Bulgaria and afterwards held it for six years. He then captured Tiberius and Leontius. He ordered them, bound in chains, to be dragged through the streets, while all the people cried after them: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 90). He himself also trod upon their necks and finally beheaded them. He caused others too, found guilty of the conspiracy perpetrated against him, to be tortured by various punishments. [Col. 0917D] Moreover, as often as he wiped away a drop of rheum falling from his mutilated nose, he ordered one of them to be killed. He also sent the patriarch Gallicinus, after tearing out his eyes, into exile at Rome; he made Cyrus, an abbot who had supplied him with necessities, patriarch, and appointed Tiberius, Cyrus’s son, his partner in the kingdom. Then he wished to seize Philippus, whom he himself had exiled in Pontus. But Philippicus was made emperor by the army and, after a battle six miles from the city of Constantinople, killed Justinian; the adherents of Philippicus also killed Justinian’s son.

Concerning Philippicus, emperor at Constantinople, and the chronicle of the kings of the Franks in the same period.

In the year 713 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Philippicus, [Col. 0918A] sixty-first from Augustus, received the empire. Then the younger Dagobert reigned in Francia in name alone. But Pippin the Fat, mayor of the palace, possessed all the honour and power of the kingdom. At that time the Roman people decreed that neither Philippicus’s documents nor even his commands should be received in the Church or at Rome, since he was a heretic; nor should his name be recited among the solemnities of the Mass. On the holy day of Pentecost, after coming out of the bath and lying in bed after noon, he was seized by Rufinus and Theodore, who had entered through the Golden Gate, and blinded, after he had begun to reign for one year and eleven months.

Concerning the Emperor Anastasius, sixty-second from Augustus, and the chronicle of his time.

[Col. 0918B] In the year 714 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Artemius, who after changing his name was called Anastasius, sixty-second from Augustus, received the empire and reigned three years.

Then, after the death of the younger Dagobert, king of the Franks, and of Pippin the Elder, Charles Martel, son of Pippin the Fat by Alpaida, who was grandfather of Charlemagne, became mayor of the palace. He administered the kingdom of the Franks for twenty-seven years, while the kings still remained there, but without honour or usefulness. This Charles Martel crushed in many wars a certain Ragenfrid, who wished to invade the kingdom; he subdued Bavaria and Swabia; conquered Gascony, Saxony, and Frisia; and killed 385,000 Saracens. Therefore, while the Frankish kingdom was enlarged in many ways under the most warlike prince Charles Martel, [Col. 0918C] the empire of the Greeks diminished. The soldiers set up Theodosius as emperor against Anastasius, though unwilling; in battle he defeated Anastasius and had him ordained a priest.

Concerning the Emperor Theodosius II, sixty-third from Augustus.

This Theodosius, having obtained the empire, sixty-third from Augustus, ruled one year. Leo, sixty-fourth from Augustus, succeeded him, while Charles Martel still remained in Francia.

Concerning Leo, emperor of the Greeks, sixty-fourth from Augustus.

This emperor, sixty-fourth from Augustus, called Leo, ordered the images [Col. 0918D] of the Lord to be burned and holy persons resisting his iniquity to be beheaded. Among them Saint Theodoxia suffered; her body, still entire, is preserved at Constantinople with immense veneration.

When Pope Gregory saw that the Emperor Leo was wicked and incorrigible, he persuaded all Italy to withdraw from his empire. At that time the relics of Saint Augustine were transported from Sardinia to Pavia by Liutprand, king of the Lombards. Then also the venerable priest Bede rested in peace. In these days the Saracens surrounded Constantinople in a siege for three years; at last they withdrew without victory. At Rome too 300,000 then perished by plague. Leo the emperor died in the fourth year of his reign; his son Constantius succeeded him.

Concerning the last Constantius, emperor of the Greeks, sixty-fifth from Augustus.

[Col. 0919A]

Constantius therefore became emperor in the year 742 from the Incarnation of the Lord, sixty-fifth from Augustus. This evildoer, sacrificing to demons and made worse than his father, given over to luxury and every impurity, afflicted God’s Church. Therefore he and his father appear to have deserved by their iniquities that their kingdom should be divided. In the first year of that Emperor Leo’s reign, Charles Martel, son of Pippin the Fat, died, leaving three sons: Carloman, Pippin the Short, and Grifo. Grifo, the younger, being troublesome, was captured by his brothers in Auvergne and held after battle, and remained with his wife Swanahild in a certain castle.

The rest our page relates in verse. Likewise, concerning the Emperor Theodosius in verse, and the pope of his time.

[Col. 0920A]

Theodosius’s life lasted twice twelve years,

And in his time adornment came also to the Churches;

He likewise ordained that images should stand in their proper order.

Pope Gregory II stands with Caesar Theodosius;

For ten years he was a fosterling of City and World,

He endured three times three months and three times eight days.

In Gregory’s time Bishop Boniface appears;

From the see of Mainz he performs many miracles;

By baptismal grace he brought the German kingdoms.

**GODEFROY OF VITERBO, PANTHEON.**

[Col. 0919]

**PART SEVENTEEN. THE EMPIRE IS TRANSFERRED TO THE FRANKS.**

**Author’s prologue.**

[Col. 0919B]

I remember that above I promised to relate how the Franks, of whom we make mention here, came into Gaul, and how, separated from Roman rule, they began to remain under their own authority and power.

Therefore, at the time when Aeneas came into Italy after the destruction of Troy, the younger Priam, nephew of the great Priam through his sister, and with him Antenor, prince of the Trojans, came with 13,000 men by the Illyrian Sea into Venetia. There, building the city of Padua—in which Antenor himself is today found honourably buried in royal fashion—they established their dwellings in the region of Scythia beyond the Maeotian marshes, building the city of Sicambria, from which they were also called Sicambri. [Col. 0919C]

When the whole world had been subdued into a province of the Romans, and they too had been subdued among the others, after time had passed they occupied Germany, where they were thereafter also called Germans.

Then, when the Emperor Valentinian could not destroy the Alans, who had been attacked and had withdrawn among the Maeotian marshes, he issued an edict that whatever people should conquer and destroy the Alans would be free from every tribute for the next ten years. Therefore the Germans, desirous of that glory, moved an army against the Alans, conquered and utterly exterminated them; consequently they were free of tribute for ten years. Because of this same victory they were perpetually called *Franci*, that is, “the fierce,” by the Emperor Valentinian.

[Col. 0920B] But when the ten years had elapsed and the Romans demanded from the Franks their customary tributes, the Franks, now made unrestrained by that very freedom, refused to pay the tribute. They had among themselves ancient leaders, as I have said, Priam and Antenor. Therefore, when the Romans fought against them, and Priam their king was killed in battle, they withdrew into the regions of the kingdom of Thuringia with their leaders, namely the sons of Priam and Antenor, Marcomer and Sunno. After Sunno’s death, they took counsel together and made Marcomer’s son, named Pharamund, their king.

They also began from that time to possess laws composed by their lawgivers Wisogast and Salogast. From that Salogast the Salic Law received its name; [Col. 0920C] the Franks, who are also called Salian, use this law even today. When Pharamund died, his son Crinitus succeeded, and from him the kings of the Franks were called the Long-haired.

In these times Francia began to grow and Rome to decline, as I said above. For the peoples subdued by the Romans had now learned to rule by themselves. Conversely, the Romans, who had always ruled, were compelled to serve the peoples. For after the Goths had ravaged the City itself, they settled in Gaul beyond the river Loire. The Burgundians likewise dwelt beside the Rhône, and they too shortly began to have kings. So also the Franks, crossing the Rhine, drove out the Romans who lived there. Afterwards, having taken the cities of Tournai and Cambrai and gradually advancing from there, they claimed and subjected Rheims, [Col. 0921A] Soissons, Orléans, Cologne—then called Agrippina—Trier, almost all Gaul and Germany, from Aquitaine as far as Bavaria.

When Clovis, king of the Franks, died, his son Merovech, from whom the Franks were called Merovingians, succeeded to the kingdom. Upon his death Childeric succeeded. Since he lived luxuriously, his people expelled him from the kingdom, and he withdrew to the king of the Thuringians, named Bisinus. Received humanely by him, he secretly slept with his wife Bisina, a most beautiful queen. Afterwards that same Childeric was restored once more to the Frankish kingdom through the intervention of his friends. Queen Bisina followed in his wake; when King Childeric asked why she had come, she answered: [Col. 0921B] “I come to you, to remain with you.” The king therefore took her as his wife and begot by her a son, Clovis. But while Childeric, expelled from the kingdom, was staying in Thuringia, as we have said, a certain Roman named Aegidius was put in his place in the kingdom of the Franks. After eight years Childeric was recalled to the kingdom. He invaded the city of Agrippina and, having driven out all the Romans there who seemed to favour Aegidius, installed his Frankish supporters. Accordingly, he commanded that the same city, which until that time had been called Agrippina, should forever be called Cologne because of its Frankish inhabitants. When Aegidius died, his son Syagrius reigned in the city of Soissons.

King Childeric, departing this life, left the kingdom to his son [Col. 0921C] Clovis. This Clovis was the first Christian among the kings of the Franks, baptized by Saint Remigius. Syagrius, son of Aegidius, being unable to reign or contend against Clovis, withdrew to Alaric, king of the Visigoths. This Alaric was ninth from Alaric the Great, king of the Goths, by whom, as we said above, Rome was captured and ravaged. Clovis demanded Syagrius back. Alaric handed him over. Once delivered up, he was killed; and all the Romans then living in Gaul were so exterminated that not one could be found in all Gaul.

It seems to me that in those times the Franks learned from those Romans who had lived there the Roman language that they use to this day. [Col. 0921D] What language they had naturally before that, we do not know. Thus Clovis, having subdued the Alemanni and now become Christian, declared war on the Goths and Aquitanians. As he set out, he made a vow to Saint Martin at Tours, who had already been dead 112 years. When he had triumphed over the Goths and killed their king Alaric, he returned to Tours and gave thanks to God and Saint Martin. The church of Saint Martin was then enriched; wishing to redeem with his own money his horse, which he had earlier, while going to battle, given to Saint Martin, he sent one hundred solidi to the church’s keeper as redemption for that horse. But the horse stood immovable. Hearing this, the king perceived that Saint Martin had thought the horse’s [Col. 0922A] price too little. Therefore he offered a further hundred solidi for its redemption. When these had been given, the horse at once followed and was presented to the king. Hence Clovis is said to have remarked: “Saint Martin is a good helper, but an expensive dealer.”

We set down all this concerning the origin of the Franks here under the heading of the Emperor Leo, in whose time the Greeks altogether lost dominion over Rome and the Franks began to possess the Roman Empire in the West: first through Charles Martel, duke of the Franks, whom Pippin the Fat, mayor of the palace, begot by a secret union with Duchess Alpaida; then through Pippin the Short, son of Charles Martel; afterwards through Charlemagne, son of [Col. 0922B] Pippin the Short, the first emperor of the Franks; then through Louis, son of Charles; and thereafter down to the present day, as, with God as author, we shall relate in the future in distinct chapters, at their respective places and times.

Concerning the last Leo, emperor of the Greeks, sixty-sixth from Augustus; in whose time the empire of the Greeks passed to the Franks; and concerning the Roman pontiffs of that time and sundry chronicles.

The empire of Caesar Leo is now said to be present;

For sixteen completed years he bears the reins of glory;

He is the last whom his Rome venerates.

Pope Gregory sat with Caesar Leo;

For ten years he duly exercised Roman honour,

And life cherished him for a further three times three months.

[Col. 0922C] Moreover, he endured eight days until his rest.

Charles Martel, duke of the Franks, governed kingdoms;

Pippin the Short then sat as duke with his father;

There were very frequent wars with the Goths.

Up to this point the Greek kings may be recalled,

Whom I have said then ruled Italy by imperial authority;

Now the Greek crown falls in Italy also.

We turn to the Franks, by whose strength

The Italian people can be protected and Rome held secure:

Charles Martel shall be protector and founder.

Thereupon Pippin the Short deserves to become king;

After Martel he defends papal rights;

He also becomes patrician and bears honour in the City.

After these things Charles shall be able to deserve the empire,

And by his power defend the Church;

[Col. 0922D] By his empire the Greek crown perishes.

Concerning the genealogy of Charlemagne, from the times of his great-grandfather Pippin the Fat, and how this line obtained the kingdom of the Franks, thereafter receiving the Roman Empire and the whole world.

In the year 710 from the Incarnation of the Lord, when the younger Dagobert, king of the Franks, died, his little son remained under the guardianship of Pippin the Fat, who was mayor of the palace. He too shortly afterwards perished through the plots of certain persons. Then Grimoald, legitimate son of Pippin the Fat, having usurped the kingdom, was captured by the relatives of the deceased King Dagobert and held in strict custody until he died there.

At the same time, that part of Gaul in which lie the rivers Seine and Loire was called Gaudina. There [Col. 0923A] two petty kings who were brothers, on their mother’s counsel, invaded the kingdom of the Franks—that is, of the Germans—beyond the Rhine, since there was then no king there. In their first onset they attacked the city of Worms. Repelled by the Franks in battle, they renewed their strength and surrounded the city of Mainz with a siege. Since the Franks had no king, they determined to make Charles Martel, son of Pippin the Fat and born of Alpaida, king. He refused indeed to receive the crown, but took up their standard against the Gaudinians; joining battle with the aforesaid kings, he killed both kings with his own hand in battle, and, advancing with that victory, subjected all the province of Gaudina, including Rheims and Paris.

Then the same Charles Martel by perpetual decree [Col. 0923B] ordained that this province should not be called Gaudina by that name, but should be called *Francigena*; in the German tongue he commanded the province to be called after his own name *Carlinga*, and its people *Carlingi*, after his own name, just as Caesarea is named from Caesar. All Germans preserve this term even today. For they say: “I am going to Carlinga; I come from Carlinga; that man is a Carlingus; and he has the Carlingan language.” In Latin, however, they call them *Francigenae*, as though born from the Franks. They call the western Germans—that is, those on this side of the kingdom and beyond it—Franks. They likewise call the land itself Francia from the Franks. They are also accustomed to call Franconia after a certain duke of theirs, Francon. Therefore let us speak of Charles Martel himself, [Col. 0923C] what kind of man he was and how many sons he left.

Concerning Charles Martel.

Therefore, in the year 714 from the Incarnation of the Lord, this aforesaid Charles, surnamed Martel, was mayor of the palace. He was father of Pippin the Short and grandfather of Charlemagne. As duke and mayor of the palace of the Franks, born by concubinage to Duke Pippin the Fat and Duchess Alpaida, he conquered and subjected by his prudence all Gauls and Spains; freed the Roman Church and Italy from the Goths; and he was the first, with the consent of Pope Zacharias, to give the tithes of churches in fief to soldiers for the necessity of God’s Church. At that time the priest Bede died, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, and bestowed many writings [Col. 0923D] upon the Churches.

Charles Martel left two sons, Pippin and Carloman, who were jointly called dukes and mayors of the palace of the Franks. But after four years Carloman became a monk at Monte Cassino. Pippin, however, through Pope Zachary and by election of the Franks, was made king of the Franks, when King Childeric, being incompetent, was made a monk by the Franks and sent into a monastery. Charles the Great was born to Pippin. The remaining verses concern Emperor Leo and Charles Martel:

## On the First Coming of the Goths into Italy, in the Time of Leo, Emperor of the Greeks, When Charles Martel Freed Italy from the Goths

While Leo wore the diadem of the Greeks’ Caesar,

A scourge came upon Rome; peace departed from the land.

[Col. 0924A] For Gothic madness stirred up dreadful battles.

Gascony bore Goths trained for crime;

A multitude of Goths—a race and embodiment of evils—

Made every land their prey by their strength.

They press upon the Ligurians with war, bringing sufferings on every side;

Tuscany is laid waste, and Rome too feels their fury;

The Italian land mourns: death stood before its doors.

Rome seeks aid; Leo gave none. Therefore the Romans

Thereafter strive through the Franks to remove these conflicts;

The Germans come, and the standards of Francia gleam.

At the request of Pope Gregory and of the whole senate,

Charles Martel is summoned to undertake war,

That he may free his fatherland; the charge is granted by the City.

The commonwealth grants tithes as the soldier’s reward;

[Col. 0924B] The pope summons the nobles: let them come to defend Rome.

Then the Church gave them its tithed possessions.

The multitude of Goths is driven away by Martel’s warfare;

Rome is restored, the Church’s peace repaired,

And the glory of the Franks shines in the chief city.

## On the Death and Burial of Charles Martel, and on His Son Pippin the Short, Together with His Two Brothers

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 743, Charles Martel having died and been buried in the city of Liguria called Aix, his son Pippin, called the Short, and his brother Carloman, having driven their third brother Grifo from the kingdom as though he were their enemy, divided the kingdom between themselves. Carloman received Austrasia—that is, *Osterrich*—and Alamannia, that is, Swabia and Thuringia. Pippin [Col. 0924C] received Burgundy, Neustria, and the province on this side of the Rhône.

Then, after many battles undertaken by them against their enemies, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 746, when the monastery of Fulda was being founded, Carloman left all the land to his brother Pippin. He himself received the monastic habit, through Pope Zachary, on Mount Soracte, where blessed Sylvester had formerly hidden; and thence, because of the excessive crowding of people, he moved to Monte Cassino. Having become a cleric, he awaited the end of his life there. There also, as is said, he at one time tended swine; and there, at the entrance of the church, he received a blessed burial.

In these times Pippin, duke of the Franks, was made patrician of the Romans.

[Col. 0924D] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 751, when the kings in the Frankish kingdom ruled in name alone, while the mayor of the palace held all the administration and power of the kingdom, and when the Church, afflicted by the Goths and Lombards, had urgently sought assistance from the Franks, Pippin, called the Short, while mayor of the palace, sent envoys to Pope Zachary—namely Burchard, bishop of Würzburg, and his chaplain Fulrad—to inquire, and asked what Zachary considered should be done concerning the kingdom of the Franks.

The pope replied that it was better for the man who possessed the care and power of the whole kingdom to be king than for the man who was king in name alone. For in the king there remained only the shadow of a name, whereas power and dignity appeared effectively in Pippin. At that time [Col. 0925A] Childeric was king, incompetent and useless, from the genealogy of the ancient kings of the Franks, who had all been called Merovingians after Merovech, son of Clodio, and who likewise possessed the empty name of king. Pippin’s envoys therefore returned from the City, and all Gaul willingly consented to Pope Zachary’s counsel.

## Pippin Is Made King of the Franks

Therefore, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 752, by the authority of Pope Zachary, Pippin was chosen for the kingdom in the city of Soissons by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, and the other princes of the realm. In the following year, Pope Zachary having died, Pope Stephen succeeded him. Since he suffered many evils from Aistulf, king of the Lombards, he met Pippin as the latter returned from a battle with the Saxons, in which [Col. 0925B] he had also received news of the death of his brother Grifo. He met him at the estate called Carisius, begging him to come to the aid of the Roman Church. The remaining verses state:

## On the Goths and the Lombards, from Whom Pippin Freed the Roman Church and All Italy

After the Goths had first been removed by war far from the land,

A people of the Huns came, hostile to the wishes of the Ligurians,

Destructive to every region of Italy.

While this people makes war and fights a threatening enemy,

A woman, fighting, lets her hair hang down before her,

And an artificial beard hangs down in like fashion.

The Ligurians marvel at the long beards upon their breasts;

When they see the beards, they are afraid, as beasts fear apparitions.

[Col. 0925C] The Ligurian people feared, yielded, and gave up their arms.

Thus that people deserved to be called Lombard,

Having contrived by this device to rule over the Ligurians;

It conquered Apulia—shore, countryside, and sea.

Luitprand was king of the Lombards in the city of Pavia;

He oppresses the Church and presses Rome as far as Sutri,

Nor does he allow the homeland to possess the path of peace.

The pope is hemmed in. Caesar Leo is called upon for these matters;

No hope is offered there; the king of the Franks is asked,

But the king does not come, since the head was but a shadow.

At that time incompetent Childeric is regarded as having reigned,

Who neither protects the kingdom of the Franks by courage

Nor knows well how to maintain royal halls.

Pippin, duke of the Franks, takes care to protect his kingdoms,

[Col. 0925D] And he himself is regarded as mayor of the palace,

A king and patrician who will soon be great.

Pippin, duke of the Franks, then governed the realms,

And fully held the office of king beneath the king;

The king there was contemptible, with an empty title.

While the king sat before the princes upon the throne,

He commanded nothing unless that duke first ordered it;

The duke himself bore the laws and the power.

The king was Childeric, who is thought to have then reigned;

He was the shadow of a king, not a king, if he is rightly described.

If Francia can do so, a shadow shall not be its head.

Then King Luitprand reigned in the city of Pavia,

And oppressed Rome and likewise Pope Zachary,

Ever gaping greedily to destroy the Church altogether.

While the Short held the government of the Frankish realm,

[Col. 0926A] Yet King Childeric sat empty and contemptible,

The Short wrote, conveying these words to the Apostolic See:

“If you desire the churches to be aided by the kingdom’s strength,

Command that a vigorous and strong king be raised up;

‘We retain the strength for these matters of the fatherland,’ he says.

For King Childeric, to whom Francia supplies the name,

Is like a funeral thing, to whom no power is given;

He has a bare name, but the land supports me.

Write, Father, to the Franks; ask, urge, and always command them

To make a king powerful in homeland and sword;

For the shadow of a ruler gives no assistance.”

A papal letter of the greatest renown comes to the Franks;

The throne is raised up, glory falls to Pippin.

For all Francia gave the kingdom to him.

[Col. 0926B] Childeric became a monk and had his head shorn;

He hid himself under religious observance in a monastery.

Such was fortune; thus the wheel turned and fell.

From the see of Mainz Boniface anoints the king;

Francia, made subject, joins itself to the king’s service;

Everywhere safety gives way to King Pippin the Short.

Thus Pippin gained the kingdom by his worth,

He who was least in body restored affairs to a better state,

And governs subject realms better than the rest.

His wife was Bertha, great of foot by name;

She came from Hungary, but was found to have a Greek mother,

For she was the daughter of Emperor Heraclius.

From this union the future supreme crown comes about:

Charles the Great, whom Bertha was to bear;

Having first written what was seen, she is joined by her art. [Meaning uncertain.]

### Chronicle

[Col. 0926C]

The Trojan offspring was once divided into two lines of kings, namely into Aeneas and the younger Priam. Aeneas came into Italy, and from him descended all Roman kings and emperors. But the younger Priam went into Germany, and from him all German, or Teutonic, kings were born. These two lines, therefore, coming from Troy, converge in the one Charles the Great, since he was German on his father’s side and Roman or Greek through his mother Bertha.

## Pippin’s Descent

The Trojan offspring, divided into two parental lines,

Is joined in the womb of Bertha, in Pippin’s seed;

[Col. 0926D] In Pippin’s seed Troy becomes one for itself.

If now you seek German and Roman branches,

Charles stands forth, the sole heir, the jewel of the lineage:

Roman through his mother, German through his father.

Let the written digression on King Pippin now rest;

Let Pippin’s deeds against the Lombards be made clear:

Behold, I shall sing how he aided the Church.

## Again, on How Pippin Is Made King of the Franks through Pope Zachary

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 754, Pippin was released by Pope Stephen, together with all the princes of Francia, from allegiance to the aforesaid Childeric, king of the Franks. Then also, Childeric having been shorn, made a monk, and thrust into a monastery, Pippin received royal anointing. At that time the kingdom [Col. 0927A] of the Merovingians came to an end, and the kingdom of the Carolings began, who afterwards obtained the Greek Empire at Rome. From this act also the Roman pontiffs derive authority to change a kingdom. Pippin thereafter governed the kingdom of the Franks laudably both in name and in reality.

### Chronicle

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 755, Pippin, requested by Pope Stephen, raised an army against Aistulf, king of the Lombards, and prepared to enter Italy. The Lombards had prepared their defense by placing strong walls before them in mountain narrows. Pippin killed many of them, broke down the barriers of the walls, passed through, and encamped on the Lombard plain. King Aistulf gathered himself into Pavia, [Col. 0927B] where, besieged by Pippin, he was compelled to provide forty hostages and moreover swear that he would no longer harass the Roman Church. Pope Stephen was honorably sent back to Rome with a Frankish escort, and Pippin himself returned to Francia.

In this year Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, who had founded the Church of Fulda and many others, received the crown of martyrdom from the Frisians to whom he had preached.

Whatever else pleases is set forth in verses concerning these deeds.

## On the Death of King Luitprand of the Lombards, the Elevation of King Aistulf, and Pippin’s First Entry into Italy

Luitprand dies; Aistulf is raised to the throne,

And the Church is burdened by a more grievous fury under him;

Through his leadership Rome is given over to destruction.

[Col. 0927C] The Roman is ordered to bring him golden tribute;

The Roman bishop nowhere maintains his rights;

The Greeks dissemble and do not aid their own realms.

Now, at prayer, they call Pippin for the first time to battle,

To conquer Pavia and cast down the king,

To free Italy and Rome’s own bosom.

He comes, besieges the king, and compels him at once

To restore to the Romans what Aistulf had then carried off;

Grace is shown to the king who rules the holy places.

Pippin visits bountiful Rome with his army,

Yet he did not wish to wear the imperial crown in Rome;

He becomes patrician: name and honor resound.

Thence he returned to the Mainz halls of his homeland,

The royal seat of the Franks, then renowned,

[Col. 0927D] Where the supreme glory of the Germans resides.

While King Luitprand reigned in the city of Pavia.

The pope previously mentioned, Zachary, met his fate;

He sat for ten years and twice a month in life.

Adding eighteen days to the years,

Stephen, the venerable bishop, is raised at Rome,

And through his efforts peace returned to life.

## On the Second Rebellion of King Aistulf and Pippin’s Second Victory over Him

After Pippin’s departure, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, broke his promises and showed himself more savage than usual against the Church. Therefore Pippin again entered Italy with force; and Aistulf, again besieged in Pavia, was compelled to set everything right through stronger promises and more hostages. Moreover, [Col. 0928A] he was forced to surrender Ravenna to the Church, together with certain other cities. Pippin himself returned to Gaul.

In the following year, while the Greek kingdom, as noted above, was declining, and the kingdom of the Franks had now been greatly exalted, envoys of Emperor Constantine came from Greece with great gifts to Pippin at Compiègne. Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, likewise then rendered fidelity and submission to King Pippin with his princes. After this Pippin defeated the Saxons in a very severe war and made them tributaries. Not long afterward he crushed Waifar, the great duke of Aquitaine, in battle and compelled him to give hostages. Duke Waifar of Aquitaine and Duke Tassilo of Aguaria then began again to rebel. Pippin [Col. 0928B] killed Waifar after various battles. He also subdued Tassilo, having sufficiently crushed him. Then Pippin fell ill at Tours and, having been carried to Paris, died in the fourteenth year from the day on which he had been anointed king, but in the twenty-third year after he had received the principate following his father, leaving two sons, Charles and Carloman.

Our page relates the rest in verse.

## Again, We Relate in Verse Concerning the Same Pippin

While the senate thinks that it has escaped Aistulf’s crime,

The king of the Lombards soon prepares for worse things,

And his designs now allow no rest.

The bishop complains that Aistulf inflicts torments;

The clergy’s life begs Pippin to defend it in his accustomed way:

If he delays, Rome, hemmed in, perishes.

[Col. 0928C] Pippin, carried over the Alps through a swift pass,

Engages with his soldiers; Aistulf is driven away in war,

Shut within his city and constrained to seek terms.

He swears, and the whole matter is bound by hostages:

If henceforth the pope is afflicted by the Lombard plague,

Let royal punishment take the hostages’ heads.

Peace having been restored, a pleasing offering is given to Peter;

Trousered Francia visits those blessed places,

And returns to its homeland, the settled peace remaining firm.

## On the Elevation of Desiderius, King of the Lombards, and His Opponent Ratchis

When King Aistulf’s life is shortened by its brief day,

His brother Ratchis, a monk, prepares to reign;

Desiderius’ party was hostile to him.

The peoples being divided and these kings troubled,

[Col. 0928D] Arms press against arms, and many are slain;

With opposing battle-lines each fights fiercely enough.

Now Pope Stephen gives his favor to Desiderius;

And he swears to him not at all to harm the honor

Which the pope is accustomed to hold over the Italians.

Ratchis yields as a monk; the other party takes its seat;

The Ligurian people reverently obey Desiderius,

For the pope gave him a time of assistance.

Rare is the Ligurian’s faith: the king violates the treaty of peace,

The bonds of the treaty formerly given now rendered void;

The pope is violently shaken by grief without cause.

When Rome learns this, it grieves at altered circumstances;

It stands like a broken ship or prey prepared for pirates,

Its affairs shaken on every side and given to the flames.

## Charles the Great, Son of Pippin, Is Raised to the Kingdom of the Franks upon Pippin’s Death

[Col. 0929A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 768, while Constantine V still ruled in Greece, Charles the Great, son of Pippin the Short, divided the kingdom with his brother Carloman and began to reign. First he drove Hunald, who, after Duke Waifar had been killed, was renewing war in Aquitaine, to Lupo, duke of Gascony; afterwards he received into submission both Hunald himself and Lupo. Then, in the following year, after celebrating a general assembly at Worms, he prepared to visit the thresholds of the apostles for prayer. In the third year of his reign, his brother Carloman died, and Carloman’s wife with her sons fled to Desiderius, king of the Lombards.

[Col. 0929B] Charles, therefore, having now gained the kingdom alone, entered Saxony with an army. Having laid everything waste with sword and fire and taken hostages there, he returned. Then, at the request of Pope Hadrian, he entered Italy and enclosed Desiderius, king of the Lombards, in a siege at Pavia. Leaving his army there, he proceeded to Rome for prayer. Returning thence, he compelled the exhausted city to surrender and carried off the king as a captive.

Meanwhile the Saxons, emboldened by the king’s absence and abandoning their allegiance, ravaged places adjoining their land. The king, however, having subdued Italy, returned to Francia and entered Saxony with his soldiers arranged in three divisions. Having ravaged the land with fires, he plundered an immense quantity of booty; and, returning not long afterward, he again took hostages from them.

[Col. 0929C] In these days Constantine the persecutor died in the thirty-fifth year of his reign, and his son Leo succeeded him, holding the Greek monarchy in Greece rather weakly for six years.

## On Leo, the Sixty-First Emperor of the Greeks Mentioned Above, and the Chronicle of His Time

Therefore, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 776, Leo, the sixty-sixth from Augustus, received the Greek Empire. At first he appeared milder; hence the princes requested that his son be made emperor.

During the same time the Saxons, as was their custom, broke the agreement not once but often. Charles crushed them in various battles and persuaded very many of them to receive the Christian faith. Leo the emperor, however, died in the sixth year of his reign.

It is pleasing to relate the remaining deeds in verse:

## Again, We Relate in Verse of Pippin and His Lineage, and How Charles Was Called into Italy to Aid the Roman Church

Pippin dies; vigorous Charles arises,

Born at Ingelheim, whose mother Bertha was Hungarian,

And whose father was Pippin: the chronicles disclose the truth.

The youth’s stature was twice that of his small father;

Greater were his excellence, appearance, and courage of spirit;

His renown was famous, his glory exceedingly great.

Now the aforesaid second Pope Stephen dies;

[Col. 0930A] The world flourished under his teaching for five years.

He lived, besides, to the end eight days.

The venerable third Stephen succeeds at Rome,

Whom the tyrant Desiderius troubles everywhere;

He was pope for only a short time.

For he sat three years and five months;

I add eighteen days during which he sat,

And Desiderius gave him grim times.

After him blessed Pope Hadrian is raised,

Whose pontificate Desiderius troubles;

Pressed on every side, he too seeks Charles’s aid.

Hadrian lived twenty-four years;

I add ten months and ten days to be counted,

And I further add seven days.

Excellent Charles rereads the papal letters;

[Col. 0930B] The pope writes him the evils which the Lombard has committed,

And asks that he bring Christ’s weapons to the flock.

The Frankish nobles are asked along with the king

To defend the Church together by their strength;

Pippin’s deeds are recalled there.

Such, it is reported, was the judgment of the nobles:

If the Church wishes to be defended by Frankish warfare,

Charles must be set over the Empire.

For it is futile thus to conquer Italy,

Unless a ruler remains who can govern it

And bear the rights of empire in like form.

He who holds the offices that often relapse and fall again

Has passive times for himself, but grants few active ones;

For he punishes evils but does not bind them.

Let the king of the Franks be lord of lords at Rome;

[Col. 0930C] Let him hold the Empire, bring down the land of the Italians,

And take all the land from the Danes.

While Rome seeks the king’s aid in every entreaty,

While it asks him to deign to defend the homeland from the enemy,

It says that he should take up the Empire as another lord.

The king says: “I refuse to bear Italian labors

Unless I likewise steadily possess Italian honors,

Which, if they became mine, would establish peace for me.

I weigh the battles of Pippin, my father,

How great were the weapons which that worthy man brought in anger against the Ligurians;

Yet the resisting crowd did not cease from its deceits.

Italy cannot be held without a ruler;

If you wish to preserve the clergy’s peace without a king,

What was yesterday’s error will be greater tomorrow.

[Col. 0930D] No archate avails while no one rules it,

Nor does empire avail unless it is governed by Caesar’s sword;

Royal rule establishes a subjected homeland.

Mighty Rome flourished while Caesar sat in the City;

The commonwealth grew, the Italian people rested in peace,

And the land paid fitting tribute to its lords.

If Rome wishes the times that I recall to be restored,

Or the crime of King Desiderius to be undone,

It is expedient that the rights of empire for which I ask be granted.”

When the king had spoken, the people demand that arms be taken up;

They seek the rights of their clergy and themselves desire to defend them,

For Rome perishes through Desiderius’ fury.

The court of the Franks agrees to their prayers,

That the victory of the Germans may assume the Empire,

And that the treasury may everywhere seize Italian land.

[Col. 0931A] The nobles move their standards; the king orders arms to be prepared.

He crosses over to the Ligurians, over whom he now wishes to rule,

But Desiderius brings on dreadful battles.

A field among the Ligurians is rightly called Mortaria,

Where the king engages; the defeated Ligurian force flees,

Thus Desiderius’ host turns its back.

Because of the slaughter of many peoples that was done,

That tract of land is said to bear the name Mortaria,

Which now stands as a great market for travellers.

Then two companions, blessed in merits and life,

Amis and Amelius, were killed in the same battle;

Charles granted them fitting tombs in abundance.

Now the king besieges noble Pavia with his army,

And orders it to be made subject to Frankish swords,
