[Col. 0931B] And to restore to the Church what it unjustly holds by seizure.

The heavily besieged city suffers, restrained by fire and hunger.

Lombard pride, wearied by wounds, yields,

And, though unwilling, remains shut in.

There the remarkable duke Roland bore the standards,

And Oliver, likewise notable for companionable worth;

The fierce men then had these as commanders for their king.

Meanwhile the queenly power visits Rome;

Nor did it then wish to claim the imperial crown.

It prays, and the standards fly back to the Ligurians.

After Charles returned from the City, he visits and conquers Italy,

Presses it to be subject to the treasury,

And restores fitting estates to its churches.

[Col. 0931C] King Desiderius, whom he had shut within by warfare,

Is handed over to exile in chains together with his wife;

His life ends in prison at Aachen.

When King Charles harassed King Desiderius,

Two hundred and five passing years earlier

The Italian land had been subject to the Lombards.

## History of the Lombards, Who Were Formerly Called Vinuli

Two dukes of the Lombards came from the island of Scatinavia, namely Hibor and Hangio; their mother was the very wise Gambara. Having then set out, they found, on the coast of the Ocean Sea beneath a rock called Altissima, seven men who had been placed there from most ancient times, sleeping. They were expensively dressed in Roman fashion and incorrupt both in clothing and in body. [Col. 0931D] When one man attempted to strip one of them of his clothes, the hand of the person touching them immediately withered; therefore none of the others afterwards ventured to touch them.

That place, the province itself, and those peoples are called Vinuli. They eat raw flesh and drink blood, as the *History of the Lombards* attests. They are also clothed in raw, shaggy hides of beasts, resembling stags; and they never walk without a drawn bow and arrows. They have snow at all times, and in some of their places, during their summer, there is clear daylight in the middle of our night, so that they seem then to be without nights. When it is the solstice among us, the sun is not seen there. The days there are shorter than elsewhere, but the nights longer; because the farther [Col. 0932A] one goes there from the sun, the nearer the sun itself appears to the earth, and the longer the shadows grow.

The Lombards, leaving Scantinavia with the aforesaid dukes, settled for some time in the region of Scoringa. At that time Ambrietasius, duke of the Vandals, was oppressing every neighboring province with wars. Therefore, elated by many victories, they sent envoys to the Vinuli: either let them pay tribute to the Vandals or prepare themselves for a contest of war. Thus Hibor and Angio, leaders of the Vinuli, together with their mother Gambara, determined that it was better to defend liberty with arms than to defile liberty by payment of tribute. Through envoys they sent word to the Vandals that they would rather fight than serve.

Toclacus the historiographer recounts the ridiculous ancient tale [Col. 0932B] that the Vandals approached their idol Godam and asked victory over the Vinuli. He replied that he would give them victory when he first saw the rising sun. Conversely, Gambara is said to have approached a goddess called Feria, namely Godam’s wife, and to have requested victory for the Vinuli. The same goddess Feria gave advice that the Vinuli women should place their loosened hair before their faces and, early in the morning, appear with the men and stand so as to be seen together through the window through which Godam would look at them. This is said to have been done.

When Godam, looking at the rising sun, saw them, he said: “Who are these Longibarbi [‘long-beards’]?” The goddess Feria answered him: “That he might also grant victory to those to whom he himself had given a name.” Thus, they say, he granted victory to the Vinuli. These accounts indeed appear fabulous.

But the true name of the Lombards is derived from the long beard, untouched by iron: the same Vinuli are called Longobards. In the language of the Vinuli, *lang* means “long,” and *bart* means “beard.” Some, adding a letter, called Gotham “Votam.” He is the one whom the Romans call Mercury, and was then worshipped as a god by all the Germans; hence even today *Goth* in German is called *Deus*, “God,” in Latin. The Vinuli therefore are still called Lombards today.

Accordingly, after fighting the Vandals ten times and contending for liberty, the Vinuli were victorious. Later, compelled by a great famine, they were dismayed in the same province of Scoria. Leaving it, they prepared to cross into the province of Moringa, but the Assipidi obstructed their path, refusing them passage through their territories. When the Lombards saw the great number of their enemies and did not dare to engage them because of the smallness of their own numbers, necessity at last devised a plan. The Lombards pretended that their camp contained cynocephali, that is, men with dogs’ heads. They further spread among the enemy that these fought battles stubbornly, drank human blood, and, if unable to reach an enemy, drank their own blood. Hearing this, the enemy believed it and feared to undertake the war that they had declared. Yet they had among them a very brave man, in whose strength they had complete confidence. They put forward this man alone to fight for all, sending word to the Lombards that they should set one of their men against him to enter single combat with him on behalf of all, on the following condition: if he defeated the Lombards’ champion, they themselves would obtain free passage; but if the other defeated him, they would turn back as they had come.

[Col. 0933A] In response, a certain man of the Lombards’ servile class offered himself to fight for all, on the condition that, if victorious, he would be granted freedom. The Lombards gladly promised what he requested. Thus, when the slave had defeated his enemy, the Lombards reached Mauringua and passed into Rugulanda. There [Col. 0933B] they stayed a short while, then moved into the province of Anthap and from there to the land of Bathaib, then into Burgunda, which they held for several years. Meanwhile, when the two Lombard dukes—Hibor and Angio—had died, they made a king for themselves.

Agelmund, son of Angio, of the Vinuli lineage, who was counted the noblest among them, therefore reigned. He ruled the Lombards for thirty-three years.

In his time a certain prostitute bore seven infants in one birth and cruelly threw them all into a pool to be killed. King Agelmund, riding on horseback, happened to come to the pool and touched the wretched infants with the spear he carried. One of them grasped the spear with his outstretched hand. Moved by pity and greatly marveling at the event, the king immediately ordered him to be raised from the water and entrusted him to a nurse to be brought up with the greatest care. From the pool, which is called *lama*, he named him Lamis. When he had grown up, he became a warlike young man, distinguished by great courage, so that after King Agelmund’s death he himself governed the kingdom with praise.

Meanwhile, while the Lombards thought themselves secure from every enemy, the Bulgars attacked them at midnight, killed King Agelmund and a great part of his people, and carried off the king’s only daughter captive.

Afterwards the Lombards recovered their strength and made the aforesaid Lamision their king. He immediately turned his arms against the Bulgars. In the first battle, when the Lombards had turned their backs, King Lamissio encouraged them, promising freedom to the slaves if they fought well, and generous rewards to all. Therefore, all armed, they turned their hands against the Bulgar enemy, cut down nearly all of them, plundered limitless spoils and weapons, and won a most glorious triumph. From then on, the Lombards began always to be bolder in fighting battles.

[Col. 0933D] After the death of King Lamision, who had reigned second, Letha reigned in his place as their third king. After he had reigned forty years, his son Gildehoc succeeded him, fourth from their first king. After his death, Gildehoc received the kingdom as fifth king. A little later the Lombards left those territories and passed [Col. 0934A] into Rugulanda, that is, the homeland of the Rugii, where they remained for some time because of the land’s fertility. Meanwhile King Gildehocus died, and his son Classo succeeded him. After King Classo’s death, his son Guado succeeded, the seventh king of the Lombards. They then left Rugulanda and settled in open plains, which in their language they called *felda*; they remained there for three years.

After Guado’s death, his son Gualtarius succeeded him as the eighth in the kingdom. All those kings were Adelingi, that is, of the nobler lineage, which among them is called *Adelinga*. King Gualtarus died after reigning seven years. Alduin succeeded him as ninth king, and led the Lombards into Pannonia. Aldoin had a son, Alboin, a most bold warrior, [Col. 0934B] who, when the king of the Gepids fought against the Lombards, struck down the Gepid king’s son with one blow of his sword and won a glorious victory over the Gepids.

At that time Emperor Justinian abridged the multiplicity of laws and wonderfully extended the Empire in various parts of the world, as has been sufficiently recounted in the treatment of him when we wrote of the other emperors.

In these days blessed Abbot Benedict was at the place called Subiaco, and shortly afterward moved to Monte Cassino.

When Aldoin, king of the Lombards, died, his aforesaid son Alboin—born to Queen Rudulinda, a most warlike and altogether vigorous man—succeeded [Col. 0934C] his father in the kingdom as the tenth king of the Lombards. He took as wife the daughter of Chlothar, king of the Franks, named Glotsuinda. By her he had only one daughter, named Abbisinda.

Meanwhile Thurisind, king of the Gepids, died; Cunimund succeeded him. Having broken the treaty with the Lombards, he chose war with them rather than peace, in order to avenge the ancient wrongs done to his father and the death of his brother. Therefore King Alboin made a perpetual alliance with the Avars, who had formerly been Huns but were afterwards called Avars after their kings; he then hastened to the battle with the Gepids that had been declared against him. While the Gepids advanced to battle, the Avars, as they had agreed with Alboin, invaded the Gepid kingdom. [Col. 0934D] Hearing this, the Gepids were placed in straits and lost heart. By their own counsel they chose first to fight the Lombards, and then to remove the Huns—that is, the Avars—from their homeland.

Thus the Gepids and Lombards joined battle. In this battle the Gepids were exterminated so thoroughly that not one messenger remained among them. In that battle Alboin killed Cunimund, king of the Gepids, and made a drinking cup from the skull of his head. This kind of cup is called a *scapha* among them, but in Latin it is called a *patera*, “bowl.”

Alboin carried off captive Cunimund’s slain daughter Rosamund. Since his former wife, Glotsuinda, daughter of King Chlothar, had already died, he took the captive woman as his wife, to his own ruin, as later became evident. From that time the Lombards were enriched and exalted beyond measure. The Gepids, however, being as good as exterminated, were consigned to the perpetual servitude of the Huns, that is, the Avars.

Therefore, as reports of Lombard victories rang out everywhere, Narses, the imperial *chartularius*, who then governed Italy, prepared war against Totila, king of the Goths. Since he had long had the Lombards as allies, he sent envoys to King Alboin, asking that he provide assistance in his coming battle with the Goths. Alboin then sent him an army to aid the Romans against the Goths. After receiving them, the Romans joined battle with the Goths. The Goths, together with their king Totila, were destroyed to the last man; the Lombards, honored with many gifts, returned victorious to their own country.

[Col. 0935B] From that time onward, the Romans were always friends of the Lombards in Pannonia. Therefore Narses, after the Gothic people had been destroyed and the enemies of the Romans overcome in various parts of the world, incurred the Romans’ envy. The Romans accused him most gravely before the emperor Justinian and the empress Sophia by false denunciations. Justinian ordered Narses to depart from Italy and return to Constantinople, appointing the prefect Longinus in his place in Italy. Queen Sophia also, violently enraged against him, uttered very grave threats, saying that she wished to humble the eunuch Narses so far that he would have to live with the other women in spinning wool and weaving cloth. To these words the eunuch Narses is said to have replied that he would set her such a warp as she could not complete in all the days of her life. Thus, harassed by hatred and fear, he withdrew to Naples, a city of Campania, and soon sent envoys to the Lombard nation, bidding them abandon the very poor fields of Pannonia and come to possess Italy, filled with every kind of wealth. At the same time he sent various kinds of fruits and specimens of other things in whose abundance Italy rejoices. By these and other words Narses strongly enticed the Lombards to enter Italy.

The Lombards gladly received the embassy, were elated at their future advantages, and prepared to enter Italy. [Col. 0935D] At the same time fiery battle-lines appeared in the sky, flashing forth the blood of Italy that was afterward to be shed.

King Alboin of the Lombards, about to enter Italy, sought assistance from all his Saxon friends, so that he might enter spacious Italy with a larger force and possess it. Twenty thousand men among the Saxons, with their wives and children, came to him, intending to remain permanently with the Lombards. Hearing this, the Frankish kings Chlothar and Sigibert settled Suebi and other peoples in the places from which the Saxons had departed.

Alboin left his seats—that is, all Pannonia—to his friends the Huns, that is, the Avars, on this condition: that, if the Lombards should at any time need to return, they might be permitted to go back to their possessions in Pannonia.

The Lombards had inhabited Pannonia for forty-two years. They departed from it in April, in the second indiction, with wives and children, intending to possess Italy.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 588, Alboin entered Italy at Forum Julii near Venice, appointed his nephew Gilphuls as duke there in the first place, and entrusted those regions of Italy to him.

At the same time Chlothar, king of the Franks, died, and the kingdom of Gaul was divided fourfold among his sons. The first of them, Aribert, held Paris; the second, Guntram, held Orléans; the third, Chilperic, held at Sens the seat of his father Chlothar; [Col. 0936B] the fourth, Sigibert, held his seat in the city of Metz. At Rome there was then Pope Benedict; at Aquileia Paul was patriarch, who, in fear of the Lombards, fled with all the treasure and furnishings of his church to Grado—that is, Venice. At the same time the Avars, who are also Huns, or Hungarians, hearing of the death of Chlothar, king of the Franks, turned their arms against his son Sigibert. He met them in Thuringia and triumphed splendidly over them near the river Elbe; when they sought peace, he granted it.

When Alboin had reached Treviso, Felix, bishop of that church, met him; and, at the bishop’s request, the king granted the confirmation of his privilege concerning all the Church’s possessions. Alboin conquered Verona and all the other [Col. 0936C] cities of Venice, except Padua, Mantua, and Monselice. For Venice does not consist merely of a few islands, as some suppose, but extends its boundaries from the frontiers of Pannonia as far as the river Adda, in the territory of Lodi and Milan. This is proved by the annalistic books, in which the city of Bergamo is numbered among the other cities of Venice. The district about Milan and Pavia is called Liguria, as it were from gathering legumes, in which it seems to abound at all times more than the other provinces. The Ligurians extend their boundaries as far as the frontiers of the Suebi and Burgundians.

Alboin, king of the Lombards, forced his wife Rosamund to drink from the skull of her father Cunimund, king of the Gepids, which he had caused to be fashioned in the likeness of a drinking-cup.

[Col. 0936D]

King Alboin, seated ceremonially at a banquet during one of his great festivals, ordered that the cup which he had caused to be prepared from the head of Cunimund, king of the Gepids, his father-in-law, should be offered to the queen in the presence of all. As she, unaware of the wicked deed, took the cup intending to drink, King Alboin said to her: “Drink with your father.” At these words Queen Rosamund, more deeply grieved than can be believed, turned her ingenuity and her mind toward avenging this crime.

She therefore enlisted in this undertaking the king’s cupbearer, named Helmichis, and another soldier, named Peraedeus. Helmichis was the king’s foster-brother and milk-brother, a very brave soldier. When at first he did not consent, the queen, using subtler cunning, ordered a very beautiful maidservant to submit herself to the cupbearer for intercourse on the following night. After the girl had done this once or twice, the queen, on the night itself, secretly removing the girl, gave herself to the unsuspecting soldier; and, after satisfying her desire with him, said: “What woman do you think I am?” He replied by naming the girl. She said: “Know that I am the queen. Unless, therefore, you obey my commands, you will perish when Alboin himself strikes you down. Choose, then, rather to kill him and reign happily with me than, while he lives and I accuse you, to perish.” Thus Helmichis the cupbearer, placed in distress, followed the woman’s command as though unwillingly, [Col. 0937B] and at last this wicked counsel met with a most evil outcome.

How the queen and Helmichis, the king’s cupbearer, together with the soldier Peraedeus, began and completed these crimes, and how they themselves afterward perished, the following page will explain in heroic verse. After reading it, we shall return again to the histories of the emperors and set forth accounts of Charles and his successors.

Likewise, concerning Alboin and Rosamund in verse: how she avenges herself and finally dies by poison.

Six hundred years had passed since the time of Christ  
when the Lombard established warfare throughout Italy;  
the Lombard formerly bore the ancient name of Vinulus.

[Col. 0937C] After nine kings of the Vinuli had already passed away,  
their king Alboin came into Italy;  
thus the earlier writings of the Lombards declare.

The Lombard crown, once led through Hungary,  
occupied Italy and held its seat in the city of Verona;  
so the earlier records of history relate.

Their king Alboin was the first to enter Italy;  
he conquered in war the people of the Gepids from Hungary,  
killing their king and plundering their market-place.

Then he carried away the head of Cunimund, king of the Gepids,  
and, in the form of a cup, prepared the bones of the round head;  
as victor, he then drank the cups dear to him.

Meanwhile his first bride, Glodosunda, died;  
the daughter of the king of the Gepids became his second bride.  
This was Rosamund, by whose contrivance he paid the penalty.

[Col. 0937D] The head of his father-in-law, whom he had caused to be killed by the sword,  
he ordered to be made into a cup by craft and bound with gold;  
then he commanded wine to be given to his bride.

The woman would not have known that it was her father’s skull,  
nor would she have drunk the wine, unless that impious man had said:  
“It is the skull of your father: drink with the father who begot you.”

As Rosamund groaned while drinking the foul wine offered her,  
she crushed her breast, and tears poured forth violently;  
the fate of her slain father became bitter indeed.

She shuddered at the unheard-of crime and the wicked king;  
the queen prepared to kill her hateful husband  
when she learned that the severed head was a drinking-cup.

She instructed a maidservant, beautiful in form and appearance,  
to join the cupbearer to herself in the hour of intercourse;  
the girl promptly accomplished what she was asked.

[Col. 0938A] On the following night the queen came, saying to the woman:  
“I wish you to withdraw from this soldier’s bed;  
I wish to be done to me what he did to you yesterday.”

She went away; the queen secretly prostituted herself,  
herself receiving the unwitting man willingly;  
and after the games were completed, she began to speak:

“How do you not fear that you have touched the queen?  
Behold, you shall deservedly die by your king’s sword;  
unless you trust me, you shall be a victim of death.”

The man thought her a maidservant, but the voice was Rosamund’s;  
therefore the man was terrified, while the woman strengthened him  
and began to unfold the man’s future deeds.

“Choose what you desire: two things lie before you:  
either you will kill the king,” she says, “or the king will kill you.  
Choose by the lot of the court: to live or to die.”

[Col. 0938B] “Though unwilling, I seek you,” she said, “as my husband.  
You shall be king, and with the sword you shall cut down the wicked king;  
if you trust me, how soon you shall be supreme!”

While the queen grieved excessively for her father’s death,  
the avenging cupbearer swiftly avenged the recent deed;  
when the king slept, he took off his head.

The woman gave herself as the price of death to fate,  
and soon afterward turned her treasures over to him;  
then, after further events, they made their escape.

For they took their way to Ravenna in vessels;  
the duke of the city received them and gave them the theatre;  
then great Ravenna was their native land.

The queen seeks secret compacts with the duke:  
if the cupbearer perishes, if he can be removed by death,  
[Col. 0938C] the duke alone shall be the queen’s husband there.

When the cupbearer came, she prepared a poisoned drink;  
drinking, she offered it to him and compelled him also to drink;  
the adulterous woman drank poisons known to her.

She dies first; he dies afterward.  
There fraud perishes by fraud; death, bitten, dies fittingly;  
thus the heavy wrath of God repaid her what she deserved.

Concerning Constantine, emperor of the Greeks, sixty-seventh from Augustus, while Charlemagne reigned in Francia.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 781, while Charlemagne reigned in Francia, Constantine, son of Leo and sixty-seventh from Augustus, succeeded to the empire of the Greeks. His daughter, who had been betrothed to Charlemagne by her mother, [Col. 0938D] was given to another. In the third year of his reign, the same King Charles came to Rome and was honorably received by Pope Adrian. Having celebrated holy Easter there, his son Pippin was anointed king of Italy, and his other son Louis king of Aquitaine. Charles himself, amid the acclamations of the whole Roman people, was called Roman patrician.

About the same time, while Charles was celebrating the Lord’s Easter at a place called Ingelheim, four miles from the city of Mainz, Tassilo came with the leading princes of Bavaria. There, accused by the Bavarians of not having kept faith with Charles—indeed, of having brought the Avars in to devastate the kingdom—he was found guilty of these and other crimes against majesty and was to be punished by death. Yet the king, moved by mercy, permitted him to assume the monastic habit in the monastery [Col. 0939A] of Lorsch, which he himself had built, and there to do penance for his sins.

Meanwhile Emperor Constantine, by the counsel of his mother Irene, as they say, was blinded not long afterward and died in the first year of his reign. His mother then reigned after him for five years. Since the empire had thus come into a woman’s hand, it was fitting that it should be transferred to the Franks, most powerful men.

Pope Leo was blinded and had his tongue mutilated at Rome, and was restored again by God.

At the same time Pope Leo, succeeding after the death of Pope Adrian in the year 799 from the Incarnation of the Lord, was treated most outrageously by the Romans. Thus he was twice blinded in one day, [Col. 0939B] and his tongue was twice cut off, and he was shut up in a certain chapel. On the following night certain faithful persons brought him to the basilica of St Peter, where by the power of God he received his eyes and the sight of his eyes, and his tongue together with speech. Then he went to King Charles and lamented the course of events. Therefore Charles, having already subdued the Bavarians, Danes, Saxons, Aquitanians, Normans, Britons, Pannonians, and many other provinces, was making his way to the city of Rome to avenge the pope. Pope Leo, first restored to his see by envoys, then met Charles as he approached at the tenth milestone and received him honorably. Ten days later the king addressed an assembly of the people and explained the reason for his arrival. There Pope Leo, of his own free will and with no one [Col. 0939C] compelling him, cleared himself of the accusation brought against him by touching the most holy Gospels. The rest is contained in verse.

Likewise, concerning the same Pope Leo III, in verse: how he was blinded and his tongue cut off.

Now that the plague had been removed from the Church of the Ligurians,  
and the whole Roman people rejoiced in every respect,  
the wheel turns, driven by ambiguous fortune.

Pope Leo is seized while a procession is being celebrated;  
his body is battered, his eyes are plucked out by the roots,  
and the blind pope lies in a dreadful prison.

That malignant people also utterly removed his tongue,  
though they were unworthy to touch the papal emblems;  
having torn away the tongue, they carried it off again.

At dawn the matter turns for the better,  
[Col. 0939D] while the people weep and the pope suffers in prison:  
by skill he is taken out from the middle of the prison.

When the sorrowing Church seeks to see the Lord,  
true Mercy restores his mortal wounds;  
he who was lately blind shares again in the light.

The prelate, possessing eyes, sees all things in his former light.  
Glory be to Christ, who wrought wonders in him,  
whereby the blind man deserved to possess the adornment of his brow.

He also recovers his own tongue as speech returns;  
the Church hears the pope reciting his complaint,  
powerful in eloquence though lately mute.

Reader, if you seek the names of the authors of the crime:  
Campulus, the Church’s primicerius among the clergy,  
was the author of the crime, whom the punishment imposed struck down.

[Col. 0940A] A singer named Paschal, the pope’s sacristan,  
laid sacrilegious snares; for he perpetrated these deeds.  
Both are equal in guilt, and together they shall pay the penalty.

Leo’s complaint before Charles, and concerning Campulus and Paschal, the accused.

The people reveal the torments Leo had suffered;  
meanwhile Charles received the complaint from the city  
and ordered the prelate to come, and he came.

When the pope did this, he sought royal comfort  
and brought with him many ranks of the Roman clergy.  
There shall be vengeance for the martyrdom that Leo endures.

The Frankish court pities their prayers  
and asks what now is the cause of their sufferings.  
Leo stands and complains, himself recounting the treachery.

When the occasion demanded it, Leo related everything to the king:  
[Col. 0940B] all the evils he had suffered, all that Campulus had done.  
He who wears the crown has compassion for the afflicted.

The gentle men grieve in heart; the Romans weep in pity;  
they hasten to suppress the prelate’s terrible grievances.  
The nobles move their camp; the royal standards shine.

A host of magnates received the senate from the City;  
the pope receives the reconciled archons for himself;  
at the king’s command, the peace desired is granted.

Campulus and the others marked by guilty wrongdoing  
are given over to exile because they committed foul crimes;  
the prelate and the Church enjoy lasting joy.

How and when Charlemagne was made emperor of the Romans, sixty-eighth.

In the year 801 from the Incarnation, and 1552 from the founding of the City, Charlemagne, in the thirty-third year of his reign, was crowned by Leo III, supreme pontiff, [Col. 0940C] while all the Roman people acclaimed and sang imperial praises. Thus Charles was called emperor, the sixty-eighth from Augustus.

Charles Augustus therefore allowed those who had committed sacrilege against the pope—namely Campulus the primicerius and Paschal the sacristan—to live, although condemned to capital punishment; at the pope’s intervention, he banished them to perform penance.

Moreover Irene, empress of the Greeks, sent envoys asking that peace be arranged between Greeks and Franks. Charles sent his own messengers with them and asked Irene to be his wife. When Irene had assented, Eutius the patrician, in the presence of Charles’s envoys, made his brother [Col. 0940D] Nicephorus emperor and thrust Irene into a monastery. Nicephorus, now made emperor, sent his envoys along with Charles’s envoys, and they then confirmed a treaty between themselves by letters and messengers. The king of the Persians also honored Emperor Charles at that time with gifts. The rest concerning Charles’s coronation is contained in verse.

Likewise, the coronation of Charlemagne is related in verse.

Leo rejoices everywhere to be blessed with papal peace.  
While he busies himself at the altar arranging the divine rites,  
the royal palace sings regal measures in due order.

The Church praises the crown as the people applaud;  
illustrious Rome has freely offered the girdle of empire;  
the hall resounds mightily with imperial praises.

[Col. 0941A] When the king is praised and called Caesar in the City,  
he marvels at the songs with which the people echo;  
and he gives these words to be reported to the princes:

“Rome, which wishes to bestow on me the name of empire,  
will bestow it in vain unless it confers an omen with the name.”  
Nothing is done for me unless words of power accompany it.

“The world cannot be possessed merely by imperial praise;  
the commonwealth seeks that the deed be accomplished along with praise.  
If praise proves empty, glory will be a mockery.

“But since the people have been pleased to raise me by praise  
and the pope has wished to consecrate me to Caesar’s lot,  
lest I appear fearful, we shall accept it,” he says.

“What Rome does not hold, my right hand shall seek by the sword.  
I desire to extend the power of the nobles over the Greeks;  
let this day confer on me the riches of the City and the world.

[Col. 0941B] “I do not refuse to take Rome’s name of empire,  
for over the Greeks we shall gain the rights of the crown;  
thus the whole court urges me to take the name.”

Charles received the imperial crown in the City,  
and by his aid Rome restores her times,  
as our page likewise declares in its titles.

Charles, crowned at Rome, considers invading the empire of the Greeks.

When Charles resolved to wear the diadem of the world,  
he decreed that he should be anointed by the hands of the supreme pontiff;  
he took the name and burden of the imperial eagles.

The clergy sang for him; the people subjected their rights;  
yet he had not then attained the empire’s full summit,  
for Leo, king of the Greeks, wore the diadem.

And since his fame as a great terror was throughout the world,  
[Col. 0941C] because Charles now held Rome, the head of Italy,  
his ambition grew so that he might possess new Rome as well.

It was not enough for the king to have sought Rome’s favor;  
nor did he think he held the empire in full splendor.  
Therefore he immediately moved arms against the Greeks.

He went into Ausonia, pressing the matter with full severity,  
that the Greek might surrender the empire to him without delay.  
Fearing death, the latter proposed suitable terms.

Nicephorus, emperor of the Greeks, is killed by the Bulgars; his son-in-law Michael is raised up, while Charles already rules at Rome.

In the year from the Incarnation 812, Nicephorus, emperor of the Greeks, was killed by the Bulgars in open battle. His son-in-law Michael succeeded him in the kingdom. [Col. 0941D] He honorably dismissed Charles’s messengers, who had been sent to his predecessor, and sent his own envoys with them to Charles, confirming the renewed peace with him. He too, when he led an army against the Bulgars and met with no success, returned; after laying down the kingdom, he became a monk.

Concerning Leo, emperor of the Greeks, while Charles already ruled at Rome.

Leo, son of the patrician Bard, emperor in Greece, again concluded a perpetual peace with Charles on these terms: each should always be called the other’s brother, and each should always assist the other; the Greek emperor should possess the East, while Charles and his successors should possess Rome with the entire West. When all this had been settled in peace, Charles traveled through Constantinople to Jerusalem for prayer. [Col. 0942A] Having prayed there, he returned, as they say, through Sicily, and from there returned to Rome through Calabria and Apulia. Having received a blessing, he returned to Gaul; at Aachen he built, with marvelous workmanship, the church of Blessed Mary.

Likewise, Charles, warned by an angel, prepared an army for Spain. There, as they say, he labored for fourteen years, converted very many peoples, and lost very many men. Returning thence to Aachen after countless victories, he ended his life in the palace at Aachen, where he had established the chief seat of the Frankish kingdom: in the forty-sixth year of his reign, the forty-third year after Italy’s subjugation, the fourteenth year of his empire, and the seventy-second year of his age. He received honorable burial in that same church of St Mary, according to imperial custom.

Charles, as some writers recorded, was large and robust in body, tall in stature, with a rounded crown of the head. His eyes were very large and lively, his nose somewhat longer than average, his hair beautifully gray, and his face cheerful and pleasant. He was abundant and overflowing in speech, moderate in food, and more temperate still in drink. The boundaries of his realm then extended from Bulgaria or Illyricum to the Spaniards, and from the Danes to the Pharos of Sicily, apart from adjacent regions, namely Bohemia, Poland, Dalmatia, Istria, Venice, Brittany, and other provinces.

[Col. 0942C] It is pleasing to recount the remaining deeds in verse.

Likewise, we explain in verse the treaty made between Charles and the emperor of the Greeks.

The kings establish a treaty, that each may be called brother;  
they divide the empire, but the honor is held in common.  
The Greek holds Greece; ancient Rome becomes his.

Thus two supreme crowns are borne in the world;  
if Rome was once one, now in due order there are two Romes.  
There was one Caesar; now two shall observe the rights.

There was one lord of the world, pre-eminent in honor;  
now two brothers are adorned with double rank,  
though they often continue to fashion the title “brother.”

Greece agreed; the settlement pleased the king.  
With Greek consent Charles attained the summit for himself;  
by laws he secured what was almost a spoil.

[Col. 0942D] By this treaty the brothers were made after their own manner,  
so that they might jointly hold the empire, constrained by peace:  
ancient Rome was ours, but new Rome yielded to them.

By counsel and sword each promises to aid the other;  
each is adjudged to be called by a brotherly name;  
each wishes the summit to be granted to him by equal right.

Concerning the four principal seats of the Roman empire in the West.

Wishing to write the truth of how many places are foremost for the crown,  
I judge that there are four seats of empire:  
I shall set forth their names as the deeds also declare.

The first place is at Aachen; next comes Arles;  
then at Monza the royal seat is established;  
afterward Italy’s supreme crown is customarily bestowed,

when Caesar wishes to wear the Roman diadem.  
[Col. 0943A] He must reverently be anointed by apostolic hands,  
and he shall receive as father him to whom the holy places are open.

Without the hand of the pope, whom golden Rome has produced,  
it is not fitting that the sole ruler receive the crown in the City.  
Then the highest grace thunders forth heavenly gifts.

We acknowledge that this is customarily done by the empire,  
for in receiving sacred things we are accustomed to please God.  
The king appeases the pontiff and cherishes him with honor.

Such things, by the law of the court, are granted to no dignity;  
by the law of heaven they are bestowed solely on Peter’s love,  
for it is fitting that they be revered by heaven’s ordinance.

The bishop anoints him, but Christ is regarded as the anointer—  
the divine hand from heaven, which is perceived in the heart—  
to whom the king rightly offers this and every honor.

While the sacred hand of the pontiff pauses to bless him,  
[Col. 0943B] Christ’s extended hand directs its gifts to him;  
the anointer offers him the gifts sent by God.

He is anointed as the Lord’s Christ, but God anoints him.  
The pontiff’s anointing grants him the right to wear the diadem;  
the pope who blesses him acts in God’s stead.

For the Psalm will be my witness, which has joined these words:  
“I have found David my servant, whom I, God, have anointed.”  
The letter there says, “I have anointed,” not “he anointed.”

Samuel himself indeed then performed the anointing in person;  
yet it is not written, “Samuel anointed,” but “I, God, anointed  
him myself from heaven with my holy oil.”

Thus the diadem is consecrated by non-bodily oil,  
though material oil is thought to consecrate it;  
the gracious hand of the pontiff performs the sacred rite.

[Col. 0943C] If you ask what the pope does, what honor he possesses:  
I speak of the heavenly key-bearer, to whom the world obeys,  
to whom God himself gave earthly things together with heavenly.

Charles journeys as a pilgrim to Jerusalem by way of Constantinople, but returns through Sicily, Calabria, and Apulia.

Charles, having at last gained the honors of Ausonia,  
undertook Jerusalem’s labors in peace,  
now wishing to fulfill his vows to the life-giving cross.

He visits the holy traces of those places  
where the God of gods was born, where he suffered,  
where the Virgin Mary bore the heavenly bridegroom.

When the king had worshipped and desired to wash in the Jordan,  
he honored David’s royal walls with gifts;  
then, returning by ship, he came to the Sicilian kingdom.

Charles returns from Jerusalem.

[Col. 0943D]

While the swift ship bore the king on the sea-wave,  
he reached the harbor of the city of Palermo without mishap;  
the whole land of Sicily paid him tribute.

Here Charles restores the Sicilian king by baptism,  
whom he orders to adopt the law of the Roman Church;  
the Catholic people received God’s doctrine.

There stands a great mountain, said to be Roland;  
another is called Oliver by the same reasoning;  
the fierce leaders established these memorable things.

There is also a mountain called Etna, which emits flames,  
into which burning stone falls with sulphur;  
this is said to be the head of Tartarus.

Scylla barks there; Charybdis inflicts many losses;  
ships perish there, and men are drowned in them;  
[Col. 0944A] the wave of Pharos’ whirlpool brings destructive dangers.

Charles, seeing in those places the losses said to be caused by them,  
marvels that Etna’s native regions gleam with ashes,  
and says to the city of Messina: “Farewell, my friend.”

Likewise concerning the same.

From there he crosses Pharos, which he had found bitter with its whirlpool,  
seeing there many losses among his possessions;  
and they say the king did not grieve a little because of this.

Calabria receives him; the standards of the mighty hasten on;  
they seize and retain the whole land by sudden prowess,  
and everywhere the conquered land lies at peace.

From there, through Apulia, the marvelous power came to Rome  
and bore the imperial crown in the City;  
organ, lyre, pipe, and trumpet resound.

[Col. 0944B] Then Aaron, king of the Persians, as Charles returned,  
won his favor with gifts, sending an elephant  
and also sending him many vessels of gold.

An angel of the Lord commanded Charles to go against the Spaniards.

With peace given at Rome and Pope Leo seated there,  
Charles, increased in honor by the customary diadem,  
returned to his country, ruling his ancestral realms.

As Charles wished to renew the joys of empire,  
at Easter time he sat upon the imperial throne  
and bestowed royal gifts upon kings and dukes.

To the king as he slept a heavenly voice spoke,  
commanding him to subject the Spaniards to Christ’s law.  
He who wore the diadem heard and was astonished.

[Col. 0944C] In the morning the royal vision was disclosed and received with joy;  
the court, applauding, was sufficiently prepared for the command;  
the heavenly mandates stand established by reason.

While Charles wished arms to be prepared against the Spaniards,  
Gaino, foremost among the counts, proposed a different counsel  
and requested that the campaign be delayed.

Then he said: “O Caesar, rain and cold now abound;  
the rivers are strong, and the torrents of rain overflow;  
the harshness of winter is far too much to be feared.

“Spare the nobles; let the knights rest through the winter;  
let the rivers subside and ice and snow melt;  
then move your standards in the heat of the sun.

“If it please you, meanwhile send a powerful envoy  
who may see whether perhaps he can convert the people,  
lest a great multitude perish by your sword.

[Col. 0944D] “You may send the magnificent Roland for peace;  
I think the people can be recalled by his speech.  
If he returns with peace, your praise will be greater.”

As he ceased speaking, the illustrious court favored the proposal;  
yet Charles feared the future dangers to his nephew,  
lest he deliver his forces into deadly places.

Roland rose and, filled with fury, roared:  
“Out of envy Gainus seeks to betray me;  
his hostile mind lies hidden, but now its curses are apparent.”

“I shall go, nor does my right hand despise dreadful labors;  
I hope that we shall bring many honors back to the empire.  
May God be among us.” The leader moves his standards.

The king fears the outcome, for the dangers are a hundred;  
a multitude of dukes and an assembly of mighty men accompany him;  
the leader’s army then numbered thirty thousand.

[Col. 0945A] When the leader sets out, the Romans proceed without peace;  
the most grievous road produced manifold conflicts everywhere;  
the peoples settled in that region prepare war.

In the dark night an angel of gracious appearance comes;  
he foretells hard battles everywhere in the leader’s future  
and promises aid, lest the leader’s forces fall.

“Gather your mighty battle-lines,” says the angel.  
“Behold, I see six kings bearing hostile standards;  
when you strike them in battle, you shall conquer under my guidance.”

He spoke, and the mountains gleam with golden shields;  
the encircled Frankish hosts press fiercely into battle;  
wounds resound and slaughtered bodies fall.

Roland’s skilled hand cut down wondrous ranks;  
by the great leader’s sword the tyrant kings perished;  
the evil men perished by the triumphant sword.

[Col. 0945B] They relate that five kings stood in the front line,  
whom, they say, were killed here by five strokes of the leader.  
This angel of light protects the leader’s forces.

A brighter angel from heaven strikes the ranks with missiles;  
by his aid the illustrious company of the faithful stood firm,  
and the enemy yielded to it by God’s disposing lot.

Such battles were fought in many places;  
this was wrought by the victory of Teutonic arms;  
every land was conquered by their strength.

At Pamplona then was the supreme crown,  
to which Barcelona and the region of Aragon were subject,  
together with Tarragona, or good Gerona.

The supreme king David, rushing to arms from this city,  
pressing the Frankish hosts in a battle-position,  
[Col. 0945C] wages terrible fights and then returns defeated.

King David, defeated among the host, is driven within;  
sharply afflicted because he endured the leader’s blows,  
the leader deploys his standards before the king’s palace.

The leader requests that a parley be held under a brief peace;  
the king agrees and asks in order for the reasons why he has come.  
The affair is serious; the speech must be sustained.

The leader of the Roman empire sets forth his honor  
and commands him to grant the crown’s fiscal rights.  
When this demand stirs him, the king swells with anger and grief.

Anger moves the king because he has received bitter demands;  
such fiscal claims were unusual among his equals.  
He again rushes to arms and prepares war in fury.

The very brief truce of arms is dissolved;  
[Col. 0945D] the king, once the leader’s enemy, rejects his threatening demands;  
each enemy makes abundant use of ambushes.

The dispute becomes open without delay; they return to their former wars.  
The king cannot go out, shut up within;  
the standards of Francia fly into Caesar’s land.

Roland fought countless marvelous battles,  
pre-eminent in the world and notable in the office of a soldier—  
a star of honor, fully worthy of honor.

* Charles receives the returning standards of his nephew;  
the wicked people are too opposed to Catholic purposes;  
the king prepares to carry war back to the lands of heretics.

The king commands the victorious standards of empire to move;  
the Spanish kingdoms shall no longer be able to stir,  
and by heaven’s judgment the wicked multitude perishes.

How Charles once conquered the Spaniards,  
[Col. 0946A] I am unwilling to append to this book’s headings;  
another work of a different measure shall have the fortune to treat it.

Away, my Muse, from this slaughter;  
sit joyfully with me and bring forth Caesar’s offspring for me;  
turn your dactylic foot toward Caesar’s sons.

Louis, son of Charles, is raised to the empire, sixty-ninth from Augustus.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 815, Louis, son of Charlemagne—whom Charles, while still young, had appointed his successor and emperor—hastened back from Aquitaine to the palace at Aachen when he learned of his father’s death. There, with the consent of all the princes, he was made emperor, the sixty-ninth from Octavian Augustus. In the first year of his reign, through the reports of certain persons, he learned that some leading men of the kingdom had been killed for conspiring against Pope Leo. In order to investigate this, he summoned his nephew Bernard, king of Italy. Bernard set out for Rome, but there fell ill and reported the state of affairs to Augustus through Count Herold. Pope Leo too, sending messengers to Louis, cleared himself of the charges then brought against him. A little later Leo died and Stephen was appointed in his place. Stephen immediately sent ahead messengers to say that he would come to the emperor; then, setting out at once, he followed them. The emperor honorably received him at Reims, where, after the pope had celebrated the solemnities of the Mass, he proclaimed Louis emperor of the Romans amid imperial praises.

[Col. 0946C] Later at Aachen the emperor chose his son Lothar as his colleague in the empire. He placed his other two sons, who were called kings, one over Aquitaine and the other over Bavaria. But shortly afterward he found that his nephew Bernard, king of Italy, together with other cities of Italy, had conspired against him. While Louis was preparing an army against him, Bernard, his courage broken, came forward and surrendered himself to the emperor. Then, at Aachen, after judgment had been pronounced upon Bernard and the other conspirators of his faction, although they were to be punished with death, the emperor ordered them all to be blinded.

Then he sent his son Lothar into Italy. Lothar, after arranging matters there, was invited by the Roman pontiff at holy Easter and crowned to the empire by him.

[Col. 0946D] Later Louis was driven from the kingdom, because of the evil deeds of his wife, as is said, and was restored again. Then, a short time afterward, in the sixth year of his empire, he died. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 841, when Lothar, son of Louis, returning from Italy, proposed to hold sole rule, his brothers Charles and the younger Louis, unwilling to be deprived of imperial rank and title, declared war on Lothar. Having gathered all the forces of the kingdom on both sides, they fought a remarkable battle at Fontenoy, where the strength of the whole Frankish kingdom was so diminished that no one could henceforth think of extending their kingdom, but scarcely of holding his own against the surrounding peoples. There Charles and Louis gained only a bloody and lamentable victory. Then, peace having been made among them, the empire was divided between the three brothers as follows. Charles obtained the portion from the British Sea to the river Meuse; to Lothar was assigned Belgic Gaul from the Meuse to the Rhine, which even to this day has customarily been called Lotharingia after his name; while Louis received by lot all Germany, Alemannia, and Bavaria eastward from the Rhine.

Likewise we relate in verse concerning the same Emperor Louis.

Charles begot the excellent King Louis,  
whom God made a life-giving friend conformed to himself;  
by his law the clergy are rightly called lord.

This father advanced the Church with varied honor—  
[Col. 0947B] with clothing, houses, and grain—whose favor increased it,
By his own right he is everywhere reckoned great.

He causes us to dwell in our own houses and to maintain knights,  
and to shine in varied and grey clothing;  
by this same law the goshawk and the hawk are kept.

Such honour would not come to the clergy unless Caesar granted it;  
no yokes of the great race of counts would be borne by the clergy;  
lest it become rustic, it flourishes in nobility.

A Catholic king, a man who cherishes, increases, and loves the blessed,  
he receives three sons by divine gift  
and makes them sharers in his kingdom.

This offspring divides, and subdivides the regions;  
yet one alone possesses the highest honours of the empire,  
[Col. 0947C] But the other two grieve at being without a throne.

They are separated by climate, not endowed with a diadem,  
nor are they anointed by the hands of a pontiff;  
thus there was grievous and great war among the sons.

One Lothair sat among the Franks in the world’s high place;  
Charles is the other, to whom Gaul of the Seine falls;  
thus Louis possesses the regions of Bavaria.

### Concerning the Emperor Lothair, son of Louis, seventieth from Augustus

After the Frankish kingdom had been divided, Lothair—upon whom, as I have said, the Roman Empire had devolved together with Lotharingia—ruled as the seventieth from Augustus. When Theophilus had died and his son Michael was ruling among the Greeks in the imperial city, the Northmen entered by the river Loire, stormed certain cities, and, on Holy Saturday of Easter, killed a bishop who was, according to custom, celebrating the general baptism with his clergy. Spreading in every direction and laying waste the whole province with sword and fire, they seized also the cities of Angers and Tours, and did not shrink from burning the church of Saint Martin. [Col. 0947D]

At that time Charles, to whom, as I said above, the western kingdoms had fallen in the division, captured Charles, king of Aquitaine, and, on the advice of bishops, had him shorn and made a monk at Soissons in the monastery of Saint Medard.

Moreover, the emperor Lothair divided among his three sons the kingdom that had fallen to him: he gave Italy, together with the imperial title, to Louis; Lotharingia to Lothair; and Provence to Charles. He himself, having arranged all matters in the monastery of Prüm, became a monk in the sixteenth year of his empire after his father’s death. [Col. 0948A]

See to what a decline the Roman Empire had come: when the kingdom of the Franks had been divided into three parts, its empire was but a third part of one third.

Accordingly, when Lothair became a monk after laying aside the belt of military service, in the year 845 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Louis, son of this same Lothair, the most serene sixty-third from Augustus Octavian, assumed the empire. At that time Basil, who had killed Michael, was ruling at Constantinople.

Then Lothair, his brother, who had received Lotharingia as his portion of the kingdom, took as wife Theutberga, sister of Abbot Hucbert. [Col. 0948B] Not many days later Charles, Lothair’s brother, who had received Provence as his portion of the kingdom, died. Therefore Lothair, his brother, who held the kingdom of Lotharingia, contended against his uncle Charles, who held Aquitaine. Meanwhile this same Lothair entrusted the duchy between Mont Joux and Mont-Jovis to Abbot Hucbert, that is, the brother of his queen and wife.

Moreover King Louis, Lothair’s other uncle, who held Germany and Bavaria, fought many splendid battles against the Slavs and deprived their captured prince, Rastislav, of his eyes. Then this same King Louis, namely king of the Germans and Bavarians, was summoned by certain princes of Gaul to the kingdom of Gaul which his brother Charles had received in the division of the kingdom. He crossed with an army into those regions, invaded the kingdom of his brother Charles, and advanced as far as Sens. But when, leaving his army there, he had returned to Germany and Bavaria, the princes who had invited him there returned to the favour of their own king. Hence Louis’s army, which had remained there, was compelled to depart from Gaul. [Col. 0948C]

In these days Saracens advancing from Africa were ravaging the region of the Beneventans, formerly called that of the Samnites. Against them Emperor Louis, suddenly gathering forces from every quarter, summoned his brother Lothair to help him. Lothair entered Italy with an army; but as he proceeded wickedly and outrageously, he lost many of his people, in punishment for his sins, both from the heat and from spider bites. Lothair himself also was struck by illness on the road and died near Piacenza. [Col. 0948D]

King Charles of Gaul, on hearing of Lothair’s death, invaded his kingdom, namely Lotharingia. In response, Emperor Louis divided the kingdom of Lotharingia with his uncle Charles by an agreement between them, provided that Louis the emperor should possess the palace at Aachen with his share. Not long afterward, Duke Adelchis of Benevento, trusting in the Greeks and joined by Campanians, Lucanians, and Samnites, planned rebellion against Emperor Louis. The emperor therefore gathered forces and attacked Benevento in war. Adelchis persuaded him to withdraw from his territories by gifts deceitfully bestowed for that purpose. On his return, the emperor captured all the cities of Campania and Lucania, except Capua, without severe exertion. Capua too was afterwards captured; and when its bishop, with the clergy, carried relics before the emperor’s feet and sought pardon in tears, he restored them to favour and cleared all Campania and Apulia of Greeks. [Col. 0949A]

Shortly afterward, on Duke Adelchis’s advice, the emperor dismissed his army and entered Benevento. At about midday the duke and citizens attacked the sleeping emperor and threatened to burn him together with the palace unless he swore that he would never again enter their territories. After this shameful agreement the emperor came to Rome. There, before Pope John, who had succeeded Adrian, and in the presence of the senate, he set forth his case; for this reason Duke Adelchis was judged an enemy by the senate. The emperor was absolved by the Apostolic See from the oath which he had made not voluntarily but to save his life. [Col. 0949B] Yet, although he had been absolved, he did not go to Benevento in order to avoid scandal; nevertheless, he sent the queen there with an army. Adelchis, terrified, fled to Sardinia and escaped Caesar’s wrath. In these days the Franks made Otto, son of Robert, their king.

### We also relate the same Emperor Lothair in verse

Lothair alone sat in the citadel of empire,  
and by right the Roman monarchy fell to the Germans;  
the German Caesar gave laws in the City. [Col. 0949C]

Then Herold, king of the Danes, received baptism,  
and his son Manigold, a boy, with his mother;  
and the rest of his people received the chrism.

Louis obtained the empire together with his father;  
having received the governance of Italy beneath his father,  
the royal standards were borne as far as the Sicilian Pharos.

### Concerning Charles the Second, Emperor of the Romans, seventy-first from Augustus

In the year 874 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the most gracious Emperor Louis died, in the nineteenth year of his empire. In the same year Charles, his elder uncle, king of western Francia, came to Rome with his Franks and, as is said, obtained the empire from the Romans by money. He thus ruled as the seventy-first from Augustus. [Col. 0949D]

Not long afterward his brother Louis, king of the Germans and Bavarians, died in the fortress of Frankfurt, leaving three sons: Carloman, Louis, and Charles.

Moreover, when Emperor Charles heard of his brother King Louis’s death, he endeavoured to invade the kingdom of Lotharingia. First he occupied the palace at Aachen and advanced as far as Cologne. Meanwhile Carloman, eldest son of the deceased Louis, king of the Bavarians and Germans, entered Italy and attempted to seize the empire. His brother Louis, however, had already begun to rule among the Germans and Bavarians. When he heard that his uncle Charles had entered the territories of his kingdom, namely Aachen and Cologne, he sent an embassy warning him to withdraw from the kingdom. Since Charles did not desist, Louis advanced to battle; and the two fought near the Rhine at Andernach. Charles was put to flight, with many slain on either side. [Col. 0950A]

After this, the three sons of Louis made an agreement and divided the German kingdom left them by their father in this way: Carloman received Bavaria, Pannonia, Carinthia, Bohemia, and Moravia; Louis received eastern Francia, namely the region about the Rhine, together with Thuringia, Saxony, Frisia, and Lotharingia; Charles received Alemannia, that is Swabia, and certain cities of Lotharingia because of their abundance of wine.

Meanwhile the aforesaid Emperor Charles II went from Gaul to Rome and, returning from there, made his way to Pavia. There he was informed that Carloman, son of his brother Louis, who held Bavaria, had entered Italy with a great army. The emperor, wishing to return to Francia, died by poison. [Col. 0950B]

In the second year Louis, son of the younger Charles, called the Bald, died, leaving two sons, Louis and Carloman, since their third brother, afterwards called Charles, was then still carried in his mother’s womb. Boso invaded their kingdom of Provence, which their father Charles, son of Emperor Lothair, had received as his portion in the division of the kingdom, and which Emperor Charles had recently entrusted to him among the Gauls. Boso first came to Lyon, [Col. 0950C] where the archbishop of Lyon anointed him king of Burgundy and Provence; he was resisted by the said youths Louis and Carloman.

### Concerning the birth of Arnulf, King of the Franks, seventy-second from Augustus

In the year 880 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Carloman son of Louis, to whom Bavaria had fallen by lot, died after the many triumphs he had accomplished, and was buried at the place called Ötting in Bavaria. He left a son by a noble but not lawful woman; because he was descended from the Carolingian stock, they called him Arnulf. To this Arnulf the monarchy later fell.

But Louis, king of eastern Francia, hearing of his brother’s death, came to Bavaria and subjected it to himself, [Col. 0950D] granting the aforesaid Arnulf the duchy of Carinthia together with the castle called Mosaburg.

### Concerning that King Charles who had received Alemannia as his portion from his brothers, seventy-third from Augustus

In the year 881 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Charles, who had received Alemannia as his portion, moved an army into Italy. Having received all Lombardy in submission, he came to Rome, where Pope John consecrated him to the empire as the seventy-third emperor from Augustus.

At that time the Northmen entered King Louis’s kingdom by ship on the river Waal, burned the palace at Nijmegen, and then ravaged Cologne and Aachen together with that entire province. In the midst of these events Louis himself died at Frankfurt and was buried in the monastery of Lorsch. [Col. 0951A]

When the Northmen learned of King Louis’s death, they became more secure and invaded Trier, the noblest city of the Gauls. On Maundy Thursday they consumed it, together with the neighbouring province, by fire and killed the bishop of that city; then, laden with Frankish spoil, they returned to their ships.

While these things were happening in Gaul, Emperor Charles III remained in Italy. The princes of both Gaul and Germany urgently petitioned him all together that, since his brother Louis, king of the Germans, had died, he should return, take up his paternal kingdom, and free his country from the Northmen’s incursion. He returned swiftly and, taking Lombards, [Col. 0951B] Bavarians, Saxons, Frisians, Alemanni, Thuringians, and many others, moved an army against the Northmen, who were still remaining in the kingdom.

Thus Godfrey, king of the Northmen, became a Christian and was received by the emperor from the sacred font. He also took as his wife Gisela, daughter of Lothair, and received the whole land of the Frisians as her dowry; and so he departed with his men from the kingdom’s borders.

The following year Louis, son of Charles, king of the Franks, died and was buried in the monastery of Saint-Denis, leaving his brother Carloman heir to the kingdom. Not long afterward Carloman, struck by a boar while hunting, died.

The princes of western Gaul having thus been lost, [Col. 0951C] they voluntarily invited Emperor Charles, who then seemed the only survivor of the Carolingian line, and all submitted to him when he came. Shortly afterward this same Emperor Charles became so ill in body and mind that he was judged useless by men. Therefore the aforesaid Arnulf was elected emperor by all in the year 886 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

The sick Emperor Charles fell into such poverty that, lacking even bread, he gratefully accepted from Arnulf a few revenues for the comfort of life. From this time until the Emperor Otto I, we find that the empire was ruled in confusion. For when this Charles died—after ruling seven years and then living a private life in the seventh year, having relinquished the empire—the empire was divided in various ways, as individual provinces strove to create individual kings. Yet the greater part fell to Arnulf. [Col. 0951D]

Then Italy and Lombardy set up Berengar of Friuli as their king, and made Guy of Spoleto another king. King Berengar was then driven out by King Guy and fled to Arnulf.

In these days the Hungarian people, having departed from Scythia and been driven out by the Pechenegs, first came into Pannonia; after expelling the Avars from it, they remained there permanently. This Hungarian people is said at that time to have been so beast-like and uncivilized that they used raw flesh for food and human blood for drink, as did the Phalagi [identity uncertain]. The Pechenegs even to this day desire the blood of beasts and use raw flesh of horses, foxes, wolves, and cats. [Col. 0952A]

Moreover Arnulf ruled all eastern Francia, which today is called the German kingdom—that is, Bavaria, Swabia, Saxony, Thuringia, Frisia, and Lotharingia—and the entire Rhine; while Odo held western Francia by Arnulf’s authority.

After this the Northmen invaded Arnulf’s kingdom and destroyed the dukes who met them. Arnulf later struck them down with such force that few survived. Then, in the year 854 from the Incarnation of the Lord, after arranging all affairs in Germany, [Col. 0952B] Arnulf entered Lombardy with an army. Having captured the city of Bergamo, he hanged Count Ambrose on a gallows; Italy was so terrified that the whole country submitted to his authority. Arnulf returned to Gaul by Mont-Jovis.

At that time Guy, who had usurped the kingdom of Italy, died. His son Lambert came to Rome and had himself called emperor. Arnulf then gave Lotharingia to his illegitimate son Cendebald. Subsequently, summoned by Pope Formosus, Arnulf again entered Italy and came to Rome, which he then captured by arms; he was crowned by the same pontiff and received the name Augustus. Afterwards he ordered those who had stirred up sedition against the pontiff to be beheaded. When Arnulf had returned from the City, Lambert, son of Guy of Spoleto, [Col. 0952C] who had seized the empire, died; and Louis, son of Boso, was invited by the Lombards to the empire.

I, Gotfrid, have found in certain histories of the Romans that after Charles III, as though the empire had been transferred from the Franks to the Lombards, Arnulf is not named in the catalogue of emperors, while Louis and those after him are placed among the Augusti. Others, however, put Arnulf in the catalogue; and those who ruled confusedly after him until Otto they customarily call not emperors and Augusti, but usurpers and Augusti. Not long afterward, when Otto, king of the western Franks, had died and been buried in the church of Saint-Denis, Charles was made king there. [Col. 0952D] Arnulf, emperor in the twelfth year of his reign according to the reckoning given above, died and was buried beside his father Louis at Ötting in Bavaria. His tomb, however, is shown in the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg.

### Concerning King Cendebald, son of Emperor Arnulf

Cendebald was a king, born not of a wife,  
son of King Arnulf, ruler of a kingdom,  
yet at that time he did not wear the diadem of empire.

He was an impatient man, above all devoted to anger.  
He is said to have struck his lord of Cologne with such a staff  
that the bishop was lifeless night and day.

Cendebald dies, a friend of crooked truth;  
a legitimate boy is raised up, called Louis,  
his brother, likewise a legitimate boy. [Col. 0953A]

### Concerning Louis the Child, King of the Franks, son of King Arnulf, seventy-fifth from Augustus

In the year 901 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Louis son of Arnulf was made king at the place called Forchheim, and was invited by the princes of Lotharingia, who had been offended by Cendebald, to the kingdom of all Belgium. For that region is called Belgic Gaul. When Cendebald learned this, while committing many evils and staining the kingdom with much plunder, fire, and slaughter, he was finally killed in battle by Counts Stephen, Gerard, and Mafrido. Thus Louis, Arnulf’s son, freely obtained the kingdom.

In these days the Hungarians ranged through Lombardy, killed with their arrows the inhabitants of the land who met them, and, after cruelly depopulating the province, returned to their own country. [Col. 0953B] In the year 905 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Louis son of Boso, having obtained the empire, expelled Berengar. When he held the entire kingdom at his own discretion, he dismissed his soldiers and went with a few men to Verona. There he was captured through treachery by the citizens; Berengar was recalled, and Louis was blinded. From that time Berengar held the kingdom of Italy together with the Roman Empire.

At about the same time Albert, a most noble count of the Franks, grandson through a daughter of Otto, duke of the Saxons, killed Conrad, whom some say was son of King Louis. Therefore the king attacked the aforesaid Albert in war at the castle of Bamberg, where there is now a distinguished bishopric. [Col. 0953C] But Albert, unable to resist the king, sought counsel from Otto, archbishop of Mainz. The archbishop went to the then very strongly fortified castle of Bamberg to Albert and persuaded him to come into the king’s presence, giving him his hand in pledge that he would bring him back safe and unharmed to his own castle.

Having received the archbishop Otto’s pledge and promise, Count Albert went with him. When he had gone a little way out from his castle, he said to the archbishop: “Lord, we ought to have taken dinner in the castle before proceeding to the king’s court, for we shall have to fast throughout this whole day.”

The archbishop replied: “You have spoken rightly. Let us return to the castle and eat a little.” [Col. 0953D]

Count Albert accepted in the ancient manner with simple ears the priest’s words, which were spoken deceitfully. He quickly returned to the castle with the bishop, and, having received and given a meal, proceeded under the bishop’s escort to the king without demanding any other assurance from him. There, when put on trial, he was condemned to the capital sentence. When condemned, he reminded the archbishop of the promise made for his safety. The archbishop answered that he had kept his pledged promise, having brought him, after he left the castle, back safe and unharmed into his castle. Thus outwitted by such fraud, Albert himself was beheaded in that same court. From his possessions, it is said, the church of Bamberg was afterward built and enriched with wealth.

[Col. 0954A] Whether Archbishop Otto, who is said to have done this for the safety of the kingdom, sinned in this matter should be left to the judgment not of myself but of my hearers. Yet if I had done it, I should consider that I had sinned even by employing a Saracen. From this Albert’s blood another Albert is said to have derived his origin, who later added to the Roman Empire the eastern march—commonly called Austria (*Osterich*), and called by others Upper Pannonia—after it had been wrested from the Hungarians.

Louis, king of eastern Francia, died in the twelfth year of his reign without an heir. According to the writings of some, the genealogy of the Carolingians came to an end for a time in this King Louis and in his above-mentioned brother Cendebald. Hence someone wrote: “The last of the Augusti in Rome was Augustulus; [Col. 0954B] but the last of the Carolingians in Francia was Cendebald.” Therefore, Louis having now died, Otto, duke of the Saxons, was sought by all. But the most illustrious prince Otto, as though burdened by old age, refused to be made king.

### The same King Louis the Child is likewise related in verse

This boy, strong in piety, rules for three years;  
he is the last blood of the seed of the Carolingians,  
yet Charles has offspring from his side.

### Concerning Conrad I, king after Louis the Child, seventy-seventh from Augustus

In the year 913 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Conrad I, son of that Conrad whom the aforesaid Count Albert had killed, was made king by the counsel of the aforesaid Duke Otto, who had refused to accept the kingdom, and with the agreement of all the Franks. [Col. 0954C] Some assert that he was the son of the brother of the late King Louis, and therefore count him as the last of all the Carolingians. In the first year of his reign the Hungarians once more spread out to ravage the land, but were defeated by the Swabians and Bavarians near the river Inn. Afterwards Arnulf, duke of the Bavarians, rebelling against King Conrad, fled with his wife and sons to the Hungarians.

King Conrad died in the seventh year of his reign, and by his counsel Henry, son of Duke Otto, was appointed in his place as king in the year 920 from the Incarnation of the Lord. From that time some say the empire was German rather than Frankish. [Col. 0954D] Hence they also say that Pope Leo called this Otto the first king of the Germans. For Henry, the duke of whom we are speaking, is reported to have refused the dignity of empire offered him by the supreme pontiff; for that reason he is not counted in the catalogue of German emperors.

But from many authoritative writings it has become clear to me that the German kingdom, which Emperor Frederick possesses in our time, is a part of the kingdom of the Franks. For the first Franks lived on both sides of the Rhine, in the region now called eastern Francia as far as Bavaria’s borders. Western Francia, however, is that kingdom on both sides of the Seine and Loire; this province was formerly called Gaudina, but was first called Francia, or *Francigena*, that is, “born of the Franks,” by Charles Martel, grandfather of Charlemagne. [Col. 0955A] In the German tongue, from which Charles Martel himself was descended, he called it after his own name *Carlinga*, just as Caesarea is named from Caesar and Alexandria from Alexander. He did this because he subdued them with his sword and joined them to the kingdom of the Franks.

Another quite manifest reason for this is shown. Finally, as appears above, in the time of Charlemagne, king of the Franks, all Gaul—that is, Celtic Gaul and Belgic Lyonnaise—and all Germany, extending from the Rhine to Illyricum, constituted one Francia. But afterward, when the kingdom was divided among the sons of sons, one kingdom was called eastern Francia and another western Francia. Nevertheless, both were called the kingdom of the Franks.

[Col. 0955B] Thus in the eastern kingdom of the Franks, commonly called German, when the Carolingian line failed, Henry I of the Saxon people succeeded to the kingdom. Yet in western Francia—that is, at Paris and Rheims—there still remained a certain King Charles, likewise of Carolingian descent. Henry’s son Otto later restored the Roman Empire to the Franks, after it had been usurped by the Lombards. Hence perhaps Otto himself was called the first king or emperor of the Germans because, though he was not the first to rule among the Germans, he was the first king of Saxon blood outside the Carolingian line and the first to bring back the Roman Empire from the Lombards to the Germans.

[Col. 0955C] Here the changing names of the kings of the Franks should be noted: first, from King Merovech his successors were called Merovingians; later, from Charlemagne, his successors were called Charleses or Carlings; from Emperor Otto they were called Ottos; and then, from Henry, Henrys.

### Concerning the same King Conrad I, though the last of the Carolingians, in verse

Now that the male seed of the Charleses had failed,  
Conrad arose, a kinsman from their side,  
and obtained the empire and the German land.

The distinguished King Conrad sits first in order;  
he attacks his enemies and drives adversaries to the depths;  
he subjugates the Hungarian and Illyrian regions.

[Col. 0955D] No heir was born to Conrad I.  
The nobles wonder who deserves to possess the sceptres;  
life is yielded to fate, and the people grieve greatly.

### Concerning Henry I, King of the Franks, surnamed the Fowler

In the year 920 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Henry, called son of Otto, ruled in eastern Francia, while a certain King Charles was then ruling western Francia at Paris. Some Celtic writers assert that at first he was merely duke of the Saxons and was then subject to Charles. Afterwards, by the counsel of his son-in-law Duke Giselbert, who held Belgium, he withdrew with all the easterners from the kingdom of that Charles and assumed the royal title. Others say that after the death of Conrad I he was elected king by all the easterners [Col. 0956A] and never received anything from the hand of that Charles.

After this King Henry inflicted an incredible slaughter upon the Hungarians who had violently entered Saxony. This King Henry wrested the sacred lance of the empire, which is borne before the emperors, from King Rudolf of Burgundy by great exertions. Others say that it had been transferred to the empire from Boso, king of Provence. But King Henry, after many deeds of prowess, was on his way to Rome to obtain the Roman Empire when, before he reached Rome, he died, leaving his son Otto I, who became emperor, in the seventeenth year of Henry’s reign.

### The same Henry I is set down in verse

[Col. 0956B] Henry, duke of the Saxons, is called to reign;  
envoys are sent to him, and though often asked,  
he refuses to accept the empire duly offered.

They found the duke, seated in the old manner,  
making his nets in the work of a bird-catcher  
so that he might cunningly catch small birds.

And because he was simply bird-catching in their presence,  
from then on and forever he is called by the surname Fowler,  
although the world had in him an outstanding man.

Therefore, when he is further asked to take Rome for himself,  
the duke swears never to wear a crown upon his head,  
since the ample possessions he holds suffice him.

Henry is compelled to exercise royal authority;  
at last he is compelled to be reverently anointed king,  
yet no crown is placed upon his head.

[Col. 0956C] The diadem is ordered to be carried before, rather than upon, the king,  
so that whatever he seems to have sworn may be duly kept;  
yet everywhere he possesses the full insignia of a king.

From this Henry, Otto, the first king, is born;  
I now greatly desire to recount his illustrious deeds,  
and the Muse bids me bring forth three Ottos.

### Concerning Otto I, Emperor of the Romans, seventy-eighth from Augustus

In the year 936 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Otto I, noble heir of Henry I, succeeded to the kingdom and was crowned at the palace of Aachen by Hildibert, archbishop of Mainz. He subdued the Slavonic Bohemians who resisted him. When the Belgians prevented his crossing of the Rhine, he put them to flight; and after all Belgic territory had been ravaged with fire and sword, [Col. 0956D] he besieged the fortress situated on Mont-Capri. Louis, son of King Charles of western Gaul, intending under this pretext to recover the Belgic land which his father had lost, entered the province of Alsace. When Otto heard this, he raised the siege of Mont-Capri and, having expelled King Louis from Alsace, besieged Breisach.

Meanwhile Duke Giselbert, who had Otto’s sister as his wife, advanced against the Franks as an enemy of King Otto as far as Andernach. There he was defeated by the Franks and, fleeing, drowned in the Rhine, all his men having been killed or scattered in flight. King Otto again entered Belgium, reduced the whole country to submission, and from that time all German kings held Belgium without opposition. [Col. 0957A]

After this King Louis married the widow of Duke Giselbert, who was Otto’s sister. Not long afterwards he himself was expelled from his kingdom by his own people and came to Otto seeking help. Having obtained it, he defeated his enemies and was restored to his kingdom by Otto.

After this a synod was held at Ingelheim in the presence of both kings, together with Marinus, legate of the Apostolic See.

At that time Berengar oppressed Italy with excessive cruelty and held Adilinda, widow of the deceased Emperor Lothair, captive.
