Otto entered Italy in strength, freed the queen, [Col. 0957B] married her, and, having driven Berengar out, celebrated Christmas at Pavia. Leaving Duke Conrad there against Berengar, he himself returned to German Gaul. By Duke Conrad’s advice Berengar went to Otto, seeking pardon through Conrad and through Letulph, son of King Otto. Since the king had denied him an audience for three days, he finally obtained with difficulty, through the duke and the royal son, an appointment to come to Otto at Reggio in Lombardy. There he was later presented and received the kingdom of Italy from Otto’s hand, except for the march of Verona and Aquileia. When Berengar returned to Italy, his tyranny provoked all Italy’s hatred against him. Then Letulph, the king’s son, attempted to plot against his father, but soon changed course and received the king’s favour.

At that time the Hungarian people broke forth and covered the entire land like locusts, encamping beside the river Lech near Augsburg, the city of Swabia. At the prayers and exhortation of Ulrich, the most holy bishop of that city, Otto met them trusting in the Lord and struck them down with such force that they not only ceased from harassing others but, fearing for themselves, fortified their own land with rampart and marsh. In that battle King Conrad’s son-in-law and the duke of Worms fell; all the barbarians except six surviving men are said to have been destroyed by the sword. [Col. 0957C] A certain count of Styria in Bavaria is said to have been the author of this disaster; the Hungarians killed him as one who had led them forth to death, and his land was reduced to the royal fisc.

At that time legates came from the Apostolic See, complaining of Berengar’s tyranny and requesting Otto’s protection in Italy. Guabert, bishop of Milan, and Gualdo, bishop of Como, came to the king with other princes of Italy on the same matter. [Col. 0957D]

Otto then elevated his son Otto to the kingship in the palace at Aachen. Afterwards, gathering an army, he entered Italy through the valley of Trent. Having subdued all Italy to himself, he advanced to the City, was received with the highest honour by Pope John and all the people, and received the name and dignity of emperor. [Col. 0958A] According to those historians who place Arnulf in the catalogue of emperors and exclude from it the others who meanwhile held the empire in Italy, this Emperor Otto is the seventy-seventh from Augustus Octavian. But according to Roman historians, who exclude Arnulf from the catalogue of emperors and include Louis, the two Berengars, Hugh, Berengar, and Albert in the number and catalogue of earlier rulers, Otto is the eighty-fourth from Augustus.

From that time the kingdom of the Romans returned to the Germans and to the eastern Franks, from whom it had in some manner seemed already to have slipped away, after the aforesaid Frankish and Lombard emperors. I do not say, however, that the empire was at any time taken from the Franks; rather, it suffered an eclipse for as long as so many and such various usurpers held the empire in confusion. [Col. 0958B]

Returning from Rome, Emperor Otto celebrated Easter at Pavia; but Berengar fled the emperor and lay concealed. In the following year Otto besieged Berengar on Mount Saint Leo. Berengar’s son Albert fled to the island of Corsica and later approached Pope John of Rome, winning him to his side by many promises. When Otto learned this, he raised the siege and led an army to Rome. There certain Romans, afraid, fled with Pope John, while others submitted to Otto after giving hostages. The emperor then sent an embassy, writing to Pope John that he should return. When John refused to return, Otto summoned a synod [Col. 0958C] and appointed Leo in his place. Seeing this, Albert, Berengar’s son, again fled to Corsica.

Whether all these things were then done lawfully or unlawfully does not pertain to this work to explain; for I have undertaken to describe deeds done, not to render an account of those deeds. The emperor accepted Berengar’s surrender and banished him to Bavaria.

While Otto remained in Rome, the Romans, having conferred with the neighbouring fortresses, resolved to kill him. But since betrayal had forestalled their plans, the emperor strove to guard against the ambushes and killed many Romans; then, after oaths had been exchanged, he took from them one hundred hostages. Afterwards, at the pope’s request, he released the hostages at Spoleto, as Otto departed. [Col. 0958D]

The Romans received Pope John back into the City after expelling Leo. Leo swiftly went to the emperor at Camerino, and there celebrated Easter with him. Meanwhile John died, and the Romans appointed Benedict in his place. Otto, angered both by Leo’s expulsion and by Stephen’s substitution, hastened to the City, which he forced to surrender after hemming it in with siege and exhausting it with incredible famine, on this one condition: that they open the gates to receive him and deliver Benedict into his power. Then the emperor restored Leo to the chair; taking the deposed Benedict with him, he returned to his own Francia. Not long afterward, when the Italians defected from him, the emperor crossed the Alps; and, after celebrating Christmas at Rome, he hanged in a single day thirteen of the leading Romans, besides the prefect, who had stirred up the faction against Pope Leo. Then he had his son Otto crowned by Pope Leo and called Augustus, and joined him in marriage to Theophano, daughter of the emperor of Constantinople. Then, in the thirty-seventh year of his reign and the thirteenth of his empire, he ended his last day. This is that Otto who defeated the Greeks in Apulia and Calabria and transferred the Roman Empire to the eastern Franks.

[Col. 0959A]

He was the first to discover silver mines at Goslar in Saxony. He also adorned Magdeburg, the metropolitan see where he was buried, with very many ornaments and treasures. Berengar the exile and his wife died at Bamberg. [Col. 0959B] The denarii called *Otholini* were introduced in Italy by this Otto.

Likewise, verses are supplied concerning the same Otto the First.

Otto, crowned, celebrated the Paschal feast;

The renowned court of magnates attended the king,

And the royal table bore the dishes it had prescribed.

That table had first held cooked food already prepared

Before the lords arrived or, in the custom of dukes, took their seats;

That food was given to wretches and to the poor.

A boy duke approached, the sole heir of a great duke;

Being hungry, when he saw the dishes ready,

He took some to eat, having a child’s heart.

According to his custom, the server—changeable in the vice of anger—

Did not fear to strike the boy with a heavy stick;

[Col. 0959C]

Then the boy fell to the ground, laid low by the blow.

A knight was present, appointed the boy’s guardian and instructor;

He nobly avenged the lord whom this man struck,

For the server himself lay dead from the wound.

The crowd groans; King Otto comes and asks the cause.

The man lies there; while the crowd is silent, he orders it disclosed—

What had been the boy’s cause, and what now was the man’s.

He asks also for the author of the death: who was he?

The man stood in the midst, in spirit as though greater than Achilles,

And did not deny that he himself had killed the man with a stick.

The king said: “Therefore, by right, you seem worthy to die,

Since with your own mouth you fully confess yourself the author

Of the crime; you shall be a victim of death deserving your deeds.”

The knight said: “Discern more carefully what law requires,

Lest the matter be judged in a hasty judgment;

[Col. 0959D]

For it is God’s Easter, O king: have mercy on me.”

Anger moves the king; the man fears to die without law.

When the king refuses what is just, the knight immediately seizes the king;

Otto, thrown to the ground, pays for having denied justice.

As he holds Otto, he pulls his beard and moustache,

Pressing throat and face, fiercer in savagery than a lion;

Had aid not come, Otto would have died.

Beneath the bench-seat he cruelly torments the king;

With nails fixed in, he strives to break his throat;

Now with foot, now with hands, the crowd dragged him away.

Otto sits stunned, raised from his shameful position;

His beard is stripped of hair; his scraped throat hurts;

A head crowned with praise stands without praise.

The grieving crowd, standing before the doors, wants the man tortured.

[Col. 0960A]

Otto defends the accused and orders him summoned.

The man stood and was silent; Otto begins to speak:

“You asked to be brought before judgment by the rule of law.

When that was denied you, the hand of Christ touched me;

I have suffered blows deserved not from you but from the Lord.

I deserved them, because it was Easter, when I might have spared you.

What I wished was not lawful; vengeance made this known to us.

I bear in my anger the deserved lashes of God.

Yet you could have punished this more mildly

Than by plucking out my beard with your hands without a razor.

Henceforth, make what requests you wish in due order.”

When the knight explains what was then the cause of his rage,

He mitigates Otto’s symptoms by the force of reason;

Thus the knight is allowed to depart unharmed.

Nor is he allowed to go in such a way that he must return:

[Col. 0960B]

For when an injured person returns, we remember anger;

When evils lie hidden, resentment and anger are silent.

Thereafter came a time when the king himself would have been killed

Or harshly held captive, but was redeemed by the knight’s sword;

He stands sound in body, whose deeds I also sing.

When, beneath the citadel of heaven, the Dog is joined to the Lion,

As Otto pleases, a fortress is put under siege;

Otto decrees that those shut in be put to death by the law of the court.

While the king himself was accustomed to sleep at midday,

And rest in sleep held the nobles on every side,

The man sits in the bath, duly taking his bath.

While the king slept, the enemy swiftly rushes from the city;

To kill the king, they press forward in stealthy haste;

The knight who is bathing alone sees them.

Leaping from the bath, he snatches shield and sword;

[Col. 0960C]

With Otto lying down, he forestalls the hostile fury;

He cries out and, as was his way, raises grim battle.

The royal party increases; the enemy fears and retreats.

As the naked knight pursues, the true battle heats up;

He is seen naked far and wide, and his deeds are plain.

Caesar marvels that a naked man leads brave warriors,

For he sees the naked man alone overcome cohorts;

Everywhere the praise of the naked knight was great.

The next morning King Otto orders the knight to come.

The knight fears to approach, lest the king remember his anger

And recall against him the man’s former offence.

When the knight comes under compulsion, the king says to him:

“Was it not by your hands that our hairs perished?

Was not my beard plucked in your rage?”

[Col. 0960D]

The knight says: “I admit it; but my offence had been forgiven.

It is not fitting that a king revive offences themselves a second time;

I come secure, summoned by the king.”

Wonderful Otto rises to embrace the knight

And says to him: “Rejoice: I adopt you into my household;

You perform royal deeds; you shall always be my friend.”

## Concerning Otto the Second, emperor of the Romans, the seventy-ninth from Augustus

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 975, Otto the Second, son of the great Otto, who had been crowned by Leo, Roman pontiff, succeeded his father in the empire; he ruled as the eighty-fifth from Augustus. While he was heedlessly pursuing the Greeks through Calabria, after losing his troops he leapt from a ship and escaped by swimming. Afterwards, in the ninth year of his empire, he died at Rome and received an honorable burial before the church of Saint Peter, in a marble basin.

[Col. 0961A]

The Romans relate of him that this Otto, after taking Benevento, carried off from there the bones of Saint Bartholomew and placed them at Rome, on the island in the Tiber called Lycaonia, in the church now called Saint Bartholomew’s, in a porphyry basin. Later he planned to convey those same relics, together with that sarcophagus, down the Tiber to the sea and across the sea into his own Francia; but death forestalled him, and thus the relics remained at Rome.

Likewise, we set down in verse something concerning the same Otto the Second, emperor.

Otto the Second is present, invested with the diadem at Rome;

Glad, he departs anointed by apostolic hands;

[Col. 0961B]

He granted the Italians the right to enjoy peace everywhere.

When the king departed, the Italian people took up wars;

Authority became cheap, discord among the nobles increased,

For royal peace lay hidden—there was none.

The land perishes, the oppressed people groan and are burdened by war;

The angered king comes; the senate hastens from the City;

Royal Rome, capital of empire, receives him.

Otto summons the powerful dukes and counts of the empire;

He receives also the bishops of the Church as they arrive together,

And complains that his peoples lack peace.

In a judge’s office he enumerates those marked by guilt,

And orders a fitting punishment prepared for the dukes;

Terrible vengeance produces dreadful scourges.

Before the steps at Rome Otto orders tables set out,

[Col. 0961C]

And many benches arranged in a circuit and in order,

With places assigned everywhere to the princes according to custom.

While food is being laid out, drink and fare prepared,

While the nobles eat, while the hour is thought happier,

Otto surrounds both sides with armed men.

The herald orders silence, and that no one move from there:

Whoever speaks or stirs himself is to be struck with the sword.

The crowd fears; terror of the nobles is everywhere.

Otto orders the written crimes of the dukes, which he had earlier had recorded,

To be read aloud before their tables,

And condemns those convicted of guilt under equal law.

He who deserved it is condemned there to capital punishment;

Now the table may be stained with noble blood;

Otto wishes heads brought to him as though they were dishes.

While the table is drenched with the blood of human heads,

[Col. 0961D]

The king nevertheless orders them all to eat the fare set before them,

And sends abundant cooked dishes to the unwilling guests.

Thus he mocks their crime; thus he pours out bodies;

Thus he excludes crime; thus he forges the advantages of peace;

Thus his peace prevailed; thus the guilty man paid for his deeds.

## Concerning Otto, the third emperor, the eightieth from Augustus

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 984, Otto the Third, still quite a boy, succeeding his father to the kingdom, eighty-sixth from Augustus, assumed the empire. In his days Bishop Albert, preaching Christ to the Prussians, was crowned with martyrdom.

The Emperor Otto the Third ended his last day in the seventeenth year of his empire and was buried at Aachen in the church of Saint Mary. These latter two Ottos, [Col. 0962A] although for brevity’s sake we have said little about them, were so fierce and so remarkable that one was customarily called the pale death of the Saracens, or “the Bloody”; the other Otto, “the Wonder of the World.” Yet concerning this third Otto we have described certain other matters in verse, which we set down in the present chapter.

Likewise, verses are supplied concerning Otto the Third, emperor.

Near Modena is the house of a count, called Amula,

Then exempted from the services and commands of the empire,

And often available for Otto’s lodging.

When the queen sees the count, noble in body and handsome in face,

She is urged by love’s goads

And wishes secretly to violate the king’s bed with him.

[Col. 0962B]

While the queen thinks to bend the man to vice,

She pulls the count by his garment; dragged, he withdraws without his garment.

The spurned woman, grieving, makes her wicked wish.

At once the queen complains to her summoned husband,

Urging him to have the count’s head cut off by a drawn sword.

Otto quickly believed the fabricated charge.

While the count is deemed guilty upon his lady’s testimony,

The deceit is affirmed; an undeserved death is swiftly prepared,

And no opportunity is given to the innocent man to reveal the truth.

The count tells his own wife what had occurred to his shame:

“I prefer to die rather than depart from the king’s honor;

This woman, worthy of death, offered herself to me.

And because, fleeing the woman’s lust, I hid myself,

I am judged to death; I am not permitted to state what happened.

After my death, you will be my witness who knows the truth.

[Col. 0962C]

If what you prove by testimony should seem doubtful to them,

You shall overcome them by the ordeal of glowing iron;

Thus after my death fame will give me joy.”

His wife says: “Flee, if you can, lest you die thus.”

He replies: “I prefer death to being thought guilty;

He who flees draws greater suspicion upon himself.”

He spoke, and, as the herald dragged him away, he was called to his doom.

The countess follows her husband, for he is killed by deceit;

When the count was put to death, she carried off his head.

When Otto orders the grounds of judgment prepared

And commands widows to be summoned by a public herald,

Desiring justice to be given through these pious proceedings,

The countess stands weeping beside her slain husband

And complains that Caesar gives an unjust judgment,

[Col. 0962D]

Striving, according to the custom of the place, to address him skilfully.

She says to him: “Tell me: by what law is punishment prepared for the guilty

If a man is killed by fraud when faith has at some time been broken?”

Otto replied: “By law, the penalty is the loss of one’s head.”

She added: “Your own sentence condemns you, Caesar;

I shall show that you cut down my husband by fraud as a criminal.

If you wish laws to be observed, it is fitting that you therefore die.”

She fell silent. The king was astonished, saying to the woman:

“I do not know what you seek, nor do you seem to have stated the truth;

Who, indeed, will be your witness to this crime?”

“Behold,” said the countess, “the count’s head is ready:

He perished through your fraud; acknowledge your own guilt;

Receive the judgment pronounced by yourself.”

The king said: “This count deserved death for his crime.”

She denies it, wishing to undergo the ordeal of fire;

[Col. 0963A]

The king prepares the fiery ordeal; thus the woman prevails.

When Otto sees himself caught in the noose of law,

The wonderful goodness of the man can be overcome by reason;

He allows himself to be delivered into a woman’s hands.

While the countess holds the king, the king’s honor grants

That full power over his head be assigned to her,

So that he himself may stand or fall at her discretion.

She considers how she may destroy the king;

Then the king requests a short truce for a time,

And the nobles add their prayers with compassion.

Through innumerable prayers of nobles and women alike,

The royal life is granted a term of ten days;

Thus by reason the woman overcame her lord.

Now, with the tenth day coming and threatening disaster,

Otto returns; the countess comes, she who had come before.

[Col. 0963B]

When the king said, “Hail,” she replied, “Beware.”

The countess, that wondrous lioness, takes him as an accused man.

As he is led off and commanded to submit to punishment,

The woman, overcome by entreaty, herself postpones the death.

She postpones it and says: “Thus I now spare you, most miserable man,

On condition that in eight days’ time the monarch’s punishment be by the sword.”

Thus life was granted him, yet he hangs in suspense.

When Otto returns and completes eight days in peace,

Then, with the princes, he again asks for eight days by prayers;

After counting them, the seventh day grants respite.

The seventh passes; again he wishes to obtain eight,

So that he may have six days kept in peace;

At the clergy’s counsel the woman says: “It shall be so.”

Yet she did not grant it unless the king promised her

That first the queen should perish in burning flames;

[Col. 0963C]

When this was agreed, life restored returned.

For three truces the monarch granted three castles,

Nor was he sparing in granting much besides;

We know the names and sites of the castles.

If you wish to know the boundaries of those places,

The people of the Tuscan region point them out;

Nor has the ground itself often escaped my own sight.

## Concerning Henry the Second, namely “the Lame,” emperor of the Romans, the eighty-seventh from Augustus

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1001, after Otto the Third had died without an heir, Henry the Lame, son of Hezilo, a Norican by nationality and duke of the Noricans—that is, of the Bavarians—was elected by all the princes of the realm and made king, the eighty-seventh from Augustus.

[Col. 0963D]

Having successfully waged many wars in Germany, Bohemia, Italy, and Apulia, he was at last granted rest by the Lord. Being most Christian, he gloriously founded and richly endowed the most noble bishopric of Bamberg. By giving his sister in marriage to Stephen, king of the Hungarians, he called both the king himself and all his kingdom to the faith. All Hungarians venerate this Stephen as a saint because through him they received the beginning of the faith.

The most pious Emperor Henry, having completed the twenty-fourth year of his reign and the eleventh year of his empire, died and was buried in the church at Bamberg. There his tomb, often and manifestly adorned by frequent miracles, is magnificently venerated throughout that province. The remaining matters [Col. 0964A] concerning Emperor Henry himself, and the city and church of Bamberg—I, who learned there my first lessons in the art of grammar, as one reared by them—have set forth in verse.

Likewise, let us speak in verse concerning the same Henry the Second, surnamed the Lame, emperor of the Romans, and concerning the city and its glorious church called Bamberg, that is, Peacock Mountain.

The Bavarian river, commonly called the Radiant,

Nourishing the Norican fields and winding in diverse courses,

Flows beside the lovely city of Peacock Mountain.

By its common name the mountain is called Babenberg;

It is enlarged by the river, and the neighboring land is watered,

And a bridge laid across it joins either bank.

A city most worthy of praise rises from the mountain’s base,

And thus becomes lofty, planted with its foremost towers;

[Col. 0964B]

Yet in the mountain city the clergy hold the heights.

A line of houses encircled by a host of walls

Becomes a stronghold for lords, with laymen excluded;

Their cleric disdains to enter the marketplace.

That clergy is customarily blessed with grammatical learning;

No vulgar speech dares sound within the city;

Latin alone is customarily spoken by all.

### Concerning the church of Bamberg

The church’s form heightens and adorns the mountain’s summit;

There the great rule of the clergy is renewed;

Wealth is displayed widely in possessions and workmanship.

Otto, father of fathers, holds the pontificate in order;

He enlarges the assembly of noble brethren with honor;

Himself sacred, he renders sacred things and matches one to the other.

In the church gold of marvelous weight gleams—

[Col. 0964C]

Gold less than that which the Moor was accustomed to pay the Danes;

Who could count the purple coverings?

### Concerning Peacock Mountain, its form and location

Peacock Mountain has neighboring hills,

Three, as it were, alike and sharing in the city;

Itself shining in the middle, it rises preeminent without equal.

The more beautiful of them provides the greatest precincts for monks;

The others provide churches for many canons;

And a fourth part provides a marketplace on either side of the river.

Thus in the shape of a cross Peacock settled his colony,

That it might venerate, cherish, and celebrate him as patron;

He himself provides good things from the city for his servants.

Peter stands in the middle; Stephen is on his right;

James stands on the summit; Michael holds the left;

[Col. 0964D]

And alongside the river the Virgin Mary bears splendor.

### Concerning the burial of Emperor Henry

Reader, hear of the riches of the holy Emperor Henry, surnamed the Lame:

By what gift can they be enclosed? These and greater things are his many good works.

His good bones too are ready to work miracles;

His gracious crown bestowed this work and these gifts,

Whence worthy songs resound through the churches.

### The author first studied at Bamberg

Leaving this praise, I recall my former times:

In my childhood Bamberg was my former teacher;

What my mind learned there, in friendship it gives back to her.

I could not repay as much, but I could repay what I could.

Behold, my wings fly more swiftly toward other matters;

History calls me. Blessed Peacock, farewell.

Likewise praises are written concerning the same Henry the Lame.

[Col. 0965A]

Solemnly hear of the merit of Henry the Lame,

Whom it is fitting to applaud, to whose praise I offer verses:

Taken from the fortress of earth, he reigns in the fortress of heaven.

With a virgin wife, he too remained a virgin;

He gave almost a thousand Catholic churches;

To the poor and widows he was hope, way, and life.

Now we see his bones consecrated upon the altar,

And fitting solemn rites prepared in saving fashion;

Very many bodies of the infirm are restored to health.

## Concerning Conrad the Second, emperor of the Romans, the eighty-second from Augustus

[Col. 0965B]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1020, when the Emperor Henry the Lame died without sons, Duke Conrad, a Frank by nationality, was elected to the empire by all, on the counsel of Emperor Henry himself—though he did not enjoy Henry’s favor—and was the eighty-second from Augustus Octavian. Through his mother he traced his origin from the first Frankish kings, who had come from Troy and had been baptized by Saint Remigius. He had as wife, named Gisela, of the Carolingian line, the niece of his predecessor, Emperor Henry the Lame, whom he had married against the emperor’s will. As someone indicated at that time by these little verses:

When, after the tenth, the fourth is counted in the line,

Prudent Gisela descended from Charlemagne.

This Gisela was first married to Arnulf, duke of the Swabians, [Col. 0965C] and bore him twins, namely Ernest and Hermann. After he died, she married this Conrad, of whom we are now speaking.

This Conrad, therefore, was vigorous in arms, prudent in counsel, flourishing in wisdom, skilled in civil law, and devout in the Christian religion. At the beginning of his reign, Bolesław, duke of the Poles, whom his predecessor Henry had recently subjected to the realm, sought to be called king in his own right and resolved to separate completely from the empire. But death forestalled his purpose, and he left his son Mieszko as his successor. When the latter planned to imitate his father and had moreover expelled his own brother Otto from the country, the king crossed into Poland both to restore the expelled brother to his country [Col. 0965D] and to avenge himself and the realm for Mieszko’s defiance.

Since Mieszko could not resist, he fled to Ulrich, duke of the Bohemians, who was then also an enemy of the empire. When Ulrich intended to surrender him to the king and thereby return to favor, the king scorned to receive him through such treachery. But Mieszko, having received the duchy of Poland from the king, surrendered to Conrad the crown which his father had planned to place upon himself against the empire, and subjected himself to Conrad’s authority. This Mieszko afterwards was killed by his own squire.

From that time the province of the Poles paid tribute to our empire. Conrad designated his still boyish son Henry to reign after him. [Col. 0966A] Having done this, he entered Italy. His stepson Duke Ernest came to him, at the counsel of his mother Queen Gisela, and obtained the king’s favor, promising to cross into Italy with him.

Conrad came to Rome and, on Easter Day, proceeding between two kings—namely Cnut of the English and Rudolf king of Burgundy, uncle of his queen Gisela—was crowned by John, supreme pontiff, and received the dignity of empire amid the applause of all the people. In the same week war arose between quarreling Romans and Germans; after many Romans had been put to flight and slain, the emperor triumphed.

Emperor Conrad returned to his Francia across the Pyrenean mountain. There, when he heard that his aforementioned stepson Duke Ernest was now intending to rebel against the realm, he drove him out by the forces of the empire on land and sea, [Col. 0966B] forcing him to live in the forests. There he was later killed by those faithful to the empire, and his brother Hermann assumed his duchy.

At that time, King Rudolf of Burgundy, as he was dying, left by testament to Henry, son of Emperor Conrad and his own nephew, the kingdom with its crown and other insignia. Therefore Count Otto the Celt, asserting that the kingdom of Burgundy, or Lyonnaise Gaul, belonged to him, invaded it. Indignant at this, the emperor entered that kingdom with an army, compelled Otto to surrender, and received all those princes into his allegiance.

Then, as the people of Italy plotted against the empire, [Col. 0966C] he came to Milan and sent into exile at Aquileia the bishop of that city, who had been captured and was said to be guilty of that faction; he later escaped secretly. As the emperor proceeded to Cremona, he encountered the Roman pontiff there. After dismissing him with great honor, the emperor withdrew to the mountains because of the heat. Meanwhile Count Otto, having broken his oaths, rebelled again in Burgundy. There he was killed by the empire’s faithful supporters, and his banner was sent to the emperor as a sign of victory. Conrad went to Rome for prayer; then, having visited many cities in Apulia, he intended to return by way of the Adriatic Sea, where he lost many princes through an unhealthy condition of the air. Then he returned to Francia and reached the city of Lower Trajectum [Col. 0966D]; there he fell ill and died, in the seventeenth year of his reign and the fourteenth of his empire. Let us set forth the remaining matters concerning Emperor Conrad the Second in verse.

Likewise, the same Emperor Conrad is described in verse.

He was duke from the town rightly called Guebelinga;

From it is generated the illustrious nobility of kings,

Supreme in the world in the office of knighthood.

Everywhere his power was hostile to enemies;

The duke’s deeds were great, but greater was his integrity—

Eloquent, worthy of his honor.

She was the kinswoman of Henry, whom I have now mentioned;

She herself, beautiful, then secretly loved the duke,

And from his embrace bore illustrious offspring.

[Col. 0967A]

The duke carried her off and held her as his bride for many years;

For a time he lay under imperial ban,

An outlaw in hiding, paying a long penalty.

When Caesar recognized that his own time of death was near,

He instructed the magnates to set the king above the host

And persuaded them together to hand over the kingdoms to the duke.

“Though,” he said, “he has for years been outlawed under ban,

This man is able to defend the kingdoms against mighty tyrants

And to maintain well the Roman realm.”

King Henry the Lame dies; the duke is recalled by the lords.

The nobles meet to establish another king;

Among them was this young man, at the people’s request.

### Concerning Duke Cuano, and his jesting remark accepted as valid

Duke Cuano was foremost among the princes and hoped without doubt to obtain the empire. When the other princes [Col. 0967B] asked him who seemed most suitable for the empire, he replied in a seemingly mocking manner: “My nephew Duke Conrad seems most suited to the empire.” For he believed this impossible and named him for that reason. On hearing this, they all praised Conrad and elected him. Duke Cuano objected; nevertheless, the choice of all prevailed. In this manner Conrad then came to rule.

Likewise, concerning the same Duke Cuano and his nephew Conrad.

There was in the land an exalted duke named Cuno;

He confidently expects to obtain the crown beyond doubt,

But now no hope is spoken of Conrad.

The dukes sat down; they wished an election to be conducted;

That duke seeks for Conrad a diadem to be prepared;

[Col. 0967C]

He sought it indeed by deception and did not wish it done.

As he asks, they praise; he resists those praising;

Yet, despite the duke’s prohibition, the kingdom is handed to him.

Thus a voice uttered in deceit stood valid by reason.

### Concerning Emperor Conrad’s edict and the affair of Lupold

Emperor Conrad the Second spared no violator of the peace. Therefore Count Lupold, a violator of the peace, fearing execution by the emperor, fled into a very remote forest, where he hid alone in a hut with his wife. By chance the emperor, returning from hunting, turned aside there and stayed there that night. That same night the count’s wife gave birth to a boy. When he cried, a voice from heaven said: “O emperor, this infant shall be your son-in-law and heir.” When this voice had been heard a third time, [Col. 0967D] the emperor rose at dawn and, having found two of his servants, said: “Go and kill that infant.” They went and took the child; but pitying him, they did not kill him, but placed him in a tree and left him. To the king, however, they presented a hare’s heart as the infant’s heart. The king rewarded them. Some time later a certain duke passed by and found the child, carried him away, and adopted him as a son. Much later the emperor saw the boy in the duke’s house and suspected he was the one whom he had ordered killed. He took him as if for his retainer and commanded him to carry his letters to the queen, ordering the queen in the letters, once she had seen them, immediately to have him killed. The boy, unaware of the matter, went on and lodged in the house of a certain priest. While he slept, the priest [Col. 0968A] stole and opened the letters; seeing there the boy’s death, he wrote another letter as follows: “When you see this boy, O queen, immediately give him our daughter as wife, as you love your life.” He put these letters back in the boy’s purse. The boy went away unaware, and thus the king’s daughter was immediately given to him.

Likewise, we expound in verse concerning the same Emperor Conrad and the peace of his time.

For peace Conrad strips dukes of their honor,

And makes the enactments of peace stand through its favor;

Every duke fears lest punishment be his.

One of the counts was marked as having violated the peace;

A small house was secretly prepared for him in the forest’s hiding places,

For he feared the king while hiding there.

The count and his wife, grieving, hid in this manner.

[Col. 0968B]

The count sees King Conrad coming;

His companions scattered, he too was alone.

He sought lodging because dark evening compelled him;

The wretches offer the king such comforts as they can;

The generous hostess gave whatever his horse desired.

That same night a son is born to the count;

They receive the boy, blessed in form and appearance;

In sleep a great vision came to the king.

A voice says: “Behold, this boy shall be your only heir;

He shall receive all that you are seen to possess;

In later time you shall have him as your son-in-law.”

At dawn the king goes farther on,

And grieves and weeps that such a son-in-law should take up the reins;

Without delay he considers how this boy may perish.

At once, following his tracks from the forest during the night,

[Col. 0968C]

Behold, the dogs and servants remain, seeking the king again,

Wondering that their lord had disappeared by night.

Then the king calls two young men, leaving the others behind.

With a wicked heart he speaks constrained words:

“Go together, boys; quickly bring me a heart.”

As they seek the boy, God himself takes care to protect him,

For the young men in pity wish to spare the boy;

By heaven’s judgment he is to be saved.

While the parents held their own creature in their hands,

The armed servants came, carrying off the boy,

So that he might leave his life in the midst of the woods.

When they look upon the boy, their minds change,

For wherever he looks he smiles, and by his smile begs

That so childlike a little head not fall.

[Col. 0968D]

As the armed servants now wish to pity the boy,

They begin to speak aloud what they conceive:

“Look how beautiful he will be, born yesterday!”

One says: “I would rather grant you life

Than have your little limbs struck by my sword,

And so you shall remain by a feigned death.”

The other says: “I wish to abandon the whole plan:

Let us place the boy in a remote place in the forest,

Lest a wolf eat him; I shall make a nest-like place.

“But by what cunning shall we bring tokens of death?”

He replies: “We shall catch a hare in the field with dogs

And take its heart, by which I shall feign the crime.”

He spoke; and behold, a hare sprang up beneath the young men’s feet.

The armed servant pursues it crying out and urges on the dogs;

Thus, by God’s mercy, the victim is brought to him.

[Col. 0969A]

Weeping, they leave the boy on a branch of a tree;

Showing the hare’s heart, they invent lies

That the crime has now been done in accordance with the command.

Caesar gives thanks and bestows great joys on the two,

Granting both power as a reward for the crime;

For the work of destruction greatly pleased him.

It happened that a duke passed by where the infant now lay.

He heard him and was amazed; the child’s cry persisted loudly;

When he saw the child, the duke quickly picked him up.

The duchess, exceedingly rejoicing, receives the infant.

While she had been playing with the duke in the darkness of night,

The great duchess complains that she is barren.

The duke says: “You may pretend that this boy was born there;

Pretend, I pray, that you gave birth; declare that he was born of you.

For I suspect that he has been given by the hand of the Lord.”

[Col. 0969B]

The beautiful woman agrees when she hears her husband.

“Go out from here,” she says, “leave the chamber swiftly;

Tell everyone at once that I have given birth.

Thus I shall imitate the labor of childbirth according to custom;

You, govern my words and grant your support,

So that they may believe the boy was born from me.”

The report flies that the duke has begotten and the duchess given birth.

In appearance, face, and form the boy resembles his father;

He grows and brings great joy to the duke.

When the boy Henry had risen to his fifteenth year,

He was judged worthy to be raised to the honor of knighthood,

For his appearance, body, and deeds wholly pleased.

Meanwhile the king himself comes; the boy stands before him.

Fresh beauty and face shine; his hair is fair;

[Col. 0969C]

As he shines like a flower, the king calls the duke himself:

“Tell me, whose boy is this?” The duke answers him: “He is mine.”

Caesar says: “In every respect his form resembles Achilles;

I shall attach him to my own service.”

The duke says: “I pray, father, spare the tender boy for now;

When he is strong, when he is a knight, call the young man back,

So that he may then be free for service given in a better manner.”

While the father entreats and strives so to retain him,

The fierce king entirely rejects all that he asks

And takes the boy away for himself without delay.

The king’s anxious mind diligently presses the youth

To tell who his father or mother is.

“I am the duke’s,” he replies; “the duke’s household rules me.”

Because the king now knew that the duchess was barren,

[Col. 0969D]

He concludes that she had not borne the boy;

and, since he thus suspects, devises evil in his heart.

For he thinks this is the boy whom he had earlier ordered killed,

And fears that he may be called to the imperial diadem;

Therefore he swiftly devises deadly peril for the boy.

He himself hurries to write a letter with his own hand,

By which he compels the boy, through deception, to carry his own death;

Thus the boy becomes Uriah and takes the roads.

He is said to have hurried to Aachen in seven days.

He lacks companions and has not sufficient resources for everything;

A priest receives him, as God himself commands.

Weary and hungry, he takes sleep upon a bench.

The priest, seeing the youth shine with beauty,

[Col. 0970A]

Arranges that a delicious meal be provided.

The letter hung from the good boy’s purse;

The priest opens it and seeks to discover its content,

And quickly sees there, by chance, the boy’s death.

When the priest is able to perceive the boy’s death,

He immediately strives to change his lot for the better;

He erased the evil text and then wrote this good text there:

“When you, queen, read this writing of the king, you shall see this boy;

You shall make him your son-in-law and hold him dear.

If you delay in giving him, you shall be a victim of death.”

In the morning, rising, the boy says: “Dear host, farewell.”

The priest replies: “Keep me always as your servant, lord;

When you are king, remember me, I ask.”

The youth laughed at this and thought it had been a joke;

Hastening toward Aachen, he completed the journey,

[Col. 0970B]

Unaware what the letter’s writing was bringing about for him.

The queen, looking out, sees the youth coming;

She marvels at his figure, face, and shining countenance.

As soon as the boy arrives, he gives her the royal letter.

She reads it, but conceals what she has read, keeping it secret;

Seeing her daughter, she remains silent, her blush revealing her distress.

Her mother urges her swiftly to see the written message.

The royal commands, read with their excessive severity,

Show that the lady fears the king’s anger;

The youth’s appearance urges that these things be done.

It was impossible for the king’s commands to be refused;

The court orders a marriage chamber prepared for the young man according to custom;

The daughter is ordered promptly to be given as his bride.

After a little while another letter comes from the king, asking

Whether the queen reverently obeys his commands.

[Col. 0970C]

She replies: “I have ordered all things to be performed.

Indeed, I reread the harsh letter at your command;

But because I feared quickly to contradict the king,

I supplied all that your letter directs.

Our daughter is married, the wedding celebrations have been held,

The court has rejoiced, great ceremonies have been prepared;

Our daughter rejoices to have a husband equal to her.”

Caesar reads this and is astonished, considering all these things.

He spurs his horses, hastens on his way, and quickens his course;

Deeply troubled, he sits down again at Aachen.

The daughter stands with her mother, accompanied by a crowd of nobles,

And her mother presents the son-in-law whom she had formerly preferred.

The beloved bride leads her bridegroom by the hand.

Turgidly seated, he does not know what to do with her or what to say to her;

[Col. 0970D] he swells up, glowing and smoldering with rage;

Fury and reason stand within his battered breast.

Anger, the frenzy of the heart, stands opposed to reason,

And reason, allied with compassion, confronts fury;

The son-in-law, standing between them, believes that he will die at once.

The daughter, with her mother, while her father’s savagery boils,

Silent and full of fear, watches his threatening, changing face;

Death and life alike lie in the king’s mouth.

Fresh anger strives to inflict death and punishment;

“Spare him, father; delay,” nature pleads;

He is conquered without delay by nature’s entreaties.

While a grievous struggle of mind took place in the king,

Reason prevailed in the case, and the mighty man’s anger fled;

Joyfully he looks upon his wife as he had formerly been accustomed to do.

He says to her: “What God has ordained cannot be annulled.

[Col. 0971A] What I wished, I can no longer accomplish; God himself has forbidden it.

What God has established, we shall endure,” he says.

His wife presses him on this point: “God,” she says, “has granted these things;

Heavenly wisdom is altogether removed from human wisdom;

These are God’s deeds: let your mind yield to him.

Yet if nature marked the son-in-law as freeborn,

Neither fortune nor my daughter would bring me harm;

But if the son-in-law is otherwise, he would give no joy.”

The duke is therefore compelled to inform the king what he had done;

Then he compelled the two young men to recount the truth,

And compelled also the count whom the Black Forest conceals.

When the count is brought in, he believes his grief is increasing;

But, recognized as the father, he receives immediate recompense,

For his son will be son-in-law to the empire.

When Caesar was able to learn of his nobility,

[Col. 0971B] the king can enjoy peace, and the son-in-law himself deserves it:

“This man,” he says, “shall be both my companion and my son-in-law.”

And when he sees that he himself too had broken faith with the boy,

He applauds the man whom God’s right hand saved and loved:

“You are son-in-law to the empire; you are my son,” he says.

The king falls into his allotted fate; that man is called the king’s son-in-law;

He is praised in due order and joined to his father-in-law as son-in-law:

Thus Fortune’s wheel is permitted to have altered their circumstances.

That woodland place where the man was brought up

Is the noble church called Hirsau, home of monks;

There great ceremony is now offered to the Creator.

### Concerning Henry III, emperor, son of Emperor Conrad II, the eighty-third from Augustus

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1040, Henry III, son of the aforesaid Empress [Col. 0971C] Gisela, who had begun to reign while his father was alive, after his father’s death began to rule as the eighty-third from Augustus. In him the imperial dignity, which for a long time, having been drawn outside the genealogy of the Carolingians, had already been in exile, was restored through his mother Gisela to the most noble stock of the Carolingians.

This Henry is said to have been equal to his father in virtues and even more eminent. First, he received in submission the duke of the Bohemians, then hostile to the empire. He received Peter, king of the Hungarians, driven from his kingdom and exiled; and, having joined battle with the Hungarians, he routed an innumerable multitude of them. Entering Pannonia, he restored Peter himself to his kingdom. Later he took as wife Agnes, sister of the most noble prince of the Gauls, William, duke of Poitou and Aquitaine. When he celebrated the wedding in royal fashion at Ingelheim, he allowed all the minstrels to depart empty-handed, and gave to the poor all that was to have been bestowed upon them.

At about the same time a grave confusion arose in the Roman Church, three usurpers occupying that see. One of them was called Benedict. To increase the misery still further, they divided the patriarchates and their revenues among themselves: one sat at Saint Peter’s, another at Saint Mary Major’s, and the third—that is, Benedict—at the Lateran palace. All, as we have learned, lived shameful and depraved lives. Then a certain priest named [Col. 0972A] Gratian, pitying God’s Church in such confusion, approached the aforesaid men and persuaded them with money to withdraw from the holy see. Benedict, who seemed to possess the greatest authority among them, was left the revenues of England as part of the peace settlement. For this reason the Romans unanimously chose that priest Gratian as supreme pontiff, as the liberator of the Church, and called him Gregory VII.

On hearing this, the emperor hurried to Rome. Gratian met him at Sutri and gave him a precious crown, to win his favor. The emperor then received him kindly; but later, after convening a synod, he persuaded him to resign because of the stain of simony. With the Church’s consent he substituted for him Suidger, [Col. 0972B] bishop of Bamberg, whom it pleased them also to call Benedict.

From this time it is said that the canonical election of Roman pontiffs was so stifled that this Benedict, Aldibrand, and the four others following them are found entered in the catalogue of Roman pontiffs as appointed by the emperor. How God’s Church, partly under the younger Leo and fully under Alexander, recovered free election—as we have learned from the testimony of trustworthy men—we shall, with the Lord as author, relate later. We set forth the rest concerning Henry III in verse.

### Concerning the same Henry III

They called Henry “the Black,” because of his dark beard;

Through the pope’s mediation he received the Roman empire,

[Col. 0972C] And watched over his peoples with integrity.

The pope Benedict then called a German,

Who, leaving the Roman princes in peace,

Returned to the homeland from which he nobly sprang.

The Roman court proceeds together with Caesar;

A German host serves under worthy governance,

And at the city of Worms he finds his first rest.

After many conversations the pope travels with Caesar;

The pope dies at the place called Bamberg;

Then Leo the German received the papal burden.

### Concerning Henry IV, emperor of the Romans, the eighty-fourth from Augustus

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1047, Henry IV, a victorious king, was crowned at Rome by Pope Clement on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, [Col. 0972D] and received the name and dignity of the empire, the eighty-fourth from Augustus. Thereupon, having led his army through Apulia, he returned honorably to his homeland.

In the same year, after the death of Suidger—that is, Pope Clement—Poppo, patriarch of Aquileia, was installed in his place at Rome. Not long afterward Peter, king of the Hungarians, was deprived of both his eyes and his kingdom by one of his retainers, named Andrew. Then Poppo died—that is, Pope Damasus. Bruno, bishop of Toul—that is, Pope Leo—succeeded him at Rome. Descended from noble Frankish stock, he had been appointed to the see of blessed Peter by imperial authority. As he traveled through Gaul after assuming the purple, he happened to come to Cluny, where the aforesaid Pope Aldibrand [Col. 0973A] was carrying out the office of prior. Aldibrand approached him, filled with zeal for God, and firmly rebuked him for his undertaking, declaring it unlawful for a supreme pontiff to enter the government of the universal Church through the hand of a layman. “Nevertheless,” he said, “if you are willing to trust my counsel, you can accomplish this: you will neither embitter the king’s mind nor take from the holy Church its freedom in the election of a pontiff.” Bruno yielded to Prior Aldibrand’s admonition, laid aside the purple, assumed a pilgrim’s dress, and set out on his journey, taking Aldibrand with him. Thus, when both had come together to Rome, Bruno was elected supreme pontiff on Aldibrand’s advice. In this manner the Roman Church then began, in whatever measure, to be newly formed toward the election of its own pontiff.

Meanwhile the emperor entered Belgium and compelled Dukes Godfrey and Baldwin to submit. After this, a synod was celebrated at Mainz in the presence of Pope Leo himself and Emperor Henry IV.

The emperor then moved an army against Andrew, who, as we have narrated above, had deprived his lord Peter, king of the Hungarians, of his eyes and kingdom, and entered Pannonia. But since the inhabitants of the land hid everywhere, and all Hungary’s provisions had either been concealed, contaminated, or poisoned, he was unable to maintain his army there; after devastating Pannonia, he returned. Again, in the following year, attacking Pannonia in war, he took Pope Leo [Col. 0973C] with him, put Andrew to flight, and arranged all matters successfully.

### The land of Robert Guiscard in Apulia

At that time the Norman people arose under Robert Guiscard, a most vigorous man and a duke of great renown, and entered Apulia. There they afflicted the inhabitants in various ways, now by force, now by trickery and fraud. When Pope Leo, returning to Rome from Gaul with an army, began to restrain them and intended to expel them from Apulia, he joined battle with them. Though many were struck down, he was defeated and compelled to flee to Benevento. Such a multitude fell there on both sides that a heap later made from the bones of the dead is still customarily shown by the inhabitants to travelers.

[Col. 0973D] In the following year Pope Leo died and, buried in the church of Saint Peter, was shown to shine with miracles. He was succeeded by Gebhard, bishop of Eichstätt, who was called Pope Victor. Stephen, a German by nation, succeeded him in turn.

The emperor again entered Italy and took with him Countess Beatrice, mother of Countess Matilda, his kinswoman and widow of Marquis Boniface.

### Concerning the recovery of the Holy Sepulchre, in the year of the Lord 1067

After Gregory VII, pope at Salerno, had died, while Gilbert held the papal throne and city at Rome through the emperor, a few Romans, fearing the emperor, drew Abbot Desiderius of Monte [Col. 0974A] Cassino unwillingly to the papacy. Having secretly bribed the guards who guarded the Leonine City, they placed him, in the silence of night, in the chair at Saint Peter’s and named him Victor. But he was immediately seized by diarrhea and ended his life. In his place they appointed Otho, bishop of Ostia—that is, Pope Urban.

At the same time the city of Jerusalem was being trampled upon and held by pagans; but they kept the Lord’s sepulchre reverently for the sake of profit, while Emperor Henry IV and Alexius, king of the Greeks, were still alive. Then the aforesaid Pope Urban, traveling into Gaul because of the misery of the Jerusalemites, stirred up Christian arms [Col. 0974B] for the defense of the Holy Sepulchre. He gathered one hundred thousand men under arms from different peoples and set over them the following leaders: Godfrey of Bouillon, duke of Lorraine; the count of Saint-Gilles; Raymond, count of Flanders; Robert; and Hugh, brother of Philip, king of France. He entrusted the care of all of them to the bishop of Le Puy in Christ. Other Christians, hearing these reports, flocked in an inestimable multitude from every Christian region, language, and island, asserting that they were apostles and preachers of Christ, and fighters against the enemies of Christ’s cross.

With Duke Godfrey as leader, they came through Bulgaria to Constantinople with great difficulty. There they endured much deceit and obstruction from King Alexius; after joining battle with the Greeks, they captured the bridge of the imperial city and, crossing over, set fire to the suburbs. There, after mustering three hundred thousand warriors, they came to Nicaea, once a Christian stronghold, captured it from the pagans, and gave it to the emperor. Then, proceeding along the coastland of the Ruthenians, they found such an abundance of goods that, according to Count Robert’s testimony, an ox was sold for a shekel and a ram for a coin. They also overwhelmed in battle Saracen princes who met them. Elated by these successes, they surrounded Antioch with a siege. Remaining there for nine months, with supplies failing and the army weakened, they were greatly humbled. But God had mercy on them and delivered the city, with all the Turks’ abundance, into [Col. 0974D] their hands.

When news of them terrified the whole East, the king of the Babylonians sent envoys to them, seeking their alliance deceitfully. With these envoys Frankish envoys went to Babylon and were honorably received. When their stature and beauty were observed, when their strength and greatness of spirit were considered, and when the natives of that land declared them to be more than men, the king of Babylon, having received counsel from his men, immediately moved an army and surrounded Jerusalem by siege. He told its inhabitants that he had made a treaty and friendship with the Franks, with whom he wished also to destroy them unless they surrendered themselves and their city to the king of Babylon. Therefore the Turks holding the city, from fear of the Christians, [Col. 0975A] surrendered themselves and the city into the king’s hands. Having expelled all the Turks, he fortified the city with Saracens and thus, by his stratagem, hindered the Christians’ purpose.

Meanwhile, after capturing Antioch, as we have said, the Christians appear not to have glorified God worthily. They were therefore surrounded by so great a multitude of Saracens that their former abundance was followed by a famine so unbearable that they scarcely abstained even from human flesh. But the Lord, looking upon his people’s distress, revealed to them in those places, by revelation, the lance by which Christ’s most holy side is said to have been pierced. Trusting in its power, the Christians, though weak and hungry, joined battle with the Saracens and, courageously routing them all, overcame their enemies not by their own strength but by Christ’s.

Proceeding thence into Syria, they captured the cities of Barra and Maat; while remaining there, they are said again to have been so worn down by scarcity that some starving men devoured even fetid human bodies. After this they directed their battle-lines against the Holy City, then inhabited and fortified by Saracens. Unable to capture it under siege, they took religious counsel and, imitating Christ, the teacher of humility, resolved to walk around it barefoot. Thus, on the day called the Division of the Apostles, the city was taken; and the enemies seized there were slaughtered in such numbers that, in Solomon’s Portico, the blood of the slain reached the knees of our horses. From that time Jerusalem, with God as its author, has remained in our possession until now.

[Col. 0975C] Moreover, the admiratus* of the Babylonians—who is also called king of the Memphites and Alexandrians—while staying at Ascalon assembled an innumerable army, intending by his power to recover Jerusalem and Antioch. He still held the Frankish envoys with him at Ascalon. The Christians, leaving their baggage and sick persons in the city, met the Babylonian army in the field. When they saw the infinite multitude of enemies, they poured out prayers to the Lord and advanced against the enemy with few men. Marvelously, through divine aid, with five thousand horsemen and fifteen thousand foot soldiers, they compelled one hundred thousand Saracen horsemen and three hundred thousand infantry to turn their backs, [Col. 0975D] and they seized immense spoils. More than one hundred thousand Saracens were slain by the sword in that battle, while around the gate of Ascalon two hundred thousand were suffocated at the city’s entrance. Countless others, it is reported, perished by drowning or entanglement in thorns.

When the victory was accomplished and the princes returned to their own lands, Duke Godfrey led the army remaining behind vigorously and wisely. Since Romans and Germans frequently quarreled among themselves through envy, he, being skilled in both languages, beneficially trained them by his own efforts toward peace and concord, so that they might remain together. Meanwhile Pope Urban, who had sent the army beyond the sea, after holding a council at Clermont returned to Rome and expelled Gilbert, who [Col. 0976A] held the Roman chair through the emperor, from the city; only Crescentius’s house—that is, the castle of Saint Angelo—remained to him. Thereafter, having recovered his chair, Urban left the city and traveled through Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily. Having gathered very much money there, he returned to Rome, bribed the guards of Crescentius’s castle with money, and, having thus expelled Gilbert, at last freely possessed both the City and the papal chair. Not long afterward he died and left the chair to Pope Paschal.

Meanwhile, as Christians flocked to the Lord’s Holy Sepulchre, Duke Godfrey died in Jerusalem. His brother Baldwin was installed there in his place and, by the authority of the supreme pontiff, was called king in the year of the Lord 1100.

[Col. 0976B] At the time when the first Baldwin was made king of Jerusalem, Gilbert’s death brought an end to the most dreadful schism, like Egypt’s thickest darkness.

In the following year Conrad, son of Emperor Henry IV, to whom his father had entrusted Italy, died, namely in the ninth year after he had departed from his father; he was honorably buried in the city of Florence. After this his father, the emperor, having celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Mainz, designated to the princes his son Henry, the fifth of the Henries, as his successor. He vowed and publicly declared that he would go to Jerusalem. In the second year, while the emperor was again at Mainz, [Col. 0976C] his son Henry, acting on Bavarian counsel, began to plot rebellion against him at Regensburg, taking as his pretext that his father was held excommunicated by the Roman pontiff. Having taken the princes with him, he entered Saxony, which was easily stirred against the empire, and there at Quedlinburg joined all the Saxons to his cause.

Then Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz, who had long been expelled from his see by the father-emperor, attached himself to his son Henry V. At a council held at the village of Nordhausen, he condemned the emperor as a simoniac. He then consecrated Henry, elected to Magdeburg but rejected by the emperor. Next he planned to return to Mainz with the son’s help. But the father, remaining at Mainz [Col. 0976D] with his army, frustrated the plan. After this, the son captured the castle of Noricum, that is, Nuremberg.

### Again, concerning the same Emperor Henry IV

When Henry IV was a boy, after his father’s death he was under the guardianship of his mother, Empress Agnes, who governed the empire wisely for some time. Later the son, alienated from his mother by the counsel of libertines, began to rule on his own. This separation was the seedbed of the greatest discord. The empress, seeing the wicked changes of circumstances and unwilling to be swept up in the waves of disturbance, chose the religious life and withdrew to the monastery of Fruttuaria. Later she went from there to Rome and, having stayed there for some time, died. She was honorably buried in a marble tomb in the church of Blessed Petronilla.

In these days Alexander, first bishop of Lucca and afterward raised to the supreme pontificate by common vote and election, restored the Roman Church, long since enslaved, to its former liberty. For he firmly restrained Cadalus, bishop of Parma, who sought to seize the Roman see by armed force. A verse concerning this Cadalus and this Alexander was written in the Lateran chamber:

> Alexander reigns; Cadalus falls and is defeated.

Accordingly Henry’s empire was divided against itself; with the Saxons conspiring, rebellions arose. Many slanders and shameful reports concerning the emperor were brought to the ears of the supreme pontiff. Hanno, archbishop [Col. 0977B] of Cologne, and Germanus, bishop of Bamberg, were sent to Rome. When they returned after accomplishing their embassy, they delivered apostolic letters to the king, by which he was admonished to make satisfaction concerning simony and other enormities. At the same time the Saxons openly rebelled, seized the cities and castles which the king had built in Saxony, and utterly destroyed them.

In the second year Pope Alexander died and left the apostolate to his archdeacon Hildebrand, who became Gregory VII. Since this was done without the emperor’s consent, a most grievous schism is said to have arisen. Pope Gregory, therefore, seeking to uproot simony and restrain the incontinence [Col. 0977C] of clerics, repeatedly summoned the emperor himself to synods on such matters. By a decretal edict he prohibited forever throughout the whole Roman world marriages of clerics from the subdiaconate upward; and he made himself God’s champion, a wall for the house of the Lord.

The emperor attacked the Saxons in war and, near the river Hunstrot, in an indecisive battle, after very many had been slain on both sides, barely obtained a bloody victory. There fell Gebhard, father of Duke Lothair, who afterward ruled, and Ernest, father of Margrave Albert.

In the same year William, count of Normandy, conquered Greater Britain, which is now called England, and killed its king Harold. Then, after stationing Normans there and reducing the entire province [Col. 0977D] to servitude, he ruled there himself.

In the following year the emperor took as wife Bertha, daughter of Otto, margrave of Italy. The pope excommunicated so great an emperor; by his counsel the Saxons made Rudolph their king. When Rudolph was later killed in battle, they substituted for him Herman, prince of Lorraine, who himself was also soon slain. Before this emperor, we do not read of anyone excommunicated or deprived of the empire by the Roman pontiff—unless perhaps it is considered an excommunication that Philip, the first Christian emperor, is said to have been placed among the penitents for a short time by the Roman pontiff; or that Theodosius, because of a bloody slaughter of men, is said to have been excluded from the thresholds of the Church.

[Col. 0978A] Meanwhile Pope Gregory VII was driven from the City by imperial power. Gilbert of Ravenna was intruded in his place.

### Again, concerning the same Henry IV, set down in verse

Henry IV, arising from the Ghibelline stock,

Pressed many kingdoms throughout Italy with great savagery,

That they might render fitting tribute to their Lord.

While he recovered all that he considered seized or increased,

He very often burdened the possessions of the Roman pontiff;

The pope, grieving over these deeds, said, “We shall not endure this.”

Why Caesar seeks what is unlawful, the pope soon asks;

By what right does he wish to possess the Church’s goods?

“My peace has now perished through the man’s savagery.”

Henry despises every complaint of the pope,

[Col. 0978B] Nor does he desire to placate the Church by any remedy,

For he was powerful in arms and great in heart.

He is said to have been marked by excessive envy

And judged wicked through his excessive brutality;

Of these things a brief page will give examples.

If he thought a man or horse remarkable for excellence,

He would devise whatever wicked thing could bring about its death,

And lay snares of death by fraud and deceit.

There was a soldier, handsome and lofty in honor before the king;

He is said to have killed a lion with his bare fist,

The foremost man in the world in a soldier’s office.

The unwilling king sees him, a wicked plotter,

Envious Henry, fierce enemy of excellence;

That man soon perishes through his plots.

A rider is said once to have belonged to the king

To whom nature had given no equal in prowess;

At the king’s command, this man perishes in the waters of the Rhine.

[Col. 0978C] While the king’s evil reputation is widely noted throughout the empire,

Anger moves the nobles and the whole German people is oppressed;

The empire grieves to sustain a shameful head.

The court of Frankish lords gathered together

Condemns the king’s crimes and deeds,

And wishes now to reject proven deceit.

Now the judgment of the magnates seeks an answer from the apostolic see:

“Can a king, the chief of crimes, lawfully be removed?”

The pope replies: “He ought rightly to be deposed.”

Pope Gregory VII now stands in the City;

Then Urban comes, who presses hard against the king’s deeds;

Paschal too brings times full of evils.

[Col. 0978D] Henry, badly fated, is thereafter made anathema;

Rudolph with the Saxons took up this diadem,

With whom the Church presses royal claims.

Noble Rome too joins in agreement with the Saxons;

A golden crown is sent thence to Rudolph;

Wars multiply and thunder throughout the empire.

A verse was written and inserted in the diadem:

> The Rock gave Peter; Peter gave the diadem to Rudolph.

This crown is thus sent to the Saxons.

Albert, then first in rank among bishops by the see of Mainz,

Was fierce and cruel in savage brutality,

Yet not inferior in intelligence or integrity.

He was more hostile than all others to Henry;

So too the archbishop of Cologne, the renowned Frederick,

And Albert * of Trier, became a grievous enemy to him.

[Col. 0979A] They conspire from every side; wondrous battles come;

Standards, matched with eagles, come to dreadful conflicts;

Three times the Saxon repelled him in battle.

The battle returns a fourth time; the Saxon hard presses the king,

For a fourth victory had, as it were, already been won;

But as the new king wages war, he perishes by the sword.

While Henry flees, his troop of counts fleeing,

A soldier preserves his standard in the midst of the position,

Saying: “Where are you going? Look back: you shall be victor.

“For I tell you that Rudolph has been killed by the sword.”

The king denies the event, but the soldier draws him back as he resists.

When the king laments this fate, public report arrives.

The soldier says: “Rise; your great glory shall rise again.

“The Saxon flees because the king has fallen; run, press on!”

When he had been drawn back, he returned and was himself victorious.

[Col. 0979B] Yet the punishment did not leave him victorious for long;

His enemies bring it about that the king is consigned to death;

His son desires to take the kingdoms from him.

### Henry the Younger takes the empire against his father

An ungrateful bishop and senate of nobles bring it about

That the son possesses the diadems for his father’s destruction,

Believing that through the pontiff’s aid he can do all things.

The father, as he had been before, is made anathema under the pontiff;

The son Henry is raised up holding the diadem,

And strives utterly to suppress his father’s rights.

The father is therefore driven out by the excessive savagery of the nobles;

Yet the son was not altogether without pity for his father:

At Liège the father hides, poor and destitute.

Henry the Great, reckoned fourth by number,

[Col. 0979C] had completed fifty-two years of life,

During which he is said to have suffered the bitter wars of his son.

Then he died; then he wished to be buried at Liège;

His canons sought to honor his body

And to lay his limbs in a royal tomb according to royal custom.

But because the king had deserved, while living, to be anathema,

The pope promptly orders the body to be removed from there,

And immediately strikes all Liège with anathema.

He banishes the body also from sacred places. With circumstances changed,

The son grieved that his father’s bones should be among the wicked;

Having quickly removed them, he caused them to be taken farther away

To his homeland, Speyer, which encircles the banks of the Rhine.

Moved by excessive anger, he threatens his father’s bones;

The chapel of Saint Afra was that which received the father’s bones.

[Col. 0979D] Thus transferred and enclosed in a new bier,

For five years he remained unburied in the bier,

Hated by all and subjected to mockery.

This kind of horror becomes a cause of grief to the son;

His father’s bier renews the time of mourning,

While he himself lies outside, expelled from the churches.

Sacred burial is denied while the pope forbids it,

Unless the ring and staff are restored to the pope,

With which he had sold his churches.

He sold them, because he was seldom free from simony;

Lest this disgrace be exposed, divine wisdom forbade it,

And the pope eagerly longs altogether to abolish it with such purpose.

Henry, true heir of the deceased Caesar,

Is henceforth forbidden to possess the pontiffs’ staffs:

No rule will permit this to be done.

[Col. 0980A] Kings may no longer sell bishops;

For sacred laws forbid this through the ages;

It is fitting that each person reject Simon’s crimes.

Henry V then falls into a labyrinth;

Bound by this snare, he is constrained outside and within;

He yields to the Church and grants gifts under compulsion.

Caesar relaxes only these two demands repeatedly made:

He no longer disturbs churches that have endured rage;

War gives rest, and renewed peace is pleasing.

Ring and staff follow papal rights;

Thus worldly matters too are rightly governed by the empire;

Their respective rights stand established in equitable reason.

Now the emperor’s sacred burial becomes valid;

There is a golden structure for his father, yielding greater joys,

And holy Speyer receives and inters his limbs.

### The Normans invade Apulia in the time of Emperor Henry IV

[Col. 0980B]

While Henry IV’s glory declines to its lowest point,

Apulia first experiences Norman warfare,

And Calabria and the Sicilian gulf are conquered.

There William, the Norman duke, must first be noted,

And afterward * Robert the Great Guiscard must be remembered,

Whose greatest deeds I shall set forth briefly.

He brought the pagan Sicilians under his authority;

Apulian and Calabrian alike, conquered, bent their necks to him,

Whom King William now governs by his excellence.

### Robert Guiscard burned the Lateran while Emperor Henry held Pope Paschal captive at Rome

Henry was not permitted to defend the land,

For throughout the empire there had been a very mighty war,

[Col. 0980C] And Pope Paschal entered into captivity and chains.

While Henry V bore the crown in the City,

Guiscard dared partly to burn Rome;

Thus the burning of the Lateran gate resounds.

When he crosses to the Danes, the Greeks recount his battles;

There a portion of the Danish king’s men became victims of death;

There is an abundance of plunder and a wondrous mass of slaughter.

The duke was poor in resources, rich in excellence;

He had coins of leather issued and spent them widely,

With which the defeated abundance of the Danes lies subdued.

After defeating the Danes, after times of abundance,

He repaid silver for the leather pennies

And generously bestowed abundant gifts upon his soldiers.

Robert Guiscard at last dies without offspring;

[Col. 0980D] Roger the German succeeds him in honor

And possesses and protects the regions of Sicily.

Roger was customarily called a pagan;

Count Roger was begotten by Roger,

A jewel of his race and foremost in excellence.

He was a jewel and deserved to rule through his excellence;

Apulia, Calabria, and Africa became subject to him:

What I say is plainly evident: the land lies conquered.

Here I shall leave the time and deeds of King Roger;

First I shall relate the affair of Emperor Henry V,

And afterward I shall give the time and deeds of Roger.

### Again, concerning Henry V the Younger, son of Henry IV, the eighty-fifth from Augustus

Henry the Younger moves an army against his father, and the father against him. The armies of both, [Col. 0981A] with the Rhine between them separating one from the other, encamp above the River Rhine. The father’s greatest strength lay in the Bohemian army and in Leopold, margrave of Austria. When the son recognized this, he turned both the Bohemian duke, named Boroez, and Margrave Leopold away from aid to his father by most lavish promises. When they departed, the father was weakened and compelled to withdraw from the field; he departed in confusion. From that day, therefore, the father’s power declined and the son’s increased.

Afterward father and son meet at the castle of Pinguium, where the son advises his father to emerge from excommunication through the apostolic see. The father asks that the princes be assembled at Mainz and that the same matter be considered there before them. Therefore, at the father’s request, a general court is proclaimed at Mainz, and there father and son are presented before all the princes.

### Concerning the people of Jerusalem

At about the same time Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, made besieged Ascalon tributary to himself. Having joined battle with the Saracens, though he had only four thousand warriors, he overthrew fifty thousand enemies by God’s power rather than that of men, capturing one Saracen leader and killing another.

Then Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, an adversary of Christian prosperity, allied with his friendship the Turks, now reduced to desperation, and granted them the tower of Nicaea, won with Christian blood.

[Col. 0981C] Meanwhile, when the general court had assembled at Mainz and the legates of the apostolic see were present, the emperor was pronounced excommunicated before all. He was then confined under guard in a certain castle. When the princes seek an audience with him there, they circumvent him by deceit and in some fashion compel him not to delay surrendering the royal insignia to his son: namely, in the fifty-third year of his reign and the fortieth of his empire. The princes therefore returned from the father to the son, carried the imperial insignia to him, and, declaring that he had then been chosen by his father, created him emperor through the hands of the Roman pontiff’s legates, the ninety-second from Augustus Octavian.

### The Author

[Col. 0981D] Up to this point, supported by the authorities both of the books of Orosius and Eusebius and of others who wrote after them, we have set down our writings. But the matters which follow, being of recent memory and, as it were, of our own times, we shall present to readers, as truthfully as we can with the Lord’s favor, as handed down to us by trustworthy men and partly seen by us with eyewitness faith and heard by our own ears.

Know that I, Godfrey, author of this book, was chaplain and notary of King Conrad III, of Emperor Frederick, and of his son Henry VI. During their times I investigated all these matters, on both sides of the sea, for forty years, from every archive—Latin, barbarian, Greek, Jewish, and Chaldaean.

### Concerning Henry IV

[Col. 0982A]

Emperor Henry IV, having surrendered all royal insignia to his son, abandoned by the support of all the princes and reduced to poverty, came by the River Rhine to Cologne. There he was received by the citizens, not as an exile but as emperor. Going on from there to Liège, he made known to all, in speech and in letters, that the princes had deceived him and compelled him to surrender the royal insignia to his son. After a short interval the father died at Liège and was buried there in royal fashion. But later, by order of the Roman pontiff, he was expelled from the cemetery and denied every Christian burial. His body was carried in a bier from Liège to the city of Speyer, above the Rhine, where he had founded, though not completed, a church of marvelous construction in honor of Saint Mary. There, in the chapel of Saint Afra, [Col. 0982B] it was kept unburied in its bier for five years. What was afterward done with him we shall relate below in verse at the end of this chapter. Let us now see what the son does.

### Henry V captures Pope Paschal
Henry V, after his father’s death, having assembled a remarkably large army, in the third year after his father’s death crossed the Pyrenean Mount Jovis, setting out for Rome. When he had encamped above the Po and ordered the army to be counted, thirty thousand soldiers were found, apart from all those who had flocked to him from Italy. Then, crossing the Apennines, he captured and destroyed Barga of Pontremoli, strongly fortified with towers and walls, because it had attempted to bar the army’s passage.
