Proceeding thereafter through Perugia as far as Arezzo, he destroyed that city because its citizens had destroyed the church of Saint Donatus—that is, the bishop’s seat—which lay outside the city, intending to establish the episcopal see within the city walls. Having done these things, he came to Rome and was received on the steps of Saint Peter’s by Pope Paschal, all the cardinals, and the Roman people, with crosses in procession, with rejoicing and great joy. Yet, on the advice of certain wicked men, he seized and held Pope Paschal captive, entrusting him to the keeping of Ulrich, Patriarch of Aquileia, with due respect. Then, when a sudden tumult arose, and the ornaments of the Church and all the clergy’s goods were seized and scattered, those who had expected joy encountered mourning.

The occasion and cause of this captivity is said to have been as follows. As the emperor was making for Rome, the pope had agreed with him on this compact: that the emperor should surrender the investitures of bishops, while the pope, conversely, should release to the emperor all episcopal regalian rights. This agreement is said to have been secured between pope and emperor by oaths and hostages. Since the pope could not carry it out because the bishops resisted, though he was entirely innocent in every respect, he was committed to custody as though guilty. The chief adviser of this faction is said to have been Albert, then the emperor’s chancellor, who later became Archbishop of Mainz; the emperor afterwards found him, by divine judgment, an exceedingly formidable enemy.

After the pope had been captured and detained for some time, the emperor was recalled by the citizens. Receiving from the pope the investiture of bishops—that is, the ring and staff—he took care to reconcile both the pope and the Roman citizens to himself with gifts. Crowned by the pope, he obtained imperial favor and title in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, the sixth year of his reign from the time when his father had resigned the regalian rights to him.

After these events, a synod of bishops was later held and rejected as a *pravilegium*—an evil privilege—the privilege extorted from the emperor by threats and terrors. Returning from the City into Francia, the emperor took as wife Matilda, daughter of Henry, king of the English, and celebrated splendid nuptials at Mainz. At this court Lothair, Duke of Saxony, who later became emperor, clothed in a woollen tunic as penance and barefoot, fell at the emperor’s feet. Such terror had seized everyone that no one dared resist his will. Yet at the very celebration of the marriage, where all had assembled, many conspiracies of princes were formed against his terrifying power; from that time many began to rebel, both openly and secretly. At the counsel and instigation of the archbishops Frederick of Cologne and Albert of Mainz, and certain others, Pope Calixtus, who had received the Roman pontificate after Paschal and Gelasius, bound the emperor with the bond of excommunication.

The schism having thus been renewed, the emperor went to Rome and, by force, installed in the see Burdinus, a Spaniard by birth. The Romans later captured him at Sutri and, as is said, placed him upon a camel, carried him off in disgrace, and consigned him to perpetual confinement in a cage near Salerno. Seeing that the kingdom was gradually slipping away from him, reflecting on his father’s example, and fearing the anathema that pressed upon him, the emperor summoned a general court at Worms. There he publicly resigned the investiture of bishops—the ring and staff—into the hands of the apostolic legate Lambert, later Pope Honorius; through him he was also absolved from the anathema. The pope likewise issued the emperor a privilege: that all bishops, both on the far side of the Alps and on this side, should not be ordained bishops until they had received investiture of their regalian rights from the emperor’s hand.

Wishing to avenge himself upon the Romans, the emperor hurried into Italy and besieged the City. When they rashly sallied out against him, he captured many of them, nearly all of whom he either blinded or mutilated by cutting off their noses. He then returned to his native land, was seized by illness, and died. He was buried in the city of Speyer, where he had completed and enriched the church mentioned above, beside his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, in the nineteenth year of his reign and the fourteenth of his empire.

It now pleases us to recount the remaining events in verse.

Likewise, concerning the captivity of Pope Paschal and the war between Empire and Church, composed in verse.

[Col. 0984A]

When Rome in every respect was subject to Henry,  
Anointed by apostolic hands and having received the crown,  
He seized the apostolic lord: the report resounds through the City.

The people prepare war; the senate comes to aid from the City.  
Henry prevails; the party of the prelate is stripped;  
The pope, deprived of his mantle, is captured by his enemy.

Now the question arises: why is the pope held in prison?  
The answer given is: “Because the prelate has taken everything;  
He has taken from the Empire the pontifical dignity.

“The property of bishops which he himself strives to retain  
The Empire bestowed—property which Caesar ought to possess;  
Henceforth whoever holds it shall hold it by Caesar’s grant.

“The ring and staff come from our gift;  
Everywhere bishops are furnished by kings’ benefaction.  
How does the pope exercise Caesar’s office?”

The Church replied: “If we seek to confess what is just,  
The ring and staff never came from Caesar,  
For God gave these things from heaven to the Churches.

“All that kings gave in former times  
Is no longer the kings’ property, but belongs to those to whom the rights were given;  
Neither God nor your own laws permit otherwise.

“Since yours is the kingdom and yours is the guardianship of law,  
By our imprisonment you set evil examples for the future,  
When in your savagery you rage against the Lord’s holy one.

“You are a maker of law, though you seem to scorn laws;  
Now you fear neither God’s laws nor royal laws.  
You torment the Church, though you shall be tormented.

[Col. 0984C]

“It is a disgrace to confuse the fountain of law with lawlessness,  
And more fearful still to scorn the King of Heaven.  
When you deny sacred laws, you rule a sorrowful realm.

“Why does a layman demand that heaven’s gifts be handed over to him?  
The harmonious election of the clergy, as God established it,  
Shall always remain free by heaven’s judgment.

“If you reclaim what is yours, reclaim what you gave;  
Since you did not give these things, why have you proposed to take them?  
It was fitting for you to give; it is not for me to take away.

“If reason teaches that whatever is given should be reclaimed,  
Let your dowry be taken away and ours likewise restored to us;  
If you desire this, we ask that it be held valid.

“We gave the Empire; you seem to have given little.  
By the pope’s support you are called Roman Caesar:  
Why, then, do you impose chains upon the pope?”

[Col. 0984D]

“Whatever the prelate may do, whatever the sacred company declares,  
He shall be compelled to restore what appears to belong to Caesar.”  
And each party confirms the contrary in writing.

The ring and staff, and the other things mentioned,  
Are prepared to be wholly restored at Caesar’s command;  
And Pope Paschal goes away thus despoiled.

Concerning the excommunication of Emperor Henry V for the captivity of Pope Paschal.

The grieving pope raises lamentation and by his letter quickly summons  
The Church from throughout the world to the City.  
When it has assembled, he lays before it Caesar’s acts.

Then he says: “O fathers, take note of what Caesar has written,  
And issue whatever decrees you judge fit concerning it;  
Command that I too should no longer be pope.

[Col. 0985A]

“I have recognized that your misfortunes came through my sins;  
I have judged myself worthy to be deprived of my office.  
I have deposed myself too, lest you perish,” he says.

He speaks thus, casts aside the mitre, and leaves the mantle:  
“Let the Church ordain whatever it pleases without me,” he says,  
“And let it judge for itself according to the pope’s custom.”

The clergy read the documents: the king claims the pontifical rights;  
The ring and staff are said to be held under Caesar’s authority.  
“There shall not be such a multitude of bishops,” he says.

The document extorted from the pope contrary to justice  
Is burned, and we restore to you your ancient honor.  
“Take up the mantle, Father,” the whole assembly urges.

Again new wars are waged against Henry V;  
The former torments inflicted upon his father now assail him.  
As his father had been before him, so he suffers anathema.

[Col. 0985B]

A papal letter and papal seal alike,  
Sent throughout the Empire, solemnly excommunicate him  
And all the nobles who uphold his commands.

Now Paschal dies and Calixtus succeeds to the dignity,  
From the see of Vienne and mingled with royal descent;  
By Frankish lineage he was an enemy of Caesar.

A disputation between the imperial and papal courts: which was greater at that time.

The papal and imperial courts contend  
Whether one is unequal to the other or ought to be made equal.  
The king’s court, taking the opposing side, says:

“The pope is a spirit enclosed in the covering of flesh;  
Who would dare describe him as though he were earthly?  
What equality has earthly matter with heavenly things?

“He is also equal to the heavenly powers; heaven is granted to his speech,  
By which he binds and looses, by which he seems to possess kingdoms;  
Though a spirit exiled in flesh, he holds the stars.”

Argument to the contrary concerning the emperor.

Caesar stands as the living law, commanding kings;  
Under the living law are all laws that confer rights.  
That law punishes, absolves, and itself binds.

He is the maker of law and ought not to be held under law;  
Yet he has been pleased willingly to be held under law.  
Whatever pleases him shall have the force of law.

God, who binds and looses, brought him forth into the world;  
May divine power be with him in the kingdom of the saints.  
He gave the stars to the heavenly powers, all other things to him.

Response of the Roman court against the emperor.

The papal party likewise answers the imperial party:

[Col. 0985D]

“We grant that you reign, provided that you are subject to Peter;  
Christ grants both jurisdictions to us.

“Spirit and body are powerfully subject to me:  
Through the body I hold earthly things, through the mind heavenly things;  
Thus, holding the pole, I loose and bind the world.

“The pope seems to open the heavens and touch celestial things;  
For he is worthy to give, govern, bind, and loose all things—  
He to whom the New Law and the Old Law gave every dignity.

“Though the ring and staff are thought earthly things,  
They belong to heaven’s right, since they seem to signify it.  
Consider God’s laws; let your mind yield to them.”

Caesar restores to the apostolic see all that it demanded;  
A good peace is concluded. Having restored to God what had been taken away,  
Each joyfully claims the rights of his own party.

Concerning Emperor Lothair, eighty-sixth from Augustus, after Henry V.

[Col. 0986A]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1125, Henry V having died without an heir, the princes assembled at Mainz. After deliberating there concerning a successor, four leading men of the realm were nominated for the kingship: Lothair, Duke of Saxony; Frederick, Duke of Swabia; Leopold, Margrave of the East; and Charles, Count of Flanders.

At length Lothair, a Saxon by birth, son of Gebhard, was drawn to the kingship by the unanimous vote of all, though resisting, crying out loudly and vehemently. In the presence of the legate of the Apostolic See, he reigned as the ninety-second from Augustus.

He humbled in every respect the descendants of Emperor Henry. Against him Duke Frederick and his brother Conrad, nephews of Emperor Henry through his sister, rebelled for a long time. For this reason Pope Honorius, successor of Calixtus, excommunicated them.

Nevertheless the aforesaid Conrad was made king against Lothair by his brother Frederick and certain others. With a small army he entered Italy and at Monza, near Milan, wore the crown. Then he advanced toward the Roman regions, but at last, his resources exhausted, returned to his own country; making peace with Lothair, he relinquished the kingship and remained at rest. At the same time, Honorius having died at Rome, a schism arose between Innocent and Anacletus. Innocent crossed into Gaul and came to Liège, where Lothair met him and promised assistance. Therefore Pope Innocent, after holding a council at Clermont,

[Col. 0986C]

returned to Rome and crowned King Lothair in the Lateran palace at Saint Saviour’s. For he could not remain at Saint Peter’s because of the power of Anacletus, son of Peter Leo.

Lothair returned to his native land; then, having renewed his army, he came back to Rome after two years. There he took Innocent with him, crossed into Apulia, drove thence Roger the Sicilian, who was then called Duke of Apulia, and established Count Raino as duke there. He captured the city of Bari and occupied all Apulia. Returning from there, he was seized by illness at Verona and ended his life in the twelfth year of his reign. The aforementioned Conrad succeeded him in the kingship by election of the princes.

Likewise concerning Lothair in verse, and concerning Duke Conrad raised against him but finally reconciled.

Henry V then had no male heir,  
But his sister bore one worthy to possess kingdoms:  
Conrad III, the king, would wear the diadem.

Duke Conrad prepares to grasp the Empire;  
Lothair, Duke of Saxony, is raised against him—  
Granted more through envy than reason.

Jealousy and envy recalled the deeds of former times,  
Whom the fortune of Henry’s loved ones had suppressed;  
Thus Lothair now takes and holds the throne.

Conrad crosses into Italy and, received there,  
Mightily gains the diadem at Milan;  
Strongly, king against king, he wages war on either side.

[Col. 0987A]

There was schism in the realm, and new schisms at Rome;  
For there were two popes and two crowns.  
The world grieves that errors of schism are present.

Anacletus was one prelate in the schism;  
Innocent was the pope maintained against him.  
Ancient Rome bears these two schisms with her.

Anacletus yields, and the other deserves to sit;  
Lothair reigns, Conrad is regarded as his friend,  
And he himself was the supreme standard-bearer of the Empire.

Lothair grew old; Conrad’s youth was long.  
He offered obedience, but after the old man was entirely removed,  
The young successor received royal rights.

Meanwhile the young man held the kingdom’s standards;  
He was always foremost among the dukes and sat first.  
Nobility and a worthy appearance gave this to him.

[Col. 0987B]

Thus Lothair ruled for twelve years;  
Twice he saw Italy and again came to Rome,  
And once harshly subdued Apulia.

Roger, now Duke of Sicily, is thought to reign;  
Driven from Apulia, he flees Caesar’s sword.  
Caesar holds Bari and conquers as far as the Pharos.

He makes Raino duke, leaving everything to him;  
Duke Roger afterwards conquers him in this struggle  
And makes himself duke of Apulia without end.

Then he ordered himself to be called king and lord,  
To have royal insignia prepared according to royal custom,  
And great tributes paid throughout Apulia.

Pope Innocent proves a sufficiently strong enemy to him:  
He enters Apulia and sets matters against the king;  
Captured there, he yields and grants royal rights.

Concerning the elevation of Conrad III after Emperor Lothair, eighty-seventh from Augustus.

[Col. 0987C]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, the aforementioned Conrad, the ninety-third from Augustus, was elected king at Koblenz, between Mainz and Cologne, in the presence of Theodwin, Bishop of Porto and legate of the Apostolic See. He was immediately installed by the princes at Aachen, in Charlemagne’s seat, and crowned by the same legate.

Yet the Saxons and Henry, Duke of Bavaria, did not then consent to him. They further asserted that he was not a lawful king but had been created by fraud. The king appointed a general court for them all at Bamberg.

[Col. 0987D]

When they came there, all were received into the king’s favor and peace together with the empress, Lothair’s widow, except only Henry, Duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Proud, who still stubbornly retained the royal insignia. For he was son-in-law of the deceased Emperor Lothair and, holding the regalia on this account, aspired to the kingship as far as he could. At last compelled, he restored the regalia—that is, the cross, lance, and crown—but did not obtain the king’s favor. Later, proscribed by the king upon the judgment of the princes, abandoned by all his followers, and attended by scarcely four knights, he withdrew miserably into Saxony. Not long afterward he died.

At this time Roger the Sicilian again entered Apulia and fought with Duke Raino, whom Lothair had appointed there; defeated, he fled. Meanwhile Anacletus, son of Peter Leo, died at Rome, and with his death the schism ended. Shortly afterward Duke Raino, or Rainald, of Apulia died. Roger returned to Apulia and occupied the land, deprived of its duke and offering no resistance. He expelled Prince Robert of Capua with all the nobles and afflicted those remaining with various tortures. Finally, he ordered himself styled king of Sicily and Apulia. Prince Robert of Capua, together with all the expelled counts, withdrew to King Conrad. The king received them all kindly and kept them with him for a long time in Germany, but could not cross into Apulia because a grave necessity of the Empire impeded him.

[Col. 0988B]

Moreover Pope Innocent, a high-minded man, having assembled an army with the Roman people against Roger, entered Apulia. There, having been rashly led into a place called Galluzu, he was captured by Roger. Roger compelled him, though treating him with respect, and fully obtained, as he wished, royal title and authority in both Sicily and Apulia, with apostolic blessing.

Roger, thus elevated as king by apostolic authority and having no obstacle save King Conrad, stirred up against Conrad in Germany Duke Welf, brother of the aforesaid Henry the Proud, whom he had hired with his money. The king handsomely defeated him in one battle near the castle of Weinsberg and struck down his men in great slaughter.

[Col. 0988C]

On another occasion Henry, Conrad’s son—who, had he lived, would have reigned after him—defeated the same Welf in war. Yet Welf, as long as Conrad lived, stood for Roger and obstructed the kingdom to the best of his ability.

At this time the Romans began to restore the senate, which had ceased so long before that there was not even mention of it in Rome. Pope Innocent attempted, by ingenuity, money, and threats, to dissolve it, but could not. Overtaken by illness amid this discord, he ended his last day. The praiseworthy priest Celestine succeeded him; when he died within the year, Pope Lucius took his seat.

Lucius II, therefore, attempting to extinguish the senate, climbed the Capitol at Rome with a great armed force in order to remove in disgrace the senators then sitting there.

[Col. 0988D]

But the senate and Roman people took up arms and immediately drove the pope and all his men from the Capitol. There, as we heard at the time, the pope was struck by large stones and did not sit in his seat until the day of his death, which followed shortly afterward. Eugenius, abbot of Saint Anastasius at Rome, of the Cistercian order, then succeeded him.

During his time King Conrad died at Bamberg, and his nephew Frederick, Duke of Swabia, succeeded him. Then Manuel ruled at Constantinople, having as wife a German woman, namely the sister of King Conrad’s wife, born of Sulzbach, daughter of a most noble count in the land of the Bavarians. The rest concerning King Conrad—how he went overseas—and concerning King Roger and his son King William, and likewise concerning King William, son of William, we record in verse.

Likewise concerning Conrad III: how King Roger took Apulia from him and harassed the German kingdom through Duke Welf.

As Lothair died, worthy Conrad came,  
Hostile to enemies, wise, and moderate in all things;  
The Empire and every land greatly praise him.

While the Sicilian fears him and fears losing his kingdoms,  
He gives gifts to Duke Welf, by whom he is often restrained;  
By this duke he maintained his dignity amid war.

Conrad threatens from every side to hem in the Sicilians;  
The other prepares rather to render rewards to Welf,  
And Welf raises dreadful battles against the king.

[Col. 0989B]

The royal mind, full of rage, turns against Welf;  
By the strength of his Empire it defends its honor.  
With hostile faces they move arms against each other.

Conrad’s right hand, like Achilles’ sword,  
Cuts off the head of the duke’s standard-bearer as he advances;  
When he falls in battle, Welf departs repulsed.

After manifold slaughter and the taking of a trophy,  
Conrad, by his valor, is deemed greater than Maccabaeus;  
Welf loses every honor at that time.

The final day of Roger, Sicilian king, comes;  
His son William receives the kingdoms he desired  
And rules thus during his lifetime.

Time passes; Conrad dies—wondrous power.  
Frederick succeeds him; dignity is raised again;  
Meanwhile the Sicilian king suffers no disaster.

[Col. 0989C]

Frederick wages no wars against the Sicilian king,  
For then he waged a long war at Milan.  
Thus King William rules a peaceful kingdom.

Concerning the two Williams.

William succeeds William in dignity,  
Handsome, proven with the sword, and supreme in beauty—  
Who would be more worthy of honor in Italy?

When William had already completed thirty years,  
The memorable Caesar Manuel dies among the Danes;  
Then too King Louis dies among the Franks.

That tyrant seizes the Empire of the Greeks,  
Andronicus, chief of crimes, a man not even worth remembering;  
The Greek nobles fall by his sword.

Concerning the peace between Emperor Frederick and the Lombards.

[Col. 0989D]

Here it should be said that in Frederick’s Empire  
All the Lombards become his friends,  
As he wished; the matter is clearly accomplished for him.

His son Henry is raised to high station,  
Lawfully crowned, blessed with a wife’s distinction:  
The daughter of the Sicilian king becomes betrothed to him.

The bride was exceedingly beautiful, named Constance,  
Posthumous, left in her mother’s womb after her father’s death,  
And already a virgin thirty years of age.

Likewise concerning Conrad III: how he went overseas with an army of Christians.

Wise in counsel as Seneca, in appearance Paris, in arms Hector,  
King Conrad had ruled the realm for twice six years  
When he bore the implanted signs of the cross upon his shoulders.

Therefore all the people beyond the Alps were pilgrims.

[Col. 0990A]

No seagoing ship carried them across the seas;  
Rather, they hastened along the road through Hungary.

Then Louis, king of the Franks, of tranquil mind,  
Had taken up the signs of the cross. If you ask the number:  
The host amounted to a thousand thousands of soldiers.

The fortune to come lay hidden from kings and peoples,  
For our men were destined to die for God’s law.  
Both armies came to Constantinople.

From there a direct route through Iconium was prepared for the kings,  
But through Greek treachery they wandered grievously in deserts;  
There they perish from hunger, with no good hope offered.

Thousands of Turks come to war against the men;  
A host of Moors strikes the German ranks,  
Piercing their breasts and their tents.

Now the king of the Franks, as companion, stands by the Germans.

[Col. 0990B]

The array of weapons and trappings of horses is lost;  
Meadows, streets, and market-place lie full of biers.

While hardship assails and heat brings plagues from every side,  
Those who had been knights proceed on foot, dying;  
Everywhere the sick lie down; our battles fall silent.

Then King Conrad bore arms for many days,  
Leading the cavalry with his sword while all else failed;  
Thus the German standards make for peaceful places.

The distinguished Frederick, Duke of Swabia, was present,  
Ruling the German companies equally with his uncle;  
He attacks the enemy and himself protects the camp.

As they hasten to avoid utter ruin,  
By chance they find two ships along the shore,  
By which they hastened on their way to Jerusalem.

Then they strove more fiercely against the city of Damascus.

[Col. 0990C]

They joined battle and victory began to arise;  
The city was besieged, for it was almost captured.

Had the enterprise not been sold for money through treachery,  
The city would have perished and bestowed honor on our men.  
The king, grieving at the betrayal, turns his standards back.

The great king was so much a fighter with his own hands  
That none could withstand his sword as it struck;  
Bodies fall cut through the middle.

He returns to his kingdoms and lives a little while afterward;  
Few palm-bearing men return alive again,  
And the king dies in peace, for there he rests.

In the year one thousand, one hundred, thirty,  
And forty, he gives his time back to heaven—  
He whom I served, who recite these verses of mine.

Concerning the elevation of Emperor Frederick I, nephew of Conrad III, eighty-eighth from Augustus.

[Col. 0990D]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, likewise in the 1918th year from the founding of the City, and after 6,335 years had elapsed from Adam, Frederick I, son of Frederick, Duke of Swabia and brother of King Conrad, born from the most illustrious stock of the Carolings, was elected to the Empire at Frankfurt after Conrad III by the common vote and consent of all the princes: the ninety-fourth from Octavian Augustus. Here we make a brief account of him in order to maintain the catalogue of emperors, lest the order of their names be interrupted if his name should perhaps not be assigned in this catalogue. Elsewhere, however, where we speak of the destruction of Milan and other matters, we have set down in verse nearly all the principal deeds he performed in Italy, narrating them rather briefly.

We therefore give thanks to the Creator, from whom all good things proceed, because, as we promised at the beginning of this book, we have set forth in verse a summary embracing the whole Old and New Testament. From the beginning of the world down to the present day, in the time of Lord Emperor Frederick and Lord Pope Urban III, we have briefly described all kingdoms of the world, all kings and their deeds, their names, dates, and years; likewise all Roman pontiffs, with their years, months, and days in order, and also which emperors lived with which popes. We have distinguished all the chronicles that we inserted into the Catholic Church’s history.

[Col. 0991B]

In all these matters we have knowingly added nothing fabulous, but have followed Catholic and authoritative writers: Eusebius, Pope Clement, Dionysius the Areopagite, Origen, Jerome, Augustine, Josephus, Orosius, Hegesippus, Strabo, Hionius, Solinus on marvels, and Suetonius on the lives of the emperors.

Likewise we record the same Emperor Frederick in verse.

We have described all things fully concerning ancient kings;  
You, Frederick, younger in age but first in virtue,  
Now display deeds that it pleases us to recount.

For I have learned Frederick’s times, battles, and deeds,  
And have vowed to bring forth the greatest—or rather the best—of them:  
What he endured, stirred up, or received in consequence.

[Col. 0991C]

My Muse, while we strive in brief compass to touch  
The lofty summit of the great king,  
Begin on a higher note; our instruments swell.

Now my tongue shall compose your trophies, Frederick;  
Let every chorus throughout the world sing gigantic deeds.  
Rise, my Muse: let us sing them too.

Frederick was a flower sprung from the flower of kings in honor;  
Germany, full of favor, chose him king,  
Always desiring to have him as lord of the Empire.

When the king sat at Aachen in the seat of the Carolings,  
Germany wholly obeyed in lawful order;  
The king carried his standards to Italy’s borders.

Concerning the city of Milan and its war with Emperor Frederick.

Mighty Milan, rightly called a lioness for its merits,

[Col. 0991D]

Outstanding in strength, full of people and soldiers,  
Cruel, proud, fierce, wholly rebellious, it was.

It had allied cities by which it troubled all things.  
It remains to give the cities’ names:  
Brescia, Tortona, Crema, noble Piacenza.

When the king had succeeded in gaining the German crown,  
He sought the Italian one too, because illustrious Rome so teaches;  
The royal standards fly through the midst of the Ligurians.

Milan scorns to fear its king’s standards,  
But wishes to defend its countryside by its own strength,  
Not knowing that King Frederick would be its death.

When the king presses it on every side with royal proclamations,  
He scatters and breaks it in six flowing years of war;  
The city that had been supreme suffers, subdued by war.

[Col. 0992A]

(The king for the moment overlooks the evils Milan deserves;  
The army is ordered to march against the other cities,  
And the commanders bear arms against the Astesans.

The king departs; Milan does not grant him honor.  
The time will come when, crushed in fury, it will pay for its acts.  
Rome calls the king; the king moves his standards.)

Concerning the city of Asti.

Greatly fearing the king, Asti soon abandons its inhabitants;  
All carry all their possessions into the new castle,  
And so Asti leaves its own site empty.

Yet Asti is not left altogether empty or deserted:  
After the towers are overthrown, they ravage the provisions found there;  
There was no destruction of the other wall.

As the king departs, better fortune is prepared;  
The people swear allegiance and Asti is thus reconciled to him.

[Col. 0992B]

The offense was slight; full pardon is granted.

Likewise concerning the same city of Asti.

In the Ligurian land stands a city called Asti,  
Renowned for riches, vast though lightly defended;  
It quickly yielded, yet did not itself fall.

Concerning the city of Tortona, three times devastated by Frederick.

Now it remains to recount Tortona’s suffering,  
Which, relying on ancient Milanese fury,  
Wishes in its accustomed way to be an enemy.

When the king moves camp, the fierce crowd fears the lion;  
Tortona is encircled by the dreadful labor of the nobles;  
As the soldiers attack, the fleeing people grieve.

The king blocks every side; the people withdraw into the citadel.  
Nor does a knight, hemming in every quarter, thus leave it open for them—  
The city is plainly captured; the crowd occupies the summit.

[Col. 0992C]

Here food is cut off, there the spring is taken away;  
The tunnelling mole, the battering ram, and missiles from mangonels are prepared;  
They pierce within and break through both sides.

Now near death, the people, subject to fate, yield;  
They give the king entrance through gates thrown open on every side,  
Yet the lives and limbs of the populace remain safe.

The king orders the walls rooted in the ground to be burned;  
Then the walls fall, and the people deservedly doomed perish.  
Thus Tortona falls, which had been sufficiently lofty.

Illustrious Tortona, while the crown is greatly enraged,  
Falls conquered and prostrate, receiving three sorrowful gifts:  
For three times it is wholly destroyed and subdued.

How he proceeded from Tortona to Rome to be consecrated.

When he had completed these things, a distinguished embassy came,  
That he should hasten from there to defend papal rights;  
By the pope’s aid he would now be sole ruler.

And to remove delay, the pope urgently presses him.

[Col. 0992D]

The good king rises and directs the eagles toward the City;  
The burned fields of Piacenza give him passage.

Parma serves him; he crosses the Bolognese fields;  
Florence, beneath a rather small mountain pass, bears arms;  
The messenger of Achaea, Palaeologus, is present.

Arnold is captured—the man Brescia had known as a native—  
Whose teachings were as though they subverted the world.  
The noose strangles him; fire and water carry him away.

All Tuscany, devoted throughout, gives itself to him;  
Known and unknown distant kingdoms are subject;  
The camps lie in the estates at Acquapendente.

The standards come to Viterbo, worthy for the merit of life.

[Col. 0993A]

There open Erebus makes a fiery, violent spring;  
There the people are brave and soldiers valiant in arms.

An excellent spring has made many baths for the natives;  
The land is fertile, enriched by abundant plenty;  
For it produces kinds and species through fertility.

There Rome wished her weary veterans to rest,  
Knights discharged from service, oppressed by old age or wounds;  
Thus the place itself makes it worthy of life’s reward.

The author’s words.

When life is burdened by long service and labor,  
When it is pressed by old age or weakened by wounds,  
Let aged dignity often find rest here.

If Caesar wishes his splendid deeds to be cherished,  
This honor of Empire ought in every way to be maintained:  
That a tranquil life should be led by old men.

[Col. 0993B]

This is not glory for slaves but for lords,  
If the honorable old age of retired men remains safe,  
If street and market-place shine with their garments.

If divine power makes a wretched servant,  
Poverty brings disgrace upon the lord whom it serves;  
That wretched man stands not for himself but for his lord.

Many royal tents advance upon Rome,  
So that the Empire may bear the crown in the Roman seat.  
The public standards thunder, for the Church favors him.

The Roman people resume their ancient customs;  
Secure in his soldiers, the king scorns their supremacy.  
He asks nothing; rather, he commands. Rome swells with rage.

The senate, badly frustrated in hope, departs thence;  
The Roman people, fiercely angered, prepare for arms,  
Thinking themselves able to conquer the king’s chiefs and forces.

[Col. 0993C]

The king, strong in spirit, moves many cohorts;  
The pope gives access through open gates by secret paths.  
By night he seeks blessed Peter’s sanctuary under the sword.

At dawn he takes the seat and crown,  
Reverently honors Peter’s basilica with a gift;  
Rome laments and weeps; the report resounds through the City.

How the emperor was crowned by Pope Adrian at Saint Peter’s without the Romans’ consent; whence battle was fought with the Romans, but the emperor prevailed.

Rome is deceived when he thus receives the crown;  
The royal person receives the papal gifts;  
He is anointed and raised up: the report resounds through the City.

Prelate Adrian and the whole Roman court

[Col. 0993D]

Then fulfilled the royal vows without the Romans,

[lacuna]

The senate, fiercely angered, rises to arms;  
Caesar, armed and spurred by ferocity, leaps forth.  
On either bank of the Tiber battle rages.

The people attack; the king prevails, and many are slain.  
For the fugitives the Tiber’s waters are their only defence;  
The blood-stained crowd swims in the waters.

Concerning the destruction of Spoleto.

When these things had been completed, relying on the papal favor,  
As they return rejoicing, they halt in Spoleto’s fields.  
From them Caesar demands tribute due.

False coinage appears; Caesar quickly removes the fraud.  
For he wages war and kills many of the people;  
The conquered people groan both within and without.

[Col. 0994A]

Augustus commands that the place perish, consumed by fire.  
The soldier who had gone away empty returns laden;  
He who scorned to pay what was due gives everything.

Concerning the treachery of the Veronese among the Alps, where they planned to destroy the emperor and his whole army trapped in the mountain narrows.

The royal eagles come to the plains of Verona.  
As the king crosses rivers, he finds a harsher omen;  
Verona, hemming him in among mountains, raises war.

Encircled by narrow mountains and the course of a river,  
The king and his nobles were as though bound in a prison;  
Trapped, they had no routes of escape.

Weapons rush forth because loosened rocks rain down from the mountain;  
Rocks from the summit kill and batter the nobles;  
No weapons can avail the soldiers.

[Col. 0994B] For four days they endured these punishments,  
during which, without hope of life, they bore the hazards of fortune;  
they received wounds, yet inflicted none.

By hidden paths they climbed over the lofty summits,  
whence they repaid the people of Verona for their evil deeds;  
and the populace returned from the mountain’s brow to the depths below.

Now the noble king commands one man’s foot to be cut off, another’s eyes wholly torn out, another to be raised aloft by a noose;  
such honour ought for these deeds to be bestowed upon the wicked.

### On the messenger concerning the schism between Alexander and Octavian, in the time of the aforesaid emperor

Then Adrian, bishop of Rome, died;  
Alexander came, and Octavian opposed him.  
A schism arose in the Church; forces fought on both sides.

While the schism raged, Frederick’s power advanced,  
[Col. 0994C] and after much conflict forcibly took Milan.  
When it had been sufficiently overwhelmed, the recurring quarrel returned.

The Ligurians conspired; the king fled thence;  
and Lombard pride crushed every royal right,  
itself ruling itself then almost as though it were Caesar.

The king returned; Moriana paid the penalty; Cilenia, shut in,  
gave the king an entrance when Susa perished,  
and the remaining Ligurians feared the royal standards.

### On the city of Alexandria, now called Caesarea, in Lombardy

Bormida together with the Tanaro had made a city of straw,  
which the king, arriving suddenly, pressed with siege.  
The Ligurians came to its aid; the standards of war were displayed.

Caesar, on the opposite side, immediately abandoning the siege,  
[Col. 0994D] met them. The populace, standing as though defeated, was astonished  
and sought terms of peace, thoroughly filled with fear.

Bearing bare swords against their bare necks,  
they came before Caesar’s feet, asking pardon;  
Caesar resolved, for the love of God, to spare them.

The people, having made peace, swore the royal commands.  
Before eight days had passed, the peace was dissolved and made void;  
war returned, established anew just as it had been.

The city of Milan rose again, restored more splendidly;  
Lombard power, made stronger, swelled.  
Both proud and powerful parties flew to arms.

The king prevailed at first; but afterwards he withdrew in flight.  
Yet he did not depart from the country; but, wearied by blows,  
both king and Ligurians were now silent concerning arms.

After three times six troubled years, the schism ended;  
[Col. 0995A] Alexander at last prevailed, and Caesar obeyed him;  
he settled in peace and gave counsel.

### On King Henry VI, son of Lord Emperor Frederick, the eighty-ninth from Augustus

Concerning Lord King Henry, son of Lord Frederick Augustus, while still an adolescent, we do not possess accounts of deeds. Yet we see his most elegant appearance, praiseworthy knighthood, courage and liberality, goodwill, piety, justice, and truthfulness; indeed, every royal virtue which we could desire in one of youthful age. Although by natural ability and learning he seems to excel all his contemporaries in wisdom and subtlety of perception, nevertheless—saving his majesty—we, if we know no more, have at least observed more through the passage of time, and have experienced and reflected upon more. Therefore we propose to set forth for him certain admonitions, by which he may be formed toward praiseworthy morals, justice and judgment, and encouraged in heroic verse toward those royal virtues by which he has been granted to govern the empire gloriously and honourably.

### Again, concerning King Henry VI, still an adolescent: a model of kingship is proposed, showing how he ought laudably to govern the empire

For Henry VI the sacred diadems stand ready.

Be present, Frederick, father and monarch, at this festival;  
O father, O son, royal verses lie open.

Henry, monarch, you are heir to ancient kings;  
you shall bear the diadem, heir of the Roman summit;  
you shall bear Romulus’ standards; you hold our age.

[Col. 0995C] Star of empire, the nones and ides applaud you;  
faithful Godfrey gives you royal verses,  
which you should read often, that you may rule kingdoms well.

O youth, flower of the youths of the world, glory of kings,  
honour of city and world, whom the times of events applaud,  
receive the counsel which my verses convey.

Beware friends entangled in filth and perversity.  
Be equitable toward all, but chastise the unjust.  
Consider whatever you do; know yourself more fully for yourself.

It is more splendid for you to bind yourself alone under law  
than to conquer diverse peoples or great kings.  
If you read these things in your mind, king, you will rule kingdoms well.

If you are unwilling to respect your own wishes or public wishes,  
by what reasoning will you be able to claim that you are king?  
If you are not a ruler to yourself, neither will you be a ruler to me.

[Col. 0995D] Alexander the Great’s teacher fashioned corrupt habits for himself  
and indecorous manners of walking;  
the boy king learned them, but regretted having learned them.

Alexander conquered Darius and Babylon alike;  
but he could not conquer the habit impressed upon himself:  
what a vessel has once been steeped in, it is accustomed to retain.

As a boy, examine whether a depraved mark stains you,  
and strive wholly and without delay to remove the fault;  
for an old vice does not know how to depart.

Although everything is permitted to you, do not seek to have everything permitted;  
for things often permitted may, when tried, cause harm.  
For lawful things often produce harmful consequences.

Holding the reins of laws, curb yourself strongly with the rein;  
spare others more, yourself less, as occasion requires;  
while you fear no one, be yourself a fear to yourself.

[Col. 0996A] The life of Pharaoh, Nero’s criminal deeds,  
and the transgressions of Solomon show  
what evils are born for the wicked and what goods for the good.

I set before you these severe examples of the ancients,  
so that Holy Scripture may become your instruction for the future:  
by this art you will be able to cherish your fatherlands.

In the office of judge, honour sacred places fittingly;  
strive, Henry, to enjoy peace and punish the wicked;  
if you investigate crime, peace will be without delay.

Command that churches be supported with abundant piety;  
the diadem desires always to be defended in adversity  
by your aid and by the prayers of the Church.

If you desire to deserve the promises of a true king,  
strive, Henry, to be instructed through the help of the clergy,  
that you may please the Lord tomorrow as also yesterday.

[Col. 0996B] Whenever you see the complaints of a poor man or widow at hand,  
offer remedies the more promptly, full of compassion;  
administer the judgment of the wretched with mercy.

Thus make the laws of heaven first and those of the court last equal,  
so that justice may prevail as far as your age permits;  
cut off every evil; forbid all harmful things.

It is sometimes expedient to relax the enacted laws,  
lest evil clemency of kings perish through harshness;  
for I think God often wishes the guilty person to live.

May your honour deign so to pardon your subjects  
that kindly authority acquits more often than it punishes;  
if you strike while showing mercy, you will be a ruler loved.

Sitting in judgment, judge, restrain your mind thus:  
let not your face, avenging crimes, be the indicator of your heart,  
and keep hidden those things which are nearest to punishments.

[Col. 0996C] Let the good man be equally advocate for either side of a case;  
let foreigner and resident alike bear an equal burden;  
and let no secret practice pollute the hand.

Let lawsuits run their course with equal hazard on either side,  
nor let citizens, under the majesty of office, oppress the wretched;  
let litigations fall by the judge’s skill in settling them.

If the parties wish to produce diverse witnesses,  
lest fraud intervene, test and constrain everything by examination;  
then you will be mindful of the boy Daniel.

If a document remains, confine the case by written evidence;  
do not spare crime if the record proves false;  
let no man win your approval by falsehood, fraud, or deceit.

If certain reasoning can avenge a crime,  
king, act so that your vengeance may be known at once;  
[Col. 0996D] delayed vengeance fosters crimes and brings losses.

If my bonds had earlier been punished at once,  
no capture at Mainz would have inflicted loss upon you:  
royal punishment causes crimes not to be committed.

### Again, an admonition to King Henry

Having considered the praises which you hear recounted,  
I do not wish you to desire to be exalted by the truth of the proud;  
for a proud life breeds weariness among peoples.

Perhaps by this praise you may think yourself near to the gods.  
King, you are mortal flesh: take care not to be deceived;  
because you are mortal, death brings you your destiny.

Mortal in body, govern mortal things so  
that you, as king, may die by equal law with the poor;  
the lives of rich and poor alike come to an end at the same time.

### On the marriage of Henry VI

[Col. 0997A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1186, in the sixth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January], King Henry VI celebrated his glorious marriage at Milan, at Saint Ambrose, with Queen [Col. 0998A] Constance, daughter of Roger, king of Sicily. He was in the twenty-first year of his age and the seventeenth year of his reign.

[Col. 0997] End of the seventeenth part.

# Godfrey of Viterbo’s *Pantheon*

## Part Eighteen: On the Angles and Saxons

### On certain persecutors of the Church

[Col. 0997B]

The chronicles that declare Diocletian to have ruled,  
when they report that Maximian then ruled with him,  
sing that he held the regions of Britain.

Among these people Rome had made him patron of the land;  
they report that he held it quite peacefully as a settler,  
and they always wish to regard him as lord of their country.

Yet he burned with rage against the saints,  
and therefore had destroyed the Christians from the region,  
wishing to burn all Catholic writings.

### On Maximian’s offspring

[Col. 0997C]

Maximian dies, most criminal lover of crimes,  
and leaves behind twin sons by his own wife,  
given the names Uther and Aurelius.

The mother, having the boys, withdraws far from the region,  
to that part of Britain which secretly obeys her reverently,  
knowing that the paternal land would return to her sons.

With all enemies removed under such government,  
the boys live safely, far away from there;  
but a new and ruinous fate arises for those places.

The island makes the dead king’s brother king,  
a monk named Constans, living under the Rule,  
who after a short time rules the British kingdoms.

### On Vortigern, leader of the Angles

Vortigern is regarded as the foremost leader of the Angles;  
[Col. 0997D] throughout the whole region he is held dear by the nobles,  
and through his assistance the monk holds the kingdoms.

He advises the king to summon many armed men,  
so that he may be able to punish whichever of his own people are evil  
and, subjecting the land to himself, wield power everywhere.

The record calls them Romans whom he hires for payment throughout the kingdoms;  
and, as is customary, troubled Britain stirs up disputes;  
the peoples dwelling in the region foster wars.

### Why the Saxons crossed the Ocean

Saxon is summoned for these royal wars and exhorted,  
and an innumerable crowd of peoples is set in motion with him;  
they carry arms and military service across the Ocean.

The king now wonders why so great a multitude has come.  
Saxon answers that all of them could not remain at home;  
the land was small, the place full of soldiers.

[Col. 0998B] The land, full of men, was now almost without even grass;  
this land of yours, since it is exceedingly rich, preserves us.  
Keep us, warlike men, for yourself.

We are a multitude driven out by the land allotted to our fathers;  
a multitude of mighty men wishes to remain in a home allotted by equal lot;  
fate has sent us also to hold kingdoms for you.

### The Saxons are humanely received by Vortigern, their leader

Vortigern says: “Let new joys be yours, O king,  
for fortune, by the kindness of fate, has subdued cruel men for you;  
[Col. 0998C] thus now, king, rule your kingdoms in peace.

Grant that your strongest castles be maintained by the Saxons;  
let rights and powers be held under the Saxon stronghold;  
by Saxon service let your wars be waged.

The friendship of heart which Vortigern had  
so cherished Saxon deeds among the Saxons  
that Saxon too was faithful to the leader in his heart.

Saxon, holding the country through the king’s kindness and elevated by it,  
is suddenly changed by the leader’s hidden cruelty;  
the king loses his head by the leader’s sword.

Then the knights with the leader groaned in feigned grief  
and determined, under a false appearance, to avenge the killing;  
with rejoicing hearts they set sad deeds in motion.

They established the leader as king in the cruel stronghold;  
sitting there, by Saxon strength he held everything under Saxon law,  
[Col. 0998D] and ruled his world with a Saxon sword.

There was born from the line of this king a soldier,  
Duke Volgimer, as he was called in popular speech,  
a famous commander of military service, mighty in arms.

He grieves that Saxon is accustomed to hold his kingdoms;  
for, should Saxon perish, he wishes the royal heir to rule.  
For this reason and through envy he was then a grievous enemy to them.

### On Orsus and Hengist

At that time the royal union of the Angle brothers  
was Orsus and Hengist, as they were called in the Angle tongue;  
these two were rightly the heads of the Saxons.

While Duke Volgimer separately stirs arms within,  
Hengist and Orsus leap up and wholly resist them.  
The island of the Britons furnishes each party’s treachery.

[Col. 0999A] While Volgimer and Saxon engage in their conflicts,  
both parties suffer, and Britain’s lands are shaken;  
with wounds inflicted, death is abundant on both sides.

As Volgimer strives to harass his ancestral kingdom  
and desires to annihilate the Saxons’ present place,  
Saxon offers words of peace, through the favour of the fathers.

The king summons his angry son, dear in his homeland,  
and, as if pacified, voluntarily reconciles himself with him;  
by such speeches he moderates the matter for him.

### Commendation of the Saxons

“Why, son, do you oppress the forces of the Saxon people,  
when they are friends of my kingdom and guardians of my chamber,  
faithful men and warriors?

They have, as I attest, secured the diadem of my kingdom;  
by their valour they have greatly lightened hostile days.  
[Col. 0999B] ‘You persecute badly what has done well,’ he says.

Grant peaceful days; lay down your rage;  
steadfastly restore your affection to the Saxons.  
This would benefit you when I am dead.

Since, son, you are the distinguished heir of my kingdom,  
by Saxon valour you can maintain your rights;  
they will uphold your rights and wage your wars.”

Volgimer does not receive his father’s actions in a spirit of peace;  
the Saxon wages war against the threatening youth as though freely;  
yet he strongly resisted the enraged man with the sword.

Orsus and Hengist cannot endure this from Saxon;  
everywhere through the country they set opposing battles in place,  
and, as the leader’s passion moves war, they make war.

While the British land rages utterly within,  
[Col. 0999C] the leaders Hengist and Orsus cross the ocean  
and each brother returns to his own homeland.

Angria reveals that the Saxon lords have returned;  
a great complaint is proposed in Macedonian fashion,  
telling what evil wars of Volgimer Saxon endures.

Everywhere through the land, amid the resounding complaint,  
women together with men strive to take up arms;  
the island of the Britons will now bear new wars.

Orsus and Hengist brought their own sister,  
who was endowed with beauty of form and appearance;  
Corinna was worthy to share the king’s bed.

### On Angria, the queen, the region, and the other deeds

The queen took the name Angria from the region,  
a German woman supported by rosy complexion,  
to whose service Macedon moves his standards.

[Col. 0999D] A famous ship, full [of people], is borne across the sea’s waves;  
the British island sees scant mourning on every side:  
while the ship bears arms, the subjected land perishes.

King Vortigern, lover of the Saxon people,  
giver of peace to both sides, desires to be reconciler  
and asks that the wars fall silent through a conference.

The wars fall silent as they see the agreements; the standards rest.  
With discussions held on either side, savage hearts grow warm.  
The king prepares firm treaties for the angry parties.

While from this hour the king labours to give terms of peace,  
quarrelling renews wickedness; they contend still further;  
the soldier flies to arms, and peace perishes without delay.

The Saxon people stand supported by the strong spear;  
therefore their enemies are slain by their knives without revenge;  
all the glory of the country lies fallen by the Saxon sword.

[Col. 1000A] Their strength overcomes the strength of the Angles;  
Macedon overcomes and kills the worthy settler by the sword;  
Saxon takes the country and plunders the land.

Volgimer, driven out thence as an enemy despite his pride,  
fears to encounter the fate of his fathers, whose death he has seen;  
he slips and flees through the middle of the forest.

After a short time, he is said to have perished by poison.  
Everywhere through the land Saxon flourishes in full order;  
henceforth I bear full trophies to the Saxons.

The king’s friendship, by which Macedon had often revived,  
fixed the hearts of the conquerors in service to the king;  
therefore Saxon remained there subject to him.

Everywhere the king’s will accords with the Saxons;  
wherever he triumphs, Saxon regards the king as a father;  
indeed, the king governs the conquered regions for his king.

[Col. 1000B] Orsus and Hengist seem almost to reign jointly,  
for together with the king they guard the shared kingdoms:  
the king is father; these are sons, with their descendants.

A delightful feast is ordered to be prepared for the princes.  
As the king sits in his hall, the maiden Angria is summoned;  
more splendid than a star, her beauty gives joy.

Queen Angria, conveyed here in a ship of the sea,  
bows to her brothers and offers adornment to the king;  
and swiftly binds the royal heart in love.

The sight of the maiden penetrates his breast without a wound;  
love, once cast in, soon lies hidden beneath his breast;  
in the burning of his mind, the girl discharges her darts.

Her golden hair shone amid gilded garments;  
as she received the cups, the king fixed his eyes upon her,  
and, desiring to look, said, “Friend, drink.”

[Col. 1000C] She tastes it and replies: “Drink with me, divine power.”  
The king says: “Then sit down; your nobility binds me.  
You deserve,” he says, “to be nourished beneath the royal roof.”

The mouth of the mighty cupbearer is made sweet by the cups;  
then the heat of his mind urges him toward desired deeds:  
the more wine he drinks, the more he wishes to love.

The meal is brief; fickle fortune comes for the maiden;  
the king’s heart, which the maiden carries, rages in his breast.  
Taking her gently by the hand, he says: “Come, beloved.”

Having thus foreseen these things, the renowned maiden laughed;  
having summoned her brothers, she returned her words to the king:

“If he wishes, according to the law of the Angles, to prepare a marriage-bed,  
and wishes by good law to share the crown with me,  
[Col. 1000D] let the Saxon forces be obedient to the king’s commands.”  
Her words please the brother; she becomes his bride without delay.

Orsus and Hengist, with their sister ruling beside the king,  
henceforth enjoy greater favour everywhere;  
the whole island favours them, and the kingdoms remain quiet.

The Briton fears what has happened, because Saxon holds dominion,  
lest he claim for himself the pre-eminence he has prepared by conquest;  
Saxon claims the empire granted through labour.

The land began to be grievously oppressed by the strength of the Angles;  
in common speech it was called Angliterra [England],  
and it draws the name of the Angles from the city.

It is assimilated to its conquerors in customs and languages.

Angria is perpetually called by the victorious name;  
Angria was then said with *R*: there was no *L* there.

Pope Gregory, by whose baptism they flourish,  
[Col. 1001A] gave the name an *L*, first removing the *R* from it;  
thus the pope called them, as it were, angelic people.

There was then in the country a mountain with a beautiful summit,  
upon which the king of the Angles prepared an imperial castle;  
but the place could not bear the weight of the stones.

For however many walls are joined together there today and seem destined to stand,  
they fall empty in the morning, only to fall again after some time;  
the earth beneath swallows whatever he puts there.

The peoples wonder, and masters of the craft wonder,  
for whatever stones the builders are able to throw there  
perish without delay: the earth, like a she-wolf, devours them.

The king commands soothsayers to be summoned after long attendance  
and orders them promptly, by magical art, to disclose to him  
why the walls collapse, which the earth draws down.

Why they fall they do not know; but how they might stand,  
[Col. 1001B] they immediately seek to devise deceitful advice;  
having found it, they present it at the king’s command:

“This mountain,” they say, “the gods have established for themselves;  
kings have often brought them great offerings.  
Unless you give these, no walls will stand.

The sacred gifts for the gods which we now command you to bring  
neither you can bring, nor we possess among our resources,  
nor can island, land, or forest provide them at all.

This place demands consecration by a torrent of human blood,  
a foundation made with a body, and building above it afterward;  
from then on the wall will stand, if you supply the things named.

Yet your victim does not require a human body  
whose origin has been conceived from human seed:  
there must be a son born to a mother without a father.”

The king, now instructed by the counsel of the seers,  
sent envoys everywhere, equipped for this purpose;  
the desired one is sought and, by fate’s leading, found.

[Col. 1001C] They find a boy created by the art of a phantom,  
Merlin by name, a seer of seers without teaching,  
born in female childbirth but without a father.

A great company of nobles receives the found boy;  
at his arrival they think the castle will be redeemed  
if Merlin’s body is buried there.

They ask his mother by what seed, by what novelty,  
her son could be born of a mother without a father.  
She answers: it is clear that an incubus is the father.

Merlin says to the king: “You accomplish nothing here;  
beware of being deceived by ignorant seers:  
the evil crowd brings you no benefit.

[Col. 1001D] Behold: if my body is put separately [there] by art,  
it will immediately be swallowed up; your city will fall, broken backward.  
By multiplying deceit, you lose both goods.

“Bring,” he says, “the soothsayers and command the crowd of magicians  
to say what is now the cause of your walls,  
what the fates intend, and what deceit lies in their art.

If they know how to speak, you shall retain their teaching;  
if they deceive wickedly, let the sword be the penalty for their wickedness.  
Afterward I will make firm the ground of your walls.”

The boy’s words please him; the king immediately demands what he has said.  
The soothsayers cannot attain by art what is required;  
there the penalty is given to their crime, as the boy had said.

The king releases the necks of many magicians from prison,  
so that, should the boy perhaps overcome their deceit,  
a tribunal of death may everywhere be made for the soothsayers.

[Col. 1002A] Henceforth Merlin is asked through his words  
why the stone falls there where the king orders lofty things to be built,  
and why hollow earth draws down the craftsman’s work.

“If you wish,” says the boy, “I shall tell the strange riddle:  
at the mountain’s summit stands a body of water sought from above;  
the earth placed over it hangs suspended thus.

It bears the earth’s burden, upon its floating crust;  
the little wave can bear no further load you allow to be added;  
it swallows the weights which you lay upon it.

That the uncertainty may be made clear, let the mountainside be dug;  
then let a river which you do not know come forth for you;  
after that a dry lake and dry earth are obtained.”

At Merlin’s command the king orders it opened;  
a great river, opened there, is shown and approached;  
there the king will build a fortress for his people.

[Col. 1002B] It remains for the king to punish the deeds of those magicians,  
whose deceit had often been the cause of his pains:  
let him burn the bodies of those hidden in their beds.

While the soothsayer falls, while we come to the mountain’s events,  
Merlin becomes seer both greatest and least everywhere,  
as Ocean and the gulf of Scotland teach.

As the lake flows out, a heavy wave terrifies the inhabitants;  
from the middle of the whirlpool rises the grim shape of dragons.  
They make noise on every side and shake the ground.

Two dragons make for the regions of Cornwall;  
one was red and the other white; through their conflict they oppress the regions.  
The terrified people will cultivate the countryside in fear.

Uther and Aurelius, whom the record above mentioned,  
offspring of the Italian prince Maximian,  
then grew stronger in military service.

[Col. 1002C] Uther, raging to arms, himself attacks the dragon;  
he is said to have driven in his sword for its destruction,  
and then the people of the country give vent to great joy.

He who had formerly been the youth and handsome soldier Uther  
is called Uther Pendragon according to their law;  
they wish him to have the name of the serpent.

Fresh, wandering report carries news of the dragon’s death:  
Uther is said to have cut down the guilty creature with the sword’s edge;  
fear is in the king, and joyful report among the good.

When the report came to King Vortigern,  
he says: “Merlin, I beg you, seek out the future,  
for the queen fears when she sees such great novelties.

Tell us, I pray, Merlin, the omen of the dragons:  
what report, what rumour, speaks of the regions’ party?  
[Col. 1002D] What rights do Uther and Aurelius claim for themselves?”

Merlin says: “If you desire eagerly to know greater things to come,  
you will now learn the fearful signs of your kingdom  
and will know that chance days have come upon you.

I say that these two serpents are the mighty men  
Uther and Aurelius, now claiming their paternal kingdoms;  
by God’s judgment the land will return to them.

They will take away the possessions of the Saxons, or those subject to you;  
they are strong in military power and their country’s aid;  
either might be Caesar in Rome.

They are sons of mad Maximian,  
of Roman stock, burning with savage ferocity.  
Look to yourself, if you can,” Merlin says:

“The island is divided; two peoples follow sceptres;  
royal rights are governed by uncertain kings;  
[Col. 1003A] and new wars have arisen in Saxon places.

Aurelius prevails and gains the kingdom for himself;  
Vortigern’s force falls and is driven away by the sword;  
he loses his bishopric and loses his head as well.

Queen Angria, widowed by the king’s downfall,  
renews the earlier wars and does not prove weak in strength;  
she brings varied battles, losses, dangers, and threats.

Orsus and Hengist, with the rest of the Saxon force,  
resist fiercely those seizing this kingdom,  
suffering bitterly over the death of the overthrown king.

When Uther and Aurelius take possession of their paternal kingdoms,  
they grow in strength, but English wars also swell;  
the angry kings bear arms in abundance.

After various killings, houses are burned on either side;  
the peoples, weary of enduring dangers, assemble,  
[Col. 1003B] and decide to make a covenant of peace among the nobles.

This is the peace settlement: that, once properly reconciled,  
the king freely grant the Saxons treaties of peace,  
giving cities and fiefs, possessions and honour.

Queen Angria, having taken the remedy of peace,  
bows to the kings and withdraws to the maritime fields,  
asking that they allow her to hold peaceful strongholds there.

Aurelius, the first-born and monarch of the kingdom,  
thus makes the ordinances of peace, thus attends to affairs,  
so that he may restore his country’s joys and broad tranquillity.

He cherishes the best things, scatters dreadful things, restrains wars,  
rejects hidden things, reforms what is fitting:  
he was a king—indeed, a father; his father’s deeds are evident.

Yet he imitates his father in his admitted cruelty,  
renewing punishments previously inflicted and remitted,  
[Col. 1003C] and he holds teachings of error full of deceits.

He is himself a rival of God and becomes protector of the Jewish people;  
he carries written courts and fosters the sect of Mani;  
and he is held wholly opposed to the Catholic cause.

After a few years, after many perils of events,  
Aurelius receives his fate and the end of his days,  
just among the nobles, but guilty before God.”

### When Aurelius, king of the Angles, has died, Uther, also called Pendragon, is raised up

After the king’s fate, the lordship of the land is changed;  
King Aurelius dies, and his brother is called to high rank;  
the throne is raised, and the crown is transferred.

The king is called by the additional name Uther Pendragon,  
unconquered in strength, whose dragon falls by a blow;  
his royal figure pleases in character and appearance.

[Col. 1003D] It was his custom to summon the nobles at Easter,  
to prepare great feasts, messengers of joy,  
and from the royal throne to give royal gifts.

It is not permitted for a husband to bring gifts without his wife;  
rather, they come together to praise the Lord,  
and the prince’s hall affords them its customary place.

The lord divides the feasts of the company into two;  
the nobles form the right-hand side and women the other;  
the king sits in the middle, and worthy dishes are served.

There the duke of Cornwall sat first in rank;  
opposite him his wife ate, named Hierna,  
upon whom the king quickly cast lustful eyes.

As she sat lofty, a rose more beautiful than all others,  
the king multiplied dishes envied by all;  
[Col. 1004A] the rest of the company observed through various eyes.

When she smiled, she returned eyes intoxicated [with love];  
their glances resting upon one another, they seemed bound in heart;  
touched by love, he thirsts for feminine secrecy.

The court of great ladies sits disturbed,  
for, as though unaware, the king does not see their company:  
he looks too much upon this woman, too little upon all the rest.

Love envelops him; the king quickly ends the feast.  
While he wishes to remove this cause, the wheel turns back;  
the duke rises in alarm, and Hierna flees.

At dawn they flee from the place where they had stayed;  
the duke’s loose reins seize more favourable places;  
Hierna is borne flying to the regions of Cornwall.

When news of the flight is heard, the king, burned by love, suffers;  
he commands them to return, but the duke proceeds farther,  
[Col. 1004B] and while she flees outward, the king rages without delay.

The law was that nobles should never depart from the king  
unless they first sought leave granted for their return  
and, returning home, bore royal letters.

When the aforesaid rule had now been violated,  
royal wars were prepared for the duke’s destruction,  
and the land was deemed condemned to ruin.

By very strong skill the duke prepares to resist his fate;  
he often waged royal battles from open gates,  
often freely inflicted very fierce battles.

The king holds him besieged, restrained by the strength of the nobles;  
he removes access, blocks return from the city,  
and orders many battles to be brought against the duke.

Thus hidden love, lodged in the royal breast,  
brings attacks and itself stirs up the tumult of knights;  
[Col. 1004C] it also makes the royal limbs languish, wearing them down.

Now love cast in penetrates the breast without a wound;  
the love hidden in his entrails is revealed by pallor;  
he does not escape its darts and, oppressed by love, falls.

In this condition he seeks the help of Gothic physicians,  
but no antidote can remove the causes of his pains,  
for the physician does not know that the burden is love.

When he fears death, the best care is directed to the task;  
Merlin offers counsel through better skill,  
marvellous in his assistance and cultivating marvellous deeds.

He asks the physicians what is now the cause of the pain.  
When they cannot speak, a severe penalty of disgrace is theirs;  
the anger hidden within is brought forth openly.

Merlin says to the king: “Love presses you as the cause.  
Go outside, physicians: everywhere you are a burden upon the task;  
[Col. 1004D] leave the royal court; seek the law courts.

I beg you, conform to our law in the king’s bed.”

Having expelled the physicians, Merlin brings consolations;  
then he brings fitting joys to the king’s house.

### On Merlin, prophet of the Angles

The king asks what Merlin’s remedy may be.  
He answers: “I wish you to take up a position in the woods,  
and by my arts you will see marvels there.

Behold, I shall make you pass into the duke’s appearance,  
an appearance which will now remain and return to you again:  
let the duke’s true appearance now be your appearance.

By this lot I turn his servants into ours;  
behold, whoever sees these servants will think them the duke’s;  
you will see me too in a servant’s skin.

[Col. 1005A] With faces given by art, varied according to your will,  
and called by various names as their appearance changes,  
you will be able to indulge your desire as you wish.

Henceforth let us take care to go to Cornwall, to the duchess,  
so that she herself may heal the wounds fixed in your breast;  
once sufficiently summoned, you will return thus.

Though you are at war, climb the upper part of the castle.  
Meanwhile lovely Hierna, whom you desire, will see you,  
while the feigned appearance of her husband sits there.”

### On the same subject

At the prophet’s sign the king rejoices, rising at once  
and urgently ordering his companions to carry out the commands given;  
he goes to do these things, though he had previously been sick.

The beautiful Corinna was not then in the castle with the duke;  
[Col. 1005B] another part of the mountain opens the duke’s other fortress,  
where Hierna always lives in full residence.

Here the king orders armed attendants to remain,  
promising to lead more knights above these;  
thus the king’s feigned route is arranged.

When the king begins his journey, accompanied by a few followers,  
he enters the mountains over their highest summits,  
so that the great duchess receives her own husband.

At the king’s arrival, a crowd of nobles expresses joy;  
a hundred organs resound in restrained praise;  
town, street, and marketplace sing praise to the Lord.

In the king’s embrace, the woman gives her embrace as though to the duke;  
she lays kisses and tears upon the face stamped by art  
with the duke’s features, applying lips to the duke’s seeming lips.

Then they make him explain news about the king;  
[Col. 1005C] he says that the king follows a wicked law,  
for he who rules kingdoms himself destroys the flock.

“The king,” he says, “makes war upon me without cause with armed men;  
he destroys and takes my castles by his completed wars;  
yet he knows that our arms are sufficiently harmful.

The unjust man oppresses me; the place around me is burned;  
an attack threatens; I am wholly burdened with war.  
Let this one day now grant me rest.”

Hierna groaned deeply when she saw her husband  
worn down by enemies and oppressed by excessive labour;  
she grieves that the place inflamed by war is perishing.

They sit through the whole night; a celebrated feast summons the king.  
The king hastens enough; serene Hierna sits down;  
but the heart of him who eats was more set upon Venus.

[Col. 1005D] Now the meal is brief; his mind is wounded and he eats little.  
He is shut within, and, with the lady’s favour, remains seated;  
Corinna generously grants the other things he sought.

They lie together through the night; consolation comes in the morning.  
She reports that offspring has plainly lodged in her womb;  
he becomes the father and therefore remains more joyful.

Night, day, and hour are all at once marked.  
The father, full of joy, labours to depart  
and promptly gives the king’s memorable tokens.

The tokens which the father bears the knowing mother keeps for herself,  
and what the mother has, the ardent king carries away with himself;  
nor was the father’s deceitful appearance disclosed to the mother.

The feigned duke departs from his wife and goes to his task;  
when he returns to the ancient forest, his former appearance is restored.  
“It now pleased me to write what his force does.”

### Uther Pendragon, returning from his deception of the duchess, finds the duke slain and his castle captured

[Col. 1006A]

When the king departed from the castle accompanied by Merlin,  
the soldiers slightly withdrew their forces from their undertaking  
and lay hidden thus after setting ambushes.

When the duke’s men saw the army had left the castle,  
they rushed upon the few, trusting to obtain spoil;  
the duke too, with the rest, leaps forth bearing arms.

The king’s army from the ambush meets them;  
it defends its lord’s rights with the hands of Achilles.  
The unfortunate duke is captured and loses his head by the sword.

The other part of the knights who came from the castle with the duke  
lies wholly scattered; the king’s force occupies the castle,  
and royal standards crown its summit.

When the king returns from the forest to confront the enemy’s undertaking,  
[Col. 1006B] seeing the castle’s standards, he recognizes his own victory;  
then, quickening his journey, he expresses fitting joy.

He praises without end the battles of his victorious men;  
he enriches each of their companions according to his desire,  
and then desires to take the rest of the land by war.

### Again, on Duchess Hierna, besieged in her castle

Uther Pendragon orders the English standards to advance.  
Hierna seeks to defend herself by strength of arms,  
not knowing that she will be the king’s companion and wife.

Under a show of peace she receives the threatening commands:  
that she come into the meadows between them to conclude a treaty,  
lest she perish uselessly with her possessions and castle given up.

She answers: “I have a strong husband above in the castle;  
let this conference requested for peace remain for you.  
It is not fitting that a woman seek a position in the fields.”

[Col. 1006C] The king says: “Know that your ungrateful duke has been slain;  
abandon him, delivered to death; receive a better fate now.  
That you may not doubt, look—raise your head.”

Wounded by deadly reports and pierced by darts,  
the faithful, troubled woman falls lifeless,  
and only when scarcely restored to life does she speak.

“King,” she says, “the unjust death of my duke profits you nothing.  
He leaves me with the child I bear in my womb.  
If the father perishes by the sword, the son will be your enemy.

My city, so strong, does not fear the arms of your cohort;  
nor does it fear the hazards of fate from open gates.  
While this child lives, he himself will remain there.”

The king says: “O lady, I pray, let us speak more privately.  
I shall tell you deeds which we think dear for you to hear,  
from which we give worthy proofs of favour.

[Col. 1006D] Lay aside your haughtiness and abandon the anger you have begun.  
If you believe me, you will retain the highest honour;  
you will receive joys for which you sorrowfully grieve.”

The most courageous woman, scarcely overcome by the king’s entreaty,  
yielded, and reverently brought her mind to discourse.  
Henceforth Merlin’s marvels will speak there.

### He speaks with the duchess

The appeasing king says: “For you I prepared my wars,”

I longed for you too greatly, and under compulsion loved you too greatly;

Bound by your cord, I was able to be drawn by love for you.

In the likeness of the duke I once sat with you;

Devoted to intellectual pursuits, I rested upon the gleaming bed;

With my mouth I gave kisses along with the other acts.

From your mouth I learned that your womb bore offspring.

[Col. 1007A] Therefore it pleased you to keep my tokens as your own;

Behold what is yours, which I hold: look upon them, recognize them, wear them.

He whom you bear in your womb is mine; him I desire to hold.

He shall be king of my country and co-heir of the kingdom;

You shall sit as queen and wear the diadem.”

Here the duchess recognizes the king’s words and yields herself to him.

Without delay she believed, and recognized the earlier deeds;

At once she receives the greater things and despises the lesser;

She wipes away her tears and drives bitterness out.

Her countenance becomes radiant; at once she happily takes on colour;

She who had been pale, the queen regains her blush;

She is brighter than a flower, though she had previously been sick.

When the knight asks what purpose is required of him,

She commands that the fortress be opened swiftly to the king,

[Col. 1007B] Receiving from every side the commands of the man which must be obeyed.

A wondrous royal wedding is immediately prepared;

[Col. 1008A] She is betrothed, and is called supreme queen;

The peoples enjoy peace on river, countryside, and sea.

At Merlin’s direction the king and queen inquire

What honour the creature lying in her womb is to obtain,

Whether it will be a woman, or a man of worthy form.

Joyful, the prophet says: “Behold, prepare great rejoicings;

Hasten, nobles, and offer thanks to heaven;

For wonderful future things, now hidden in the womb, shall be made manifest.

This man shall be Arthur, destined to be the greatest king in the world,

To wage wars, a king who shall possess the lands of Gaul;

He shall be great in name, and shall perish by wounds.

Yet he shall not perish altogether: he shall be kept in the depths of the sea.
