From his original condition he will be able to live for ever:

These things I tell you; the rest I keep enclosed in my breast.”

If you inquire what wars Arthur, so great a man, fought,

[Col. 1008B] He was able to conquer every land by diverse marvels,

And himself was pre-eminent over men in strength and swordsmanship.

## Godfrey of Viterbo’s *Pantheon*

[Col. 1007]

## Part Nineteen

Concerning the royal insignia: namely, the holy cross, the sword, the sacred lance, the sceptre, the golden orb, the crown, and the diadem; what the jewels in the crown signify; what the gold in the crown signifies; and what the crest in the crown signifies.

[Col. 1007C]

Caesar commanded yesterday that inquiry be made what insignia there are

Which are rightly said to belong to the head of the empire,

And why he bears these signs, and what their rationale may be.

As Scripture proclaims, the cross, sword, sceptres, crown,

Lance, orb—these provide us with noble insignia;

It remains for me to explain what their respective signs mean.

### What that cross signifies

The cross is the head of the empire; it is given also as a remedy for diseases;

By its arms it contains the regions of the four-cornered world;

The cross is the ladder of God, hope, the way, and life for the condemned.

[Col. 1007D] By it ascent is given to the righteous, rewarded with their due recompense;

By it the thief hangs, and receives a reward for his crime;

The empire is accustomed to bear it throughout every land.

Its outstretched arms embrace and hold the world,

And, by Christ’s power, hold back all prodigies;

The cross, like an athlete, forbids every harmful thing.

Therefore, through this sign, by which every evil is removed,

It is a venerable sign worthy of the head of empire;

The battles of virtue take for themselves the signs of the cross.

The cross is granted to the empire to be borne by special right,

Since this ruler holds Christ’s place in defending kingdoms,

And bears on earth the venerable signs of the cross.

### What the royal or imperial sword signifies

The sword appears to display the sign of judgment,

[Col. 1008C] By which the savagery of evildoers is commanded to cease,

So that the robber may be thwarted; the king accordingly bears arms.

It is commanded that the drawn sword always be kept ready,

That it may swiftly punish what guilt has deserved:

For if it is slow, peace, emptied of protection, perishes.

God alone establishes and enacts laws for himself,

So that evils, restrained by his sword and noose, may be at rest.

If he did not suppress evils, the prince would be a mere shadow.

Thus God subjects kingdoms and the disputes of laws to himself,

Because heaven may be gained by human blood,

And, when the guilty man perishes, gifts acceptable to God are given.

With the sword at rest, he cannot restrain the world;

He can govern by a torrent of human blood:

He who wishes to rule shall uphold laws by blood.

### What the royal sceptre signifies

[Col. 1008D] While royal sceptres are held in the hands of kings,

Then they seem, as it were through a rod, to restrain all things,

And the penalty is inflicted which reason prescribes.

Supported everywhere by innumerable usages and laws,

This ruler instructs men to maintain worthy observances,

Yet he has the royal rod by which they may be governed.

Men are accustomed to devise many laws in different regions;

Caesar, holding the sceptres, knows how to distinguish many laws,

And by his rod commands that his laws be valid.

Life, descent, diverse languages, and regions vary;

One rule cannot distinguish all customs;

Therefore through the empire he sets many laws in motion.

One law stands above many laws; one king above many kings;

One equal above equals, one custom above customs, one usage above usages;

[Col. 1009A] The one man in whose world we dwell commands these.

Roman law deserves precedence over every body of law;

Yet it does not annul whatever reason contains in those laws;

Caesar wishes rather to retain both greater and lesser laws together.

### What the imperial lance signifies, and whence it came

The Lance of Maurice, greatest among the remaining insignia,

Has wrought very many miracles for worthy Christians;

For the nail of God is held to be joined to it.

Borne in war, it subjects mighty men to the empire;

Nations cannot resist its movements;

Wherever it stirs up wars, it is accustomed to conquer all things.

The holy lance is accustomed to overcome the contests of kingdoms;

It makes Roman nobles into citizens of Rome;

From it Caesar has the favour of kingdoms toward himself.

[Col. 1009B] When Boso, king of Arles, held it,

And fortune always favoured him in battle,

He became a grievous terror to the needy.

Now let the book set forth on what occasion and for what reason

After these events this sacred lance was delivered to the empire at Rome,

And why our letter recounts Boso.

Boso, handsome, a great king and a spirited king,

Once became wholly sleepless and frenzied;

Then, having fallen asleep, he bound his side with a sword.

Whoever called him while he rested in sleep,

The king’s right hand, immediately filled with fury, would kill;

He slept alone and without companion in his dwelling.

At Christmastide the king was at Arles;

The holy bishops rise, prepared for the feast,

Devoted to the offices of the night with praise and song.

[Col. 1009C] And while the bishop performs the sacred rite by which Mass is sung,

The king comes in anger because he had not been summoned beforehand,

And strikes the mitred head with a staff.

A deed grievous enough: the bishop is struck without cause

Together with the consecrated elements, the solemn rites being rendered void.

Henceforth learn what God then does.

The bishops of Arles, thus badly treated,

Gather soldiers and come prepared for war,

To bring about things worthy of the heavenly decree.

Therefore the king, hemmed in, rises when called to arms;

He is conquered and expelled, while the bishop stands honoured;

The king grieves in anger, subjected to mockery.

His defeated mind grieves, overwhelmed by excessive shame,

Nor does he wish to reign, because in war he lost his honour.

[Col. 1009D] He wishes that the life of a monk might now be his.

While the great Otto held the imperial throne,

And the powerful fortune of the world sufficiently favoured him,

King Boso, speaking to him, recounts these words with tears:

“I surrender to you my kingdom; I lay aside all honours;

Henceforth may our sacred lance confer honours upon you;

For me, the life of a monk alone should be cultivated.

I give you Vivarium; you shall dwell at Lyons;

You shall hold these two fortresses on this side of the Rhône, after I have crossed over;

There the king claims no estates from the Franks.

The Lance of Maurice, which my right hand gives you,

Is the chief of those things which I have now named as my kingdoms;

Now the holy lance shall give you the headship of the empire.

Where the Saône and Rhône flow uncertainly is Vienne;

On this side of the Tyrrhenian Sea lay Boso’s kingdoms;

Together with it, the Allobroges and Morienna favour this ruler.”

### What the golden orb, borne in kings’ hands, signifies

[Col. 1010A]

That golden orb is called an apple or a *palla* [ball],

By which he is understood to bear the world represented in figure;

When he is crowned, the *palla* to be borne is given him.

It signifies the world, whose form is said to be round,

And said to contain within a full foundation of earthly weight,

Which the hand bears as a secret orb.

It was gathered clean from the four regions of the earth,

So that it might be borne in the exalted hands of empire;

By this device Julius bore his empire.

Thus one hand bears this rounded world;

Thus the royal fist encloses every region,

Thus royal splendour holds everything that exists.

### What the cross placed above the golden orb signifies

[Col. 1010B]

The cross stands above the orb, set upon it by heaven’s gift;

Receive with a good heart, O king, what mystical things I offer you,

And, seated upon your throne, consider what man is.

The cross and orb are held joined together;

The former appears more, the latter less, in the venerable part;

The former strikes and heals; it perishes, while the latter remains.

If you desire to enclose earthly kingdoms in your fist,

You must reverently observe the things signified by the cross;

Be a servant of God, who rules your sceptres.

### What the imperial diadem signifies

This diadem signifies the conferring of a double crown,

Because it grants ancient Rome and the regions of the world;

Whoever holds it sits highest in the world.

The crown is double because, while it encompasses the city,

[Col. 1010C] It also contains the remaining world by the majesty of the diadem;

Thus one crown makes its own two things.

I do not speak of two in numerical respect, but in effect:

The diadem possesses the dominion of the conquered city and world;

Caesar, joining these two, was master of all things.

### What the precious gems in the crown signify, and who instituted them

Julius instituted gems to be set upon the crown,

So that it should be precious, laden with the splendour of stones;

Now the book shall explain what a gem signifies.

Four mystical properties are implanted in all gems:

Hardness, virtue, brightness, and perpetual warmth;

He who is to be Caesar should desire to know these mysteries.

Steadfastness is represented by hardness, honour by virtue;

A good reputation is colour, brightness is gain without crime;

[Col. 1010D] He who wears the diadem shall possess these four things.

### What gold in crowns signifies

Golden material is suited to royal crowns;

It indicates that sovereignty over the world belongs to its rulers;

The circle is the round form of the earthly globe.

Gold surpasses all metals by its brilliance;

The empire surpasses those whom the world contains within its domain,

And rightly governs them by Romulean law.

Malleable gold receives innumerable forms;

The Roman monarchy likewise receives various regulations,

Flexible and accommodating, a golden form for its subjects.

### What the crest in the imperial crown signifies

The imperial crest is placed above the circle;

In it the enlarged commonwealth is plainly shown:

He who wears the diadem shall be conqueror and founder.

[Col. 1011]

A catalogue of all Roman pontiffs and all Roman emperors; and likewise of all kings who existed from the beginning of the world down to Pope Urban III, Emperor Frederick I, and his son King Henry VI.

Pope Stephen the German held office for eight months. Pope Benedict held office for ten years. Pope Nicholas held office for three years, six months, and twenty-five days. Pope Alexander held office for nine years and six months. Pope Gregory VII held office for fifteen years, one month, and eight days. Pope Victor held office for four months and seven days. Pope Urban held office for eleven years, six months, and eighteen days. Pope Paschal held office for nineteen years. [Col. 1019C] Pope Gelasius held office for one year and six days. Pope Callistus held office for five years, ten months, and thirteen days. Pope Honorius held office for five years, six months, and twenty-nine days. Pope Innocent held office for thirteen years, six months, and fourteen days. Pope Celestine held office for five months and eleven days. Pope Lucius held office for eleven months. Pope Eugenius held office for eight years, five months, and ten days. Pope Anastasius held office for one year and five days. Pope Adrian held office for four years and nine months. Pope Alexander held office for twenty-two years. Pope Lucius III held office for three years. Pope Urban III is pope now.

## Emperors

[Col. 1012]

[Col. 1012A] Julius Caesar reigned for four years and six months. Emperor Octavian reigned for fifty-six years. Emperor Tiberius reigned for thirteen years. Emperor Gaius Caligula reigned for three years and ten months. Emperor Claudius reigned for fourteen years and five months. Emperor Nero reigned for thirteen years and nine months. This was the first persecution. The emperors Galba, Vitellius, and Otho reigned for one year. Emperor Vespasian reigned for nine years and eleven months. Emperor Titus reigned for two years and two months. [Col. 1012B] Emperor Domitian reigned for fifteen years, five months, and two days. This was the second persecution. Emperor Nerva reigned for one year and four months. Emperor Trajan reigned for nineteen years, five months, and fifteen days. This was the third persecution. Emperor Adrian reigned for twenty years and eleven months. This was the fourth persecution. Emperor Antoninus Pius, with his sons, reigned for twenty-two years and three months. Emperor Marcus Verus Antoninus, with his brother Aurelius Commodus, reigned for twenty-nine years and four months. This was the fifth persecution. Emperor Commodus reigned for thirteen years. Emperor Aelius Pertinax reigned for [Col. 1012C] six months. Emperor Severus reigned for nineteen years. Emperor Antoninus Caracalla reigned for seven years. Emperor Alexander reigned for twelve years. Emperor Macrinus reigned for one year. Emperor Marcus Aurelius reigned for four years. This was the sixth persecution. Emperor Maximinus reigned for three years. Emperor Gordian reigned for seven years. Philip, with his son Philip, the first Christian emperor, reigned for seven years. [Col. 1014A] Emperor Decius reigned for one year. This was the seventh persecution. Emperor Gallus, with his son Volusianus, reigned for two years. Emperor Valerian, with his son, reigned for fifteen years. This was the eighth persecution. Emperor Claudius reigned for one year. Emperor Aurelian reigned for five years and six months. This was the ninth persecution. Emperor Tacitus reigned for six months. Emperor Probus reigned for six years and four months. Emperor Carus, with his sons Carinus and Numerian, reigned for three years. The emperors Diocletian and Maximian reigned for [Col. 1014B] twenty years. This was the tenth persecution of Christians. The emperors Constantius, Galerius, and Licinius reigned for two years and six months. Emperor Constantine reigned for thirty years and ten months. The emperors Constantius, Constantine, and Constans, brothers, reigned for thirty-four years, five months, and twenty-three days. Emperor Julian reigned for two years and six months. Emperor Jovinian reigned for eight years. Emperor Valentinian reigned for eleven years. [Col. 1014C] Emperor Valens reigned for four years. Gratian and his brother, emperors, reigned for six years. Emperor Valentinian reigned for twelve years. Emperor Theodosius reigned for twenty-seven years, with both his sons and after both his sons. Arcadius and Honorius, Theodosius with Valentinian, emperors, reigned for thirty-two years. The emperors Honorius and Arcadius reigned for twenty-five years. The emperors Valentinian and Martian reigned for nine years. Emperor Marcian reigned for six years after Valentinian. Emperor Leo reigned for seven years. Emperor Zeno reigned for seventeen years. [Col. 1014D] Emperor Anastasius reigned for seventeen years. Emperor Justin the Elder reigned for seven years. Emperor Justinian reigned for thirty-four years. [Col. 1016A] Justin the Younger, emperor, reigned for seven years. Emperor Tiberius reigned for six years. Emperor Maurice reigned for thirty-one years. [Col. 1016B] Emperor Phocas reigned for eight years. Emperor Heraclius reigned for thirty-six years with his son Constantine. Constantine, son of Heraclius. [Col. 1016C] Constantine the Younger. Justinian the Younger. Leo. Tiberius. [Col. 1016D] Emperor Justinian. Emperor Philip. Emperor Anastasius. Emperor Theodosius. Leo, son of Constantine. Constantine with his son Leo. Pippin, now king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans. Leo, emperor after his father’s death. Charlemagne, now king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans. [Col. 1018A] Constantine with his mother Irene, empress after her son.

### Now the empire is transferred to the Franks

That Charles, emperor of the Franks. Louis, with his son Lothair. Lothair, emperor after his father. Likewise Lothair, emperor with his son Louis. [Col. 1018B] Louis II, emperor after his father [the final word is uncertain]. Charles II, emperor. Charles III, emperor. Arnulf, according to some.

### According to the Romans, these are emperors in Italy

[Col. 1018C] Louis, emperor in Italy. Berengar, emperor in Italy. Hugh, emperor in Italy. Guy, emperor in Italy, and his son Lambert. Berengar rules in Italy. Lothair in Italy. Berengar in Italy with his son Albert.

[Col. 1018D]

### Now the Germans rule

Otto I, German emperor. Otto II, German emperor. [Col. 1020A] Otto III, German emperor. Henry I, emperor. Conrad I, emperor. Note that before this Emperor Henry there was another Henry, king and Saxon; he is called Henry I as king, but not emperor. Likewise there was another King Conrad I, but not [Col. 1020B] emperor. These, however, are the first Henry and first Conrad as German emperors. Henry III in the kingdom, but in the empire Henry II, in reckoning the Henrys. Henry III as emperor; but in the kingdom he is Henry IV, in reckoning the Henrys. Henry IV as emperor; but in reckoning the Henrys [Col. 1020C] he is Henry V. This Henry captured Pope Paschal; and this man rejected the Church’s ring and the bishops’ staff. Lothair II. Conrad III. Frederick I. Henry VI rules with his father Frederick.

[Col. 1019] End of the catalogue of Roman pontiffs and emperors.

## Catalogue of Italian Kings

[Col. 1019D]

Italus, first king of Italy, reigned for forty-one years.

Janus, king of Italy, reigned for twenty-seven years.

Saturn, king of Italy, reigned for thirty-four years.

Picus, king of Italy, reigned for thirty-one years.

Faunus, king in Laurentum—that is, in the province of Sabinia—reigned for twenty-nine years.

[Col. 1020D] Latinus, king in Latium, reigned for thirty-two years.

Aeneas, king of Italy, reigned for thirty-six years.

Ascanius, king of Italy, reigned for thirty-six years.

Posthumus Silvius, son of Lavinia, reigned for thirty-nine years.

Aeneas Silvius reigned for twenty-two years.

Latinus Silvius reigned for fifty years.

Alba Silvius reigned for thirty-four years.

[Col. 1021A] Capetus Silvius reigned for thirty-four years.

Capys Silvius reigned for twenty-seven years.

Calpetus Silvius reigned for thirteen years.

Tiberinus Silvius reigned for eight years.

Agrippa Silvius reigned for forty-one years.

Alladius Silvius reigned for twenty-four years.

Aventinus Silvius reigned for thirty-six years.

Procas Silvius reigned for twenty-three years.

Amulius Silvius, the last king in Latium, having expelled his brother Numitor, reigned in Alba for forty-four years.

Then, when the city of Rome was founded in Numitor’s time, Remus and Romulus ruled at Rome. Their mother was Rhea Silvia, a Vestal virgin, whom others [Col. 1021B] call Aelia.

### Roman Chronology

Rome was founded in the 3,484th year from Adam; in the 1,300th year from the empire of Ninus; in the 414th year after the destruction of Troy; in the third Olympiad, while Hosea was then also reigning in Israel.

After Romulus, Numa Pompilius ruled at Rome for forty years.

Tullus Hostilius ruled for thirty-two years.

Ancus Marcius ruled for twenty-four years.

Tarquinius Priscus ruled for thirty-seven years.

Servius Tullius ruled for forty-four [Col. 1021C] years.

Tarquinius Superbus ruled for twenty-five years.

After Tarquinius Superbus was expelled, consuls, senators, dictators, tribunes, and masters of the soldiers ruled for 464 years.

Thereafter, from Julius Caesar, who succeeded them, there were emperors and Roman pontiffs, as we have described above.

We shall now speak of the kingdom of the Assyrians, which began in the fifteenth year of Serug, Abraham’s great-grandfather. It endured until the fifth year of Uzziah, king of the Jews. That kingdom had thirty-eight kings, whose names follow in order. Their kingdom endured in its condition for 1,302 [Col. 1021D] years.

## Catalogue of Assyrian Kings

These are the kings of the Assyrians. Nembrot, king of Babylon, a giant ten cubits tall. Belus, king of the Assyrians. Ninus, king of the Assyrians. Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians, wife of Ninus after him. Zameis, also called Ninias, son of Ninus and Semiramis, king of the Assyrians. Arius, king of the Assyrians. Aralius, king of the Assyrians. Baleus Xerses, king of the Assyrians. Armamitres, king of the Assyrians. [Col. 1022A] Belochus, king of the Assyrians. Baleus the Younger, king of the Assyrians. Altadas, king of the Assyrians. Mamitus, king of the Assyrians. Mancaleus, king of the Assyrians. Spherus, king of the Assyrians. Another Mancaleus, king of the Assyrians. Sparetus, king of the Assyrians. Ascatades, king of the Assyrians. Amyntas, king of the Assyrians. Belochus the Younger, king of the Assyrians. Belopares, king of the Assyrians. Lamprides, king of the Assyrians. Sosares, king of the Assyrians. Lampares, king of the Assyrians. [Col. 1022B] Pannias, king of the Assyrians. Sosarmus, king of the Assyrians. Mitreus, king of the Assyrians. Tautanius, king of the Assyrians. Teuteus, king of the Assyrians. Tyneus, king of the Assyrians. Dercillus, king of the Assyrians. Eupales, king of the Assyrians. Laosthenes, king of the Assyrians. Pyridiades, king of the Assyrians. Ophrateus, king of the Assyrians. Ophraganeus, king of the Assyrians. Astrasapes, king of the Assyrians. Tonos Concoleros, who is commonly called Sardanapalus.

[Col. 1022C] Under this Sardanapalus the kingdom of the Assyrians perished, and the Medes subdued it, in the 1,226th year from the empire of Ninus; in the 1,305th year from the reign of his father Belus; and in the 1,164th year from the beginning of Babylon, or from its restoration under Queen Semiramis. Then the aforesaid Sardanapalus, the last and basest king of the Assyrians, invented the first mattress or first cushions, and made them with his own hands. For this reason his princes, moved by shame, wished to kill him; but he said to them: “You shall not have a triumph over me.” Having said this, he threw himself into the fire and was consumed in it.

## Catalogue of Median Kings

[Col. 1022D]

These are the names of the Median kings after they had subjected the Assyrian kingdom to themselves:

Arsaces, the first king of the Medes, reigned for twenty-eight years. He was succeeded by Sosarmus, king of the Medes; in the fifteenth year of whose reign the Olympiad first began to be named at Elis, a city of Greece. King Medidus succeeded King Sosarmus. After him there was Cardiceas, king of the Medes, and he was succeeded by Dejoces, king of the Medes. After him Phraortes, king of the Medes, reigned; he reigned for twenty-two years. He was succeeded by Cyaxares, king of the Medes. After him came Astyages, king of the Medes.

[Col. 1023A] Cyrus, king of the Persians, the grandson of this Astyages through his daughter, defeated that same grandfather Astyages in war and subjected the kingdom of the Medes; he made his grandfather King Astyages governor over the Hyrcanians, and himself established the kingdom of the Medes under the Persian empire. The empire of the Medes had endured for two hundred and fifty-seven years.

Catalogue of the Kings of the Persians.

These are the kings of the Persians:

Cyrus, King of the Persians. He was succeeded by Cambyses, King of the Persians, bearing four names: Xerxes in 2 Esdras; Nebuchadnezzar in the history of Judith; and Ahasuerus in the history of the Book of Esther. After this Cambyses there succeeded [Col. 1023B] Darius, King of the Persians, son of Hystaspes, who restored the Temple of the Lord. Darius was succeeded by his son Xerxes, King of the Persians. He was succeeded by another Artaxerxes, King of the Persians, after whom came Darius Nothus, King of the Persians. Then came Artaxerxes the Great, King of the Persians. He was succeeded by Darius Ochus, King of the Persians. This Darius was succeeded by Arsames, King of the Persians, also called Arses. He was succeeded by the last King of the Persians, Darius Codomannus.

Alexander of Macedon defeated this Darius, and subjected the Persians and the whole East.

After Alexander the Great died, his commanders divided the empire among [Col. 1023C] themselves as follows: Ptolemy received Egypt; Antipater, Greece; Seleucus, from whom Seleucia takes its name, received Syria and Babylonia; Cassander received Lycia and Pamphylia; Antigonus, Greater Phrygia. Each of them placed a diadem upon his own head.

Catalogue of the Kings of the Hebrews.

Saul. David. Solomon, king of all Israel. Rehoboam in Judah. Jeroboam in Israel. Baasha in Israel. Abijah in Jerusalem. King Asa in Jerusalem. [Col. 1023D] King Jehoshaphat in Jerusalem. Elah, king of Samaria. Zimri, king in Samaria. Omri, likewise king in Samaria. Ahab, king in Samaria. Ahaziah, king in Samaria. Jehoshaphat, king in Judah. Joram, king in Judah. Azachias, king in Judah. Joachim, king in Judah. Ahaz, king in Judah. Hezekiah, king in Judah. Jehu, king of Samaria. Joash, king in Samaria. Jeroboam, king in Samaria. [Col. 1024A] Zechariah, king in Samaria. Shallum, king in Samaria. Menahem, king in Samaria. Pekahiah, king in Samaria. Hoshea, king in Samaria.

While this same Hoshea was reigning, Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, seized that same Hoshea and led him captive with all the people of Samaria; and he settled them by his river Mosim, in the land of the Medes.

Hezekiah was then king in Jerusalem. Manasseh, king in Jerusalem. Amon, king in Jerusalem. Josiah, king in Jerusalem. Joash, king in Jerusalem. Joachim, king in Jerusalem.

[Col. 1024B] Nebuchadnezzar led this man captive, together with all the people of the Jews, in the Babylonian deportation.

From this point onward all the kings of the Hebrews, both in Jerusalem and in Samaria, cease, because they are in captivity.

But after four hundred years they again had kings in Jerusalem, after the times of the Maccabees:

Namely, King John Hyrcanus; King Aristobulus; King Alexander; again King Aristobulus; again King Hyrcanus; King Herod, a foreigner, son of Antipater, [Col. 1024C] a pagan man, by a Jewish mother. In his time Christ, the King of kings, was born.

Catalogue of the Kings of Troy.

King Jupiter and his sons. Dardanus, first king in Troy. Tros, second king in Troy. Laomedon, king of Troy. Priam, king of Troy. Anchises, king of Troy. Hector, king of Troy. Paris, king of Troy. The younger Priam, king of Troy. Antenor, king of Troy. Aeneas, king, from Troy.

Catalogue of the Kings of the Greeks.

[Col. 1024D]

King Jupiter at Athens. King Danaus, his son. King Pelops in Greece. King Atreus in Greece. King Menelaus in Greece. King Agamemnon in Greece. King Philip, father of Alexander the Great. King Alexander the Great.

Then that kingdom itself was subdivided among Alexander’s twelve commanders, until the times of the Romans, who obtained all kingdoms.

Catalogue of the Kings of Sicyon.

Sicyonia is a region which was first called Api and [Col. 1025A] afterwards, when its name was changed, was called the Peloponnese.

The kingdom of the Sicyonians began in the twenty-fourth year of Nahor, Abraham’s grandfather, and endured until the year of Eli, priest of the Lord at Shiloh. This kingdom lasted for nine hundred and sixty-two years. It had these twenty-six kings:

1. Aegialeus — reigned 52 years  
2. Europs — 45 years  
3. Selchin — 20 years  
4. Apis — 25 years  
5. Thelasion — 52 years  
6. Aegydius — 34 years  
7. Thurimachus — 45 years  
8. Leucippus — 53 years  

[Col. 1025B]

9. Messapius — 47 years  
10. Heratus — 46 years  
11. Plemnaeus — 48 years  
12. Orthopolis — 63 years  
13. Marathius — 30 years  
14. Marathus — 20 years  
15. Erichthreus — 55 years  
16. Choar — 30 years  
17. Epopeus — 35 years  
18. Laomedon — 40 years  
19. Sicyon — 45 years  
20. Polybus — 40 years  
21. Inachus — 42 years  
22. Phaestus — 8 years  
23. Adrastus — 4 years  

[Col. 1025C]

24. Polyphides — 31 years  
25. Pelasgus — 20 years  
26. Zeusippus — 32 years  

Catalogue of the Kings of the Egyptians.

The kingdom of the Egyptians began under Belus, father of Ninus, and also existed under Ninus and his wife Semiramis. When they died, it remained among the princes of Egypt, who by election established a king for themselves under the title “dynasty.” His successors too were each similarly called dynasts. Before Abraham’s time the kingdom of Egypt had fifteen dynasties, that is, kings of Egypt.

At Abraham’s birth there were already seventeen dynasties. From that time the kings of Egypt began to be called [Col. 1025D] Thebans. Later, when the name was changed again, those kings were called Shepherds.

In the twentieth dynasty they began to be called Pharaohs. They were also called by another name, Diapolitans.

There were seventeen Pharaohs at their different periods, down to Cambyses, son of Cyrus, King of the Persians, who was the first to subject Egypt. It should be noted that from the time when Joseph went down into Egypt to the birth of Moses, there were five kings—that is, Pharaohs—in Egypt. Their names are these:

King Amois reigned fifteen years. King Nembrot reigned thirteen years. King Amenophis reigned twenty-one years. King Memphres reigned twenty-two years. [Col. 1026A] King Mesphat reigned twenty-six years.

Under this king, Aram, son of Levi, at the sixty-fifth year of his life begot Moses. Pharaoh’s daughter, named Termut, drew him from the river and brought him up. He also led Israel out of Egypt.

Catalogue of the Kings of Egypt and Antioch after the Death of Alexander the Great.

After Alexander’s death, then, Ptolemy, surnamed Soter, first succeeded in Egypt. He reigned in Egypt for nineteen years. The second king of Egypt, Ptolemy, was called Philadelphus. The third Ptolemy was called Euergetes. The fourth Ptolemy was called Philopator. Antiochus the Great rose up against this Philopator; he killed him and subjected Egypt, Judaea, [Col. 1026B] and Persia, and reigned for thirty-six years. He had two sons, Seleucus and Soter. While that Seleucus, the elder by birth, was at Rome as a hostage, his brother Seleucus, the younger, succeeded his father in the sovereignty of Antioch and was surnamed Epiphanes. This Epiphanes expelled his brother’s son Demetrius from the kingdom. This Epiphanes so oppressed the Jews that they placed idols in the Temple of the Lord and worshipped them. Then Mattathias, father of the Maccabees, rose against Antiochus, and after him Judas Maccabaeus. Antiochus Epiphanes reigned twelve years; his son Eupator succeeded him and reigned twelve years. Demetrius, son of Soter, succeeded him as king in Antioch. Under the rule of this Demetrius Judas Maccabaeus was killed. Alexander killed this Demetrius, [Col. 1026C] having himself killed his aforementioned father Eupator, and he reigned in his place. Afterwards Demetrius of Crete, son of the aforementioned Demetrius, killed this Alexander and reigned in his place. Later Antiochus the Great, son of this Alexander, was received into the kingdom of Antioch and drove Demetrius out from it. Tryphon, the leader of the boy Antiochus, killed that boy, his lord; and therefore he himself reigned in his place, while Demetrius, whom that boy had expelled, was still held captive by Artaxes, king of the Arabs. When Tryphon had been hard pressed by arms in battle, Demetrius, son of the captive Demetrius, rose up, was received into the kingdom of Antioch, and ruled. In the time of this Demetrius, John Hyrcanus, of Maccabean stock, was [Col. 1026D] high priest. His son Aristobulus was established as the first king of the Jews after the Babylonian captivity. His son Alexander, king of the Jews, succeeded him. Aristobulus, Alexander’s son, succeeded Alexander.

And he himself reigned in his place while King Demetrius, though expelled, was still held captive among the Arabs. But when Tryphon had been severely defeated in battle by the Maccabees, Demetrius, son of the captive Demetrius, was restored to the kingdom. Tryphon, having fled, went into Persia.

At that time Aristobulus, of the line of the Maccabees, became the first king of the Jews, namely four hundred and forty-seven years after the Babylonian deportation.

[Col. 1027A] Aristobulus was succeeded by another Aristobulus, whom the consul Pompey killed and made Antipater procurator of Judaea.

His son Herod succeeded to the kingdom.

At that time Christ the Lord was born, and the kingdom of the Jews was subdued; Antioch having long since been subjected by the Romans.

Catalogue of the Kings of Argos.

The kingdom of the Argives began in the year in which Jacob and Esau, sons of Isaac, were born, under their first king Inachus. It lasted until the fifteenth year of that woman prophet who was called Deborah in Israel. The kingdom of the Argives remained in its condition for two hundred and sixty-four years. It was dispersed and destroyed [Col. 1027B] under Danaus, king of the Greeks, from whom all Greeks, even to the present day, are called Danaans.

At the same time King Phoroneus, son of Inachus, the first king of the Athenians, and his wife Niobe gave the first laws to the Greeks at Athens; and they were the first to establish that cases should be tried before a judge, and they called the place of judgment the forum.

Catalogue of the Kings of the Babylonians.

The kingdom of Babylonia was counted under the kingdom of the Egyptians or of the Assyrians. Yet in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, who was not of the line of the kings of Babylonia or Assyria, but was, as it were, an extraordinary ruler—namely a bastard, begotten from an uncertain union—the empire of Babylonia began to take precedence, until the time of Cyrus, King of the Persians and [Col. 1027C] Medes, who subjected Babylonia and joined it to the Persian empire. We shall therefore set down a catalogue of the kings of the Babylonians from Nebuchadnezzar himself to Cyrus:

King Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed Jerusalem and took all the Jews captive. King Nebuchadnezzar, son of the first. King Evilmerodach, likewise his son. King Regusar, son of Evilmerodach. King Labosar, likewise son of Evilmerodach. King Belshazzar, likewise son of Evilmerodach.

This Belshazzar saw the hand writing upon the wall. Daniel interpreted that vision, saying that his kingdom would be divided and that the king himself would perish [Col. 1027D] by the sword. When this had been said, on the following night Darius, king of the Medes, and Cyrus, his grandson through his daughter—the King of the Persians, that is—came and killed King Belshazzar, and obtained the whole kingdom of Babylonia.

Catalogue of the Kings of the Franks.

We shall arrange in a catalogue the most noble genealogy of the kings of the Franks, though unknown to many authors, beginning from Adam to Noah; from Noah to Nembrot, the first king of Babylonia; from him, from king to king, to the Trojan kings; thence to Charlemagne; and from him to the Emperor Frederick and his son King Henry. Let us therefore begin with Adam.

Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Malalchel, Jared, [Col. 1028A] Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem son of Noah, Arphaxad son of Shem. Arphaxad begot Salem; Salem begot Heber; Heber begot Peleg and Irari, father of Nembrot, the first king, at the division of languages. Nembrot, the first king of this world in Babylonia, begot eight sons. The first of them was Cres, from whom the island of Crete took its name. Cres, first king of the Cretans, begot Caelius.

Caelius begot Saturn. King Saturn begot Jupiter. King Jupiter begot Dardanus and Tros. King Tros built Troy in his own name and begot Laomedon. King Laomedon begot Priam and Anchises. King Anchises begot Aeneas, from whom all the nobility [Col. 1028B] of the Alban and Roman kings descends.

The elder King Priam had through his sister a nephew, the younger Priam. This Priam, and Antenor with him, after the destruction of Troy crossed the Illyrian Sea by ship through the Veneto with thirteen thousand armed men. There they built the city of Padua, in which Antenor also has an honourable tomb. From there they crossed to the Maeotian marshes; there they built the city of Sicambria, from which they themselves were called Sicambrians. Then, as time passed, they occupied Germany and were called Germans from it. Later they were called Franks by the Emperor Valentinian—that is, “fierce ones.” While reigning in Germany, they first had as their king [Col. 1028C] the son of the aforesaid Priam, named Priam, whom the Romans killed in battle because he rebelled against the Roman empire. Priam’s son then remained, called Marcomir; the Germans made his son Pharamund their king. They then began to possess laws composed by their lawgivers Guisogastald and Salagast. From that Salagast the Salic Law received its name. The Franks have used this Salic Law to the present day; hence they themselves are called Salian Franks.

When King Pharamund died, his son King Crinitus succeeded, from whom all the remaining kings of the Franks were called Criniti.

In these times the Franks began to increase, whereas the Romans [Col. 1028D] began to decline. For the peoples who had been subject to the Romans began to rule themselves, while the Romans, on the contrary, were compelled to serve the peoples.

For after they had already plundered the City itself, the Goths settled beyond the river Loire in Gaul. The Burgundians then began to have a king. The Franks likewise drove out the Romans who then lived around the river Rhine. When King Crinitus died, King Gildibert succeeded; by Queen Bissina he begot Clovis.

King Clovis begot Meroveus.

King Meroveus begot another Meroveus, from whom all the remaining kings in Francia were called Merovingians.

[Col. 1029A] King Ildricus, son of Meroveus, begot another Clovis.

This Clovis was the first Christian king of the Franks, and Saint Remigius baptized him.

This Clovis subjected the Alamanni and defeated the Goths, that is, the Vascones.

In the year 751 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the kings of the Franks ruled in name alone. Among them there was a prince of their own kindred who was called, from his office, *majordomus*; for he governed that whole kingdom. The first of these is said to have been Arnulf, who later became bishop of Metz.

His son Ansgisus was *majordomus* after him. After him came his son Pepin, [Col. 1029B] *majordomus*, surnamed the Fat. His son was Charlemagne’s grandfather, Charles Martel, from whom was born Pepin the Short, duke also of the Franks, king, and *majordomus*; from him was born Charlemagne, first emperor of the Franks.

From that time there have been emperors in Francia up to the present day. They are:

Charlemagne, the first emperor; Louis II, Emperor of the Franks; Lothair I; Lothair II; Charles II; Charles III; Arnulf; Cendebuldus; [Col. 1029C] Louis the Child; Conrad I; Henry I; Otto I; Otto II; Otto III; Henry II; Conrad II; Henry III; Henry IV; Henry V; Lothair the Saxon; Conrad III; Frederick I; Henry VI, son of Frederick.

[Col. 1029D] Behold, reader: from Adam to Frederick and his son Henry you have the full genealogy and complete catalogue of the kings, or emperors, of the Franks. Thanks be to God.

Catalogue of the Kings of the Goths.

The Gothic people are diverse. There are Visigoths, whom we call Vascones, around the provinces of Catalonia and Aragon. There are also Ostrogoths in the southern region. All of these have one origin; but because of their different climates, their names or surnames differ. Their kings were these:

King Theoderic I; [Col. 1030A] King Theoderic II; King Theobald; King Alaric; King Dalaric; King Witigous; King Vigivus; King Sigismund; and certain others.

Catalogue of the Kings of the Lombards.

The Lombards were once called Vinuli in their native country, from which they first came, in the southern region of the province of Scandinavia. On coming thence, at the beginning they had two dukes, Ivor and Agion, and their mother Gamara. After these died, the Lombards made Agilmund, son of Agion, their king; he [Col. 1030B] reigned thirty-three years. When he died, they made Lamison king. When he died, King Lecha reigned in his place. After he had reigned for forty years, his son Gildeoc succeeded him.

When he died, his son Classo succeeded as king. When he died, his son Guado succeeded him. When he died, his son Gualtaris succeeded him, the eighth in the Lombard kingdom.

King Gualtaris died after reigning seven years. Aldoin, the ninth king of the Lombards, succeeded him. This Aldoin first led the Lombards into Pannonia. At that time the Emperor Justinian abridged the multitude of laws. In these days Saint Benedict was abbot at Subiaco. When King Aldoin died, his son Alboin succeeded as the tenth [Col. 1030C] of the Lombard kings. He killed Cunimund, king of the Gepids, and took his daughter Rosimund as wife. From the head of that same King Cunimund he had a drinking cup made for himself. He even made the daughter serve drink in it, saying to her, “Drink with your father.” But she, beyond the injury done to herself and her father, caused him to be killed, as is contained in the body of this book.

Therefore, when Lombard victories were celebrated everywhere and King Alboin was still remaining in Pannonia, Narses, prefect of Italy and imperial *chartularius*, summoned Alboin himself with all the Lombards into Italy. There, after Alboin’s death, Liutprand succeeded. After his death, Aistulf succeeded. After his death, [Col. 1030D] Desiderius succeeded.

The Emperor Charlemagne captured that Desiderius and carried him into exile. From then on the emperors and kings of the Franks held Lombardy in subjection, down to the times of the Emperor Frederick and his son King Henry VI.

In their times I, Godfrey, composed and wrote this sort of book, to the honour of God, the Church, and the Empire, and for the lasting benefit of all readers. I therefore pray all readers of this book, for the love of God and in view of the highest charity, to bless my soul and the souls of my parents. Amen.

[Col. 1029] End of the catalogues of all kings.

SYNCHRONOUS CATALOGUE OF POPES AND EMPERORS.

[Col. 1031]

[Col. 1031A] The Lord Jesus Christ, the first and supreme pontiff, sat in this world for thirty-two years and three months before his Ascension.

The apostle Peter, preaching in the regions of the East, held office for four years. In the bishopric of Antioch he held office for eight years. At Rome, however, in the papacy, he held office for twenty-five years, two months, and four days.

Division of Times.

The Emperor Octavian Augustus lived in the time of the apostle Peter and ruled for fifty-six years.

Tiberius, Octavian’s stepson, lived in Peter’s time and ruled for thirteen years.

Gaius Caligula lived in Peter’s time and ruled for three years, ten months, and eight days.

[Col. 1031B] Claudius ruled in Peter’s time for fourteen years and eight months. In Claudius’s time the apostle Peter came to Rome, where he held office for twenty-five years. Linus was Peter’s assistant in the papacy with him for nine years, three months, and twelve days.

Cletus, Peter’s assistant together with Linus, held office for twelve years, one month, and ten days. These two, namely Linus and Cletus, were co-bishops and Peter’s assistants. Hence the apostle John writes as follows in his third letter to all the bishops of Gaul and Germany: “Peter, prince of the apostles, chose Linus and Cletus as his assistants; yet he did not hand over to them the pontificate or the power of binding and loosing, but they assisted him [Col. 1031C] in external matters.”

The Emperor Nero lived in Peter’s time and ruled for thirteen years and nine months.

Galba, Vitellius, and Otho seized the empire after Nero, and quickly destroyed one another in wars and conflicts. Vespasian succeeded them.

Division of Times.

Pope Clement I, after Peter, held office for nine years and one month. After his death the papacy was vacant for twenty-one days.

Vespasian, in Clement’s time, ruled for nine years, eleven months, and twenty-two days. In his time the Colossus was erected, one hundred and eight feet high. Then the city of Adventia was founded [Col. 1031D] among the Allobroges, on the river Saône. Vespasian died from diarrhoea.

Titus, in Clement’s time, ruled for two years and two months, and was most eloquent.

Domitian, Titus’s brother, in Clement’s time ruled for fifteen years, five months, and two days. In his pride he ordered that he be called God and Lord; he persecuted Christians and banished John the Evangelist to the island of Patmos. He killed the entire family of King David. In his time the Capitol at Rome, the forum, porticoes, stadium, Baths of Trajan, and Pantheon were built. Domitian was [Col. 1032A] killed by his own people in the palace. His corpse was shamefully dragged through the streets by the Roman people.

Nerva, in Clement’s time, ruled for one year and four months. He condemned everything Domitian had done, and restored what Domitian had condemned. John therefore then returned from exile, where he had written the Apocalypse.

Division of Times.

Pope Anacletus held office for nine years, two months, and eleven days. There was a vacancy of thirteen days.

Trajan, in Anacletus’s time, ruled for nineteen years, six months, and fifteen days.

Division of Times.

Pope Evaristus held office for nine years, ten months, and two days. There was a vacancy of nineteen days.

[Col. 1032B] The Emperor Hadrian, in Evaristus’s time, reigned for twenty years and eleven months. Then occurred the third persecution of Christians, sufficiently severe.

Division of Times.

Pope Alexander held office for ten years and seven months. After him the Roman papacy was vacant for twenty-five days.

The Emperor Aelius, in Pope Alexander’s time, reigned for twenty years and eleven months. He rebuilt Jerusalem and called it after his own name Aelia; and he banished all the Jews into the remotest regions, so that they might no longer dwell there and so that the city might never again be called Jerusalem, but Aelia.

Division of Times.

[Col. 1032C] Pope Xystus, under the Emperor Decius, held office for ten years and five months. There was a vacancy of two days.

The Emperor Decius, in Xystus’s time, reigned for one year. Orosius says three years.

Division of Times.

Pope Telesphorus, under Antoninus, held office for eleven years, five months, and twenty-one days. There was a vacancy of seven days.

The Emperor Antoninus Pius, under Pope Telesphorus, ruled for twenty-two years and three months. In his time the physician Galen, born at Pergamum, flourished.

Pope Hyginus, under the Emperor Antoninus, held office [Col. 1032D] for four years, one month, and four days.

Division of Times.

Marcus Antoninus, in Anicetus’s time, ruled for nineteen years, four months, and one day, together with his brother Lucius Aurelius. This Lucius died of apoplexy. Antoninus, however, summoned his son Commodus to the empire. They moderated harsh laws and burned all fiscal records in the public forum.

Pope Anicetus, under the Emperor Marcus, held office for eleven years, six months, and three days. The papacy was vacant for ten days.

Likewise under Marcus, Pope Pius held office for ten years, [Col. 1033A] four months, and four days. After his death the see was vacant for thirteen days.

Likewise under the same Emperor Marcus, Pope Soter held office for nine years and seven months. There was a vacancy of twenty-one days.

Pope Eleutherus held office for fifteen years, nine months, and three days. After him, under Commodus, the papal see was vacant for ten days.

The Emperor Commodus, in Eleutherus’s time, reigned for thirteen years.

The Emperor Aelius Pertinax, under Eleutherus, was killed within six months. After him Julian ruled for seven months; Severus killed him and himself became emperor.

Division of Times.

[Col. 1033B] Pope Victor held office for eleven years. Under Severus the chair of Peter was vacant for twelve days.

The Emperor Severus, under Pope Victor, reigned for nineteen years. In Britain he fortified part of the island from sea to sea with a wall one hundred and thirty miles long, strengthened with many towers. That Emperor Severus was buried at York.

Division of Times.

Pope Severinus held office for eight years, seven months, and ten days, under Aurelius. There was a vacancy of six days.

Antoninus Aurelius Caracalla, in Severinus’s time, ruled for seven years. He was harsher than his father Severus and was killed by the Persians.

[Col. 1033C] Division of Times.

Pope Callistus I held office for six years, two months, and ten days. There was a vacancy of six days.

The Emperor Alexander, in the time of Pope Callistus I, reigned for twelve years. He defeated Xerxes, the great king of the Persians, in battle.

Division of Times.

Pope Urban I held office for four years, ten months, and twelve days. The see was vacant for thirty days after his death.

Macrinus, in Urban’s time, ruled for one year. His history is not available.

Division of Times.

Pope Pontianus held office for nine years, [Col. 1033D] six months, and two days. There was a vacancy of ten days.

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, in Pontianus’s time, ruled for three years. He died amid sexual immorality and every disgrace, leaving behind an infamous reputation.

Pope Anterus held office for twelve years, one month, and twelve days. There was a vacancy of eight days.

The Emperor Maximus, in Anterus’s time, reigned for three years and persecuted Christians.

Division of Times.

Pope Fabian held office for fourteen years, eleven months, and eleven days.

Gordian, in Fabian’s time, ruled for seven years. This boy was betrayed by his own people and killed in the Parthian war. In that time Origen flourished.

[Col. 1034A] Division of Times.

Pope Cornelius held office for two years, two months, and three days. After him the see was vacant for thirty-one days.

The Emperor Philip, together with his son Philip, was the first Christian emperor. In Pope Cornelius’s time he ruled for seven years. In the fourth year of his reign the thousandth year from the founding of the City was completed, on account of which theatrical games were held at Rome in the Campus Martius for three days and three nights. Decius treacherously killed this Philip and his son Philip, became emperor himself, and persecuted Christians out of hatred for that Philip.

Division of Times.

[Col. 1034B] Pope Lucius I held office for three years, four months, and three days. There was a vacancy of thirty-one days.

The Emperor Decius, in Lucius’s time, ruled for three years and persecuted Christians. This was the seventh persecution.

Division of Times.

Pope Stephen held office for eight years, six months, and two days. There was a vacancy of twelve days.

Gallus together with Volusianus, in the time of Pope Stephen I, ruled for two years and four months. These two emperors were treacherously killed by Aemilianus. Aemilianus himself too was later killed in the fourth month. In that time Pope Cornelius removed the bodies of the saints from the Catacomb and dedicated them.

[Col. 1034C] Division of Times.

Pope Xystus II held office for two years, six months, and fifteen days. There was a vacancy of thirty-five days.

Valerian together with his son Gallienus now ruled for fifteen years. The eighth persecution of Christians was carried out by them. In that time the Germans—that is, the Teutons—ranged through Gaul and devastated Italy. The Gothic people also now ravaged Macedonia, Greece, Pontus, and Asia. The Emperor Valerian was captured and blinded by Sapor, king of the Persians. So long as he lived, he endured this punishment: whenever the king of the Persians mounted his horse, Valerian himself always lifted him onto it with his own [Col. 1034D] back.

Pope Dionysius, under the same Valerian, held office for five years and two months. After him the pontificate was vacant for five days.

Pope Felix, under the same Emperor Valerian, held office for four years, four months, and five days. After him the papal see was vacant for five days.

Division of Times.

Pope Eutychianus held office for ten months and one day, in the time of the Emperor Claudius.

Claudius, in Eutychianus’s time, ruled for one year and nine months. He destroyed with incredible slaughter the Goths who were devastating Macedonia and Illyricum. On this account the senate decreed that a golden shield and a golden spear should be given him in the Capitol.

[Col. 1035A] Division of Times.

Pope Gaius held office for eleven years, four months, and twelve days. The papal see was vacant for six days after him.

Aurelian, in Pope Gaius’s time, ruled for five years and six months. He crushed the Goths with the greatest valour, encircled Rome with stronger walls, and built a temple of the Sun. He stirred up the ninth persecution against Christians. At length he himself was killed.

The Emperor Tacitus likewise ruled for six months in Pope Gaius’s time.

Likewise Florianus, under the same Gaius, ruled for three months.

Probus, under the same Pope Gaius, ruled for six years [Col. 1035B] and four months.

Division of Times.

Pope Marcellinus held office for nine years, five months, and twelve days. There was a vacancy of six days.

The Emperor Carus, together with his sons Carinus and Numerian, in Pope Marcellinus’s time, ruled for three years. After he had defeated the Persians and was beyond the river Tigris with his two sons, he was killed by a thunderbolt.

Pope Marcellus held office for nine years, five months, and twenty-one days. The papal see was vacant for twenty days.

Diocletian and Maximian, in Marcellus’s time, ruled for twenty years. Diocletian took his colleague [Col. 1035C] Maximian into the imperial office and sent him into Africa to defend it against the Quingentiani. Moreover, he selected several Caesars for himself, namely Constantius, Licinius, and Galerius. Diocletian also commanded that he be worshipped as a god, and he was the first to wear gems on clothing and footwear. For earlier kings had used purple alone. This Diocletian in the East and Maximian in the West ordered all Christian churches to be destroyed, books burned, and all Christians killed. This tenth persecution was more savage and more prolonged than all the others. Diocletian laid down the purple at Nicomedia, and Maximian at Milan.

Division of Times.

[Col. 1035D] Pope Eusebius held office for two years and two months. He himself and all the popes named above were martyrs.

Constantius, Galerius, and Licinius, Caesars of Diocletian, lived in the time of Pope Eusebius and governed the Roman Empire.

Division of Times.

Pope Miltiades held office in the papacy for seven years and seven months.

The aforesaid Caesars Valerius, Constantius, and Licinius ruled in Pope Miltiades’s time for two years. Constantius subdued Spain, triumphed over the Alamanni, and, after the death of her father [Col. 1036A] Johel, king of Britain, took as wife the king’s daughter Helena, by whom he begot Constantine. Others, however, maintain that Constantine himself was the illegitimate son of Helena, a tavern-girl, born in the regions of Persia, while his father Constantius was serving as an envoy in Persia to collect public taxes. Constantius the father is said to be buried in England at York.

At the same time Maxentius, son of Maximian, was made emperor at Rome. Constantius, later summoned by the Romans, killed him near the Milvian Bridge; and he himself ruled for thirty years and ten months. He left the kingdom of Britain to his maternal uncle Tacherio. At first he persecuted Christians; later, however, through Pope Sylvester he received [Col. 1036B] sacred baptism.

Pope Sylvester held office for twenty-three years and ten months. There was a vacancy of fifteen days.

This Sylvester became pope in the fourth year of Constantine’s reign and baptized him. But, as the Tripartite History relates and Eusebius of Caesarea testifies in the *Chronicles*, he was afterwards rebaptized by a certain Arian Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, at a country estate called Aquilona.

Constantine, in the time of Popes Sylvester and Martin, ruled for thirty years and ten months. We have discussed him at sufficient length in the body of this book, under the treatment of the emperors.

Pope Marcus held office for two years, eight months, [Col. 1036C] and twenty days. There was a vacancy of fifteen days. This Pope Marcus lived in the time of the Emperor Constantine.

Division of Times.

Pope Julius held office for eleven years, two months, and six days. There was a vacancy of fifteen days.

Constantius, together with Constantine and Constans, ruled in the time of Pope Julius for twenty-four years, five months, and twenty-three days. Constans, having subdued the Gauls and received them into peace, was killed in Spain. Constantine, however, while preparing to make war upon his brother Constantius, was killed near Aquileia. Thus sole rule passed to Constantius; having fallen into the heresy of the Arians and been rebaptized by them, he inflicted a most severe persecution upon the Catholics. With his support, the Arians destroyed all the Catholic bishops by imprisonments and various other tortures. In this persecution Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, Hilary of Poitiers, and Eusebius of Vercelli appeared most steadfast and unconquerable. At that time Basil of Caesarea, Victorinus the rhetorician, and Priscian and Donatus the grammarians flourished.

### Division of Times

Pope Felix, while Pope Liberius was still living and had been sent into exile, was appointed by the heretics and sat for one year, four months, and two days. The see was vacant for thirty-eight days.

When Liberius returned from the exile imposed by the Emperor Constantius after two years and was restored to the papacy, Felix, who had been substituted for him while he was alive, was transferred to another city. Why this same Felix was entered in the catalogue of Catholic apostolic men, I do not know. Ask the Romans, if you please.

### Division of Times

Julian the Apostate ruled in the time of Popes Liberius and Felix for two years and six months. From childhood he had been a Christian and a subdeacon of the Roman Church. But afterward he turned to the worship of idols, became a most wicked apostate, persecuted Christians, and, in hatred of Christ, ordered the Temple at Jerusalem to be rebuilt. A fuller account of Julian’s life and death is contained in the body of this book. In Julian’s time Didymus and Basil, bishop of Caesarea, flourished.

[Col. 1037B] ### Division of Times

Pope Damasus sat for eighteen years, four months, and one day. After him the papal see was vacant for twenty days.

Jovian ruled in the time of Pope Damasus for eight years. He recalled the whole army of Constantius to the Catholic faith.

### Division of Times

Pope Siricius sat for fifteen years and eleven months. The see was not vacant.

Valentinian ruled in the time of Siricius for eleven years.

Valens, son of Valentinian, ruled under the same Pope Siricius for four years.

The Emperor Gratian, together with his brother Valens, ruled under the same pope for six years.

### Division of Times

Pope Anastasius sat for three years, ten months, and twelve days. After him the pontificate was vacant for twenty-one days.

Valentinian II ruled in the time of Pope Anastasius for twelve years.

### Division of Times

Pope Innocent sat for eleven years, two months, and twenty-one days. Then Rome was captured by Alaric, king of the Goths, while the pope himself was staying at Ravenna.

Theodosius ruled for twenty-seven years in the time of Pope Innocent I.

[Col. 1037D] ### Division of Times

Pope Zosimus sat for one year and eleven days. The see was vacant for eleven days.

Arcadius, together with Honorius, Theodosius, and Valentinian, ruled for thirty-two years under the same pope.

### Division of Times

Pope Boniface sat for three years, eight months, and seven days. The see was vacant for nine days.

Honorius and Arcadius ruled in the time of Pope Boniface for twenty-one years.

Pope Celestine sat for seven years, ten months, and seventeen days. The see was vacant for twenty days. He was the first to send to the Scots, who believed in Christ, a bishop named Palladius.

[Col. 1038A] ### Division of Times

Valentinian, together with Marcian, ruled for nine years.

Pope Sixtus, under the same Valentinian, sat for eight years and one month. The see was vacant for twenty-two days.

### Division of Times

Pope Leo sat for eleven years, one month, and thirteen days. The see was vacant for seven days. Then the Fourth Synod of six hundred and thirty Fathers was held under the Emperor Marcian against Eutyches; there it was granted that Mary is *Theotokos*, that is, Mother of God, and it was forbidden to say that there are two persons in Christ. At that time Attila entered Italy; Pope Leo went out to meet him and obtained from him that he should not enter the City. Therefore Attila turned his reins back.

[Col. 1038B] ### Division of Times

Marcian, after Valentinian, ruled under Pope Leo for six years.

### Division of Times

Pope Hilary sat for seven years, three months, and ten days. The see was vacant for ten days.

The Emperor Leo ruled at Constantinople for seven years.

### Division of Times

Pope Simplicius sat for fifteen years, one month, and seven days.

The Emperor Zeno ruled in the time of Pope Simplicius for seventeen years.

Pope Felix sat for eight years, six months, and seven days. The see was vacant for five days. He was under Zeno.

### Division of Times

Pope Gelasius sat for four years, eight months, and eighteen days. The see was vacant for seven days. At this time Genseric, king of the Goths, captured the city of Rome and stripped it of all its goods for fourteen days; but he spared those who fled to the churches, and so departed enriched.

The Emperor Anastasius ruled in the time of Gelasius for seventeen years.

Pope Symmachus sat under Anastasius for nine years and seventeen days.

### Division of Times

Pope Hormisdas sat for nine years and seventeen days. The see was vacant for six days.

[Col. 1038D] Justin the Elder ruled under Hormisdas for seven years.

Pope John sat under Justin for two years, nine months, and sixteen days. The see was vacant for fifty-eight days. He was worn down by imprisonment and hunger at the hands of Theoderic, king of the Goths, and after prolonged suffering was put to death.

Pope Mercurius sat under Justinian.

Pope Boniface sat for two years and twenty-six days. The see was vacant for seventy-six days.

### Division of Times

Pope John II sat under Justinian for two years, four months, and six days. The see was vacant for six days.

[Col. 1039A] Pope Agapetus sat under him for eleven years, ten months, and eleven days. The see was vacant for twenty-seven days.

Pope Silverius sat for one year, five months, and eleven days. The see was vacant for six days.

Pope Vigilius sat for seventeen years, six months, and twenty-one days. The see was vacant for twenty-five days. The Fifth Synod was now held under Justinian, against Theodore.

Pope Fabian sat for one year, five months, and thirteen days.

### Division of Times

Pope Pelagius sat under the Emperor Justin for eleven years, ten months, and twenty-seven days.

[Col. 1039B] Pope Benedict sat under the same Justin for four years and two months. The see was vacant for three months.

Justin ruled for seven years.

Pope John sat under Justin for twelve years, eleven months, and twenty-six days.

### Division of Times

Tiberius ruled for six years.

Pope Benedict sat under Tiberius for four years and two months.

### Division of Times

Maurice ruled for twenty-one years.

Pope Pelagius II sat under Maurice for ten years, two months, and ten days. The see was vacant for seven months.

[Col. 1039C] Pope Gregory sat under Maurice for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. The see was vacant for five months. He converted the English.

### Division of Times

The Emperor Phocas ruled for eight years.

Pope Boniface III sat for nine years and twenty-two days. The see was vacant for thirty-six days. Then the Pantheon was consecrated.

### Division of Times

The Emperor Heraclius, together with his son Constantine, ruled for thirty-six years. Through the same Heraclius the Exaltation of the Holy Cross took place.

Pope Boniface IV sat under Heraclius for five years and ten months. The see was vacant for fourteen days.

[Col. 1039D] Pope Deusdedit sat under Heraclius for three years and one month. The see was vacant for sixty-seven days.

Pope Honorius sat for twelve years, eleven months, and sixteen days. The see was vacant for one year, seven months, and eighteen days.

Pope Severinus sat for two years and four days. The see was vacant for four months and twenty-six days.

Pope John sat for one year, eight months, and nineteen days. The see was vacant for forty-three days.

### Division of Times

The Emperor Constantine, son of Heraclius.

Pope Theodore sat for six years, five months, and eighteen days. The see was vacant for one year and two days.

[Col. 1040A] Pope Martin sat for six years, two months, and twenty-seven days. The see was vacant for one year and twenty days.

Pope Eugenius sat for two years, nine months, and twenty-four days. The see was vacant for two months and one day.

Pope Vitalian sat for fourteen years and six months. The see was vacant for one year and thirteen days.

### Division of Times

Constantine the Younger, emperor.

Deodatus sat for three years, two months, and five days. The see was vacant for eight days.

Pope Donnus sat for one year, five months, and ten days. The see was vacant for two days. He built the place called Paradise before the church of St. Peter.

[Col. 1040B] Agatho sat for two years and four days. The see was vacant for one year, five months, and five days. The Sixth Synod was now held at Constantinople, of one hundred and fifty bishops, under Constantine, the emperor’s great-grandson, against George the patriarch.

Pope Leo sat for ten months and sixteen days. The see was vacant for twelve days.

Pope Benedict sat for two months and twenty days.

Pope John sat for one year and nine days. The see was vacant for two months and eighteen days.

[Col. 1040C] Pope Conon sat for eleven months. The see was vacant for four months and twenty-two days.

### Division of Times

Justinian the Younger, emperor.

Pope Sergius sat for thirteen years and nine months.

Pope Leo sat under Justinian the Younger for two years and nine months.

### Division of Times

Pope John sat for three years, two months, and sixteen days. The see was vacant for one month and thirteen days.

Another Pope John sat for two years and seven months. The see was vacant for eight months.

[Col. 1040D] Pope Sisinnius sat for twenty days. The see was vacant for one month and nineteen days.

### Division of Times

Justinian, emperor.

Pope Constantine sat for seven years and twenty days. The see was vacant for one year and forty days.

The Emperor Philippicus ruled in the time of this Pope Constantine.

### Division of Times

The Emperor Anastasius ruled in the time of Pope Gregory.

Pope Gregory sat under this Anastasius for fifteen years and twenty-two days. The see was vacant for thirty-five days.

[Col. 1041A] ### Division of Times

The Emperor Theodosius. Under him Pope Gregory III sat for ten years, nine months, and twenty-four days. The see was vacant for eight days.

The Emperor Leo, together with his son Constantine, ruled in the time of this Pope Gregory.

### Division of Times

While Constantine ruled together with his son Leo:

Pope Zacharias sat for ten years and eight months.

### Division of Times

Pope Stephen sat for five years and three months. The see was vacant for thirty-five days. In the time of Pope Stephen, Pippin, duke of the Franks, was made king of the Gauls and patrician of the Romans. Childeric, formerly king of the Franks, being idle and useless, was tonsured and made a monk.

[Col. 1041B] Pope Paul sat in the time of King and Patrician Pippin for five years and one month. The see was vacant for one year. In the time of Paul and Pippin, Leo ruled.

### Division of Times

Pope Stephen sat for three years and six months in the time of Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans.

Pope Adrian sat for fourteen years, ten months, and twenty-seven days in the time of Charles, king and patrician.

Pope Leo III sat for twenty years and six months, while Constantine ruled in Greece together with his mother Irene and Charlemagne ruled in Francia. He was the first to receive Charlemagne as emperor and solemnly sang for him the imperial acclamations at Rome. The Seventh Synod of Nicaea was now held concerning images of the saints under Constantine and his mother, the Empress Irene. Charlemagne ruled as emperor, in the time of Pope Leo and thereafter, for forty-six years.

[Col. 1041C] ### Division of Times

The Emperor Louis, son of Charlemagne, ruled after his father together with his son Lothair.

Pope Stephen III sat under Louis and Lothair for seven years.

Pope Paschal sat for six years.

Pope Eugenius sat for six years.

[Col. 1041D] Pope Valentine sat for eleven years under the same emperor.

### Division of Times

Lothair ruling after his father Louis:

Pope Gregory IV sat for fourteen years.

Pope Sergius sat for three years.

Pope Leo sat for eight years and five months under the same Lothair and his son Louis.

Pope Benedict sat under the same ruler for two years.

### Division of Times

The Emperor Louis ruled after his father.

[Col. 1042A] Pope Paul sat under the same Louis for ten years and two months. The see was vacant for one year.

Pope Stephen sat for four years.

Pope Nicholas sat for ten years and one month.

Pope Adrian sat for four years and eleven months.

### Division of Times

Charles II, emperor, ruled after Louis II.

Pope John sat under Charles II for ten years and one month.

### Division of Times

Carloman ruled after Charles II.

Pope Marinus sat under Carloman for one year and three months.

[Col. 1042B] Pope Adrian III sat for one year and three months.

Pope Stephen sat for four years.

### Division of Times

Under the Emperor Arnulf, according to some.

Pope Formosus sat for four years and seven months.

Pope Boniface sat for twelve years.

Pope Stephen sat for one year, one month, and eighteen days.

Pope Romanus sat for four years.

Pope Theodore sat for one year.

Pope John sat for two years.

### Division of Times

[Col. 1042C] From this point onward, according to the opinion of the Romans, we set down those emperors who are said to have ruled in Italy alone. Louis rules in Italy.

Pope Christopher sat under Louis for six months.

Pope Sergius sat under the same Louis for six years and four months.

### Division of Times

While Berengar ruled in Italy, Pope Anastasius sat for one year and one month.

Pope Lando sat for five months under this Berengar.

Pope John sat for four years and two months under Berengar I.

[Col. 1042D] ### Division of Times

While Hugh ruled in Italy:

Pope Leo sat for seven years and fifteen days.

### Division of Times

While Guy ruled in Italy together with his son Lambert:

Pope Stephen sat for two years and one month.

Pope John sat under the same rulers for four years and ten months.

### Division of Times

While Berengar II ruled in Italy, Pope Leo sat for three years and six months.

[Col. 1043A] ### Division of Times

While Lothair ruled in Italy:

Pope Stephen sat for three years and four months.

### Division of Times

While Berengar III ruled in Italy together with his son Albert:

Pope Marinus sat for three years and six months.

### Division of Times

From this time onward the Germans alone begin to rule.

Under Otto I, emperor of the Germans:

Pope Benedict sat for one year and five months.

Pope Leo sat under the same Otto I for one year and three months.

Pope John sat under the same Otto for five years and eleven months.

[Col. 1043B] ### Division of Times

Under Otto II, emperor:

Pope Benedict sat for one year and five months.

Pope Donnus sat for one year and six months.

Pope Boniface sat for one month.

Pope Benedict sat for nine years.

Pope John sat for eight months.

Pope John sat for four months.

### Division of Times

Under Otto III, emperor of the Germans:

Pope John sat for ten years and six months.

Pope Gregory sat for one year and six months.

Pope John sat for ten months.

[Col. 1043C] Pope Silvester sat for four years and five months. He was called Gilbert.

Pope John sat for ten months.

Pope John sat for three years.

Pope Sergius sat for three years.

### Division of Times

Note that there are more kings named Henry than emperors named Henry. Hence when Henry I, emperor, is read of, he is indeed first in reckoning by the empire; but in reckoning among the Henrys he is second, for there was one King Henry before him. Understand the same of the Conrads.

Henry I, emperor, surnamed the Lame, who is reckoned second among the Henrys. In his time Pope Benedict sat for eleven years and eleven months. Pope John sat for six years and nine months.

[Col. 1043D] ### Division of Times

While Conrad I ruled—he is reckoned second among the Conrads—Pope Benedict sat for fourteen years.

Pope Silvester sat under the same Conrad for two months.

Pope Gregory sat under the same ruler for one year and six months.

Pope Clement sat under the same Conrad for nine months.

Pope Damasus, a German, sat for one month.

Pope Leo, a German, sat for five years and five months.

Pope Victor, a German, sat for two years and four months.

Pope Stephen, a German, sat for eight months. All were under this same Conrad II.

[Col. 1044A] ### Division of Times

Henry II, emperor; but, reckoning by the kings named Henry, he must be counted third. For before all the Henrys and before all the Ottos there had been, as we have said, a certain King Henry, but not an emperor, of Saxon stock; he was surnamed the Fowler. Likewise, before all the Conrads there was the first Conrad, king of the Germans, but he was not emperor. In the time of this Emperor Henry II, Pope Benedict sat for ten years.

Pope Nicholas sat for three years, six months, and twenty-five days.

### Division of Times

Henry III, emperor; but, reckoning among the Henrys, he must be counted fourth. In the time of this Henry, Pope Alexander sat for nine years and six months.

[Col. 1044B] Pope Gregory VII sat for fifteen years, one month, and eight days.

Pope Victor sat for four months and seven days.

Pope Urban sat for eleven years, six months, and eighteen days.

### Division of Times

Henry IV, emperor, who in reckoning among the Henrys was counted fifth. This is the Henry who seized Pope Paschal at Rome; and he rejected the ring and staff of bishops belonging to the Roman Church.

Pope Paschal sat under him for nineteen years.

Pope Gelasius sat for one year and six days.

Pope Calixtus sat for five years, six months, and thirteen days.

[Col. 1044C] Pope Honorius sat for five years, six months, and twenty-eight days.

### Division of Times

Lothair II, emperor, reigned for twelve years; he was a Saxon.

Pope Innocent sat for thirteen years, six months, and fourteen days.

Pope Celestine sat for five months and eleven days.

Pope Lucius sat for eleven months.

### Division of Times

Conrad, king of the Germans and Romans, ruled for fourteen years.

Pope Eugenius sat in the time of Conrad III for eight years, five months, and ten days.

[Col. 1044D] ### Division of Times

Frederick I, emperor, now rules in his thirty-seventh year.

Pope Anastasius sat in Frederick’s time for one year and five days, while the aforesaid Eugenius was still alive.

Frederick II rules.

Pope Adrian sat for four years and nine months. He anointed Frederick as emperor.

Pope Alexander sat for twenty-two years while Frederick ruled as emperor and his son Henry VI ruled jointly with his father.

Pope Lucius sat for three years while Frederick ruled as emperor and his son Henry ruled.

Pope Urban III likewise sat while Frederick ruled as emperor and his son Henry ruled; he now happily occupies the see. Amen.

**In the Year of the Lord 1179: Peter Comestor**

[Col. 1045]

## NOTICE  
*(Oudin, Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Writers and Writings, II, 1526)*

[Col. 1045A] Peter Comestor, canon and dean of Blessed Mary’s at Troyes, is wrongly said by some to have been the brother of Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, Master of the *Sentences*, and of Gratian, as he is called, prince of canonists, both Italians. Gratian was an Etruscan from the town of Chiusi, and Peter Lombard was a Lombard, native of Novara; Peter Comestor, however, was a Frenchman. Yet where in France he was born remains uncertain. Some write that he was a Parisian, relying upon the authority of Aegidius in the *Carolinus*, where he says:

> I could also set forth him who was snatched from our midst,  
> Whose titles his successor, the Poitevin, now holds with the honour of second place, etc.

Here Aegidius speaks of Peter of Poitiers, who succeeded Hilduin, Comestor’s successor, in the chancellorship of Paris and the chair of theology; and he counts Comestor among the Parisians. By contrast, Henry of Ghent calls him a man of Troyes: “Peter, called Manducator [‘the Eater’], born at Troyes, seeking the benefit of students in theology, abridged all the histories of the Old and New Testaments into one work, which they call the *Scholastic History*.” Nor was this name given to him merely because he was dean at Troyes, but because he was himself born in that city.

Whatever the case, he was a man of great reputation, especially in theological matters. Cardinal Peter of St. Chrysogonus commended him to Alexander III in these words: “We do not think you are ignorant of the learning and uprightness of Master Peter Manducator, dean of Troyes.” Likewise Vincent of Beauvais, at the year 1151, commemorates Peter Lombard and Comestor as distinguished masters; and especially says of the latter: “About the same time I judge that Master Peter Comestor flourished, who composed the *Scholastic History*, briefly and profitably tracing the history of Holy Scripture and prudently explaining difficulties in very many places. Moreover, he inserted in suitable places certain incidental matters from the history of Josephus the Jew and from some Gentile authors.”

[Col. 1045C] He also published certain other little works, and elegantly composed the following verses in praise of the Blessed Virgin:

> If it were possible that the dust of sand and the waves,  
> The drops of the waves, dew, gems, lilies, flames,  
> The heavens, the dwellers in heaven, snow, hail, both sexes,  
> The wings of winds, every kind of bird and beast,  
> The branches and foliage of forests, and the feathers of birds,  
> Dew, grass, stars, fishes, serpents, and ears of grain,  
> And stones, mountains, valleys, earth, and dragons  
> Were all tongues, they could never express  
> What the Virgin Queen Mary is, or how great she is;  
> Neither letter nor age could set forth what your mercy is.

These are Vincent’s notable remarks concerning Comestor, who was chancellor of the University of Paris from 1164 until his death. He wrote four books of *Ecclesiastical History*; and a work, or collection, of sermons on the solemnities of feasts throughout the yearly cycle.
