He presented the *Scholastic History* to William called “of the White Hands,” archbishop of Sens, the most generous patron of all learned men, who afterward became cardinal and archbishop of Reims.

Concerning his works, Otto of St. Blasien, a contemporary writer, says:

> He compiled the most useful book of *Scholastic History*, beginning from the start of Genesis. He continued through the Pentateuch, the book of Joshua, Judges, and Ruth; and, incorporating Chronicles into the book of Kings, he embraces Tobit with the final portions of Isaiah. Having described the captivity together with the death of Gedaliah and the visions of Daniel, he carefully proceeds through Ezra, Esther, Judith, and the book of Maccabees. Thereafter, following Josephus, he carried the history from John Hyrcanus to the reign of Herod and the birth of Christ; and, having included the Gospel, concludes the whole in the Acts of the Apostles. He elucidates every obscurity, makes uncertainties certain, and introduces diverse forms of ecclesiastical tradition. Besides this, he composed a book of sermons with remarkable subtlety, in which, along with other useful matters, he impresses morality upon the minds of mortals in a wonderful way.

[Col. 1046B] The fourth age of the *History of the University of Paris*, p. 374, speaks very fully of his sermons, maintaining that he delivered many of them in the public schools of Paris, according to the practice of those times. These sermons are by no means arranged in the order in which they are written today, but occur in a disorderly and confused fashion, as they issued from the pulpit at various times.

I add that 114 sermons of this Peter are found in manuscript, in folio, in the library of Longpont, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Soissons. They begin with these words: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline thine ear,” etc.; “We read of three hearers of the heavenly word,” etc. It should be observed, however, that the sermons published by John Buseus of the Society of Jesus under the name of Peter of Blois, and found in the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, thirteenth century, part or volume II, p. 837, are not truly by Peter of Blois but by Peter Comestor, as Peter de Goussainville rightly noted. He therefore omitted these sermons from that edition of Peter of Blois, thus restoring them to their legitimate author.

The sermons of Peter Comestor in manuscript codices are sometimes more numerous, sometimes fewer; they neither begin in the same way nor proceed in the same order. Some occur in manuscript codex 381 of the library of St-Germain-des-Prés, beginning: “Be instructed, you who judge the earth. Do not suppose that I have taken an opening unrelated to yourselves; for, unless you wish to conceal it, you are those who judge the earth,” etc. They are found among the printed sermons in the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, under the false name of Peter of Blois.

[Col. 1047A] Others are in the library of St Victor of the Regular Canons of St Augustine, letter QQ. 19, a codex of excellent quality. They are entitled *Sermons of Master Peter Comestor* and begin: “Today, dearest brethren, the season of the Lord’s Advent begins, from whose holiness of season,” etc. Others likewise occur there, letter QQ. 22: *Sermons of Master Peter Comestor*. They begin: “First sermon on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin. Adorn thy bridal chamber, O Zion,” etc.; “We read that where there is a greater gift of knowledge, there is a graver danger of fault,” etc.

For, as can be seen, they proceed in one way and another in different manuscript codices: for example, at Cambridge in Pembroke Hall, MSS 48, nos. 1 and 3; 76, no. 1. Sermons are likewise found in the Séguier Library of France, MSS 4389, 4390, 4391; in the Colbert Library at Paris, MSS 3690 and 4028; and elsewhere, as three times in the library of Marmoutier at Tours, MSS D.2, D.3, D.4; in the library of Conques, letter M.1; and in the library of the monastery of Golden Valley, of the Cistercian Order in the duchy of Luxembourg, MS 69.

Peter Comestor’s sermons have a distinctive concluding formula, by which they may easily be distinguished from all others: they always end, by their author’s special preference, with these or equivalent words: “By the granting of Jesus Christ our Lord, our King, our Judge, who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire”; or alternatively: “May Jesus Christ himself deign to grant this, our Lord, our King, our Judge, who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.” Those who wish may test whether I have spoken truly in the sermons found under the name of Peter of Blois in the twelfth century, part I, of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, Cologne edition of 1618, which truly belong to Peter Comestor. For, of the fifty-one read there, one alone does not end in this manner of Comestor’s; and this is undoubtedly due to the error of a copyist.

[Col. 1047C] There is great dispute concerning the year in which Comestor died. Vincent of Beauvais, with others, maintains and writes that he died in 1160; but this is entirely false. Robert of Auxerre, however, relates in his *Chronicle* that Master Peter Comestor died in 1178, though some dissent, maintaining that he lived until 1198. This latter view is held by the Regular Canons of St Victor outside the walls of Paris, among whom he was buried, on the authority of their own domestic records, which are nevertheless late and erroneous. The recent Jesuit Labbe also agrees with them in his historical dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

But, as Caesar Egassius Bulæus rightly observes in his history of the fourth age of the University of Paris, fol. 443, who would believe that Robert erred by nearly twenty years in his reckoning? Especially as he knew Peter Comestor at least by reputation, if not by sight, and flourished in the same period. Add that Peter Comestor, chancellor of the University of Paris, died while holding the chancellorship; therefore he died before 1198, since in 1196 Peter of Poitiers, his successor after Hilduin in the chancellorship, subscribed a certain document, as the fourth age of the said *History of the University*, p. 767, records in its Catalogue of Distinguished Academics. Finally, Hilduin must be placed between Peter Comestor and Peter of Poitiers. Hence the canon Robert of St Marian at Auxerre rightly concludes that Peter Comestor’s death should be assigned to 1178.

But however that may be, Robert writes of him under the aforesaid year: “Peter Comestor, a most famous doctor, died. By a wisely framed will, he distributed all that he possessed wholly among the poor and churches.” On his tomb among the Victorians is inscribed this epitaph:

> I was Peter, whom a stone covers, and I was called Comestor.  
> Now I am eaten. Living, I taught, nor do I cease to teach  
> Though dead, so that whoever sees me reduced to ashes may say:  
> “What we are, this man was; what he is, we shall one day be.”

[Col. 1048B] Very many writers speak of Peter Comestor: Henry of Ghent in his book *On Illustrious Men*; Aubertus Miraeus in his scholia to that book in the *Ecclesiastical Library*; Robert Bellarmine and Philip Labbe, each in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, to whom we add much here; Antonio Possevino in the *Sacred Apparatus*, vol. II, p. 247, under “Peter Comestor,” whom he says flourished in 1160; and, returning to the chronology here established, we retract what we wrote concerning him in the *Supplement to On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 462, where we had placed him in 1190; Gerard John Vossius, book II of *On Latin Historians*, chapter 53; the fourth age of the *History of the University of Paris*, under the year 1151, p. 261, and under 1169, p. 374, and finally under the year 1178, p. 445, when it judges him to have died, as also in the *Catalogue of Distinguished Academics*, p. 764; William Cave in the *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1170, p. 682, where, following the common error, he thinks that Comestor died in 1198.

[Col. 1047]

## SECOND NOTICE  
*(Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin, vol. V, p. 404)*

[Col. 1047D] Peter, surnamed Comestor or Manducator—called *Mangeur* (“Eater”) by the French, whence the name—if we believe Trithemius, because, by very frequently citing authorities from Scripture in his sermons and little works, he had, as it were, eaten them into the belly of his memory.

> **[Note: Col. 1047]** Chapter 380, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Labbe thinks this ridiculous, vol. II, p. 199. Yet we sometimes see that things which are ridiculous are also quite true.

A native of Troyes, formerly priest and dean of the church of his native city, then chancellor of Paris, he finally died in retirement among the Canons of St Victor at Paris, in the year 1178, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October]. There this epitaph was set up for him, reported by Germain Brice in his *Description of Paris*, vol. II, p. 188, and by many others:

[Col. 1048D] “I was Peter,” etc. (See above.) [lacuna] He wrote the *Scholastic History* for William, archbishop of Sens from 1169 to 1175: that is, a kind of abridgment of the historical books of the Old and New Testaments, approved for use in schools, with various materials added from time to time besides exposition—not only from Josephus and authorities of approved reliability, but also from apocryphal and pagan writers. See John Rainolds, *Censura of Apocryphal Books*, vol. I, pp. 477 and 1239 ff. It appeared at Reutlingen in 1473, in large folio, and at Strasbourg in 1483 and 1502; at [Col. 1049A] Basle in 1486, folio; at Paris in 1513, quarto; at Haguenau in 1519, folio; at Lyons in 1526, quarto, and in 1543, octavo. In the old editions there is no trace of books—whether sixteen, as Labbe and Cave say, or twenty, as Trithemius and Simler say—but only the histories of the historical books are divided: thus the history of Genesis into 115 chapters, the history of Exodus into 78 chapters, and so forth. Likewise, in the New Testament, the Gospel history into 198 chapters and the history of the Acts of the Apostles into 127.

Most recently this work was reprinted at Venice in 1728 and dedicated to the most reverend and most holy Fathers of the council then being held at Benevento. There is also a French translation [Note: [Col. 1049B] Richard Simon, vol. II, *Critical History of the New Testament*, p. 320: “At that time there was nothing greater or more esteemed for Holy Scripture than Peter Comestor, who was translated into several languages of Europe. The Bible was read [Col. 1050B] only in the manner in which it appeared in this compiler, and with his glosses. This practice lasted a long time in France.”] printed two hundred years ago, without date or place, with woodcut illustrations, in folio, in two volumes, dedicated to Charles VIII by its translator Guiars de Moulins. See Richard Simon’s *Critical History of the New Testament*, book II, pp. 19 and 320, where he notes that the same translation, in a more recent revision and interpolation, appeared at Paris in 1545.

It was rendered in Saxon rhyming verse [Col. 1049B] by command of Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia, in the thirteenth century, as far as the time of Samuel; it survives in manuscript and is mentioned in the catalogue of the Pauline Library at Leipzig, p. 163. Sander also mentions it in the manuscript *Bibliotheca Belgica*, p. 285: a *Scholastic History* rendered in German rhyming verse by Jacob van Maerlant, about the year 1271. Finally, Walter Hunte, an English Carmelite, reduced it to an epitome. See Vossius, pp. 434 and 635.

[Col. 1050A] James le Long testifies in his *Bibliotheca exegetica*, p. 683, that a manuscript commentary on the Epistles of Paul exists in the Sorbonne Library at Paris.

From the brief treatise *On Penance*, in manuscript in the Lambeth Library in England, and from a volume of Sermons in the same library, which he calls very beautiful, Henry Wharton cites certain passages in the supplement to Ussher’s *Dogmatic History*, pp. 407 and 353.

Concerning Comestor’s sermons—whether those read under the name of Peter of Blois [Note: [Col. 1050B] *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. XXIV, Lyons edition, p. 1385.], or others, including the 114 preserved in the library of Longpont, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Soissons, and in other libraries of France and England—see Oudin, vol. II, p. 1527 ff.; Du Boulay, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. IV, p. 374 ff.; *Nova Litteraria Maris Baltici*, 1678, p. 246.

Sixty-eight sermons were recently sold at Copenhagen, in the Rostgaard Library, p. 461.

Labbe notes, in vol. II of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 200, that a sermon on the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin [Col. 1050B] was published at Antwerp in 1536 from a manuscript codex of an English library.

To offer the reader a specimen also of Comestor’s vein, here is a ten-line poem in praise of the Blessed Virgin Mary, preserved by Vincent of Beauvais, *Speculum historiale* XXIX.1, and Antoninus of Florence, *Summa historica*, title 18, chapter 8, vol. III, p. 77.

“If it were possible,” etc.; see the earlier notice, col. 1045.

[Col. 1049]

# THE SCHOLASTIC HISTORY OF THE MOST LEARNED MASTER PETER COMESTOR

An outstanding work, briefly comprehending a large part of Holy Scripture, which had been widely dispersed both in the continuous text and in glosses; now once again brought to light, purged of many errors, abbreviations removed, and carefully corrected; dedicated to the Most Reverend Father Master Friar Emmanuel Navarro, Benedictine, doctor of theology in the University of Salamanca, holder of the evening chair, abbot of the College of St Vincent, and preacher to His Catholic Majesty.

(Madrid, from the press of Antonio González de Reyes, 1699, quarto. With privilege.)

## Dedicatory Epistle

To the Most Reverend Father Master Friar Emmanuel Navarro, Benedictine, doctor of theology in the University of Salamanca, holder of the evening chair, abbot of the College of St Vincent, and preacher to His Catholic Majesty, etc.

The *Scholastic History*, most reverend Father and most wise Master—an undertaking compiled by Master Peter Comestor more than [Col. 1051] five hundred years ago—lay hidden, so to speak, not merely from the unlearned but from very many scholars, who were wearied by its printing and nauseated by its abbreviations. It now sees the light in a new printing and shines forth dedicated to your name. Accept this welcome gift, a token of affection and gratitude, and embrace with all your strength so outstanding a work. It needs not merely a herald, but a patron—and such a patron as you, who are distinguished by integrity of character and by the renown of learning and wisdom: “Who could be more reverent toward this work than you, or a kinder judge of it?” [Note: [Col. 1051] Pliny, book VI, letter 17.] This was the consideration which led me to resolve especially to dedicate it to you.

But I spare your praises—or rather, I confess myself unequal to them—especially because I have learned that “silence is sometimes no less an act of eloquence than speech,” [Note: [Col. 1051] The same, book VII, letter 6.] and know that virtue,

> Desiring no external aid, needing no praise,  
> Courageous in its own resources,

[Note: [Col. 1052] Claudian, *Panegyric on Theodoric*.]

May you live long and happily, to the glory of our Spain, an ornament of the Benedictine family, an honor of the University of Salamanca, and a refuge of those devoted to you; and, after Nestor’s years, may you endure forever in eternity.

Thus your own, Francisco Sacedón, prays from his heart.

## [Epistle]

Censure issued by commission of the Supreme Council of Castile, by the Reverend Father Master Friar Juan de Argüelles, of the Order of Hermits of St Augustine, general definitor and procurator-general of the Peruvian province, invested with the master’s degree at the University of Lima, theological examiner in the sacred tribunal of the nunciature at Madrid, bishop-elect of Panama.

[Col. 1051A] By command of the royal and supreme Council of Castile, I have diligently examined this volume of Peter Comestor, of extraordinary learning and elegance; it requires no approval other than the author’s most celebrated name, spread throughout the world. Indeed, the place which Gratian has happily attained among jurists, and Peter Lombard among theologians, Peter Comestor—most closely united to both as their brother in blood, intellect, and vigor—clearly claims among historians. Each is a standard-bearer in his own class; professors of every science venerate one or another of them as their master.

This triple offspring of Jupiter was prefigured in the prophecy of the Cumaean Sibyl:

> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.

Or, better and more clearly, it arose in the three Graces born of Eurynome, whose bounty spreads widely through all the pathways of the earth, advancing whatever everywhere shines forth as praiseworthy and outstanding in every kind. Hesiod sang thus:

> Eurynome, daughter of Ocean, bore them three fair-cheeked Graces.

[Col. 1052A] In a not dissimilar way, whatever shines in the field of letters with elegance, clarity, and truth is found most abundantly in the divine bounty of each of the three. And, to come individually to the matter at hand, this author has been received by all with the highest reverence. From his mouth discourse bursts forth more violently than a torrent, more weightily than a river, more deeply than the Ocean, more clearly than water. With subtlety he treats humble matters, with moderation middling matters, and with magnificence and splendor the highest matters, surpassing the limits of admiration, eloquently and copiously. Therefore he is deservedly extolled by all and raised to the summit of authority; and accordingly he is judged worthy to be entrusted anew to the press for the ornament and advancement of the republic of letters. This is my opinion, subject to better judgment. In this royal convent of St Philip, 2 May, in the year of the Lord 1698.

Master Friar Juan de Argüelles.

## Preface to the Reader, on the Author, the Work, and the Printing

[Col. 1051]

Peter Comestor, a Frenchman by birth, was a priest of the Church of Troyes. He was called *Comestor*, or “Eater,” because he seemed to have devoured all learning, or because, by very frequently citing authorities of Scripture in his sermons and small works, he had, as it were, eaten them into the belly of memory [Note: [Col. 1051A] Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers.*], especially in the *Scholastic History*; hence he was called, by excellence, Master of Scholastic History.

The popular belief that Gratian, compiler of the *Decretum*, and Peter Lombard, Master of the *Sentences*, were his brothers has gained currency. But this opinion does not please Genebrard, Bellarmine, or Stephen Menochius, since their native places oppose it: Comestor was a Frenchman from Troyes; Gratian a Tuscan from Chiusi; and Lombard a Lombard from Novara [Note: [Col. 1051A] Genebrard, *Chronology*, book IV, year 1163; Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Peter Lombard; Menochius, [Col. 1052A] *Nelle stuore* [probably *Storie*], century 12, chapter 3, *On Writers*, under Comestor.].

The *Scholastic History* briefly embraces, from the beginning of the world to the deaths of Saints Peter and Paul, the historical books of both Testaments, with singular skill and remarkable learning. It adds various readings, interpretations, and sayings of the Fathers, interweaving many secular histories, many traditions, and diverse opinions.

The eminent Bellarmine adds that it not infrequently intermingles uncertain stories. But the reader will see that in traditions and weakly established accounts the author approves nothing; rather, he rejects very much, adding in nearly all such cases the words: “they hand down,” “the Hebrews relate,” “others say,” thus withholding belief from their authors.

It is evident that the additions scattered throughout the *History* are not Comestor’s, or at least not all of them. We have transferred these to the ends of the chapters, so that they may not delay the reader.

[Col. 1053] We have omitted to mark the words of Holy Scripture in a different typeface, because, since the author’s purpose is historical, he sometimes contracts them and sometimes expands them, so that they do not in every respect regularly conform to the wording of our Vulgate.

How many and how great the corrections we have made will be apparent to anyone comparing the old edition with the present printing. Yet we do not deny that matters still remain to be corrected; let the negligence of the typesetters be our excuse. Human labor readily goes astray, and God’s works alone are perfect.

Walter Hunt, an Englishman of the Carmelite Order and doctor of Oxford, said to have flourished in 1478, is said to have compressed an abridgment of this work into a single book under the title *Abbreviations of Peter Comestor*.

Peter Comestor died at Paris in 1178, or thereabouts; for his death is recorded in that very year by the Monk of St Marian in his Chronicle of Auxerre, in these words [Note: [Col. 1053] Possevino, *Bibliotheca*, and Saussay, *On the Mystical Writers of Gaul*, p. 714.]:

> Peter Comestor, a most famous doctor, died. By a wisely arranged will, he distributed absolutely everything he possessed to the poor and to churches.

He was buried in the church of St Denis in the city of Paris itself, with an epitaph inscribed beforehand by himself before the day of his death; we give it below.

“I was Peter,” etc. It appears above, col. 1048.

We have not judged it superfluous, kindly reader, to inform you of these matters. Farewell, and enjoy

# THE SCHOLASTIC HISTORY OF THE MOST LEARNED MASTER PETER COMESTOR

## Epistolary Prologue

To the reverend Father and his lord, WILLIAM, by the grace of God Archbishop of Sens, PETER, servant of Christ and priest of Troyes, wishes a good life and a blessed end.

The cause of undertaking this labor was the urgent request of my companions. As they used to read the history of Holy Scripture, diffusely presented in the continuous text and glosses, they compelled me to undertake a work that they might consult for the pursuit of historical truth—though it was very brief and unexplained. In this work my mind so ruled my pen that I did not depart from the sayings of the Fathers, although novelty is attractive and soothes the ears.

Beginning, therefore, with Moses’ cosmography, I have conducted the little stream of history down to the Ascension of the Savior, leaving the sea of mysteries to those more skilled, among whom it is permissible both to pursue old matters and to forge new ones. I have also inserted certain incidental accounts from pagan histories, according to chronological fitness: like a stream which, while filling the channels it finds beside its bed, nevertheless does not cease to flow onward. Yet because a rough style needs the file, illustrious Father, I have reserved the file for you, so that, God willing, your correction may give this work brilliance and your authority permanence. God blessed above all things.

# THE SCHOLASTIC HISTORY OF THE DISCIPLINE OF THEOLOGY BEGINS

[Col. 1053]

It belongs to imperial majesty to have three chambers in its palace: an audience hall, or council chamber, in which it decrees laws; a dining room, in which it distributes food; and a bedchamber, in which it rests. In this manner our Emperor, who commands the winds and the sea, has this world as his audience hall, where all things are ordered at his command. Hence that saying of Isaiah: “I fill heaven and earth” (Isa. XXV). In this respect he is called Lord. Hence: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. XXII).

He has the soul of the righteous as his bedchamber, because it is his delight to rest there and to be with the children of men (Prov. VIII). In this respect he is called bridegroom, and each soul bride (Hos. II). He has Holy Scripture as his dining room, in which he so intoxicates his own that he makes them sober. Hence: “We walked in the house of God with one accord” (Ps. LIV), being of one mind in Holy Scripture. In this respect he is called the master of the household.

This dining room has three parts: foundation, wall, and roof. History is the foundation, and it has three kinds: annual, monthly, and ephemeral history. [Note: [Col. 1055] Addition 1. An ephemeral is a fever lasting only for a day, so named from the worm which dies on the same day on which it is born. Annual history is an event accomplished in the course of a year; monthly history is a history occurring within one month—that is, some notable event occurring within one month. Ephemeral history is something suddenly done, that is, within one day or part of a month. By the same analogy, an *ephemera* is a fish which dies on the same day on which it is born.]

Allegory is the wall resting upon it, which signifies one event through another event. Tropology is the roof laid upon the summit, which indicates through what has happened what ought to be done by us. [Note: [Col. 1055] Addition 2. We shall take the beginning of our discourse from the foundation—indeed, from the beginning of the foundation itself—with the help of him who is the ruler and beginning of all things.] The first is plainer, the second more acute, the third sweeter. Allegory is sometimes drawn from a person, as Isaac signifies Christ; David too sometimes signifies Christ in this manner. Sometimes it is drawn from a thing which is not a person, as the slain ram signifies suffering humanity, and a stone hardness of heart. For a person is an individual substance of rational nature.

[Col. 1055] Sometimes it is drawn from a number, as: “Seven women shall take hold of one man,” etc. (Isa. IV), that is, the seven gifts of the graces of the Holy Spirit. Sometimes from a place, as the mountain on which Christ taught signifies the eminence of virtues (Matt. V); sometimes from a time, as: “May your flight not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. XXIV), that is, in the cooling of charity; sometimes from an action, as David’s killing of Goliath (1 Kings [1 Samuel] XVII), that is, Christ’s killing of the devil.

Tropology is discourse directed toward conversion, concerning the morals of the soul; and it moves more strongly than allegory, which concerns the Church militant; anagogy concerns the Church triumphant and the Trinity of the Lord.

# [BIBLICAL HISTORY]

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF GENESIS

[Col. 1055]

## Chapter I. On the creation of the empyrean and the four elements

[Col. 1055A]

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was the beginning,” in whom and through whom the Father created the world (John I). “World” is used in four ways. Sometimes the empyrean heaven is called a world because of its purity; sometimes the sensible world, which the Greeks call *pan* and the Latins *omne* (“all”), because the philosopher did not know the empyrean; sometimes the sublunary region alone, because it alone contains animals known to us—of which it is said, “The prince of this world shall be cast out” (John XII); sometimes man is called a world, because in himself he represents the image of the whole world. Hence man is called by the Lord “every creature,” and the Greek calls man *microcosmus*, that is, the lesser world.

God created the empyrean, the sensible world, and [Col. 1055B] the sublunary region—that is, he made them from nothing; but he created man, that is, he formed him. Concerning the creation of those three, therefore, the lawgiver says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I), that is, container and contained: namely, the empyrean heaven and angelic nature. By “earth,” however, he means the matter of all bodies, namely the four elements, that is, the sensible world consisting of them. Some understand “heaven” as the higher regions of the sensible world, and “earth” as the lower and tangible regions.

Where we have “God,” the Hebrew has *elohim*, which can be both singular and plural: “God” or “gods,” because the three persons are one God, the Creator. When Moses said “created,” he refuted three errors: those of Plato, [Col. 1055C] Aristotle, and Epicurus. Plato said that three things existed from eternity: God, Ideas [Note: [Col. 1055C] Ideas: in Greek, exemplars or forms.], *hyle* [Note: [Col. 1056C] *Hyle* is prime matter and is interpreted as “wood” or “forest.”], and that at the beginning of time the world had been made from *hyle*. Aristotle posited two things: the world and its maker, who works from two principles, matter and form, without beginning and works without end. Epicurus posited two things: void and atoms; and at the beginning nature compacted certain atoms into earth, others into water, others into [Col. 1056A] air, and others into fire. Moses, however, proclaimed God alone to be eternal and the world to have been created without pre-existing matter.

It was created “in the beginning,” that is, in the Son; and “in the beginning” must be repeated thus: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”—namely, at the beginning of time. For the world and time are coeval. Yet, as God alone is eternal, so the world is everlasting—that is, eternally continuous, eternal in time—and the angels are likewise everlasting. Or: in the beginning of all creatures he created heaven and earth, that is, he made these primordial creatures, and made them simultaneously. But what was made simultaneously could not be spoken of simultaneously. For although heaven is named here before earth, it is nevertheless written: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens [Col. 1056B] are the works of your hands” (Ps. CI).

Having anticipated this creation of the world, Scripture unfolds it under the works of six days, indicating three things: creation, ordering, and adornment. On the first day, creation and a certain ordering; on the second and third, ordering; and on the remaining three, adornment.

## Chapter II. On the primal confusion of the world

“But the earth was empty and void” (Gen. I): that is, the structure of the world was still useless, unfruitful, and devoid of its adornment. “And darkness was upon the face of the deep.” The same structure which he had called earth he calls “the deep” because of its confusion and obscurity. The Greek therefore called it *chaos*. Because it was said, “darkness was,” some taught [Col. 1056C] that darkness was eternal, since it already existed when the world was made. Others, mocking the God of the Old Testament, say that he created darkness before light. But darkness is nothing other than the absence of light.

Yet a certain obscurity of air was created by God and called darkness. Hence it is said in the catalogue of creatures: “Bless the Lord, light and darkness” (Dan. III).—“And the Spirit of the Lord,” [Col. 1057A] that is, the Holy Spirit, the Lord, or the will of the Lord, “was borne over the waters,” as the will of an artisan who has before his eyes all the material of a house to be made is borne over it while he determines what he will make from what.

He calls the aforesaid structure “waters,” as material pliant for working out of it. Its names are varied in this way lest, if it were designated solely by the name of one element, it should be thought more suited to that element. The Hebrew has, in place of “was borne over,” “brooded,” or, in the Syriac language, “cherished,” as a bird does its eggs. In this, too, the beginning of all governance of the nascent world is indicated. Plato misunderstood this passage, thinking that it was spoken about the soul of the world. But it was spoken of the creating Holy Spirit, concerning whom we read: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created” (Ps. [Col. 1057B] CIII).

## Chapter III. On the work of the first day

“And God said, ‘Let there be light.’ And light was made” (Gen. I): that is, he begot the Word in whom there was that light should be made—so easily as if someone were to say it with a word. [Note: [Col. 1057D] Addition 1. As the Word is the Son, so speaking is begetting and being begotten.]

He calls light a certain luminous cloud, illuminating the upper parts of the world, though with a faint brightness, as commonly happens at dawn, and this cloud circling very near the sun. By its presence it illuminates in turn the upper hemisphere and the lower. [Note: [Col. 1057D] Addition 2. As soon as I open my eyes, my gaze immediately casts itself upon the sun in the East; it could not do this unless it flew across the many spaces of air between me and [Col. 1058A] the sun. If I wished to explain that instantaneous flight, I would often add “first” and “afterwards.” Thus my gaze first passes through the adjacent air; afterwards through the air above the Alps; afterwards through the air above other lands as far as the ocean; afterwards through the air above the ocean; and finally it touches the sun.]

By “let there be” is understood the presence or foreknowledge of light in God before it was made; its perfected essence was in act when it came forth into existence. “And God saw the light, that it was good”: that is, what had pleased him in presence or foreknowledge to be made, pleased him in its essence to remain. [Col. 1057C] Or, tropologically, “he saw” means “he caused to be seen.”

“And he divided the light and the darkness.” Here ordering begins. Yet he says something concerning creation, as though with light he created darkness: that is, the shadow produced by bodies obstructing light; and he divided those created things by spatial distance and quality, so that the different hemispheres might never simultaneously but always alternately claim them from opposite directions. The division of angels is also understood here: those who stood are called light, those who fell darkness.

He called light “day,” from the Greek *dia*, which is “brightness,” just as *lux* (“light”) is so called because it *luit*, that is, washes away darkness. He called darkness “night,” from *nocendo*, “harming,” because it harms the eyes so that they cannot see; just as darkness is so called because it holds the eyes so that they cannot see. Yet, as day is derived from Greek *dia*, [Col. 1057D] so night is from *nyctim*. “And evening came, and afterwards morning came.” Thus one natural day was completed. For light was first created with heaven and earth. As it gradually set, evening of the first ordinary day came; and, when the same light passed beneath the earth and came to the east, morning came—that is, the night ended and the second day began. Thus, with the day’s light preceding and the following night concluded, one day existed. The light itself displayed the divided regions but did not divide them.

## Chapter IV. On the work of the second day

[Col. 1058A]

On the second day God ordered the upper regions of the sensible world. For as soon as the empyrean heaven was made, it was immediately ordered and adorned—that is, filled with holy angels. On that day, therefore, God made the firmament in the midst of the waters (Gen. I): that is, a certain outer surface of the world, made of frozen waters, solidified like crystal and translucent, containing within itself the other sensible things, after the image [Col. 1058B] of the shell in an egg; and in it the stars are fixed.

It is called a “firmament” not merely because of its solidity but because it is the firm and impassable boundary of the waters above it. It is also called heaven because it conceals—that is, covers—all invisible things. When “the firmament of heaven” is read, it is a hendiadys: that is, the firmament which is heaven, as when one says “a creature of salt.” Because of its vaulted shape it is called in Greek *ouranon*, that is, “palace.” Or it is called *coelum* as though *casa helios*, “the house of the sun,” because the sun placed below it illuminates it. Yet the philosopher understood this revolving vault as the highest region of fire. When fire has nowhere to rise, it revolves, as is clear in an oven; so also fire revolves around the outer parts of the world. This is the [Col. 1058C] starry or ethereal heaven.

There is also a third heaven below, called the aerial heaven, concerning which it is said: “The birds of heaven ate it” (Mach. XIII). Some suppose that there is a fourth heaven above the empyrean, because Lucifer, while in the empyrean, is read to have said: “I shall ascend into heaven,” etc. (Isa. XVI). In this way, they say that Christ as man is there above the angels who are in the empyrean.

Certainly the firmament divides the waters beneath it from the waters above it, of which the Psalms say: “You roof its upper regions with waters” (Ps. CCIII). These waters are frozen like the firmament itself, like crystal, so that they cannot be melted by fire, or they are vaporous after the manner of mist. Why they are there, God knows, unless it be that some suppose that dew [Col. 1058D] descends from them in summer.

The statement, “Let there be a firmament,” followed by “God made the firmament,” and thirdly “the firmament was made,” is not superfluous. For just as, in building a house, the house is first made in the artisan’s knowledge, then materially when wood and stones are smoothed, and then essentially when the smoothed materials are arranged into the structure of a house, so “let there be” refers to God’s presence or foreknowledge; “he made,” to the work in matter; and “it was made,” to the work in essence. The work in matter was done on the first day, and the work in essence on the second.

Although the work of this day was good, like the others, it is nevertheless not written of it, “God saw that it was good.” For the Hebrews hand down that on this day the angel Satanel was made the devil [Note: [Col. 1059A] Addition 1. He is called Satanel, and also Lucifer. This is found in the *Life of Blessed Clement* and perhaps, since it resembles other angelic names, such as Raphael, it is so called. He was thus named before his fall; or perhaps after his fall: Satan, as adversary; El, that is, to God.], that is, Lucifer. Those Hebrews seem to be agreed with by persons who are accustomed to sing [Col. 1059A] a Mass of the Angels on the second weekday, as though in praise of the angels who stood.

But the saints teach that this was done as a sign, because two is a disreputable number in theology, since it is the first to depart from unity. God, however, is unity and detests division and discord (Prov. VI). We may nevertheless say that the work of the third day still belongs, as it were, to the work of the second day, as will later appear. Therefore it is not commended until the third day, as though after its completion.

## Chapter V. On the work of the third day

[Col. 1059B]

On the third day God gathered the waters under the firmament into one place (Gen. I). Although they occupy many places, they are said to be gathered into one place because all are contained in the bowels of the earth. It may be that the waters which, in vaporous form, occupied all the space of the air, having been solidified occupied a small place; or that the earth subsided a little, so as to enclose them as in a womb. Thus dry land appeared, which, while concealed beneath the waters, was properly called *humus*; but when it appeared dry, it was called *terra*, because it is worn by the feet of living creatures. Or, surrounded by the three elements, it is called *solum*, because solid. It is called *tellus* because it bears human labors.

[Col. 1059C] He called the gatherings of waters “seas,” according to the idiom of the Hebrews, who call any gatherings of waters seas. When the work concerning the waters was completed, it is added: “And God saw that it was good.” He added another work to it when he said, “Let the earth bring forth.” This is to be understood not only of the act of bringing forth but also of the capacity, as though it were capable of bringing forth. For from the earth he brought forth green grass bearing seed and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit according to their kinds.

It is clear that the earth did not bring forth its plants gradually over periods of time, as it now does, but immediately in green maturity, so that the herbs were laden with seeds and the trees with fruits. Note that it says “green.” Some say that the world was made in spring, because that season is green and fruitful. [Col. 1059D] Others, because they read “a tree producing fruit,” and find added “herb having seed,” say that its making occurred in August under Leo. But the Church teaches that it was made in March.

Observe that it first says “bearing seed” and adds “each having seed,” because *sementis* is properly said while it is still in the seed-bearing plant. [Note: [Col. 1059D] Addition 1. That is, in the herb itself producing the seed, [Col. 1060A] because *sementinum* is called, as it were, “holding seed”; *sementis*, as it were, “seed held” or “retained.”] *Semen*, however, is said when it is sown; and *seminium*, or *sementum*, when it has been sown. Yet *sementis* is otherwise distinguished as applying to grain and trees, *semen* to animals, and *seminium* to the beginning of any thing.

Nor should it trouble us that, in the ordering of the elements, the air seems not to have been ordered because it was not named. It was ordered when the air, freed from the waters, received the form known to us.

## Chapter VI. On the work of the fourth day

[Col. 1060A]

On the fourth day he began to adorn what he had arranged, with those things which move in fitting motions beneath the whole universe. For plants, because they cling to the earth, belong, as it were, more to the ordering of the earth; and, just as he had begun the ordering from the higher things, so he began the adornment from the higher things. For on that same day he made the luminaries: the sun, the moon, and the stars. The sun is so called because it shines alone—that is, with none together with it; the moon, *luminum una*, “one of the lights,” that is, the first, as “one of the days” or “one of the Sabbaths” is said (Luke v and xxiv). The sun and moon are called the two great lights in two respects and by comparison with two things: not only because of the magnitude of their light, but also of their bodies; and not only in comparison with the stars, but also in themselves. For the sun is said to be eight times greater than the earth.

> [Note: Col. 1061C, Addition 1. This is inferred from the fact that it appears equally large to everyone everywhere on earth; this could scarcely happen unless it were greater than the earth.]

The moon too is said to be greater than the earth. He willed that the moon and the stars should illumine the night, lest night, without light, should be excessively unseemly, and so that those working by night—such as sailors and travellers—might have the comfort of light. There are also certain little birds which cannot endure sunlight and feed almost entirely at night.

> [Note: Col. 1061C, Addition 2. Especially such birds occur in the sandy deserts of Ethiopia, where a slight gust of wind levels the tracks left by travellers.]

Nor is the sun superfluous, although a bright cloud took its place (Matt. xvii), since that cloud had a weak and insufficient light and perhaps illuminated only the upper regions, just as a star does not now illuminate more. Concerning that aforesaid bright cloud, however, it is handed down that either it returned to the matter from which it had been made—as did the star which appeared to the Magi (Matt. ii), and the dove in which the Holy Spirit was seen (Matt. iii)—or that it always accompanies the sun; or that the solar body was made from it.

Nor did he will these things to exist merely for beauty and for the use of light, but also that they might serve for signs, seasons, days, and years: namely, that they might be signs of fair and stormy weather. Or, that from them should arise the twelve greater signs and certain smaller signs, more numerous than these, which are called signs or constellations. This is so both because antiquity marked or observed them with great diligence, and because people still mark and observe them for the designation of times. Nor should it be said, as the astrologers, or *genethliaci*, dream, that they were set as signs of our events and actions, or that they indicate and govern the condition of our life—a claim which they teach through certain experiments that they call *apotelesmata* [astrological prognostications]. For this must not be believed about heaven except by those alienated from the Father who is in heaven.

What follows, “for seasons,” should not be understood to mean that seasons then first began through them; seasons began with the world. Rather, through them there are four divisions of the seasons. The sun, descending toward Capricorn, makes the winter solstice; ascending toward Cancer, the summer solstice. Between the two, at equal distance from each, it makes the equinoxes. Or there is here a hendiadys: “for signs and seasons,” that is, signs of the seasons.

“For days” is said in the plural because “day” is used in several senses: of the natural day, namely a space of twenty-four hours, and of the customary day. “Day” is also used for a time undetermined and unknown to us, as in: “On that day the mountains shall drip sweetness” (Amos ix). “For years” too is said in the plural because “year” likewise has several meanings. I do not say this merely because different nations certainly have different divisions of greater and lesser years, and the planets have their own years. We say it also according to the usage of the Church. There is a lunar year of 354 days; a solar year consisting of 365 days and a quarter, that is, six hours; a leap year consisting of 366 days; and an embolismic year, consisting of 380 days or more and containing thirteen lunations. A year is also called from *ana*, meaning “around,” because it turns back upon itself. Hence the ancients, before the use of letters,

[Col. 1061B]

represented the year under the image of a serpent whose tail was turned back into its mouth.

Therefore, when the luminaries had been made, God placed them so that they might shine in the firmament of heaven, illuminate the earth—but not continually—and divide light from darkness. That the moon was made at the full is inferred from another translation, which reads: “And the lesser light at the beginning of the night.” For at the beginning of the night the moon rises only when it is *panselenos*, that is, round. It is called from Greek *pan*, “all” in Latin, and *selēnos*, “moon,” or *mēnē*, “moon”—what we call the full moon. From this it is inferred that the sun was made in the morning in the east, and, when evening came, the moon was made at the beginning of the night, likewise in the east. Some, however, hold that they were made simultaneously in the morning: the sun in the east and

[Col. 1061C]

the moon in the west; and that, when the sun set, the moon went back beneath the earth to the east at the beginning of the night.

## Chapter VII. On the work of the fifth day

On the fifth day God adorned the air and the water, giving flying creatures to the air and swimming creatures to the waters; and both arose from the waters (Gen. i). For the transition of water into air, by rarefaction, and of air into water, by condensation, is easy. Moses called fish creeping things because with a certain impetus they propel their whole bodies, like serpents; they are not borne upon feet, like beasts.

Observe that, from the statement, “He created the flying creature of heaven above the earth,” Plato erred. Having gone down into Egypt, he read the books of Moses and thought Moses meant that birds were an adornment only of the air around the earth, while the adornment of the higher air consisted in good demons and evil demons.

> [Note: Col. 1062B, Addition 1. Since good angels may more truly be called demons than evil angels, nevertheless, in mockery of their promise—“You shall be as gods” (Gen. iii)—this name was given to them.]

But this is not so. Good demons, as has been said, are in the empyrean; evil ones, however, were cast down into this darksome air as punishment, not as its adornment. For God did not spare the angels that sinned (II Pet. ii).—“God created,” that is, fashioned, the great sea-creatures. *Cete* is an indeclinable neuter noun, though *cetus, ceti* is also declined. “And every living and moving soul”

[Col. 1062A]

which the waters had produced. The souls of fish and birds are called movable in comparison with the soul of man. For they move from being to non-being; the human soul does not, since it is perpetual—or perhaps because they do not have souls, but nevertheless have vegetative spirits, since this is extinguished together with them.

> [Note: Col. 1062B, Addition 2. Augustine seems to hold that fish have souls. For he says that they have memory. He says that there is a spring in the region of Bulla full of fish; when people walk above it, the fish swim in groups, go and return with them, and stand still with those who stand still, waiting for something to be thrown to them, because they have become accustomed to this.]

He called the animal itself “soul,” that is, a living thing. Hence the Greeks also divide animals into *zōa* and *psychēia zōa*: *zōa* means living brute creatures, while *psychēia* means ensouled creatures, from *psychē*, “rational soul.” Yet a creature is also called movable when it was created in such a way as to move from life to death. Man was not so created, for he was created not to die if he so willed. But these creatures were made either to become food for others or to fail through old age. God blessed them: “Increase and multiply.”

## Chapter VIII. On the work of the sixth day

[Col. 1062B]

On the sixth day God adorned the earth. For the earth produced three kinds of animals: cattle, creeping things, and beasts (Gen. i). Since God knew that through sin man would fall

[Col. 1062C]

into the punishment of labour, he gave him cattle as a remedy for labour, as helps, for work or for food. Creeping things and beasts, however, are for his exercise.

There are three kinds of creeping things. There are drawing creatures, such as worms, which draw themselves along with their mouths; serpentine creatures, such as snakes, which propel themselves by the force of their ribs; and creatures that crawl on feet, such as lizards and frogs. Beasts are so called as though *vastiae*, from laying waste—that is, from harming and raging.

A question is raised about certain tiny living creatures which are accustomed to arise either from corpses or from moisture: whether they arose at that time. There are six kinds of these. Some have their being from exhalations, such as gnats; worms that arise before the water-clock; gnats from wine; butterflies from

[Col. 1062D]

water. Some arise from the corruption of moisture, such as worms in cisterns; some from corpses, such as bees from young bulls; beetles, hornets, and large flies that buzz in flight arise from horses; some from decaying wood, such as woodworms; some from the decay of herbs, such as caterpillars from vegetables; and some from the corruption of waves, such as weevils from beans. It is said of these that those born without corruption—such as those arising from exhalations—were made then; but those arising from corruptions arose after sin, from things that had become corrupt.

A question is also raised about harmful living creatures: whether they were created harmful, or whether they were at first gentle and later made harmful to man. It is said that before man’s sin they were gentle, but after sin they became harmful

[Col. 1063A]

to man for three reasons: for man’s punishment, correction, and instruction. Man is punished when he is harmed by them or fears being harmed, for fear is a very great punishment. He is corrected by them when he knows that these things have happened to him because of his sin. He is instructed by admiring the works of God, admiring the works of ants more than the burdens of camels; or, when he sees that these very small creatures can harm him, he remembers his frailty and is humbled.

But someone might say that certain animals harm others, which are neither punished, corrected, nor instructed thereby. Yet through these things and in them man is instructed by example. They were also created in order to become food for others. But if it is again said that they even rage against dead human beings: man is instructed in this too, not to shrink from any kind of death,

[Col. 1063B]

because, by whatever passages he goes, not a hair of his head shall perish (Luke xxii).

In this way a question is commonly raised about unfruitful herbs and trees: whether they too arose in those days, since Scripture mentions only seed-bearing herbs and fruit-bearing trees, which now exist. It may be said that those now unfruitful bore some fruit before sin; after sin they arise more for man’s toil than for his advantage. Or they arose for man’s sake and after sin, because it was afterwards said to man: “Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for you” (Gen. iii). Or whatever clings to the earth produces fruit, that is, some manifest or hidden usefulness.

Because fish and birds were told, “Increase and multiply,” this is to be understood also of these, though it was not expressly said. For this is the common purpose of their creation.

## Chapter IX. On the creation of man

Then the creation of man is added in this manner: “Let us make man,” etc. (Gen. i). The Father speaks to the Son and the Holy Spirit. Or it is, as it were, the common utterance of the three persons: “Let us make,” and “our.” Man was made in the image of God with respect to the soul.

> [Note: Col. 1064B, Addition 1. That is, with respect to essence and reason, he was made in the image; with respect to virtues, in the likeness of God.]

The image of God is the soul in its essence and reason, because it was made spirit and rational, like God. The likeness is in virtues, because it is good, just, and wise. “Man passes away with an image” (Ps. xxxviii), because even a sinful man retains that image, but he is often deprived of the likeness. “Male”

[Col. 1063D]

“and female he created them.” This concerns the body; yet he is said to have created them because of the soul.

> [Note: Col. 1064B, Addition 2. Lest someone think that he had made man only spirit, and thus without a body. *Andros* is interpreted “man,” *geos* “woman,” or *gama*, whence *bigamus*, “twice-married.”]

He says “them” in the plural, lest we should think that *androgei*—that is, hermaphrodites—were made. Nevertheless, with respect to his body man was in some fashion made in the image of God, as:

> He gave man a lofty face, etc.  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I.85)

so that he might behold and imitate God and heavenly things. Hence, when a certain philosopher was asked for what purpose he had been made, he replied: “To contemplate heaven and the divinities of heaven.”

God gave man power to preside over the other living creatures. Thus man’s dignity is indicated in three respects. First, because he was not only made according to his kind, as were the aforementioned creatures, but also because he is the image

[Col. 1064A]

of God. Secondly, because he was made with deliberation: in the other works, indeed, “he spoke and they were made” (Ps. xxxii), but in this case the persons, as though deliberating among themselves, said, “Let us make.” Thirdly, because man was established as lord of the animals, so that they might serve him—whom God knew would become mortal—for food, clothing, and assistance in labour.

Before sin, God gave only herbs and the fruit of trees as food to men and animals. This is inferred from the fact that before sin the earth produced nothing harmful or barren. Note that man lost dominion over the greatest creatures, such as lions, so that he might know that he had lost it; and he lost it even over the least, such as flies, so that he might know his own lowliness. Over the intermediate creatures he retains dominion, for comfort and so that he may know that he had possessed it also in other creatures.

And God blessed them thus.

## Chapter X. On the institution of marriage

“Increase and multiply” (Gen. i). Since this could not take place without their union, it is clear that God instituted the marriage of man and woman. This refutes certain heretics who say that intercourse cannot occur without sin. If it is asked why food was given to man before sin, when he was immortal,

[Col. 1064C]

we reply that the immortality in which he was created had to be sustained by food. It was not such as the immortality to come, which will not need food. The former was the ability not to die; the latter will be the inability to die.

“And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good”: each thing separately was good. But in their totality all things were very good, just as an eye is more beautiful in an animal than when separated from it. Or all things were very good, that is, the whole assemblage of good things was excellent; for although some things in it have now in themselves been turned to disgrace, they are useful to others. God himself, however, is the highest good.

But regarding man, unlike the other things, he did not say, “And God saw that it was good,” because he knew that man would soon fall; or because man was not yet complete until woman should be made from him. Hence it is afterwards read: “It is not good for man to be alone” (Gen. ii).

## Chapter XI. On the rest and sanctification of the Sabbath

“Thus the heavens and the earth were completed” (Gen. ii). Here is the conclusion of the works: because they were created, ordered, and adorned, they were therefore completed. They were made in the number six, the first perfect number encountered in counting, because, when its constituent parts are added together, it produces the same sum—a property which among the numbers of units you will find only in this number. A number of units is called one beginning with one and continuing to ten. Nor among tens does this occur except in twenty-eight.

“God completed on the seventh day the work which he had made.” Another translation reads “on the sixth,” and then there is no difficulty. But the Hebrew truth reads “on the seventh,” and therefore the question is raised: if “to complete” means to do some final part of a work, how can what follows be true: “God rested on the seventh day,” etc.?

> [Note: Col. 1065C, Addition 1. By parts of a number we mean those of which each can be assigned what fraction it is of that number. Although six consists of one and five, and of two and four, one cannot say what fraction of it either a fourth or a fifth is.]

It is true that he made the seventh day and also blessed it, and afterwards rested. Or “he completed” means “he showed it to be complete,” since he made nothing new on it, and then rested from new kinds of works. For afterwards he made nothing whose matter he had not then made, as in the case of bodies; or whose likeness he had not then made, as in the case of souls. He is not said to have rested as though weary, but because he ceased. Thus Isaiah says that the seraphim had no rest, saying, “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. vi), that is, they did not cease. Or he rested from work, or in his works: that is, he has no need of his works, and the statement is, as it were, negative. Or he rested from work in himself, that is,

[Col. 1065B]

in the changeability of his works he appeared unchangeable.

> Remaining stable, he sets all things in motion.  
> (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*)

The phrase “from all the work which he had accomplished” indicates that there was a work which he had not yet done and from which he has not yet rested. For he had performed three works: he created, ordered, and adorned. He does not cease to perform the fourth work, propagation. He will perform the fifth: “he will gird himself, and passing by, will minister” (Luke xii), where rest will chiefly be found.

“And he blessed the seventh day,” that is, he sanctified it: he willed it to be holy and celebrated. For it is always said that among certain nations the Sabbath was observed even before the Law. In the Law he also called its observance sanctification: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. xx).

## Epilogue

“These are the generations of heaven and earth” (Gen. ii). Some end the works of the six days here; some at “Adam knew his wife” (Gen. iv); others at “This is the book of the generation of Adam” (Gen. v). Leaving aside what is uncertain, let us attend to the text.

Since it had spoken briefly of the creation of man and woman together, though they were not in fact made together, it repeats certain matters in order to explain what it had compressed. “Generations” may be understood actively, that is, as God’s operations; or passively, as things generated.

Nor should we pass over the statement that he made every shrub before it arose in the earth, and every herb before it sprouted, although above it said that a shrub, as soon as it was made, was immediately mature and bore fruit, and that herb arose bearing seed. To this it is said that there were two modes of divine operation, as has been stated: the material and the essential. Therefore, he made them materially before they arose and sprouted essentially.

Or otherwise, as the following text indicates when it says: “For the Lord had not caused it to rain upon the earth.” He indeed then made them perfect and essentially before they arose and sprouted,

[Col. 1066A]

as now they come gradually to growth and maturity through the benefit of poured-out dew and the application of human labour. For then a spring watered the earth, as the Nile waters Egypt (Deut. xi; Isa. xxiii), by turns in different regions; just as it is said that the Jordan, before the overthrow, watered the whole Pentapolis in turn. That is, just as Augustine says of certain springs that by a wonderful alternation they water an entire region, lest, if we say that at that time all the earth was watered simultaneously by a spring, we should call it a flood. Or because the text there reads “a spring,” not “one spring,” it implies a multitude, as in “the locust came” (Exod. x).

## Chapter XII. On the creation of the soul of the first-formed man

“Therefore the Lord God formed man from the clay of the earth” (Gen. ii). Here he first calls God “Lord,” because then he first properly had a servant, namely one who laboured (Wis. x). After the recapitulation, he treats more fully of the formation of the two human beings, first of the man. Since man has two parts, he treats of each. The statement “he formed man from the clay of the earth” concerns the flesh; “he breathed,” etc., concerns the soul. It is as though he said: He made the body from earth, the soul from nothing.

Another translation reads “he breathed into” or “breathed,” which is not inappropriate of God, as some thought, though he has neither throat nor breath. For God “breathed,” that is, he made a spirit. Likewise, “he breathed into” means that he immediately made the soul. Hence in Isaiah: “I have made every breath” (Isa. lvii). The words “into his face” are a synecdoche, the whole being understood from a part. For he gave life to the whole

[Col. 1066C]

man. Yet he named only the face as the more worthy part, because it is capable of the senses.

He also calls this same soul the “breath of life,” because through it man breathes and lives. Afterwards he calls him “a living soul in himself,” that is, living in perpetuity of life, not movable like the soul of a beast. Plato did not soundly understand this passage when he said that God created souls but angels formed the body, as in: “Gods of gods, whose maker and father I am,” etc.

The assertion of some that the soul was made from the divine essence cannot stand, because then it could in no way sin. Others distinguish between the breath of life and the soul, saying that the breath of life is a spirit which they also assert was then given to man for prophecy, when he said: “This now is bone of my bones.” Others make a different distinction, calling “breath” a certain bodily spirit in the body of an animal, which also produces the five senses in it. This spirit is gradually extinguished; and while an animal is dying, that spirit is still felt in one part of the body when it has been extinguished in another.

Man was made in mature manhood, mortal and immortal—that is, able to die and able not to die—and the soul was infused into the body after it had first been formed. But it is asked whether, when it was infused into the body itself, it was created there, or whether it was created outside the body and was naturally given the will to be embodied. Whatever happened in the case of that soul, it is said of souls created afterwards that they are created in their bodies when they are infused.

## Chapter XIII. On paradise and its trees

[Col. 1067A]

“Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning.” Someone might, as it were, ask: Did man remain in the place where he was made, namely in the field of Damascus? No. Where, then, was he transferred? Into paradise, which God had planted on the third day—that is, furnished with plants, planted with herbs and trees—from the beginning of creation, namely when dry land appeared and he caused the earth to germinate; or “from the beginning” means from the first region of the world. Hence another translation reads, “a paradise in Eden toward the east.” *Eden* is Hebrew and is translated in Latin as “delights.” Therefore “a paradise of delight” is the same as “a paradise in Eden,” that is, in delights. But “from the beginning” is the same as “toward the east.”

It is a most pleasant place, separated from our inhabited zone by a long expanse of land and sea, and so elevated that it reaches to the lunar sphere. Hence the waters of the flood did not reach it. Paradise is also the empyrean heaven, and is called spiritual because it is the region of spirits. Spiritually, paradise also means the blessed life or the Church.

And God produced in paradise, from the ground, various trees by the sight of which man might delight and by eating of which he might be sustained. “He produced” means that he led them far upward into height; or “he produced” means that he brought them forth for man. In the midst of them, as more worthy, he placed the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

The tree of life was named from its effect, which it had by nature: if eaten often, it strengthened man in perpetual soundness, so that he should decline for the worse or toward decay through no illness, old age, or anxiety. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was named from what followed its eating. For man did not previously know what evil was, because he had not yet experienced it. We call health and soundness good; illness and weakness evil. Man had not yet felt these. He knew them indeed by knowledge, since the other contrary is known from one of the contraries, but not through experience: as a physician, while healthy, knows diseases, but knows them more fully when he is ill, because he both knows and feels them. Thus a delicately reared child is said not to know what evil is; rather, he does not yet know how great good or evil is. Or evil means disobedience,

[Col. 1067D]

and good obedience, because after eating he knew how great was the good of obedience and how great the evil of disobedience.

Plato, thinking that it could not apply to trees that there should be a tree of life and a tree of the knowledge of good and evil, therefore thought both statements were said of man, because man lives and knows good and evil. He said that man himself was called a tree, that is, bodily, in distinction from spirits, that is, angels, who also live and know good and evil. He further handed down that the tree was placed in the middle because man is, as it were, midway between the Creator set above him and sensible things set beneath him. He said that the creation of that man differed from the creation of all other human beings through those two added words, “of life” and “of the knowledge of good and evil.”

For just as in the Samian figure—that is, the Pythagorean figure, which came from the island of Samos, for this figure was invented by Pythagoras—there is first an unbroken trunk and afterwards, at the top, a forked way, so man now in his earliest ages, as it were, merely lives, not using the powers given for understanding. But when he reaches years of discernment, he then distinguishes good from evil, and only then are his actions good or evil. But Adam was not made thus. Rather, with life there was given to him knowledge of good and evil. It is as though he said: Man was made bodily, subject to God, set over living creatures; and at the same time he lived and knew good and evil.

## Chapter XIV. On the spring of paradise and its four rivers

“And a spring, or river, went out to water”

[Col. 1068B]

“paradise,” that is, the trees of paradise (Gen. ii). “Spring” may mean the abyss, that is, the womb of all waters; or springs, by syllepsis, the singular being used for the plural. “To water” is used to mean “to supply moisture.” For the surrounding earth is said to be moistened by rivers through *tracones*, that is, underground passages, or through channels fourteen or sixteen stadia long.

That spring is divided into four rivers. One is called Phison, which was named Ganges after Gangarus, king of India. According to Isidore, *Phison* means “a multitude,” because it receives ten rivers; or “a change of mouth,” because it is changed from the appearance it has in paradise. It also changes in three ways according to different places: in colour, because it is clear in one place, dark in another, and muddy in another; in volume, because it is small in one place and broad in another; and in sensation, because it is cold in one place and warm in another. This river surrounds the land of Hevilath, that is, India, and carries golden sands.

Another is called Gehon, or Gihon, or Igion; it is also the Nile, and means “a cleft of the earth,” or “earthy,” because it is muddy. This surrounds Ethiopia. The other two are called by their original names, Tigris and Euphrates. The tiger is a very swift animal, and therefore that river was named Tigris from its swiftness. It flows toward the Assyrians. Josephus says that the Tigris is called Diglat, meaning “sharp” or “narrow.” Euphrates means fruitful or fertile. Moses was silent about the regions through which it passes, as though they were known, because it is in Chaldaea, from which Abraham had come.

These four rivers, as we have said,

[Col. 1068D]

flow from the same spring and divide; then some of them mingle with one another and divide again. They are also often swallowed up by the earth and emerge again in many places. Hence various accounts are read concerning their sources. The Ganges too is said to rise in the regions of Mount Caucasus, the Nile not far from Atlas, and the Tigris and Euphrates in Armenia.

## Chapter XV. On the command and prohibition concerning food

Therefore God took man from the place of his formation into paradise, namely the earthly paradise, in order that he might work there (Gen. ii). Yet this was not labouring from necessity, but working with delight and refreshment; and thus God would keep him, namely man. Or both clauses refer to man: namely, that man should keep paradise and work it, as has been said. Some manuscripts do not have *illum* (“him”) but *illud* (“it”); then the sense is “and he should keep it,” that is, man should consider his own work, so that what he did on the earth through cultivation, he should observe in himself through discipline: as the earth obeyed him, so he himself should obey his Creator.

And he commanded him, saying, etc. In order that man might know himself to be under a Lord, he received a command from the Lord. Every command consists in two things, command and prohibition; and therefore the Lord used both. He commanded: “From every tree of paradise eat.” He forbade: “From the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat.” The command was given to the man so that it might also pass through the man to the woman; or perhaps this is anticipation, because, once the woman had been made, it was given to both together.

He adds the penalty if man should despise it:

[Col. 1069B]

“On whatever day you eat, you shall die by the death,” namely the death of the soul, and you shall incur the necessity of death. Hence another translation reads more plainly:

> [Note: Col. 1069B. On the various translations we speak once for all. Before the incarnation of the Lord, in the 341st year, in the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus, the Seventy interpreters flourished. After the Lord’s ascension, in the 124th year, Aquila, a Jew who became a Christian, the first translator from Hebrew into Greek, flourished under Hadrian’s reign; then, fifty-four years later, under Commodus, Theodotion; then, thirty years later, under Severus, Symmachus; then, eight years later, the fifth edition was discovered at Jerusalem. Because its author is unknown, it is called the Vulgate. Origen’s edition too is called the common edition because we use it, as it were, commonly. Then, twenty-eight years later, under Alexander, Origen corrected the Seventy by means of the asterisk and obelus; afterwards he translated without these signs. All these translated from Hebrew into Greek; some translated from Greek into Latin. Many in the early Church, with a slight knowledge of both languages, translated the text from Greek into Latin. Finally Jerome translated from Hebrew into Latin, and his edition is now preserved everywhere among us. *Periarchon* means “On First Principles.” It is the book in which Origen says that Christ still suffers in the air for demons, just as he suffered on earth for human beings, on the authority of: “You hate nothing that you have made” (Wis. xi).]

“You shall be mortal.” The Septuagint put it in the plural: “On whatever day you eat, you shall die by the death.” Therefore some believe it was said to both, and that this is anticipated here. This command, moreover, was given through some subject creature, just as commands are given to us through prophets and angels.

## Chapter XVI. Principally on the giving of names to living creatures, and on the formation of woman

[Col. 1069D]

God also said: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper for the begetting of children, who may be like him.” For like things naturally arise from like. But lest the formation of woman should seem superfluous to Adam, who might think that among the animals there was one like himself, God therefore brought to Adam all the living creatures of earth and air. The creatures of the water are to be understood among these as well. Take the whole from a part.

Or all are earthly because even those formed from water have something earthly in themselves; or rather, fish were only later recognized and named by human beings. This is evident because they bear the same names as land animals, having been found similar to them. He caused them all to come together by that nod by which he created all things; or perhaps it was done through angels.

He brought them for two purposes: that man might give them names, through which they might know him to be set over them; and that Adam might know that none of them was like him. Adam gave them names in Hebrew, the only language at the beginning. This is inferred from the fact that the names read until the division of languages are Hebrew. When no one like himself had been found, God cast Adam into a stupor—not sleep, but ecstasy—in which he is believed to have been present at the heavenly court.

[Col. 1070B]

Hence, on awakening, he prophesied concerning the union of Christ and the Church; and there he learned of the coming flood and the judgment by fire, and afterwards made these known to his children.

## Chapter XVII. On Adam’s sleep and the formation of woman from his rib

When he had fallen asleep, the Lord took one of his ribs—both flesh and bone—and by the ministry of angels built it into a woman, making flesh from flesh and bones from bone, and set her before Adam. He said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” This adverb “now” led the Jews into error, so that they say another woman had first been made, of whom it is said: “Male and female he created them” (Gen. i), and that this one was now a second woman. It is as though Adam said:

[Col. 1070C]

“The former woman was made from the clay of the earth with me, but this one now from my flesh.”

Josephus says that the woman was formed outside paradise and transferred into paradise with the man, saying: “God brought Adam and his wife into this garden, commanding them to care for the planting.” From Adam’s two wives they invent innumerable, or endless, genealogies; but they appear to be refuted by the text itself, in which speech is always in the singular concerning his wife.

Observe that, when speaking of the formation of woman, the text speaks only of the body. Hence some wished the soul to be passed over in silence so that it might be understood that the woman’s soul was propagated from the man’s soul, as flesh from flesh. Augustine too seems uncertain what should be thought about the soul: whether it comes by propagation or from nothing. But the very fact that the soul is passed over in silence is rather against them. For if the woman’s soul came by propagation, it was made differently from the man’s soul, which came from nothing. And if it was made differently, this ought not to have been passed over, lest it be thought to have been made as we had already heard concerning the man’s soul. Thus by silence it indicates that it should not be thought to have been made otherwise than we had learned before.

## Chapter XVIII. On the names of woman
Adam gave his wife a name as her lord, and said: “She shall be called *virago*” (Gen. 2), that is, “made from man”; and the name was taken from the name of man, just as her material had been taken from his material. The derivation also exists in Hebrew. For “man” is called *ish* [Col. 1071A], from which she is named *ishah*, as *virago* from *vir* [man]. This was the proper name of that woman; now it is common to all women. Its shortened form is *virgo* [virgin]. Women are called virgins so long as they remain in the integrity of their birth; afterward, once that integrity is broken, they are called women. Similarly, Adam was the proper name of that man, but is now common; and Adam means “red” or “red earth,” because, according to Josephus, he was made from earth mixed with red earth.

> [Note: Col. 1071B, Addition 1. The earth was properly still virgin soil, because it had not yet been corrupted by human work or stained with blood.]

For such is virgin earth: true, or red—that is, animated, because the seat of the soul is in the blood; or red in respect of what it was to become, namely bloody, that is, sinful (Gen. 3). Sin is often denoted by the name of blood, as in: “A garment clotted with blood” (Isa. 9), and “Blood has touched blood” [Col. 1071B] (Hos. 4). He also gave her another name, Eve, namely after the sin; it means “life,” because she was to be the mother of all the living.
