Yet, since it is not read here that he gave this name, but below, after the curse, perhaps, lamenting human misery, he called her Eve, as though alluding to the wailing of little children. For a newly born boy cries out “a,” while a girl cries “e,” as if to say: all who are born from Eve will say “e” or “a.”

## CHAPTER XIX. Adam’s Prophecy

Having bestowed the name, Adam immediately prophesied, saying: “For this reason,” namely because she was taken from the side of the man, [Col. 1071C] “a man shall often leave father and mother for his wife and shall cleave to his wife” (Gen. 2), as to a little portion of himself. Or, pointing to the wife, he says “for this reason,” that is, because of this woman, a man shall leave, etc. This happens daily among men, because they leave their parents in bodily cohabitation, or spiritually, because zeal for one’s wife is greater than children’s love for their parents—not, I say, parents’ love for their children. For moisture rises from the trunk to the branches, but does not return.

> [Note: Col. 1071D, Addition 1. This should especially be understood as “he shall always leave,” that is, he shall not be joined to them in marriage. Here two persons, in the Law eleven persons, and in the Gospel more persons, are excluded from marriage. This means: because of this—that is, marriage—a man shall leave father and mother.]

Therefore he did not say that, because of this, parents will leave their children. “And the two shall be one flesh”: that is, both shall be united in one fleshly act. Or, the two shall be one flesh in begetting children. For a child’s flesh is co-created not from one blood but from two bloods. Or, although they are two persons, [Col. 1071D] they will nevertheless be one flesh in marriage; in other respects they are two, because neither has power over his or her own flesh.

## CHAPTER XX. Their State of Innocence before Sin

“Both were naked, and they were not ashamed” (Gen. 2). They thought that nothing needed to be covered, because they had experienced nothing needing restraint, just as we do not blush if someone sees our hands, head, or feet. For the disorderly movement of the members itself makes them shameful parts. [Col. 1072A] Thus little children, if their private parts are seen, do not blush, because by the benefit of their age they have not yet experienced the shameful movement. This movement is shameful and disorderly because it does not occur without sin—except rarely, when excused by the hope of offspring. Yet even when it can be excused from sin, it cannot lack shame. Hence, although holy Zacharias knew holy Elizabeth in order to beget the Lord’s holy forerunner, he nevertheless did not wish to be seen (Luke 1). Some have therefore thought that here God commanded each of them to abstain from the fruit, although the matter has been anticipated.

## CHAPTER XXI. The Suggestion of the Serpent or the Devil

“The serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth” (Gen. 3), both naturally and accidentally. Accidentally, because it was filled with the devil. Lucifer, cast down from the [Col. 1072B] paradise of spirits, envied man because he was in the paradise of bodies. He knew that, if he caused man to transgress, man too would be cast out. Fearing discovery by the man, he undertook to bend the woman—less wary and less steadfast—toward vice.

He did this through a serpent, because at that time the serpent stood upright like a man, for in the curse it was cast down; and even now, as they relate, the *phareas* walks erect. As Bede says, he also chose a particular kind of serpent having a virgin-like face, because like delights in like. He moved its tongue to speak, though it did not know what it was saying, just as he speaks through fanatics and the possessed, who likewise do not know. And he said: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?”—that is, that you should eat from a tree, but not from every tree. He asks in order to find from [Col. 1072C] her answer an opportunity to say what he had come to say.

And so it happened. For when the woman, as if doubting, said, “Lest perhaps we die,” because one who doubts is easily bent to either side, he confidently declared: “You certainly shall not die. Rather, God, unwilling that you should become like him in knowledge, and knowing that when you eat from this tree you will be like gods, knowing good and evil, prohibited it out of envy.” And the woman, lifted up and wishing to become like God, consented.

## CHAPTER XXII. Eating the Fruit and the State after Sin

The woman first saw that the tree was beautiful to look upon (Gen. 3), that is, clean; and, judging from its smell or touch that it was pleasant for eating, she ate and gave to her husband—perhaps first persuading him with convincing words, [Col. 1072D] which the lawgiver passes over for brevity. He too readily agreed, because, having believed that the woman would immediately die according to the Lord’s word, and seeing that she had not died, he judged that the Lord’s saying was merely intended to frighten them, and he ate.

“And their eyes were opened”: that is, by sight they perceived something they had not perceived before, namely the unbecomingness of nakedness. Or this is not to be understood of bodily eyes, since it has been said, “The woman saw the tree,” etc. They did not approach the tree as blind men feeling their way. By “their eyes,” then, we mean desire and awareness of it. Natural motions of desire were indeed in them, but suppressed and shut up, as in children until puberty; [Col. 1073A] then they were opened like little streams and began to move and spread. Since they had not previously felt these movements within themselves, they then experienced and recognized them. And just as they had been disobedient to their superior, so their members began to move against their own superior, namely reason. They first felt in their genitals the movement of desire contrary to reason; seeing their own parts move against them, they blushed. Hence those parts are called shameful.

The other members stand still or move at a human being’s command; the shameful parts do not. Since these are the gateway of propagation, the disobedience of the members was, as it were, written upon the gateway as a sign of the parents’ disobedience. “They knew that they were naked,” that is, that the private parts were unbecoming; in other words, they were ashamed for their private parts to be seen. [Col. 1073B] Josephus nevertheless relates that they gained the knowledge that they were naked and the understanding of their shame from eating the tree, as though it naturally possessed this effect, saying: “For this plant was a cause of acuteness and understanding.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. The Curses of the Serpent, Man, and Woman

Then they made themselves girdles (Gen. 3), that is, loincloths, like short breeches, such as athletic garments.

> [Note: Col. 1074D, Addition 1. That is, thigh-coverings from Campania, where men are runners, so that they may run more freely.]

Nor was it without reason that these were made from fig leaves, for if their juice is ground and a human body is anointed with it, the flesh immediately feels there an itch of pleasure, so that it might thereby be shown that they had already felt the itching of pleasure in their flesh. This itch signifies the itch of pleasure [Col. 1073C] which they themselves experienced. Hence some say that the fig was the forbidden tree.

They heard the voice of the Lord walking, so that his very movement seemed already to accuse them because they had not stood firm in the commandment. He spoke through a created thing subject to him. They hid themselves from the face of God among the trees. The Lord called the man, namely him to whom he had given the commandment, and, reproving rather than seeking information, said: “Adam, where are you?”—as if to say, “See in what misery you are.” He said: “I hid myself because I was naked.” A foolish answer, as though nakedness displeased him who had been made such. And the Lord said: “Who told you this, unless it was because you ate from the tree?”

But he did not humbly confess; instead, turning the sin back upon his wife—indeed upon the giver of the woman herself—he said: [Col. 1073D] “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate.” He said to the woman: “Why have you done this?” Nor did she accuse herself, but shifted the sin to the serpent, and silently to the serpent’s Creator. The serpent, however, is not questioned, because it had not done this by itself, but the devil through it.

In cursing them, he began with the serpent, observing the order and a fitting number of curses. The serpent had sinned first and more greatly, in three ways; the woman afterward and less than it, though more than the man, in two ways; the man last and least, in one way. The serpent envied, lied, and deceived. For these three acts it received three curses. Because it envied human excellence, [Col. 1074A] it was told: “You shall go upon your breast.” Because it lied, it was punished in its mouth: hence, “You shall eat earth all the days of your life”; indeed, its voice was taken away and venom placed in its mouth. Because it deceived, it received this: “I will place enmities between you and the woman.” From this it is implied that Eve repented: “She shall crush your head,” which the serpent naturally guards as the seat of life. “And you shall lie in wait especially for her heel.”

And as there is a natural hatred between horses and griffins, wolves and dogs, so also between man and serpent. For as a serpent’s venom kills a human being, so a fasting person’s spittle kills a serpent. And because they were still naked, a serpent now fears a naked person and flees, but leaps upon one who is clothed.

The woman sinned in two ways: she grew proud and ate what was forbidden. [Col. 1074B] Because she grew proud, he humbled her, saying: “You shall be violently under the power of a man,” so that he may even afflict you with wounds in defloration. Now she is subject to her husband by condition and fear, whereas before she was subject to him by love. Because she sinned in her fruit, she was punished in her fruit. Therefore it was said to her: “You shall give birth in pain.” “In pain” is the curse; “you shall give birth” is the blessing. For the barren woman is cursed (Exod. 23). Thus, even in punishing, God did not forget to show mercy—a point also to be noted in the other curses of human beings.

Adam, because he sinned solely by eating, was punished with the labor of seeking food for himself: “Cursed is the earth in your work,” namely for your work—that is, for your sin. On account of this [Col. 1074C] it came about that the earth, which previously produced good and abundant fruits spontaneously, would henceforth produce them rarely and not without human labor, and would sometimes bring forth thorns and thistles instead of fruits. He added: “And you shall eat the herbs of the earth,” as though even in this you would be equal to a beast.

He cursed the earth because the transgression occurred through the earth’s fruit, not through the waters. Hence the Lord ate fish, but is not read to have eaten flesh of living things from the cursed earth—except perhaps the Paschal lamb, in obedience to the command of the Law. He therefore adds concerning labor: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth,” that is, until you die, because you are earth and shall go into earth. “You shall go” is well said: you who, if you had remained in the same state, could have passed to a better one if you wished, will now go from misery to misery, [Col. 1074D] like flowing water. And then Adam, lamenting the misery of his posterity, called his wife Eve, as has been said.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Their Expulsion from Paradise and the Flaming Sword

God made Adam and his wife garments of skins, that is, from the skins of dead animals, so that he might carry with himself a sign of his mortality.

> [Note: Col. 1073. “Made,” according to some, means “commanded that he should make for himself.”]

And he said: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3): this is irony, as if he wished to be like God, but [Col. 1075A] it is now evident that he is not. Nor is it the voice of God mocking him, but a voice correcting him from pride; and it is the voice of the Trinity. Or it is God’s voice to the angels, and a voice of lamentation, as is clear from this: he was made by me so that he might be as one of us, if he had stood firm. “Now therefore, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand and take from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.”

> [Note: Col. 1075D, Addition 1. The words “live forever” should be understood according to human opinion, as though he said: “and eat with the expectation of living forever”; or “forever” is understood to mean a long time. Some relate that they were in paradise for seven hours.]

This is aposiopesis—as though: “See to it,” “beware,” or “cast him out.” God’s judgment seems severe, adding the punishment of expulsion to the punishments already stated.

> [Note: Col. 1075D, Addition 2. The Church represents the expulsion of the first parents on the beginning of the fast, when it expels penitents from herself. It gives sackcloth as a sign of the garments of skin [Col. 1076A], and ashes with the words, “You are ashes,” etc. In remembrance of the curse, those expelled carry burning candles, because, on account of the deed in which they stretched out their hands toward the forbidden fruit, a flaming sword was placed at paradise. They also go to another church, and the doors are shut before them as a sign of paradise’s entrance, once closed. They eat not at a table but upon the ground, because “cursed is the earth in your work.” No one says *ave* to them, because the name Eve had not yet been changed into *ave*, as happened in the greeting of the Blessed Virgin Mary.]

But the contrary is true. For he mercifully tempered the punishment he had given, so that this may truly be said of him: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. 3). Since they were to live in misery, the longer life lasted, the more miserable it would be. Therefore, if they had tasted of the tree of life and lived longer, they would have been miserable longer.

Nor is it surprising that even after sin they might have lived longer by eating from that tree, since there are still certain islands of the living in which no one dies. Likewise, among the Seres, there is a down on the leaves of trees whose consumption prolongs life. Alexander also wrote to Aristotle concerning the priests of the trees of the sun and moon that they live an exceedingly long life through eating their fruits. And, as he had said, the Lord sent him out of the paradise of delight to work the earth from which he had been taken—namely, the field of Damascus, from which he had been taken. There Cain killed his brother Abel (Gen. 4), and near it Adam and Eve are buried in the double cave.

He placed before the paradise of delight cherubim [Col. 1075C] and a flaming, turning sword: so that the angel might bar the devil and the fire the human being. Or, through the ministry of angels, he placed there a fire which blocked entrance to paradise. It is called a sword—not merely any sword, but a turning sword, that is, one cutting on both sides—because it was fitting that a human being be punished in both parts of himself, namely soul and body. Or it is called turning, that is, capable of being turned away, namely removed when God should wish. For it was removed temporarily when Elijah and Enoch entered, but not completely, until it was extinguished at Christ’s death.

If it is asked what that fire consumed, it may be said that there is a kind of fire—as is read in the Life of Saint Nicholas—to which, if you put your hand, you feel heat but do not suffer burning. It needs no material [Col. 1075D] to consume, and in this way it burns the spirit. Again, if it is asked why God permitted man to be tempted although he knew he would fall, and many questions of this sort, we say, so far as the present work concerns us: because he so willed. If one asks why he willed it, it is a foolish question to seek a cause for the divine will, since it is itself the highest cause of all causes.

## CHAPTER XXV. The Generations of Adam

[Col. 1076A]

“Adam knew his wife” (Gen. 4), but not in paradise: rather, now guilty and expelled. The lawgiver briefly passes over Adam’s generations, hastening to the times [Col. 1076B] of Abraham, father of the Hebrews, and passes over many sons and daughters of Adam in silence. But Methodius the martyr prayed while he was in prison, and the Spirit revealed to him the beginning and end of the world. He both prayed for this and left it in writing, though simply, saying that they left paradise as virgins.

In the fifteenth year of Adam’s created life, Cain and his sister Chalmana were born to him. Although Adam was made as though at the age of thirty, he was nevertheless one day and one year old, then two years and three years old, and so on. He could therefore have begotten many children before Cain, who are passed over here. After another fifteen years Abel and his sister Delbora were born to him. In the one hundred and thirtieth year of Adam’s life, Cain killed Abel; and Adam and Eve mourned [Col. 1076C] him for one hundred years. Then Seth was born to him in the thirtieth year of the first chiliad, that is, of the first age. We call a period of a thousand years one age, a chiliad. For Methodius begins the ages after Adam’s two hundredth year and calls one chiliad an age.

The Septuagint agrees in this, saying that Adam was two hundred and thirty years old when he begot Seth, whereas the Hebrew has one hundred and thirty. The Hebrews, however, omit the one hundred years of mourning.

> [Note: Col. 1076D, Addition 1. The place where they mourned is called the Valley of Tears near Hebron. *Chilios* is interpreted as “two thousand”; and where we speak of six ages, the Greeks speak of six chiliads—not because every age had a thousand years. Some had more years and some fewer.]

But let us return to the brevity of Genesis. Eve conceived and bore Cain, whose name means “possession”; she bore Abel again, whose name means “mourning,” “grief,” or “vapor,” as though he would soon pass away, as if what was to happen to him had been prophesied in his name. Yet according to Josephus, [Col. 1076D] it means “nothing here,” because he left no seed upon the earth. Abel was a shepherd and Cain a farmer. Since he was most wicked, Cain first cultivated the soil also to provide for his avarice.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The Brothers’ Offerings

“After many days they offered gifts to the Lord” (Gen. 4): Cain offered from the crops; Abel, according to Josephus, milk and the firstborn of the lambs. Moses says that he also offered from their fat, that is, from the fattest of the flock. [Col. 1077A] Adam is believed to have taught his sons in the Spirit to offer tithes and firstfruits to God.

God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but did not look upon Cain and his gifts, because Abel pleased God, and his offering pleased God on Abel’s account (Heb. 2). Another translation explains how this became known: “God kindled fire over Abel and over his gifts.” For fire from heaven burned up his offering, as is read to have happened to Elijah on Carmel (3 Kgs. 18), and under Moses in Leviticus (Lev. 10; 2 Chr. 7). Cain’s gifts, however, born from the man’s avarice, did not please God.

Cain became angry, and his face fell in shame, seeing one inferior to himself preferred. Therefore the Lord, reproving Cain, said: “Why are you angry? If you do well, will you not receive a reward [Col. 1077B] in me?” Or, instead of “you will receive,” Theodotion has, “your gift will be acceptable.” “But if you do evil, sin will immediately be at the door,” that is, present and ready, and in the will through which it entered into action. Yet because you possess free choice, its appetite—that of sin—will be under you, that is, in your power, and you will rule it if you wish.

Another translation has: “Why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still. Its turning is toward you, and you shall rule it,” that is, it lies within you to turn away from sin. He had offered rightly because he offered to God, the creature to the Creator; but he had not divided rightly because he had offered himself, who was better, as an offering to the devil. Or he did not divide rightly because he kept the better things for himself [Col. 1077C] and offered the Lord ears of grain rubbed bare and gnawed away beside the road.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Death of Abel

Cain, therefore, envying his brother, said to him: “Let us go out into the field,” or “Let us cross over” (Gen. 4). Jerome says that this is found secretly in Samaritan books and in our own.

> [Note: Col. 1078C, Addition 1. The Samaritans had received the Pentateuch in order to be delivered from wild beasts, but had corrupted it in many places by adding according to number.]

For it is not read what Cain said to him, but it should be understood that he spoke to him the words of the Lord’s rebuke. Then he rose up against Abel and killed him. And the Lord said to him: “Where is Abel your brother?” He did not ask from ignorance, but reproved and condemned the fratricide. When Cain wished to conceal what he had done, God said: “The voice of your brother Abel’s blood cries to me from the earth,” that is, what you have done is evident, because the shedding [Col. 1077D] of blood reveals it, and what is plainly apparent needs no accuser.

Hence in the Church there is a custom among some that, even if no one accuses them, persons suspected of shedding blood are summoned to answer in a sacred place, because the blood cries out. If they deny it, they are tested by the judgment of God and by oath. “Now therefore you shall be cursed upon the earth, wandering and a fugitive.” This man is rightly cursed, and not Adam, because he knew the punishment of the first transgression and then added fratricide.

Cain, fearing that beasts might devour him if he went away from people, or that people might kill him for his sin if he remained with them, condemned himself and despaired, saying: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve pardon for.”

> [Note: Col. 1078C, Addition 2. “My iniquity is greater than that by which I may deserve pardon,” as though he said: my iniquity is greater than every merit.]

“Everyone who finds me will kill me.” He said this from fear, or he said it as a wish, [Col. 1078A] as though saying: “Would that they might kill me!” And God said to him: “It shall certainly not happen so.” That is, you shall not die quickly; but “whoever kills Cain”—one must supply: “will free him from fear, pain, and misery”—“shall be punished sevenfold.” Then it is added impersonally: punishment shall be inflicted upon him while he lives in punishment, until the seventh Lamech. This agrees with the Septuagint translation: “Whoever kills Cain will pay seven acts of vengeance.”

Some relate that his punishment lasted until his seventh generation because he committed seven sins: he did not divide rightly; he envied his brother; he acted deceitfully; he called him into the field and killed him; he brazenly denied it; he despaired; and, condemned, he did not repent. Or “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold” means that he will be punished more than Cain himself, because the prohibition of homicide had not yet been given to Cain.

God placed a sign upon Cain: trembling of the head, because he had killed his brother, who was head of the Church. Thus it might be known that he had been punished by the Lord, excommunicated, and was unworthy of mercy, and yet not be killed. Then he went out from the face of the Lord.

> [Note: Col. 1078C, Addition 3. The Church represents Cain’s expulsion by excommunicating those who shed blood, especially with extinguished candles, because both Cain and such persons have extinguished the lives of their brothers.]

He lived toward the eastern region of Eden, that is, of delights—not in delights, but toward the land of delights. Josephus says: “After traveling over much land with his wife Chalmana, he settled in a place called Nayda, where sons were also born to him.” Jerome, however, says: “It is not the land Nayda, as our common people suppose; rather, he lived in the land of Nod, that is, ‘unstable’ and ‘wandering,’ for *nod* has this meaning. Thus Cain is called [Col. 1078C] *nod*.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Generations of Cain

Cain knew his wife, who bore him (Gen. 4) Enoch. He built a city and named it Enoch after his son Enoch. This shows that there were already many [Col. 1078D] people, though their descent is not stated, whom Cain summoned to build the city and by whose help he made it.

Josephus says that, gathering wealth through robbery and violence, he invited his own people to brigandage; he changed the simplicity of human life into invention and inequality, introducing measures and weights, craftiness, and corruption. He first marked out boundaries of land. He fortified or walled cities; and, fearing those whom he injured, he gathered his own people into cities for safety.

Enoch begot Irad; Irad, Maviael; Maviael, Mathusael; Mathusael, Lamech. Lamech, seventh from Adam and most wicked, first introduced bigamy and thereby committed adultery against the law of nature and God’s decree. For at the first creation one woman had been made for one man, and [Col. 1079A] God had decreed through Adam’s mouth: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). Lamech took two wives, Ada and Sella.

Ada bore Jabel, who invented portable shepherds’ tents for changing pastures; he organized flocks and distinguished them with marks. He separated sheep from goats according to kinds; according to quality, separating single-colored animals from the flock of spotted fleece; and according to age, yearlings from older animals. He understood that mating should take place at fixed times. His brother’s name was Tubal, father of those who play the lyre and organ. These were not, indeed, instruments, which were invented much later; rather, he invented music, that is, harmonies, so that pastoral labor might be turned as it were into delight.

Because he had heard Adam prophesy about two judgments, lest the art be lost, he wrote it upon two columns, the whole art on each, as Josephus says: one marble, the other brick, so that one would not be washed away by the flood and the other would not be destroyed by fire. Josephus says that the marble column still stood in the Syrian land. Sella bore Tubalcain, who first invented the smith’s art, skillfully practiced military matters, and fashioned carved works in metals for the lust of the eyes.

While Tubalcain was making such objects, Tubal, mentioned above, delighted in the sound of the metals and discovered from their weights the proportions and harmonies arising from them. The Greeks fabulously attribute this discovery to Pythagoras. Similarly, from the action of shrubs he devised the practice of working—that is, carving—in metals. [Col. 1079C] For when he had burned shrubs in the pastures, veins of metal flowed into little streams; and when sheets were lifted out, they bore the forms of the places in which they had lain.

Tubalcain’s sister was Noema, who invented the art of variegated weaving. Lamech, however, according to Josephus, wisely knowing divine matters, and seeing that Cain was subject to a common punishment while a greater punishment was due to himself, foretold this to his wives: “Because I killed a man to my wound and a young man to my bruise, vengeance upon Cain shall be sevenfold, but upon Lamech seventy-sevenfold.”

Lamech, an archer, became dim-sighted through long life. Having a young man as his guide, while hunting merely for pleasure and for the use of skins—for there was no use of meat before the flood—he accidentally killed [Col. 1079D] Cain among the shrubs, believing him to be a wild beast. Guided by the youth’s signal, he directed an arrow and killed him. When he learned that he had killed a man, namely Cain, he angrily beat the youth to death there with his bow.

Thus he had killed Cain to his wound, and the young man to the bruise of the wound. Or he had killed both to his own wound and bruise, that is, to his own condemnation. Therefore, since Cain’s sin was punished sevenfold, as we have said, his own was punished seventy-sevenfold: that is, seventy souls and seven who descended from Lamech perished in the flood. Or this number merely denotes the greater severity of the punishment.

The Hebrew says: His wives often treated him badly. Hence he angrily told them that he suffered this for the double homicide he had committed; yet he frightened them by adding the punishment, as if to say: [Col. 1080A] “Why do you wish to kill me? Whoever kills me will be punished more severely than he who killed Cain.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. Seth and His Descendants

Adam again knew his wife, who bore a son and called him Seth (Gen. 4). Strabus says that after Abel’s death Adam vowed never again to know his wife, but, commanded by God through an angel, broke the vow so that the Son of God might be born from him.

> [Note: Col. 1080B, Addition 1. It is read that Adam had thirty sons and an equal number of daughters besides Cain and Abel.]

Josephus, however, says that after Abel had been killed and Cain had fled, Adam considered the procreation of children and was greatly troubled by his desire for offspring. Strabus could call this thought of propagation a command of the Lord, because he had commanded: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1).

Seth also had a son, whom he called Enos, a name meaning “man” or “male,” as though rational and strong, because he was the first to begin to call upon the name of the Lord. Perhaps he invented words of prayer for invoking God. But most Hebrews suppose that he had devised images for the honor of God, and they are mistaken. Or perhaps, to stir up sluggish remembrance of God, he portrayed the Lord, as is now done in the Church.

## CHAPTER XXX. He Inserts an Epilogue

“This is the book of the generation of Adam” (Gen. 5). He repeats the account of Adam’s generation in order to continue the complete order of genealogies. Hence some begin the [Col. 1080C] first age from Adam; others from Seth. Methodius agrees with the latter, and says this because no one was born from Abel and Cain’s entire line perished in the flood.

Adam lived one hundred and thirty years and begot Seth in his image and likeness: Adam himself in God’s image, the rest in Adam’s image—which is nearly the same thing. Or rather: mortal beings beget mortal beings. Hence: “As is the earthly man, such also are the earthly” (1 Cor. 5). Perhaps Moses omitted Adam’s hundred years of mourning because, as we have said, the Septuagint, Methodius, and Josephus write that he was two hundred and thirty years old when he begot Seth.

Seth begot Enos; Enos, Cainan; Cainan, Mahalaleel; Mahalaleel, Jared; Jared, Enoch; Enoch, Methuselah; Methuselah, Lamech; Lamech, Noah. Thus, as in Cain’s line the seventh, namely Lamech, was the worst, so in Seth’s line [Col. 1080D] the seventh, namely Enoch, was the best. God transferred him temporarily to the paradise of delight, so that at the end of time, with Elijah, he might turn the hearts of fathers toward their sons (Mal. 4).

> [Note: Col. 1081A, Addition 1. Enoch invented certain letters and wrote certain books, under whom Adam is understood to have died.]

The Jews, however, attribute the cause of this translation more to the number seven than to Enoch’s holiness, because, they say, many are read to have been holier than he, and none of them was translated. Indeed, they say that God arranged all things according to the number seven: that he created seven heavens, gave each its own name, and created seven earths, which David calls the foundations of the mountains (Ps. 17).

There are differing opinions concerning Methuselah’s years. According to the calculation of the Septuagint, he lived fourteen years after the flood; yet he is not read to have been in the ark, nor translated like Enoch. [Col. 1081A] Some say that he died six years before the flood. Jerome asserts that he died in the same year in which the flood occurred; a careful calculation of his years according to Genesis also shows this. Yet all agree about the total number of his years, because he lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years.

Noah, moreover, was the tenth from Adam, in whom the first age ended, so that he himself belonged to it. The Septuagint assigns to this age two thousand two hundred and forty-four years; others, two thousand two hundred and sixty-four. Jerome gives not quite two thousand; Methodius, two thousand. Yet Methodius arranges the ages by chiliads and does not add any surplus years; thus he handed down nothing certain concerning the number of years.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The Cause of the Flood

[Col. 1081B]

Noah, when he was five hundred years old, begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth (Gen. VI). Moses, intending to speak of the Flood, first states its cause: “When human beings began to multiply upon the earth,” the sons of God—that is, the devout descendants of Seth—saw the daughters of men—that is, those of Cain’s line—and, overcome by desire, took them as wives; and giants were born from them. He does not specify whether this occurred in Noah’s time, before it, long before, or shortly before.

Josephus, however, says that the sons of Seth remained good until the seventh generation; afterwards they turned to evil, abandoning their fathers’ observances, and thereby provoked God against themselves. For many angels of God—that is, sons of Seth, namely those previously called sons of God—having intercourse with women, begot violent sons, who, because of their confidence in their strength, were called giants by the Greeks. [Col. 1081C]

Methodius gives a fuller account of the cause of the Flood, namely human sins. He says that, in the five-hundredth year of the first millennium—that is, after the first millennium—the sons of Cain abused the wives of their brothers through excessive fornications. In the six-hundredth year, women, given over to madness, exceeded men in debauchery. After Adam’s death, Seth separated his own kindred from Cain’s kindred, which had returned to its native soil. For while he lived, their father had forbidden them to intermingle; and Seth dwelt upon a mountain near Paradise. Cain lived on the plain where he had killed his brother. In the five-hundredth year of the second millennium, human beings burned with desire, coupling with one another. In the seven-hundredth year of the second millennium, the sons of Seth desired the daughters of Cain, and giants were born from them. And when the third millennium began, the Flood poured forth. Thus Methodius arranges the matter. [Note: [Col. 1082C] Addition 1. Augustine condemns this opinion elsewhere.]

It could also have happened that incubus demons begot giants, so called from the greatness of their bodies, or from *geos*, “earth,” because incubi or demons are accustomed to oppress women at night; but their monstrous bodies corresponded also to monstrous minds. Yet after the Flood other giants were born at Hebron; later there were giants in Tham, a city of Egypt, from which they too were called Titans. [Col. 1082A] From their stock came Enachin, whose sons dwelt in Hebron; from them arose Goliath and certain others.

God, angered by human sins, said: “It repents me that I have made man,” as though he said: “I shall do what a human being remorseful for his work customarily does: he destroys what he has made.” The meaning is: “I shall destroy the man whom I made.” “My spirit”—that is, my indignation—“shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh,” as though he said: “I shall not punish him eternally as I do the devil, because he is frail. But here I shall render what he deserves.” Yet before I destroy him, I shall give him time for repentance, should he wish it; and his days for repentance shall be one hundred and twenty years. This should not be understood of the human spirit, but of God’s indignation.

Nor is this [Col. 1082B] the limit of human life after the Flood, since after the Flood people are found to have lived longer. As Jerome says, the Lord spoke this twenty years before the ark began to be made, though it is recorded as having been made in one hundred years. Or, according to Strabo, he spoke from the year in which the ark began to be made; but because they persisted in evil before the appointed time, they were destroyed in the hundredth year. Josephus, nevertheless, says that this term of life was established for human beings.

The statement that God was inwardly touched by grief of heart perhaps means nothing other than that the magnitude of the divine offence was hidden from men. Or it is *anthropopathos*, that is, a human emotional condition when something belonging to a human being is attributed to God.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Noah’s Ark, and How the Lord Spoke to Noah

[Col. 1082C]

Noah was perfect in his generations (Gen. VI): not, as it were, with that perfection which belongs to the heavenly homeland, but according to the condition of his generation, namely the earthly one. And the Lord said to Noah: “The end of all flesh has come before me. Except those who are to be saved in the ark, I shall destroy them with the earth,” that is, together with the earth’s fertility.

They also maintain that the earth’s vigour and fruitfulness were far less after the Flood than before it. Hence the eating of flesh was granted to human beings, whereas previously they lived on the fruits of the earth. In accordance with the Lord’s command Noah made an ark of [Col. 1082D] smoothed—that is, polished—or squared timbers. [Note: [Col. 1083C] Addition 1. The Lord spoke as it were to a farmer, directing him to make a vessel in the form of an *arconium*, that is, one tending towards a cone; or perhaps from *arcendo*, “enclosing,” because it was closed on every side.] Another text reads “pitched timbers,” three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high. [Note: [Col. 1083C] Addition 2. The statement that the ark was thirty cubits high should be understood of its body, that is, from its bottom to the deck. For it would be impossible for its covering not to have risen higher, and for timbers only thirty cubits long to cover its length and breadth.]

This was patterned upon the human body, in which the length is six times greater than the width and ten times greater than the height. Length extends from sole to crown; width from one side of the ribs to the other; height from back to belly. Many, however, wish this to have been said only of Christ’s body, since this is read in Isidore, who displays the likeness of the human body in which Christ appeared.

Thus the ark was square at its base, but, with one side longer, it rose inward from the corners until its summit was completed in a cubit. It was coated within and without with pitch, [Col. 1083A] a very hot adhesive; timber coated with it is not broken apart by any force or art, nor can material or a wall treated with pitch be dissolved except by a woman’s menstrual fluid. It is gathered floating in the lakes of Judaea. In Syria it is mud seething up from the earth.

Rooms and three storeys were made in it, called divisions from *trita*. Another translation says “two-chambered and three-chambered.” For it had five chambers, which Augustine also says were there besides the bilge; he says that above the bilge’s deck it was two-chambered. One chamber was for dung, another a storeroom; above this dwelling was another, three-chambered. The side chambers were respectively for fierce and tame animals; the middle chamber was for human beings and birds. It had a door where the two-chambered and three-chambered sections [Col. 1083B] met.

Others, however, arrange these five chambers only in height. They call the lowest, together with the bilge, the dung chamber; the second above it, the storeroom; the third, that of fierce animals and serpents, placing the door where these join; the fourth, that of tame animals; and the highest, that of humans and birds. Josephus nevertheless says that the ark had four chambers, perhaps not including the dung chamber or the bilge.

Noah made in it a window, which the Hebrews hand down to have been crystalline; in Hebrew it is called “midday,” and by Symmachus “daybreak.” Rabanus says that the ark’s cubits were geometric cubits, otherwise it could not have held so much. A geometric cubit contains seven or nine of ours. Strictly speaking, [Col. 1083C] a cubit is a foot and a half.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Entering the Ark

When the ark had been completed, the Lord said to Noah: “You shall enter the ark—you and your sons, your wife and your sons’ wives” (Gen. VI). In these eight was preserved [Col. 1083D] the seed of the human race. [Note: [Col. 1084C] Addition 1. Noah’s wife: Phuarphara; Shem’s wife: Pharphia; Ham’s wife: Cathaflua; Japheth’s wife: Fliva.] When he spoke of entering, the Lord named the men separately and the women separately, as though he said: “In a time of affliction one must abstain from women’s embraces.”

“And from every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two into the ark,” that is, a pair: male and female. Of unclean animals there were only two of each kind; but of clean animals, seven. Moses calls those animals unclean in accordance with his own time, namely those which the Mosaic Law calls unclean. Or they were called unclean even then, because by nature they were unfit for human food. I say “by nature,” because none had yet been granted for eating. “You shall take with you from every kind of food that can be eaten, that it may serve as food both for you and for them.”

If it is asked [Col. 1084A] whether any tiny or unclean creatures were brought in under this number, Augustine says that those not produced by intercourse did not need to be in the ark—those, namely, born from dust, such as fleas, or from moisture or corruption. That only creatures capable of generation through intercourse were brought in is indicated when he adds “according to its kind,” or “in its kind.”

It is further asked: if some creatures had been enclosed there without transgressing the command, what necessity would have compelled the inclusion of those that feed on flesh, since they needed to be fed? Augustine says that foods other than flesh might be shared in common, especially since creatures that eat flesh can eat figs and chestnuts; above all, hunger compels them to eat everything. Perhaps animals did not yet eat flesh, [Col. 1084B] any more than human beings did.

And Noah did all that the Lord commanded him. In the six-hundredth year of his life Noah entered the ark with all that the Lord had told him—creatures brought by divine will and the ministry of angels—in the second month, on the seventeenth day, called Nisan by the Hebrews, May by the Latins, and Dion by the Macedonians. Moses, however, according to Josephus, establishes Nisan—that is, April—as the first month in legal matters. But in contracts—that is, in conducting business—and in other arrangements of secular government, he retained the decrees of the seasons and the customary order of months.

Josephus says that from Adam to this time there were two thousand six hundred and fifty-six years, as is written in the sacred writings, and the account has been marked with integrity. [Col. 1084C]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Inundation and the Cataclysm

After Noah had entered the ark, the fountains of the deep—that is, the waters within the bowels of the earth—were broken open, and the cataracts of heaven—that is, the windows, namely the clouds—were opened (Gen. VII). Properly speaking, cataracts are channels of the Nile, when the Nile is divided through seven mouths, or places of the same sort called *catadupla*. Improperly, any channels of water are called outlets, that is, cataracts.

It rained upon the earth for forty days and nights. The ark was lifted up and borne on high, and the water rose above all the mountains by fifteen cubits, [Col. 1084D] in order to wash away the pollution of the air, as high as human works had ascended. The fire of judgment will rise to the same place in order to purify the air.

Yet human works do not seem able to have risen so high, since Olympus reaches into the clear air. On its summit letters inscribed in dust have been found to remain unmoved for a year, because the winds cannot erase them owing to the mountain’s height. There, because of the air’s excessive thinness, even birds cannot live; nor could philosophers who climbed it remain there for any length of time without sponges full of water, which they held to their nostrils in order to draw from them denser air.

But some think that the mountains were not then as high as they are now. Or perhaps people sacrificed on heights and kindled fire, whose vapour and [Col. 1085A] ashes might have risen very high and defiled the air.

When Noah had entered, God shut the door and pitched it on the outside. Every living soul upon the earth died, and the waters prevailed over the earth, so raised, for one hundred and fifty days, namely from the day on which Noah entered. After one hundred and fifty days the waters began to diminish in the seventh month, so that on the twenty-seventh day of the month the ark rested upon the mountains of Armenia. The people of that province still point out the remains of the ark there.

Josephus says that writers even of barbarian histories preserve the memory of this Flood and ark. Berosus the Chaldaean says of it:

> “It is said that some part of his vessel, which came to Armenia near the mountain of the Cordyaeans, still remains; and that a certain pitch is taken from it, which people use especially for expiations.”

Hieronymus the Egyptian, who wrote on antiquity, mentions the same matter. Manasseh of Damascus says concerning it:

> “Above Numidia there is a high mountain in Armenia called Baris, upon which, it is said, many who fled were saved at the time of the Flood, and someone carried along in the ark came ashore.”

Finally, in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the mountain tops appeared. After forty days Noah opened the window and released a raven, which did not return (Gen. VIII), perhaps carried off by the waters, or enticed by finding a corpse floating upon them. Josephus, however, says that, finding everything still flooded, it returned to Noah.

After it Noah released a dove, which, [Col. 1085C] since it found no place where its foot could rest, returned to Noah. But had not the mountain tops already been uncovered? Perhaps they were not yet dry, and so it could not rest in a marsh any more than on water. Or this may be understood as having occurred earlier, though stated later, by recapitulation.

After seven days he sent it out again, and it returned in the evening carrying a green olive branch. After another seven days he sent it out, and it did not return to him again. Thus, in the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life, in the first month, on the first day of the month, Noah opened the roof of the ark and saw that the surface of the earth was dry; but he waited for the Lord’s command to leave.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Noah’s Departure and the Rainbow

In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the Lord said to Noah: “Leave the ark, you and your wife, [Col. 1085D] your sons and your sons’ wives” (Gen. VIII). Those who had entered separately are ordered to leave together, as though he said: “Now the time for embraces has returned, that you may multiply upon the earth.” For immediately he added: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. IX).

Noah went out with everything that was with him, on the same day on which he had entered, when the year had come full circle. He had entered on the seventeenth moon of the second month, although another translation has the twenty-seventh; and he departed on the twenty-eighth moon. For whatever the moon is today, if you add eleven, it will be the same on that day when the year has turned: if it is the first moon today, on the same day of the following year it will be the twelfth.

Do not be troubled that I said he left on the [Col. 1086A] twenty-eighth moon, while the book says the twenty-seventh. It could be that he left in the evening of the twenty-seventh day, and at the twenty-seventh moon, with the twenty-eighth already imminent. Intermediate times are often called by the name of either extreme, as when the Lord was crucified between the third and sixth hour: one evangelist says the third hour and another the sixth.

Or rather, according to the names of the seven days: if, in the third weekday, the moon is twenty-seven, then after a year, on the same third weekday, the moon will be twenty-eight, because the reckoning given by one day declines in the martyrology. For example, if the Kalends of January fall on Sunday and the moon is seven, then after a year, on the Kalends of January, the moon repeated will be seventeen, but the Kalends will fall on Monday. Therefore on the Sunday before the Kalends the moon will be seventeen; and thus, from Sunday to Sunday after a year, only ten moons are added, but from Kalends to Kalends, eleven.

Noah built an altar to the Lord and offered the seventh of the clean creatures to the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1085] The seven clean creatures admitted signify the seven gifts which a perfect person ought to possess.] The Lord had ordered seven of every kind to be brought in so that, when the seventh had been offered, six might suffice for propagation.

The Armenians call the place where they departed *Egressorium*, “the Place of Departure.” Noah’s sons called it Thenon, that is, “eight,” after the number of those who departed. For this reason also, as some report, Noah built the altar of eight stones.

The Lord smelled the sweet savour and said to Noah: “I shall no longer curse all the earth because of human beings, for they are inclined to evil. [Col. 1086C] Seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, night and day shall not cease.” Perhaps the four seasons were not yet so fully distinguished, because until the Flood the waters had not been gathered into clouds.

The Lord blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply; and let fear of you be upon every living creature of the earth.” This was said to comfort them, lest the few human beings should fear being overpowered by the many beasts. It was as if God said: “Previously I gave green plants for food; now I hand over living creatures to you, [Note: [Col. 1086D] Addition 1. The eating of flesh did not exist before the Flood, but was allowed immediately afterwards.] except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood,” that is, an animal that has been strangled.

God prohibited them from committing homicide, because they especially feared that the Lord might again flood the earth with the waters of the Flood. Noah prayed every day that this might not occur, as Josephus relates. God covenanted with them [Col. 1086D] that there would be no further Flood, and, as a sign of this covenant, placed his bow in the clouds. [Note: [Col. 1087A]

Addition 2.

That they might not fear rains, a pledge was given in the clouds.]

It is the sign of two judgments: the past judgment by water, which need not be feared, and the future judgment by fire, which is to be expected. Therefore it has two colours: blue, which is watery and outer, because it is past; and red, which is fiery and inner, because the fire is future. The saints also hand down that for forty years before the Judgment the rainbow will not be seen; this will naturally show that the drying of the air has already begun.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Noah’s Drunkenness and Ham’s Curse

[Col. 1087A]

Noah began to cultivate the earth and planted a vineyard, bringing wild native vines under cultivation for vineyard use. He drank wine, but did not know its power, became drunk, and lay asleep naked in his tent (Gen. IX). For the uncovering of the thighs follows drunkenness, just as lust follows satiety.

When Ham saw his father’s naked shame, he mockingly reported it to his brothers. But they put a cloak upon their shoulders and, walking backwards so that they might not see, covered their father’s shame. It is clear that people did not yet use breeches. [Note: [Col. 1087D] Addition 1. Semiramis was the woman who first invented breeches and their use.]

When Noah awoke and learned what [Col. 1087B] his younger son had done to him, he said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a slave, a servant to his brothers.” But how is Ham called the younger son, when he was middle-born? He may be called younger, that is, less worthy; or perhaps shorter in stature. Or this is said of Japheth, who, though younger, was wiser than Ham, his elder.

He cursed not the son but the son’s son, because he knew in the spirit that the son would not serve his brothers, but his seed would—not all of the seed, but those descended from Canaan. The sins of fathers are indeed often punished temporally in their children. The sense is: “You do not rejoice in your son, just as neither do I rejoice in you.”

And he added: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant.” This is prophecy, for he foresaw that the worship and name of the one God would remain among Shem’s sons. And again: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant.” This too is prophecy. For the nations descended from Japheth, enlarged in number through God’s agency and in the worship of gods by God’s permission, were afterwards grafted into the trunk of the olive tree.

The days of Noah came to nine hundred and fifty years, and he died. Josephus says that no one should think false what has been written of the ancients’ long lives, because God granted them longer spans of life on account of the virtues and glorious pursuits they constantly investigated—that is, astronomy and geometry—which they could not otherwise have learned unless they had lived for six hundred years. For through so many years’ revolutions the great year is completed. [Note: [Col. 1087D] Addition 2. The great year is completed when all the planets return to the places of their creation.]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Dispersion of Noah’s Sons and Nimrod

[Col. 1087D]

Moses returns to the beginning of Noah’s genealogy, saying: “These are the generations of Noah’s sons” (Gen. X). He begins with Japheth, the younger, in order that Shem, whose succession he intends to trace, may be placed last.

From them seventy-two generations are traced: fifteen from Japheth, thirty from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem. According to Alcuin, these three were scattered through the three parts of the world: Shem received Asia, Ham Africa, and Japheth Europe. Or, more specifically, Josephus says: [Col. 1088A] Japheth’s sons possessed the northern region, from the Taurus and Amanus Mountains of Cilicia and Syria to the river Tanais, and, in Europe, as far as Gades. Ham’s sons held all the lands from the province of Syria and the mountains of Amanus and Lebanon which lie beside the sea, taking possession also of those extending to the Ocean and giving them their own names. Shem’s sons separately inhabited Asia as far as the Ocean, beginning from the Euphrates.

We shall follow Shem’s generation, passing over the others, but adding this: Cush is called Ham’s son, and Nimrod the son of Cush. Nimrod first began to be mighty upon the earth, a mighty hunter of men before the Lord—that is, an exterminator and oppressor through his love of dominion—and [Col. 1088B] compelled human beings to worship fire. [Note: [Col. 1088D] Addition 1. The Chaldaeans worshipped fire and compelled others to do the same, burning other idols. But the priests of Canopus, hearing this, had made a great idol in honour of Bel. Removing its golden crown, they put in its place an earthen vessel shaped like a crown, perforated with holes and stopped with wax. When the Chaldaeans came, they set fire against it; and, as the wax melted, the water that was in the crown flowed out and extinguished the fire, and the idols of Canopus prevailed.]

From this arose the proverb used of someone who is strong and wicked: “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.” We have said this because Methodius says that he was among the sons of Hirom, son of Shem. Explaining why he first began to rule, Methodius speaks as follows of a son of Noah whom Moses does not mention:

“In the hundredth year of the third millennium a son was born to Noah in his likeness, and he named him Jonithus.” [Note: [Col. 1089A] Addition 2. An objection is made from Methodius concerning Jonithus: Noah had not begotten him before the Flood, since Jonithus was not in the ark; neither had he died before it, since after the Flood he instructed Nimrod. Perhaps Methodius’ reasoning is not sound.] “In the three-hundredth year Noah gave gifts to his son Jonithus and sent him into the land of Ethan. Jonithus entered it as far as the eastern sea, called Elioschora, that is, ‘the region of the sun.’ There he received from the Lord the gift of wisdom and discovered astronomy.”

Nimrod, a giant ten cubits high, came to him, was instructed [Col. 1088C] by him, and received his counsel as to the places in which he should begin to reign. This Jonithus foresaw certain future events, especially the rise of four kingdoms and their successive fall. Daniel also plainly prophesied this. Jonithus foretold to his disciple Nimrod that those first ruling would be from Ham, from whom Belus descended; then from Shem, the Medes, Persians, and Greeks; and afterwards, from Japheth, the Romans.

Returning from him, Nimrod, inflamed by desire for rule, urged his own people from Shem to rule over the others as though he were first-born. But they refused. Therefore he passed to Ham, who consented; he ruled among them at Babylon, and from that point was called one of Ham’s sons. But if he really was one of Ham’s sons, there is no question why he ruled among them. Following his example, Jectam, or Jetram, or Uram began to rule over Shem’s sons, and Suphene, or Sustene, over Japheth’s sons.

Philo the Jew—or, as others hold, a Gentile philosopher—relates in his *Book of Questions on Genesis* that, while Noah was still alive, twenty-four thousand one hundred men were born from his three sons, apart from women and little children; and they had three leaders over them, whom we have mentioned.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Tower of Babylon

[Col. 1089A]

After Noah’s death, moving their steps from the East, the leaders assembled in one place, on the plain of Shinar. Fearing a flood, and following the counsel of Nimrod, who wished to rule, they began to build a tower reaching up to heaven, using bricks instead of stones and pitch instead of mortar. The Lord descended [Col. 1089B] to see the tower (Gen. XI): he took notice in order to punish, and said to the angels: “Come, let us confuse their language, so that no one may understand his neighbour’s speech.”

In this division God left nothing undone, for the sounds are the same among all nations; rather, he divided ways and forms of speaking among different peoples. Josephus says of this tower that its width was so exceptionally great that, to those looking at it nearby, its height seemed lessened. But the gods sent winds, overthrew the tower, and allotted a distinct speech to each person. Consequently the city came to be called Babylon, for the Hebrews call confusion *Babel*.

The Sibyl mentions this tower, saying:

> “When all people had one speech, some built a lofty tower, as though they would ascend to heaven by it.”

Hesychius mentions the plain of Shinar in the region of Babylon, saying: “Those who were rescued from among the priests, taking up the sacred rites of Jupiter, came into Babylonian Shinar; and afterwards, divided by the diversity of languages, they made migrations, taking possession together of inland and maritime regions.”

Nor do I think it should be passed over that Moses says that Raamah, Cush’s son, had two sons, Sheba and Dodan. Josephus says Sheba and Judah, and that Judah, inhabiting the Egyptian nation of the Hesperians, left his surname to the Jews.

The statement that Asshur went out from the land of Shinar should be understood to mean that Nimrod drove him by force from that land and tower, which were his by hereditary right. Or it should not be understood of Asshur, [Col. 1089D] Shem’s son, who invented purple dye and hair or body ointments, and from whom Chaldaea [Note: [Col. 1089D] Addition 1. Chaldaea, Babylon, and Shinar are the same.] and Assyria were named; rather, “Asshur” means the Assyrian kingdom, which departed from there in the time of Serug, Abraham’s great-grandfather. The Babylonians, descended from Nimrod’s seed, held the kingdom until the fourth millennium and the last *cusmides* [uncertain reading].

## CHAPTER XXXIX. First Digression

Meanwhile the Egyptians and Assyrians gained dominion as follows. In the days of Serug, Belus Nerothides, king of Babylon—there was another Belus, king of Greece—entered Assyria, but held little of it. After his death, his son Ninus possessed all Assyria and enlarged the city in [Col. 1090A] which the capital of the kingdom stood to a circuit of three days’ journey; from his own name he called it Nineveh.

Hence some histories say that the kingdom of the Assyrians began with the ancient Belus; this is true as regards its beginning. Others say that it began with Ninus; this too is true as regards the expansion of the kingdom. Ninus defeated Ham, who was still alive and ruled in Bactria [variant: Thrace], and was called Zoroaster, the inventor of magical art. He wrote the seven liberal arts upon fourteen columns, seven of bronze and seven of brick, against both judgments [variant: flood]. Ninus burned his books. Idols arose from the same peoples in this manner. [Note: [Col. 1090A] Addition 1. Syrophanes was the first idolater of Egypt; Diothatus, of the Lacedaemonians; according to the *Poetria* of Master Anselm. [Col. 1090B]]

## CHAPTER XL. On Belus’ Death and the Rise of Idols

[Col. 1090B]

After Belus died, Ninus, to console himself in his grief, made an image of his father. He showed it such reverence that he spared any criminals who fled to it. Therefore people in his kingdom began to pay divine honours to its image. Following this example, very many dedicated images to their illustrious dead; and just as the other idols derived their origin from Belus’ idol, so they derived the general name for idols from his name.

For just as the Assyrians called him Belus, so other nations called him in accordance with the idiom of their own language: some Bel, others Beel, others Baal, others Baalim. Indeed, they also made the names specific: some calling them Beelphegor, others Beelzebub. But let us at last [Col. 1090C] resume the sequence of Shem’s genealogy.

## CHAPTER XLI. On Shem’s Generation

Shem was one hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad, two years after the Flood (Gen. II). This seems inconsistent with what was said above, that Shem was born in Noah’s five-hundredth year and that the Flood came in his six-hundredth. Therefore Shem was one hundred years old after the Flood, and two years later he was one hundred and two. But it is customary for Holy Scripture often to state round numerical limits, leaving unmentioned a few remaining years.

It may therefore be said either that Shem was one hundred and two years old but Scripture omitted the two; or that Noah was five hundred and two when he begot him; or that two years were lacking to Noah’s six hundred when the Flood came. Or the text should be read thus: “Shem was one hundred years old after the Flood, and it was two years after the Flood when he begot Arphaxad.”

Josephus, however, says that Shem’s son Arphaxad was born twelve years after the Flood; perhaps this is a scribal error. Arphaxad begot Salem, to whom Luke (ch. III) adds Cainan [Note: [Col. 1091C] Addition 1. He is found in the gloss on Luke. In a certain enumeration of Christ’s genealogy you will find Cainan, through whom the Master corrected this passage.] according to the Septuagint; he founded Salem; and Heber, from whom the Hebrews are named, according to Josephus.

Augustine nevertheless says: “It is rightly asked whether the Hebrews were named from Heber, or from Abraham, as though *Abrahaei*.” Heber begot Peleg and Joktan. *Peleg* in Hebrew means “division,” because in his days, through the division of languages, the nations were divided and the division of the lands took place. But this is said to have occurred especially under him because, while the ancient language remained in him and his sons, the others were divided off from him, as it were. [Col. 1091A]

Peleg begot Reu, or Regau; Reu begot Serug; Serug, Nahor; Nahor, Terah. When Terah was seventy years old he begot Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and the order is reversed. Haran was the first-born, and Abram the last. Perhaps he did not beget them at this age, but then began to beget children and begot them in their respective times—that is, at different times—so that he was already one hundred and twenty years old when he begot Abram, who was the last. [Note: [Col. 1091C] Addition 2. Thus the Hebrews do not make this age short.]

In Terah the second age ends: according to the Septuagint, it contains one thousand and seventy-two years; according to Methodius, one millennium; according to the Hebrew truth, one thousand two hundred and ninety-two years. Josephus gives this number of years down to Terah’s birth, but this age extends down to Abraham’s birth. [Col. 1091B]

Haran begot Lot, Iscah (that is, Sarai), and Milcah, and died before his father in Ur of the Chaldaeans. According to Josephus, Ur is the name of a city where his tomb is still shown. The Hebrews call *Ur* “fire,” and hence invent the tale that the Chaldaeans threw Abram and Haran into a fire through which they made little children pass, because they refused to worship fire. Haran died there, but Abram was delivered with God’s help. Hence it is said: “I am he who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldaeans” (Gen. II). [Note: [Col. 1091D] The Church sings this chant.]

Terah therefore, hating the land because of his grief for Haran, and unable to endure the injuries inflicted upon him to make him worship fire, [Note: [Col. 1091D] Gloss. Since the Chaldaeans worshipped fire and others idols, [Col. 1092D] all were idolaters except Abram and his household.] resolved to become a wanderer. He gave Melcham to Nahor as wife, and Sarai to Abram; Abram also adopted Lot, his wife’s brother, as a son, because Sarai was barren. [Col. 1091C]

## CHAPTER XLII. On Terah’s Departure from Chaldaea with His Household

Terah therefore went out with them to go into the land of Canaan, and they came as far as Haran, a city of Mesopotamia (Gen. XI). The Septuagint translators write Charran, because it has an aspiration in both places and they could not render it in Greek; they used *ch* for both aspirations. Hence they also called Noah’s son Habam, Cham. Accordingly one reads Oreb or Choreb, Raab or Rachab.

Mesopotamia received its name from the waters flowing around it. For *meso* means “middle” and *potamos*, “water,” just as Aquilegia is called “bound by waters.” Terah’s days came to two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Abraham’s Years after His Father’s Death and His Departure from His Land
And the Lord said to Abram: “Go forth from your land,” etc. (Gen. 12). Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran. Josephus says: “At the Lord’s command, when he was seventy-five years old, he left Chaldaea in order to migrate into Canaan” [Col. 1092A]. If, then, Abram was seventy-five after his father’s death, it is clear that Thare was more than seventy years old when he begot Abram, as we have said. For if he begot Abram at that age, Abram would have been one hundred and forty-five years old after his father’s death. Augustine, however, said that this was stated by recapitulation. For while his father was still alive, when Thare was one hundred and forty-five and Abram seventy-five, he left Haran, leaving his father and brother there; and on the journey, as he was going into Mesopotamia, the Lord spoke to him and said: “Go forth from your land,” etc.—not because he had not already departed bodily, but because he still had in mind a return to it: as if He said, “You who have gone out in body, go out also in mind.”

Jerome [Col. 1092B] said that the tradition of the Hebrews is true: they place Thare at seventy years old when he begot Abram, and say that Abram left Haran after his father’s death, being then older than Moses says. Yet his years were counted from the time when, by God’s help, he escaped the fire of the Chaldeans, so that his age was reckoned from the time at which he confessed the Lord, despising Chaldean idols.

[Note: [Col. 1092B] Addition 1. Thare was therefore one hundred and thirty years old [Col. 1092C] when he begot Abram; Abram was seventy-five when his father died.]

“Behold,” says Josephus, “the lifespan of human beings was now gradually being cut down, declining until Moses, in whom the Lord confirmed the limit of life that He had established.” Moses indeed died at one hundred and twenty years of age.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On Abram’s arrival in the land of Canaan

[Col. 1092C]

Abram therefore took Sarai and Lot, and “the souls which they had made in Haran” (Gen. 12), that is, the living creatures which he had acquired there; and he entered the land of Canaan. He came to Shechem, which is often corruptly read as Sichar, and to the illustrious valley, which was then called the Pentapolis from the five cities of the Sodomites. It is now called the Salt Sea or the Dead Sea, because nothing lives in it and nothing having life can sink in it; or it is called the Lake of Asphalt—that is, of bitumen, called Judaic bitumen—or the Valley of Salt.

[Note: [Col. 1093A] Addition 1. It is now called the Sea of the Devil, at whose prompting sin was committed there; much alum is found there.]

And the Lord appeared to him and said: “To your seed I will give this land.” There he built an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him. Josephus says of him [Col. 1092D]:

> “He was the first to venture to declare that God is the one Creator of all things; and he prevailed in renewing and changing the opinions which others held concerning God. He inferred this from the conditions of earth and sea, from what happens concerning the sun and moon, and from all that continually occurs in the heavens.”

Berosus also mentions him, saying that in the tenth generation after the Flood there was among the Chaldeans a man skilled in heavenly matters.

Passing on from there, Abram pitched his tent between Bethel and Ai, and there again built an altar to the Lord. Abram went on, advancing farther toward the south; but Moses, for brevity’s sake—or as though it were known—does not say where he went [Col. 1093A]. He dwelt in Damascus. Thus his name is still held in honor in the city of Damascus, and a village is pointed out which is called “the dwelling of Abram.” Hence Nicolaus of Damascus says:

> “Abram reigned in Damascus, arriving as a foreigner with an army from the land above Babylon called Ur of the Chaldeans.”

## CHAPTER XLV. On Abram’s descent into Egypt and his return

There was a great famine in the land of Canaan, and Abram went down into Egypt. Fearing the lust of the Egyptians, lest they should kill him because of his wife’s beauty [Col. 1093B], he said that she was his sister. The woman, exceedingly beautiful, was taken into Pharaoh’s house. The Egyptians treated Abram well because of her. But God restrained the king’s desire, so that he did not touch her, by illness and a disturbance of affairs. When the priests offered sacrifice for the king’s health, they declared that this had happened through God’s wrath because he had wished to wrong a foreigner’s wife.

Pharaoh summoned Abram and said to him: “Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? Behold your wife: take her and go” (Gen. 12). The king commanded his men to conduct him away. For he was very rich in gold and silver, male and female servants, and beasts of burden. He taught the Egyptians arithmetic and the matters pertaining to astronomy, previously unknown to them, from whom these afterward passed to the Greeks.

Abram returned as far as the place where he had pitched his tent, between Bethel and Ai. He divided the land with Lot when their herdsmen quarrelled with one another over pasture. He also granted Lot the choice; and Lot, lifting up his eyes, saw that the region of the Jordan suited him, and settled in the towns of Sodom. Abram, however, went down to the valley of Mamre near Hebron [Col. 1093C] and dwelt there; and there he made an altar to the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Addition 1. Hebron means “marriage” or “of marriages,” because the four patriarchs with their wives were reduced to ashes there. This interpretation is found in a certain gloss on the Acts of the Apostles, which the Master, while reading, consulted so that it might be included in the histories; he said that he had done so.]

Hebron is a city also called Cariatharbe, that is, “the city of four.” For *Arbe* means four, and *Cariath*, city. There Adam the greatest, and Abram, Isaac, and Jacob with their wives were buried. Mamre, Aner, and Eshcol were brothers and allies of Abram. The valley was named after their firstborn [Col. 1093D]. Abram lived there beside an oak, or a terebinth, whose roots are still visible. Josephus called it by name, saying:

> “Abram dwelt near an oak called Agyga, or Ogig, or Dirpsi; there God promised him that He would give him and his seed all the surrounding land, through the four regions of the world.”

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Addition 2. According to Jerome, that tree endured until the time of the Emperor Theodosius; and [Col. 1094A] the present tree is said to have sprung from it. Though dry, it is nevertheless medicinal.]

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Abram’s victory and Melchizedek’s meeting with him

[Col. 1094A]

It came to pass at that time that Amraphel, king of Sennaar—that is, Babylon—etc. (Gen. 14). The lust for domination had already advanced so far that every city had its petty king, most of whom served some greater king. In the end, all were subject to the monarch of the Assyrians.

The five cities of the Sodomites—Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela, which is also Zoar—had five kings. Chedorlaomer, king of the Elamites, had subdued them and made them tributary to himself; for twelve years they served him by paying tribute [Col. 1094B]. But in the thirteenth year they refused to pay him. Therefore, in the fourteenth year, Chedorlaomer, taking with him three kings of Babylon, Pontus, and the nations, assembled an army and came to the illustrious valley, where there were pits of bitumen. By God’s wrath this was afterward turned into the Dead Sea. They ravaged the surrounding lands.

The five kings went out to fight against the four; they turned their backs, many fell, and those who remained fled to the mountains. The victors took all their possessions and captives, including Lot and his goods. And behold, one who had escaped reported this to Abram the Hebrew, or “the one from beyond the river,” because he had come from beyond the Euphrates. Abram counted three hundred and eighteen trained members of his household [Col. 1094C], together with the three aforementioned brothers, Mamre, Aner, and Eshcol; and he pursued them as far as Dan, one of the sources of the Jordan. The town of Dan was named from it and is now called Paneas. For the other source is called Jor; when the two are united, they are called Jordan.

He fell upon them by night, divided his companions into three companies, slaughtered them while they slept, and those who were awake, unable to fight because of drunkenness, fled. Abram pursued them as far as Hobah, which lies to the left of Damascus; and he brought back Lot, the women also, the people, and all their possessions.

The king of Sodom met him at the place called the King’s Valley, on the road to the city of Solyma, or Salem, later called Jerusalem. But Melchizedek, king of Salem [Col. 1094D], offered him bread and wine. Explaining this, as it were, Josephus says:

> “He supplied the army with gifts of hospitality and likewise furnished a great abundance of needed things; and over the meal he blessed God, who had subjected Abram’s enemies to him.”

For he was priest of God Most High. Abram gave him tithes from all the spoils; this is the first occasion on which tithes are recorded as given, whereas firstfruits were given by Abel. The king of Sodom said to him: “Give me the persons; take the rest for yourself.” Abram refused to take even the smallest thing, except what the young men had eaten and the shares of the three brothers who had come with him.

The Hebrews say that this Melchizedek was Shem, Noah’s son, and that he lived until Isaac.

[Note: [Col. 1095A] Addition 1. Josephus says at the end of his book: “The mightiest of the Canaanites, who in the native tongue was called ‘righteous king,’ was the first to offer priesthood or sacrifice to God, built a sanctuary, and established the city which he called Jerusalem. When it was called Solyma, after the Canaanites had been expelled, Leobius, or Theobitus, was the first of the Jews to reign in it.”]

They also say that all firstborn sons from Noah to Aaron were priests: they blessed the people at feasts and offerings [Col. 1095A], and possessed the rights of primogeniture, which will be explained later.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the origin of the Jubilee

They relate that the Jubilee had its beginning from this victory, because of this release of captives. For *jubel* means “release” or “beginning”; hence *jubileus*, “releasing” or “initiating.” It was instituted as the fiftieth year [Col. 1095B] because, according to some, Lot was then fifty years old; or because it was the fiftieth year from the time when the Lord had spoken to Abram on the road, or from the time when he left Haran. Or Abram, skilled in the stars—among which, according to some, he also instructed Zoroaster, the inventor of magical art—knew that atmospheric disturbance caused by planets being elevated or depressed always returns to moderation within fifty years; and what he saw take place in the stars he wished to imitate on earth.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On Abram’s sacrifice after the promise of an heir

After these things, the Lord spoke to Abram, saying: “I am your protector, and your reward exceedingly great.” Abram said: “What will You give me? I shall go [Col. 1095C] without children, and Damascus, son of my steward Eliezer, will be my heir” (Gen. 15). It is as though he said: “What is the promise of land to me when I lack an heir?” They say that Damascus was founded and named after this Damascus, and that he reigned there.

The Lord said to him: “This man shall not be your heir, but one who shall come forth from your womb.” Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Since what was promised was beyond hope, Abram asked for a sign by which he might know it would happen to him—not from distrust, but in hope and inquiring after the manner of its fulfillment. From this especially grew the Jewish custom of seeking signs.
