The Lord said: “Take for me tomorrow a heifer, a she-goat, and a ram, each three years old, and a turtledove and a dove.” It is as though He said: “You shall sacrifice these to Me, and I shall show you a sign.” Taking these animals [Col. 1095D], he divided them in the middle and set the parts opposite each other, one on either side; but he did not divide the birds. While he awaited the Lord’s instruction concerning the manner of sacrifice, birds descended upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away.

When the sun had set, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, along with a great horror, which was part of the sign. It was said to him: “Know beforehand that your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own; strangers will reduce them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years. But you shall go first to your fathers; and in the fourth generation they shall return here.” It is as though He said: “Do not expect that you, or your seed after you, will now reign in this land. After you first die, my promise will be fulfilled four hundred years later.”

This is not to be understood as meaning that they served in Egypt for all those years; rather, the number of years was completed in that affliction. According to Isidore, they are counted from the time when these things were promised to Abram. Augustine counts from Isaac’s birth, because it was said, “your seed.” From the year of Isaac’s birth to the year of the departure from Egypt he counts four hundred and five years. But Scripture passes over the five and reads thus: “Your seed shall be a stranger for four hundred years.” Whether in Canaan or in Egypt, it was a stranger until it received its inheritance through God’s promise. The inserted words, “they will reduce them to slavery and afflict them,” do not refer to the four hundred years.

The statement that they would return in the fourth generation must be understood according to [Col. 1096B] the priestly tribe.

[Note: [Col. 1096C] Addition 1. There were two tribes: the priestly, which took its beginning from Levi; and the other, the royal, from Judah.]

For Levi begot Kohath, who begot Aram, or Amram, who begot Aaron, who begot Eleazar, who departed with Aaron. Do not say that four generations mean four persons, but four successions, so that there are as many generations as there are occurrences of “begot.” Another text has five generations, according to the royal tribe: Judah begot Phares, who begot Efron, who begot Aram, who begot Aminadab, who begot Naason, who departed with his father.

Darkness came, and fire like that of a furnace appeared, passing between those divided pieces and consuming them. Behold the sign. The Lord defined for him the boundaries of the promised land, from the brook Corula, the river of Egypt, as far as the Euphrates, and named its peoples.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On Hagar’s flight and Ishmael’s birth

[Col. 1096C]

Sarai therefore had no children, and said to Abraham: “Go in to my maidservant Hagar; perhaps I may receive children from her” (Gen. 16). He went in to her. When she had conceived, she despised her mistress, while Abraham overlooked it. Sarai said: “You act unjustly toward me. May God judge between me and you.” Abraham replied: “Behold, your maidservant is in your hand; use her as you please.”

Sarai afflicted her, and Hagar fled, wishing to return to her homeland because she was Egyptian. The Angel of the Lord found her as she fled, thirsty and not knowing the way, wandering alone beside the well which is [Col. 1096D] on the road to Shur in the wilderness. He said to her: “Where have you come from, and where are you going?” She replied: “I flee from the presence of my mistress Sarai.” The Angel said: “Return to your mistress and humble yourself beneath her.” And again: “You have conceived and will bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael.”

Here for the first time a name is recorded as foretold by the Lord, which is very rare. “His hand shall be against all, and the hand of all against him; and he shall pitch his tents opposite his brothers.” Yet this is not read of Ishmael himself but of his son Kedar. Nevertheless, this was foretold concerning his race, because the Saracens, wandering with no fixed settlements, attack the peoples adjoining the desert and are attacked by all.

According to Methodius, this was especially to happen [Col. 1097A] when four rulers from Ishmael’s race—whom he also calls “sons of the vine,” perhaps on account of madness, as though drunken—namely Oreb, Zeb, Zebee, and Salmana, came out of the wilderness against the children of Israel (Ps. 82). Defeated by Gideon, they were driven back into the wilderness from which they had emerged.

Where Genesis reads, “He shall be a wild man,” the Hebrew has *Phara*, which means “wild ass.” For this reason, Methodius says: “The wild asses and gazelles will surpass every rage of the beasts from the wilderness, and the number of the meek will be crushed by them.” For he says concerning Ishmael’s children:

> “It shall come to pass that they will come forth yet once more and possess the world for eight weeks of years; and their journey will be called the way of affliction, because the Lord called their father Ishmael a wild ass. In holy places they will kill priests; there they will sleep with women; at the tombs of the saints they will tether their beasts of burden. And this will be because of the wickedness of the Christians then living, of whom it is said: ‘In the last days men shall be lovers of themselves,’ etc. (2 Tim. 3).”

Then will be fulfilled what was spoken through Ezekiel: “Son of man, call the beasts of the field and exhort them, saying: ‘Assemble and come, because I sacrifice a great sacrifice for you. Eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the high gods’” (Ezek. 39).

While the Lord spoke with Hagar, He passed by in a whirlwind, and she saw God’s back parts. She said: “I have seen the back parts of the One who sees me.” She called the place the Well of the Living and Seeing One, because the Lord had seen her [Col. 1097C] and, as it were, restored life to the thirsty woman by showing her the well. Hagar’s well is still shown between Kadesh and Barath. When she had returned, she bore a son and called him Ishmael.

[Note: [Col. 1097C] Addition 1. It is read in the Life of Clement that Abram had another son by Hagar, called Eliesdros, from whom the Persians derived their origin.]

Abram was eighty-seven years old when Ishmael was born.

## CHAPTER L. On the covenant of circumcision and the change of Abram’s and Sarai’s names

After Abram had begun to be ninety-nine years old, the Lord appeared to him, saying: “I will multiply your seed, and you shall keep my covenant,” namely this: “Every male among you shall be circumcised,” etc. (Gen. [Col. 1097D] 17). But before explaining the covenant, He changes his name.

He was called Abram, from *Abba* and *ram*, as though *Abbaram*, that is, “exalted father.” With the addition of the letter *a*, he was called Abraham, as though *Abbaraam*, which means “father of many,” with “nations” understood. The Hebrews, however, say that God added to Abraham the letter *e* from His own tetragrammaton, though it is pronounced *a*: for it is their idiom to write *a* and pronounce *e*, and conversely. The aforementioned *r* is for euphony. Since his name was changed at the time of circumcision, the Hebrews give names when they circumcise.

[Note: [Col. 1098C] Addition 1. This applies to the interpretation, not to the form “Abram.”]

The Lord wished, as it were, by a certain mark to distinguish His people from others, and so imposed circumcision upon them: “Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh [Col. 1098A] of your foreskin. An infant of eight days shall be circumcised, both one born in the household and one bought; the person whose flesh has not been circumcised shall perish from among his people.” No command was given concerning the knife to be used. Why it was performed with a stone knife will be stated later.

It should be noted that a slave was first called *servus* from *servando*, “preserving.” For victors called conquered enemies whom they preserved alive *servi*, slaves. A *verna*, *vernaculus*, or *vernula* is one raised in the household. An *emptitius* is one purchased in his own person. An *originarius* is a serf of the soil, that is, a tenant farmer.

The Lord said to Abraham: “You shall no longer call your wife Sarai, but Sarah.” Some say Sarah’s name was changed because it had previously been written with two *r*’s and then with one, or the reverse; they are mistaken. Rather, while she was called Sarai, that is, “my princess,” and as though the princess of one people, she was called Sarah, that is, “princess” absolutely, as one destined to be princess of all peoples. Observe that, as it appears to us, the letter *i* is removed and none added; but among the Hebrews an *a* is added and written by means of *e*. Some, because *Sarath* in Hebrew means leprosy, wrongly thought that she was first called “leprosy.”

The Lord said: “From her I will give you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac.” Abraham fell upon his face and laughed for joy, clapping his hands, and said: “Do you think a son will be born to a man of a hundred years, and will Sarah, ninety years old, give birth?” The Lord said: “Sarah shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac,” which means “laughter,” from his father’s laughter. Behold, for the second time a future child’s name is announced by the Lord. This is further recorded of two persons in the Old Testament—Samson and Josiah—and in the New Testament of only two, Jesus and John. The Lord also promised him the multiplication of Ishmael.

When the Lord’s speech was finished, Abraham circumcised himself, Ishmael, and all the males of his household. Abraham was then ninety-nine years old, and Ishmael thirteen.

## CHAPTER LI. On the three angels received by Abraham

The Lord appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre. When he raised his eyes, he saw three men; running to meet them, he worshipped one of them (Gen. 18). Josephus says [Col. 1098D] that three angels in human appearance were sent: one to announce to Abraham God’s word concerning his son, and two to overthrow Sodom. Eusebius, however, says: “To Abraham, the first of all the prophets, the Word of God, appearing in human form, promises the calling of the nations.” Thus the Son appeared to him, and Abraham worshipped Him.

But because nowhere is the Father read to have appeared in a subordinate creature, it is said that two angels appeared as figures of the two heralds, Moses and Elijah: one of whom preceded the first coming, while the other will precede the second.

[Note: [Col. 1099B] Addition 1. The Anthropomorphites are heretics from among the Jews who say that God the Father has a human body, whose upper part they place in heaven and whose feet they place on earth.]

Abraham asked them to turn aside to him and refresh themselves by eating a little. They agreed. Judging them to be men, Abraham ordered Sarah to make cakes baked under the ashes from three measures of fine flour. He himself [Col. 1099A] took a choice calf from the herd, butter and milk, and roasted calf, and set them before them. It is probable that he first believed them to be men, for whom he prepared these gifts of hospitality, and afterward proved them to be angels of God. Of the food which they took, one may say that it was consumed in the act of chewing, as water is by the heat of fire. Abraham stood beside them.

[Note: [Col. 1099B] Addition 2. Augustine seems to approve this order in his work on Genesis at this passage: “When Sarah heard it, she laughed.” That is, Abraham first thought them men in whom God nevertheless spoke, because certain signs of divine majesty appeared in them. Therefore, prostrate upon the ground, he worshipped not them but God in them. Later he understood from certain figures, or by divine inspiration, that they were angels. Yet seeing that they had human bodies, he prepared food for them.]

Sarah was behind the tent door. The angel said: “Returning, I shall come to you at this time”—that is, on the same day of the following year—“and Sarah shall have a son.” Hearing this, Sarah laughed. For they were both old, and Sarah’s womanly functions—that is, menstruation—had ceased; when these fail, the power of bearing children fails. If one of them were young, it would not be impossible for offspring to arise from an old and a young person. But both were advanced in age. Moreover [Col. 1099B], Sarah herself was barren. She therefore laughed because she doubted, saying: “After I have grown old, and my lord is aged, shall I give myself to pleasure?”

The Lord said to Abraham: “Why did Sarah laugh?”

[Note: [Col. 1099C] Addition 3. Perhaps she believed it had been said flatteringly because she had fed them well.]

“Is anything difficult for God?” Sarah, terrified, denied that she had laughed. Behold, He who knows hearts could judge with what intention each person had laughed.

## CHAPTER LII. On the two angels descending to Sodom

[Col. 1099C]

When they had risen, those three men turned their eyes toward Sodom, and Abraham walked with them. The Lord said: “I cannot conceal from Abraham what I am about to do” (Gen. 18). He said to him: “The cry of Sodom [Col. 1099D] and Gomorrah has come to me.” Sin “with a cry” means fault joined to freedom: when someone sins openly and according to his own pleasure. Their sin was pride of life and abundance of bread (Ezek. 16), through which they broke out into shameful lust.

He added: “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the cry which has come to me.” He who knows all things left this as an example for us, as though saying: “Do not believe evil reports about people before you have tested them.” Hence a judge cannot punish a crime known to himself alone. Thus it was said: “No one has condemned you; neither will I condemn you” (John 18).

But Abraham, remembering Lot, his brother’s son, drew near to the Lord and said: “Will You destroy the righteous with the wicked?” (Gen. 18). This [Col. 1100A] is not Your way, You who judge all the earth. “If there are fifty righteous men there, will You not spare the people for their sake?” The Lord said: “I will spare all the people for their sake.” Then Abraham, descending gradually, as it were, said: “If there are forty-five? Again, if forty? What if thirty? What if twenty? What if ten?” The Lord said: “I will not destroy them for the sake of ten.”

The Lord departed—that is, He no longer appeared—after He had ceased speaking with Abraham; and Abraham returned to his place. The two angels who had been with the Lord, or others according to some, came to Sodom at evening. Lot was sitting in the city gate, waiting for some guest to arrive. Meeting them, he worshipped and asked them to turn aside into his house. Though they resisted, he urgently compelled them. When they had entered, he made a feast, baked unleavened bread [Col. 1100B], and they ate.

Then the men of the city, from boy to old man, surrounded the house and said to Lot: “Bring out those men here, that we may know them.” He said: “I have two daughters who have not yet known a man; abuse them as you please. Only do no harm to these men, who have entered under the shade of my roof.” For it was the custom of the faithful to protect their guests against every injury. What he said, however, arose from disturbance of mind, not from deliberation. Deliberation, indeed, is when someone does a lesser thing so that he himself may not commit a greater. Yet one must in no way commit a lesser mortal sin lest another commit a greater one.

But they refused and pressed violently upon Lot. Behold, the angels brought Lot inside and shut the door. They struck those men with blindness—not with deprivation of sight [Col. 1100C], but with *acrisia*.

[Note: [Col. 1100D] Addition 1. *Acrisia* is when someone has open eyes and yet does not see, as magicians bring about by enchantments. It also occurs when someone at times has an object in his hand and does not see it; that too is *acrisia*.]

In Latin we may call it *audientia*: it causes one not to see, not everything, but what is needed. With this were struck those who sought Elisha when he was among them (4 Kings 6), and the disciples walking with the Lord to Emmaus (Luke 24). Perhaps this is why we sometimes look for what we are holding in our hand.

The angels said to Lot: “Bring all who are yours out of this city, for we shall destroy this place.” Lot went in to his sons-in-law and said: “Rise and go out, for the Lord will destroy this city.” One should not believe, as Jerome says, those who assert that Lot had other daughters besides the aforementioned virgins, married to husbands and drowned with them. Rather, he calls them sons-in-law because they were to be his sons-in-law. Hence [Col. 1100D] the Hebrew truth has: “Lot went out to the bridegrooms.” They refused to leave, saying that this was Lot’s customary manner of speech, since he always foretold evils.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the overthrow of the Sodomites

In the morning, when Lot delayed to leave, the angels seized him, together with his wife and daughters, and set them outside the city, saying: “Do not look back, but save yourself on the mountain” (Gen. 19). In his confusion, not yet fully trusting the Lord, he said: “I cannot [Col. 1101A] be saved on the mountain, lest evil overtake me and I die.” Perhaps, as an old man, he dreaded the cold of the mountains and the labor of the journey. “But this city is small, and I can flee to it and be saved there.” The Lord said: “I will not overthrow the city for which you have spoken.” Therefore, because he called it small, the city was named Zoar, that is, “small.”

The Hebrews relate that this city was first called Bela, afterward Salisa, and in Isaiah “the frightened heifer” (Isa. 15), because after the overthrow of the other four cities it was swallowed by a dreadful earthquake. It is now called the City of Palms. So long as Lot was in it, the Lord spared it. But, as Jerome says, Lot, fearing its customary earthquake, went out and remained on the mountain.

After Lot had left Sodom, the Lord rained sulfur and fire upon those cities [Col. 1101B]. The Lord, being on earth, rained them from Himself who was in heaven: He who judged—that is, punished—did so from Him who commanded. He rained these things so that the earth might be dry forever, with no hope of producing again. Thus He punished these people more severely than the first sinners by the Flood. For although they had exceeded the measure of sin, they nevertheless sinned, as it were, naturally; and He overthrew all, even the little children, for their parents’ sins. In this provision was made for them, lest by living long they should follow their fathers’ examples. There is some good in not being guilty when one cannot be glorious. For it is advantageous not to be poor for one who cannot be king.

Lot’s wife looked back and was changed into a pillar of salt, which Josephus says he saw and which still remains.

[Note: [Col. 1101D] Addition 1. This lake separates Judaea from Arabia—not the greater Arabia, but that which formerly was the pathless and waterless wilderness in which the children of Israel spent forty years. Josephus says that because of its extraordinary buoyancy, even very heavy objects thrown into it are borne upward. Therefore Vespasian ordered some persons, with their hands bound behind their backs, to be thrown high into it; all were driven back upward, as though by a breath of air, and floated on the surface.]

The region was thus turned into a salty and barren lake, called the Dead Sea [Col. 1101C], because neither fish nor birds live in it as in other waters. It does not admit a ship, nor does it support any material so that it may float entirely upon the surface, unless it is coated with bitumen for the sake of people living within it. For everything without life sinks to the depths. If you immerse something living by some art, it leaps back up. A burning lamp floats; when extinguished, it sinks. In many places it casts up black masses of bitumen, and for this reason is called the Lake of Asphalt, or Asphaltitis. It is also said that apples growing on the trees around it are green until their color ripens; if, when ripe, you cut them open, you find ashes within. Therefore, as Josephus says, the ash of the Sodomitic land bears witness. It is also called the Valley of Salt. Perhaps salt is produced there, or salt stones are found around it [Col. 1101D].

## CHAPTER LIV. On Lot’s incest

Lot left Zoar and remained in a cave on the mountain with his two daughters (Gen. 19). Lot’s daughters had learned that the world was to be consumed by fire; and they suspected that something like what had occurred in Noah’s days had happened [Col. 1102A], and that they alone had been preserved with their father as survivors in order to restore the human race. They therefore formed a plan. Softening their father’s grief and sternness with wine, each, though a virgin, conceived on a separate night by her unaware father; nor did they repeat it.

The Hebrews, however, mark this above as incredible, because the nature of things does not allow anyone to have intercourse unknowingly. Or it is said that he did not know that she was his daughter, thinking her to be his wife. It is also said that conception at defloration is impossible. For this reason Antichrist will say that he is the son of a virgin.

The elder daughter bore a son and called him Moab, father of the Moabites. The younger bore a son and called him Ammon, father of the Ammonites. Moab means “from the father”; by this name the mother openly proclaimed her father’s incest. Ammon means “son of my people.” She concealed it somewhat, as though he were the son of some man from among my people.

Jerome says that the daughters may be excused because they believed the human race had perished; concern for posterity excused the impiety of incest to a considerable degree, though not entirely. But this does not excuse their father; his unbelief was the cause of the incest. Strabus says of the same matter: “Lot is inexcusable: first, because he did not believe the angel that he could be saved in Zoar; then because he became drunk, and sin was the cause of sin.”

## CHAPTER LV. On Abram’s sojourn with Abimelech, king of Gerar
Abraham departed from the valley of Mamre for the southern country and sojourned at Gerar, between [Col. 1102C] Kadesh, whence the waters of contradiction flowed, and Shur. There, again representing Sarah as his sister, he repeated the earlier deception out of fear; but Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for her and took her (Gen. 20). In this, the remarkable vigor of her beauty is noted: even at ninety years of age she could still be loved. But, as Josephus says, by God’s will the king fell ill, so that he would not touch her. At the end of this chapter, however, another punishment is mentioned: namely, that God had closed every womb of Abimelech’s household because of Sarah, so that no female in his house could meanwhile conceive.

When the physicians despaired, he fell asleep and heard from the Lord that these afflictions had been brought upon him because of the foreigner’s wife. God commanded him to restore the wife to her husband, because he was a prophet and would pray [Col. 1102D] for him, and he would live. Rising at once, he summoned his servants, summoned Abraham also, and said to him: “What have you done to us? What did you see that made you do this?” Abraham said: “I thought that the fear of God was not in this place and that they would kill me on account of my wife. Besides, she truly is my sister, the daughter of my father.”

Here “my father” is distinguished—namely, his own father. What follows is understood as “mine,” that is, “who is my brother,” or: “the daughter of my father and not of my mother”; that is, she is my niece and kinswoman on my father’s and my brother’s side, not on my sister’s side. Hence another translation reads: “She is my sister by her father, not by her mother.” For just as they called male relatives brothers, so they called female relatives sisters. He called Aram, his brother, his father because Aram was older than he, following the manner of speech by which we call elders fathers [Col. 1103A] and younger persons sons. And because kinship through men is customarily considered more worthy and more strongly felt than kinship through women, he called his female relative by the more honorable designation—sister rather than niece.

Or he pretended that she was his father’s daughter and nevertheless did not lie, just as the Lord did not lie when he pretended to be going farther (Luke 24); especially since he is believed to have said this at the Lord’s command, and was thus a reporter of the Lord’s words, just as Elisha concealed himself from those who did not recognize him. Some, however, say that Terah, after Abraham’s mother had died and Aram had died, took his son’s wife and begot Sarah by her. Thus here she is called Terah’s daughter according to the flesh, and above Aram’s daughter according to the raising up of seed, because Aram left only a male child.

Abraham prayed for him, and he was healed; [Col. 1103B] his wife and maidservants also bore children. Abimelech gave Abraham gifts and land to dwell in wherever he chose. But to Sarah he said: “Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver for you. This shall be a covering of the eyes to you before all who are with you”—that is, a reminder of shame, because you have been caught in a lie. Hence he adds by way of explanation: “Wherever you go, remember that you were exposed.” Or it is an elegant mockery: “This shall be a covering of the eyes to you,” that is, provision for burial. As though he said: “You are an old woman, near to death; yet you lied and deceived. Take this, then, for the expenses of your funeral.” Such funerals were customarily conducted at great expense, especially among the Jews. Or the money was for buying veils, that you might cover your face and not be loved.

## Chapter LVI. On the birth of Isaac and the expulsion of Hagar with her son

[Col. 1103C]

The Lord visited Sarah; she conceived and bore a son, and Abraham circumcised him on the eighth day (Gen. 21). From that time Jews likewise circumcise after the same number of days. Arabs, however, do so after thirteen years, because Ishmael, founder of that people, was circumcised at that age. He called him Isaac, that is, “laughter,” because the Lord had given laughter—that is, unexpected joy—to his parents.

The boy grew and was weaned at the age of three. His father made a great feast on that day, because it was then that the son first came to his father’s table. While Ishmael and Isaac were playing together, the older injured the younger. The mother perceived persecution in the play: namely, that after their father’s death the elder would wish to rule over the younger. Or, as the Hebrews relate, Ishmael compelled him to worship [Col. 1103D] clay images which he had made. Since this displeased the mother, she said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son.”

Abraham took this hard and concealed his intention; but the Lord said to him: “Hear Sarah’s voice.” Taking bread and a skin of water, he put them on Hagar’s shoulder and gave her the boy. When the water was consumed in the wilderness and the boy was failing from thirst, the mother threw the boy under a tree and sat at a distance, as far as a bow can shoot.

> [Note: [Col. 1104A] Addition 1. That is, she left him lying as if at the distance of a throw; not that she carried him when he was already thirteen years old. Or the statement is made by recapitulation.]

So that she would not see her son dying, she wept; and God heard the voice of the boy—that is, the mother’s weeping for the boy. The angel said to the mother: “Rise; take the boy.” God opened her eyes, and she saw a well. She gave the boy drink and, having filled the skin, went away. The boy grew, lived in the wilderness of Paran, and became an archer. His mother took for him a wife [Col. 1104A] from the land of Egypt. By her were born to him twelve sons, chiefs of their tribes, whose names are celebrated in towns, districts, and tribes.

Nebaioth, the firstborn, is more prominently named; after him, the part of Arabia extending from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is called Nabataea. Kedar was the second, after whom Kedar in the wilderness is named; Dumah the sixth, after whom the region of Duma is named; Tema the ninth, after whom Tema to the south is named; and Cethuma the last, after whom Cethema to the east is named.

## Chapter LVII. On the well of the oath

[Col. 1104B]

At that time Abimelech saw that Abraham had become numerous, feared him, and came to him with Phicol, commander of his army. He said: “Swear to me by God that you will not harm me or my descendants, but will always deal with me according to the kindness which I have shown you” (Gen. 21). Abraham brought them to the well which God had shown Hagar, a well Abraham had dug before Hagar was expelled. But Abimelech’s servants had taken it from Abraham and had made it a watering-place in the wilderness for flocks which grazed far from his dwelling in the desert.

Abimelech restored the well to him. But, as testimony that Abraham himself had dug the well and that Abimelech restored what had been taken away, Abraham gave the king seven ewe-lambs and called the well Beersheba, that is, [Col. 1104C] “the seventh well.” For *sabee* means “seven” in Hebrew, and there they both struck a covenant. Therefore they think it was also called Beersheba, that is, “the well of the oath”; for *sabee* likewise means “oath” in Hebrew. Josephus, however, interprets Beersheba as “covenant of the well.” The surrounding region also took the name Beersheba from the well.

Abraham planted a grove around the well and remained there many days as a settler, not as a permanent inhabitant. For Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles that he received no inheritance there, not even the space of a foot (Acts 7).

## Chapter LVIII. On the offering of the ram in Isaac’s place

While he lived in Beersheba, and Isaac was, as Josephus says, twenty-five years old, the Lord said to Abraham: “Take your only son Isaac, whom [Col. 1104D] you love; go to the land of vision, and offer him to me as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall show you.”

By “land of vision” he meant that mountainous part of Judea, because it can itself be seen from afar and one can see far from it. Isaiah also calls it “the valley of vision” (Isa. 22). On the summit of the mountains of Judea was a more prominent hill, called Mount Moriah, which God showed Abraham for sacrificing his son. The Hebrews relate that the Temple was later built there, and the altar was made on the spot where Abraham made his altar and where David saw the angel sheathing his sword on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Hence Isaiah says: “The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be on the summit of the mountains, and all nations shall flow to it” (Isa. 2). The Lord also commanded the Jews not to sacrifice [Col. 1105A] for themselves in every place, but only in the place which the Lord would show them (Deut. 34).

Abraham therefore rose in the night, telling no one what he intended to do, saddled his ass, took two young men and his son, and traveled for two days. On the third day, lifting up his eyes, he saw the place at a distance. This proves that those who place it between Bethel and Ai are mistaken, for that place is not a day’s journey from Mount Moriah. Taking the wood and fire, and leaving the young men below with the ass, he went up alone with his son.

His son said: “Look, here are the fire and the wood; where is the victim for the burnt offering?” His father answered: “God will provide himself a victim.” He set up the altar, laid on the wood, and applied the fire. Josephus reports the father’s words to the boy: because, by God’s will, he had entered [Col. 1105B] the world wondrously, so by God’s will he had to leave it wondrously. The Lord had judged him worthy to end his human life not by illness, war, or any suffering, but to summon his soul to himself with prayers and sacrifices, and would raise him to fulfill the promises. Thus Isaac willingly approached both the altar and death.

Of this Alcuin says:

> [Note: [Col. 1106A] Addition 1. Alcuin was the teacher of King Charles and abbot of Saint Martin of Tours.]

“With an unwavering mind Abraham wished to sacrifice his son, praiseworthy both in the steadfastness of his offering and in his faith that his son would be raised.”

But when he seized the sword to sacrifice his son, the angel cried to him: “Do not stretch out your hand against the boy. Now I know that you fear the Lord.” For the Lord did not thirst for the boy’s blood, but wished [Col. 1105C] it to be known how greatly Abraham feared the Lord. Abraham saw behind him a ram caught by its horns among the bushes, and offered it in place of his son.

The Hebrew has: “caught by its horns in the thickets, *Sabech*”; and *Sobech* is a kind of shrub. Eusebius erred in saying that *Sabech* was a goat standing upright to crop leaves. He thus called the ram *Sabech*, that is, as it were, an upright goat. Rabanus says that it was not newly created but brought from elsewhere by an angel. Abraham called the place: “The Lord sees.” Even now, as a proverb, Jews in distress say: “On the mountain the Lord will see,” as though saying: “As he looked upon Isaac on the mountain, so may he look upon us in this affliction.”

The Hebrews say that the day of Isaac’s deliverance was the first day of September. They therefore keep it as a feast [Col. 1105D] and sound animal horns in memory of the ram. The Lord swore by himself that Isaac’s seed would be multiplied and that land would be given to his seed. On the following day Abraham returned to Beersheba. He was told that Milcah had borne eight sons to his brother Nahor: the firstborn Uz, from whose line Job descended, as it is written: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job” (Job 1); and Uz’s brother, from whose line came Balaam, who, according to the Hebrews, is called Elihu the Buzite in Job.

Those who say that Job was of Esau’s line are therefore mistaken. For the statement at the end of his book that it was translated from Syrian speech, and that he himself was the fourth from Esau, is not found in the Hebrew. By his concubine Roma, otherwise Rema, Nahor had four sons.

## Chapter LIX. On Sarah’s death

[Col. 1106A]

Abraham returned to the valley of Mamre. Sarah died at one hundred and twenty-seven years of age and was buried at Hebron in the double cave (Gen. 24), which Abraham bought from Ephron for four hundred silver shekels, the Hittites—that is, the people of the land—interceding for him. The double cave was a rock naturally or artificially containing two caves.

> [Note: [Col. 1106B] Addition 1. This is the same as Kiriath-arba, that is, the city of the four patriarchs: Isaac, Abraham, Jacob, and Adam.]

Abraham bought it as a burial-place for his family. Men were buried in the upper cave and women in the lower. Yet Adam and Eve had already been buried there. Abraham did not sin in buying it, nor did Ephron in selling it—just as one does not sin today by buying [Col. 1106B] a field to make a cemetery, unless perhaps the issue was that the first-created human beings were buried there. Jerome nevertheless says that Ephron deserves censure and that therefore his name was changed from Ephron to Ephran.

## Chapter LX. On Eliezer’s embassy to Mesopotamia

Abraham was old and said to Eliezer, the steward of his house: “Put your hand under my thigh and swear to me by the God of heaven and earth that you will not take for my son Isaac a wife from the daughters of the peoples among whom I dwell; but you shall go to my kindred and take a wife for him from there. Yet if any woman among them is unwilling to follow you, you shall not be bound by the oath.” The servant swore, placing his hand under Abraham’s thigh.

The Hebrews relate that he swore by Abraham’s sanctification—that is, by circumcision. But since it says “under the thigh,” we say that he swore by Abraham’s seed, that is, by Christ, whom Abraham knew would be born from him. Thus Abraham said: “Swear to me by the God of heaven and earth.” His desire that the hand be placed under his thigh indicates that Christ’s flesh would surpass all others.

Eliezer therefore took ten camels and departed, carrying with him goods of every kind belonging to his master, especially things which he knew to be rare in the land to which he was traveling. He went to Mesopotamia, to Charbem, [Col. 1106C] the city of Nahor.

> [Note: [Col. 1107C] Addition 1. Or to Haran: for the Hebrews aspirated vowels both before and after.]

According to Josephus, the journey required much time and labor: in winter Mesopotamia has deep mud, in summer a lack of water, and in wooded places robbers. He made the camels kneel by the well before the city, unwilling to take them in unwatered. When women went out in the evening to draw water, he prayed that among them the wife of his master might be found, if any woman of that people was owed to his master; and that she might be recognized by this sign: while others refused water, she herself would offer it to him when he asked.

And behold, Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel, came down, filled her pitcher, and, while the others turned away, gave water to the traveler. She added: “I will draw water for your camels also.” Having drawn the water, she poured it into the troughs and gave the camels drink. Silently observing her, to see whether she was suitable for his master, he asked whose daughter she was and whether there was room in her father’s house for him to stay.

> [Note: [Col. 1107C] Addition 2. Lest perhaps she should be one-eyed, hunchbacked, crooked-nosed, or large-nosed.]

When he learned that she was the daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor and Milcah, and Laban’s sister, he brought out golden earrings and bracelets and gave them to her. The girl ran to her mother’s house [Col. 1107A] and reported what she had heard.

> [Note: [Col. 1107C] Addition 3. The fact that it does not say “her father’s house” is taken to show [Col. 1107D] that he was dead, as Josephus held.]

Laban came out, brought the man into the lodging, unsaddled the camels, gave them straw and fodder, washed the guests’ feet, and set bread before them. Eliezer refused to eat until he had spoken the words for which he had come. When he had identified himself as the servant of Abraham, their brother, praised Abraham highly, and set before them Abraham’s request, the oath he himself had sworn, and his prayer at the well answered by the Lord, Laban and Bethuel replied:

> [Note: [Col. 1107D] Addition 4. That is, his wife, acting under the charge she had received from him when he was dying, if it is true that he was dead, as Josephus says.]

“This matter—namely, Abraham’s request and your prayer—has come from the Lord. We cannot speak to you anything contrary to [Col. 1107B] his will. Behold, Rebekah is before you: take her, and let her be the wife of your master.”

But it should be noted that Josephus says Bethuel had already died, that the maiden was under the care of her mother and brother, and that at the well, when asked whose daughter she was, she had already mentioned her father’s death. Moses too appears thus far to mean that she had no father even then. Above, he said: “The girl ran to her mother’s house.” Perhaps the mother is here called father because she now declared the father’s command concerning the giving of his daughter, which he had left when dying. For he could have designated that she was to be given to his own kin.

Hearing this, Abraham’s servant worshiped the Lord who had directed his journey. He brought out gold and silver vessels and clothing, gave them to Rebekah, and gave gifts also to her mother and her brother [Col. 1107C]. Rising in the morning, the servant asked to be dismissed, pleading the delay he had made on the road and his master’s old age. When they asked him to remain with them ten days, he refused. They said: “Let us call the girl and ask her will.” When they asked whether she wished to go, she said: “I will go.” Here a woman’s consent is first recorded as having been sought; afterward it was held by law that it must be sought. And they sent her away.

## Chapter LXI. On Rebekah’s arrival to Isaac

[Col. 1107D]

At that time Isaac lived at Gerar and was perhaps walking along the road that leads to the well of the Living One who sees. He had gone out to meditate in the field, perhaps on account of the servant’s delay (Gen. 24). Another text has “to exercise,” perhaps laboring in the field or undertaking some work to relieve the time. When Rebekah saw Isaac and learned that he was her husband, she descended from the camel, took a *teristrum*, or white mantle, covered and adorned herself. A *teristrum* is a kind of Arabian women’s garment. Isaac [Col. 1108A] brought her into his mother’s tent and loved her so deeply that her presence moderated the grief occasioned by his mother’s death.

## Chapter LXII. On Abraham’s death after he fathered children by Keturah

Abraham took another wife, named Keturah (Gen. 27). The Hebrews say that Keturah is an appellative name, meaning “joined” or “united.” They say that she was Hagar: previously a concubine, she became a wife after Sarah’s death, changing from one not joined to one joined, lest the old man be accused of lusting after a new marriage. Josephus, however, says that Abraham took her before he sent for his son’s wife. She bore him six children; for a young woman can bear children by an old man.

While he still lived, Abraham separated them from Isaac to the eastern region, [Col. 1108B] and gave Isaac everything that he possessed, but bestowed gifts on the others. Nevertheless Keturah’s sons called themselves Saracens after the name of a free woman. They first occupied Trachonitis, Phoenicia, and Arabia as far as the borders of the Red Sea.

Josephus reports that one of them was the father of Afer, who established his camp in Libya; his descendants lived there and named it Africa after him. He also says that the prophet Eldeus, also called Malcus or Malchus, wrote a history of the Jews, just as Moses wrote one. He reports that this writer said Syria was named after one of Keturah’s sons, Surim or Syrim; Africa, after another, called Apher. Hercules assisted this Apher when he went down into Libya, married his daughter Ethaea, [Col. 1108C] and fathered Dodorim by her, whose son was Phorom.

Abraham’s days were one hundred and seventy-five years, and he declined and died:

> [Note: [Col. 1108C] Addition 1. “Failing” occurs in the text; and in the Gloss there is Jerome’s comment on this passage, saying that “failing” was wrongly added in the Septuagint, both because it is not so in the Hebrew truth and because it seems unfitting to say of so great a patriarch that he failed or diminished. Since our text contains “failing,” concerning which Jerome criticizes the Septuagint, it is evident from this and many other passages that this is not our pure translation of Jerome. Rather, perhaps, it is some earlier version which he compiled from Greek into Latin out of the Septuagint translation and other translations. Because that version perhaps did not seem sufficiently authoritative, he set his hand to make a pure translation from Hebrew into Latin, which we possess only in the Twelve Prophets. Or perhaps it may be said that ours is that Vulgate which was miraculously discovered at Jerusalem.]

He died and was gathered to his people in the bosom of hell. Ishmael and Isaac buried him in the double cave with his wife.

## Chapter LXIII. On the rise of kingdoms

[Col. 1108D]

In Abraham’s eleventh year, Ninus died. His wife Semiramis, so that she could reign after him, married her own son, whom she had borne by Ninus, and bore by him a son who also enlarged Babylon. In Abraham’s seventy-fifth year, the promise was made to him. In his eighty-sixth year, Ishmael was born to him. In his one hundredth year, [Col. 1109A] Isaac was born to him. In his one hundred and thirty-seventh year, Sarah died.

## Chapter LXIV. Another digression

The kingdom of the Assyrians arose in the twenty-fifth year of Serug, Abraham’s great-grandfather, under Belus, and continued until the seventh year of Uzziah king of Judah, for 1,300 years—others say 402 years—through thirty-seven kings, down to Sardanapalus, who was the first to invent cushions. After him the kingdom was transferred to the Medes.

The kingdom of the Sicyonians arose in the twenty-fourth year of Nahor, Abraham’s grandfather, under Euryalus, otherwise Aegialus, and continued until the seventeenth year of Eli, priest and judge of Israel, for [Col. 1109B] 971 years and through thirty-one kings, down to Zeusippus. After him the priests of Charmi governed Sicyonia. Sicyonia is the region formerly called Apia and afterwards the Peloponnese.

Before Abraham’s time there had already been fifteen dynasties in Egypt. The Egyptians call supreme authority a “dynasty.”

> [Note: [Col. 1109C] Addition 1. A dynasty properly means a principate that continues in a particular province by virtue of choosing an emperor or another ruler who is preeminent in that province. For example, emperors were once chosen in Saxony, and this arrangement continued there, and then for a long time in Franconia; afterwards in Bavaria, and now in Swabia. These are nevertheless the principal provinces of the German land, though many others adjoin them. What has been said of these is to be understood likewise of others.]

From Abraham’s birth, the sixteenth dynasty was held by the Thebans; the seventeenth by the Shepherds, so-called kings; and the eighteenth by the Thebans, or Thiopolites, who were also Pharaohs, through seventeen kings. Dynasties also often changed, passing from the families of certain kings to others, down to Cambyses, son of Cyrus, under whom they first ruled Egypt independently.

## Chapter LXV. On Ishmael’s death

[Col. 1109C]

Ishmael also lived one hundred and thirty-seven years and died (Gen. 25). The Hebrews relate that he died of dysentery “before all his brothers,” that is, he died while his brothers were still living. His descendants lived from Havilah to [Col. 1109D] Shur. Havilah is India, so called from Havilah, Noah’s grandson. Shur is the wilderness between Kadesh and Barath, extending through the desert as far as the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt.

## Chapter LXVI. On Rebekah’s travail in bearing twins

The narrative continues with Isaac. Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah as his wife. She was found barren for a long time. Since Isaac knew of the promise made to his father that his seed would be multiplied through himself, he prayed to the Lord that he would fulfill what he had promised. The woman conceived, having two children in her womb.

But when she drew near to giving birth, the little ones collided in her womb. The Seventy Interpreters rendered it, “they played” or “kicked”; Aquila, “they were crushed together”; Symmachus, “they were borne on the surface,” in the likeness [Col. 1110A] of a ship lacking its proper weight. The children moved in confusion, so that each appeared in turn able to emerge first at birth. This should not be understood, as some have thought, as resulting from the narrowness of a mother’s womb scarcely able to contain twins, but solely from God’s will, already showing in those not yet born what would occur in the grown men. It prefigured the birthright which one possessed by nature but the other received by grace, and the future conflict even between their descendants.

Jacob is believed to have been sanctified already in the womb; and this movement prefigured that there would be no agreement of Christ with Belial (2 Cor. 6). The mother, grievously afflicted, wished she had not conceived and, almost despairing of childbirth, went to consult the Lord. Yet, since no place, manner, or persons through whom to consult the Lord had yet been instituted, perhaps she went to Mount Moriah, where Abraham had made an altar to the Lord; and, after victims had been sacrificed, lay upon their skins and received an oracle in a dream. Perhaps, according to the custom of the nations which she had seen among her relatives, she put beneath her head a kind of laurel which they call a tripod, and lay down amid the branches of the tree called chaste-tree, so that, sleeping, she might not experience phantasmal visions of the head. Or she consulted Melchizedek, who was still alive.

However she did so, she received this answer from the Lord: “Two nations are in your womb,” that is, the fathers of two nations which will later be divided and fight one another; “and the greater shall serve the lesser.” This was not said of the children, since the older is always set over the younger, but of the peoples. For the Idumaeans, who would descend from Esau, were tributary to David, who descended from Jacob. Unless perhaps Esau is understood to have served Jacob when he persecuted him, as a file contributes to iron, a furnace to gold, and a flail to grain.

When she bore the two, the one who came out first was red and entirely hairy like a skin; on this account he was called Seir. For the Hebrews call hairiness *Sciron*. His proper name was Esau, that is, “strong.” Immediately the other came out, holding his brother’s heel in his hand, as though wishing to draw his brother back from the birthright; and on this account he was called Jacob, that is, “supplanter.” Isaac was therefore sixty years old when the children were born to him. Abraham was still alive [Col. 1110D] and survived fifteen more years. For after the hundred years Abraham had lived when Isaac was born, fifteen years still remained to Abraham’s life.

We have said this because Josephus says: “Moreover, after Abraham’s death, Isaac’s wife conceived,” and perhaps calls this his death when his body had become wholly exhausted and he ceased to beget children. The wording of the text itself indicates that this is not said by recapitulation.

## Chapter LXVII. Third digression

In the same year in which Isaac’s twins were born, the kingdom of the Argives arose under Inachus, father of Isis, its first king. It continued until the fifteenth year of Deborah and Barak, judges of Israel. It lasted down to Acrisius, the last ruler, through fourteen kings and for 544 years—others say 564. Although Perseus did not deliberately kill Acrisius, he nevertheless fled Argos in fear and transferred the kingdom to Mycenae. If you read in histories that this kingdom proceeded from Inachus down to Telenus, it means that descendants of Inachus’ family ruled down to that time, and that the kingdom was then given to Danaus, who was not of royal stock.

## Chapter LXVIII. On Esau’s sale of the birthright

When Isaac’s sons had grown up, Esau became a hunter, while Jacob was a farmer and a shepherd who lived in tents. Their father loved Esau, both because he was the firstborn and because he gladly ate his game. Their mother loved Jacob, both for his simplicity and through God’s inspiration.

It happened [Col. 1111B] that Jacob had cooked a lentil stew. Esau returned exhausted from the field and said: “Give me some of this red food, for I am exceedingly weary.” It is as though he said: “I am hungry and, in my weariness, cannot manage to prepare food for myself.” Jacob said to him: “Sell me your birthright.” Esau, setting little value on the birthright and thinking that he would die unless he ate immediately, gave Jacob his birthright for a meal of lentils. He swore that he would hold such a sale valid (Gen. 25). Because lentils are tawny, in Hebrew this is *Edom*, after whom the region was later called Idumaea.

The birthright consisted of certain dignities which firstborn sons held within their kindred until Aaron. The firstborn had a special garment which he wore only when offering sacrifice and when receiving the final blessing from his father. At solemnities and feasts, he blessed the younger members; and on such occasions he received a double portion of food. They also relate that in the division of the inheritance he likewise received twice as much.

## Chapter LXIX. On Isaac’s descent to Gerar

When a famine arose, Isaac wished to go to Egypt but remained at Gerar by God’s command. Through friendship for Abraham, Abimelech received him. Following his father’s example, Isaac said of his wife: “She is my sister.”

> [Note: [Col. 1112C] Addition 1. This appears to be said by recapitulation: that is, it happened before it is narrated here. For Abimelech does not seem to have lived so long, namely, beyond the aforesaid sale.]

Perhaps after many days, Abimelech saw Isaac through a window playing with his wife. He summoned him and said: “Why have you imposed upon us?” (Gen. 16). Here *imponere* is used absolutely, meaning to practice an imposture—that is, to commit deceit. The sense is: “Why did you deceive us? Why did you lie that she was your sister? You could have brought great evil upon us if someone, considering your wife free of a husband, had known her.” He said to his people: “Whoever touches this man’s wife shall surely die.”

Isaac sowed in that land and found a hundredfold, estimated—that is, he reckoned that, according to his memory, the seed he had formerly sown had yielded a hundredfold. This could not have been true of one kind of crop alone; perhaps he was increased a hundredfold in every kind of wealth. Hence another translation reads: “In that year he found a hundredfold.”

For this reason the Philistines envied him and stopped up the wells which his father had dug, filling them with earth. Abimelech too, fearing him, said: “Depart from us, [Col. 1112A] for you have become more powerful than we.” Isaac departed and came to a field called Phata, that is, “valley.” He lived beside a channel through which a torrent sometimes flowed, and there he cleared out the wells which his father had formerly dug in that same place but which the Philistines had stopped up after his death.

When he found living water, the shepherds of Gerar disputed with him, saying: “The water is ours.” He therefore called the well Eschom, that is, “accusation” or “quarrel.” Moving from there, he dug another well, and they disputed over that too. He therefore called it Satanam, that is, “adversary” or “hostilities.” As Josephus says, he left the work on both wells unfinished, unwilling to contend with the natives, awaiting and hoping for their goodwill [Col. 1112B] and permission.

Departing from there, he dug a third well, over which they did not dispute. Therefore he called it Rehoboth, that is, “breadth,” because he had expanded and grown in the land. From that place he went up to Beersheba. The Lord appeared to him that night, promising what he had promised his father. Isaac built an altar, called upon the Lord’s name there, and ordered his servants to dig a well there. It is probable that they cleared out Abraham’s well.

At that time Abimelech and Phicol, commander of the army, came to him; and, swearing to one another, they established a covenant. On that same day Isaac’s servants returned to him, reporting that they had found water in the well which they had dug. He called it Beersheba, that is, “the well of satiation” or “abundance.” This name was given to the city down to the present [Col. 1112C] day.

Note that this name differs slightly in sound and spelling from the name Abraham had formerly given it. For *sabee*, written with the Hebrew letter *sin*, means “seventh” or “oath” and has a harsher sound; but the form written with Greek sigma means “satiation” and has a softer sound.

## Chapter LXX. Fourth digression

At that time Phoroneus, son of Inachus and Niobe, first gave laws to Greece and established the practice of trying cases before a judge. He named the designated place of judgment a *forum* after [Col. 1112D] himself. His sister Isis sailed to Egypt, gave the Egyptians certain rudiments of letters, and taught them much concerning agriculture. Hence, since she was called Io, the Egyptians called her Isis, because in their language it means “earth.” Therefore after her death she was admitted among the gods in Egypt.

Phoroneus’s son, also called Apis, sailed to Egypt at the same time. They say that he was Isis’s husband; he too was deified by the Egyptians and called Serapis.

## Chapter LXXI. On Esau’s wives

Esau, at forty years of age, took as wives Judith and Bethsameth (Gen. 26), daughters of powerful men among the Canaanites, acting as his own master in the choice of wives. Both offended [Col. 1113A] Isaac’s and Rebekah’s hearts. Although Isaac did not wish those native to his province to be joined to his kindred, he nevertheless decided that it was better to remain silent.

## Chapter LXXII. On Jacob’s blessings
Isaac grew old and could not see. And he said to Esau: “Prepare for me food from your hunting, that I may eat, and that my soul may bless you before I die” (Gen. 27). When Esau had gone out hunting, Rebecca said to Jacob: “I heard your father speaking thus and thus with your brother Esau. Bring me quickly, therefore, two choice kids, so that I may prepare for your father foods which he gladly eats, and that he may bless you in Esau’s place.” He went and brought them, and gave them to his mother. When she had prepared the food, she clothed Jacob in Esau’s very fine garments, which, as we have said, the firstborn used. Jacob feared [Col. 1113B] that, if detected by his father, he would receive a curse rather than a blessing. His mother then wrapped the skins of the kids around his hands and neck, so that they might imitate the appearance of his hairy brother. In other respects they were very much alike, like twins. Jacob brought the food he had received to his father, saying: “I am Esau; eat of my hunting, that your soul may bless me.”

[Note: [Col. 1114A] Addition 1. That is, “I am he to whom the birthright and the blessing belong,” as they formerly belonged to Esau. Nor does he lie, any more than Christ lies when he says that John is Elijah—not personally, but in resemblance, as Gregory says in a Homily.]

Isaac said to him: “Come near me, that I may touch you and test whether you are my son Esau or not.” Having felt him, he said: “The voice indeed is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.” When he had eaten and drunk wine, he kissed his son and blessed him, saying: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth, an abundance of grain, wine, and oil.” In these three things the entire fertility of the earth is customarily understood: through [Col. 1113C] grain, food; through wine, drink; through oil, prepared dishes. And he added: “Let peoples and tribes serve you; be lord of your brothers. Let him who curses you be cursed, and let him who blesses you be filled with blessings.”

Note that the three things promised in the blessing—abundance, power, and the birthright—belong to the present time. But the fourth, namely blessing, belongs to the future; and therefore it is customarily said in our priests’ blessings. Jacob was blessed according to the words, not according to his father’s intention, just as a bishop ordains another man whom he believes to be his own candidate, and the man is nevertheless ordained.

The father had scarcely finished speaking when Jacob departed and Esau came, bringing food to his father and requesting a blessing from him. [Col. 1113D] Isaac was exceedingly alarmed; and in this ecstasy he saw in the spirit that this had been done by the Lord, and understood the significance of the pious deception. Therefore, not becoming angry but confirming what he had done, he said: “Your brother came deceitfully and received your blessing, and he shall be blessed.” Esau said to him: “Jacob has rightly been called Jacob. Behold, this is the second time he has supplanted me—that is, deceived me twice: first by taking the birthright, and then by stealing the blessing.”

When he too asked his father for a blessing, and pressed him urgently while his father hesitated over how to bless him, Isaac, moved with pity, said: “In the richness of the earth and in the dew from heaven above shall your blessing be”; and so it was. For Idumaea is pasture-land. And, prophesying concerning his descendants, he added: “You shall live by the sword,” that is, you shall be warlike, “and you shall serve your brother,” namely when [Col. 1114A] Idumaea was made tributary to the house of Israel; “but the time will come when you shall shake his yoke from your neck.” This was fulfilled when the Idumaeans rebelled so as not to be subject to Judah.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On Jacob’s Dream while Fleeing to Mesopotamia, and on the Separation of Jacob and Esau

Esau therefore hated Jacob and said in his heart: “The days of mourning,” that is, of my father’s death, “will come, and I shall kill Jacob.” These things were reported to Rebecca (Gen. 27). By the same spirit through which she had instructed Jacob to deceive his brother, Rebecca knew Esau’s thoughts. Jacob is therefore excused for lying to his father and deceiving his brother by his mother’s command; and his mother by the familiar counsel of the Holy Spirit. She said to Jacob: “Flee to my brother Laban and remain there until your brother’s anger subsides.”

So that this might not be done without his father’s permission, Rebecca said to her husband: “If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters [Note: [Col. 1115A] Addition 1. From whom came the Hittite, one of the seven peoples; for whom they sometimes found the form *Cethaeus*, [Col. 1115B] because, where the Hebrews use an aspirated vowel in both cases, we employ *ch* to soften the harshness. They say *Haraham*, we *Charam*; they say *Hethaeus*, we *Chetaeus*.] of Heth, I do not wish to live.” Isaac summoned Jacob, blessed him, and commanded him to go into Mesopotamia and take a wife for himself from the daughters of Laban.

But Esau, believing that he had offended his father by his marriages with foreign women, went to Ishmael, his uncle, taking as wife his daughter Meleth, Nabajoth’s maternal half-sister, in addition to those whom he already had. Thus Jacob left [Col. 1114C] Beersheba and was making his way toward Aram (Gen. 28). While passing through Canaan, he feared the inhabitants of the land because, as Josephus says, the Canaanites were hostile to Isaac, having been severely harmed in his earlier wars, especially when he captured Kiriath-jearim, around which they had suffered most severely. Jacob therefore feared to enter the house of any inhabitant of the country and lay out under the open sky.

When he came near Luz in the evening, he placed a stone beneath his head and fell asleep. In a dream he saw a ladder standing from earth and reaching heaven, with angels descending and ascending by it. Josephus says: “He saw figures descending by it, having a more noble nature than human beings”; and the Lord leaning upon the ladder, saying to him: “I am [Col. 1114D] the God of Abraham and Isaac. I shall give this land to you and to your seed. In you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed. I shall be your guardian on this journey and shall bring you back to this land.”

The Lord used a reversed order. First he guarded Jacob in his own person; afterwards, under Joshua, he gave that land to Jacob’s seed (Josh. 13); and at the end of time, in Christ—who was descended from Jacob—the tribes of the earth were blessed. When Jacob awoke, he said: “Truly, the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it. This place is awesome; it is the house of God, and the gate of heaven.” And he prophesied concerning the Law, the Temple, and Christ’s Passion, which were to take place in that land. For the Law is awesome; the house of God is the Temple; and Christ’s Passion is the opening of heaven’s gate.

He set up as a monument the stone which he had placed beneath his head, [Col. 1115A] that is, as a praiseworthy memorial of this vision; he poured oil upon it for the Lord, vowing that the Lord who had appeared to him would always be his God, that the stone—that is, the place of the stone—would always be honourable to him, and that upon his return he would offer him tithes and sacrifices. He also decreed that the neighbouring city should be honoured, calling it Bethel, that is, “house of God,” or, according to Josephus, “sacrifice of God.” It had first been called Jebus, from the Jebusites who founded it; afterwards Luz, that is, “nut” or “almond tree,” because when its foundations were first laid an almond root was found there. Or perhaps there is an abundance of trees of this kind there.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On Jacob’s Two Wives

[Col. 1115B]

Proceeding into Mesopotamia, he eventually arrived, after a long time, in Aram and came to a well in a field, covered by a large stone, beside which three flocks were lying down. When he told the shepherds to water the flocks and take them back to pasture, he learned that the custom there was not to remove the stone until all the flocks had assembled, and that it was not permitted to water the flocks separately. As he asked every question about Laban, the shepherds said: “He is well; and behold Rachel, [Col. 1115C] his daughter, is coming with her flock” (Gen. 29).

When she arrived, Jacob removed the stone from the mouth of the well. It is clear that Jacob did not go alone, and he watered her flock; and, declaring himself her cousin, he kissed her. She reported this to her father. Laban came to meet him, brought Jacob into his house, and, having heard the reason for his flight, said: “You are my bone and my flesh; therefore you shall safely hide with me.” At length he decided that Jacob should tend the flock.

After a month Jacob offered a choice of wages for his pastoral service. Laban had two daughters: Leah, with weak eyes, and Rachel, beautiful in appearance. Jacob loved her and said: “I shall serve you seven years for Rachel.” He therefore served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him only a few days because of the greatness of his love. It was not said that they seemed *short*, [Col. 1115D] because to a soul in longing even speed itself is slow; but they were called *few*, because he seemed to have bought so lovable a thing for few days. For he would have served many more years for her before he could endure to be without her. Or “days” refers to the toil of those days, which seemed slight to him because love lightened the labour.

When the seventh year was complete, Laban held a wedding feast for his son-in-law. But when evening came, he secretly brought in Leah and gave his daughter a maidservant named Zilpah. Jacob, as Josephus says, through drunkenness and the darkness of night lay with Leah; when day came, he complained to Laban of the wrong. Laban asked pardon on grounds of necessity, asserting that it was the local custom to give the elder daughters in marriage first. He said that after another seven years he would give Rachel to him, and approved the reason for the delay, saying that he would not [Col. 1116A] willingly send his daughter among the Canaanites, since he even regretted having sent her sister there.

Jerome, however, says that those were mistaken who said Rachel was given to Jacob after another seven years; rather, she was given after the seven days of feasting, which it was not lawful, by bringing in another bride, as it were, to disturb. When those days were finished, Jacob obtained the marriage he desired, preferred his love for the latter to the former, and served another seven years for Rachel.

## CHAPTER LXXV. On Leah’s Four Sons, and the Sons of the Maidservants

The Lord opened Leah’s womb, her sister having been made barren, so that she might gain her husband’s love through fruitfulness. She bore a son and said: “The Lord has seen my humiliation” (Gen. 29), namely, my lowly standing in my husband’s eyes; and therefore she called her son Reuben, that is, “son of vision.” Again she bore another son and said: “The Lord has heard that I am held in contempt”; and therefore he was called Simeon, that is, “hearing.”

She bore a third and said: “My husband will be joined to me, because I have added sons to him”; and for this reason he was called Levi, that is, “addition,” or “the confirmer of union,” according to Josephus. She also bore a fourth and said: “Now I shall confess the Lord”; and for this reason he was called Judah, that is, “confession.” Then she ceased bearing.

Rachel therefore envied her sister and said to Jacob: “Give me children, or else I shall die.” He said: “Am I God?” And she said: “If not from me, then at least from my maidservant.” She gave Bilhah to him in marriage, not as a wife, but to be joined to him. Bilhah bore a son, and Rachel said: “The [Col. 1116C] Lord has judged me,” that is, has made me equal to my sister; and therefore the boy was called Dan, that is, “judgment.” She bore another, and Rachel said: “I have been compared with my sister and have prevailed”; and therefore the boy was called Naphtali, that is, “comparison,” or “delay.”

Leah also gave Zilpah to her husband. She bore a son, and Leah said: “Happily!” Therefore the boy was called Gad, that is, “good fortune.” She bore yet another, and Leah said: “All women will call me blessed”; therefore the boy was called Asher, that is, “blessed.”

## CHAPTER LXXVI. Fifth Incidental Event

In these times there was a local flood in Achaia, under King Ogyges, who renovated the city called Acta and named it Eleusis. At that time also, beside Lake Trichonis, a virgin appeared whom the Greeks called Minerva. She invented many arts, especially wool-working. She was also called Pallas, either from the Thracian island Pallene, where she was reared, or from the giant Pallas, whom she killed.

It is also related that, when the Cyclades had long been obscured by that flood, Delos was the first among them to be lit by the sun as the waters diminished; therefore it was called Delos, a name meaning “manifest.”

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On Leah’s Remaining Sons and Joseph’s Birth

At the time of the wheat harvest—that is, either after the barley had already been gathered, or perhaps because three gatherings, from *metere*, “to harvest” or “to gather,” are called harvests: the fruit harvest, which is first; the wheat harvest, which is second; and the vintage harvest, which is third—at this [Col. 1117A] time, I say, Reuben returned from the field carrying mandrakes and gave them to his mother (Gen. 30). Rachel desired to eat them and said to Leah: “Give me some of your son’s mandrakes.”

Some suppose that this kind of fruit, when eaten, brings fertility to barren women; Augustine says that this is false. Having seen a mandrake on the occasion of this reading, he says that he carefully investigated all its nature and power, and found nothing of the sort in it. Leah said: “Does it seem a small matter to you that you have taken away my husband, unless you also take his mandrakes with him?” Rachel, softening her sister’s anger, said: “Let him sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son’s mandrakes.”

Leah met Jacob as he returned from the field, indicating that she had hired him for a wage. She conceived that night and bore [Col. 1117B] a fifth son, saying: “God has given me my reward, because I gave my maidservant to my husband”; therefore she called the boy Issachar, which means “reward.” For *achar* means “reward.” She also so named him because she had bought her husband’s entrance with the mandrakes.

Again Leah conceived and bore a sixth son, saying: “My husband will dwell with me, because I have borne him six children”; therefore she called the boy Zebulun, that is, “dwelling.” In the Book of Hebrew Names, however, it is forcibly interpreted as “flow of the night.” Afterwards she bore a daughter named Dinah.

But the Lord remembered Rachel and opened her womb. She bore a son, saying: “May the Lord add another son to me.” Therefore the boy was called Joseph, that is, “increase.”

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On the Parti-Coloured Rods and the Offspring

[Col. 1117C]

When the fourteen years of service for his wives were completed, Jacob said to his father-in-law: “Give me my wives and children, that I may return to my own land.” Laban said: “May I find favour in your sight, so that you may still serve me seven years; set the wage which I should give you. For I know that God has blessed me because of you” (Gen. 30).

Jacob said: “It is just that I should at some time provide for my own household. If you do what I ask, I shall still pasture your livestock: separate the variegated and speckled flocks and place them in the care of your sons; but give me the solid-coloured animals. Whatever is born variegated from the solid-coloured animals shall be my wage, and whatever is of one colour shall be yours. My righteousness shall answer for me [Col. 1117D] tomorrow,” that is, in the future. As if he said: “Nature works for you, so that white are born from white, black from black; but my righteousness works for me, when God, in return for my labour, gives me against nature whatever seems just to him.”

Laban accepted this gladly, separated all the differently coloured animals, and gave them to his sons to guard. He gave the solid-coloured flock to Jacob and placed a journey of three days between Jacob and his sons, lest any fraud arise through the proximity of the animals. Thus this statement is clear, except that the text says Laban gave the solid-coloured flock into the care of his sons, namely Jacob’s sons, which seems contrary to what we have said. It may be said that he gave it into the care of his sons—that is, his grandsons, Jacob’s sons, who were shepherds under their father. Or it was said by anticipation: after the solid-coloured flock had been born under Jacob’s care, he gave it to his sons, having first given him the variegated flock.

Jerome also says that this passage had remained confused until his time. Jacob, however, devised a new turn of nature, that is, a reversal, and with natural art contended against nature. He took green poplar rods, which the Septuagint calls storax rods, and almond and plane-tree rods; stripping their bark in places, he made the rods variegated in colour. Perhaps there were three troughs and he took only three rods, each of the same length as a trough, putting one rod in each trough. Perhaps there were many rods in the troughs.

Jacob observed the season when the livestock mated, and in the heat of the day, when they eagerly went to drink, he made the sheep and goats be mounted during that very eagerness of drinking, so that they might conceive offspring like the images of the rams and he-goats mounting them which they saw reflected in the water. For the colour of the reflections was variegated because of the rods placed there.

But lest all the offspring become parti-coloured and the fraud be detected, Jacob moderated the matter thus: at the first time when the sheep mated, because spring offspring are better, he set the rods before them so that they might conceive in their sight. For in the later mating, that is, in the mating occurring at the end of spring, the offspring are inferior, because nature is less vigorous in those slow to seek intercourse; therefore he did not set the rods then. Thus the late-born animals belonged to Laban, and those of the first [Col. 1118C] season to Jacob. Or perhaps the late mating is called that of autumn, because the nature of the sheep of Mesopotamia and Italy is said to be the same, so that they give birth twice a year; hence the poet:

> “Twice pregnant with offspring …”

As for the statement that they conceived at the rods, Jerome says that the force of the Hebrew word cannot be expressed except by circumlocution. For it denotes the extreme convulsion of the whole body at the height of intercourse. Nor is it remarkable that offspring should resemble an image seen at the climax of pleasure, since Jerome says that this very thing happens among herds of mares in Spain; and Quintilian defends a woman accused of having borne an Ethiopian child by arguing that it happened from an image she had seen. In the books attributed to Hippocrates [Col. 1118D] it is also found that a certain woman was to be punished because she had borne a very beautiful child, unlike both parents and indeed their entire family, unless Hippocrates had advised them to inquire whether perhaps there was such a painting in the bedroom.

Jacob therefore became exceedingly rich. After he heard Laban’s sons saying, “Jacob has taken what was ours, and has made himself illustrious from our father’s property,” and also observed that Laban’s face was no longer toward him as it had been yesterday and the day before—especially because the Lord had said to him, “Return to your own land, and I shall be with you”—he sent for Leah and Rachel and called them into the field where he was pasturing the flock. He said: “Your father’s countenance is not toward me. You know that he has cheated me and changed my wages ten times” (Gen. 31). The Septuagint says “for ten years.” But this must be understood as ten years, as though ten cycles, which tenfold alteration occurred in six years. For Josephus says that the entire time Jacob was with Laban was twenty years.

Jacob did not wish to complete a third period of seven years—twenty-one years—in Laban’s service, because of Laban’s wickedness. For when Laban saw that more parti-coloured animals were being born, he said: “Henceforth let the solid-coloured animals be your wages.” Again, when he saw the solid-coloured animals multiplying, he changed the wage. Jacob added: “God has taken your father’s substance and given it to me. In dreams he showed me what sort of offspring would be born, and he said to me: ‘Arise and depart from this land.’” Leah and Rachel answered: “Our father has treated us as foreigners. Shall we have anything left from his property and inheritance? Do [Col. 1119B] whatever the Lord has commanded you.”

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On Jacob’s Flight and the Covenant Made with Laban

Jacob therefore rose with his wives and children and departed, taking all his possessions, flocks, and everything that he had acquired in Mesopotamia (Gen. 31). Jacob also took, as Josephus says, half the flock, without Laban’s knowledge, while Laban had gone to shear the sheep. Rachel, likewise without her husband’s knowledge, stole her father’s valuable idols and took them with her—not in order to worship them, for, instructed by her husband, she knew that they were not to be worshipped, but so that if they were caught and her father pursued them, they might obtain pardon by fleeing to these objects.

Jacob crossed the river and went toward Mount Gilead. On the third day Laban was told [Col. 1119C] that Jacob had fled. Taking his sons and relatives, he pursued him for seven days. Josephus, however, says that Laban discovered Jacob’s and his daughters’ departure after the first day, pursued them, and found them encamped at a distance on a hill. It may be said that, if he learned of it on the third day, he is said to have learned it after the first day because the messenger then set out and came to him on the third day, where his sons were pasturing the flocks, which had been separated from Jacob by a three-day journey, as stated above.
