Laban saw God in a dream, saying to him: “Beware of saying anything harsh against Jacob.” Rising, he said to Jacob: “Why did you flee without my knowledge? And why did you steal my gods? You are my cousin, my son-in-law, and my kinsman-by-marriage; you ought not to have done this.” Jacob answered: “I feared that you would violently take your daughters from me, though they follow not so much me as their children. As for your accusation of theft: with whomever you find your gods, let that person die before our brothers.”

Laban entered Leah’s and the maidservants’ tents but found nothing. When he entered Rachel’s tent, she hid the idols beneath the camel’s saddle-gear and sat upon them. To her father, who was searching, she said: “Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, because what happens to women according to their custom has now happened to me.” Thus the searching man’s concern was deceived.

Jacob became angry and reproached Laban because, despite twenty years of diligent service, he had not deserved that Laban should search all his household goods himself. Laban said: “Everything you have is mine, [Col. 1120A] but what can I do for my children and grandchildren? Come, let us make a covenant.” Jacob took a stone and set it up as a monument of the covenant, and said to his kinsmen: “Bring stones.” They gathered them, made a heap, and ate upon it.

Laban said: “Let this heap be a witness of our covenant: that I shall not cross beyond it to come against you with evil intent; and that you shall not cross over to me with hostile purpose, nor afflict my daughters, nor bring other wives in above them.” For this reason Jacob called the hill in his own language Galaad, that is, “heap of witness.” For *gal* means “heap”; *ad* means “witness.” But Laban, in the Syrian language, called it Igar-sahadutha. Laban rose by night, blessed them, and returned to his own place. Josephus, however, says that they set up a pillar on the mountain in the form of an altar. Perhaps he called the heap a pillar [Col. 1120B] without distinguishing the name.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On Jacob’s Vision of Angels and the Gifts Sent Ahead to Esau

Jacob proceeded upon the journey he had begun, and a multitude of angels met him. For this reason he called that place Mahanaim, that is, “camps,” because there he saw angels as though prepared to defend him against the brother whom he feared. From that place he sent messengers to his brother to discover Esau’s disposition (Gen. 32). When they returned, they reported that Esau was peacefully coming to meet him with four hundred men.

Jacob therefore was afraid, not because he distrusted the angels’ promise, but because he was troubled in the manner of human beings. He divided the people with him into two companies: the maidservants and their children in the first company; the free women and their children in the second; but at the rear of the latter he placed Rachel and Joseph, as dearer to him. Hence some were mistaken in thinking that Rachel and Joseph formed a third company. He divided them so that, if Esau came to harm them and struck the first company, the remainder might flee and be saved.

He also set apart from his possessions gifts for his brother: the more beautiful and rarer animals, and animals of different kinds. He sent them by separate messengers, leaving a space between flock and flock, so that the frequent succession of gifts would make them appear numerous, and so that, if any indignation yet remained in Esau, it might be appeased by the gifts. Thus the gifts went ahead, while Jacob himself was still [Col. 1120D] in Mahanaim.

Rising before dawn, he took his wives and children, together with everything belonging to him, across the ford of Jabbok.

[Note: [Col. 1120D] Addition. At the second milestone from the Jordan, on the borders of Idumaea, is the torrent Jabbok, which Jacob crossed by fording.]

Josephus says that they crossed a torrent named Jabbok. Since Genesis records that Jacob, praying in fear of his brother, said: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies,” perhaps the stream which he crossed is called Jordan because it is stony there and is a torrent, and is called the ford of Jabbok. Or perhaps through a scribal error *Jabbok* is read in place of *Jacob*, and the ford received its name from that crossing: “Jacob’s ford.”

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On Jacob’s Wrestling with the Angel and the Change of His Name

[Col. 1121A]

While the companies went ahead, Jacob remained alone on the bank of the river in order to pray. And behold, a Man wrestled with him until morning. He touched his side—or, according to another reading, the sinew of his left thigh—and it withered (Gen. 32). Jacob therefore resolved thereafter not to eat that sinew, and his descendants observe the same practice.

When dawn was rising, the Man said to him: “Let me go.” Jacob said: “I shall not let you go unless you bless me.” When the Man asked his name, Jacob said that he was called Jacob. “Your name,” he said, “shall no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because if you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men?” Thus he blessed Jacob by changing [Col. 1121B] his name and strengthening him so that he would not fear his brother. For his standing undefeated against God became a sign to him that he would stand undefeated against his brother.

Josephus says that the Hebrew name Israel means “a sacred angel resisting”; but in the Book of Hebrew Names it is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” For *is* means “man,” *el* is the name of God, and *ra* is said to mean “seeing”: or, “a mind seeing God.” Jerome says that this interpretation is made not so much truthfully as forcibly. Josephus says that he did not find the former interpretation in Hebrew, and says that the name means “prince with God.” For he maintains that the angel interpreted it thus: “If you have been a prince or strong against God,” and so forth.

Jacob called that place Penuel, that is, “face of God,” and said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, [Col. 1121C] and my soul has been saved”—that is, from being greatly terrified it has been very greatly strengthened. When he passed beyond Penuel, the sun rose upon him, and he limped.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. On Esau’s Meeting Jacob and the Purchase of Land at Shechem

Raising his eyes, Jacob saw Esau and the four hundred men with him. Going ahead of both companies which he had formed, he bowed down seven times with his face to the ground. Esau ran to him, embraced him, kissed him, and wept (Gen. 33). Asking to whom the women and little children belonged, and being told that they belonged to Jacob, Esau approached and kissed them.

When Esau did not wish to keep the gifts sent ahead, saying that he had very great abundance, Jacob said: “If I have found [Col. 1121D] favour before my lord, accept this small gift from my hand. I have seen your face as though I had seen the countenance of a god,” that is, of someone most powerful. For Jacob either did not believe Esau to be God, or he would have burst into such madness or flattery.

Esau returned that day to Seir, namely, the settlement which he had so named from his own name. Jacob proceeded from there and pitched tents in the place which for that reason he called Succoth, that is, “tents.” Jerome says of it: “Succoth is to this day a city beyond the Jordan, in the district of Scythopolis, where Gideon crossed the Jordan when he spoke to the men of Succoth.” But it is surprising that he said “beyond the Jordan,” since, according to some, Jacob has already been said to have crossed the Jordan when he was in Succoth. Perhaps “beyond the Jordan” was said with reference [Col. 1122A] to Mesopotamia, from which Jacob was returning; or rather, he had not yet crossed the Jordan but the Jabbok. When he said above, “this Jordan” (Gen. 32), he did not point to the present stream but indicated the familiar boundary of Judaea.

He went from Succoth to Salem, the city of the Shechemites—that is, to Shechem. For from Shechem they were called Shechemites, or perhaps Shechem had two names. Or, as the Hebrews relate, Moses only then called it Salem, that is, “completed and perfected,” because there Jacob’s limping thigh was healed. Jacob bought a portion of the field near the town from Hamor, king of the Shechemites, and his sons, for one hundred lambs; he lived there and, after erecting an altar, invoked the mighty God of Israel.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. On the Death of the Shechemites for the Abduction of Dinah

[Col. 1122B]

Dinah went out to see the women of that region (Gen. 34), because, as Josephus says, while the Shechemites were holding a festival, she went alone into the city to buy the ornaments of the local women. Shechem, the king’s son, saw her, loved her, abducted her, and violated the virgin by force. His soul became attached to her, and he said to his father: “Take this girl for me as a wife.”

The king went out with his son to Jacob. Jacob’s sons were coming in from the field; angered, they were silent. When the king asked for reciprocal friendship and alliance, for intermarriage between them, and when Shechem offered much and promised greater things, they replied deceitfully: “It is unlawful for us to form an alliance with uncircumcised men; but be circumcised, and we shall be one people.” The proposal [or: choice] pleased Hamor and his son, and the young man did not delay but immediately fulfilled it. Entering the city, they persuaded the people, and all were circumcised.

Then, behold, on the third day, when the pain of the wounds was most severe, Simeon and Levi, having taken swords, confidently entered the city and killed every male in it. They took their sister from Shechem’s house; but the other brothers fell upon the slain, plundered the city, and led away the little children and women as captives. Josephus says only: “When there was a festival and the Shechemites were engaged in rest and feasting, they immediately attacked at the first watches and killed them while they slept.”

When he learned this, Jacob said to Simeon and [Col. 1122D] Levi: “You have troubled me and made me hateful to the inhabitants of this land. They will strike me, and I and my household shall be destroyed.” But the Lord, strengthening him, said: “Arise, go up to Bethel, dwell there, and make an altar where I appeared to you” (Gen. 35); but first sanctify your people.

Jacob summoned his household. While purifying them, he found Laban’s gods, as Josephus says; for he had not known of them because Rachel had hidden them in the ground beneath a tree. He said to his people: “Cast away the foreign gods, purify yourselves, and let us go up to Bethel.” For they had also brought idols from Shechem, and earrings—that is, ornaments of idols. Jacob buried all these beneath the terebinth which stands behind the city of Shechem. Some relate that David took them to Jerusalem and melted them down into material for the Temple [Col. 1123A] which he intended to build.

A terror from God seized the neighbouring peoples so that they did not pursue Jacob. He departed, came to Bethel, built an altar there for the Lord, and offered to him, in accordance with what he had previously vowed. At that time Deborah, Rebecca’s nurse, died and was buried near Bethel beneath a terebinth. The place was called the Oak of Weeping. Note that here it seems that oak and terebinth are the same thing.

The Lord appeared to Jacob again and said: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.” And he called him Israel. It is clear that above he only promised the name (Gen. 32), but here he imposed it.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. On Rachel’s Death in Benjamin’s Birth

Jacob departed from there and came in the springtime to [Col. 1123B] the land which leads to Ephrath (Gen. 35), that is, Bethlehem. This is an anticipation, for it was called Ephrath only later, from Caleb’s wife, who was buried there. There Rachel, while giving birth, began to be in danger; nevertheless, she bore a son. As her soul was leaving because of the pain of childbirth, while dying she called her son Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow.” But his father circumcised him and called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.”

Rachel was therefore buried on the road leading to Bethlehem; alone among her kindred, she did not obtain the honour of burial with Abraham. Jacob set up a monument over her tomb, which remains visible to the present day. Departing from there, he pitched his tent beyond the Tower of Eder, that is, “Tower of the Flock.” The Hebrews say that this is the place where the Temple was afterwards built, and that it was called, as by a certain prophecy, “Tower of the Flock,” that is, of the congregation that was to gather at the Temple. But Jerome says that the place is near Bethlehem, where either the flock of angels sang at the Lord’s birth, or Jacob pastured his flocks, leaving the place its name from that fact. While he lived there, Reuben slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine; yet this did not escape Jacob’s notice.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. On Isaac’s Death and the Kings of Edom
He also came to Isaac, his father, in the city of Hebron (Gen. 35), and found his mother already dead. Not long after his arrival, Isaac’s days were completed: he was one hundred and eighty years old, or, according to Josephus, one hundred and eighty-five. And he was gathered to his people, full of days, and [Col. 1123D] his sons Esau and Jacob buried him in the double cave. Here ends Joseph’s first book.

Moreover, when their father had died, Esau and Jacob became so wealthy that the land could not contain them. Esau returned to the hill country which he had left, and the land was called Idumaea from Edom; it had previously been called Bozrah. For Moses, enumerating the twelve kings of that land from the first to the last whom he could have seen, says: “And after Bela reigned Jobab, son of Zerah of Bozrah” (Gen. 36). Some then say that Jobab was Esau’s great-grandson; but the Hebrews disagree, as was said above.

[Note: [Col. 1124B] Addition 1. Since Moses was fourth from Jacob and fifth from Esau, he did not see the twelve kings of Edom. Resolve this by what follows: “Some nevertheless say,” [Col. 1124C] etc.]

It also appears in Genesis that the same land was called Seir before Esau as well.

[Note: [Col. 1124C] Addition 2. Damascus lies beneath Mount Seir; Idumaea is in the land of Damascus, for Esau also lived in Damascus. Teman is the metropolis of Idumaea, whence Eliphaz the Temanite; and Shua, whence Bildad the Shuhite. Lebanon divides Idumaea and Phoenicia. At its foot rise the rivers Albana and Pharpar, flowing beside Antioch.]

For, after enumerating Esau’s sons, Moses enumerates the princes of the Horites, who were in the land before Esau, beginning thus: [Col. 1124A] “These are the sons of Seir the Horite, inhabitants of the land,” etc. Esau expelled the Horites, as is read in Chronicles (1 Chron. 1). Some nevertheless say that the kings here enumerated were kings in Edom before the children of Israel had a king—namely Saul—and that this enumeration was added by Ezra, who could have known it.

In the enumeration of these persons there is mention of Anah, son of Zibeon, whose daughter Esau took as wife. He discovered hot waters in the wilderness while tending his father’s asses. The Hebrew expression is, “he found Jamnum”; concerning this, Jerome says, the Hebrews dispute in various ways. Some say that *Jamnum* means “seas,” because he found a lake in the wilderness. Others think that hot springs are called by this name in the Punic language, which is akin to Hebrew, and which the Greeks call θερμαί (*thermai*, “hot springs”). Others say that he bred wild asses with she-asses, so that swift asses were born from them, called *jamnum*. Others say that *jamnum* means “pairing,” because he was the first to make mares mount asses, so that mules might be born.

It should be noted that, in the recapitulation of Esau’s sons, Moses gives different names for Esau’s wives from those he had given earlier. Josephus also says that Amalek, Esau’s natural son by a concubine, lived in the part of Idumaea called Gabolitis, and named it Amalekite. But leaving these matters aside, we must proceed to Jacob’s descendants.

## Chapter LXXXVI. The Sixth Incidental Event

[Col. 1124C]

At that time Prometheus, brother of Atlas, was said to have been the first to make men: both because he made the unlearned learned, and because he is said to have made images of men which, by a certain art, he made to walk. He also first invented [Col. 1124D] the ring, though it was of iron, and set a gem in it. Hence he called it also an *ungulus* (“little nail”), because, as a nail is surrounded by flesh, so a gem is surrounded by metal. He further ordained that it should be worn for ornament on the finger called the middle finger, judging it worthier than the others because a certain vein extends from it to the heart.

It is also said that in that period Triptolemus came into Greece in a ship upon which a dragon was painted, and enlarged agriculture. Ceres, besides implements for ploughing, also invented the measuring of grain; previously crops were stored in bins and wheat was counted by heaps. Hence the Greeks also called her Demeter. At that time likewise the defeated Telchines, as exiles, founded Rhodes.

## Chapter LXXXVII. On the Sale of Joseph

[Col. 1125A]

When Joseph was sixteen years old, he tended his father’s flock (Gen. 37). It should be known that Joseph was sold twelve years before Isaac’s death. This is proved as follows. Isaac was sixty years old when Jacob was born, and died at one hundred and eighty; therefore Jacob was one hundred and twenty at his father’s death. But he was one hundred and eight at the sale of his son. For when he came to Joseph in Egypt he was one hundred and thirty, while twenty-two years elapsed between Joseph’s sale and the descent into Egypt. Joseph was sixteen when sold into Egypt, and thirty-nine when his father came to him.

Moses therefore returns to what he had passed over. Thus, while Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia and had not yet come to his father—while Rachel was still alive, according to Josephus—Joseph was sold in the following manner. His brothers hated him because he was loved by his father more than the others (Gen. 37): partly because he had begotten him in old age, and partly because Joseph was more distinguished in appearance and wiser than the rest. Joseph had accused his brothers before their father of a very grave offence: either of hatred toward himself, or of intercourse with beasts, according to the opinion of some who follow the order of Genesis—only Reuben being accused concerning his father’s concubine.

His father made him a many-coloured tunic.

[Note: [Col. 1126C] Addition 1. Some pronounce *polymitam* with a short penultimate syllable, because it is compounded of *polys*, “many,” and *micos*, “thread”; just as *hexaminatum* derives from *hexa*, “six,” and *licia aminatum*, “threaded,” as though possessing six threads—and thus its penultimate is short.]

Or it was embroidered by hand or needle; or, according to Aquila, an *astragolean* tunic—that is, one reaching to the ankles; or, according to Symmachus, a sleeved tunic, that is, one having sleeves. Others used sleeveless garments, so that they might be more unencumbered. Yet it may be called *manicata*, “hand-painted,” namely with needlework overlaid upon it.

The greater cause of hatred, however, was the revelation of dreams. He told his brothers the dream he had seen, saying: “I thought that we were binding sheaves in a field, and that your sheaves were worshipping my upright sheaf.” They said: “Will you be our king, or shall we be subject to your dominion?” He also told them another dream in his father’s presence: “I saw, as it were, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars worshipping me.” His father rebuked him and said: “Shall I, your mother, and your brothers worship you upon the earth?” He could fittingly say this, because his mother was still alive. Yet his mother did not worship him, because she did not go down to Egypt. [Col. 1125D] Nor is his father recorded as having worshipped him, because Joseph would not have endured it; but his brothers worshipped him, and the parents did so in their sons.

When his brothers were staying at Shechem while tending the flocks, his father sent him from the valley of Hebron to see how his brothers and livestock were faring. When he did not find them at Shechem, he pursued them to Dothan. Seeing him from afar, they said to one another: “Behold, the dreamer is coming. Come, let us kill him and cast his body into an old cistern; then we shall say: ‘A savage beast has devoured him.’” But Reuben, wishing to save him, said: “Let us not shed his blood, but cast him alive into the cistern, lest the father be destroyed together with him and the mother in mourning.” Here Josephus maintains that the mother was still alive.

So, stripping him of the many-coloured tunic, [Col. 1126A] they threw him into a cistern in which there was no water. Reuben went away in search of better pasture. While they sat eating bread, they saw Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, carrying on camels spices, resin, and stacte—that is, myrrh—into Egypt. Judah said to his brothers: “It is better that the boy be sold to the Ishmaelites and that our hands not be defiled by concealing his blood. For he is our flesh and blood.” And they sold him to Midianites for twenty pieces of silver.

He calls the same persons Midianites whom he also calls Ishmaelites. Yet Midian was Abraham’s son by Keturah, and Ishmael by Hagar; and Abraham is recorded as having separated the sons of the different wives from one another. Perhaps, having first been separated, they afterward came together and became one people, retaining the name of each parent. Or the opinion of the Hebrews is true: they say Hagar and Keturah were one woman, and thus perhaps they were never separated.

When Reuben returned to the cistern, he did not find the boy. Believing him dead, he wailed and tore his garments. But when he learned that Joseph was alive, he was quieted. They took Joseph’s garments and dipped his tunic in the blood of a kid. They sent certain men to carry it to their father and say: “We found this; see whether it is your son’s tunic.” When the father recognized it, he said: “A savage beast has devoured my son Joseph.” Tearing his clothes and clothing himself in sackcloth, he mourned his son a long time. When his sons gathered to ease their father’s grief, he would not listen to them, but said: “I shall go down mourning to my son in hell.”

For there was then [Col. 1126C] in hell a certain place for the blessed, far removed from the places of punishment, which because of its rest and separation from others was called a “bosom,” as we speak of a gulf of the sea. It was also called Abraham’s bosom, because Abraham too was there, from his trial onward until Christ’s death.

[Note: [Col. 1126C] Addition 2. He was called the first way of believing, not because he was the first to believe, but because he was the first to suffer persecution for faith in the one God, having been expelled from Chaldaea [Col. 1126D].]

## Chapter LXXXVIII. On Joseph’s Entry into Egypt

[Col. 1126D]

The Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and commander of the army (Gen. 37). Others call him *archimachirus*, that is, chief of cooks. For *machera* means “kitchen,” or “the cooks’ axe,” from *machere*, “to kill.” Nor is this inconsistent with truth, because among many nations the ruler’s steward is both more honourable and commander of the soldiers.

Josephus calls him Petephres, but Jerome asserts that the name was not translated well. He had a wife and children, since Joseph also took his daughter as wife; nor was he one of the king’s eunuchs who were castrated in childhood. But the Hebrews relate that, seeing Joseph’s beauty, he bought him in order to have intercourse with him. [Col. 1127A] The Lord, however, protecting Joseph, so chilled him that thereafter he was incapable of intercourse and was as though a eunuch. When the hierophants saw him withered, according to their custom they made him priest of Heliopolis, that is, the House of the Sun; and he was more honoured than before in his office of command.

## Chapter LXXXIX. That Judah Begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar, etc.

At that time—before Joseph was sold, since this also is inserted by recapitulation—

[Note: [Col. 1128A] Addition 1. Recapitulation is one thing: when something that happened earlier is narrated later. Anticipation is another: when something is narrated before it happened.]

Judah went down from his brothers to a man of Adullam named Hiram (Gen. 38). There he took a wife named Shua, daughter of a Canaanite, who bore him his firstborn son Er, then Onan, and afterward Shelah. Judah gave his firstborn Er [Col. 1127B] a wife named Tamar. Er was wicked—that is, he abused his wife’s vessel—and was killed by the Lord; that is, he was found dead in bed beside his wife.

Judah told Onan to go in to her and raise up seed for his brother. Here certain things written later in the Law are plainly observed before the Law. But Onan, resenting the prospect that children should not be born for himself, spilled his seed upon the ground; that is, he strove to have intercourse with his wife without effect. And the Lord struck him down. Judah sent Tamar back to remain a widow in her father’s house until Shelah should grow up. When he was grown, Judah feared to give him to Tamar and kept delaying.

Shua, Judah’s wife, died. After receiving consolation following the mourning, Judah went with Hira his shepherd to shear sheep. Tamar heard this; laying aside the garments [Col. 1127C] of widowhood, she put on a veil and sat at the fork in the road leading to Timnah. The Hebrew means “she sat at the eyes.” For this is how it calls a crossroads, where the traveller ought to look more carefully where he is stepping. When Judah saw her, he supposed her to be a *cadesa*, that is, a prostitute. He said to her: “Allow me to have intercourse with you.” She said: “What will you give me?” He replied: “I shall send you a kid from the flock.” And she said: “I will permit what you wish if you give me a pledge.” He gave her as earnest a ring, bracelet, and staff which he carried.

By this single intercourse the woman conceived twins. Then she went away, resuming the garments of widowhood. Judah sent the kid through the shepherd. When he came and did not find her, he returned to Judah without the pledges. After three [Col. 1127D] months it was reported to Judah: “Tamar has committed fornication, and her womb has swollen.” He said: “Bring her out to be burned.” As she was being led to punishment, she sent the pledges to her father-in-law, saying: “I conceived by the man to whom these things belong.” He said: “She is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah. She did this lest my son’s seed perish.” Judah did not know her again.

When the time of delivery came, two appeared in the womb. At the very birth one put out his hand, and the midwife tied scarlet thread on it, saying: “This one will come out first.” But he drew back his hand and the other came out. The mother said: “Why has the barrier been divided from your brother because of you?” Therefore she called him Perez. By “barrier” she meant the membrane of the afterbirth, or placenta, in which the child is wrapped in the womb, which is divided [Col. 1128A] at birth and follows the child. Afterward the other came out with the scarlet thread and was called Zerah, that is, “rising” or “dawn,” because he appeared first, or because very many righteous persons were born from him, as is read in Chronicles (1 Chron. 2).

Yet in the gloss on the Book of Kings at the beginning of the third book it is read: “In Genesis the midwife tied scarlet thread on the hand of Perez; and perhaps he received the name Perez from having divided the wall. Perhaps afterward she took the scarlet thread from Zerah’s hand and tied it on Perez, so that he might be distinguished as firstborn from twins who resembled one another.”

## Chapter XC. On Joseph’s Imprisonment

[Col. 1128B]

Thus Joseph was brought into Egypt and bought by Potiphar the eunuch. The Lord was with him, and he administered his master’s household entrusted to him. The Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house because of Joseph; his master knew nothing of all that he possessed except the bread which he ate (Gen. 39).

It happened that his mistress cast her eyes upon Joseph and said: “Sleep with me.” He replied: “My master has entrusted all his possessions to me except you. How then can I do this—and indeed sin against my God?” It happened, as Josephus says, that a public festival was at hand, at which women too had to be present. She then feigned illness before her husband, thereby seeking solitude and silence so as to persuade Joseph. Seizing [Col. 1128C] the hem of Joseph’s cloak, she said to him: “Sleep with me.” Angrily, he left the cloak in her hand and went outside.

Grieving that she had been scorned, she showed the retained cloak to her returning husband as proof of her accusation, saying: “The Hebrew servant came in to mock me.” He, excessively credulous toward his wife, handed Joseph over in bonds to the royal prison. But the Lord was with him and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison, who placed the prison and its prisoners in Joseph’s charge.

## Chapter XCI. On the Interpretation of the Cupbearer’s and Baker’s Dreams

It happened that the king’s cupbearer and baker were sent to the same prison, and Joseph attended them. Both saw a dream in one night. When Joseph saw them sad in the morning (Gen. 40), [Col. 1128D] he asked the cause of their distress. Learning that they grieved because of a dream, he said: “Tell me what you saw. Does interpretation not belong to the Lord?” That is: “Can it not be interpreted by God’s help?”

The chief cupbearer said: “I saw before me a vine, and in it three *fundos oculos* [probably ‘branching shoots,’ literally ‘fountain-eyes’], that is, places from which the vine-shoots flow forth. Others read three branches, or three offshoots, which is the same. The buds gradually grew; then, after the flowers, grapes ripened. I pressed the grapes into Pharaoh’s cup, which I held, and gave the cup to Pharaoh.”

Joseph said: “God gave humankind the use of wine for good: it is even poured out to him in libation; it settles disputes and sorrows, and the dream is favourable. [Col. 1129A] The three offshoots are three days, after which Pharaoh will restore you to your former rank. Remember me when things go well for you, so that you may speak to the king and have me brought out of this prison. For I was stolen from the land of the Hebrews, and here I was thrown innocently into the pit.”

Then the baker said: “I saw that I had three baskets of flour upon my head, and that in the uppermost I carried foods made by the baker’s art, while birds ate from it.” Josephus, however, says: “Two baskets were full of bread, while the third contained provisions and various foods such as are customarily served to kings.” The Greek has “three baskets of *kodritoi*,” that is, second-quality loaves. It may have been that even the upper basket contained second-quality loaves, above which lay first-quality loaves, from which Pharaoh ate.

Joseph said: “I would rather be an interpreter of good things. Three days remain, after which Pharaoh will hang you upon a cross, and birds will eat your flesh.” Thereafter the third day was Pharaoh’s birthday; amid the banquet he remembered the chief cupbearer and the chief baker. He restored the cupbearer to his position, but hanged the baker on a gibbet. The cupbearer forgot his interpreter.

## Chapter XCII. On Joseph’s Exaltation through the Interpretation of Dreams

After two years Pharaoh saw a dream. He thought he was standing beside a river, from which seven fat cows came up, with plump flesh—that is, full-bodied, as though raised for eating. Then seven others emerged from the river, exhausted by extreme leanness, and devoured [Col. 1129C] the first. Pharaoh awoke, fell asleep again, and saw another dream. Seven full ears of grain sprang up on one stalk; beside them there arose seven others, equally numerous, thin and blasted by scorching wind, and they devoured the first. Pharaoh, terrified, summoned the interpreters and wise men of Egypt, but there was no one who could interpret it (Gen. 41).

Then the cupbearer remembered Joseph. At his suggestion and by the king’s command, Joseph was brought out of prison and shaved; prisoners and exiles let their hair grow. After changing his clothes, he was brought before the king. Taking Joseph’s right hand, the king said: “I saw dreams. Do not fear to explain whatever they may be.” He related what he had seen.

Joseph said: “The king’s dream is one,” that is, it has one meaning. “God has shown Pharaoh what [Col. 1129D] he is about to do. Behold, seven years of great fertility will come throughout all the land of Egypt. They will be followed by seven years of such sterility that all former abundance will be forgotten. The cows and the farmers, and the ears of grain, point to the same thing; the repetition of the dream is an indication of its certainty. As for what you saw beside the river, the cause of this fertility and sterility will arise chiefly from the river. Therefore let the king now appoint a man who shall gather a fifth part of the crops during the seven fertile years into the king’s granaries, that they may be preserved against the famine prepared to come.”

Pharaoh marvelled at both things in Joseph: the explanation of the dream and the discernment of his counsel. He entrusted to him the administration of this matter, saying that he was full of God’s Spirit. Behold, the Spirit of God has now been indicated three times: first, in the words, “The Spirit of God moved over the waters” (Gen. 1); second, “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings” (Gen. 6); and third, here.

[Col. 1130A] Pharaoh then took the ring from his own hand and put it on Joseph’s hand, placed a gold chain around his neck, and made him second in the kingdom. Joseph mounted the king’s chariot, while the herald cried out that all should bend the knee before him, as before the king. The Hebrews, however, relate that the herald did not call for kneeling, but cried *abrech*, meaning “most tender father.” For *abba* is “father,” and *rech*, “delicate” or “most tender”; as if he said: “Although tender in age, he is nevertheless a father in wisdom.”

The king said to Joseph: “I am Pharaoh.” This is an oath, and its sense is: “As it is true that I am Pharaoh, so it is true what I shall say: without your command [Col. 1130B] no one in Egypt shall move foot or hand”; that is, no one shall depart from here without your authorization, nor exercise public office. In the Egyptian language he called him Phanecphane, that is, “Saviour of the world,” which in Greek is called Pontiphanec; in Hebrew, however, it means “discoverer of hidden things.” He gave him Aseneth, the virgin daughter of Potiphar his master, as wife.

[Note: [Col. 1130B] Addition 1. To excuse Joseph’s marriage to a foreign woman, the Hebrews say that Job, after his afflictions, married Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, and received by her a daughter, from whom Aseneth, Potiphar’s daughter, was born. [Col. 1130C]]

Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh. Before the famine came, two sons were born to him. He called his firstborn Manasseh, which means “forgetfulness,” saying: “God has made me forget my labours and my father’s house.” He called the second Ephraim, which means “fruitfulness,” saying: “God has made me increase in the land of my poverty.”

## Chapter XCIII. On Joseph’s Brothers’ Entry into Egypt

[Col. 1130C]

Joseph gathered grain for seven years. When these had passed, the years of want came. The people cried to Pharaoh, asking for food. He answered them: “Go to Joseph.” Joseph opened the granaries and sold grain to the Egyptians. Other provinces also came into Egypt to buy food (Gen. 41). The money was handed over to the king’s treasurers.

When Jacob heard that food was being sold in Egypt, he sent ten of his sons there, keeping Benjamin at home. [Col. 1130D] Having entered the land of Egypt, they came to Joseph, but did not recognize him. When they had worshipped him and he recognized them, he spoke harshly to them: “Where have you come from?” They said: “From the land of Canaan, to buy food.” He said: “You are spies; you have come from various directions to see the weaker parts of the land.”

They replied: “It is not so, lord. But your servants are all sons of one man; the youngest is with our father, and the other is no more.” He said: “This is what I said: you are spies. For it is impossible for an ordinary man to have such sons, since even for kings such abundance of sons is very difficult. By Pharaoh’s life, none of you shall leave here until your youngest brother comes. Send one of yourselves to bring him.” For he feared that perhaps they had also committed some wrong against him. [Col. 1131A] He handed them over bound to custody for three days.

On the third day he brought them out. Holding Simeon back and binding him before their eyes, he allowed the others to depart. They complained to one another: “We deservedly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother.” They did not know that Joseph understood them, because he spoke to them through an interpreter. Joseph ordered his servants to fill their sacks, replace each man’s money in his own sack, and give them provisions for the road besides.

## Chapter XCIV. On the Brothers’ Return to Their Father

They departed and came to their father in the land of Canaan, and told him everything that had happened to them. When they poured out the grain, each found tied money in the mouth of his sack. [Col. 1131B] All were terrified, and their father said: “You have made me childless: Joseph is no more, Simeon is held in bonds, Benjamin will be taken away. These evils have fallen upon me.”

Reuben said: “Entrust him to me; kill my two sons if I do not restore him to you.” But he said: “My son shall not go down with you” (Gen. 42). Meanwhile, when the food had been consumed, famine pressed upon them. Jacob said to his sons: “Return to Egypt, that you may buy a little food.” Judah said: “If you are willing to send the boy with us, we shall go; otherwise, we shall not go.”

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Addition 1. From Jacob’s not entrusting the boy to Reuben, who offered his two sons, but to Judah under the condition of liability, they wish to infer that it is a greater sin to kill a soul than a body.]

“I shall take responsibility for the boy; require him from my hand. Unless I bring him back, I shall be guilty of sin forever.” Israel said: “If it must be so, do what you wish. Take with you some of the best fruits of our land: a little resin, honey, storax, and stacte; terebinth fruit and [Col. 1131C] almonds. Carry gifts to the man. Take back the money which you brought back, and other money to buy food. May God make the man favourable to you and send your brothers back with you” (Gen. 43).

Resin is called any liquid or dry gum, from the Greek *resin*, “to flow.” The first and more precious kind is called terebinth resin—which perhaps he explains by adding “and terebinth fruit.” The second is mastic resin, which comes from the island of Chios; the third, pine resin. Perhaps he called balsam by this name, for Josephus places balsam ointments at the beginning of the gifts and says nothing of resin. Some say storax is a species of resin. Jerome says that the Hebrew has *nethota*, which generally means “incense”; and in Isaiah, for “the house of Nethota,” [Col. 1131D] some translated “house of incense,” others “house of storax.”

## Chapter XCV. On the Brothers’ Entry into Egypt with Benjamin

Thus Jacob’s sons went down into Egypt and stood before Joseph. He ordered his steward to bring them in and prepare a banquet, because they would eat with him. Fearing that they had been brought in because of the money which had been returned, they told the steward that they had brought back the same money, and that, without their knowledge, it had also been placed in their sacks. He said: [Col. 1132A] “Peace be with you. Your God gave you that money; I have the money which you gave me, verified.” Then he brought Simeon out to them. They prepared the gifts until Joseph came in at noon (Gen. 43).

When he entered, they offered the gifts and worshipped to the ground. When he learned that their father was well, and blessed Benjamin, his heart was stirred. He entered his chamber and wept. Having washed his face, he went out, restrained himself, and said: “Set out the bread.” Joseph sat apart, as a foreigner; the Egyptians apart, as natives; and the brothers apart, as strangers. The Egyptians consider it profane to eat with Hebrews, perhaps because of their differing worship.

Joseph arranged the brothers according to their ages, as they were accustomed to sit in their father’s house. When portions were given, [Col. 1132B] they marvelled that Benjamin’s portion exceeded five portions. Josephus, however, says: “He honoured Benjamin with double portions.” Both can stand, if there were five servings of foods and Joseph gave him double from each. They drank and were intoxicated with him—that is, satisfied with food, according to the Hebrew idiom.

Joseph ordered his steward to fill their sacks, replace their money as before, and put his own silver cup in the youngest brother’s sack. It was done. At dawn they were dismissed. Then, at Joseph’s command, the steward pursued and overtook them, saying: “You have done a very wicked thing. You have stolen the cup from which my lord drinks and in which he customarily practises divination” (Gen. [Col. 1132C] 44).

They said: “Whoever is found to have what you seek shall die, and we shall be your lord’s servants.” He searched, beginning with the eldest and continuing to the youngest, and found the cup in Benjamin’s sack. They returned to Joseph, who said: “Do you not know that no one is like me in knowledge of divination?” Perhaps this was said in jest and should not be imputed to him. Judah earnestly pleaded that Joseph retain him as a better servant in place of the boy, because he had taken Benjamin into his own charge from his father.

## Chapter XCVI. That Joseph Revealed Himself to His Brothers

Joseph could no longer restrain himself. Sending the others outside, he cried aloud while weeping, so that those who had gone out [Col. 1132D] heard: “I am Joseph. Do not be afraid. The Lord sent me before you for your salvation. Two years of famine have now passed; five years remain in which there can be neither ploughing nor reaping” (Gen. 45). This is believed to have happened because of an excessive inundation of the river.

He added: “Hurry, tell my father of my glory, and bring him to me, that I may feed you and your livestock, lest you die. You shall live in the land of Goshen. Your eyes see that my mouth speaks to you”; that is, what I say is true. Joseph kissed all his brothers and wept over each of them.

The report was heard in the king’s court: “Joseph’s brothers have come.” Pharaoh rejoiced and said to Joseph: “Concerning your brothers: take wagons from Egypt to transport your wives and little ones. [Col. 1133A] Bring all your possessions with you. I shall give you all the good things of Egypt, and you shall eat the richness of the land.” It was done. Joseph gave each of them two garments. A *stola* is so called from *telon*, “long,” as though it were an ankle-length tunic. But to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five excellent garments. He sent the same number to his father, along with ten asses carrying every good thing of Egypt. As they departed, he said: “Do not quarrel on the way.”

When they came to their father, they said: “Joseph is alive, and he rules in Egypt.” Jacob, as though waking from a deep sleep, did not believe them. But when he saw all that Joseph had sent him, he said: “It is enough for me that my son Joseph lives.” As though he had said: “I care little about punishment or glory. If he lives, I shall go and see him before I die.”

## Chapter XCVII. On Israel’s Descent into Egypt

[Col. 1133B]

Thus Israel set out with all that he had and came to the Well of the Oath. Having sacrificed victims to God, he heard God say to him in a vision of the night: “Do not be afraid; go down into Egypt. There I shall make you into a great nation, and I shall bring you back from there. Joseph also shall place his hand upon your eyes.”

Rising from the Well of the Oath, he came into Egypt with all his offspring. All the persons who entered with him and came from his thigh—though not because souls are propagated by transmission, but because the whole is understood from a part—were sixty-six (Gen. 46), apart from Jacob himself, Joseph, and Joseph’s two sons who were in Egypt. [Col. 1133C] Thus all together were seventy.

Yet the Septuagint translated seventy-five, and Luke likewise in the Acts of the Apostles. Jerome maintains that this was said by anticipation, and that five sons of Joseph’s sons were counted with them, because those sons were to make two tribes. Luke, writing the Acts of the Apostles for Gentiles, did not dare to alter the Septuagint’s wording, because its authority was strong among the Gentiles, while he himself was still unknown to them. The Septuagint itself also translated in Deuteronomy that Israel entered with seventy persons (Deut. 10).

Observe that Er and Onan, Judah’s sons, are counted among these, though they died in the land of Canaan. Perhaps Jacob’s two maidservants are counted in place of the dead, if indeed they also entered. Or Scripture gives the rounded total, though a small number is lacking. Again, observe that if Dinah is counted among the sons and grandsons, there are seventy apart from Jacob. Leah’s children are thirty-three, Zilpah’s sixteen, Rachel’s fourteen, and Bilhah’s seven.

Observe that, since Joseph had only two sons, Benjamin must have had ten; but only nine are read in the book. Perhaps through scribal error two names were written for one. Thus Master Hugh divided Asbel into Asa and Belum. But this does not seem possible, because when the tribal families are enumerated in Numbers after the Midianites had been defeated, it is read: “Asbel, from whom came the family of the Asbelites” (Num. 26). But in the Hebrew truth, Rosh and Muppim are two names which in our text have been wrongly joined, [Col. 1134A] perhaps because Josephus wrote Asbela for Asbel; therefore he divided it thus.

## Chapter XCVIII. That Joseph Met His Father and Introduced Him to the King
Jacob therefore sent word ahead to Joseph, that he might meet him. Joseph, having yoked his chariot, met him in Goshen (Gen. 46). Others say, at the city of Heroon in the land of Rameses, which was then called Goshen and afterwards Thebaïs, from the water of Thebes, whose legion was commanded by blessed Maurice. There are other Thebes, whence the Thebans. Afterwards, when kings came from it, it was called the City of Heroes, because the heroes of Egypt owed it protection. On the borders of that land the Hebrews later built, under Egyptian compulsion, the City of Tabernacles, which was called Rameses and was afterwards named the district of Arsenoires, which [Col. 1134B] means “without sex,” so called when both sexes began to rule Egypt indiscriminately, without distinction.

Joseph said to all his father’s household: “I shall go and report to Pharaoh that you have arrived, and that the men are shepherds. And when he asks you, ‘What is your occupation?’ you shall say, ‘We and our fathers are shepherds.’ Say this so that you may live apart from the Egyptians, in the excellent land of Goshen; for all Egyptians detest sheep-herders, because they do not eat sheep but worship them as Ammon.”

Joseph then entered before the king and set before him the last of his brothers—that is, the five highest-ranking men. When they said that they were shepherds of sheep, they added: “There is no grass in the land of Canaan, and we ask that you command that we, your servants, [Col. 1134C] may be in the land of Goshen. For we do not wish to be separated, but to carry out every provision for our father” (Gen. 47).

If it is asked how Egypt abounded in pasture during a time of famine, we say that Egypt, contrary to the nature of other regions, is barren in pasture when it abounds in crops, and conversely. For a longer, or more prolonged, stay of the river upon the land hinders the season for cultivation or destroys the crops, but nourishes the pastures.

After this Joseph brought his father before the king. He blessed the king. When the king asked him concerning the days of his years, he said: “The days of the pilgrimage of my life are one hundred and thirty years: few and evil; nor have they reached to the days of my fathers.” He said “pilgrimage” because the saints regard this life as a sojourn. He called them “evil” because [Col. 1134D] “the wise man is the accuser of himself” (Prov. 18); and in saying “few,” he defined this by adding, “nor have they reached,” and so forth.—Joseph therefore gave his brothers a possession in the best soil of the land of Rameses.

Josephus nevertheless says: Pharaoh granted them permission to dwell in the Heliopolitan district; for there his shepherds had their pastures, and he knew that it was pleasing to the Egyptians for shepherds to be kept separate from them, and that nothing belonging to the Egyptians had been given to these men. Perhaps the land of Goshen belonged to the territory of Heliopolis.

## CHAPTER XCIX. On the institution of the tax, or provision, of a fifth part of the crops

The famine increased in Egypt. When the buyers’ money had failed, Joseph sustained them that year in exchange for livestock (Gen. 47). In the following [Col. 1135A] year, when they were again perishing from famine, Joseph bought all the land of Egypt in exchange for food and subjected it to Pharaoh’s servitude, except the land of the priests. The kings had given this to them, and fixed provisions from the public granaries were owed to them; therefore they were not compelled to sell their possessions.

But near the end of the barrenness Joseph said to the people: “Behold, you, your livestock, and your land are in Pharaoh’s hand. See, I restore the land and livestock to you, and I shall give you seed; cultivate the land for the king. You shall give a fifth part to the king; I leave the remaining four parts to you for sowing and for food.” They said: “Our salvation is in your hand.” From that time until now a fifth part has been paid to the kings of Egypt. And it became, as it were, a law.

## CHAPTER C. On the oath Joseph made to his father

[Col. 1135B]

Israel therefore dwelt in the land of Egypt, increased exceedingly, and lived there seventeen years; and his days came to one hundred and forty-seven years. When he saw that the day of his death was near, he called Joseph and caused him to put his hand under his thigh and swear—according to the Jews, that is, he swore by the holiness of circumcision, or by Christ—that he would bury him in the tomb of his ancestors, called the Abrahamic tomb. By way of insertion he said, “where Rachel died,” as though excusing himself for not having buried her where he himself wished to be buried.

The saints were concerned to be buried in the land where they knew Christ would rise again, so that they might rise with him there. For the Abrahamic tomb is almost thirty [Col. 1135C] miles from Calvary. After Joseph had sworn, Israel turned toward the head of the bed, which was toward the east, and worshipped God.

Some manuscripts read, “he worshipped upon the head of his staff,” or, “at the head of his staff”; and either may stand. For the old man may have had a staff, as is customary at that age, and, leaning upon it, have worshipped; or he may have held the sceptre which Joseph bore until he had sworn. Once Joseph had sworn, leaning on the top of the staff not yet returned, he worshipped God. For one must not believe those who say that he worshipped Joseph’s sceptre.

## CHAPTER CI. On the blessing of Ephraim and Manasseh

Again Joseph was told that his father was ill; and, taking his two sons, he went. When the old man heard that his son had come, he gathered strength and sat upon the bed. Seeing Joseph and his two sons, Jacob said: “Who are these?” For he could not see clearly. Joseph said: “These are my sons, whom God has given me in this place.” And Jacob said: “These two shall be mine. They shall be reckoned to me as Reuben and Simeon”—that is, each shall form a tribe.

> **[Note: Col. 1136B, Addition I.]** Each of Jacob’s sons, except Joseph, formed a tribe; in Joseph’s place his two sons formed two tribes, although the tribe of Levi is seldom counted.

“Those whom you father hereafter shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritances”—that is, they shall not form tribes but shall be content with their inheritances (Gen. 48). Or otherwise: “they shall be called by the names of their brothers,” that is, they shall be numbered among the tribes of their brothers, so that some shall be Manassehites and some Ephraimites.

Joseph brought Manasseh to his father’s right hand and Ephraim to his left, bowing down and asking him to bless them. But Jacob, [Col. 1136A] by the Spirit, crossed his hands, placing his right hand upon the younger. Joseph took this badly and said: “Not so, father, for the other is the firstborn.” But he said: “I know, my son, I know. He too shall become a people; but the younger shall be greater, and his seed shall grow into nations.” This was fulfilled in Jeroboam, who first ruled the ten tribes and was an Ephraimite.

And he said concerning Ephraim: “In you Israel shall bless, and it shall be said proverbially: ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” And to both he said: “May the God of our fathers bless these boys; and may my name be invoked upon them”—that is, the names of Abraham and Isaac—“and may they increase into a multitude upon the earth.”

And he said to Joseph: “God will bring you back to your land. Beyond your brothers I give you Shechem, which I took by my sword [Col. 1136B] and bow from the hand of the Amorite.” To be sure, he had bought it from Hamor’s king for a hundred lambs; but when it should have been taken from him because of the slaughter of the Shechemites, he retained possession of it by force.

## CHAPTER CII. On the blessings of the twelve tribes

Jacob called his sons and said to them: “Gather together, that I may declare to you what shall happen in the last days.”

> **[Note: Col. 1136B–C, Addition I.]** Not that he blessed all of them, as is evident in Reuben’s case, but because he prophesied concerning all.

(Gen. 49). In the literal sense he prophesied concerning the division of the land and the future condition of the tribes; but most plainly, concerning both advents of Christ.

## CHAPTER CIII. On Reuben

[Col. 1136C]

“Reuben, my firstborn, my strength”—that is, whom I fathered while vigorous in age—“the beginning of my sorrow,” that is, of my anxiety concerning my sons; whence others read, “the chief among my children.”

> **[Note: Col. 1136D–1137A, Addition I.]** Jerome, in Book I of the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, chapter 207, says thus: “In Hebrew it is written: ‘Reuben, my firstborn, my strength, and the chief among my children, greater in bearing and greater in strength: you have been poured out like water; let there be no addition, for you went up to your father’s bed and defiled the couch by your ascent.’ The sense is this: You are my firstborn, the greatest among my children, and according to the order of birth and inheritance—which was due by right to firstborn sons—you ought to have received the priesthood and the kingship; this is also shown by the burden you were to bear and by your preeminent strength. But because you sinned, and, like water which is not held in a vessel, were poured out in the rush of desire, I therefore command you to sin no further and to remain among the number of your brothers, bearing the punishment for sin, because you have lost the rank of the firstborn.”

“First in gifts, greater in rule” [it should be supplied: “you ought to have been”], “you have been poured out like water,” that is, into base lust. “Do not increase, because you ascended your father’s bed” (Gen. 49). Or distinguish it thus: “You have been poured out like water; do not increase, because you ascended your father’s bed,” as if he said: By the law of primogeniture honour above the others and a double portion in the inheritance were owed to you; but let it suffice for your crime that you are equal to the rest. Therefore you shall not grow above them, as boiling water overflows, or as an inundating river [Col. 1136D].

## CHAPTER CIV. On Simeon and Levi

[Col. 1137A]

“Simeon and Levi, instruments of iniquity, because in their fury they killed men,” namely the Shechemites, “and in their self-will they dug through a wall” (Gen. 49). Here he makes clear that this was done against his will. Others read, “they overthrew a bull,” which some understand of the king’s son who had carried off Dinah; some of Christ; while others think it said, by syllepsis, of their bulls.

“Let not my soul enter into their counsel”: this plainly concerns Christ. For the scribes were from Simeon and the priests from Levi, by whose counsel Christ was killed. “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” Literally, Levi received no territorial allotment [Col. 1137B], but, distributed among the others, had villages for the grazing of livestock. Simeon likewise, because it was small, received no allotment, but was received within Judah’s allotment.

## CHAPTER CV. On Judah

There follows the passage concerning Judah, where he prophesied about the future kingdom in Judah and plainly about Christ. “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. 49). This happened when, while the others hesitated, he was the first after Moses to enter the Red Sea, and there he earned the kingship. “Your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies, and your father’s sons shall worship you.” Here he indicates that a king is to come.

“Judah is a lion’s cub.” This concerns the beginning of the kingdom: David, the least of his brothers, was chosen king. “You have gone up from the prey, my son,” because David at first had very many enemies. [Col. 1137C] “Resting, you lay down like a lion, and like a lioness,” because afterward he reigned in peace and was greatly feared. “Who shall rouse him to prophesy?”—as though to say: only the Spirit that was directed into David. Or it may be said concerning Solomon’s succession: “The sceptre shall not be taken away,” that is, a king from Judah, “nor a ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent,” namely Christ, sent by the Father.

Until the Babylonian captivity there were twenty kings from Judah; thereafter there were rulers until Hyrcanus. Again there were kings about the time of Christ; both lines failed, and Herod, a foreigner, reigned. “And he shall be the expectation of the nations,” namely the salvation long desired, not only by the Jews but also by the Gentiles.

Finally he turns his speech to his son Judah concerning that Christ who was to be sent, thus: “O my son, he shall be [Col. 1137D] binding his colt to the vine and his she-ass to the vine-stock”—that is, the Gentile and Judaea—to himself, who is the vine. “He shall wash his garment in wine and his cloak in the blood of grapes,” that is, he shall make his flesh bloody with the blood of the Passion. “His eyes are more beautiful than wine,” that is, the apostles; “and his teeth whiter than milk,” that is, the preachers.

The Hebrew interprets all this concerning Judah as follows: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah,” that is, a certain dominion, because he was the first to enter the Red Sea, the first to offer when the tabernacle had been made, and the like, “until he comes who is to be sent.” The Hebrew says: “until Shiloh comes,” that is, until Saul was anointed at Shiloh. Yet it afterward returns to Judah, who rescued Joseph from his brothers’ hands. “He shall be the expectation of the nations,” that is, of the tribes; whence: “Judah, the Lord will go up for you into battle.” “Binding his colt to the vine and his she-ass to the vine-stock” means that he shall have such abundance of wine that a donkey will be laden from one vine; and for this reason it also calls his eyes ruddy, because this is how the eyes of drinkers appear. In the whiteness of the teeth it indicates an abundance of sheep and milk, because milk that has been consumed appears in the teeth.

## CHAPTER CVI. On Zebulun

“Zebulun shall dwell by the shore of the sea, at the station of ships, extending as far as Sidon” (Gen. 49). Literally, this tribe possessed a maritime territory.

## CHAPTER CVII. On Issachar

“Issachar is a strong, or bony, ass,” that is, a man of agriculture, “lying down in the borders,” because he possessed the inland region between the coastland and the mountains. “And he saw rest [Col. 1138B] to be good,” that is, fertile land; hence follows, “and the land, that it was excellent.” “And he bent his shoulder to bear,” because he laboured in carrying to the sea the merchandise that abounded in his territory; “and he became a servant under tribute,” that is, to ships carrying tribute.

The Hebrews interpret this metaphorically, saying that he laboured in study night and day, and therefore all the tribes served him as a teacher, bringing gifts.

## CHAPTER CVIII. On Dan

“Dan judged his people, as also another tribe of Israel. Let Dan become a serpent in the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hoofs so that its rider falls backward” (Gen. 49). This was fulfilled in Samson, as if he said: Although Dan is the smallest tribe, nevertheless from it shall arise a judge in Israel, as from the others, who, in the manner of a serpent, watched the roads so that enemies might not range through Judaea and plunder it as before; and he shall make the pride of the Philistines retreat.

But, great though he may be, he shall not be Christ. Hence he adds: “Yet after him I shall await your salvation, O Lord.” This is also interpreted of Antichrist, whom they maintain will come from Dan. He shall be armed against the saints with the bite of deadly persecution and with the horn of power. He will cast backward many who have ascended to the summit of virtues; and then the Saviour, awaited before the judgment, shall come.

Others refer this to Judah, who cast down into death the horse—that is, Christ’s flesh—and its rider—that is, his soul—by the bite of betrayal; yet the awaited [Col. 1138D] Saviour shall rise again. But Judas is believed to have been from Issachar.

## CHAPTER CIX. On Gad

“Gad, armed,” or “a bandit,” “shall fight before him, and he himself shall arm himself behind” (Gen. 49). Gad, with Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh, left his wives and children beyond the Jordan in their own territory and went armed before Israel into the land. In accordance with the agreement made with Joshua—that he should return to the land which he had occupied, namely after fourteen years—when he returned first, he found the war of neighbouring nations against his own people which he had left behind; and fighting bravely, he struck down the enemies.

## CHAPTER CX. On Asher

“Asher’s bread is rich, and he shall provide delicacies for kings” [Col. 1139A] (Gen. 49). For this tribe’s possession was fertile and abounded in luxuries.

## CHAPTER CXI. On Naphtali

“Naphtali is a released hind, giving words of beauty” (Gen. 49). By the swiftness of the hind is signified the rapid productivity of its richer land, which bears precious fruits beyond the others. Others read, “an irrigated field,” because it is watered by the Jordan above Lake Gennesaret, or because hot springs are there.

They refer the praise of its words to Mount Tabor, which lies within its territory, because prophets dwelt there; or because the first of its fruits was offered at Passover, whence praise of God arose, which is a word of beauty. Yet it is more truly referred to Christ and the apostles, because he taught there especially.

## CHAPTER CXII. On Joseph’s blessings

[Col. 1139B]

“Joseph is an increasing son,” namely in power and dignity, or because he has two portions among the tribes. “The daughters ran about upon the wall” (Gen. 49). Here he indicates that, as Joseph passed through Egypt, women climbed the walls to behold his beauty.

“They embittered him, quarrelled with him, and envied him, those who had arrows.” This concerns his brothers, or Egyptian men armed against him with the arrows of envy. “His bow rested in strength,” that is, in the Lord; and therefore “the bonds of his arms and hands were loosed by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob,” that is, God, who is Jacob’s power, loosed the bonds with which his brothers had bound him.

“From there came forth the shepherd, the stone of Israel,” because from him came Jeroboam, [Col. 1139C] who ruled Israel—that is, the ten tribes—strongly; or because he was shepherd of his father’s whole household in Egypt. The Hebrew has more correctly: “From there, the shepherds’ stone in Israel.”

After praising him, he blessed him thus: “The God of your father shall be your helper. The Almighty shall bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep lying below, blessings of breasts and womb”—the order is reversed, because this is said for conception and nourishment. He wishes him the dew of heaven, the fruitfulness of the earth, abundance of milk, and fertility of livestock.

“Your father’s blessings have been strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the eternal hills should come.” Here nothing is explained literally. Perhaps it may be understood thus: It is written in Numbers, “The rocks of Arnon bent down,” or, “the rocks of Arnon rejoiced” [Col. 1139D] (Num. 21); and in the Psalms: “The mountains leapt like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep” (Ps. 113). And this he calls “the desire of the eternal hills.” These three things refer to the same matter. Elsewhere they are called the eternal four-sided hills.

We say, therefore, that near the Arnon there were very rugged and rocky hills, and therefore they were called eternal. They had four *ceraunia* [thunderstones], whence they were also called four-sided. Some part of them bent down before Israel so that it might pass easily, and, as it were, applauded their arrival; and perhaps the half-tribe of Manasseh received its allotment around those hills. The sense is: Joseph shall thus be blessed until he enters the promised land through hills that leap for joy, and beyond it, because “until” here is inclusive.

Perhaps he prophesied concerning Mount Ephraim and the mountain of Samaria, where [Col. 1140A] Israel reigned; or concerning the mountains of the Medes and Persians, beyond which Ephraim and Manasseh are still exiled, while the land rejoiced at its enemies’ exile. In that case “until” is exclusive; for then Israel’s glory came to an end.

The Hebrew supplies this sense: “Until the eternal hills are joined to heaven.” The sense is: May Joseph be blessed everywhere, according to a customary manner of speaking. For so people commonly say, “until heaven and earth come together.” And may all these blessings be upon Joseph’s head, and upon the crown of the Nazirite—that is, the holy one—among his brothers.

## CHAPTER CXIII. On Benjamin

“Benjamin is a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Gen. 49). Some refer this to Jerusalem, which lay in Benjamin’s territory. It is called a ravening wolf because it shed the blood of the prophets [Col. 1140B] and of Christ; and in the morning of the departure from Egypt it received prey—that is, the Law—as though it had risen from God, and still consumes it; but at the evening of the world it shall divide the life-giving Spirit from the killing letter.

The Hebrews refer it to the altar which was in Jerusalem. It is called a ravening wolf because of the devouring fire, upon which the priests in the morning set the victims to be burned; in the evening they divided among themselves their respective portions of the sacrifices.

But it is more truly understood of Paul, who was of Benjamin: at first he persecuted the faithful; afterward, being faithful, he dispensed the sayings of God and the ranks of the Church. Or it may be so because this tribe was very warlike. “And he blessed each with his own blessings”: not because he spoke good things of each one, but because he spoke well and prophetically; or because for the most part [Col. 1140C] he blessed them.

## CHAPTER CXIV. On Jacob’s death and his removal to Hebron

Jacob spoke these things, drew his feet up upon the bed, died, and “was gathered to his people,” that is, to the angels, in certain hope that would at last become reality (Gen. 49). It is indeed known that he was gathered to Abraham and Isaac, but so few cannot be called a people. Or all those predestined from Adam, who were in Abraham’s bosom, may be called a people.

Joseph commanded the physicians to embalm him with spices, and the Egyptians kept him for forty days (Gen. 50). It was the custom of pagans to keep bodies unembalmed for nine days, mourning each day and warming them with hot water, in order to discover whether the soul had departed or was merely asleep; but embalmed bodies they kept for eleven days. The Hebrews’ custom was to keep bodies unembalmed for seven days and embalmed for thirty days. Thus they also kept Jacob for thirty days, and so the seventy days passed under the observances of both peoples.

The faithful now, because they say that their dead are embalmed with faith and virtues, mourn them for thirty days; that is, they celebrate special Masses for them during that number of days. Some observe especially the third day, for spirit, soul, and body. Others observe the seventh, because the dead pass into the seventh rest, or because of the sevenfold nature of soul and body.

Joseph informed Pharaoh through intermediaries that he had sworn to his father concerning burial. Having received Pharaoh’s permission, accompanied [Col. 1141A] by his brothers and many Egyptian elders, he carried his father to be buried in Hebron. But, fearing wars, they departed from the direct route and came to the threshing floor of Azad, where later the people, murmuring against God, were consumed by divine fire. There they mourned seven days. For this reason the natives called it “the Mourning of Egypt.” Finally, returning to the road and crossing the Jordan, they buried him in the double cave. Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and the whole escort.

## CHAPTER CXV. On Joseph’s return and death

But his brothers, fearing that after their father’s death he would remember their wrong against him, said: “While your father was still alive, he commanded us to say these words to you: ‘I beg you to forget your brothers’ crimes.’ We too ask you to forgive this iniquity for your father’s sake.” And they bowed down before him, prostrate upon the ground.

Joseph wept and said: “Do not be afraid,” and he comforted them. He lived one hundred and ten years and saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation. Children were also born from Machir, Manasseh’s son, upon Joseph’s knees. He said to his brothers: “God will indeed visit you and bring you back to the land for which he swore to your fathers. Carry my bones with you from this place.”

After he had bound them by oath concerning this, he died; and, embalmed with spices, he was laid in a place in Egypt and was not moved until the children of Israel departed from Egypt (Exod. 13; Josh. 24). According to Josephus, each of the other brothers, at his death, was carried away and buried in Hebron; afterward they were transferred to Shechem.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF EXODUS

[Col. 1141]

## CHAPTER I. Preface

[Col. 1141B]

The history of Exodus follows. It is not different from the history already related, but is the same history continued. Yet, to remove weariness, it has been divided into five parts, each of which has received the proper title of a book. These five are also divided by the Hebrews into fifty-four volumes, thirteen of which came before in Genesis. This second part is called in Greek *Exodus*, in Latin *Exitus* (“Departure”). For *hodos* means a journey or road. It treats of Israel’s departure from Egypt. In Hebrew it is *Elesmoth*, from the beginning of the book, and means “These are the names,” just as we name the Psalms from their opening words.

## CHAPTER II. On the servitude of the children of Israel

“Then a new king arose in Egypt” (Exod. 1), a long [Col. 1141C] time after Joseph’s death. The eighth ruler after the one under whom Joseph lived—who was called by his own name Nephres—was Ammonaphis, under whom Moses was born. But when the kingdom had passed to another house, that king, as though new in relation to the former, did not know the benefits Joseph had conferred upon Egypt. He hated Israel especially, as Josephus says, because the Egyptians envied them for their strength of intellect, industrious labour, abundance of wealth, and nobility of offspring.

The king said to his people: “The people of Israel are almost stronger than we are. Let us oppress them wisely, lest, when multiplied, they themselves rise against us, join our enemies, and depart free.” He therefore imposed heavy compulsory labours upon them, so that, broken by toil, they would have no leisure for sexual embraces. He appointed Hebrews as work-masters over them, but Egyptians over the work-masters, so that they might oppress them more harshly.

Thus they baked bricks from which “they built for the king the store-cities, Pithom and Rameses.” The cities existed previously, but were not store-cities. They lay on Egypt’s frontier; therefore Pharaoh fortified them, so that he might station armed men there, as in encampments constantly keeping watch, lest anyone enter or leave without the king’s command. Or “store-cities” means formerly cities of the poor, which their labour enriched; or, as another text has it, “cities of depots,” where the treasury was stored.

He imposed another task upon them, less onerous but servile: they were to carry away in baskets the mud of the streets and the filth of the lanes. Of this it is written: “His hands served in the basket” (Ps. 80). According to Josephus, he added a third task: they were to divide the river through many channels and surround the cities with ditches, so that the river could not flood them. They had now spent—that is, completed—four hundred years in these miseries. But the more they were oppressed, the more, by God’s action, they multiplied.

## CHAPTER III. On the deceit concerning the midwives

[Col. 1142C]

When Pharaoh saw this, he devised another stratagem. He ordered the Hebrew midwives Sephora and Phua, who were set over the multitude of midwives, to kill Hebrew boys at their delivery and to lie that a miscarriage had occurred, but to preserve the girls: partly because the weaker sex could do no harm and would serve Egyptian lust; partly because a certain scribe of sacred matters had foretold to the king that at that time a male would be born in Israel who would humble Egypt’s kingdom and surpass all others in power.

“But the midwives feared God and preserved the males” (Exod. 1). When the king rebuked them, they lied, saying: “The Hebrew women [Col. 1142D] possess skill in midwifery; before we come to them, they give birth.” “And because they feared God, he built houses for them,” that is, he made them wealthy when they had been poor, or fruitful when they had been barren.

Augustine says that the midwives sinned venially. Gregory seems to hold that they sinned mortally. For he says that the reward for their kindness could have been given in eternal life, but, because of the fault of their falsehood, it was reduced to temporal recompense.

## CHAPTER IV. On the drowning of the children

Pharaoh, seeing that his stratagems did not profit him, openly attacked them. He commanded that every male child born among Israel should be thrown into the river, and many were drowned and perished at that time (Exod. 1). For this sin God is believed to have handed the Egyptians over to this error: that they worshipped Apis as God.

Apis, according to Pliny, who also testifies that he saw it, was a certain bull which suddenly emerged from the river, having on its right shoulder a white mark like a horned moon. Immediately the Egyptians flocked to it, chanting with every kind of musical instrument. It was lifted into the air and borne above them, as though singing; and at its movement or halt they themselves moved or stood upon the ground. That same day it vanished.

Some say that it emerged yearly at the festival of Serapis, and hence they think that it was called Serapis—that is, consecrated to Serapis. Others say that it appeared once every ten years. Others say that it appeared only in the time of a just priest of Heliopolis, not of an unjust one, so that the justice of priests might seem to be divinely indicated. Thus God punished the sin committed in connection with the river by the error concerning the river.

## CHAPTER V. On Moses’ birth and upbringing

“After this a Levite man went out” (Exod. 2), named Aram, or Amram, and took as wife a woman of his own tribe named Jochebed. After the edict he did not wish to approach his wife, preferring to lack children rather than beget them for death. But God appeared to him in a dream, as Josephus says, telling him not to fear to know his wife, because the child whom the Egyptians feared would be born from her; he also revealed to him concerning Aaron’s priesthood.

At last “the woman conceived and bore a son” quietly, because the pains of childbirth did not press heavily upon her. “Seeing the child was beautiful, she hid him for three months. But when she could hide him no longer, she took a little basket of rushes,” formed like a *fiscus*, that is, a round basket, woven with twigs, “coated it with bitumen and pitch, and, placing the baby within, set him out among the reeds on the riverbank,” lest he be carried away by the current. The child’s sister Mary stood at a distance, waiting to see the outcome, by her mother’s command.

“Then Terimith, Pharaoh’s daughter, came down to wash herself in the river. Seeing the little vessel, she ordered it brought to her, saw the crying infant, and, moved with pity, said: ‘This is one of the Hebrew children.’” For God had made him so beautiful that even enemies considered him worthy to be nourished. Although several Egyptian women put their breasts to him for nursing, he turned his face away.

Mary said: “Do you wish me to bring a Hebrew woman? Perhaps he will take the breast of one of his own people.” By Terimith’s order she went and brought the child’s mother as though she were a stranger; and the boy took her breast. Terimith therefore took the child to be raised and, once he was weaned, returned him to Pharaoh’s daughter, who adopted him as a son. He was called Moses. For the Egyptians call water *moys*, and one saved, *is*.
