One day Terimith brought him to Pharaoh so that he too might adopt him. Admiring the child’s beauty, the king put upon his head the crown which he happened to be wearing. It bore a crafted image of Ammon. But the child threw the crown to the ground and broke it. The priest of Heliopolis rose from beside the king and cried out: “This is the child whom God showed us must be killed, so that from now on we may be free from fear!” He wished to rush upon him, but the king’s protection saved him, together with the persuasion of a certain wise man, who asserted that the child had done this in ignorance.

To prove the point, he had coals brought and offered them to the child. The child put them to his mouth and burned the tip of his tongue with fire. [Col. 1144B] Hence the Hebrews think that he had a speech impediment. He was of such great beauty, Josephus says, that no one was so stern as not to linger over the sight of him; and many, seeing him carried through the streets, abandoned the tasks on which they were engaged.

## CHAPTER VI. On Moses’ Ethiopian wife

When Moses had become an adult, the Ethiopians devastated Egypt as far as Memphis and the sea. The Egyptians therefore turned to divination and received the response that they should employ a Hebrew as their helper. They barely obtained Terimith’s consent for Moses to be made commander of the army they had prepared, after they had first sworn that they would not harm him.

[Col. 1144C] Moses was a warlike and highly skilled man. Avoiding the river route as longer, he led the army by land on a shorter path, in order to overtake the Ethiopians unawares. But because he travelled through places full of serpents, he carried ibises—Egyptian storks naturally hostile to serpents—in papyrus crates on wagons. They cleanse their own bellies by thrusting their beaks into their hind parts. When he was to pitch camp, he sent the birds ahead, so that they might drive away and devour the serpents; and thus the army crossed safely by night.

At last he defeated the Ethiopians, caught them as they fled, and shut them up in the royal city of Saba. Cambyses later named it Meroë after his sister. Because it was impregnable, Moses besieged it for a long time. Then Tarbis, daughter of the Ethiopian king, set her eyes upon him; and, by agreement, she surrendered the city to him if he would take her as his wife. So it was done. This is why Mary and Aaron quarrelled with Moses over his Ethiopian wife (Num. 12).

When he wished to return, his wife would not consent. Therefore Moses, as a man skilled in astronomy, carved upon gems two images possessing this effect: one bestowed memory, the other forgetfulness. He set them in matching rings and gave his wife the ring of forgetfulness, while retaining the other himself, so that they might be marked by equal love and by matching rings. The woman therefore began to forget her husband’s love, and at last he returned freely to Egypt.

## CHAPTER VII. On Moses’ flight and his kinship with Jethro

[Col. 1145A]

In those days Moses went out to his brethren in the land of Goshen. He saw their affliction, and an Egyptian overseer striking one of the Hebrews; and, having struck the Egyptian in secret, he hid him in the sand. Going out on the following day, he saw two Hebrews quarrelling. When he rebuked the one who had committed the wrong, he replied: “Who appointed you judge over us? Do you mean to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” Moses was astonished that this matter had become known publicly, and was afraid, especially when he heard that Pharaoh had heard of it and was seeking to kill him. Fleeing through the wilderness, he came into the land of Midian and, as Josephus says, overcame want of food by steadfast endurance. He came to the city of Midian by the Red Sea, so named after a son of Abraham by Keturah, and sat beside a well.

Now the priest of Midian—that is, its chief man, for in ancient times such men were called priests—had seven daughters. He was called Raguel, surnamed Jethro and also called the Kenite. They had come to draw water for their flocks. For the tending of flocks was then also women’s work, especially in the country of the Troglodytes. But shepherds arrived and drove them away; Moses prevented them from wronging the maidens and watered their flocks. When they returned earlier than usual, they asked their father not to leave the kindness of the stranger without recompense. “When Moses had been summoned, he swore that he would dwell with him. And he took as wife his daughter Zipporah, who bore him [Col. 1145C] Gershom,” a name meaning “sojourner,” because he had begotten him in exile. She also bore another, whom he called Eliezer, that is, “the help of my God.” His father-in-law entrusted to him the whole care of his flocks, in which lay all the property of the ancient barbarians.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the vision of God in the bush

At last the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel cried to the Lord; and He remembered the covenant which He had made with their fathers (Exod. II–III). “Now Moses was feeding flocks of sheep in the wilderness. And when he had driven the flock to the inner part of the wilderness, he came to the mountain of God,” Sinai, which is also called Horeb in one part of it; “and the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire in the midst of a bush” (Exod. III).

The fire fed upon the green growth of the bush without harming it. The mountain was especially good for pasture and abounded in grass, because shepherds did not dare to go up there, both because the mountain was lofty and because it was thought that God dwelt there. And Moses said: “I will go and see this great vision.” The Lord called to him from the bush and said: “Moses, Moses.” He answered: “Here I am.” And the Lord said: “Take off your shoes, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.”

And He said: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have come down to deliver them and bring them into a land flowing with milk and honey, to the places of the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite.” He omitted the name of the seventh nation, the Girgashite [Col. 1146A]; and it is omitted almost everywhere except in Deuteronomy. “But come: I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may bring my people out of Egypt.”

Moses said to Him: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh?” And the Lord said: “I shall be with you, and you shall have this sign that I have sent you: when you have brought my people out of Egypt, you shall sacrifice to God upon this mountain.” As though He said: Then you will see that I was with you and brought you out of the land of Egypt.

The Hebrews, however, end the verse here: “that I have sent you.” “And Moses said: If the children of Israel ask, ‘Who is it that has sent you? What is his name?’ what shall I say to them?” To this the Lord replied: “I am who I am.” As though He said: My name is “He Who Is.” “And you shall say to them: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you.’ You shall say also: ‘The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, [Col. 1146B] and the God of Jacob has sent me to you. This is my name for ever,’” because these three witnesses live for ever.

Josephus says: He told him His own appellation, which men had not previously heard, and which it is not permitted for me to utter. “Go, gather the elders of Israel, and tell them that I appeared to you in the bush and sent you to deliver them. They will go with you to the king of Egypt. And you shall say to him: ‘The God of the Hebrews has called us. We shall go three days’ journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to our God.’ Yet I know that he will not let you go except by a strong hand; and I shall strike Egypt with my wonders. Nor shall you go out empty: you shall ask the Egyptians and your fellow lodgers for precious vessels and garments, and you shall despoil Egypt.”

The Hebrews say that they asked to receive these things as a gift; but it is more likely [Col. 1146C] that they asked to borrow them. They are, however, excused by the Lord’s command.

## CHAPTER IX. On the signs given to Moses

“Moses said: ‘They will not believe me.’ The Lord said to him: ‘What is that which you hold in your hand?’ He answered: ‘A rod.’ And He said: ‘Throw it on the ground.’ He threw it down, and it became a serpent. Moses was so frightened that he fled. And the Lord said: ‘Take hold of its tail.’ When he seized it, it became a rod again” (Exod. IV). For in Hebrew the word for serpent is feminine.

And He said: “Perform this sign, that they may believe you.” And He added: “Put your hand into your bosom.” He did so, and it became leprous—that is, white like snow. Again He said: “Draw your hand back into your bosom.” He drew it back and [Col. 1146D] brought it out, and it was like the rest of his flesh. And again: “But if they do not believe even these two signs, take water from the river and pour it upon dry ground, and it shall become blood.”

Moses said: “I pray you, Lord, send another; for I have become more slow of speech since you spoke to your servant, and I have not been eloquent since yesterday or the day before.” The Lord said: “Who made the mouth? Who makes one mute or deaf, seeing or blind? Is it not I? Go, therefore: I shall teach you and shall be with you.” But he said: “I pray you, Lord, send whom you will send.” Then the Lord, as though angry, said: “Your brother Aaron is eloquent; he too will come out joyfully to meet you. Put my words in his mouth, and I shall show you what you ought to do. Take the rod with which you shall perform the signs.”

Thus Moses came [Col. 1147A] to Jethro and said: “I shall return to my brethren in Egypt, to see whether they are alive.” Jethro said to him: “Go in peace.” When he delayed, the Lord again said to Moses: “Go into Egypt; those who sought your life are dead”—namely Pharaoh and his accomplices. Or the plural is used for the singular, if Pharaoh alone sought him.

## CHAPTER X. On Moses’ return to Egypt and the dismissal of his wife

“Moses therefore took his wife and children, placed them upon an ass, and set out. When he was on the journey, at an inn, to eat, the Lord—that is, an angel—met him with drawn sword and wished to kill Moses, namely because he was taking wife and children contrary to God’s will, for they would be [Col. 1147B] a hindrance. Or because he was taking a child who was uncircumcised. Perhaps Moses had already circumcised the other. For one should not believe those who say that the other remained with Jethro, since above it says ‘children.’

“Immediately Zipporah took a very sharp stone, circumcised the foreskin of her son, touched his feet, and said: ‘You are a bridegroom of blood to me’; and after she had said this, He let him go” (Exod. IV). As Augustine says, this passage has been obscured by its brevity. Where, then, it says, “she touched his feet,” one must understand that the blood touched the feet either of the child or of the angel. Hence, in anger, she said to her husband: “Are you a man of blood to me? That is, am I bound through marriage to you to do so dreadful a deed as to shed my son’s blood?” And either she withdrew from him, or the angel did.

The Hebrew reads thus: “And she touched his feet,” [Col. 1147C] that is, Zipporah touched Moses’ feet. “For in anger she threw the foreskin at Moses’ feet and said: ‘You are a bridegroom of blood to me,’” that is, you became the son-in-law of my father in order to be to me—that is, to my flesh, in my son—unto blood, that is, unto death. Or: “My blood has been shed to appease the angel who threatened you with death.”

“And the angel let Moses go,” which is clear in the Hebrew. Yet the Hebrew says, “the angel released him,” whom, namely, he had previously been constraining unto death. From this some wish to conclude that the custom of circumcising with stone knives began here, or with Joshua at Gilgal. Yet where we have “stone,” the Hebrew has “edge,” and says “a very sharp cutting-edge, a razor.” Hence the Jews also circumcise with razors.

Some Hebrews relate the fable that circumcision was performed with stone down to David. But because, when Goliath was cast down, the iron of his breastplate and helmet yielded to the thrown stone, as though giving it place, thereafter stone yielded to iron in circumcision.

## CHAPTER XI. On the first approach to Pharaoh

Moses therefore went away alone, carrying the rod. By the Lord’s command Aaron entered the wilderness of Sinai; “and he met Moses on the mountain of God. Moses told him the words of the Lord and the signs which He had commanded. They came together and assembled the elders of Israel. Aaron spoke to them all the words of the Lord and performed the signs before them, and they believed” (Exod. IV).

After this, they entered Pharaoh’s presence with the elders of Israel and said to him: “Thus says the Lord, [Col. 1148A] the God of Israel: Let my people go, that we may sacrifice to our God” (Exod. V). No inconsistency or duplicity is to be understood here. For perhaps the people would have been brought out in that order, had Pharaoh dismissed them.

Then Moses, according to Josephus, reminded him how much he had done for the Egyptians when they were oppressed by the Ethiopians; he recalled the labours and dangers that he had borne for them, and that he had not received from them a fitting recompense. At the same time he explained the signs that had happened to him. The king mocked him, calling him his fugitive slave and saying that he had returned to stir up rebellion.

Then the king said to his servants: “The people are numerous: how much greater will they become if you give them rest from their labours?” He ordered that straw should no longer be supplied to them for making bricks, [Col. 1148B] since chopped straw was mixed with clay in order that the bricks might be stronger; or rather, the bricks were baked because wood was scarce in Egypt.

## CHAPTER XII. On the affliction of the children of Israel

The Hebrews were therefore oppressed with labour: by night collecting straw and by day making bricks. The same number of bricks as before was demanded from them. The foremen from among the children of Israel, who were set over their working brethren, were beaten by Pharaoh’s overseers because of the nightly collecting of straw. For the Hebrew officials were the workmasters, but the Egyptians were overseers over the workmasters.

The rulers of the children of Israel came to Pharaoh and said: “Why do you deal unjustly with your servants?” He said: “You are idle, and therefore you say: [Col. 1148C] ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord.’ Go therefore and work: straw shall not be given you.” As they went out, “they met Moses and Aaron and said to them: ‘May the Lord look upon your injury done to us and judge, since you have made us stink’”—that is, rendered us detestable—“before Pharaoh.”

Moses said to the Lord: “Why have you sent me, to afflict this people?” (Exod. V). The Lord said to him: “With a strong hand I shall drive them out” (Exod. VI). And He added: “I am He who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty”—that is, as the Almighty—“and I did not make known to them my name Adonai,” that is, the strength and power belonging to this name, but rather mercy and wisdom, to which *Eli* and *Eloi* belong. Or, “I did not make it known as I did to you.” For the Lord appeared to Abraham, but spoke with Moses face to face.

Again He said: “I shall bring you into the land over which I lifted my hand”—that is, swore—“that I would give it to your fathers: I, the Lord.” As though He said: This is as true as that I am the Lord; and it is a form of oath. “Moses told all these things to the children of Israel, but they did not heed him because of anguish of spirit” (Exod. VI).

The history here enumerates the heads of households according to their families, but only from three tribes, namely Reuben, Simeon, and Levi. It is enough for us to speak of Levi alone. Levi’s sons were Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. From them arose the three Levitical families: the Gershonites, Kohathites, and Merarites. Kohath’s sons were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Amram’s children by Jochebed were Aaron, Moses, and Miriam. [Col. 1149A] Aaron took as wife Elizabeth, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon; she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Eleazar took a wife from the daughters of Phanuel, and she bore him Phinehas. “This is Moses and Aaron,” to whom the Lord spoke in the land of Egypt. This was added by Ezra, as some say. Or Moses spoke of himself as though of another.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the changing of rods into a serpent

“Again the Lord spoke to Moses: Speak to Pharaoh everything that I speak to you, and do not fear him. Behold, I have made you God to Pharaoh,” that is, powerful over him and in his land, to perform signs in the manner of God (Exod. VII). “Aaron shall be [Col. 1149B] your prophet,” that is, your spokesman. Yet Moses was not God, nor Aaron a prophet.

Moses and Aaron entered Pharaoh’s presence. Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh. Aaron took Moses’ rod and threw it on the ground before Pharaoh, and it became a serpent. Pharaoh summoned sorcerers, and they did likewise: each threw down his rod, and they became dragons; but Aaron’s rod swallowed their rods. One should know that the magicians deceived the eyes of the spectators. Or, according to Augustine, demons run throughout the world and suddenly bring the seeds of things from which such effects are produced.

## CHAPTERS XIV AND XV. On the plagues of Egypt and water changed into blood

“The heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not listen to them. The Lord said to Moses: Go out to meet Pharaoh when he goes out to the waters, and say: ‘By this you shall know that I am the Lord: I shall strike the water of the river with the rod, and it shall be changed into blood. The fish shall die, and the Egyptians shall suffer’” (Exod. VII). And it happened so.

> **[Note: Col. 1149D]**
>
> **Addition 1. Verses on the ten plagues**
>
> First, the reddened wave; the plague of frogs, second.
>
> Then the grievous gnat; after it, the fly more harmful than these.
>
> [Col. 1150A] Fifth laid low the cattle; the sixth produced blisters.
>
> Then hail comes; then the locust with its baneful bite.
>
> The ninth covers the sun; the last kills the firstborn.

“And Aaron struck the water of the river, and it was changed into blood”; and there was blood throughout all the land of Egypt—in rivers, streams, and marshes. Perhaps not in all waters, but in those flowing from the Nile, and in vessels in houses, whether of wood or stone. “The Egyptians dug wells around the river and found blood.” The magicians Jannes and Jambres did likewise. And [Col. 1149D] they say that water was brought from the land of Goshen, which the Lord had not struck with plagues because the children of Israel lived there.

Josephus, however, says that the river was drinkable for the Hebrews although it had been changed; for the Egyptians it presented not only the colour but also the bitter taste of gore. Hence it seems more likely that elsewhere besides the Nile there was water in Egypt. This was the first plague with which the Lord struck Egypt for seven days. Josephus says that Pharaoh, fearing because of it and wavering, allowed the Hebrews to depart; but when the evil had been relieved, he changed his decision.

## CHAPTER XVI. On frogs

“Again the Lord spoke to Moses: Go in to Pharaoh; and if he refuses to dismiss the people, tell Aaron to stretch out his hand over the rivers, streams, and marshes” (Exod. VIII). He did so. “And frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.” As Josephus says, once produced, they soon died; and from their decaying bodies an exceedingly harmful stench rose from the water. Indeed, certain ones, as though household creatures, entered houses and were often found in foods, drinks, and beds. “The sorcerers [Col. 1150B] also did likewise.”

There are three kinds of frogs: one, living in rivers, is vocal; another is very small and is also called a reed-frog, and if it is thrown into a dog’s mouth, the dog becomes mute; the third is large and poisonous, called the *rubeta* [toad], and popularly *exassantium* [reading uncertain]. Pharaoh said to them: “Pray to the Lord, and the frogs shall be removed from us, and I shall let the people go.” Moses cried to the Lord, and the frogs died. But Pharaoh, seeing that relief had been granted, did not dismiss them.

## CHAPTER XVII. On gnats

“The Lord said to Moses: Tell Aaron: Stretch out the rod and strike the dust of the earth, and let there be gnats throughout all the land of Egypt” (Exod. VIII). It happened so. Gnats are flies so [Col. 1150C] small that they escape the sight unless it is very sharp, and they bore into the body upon which they alight with a painful sting. “The sorcerers attempted likewise, to bring forth gnats, but were unable. And they said to Pharaoh: ‘This is the finger of God,’” that is, the Spirit of the Lord God. For as the Son is customarily understood through the right hand, so the Holy Spirit through the finger.

Augustine asks why they failed at this point, though not at the first or second plague. He says that it was done to signify that, although philosophers had knowledge of the Father and the Son, they did not have knowledge of the Holy Spirit. These three signs were performed through Aaron’s hand; those which follow were performed by the Lord alone, while some were performed through Moses.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the dog-fly

[Col. 1150D] “The Lord therefore said to Moses: Go out to the waters to Pharaoh and tell him that, if he refuses to dismiss my people, I shall send every kind of fly throughout all the land of Egypt and shall make the land of Goshen marvellous on that day, for it shall have tranquillity” (Exod. VIII). It happened so. “A most grievous fly came into all the land of Egypt.” This is figurative speech, meaning a multitude of flies; and it is expressed more forcefully than if the plural had been used.

> **[Note: Col. 1151A] Addition 1.**
>
> That is, by a customary mode of expression he says this, according to which Augustine says: “I know not how the singular number signifies more than the plural; as in ‘he fills with an armed soldier.’” Through this clause the manner of speech is indicated, the figure is noted, and this is its sense and the propriety of the expression. [Col. 1151B]

For this the Septuagint used “*coenomyia*,” that is, the dog-fly, as is also found in the Psalms (LXXVII and CIV). “Then Pharaoh summoned them and said: ‘Go, sacrifice to your God in this land.’ They said: ‘We cannot. We shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians. If we kill before [Col. 1151A] them what the Egyptians worship, they will stone us.’” For they worshipped the bull in honour of Apis, the cow for Isis, and the sheep for Ammon; therefore it was abominable to them for these animals to be killed or eaten.

Pharaoh said: “Go into the wilderness, but do not go too far; pray to the Lord for me.” Moses prayed, and the fly departed. “And Pharaoh’s heart was again hardened.” Josephus says that in connection with these two plagues an innumerable multitude of lice sprang up among the Egyptians, boiling forth from within; they could not eradicate them either by washing or by medicinal ointments. For it is credible that the Egyptians were struck with many plagues besides the ten famous ones.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the death of livestock

[Col. 1151B] “Then the Lord said to Moses: Tell Pharaoh that if he holds my people back tomorrow, I shall bring a grievous pestilence, and all Egypt’s animals shall die; but nothing of what Israel possesses shall die. And the animals of Egypt died” (Exod. IX)—namely those which were in houses, because those in the pastures afterwards perished in the hail. Or perhaps this is not specified because these events may not have occurred without a long interval of time, and they could have obtained animals again from elsewhere.

Josephus also says in connection with this plague [Col. 1151C] that the Lord filled their country with beasts of many kinds, whose appearance no one could endure; the Egyptians themselves were consumed by them, and the land was deprived of cultivators. “And Pharaoh’s heart was made heavy, and he would not dismiss the people.”

## CHAPTER XX. On sores and blisters

“Again the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Take ashes from the furnace, and let Moses scatter them into the sky before Pharaoh; and there shall be sores and blisters upon human beings and beasts throughout all the land of Egypt” (Exod. IX). It happened so. Even the sorcerers could not stand before Pharaoh because of the wounds in them, which came from inward corruption.

## CHAPTER XXI. On hail

[Col. 1151D] “The Lord also said to Moses: Tell Pharaoh: Thus says the Lord: For this reason I have set you up, that I may show my power in you and that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. At this very hour tomorrow I shall rain such hail as has not been in Egypt until this day” (Exod. IX), nor even in the Hyperborean regions. “Gather in what you have in the field; for men and animals found outside will die from the hail.” Whoever among Pharaoh’s servants feared the Lord caused servants and animals to take refuge in houses.

Moses stretched out his rod toward heaven, and the Lord gave thunder, hail, and lightning; fire and hail mingled together were borne along. The hail struck everything that was in the fields, shattered the grass, and [Col. 1152A] broke the trees of the land. The barley was damaged because it was already green, and the flax because it had already put forth seed-pods. But “the wheat and *far*,” a kind of grain coarser than wheat, “were not damaged, because they are late crops,” not yet green, since they had not yet emerged into ear. “Nevertheless, hail did not fall in the land of Goshen.”

Pharaoh summoned them and said: “I have sinned even now. Pray to the Lord for me, and I shall let you go.” Moses went out from the city and stretched his hands to the Lord; the storm ceased, and rain did not even drip upon the earth. “And Pharaoh’s heart was made heavy.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On locusts

“The Lord said to Moses: Go in to Pharaoh, and I shall perform signs which you may recount to your children and [Col. 1152B] grandchildren, that you may know that I am the Lord. And, having entered, they said to the king: ‘Thus says the Lord: Behold, tomorrow I shall bring locusts into your territory, to consume what the hail has left behind’” (Exod. X).

When Moses had gone out, Pharaoh’s servants said to him: “How long shall we endure this calamity? Let the men go, for Egypt is perishing.” When they had been recalled, Pharaoh said: “Who are those that are going to sacrifice?” Moses said: “Men and women, old and young, with sheep and herds.” He replied: “Who can doubt that you intend the worst? It shall not be so: only the men may go, for that is what you requested.” And they were driven from his presence.

Moses stretched out his hand over the land of Egypt, and the Lord brought a south wind all that day and night. It bore up locusts, which settled innumerably [Col. 1152C] throughout all Egypt’s borders and consumed every green thing on the trees and herbs. The locust is so called as though from a “long spear,” because it has longer hind legs.

Pharaoh hurriedly summoned them and said: “I have sinned against your God and against you. Pray that the plague may be removed this one time also.” Moses went out and prayed to the Lord. A west wind blew and cast the locust into the Red Sea. “And the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let Israel go.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On darkness

“Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and palpable darkness came to pass, so that the Egyptians could neither see nor move from place to place” (Exod. X); [Col. 1152D] many were even wondrously compelled to die. “But wherever Israel was, there was light.” Pharaoh summoned them and said: “Go, all of you; only let the sheep and herds remain.” Moses said: “Not a hoof shall remain of them, especially since we do not yet know what we ought to sacrifice.” Pharaoh said: “Take care not to see my face again, lest you die.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Egyptian days

Moses therefore went to his brethren, and the Lord said to him: “I shall yet strike Pharaoh with one plague, and he will let you go” (Exod. XI). It should be noted that there were more plagues in Egypt than the ten which Exodus enumerates, but perhaps they were not so severe and are therefore passed over in silence. From this come the so-called Egyptian days, because Egypt suffered upon them; yet we note only two in each month in remembrance, although perhaps there were more. Nor should it be believed that the Egyptians, although skilled in astronomy, discovered these unlucky days for beginning a work, a journey, or bloodletting.

Note also that certain Egyptians, fearing Egypt’s destruction, departed; for example Cecrops, who entered Greece and founded a city which he called Acte, later called Athens, which some Greeks called Diades and others Orchomenus. He was called Diffres. This is an Egyptian name, rendered in Latin approximately as “two-man,” either because, as Pompeius Trogus says, he gave the Greeks the institution of marriage between man and woman, or as “two-bodied,” or because of his great height, or his immense strength, or his skill in the two languages, Greek and Egyptian, under whom the olive first sprang up on the citadel.

It is also believed that Dionysius Bacchus left at the same time; he cultivated fields and gave the Greeks the use of the vine. A flood in Thessaly under Deucalion, and a conflagration under Phaethon, are likewise said to have occurred about the time of Moses; and in his time Hercules defeated Antaeus. Erichthonius son of Vulcan is said to have invented the chariot, and Troilus first to have yoked a four-horse team. Egypt, formerly Mesraim and later Aerea, was called Egypt after King Aegyptus was drowned. Lacedaemon, son of Semele, founded Lacedaemon; Panthus, son of Triopas, Lesbos. Epidaurus and Corinth, formerly Ephyra, were founded. According to some, Isis bore Epaphus by Thelenus; he founded Memphis, while he ruled in Lower Egypt. [Col. 1153C]

But the Lord, specifying the plague that remained, said: “I shall enter Egypt, and every firstborn shall die, from Pharaoh’s firstborn to the firstborn of the female slave at the mill, and even the firstborn of livestock. Yet among you not even a dog shall bark; and you shall ask the Egyptians for precious vessels, and they shall give them to you” (Exod. XI).

## CHAPTER XXV. On the days of unleavened bread and the paschal lamb

“Again the Lord said to Moses: ‘This month shall be for you the first among the months of the year’” (Exod. XI). This is April—that is, the April lunar month, which often begins in March. The Hebrews call it Nisan, the Egyptians Pharmuthi, and the Macedonians Xanthicus. [Col. 1153D] For the Lord wished the Jews to differ from other nations not only in religion and the mark of circumcision, but also in their reckoning of time.

The Romans, following the tradition of Numa Pompilius, make January the first month, because then the sun begins to rise after the winter solstice. The Arabs begin the year after the summer solstice. The Hebrew observance in March seems more fitting, since the world is read to have been created in that month. Thus in the ceremonial April they differ from us; in the civil reckoning they agree with us.

The Lord added: “On the tenth day of this month every household shall take a lamb,” or, if it cannot obtain a lamb, at least a kid. “But if the number of a household is insufficient for eating the lamb, it shall take from the neighbouring household, according to the number of persons sufficient [Col. 1154A] for eating the lamb. It shall be a male, a year old”—that is, one year of age—“without blemish,” not a blemish of fleece but of body, as is specified in Leviticus: “if it be blind, if broken,” and so forth (Lev. XXII). Taken from the flock, “you shall keep it in the house until the fourteenth day, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it”—that is, each household its own—“at evening. With a bundle of hyssop you shall stain both doorposts and the lintel with blood, eating the flesh that night roasted by fire; and nothing of it boiled in water or raw”—that is, half-cooked through haste—“and unleavened bread with wild lettuces,” whose bitterness might recall the bitterness of slavery for ever.

[Col. 1154B] “You shall consume the head with the entrails and feet. If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire.” For, as Josephus says, what is burned is accustomed to rise upward; and the rising of the fire signified the lifting from them of the plague which devastated the Egyptians. No uncircumcised person shall eat of it. Concerning the manner of eating, He also said: “You shall gird your loins, have shoes upon your feet, hold staffs in your hands; you shall not break a bone, nor carry any of the flesh outside, and you shall eat hurriedly. For it is *Phase*, that is, the passage of the Lord.”

That night was called the passage because on it the angel passed through Egypt, striking the firstborn from human beings to cattle, and passed over the roofs of the Hebrews that had been smeared or daubed with blood. Israel also set out on the journey of passage from Egypt. Again the Lord said: [Col. 1154C] “You shall keep this day as solemn and memorial, observing it throughout your generations in perpetual worship. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; the first day shall be holy and venerable, and likewise the seventh. You shall do no work on them except what pertains to eating.”

It is clear that they could work on the intermediate days. From this it is also clear that the Sabbath was more solemn to them than any festival with respect to rest, since on it even work connected with eating was not permitted. Hence it could be that women were able, on the solemn day of Passover itself, to prepare ointments for anointing the Lord, which would not have been permitted on the Sabbath. In Ezekiel a feast is read on the first day of April and another on the seventh, which is not found here.

The children of Israel returned and did as the Lord commanded Moses and Aaron; and they gathered on the fourteenth moon in Egypt’s borders near Rameses. Josephus, however, says they gathered on the tenth [Note: Col. 1154D]

> **Addition 1.**
>
> By “the tenth moon,” elsewhere “the fourteenth,” it is indicated that the lamb which was taken signified something eternal. For the moon is said to have been created on the fourth day, as though it were the eleventh day of the world on the first day, and the tenth before the world. Some say that ten persons ate one lamb. Observe carefully this point: the moon was created on the fourth weekday and on that day was the fourteenth; thus the third weekday was the thirteenth, the second weekday the twelfth, and the first weekday the eleventh.

moon, and scarcely waited for the fourteenth.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the death of the firstborn

[Col. 1155A] “And it came to pass at midnight that the Lord struck every firstborn in Egypt; nor was there a house in which a dead person did not lie” (Exod. XII). Perhaps the Lord so arranged it that there was no house without a firstborn. Pharaoh, compelled, sent messengers to Moses, telling him to depart with all his people; indeed, the Egyptians pressed them to leave.

> **[Note: Col. 1155B] Addition 1.**
>
> Pharaoh, or Egypt, beaten by ten plagues, did not yield; conquered by the blood of the lamb alone, it let the children of Israel go.

“The people therefore took kneaded dough upon their shoulders, bound in cloaks. They asked the Egyptians for vessels and an abundance of clothing, and despoiled the Egyptians,” by the Lord’s command: partly as wages for the labour of which they had been defrauded, and partly so that the tabernacle might be made from it. There were about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides little children and an innumerable common crowd serving them; and [Col. 1155B] they took with them a very great number of animals of various kinds.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Israel’s departure from Egypt

It came to pass that the Nile, beyond its usual measure, was still flooding the land in which Joseph’s tomb was situated. They were bound by oath to carry away his bones. Moses took the name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, written upon a gold plate; when it was placed upon the water, it floated until, coming to the place of the tomb, it stopped above it. They dug it up and took away the bones, which, after being taken up, are said to have prophesied to them—perhaps concerning the difficulty of the journey.

The Hebrews, however, relate that a sheep suddenly [Col. 1155C] stood beside them and spoke to them. For this reason they led it with them for a long time through the wilderness and called it Joseph’s sheep, concerning which it is said: “You who lead Joseph like a sheep” (Ps. LXXIX). At their departure, an earthquake occurred, and many Egyptian temples fell down with their idols.

“Now the dwelling of the children of Israel in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years” (Exod. XII). But by the name Egypt is to be understood the whole duration of their sojourning, which began with the promise made to Abraham on the road in Mesopotamia; from that promise until the giving of the Law so many years elapsed. For Israel served in Egypt only one hundred and forty-four years after Joseph’s death. When these had been completed, the entire multitude departed [Col. 1155D] from Egypt on the same day—something also marvellously accomplished by God, or perhaps on the very day on which Abraham departed to live as a sojourner.

Note that here it says, “On the day when they went out” (Exod. XIII), and below, “Remember this day, on which you went out of Egypt, on the first day,” namely of unleavened bread; while above they are also said to have been told, “Let no one go out of the door of his house until morning.” Conversely, immediately here it is read: “That night is to be observed to the Lord, when He brought them out of Egypt”; and in the blessing of the Paschal candle they are said to have been “led out by night.” Perhaps “led out by night” should be understood as: compelled by the Egyptians at night to leave in the morning.

“They departed from Rameses for Succoth,” and the Egyptians did not follow them, being occupied with burying their dead. Many Egyptians also [Col. 1156A] wept in repentance because they had been so cruel to them. “They baked the dough which they had brought from Egypt and made unleavened cakes baked under ashes,” though the dough had set from only a little time. They used these for thirty days. For what they had brought from Egypt did not suffice beyond that time, even though it was preserved out of necessity and they did not eat it to satiety.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the sanctification of the firstborn
“Again the Lord said to Moses: ‘Consecrate to me every firstborn male that opens the womb, both among human beings and among beasts’” (Exod. XIII), because he had struck down the firstborn of Egypt in their deliverance, and because for this reason he wished only males to be consecrated to himself. It may be said that only males were struck down; or perhaps because he had delivered [Col. 1156B] their firstborn from the destroying angel, and in this way they were his, he wished henceforth that all firstborn should be his; or because God ought to be honoured with the first of every fruit.

The firstborn who belonged to the sons of Levi were offered and were not redeemed, but served the Lord continually. The firstborn of the others were offered and redeemed for five shekels (Num. III and XVIII). The firstborn of animals fit for sacrifice, once offered, belonged to the priests. Of unclean animals, however, which were not offered, some were redeemed: for example, the firstborn of an ass was exchanged for a sheep, which was offered in its place. Others, not even being redeemed, were killed, such as the firstborn of a dog.

And the Lord added: “When the Lord brings you into the promised land, you shall declare these things to your children, to be observed as an everlasting rite. [Col. 1156C] And this shall be as a sign upon your hand and as something fastened before your eyes,” so that the memory of this deliverance should no more be forgotten than are things carried in the hand or hung before the eyes. The Pharisees, observing this literally, wrote these things and also the Decalogue on slips of parchment; they bound them about their left arms and hung them between their eyes. The Lord calls these in the Gospel *phylacteries*, from *phylace* and *thorax* (Matt. XXIII).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the wilderness of Egypt

“Therefore, when Pharaoh had sent forth the people, Moses did not lead them out through Palestine, which borders Egypt,” because of the ancient injury and hatred of their fathers [Col. 1156D], lest the Philistines rise against them; “but he led them round by the wilderness which is beside the Red Sea” (Exod. XIII). This was both because of the Lord’s command that the people be led to Mount Sinai to sacrifice to him, and so that, should the Egyptians repent and wish to pursue them, they would endure the serious hardship of the journey.

“And the children of Israel went up armed from the land of Egypt,” that is, equipped with much baggage. Yet another translation has: “The children of Israel went up in the fifth generation.” Moses was fifth from Jacob; or, through the tribe of Judah, from Phares to Salmon, there were only five generations. The Hebrew has: “The children of Israel went up in five generations.” — “And setting out from Sochoth, they came to Etham.”

Etham was then a deserted city [Col. 1157A] at the edge of the wilderness. Josephus calls it Lycus, and says that Babylon was later built there, while Cambyses was devastating Egypt.

> [Note: [Col. 1157A] Addition 1. Not that famous Babylon of Nebuchadnezzar, but another Babylon, which was inhabited even then. Blessed Catherine is said to rest there on Mount Sinai; religious monks live there, and only oil burns in their lamps, flowing from the tomb of that blessed Virgin.]

## CHAPTER XXX. On the guidance of the pillar and the Red Sea

“The Lord, as guide of their journey, went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, against the heat of the sun, and by night in a pillar of fire” (Exod. XIII), against darkness and so that they might protect themselves against serpents.

And the Lord commanded that, having “turned back” somewhat [Col. 1157B] toward Egypt, they should encamp in the region of Phihahiroth, which lies between Magdalum and the sea, opposite Beelsephon (Exod. XIV). Magdalum is a city on the Egyptian frontier, to which the Jews first fled when Gedaliah had been killed in the time of Jeremiah; and they pitched camp by the Red Sea (Jer. XLI).

The water of this sea is not red; rather, all the surrounding land is red, and from it the current is tainted and coloured, whence exceedingly bright vermilion is obtained. Whatever in its fruits is suitable for food takes on this colour. For this reason red gems are found there; buried in the ground and worn among the earth’s sands, they have the colour of the soil and of the sea.

This sea divides into two gulfs. The eastern one is called the Persian Gulf because the Persians inhabit its shore; [Col. 1157C] the other is called the Arabian Gulf, though we call it the Red Sea. The Hebrew calls it *Cannosum* (“Reedy,” i.e. the Reed Sea), because reeds abound on its shores. There the children of Israel were indeed hemmed in: on one side were exceedingly rugged, impassable mountains, and on the other side the sea.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the crossing of the Red Sea

“Pharaoh’s heart was changed” (Exod. XIV). He took three hundred chariots of his own and three hundred from the Egyptians and pursued them. He also led fifty thousand horsemen and two hundred thousand armed infantry. “And the Hebrews raised their eyes, saw the Egyptians behind them, and were greatly afraid.” They had no opportunity for flight, could not fight because they were unarmed, and could not remain there because of the scarcity of provisions.

[Col. 1157D] When they sharply reproached Moses, he said to them: “Do not be afraid. The Lord has done these things so that today you may see his mighty works. He himself will fight for you, and you shall be silent. The Egyptians whom you now see, you shall not see for ever.” The Hebrew is fuller: “You shall not see for ever as you now see them”—that is, alive.

Moses prayed to the Lord, who said: “Why do you cry to me? Lift up your rod, stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it, so that the children of Israel may enter upon dry ground. And the angel who went before them moved away and stood” behind them, between the Egyptians and Israel, “and the cloud was dark”—dark to the Egyptians but bright to the Hebrews.

“And when Moses stretched out his hand,” a violent wind blew “and turned the water into dry land”; [Col. 1158A] and the sea was divided into twelve divisions, so that each tribe might proceed in its own companies. Moses called each tribe in the order of its birth and urged them to follow him as he went before them. When Reuben, Simeon, and Levi feared to enter, Judah was the first to undertake the journey after him; hence he deserved kingship there also.

“Therefore they went through the midst of the sea, and the water was like a wall on their right hand and on their left.” Seeing this, the Egyptians judged them mad. But when they saw that they departed unharmed, they entered after them.

“And now the morning watch had come.

> [Note: [Col. 1158D] Addition 1. Four morning watches are said to exist: the first, midnight; the second, the dead of night; the third, cockcrow; the fourth, before dawn. They entered the Red Sea in the fourth.]

“And the Lord looked upon the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud,” that is, he sent upon them intolerable rains, heavy thunder, flashes of lightning, and fiery gleams. Therefore [Col. 1158B], terrified, they said: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them.”

According to Josephus, however, the children of Israel came to the opposite shore. The Hebrews, on the other hand, maintain that when they reached the end of a mountain projecting into the sea, they turned aside along a long route through the sea and, going round the mountain, returned to the same Egyptian shore. They prove this as follows: it is the nature of the sea to cast up upon the nearest shore what perishes in it. Therefore, since the Egyptian dead lay miserably upon the shore, it is clear that it was the same shore on the other side of the mountain. For in the span of a night, nearly equal to the night of the equinox, neither group could even have crossed to the middle of the sea, since it is broad there.

While the Egyptians were thus thrown into confusion, Moses, at the Lord’s command, stretched out his hand over the sea, and the waters returned [Col. 1158C] to their former place and covered the Egyptians: “not even one of them survived.” Israel took the weapons of the dead.

Moses composed a song to the Lord in hexameter verse: “Let us sing to the Lord,” etc. (Exod. XV). Because it is read before the others, it is called the Song of Songs. Josephus says that this ought not to be disbelieved, since it is recorded that the Pamphylian Sea was divided for Alexander of Macedon and his army while he pursued Darius, at the Lord’s command, because through him he wished to destroy the Persian kingdom.

Israel remained beside the seashore for seven days. With drums and musical instruments, each day they came to the shore and sang the song of Moses to the Lord, the men separately and the women separately. In memory of this, during the seven Paschal days [Col. 1158D] we return in song to the fonts. Here ends the second book of Josephus.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the sweetening of the waters of Marah

After this, “they went out into the wilderness of Shur” (Exod. V). Yet the Hebrew has “into the wilderness of Etham.” For we say that before the sea they were in the wilderness of Etham; after the sea, in the wilderness of Shur; after Elim, in the wilderness of Sin.

“They travelled for three days through the wilderness and found no water,” until they came to Marah. There they found water, but because of its bitterness [Col. 1159A] they could not drink it. Hence they called that place Marah, from this bitterness of the water—or rather from bitterness of spirit. For one who thirsts is more distressed if he cannot drink water he has found than if he finds no drink at all.

“But the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood, which, when he cast it into the waters, made them sweet.” Perhaps that wood possessed such efficacy; perhaps it was miraculously brought about that wood should be found in a wilderness where there was no wood. The Hebrew says that the wood was naturally most bitter, and that, in order that divine power might be wonderfully displayed, bitter added to bitter produced sweetness.

Josephus seems to wish that the waters acquired this defect because they had always remained motionless, in accordance with the saying:

[Col. 1159B]

> And waters acquire a fault unless they are stirred.  
> (OVID)

For he says that there was a small well there. Moses took the rod that he had, immediately split it lengthwise down the middle, and threw it into the well. He ordered strong men to draw water and first pour out a great quantity, so that what remained at the end, agitated by repeated disturbance and cleansed, might become drinkable.

There also he gave them ordinances—not yet in actual deed, but by promising that he would give them if they would obey him.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the twelve springs and seventy palms of Elim

After this, “they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palms” (Exod. XV). Josephus says [Col. 1159C] that there was little water in the springs, so that the small quantity drawn from them by hand was muddy and useless. For this reason the palms did not rise far from the ground, because there was insufficient moisture to bind the soil together.

From there, “they came to the wilderness of Sin, which lies between Elim and Sinai” (Exod. XVI), where they made several encampments, which are set out in Numbers.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On quails and manna

“On the fifteenth day of the second month” (Exod. XVI)—that is, May; namely, on the thirtieth day after their departure, the Passover was celebrated—

> [Note: [Col. 1160D] Addition 1. The Lord commanded Moses that if anyone, whether because of a journey or because of uncleanness, could not celebrate the Passover in the first month, namely April, he should celebrate it on the tenth day of the second month, namely May.]

—the provisions which they had brought from Egypt failed them. They said: “Would that we had died in Egypt, when we sat [Col. 1159D] over pots of meat and ate bread to the full.”

When Moses prayed to the Lord, he said to them: “The Lord has heard your murmurings against him and will give you meat in the evening and bread in the morning to the full.” And it came to pass in the evening. A quail rose from the Arabian Gulf, where it is especially reared, crossed the middle of the sea, covered the camp, and was caught as the people pleased.

The quail is a royal bird, which Josephus calls *ortygia*, the Greeks call it *orthogometrum*; in common speech we call it *curlegium*, from its running. In the morning, after Moses had prayed, dew descended and clung to his hands. At first he supposed it to be rain, but when he tasted it he perceived the sweetness of honey and understood that the promised bread had been given. The dew lay around the camp, and [Col. 1160A] it was a small grain like coriander seed, white like hoarfrost, and as if hairy.

Seeing this, the children of Israel said, “Manhu”—that is, “What is this?” From this it was thereafter called *manna*. Some consider it indeclinable; others place it in the first declension; others in the third, like *Pascha*, *Paschae*, or *Paschatis*.

Moses said: “This is the bread given you by the Lord. Gather for yourselves one *gomor* for each head.” Some gathered more, others less; and they measured it by the measure of a *gomor*. “He who had gathered more had no excess, nor did he who had prepared less find less.” Perhaps what was gathered was placed in heaps, and a *gomor* was issued to each person. Josephus calls this an *assarius*, and it is a tenth part of an ephah. Or perhaps, however much someone collected, on coming to his own place he found only a *gomor*, though others also ate from it.

> [Note: [Col. 1160D] Addition 2. It happened miraculously that a *gomor* was sufficient even for the gluttonous.]

It was gathered in the morning because, when the sun grew hot, it melted—something miraculous, since at the fire it became hard. They ground it into powder and, having kneaded it together, formed it into loaves. Its flavour was exceedingly sweet; hence it is said to have been “fine flour with honey.” Elsewhere it is called “the taste of bread made with oil” (Num. XI; Wisd. XVI).

The statement that it tasted in each person’s mouth like whatever he desired is not very authoritative.

> [Note: [Col. 1160D] Addition 3. Yet this agrees with what is said in the Book of Wisdom: “You gave us bread from heaven, possessing every sweetness of flavour” (Wisd. XVI).]

Josephus says that even to this day that place is moistened by dry rains.

Moses said to the people: “Let no one leave any of it until morning.” Some nevertheless kept some back, and it swarmed with worms and rotted. Moses commanded them to gather double food on the sixth day, because [Col. 1160C] it was not found in the field on the Sabbath. Yet what was kept for the Sabbath did not spoil.

Some also think that no one gathered even on the sixth day more than one *gomor*, but that it was miraculously multiplied so as to suffice for two days. They infer this from what is read below: “For this reason the Lord has given you double food on the sixth day.”

The Lord said to Moses: “Fill a *gomor* from it, that it may be kept for generations to come”—that is, for generations afterwards, to preserve its memory. “And Moses did according to the word of the Lord, and Aaron placed it” in a golden vessel “to be kept in the tabernacle.”

The Hebrews say that at first they had a small tabernacle in which they consulted [Col. 1160D] the Lord, concerning which it is said below: “Moses took the tabernacle and pitched it outside the camp, far off” (Exod. XXXIII). Or this was said by prolepsis, of the future tabernacle. The children of Israel were nourished by this food for forty years, until they reached the borders of the land of Canaan (Exod. XVI).

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the water given at Rephidim

[Col. 1161A]

“Therefore the whole multitude set out from the wilderness of Sin, according to their encampments, at the command of the Lord, and came to Rephidim” (Exod. XVII). This does not mean that the Lord verbally assigned them their encampments, but that when the cloud, which they always followed as it went before them, came to a halt, they encamped by its direction.

There water failed altogether, and they murmured against Moses. He said to the Lord: “What shall I do with this people? In a little while they will stone me.” And the Lord said to him: “Take elders from Israel and go to the rock of Horeb; strike it with your rod.” This is a part of Mount Sinai so called. There is elsewhere another rock of Horeb, named after King Horeb, who was slain on it.

And it happened so. Waters came forth, and the people drank. “And [Col. 1161B] Moses called the name of the place Temptation, because they tempted the Lord, saying: ‘Is the Lord among us or not?’” Other waters of contradiction came later.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the battle against Amalek

“Then Amalek came out to fight against Israel at Rephidim” (Exod. XVII). Strabo says: Amalek was a son of Ishmael, from whom came the Amalekites, who are themselves Ishmaelites—that is, Saracens. Josephus calls them warlike, dwelling in Goboch or Jaboth and Petra, and hired by their neighbours to wage war against the Hebrews. On the other hand, it is read in Genesis that Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn, begot Amalek by a concubine (Gen. XXXVI).

Hence in the Book of Kings, where the son of Doeg the Idumaean [Col. 1161C] announces Saul’s death to David, he says: “I am an Amalekite” (III Kings I). Perhaps there were two men of the same name, and from them two peoples.

Moses chose Joshua, of the tribe of Ephraim, a warlike man, to fight the enemy. He gave him only a few armed men, retaining most to guard the camp. Moses himself went up the mountain, holding the rod of God in his hand. Aaron and Hur, Mary’s husband, went up with him. Yet according to Chronicles, Hur was the son of Caleb and the grandfather of Bezalel (I Chron. II).

“When Moses raised his hands to the Lord, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them a little, Amalek prevailed” (Exod. XVII). When this was discovered, “Aaron and Hur placed a stone beneath him and supported his hands on either side, for they were heavy,” from the labour of prayer. [Col. 1161D] In figure of this, the priest raises his hands in the Mass, also as a figure of Christ praying on the cross.

“Moses did not lower his hands until sunset. And Joshua put Amalek to flight by the edge of the sword. And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Write this in a book as a memorial. For I shall yet blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.’” This was fulfilled in the days of Saul.

“And Moses built an altar and called it: ‘The Lord is my exultation.’”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the appointment of leading men for judgment, at Jethro’s counsel

“Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, came out to meet him in the wilderness and brought with him Zipporah and her two sons. When he had entered Moses’ tabernacle, Moses related to him the signs which the Lord had performed for [Col. 1162A] them and all the hardship of his journey. Rejoicing with him, Jethro said: ‘Blessed is the Lord, who delivered his people from the land of Egypt. Now I know that the Lord is great above all gods.’ Therefore Jethro offered sacrifices to the Lord, and Moses, Aaron, and the elders of Israel ate with him before the Lord” (Exod. XVIII).

Augustine, however, does not wish a Gentile to have offered sacrifice to the Lord, but Moses to have done so, according to another translation: “Jethro took sacrifices from those offered by Moses; he took them from him and ate.” Perhaps Moses then sacrificed near the mountain, as the Lord had foretold. Josephus says that Jethro came near the mountain where Moses had seen many visions in the bush.

“On the following day Moses sat to judge the people, who stood before [Col. 1162B] him from morning until evening.” Observing this, Jethro said: “You will be worn out by foolish labour; the task exceeds your strength. But hear my words, and God will be with you. Represent the people in matters concerning God, show them the ceremonies and the way of conduct, or of the journey. But for deciding cases choose strong men, fearing God, lovers of truth, hating avarice.”

Observe that among these four qualities, which he says should be considered in choosing a judge, he includes power, which is highly valuable if the other three follow; otherwise oil is added to the furnace and a sword to poison. Another translation has “wise men,” whom perhaps it calls powerful for judging.

He added: “Appoint from among the chosen some tribunes—that is, set one over each [Col. 1162C] tribe. He is called *tribunus* from *tribus*, ‘tribe’; in Hebrew, [term uncertain]; in Greek, *chiliarch*, ‘commander of a thousand’; in Latin, *millenarius*, ‘commander of a thousand.’ This does not mean that there were only a thousand in a tribe, but a definite number is put for an indefinite one. Or the highest number is used for an abundant multitude. Perhaps because each tribe already had its own leader, he wished there to be commanders of thousands under the leader, each presiding over a thousand.

Under the commanders of thousands he ordered ten *hecatontarchs*, that is, commanders of hundreds or centurions, to be appointed; under each centurion, two *pentacontarchs*, that is, commanders of fifty; under each commander of fifty, five leaders of ten. Thus, when a dispute arose among ten persons, the leaders of ten stood in judgment; and so it was easy to settle the disputes of a few. If they could not decide them, they went up to the commander of fifty, and so on up to Moses; this, however, was rare. Greater matters they reserved for Moses, while they themselves judged smaller ones.

In this manner the Roman Church called many to share its burden of care: primates or patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, and archpriests. Lesser priests judge lighter sins and certain grave but hidden ones; more serious and public sins they refer to the bishop.

Moses accepted this and did not blush, though a man full of God, to follow a Gentile’s advice. “And he dismissed his kinsman”; the Hebrew everywhere has “father-in-law.” “And Jethro returned to his own land.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On arrival at Mount Sinai

“Therefore, in the third month after their departure from Egypt, that is [Col. 1163A] June, on this day—the Kalends of June—they came to Mount Sinai and pitched their tents opposite the mountain” (Exod. XIX), namely on the forty-seventh day from the Passover.

In expounding the Scriptures, we reckon thirty days for a month, choosing, as it were, a middle way between lunar and solar months. Some lunar months are fewer than thirty days, but none more; solar months, however, are more often longer than this number. Sixteen days of the first month remained after the Passover, and thirty days of the second month then passed. It follows that the first day of June was the forty-seventh.

At dawn on the following day Moses went up the mountain to God, who said to him: “You shall say to the house of Jacob: ‘You have seen what I have done for you.’ Now I shall add what I shall also say to you: ‘If therefore you keep [Col. 1163B] my covenant, you shall be my special possession above all peoples.’”

When Moses reported these things to the people, they replied: “All that the Lord has spoken we will do.” When Moses returned to the Lord, the Lord said to him: “I shall come to you in darkness, that the people may hear me speaking with you. Go and sanctify the people today and tomorrow—that is, let them wash themselves and their garments. Let them abstain from embraces and be ready for the third day. You shall set boundaries around the mountain; whoever then crosses them and touches it shall die. No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or pierced with darts, whether beast or man.”

Josephus says that during these two days they enjoyed abundant feasts and fitting adornment.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the giving of the Law by spoken word

[Col. 1163C]

“The third day had now come, and before sunrise thunder began to be heard, lightning to flash, and a thick cloud to cover the mountain; and the blast of a trumpet resounded loudly. The mountain smoked because the Lord had come down in fire, and smoke rose like smoke from a furnace” (Exod. XIX). The mountain also trembled, as the Hebrews say.

“The people were afraid,” and even thought that Moses had perished through God’s wrath. At length Moses appeared joyful, and the air serene with him; he returned among them and said: Today you will not hear Moses, son of Amram and Jochebed, but him who struck Egypt for you, who made a way through the sea, who sent food from heaven and gave drink from the rock; through whom Adam ate from the fruits [Col. 1163D] of the earth, Noah was delivered or received from the floods, Abraham obtained Canaan, Isaac was born to old people, Jacob was enriched with offspring, and Joseph was exalted. Therefore let these words be more beloved to you than sons or wives.

And he led the people out to meet the Lord at the foot of the mountain. At the Lord’s command Moses and Aaron ascended beyond the boundaries; the priests—that is, the leading men—and the people did not cross them. The Lord spoke to them so that the voice escaped none of them. Thus, on the fiftieth day he gave them the Law by word alone, as a figure that he would give it through the Holy Spirit on the fiftieth day.

## CHAPTER XL. Explanation of the Decalogue (Exod. XX)

“You shall have no strange gods before me.” All the saints maintain that the Lord gave only ten commandments, [Col. 1164A] but they differ in how they divide them. Origen divides into two what Augustine considers the first and one commandment; and he combines into one what Augustine regards as the final two. Josephus agrees with him.

Moreover, Augustine says that three were on one tablet and seven on the other.

> [Note: [Col. 1164A] Addition 1. Josephus says that he saw the two stone tablets of the Law, each of which contained two and a half commandments, both the outer and the inner tablet.]

Josephus and the Hebrews, however, assign five to each tablet. Perhaps Augustine wished three to pertain to the love of God and seven to the love of neighbour; and by rank rather than by Scripture, he called them the first and second tablets, just as we customarily call people of the first class and the second class. Yet however they are distinguished, the meaning is the same.

[Col. 1164B]

### First commandment

“You shall have no strange gods before me,” that is, you shall have me alone as God. *Non habebis* (“you shall not have”) is put for *non habeas* (“do not have”), imperatively, according to the idiom of the Hebrews. For God is not making an assertion here, since at times they did have other gods.

“You shall not make for yourself a graven image,” or an idol. Another text has, “that which is nothing in the world,” that is, representing no natural thing, such as Ammon with a ram’s head, or Anubis—that is, Mercury—with a beardless dog’s head. “Nor any likeness which is in heaven, or on earth, or in the waters, or beneath the earth”: that is, do not make for yourself as God an image of the sun, moon, [Col. 1164C] and things of that kind; nor of a human being, beast, and the like; nor of a dragon or any creeping thing, which the varying error of human beings worshipped. “You shall neither worship nor adore them.”

To worship is to adore mentally. To adore is to perform outward reverence, even if not in one’s heart, whether from fear or from flattery toward kings. Afterwards, to impress upon them the observance of what had been said and what would be said, he incidentally added: “I am the Lord your God, strong and jealous—

> [Note: [Col. 1165A] Addition 1. God is so called by essence, power, participation, and designation.]

—visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.”

Jealousy is called envy; it is also called love, but properly the love of a husband for his wife, by which he cannot endure another’s approach to her. In this manner [Col. 1164D] the Lord says: “I am jealous,” that is, I shall not allow you to commit fornication after strange gods.

Because he added that he visits the fathers’ sins upon the children, heretics say: “This is not a good saying, that someone should be punished for another’s sin.” They say that the Old Testament was not given by God. Yet God is not so cruel; rather, he appears gentle even in this, as is implied by the very term “visiting.” For we visit the sick out of compassion, and he in gentleness does not immediately punish the sinner, but waits even until the fourth generation, as long as fathers normally live. If the father is corrected, or his children do not imitate him, he spares them; otherwise, after a long waiting, he punishes more justly. This must be understood only of temporal punishment.

Thus we read that vengeance was taken on the descendants of Ahab and Jehu [Col. 1165A] (III Kings XXI). Or the severity of a just judge may be expressed. Those who sin are punished more severely if they see their children also punished on their account, and more justly because of the delay.

Origen, however, understands “fathers” here as demons; and “descendants” as the accomplices whom we sometimes join to ourselves in sinning. Thus: first, the devil entered Judas’s heart (Luke XXII): behold the father. Afterwards, “he went to the chief men” (ibid.), so that they too might sin in this matter: behold the children. Afterwards, “he received from them a cohort and officers” (John XVIII): behold the third and fourth generation. But here the Lord does not visit the sins of the fathers, who are reserved for eternal fire; nevertheless, he now often punishes human beings.

[Col. 1165B]

### Second commandment

“You shall not take the name of your God in vain,” that is, you shall not swear by God’s name falsely, superfluously, or deceitfully; nor, so far as lies in you, make his honour vanish by holding perverse opinions concerning him.

### Third commandment

“Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day,” that is, keep it holy and as a holiday. “You shall do no work on it—you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, your beast, or the stranger who is beside your gates,” that is, serving with you in your house—because “God rested on the seventh day” (Gen. II). We too observe the seventh day, although not the same day as they did. For Josephus likewise says: “The fourth saying concerns the observance of weeks, when they were to cease from all work”; therefore we say that it is to be understood of servile work.

### Fourth commandment

“Honour your father and mother” with a twofold honour: namely, by reverence and by supplying necessities. In the commandments that follow, indeed almost everywhere, the whole is understood from a part. Therefore the Lord, teaching that they were to be understood comprehensively, fulfilled the Law.

### Fifth commandment

“You shall not kill” by hand, mind, or consent. Do not lay a violent hand upon an innocent person; do not withhold life-saving aid from one to whom you can and ought to give it. A judge, however, does not kill; the law does.

### Sixth commandment

“You shall not commit adultery,” that is, do not have intercourse with anyone outside the covenant of marriage.

### Seventh commandment

“You shall not commit theft,” nor even seize what belongs to another.

### Eighth commandment

“You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour.” Here he prohibits every lie, although some have wrongly thought that God silently permitted a lie that benefits someone if it harms no one.

### Ninth commandment

“You shall not covet your neighbour’s house.” According to Augustine, this prohibits coveting another’s immovable property.

[Col. 1166A]

### Tenth commandment

“You shall not desire his wife, male servant, female servant, ox, ass, or anything that is his.” Here he prohibits coveting movable property. According to Origen, this is one commandment.

## CHAPTER XLI. On making an altar

“The people saw voices, flashes of fire, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain; and, standing at a distance, they said to Moses: ‘Let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.’ Therefore the people stood far away, and Moses approached the darkness. The Lord said to him: ‘You shall make an altar of earth for me’” (Exod. XX).

Perhaps, before the construction of the portable altar, he wished this to be done; or perhaps that portable altar was of earth, as we shall say below [Col. 1166B]. “But if you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of cut stones. If you raise your tool upon it, it shall be defiled.” As if to say: I do not wish you to build for me something holy with an instrument for shedding blood. Hence we too construct an altar from a single stone. Perhaps he prohibited the killing of sacrificial victims upon the altar.

He added: “You shall not ascend to my altar by steps, lest your nakedness be exposed.” Perhaps the ancients did not yet use breeches.

## CHAPTER XLII. On judgments (Exod. XXI)

Thereafter the Lord added certain judicial ordinances to determine disputes. We shall not pursue all of them, but those that are relevant, as follows.

“If you buy a Hebrew servant”—that is, one who is not already a servant—“he shall serve you for seven [Col. 1166C] years,” unless a jubilee intervenes. “In the seventh he shall go out free and without payment, wearing the sort of clothing in which he entered. If he entered with a wife, he shall leave with wife and children. If his master gave him a wife, the woman and the children she bore shall belong to the master. But if the servant chooses to remain in slavery, ‘his master shall bring him to the gods’”—that is, present him to the priests—“and he shall be brought to the door of the tabernacle, and his ear shall be pierced with an awl,” as a sign of perpetual servitude; “and he shall be a servant for ever,” that is, while he lives, or until the jubilee. The same is to be understood concerning a female servant.

### On the female servant

“If anyone sells his daughter as a female servant,” [Col. 1166D] not as a slave woman, of course, but as a concubine—whom the Greeks call *Moypheton*, others *Moypheten*—“she shall not go out in the seventh year as a slave woman,” namely, without payment. Because he has humbled her, he shall provide her “a dowry, clothing, and marriage”—that is, a husband—as the price of her chastity. If before the seventh year she displeases him, he shall not have power to sell her to another, nor shall he deny the price of her chastity.

“If in the meantime he has named her to himself,” that is, has taken her as wife, he shall deal with her according to the law of wives, “nor shall she go out without a bill of divorce.” But if he bought her not for himself but for his son, he shall do for his son, as for himself, in the manner stated above. “If he does not do these three things,” that is, if he neither humbles her himself without naming her, nor names her, nor takes her for his son, [Col. 1167A] “she shall go out free, in the manner of slave women, and without any payment given to her.”

### On a homicide

“He who kills a human being intentionally shall die; but if unintentionally, he shall flee to one of the six cities of refuge,” and there preserve his life, lest he be killed by the slain person’s relatives. He shall remain there until he is reconciled to the dead person’s relatives by the judges of that city, or until the death of the high priest. Then he shall safely return to his own home. “But one who kills deliberately shall be torn away even from the altar.” This is recorded as having been done to Joab (III Kings II).

In place of these cities we have places dedicated to God, which nevertheless grant greater immunity than those cities did. For even an intentional killer and any fugitive are protected in them. [Col. 1167B] Yet some make an exception: if someone flees to a church for a homicide, theft, or the like committed in the church, they say that he ought to be removed and punished.

### On retaliation

The Lord also added laws of retaliation, commanding that there be rendered “life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, wound for wound, bruise for bruise, burn for burn.”

### On the goring ox

“If a goring ox kills a servant, it shall be stoned and its flesh shall not be eaten. But the owner of the ox shall pay thirty shekels of silver to the servant’s master.” The Hebrews say that the value of a servant was assessed thus [Col. 1167C] because thirty generations descended from Ham, whom Noah assigned to slavery.

### On tithes and first-fruits

“You shall not delay to offer tithes and first-fruits” (Exod. 22). “Yet you shall leave a lamb or kid with its mother for seven days; on the eighth day and thereafter you may give it.”

### On the seventh year

“For six years you shall sow your land and gather its produce; in the seventh year you shall let it rest” (Exod. 23). Hence it was called the year of rest.

> [Note: Col. 1167D, Addition 1. Augustine, in his commentary on Exodus, says that in that year they sowed, but did not harvest.]

It was also called the year of remission, because during it no one was permitted to demand any debt until it had ended. “And whatever grows in it during that year from the preceding crops, the poor of the people shall eat; and what remains after the poor, the beasts of the field shall eat. You shall do likewise with your vineyard and your olive grove.” While this observance was maintained, Josephus says, the crops in the sixth year were so abundant that they sufficed for the use of the seventh and eighth years, even for sowing.

### On the three festivals

He also added provisions concerning the three principal annual festivals, at which He wished every male to appear before Him, but not empty-handed (ibid.). These will be discussed below.

[Col. 1168A]

### On not boiling a kid in its mother’s milk

“You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (ibid.). Josephus explains this as follows: You shall not eat it before the eighth day, because it is not yet distinct from milk. The saints explain it with reference to Christ: Do not kill Christ on the day of His conception.

> [Note: Col. 1168C, Addition 1. Or it is a prophecy that Herod would not kill Christ as an infant, or that the apostles would not endure persecutions until they had first been strengthened.]

Yet they transgressed this. The day of conception is called the mother’s milk because, from that point, the material of milk is prepared in the mother. The Hebrew has: “You shall not boil what has been separated in its mother’s milk”; and the sense is: What has been separated from the flesh of its parents—that is, what has been conceived and born by bodily generation—you shall not eat cooked with milk, or with any milky food, namely cheese or butter. This was said because birds are separated not from flesh but from eggs, and they eat them cooked in milk, or with milk.

[Col. 1168B]

Nor do they say that the prohibition of the mother’s milk means that it is permissible to boil it in another milk; rather, because that milk could more readily be found together with the animal, by this means He prohibited cooking in every kind of milk. Some, however, understand this to refer to things offered to the Lord: as though one should not offer a lamb or kid before the eighth day, because it is not yet edible and is not distinct from its mother’s milk. For above He had also spoken of the first-fruits of lambs and of tithes.

At the end of the judgments the Lord added: “If you do this, I shall destroy every people into whose land you enter, and I shall send ahead hornets and wasps, which will drive them out.”

> [Note: Col. 1168C, Addition 2. This is never recorded as having occurred literally; therefore understand the stings as terrors.]

That is, “the terror of your name. But I shall drive them out gradually, lest the land be reduced to desolation and the beasts increase against you. And I shall set your boundaries from the Red Sea,”

[Col. 1168C]
