which is in the east, “to the Palestinian Sea,” called the Tyrrhenian Sea, which is in the west; “and from the wilderness,” which lies beyond Bethlehem and begins beyond Tekoa, “to the river,” namely the Euphrates. This entire region was at one time called Judaea.

## Chapter XLIII. On the covenant confirmed by the sprinkling of the blood of calves

[Col. 1168D]

“So Moses came and recounted to the people the judgments of the Lord, and they all said with one voice: ‘All that the Lord has spoken we shall do and hear’” (Exod. 24). This was said in an inverted and disorderly manner, foreshadowing that they would become transgressors and liars in this very statement.

“And Moses wrote all the words of the Lord,” apart from the Decalogue, “and, rising early in the morning, built an altar to the Lord, and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel”—perhaps he called twelve altars “pillars.”

> [Note: Col. 1169B, Addition 1. A *titulus* may be triumphal, proclamatory, or commemorative.]

Or, more probably, he set up one [pillar] from twelve stones, and wrote upon each [stone] one of the names of the sons of Israel, as a monument of the twelve tribes. “And he sent young men,” namely Nadab and Abihu, who were to be priests, “and they sacrificed to the Lord twelve calves as peace offerings.”

[Col. 1169A]

“And Moses took half the blood and put it into bowls,” that is, wicker vessels with handles, called *craters* from *cratin*, “to weave”; “and he poured the remaining blood upon the altar. Then he read the book of the covenant while the people listened. They said: ‘All that the Lord has spoken we shall do.’ Then he took the blood and sprinkled it upon the people, saying: ‘This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you.’”

It was as though he said: Thus shall the life perish and the blood be shed of whoever violates this covenant—that is, the agreement between you and the Lord. Indeed, they had this sign for confirming the covenant from the Gentiles, who, shamefully tearing apart the covenant-sow, thus confirmed that the violator of the covenant was to be shamefully torn apart. Yet the Jews also had another, more terrible sign of covenant from among themselves:

[Col. 1169B]

the pouring out of water, performed by Joshua and Samuel. For just as water is wholly poured out, so that nothing remains in the vessel—which is not true of other liquids—and indeed it itself perishes when poured upon the ground, so whoever broke the covenant would utterly perish, together with his offspring.

## Chapter XLIV. On Moses’ first ascent of the mountain

“After this Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, according to the Lord’s command, ascended as far as the limits of the mountain, and they saw the Lord. Beneath His feet was something like sapphire work, and like the sky when it is clear. Yet He did not lay His hand upon those who were in the camp”

[Col. 1169C]

(Exod. 24), that is, He did not hide Himself from them; rather, seeing the majesty of the Lord, though not Himself, they joyfully feasted. And the Lord called Moses, intending to give him the stone tablets inscribed with the Decalogue. Taking only Joshua with him, he crossed the boundary, saying to the elders: “Wait here,” that is, in the camp and as far as the boundary. “If any question arises, refer it to Aaron and Hur.” And the cloud covered the mountain.

Again, having left Joshua upon a certain plain of the mountain, Moses alone ascended into the darkness. “But on the seventh day the Lord called him from the midst of the darkness.”

## Chapter XLV. On making the tabernacle

“And Moses entered the midst of the cloud and was with the Lord forty days and forty nights”

[Col. 1169D]

(Exod. 24), neither eating nor drinking. “And the Lord said to him: Take first-fruits” (Exod. 25), that is, every precious thing from the people of Israel, but only “from one who offers voluntarily”: namely gold, silver, bronze, blue, purple, and scarlet twice dyed—that is, silk of blue, purple, and scarlet colour—fine linen, which is a soft and white kind of Egyptian flax; goats’ hair; “rams’ skins dyed red,” which we call Parthian, because the Parthians devised this way of colouring them; “blue skins; acacia wood.”

(Setim is the name of a mountain, a region, and a tree. Its leaves resemble those of the white thorn; its wood is very light, imperishable, and incombustible.) “Oil also for lamps; spices

[Col. 1170A]

for ointments and sweet incense; onyx stones, sardonyxes, gems; and let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst,” so that it should not be burdensome for them to return repeatedly to this mountain. “You shall make it according to the pattern of the tabernacle which I shall show you.”

## Chapter XLVI. On the design of the ark

“You shall make an ark of Setim wood” (Exod. 25), which in Hebrew is called *beron*. Note that Moses recounts in this order: first the things made in the tabernacle; second, the tabernacle; third, the court. Josephus, by contrast, does the reverse: he follows the order of construction, whereas Moses follows the order of placement.

The ark’s length was two and a half cubits; likewise its width was one and a half cubits.

[Col. 1170B]

The cubit meant is the human rather than the geometric cubit, as appears from the Lateran altar, beneath which the ark is said to be. Josephus also here calls a cubit two palms. The ark is said to have had no feet, and it was overlaid inside and out with the purest gold. A golden rim was made on top, like the lip commonly made on tables and chessboards.

On each of the two long sides were two golden rings, passing through the whole wood. Through them were placed gilded poles of Setim wood by which the ark was carried, and they were never removed. Later the testimony was placed in it: that is, the tablets on which the covenant was written. Yet whatever testimonies were deposited there may be called testimonies. A golden urn full of manna was placed there, as testimony that He had given them bread

[Col. 1170C]

from heaven; the tablets, as testimony that He had awakened in writing the natural law which had lain dormant in their hearts; Aaron’s rod, as testimony that all authority is from the Lord God; Deuteronomy, as testimony of the agreement by which they had said: “All that the Lord says to us we shall do.” For this reason it was called the ark of the covenant, or of testimony. For this reason the tabernacle was also called the tabernacle of testimony; and likewise because cases were heard before its doors.

## Chapter XLVII. On the mercy-seat and the cherubim

A golden mercy-seat was also made over the ark—that is, a golden slab of the same length and breadth as the ark, sufficient to cover it (Exod. 25). Its thickness is not recorded.

[Col. 1170D]

This same object was called the oracle, because the Lord gave responses from that place. A divine response is called an oracle because it is given to those who pray. It was also called the mercy-seat, because the Lord, speaking from there, was propitiated toward the people; or because on the Day of Atonement they said that the glory of the Lord always descended there.

At each side of the oracle—

> [Note: Col. 1171A, Addition 1. They may also be said to have stood upon the ground beside the ark, five cubits high, as was later done in Solomon’s Temple, except that there they were twice as large.]

—that is, at its two front corners, were placed two golden cherubim, fashioned by hammering, not cast but formed by hammer-strokes. Josephus says that they were winged creatures of a form no human being has seen. Moses said that he had seen them depicted upon the seat of God. The cherubim faced one another, though their faces were turned toward the mercy-seat; with two wings spread out and touching each other,

[Col. 1171A]

they covered the oracle, extending their wings toward each other.

## Chapter XLVIII. On the table and its columns

The Lord likewise said: “You shall make a table of Setim wood, two cubits long, one cubit wide, and one and a half cubits high” (Exod. 25); He says nothing about its thickness. “And you shall overlay it on every side with pure gold.”

According to Josephus, this table was somewhat like the Delphic table of Apollo. It had four feet, constituting what is called its height. From the middle of their lower portion they were rounded like shins and turned on a lathe. The upper part was square, like a thigh. In each foot was a golden ring, and there was a socket in the foot into which the ring was set. In the rings were gilded poles by which the table was carried. It had a rim all round, as did the ark; and attached to the rim was a golden crown four fingers high, so that half of it projected above the table,

[Col. 1171B]

lest what was placed upon it should fall off. The other half hung below for ornament. This crown was *interrasilis*, that is, worked alternately in carved and plain portions.

The Hebrews say that those carvings were like images of kings and were prophetic: as many images were made there as there would be kings in Jerusalem from David to Zedekiah. Josephus, however, seems to mean that it had no rim other than this *interrasilis* crown—that is, a lattice-work crown.

> [Note: Col. 1171C, Addition 1. Just as Ezekiel’s Ariel rose from the lattice-work by means of something interposed (Ezek. 11), so Ariel is interpreted “altar of God,” or “devouring lion,” because the altar of burnt offerings devoured everything.]

A second crown, smaller than this one, was placed upon it. But how large it was, how it was placed above, and whether it was plain or lattice-work, we do not know; nevertheless it is called a little crown. The Hebrews say that this too was prophetically added to foreshadow the division of the kingdom into two kingdoms. For the kingdom of Israel was more populous than that of Judah, but less worthy; therefore the little crown was set above, and yet was smaller. This table stood in the tabernacle on the north side, not far from the entrance.

## Chapter XLIX. On the loaves of the Presence

[Col. 1171D]

Twelve very pure unleavened loaves of fine flour were placed upon it, six on either side, each consisting of two tenths of an ephah.

> [Note: Col. 1172A, Addition 1. The ephah and the bath are measures of two [uncertain]. Either, then, ephahs arising from tithes were measured out, one on this side and one on that; or the ephah was tithed, and that [portion] was given as a tithe; or, just as the Levites first received tithes of all things, so the high priests received tithes of these tithes. Perhaps, therefore, those loaves of three modii were made from that secondary tithe. The passage may be explained in any of these ways.]

(Exod. 25), which Josephus calls two *assarii*. A golden plate was placed upon each loaf, and upon the plate a handful of incense. Josephus says that golden bowls full of incense were placed on them. Early on the Sabbath, fresh and warm loaves were placed upon the table, and they remained there untouched until the following Sabbath. Then, when they had been removed and all the incense burned upon the altar, new ones were substituted with other incense. The loaves that had been removed were eaten by priests alone; whence they were called priestly loaves.

[Col. 1172A]

Or they were so called, Josephus says, because the Lord commanded that priests alone should form, bake, place upon the table, and remove those loaves; yet after they had become rich, they did not observe this. They were also called loaves of the Presence because they were set before the Lord as an everlasting memorial of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel; or because they were placed there throughout the whole week, or were to be set there for ever in succession.

## Chapter L. On the vessels for libations

[Col. 1172B]

The Lord therefore commanded four kinds of vessels to be prepared from the purest gold, for offering libations, both by offerers to the priest and by priests to the Lord (Exod. 25). They are called *libamina* from *libare*, “to taste,” in the first case, and from *libare*, “to pour,” in the second. They were to be placed upon the table: dishes, bowls, censers, and cups. In them the wine which was to be offered was inspected beforehand and tasted, to determine whether or not it was fit to be offered.

But because wine is recognized by colour and taste, it is said that, besides the golden bowls, there were glass bowls there; hence they were called *phialae*, from *phialim*, which is said to mean “glass” in Greek. They were narrow below and broad above,

[Col. 1172C]

so that colour and taste could be recognized in them; the Hebrews call them little bowls. The cups were smaller, narrower, and golden; with them wine was poured over the altar as a libation for the sacrifice. In the censers, also called little mortars, incense was examined beforehand and offered. Likewise vinegar was examined in the dishes.

But because one never or rarely encounters an offering of vinegar, some say *acceptabula*, receptacles in which the priests inspected beforehand things to be offered, to determine whether they were acceptable—that is, suitable—or not. They then subdivide the dishes into three kinds: bowls, containing wine; censers, containing incense, fine flour, grain, and salt; and cups,

[Col. 1172D]

containing oil. For the priests first took small portions of the things to be offered, put them into such vessels for tasting, as it were tasting from each individual offering. These Moses called *libamina* to be offered: that is, portions to be taken from things offered.

## Chapter LI. On the golden lampstand

The Lord also commanded a lampstand to be made of pure beaten gold (Exod. 25). Josephus, however, calls it cast. Its shaft was fixed in a base, and was of iron overlaid with five jointed golden reeds, like a cane. Where the tops of the reeds were joined together, they had swelling heads, each like a cup—which we call a *cuppa*. They were joined like two cups in the form of a nut; and from the base

[Col. 1173A]

of each cup issued curved flowers like lilies. In that same base, between the cup and the lilies, was a movable little sphere, as movable spheres are set below the heads of chairs. Thus, since there were five reeds joined together in this fashion on the shaft, there were four joints, each having, as it were, two cups joined together, along with spheres and lilies. This is what Moses means when he says that there were four cups in the shaft in the form of a nut.

The Hebrew, however, does not say “cups,” but rounded ornaments marked out in black (*nigellatae rotunditates*). From this shaft proceeded three branches on one side and three on the other, of iron, each overlaid with golden reeds like the shaft. At their joints the tops of the reeds came together like cups in the form of a nut, with spheres and lilies.

[Col. 1173B]

Since Moses says that each had four cups, each seems to have had four reeds. Some, however, think that there were no little spheres in the bases of the cups, as stated, but that a movable little sphere was set upon the middle flat surface of each reed. Thus, if it was cast, the lampstand was made of iron overlaid with golden reeds; but if it was simply beaten work, it was made wholly of gold and was hammered with wonderful workmanship into this shape.

Josephus says that it was composed of seventy parts, rising from one base. Thus there were twenty-nine incomplete reeds in the shaft and branches; but, where two parts were joined in the middle, a little sphere was placed over them so that the joint would not be seen and the reed would appear to be one. Thus there were twenty-nine reeds, with as many little spheres, fifty-eight [parts], five [other] parts, and seven seats for lamps in the base.

[Col. 1173C]

Whatever its construction, it had seven equal tops at its summit, upon which were placed seven golden lamps. There were also seven golden oil-pourers, by which oil was poured into the lamps. There were golden tongs, called snuffers, for trimming or extinguishing the wicks. There were also golden vessels for putting into water what had been trimmed, lest it give off a foul smell; these were called extinguishers.

Its total weight with its vessels was one talent of gold by the sanctuary standard. For they had three talents: the lesser, of fifty pounds, which was that of merchants; the middle, of seventy pounds, which was that of citizens; and the greatest, of one hundred and twenty pounds, which was that of the sanctuary. Josephus, however, says that it had one hundred minas, which the Hebrews call *cithares*; translated into Greek, this is called a talent. It was placed to the south, opposite the table—not directly, but obliquely.

[Col. 1173D]

## Chapter LII. On the walls of the tabernacle

The Lord also commanded the tabernacle to be made in this manner (Exod. 26). The tabernacle was a rectangular oblong house dedicated to God, enclosed by three walls: north, south, and west. The entrance on the east stood open, so that at sunrise it might be illuminated by its rays. Its length was thirty cubits, its width ten, and its height ten.

On the south side were twenty upright boards of Setim wood. Each was ten cubits long, four fingers thick, and one and a half cubits broad.

[Col. 1174A]

They were joined to one another by interlocking joints, so that there should be no crack or unevenness in the surface of the wall. They were gilded on both sides. Each was set upon two perforated silver bases, into the holes of which golden pivots were inserted, projecting from the two corners of the board, as is commonly done in chests.

Augustine, however, seems to hold that one base was beneath the board and the other above as a lintel; but the text is contrary, for it says that two bases were placed beneath each board at its two corners. Whether the boards were suspended above the ground upon the bases,

[Col. 1174B]

or reached the ground between the bases, is not recorded. The north wall was constructed by the same plan.

On the west were seven boards, in every respect like the others and standing in the bases in the same way. But because they filled only nine cubits, half a cubit stood empty on each side. Therefore a board one cubit wide was cut in half, making half-cubit boards, which were added on both sides and completed the western wall with the other two; each of these also was fitted into two bases.

To prevent the walls from being shaken by gusts of wind or any other cause, each board had golden rings set in order like certain roots, through which bars were inserted horizontally across the wall to hold the boards firmly together.

[Col. 1174C]

The bars were of gilded Setim wood, each five cubits long. The end of one bar was fitted into the end of another like a joint, so that several thus linked together appeared to be one bar of immense length, as is commonly done in the ivory staff of a bishop’s crozier.

This would clearly be so, had not the Lord added that there were five bars on the north side, as many on the south, and as many on the west—which seems less suitable. For since every bar was five cubits long, five laid out along a side extended only twenty-five cubits. Thus five cubits of that side were left untouched; whereas on the western side two would have sufficed.

Some say that of the three superfluous bars, one was added to the five bars on the north side and another on the south, so that what was lacking was supplied. They say that the third was cut into two and placed at the two corners of the walls, so that, bent back, they bound the corner-joints, as the corner-joints of chests are commonly fastened by straps.

[Col. 1174D]

But this cannot be inferred from the text. Since, therefore, the text says that five bars were inserted through the middle boards from end to end, it may be understood of the height of the wall. Thus, near the topmost edge of the wall, one row of bars was extended lengthwise along the whole wall; near the bottom edge another row was similarly extended; and on the middle surface there were three rows. Hence the statement that there were five bars on one side refers rather to the number of rows than to the number of individual bars.

Each board had five rings.

> [Note: Col. 1175B, Addition 1. One board was cut and hollowed out on its face at one side; likewise the other board was cut and hollowed out on the opposite side; on their faces they were joined together.]

In each of the two walls there were thirty bars, because each of the five rows had six bars. On the western side there were ten bars, two in each row. Some say that not all the bars were of the same length: each of the five bars on the long sides was six cubits long, and so five sufficed to span thirty cubits; and each of the five bars on the west was two cubits long. But Josephus, speaking of these bars, says that each was five cubits long.

## Chapter LIII. On the division of the tabernacle and the two veils

[Col. 1175B]

This tabernacle was divided into two parts (Exod. 26). The rear part, toward the west, extended ten cubits, and was therefore square—ten cubits in length, breadth, and height. This part was called the *adyton*, or the Holy of the Holy, the sanctuary of the sanctuary, or the Holy of Holies. The front part, toward the east, extended twenty cubits. It was common to the priests and was called the Holy Place, or sanctuary.

[Col. 1175C]

In relation to this, the rear portion was called “Holy of the Holy,” as a genitive of succession, like “age of ages.” Or it was called “Holy of the Holy,” that is, holier than the holy, like “Lord of lords” or “King of kings.”

To separate the two parts from one another, four gilded columns of Setim wood stood in the middle, having golden capitals and silver bases. Josephus, however, says that there were four boards worked like the others, equally spaced from one another, with three narrow entrances between them. Upon the capitals of the columns were laid two bars, ten cubits long, extending from wall to wall. From them, through golden rings, hung a veil stretched before the four columns, square on every side, namely ten cubits in each dimension, so that it prevented a view of the inner things from every side.

[Col. 1175D]

The veil was made from twisted fine linen—a very white and soft kind of flax—and blue, purple, and scarlet twice dyed: that is, silk threads of blue, purple, and scarlet colour. It was made in *opus plumarium*, that is, work painted with a needle. For in a certain language—namely, one of the various languages of the Egyptians, as the Greeks have various languages—*pluma* means “needle.”

This kind of veil is popularly called *distratum*, as though “twice laid.” For first a fabric is made, beneath which various pictures are worked by hand with a needle. Some say that *opus plumarium* is named from the likeness of birds, upon which the variety of feathers is superadded. The same work is also called *polymitum*, from Greek *polu*, “much,” on account of the multitude of its pictures.

[Col. 1176A]

According to Josephus, this veil was beautifully woven with all the flowers produced by the earth and with other pictures which painters could interweave, except representations of animals.

At the entrance of the tabernacle were five gilded columns of Setim wood, with golden capitals but bronze bases. Over them two bars, or one bar ten cubits long, were extended from wall to wall. Each end was inserted into its respective wall, like a beam in a house. From this hung another veil, inserted by golden rings and worked like the preceding one. According to Josephus, however, it hung only to the middle of the columns, covering them for five cubits; the remaining five cubits to the ground stood open as an entrance for the priests.

[Col. 1176B]

Concerning this, Josephus says that another woollen curtain was placed over it, reaching to the ground and drawn and pulled back by ropes through rings, so that on feast days, when pulled back, it afforded a view of the tabernacle, while on other days, when drawn across, it prevented the view—especially when the sky appeared cloudy. For it was a strong covering and could easily bear the strain. He says that a similar hanging was suspended at the entrance of Solomon’s Temple.

In the inner sanctuary was the ark of the covenant with the things which, as we have said, were deposited in it, and with those placed upon it. In the front part were the lampstand on the south and the table on the north. In the middle, not far from the entrance, was the golden altar, which Josephus also calls the golden censer; of this we shall speak later.

[Col. 1176C]

## Chapter LIV. On the curtains and the goat-hair covering

The roof of the tabernacle was not vaulted—that is, curved, as in churches—but flat, in the Palestinian manner. It was fitted with four coverings (Exod. 26). The first covering consisted of ten curtains, also called veils, tents, or sometimes “the tabernacle.” They were made of the four colours mentioned above, in needlework. Each curtain was twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits broad. Five were joined to one another, and likewise five, producing, as it were, two curtains, which in turn were joined together.

[Col. 1176D]

They were joined by blue loops arranged along the side of each curtain, one coming opposite another, with pairs fastened by a golden ring, as silver or golden clasps used for ornament at the neck commonly join the two edges of a garment’s collar. Josephus nevertheless says that they were joined by golden rings and hooks.

The second covering consisted of goat-hair cloths, also sometimes called veils or hair-cloths. They were made of goats’ hair, which we sometimes call “hair” in distinction from sheep’s wool, and from which haircloth is made. Therefore these goat-hair cloths were called *cilicina*. Because of their roughness they were called *saga*, whence we call certain rough cloths *sagiae*. Or perhaps *saga* were so called from their squareness.

> [Note: Col. 1177B, Addition 1. It is said that the kings of the Franks use this when they are first crowned. It is square, fastened at the neck, and has no seam.]

Hence the military cloak, invented by the Gauls, was called a *sagum* because it was square.

[Col. 1177A]

Yet it was made from rough cloth against the inclemency of the weather, and may have been called a *sagum* for that reason. There were eleven of these cloths. Each cloth was thirty cubits long and four cubits broad. Five were joined to one another, making as it were one cloth, and the other six were similarly joined as one cloth. They were joined by golden rings inserted into opposing loops.

Whether each individual curtain or cloth was thus joined to the next, or whether six curtains were sewn inseparably by thread into one curtain, and likewise the other five, while only these two large curtains were joined by rings and loops to cover the tabernacle, is not clear.

## Chapter LV. On Bede’s method of covering

[Col. 1177B]

Let us first see how the tabernacle was covered with these. According to Bede, the ten joined curtains were stretched crosswise over the tabernacle, covering the whole tabernacle and descending along its sides, one cubit short of the ground on every side. Because together they made forty cubits, they covered the thirty-cubit length of the tabernacle.

> [Note: Col. 1178B, Addition 1. Observe that he says: “Five cubits hung down.” He does not say this because five cubits hung down along the whole western and eastern sides together, but because the portion of the curtain hanging along the sides, in relation to the tabernacle’s length, was only five cubits; in relation to its breadth, however, it was nine cubits. Consequently, when the cubits coming from both sides were joined, the tabernacle was covered in those two parts as well—namely the west and east—except for one cubit.]

Five cubits hung down alongside the western wall, and another five descended only before the eastern opening. Yet, lest they hang disorderly on either side,

[Col. 1177C]

the curtains extending beyond the two great sides of the tabernacle were drawn as far as the middle of the opening and joined to each other there; and likewise on the western side. Thus the tabernacle was covered by curtains on every side, except for one cubit near the ground, which remained uncovered all round.

The goat-hair cloths were laid over it crosswise in the same fashion; but because they were thirty cubits long, they descended to the ground along the sides and so covered the cubit not covered by the curtains. Since they measured forty-four cubits across, being eleven joined cloths each four cubits wide, they covered the thirty-cubit length of the tabernacle. Of the fourteen cubits remaining, seven descended to the west and seven to the east.

[Col. 1177D]

The portions of the cloths left over, hanging down along the two large sides to the ground, were turned back on each side to cover the eastern entrance. But because seven cubits came from each side, while the entrance-space was only ten cubits, one cloth was sewn over another. Or perhaps, at the top of each, two cubits were folded back and sewn, like the hems of a garment; then the cloths coming equally from the sides were joined in the middle of the entrance, at the same place as the curtains, and likewise on the western side.

On account of such sewing-over or folding of the cloths, Bede says that the Lord first told Moses: “You shall double the sixth cloth at the front of the roof” (Exod.

[Col. 1178A]

26); that is, you shall sew over or fold back half a cloth, which exceeds the curtains at the entrance. Then He added more plainly: “What remains of the cloths”—that is, the one additional cloth—“with half of it you shall cover the rear of the tabernacle,” that is, the western side.

They were doubled so that they could withstand the force of the winds. According to this arrangement, the tabernacle was covered on every side by the goat-hair cloths down to the ground, and nothing of it could be seen. Thus the costly curtain at the entrance was useless; and when priests entered the tabernacle, they either had to lift the cloths and curtains to go inside, or else they were joined by hooks and rings in the middle and undone for their entrance.

## Chapter LVI. Josephus otherwise

[Col. 1178B]

Josephus’s arrangement is different, and Origen agrees with it; it seems the more probable. For he says that the ten curtains joined together, as stated, were stretched transversely from the front of the tabernacle [Col. 1178C] over the entrance, covered the whole tabernacle, and descended beside the western side as far as the ground. The entrance, however, was not covered by any part of the curtains, since it had its own veil. Likewise, concerning the goat-hair coverings, he says that they covered the whole tabernacle except the entrance. But because the goat-hair coverings exceed the curtains by two cubits on each side, he says that these were folded back beneath the curtain, lest a wind entering between the coverings and the curtains should shake the entire covering. For this reason, too, he thinks it was said: “You shall double the sixth covering at the front of the roof.” Yet even under this arrangement, however handsome and exceedingly costly it was, the outer part of the tabernacle was not visible, nor was that portion of the curtains which hung down around the tabernacle. [Col. 1178D] Thus things made at such expense would seem to have been made in vain. Therefore perhaps on every side the curtains and coverings were stretched around the tabernacle by ropes, and the ropes were fastened to bronze pegs; for Moses says below that the tabernacle had pegs. They were raised all around in the manner of a hanging roof, so that the tabernacle could be seen from every side and entered by those passing beneath the curtains.

## CHAPTER LVII. On the Skins Laid Over It

However these two coverings may have been arranged, there is no question concerning the remaining two. Indeed, the third covering was of red-dyed rams’ skins. Covering only the upper parts, they did not descend to the sides, but were bound around with ropes fastened to the ground by bronze pegs (Exod. XXVI). The fourth [Col. 1179A] covering likewise was laid over it in the same manner, of hyacinth-blue rams’ skins. These two were laid over it as protection from heat and the pouring of rain. Thus, as Josephus says, many who looked on it from afar were struck with wonder; for they thought its color differed in no respect from that of the sky.

## CHAPTER LVIII. What the Things Mentioned Above Signified

In this construction of the tabernacle it is evident that God, not man, so arranged it; for, as Josephus says, anyone willing to consider these matters without envy will find that each of these things was made in correspondence with the form of realities. The hidden place, accessible only to the high priest, represented heaven, assigned to God and the angels. The sanctuary, which was twice as large, represented land and sea, open to the tread of all, just as that part was common [Col. 1179B] to the priests. The curtains represented the starry heaven; the goat-hair coverings, the waters above the firmament; the red skins, the empyrean heaven in which the angels are; the hyacinth-blue skins, the higher heaven, where God is above all things.

Yet Josephus says that the four elements were signified in the four colors of the veils: by linen, the earth, because linen comes from the earth and initially has an iron-gray and green color; by purple, the sea, because it is dyed from marine shells; by hyacinth-blue, the air, because it resembles it in color; by scarlet, fire, because it is like it in color. By the table, time or the year [Note: [Col. 1179C] Addition 1. There is a legal year, a customary year, and an emergent year. The legal year begins with the April new moon; the customary year begins with the Kalends of January; an emergent year begins on any day whatever.]; by the loaves, the twelve months; by the crown four fingers broad, the solar year of four seasons; by the smaller crown, the [Col. 1179C] lunar year; by the seven lamps of the lampstand, the seven planets; by its seventy parts, the *decarmonia* [Note: [Col. 1179D] Addition 2. *Deca* means “ten,” and *harmonia* means “concord.” Hence *decarmonia* means the consonance of the planets.] of the planets—perhaps because each planet has ten dignities or powers, five natural and five accidental, in which they stand harmoniously, that is, proportionately. This is indicated in the lampstand, because the things beneath them tend toward them; that is, they derive their natural motions and effects from them. Its ornamentation also indicates this: the cups, that is, vessels for liquid, signify water; the little spheres, the spherical sun; the lilies, the air, which alone is affected by odors.

## CHAPTER LIX. On the Altar of Whole Burnt Offerings

[Col. 1179D]

The Lord also commanded an altar to be made from *setim* wood (Exod. XXVII). This altar was called the altar of the whole burnt offering, or of whole burnt offerings, or of holocausts; it might be called the altar of sacrifices, but it received its name from the more eminent sacrifice. It was five cubits in length and breadth, that is, square, and three cubits high. Since it was rather high, something was placed beside it during the time of ministry for the minister to stand upon; when the ministry was completed, this was removed. For elsewhere the altar is forbidden to have steps.

It was hollow [Col. 1180A] like a chest without a lid: its walls were wooden, but covered with bronze inside and out. Yet they could not be burned, just as neither *antiton* [uncertain reading], nor any wood of Paradise, can be burned; rather, it becomes cleaner by burning. Its hearth, or little bronze altar, was like the bottom of a chest, upon which fire was made; the fire was laid through a window situated on the eastern side. At the four upper corners, outside, were four curved horns, in which four chains were inserted through rings. From these hung a bronze grating, made in the form of a net, which descended inside as far as the middle of the altar. The things to be burned as a pleasing odor to the Lord were placed upon it, and the fire, rising from the hearth through the circles of the grating, consumed them. Around the four lower corners were bronze rings, in which were placed poles [Col. 1180B] of *setim* wood covered with bronze, for carrying the altar.

Yet concerning this altar and its grating there is uncertainty, not only among us but even among the Hebrews, especially since the Hebrew text seems to differ in nothing from our translation. We indeed have it thus: “You shall make a bronze grating in the form of a net, at whose four corners there shall be bronze rings, which you shall place beneath [Note: [Col. 1181A] Addition 1. According to the opinion stated above, this is explained as “beneath” or “above”; or the wording is arranged thus: “which you shall place beneath,” that is, beneath which you shall place.] the hearth of the altar; and the grating shall reach to the middle of the altar.” But the Hebrew has it thus: “You shall make for it a *michar*, that is, a grating, a network of bronze; and upon the network four bronze rings; and you shall place it as the base of the altar beneath; and the network shall reach to the middle of the altar.”

Josephus, however, says: “Beneath it was a grating made in the manner [Col. 1180C] of a net. For the earth received the fire which was carried from the grating, since it had no bases beneath it.” Cassiodorus the senator, however, in the illustration which he made, and which he mentions in his *Exposition of the Psalms*, gave four feet to each altar. Accordingly, some think that meat to be roasted was not laid upon the grating; rather, it was a kind of vessel in which the altar rested, whose walls surrounded the altar and rose to its middle. At its upper corners hung four rings, through which, when poles were inserted, the altar resting upon it could be carried. For the altar is not said to have had other rings.

But whether this net-like vessel was separate from the altar, so that the altar could be removed from it and set upon it whenever desired, or whether it was so skillfully fashioned in cast work from [Col. 1180D] the altar itself that it appeared, as it were, attached to it, is uncertain. They maintain that upon the little hearth of the altar, which they say was placed in its middle, a pile of wood was laid through the eastern window, and meat to be roasted was placed upon the wood. Or perhaps there was no little hearth there, but fire was made upon the grating laid over it, which Josephus seems to mean in the words quoted above.

Others think that it had neither a covering nor a base, but that only its walls were filled with earth, according to the Lord’s words: “You shall make me an altar of earth.” Fire was made in its upper chest, where the things to be burned were placed. They hold the same view concerning the grating laid over the altar [Note: [Col. 1181A] Addition 2. This has not been observed according to the opinions stated above, but mystically.]. The little hearth beneath which the grating is said to have been placed, the Hebrew calls an *aruncula*, or a groove, [Col. 1181A] which he says was in the middle of the altar’s walls [Note: [Col. 1181A] Addition 3. Perhaps because it was a hollow place for receiving the ashes of the victims.], as far as which point the height of the grating extended.

## CHAPTER LX. On the Position of the Altar and Its Vessels

The altar was placed in the open air before the tabernacle, not directly before the entrance but somewhat farther south (Exod. XXVII), so that those sacrificing before it, while standing to the north, could look into the tabernacle itself, as far as the holy of holies. [Col. 1181B] And because they stood to the north, that is, on the northern side of the altar and facing south, one sometimes reads that they sacrificed to the north and sometimes to the south.

Its implements included basins for collecting and carrying away the ashes when they became abundant; these were deposited in a hidden and clean place. There were also tongs for tending the altar’s fire; and forks, which we call in Greek *creagrae*, because cooked meat was drawn out of cauldrons with them; and little pans, as it were fire-shovels, from *vehendo*, “carrying,” by which coals were carried from this altar to the altar of incense; besides kettles and pots for boiling meat—though these were not boiled beside the altar. All these things were bronze. The Hebrew, however, has it thus: “You shall make its [Col. 1181C] pots, its shovels, its basins, its hooks, and its receptacles for fire.”

## CHAPTER LXI. On the Court Around the Tabernacle

The court around the tabernacle was one hundred cubits on the southern side, one hundred on the northern, fifty on the eastern, and the same on the western side (Exod. XXVII). Thus it was four-sided, or quadrangular, but not square: one dimension was longer than the other. On the southern side there were twenty columns, five cubits high, covered with silver plates, having silver capitals with carved work and bronze bases. They stood five cubits apart, and each had rings upon it [Note: [Col. 1182A] Addition 1. There were projections at the tops of the columns, themselves perforated; and in the opening were two cords, one on this side and one on that, to keep the column upright. In the glosses on Exodus VI, they are called little tongues; and because they were stripped smooth and somewhat rounded at the top in the manner of a tongue, Josephus calls them corners. It is also credible, he says, that beneath each base of the columns a peg was fixed, by which the whole column was firmly attached to the earth.]. Ropes extended from the rings to the heads of pegs, which were one cubit in size, [Col. 1181D] and were firmly driven into the ground at each column to keep the court immovable.

A curtain of the finest linen, one hundred cubits long and five broad, hung from the columns, extending from capital to base, so that it seemed no different from a wall—unless perhaps, because of inclement weather, it was sometimes drawn back by ropes and pegs so that the people might take shelter beneath it as under a roof. In the same manner, the northern side had twenty columns and an extended curtain. On the western side, ten columns and a curtain fifty cubits long enclosed the court. At the eastern entrance three columns stood on this side and three on that, with curtains spread beside them, differing in no respect from the former ones. In the middle of that side were four columns in the form [Col. 1182A] of gates, from which hung a veil of the four precious colors, woven in embroidered work, which could easily be raised and lowered for exit and entry.

It should be noted, however, that on the longer sides there were twenty columns, between which were openings amounting to one hundred cubits; on the two shorter sides, nine. Yet because the corner columns were common to two sides [Note: [Col. 1182B] Addition 2. If there were only twenty columns on the southern side, and each stood five cubits from the next, then, since there were nineteen spaces between them, they would extend only ninety-five cubits in length. Understand the same concerning the northern side. The master resolves this objection.], they are said there to be twenty and here ten. The Lord designated by the number of columns the number of intervals. Each large side therefore had twenty columns, that is, twenty intervals. Another text has ten columns, that is, ten intervals.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the Lamps of the Tabernacle

[Col. 1182C]

The Lord also commanded the children of Israel to offer the purest olive oil, beaten in a mortar (Exod. XXVII). For this is purer than nut oil, linseed oil, myrtle oil, or radish oil, so that a lamp might always burn from it in the tabernacle of testimony. Aaron and his sons lit it in the evening, and the seven lamps burned upon the lampstand before the Lord until morning; in the daytime, however, only three did so. The lamp-wick was made of papyrus; the little vessel, which we call a *mergus*, was golden.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the Common Garments of the Priests

Again the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: [Col. 1182D] “Bring near to yourself Aaron your brother, with his sons, from among the children of Israel, that they may perform the priesthood for me; and you shall make a holy garment for your brother” (Exod. XXVIII), in which, once sanctified, he may minister to me.

Since the narrative treats these garments confusedly, let us set them forth in a suitable order for clarity. Four garments were common both to the lower priests, called *chaneos*, and to the chief of the priests, called the *arabarchus*; and after these there were four others, worn by the *arabarchus* alone, that is, the chief priest. He was clothed in them in this order.

First, after hands and feet had been purified with water, the priest put on the *manachasim*, a word meaning “a binding garment,” which may be called in Greek *brachae* and in Latin *femoralia*, “breeches” [Note: [Col. 1183C] Addition 1. Origen: “A breech-garment is a garment in which the private parts of the body are customarily covered and contained. And lest indecency be revealed when the breeches slip down, the thighs are bound by a belt.”]. It was woven of twisted [Col. 1183A] linen. The feet passed through it, and it rose as far as the loins; there it was tightly fastened, and it descended only to the knees.

Our high priest, however, because he possesses continual continence, covers only his feet with sandals (John XIII), as though it were said to him: “He who has been washed does not need except to wash his feet” [Note: [Col. 1183C] Addition 2. That is, he should restrain the first movements, which he cannot entirely suppress.].

Second, he was clothed in a double linen tunic, called *ceetomone*, that is, “linen,” which we call a close-fitting linen garment, or shirt, or under-tunic. Moses called it *abanech*, but later the Hebrews, having learned from the Babylonians, called it *emissan*. It descended to the ankles and was suitably fitted to the body, but tightly confined the arms with sleeves; the neck-opening was bound on either side above the shoulders by clasps or little fastenings [Col. 1183B].

Third, he was bound with a belt about four fingers broad, so netted that it looked like the skin which a viper sheds in summer. It was woven with scarlet, purple, and hyacinth-blue flowers, but its warp was linen. It began to be girded at the breast, was carried around the sides, returned again before the navel, and there was moderately fastened; it hung as far as the shins as an ornament while the priest performed no work. But when he sacrificed, lest it hinder him, he threw its hanging ends over the left shoulder. Hence perhaps the deacon sometimes places the folded chasuble upon the same shoulder.

Fourth, he wore upon his head a simple tiara, very different from the high priest’s *cidaris*. [Col. 1183C] It was in the form of a small tube or modest helmet, rising above half the crown of the head, and was called *manephei*. It had bands, repeatedly wound and tied so that it would not easily slip; above it was another linen covering, descending to the lower edge of the beard, concealing the bindings of the cap and the whole surface of the head, and fitted securely so that it would not fall off while the priest was at work.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the High-Priestly Garments

[Col. 1183D]

Over these, the *arabarchus* wore four garments peculiar to himself. The first was a hyacinth-blue tunic, a full-length garment called *poderis* or *impoditis*, which the Hebrew calls *michir* (Exod. XXVII). It was made from two cut pieces sewn together over the shoulders and along the sides in the manner of a dalmatic, with sleeves of the same color sewn on. Its neck-opening did not run crosswise over the shoulders, but had a lengthwise slit from the breast to the middle of the shoulder-blades. To prevent this opening from showing indecently in front and behind, a band was sewn on, fastened on either side above the shoulders with clasps. Instead of fringes, it had seventy-two little golden bells, intermixed with an equal number of small pomegranates (*nastusi*), made from hyacinth-blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, so that after each bell [Col. 1184A] came a pomegranate, arranged, as it were, alternately. Thus the sound might be heard when the priest entered or departed from the sanctuary alone, and he might not die [Note: [Col. 1185C] Addition 1. Although it was not literally true that the priest would die if the sound was not heard, nevertheless this allegorically teaches that priests who must care for their flock ought not to be mute; hence it is said: “Woe to the dog that does not bark.”].

Josephus seems to hold that over this tunic the high priest was girded with the belt mentioned above, with which the other priests girded themselves over the linen tunic. Others say that he was not yet girded with it, but was girded over the ephod, so that he might finally be girded over all the garments. There were also those who said that the high priest had two belts: the first like that of the priests, the second over the ephod; nevertheless, the two were reckoned as one garment.

The second garment was the ephod, like the Greek shoulder-garment, woven of the four colors mentioned above and gold. It had no sleeves and was like a short tunic, descending to the loins so that it could be girded [Col. 1184B] over. It covered the upper part of the hyacinth-blue tunic, leaving the lower part untouched. The edges of its sides were joined by golden hooks and rings. It had upon the breast a square opening the size of a palm [Note: [Col. 1185D] Addition 2. A *palmus* is the fourth measure, made with the fist, the thumb extended and the remaining fingers bent; it contains half a foot.], into which the *logion* was set. On its upper part, over both shoulders, two onyx stones—sardonyxes according to Josephus, emeralds according to the Septuagint—were fastened with gold. On these were engraved the twelve names of the sons of Israel in provincial letters [Note: [Col. 1185D] Addition 3. That is, in letters and figures marked by certain signs known to all. There are certain characters commonly known, which even laymen are said to use upon their fingers in calculations; or “provincial letters” may mean Egyptian letters, which they knew because of their dwelling among the Egyptians. But however one understands this, they were written in the Hebrew language.], in Hebrew, according to their order of birth: the six names of the elder sons on the right shoulder, those of the younger on the left, in remembrance of the children of Israel. It had a neck-opening across the shoulders, woven with strong straps [Col. 1184C].

The ephod which Samuel (II Kings II) and David (II Kings VI) are said to have worn was another garment, properly called an *ephotar*, and it was linen; this other one, however, was variegated with remarkable beauty.

The third ornament was called by the Hebrew *essin*, by the Greek *logion*, and by the Latin *rationale*, “breastpiece.” It was square and double, so that it would not be torn by the weight of the gems. It measured a palm, sufficient, that is, to fill the opening of the shoulder-garment. It was woven from the four colors mentioned above and gold, in the same pattern as the shoulder-garment. It contained twelve stones firmly set in gold, three in each of four rows. In the first row: sardius, topaz, emerald. In the second: carbuncle, sapphire, jasper. In the third: ligure, agate, amethyst. In the fourth: chrysolite, onyx, [Col. 1184D] and beryl. On these were engraved the twelve names of the sons of Israel, each name on its own stone and according to their order of birth.

Thus the priest bore a memorial of the children of Israel, and bore the children of Israel upon his shoulders and breast, for remembrance of three things: the people were to remember one, and he himself two. That is, the people, seeing the names of their fathers, should strive not to degenerate from the virtue of their forebears; while the priest should remember to imitate the life and faith of the patriarchs, and should also remember to commend to God in sacrifices and prayers the people descended from those fathers.

It was called the breastpiece of judgment because these two words were written in it: “judgment” and “truth,” or “doctrine” and “truth.” Indeed, where we have, “You shall place in the breastpiece of judgment judgment and truth,” [Col. 1185A] the Hebrew has *phurim* and *thumim*. Hence they also call *phurim* the lots by which the judgment of truth is customarily sought. They say that in the middle of the breastpiece there was a square stone two fingers wide, by the alteration of whose color they discerned whether God was favorable or offended.

Josephus says that the sardonyx worn on the right shoulder shone with such splendor when the high priest’s sacrifice pleased God that its ray could be seen even by those standing far off. When they were about to go out to battle, if God was with them, such a radiance appeared in the stones of the breastpiece that it became manifest to the whole multitude that God was present with them in that aid; and for this reason it was called the breastpiece of judgment.

Josephus further asserts that this sardonyx and the radiance [Col. 1185B] of the sardonyxes in the breastpiece had ceased two hundred years before he wrote these things, because God bore with displeasure the transgressions of the Law.

At the four corners of the breastpiece were four golden rings. Into the two upper rings were inserted two golden chains joined to each other: that is, crossed and joined in the middle in the shape of the letter X; or rather, this describes the making of the chain [Note: [Col. 1185D] Addition 4. The master says that in likeness of this chain, the stole hanging from the neck on both sides ought to cross on the breast; but this is not done from it.], in which link is joined to link. For this the Hebrew has, “woven chains, the work of intertwining.” Josephus says that they came through tubes, which, according to the Chaldean, means “finished,” that is, made to the measure of the space over which they extended. They were carried upward as far as the high priest’s shoulders, and there inserted into two [Col. 1185C] golden hooks firmly fixed in the shoulder-garment. To the two lower rings were sewn two hyacinth-blue bands, which were carried around the sides and inserted into two golden rings between the shoulders. These were fixed in the ephod beneath each sardonyx, so that both fastenings held ephod and *logion* firmly together.

Concerning this Josephus says that there was a belt thickly woven with the four colors and gold, carried around from either side and turned back again before the breast, its two ends hanging below, and having fringes composed with marvelous beauty from golden tubes.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Mitre and Tiara

[Col. 1186A]

The final ornament was for the head. More generally it may be called a tiara, mitre, or fillet; more particularly, a *cidaris* (Exod. XXVIII). The tiara was made in the manner described above, common to the priests. Sewn over it was another covering, entirely hyacinth-blue, encircled by a golden band made in three rows. Upon it, from the back of the head onward, stood golden flowers like plantain, set at intervals. Above the forehead stood a golden flower like the plant which the Greeks call *jusquiamum* (henbane), one finger in size. On the upper surface of the tiara, all around and up to its summit [Col. 1186B]—which ended in a very sharp point—there were, at intervals, golden pomegranates skillfully made with their thorny tips.

Over the forehead hung a golden plate, called the *petalum*, made in the shape of a half-moon. It curved upward and, by a golden ring in the middle, was inserted into a golden hook fastened to the tiara. On it was engraved *Aioth Adonai*, namely the holy name of the Lord: that is, the Tetragrammaton, which is called ineffable, not because it cannot be spoken, but because it signifies an ineffable reality. It is written with these letters: *iod, he, vau, he* [Note: [Col. 1186C] Addition 1. Yet these letters do not represent their own alphabetic elements in that name, as the other letters sometimes do.]. They signify “the beginning of the life of this suffering one”: that is, through the passion of him whom this priest prefigures, [Col. 1186C] life lost in Adam will be renewed and recovered.

Lest, when the high priest moved, the holy plate should also move, it was tied upward with a transparent hyacinth-blue band concealing the hook and ring. This band was carried around the head and tied at the back, while its hanging ends fell over both shoulders.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On the Figure of the Garments

Clothed in these garments, the high priest bore upon himself an image of the whole world. The breeches and close-fitting linen garment, because they were linen, represented the earth; the belts, however many there were [Note: [Col. 1187A] Addition 1. Because some thought there was one and others several, they say “however many there were.”], represented the encircling [Col. 1186D] Ocean. The hyacinth-blue tunic represented the air by its very color; the bells signified the sounds of thunder; the pomegranates, flashes of lightning. The variety of the ephod represented the starry heaven; its interweaving with golden colors signified that vital heat penetrates all things. The two sardonyxes represented the sun and moon, or the two hemispheres; the twelve gems of the breastpiece, the twelve signs of the zodiac.

It is fitting that the central ornament was called the *rationale*, “reason.” For all things are full of reason, and earthly things adhere to heavenly things. Indeed, the ordering of earthly things and of seasons, of heat and cold, and the twofold tempering between them, descends from the course and reason of heaven. The *cidaris* represented the empyrean heaven, and the plate laid upon it, God presiding over all things.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On the Construction of the Altar of Incense and Its Position

[Col. 1187A]

After the description of the garments, the Lord spoke to Moses concerning the manner of consecrating Aaron and his sons. We have postponed this until the consecration itself, while proceeding to discuss the golden altar. This altar was made of *setim* wood, one cubit long and one cubit broad—that is, square—and two cubits high. It was covered in the purest gold and had horns, a golden grating, chains, rings, and golden poles like the former altar (Exod. XXX). Whether it had a little hearth or whether the earth received its ashes is uncertain. Josephus [Col. 1187B] adds that it had six crowns of the purest gold at each corner; perhaps this is what is expressed singly in Exodus: “You shall make for it a golden crown around it” [Note: [Col. 1187C] Addition 1. A projection in the form of a rim.].

This altar was called the altar of incense, or of *thymiama*, because every day, morning and evening, incense was burned upon it to accompany the continual sacrifice offered from two lambs, sanctified to the Lord. Some, however, said that incense—that is, frankincense—was laid on only in the morning, whereas in the evening, because of the dignity of the evening sacrifice, *thymiama* was offered.

Furthermore, the saints seem to have doubted whether this altar was within the holy of holies or in the sanctuary with the lampstand and table. Yet it must not be supposed that there was uncertainty that it was in the sanctuary, since the Hebrew says this and Josephus [Col. 1187C] states it plainly, and Moses’ initial arrangement of the tabernacle suggests it—except that Paul, in Hebrews, places a golden censer within the holy of holies alone [Note: [Col. 1187C] Addition 2. Origen, in the homily *On the Tabernacle*: “Moreover, certain places are made distinct by veils, which are called holy; and others, likewise divided by a second veil, are called the holy of holies. Within is placed the ark, above which the cherubim stand with outstretched wings touching one another; and there a certain plate with a golden base [reading uncertain] is placed, which is called the propitiatory; but the golden altar of incense. Furthermore, in the outer place a golden lampstand is set on the southern side, facing north; on the northern side is placed the table and the presentation of the loaves upon it; and the altar of whole burnt offerings is placed beside the inner veil.”] (Heb. IX).

It could indeed be that in the Temple, where all things had been enlarged and multiplied, in addition to the golden altar which stood outside the veil and which had to be entered twice daily, a censer was placed in the entrance. In it the high priest would burn the coals and incense which he carried with him when he was about to enter the inner place itself.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the Composition of the Incense

[Col. 1187D]

Concerning the composition of the holy incense, the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Take for yourself spices: [Col. 1188A] stacte, onycha, sweet-smelling galbanum, and the purest frankincense; all shall be of equal weight, and you shall grind them into the finest powder” (Exod. XXX).

Onycha is said to be a small, sweet-smelling shellfish, the size of a human fingernail; hence it is called *onycha*, because *onyx* in Greek means “nail.” Stacte is the gum which flows from myrrh, and is also called myrrh. Galbanum is the sap of ferula; the best kind grows in Syria, being cartilaginous, that is, less woody, and snakes are driven away by its odor. Ferula, also called fennel, grows in Gargano; its sap is cheaper. The purest frankincense is the best, and is called “male” because it is round like a human testicle. It is also called *Libanum* from Mount Lebanon in Arabia, where [Col. 1188B] the frankincense tree grows, with branches tangled and twisted like those of a maple.

From these four substances the powder of holy incense was made. The Lord forbade such a composition to be made for human use; if anyone made something similar in order to enjoy its fragrance, he would perish from among his people (ibid.). Hence in the Church the fragrance of blessed incense is not given to bridegroom and bride. Hence also, after blessed incense has been offered upon the altar, if the censer is brought down to the clergy in choir or to the laity, other incense, without blessing, must be placed in it and offered to people.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On the Preparation of the Holy Anointing Oil

The holy ointment was also made from four spices [Note: [Col. 1189C] Addition 1. Note that according to Chronicles, Bezalel does not appear to have had more than two years.] (Exod. XXX). A spice is any fragrant substance that affects the air by its odor, as though from *aerioma*, “an affecting of the air.” [Col. 1188C]

Five hundred shekels of the finest myrrh branches were taken—that is, the choicest myrrh. Myrrh is a tree, called *smyrna* in Greek, five cubits high, found in Arabia. The Arabs burn its branches so that it may put forth shoots and bear fruit more abundantly; through their vapor they would contract many intolerable diseases unless they counteracted it with the smoke of storax. There were two hundred and fifty shekels of cinnamon, and the same quantity of calamus, but five hundred of cassia.

Cinnamon is a shrub of India or Ethiopia, two cubits high, called, as it were, *cannamomum*, because it has thin, bent, reed-like stalks; when broken, these emit a visible vapor. Calamus is an aromatic species growing near Lebanon. Cassia grows in watery places, grows to immense size, and yields a fragrance. These things, reduced to powder with olive oil in the measure of a *hin*, were prepared by the work of a perfumer. It was called the oil of holy anointing, or holy ointment; concerning its use we shall speak in its place. Josephus also says that balsam was added.

## CHAPTER LXX. On the Bronze Laver

“The Lord spoke again to Moses: ‘You shall also make a bronze laver with its base’ (Exod. X),” that is, a washing vessel, also called a *luter*. It stood between the tabernacle and the altar of whole burnt offerings. Water having been put into it, the priests washed their hands and feet before receiving the holy garments in order to sacrifice; likewise before entering the tabernacle and upon leaving it. It is said to have been made from the mirrors of women [Col. 1189A] who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle. Perhaps it was made from bronze mirror-stands. Or rather, after it was made, mirrors were placed around the upper rim of the laver, in which the priest could see whether he had some stain, on his face or on his garment, that needed to be washed away.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On the Ransom of Those Numbered

Again the Lord said to Moses: “When you number the children of Israel, each shall give the price for his own life, that no plague may be among them: half a shekel according to the measure of the sanctuary” (Exod. XXX). A shekel contains twenty obols. “They shall give it from twenty years of age and upward,” for from that time they passed under the name of the family. “The rich shall not add, nor the poor diminish.” This money was set aside for the uses of the tabernacle.

This was punished in [Col. 1189B] David, because he acted otherwise than God had commanded. For, reigning in peace, he numbered the people as though proudly, and did not make those numbered offer according to the Lord’s command; thus he sinned in two respects (II Kings XXIII).

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the Selection of Craftsmen and the Giving of the Tablets
“Moreover, the Lord called by name,” that is, he chose by name the chief craftsmen for this work: “Bezalel [Note: [Col. 1189C] Addition 1. Note that, according to Chronicles, Bezalel seems to have been no more than two years old.] son of Uri, of the tribe of Judah, and Oholiab his associate [Note: [Col. 1189C] Addition 2. Scribal error is especially to be considered in two matters: proper names and numbers. Since Chronicles consists almost entirely of these two, it may have been a scribal error: when they ought to have recorded a certain number of Bezalel’s years, they wrote an uncertain number as certain.], though less skilled, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan” (Exod. 31). He filled him with the Spirit of God, that is, with knowledge for devising every kind of craftwork.

[Col. 1189C] “And when these words had been completed, he gave Moses two tablets of stone, written by the finger of God.”

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On the molten calf

“When the people saw that Moses delayed, they said to Aaron: ‘Make us gods to go before us; for we do not know what has happened to Moses’” (Exod. 32).

[Col. 1189D] The Hebrews excuse themselves by saying that *Elohim* signifies not only “gods” but also “lords,” and that they asked for leaders for the journey. But Aaron and Hur resisted. The enraged people spat in Hur’s face and, as is related, suffocated him with their spittle. Aaron therefore, in fear, said: “Take the earrings of your wives and children, and bring them to me.” These were the things they held most dear and precious; he thought that, yielding to their avarice, they would be unwilling to bring them. “When he had received them, he fashioned from them a molten calf by the work of casting.”

Perhaps they would accept nothing else, because they had worshipped a bull in Egypt. Some relate that Aaron threw the earrings into the fire, and that through demonic agency only a calf’s head was cast from them. Yet it is sometimes called a calf and sometimes a calf’s head, because Aaron, in his own defence, is later [Col. 1190A] recorded as saying to Moses: “I threw it into the fire, and this calf came out.” “And the people said: ‘These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.’” Aaron made an altar before it and proclaimed a festival for the next day. Rising early in the morning, they offered sacrifices; “and the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play,” that is, to worship.

“Then the Lord said to Moses: ‘Go down; your people have sinned.’” As if to say: they are no longer mine. “Let me alone, that I may destroy them and make you into a great nation.” To this Moses replied: “I beg you, Lord, let your anger be quieted, lest the Egyptians say: ‘He brought them out craftily in order to kill them in the mountains,’” being unable to give them the land which he had promised. “Remember also your servants, to whom you swore, saying: ‘I shall give this land to your seed.’”

[Col. 1190B] When the Lord had been appeased, Moses descended carrying the tablets, written on both sides by God’s finger. Joshua met him—perhaps because he went out each day to meet him. For it is not credible that Joshua fasted with Moses. He said to Moses: “There is the sound of battle-cry in the camp.” Moses replied: “No, it is the voice of singers.” When he drew near, he saw the calf and the dances; angered, he threw down the tablets, and they were broken. He burned the calf, reduced its mass to powder, scattered it in water, and gave the children of Israel drink from it.

When he accused Aaron for having listened to the people, Aaron excused himself by saying what has been stated above: that he had feared the people, because they were inclined to evil. “Moses therefore saw that the people had been stripped of their ornaments [Note: [Col. 1190D] Addition 1. “Stripped” is explained in four ways: despoiled, deprived, exposed, marked out.],” namely, either of God’s help, or rather that they had finally made manifest [Col. 1190C] the idolatry which they had long before conceived. Or perhaps he saw that God had identified for him the instigators of the crime by means of the powder they had drunk, which miraculously appeared in their beards. Standing at the gate of the camp and summoning the Levites, he said: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, join me. Let each man put his sword upon his thigh; pass through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his friend and his brother”—that is, whomever he found marked by the powder. “And about three thousand fell that day.” Another translation has twenty-three thousand.

Josephus says nothing of all these matters concerning the calf; he only recounts their opinions about Moses’ delay. Some said that he had been devoured by wild beasts, others that he had been taken away by the Lord, still others that, sound of mind, he was philosophizing with the Lord.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On Moses’ prayer and God’s threats

“On the next day Moses spoke to the people: ‘You have committed a very great sin. I shall go up to the Lord, if I can perhaps entreat him for you.’ And when he had gone up, he said: ‘I beseech you, Lord, either forgive them this offence, or blot me out of your book which you have written’ [Note: [Col. 1191B] Addition 1. According to predestination, Paul was written in the book of life when he was persecuting the Church.]” (Exod. 32).

Some maintain that this was spoken in an outburst of feeling rather than from reason; or that it was said from great confidence in God, as an impossible proposition, as if he meant: “Just as it is impossible for you to blot me out, so I pray that it may be impossible for you not to forgive them.” Augustine says that the reasoning should be concluded from what follows, so that [Col. 1191A] the following should be placed first: “Either blot me out, or forgive them.” This is put in place of its equivalent, as if he meant: “If you do not blot me out, forgive them.” For the disjunctive is turned into a conjunctive, when what comes first is denied and what follows remains.

A person is said to be written in or blotted out from the book of life in two ways: according to foreknowledge [Note: [Col. 1191B] Addition 1. According to predestination, Paul was written in the book of life when he was persecuting the Church.], or according to present righteousness [Note: [Col. 1191B] Addition 2. According to present righteousness, Judas was written in the book of life.]. “To him the Lord said: ‘Whoever has sinned against me, unless he repents, I shall blot him out,’” as if to say: not you, because you have not sinned. “Go, lead this people; my angel shall go before you. For I shall not go up with you, because the people are stiff-necked, lest perhaps they destroy you on the way” (Exod. 33).

The Hebrews relate that previously God himself had been their guardian; thereafter he gave them Michael as their own guardian, just as other nations have proper guardian angels appointed to them. The Lord also added: “Once I shall go up in your midst, and destroy you.” This is a threat of Babylonian or Roman captivity. Note that “going up” is said in two ways: from lower things to higher, or from hidden things to manifest; and the meaning is: “I shall reveal myself to you through your calamity.”

## CHAPTER LXXV. On the removal of the former tabernacle

“Hearing these things, the people mourned, and no one put on his ornament. They laid aside their adornment from Mount Horeb” (Exod. 33). Moses then took the tabernacle—[Col. 1191C] which may suitably be understood as the earlier tabernacle that they had made for themselves, in order to deliberate about legal matters before it. Since until then it had stood at the foot of the mountain, that it might be nearer to the Lord, the Lord wished it to be removed away from himself [Note: [Col. 1191C] Addition 1. As though he were turning his face away from them.]. Moses pitched it on the other side of the camp, far from the camp.

Moses would go out to it [Note: [Col. 1191C] Addition 2. Moses himself entered the tabernacle, speaking with God.], and the people stood at the doors of their own tents and worshipped from afar. “The pillar of cloud came down, and the Lord spoke with Moses, while all saw, face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend”: that is, plainly.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. That Moses saw the Lord’s back parts

[Col. 1191D]

“Moses again prayed to the Lord: ‘Look upon your people, this nation. You wish me to lead out the people; tell me whom you will send with me.’ And God said: ‘My face shall go before you’” (Exod. 33). Behold, Moses had now obtained something greater: more is signified by “face” than by “angel.” But because Moses understood that, by “face,” someone most like God was being promised, he added: “If you yourself do not go before us, do not lead us out of this place [Note: [Col. 1192B] Addition 1. He shows himself familiar to one whom he calls by his own name; this is especially commended in the greater persons.].”

The Lord said to him: “I shall also do the thing which you have spoken, and I have known you yourself by name”—that is, you have pleased me in a proper and special manner. “I shall be called in the name of the Lord before you,” that is, I shall cause myself [Col. 1192A] to be called God and your leader. This will be through the miracles I shall perform, and for no reason other than because I will it: “for I shall have mercy on whom I will.”

Moses said to him: “Show me your face.” The Lord said to him: “You cannot see my face. For no human being shall see me and live. You shall stand in the cleft of the rock, and I shall pass before you in my glory. Since you could not endure it, I shall place my hand before you. When I have passed by, I shall remove my hand, and you shall see my back parts.” This is said by way of likeness. For just as, when a man is seen from behind, one knows that he is a man but not which man he is, so now we know that God exists, but we do not yet know what he is.

It may be that the Lord passed by in such great brightness as human sight could not endure, and a cloud was placed over Moses. Afterwards, when he had gone farther away, he could be seen by Moses. Literally, the Hebrews relate that he saw a man’s back parts and certain fastenings on the back of his head.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On the second tablets and the glory of Moses’ face

And the Lord said to Moses: “Cut for yourself two tablets like the former ones, and I shall write upon them the words which the tablets that you broke contained” (Exod. 34). Deuteronomy also says that God wrote them (Deut. 9). But subsequently he says: “Write these things for yourself,” and so on. A little later: “Moses was with the Lord [Col. 1192C] forty days,” and so forth, “and he wrote on the tablets the ten words of the covenant.” It may be said that the authority for writing was in the Lord, but the ministry was in Moses.

After Moses had cut out the tablets, he rose in the night and ascended the mountain. When the Lord passed before him in a whirlwind, he fell face down upon the earth in worship and said: “I beseech you, go with us, take away our iniquities, and take possession of us.” The Lord briefly reminded him of certain things which he had already foretold concerning the three festivals, the offering of first-fruits and firstborn, and added that they were to have no fellowship with the nations of the promised land.

“Moses was with the Lord a second time for forty days and forty nights. He did not eat bread or drink water. When he came down from the mountain with the tablets, his face appeared horned, and he [Col. 1192D] did not know it.” That is, rays of wondrous brilliance issued from his face and dazzled the eyes of those who looked at him [Note: [Col. 1193A] Addition 1. As in Christ, when he drove out from the Temple those selling and buying.]. The apostle Paul calls this “the glory of Moses’ face.” Moses put a veil over his face when he spoke to the children of Israel. He also told them all that had been commanded him.

How long this glory lasted, and whether this happened once or more often, we do not know. The Hebrews relate that he went up to the Lord a third time to obtain certainty of forgiveness for them, and again remained with the Lord for forty days and forty nights in fasting. When he returned with assurance of forgiveness, it was the ninth day of the seventh month. The following day, celebrating the forgiveness granted, they afflicted their souls by fasting; [Col. 1193A] and thereafter the tenth day of this month was called the Day of Atonement [Note: [Col. 1193A] Addition 2. These forty [Col. 1193B] days had already elapsed from the fiftieth day after their departure from Egypt. Because they had God propitious, modern Jews still celebrate this feast.].

If this is true, it may be that for this reason the Church also appoints three forty-day fasts each year, though this practice is said to be instituted because three persons are read to have fasted for forty days: Moses, Elijah, and Jesus [Note: [Col. 1193B] Addition 3. Note that one Church observes three fasts because of Moses, Elijah, and Jesus, but observes two of them at dissimilar times. Another observes four because of Moses’ two fasts, Christ’s one, and Elijah’s one, again at different times.].

Whether this were so or not, after the second return Moses gave them commands concerning the construction of the tabernacle, according as he had received them from the Lord. He prefaced them with the observance of the Sabbath, lest they should think themselves permitted to work on the Sabbath in this undertaking.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On the construction and erection of the tabernacle

[Col. 1193B]
