The entire multitude went out and, in accordance with Moses’ words, offered with the readiest spirit whatever each had that was most precious. Their abundance was so great that the craftsmen were compelled to have a herald proclaim that no one should offer anything further. Bezalel and Oholiab made everything [Col. 1194A] that had been commanded them, and as it had been commanded (Exod. 35).

According to Josephus, the whole period required for the work was seven months. All the gold expended in the work of the sanctuary amounted to twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels, by the weight of the sanctuary. There were also one hundred talents of silver, from which were cast one hundred bases of the sanctuary [Note: [Col. 1194B] Addition 1. Annas, Caiaphas, and others who pronounced Christ worthy of death and shed his blood at the base of the altar were of Aaron’s stock. For there he was killed, where the altar and its base were. Hence: “It is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13).]. From one thousand seven hundred seventy-five further shekels were made the capitals of the columns, which were also covered with silver. There were likewise offered seventy talents of bronze and two thousand four hundred shekels.

Those who offered, from twenty years old and upward, numbered six hundred three thousand five hundred and fifty. Therefore, in the seventh month of the second year, on the first day of the month, Moses erected [Col. 1194B] the tabernacle. A cloud covered it while the light was clear—not stormy, but bright—yet not such that sight could pass through it, but such as befitted God’s presence. Thereafter, when that cloud rose, they moved camp; when it settled, they halted. While it stood over the tabernacle, they too remained still; and there was fire by night.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS

[Col. 1193]

## CHAPTER I. Preface

[Col. 1193C]

The third division of the history written by Moses is called in Greek *Leviticus*, because it deals with the election and ministry of the Levites; in Latin, *Offertorius* or *Sacrificaticius*, because it treats of sacrifices and of the things offered according to the Law. In Hebrew, however, it is *Vaiacra*, which means “ministerial matters.” Moses gave it this name according to Hebrew custom, because they name books from their beginnings, just as we name Masses and Gospels—for example, when we say, “the Sunday on which is sung: ‘People of Zion,’” or “is read: ‘There will be signs in the sun and moon.’”

This book begins as follows [Note: [Col. 1193D] Addition 1. Moses composed this book, the two preceding, and the two following; but he did not divide them as they are now divided. Rather, after composing them, he brought the entire work together as though into one body and one volume. Ezra, however, who was called the swift scribe and restored the entire library burned by the Babylonians [Col. 1194C], divided this work into five sections, or five books, called the Pentateuch.]: “Moses called, and the Lord spoke to him from the tabernacle of the covenant, saying: ‘The man who offers a sacrifice—if it is a burnt offering, and from the herd—shall offer a male.’” For “however,” the Hebrew has *va*, meaning “and,” and *yiqra*, “he called.”

## CHAPTER II. A useful division is permitted

[Col. 1194C]

To consider the teaching and tradition concerning sacrifices which follows, certain preliminary matters must be set forth in this manner. Five things must be considered here: the sacrifices offered to God; the persons by whom they are offered; the times when they are offered; the places where they are offered; and the reasons for which they are offered.

There is properly a threefold distinction among things offered. Either there was an offering from animals, and this was called a sacrifice; it could not be offered before the eighth day after birth, nor could a mother and her offspring be offered on the same day. Or it was from dry material, such as fine flour, bread, [Col. 1194D] and incense, and was properly called an offering. Or it was from liquids—wine and oil—which was properly called a libation or drink-offering, although Scripture sometimes uses these names interchangeably.

There were two classes of offerers: an individual person or the Synagogue. Among individual persons, one was a priest, another a ruler, another a private person; these will be discussed in their places, as likewise places and times in their proper places. There was also a threefold distinction of causes. They offered sometimes of necessity, sometimes voluntarily, and sometimes by occasion. Necessarily, they offered either by vow or by command. By command they offered first-fruits of grain, grapes, and fruits [Note: [Col. 1195A] Addition 1. There were two first-fruits: the first first-fruits of crops, from rubbed ears, on the first day of Unleavened Bread; the second in loaves, on the day of Pentecost.]. They also offered tithes of the same things, and additionally of animals; likewise the firstborn of animals and children; and the offerings of the three festivals, and so forth [Note: [Col. 1195B] Addition 2. If a human firstborn belonged to the Levites, he remained at the Temple; otherwise, he was redeemed for five shekels.].

Honey and leaven were never offered to the Lord, although their first-fruits were offered to the priest at their appointed times; nothing from them, however, was placed upon the altar. In every sacrifice, salt was never to be absent; for this reason it was called “the salt of the covenant,” because it was unlawful to transgress this rule. Now, following the order of the book, we must begin with sacrifices.

## CHAPTER III. On burnt offerings and their manner of offering

[Col. 1195B]

Of sacrifices, some were burnt offerings and others sacrifices in the narrower sense. Let us first consider the burnt offerings. Burnt offerings were those sacrifices which were wholly burned. For *holon* means “whole,” and *cauma*, “burning.” They were made only from three classes: from cattle; from flocks, but only sheep and goats; and from birds, but only turtledoves and pigeons.

From cattle and flocks they were offered thus: only a male of one year [Col. 1195C] (Lev. 1), that is, one year old or approximately so, but not older than a year. Hence the victim is sometimes called a lamb and sometimes a ram. A bull, however, could be offered when older than a year, as Josephus says. It was also to be without blemish, which must be understood not of a mark in the fleece but of the body: namely, it was not to be weak, have a broken limb, sores [Note: [Col. 1196B] Addition 1. A *papula* is an ailment of the mouth, called *lampast* in French.], scabies, blindness, or anything similar.

It was first presented to the priest at the entrance of the court, so that he might see whether it was fit to be offered. Afterwards it was offered to the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle through the laying on of hands upon its head, after the hands had first been washed. For besides the priests’ laver, there were in the court two basins, one for men and the other for women. Hence the Hebrews called the victim from the place of offering [Note: [Col. 1196B] Addition 2. Hence *hostia* according to the Hebrews has one derivation, according to the Gentiles another.].

The Gentiles, however, customarily called a sacrificial offering *hostia* from enemies to be conquered, [Col. 1195D] and *victima* from conquered enemies [Note: [Col. 1196B]

Addition 3. A *victima* is so called because it falls beneath the conquering right hand.

[Col. 1196C] A *hostia* takes its name from subdued enemies. (OVID.)

He used *domitis* (“subdued”) in place of *domandis* (“to be subdued”), from metrical necessity.].

The Hebrews called it *victima* from binding, because the animal was brought bound. The victim having thus been offered, the priest led it back to the altar of burnt offerings. Standing to the north, he slaughtered it before the Lord at the side of the altar and in the sight of the holy persons, and poured its blood all around the rim of the altar [Note: [Col. 1196C] Addition 4. One victim, which was somewhat large, was slaughtered by the priest, and its blood was poured at the altar’s rim. Another, larger victim was killed in such a way that the priest sprinkled the walls of the altar with its blood. There was also a very large victim, sacrificed so that its blood was poured by the one slaughtering it upon the altar’s horns.]. The Hebrew has “wall”; Josephus, “edge”—perhaps its projecting lip.

After the skin of the victim, which belonged to the priest, had been removed, he cut the limbs into pieces. After these were washed, he burned them all—together with the head, feet, and entrails—upon the altar as a burnt offering, a pleasing odour to the Lord. One must not believe that the Lord delighted in the stench [Col. 1196A] or smell of meat, but rather in the things signified and in the devotion of those offering.

But if a burnt offering was made from birds, it was done thus. When the two persons offered, as has been stated—first the Israelite, then the priest—how the little bird was offered by the person is not stated. Perhaps it was in the same manner as livestock, or perhaps only to the priest. A young turtledove or pigeon was offered; the priest broke its neck by hand alone. Priests were not allowed to raise iron against a bird. With its neck twisted back and its head beneath its wing, he tore with his nail the skin of the neck where it had been broken. Having poured out the blood around the altar’s rim, he threw the crop and feathers eastward in the secluded place where the ashes were poured out. Then, after breaking the wings by hand, [Col. 1196B] he burned it on the altar as a burnt offering.

These were the smaller and simpler burnt offerings, made voluntarily. There were certain greater ones, required by a certain necessity, and in a certain way holier because the entire animal was burned, including its skin and dung. These will be discussed later. Yet in a certain way they were less worthy, because they were not burned upon the altar. Let us now proceed to the voluntary partial sacrifices.

## CHAPTER IV. On peace offerings and salutary offerings

[Col. 1196C]

Some of these were peace offerings and some salutary offerings: that is, offerings made for health to be granted, received, or preserved; likewise for peace, whether toward God or toward human beings, or because they were performed for the good of peace, when each received what was his own—God, the priest, and the offerer.

When made from animals, they were from cattle only, and from the aforementioned flock animals, but not from birds. In the manner in which the person or priest offered them, the same procedure was followed as with a burnt offering. But there was this difference: here a male or female could be offered, one year old or older, though still without blemish. Part of the victim was offered to the Lord, part belonged to the priests, and the rest to the offerers.

From cattle, the following were offered to the Lord. All *adeps*, that is, the fat of the internal organs, was offered. The fat above an animal’s flesh is called *arvina* or lard; that mixed with flesh is properly *pinguedo*, while that of the intestines is *adeps*. There are three kinds of *adeps*: the fat of the vital organs, that is, the heart and belly; the fat of the liver—that is, of the *hepar*—which we call the *reticulum*, because it is wrapped like a net; and the fat of the kidneys. The priest burned these three fats and the two kidneys—that is, the loins and little kidneys—upon the altar. The same things were offered to the Lord from a goat.

If the offering was from sheep, in addition to the things already named, its entire tail was offered; the Septuagint calls this the loin. The skin belonged to the priest who offered it. The right shoulder, called the “portion of separation,” and the breast, called the “portion of elevation”—why they were so called will be explained below—fell to the use of the priests; likewise, according to tradition, the tongue with the throat, though I do not recall reading this in the text. Perhaps these adhered to the breast and were removed from the animal with it.

[Col. 1197B] It was therefore enough to name the breast. The priests ate these portions in their houses with their wives, children, and entire household, provided only that they were clean [Note: [Col. 1197B] Addition 1. They became unclean in various ways: by touching the dead and in many other ways, which will be explained [Col. 1197C] below.]. Even from animals slaughtered at home for a feast or on religious grounds, they gave the breast and shoulder. The remainder belonged to the offerers, who feasted from it before the Lord in places assigned for this, in the court itself or nearby.

Both priests and others were permitted to eat these portions for two days. If anything remained on the third day, it was burned. Note that no animal was offered either as a burnt offering or as a sacrifice without its accompanying libations; but the libations will be discussed more properly below.

## CHAPTER V. On the offering of inanimate things

[Col. 1197C]

If a person’s means could not procure an animal, he offered for health or peace fine flour—that is, the very finest flour—pouring oil over it. It was called fine flour with oil, or flour moistened with oil; incense was offered with it. The priest burned upon the altar all the incense and a full handful of the oiled fine flour as a memorial—that is, in remembrance of the offerer, so that the Lord might remember him, or that the priest might remember him before the Lord. The remainder belonged to the priests (Lev. 2).

The Hebrews relate that a full handful was not always offered; according to the amount of flour, less might be offered, so that even when his handful was full, [Col. 1197D] the priest could open all his fingers except the middle one, and that tiny amount which remained between that finger and the palm was sufficient [Note: [Col. 1198A] Addition 1. When the flour was made into bread, some say that there were four kinds of bread: baked in an oven, on a griddle, cooked in water—which they call unleavened *lagana* [Col. 1198B]. Some, however, understand this as a form of bread; on that interpretation, the third kind was baked in a frying-pan.]. Josephus, however, says that one drachma was to be offered.

If he offered a sacrifice of cooked fine flour, he offered unleavened loaves mixed with oil, baked in an oven or on a griddle, and unleavened *lagana*, that is, broad, thin loaves, not mixed with oil but spread with it. Some, however, understand *lagana* as bread cooked in water, making it a third kind of bread, distinct from that baked in an oven and on a griddle. If he offered it cooked in a frying-pan, it was mixed with oil and unleavened, and was divided into small pieces.

From these offerings the priest burned the memorial before the Lord: one loaf from the loaves, and one piece from the fragments. The remainder belonged to Aaron and his sons, to be eaten with all their household, and was divided among them in equal shares. In Hebrew, besides the oven, three terms occur: *Marchesilis*, *Mahebach*, and *Michar*. *Marchesilis* means “reconciling woman,” which suits a frying-pan because of the crackling and whispering of frying. *Michar* means “net” or “sieve”; *Mahebach*, perhaps “bubbling,” may be a pan in which liquid cooking is done [Note: [Col. 1198B] Addition 2. He means that *Mahebach* can be understood as the third species of sacrifice.].

It can also be a third kind of sacrifice: namely, a salutary or peace offering for thanksgiving or victory, that is, for some unexpected favourable event. It may be said to occur by occasion, making it one kind of sacrifice performed by occasion.

## CHAPTER VI. On sin offerings

[Col. 1198B]

After the salutary offerings, the Lord gave commands concerning sacrifices for sin and for trespass [Note: [Col. 1198B] Addition 1. Nevertheless, all these sacrifices are often indiscriminately called [Col. 1198C] peace offerings.] (Lev. 4). *Peccatum* (“sin”) is called the more serious offence, namely one committed deliberately. *Delictum* (“trespass”) is lighter, namely one committed in ignorance. Or sin is committed when one does what ought not to be done; trespass, as though “a leaving undone,” is committed when one does not do what ought to be done [Note: [Col. 1198C] Addition 2. A *delictum* is also specifically a sin against God, that is, against what has been consecrated to God. For this is “to leave,” that is, to leave God; or a *delictum* is an acknowledged sin.]. There was a diversity of sacrifices according to the persons sinning.

## CHAPTER VII. For the sin of a priest

[Col. 1198C]

Here four classes of persons are distinguished: the priest, the Synagogue—that is, the people—the ruler, and an individual person. “If therefore the priest who was anointed should sin, causing the people to trespass” (Lev. 4), he did as follows. The words “who was anointed” are added not because all priests were anointed, but to distinguish those who, though of priestly descent, could neither be anointed nor minister because of bodily blemish.

The added words “causing the people [Col. 1198D] to sin” may be general, because any sin of any priest is drawn into imitation; this is said to intensify the sin. Or it is said specially when, by word or in some manner, he has provoked the people to sin. Or indeed, as the Hebrew has it: “If the priest who is anointed sins to the guilt of the people”—that is, so basely and openly, as though he were one of the people, which is very unbecoming—then he offered for his sin, by laying on of hands at the entrance of the tabernacle, an unblemished calf [Note: [Col. 1199A] Addition 1. Because a calf was the particular victim of priests.].

He slaughtered it before the altar; taking some of its blood, he brought it into the tabernacle and, dipping his finger in it, sprinkled it seven times toward the veil of the sanctuary. [Col. 1199A] From the same blood he put some upon the horns of the altar of incense. Going out, he poured the remainder of the blood around the rim of the altar of burnt offering. He burned all the fat, together with the kidneys and little kidneys, upon the altar, as also with the calf of the peace-offering sacrifice. But the skin and all the flesh, with even the dung, he carried outside the camp to a clean place where ashes were customarily poured out, and burned them there upon a pile of wood.

## CHAPTER VIII. For the sin of the Synagogue

“If the whole assembly through ignorance has done what is against the Lord’s commandment, the elders of the people offered at the entrance of the tabernacle, through the laying on of hands, a calf” (Lev. 4). The procedure for [Col. 1199B] this calf was the same as for the earlier one offered for the priest’s sin. When the priest prayed for them, the Lord was favourable to them.

Only two differences between the priest’s sin and that of the people are indicated here. First, the priest is not said to sin through ignorance, for he is not permitted to be ignorant of the Lord’s commandments. Second, one does not read that anyone prays for the priest, because “if the enchanter is struck by a serpent, who shall heal him?” (Ecclus. 12).

Here the difference between these burnt offerings and those mentioned earlier is evident: none of these belonged to the priests, but all was burned for the Lord [Note: [Col. 1199C] Addition 1. This had also been noted above at the end of a certain chapter.]. Nor were the limbs of these offerings, together with the head, feet, and washed entrails, placed upon the altar [Note: [Col. 1199C] Addition 2. You have this same rule in the Apostle and in the Epistle to the Hebrews.]. For the general rule was that, from an offering whose blood was brought into the sanctuary, nothing might remain, nor [Col. 1199C] was anything from it burned on the altar except the fat with the kidneys and little kidneys.

There was also a difference in the manner of offering and in the number of priests who made the offering. For the flesh of a salutary burnt offering was divided into nine parts, which nine priests placed upon the altar, each his own portion. One priest offered four things together: the head, feet, liver, and entrails washed in water. Two others offered the blood, so that they were twelve in all.

## CHAPTER IX. On the sin offering of a ruler

[Col. 1199D]

If a ruler—also called a chiliarch or tribune—sins through ignorance and afterwards recognizes his sin, whether by himself or through another, he is to offer at the entrance of the tabernacle, by laying on of hands, an unblemished male goat (Lev. 4). Once it has been slaughtered, the priest dips his finger in its blood and touches with it the horns of the altar of burnt offering, pouring the rest at its base. He burns the fat, kidneys, and little kidneys; the rest belongs to the priests.

But because it was a sin offering, and because the horns of the altar of burnt offering had been touched by its blood, its flesh was holy and sanctified whatever it touched—not indiscriminately, but within its own kind: flesh, flesh; fine flour, fine flour; bread, bread. Only a priest who was anointed and clean could eat it, and only in a holy place [Col. 1200A] and on the very day on which it was offered. If any remained, it was burned with fire [Note: [Col. 1200A] Addition 1. This is not said on account of this sacrifice, since it contained no fine flour or bread; rather, it looks forward to the following matters, namely the sacrifice of the poor.].

If a garment was stained with its blood, it was washed so that no trace of blood remained; otherwise it was burned. An earthen vessel in which the flesh was cooked was immediately broken; a bronze vessel was scoured and washed with water.

## CHAPTER X. On the sin offering of an individual

When an individual from the people of the land sinned through ignorance, he offered an unblemished female goat in the same manner as the others, or a lamb (Lev. 4). The procedure for [Col. 1200B] this offering was the same as for the ruler’s male goat. But if his means could not procure livestock, he offered two young turtledoves or pigeons. One was offered to the Lord as a burnt offering; the other belonged to the priests, although its blood was dripped at the base of the altar of burnt offering because it was for sin.

If he could not procure even small birds, he offered fine flour, one-tenth of an ephah, and put neither oil nor incense upon it, because it was for sin. The priest burned its memorial portion upon the altar; the remainder he retained as his priestly due.

## CHAPTER XI. On the perpetual fire and the removal of ashes
“Again the Lord spoke to Moses: ‘Fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall feed it by placing wood upon it every morning, day by day; and the fire shall be [Col. 1200C] from that same altar’ (Lev. VI),” that is, it was not to be brought and added from elsewhere. When the ashes became excessive, the priest put on the four priestly garments mentioned above; and, taking the ashes from the altar, he placed them in a basin beside the altar. Then, having removed the sacred garments and put on others—perhaps assigned for this purpose, or even his own—the priest carried the ashes outside the camp and caused them to be consumed there into ash in a most clean place.

## CHAPTER XII. On the prohibition of eating fat and blood.

Let what has been said here concerning offerings suffice. In Numbers one reads concerning the offerings of the seven legal festivals, with this addition: that all fat belonged to the Lord (Num. XXIX). “You shall not eat any fat or blood at all” (Lev. III–IV), which is understood of animals offered in sacrifice; nevertheless, because of this, the Jews abstained from every kind of fat. More truly, however, the Lord prohibited them from eating the fat which was to be offered, expressly naming the fat of ox, sheep, and goat.

> [Note: [Col. 1201A] Addition 1. Observe that Augustine states it thus here; nevertheless, the Jews do not eat the fat of a clean animal which may not be offered—for example, that of deer, gazelles, and the like. They do not eat the fat which was customarily offered, but employ it for various uses, as they do the fat of an animal that died of itself.]

But the fat of an animal that had died of itself, or had been killed by a beast, he permitted them for various uses: for lamps or for external anointings. What, then, do they do with the fat of a clean animal which was not offered, which did not die of itself, and which was not taken by a beast, if it belongs to the Lord? Perhaps they throw it away or give it to foreigners to eat. But how can they do either this or that with it, if it belongs to the Lord?

The Lord also prohibited them from all consumption of blood (Lev. III). Josephus says that Moses thought the soul and spirit to be in it. By this prohibition, only the eating of strangled animals is understood to be forbidden.

> [Note: [Col. 1201A] Addition 2. Or by the name “spirit” he means that through which the soul is joined to the body, and through which the flesh also pulsates when the soul is absent. Hence: “Bless the Lord, spirits [Col. 1201B] and souls of the righteous” (Dan. III).]

Yet he prohibited eating blood so strictly that he wished even a bird or wild animal caught by fowling or hunting to be eaten only after its blood had been poured upon the earth and covered. And he added: “For the life of all flesh is in the blood” (Lev. XVII).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the consecration of the high priest and the lesser priests.

[Col. 1201B]

Again the Lord commanded Moses to initiate Aaron and his sons as priests (Lev. VIII). At that time all Aaron’s sons were consecrated, though afterward not all those of his lineage were. For if anyone of Aaron’s seed were blind, lame, had a large, small, or crooked nose, were hunchbacked or ruptured, had a persistent scab or an eruption, he could not minister or enter the sanctuary; nevertheless, they ate the breads offered in the sanctuary (Lev. XXI).

Therefore Moses, according to the Lord’s command, took Aaron and his sons, the sacred garments, the oil of anointing, a calf, two rams, [Col. 1201C] and a basket containing three kinds of unleavened bread: cakes of bread, what is called a *collyrida*, a flat cake (*laganum*), and a crusty loaf (*crustulum*). A *crustulum* is bread hardened almost into a crust. And he assembled the entire multitude at the entrance of the tabernacle. For in the election of a high priest the people’s assent is desired.

Josephus relates that Moses inclined the people’s minds toward Aaron’s priesthood in this manner. He said that he himself had considered himself worthy of the priesthood: both because of the familiarity he had with the Lord, because he had laboured greatly for the people, and because everyone is naturally his own friend. But the Lord had judged Aaron worthier. Therefore, when it pleased the people, he presented Aaron and his sons to the Lord.

After he had washed them with spring water, and Aaron had put on the breeches, Moses clothed him with the seven other garments mentioned above. Pouring the oil of anointing upon his head, he anointed his head and hands, so that the oil dripped down his beard to the hem of his garment. He clothed Aaron’s sons in linen garments, girded them with belts, placed mitres upon them, and sanctified their hands with oil. He likewise anointed the tabernacle with holy oil and all its furnishings. Having sprinkled both altars seven times with water, he anointed them and all their vessels, and sanctified the bronze laver and its base with oil.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the authority granted them to offer, and to receive their portions.

Aaron and his sons offered a calf for [Col. 1202A] their sin, laying their hands upon its head (Lev. VIII). After Moses had sacrificed it, he dipped his finger in the blood, touched with it the horns of the altar all around, and did with it as we said above was to be done with the calf for the priest’s sin. They offered also a ram as a burnt offering, namely, a peace offering; and Moses did with it as the Lord had commanded to be done with peace burnt offerings.

By the laying on of hands they offered a second ram, namely, the sacrifice of their own consecration. After Moses had sacrificed it, he took some of the blood and touched the tip of their right ear, the thumb of their right hand, and likewise that of their right foot. He poured the rest of the blood all around upon the altar. He set apart all the fat, the tail, the kidneys with their surrounding fat, [Col. 1202B] and the right shoulder. Then he took one *collyrida*, one flat cake, and one crusty loaf from the basket and gave them all together to Aaron and his sons, as if to say: Receive authority to take these things from the people, some for offering to the Lord, others for your own use.

While they held them in their hands, Moses placed the breast upon all of them. Hence it was called the “breast of elevation,” because it was placed over everything; yet it was so placed as a sign that wisdom is above all things. It is also read as being so called because of the elevation performed by those who offered it. For in peace offerings and salutary offerings, the offerers first raised the shoulder and breast before the Lord, and then gave them to the priests as their allotted portions [Col. 1202C] respectively.

The right shoulder was called the “shoulder of separation,” because in separating the members of the victim it was first separated from it, and because Moses set it apart as the priests’ portion, as worthier than the other members. Some relate that the formation of an animal’s body in the mother’s womb begins from the right shoulder. Therefore Aaron’s sons, holding all these things in their hands, raised them before the Lord and gave them to Moses, who burned them all for the Lord upon the altar, because it was the offering of consecration.

Taking ointment and blood that was on the altar, mixing in spring water, he sprinkled them and their garments. Once they had been sanctified in this manner, they cooked the remaining flesh of the ram before the entrance of the tabernacle. There they ate it [Col. 1202D] with the breads left in the basket; and whatever remained of these in the basket the fire consumed.

For seven days Moses repeated in the same manner each thing we have described; yet he did not clothe them again, since, once clothed, they did not remove the sacred garments for seven days, nor did they leave the court of the tabernacle. Some nevertheless relate that all things proceeded on the first day as we have said, while during the six ensuing days of consecration the offerings alone were repeated daily, not the anointing. Josephus, however, says that on the following days all things proceeded just as on the first day.

## CHAPTER XV. On the priests’ first offering and the fire given from above.

On the eighth day Moses announced a solemnity to the people, on which the consecrated priests were to begin to offer [Col. 1203A] for themselves and the people (Lev. IX). During the preceding seven days Moses had performed the priest’s office: he had received from Aaron and his sons what they were afterward to receive from the people, and he had ministered at the altar. On the eighth day they themselves undertook the ministry to which they had been appointed, and Moses ceased.

Some relate that the eighth day was the first day of the second year after their departure. When it is objected that the tabernacle is said to have been erected on the first day of the second year, they say that its erection was on that day, but the completion of its consecration followed. Moses commanded that the earthly fire, which had been used upon the altar during those days, be removed, because the Lord would appear to them that day.

When the children of Israel had assembled, Aaron first offered for his own sin a calf, [Col. 1203B] whose fat, kidneys, and surrounding fat he placed upon the altar without fire being put beneath; the rest he burned outside the camp. He also sacrificed for himself a peace offering, a ram as a burnt offering, and placed it upon the altar, but without fire.

Then, intending to offer for the people, he took from them five victims: a calf for the people’s sin, a goat for the ruler’s sin, a lamb for an individual’s sin, an ox for a burnt offering, and a ram for peace offerings. Yet in the account of slaughter he is said to have slaughtered only three: the goat for the people’s sin, the ox, and the ram for the peace offerings. Perhaps because they had been enumerated earlier, the other matters were passed over for brevity. And because he was not treating separately, as before, of the sin of the Synagogue, the ruler, and the individual, any of the three could be said to have been offered for the people’s sin.

Augustine, however, rejects [Col. 1203C] the text which says that only five were taken, and says that with those five was taken a yearling lamb for *holocarposis*, a word meaning “fruitful whole burnt offering.” That burnt offering was called *holocarposis* which the Lord showed, by some visible sign, to be pleasing to him.

After Aaron had placed upon the altar those portions which were to be burned, he set apart for the Lord his own portion from the peace offerings, the right shoulders and breasts; and, extending his hands, he blessed the people. Moses and Aaron entered the tabernacle and, coming out again, blessed the people. When the offerings were upon the altar, together with the continual morning sacrifice—

> [Note: [Col. 1203D] Addition 1. The continual sacrifice was that offered every day: namely, two lambs, one in the morning and the other in the evening.]

—fire came forth from the Lord and devoured what was upon the altar. This [Col. 1203D] fire was preserved perpetually until the Babylonian deportation, and thereafter it was not permitted to add foreign fire.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the death of Nadab and Abihu.

On the same day Nadab and Abihu, having seized censers, placed foreign fire upon them and offered incense over it (Lev. X). Fire came forth from the Lord—either the fire already upon the altar, or another coming again from above—and devoured them, that is, extinguished them. Moses said to Aaron: “This is what the Lord said: ‘I shall be sanctified in those who draw near to me,’” that is, even in those who minister to me I shall show myself [Col. 1204A] holy, sparing not their sins.

He summoned Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Uzziel, Aaron’s uncle, their kinsmen, and said to them: “Carry your brothers outside the camp.” They carried them out as they were, clothed in linen garments and tiaras, and buried them, just as ministers of the altar are buried clothed in the garments of their ministry.

When Aaron and his two remaining sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, wished to mourn their brothers in the customary fashion, Moses forbade them, saying: “Holy oil is upon you. Do not uncover your heads; do not tear your garments, lest perhaps you die; you shall not go out from the entrance of the tabernacle.”

Josephus, however, tells it differently: while they were carrying over the altar victims which the Lord had not commanded, but which they had used at first, they were suddenly set aflame, and no one could extinguish them. Moses commanded their father and brothers to carry the bodies outside the camp and bury them with fitting honour. Moses also told Aaron and his sons to take their portions of the peace offerings and the sin offering, whose blood had not been brought into the tabernacle, and eat them. When they sought the goat offered for the ruler’s sin, it was found burned up. Moses became angry and rebuked Aaron and his sons for this, but Aaron excused himself, saying: “What you see has happened to me”—as if to say: This was done because of distress of mind.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the distinction of foods.

The Lord commanded Moses and Aaron to deliver to the children of Israel a law concerning the distinction of foods (Lev. [Col. 1204C] XI). In its literal sense, the Lord restricted for them the foods granted to humankind because of their gluttony. Its summary may be given thus. Some animals live on land, others in water, and others in the air. Of those on land, some are creeping things, all of which are unclean; others lurk beneath the ground, such as the mole, which is born from mud, and all these are unclean. Others walk upon the earth; regarding these, the general rule is: clean is only what chews the cud and divides the hoof.

> [Note: [Col. 1204D] Addition 1. He says “chews the cud” because of the pig, which nevertheless divides the hoof; he says “divides” because of the camel, which chews the cud.]

There is likewise a general rule for fish: only that which has scales and fins is clean. He specified by name which birds were unclean. This alone was said generally concerning birds:

> [Note: [Col. 1205A] Addition 2. For example, the griffin, and anything else similar.]

A winged creature that walks on four feet is unclean [Col. 1204D] unless it has longer hind legs upon which it leaps.

> [Note: [Col. 1205A] Addition 3. Such as locusts and the *bruchus*; and the *opimachus* is a bird which fights serpents.]

Whoever touches their carcasses shall wash his garments and be unclean until evening, even if it is necessary for someone to carry one of them dead. Whatever any part of their carcasses falls upon shall be defiled, whether a wooden vessel or any garment; they shall be cleansed with water at evening. An earthen vessel into which it falls shall be broken. Ovens or *citropedes*, which we call *strapas*, shall be destroyed.

> [Note: [Col. 1205A] Addition 4. Understand oven and *citropes* as the same thing: namely, earthen vessels with which bread-baskets are covered at the hearth; among us it is called a clay cover.]

But springs, cisterns, all bodies of water, and seed grain not yet sown are not defiled by their touch.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the purification of a woman after childbirth.

[Col. 1205A]

The Lord also added the following law concerning the purification of women: “If a woman gives birth to a male, she shall be unclean for seven days, according to the days of her menstrual separation” (Lev. XI); that is, she shall be judged subject to the same uncleanness as when she is separated from clean persons while suffering menstruation. For she is so unclean that whatever she touches she makes unclean: food, bed, garment, or seat. Hence no one may share with her either bed or food.

On the eighth day the boy was circumcised. After the seven days of defilement, she remained thirty-three days in the blood of her purification, so that all the days of her purification were forty. For physicians say that a male body is formed in the womb in so many days. During the thirty-three days of purification, she might rise and walk about within the house, but not go out or work. By touching she did not defile; others could share food and a seat with her, but not a bed. Yet she could not approach the tabernacle until the forty days had been completed.

If she gave birth to a female, the earlier days of defilement were doubled—

> [Note: [Col. 1205C] Addition 1. That is, she was unclean for two weeks, [Col. 1205D] according to the rite of menstrual flow.]

—and afterward likewise the days of purification, making eighty days in all, [Col. 1205C] because a female is formed in the womb in so many days. When the days of purification were complete, she offered for a son or daughter a yearling lamb as a burnt offering, and a young pigeon or turtledove for sin—

> [Note: [Col. 1205D] Addition 2. This offering was also called purification.]

—because she had conceived in sexual desire; it belonged to the priest. If her means could not provide a lamb, she offered two turtledoves or two young pigeons: one as a burnt offering for the child, the other for her own sin, or for the daughter’s original sin, because it had been remitted to a son in circumcision.

> [Note: [Col. 1205D] Addition 3. Augustine nevertheless says that they offered for the sin of children, which, although remitted in circumcision, was then remitted more fully.]

The Hebrews, however, maintain that little children have no sin. Besides this, Josephus says that a firstborn was redeemed with five shekels.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the recognition of leprosies.

[Col. 1205D]

The Lord also delivered to them a law concerning leprosy (Lev. XIII). There are four kinds of leprosy: in the skin, in the hair, in a garment, and in a house.

> [Note: [Col. 1206D] Addition 1. From what is said about the varieties of leprosy, it is clear that not everything can be understood literally. Origen: We find five forms of human leprosy set forth. Either a scar and a mark of whiteness occur in the body, and a contagious leprosy arises in the skin of its body; or spreading leprosy spreads and covers all the skin with contagious leprosy from head to foot; or an ulcer occurs in the skin of the flesh and becomes wounded, and at the site of the ulcer there arises a white scar; or there is in the skin of the flesh a burn from fire, bright white or white tinged with red. The fourth form occurs when a man or woman has contagious leprosy on the head or beard. The last is when, on baldness or on the receding forehead, there is a reddish contagious leprosy: this is spreading leprosy in baldness or on the receding forehead. [Col. 1207A]]

Leprosy of the skin is recognized if there is whiteness—that is, a pale white spot—or pustules, or a scar; especially if it is white or reddish-white, if the place of leprosy lies lower than the rest of the flesh, or if the hairs have turned white and become thinner than usual. Leprosy in the hair [Col. 1206A] is called alopecia, when the hair falls out. If a white or reddish colour is found in baldness or a receding forehead, it is a leprous lesion.

When, therefore, a leper was brought to the priest—without whose judgment he was not excluded—if the leprosy was not yet evident, the priest shut him up in his house for seven days. When these were completed, if the leprosy had not increased, he shut him up again for another seven days. If the leprosy still had not increased, he cleansed him, that is, judged him clean, because it was merely a scab; and the man washed his garments and was clean.

But when the leprosy was evident, he was separated at the priest’s judgment. His garments were loose, that is, easy to put on or take off—

> [Note: [Col. 1207A] Addition 2. There was a garment which had an opening from the neck down to the navel and was fastened with little buttons.]

—or he wore only his outer garment, so that he might be recognized; his head was uncovered, that he might be recognized; and his mouth was covered with a garment [Col. 1206B] lest he spread the stench while speaking. He lived alone outside the camp, so that he seemed in no way different from a dead man.

As Josephus says, this shows the absurdity of those who alleged that Moses suffered from leprosy and, having become leader of persons cast out for the same reason, came with them into Canaan—when he was so regarded as almost merciless toward lepers, precisely those most in need of mercy.

Leprosy of a linen or woollen garment, or of leather, was a whitish or reddish spot lying lower than the rest of the surface, because it is corrosive. When it appeared, the priest examined it. If the leprosy was evident, the garment was burned; if doubtful, it was shut away for seven days. If the spot increased, it was judged leprosy. If it had not increased, the garment was washed and shut away for another seven days. If [Col. 1206C] it was still doubtful, he tore that part away from the sound fabric. If, however, a spot appeared again elsewhere, it was a spreading leprosy and the garment was burned.

If a similar corrosive spot appeared in a house, the priest first commanded everything to be taken out of the house. Examining depressions in the wall disfigured by paleness or redness and lying lower than the rest of the surface, he shut the door of the house for seven days. After these, if he found that the leprosy had increased, he ordered the leprous stones to be removed and thrown outside the city; the house to be scraped all around inside; the dust from the scraping to be scattered outside the camp or city in an unclean place; other stones to be put in the house; and the house to be plastered with different mortar. If the spot returned again, it was a persistent leprosy, and [Col. 1206D] the house was to be destroyed, with its timbers and stones, and its dust thrown outside the town into an unclean place.

## CHAPTER XX. On the purification of a leper.

[Col. 1207A]

If a leper was cleansed, he was restored to common habitation in this manner. He came as far as the common entrance of the camp or town, bringing with him two live sparrows—

> [Note: [Col. 1208A] Addition 1. Perhaps they were two species of sparrow, one of which was permitted as food under the Law, while the other was forbidden. The Master and Hugh say that no distinction is made between them. Origen says: Two live hens were taken for the person being cleansed, together with cedar wood, scarlet dye—that is, a red thread with which he bound the living sparrow—and hyssop upon the cedar wood.]

—which were permitted as food, cedar wood, hyssop, scarlet worm, that is, a scarlet thread, and living water in an earthen vessel (Lev. XIV). Meeting him, the priest killed one sparrow and allowed its blood to drip over the water. Binding the other, the living one, with the [Col. 1207B] scarlet thread, together with the hyssop, to the top of the cedar wood, as though making an aspergillum, he dipped it in the reddened water, sprinkled the man seven times, and released the living sparrow to fly away into the field.

After the man had washed his garments, he shaved all the hair of his body and, having washed with water, entered the camp; but he remained outside his own tent for seven days. On the seventh day he again shaved all the hair of his body, including his eyebrows. After washing his garments and body, on the eighth day he took two unblemished lambs, a year-old ewe, three tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, and a sextary of oil, and offered all these at the entrance of the tabernacle.

Then the priest sacrificed one lamb as a guilt offering; taking some of its blood, he placed it upon the tip of the [Col. 1207C] man’s right ear, upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon that of his right foot. Taking the sextary of oil, he poured some into his left hand and, dipping his right thumb in it, sprinkled seven times toward the tabernacle. The rest of the oil in his left hand he poured upon the tip of the man’s right ear, upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon his right foot—that is, upon the blood which he had first applied—and upon his head.

The priest prayed for him, making a special prayer instituted for that purpose. Then he offered the sin sacrifice, and afterward sacrificed the burnt offering with its libations, placing it upon the altar. Observe that here the guilt offering, with whose blood the man was anointed, is properly distinguished from the sin offering—

> [Note: [Col. 1208A] Addition 2. “For sin” stands, as it were, in place of an accusative expression. Hence: “And you did not require a sacrifice for sin” (Heb. X).]

—[Col. 1207D] concerning which nothing was done to him. Thus Moses here says, as though distinguishing them, that the victim for guilt belonged to the priest in the same way as the victim for sin. For after he had distinguished the lamb for guilt, and had not specified which of the remaining animals was for sin and which was to be made a burnt offering, he indicated that it lay within the priest’s discretion to make one a sin offering and the other a burnt offering, as he wished.

> [Note: [Col. 1208A] Addition 3. Observe that Moses truly distinguishes between a guilt offering and a sin offering, but by no means distinguishes between guilt (*delictum*) and sin (*peccatum*). The saints, however, distinguish them in three ways: guilt is what is done deliberately, sin what is done through ignorance; or guilt is what is done against God, sin what is done against one’s neighbour; or guilt lies in omitting what ought to be done, sin in committing what ought not to be done. [Col. 1208B]]

If his means could not provide these things, the lamb for guilt and the sextary of oil were nevertheless not reduced, since by them the man was purified as before. But instead of the ewe and the remaining lamb he offered a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, one of which was made a sin offering and the other a burnt offering. He also offered a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the man with a seminal discharge and the woman with a bloody flux.

[Col. 1208B]

Next the Lord added provisions concerning a man suffering a discharge of semen (Lev. XV). A man is judged subject to this disorder when a foul seminal fluid adheres to and coagulates upon the flesh intermittently, which he discharges involuntarily because of corruption. Such a man, being unclean, rendered unclean whatever he touched: his bed, his garment, his seat, even the pack-saddle upon which he sat—

> [Note: [Col. 1208D] Addition 1. A *sagma* is an ass’s pack-saddle, that is, its saddle.]

—that is, the ass’s covering. An earthen vessel that was touched was broken; [Col. 1208C] a wooden vessel was washed. Whoever touched his bed, garment, or seat, or upon whom he cast saliva, washed his garments and was unclean until evening.

When he had been healed, he counted seven days after his cleansing; and, having washed his garments and body in living water, he was clean. On the eighth day he offered a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, and the priest made one a sin offering and the other a burnt offering. The same law of uncleanness and purification applied to a woman suffering a flow of blood from illness.

> [Note: [Col. 1208D] Addition 2. The Hebrews relate that if anyone sleeps with a woman on the first day of her menses, and a child is conceived thereby and lives, it will become leprous within ten years; if on the second day of menstruation, then [Col. 1209A] within twenty years, and so on through the seventh day.]

A menstruating woman was similarly subject to the same uncleanness, but she was not formally purified; it was enough for her to wash herself with her garments. For uncleanness through illness is also wont to arise because of sin, and [Col. 1208D] therefore a peace offering for sin was offered for such cases; this was not done for menstruation, because it is natural.

> [Note: [Col. 1209A] Addition 3. Hence the woman with a bloody flux was told by the Lord, after she had been healed: “Go, and sin no more” (John VIII). This makes clear that her illness had befallen her because of her sin.]

Observe that the one who approaches a menstruating woman is here said to be unclean for seven days, and purification is granted him; this must be understood of one approaching unknowingly. Below, it says that both are to be put to death if this is done deliberately. Nor is this surprising, since the Lord even required a man lawfully knowing his wife to wash his garment and his whole body, and to be unclean until evening; the same applies to the wife.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the red heifer, the scapegoat, and the ashes for sprinkling.

[Col. 1209A]

“Again the Lord spoke to Moses—

> [Note: [Col. 1211A] Addition 1. Since Aaron’s two sons, Nadab and Abihu, had died when they brought foreign fire to the altar of God, heavenly teaching had to be imparted to Aaron concerning how he ought to approach the altar, by what rite of supplication he should render God favourable, and how he should beware of what had befallen his sons. Therefore the following law is prefaced here concerning these matters: “Again God spoke,” etc.]

—Speak to Aaron, lest he enter the sanctuary, which is within the veil, at every time, lest he die; for I shall appear in a cloud over the oracle, unless he does these things” which follow (Lev. XVI).

It must not be understood that whenever he wished to enter, he performed these things and entered; rather, when he was to enter only on the tenth day of September, he first performed them. This day was solemn in Israel and was called the Day of Propitiation for the reason stated above; or because on that day the ash of expiation was prepared, just as Thursday is called holy because holy chrism is made on it. An offering was made that day for the common or unknown sins of the entire year.

It was also called the Day of Affliction, because on that day people and beasts fasted, as did even children of seven years, and the commemoration of the dead was observed. It was also called the Day of Expiation, because on that day the whole tabernacle and the altars were purified by the sprinkling of blood from the defilements contracted throughout the year through the sins of the ministers.

That day the high priest took from his own property a red heifer, three years old, unblemished, which had not drawn a yoke. Let us not be disturbed if it is sometimes called a calf, for it must be understood only in the feminine gender, because it was offered for sins of frailty. From the entire multitude he took two goats for sin and a ram for a burnt offering. After washing himself, he put on linen garments only, according to the rite of the lesser priests. When the animals had been offered and an offering or special prayer made for himself and his household, he set the two goats at the entrance of the tabernacle and cast lots over both, that it might be known which was the Lord’s and which became the people’s.

One should not believe certain persons who said that lots were cast in order to discover which goat was to be sacrificed to the Lord and which sent to the devil into the wilderness with the sins. For the Law permits sacrifice to none but God. Certainly, the goat whose lot came out “for the Lord” he offered for the people’s sin; perhaps this was properly called “for sin.” The goat whose lot came out “for the people” he kept alive. He sacrificed the red heifer for his own sin and that of his household; and, taking some blood of the goat and heifer, a censer full of coals, and much incense, he entered beyond the veil. He put on only so much incense that mist and vapour covered the oracle, lest he die on seeing the Lord’s majesty.

He sprinkled with his finger seven times from the blood before the mercy-seat, toward the east, and sprinkled the pavement the same number of times. By a similar sevenfold sprinkling he expiated the outer sanctuary and the pavement. He poured some of the same blood upon the horns of the golden altar and sprinkled it seven times with his finger, [Col. 1210A] thus expiating the whole tabernacle and altar from the uncleannesses of the children of Israel and from all their transgressions—that is, from the defilement contracted by the tabernacle, situated among sinners.

No one was with him in the tabernacle when he expiated it. In this manner we too wash altars with wine once a year. Observe that here the priest is read to go out from the oracle to the altar; hence it is clear that the altar was outside. Nor can it be said that he went out to the altar before the tabernacle, when the altar here is called the altar “before the Lord.”

After this expiation the priest went out to the living goat. Placing both hands upon its head, he confessed in general all the iniquities of the children of Israel and imprecated them upon its head. Some relate that he also put upon its head a paper inscribed with the people’s sins, [Col. 1210B] and sent it into the wilderness by a man appointed for this purpose. The Hebrews relate that certain children were prepared for this by tribe—that is, from a tribe assigned for this purpose—and had their spleens medically removed, so that the people might thus be expiated from the sins of that year, contracted through ignorance or frailty, which the goat bore away with it. Because it was sent out not to return, it was called in Greek *apompeius*, in Latin *emissarius*, “the sent-away one.”

When Aaron had led the man with the goat outside the camp, he returned to the tabernacle of testimony. Having removed the linen garments in which he had expiated the sanctuary and sent away the goat, he washed his body in a holy place and put on his own garments—namely, the precious pontifical garments. Then [Col. 1210C] he offered the ram as a burnt offering, and the fat of the heifer and goat for sin, with the kidneys and surrounding fat.

In the same manner, the evangelical high priest, in the sprinkling at the dedication of a basilica, as though in an expiation, uses linen and lesser vestments. He also uses similar vestments on Baptismal Saturday, in the consecration of fonts and in the immersion of catechumens, when their sins are transferred. But when, these matters having been completed, he approaches the administration of the altar, he is adorned with pontifical and precious garments.

The calf and goat whose blood had been used for expiation were carried outside the camp and burned with fire, their skins, flesh, and dung alike. The priest cast them [Col. 1210D] into the fire that consumed them. Having changed his former garments and put on his own, he cast cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet twice-dyed into it, because these were efficacious in purifications; then, returning after washing his garments and body, he entered the camp and was unclean until evening.

The priest who remained by the fire to have everything burned to ashes likewise entered the camp only after washing his garments and body, and was unclean until evening. Likewise the third priest, who collected the ashes and kept them for the water of sprinkling, entered the camp only after washing and was unclean until evening. From these ashes was made the water of sprinkling, by which the unclean were purified throughout the year.

Hence it is difficult to find a reason why those who handled this ash were unclean, as stated, when the ash was made to purify the unclean and when the Lord calls this sacrament, as it were most holy, “the rite of the victim.”

> [Note: [Col. 1211B] Addition 2. Since even the Jews openly confess that they do not know how to answer this question at all, nor does Gamaliel teach them anything here.]

The one who released, or rather led, the goat into the wilderness was also unclean. Yet the reason for him is easily found. It is probable that these ashes were made yearly, as chrism is now made. Some Hebrews, however, say that they remained effective and lasted for several years, and were made only when the prior supply failed.

> [Note: [Col. 1211] This chapter seems to belong to the historical narrative of the book of Numbers.]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the purification of the unclean.

[Col. 1211B]

These ashes purified the unclean in the following manner. If anyone touched the corpse of a dead person in a tent, or in a field, whether one slain or one who had died naturally, or touched that person’s grave, he was unclean for seven days (Num. XIX). The tent in which a person had died, and all the vessels in it, were unclean for seven days. [Col. 1211C] A clean man took ashes from the burning; pouring living water over them, he dipped hyssop in it and, on the third and seventh days, sprinkled the tent, all its furnishings, and persons defiled by such contagion. Once their clothes and bodies had been washed, they were clean. If the unclean person had not been sprinkled on the third day, he was not cleansed on the seventh. But anyone not thus expiated perished from the midst of the congregation, because he defiled the sanctuary—that is, his soul perished from Israel because he sinned and was barred from entering the holy place. Yet the person who cleansed the unclean by this water, because he had touched the ashes, washed his clothes and was unclean until evening. We do not believe that a person was expiated by these ashes for the uncleannesses by which he was unclean for only one day—for example, because of a nocturnal emission or because he had slept with his wife—but at least for the uncleanness lasting seven days, since such expiation is said to be performed on the third and seventh days. Concerning the expiations made with offerings, as was said above concerning the leper, the man with a seminal discharge, and the menstruating woman: because they are said to count seven days and be purified on the eighth, we believe that they were expiated with these waters on the third and seventh days.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On persons excluded from marriage

The Lord also delivered to the children of Israel a multitude of commandments, recapitulating those previously given and adding new ones. Of these we have touched only upon those [Col. 1212A] necessary for understanding the reading of Sacred Scripture. The Lord indeed forbade a man to approach one of his own flesh, or to uncover her nakedness—that is, to uncover and enter her private parts. In the marriage of the first parents, because of the scarcity of humankind, the Lord excluded only two persons from marriage, saying: “Therefore a man shall leave father and mother” (Gen. II); that is, neither may a son be joined to his mother nor a daughter to her father. Under the Law, however, he excepted more persons—about twelve (Lev. XVIII): mother, stepmother, sister, granddaughter, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, uncle’s wife, daughter-in-law, and brother’s wife.

[Note: [Col. 1212B] Addition 1. For if a man having a wife died without having children by her, his brother married her and thereby raised up offspring for his deceased brother.]

This list also includes a stepdaughter, the daughter of a stepson or stepdaughter, and the wife’s sister. He excluded few persons then, so that people might multiply [Col. 1212B] and fill the earth. Under grace very many are excluded, where continence has a place; and this is the prohibition of marriage. For every woman is excluded from fornication.

## CHAPTER XXV. A catalogue of certain commandments (Lev. XVIII–XXIII)

He also prohibited intercourse with a male or with an animal, under threat of death; he commanded that they should not gather the ears of grain or clusters left behind, nor fallen grapes, but should leave them for the poor of the land; [Col. 1212C] that they should not withhold a hired laborer’s wages until morning; that they should not show partiality; and that they should love a friend as themselves—where the Septuagint has “neighbor.” He prohibited the observance of dreams, omens, and divinations; sowing a field with mixed seed; breeding together animals of different kinds; and wearing a garment woven of two materials. He prohibited cutting the hair in a rounded shape, shaving the beard, cutting one’s flesh for the dead, and making figures or marks upon one’s flesh. With these and similar commands, it must be understood literally: “according to the rite of the nations,” especially of the Egyptians among whom they had lived.

[Note: [Col. 1213A] Addition 1. They even caused different animals to mate, so that an animal might be born from them especially suited to sacrifice to the gods or dedicated in their honor; thus the mule, from horse and ass, was fitting for Mars and Silenus.]

For David is also recorded as having possessed a mule; Solomon was set upon it and brought to the spring of Gihon to be anointed (III Kings I). But Egypt, venerating monsters of every kind as gods, [Col. 1212D] associated different seeds in one field and different materials in one garment in honor of different gods, whom it believed to preside over such things; it also sacrificed different locks of hair to different gods. Hence, at the beginning of these commandments, the Lord said: “You shall not act according to the custom of the land of Egypt in which you lived; nor shall you act according to the practice of the land into which I shall bring you.”

He also added a special command for their entry into the promised land: that they should remove the “foreskins” of the trees they planted. Explaining this, as it were, he adds: “The fruits that they produce shall be unclean to you”; yet this is not in the Hebrew. He seems to mean that the fruit of the first three years [Col. 1213A] was unclean and to be cast away; the fruit of the fourth year was holy to the Lord and shared with the poor; but in the fifth year and thereafter it belonged to its owners and was edible.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On three kinds of bread

For clarity concerning what is handed down here in Leviticus (Lev. XXIV), it should be known that the priests had three kinds of bread: priestly, Levitical, and lay bread. Priestly bread was the bread of the Presence, made at public expense, which [Col. 1213B] only priests were permitted to eat. Levitical bread, also called offertory bread, was eaten only by those of Levitical stock, including those unable to minister because of a blemish, and a daughter of the household—but not if she was married, widowed, or divorced, unless necessity caused her to return to her father’s house, so that she might be as a daughter of the household. A stranger did not eat of this bread.

[Note: [Col. 1213B] Addition 1. “Stranger” is a general term, including the foreigner, who merely passes through, and the resident alien, who, although from the same region, rents a dwelling.]

Nor did the priest’s resident alien or hired servant eat it; but his home-born slave or purchased slave could eat it. Lay bread—that is, common bread—could be eaten by anyone.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the holiness of priests

[Col. 1213C]

In treating the holiness of priests, the Lord first deals with the lesser priests (Lev. XXI). They were not to be defiled by the deaths of their fellow citizens, nor even by that of the ruler of the people, except only in the case of mother, father, son, daughter, brother, and virgin sister: that is, they were not to wash, bury, or touch other dead persons in mourning. Nor did he merely forbid them wives forbidden to others; he also forbade them to have concubines or to take as wives a prostitute, a slave woman, a captive woman, a widow, a divorced woman, or women who make their living from tavern-keepers and innkeepers—that is, from shops where goods are sold.

But he willed that the high priest should enter to no dead person whatsoever.

[Col. 1213D] Hence it is said that the lord pope attends no funerals. Nor was he to take a wife except a virgin, and only one from his own people. Nor does the parish of the lord pope extend beyond the city walls. In general, however, he commanded that a priest, on the days of his turn when he ought to minister, should not drink wine or anything capable of intoxicating, so that he might know how to distinguish holy from profane, clean from unclean, and teach the children of Israel the ordinances of the land which the Lord had spoken (Lev. X); and so that a priest, when he happened to be unclean, should not approach even to touch the things offered by the children of Israel.

[Note: [Col. 1214B] Addition 1. The Jews had seven feasts: the Sabbath, the New Moon, Pentecost, Passover, the Feast of Trumpets, the Feast of Atonement, and Tabernacles.]

(Lev. XXII–XXIII). It is also plain that, if an evangelical priest ministers daily, he ought to maintain continual purity. The Lord also added regulations concerning the legal solemnities. But since these are set forth more fully in the book of [Col. 1214A] Numbers, we shall deal with them there. On the first day of September was the Feast of Trumpets, or the trumpet-blasts for Isaac’s deliverance, called the feast of candles; on the tenth day of the same month, the Feast of Atonement, because, when they had made the calf, God was appeased by Moses’ prayer; on the fifteenth day, the Feast of Tabernacles, which means the pitching of tents, the feast of the Father (Num. XXVIII–XXIX). For since power is ascribed to the Father, God’s power was great in that their garments did not wear out for forty years. They now also have other feasts: Purim, that is, “of lots,” because the lot fell out contrariwise, as is read in Esther (Esther IX), because they killed those who were going to kill them; and three Encaenia, that is, dedications: one in autumn, performed by Solomon (III Kings VIII); one in spring, performed by Zerubbabel [Col. 1214B] and the others returning from Babylon (I Esdras III); and one in winter, performed by the Maccabees (II Macc. VIII). Of this the Gospel says: “The feast of the Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter” (John X).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the punishment of the blasphemer

“Behold, the son of an Israelite woman, whom she had borne by an Egyptian man, went out; and, quarrelling with an Israelite man, he blasphemed the name of the God of Israel, cursing him” (Lev. XXIV). Moses confined him in prison until he had consulted the Lord concerning this matter. The Lord [Col. 1214C] said to Moses: “Whoever curses his God, all who heard him shall lay their hands upon his head,” as if testifying against him; “and, when he has been led outside the camp, the whole multitude shall stone him,” whether citizen or stranger.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the law of retaliation

The Lord further laid down the law of retaliation (Lev. XXIV): whoever injured a person was to be injured in the same manner in which he had injured him—namely, he was to render life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, fracture for fracture, bruise for bruise, burn for burn. Note that retaliation did not apply to injuries to property, but only to bodily injuries, because thefts were repaid double or fourfold. Retaliation was also limited by necessity: [Col. 1214D] if a woman injured a man in his male sexual organs, she was punished in the hand, because she did not have male sexual organs; and a man who injured a pregnant woman so as to cause the abortion of a fetus not yet ensouled was fined money. It is uncertain, however, whether retaliation extended as far as judicial action, or had force only between the injured person and the offender. That an injured person might avenge himself without a judge may perhaps be inferred from the fact that an involuntary manslayer fled to cities of refuge, lest he be killed by the relatives of the slain person.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the observance of the jubilee year

The Lord also added regulations concerning observance of the jubilee, which followed a week of weeks of years (Lev. XXV). As a prefiguration of it, some report, they sounded trumpets at each [Col. 1215A] new moon during the preceding seven years, and solemnized the seven continuous days before it with trumpet-blasts. Yet the book of Numbers says that trumpets were sounded throughout the land on the tenth day of the seventh month (Num. X–XXIX). In this jubilee year, all alienations of property returned to their original owners, except houses in walled cities; these, however, the seller was permitted to redeem during the first year after the sale. The houses of Levites were excepted, since wherever they might be situated they returned in the jubilee. In that same year the land rested, debts were remitted, and slaves were set free. For although they were fellow-tribesmen, the Lord nevertheless wished to punish them through the division of servitude because of transgressions of the laws.

Josephus says that at the jubilee the seller of a field and [Col. 1215B] its purchaser met; and, reckoning the produce and the expenditures made on the field, if they found that the produce exceeded the expenditures, the seller received back the field; but if the expenditures exceeded the produce, the purchaser received what was lacking and departed from the possession. This reckoning could, however, be made before the jubilee year—not only in the jubilee itself—if the seller wished earlier to recover what he had sold. The text of Leviticus seems to mean that the field was to be sold at a higher or lower price according to the number of years remaining until the jubilee: so that the seller would not be burdened by selling cheaply when many years remained before he recovered what he had sold, nor the purchaser burdened by buying dearly what he was soon to lose. Having fixed this calculation of produce and expenditures within the jubilee period, it adds that, if the seller could not repay what remained [Col. 1215C] of the expenditure, the purchaser should hold the field until the jubilee. For in the jubilee itself [Col. 1216A] every seller returned to the original owner. The Lord willed that land should be sold by them subject to the condition of recovery, because it was his and not theirs. Foreigners, however, he willed that they should possess as slaves forever.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On blessings and curses

To observers of such commandments the Lord prefaced his blessings, saying: “I shall give you rains in their seasons,” etc. (Lev. XXVI), where the clauses of the promises are found. But for transgressors he repeatedly heaps up many lengthy curses.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On tithes and votive offerings

In the tithing of animals, whichever animal came tenth, whether by birth or by counting, was consecrated to the Lord, [Col. 1216B] and it was not lawful to exchange it for something better or worse (Lev. XXVII). Likewise, an animal vowed by its owner was not permitted to be exchanged; if anyone exchanged what he had vowed, both the vowed animal and the replacement belonged to the Lord. But a distinction must be made concerning vows of this kind. Sometimes something was so consecrated to the Lord by a vow that it was devoted under the ban; this could not be sold or alienated by the priests. At other times votive things were not so bound, but could be sold by the priest at a fixed price according to the benefit which might arise from them, whether it was a person or an estate. Yet if the person who had given it by vow wished to buy it for more than the valuation at which it would be given to another, he was to add a fifth part. This was established so that one who had vowed might not aspire, as though led by repentance, [Col. 1216C] nor consider himself worthier than others in purchasing that thing because he had given it.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF NUMBERS

[Col. 1215]

## CHAPTER I. Preface

[Col. 1215C]

The fourth division of this history is called in Hebrew *Vajedabber*, which means “and he spoke.” Among us, however, this name is not used. We do not have its Greek name in our writings; for in Greek it is *baresmoth*, otherwise *ellesmoth*. In Latin it is called the Book of Number, or Numbers. It is sometimes called *Numeri* in the plural; hence people commonly say, “This is read in Numbers.” It is properly designated by this title because four things are chiefly numbered here: the whole people, the men fit to bear arms, the Levitical firstborn—who are also numbered twice—and the encampments through which they travelled. Neither women, persons under twenty years old, nor the mixed multitude, nor those disabled for war, are numbered.

[Note: [Col. 1217A] Addition 1. The “mixed multitude” means certain Egyptians who had followed them when they departed.]

Josephus thus passes to this part of the history. While they remained by Sinai, Moses learned from God the aforementioned constitution of laws and delivered it to the Hebrews in writing. Thinking these matters sufficient concerning legislation, he turned to the rules of military service and counted the heads of the peoples, namely those able to fight. Moses says that the Lord spoke concerning this, saying: “The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the tent of the covenant, on the first day of the second month, in the second year after the departure from Egypt” (Num. I). Note that he omits here certain things that were done in the first month of the second year: namely, the offering of the twelve [Col. 1216D] princes, which each made on successive days at the dedication of the tabernacle; the Passover solemnity, properly called Passover in the wilderness; and perhaps the consecration of the Levites.

[Note: [Col. 1217B] Addition 2. Note that they celebrated the first Passover in Egypt; the second in the wilderness, of which he speaks here; the third at their arrival and entry into the promised land at Gilgal; and the fourth in the promised land.]

He will, however, deal with these below by way of recapitulation. Following the order of the book, then, we say that Moses, Aaron, and the twelve tribal leaders, by the Lord’s command, in the second year, second month, and on the first day of the month, numbered the men, excluding the tribe of Levi, from twenty years old and upward. Josephus set a definite limit, namely up to the fiftieth year. They were numbered by generations, families, houses, names, and individual heads. Some say that these five terms were added only for emphasis, both here and in Joshua; yet “generations” or kindreds may properly be distinguished [Col. 1217A]. Here he calls the twelve tribes themselves families, descended originally from the sons of the patriarchs. For example, within the one tribe of Levi there were three families: the Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites. Each family had many houses, in which there were their own household heads. The added words “names and heads” should be read intransitively, that is, “the names of the heads”: namely, the individual persons in the same house. The total number, from twenty years old and upward, able to go out to war, was six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty men. The tribe of Levi was not counted with these children of Israel.

## CHAPTER II. On the watches around the tabernacle

[Col. 1217B]

The Lord also commanded that the tabernacle should always be set in the middle of the camp, and that the children of Israel should keep watch around it in companies and wedges (Num. II), terms here taken in the same sense.

[Note: [Col. 1217D] Addition 1. A multitude is called a *cuneus* (“wedge”), as though *coneus*, from “coming together” and “uniting.”]

A company properly consists of thirty thousand. A *cuneus* is so called as a gathered multitude. “Keeping watch” is used broadly here; properly, watches are night vigils. Three tribes kept watch on each of the four sides of the tabernacle, yet at such a distance that they had very broad streets in the middle. [Col. 1217C] There was an arrangement like that of a market for goods for sale, with each person placed in order. Craftsmen too stood at their stations, so that their camp appeared very much like a suitably built city. Thus Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun pitched camp to the east; Reuben, Simeon, and Gad to the south; Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh to the west; Dan, Asher, and Naphtali to the north. Between the tabernacle and the camp the Levites kept watch in their tents, closer to the tabernacle than to the camp. They likewise kept watch in four directions: Moses and Aaron with their own people on the east; the remaining Kohathites on the south, under the charge of Eleazar son of Aaron; the Gershonites on the west; [Col. 1217D] and the Merarites on the north, both groups under Ithamar’s charge.

## CHAPTER III. On the exchange of firstborn for Levites

The Lord set apart the tribe of Levi for the firstborn then belonging to the Israelites, and the Levites’ livestock for the firstborn livestock, making, as it were, an exchange with the people (Num.
