III). For all the firstborn were then especially his, because, when he killed the firstborn of Egypt, he spared their firstborn and reserved them for himself. Thereafter, on that very account, he consecrated all their firstborn to himself forever, especially because the first fruits of all produce are owed to the Lord. In exchange for the firstborn they then possessed, therefore, he took for himself the tribe of Levi and their livestock; and the people held those firstborn in place of the Levites and their livestock. So that the number twelve of the tribes should not be diminished, he established the tribe of Manasseh, as it were, in place of the Levites, and Ephraim in place of Joseph.

[Note: [Col. 1218B] Addition 1. For Jacob, in blessing his sons, had promised Joseph’s sons that each would become a tribe.]

Lest the number of Levites seem greater than that of the firstborn, and the exchange thus unequal, the Lord said to Moses: “Number the male sons of Levi from one month old and upward.” When they were counted, they were found to be twenty-two thousand. Yet note that, if you examine the book of Numbers closely, you will find their number by families to be twenty-two thousand three hundred. A Hebrew says that three hundred of them were firstborn, and thus already belonged to the Lord [Col. 1218B].

[Note: [Col. 1218B] Addition 2. Therefore, lest that exchange be disadvantageous to the Lord if what was lacking among the Levites were not restored to him in place of the firstborn, he receives five silver shekels for each firstborn. [Col. 1218C]]

Again the Lord said to Moses: “Number the male firstborn from one month old and upward.” They were found to be twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three. For the two hundred and seventy-three who exceeded that number, Moses took as a price five shekels for each head, by the sanctuary measure, and gave them to Aaron and his sons according to the Lord’s word.

## CHAPTER IV. On the age of those ministering in the tabernacle, and the distinction among ministers

[Col. 1218C]

Again the Lord said to Moses: “Number the Levites from the thirtieth year to the fiftieth, that they may serve me in two capacities: these by carrying and setting up the tabernacle, and the retired elders by guarding it.”

[Note: [Col. 1219A] Addition 1. All those from thirty years to fifty carried the tabernacle and set up its appurtenances. Those above fifty were called retired.]

When counted, they were found to number eight thousand five hundred and eighty. The Septuagint, however, says from the twenty-fifth year, an age which we too observe in the ordination of priests. They transported the tabernacle in this manner. Since the things beyond the veil were not permitted to be seen uncovered, the priests entered first and wrapped the ark, the mercy-seat, and the cherubim—first with the veil that hung before it, [Col. 1218D] then with a violet-blue covering; and they wrapped the golden lampstand, altar, and table with their utensils in coverings. Then the Kohathites entered and carried all these wrapped items upon their own shoulders. Likewise, as some think, they carried the altar of burnt offering with its utensils. The Gershonites, to speak briefly, took down the tabernacle’s covering and carried the soft articles in carts: curtains, tent-cloths, red-dyed and violet-blue skins, the tent which stood before the tabernacle, also the curtains of the court, cords, and the vessels of ministry pertaining to the bronze altar.

[Note: [Col. 1219A] Addition 2. But because they also cleansed the altar of its ashes there, it is said that the Kohathites carried the altar upon their shoulders and its vessels. It may more properly be said that the Gershonites carried the vessels used in the ministry of the altar, not the altar’s vessels: perhaps certain containers into which they put items pertaining to the altar that they carried, and these vessels were placed upon [Col. 1219B] carts.]

The book is silent concerning who carried the altar of burnt offering. Yet it may be said that the Gershonites carried its vessels, as the book states, while the Kohathites carried the altar itself upon their shoulders. The Merarites, [Col. 1219A] to speak briefly, carried in carts all the hard components of the tabernacle and court: boards, bases, bars, pillars, pegs, and the rest. The retired Levites did not serve in this work; once the tabernacle had been set up, they sat as guards.

## CHAPTER V. On one method of restoring another’s property

[Col. 1219B]

The Lord then commanded that lepers and those with seminal discharges be expelled from the camp through the priests (Num. V). And it was done. The Lord also added a rule concerning restoration of another’s property: restoration was to be made with an additional fifth of the principal.

[Note: [Col. 1219C] Addition 1. The thing restored with a fifth of the principal was restored with a fifth part of its own value. [Col. 1219D]]

But because Exodus seems to say the contrary, namely that restoration should be fourfold (Exod. XXII), we have postponed the matter until now in order to resolve it here. We say that possession of another’s property sometimes arose deliberately, by theft or robbery; sometimes through negligence; and sometimes in ignorance.

[Note: [Col. 1219D] Addition 2. For the thing is presumed to remain in existence, preserved for restoration.]

Concerning something knowingly taken, Exodus says that it is to be restored fourfold if the thing has perished; but if it remains, twofold. If you read there of five [Col. 1219C] oxen for one, that is, according to some, another translation; and that “fourfold” is the truer reading is proved from Zacchaeus’ words. This passage deals with something taken in ignorance: the principal is to be returned with an additional fifth. Or it concerns stolen property when the matter is wholly hidden and the repentant thief voluntarily confesses and restores it. If there were no person to receive it, it was to be restored to the Lord and belonged to the priest. For the sin of theft or negligence, moreover, some offering was made in proportion to the value of the property. Josephus says that gold and silver were restored twofold, livestock fourfold, but an ox fivefold, because the more useful it is than other possessions, the more damaging its loss.

## CHAPTER VI. On the ordeal of jealousy

[Col. 1219D]

The Lord also added the law of jealousy. Jealousy properly means a husband’s love for his wife, through which he cannot endure her being joined to another (Num. V). Hence the husband is called *zelotes* (“jealous”); *zelotypia* is sometimes called adultery, and *zelotypus* an adulterer. Thus *zelotypia* commonly means mere suspicion of adultery, of which the following is read here. If a spirit of jealousy stirs a husband against his wife, who has been defiled but cannot be proved guilty, or against one accused on false suspicion, he shall bring her to the priest and offer for her an *assarius* of barley flour, which is one tenth [Col. 1220A] of a *satum*. He shall pour no oil upon it nor put frankincense on it. The priest shall set her before the Lord, put living water in her hands in an earthen vessel, together with a little of the flour offering, and burn the frankincense upon the altar. He shall cast into the water a little dust from the floor of the tabernacle, uncover her head, and, as Josephus says, write upon a parchment the name of God, namely the Tetragrammaton.

He shall make her swear that she has done her husband no wrong in the matters alleged against her. If this does not satisfy the husband, the priest shall add curses also written on the parchment and say: “If you have not been defiled by forsaking your husband’s bed, may these most bitter waters not harm you. But if you have turned aside from your husband, may the cursed waters enter your belly and make it swell, [Col. 1220B] and may your right thigh rot.” And the woman shall say: “Amen, amen.” The priest shall erase all the writing of the parchment in the water and give it to her to drink. Then the priest shall take from her hand the sacrifice of jealousy, elevate it before the Lord, and place it upon the altar. If the woman is guilty of adultery, her thigh will rot and her womb swell with dropsy—not immediately, however, but as long as ten months afterward. But if she has not been defiled, the water will not harm her; indeed, she will often conceive and bear a male child in the tenth month. These waters were called holy because the name of the Lord had been dissolved in them; cursed because curses had been put into them; and most bitter because of the effect that sometimes followed. This law was introduced because of the hardness [Col. 1220C] of their hearts, just as a bill of divorce was permitted, since they were ready to shed blood.

## CHAPTER VII. On the holiness of Nazirites

The Lord spoke to Moses concerning the law of Nazirites (Num. VI). “Nazirite” means holy, or flourishing, or sprouting. Certain persons were called Nazirites who, by a vow, bound themselves to holiness for a fixed period or continually, as Samuel did. They consecrated themselves to the Lord and were, as it were, separated from the common life of humankind, as someone today serves by vow for one or two years in the hospital at Jerusalem. The law of their holiness was this: throughout the period of his separation, a razor was not to pass over his head. Hence perhaps some depict the apostles [Col. 1220D] and Christ with long hair—not in reality, but to signify holiness. They drank nothing that could intoxicate; they ate nothing from the vine, from the raisin to the unripe grape; and they approached no dead person.

[Note: [Col. 1221A] Addition 1. That is, an unripe grape, which, gathered before maturity and preserved, eventually swells when put in water. [Col. 1221B]]

If someone suddenly died before a Nazirite, the head of his consecration was defiled. He immediately shaved his head and, on the seventh day, again offered a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, one of which the priest made a sin offering and the other a burnt offering. The days he had already observed were invalid, and he began again the holiness of his vow. Perhaps it was not for any dead person, but for one killed in his presence, that everything he had done for holiness was defiled. When the days of his vow were completed, he offered a year-old lamb as a burnt offering, [Col. 1221A] a year-old ewe as a sin offering, and a ram as a peace offering. Note that, when “ram” is simply stated in this way, the Hebrew says that it must be at least two years old. He also offered a basket of various unleavened breads, apart from things he voluntarily offered according to the perfection of his holiness; this offering was called *corban*, that is, “gift.” A woman offered thirty shekels if she could; a man, fifty; otherwise a poor person offered at the priest’s discretion. Once the priest had sacrificed the victims according to his rite, the Nazirite returned to the entrance of the tabernacle. The priest placed his hair in the fire of the sacrifice, and he could then return to the ordinary life of a human being.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the blessing over the people

[Col. 1221B]

[Note: [Col. 1221B] Addition 1. What was done in the first month of the second year, though omitted, will be explained here.]

Again the Lord spoke to Moses: “Aaron and his sons shall invoke my name upon the children of Israel, and I shall bless them.” This is done in all the sacraments of the Church. They shall invoke it thus: “May the Lord God bless you and keep you; may he give you peace and show you his face.”

[Note: [Col. 1221B] Addition 2. In Numbers, in the form of this blessing, the name of the Lord occurs three times.]

(Num. VI).

## CHAPTER IX. On the offerings of the twelve days at the dedication of the tabernacle

[Col. 1221C]

Now on the day when Moses anointed the tabernacle and sanctified it, the twelve tribal leaders offered for the altar’s inauguration, as the Hebrew has it, six wagons drawn by twelve oxen—each leader one ox, and every two leaders one wagon. Two wagons were given to the Gershonites, to carry the burdens of which we have spoken; and four were given to the Merarites. Afterwards, each leader on his own day offered the vessels necessary for the altar. For the solemnity of the dedication was extended through twelve days. On the first day Nahshon of the tribe of Judah offered a silver dish of one hundred and thirty shekels. The Hebrew has, “a silver bowl and a basin of seventy shekels,” each filled with fine flour; [Col. 1221D] incense was placed in the basin. He also offered a golden mortar of ten shekels, full of incense. Spices were ground in this vessel. The Hebrew has “spoon,” namely that by which incense was placed in the censer. He also offered an ox, a ram, and a year-old lamb as a burnt offering; a he-goat as a sin offering; and, as a peace offering, two oxen, five rams, five he-goats, and five year-old lambs.

[Note: [Col. 1222B] Addition 1. According to the Hebrew, an ox had to be at least three years old and a ram two years old.]

The other leaders offered vessels of the same sort and the same victims, each on his day; and thus the dedication was completed in twelve days. It is clear that this is said by way of recapitulation. For, according to what the text seems to mean, the dedication began on the eighth day of the first month: during the preceding seven days of that month the priests were consecrated [Col. 1222A] and the tabernacle anointed, but not yet dedicated. If this is so, the priests’ consecration and the tabernacle’s dedication were prolonged for nineteen days.

[Note: [Col. 1222B] Addition 2. For it was not permitted to hold two general feasts simultaneously.]

Therefore they did not celebrate Passover in that year at its proper time, namely on the fourteenth day. Yet this was commanded them by the Lord on the first day of that same year. Therefore, as we said above, some have held that the seven days of the priests’ consecration were the final days of the first year; that on the first day of the second year the tabernacle was anointed; on the twelfth day its dedication finished; and on the fourteenth day Passover was celebrated.

[Note: [Col. 1222B] Addition 3. It may plainly be said that, on the same day, the priests’ consecration or anointing, the tabernacle’s dedication, and the offering of the leaders began, and ran concurrently for seven days. After these, the offering continued for five days; on the thirteenth day the Levites were consecrated; and on the fourteenth day they observed [Col. 1222C] the solemn Passover.]

Yet it may be said that this twelve-day offering was made in the second month of the second year, and that these matters are not said by way of recapitulation. When it is read that it began on the day the tabernacle was anointed, they take “the same day” in a similar sense: because, just as the tabernacle was anointed on the eighth day of the first month, so this offering began on the eighth day of the second month. Thus, during the first eight days of the third year, the priests and tabernacle were consecrated.

## CHAPTER X. On the consecration of the Levites

[Col. 1222C]

> “Again the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Take the Levites from among the children of Israel, and you shall consecrate them to me’ (Num. VIII).” Accordingly, at the Lord’s command, the Levites were first sprinkled with the water of purification; all the hair of their bodies was shaved—though this did not include the hair of their heads—and their garments also were washed. Then, before the Lord, they stood at the entrance of the tabernacle, with the whole multitude assembled. The children of Israel laid their hands upon them, and Aaron presented them to the Lord as an offering, that they might serve in his ministry. The Levites also presented two bulls, one of which Aaron offered for sin and the other as a burnt offering; thus they were set apart for the Lord from among the children of Israel.

Thereafter they possessed for their use those things that belonged to the Lord. For they lived from the tithes and were content with these. The priests, moreover, had sacrifices, firstfruits, firstborn offerings, and vows. They ate all these with their households, provided that they were clean, except for offerings for sin, because the priests alone ate the sins of the people. The Levites gave the high priest a tithe of their tithes, and they gave from the best portions. Therefore they had no allotted portion in the land, and this turned out better for them: otherwise they would have possessed only a twelfth part of the land’s goods, whereas now they possessed a tenth.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning those who cannot keep the Passover in the first month, so that they may keep it in the second.

> “The Lord spoke to Moses in the second year, in the first month [Note: **[Col. 1223B] Addition 1.** As though to say: From the fact that it is said there, ‘in the second year,’ it is clear that this statement—namely, ‘Let the children of Israel keep the Passover,’ etc.—is spoken by recapitulation. For it must have been said earlier, since it was done earlier in the month, namely in the first month, before the offering of the princes set forth above.] (Num. IX).”

Here it is plainly determined [Col. 1223A] that this is said by recapitulation: “Let the children of Israel keep the Passover at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of the month until evening.” And they kept the Passover.

But there were certain persons unclean through contact with a human being [Note: **[Col. 1223B] Addition 2.** By the better part, the whole human being is denoted [Col. 1223C]—that is, both body and soul—which is frequent in Sacred Scripture.], that is, through a human being, who is called a “soul”; having touched his corpse, they could not keep the Passover. They said to Moses: “Why are we deprived of the ability to offer among the children of Israel?” Perhaps they were indignant because such uncleanness is at times unavoidable. Moses consulted the Lord about this. He answered him: “Any man of your people who has become unclean through a human being, or is on a distant journey, shall keep the Passover in the second month, on the fourteenth day, observing the whole rite of the Passover.” But if, without causes of this kind, he does not keep the Passover at its appointed time, his soul shall be cut off [Col. 1223B] from his peoples. A foreign resident also, if he is among you, shall keep the Lord’s Passover.

If it is asked what a person should do if, again in the second month, because of uncleanness he could not keep the Passover: it may be said that he would keep it in the third month, because what is said in one case is to be understood similarly in others; or perhaps, if he did not keep it later that year, he would not sin.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the silver trumpets and the manner of sounding them.

[Col. 1223C]

> “Again the Lord spoke to Moses: ‘Make for yourself two hammered silver trumpets’ (Num. X),”

by which you shall summon the multitude. They had these two trumpets for four uses: summoning the multitude, moving the camp, war, and festivals. The trumpet, as Josephus says, was a musical pipe, almost a cubit in length, wider than a reed, having at its beginning a breadth suitable for the mouth to receive breath; in Hebrew it is called *asora*.

There was, however, a difference in summoning the multitude. To summon all the people, both trumpets were sounded together in a simple blast. To summon only the princes, they sounded once [Col. 1223D]. This may be understood in two ways: either with only one trumpet, or with one blast. Also, as Josephus adds, they sounded once if the princes wished each to summon his own people in the assembly, or if Moses summoned the people through the assemblies.

For moving the camp, however, the trumpets were sounded not simply, but in short and more prolonged signals. At the first signal, the camps of the three tribes on the east moved; at the second, those on the south; at the third, those on the west; and at the fourth, those on the north. The manner of sounding in war is not distinguished, perhaps because among them it was done as among other nations. They also sounded when they held a solemn feast, on festival days, and at the calends; but the manner is not specified. The priests, however, sounded them.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Israel’s departure from Mount Sinai.

[Col. 1224A]

> “In the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud was lifted from the tabernacle of the covenant, and they set out from the mountain of the Lord on a journey of three days” (Num. X).

The Hebrews say that the ark went ahead of them for three days; when the cloud stood over it, they gathered gradually, as though to a fixed place—some sooner and some later. But it is better to say only this concerning the journey: when they left Mount Sinai, the cloud went before them and did not rest for three days and nights. Hence they immediately murmured because of the hardship of the journey, since they did not pitch camp even at night; and then the cloud rested in the wilderness of Paran, that is, at the first stopping-place which they made [Col. 1224B] in Paran.

For Paran is a vast wilderness now inhabited by Saracens. Therefore, since in the first year, on the first day of the third month, they came to the mountain of the Lord, and departed from it in the second year, on the twentieth day of the second month, it is clear that at this stopping-place—which was approximately the twelfth—they stayed for a year. Jerome says that they were there for a year and four days. This is extremely difficult to establish unless perhaps it was an embolismic year.

It may nevertheless be said that, when a natural year had elapsed, they departed on the same day on which they had received the Law. Thus, since they came to the mountain on the day before the Kalends of June, and received the Law on the fourth day of June, if they departed on that same fourth day when the year had elapsed, it is clear that they remained at the mountain [Col. 1224C] for a year and four days; and thus, in the third month of the legal year, on the fourth day, they departed.

Nevertheless, it is still true that they departed in the second month of the second year, on the twentieth day. For besides the natural year, they reckon years in three ways. There is the customary year, beginning in January, which they share with us in their contracts and ordinary business. But in what month of the fifth day of this year they departed is not recorded. There is also among them the legal year, which they use in legal matters. In this year, as we have said, they departed in the third month, on the fourth day. There is also among them the year of the Exodus. For in remembrance of their deliverance, they began to count their years from the departure out of Egypt, just as Greece did from the first Olympiad, the Romans [Col. 1224D] from the founding of the city, and Christians from the Incarnation of the Lord. In the second month of this year, on the twentieth day, they departed.

For one Passover-to-Passover year had already elapsed, and from the second Passover until that Passover fifty days had passed. Therefore one month of thirty days had elapsed, and the second had already reached twenty days. This distinction of years is necessary in many places. In this stopping-place, the latter half of Exodus, the whole of Leviticus, and a considerable number of the prescriptions of Numbers were written.

Note that there are four kinds of year: legal, exodus, customary, and natural. In the legal year, they departed in the third month of this year—June—on the fourth day of that month. Count this one from Kalends to Kalends. In the exodus year, they departed in the second [Col. 1225A] month of this year, namely on its twenty-second day, which was the fourth day of June. Count this one from Passover to Passover. First take the fifteen days of the first month and join them to the fourteen days of the following May: behold, you have the first month of the second year. Again, take the sixteen days remaining in May and join them to the four days of June, and you will have twenty days of the second month from Passover. Thus both calculations—the legal year and the exodus year—will be correct, as the text itself contains.

The customary year began in January, and the Hebrews share it with us in their business affairs. In the natural year, they departed in its third month, on the fourth lunar day, which was the fiftieth day from the fourteenth lunar day of April.

Moses took with him Obal, otherwise Obad [Col. 1225B], his wife’s brother, who knew in what places through the wilderness camps could conveniently be pitched. Moses promised him a share in the best things which the Lord would give them. And when the ark was lifted up, Moses said: “Rise, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered; let those who hate you flee before your face.” But when it was set down, he said: “Return, O Lord, to the multitude of the children of the host of Israel.”

[Note: **[Col. 1225B] Addition 1.** “It is better,” says the Master, “that we say only that, when they departed from Sinai, the cloud went before them.”]

[Note: **[Col. 1225B] Addition 2.** The solar year exceeds the lunar year by eleven days. When these have accumulated, they make up one lunation of thirty days, or indeed twenty-nine days, with the remainder reserved; and the year in which that lunation occurs is called embolismic, while the others are called common years. It sometimes happens that two common years intervene before an embolismic year, and sometimes one, according as only one occurs twice in a nineteen-year cycle. This, then, is why Jerome said, “unless it was an embolismic year.” It is impossible that they were there for a natural year and four days if they departed on the fiftieth day from Passover, because the day of Passover is never the same in the preceding and following years, and the Passovers of one year and the next never coincide. Likewise, the fiftieth day is never the same. Therefore they did not depart, after a natural year had elapsed, from the day on which the Law was given; rather, having come to the mountain on the first lunar day of June, after the lunations had run their course to the first lunar day of June [Col. 1225D], they departed on the fourth day of that same lunar month, which was the fiftieth day from the fourteenth lunar day of April.]

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the election of the seventy elders.

[Col. 1225D]

A murmur arose among the people against the Lord, as they grieved over their hardship; and fire, kindled in the Lord’s wrath, consumed the outermost part of the camp (Num. XI), namely those who were far behind. “Moses prayed before the Lord, and the fire was extinguished; and he called the name of that place Burning.” Yet this was not the name of a stopping-place.

At the same stopping-place, the mixed multitude that had gone up with them—that is, Egyptian male and female slaves—and many Israelites together with them burned with a desire for meat. By “meat” we understand not flesh alone, but abundance of other [Col. 1226A] foods as well. Thus, in their complaint, no mention is made of meat when they said: “We remember the fish that we ate freely in Egypt; let cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic come to our minds. Our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing but manna.”

Moses heard the people weeping, and it seemed an unbearable thing to him because they demanded food from him as well. He said to the Lord: “Why have you laid the burden of this people upon me? Did I conceive and bear this entire multitude? I beg you, either provide otherwise, or kill me.” The Lord said to him: “Gather for me seventy men from among the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the best, at the entrance of the tabernacle; and I will take from your spirit and give it to them, so that they may bear [Col. 1226B] with you the burden of the people. And you shall say to the people: ‘Tomorrow I shall give you meat for a month of days,’” that is, enough for a month, even to nausea. “Nausea” is used broadly for vomiting. Properly, it is the vomiting induced by the stench of bilge-water.

The taking away of Moses’ spirit and its giving to others is not to be understood as a division of his spirit into portions, or as a diminution; rather, it is the enlightenment of others for governing the people through the same special grace by which Moses himself was enlightened, just as many lamps are lit from the fire of a single lamp without diminishing it.

Moses therefore brought the seventy chosen men to the entrance of the tabernacle, except for two who had remained in the camp—not from contempt, but because they considered themselves unworthy. One was called Eldad and the other [Col. 1226C] Medad. As the Hebrews say, they were Moses’ brothers through their mother, but not through their father [Note: **[Col. 1226C] Addition 1.** Jerome says in his commentary on Chronicles that they were not brothers through their father, but through their mother, because after receiving the Law Amram, at Moses’ command, dismissed Moses’ mother, since she was his relative, and took another wife, by whom he received these two. But on this account they would not yet have been two years old. The Master resolves this thus: it may be said that the Law was received by Moses through knowledge in the spirit much [Col. 1226D] earlier than through its public giving, perhaps thirty or forty years earlier. Thus these two could have been included among the seventy.].

The Lord descended in a cloud, and the spirit rested upon those who stood with Moses, and they prophesied. But the two who had remained in the camp also prophesied and afterwards did not fall silent; that is, thereafter they were always called prophets. Moses returned with them to the camp.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the giving of meat and God’s wrath upon them.

[Col. 1226D]

A wind went forth from the Lord, catching at his command quails from across the sea in the Ortygian islands, and carried them to the camp all around it for a day’s journey. They flew two cubits above the ground (Num. XI). The people rose and gathered quails for themselves during two days, and dried them. Even the one who gathered least had ten *cors*.

These quails, according to tradition, were not the small ones found among us; rather, they were larger birds, called royal birds, which we call *curleios*, from their running. Before the food was exhausted, the Lord’s wrath struck the people [Col. 1227A] with a very great plague. The kind of plague is not specified here, but the Psalms seem to indicate that it was fire. The people who had desired meat were buried there. Thus the place was called Cabroth, otherwise Cabaioth, meaning “the desire of burial” or “graves of craving.”

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Miriam’s affliction and the cause of her leprosy.

> “After departing from the graves of craving, they came to Hazeroth; and there Miriam and Aaron contended with Moses because of his Ethiopian wife” (Num. XII).

As though quarrelling with him, they reproached him because he had married the queen of Ethiopia, or because he had dismissed her after marrying her; or rather, because of his wife Zipporah, who had quarrelled with Miriam. For the Midianites were formerly called [Col. 1227B] Ethiopians, as is read in Chronicles. Indignantly they said: “Has the Lord not spoken to us as well as to Moses?” (II Chron. XIV). As if to say: Why does Moses wish to rule over us because the Lord has spoken to him?

The angry Lord said to them: “Come out, you three alone, to the tabernacle.” And when they stood there, the Lord descended in a pillar of cloud. Calling Aaron and Miriam, he said: “If there is a prophet among you, I shall speak to him in a vision, or through a dream, or through riddles, or through figures. But to my servant Moses, who is most faithful in all my house, I speak mouth to mouth. Why then did you speak against him, setting yourselves as his equals?” The cloud departed, and behold, Miriam appeared leprous.

Aaron said to Moses: “I beg you, my lord, do not lay this sin upon us.” [Col. 1227C] Moses prayed to the Lord: “God, I beg you, heal her.” The Lord said to him: “If her father had spat in her face, would she not have had to be ashamed for at least seven days? Let her be separated outside the camp for seven days.” As though to say: If her father had disgraced her because of some offense of hers, should she not be ashamed for some time?

“Miriam was therefore excluded outside the camp for seven days, and the people did not move until she was recalled.”

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the twelve spies.

> “After the people departed from Hazeroth, they pitched their tents in the wilderness of Paran” (Num. XIII).

Paran is not the name of a stopping-place but of a wilderness containing many stopping-places, as will be evident in the catalogue of stopping-places. [Col. 1227D] For it contains all the stopping-places from Hazeroth, which was the fourteenth, through Ezion-geber, which was the thirty-second; through all these they passed in the second year.

From Ezion-geber, at the Lord’s command, Moses sent twelve men [Note: **[Col. 1228B] Addition 1.** These are the names of the twelve spies whom Moses sent: “From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua; from the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat; from the tribe of Judah, Caleb; from the tribe of Issachar, Igal; from the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea, or Joshua; from the tribe of Benjamin, Palti; from the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel; from the tribe of Joseph, Gaddi; from the tribe of Dan, Ammiel; from the tribe of Asher, Sethur; from the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi; from the tribe of Gad, Geuel. These are the names of the men whom Moses sent to examine the land of Canaan” (Num. XIII).], one from each tribe, to examine the land which they were to possess. Chief among them were Caleb son of Jephunneh, from Judah, and Hoshea son of Nun, from Ephraim. Moses called Hoshea Joshua; he was Moses’ minister.

Hence some say that the previously mentioned name Joshua was used by anticipation, because this name was first given to him here. It may also be said that Moses entrusted to him the care and safety of the other eleven. Since he was called Joshua or Hoshea, names that mean “savior,” Moses then first applied these names to him in a special sense when he appointed him as the savior of the others.

Moses commanded them to examine the character of the land, its people, and its cities, and to bring back fruits of the land. It was the season when early grapes could be eaten. Going up, they explored the land; and when they came to Hebron, they saw three men of the race of Anak, or Anakim—that is, of giant stock—such as they had also seen in the Egyptian city of Tanis. These were also called Titans from Tanis. Hebron had been built seven years before the city of Tanis. Hence it is believed that the race of giants descended into Egypt from Hebron.

Going down as far as a most fertile valley and stream, they took pomegranates [Note: **[Col. 1228B] Addition 2.** *Malagranatus* is the pomegranate tree; *malum granatum* is the pomegranate fruit.] and figs from that place. They also cut off a vine-branch with a cluster of grapes, which [Col. 1228B], because of its size, two men carried on a pole. For this reason that place was called Nehelescol, that is, “the stream of the cluster.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the people’s murmur, for which they perished in the wilderness for forty years.

[Col. 1228C]

After forty days, they returned and came to their people at Kadesh (Num. XIII). In the meantime the people had departed from the thirty-second stopping-place and were dwelling at the thirty-third. Yet some maintain that the spies were sent from Kadesh and that the people awaited them there. Josephus calls this stopping-place a valley near the borders of the Canaanites, difficult to inhabit [Note: **[Col. 1229C] Addition 1.** Seven peoples lived in the land of promise, one of whom was the Canaanite.].

Commending the land which they had seen, the men added [Note: **[Col. 1229C] Addition 2.** So too, when we envy someone, we attach faults to his praises, accompanied by an objection.]:

> “But it has very strong inhabitants, great and fortified cities, and we saw there the offspring of Anak, compared with whom we seemed like locusts; [Col. 1228D] the land which we surveyed devours its inhabitants.”

A Hebrew explains this as follows; observe his threefold exposition of the statement, “The land which we surveyed devours its inhabitants.” The land is weak and cannot sustain long-lived people; or, no nation was permitted to live in it long because of the frequent attacks of those who came upon it. Thus, when the prophet promises security of permanent residence in that land, he says that this reproach will be removed from it: it will not be called a land that devours its inhabitants. Yet this can also be said in praise of the land: it is so good that no one wishes to leave it as a foreigner, but whoever is born in it dies there.

When the entire crowd heard this, they wept, saying: “Would that we had died in Egypt! Is it not better to return to Egypt than to fall by the sword and have our wives and children handed over as captives? [Col. 1229A] Let us appoint for ourselves another leader than Moses and return to Egypt.”

But Joshua and Caleb tore their garments and said: “Do not rebel against the Lord,” that is, do not judge him false in what he has promised, “for we shall devour the people of this land as bread.” As the other ten who had terrified the people shouted against them, and the entire multitude wished to crush them with stones, the glory of the Lord appeared over the covering of the covenant. The Lord said to Moses: “How long will this people not believe me? I shall strike them and make you into a great nation.”

Moses said: “I beg you, Lord, do not do this, lest perhaps the Egyptians mock you and say: ‘He could not bring the people into the land which he had promised.’” The Lord said to him: “According to your word, I have forgiven. [Col. 1229B] Yet, as I live, none of those who saw the signs which I performed in Egypt”—namely those counted from twenty years and above, who had already tested me ten times, that is, many times—“shall see the land concerning which I swore to their fathers, except Joshua and Caleb.”

But because [Note: **[Col. 1229C] Addition 4.** But because mercy is joined to justice in every work of God, he adds “but because.”] the Amalekites and Canaanites dwell near you, lest they come upon you, move camp tomorrow and return to the wilderness. According to the number of the eleven days [Note: **[Col. 1229D] Addition 5.** Again there follows a statement concerning the justice of God: “according to the number,” etc. Hence the prophet David: “For forty years I was offended with this generation” (Ps. XCIV).] in which you examined the land, you shall bear your iniquities for forty years.

Moses spoke all these words to them, and the people mourned exceedingly. Behold, rising in the morning, they said to Moses: “We have sinned in despairing; we are ready to go up to the place which the Lord promised.” Moses said to them: “Do not go up; [Col. 1229C] for the Lord is not with you.” But they, blinded, thinking that they could conquer without God, went up, while the ark, Moses, and the Levites remained in the camp. The Amalekite and Canaanite pursued them, striking them down as far as the place which for this reason was called Hormah, that is, “the ban,” and they returned to the wilderness (Num. XIV).

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the stoning of the man gathering wood on the Sabbath.

[Col. 1229D]

> “When they were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath. Moses detained him until he consulted the Lord. The Lord said of him: ‘This man shall die outside the camp; let him be overwhelmed with stones’” (Num. XV).

And it was done so. Some think that this man was Shaphat, because [Col. 1230A] his daughters later said: “Our father died in the wilderness in his sin” (Num. XXVII).

There also the Lord commanded them to place blue fringes at the four corners of their cloaks, so that even the least commandments of the Lord might be remembered and observed. The Pharisees magnified these to such an extent that they even tied thorns into them, in order that the frequent prick of the thorns might awaken them to continual remembrance of the Lord’s commandments. The Jews then wore square cloaks; and even now, at the corners of their square garment in their synagogues, they have blue fringes in remembrance of the Law given from heaven. They did this so that they might be distinguished from other nations even by their dress.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the schism of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, and their punishment.

[Col. 1230B]

Now Korah, son of Izhar, Amram’s brother [Note: **[Col. 1231A] Addition 1.** Note that Izhar and Amram were brothers. Since one of them, namely Izhar, was the firstborn, it seemed to his son Korah that he rather than Moses, Amram’s son, ought to hold the high priesthood. He wished to persuade Dathan and Abiram of the same thing concerning the dignity of leadership, because they were foremost among the Reubenites.], when he saw his cousins honored, one with the priesthood and the other with leadership of the people, grew envious (Num. XVI). Murmuring against Moses and Aaron, he had as accomplices two hundred and fifty of the leading Levites, whom he even considered worthy of the priesthood. He had also joined to himself Dathan and Abiram, the more powerful Reubenites, to whom, he said, leadership of the people was due because they belonged to Reuben, the firstborn.

Moses said to them: “Let each of you take his censer; tomorrow, having taken fire, place incense upon it—Aaron also with you—and the one whom the Lord chooses, he shall be holy.” Moses therefore sent in the morning to summon Dathan and Abiram; they said: “We [Col. 1230C] will not come.” Having summoned the whole multitude, Moses said to Korah and the two hundred and fifty: “Take your censers, put incense on them, and stand before the Lord.”

While they stood thus, Moses went down with the elders of the people to Dathan and Abiram to summon them. For Abiram also, according to Josephus, was in part a Levite. But they stood with their wives, children, and all their household company at the entrances of their tents, prepared rather to resist if Moses wished to use force than to obey. Seeing this, Moses prayed to the Lord that they might perish by an unprecedented death, and that it might thus become clear that the Lord had sent him.

While he prayed and wept, the earth shook, the people were terrified by the great roar raised through their tents [Col. 1230D], and the earth split beneath their feet. Opening its mouth, it swallowed them with all their possessions; they went down alive into hell, that is, into the open chasm of the earth. Then the earth closed again, as though none of these things had happened.

But fire also went forth from the censers of Korah and his company, such as had never been seen to leap up either from the earth, from the collision of thunderbolts, or from the violence of winds; and it devoured them, while Aaron stood unharmed. At the Lord’s command Eleazar took their censers, with the fire scattered here and there, and beat them into plates. Fashioning small golden crowns from them, he fastened them to the bronze altar, to warn the children of Israel that no one except one of Aaron’s seed should approach to offer incense [Col. 1231A] to the Lord, lest he suffer like things. Yet they were also so crafted that they remained there as an ornament.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the burning of the people, extinguished through Aaron.

The next day, however, “the entire multitude again murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘You have killed the Lord’s people’” (Num. XVI). When they [Col. 1231B] wished to overwhelm them with stones, Moses and Aaron fled to the tabernacle. The cloud covered them, and the glory of the Lord appeared. Fire went forth from the Lord and devoured the people.

Moses said to Aaron: “Take a censer; having taken fire from the altar, put incense upon it and hurry quickly to the people, that you may pray for them.” Aaron hastened with the censer, stood between the living and the dead, and prayed to the Lord; and the plague ceased. Fourteen thousand and seventy of them were struck. Elsewhere the reading is seven hundred, apart from those who had perished in Korah’s rebellion.

[Note: **[Col. 1231B] Addition 1.** Aaron’s priesthood had been confirmed by the preceding sign. Two further signs follow, one of which is supplied here.]

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning Aaron’s rod, which in one night flowered, put forth leaves, and bore almonds.

[Col. 1231C]

Nevertheless, the tumult over Aaron’s priesthood had not yet ceased. For they said that, even if the Lord had not chosen the aforementioned Levites, there might be persons from some of the remaining tribes worthy of the priesthood; and perhaps the Lord wished to have some priests from every tribe, lest so great a dignity of ministry should be entrusted to one household and so few ministers (Num. XVII). They also accused Moses of causing the scarcity of the wilderness, so that they might always seem to need his assistance [Note: **[Col. 1231D] Addition 1.** They said that Moses had led them through the wilderness of his own accord, so that they might need his help.].

Therefore, at the Lord’s command, Moses took the rods of twelve princes and wrote upon each the name of its tribe, or rather of its prince. Upon Aaron’s rod [Col. 1231D] he wrote the name of Levi. Besides these twelve he took one separately, containing all the families, in order to test whether God wished to have priests from all the tribes. In Numbers, however, it is read that there were only twelve rods; this should be understood to refer to the individual rods, the general one being excepted.

When Moses had placed them in the tabernacle before the Lord, he returned the next day and found that Aaron’s rod had sprouted, spread out leaves, and produced almonds. Thus, by God’s ordinance, Aaron possessed the priesthood most securely for the third time. For as a sign against rebels, the Lord commanded that Aaron’s rod be kept in the tabernacle for the future.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the return to Kadesh in the fortieth year.

[Col. 1232A]

The children of Israel were therefore in the wilderness for a long time. They remained for a long time at Kadesh-barnea, wandered long around Mount Seir, returned almost as far as the Red Sea and the region around Sinai, and their corpses lay strewn in the wilderness. At last, after many hardships and thirty-eight years, they returned to Kadesh, whence they had sent the spies, or to which the spies had returned to them, as stated above. This is in the wilderness of Zin [Note: **[Col. 1232C] Addition 1.** Zin, of which the present passage speaks, either is Kadesh or contains Kadesh. Hence it is said, “Zin in which Kadesh is,” etc.], and it is not the wilderness to which they came at the eighth stopping-place, as Jerome says.

For the earlier wilderness is written Sin with *samech* and is interpreted “thornbush” or “hatred.” But Zin, in which Kadesh is, or which is Kadesh, is written with *sade* and is interpreted “commandment” [Col. 1232B] or “holy”; and, according to some, it is part of the wilderness of Paran.

Therefore, at the end of the thirty-ninth year, they came from the region of Sinai to Kadesh in eleven days. It may be that in eleven days, travelling rapidly, they covered as much as they had travelled slowly, or by another route, through twenty-one stopping-places. Thus in the fortieth year, in the first month, the children of Israel returned to the wilderness of Zin, and the people remained in the wilderness of Kadesh (Num. XX).

Thus the forty-two stopping-places of the children of Israel, by which they are said to have travelled from Egypt to the plains of Moab by the Jordan, were completed in only three years. They travelled from Egypt to Mount Sinai in the first year, from the fourteenth day of the first month to the first day of the [Col. 1232C] third month. Then in the second year, departing Sinai on the twentieth day of the first month, they completed twenty-one stopping-places as far as Kadesh within the second year; but the interval of that year is not specified, as it is in the first year. For thirty-eight years [Note: **[Col. 1232C] Addition 1.** As though to say: In the stopping-places of the second year, the amount of time [Col. 1232D] which elapsed between one stopping-place and another is not distinguished as it is in the stopping-places of the first year.] they wandered and fell; in the fortieth year they returned to the same Kadesh. In that year they passed through the remaining nine stopping-places. If you find that there were ten stopping-places in this year, know that the repeated Kadesh is again counted among them.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the death of Miriam and the waters of contradiction.

[Col. 1232D]

Mary died at Kadesh (Num. 20), when, as Josephus says, she had completed the fortieth year since leaving Egypt, at the beginning of the month Xanthicus, which is also Nisan, according to the lunar calendar. They buried her on the mountain called Zin. After the thirty days of mourning had passed, Moses purified the people in this manner: he burned outside the camp a three-year-old heifer, entirely red. Here Josephus continues the order of the ashes of purification, which the Lord commanded to be performed on the tenth day of the seventh month; and he seems to mean that Moses first performed this kind of burning now [Col. 1233A]. Hence he adds: “He commanded that those to come should observe this also.” It may be that, being hindered, they had deferred it until now, since they are not recorded as having celebrated the Passover in the intervening time. But when they entered the promised land, they carried out their ordinances according to the Lord’s commands.

Here also Josephus says that, before they returned to Kadesh, they came to the borders of Idumea and sent messengers to Edom [Note: [Col. 1233C] Addition 1. This Edom was Jacob’s brother.], requesting freedom of passage through his land. When he refused it, Moses withdrew from there, making his journey through the wilderness. The history in Numbers says that Israel sent to Edom after Mary’s death. It is not clear whether Josephus says this by anticipation, or the book of Numbers by recapitulation. But we, following the order of the history, say that when Mary died the people needed water [Col. 1233B]; and, when a sedition arose among the people against Moses and Aaron, both prayed to the Lord. The Lord said to them: “Take the rod, and gather the people to the rock; and when struck, it will give you water.” Whether Moses used the rod that had blossomed or another rod is uncertain. Yet because Numbers says “the rod which was before the Lord,” it seems to have been the rod that was in the ark.

“And when the multitude had gathered before the rock, Moses said: ‘Hear, rebels and unbelievers: shall we be able to bring water out for you from this rock?’” Here, whereas Moses and Aaron had acted confidently on other occasions, disturbed by the people’s murmuring they acted distrustfully; this became known when the Lord revealed it. For it could not have been discerned from any act or word of theirs [Col. 1233C], unless perhaps because Moses, as though doubting, said, “Shall we be able,” etc. From this an affirmative meaning might be drawn—“we shall be able”—or a negative one—“we shall not be able.” Therefore, when he first struck the flint with the rod, because he had despaired, the waters did not flow. But at the second blow they came forth so abundantly that the people and their beasts drank.

“And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: ‘Because you did not believe me, you shall not bring this people into their land.’ This is the water of contradiction,” because even the chosen men despaired of the promises and of God’s power, as though contradicting the one who promised.

## Chapter XXV. On the circuit of Idumea

[Col. 1233D] “Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, saying: ‘Your brother Jacob sends you these words: I beg that we may be permitted to pass through your land. We shall not go through cultivated places; we shall travel by the public road; we shall turn neither to the right nor to the left. If we drink your waters, we shall give what is just.’ And he answered: ‘You shall not pass through me.’” Yet, fearing that they might pass through, he came out against them with a strong force. “Therefore Israel turned aside from him,” especially because God had commanded: “You shall not fight against your brother.”

Israel went around Idumea; leaving Kadesh and proceeding through the wilderness of Arabia, and passing through Archim, the metropolis of the Arabs, now called Petra, it came to Mount Hor, which is on the borders of the land of Edom.

## Chapter XXVI. On Aaron’s death

[Col. 1234A]

“There the Lord spoke to Moses: ‘Let Aaron,’ he said, ‘go to his people. He shall not enter the land of promise, because he was unbelieving toward my word. Take Aaron and his son with him, and lead them before all the people up Mount Hor. When you have stripped the father of the high-priestly robe, you shall clothe Eleazar with it’” (Num. 20), to whom the high priesthood came by age, his firstborn having been consumed by fire. “And Moses did as the Lord had commanded him, and Aaron died on Mount Hor.”

In Deuteronomy Mosera is said to be the place of Aaron’s burial (Deut. 10), which is shown even today on the summit of the mountain. The people mourned him for thirty days. He died in the fortieth year after the departure, when he was one hundred and twenty-three years old [Col. 1234B], in the same year as Mary, on the first day of the fifth month—called Sedebach among the Hebrews and August among the Romans—according to the lunar calendar.

## Chapter XXVII. On the victory after the vow of anathema

“When the Canaanite who lived in the south heard that Israel had come there, he fought against it, prevailed, and took spoil from it” (Num. 21). But Israel vowed to the Lord that, if the Lord delivered him into its hands, it would devote his cities to destruction; and it did so. It called the name of that place Hormah, that is, “anathema” or “thing devoted.”

Perhaps this is the place that above was called Hormah by anticipation. *Anathema* is said to derive from *anathene*, that is, “to set up above”; this is “to devote,” that is, by a vow to set something apart from our use below [Col. 1234C], when the vowed and rendered thing was placed above in the temples. Note that in old times the people of the promised land were generally called Canaanites [Note: [Col. 1234C] Addition 1. They are read as defeated a third time by the Cappadocians, in Deuteronomy, chapter 2.]. Hence here he calls by the general name those who were in the south. For at that time the seven peoples there were called by their proper names, and the one properly called Canaanite was he who inhabited the coastland.

## Chapter XXVIII. On the bronze serpent against the fiery serpents

Leaving Mount Hor, they came to Salmana, where the people began to be weary of the journey and its toil while they were going around the land of Edom [Col. 1234D], and they murmured against Moses (Num. 21). Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people. They were called fiery because they were very small and swift, like sparks. Or, as others report, their venom made the person touched swell until there was a fiery swelling and redness.

They begged Moses to pray for them. The Lord said to him: “Make a bronze serpent, and set it upon a pole raised high in the midst of the people; and whoever has been struck by a serpent shall look upon it and live.” And it was done so. The children of Israel always had it with them, and it was splendidly preserved in Jerusalem. At length, because of the superstitious worship which the people offered it, the king of Judah ground it into dust [Note: [Col. 1234D] Addition 1. Because the histories contradict one another on this point; [Col. 1235A] therefore the king’s name is not given, though it will be determined later.].

## Chapter XXIX. On the rocks of the torrents that leaped

[Col. 1235A]

From there, after travelling through some stopping-places, they came to the torrent Zared, which they crossed dry-shod, as they had crossed the Red Sea (Num. 21). Leaving it, they encamped opposite the Arnon, which, as Josephus says, is a river descending from the mountain of Arabia and flowing through the wilderness into Lake Asphaltitis, dividing Moabitis and Armonica. Some maintain that Armonica is a city in the wilderness, projecting into the borders of the Amorite.

The book of Numbers continues concerning this crossing of Israel through that land in this manner: “Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars [Col. 1235B] of the Lord: ‘As he did at the Red Sea, so he will do at the torrents of Arnon. The rocks of the torrents bent down,’” or “leaped,” “‘so that they might rest in Arnon and lie down at the borders of the Moabites.’”

I do not remember reading a sufficient explanation of this passage. Augustine says that perhaps there was a book so called among the Chaldeans, from whom Abraham had come; or among the Egyptians, among whom Moses had learned wisdom; in which this crossing had been prophesied. Others think that, in order to establish boundaries there between two peoples, a war was waged, which, because of its magnitude, was called the Lord’s war, and that this book recorded that war.

Some say that the entire history concerning the children of Israel is called the Book of the Wars of the Lord, in which it is frequently said that the Lord fought for them [Col. 1235C]. The Hebrews especially say that in that land the Amorites were destroyed by the mighty hand of the Hebrews; and they read “it is said” for “it shall be said,” because the Hebrew also has this: “Concerning this it shall be said in the Recollections of the Wars of the Lord.” It is read thus: “Therefore,” that is, concerning Arnon, “it is said,” that is, it shall be said, and memorial will be made “in the Book of the Wars of the Lord,” that is, in this history, when it is read by posterity. The mention of it will be this: “As the Lord did at the Red Sea,” destroying the Egyptians, “so he will do at the torrents of Arnon,” destroying the Amorites. Moses spoke of the future: “he will do”; we speak of the past in this way: “he did.”

What follows—“The rocks bent down,” etc.—is likewise interpreted ambiguously. The Hebrews relate [Col. 1235D] that an immense multitude of Amorites laid ambushes for the Israelites in the valleys of the torrents and rocks of Arnon, in order to destroy the unsuspecting travellers; but the Lord crushed those lying hidden by rocks that bent down from both sides, so that the falling masses of rock extended into the Arnon and there rested, that is, came to an end.

Some said that the position of the Arnon is being described: since there are steep and very high rocks in the wilderness, they gradually slope downward, diminishing in height [Note: [Col. 1236A] Addition 1. A collapsing fall of a mountain, something seen in certain snowfalls; and it is called *labentia* from *labendo*, “falling.”], until they rest, that is, end, near the Arnon. It may be that some rocks of mountains—lower and smaller ones—bent down before the Israelites so that they might cross easily. Perhaps this was foretold in Joseph’s blessing: “Until the desire of the everlasting hills should come” (Gen. 49). And perhaps David said the same thing [Col. 1236A]: “The mountains leaped like rams,” etc. (Ps. 113).

## Chapter XXX. On the song at the well

From that place a well appeared to them—that is, from this place they came to another place where, at the Lord’s direction, they dug a well (Num. 21). Hence it is added: “For the princes, the leaders of the multitude, dug this well in the lawgiver,” that is, in the Lord. This, however, is not found in the Hebrew. And water rose up from the well until it overflowed above: perhaps as a sign that from then on they would fight, overcome their enemies in this way, and overwhelm them. Seeing this, Israel sang this song: “Rise up, O well,” etc.

## Chapter XXXI. On the death of Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan

[Col. 1236B]

Leaving that place, the people passed through several stopping-places and arrived as far as Bamoth (Num. 21). This is not the name of a stopping-place, but a valley in the region of Moab, on the summit of Pisgah, that is, beside that mountain [Note: [Col. 1236D] Addition 1. He explains what he had said: “a valley on the summit of Pisgah.”]. Or perhaps the mountain is so great that it has hills and valleys on its summit.

From there Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, asking him to grant passage through his land [Note: [Col. 1236D] Addition 2. Or at least around his land, as Esau and Moab had done; this is read in Deuteronomy.]. He refused; indeed, coming out with an army against Israel into the wilderness, he fought Israel and was struck by the edge of the sword, that is, in the encounter. Josephus says that very many of them perished of thirst; others, rushing to the river, were pinned to the ground by javelins; those fleeing to the walls were overtaken by slingers [Col. 1236C].

Sihon was therefore killed, and Israel took all his cities from Arnon as far as Jabbok [Note: [Col. 1236D] Addition 3. There are cities, one of which is the capital of the kingdom, the other its boundary.]. Among them Heshbon was the capital of the kingdom, and Israel lived in them. Josephus says that this land, situated between three rivers, had as it were the nature of an island and was exceedingly fertile. Arnon flows from the south; Jabbok from the north, descending into the Jordan; and the Jordan, to the west, gave it its name.

When Israel had crossed the river Jabbok and went up by the road of Bashan, Og king of Bashan met it at Edrei. They struck him and his people until total destruction, and possessed his land. Yet this land which they held beyond the Jordan was not part of the promised land; this is clear because Moses entered it [Col. 1236D]. “And they departed and encamped in the plains of Moab, where Jericho lies across the Jordan” (Num. 22).

## Chapter XXXII. On Balaam’s journey and the ass that spoke to him

Balak son of Zippor, then king in Moab, saw what Israel had done to the Amorite and was afraid. Calling together the elders of Midian, who were near his kingdom and his friends, he consulted them concerning what ought to be done, saying: “This people will destroy us, as an ox is accustomed to crop grass down to the roots” (Num. 22). By their counsel he sent to Balaam son of Beor, a diviner who lived by the river of the Ammonites, asking him to come and curse this people.

For they had heard that whomever Balaam blessed was blessed, and whomever he cursed was cursed. They had also heard that Israel prevailed not by bow and sword but by prayer poured out to its God; and it seemed expedient to them to contend with curses against prayers. When the elders of Moab and Midian came to Balaam, carrying in their hands the gifts of divination and explaining the reason for their journey, Balaam said to them: “Stay here this night, until I see what the Lord will say to me.” For he falsely claimed to be the Lord’s prophet [Col. 1237B], although in offering sacrifices he consulted demons. Perhaps he called “Lord” the demon that spoke to him.

In the night the Lord, caring for his people, said to him: “Do not go with them, nor curse this people, for it is blessed.” Rising in the morning, Balaam said that he had been forbidden by the Lord. Again Balak sent him more numerous and more honourable men, and promised greater and ampler gifts if he would curse the people. Balaam told them: “If Balak gave me his house full of gold, I could not change the word of the Lord. I beg you, stay here also this night.” And in the night the Lord said to him: “Rise, go with them; but only on condition that you do what I command you.”

In the morning he set out with them, mounted on an ass. “And the Lord was angry with him, and the angel [Col. 1237C] of the Lord stood in the way against Balaam, with a drawn sword.” For he had changed his purpose; seized by desire for the promised gifts, he was considering how to curse the people, although the Lord had forbidden it. Josephus seems to hold that, angry with him, the Lord said to him, as it were ironically, “Go with them.” Since Balaam did not understand this, the angel opposed him.

When the ass saw the angel, whom Balaam nevertheless did not see, she turned aside in fear into a field. Balaam beat her and brought her back to the path; again the angel stood in a narrow place between walls enclosing vineyards, and the frightened ass pressed herself against the wall and crushed the rider’s foot. But he beat her. Again the angel stood in a narrow place where she could turn neither right nor left [Col. 1237D]. The ass, afraid, fell beneath the feet of her rider. When he struck her sides violently with a staff, the Lord opened the ass’s mouth, and she said: “Why do you strike me? Behold, this is now the third time.” He answered: “You have mocked me. If only I had a sword, I would strike you!”

Accustomed as he was to marvels, he was not alarmed at the ass’s voice. “Immediately the Lord opened Balaam’s eyes; and he saw the angel standing in the way with a sword, and he worshipped him.” The angel said to him: “Your way is perverse before me; and unless the ass had turned aside, I would have killed you.” Balaam said: “I have sinned; and now, if my way is contrary to you, I will return.” The angel said: “Go, but beware lest you speak anything other than what I command you.”

## Chapter XXXIII. On Balaam’s divination and his prophecy

[Col. 1238A]

As he went, Balak met him at the extremities of the Moabites’ borders, received him magnificently, and gave him gifts (Num. 22). Balaam declared to him: “I cannot speak except what the Lord puts into my mouth.” Together they went up to a high place on the mountain, from which they looked upon the furthest part of the people. They were forty stadia away from the army of the Lord.

Balaam said to Balak: “Build here seven altars and prepare as many bulls and the same number of rams” (Num. 23). When they had both placed a bull and a ram upon an altar, Balaam said to the king: “Stand beside the burnt offering; I shall go, in case the Lord may meet me, and I shall tell you what he commands [Col. 1238B].” When he had departed, the Lord put words in his mouth. Returning before them all, having taken up his parable—or, as the Hebrew has it, having begun his discourse—he said: “How shall I curse a people whom the Lord has blessed? It shall dwell alone among the nations and shall not be reckoned,” that is, it shall be singular beyond all others and innumerable. “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last things be like theirs.”

Grieved, Balak said: “What are you doing?” He led him to another high place on Mount Pisgah, from which he could see another part of the people. According to the error of the Gentiles, Balak thought that all things were inherent in places and times, and that God, like a human being, could change. Having set up seven altars there according to the manner already described and placed the burnt offering upon them, the Lord again put words in Balaam’s mouth. Returning, he said: “There is no idol in Jacob, nor image in Israel. The Lord his God is with him. There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. He shall rise like a lion; like a lioness he shall not lie down until he devours the prey,” that is, the land of the Canaanites.

Then Balak said: “At least neither bless them nor curse them.” Again he led him up Mount Peor and set up seven altars. When burnt offerings had been placed upon each, Balaam did not go away as before to seek augury. Instead, raising his eyes, he saw Israel dwelling in tents according to its tribes; and, as the Spirit of God rushed upon him, he said, speaking of himself: “Balaam son of Beor has spoken: the man whose eye is darkened [Col. 1238D], the hearer of God’s words. How beautiful are your tents, O Jacob” (Num. 24).

The Hebrew and Origen’s translation have: “whose eye is unveiled.” Yet the sense is the same, because, while asleep, he saw in dreams the things he said. Thus the eye of the flesh was closed, and the eye of the mind unveiled. Hence it follows: “He who falls, and whose eyes are opened.” The Hebrew has more fully: “He who places himself,” that is, lies down in bed.

He also added an explicit prophecy concerning Saul: “His king shall be raised up because of Agag, and his kingdom shall be taken away.” This happened to Saul because he spared Agag, king of the Amalekites. Afterwards he addressed the people: “Whoever blesses you shall himself be blessed; whoever curses you shall be accounted under a curse.”

When Balak became angry, Balaam said that as he departed he would give him advice about what to do against this people. Again taking up his parable, he said: “A star shall arise from Jacob and a rod shall rise,” that is, Mary, “from Israel; and he shall strike the leaders of Moab and lay waste all the sons of Seth” [Col. 1239A]. As though to say: he shall lay waste the entire human race—namely, he shall crush the carnal in the good and destroy the wicked. For from Seth came the whole human race, including Noah; Cain’s children perished in the flood.

According to this oracle, the Magi are said to have come into Judaea when they saw the star (Matt. 2), and writings of Balaam on this subject are said then to have existed among them. He also prophesied that Israel would subject to itself the Idumeans and Amalek, who was the first to fight against them. He also prophesied that the Assyrians would ravage the land, including the Kenites, who were from a very strong stock, namely from Jethro. He added: “They shall come in triremes from Italy, overcome the Assyrians, ravage the Hebrews, and at the end they themselves shall perish.”

He foretold the monarchy of the Romans [Note: [Col. 1239B] Addition 1. Namely, when all kings were subject to the Roman Empire.] and, at the end of time, their destruction. Josephus says that he further prophesied that the whole world, including islands, would be their habitation forever. Since part of the prophecy has been fulfilled, we firmly believe that the rest will be fulfilled.

## Chapter XXXIV. How Israel was initiated into Baal-peor through love of women

[Col. 1239C] Balaam rose to return to his own place (Num. 24). As Balak took leave of him and his own people at the borders of Midian, Balaam gave them the advice to send around Israel’s tents young women whose beauty might deceive chastity, with saleable gifts [Note: [Col. 1239D] Addition 1. *Exenia*: travellers’ dishes or gifts; hence *xenodochium*, a hospice.]. They were to strive to entice again those young men who turned toward them, so as to make them transgress their ancestral laws and worship foreign gods. Thus, with their God angered against them, they would be humbled, at least for a short time; for while God was favourable to them, neither wars nor any pestilence could overcome them (Num. 25).

The Midianites did so. Yet some Moabite maidens were also sent, though few, because they are naturally ugly. At that time Israel was staying at Shittim, and it committed fornication with the daughters of Moab [Col. 1239D]. They invited the Israelites to their sacrifices; they ate their idol-sacrifices and worshipped their gods; and Israel was initiated [Note: [Col. 1240A] Addition 2. *Initio, -as*, not *initior*; whence: “I initiate a pupil into letters.”], that is, consecrated, to Baal-peor, the idol of the Midianites—the idol of sexual lust, whom Greece called Priapus.

The Lord, angered, said to Moses: “Take all the leaders of your people and hang them on gibbets before the sun, so that my wrath may be turned away from Israel” [Note: [Col. 1240A] Addition 3. Some punishment or plague inflicted by the Lord must be understood, although we do not have it explicitly stated.]. Perhaps he wished the tribal leaders to be hanged because they did not correct their subjects. Or rather, “the leaders” means the authors of this idolatry. Hence, immediately adding, Moses said to Israel’s judges: “Let each kill his neighbours who have been initiated to Baal-peor.”

## Chapter XXXV. On the zeal of Phinehas

[Col. 1240A]

Josephus relates that Zambri, a leader in the tribe of Simeon, had taken as wife the daughter of a certain powerful Midianite, named Corbi. At her urging, during a certain solemnity, when the other leaders were offering sacrifice to God, he himself did not sacrifice. Therefore, when Moses had assembled the congregation and reproved them—though not by name, because the crowd was implicated—Zambri confessed before all that he had taken a foreign woman, worshipped idols, and was not subject to the tyrannical laws which Moses had imposed upon himself [Col. 1240B]. Under the pretext of law and God, he said, Moses oppressed the people with a heavier servitude than the Egyptians did, depriving them of their own free choice of life.

Leaving, before the entire crowd which was weeping at the doors of the tabernacle of the Lord, he entered his wife’s tent. All marvelled that he had not died. Then Phinehas [Note: [Col. 1240C] Addition 1. Hence in the Psalm: “Phinehas stood and appeased, and the shaking ceased” (Ps. 105).], son of Eleazar, rose from the midst of the multitude. Taking a dagger, he entered after him into the brothel; finding them in intercourse, he pierced both in their genitals. The plague ceased, and about thirty-four thousand were killed—perhaps by the Lord through some preceding plague, which then ceased. But Josephus seems to mean that very many young men, inflamed by Phinehas’s zeal, struck down many thousands of the people.

The Lord said to Moses: “Let the Midianites know that you are enemies; strike them.” This happened afterwards, when Moses sent an army and struck the Midianites. Or perhaps, just as the children of Israel had been struck, the Lord also then wished the women who had overthrown them to be killed.

## Chapter XXXVI. The second census of fighting men

After the blood of the guilty had been shed, the Lord said to Moses and Eleazar: “Count the total number of the children of Israel able to go out to war, from twenty years old and upward, by their households and clans” (Num. 26). They did so [Col. 1240D], and six hundred and one thousand seven hundred and thirty were found. Among these was none of those who had been counted by Moses and Aaron except Joshua and Caleb. And the Lord said: “The land shall be divided among these; to the more numerous you shall give a greater part, and to the fewer a smaller.”

This is not to be understood of tribes or families, but of households [Note: [Col. 1240D] Addition 1. We continued this chapter thus: After the Lord had now destroyed, on account of their wickedness, all those earlier counted and fit for war [Col. 1241A], and after they had wandered in the wilderness for a long time because of their unbelief, the Lord commanded that those fit for war should be counted anew.]. For the land was divided equally among the tribes according to lots, and each tribe allotted equal portions by lot to the families [Note: [Col. 1241A] Addition 2. Things to be distributed by lot must be divided equally, lest by chance a smaller portion be assigned to the more numerous, and conversely.]. But the families divided their portions among the households without lot, according to the number of persons, giving larger and smaller shares [Note: [Col. 1241A] Addition 3. Recall what was distinguished above between tribe, family, and household, and you will understand what is said, which otherwise is not to be understood.]. The Levites too were counted, from one month old and upward: twenty-three thousand males.

## Chapter XXXVII. On the law of hereditary succession

[Col. 1241A]

The household of Salphaad, because he had left no son, was not counted (Num. 27). But when his five daughters heard that land would be given to those counted [Col. 1241B], they stood at the door of the tabernacle before Moses, Eleazar, and the entire multitude, and said: “Our father died in the wilderness for his own sin and had no male sons. Why is his name removed from the family? Give us a possession among our kinsmen.”

Moses referred their case to the Lord, who said: “The daughters of Salphaad ask for a just thing. Speak to the children of Israel: if a man dies without a son, the inheritance shall pass to his daughter.” This custom remains in force to this day. “But if he has no daughter, it shall pass to his brothers. If he has no brothers, it shall pass to his paternal uncles. If he has none of these, it shall pass to those who are nearest.”

## Chapter XXXVIII. On Joshua’s appointment

[Col. 1241C] “The Lord also said to Moses: ‘Go up Mount Abarim and look upon the land which I shall give to the children of Israel; afterwards you shall go to your people, for you shall not enter it.’ Moses said: ‘May the Lord, God of the spirit of all flesh, appoint a man over this multitude, lest the Lord’s people be like sheep without a shepherd.’ The Lord said: ‘Take Joshua and set him before Eleazar and the entire multitude, and lay your hand upon his head, so that it may obey him, as the whole congregation of the children of Israel obeyed you.’ And Moses did as the Lord commanded him” (Num. 27).

The entire multitude knew that Joshua would lead them after Moses’s death. Whether Moses went up then or later to see the land is uncertain [Col. 1241D]; but it is certain that he went up and was able to see part of the land. If he saw all of it, that was done miraculously.

## Chapter XXXIX. On libations

The Lord commanded Moses concerning the perpetual sacrifice and the sacrifices of the legal solemnities. But because no victim was offered without libations, something about these must first be said briefly. A libation or offering was fine flour mixed with oil and wine; these were burned with the victim, so that bread, wine, and flesh, as it were, might be offered to the Lord. A proper libation was prescribed for each victim.

For a lamb there was offered a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour, and a fourth part of a hin, or ephah, of wine (Num. 28). Ephah and cor [Col. 1242A; Note: [Col. 1242A] Addition 1. A cor contains thirty modii; an ephah, three measures of dry goods; a hin and a bath, of liquids. First a tenth was taken. Then the nine parts were tithed, and the remainder was tithed a third time; thus there were three tenths of one ephah. For a ram: two tenths of fine flour and a third part of a hin of wine. The libations for a he-goat were the same.
