If you ever read that for a lamb there is given “a tenth of a tenth” of fine flour, it must be understood of the customary tenth to be tithed, as though “a tenth of the tithing” or “a tithing tenth.” Or the tenth of an ephah itself was again tithed, and this tenth of the tenth was given for a lamb, according to some; or rather “a tenth of a tenth” means the same as “a tenth of an ephah.” For an ephah is a tenth part of a cor.] were measures for dry goods; hin and bath, for liquids. For a ram: two tenths of fine flour and a third part of a hin of wine. The libations for a he-goat were the same. For a calf: three tenths of fine flour and half a hin of wine. Perhaps the three tenths were whole tenths, from three ephahs or from one ephah.

## Chapter XL. On the perpetual sacrifice

[Col. 1242B]

First let us consider the perpetual sacrifice. The perpetual, or unfailing, sacrifice was offered daily at public expense (Num. 28). In the morning a year-old lamb was offered as a burnt offering with its libations, so that it might burn throughout the day as a sweet savour to the Lord. After it had been placed on the altar, the priest, with live coals and incense and after washing, entered the tabernacle and placed the coals with the incense on the altar of incense; this was called the completion of the sacrifice. Then he also extinguished four of the seven lamps.

In the evening another lamb was placed in the same manner [Col. 1242C]. Entering with incense, the priest lit all the lamps; and thus throughout the night there was on the altar a sweet savour to the Lord. The evening sacrifice, however, was better and richer than the morning one, because often several additional offerings were placed upon it during the day. It was therefore said to be more pleasing to the Lord, because we call what is richer more pleasing; for it signified the Lord’s death, which took place in the evening.

Some report that these lambs were supplied at the priests’ expense. Josephus, however, says they were at public expense; he also specifies the daily offering at the priests’ expense. For on the days of his course a priest offered an *assarium* of flour mixed with oil and hardened by slight baking, half in the morning and half in the evening upon the altar.

In this manner the Church offers the Lord praises and compline in the morning and evening—or rather, at Prime and Compline, confession for mutual prayer—as a perpetual sacrifice, because our sacrifice to God is a contrite and humbled spirit (Ps. 50) [Col. 1242D].

## Chapter XLI. On the Sabbath and its offerings

There were seven legal solemnities: the Sabbath, the New Moon, Passover, Pentecost, the Feast of Trumpets, the Feast of Propitiation, and Scenopegia, the Feast of Tabernacles. Sabbath means “rest,” and it may be called the Lord’s feast. While the other feasts were instituted and named from some event or activity connected with them, this one is called Sabbath because God rested on it. Perhaps this is why it has two privileges: on it food may not be prepared, nor may one travel more than a thousand paces.

This feast is called legal, not because the Sabbath had been observed before the Law, even by certain foreign nations, but because under the first Law it was observed by command. On that day, besides the perpetual sacrifice, two unblemished year-old lambs were offered as a burnt offering with their libations (Num. 28) [Col. 1243A].

## Chapter XLII. On the New Moon

*Neomenia* means “newness of the moon.” For Greek *neos* means “new,” and *mene* means “moon.” Since the Jews, by the Law, used lunar cycles as months in their observances, they called the day of the new moon the legal Kalends; among them it was a feast day. On that day they offered two calves, one ram, seven year-old lambs, each with its libations, and a he-goat for the removal of sin with its libations: all these as a burnt offering (Num. 28) [Col. 1243B].

## Chapter XLIII. On Passover

On the fourteenth day of the first month, in the evening, they ate the paschal lamb; that night was called *Phase* (Num. 28), that is, “Passage,” for the reasons given above. It was also called *Pascha*, that is, “sacrifice.” On the following day the Feast of Unleavened Bread began, extending for seven days. Its first and last days were solemn feast days, free from all servile work.

Ezekiel adds matters concerning the feast of the first day of April and elsewhere concerning the tenth day, on which the lamb was taken (Ezek. 45, 46). Hence the first month is customarily compared with the seventh in the solemnities. Perhaps Moses passed this over for brevity’s sake. Or many things were added to enlarge God’s worship, which Ezekiel sets forth, as on the Sabbath concerning the opening of the gates and the prince’s prayer [Col. 1243C].

After the first solemn day—that is, on the sixteenth lunar day—they roasted fresh ears of grain in fire and offered to the Lord, in the manner of crushed spelt, grains rubbed by hand, one *assarium*. The priest burned a handful, or one drachma, of this upon the altar; the remainder was his. Because of this offering, some thought that this feast was called not only the Feast of Unleavened Bread but also the Feast of New Things. They err because they read that Nisan is sometimes called the month of new things.

Josephus says that seven weeks were counted from this sixteenth day, immediately after which came Pentecost. Others say that they were counted from the day after the Sabbath, which fell in the days of Unleavened Bread, because the letter of the history seems to say this [Col. 1243D]. Others say that they were counted from the first day of Unleavened Bread itself, lest more than fifty days be found between Passover and Pentecost. During these seven days, on each day, the same victims as at the New Moon were offered as burnt offerings with their libations.

## Chapter XLIV. On Pentecost
Pentecost means “fiftieth.” For *pentacon* is “fifty” in Greek, and in Hebrew *Asarta*, or Pentecost. The fifty-day period itself, when completed, with the final day imminent, was called the feast of Pentecost, that is, the day following fifty days. [Note: [Col. 1244B] Addition 1. Accordingly you find: “When the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled” (Acts II).] It was observed in remembrance of the giving of the Law, which was given on the fiftieth day after the departure from Egypt. The same solemnity was called the Feast of Weeks [Col. 1244A] (Num. XXVIII), because, as stated, after seven weeks had been counted from the day after the Sabbath of Unleavened Bread, it took place. [Note: [Col. 1244B] Addition 2. The more certain opinion is that Pentecost falls on the fiftieth day from the first day of Unleavened Bread, and its second day on the fiftieth day from the second; on that second day new loaves were offered, just as grain was offered on the second day of Unleavened Bread. Thus two fiftieth days are counted in the reading.]

But if we wish to follow Josephus, we shall say that “Sabbath” here means the first solemn day of Unleavened Bread. It was also called the Feast of Firstfruits, because then, from the new crops, [Note: [Col. 1244B] Addition 3. Three firstfruits of crops were offered to the Lord: those to be gathered, those to be eaten, and those to be stored. Those to be gathered were offered in sheaves, at Passover; those to be eaten, in loaves, at Pentecost; and of those stored away, at most a fortieth part and at least a tenth part was given.] two loaves, each of two *assarii*, made from dried parched grain according to Josephus, and leavened, were offered. Therefore nothing from them was placed upon the altar. With them two lambs were offered, solely for the food of the priests; and none of these things was allowed to remain until the next day. This too was a feast of seven days, and on each day the same victims were offered as at the New Moon and during the days of Unleavened Bread, together with their libations. Yet Josephus seems to say that three bulls, [Col. 1244B] two rams, and fourteen lambs were then sacrificed.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the Feast of Trumpets

[Col. 1244C]

On the first day of the seventh month there was a double solemnity: the New Moon and the Feast of Blasting, or of Trumpets (Num. XXIX). Hence: “Blow the trumpet at the New Moon” (Ps. LXXX). On this occasion they sounded trumpets made from animal horns, because on that day Isaac was delivered from being sacrificed, an animal being substituted for him. It was also called the Feast of Sevenths, or the Sabbath of Months, because this seventh month was almost wholly solemn. On that day, besides the offerings of the New Moon, one bull, one ram, and seven yearling lambs were offered as burnt offerings, together with a goat for sin, with their libations. It is reported that the Jews introduced [Col. 1244D] the use of candles, in order to signify by fire the sacrifice of Isaac that had been prepared. Likewise, more recent people transferred candles to the tenth day, which perhaps concerns the dead because of the hope of resurrection.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the Feast of Atonement

On the tenth day of the same month was the Feast of Atonement (Num. XXIX), because on that day Moses returned to them, reporting that God had been appeased concerning the offense of the molten calf. [Note: [Col. 1245A] Addition 1. Above, in different chapters of Exodus: “And the Lord said to Moses” (Num. XXXII).] On that day men, beasts of burden, and children of seven years fasted, from evening to evening, in remembrance of the dead. Hence it was also called the Day of Affliction. It was likewise called the Day of Expiation, because on that day the tabernacle and altar were expiated by the blood of the red heifer, as stated above. Ashes were also made from it for the expiation of the unclean; [Col. 1245A] and they themselves were cleansed from the sins of that year by the sending away of the scapegoat. The offering of that day was one bull, one ram, seven yearling lambs, and a goat for sin, with their libations.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Scenopegia

On the fifteenth day of the same month was *Scenopegia*, meaning “the setting up of tents” (Num. XXIX). During it they dwelt for seven days beneath shelters, in remembrance of the forty years during which they lived in tents in the wilderness. Hence it is commonly called the Feast of Tabernacles. It was prolonged for seven days, the first and last of which were solemn. [Col. 1245B] The eighth day was also solemn, not because it belonged to Scenopegia, but because on that day they assembled to make a collection, perhaps for the use of the poor or for other common purposes.

Thus Scenopegia is sometimes read as a feast of eight days. But those fathers did not keep an octave. It is also reported that, during the four intervening days from the tenth day until this feast, the Hebrews observed fasts. Josephus reported that during these seven days they carried in their hands branches of myrtle and willow, palm-tops, and twigs of the Persian apple tree. An offering from all the fruits of the earth was made to the Lord in thanksgiving.

The offering for the seven days was as follows. On the first day, thirteen bulls, two rams, and fourteen yearling lambs were offered as burnt offerings [Col. 1245C], together with a goat for sin, with their libations. The same offering of rams, lambs, and goat was made on each following day; but one was subtracted daily from the number of bulls. On the second day, twelve; on the third, eleven; on the fourth, ten; on the fifth, nine; on the sixth, eight; on the seventh, seven. On the eighth day, which was solemn, one ram, one bull, and seven yearling lambs were offered as burnt offerings, together with a goat for sin, with their libations. Perhaps the number of bulls was reduced during the seven days so that their total would be seventy, in remembrance of those who entered Egypt in seventy souls.

These are the burnt-offerings at the seven solemnities, and they were made from public funds. This did not cause [Col. 1245D] the continual sacrifice, nor voluntary or required victims, to cease. Note that the three solemnities which lasted seven days were called the principal ones. And a Sabbath falling within those days was called the Sabbath of Sabbaths, as it were, the Sabbath of festivals. The Hebrews added other festivals on account of various events, such as the Dedication and *Phurim*, that is, the feast of Esther; but these are not called legal—that is, they were not instituted in the Law.

Note that the three solemnities mentioned above—Passover, Pentecost, and Scenopegia—are called *ceremonies*, either from candles, that is, lights; or from *caries* (“decay”) and *mene* (“deficiency”), because then defilements ought to fail in us, as it were *carimeniae*; or from abstaining from *munia*, that is, servile duties, as it were *carimoniae*; or from Ceres, to whom [Col. 1246A] the highest reverence was paid when Roman sacred rites were brought there after the city had been captured by the Gauls.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On Vows

The Lord also added concerning women’s vows: “A widow or divorced woman shall fulfill whatever they have vowed or bound themselves to by oath” (Num. XXX). A daughter or wife is bound by a vow or oath unless her father or husband objects as soon as he hears it. For if he objects immediately, their promises are void. But if, having heard, he keeps silent and later objects, he himself shall bear the guilt. A man, however, shall fulfill every oath or vow, except perhaps one concerning continence.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the Destruction of Midian and the Division of the Spoil

[Col. 1246B]

“Again the Lord spoke to Moses: ‘Take vengeance for the children of Israel upon the Midianites, and then you shall be gathered to your people’” (Num. XXXI). Therefore Moses armed a thousand chosen men from each tribe—twelve thousand in all—and set Phinehas son of Eleazar over them. He also gave them the sacred vessels and trumpets for sounding. They set out and defeated their enemies. They killed five kings and all their men; they consumed cities, villages, and forts with fire; they also killed Balaam with the sword; and they carried off as spoil the women and children, livestock, and all household goods.

When they were returning, Moses, Eleazar, and all the princes of the Synagogue went out to meet them beyond [Col. 1246C] the camp. Seeing the women, Moses angrily said to them: “Why have you spared the women? Are not these the very ones who deceived the children of Israel? Kill all who have known men, every male; but preserve the virgins.” And they did so, and thirty-two thousand virgins were preserved.

Moses said: “Because you have sinned, you shall be unclean. Those who killed or touched the dead shall remain outside the camp for seven days, and shall be purified on the third and seventh days with water of sprinkling. The spoil which you carried off shall likewise be purified. Gold, and whatever can pass through fire, shall be purified by fire. But whatever cannot endure fire shall be cleansed with water of expiation.”

And the Lord said to Moses: “Take the total of what was captured, from human beings to livestock, and divide the spoil equally [Col. 1246D] between those who fought and the remaining multitude. From the share of those who fought, set apart for the Lord one life out of every five hundred, and give them to Eleazar. From the half belonging to the multitude, take every fiftieth head and give them to the Levites.”

When this had been done, the commanders of the army came to Moses and said: “We have counted the number of fighting men whom you gave us, and not one of them is missing. Therefore we offer as gifts to the Lord whatever gold we were able to find in the spoil: anklets, [Note: [Col. 1246D] Addition 1. From *peri*, meaning “around,” and *scele*, [Col. 1247A] meaning “arm,” they are called *periscelides*, as it were an ornament of the arm.] bracelets, rings, armlets, and necklaces, that you may entreat the Lord for us.” Moses and Eleazar received the gold and brought it into the tabernacle.

## CHAPTER L. On the Allotment of Two Tribes and a Half

[Col. 1247A]

Now the children of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh possessed very great quantities of livestock (Num. XXXII). Seeing that Amorite territory, Bashan, and Gilead were suitable for feeding livestock, they asked Moses to give this land to them. But Moses, thinking that they had sought this out from fear of battle and labor, called them wicked because, while their brothers stood in hardship, they themselves wished to live in luxury.

They promised, however, that they would place their women and children in safe locations, build sheepfolds for the sheep and stables for the beasts of burden, while they themselves would go armed before their brothers until they had brought them into their own territories. On this [Col. 1247B] condition they received the land of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. Moreover, the children of Machir son of Manasseh obtained Gilead. Jair, son of Manasseh, captured its villages and called them Havvoth-jair, that is, “the villages of Jair.”

## CHAPTER LI. Catalogue of the Forty-two Encampments

Here is set down the catalogue of encampments from the departure out of Egypt (Num. XXXIII). Before the crossing of the Red Sea there were four: Rameses, Succoth, Etham, and Pi-hahiroth. From the Red Sea to Sinai there were eight: Marah, Elim, Yam-suph, meaning the Red Sea, or Sea of Reeds—for *yam* means “sea,” and *suph* “red” or “reedy”; and it could have been the Lake of Reeds, because the Hebrews call every collection [Col. 1247C] of waters a sea—then after Yam-suph, the wilderness of Sin, Dophkah, Alush, Rephidim, and the wilderness of Sinai.

From Mount Sinai to Kadesh there were twenty-one: Graves of Craving, Hazeroth, Rithmah, Rimmon-perez, [Col. 1248A] Libnah, Rissah, Kehelathah, Mount Shepher, Haradah, Makheloth, Tahath, Terah, Mithkah, Hashmonah, Moseroth, Bene-jaakan, Mount Gidgad, Jotbathah, Ebronah, Ezion-geber, and Kadesh. From Kadesh to the plains of Moab there were nine: Mount Hor, Zalmonah, Punon, Oboth, Iye-abarim, Dibon-gad, Almon-diblathaim, the mountains of Abarim, and the plains of Moab.

## CHAPTER LII. On the Cities of the Levites and Their Suburbs

Again the Lord spoke to Moses and marked out the boundaries of the promised land from east and west, south and north (Num. XXXIV). He named the princes of the tribes who, after crossing the Jordan, were to divide the land with Joshua and Eleazar. He commanded that the Levites, dispersed among all the tribes, should have [Col. 1248B] cities in which to live; and that, outward from the walls all around, they should possess a thousand paces of land, in which there would be pasturelands for feeding their livestock (Num. XXXV). Six of these cities were to be cities of refuge, three beyond the Jordan and three on this side, concerning which Deuteronomy speaks (Deut. XIX).

## CHAPTER LIII. On Marriage within One’s Tribe

“The children of Machir, son of Manasseh, came to Moses and said: ‘The daughters of our brother Zelophehad have an allotment with us by command of the Lord. If, therefore, they marry men of another tribe, because their children will follow their father’s tribe, our inheritance will be diminished and the distribution of allotments thrown into confusion at the Jubilee’” (Num. XXXVII).

On account of the daughters of Zelophehad, therefore, this law was promulgated by the Lord through [Col. 1248C] Moses: all men shall take wives from their own tribe and kindred, so that inheritance may remain within families; tribes are not to be mingled, but are to remain as they were separated by the Lord, etc.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF DEUTERONOMY

[Col. 1247]

## CHAPTER I. Preface

[Col. 1247C]

The fifth and final division of this history is called *Hadde debarim*, meaning “These are the words.” In Greek it is called *Deuteronomy*, that is, “second law”: for *deuteron* means “second,” and *nomia*, “law.” Some, in error, have used this name to say that there are two laws: one given by God, contained in the preceding books, and another given by Moses, contained in this book. To support their error, they observe that in many passages above it is written of the former: “The Lord spoke to Moses and to all Israel,” whereas of this one it is said: “Moses spoke.” They also said that many things are read here which are not found above, some apparently contrary; and that this would not happen if this were a repetition of what preceded.

The truer judgment is that this Pentateuch is but one Law, which the Apostle and others often call the Law of Moses rather than the Law of God. The Hebrew also calls these five books *thorath*, that is, “Law.” Nor is this book called the second law for any reason except that what was stated before is here repeated, [Col. 1248C] as it were, as a law repeated. Three things are repeated here for three reasons: commandments and ceremonies, to commend them to memory and confirm them; God’s benefits, to strengthen love of God in them; and the punishments they endured when they murmured, [Col. 1248D] to instill fear.

If in this repetition some contradiction with the preceding material seems to be present on the surface of the words, nevertheless none exists in meaning. There were also those who said that this book was made by Joshua after crossing the Jordan, because at the beginning it is read: “These are the words which Moses spoke beyond the Jordan” (Deut. I). For Scripture customarily says “beyond the Jordan” or “on this side of the Jordan” according to the position of the promised land. Yet it is called the book of Moses or Joshua because Joshua committed to writing what Moses transmitted orally. Jerome also seems to hold that Joshua wrote a large part of this book. It seems truer that it was written by Moses, who speaks of himself as of another person. Or Ezra added this at the beginning, [Col. 1249A] just as he did at the end concerning Moses’ death—especially since near the end of the book we read: “Moses wrote this law” (Deut. XXXI), and shortly thereafter: “After Moses had written the words of this law in a scroll, he commanded the Levites: ‘Take this book and place it at the side of the ark of the covenant’” (ibid.). It is read that, a long time afterward, Deuteronomy was found in Jerusalem in the ark.

## CHAPTER II. Epilogue with Additions and Explanations

In the fortieth year after the children of Israel departed from Egypt, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, Moses, seeing that the day of his death was approaching, spoke to all the children of Israel and began to expound the Law. According to Josephus, he assembled them by the [Col. 1249B] Jordan, at the place where the city of Abidal now stands, the place of palms (Num. I).

As we follow Moses’ recapitulation, we shall omit what has already been stated; we shall say something about the additions, and we shall mention and resolve matters which seem contradictory. Thus Moses says in recapitulating: [Note: [Col. 1249C] Addition 1. Above, in Exodus, chapter XVIII: “Now Jethro went out.”] “I said to you at that time: ‘I cannot bear your affairs alone; choose from among yourselves wise men, and I shall appoint them as commanders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.’” This seems contrary to what was stated earlier. For above it was said that this was done by Jethro’s advice; but both took place. First, at the advice of his father-in-law, Moses privately decided to do it; afterward, he carried it out with the authority and consent of the people.

Likewise, where Moses says here, [Col. 1249C] “You said to me: ‘Let us send men to examine the land,’” whereas above the Lord is read to have said, “Send men” (Num. XIII), there is no contradiction. For at the people’s suggestion Moses consulted the Lord, who said, “Send.” In order also to strengthen their faintheartedness, Moses repeated the account of the victory over Og king of Bashan (Deut. III), who had resisted them, being of the race of giants; and as proof of his size, his iron bed is shown at Rabbath of the children of Ammon, nine cubits long and four broad.

## CHAPTER III. On the Cities of Refuge beyond the Jordan

Moses set apart three cities of refuge beyond [Col. 1249D] the Jordan: Bezer in the tribe of Reuben, Ramoth-gilead in the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan in the tribe of Manasseh (Deut. IV). Their use was this: if anyone killed a person unintentionally, he fled to one of them, and there was safe from the relatives of the slain person. For if the person who was to avenge the shed blood found him outside the boundaries of one of these cities, he could strike the killer with impunity. The fugitive remained there until reconciliation with the relatives, or until the death of the high priest; at that point all such fugitives returned safely to their homes. Yet if the relatives of the slain wished to charge him with having killed deliberately, and proved this before the citizens of his city, he was handed over to them to be killed.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Commandment of Love

[Col. 1250A]

Moses also added: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength.” [Note: [Col. 1251A] Addition 1. Elsewhere ten commandments are set forth. But note that these are contained under these two: the first of them embraces three, and the second contains seven.] (Deut. VI).

He also added, when repeating the account of manna: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. VIII). Here he called every kind of human food “bread.” Scripture is accustomed to use “bread” for food; and the sense is: Do not wonder that the Lord gave you unfamiliar food, for human life is not established with God only by customary foods; by his word alone he can create new things by which human beings may live.

Among the benefits Moses also added that for forty years in the wilderness their clothes had not worn out [Col. 1250B] with age, nor had their sandals become worn; and that they escaped the surrounding fire-breathing serpents, which perhaps for this reason he previously called fiery, and scorpions and dipsads (Deut. VIII), which in Latin are called *situlae* (“buckets”), because they kill a person through thirst and are so small that when trodden upon they can scarcely be seen. Their poison kills before it can be felt, and one who is dying feels no pain. Yet it is called *situla* by contrariety: the vessel called a *situla* takes thirst away, whereas this creature brings it. So too *pharetra* (“quiver”), which brings death, is called *feretrum*, because it bears—or carries away—the dead.

To show as well what necessity would rest upon them to observe the Lord’s commandments in the promised land, he added that this land was not like Egypt, which is made fruitful by the benefit of a river, where waters are channelled through gardens [Col. 1250C] for irrigation. Rather, it was mountainous and low-lying country, awaiting rain from heaven; and therefore God had to be worshipped there all the more, so that he might give rain in its seasons: the early rain, namely in autumn, spring, or winter, to nourish the seed once sown; and the latter rain, for growth in spring or summer.

Moses also added concerning the boundaries of the promised land: “Every place which the sole of your foot has trodden shall be yours: from the wilderness, which is in the south, and Lebanon, which is in the north, and the great river Euphrates, which is in the east, to the Mediterranean shall be your boundaries” (Deut. II), that is, the sea called the Tyrrhenian. He also added that after crossing the Jordan, [Col. 1250D] when they came out, they should pronounce the blessings and curses written in this book in the following manner: six tribes, the elder ones, should ascend Mount Gerizim with the priests and Levites, and six younger ones Mount Ebal opposite them. Those on Gerizim should pronounce all blessings upon the observers of the Law, and those on Ebal should answer, “Amen.” Then the priests and Levites with the other six tribes should ascend Ebal, and together pronounce all curses against transgressors, while those on Gerizim should answer, “Amen.”

Note that, when he lists the nations whom they drove from the promised land, he almost everywhere names six: the Canaanite, Amorite, Perizzite, Jebusite, Hivite, and Hittite. But in this recapitulation he names a seventh, the Girgashite. Note also that Abraham was promised that ten nations would be destroyed, and ten were indeed then there. But when the children of Israel came there, three had already been destroyed: the sons of Lot destroyed the giants, the sons of Esau the Horites, and the Cappadocians part of the Hivites.

## CHAPTER V. On the Second Tithe

Moses added that they were not permitted to eat in their own towns the tithe, the firstborn of livestock, the firstfruits of their labors, vowed offerings, or voluntary offerings, but only before the Lord in the place which the Lord should choose; there they were to eat them with wife, children, male servant, female servant, and the Levite who lived in the same place (Deut. XII). In this command [Col. 1251B] the Levites, to whom the aforementioned things were due, seem to be defrauded. Therefore some say that this happened once only, namely when they first obtained the land. For then they offered the aforesaid things to the Lord, and afterward gave them to the Levites. But this is nothing, because the Lord had not yet chosen a place for himself in the promised land.

Others say that this was done every year as follows: the person who gave the tithe to the Levites separated for himself the first portion of the entire tithe—for example, the first basket of grain, the first amphora of wine or oil—and carried that small part of the tithes with him to Jerusalem, where he feasted on it before the Lord. They infer this because this tithe is commanded to be placed in a basket, which is a small vessel and could not hold a true tithe. But they provide no explanation here concerning firstborn animals, firstfruits, vowed, and voluntary offerings.

Therefore the more correct teaching of the Hebrews is this: every year Hebrews made two tithings of their possessions. They separated the first for the Levites. Of this it is said: “Let alms sweat in your hand until you find the righteous person to whom you should give,” that is, the one to whom you owe it. Then they tithed the remaining nine parts again; this second tithe they kept for themselves. From it, three times a year when they went up to Jerusalem, they made offerings and feasts for themselves and their household, inviting the Levite who lived with them and who likewise went up with them. For the same uses they reserved for themselves the second animal after the firstborn, as it were a second firstborn; likewise, after the firstfruits, they set aside an equal amount for themselves as it were second firstfruits. [Col. 1251D]

Whoever wished to spend more than these things at those three feasts set aside something further from his possessions and reserved it with the aforesaid things, vowing it to the Lord. Moreover, at those solemnities some people voluntarily spent certain things, besides those already mentioned, in honor of the Lord; and Moses commanded that these secondary offerings be carried to the holy place and eaten before the Lord (Deut. XIV and XV). Those who lived farther away, however, were allowed to sell these things in their own place, carry the price with them, and buy in Jerusalem whatever their soul desired.

Further, in the third year, after subtracting the two tithes as described, they made a third tithing for the uses of the poor. They kept it at home, so as to have something to give to the needy stranger, resident alien, orphan, and widow, [Col. 1252A] and also to Levites if they were in need. They spent none of this upon their own uses; and of this it is said: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke VI).

He also adds that if even a brother, wife, son, or intimate friend persuaded anyone to idolatry—perhaps because of the abundance enjoyed by the Gentiles—he was not to conceal him; rather, once convicted or confessed, the people were to stone him, and the person whom he had persuaded was to be the first to lay hands upon him. In the same way, city was to rise against city and destroy it if it persuaded others to depart from the worship of God.

He also forbade cuts and baldness to be made over the dead (Deut. XIV), that is, the shedding of one’s own blood, cutting of hair, and sacrifice to the dead, as the heathen do. [Col. 1252B] He also forbade the eating of carrion, but added that they could give or sell such things, which were unclean to themselves, to strangers and resident aliens, because other nations lawfully eat many things forbidden to the Hebrews.

To the seventh year of the land’s rest Moses also added that a creditor was not to demand a debt from a Hebrew debtor only. He could demand it from a stranger; and for that reason he called that year a year of remission, though not the remission of the Jubilee. For at the Jubilee debts were forgiven; in this year they merely deferred demanding them.

He forbade ploughing with firstborn oxen and shearing the fleeces of firstborn animals. By this he indicates that nothing from the firstborn was to be taken or used for private purposes, because it belonged to the Levites. If, however, a firstborn had a blemish, it could be eaten in its own place, but not before [Col. 1252C] the Lord.

Repeating the matter of Pentecost, Moses says: “You shall count seven weeks from the day on which you put the sickle into the grain, and you shall celebrate the feast day of weeks to the Lord your God” (Deut. XVI). As Jerome says, the Hebrews observe this neither according to the letter nor according to the spirit, for Pentecost would not then occur on the same day: some reap earlier and others later, according to the conditions of their regions. There were also those who said that each farmer counted fifty days from the first day of his own harvest, and on that day prepared a solemn feast for himself and his household and observed a festival. They did not regard it as the legal Pentecost, but celebrated it as a solemn day, as it were, for all their gathered crops.

Josephus reported that on the fifteenth moon of Passover, namely the solemn day of Unleavened Bread, they offered rubbed grain to the Lord. This was the first putting of the sickle into the grain, and from the sixteenth moon they counted seven weeks, after which they observed Pentecost. [Note: [Col. 1252D] Addition 1. In truth, the first day of Pentecost is the fiftieth day from the first day of Unleavened Bread; on the second day of that feast two new loaves were offered. Thus understand two fiftieth days: in the first case, the first day of Pentecost; in the second, the second day of the same feast.] Yet some say, as was stated above, that seven weeks ought to be counted from the Lord’s Day occurring during the feast of Unleavened Bread, because Leviticus reads: “You shall count from the day after the Sabbath” (Lev. XXIII).

## CHAPTER VI. On Appeal by the People to the High Priest

[Col. 1253A]

He also commanded that the judges of the cities sit in the gates, as though judging matters within and without, concerning the boundaries of the city; that a person put to death by them should perish on the testimony of two or three witnesses; and that the hands of the witnesses should be first against him (Deut. XVI). If those judges happened to be uncertain about a judgment, they were to go up to the high priest, and whatever he judged was to be done. If anyone did not obey his judgment, he was to be killed.

Josephus says of these city judges that seven were chosen in each city, esteemed for virtue and zeal for justice. Two men of Levitical stock were assigned to each of them as assistants. They did not admit women’s testimony [Col. 1253B] because of fickleness, nor that of slaves because of lowliness of spirit, on account of which they could easily be corrupted by fear or profit. In appeals the high priest was not permitted to judge without a prophet and the elders of the place which the Lord had chosen.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Justice of a King Chosen by Them

He also added that if at some time they established a king for themselves, they should choose not a foreigner but a member of their own tribe, who should ordain nothing without the counsel of the high priest and elders (Deut. XVII); that in leisure he should always read Deuteronomy; that he should not multiply wives for himself, lest they turn him from the right way; that he should not multiply horses or great stores of wealth, lest, becoming more powerful, he become cruel toward his subjects; [Col. 1253C] and that he should not alter the boundaries of his own or another’s land. For one who changes the boundaries of lands is not far from transgressing laws.

Solomon greatly violated this command, boasting that he had left as much gold and silver in Jerusalem as he had found bronze and iron there. Yet at last, as they report, he repented; this will be discussed later.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Rejection of Sorcerers

He forbade them also to have among them diviners, that is, inspectors of entrails at altars for knowing the future; interpreters of dreams; augurs, that is, observers of birds’ movements or cries; sorcerers, that is, those sacrificing children to demons or at least performing purifications; enchanters, that is, illusionists who deceive by looking; [Col. 1253D] Pythons, that is, ventriloquists who speak through an evil spirit, so called from Python, that is, Apollo; diviners, that is, haruspices, inspectors of the stars; nor necromancers, who summon the dead by sacrifices or incantations. For God would raise up for them a prophet from their own nation, and they were to hear him.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Law of Retaliation

Concerning the law of retaliation, on the occasion of a false witness, he added that if, after most diligent inquiry, they discovered a false witness, they should do to him what he had intended to do to his neighbor: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, foot for foot (Deut. XIX).

## CHAPTER X. On Removing the Fearful and Anxious from the Army

[Col. 1254A]

He also added concerning an army going forth to battle that first the priest should exhort the army not to fear its enemies and to hope only in the Lord, not in weapons and its own strength. Next, the commander of each company was to speak and say: “Whichever of you is fearful, let him return, lest, terrified himself, he make his brothers afraid.” He also commanded that those anxious about unfinished affairs which they had left behind should return (Deut. XX).

He specified three affairs to which human affection is most strongly attached, saying: “What man is there who has built a new house and has not dedicated or inaugurated it? Let him return, lest perhaps he die in battle and another dedicate it. What man is there [Col. 1254B] who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him return, lest perhaps he die and another take her. What man is there who has planted a vineyard and has not yet made it common, so that all may eat of it? Let him return, lest perhaps he die and another perform his office?”

This is understood as follows. If a newly planted vineyard bore fruit before its fourth year, it was unclean, because nature seemed to have exerted force before the proper time; and it was not lawful either to offer its firstfruits to God or to eat anything from it. In the fourth year it was harvested for the Lord. A person carried all the fruit of that year to the holy city, along with the second tithe of other crops, to feast on them before the Lord. In the fifth year the person became master of the vineyard and harvested [Col. 1254C] for himself. In the sixth year and thereafter it became, as it were, common to all, according to their custom. Travelers were allowed to enter vineyards and orchards and satisfy themselves as from their own property, but it was not lawful to carry anything out. Nor did those whom they met forbid grape-gatherers to taste from what they were carrying to the winepress.

Another translation is straightforward: “What man is there who planted a vineyard and has not drunk from its young growth?” etc.

## CHAPTER XI. That They Were Not to Make a Covenant with the Nations

He also added that they were not to make a covenant with the nations of the promised land, but that they were to be utterly exterminated (Deut. XX). In this they later sinned grievously. But with neighboring nations they were to be peaceable, insofar as possible, and allied. He also added that in a siege [Col. 1254D] they were not to cut down fruit-bearing trees to make siege engines.

Likewise, if a slain person were found but the killer was unknown, the elders of the nearest city were to kill a heifer and, after washing their hands over it, swear before the priests to their own innocence (Deut. XXI). When going out to battle, if anyone saw among the captives a beautiful woman, virgin or already married, and wanted to have her as a wife, he was not to enter her bed until she had shaved her head, cut her nails, and, putting on mourning attire, mourned for thirty days for her parents and friends whom she had lost in war, so that, having at length had her fill of grief, she might turn to the wedding feast. Then the man might humble her. But if he had had his fill of her and she no longer pleased him, he was to send her away free. For he was not permitted either [Col. 1255A] to reduce her again to slavery or to sell her to another.

He also commanded that an evildoer hanging on a gibbet be taken down that same day and that the corpse be buried the same day, because everyone hanging on wood was accursed; that is, it was enough punishment that he had undergone a shameful and accursed death, lest punishment be extended beyond what was right. He also said it was abominable before the Lord for either a woman to wear male clothing or a man female clothing.

## CHAPTER XII. On Those Who Were Not Permitted to Enter the Church of God
He further added, concerning the distinction among those entering the Church of God, as follows: “No eunuch whose testicles have been crushed or cut off, nor anyone whose male organ has been severed, shall enter the Church of God; nor shall a mamzer enter, even to the tenth generation. Ammonites and Moabites shall not enter after the tenth generation, for ever, because these peoples, related to the Hebrews when they came out of Egypt, met them only with bread, although they knew that they were suffering thirst in the desert; and they hired against them Balaam son of Beor” (Deut. 23).

Moreover, very many of them were led astray by the women of those same peoples. “Entrance into the Church” may be understood as entrance into the court [Note: [Col. 1256A] Addition 1. There were four courts: one for the Levites; a second for clean Israelites, who were not rendered unclean by contact with the dead or otherwise; a third for the unclean; and a fourth for Gentiles.] of the clean, from which some were barred forever and others temporarily—namely, either until some limit of their lifetime, of whom elsewhere, or until the limit of their descendants, which is the matter here.

The Hebrew more correctly states that to enter the Church of God is to take a wife from among the daughters of Israel and thus to become, in oneself and in one’s lineage, part of the people of God. Yet on this interpretation the preceding provision concerning the eunuch seems pointless, since he cannot take a wife; but neither, if he wished to take an Israelite wife for money, inheritance, or any other reason, would this be permitted him. Perhaps this is because, unless he had named only the mamzer, the spurius and the nothus would not have been excluded from the Church. A mamzer, properly speaking, is one born of a prostitute; a spurius, one born of a concubine because of the filth of incontinence; a nothus, one born of an adulteress. For he seems not to be a true son of marriage, just as we speak of “spurious fevers” which appear to be genuine quartan fevers or the like, but are not.

Therefore a mamzer shall not marry the daughters of Israel; nor may his son, even by a lawful wife, nor his grandson, do so until the tenth descendant. At that point he might enter the Church [Col. 1255D] of God, because the memory of the ancient disgrace had been entirely extinguished. The Church excludes not only mamzers but also spurii from holy orders.

Concerning the prohibition against the entry of the two aforementioned peoples, Augustine says that they could enter in the tenth generation, on account of Ruth the Moabitess, who entered; from her Boaz, son of Salmon, begot Obed. But since we do not know Ruth’s generation, we have counted ten generations from Abraham, the contemporary of Moab, to Ruth’s marriage. The words added to the prohibition, “for ever,” must be explained by what is promised in the same place: namely, except after the tenth generation. Or, because it says “Ammonites and Moabites,” names of masculine gender, and does not say “Ammonite women” or “Moabite women,” the prohibition was made concerning men, not women—perhaps because perhaps not even the women met the Hebrews in the wilderness.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the prohibition of prostitution and the bill of divorce

He further added: “There shall be no harlot, nor male prostitute, in Israel. You shall not offer the wages of a prostitute, nor the price of a dog, in the house of the Lord your God” (Deut. 23). For, as Josephus says, it was not lawful to offer payment received for the mating of a hunting dog or a dog guarding flocks, because the Divinity takes no pleasure in things arising from disgrace.

Likewise: “You shall not lend money [Col. 1256B] at interest, nor grain, nor anything else, to your brother, but to a foreigner.” But what is said regarding a brother is a command; what is said regarding a foreigner is a permission—just as the following provision concerning the bill of divorce was a permission.

A man whose wife did not find favor with him because of some indecency—which may arise in many ways—wrote that he would never again live with her, together with the reason why the woman displeased him, so that he might not live with her; and he gave the woman a document in which these things were written, to be read before the priests. When he had sworn that what he had written was true, each of the two was permitted to marry another. But if the woman went in to another man, who in turn gave her a bill of divorce, the first husband was not permitted to receive her back, because he had made her abominable before the Lord.

Now a wife is not put away for any indecency except fornication alone; nor, even so, is either of them permitted to proceed to second vows. Nevertheless, some churches have now introduced an exception for leprosy, because the disease spreads and is contagious.

Likewise, one who has recently taken a wife shall not be sent out to war, nor shall any public necessity be imposed upon him, so that for one year he may rejoice with his wife (Deut. 20). This year, however, may be understood as a nuptial year rather than the usual year of ten months, according to which number the year of mourning is reckoned. For after her husband’s death a wife may not pass to another man before ten months, because she may perhaps have conceived by the first husband, and uncertainty could arise as to to which man the child should be ascribed.

Likewise, he prohibited free men from taking maidservants as wives.

## CHAPTER XIV. On punishments by stripes, of which the greatest was forty

Again, if the judge sees that the accused deserves only stripes, he shall lay him down before himself and have him beaten (Deut. 25). The measure of the stripes shall correspond to the measure of the offense, provided that it does not exceed forty. Thus we also strike excommunicated penitents according to the number of verses in a psalm, which we sing while striking them. Josephus says that he was to be beaten with the public strap with forty lashes less one. It was most disgraceful for a free man to undergo this punishment.

## CHAPTER XV. On raising up seed and the ways of removing the shoe

Likewise, a woman left without children by her husband shall be taken [Col. 1257A] by his brother; and he shall name the firstborn son by her after his deceased brother (Deut. 25)—that is, he shall call the son the son of his deceased brother, not his own, and shall leave as heir the one whom he raises up. But if the brother does not wish to receive the widow who is owed to him by law, the woman shall summon the judges at the gate. When he has been called, if he refuses to take her, the woman shall remove his shoe from his foot before them and spit in his face; and his house shall be called the house of the unshod man, a reproach in Israel.

Elsewhere it is read that another, the man who was going to take her, unshod him, in accordance with what John said: “I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal” (Luke 3). This perhaps happened if another man was present to take her when the brother rejected her. For sometimes no one was going to take her [Col. 1257B], and then the woman removed the shoe. Sometimes, too, the brother, without being summoned by the woman, declared before the judges that he did not wish to have her, and then he unshod himself. Hence elsewhere it is read that one unwilling to raise up his brother’s seed unshod himself.

Likewise: “If a woman seizes the genitals of another man who is fighting with her husband, you shall cut off her hand; and you shall not bend in any mercy toward her.”

Likewise: “You shall not have a weight and a weight, a measure and a measure”—that is, a larger one with which to buy and a smaller one with which to sell; for this is an abomination to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the sowing of fields

Moses also added concerning certain mixtures of things of different kinds that must be avoided, saying: [Col. 1257C] “You shall not sow your vineyard with another seed of grain or pulse, lest both the crop that you have sown and what grows from the vineyard be consecrated together” (Deut. 22)—that is, lest you give one tenth and individual firstfruits as though from one field, although these must be given separately from each kind of produce; or lest on this pretext you wish not to give the firstfruits of the crop or of the wine, because they are not consecrated together. For the crop is consecrated in the first year, the vineyard in the fourth. Once the other consecration had been performed, you might perhaps think it sufficient for the consecration of one field.

Another text has: “Lest they be choked together.” This appears to be Josephus’s meaning when he says that this mixture is prohibited because nature does not delight in the union of dissimilar things.

Likewise: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together.” Josephus gives its meaning: namely, that the earth is to be plowed only by oxen, so that under the name “ass” we understand every other animal to be excluded. The Hebrews teach that this was said because the Lord did not wish a servile beast—that is, an ass—to be joined to the king of beasts of burden. For the Lord showed Ezekiel four animals as it were royal ones (Ezek. 1): man is king of all animals; beneath him, the lion is king of wild beasts, the eagle king of birds, and the ox king of beasts of burden.

Some Hebrews explain it more childishly: namely, because the ox chews the cud, the ass would think that it was eating and would be afflicted by hunger and fail.

Likewise: “You shall not wear a garment woven from linen and wool.” For, as Josephus says, this garment was granted to priests alone. The Jews observed this so strictly that they did not even sew skins or any woolen garment except with woolen thread. Josephus further relates that beasts of different kinds were forbidden to be mated, lest this wrong pass on to human beings, so that they might think it lawful to mate with animals. He says that many things are prohibited only among lesser matters, lest by analogy an approach be made to greater ones.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the destruction of the Amalekites

The Lord also commanded that, when they held dominion in the land of promise, they should blot out Amalek from under heaven (Deut. 25), because they had done them great harm as they passed through the wilderness (Deut. 26): namely, by killing the rearmost of the column, that is, the weary, the leprous, and those with discharges of seed—those, that is, who were not allowed to enter the camp. And the Lord added to this command: [Col. 1258B] “Take care lest you forget.” Because Saul transgressed this, the kingdom was transferred from his house.

Likewise: “When you enter the land of promise, you shall take firstfruits from all your produce and put them in a basket,” namely a wicker vessel, “and you shall go to the place which the Lord has chosen. Having made the offering, standing opposite the altar, you shall give thanks to God before the priest because he delivered your father Jacob from the Syrian pursuing him,” namely Laban, “and his sons from Egypt, and finally gave you a land flowing with milk and honey.”

Some say this was done once, upon entering the land; but Josephus says that these thanksgivings were to be performed every year at the Feast of Tabernacles. [Note: [Col. 1258D] Addition 1. In memory of this matter, Jews even now, when entering their synagogue, sing this psalm: “Bless the Lord, O my soul” (Psalm 102), which contains the benefits granted to them.] Indeed, he says that God’s gifts must be continually attested by them twice daily, evening and morning.

Likewise: “When you cross [Col. 1258C] the Jordan, you shall build an altar to the Lord from stones that iron has not touched, and you shall offer sacrifices to the Lord; and you shall write upon the stones all the words of this law plainly and clearly” (Deut. 27).

Likewise, after Moses had set out the blessings of those who observe the law and the curses of transgressors, at the end of the curses he says prophetically: “The Lord will bring you back to Egypt in ships; there you shall be sold to your enemies as male and female slaves, and there shall be none to buy” (Deut. 28). This prophecy was later fulfilled, when thirty Jews could be bought even for a single denarius. For in Alexandria, as Josephus says, many thousands of Jews were sold and scarcely found purchasers.

In this recapitulation Josephus lays down that no Israelite should possess poison or anything deadly; and whoever is found to possess it shall die, suffering what the one against whom it is proved to have been prepared would have suffered.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That Moses delivered Deuteronomy to the Levites

Having made the recapitulation, Moses delivered Deuteronomy to the Levites, that they might place it [the text has *illud*, “it”] in the Ark of the Lord’s covenant, so that it might be read in the seventh year of remission, while all persons of both sexes listened, during the days of the Feast of Tabernacles, by the high priest standing on a raised platform, as Josephus says [Col. 1259A].

Moses likewise said: “I know your disposition and your exceedingly stiff neck. While I still live with you, you have always acted contentiously against the Lord; how much more when I am dead” (Deut. 31). Therefore I again warn you not to do so. And because human testimony is lacking to me as a witness of this warning, or would be useless because men are mortal, I call the immortal elements as witnesses.

## CHAPTER XIX. The song of testimony

And Moses spoke, with the whole assembly listening, the words of this song: “Hear, O heavens, what I speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth,” etc. (Deut. 32). Of this song we explain only this verse literally: “He set the boundary of the peoples according to [Col. 1259B] the number of the children of Israel,” that is, according to the number of persons who entered Egypt the Lord had assigned the nations of tongues.

The Hebrew reads thus: “The Lord set the boundaries of the peoples, but he set the boundaries of the children of Israel according to number”—as though saying: he counted Israel as precious, while he did not distinguish the others, as worthless, by number. Another edition has: “according to the number of the angels of God.”

## CHAPTER XX. On the death of Moses after he had blessed the people

“And the Lord spoke to Moses on that same day: Go up Mount Abarim, to Mount Nebo—that is, pass through the former to the latter—and see the land of Canaan, and die” (Deut. 32). But before [Col. 1260A] Moses went up, he blessed the children of Israel. He began the blessing in this manner: “The Lord came from Sinai, and rose for us from Seir. He appeared from Mount Paran; at his right hand was a fiery law” (Deut. 23).

The Hebrews teach that the Lord sent his angels to the Edomites and to the Ishmaelites in Paran, and offered them his law. When they would not receive it, he came to the Jews on Mount Sinai with many thousands of angels. After the blessings of the individual tribes had been given, “Moses went up upon Nebo to its summit, called Pisgah, and the Lord showed him all the land of promise, as far as the western sea, and the southern region, and the breadth of the plain of Jericho” (Deut. 34), which by another name was called the City of Palms, as far as Zoar.

And Moses died there in the land of Moab at the Lord’s command, and the Lord buried him by the ministry of angels “in the valley in the land of Moab; and no man knew his grave to this present day.” The Hebrews maintain that this was done so that they might not worship Moses as God, since they were prone to idolatry.

“Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died; yet his eye had not grown dim, nor had his teeth become loose. And the children of Israel mourned him thirty days. And there did not arise again a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face”—that is, so familiarly. This final chapter, they say, was added by Ezra, just as, from the words “Moses went up” to this place, they say that Joshua added it.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF JOSHUA

[Col. 1259]

The preface to the history of the book of Joshua begins.

[Col. 1259C]

The Book of Joshua is named after its author, who was also called Jesus. For Joshua and Jesus are the same name. He was surnamed Jesus son of Nave, or Joshua Bennun—that is, son of Nave or Nun, which is the same. He was so surnamed to distinguish him from Jesus son of Sirach, the great-grandson of Jesus the high priest, who wrote Ecclesiasticus.

Note that, according to the Hebrews, the second division of the Old Testament begins here. They divide the Old Testament into three divisions. The first they call the Law, the second the Prophets, and the third the Hagiographa. In the Law they place the five books of Moses; among the Prophets, eight: Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve Prophets. In the Hagiographa [Col. 1259D] [Note: [Col. 1260C] Addition 1. Job, David, the three books of Solomon, Daniel, Chronicles, Ezra, Esther, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, and Maccabees are Hagiographa, because their author is unknown; but because their truth is not doubted, they are received by the Church. [Col. 1260D] But if neither author nor truth were known, they would not be received, as, for example, the book *On the Childhood of the Savior*.] they place the nine remaining books of the Old Testament. These are called Hagiographa, that is, writings of the saints; this name is common to all books of Sacred Scripture. And because these nine did not possess an eminence above the others by which they might be designated, they are content with a common name, just as the name “confessor” is general to all saints; yet some of them, according to some particular eminence that they possess, are designated by other names: some are called apostles, others martyrs, and so forth. In this way also the lowest order of angels is named by the common name of all.

Origen, however, following the Greeks, places seven books in the first division, adding Joshua and Judges to the Pentateuch, and calls that division the Heptateuch, from *hepta*, “seven,” and *teuchos*, “volume.” But whatever division this book occupies, its history is not changed.

## CHAPTER I. On Joshua

[Col. 1260D]

“And it came to pass after the death of Moses,” and after the mourning of the people that had taken place for him had ceased, “that the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun: Moses my servant is dead. Arise and cross this Jordan, you and all the people with you; as I was with Moses, so I shall be with you” (Josh. 1).

In almost the same words he promised Joshua the same things that he had promised Moses, and described the same boundaries of the land of promise. Note that when he said, “Moses is dead,” he refuted the error of certain persons who say that Moses was taken up with Elijah and Enoch, because no trace of his death remained. And by adding “my servant,” he destroyed the error of others who say that Moses was eternally damned because of the waters of contradiction.

When he said “arise,” this is a manner of speaking, not the literal sense. We ought not to suppose that he was sitting or lying down when the Lord spoke to him.

Then Joshua commanded the people through heralds: “Prepare provisions for yourselves, for after the third day you shall cross the Jordan.” This must be understood of provisions other than manna, which could not be kept for a third day. Joshua said this by human judgment, for they did not cross the Jordan until the seventh day. The scouts whom he then sent remained away for three days; after their return the people waited three days for the waters to diminish and prepared provisions according to Joshua’s command.

Thus, as Augustine says, the Lord permitted Joshua to err, so that thereafter he would not undertake anything similar without divine counsel—especially since the Lord had said to Moses at Joshua’s appointment: “Joshua shall succeed you; if he wishes to do anything, Eleazar shall consult the Lord for him” (Num. 27). That he erred is clear, for he did not know whether on the third day the cloud would rise, without whose movement the camp would not move. Some nevertheless maintain that this was said by anticipation, and that Joshua did not give the command until the messengers had returned.

## CHAPTER II. On the scouts and Rahab

Joshua therefore sent two scouts from Shittim to Jericho (Josh. 2). Meanwhile he himself moved the camp and pitched it forty stadia from the Jordan. Under the pretense of stupidity, the scouts carefully inspected the city and its unfortified places. At evening they turned aside into the house of Rahab the prostitute, which adjoined the city wall and gate.

The king of Jericho, while dining, was informed that men who were scouts were present. When he sent to Rahab to bring them out, she had hidden them in stalks [Col. 1261D] of flax which she was drying on top of the wall, falsely saying that they had gone out when the gate was being shut. And she said to the messengers: “Pursue them on the road to the Jordan, and you will catch them.”

Then she went up to the men whom she had covered and said to them: “I know that he will deliver this land to you from what we have heard of the things the Lord has done for you. Swear therefore to me by the Lord that, as I have shown mercy to you, so you shall show mercy to me and to all my father’s house, so that you may save our lives and everything we possess.” And they swore.

Then the woman let them down by a scarlet cord from the window of the house that clung to the wall, and said to them: “Hide in the hill country for three days, until those pursuing you return.” They said to her: “We shall not be bound by the oath if, when the city is taken, you do not gather into your house all your household with you and tie this cord in the window, so that by this sign we may recognize your house. Whoever has entered the door of your house, his blood shall be upon his own head, and we shall be free.”

Accordingly, after three days the scouts returned to Joshua, reporting all that had happened to them. Joshua, Eleazar, and the elders of the people ratified their oath.

## CHAPTER III. On the crossing of the Jordan

After three days had passed, Joshua said to the people: “Sanctify yourselves, for tomorrow the Lord will perform wonders among you” (Josh. 3). At dawn he said to the priests: “Take up the Ark and go before the people at a distance of two thousand cubits, so that you may be seen [Col. 1262B] by all. When you enter the edge of the Jordan, it shall dry up like pavement.”

As the priests went ahead with the Ark, the entire multitude followed, with children and women placed in the middle. Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh went in front, according to what they had promised Moses. There were sixty thousand armed men. Chronicles reads only fifty thousand; in that book many things have been corrupted through scribal fault.

When they came to the Jordan, they found it impassable. For it had risen beyond its usual level at the time of the wheat harvest, both because snow had melted in the mountains and because late rain had recently fallen. When the priests entered the water, the waters rising upstream stood still and appeared swollen like a mountain, far off from the city called Adam, as far as the place called Zarethan. The lower waters descended into the Dead Sea, where five cities—Sodom and the others—were submerged (Gen. 19).

The priests stood with the Ark in the middle of the river until the entire people had crossed through the dry channel. Then Joshua chose twelve men, one from each tribe, who took from the place where the priests had stood twelve stones, according to the number of the children of Israel, onto dry ground (Josh. 4). From the dry ground they carried back into the riverbed another twelve stones, as a memorial heap of their crossing; and they remain there to this day. John is believed to have pointed to these when he said: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3). Yet in the commentary on Matthew it is read that he referred to those stones which Joshua had caused to be carried from the Jordan.

When the people had crossed, and the Ark after them, the waters returned to their channel. The people came up from the Jordan in the first month, on the tenth day of the first month; and taking with them the twelve stones of the river, they camped at Gilgal, ten stadia east of Jericho and fifty stadia from the Jordan. Joshua built an altar to the Lord from the stones which they had taken from the Jordan, and later sacrificed to God upon it.

Note that this is how it is read in Eusebius’s *Chronicles*. According to the Hebrews, that year was a jubilee, and it was the fifty-first among jubilees, as though two thousand five hundred and fifty years had elapsed from the beginning of the world, with every jubilee reckoned by fifty years. According to the Septuagint, far more years had elapsed from the beginning of the world. Bede also, in his *Chronicles*, setting out the number of years according to Hebrew truth, proves that seven years were lacking from the aforementioned total [variant: “had elapsed”].

## CHAPTER IV. On circumcision at Gilgal

At that time, at the Lord’s command, Joshua circumcised the people a second time “with stone knives” (Josh. 5); yet the Hebrew has “sharp razors.” This must not be understood as though the same man were circumcised again. Rather, the children born in the wilderness during the forty years were uncircumcised: some by the Lord’s command, others through their parents’ negligence, and others because of their parents’ caution, lest perhaps, immediately after they were circumcised, the cloud should rise and they would have to move on, so that the children would be endangered.

After the circumcision the Lord said to Joshua: “Today I have taken away from you the reproach of Egypt,” that is, the foreskin, which among the Hebrews was a reproach, the uncleanness of Gentiles. Therefore that place was called the hill of foreskins, or Gilgal [Note: [Col. 1263D] Addition 1. Note that *Gilgal* is sometimes used as indeclinable, sometimes as a first-declension word—*Galgala, Galgalae*—and sometimes as a neuter of the second declension—*Galgala, Galgalorum*.], that is, “revelation,” as though “sanctification,” according to the words: “Judah became his sanctification” (Ps. 113). Yet the reproach taken from them may be said to be Egyptian servitude and the labor of the wilderness, which accords with another interpretation of the name. For *Gilgal* means “freedom.”

The people remained in the place of encampment until they were healed, and they celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day at evening in the plains of Jericho. This had previously been done only twice: first at the borders of Egypt near Rameses; second, at the foot of Mount Sinai, in the second year after the departure. From then until the land of promise it had been omitted together with circumcision.

“And on the following day they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened bread and parched grain of that same year.” Parched grain is roasted grain rubbed by hand, like grain crushed with a pestle. It is called *polenta*, as though *polrenta*. Some, however, teach that *polenta* is porridge made from the most refined flour, and is called *pollenta*, as if from *pollen*, “the most refined flour,” whose nominative is *pollen* or *pollens*. Immediately the manna with which they had been nourished for forty years failed them.

## CHAPTER V. On the angel appearing to Joshua and the overthrow of Jericho

That same night, while Joshua was in the plain of Jericho to reconnoiter, “he saw a man standing opposite him” with a drawn sword, “and said: Are you one of us or of our adversaries? He answered: No; rather, I am captain of the army of the Lord, and now I have come” (Josh. 5).

The angel taught him how to take the city and that he should make it [Col. 1264A], with all it contained, an anathema. [Note: [Col. 1264C] Addition 1. *Anathema* means, as it were, “set apart.” Thus a city was called an anathema when everything captured with it was burned and made into a heap of ashes offered to the Lord. Nothing was taken from it except things which pass through fire and are not reduced to ashes but rather are purified in fire—namely, all metal objects—which, when purified by fire, were reserved for the use of the tabernacle, temple, and vessels.] An anathema means removed from human use and set apart.

When Joshua had prostrated himself in worship, the angel said to him: “Remove the shoe from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy”—that is, it has been sanctified. For a place defiled by the dwelling of Gentiles was sanctified by the Lord’s presence through the angel. Moreover, by the bareness of the feet in holy places of this kind and among penitents, innocence may be signified, which is fitting for such persons. For the first parents possessed it when naked.

At dawn, according to the angel’s counsel, seven priests sounded seven trumpets before the Ark; all the armed people went before the Ark, and the remaining multitude followed it. They went around the city once on the first day of Unleavened Bread [Col. 1264B], in silence, and returned to camp (Josh. 6). They did so for six days. On the seventh day they went around it seven times, and on the seventh circuit Joshua said to the people: “Shout and go up; and let this city be an anathema,” as though devoted to death, except for the gold, silver, bronze, and iron, which shall be preserved for the Lord as the firstfruits of our works. Rahab alone with her household shall be saved.

Therefore, as the people shouted and the priests sounded their trumpets, “the walls fell completely to the ground. Each man went up by the place opposite him; and they killed every living thing in it and burned it, and all its furnishings, into an everlasting heap for the Lord.” Rahab, however, honored with gifts together with all her household, they received into Israel forever. In the course of time Salmon, a leader in the tribe of Judah, took her as wife. [Note: [Col. 1264D] Addition 2. He begot Boaz, the grandfather of that Boaz who begot Obed. For three successive persons—father, son, and grandson—were called Boaz; and therefore Matthew mentioned only one (Matt. 1).]

Then Joshua pronounced a curse, saying: “Cursed is whoever rebuilds Jericho: he shall lay its foundations in his firstborn and set up its gates in his youngest child,” which was fulfilled, as will later appear.

## CHAPTER VI. On the stoning of Achor

Now Achor, or Achar [otherwise Achim], son of Carmi, of the tribe of Judah, took something from the anathema (Josh. 7): namely, a scarlet cloak woven with gold, having, according to Josephus, the weight of a *maza*, that is, a *massa*, that is, two hundred shekels of gold. He also took as many shekels of silver and a gold bar, or plate, of fifty shekels.

Joshua sent men [Col. 1265A] from Jericho to explore the city of Ai, which is near Bethel. On their return they said: “Let not all the people go up. Three thousand are enough to take the city.” Josephus, however, says thirty thousand. When they went up, they were struck while turning their backs by the men of Ai, and thirty-six men of them fell.

Joshua tore his garments and lay prostrate before the Ark until evening, and the elders of the people with him, clothed in sackcloth; and the heart of the people melted. For they feared that the terror which had seized the Canaanites might turn into boldness, so that they would attack them.

The Lord said to Joshua: “The people have been defiled by the anathema, and I shall not be with them until they are cleansed. Bring the people near to you tomorrow, and cast lots by tribes, families, houses, and heads. Whoever is found by the lot shall be burned with fire together with all his property.”

When this was done, the lot found the tribe of Judah, then the family of Zerah, then the house of Carmi, and finally Achor himself. Joshua said to him: “My son, give glory to God by confessing what you have done.” After he had confessed, messengers were sent to his tent; they brought back to the people the aforesaid money hidden in the ground.

Joshua therefore took him with all his household, all his possessions, and his animals, led him into a deep valley, and all the people stoned him; and everything that belonged to him was consumed by fire. “And they made over him a heap of stones which remains to the present day. And the place was called the Valley of Achor.”

We should not suppose that the people neglected the Lord’s command [Col. 1265C] that he should be burned. For in Sacred Scripture “fire” is often understood as severe punishment, as in the passage concerning Egypt’s iron furnace (Jer. 11). The Hebrews nevertheless think that the Lord commanded him and such other things as could be covered by stones to be stoned, while the remaining things, which did not feel stones, were to be burned with fire.

Augustine, however, teaches that Joshua did this with a certain discernment. Either Achor repented, and thus was not worthy of the fire of Gehenna, and Joshua did not wish to burn one who was not worthy of fire; or, if he did not repent and was worthy of eternal fire, Joshua reserved the punishment of fire for the Lord. He punished him by another kind of penalty, lest he seem to be punished twice for the same thing.

## CHAPTER VII. On the burning of Ai

[Col. 1265D]

Afterward Joshua rose, and all the people with him, to go up to Ai; and he sent thirty thousand men between Bethel and Ai, to the west (Josh. 8). Having left five thousand in the place of ambush, they returned to the army that was to the north. The king of Ai hurried out in the morning with all his people, unaware that an ambush lay hidden behind him.

But when Joshua fled and had drawn them far from the city, he raised the shield which he carried. [Note: [Col. 1266A] Addition 1. From the fact that they had shields, it may be inferred that they had horses, since infantry could scarcely carry shields.] When they saw it, those in ambush arose, entered the city, and set it on fire. When they came out after the enemies, and Joshua attacked them, the adversaries were cut down from both sides. They killed them all, from man to woman, twelve thousand persons; but they divided the spoil among themselves.

They hung the king of Ai on a gibbet until evening; then they took him down and threw him at the entrance of the city, heaping a mound of stones over him. They set the city on fire and made it an everlasting ruin.

Here he anticipates the narrative of the altar which was made between Gerizim and Ebal, upon which Joshua wrote Deuteronomy, and of the blessings and curses pronounced upon those mountains; these we shall discuss in their proper place.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the deceit of the Gibeonites and the penalty
The Gibeonites, however, hearing what Joshua had done to the two cities, and that by the Lord’s command he spared none of those dwelling in the land of promise [Col. 1266B], nor made alliances with them, cunningly devised a plan to enter into a treaty with Israel. They sent messengers as though coming from a distant place; as proof of their long journey they carried skins, old shoes patched with pieces of leather, and bread in their bags that was hard, mouldy, and crumbled into pieces (Josh. IX). When they came to Gilgal, they said to Israel: “We have come from a far country, which lies outside the land allotted to you by lot. We are your servants; make a treaty with us.”

The children of Israel believed them and did not inquire of the Lord. Having made a treaty with them, Joshua, Eleazar, and all the princes of the multitude swore an oath to them. But after three days Israel learned that it had been deceived by the Gibeonites. They broke camp [Col. 1266C] and came to destroy their cities; and the Gibeonites came out to meet them. Joshua said, “Why have you deceived us?” They replied: “We were greatly afraid and took counsel for our lives. Do whatever seems good and right to you.”

Then the people cried out that the oath, obtained by deceit, ought not to be kept—especially since the Lord had forbidden alliances with such people. But the elders who had sworn, in order to preserve the sanctity of the oath and to quiet the people’s murmuring, made this arrangement: they would not have them as allies, but as servants—drawers of water and hewers of wood. They were called Nethinim, because they were to cut wood and carry water for the service of the altar, in the place which the Lord [Col. 1266D] should choose for himself. This done, Israel returned to Gilgal.

## CHAPTER IX. Of the Five Kings Hanged

At that time Adonizedek reigned in Jerusalem (Josh. X), a name interpreted “the Lord is righteous”; perhaps the kings of Jerusalem were so named. For Melchizedek likewise means “righteous king.” When he heard that the Gibeonites had allied themselves with Israel, he was greatly afraid. He summoned four kings to join him, and the five kings of the Amorites went up and besieged Gibeon.
