The besieged sent to Joshua, saying: “Come up quickly and deliver us.” Gathering an army, Joshua suddenly fell upon the enemies, who were turned to flight down the descent of Beth-horon. The Lord sent hail upon them, and more were killed by the hail than by the sword. Joshua, seeing the sun descending toward its setting [Col. 1267A] and the moon rising, feared that the enemies might escape under cover of night. He cried to the Lord, saying: “Sun, do not move over against Gibeon; and moon, over against the valley of Aijalon.” The sun and moon stood still for the space of one day.

> [Note: [Col. 1267B] Addition 1. Under Hezekiah ten hours were added (IV Kings XX; Isa. XXXVIII); here, one day.]

Nor before nor afterward was there so long a day. The five kings hid themselves in a cave of the city of Makkedah. Joshua commanded his companions: “Roll stones against the mouth of the cave and set guards there; but you pursue the enemy.” Therefore, after the adversaries had been struck down with a great slaughter, the army returned to Joshua at Makkedah, where the camp was then safe and its numbers intact. Joshua said: “Bring the five kings out of the cave.” When they had been brought out, he said to the commanders of the army: “Put your feet upon the necks of these kings. Do not be afraid. Thus shall the Lord do to all [Col. 1267B] your enemies.”

This done, they hanged the kings on gibbets; at evening they took them down and threw them into the cave in which they had hidden, placing stones over its mouth as an everlasting mound. That same day he struck Makkedah and its king with the edge of the sword. Afterwards he devastated Libnah and Lachish, Eglon also, Hebron, and Debir; and he returned with all Israel to the place of the camp at Gilgal.

## CHAPTER X. Of the Twenty-Four Kings Struck Down by Joshua

When Jabin king of Hazor heard this, he sent to all the surrounding kings [Col. 1267C] (Josh. XI). Twenty-four kings came out with their troops, having with them three hundred thousand armed men and two thousand chariots. They assembled at the waters of Merom, also called Meros, to fight against Israel. The Lord said to Joshua: “Do not fear them. Tomorrow I shall deliver all of them to you to be wounded; you shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire.” And so it came to pass.

All the children of Israel struck them down, except those who had taken refuge in strongly fortified cities. For from the day when the Canaanites heard that Israel was coming out of Egypt against them, they had made for themselves many exceedingly strong fortifications; Israel did not gain possession of these except over a long time and with grievous labor. Nevertheless, it devastated the whole surrounding country, sparing no age or sex, and became exceedingly rich [Col. 1267D] from the enemies’ spoil.

## CHAPTER XI. Of the Altar on Ebal, and the First Distribution of the Land

The fifth year had now passed. Joshua transferred the place of the camp to Shiloh and moved the tabernacle there with all its furnishings, because of the suitability of the place. From there he proceeded to Shechem with all the people and set up on Mount Ebal an altar to the Lord of unhewn stones; upon it he offered burnt offerings and peace offerings (Josh. VIII). He wrote upon it the Deuteronomy, which some understand to mean only the commandments of Deuteronomy.

He placed one half of his people on Mount Ebal with the priests and Levites, and the other half on Mount Gerizim [Col. 1268A] with the priests and Levites. They proclaimed blessings and curses alternately to one another, as Moses had commanded them. Josephus, however, relates that they left the curses and blessings inscribed upon the altar. This done, they returned to Shiloh.

Joshua granted to the tribe of Judah the southern highlands which they had already acquired, though he had not yet delivered them by lot. He likewise granted the northern highlands to Ephraim, placing half the tribe of Manasseh between the two. He entrusted the land to these tribes while the others remained in camp, both because they were warlike and because they were more worthy. For he knew that the kingdom had been promised from them, and that Jacob had blessed Manasseh and Ephraim because of Joseph their father’s service. Joshua himself was also an Ephraimite.

But he gave Ephraim, apart from the allotments of the others, the field of Shechem, which Jacob had given especially to Joseph his son; and there he buried Joseph’s bones. Jerome, however, testifies that he saw at Shechem the tombs of the other eleven patriarchs; and it is credible that each tribe brought its own patriarch into its own allotment.

## CHAPTER XII. That Hebron Was Given to Caleb

Caleb son of Jephunneh came to Joshua before all the people and said: “You know what the Lord said concerning me and you to Moses, and how Moses swore to me on our return from the reconnaissance, saying: ‘The land which your foot has trodden shall be your possession forever.’ The Lord promised me the land in which we found the Anakim, and you heard it. Forty-five [Col. 1268C] years have passed since the Lord spoke this word, and today I am eighty-five years old, as strong as I was at that time” (Josh. XIV).

Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron as a possession, and the land rested from warfare.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Joshua Divided the Land by Lot among the Ten Tribes

Joshua again assembled the congregation at Shiloh and said: “I have grown old. It is good that we divide by lot the land which the Lord promised us” (Josh. XXIII). From each tribe he took three capable men to survey the land. He gave them ten men skilled in measuring, so that the truth might not escape them through lack of skill. He commanded them not to measure the land according to its extent, but according to the value [Col. 1268D] of productive land and of that which was less suitable. For ten acres are often worth more than a hundred. He commanded them to put in writing the division of the land.

The men surveyed and assessed the land, and in the seventh month returned to him at Shiloh. Lots were cast: the first lot came out for Judah, the second for Simeon, the third for Benjamin (Josh. XXI). This allotment was very small because of the fertility of the land; for they received Jericho and Jerusalem. The fourth was for Ephraim; the fifth, for half of Manasseh; the sixth, for Issachar; the seventh, for the Zebulunites; the eighth, for the Asherites; the ninth, for Naphtali; and the last, for the Danites.

It should be noted that, according to the earlier grant of land to two and a half tribes and the later delivery by lot to nine and a half tribes, authors sometimes speak in differing ways [Col. 1269A]. For it is said that Judah had land without a lot and that it possessed Jerusalem but could not drive out the Jebusite from it: these statements concern the grant. Elsewhere it is said that Benjamin possessed Jerusalem: this concerns the delivery. Again, Joshua is said to have addressed seven tribes: “How long do you languish in idleness? Give me men to divide the land for you” (Josh. XVIII). Although he said this to all, he is recorded as saying it only to seven, because the two tribes and the half tribe possessed the land granted to them as though it had already been delivered.

Hence the name Judaea is understood in different ways. Sometimes Judaea means the entire land of promise, and is then called Judaea after the Jews, as when Pompey is said to have made Judaea tributary. Sometimes Judaea means only [Col. 1269B] the kingdom of Judah, as in: “Joseph heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judaea” (Matt. II). Sometimes it means the allotment of Judah alone, as in “Judaea and Jerusalem,” that is, the allotment of Judah and that of Benjamin. Therefore, if authors appear to contradict one another on this matter, the distinction must be made according to land granted or land delivered. For Judah and Ephraim had the larger grant or allotment.

Joshua and Caleb alone, as it were by special privilege, had land without a lot.

> [Note: [Col. 1269C] Addition 1. It may have been, as it is now, that different persons in the same city possessed what was their own by right, as we often see happen within individual places.]

Caleb had Hebron; Joshua had Timnath-serah, or Tannasara, and also Shechem, according to Josephus. Joshua chose this portion for himself after the distribution had been made to all, as a good steward (Josh. XXI). He also set apart for the Levites forty-eight cities [Col. 1269C] to inhabit, ten of which they had previously received in Amorite territory. Of the remaining thirty-eight, he established three cities of refuge: Hebron in Judah, Shechem in Ephraim, and Kedesh in Naphtali (Josh. XV).

Then the sons of Joseph said to Joshua: “Why have you given us, as it were, the possession of a single measuring-cord, when we are so great a multitude?” Joshua replied to Ephraim and Manasseh: “You are a numerous and strong people. You shall not be content with your lot, but shall go up to the hill country; you may advance beyond the boundaries of the land of promise and prepare a place for yourselves” (Josh. XVII).

## CHAPTER XIV. Of the Watered Lands Given to Achsah by Her Father Caleb

[Col. 1269D] At that time Caleb went up into the land delivered to him and struck down in Hebron three sons of Anak.

> [Note: [Col. 1270A] Addition 1. In Chronicles Hebron is called Kiriath-arim, that is, “city of forests,” or Kiriath-baal, that is, “city of flies,” or “of men.”]

Going up from there, he besieged the city of Debir, which had formerly been called Kiriath-sepher, that is, “city of letters.” Its citizens were scribes. Finding it fortified, he said: “Whoever first strikes this city and captures it, I shall give him my daughter Achsah as wife with it.” Othniel, son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it. They were brothers only through their mother.

> [Note: [Col. 1270A] Addition 2. This note resolves the objection that may be raised here: Caleb appeared to oppose the law already given by giving his daughter to his brother’s son.]

For the former is called son of Jephunneh, the latter son of Kenaz—unless perhaps their father bore two names. Caleb therefore gave his daughter Achsah to his brother as wife.

> [Note: [Col. 1270A] Addition 3. Note that Caleb preferred to keep his vow rather than the law which forbids marriage with a brother’s daughter, unless perhaps the law is understood to concern a brother’s daughter [Col. 1270B] by the same father.]

As she was going with her husband to the city given to her, she was persuaded by her husband to ask her father for a field in the valleys. [Col. 1270A] She sighed and wept as she sat on the ass. Caleb said to her: “What is the matter?” She replied: “Give me a blessing. You have given me dry land; add also watered land.” Caleb gave her the upper watering-place and the lower watering-place.

> [Note: [Col. 1270B] Addition 4. “The redemption of the heights” and “the redemption of the lowlands”: the word “streams” is understood.]

That is, he gave her irrigated fields around the city on its eastern and western sides.

## CHAPTER XV. Of the Return of the Two and a Half Tribes

[Col. 1270B]

At the same time, when the fourteenth year had already passed, Joshua said to Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh: “You have done what Moses, servant of God, commanded you. And because the Lord has given rest to your brothers, return to the land of your possession—provided only that you keep God’s law, worship him, and do not go after foreign gods. For you will not have the ark and the tabernacle. We are brothers and servants of one God, though we are separated by the river between us. You return with much wealth; divide it with the brothers who remained behind.”

As they returned, they came [Col. 1270C] to the mounds of the Jordan (Josh. XXII). For this was the name of the place by which they crossed; another place by which the children of Israel crossed is called the fords of the Jordan. Beside the Jordan they built an altar of immense size, calling it by this name: “Our witness that the Lord himself is God.” Josephus seems to mean that they inscribed this upon the altar.

When they had returned to their own territory, Joshua and those who remained were informed that the altar had been built. They thought that the others had erected it in order to offer sacrifices upon it, though this was lawful only upon the altar which God had established before the tabernacle. As Joshua was taking up arms to destroy them, Phinehas was sent to them on counsel, together with ten distinguished men [Col. 1270D]. They said: “What is this transgression? Why have you abandoned the God of Israel and his worship, building for yourselves a sacrilegious altar?”

They replied: “Far be this crime from us! Otherwise may God himself inquire and judge. But we feared lest tomorrow your children should say to our children: ‘What have you to do with us? What have you to do with the Lord God of Israel? The Lord has set a boundary between us and you.’ Therefore we raised this memorial as a sign that we are your brothers and worshippers of God with you.”

When Phinehas heard this, he was appeased. When he reported these words to all the people, they praised God. Some think that this is the event referred to in the book of Judges, where the angel of the Lord is said to have gone from Gilgal to the place of weeping (Judg. II). But since [Col. 1271A] Augustine thinks it more likely that this took place after Joshua’s death—for the children of Israel did not dare openly to depart from God while he lived—we shall explain it in its proper place.

## CHAPTER XVI. Of the Covenant Which the People Made with God

After much time had passed, Joshua assembled all Israel at Shechem and said: “Today I enter upon the way of all flesh, and I know that you are prone to provoke God. Choose today what pleases you, whom you ought especially to serve: whether the gods whom your fathers served in Mesopotamia, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But I and my house will serve the Lord.”

The people said: “We shall serve the Lord; far be it from us to depart from him!” Joshua said: “You are witnesses that today you have chosen the Lord for yourselves.” They replied: “We are witnesses” (Josh. XXIV). They went up to Shiloh to stand before the Lord. On that day the people made a covenant with the Lord; and as a sign of the covenant Joshua poured water upon the ground.

It was the custom among the nations, as a sign and ratification of a treaty made, to pour out swine’s blood, as if to say: “Thus shall the blood of whoever violates this treaty be poured out.” But when the Hebrews poured out water, they indicated a harsher punishment upon the violator. Other liquids cannot be poured from a vessel without leaving some trace of themselves in it. Water alone is entirely poured out. Thus the Hebrews acted when making a covenant with the Lord, as if to say: not only shall the violator of this covenant perish, as in other treaties, but his entire offspring [Col. 1271C] shall perish with him, so that no trace of him may appear upon the earth.

“And Joshua wrote these words that day in the book of the law of God,” that is, in this book [Col. 1272A], “and took a very great stone and placed it under the oak which was before the sanctuary of the Lord. And he said: ‘Behold, this stone shall be a witness to you.’” For the ancients used to set up durable objects of this sort, so that by their lasting character they might call to posterity’s mind the covenant that had been made. Joshua dismissed the people, each to his own possession.

## CHAPTER XVII. Of the Death of Joshua and Eleazar

“After these things Joshua died, when he was one hundred and ten years old” (Josh. XXIV). He was forty-four years old when he came to Moses, and he served him forty years in the wilderness. From this it is inferred that he governed the people for twenty-six years beyond the Jordan. They buried him in Timnath-serah [Col. 1272B], situated on Mount Ephraim.

Eleazar also died, and they buried him in Gibeah of Phinehas, his son.

> [Note: [Col. 1272B] Addition 1. “Gibeah of Phinehas” may be the name of a city from Phinehas being buried there, or it may consist of two words.]

This place had been given to him on Mount Ephraim. Phinehas succeeded his father in the priesthood.

### Incidental Matters

In the days of Joshua, Erichthonius was the first to yoke a four-horse chariot in Greece, although it had already existed among other nations. Busiris exercised tyranny over strangers. Phoenix and Cadmus departed from Egyptian Thebes for Syria and reigned in the region of Tyre and Sidon. But when Cadmus withdrew to Greece, the land was called Phoenicia after Phoenix. Jupiter coupled with Europa, daughter of Phoenix. Danaus, through his fifty daughters, killed the fifty sons of his brother Aegisthus; only one survived, and he reigned after him.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF JUDGES

[Col. 1271]

## CHAPTER I. Preface

[Col. 1271C]

The Book of Judges is called in Hebrew *Sophetim* (“Judges”). It describes the judges down to Eli the priest, and for this reason is called “Judges,” as from its subject matter. Yet some think it was so named from its authors: each judge, writing after the manner of a chronicle, recorded the events of his own time. But who compiled these into one work is uncertain. Some say Samuel, others Ezra. It seems more likely that it was Hezekiah, who collected into one the Proverbs of Solomon and the Book of Kings.

If it is asked why Joshua and Moses are not counted among the judges, we say that they not only judged the people but also ruled them. The others had no authority over the people except that, in their troubles, the people made use of their counsel and prudence.

## CHAPTER II. How Judah Fought against the Canaanite

After the death of Joshua, the people consulted the Lord through Phinehas: “Who shall go up before [Col. 1272C] us against the Canaanite and be leader of the war?” And the Lord said: “Judah” (Judg. I)—indicating not a person but the tribe. Yet Caleb is believed to have presided over the people; but because of the shortness of his time, he was numbered neither among the rulers nor among the judges.

Judah said [Col. 1272D] to Simeon: “Come up with me into my allotment and fight against the Canaanite, and I will go with you into your allotment.” Yet Simeon is not subsequently recorded to have had an allotment of his own, but adhered to Judah, so that what Jacob had foretold concerning Simeon and Levi might be fulfilled: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Gen. XLIX).

Judah and Simeon went up to Bezek and struck down ten thousand men there. Having captured Adoni-bezek—that is, “lord of Bezek,” for *adonai* means “lord”—they cut off the extremities of his hands and feet. Yet the Hebrew expression seems to mean his thumbs. Once these are cut off, a man is unfit to bear arms. Adoni-bezek said: “I suffer this deservedly, for I had done this very thing to seventy kings, who gathered scraps of food beneath [Col. 1273A] my table.”

Going up to Jerusalem, they struck it, gave it to the flames, left Adoni-bezek there, and he died. It must not be understood that the children of Israel then had Jerusalem under their dominion after driving out the Jebusite. This did not take place until David’s time, when, after expelling the Jebusites, he dwelt in it and transferred it from Benjamin to the royal allotment.

Some think this was stated by recapitulation and happened while Joshua was alive, before the lots were distributed, when Judah possessed Jerusalem by grant; and that all is spoken by recapitulation down to the words: “And others arose who did not know the Lord” (Judg. II). Others maintain that it is related in the order in which it happened, and that recapitulation begins only at: “So the people departed, [Col. 1273B] etc.” (Josh. XV).

> [Note: [Col. 1273B] Addition 1. Augustine also holds that this was said in its proper order, though anticipated in Joshua.]

Caleb went up into Hebron, the land, that is, of the giants; and after striking down the enemies, he possessed it more fully. Here the history is recapitulated which we said above happened at Kiriath-sepher. Judah captured Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron with their territories. But it could not destroy the inhabitants of the valleys, because they had many scythed chariots.

## CHAPTER III. Of the Kenites and the People’s Transgression

“The children of Jethro the Kenite, kinsman of Moses, went up from the city of palms with the children of Judah into the wilderness of his allotment, which lies to the south” (Judg. I). These are the children of Hobab, brother of Zipporah, Moses’ wife [Col. 1273C], who, leaving father and homeland, followed Moses and thereafter dwelt among the children of Israel.

The city of palms here is called En-gedi; or the city customarily so called is Jericho, and perhaps they moved from its plains, where they were with Benjamin, to Judah. Benjamin went up to Jerusalem after Judah. Hence some think Jerusalem was common to both. Benjamin could not drive out the Jebusite, but permitted him to dwell with it under tribute.

Ephraim likewise went up to Bethel, which had formerly been called Luz. Seeing a man coming out of the besieged city, they said to him: “Show us the entrance to the city, and we will show you mercy.” When he showed it, they struck the city; but they enriched the man and his household. He passed into the land of the Hittites and built [Col. 1273D] a city there, calling it Luz. Ephraim did not destroy the Canaanite but allowed him to live under tribute.

Likewise, when the remaining tribes had become strong, they preferred to have the Canaanites as tributaries rather than destroy them, transgressing the Lord’s command. They turned to agriculture. Giving themselves over to wealth, feasting, and lust, they became unfit for war and were no longer upright in their observance of the laws.

## CHAPTER IV. Of the Place of Weeping at Gilgal

“The angel of the Lord appeared at Gilgal; and when the children of Israel had assembled to him from the territories, he moved to another place, and they followed him” (Judg. II). Having reproached them through the angel for the benefits he had bestowed upon them, the Lord added: “Why have you made a treaty with the inhabitants of this land [Col. 1274A], preserved their altars, and refused to obey my voice? Therefore their gods shall be your ruin.”

While the angel spoke these things, they raised their voices and wept; and the place was called the Place of Weeping, so named from the event, just as Gilgal means “Hill of the Foreskins.” “And there they sacrificed victims to the Lord.”

Here, moreover, he recapitulates the history from Joshua in order to preserve the sequence of the narrative, saying: “Joshua therefore dismissed the people, and the children of Israel went, each to his own possession. They served the Lord all the days of Joshua and of the elders who lived after him and knew the works which the Lord had done with Israel. Joshua died, and the whole generation of elders was gathered to its fathers.”

## CHAPTER V. Of Othniel, Deliverer of the People, and His Death

[Col. 1274B]

“And others arose who did not know the Lord” (Judg. II), that is, who had not seen the mighty works which he had done for them in their departure from Egypt, in the wilderness, and upon entering the land of promise. “They did evil in the sight of the Lord, served Baal, Ashtaroth, and the gods of the land, and contracted marriages with foreigners” (Judg. III).

Therefore the offended God did not destroy the nations from among them, so that they might be a goad and affliction to them. “The Lord delivered them into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia and Syria. They served him eight years and cried to the Lord, who raised up for them a deliverer, Othniel, brother of Caleb.” Josephus calls him Kenaz, as though he bore the same name as his father. He is called Kenaz, as though “Kenizzite,” from a place. The Lord was with him; he fought against Chushan-rishathaim and subdued him, and the land rested forty years. Othniel died.

Here Josephus places the killing committed in Benjamin on account of the Levite’s wife; we shall set it forth below, following the order of this book. Note that the Hebrews included the years of servitude and rest under this number, and similarly under the other judges; otherwise the chronology would not stand.

### Incidental Matters

In the days of Othniel, Cadmus reigned at Thebes; from his daughter Semele was born Dionysus, Liber Pater. Bithynia was founded by Phoenix, who gave certain letters to the Phoenicians and introduced the purple dye for writing. Hence that color was called Phoenician; later, with a changed letter, it was called Punic. Ephyra, now called Corinth, was founded by Sisyphus. Minos, son of Europa, reigned in Crete.

## CHAPTER VI. Of Ehud and Shamgar, Deliverers of Israel

“The children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord. He raised up against them Eglon king of Moab and joined to him the children of Ammon and Amalek” (Judg. III). Crossing the Jordan, he struck Israel, placed his idols at Gilgal, made his residence in the city of palms—that is, Jericho—and the children of Israel served him eighteen years. They cried to the Lord, who raised up for them a savior, Ehud, son of Gera, son of Gemini. He used either hand as his right hand.

> [Note: [Col. 1275D] Addition 1. In the Book of Kings, where it begins to treat of Saul, he is called “a man mighty in strength” (I Kings XVI); for this reason some think he was called *geminus*, “double,” as though he had two names.]

Some say [Col. 1275A] that Gemini was a certain base man in Benjamin, whose descendants were often reproached for his disgrace. The Hebrews relate that this was Benjamin. As though by aphereses, where we write *geminum* (“twin,” “double”), they write *Jemin*, which means “right-handed” or “of the right side”; in Latin he might be called *geminus*, because he is doubled with the one who draws [the word], unless *geminus* were written from *Jemin* with consonantal J. From *Jamin* comes properly *Jeminus*, just as from *dextera* (“right hand”) comes *dextrarius* (“right-handed”).

The children of Israel sent gifts through Ehud to King Eglon. Ehud made himself a two-edged sword a handbreadth long and girded it on his right thigh beneath his cloak, a military garment of square form. Eglon was exceedingly fat. After offering him the gifts, Ehud dismissed the companions who had come with him, then returned [Col. 1275B] to the king and said: “I have a secret word for you, O king.” When all who were with him had gone out, Ehud approached and said: “I have a word of God for you”—which is to be understood of a dream received by God’s command. Eglon immediately rose from the throne.

Ehud stretched out his left hand, drew the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it forcefully into Eglon’s belly. He did not draw it out, but left it in the body. Ehud carefully shut the doors of the upper chamber, went out through the rear exit, and escaped. After a long delay the king’s servants entered and found him dead, lying on the ground.

Ehud came to Seirah and sounded the trumpet on Mount Ephraim. The children of Israel came down with him to the fords of the Jordan [Col. 1275C] leading into Moab. When the Moabites wished to cross, they struck down about ten thousand. On that day Moab was humbled beneath Israel’s hand, and the land rested eighty years. Ehud died. Then, when the Philistines wished to enter Israel’s land, Shamgar killed six hundred men with a single ox-goad. He too defended Israel and ended his life in the same year.

### Incidental Matters

In the days of Ehud, the city of Cyrene was founded in Libya; Triptolemus came in a long ship to Eleusis and distributed grain there. Orchus, king of the Molossians, abducted Proserpina. His huge dog Cerberus devoured Pirithous, who had come with Theseus to abduct Proserpina; and Cerberus would also have devoured Theseus, had Hercules not arrived and freed him. Phrixus and Helle escaped the snares of their stepmother in a ship whose emblem was a ram. Tros reigned in Dardania, and Troy is said to have been founded from his name. Perseus killed Gorgon, a courtesan who by her excessive beauty deprived her beholders of their wits. Dionysus founded Nysa in India and called it after his own name.

## CHAPTER VII. Of Deborah the Prophetess, and Barak, Sisera, Jael, and Jabin
> “After the death of Ehud the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord. And he delivered them into the hands of Jabin king of Canaan [Col. 1276A], who reigned at Hazor and had Sisera as commander of his army. Sisera lived at Harosheth of the nations (Judith IV),” so called because it was inhabited not by one people, but by peoples gathered from many nations. And he oppressed the children of Israel for twenty years. They cried out to the Lord.
>
> Now Deborah was a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth. She had set up her tent on Mount Ephraim beneath a palm tree called Deborah’s palm, and the children of Israel went up to her for every judgment. She summoned Barak, son of Abinoam, from Kedesh—or, alternatively, Kadesh—of Naphtali. For the woman who was to go into battle summoned her husband, who, as stated above, was Lapidoth. For Barak and Lapidoth are believed to have been the same person, because both names have the same interpretation [Col. 1276B]. Each is interpreted “lightning-flash,” while Deborah in Hebrew means “bee.”
>
> She said to him: “The God of Israel has commanded you: Lead an army to Mount Tabor, ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun; and I will deliver Sisera into your hand beside the torrent Kishon.” Barak replied: “Unless you come with me, I shall not go.” She said: “I will go, but the victory will be delivered into the hand of a woman.”
>
> Sisera was informed that Deborah and Barak had gone up Mount Tabor to fight. He assembled his army at the torrent Kishon: three hundred thousand armed men, according to Josephus; ten thousand cavalry; nine hundred scythed chariots; and another two thousand one hundred chariots. Deborah said to Barak: “Go down, for on this [Col. 1276C] day the Lord will deliver Sisera into your hands.” He went down with ten thousand men, while Deborah remained on the mountain in prayer.
>
> The Lord terrified Sisera and all his multitude. Wind, hail, and rain rushed into their faces; bows and slings became useless; many, thrown from their horses and chariots, were crushed. Thus, when the army had been turned to flight, Sisera leapt from his chariot and fled, reaching the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite. For Heber, with all his household, had withdrawn from his brothers—who, as we have said, dwelt in the allotment of Judah—and had pitched his tents in the valley of Zaanannim beside Kedesh. There was an alliance between the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.
>
> Jael received the fugitive, who asked her to hide him; and when he asked for a drink [Col. 1276D], she gave him milk, so that he might fall into a deeper sleep. But while he slept, she drove an iron peg, struck with a hammer, through both temples and into the ground. Soon afterward, she showed him to Barak as he came, pierced through upon the ground. Thus was fulfilled what Deborah had said: that triumph would come through a woman.
>
> Barak then led his army against Hazor; he killed Jabin when he came out to meet him and utterly destroyed the city, according to Josephus. Deborah and Barak sang a song to the Lord, in which they exhort the victors to bless God, recalling the benefit which the Lord had bestowed upon Israel when he gave the Law amid earthquake and rain. They add also that, through Shamgar, as we have said, the enemies had withdrawn from the roads of Israel, and how Israel’s strength failed until [Col. 1277A] Deborah arose, when the Lord chose new wars so that a woman might triumph over men.
>
> What follows in the song—“Arise, Deborah, and utter a song”—is not in the Hebrew. She also added concerning Amalek,

> [Note: [Col. 1277C] Addition 1. Amalek, who was the first to attack Israel in the wilderness.]

> conquered at Rephidim by Ephraim—that is, by Joshua the Ephraimite—and she prophesied that the same people would afterward be conquered by Saul of Benjamin. She commended those from Manasseh, Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali who had come with them to battle, reproaching Reuben, Gad, Dan, and Asher, who refused to come with them.
>
> When it is also said that Reuben was divided against himself, this means either that he separated himself from those who were going to fight, or that the Reubenites were divided among themselves: some urging that they should go to battle, others dissuading them. When it says that they fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, it should be understood that this is a region beside the Kishon, which flows past Megiddo. The Hebrew has *in Ramazache*, interpreted “upon the height of the plain”; it signifies that on the plain where the battle was fought they became superior to their enemies [Col. 1277B].
>
> The following words, “The stars fought against Sisera,” must not be understood astrologically, as though this happened through a fated conjunction of stars. Rather, flashes and bolts of lightning were hurled down upon them from above as if stars were falling; this is a hyperbole.
>
> It follows: “The torrent Kishon swept away their corpses like the torrent Kedumim”; supply, “it swept away the corpses of the Egyptians.” *Kedumim* means “of the ancients,” and is used for the Red Sea because ancient miracles were performed there [Col. 1277C].
>
> The words that follow, “Trample down the mighty, O my soul,” are the voice of the people exhorting itself. Next comes: “Cursed be the land of Meroz, said the angel of the Lord.” Meroz was one of the princes of Canaan. But Deborah called herself the Angel of the Lord, or Michael, who presided over Israel, and said that he commanded Meroz to be cursed. Meroz signifies “secret,” that is, the apostate angels who opposed him in secret. Afterward she blessed Jael because she acted courageously; and the land rested for forty years.

### Incidental Matters

At that time the kingdom failed at Argos and was transferred to Mycenae. Father Liber died; his tomb is at Delphi beside the golden Apollo. He is depicted with a woman’s body because he had women serving as soldiers together with men in his army. Ilium was founded by Ilus; Miletus was founded.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning another messenger, and Gideon

The children of Israel again did evil before the Lord, who delivered them into the hands of Midian for seven years (Judges VI). Each year Midian and Amalek came up against Israel, ravaging their crops and carrying away all their beasts as plunder. When Israel cried out to the Lord, he sent them a man, a prophet, through whom the Lord reproached them with the benefits he had bestowed upon them; yet they would not hear his voice.
>
> “Then the angel of the Lord came and sat beneath an oak which was in Ophrah.” This was the man [Col. 1278A] whom the Lord had sent. The stone on which he sat, the oak, and the field belonged to Joash, head of the family of Ezri—that is, the most honorable man among the rest of that family. Gideon,

> [Note: [Col. 1280D] Addition 1. For the sixth time the Lord stirred up the spirit of Gideon in Israel.]

> his son, fearing the enemies who had invaded the land, was secretly threshing grain in a winepress in order to have provisions for flight. Josephus says that this was a very great indication of divine favor: at that time he used a winepress as a threshing floor, for through him threshing floors and winepresses would afterward be filled.
>
> The angel said to him: “The Lord is with you, bravest of men.” Gideon replied: “If the Lord is with us, why have these evils overtaken us?” The Lord looked upon him in the angel and said: “Go in this strength of yours—that is, the strength which I confer upon you by looking upon you [Col. 1278B], or by sending you—and you shall strike Midian as one man.” Gideon said: “If I have found favor before you, do not depart until I return.”
>
> Gideon cooked a kid, put the meat and unleavened bread in a basket, poured the broth into a pot, and offered them to the angel. The angel said: “Put the meat and bread upon the rock, and pour the broth over them.” When he had done so, the angel touched them with the tip of the staff he carried. Fire rose from the rock and consumed everything. The angel vanished from his sight.
>
> Gideon, afraid, said: “Alas, Lord, for I have seen the angel of God!” The Lord said to him: “Do not fear. You shall not die.” That same night the Lord said to him: “Destroy the altar of Baal which your father erected; cut down the grove around it; kill the bull which he fattens for idols; and offer to me as a burnt offering the other, seven-year-old bull [Col. 1278C], which the citizens have dedicated to the idol, upon the altar which you shall build for me on the top of the rock upon which you previously placed the sacrifice.”
>
> Gideon, fearing his father and the citizens, completed everything by night with ten servants; he called the altar “Peace of the Lord,” and concealed himself. The next day the citizens said to Joash: “Bring out your son, that he may die, because he has done this.” He answered them: “Are you Baal’s avengers? If Baal is a god, let him avenge himself.” From that time Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is, “the strength of Baal,” as though “strong against Baal.”
>
> Midian and Amalek crossed the Jordan and encamped in the valley of Jezreel like locusts. But the Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon, and he summoned the house of Abiezer, from whose family he was descended. He also sent [Col. 1278D] messengers to Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali. Thirty-two thousand men came to him.
>
> Gideon asked the Lord for a sign of victory by placing a fleece on the threshing floor: if during that night the fleece should be wet with dew while the floor remained dry. And so it happened. When the fleece was wrung out, it filled a bowl with dew. The following night, lest it be thought to have happened by chance, he asked for the opposite sign: that the floor should be wet and the fleece dry. This happened.
>
> Gideon came with his men to the spring called Harod (Judges VII). The Lord said to Gideon: “You have too many people with you, lest Israel say, ‘I have delivered myself by my own strength.’ Proclaim to the people: ‘Whoever is afraid, let him return.’” Yet it must be understood that he did not omit the other three proclamations which the Lord commanded to be made to the people [Col. 1279A], and which Moses set forth in Deuteronomy: “Whoever has built a house and has not dedicated it, let him return.” Likewise: “Whoever has planted a vineyard and has not yet made it common, and whoever has betrothed a wife and has not yet taken her” (Deut. XX).
>
> Twenty-two thousand of the people returned, and only ten thousand remained. The Lord said to Gideon: “There are still too many people. Lead them down to the water in the noonday heat. Separate those whom you judge spirited and courageous, who lap water with hand and tongue like dogs.” Only three hundred men were found among them. The Lord said: “By these three hundred I will deliver Midian into your hands.”
>
> Taking these men, provisions in proportion to their number, and trumpets, Gideon gave himself to the contest. “That same night the Lord said to Gideon: Go down into the camp [Col. 1279B] of Midian, you and your servant Purah with you; hear what they are saying, and your hands will be strengthened.” For his heart had grown faint.
>
> Going down, he stood at the edge of the camp where the watches were posted, and he heard a man telling his fellow soldier a dream in this manner: “It seemed to me that a baked barley loaf, fit to be eaten, descended into the camp of Midian as far as the tent

> [Note: [Col. 1280D] Addition 2. Perhaps by their “tent” he means the standard by which they were led, or they had a tent in which they sacrificed to their idols.]

> —that is, the king’s tent—and overturned it, levelling it utterly to the ground.” The man to whom he spoke said: “Barley is insignificant among grains, and among the peoples Israel appears contemptible; and in Israel Gideon’s family is lowly. This is nothing other than Gideon’s sword: the Lord has delivered Midian into his hand.”
>
> Gideon heard this and worshipped. [Col. 1279C] Returning to his companions, he said: “Let us go: the Lord has delivered the camp of Midian to us.” He divided them into three groups, placed trumpets in their right hands, empty jars and lamps within the jars in their left hands, and said: “Do what you see me doing.”
>
> They entered around the camp in three places during the middle watch of the night. When they broke the jars, they held the lamps in their hands, sounded the trumpets, and cried: “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!” According to Josephus, they also carried empty amphorae. When these were struck together at once, a terrible sound was heard. Suddenly awakened, the enemies were confused; not recognizing one another, many fell by mutual wounds, while others fled as far as Beth-shittah.
>
> The men of Naphtali, Asher, and Manasseh who had returned were called out and pursued Midian [Col. 1279D]. Ephraim also came down to confront the fugitives and occupied the Jordan as far as Beth-barah. They killed two kings of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb: Oreb at a certain rock, and Zeeb in a winepress. The place was called the Winepress of Zeeb, and the other place the Rock of Oreb. The latter differs by only a small stroke of a letter from the name Horeb, whence waters flowed through Moses’ hand; perhaps there is a difference in interpretation.
>
> Ephraim brought the heads of the kings to Gideon, and angrily said to him: “Why did you disdain to summon us to battle?” He replied: “Lest you perhaps become angry: the gleaning of Ephraim is better than the vintage of Abiezer, for the kings of Midian have been delivered into your hands. What could I do like what you have done?” (Judges [Col. 1280A] VIII). When they heard this, their spirit was calmed.
>
> Gideon crossed the Jordan with three hundred men. Because of exhaustion, they could not pursue the fugitives. He said to the men of Succoth: “I beg you, give us bread, that we may pursue Zebah and Zalmunna.” They denied him and mocked him. The men of Penuel gave him the same answer when he asked them for bread.
>
> Zebah and Zalmunna were resting in the valley, suspecting nothing adverse, with only twelve thousand men, after one hundred and twenty thousand had been slain from their army. Gideon suddenly fell upon them; he threw their army into confusion, captured the two kings, and brought them back with him. On his return he seized a boy from Succoth and asked him the names of the elders of Succoth. He wrote down for him seventy-seven men, whom Gideon crushed with thorns and briars [Col. 1280B] as the authors of the aforementioned mockery. He also overthrew the tower of Penuel and killed the inhabitants of the city.
>
> When he returned to Ophrah, his own region, he said to Zebah and Zalmunna: “What sort of men were those whom you killed on Mount Tabor?” They answered: “They were like you.” He said to them: “They were my brothers by the same mother.” He said to his firstborn: “Kill them.” But the boy did not draw his sword, because he was afraid, being still a child. Gideon arose and killed them.
>
> “Then all the children of Israel said to him: ‘Rule over us—you, your son, and your grandson.’” He replied: “I shall not rule over you, nor shall my son; but the Lord shall rule over you. I ask only one thing of you: give me the gold earrings from the spoil.” They gave them to him. The weight of gold was one thousand [Col. 1280C] seven hundred shekels. Gideon made from it an ephod and placed it in the city of Ophrah; and all Israel prostituted itself to it. It became a ruin to Gideon and to all his household.
>
> By the ephod, which is the chief garment of the high priest, it is understood that Gideon made all the priestly vestments; he made at Ophrah a tabernacle and an altar besides the one at Shiloh. He became a priest and sacrificed victims to the Lord upon it. Therefore the Lord, being offended, almost destroyed his entire house. Gideon had seventy sons by his wives and one illegitimate son, Abimelech, by the concubine Dyohoma, whom he had at Shechem.

> [Note: [Col. 1280D] Addition 3. From this it is inferred that he afterward repented, since he sacrificed somewhere other than where the Lord had appointed.]

> Abimelech killed all his brothers except one. The land rested forty years, during which Gideon presided. He died in a good old age [Col. 1280D] and was buried in his father’s tomb at Ophrah.

### Incidental Matters

In Gideon’s time Mercury invented the pipes, deriving their name from Syrinx, the wife of Cadmus, who had left her husband because of jealousy of Harmonia. He also invented the lyre in this way: he found the shell of a dead, decayed tortoise, whose dried and stretched sinews in the mouth of the shell gave out a sound at a light breeze [Col. 1281A]. It is uncertain who this Mercury was: Hermes, the philosopher Trismegistus, or the lesser Mercury. For Josephus records that there were three.
>
> Tyre was founded two hundred and forty years before the Temple of Jerusalem. Daedalus made metal birds which he caused to fly artificially by enclosing a spirit within them. He is also said to have made self-moving statues. For he was the first of all to separate the feet of statues from each other, whereas others made them joined together. When he fled by ship with his son, people thought that he had flown away on wings because his escape could not be traced.
>
> The story of the Argonauts occurred; Orpheus was held famous. His disciple was the poet Musaeus. Linus, Hercules’ teacher, flourished. Minos is believed to have given laws to the Cretans, though Plato denies this. Plato also maintains that the Hydra was a most subtle sophist.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Abimelech, who killed his seventy brothers

After Gideon’s death, the children of Israel prostituted themselves to the Baals and did not show mercy to the house of Jerubbaal (Judges IX). Abimelech went up to Shechem, to all his mother’s kindred, and said: “Consider that I am your bone and your flesh. Speak to all the men of Shechem thus: Which is better for you—that seventy men, the sons of Jerubbaal, should rule over you, or that one man should rule?” They spoke concerning him to all the people; they inclined the people’s heart after Abimelech; and all swore allegiance to him [Col. 1281C] in Baal’s shrine. Therefore the idol was thereafter called Baal-berith; for *berith* means “conspiracy.”
>
> Taking seventy pounds of silver from the shrine, they gave it to him. With it he hired needy and wandering men. Going up to Ophrah, he killed all his brothers upon one stone, except one, Jotham. Then all the Shechemites made Abimelech king beside the oak at Shechem.
>
> If it is asked how Saul, then, is said to have been the first king in Israel, one may answer that this is said because of the universal kingdom; Abimelech ruled only over the Shechemites. When this was reported to Jotham, he stood upon the summit of Mount Garam, or Gerizim, and cried out to all the Shechemites who had gathered for Baal’s feast day: “Hear me, men of Shechem: ‘The trees of the woods went to anoint a king [Col. 1281D] over themselves, and they said to the olive tree: Rule over us.’”
>
> The olive would not forsake its fatness, which gods and human beings use. They said the same to the fig tree, which would not forsake the sweetness of its fruit. They said the same to the vine, which would not forsake the wine that gladdens God and human beings. Then they said to the bramble: “Rule over us.” It replied: “Come, then, and rest beneath my shade; otherwise, let fire come forth from the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.”
>
> The bramble is a kind of thornbush, commonly called a brier, extremely rough and prickly like thorns. Josephus says that among trees it has the nature of producing fire. Then Jotham explained the parable to them, saying: “You have killed the sons of Jerubbaal and have made the son of his slave-woman king over yourselves. If [Col. 1282A] you have acted rightly toward Jerubbaal, his house, and his sons, may it go well with you; but if perversely, let fire come forth from Abimelech and devour both him and you.” Having said this, he fled.
>
> After Abimelech had reigned over Shechem for three years, the Lord gave him an evil spirit against him, and they expelled Abimelech from the city and tribe. He carried out brigandage against them, taking plunder from them.
>
> At vintage time Gaal entered Shechem with his brothers. When he came down among them, the Shechemites went down, gathered the vineyards and grapes, and entered the shrine of their god. Amid feasting and drinking, they cursed Abimelech. Gaal also said: “Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal?” This was said ironically—as though he were not, but was [Col. 1282B] illegitimate. He added: “Would that this people were put into my hand, so that I might remove Abimelech from the midst!”
>
> Zebul, whom Abimelech had made ruler in the city, secretly reported everything to Abimelech. Abimelech therefore rose at night with his army and laid ambushes beside the city. Gaal went out in the morning, and Zebul stood with him at the gate. When Abimelech came up with his army, Gaal said to Zebul: “Behold, a multitude is coming down from the mountains.” Zebul replied: “You see the shadows of the mountains as though they were men’s heads, and are deceived by this error.” Again Gaal said: “Behold, people are coming down as if from the navel of the earth.” Zebul said: “Where is your mouth now, with which you spoke against Abimelech? Go out and fight him.”
>
> He fought [Col. 1282C], was defeated, and fled back into the city. Zebul expelled him and his companions. “On the following day Abimelech took the city by storm, killed its inhabitants, destroyed it, and scattered salt over it. But the inhabitants of the tower of the Shechemites entered the shrine of their god because it was a fortified place.”
>
> Josephus, however, says that the refugees from throughout the district gathered upon a most strongly fortified rock and tried to fortify or wall it. Seeing this, Abimelech went up Mount Zalmon. Carrying a cut branch, he said to his companions: “Do what I do.” They took branches, surrounded the stronghold, set it on fire, and a thousand men perished there by fire and smoke, besides women and children.
>
> Leaving there, Abimelech besieged the town of Thebez. In its middle was a tower into which the Thebezites had withdrawn [Col. 1282D]. Note that inhabitants of Egyptian Thebes are called *Thebaei*; inhabitants of Greek Thebes, *Thebani*; and inhabitants of Jewish Thebez, *Thebitae*. As Abimelech attacked the tower and attempted to set fire beneath it, a woman threw down a piece of millstone and shattered his skull. He said to his armor-bearer: “Strike me, lest I be said to have been killed by a woman,” for she killed him.
>
> Josephus says that this calamity came upon the Ephraimites because they had quarreled with Gideon at the waters of the Jordan.

### Incidental Matters

At the same time the *chorus* was invented in Greece. Strabo says that this instrument was a skin with two reeds: one is used for blowing into it, and through the other it produces sound. According to some it is written without aspiration [Col. 1283A]; but when it denotes the voice of singers, metre, and wind, it is written with aspirated *ch*.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Tola, leader of Israel

After Abimelech, Tola of Issachar, son of Puah, Abimelech’s uncle, judged Israel for twenty-three years (Judges X). Let it not trouble you that Puah and Joash are brothers although one was born of Issachar and the other of Manasseh. They were sons of one mother and two fathers, from different tribes. Tola judged Israel at Shamir for twenty-three years and died.

### Incidental Matters

At that time Hercules defeated Antaeus in wrestling and destroyed him. There was war between the Lapiths and Centaurs, whom Palaephatus, in his book *On Incredible Things*, describes as noble Thessalian cavalrymen. Priam [Col. 1283B], son of Laomedon, ruled at Troy. Androgeus was treacherously killed at Athens. Theseus killed the Minotaur in a contest, on account of which the tribute-paying Athenian boys were freed from punishment. The Minotaur was a certain inhuman man, powerful in wrestling, a magistrate of Minos. Hence he was so called, as though *Minos taurus*, “Minos’ executioner.”

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Jair the Gileadite, leader of Israel, and his death

After Tola, Jair the Gileadite, of the tribe of Manasseh, judged Israel for twenty-two years. He had thirty sons, whom he made rulers of thirty cities, which he called by his own name, Havvoth-jair—that is, “the towns of Jair”—and he died (Judges X).

### Incidental Matters

[Col. 1283C] At that time Theseus carried off Helen, whom her brothers Castor and Pollux recovered, after capturing Theseus’ mother while he was abroad. Philistus writes that Carthage was founded by Tyrian citizens, Zorus and Carthage. The nymph Carmentis invented Latin letters.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the repentance of the children of Israel for their idolatry, and concerning Jephthah

Again the children of Israel served the idols of the surrounding nations, and the Lord delivered them into the hands of the Philistines and Ammon (Judges X). All who lived beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorite were grievously afflicted for eighteen years. The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan and ravaged Judah, Benjamin, [Col. 1283D] and Ephraim. In their affliction they cried out to the Lord. When he sternly answered them, “Go and invoke the gods whom you have chosen,” they cast all idols out of their borders, and the Lord was grieved at their miseries.
>
> The children of Israel assembled at Mizpah against the Ammonites, who had pitched their tents in Gilead. “At that time Jephthah the Gileadite was a most valiant fighting man” (Judges XI), but the son of a prostitute. Gilead had a wife, by whom he had sons. When they had grown up, they expelled Jephthah as illegitimate, saying: “You cannot be heir in our fathers’ house.” He went into the land of Tob. “Needy men and brigands gathered around him and followed him as their leader.”
>
> The elders of Gilead went down to him and said: “Be [Col. 1284A] our leader and fight against the sons of Ammon.” He replied: “Are you not those who hated me and expelled me?” They said: “We do not hate you, nor have we come to pursue you, but to follow you.” Jephthah said: “Then swear to me.” And they swore.
>
> Going up with them to Mizpah, he humbled himself before the Lord and became leader of the people. He sent messengers to the king of Ammon with these words: “Leave my land. Why do you ravage it?” The king replied: “Israel took my land when it came up from Egypt; restore it to me.” Jephthah said it had been acquired by right of war and possessed for three hundred years, but Ammon would not consent to depart. Jephthah said: “May the Lord judge today between Israel and Ammon.” The Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah.
>
> Going out to battle [Col. 1284B], he made a vow to the Lord: “If you deliver the sons of Ammon into my hands, whoever first comes out from my house to meet me as I return, I shall offer him as a burnt offering to the Lord.” Jephthah struck the sons of Ammon with a very great slaughter, and they were humbled before the children of Israel.
>
> As Jephthah returned to Mizpah, his only daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dances. On seeing her, he tore his garments and said: “Alas, my daughter, you have deceived me, and have been deceived. I have opened my mouth to the Lord against you.” But the daughter, not grieving in this situation over her father’s victory, said: “Father, do to me whatever you have promised. Only grant me this: let me go about the mountains for two months and lament my virginity with my companions.” Her father said: “Go.” When the two months were completed, she returned to her father [Col. 1284C], and he did to her as he had vowed.
>
> Thereafter the custom grew in Israel that the children of Israel should come every year and lament Jephthah’s daughter for four days. Josephus reproves Jephthah because he offered a burnt offering neither lawful nor pleasing to God. What if a dog had come to meet him? Would he have sacrificed it to the Lord? He was therefore foolish in making the vow and impious in fulfilling it. Yet he could have been good before the vow, since the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and even after the vow; for the Apostle includes him in the catalogue of the good (Hebrews XI). Some, however, excuse him, saying that he did this by the familiar counsel of the Holy Spirit.
>
> Then the Ephraimites came to him and said: “Why did you disdain to summon us to battle? We shall burn your house.” [Col. 1284D] He replied: “I summoned you, and you would not come” (Judges XII). Calling together the men of Gilead, he fought against Ephraim. The Gileadites occupied the fords of the Jordan. When an Ephraimite fugitive came to them and begged to be allowed to cross, they said: “Are you an Ephrathite?” When he answered, “I am not,” they asked him: “Then say *Shibboleth*, which means ‘an ear of grain.’” He replied, “Sibboleth,” unable to pronounce the same letter in the word for “ear of grain.” They immediately cut his throat. At that time forty-two thousand men of Ephraim fell.
>
> Note that *Ephrathite* is used here for Ephraimite; properly speaking, however, an Ephrathite is a Bethlehemite. Jephthah judged Israel for six years, died, and was buried in his own city, Sebeth, which is in Gilead. He says that three hundred years are reckoned from the age of Moses [Col. 1285A] down to himself. The preceding eighteen years of affliction are not added to these years.

### Incidental Matters

At that time Hercules threw himself into the flames, for he had fallen into a pestilential sickness.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Abessan, leader of Israel

After Jephthah, Abessan, or Essebon, a Bethlehemite of Judah, judged Israel for seven years (Judges XII). At that time Agamemnon reigned at Mycenae and Menelaus in Lacedaemon.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Ahialon

After Abessan, Ahialon the Zebulunite judged Israel for ten years (Judges XII). He, together with his ten years, is absent from the Septuagint. To make good this deficiency, Eusebius assigned to Joshua, Samuel, and Saul—whose years Sacred Scripture does not state—more years than he found in Josephus, so that he might attain the total of four hundred and eighty years proclaimed by Scripture from Israel’s exodus from Egypt until the building of the Temple [Col. 1285B].

### Incidental Matters

At that time Paris carried off Helen and the ten-year war arose. Memnon and the Amazons brought aid to Priam.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning Abdon, leader

After Ahialon, Abdon the Thekoite of Ephraim judged Israel for eight years (Judges XII). Under these three judges Israel did not depart from the Lord, and the land rested [Col. 1285C]. Therefore they are recorded as having done nothing memorable. Yet some relate that under Abdon the disaster in Benjamin occurred on account of the Levite’s wife.

### Incidental Matters

In his third year Troy was captured, and three hundred and six years elapsed until the first Olympiad. Then the Greeks, in glory over their victory, began to date their times thus: “In the year from the capture of Troy.” Once the Olympiad had begun, they thereafter dated time by the number of Olympiads.

> [Note: [Col. 1285D] Addition 1. Note that an Olympiad was so called from the games held beneath Mount Olympus at the city of Elis, where the Eleans conducted contests. They called the contest a quinquennial one, counting the four intervening years; and for this reason they called the period of the Elean contest an Olympiad, reckoning four years in one Olympiad. An Olympiad is a period of four years.]

> At last the Romans, when they flourished, dated time thus: “In the year from the founding of the City.” Finally Christians date it thus: “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord.” After Troy had been captured, Menelaus and Helen came to Thueris, king of Egypt, whom Homer calls Polybus. In the third year after the capture of Troy—or the fifth, according to some—Aeneas ruled in Italy for three years. Before him Janus, Saturn, Picus, Faunus, and Latinus had ruled there for about one hundred and fifty years [Col. 1285D].

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Samson

> “Again the children of Israel sinned before the Lord, and he delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty [Col. 1286A] years” (Judges XIII).

They were delivered from that servitude as follows: “There was a man of the tribe of Dan named Manoah, who had a beautiful but barren wife. As she often prayed in the field for her barrenness to be removed, an angel appeared to her and said: ‘You shall conceive and bear a son. Take care henceforth neither to eat nor drink except according to the law of the Nazirites.’

> [Note: [Col. 1286C] Addition 1. Seek in the history of Numbers the law by which Nazirites lived (Num. VI). The Master inserted this in order to satisfy Jerome, who says that his name was foretold by the Lord, although it has been determined above how many persons there were whose names were foretold, because the name given to him was Samson. Jerome says that, by the equivalence of these words of the Lord, his name was foretold.]

> ‘For your son will be a Nazirite of God from his mother’s womb and thereafter; he himself shall deliver Israel.’ Another text reads: ‘And Samson shall be called the mighty deliverer of Israel.’
>
> When she had told her husband everything and had commended the angel’s beauty, the man was saddened because he was jealous. To soothe her husband’s irrational grief, she suggested that they should both pray to the Lord for the angel to come again and instruct them both regarding the child. The angel appeared again to the wife. When she summoned her husband, Manoah said to him [Col. 1286B]: “Are you the one who spoke concerning the child?” The angel replied: “I am.” Manoah said: “What do you wish the child to do?” The angel said: “He shall be a Nazirite all the days of his life.”
>
> Manoah brought a kid and loaves. The angel said: “I shall not eat. If you wish to make an offering, offer them to the Lord.” Manoah said: “What is your name?” The angel answered: “Why do you ask my name, which is wonderful?” Manoah offered what he had brought to the Lord upon the rock, to him who works wonders. The angel ascended in the flame of fire and appeared no more.

> [Note: [Col. 1286D] Addition 2. Note that in the Old Testament the names of four persons were announced through an angel: Ishmael, Isaac, Josiah, and Samson; in the New Testament, two: John and Jesus.]

> Understanding that he was an angel of God, Manoah said: “We shall die, because we have seen the Lord.” The woman said: “Not at all. For the Lord has accepted our burnt offering and has revealed the things that are to come.” They called the son who was born [Col. 1286C] Samson, a name meaning “mighty.” The child quickly grew, so that he was already recognized as one destined to be a prophet; and the Spirit of the Lord began to be with him in the camp of Dan—that is, in the army of his tribe. Or this was the place in which Samson first lived, called “the camp of Dan” by anticipation, for the tribe of Dan had not yet received its own allotment.

## CHAPTER XVII. How Samson took a wife and killed a lion
Samson therefore went down to Timnah of the Philistines to see the festival being held there (Judg. 14). There he saw a virgin and desired her; and he said to his father and mother, “Please get her for me as a wife, a woman of Timnah, for she has pleased my eyes.” They said, “Why do you disregard the daughters of your own kinsmen and go over to the daughters of the uncircumcised?” Not knowing that the matter was brought about by the Lord.

As they went down with him, [Col. 1287A] a lion’s cub appeared to him among the vineyards of the town. Samson rushed upon it in the Spirit of the Lord, having nothing in his hand, and tore it limb from limb as though it were a kid of the goats; but he did not tell his parents. After he had betrothed the woman, when after some days he returned to take her, he turned aside to see the lion’s carcass. And behold, bees were in the lion’s mouth, with a honeycomb. He took it and ate on the way; he gave a part to his father and mother, and they ate; he also gave a part to his betrothed.

When the citizens of Timnah were at the wedding feast, fearing the young man’s strength, they gave him thirty strong young men—companions in speech, but guards in fact—lest perhaps, as the guests’ fullness increased, he might attempt something. Samson said to them: “I shall set you a riddle: if you solve it for me within the seven days of the feast, I shall give you [Col. 1287B] thirty linen garments and as many tunics; otherwise, you shall give me the same number.” They said, “Set it forth.” Samson further said: “From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness.”

Josephus gives different words: “He who devours all things produced sweet food from himself, although he himself is not sweet.” They could not solve the proposition for three days. When the seventh day was at hand, they said to the bride: “Coax your husband so that he may tell you the riddle, and tell us; otherwise we shall burn you and your father’s house.” Troubling her husband with tears, she said: “You hate me, and therefore you do not explain it to me.” Thus during the seven days of the feast she wept before him.

But how did she weep for seven days, when it was said above that the young men came to her on the seventh day of the feast? One may say, “When the seventh day was at hand,” that is, when the first day among the seven was still present. This is specified so that one might not think that they came after the three days of which it was said that they could not solve the riddle during those three days. Another explanation is possible: “When the seventh day was at hand,” that is, it was approaching but had not yet arrived; “was at hand” is said as though it were near. Thus, after their three days of inquiry, they came to her on the fourth day, and she spoke to her husband. The statement that she wept for seven days means that she wept within those seven days, not throughout them. Some, however, correct the text thus: “When the first day was at hand.” I think this resulted from a copyist’s error: seeing *septem* (“seven”) abbreviated, he thought that *unum* (“one”) should be read.

At last, on the seventh day, when she had become troublesome to him, [Col. 1287D] he explained it; and she immediately told her fellow citizens. Before sunset on the seventh day they said to Samson: “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” He replied: “What is more deceitful than a woman? Had you not ploughed with my heifer, you would not have found my riddle.” Then the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon. There he struck down thirty men, took their garments, and gave them to his wedding-companions. In anger Samson returned to his father’s house. His wife, however, married one of his wedding-companions.

When the days of the wheat harvest were approaching, Samson came to visit his wife, bringing a kid (Judg. 15). When he wished to enter her chamber, her father prevented him, saying: “I thought that you hated her, and so I gave her to your friend. She has a sister who is more beautiful than she; let her be your wife instead.” Samson said to him: [Col. 1288A] “From this day onward I shall be without blame against the Philistines; for I shall do you harm.”

He caught three hundred foxes, joined tail to tail, and tied torches between them. Setting fire to the torches, he let them run about; and they burned the Philistines’ crops so thoroughly that the fire consumed even the vineyards and olive groves. Knowing that it was Samson’s work, the Philistines burned his wife and her parents as the authors of this evil. Samson said: “I shall yet seek vengeance, and then I shall rest.” And he struck them with a great blow, so that in astonishment they put shin upon thigh.

The Septuagint translators say: “Samson struck the foreigners shin upon thigh.” This returns to the earlier sense: he struck them so wonderfully that, in astonishment, they placed the shin of one foot upon the thigh of the other. Yet, since we walk with the shins and sit upon the thigh, some [Col. 1288B] explain it thus: “He struck shin upon thigh,” that is, foot-soldiers as well as those sitting on horseback. “And Samson lived in the cave of the Rock of Etam, as though in a fortified place.”

## Chapter XVIII. How he killed many with the jawbone of an ass

“Then the Philistines went up into the land of Judah and encamped in the place afterward called Lehi, that is, ‘jawbone.’ The men of Judah said to them, ‘We are your servants. Why have you come up against us?’ They said, ‘To bind Samson.’ Three thousand men of Judah went up to Samson, and, reproaching him, said: ‘Do you not know [variant: *nosti*, “you know”] that the Philistines rule over us? We have come to bind you and hand you over [Col. 1288C] to the Philistines.’ He said: ‘Swear that you will not kill me.’ And they swore” (Judg. 15).

He allowed himself to be bound with two new ropes. As they dragged him along and the Philistines shouted with joy, the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and his bonds came loose like strands of flaxen tow—that is, like a thread of flax twisted with its husk when exposed to the heat of fire. Taking up the jawbone of an ass lying on the ground, he killed a thousand men with it, putting the others to flight.

In triumph Samson sang in verse: “With an ass’s jawbone, with the jawbone of the foals of she-asses, I destroyed them and struck a thousand men.” The Hebrew has: “With an ass’s jawbone, *ḥămôr*.” And *ḥămôr* means “a heap upon heaps”: that is, with the jawbone of an ass I made a heap of dead bodies. [Col. 1288D] He threw away the jawbone and called the place Ramath-lehi, or Ramath-lebi, meaning “the elevation of the jawbone.” For *Ramah* means “high place.”

He was thirsty to the point of death. The Hebrews relate that this happened because he gave glory to himself rather than to God. He cried to the Lord: “I beseech you, Lord: behold, I am dying and shall fall into the hands of the uncircumcised.” The Lord opened the molar tooth in the ass’s jawbone, and water came out; having drunk, he recovered his strength. The former name was changed, and the place was called “The Spring of the One Who Calls from the Jawbone.”

Since he did not fear the Philistines, he went to Gaza, saw a prostitute, and went in to her (Judg. 16). When this became known, the Philistines placed guards at the city gate, intending to kill him when he went out in the morning. But Samson arose at midnight, seized both [Col. 1289A] doors with their posts and bar, carried them on his shoulders, and bore them to the top of the mountain facing Hebron.

## Chapter XIX. How Samson was finally deceived

After this he loved Delilah, who lived on Mount Sorek (Judg. 16). Sorek is either a place or a kind of vine. Five satraps—that is, the leading Philistines—came to her and said: “Learn from him where his strength lies and how we may overpower him when bound, and each of us shall give you eleven hundred pieces of silver.”

> [Note: [Col. 1290A] Addition 1. For nearly every woman is by nature greedy and fickle. Hence I shall add: What is lighter than a river? A breeze. What is lighter than a breeze? Rumour. What is lighter than rumour? A woman. What is lighter than a woman? Nothing.]

This makes five thousand five hundred; some, however, punctuate it thus: “Each of us shall give you one thousand and one hundred pieces of silver.” Delilah coaxed Samson. He deceitfully answered her: “If I am bound with seven new sinew-ropes still damp, [Col. 1289B] I shall become like other men.” Josephus calls these fresh vine-shoots. They brought her seven ropes, with which she bound him while he slept, drunk, with Philistines hidden nearby.

> [Note: [Col. 1290A] Addition 2. He is said to have been drunk not with wine but with love, or else satisfied; otherwise he would have violated the law of the Nazirite before his shaving, and the Lord would have departed from him.]

The woman cried, “The Philistines are upon you, Samson!” He broke the bonds as if they were tow. The same thing happened a second time, with seven new ropes. On the third occasion she tied the seven locks of his head with a weaver’s web and drove it into the ground with a peg. Awakened by her, Samson pulled out the peg together with the locks and the web.

When Delilah pressed him and his soul was weary unto death, he revealed the truth to her: “I have been a Nazirite from my mother’s womb. If my head is shaved, my strength will depart from me.” Then Delilah summoned the satraps to come with the money which [Col. 1289C] they had promised. She caused him to sleep upon her knees and, through a barber, shaved his seven locks—that is, all of them. Or, because a razor had come upon his head, the Lord departed from him even when only the seven locks were shaved. Then the woman cast him off.

When the Philistines seized him, they gouged out his eyes, led him about through the land, and, imprisoned at Gaza, made him grind, afflicting him with servile labour. The Hebrews, however, relate that the Philistines compelled him to sleep with strong women, so that they might obtain strong offspring from him.

As time went on and his hair began to grow again, at the time of a public festival the princes entered their temple to offer magnificent sacrifice to their god Dagon, [Col. 1289D] because he had delivered their enemy into their hands. As the banquet guests rejoiced, Samson was brought in so that he might entertain them and they might mock him. He stood between the two pillars on which the house rested. He said to the boy guiding him: “Let me touch the pillars and rest a little.” Seizing both pillars with his hands, he said: “Let my soul die with the Philistines.” When he shook the pillars, the house fell upon them all; and by dying he killed far more than he had killed while alive.

Apart from the banquet guests, about three thousand persons of both sexes, who were waiting upon the roof for his performance, perished. All his kindred took him and buried him in his father’s tomb. He judged Israel for twenty years. Thus far the Book of Judges marks a period of two hundred and ninety-nine years [Col. 1290A], and has twelve judges besides Shamgar and Barak.

## Chapter XX. Incidental matter

At that time Ascanius, the second king of the Latins, founded Alba. Palefatus, in his book *On Incredible Things*, relates that Ulysses fled Scylla, who was accustomed to plunder guests, in the trireme of the Sirens. He also relates that the Sirens were women who deceived sailors.

## Chapter XXI. On Micah and his priest

[Col. 1290B]

There follows the story of Micah’s idol (Judg. 17). Josephus says that this event, and the other concerning the Levite’s wife, occurred after Joshua’s death and before Othniel, when Israel had sinned exceedingly before the Lord and the Lord had given them into the hands of the Canaanites. They took Ashkelon and Ekron from Judah, along with many cities in the plains, and compelled the Danites, driven out, to flee into the hill country.

At that time there was a man from Mount Ephraim named Micah, who received from his mother eleven hundred pieces of votive silver. At his mother’s command he made from them an ephod and *teraphim*, that is, a priestly garment and idols. He set apart for them a shrine in his [Col. 1290C] house, filled the hand of one of his sons, and he became his priest. He invested him with the priesthood by placing something in his hand, or “filled his hand,” that is, he frequently made offerings to him as to a priest. In those days there was no king in Israel, but everyone did what seemed right to himself.

There was another young man, a Bethlehemite, related to Micah and a Levite, but poor. He wished to travel abroad wherever he might find advantage for himself. When he turned aside into Micah’s house, and Micah learned the reason for his journey, he appointed him his priest, granting him each year ten pieces of silver and a double garment, besides food.

In those days the tribe of Dan was seeking a possession for itself. They sent five men to explore a land in which they might live [Col. 1290D] (Judg. 18). Entering Micah’s house, they rested in the Levite’s lodging. After examining the garments and idols, they departed and came to Laish.

Seeing the place to be fertile and very wealthy, and its inhabitants without fear and unwarlike, they returned to their brethren and said: “Let us go and take possession of the land that we saw. There will be no difficulty.” Six hundred armed Danites set out and first stayed at Kiriath-jearim of Judah. From this they called the place the Camp of Dan. Another place bore the same name, the one mentioned in connection with Samson. A third place bore the same name, where Jeroboam sacrificed to the calves (3 Kgs. 2).

As they passed Micah’s house, the five men mentioned above entered to take the garments and idols. When the priest cried out, [Col. 1291A] they said to him: “Come with us. It is better for you to be a father in one tribe than in the house of one man.” He went with them, carrying all things with him. When Micah pursued them with his entire household, he saw that they were stronger and were threatening him with death, and he turned back.

They came with their women, children, beasts of burden, and all their possessions to the people of Laish; they struck them down and burned the city. They built a city for themselves not far from Lebanon, near the springs of the Jordan, by the great plain of Sidon in the region of Rehob. They called it Dan; formerly it had been called Laish. They set up Micah’s idol as their god throughout all the time that the house of God was at Shiloh. Jonathan, the son of Gershom, of the line of Moses, and his sons, they appointed as priests [Col. 1291B] in the tribe of Dan until the day of their captivity.

When the history repeats, “In those days there was no king in Israel,” it appears to agree with Josephus, who says that the event which follows took place about the same time.

## Chapter XXII. On the Levite’s wife

There was a Levite living on the side of Mount Ephraim who had a wife from Bethlehem. When her husband was angry, she returned to her father’s house in Bethlehem (Judg. 19). Her husband followed her with his servant and two asses, and he was reconciled with his wife. On the fourth day, when he wished to return, his father-in-law detained him until the next day. On the fifth day, after taking food about noon, he departed, leading two laden asses and [Col. 1291C] his concubine—for “wife” is sometimes so called.
