And, as Josephus seems to intend, he undertook the ill-fated journey on the fifth day of the moon.

As they passed near Jebus, when day was declining, he did not wish to enter a town of a foreign nation. He went on to Gibeah, in the tribe of Benjamin; and, since no one received him, he sat in the street. Behold, an old man was returning from the field. He was from Mount Ephraim and lived as a resident alien in Gibeah. He brought them into his house.

While they were dining, men of the city, sons of Belial, came and said to the master of the house: “Bring out the man who has entered your house, that we may abuse him.” Josephus, however, says that they did not come for him, but to seize his wife. When the old man offered them his virgin daughter and the man’s wife in the man’s stead, they brought out the man’s wife. After they had abused her all night, [Col. 1291D] they released her in the morning. Returning to the lodging, she died before the door.

Her husband carried the corpse on an ass and returned home. Cutting her into twelve parts, he sent them throughout all the borders of Israel. Each cried out: “Nothing like this has ever happened in Israel since our fathers came up out of Egypt.” All went out as one man to Mizpah, four hundred thousand fighting men, [Col. 1292A] and said: “No one shall return to his home until we have avenged ourselves upon Gibeah” (Judg. 20). They chose one man out of ten

> [Note: [Col. 1292D] Addition 1. Understand a tenth part of the men. The sense is: they chose a tenth part of the men to bring provisions.]

to bring provisions. They sent to the entire tribe of Benjamin, saying: “Hand over to us the wicked men of Gibeah, that they may die.” They refused; indeed, they gave them thirty-five thousand Benjaminites as reinforcements. There were in Gibeah seven hundred men, so left-handed that they fought with the right; likewise they cast stones from slings so precisely that they could strike even a hair.

The army of Israel went up to Shiloh and consulted the Lord: “Who shall go up as leader of the battle against Benjamin?” The Lord answered: “Judah.” This perhaps appears to support Josephus concerning the date of this disaster. They went up and from there attacked [Col. 1292B] Gibeah. On the first day the Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and struck down twenty-two thousand Israelites; on the following day, eighteen thousand. On the third day, surrounded by ambushes, they fell; and the Israelites burned the city, killing men, women, and children, and doing the same to the other cities of Benjamin.

Of all Benjamin’s number only six hundred remained. They stayed at the Rock of Rimmon and mourned with great mourning for four months.

> [Note: [Col. 1292D] Addition 2. This rock was high. *Ramah* means “high.” Therefore, concerning the mourning of these people who bewailed their children, the Gospel says: “A voice in Ramah,” etc. (Matt. 2).]

The Israelites swore at Mizpah that none of them would give his daughters in marriage to the sons of Benjamin (Judg. 21). At last, repenting of the destruction of one tribe, they asked which Israelites had not come up with them or taken the oath. They found that the people of Jabesh-gilead had not [Col. 1292C] participated in the battle. They struck them down, from man to woman, preserving only four hundred virgins. Calling the six hundred men from the Rock of Rimmon, they restored to them the inheritance of Benjamin and gave them those four hundred virgins as wives.

Taking counsel concerning wives for the remaining two hundred, they said to them: “Behold, there is a feast of the Lord at Shiloh. The daughters of Israel will come up leading dances. You, hidden in the vineyards, come out and let each of you seize one wife.” And it was done so. The tribe of Benjamin was restored. “In those days there was no king in Israel, but everyone did what seemed right to himself.” This is the same concluding clause as above. Therefore it seems likely that both events happened about the same time.

# History of the Book of Ruth

[Col. 1293]

## Chapter XXIII. On Ruth

[Col. 1293A]

After Samson, Eli the priest judged Israel. He is called not merely judge, but priest, from the more worthy office. When the priesthood had been transferred from the sons of Eleazar, he was the first of the sons of Ithamar to receive it.

> [Note: [Col. 1295B] Addition 1. This is certain: when Aaron had four sons, two of them perished by fire in the wilderness. Of those who remained, Eleazar was the elder, and the priesthood belonged to him. It continued until Eli, who was of Ithamar, his brother.]

In his days there was famine in the land. Elimelech, an Ephrathite from Bethlehem, rose up with his wife Naomi and his two sons Mahlon and Chilion, and entered the land of Moab in order to find food there. After he died, his sons married Moabite wives, Orpah and Ruth. Josephus, however, says that the father himself took wives for his sons. They remained there ten years, and both died childless.

Naomi, widowed and bereft of her sons, rose up to return to her homeland, for she had heard [Col. 1293B] that the Lord had given food to his people. Her daughters-in-law accompanied her.

> [Note: [Col. 1295B] Addition 2. Jerome says in his commentary on Chronicles that, in Elimelech’s days, the sun stood still because of transgressors of the law. But because they did not fear God, the famine became so severe that a leading man in the tribe of Judah fled with his wife and children.]

She said to them: “Return, my daughters, to your mother’s house. For you can no longer hope for husbands from my womb.” Note that among the Moabites the law of raising up seed was observed. Orpah consented and returned, but Ruth followed her. Naomi said to her: “Listen, daughter: our God is not like the gods of the nations, nor does our people live according to the custom of the nations. It is better for you to return to your people and your gods.” Ruth said: “Your people shall be my people; your God, my God.”

They travelled together and came to Bethlehem, which was formerly called Ephrathah after Caleb’s wife.

> [Note: [Col. 1296A] Addition 3. Several opinions are given. Hence the city now called Bethlehem was formerly called Ephrathah, according to the first opinion, which says that Miriam, Moses’ sister, was carried there, because she died in the wilderness. Jerome, however, says that Caleb begot, by Ephrathah, Hur, the husband of Miriam; and Hur begot Bezalel.]

According to some, this was Miriam, Moses’ sister, transported from the wilderness. After she was struck with leprosy, she was called Ephrathah—that is, “she saw wrath,” meaning that she learned God’s anger by experience. Or it is interpreted “mirror,” because her punishment was set before all as an example. But Bethlehem then first began to be called so because of the incredible abundance restored to it; *Bethlehem* means “house of bread.”

The report spread through Bethlehem, and people said: “Is this that Naomi?” She said to them: “Do not call me Naomi, which means ‘beautiful’; call me Mara, which means ‘bitter.’ I went out full, and the Lord has brought me back empty, full of bitterness.” At that time they were first reaping barley. There was there a powerful and wealthy man, Boaz, a kinsman of Elimelech (Ruth 2).

With Naomi’s permission Ruth went into his fields [Col. 1293D] and gathered ears after the reapers. It happened that Boaz came out to the field and said to the reapers: “The Lord be with you.” He asked whose girl this was. They said: “This is the Moabite woman who came with Naomi.” Boaz said to her: “Daughter, do not go into another’s field. None of my young men shall trouble you. If you are thirsty, go to the water-containers of my servants, drink; and, at mealtime, come here, eat, and dip your morsel in vinegar.”

> [Note: [Col. 1296A] Addition 4. Since that land is extremely hot, the people of that region use vinegar, which is cold, in their seasonings as a remedy against the heat. Contraries are cured by contraries, because even the most intense heat is thereby moderated.]

“May the God of Israel repay you, because you have taken refuge under his wings.” He also told his servants: “Deliberately pull some out from your sheaves, so that she may gather without embarrassment.” When Ruth ate beside the reapers, she set aside parched grain, which Josephus calls *alphita*, and kept it for her mother-in-law.

In the evening, beating out with a rod what she had gathered, she found about an ephah of barley, that is, three modii. When she returned to her mother-in-law, she told her what Boaz had done for her. Naomi said: “The man is our kinsman; blessed be he by the Lord.” Ruth did the same in the following days, until the winnowing of the threshing-floor.

It was the custom in Israel that, at the winnowing of the threshing-floor, the master prepared a great feast for his servants and reapers. He slept on the threshing-floor and, as though observing a festival, abstained from embraces. The same was done at sheep-shearing. Whether it was done after the vintage I have not read. Naomi said to Ruth: “Wash yourself, daughter, anoint yourself, put on more elegant clothing, and go up to the threshing-floor with the others. Let the man not see you until he has become drunk. When he falls asleep, lie down at his feet and remain there” (Ruth 3).

She did everything that her mother-in-law commanded. Behold, at midnight the man awoke and, startled, said: “Who are you?” She replied: “I am your servant. Spread your cloak over me, because you are a kinsman.” Boaz told her that chastity must be preserved in such advances, and added: “Another kinsman is nearer than I. If he wishes to take you under the right of kinship, [Col. 1294C] well and good; otherwise I shall take you, as the Lord lives.”

Boaz rose from the place where he had been lying beside the *arconium* of sheaves before people could recognize one another.

> [Note: [Col. 1296A] Addition 5. *Arconium* is said to derive from *arcere*, ‘to keep apart,’ because there the *gelimae* are kept separate from one another.]

He filled her little cloak with barley—about six modii. Ruth returned burdened with it to her mother-in-law and told her what Boaz had said. Boaz went up to the gate, sat with the judges, called ten of the city elders, and summoned the nearer kinsman of whom he had spoken. He said to him: “Naomi intends to sell the portion of our father Elimelech’s field. We two alone are kinsmen, but you are the nearer. Buy it, then, if you please.” The other said: “I shall buy it.” Boaz said to him: “Then you must not remember the laws only by halves: with the field you must take Mahlon’s widow, in order to raise up [Col. 1294D] the name of your kinsman.” He said: “I yield the right of kinship; use my privilege.” Boaz said: “Then take off your shoe, so that the renunciation may be binding” (Ruth 4).

Josephus, however, says: “Boaz, having called the elders as witnesses, ordered the woman to remove his shoe according to the law and spit in his face.” John says: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of whose shoe.”

> [Note: [Col. 1296B] Addition 6. One explanation of John’s words is this: John was thought to be the bridegroom of the bride, that is, of the Church. It was customary that, when one died childless, his nearest kinsman should take his wife. If the nearest refused, she removed his shoe, and the next kinsman took her. John therefore says: I am not the bridegroom, but Christ is; I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his shoe in order to take his bride. Yet he himself was not the one who removed the shoe of the man who refused and then took her. This is what is indicated here.] (Mark 1).

From these three cases one infers that, according to differing circumstances, sometimes the man refusing removed his own shoe; sometimes the woman removed it; sometimes the man who took her did so. But however it was done, as a reproach for refusing contrary to the law, his house was called “the house of the unshod.”

Boaz said to those standing by: “You are witnesses of this matter.” They said: “We are witnesses. May the Lord make this woman for you like Rachel and Leah, who built up the house of Israel.” Boaz took Ruth as his wife. After a year a son was born to him. Naomi placed him in her bosom, performing the office of nurse and bearer. Her neighbouring women congratulated her: “Behold, you have one who will nourish your old age and serve you more than seven sons.” Therefore she called his name Obed, which in Hebrew is interpreted [Col. 1295B] “serving.” He was the father of Jesse, the father of David.

# History of the First Book of Kings

[Col. 1295]

## Chapter I. Preface

[Col. 1295C]

The Book of Kings is divided among us into four volumes; among the Hebrews, however, into two. They call the first *Samuel*, after its author’s name. They call the second *Melachim*, that is, “Kings,” after its subject matter. Some call it *Melachoth*, meaning “Kingdoms,” but incorrectly. For it concerns only the one kingdom of the Jews and its kings, although it was divided in two. This book was written chronologically under those kings and compiled into one by Jeremiah. This is evident because the ending of this book and that of Jeremiah are the same. To commend Samuel, however, a commendation of his father is first supplied in this form.

## Chapter II. On Samuel’s parents

[Col. 1295D]

There was a man from Ramathaim-sophim, in the hill country of Ephraim, named Elkanah the Ephrathite (1 Sam. 1). Here “man” is used not for sex but for strength of virtues; nor does “one” refer to number but to exceptional religious devotion beyond others. His city is called Ramathaim, which in the Gospel is called Arimathea (Matt. 27); Josephus calls it Ramath, because it was situated on high ground. *Sophim* is interpreted “observation,” and stands in the genitive case, as though one said “Ramathaim of observation,” because the surrounding [Col. 1296C] country could be seen far off from it. So Jerome relates.

Others divide the name thus: Ramathaim-sophim. “Mount Ephraim” is not the name of a mountain, but of a region. Hence later, where twelve governors of regions are mentioned, who served Solomon month by month, Dechar is listed as governor of Mount Ephraim.

Elkanah was a Levite, the nineteenth descendant from Levi, descended from him through Kohath, Izhar, and Korah. Hence it is clear that Samuel was not an Aaronite. He is called an Ephrathite, that is, a Bethlehemite, for through his mother he was from the tribe of Judah. Therefore Samuel later appointed one of his sons judge in Bethlehem, as among fellow tribesmen.

Note that some distinguish three names thus: *Effrataeus*, referring to Ephraim, is written with two *f*s; *Euphrathaeus*, referring to Ephrathah, with *ph*; and *Ephrathaeus*, referring to the Euphrates, means “fruitful,” with *eu*. As they say, this is a boundary of Judea near the Euphrates.

## Chapter III. On Peninnah and Hannah, the wives

“Elkanah had two wives: the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah” (1 Sam. 1). Although he ought to have said “of the other” when speaking of two, he said “of the second,” indicating that, although they were equal in the name of wife, Peninnah was second in her husband’s affection. Hannah was beautiful but barren; Peninnah fertile.

That man went up on the three appointed days, according to the Law, to worship at Shiloh. Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas were priests at Shiloh. When Elkanah had sacrificed, he gave “to Peninnah and her sons and daughters portions, but to Hannah he gave one portion in sorrow.” Some think this means new garments, which he distributed to his wives and children on the feast day. But it is more likely to refer to the portions of sacrifices that fell to those making offerings, which the Levites distributed to others as holy things.

The Hebrew expression seems rather to mean: “he gave one double portion before sending [them away],” as though one portion equal to two. Hannah, moreover, was grieved by barrenness and did not take food. She went out to the doors of the tabernacle to pray, while Eli sat before the entrance, so that those seeking counsel might find him ready. Hannah, weeping, made a vow to the Lord: “Lord of hosts, if you give me a male child, I shall give him to you as a Nazirite all the days of his life.”

Eli watched the motion of her lips but did not hear her voice. Thinking that she was drunk, he said: “Digest for a little while the wine with which you are soaked.” She answered: “By no means, my lord. Rather, I am an unhappy woman, even until now. Pray for your servant.” Understanding that she was barren, Eli said: “May the God of Israel grant you your petition.” The Hebrew, however, has “will grant.” Thus secure because of the priestly promise, the woman departed, “and her countenance was no longer changed in different ways”: that is, her mind was no longer distracted by varying doubts.

## Chapter IV. On Samuel’s birth

[Col. 1297C]

It came to pass that she bore a son and called his name Samuel, that is, “petition of God,” because she had received him after asking God for him. The woman did not go up to Shiloh with her husband until she had weaned the child (1 Sam. 1). When she brought him, now weaned, to Shiloh, she brought three calves and three modii of flour. The Hebrew, however, has “a modius of flour and a jar of wine,” which is a measure of three modii.

She did not bring fine flour and wine merely for libations, since less would have sufficed for the libations of calves—especially since she offered only one calf—but it should be understood that she gave the remainder to the household of priests. It seems remarkable that a two-year-old boy, as though newly weaned, was brought to minister in [Col. 1297D] the tabernacle. Therefore some say that there are three weanings: the first is from the milk of the breast, occurring in the third year; the second from the milk of childhood, occurring in the seventh; the third from the milk of boyhood, occurring in the twelfth. Thus the boy is removed from the nurse, the pedagogue, and the guardian.

Some therefore say that he was brought after the second weaning to be instructed in letters. Hence it is later read that his mother sent him a little tunic every year (1 Sam. 2). Others say that he was brought after the third weaning, as already fit for ministry. Hence it immediately follows: “But the child was ministering in the presence of the Lord” (ibid.).

When she had presented the child to Eli, Hannah said: “As your soul lives, my lord, I am the unhappy woman for whom you prayed; and behold the son whom the Lord gave me.” This was a form of oath for confirmation, as if to say, “By your soul, my lord.” Some think that it is sometimes said there by imprecation—for example, “As your soul lives, king, if I know him,” meaning, “May your life destroy me, king, if I know him.”

Hannah prayed to the Lord and said: “My heart has exulted,” etc. (ibid.). Yet this is properly a song, not a prayer. The song contains three things: first, thanksgiving for the benefit granted to her; second, an attack upon the proud, occasioned by Peninnah, as in “Do not multiply speech”; third, prophecy concerning Christ’s kingdom, as in “The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth.”

What is read in the song, “Until the barren bore many, and she who had many children became weak,” is rendered in the Hebrew with “seven” instead of “many,” and “was cut off” instead of “became weak.” Tradition holds that as each of Hannah’s children was born, one of Peninnah’s children died. It counts Samuel’s two sons among Hannah’s five children, making seven. Elkanah returned to his house, while Samuel ministered before Eli. Josephus says that he prophesied when he had completed his twelfth year.

## Chapter V. On Eli’s sons
Moreover, the sons of Eli, not knowing the Lord, took from those offering sacrifice the priests’ portion of the sacrifices before the fat had been burned: they took it raw, so that they might prepare it more elegantly for themselves. [Col. 1298C] The priest’s servant would put a flesh-hook into the pot, and whatever the flesh-hook brought up belonged to the priest (1 Sam. 2). This was not a portion, but robbery.

“But Samuel ministered, girded with a linen ephod,” not a priestly but a prophetic one; “and his mother brought him a little tunic every year.” And the Lord visited Hannah, and she had three sons and two daughters.

“Now Eli was very old,” and he heard of the sins of his sons, who lay with the women keeping watch at the entrance of the tabernacle, and defiled those who had come for purification. Some, however, maintain that they did not have intercourse with the women, but, corrupted by money, gave women permission to consort with their husbands during the days of purification. Hence their father said to them: “You make the people of the Lord transgress,” and he rebuked them lukewarmly.

[Col. 1298D] But a man of God came to Eli and said to him: “I expressly declared that the house of your father should minister to me for ever. Far be this from me! But those who honour me I will glorify, and those who despise me I will cast away. Behold, I shall cut off the arm of your father’s house,” that is, I shall take the priesthood away from your house, for which the right shoulder was due to it, “and you shall see your rival in the temple.” This occurred in Solomon’s days, when Zadok, who was descended from Eleazar, was made priest after Abiathar, who was descended from Ithamar, had been expelled (1 Chron. 24).

Some nevertheless suppose that the priesthood was transferred to Samuel, who was not an Aaronite. But neither is Samuel said to have been a priest, nor were the Aaronites removed from the priesthood until about the time of the Maccabees. What the man of God further said, [Col. 1299A] “a great part of your house shall die,” was perhaps fulfilled shortly afterwards, when his sons fell in battle, or when Saul killed the priests of Nob; and, as a sign that the prediction would prove true, he foretold that his sons would die on one day.

“Now in those days the word of the Lord was precious” (1 Sam. 3), that is, rare.

## CHAPTER VI. That the Lord called Samuel a third time

“And it happened one day that Eli lay in his bed, and his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp by day before it was extinguished” (1 Sam. 3). This seems strange. For no one is so nearly blind that he sees a burning lamp less clearly than an extinguished one, especially since dim eyes see more clearly by lamplight than by day.

Some punctuate it thus: “He could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished,” that is, before he died. “But Samuel was sleeping”; and the word “but” is superfluous. The Hebrew seems to support this interpretation, for it pauses after “he could not see,” and then adds, “the lamp of the Lord was not yet extinguished.” Thus the sequel is fitting: “But Samuel slept in the temple of the Lord,” that is, in a chamber beside the tabernacle, where he alone slept with Eli the priest.

Therefore, when the Lord called him, he ran to Eli, saying, “You called me.” He spoke falsely, but did not lie. Eli said, “I did not call you. Go back and sleep,” and it happened similarly a second time. “For Samuel did not yet know the Lord,” [Col. 1299C] that is, he did not yet have the habit of hearing the Lord.

When the Lord called him a third time, he again went to Eli. Eli understood that the Lord had called him and said: “If he calls you again, say, ‘Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening.’” When the Lord called him as he slept, he said, “Speak, Lord,” and the Lord disclosed to him the same threat against Eli’s house that He had earlier made through the man of God.

Yet one must not suppose that the promise the Lord had made to Aaron concerning an everlasting priesthood had been rendered void. For promises of this kind must always be understood with the condition sometimes expressly stated: “If your sons keep my covenant,” etc. (Ps. 131 [132]). Josephus seems to hold that the Lord called Samuel three times in order to prefigure [Col. 1299D] his three future dignities. For he was a prophet, a status which Josephus says he possessed from this calling; he was also a judge; and he offered sacrifice, as a priest might, because Ichabod, Eli’s grandson, was a little child.

In the morning Eli adjured Samuel to tell him the entire word of the Lord, and he told him everything. Eli said: “He is the Lord; let him do what is good in his own eyes.” Samuel grew, and all Israel knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord; and all the people consulted him, according to the word of the Lord. For the Lord had commanded them to reject diviners, soothsayers, and such persons, and to inquire of their brethren for the word of the Lord.

## CHAPTER VII. On the death of Eli and his sons, and the capture of the Ark by the Philistines

[Col. 1300A]

And it happened that the Philistines assembled for battle at Aphek (1 Sam. 4), which is said to be a place of Jezreel belonging to Israel, and which Josephus calls the city of Ampheolbenitis. Israel too went out to battle beside the Stone of Help—so named by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation, as will become clear later. Israel was defeated, and about four thousand men fell. The elders said: “Let us bring from Shiloh the ark of the Lord, who sits above the cherubim.” This is said, as also in the Psalm, “You who sit above the cherubim” (Ps. 79 [80]), because the glory of the Lord sometimes appeared there.

They took the ark, and Eli’s two sons went with it. [Col. 1300B] For Phinehas was already performing his father’s office; and they had received Eli’s command lest perhaps they return to him without the ark. The Philistines were afraid and fought more fiercely. Israel fled; thirty thousand foot soldiers were slain; the ark of the Lord was captured; and Eli’s two sons died.

A young Benjaminite ran from the battle line and reported in Shiloh what had happened. Eli was sitting opposite the road leading to the camp, watching—that is, listening. For he was already blind, according to the Hebrews, or rather nearly blind. When he heard of the slaughter of the people and the death of his sons, he remained still. But when he heard that the ark had been captured, he fell backward, broke his neck, and died.

His daughter-in-law, Phinehas’s wife, was pregnant. Overcome by grief, she bent herself and gave birth to a son of seven months, as Josephus says. [Col. 1300C] She called him Ichabod, that is, “inglorious,” saying: “The glory of the Lord has departed from Israel.”

Eli judged Israel for forty years. Josephus agrees; but the Septuagint and Chronicles say twenty. It may be said that after Samson twenty years passed without a judge, which were added to the years in which Eli judged. Some, however, say that the twenty years during which Samuel judged are to be added to the years of Eli, his master. But it is truer that Samuel’s years are counted with Saul’s years.

Certainly it may have happened that, when Eli was made judge, he transferred the priesthood from the house of Eleazar. Eleazar succeeded Phinehas; Abiezer succeeded Eleazar; Buzi succeeded Abiezer; Ozi succeeded Buzi; and [Col. 1300D] the priesthood was transferred.

### Incidental matters

In Eli’s days the third king of the Latins was Silvius Posthumus, son of Aeneas and Lavinia; from him onward the Latin kings were called Silvii. Ascanius left him as heir while his own son Julius was still a little child; from Julius the Julian family drew both its origin and its name. The sons of Hector recovered Ilium after expelling the descendants of Nestor.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the return of the Ark

The Philistines took the ark of the Lord to Ashdod and set it beside Dagon, as though it were a trophy (1 Sam. 5). Rising early, they found Dagon lying prostrate on the ground before the ark and, as Josephus says, as though worshipping it; and they restored him [Col. 1301A] to his place. Again, on the following morning, they found him prostrate: his head and hands, cut off from the trunk, lay upon the threshold. For this reason, to this day no one entering the temple at Ashdod treads upon the threshold.

The hand of the Lord lay heavily upon the Ashdodites. He struck them in the more private region of the buttocks, and their projecting haemorrhoids rotted. Josephus says this occurred through the cruel affliction of dysentery, so that they discharged decaying intestines; and mice swarming out of the fields gnawed away their haemorrhoids. Having summoned the satraps, they said to them: “What shall we do with the ark?” They replied: “Let it be moved around.”

Wherever it was moved, it struck everyone in their hinder parts; and they made themselves leather seats. The rulers of the five cities assembled to deliberate what they should do. Some said that the ark caused their afflictions; others, that they came by chance; others, from corruption of the air and the fruits of the earth.

[Col. 1301B] The priests and diviners said: “Why do you harden your hearts like Pharaoh and Egypt?” (1 Sam. 6). “Send back the ark, but not empty. Put in a little box beside the ark five golden rings and five golden mice, according to the number of cities that have been struck.” Josephus, however, says that there were five golden human images.

“And you shall place the ark on a new cart, and yoke two milch cows upon which no yoke has been placed; shut up their calves at home; and if they go straight up toward Beth-shemesh, then it was the ark itself that did us this harm; otherwise it happened by chance.” The cows went straight ahead, lowing, and did not turn aside either right or left from the road leading to Beth-shemesh.

[Col. 1301C] This is one of the priestly cities in the tribe of Benjamin. There is another Beth-shemesh in the tribe of Naphtali. “Now the Beth-shemites were harvesting wheat, and the cart came into the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite and stopped there. They placed the ark upon a great stone,” which the Hebrews think was an altar built by Abraham, “and they placed the little box, which was beside it. The Levites cut up the wood of the cart and laid the cows upon it as a burnt offering to the Lord. And the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrifices on that day.”

Some maintain that there were only five Philistine cities, and that this is why they sent only five golden rings and five mice. But later Ziklag is read to have been a Philistine city (1 Sam. 27). Therefore Isidore’s statement appears preferable: there were only five chief cities; “each offered a golden ring and a mouse, while the others offered mice only, as far as Great Abel, upon which they placed the ark of the Lord.”

This wording seems to indicate that Abel was the name of the stone upon which the ark was placed. Others maintain that it was a city then called Beth-shemesh and afterwards Abel—meaning “mourning”—because of the mourning of the Beth-shemites that followed. “Great” was added to distinguish it from another Abel, called Abela later on, where the wise woman cried out to Joab (2 Sam. 20): “Those who inquire [Col. 1302A] should inquire at Abel.”

> [Note: Col. 1302B, Addition 1. When Joab wished to capture it, the sense is: Do not destroy it, because everyone there takes counsel concerning what should be done.]

Then it is read, “upon which they placed the ark,” that is, beside which they placed it. “Seventy men of Beth-shemesh and fifty thousand of the people were struck, because they looked upon the ark uncovered.” Those seventy are thought to have taken down the ark when they were not priests. If it is asked why not all the Philistines who saw the ark died, it may be answered that they did not sin by seeing it, since they were not forbidden to see it.

The frightened Beth-shemites sent to the men of Kiriath-jearim, asking them to take the ark away from them (2 Sam. 2). They brought it back and took it into the house of Abinadab, a righteous man, at Gibeah.

> [Note: Col. 1302B, Addition 2. Samuel moved it from Kiriath-jearim to Mizpah; afterwards he and Saul moved it to Gilgal; afterwards Saul moved it to Nob, and from Nob to Gibeah; afterwards David moved it to the house of Obed; afterwards to Zion; and afterwards Solomon moved it into the Temple. The diligent reader will be able to observe all these transfers in this book.]

They appointed his son Eleazar as priest to guard the ark, and it remained there for twenty years, until the eighth [Col. 1302B] year of Saul’s reign, when he himself took it into the camp. It had remained with the Philistines for seven months; and then Israel rested after the Lord, the Lord’s anger against them having been calmed.

## CHAPTER IX. That Israel defeated the Philistines while Samuel prayed

[Col. 1302C] Samuel observed this and saw their trust in the Lord. He said: “Let us go up to Mizpah, that I may pray for you” (1 Sam. 7). When they had gone up to Mizpah, he poured out water before the Lord, water in which accumulated curses had been cast; if an idolater drank it, his lips adhered to one another inseparably—perhaps as a sign of the covenant, as Joshua did. Samuel judged them there, that is, taught them God’s judgments.

Some, however, assert that Samuel ground a certain idol into powder, mixed it, and gave it to the people to drink; and that he identified in their beards those guilty of idolatry from those who were innocent, just as Moses had once done.

The Philistines heard that unarmed Israel had assembled at Mizpah, and they came up armed against them. [Col. 1302D] Israel, afraid, said to Samuel: “Cry out for us to the Lord.” Samuel offered a suckling lamb as a burnt offering. While Samuel cried to the Lord, battle began. The Lord thundered with a great crash over the Philistines; the earth shook and opened chasms in places; the Philistines were put to flight and were slain by the sons of Israel, who struck them down as far as the borders of their land.

Samuel took a stone and set it at the boundary, calling that place “Stone of Help.” The Philistines did not again attempt to enter Israel’s borders while Samuel lived.

Samuel judged the people, making a circuit each year through Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. He returned to Ramah, built an altar there, and [Col. 1303A] judged Israel there also. Those three cities were famous: Bethel because of Jacob’s dream; Gilgal because of the second circumcision; and Mizpah because Joshua frequented it. Samuel went up to them in turn at the three weekly festivals and judged the people there. On other days the people went up to him at Ramah for judgment.

## CHAPTER X. On Samuel’s wicked sons and Israel’s request for a king

When Samuel had grown old, he appointed his sons Joel and Abiah, one at Bethel and the other at Beer-sheba, to sit there and judge the people (1 Sam. 9). They turned aside after greed and perverted justice.

Unable to bear this, the people said to Samuel: “Give us a king to judge us, as the other nations have.” Samuel took this badly because of his innate justice and his aversion to kingship. When he consulted the Lord, the Lord said: “Hear the voice of the people. They have rejected not you alone, but me, so that I should not reign over them. Yet warn them of the right of the king over them.”

Samuel said to the people: “This shall be the right of the king: he will make your sons his servants—horsemen, runners, farmers, and makers of weapons. He will make your daughters perfumers, cooks, and bakers. He will put your male and female servants and your beasts to his own work; he will give your best things to his servants; and you will be his slaves.”

The people said: “We shall not listen to you; a king shall be over us, [Col. 1303C] and he shall fight before us.” Samuel said: “Go each to your own home; at a suitable time I shall summon you, when I learn from the Lord that he will give you a king.”

## CHAPTER XI. On Saul’s anointing and election

“There was a man of Benjamin named Kish, from the stock of Jemini; his son was Saul, and there was no man better than he in Israel. When Kish’s she-asses were lost, he said to his son: ‘Take one of the servants and look for the she-asses’” (1 Sam. 9).

After they had passed through Mount Ephraim, the land of Shalim, and the land of Benjamin without finding them, they came to the land of Zuph, who was Samuel’s great-grandfather. Saul said to the servant: “Let us return, lest my father be anxious about us.” The servant replied: “There is a man of God in this city who speaks without uncertainty. Let us go to him, in case [Col. 1303D] he may tell us about our way.”

Saul said: “What shall we bring him? Bread has failed from our packs, and we have no little bag”—that is, no silver in a bag. As Josephus says, he was mistaken in thinking that the prophet would accept gifts, since Saul is not said to have offered any, nor Samuel to have accepted them. The servant replied: “I have in my hand a quarter of a silver stater.”

They went up to Ramah, where the man of God was, and said to girls going out for water: “Is the seer here?” They answered: “He is here today, sacrificing at the high place.”

> [Note: Col. 1305B, Addition 1. The sacrifice means the meal that Samuel had prepared for them.]

As they walked in the middle of the city, Samuel appeared to Saul. On the previous day the Lord had said to him: “Tomorrow, at this hour, I shall send you a man from Benjamin, whom you shall anoint over my people.” When Samuel saw Saul, the Lord said to him: [Col. 1304A] “Behold the man of whom I spoke to you.”

Samuel said to Saul: “I am the seer. Go up and eat with me; tomorrow I shall dismiss you, and I shall tell you what is in your heart. And do not be anxious about the she-asses, for they have been found.” Saul might seem to have had concern in his heart about the she-asses, had the prophet not specified this. Hence the Hebrews say that Saul saw in a dream that he was placed on top of a palm tree, a sign that he would reign; this made him anxious. For this reason Samuel said to him: “To whom shall belong every good thing in Israel? Shall it not be yours?”

They went up to the high place, for before the Temple it was permitted to sacrifice at a high place.

> [Note: Col. 1305B, Addition 2. Since those who sacrifice at high places are condemned in many passages, how is it that Samuel is said to have sacrificed at a high place? Answer: the Temple had not yet been built.]

When they reclined in the dining room, Samuel gave him a place at the head of the thirty men who had been invited. He set before him the shoulder, as though it were a royal portion, which he had deliberately reserved for him.

[Col. 1304B] In the morning, after they had risen and left the city, Samuel said: “Let the servant go on before us, but you stand still, that I may tell you the word of the Lord.” Samuel took a flask of oil—a clay vessel, square, with an opening in its side—and poured it upon Saul’s head. He kissed him and said: “God has anointed you ruler over his inheritance. This shall be your sign: when you leave me, you will find two men near Rachel’s tomb, who will tell you that the she-asses have been found.

“When you come to the oak of Tabor”—and Tabor is the name of a man, not a mountain—“three men will meet you: one carrying three kids, another three loaves of bread, and another a flask of wine; and you will receive two loaves from [Col. 1304C] their hand. After this you will come to a place called the Philistine garrison, because the Philistines once encamped there; and you will meet a band of prophets coming down from the hill of God, playing instruments and prophesying. The Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them” (1 Sam. 10).

Note that Samuel was the first to establish communities of religious men continually singing psalms to the Lord. Their communities were called a *cuneus*, a “band,” as it were a “wedge.” They were said to prophesy, that is, continually to praise God; and perhaps some of them sometimes did prophesy.

Samuel added: “When you see these signs, know that the Lord is with you, and go down before me to Gilgal, for we shall meet there when necessary. I myself shall come down [Col. 1304D] to you, that you may offer an offering for seven days.” According to some, offerings were made for that number of days at the consecration of a priest and king. He added: “Wait here until I come to you, and I shall show you what you must do.”

Some, however, refer the seven days to waiting, so that the meaning is: “You shall wait seven days until I come”; this will be explained later. When Saul came to the band of prophets, he prophesied with them. The Hebrews say that he prophesied concerning Gog and Magog, the rewards of the righteous, and the punishments of the wicked.

Those who knew him wondered and said: “Is Saul also among the prophets—and is Kish his father?” That is: since he is not of prophetic stock. Another reading has: “And who is his father?” with the same sense; or: [Col. 1305A] “And who is their father?” That is, God alone is the father of prophets, and “the Spirit breathes where it wills” (John 3), not only upon the sons of prophets. Hence it became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” This was perhaps said of Saul alone, or of anyone suddenly elevated.

He went in to Ner, his paternal uncle. When Ner asked him about Samuel’s words, Saul was silent about the matter of kingship, but told him the rest. Samuel summoned the people to Mizpah and said: “Stand before the Lord, and we shall proceed by tribes, families, and heads.” The lot found the tribe of Benjamin and came down to Saul son of Kish. Samuel is believed to have managed the lots according to his own purpose. Saul, knowing that he would be sought, hid himself, as though unwilling to accept the rulership.

[Col. 1305B] When he was found, they set him in the midst of the people. “He was taller than everyone else from the shoulder upward.” Samuel said: “Behold him whom the Lord has chosen; there is none like him among all the people.” All the people cried: “Long live the king!”

Samuel wrote the law of kingship and read it aloud before all the people and the king. He put the book in the tabernacle, which was still at Mizpah with the altar. They returned to their homes, and Saul went to his house in Gibeah. Some despised him, but Saul took no notice.

## CHAPTER XII. On Nahash and Saul’s second anointing after victory over Ammon

[Col. 1305C]

“It happened about a month later that Nahash the Ammonite besieged Jabesh-gilead” (1 Sam. 11). When those under siege requested a covenant from him, he said: “On this condition I shall make a covenant with you: that I gouge out the right eyes of all of you.” For he gouged out the right eyes of those captured in war, so that, covering their left eyes with shields, they would be useless in battle.

They answered him: “Grant us seven days, and we shall send throughout all the borders of Israel; if there is no defender for us, we shall come out to you.” The messengers came to Saul’s Gibeah. When they reported this, the people wept. Saul himself was coming from the field, following oxen. [Col. 1305D] He promised the men of Jabesh that on the third day he would come to their aid, and ordered some of them to remain in order to guide the way.

Divinely inspired, he cut both oxen into pieces and sent them throughout all Israel, saying: “Whoever does not go out after Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen.” All went out as one man, three hundred thousand men. Saul arranged the people in three divisions, entered the camp during the morning watch, and struck Ammon with a great blow.

The people said to Saul: “Who said, ‘Saul shall not reign over us’? Give them to us, that they may be killed.” Saul said: “No one shall be killed today, because the Lord has brought deliverance in Israel.” Samuel said: “Let us go to Gilgal, [Col. 1306A] and renew the kingdom there.” They anointed Saul king a second time at Gilgal.

Samuel said to the people: “Behold, the king goes before you. You rejected me and the Lord. This is your sign that the Lord gave you a king in anger: behold, today is the wheat harvest. I shall call upon the Lord, and he will send thunder and lightning, hail and rain” (1 Sam. 12). It immediately happened, contrary to the nature of that land.

The frightened people said: “Pray for your servants. For we have added evil to our sins by asking for a king.” Samuel said: “You have sinned; do not henceforth depart from the Lord, and you shall live. Otherwise both you and your king shall perish.”

“Saul was a son of one year when he began to reign,” that is, humble like a small child; “and he reigned two years over Israel” [Col. 1306B] (1 Sam. 13), that is, he ruled the people justly. In the remaining years of his reign he was like a tyrant, not a king.

Some read this of his son Ish-bosheth, saying that he was one year old at the beginning of his father’s reign. They likewise understand it of him that he reigned two years in Israel. That Ish-bosheth reigned two years is certain; but that he was an infant when his father began to reign cannot stand. Saul reigned about twenty years; Ish-bosheth, when he reigned after his father, was already forty years old. Yet they try to settle this by saying that Saul began to reign after Eli and by assigning Samuel’s years to Saul’s reign. The Hebrew reads thus.

## CHAPTER XIII. That Samuel foretold to Saul the transfer of the kingdom

[Col. 1306C]

“Saul was a son of one year [Note: Col. 1307C, Addition 1. This chapter may be understood in two ways: either *Saul* is nominative, or it is dative.] when he was in the kingdom, and he reigned two years. He chose for himself three thousand in Israel” (1 Sam. 13), that is, when he had reigned for a year and then two years—thus after about three years—he chose for himself, etc.

“Two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and Bethel, but a thousand were with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin,” which was a city of Phinehas son of Eleazar. “Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison that was at Gibeah,” that is, the fortified place where the Philistines had stationed guards as masters in Israel; and then Israel rose against the Philistines.

When this was heard, the Philistines assembled to fight Israel: thirty thousand [Col. 1306D] chariots, six thousand horsemen, and an innumerable multitude. Saul went up to Gilgal and summoned the people and Samuel to consult the Lord. While he waited for Samuel seven days, as agreed, the people dispersed from him. In fear, “they hid in caves, secret places, and caverns; and the Hebrews also crossed the Jordan.”

Some were called Hebrews in Israel by this special designation. They are believed to have gone down in fear to the Philistine camp to serve them. When Saul saw that delay on the seventh day harmed him, he offered the burnt offering and peace offerings. As soon as he had finished, Samuel came. Rebuking Saul, he said: “What have you done?”

Saul answered: “The people were slipping away, and you had not come by the appointed days. I feared that the enemies [Col. 1307A] would come up against us before I had appeased the face of the Lord; compelled by necessity, I offered to the Lord.”

Saul seems to have sinned by offering a burnt offering to the Lord to consult him without Samuel. Hence some, as stated above, say that the seven days Samuel mentioned were not days of waiting but days of offerings at the consecration of a king; and they say that an offering to consult the Lord must never be made without him. Yet, while it is read that offerings were made for seven days “for the priest,” I do not recall reading “for the king.” It is highly remarkable that, although Saul had already twice been anointed king, neither occasion involved such an offering for a king.

It may therefore be said that Samuel gave this command in this sense: whenever Saul wished to sacrifice in order to consult the Lord, he was to summon Samuel, so that Samuel might show him what he should do; and if Samuel delayed after being summoned, Saul was to wait for him seven days. Saul, however, counted the day on which he summoned Samuel among the seven, [Col. 1307B] and did not wait for him except six days.

Samuel added: “Your kingdom shall by no means continue; the Lord has sought for himself a man after his own heart, to rule his people.” Samuel went to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul went out with the people to meet the Philistines, and only six hundred men were with him, together with his son Jonathan.

“Now there was no blacksmith in Israel; for the Philistines had taken care that the Hebrews should not make sword or spear. Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen all the edges of their tools, even to mend the goad,” that is, to repair and sharpen it. Or: “even to the goad which is for correcting,” namely, oxen. “When the day of battle came, neither sword nor spear was found in the hand of the entire people, except the sword of Saul and Jonathan.”

Saul had the ark of the Lord brought beside the camp, and Ahijah son of Ahitub, brother of Ichabod, carried the ephod.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the defeat of the Philistines and the honeycomb Jonathan ate

One day Jonathan went out with his armour-bearer to scout the Philistine garrison, without his father’s knowledge (1 Sam. 14). [Col. 1307D] Jonathan wished to cross over to the Philistines through a steep valley, with projecting rocks on either side shaped like teeth. Jonathan said to the young man: “When we show ourselves to them, if they say, ‘Wait until we come to you,’ let us stand still. But if they say, ‘Come up to us,’ let us go up, for the Lord has delivered them into our hands; this shall be our sign.”

When the Philistines said: “Come up to us,” Jonathan climbed up on hands and feet, with his armour-bearer behind him. The Lord struck terror among them before Jonathan, and Jonathan and the young man struck down twenty of them in half an acre. The camp was thrown into confusion; they fled and killed one another. Saul’s watchmen reported the enemies’ flight.

When Saul asked, “Who has gone away from us?” [Col. 1308A] Jonathan and his armour-bearer were found to be absent. Saul said to Ahijah: “Bring forward,” that is, prepare, “the ark of the Lord for consulting the Lord.” But as the tumult increased in the camp, he said to the priest: “Withdraw your hand.” Saul and the people shouted and began to pursue the fugitives.

The Hebrews who had gone over to the Philistine camp also returned, to join Israel; and all who had hidden themselves earlier came back into the battle. There were now with Saul about ten thousand. Saul, seeing that eating would cause harmful delay, put the people under oath: “Cursed is the man”—that is, he shall deserve death—“who eats bread before evening, until I take vengeance on my enemies.”

As the people passed through the wood, flowing honey appeared, but no one tasted it. [Col. 1308B] Jonathan, who had not heard his father’s curse, dipped his staff into a honeycomb. When he tasted it, “his eyes were enlightened,” that is, his face became cheerful as his strength returned.

It is said that honey is so abundant there in hollow trees, rock caverns, and hidden places in the ground that many honeycombs are found falling upon the earth. Josephus says Jonathan found it by the dens beneath an oak in Ephraim’s allotment. When someone told him of his father’s curse, he ceased eating, not approving his father’s curse: “Would not a greater blow have been inflicted upon the enemy if the people had taken food?”

In the evening the people, extremely weary and unable through hunger to endure delay, slaughtered livestock on the ground and ate with the blood. That is, they killed and cooked it in whatever fashion, before the blood had been thoroughly drained, eating the flesh before it was cleansed. Contrary to their ancestral custom, they cut the throats with a knife and drained the blood.

> [Note: Col. 1309B, Addition 1. The practice was that in battle they did not eat until the evening sacrifice had been made for it. Otherwise, they ate with the blood which they had shed in battle.]

Some say that no one was permitted to eat from the enemies’ spoil until he had offered a victim to the Lord; anyone eating otherwise ate, as it were, with blood. Saul said to the people: “You have sinned; roll a great stone to me.” He ordered everyone to cut up livestock upon that stone and before him, according to ancestral custom, lest anyone secretly do otherwise.

“Then Saul first built an altar to the Lord.” From this it is evident that Saul had not already offered twice at Gilgal upon an altar newly built. Some nevertheless think that every time he offered, he built a new altar. But this “first” is said because [Col. 1308D] now he offered fully in accordance with God’s pleasure.

When Saul wished to rush upon the enemies at night, the priest said: “Let us consult the Lord.” But when he consulted, “the Lord did not answer him on that day,” that is, neither by night nor on the following day. Saul said: “This silence is due to a hidden sin. By the living Lord, even if it was done by Jonathan, he shall die without reprieve.”

He put the people on one side and himself and Jonathan on the other. The lot fell upon Jonathan. Saul said: “What have you done?” Jonathan replied: “I am conscious of nothing except that yesterday, unaware of the curse, I ate honey.” Saul said: “You shall die, Jonathan; for unless I do this, may God do this to me and add this besides.”

The people said: “Then shall Jonathan die, who brought deliverance in Israel? As the Lord lives”—[Col. 1309A] that is, by the living Lord, or, as God is living and not like the gods of the nations—“not a hair of his head shall fall to the ground.” This is aposiopesis; or *if* is read for *not*. They rescued Jonathan from his father’s hands and returned to their homes.

“But Saul, established in the kingdom, overcame Israel’s enemies wherever he turned, and struck Amalek.” This is prolepsis. Or perhaps he struck them earlier than he destroyed them completely, by the Lord’s command. Saul’s sons were Jonathan, Jishui, and Malchishua. His fourth son, Ish-bosheth, is omitted, either because he was a child and not yet a soldier, or because he was incapable. His daughters were Merab and Michal; his wife, Ahinoam; and the commander of the army, Abner son of Ner, his cousin. For Kish and Ner were brothers and sons of Abiel. Yet Chronicles reads [Col. 1309B] that Ner was Kish’s father (1 Chron. 8), which is said on account of age and because he raised him.

## CHAPTER XV. That Saul defeated Amalek
“Then Samuel said to Saul: Thus says the Lord: ‘Destroy Amalek and all that belongs to him, because he opposed Israel when it came up from Egypt’” (1 Sam. 15). The Lord wished even the beasts to be killed, so that no remembrance of Amalek might survive in anything. Some say that they were sorcerers and possessed the skill of changing themselves into cattle; and therefore, lest they escape under the form of cattle, the cattle too perished. [Col. 1309C] “And Saul reviewed two hundred thousand foot-soldiers and ten thousand men of Judah.” Observe that almost everywhere the men of Judah are spoken of as superior to the rest. Hence elsewhere: “Judah, a lion’s cub” (Gen. 49). When Saul invaded Amalek, he said to the Kenite: “Withdraw from Amalek, lest I sweep you away with him, because you showed kindness to Israel.” For Jethro, who was also called Reuel and Cis, gave good counsel to Moses (Exod. 18). His household dwelt among Amalek, except for the sons of Hobab; and the Kenites departed and thereafter dwelt in Israel. From them Rechab was descended, as is read in Chronicles: “These are the Kenites who came from the warmth of the house of the father of Rechab” (1 Chron. 2).—“Then Saul struck Amalek with the edge of the sword,” that is, in devastation as though by devouring; [Col. 1309D] or it is an idiom, meaning “with the sword.” “And Saul spared Agag, king of Amalek, and the best of the herds. And the Lord said to Samuel: ‘I regret that I made Saul king.’” And Samuel prayed to the Lord for him throughout the night.

When he learned that Saul had set up for himself a triumphal arch at Carmel, in accordance with the pride of the Gentiles, who used to have an arch of myrtle, palm, and olive branches erected as a sign of victory, he went down to him at Gilgal, and Saul met him. When Samuel reproached him for having kept back anything from Amalek, Saul excused himself by saying that the people had preserved the best things in order to offer them to the Lord in thanksgiving. Samuel said to him: “Obedience is better than sacrifices.” God delights in good deeds, not in sacrifices—especially when they offer [Col. 1310A] what God had decreed should perish.

And Saul said: “I have sinned; but this once bear my sin,” that is, pray and make satisfaction for me, or forgive me. Samuel said to him: “God has cast you away, so that you shall not be king over Israel.” When Samuel wished to depart, Saul seized the edge of his cloak, and it tore. Samuel said: “Thus has the Lord today torn the kingdom from you,” that is, from your posterity. After they had worshipped the Lord together, Samuel ordered King Agag to be brought to him. He was brought, fat and trembling. Agag said to Samuel: “Does bitter death separate in this way?”—as though saying: It is strange that death so shakes you and has separated your soul from you. Some read “it has separated two words,” supplying “against you”; or, according to another reading, “Agag said: ‘Thus bitter death separates me.’” That is: Death, which had separated my own people from me, most bitterly separates me from humankind. Samuel cut him to pieces, and went to Ramah. Saul, however, went up to his house at Gibeah; and Samuel saw Saul no more in royal attire, though he afterwards saw him in a prophetic capacity.

## Chapter XVI.—On David’s anointing in his father’s house

Samuel mourned for Saul, and the Lord said: “How long will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him? Fill your horn with oil and go to the house of Jesse, that you may anoint one of his sons as king; and because you fear Saul, take a calf as though to sacrifice it” (1 Sam. 16). When he came to Bethlehem, the elders said to him: [Col. 1310C] “Is your coming peaceful?” For they feared that the king had sent him on some punitive business, or that, perhaps having offended the king, he had fled and they would not dare receive him. When he said that he had come to sacrifice, he consecrated Jesse and his sons and placed them before the altar. Seeing Eliab, the firstborn, tall and excellent, he thought he would become king; but the Lord said to him: “I do not make bodily beauty the summit of royal rank, but strength of character.” The Lord tested the others in the same manner.

Jesse had set seven sons before Samuel—seven of his own—and Nathan, his adopted son, the son of Shammah his son. Samuel said to him: “Are these all the sons?” He answered: “There remains the youngest, who is tending the sheep.” At Samuel’s command he was brought: [Col. 1310D] “David, ruddy,” that is, reddish; “and handsome.” He was anointed in the midst of his brothers, and the Spirit of the Lord was directed upon David from that day onward. “And the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit,” sent “by the Lord,” tormented him.

Josephus says that David then received the prophetic spirit, just as Saul himself had begun to prophesy when the Holy Spirit came upon him. But because it is said that the spirit departed from Saul and was directed upon David, this appears to refer to the same spirit—that is, the grace of the Spirit, through which Saul had until then been victorious over his enemies. Then Saul’s servants said to him: “An evil spirit torments you. Employ a psalmist skilled on the lyre, and you will bear it more lightly.” Physicians report that harmony makes the cheerful more cheerful and the sad sadder. Mathematicians report [Col. 1311A] that many demons cannot endure harmony, and sometimes none can; and the king was told that David knew how to play and was a man of war.

When the king sent to Jesse for his son, “Jesse took an ass loaded with bread, wine, and a kid, and sent them to the king by David’s hand.” The phrase “an ass loaded” means sufficiently burdened; or perhaps, just as wineskins are made from oxen and goats, sacks for carrying things were made from an ass’s hide. “Therefore, whenever the spirit seized Saul, David played upon the lyre, and it became lighter for him, and at times the spirit withdrew from him.” When Saul’s spirit had ceased for a while, David was sent back to his father.

## Chapter XVII. On the war of the Philistines against Israel and the death of Goliath

[Col. 1311B] It came to pass that the Philistines assembled against Israel for battle. Saul and Israel encamped in the Valley of the Terebinth, beneath which Jacob hid the idols. “And a bastard man came forth from the Philistine camp, Goliath of Gath,” of giant stock, “six cubits and a span in height” (1 Sam. 17). He is called a bastard because he was born of an ignoble father—that is, a Gentile—and a noble mother—that is, a Jewish woman. A *spurius* and a hybrid is one ignoble on his father’s side, as a *mamzer* is; a *nothus*, on his mother’s side.

He reproached Israel for being servants of the Philistines and proposed a single combat, such that the people whose champion was defeated should be slaves of the other. The Hebrews were astonished and exceedingly afraid of him. Goliath spoke thus for forty days. David’s three eldest brothers were in the army; and Jesse sent them, by David’s hand, an ephah of parched grain and ten loaves, and to the tribune under whom they served ten little cheeses—that is, ten small fresh cheeses. The Hebrew has “ten portions of cheese,” meaning ten kinds and varieties of cheese. Jesse commanded David to bring back assurances from his brothers—that is, bills of divorce. It was the custom for those going to war to give their wives bills of divorce, so that, if they were captured and did not return within three years, the wives might marry whomever they wished.

When David came to the place of combat—for every day some combatants came forth—behold, Goliath came up, uttering reproaches as yesterday and the day before; and the Israelites fled before him. [Col. 1311D] David, wondering, heard several men say: “Whoever strikes this man down, the king will enrich and give him his daughter.” When Eliab, David’s brother, heard him asking such questions, he rebuked him, fearing that he might fight and be killed. David answered: “What have I done? Is it not merely a word [above, worthy of rebuke]?” That is: Why do you rebuke me for a mere word? Or thus: It is only speech and not action; I do not say it because I intend to fight, but in order to know the matter.

David’s words were reported to Saul, and he said to the king: “I, your servant, will fight against the Philistine.” When Saul forbade him because he was a boy, David added: “I, your servant, killed a lion and a bear when they attacked the flock. Therefore this uncircumcised man will be like one of them,” with the Lord delivering me. Then [Col. 1312A] Saul clothed him in his own armor; but David laid it aside because he was unaccustomed to armor. “He took in his hand a shepherd’s staff, chose five very smooth stones from the torrent,” that is, flat and rolling stones, “put them in his shepherd’s bag,” that is, the vessel in which he milked or carried bread, “took a sling in his hand, and advanced against the Philistine.”

Goliath despised David and said: “Am I a dog, that you come against me with a staff?” David answered: “You come against me with weapons, but I come against you in the name of the Lord, so that today this whole assembly may know that the Lord does not save by the sword.” When he cast a stone, he struck him in the forehead with the sling. He struck him in the same place with the second and third stones as well; [Col. 1312B] on the third cast he brought him down, then ran, drew Goliath’s sword, and cut off his head.

Some Jews here tell the tale that the iron of the helmet and breastplate rendered obedience to the Lord, making room for the stone to enter and kill the man; and for this reason circumcision was thereafter performed with an iron knife, though previously it had been done with a stone one. The Philistines fled, and Israel pursued them as far as the gates of Ekron. “David took the head and the sword and put them in his tent.” Much later he took them to Jerusalem; the Hebrew does not have “his.” It is therefore believed that he placed them in the tabernacle of the Lord as a trophy. Hence Abimelech afterwards received the sword.

When David returned from battle, Saul said to Abner: “Of what stock is this young man?” Perhaps he wished to know to whom [Col. 1312C] he would give his daughter. Saul did not recognize him because he had been absent for some time and, altered by the devising of the evil spirit, had become weak in memory.

> [Note: [Col. 1312C] Addition 1. Although he had often previously been present with the king [Col. 1312D] and soothed him with the lyre, he did not recognize him now.]

Abner answered: “As your soul lives, O king, I do not know him”—that is, by your life I do not know him, or by way of an imprecation. For the Hebrews often name evils by their opposites, as in: “Bless the Lord, and die” (Job 2). When Saul asked David who he was, he said: “I am the son of your servant Jesse.” Then Jonathan’s soul was bound to David’s soul, and they made a covenant; Jonathan gave David his garments, even his bow, sword, and belt (1 Sam. 18).

## Chapter XVIII. On Saul’s persecution of David

[Col. 1312D]

It came to pass, when they returned triumphantly from battle and David planned to carry Goliath’s head to Jerusalem—for, as Josephus says, he had it with him, but had already dedicated the spear to God—that women came out from all the cities. The women sang with instruments: “Saul struck down thousands”; and the maidens replied: “And David, tens of thousands” (1 Sam. 18). Hearing that the cause of victory was attributed more to David than to himself, Saul said sorrowfully within himself: “What remains for him except the kingdom alone?” He feared that the kingdom would be transferred from his house. “He envied David and no longer looked upon him with kindly eyes.”

After [Col. 1313A] a few days an evil spirit seized Saul, and he behaved as though prophesying. Throwing the spear he held, he thought to pin David, who was playing, to the wall. David avoided him for the second time. For the first time he had withdrawn when war threatened; afterward Saul made him a chiliarch and said: “I will give you my daughter Merab; only be a brave man and fight the Lord’s battles.” For he reasoned within himself: “Let not my hand be against him, but the hand of the Philistines.” Yet when Merab ought to have been given to David, she was given to Hadriel the Meholathite.

Michal, however, loved David, and Saul was pleased. He said to him: “Today you shall be my son-in-law in two respects,” meaning, through my two daughters.

> [Note: [Col. 1313C] Addition 1. Jerome says that the two things were the hundred foreskins which he had previously given the king for Merab, and the two hundred which he afterwards gave for Michal.]

For you had one as your betrothed and shall have the other as wife. Or thus: In return for two things—because you struck down the giant and will give [Col. 1313B] a hundred foreskins. Saul conveyed this to him through his servants: the king had no need of a bridal gift—that is, gifts or a marriage payment—except one hundred Philistine foreskins. David went with the men whose tribune he was at Ekron and struck down two hundred Philistines. Bringing their foreskins, he counted them out to the king. Josephus, however, says that he cut off six hundred heads and came to the king, demanding the marriage; Saul gave him his daughter, though unwillingly.

When Saul saw that David was approved by the Lord and by men, he was afraid and plotted his death. No longer wishing to conceal his fear, “he told Jonathan and his servants to kill David” (1 Sam. 19). Jonathan informed David, saying: “Hide yourself until morning; tomorrow I shall speak to my father for you.” The next day Jonathan spoke to his father: “Why do you sin against innocent blood? He has brought salvation to Israel; his works are very necessary for you, and by his death your daughter will be afflicted as a widow.” Saul was appeased and swore: “As the Lord lives, he shall not be killed.” Jonathan brought David to the king, and he stood before him as formerly.

## Chapter XIX. How Michal let David down through a window when Saul was pursuing him

After battle had again commenced, David struck the Philistines with a great blow. Saul envied him, and the demon again tormented him. He wished, as before, to pierce David as he played, [Col. 1313D] but David fled to his own house (1 Sam. 19). Saul sent officers by night around the house in order to kill him when he came out in the morning. When Michal perceived this, she let him down through a window, and he escaped.

Michal spread out her bed as though occupied by a sick man. In it she placed an image, with a goat-skin at its head to represent hair; and she put coverings over it, with the breathing liver of a goat to imitate panting. When Saul discovered that he had been deceived, he said to Michal: “Why did you let my enemy go?” She answered: “I was afraid, for he said to me: ‘Let me go, or I shall kill you.’”

David, fleeing, came to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that the king had done [Col. 1314A] to him. They both went to Naioth, a hill at Ramah where there was a band of prophets. When Saul learned this, he sent officers to Naioth to seize David. When they saw the prophets and Samuel standing over them, the Spirit of the Lord came upon them and they prophesied. He sent second and third messengers, and they too prophesied. Enraged, Saul went after them. Before reaching Naioth he began to prophesy, and became as though mad. Stripped of his royal clothing, he sang with the rest throughout the whole day and night, while David and Samuel watched in secret.

> [Note: [Col. 1315A] Addition 1. What, then, is meant by the statement above that Samuel did not see Saul until the day of his death, except that he did not see him in royal dress?]

David fled from there and came to Jonathan, who was being sought. Jonathan said to him: “You shall not die. My father will do nothing great or small without telling me.” David replied: “Your father knows [Col. 1314B] that you love me, and he will say, ‘Let Jonathan not know this.’ As your soul lives, only one step, so to speak, separates me from death” (1 Sam. 20). By “one step” he means the wall of his house, which had intervened when he escaped the hands of the officers. The Hebrew has “only one pace,” and the sense is: There was the smallest interval between me and death.

“Therefore, I beg you, do what I say. Tomorrow will be the Kalends, and I shall hide in the field until the evening of the third day. If the king asks for me, since I customarily sat beside him to eat, [Col. 1315A] say to him: ‘David asked leave to go to Bethlehem, because there are solemn sacrifices there for all his fellow-tribesmen.’”

> [Note: [Col. 1315A] Addition 2. The Hebrews maintain that David did not eat, nor is it plainly read that he did eat.]

Perhaps there was some new-moon festival lasting three days. “If the king says to you, ‘Good,’ there will be peace for your servant. But if [Col. 1314C] he is angry, his malice against me is complete.” Jonathan said: “Let us go out into the field.” When they had gone out, Jonathan swore to David that whatever good or evil he found in his father he would report; and they mutually swore a covenant between themselves and their offspring.

“Jonathan also continued swearing,” that is, swearing very earnestly. But the inserted words, “The Lord required it from the hand of David’s enemies,” were added by the writer of his own accord in the Spirit.

> [Note: [Col. 1315A] Addition 3. Ezra, or another writer, because David afterwards disinherited Jonathan’s son.]

Jonathan added: “On the day on which it is lawful to work,” that is, the day before the Kalends, as some wish; but it is better understood of the following day: “You will go out and sit hidden by the stone Ezel. When I come to you after the festivities, I shall shoot three arrows beside it, as though [Col. 1314D] practising at a mark. If I say to the boy who will fetch them, ‘Look, the arrows are on this side of you,’ there is peace for you; come to me. But if I say, ‘The arrows are beyond you,’ go, and may the Lord be between me and you forever.”

On the first day of the festival David’s place was seen to be empty, but Saul said nothing, thinking David not yet purified. On the second day, when the king asked for him, Jonathan excused him. Saul angrily said to him: “Son of a woman who seizes men of her own accord, I know that, to your shame, you love the son of Jesse. So long as he lives, neither you nor your kingdom will be established. Bring him to me, for he is a child of death.” Jonathan said: “Why should he die?” Saul seized a spear to strike him; Jonathan avoided him in grief, ate no bread that day, and went out to the field. He did [Col. 1315A] as he had told David. When he said to the boy, “The arrows are beyond you,” he sent the boy into the city with the bow and arrows. David rose from his hiding-place and bowed three times—either to God or to Jonathan himself. “They wept greatly, and Jonathan said: ‘Whatever we have sworn shall stand forever between us and our offspring. Go in peace.’”

## Chapter XX. On David’s flight to Nob

[Col. 1315B] David fled to Nob, to Abimelech the priest, brother of Ahiah. The priest wondered that the king’s son-in-law had come almost alone. David said to him: “A secret command of the king pressed me, and I have appointed the servants to such-and-such a place; therefore I came privately and with few, or almost no, companions. Now if you have anything at hand, give me at least five loaves” (1 Sam. 21). Perhaps the number of his companions is understood from the number of the loaves; and David does not lie, for he did not say this with intent to deceive.

The priest answered: “I have no common bread at hand, but only holy bread, namely the loaves of presentation. If the young men are clean, especially from women, let them eat”—as though saying: Necessity has no law; yet, if they are unclean through intercourse, I shall not give it to them even in necessity. David said [Col. 1315C] to him: “We have abstained from women since yesterday and the day before, and the vessels of the young men have been holy,” that is, their bodies, in which souls are contained, or the young men themselves. “Moreover, this way is unclean, but it shall itself be sanctified today in the vessels.” That is: perhaps we contracted some uncleanness on this journey, but bodily cleanliness suffices to cleanse it.

The Hebrew has: “The vessels of the young men are holy,” and they interpret this as vessels for eating—as though saying: You may put the clean loaves in clean vessels. It follows: “Moreover, this way is common,” that is, your question is common.

> [Note: [Col. 1315D] Addition 1. They again say that he was Ahiah himself, son of Ahitub, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar.]

That is: Why do you inquire about cleanliness, when even if they were clean they ought not to eat? “But it shall itself be sanctified today in the vessels,” [Col. 1315D] that is, in our consciences. For we know that necessity, which has no law, excuses and, as it were, sanctifies us. He gave them the loaves of presentation which had been removed in order that hot ones might be set out. From this it may be inferred that it was the Sabbath.

When David asked whether he had weapons, the priest gave him Goliath’s sword. Josephus says it was the spear, wrapped in a cloak in the tabernacle. For the ark was then there with one of its tabernacles. Doeg the Idumean, Saul’s chief shepherd, who was bound to prayer by a vow, observed all this.

## Chapter XXI. On David’s flight to Achish

David fled that day to Achish, king [Col. 1316A] of Gath (1 Sam. 21). His servants told the king that the man concealed with him was virtually king in Israel; that he would receive a neighboring enemy if he kept him safe. David was afraid, especially because Saul had sent to Achish to demand that he return his fugitive servant. When he was being brought before the king, he feigned madness. He struck against the doors of the gate, as though seeking to enter through a closed gate, and performed the acts of a madman so as to convince the king that his affliction was genuine. The king said: “This possessed man shall not enter my house,” and dismissed him.

David went from there and hid in the cave of Adullam (1 Sam. 22), though not immediately. First he came to Nahash, king of the Ammonites, as Jerome says in a gloss on the following passage. “All his kindred gathered to David there. Others also gathered to him—those oppressed either by Saul’s hatred or fear, or by debt—and there were with him about four hundred armed men. David went with them to Mizpah, which is in Moab.” There is another Mizpah in Judah. He left his father and mother with the king of Moab, and they remained with him for as long as David was in the stronghold—that is, on the expedition in which he sought fortified places to live.

## Chapter XXII. On the death of Abimelech and eighty-five priests

At the prophet Gad’s warning to depart from there and go into the land of Judah, David went into Judah and came to the forest of Hereth (1 Sam. 22). Saul heard that David had appeared. While Saul was in [Col. 1316C] the grove at Ramah, holding a spear, he said to his servants: “Will the son of Jesse enrich all of you sons of Benjamin? Is there none among you who grieves for my condition?” Doeg the Idumean said: “I saw him at Nob, with Abimelech son of Ahitub, who consulted the Lord for him, gave him provisions and Goliath’s sword.”

The angry king summoned Abimelech and all the priests at Nob and said to him: “Why have you conspired against me with the son of Jesse? For you gave him bread and a sword.” He answered: “Far be this from me! Let not the king suspect anything of this kind throughout all my father’s house. I did not know that he had fled from you.” The king said to the guards: “Fall upon the priests.” They refused to raise their hands against the anointed of the Lord. [Col. 1316D] The king said to Doeg: “Fall upon them.” That day he slaughtered eighty-five men wearing the linen ephod. Perhaps they were then clothed in it to move the king’s mind by the garb of religion. The Hebrews say that not all were priests, nor all clothed in the ephod, but that all were worthy men.

Saul also struck Nob, the village of the priests, its women, men, and beasts, according to what God had prophesied to Eli the priest: that his offspring would be uprooted to the very root. Abiathar, the priest and son of Abimelech, alone escaped. He fled to David carrying with him the ephod made by Moses, and reported to him the death of his father and family. David said: “I am responsible for all the lives of your father’s household. Remain with me. Whoever seeks your life seeks mine also.”
