It was reported [Col. 1317A] to David that the Philistines were attacking Keilah and plundering the threshing-floors—that is, the grain from the floors—or ravaging the crops. “Therefore he consulted the Lord: ‘Shall I go and strike the Philistines?’ And the Lord said: ‘Go, strike them, and save Keilah’” (1 Sam. 23). When David’s men were afraid to go with him, he consulted the Lord again and received the same answer as before. David went, struck the Philistines with a great blow, and entered Keilah.

When Saul heard this, he said: “David is shut up in a city.” He assembled an army to besiege David and his men. When David learned this, he consulted the Lord through Abiathar: “Will Saul come down here, and will the men of Keilah hand me over to him?” The Lord said: “He will come down, and they will hand [Col. 1317B] you over”—as though saying: This is the king’s intention, and theirs, which could not be hidden from God. David and his men, about six hundred, departed and wandered uncertainly. When Saul learned this, he pretended not to go out.

David went into the mountain of the wilderness of Ziph. Jonathan went to him at the wooded place called Nava and strengthened his hand in God. He said: “You will reign over Israel and I shall be second to you. My father knows this too.” They renewed their covenant oath before the Lord—that is, before Gad the prophet and Abiathar.

## Chapter XXIII. On the Ziphites, and how David hid in a cave while fleeing Saul

The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah [Col. 1317C] and said: “David is hiding among us on the hill of Hachilah. Come, and we shall hand him over into your hands.” Saul blessed them and said: “Examine more carefully where his foot is, report it to me, and I shall follow you. David and his men, however, were in the wilderness of Maon” (1 Sam. 23). When Saul went out to seek him, David ascended to the Rock, a very well-fortified place, as Jerome says, where he set down what burdened him. David moved about in the wilderness of Maon on the shady mountain. Saul’s men surrounded the mountain in the manner of a circle.

When David despaired of being able to escape, a messenger came to Saul: “Return quickly, for the Philistines have poured into the land.” Saul ceased pursuing David and went to meet the Philistines. Therefore they called that place the Rock of Division, because Saul had been separated there from David. “David then went up from there and lived in the very secure places of En-gedi” (1 Sam. 24), a town containing a balm vineyard. Saul took three thousand chosen men and pursued David even among the precipitous rocks accessible only to ibexes.

> [Note: [Col. 1318B] Addition 1. *Ibex* is equivocal: it may mean a bird, like a stork, or a she-goat.]

Saul entered a cave to relieve his bowels. David and his men were hiding in the inner part of the cave. David’s servants said: “The Lord has delivered him into your hands.” David silently cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak. Returning to his men, he struck his heart “metonymically,” that is, his breast, in which the heart is contained; or his conscience [Col. 1318A] reproached him for what he had done. When his companions murmured against him, fearing that they would fall upon Saul, he said: “As the Lord lives, unless the Lord himself strikes him, or at his death, or in battle”—an aposiopesis, as though he meant: thereafter I shall not spare him. “May the Lord be merciful to me,” that is, may he grant me this mercy, that I do not stretch out my hand against the anointed of the Lord. “And he restrained his men with these words.”

Saul went out and continued on his journey. David went out after him and cried: “My lord the king.” When Saul looked back, David bowed to the ground and said: “Why, my lord the king, do you listen to the words of men speaking evil against me, saying, ‘David seeks evil against you’? Recognize the edge of your cloak in my hand: when I cut it off, my eye spared you. Whom do you pursue? A dead dog and one living flea.” Hearing this, Saul wept and said: “You are more righteous than I. May the Lord repay you. I know that you will reign. Swear to me by the Lord that you will not destroy my descendants after me.” David swore to Saul. Saul went to his house; David went up to safer places in the narrow passes of Mizpah.

## Chapter XXIV. On the death of Samuel and Nabal

At that time “Samuel died,” and all Israel mourned him, each person grieving as for his own son, “and they buried him at Ramah” (1 Sam. 25). It is certain, therefore, that Samuel did not write from this point to the end of the second book. Why then do these two books bear his name as their title? Because one of the prophets among his disciples wrote the remainder, and the work is ascribed to the master. Some nevertheless say that Nathan wrote what follows; others, David.

“David went down to the wilderness of Paran.” Paran is a town in Arabia. There was a man in the city of Maon, in the wilderness of Maon, and his property was at Carmel. This is a mountain in the territory of Judah. There is another Carmel on the border of Palestine and Phoenicia, where Elijah killed the prophets of Baal; and this man was from the family of Caleb. Chronicles reads: “Caleb begot Orham”—others have “Archam”—“Orham begot Jezeni”; this, the Jews think, is Nabal [Col. 1318D] (1 Chron. 4).

When David heard that Nabal had gone up to shear his flocks, he sent ten young men to ask him to send some blessing on the festive day. For the Jews rejoiced and feasted at sheep-shearing, in remembrance of their forefathers who had been shepherds. Nabal said to David’s messengers: “I will not send anything. Who is the son of Jesse? Today fugitive slaves have multiplied. I do not know them.” When David heard that Nabal had insulted him, he girded on his sword with four hundred men and said: “May the Lord do so to my enemies and more besides, if I leave of all that belongs to him even one who urinates against a wall”—that is, not even a dog or an infirm person.

Nabal’s wife Abigail was beautiful and prudent, and did not know of this. A keeper of the sheep told her [Col. 1319A] how much protection David had provided in the wilderness. Abigail therefore hastened and took to meet David bread, wine, cooked rams, measures of parched grain, bundles of raisins, and cakes of figs. Bowing to David, she said: “Let this iniquity, my lord, be upon me,” that is, forgive me this wrongdoing of my husband. Or thus: If you think it wrongdoing not to destroy him because you have sworn, let it be imputed to me. My husband acts in accordance with his name; for *Nabal* means “fool.” “The Lord has appointed you ruler over Israel; you ought not to shed innocent blood. He has done you no harm, but has not given you what was his; and your life shall be kept as though in the bundle of the living.”

The Hebrew has “in the bond of life,” which is the same thing—that is, in the fellowship of the saints. [Col. 1319B] Another reading has “in a bundle of strength.” That is: The Lord will preserve your life for increase just as a bundle of vines is kept in water for transplanting. David answered: “Blessed is the Lord, who sent you today to meet me. Go in peace. I have heard your voice,” namely by remitting the insult, “and honored your face,” by accepting the guest-gifts from your hand.

When Abigail told her husband all these things, his heart died within him from fear; for he feared that David might perhaps not be willing to break his oath. He died after ten days. When David heard it, he said: “Blessed be God, who kept my hands from blood and returned Nabal’s wickedness upon his head.” He summoned Abigail and took her as wife. David also took a third wife, Ahinoam of Israel.

## Chapter XXV. On David’s flight to Achish
Again the Ziphites reported to Saul: “Behold, David is hiding on the hill of Hachilah” (I Kings [1 Samuel] 26). And Saul went after him with three thousand chosen men. David went down by night to Saul’s camp, taking with him Abishai, son of Zeruiah, his sister. She had three sons: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel, David’s nephews. When they had secretly entered the king’s tent while all were asleep, Abishai said: “I will pin Saul to the ground with the spear.” But David restrained him, saying: “Who shall stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be innocent? Rather, take the spear fixed in the ground at his head, and the vessel of water [Col. 1319D], and let us go.” They departed without anyone waking, for a sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them.

When they had crossed the torrent and stood on the summit of a mountain, from which they could be heard, David cried out to Abner and to all the people: “You are sons of death, because you have not guarded your lord, the Lord’s anointed. Someone entered in order to kill the king. Look where the king’s spear is, and the cup of water.” Saul, recognizing the negligence of his men and David’s kindness, cried out: “Is this your voice, my son David?” He replied: “Why does my lord persecute his servant? What have I done? If the Lord incites you against me, let him smell the sacrifice”—that is, he must be appeased by sacrifice and prayer, so that he may show us what he wills concerning this matter. Or thus: You yourself should kill [Col. 1320A] me, and it will be like a sacrifice to God, a pleasing fragrance. Some read it in this way: “Let him smell the sacrifice, if the Lord incites you against me,” that is, let us test by God’s judgment, while sacrificing, whether the Lord will do this. But if the sons of men incite you, cursed are they, who compel me to pass over to idolaters, so that I may not serve the God of Israel.

And Saul said to David: “I have sinned. Return, my son; I will do you no further harm.” David replied: “May the Lord judge between us. Behold the king’s spear: let someone come and take it.” To him Saul said: “Blessed are you, my son. You shall indeed accomplish what you do, and you shall be mighty in strength.” And Saul returned to his own place.

David said in his heart: “One day I shall fall into Saul’s hands; it is better that I should save myself among the Philistines.” Therefore David went, and six hundred men [Col. 1320B] with him, to Achish, son of Maoth, king of Gath (I Kings [1 Samuel] 27). This was the son of the aforesaid Achish, whose mother was called Maoch. David’s two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, were with him. David said to Achish: “I do not wish to be a burden to the king; let the king give me a place in which to live.” Achish gave him Ziklag, which thereafter became the property of the kings of Judah. David lived there for four months and twenty days, and raided the surrounding Philistine villages which were not under Achish’s power. He did not bring back man or woman as a captive, lest they perhaps speak against him. When Achish asked whom he had struck, he said that they had ravaged those dwelling in the south of Judah and in the lowlands.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the gathering of the Philistines against Israel, the destruction of the Pythonists, and the raising of Samuel

[Col. 1320C]

It came to pass at that time that the Philistines gathered for battle against Israel. Achish said to David: “You and your men shall go out with me to the camp. I appoint you guardian of my head above all others” (III Kings [1 Samuel] 28). Saul too gathered all Israel and came to Gilboa. But Samuel was dead. This is repeated here in order to show Saul’s distress, in which Samuel was especially necessary to him; or to show that Samuel had died recently and was soon to be raised. For they maintain that no one can be raised by the art of Pythonism unless he has died recently [Col. 1320D] and his vital parts are still intact.

Saul therefore became afraid and consulted the Lord, who did not answer him, neither through dreams nor through prophets—that is, through Samuel’s disciples—nor through priests. The Hebrew has: “nor through the teaching of the ephod,” namely, that in which were doctrine and truth. Saul said to his servants: “Find me a woman who has a python.” For he himself had slain magicians, diviners, and practitioners of Pythonism. Jerome relates that one had been preserved, because she was Abner’s mother; she lived hidden in Endor, a city beside the spring of Endor.

Some maintain that a *python* is the art of raising the dead, invented by Pythius, as if he said: “Find me a woman skilled in that art.” This agrees with the Hebrew, in which one reads “a woman of Baladoph.” *Balad* is interpreted “mistress”; *oph* is the name of that art. Saul therefore changed his clothing and came to the woman by night with two men. He said: “Raise up for me whomever I shall name to you.” She answered: “You know how much Saul has done against magicians. Why then do you lie in wait for my life?” Some maintain that Saul destroyed them for this reason: because they proclaimed that David would become king.

Saul swore to her that she would suffer no harm on account of this matter, and told her to raise Samuel. But when the woman saw the holy man, she was troubled and said: “Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul.” For Samuel had revealed this to her, as Josephus says. Some tell the tale that a dead man raised by magic first moves from the feet and rises, except when he is raised at a king’s request [Col. 1321B]: then he rises from the head. Others say that a prophet cannot be raised unless a king makes the inquiry.

Then Saul told her that he was Saul, and said: “Do not be afraid. What did you see?” She answered: “An old and glorious man, clothed in a priestly mantle.” Saul, understanding that it was Samuel, worshipped him. And the soul of Samuel, as Josephus says, asked: “Why have you disturbed me?” Saul answered: “I am greatly distressed. The Philistines are fighting against me, and the Lord has not answered me. I beg you, tell me what I should do.” He replied: “Why do you ask me, when the Lord has departed from you? The Lord will do to you as he has spoken. He will take the kingdom from your hand and give it to David. Tomorrow, moreover, you and your sons shall be with me”—[Col. 1321C] that is, among the number of the dead, “as I am,” or in hell.

Concerning this raising, some say that an evil spirit appeared in Samuel’s form, or that his image appeared there phantasmatically and was called Samuel. Some maintain that, by God’s permission, Samuel’s own soul appeared there, clothed with a body only for the sake of giving counsel. Others, however, say that only the body was raised, with a life-giving spirit, while the soul remained and rested in its own place.

On hearing this, Saul fell prostrate on the ground from fear. He had eaten no bread that day, and the woman and his servants compelled him to eat. When he had eaten, he returned to the camp during the night; for he did not wish it to become known that he had consulted the Pythoness.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That David defeated Amalek

[Col. 1321D]

“The Philistines therefore gathered at Aphek, and Israel encamped beside the spring that was in Jezreel” (I Kings [1 Samuel] 29). But the Philistine satraps, seeing David and his men with Achish, said: “Let these Hebrews return to their own place, lest perhaps when we begin to fight they become our adversaries and earn their lord’s favor by means of our heads.” Then Achish said reluctantly and sorrowfully to David: “You are good in my sight, but you do not please the satraps. Rise during the night and depart at daybreak.”

David therefore departed with his men for Ziklag, arriving on the third day. Meanwhile the Amalekites had attacked Ziklag. They had burned it and carried off captive the women, the little children, and all the spoil (I Kings [1 Samuel] 29–30). David therefore and the people who were with him wept [Col. 1322A] until they had no tears left; and his own men wished to stone him.

But David strengthened himself in the Lord and consulted the Lord through Abiathar, saying: “Shall I pursue these raiders, and shall I overtake them?” He answered: “Pursue them, and you shall overtake them and recover the spoil.” David therefore went, with six hundred men, and came to the torrent of Bethor [or: Besor]. There two hundred weary men remained with the baggage, by David’s command.

When the others had crossed, they found an Egyptian boy faint from hunger, whom his master, an Amalekite, had abandoned when he saw that he had fallen ill. They gave him food, and his spirit returned. David said to him: “Can you lead me to this band?” He replied: “If you swear to me that you will not kill me or hand me over into the hands of my master, [Col. 1322B] I will lead you.” David swore to him. Under his guidance they found the enemy feasting and, as it were, celebrating a festival day. David struck them from evening until the evening of the next day, and only four hundred young men escaped on camels.

David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, from man to beast. It is said that in this victory nine military leaders from Manasseh gave him assistance; they had fled to him when he was returning to Ziklag. Previously, only men of Judah and Benjamin had come to him.

When they returned to the two hundred men who had remained behind exhausted, David greeted them peacefully. But some who had gone with him were angry and said: “Let each have his own wife and children; we shall give them nothing from the spoil.” David said: “No one, my brothers, shall listen to you [Col. 1322C] in this matter. The share of the one who goes down to battle shall be equal to that of the one who remains with the baggage.”

Jerome says: He did not say “those who remained exhausted,” because nothing ought to be given to the exhausted from the value of the spoil. This became the rule from that day onward, as though a law in Israel, until this day. David then came to Ziklag and sent gifts from the spoil to the elders of Judah who were near him, and to the rest among whom he and his men had sojourned.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the death of Saul and his sons

Now the Philistines were fighting against Israel (I Kings [1 Samuel] 31). Saul, however, knowingly and deliberately hastened toward death and fought courageously. For only the great-souled despise terrible things. [Col. 1322D] Such greatness of soul especially befits kings, who, because of the height of their office, are not permitted to be evil toward their subjects, nor even merely moderately good.

“The sons of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell on Mount Gilboa; and Saul’s three sons, Jonathan, Aminadab, and Melchisna, were struck down.” Ish-bosheth was at home. When Saul had been badly wounded, he said to his armor-bearer: “Strike me with your sword, lest these uncircumcised men mock me while I live and then kill me.” But the armor-bearer refused. Saul therefore fell upon his sword. He had become so weak that he could not pierce himself through. Seeing this, his armor-bearer likewise fell upon his sword. This was Doeg the Edomite, as the Hebrews suppose; he feared that he would remain alive after [Col. 1323A] Saul because of David. And all Saul’s household who were with him died.

When the Israelites beyond the valley of the Jordan saw the slaughter of their men, they left their cities and fled. On the following day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they stripped Saul and his sons of their weapons. They sent their severed heads, together with the weapons, around throughout their land, so that this might be proclaimed in the temple of the idols and among the people. They placed Saul’s weapons in the temple of Astaroth, but his head in the temple of Dagon, as is read in Chronicles (I Chronicles 10). They hung his body and those of his sons upon the wall of Beth-shan, as it were before the eyes of Israel. For it is a Philistine city on Israel’s border.

But the men of Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul had delivered from the Ammonites, went [Col. 1323B] all night and took the corpses from Beth-shan’s wall. They burned them with fire, buried their bones in the grove of Jabesh, and mourned for Saul while fasting seven days.

Note that in Chronicles one reads: “Saul died because of his iniquities” (I Chronicles 10), and it is added, as though to increase the weight of his sin: “but moreover he consulted a Pythoness, on account of which the Lord killed him.” Many fail to consider the greatness of this sin. Saul reigned eighteen years while Samuel lived, and two years after Samuel’s death. Yet Sacred Scripture does not record these years. Properly speaking, the periods of the named prophets begin with Samuel, just as the periods of Israel’s kings begin with Saul.

## Incidental matters

In these days, among the Latins, the fourth king was Silvius Aeneas, son of Posthumus. Another history, however, makes Silvius Latinus, the maternal brother of Posthumus, the fourth, and Silvius Aeneas the fifth. Some say that Homer lived in these times, concerning whom there is great disagreement among the ancients. Crates [Col. 1324B] places him before the descent of the Heraclidae into the Peloponnesian city. Cristodenes places him in the hundredth year after the capture of Troy. Aristarchus and Philochorus place him in the time of the Ionian migration. Apollodorus of Athens places him in the two hundred and fortieth year after the destruction of Ilium; others, a short time before the Olympiads began.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF II KINGS

[Col. 1323]

## CHAPTER I. On David’s lament over Saul and Jonathan

[Col. 1323B]

After Saul’s death, a young man fleeing from the battle came to David at Ziklag and bowed down. Having reported to him that the people had been defeated and that Saul and his sons were dead, David said: “How [Col. 1323C] do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?” He replied: “I saw Saul leaning upon his spear, and the enemy was approaching him.” When he had asked who I was, and I said, “I am an Amalekite,” he said: “Kill me, because you are a proselyte [Note: [Col. 1325B] Addition 1. A proselyte was one who came from Gentile life to Judaism.]; lest the uncircumcised kill me.” And I killed him, because he could not live; and I took the diadem which was”—that is, which was accustomed to be—“upon his head, and the bracelet from his arm, and have brought them to you, my lord” (II Kings [2 Samuel] 2).

The Hebrews say that this man was the son of Doeg the Edomite. Before his father fell upon his sword, he gave him the royal insignia which he had kept, so that, by bringing them to David, he might render David favorable to himself. Nor is there any objection to calling the father an Edomite and the son [Col. 1323D] an Amalekite, since the Amalekites are Edomites. For Amalek was the son of Eliphaz, son of Esau, and thus of Edom.

David therefore and all who were with him tore their garments, mourning and fasting until evening according to the Law. David said to the messenger: “Why were you not afraid to stretch out your hand against the Lord’s anointed? Your own mouth has spoken against you.” At David’s command, one of his young men killed him.

“David commanded that fathers should teach their sons the song of the bow”; elsewhere it reads, “should teach their sons the bow”—[Col. 1324B] that is, the art of archery—because he had heard that the people had been killed by archers, as is written in the Book of the Just. This book is not extant, like very many books mentioned in the Old Testament, which we believe were burned by the Babylonians.

Some have said that it is called the Book of the Just because it treats of just men, namely Samuel and David. Others call the Pentateuch the Book of the Just, in which it may be inferred that archery is useful, because Jacob says that he took a field from the hand of the Amorite with sword and bow (Genesis 48). Some read *Justorum* as a neuter and call it the Book of Just Things, because it speaks of things which are just, like a book of judgments. The sense, then, is: David commanded that art to be preserved as that which is written in the Book of the Just is preserved.

“Then David lamented with a mournful song over Saul and Jonathan,” and it is believed to have been composed in meter. The structure of this poem is threefold. First, it treats of the place [Col. 1324D] where the slaughter occurred and curses it; second, it praises Saul and Jonathan; third, it especially praises Jonathan, showing how greatly David loved him. Nor does it matter that at one time it speaks in the plural and at another in the singular of the same mountain: it is one mountain having several hills.

Where it reads: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you,” some read “upon you” in the singular, following that reading. “Mountains of Gilboa”—understand: woe to you; afterward they add: “let neither dew nor rain come upon you.” [Col. 1325A] These mountains, they say, had previously been very fertile; David curses them not with dryness but with barrenness, as though they were dry. Hence he added: “Nor let there be upon you fields of first-fruits,” that is, of the choicest fruits as before.

Others say that this is a prophecy fulfilled in Elijah’s days, when rain did not fall upon the earth for three years and six months. Others say that it neither rained upon the mountain’s summit before nor afterward, but that this was confirmed by the curse.

David mourned Saul because he had been killed disgracefully, although he had been anointed with oil. He adds the cause of this death: “because of the blood of the slain and the fat of the mighty,” that is, because of the blood of the priests whom Saul killed at Nob. The Hebrew, however, begins the verse thus: “From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, Jonathan’s arrows,” [Col. 1325B] and so forth.

## CHAPTER II. On David’s first anointing as king over the tribe of Judah at Hebron

After this, in response to the Lord, David went up to Hebron and lived there with his two wives in his own house; and his men stayed in the towns of Hebron. The men of Judah anointed him king over the tribe of Judah (II Kings [2 Samuel] 2).

Here begins the fourth age, not because of the proclamation of the kingdom of the Jews, as some wish—for then it would have begun with Saul—but because of the renewal of the promise formerly given to the fathers concerning the Christian kingdom, which was prefigured in David. The Lord swore truth to David [Col. 1325C] that one from the fruit of his womb would sit upon his throne (Psalm 131 [132]).

It was reported to David that the men of Jabesh had buried Saul, and he sent them word: “Blessed are you by the Lord, who have shown this mercy to your lord. May the Lord repay you; and I too shall repay you. Do not be afraid as though you had no king, for the house of Judah has anointed me king for itself.”

## CHAPTER III. On the kingdom of Ish-bosheth

“But Abner, Saul’s commander of the army, took Ish-bosheth and led him through the camps”—that is, wherever the army was dispersed—“and made him king over the remaining tribes” (II Kings [2 Samuel] 2). Or by “the camps” understand Mahanaim, a very fortified place, where he anointed him king.

“Ish-bosheth was then forty years old, and he reigned two years over Israel. But David reigned seven years and six months in Hebron over the house of Judah.” At that time civil war arose among the Hebrews. Abner and his young men went out from the camp to Gibeon. Joab and David’s young men met them at the pool of Gibeon. It was agreed between them that only twelve on each side should fight in the midst of the armies. Each seized his counterpart by the head and drove his sword into the other’s side; and they fell together. Therefore that place was called the Field of the Strong. Josephus, however, seems to hold that David’s young men who survived killed [Col. 1326A] their counterparts.

Battle then arose among the rest, and Abner fled with his men. Joab had with him his two brothers, one of whom, Asahel, was exceedingly swift, like one of the gazelles. Asahel pursued Abner and his men most urgently. Abner said to him: “Do not follow me, lest I be compelled to pierce you through, and I shall not be able to lift up my face before Joab.” But Asahel would not turn aside. Abner struck him in the groin with the reversed spear—that is, with the rear wooden end rather than with the spear’s point, or with the spear turned toward him.

As Joab and Abishai pursued and Abner fled, the sun set, and they came to the hill of the aqueduct. On its summit the sons of Benjamin gathered around Abner into one band. Abner said to Joab: “Do you wish to rage on until your brothers are destroyed? But do you not know that he who provokes an enemy does not have his throat cut for nothing?” Joab therefore ceased, and the whole army ceased pursuing them.

Abner and his men crossed the Jordan that night and came to Ish-bosheth at Mahanaim. Joab and his men took Asahel and buried him in his father’s tomb at Bethlehem, then returned to David at Hebron.

## CHAPTER IV. On David’s sons

There was therefore a long struggle between these kings; David increased, while the other declined (II Kings [2 Samuel] 3). David’s sons were born in Hebron: his firstborn, Amnon, by Ahinoam; the second, Chileab, or Chelaph, by Abigail; the third, Absalom, by his foreign wife Maacah, namely the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth, [Col. 1326C] Adonijah, son of Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah, son of Abital; the sixth, Jethraam [Note: [Col. 1326C] Addition 1. That Jethraam was born to David in Hebron does not seem true; hear the reason and its solution.], whom Josephus calls Nathan, by his wife Eglah. The Hebrews say that Eglah was Michal, who alone is called his wife because in his youth she was the first wife whom he had obtained.

This does not seem able to stand with what is read later: that Michal mocked David in Jerusalem, and that no son was born to her by David until the day of her death, because she died in that very childbirth. But it could have occurred that, near the time of giving birth, she came down from Jerusalem to Hebron so as to give birth there, as in the original place of the kingdom.

## CHAPTER V. On the killing of Abner

[Col. 1326D]

At that time Abner entered in to Saul’s concubine Rizpah, exceedingly beautiful (II Kings [2 Samuel] 3). Ish-bosheth rebuked him for this as an affront to his house, fearing that perhaps by means of the concubine Abner would claim the kingdom for himself. Enraged, Abner said to him: “Am I today a dog’s head against Judah because of you?” As if to say: Because of you, Judah regards me as the head of a dead dog. Or thus: Because of you, I have become the head of dogs—that is, ruler of those irrationally barking against the Lord’s anointed.

Abner sent messengers to David, saying: “Whose is the land?” As if to say: Is not the land in [Col. 1327A] my hand? “Make friendship with me, and I shall bring all Israel back to you.” David replied: “Very well. I shall make friendship with you, but you shall not see me until you bring Michal back.” David also commanded Ish-bosheth to return his wife Michal to him.

They took her from her husband Phaltiel [Note: [Col. 1327C] Addition 1. This Phaltiel was learned in the Law, and therefore did not wish to violate another man’s wife; for this reason *el*, which is the name of God, was fixed to his name, because, through fear and reverence for God and the Law, he abstained. This is what the Hebrews say.], who followed her weeping as far as Bahurim. For he had not known her, because she, loving David, was always sorrowful.

Abner spoke to the elders of Israel, and especially to Benjamin, that they should go over to David, whom the Lord had chosen. Abner went up to David at Hebron, was received magnificently by him, and said: “I shall rise and gather all Israel to you.” When he had departed in peace, behold, Joab and David’s young men returned from striking raiders, with very great spoil. Joab was told [Col. 1327B] of Abner’s arrival and of his peace with the king. When he tried to change the king’s mind, saying, “Abner has sworn this in order to deceive you,” and the king did not agree, he sent messengers after Abner, as though the king were recalling him, and brought him back. Meeting him as he returned, Joab led him aside as though to speak more privately, struck him in the groin, and he died, apparently in revenge for his brother. But it is truer that Joab feared Abner would become second to the king.

When David heard this, he said: “I and my kingdom are innocent of Abner’s blood; may it come upon Joab’s head. May there never fail from Joab’s house one suffering a discharge of seed, a leper, one holding a spindle”—that is, an effeminate man—“one falling by the sword, and one needing bread.” According to this, [Col. 1327C] David seems to curse him with seminal discharge, leprosy, emasculation, slaughter in war, and beggary.

Some read “a leper holding a spindle” as one expression, meaning a short fan for driving away flies, made of palm leaves and wound between the fingers like a spindle. David therefore tore his garments and wept over Abner, as did all the people with him. He commanded all to fast until evening and said: “Do you not know that a very great prince has fallen today in Israel? But I am a weak king.” As if to say: Since I am a new king, I especially needed this man’s help. “Moreover, the sons of Zeruiah are harsh toward me.”

## CHAPTER VI. On the death of Ish-bosheth and David’s second anointing over all Israel

[Col. 1327D]

“When Ish-bosheth heard of Abner’s death, his hands were weakened, and all Israel was troubled. There were two men, leaders of raiders, with Ish-bosheth: Baanah and Rechab, of the sons of Benjamin” (II Kings [2 Samuel] 4). They had angrily withdrawn from Ish-bosheth and gone to Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, in order to make him king. He refused, indeed he betrayed their plan. Some relate that Ish-bosheth was offended with them because they told him that Mephibosheth ought to be king, since he was the son of Saul’s firstborn [Col. 1328A] son.

This Mephibosheth was lame in both feet. For he was five years old when he was told of Saul’s and Jonathan’s death; as his nurse took him up to flee, he fell and was crippled.

Baanah and Rechab entered Ish-bosheth’s house carrying ears of wheat, as though first-fruits for the king. But the female doorkeeper of the house had fallen asleep. Finding Ish-bosheth asleep at noon, they killed him and brought his head to David at Hebron, saying: “Behold the head of the man who sought your life,” thinking that they would receive rewards from David. David said to them: “You have killed an innocent man; you have shed your lord’s blood, and therefore I shall remove you from the earth.” Their hands and feet were cut off, and they were hung [Col. 1328B] over the pool, or the thorn, at Hebron; but Ish-bosheth’s head was buried in Abner’s tomb.

The leading men of Israel came to David. He made a covenant with them, and they anointed him king over all Israel (II Kings [2 Samuel] 5). Thus he was first anointed as a sign of kingship; second, as king over Judah; third, as king over Israel. David was thirty years old when he began to reign. “Son” is superfluous, in the Hebrew idiom. He reigned forty years: in Hebron, seven years and six months over Judah—understand, especially over Judah. For if he reigned in Israel immediately after Ish-bosheth, he reigned in Judah for only two years.

But the Hebrews say that he reigned at Hebron for some years while Saul was still alive, because the house of Judah was already desiring him as king and he sent [Col. 1328C] them gifts as though they were his own people. In Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all the people. If one asks why six months are subtracted from the total of his reign, the Hebrew says that David was ill for six months and did nothing worthy of a king. Or because Absalom pursued him for six months, when David was, as it were, not reigning.

## CHAPTER VII. That David captured and fortified Jerusalem

Afterward, having assembled an army, David went up to Jerusalem to expel the Jebusite. They placed blind men and lame men upon the wall in mockery, saying to David: “You shall not enter here unless you remove the blind and lame [Col. 1328D]” (II Kings [2 Samuel] 5). That is, the city is so strong that we do not need the help of strong men.

Others say that they set images on the wall which they called blind and lame—that is, doing nothing—as if to say: Even while we do nothing, you will not be able to enter. Or they called themselves blind and lame because David considered them weak and like such people. Thereafter it became proverbial: “The blind and lame shall not enter the temple of God.” At first, the Law simply prohibited blind and lame persons from entering the temple to make offerings; afterward it became a proverb. Perhaps when gatekeepers kept out the unclean, they said enigmatically: “The blind and lame shall not enter,” using blindness and lameness for any impurity.

David gained possession of [Col. 1329A] the lower city when Ornan the Jebusite handed it over to him. Since he could not take the citadel of Zion, he offered the command of the army as a reward to whoever first struck the Jebusite and reached the water-channels of the roofs—that is, the roof-gutters through which dripping water flows. Others call the *fistulae* underground tunnels through which there was an ascent to the roof.

When many hastened, Joab surpassed them all and cried out to the king, demanding the command of the army. David took the citadel, having expelled the Jebusites except Ornan. He built around it, beginning inside from the Millo, and called that part of the city the City of David. Joab built the rest of the city. The Millo was the chief place, and as it were a deep chasm of a valley. The City of David itself was afterward called [Col. 1329B] Millo.

David built a house in it, Hiram king of Tyre giving him assistance by sending cedar wood and craftsmen. David took other wives, and eleven sons were born to him in Jerusalem, among whom Nathan is listed, namely another Nathan than the prophet Nathan, whom David had adopted after his father’s death.

Note that Jerusalem was called Jebus until Melchizedek, from whom it was called Salem. David afterward called it Jebusalem. Then, changing *b* to *r*, he called it Jerusalem, as though “fortified Salem.” For *hiero* means “fortification” in Hebrew. Josephus relates that some believe Homer made this change of letter. It was afterward called Jerosolymia from Solomon, and finally, by syncope, Jerosolyma.

## CHAPTER VIII. That David defeated the Philistines

[Col. 1329C]

When the Philistines heard that David reigned over Israel, they all came up to seek David and encamped in the Valley of Rephaim, not far from Jerusalem (II Kings [2 Samuel] 5). In response to the Lord, David went out against them, struck them with the edge of the sword, and scattered them in flight in every direction. Therefore the place was called Baal-perazim, that is, “division of men”; or because there the fleeing men had left their idols, which David took away and melted down.

The Philistines again came up into the Valley of Rephaim and placed their idols beneath pear trees. The Lord said to David: “You shall not go to meet them, but go around behind them and come opposite the pear trees.” [Col. 1329D] The Hebrew has “of those who weep,” that is, of idols, which are worthy of weeping and draw their worshippers into eternal weeping. When the angel of the Lord, walking over the tops of the pear trees, made a sound, David rushed upon them and struck them as far as Gezer.

## CHAPTER IX. On bringing the ark back to Jerusalem

David made a tabernacle beside his own house for placing the ark in, and put in it some of the old curtains (II Kings [2 Samuel] 6). He preserved the former boards, columns, and bases. David went down with thirty thousand men, and “they placed the ark upon a new cart and carried it from the house of Aminadab, which was at Gibeah,” that is, on a hill beside Kiriath-jearim. Here Gibeah is not [Col. 1330A] the name of a city or place but, according to its meaning, denotes a hill.

Two sons of Aminadab drove the cart: Ahio went before, and Uzzah followed. David and all Israel made music before the ark with musical instruments. But when they came to the threshing-floor of Nachor, the oxen kicked and the ark tipped. Uzzah stretched out his hand and held it; his right hand, with which he ought to have carried the ark as his father had commanded, withered, and he died. The place was called the Striking of Uzzah.

Josephus says that he was struck because he touched the ark though he was not a priest. Others say that it was because he had placed the ark upon a cart when it ought to have been carried upon shoulders. The Hebrews maintain that he had slept with his wife that night.

David therefore feared to turn the ark aside to himself and placed [Col. 1330B] it in the suburb, in the house of Obed the Levite, son of Edom the Gittite. It remained there three months, and the Lord blessed Obed’s house [Note: [Col. 1330C] Addition 1. The Hebrews say that his wives, concubines, and daughters-in-law gave birth to males, and that the livestock bore double offspring.]. When David heard this, he went to bring the ark into the City of David with joy.

David, girded with a linen ephod, made music before the ark with instruments bound to the shoulder—that is, tied to the shoulder. Or, according to some, this is a kind of instrument made in water. Michal saw him making music from a window and despised him in her heart.

When they had placed the ark in its place, David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, blessed the people, and distributed to every person one small cake of bread, a portion of roasted beef, and flour fried in oil. When David returned to his house, Michal mocked him, saying: “How glorious today was the king of Israel, [Col. 1330C] stripped naked as though he were one of the buffoons.” David answered: “As the Lord lives, I will play and become still more humble before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father.”

Therefore “no son was born to Michal until the day of her death.” This may be read inclusively—that is, until she died in childbirth—or exclusively, that is, never. Josephus seems to mean the latter, saying that she bore no children at all by David, but had five children by the man to whom her father had given her after taking her away from David; these are to be understood as adopted children. For after the death of her sister Merob, Michal adopted her five children.

## CHAPTER X. On David’s victories and his officials
“And it came to pass, when the king was sitting in his house and had rest from his enemies, that he said to Nathan: ‘You see that I dwell in a cedar house, while the ark of God is placed amid skins. I will make a house for it.’ And Nathan said, ‘Do so, for the Lord is with you’ (II Kings 7),” not knowing what he was saying—that is, he was not speaking this by the Holy Spirit. That same night the word of the Lord came to Nathan: “Say to my servant David [Note: [Col. 1331C] Addition 1. Observe that it is said to David [Col. 1331D] through Nathan: ‘when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you,’ etc.; this cannot be said of Solomon, who reigned while his father was alive. The Jews still await its fulfilment.]: ‘He shall not build me a house, because he is a man of blood; but his son, succeeding him in the kingdom, shall make a house for my name, and I shall establish his throne for ever, and I shall be a father to him, and [Col. 1331A] he shall be a son to me.’” From this promise it is inferred that Solomon is saved.

On hearing this David rejoiced at the succession to the kingdom, and especially gave thanks to God thereafter, adding: “For this is the law of Adam, O Lord God”—that is, the law of man: that he should be concerned for the succession of his sons, or that he should give thanks to God for his benefits.

“And it came to pass after these things that David struck the Philistines and took away the bridle,” that is, the authority to exact tribute which they had over Israel, “from their hand. And he struck Moab; and David measured them with a cord,” that is, he gave an inheritance to whomever he wished; “leveling them with the ground,” that is, greatly humiliating them; “and he measured two cords, one for putting to death and one for keeping alive,” that is, at his own discretion he killed whom he wished and spared whom he wished. “And [Col. 1331B] Moab became tributary to him.” And he struck Hadadezer, king of Zobah (II Kings 8). When Syria and Damascus brought him reinforcements, he struck thirty thousand of them; and, stationing a garrison in Syria, made it tributary.

When Thou [otherwise Theno], king of Hamath, heard that Hadadezer, his enemy, had been struck down, he sent his son Joram to David with gifts and thanksgiving because he had struck his enemy. And when David was returning from Syria, the Edomites met him [Note: [Col. 1331D] Addition 2. The Edomites derive from Edom, that is, Esau, who was older than Jacob; both were from Rebekah.] in the Valley of Salt; and he struck twelve thousand of them. Jerome corrects this to eighteen thousand; and at Jebetzel he struck as many as twenty-three thousand, and, placing a garrison there, made it tributary. Then was fulfilled what had been said to Rebekah: “The greater shall serve the lesser [Note: [Col. 1331D] Addition 3. The Hebrews say that Jacob’s wives, concubines, and daughters-in-law bore males, and that the livestock bore double offspring.]” (Gen. 25).

And he brought into [Col. 1331C] Jerusalem exceedingly much gold and silver, which he consecrated to the Lord for the building of the future house. He also consecrated Corinthian bronze [Note: [Col. 1331D] Addition 4. At Corinth there was a certain temple built with the silver, bronze, and gold of idols. When it was burned, the metals melted and were mingled; and [Col. 1332A] because the greater part was bronze, such a mixture was generally called Corinthian bronze.], from which Solomon made the bronze sea, the columns, and the altar.

“Moreover Joab was over the army [Note: [Col. 1332A] Addition 5. In Chronicles it is read (I Chron. 6) that on that day David appointed the brethren of Asaph as singers, Asaph himself as precentor, and others who sang psalms compiled from different psalms.];” Jehoshaphat was over the records [Note: [Col. 1332A] Addition 6. The officer over the records acted in the king’s stead; laws were written by his judgment.], that is, the recorder of deeds. For individual kings wrote chronicles of their deeds. Zadok and Abiathar were priests; Saratas was secretary, that is, chancellor. Benaiah was over the Cherethites and Pelethites, who were David’s bodyguards [Note: [Col. 1332A] Addition 7. These are said to have been two very mighty men; others say that they were two families.]. David’s sons, moreover, were priests, that is, more eminent than the rest after the king [Note: [Col. 1332A] Addition 8. These are said to have been seventy judges of places, as Moses chose seventy. Hence Celeti means “destroyers,” and Phelethi “wonderful men.”]. Thus Jethro is called priest of Midian.

## CHAPTER XI. On Mephibosheth, and how Ammon dishonoured David’s messengers

[Col. 1332B]

David remembered the covenant which he had made with Jonathan and said: “Does anyone remain of the house of Saul to whom I may show kindness for Jonathan’s sake?” (II Kings 9). When he learned that Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, remained and was lame in his feet, he summoned him, restored to him all the property of Saul his grandfather, and made him his table-companion, as one of his own sons. Ziba, Saul’s servant, who had fifteen sons and twenty servants, by David’s command cultivated the land and brought its produce to Mephibosheth in Jerusalem. Mephibosheth had a son, Micha.

“And it came to pass that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, died, and his son Hanun reigned in his place” (II Kings 10). David sent messengers [Col. 1332C] to console him over his father’s death, urging that the friendship which he had had with his father should continue. For when David had fled to Achish while feigning madness, he had been kindly received by this man’s father. But Hanun’s princes incited their king, saying: “Do you not know that David sent men to inspect your entrance and departure, so that he might strike you and your land?” Hanun therefore took David’s servants, shaved half their beards, and cut off their garments to their buttocks.

When the Ammonites saw that they had provoked David, they hired soldiers from Syria of Rehob and of Sobach, and from King Micha and King Istob. David sent Joab and the whole army against them. The Ammonites stood [Col. 1332D] before the entrance of the city, while the Syrian army was in the open country. Joab divided his army: he entrusted one part to his brother Abishai and kept another part for himself. He charged the Syrians and put them to flight by the sword. Seeing this, the Ammonites too turned their backs before Abishai and withdrew into the city. Joab returned triumphantly to Jerusalem.

When the Syrians saw how they had fallen before Israel, they again assembled a larger army. David gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, drew up his battle-line against the Syrians, and struck down chariots and forty thousand horsemen among them, and Sobach, commander of the army. The Syrians feared thereafter to give aid to the sons of Hanun; they made peace with Israel and served them.

## CHAPTER XII. On David’s adultery, Uriah’s death, and David’s repentance

[Col. 1333A]

“And it came to pass, at the turning of the year, at the season when kings usually go out to war, that David sent Joab and all Israel; and they ravaged the sons of Ammon and besieged Rabbah. But David remained in Jerusalem. It happened that David rose from his bed after noon and walked upon the roof. Opposite him he saw Bathsheba, wife of Uriah, daughter of Eliah, son of Ahithophel, washing herself with cold water” (II Kings 11). Inflamed by her beauty, he summoned her and knew her; “and immediately she was cleansed from her uncleanness”—that is, after intercourse she washed herself; or she conceived and her menstrual flow ceased, which nature is said to reserve after conception to nourish the fetus.

Some report [Col. 1333B] that she was then menstruating and that her menses ceased at the king’s touch. Epiphanius says that, when David summoned Bathsheba, Nathan knew it in the spirit and hurried to David to prevent him before the woman came, but Belial hindered him. For on the way he saw a naked slain man lying there and delayed. That night the king completed his sin, and Nathan mourned.

When David learned that she had conceived, he recalled Uriah, Joab’s armour-bearer according to Josephus, from the campaign, so that he might go in to his wife and the child might be attributed to him. David asked Uriah about the state of the war, urging him to go in to his wife and refresh himself a little. Uriah did not comply and slept with the servants. Therefore David summoned him again and set him [Col. 1333C] with himself at table, inviting him to drink until drunkenness. Yet not even thus was the man aroused by desire for his wife, and he said: “The ark of the Lord and Israel dwell in tents, and my lord Joab remains upon the face of the earth; and shall I enter my house? By your welfare, O king, I will not do this thing.”

David, being certain that he would not enter, wrote to Joab as though Uriah had offended him, instructing him to place Uriah in that part of the battle where he would be struck down and die. When Uriah carried the letter of his own death, he died according to the king’s command. Bathsheba, on receiving news of her husband’s death, mourned him. When the mourning was over, David summoned her; she became his wife and bore him a son.

Then the Lord sent Nathan to [Col. 1333D] David (II Kings 22). Nathan set before him a parable about a rich man who had many sheep and seized the one little ewe of his poor neighbour, in order to prepare food from it for a guest who had arrived. The king was indignant with that man and said: “As the Lord lives, the man who did this is a son of death. He shall restore the sheep fourfold.” Nathan replied: “You are that man. You took Uriah’s wife for yourself; and, to conceal the adultery, you killed him by the sword of the sons of Ammon. Therefore the Lord says this: ‘The sword shall not depart from your house until the day everlasting. Behold, I shall raise up evil against you from your own house.’”

The latter happened when Absalom pursued him, but the former in the division of the kingdom after Solomon. “And David said to Nathan: [Col. 1334A] ‘I have sinned against the Lord.’” Descending from the throne of judgment, he sat upon the ground, and, as a worshipper of God, was not ashamed to confess his sin before all. Nathan said to him: “The Lord has taken away your sin. You shall not die, nor shall you lose the kingdom. Nevertheless, the son born to you shall die, because you have caused the enemies of the Lord’s name to blaspheme.” For idolaters said, or could have said: “The God of Israel is not just, since he removed Saul from the kingdom and put David in his place, although David sinned more grievously than Saul.”

The Lord struck the little child, to the point of desperation for his life. David prayed to the Lord for the child, fasted, lay upon the earth, and would not be comforted. “But on the seventh day the child died. And when David [Col. 1334B] saw his servants whispering, he understood that he was dead.” On learning it, he washed his face, changed his garment, entered the house and worshipped; then, made cheerful, he ate. The servants wondered that he had acted contrary to custom, and he said to them: “While the child was still alive, I wept and worshipped the Lord, that he might live. Now that he is dead, why should I weep? Shall I be able to bring him back? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.”

David said this to console Bathsheba because he loved her. In the course of time he begot by her a son whom he called Solomon, and entrusted him to Nathan, who called him Jedidiah, that is, “beloved of the Lord.” Joab was then fighting against Rabbath and captured it. He sent to David, saying: “Come and take the city, lest the victory be ascribed to my name.” David assembled all the people, set out, took the city, ravaged it, and took the crown from the head of Melchon—meaning “their king,” the idol of the Ammonites. The crown contained precious gems and a talent of gold. David melted it down and fashioned it into a crown for himself, setting an incomparable sardonyx among the gems. He ravaged the remaining cities of the Ammonites, sawed many of their people with iron implements, cut up many more with knives, and put them to work in brick-making.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Tamar, whom Amnon violated

After these things the Lord raised up evil [Col. 1334D] in David’s house in this manner. His firstborn Amnon loved Tamar, Absalom’s sister by both parents, so greatly that he pined away and fell ill because of her (II Kings 13). His kinsman and intimate friend was Jonadab, son of Shimeah, David’s brother, a very shrewd man, whom Josephus calls Jonathan. Some suppose that he was Nathan; but far be it that the prophet should have given disgraceful counsel.

He said to Amnon: “Why are you wasting away in such emaciation, son of the king?” As though to say: you who ought to succeed the king in the kingdom. Amnon replied: “I love Tamar beyond measure.” He answered: “Feign illness. When your father comes to visit you, say to him: ‘Please let Tamar my sister come and make me a dish of food, so that I may eat more pleasantly from her hand.’”

When Tamar, sent [Col. 1335A] by the king, arrived, she cooked before his eyes little soups, or, according to Josephus, fried cakes. Amnon dismissed everyone. When Tamar brought him food in the inner chamber [Note: [Col. 1335B] Addition 1. An inner chamber is called a room which cannot be reached except through another room.], he seized her and said: “Lie with me, my sister.” She replied: “Do not, brother, violate me and bring disgrace upon your family in Israel. Rather, speak to the king, and he will not refuse me to you.” She said this to escape his hands. For according to the law it was not permitted for a man to take a sister by the same father.

Yet some explain that this was said if both were of the same people; but she had a Gentile mother, namely Maacah, whom David captured in battle and, after cutting her hair and nails, married according to the law. Thus, it is said, they could have become spouses.

[Col. 1335B] “But Amnon would not comply; he violated her, and immediately hated her more than he had previously loved her. He drove her away though she begged to remain with him and become his wife. When Amnon’s servants put her out, she scattered ashes upon her head and tore the long robe worn by virgin daughters of the king, which Josephus calls a sleeved tunic. With her hands placed upon her head, she went crying to her brother Absalom.” Her brother said to her: “Be silent, sister; he is our brother.” And she remained a long time in Absalom’s house, enduring widowhood.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Amnon’s death, Absalom’s flight, and his return to David

[Col. 1335C]

After two years Absalom went up for the shearing of sheep and said to the king: “Please let the king come with his servants to his servant’s feast” (II Kings 13). When the king declined, lest he burden him, Absalom said: “At least, I beg you, let my brother Amnon and the king’s sons come with him.” They went with Absalom. As Absalom’s servants reclined, they killed the drunken Amnon at his command. The king’s sons mounted their mules and fled; and a report came to David saying: “Absalom has struck all the king’s sons.” The king tore his garments and fell upon the ground.

But Jonadab, [Col. 1335D] from whom the truth was not concealed, said to the king: “Let not my lord fear, for Amnon alone is dead—the one whom Absalom hated from the day on which he violated his sister.” And behold, the king’s sons appeared, and they wept with the king in exceedingly great lamentation. Absalom fled to his grandfather, Talmai, king of Geshur, and was with him for three years. When the king had been consoled over Amnon’s death, he ceased wishing to pursue Absalom, since he knew him to be wicked and deserving of death.

When Joab, who loved Absalom, understood this, he sent to the king a wise woman from Tekoa, who is thought to have been the great-grandmother of Amos the prophet; and Joab put his words in her mouth (II Kings 14). When the woman came before the king, she prostrated herself and said: “Save me, king. My husband is dead, [Col. 1336A] and I had two sons; one killed the other in the field [Note: [Col. 1336D] Addition 1. The Hebrews say that the matter happened thus, which the woman turned into a parable.], and the whole kindred rises against the killer, seeking his life for the life of the slain, and they seek to extinguish my spark upon the earth.”

This woman placed herself in David’s position, her sons in the position of Amnon and Absalom, and her kindred in the position of David’s other sons. David said to her: “Go in peace; I shall see to your case.” Since this did not suffice the woman, she said to the king: “Let this iniquity be upon me, my lord, and upon my father’s house; but let the king be innocent.” As if to say: if you think it unjust to spare the killer, let it be charged to me and my household. Though the king repeated his promise, it did not suffice the woman, and she begged the king more insistently. He said: “As the Lord lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground.”

Then the woman explained the comparison to him and said: “Therefore let my lord bring back his outcast. For God does not will a life to perish, and all of us flow away like waters which do not return.” As if to say: you cannot restore your dead son to life. It is better to restore the living one than, in avenging the other, to lose both. The king said: “Is Joab’s hand with you in these matters?” She answered: “He himself put these words in my mouth, so that I might turn this saying into a comparison.” The king said to Joab: “Bring back the boy Absalom.”

When Joab had brought Absalom back to Jerusalem, the king said: “Let him not see my face until I summon him,” lest, on seeing him, grief for his son revive in me. Absalom remained in Jerusalem [Col. 1336C] two years and did not see the king’s face. Absalom was exceedingly handsome; according to Josephus, his hair was so abundant that it could scarcely have been shorn in nine days. When it was cut once a year, it weighed two hundred shekels. Perhaps this was the weight of his hair when cut. Or women bought it at this price in order to adorn their own hair.

Three sons and one daughter, named Tamar, were born to Absalom. He repeatedly sent for Joab, that he might intercede for him with the king, but Joab would not come to him. Absalom therefore sent his servants to burn the crops in Joab’s field. When this was done, Joab came to him and said: “What have your servants done?” He replied: “They could not get you otherwise. I beg you, go in to the king, that I may see his face; otherwise let him kill [Col. 1336D] me.” When Joab had gone in to the king, Absalom was summoned, and the king kissed him.

## CHAPTER XV. How Absalom pursued David his father

Then Absalom began to aspire to the kingdom, for Calech, born before him, was either incapable or dead. “He made for himself chariots and fifty horsemen to run before him. Rising early in the morning, he stood at the gate and flattered those going up for the king’s judgment, saying: ‘What you say is good, but there is no one appointed by the king to hear you. Who will appoint me king, that I may judge justly?’” And he inclined the hearts of the men toward himself (II Kings 15).

After four years of his return, he said to the king: “While I was in exile, I vowed: ‘If the Lord brings me back to Jerusalem, I shall sacrifice to the Lord in Hebron.’ I shall therefore go and pay my vows.” The king said: “Go in peace.” Another reading has “after forty years”; for forty years had passed since the priests of Nob were killed. These years are set down here in order to show that divine vengeance was being raised against David because he deceived Abimelech the priest.

Absalom therefore went to Hebron, using the counsel of Ahithophel the Gilonite, who had been David’s counsellor. Many went out from Jerusalem without knowing the matter. When he had sacrificed victims, the conspiracy became strong, and the people with Absalom increased. When David learned this, he said to his servants: “Let us leave quickly, lest Absalom come [Col. 1337B] and seize us, strike the city.” David the king departed, and all his household, barefoot, leaving ten concubines to guard the house. Before the king went six hundred fighting men, Cherethites and Pelethites, who had followed him from Gath. These are believed to have rendered David services when he hid in Gath, and in return he had given them a place in Jerusalem. Josephus says that those six hundred who went out with him had once stood by him during Saul’s persecution. It could be that both these and those others were with him.

The king said to Ittai the Gittite, son of Achish, who was foremost among the six hundred: “Take your brothers back to Jerusalem and dwell with King Absalom. You came yesterday, and today you are compelled to leave.” He replied: “As the Lord lives, neither in death nor in [Col. 1337C] life shall I leave you.” All crossed the brook Kidron weeping with the king. The Levites carrying the ark set it down until the people had crossed; Abiathar went up to consult the Lord, who did not answer him. Therefore David said to Zadok: “Return to the city with the ark. I shall hide in the wilderness. Your son Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar shall be with you; through them a word from you shall come to me.” They returned with the ark.

When David had gone up the slope of the Mount of Olives, Hushai the Archite, his counsellor, met him. David said: “Return, and be with Absalom. You will frustrate Ahithophel’s counsel; and whatever you hear in the king’s house, you shall report to the priests, who will send their [Col. 1337D] sons to me.” Hushai came to Absalom at Jerusalem.

When David had gone a little farther, Ziba appeared before him with two asses, carrying bread, raisins, and cakes of figs—or pressed figs, that is, figs compacted between boards called *palae* (II Kings 16). Ziba said to the king: “I have brought the asses for the king’s household to ride upon, and I have brought provisions for them to be fed in the wilderness.” The king said: “Where is Mephibosheth?” He replied: “He remained in Jerusalem, saying: ‘Today the Lord will restore to me the vengeance of my father.’” The king said to Ziba: “Let everything that belonged to Mephibosheth be yours.”

David came as far as Bahurim, and a man of Saul’s kindred, named Shimei, came out, throwing stones and mud and cursing the king, saying: “Get out, man of blood. [Col. 1338A] Behold, the evils which you did to the house of Saul oppress you.” When Abishai wished to strike him, David forbade him, saying: “The son of my womb seeks my life; how much more the son of Jemini. The Lord has sent him to curse me. May the Lord regard this affliction of mine.” The Hebrews invent the tale that this Shimei was Nebat, Jeroboam’s father, and that Jemini was the name of his grandfather. David went down as far as the Jordan.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Hushai’s counsel and Ahithophel’s death

It came to pass that Hushai, coming to Absalom, prostrated himself and said: “Hail, king.” Absalom said to him: “Why did you not go with your friend?” He answered: “I shall belong to the one whom the Lord and all [Col. 1338B] Israel have chosen. Whom shall I serve? Shall it not be the king’s son? As I obeyed your father, so shall I obey you” (II Kings 16).

Then Absalom went in, before all, to his father’s concubines, by Ahithophel’s counsel, so that all Israel might understand that he was pursuing his father wholeheartedly and might be strengthened with him. After this Ahithophel said (II Kings 17): “I shall choose twelve thousand men for myself, pursue David tonight, and strike him, because he is weary; and all shall return to you as though one man.” Absalom said: “Let us summon Hushai and consult him.” Hushai said: “Ahithophel’s counsel is not good this time. You know that your father and his men are very mighty. If he now strikes some of your men, whoever hears it will say: ‘A slaughter has [Col. 1338C] occurred among the people who followed Absalom,’ and they will fear to be with you. But this is good counsel: let all Israel be gathered to you, and let us rush upon him. Wherever he is, we shall cover him.”

Hushai’s counsel pleased them all. Hushai told the priests to notify David that he should not remain in the wilderness that night, but cross the Jordan. A maid went to the priests’ sons, who were hiding near the spring Rogel, carrying a cloth as if to wash clothes, and told them Hushai’s message. But a certain boy, the maid’s son as it is said, saw them and told Absalom. Josephus, however, says that certain horsemen saw them and informed Absalom. He sent after them to have them seized. They entered a woman’s house in Bahurim and asked her to conceal them. She [Col. 1338D] lowered them into a well and spread a covering over its mouth, as though drying *ptisanae*, that is, barley for barley-gruel; and so the matter was concealed.

When those who had been sent returned, the men came up from the well and reported to David what had been conveyed to them. David and his followers crossed the Jordan before dawn and came to Mahanaim. Ahithophel, knowing that the kingdom would return to David and fearing that he would fall into his hands, went down to his house in Shiloh and hanged himself with a noose.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Absalom’s death

Absalom assembled an army, crossed the Jordan, and appointed Amasa over the army in Joab’s place (II Kings 17). He was the son of Abigail, daughter of [Col. 1339A] Nahash—that is, Jesse—David’s sister; Josephus calls her Abigea. He was Joab’s cousin. The men beyond the Jordan, especially Barzillai the Gileadite, offered David an exceedingly great abundance of provisions, bedding, rugs, and earthenware.

David divided the people with him into three parts: he gave one to Joab, the second to Abishai, and the third to Ittai the Gittite, who is thought to have been the son of Achish, David’s friend (II Kings 18). When the king wished to go out with them to battle, they said: “You shall not go; they seek you alone and do not care for the others.” As the divisions went out to battle, numbering about seven thousand, David stood beside the gate and said: “Spare the boy Absalom for me.”

That day battle took place beside the forest of Ephraim. Absalom’s army fled, twenty thousand of them being slain; and the beasts of the forest killed more than the sword. Absalom fled upon a mule and came beneath a thick oak. His head was caught by its branches; the mule passed on, leaving him hanging. When someone reported this to Joab, he said: “Why did you not pierce him?” The man replied: “I would not lay my hand upon the king’s son,” especially since I heard him say: “Spare the boy Absalom for me.”

Joab fixed three arrows in Absalom’s heart. While he was still struggling, Joab’s armour-bearers killed him, threw him into a great pit, and heaped a pile of stones over him, so that, as a criminal, he might perish by a double death. Israel fled to their tents.

“While still alive, [Col. 1339C] Absalom had raised for himself a monument in the King’s Valley,” which is two stadia from Jerusalem, as a memorial of his name. The monument bore the name “Absalom’s Hand.” Some think this monument was a triumphal arch on which Absalom’s hand was carved. But Josephus says that it was a marble statue.

Then Ahimaaz said to Joab: “I shall run and announce it to the king.” He replied: “I do not want you to bear news today, for the king’s son is dead.” Joab said to Hushai: “Go and report to the king what you have seen.” Ahimaaz also ran after him by a shorter road and passed him.

David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman on the roof of the gate cried out: “I see one man running alone.” The king said: “If he is alone, he is a good messenger.” The watchman said again: “A second man appears [Col. 1339D] to me, running alone.” The king said: “He too is a good messenger.” Ahimaaz came, prostrated himself, and said: “Blessed be God, who has shut up the men who rose against the king.” The king asked: “Is there peace for the boy Absalom?” But he would not tell him. Hushai, arriving afterward, told him.

Grieved, the king went up into the upper room over the gate, weeping with his head covered and crying: “My son Absalom, who would grant that I might die for you? Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!” When the people heard this, they feared to enter the city (II Kings 19). Joab entered to the king and said: “Today you have put to shame the faces of those who saved your life. You love those who hate you and hate those who love you. Go out and speak to your servants, otherwise not one will remain with you this night; and this evil will be [Col. 1340A] worse for you than all that you have ever suffered.” The king therefore sat in the gate with his face washed, and the whole multitude came to him; and he spoke kindly to them.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On David’s return to Jerusalem

Those who had followed Absalom encouraged one another to recall the king, remembering his benefits to Israel (II Kings 19). David sent to Zadok and Abiathar to speak to the men of Judah: “Thus says the king: ‘You are my bone and my flesh. Why are you the last to bring back the king?’” As though to say: See that you are not slower than the others. Through them he also swore to Amasa that he wished to appoint him commander of the army in Joab’s place. The men of Judah sent to the king that he should return. The king came as far as the Jordan, and all [Col. 1340B] Judah came to meet him at Gilgal.

Shimei too came down from Bahurim with them, accompanied by his fellow tribesmen and a thousand men of Benjamin. Ziba also, with his sons and servants, crossed the Jordan to him in order to bring over his household. According to Josephus, these men made a bridge over the Jordan, so that the king might cross more easily with the army. When the king had crossed, Shimei prostrated himself, saying: “Do not remember, my lord, the injury of your servant. For I know my sin, and therefore today I came to meet you, first of all the house of Joseph”—not because he was of Joseph’s tribe, but because he lived in Ephraim’s allotment.

When Abishai said that Shimei should be killed, David said: “Do you not know that today I have been made king over [Col. 1340C] Israel? Therefore no man shall be killed in Israel today.” As though to say: I shall kill those who today made me king over themselves. He also feared that, if Shimei were killed, the rest who had similarly offended the king would not wish to make him their king. Shimei said: “You shall not die.”

“Mephibosheth also came to meet the king with his feet unwashed and his beard untrimmed; for he had not washed his clothes from the day on which the king departed.” The Hebrew has “with his feet unadorned,” explaining that he had made himself wooden feet. The king said to him: “Why did you not come with me?” He replied: “My servant despised me, refusing to saddle an ass for me that I might go with the king; moreover he accused me. But you, being just, do what seems good to you.” The king said: “What I have spoken is settled. You and Ziba shall divide the possessions.” [Col. 1340D] As though to say: I had given them to both of you; but because neither can possess all of them, let them be divided between you.

It is said that David, forgetful of his oath to Jonathan, judged unjustly; and therefore Rehoboam and Jeroboam divided his kingdom. For after Solomon’s death, Rehoboam his son and Jeroboam his armour-bearer divided the kingdom which David had possessed.

Barzillai also, who had supplied the king with food, came down with him. “The king said to him: ‘Come with me to Jerusalem, and I shall honour you.’ He replied: ‘Today I am eighty years old; I do not need this change. Let my son Chamas, otherwise Chanaam, go with you; do for him what seems good to you.’ The king said: ‘Let him come, and I shall do for him whatever pleases you.’” Barzillai returned to his own place.

Then all the men of [Col. 1341A] Israel came running to the king and angrily said: “Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away and brought you across without us?” Judah replied: “Because the king is nearer to me.” Israel said: “I am greater by ten [Note: [Col. 1341A] Addition 1. Observe here something which you will scarcely find elsewhere: by the name Israel only eleven tribes are designated. For though there had been twelve, David was king from the tribe of Judah; resenting this, the eleven came to David’s tribe saying:] parts; therefore David belongs more to me than to you, especially since I am the firstborn.”

When the men of Judah replied more harshly, Sheba son of Bichri, son of Jemini, sounded the trumpet and said: “We have no share in the son of Jesse. Return to your tents, Israel” (II Kings 20). Departing from David, they followed Sheba. But the men of Judah brought their king back to Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the death of Amasa and Sheba

[Col. 1341B]

King David confined the ten concubines whom Absalom had entered to a seclusion of widowhood, and did not go in to them (2 Sam. 20). The king said to Amasa, who was commander of the army: “Gather the men of Judah for me within three days.” Amasa therefore went, but delayed beyond the appointed time. Then the king said to Abishai—not to Joab, whom he had already removed from the command; nevertheless, Josephus says that he said it to Joab—“Take your lord’s servants and pursue Sheba, lest he escape you.” All the mighty men went out from Jerusalem with him; and they encountered [Col. 1341C] Amasa sitting beside the great stone which is at Gibeon.

“Now Joab was clothed in a close-fitting tunic”—Josephus, however, says a breastplate—“and was girded with a well-made sword, which could come out with a slight movement.” By a certain trick, pretending that the sword had fallen, and that he had “caught it in his right hand,” he seized Amasa’s chin as though to kiss him, and struck him in the side with his left hand, spilling out his entrails. Joab and Abishai pursued Sheba; but those who came upon the dead man in the road stopped there. A certain man removed him into a field and covered him, so that passers-by might not stop, crying that the man who treacherously delayed returning to the king had been justly killed.

Joab, with the army, then besieged Sheba in [Col. 1341D] Abel and began to demolish the city’s walls. A wise woman of the city cried out to him: “A saying was spoken in the ancient proverb: ‘Let those who inquire, inquire at Abel.’” As if to say: this has from ancient times been a city of counsel. “Why do you seek to overthrow a mother-city in Israel? Why do you cast down the Lord’s inheritance?”

The Hebrew does not contain “proverb”; and its sense is, according to the Hebrew: “A saying was spoken in ancient times,” that is, it was once said in the Law that Israel should first offer peace to its enemies before attacking them. “Why then do you cast down the Lord’s inheritance?” That is: why do you not observe among Israelites the law which has been observed toward foreigners? Afterwards the Hebrew reads the material inserted in praise of the city, in accordance with the earlier explanation.

[Col. 1342A] Joab replied to her: “I do not seek to overthrow the city, but Sheba son of Bichri, who raised his hand against David.” The woman spoke wisely to the citizens. “They threw Sheba’s severed head to Joab.” Then the army returned to the king at Jerusalem; and the king restored Joab over the army, and the other officials to their offices as above, adding this: that he appointed Adoram over the collection of tribute, and that Ira was made David’s own priest.

## Chapter XX. On the three-year famine and the hanging of seven men in vengeance for the Gibeonites

There was also a famine in David’s days for three consecutive years, and David consulted the Lord (2 Sam. 21). He answered that this had happened because of Saul and [Col. 1342B] his house: in killing the Gibeonites, as though out of zeal for the children of Israel, Saul had annulled Joshua’s oath and that of the elders. David said to the Gibeonites: “What shall I do for you, that you may bless the Lord’s inheritance?” They said: “We must destroy the man who crushed us, so that not even one survivor may remain of his stock.” But because David could not do this on account of the oath which he had sworn to Jonathan, they moderated their request, saying: “Let seven men from his sons be given us, that we may crucify them before the Lord.” The king spared Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, and handed over to them two sons of Saul, whom Rizpah had borne to him.

These, still boys, had joined Doeg in killing the priests of Nob, and afterwards the Gibeonites. He also gave them five adopted sons of Michal, whom Merab had borne to Adriel.
