The Gibeonites crucified them in the days of the first harvest, that is, at the beginning of the barley harvest. Rizpah, putting on sackcloth, spread it beneath herself upon a rock and lay beside them day and night, to keep birds and beasts away from them, from the beginning of the harvest until water dripped upon them—that is, until about the Kalends of September. For then, according to the nature of that land, rain first falls after the harvest. Some incorrectly suppose that this Rizpah was Orpah, Naomi’s daughter-in-law.

When David heard what Rizpah had done, he took them down from the gibbets; and, taking the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh-gilead, together with the bones of those who had been fastened up, he buried them in the tomb of Kish their father. When this was done, God restored fertility to [Col. 1342D] the land.

## Chapter XXI. On David’s four battles

“Again there was war between the Philistines and Israel, and David fought against them with his men. And when David had nearly collapsed from fighting with Ishbi-benob, who was of the race of Arapha, that man attempted to strike David; but Abishai intervened and killed the Philistine” (2 Sam. 21).

The Hebrews maintain that he was of the race of giants; they say that Arapha was Orpah, Naomi’s daughter-in-law, who bore to a man of Gath four giants mentioned here: Ishbi-benob, Saph, Goliath, and a fourth having six fingers on his hands and feet. “Then David’s men swore to him, saying: ‘You shall no longer go out [Col. 1343A] with us to battle, lest you extinguish the lamp of Israel.’”

On the occasion of this last battle, the history here recapitulates three earlier named battles of David, though not in the order in which they occurred. The first was at Gob, a city also called Isaer, where Sibbecai struck down Saph, of the race of giants. Another battle likewise occurred at Gob, in which, according to Josephus, the mighty Ephron, David’s kinsman, appeared; when his own men had been put to flight, he alone killed very many enemies and turned the rest to flight.

But the Book of Kings here gives David’s battle against Goliath in this form: “In it Adeodatus, son of the forest, the embroiderer, the Bethlehemite, struck Goliath of Gath.” By these four names David is designated. He is called Adeodatus, “God-given,” because he was given by God as king for Israel’s deliverance; “son of the forest,” because he was taken from pastures and woodland; “embroiderer,” because his mother was of the line of Bezalel the embroiderer—or because in many ways he enlarged the worship of the Lord; and “Bethlehemite,” from his homeland.

[Col. 1343B] Another battle is also mentioned in which Jonathan, son of Shimeah, David’s brother, struck down a man having six fingers on his hands and feet. David, therefore, being freed from warfare, spoke to the Lord the words of his song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul; and he said: “The Lord is my rock” (2 Sam. 22), and so forth. In the Psalms, according to our translation, it reads: “I will love you, O Lord, [Col. 1343C] my strength; the Lord is my support and my refuge” (Ps. 7), and so forth. Ezra took its title from the words set down above: “on the day when the Lord delivered him,” and so forth.

Josephus says here that, when David enjoyed the deepest peace, he composed songs and hymns: some in trimeter, others in five-meter verse; and made different instruments, upon which the Levites might sing hymns on Sabbaths and other feasts. Josephus also sets out the difference between the psaltery and the nabla. The psaltery is a melodious lyre fitted with ten strings and struck with a plectrum. The nabla, having twelve tones, is played with the fingers.

After the aforesaid song David added, speaking of himself as though of another: “These are the last words which David son of Jesse spoke: the man [Col. 1343D] to whom it was appointed”—that is, to whom the promise was made—“concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob” (2 Sam. 23). The Hebrew has it thus: “The man exalted above the Christ of the God of Jacob spoke,” that is, the Christ exalted above others and anointed by God. Because of these words, some say that the preceding psalm was the last written by David. But it is safer to say that the “last words of David” are those which follow: “The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me,” and so forth. Perhaps this psalm was indeed the last written, but was not numbered among the other one hundred and fifty.

## Chapter XXII. Catalogue of David’s mighty men

Now about the king were all the mightiest men, of whom the more distinguished were thirty-six (2 Sam. 23). [Col. 1344A] Yet David was more distinguished than the rest, “sitting in the seat as the wisest”; thus, with David included, there were thirty-seven. After David, among those six who stood above the thirty, three were most mighty; the other three were not so strong, though still stronger than the remaining thirty. Thus one might say that thirty were strong, three stronger than they, and the remaining three most mighty.

According to this interpretation, the catalogue of the thirty-six mighty men begins here: “He is chief among the three, like the tenderest wood-worm, who killed eight hundred in one assault.”

> [Note: [Col. 1345B] Addition 1. Note that the text found in the Book of Kings is difficult: “David, sitting in the seat, the wisest; chief among the three, he is [Col. 1345C] like the tenderest wood-worm, who killed eight hundred in one assault.” It is distinguished in this one way: “wisest” is the end of the sentence, and “chief” the beginning of the following sentence.]

Josephus says nine hundred; Chronicles says three hundred. This man is not named here by the history. Chronicles calls him Jashobeam; Josephus, Eusebius. It is not read where this occurred, except insofar as it is [Col. 1344B] commemorated here.

After him was Eleazar, David’s uncle’s son, who struck down the Philistines until his hand failed and became stiff upon the sword. After him was Shammah the Hararite, whom Josephus calls Semeias. When the people fled, he stood alone in a field of lentils, struck down the Philistines, and wrought deliverance in Israel. Josephus attributes to these three the bringing of water from the cistern of Bethlehem. But the history of Kings refers this to the following three, whom we called stronger; the first was Abishai, Joab’s brother. “He is the one who raised his spear against three hundred whom he killed; indeed excellent, but he did not attain to the first three.”

After him was Benaiah, who struck down two lions of Moab—that is, princes—whom Chronicles calls rams (1 Chron. 2). “He [Col. 1344C] also killed an Egyptian man,” that is, an imitator of the Egyptian who blasphemed the Lord and whom Moses killed. The Hebrews say that this was Shimei, whom he later killed under Solomon. “He also killed another Egyptian man, a man worthy of spectacle,” five cubits tall, “who had a spear in his hand; Benaiah came to him with a staff, wrenched the spear from his hand, and killed him with his own spear.”

Jerome, however, says that what we have said concerning the other Egyptian applies to Shimei, who had a spear in his hand—that is, the law of God—which, if he had meditated upon it by remaining in Jerusalem, he would not have perished. The same man killed a lion in this manner. In snowy weather a lion slipped into a cistern. Seeing no way out, because the cistern’s opening was blocked by snow, it roared. Hearing it while he was travelling, Benaiah descended to it with a staff and threw it down with his hands.

Neither the Book of Kings nor Josephus names the third of the stronger men here. But one must return to Sabochai, of whom mention was made shortly before. These three performed the great deed which follows. The Philistines once pitched their camp in the valley of Rephaim as far as the city of Bethlehem; and there was a shortage of water in Jerusalem. David had gone up to the stronghold to consult the Lord, and before those standing by he expressed a longing for the water of Bethlehem, especially that which was in the well by the gate. Then these three made their way through the midst of the enemies to Bethlehem; drawing water, they returned again to the king through the enemy camp. [Col. 1345A] The Palestinians, astonished at their boldness, ceased fighting.

The king refused to drink the water brought to him, saying: “Shall I drink the blood of these men and the peril of their lives?” He poured it out as a libation to the Lord,

> [Note: [Col. 1345C] Addition 2. Jerome says on this passage in Chronicles: “It should be noted that the wine offered to God was mixed with water.”]

giving thanks for the men’s safety.

The Hebrew differs from this enumeration of the mighty men, counting only thirty-six strong men. Among the first three, whom we called most mighty, it counts David himself thus: “David sitting in the seat, the wisest, chief among the three; he is like the tenderest wood-worm,” and the remaining words, which are unchanged. It says that he killed many in one assault because, as punishment for the sin when he acted impetuously in the matter of Bathsheba, many were killed.

David is compared to the wood-worm, called [Col. 1345B] *teredo* or *terebella*, which, though soft, pierces hard wood: when it is touched, nothing is softer than it; when it touches, nothing is harder. So David, in afflictions, at home, and toward subjects, was gentler than the rest; upon the throne and against enemies, none was keener. David is here commended in three respects: wisdom, humility, and strength. The remaining thirty whom we called strong are subsequently enumerated; Joab is not counted among them, either because he was the leader of the others or because he was unworthy on account of the deaths of Abner and Amasa.

## Chapter XXIII. On the census of the people and the altar erected by David

[Col. 1345C]

“After the famine previously sent by the Lord, the anger of the Lord again burned against Israel” (2 Sam. 24). Chronicles seems to explain the Lord’s anger by saying: “Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to number [Col. 1345D] the people” (1 Chron. 21). The king said to Joab: “Go through all the tribes of Israel and number the people, that I may know their number.”

> [Note: [Col. 1347A] Addition 1. The Hebrew says this: The Lord had already taken vengeance on David for Uriah’s death through the persecution by his son Absalom, but not yet on the people and rulers who had not opposed him. Therefore he now wished to exact vengeance against Israel, that is, against the people. At the devil’s suggestion David caused the people to be numbered, which should not have been done except when he was about to proceed to war; and then five shekels were to be received from every head as an offering to the Lord. David did this from the haughty arrogance of pride.]

Joab, understanding that he said this from pride, replied: “May God increase your people; but what does my lord the king intend in this matter?” As if to say: Take care lest you offend the Lord. When the king would not change his purpose, Joab and the commanders of the army went out, numbered the people, and returned after nine months and twenty days to Jerusalem with the census committed to writing.

“There were found of Israel eight hundred thousand strong men, and of Judah five hundred thousand fighting men.” The Benjaminites are said not yet to have been [Col. 1346A] counted, because they were few. In Chronicles far more are recorded, namely one million one hundred thousand (1 Chron. 6:21); and Joab is believed to have withheld part of the people’s number from the king. David sinned in two respects: he numbered them proudly, and each person numbered did not pay money to the Lord, namely five silver shekels, as is written in the Law of Moses. Recognizing this, David said to the Lord: “I beseech you, Lord, take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have sinned exceedingly.”

At daybreak the Lord sent to him the prophet Gad, bearing three alternatives of punishment.

> [Note: [Col. 1348A] Addition 2. For it is written in Exodus: “When you take the sum of the children of Israel, each shall give the Lord, according to their number, a price for his soul; and there shall be no plague among them.”]

He said: “Either famine will come upon your kingdom for seven years, or you will flee your enemies for three months, or there will be pestilence among the people for three days.” David said: “I am greatly distressed.” That is: [Col. 1346B] If I choose famine, the punishment will be the poor’s, not the rich’s. If I choose victory for our enemies, the punishment will be the army’s, not mine, since I am surrounded by the strongest men. Therefore I shall choose a blow common to king and people. “For it is better that I fall into the hands of the merciful Lord than into the hands of man.”

The Lord therefore sent pestilence in Israel from morning until the appointed time—that is, until the dinner hour according to Josephus, or until the time of the evening sacrifice according to others—and seventy thousand men of the people outside Jerusalem died. Chronicles (1 Chron. 21) reads “almost three hundred thousand.”

> [Note: [Col. 1345D] Read “seventy thousand,” as above in the Book of Kings.]

The Hebrews say that there the number of common people is given, but here that of the nobles. When the destroying angel had stretched out [Col. 1346C] his hand over Jerusalem to destroy it, and stood by the threshing-floor of Araunah the Jebusite, also called Ornan, David saw him standing with drawn sword and cried: “I am the one who sinned; what have these sheep done? Turn, I pray, your hand against me and against my father’s house.” The Lord had mercy and said to the angel: “Enough; restrain your hand.”

“On that day Gad said to David: ‘Set up an altar to the Lord on the threshing-floor of Araunah the Jebusite.’” David went up and said to Araunah: “Sell me your threshing-floor, that I may build there an altar to the Lord and the slaughter may cease.” He replied: “Let my lord take it freely. Let him also have oxen for a burnt offering, and the carts and yokes of oxen to use as wood.” But the king said: “By no means; I will buy it for a price, and I will not offer free burnt offerings to the Lord.”

[Col. 1346D] David therefore bought the threshing-floor for “six hundred shekels of gold,” as Chronicles records (1 Chron. 21), and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver; and he built there an altar to the Lord, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the Lord was appeased toward the land. This is Mount Moriah, the Hebrews say, where Abraham intended to offer his son and offered a ram in his place (Gen. 22). At that time the tabernacle and altar made by Moses were on the high place at Gibeon, although the ark was in Jerusalem. When Gad prophesied that the Temple would be there, David decreed that the place should be called the threshing-floor of the people.

# History of the Third Book of Kings

[Col. 1347]

## Chapter I. On Solomon’s anointing as king

[Col. 1347B]

According to the Hebrews, this begins *Malachim*, meaning “Kings.” For although the preceding work dealt with two kings of the Hebrews, who did not reign at the same time, this work deals with kings who reigned simultaneously in Judah and Israel; therefore it is rightly called *Kings*.

“King David had grown old; and though he was covered with garments, he was not warmed” (3 Kings 1). They found for him Abishag the Shunammite, an exceedingly beautiful young woman, who slept with the king, warmed him, and attended him. “But the king did not know her.”

Adonijah, David’s fourth son, being the eldest among the surviving sons of the king, was confident of becoming king and procured chariots and horsemen for himself. His father did not rebuke him, and Joab [Col. 1347C] and Abiathar the priest supported him. The other royal officials and the strength of the army were not with him. Adonijah prepared a solemn banquet in the royal garden near the spring of Rogel. He invited the king’s sons and servants, but did not invite the mighty men who did not favor him, nor Solomon.

Nathan warned Bathsheba to go in to the king, and put words into her mouth. Entering before the king, she said: “My lord, you swore to your handmaid: ‘Your son Solomon shall reign after me’; and now, behold, Adonijah reigns without your knowledge. Since he has invited others to the banquet but has not invited my son, I know that, ‘when you sleep with your fathers, my son and I shall be sinners’”—that is, judged worthy of death: I as an adulteress, he as the son of an adulteress.

“While she was still speaking, [Col. 1347D] Nathan entered and said: ‘My lord the king, did you say: “Adonijah shall reign after me,” and did you not make it known to me, your servant?’” The king said to Bathsheba: “As the Lord lives, who has rescued my soul from every distress, as I swore to you, so I shall do today.” He said to Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah: “Take with you your lord’s servants, set my son Solomon upon my mule, and let Zadok and Nathan anoint him king at the spring of Gihon. With singing set him upon my throne.” Benaiah answered: “Amen.”

Zadok took the horn of oil from the tabernacle [Col. 1348B] and anointed him. They sounded the trumpet and all the people said: “May King Solomon live!” The earth resounded with their cry. Solomon sat upon the throne, and David, on his bed, worshipped God, who had granted him to see one sitting on his throne.

When Adonijah and those whom he had invited perceived the disturbance that had arisen in the city, Jonathan son of Abiathar ran to them and reported what had occurred; and each went to his own house. But Adonijah, fearing Solomon, went to the tabernacle and seized the horn of the altar of incense, saying that he would not leave unless the king swore to preserve his life. Solomon swore to him, saying: “Go to your house.”

## Chapter II. On Solomon’s second anointing

[Col. 1348C]

> [Note: [Col. 1347] What follows has been collected from various chapters of the last book.]

David, wishing to show the people that he had made his son king, gathered all the princes of Israel, priests, and Levites. Solomon was anointed a second time, and Solomon’s kingdom was confirmed by all. Before all the people David instructed Solomon concerning the observance of the laws, justice, and piety. He commanded him to build a temple to the Lord, saying that he had already prepared for it ten thousand talents of gold, one hundred thousand of silver, iron and bronze beyond number, and a very great abundance of stones and wood (1 Chron. 29).

He also divided the Levites into three orders: Aaronites, Mosaic Levites, and Levites. He divided the Aaronites by descent and found sixteen from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar. From each of these he chose one high priest, commanding that each should minister from Sabbath to Sabbath; yet Zadok and Abiathar were to preside over all. They cast lots before the king to arrange the weekly courses.

> [Note: [Col. 1349B] Addition 1. He who was of the line of Eli held the primacy.]

Among the Levites he appointed twenty-four overseers of the Temple works; others read twenty-three thousand. These were called Nethinim. He appointed six judges and scribes of the people; seven gatekeepers of the house of God—others read four thousand—and as many more to sing hymns. Afterwards he divided the army into twelve cohorts. Each cohort contained twenty-four thousand men, whom he commanded Solomon to maintain for three hundred [Col. 1349A] days. He honored the Mosaic Levites to some extent, making them keepers of God’s treasuries and of the vessels which kings might dedicate to God.

He set before the entire assembly the whole plan and arrangement of the Temple’s construction, urging his sons not to resent the elevation of the least among them—that is, Solomon—because God had so commanded, just as David himself, the least among his brothers, had been anointed. He delivered to Solomon the whole design and plan of the building, all encouraging this. Then, making an offering of firstfruits, he offered three thousand talents of gold for the entrance and for making the chariot of God,

> [Note: [Col. 1349B] Addition 2. By “chariot” he means the *ciborium*, that is, the covering. A *ciborium* is raised on four columns, beneath which are the ark and cherubim, as in many places above the bodies of saints.]

under which they placed the ark. The princes, priests, Levites, and elders of the people offered five thousand talents of gold and ten thousand staters, ten thousand talents of silver, and many precious stones. Their custody was held by the great-grandson of Moses, Jabez—or Jabus, as others say.

## Chapter III. On David’s death

“David’s days drew near for him to die” (3 Kings 2). He repeated to Solomon his commands concerning the worship of God, observance of the Law, piety, and justice toward his own people; and recalled God’s promise [Col. 1349C] to him that his seed would reign continually, if his sons kept his covenant and the testimonies which he would teach them (Ps. 131).

He added three commands concerning Joab, the sons of Barzillai, and Shimei. He said: “You know what Joab did,” out of envy, “to the two commanders Abner and Amasa, whose blood he shed—the blood of war—in peace.” That is, he shed in a time of peace blood which ought not to be shed except in war, the blood of men with whom he was at peace; “and he put the blood of war upon his belt and upon his shoe.” That is, the blood was not spattered upon his weapons, because he did not fight them; it was on his clothes when he was speaking peaceably with them. The meaning is: he killed them, not by force, but by deceit.

Or otherwise: men of war inscribed on their weapons the marks of their exploits, as a display of glory. But since Joab did not dare publicly to display these acts as achievements, he at least depicted them on his belt and shoe. David added: “Deal with him according to your wisdom; do not let him go down peacefully to the underworld. But show kindness to the sons of Barzillai, and let them be your table-companions. Nor shall you allow Shimei the Benjaminite, who cursed me, to remain unpunished.”

David died and was buried in the City of David, having reigned forty years. Near his tomb Solomon made eight treasure-chests, one of which the high priest Hyrcanus opened after thirteen hundred years, and another Herod opened, as we shall say below. The others have not yet been revealed,

> [Note: [Col. 1350A] Addition 1. Some writings appear to say that they will not be revealed until the time of Antichrist.]

having been hidden by an arrangement of mechanical art.

[Col. 1350A] **Incidental matters.**

In David’s days Carthage was founded, as some hold, by Chalcedon of Tyre, or, as others say, by his daughter Dido. The fifth king of the Latins was Silvius Latinus. Under him Nathan, Gad, and Asaph prophesied.

## Chapter IV. On the deaths of Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei

Solomon sat upon the throne of David his father. In the course of time Adonijah begged Bathsheba to obtain from the king that Abishag [Col. 1350B] the Shunammite be given to him as wife (3 Kings 2). When she entered the king’s presence, a throne was placed for her at the king’s right hand, and she said: “I ask a small favor of you; do not put me to shame. Let Abishag the Shunammite be given as wife to your brother Adonijah.”

The king indignantly replied: “Why do you ask this of me, mother? Ask the kingdom for him as well. For he is my brother and older than I, and he has with him the powerful Abiathar and Joab.” Abishag was, as it were, a queen and a person of power. Adonijah had spoken against his own life and to the dishonor of his father. “As the Lord lives, Adonijah shall be put to death today.” He killed him by the hand of Benaiah son of Jehoiada.

The king also said to Abiathar the priest: “Go to your field and do not again come into my presence. You are a man deserving death; but this spares you, that you often labored with my father and bore the ark before him.” Thus Abiathar was removed, and the priesthood passed to Zadok, from the house of Ithamar to the house of Eleazar, as Samuel had foretold to Eli (1 Sam. 2).

There had been five descendants of Eleazar deprived of the priesthood after Phinehas: Joseph, who begot Joathan; Joathan, Mareoth; Mareoth, Asophi; Asophi, Achitob; and Achitob begot Zadok. Joab fled to the tabernacle of the Lord and grasped the horn of the altar. The king sent Benaiah to summon him. Joab said: “I will not go out, but shall die here.” When Benaiah reported this to the king, the king said: “Do to him as he has said.” Benaiah killed him at the horn of the altar, and “he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.” The king appointed [Col. 1350D] Benaiah over the army in his place.

The king also summoned Shimei and said: “Live in Jerusalem; do not go out from it. On whatever day you cross the Kidron torrent, know that you shall be killed.” He answered: “The king’s word is good; I shall do so.” He lived in Jerusalem for three years. Afterwards Shimei’s slaves fled to Achish king of Gath; Shimei went down to Gath and brought them back. When this was reported to Solomon, he said to him: “Why have you despised the king’s oath and transgressed his command? May the Lord return upon your head the evil which you did to my father.” The king killed him by the hand of Benaiah. And the kingdom was established in Solomon’s hand (3 Kings 3).

## Chapter V. On Solomon’s dream

[Col. 1351A]

Solomon took as wife the daughter of Pharaoh king of Egypt (3 Kings 3). Of her, as the Hebrews say, he begot a son almost against nature, while he himself was still in his eleventh year; and he brought her into the City of David. He had not yet built a house for himself.

He had proposed three works to accomplish: a house for the Lord, a house for himself, and to surround Jerusalem with a triple wall. Within the first circuit were to be the Temple and dwellings for those serving weekly; also the royal house with the residences of its household. In the second were to live mighty men and prophets; hence it is later read of the prophetess that she lived in the second district. In the third lived craftsmen.

After this Solomon went up to Gibeon to sacrifice there upon the high place. When it says [Col. 1351B] “Gibeon,” it is not a proper place-name but a common noun, and means “high hill.” Josephus says that he went up to Hebron and offered a thousand victims as burnt offerings on the altar which Moses had made. The Lord appeared to him in a dream by night and said: “Ask what you wish, that I may give it to you.” He answered: “Lord God, I am a little child and do not know my going out and coming in. Therefore give your servant an obedient heart, that I may be able to judge your people and distinguish good from evil.”

The word pleased the Lord, and he said to him: “Because you have not asked, according to the desire of men, for long life, riches, or the life of your enemies, I have done according to your words and given you a wise heart, so that none before you has been like you. Moreover I have given you even those things which you did not ask, provided that you walk in my ways as your father did.” Solomon awoke and understood that it was a dream—that is, a revelation granted through a dream. Returning to Jerusalem, he gave thanks before the ark of the Lord and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

## Chapter VI. On Solomon’s judgment in the dispute of the harlots

Then two harlots came to the king (3 Kings 3). One said: “This woman and I lived alone in one house. After I had given birth, she too gave birth on the third day. Her son died; in the silence of the night she placed him in my bosom and placed my living son in [Col. 1351D] her own bosom. When morning came, looking more closely, I discovered that the dead child was not mine.” The other replied: “It is not so; your son is dead, but mine is alive.”

While all minds were uncertain in deciding this matter, the king unexpectedly resolved the case. When a sword had been brought, Josephus says, he ordered the infant divided, so that each might receive half of the living child and half of the dead. Hearing this, the mother of the living child’s heart was stirred within her for her son, and she said: “I beg you, my lord, give her the living child. It is enough for me if I see him live.” The other said: “By no means; let him be divided.” The king, recognizing the words of each as uttered from the true source of her heart, said: “Give this woman the living child. She is his mother.”

All Israel, perceiving that divine wisdom was in [Col. 1352A] the king, feared him; and his counsellors, who had formerly mocked the judgment as though it came from an adolescent, were astonished.

Benaiah was over the army. Zadok was priest; Azariah son of Nathan was over the king’s officers; Zabud son of Nathan was the king’s priest, that is, chancellor; Ahishar was over the household, that is, steward; and Adoniram was over the tribute (3 Kings 4).

## Chapter VII. On Solomon’s governors and the discovery of exorcisms
Solomon had twelve governors over all Israel; each, in turn, supplied the necessities for the king and his household for one month (1 Kings 4). One of them presided over the rest, namely Ahimaaz, who had Basemath, Solomon’s daughter, as his wife, [Col. 1352B] although one of the others also had a daughter of Solomon. “Solomon’s daily provision was thirty cors of fine flour and seventy cors of meal; ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and one hundred rams, besides venison—stags, goats, buffaloes, and fattened birds.” Fish too were brought daily by foreigners. There was complete peace in the land; Solomon had forty thousand chariot-horses and twelve thousand horsemen. Half of these served the king at Jerusalem, while the rest remained distributed among the royal towns. The governor who supplied the expenses of the table also furnished the horses with barley and straw, bringing everything to the place where the king was staying.

[Col. 1352C] The king surpassed in wisdom all the Easterners, Egyptians, and even the four most celebrated Hebrew sons of Moal: Heman, Ethan, Chalcol, and Darda. He wrote a book on Songs, and five thousand verses of musical compositions; and three thousand parables. He discussed the nature of trees and herbs, from the cedar to the hyssop. He likewise philosophized concerning the nature of every kind of living creature, setting forth a parable for each genus. He also devised adjurations by which illnesses are usually alleviated; others by which demons are expelled; and still others by which those bound by them do not return. He also devised characters inscribed on gems: when such a gem was placed in the nostrils of a demoniac, together with the root shown by Solomon, it immediately freed him from demons.

[Col. 1352D] This knowledge was of very great value among the Hebrew people and was especially necessary. For before Christ’s coming people were more often harassed by demons, which at times thrust living human beings down into hell. Josephus too testifies that he saw a certain exorcist, Eleazar, before Vespasian, his sons, and the rulers, curing persons afflicted by demons in the manner described above. To prove to them that the demon had gone out through the nostrils with the breath of the panting person, he placed a vessel in the middle and commanded the departing demon to overturn it as evidence of its departure; and so it happened.

> [Note: Col. 1352D, Addition 1. Josephus names neither a gem nor a herb. But it was a crystal gem; between the ring and the gem was placed the root of a certain herb, [Col. 1353A] called by some *portagon*, by others “gall of the earth” (*fel terrae*) or *felterna*, and by others “Saracen herb” (*sarracenica*). Around the bezel, engraved in silver, were the seven chief names of God through which, as is said, he created heaven and earth, as is found in the *Book of Images*; and three other names, different from these, were engraved on the stone. If you wish to know the method of treatment, read the *Book of Images*, and there you will find everything.]

## Chapter VIII. On the workers of the Temple

[Col. 1353A]

Solomon sent to Hiram, king of Tyre, saying: “I wish to build a temple to the Lord, as he spoke to my father. Therefore command your servants to cut cedars for me from Lebanon, and I shall give you whatever wages you ask for them” (1 Kings 5). Hiram replied to him, [Col. 1353B] saying: “My servants shall bring down the timber from Lebanon to the sea [Note: Col. 1354A, Addition 1. In Chronicles it is read: “as far as Joppa” (2 Chronicles 2).], and shall convey it on rafts to the place you designate for me; you shall take it from the harbor and provide food supplies for my household.”

Thus Hiram gave Solomon cedar and fir timber, with which the Sidonians abound. Solomon, however, supplied their lack of food, giving Hiram every year twenty thousand cors of wheat, the same quantity of barley, and the same number of baths of oil and the same measure of wine. Now “Solomon levied workmen from Israel,” namely proselytes; for he made none of the Israelites serve. “The levy was thirty thousand men,” that is, the total number upon whom this service was imposed. Or perhaps “levy” means a designated body of men, [Col. 1353C] like a cohort or legion. “He sent them to Lebanon with Hiram’s servants, ten thousand each month in rotation, so that, returning home for two months, they might rest”—so that in the fourth month the first men would return again to the work. “Aduram was in charge of this levy.”

Solomon also appointed eighty thousand quarrymen—that is, stonecutters—on the mountain; over them he set three thousand three hundred Israelites who gave orders to the workmen. In the quarry the quarrymen extracted and squared great, precious—that is, marble—stones.

> [Note: Col. 1354A, Addition 2. Quarrymen (*latomi*) properly are those who dig stones and rocks out in the quarry; masons (*caementarii*) are those who dress and set them; while Byblians (*Biblii*) carve images.]

These stones in the foundation were so large, Josephus says, that many of them measured twenty cubits in length, ten in breadth, and five in height. Solomon’s masons [Col. 1353D] and Hiram’s masons dressed the squared stones. The Byblians prepared the dressed material by polishing and carving not only stones but timber as well. Byblos is a city of Phoenicia, of which Ezekiel says: “The elders of Byblos and its wise men” (Ezek. 27). Thus everything was dressed and finished outside the city, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any iron tool was heard in the house of the Lord while it was being built.

There were seven thousand pack-horses carrying burdens.

> [Note: Col. 1354A, Addition 3. Chronicles states that there were seventy thousand proselytes (2 Chronicles 2) carrying burdens on their shoulders, and says nothing of horses; Kings speaks of horses and says nothing of men.]

The Jews tell a tale that, in order to extract the stones more quickly, Solomon possessed the blood of a little worm called *tamir*, with which sprinkled marble was easily cut. It was discovered in this way. Solomon had an ostrich with a chick, and the chick was shut beneath a glass vessel. When the ostrich saw it but could not reach it, it brought from the desert [Col. 1354A] a little worm, smeared the glass with its blood, and the glass broke. When Solomon saw that the summit of Mount Moriah, where he built the Temple, was narrow, he threw it down and spread it out into a broader level area.

## Chapter IX. On the building of the Temple

[Col. 1354B]

“It came to pass, four hundred and eighty years after Israel’s departure from Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign, in the second month, called Ziv among the Hebrews and May among us, that Solomon began to build the house of the Lord” from white marble called Parian marble (1 Kings 6). Josephus, however, says that it was in the five hundred and second year after the departure from Egypt. He also reckons the years of the preceding ages, saying that 1,020 years had elapsed from Abraham, 1,400 from the Flood, and 3,102 from Adam.

The house was sixty cubits long and twenty cubits broad. The front part, called the Holy Place [Col. 1354C] and situated on the east, was forty cubits long. The remaining western section was twenty cubits long and was called the Holy of Holies. Its height was thirty cubits up to the first storey; above this a second level rose thirty cubits, up to the second storey. The third level was sixty cubits up to the third storey, which was the roof of the house. Thus the Temple’s total height reached one hundred and twenty cubits.

Josephus, however, mentions only two levels, assigning sixty cubits to each, but includes the two lower ones under a single level. Before the Temple façade was a porch, sixty cubits long, corresponding to the Temple’s length, [Col. 1354D] and ten cubits broad, rising, as Josephus says, to the Temple’s height. Solomon made slanting windows in the Temple—that is, narrow on the outside and widening obliquely inward; these were Solomon’s invention.

He placed beams across the house at three points, at the tops of the three levels, so long that their ends projected externally on both sides. Upon the externally projecting ends he built three storeys for walking around the Temple; these are called the pinnacles of the Temple in the Gospel (Matt. 4). How they were made on either side is sufficiently clear. But how they stood on the eastern and western fronts, I do not remember having read, nor do I either wish or presume [Col. 1355A] to speculate about it. Yet it is believed that they were there, as Josephus seems to imply when speaking of the Temple’s destruction.

The width of the storeys differed. “The lowest storey was five cubits wide, the middle six cubits, and the third seven.” Some understand this literally: those living in the upper storeys were not obstructed, when looking downward, by the projection of the lower ones. The Hebrew, however, says that the three storeys had equal width, so that if the masons dropped a plumb-line from the top to the bottom, their equality could be measured. Nevertheless, the lowest storey was five cubits broad and the middle six, because the upper wall was made narrower, as though set back by one cubit. The top [Col. 1355B] storey was seven cubits wide because of a similar recession of the wall above.

Some said that the lower storey was seven cubits wide and the middle six, so that the storeys narrowed as they rose, like the wall; and they correct the text, putting “above” in place of “below.” Or they retain “below,” saying that “the storey which was below” refers not to position but to number. For just as “high,” “deep,” and “highest” may be said, so “below” may denote what is lower in position; but in numerical order it denotes that which one reaches in counting upward.

These storeys were joined to the wall so as not to adhere to it—that is, they were not inserted into the wall—though the beams projected from the walls. At the outer edges [Col. 1355C] of each storey, so that those walking there might be protected from the danger of falling, he built small parapets, like supporting rails. In Kings these are called “sides”;

> [Note: Col. 1355. Hardly anything of this sort, even in sense, is found in Chronicles.]

in Chronicles they are called railings (2 Chronicles 3). We do not know their height except that of the uppermost, which was five cubits high.

## Chapter X. On the ornamentation of the lower house

The wall of the lower level was lined everywhere inside with cedar boards, while cedar ceilings were fastened to the beams of the floor above (1 Kings 6). The floor of the house was covered with fir boards; the side storeys, the beam ceilings, and the floors were overlaid with gold plates fastened by gold nails, each weighing fifty shekels. [Col. 1355D] Nothing in that lower portion of the Temple was not covered with gold, so that the radiance of the gold made the faces of those entering shine.

At the joining of the boards he made relief work—that is, carvings or turnings—so skillfully finished at the joints that the place of joining could not be detected. In the middle of the panels were projecting figures: cherubim and palms. These were carved in cedar panels but covered with gold, or else formed in the gold panels themselves.

The oracle, called the Holy of Holies,

> [Note: Col. 1357C, Addition 1. That is, “successive holies,” namely a place of holies, just as one says “age,” “successive of an age”; or “Holy of Holies” comparatively, that is, holier than holy things.]

was twenty cubits long, twenty broad, and thirty high. The text, however, gives it also twenty cubits of height; this must be understood [Col. 1356A] of the partition wall between the Holy Place and the oracle. For just as columns were placed in the tabernacle from which the veil was hung, so in the Temple a cedar partition was placed, rising only twenty cubits high and leaving the remaining ten cubits up to the ceiling open, so that the smoke of incense rising from the altar could freely enter the oracle through the upper opening.

The entire wall was overlaid with gold and bore reliefs of cherubim and palms, arranged in keeping with the movement of the panels. From this wall hung a veil of four colours, woven with cherubim so delicate that they did not obstruct the view of the wall. Covering the entire wall, it perhaps rose to the ceiling; it is this veil that the Gospel says was torn [Col. 1356B] from top to bottom (Matt. 27).

I have not read anything concerning the internal design of the upper levels, except that, when the building was being completed, a stone was placed in the upper corner, not without great wonder from all. For when the builders tried to set it both in the foundation and in the wall, no place for it was found, until it was most fittingly placed in the upper corner, last of all, in accordance with David’s prophecy: “The stone which the builders rejected, this has become,” etc. (Ps. 17).

At the top of the wall, all around, golden spikes the height of a man were fastened to drive away birds, so that to those looking from afar it seemed like a golden forest. Around the wall was an outer rim, from which hung great [Col. 1356C] golden clusters of grapes with golden vine-leaves, so skilfully made that people looking upward often thought they saw them move like birds.

> [Note: Col. 1357C, Addition 2. A *pampinus* is the leaf or sheath beneath which the fruit of the vine is protected from cold or heat and guarded against every injury; it is therefore cut through in places, both to admit sunlight for ripening the fruit and to provide shade. It is called *pampinus* because it hangs from the vine-shoot (*palmes*). It is feminine: *haec pampina*, with the genitive plural *harum pampinarum*.]

Near ground level, in the wall of the right—that is, southern—side of the house was a side-door.

> [Note: Col. 1357C, Addition 3. The meaning is that, in the southern wall, called the right side in contrast to the northern [Col. 1357D] side, which was the left, there was a door through which one ascended to the upper chamber.]

By a winding stair they went up to the middle upper chamber and from the middle one to the third—that is, by a twisting ascent commonly called a “vine,” made in the likeness of a snail shell. Josephus, however, describes a hidden ascent made through the thickness of the wall, easy and safe, adequately lit by windows in the outer portion of the wall. The entrance to the stair is said to have been near ground level at the front corners of the two walls.

At the Temple entrance he made square doorposts of olive wood [Col. 1356D] and two doors of fir wood, one on each side. Each door was double and opened in interlocking folds.

> [Note: Col. 1357D, Addition 4. Observe that there are two opinions regarding these doors. Some say that on each side of the entrance, which was ten cubits wide, there was one door, each with a second door joined to it, as we see in certain windows. Both the main door and its attached leaf were five cubits wide. Thus, on each side there were, as it were, folding leaves, each ten cubits wide; when opened on either side, they covered the width—or rather the thickness—of the wall and appeared like a continuous adjoining wall. When closed, the two attached leaves on each side folded back.
>
> The other opinion is that there were two doors, one on either side, in the corners of the wall itself, [Col. 1358A] such that each of the four corners had its own door, each one cubit wide; and, when the two outer doors were shut, the inner ones were closed by some mechanism. The text can be applied to either of these views, though more plainly to the following one.]

He carved on them cherubim, palms, and very prominent relief work, and covered everything with gold plates, squared and aligned by rule. These doors were of such beauty that David, prophesying the Temple’s destruction, expressly mentioned them: “They have cut down its doors together” (Ps. 73). And, as Josephus says, there was no piece of wood in them larger than a palm. Perhaps this is what Kings indicates in saying, “in squared work according to rule.”

Their height was thirty cubits, corresponding to the height of the lower [Col. 1357A] upper chamber. But Josephus’s statement that they were twenty cubits high seems false, because that was the Temple’s width; therefore on the east there would have been no wall. Yet Kings supplies the explanation when it says: “The door was double and opened in interlocking folds.” The wall was ten cubits thick on either side, and the opening in which the doors stood was likewise ten cubits wide; thus five cubits remained on either side in the eastern wall. In the opening were four doors, two outside and two inside, each five cubits wide. They were so skilfully fitted that when shut they made what seemed a continuous wall inside and out. When opened they met one another in the middle of the wall’s thickness and covered its entire width.

[Col. 1357B] They adhered to one another so ingeniously that when the outer doors were shut, the inner ones were shut at the same time. No one remained in the Temple at night to close them from within. When the outer doors were opened, the inner ones likewise opened at once. This is why it is said: “The door was double and opened in interlocking folds.”

In the oracle wall he made two small doors of olive wood, with five-cornered doorposts, so that hinges were fixed at the middle fifth corner, around which the small doors moved. On the doors were reliefs of cherubim and palms. Some, however, say that “doorposts of five corners” means five cubits, with “cubits” understood. In the oracle were the Ark, the mercy-seat, and the cherubim made by Moses in the wilderness.

## Chapter XI. On the two cherubim

[Col. 1358A]

“Solomon made two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high” (1 Kings 6), standing on the pavement at the sides of the Ark. Their feet were set obliquely, raised as if for walking. They were covered in pure gold and had golden wings, each five cubits long. Two wings extended over the Ark, met one another above it, and covered the sanctuary [Col. 1358B] below them. Their other two wings stretched outward toward the walls, so that one wing of one cherub touched one wall and a wing of the other touched the opposite wall.

Outside the partition, in the Holy Place, he placed the table on the north and the lampstand on the south; between them stood the golden altar made by Moses in the wilderness. But besides that lampstand, he placed ten other golden lampstands of the same form but larger size, five on one side and five on the other. Likewise, besides the table made by Moses, he placed ten other tables of the same form but larger size, five on one side and five on the other.

Between these he placed the altar of incense and covered it with cedar. It is also called the altar of the oracle, that is, before the oracle. This indicates that it was another altar [Col. 1358C] than the one Moses made. Moses’s altar was of shittim wood and covered on every side with gold; this one was covered with cedar. Therefore it is understood that this altar was made of stones untouched by iron, and was covered around with cedar boards. These too were overlaid on every side with gold plates. I do not recall having read its measurements.

Perhaps the small altar made by Moses in the wilderness was placed in the Holy of Holies, not for the daily use of incense, but for certain special uses, when the priest entered once yearly with blood. This may be inferred because the Apostle says that the Holy of Holies contained a golden censer (Heb. 9). Such was the Temple’s interior adornment.

## Chapter XII. On the porch

[Col. 1358D]

At the front of the Temple was a porch (1 Kings 7), called in the Gospel the Temple vestibule. It had bronze columns arranged along its length; among them, before the Temple doors, were set two more remarkable than the rest, with a space of ten cubits between them, corresponding to the width of the Temple gate. Their construction was as follows.

The shaft, or upright, of each column was eighteen cubits high.

> [Note: Col. 1360A, Addition 1. Thirty-five cubits high, as Chronicles states.]

It was not smooth but fluted, with channels four fingers deep around its circumference. It was cast, and a line of twelve cubits encircled it. If anyone wished to touch its roundness, perhaps [Col. 1359A] a line was cast around the middle of the column. The abacus of the column, upon which the capital was placed, was broader than the shaft and round, carved in openwork. The capital set upon the abacus was cast and five cubits high; at its upper part it was shaped like a lily. Its sides were woven everywhere in a pattern of netting and chains, so skilfully that nets and chains seemed added rather than carved; or perhaps, because they were not solid, they were cast perforated throughout, so that the connections expressed the form of a net.

“There were seven rows of netting on one capital”: that is, seven bands bearing the same carving, occupying the entire circumference of the capital; or these seven [Col. 1359B] rows ascended from the lower part of the capital to the top. Above the capital was something like a cord, upon which lay netting that held its summit and descended a little around the sides of the capital. At its edge hung two hundred pomegranates in two rows. Pomegranates also hung from the abacus of the column on which the capital rested, for it is written that the capitals were above the top of the pomegranates. The other column had the same construction. I have not read about the construction of the bases.

These two columns were called by their own names, both because of their magnificence and because of their abundant prefiguration of future things. The right-hand one was called Jachin, that is, “firmness”; Josephus calls it “Jachin’s chamber.” [Col. 1359C] The left was called Boaz, or Boz, meaning “strength” or “in strength.”

The narrative deals with the other, smaller columns of the vestibule, saying: “The capitals upon the tops of the columns were made like lilies, in the porch, four cubits [high]; and again there were other capitals upon the tops of the columns above, corresponding to the dimensions of the columns, opposite the netting.” It says nothing concerning the construction of the columns. It says that their capitals were one cubit smaller than the earlier capitals. Of their form it says only that they were lily-shaped and had netting laid over them. What follows—“there were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital”—is ambiguous: whether this is said of the smaller capitals, or is a recapitulation concerning the earlier capitals.

[Col. 1359D] Hiram of Tyre cast these columns. He was full of wisdom for making every work in bronze, the son of a widowed woman of the tribe of Naphtali and a Tyrian father. Hiram also cast all the bronze vessels of the Temple and everything made of bronze in it, in the plain of the Jordan, in clayey ground, between Succoth and Sarchan. Do not be troubled that they are sometimes said to have been made of bronze and sometimes of *aurichalcum*, for it is the same material, whose brilliance and beauty were like gold, as Josephus says.

One ascended to this vestibule from the court of the priests by twelve steps, according to Josephus. Some, however, say seven, according to Ezekiel’s vision; for they say that in many respects the plan of the material Temple agrees with the plan of the spiritual Temple seen by Ezekiel.

## Chapter XIII. On the chambers and upper rooms of the weekly courses

Solomon built thirty small houses around the Temple behind the vestibule; by their connection with one another they surrounded the whole interior area of the Temple (1 Kings 7). Each was five cubits wide, five cubits long, and fifteen cubits high. Their entrances were so arranged that one entered from one chamber to another, with some interval between. Above them other chambers, equal in size and number, were built, so that the three sides of the Temple were covered all around [Col. 1360B] with small rooms up to the first external storey.

> [Note: Col. 1360B, Addition 1. If the outer length of the Temple was only forty cubits and its breadth thirty, then the circuit of the three walls was only one hundred and forty cubits. Twenty-eight small rooms would suffice to enclose it, because five times twenty-eight is one hundred and forty. But one must believe that the previously stated dimensions of the Temple were measured between the inner walls, and that the wall was ten cubits thick. Thus the outer length was seventy cubits from side to side and the western width forty, making one hundred and eighty. Thirty-six small rooms would be needed to fill this length if they were continuous.]

The remaining upper part of the Temple was not built around, but could be seen freely. These small rooms were not *pastophoria* or exedrae, as some suppose—of which we shall speak later—but sleeping quarters and upper rooms for the weekly courses, and treasuries for Temple vessels and vestments.

## Chapter XIV. On the court of the priests

[Col. 1360C]

He built the inner court with three rows of polished stones and one row of cedar beams (2 Kings 7). There were, however, several courts around the Temple, as the Psalm says: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. 133). Kings mentions only the inner court; Josephus treats of that same court and of a second one. But besides these two there were also two others.

The inner court [Col. 1360D] was a large open square spread around the Temple on every side, extending very far in front of the Temple doors to the east, since there stood the bronze altar and the lavers, and there Levites and priests ministered before the Lord. It did not extend so far around either side of the Temple, and was narrower on the west. Its pavement was laid with variegated marble and decorated with diverse images.

This court was enclosed by a low wall only three cubits high. One cubit consisted of stones of one colour, the second of stones of another, and the third of stones of a third colour. Inside it was lined with cedar. The wall stood all around at the boundary of this court, to prevent all others from entering it beyond the ministers. [Col. 1361A] Those singing psalms leaned upon it; turning toward the people, they spoke while bent over it.

At regular intervals columns stood in the same wall, warning the people standing outside by inscriptions—some in Hebrew, some in Greek, and some in Latin—about the law of holiness and prohibiting them from passing into the sacred place. This circuit of the wall was properly called the *gion*, in Latin *cancellus*, “railing.” It had a single entrance on the east, opposite the Temple gate, an opening twenty-five cubits wide without doors. Men and women bringing their offerings went up to this entrance to meet the ministers who came out to receive them. They were not allowed to pass farther except in certain cases.

> [Note: Col. 1361B, Addition 1. Perhaps when the judgment of jealousy was performed, or when a Nazirite completed the period of his vow.]

They ascended to it by fourteen [Col. 1361B] steps. This court was called the inner court or the court of priests. Even Aaronites who could not offer because of some blemish did not enter it, although they were supported from portions of the sacrifices.

## Chapter XV. On the court of the clean

> [Note: Col. 1361D. The following material is taken from Josephus.]

Beyond that court, and below it on the mountain’s sloping side, lay the second court, called the holy court, which Josephus calls a great hall or basilica. It extended [Col. 1361C] around the inner court, though it was much larger. Its pavement was variegated marble. It was surrounded by a wall twenty-five cubits high on the inside and forty cubits high on the outside, in accordance with the slope of the hill. Although it was thus high, it did not rise to the Temple structure or obstruct the view of it.

The wall on the west was plain and had no gate. On both sides and on the eastern front it had surrounding porticoes like a monastic cloister. In them stood columns, each made of a single stone of a different colour, with silver bases. The vaults of the porticoes and their ceilings were of cedar. The porticoes were thirty cubits broad.

On the southern side [Col. 1361D] were four gates with double leaves, ornamented in marvellous work with gold and silver plates. Gates of the same number and construction stood on the northern side. Gatekeepers sat in them to keep the unclean from entering this court. On the eastern front was the gate called Beautiful, with doors made of Corinthian bronze. At the corners of this front were two small gates, through which women went up to offer; or perhaps the ministers descended there to meet them and receive their offerings.

[Col. 1362A] Through the gates mentioned above, clean men ascended from every side into the second court, to pray in the open during fair weather and beneath the porticoes during stormy weather. In the eastern open area of this court animals and birds for offering were sold, and there stood the tables of the money-changers, which the Lord overturned (Matt. 21; John 2). In the porticoes around the gates stood treasuries of various kinds for receiving the offerings of those entering.

In the side porticoes were *pastophoria*, that is, separate places for eating, where those making sacrifices ate before the Lord the portions of the sacrifices allotted to them. Some, however, hold that only those coming from outside, from the regions of Israel, ate there, and that this is why they were called *pastophoria*. In these same porticoes [Col. 1362B] were chairs, *synedrae*, and exedrae—that is, three kinds of seats, as Isidore says. Teachers sat in chairs in the school; hearers sat in *synedrae* in the assembly hall. They were called *synedrae* as though “sittings together.” In exedrae assessors sat with the judge when something was discussed more privately, as in a consultation-room. They were called *exedrae* as though “sit-tings beside,” although *exedra* is more often used for a chamber.

This second court is often called “the Temple” in the Gospel: where it says that sheep and animals were sold in the Temple (Matt. 21), that Jesus taught in the Temple (Luke 19), that the children of Israel prayed in the Temple, and so forth in this manner.

## Chapter XVI. On the court of women

[Col. 1362C]

> [Note: Col. 1361D. Ibid.]

Below this court was a third court, likewise situated on the mountain’s slope. Its construction was the same as that of the second, though not of such beauty or costly ornamentation. In it only clean women prayed.

## Chapter XVII. On the court of the unclean

> [Note: Col. 1362D. Ibid.]

Below that court was a fourth, in which unclean men, women, and Gentiles prayed. Its outer wall stood at the foot of the hill, and from it one ascended four hundred cubits to the summit of the hill alone, on which the Temple stood. Thus the walls of the courts in no way obstructed the view either of the Temple or of those ministering in the inner court.

## Chapter XVIII. On the altar and the bronze sea

[Col. 1362D]

[Note: [Col. 1362D] Ibid.] Moreover, in the inner court there was a bronze altar. It was made of unhewn stones and clad on that side with bronze, and was far larger than the portable one made in the wilderness: twenty cubits in length and as many in height. Beneath it was a great pit, into which ashes flowed through an opening in the middle of the altar, while the blood poured at the base of the altar ran into it. The pit was sometimes cleaned through a window [Col. 1363A] on the east. The altar which Moses had made was preserved in some part of the court out of reverence for it. Some relate that it remained there until the Temple’s destruction by the Romans. Indeed, afterward, when pagans lived in Jerusalem, they made it into a clock for themselves. Concerning the position of this altar, and how those sacrificing at its side sacrificed before the Lord, enough has been said above.

Moreover, Solomon placed in the same court the molten bronze sea (III Kings VII; II Chronicles IV), which we may call a washing-vessel, so that the priests who were to minister might wash their feet and hands in it. Josephus calls it an immense basin, made in the form of a hemisphere, whose breadth was ten cubits in diameter, from rim to rim. [Note: [Col. 1363C] Addition 1. That is, a line drawn diametrically from one rim to the opposite rim measured ten cubits.] [Col. 1363B] Its height was five cubits from the rim to the bottom, and its thickness three fingers. At its upper part it was so broad that “a cord of thirty cubits encircled it round about”; but it gradually narrowed in its descent, so that around the bottom a cord of ten cubits would encircle it. Its upper rim was flared outward in the manner of a lily. On its outer sides were two rows of carved representations—that is, bearing certain scenes. “It held two thousand baths,” that is, three thousand metretae. For a bath holds a metreta and a half. A bath is a measure of three modii, of the same capacity as an ephah. But the bath is a measure for liquids, whereas the ephah is for dry goods. Moreover, the base on which it stood had twelve bronze, cast oxen: three facing north, three west, three south, and three east. Only their foreparts projected beneath the sea; their hindquarters were concealed within.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Lavers

“Solomon also made ten bronze, cast lavers,” four cubits high (III Kings VII). At the top of a laver was an inward-curving mouth, so narrow that its [Col. 1363D] breadth was one cubit. Its bottom, corresponding to the size of the base on which they stood, was a cubit and a half wide. [Note: [Col. 1364D] Addition 1. “Cubit” is used in three ways: either for the bend of the arm itself; for the measure from there to the tips of the fingers; or for the distance from one hand to the other when the hands are stretched out. It is called a cubit because, when taking food, we recline upon it.] “One laver held forty baths.” In them the entrails and feet of the burnt offerings were washed. All were of the same construction, as were the bases in which they were set.

A base was four cubits square in length and breadth at its lower part, and three cubits high. As it rose, it gradually narrowed to a cubit and a half, corresponding to the size of the laver’s bottom. It was composed of four panels, upon which a fifth, square panel was placed. This projected slightly beyond the tops of the others on every side, and had in its middle a raised round hollow in which the laver stood. The work [Col. 1364A] on the base was openwork; and at the junctions of the panels, at the four corners, were projecting carvings in the form of columns. Some call these *media intercolumna* [intermediate intercolumns]; yet some read there *media intercolumna quadrata*, “square intermediate intercolumns,” calling the central panel, laid over the four panels, a column. The upper half of the sides of the base had engraved little garlands and braided wreaths, [Note: [Col. 1364D] Addition 2. A *coronula* may be called something made of a solid material, such as gold; but a braided crown is made of joined flowers or branches, as is done with laurel and myrtle.] with lions, oxen, and cherubim in their midst. Above the necks of the lions and oxen, and below them, bronze straps hung down, by which they appeared to be bound.

At the top of the four corner columns were outspread shoulders, in the likeness of a human hand and an eagle’s foot. Upon these the panel supporting the laver was fitted so as to seem naturally joined to them. Those [Col. 1364B] columns had their own carvings: human beings, trees, and birds. Moreover, the other, lower half of the base, which was close to the ground, had projecting wheels all around, a cubit and a half in diameter, with the axles, spokes, and hubs customary in a wheel, all cast. Around them were placed various carvings. All this was fashioned so that it seemed not carved but as though attached all around; and the base appeared to be carried on the wheels surrounding it. The casting, measurements, and carving of all ten bases and lavers were alike. Yet I do not recall reading anything concerning the carving of the lavers themselves.

Five of these stood in the Temple court on the right and five on the left, for this use. The Nethinim first washed the members of the sacrificial victims in the sheep-pool [Col. 1364C] and handed them, once washed, to the priests. The latter immersed them in the lavers, lest any dirt had meanwhile adhered to them, so that they might place them, cleansed anew, upon the altar. These washing-vessels were arranged as follows: for persons entering the priestly court, the bronze sea first met them on the south, for washing their hands; then, farther on, came the ten lavers for immersing the portions of the victims; and farther upward came the bronze altar, likewise on the south. Once the victims had been laid upon the altar, the priests performing the offering returned to the bronze sea and washed their feet and hands there, so that, washed in this way, they might complete the sacrifices—that is, enter the Temple with coals and incense, to burn it upon the altar as a pleasing odor to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Vessels of the Altar

[Col. 1364D]

Hiram made the utensils of the bronze altar from bronze: basins for receiving the altar’s ashes and coals; pots and cauldrons for cooking meat; hooks—that is, little flesh-hooks—for taking out [Col. 1365A] or arranging meat; fire-forks, that is, forks for arranging the fire and laying the portions of victims upon it; and pans, vessels of equal width at mouth and bottom, for heating things (III Kings VII). Josephus also adds trowels, perhaps for gathering or removing ashes, or for turning over the pavement.

The Temple vessels, moreover, were of gold or silver. The utensils of the lampstands were of gold, concerning which Exodus speaks (Exodus XXXVII). Josephus gives the number of the vessels which Solomon made in the course of time: namely, tables upon which stood bowls, dishes, little mortars, and plates for offering fine flour; mixing bowls in which flour was mixed with oil; and *assarones*, in which libations were measured. Also censers [Col. 1365B] in which incense was carried, and other censers in which fire was carried from the greater altar to the lesser. Solomon offered all these in gold, and likewise other such objects in silver, but twice as many. I have been reluctant to give their number according to Josephus, lest it appear unbelievable, especially since scribes’ errors occur very frequently in numbers.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Dedication of the Temple

Therefore, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign, in the second month, the house of the Lord was founded; and in the eleventh year, in the month Ebul—that is, October—it was completed in all its workmanship and in all the utensils immediately necessary. For more things were made and added after the dedication. He built it in seven years and seven months.

In the eleventh year Solomon summoned the elders of Israel, the princes of the tribes, and the heads of families for the dedication of the Temple and for carrying the ark into it (III Kings VIII). All assembled in the seventh month, that is, the seventh lunar month, which had entered October. It was the solemn day, namely the tenth day, on which expiation was made. Yet one may say that the Temple was dedicated in September, because nearly the whole month is festive, the king hastening matters; and that after the dedication he made some utensils which were lacking in the eighth month. Thus both are true: in the eighth month the house was completed in all its workmanship and utensils, yet it was dedicated in the seventh month.

The priests [Col. 1365D] and Levites carried the ark of the Lord and all its vessels from the City of David; and, as Josephus says, the voice of those rejoicing could be heard from far away. The king and the whole multitude went before the ark, or rather rejoiced before it, and sacrificed victims beyond estimation and number; the smoke of the spices could be smelled by those at a distance. The priests brought the ark of the Lord into its place, into the oracle beneath the wings of the cherubim, by which it was covered as if by a kind of ciborium. The heads of the poles, upon the shoulders of those carrying them, were visible to the people standing behind, until, once the ark was set down, they were withdrawn forever from human sight. The ark itself was covered lest it be seen. “And in the ark there was nothing except the two stone tablets of the covenant.” But one must add the golden urn [Col. 1366A] full of manna and Aaron’s rod; for the Apostle testifies that these were in it (Hebrews IX).

When the priests came out from the oracle and said, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever” [Note: [Col. 1367A] Addition 1. When David brought in the ark, they sang another psalm: “Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon his name” (Psalm CIV).] (Psalm CIV), “a cloud filled the house of the Lord”—not a fearful cloud, but mild and shining. It overshadowed the faces of the priests so that they could not see one another or minister. Solomon said: “The Lord has said that he would dwell in the cloud.” Nowhere is the Lord recorded as having said this. But because he appeared on Mount Sinai in a cloud, went before Israel in a cloud, and passed before Moses, who had been placed in the cleft of the rock, in a cloud, Solomon stated as a saying what had been shown by the deed. The sense is: “The Lord has said”—that is, he has demonstrated by his action.

A certain fanciful opinion had come upon everyone, that the Lord had locally descended into the Temple. Solomon removed it, saying: We know, Lord, that you have made for yourself an everlasting dwelling: heaven, earth, and sea together. Then, bending both knees upon the ground before the whole assembly, [Col. 1366B] he raised both hands to the Lord, praying for sins or giving thanks for the fulfillment of the Lord’s promise, who had promised David that a house would be built for him through the hand of his son. He also prayed that whatever Jew or gentile came up to this house, supplicating for sins or crying to the Lord in some affliction, might be heard by the Lord in the things he justly asked. Rising from prayer, he stood and blessed the whole people; and on that day the Temple was dedicated with its vessels.

Thereafter, on that same day, a fourth feast was observed: namely, the feast of dedication. For on that day there were three other feasts: the feast of propitiation, of affliction, and of expiation. Do not be troubled that we said he bent his knees upon the ground, whereas Chronicles says that Solomon made a bronze platform four cubits high, which he placed in the middle of the basilica, and that, standing upon it, he blessed the people. For he could have done both. Or, if the two statements are taken as referring to the same thing, it should be understood that he bent his knees upon the ground—that is, upon the place where he stood.

“And Solomon sacrificed peace offerings: twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep.” Since the bronze altar was too small to receive the burnt offerings and the fat [Col. 1366D] of the peace offerings, the king consecrated the middle of the inner court, so that what could not be burned upon the altar might be burned there. [Note: [Col. 1367A] Addition 2. Chronicles records that fire came down from heaven and consumed the offerings (II Chronicles VII).] Solomon therefore held the festival of dedication, with all Israel, for fourteen days. This is to be understood as follows: the dedication was celebrated for five consecutive days; on the sixth day, the fifteenth of the month, the Feast of Tabernacles occurred, interrupting it for seven days. When that feast was finished, the dedication was again celebrated for the two days which had been omitted; and on the eighth day—that is, after two periods of seven days—the king dismissed the people. Or else the dedication was held for seven consecutive days; after the seventeenth day the Feast of Tabernacles began, ending on the twenty-third; and on the eighth day of Tabernacles, after the assembly, he dismissed the people.

[Col. 1367A] “And the Lord appeared to Solomon a second time in a dream, saying: I have heard your prayer; I have sanctified this house, and my eyes shall be upon it every day, and upon you and upon the people of Israel, if you keep the commandments which I have set before you. Otherwise I shall remove you from the land which I gave you, and I shall cast this Temple from before my face, and your calamities shall become a tale told by narrators” (III Kings IX).

## CHAPTER XXII. On the House of the Forest

[Col. 1367B] After the Temple had been built, Solomon began the construction of the royal residences (III Kings II), which he scarcely completed in thirteen years. The people’s zeal was not so ardent in regard to these as it had been concerning the Temple, nor had their wealth for them been prepared by his father. He made three houses: one for himself, one for his wife, Pharaoh’s daughter, and the House of the Forest.

Concerning the king’s house, this alone is said in this book of Kings: “Solomon built his own house in thirteen years and brought it fully to completion” (III Kings VII); and shortly afterward, “also the porch of the throne, in which he made a tribunal” (ibid.). He called the porch itself the house in which were the throne and tribunal: the throne belongs to the king, the tribunal to the judge. [Col. 1367C] In that same small house was the place where one sat to judge—that is, where matters were discussed with assessors in reaching a verdict. The book of Kings is silent concerning the construction of this house, perhaps because it was the same as the House of the Forest, which it describes more fully.

It is said in Kings that he made the queen’s house with work such as that of the royal house. The House of the Forest, however, was double and made of two materials. Its lower part was of stone and was called *nephota*, that is, the spice-store, where spices and aromatics for the use of the Temple and royal house were kept, so that through the properties of earth and sea they might long retain their freshness. The upper part of the house was wooden, made from Lebanese timber; whence it was called the House of the Forest, the House of Lebanon, or the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Some, [Col. 1367D] however, think it was so called because it was planted all around with trees and pleasure gardens of marvelous delight, resembling the density of the forest of Lebanon.

Weapons were kept there, so that by the benefit of the wood they might not rust—not only weapons for warfare, but also arms for ornament and for display of royal magnificence. “For King Solomon made two hundred golden shields, and six hundred shekels were in each shield” (III Kings X). Chronicles adds an equal number of golden spears (II Chronicles IX). “He also made two hundred golden bucklers,” some round and others shaped like a half-shekel. The king’s guards, keeping watch before the entrance of the house, used these (III Kings XIV). When the king went out, riders carrying such weapons also went before him: fair-haired youths, their long hair flowing down to the saddle of their horses, who applied a golden dye to their hair so that their heads shone when struck by the sun. The king followed them, riding in a chariot, and was accustomed to go out to a certain place two cords distant from Jerusalem, called the Garden of Eden—that is, of delights.

The upper part, called the House of the Forest, was one hundred cubits long, fifty broad, and thirty high; its whole ceiling was covered with cedar boards. It was supported by three rows of columns. Each row had fifteen columns facing one another and equally spaced; thus, between the walls and the three rows of columns were four walkways. [Col. 1368B] Before the doors of the house he made a colonnaded porch fifty cubits long and thirty broad. The book of Kings is silent concerning the composition of the lower stone part of the house, perhaps because it was of the same construction as the upper part.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Basilica and the Royal House

Opposite stood the royal house, with a large intervening garden; it was of the same length, breadth, and height, and similarly furnished with columns (III Kings VII). Yet it was a single, one-storey wall, whose height had four divisions. Three were varied with different colors, while the fourth, uppermost division was decorated with carvings. There were carved trees of various kinds, shaded by branches, [Col. 1368C] leaves, and fruit, so finely wrought that they seemed somehow to move.

In the middle of the entire expanse was a small house thirty cubits wide, in which was a throne supported by strong columns, upon which the king sat to pronounce judgments. On the rear front of the house, the ceilings and walls were covered with gold, where “the king made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with gold” (III Kings X). Its ascent was easy by six steps of porphyry marble; twelve little lions stood upon the six steps, on either side. The rear, rounded back of the throne rested upon an ox facing forward; two hands held it on either side, and two lions stood beside each hand. “There was no such work in [Col. 1368D] all kingdoms.” Around the house he also made other dwellings and seats, where, after cases had been heard, they sat down; all were floored with marble and cedar panels.

He also made the queen’s house on the descending side, most richly adorned with marble, cedar, gold, and silver. He made splendid furnishings for both houses, and all vessels suitable for banquets, all of gold. Thus Solomon completed the Temple and the royal houses with all their furnishings in twenty years, Hiram king of Tyre assisting him with timber and gold (III Kings IX).

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Towns Given to Hiram
