“Then Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in [Col. 1369A] the land of Galilee” (III Kings IX), in the coastal allotment of Naphtali. But they did not please the king of Tyre, although they were situated not far from Tyre. “And he called that land Cabul,” which in the Phoenician language means displeasing; and then for the first time that land was called Galilee of the Gentiles, not because gentiles lived there, but because it was under the authority of a gentile king.

Josephus reports that Menander, a Phoenician historian, wrote that Solomon and Hiram sent one another riddles and figures, and whoever did not solve them was to pay the other a fixed penalty. When Hiram was hard pressed in solving them, he consulted a young Tyrian, Abdemon son of Abdemon, because he readily explained everything.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Solomon’s Works

[Col. 1369B]

Moreover, Solomon turned his mind to building the city walls, which he enlarged with marvelous strength (II Kings IX and II Chronicles VIII). He paved with black stone the royal roads leading to Jerusalem. In many places he restored the ruins of cities. He also founded new cities as locations required: some against the harshness of winter, some against summer heat, some against the changeability of spring and autumn. At the borders of the land he built garrison towns; indeed, beyond the borders of the land of promise he had occupied very many cities, Pharaoh, his father-in-law, king of Egypt, assisting him.

Josephus says that this Pharaoh was the last of Egypt’s [Col. 1369C] kings to be called Pharaoh, a name meaning “reigning.” Admiring Solomon’s works, he especially praised the House of the Forest, the sacrifices, and the number of Levites engaged with them. Solomon made no Israelite a slave; rather, they were fighting men and his ministers. Of them, five hundred and fifty were appointed over all Solomon’s works. But he made the Canaanites, from Mount Lebanon as far as the city of Hamath, tributary slaves.

King Solomon also made a fleet on a certain Egyptian island in the Red Sea called Ezion-geber. Seamen from Tyre—which was then an island—sailed with Solomon’s servants. They brought much gold from Ophir; and, after sailing around India and Sicily, they returned after three years had elapsed, bringing [Col. 1369D] Solomon four hundred and twenty talents of gold, silver, elephant tusks, apes, peacocks, gemstones, and very much *thina* wood, similar to shittim wood and fragrant. From it King Solomon made supports and seats for the house of the Lord and the royal house, and harps and lyres for the singers; for he made the *cynara* and *nabla* of electrum. Silver was regarded as of virtually no value in his days; indeed, in Jerusalem very many seats before the doors of houses were of silver. Cedarwood too was as abundant there as sycamore wood.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Queen of Sheba

Moved by the astonishing report of these things, the queen of Sheba came to test him with riddles (III [Col. 1370A] Kings X and I Chronicles IX). She entered Jerusalem with a great retinue and immeasurable riches. Sheba is sometimes the name of a region, but here it is a royal city of Ethiopia; the meanings of these names are distinguished among the Hebrews by the pointed forms of the letters *sin* and *samekh*. Herodotus says that after Minos, who founded Memphis, the kings of Egypt were called Pharaohs, a word meaning “reigning.” They were succeeded by Nichaula, queen of Egypt and Ethiopia, whom Josephus thinks came to Solomon.

Having entered to him, she spoke all that was in her heart. There was no word hidden from the king; rather, he instructed her in all the matters she had proposed. In amazement she was left breathless, saying that the king’s fame was less than the truth. Yet she admired three things above all: the House of the Forest, above the Temple’s construction; the arrangement and number of those ministering in the Temple; and, thirdly, the arrangement and distinction of those serving the king at table. The cupbearers were adorned in like fashion, yet distinctively from the others; likewise the bread-bearers and food-servers, so that amid such a great multitude of attendants no one could be uncertain which service each performed.

The queen gave the king gifts of one hundred and twenty talents of gold, precious stones, and spices in quantities and of qualities never seen in Jerusalem. Josephus also says that she gave the king a balsam root, [Note: [Col. 1370C] Addition 1. Which Cleopatra, the most wicked [Col. 1370D] queen of Egypt, afterward took away.] from which the balsam vines of Engedi were propagated. Solomon in turn gave her many gifts, and there was nothing that he did not grant her when she asked. [Col. 1370C] The queen, having received these freely, returned to her own country.

Some relate that she wrote back to Solomon what she was afraid to tell him in person: namely, that she had seen a certain piece of wood in the House of the Forest upon which someone was to be hanged, and through whose death the kingdom of the Jews would perish; and she indicated this to the king by certain signs. Solomon, fearing this, concealed it in the deepest bowels of the earth. By its power, stirred water healed the sick; yet the Hebrews deny that this is contained in their books. But how it floated to the surface in the sheep-pool around the time of Christ is uncertain (John V); it is believed to have been the wood of the Lord’s cross.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Solomon’s Foreign Women and His Death

[Col. 1370D]

As time went on, “King Solomon loved foreign women” contrary to the law, and placed a blemish upon his glory and schism within his race (III Kings II). “He had queens as wives, about seven hundred.” Josephus, however, says seventy, and three hundred concubines. These turned his heart away when he was already old, and he followed foreign gods so as not to grieve his pleasures. He built three shrines to idols upon high places around Jerusalem: one to Astarte, goddess of the Sidonians, called Juno; a second to Chemosh, idol of the Moabites; and a third to Moloch, idol of the Ammonites. [Col. 1371A] Moloch’s shrine he established on the Mount of Olives, opposite the Temple, which greatly displeased God. Hence that place was afterward called the Place of Offence.

Therefore Nathan, or another prophet, was sent to him by God, saying: “Thus says the Lord: Because you have broken my covenant, I shall tear your kingdom apart and give it to your servant—not all of it, however. I shall give one tribe, besides the tribe of Judah, to your son, for the sake of David my servant; for his sake I shall not do this in your days.” Although Solomon had lived in the greatest peace, toward the end of his life the Lord raised up against him an adversary, Hadad the Edomite, of royal lineage. When Joab raged in Edom, Hadad escaped as a boy to Egypt. Later the king of Egypt gave him as wife the sister of [Col. 1371B] his own wife, who bore him a son, Genubath. When Hadad heard that David and Joab had died and that Solomon had fallen into ill repute—or had become foolish—he left Egypt and harassed Israel.

The Lord also raised up against him another adversary: Rezon, leader of brigands in Damascus. Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah, who served Solomon, likewise raised his hand against the king in this manner. Solomon built the Millo, raising the walls from the base of the ravine so as to make them level with the City of David. Seeing that Jeroboam was of good character and industrious, Solomon made him overseer of the work and then set him over the labor-gangs of the whole house of Joseph.

One day, as Jeroboam was leaving Jerusalem, Ahijah the Shilonite prophet met him on the road, wrapped in a new cloak. [Col. 1371C] He tore it into twelve pieces and said to Jeroboam: “Take ten pieces for yourself. For thus says the Lord: I shall give you ten tribes, and you shall be king over Israel; but I shall give one to Solomon’s son, so that David may remain a lamp before me in Jerusalem, which I have chosen for my name to be there.” On hearing this, Jeroboam became swollen with pride and persuaded the people to withdraw from Solomon. For this reason, “Solomon sought to kill him. Then Jeroboam fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, until Solomon’s death. The rest of Solomon’s words, and all that he did, are written in the Book of Words, or in the Book of the Days of Solomon.”

Some think this book is Chronicles; but since Solomon’s remaining works are not written there either, it is more correct to suppose that this book has not survived. [Note: [Col. 1372A] Addition 1. Note that Holy Scripture mentions several books which have not survived, such as the Book of the Wars of the Lord, mentioned in Numbers; likewise perhaps the Book of Words (Numbers XXI), of which it speaks here and often elsewhere. Some nevertheless wish Chronicles to be meant, since it is called the Book of Things Left Over, because what is said less fully in the books of the Old Testament is supplied there.]

“And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the City of David,” having reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years. The question is asked why Solomon is said to have been old, when he is read to have lived little more than fifty years. For Rehoboam was forty-one years old when his father died, and Solomon is said to have begotten him when he was eleven. Josephus speaks more fully on this point: Solomon died at a very great age, having reigned eighty years. He lived ninety-four years; but divine Scripture records only those years during which he reigned before he transgressed.

[Col. 1372A] Incidental Notice

In Solomon’s days, the sixth king of the Latins was Silvius Alba, son of Silvius Aeneas.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Rehoboam and the Division of the Kingdom

After Solomon’s death, Rehoboam succeeded him, and [Col. 1372B] his mother was Naamah the Ammonite (III Kings XII). When Jeroboam heard of Solomon’s death, he returned from Egypt and came to Rehoboam at Shechem with the entire multitude of Israel, which had summoned him. When they wished to establish Rehoboam as king, they said to him: “Lighten somewhat the heavy yoke which your father imposed on us, and we will serve you.” This should not be understood of the burden of tribute, but of the imposts for expenditures, over which Ahimaaz had presided under Solomon. He replied: “Go, and return to me on the third day.”

Meanwhile he consulted the elders: namely Zadok, Benaiah, Jehoiada, and Solomon’s other princes. They said: “If today you listen to them and speak gently to them, they will serve you forever.” After this he consulted the young men—not merely young in age, but in character. [Col. 1372C] They said: “Speak imperiously and threaten the people; then, being afraid, they will serve you.” When the people returned on the third day, he said to them: “My little finger is thicker than my father’s shoulder. My father struck you with whips; I shall strike you with scorpions.” That is: I am more powerful than my father and shall do greater things against you. A scorpion is a thorny bramble, or a knotted whip of rods, or a scourge having lead balls at its tip.

The outraged people said: “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” That is: each tribe has received its own hereditary portion from the Lord; what necessity is there that one man be chosen from one tribe to rule the others? Let each tribe govern [Col. 1372D] its own inheritance. And the ten tribes withdrew from him. He sent after them Adoram, who was over the tributes, and they stoned him. Rehoboam, in fear, then fled to Jerusalem. The ten tribes made Jeroboam king over themselves. Judah and Benjamin, however, followed Rehoboam, and the Levites were with them because of the Temple in Jerusalem.

Thus the monarchy of the Hebrew kingdom was divided into two kingdoms and never again returned to unity. The kingdom of the ten tribes was called the kingdom of Israel because of its multitude, retaining for itself the name of Jacob, its father. It was also called Ephraim, because Jeroboam, the first to rule them, was from Ephraim—as though the blessing upon Ephraim had then first been fulfilled. The other kingdom was called the kingdom of Judah because of the dignity [Col. 1373A] of the royal tribe. The history treats of both kingdoms in a manner that is, as it were, intercalated and episodic, now speaking of one and now of the other. A careful reader will readily perceive this.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Jeroboam, Abdo, and the Calves
Moreover, Rehoboam assembled an army of one hundred and eighty thousand chosen men to fight against Israel (3 Kings 12). But the Lord sent to him the prophet Shemaiah, saying: “Thus says the Lord: ‘You shall not fight against your brothers, for this thing has come from me.’” This is to be understood concerning the schism of the kingdoms. And they ceased from battle.

But Jeroboam said in his heart: “If this people goes up to Jerusalem three times a year, its heart will turn back [Col. 1373B] to its lord Rehoboam, and they will kill me.” Then, having devised a plan, he made two golden calves—Josephus calls them heifers—and established a shrine for each, one in Dan and the other in Bethel. And he said to the people: “Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” As though he said: Every place has God; you need not go up to the city of your enemies to seek God there. I have made you calves bearing the same name as God, so that in them you may worship the Lord; and I shall appoint priests and ministers from among you, so that you need not depend upon the sons of Levi.

When the Feast of Tabernacles was approaching, “he appointed for them a solemn day in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month.” Perhaps he transferred the feast from the seventh month into the eighth; or the lunar month of September had extended into October. Then he went up with [Col. 1373C] the people to Bethel for the feast-day.

The Lord sent a prophet from Judah to Bethel, who in Paralipomenon is named Abdo; some believe that he was Gad. While the king stood by the altar to offer sacrifice, he cried out: “Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: A son shall be born to the house of David, named Josiah; upon you he shall burn the bones of your priests, dug up from their tombs.” And he said to the people: “I shall give you a sign that the Lord has spoken through me: behold, the altar shall be split apart, and the offering upon it shall be poured out” (3 Kings 13).

Then the king stretched out his hand, commanding that he be seized; and immediately his hand and arm withered. The altar too was split, and everything upon it was poured out. The frightened king [Col. 1373D] said to the prophet: “Pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me.” When he prayed, the king’s hand was restored to him.

When the king said to him, “Come and dine with me, and I shall give you gifts,” he answered: “I cannot. For thus the Lord commanded me: ‘You shall not eat bread, nor drink water, nor return by the road on which you came.’” Therefore, leaving Bethel, he was returning to Jerusalem by another road.

Now there was at Bethel a certain old prophet, lying in bed. When his sons told him what they had seen and heard, he said to them: “Saddle the donkey for me.” Mounting it, he went after the man of God and said to him: “Return with me and eat.” He answered: “I cannot, because the Lord has forbidden me.” But the other said: “I too am a prophet, as you are; and the Lord [Col. 1374A] said to me: ‘Bring him back with you, that he may eat.’” Thus he deceived him and brought him back.

As they sat at table, the word of the Lord came to the prophet who had brought him back, and he said in the Spirit: “Because you have not kept the commandment of the Lord, your corpse shall not be brought into the tomb of your fathers.” Note that the Holy Spirit spoke justly through an unjust man, so that the prophet received his punishment from the very mouth from which he had received his fault.

When the man of God departed after the meal, a lion killed him on the road. But the donkey stood beside him, and the lion guarded the corpse, touching neither the donkey nor it. When that old prophet heard this, he brought back the corpse and placed it in his own tomb, saying to his sons: “When I have died, place my bones beside his bones,” [Col. 1374B] so that my bones may be spared for his sake when the word of the Lord concerning the burning of bones upon the altar comes to pass.

But Jeroboam did not turn back from his wicked course. For that old prophet persuaded him that the man whom the Lord had killed had not been a true prophet; that his right hand had gone numb through the exertion of sacrificing and, when it had rested, had returned to its natural condition; and that the altar had broken because of the weight placed upon it.

## Chapter XXX. On the death of Abijah and Jeroboam

In those days Abijah, Jeroboam’s son, became ill; and the king said to his wife: “Change your appearance, lest you be recognized as my wife, and go to Shiloh to the prophet Ahijah, who formerly spoke to me concerning the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1375A] Addition 1. Ahijah saw in the Spirit the people trampling the yoke of oxen, and foretold that priests would be trampled by the people; he also foretold to Solomon that he would be overthrown by women, and he was buried beside the oak of Shiloh.], [Col. 1374C] for he will tell you what will happen to this boy” (3 Kings 14).

The woman went up to Ahijah, who could not see because of old age; but, forewarned by the Lord, he said: “Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? Go and tell Jeroboam: Thus says the Lord: ‘I raised you up from among the people; but you cast me behind your back and made for yourself foreign gods and molten images. Therefore I shall strike down from Jeroboam everyone who urinates against the wall, and the confined,’ that is, the imprisoned, ‘and the last in Israel’; that is, I shall destroy from his house even the most insignificant persons, who, because of their lowliness, are thought not worth noticing. ‘And I shall give their corpses to dogs and wild beasts. But you, return home; and as you enter, the child shall die.’”

He alone of Jeroboam’s house [Col. 1374D] would be brought to burial. The woman returned to Tirzah, and the boy died; and they buried him. The rest of Jeroboam’s acts are written in the book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. Jeroboam died after reigning twenty-two years.

Now Rehoboam reigned in Judah, which comprised the tribe of Judah and Benjamin. He was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-six years in Jerusalem. But Judah too—that people—sinned before the Lord and made for themselves altars, statues, and groves upon mountain heights. “And there were effeminate persons in the land of Judah”: that is, worshippers of Cybele, emasculated by nature or by act, as is read concerning the hierophants [Note: [Col. 1375B] Addition 2. From *hiera*, meaning “sacred things,” and *phanum*, meaning “temple”: as it were, “a sacred temple.”].

The Lord, offended, stirred up against Judah Shishak king of Egypt in the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign. [Col. 1375A] Entering Jerusalem, although previous agreements meant that Rehoboam could not resist him, he did not keep the treaty. For he had made an agreement with Rehoboam concerning the demolition of certain walls, which he violated. “He plundered the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the royal house; he also carried off the golden shields which King Solomon had made [Note: [Col. 1375B] Addition 3. The Hebrews say that for fifty-two years no bird flew over Jerusalem, and that the Jews almost despaired.], in place of which King Rehoboam made bronze shields.”

Rehoboam had eighteen wives and thirty concubines; twenty-eight sons and forty daughters were born to him. “The rest of Rehoboam’s acts are written in the book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.” The prophet Shemaiah wrote his earlier and later deeds. “And Rehoboam died and was buried in the city of David, and his son Abijah reigned in his place.”

[Col. 1375B] Incidental matters

In the days of Rehoboam, the seventh king of the Latins was Silvius Achis, or Silvius Aegyptius. Herodotus reports that Shishak, king of Egypt, subdued many peoples and captured some without battle. In mockery [Col. 1375C] of them, on the statues borne before him in triumph he carved women’s genitals, signifying that they had been emasculated. He also reports that the Ethiopians and Phoenicians learned circumcision from the Egyptians.

## Chapter XXXI. On Abijah, king of Judah

“Therefore, in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam’s reign, Abijah reigned over Judah. He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah, daughter of Tamar, daughter of Absalom. And he walked in all the sins of his father” (3 Kings 15).

There was a battle between Jeroboam and Abijah at a place called Mount of the Amorites, and Abijah gained an incalculable victory beyond expectation. “And Abijah died, and [Col. 1375D] they buried him in the city of David; and Asa his son reigned in his place. In the twentieth year of Jeroboam Asa reigned over Judah, and he reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name,” that is, his grandmother’s, “was Maacah.”

Note that Rehoboam and Jeroboam are said to have reigned concurrently for seventeen years; then Abijah reigned concurrently with Jeroboam for three years, and thus the twenty years of Jeroboam’s reign were completed. Therefore Asa did not begin to reign in Jeroboam’s twentieth year, as was stated, but rather in the twenty-first—an expression made by synecdoche. For Abijah is said to have reigned three years because he reigned two full years and part of a third; in the remaining part of that same third year his son Asa began to reign, namely in the twentieth year of Jeroboam’s reign. [Col. 1376A]

Such discrepancies frequently occur in what follows; some are resolved through synecdoche. Or they arise because sons sometimes reigned jointly with their fathers, as we shall say later. Those that cannot be resolved are attributed to the fault of copyists.

## Chapter XXXII. On Asa, and the kings of Israel Nadab, Baasha, and Elah

“Therefore Asa did what was right before the Lord, like David his father. He removed the effeminate persons from the land and the filth of idols; and he removed Maacah his mother, so that she should not be chief in the rites of Priapus. He overthrew her shrine and burned the shameful image in the torrent Kidron [Note: [Col. 1377B] Addition 1. The Hebrews say that Asa ground the idol into powder and secretly scattered it in the torrent Kidron; and that, in order for this to become public, fire proceeded from the water [Col. 1377C] by the Lord.]. He did not, however, remove the high places.

Now [Col. 1376B] Nadab, son of Jeroboam, reigned over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah (3 Kings 15). Here it is evident that Jeroboam died at the beginning of the twenty-second year of his reign; this year was Asa’s second regnal year. “And he reigned over Israel two years,” that is, one year and some part of another year is called a year by synecdoche, just as the Gospel says that Christ preached for three and a half years, where part of a half-year is called a half-year.

The reverse also often occurs: the entire total period is called by the name of one of its parts through synecdoche, as in: “When Noah was five hundred years old, he begot Shem” (Genesis 5), although Noah was five hundred and two years old. This double synecdoche occurs very frequently below. But let these observations suffice.

[Col. 1376C] Nadab walked in the ways of his father, by which he made Israel sin. While he was besieging Jebbethon, a city of the Philistines, Baasha plotted against him, killed him, and reigned in his place in the third year of Asa king of Judah. He struck down the entire house of Jeroboam, according to the word of Ahijah the Shilonite, and reigned at Tirzah for twenty-four years, though not completed. “And there was war between Asa and Baasha all their days.”

In the tenth year of his reign Asa struck Zerah king of the Ethiopians with a great blow, when he had invaded the land of Judah. As Asa returned from victory, the prophet Azariah met him and said that the victory had been granted him by God because he observed His laws. Asa then wrote throughout the whole province that all should carefully [Col. 1376D] observe the laws.

But Baasha king of Israel sinned before the Lord, walking in Jeroboam’s ways and beyond them [Note: [Col. 1377C] Addition 2. Note that this Baasha was not of Jeroboam’s family; for among the kings of Israel, a son did not always succeed his father, but only rarely. The kingdom of Judah, however, never departed from its lineage, because a son always succeeded his father.]. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani came to him, saying: “Thus says the Lord: ‘I raised you from the dust, but you walked in the ways of Jeroboam and caused my people to sin grievously; therefore I shall cut off your descendants and make your house like the house of Jeroboam.’”

Yet Baasha did not desist because of this, but went up against Judah and built Ramah forty stadia from Jerusalem. When Asa king of Judah saw himself hemmed in, he took gold and silver from the house of the Lord and the royal house and sent it by his servants to Ben-hadad king of Syria at Damascus, saying: “There was a treaty between my father and your father, and between me and you. I ask you to break the treaty [Col. 1377A] which you have with Baasha, that he may withdraw from me.”

Ben-hadad consented and sent an army against the cities of Israel. Hearing this, Baasha stopped building Ramah and returned to Tirzah. Then King Asa sent throughout all Judah, saying: “Let no one be excused.” They carried away the stones and timber of Ramah, and with these King Asa fortified Geba and Mizpah.

The prophet Jehu came to him—or, as some maintain, Hanani, Jehu’s father—rebuking him because, having abandoned the Lord, they had placed their hope in the king of Syria. The king put him in stocks; for this reason “in the time of his old age his feet became diseased. And he died and was buried in the city of David, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.”

Under Asa, the eighth king of the Latins was Silvius Capis. Yet while Asa was still alive, according to some, the prophet Jehu went down to rebuke Baasha king of Israel, and Baasha killed him. Baasha therefore died and was buried in Tirzah. But, as Josephus says, he was killed by Creon, his fellow-soldier. His son Elah reigned in his place at Tirzah in the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah. “And he reigned over Israel two years,” that is, a year and part of a year. While he reclined in the house of Arza, his steward, Zimri his servant, commander of half the cavalry, struck him down while drunk. He also struck down the entire house of Baasha, according to the word of the prophet Jehu.

## Chapter XXXIII. On Zimri and Omri

[Col. 1377C]

In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned in Tirzah for seven days. Now the army of Israel was besieging Jebbethon. When it heard that Zimri had killed the king, it made Omri—who was commander of the army in the camp—king for itself, in Asa’s twenty-seventh year. Omri therefore went up, and [Col. 1377D] all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah (3 Kings 16).

But Zimri, afraid, fled into the royal house and set it on fire over himself. “Then the people of Israel were divided. One half followed Tibni, and the other half Omri.” This struggle lasted three years and more. Yet Omri, as though he were already reigning, prevailed; Tibni was killed in the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, and Omri reigned fully over Israel, reigning twelve years.

From his first election at Tirzah he reigned six years. He bought from Shemer, for two talents of silver, a part of the mountain on which stood the city of Mareon; he rebuilt it and named it Samareon, as it were from Shemer and Mareon, which in Greek is called Samaria. There he established the seat of the kingdom, which had previously [Col. 1378A] been at Tirzah. “Omri did evil before the Lord beyond all who had been before him; and he died and was buried in Samaria [Note: [Col. 1378A] Addition 1. Samaria is the name both of a city and of a region, as is evident here.].”

His son Ahab would reign in his place in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah. Here perhaps the copyists’ error is evident. For Omri, Ahab’s father, reigned twelve years, as stated; he began to reign in the thirty-first year of Asa, who reigned forty-one years. Thus Asa died while Omri was still alive. But Josephus correctly says that Ahab began to reign when Jehoshaphat, Asa’s son, was already reigning. Nevertheless, we shall give the customary resolution of this point at the end of the kings.

## Chapter XXXIV. On Ahab, Jezebel, and the prophet Elijah

[Col. 1378B]

“And Ahab reigned over Israel twenty-two years” (3 Kings 16). Josephus, however, says twenty years and two months. “It was not enough for Ahab to walk in Jeroboam’s ways: he introduced the idols of the nations into Israel, married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, built a shrine and altar to Baal in Samaria, and worshipped him.

“In his days Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho.” When he laid its foundations, his firstborn son Abiram died; when he fortified its gates, his youngest son Segub died, according to Joshua’s curse.

“And the Lord sent Elijah the Tishbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead, to Ahab” (3 [Col. 1378C] Kings 17). He said to the king: “As the Lord God of Israel lives, in whose presence I stand, if in these years there shall be dew or rain except according to the words of my mouth.” This is aposiopesis; or *if* is used for *not*. Ahab sought Elijah’s life.

At the Lord’s command Elijah fled and hid by the brook Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan. “Ravens brought him bread and meat morning and evening, and he drank from the brook. But after some days the brook dried up, for it had not rained upon the land. And the Lord said to Elijah: ‘Go to Zarephath of the Sidonians; for there I have commanded a widow woman to feed you.’”

Zarephath was a small city between Tyre and Sidon. A forest was also visible beside the city of Zarephath. When Elijah came to the city gate, a widow woman appeared, gathering sticks. After he asked her for a cup of water, he also asked her to bring him a morsel of bread. She answered that she had only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil with which to moisten it; she would make bread from it and eat it with her son, but afterwards, when the food failed, they would waste away.

Elijah said to her: “Do not fear. First make me a hearth-baked cake; afterwards you shall make one for yourself and your son. For thus says the Lord: ‘The jar of flour shall not fail, nor shall the cruse of oil diminish, until it rains upon the earth.’” Elijah remained with the widow for some time.

After this the woman’s son died. She said to Elijah: “Why have you come in to me, man of God? That my sins might be remembered”—that is, might appear more plainly by contrast with your righteousness—[Col. 1379A] “and therefore my son be killed?” Elijah placed the boy on his bed in the upper chamber, stretched himself over him three times, and cried to the Lord; and the boy came back to life. Receiving him, the woman said: “Now I know that you are a man of God.” The Hebrews maintain that this boy was the prophet Jonah.

## Chapter XXXV. On the priests of Baal whom Elijah killed

After the third year of drought and famine the Lord said to Elijah: “Go, show yourself to Ahab, that I may give rain upon the earth” (3 Kings 18). There was a severe famine in Samaria, also mentioned by [Col. 1379B] Menander in his *Deeds of the Sidonians*.

Ahab had as steward of his household Obadiah. When Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah hid one hundred prophets in two caves, fifty in each, and fed them with bread and water. For this reason he was afterwards granted the spirit of prophecy. Ahab said to him: “Let us go down into the valleys and seek fodder for the horses and mules.” They divided the regions between themselves.

Elijah met Obadiah on the road and said: “Go tell your master: Elijah is here.” But he said: “What sin have I committed? When I tell Ahab, ‘Elijah is here,’ the Spirit of the Lord will carry you to a place I do not know; and Ahab, not finding you, will kill me. Yet your servant has feared the Lord from his youth.” Elijah said: “As the Lord lives, today I shall appear to [Col. 1379C] Ahab.”

Ahab, summoned by Obadiah, met Elijah and said: “Are you the man who troubles Israel?” He answered: “It is not I who have troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house, because you have forsaken the Lord and followed Baal. But gather to me all Israel on Mount Carmel, along with the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of the groves who eat at Jezebel’s table.”

The people and prophets assembled on Mount Carmel. Elijah said to the people: “How long do you limp between two sides? If the Lord God of your fathers is God, follow him; but if Baal, follow him.” Since the people did not answer, Elijah continued: “I alone remain here a prophet of the Lord, while Baal’s prophets are many. Let two bulls be given to us. Let them choose one bull, cut it in pieces, and place the pieces upon wood without putting fire beneath it; and I shall do likewise with the other bull. They shall call upon their gods, and I upon my God; and the one who answers by giving fire from heaven, he shall be God.”

Elijah’s proposal pleased the people. When Baal’s priests had done as he directed, “they called upon Baal from morning until noon; they leapt about the altar which they had made and cut themselves, according to their custom, with little lances, until they were drenched in blood.” Demons take particular delight in an offering of human blood [Note: [Col. 1380C] Addition 1. Isidore says, chapter 58, that demons love human blood: therefore, whenever necromancy is performed, blood is mixed with water so that they may be provoked more easily by the colour of blood.].

“Elijah mocked them, saying: ‘Raise your cry! Perhaps your god is asleep, or is speaking with someone else, or is in an inn.’” Elijah then said to the people: “Come near.” In the presence of [Col. 1380A] the people, he repaired the altar of the Lord that had been destroyed—that is, he destroyed their altar and cleared the place in order to make a new altar there before the Lord. “He took twelve stones, according to the number of Israel’s tribes, and built from them an altar in the name of the Lord God of Israel. He made a water-channel around the altar, of two measures. He laid the wood on it and the pieces of the bull, commanded water to be brought”—perhaps from the nearby sea—“and poured it over the burnt offering and the wood.

“The water was poured out three times, until the channel was filled, lest anyone suppose that by magical art he had brought up fire from the depths of the earth. Elijah cried to the Lord in the people’s hearing: ‘Lord God of our fathers, hear me today, that this people may learn that you are the Lord God.’ Fire descended from [Col. 1380B] heaven and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, the dust, and, lapping it up, the water in the channel. The people worshipped and said: ‘The Lord himself is God.’”

At Elijah’s command they seized all the prophets of Baal and brought them to the brook Kishon, “and Elijah killed them there. And he said to Ahab: ‘Go up and eat before the rain comes down.’”

While Ahab ate, Elijah ascended to the summit of Carmel. Bowed down to the earth with his head between his knees, he prayed, and said to his servant: “Look toward the sea, to see whether a cloud is rising.” For the sky was perfectly clear. The servant said: “There is nothing.” He sent him seven times. But on the seventh occasion a small cloud was rising from the sea, growing to the size of a man. Elijah said to Ahab: “Go down quickly to Jezreel, lest the [Col. 1380C] rain overtake you.”

And behold, the heavens became dark, with clouds and wind, and there was heavy rain. Ahab hurried to Jezreel, while the hand of the Lord came upon Elijah, and he ran before Ahab until he entered the city.

When Jezebel heard what Elijah had done to her prophets, she angrily sent messengers to Elijah, saying: “May the gods do these things to me, and add these things [Note: [Col. 1380D] Addition 2. As in greetings, a word is omitted because of excessive feeling, so that one may understand whatever is wished; thus in expressions of this sort a demonstrative pronoun is used, so that the speaker may invoke upon herself whatever evil she pleases if this does not happen.], unless tomorrow at this hour I make your life like the life of one of them” (3 Kings 19).

## Chapter XXXVI. On Elijah’s flight and Elisha’s calling

[Col. 1380D]

“Elijah, afraid, fled to Beersheba and left his servant there”—Jonah, according to tradition—“and entered the wilderness alone, a day’s journey. Sitting beneath a juniper tree, he prayed to die there,” saying that he was not better—that is, not more worthy of life—than his fathers, so that, after they had perished, he should desire to live. “Then, throwing himself down, he fell asleep. The angel of the Lord touched him and said: ‘Arise, eat.’ And behold, at his head [Col. 1381A] was a hearth-baked cake and a vessel of water. He ate and drank and fell asleep again. The angel awakened him a second time, saying: ‘Arise, eat, for a great journey remains for you’” (3 Kings 19).

Josephus, however, says that it was not an angel who awakened him, but someone. “Elijah ate and walked in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights, as far as Horeb, the mountain of God,” where the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush. Elijah remained there in a cave.

The Lord said to him: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” He replied: “I have been zealous against Israel for you. For they have destroyed your altars, killed your prophets, and I alone remain; they seek my life, and I have fled.” The Lord said to him: “Go out, and the Lord will pass before you.”

But first three things visibly [Col. 1381B] passed by, in none of which the Lord passed. First there came a strong wind, shattering rocks; but the Lord was not in the wind. Second came an earthquake; but the Lord was not in it. Third came fire; but the Lord was not in the fire. Fourth came the whisper of a gentle breeze, and the Lord was with it.

Elijah covered his face with his cloak and stood at the entrance of the cave. The Lord, passing by, said to him: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” He answered him as above. The Lord said to him: “Return through the wilderness and go to Damascus”; and, in vengeance on my behalf, “anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu son of Nansi king over Israel, and Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel as prophet in your place [Note: [Col. 1381D] Addition 1. This accords with an oracle. For when Elisha was born in Gilgal, the image of the golden calves bellowed. On hearing this in Jerusalem, a priest said: ‘A prophet has been born in Israel who will destroy their carved images, even their molten ones.’]. These three will kill [Col. 1381C] the idolaters of Israel: some Hazael, others Jehu, others Elisha. And I shall leave for myself in Israel seven thousand men whose knees have not bent to Baal, nor have they kissed his hands.”

Note that Elijah anointed Hazael only in the sense that he foretold through Elisha that he would become king. Neither Elijah nor Elisha anointed Jehu; rather, one of the prophets sent by Elisha did so. Nor did Elijah anoint Elisha except by placing his cloak over him. For under the Law only king and priest were anointed.

Therefore Elijah found twelve men ploughing with twelve yokes of oxen, one of whom was Elisha. “Elijah cast his cloak over him,” and Elisha immediately prophesied, according to Josephus. Running after Elijah, he said: “I beg you, let me kiss my father and mother, and I shall follow [Col. 1381D] you.” He returned, slaughtered a pair of oxen, cooked it with the wood of the plough, gave food to his fellow labourers, then rose and followed Elijah, ministering to him.

## Chapter XXXVII. On the first siege of Samaria, and subsequent events

“Ben-hadad king of Syria was besieging Samaria, with thirty-two kings accompanying him. He sent to Ahab in Samaria, saying: ‘If you want me to withdraw from you, tomorrow at this same hour I shall send my servants, and they shall take everything [Col. 1382A] pleasing to them from your house and from the houses of your servants, including wives and children’” (3 Kings 20).

Ahab took counsel with the elders, who said: “Do not yield to him.” Ahab replied to Ben-hadad’s messengers: “Tell my lord: Everything that you commanded in your message I can do; but this thing I cannot do”—namely, concerning wives and children.

Ben-hadad angrily sent back word: “May the gods do these things to me, and add these things, if the dust of Samaria will suffice for the handfuls of all my people who follow me.” Samaria had ground within it almost level with the walls; the meaning is this: I have such a multitude with me that, if each person brought together but one stone, log, or turf, they would build an embankment equal to Samaria’s walls and [Col. 1382B] to the ground within, and would fight against you from it.

The king of Israel answered: “Tell him: ‘Let not one who is girded boast as one ungirded.’” The meaning is: You are still girded with arms, and the matter is undecided. Therefore do not boast as though you were already victorious and had laid aside your weapons. That is, a combatant cannot boast as a victor can; or, according to another reading: “Let not the girded boast equally with the ungirded.” That is: Before victory, the one equipped with a multitude cannot boast, nor the one ungirded—that is, lacking a multitude—because a few often conquer many.

Now Ben-hadad was drinking with his kings in tents and said to his servants: “Surround the city.” As they attacked it, Ahab became greatly afraid. But behold, one prophet—Micaiah, as some report—encouraged him, saying: “Thus says the Lord: ‘Today I shall give all this multitude into your hand, that you may know that I am the Lord.’” Ahab said: “By whom?” He answered: “By the foot-soldiers of the provincial commanders.” Ahab said: “Who shall be their leader?” He answered: “You.”

Ahab found two hundred and thirty-two sons of the commanders, and went out with them. When Ben-hadad was told that they had come out from Samaria, he sent men to meet them, saying: “Whether they have come for peace or for war, seize them alive.” But the sons of the commanders struck down each man the man who came against him. The Syrian army fled, and Israel went out and struck the horses, chariots, and Syria with a great blow.

Then [Col. 1382D] the prophet came to Ahab, saying: “The Lord has strengthened you; consider what you will do. Next year the king of Syria will come up against you.” That is: You must have the Lord favourable to you. Then Ben-hadad’s servants said to him: “Their gods are gods of the mountains, and we fought them in the mountains; therefore they defeated us. Let us fight in the plains, where their gods can do nothing, and we shall overcome them. But do this: remove the kings from the army, because they are ineffective; appoint commanders in their place; and restore the number of fighting men which you had before.”

## Chapter XXXVIII. On Ahab’s victory

Accordingly, after a year Ben-hadad came with an army to Aphek, which is in the plains (3 Kings 20). [Col. 1383A] “The children of Israel were encamped opposite them like two small flocks of goats, while the Syrians filled the land.” A man of God said to Ahab: “Because the Syrians have said, ‘The Lord is God of the mountains and not of the valleys,’ I shall give them into your hand.”

They drew up their battle lines opposite one another for seven days. On the seventh day, one hundred thousand Syrian infantry were struck down; the rest fled to Aphek, and a wall fell upon those who remained. Ben-hadad fled into the city and hid in a chamber within a chamber.

His servants feared that Ahab would come upon them and spare no one. Knowing that the kings of Israel were merciful, they girded their loins with sackcloth, put ropes upon their heads, and came to meet Ahab, saying: “Your servant Ben-hadad says: [Col. 1383B] ‘May my life, I pray, be spared.’” That is: Whatever great ransom you impose, I shall accept it for my life.

Ahab answered: “If he is still alive, he is my brother,” that is, I shall make a treaty with him. “Seizing upon the word from his mouth as an omen, they hurriedly brought Ben-hadad to him.” Ahab raised him into his chariot with him.

Ben-hadad said to Ahab: “The cities which my father took from your father I shall restore to you. Make streets for yourself in Damascus”—that is, a market for merchandise—“as my father did in Samaria.” When they had made a treaty, they returned home.

Then Micaiah said in the Spirit to his companion: “Strike me.” But he refused. He said to him: “Because you did not obey the voice of the Lord, when you depart from me a lion will strike you.” This happened. Finding another [Col. 1383C] man, he said to him: “Strike me” on the head. The man wounded him.

Then the prophet, changing his appearance with sprinkled dust and blood, cried to the king on the road: “When we were in battle, a man brought his captive to me, saying: ‘Guard this man; if he escapes, your life shall be for his life,’ that is, you shall be my servant in his place, ‘or you shall weigh out a talent of silver for me.’ But while I was turning this way and that, suddenly he was gone.”

The king said: “Your judgment is your own,” which you yourself have decreed: you must do one or the other for him. Then, his face washed, the prophet was recognized by the king and said: “Thus says the Lord: ‘Because you let go a blasphemous man worthy of death, your life shall be for his life,’” [Col. 1383D] that is, he himself will kill you.

The king, angry with the prophet, ordered him kept under guard, and came to Samaria.

## Chapter XXXIX. On Naboth’s vineyard
Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard beside the king’s palace (III Kings 21). The king said to him: “Give me your vineyard, that I may make it into a vegetable garden; and I will give you a better vineyard for it, or its price.” He replied: “May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should not give you the inheritance of my fathers.” As though he said: I cannot; the inheritance was left me by my fathers, that I might leave it to my descendants.

The king, grieved, threw himself upon his bed and would not eat. Jezebel encouraged him, saying: “Be of good courage [Col. 1384A]; I will give you Naboth’s vineyard.” Secretly she wrote letters in Ahab’s name, sealed with his ring, and sent them to the judges of Jezreel, ordering them to convene an assembly and proclaim a fast, as though they were about to hold God’s judgment; and to produce witnesses against Naboth who should say: “Naboth has blessed God and the king”—that is, cursed them, according to the Hebrew idiom—and, having condemned him as guilty of treason, to stone him.

So it was done, and Naboth was stoned outside the city of Jezreel. When Ahab learned of Naboth’s death, he went down to the vineyard in order to possess it. Elijah the Tishbite met him and said: Thus says the Lord: “You have killed, and moreover taken possession.” The Hebrew has: “You have killed, and after this you shall inherit.”—“In the place where the dogs licked Naboth’s blood [Col. 1384B], they shall lick your blood also,” that is, in the same region. This must not be understood as the identical spot in the strict sense.

He replied: “Have you found me, my enemy?” that is, Why are you hostile to me? Elijah said: “Because you have sold yourself to the devil,” to do evil in the sight of the Lord; therefore the Lord will cut off your posterity and make your house like the house of Jeroboam and Baasha. And the Lord also says of Jezebel: “Dogs shall eat Jezebel in the field of Jezreel.”

Ahab, therefore, greatly afraid, tore his garment, covered himself with sackcloth, slept in sackcloth, and walked with bowed head. The Lord said to Elijah: “Because Ahab has humbled himself before me, I shall not bring this evil in his days, but in the days of his son.” Perhaps his sin was forgiven because of his present [Col. 1384C] righteousness.

“Thus three years passed without war between Syria and Israel (III Kings 22),” because of the treaty they had made. Meanwhile Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, took for his son Joram Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, as wife; and through this relationship the king of Judah and the king of Israel were allied.

Then Jehoshaphat went down to visit the king of Israel. While he was present, Ahab said to his servants: “Ramoth, which is in Gilead, is ours; why do we neglect to take it from the hand of the king of Syria?” And he said to Jehoshaphat: “Will you come with me to fight at Ramoth-gilead?” He replied: “As I am, so are you; my people are your people. But let us seek today, I pray you, the word of the Lord.”

About four hundred prophets of Baal were summoned [Col. 1384D]. The king said to them: “Shall I go to Ramoth-gilead to fight, or shall I remain?” They said: “Go up, and the Lord will give it into the king’s hand.” Jehoshaphat said: “Is there no prophet of the Lord here?” Ahab replied: “One remains, Micaiah son of Imlah, but I hate him, because he does not prophesy good to me.” He supposed that the rest had been killed by Jezebel.

At Jehoshaphat’s request Micaiah was summoned. The messenger urged him to say favorable things to the king, as the others did. He replied: “As the Lord lives, whatever the Lord says to me, that I shall speak.” Now among the false prophets was Zedekiah, bearing iron horns and saying to Ahab: “Thus says the Lord: With these you shall thresh Syria until you destroy it”; that is, I give you this sign that you shall thresh Syria.

Then Ahab asked Micaiah [Col. 1385A] the same question he had asked the others. He replied: “Go up, and the Lord will deliver them into the king’s hand”; yet he did not say whom, or into whose kingly hand. Ahab said to him: “I adjure you to speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the Lord.” Then Micaiah said: “I saw Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd. And the Lord said to me: These have no master; let them return.”

Ahab understood that he was foretelling his death and said to Jehoshaphat: “You see that he does not prophesy good to me.” Micaiah then added: “I saw the Lord seated, with angels standing by him—the good on the right, the evil on the left—and he said: Who will deceive Ahab, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” For this his merits required. One on the left said: “I will be a lying spirit in the mouth [Col. 1385B] of his prophets.” The Lord said to him: “You shall deceive him and prevail.”

Then Zedekiah struck Micaiah on the cheek and said: “Has the Spirit of the Lord left me and spoken to you?” Micaiah said to him: “You will see when you hide yourself in an inner room, as one caught in a lie.” Zedekiah saw that the king was wavering and secretly encouraged him: “If this man were a prophet, my hand would have withered, as Jeroboam’s hand did. Moreover, he has spoken against Elijah, who foretold that you would die where Naboth died.”

Then the king ordered Micaiah to be imprisoned until his own return.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning Jehoshaphat and the death of Ahab and Ahaziah

The two kings therefore went up with the army to Ramoth-gilead, and Jehoshaphat was in royal dress [Col. 1385C] (III Kings 22). Ahab, by contrast, wore military clothing, either so that he might not be recognized by the Syrians; and the king of Syria had ordered his commanders to disregard the others and seek the blood of Ahab alone.

“Accordingly, when they made an attack, they fought against Jehoshaphat. But when he cried out, summoning his servants, the Syrians realized that he was not Ahab and withdrew from him. Yet one man, aiming an arrow at random, struck Ahab between the lung and the stomach; and blood flowed into his bosom,” that is, into the interior of the chariot. The army was recalled from battle by heralds.

Ahab died, was carried to Samaria, and was buried there beside the ivory house which he had built. While women washed the chariot and its reins in the pool of Samaria, dogs licked [Col. 1386A] his blood, according to Elijah’s word. “And his son Ahaziah reigned in his place.”

As Jehoshaphat returned, Jehu son of Hanani met him and rebuked him because he had aided an ungodly man. Jehoshaphat, however, reigned in Jerusalem. “He was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty years. He began to reign in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.” Here too there arises a question concerning chronological comparisons, all of which we shall discuss separately after the Book of Kings.

“And Jehoshaphat walked in the ways of Asa his father.” In the third year of his reign he ordered the princes and priests of his kingdom to travel through every city and teach the people the law of Moses. The Ammonites, Moabites, and Arabs invaded Judah near En-gedi. As Jehoshaphat prayed [Col. 1386B] in the Temple, as is read in Chronicles, the prophet Jahaziel son of Zechariah strengthened him, saying: “O Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear [Note: [Col. 1386C] Addition 1. Note that “Judea” sometimes denotes the whole land of the Jews, as in: “The God of Judea, unknown” (Acts 17), and: “God is known in Judea” (Psalm 75). At other times “Judea” means only the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, as when it says that Rehoboam reigned over Judah and Jeroboam over Israel (III Kings 14). At other times the tribe of Judah alone is called Judea, as where it says: “Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear.”], tomorrow go out, and the Lord will be with you” (II Chronicles 20).

Going out, he struck and routed the enemies. When Israel plundered the enemy camp for three days, he called that place the Valley of Blessing; afterward his heart was upright with the Lord. He also removed the remaining effeminate persons from the land; nevertheless, he did not remove the high places, and Edom was still tributary to the king of Judah.

Jehoshaphat also sent fleets to Ophir for gold, but they were wrecked at Ezion-geber. Eliezer the prophet, son of Dodam, had foretold this wreck, because Jehoshaphat had made an alliance with Ahaziah. “Jehoshaphat died [Col. 1386C], was buried in the city of David, and his son Joram reigned in his place.”

### Incidental notice

Under Jehoshaphat, the ninth king of the Latins was Silvius Carptemus; the tenth, Silvius Tiberius, from whom the river Tiber—previously called Albula—received its name; the eleventh, Silvius Agrippa.

# HISTORY OF THE FOURTH BOOK OF KINGS

[Col. 1385]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning Ahaziah, king of Israel

[Col. 1385D]

Ahaziah, son of Ahab, began to reign in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat, reigned two years, and walked in the ways of his father and mother. “Moab rebelled against Israel,” that is, it withdrew from paying him tribute (IV Kings 1).

Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper room, became ill, and sent [Col. 1386D] messengers to consult Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, concerning his illness. Josephus says that he sent to the god of Ekron, the Fly [Note: [Col. 1387B] Addition 1. Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, is called “the fly.”]. The Lord sent Elijah to meet the messengers. He said to them: “Is there no God in Israel, that you go to the god of Ekron? Therefore Ahaziah shall not rise, but shall die.”

When the messengers returned to the king and said that they had returned because of such a prohibition, he asked them about the appearance of the man who had appeared to them. They said: “He is a hairy man, girded with a leather belt.” He said: “It is Elijah.”

The king sent a captain of fifty with his fifty armed men, to summon Elijah or drag him away against his will. The captain of fifty said to Elijah, sitting on the top of a mountain: “Man of God, the king orders you to come down.” He replied: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and yours.” And so it happened.

The king also sent another captain of fifty with his men, who spoke the same things and suffered the same things. He then dispatched a third captain of fifty, believed to have been Obadiah. Bending his knees before Elijah, he said: “I beg you, have mercy on my life and on the lives of my servants.” The angel said to Elijah: [Col. 1387B] “Go down with him; do not fear.” He went down to the king and said: “Because you sent to Baal-zebub, as though there were no God in Israel, you shall die.”

Ahaziah died, and his brother Joram reigned in his place, in the second year of Joram son of Jehoshaphat. At that time the king of Judah and the king of Israel bore the same name and were related.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Elijah’s assumption

“It came to pass, when the Lord wished to take Elijah up into heaven by a whirlwind, that Elijah and Elisha came to Gilgal. Elijah said to Elisha: ‘Remain here, for the Lord has sent me to Bethel.’ He replied: ‘As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I shall not leave you’” (IV Kings 2). For he knew in the Spirit that Elijah was to be taken up.

The sons of the prophets who were at Bethel met them [Col. 1387C] and secretly said to Elisha: “Do you know that today your master will be taken from you?” He replied: “I know; be silent.” Elijah said: “Remain here.” But he refused.

When he came to Jericho, the sons of the prophets there said to Elisha the same thing as those mentioned before. Elijah wanted him to remain there, but he would not. When both came to the Jordan and fifty of the sons of the prophets watched from afar, Elijah wrapped up his cloak and struck the waters; they divided, and they crossed on dry ground.

After they crossed, Elijah said to him: “Ask what you wish, and I shall do it for you before I am taken from you.” He replied: “I beg that your spirit may be double in me.” He answered: [Col. 1387D] “You ask a difficult thing; nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken from you, it shall be so; otherwise it shall not be.”

Elijah had a double spirit, that is, directed toward two things: prophecy and miracles. Elisha also had the spirit for the same two things; thus the disciple did not ask to be above the master. Some, however, distinguish the phrase thus: “May your spirit be double in me,” that is, may it be doubled in me. They relate that this was fulfilled in this way: Elisha raised a dead person while living, and, though dead, raised a dead person too; Elijah did not do this.

“As they went on, behold, a fiery chariot and fiery horses divided the two of them; and Elijah went up, carried in a whirlwind into heaven.” It is read that Sabacha, Elijah’s father, while Elijah was not yet born, saw in a dream white-clad men saluting him. When he reported this in Jerusalem, he received the answer: “This boy shall judge Israel by sword and fire.”

Elisha watched and cried: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” that is, the sustainer and ruler of the people. Elijah threw down his cloak to him. Then Elisha tore his own garments, either in grief or by casting off his own clothing in order thereafter to use Elijah’s garment.

“Returning to the Jordan, he struck the waters with Elijah’s cloak; they did not divide, and he said: ‘Where is the God of Elijah even now?’ He struck again, and they divided. He crossed over. When the sons of the prophets saw this, they said: ‘The spirit of Elijah has rested upon Elisha.’ Coming to meet him, they bowed down to him.”

Although he resisted, they sent fifty men to seek Elijah, in case the Lord had perhaps thrown him upon one of the mountains or into one of the valleys. After searching for three [Col. 1388B] days and not finding him, they returned.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning Elisha’s salt

“Then the men of Jericho said to Elisha: ‘This land is excellent, but the water of the spring makes the land barren’” (IV Kings 2). Taking a new earthen vessel, he put salt in it; then he went out to the spring and cast the salt into it. After praying, he said: “Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters; there shall no longer be death or barrenness in them.” Perhaps the water made those who drank it sick, as well as causing barrenness. “And the waters were healed to this day.”

As he went up to Bethel, forty-two boys mocked him, saying: “Go up, baldhead!” “And he cursed them in the name of the Lord,” that is, through the Lord’s name or by invoking the Lord’s name. “Then two bears came out of [Col. 1388C] the wood and devoured them.” After passing through Mount Carmel, he returned to Samaria and lived there.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the three kings who besieged the king of Moab

“Joram son of Ahab began to reign in Samaria in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat and reigned twelve years (IV Kings 3). He removed the idols of the nations which his father had introduced; nevertheless, he did not depart from the worship of Jeroboam’s calves. When Micaiah reproved him, he killed Micaiah by throwing him over a precipice, as Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, says. Micaiah was buried in Moresheth, alone beside the tomb of Senachim. Another Micaiah, likewise a Moreshethite, was the sixth of the Twelve Prophets.

Now the king [Col. 1388D] of Moab paid tribute to the king of Israel: one hundred thousand lambs and an equal number of rams with their fleeces. But when Ahab died, he withdrew from tribute. Therefore Joram king of Israel went up against him in battle, taking Jehoshaphat king of Judah with him; and Jehoshaphat brought the king of Edom as well.

After they had traveled seven days through the wilderness of Edom, they had no water. Jehoshaphat said: “Is there a prophet of the Lord here?” Someone replied: “Elisha is here, who poured water over Elijah’s hands.” The three kings stood before Elisha. He said to the king of Israel: “What have I to do with you?” that is, Since you are an idolater, why do you come to the prophet of the Lord? Nevertheless, for Jehoshaphat’s sake, I shall look upon you.

He said: “Bring me a minstrel,” that is, one who plays music. As the minstrel played, [Col. 1389A] his spirit was stirred by the harmony, the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he said: “Make ditches and pits in the bed of this dry torrent,” so that they may hold the abundance of water which is coming. For the Lord will give you water in abundance without wind or rain. “Moreover, the Lord will deliver Moab into your hands. You shall strike their chosen cities, cut down their fruit-bearing trees, stop up their springs, and cover their fine fields with stones.”

“It came to pass in the morning, at the hour of sacrifice, that waters rushed through the bed of the torrent.” For, as Josephus says, it had rained heavily for three days in the upper parts of Edom. The Moabites stood at the borders of their land to prevent the enemy from entering. When in the morning they saw, opposite them, the muddy waters of the torrent reflecting the sun, they supposed [Col. 1389B] that they were stained with blood and said: “Let us rise for the spoil; the enemy have slain one another.”

As they rushed in headlong, Israel struck them, and they fled. Israel devastated Moab and did the four things which Elisha had foretold. They surrounded the city where the royal seat was, and it was largely battered by slingers. Despairing, the king of Moab took seven hundred chosen men with him, intending to break through the section of the army where the king of Edom was and escape. But the enemy drove him back into the city. Forced by necessity, he offered upon the wall before the enemy his son who was to reign after him as a burnt offering, so that God might deliver him. Seeing this act of desperation, the kings withdrew from him out of human compassion.

Jehoshaphat returned to [Col. 1389C] Jerusalem, and the prophet Jehu son of Hanani met him and blamed him because he had given support to an idolatrous man.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the abundance of oil

It happened that a certain woman of the wives of the prophets—namely, the wife of Obadiah—cried to Elisha: “My husband is dead, and he was burdened by debt because of the support of the prophets. Behold, the creditor is coming to take my two sons to serve him.” Elisha replied: “What do you have in your house?” She said: “I have nothing except a little oil with which I anoint myself.” He said: “Borrow empty vessels, not a few; then, having shut the door with your sons, pour from it into all the vessels.”

As the woman poured, [Col. 1389D] the oil increased; when the vessels were filled, it stopped—that is, it ceased to increase. When Elisha learned this, he said to her: “Go, sell it and pay the creditor; you and your sons shall live on what remains.”

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the restoration of the Shunammite’s son

It happened that Elisha passed through the city of Shunem. There was there a great woman—not so much in bodily size as in wisdom—who, recognizing him as a man of God, prevailed upon him to eat bread (IV Kings 3). As Elisha frequently turned aside to her house, the woman persuaded her husband to make a small upper room for him and place in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand.

Elisha returned and rested there. He said to Gehazi: “Call this Shunammite woman and speak to her: What do you wish my lord to do for you? [Col. 1390A] He will speak for you to the king or to the commander of the army.” She replied: “I dwell among my own people,” as though to say: I am surrounded by relatives, and no one troubles me.

When Elisha asked what she wanted, Gehazi said to him: “She has no son, and her husband is old.” Then Elisha said to her: “At this season, at this very hour, if life remains with you, you shall have a son in your womb.” The Hebrew has: “At this season, when there is still a time of life for you,” understood: you shall have, and so forth. She replied: “Do not lie to your servant, man of God.” Yet the woman conceived and bore a son, according to Elisha’s word.

When the boy had grown, he went out to his father among the reapers and became ill. After crying twice, “My head hurts,” his father sent him back to his mother; “and he died.” His mother laid him [Col. 1390B] on the bed of the man of God, shut the door, called her husband, and said: “I shall run to the man of God and return.” He replied: “Today is neither a new moon nor a Sabbath; why will you go?” For on those days prophets and teachers were customarily visited and heard.

Taking one of the servants with her and riding upon an ass, the woman came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When he saw her, he said to Gehazi: “Behold that Shunammite woman. Run to meet her and say: Is all well with you, your husband, and your son?” She replied: “Well.” Note that Elisha always called his hostess “the Shunammite.” He had not become so familiar with her as to know even her personal name.

The woman threw herself down and seized Elisha’s feet. Elisha said to Gehazi, who wanted to remove her: “Leave her alone. Her soul [Col. 1390C] is bitter, and the Lord has hidden it from me.” The woman said: “Did I ask you for a son?” As though she said: Though I did not ask for one, you gave me a son to my ruin. “Did I not say to you: Do not deceive me?” She calls it deception for a son to be given by the Lord and taken away so quickly.

Elisha said to Gehazi: “Take my staff and go. Do not delay, whether by greeting anyone or answering one who greets you; put my staff upon the boy’s face.” When he had left, the woman said to Elisha: “As the Lord lives, I shall not leave you.” He followed her. Gehazi returned to meet him, saying: “The boy has not risen.”

Elisha entered, lay upon the boy, and, drawing himself close, fitted his limbs to the boy’s limbs. When he had prayed, [Col. 1390D] the boy’s flesh grew warm; the boy yawned and opened his eyes. Elisha restored him alive to his mother and returned to Gilgal.

Elisha often visited this place, both because of its religious significance and because he had been born there. At his birth such a prodigy occurred there that an image of one of the golden calves gave a shrill bellow. When this was heard in Jerusalem, a priest, by divine prompting, said: “A prophet has been born in Israel who will destroy their carved images and molten images.”

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning colocynths and the abundance of loaves

“Now there was famine in the land, and ten sons of the prophets had come to Elisha. He said to one of the servants: ‘Cook a stew for the sons of the prophets.’ Going out to gather wild herbs, he found what looked like a wild vine [Col. 1391A], gathered colocynths from it without knowing what it was, and cut them into the stew-pot” (IV Kings 4).

These are wild gourds, very bitter and smaller than those growing in gardens; or, as some say, it is a plant spreading like a vine along hedges, with a small, purple, round fruit when ripe. When those reclining at table tasted this cooked food, they cried: “Death is in the pot, man of God!” that is, bitterness as though in death, or deadly bitterness. He brought flour and put it into the pot, and the food became sweetened.

A certain man brought the man of God loaves of first fruits: twenty barley loaves and fresh grain in a bag, that is, rubbed grain. This must not be understood of the first-fruit loaves offered at Pentecost, nor of the gruel offered at Passover. Rather, [Col. 1391B] because there was famine in the land, this man had quickly made bread from wheat still fresh; Elisha ordered it set before the people.

Some say it was for one hundred men, because the servant said: “How much is this, that I should set it before one hundred men?” But it should be understood: that I should set it before even one hundred men, much less before the people. Or perhaps he set only two first-fruit loaves before a hundred men, saying: “Thus says the Lord: They shall eat, and there shall be left over.” And so it happened miraculously, according to the word of the Lord.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Naaman

“Naaman was commander of the army of the king of Syria, a rich and distinguished man, but leprous. Raiders from Syria had taken captive an Israelite girl, who was in the service of Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress [Col. 1391C]: ‘Would that my master were with the prophet in Samaria; he would cure him.’ Naaman took much silver and gold, and ten changes of clothing” (IV Kings 5), that is, ten pairs, or new garments, so called because they replace old clothes.

“He also took with him letters from the king of Syria to the king of Israel, in these words: ‘Know that I have sent Naaman to you, that you may cure him of leprosy.’” Hearing this blasphemy, the king of Israel tore his garments and said: “Am I God, that I should cure a leprous man? He seeks pretexts against me.”

Elisha sent to him, saying: “Why have you torn your garments? Let him come to me and know that there is a prophet in Israel.” Naaman and his cavalry therefore stood at Elisha’s door. Elisha sent out word to him: “Wash [Col. 1391D] seven times in the Jordan, and you shall be clean.” Naaman departed angrily because Elisha had not touched him while invoking the Lord’s name. But his servants said: “If the prophet had told you to do some great thing, you ought to have done it; how much more, then, when it is a small thing?”

So he went down, washed himself seven times in the Jordan, and was cleansed. Returning, he stood before Elisha and said: “I know that there is no other God in all the earth except in Israel.” And he offered him a blessing—that is, a gift. Although he pressed him strongly when Elisha refused, Elisha said: “As the Lord lives, I shall not accept it.”

Naaman said: “I beg that I may take a load of earth for two mules from this land.” A mule is the offspring of a horse and a she-ass. According to some, he took the earth in order to spread it in the temples of idols, so that, standing on it, he might worship the God of Israel’s land and not offend his master if he did not worship along with him. But it seems truer that he made from it an altar to the Lord for sacrifice. Hence he adds: “Your servant shall no longer offer burnt offering or sacrifice to foreign gods, but only to the Lord. One thing I cannot alter: when the king leans upon my hand and worships in the temple of Rimmon, I must worship with him. Pray to the Lord that he may not impute this to me.”

“And Naaman departed at a chosen portion of land,” that is, after he had chosen earth to carry away. The Hebrew has: “He departed from him a little way,” literally, “some space of land.” The same ambiguity occurs in Genesis: “It was the spring season, and Ephrath was being entered” (Genesis 48). The Hebrew has: “There was still a space of land, and Ephrath was being entered.” Thus the Latin translator rendered “a chosen time” or “springtime” for “space.”

Gehazi ran after Naaman to receive something from him and said: “My master has sent me to you, saying: ‘Two young men of the sons of the prophets have come to me; give them a talent of silver and two garments.’” Naaman gave him two talents and garments, and assigned servants to carry them. Gehazi hid them in the house.

When in the evening he stood before Elisha, Elisha said: “Where have you come from, Gehazi?” He replied: “Your servant has not gone anywhere.” Elisha said: “Was not my heart with you when the man turned back to meet you? You have taken silver in order to buy possessions. But Naaman’s leprosy shall cling to you and your seed forever.” He went out from Elisha leprous.

It is not literally recorded that Gehazi had a leprous son or descendants. Yet concerning the Gehaziites it is certain that they were infected with the leprosy of simony.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the axe and the *acrisia* of the Syrians

While Elisha was with the sons of the prophets cutting timber at the Jordan, the iron head of one man’s axe fell into the water (IV Kings 6). When the man cried out, Elisha threw a piece of wood into the water where the iron had fallen; the iron floated, and he took it up.

“Now the king of Syria fought against Israel” and often stationed his servants in ambushes, which the king of Israel avoided because Elisha disclosed to him the Syrians’ hidden plans. Troubled, the king of Syria said to his servants: “Which of you is betraying me to the king of Israel?” One replied: “Not at all; but Elisha tells the king of Israel whatever you say in your inner chamber.”

He said: “I will send [Col. 1392D] and seize him.” Learning that Elisha was at Dothan, he sent there a strong force. Arriving at night, they surrounded the city. In the morning Elisha’s servant saw the army and cried out in terror: “Alas, my lord, what shall we do?” He replied: “Do not fear; those with us are more numerous.”

When Elisha prayed, the Lord opened the servant’s eyes, and he saw the mountain full of fiery chariots, that is, companies of angels. As the enemies came toward him, Elisha prayed, and the Lord struck them with blindness—not complete blindness, but *acrisia* [Note: [Col. 1393A] Addition 1. *Acrisia* is a derangement of sight: namely, when we look for what we are holding in our hand.], so that they did not recognize him.

Elisha said to them: “This is not the road, nor is this the city,” that is, Elisha does not live here. “Follow me, and I will show you the man you seek.” And he led them into Samaria. When Elisha prayed, “the Lord opened [Col. 1393A] their eyes, and they saw themselves in the middle of Samaria,” surrounded by enemies.

The king of Israel said to Elisha: “Shall I strike them down, my father?” He replied: “By no means.” For the Lord had brought them there; instead, give them abundant hospitality. When this was done, the Syrians returned home; and in Elisha’s days Syrian raiders came no more into Israel.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the famine and the second siege of Samaria

“After this, Ben-hadad besieged Samaria, and a famine arose in Samaria, so severe that an ass’s head was sold for eighty silver coins and a fourth part of a *cab* of dove’s dung for five silver coins” (IV Kings 6). With this, [Col. 1393B] as Josephus says, they seasoned food in place of salt. Some relate that “dove’s dung” denotes the crop of a dove, in which grains carried from outside were found.

As the king of Israel passed along the wall and inspected the wall guards, a woman cried to him: “Save me, my lord king.” Supposing that she sought something from him, he answered in agitation: “The Lord does not save you; from where can I save you? From the threshing floor or from the winepress?” She replied: “Not at all, lord; rather, this woman and I had agreed to eat our sons. We ate my son, but she has hidden her son.”

The king was deeply grieved, tore his garments, exposed the sackcloth which he wore next to his flesh [Col. 1393C], and said: “What further evil can we expect from the Lord? May God do this to me and more besides if Elisha’s head remains upon him today.” For he blamed Elisha for this calamity, on the ground that he did not free his fellow citizens though he could do so.

Having sent an executioner, the king, moved by repentance, followed him in order to prevent him. Elisha sat in his house with elders, whom Josephus calls his disciples. Elisha said: “Do you not know that the son of a murderer”—that is, of the man who killed Naboth—“has sent to cut off my head? Keep the messenger from entering until the king comes,” for he will prevent what he has ordered.

When the king arrived, Elisha said: “Tomorrow at this hour, at the gate of Samaria, a measure of fine flour shall be one stater, and two measures of barley likewise” (IV Kings 7). [Col. 1393D] One of those upon whose hands the king leaned mocked him, saying that this was impossible. Elisha said to him: “You shall see it, but shall not eat of it.”

There were four lepers at the entrance of the gate, dying of hunger. In the evening they went to the Syrian camp and found no one there. For the Lord had terrified the Syrians with the sound of a great army sent upon them; they fled, wishing only to save their lives. The lepers entered, ate, took from the booty according to their desire, and told the city gatekeepers that the Syrians had gone away.

The king of Israel suspected that the Syrians had feigned flight and lay in hiding. He therefore sent two men on horses to explore everything as far as the Jordan. When they returned and reported that the Syrians had fled, the people went out and plundered the camp. Fine flour and barley were sold [Col. 1394A] according to Elisha’s word. The officer who had mocked him was appointed by the king at the gate; the crowd trampled him, and he died.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the seven-year famine and the Shunammite woman’s sojourn

“After this Elisha spoke to the woman whose son he had raised: ‘Go with your household and live as a resident alien wherever you can. For the Lord has summoned a famine upon the land for seven years,’” that is, the angel set over famine (I Kings 8). As though he said: Famine will come; or this is a manner of speaking. It is uncertain whether this famine preceded or followed the siege mentioned above.
