The woman therefore went into the land of the Philistines, and her fellow countrymen occupied her possessions. When the famine ended, she returned and went to petition [Col. 1394B] the king concerning her house and fields. At that moment the king was speaking with Gehazi, asking him about Elisha’s great deeds. Seeing the woman, he said: “My lord, this is the woman, and this is her son, whom Elisha raised.” After she recounted the course of events to the king, he restored to her all that she had lost from the day when she left the land.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the death of Ben-hadad

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, heard that God, not man, had driven him away from the siege, and he fell ill in grief (IV Kings 8). Elisha came to Damascus, and the king sent Hazael to meet him with gifts, to ask him about his illness. Elisha answered his inquiry: “Say to him: You shall recover.” He did not say, “He shall recover,” because the king would die. Yet after telling Hazael, “You shall recover,” he drew [Col. 1394C] him aside and said: “The Lord has shown me that he shall die, and that you will be king of Syria.”

Thus was fulfilled what the Lord had said to Elijah. Elijah did not otherwise anoint Hazael, except in that he foretold through Elisha that he would become king. Elisha wept, seeing in the Spirit the evils Hazael would inflict upon the children of Israel, which he also told him.

Hazael returned to the king and said: “You shall recover.”—“The next day he took a covering, poured water upon it, and spread it over his face.” A *stragulum* is properly a coverlet spread over a bed or a seat. It is said that Hazael placed a cloth soaked with water upon him to cool him.

The Hebrew has: “He spread the covering over his own face,” so that it is understood not that Hazael did this, but Ben-hadad himself; yet the king died and Hazael reigned in his place. Some, however, explain this as attendance upon the dead, saying that Hazael washed the dead man with water and spread a covering over the dead man’s face.

Josephus plainly says that Hazael, on the next day, strangled him with a noose drenched in water. Some refer the preceding text to this sense, saying that Hazael placed the moistened garment upon his face while pretending to cool him, but immediately poured water over his mouth until he suffocated him.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Joram, king of Judah
Moreover, in the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel—in which Jehoshaphat king of Judah had reigned jointly with him—Joram son of Jehoshaphat reigned in Jerusalem for eight years [Col. 1395A] (IV Kings VIII). At his wife’s counsel he did evil before the Lord, following foreign gods. Yet the Lord did not destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant. Then Edom revolted, so as no longer to be subject to Judah. For the Idumeans killed their own tributary king and created a new one, who would not be obliged to pay tribute.

And when Joram had killed his six brothers and was compelling the people of Jerusalem also to practise idolatry, a certain prophet Elijah sent him a letter of rebuke, threatening punishment. The threat was fulfilled as follows: the Arabs, invading Judah, devastated the province and the royal houses, carried away the king’s wife, and killed his sons, except Ahaziah. At length he himself fell into a chronic illness, his bowels pouring out through internal corruption, so that [Col. 1395B] daily he saw himself, as it were, perishing. He died and was buried in the city of David. Yet, as Josephus says, they did not place him in the tomb of his fathers, but assigned him a private grave, without royal funeral rites. And his son Ahaziah, or Azariah, reigned in his place.

Matthew omits this king and the rest down to Uzziah (Matt. I). Joram son of Ahab reigned twelve years. Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem; and he walked in the ways of Ahab his grandfather. He went with Joram son of Ahab, his uncle, to fight against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. Joram was wounded; leaving the army under siege and under Jehu its commander, he went down to Jezreel to be healed, and Azariah went down [Col. 1395C] with him.

## CHAPTER XIV. Jehu, king of Israel, anointed in the time of Elisha

Elisha sent one of the sons of the prophets with a flask of oil to the army at Ramoth-gilead, in order that there he might call Jehu aside and anoint him king over Israel (I Kings IX). When he found Jehu sitting with the commanders, he said: “I have a word for you, commander.” And Jehu said: “For whom among us?” He replied: “For you, commander.” Perhaps Jehu, not recognizing him, took it in his mind as a sort of foretelling that he himself was the Jehu whom the first answer had identified.

When he had led him into an inner room, he poured oil upon his head and said: “Thus says the Lord: [Col. 1395D] I have anointed you king over Israel, and you shall strike down the whole house of Ahab, in vengeance for the blood of my servants at the hand of Jezebel.” Having done this, the prophet fled away very quickly.

When Jehu returned to his master’s servants, they said: “Why did this madman come to you?” For they regarded the sons of the prophets as madmen; or perhaps because he had fled away as quickly as a madman. Jehu said: “You judged correctly. For he spoke mad words, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord: I have anointed you king over Israel.’” They hastened therefore to take their garments and spread them beneath him in the manner of a tribunal; and, sounding the trumpet, they said: “Jehu shall reign.”

Jehu therefore conspired against Joram and said: “Let no one report this in Jezreel, but let us all go up together.” As they went up, the watchman in Jezreel [Col. 1396A] said: “I see a mass of people coming.” Joram, suspecting either that the city had been captured or that peace had been made, sent a messenger to meet them. He said: “Thus says the king: Is all well?” Jehu said: “What have you to do with peace?” As though he said: “What is that to you? Follow me.” Or perhaps Jehu replied to this man as though he himself were king, as if to say: “Why do you inquire about peace, you who trouble the land and its peace?” And the messenger joined him.

Joram sent a second messenger also, who likewise did not return to him. Then Joram king of Israel, with the king of Judah, went out to meet Jehu as far as the field of Naboth the Jezreelite. Joram said: “Is there peace, Jehu?” He answered: “What peace? The prostitutions of your mother are still flourishing.” That is, what peace can there be between us while we continually offend [Col. 1396B] God through your mother’s idolatry?

As Joram fled, he said to his kinsman: “There is treachery here, Ahaziah!” Then Jehu struck Joram between the shoulders; the arrow passed through his heart, and he fell dead. Jehu said to the commander of a third part of the army: “Throw him into Naboth’s field. Remember that you and I were following Ahab, this man’s father, when the Lord threatened him through Elijah that he would repay him in Naboth’s field for the blood of Naboth and for the blood of his sons.”

Yet above no mention was made of Naboth’s sons; what was left unspoken there is supplied here. Perhaps the dogs licked Joram’s blood in accordance with Elijah’s word. For they licked Ahab’s blood when they licked the blood of his son.

Jehu pursued Ahaziah as he fled and wounded [Col. 1396C] him on the ascent of Gaber. Wounded, he fled to Megiddo and died there; they carried him to Jerusalem, and he was buried in the city of David.

After this Jehu entered Jezreel. Jezebel was in the fortress of the tower. She painted her eyes with antimony and adorned her head, so that she might appear more beautiful to those approaching; and through the window she said to Jehu: “Can there be peace for Zimri, who killed his master?”—as though she said: “You have killed your master, like Zimri, and must be punished with the same penalty.”

Then Jehu said to the two eunuchs standing around her: “Throw her down.” They threw her down from the tower, and horses’ hooves trampled her. When Jehu sat down at table, he said to his servants: “Go and bury [Col. 1396D] that cursed woman, for she is a king’s daughter.” When they came to her, they found nothing except “the skull”—that is, the upper chamber of the brain—“and the feet and the palms of the hands.” When Jehu heard this, he said: “It is the word of the Lord which he spoke through Elijah” (III Kings XXI).

## CHAPTER XV. The seventy sons of Ahab, their death, and the death of Jehu

Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. Jehu wrote to their guardians and to the leading men of the city, saying: “Choose whichever of Ahab’s sons you wish, appoint him king over yourselves, and fight for the house of your lord” (IV Kings X). Terrified, they wrote back: “We are your servants; do what pleases you.” He wrote to them a second time: “If you are on my side, [Col. 1397A] take the heads of your lord’s sons and come to me tomorrow at Jezreel.” And so it was done.

They brought the heads in baskets to Jehu. He commanded that they should not be brought in to him, but placed by the entrance of the gate in two heaps until morning. When in the morning they looked upon the heads, Jehu said to the people: “You are righteous.” That is, by comparison with those who killed the seventy, you are righteous, who killed only Joram and Jezebel with me. Or, rather, he commended the Samaritans who had killed them, as if saying: “You acted justly in fulfilling the Lord’s word.” The following text seems to mean this, for it adds: “If I killed my lord, who struck him and these others? The Lord did what he spoke by the hand of Elijah.”

Then Jehu struck down all who remained of the house [Col. 1397B] of Ahab in Jezreel—his nobles, acquaintances, and priests—and he was proceeding to Samaria. On the way he met forty-two brothers of Ahaziah king of Judah, who were going down to greet Joram and Ahaziah, not knowing that they had been killed; and Jehu killed them.

Then Jehonadab son of Rechab came out to meet Jehu and blessed him for the Lord’s vengeance that he had carried out. Jehu put him into his chariot, brought him to Samaria, and struck down all who remained of Ahab, to the last one.

Jehu therefore gathered the people of Samaria and spoke deceitfully: “I wish to enlarge the worship of Baal. Call all his prophets and priests. Whoever is absent shall not live. For I have a great sacrifice for Baal.” All the servants of Baal came; not one was absent, and [Col. 1397C] the house of Baal was filled. Jehu said to those in charge of the vestments: “Give garments to all Baal’s servants.” And they gave them.

When Jehu had carefully searched to ensure that none was missing and that no other person was present, he said to his soldiers: “Go in and strike them down; let no one escape.” They struck them down, crushed Baal’s statue, destroyed his temple, and made it into latrines—that is, underground channels for cleansing the city’s streets. Thus Jehu wiped Baal out of Israel.

Nevertheless, he did not depart from the ways of Jeroboam. And the Lord said to him: “Because you have done what was in my heart against the house of Ahab, your sons shall sit upon the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.” Jehu died and was buried in Samaria, after [Col. 1397D] reigning twenty-eight years; and his son Joam, or Joaham, or Jehoahaz reigned in his place.

## CHAPTER XVI. Athaliah and Joash

Athaliah, seeing that her son was dead and wishing to reign, killed all the royal seed in Jerusalem (IV Kings XI). But Jehosheba, Ahaziah’s sister by the father and wife of Jehoiada the high priest, stole away Ahaziah’s infant son Joash so that he would not be killed. She hid him for seven years in the house of the Lord—that is, in the small dwellings of the weekly ministering courses.

In the seventh year Jehoiada assembled the centurions, the leaders of the Levites, and the soldiers. He secretly showed them the king’s son; all conspired for the boy against Athaliah, agreeing that they would make the boy king on the Sabbath. They acted as follows.

There were [Col. 1398A] twenty-four high priests, of whom one, during the week of his course, had with him in ministry twenty-four lesser priests, as many singers, and as many gatekeepers. At dawn on the Sabbath, the high priest who had been ministering went out with his company to his own home, while the priest who was to minister entered with his company. On this occasion, however, Jehoiada, in order to enlarge the force, retained those who were about to leave and received those who were entering, making two companies from them. He also added a third company of the centurions and Levites whom he had summoned.

Entering the house of the forest and the armoury which David had formerly made, he gave weapons to each man. He commanded those who were going out to stand round the king and guard him in the inner court. To those coming in he said [Col. 1398B] that they should go up to the royal house, lest the queen’s servants, coming out from it, should prevent the king’s anointing.

But he divided this company into three parts, commanding one to keep the king’s watch—that is, the portico of the royal house; another to guard the Gate of Sur, through which one went up from the city to the royal house; and the third to guard the House of Messa, called the Gate of the Shield-bearers—that is, of the king’s guards—through which one went up from the royal house to the Temple. He stationed the third part, which he had gathered from the centurions and Levites, to guard the Temple courts on every side.

Then he himself, with the remaining priests, Levites, and elders, brought forth the king’s son, anointed him king, placed the diadem upon him, and gave him the testimony—that is, the law of God—to hold [Col. 1398C] in his hands, so that together with the royal habit he might be entrusted with the discipline of observing God’s law.

Athaliah, running up, tore her garments and cried: “Treason! Treason!” The centurions brought her outside the Temple enclosure through the Horse Gate, and she was killed there. They led the king through the Gate of the Shield-bearers into the palace, and he sat upon the royal throne. The people of the land rejoiced because the Lord had removed the reproach that a woman should reign over them; and they destroyed the temple of Baal, its altars, and the images which Joram and Athaliah had made. They also killed Mattan, Baal’s priest, before the altar.

“Joash was seven years old when he began to reign,” in the seventh year of Jehu king of Israel; and he reigned in Jerusalem forty years [Col. 1398D] and did what was right before the Lord throughout all the days of Jehoiada the priest.

## CHAPTER XVII. The treasury chest

There were ruins in the house of the Lord, not only from age and neglect, but also those caused by Athaliah, who had used consecrated things to furnish the house of Baal. Joash therefore commanded the priests to restore the fabric of the house, receiving the offerings of those who passed by and those offered as the price of a life—that is, what were given by those counted when about to go to war (IV Kings XII). For the offering for transgression and sin belonged to the priests. Although the priests had received these funds until the twenty-eighth year of King Joash, they had nevertheless not repaired the fabric of the Temple. Angered, the king forbade the priests to receive money any further.

[Col. 1399A] Josephus, however, says that the priests collected half a shekel per head throughout the whole region. Jehoiada, seeing that this did not please the people, ceased collecting it, and for this reason the ruins were not repaired.

Then Jehoiada made a secure treasury chest with an opening at the top and placed it to the right of those entering the house, not far from the altar. “When a great quantity of money appeared in the treasury, the king’s scribe and the high priest poured it out and gave it to those set over the masons of the house of the Lord. No accounting was made with them, but they dealt faithfully” (II Chronicles XXIV). No vessel for the house of the Lord was made from that money, except out of what remained after the repair of the fabric, as is read in Chronicles.

Jehoiada the priest died. He alone, after Moses, is recorded to have lived [Col. 1399B] one hundred and thirty years. He was buried in the city of David because he had restored David’s dynasty through his son-in-law. After his death Joash turned aside from God’s lawful ways, and the nobles too were corrupted by his example.

When Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, rebuked him, Joash caused him to be stoned between the Temple and the altar (Matt. XXIII).

> [Note: [Col. 1399C] Addition 1. Let it not trouble you that the Gospel reads: “unto the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah” (Matt. XXIII). Perhaps Jehoiada had two names. Or it may be because Barachiah means “blessed of the Lord,” which this man was.]

From that time, as Epiphanius says, the people did not receive a manifest answer in the Temple as they had before, neither from the *dabir* [Note: [Col. 1399C] Addition 2. *Dabir* means the stone placed in the breastpiece of judgment. Hence by the *dabir*, that is, by the breastpiece, they discerned whether God was favourable or offended. Or *dabir* is interpreted “word,” and the sense is: He spoke to [Col. 1399D] them neither through a word nor through signs.] nor from the ephod. Not long afterward the king paid the penalty.

For Hazael king of Syria, having captured Gath, went up against Jerusalem (IV Kings XIII). Joash sent him the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the royal house—not from the hidden stores of the tombs [Note: [Col. 1399D] Addition 3. All Zechariah’s sons were stoned with him except one posthumous son, who was afterward called Zechariah.]—and Hazael withdrew from him. When Joash contracted a most severe illness, because, as the Hebrews say, he wished divine honours [Col. 1399C] to be bestowed upon himself, “two of his servants struck him down; he died and was buried in the city of David, though not in the royal monuments, and his son Amaziah reigned in his place.”

[Col. 1399D] **Incidental matter.**

Under Joash, the twelfth king of the Latins was Silvius Aremulus, who established an Alban stronghold among the hills where Rome now stands. His son was Julius, the great-grandfather of Julius Proculus, who, migrating to Rome with Romulus, founded the Julian family.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The death of Elisha

In the twenty-third year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu reigned over Israel for seventeen years, and walked in the ways of Jeroboam. The Lord was angry with Israel and gave them into the hand of Hazael and into [Col. 1400A] the hand of Ben-hadad his son; and of Jehoahaz’s people there remained only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers (IV Kings XIII).

Jehoahaz cried to the Lord, and the Lord in his mercy gave him peace during his days. He died and was buried in Samaria. His son Joash reigned in his place in the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, and reigned over Israel sixteen years. He walked in the ways of Jeroboam, though not as greatly as his fathers had done.

Elisha was ill, and Joash king of Israel went down to him. Weeping, he said: “My father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer.” Elisha said: “Bring a bow and arrows, and put your hand upon the bow.” When this had been done, Elisha placed his own hands upon the king’s hands and said: “Open the eastern window, [Col. 1400B] and shoot an arrow.” He shot it. Elisha said: “It is the Lord’s arrow against Syria; you shall strike the part of Syria which is at Aphek, until you consume it.”

Taking up the bow and arrows, Elisha said to the king: “Strike the ground with the missile.” When he had struck it three times and stopped, the man of God became angry and said: “Had you struck up to seven times, you would have struck Syria that many times; but now you will strike it three times.”

Elisha died and they buried him near Obadiah. In that year Moabite raiding bands had entered the land. Some people burying a man saw the raiders; frightened, they threw the corpse into Elisha’s tomb. When it touched Elisha’s bones, the man came back to life. Josephus, however, says that the raiders threw into Elisha’s [Col. 1400C] tomb a dead man whom they themselves seemed to have killed.

“Hazael king of Syria died, and his son Ben-hadad reigned in his place.” Joash king of Israel fought him in three campaigns, defeated him, and recovered from his hand the cities which Hazael had taken from Israel, according to Elisha’s word.

## CHAPTER XIX. Amaziah and Joash king of Israel

“In the second year of Joash king of Israel [Note: [Col. 1400C] Addition 1. From this point, king of Judah and king of Israel were equally called by the same name.], Amaziah son of Joash reigned in Jerusalem. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign and reigned twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Jehoiada of Jerusalem. He did what was right before the Lord, according to [Col. 1400D] the things which Joash his father had done, except only that he did not remove the high places”—it must be understood that this applies to both of them (IV Kings XIV). For Joash did not remove the high places either, although the wording seems to say otherwise.

He killed the servants who had killed his father, but not their sons, because of the Mosaic law which says: Fathers shall not die for sons, nor sons for fathers [Note: [Col. 1401C] Addition 1. Since a human being does not know the magnitude of anyone’s sin, it is sufficient, so far as human judgment is concerned, that one should die for one’s own offence, according to God’s justice; perhaps not even the death of a son is ever for his father’s offence.] (Deut. XXIV).

He assembled an army to defeat the Amalekites and Idumeans, and hired from the king of Israel one hundred thousand armed men for one hundred talents of silver. When he was ready for battle, a prophet advised him to dismiss the Israelites because they carried idols, and because God would give him victory. He agreed, though reluctantly, because he had paid wages to the Israelites.

“He struck down ten [Col. 1401A] thousand of Edom in the Valley of Salt and captured Petra,” the famous city of Arabia. He called it Jectehel, which means “God’s help.” Josephus, however, says that he brought the prisoners he had captured alive to the lofty Petra of Arabia and threw them down from it. Chronicles says the same (II Chronicles XXV); for Josephus and Chronicles agree in nearly everything.

Yet afterward he worshipped the gods whom he had taken from Amalek, because he heard them giving responses: Amalek, they said, had perished because its people had been negligent in their worship. For this he was struck with such a punishment. Inflated with pride, he wrote to Joash king of Israel: “Be subject to me, as your fathers were subject to David and Solomon.” Or else: “Come, and let us look one another in the face”—that is, “Let us fight.”

Joash replied to him in a riddle: “The thistle [Col. 1401B] of Lebanon sent to the cedar, saying: ‘Give your daughter to my son as a wife.’ But the wild beasts of the forest, angered, trampled the thistle. Your heart exalts you because of victory. Why do you provoke evil, so that you and Judah with you may fall?”

When Amaziah would not yield, they met near Beth-shemesh. Judah fled before Israel; Amaziah was captured, and the king of Israel threatened him with death unless he surrendered Jerusalem. When it had been surrendered, Joash broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate, called the Valley Gate, to the Corner Gate, for four hundred cubits. “He took the gold and silver, the vessels found in the house of the Lord and in the king’s treasuries, and hostages, and returned to Samaria.

“A conspiracy was formed against Amaziah in Jerusalem. He fled to Lachish, and [Col. 1401C] they sent after him to Lachish, killed him there, brought him back to Jerusalem, and buried him in the city of David. Then all the people took his son Uzziah, or Azariah, sixteen years old, and made him king.”

**Incidental matter.**

Under Amaziah, the thirteenth king of the Latins was Silvius Aventinus. He died and was buried on the mountain which is now part of the City, and gave his name to the place forever [Col. 1401D].

## CHAPTER XX. Jeroboam king of Israel and the prophet Amos

“Joash king of Israel died and was buried in Samaria, and his son Jeroboam reigned in his place in the fifteenth year of Amaziah king of Judah. He reigned in Israel forty-one years and walked in the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin. He restored Israel’s boundaries from the entrance of Hamath, which is Antioch, to the sea of the wilderness, which is the Dead Sea, according to the word of the Lord spoken through his servant Jonah the prophet, who was from Gath, which is in Opher,” or Ophir, to distinguish it from Gath in Palestine; it is the name of a region (IV Kings XIV). Therefore [Col. 1402A] one must not read Ophel. Ophel is the name of the misty tower which stood not far from the Temple.

We do not read in Jonah of this devastation of Syria accomplished through Jeroboam. But because of the threat of overthrow which Jonah preached and wrote, Josephus says that he foretold that after a very short time they would lose dominion over Asia. This was indeed begun through Jeroboam, but completed afterward, when the Assyrian monarchy was transferred to the Medes.

Raised up by this success, Jeroboam did evil before the Lord. Amos the Tekoaite, a prophet from among shepherds, was sent from the place where he pastured his flock into Samaria, to foretell the overthrow of Jeroboam’s house and the calamity of the people, saying: “Thus says the Lord: I shall rise with the sword against the house [Col. 1402B] of Jeroboam” (Amos VII). And again: “The son comes against my people Israel” (*ibid.*).

When Amaziah, priest of Bethel, had reported this to Jeroboam king of Israel, he forbade Amos, by the king’s command, to prophesy any longer in the kingdom of the ten tribes. When Amos refused to stop, saying that he was not a prophet but a shepherd sent by the Lord (Amos VIII), Amaziah repeatedly afflicted him with blows. At length Amaziah’s son Uzziah, repeatedly rebuking him, drove a bar through his temples. He was carried back half alive to his own land, where he died and was buried. Jeroboam died, and his son Zechariah reigned in his place.

## CHAPTER XXI. Uzziah, or Azariah, the leprous king of Judah

“In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, [Col. 1402C] Uzziah reigned in Jerusalem fifty-two years” (IV Kings XV). Jerome, however, says in his commentary on Hosea that he began to reign in Jeroboam’s twelfth year. He did what was pleasing before the Lord, although he did not remove the high places.

After defeating his enemies and making the Ammonites tributary to himself, he rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem which Joash king of Israel had destroyed. He was especially a cultivator of the land and took care concerning plantations and the sowing of varied crops. When he had grown rich in mortal possessions, he attempted to act against the immortal God. For on the feast of propitiation, clothed in a high-priestly robe, he entered the Temple to offer incense, though the high priest Azariah [Col. 1402D] with eighty priests forbade him.

There was an earthquake, the brightness of the sun shone exceedingly, and it fell upon the king’s face; he was smitten with leprosy in the face. Outside the city the middle part of the mountain to the west was split and rolled down, so as both to block the roads and overwhelm the royal gardens.

“He lived apart, dwelling in a private city and living a private life. But his son Jotham governed the palace and judged the people of the land. Uzziah died and was buried in the city of David.” Josephus, however, says that alone among the kings he had a tomb in the gardens. “And his son Jotham reigned in his place.”

Under Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel, Isaiah began to prophesy—of whom more will be said later—and Hosea, born from the tribe of Issachar at Bethomoth. But here, as [Col. 1403A] Jerome says, Hosea gave a sign while foretelling: “The Lord shall come into the land, like the oak which is in Shiloh,” etc. This is not found in his book according to our edition.

Perhaps what Jerome called a sign Epiphanius called a prodigy, saying of Hosea: “He gave a prodigy, saying: ‘The Lord shall come into the land like the oak which is in Shiloh, when it has divided itself into twelve parts and from it an equal number of oaks have been produced.’” He prophesied against the ten tribes, saying little about the two. He also historically announced that the Jews would return to Christ in the last time. He likewise foretold the third day of the Lord’s resurrection. He fell asleep in peaceful rest and was buried in his own land.

Under the same kings Joel, born of the tribe of Reuben in the district of Beth-horon, also prophesied [Col. 1403B]. He described the land of the two tribes as to be devastated by caterpillar, locust, grasshopper, and blight (Joel I). He also foretold the future outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon God’s servants and handmaids, which occurred on the day of Pentecost. He died and was buried in peace at Beth-horon.

Under the same kings Obadiah prophesied, as some hand down (Obad. I); but according to the Hebrews it is truer that he prophesied before them, for he died before Elisha. His widow, left behind, was freed from creditors by Elisha’s counsel, through oil that overflowed. He was from the land of Shechem, from the district of Beth-hamar. For he was that captain of fifty whom Elijah spared, who, leaving the king’s service, became Elijah’s disciple. His tomb, together with the mausoleum of Elisha and John the Baptist, is held in veneration at Sebaste [Col. 1403C] even to this day.

Under Jeroboam king of Israel, Jonah, son of the widow of Zarephath, prophesied. After his return from Nineveh, in a time of famine, he took his mother with him and became an inhabitant among the Gentiles. For he was ashamed to remain in his own country, saying: “Thus my reproach will be taken away, because I have been found a false prophet in prophesying against Nineveh” (Jonah IV). When the famine had passed, he returned to the land of Judah. His mother died, and he buried her beside Deborah’s bath.

> [Note: [Col. 1403D] Addition 1. *Delbora* is a kind of palm, or an oak.]

He foretold this sign of Jerusalem’s destruction: when they should see a stone crying mournfully, the end would be near; and when they should see all nations in Jerusalem, then the whole city would be overthrown beyond recovery. He died and was [Col. 1403D] buried in the cave of one of the judges of Israel; his tomb is shown in one of the towns of Gath, in a certain village near Sephoron.

Under Uzziah king of Judah, the Assyrian monarchy came to an end. For Sardanapalus, the last monarch, defeated by Arbaces the Mede, burned himself; and then Arbaces transferred the monarchy to the Medes in hope, though not yet in fact. For Darius accomplished this after killing Belshazzar. The Assyrians nevertheless had kings—if not monarchs, still powerful ones—until the overthrow of Nineveh, which Nahum foretold.

**Incidental matter.**

At that time the fourteenth king of the Latins was Silvius [Col. 1404A] Procas, after whom the fifteenth king of the Latins was Silvius Amulius.

## CHAPTER XXII. Zechariah, Shallum, and Menahem

“In the thirty-eighth year of Uzziah king of Judah, Zechariah son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel six months. He did evil before the Lord, as his fathers had done; and Shallum son of Jabesh struck him down publicly and reigned in his place” (IV Kings XV). Thus the kingdom of Israel passed from the house of Jehu in the fourth generation, according to the Lord’s word.

“Shallum reigned one month in Samaria. For Menahem son of Gadi, from Tirzah, struck him down in Samaria and reigned in his place. He struck Tiphsah and its territory because his fellow citizens had refused to open it to him. In the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah, [Col. 1404B] Menahem reigned over Israel ten years and walked in the ways of Jeroboam.

“In his days Pul king of Assyria went up against Tiphsah, and Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver so that he would withdraw from him and also be his ally. Menahem took fifty shekels of silver apiece from the powerful and wealthy men of the land.”

The Hebrews relate that among these gifts Menahem sent the golden calves which were in Dan and Bethel, but this is untrue. For the priests deceitfully removed the golden calves and hid them; they made similar bronze ones, gilded over, which Menahem sent to the king of Assyria. When this deception was afterward discovered, the kings of Assyria burned with great anger against Israel.

“Menahem died, and his son Pekahiah reigned in his place in the fiftieth year [Col. 1404C] of Uzziah king of Judah. He reigned in Israel two years. For Pekah son of Remaliah, his chiliarch, killed him in Samaria at a banquet, along with fifty men, and reigned in his place in the fifty-second year of Uzziah king of Judah. He reigned in Israel twenty years.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. The beginning of the captivity of the ten tribes

“In the days of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria went up against Israel” (IV Kings XV). It is uncertain whether he was Pul or another man. He devastated the whole region beyond the Jordan and carried away captive the two and a half tribes. Ravaging Galilee, from the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali [Note: [Col. 1404D] Addition 1. Of this captivity it was said: “In the first time the land was lightened” (Isa. IX).], he transferred with him into Assyria many who could be reckoned equal to half a tribe. [Col. 1404D] Hence it is often read that he took three tribes of Israel captive; and this was the beginning of the captivity of the ten tribes.

“Moreover Hoshea son of Elah killed Pekah king of Israel and reigned in his place.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. Jotham

“In the second year of Pekah king of Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah reigned in Jerusalem. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign and reigned sixteen years. His mother’s name was Jerusha, daughter of Zadok. He did what was good before the Lord, although he did not remove the high places. He built the loftiest gate of the house of the Lord” (IV Kings XV), which some think was the Tower of the Flock. This is what is called Beautiful in the Acts of the Apostles [Col. 1405A] (Acts III); by the Hebrews it is called the Gate of Jotham. It alone remained in the destruction wrought by the Chaldeans.

He defeated the Ammonites and imposed upon them an annual tribute of one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and as much barley. In his days Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel began to harass the kingdom of Judah.

Under Jotham, Nahum of Elkosh, of the tribe of Simeon, began to prophesy against Nineveh, proclaiming: “Thus says the Lord to Nineveh: I shall destroy you, and no descendants from you shall rule the world” (Nahum II). Jerome says in his commentary on Nahum that Herodotus stated that Nineveh was overthrown by the king of the Medes in the time of Josiah.

Nahum also foretold Nineveh’s final overthrow, which happened as follows: the marsh which [Col. 1405B] surrounded it overflowed it, while at the same time an earthquake occurred and fire was sent down from above. He seems to have written of this inundation in his book where it says: “The Lord, overflowing, will not make innocent in storm and whirlwind are his ways” (Nahum I). Yet another text there reads: “Purifying, he will not make innocent.”

He nevertheless wrote his book after the captivity of the ten tribes, under Hezekiah [Note: [Col. 1405C] Addition 1. As though to say: although mention was made of his book under Jotham, he prophesied before he wrote.], while the land of Judah was being ravaged by the Assyrians. In it he prophesied more fully of the Assyrians’ destruction, to console his own nation. At length he died and was buried peacefully in his own country.

Under Jotham Isaiah saw the Lord sitting [Note: [Col. 1405C] Addition 2. Hence it is said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne” (Isa. VI).], and a seraph cleansed his lips. Under the same king the second Micah began to prophesy. “Jotham [Col. 1405C] king of Judah died and was buried in the city of David, and his son Ahaz reigned in his place.”

**Incidental matter.**

Under Jotham, the first Olympiad was instituted by the Eleans; Remus and Romulus were born from Mars and Ilia.

## CHAPTER XXV. Ahaz
«In the seventeenth year of Pekah king of Israel, Ahaz reigned in Jerusalem. He was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years; and he walked [Col. 1405D] in the way of the kings of Israel. For he even consecrated one of his sons to an idol (IV Kings XVI),» making him pass through the fire of Tophet [Note: [Col. 1406C] Addition 1. Tophet is so called from *tophus*, meaning a porous stone, through whose cavities fire issued; through this fire they passed their little children, whom they “purified,” just as we do through the water of baptism. This fire was in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, also called Gehenna, from *ge*, “earth,” and Hinnom.] in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, near Acheldemach. There was a certain son of Hinnom whose valley this was; it was therefore called Ben-hinnom, that is, “son of Hinnom.”

“Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel went up against Jerusalem and first besieged it,” as Josephus says. Ahaz engaged them, was defeated, and his son Zechariah was killed, along with many thousands; and Dichaz [otherwise Ditham], the commander of his army, was captured. When the king of Israel returned victoriously to Samaria with a great multitude of captives, a certain prophet, Odida or Obed, met him. He said that they had not conquered by their own strength, but because of God’s wrath against Ahaz; he rebuked them because they were carrying their fellow-countrymen away captive, warning that, unless they released them, sudden destruction was ready for them. Then, on the advice of Barachiah, who was eminent in Israel, the king of Israel showed the captives great hospitality and sent them and their children back to their homes.

Moreover, the king of Syria and the king of Israel besieged Jerusalem a second time. Ahaz was exceedingly afraid, but Isaiah encouraged him, saying: “Do not fear these two tails of smoking firebrands” (Isa. VII). But Ahaz did not believe him and would not ask a sign from the Lord. He sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, saying: “I am your servant; come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and the king of Israel.” The king of the Assyrians entered Syria, devastated it, and Rezin did not return to Damascus. The king of the Assyrians [Col. 1406B] captured Damascus, killed Rezin, and transferred the people of Damascus to Cyrene, which lies toward Ethiopia. There is, indeed, another Cyrene in Africa.

Ahaz king of Judah met him in Damascus with gifts. Having seen the altar at Damascus, he sent its model to Uriah the priest in Jerusalem, ordering him to build one like it. When this had been done and Ahaz had returned, he moved the bronze altar from before the temple to the north, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings upon the new altar. From the bronze altar, as some relate, he made that famous sundial of which we shall speak later. He ordered the priests thereafter to offer upon the new altar; and Ahaz removed the basins and the bronze sea, placing it upon the pavement so that no one might use it.

He also closed up the Sabbath *musach* [Note: [Col. 1406D] Addition 2. *Musach* is also said to mean the place in which the sacrifices of feast days were stored, such as the Sabbath *corban*, where votive offerings were kept; while the treasury was that in which the sacrifices of other days were kept. Thus you may note a twofold use of these three terms.] [Col. 1406C] and the king’s entrance in the temple of the Lord, so that, together with the temple, he might profane these things and thus please the king of the Assyrians. The *musach* is the treasury of kings, just as the *corban* is that of priests. Some say that the king’s entrance was the place in which the king worshipped, or the gate through which he went up to worship. Ahaz blocked all these up, just as he had closed the temple so that the priests could not enter. Under him Isaiah saw the burden concerning Babylon; he saw ten others under Hezekiah.

“And Ahaz died and was buried in the city of David, and his son Hezekiah reigned in his place.”

[Col. 1406D] Incidental matters.

Under Ahaz, Rome was founded on the Palatine Hill, on the second day before the Kalends of May, by the twins Remus and Romulus. In the third year from the founding of the city, Remus was killed with a shepherd’s rake by Fabius, Romulus’s commander. At the consular games Sabine maidens and women were carried off, and the most beautiful [Col. 1407A] of the maidens, Thalamon, was assigned by lot to Romulus’s commander. Since this turned out well for him, the place of marriage was thereafter called the *thalamus*, or bridal chamber.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the captivity of the ten tribes

“In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea reigned over Israel for nine years. He did evil before the Lord, but not as his fathers had done” (IV Kings VII). For he is said to have granted the Israelites permission to go up to Jerusalem three times a year.

“Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians went up against him, and Hoshea became his tributary. When the king of the Assyrians discovered that Hoshea was attempting to rebel, through Susac king of Egypt, to whom he had sent gifts, he besieged him, sent him bound to prison in Nineveh, besieged Samaria for three years, captured it in the ninth year of Hoshea [Col. 1407B] and the sixth of Hezekiah, and transferred Israel to the Assyrians”—namely, the seven tribes that remained—“and placed them beside the river Gozan beyond the mountains of the Medes and Persians.”

In the first captivity of the three tribes, Tobit is believed to have been taken captive, and he remained in Nineveh; or perhaps he was taken to Nineveh with King Hoshea. His history was completed under Manasseh, son of Hezekiah. But we shall treat it after the end of the Book of Kings. The king of the Assyrians brought settlers from various regions into Samaria, few at first; but afterward Esarhaddon populated the land, and they dwelt in its cities [Note: [Col. 1407D] Addition 1. The ten tribes are still held captive beyond the Caspian mountains. Therefore, whatever is said concerning the return of the children of Israel under Cyrus or Artaxerxes must be understood of the two tribes.].

Since they came from five distant regions, they brought five idols into Samaria, each region its own. At first all were called Cuthaeans [Col. 1407C], after certain leading men among them who had come from the Persian region called Cutha, after a certain river. The Greeks, however, called them Samaritans, and they are called Samaritans in the Gospel. The Hebrews called them Jacobites, because they had supplanted the Israelites in their territories. When they came into the land of Israel, the Lord sent lions among them, which killed them. It was reported to the king of the Assyrians that his settlers were perishing because they did not know the ordinances of the God of Israel. He therefore sent them one of the priests of Israel and the Law of Moses written in more ancient letters. The priest lived at Bethel, and they accepted circumcision and the ordinances of the God of Israel; nevertheless, they still worshipped their own gods in the high places.

Thus, when things went well for the Hebrews, they sometimes called themselves their kinsmen; [Col. 1407D] but when things went badly, they said they had nothing to do with Israel. The ten tribes migrated from Judah 947 years after the exodus from Egypt. From the division of the kingdom, 240 years, seven months, and seven days had elapsed, according to Josephus. Many Israelites fled into the kingdom of Judah; many hid themselves in secret places and concealed themselves among the surrounding nations. After the return of the king of the Assyrians, they returned to their homes and lived with the Samaritans.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Hezekiah, who did what was right, etc.

[Col. 1408A]

“In the third year of Hoshea king of Israel, Hezekiah reigned in Jerusalem. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years. His mother’s name was Abi of Jerusalem, daughter of Zechariah,” the posthumous child of the Zechariah who was stoned (IV Kings XVIII).

Having summoned the priests and Levites, he opened the temple in the first year and first month of his reign, repaired the vessels of God, and restored the interrupted sacrifices. On the advice of the priests, he kept the Passover in the second month, not at its proper time, because the people could not assemble at Jerusalem in the first month and the priests had not been purified. Yet so great was the multitude that many who were impure ate the Passover, and there was such an abundance of victims that in many cases the Levites supplied the office [Col. 1408B] of the priests. After the Passover they celebrated for another seven days.

“He destroyed the high places, broke the statues, cut down the sacred groves, and shattered the bronze serpent which Moses had made, to which the children of Israel had burned incense until that time”; he scattered its dust into the brook Kidron, “and called its name Nehushtan,” which is interpreted “their mouth.” As if to say: it was called a god, but was not one. He also wrote to the children of Israel, asking them to return to the worship of God. Some ignored his messengers, while others killed some of them. For this reason they afterward deserved, as has been said, to be carried captive. He also withdrew from the king of the Assyrians, refusing to serve him.

“He struck the Philistines as far as Gaza and throughout all their borders, from the watchtower to the fortified city” [Col. 1408C]—that is, both garrisons and cities. In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, went up into Judah, captured its cities, and sent to Hezekiah at Lachish, saying: “Withdraw from me, and I will bear whatever you impose upon me.” The king of the Assyrians imposed upon him three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, and swore that he would not harm him. Since Hezekiah could not find this sum in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and in his own, he removed the plates of gold which he himself had fastened to the temple doors. But when he had sent the stated money to the king of the Assyrians, Sennacherib broke his oath and sent Tartan and Rabshakeh to besiege Jerusalem. They encamped beside the aqueduct of the upper pool [Col. 1408D], on the highway of the Fuller’s Field, and cut the citizens off from the water of the outer pool.

When they summoned the king for a conference, he would not come out, but sent to them Eliakim the high priest, Shebna the scribe, and Joah the recorder. Rabshakeh spoke to them in Hebrew; for he was a Samaritan, according to some. Some said that he was a son of Isaiah who had gone over to the Assyrians, adopted the practices of the nations, and become a chiliarch. He said: “Thus says the great king of the Assyrians to you: O Hezekiah, in what do you trust, that you dare to rebel? If you trust in the king of Egypt, you lean upon a staff of reed. If you place hope in your God, have the gods of the nations and the God of Israel delivered them from my hand? If you place hope in your people, I will give you two thousand [Col. 1409A] horses, and you will not be able to find riders among your own people.”

The messengers asked Rabshakeh to speak to them in Syriac rather than in Judean, so that the people upon the wall might not hear. Then Rabshakeh shouted also to the people: “Thus says the great king of the Assyrians: Make terms with me for your advantage, lest you eat your own dung and drink your own urine. Come out to me and enjoy your goods, until I come and transfer you to a land like your own.”

When the messengers reported these threats to Hezekiah, the king tore his garments, covered himself in sackcloth, and entered the house of the Lord. He sent the messengers mentioned above, together with elders of the priests clothed in sackcloth, to Isaiah, saying: “Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of our tribulation [Col. 1409B] and of divine rebuke. Pray for the remnant of Israel, perhaps God may hear the blasphemy of Rabshakeh and take vengeance” (IV Kings XIX). Isaiah answered: “Thus says the Lord to Hezekiah: Do not fear. Behold, I will put a spirit into the king of the Assyrians; he shall hear a report and return to his own land, and I will cast him down by the sword in his own land.”

Rabshakeh then withdrew from Jerusalem and found the king of the Assyrians attacking Libnah. The king proceeded to wage war upon Egypt, intending to return in triumph and overthrow Jerusalem. When he had besieged Pelusium, he heard that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia was coming with a great army to aid the Egyptians. Alarmed, the king said that Tirhakah was a priest of Vulcan and therefore would not fight him. He returned to Judaea and besieged [Col. 1409C] Jerusalem.

Herodotus, however, gives another reason for his return. When the king of Egypt prayed to God, a multitude of mice in a single night gnawed through the bowstrings in Sennacherib’s camp; the Assyrians were thereby left unarmed. He says that Rabshakeh remained with the army near Jerusalem, while Sennacherib returned to him from Egypt. Nevertheless, before Sennacherib’s return from Egypt to Judaea, the following events took place.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the signs of the three years foretold by Isaiah

As Sennacherib was leaving Judaea to cross into Egypt, he sent Hezekiah frightening letters full of threats, saying that the God of Israel [Col. 1409D] could not deliver him from his hand. Hezekiah then went up to the house of the Lord, spread the letters before the Lord, and prayed: “O Lord God of Israel, hear the words of Sennacherib, by which he has reproached you among us; save us, I beseech you, from his hand.”

Isaiah then sent word to Hezekiah, conveying these words of the Lord to Sennacherib: “The virgin daughter of Zion shall despise you, Sennacherib; when you flee, she shall shake her head behind your back. You have reproached the Holy One of Israel and ascribed to your own strength the devastation of Judaea. But I fashioned it from ancient days and have now brought it about”—that is, I who had ordained from eternity that I would thus scourge sinners have now fulfilled it. “I was the author; you were the minister. Therefore I shall put a ring in your nostrils, as is done to a buffalo, [Col. 1410A] and a bridle in your lips, as is done to a horse, and I shall bring you back to your own land.”

Isaiah then added his own words to Hezekiah: “But this shall be the sign of your deliverance, Hezekiah: in the third year Sennacherib will depart from you and will not return. I foretell to you what you shall do this year and what you shall do in the second, so that, when you see these things fulfilled, you may know that what I foretold concerning the third year is true. This year eat what you find,” or, according to Isaiah, “what grows of itself” (Isa. XXXVII); or, according to the Septuagint, “what you had previously sown.” The Assyrians had rushed in at the approaching harvest and devastated the grainfields, vineyards, and olive groves; yet some things had escaped beneath the hoofs of the trampling horses. Hence the Septuagint says: “Eat what you had previously sown”: even among the trampled ground some things had sprouted of themselves. [Col. 1410B] Of these Isaiah said: “Eat what grows of itself.”

Knowing already of Sennacherib’s approach, they had gathered provisions from every quarter and stored them in Jerusalem; of these the Book of Kings says here: “Eat what you find.” But in the second year eat what grows of itself, or, according to Isaiah, “eat fruits” (*ibid.*), which is the same thing. For in the second year, while Sennacherib remained in Egypt, after those provisions had been exhausted, the Lord abundantly increased for them what the earth produces of itself. “But in the third year,” once the enemy had been put to flight, “sow, reap, and eat in safety. Then a remnant shall go forth from Jerusalem, and what has been saved from Mount Zion; and what remains of the house of Judah shall send [Col. 1410C] root downward and bear fruit upward.”

He speaks by comparison with a tree: the more deeply it has sent out its root, the more abundantly and loftily it bears fruit. The meaning is this: the multitude of people who fled Judaea before the enemy and took refuge in Jerusalem so as to be saved will return to their own land once the enemy has been driven away and will populate it.

On hearing this, Hezekiah rejoiced. On the advice of Isaiah and the wise men, he stopped up the heads of the springs outside the city and the water outlets in Judaea, so that, if the Assyrians returned, they might not find an abundance of water. Hezekiah then blocked the upper spring of the waters of Gihon and diverted them underground to the west of the city of David, so that they might flow into the lower pool. Before the spring of Siloam he also made [Col. 1410D] something like a reservoir in which the waters might be collected and preserved for the citizens’ use during a siege. According to Epiphanius, at Isaiah’s prayers the waters issued from the spring of Siloam more copiously than usual. This reservoir is called in the Gospel the Pool of Siloam (John IX).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Sennacherib’s flight

After a year Sennacherib returned from Egypt and, having devastated Judaea, finally besieged Jerusalem. But on that same night an angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians (IV Kings XIX). Sennacherib, terrified, fled with ten men, as the Hebrews say, “and returned to Nineveh. While he was worshipping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer [Col. 1411A] struck him with the sword and fled into Ararat,” a level and fertile region of Armenia at the foot of Mount Taurus through which the Araxes flows. His son Esarhaddon reigned in his place. The elder sons were angry with their father because he had preferred their younger brother to them as king, since he loved that son’s mother more than their own. In this Sennacherib was shown to be more wicked than the people, in that he was spared for parricide at the hands of his sons [Note: [Col. 1411A] Addition 1. The Hebrews say that an angel shaved his head and beard to shame him, fulfilling Isaiah’s words: “On that day, with a hired razor, he shall shave the head and beard of the king of the Assyrians.”].

The Jerusalemites, seeing the slaughter of the enemy, went out and plundered the camp. As they stripped the dead, they shook from them only dust; for divine fire had secretly reduced their bodies to ashes.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Hezekiah’s illness and the sun’s return

[Col. 1411B]

After this unexpected and incredible triumph, Hezekiah—although, according to Josephus, he had offered sacrifices to God together with the people—did not give worthy thanks. He was puffed up in spirit and did not sing a hymn, as the fathers were accustomed to do on such occasions. Therefore “he fell sick unto death, and Isaiah came to him and said: Thus says the Lord: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live” (IV Kings XX).

Hezekiah was saddened because he had no son—not because he would leave his house desolate [Col. 1411C], but lest perhaps the promise made to David concerning Christ should fail in him. Turning toward the wall, he wept bitterly, perhaps that he might pray more privately and so that those standing by would not see his tears; or perhaps he was lying beside the wall of the temple portico, and, because he could not go up into the portico to pray, he prayed at least toward it, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, remember that I have walked before you in truth.” As if to say: Even if I have now sinned, spare me, lest what I have done before you perish from your sight.

Before Isaiah had gone out through the middle part of the court, the Lord said to him: “Return and say to Hezekiah: Thus says the Lord God of David your father: I have heard your prayer and seen [Col. 1411D] your tear. Behold, I have healed you; on the third day you shall go up to the temple. I shall add fifteen years to your days; I shall deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, whose return you fear, for your sake and for the sake of David my servant.”

Here it is apparent that Manasseh had not yet been born, since, after his father’s death, he was twelve years old when he began to reign. Hezekiah said: “What shall be the sign that the Lord will heal me?” Isaiah replied: “Do you wish the shadow to rise ten lines on the sundial, or to return by as many steps?” It was then the tenth hour of the day, and the shadow of the gnomon was descending through ten lines. He thus offered the king a choice of sign: whether he wished the sun to stand motionless for ten hours, or to return eastward and begin the day again. If either occurred, ten hours would be added to the day’s twelve hours. The Hebrew agrees with this interpretation: “Do you wish the shadow to stand ten lines, or to return?” In Isaiah likewise the subject is only the sun’s return to the east, not the shadow’s ascent (Isa. XXXVIII).

Nevertheless, the Book of Kings is explained thus: Do you wish the shadow to rise ten lines as the sun travels over the earth through the northern regions toward the east, just as it is accustomed to travel daily under the earth by night, and then, after the ten hours are complete, immediately return to the place where it is now and complete this day? The king chose that the sun should return to the east. For if it stood still, that might be ascribed to some natural cause, or perhaps to the fact that it had happened at another time, as under Joshua; he chose an unheard-of sign. Immediately the sun, standing in the east, returned again through the ten lines through which it had already descended [Note: [Col. 1412C] Addition 1. Sacred Scripture customarily calls progress from west to east an ascent, [Col. 1412D] and movement in the opposite direction a descent. This ascent of the sun may be understood in two ways: either that, moving by degrees and in its usual motion, it returned eastward to the point of the tenth line where it had already been, and in an instant returned from the point it had reached after sunrise to the point of the tenth hour where it was now; or that it returned in an instant to the first point of the east, and thence moved by degrees back to the point of the tenth hour.].

Isaiah then had a mass of figs brought, and they applied it as a poultice “upon his wound.” The Hebrew says more properly, “upon his ulcer.” Some suppose that it was an abscess, whose pus is drawn to the surface of the skin by crushed dried figs. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, however, say that it was the royal disease, for which all sweet things, whether taken internally or applied externally, are regarded as harmful. Thus God’s power was displayed, since health was restored through harmful things.

Hezekiah recovered and, going up to the temple on the third day, said: “I said, O Lord”—that is, while I was ill I thought to myself—“In the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. XXXVIII), that is [Col. 1412C], before I have received the offspring for which I waited, I shall descend to the underworld. While thinking this, “I sought” from you through prayer “the remainder of my years,” that you might make me a father before my soul is taken away.

The Septuagint prefixes to this song of Hezekiah the title, “Prayer of Hezekiah king of Judah”; but Isaiah gives the better title, “Writing of Hezekiah king of Judah.” For in this song he merely narrated what he had thought or prayed while ill; nor did he pray in it except in two brief expressions, as there: “Lord, answer for me,” and at the end: “Lord, save me.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Hezekiah’s death

[Col. 1412D]

“At that time Merodach, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah,” asking that he might be his ally and friend (IV Kings XX). For at that time the king of the Medes and the king of the Babylonians had withdrawn from the Assyrian monarchy under Assarodach [Col. 1413A], so that they might not be subject to him. Yet the principal reason for this embassy is believed to have been the following. The Chaldeans excelled in astronomy, but by their art they could not discover why the day had been extended nearly to twice its length. At last they heard that this had been done for the king of Jerusalem, and sent to him to inquire into the truth of the matter. Moreover, the Chaldeans worshipped the sun and sent gifts to the king to honour the man whom their god had honoured.

Hezekiah rejoiced at their arrival and again became lifted up in his heart. There was nothing in his house or in all his dominion that he did not show them, including the house of spices. Some relate that this was the spice chamber in the temple of the Lord, into which it was unlawful to introduce gentiles. According to Epiphanius [Col. 1413B], however, it was an exceedingly long building made by Solomon, according to his father’s plan, on the eastern side of Zion. Solomon made a system of secret entrances far from the city, which could not be discovered by all the people and was unknown even to many priests. There the king placed gold and spices brought from Ethiopia. In it, beyond the tombs of the kings, were the tombs of the high priests, and finally the tombs of the prophets. Hezekiah exposed this secret of David and Solomon to the gentiles and contaminated the bones of his fathers by the presence of the profane. From that day he became sterile.

After the envoys had departed, Isaiah came to the king and said: “What did these men say, and from where did they come to you?” When Hezekiah [Col. 1413C] had told him what they had asked, Isaiah said: “Thus says the Lord: Behold, days are coming when everything in your house and what your fathers have stored up will be carried away to Babylon. Even some of your sons shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” The Hebrews fabulously say that this was fulfilled in Daniel and his companions, who were captured with Jehoiakim son of Josiah. But it is more truly believed that they were eunuchs not in body but in mind.

Hezekiah answered: “The word of the Lord is good. Let there be peace and truth in my days.” And Hezekiah slept with his fathers. All Judah celebrated his funeral, and they buried him above the tombs of the sons of David; that is, because of his piety in worshipping God, they made his tomb higher than the others. For he is commended thus in the Book [Col. 1413D] of Kings: “There was none like him among all the kings of Judah, neither before him nor after him” (IV Kings). David is excepted here, because the kingdom of Judah did not yet exist under him. If Josiah is asked about, we say that Josiah was better than Hezekiah; but Hezekiah is preferred to him in this respect: he was made great by illustrious achievements in war, and the Lord did three unheard-of things for him—the return of the sun, the addition of years, and the slaughter of the enemy by an angel.

Incidental matters.

In the days of Hezekiah Syracuse and Catana in Sicily were founded. Romulus selected soldiers from the people, as though one man out of every thousand. He called the Cures, who under Statius king of the Sabines supported Romulus, Quirites. He selected one hundred elders and called them fathers. Romulus [Col. 1414A] was nowhere to be found at the Capraean Marsh and, at Lucius’s urging, was consecrated under the name Quirinus. After Romulus, the elders mentioned above, each for five days in turn, governed the commonwealth for about a year and a half. This rule was called the “interval period” (*interregnum*). Then Numa Pompilius, the second king after Romulus, reigned; he called the elders mentioned above senators. He was the first to give the soldiers a *congiarium*, that is, an imperial largesse upon his accession. He added January and February to the year and laid the foundations of the Capitol. The Erythraean Sibyl flourished.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Manasseh and Isaiah’s death

“After Hezekiah his son Manasseh reigned in his place. He was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem [Col. 1414B], and he did evil before the Lord. He rebuilt the high places which his fathers had destroyed; he set up altars to Baal and sacred groves; he built altars to the host of heaven in the two courts of the temple; he placed an idol of the grove in the temple of the Lord; he made one of his sons pass through the fire of Tophet; and he multiplied diviners, augurs, necromancers, and soothsayers, causing Judah to wander in the ways of the nations” (IV Kings XXI).

When the prophets sent by the Lord rebuked him, he spared none of them, but made the streets of Jerusalem crimson with the blood of prophets. Moreover, he shed an immense amount of innocent blood, until he filled Jerusalem to the brim. Isaiah too—his maternal grandfather, according to the Hebrews, or his kinsman—Manasseh had driven outside Jerusalem near the Pool of Siloam and caused to be sawn in half with a wooden saw [Col. 1414C]. When, at the beginning of the sawing, Isaiah was in distress, he asked for water to drink. When they refused to give it to him, the Lord sent water from above into his mouth. He died, but the executioners nevertheless did not cease sawing him. Because of this sending of water, the name Siloam, which means “sent,” was confirmed. They did not bury him in the tomb of the prophets, but beneath the oak of Rogel, beside the channel of water made by Hezekiah, in memory of the miracle which the Lord had wrought in those waters at Isaiah’s prayers.

Epiphanius relates that, when Sennacherib was returning from Egypt, he sent ahead an army to besiege Jerusalem. It encamped around the Pool of Siloam in order to use its water. The pool was, as it were, common to all: citizens could go down to it, and so could enemies. But Isaiah prayed and obtained from the Lord that, when citizens went out, the water should be there as before; while, when enemies approached, the water dried up entirely, so that the Assyrians wondered where the city obtained water. For the enduring commemoration of this event, the waters of Siloam still bubble up, not continuously, but at uncertain hours. When Sennacherib himself arrived, the slaughter described above took place in his army. In memory of so great an event the people gloriously buried the prophet in the place mentioned above, so that even after his death they might continuously obtain the benefit of this water through his prayers.

Some books contain here the Prayer of Manasseh, which is placed at the end of Second Paralipomenon; therefore it need not [Col. 1415A] be placed here, especially since many copies do not contain it in this place.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Manasseh’s death

The Lord therefore sent against Manasseh the king of Babylon, who ravaged Judah. He captured Manasseh by stratagem, carried him to Babylon, and afflicted him with many tortures (II Psalms XXXIII). Manasseh understood that this was the hand of the Lord, did penance, and prayed earnestly to the Lord. The Lord had mercy and restored him to his kingdom. When he came to Jerusalem, he destroyed the idols, sacred groves, and altars which he had made, so that nothing remained as a memorial of the former things. He restored the worship of the Lord as before and taught the people likewise. He was so changed from his former way of life that he led a blessed life not without great wonder [Col. 1415B]. He also strengthened the city walls, towers, and many outer defenses with fortification.

“And Manasseh died and was buried in the garden of his own house, in the garden of Azam; and his son Amon reigned in his place” (IV Kings XXI).

Incidental matters.

In the days of Manasseh the Sibyl Erophila flourished at Samos, and was therefore called the Samian. The Parthenii founded Tarentum. Galarphus of the island of Chios first devised iron glue within himself [reading uncertain]. Tullus Hostilius was the third king of the Romans. He was the first Roman king to use purple and fasces. After a long peace he prepared for war, defeated the Albans, Veientes, and Fidenates, and enlarged [Col. 1415C] the city by adding the Caelian Hill. At last he was consumed by lightning together with his house.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Amon and Josiah

“Moreover, Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned only two years in Jerusalem” (IV Kings XXI). The Septuagint, however, says twelve. “He did evil before the Lord, as his father had done in his youth. His servants laid snares for him and killed him in his own house. But the people struck down those who had killed the king, buried him with his father, and appointed his son Josiah king in his place. Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem, walking in all the ways of David his father. He did not turn aside [Col. 1415D] to the right or to the left” (IV Kings XXII).

In the fourth year of his reign, when he was twelve years old, as Josephus says, he was already displaying remarkable piety and justice. He was already recalling the people from idolatry and correcting wicked practices like an old man. In the eighth year of his reign he cleansed the entire city and province from the worship of idols, so that no trace of idolatry remained. They even searched houses lest anything suspect remain concealed. In every matter he cultivated justice as the medicine of his soul. He sent throughout the entire province, ordering each person to bring voluntary gifts for the repair of the temple [Note: [Col. 1416A] Addition 1. Jerome, in *Paralipomenon*, says that the ark was removed from the temple in the days of Ahaz because idols had been placed there. It was in the house of Shallum, Jeremiah’s uncle, father of Hananel, husband of Huldah, who lived in the second section of the wall, until Josiah.]. He placed over this work Hilkiah the high priest, Amasiah, who was over the city, and Shaphan the scribe; [Col. 1416A] and the temple was repaired faithfully and without delay.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the holy prophet Jeremiah

In the thirteenth year of Josiah’s reign Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, of the priests of Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, three miles from the city, began to prophesy. He prophesied for fifty-one years, until the overthrow of the city, besides the time in which he prophesied in Egypt at Tanis. When he was a boy, the Lord said to him: “I have appointed you a prophet to the nations [Col. 1416B].” When he said: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord, I do not know how to speak, because I am a boy,” the Lord stretched out his hand, touched his mouth, and said: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth” (Jer. I).

From that time, though still a youth, he began to prophesy and preach, rising early in the morning and frequently standing at the gate of the house of the Lord and in the courts of the temple. The Lord showed him signs of the overthrow of Jerusalem which he proclaimed. First, he indicated that God was the author of that overthrow. He showed him something like a watchful thief holding a rod, in order to injure sleepers. Thus the Lord was already watching to strike his people. By the second sign the Lord showed him through what minister he would accomplish this: through a boiling pot facing from the north. He said: “From [Col. 1416C] the north all evil shall be opened over all the inhabitants of this land” (*ibid.*), that is, from the Chaldeans, who, in relation to Jerusalem, came from the north. He saw these two visions under Josiah. The time of the third is uncertain; indeed, it is more truly thought that he saw it under other kings, like the remaining matters that follow.

In the third vision the Lord showed him the cause of the overthrow; nor was this vision imaginary but bodily. “For the Lord commanded him to take his girdle and hide it beside the Euphrates. After many days, returning by the Lord’s command, he found it rotten and fit for no use. The Lord said to him: As a girdle clings to a man’s loins, so I joined the house of Israel and the house of Judah to myself; but because they withdrew from me, committing fornication after foreign gods, [Col. 1416D] they shall, as it were, rot away in captivity beyond the Euphrates” (Jer. XIII).

We shall treat the remaining matters concerning Jeremiah in their proper places.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the discovery of Deuteronomy
Moreover, in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign, Josiah commanded Hilkiah to count the remainder of the money that had been offered for repairing the Temple, and to make from it vessels for the Lord’s service. While Hilkiah was carefully searching through everything, he found the book of Moses in the Temple. Perhaps he opened the Ark and found Deuteronomy, which Moses had caused to be placed in it, and sent it to the king through Shaphan. When it had been read before the king, the king tore his garments (2 Kings 22). For he heard the curses written against transgressors of the Law and God’s repeated threats: if they followed idols, He would cast them out of the land which He had given them, as He had cast the Amorites out before them. [Col. 1417A] He wondered that he was still in the land, and feared that captivity was at hand.

“Then he commanded Hilkiah and prudent men to consult the Lord concerning himself and his people. They went down to Huldah the prophetess, wife of Shallum, who lived in Jerusalem in the second quarter,” that is, within the second circuit of the wall made by Hezekiah, of which Zephaniah said: “And a howling from the second quarter” (Zeph. 1), namely because the part enclosed by the second wall was the first to be taken. Perhaps they did not find Jeremiah; or rather, he was not yet of any importance. Huldah replied:

“Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall bring upon this place and its inhabitants the evils written in the book of the Law, because they provoked me by all the works of their hands. [Col. 1417B] My wrath shall be kindled and shall not be extinguished. But to the king who sent you, say: Thus says the Lord: Because you heard the words of the scroll, and your heart was terrified and you humbled yourself, these evils shall be deferred and shall not occur in your days; and I shall gather you to your fathers in peace.”

This is not to be understood of peace for the king himself, for he was killed by Pharaoh, but of peace for the people: that is, before God brought upon the people what He had threatened. Having heard this, the king sent throughout the whole province and gathered all the people in Jerusalem (2 Kings 23). Standing on the steps, he read aloud, for all to hear, every word of the book; he made a covenant before the Lord and compelled everyone to take oaths that they would observe the Mosaic laws in every respect. [Col. 1417C] He destroyed the diviners and all sorcerers, and reduced every trace of idolatry to dust. This included certain remnants of the bronze serpent, which Hezekiah had crushed or pulverized. Thus the prologue to Zephaniah says that Josiah crushed it. He defiled the high places, the valley of Topheth, and the fire of Moloch. Perhaps he scattered human bones everywhere, or other unclean things, so that the place might appear abhorrent rather than venerable.

He also utterly destroyed the horses of the sun and the chariots which the kings of Judah had depicted at the entrance of the Temple, beside the chamber of Nathan-melech the eunuch. The Jews had made there an image of the sun in the form of a beardless boy, because it suffers no old age but is renewed daily. [Col. 1417D] They had also made horses and a chariot for it, thinking that Elijah had been carried away in this manner. The king then went up to Bethel, to the altar made by Jeroboam, and burned the bones of priests and false prophets, dug up from the tombs of the high places, in accordance with the word of the prophet Abdon. When he had read that prophet’s inscription on a tomb, he commanded that his bones should not be moved, nor those of the man buried with him.

He did the same at the high places of Samaria and in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and as far as Naphtali: digging bones out of the tombs of the high places, he burned them upon the altars and reduced both bones and altars to dust. This had been foretold of Josiah three hundred and sixty-one years before. Returning to Jerusalem, he celebrated the Passover, summoning also those children of Israel who had somehow escaped the Assyrian captivity [Col. 1418A] or had by some chance returned from captivity. It is reported that he had from these as many as eleven thousand Nethinim.

“No such Passover had been celebrated since the days of the judges.” Chronicles reads, “since the days of Samuel” (2 Chron. 35), which might be said to result from scribal error, Samuel having been written for Solomon, unless the same statement were also found in Josephus. It may therefore be understood that Samuel celebrated a Passover, even though this is not read in the history. That the judges celebrated Passover is certain, since Moses and Joshua were judges. This Passover was celebrated at Jerusalem in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign.

## Chapter XXXVII. On the Death of Josiah

“In his days Pharaoh Necho, king [Col. 1418B] of Egypt, went up against the king of the Assyrians” (2 Kings 23). He had heard that the latter had already been weakened, because the Medes and Babylonians had broken away from his monarchy; and he judged that he could easily gain Syria. He had first attacked the king at Remon, who then reigned at Carchemish. Josiah therefore went down to meet him, forbidding him passage through Judaea. Pharaoh sent to Josiah, saying:

“What have I to do with you, king of Judah? I do not come against you; I am hastening to the Euphrates. God sends me against the Medes; let me go, lest God, who is with me, kill you.”

Josiah did not comply, but drew up battle-lines with the king at Remon, to fight against Pharaoh. Perhaps while he was transferring from one chariot to another, which followed him in royal fashion, he was killed by archers in the plain [Col. 1418C] of Megiddo; and at Remon the king and his army mourned him inconsolably. Hence also that saying: “There shall be mourning like the mourning at Remon.” It is reported that he was killed beside a tree and a spring, which immediately dried up. He was carried back to Jerusalem and buried in the mausoleum of his fathers.

All Judah in Jerusalem mourned him, especially Jeremiah, who wrote mournful Lamentations for his funeral: “How the city sits solitary,” etc. Male and female singers used these at Josiah’s funeral, and for a long time they repeated them over Josiah in Judaea. Later Jeremiah added other lamentations concerning the destruction of the city.
