[Col. 1418D] **Incidental Matters**

In Josiah’s days Ancus Marcius, the fourth king of the Romans, grandson of Numa through his daughter, added the Aventine Hill and the Janiculum to the city. Sixteen Roman miles above the sea he founded the city of Ostia. Greece first made use of the Dodonaean oracle. Tarquinius Priscus, the fifth king of the Romans, built the Circus at Rome, constructed walls, sewers, and the Capitol, and instituted the Roman games. Arion was carried by a dolphin into the theatre.

## Chapter XXXVIII. On Jehoiakim, or Jehoahaz

Josiah left three sons: Eliakim, also called Jeconiah, the firstborn, twenty-five years old; the middle son Jehoahaz, also called Shallum, twenty-three years old; and the third, Mattaniah, [Col. 1419A] about eight years old (2 Kings 23). The people of the land took the middle son, Jehoahaz, and made him king in his father’s place. He reigned at Jerusalem only three months. For, as Chronicles says, Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, came to Jerusalem, removed him, imposed upon the land a fine of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold, and made his elder brother Eliakim king in his place, subject to tribute (2 Chron. 36). Having changed his name, he called him Jehoiakim, so that the change of name might be a sign of subjection. He deceitfully took Jehoahaz with him, under the pretext of honouring him in Egypt. When he came to Riblah, he bound him and sent him in chains to prison in Egypt.

“Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and [Col. 1419B] he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did evil before the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done.” When the prophet Uriah reproved him and strongly threatened him, Uriah fled into Egypt. Jehoiakim sent after him, brought him back, and put him to a most shameful death.

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim’s reign Nebuchadnezzar began to reign in Babylon. Having defeated the king of Egypt, he took everything belonging to him from the brook of Egypt to the river Euphrates; and, crossing the Euphrates, he captured all Syria as far as Pelusium, except Judaea (2 Kings 24). In Jehoiakim’s fourth year Jeremiah spoke to all the people of Judah and to the citizens of Jerusalem, saying:

“From the thirteenth year of Josiah I have spoken the words of the Lord to you, and today is the twenty-third year, [Col. 1419C] yet you have not listened to me. Therefore thus says the Lord: I shall bring my servant Nebuchadnezzar upon this land and upon all the nations around it, and they shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. When the seventy years have been completed, I shall punish the king of Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans for their iniquities, and I shall make it everlasting desolations” (Jer. 25).

They wondered that he spoke so boldly. For at the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, when he stood in the courts of the Temple and said, “Thus says the Lord: I shall make this house like Shiloh, and I shall make this city a curse,” the priests, prophets, and all the people seized him, saying, “He must die.” [Col. 1419D] The princes of Judah came up from the royal house and sat in the gate of the Lord’s house, while the priests and prophets accused Jeremiah. He answered: “The Lord sent me to prophesy against this place. Behold, I am in your hands; do what is right in your eyes” (Jer. 26).

The princes delivered him from the hands of the people, especially Ahikam son of Shaphan, saying that Micah in Hezekiah’s days had preached similar things, as had many prophets in the days of the kings; they had suffered nothing from the kings, but had been honoured. Nevertheless, the princes confined Jeremiah so that he could not preach publicly.

Then the Lord said to Jeremiah: “Take a scroll and write all the words which I have spoken to you against Judah and the other nations, from the days of Josiah until [Col. 1420A] this day.” Jeremiah summoned Baruch son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the Lord. Jeremiah said to him: “I am confined and cannot enter the house of the Lord. Therefore go in yourself, and on a day of fasting read what you have written, while the people and all who come from their cities are listening.” Baruch did as Jeremiah commanded him, repeatedly reading in the house of the Lord.

In the fifth year of Jehoiakim, in the ninth month, they proclaimed a fast for all the people in Jerusalem and for all who had come in from Judah. Baruch read Jeremiah’s words at the entrance of the new gate of the Lord’s house. When Micaiah, son of Gamariah, heard this, he went down to the princes and elders of the royal house, who were sitting in the scribe’s treasury. When he had reported [Col. 1420B] what he heard, they summoned Baruch. After he had read all the words before them, they were astonished and said to him: “Hide yourself and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are.”

They went in to the king, who was sitting in the winter house in the ninth month, with a brazier full of coals before him. When Jehudi son of Nethaniah had read three or four pages, the king cut up the scroll with the scribe’s knife and threw it into the fire until it was consumed. Although some objected, the king commanded his servants to seize Baruch and Jeremiah; but the Lord hid them. The Lord said again to Jeremiah: “Write once more in a scroll all the words which Jehoiakim burned, and add more besides, especially what the Lord says against Jehoiakim: [Col. 1420C] No descendant of his shall sit upon David’s throne, and his corpse shall be cast out to the heat by day and to the frost by night” (Jer. 36).

“They shall not mourn him, ‘Alas, brother!’ or ‘Alas, sister!’”—that is, neither brother nor sister shall mourn him, saying, “Alas!” Nor shall they cry over him, “Alas, lord!” and “Alas, illustrious one!” “He shall be buried with an ass’s burial, decayed and cast out beyond the gates of Jerusalem” (Jer. 22).

## Chapter XXXIX. On Nebuchadnezzar and the Death of Jehoiakim

In Jehoiakim’s seventh year, which was Nebuchadnezzar’s fourth year, Nebuchadnezzar went up into Judaea and ravaged it (2 Kings 24). The Rechabites, who lived in tents apart from everyone else, went up to Jerusalem in fear, in order to save their lives.

The Lord said [Col. 1420D] to Jeremiah: “Go and bring all the Rechabites into one chamber of the treasuries beside the house of the Lord.” He brought them into the store-chamber of the sons of Hanan, and set before them cups and goblets full of wine, saying, “Drink wine.” They answered:

“We shall not drink wine, because Jonadab son of Rechab, our father, commanded us: ‘You, your wives, and your children shall never drink wine; you shall not build a house, sow seed, or plant vineyards; you shall dwell in tents all your days, so that you may live many days upon the land in which you are sojourners.’”

Then the Lord said to Jeremiah: “Say to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: Thus says the Lord: Will you not receive instruction, so as to obey me, as the Rechabites [Col. 1421A] obey their father? Therefore I shall bring upon you the evils which I have spoken; but from the line of Rechab there shall not fail a man standing before me” (Jer. 35).

When Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem, he captured Jehoiakim, bound him, and was taking him with the nobles to Babylon. But on the journey Nebuchadnezzar imposed tribute upon him and sent him back to Jerusalem, while taking hostages with him: boys of royal stock, Daniel and the three youths. Jehoiakim served him for three years. But when he heard that the king of Egypt intended again to fight Nebuchadnezzar, he refused him the tribute which he had promised.

The king of Babylon then went up to Jerusalem and entered it under the terms of a treaty. But when he had entered, he did not keep faith: instead, he killed every one of the strongest young men [Col. 1421B] together with King Jehoiakim, whom he ordered to be thrown into a grave outside the walls. Since these enemies had not kept faith with him, perhaps the Book of Kings calls them brigands, saying: “The Lord sent against Jehoiakim brigands of the Chaldeans, Syria, Moab, and Ammon, to destroy him according to the word of the Lord” (2 Kings 24). For marks contrary to the Law were found on the body of the slain king: namely, the name of the idol worshipped by Codonazer.

Nebuchadnezzar made Jehoiakim’s son king, bearing the same name as his father, namely Jeconiah. “Jehoiakim was eighteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned only three months and ten days.” When Nebuchadnezzar had departed, he feared that Jehoiakim, mindful [Col. 1421C] of his father’s death, might join the Egyptians and fight against him. He therefore returned and besieged Jerusalem. But at Jeremiah’s command “Jehoiakim went out to him with his mother, his whole household, and his princes. The king of Babylon received them in the eighth year of his reign; he took all the golden vessels from the house of the Lord and the treasures of the royal house, and carried them to Babylon with the king and his mother.”

From the royal household there were about two thousand; from the princes and strong men, seven thousand craftsmen and one thousand smiths: in all, about ten thousand. Among them were Mordecai and Ezekiel, still a young man, of priestly descent. Josephus nevertheless seems to mean that Ezekiel had already written two books concerning the future destruction of the city, which he left in Judaea. Because these persons surrendered voluntarily, they were properly called the *transmigration of Judah*. Those later carried away by force are properly called the *captivity of Judah*. From this transplantation of Judah—that is, from Nebuchadnezzar’s eighth year—some begin to count the seventy years of captivity.

## Chapter XL. On Zedekiah

“Nebuchadnezzar made Mattaniah, Jehoiakim’s uncle, king in Jerusalem” (2 Kings 24), to serve him under tribute, with the religious obligation of an oath interposed; and, having changed his name, “he called him Zedekiah.” Zedekiah was thirty-one years old when he began to reign, and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. “He did evil before the Lord, as did his brother Jehoiakim.” For he was proud, intending [Col. 1422A] to attach himself to the king of Egypt and not to keep his oath to the king of Babylon. False prophets deceived him, saying that the Egyptians would shortly defeat the Babylonians.

When Jeremiah told him to place his hope in the Lord and not in man, the Lord said to him: “Go down to the potter’s house, and there you shall hear my words.” He went down. The potter was making a work upon the wheel, and the vessel was spoiled in his hands; then he turned and made another vessel from the same clay, as pleased him. The Lord said to Jeremiah: “Say to the house of Judah: Thus says the Lord: Shall I not be able, as the potter does, to deal with you—to destroy and annihilate you, and then, relenting, to build and plant?” (Jer. 18).

In the fourth year of Zedekiah’s reign, the king of Edom, king of Moab, king of Tyre, king of Ammon, and king of Sidon sent messengers [Col. 1422B] to him, asking that, allied together and acting unanimously, they might refuse tribute to the king of Babylon. The Lord said to Jeremiah:

“Make yourself wooden chains, that is, six twisted bands, and put one upon your neck; give the other five into the hands of the messengers of the five kings before Zedekiah. Say to the five kings and to the king of Judah: Thus says the Lord: I made the earth and gave it to whomever pleased me; and now I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar my servant. The nation and kingdom that will not serve him, I shall punish with sword, famine, and pestilence. Do not listen to the words of the prophets who tell you, ‘You shall not serve the king of Babylon,’ lest you perish with them.”

When Jeremiah had fulfilled the Lord’s command before Zedekiah, Hananiah, a prophet of Gibeon, took the chain from Jeremiah’s neck and broke it, saying: “Thus says the Lord: Thus shall I break the yoke of the king of Babylon from the neck of these nations after two full years; I shall cause all the vessels of the Lord to be brought back and shall bring back to this place the whole transplantation of Judah” (Jer. 27).

Jeremiah said: “Amen; may the Lord do so” (Jer. 28), as though to say: I myself should wish this, if it could happen. “Nevertheless, listen, Hananiah. The Lord has not sent you, and you have made this people rest upon a lie. Therefore, this year you shall die, after two months have passed.” Hananiah died in that year, in the seventh month (ibid.). Jeremiah had foretold this in the fifth month.

Terrified by Hananiah’s death, Zedekiah sent messengers to Babylon with tribute. Jeremiah secretly sent a letter through the hands of the messengers to the whole transplantation of Judah, saying: [Col. 1422D]

“Thus says the Lord: Build houses and plant gardens; take wives and give your children in marriage; seek the peace of the city to which I have caused you to be transplanted, and pray to God for it, because in its peace will be your peace. Let not the prophets in your midst deceive you by promising that you will return shortly. For when seventy years begin to be fulfilled in Babylon, I shall bring you back to your place. Thus says the Lord concerning Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who prophesy lies to you: I shall give them into the hands of the king of Babylon, and he shall strike [Col. 1423A] them before your eyes. From them shall be taken up a curse, as people say: ‘May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire,’ because they committed folly in Israel, committed adultery with their neighbours’ wives, and spoke in my name a word which I had not commanded them” (Jer. 29).

The Hebrews report that these two were the two elders later judged by Daniel. It does not matter that the king of Babylon is said to have roasted them, whereas Daniel says they were stoned (Dan. 13): having been convicted, they were handed over to the king for punishment, which is signified by the name of fire.

When the messengers returned from Babylon, they brought letters on behalf of the false prophets to the priests in Jerusalem, in these words: “The Lord has placed you in His house over every man seized by frenzy [Col. 1423B] and prophesying, so that you may put him in stocks and in prison. Why, then, do you not rebuke Jeremiah, who told you, ‘Build houses, because you shall not return’?”

Zephaniah read the letter before Zedekiah, in Jeremiah’s hearing. Jeremiah said: “Thus says the Lord: Concerning those whom I caused to be transplanted, I shall fulfil my good word and bring them back; but upon you, who did not go out with them, I shall send sword, famine, and pestilence, and shall make you like bad figs which cannot be eaten” (Jer. 29).

“For the Lord showed me a sign: behold, two baskets full of figs were set before the Temple. The Lord said to me: ‘What do you see, Jeremiah?’ I said: ‘Figs—good figs, very good; and bad figs, very bad.’ The Lord said: ‘As these good figs are, so shall I acknowledge the transplantation which I sent away from this place, and I shall bring them back to this land. And as the very bad figs are, so shall I give Zedekiah and the rest who remain in this city for affliction and reproach among all the kingdoms of the earth’” (Jer. 24).

## Chapter XLI. On the Earthenware Flask

The Lord again said to Jeremiah: “Go, take an earthenware flask from the potter, and take with you elders of the priests and elders of the people to the valley of the sons of Hinnom, beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate. Break the flask before their eyes and say: ‘Thus says the Lord: Thus shall I break this place and this city. This place shall no longer be called Topheth and the valley of the sons [Col. 1423D] of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. I shall fill it with corpses, because there will be no other place for burial’” (Jer. 19).

Jeremiah came from Topheth and stood in the court of the Lord’s house, saying to all the people: “Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall bring upon this city all the evils which I have spoken against it.”

The priest Pashhur, angered, struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks at the upper Benjamin Gate in the house of the Lord. At daybreak the next day Pashhur brought Jeremiah out of the stocks, and Jeremiah said to him: “The Lord has not called your name Pashhur, but Terror on Every Side” (Jer. 20). Pashhur, or Phaseor, means “blackness of mouth,” as if to say: You shall not possess blackness of mouth—that is, power to command wicked things—[Col. 1424A] but, terrified on every side, you shall be led captive into Babylon.

Jeremiah prayed to the Lord: “Lord God of hosts, who sees the reins and the heart, let me see vengeance upon them; for to you I have revealed my cause.”

## Chapter XLII. On the First Siege of Jerusalem

In Zedekiah’s fifth year, which was the fifth year of Jehoiakim’s transplantation, Ezekiel began to prophesy in Babylon to the captives, after they had received Jeremiah’s letter (Ezek. 1). We shall treat his prophecy, as also Daniel’s, later, after the destruction of the city and Jeremiah’s death.

At the beginning of Zedekiah’s ninth year Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, because Zedekiah had refused him tribute. Zedekiah sent the priests Pashhur and Zephaniah to Jeremiah, saying: “Inquire [Col. 1424B] of the Lord for us, whether perhaps He may show us mercy.” Jeremiah answered: “Thus says the Lord: I shall give Zedekiah, king of Judah, his servants, and his people into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon; he shall strike them with the edge of the sword and shall not relent, spare, or have mercy” (Jer. 21).

Jeremiah walked freely among the people, proclaiming the same things. The king of Egypt went out from Egypt with an army, as though to raise the siege of Jerusalem. The king of Babylon withdrew from Jerusalem to meet him, routed him at the edge of the sword, and compelled him to leave Syria. When Nebuchadnezzar had withdrawn from Jerusalem, the false prophets mocked Jeremiah and deceived Zedekiah, saying: “The Babylonians will not return, [Col. 1424C] but our transplantation will return to us with all the vessels of the Lord” (Jer. 37).

Jeremiah, however, prophesied the opposite, and truly: “Zedekiah shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon; his mouth shall speak with that king’s mouth, his eyes shall see that king’s eyes, and he shall take Zedekiah to Babylon.” But the ungodly said that Jeremiah had lost his mind.

Jeremiah saddled an ass to go out to Anathoth, his village, which lies twenty stadia from Jerusalem. “When he came to the Benjamin Gate, Irijah, the gatekeeper, seized him, saying: ‘You are fleeing to the Chaldeans.’” He brought him to the princes, “who, after beating him, put him in prison in the house of Jonathan the scribe.” Jeremiah sat there many days.

Hanamel, son of Shallum, [Col. 1424D] his uncle, came to him at the entrance of the prison and said: “Buy my field at Anathoth, for the right of inheritance belongs to you as the nearer relative” (Jer. 32). Jeremiah understood that this was the word of the Lord. He bought the field, weighing out seven staters and ten pieces of silver; he called witnesses, wrote a sealed deed of possession, with stipulations, validations, and external marks, and made an open copy of the deed. Before Hanamel and the witnesses he gave the documents to Baruch, saying:

“Take this sealed deed of purchase and this open deed, and place them in an earthenware vessel, that they may endure for many days. For thus says the Lord: Fields and vineyards shall again be possessed in this land, of which you say that it will be desolate. Behold, I shall gather them [Col. 1425A] from all the lands to which I cast them, to this place; they shall dwell securely, and I shall make an everlasting covenant with them.”

## Chapter XLIII. On the Second Siege of Jerusalem

“In the ninth year of Zedekiah, in the tenth month, on the tenth day, the twenty-second day of the moon, Nebuzaradan, commander of the Babylonian army, returned with Nebuchadnezzar’s princes. They surrounded Jerusalem, built fortifications around it, and the city was shut up for eighteen months” (2 Kings 25).

Zedekiah, therefore, terrified, took Jeremiah from prison and questioned him secretly in his house: “Do you think there is a word from the Lord, since the Chaldeans have returned?” He answered: “You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon. But I beg you, my lord king, do not send [Col. 1425B] me back to Jonathan’s prison, lest I die there.” The king commanded that he be placed in the prison court and given each day a loaf of bread, apart from the cooked dish, until all the bread in the city was consumed.

Jeremiah cried out in the prison court: “Those who remain in the city shall perish by famine or sword; those who flee to the enemy shall in some measure escape death.” The princes and elders of the city came together before the king, saying: “We ask that this man be put to death, for he deliberately weakens the hands of the fighting men” (Jer. 37). He plainly lies, they said, when he declares: “Zedekiah shall be led bound to Babylon.” For Ezekiel prophesied in Babylon: “Zedekiah shall not see Babylon.”

The king said to them: “Behold, he is in your hands; [Col. 1425C] for indeed it is not lawful for the king to refuse you anything.” So they took Jeremiah and lowered him with ropes into the cistern of Malchiah, in which there was no water but mud, so that he might perish by a death proper to him, suffocated. The prophet was in the mud up to his throat, which was more bitter to him than any death.

Then Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch in the royal household, secretly said to the king: “These men have caused you to sin grievously.” He replied: “Take thirty men with you and lift the prophet out of the cistern before he dies.” Taking the men, he brought old, rotted rags from the royal house and lowered them by cords into the cistern. He said to Jeremiah: “Put the old rags beneath the armpits of your hands, over the ropes.” When this was done, they drew [Col. 1425D] him from the cistern.

The king secretly summoned him three times to the third entrance, which was in the house of the Lord, and said: “I ask you: hide nothing from me.” Jeremiah answered: “If I give you counsel, you will not listen to me; and if I tell you, you will kill me.” The king swore to him: “As the Lord lives, I shall not kill you or hand you over to the men seeking your life.”

Jeremiah said: “If you go out to the princes of Babylon, you and your household shall be safe, and this city shall not be burned. If you do not go out, the city shall be burned, and you and your household shall not escape their hands.” The king said: “I would do what you say, but I fear the countrymen who have gone over to the Chaldeans, lest they accuse me, I be handed into their power, and they mock me.” Jeremiah said: “You shall not be handed over.” Then the king said: [Col. 1426A] “Let no one know these words. If they ask you, ‘What did the king say to you?’ say, ‘I made my supplication before the king, that he might not send me back to prison’” (Jer. 38).

## Chapter XLIV. On Zedekiah’s Flight and the Capture of the City

Food had failed in the city to such a degree that women ate their little children, measured by the span of a hand, as is read in Jeremiah’s Lamentations (Jer. 39; 2 Kings 25). “The city was captured in the eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month [Note: [Col. 1426C] Addition 1. The city was taken in the fourth month, June; but they sent messengers to the king at Riblah to ask what he wished done with the city, and therefore the servants delayed; it was destroyed in the sixth month.],” according to Josephus and the Book of Kings. According to Jerome, however, the city was opened on the fifth day about midnight, and the Babylonian princes sat in the middle gate.

Zedekiah fled by night with all his household and his friendly princes by the way of the king’s garden. They entered the way [Col. 1426B] of the wilderness. When this was reported by some treacherous persons to the Babylonian princes, they pursued him at dawn and captured him on the plain of the Jericho wilderness. Many of the princes were scattered and withdrew from him. Zedekiah himself, with the rest, was dragged in chains to the king of Babylon at Riblah.

The king pronounced judgment upon him, saying that he had been ungrateful for the authority received from him, had acted hostilely against a benefactor, and had sworn falsely by God; and he added: “The great God, who hates your wickedness, has delivered you to me.” “He killed Zedekiah’s sons before him, and Seraiah the high priest, whose son Jozadak he spared. He also killed the eunuch who was over the fighting men; Sophar, commander of the army, who tested recruits; five [Col. 1426C] men from those who stood before the king; three of the elders of the Temple; and six proven men from the common people—or sixty, according to Jeremiah” (Jer. 52). He put out Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in chains to take him to Babylon, together with Jozadak. Those who had taken them to Riblah then returned to the army at Jerusalem.

## Chapter XLV. On the Burning of the Temple and Cities, and on Gedaliah

Accordingly, in Zedekiah’s eleventh year, in the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month—the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon—Nebuzaradan burned the house of the Lord, the king’s house, and every house in Jerusalem; he destroyed the entire wall of Jerusalem around it and took all the vessels of the Lord’s house, the two columns, and the bronze sea, binding the people in order to bring them to Babylon (2 Kings 25; Jer. 40). These persons are properly called the *captivity of Judah*.

He took Jeremiah from the prison court, concerning whom Nebuzaradan had received this command: “Take him, keep your eyes upon him, and do with him whatever he wishes.” Nebuzaradan then appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam over the land, to govern the poor who had been left behind, the farmers and vine-dressers, so that they might pay yearly tribute to the king of Babylon.

Nebuzaradan sat at Ramah, while prisoners in chains were dragged before [Col. 1427A] him. Taking Jeremiah from among them, he said: “Come with me to Babylon, and I shall honour you. But if that displeases you, remain. The whole land is before you: dwell with Gedaliah, or go wherever you wish” (Jer. 40). Nebuzaradan gave him provisions and small gifts and released him. He similarly allowed the Rechabites to depart freely.

Jeremiah and Baruch his secretary therefore remained among the people who had been left behind. Nebuzaradan went to Babylon, taking the captivity with him. This was the end of the Hebrew kingdom. According to Josephus, it had been ruled for five hundred and fourteen years, six months, and ten days. According to the Book of Kings, it had not quite reached five hundred years; and from David it had twenty-one kings. From the building of the Temple, four hundred and seventy years, six months, and ten days had elapsed. From the people’s departure from Egypt, one thousand and sixty-two years, six months, and ten days had elapsed.

There had been fifteen high priests in succession in the Temple, from the first, Zadok, appointed by Solomon, down to the father of Jozadak, whom the king of Babylon killed.

## Chapter XLVI. On the Death of Zedekiah

When Nebuchadnezzar entered Babylon in triumph, he offered solemn sacrifices to his gods and celebrated with all the people for ten days. As they reclined in merriment, the king ordered Zedekiah to be brought into their midst, with certain singers of the Temple, to play [Col. 1427C] musical instruments before the guests and sing hymns from the songs of Zion.

The guests drank from vessels of the house of the Lord. Nebuchadnezzar consecrated some of these to idols and kept others for himself. While drink was being given to the singers, the king secretly ordered that Zedekiah be given a laxative draught. Before everyone, he disgracefully relieved himself; they mocked him and led him back to prison. Overwhelmed by extreme grief, he died a few days later. When Nebuchadnezzar heard the cause of his death, he brought him out of prison and buried him with royal honour.

**Incidental Matters.**
In the days of Zedekiah the kingdom of the Jews was destroyed, and the fifth age began; [Col. 1427D] in its second year there occurred an eclipse of the sun, which Thales of Miletus had predicted in the days of the captivity. Servius, the sixth king of the Romans, son of a noble captive woman, added three hills to the City: the Quirinal, the Viminal, and the Esquiline. He dug ditches around the walls and first established a census of Roman citizens. At last he was killed by Tarquinius Superbus, son of Tarquinius Priscus. At that time seven men among the Greeks were called sages. At this point we have thought it fitting to insert the discrepancies concerning the comparison of the years of the kings of Judah and of the kings of Israel, together with such resolutions of them as have occurred to us, so that we may at last pursue their history more readily.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Resolution of the discrepancies

In the Book of Kings discrepancies arise concerning the comparison [Col. 1428A] of the years of the kings of Judah and the kings of Israel, which can sometimes be resolved. But where no resolution is found, we believe this has happened through the fault of copyists, who often make mistakes in proper names and numbers.

Rehoboam and Jeroboam reigned concurrently for seventeen years, the one in Judah and the other in Israel. After Rehoboam, his son Abijah began to reign in Jerusalem. In the eighteenth year of Jeroboam, who reigned twenty-two years in Israel, Abijah began to reign; Jeroboam for three years—said synecdochically, that is, for two years and some part of the third, which was Jeroboam’s twentieth. In the remaining part of that same year Asa, son of Abijah, began to reign, and reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem.

In Asa’s second year Nadab, son of Jeroboam, reigned [Col. 1428B] in Israel for two years—that is, for one year and some part of the second year, which was still Asa’s third—and Baasha killed him. Baasha began to reign in Israel in his place in Asa’s third year, and reigned thirty-four years, though not complete years; for otherwise he would have reigned until Asa’s twenty-seventh year, whereas he reigned only until the twenty-sixth. Thus Elah, son of Baasha, began to reign in Israel in Asa’s twenty-sixth year. He reigned for two years—that is, for one year and some part of the second, which was Asa’s twenty-seventh year—and in that same year Zimri killed Elah and reigned in his place for seven days.

After his death the people were divided. One part followed Tibni, the other followed Omri; Omri prevailed and reigned twelve years in [Col. 1428C] Israel. Here it should be noted that the contest for the kingdom between Omri and Tibni lasted for more than three years, since Scripture immediately says that Omri began to reign in Asa’s thirty-first regnal year. For if, upon Zimri’s death, Omri had immediately begun to reign when he was chosen, he would have begun to reign in Asa’s twenty-seventh or twenty-eighth year. Yet Scripture later says that he began to reign in the year of his election, when it says that his son Ahab began to reign in Asa’s twenty-eighth regnal year. For if Omri reigned twelve years and began to reign in Asa’s twenty-first year, while Asa reigned only forty-one years, it is clear that Omri outlived Asa by one year. How then [Col. 1428D] did Ahab, succeeding his father, begin to reign in Asa’s thirty-eighth regnal year?

This may be resolved as follows. When Scripture says that Omri began to reign in Asa’s thirty-first year, it is to be understood that he then began to reign alone and over all Israel, Tibni having died. But when it says that he reigned twenty-two years, or elsewhere twelve years, it counts from Asa’s twenty-eighth year, when Israel chose him as king. This period extends to Asa’s twenty-eighth regnal year, when Ahab began to reign. The following Scriptural statement accords with this interpretation: it relates that Jehoshaphat, son of Asa, began to reign in Ahab’s fourth regnal year, which was Asa’s last, namely his forty-first.

Now Jehoshaphat reigned in Jerusalem twenty-five years. In his [Col. 1429A] seventeenth year Ahaziah, son of Ahab, began to reign in Israel, and reigned two years. Since he had no son, his brother Joram succeeded him in the kingdom; and Joram began to reign in Israel in the second year of Joram, son of Jehoshaphat. But the question arises: if Ahaziah began to reign in Jehoshaphat’s seventeenth year, and reigned only two years, how did his brother Joram begin to reign in the second year of Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, rather than in Jehoshaphat’s eighteenth or nineteenth year? Moreover, in what follows Scripture immediately adds that Joram, son of Ahab, reigned in Jehoshaphat’s eighteenth or nineteenth year.

This discrepancy may be resolved as follows. The two years during which Ahaziah is said to have reigned are those in which he reigned alone and [Col. 1429B] in health, before falling through the lattice of his house. But the remaining eight or nine years, during which his brother Joram conducted the administration of the kingdom while Ahaziah languished, are reckoned not to Joram but to his brother. Hence Joram is written to have reigned in Jehoshaphat’s eighteenth year, because he then undertook the administration of the kingdom for his ailing brother. But the Scripture which says that Joram, son of Ahab, reigned in the second year of Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, considers the time when he began to reign alone, his brother now dead.

Indeed, the account of the Book of Kings was compiled from the writings of different prophets. Hence one writer and another assigned the beginning of the reigns of the kings, both of Judah and Israel, differently, according to differing systems of reckoning. Joram, son of Ahab, reigned twenty-two [Col. 1429C] years over Israel. Therefore the Scripture which later says that, in the fifth year of Joram, son of Ahab, king of Israel, Joram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, reigned, considers the time when he began administering the kingdom for his brother, who was still alive.

Now Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and reigned eight years in Jerusalem. In the twelfth year of Joram, son of Ahab, Ahaziah, son of Joram king of Judah, reigned. He was twenty-two years old when he began to reign and reigned one year in Jerusalem. Some corrupt manuscripts say that Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, was only twenty-two years old when he began to reign, which cannot stand. For if he were only twenty-two [Col. 1429D] years old when he began to reign and reigned only eight years, he was thirty when he died; yet the son succeeding him was already twenty-two years old. Therefore Joram was eight years old when he fathered him, which is impossible.

The Hebrews nevertheless maintain that Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, reigned twenty years and lived forty-two, which seems to accord with the text stating that he was twenty-two years old when he began to reign. But they say that Scripture reckons to his reign only the eight years during which he lived innocently, before killing his brothers.

Upon Ahaziah’s death, his mother Athaliah reigned six years in Jerusalem. During those same six years Jehu reigned concurrently with her; he reigned twenty-eight years in Israel. [Col. 1430A] In Jehu’s seventh year Joash began to reign in Jerusalem and reigned forty years. Thus Joash in Judah and Jehu in Israel reigned together for twenty-two years. When these had ended, Jehu died, and his son Jehoahaz succeeded him in the kingdom. He began to reign in the twenty-third year of Joash king of Judah and reigned seventeen years in Israel.

But the question arises: if Jehoahaz began to reign in Joash’s twenty-third year and reigned seventeen years, while Joash reigned only forty years, it is clear that Jehoahaz reigned until Joash’s thirty-ninth—or rather fortieth—year. How then does Scripture immediately say in what follows that Joash, son of Jehoahaz, began to reign in the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah? Perhaps he reigned jointly with his father for three years while his father was alive. Or perhaps the negligence of copyists, who often err in numbers, has produced this difficulty.

In the second year of Joash king of Israel, Amaziah reigned in Israel for twenty-nine years. The second year of Joash, in which Amaziah began to reign, is reckoned from the time when he reigned alone, his father having died.

> [Note: [Col. 1432B] Addition 1. This is added because the resolution stated that Joash reigned jointly with his father for three years in Israel.]

Amaziah king of Judah lived twenty-five years after Joash king of Israel died. Here too a question arises. It was stated above that Amaziah began to reign in the second year of Joash king of Israel and reigned twenty-nine years. Joash, however, reigned sixteen years. Thus they reigned together for fifteen years. Upon Joash’s death, therefore, only fourteen years remained to Amaziah, or at most fifteen. Perhaps the copyist erred in writing twenty-five instead of [Col. 1430C] fourteen; or perhaps Amaziah ceased to reign while alive and lived ten or eleven years longer than he reigned.

Now in Amaziah’s fifteenth year Jeroboam reigned in Israel for forty-one years. Thus Amaziah in Judah and Jeroboam in Israel reigned together for at most fifteen years. What then is meant by the following Scriptural statement: that Uzziah, son of Amaziah, reigned in Jerusalem in Jeroboam’s twenty-seventh year? Perhaps Judah was without a king for fifteen years, because, as we have said, Amaziah gave up the kingdom while alive and Uzziah, still a boy, could not reign. But after his father died, when he was ten years old and Jeroboam in Israel had begun the twenty-seventh year of his reign, he began to reign in [Col. 1430D] Jerusalem and reigned fifty-two years.

Now in the thirty-eighth year of Uzziah king of Judah, Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, reigned in Israel for six months. Here again a question arises. It was stated above that Uzziah began to reign in Jeroboam’s twenty-seventh year; Jeroboam reigned forty-one years in Israel, while Uzziah reigned fifty-two years. Thus Uzziah and Jeroboam reigned together for fourteen years. When Jeroboam died after forty-one years, if his son Zechariah immediately succeeded to the kingdom, he would have begun to reign not in Uzziah’s thirty-seventh year but in his fifteenth. Therefore either the kingdom of Israel was without a king for twenty-three years, or rather Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, reigned throughout these twenty-three years, but these years [Col. 1431A] were not reckoned to him as reign because he lived most wickedly. Only the six months in which he lived more uprightly, in Uzziah’s thirty-eighth year, were reckoned to him.

In Uzziah’s thirty-ninth year Shallum, having killed Zechariah, reigned in Israel for one month. In that same year Menahem killed Shallum and reigned in Israel for ten years. In Uzziah’s fiftieth year Pekahiah, son of Menahem, reigned in Israel for two years. In Uzziah’s fifty-second year Pekah, son of Remaliah, killed Pekahiah and reigned in Israel for twenty years. In Pekah’s second year Jotham reigned in Jerusalem, and reigned there sixteen years. Thus Jotham in Judah and Pekah in Israel reigned simultaneously for at least fifteen years. The year which was Jotham’s last was Pekah’s tenth; and so [Col. 1431B] Pekah reigned three years after Jotham, during which Ahaz, son of Jotham, reigned jointly with him.

Therefore, when we read that Hoshea killed Pekah and reigned in his place in the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah, Scripture counts Jotham’s reign from the time when he reigned jointly with his leprous father. But where we read that he reigned in Pekah’s second year, and that he reigned sixteen years, it counts from the time when he reigned alone after his father’s death.

Now in Ahaz’s twelfth year Hoshea reigned ten years in Israel. If, therefore, Pekah and Ahaz reigned jointly for only three years, as has been stated, Pekah was killed in Ahaz’s fourth year. And if Hoshea, who killed him, did not reign in his place until Ahaz’s twelfth year, then the kingdom of Israel was without a king for eight years. Thus the aforesaid discrepancies, and any others we have omitted, may be resolved either by synecdoche, or because some reigned jointly with their fathers before reigning alone, or because kingdoms were sometimes without a king.

Here ends the history of the Books of Kings, [Col. 1432B] in which the Books of Chronicles are also included.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF TOBIT

[Col. 1431]

[Col. 1431B] The history of Tobit began with the captivity of the ten tribes carried out by Shalmaneser. But at what time it ended is not sufficiently clear. For according to the literal sense of the history, Tobit seems [Col. 1431C] to have lived after the destruction of Jerusalem and the burning of the Temple. For in his song he says: “Jerusalem, city of God, the Lord has chastised you; bless God for ages of ages, that he may rebuild his tabernacle in you and bring back to you all the captives” (Tobit 13). And at the time of his death, when he foretold to his sons the return of the captives, he said: “The desolate land shall be filled, and the house of God which was burned in it shall be rebuilt again” (Tobit 14).

But if we consider the end of the life of Tobit, son of Tobit—for the end of the history was the end of his life—we shall not find that the history extends beyond the time of Josiah. For let us suppose that the son was taken captive with his father in Hezekiah’s sixth year and was one year old: he lived only ninety-nine years and died about Josiah’s twentieth year.

Jerome translated this history [Col. 1431D] from the Chaldean language into Latin at the request of the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus. The Jews place this history among the apocrypha.

> [Note: [Col. 1432B] Addition 1. Recall what was said above at the beginning of Joshua: “apocryphal” is said either of a work whose author is uncertain or whose subject matter is uncertain. But the subject matter [Col. 1432C] of this work is evident and established. “Hagiograph” means “sacred writing,” and thus any sacred writing can be so called.]

Yet Jerome says in his Prologue that it is among the Hagiographa. If so, it would nevertheless be in the third rank of the Old Testament canon. But because it belongs to no rank, we shall say that Jerome used “Hagiographa” in a broader sense, so as to include the apocrypha as well. And because the Chaldean language is close to Hebrew speech, Jerome, possessing a speaker skilled in both languages, rendered into [Col. 1432B] Latin, in a brief labour almost of a single day, whatever that speaker expressed in Hebrew words.

## CHAPTER I. On Tobit

[Col. 1432C]

Now Tobit was of the tribe of Naphtali (Tobit 1). While the others went to the golden calves made by Jeroboam (3 Kings 12), he went up to Jerusalem to worship the God of Israel. He faithfully offered firstfruits and tithes, so that in the third year he supplied the entire tithe to proselytes and strangers; and in all things he observed the law of God from childhood.

When he became a man, he took Anna, of his own tribe, as his wife, and had by her a son, whom he named Tobit after himself. Taken captive with his wife and son, he lived in Nineveh and guarded himself [Col. 1432D] from being defiled by Gentile food. He sternly rebuked his fellow tribesmen who did not keep themselves undefiled, and the Lord gave him favour in Shalmaneser’s eyes. Shalmaneser gave him authority to go wherever he wished among the captives and to do among them whatever he wished.

As he travelled through the region with his fellow captives, giving counsels of salvation, he came to Rages, a city of the Medes, and found there a fellow tribesman of his, Gabael, who was needy. He left with him, under a written bond, ten talents of silver which he had from the possessions for which he had been honoured by the king.

After [Col. 1433A] Shalmaneser died, his son Sennacherib hated the children of Israel. Tobit comforted them and ministered to the needy. When Sennacherib returned from Judaea, his army having been struck down by an angel at night, he fled from the hand of the Lord. In anger he caused many Hebrews to be killed, and Tobit buried their bodies. When this was reported to the king, he seized all Tobit’s possessions and commanded that he be killed. But Tobit fled with his wife and son and hid, because many loved him. After forty-five days, when the king had been killed by his sons, Tobit returned to his house and what had been taken from him was restored.

Now on a certain feast day, when a meal had been prepared at Tobit’s house, he said to his son: “Go and bring some of our tribe who fear God, that they may eat [Col. 1433B] with us” (Tobit 2). Returning, he reported that one of the Hebrews lay slain in the street. Tobit sprang up, fasting, secretly brought the body into his house, and ate bread in mourning and trembling. When the sun had set, he buried it. His neighbours reproached him, saying: “You were ordered to be killed on account of this very matter, and do you bury the dead again?” But Tobit, fearing God more than the king, earnestly persisted in caring for the burial of those killed.

It happened one day that, exhausted from burial, he returned home, threw himself down beside a wall, and fell asleep. Hot droppings from a swallow’s nest fell upon his eyes, and he became blind. God permitted this to happen in order to test him and to provide [Col. 1433C] an example of patience for the future. In everything he blessed God, as blessed Job did, and rebuked those neighbours who mocked him, saying: “Do not speak thus. For we are children of the holy ones, and we await that life which God will give to his faithful.”

His wife Anna went daily to work at weaving and brought home whatever she could earn by the labour of her hands. It happened that she received a kid and brought it home. Hearing its bleating, her husband said: “See whether it is stolen.” His angry wife replied: “Your hope has plainly proved vain, and your alms have perished.” Tobit groaned with tears and said: “And now, Lord, do with me according to your will, and command that my spirit be received in peace. For it is better for me [Col. 1433D] to die than to live.”

On the same day it happened that Sarah, daughter of Raguel, in a city of the Medes, heard the reproach of one of her maidservants, whom she was rebuking. The maid said to her: “Murderess of your husbands, do you wish to kill me as you killed your seven husbands?” (Tobit 3). For she had been given to seven husbands, and the demon named Asmodeus killed them as soon as they entered to her.

Sarah therefore went up to an upper room of her house, and for three days and nights, neither eating nor drinking, persisted in prayer, saying: “I beseech you, Lord God of our fathers, either free me from the bond of this reproach, or at least take me away from the earth.” At that time the prayers of them both were heard in [Col. 1434A] the Lord’s sight, and the angel Raphael was sent to heal them.

“Therefore, when Tobit thought that he had been heard in order that he might die, he said to his son: Hear, my son, my words, and establish them as foundations in your heart. When I die, you shall bury me, and you shall honour your mother as long as she lives. When she dies, bury her beside me. Always keep the Lord in mind, my son, and keep his commandments. Give alms from your substance, because almsgiving delivers from every sin and gives great confidence before God to all who practise it. Take heed, my son, against every form of fornication and against pride, from which all destruction took its beginning. Seek counsel from a wise man; turn aside from sinners. Let not a labourer’s wage remain with [Col. 1434B] you. Do not fear, my son, because we have lived a poor life; but we shall have many good things if we fear God. Moreover, know that I gave Gabael ten talents of silver at Rages, and I have his written bond. Seek out, therefore, a trustworthy man to go with you, preserving his wage, so that you may return his bond to Gabael and he may restore the deposit to you” (Tobit 4).

“Then Tobit went out and found a young man girded and apparently ready for a journey, not knowing that he was an angel of God” (Tobit 5). When he learned from him that he knew the whole region of the Medes, the city of Rages, and Gabael who lived there, he brought him in to his father. The young man greeted him, saying: “May joy always be yours.”

[Col. 1434C] He replied: “What joy can there be for me, who do not see the light of heaven?”

The young man said to him: “Take courage; your healing by God is near.”

Tobit said: “Will you be able to lead my son to Gabael?”

He replied: “I will lead him and bring him back to you.”

When Tobit asked his tribe, household, and name, he answered: “I am of the children of Israel, Azariah, son of the great Ananias.” All this was true according to the interpretation of the names. For he was among the angels who see God; he was Azariah, that is, “helper,” and son of Ananias, that is, “the glory of God.”

Then, when all that was needed for the journey had been prepared, the two travelled together, “and a dog followed them” (Tobit 6). But his mother wept, saying to her husband: “You have taken away the staff of our old age. [Col. 1434D] Would that the money for which you sent him had never existed! Our poverty was sufficient for us, so that we might count ourselves rich because we saw our son.”

Tobit said: “Do not weep. Our son will return safely to us, for I believe that a good angel of God accompanies him” (Tobit 5).

Now the two of them lodged at their first stopping-place near the river Tigris (Tobit 6). “Tobit went out to wash his feet, and an enormous fish came up to devour him. Frightened, Tobit cried out: ‘Lord, it is attacking me!’ The angel said: ‘Take hold of its gill and draw it toward you.’ He drew it out on dry land, and it thrashed before his feet.”

On this passage Bede says that, while Christ [Col. 1435A] upon the cross washed his feet that walked upon the earth, the devil came, seeking whether he might find any sin in him. Hence: “Father, take this cup away from me” (Mark 14).

Then the angel said to Tobit: “Gut this fish, and keep its heart, gall, and liver, for they are useful for remedies.” Tobit then roasted part of the fish and they ate it; the other part they salted and carried with them. As they travelled together, Tobit said: “Brother Azariah, what remedy do the things you told me to preserve from the fish possess?”

He replied: “A piece of the heart placed upon coals, by its smoke drives every kind of demon from a man or woman.” Nor should we wonder at this, since the smoke of a certain burned tree is reported to possess the same power.

When Tobit asked where they would lodge that night, [Col. 1435B] the angel replied: “Here is your kinsman Raguel, who has an only daughter, due to you with all her property.”

Tobit said: “I hear that she has been given to seven husbands, and that they were killed by a demon.”

The angel replied: “Do not fear. The demon has power over the wanton and those who do not fear God. But when you receive her, you shall refrain from her for three days, and at night you shall both devote yourselves to prayer. On the first night, after the fish’s liver has been burned, the demon will be driven away by your prayers. On the second night you shall be admitted into the union of the holy patriarchs—that is, you shall pray to God that he may admit you to a share in the holiness and chastity of the patriarchs. On the third night you shall obtain a blessing, so that sound and healthy children may be begotten [Col. 1435C] from you.”

This blessing was bestowed either by a priest or by someone greater among them, acting in the priest’s stead. “On the fourth night you shall receive her with the fear of God, guided more by the love of children than by lust, so that in the seed of Abraham you may obtain the blessing in your children.”

“At last they entered Raguel’s house” (Tobit 7). When Raguel said to his wife that the young man was strikingly like his kinsman Tobit, the angel said to him: “This is his son.” Raguel rejoiced and prepared a feast.

Then Tobit said: “I will neither eat nor drink unless you first grant my request and promise to give me your daughter Sarah.”

When Raguel heard this, he was afraid; and while he hesitated how to answer, the angel said to him: “Do not fear [Col. 1435D] to give her to him as his wife. For she is due to him, and therefore no other could have her.”

Then Raguel said: “I know that you have come from God and that the Lord has heard my prayers and tears, so that this daughter of mine might be united to her own kindred according to the law of Moses.”

Taking his daughter’s right hand, her father placed it in Tobit’s right hand, saying: “May the God of our fathers be with you, join you together, and fulfil his blessing in you.” They drew up a marriage contract and ate, blessing God.

After supper they brought the young man into the virgin’s chamber (Tobit 8), and Tobit took from his wallet a portion of the liver and placed it upon coals. Then Raphael seized the demon and bound it in the desert of Upper Egypt. [Col. 1436A] Then Tobit said to the virgin: “Sarah, let us pray to God today, tomorrow, and the next day,” that is, on the third day. “For during these three nights we are joined to God; on the fourth night we shall be in our marriage. For we are children of the holy ones; we cannot be joined together as the nations are, who do not know God.”

They both prayed together, saying: “Have mercy upon us, Lord God of our fathers; have mercy upon us, and let us grow old together in health.”

But around cockcrow Raguel had a grave prepared, so that he might bury him before daylight, and sent one of the maidservants to see whether he was already dead. She returned and reported that they were unharmed and sleeping together. All praised God, and the servants filled in the pit which they had made before [Col. 1436B] daylight. They prepared a solemn feast for all their neighbours and friends.

Raguel made Tobit swear to remain with him for two weeks. He gave him half of all that he possessed, making a written document that the remaining half should come to Tobit after Raguel’s death.

Then Tobit said to the angel, whom he believed to be a man (Tobit 9): “Brother Azariah, you know how burdensome our delay is to my parents. I beseech you: go to Gabael, give him his bond, receive the money from him, and urge him to come to the wedding.”

Raphael then took four of Raguel’s servants and two camels, went to Gabael, and, having received the money, brought him with him to the wedding. Entering, Gabael found them reclining at table [Col. 1436C] and blessed them. When all had said “Amen,” they celebrated the wedding feast in the fear of the Lord.

Now while Tobit delayed at the wedding, his father was anxious for him because he had not returned on the appointed day. His mother wept inconsolably, saying: “Alas for me, my son! Why did we send you to travel abroad, light of our eyes and staff of our old age?” (Tobit 10). But her husband comforted her.

Raguel said to his son-in-law: “Stay here, and I shall send your father a message that you are safe.” When Tobit would not agree, Raguel gave him Sarah and half his property—in male and female servants, sheep, camels, cattle, and much money. Her parents [Col. 1436D] admonished their daughter to honour her father-in-law, love her husband, govern the household, manage the home, and show herself beyond reproach.

As they returned, they came to Charan, which lies halfway along the journey. The angel said to Tobit: “Let the two of us go ahead, while your wife and household follow at a slower pace with the animals. Take some of the fish’s gall with you; you shall anoint your father’s eyes with it, and he will regain his sight.”

Now Anna sat each day beside the road upon a mountain ridge from which she could look into the distance. Recognizing her son coming from afar, she ran to her husband and said: “Behold, your son is coming.” The dog also, which had been with them on the journey, ran ahead and rejoiced like a messenger, wagging its tail.

Then [Col. 1437A] the blind man arose, gave his hand to the boy, and went out to meet his son. Kissing their son, they wept for joy. After they had worshipped God, they sat down. Then Tobit applied the fish’s gall to his father’s eyes. He waited about half an hour, and a whiteness began to come out of his eyes like the membrane of an egg. Tobit took hold of it and drew it from his eyes, and immediately he recovered his sight. They all glorified God.

Tobit said: “I bless you, God of Israel, because you chastised me and healed me; and behold, I see Tobit my son.”

Seven days later his wife Sarah entered with all her property and the money which he had received from Gabael. Fellow tribesmen and neighbours gathered around Tobit, and for seven days they rejoiced with him, feasting gladly (Tobit 11).

[Col. 1437B] When Tobit had related to his father in order the good things which the angel had done for him on the journey, they took the angel aside and begged him to accept half of all that they had brought back. Then the angel said to them privately: “Bless the God of heaven, and confess him before all, because he has shown you his mercy. For it is good to conceal the secret of a king, but honourable to reveal and confess the works of God. I will not conceal from you a hidden saying. Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good. When you prayed, left your meal, hid the dead by day, and buried them by night, I presented your prayer to the Lord. Because you were acceptable to him, it was necessary that temptation should test you. The Lord sent me [Col. 1437C] to heal you and to free Sarah, your son’s wife, from the demon. For I am Raphael the angel, one of the seven”—that is, of all—“who stand before the Lord.”

When they heard this, trembling, they fell upon their faces. The angel said: “Peace be with you; do not fear. When I was with you, I seemed to eat and drink with you out of necessity, but I use invisible food and drink, which cannot be seen by human beings. It is time for me to return to him who sent me.” Saying this, he was taken from their sight.

Then, prostrate upon their faces for three hours, they blessed God; and rising, they told of all his wonders (Tobit 12). Tobit the elder opened his mouth, blessed the Lord, and said: [Col. 1437D] “Great are you, Lord, for ever, because you afflict and save; you lead down to hell and bring back. There is none who escapes your hand” (Tobit 13).

In this song he exhorted Jerusalem and God’s captive people to turn to the Lord after his example, do righteousness before him, and believe that he would show them mercy. He prophesied concerning Jerusalem, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall worship you; nations shall come to you from afar, and, bringing gifts, shall worship the Lord in you.” That this was spoken mystically concerning the time of grace appears from what follows: “The gates of Jerusalem shall be built of sapphire and emerald, and alleluia shall be sung through its streets.”

Tobit was fifty years old when he lost his sight; he recovered it at sixty, [Col. 1438A] and afterwards lived forty-two years. He saw the children of his grandchildren and completed one hundred and two years (Tobit 14). The Gloss, however, appears to understand mystically that he lived forty-two years after receiving sight, referring forty to the labours of abstinence and two to the love of God and neighbour.

When he saw that death was near, he summoned his son and his seven sons and said to them: “The destruction of Nineveh will be near. I see that its iniquity will bring about its end. For the word of God shall not fail; and our brothers who have been scattered from the land of Israel shall return to it, and it shall be filled, and the house of God which was burned in it shall be rebuilt.”

Yet he seems to have foretold this with prophetic certainty in the form of past tense [Col. 1438B] words, rather than narrated an accomplished event. For Jerusalem and its Temple were still standing. After admonishing them concerning the love and fear of God, the giving of alms, and the duty of commanding their own sons to do the same, he added: “But do not remain here. On whatever day you bury your mother beside me in one tomb, direct your steps from there, so that you may depart from here.”

Tobit died, and afterwards his wife. Tobit the younger departed from Nineveh with his wife, sons, and grandchildren, returned to his parents-in-law, and found them in a good old age. He cared for them and closed their eyes—that is, the eyes of Raguel and Anna.

It should be noted that five women in Sacred Scripture are called Anna: the mother of Samuel; Tobit’s wife; Raguel’s wife; [Col. 1438C] the mother of the Blessed Virgin Mary; and Anna the prophetess.

Tobit the younger also died, having completed ninety-nine years. All his kindred and all his descendants buried him. For he remained in holy conduct, so that he was acceptable both to God and to human beings.

Here ends the history of Tobit. We now return to the history of the captivity of Jerusalem, and shall expound the histories of Judith and Esther in their proper places.

## CHAPTER II. On the death of Gedaliah
When the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah over the remnant of the land, all who had escaped the hands of the enemy came to him—those who had hidden among the neighboring nations [Col. 1438D], or had saved their lives in whatever hiding-places they could; and many also from the ten tribes, to whom living alongside the Samaritans was burdensome (Jer. XL). Among them were certain leaders of the land: Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah, and Jeconiah. Gedaliah said to them: “Do not be afraid. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall go well with you. I live at Mizpah, to answer the commands of the Chaldeans who will be sent to us, so that you may not be oppressed in any respect.” Having confirmed this by oath, he dismissed them to the places in the province which each had chosen for himself.

Now there was a certain Ishmael of royal stock, a wicked man. While Jerusalem was under siege, he escaped to the king of the Ammonites and stayed there. Johanan son of Kareah said secretly to Gedaliah: [Col. 1439A] “I know that Ishmael is plotting against your life, envying you the half of the land. Or rather, the king of the Ammonites will send him to strike you down, so that he may seize the desolated land. Therefore I shall go and kill Ishmael without anyone knowing, lest he kill you and the remnant of Judah be scattered and perish.” But Gedaliah said: “Do not do this thing, to kill an innocent man. It is not credible that, amid such desolation, he would commit such wickedness.”

In the seventh month of the same year Ishmael came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and Gedaliah received them splendidly (Jer. XLI). After the meal, when Gedaliah and his guests had turned to sleep, Ishmael struck them down. Going out by night, he slaughtered the Jews who were in the city and certain soldiers left there by the Babylonians, [Col. 1439B] and threw their corpses into the cistern which King Asa had made because of Baasha king of Israel. On the next day eighty men were coming from the province with gifts for Gedaliah. Ishmael went out to meet them and said: “Come in to Gedaliah.” When they had entered, Ishmael killed them, except for ten who said to him: “Spare us, for we have treasures in the field—wheat, wine, barley, oil, and honey—and we shall give them to you.” So they withdrew from him.

Then Ishmael carried captive the remnant of the people who were at Mizpah, including the king’s daughters, whom Nebuzaradan had entrusted to Gedaliah. When Johanan son of Kareah heard this, he took men and pursued Ishmael. He found him by the waters that are at Gibeon; Ishmael fled from him [Col. 1439C] with eight men, and Johanan brought back the captives and the spoil which Ishmael had carried off.

## CHAPTER III. On the descent of the remnant of Judah into Egypt, and Jeremiah’s death

“And all the remnant of Judah, from the least to the greatest, assembled before Jeremiah” (Jer. XLII). They intended to flee into Egypt, fearing that the Chaldeans would kill them because of Gedaliah’s death. They said to the prophet: “Pray to God for us, that he may show us what we ought to do; and whatever he tells us through your mouth, we will do.”

After seven days the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah. Calling together all the people, he said: “Thus says the Lord: If you remain in this land, I shall plant you [Col. 1439D] and not uproot you. For I have now relented concerning the evil that I brought upon you. Do not fear the king of Babylon, for I am with you. But if you go down into Egypt to live there, the sword of Nebuchadnezzar, which you fear, will overtake you there, and you shall perish by sword, famine, and pestilence.”

But they did not listen to Jeremiah. Instead they said: “You lie; the Lord has not sent you. Rather, Baruch is inciting you against us, to hand us over to the Chaldeans” (Jer. XLIII). So they all went down into Egypt with their women, little children, and all their possessions, and took Jeremiah and Baruch with them. The land was desolated and kept Sabbath for many years, as Jeremiah had foretold.

> [Note: [Col. 1441B] Addition 1. Jerusalem was destroyed three times—that is, on three occasions: first, by the deportation of Jehoiachin and those deported with him; secondly, by Zedekiah’s captivity and the destruction of the Temple; thirdly, by its desolation, when it was left solitary as the remnant went down into Egypt. A fourth devastation of the land preceded these three.]

For the king of Babylon did not transfer colonists into it, as the king of Assyria had done [Col. 1440A] in the land of Israel. The remnant of Judah lived in Egypt at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and in the land of Pathros; and that is the name of the king from whom that part of Egypt was so called.

“The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah at Tahpanhes, saying: Take large stones and hide them in the hollow which is beneath the brickwork at the entrance of Pharaoh’s house. And you shall say to the Jews: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall take my servant Nebuchadnezzar and set his throne upon these stones, and he shall strike the land of Egypt, and you shall perish with the Egyptians.”

Now the Hebrew women sacrificed to foreign gods and offered cakes and libations to the queen of heaven—namely, the moon, or Juno, or Berecynthia. When Jeremiah rebuked them, they said: [Col. 1440B] “Did we do these things without our husbands?” (Jer. XLIV). When he spoke more harshly to the men, they said: “When we did these things in the cities of Judah, we had our fill of bread and were well. But since we stopped, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by sword and famine.”

Jeremiah replied: “Thus says the Lord: I have sworn by my great name that all the men of Judah who are in the land of Egypt shall perish by sword and famine, until they are utterly consumed.” Then the people rose against Jeremiah and stoned him with the stones which he had hidden beneath the brick wall.

The Egyptians, however, honored the prophet by burying him beside the tomb of the kings, remembering the benefits he had bestowed upon Egypt. By his prayer he had driven away asps and [Col. 1440C] water-beasts, which the Greeks call *crocodiles*, by which Egypt had previously been plagued. Some also relate that even now the bite of an asp is healed by dust from that place, and crocodiles are put to flight.

Epiphanius says of him: “We heard from elderly men descended from the elders of Antigonus and Ptolemy that Alexander of Macedon, coming to the prophet’s tomb and learning the mystery of the place, transferred him to Alexandria and buried him gloriously. From that time crocodiles and asps were wholly prohibited from that land. For Alexander himself had earlier introduced certain serpents there which, in place of Marsian snake-charmers, drove away the asps, but could not wholly eradicate them. Because he had brought these snakes from Argos in the Peloponnese, he called them *argones*.”

This is Jeremiah, [Col. 1440D] who gave the kings of Egypt the sign that their idols must be overthrown when a virgin should give birth. Therefore their priests, setting up an image of a virgin and child in a secret place of the temple, worshipped it. When King Ptolemy asked why they did this, they replied that it was the mystery of a paternal tradition: their forefathers had received it from the holy prophet, and they believed that it would come to pass in this manner.

This is Jeremiah who, foreknowing that the Temple was to be overthrown, took the ark of the covenant with the things within it and, by his prayers, caused them to be swallowed up in a rock. Pointing at the rock with his finger, he impressed upon it the tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God. A seal was formed like writing engraved with iron; and the Lord’s very name [Col. 1441A] was so concealed beneath a covering cloud that, from that time until this day and until the end, no one can recognize the place or read the name. Often a cloud in its former form hangs there; at night it becomes fire, because the glory of God does not cease from his law.

That rock lies in desert country between two mountains, on which Moses and Aaron lie. Jeremiah said to those present: “The Lord has departed from Zion to heaven; from there he will come again in power. The sign of his presence will be when all nations worship the wood.” He also said that no one except Aaron could bring forth this ark, and that none of the priests or prophets could open the tablets within it except Moses, God’s chosen one. In the first resurrection to come, when [Col. 1441B] the dead rise, this ark will be the first to rise; it will come forth from the rock and be placed on Mount Zion. All the saints will gather to it, awaiting the Lord’s return and fleeing the adversary who will seek to kill them in the meantime.

## CHAPTER IV. On the captivity of the remnant of Judah

[Col. 1442A]

> [Note: [Col. 1441B] What follows has been taken up from diverse sources.]

After Jeremiah’s death, in the fifth year after Jerusalem’s overthrow—the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign—Nebuchadnezzar went down into Lower Syria and gained possession of it. He also subdued the Moabites and Ammonites. At last he entered Egypt, overthrew it, killed the king then reigning there, and, appointing another in his place, [Col. 1442B] again carried the Jews captive to Babylon.

From this final captivity of the remnant of Judah some reckon seventy years until the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes. Ezekiel too foretold this captivity of the remnant while in Chaldea (ch. XXIV). We shall now pursue his account more fully, beginning higher up.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF EZEKIEL

[Col. 1441]

## CHAPTER I. Preface

[Col. 1441B]

Ezekiel the prophet, from the land of Cysare, was the son of Buzi and of priestly descent (Ezek. I). He was taken to Babylon [Col. 1441C] with Jehoiachin and his mother, together with Daniel and the three youths. He lived by the river Chebar.

In the thirtieth year—not only of his own age, but reckoned from the forty-eighth year of Josiah, when Deuteronomy was found in the Temple—in the fifth year of the deportation, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, Ezekiel began to prophesy to his fellow captives for the following reasons. They had read in Jeremiah’s letter that the captivity would last seventy years, and they wept because their exile had been prolonged. Moreover, they murmured against the Lord because he had, as they thought, deceitfully driven them out. For he had said through Jeremiah that those remaining in Jerusalem would perish, whereas he promised good things to those who surrendered to his servant Nebuchadnezzar. [Col. 1441D] Yet events had now turned out contrariwise. Those who had remained were flourishing, while they themselves were oppressed beneath the yoke of servitude.

There were also among them some who said that, while they had served the host of heaven, they had abounded in every good thing; but since they ceased, they had perished by sword, famine, and pestilence (Jer. XLIV). In answer to these things Ezekiel prophesied that the overthrow of the city and the burning of the Temple were imminent; that those remaining in the city would perish by famine, and those outside it by the sword; that those carried off alive would suffer grievous servitude; but that they themselves would remain in peace and in a servitude that was, as it were, free (Ezek. XI).

To establish his authority, [Col. 1442B] God showed him certain visions: namely, the likenesses of a man, a lion, a calf, and an eagle (Ezek. I), not only to foreshadow [Col. 1442C] the Evangelists, but also to show that the God of Israel is Lord of all creation, understanding the whole of creation through these more excellent creatures. Man rules the other living creatures; the eagle is king of birds, the lion of wild beasts, and the ox of domestic animals. Beneath the living creatures he saw a wheel within a wheel, to show that the revolutions of all the elements are in the Lord’s power. Above them he saw a firmament of sapphire color; above the firmament was the likeness of a throne, and above the throne a likeness like the appearance of a man.

The Lord said to him: “Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, because they are a provoking house, perhaps they may hear, desist, and know that there was a prophet in their midst. And behold, [Col. 1442D] a hand was stretched out to him, in which was a scroll written inside and outside; and lamentations, a song, and woe were written in it” (Ezek. II).

The Lord said: “Eat this scroll, for I have put my words in your mouth” (Ezek. III). The prophet went to the deportation beside the river Chebar, to the mound of new grain. Sitting in their midst, he placed before them a brick and drew upon it the city of Jerusalem, the siege against it, fortifications, a rampart, camps, and battering-rams all around. He set an iron pan before his eyes, so that he might not see them, and said: “Thus the Lord has hardened his face against [Col. 1443A] Jerusalem, so that he will not see it, and he will besiege it. It is a sign to the house of Israel” (Ezek. IV).

Since there were many from the ten tribes in Jerusalem who had fled there, the Lord also spoke to him concerning them: “Son of man, take wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and vetch; make from them for yourself an ash-baked loaf weighing twenty staters, and cover it before their eyes, to bake it, with human excrement.” When the prophet recoiled from this, God allowed him cattle dung in place of human excrement. “And you shall say to them: Thus shall the children of Israel eat their defiled bread among the nations to which I shall cast them out.”

Again the Lord said to him: “Take a sword that shaves hair”—that is, a razor—“and pass it over your head and beard. Burn a third [Col. 1443B] of the hair with fire in their midst; cut down a third with the sword all around; and scatter a third to the wind. For thus says the Lord concerning Jerusalem: A third of you shall die by famine and pestilence in your midst; a third shall fall by the sword around you; and I shall scatter a third to every wind” (Ezek. V).

## CHAPTER II. On Ezekiel’s elevation and vision

In the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, the Spirit lifted the prophet between heaven and earth and brought him in a vision of God to Jerusalem (Ezek. VIII). At the north, at the entrance of the gate, he saw the idol of Baal. Entering, he saw every idol of the house of Israel depicted all around throughout the whole place. Seventy elders stood there, and Jeconiah [Col. 1443C] the priest was with them; each had a censer in his hand, and a cloud of incense-smoke rose up.

Entering through the gateway at the north, he saw women mourning dead Tammuz—that is, Adonis—and praising him returned to life. Between the porch and the altar he saw twenty-five men with their backs toward the Temple, worshipping toward the rising sun.

> [Note: [Col. 1444A] Addition 1. This was contrary to their custom: since the entrance was on the east, they prayed westward toward the Holy of Holies. We, however, pray toward Jerusalem, or toward the east.]

The Lord said to him: “Son of man, have you seen what they do? Is this a light matter? Behold, I shall deal with them in wrath, and my eye shall not spare them. And behold, six men were coming, holding instruments of destruction in their hands; among them was a man clothed in linen, with a scribe’s ink-horn at his loins” (Ezek. IX). The Lord said to him: [Col. 1443D] “Pass through the midst of the city and mark a Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over the abominations committed there.” And the Lord said to the six men: “Pass through the city after him and strike down everyone upon whom the Tau is not seen. Let your eye spare no one, and begin at my sanctuary.”

As they went through, the prophet cried: “Alas, alas, alas, Lord God! Will you then destroy every remnant of Israel?” The Lord said to the man clothed in linen: “Fill your hand with coals and pour them over the city” (Ezek. X). Doing this, he burned it. But the Spirit of the Lord lifted Ezekiel and returned him to Chaldea (Ezek. XI), and he spoke to the deportation everything that the Lord had shown him.

## CHAPTER III. On the threat against Jerusalem

[Col. 1444A]

After this Ezekiel, in their sight, began by day to carry away the goods of his household, as though migrating to another place (Ezek. XII). In the evening he dug through the wall, and his servants carried him on their shoulders through the breach in the wall, his face veiled so that he saw nothing. The house of Israel said to him: “What are you doing?” He replied: “This burden concerns the king who is in Jerusalem. They will dig through the wall to bring him out; he will leave in the darkness of night; he will be taken [Col. 1444B] in a net—

> [Note: [Col. 1444D] Addition 1. For as a fish is caught by a net, so Zedekiah was captured in the plain of the wilderness of Jericho.]

—he will be brought to Babylon, yet he will not see it, and there he will die.”

Afterward he spoke to the house of Israel in a riddle: “Thus says the Lord: A great eagle with great wings, with a long reach of limbs, full of feathers and variegation”—that is, Nebuchadnezzar—“came to Lebanon,” that is, to the Temple, “and took the marrow of the cedar,” that is, the vessels of the Lord; “and carried off the topmost branches,” that is, Jehoiachin; “and took of the seed of the land,” that is, Mattaniah, “and placed it in the earth, and it grew into a vine,” that is, he made him king and received an oath from him. “And there came to be another great eagle,” that is, Pharaoh. “And behold, this vine stretched out its shoots toward it, that it might water it.
