Shall he who has done these things prosper? And shall he who has broken the covenant [Col. 1444C] escape? As I live, says the Lord, he shall die in the midst of Babylon” (Ezek. XVII).

“And the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, saying: Son of man, write down for yourself the name of this day, on which the king of Babylon has set himself against Jerusalem today. Behold, today I shall take from you the delight of your eyes; you shall groan silently, you shall neither weep nor mourn or make mourning for the dead. You shall not cover your mouth with a garment, nor eat the food of mourners, but your sandals shall remain on your feet, as for one about to depart” (Ezek. XXIV).

His wife died in the evening, and he did not mourn, but was like one about to leave. They asked him what this portended. He replied: [Col. 1444D] “Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall profane my sanctuary, the delight of your eyes, and in your overwhelming anguish you shall not mourn,” because each person will be concerned for his own death.

Afterward the prophet foretold consolation for his own people, and calamities for the surrounding nations which had either aided the enemies against Jerusalem or mocked the captives: the children of Ammon, Moab, Edom, the Philistines, Tyre, Sidon, Egypt, and Ethiopia (Ezek. XXV–XXXII).

## CHAPTER IV. On the consolation of Jerusalem

In the twelfth year of the deportation, [Col. 1445A] in the eleventh month, on the fifth day of the month, someone who had escaped from Jerusalem came to Ezekiel saying: “The city has been laid waste” (Ezek. XXXIII). Yet on the preceding evening Ezekiel had foretold the coming of the messenger. When the entire deported community heard of the city’s destruction and the Temple’s burning, they raised their voices and said: “Our hope has perished; we are cut off.” Ezekiel cried out: Thus says the Lord: “When I have been sanctified in you, I shall take you from the nations and bring you into your land; and I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. XXXVI).

## CHAPTER V. On the resurrection of the dead

“The hand of the Lord came upon the prophet, and [Col. 1445B] brought him out in the Spirit into a plain full of exceedingly dry bones.

> [Note: [Col. 1446A] Addition 1. Some Jews say that this plain was in the desert where so many Jews perished after worshipping the calf; later they wandered in that desert for forty years, and all fell there unburied.]

And he said to him: Son of man, do you think these bones will live? And I said: Lord, you know. And he said: Say to them: Dry bones, thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall lay sinews upon you, cause flesh to grow over you, spread skin over you, give you spirit, and you shall live. While he was still speaking there came a sound and a shaking, and the bones came together, bone to its own joint; and behold, sinews, flesh, and skin were upon them, but they had no spirit” (Ezek. XXXVII).

The Lord said to the prophet: “Cry out to the spirit, and say: Thus says the Lord: Come, spirit, from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.” [Col. 1445C] And so it happened. “Alive, they stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great army. And the Lord said: These bones are the whole house of Israel.”

The Spirit restored the prophet to the midst of the deportation, and he spoke to them what the Lord had shown him as a sign of two things: namely, their recall from captivity and the resurrection of bodies at the end. Ezekiel took one stick and wrote upon it, “the stick of Judah and his companions”; on the other stick he wrote, “the stick of Ephraim—

> [Note: [Col. 1446A] Addition 2. The ten tribes were called the kingdom of Ephraim because Jeroboam, who first reigned over them, was of the tribe of Ephraim.]

—and his companions.” He joined them and held them together in one hand. They said to him: “What do you mean by these?” He replied: “Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall gather the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Ephraim and make them one nation and one kingdom; and my servant [Col. 1445D] David shall be their prince forever.”

“And the Lord spoke to Ezekiel: Son of man, prophesy against Gog and the land of Magog, saying: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of Meshech and Tubal. I shall lead you astray, bring you up from the farthest parts of the north, and bring you upon the mountains of Israel. There you and all your companies shall fall. I shall say to the birds of heaven and the beasts of earth: Hasten and run together from every side to the sacrifice which I slaughter for you upon the mountains of Israel, that you may eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth. I shall give a named grave to the gnawed bones, and I shall send fire upon the land of Magog and upon those dwelling confidently in the islands” (Ezek. XXXVIII–XXXIX).

The Hebrews say that this will happen after the thousand-year kingdom—

> [Note: [Col. 1446A] Addition 3. Not that Gog and Magog are a fable—indeed, they are history—but because this is how it is termed by the Hebrews.]

—and that Gog’s army will be so great [Col. 1446A] that the Hebrews will have wood for use during seven years, not from forests but from weapons; the bones will be gathered for seven years and buried in the valley which for this reason will be called *Polyandrum*—

> [Note: [Col. 1446B] Addition 4. From *polys*, “much,” and *andros*, “man”; or from *polys*, “multitude,” and *andros*, “man.” Hence *polyandrum*, as it were “the burial-place of many men.”]

—as though it were the burial-place of many men.

## CHAPTER VI. That the hand of the Lord came upon Ezekiel

[Col. 1446B]

“In the twenty-fifth year of the deportation”—that is, the thirty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign—“in the first month, on the tenth day of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was struck down, on that very day the hand of the Lord came upon Ezekiel” (Ezek. XL). In the Spirit he brought him into the land of Israel, upon a high mountain, and showed him the plan [Col. 1446C] of the city and Temple, concerning which our authors have remained silent in the literal sense.

Now Ezekiel, in Chaldea among his fellow captives, judged transgressors of the law, especially certain persons from the tribes of Dan and Gad, because they committed impiety against the Lord by persecuting those who kept the law. As Epiphanius says, he performed a great prodigy against them: their sons and all their cattle perished from serpents. He foretold that those tribes would not return to their own country but would remain in the regions of Media. Enraged at him for this, they dragged him with horses over rocky crags, dashed out his brains, and buried him in the field of Maulim, in the tomb of Shem and Arphaxad, in a double cave. In imitation of this Abraham made a tomb for Sarah at Hebron (Gen. XXIII).

[Col. 1446D] It is called double because it is vaulted, and its summit is withdrawn below the surface of the earth on one side, while on the other it hangs in the rock above the ground. This prophet gave the people a sign at the river Chebar: when it ran dry, they were to endure the desolation of their land; when it overflowed, they were to hope for their return to Jerusalem.

A very great multitude of fellow captives once assembled with him by the river Chebar. The Chaldeans, fearing rebellion, rushed upon them. But he, by his prayers, stopped the waters of the river and, walking over the waters with the entire multitude, withdrew to the opposite bank. All the enemies who dared to follow them were drowned. By prayer he also suddenly provided the people with an abundant supply of fish for food. He frequently restored life to many who were dying.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF DANIEL

[Col. 1447]

## CHAPTER I. Preface

[Col. 1447A]

Daniel also prophesied in Chaldea. According to Josephus and Epiphanius, he was of Judah’s royal seed; but according to the Septuagint he was of the tribe of Levi, for they set out the title of the tale of Bel as follows:

> “There was a certain man, a priest named Daniel, son of Abdo, a companion of the king of Babylon; he was born in Upper Beteroth.”

> [Note: [Col. 1448A] Addition 1. The Hebrews call the writing concerning Bel a fable, not because its truth is not established, but because they deny that Daniel wrote it.]

He was so chaste that his fellow tribesmen thought him a eunuch. Jerome translated his book at the request of Paula and Eustochium, with great difficulty. It was written in Hebrew letters—

> [Note: [Col. 1448A] Addition 2. Just as we see French written in Latin letters, though it is not thereby intelligible to everyone who knows the letters.]

—but in the Chaldean language. The Church did not read it according to the Septuagint, because their edition differed greatly from the truth, but according to Theodotion, who among the Hebrews has neither the history of Susanna, nor the hymn [Col. 1447B] of the three youths, nor the tale of Bel and the dragon.

We shall begin his account more fully, first observing that some prophets prophesied concerning the captivity of the two tribes long before it occurred, such as Isaiah and Hosea; others when it was imminent and occurring, such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel; others during it, such as Daniel and Habakkuk; and others after it, such as Haggai and Zechariah.

When Nebuchadnezzar had taken to Babylon the more noble Jewish boys and some of royal stock—the handsomest and most learned among them, who could stand in the royal palace—Josephus says that he castrated them, as he is known to have done also to the peoples of other nations whom he had conquered (Dan. I). He entrusted them to the chief of the eunuchs and had them taught the letters of the provinces, together with Chaldean learning. Chaldean is the same language as [Col. 1447C] Syrian, akin to Hebrew; and he commanded that they be served food from his own table.

Among them were four excellent men from the children of Judah: Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. The king changed their names, and they were called Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Belteshazzar, Epiphanius says, was a name of royal rank, given to Daniel because the king was already considering adopting him. Over these four the chief eunuch appointed a special overseer, Malasar.

They resolved not to defile themselves with Gentile foods. When Malasar compelled them to eat the food, lest they appear thinner before the king than the others, they said to him: “Test us, we pray, for ten days. Give us vegetables and water; afterward look upon [Col. 1447D] our faces and the faces of the others who eat the king’s food, and deal with us as you see fit.” Malasar therefore took away their food and wine and gave them vegetables.

For this reason their minds were clear—not dulled by an abundance of food nor confused by variety—and their bodies better suited to exertion. They suddenly became learned, because the Lord gave them knowledge and instruction, and especially [Col. 1448A] gave Daniel understanding of visions and dreams. At the end of three years they were presented before Nebuchadnezzar.

> [Note: [Col. 1448B] Addition 3. Observe that an abundance of food dulls the mind, while variety confuses its ability.]

Of all the matters about which the king questioned them, he found them ten times superior to all the diviners and magicians in his kingdom. Daniel remained honored in Chaldea even down to Darius and Cyrus—

> [Note: [Col. 1448B] Addition 4. They reigned over the Medes and Persians, and overthrew the Babylonian kingdom.]

This concludes the first pericope of Daniel.

> [Note: [Col. 1448B] Addition 5. The first division, which is not called a vision; for Jerome divided it into ten divisions, not, I say, books.]

There follow nine or ten sections called Daniel’s visions, because in them either Daniel himself saw something or explained something seen by another.

## CHAPTER II. Daniel’s first vision

[Col. 1448B]

In the second year of his reign Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream; his spirit was troubled, and the dream escaped him (Dan. II). “The second year of his reign” must not be understood from its beginning, but from its completion. His kingdom is said to have been completed [Col. 1448C] after, having subdued the nations, he carried the remnant of Israel away from Egypt.

The king therefore summoned the Chaldean interpreters and said to them: “I saw a dream, but I do not know what I saw.”

> [Note: [Col. 1449D] Addition 1. Up to this point this book was written in Hebrew; thereafter it was in Chaldean, up to the vision which he saw in dreams under Belshazzar.]

They replied in Syriac: “Let the king tell the dream to his servants, and we shall declare its interpretation.” The king said: “Unless you tell me the dream and its interpretation, you shall perish and your houses shall be confiscated.” They said: “There is no man on earth who can fulfill your command, except the gods, whose dwelling is not with human beings.”

Then the king, in great anger, commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be killed. Daniel and his companions too were sought, that they might perish. When Daniel heard this, he went in and asked the king to give him time for the solution—only one night, Josephus says. Daniel went home with his companions and prayed to God. In a night vision the mystery was revealed to him; blessing God, he went in to the king.

The king said to him: [Col. 1448D] “Can you tell me the dream and its interpretation?” He replied: “No human being can do this, but there is a God in heaven who reveals [Col. 1449A] mysteries and has shown you what is to come in the last times. These are the visions of your head”—that is, of your heart. For wisdom is in the heart according to the Gospel, not in the head according to the philosopher.

“You were thinking on your bed who would hold dominion over the world after you, and God showed you those who would reign. You saw before you a great and terrible statue: its head and neck were of gold, its neck and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, its lower legs of iron, and its feet partly iron and partly clay. A stone was cut from a mountain without hands; it struck the statue on its feet and shattered it. It was reduced to ash, carried away by the wind, and no place for it was found. But the stone became a great mountain and filled [Col. 1449B] the whole earth.

“Now hear, O king, its interpretation. You are the golden head, with those who shall succeed you. After this another kingdom, inferior to you, shall arise”—this is to be understood of the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, as represented by two arms, through which the Babylonian kingdom was overthrown. “And another third kingdom of bronze shall rule over the whole earth”—this is to be understood of the Greek kingdom, which was more famous, that is, more renowned than the others, whether because of Greek eloquence or Alexander’s fame. “And the fourth kingdom shall be like iron, because as iron subdues all metals, so it shall crush all these”—this is to be understood of the Roman Empire.

“Moreover, because you saw part of the feet earthenware and part iron, just as iron cannot [Col. 1449C] be mixed with clay, so there will be civil discord in it: one part will become firm, the other will be crushed. Then God will raise up the kingdom of heaven, which will pulverize all these kingdoms and stand forever.”

Josephus says concerning this: “Daniel also signified to the king the meaning of the stone, but I did not think it proper to disclose it. The Hebrews, however, refer this to their kingdom, which they expect.”

Then the king fell upon his face and worshipped Daniel, saying: “Truly your God is God of gods.” He gave Daniel authority over all the provinces of Babylon and over all the wise men. Daniel obtained from the king that his three companions should have authority over the provinces, while he himself should preside in Babylon and stand at the king’s gate [Col. 1449D].

## CHAPTER III. Daniel’s second vision
The second vision of Daniel follows. It is called a vision solely because in it the king saw in the furnace a fourth figure like the Son of God (Dan. III). Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue sixty cubits high and six cubits broad, and set it up on the plain of Dura, that is, of a certain river beside which the giants built a tower. The Seventy say, “on the plain of Peribolom,” which means “enclosed.” For, once the statue had been erected, the king enclosed the plain, and summoned all the rulers of the regions to the dedication of the statue [Col. 1450A]; and a herald cried loudly: “At the hour when you hear the sound of the musicians, worship the statue.

[Note: [Col. 1450D] Addition 1.—This is why, when ordinations are performed, before the prayer of the Epistle which says, “O God, who didst deliver the three children,” etc., “Let us bend the knee” is not said.]

Whoever does not worship it shall that same hour be thrown into a furnace of burning fire.” All worshipped except Daniel’s companions. They were accused before the king; the furnace was heated sevenfold; and they were cast, bound and clothed, into the midst of the furnace. But the flame of the fire killed the men who had thrown them in. Jerome said that he had not read in the Hebrew what follows, up to “Then the king was astonished”; but, because these passages were widespread throughout the world,

[Note: [Col. 1450D] Addition 2.—That is, the passages which follow—the canticle and certain other material—were widespread because the translation of Theodotion, which was read everywhere, contained them. Jerome therefore feared to omit them, though he marked them with an obelus.]

he inserted them, placing an obelus before them, lest he should seem to unlearned readers to have mutilated part of the volume.

The furnace was heated with bundles of brushwood, pitch, tow, and naphtha, which, according to the historian Sallust, [Col. 1450B] is a kind of tinder among the Persians; according to others, it is dried olive pits mixed with amurca; according to Pliny, it flows in the land of Babylon like bitumen.

[Note: [Col. 1451A] Addition 3.—Olive pits: the dried fruit of olives, steeped in the dregs of oil.]

“And the flame burst forth and burned those Chaldeans whom it found near the furnace, and spread above the furnace for forty-nine cubits”: this was measured according to a geometrical rule. “But the angel descended with them into the furnace, shook the flame away, and brought in something like a wind blowing dew,” that is, cooling them.

Then Hananiah prayed, saying: “You are righteous, Lord; for we have sinned, and you delivered us into the hands of our enemies. But may we be received by you in a contrite mind and a humble spirit; and, as in a holocaust of fat offerings, so may our sacrifice today be in your sight, [Col. 1450C] that it may please you.”

[Note: [Col. 1451A] Addition 4.—Hence infer that one often prays in the person of the Church. For these men had not committed the sin for which they had been handed over to their enemies.]

Then the three blessed God, as though with one voice, saying: “Blessed are you, O Lord God of our fathers,” etc.; and they exhorted every creature to bless God, proceeding from the higher creatures to the lower.

From the preceding words, “in a contrite mind and a humble spirit,” and from the words in the canticle, “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous,” some fell into error by saying that in a human being, besides the Holy Spirit, there are two distinct things—spirit and soul.

[Note: [Col. 1451A] Addition 5.—The philosophers erred here in saying that spirit is a certain thing through which the soul is joined to the body.]

[Note: [Col. 1451A] Addition 6.—The theologians, however, say that the soul has two powers: the higher, which they call rationality, and the lower, which they call sensuality. Thus perhaps philosophers and theologians do not differ in their view.]

Up to this point the passage is not found in the Hebrew. Then the king was astonished, and rising quickly said: “Did we not cast only three men into the fire? Yet behold, I see four men walking in the midst of the fire, and [Col. 1450D] the appearance of the fourth is like a son of God.” This can be understood of an angel. Then the king called them, and they came out. All marvelled that not a hair of their heads had been singed, nor even their *saraballa*—their trousers—altered. The king said: “There is no other God who can save in this way.” He issued an edict that whoever spoke blasphemy against their God should perish and his house be laid waste; and he restored to them the governorship of the provinces.

## CHAPTER IV. The Third Vision of Daniel, Concerning the Tree, etc.

[Col. 1451A]

[Col. 1451B] The third vision of Daniel follows. Daniel did not write it; rather, it is the king’s letter, which he wrote to his whole kingdom after he had been restored from being a beast to being a man and to his kingdom (Dan. IV). In it he proclaimed the wonders which God Most High had performed toward him. The form of the letter, inserted by Daniel into his work, is this:

“I, Nebuchadnezzar, flourishing and lifted up in pride, saw a dream which terrified me. Having summoned all the wise men of Babylon, they did not disclose its interpretation to me, until Daniel entered—my colleague, whose name is Belshazzar—

[Note: [Col. 1452D] Addition 1.—For the king himself had made him second to himself, and, as it were, his colleague.]

—who has the spirit of the holy gods. I said to him: Upon my bed I saw, and behold, a tree in the midst of the earth, whose height reached to heaven, [Col. 1451C] and whose appearance extended to the ends of the earth. It contained food for all; beneath it dwelt animals and beasts, and in its branches were birds, and all flesh fed from it. And behold, a watcher—

[Note: [Col. 1452D] Addition 2.—We commonly call the guards of military camps “watchers,” since they keep watch by night; and he resembled such a one.]

—and a holy one descended from heaven and said: ‘Cut down the tree, its branches, and its fruit, and let the beasts and birds flee from it. Nevertheless, leave its stump in the ground, and let its portion be with the wild beasts in the grass of the earth. Let its heart be changed from a human one, and let a beast’s heart be given to it; and let seven times pass over it. The decree is by the sentence of the watchers, and the petition by the holy ones, until the living know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wills’” (Dan. IV).

Then Daniel silently reflected, troubled for about an hour, because evil things were portended for the king; and he said: “You, O king, are that tree, which grew strong, and your power extended to the ends of the earth. Through the watcher you heard the sentence of the Most High against you. They shall drive you from men, and your dwelling shall be with wild beasts. You shall eat grass like an ox; seven times”—that is, years—“shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men. Yet the shoot of the root shall be left to you, because your kingdom shall be restored to you. Therefore hear my counsel: redeem your sins by almsgiving; perhaps God will forgive you” (Dan. IV).

After a year had passed, the king was walking in his palace and speaking in a spirit of pride, saying: “Is not this Babylon, which I have built by the strength of my kingdom and for the glory of my majesty?” While the word was still in his mouth, [Col. 1452A] a voice fell from heaven: “It is said to you, Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom shall pass from you, and you shall dwell with the wild beasts for seven times, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men.” That same hour he was cast out from among men and ate grass like an ox, until his grey hair grew like eagles’ feathers and his nails like birds’ claws.

“Therefore, after the days fixed by the Lord, I, Nebuchadnezzar, raised my eyes to heaven; my understanding returned to me; and I blessed the Most High, whose power is everlasting. There is none who can say to him, ‘Why have you done this?’ My nobles sought me out; I was restored to my kingdom; and still greater magnificence was restored to me.”

From this it is evident, and Epiphanius testifies, that he underwent not a bodily transformation but an alienation of mind; he lost the use of speech, and grass was given as food to human nature. Inwardly he imagined himself an ox, but outwardly a lion, according to the mystery of tyrants: in their first stage, given over to pleasures and stubbornly subject to the yoke of Belial; but in the end they kill, plunder, and trample down.

Many people went out and saw him; Daniel alone did not go out, because throughout the time of his alienation he devoted himself to prayer for him. Through Daniel’s prayers, the seven years—called seven “times”—were changed into seven months. During forty days he suffered madness; for another forty he returned to a human mind, wept, and pleaded with God, so intensely that, from excessive weeping, the flesh of his eyes had become [unclear]; then for another forty [Col. 1452C] days he reverted to madness, until seven months were completed.

After this he was recalled, yet did not reign. Seven judges were appointed in his place, and until the end of twelve years he did penance, eating neither bread nor meat and drinking no wine. He lived on legumes and herbs, following Daniel’s counsel. When he had again become king, he wished to make Daniel co-heir with his sons. Daniel said: “Far be it from me that, abandoning the inheritance of my fathers, I should cling to the gifts of the uncircumcised.”

[Note: [Col. 1452D] Addition 3.—Although Daniel here altered the order of the history, the Master, observing the proper order, nevertheless enumerates the kings of Babylon in order to show under which king Daniel saw the fourth vision—namely, under Belshazzar, the fifth from Nebuchadnezzar.]

Josephus says here that Daniel himself translated the Hebrew books into Greek. Here Daniel changes the historical order. We, however, shall follow the order.

## CHAPTER V. Catalogue of the Kings of Babylon

[Col. 1452D]

Nebuchadnezzar the Great died, and his son Nebuchadnezzar reigned in his place. From the spoils of enemies he magnificently adorned the temple of Bel, [Col. 1453A] rebuilding the city so that besiegers could by no means divert the river. He added works greater than his father’s royal monuments. In fifteen days he completed it, beside which he placed great stones like a mountain, planted trees upon them, and made the garden called the Hanging Garden, because his wife, who had been brought up on the borders of Media, desired to see her own country from afar.

Megasthenes mentions him in his *Book of Judgments*, and declares that he surpassed Hercules in courage and in the greatness of his deeds. Diocles, too, says in his *Book of Colonies* that this Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for three years and ten months.

[Note: [Col. 1453C] Addition 1.—Tyre was then an island, and he wished to join it to the mainland; but Alexander later completed this.]

After his death, Amilitanus the commoner reigned in his place. This is Evil-merodach, who, in the thirty-seventh year of the deportation, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh [Col. 1453B] day of the month, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, from prison; set his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon; and allowed him to eat before the king all the days of his life. He showed him this mercy because his father had not kept faith with him.

Some nevertheless relate that Evil-merodach was the brother of the younger Nebuchadnezzar. During his father’s appointed absence he acted wickedly in the land; when his father was restored, he was accused before him and sent to the prison where Jehoiachin was, remaining there until his brother’s death. When he began to reign, he raised up Jehoiachin, his companion in prison. Fearing that his father, who had returned from being a beast to being a man, might rise again, he consulted Jehoiachin. At Jehoiachin’s advice he dug up his father’s corpse, divided it into three hundred [Col. 1453C] parts, and gave them to three hundred vultures. Jehoiachin said to him: “Your father will not rise again unless the vultures return as one.”

He had three sons: Egessarius, who was also called Recusatus; Labosardochus; and Nabar, who was renamed Belshazzar. After the reigns of his brothers, the kingdom devolved upon him.

## CHAPTER VI. The Fourth Vision of Daniel

The fourth vision of Daniel follows, not in the order of his book but in historical order. In it he saw, under the images of four beasts, the four [Col. 1453D] kingdoms which Nebuchadnezzar saw in the fourfold statue; but material concerning Antichrist and the Day of Judgment was added.

In the first year of Belshazzar Daniel saw a dream, the summary of which he wrote as follows: “I looked, and behold, four winds were fighting in the midst of the sea” (Dan. VII). These are angelic powers which labour for the kingdoms of the world over which they preside. “And four beasts came up from the sea. The first was like a lioness and had eagle’s wings. Its wings were plucked out; it was lifted from the earth; it stood upon its feet like a man; and a heart was given to it.” This is the kingdom of the Assyrians, compared to a lioness on account of violence and impatient lust, because a lioness is always eager for mating. It had an eagle’s wings because of its longevity; for it began in its second age under Serug, Abraham’s great-grandfather, [Col. 1454A] and continued to its fifth under Belshazzar. That its wings were plucked out, that it stood like a man, and that a heart was given it refers to Nebuchadnezzar’s overthrow and restoration.

“The second beast was like a bear in part, and there were three rows of teeth in its mouth, and three princes in its teeth; and it was told: ‘Arise, devour much flesh.’” This is the kingdom of the Persians, compared to a bear because of endurance of toil and frugality in food. For they used salt and cardamom for seasoning; but it was like a bear only in part, not wholly, because it did nothing cruel to the people of God. Hence in Zechariah they are called white horses.

[Note: [Col. 1455C] Addition 1.—Where he is read to have seen horses of four colours: white, black, red, and variegated.]

It had three rows of teeth: that is, three kingdoms at its beginning—those of the Medes, Persians, and Chaldeans [Col. 1454B]—or it had three rulers over one hundred and twenty satraps. That they said to it, “Devour much flesh,” refers to Ahasuerus, to whom Haman said that the Jews should be killed (Esth. III).

“The third beast was like a leopard; it had birds’ wings; four heads were upon it; and authority was given to it.” This is the kingdom of the Greeks, compared to a leopard, which rushes in a leap toward death, because of Alexander’s impetuosity. Its varied colours signify the diverse kingdoms beneath him. It had wings because nothing was swifter than Alexander’s victory; its four heads are Alexander’s four successors.

[Note: [Col. 1455C] Addition 2.—Alexander, unwilling that the honour he held should come to anyone after him, appointed twelve men to succeed him, only four of whom reigned.]

Alexander did not possess this power of himself; he was the rod of the Lord’s wrath against pestilential sons.

“The fourth beast was terrible and strong, with iron teeth, devouring and trampling the remainder under its feet.” [Col. 1454C] This is the kingdom of the Romans. Daniel compared it with no beast, so that whatever we can imagine fiercer among beasts may be understood of the Romans. The Hebrew, however, says that it “was like a boar,” according to the Psalmist: “The boar from the forest has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon it” (Ps. LXXVI). This kingdom trampled down the others.

What follows—“and it had ten horns”—looks to the end of the world, because then the Roman kingdom will be divided into ten kingdoms. This was signified by the ten suns in the Sibyl’s prophecy. “And behold, another little horn sprang up from among them.” This is Antichrist, of the tribe of Dan, of low birth, who is to be born in an obscure part of Babylonia. He will indeed be conceived from the seed of parents; [Col. 1454D] but after conception an evil spirit will descend into his mother’s womb, by whose power the boy will thereafter be nourished, born, and grow up. Hence he is called the son of perdition.

“And three of the first horns were plucked out before him”: that is, he will first kill three of the ten kings—the king of Africa, Egypt, and Ethiopia. Then the other seven will submit their necks to the conqueror. “And behold, he had eyes like the eyes of a man”: that is, lofty and marvellous knowledge, because by magic he will perform miracles and discover hidden treasures. “And he will have a mouth speaking great things,” because he will call himself God, will circumcise himself, will say that he is the Messiah; the Jews will flock to him; he will rebuild the temple and place his throne in it; he will turn men to himself by terror, gifts, and miracles. He will kill Elijah and Enoch.

“I looked at [Col. 1455A] these things,” that is, at his power, “until thrones were set,” of which the Gospel says, “You shall sit upon thrones” (Luke XXII), “and the Ancient of Days sat”: that is, God, the eternal judge, who in John alone sits upon the throne (Rev. VII). “His garment was white as snow, and his hair like clean wool”: these signify the glory of his majesty. “His throne was flames of fire; its wheels, burning fire.” This is what is elsewhere said in the Psalm: “Fire shall go before him” (Ps. XCVI).

“A swift stream of fire issued from before him”: this denotes the swiftness of judgment, which the Apostle says (I Cor. XV) will occur “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten hundred-thousands stood before him”: this is repetition for emphasis, since ten hundred-thousands is the same as thousands of thousands; it refers to the hosts of angels. “The judgment sat, and the books were opened”: that is, when the judges sit, each person’s conscience will be laid bare.

“And I saw that the fourth beast had been slain and that the power of the others had been removed,” because then every pre-eminence will cease, “when Christ delivers the kingdom to God the Father” (ibid.). “And behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man came,” because Christ will ascend into the air borne by clouds, according to: “He shall come in the same manner as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I); and he will come even to the Ancient of Days because Christ is in every respect equal to the Father, “and he gave him power, honour, and an everlasting kingdom.”

When Daniel had seen these things, [Col. 1455C] he approached one of those standing by and sought the truth. The latter explained everything to him, adding this concerning Antichrist: “He shall crush the saints of the Most High, and they shall be delivered into his hand for a time, times, and half a time”: that is, for one year, two years, and half a year. For in Hebrew the term “time” signifies a year, and the plural number two years. Hebrew, like Greek, has a dual number. This time will be short; but unless it had been shortened, no flesh would be saved.

## CHAPTER VII. The Fifth Vision of Daniel

[Col. 1455D]

The fifth vision of Daniel follows. It was written in Hebrew; the preceding ones were written in Chaldean. “In the third year of Belshazzar, I, Daniel, was in the region of Elam, at Susa,” the metropolis of the Elamites (Dan. VIII), which in Judith is called Ecbatana (Judith I). There, Josephus says, Daniel made the mausoleum of the kings. “And in the vision I saw myself at the gate of Ulai.” Ulai is the name either of a gate or of a lake before the gate.

“And behold, a single ram stood before the marsh, with lofty horns, one higher than the other and growing up.” This is Cyrus, more powerful than Darius. [Col. 1456A] “He thrust with his horns westward, northward, and southward, and no beasts could withstand him.” This refers to the kingdom itself, not to the individual.

“And behold, a he-goat came from the west and did not touch the earth.” This is Alexander, as if flying, travelling through every inaccessible place like a goat; or he is so called from the eyes of goats, which he had in different colours. “He came to the ram which I had seen, raged against it, struck the ram, and broke its two horns,” because he struck Darius, son of Arsames, and subjected the Medes and Persians to himself. “And four horns arose for it”: that is, four successors, of whom we shall speak in their place. “From one of them came forth a small horn and became great.” This is Antiochus Epiphanes, descended from Seleucus. [Col. 1456B] While a hostage at Rome, he escaped into the kingdom and became great “toward the south,” that is, against the Egyptians; “toward the east,” that is, against those who were plotting innovations in Persia; and “against the strength of heaven,” that is, the children of Israel.

“He cast down some of the stars and trampled them, and magnified himself even to the prince of the strength,” that is, God; “and took from him the continual sacrifice and cast down the place of his sanctification,” because he placed a statue of Jupiter in the temple. “I heard one of the holy ones speaking to another and saying: ‘How long shall the continual sacrifice, the sanctuary, and the strength be trampled down?’ He answered: ‘Until evening and morning, two thousand three hundred days; then the sanctuary shall be cleansed.’” For from Antiochus’ first entry into Jerusalem until the cleansing [Col. 1456C] of the temple by Judas Maccabaeus, six years, three months, and twenty days passed, reckoned by successive days and nights.

When Daniel sought the interpretation of the dream, Gabriel came to him and disclosed it. By visions of this kind granted to saints, as Josephus says, the error of the Epicureans is exposed: they maintain that this world is carried along by chance, without a ruler and without God’s providence. For if the world had no governor, it would long ago have perished, like a ship abandoned by its helmsman, nor would all things come to pass according to prophecies.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Sixth Vision

The sixth vision of Daniel follows. It is the fourth in Daniel, but Jerome calls it the sixth in the prologue to Habakkuk; and it was written in Chaldean. It happened [Col. 1456D] that Cyrus and Darius were besieging Belshazzar in Babylon. Belshazzar made a great banquet for a thousand of his nobles and had brought the vessels which his grandfather Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from the temple of the Lord. The king, his nobles, his wives, and his concubines drank from them and praised their gods (Dan. V).

According to Josephus, a festival had been instituted in Babylon for the protection of the city. The Hebrews relate that Belshazzar believed the seventy years of captivity foretold by Jeremiah had elapsed, while the Hebrews had nevertheless not been freed from his authority; hence he rejoiced and gave thanks to his gods.

[Note: [Col. 1457D] Addition 1.—Or perhaps because he thought that the enemies had withdrawn, since they had gone off to divide the river so as to make it fordable beside the city. Or because Darius and Cyrus were allied with him, he held the banquet for them; but they killed him during the feast.]

But those seventy years had not yet elapsed; the seventh decade was already running. At the same hour a hand appeared against him, writing on the wall. [Col. 1457A] When the king saw both the hand and the writing, it is uncertain whether those standing by saw the hand; they did see the writing. After the hand vanished, the king was disturbed and his knees struck one another. He cried out loudly that the Chaldean magicians should be brought in. He said to them: “Whoever reads this writing and tells me its interpretation shall be clothed in purple, have a golden necklace on his neck, and be third in my kingdom”—that is, one of the three rulers presiding over the satraps. But they could not read the writing.

Then the queen entered—not the wife, according to Porphyry, but the grandmother according to Josephus, or the mother according to Origen—and said to the king: “There is a man in your kingdom who has the spirit of the gods, whom your father”—that is, [Col. 1457B] grandfather—“appointed chief of the magicians. Let him be called, and he will tell you everything.”

When Daniel entered, the king promised him the same gifts as above. He replied: “Keep your gifts for yourself, or give them to another. But I shall read the writing to you, O king, and explain it. You know that God Most High gave the kingdom to your father, and he did not acknowledge it. Therefore he ate grass like an ox until he acknowledged it. You too, though you knew all these things, have lifted yourself up against the God of heaven. You profaned his vessels, delivering them into unclean hands and drinking from them; you praised gods who neither live nor feel, but did not glorify the God who holds your state in his hand. Therefore these words have been set before you: *MANE, THECEL, PHARES*—that is, ‘number, weighing, division.’

“And this is the meaning: ‘God has numbered your kingdom,’ [Col. 1457C] that is, brought it to completion; the expression is drawn from money which, once counted, is taken away and stored. ‘You have been weighed in the balance and found deficient,’ that is, by the just judgment of God you shall live less long than you supposed. ‘Your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians,’ or: ‘your kingdom has been broken’; for *Phares* means ‘a fragment.’”

The king gave Daniel the promised gifts.

[Note: [Col. 1458A] Addition 2.—Daniel was not therefore guilty of simony, because he accepted what had been freely offered.]

That same night Babylon was captured. Cyrus had divided the Euphrates far from the city into many channels, in order to make fordable the riverbed which flowed into the city. The enemy entered the city beneath the wall by this route; Belshazzar was killed; and Darius succeeded him in the kingdom, being seventy-two years old—where [Col. 1457D] other books have sixty-two, and others forty-two. Cyrus deferred to him in all matters as being the elder. That the city was captured on the same night as the vision is evident in Isaiah, who speaks to Belshazzar: “Set the table; watch from the watchtower, eating and drinking; arise, princes, seize the shields” (Isa. XXI). Some relate that Belshazzar’s mother, for whom the Hanging Garden was made, was Darius’s daughter; and, because Belshazzar had no son, Darius hastened to seize the kingdom.

## CHAPTER IX. The Seventh Vision

[Col. 1458A]

The seventh vision of Daniel follows (Dan. VI). Darius took Daniel with him into Media. He made him one of the three satraps set over the one hundred and twenty, but the Spirit of God was more abundant in Daniel. The king intended to appoint him over the entire kingdom. Therefore the princes envied him and sought an occasion to accuse him “at the king’s side,” that is, because he stood at the king’s side.

The Hebrews relate that they sought an occasion in speech, touch, gesture, or messages to the queen or to one of the king’s concubines. They found no grounds at all, because he was faithful and, Josephus says, had charge [Col. 1458B] of the treasuries, being so just that he rejected gifts offered to him. The princes said: “We shall find no occasion against him except in the law of his God.” They deceived the king, saying: “All the princes of your kingdom, the satraps, and the judges have formed a plan that whoever asks anything of any god or man for thirty days, except from you, O king, shall be cast into the lions’ den. Now therefore confirm the sentence and write the decree.” The king agreed.

Daniel entered his house and, with the windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem, prayed three times a day, bending his knees. The Jews prayed at three hours of the day—the third, sixth, and ninth. It is written of the Apostle that he prayed three times [Col. 1458C] a day; and of Peter and John that they went up at the ninth hour, the hour of prayer (Acts III).

They prayed at the third hour because the Decalogue was then given to them on Sinai (Exod. XX). The Church prays at the same hour because the Holy Spirit was then given to the apostles (Acts III). They prayed at the sixth hour because the bronze serpent was then raised in the wilderness (Num. XXI). The Church prays at the same hour because Christ was then suspended on the wood (Luke XXIII). They prayed at the ninth hour because the rock gave water at Kadesh (Num. XX). The Church prays at the same hour because blood and water came from the pierced Christ (John XIX).

When those men found Daniel praying, they accused him before the king of violating the decree. The king was grieved and set his heart on saving [Col. 1458D] him, striving until sunset. When the men understood this, they said: “Know that it is the law of this kingdom that a decree of the king may not be altered.” Then they cast Daniel into the lions’ den. The king sealed the stone placed at its entrance with his own ring and with the rings of the nobles. The king ate no supper and spent the whole night sleepless. At dawn he returned to the den and cried out weeping: “Daniel, servant of God, was your God able to deliver you from the lions?” Daniel answered: “My God sent me his angel and shut the lions’ mouths, because no iniquity has been found in me.”

Perhaps this episode is called a vision because Daniel saw the angel. Daniel was brought out of the lions’ den entirely unharmed. Those who accused him said that this had not occurred through God’s providence [Col. 1459A] but because the lions had been full. Then the king ordered much meat to be put before the lions; after they had been filled, he cast Daniel’s accusers, with their wives and children, into the den. They had not reached the pavement before the lions seized them and crushed all their bones.

Then Darius wrote to his whole kingdom: “Let all fear Daniel’s God, for he is the living God and eternal for ever.” Daniel was ill for many days. When he rose, he performed the king’s works—perhaps the mausoleum at Ecbatana, which, Josephus says, remains to this day so marvellous that on the day it is seen it is thought to have been built. The kings of the Medes, Persians, and likewise Parthians are buried there; and the person entrusted with its care is a priest of the Medes.

## CHAPTER X. The Eighth Vision

[Col. 1459B]

The eighth vision of Daniel follows (Dan. IX). “In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus,” also called Astyages, “who subdued to himself the kingdom of the Chaldeans, I, Daniel, understood from the books” of Jeremiah “that the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation were to be completed”—that is, were approaching completion—“and I prayed to the Lord in fasting, sackcloth, and ashes, saying: ‘You are righteous, Lord; we have sinned and acted wickedly, and you have brought this upon us. Turn away, I beseech you, your anger from your city Jerusalem and from your holy mountain. Show your face upon your sanctuary, which is desolate. Hear, Lord; be appeased, Lord; attend and act; do not delay.’”

While I was still speaking, behold, the man Gabriel touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice [Col. 1459C] and said: “From the beginning of your prayers, a sentence of deliverance has gone forth from God. I have come to disclose it to you, and certain other matters besides, because you are a man of desires. Therefore attend to the vision and understand the word.”

Then he disclosed to him the spiritual deliverance to come through Christ, perhaps imminent, for which he prayed. He postpones this because he will later say there that he was heard: “Do not fear” (Dan. X). He also added concerning the destruction by the Romans:

“Seventy weeks have been shortened concerning your people and your holy city, in order that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies [Col. 1459D] may be anointed. Know therefore and understand: from the going forth of the word that Jerusalem is to be rebuilt until Christ the leader, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.”

By these words the angel indicates Christ’s incarnation: he fulfilled the Law and the prophecies, bore sins, brought righteousness, and was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. XLIV). He set forth weeks not of days but of years, so that one week is seven years. He called them shortened in order that we might understand lunar years, which are eleven days shorter than solar years. Thus seventy weeks of solar years make four hundred and seventy-five years; but of lunar years they make four hundred and ninety years. The meaning, then, is that from the going forth of the word for the rebuilding [Col. 1460A] of Jerusalem until Christ the leader, four hundred and ninety lunar years elapsed.

Bede therefore began to count from the twentieth year of Artaxerxes’ reign, in which Nehemiah, his cupbearer, obtained from him permission that Jerusalem’s walls should be restored, and restored them amid great distress. From that permission received from the king until Christ’s passion, four hundred and ninety lunar years elapsed. He calculates this total according to the years of the kings who followed one another, down to the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar.

Daniel then immediately inserted a brief phrase: “The street and the walls shall be rebuilt in the distress of the times,” because of fear. Of the seventy weeks of years Daniel separated the final week, saying: “He shall confirm the covenant with many for [Col. 1460B] one week.” This is to be understood of the three and a half years in which Christ preached and confirmed what he had promised to the fathers. For three and a half years of this final week had already elapsed when the Lord was baptized; and “in the middle” of the remaining portion of this same “week,” near its end, “offering and sacrifice shall fail”: that is, when the reality comes, the shadows shall cease. “And in the temple shall be the abomination of desolation”: that is, sacrifices after Christ’s death shall be abominable and destined for desolation. “And this desolation shall endure until the end” of the world.

Earlier in the text Daniel stated the time of Christ’s death, saying: “And after sixty-two weeks”—understand, together with the seven and the final week which we divided into two parts—“Christ shall be killed, and [Col. 1460C] the people who will deny him shall not be his.”

[Note: [Col. 1462A] Addition 1.—The Hebrew does not contain “a people who will deny him”; indeed, their text cannot properly be read. “Christ shall be killed, and this shall not be his”—namely, being killed—but arise from our nature.]

“For they said: ‘We have no king but Caesar’” (John XIX). And elsewhere: “We do not know where he is from” (John VII).

What follows—“And the people shall destroy the city and the sanctuary”—does not pertain to the seventy weeks. But, having prophesied the time of Christ’s coming and death, he prophesied what would happen to the people who refused to receive him, saying: “And the people,” namely the Roman people, “shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, with its leader who is to come; and its end shall be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation” decreed by God “for ever.” Note that from the two statements read here—namely, “the Holy of Holies shall be anointed,” and [Col. 1460D] “sacrifice shall fail”—is derived the saying customarily addressed to the Jews: When the Holy of Holies has come, your anointing has ceased.

Africanus agrees with Bede’s reckoning at its beginning, but differs at its end [Note: [Col. 1462A] Addition 2.—Since this form of words is not found in Daniel [Col. 1462B].]. For he does not extend the seventy weeks beyond the fifteenth year of Tiberius, in which Christ was baptized. Tertullian, however, begins to count those weeks from the first year of Darius, in which the word went forth from the Lord to Daniel through an angel that the walls of Jerusalem should be rebuilt. He extends them to the captivity brought about by the Romans. Then the statement belongs to the seventy weeks, that “the people with their coming leader destroyed the city and the sanctuary.”

The Hebrews explain it thus: “Seventy abbreviated weeks are decreed [Col. 1461A] over your people.” As though he were saying: O Daniel, know that from this day on, when I now speak to you—it was the first year of Darius, who killed Belshazzar and transferred the kingdom of the Chaldeans to the Persians and Medes—until the seventieth year of weeks, that is, until four hundred and ninety years, these things shall happen successively to your people. First, God will be reconciled to you as you pray; sin will be wiped out and transgression will come to an end. For now, with city and Temple destroyed, the people are in mourning; but shortly they will be restored. Nor will these things alone occur in these seventy weeks: Christ, everlasting righteousness, will be born; vision and prophet will be sealed, so that no prophet will be found in Israel; and the Holy of Holies will be anointed, of whom the Psalm says: “Therefore [Col. 1461B] God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV [45]); he who says, “Be holy, for I too am holy” (Lev. XX [19]).

Know, therefore, that from this day on, when I now speak to you and declare God’s word—that the people shall return and Jerusalem be restored—there are to be counted until Christ and the desolation of the Temple sixty-two weeks, and another seven weeks. During these, in their proper order, the two things previously mentioned will occur: the people will return, and the street will be rebuilt by Nehemiah and Ezra. At the end of the weeks God’s judgment will be fulfilled in a time of distress, when the Temple will again be destroyed and the city captured. For “after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be slain, and there shall not be a people belonging to him who will deny him” [Note: [Col. 1462B] Addition 3.—Hence: “And mocking him, they said: Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. XXVII [27]).]; or, as [Col. 1461C] certain Hebrews say, his dominion will not exist—the dominion which he believed he would receive.

And why speak of Christ’s being slain and of the people who deny him, being wholly abandoned, when the Roman people with their coming leader—that is, Vespasian—were also to destroy both city and sanctuary? After Vespasian’s death, when seven weeks had elapsed, that is, forty-nine years, Aelius Hadrian—who later founded the city of Aelia from the ruins of Jerusalem—defeated the rebellious Jews while Rufus, commander of the army, fought; and then sacrifice and offering failed, and the desolation will continue until the consummation of the world.

Do not be troubled, the Hebrews say, if seven weeks are counted first, then sixty-two, and again [Col. 1461D] one is divided into two parts. This is an idiom of the Hebrew language and of ancient Latin: they place the smaller number before the greater. For example, in the normal usage of our language we say, “Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years”; the other way round, “Abraham lived five, seventy, and one hundred years.” Thus it is not fulfilled in precisely the order in which it is read; rather, it reaches its end as the whole is calculated together.

Nor should it be unknown that some of them have said that the one week of which it is written, “He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week,” is divided between Vespasian and Hadrian. Thus, according to the history of Josephus, Vespasian and Titus made peace with the Jews for three years and six months; while three years and six months are reckoned under Hadrian, when Jerusalem was utterly [Col. 1462A] overthrown and the Jews were slaughtered in masses, so that they were driven even beyond the borders of Judaea. These things the Hebrews say, without greatly concerning themselves that, from the first year of Darius king of the Persians to the final overthrow of Jerusalem under Hadrian, there are reckoned one hundred and seventy-two Olympiads—that is, six hundred and ninety-six years—which make ninety-nine Hebrew weeks and three years, when Corbas, leader of the Hebrews, was crushed and Jerusalem razed to the ground.

## CHAPTER XI.—The Ninth Vision

[Col. 1462B]

Daniel’s ninth vision follows, which some say is one with the following vision (Dan. X). Jerome, however, following the Hebrew truth, maintains that there are two, and that both are written in Hebrew in Daniel. Daniel saw both: he saw the one, but heard the other, in the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, and on the same day of that year, in this manner:

“In the first year of Darius, Daniel, understanding that the seventieth year, when the captivity was to be released, was at hand, prayed to the Lord that Darius and Cyrus might free his people. God gave the decree that permission to return should be granted; and Gabriel, as related above, announced to Daniel that this decree had gone forth from the Lord. From that time Darius planned to give the Hebrews freedom and permission, but, forestalled by death, did not accomplish it. Cyrus, however, in the first year of his reign granted them the same freedom possessed by natives of the land, together with permission to return. But because almost all of them had been born in Chaldaea and possessed property there, they chose to remain in the land of their birth. The few who intended to go up into Judaea were sluggish and dilatory, even until Cyrus’s third year. Observing this, Daniel was more violently afflicted with grief than before, and prayed the Lord that he who had first given the kings the will to liberate might give the people also the will to return.

“It came to pass [Col. 1462D] in the third year of Cyrus’s reign, in the first month, on the first day of the month, that Daniel mourned for three weeks of days. He ate no desirable bread, tasted neither meat nor wine, and used no ointment for bathing, in the Persian manner. But on the twenty-fourth day, while he was beside the river Tigris, he saw—and behold, a man clothed in linen, girded with a golden belt, whose face was like lightning, his eyes like lamps, the breast of his body like chrysolite, and the lower parts—namely, thighs, shins, and feet—like glowing bronze; and his speech was like the sound of a multitude speaking. The men who were with him fled in terror; he alone saw the vision and fell upon his face.

“But that man approached, raised him up, strengthened him, and said: ‘Do not fear, Daniel. For from the first day of the month, when you set [Col. 1463A] your heart to afflict yourself before God, your words were heard; and God’s decree concerning the return of the people went forth. On that same day I wished to come to you to announce it; but the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me for twenty-one days. When I then set out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming to oppose the prince of the Persians and me, and I delayed for a little while. But now I come to assure you concerning the people’s return; and in these matters I have no helper except Michael, your prince.’”

Jerome says that these two princes of the Greeks and Persians were evil angels, assigned to those kingdoms for their trial. The angel of the Persians accordingly laboured to prevent the Hebrews from being released from Persian dominion, both because he delighted in their afflictions and because, by afflicting them longer, the Persians might sin more grievously. The angel of the Greeks also laboured to make the Persians, together with the captivity of the Hebrews among them, pass under Greek dominion.

Gregory, however, holds that they were good angels, who strove to prevent the Jews from being freed so quickly, so that, if anything still needed purging in them, it might be purged, and they might be refined to the very last degree.

Moreover, that man added: “Now I shall return to fight against the prince of Persia; but first I shall announce to you what is set forth in the Scripture of truth,” concerning certain other matters about which you are anxious. From Darius’s first year Daniel prayed for him, that his kingdom might stand and be strengthened, and he was concerned about the successors to the Persian kingdom, wishing to know them. The tenth vision follows upon their disclosure, in which [Col. 1463C] Daniel is first introduced as speaking thus:

## CHAPTER XII.—The Tenth Vision

“I, moreover, from the first year of Darius, meditated before God that Darius himself might be strengthened and established” (Dan. II [11:1]).

There immediately occurs a change of person (*metaplasm*), frequent in the prophets; and the aforesaid man is introduced, speaking to Daniel as follows: “And then I shall announce the truth to you. For behold, after Darius and Cyrus, who are now present, three kings will still arise in Persia—Cambyses, Smerdis the Magian, and Darius son of Hystaspes—and a fourth, namely Xerxes son of Darius, will surpass them all and stir up all against the kingdom of Greece.”

Of this man it is written that he burned Athens and fought a naval battle at Salamis, [Col. 1463D] when Sophocles and Euripides were renowned, and when Themistocles, fleeing into Persia, perished after drinking bull’s blood.

Then the man who spoke to Daniel passed over all the kings down to Alexander the Great, and said: “A mighty king shall arise and do whatever pleases him; and when he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken and divided toward the four winds of heaven.” In Egypt, which lies to the south, Ptolemy son of Lagus first reigned. In Macedonia, which lies west of Syria and Babylon, Philip, also called Arrhidaeus, Alexander’s brother, reigned; Seleucus governed the upper regions lying eastward. Nicanor ruled Asia, Pontus, and the other provinces in that same quarter. Antigonus ruled in the north. This is said according to the regions of the whole world. Someone in Judaea, however, has Syria to the north and Egypt to the south.

Daniel pursues only the kingdoms of Egypt and Syria because the people of God suffered under each in turn. After Alexander, Ptolemy son of Lagus reigned in Egypt; from him the subsequent Egyptian kings were called Ptolemies. After him came Ptolemy Philadelphus; then Ptolemy Euergetes; then Ptolemy Philopator; then Ptolemy Epiphanes. In Syria after Alexander reigned Seleucus; after him Antiochus Soter, from whom his successors were called Antiochi; then Antiochus Theos; then Antiochus Gallinicus; then Antiochus the Great; then Antiochus Epiphanes.

The man speaking to Daniel continues concerning these, beginning with the king of Egypt: “And the king of the south shall be strengthened.” This is Ptolemy son of Lagus, [Col. 1464B] so powerful that he restored the expelled Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, to his kingdom; after defeating Demetrius son of Antigonus, he restored to Seleucus the part of his realm that Antigonus had taken away; and he subjected Cyprus, Phoenicia, many regions, and islands to himself.

Ptolemy Philadelphus succeeded him. He was the first to bring four hundred elephants from Ethiopia, placing wooden towers on them in which he stationed armed men for battle. Under him the Seventy translators flourished. He fought Antiochus Theos, king of Syria, but later they made an alliance. Antiochus married Berenice, daughter of Philadelphus, after repudiating his first wife Laodice. When Laodice was restored to her husband’s favour, she killed by poison both her husband and the son he had had by Berenice, while making her own son Gallinicus king of Syria.

Euergetes, who succeeded Philadelphus, devastated Syria to avenge his sister Berenice. But hearing that the princes of Egypt had conspired against him, he returned to Egypt, taking with him an immense quantity of Syrian spoil and two thousand six hundred talents of images.

Gallinicus left two sons, Seleucus and Antiochus the Great. Antiochus killed his brother and reigned; he fought the Egyptian king Philopator, was defeated, fled through the desert, and was nearly captured. Epiphanes succeeded Philopator in Egypt when he was four years old, and Antiochus the Great began to harass him. But the Egyptian leaders fought on behalf of the boy.

Under Epiphanes, Onias the priest took with him very many [Col. 1464D] Jews, fled to Egypt, and received from the king the district called Heliopolis. There he built a temple resembling that of the Jews, asserting that he fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy: “There shall be an altar of the Lord in Egypt, and an inscription of him at its border” (Isa. XIX [19]). This temple remained for two hundred and fifty years, until Vespasian utterly destroyed both the city itself, called Oniae, and the temple.

Antiochus the Great left two sons, Seleucus and Antiochus Epiphanes; but Epiphanes, having fraudulently expelled or killed his brother, reigned in Syria.

Up to this point there is no dispute concerning the sequence of history between Porphyry and our writers. What follows Porphyry expounds solely of Antiochus. He explained [Col. 1465A] Daniel in order to discredit him. We, however, have expounded it in a mixed sense, referring it to Antiochus and Antichrist; some matters specially to Antiochus and some to Antichrist—for example, the passage concerning Antiochus, “Those who eat bread with him,” and so forth, down to, “Ships shall come against him, and Romans.”

Antiochus Epiphanes gave his sister as wife to Epiphanes, king of Egypt, deceitfully; she bore him two sons. Then Antiochus entered Egypt as though intending to visit his sister and nephews, but during a banquet he had his sister’s husband killed and wished to seize Egypt. The Egyptians resisted bravely and drove him out. Two years later he returned and besieged Alexandria; and behold, Roman envoys were sent to free the Egyptians, with whom they had an alliance.

When [Col. 1465B] they had landed, Antiochus went out to meet them. While they stood on the shore, Marcus Publius Laenas said to him: “The Senate and People of Rome command you to withdraw from their allies.” When he asked for time to reply, Marcus drew a circle around him in the sand with a staff and said: “The Senate and People of Rome command you not to leave this circle until you answer.” Antiochus answered: “If this seems good to the Senate and People of Rome, we must withdraw.” And he withdrew from Egypt.

Likewise, what follows is to be understood of Antiochus alone: “And he shall be devoted to the desires of women.” For Antichrist will be chaste, through a pretence of religion. But the following applies to both: “He shall worship the god of Moazim in his place.” For *Moazim* means “stronghold”; Antiochus placed a garrison and an image of Jupiter in Jerusalem, while Antichrist will worship the devil as God and as his own ruler.

But what follows applies only to Antichrist: “And he shall pitch his tent at Apadno between the seas.” *Apadno* is interpreted “his throne.” The meaning is: He shall pitch the tent of his throne in Jerusalem, which lies between the Dead Sea and the Tyrrhenian Sea; and “upon the famous and holy mountain,” that is, the Mount of Olives, “he shall pitch his tent and come to its summit,” that is, the place from which the Lord ascended, “and no one shall help him,” because a voice will be heard in the air saying, “Die!” and immediately he will be struck by lightning.

[Col. 1465D] Afterwards the vision continues concerning the time of Antichrist, the conversion of the Jews, and the resurrection of the dead, saying: “And there shall come a time such as has not been since nations began to exist. And Michael shall stand for the children of your people, and everyone among them who is written in God’s book shall be saved. And the multitude of all who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life, others to reproach, that they may see for ever” (Dan. XII [12:1–2]). Certainly not that the good may see it, for “the wicked man shall be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI [26:10]), but that they may see their own reproach for ever.

“But you, Daniel, seal the book,” that is, write the mysteries but do not expound them. “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied.” As though he said: Leave later generations material for exercise. Daniel desired to know how long [Col. 1466A] the persecution of Antichrist would last. He saw the prince of Persia standing on one bank of the river, the prince of Greece standing on the other, and the man clothed in linen standing in the middle above the waters. He said to him: “Until when is the end of these wonders?”

Lifting both hands, the man swore by the One who lives for ever: “For a time, times, and half a time.” Daniel said: “Lord, what shall come after these things?” The man answered by repeating the same period in other words: “When the continual sacrifice has been taken away and the abomination has been set up in desolation”—that is, when the worship of God has been removed and laid waste, Antichrist will abominably offer himself for adoration—“there shall be one thousand two hundred and ninety days,” that is, three and a half years.

[Col. 1466B] He then added what would happen after this. He answers: “Blessed is he who waits and reaches one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days.” If forty-five days are added to one thousand two hundred and ninety days, the total is one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days. Thus, after the death of Antichrist, those who have fallen will be granted forty-five days for repentance. The sense is: Blessed will be the person who, after the days of persecution, reaches the additional days of repentance.

“But you, Daniel, meanwhile go to the appointed term of your life; and you shall rest, and at the end of days you shall stand in your lot,” that is, you shall rise again in your own order.

## CHAPTER XIII.—Concerning Susanna

The story of Susanna follows, which the Hebrew does not have in the book of Daniel. He calls it a fable, not [Col. 1466C] because he denies that the event occurred, but because it contains the false statement that the priests were stoned, whereas Jeremiah testifies that they were burned. He also calls it a fable because we say that it was written by Daniel, whereas it was written by a certain Greek. This is proved by the verbal play there on the names of trees: *apotoy, cymi, cyse, apotoy, primi, prise* [readings uncertain; Greek wordplay as printed]. Such plays upon words and names of trees are not found in Hebrew.

In our translation, one such wordplay is found, albeit imperfectly. When the priest said, “Under the *schinus*,” Daniel replied with a word seemingly playing upon the name: “He will split you in the middle.” It would be expressed more clearly if it were said, “Under the holm-oak,” and added, “Immediately the angel of the Lord will split you.” The same sort of pun can be made from a word and the name of a time, as if someone said, “This happened on the second feria,” and another answered, “May God strike you down.”

Origen also calls this same story a fable in the tenth book of the *Stromata*, that is, *Instructions*, perhaps according to the edition which he arranged with obelus [Note: [Col. 1468A] Addition 1.—For what the obelus and asterisk are, see above, chapter XV in Genesis, “On the Different Translations.” Since there were four translations—the Septuagint, Aquila’s, Theodotion’s, and Symmachus’s—Origen, correcting these translations, made four columns: in the first he placed the Septuagint translation; in the second, Aquila’s; in the third, Theodotion’s; in the fourth, Symmachus’s. He marked agreement among the three with an asterisk; a reading differing from the three translations he marked with an obelus.] and asterisk. He called it *Stromata* because through it he instructed us more fully.

This seems to have occurred while the captivity was still recent, because Daniel was still a young man. Susanna, the wife of Joachim, was exceedingly beautiful (Dan. XIII [13]). Two elders, judges for that year, burned with desire for her; of them the Lord says: “Wickedness has gone out from Babylon through the elder judges.” The Hebrews relate that women were deceived in this matter because these men claimed to be of David’s line and that Christ would be born from [Col. 1467A] their seed.

“They arranged together a time when they might find Susanna alone,” and hid after midday in Helcia’s orchard. Susanna entered, wishing to wash—that is, to anoint herself, according to the custom of the country—and sent her maidservants to bring oil and *smegmata*. Properly, *smegma* is barley with its husk, from which women make a decoction, perhaps for brightening the complexion.

Then the elders rushed upon her and said: “Have intercourse with us, or else we shall bear witness against you that you committed adultery.” Susanna chose to fall into their hands rather than sin against God. She cried out; the servants came running, and were ashamed when they heard the elders speak.

The next day Susanna was placed in the midst of the people. The elders laid their hands upon [Col. 1467B] her head, testified that they had seen a young man and her having intercourse together, and condemned her to death. “Susanna cried out in a loud voice to God: ‘Lord, you know that I die without knowing it.’ As she was being led away, God stirred up the spirit of a boy named Daniel.”

One must not believe those who say that Daniel had died and was then raised, and thereafter became a prophet. Rather, at that time the Lord revealed that the Holy Spirit was in him, previously resting there as though concealed. Daniel said to the people: “Return to the judgment, for they have spoken falsely against her.” When they had returned, Daniel separated the elders from one another. Calling one, he said: “Under what tree did you see them conversing?” He answered, “Under the *schinus*,” which the Latins call [Col. 1467C] a holm-oak or a mastic tree. The other, when summoned, said: “Under a holly-oak.” The people cried out against them because of their conflicting answers and killed them—that is, handed them over to the king to be killed.

“And Daniel became great among the people from that day onward. And King Astyages was gathered to his fathers, and Cyrus received his kingdom,” that is, the Persian kingdom [Note: [Col. 1468A] Addition 2.—This is a transition made here by the story, perhaps referring back to the preceding account of Susanna, or rather to the following account of Bel’s idol. For at the time of Astyages’s death, and of the succession of his adopted son Darius and of his grandson Cyrus—that is, the son of Astyages’s daughter—the episode of Bel and that of Susanna took place, while the kingdom of Babylon was still flourishing.].

Perhaps this determines the time when Susanna was delivered: namely, when Cyrus became king of the Persians and Darius king of the Medes. Or rather, it determines the time of the following story, which begins here. The kingdom of Babylon was still standing, and there was a king in Babylon, concerning whom it immediately follows:

“Daniel was the king’s table-companion and was honoured [Col. 1467D] above all his friends” (Dan. XIV [14]). Since the story does not name him, he may be understood to have been Belshazzar’s father, or Belshazzar himself. Under him occurred what Daniel did in the fable of Bel and the Dragon. The Hebrew calls this a fable because it contains falsehood, and because the bodily translation of Habakkuk is impossible.

Jerome reports that, when a Hebrew said to him that such bodily transportation had never occurred anywhere, a certain smatterer who was with them replied that Ezekiel had been transported from Chaldaea to Judaea. The Hebrew mocked him, saying: The text expressly states that Ezekiel was transported in spirit. Hence our Apostle spoke cautiously when he said: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (II Cor. XII [12:2]). The Hebrew added that [Col. 1468A] this fable relates nothing prophetic, but is only a work composed through literary ingenuity.

## CHAPTER XIV.—Concerning the Idol Bel and the Dragon

[Col. 1468B]

“There was in Babylon an idol named Bel, and every day there were expended upon it twelve artabs of fine flour, forty sheep, and six amphorae of wine” (Dan. XIV [14:2]). An *artab* among the Chaldeans is the same measure as an *ephah* among the Hebrews, namely a measure of three bushels.

“The king of Babylon worshipped it every day and said to Daniel: ‘Why do you not worship Bel?’ He replied: ‘I worship not a thing made, but the living God, creator of all.’ The king said: ‘Does Bel not seem to you a living god, who eats and drinks so much every day?’ He answered: [Col. 1468C] ‘Within he is clay, and without bronze; he never eats.’

“The king summoned the priests and said: ‘Unless you tell me who consumes these offerings, you shall die. But if you show me how Bel consumes them, Daniel shall die.’ There were sixty priests, besides their wives and little children. The king came with Daniel into the temple. The priests said: ‘We shall go outside; you, O king, put out the wine and food, shut the door, and seal it with your ring. Unless in the morning you find everything eaten by Bel, let us die.’

“The king placed the food before Bel. Daniel sifted ashes across the entire pavement before the king. The door was shut and sealed with the king’s ring. That night the priests entered, as was [Col. 1468D] their custom, with their wives and children, and consumed everything.” They had made underground tunnels and a concealed entrance beneath the table.

At dawn the king came to the temple with Daniel and found the seals intact. When they opened the door, the king looked at the empty table and cried: “Bel is great!” Daniel restrained the king from entering and said: “Observe the footprints upon the pavement.” The angry king seized the priests, and they showed him the small doors by which they entered and left. The king killed them and gave Bel into Daniel’s hands; Daniel overthrew it and its temple.

In the same place there was a great dragon hidden in a pit, and the Babylonians worshipped it. Its priests possessed *hydraulia*, that is, vessels made from calfskins, and beat them with reed-sticks in order to produce a dreadful noise like thunder. Roused by this sound, the dragon sometimes gave off smoke, sometimes fire, and sometimes appeared visibly.

The king said to Daniel: “You cannot say that this is not a living god.” Daniel answered: “Give me authority and I shall kill it without sword or club.” The king gave it to him. Daniel therefore took pitch, fat, and hairs, cooked them together, made lumps of them, and put them into the dragon’s mouth; it burst apart when suffocated.

The indignant Babylonians said: “The king has become a Jew” [Note: [Col. 1469C] Addition 1.—As though they had said: “He has become a heretic,” or “a tax collector.”].
