They said to the king: “Hand Daniel over to us, or we shall kill you and your household.” Compelled, he handed him over to them. They threw him into the lions’ den, where he remained for seven days. There were seven lions in the den, and [Col. 1469B] every day they were given two bodies of condemned persons and two sheep; then these were not given to them, so that they might devour Daniel.

Habakkuk the prophet was in Judaea, carrying stew to reapers. The angel said to him: “Carry this meal to Daniel in Babylon, who is in the lions’ den.” He replied: “I have not seen Babylon and do not know the place.” The angel took him by a hair of his head, placed him over the den, and Habakkuk cried out: “Daniel, servant of God, take the meal which God has sent you.” Daniel gave thanks and ate. Then the angel restored Habakkuk to his own place.

On the seventh day the king came to mourn Daniel. Seeing him seated among the lions, he cried: “Great are you, Lord God of Daniel!” and drew him out of the lions’ den. [Col. 1469C] He then cast in those who had caused Daniel’s destruction, and they were devoured before him in an instant.

## CHAPTER XV.—Concerning Habakkuk

Habakkuk was of the tribe of Simeon. He foresaw the coming captivity of Jerusalem and, when the Chaldeans arrived, fled to Sostratenē [uncertain place-name], living as a resident alien in the land of Israel. When the remnant of Judah went down into Egypt [Note: [Col. 1470B] Addition 1.—That is, of the two tribes. For the ten tribes had already been carried captive, and settlers had been brought into their lands. Habakkuk lay hidden among these until the Chaldeans had departed; afterwards he returned to the land of Judah and, when the others had gone away, remained as a stranger in his own country [Col. 1470C].], he lived as a sojourner in his own land and wrote.

At the beginning of his work he complains against God, asking why the ungodly had devastated God’s people and sanctuary even though he cried out and was not heard (Hab. I [1]). But for his consolation the Lord disclosed to him the future calamities of the surrounding nations, to be brought by Nebuchadnezzar—calamities far greater [Col. 1469D] than those of Judah—and that Nebuchadnezzar himself would finally perish. Thus he turned from complaint to prayer.

The Lord showed him Christ’s coming, saying: “If he delays, wait for him; for he who is coming will come and will not delay” (Hab. II [2:3]). Among many imprecations, Habakkuk said of Nebuchadnezzar: “Woe to him who gives his neighbour drink, sending gall, and makes him drunk, in order to look upon his nakedness”; this Nebuchadnezzar did to Zedekiah. Finally he wrote the hymn, “O Lord, I have heard,” and so forth (Hab. III [3]).

When he was taking stew to the reapers, he said to his household: “I am going to a far country; I shall quickly return. If I delay [Col. 1470A] for days, take food to the reapers.” When he had been in Babylon, he suddenly appeared among the reapers. He understood that the people would soon return from Babylon. From this it is clear that this took place long after Susanna’s deliverance.

He gave those who were in Judaea a sign of the return: they would see light amid the ruins of the Temple. He also foretold the Temple’s final desolation: that a western nation would bring it about. Then, he says: “The veil of the Holy of Holies shall be torn, and the architraves of the two columns shall be removed; and no one shall know where they are. They themselves shall be brought into the wilderness; and at the end the Lord will illuminate those who endure persecution from the serpent, as at the beginning.”

Habakkuk died and was buried alone in his own field. We do not know how long Daniel survived [Col. 1470B] after the people’s return to Judaea. “When he died, he was buried alone with honour in a royal cave. This is Daniel, who gave a sign in the mountains above Babylonia, saying: When the wooded part of the mountains smokes, Babylon’s end will come; but when it burns like fire, the end of the whole earth will come; when waters run toward the south, the people will return to their own land. But if it flows with blood, there will be killings of Belial throughout the whole land” [Note: [Col. 1470C] Addition 2.—These words are taken from a book of Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, to whom certain secrets of the prophets were revealed in the Spirit. For many prophecies are hidden, as someone says: “My secret is for myself” (Isa. XXIV [24:16]). That book of Epiphanius is called *The Secret of the Prophets*.].

## CHAPTER XVI.—Concerning Cyrus

[Col. 1470C]

[Note: [Col. 1469] The following is excerpted from various histories.]

After the death of Darius the Mede, Cyrus held the monarchy of the East and established his capital among the Persians, although the kingdom of the Medes was greater and more distinguished, because the Persians had elevated him to kingship. He was Darius’s nephew through his sister, and Astyages’ grandson through his daughter. Astyages had only one daughter. He dreamed that from his daughter’s genitals there sprang [Col. 1470D] a vine which covered the whole of Asia; and interpreters told him that he would have a grandson by his daughter who would rule Asia and cast him down from the kingdom. Fearing this, he gave his daughter in marriage to a common soldier, lest a son born of her should be noble and powerful.

Moreover, he summoned his pregnant daughter, and, when her son was born, entrusted him to a confidant to be killed. But this man, believing that the kingdom would pass to his own daughter, was afraid to kill her son and gave the infant to one of the king’s shepherds to be exposed in a wood. When the shepherd had exposed him and told his wife, who had given birth in those days, the woman begged him to bring the little child to her to be nursed, and to expose their own [Col. 1471A] son in his place. When the shepherd returned to the boy, he found Canis giving him her breasts and protecting him from wild beasts and birds.

[Note: [Col. 1471] Canis here is a person’s proper name, as the true history relates: she was the shepherd’s wife.]

When he brought him to his wife, the child played with her as though she had long been known to him; and she called the boy Sparticus, that is, “puppy.” For *spartos* means “dog” in Persian. When he was somewhat older, the children at play made him their king, and he harshly punished those who resisted and disobeyed him. Their fathers took this badly and reported the shepherd’s son to the king. When the king summoned him and reproved him for beating the boys, he fearlessly replied that he had acted as king. The king was astonished; perceiving in him certain marks of his own family, he secretly summoned the shepherd and learned the truth of the matter.

Yet his fear concerning his [Col. 1471B] grandson was softened, since he judged that the interpreters’ prediction concerning a kingdom had been fulfilled in the boys’ kingdom. He entrusted the boy’s upbringing to the same man to whom he had previously entrusted his killing, though he did not reveal that he was anything but a shepherd’s son. He secretly gave that official’s own son to his father to eat, because he had not obeyed his command; afterward he told him what he had done.

It happened that Astyages entrusted an army to that official to defeat the enemy, while he himself withdrew into Media. But the official, not forgetting the king’s wicked act, persuaded the army to choose Spartacus as king of Persia; and he surnamed him Cyrus, which means “heir,” as though to say: “Although Astyages resists, this man is the heir.” When this was done, Astyages, in fear, adopted his cousin Darius as his son; and [Col. 1471C] after gathering an army he met Cyrus in battle, and the Persians fled. But their wives and mothers came out to meet them and, uncovering their buttocks, said: “Do you want to enter your mothers’ wombs and be born again?” Stirred by this shame, the Persians fiercely returned against the enemy, and Astyages was defeated.

Cyrus, however, treated him more as a grandson than as a conqueror, for he granted him the kingdom of Hyrcania. To Darius, as though to his mother’s brother, he entrusted the kingdom of the Medes, yet with a definite expectation that it would return to himself.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the permission granted to the Jews to return

Therefore, when the whole kingdom had come into his hands, in the first year of this kingdom the Lord stirred his spirit, so that Jeremiah’s word might be fulfilled [Col. 1471D] (1 Esdras 1–2; 2 Chronicles 36; Jeremiah 29; Isaiah 45). He granted freedom to all the Jews throughout his realm, permission to return to Judaea and to build the house of the Lord.

He was moved by Isaiah’s words, written two hundred and ten years before concerning him, in which the Lord says: “To Cyrus, my anointed one, whose right hand I have grasped, I will subject nations and kingdoms to him. He himself will rebuild my house in Jerusalem” (Isaiah 45). Thus, in order to fulfill this generous prophecy, he issued throughout his entire kingdom a written decree of freedom and permission, saying: “The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth; I believe that he is the one whom the people of Israel [Col. 1472A] worshipped.”

In this letter he also urged the Jews to go up to Judaea; and he directed those who did not wish to go up to assist those going up with money, clothing, and beasts of burden. The most distinguished Jews lived in Babylonia, that is, in the land of ruined Babylon. Babylon, properly speaking, is the name of a city; Babylonia is the name of a region, although one is often read for the other. Among them Zechariah, born in Chaldaea, was already prophesying. He blessed Shealtiel in his son, calling him Zerubbabel, which means “master of Babylon,” as though to say: “He will be master of the Babylonian captivity.”

At the exhortation of this prophet, the men of Judah were first to rise up to go to Jerusalem; afterward the men of Benjamin and the Levites did so. Therefore, as Josephus says, [Col. 1472B] they were called Jews from Judah. There were indeed several explanations for this name: concerning the tower of Babel it is read that they were called Jews from Dedan, who was surnamed Judah; elsewhere, from Judah the son of Jacob; elsewhere, from Judas Maccabaeus.

Those preparing to go up to Jerusalem, or to Judaea, urged others to join them, but found few who agreed; therefore they spent three years both in exhortation and in preparation. Thus, in Cyrus’s third year they returned under Zerubbabel as leader and Jeshua as high priest, urged on by Zechariah the prophet and Haggai, still a young man and not yet a prophet. They numbered about fifty thousand: of the Jews there were forty-two thousand four hundred and sixty; the remainder were male and female slaves and persons of mixed descent.

[Col. 1472C] Cyrus also sent back with them five thousand and forty of the vessels of the Lord, among which Josephus includes *refrigeratoria*, vessels whose use I have not discovered. Some also went up with them claiming priestly descent for the sake of gain. When the record of their genealogy was sought and not found, they were admitted into Israel but excluded from the priesthood. They returned to Jerusalem and to the towns of Judah.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the seventieth year

This is the seventieth year for the release of the captivity, which Jeremiah foretold (chapter 23). Jerome too says that Cyrus’s first year was the seventh year of the seventh decade. Thus Cyrus’s third [Col. 1472D] year was the seventieth, in agreement with Josephus, who says: “In the first year of Cyrus’s reign, the seventieth year coincided”—that is, it was imminent.

The same is read in Chronicles (2 Chronicles 36): “Whoever had escaped the sword was carried to Babylon and served the king and his sons until the king of Persia should rule, and Jeremiah’s word should be fulfilled, and the land should celebrate its Sabbaths, until the seventy years of desolation were completed.” Daniel also refers to the same matter: “In the first year of Darius, I understood the number of years, that the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation were to be completed” (Daniel 9).

Jeremiah had plainly foretold this in the letter which he sent to the exiles: “When,” he says, “the seventy years begin [Col. 1473A] to be completed, I will visit you and bring you back to this place” (Jeremiah 29). Yet elsewhere Jeremiah seems to mean that they had been completed before Babylon’s overthrow, where he says: “These nations shall serve the king of Babylon for seventy years. And when the seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation for their iniquity, says the Lord, and I will make the land perpetual desolations” (Jeremiah 25). On the basis of this authority the Jews, as we said above, maintain that Belshazzar exulted and held a banquet.

But here Jeremiah speaks of seventy years not of captivity, but of Nebuchadnezzar’s wrongdoing, beginning from the time when he began to oppress neighbouring nations. Africanus supports this view when, discussing Nehemiah and [Col. 1473B] the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, he says: “At that time one hundred and fifteen years of Persian rule had elapsed, but one hundred and seventy-five years since Jerusalem’s captivity.”

Eusebius, however, in his *Chronicles* seems to oppose the foregoing, saying that the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes was the seventieth, according to the authority of Zechariah. Writing in Darius’s second year, Zechariah heard a man standing among the myrtles saying: “Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry?” (Zechariah 1). “This is now the seventieth year.” And shortly afterward: “When you fasted throughout these seventy years, did you fast a fast for me?” (Zechariah 7).

Clement also agrees with this in the first *Stromateis*, saying: “The captivity continued [Col. 1473C] for seventy years, until the second year of Darius son of Hystaspes.”

[Note: [Col. 1473D] Addition 1. He was a teacher in Alexandria; Origen came after him. This Clement composed the *Stromateis*, that is, certain “Instructions.”]

Eusebius seems to distinguish between the seventy years of captivity and the seventy years of the temple’s desolation, saying: “According to some, the whole period of captivity—seventy years—is reckoned from the third year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah to Cyrus’s twentieth year. According to others, seventy years of captivity are reckoned from Josiah’s thirteenth year to Cyrus’s first year, whereas the seventy years of the temple’s desolation are completed under King Darius.”

[Note: [Col. 1473D] Addition 2. Investigate which Darius he was after Cyrus [Col. 1474A]; thus you will also be able to note how many years Cyrus, Cambyses, and Smerdis reigned.]

Jerome’s gloss on Ezekiel agrees with their opinion, where, in discussing lying on the right side, he says that by Cyrus’s first year thirty years of the temple’s desolation [Col. 1473D] had elapsed. But the first opinion concerning the seventieth year is more certain and established by more authorities. Zechariah’s authority alone gives us pause: “This is now the seventieth year.” Perhaps this may be resolved by taking “now” as referring to what has already passed, as though he said: “This seventieth year is already long known and famous.” Perhaps in Zechariah it is called the seventieth year not of captivity but of the fifth age, which, according to the Hebrews, began thirty years before Cyrus’s monarchy.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the rebuilding of the temple

[Col. 1474A]

“Now in the year of their return to Judaea, the people assembled in Jerusalem as one man. Building the altar, they set it upon its bases and offered burnt offerings upon it to the Lord morning and evening. They celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles” (1 Esdras 3). We do not know where they obtained fire, unless perhaps they struck it from the stones of the old altar. “In the second year, in the second month, they laid the foundations of the temple.”

Hearing this, the Samaritans came to them and said: “Let us build with you, for we seek your God as you do” (1 Esdras 4). Israel’s leaders replied: [Col. 1474B] “It is common to us and to you to worship the Lord, but not to build him a house. For King Cyrus commanded this to us alone.” When the foundations appeared above the ground, the people raised their voices in rejoicing. Yet certain elders who had seen the former temple wailed loudly, and no one could distinguish the shout of rejoicing from the lament of those wailing.

The Samaritans, angered, hindered their work.

[Note: [Col. 1474C] Addition 1. Since Cyrus had commanded them to devote care and diligence to the building [Col. 1474D] of the temple, they were corrupted by the Samaritans and were negligent in building the temple.]

When they could not hinder them directly, they gave gifts to the Persian king’s officials who had been placed over the land. Corrupted by money, these officials sold themselves to the Samaritans so as to impede the building through negligence, though Cyrus knew nothing of it. They impeded them so thoroughly that during the thirty years in which Cyrus reigned, they raised no temple walls [Col. 1474C] beyond the supports.

After Cyrus defeated Croesus by the river Halys, he cleverly brought the highly warlike Lydian people into submission. He gave them festivals and games, ordering them to devote themselves to sport, feasting, and embraces, as though showing them goodwill. In this manner he emasculated them; and those whom he could not conquer by war, he subdued through lust. Later, after crossing the Araxes, he was defeated and killed by Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae. Throwing his severed head into a bag full of human blood, she said mockingly: “Satisfy yourself with the blood for which you thirsted.”

[Col. 1474D] Incidental material

In Cyrus’s days Tarquinius Superbus was the seventh king of the Romans. He was expelled from the kingdom because of his younger son Tarquinius, who violated Lucretia. He devised kinds of tortures: bonds, thonged whips, clubs, prisons, fetters, chains, exile, and the mines.

## CHAPTER XX. On Cambyses

After Cyrus died, following thirty years of his reign, his son Cambyses succeeded him. In Ezra he is called Artaxerxes or Ahasuerus (1 Esdras 4); in the history of Judith, on account of his wickedness, he is called [Col. 1475A] Nebuchadnezzar.

[Note: [Col. 1476A] Addition 1. While his father was still alive, Cambyses held the Assyrian kingdom of Nineveh for twelve years; consequently, upon his father’s death he held the monarchy for seven years.]

Then the rulers of the land who were hindering the Hebrews—namely Reudethleem, whom Josephus calls the recorder of all events, and others who governed Syria, Phoenicia, and all the regions beyond the Euphrates—wrote to King Cambyses that the Jews were rebuilding Jerusalem, a most wicked city, always rebellious against the Persian kings, and the temple in the likeness of a fortress. They said that it had formerly been destroyed because of rebellion and that, if these were rebuilt, the Jews would at once refuse the king tribute and provisions, and the king would no longer even have passage into Syria.

They said they recalled this to his attention because they were not [Col. 1476A] unmindful of the salt—that is, of every seasoning—they had eaten in his palace: as though, in return for benefits granted them, they were advising him to forbid the Hebrews’ rebuilding. Cambyses accepted their advice and forcefully prohibited it by letters. Then God’s work in Jerusalem ceased until Darius’s second year. Under Cambyses, moreover, the events related in the history of Judith occurred.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF JUDITH

[Col. 1475]

## CHAPTER I. Preface

[Col. 1475B]

Jerome translated this history from Chaldean into Latin at the request of Paula and Eustochium. Among the Hebrews this book is counted among the histories and among the Hagiographa, as Jerome says in the prologue beginning, “Twenty-two letters,” etc. Therefore, if it is read somewhere in the prologue on Judith as among the apocrypha, that is a copyist’s error, which may be detected from the very title; the Synod of Nicaea received it among the number of the sacred Scriptures. Because of its various and corrupt editions, Jerome translated it by following sense rather than word more closely than word for word.

After Cyrus died, a certain Mede named Arphaxad rose up at Ecbatana, rebuilt it, fortified it impregnable, and won over certain [Col. 1475C] parts of Media, until at last he ruled the whole of Media (Judith 1). Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, reigning in Nineveh, defeated Arphaxad in the plain of Ragau between the Euphrates and the Tigris in the twelfth year of his reign. This is Cambyses, to whom his still-living father had granted Nineveh and the Assyrian kingdom, and whom he surnamed Nebuchadnezzar. At his father’s death he was in the twelfth year of that kingdom; for he reigned only eight years in the monarchical kingdom. After he became monarch, his heart was exalted.

[Note: [Col. 1479D] Addition 1. Since no one was above him, he wished to be worshipped alone as God. Even when ill, he would not be carried in a litter except on the shoulders of kings, as though he surpassed them all.]

He sent to all who lived in Cilicia, Damascus, Lebanon, Carmel, Galilee, Samaria, and as far as Jerusalem, demanding tribute far heavier than that imposed by his fathers. All alike refused. Then the king [Col. 1475D] angrily swore by his throne that he would take vengeance on all of them. Accordingly, in the thirteenth year of his reign he ordered Holofernes, commander of the army, to march out against those regions and to spare neither person nor fortification. He set out with an army, and they covered the face of the earth like locusts.

After he had devastated Cilicia, Mesopotamia, [Col. 1476B] and the Midianites’ country, the provincial rulers sent to him, saying: “Let your anger against us cease. Come to us peacefully, and make use of our service as may please you” (Judith 3). He descended from the mountains with great force, occupied all the cities, destroyed them, and exterminated all the gods of the land. For Nebuchadnezzar had commanded that he alone should be called God by those nations which Holofernes’ power could subjugate.

When the Israelites heard this, they were greatly afraid that he would do the like in Jerusalem and in God’s sanctuary. They sent men to the borders of the land through which there might be a route into Jerusalem; they fortified narrow passages of the roads and humbled themselves before the Lord, at the exhortation of [Col. 1476C] Eliakim the priest, son of Jeshua, son of Jozadak—or perhaps another Eliakim, whom Jeshua himself sent about to exhort the Israelites in the mountains (Judith 4). The priests covered the altar of the Lord with sackcloth; they themselves, in ashes and sackcloth, offered burnt offerings and cried to the Lord.

“It was reported to Holofernes that the Israelites had prepared themselves to resist and had blocked the mountain routes” (Judith 5). He summoned the leaders of Ammon and Moab, saying: “Who are these people who occupy the highlands, and what is their strength?” Then Achior, leader of the Ammonites, replied, recounting how this people had first come from Chaldaea through Mesopotamia into the land of Canaan. When they had gone down into Egypt, their God brought them back [Col. 1476D] into the promised land. When he was reconciled to them, no one could resist them; but when they provoked him, he scourged them, because their God hated iniquity.

Recently, he continued, their God had brought them back to Jerusalem from the slavery of Nebuchadnezzar, to whom he had delivered them because of their sins, and now they held these highlands. Achior added: “Find out whether their God is offended [Col. 1477A] with them, and you will be able to conquer them; otherwise you will not prevail against them.” Holofernes angrily replied: “To show you that there is no God except Nebuchadnezzar, from this moment you shall be joined to that people, so that you may perish with them” (Judith 4).

[Note: [Col. 1479D] Addition 2. Cambyses bore four names: Cambyses, Artaxerxes, Ahasuerus, and Nebuchadnezzar.]

Holofernes then ordered his servants to take Achior to Bethulia, before which he had encamped. As they dragged him away, slingers came out against them. In fear they tied Achior to a tree and withdrew. The slingers untied him and set him among the elders and the people. Jerusalem had sent to Bethulia two priests and the leader Uzziah, of the tribe of Simeon. After Achior told them why Holofernes had sent him to them, Uzziah received him into [Col. 1477B] his house.

Holofernes found the channel of water flowing into the city by means of little birds that drank water from the channel, and by hidden fissures of the aqueduct; after cutting off the aqueduct, he deprived them of water (Judith 7).

[Note: [Col. 1480A] Addition 3. It seemed remarkable that little birds, thrusting their beaks into the ground in a dry place, appeared to drink; from this Holofernes perceived that water lay beneath.]

There were also small springs not far from the walls, which the citizens used secretly more for refreshment than for drinking. The Ammonites said to Holofernes: “If you want to take them without war and bloodshed, station guards at the springs.” He did so, and after twenty days the water in the cisterns failed. The people cried to those who had come from Jerusalem: “May the Lord judge between us and you. It would have been better for us to serve Holofernes than to perish of thirst.” The priests said: “Let us endure five more days; perhaps [Col. 1477C] God will show us mercy.”

Now there was in the city Judith, a widow for three years, a most beautiful but chaste woman from the tribe of Reuben. She rebuked the summoned priests because they had tested the Lord and set a limit of days to his mercy (Judith 8). She said: “I shall do a work of God which I shall not reveal to you. Stand tonight at the gates of the city, with Uzziah among you, so that I may go out through your hands.”

When they had departed, she prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord God of my father Simeon, who gave him a sword against the foreigners, direct the hand of your handmaid” (Genesis 49). She did not commend Simeon’s deed, which Jacob condemned, but the vengeance wrought by [Col. 1477D] the Lord through an ungodly man. After praying, she washed herself, anointed herself with the finest ointment, put on her festive clothing, and called her *abra*, that is, her maidservant—or perhaps *Abra* is the maidservant’s proper name (Judith 10).

“She placed on her shoulder a wineskin, a vessel of oil, meal, and *lapaces*—that is, food prepared with vegetables—together with bread and cheese, and set out.” The priests admired her beauty and prayed for her. As she descended the mountain, scouts seized her and brought her to Holofernes’ tents; he was immediately captivated by the sight of her.

Holofernes sat beneath a *canopoeum*, woven of purple, gold, and gems: that is, a silken net against flies, so called from Canopus, an Egyptian town where it was invented. Others call it a *conopoeum*, because it rises like a cone from broad to narrow. The Assyrians said: [Col. 1478A] “Who would despise the Hebrew people, who have women so beautiful that we rightly ought to fight them for these women?”

After Judith had bowed down, Holofernes said to her: “Why did you choose to come to us?” (Judith 11). She replied: “It is certain that our people will go to destruction, for they have grievously offended their God. They have spent the Lord’s vessels on provisions for foreigners. Moreover, they intend to drink the blood of their cattle, which God’s law absolutely forbids anyone to taste. Indeed, because of hunger and thirst they are already counted among the dead. The Lord sent me to announce these very things to you. He will tell me when he will repay them for their sin; then I shall come and lead you [Col. 1478B] all the way into Jerusalem, and you will possess all the people like sheep without a shepherd.”

Holofernes said: “If your God does this for me, he too will be my God”—that is, “I shall have him among the number of my gods”—“and you will be great in Nebuchadnezzar’s house.”

He had her brought to the place where his treasures were kept (Judith 12). When he ordered food from his own banquet to be given her, Judith said: “I shall eat from the things I brought with me, lest God’s wrath come upon me.” Holofernes said: “When these things have failed, what shall we do for you?” She replied: “As your soul lives, your servant will not use up all these things until God accomplishes through my hand what I have planned.”

She asked permission to go outside at night to worship her God. Thus, for three days she went out at night [Col. 1478C] and washed herself in the waters.

[Note: [Col. 1480A] Addition 4. You find a similar expression in Luke, chapter 11, where a Pharisee is said to have invited the Lord to a meal. The Pharisee began to wonder within himself why he had not been “washed” before the meal.]

She prayed to the God of Israel. On the fourth day Holofernes made a dinner for his servants and said to Vagoas the eunuch: “Persuade that Hebrew woman to consent to me willingly. For among the Assyrians it is shameful for a woman to mock a man and leave him untouched.” Vagoas said to her: “Let the good woman not be afraid to enter to my lord.” She replied: “Whatever pleases him will be best for me all the days of my life.” Having adorned herself, she stood before Holofernes. He became joyful and drank more wine than he had ever drunk in his life.

“And when evening came, the servants hurried away to their lodgings, and Judith was alone in the chamber. Holofernes lay upon his bed, overcome by excessive drunkenness [Col. 1478D]” (Judith 13). Judith told her maid to stand outside at the door and keep watch. She prayed with tears, saying: “Strengthen me, Lord God of Israel, and look in this hour upon the work of my hands.” She loosened the dagger from the bedpost at the head of the bed.

[Note: [Col. 1480A] Addition 5. It was the large knife with which he went girded, but which, on entering his bedchamber, he had hung from the post.]

Striking his neck twice, she cut off his head, gave it to her maid, took the *conopoeum*, and went out. When she reached the city gate, she cried: “Open, for God is with us, he who has displayed power in Israel.” All, from least to greatest, came out to meet her with lights. Displaying Holofernes’ head and the *conopoeum*, she said: “Give thanks to the Lord, who gave us victory by my hand and brought me back undefiled.”

Achior was summoned; when he saw Holofernes’ head, he fell [Col. 1479A] to the ground in terror. Recovering himself, he worshipped Judith. She said to the people: “Hang this head upon the walls, and at daybreak attack the enemy. Confused by the death of their master, they will turn to flight” (Judith 14). Then Achior circumcised the flesh of his foreskin and was joined to the people of Israel. Uzziah sent messengers through the towns of Judah to summon them to pursue the enemy.

The Hebrews went out in the morning, and the Assyrians said: “The mice have come out of their holes.” When Vagoas entered to awaken Holofernes, he saw the headless corpse. Entering Judith’s tent, he did not find her. He shouted to the people: “One Hebrew woman has brought shame upon Nebuchadnezzar’s house. Look: Holofernes’ head is not with him!”

[Col. 1479B] They were greatly troubled and sought the protection of flight (Judith 15). The Israelites pursued them and struck them down as far as the furthest limits of their territory. For thirty days the Assyrians’ spoils were scarcely gathered together; and everything belonging personally to Holofernes was given to Judith. Joachim the high priest came from Jerusalem with all the elders to see her, and they blessed her. Then Judith sang a song to the Lord, saying: “Begin unto the Lord with timbrels,” etc. (Judith 16).

On this song see what Jerome says on the psalm “O Lord, our Lord” (Psalm 8): when the name *Lord* occurs twice in Hebrew, as here, “Adonai, Lord God,” the first is the Tetragrammaton, [Col. 1479C] while the second is the common name for Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1480A] Addition 6. “Tetragrammaton” means “of four letters”: yod, he, waw, he. Yet these letters do not represent the sounds which ought to be represented by them, just as we sometimes represent [Col. 1480B] a sound by T.]

At the end of her song she prophesied concerning the day of judgment: “The almighty Lord will visit his own on the day of judgment, and will avenge himself on the wicked, so that they may burn for ever.” After this Judith went up with the people to Jerusalem, and they offered their vows and promises to the Lord. “Judith offered as an anathema of oblivion all Holofernes’ weapons of war and the *conopoeum*, and all the people celebrated.”

They received this day among the number of holy days, calling Cambyses the second Nebuchadnezzar. Judith, daughter of Merari, a Reubenite, returned to Bethulia. On her mother’s side she was of the tribe of Simeon, and she remained a widow throughout all her life. At the completion of one hundred and five years, she died and was buried with her husband Manasseh. She set her maid free, and [Col. 1479D] all the people mourned her for seven days.

Cambyses entered Egypt, devastated it, abhorred its religion and rites, overthrew its temples, and built Babylon in Egypt. On returning from Egypt he fell ill and was borne on the shoulders of kings. He died at Damascus.

## CHAPTER II. On the two magi and Darius son of Hystaspes

[Col. 1480B]

[Note: [Col. 1479D] From the histories of Josephus and others.]

After Cambyses, one of the seven magi who governed the Persian kingdom, named Smerdis, obtained the Persian kingdom. Taking Pantaeus, daughter of Cambyses, as his wife, he pretended that he did not wish to reign for himself, but to preserve the kingdom for Mergus, Cambyses’ brother, because he was a boy. Yet Cambyses had earlier killed this Mergus in the inner part of the temple, with only this Smerdis aware of this sacrilege and parricide.

When Smerdis died after seven months of reign, he substituted his brother, a young man handsome in form and strength, declaring that he was Mergus, son of Cyrus and brother of Cambyses. This concealment of kings could easily occur in Persia because almost no one entered before the king [Col. 1480C] except his household. One of the seven magi began to suspect him, thinking that he was not Mergus. This magus had a daughter among the king’s concubines. Speaking privately with her, he told her to feel the king’s head carefully at night and discover whether he had ears. Cambyses had formerly cut off the ears of this brother of Smerdis because he had offended him.

When the girl discovered that he had no ears, she reported it to her father. After he had told the other magi, they conspired against him and killed him; these two brothers had offered resistance for only one year. The seven magi then discussed among themselves which of them should marry the king’s daughter and reign in his place. They agreed that one of them should be chosen by the following omen: at dawn they were to come alone on horseback into the palace court before the temple gates; whichever man’s horse first neighed would, according to the oracle of the gods, be made king.

One of them was Darius son of Hystaspes. Speaking secretly with his groom, he ordered him, in the place where they were to assemble the next day, to put a mare under his horse at night. When this was done, the next day the seven magi arrived at the same place; immediately, remembering the mare, Darius’s horse neighed. Without delay Darius was elevated to kingship, and he reigned thirty-nine years over the Persian kingdom.

Zerubbabel was his intimate associate. When [Col. 1481A] Cambyses had forbidden the rebuilding of the temple, Zerubbabel went up to him and, through the intervention of this Darius, tried to change the king’s mind, but was unable to do so. He then secretly persuaded Darius to make a vow to the God of Israel: if God made him king, he would restore God’s temple and send back to Jerusalem all the Lord’s vessels still held by the king of Persia.

## CHAPTER III. On the completion of the temple, and Zechariah and Haggai
Accordingly, when Zerubbabel heard that he was reigning, he confidently undertook to rebuild the Temple, while Haggai and Zechariah exhorted the people (1 Esdras 5). They preached that God was offended with them because they dwelt in panelled houses while the house of the Lord was desolate [Col. 1481B]. They said that this was a sign of God’s wrath: they sowed much and harvested little. But the Persian king’s governors beyond the River forbade the rebuilding. When the elders of Judah answered that their God had commanded this to them, and that it was sinful to oppose Him, both parties agreed that the matter should be referred to Darius.

Zerubbabel therefore went up to the king with the governors’ messengers and was honoured by him beyond what he had hoped. For he slept in the king’s chamber with two other chamberlains. Now King Darius gave a banquet to the satraps of Persia, the governors of India and Ethiopia, and the magistrates of the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces (3 Esdras 3). That same night, waking, he passed the night sleeplessly and put a question to the three guards of his body [Col. 1481C]: which of three things seemed strongest—the king, wine, or woman—promising gifts and honour to the one who answered most wisely.

On the following day the three came before the satraps and magistrates. The first said that the king was stronger than all things. For although man rules the other living creatures, the king rules man, and everything is done at his command. The second preferred the strength of wine, because, although man rules others only through strength of mind, wine overcomes even strength of mind itself. But Zerubbabel declared woman stronger than either (3 Esdras 4). For women give life and nourishment alike to kings and to those who plant vines; they bring them even to full strength; and men do not fear to lay down their lives for women [Col. 1481D]. He also related that he had seen the concubine of a certain king striking the king on the cheeks; when she laughed, the king smiled, and when she was troubled, the king was troubled.

Above all these, however, he said that truth was stronger, since it is unchangeable and everlasting. For the truth of God had created all things; by His providence the world was governed; and nothing could resist it. When all declared truth to be stronger than all things, the king told Zerubbabel to ask whatever he wished. Zerubbabel requested that the rebuilding of the Temple be carried out and that the vessels of the Lord be sent back to Jerusalem. The king rejoiced, for he remembered that he himself had vowed this. He wrote by letter to his governors beyond the River that they must in no way hinder the Jews, but aid them from the king’s expenses [Col. 1482A], giving them daily victims, fine flour, wine, and salt, so that they might offer these to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons (1 Esdras 6). He added:

> “Whoever alters this command, let a timber be taken from his house and let him be fastened upon it; but let his house be confiscated. I, Darius, have issued the decree, and I desire that it be diligently fulfilled” (ibid.).

Darius also sent back the vessels of the Lord through Zerubbabel (3 Esdras 6). On his return through Chaldea, Zerubbabel made known the king’s commands to his fellow-tribesmen, and many went up with him to Jerusalem.

> [Note: [Col. 1482C] Addition 1. Jerome also says of this same man in a certain letter: “When he had assembled a very great and splendid army, he once went up with a few men onto a mound so that he might survey them all, and began to weep. When he was asked why he did so, since he ought rather to have rejoiced over so great an army, he replied: ‘I weep because none of these will still be alive after a hundred years; all will be dust and ashes’” [Col. 1482D].]

Thus, in the second year of Darius, in the eighth month, they pressed on with the work and completed it in the seventh year of Darius, which was the forty-sixth year of the Persian kingdom, according to what is said in the Gospel: “This Temple was built in forty-six years” (John 2) [Col. 1482B].

> [Note: [Col. 1482D] Addition 2. The Jews said this when the Lord said: “Destroy this Temple, and I will raise it up again.”]

That is, from the first permission Cyrus gave to return and rebuild the Temple until the seventh year of Darius, when it was completed, this number of years had elapsed. Haggai died and was buried beside the monuments of the priests.

The children of Israel assembled for the dedication of the Temple.

> [Note: [Col. 1482D] Addition 3. Three dedications of the Temple are recorded. One was performed by Solomon after the completion of the Temple which he had built. This occurred in September, as you have in the Book of Kings, in the eleventh year of Solomon’s reign (3 Kings 6). The second is recorded here as having taken place in spring under Darius, with Zerubbabel as its promoter. Of the third, it is recorded that it was performed by Judas Maccabaeus, who, after defeating Antiochus Epiphanes, dedicated the Temple, which Antiochus had so defiled and laid waste that shrubs are even said to have sprung up in it. It is said to have been rededicated on the twentieth day of December [Col. 1483A] (1 Maccabees 4). This dedication continued thereafter; concerning it the Gospel says: “The feast of the Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter” (John 10).]

They dedicated it in the twelfth month, called March among the Latins, on the twenty-third day of the month (3 Esdras 7). This was the second, springtime dedication of the Temple. The children of Israel celebrated the Passover according to the law of the Lord.

How or when they recovered the Ark is uncertain. But if what Epiphanius says is true—that it will not come forth from the hiding place of the rock until the Day of Judgment—then it is certain that the Hebrews made another Ark resembling the first [Col. 1482C]. For among the spoils which the Romans carried away from Judaea, the Ark of the Lord, the lampstand, and the table are said to have been taken. Zechariah died in a good old age and was buried beside Haggai. Darius, after Egypt had withdrawn from him, died.

[Col. 1483A] **Contemporary Events**

At Rome, after the expulsion of the kings, consuls first began with Brutus, and Rome scarcely held dominion as far as the fifteenth milestone.

> [Note: [Col. 1483A] Addition 1. Miles are marked off by boundary stones, and at that time Roman dominion extended no farther than fifteen miles.]

Thereafter tribunes of the people, dictators, and again consuls governed the commonwealth, until Julius Caesar. Pythagoras died. At Rome, the people, having caused a sedition, withdrew from the patricians.

## Chapter IV. On Xerxes

[Col. 1483B]

After Darius, his son Xerxes succeeded him in the kingdom. He proved himself heir to his father’s intention by honouring God. At that time Eliakim, or Joachim son of Jeshua, was chief priest; and in Judaea the management of affairs rested with the priests, as it had formerly rested with kings and judges. Xerxes recovered Egypt, which had revolted from his father, and devastated Greece. Greek history recounts much concerning his power. Josephus says that Ezra came to Judaea under this king, but Ezra himself says that he came under Artaxerxes. After Xerxes, Artabanus reigned for seven months.

> [Note: [Col. 1483B] Addition 1. It is not determined here how long Xerxes reigned [Col. 1483C].]

[Col. 1483C] **Contemporary Events**

At that time Socrates was born. A stone bearing the form of a goat fell from heaven into the Aegean Sea.

## Chapter V. On Artaxerxes and Ezra

After this, Artaxerxes, also called Longimanus, obtained the Persian kingdom. At that time Ezra the Aaronite restored the Law which had been burnt by the Chaldeans. He also devised new letter-forms, easier for writing and pronunciation, and for this reason was called the “swift scribe” (1 Esdras 7). Nor is it surprising that he restored books through the Holy Spirit, since many persons in our own day would know how to restore a Psalter, a book of Hymns, and many such books after they had been destroyed.

He also added certain things of his own [Col. 1483D], such as the titles of the Psalms and many things read in the Pentateuch. Thus it is probable that he himself removed certain things which he understood to be superfluous. Some also relate that he handed down to the Jews the practice of writing from right to left.

> [Note: [Col. 1485A] Addition 1. Some maintain that Ezra was Jozadak, the father of Jeshua, or Malachi.]

Formerly they wrote in the manner of ploughmen. Hence writing is commonly called *exaratio*, “ploughing out.” They wrote from the left-hand edge toward the right, and then, returning from the right, wrote toward the left. Perhaps by this method of writing the Holy Spirit prefigured the very thing now signified in the Mass by the transfer of the book from right to left.

> [Note: [Col. 1485A] Addition 2. Here is signified that faith in the one God, which formerly rested among the Jews on the right, now rests among the Gentiles on the left, and at the end will return to them [Col. 1485B]. For this reason it should be known that, if there is a single light at Mass, it should properly always be on the left, to signify that the light of faith now rests only among the Gentiles.]

Ezra found favour in the eyes of Artaxerxes and asked permission to go up to Jerusalem, in order to instruct his people in the Law which he had restored. The king therefore gave him permission to return [Col. 1484A] and handed him a letter to his governors beyond the River and to the keepers of the public treasury, requiring them to give Ezra without delay whatever he asked, up to one hundred talents of silver, three hundred *cors* of grain, one hundred *baths* of oil, and salt without measure (1 Esdras).

He exempted the Temple ministers—priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and Nethinim—from every tax, tribute, and provision levy. He also gave Ezra authority, according to his wisdom, to remove and appoint judges and governors beyond the River, and to punish the disobedient by death, exile, confiscation of property, or imprisonment.

Ezra read this letter to the Jews settled in Babylonia. He sent a copy of it to the children of Israel [Col. 1484B] who were beyond the Caspian Mountains, and from among them priests and Levites came to Ezra, two hundred and twenty Nethinim. There were with him one thousand seven hundred persons (1 Esdras 8). They departed from Babylonia in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, on the first day of the first month, and assembled by the river which flows to Ahava. Josephus says that it was near the Euphrates. Ahava may have been a river flowing into the Euphrates, or a stream of the Euphrates.

They remained there three days, and Ezra proclaimed a fast to them, that they might humble themselves before the Lord and ask from Him a right and safe way. For Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for an escort on the road, saying: “The hand of our God is upon all who seek Him.” Ezra selected twelve priests, to whom he entrusted [Col. 1484C] the vessels of the Lord and the gifts which the king, his princes, and his people were sending to Jerusalem. They came to Jerusalem in the fifth month and kept silence for three days. On the fourth day they brought into the house of the Lord what they had carried with them; offering burnt offerings in thanksgiving, they gave the king’s letter to the governors beyond the River, who honoured the people of God and the house of God.

Then the princes of Israel approached Ezra, saying: “The people of Israel have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands” (1 Esdras 9). For they had taken wives for themselves and their sons from among their daughters. The hand of the priests, princes, and sacred servants also was found in this transgression. Ezra then tore his garments and, weeping and praying, lay upon the ground [Col. 1484D] until the evening sacrifice. Then the princes came to him, saying: “Rise; it is yours to decide what we should do. Our hand will be with you” (1 Esdras 10).

Ezra then adjured the priests, princes, and Levites to cast away all foreign wives and those born from them. A proclamation was sent to all the children of the captivity, and they assembled at Jerusalem within three days, on the twentieth day of the ninth month, called December among the Latins. Ezra rose and accused them of having, contrary to God’s Law, mixed the holy seed with the seed of the uncircumcised; it was necessary, he said, to put away their wives. The multitude answered:

> “The people are numerous, and it is the rainy season; we cannot endure standing outside, and this is not the work of one day [Col. 1485A] or two. Choose rulers for yourself and go through all Israel; wherever you find foreign women, put them away without delay.”

They were first found at Jerusalem among the sons of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers, and they were immediately put away. For one must not believe that Jeshua the high priest had a foreign wife. And the fact that Zechariah was seen clothed in filthy garments must be referred to his sons—or else to the fact that, though he was high priest, he did not rebuke the people. They did the same throughout all Israel, and every man in whom this transgression was found offered a ram for the turning away of sin.

## Chapter VI. On Nehemiah

[Col. 1485B]

And it came to pass in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes. Nehemiah, one of the children of the captivity, was the king’s cupbearer (2 Esdras 1). While he was in the citadel of Susa, he heard travellers speaking Hebrew. Approaching them, he asked about the condition of Judaea and Jerusalem, and learned from them that the city was without walls and that God’s people dwelt in it in affliction. For by day they endured [Col. 1485C] the attacks of enemies; by night robbers entered and filled the streets with the corpses of those who had been killed.

Nehemiah wept and tasted no desirable food, crying to the Lord night and day. As he stood at table and raised wine to the king, he appeared before him as though ill (2 Esdras 2). The king said: “Why are you sad, and what evil lies hidden in your heart?” Trembling, he answered: “Because the city of my fathers’ sepulchres lies desolate. If it seems good to you, send me, and I shall rebuild it.” The queen, who sat beside the king, said: “When will you return?” And he fixed for Nehemiah a time of return.

This queen was not Esther, as some have maintained; nor does that history occur in Ezra’s days. Ezra would not have passed it over in silence in his book. The king gave Nehemiah [Col. 1485D] a letter to the governors beyond the River. In it he commanded that honour be shown to Nehemiah as to a governor and envoy sent from his side, and that expenses be supplied for rebuilding the city. He sent military commanders and horsemen with him. Passing through Babylonia, Nehemiah brought back with him many of the children of the captivity and came to Jerusalem in the twenty-fifth year of King Artaxerxes, according to Josephus.

At Jerusalem Elisaphat, son of Eliakim, was high priest. Nehemiah kept silence for three days; then, rising at night with a few companions, he went around the ruins of the walls, considering how they might be rebuilt. On the fourth day Nehemiah spoke to the multitude: “Come, let us rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, and let us no longer be [Col. 1486A] a reproach among the nations. For the hand of God is with us, as are the king’s words which he has spoken to me.”

> [Note: [Col. 1486A] Addition 1. From this rebuilding must be understood the calculation of years which is indicated in Daniel’s prophecy, above, in the eighth vision: “Know therefore and understand” (Dan. 9).]

## Chapter VII. On the Rebuilding of Jerusalem

“The priests arose and built the Sheep Gate” (2 Esdras 3). Another translation reads: “They built the gate and the Sheep Pool.” This is the gate beside the Temple through which sheep were brought in for offering. Elsewhere it is called the Tower of the Flock. There was another Tower of the Flock on the road to Bethlehem, where Jacob fed his flocks (Gen. 35), and where shepherds watching over their flock saw [Col. 1486B] a multitude of the heavenly host (Luke 2).

Second, the sons of Asnaa built the Fish Gate; they set up its doors, bolts, and bars. It faced Joppa and Diospolis, through it an abundance of fish was brought in. According to Josephus, it was later called the Gate of David. Third, the perfumers and goldsmiths built the Old Gate. Its traces existed in the days of the Jebusites and Melchizedek. Fourth, the sons of Zanoah built the Valley Gate, which led into the valley of Jehoshaphat. Fifth, Malchiah, ruler of the village of Beth-haccherem, built the Dung Gate. Through this gate the city’s filth flowed out, when streams overflowed, into the Kidron torrent. Sixth, the ruler of the district of Mizpah built the Fountain Gate and the walls of the pool of Siloam.

The people built the walls between [Col. 1486C] the gates, by villages and towns, each according to his ability. Do not be troubled if you find other names of gates: perhaps these were made in the inner wall, while some of those mentioned above later received other names. For the Merchants’ Gate may perhaps be the Sheep Gate, where merchants had placed their workshops because of the Temple’s proximity. The Judgment Gate may have been the Old Gate, which stood out first at the front of the city. The Water Gate may have been the Fountain Gate. The Horse Gate, however, was not a gate of the city, but was situated before the courts of the Temple, as far as which it was lawful to ride on horseback.

Nehemiah with his servants pressed on with the work, using neither sleep nor food for pleasure but only from necessity. The work was completed in [Col. 1486D] two years and four months, though amid great distress and very many hindrances. First, the neighbouring nations attacked them with a strong hand. Nehemiah stationed half the people armed outside the city to withstand the attackers’ assaults. The other half built, laying stones with one hand and holding a sword with the other (2 Esdras 4).

A second obstacle then intervened: famine arose in the land, and the people bound themselves by debt at interest. They were compelled to sell fields, vineyards, and olive groves; eventually, they even sold sons and daughters as male and female slaves (2 Esdras 5). Having called together the multitude, Nehemiah compelled the rich and magistrates to remit the interest and restore the vineyards, slaves, and fields which they had purchased. Shaking out his garment-fold, he said: “Thus may God shake out every man who does not fulfil this word.” And the entire multitude said, “Amen.”

He also forgave the provisions owed to the king. Although he had been sent by the king as governor, he did not consume the provisions owed to governors from the first day when he departed from the king until he returned to him. Moreover, he faced a third obstacle: the governors beyond the River, who envied him, bribed certain elders at Jerusalem so that they might deliver him to death (2 Esdras 6). When they could not do so, they frightened him by various rumours in order that he might cease from the work, saying: “Many have conspired against you; go and hide [Col. 1487B] from them.” Again they said: “It has been reported to the king that you wish to rebel and make yourself king in Judaea. Do not provoke your lord.” Though they invented many things of this kind, they did not prevail, because the hand of the Lord was with him.

## Chapter VIII. On the Discovery of Fire

After the wall had been built, because there were few inhabitants in Jerusalem, Nehemiah commanded that the gates be shut before sunset and not opened before the heat of the sun (2 Esdras 7). As the seventh month approached, which is almost wholly festive among them, they assembled at Jerusalem as one man (2 Esdras 8). Nehemiah learned that they did not have fire from above. The elders handed down to him that, in the days of the captivity, Jeremiah had hidden the logs of the altar and the embers in the depths of the earth in the valley of Jehoshaphat [Col. 1487C].

When they came to the place, they dug out a pit and found logs, embers, and thick water. Taking these, they cast them upon the heap of wood and the offerings which were upon the altar, and fire burst forth (2 Maccabees 1). Nehemiah called this day *Nephthar*, which means “purification.” Others say *Nephi*. The priests prayed, Jonathan beginning and the rest responding.

> [Note: [Col. 1487C] Addition 1. Note that what we say here—namely, that the priests prayed, Jonathan beginning, and so forth—was rather done under Nehemiah. The Roman Church, in a certain letter for a fast-day, says that it was done in the time of the Maccabees, entitling the letter “A reading from the Book of Maccabees,” who lived long after Nehemiah [Col. 1487D]. Thus what is said here seems contrary to the Church. The matter may be resolved thus: since the Second Book of Maccabees, from which that letter is taken, is not a consecutive history but only a letter sent by Judas and the elders to other dispersed Jews, Judas notifies those dispersed Jews of this event and commands them to celebrate the newly instituted festival; it is not principally narrated.]

Nehemiah also composed a special prayer.

## Chapter IX. On the Observance of Tabernacles

[Col. 1487D]

On the first day of the Feast of Tabernacles they told Ezra [Col. 1488A] to bring the book of the Law and read before the people (2 Esdras 8). Ezra stood on a wooden platform made for speaking beside the Water Gate—that is, the gate of the court—near which were the basins, and he read from morning until midday. Twelve Levites enforced silence among the people. All the people wept, but Ezra said to them: “Do not grieve, for this is the holy day of the Lord; go, eat rich food and drink mulled wine, and give portions to those who have prepared nothing for themselves.”

When they returned on the second day, they found in the Law that the Lord had commanded the children of Israel to dwell in tabernacles in the seventh month on the festival day. At Ezra’s command they went out and took branches of olive, beautiful myrtle wood [Col. 1488B], and palms. They made tabernacles for themselves in their courts, on their rooftops, and in the courts of the house of the Lord—something they had not done since the days of Joshua son of Nun. It was observed thereafter in Israel until the present day.

On the eighth day they held an assembly according to the rite, decreeing that each person should give a third part of a shekel per year for oil, the loaves of presentation, wood, continual sacrifices, festival days, and sin offerings. On the twenty-fourth day, because they had heard in the Law that Ammonites and Moabites were not to enter the assembly of God (2 Esdras 9), they separated foreigners from the assembly. In their purification they appointed a general fast for the next day, so that men and beasts, even children up to seven years old, might afflict themselves. They assembled eight times to hear the Law [Col. 1488C], four times by day and four by night. When the reading ended, the people prostrated themselves for prayer; prayers were said over them, and finally the priestly blessing.

From these things, Bede says, the Church drew an example: for readings are given from steps, Levites make proclamations among the people, and the people assemble at church eight times, though not entirely in the same way as they did. For once in the night we rise for the nocturnal office, according to: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Ps. 118), and so forth. In the daytime we chant the psalms seven times, according to: “Seven times in the day I have given praise to you” (ibid.). At each Hour a reading is given, which we call the chapter; after this, on weekdays, the people prostrate themselves for prayers, and a prayer for the blessing is added [Col. 1488D].

## Chapter X. On the Building of the Wall and the Death of Nehemiah

Nehemiah, seeing that the city had become almost empty of inhabitants, asked the leading men to dwell in Jerusalem, and he blessed those who volunteered (2 Esdras 11). The rest of the multitude cast lots, and one-tenth was made to dwell in Jerusalem. After some time they assembled at Jerusalem for the dedication of the wall. Priests, Levites, and singers came up with musical instruments; chanting psalms, they proceeded along the wall (2 Esdras 12). Ezra went before them; Nehemiah and the leading men with him proceeded, chanting psalms, upon the other part of the wall [Col. 1489A]. The remaining multitude followed them on the ground, and they led choirs.

> [Note: [Col. 1490B] These matters are outside the Bible.]

When these things had been completed, Nehemiah returned to the king in Persia in the thirty-second year of his reign. Ezra died in a venerable old age and was buried in Jerusalem with great magnificence. Some Hebrews assert that he was Malachi. But Malachi was born in Judaea, at Sophis, after the return from captivity. Because he was of most excellent life and handsome appearance, the people called him *Malachi*, that is, “Angel.” They also relate that, on the very day he spoke prophetically, an angel of God appeared and repeated the same words. He died while still young and was buried in his own field.

Near the end of his days, Nehemiah returned [Col. 1489B] to Jerusalem by the king’s favour and understood the evils being done there (2 Esdras 13). The priests, during the days of their courses, did not live in the storerooms around the Temple but in their private houses with all their households; they had placed the custody of the vessels of the Lord in houses separated from the Temple. At his own expense, Nehemiah built storerooms in which the priests kept watch and the vessels were stored.

Moreover, he found the people treading winepresses on the Sabbath and bringing into Jerusalem wine, grapes, figs, and every burden. Foreign peoples likewise brought fish and merchandise and sold them to the children of Judah on Sabbaths. He rebuked the leading men, saying: “Why do you profane the Sabbath day and bring the wrath of God upon Israel and upon this city?” He bound them by oath to observe the Sabbath and commanded the gates to be shut on the Sabbath [Col. 1490A], so that merchants might not enter. They remained outside Jerusalem once and twice. Nehemiah warned them that, if thereafter they came, he would lay hands upon them; and they withdrew.

Nehemiah established at Jerusalem a library, gathering books concerning the kings, books of the prophets and David, royal letters, and books concerning gifts. For all these things which he had done, Nehemiah prayed to God, saying: “Remember me, my God, for good.”

Up to this point the sequence of history has been taken from the Hebrew annals, apart from Esther. Events occurring afterward among the Jews are presented from the writings of Josephus and Africanus, and from the Book of Maccabees, which some maintain was written by Hebrews and others by Greeks. Nehemiah, a gracious man, died and was buried beside the wall which he had built [Col. 1490B]. After Artaxerxes, Xerxes reigned for two months; after him Sogdianus for seven months. After him Darius, surnamed Nothus, reigned; under him Egypt revolted from the Persians.

**Contemporary Events**

At that period there was an eclipse of the sun, and fire erupted from Etna. Plato was born; Hippocrates the physician flourished; Dionysius exercised tyranny in Sicily. After Darius, Artaxerxes, surnamed Mnemon, son of Darius and Parysatis, reigned. He is called Ahasuerus by the Hebrews. Under him the history of Esther was written.

# History of the Book of Esther

[Col. 1489]

## Chapter I. Preface

[Col. 1489C]

Jerome translated the Book of Esther from Hebrew into Latin at the request of Paula and Eustochium. Because it had been corrupted in Greek through various editions, he recovered it from the Hebrew archives and carefully translated it word for word.

Ahasuerus reigned from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, and the throne of his kingdom was in the city of Susa. In the third year of his rule he gave a great feast for all his princes and the eminent men of the provinces before him, lasting one hundred and seventy days (Esther 1), in that wonderful palace of which one reads in the history of Alexander. Its columns were silver; its vaulted roof, like a firmament, had gems of various colours arranged in the forms of stars [Col. 1489D] and constellations.

“After these days of feasting, he invited all the people who were in Susa. They reclined outside the palace for seven days, in the entrance court of the pleasure-garden. In the garden was a vineyard with silver vines, golden branches, and clusters distinguished by a variety [Col. 1490C] of gems. Tents were spread above the guests, hanging from silver and marble columns, fastened with ivory rings and cords of fine linen and purple. Golden and silver couches were arranged upon pavement laid with emerald-green and Parian stone. All drank excellent and abundant wine from golden cups. No one compelled those unwilling to drink, although this was the Persian custom.

“Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women in the king’s palace. On the seventh day, when the king had grown warm with wine, he commanded the seven eunuchs to bring in the queen in her finery, so that she might display her beauty to all. She disdained to come at the king’s command. The enraged king asked the seven wise men [Col. 1490D] who saw his face what penalty Vashti deserved. Mamuchan replied: ‘Vashti has wronged not you alone, but all the men of your kingdom. For by her example women will make light of their husbands’ commands. Let an edict therefore go forth from you that Vashti shall no longer enter before the king [Col. 1491A], but that another, better woman shall reign in her place.’ And an edict went out to all the provinces by the king’s letter.

“The king’s servants said to him: ‘Let beautiful virgin girls be sought for the king, and let them be committed to the eunuch Hegai for safekeeping and receive the women’s adornment (*mundus muliebris*)’” (Esther 2)—that is, garments, dress, and ornaments. Hence we call the attendants of such adornment *mundibordi*. “And whichever pleases the king’s eyes shall reign in Vashti’s place.” The proposal pleased the king, and he ordered it done.

There was then in Susa a Jew named Mordecai, of the tribe of Benjamin, who had come down in the captivity of Jeconiah. He was the guardian of the daughter of his brother, Hadassah, who was also called Esther. Having been orphaned of both parents, she had been adopted by Mordecai as his daughter. She [Col. 1491B] was entrusted to the eunuch among the other women and did not disclose her people, for Mordecai had commanded her to do so. She found favour in the eunuch’s eyes; he hastened her women’s adornment and gave her seven girls to dress and attend her.

The virgins were anointed with oil of myrrh for six months, and for another six months used certain perfumes and aromatic substances, so that after a year they might enter before the king. The woman who entered in the evening went out in the morning and could not return unless the king summoned her by name. Mordecai remained in the entrance court of the royal house, concerned for his daughter’s safety.

At length came the day when Esther, daughter of Abihail, was to enter before the king. She did not ask Hegai for women’s adornment, but left it [Col. 1491C] to his discretion; he was charged with giving the women whatever they requested. She entered before the king in the seventh year of his reign, in the tenth month, which is called *Thebeth* in Hebrew and January in Latin. She found favour with the king, who made her queen in Vashti’s place. He celebrated the marriage for a month and, through those called *Aggari*, that is, couriers, ordered a respite throughout the kingdom for the time of the marriage.

Mordecai, who had more frequently lived in Babylonia, from which Esther too had been brought, moved to Susa. At that time two eunuchs, gatekeepers of the king, became angry and plotted to kill him. This did not escape Mordecai; he informed Esther, and she reported it to the king in Mordecai’s name. An inquiry was made, the plot was found out, and they were hanged on the gallows [Col. 1491D]. The matter was entered before the king in the annals, in which kings recorded the events of their times.

After this Ahasuerus exalted Haman the Amalekite, who was of the stock of Agag, whom Samuel slew. The king’s servants worshipped him, except Mordecai, who, because of his ancestral laws, did not bend the knee before him. Observing this, Haman grew angry. Learning that Mordecai was a Hebrew (Esther 3), he said: “Free Persians bend their knees; this slave refuses in disdain.” He planned to destroy the Jews in Ahasuerus’s kingdom, stirred by an old hatred because the Jews had exterminated the Amalekites.

Therefore, in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus’s reign, in the first month, the lot was cast into an urn—called *phur* in Hebrew—before Haman, to determine on what day and in what month the Jewish nation should be killed; and the twelfth month came forth [Col. 1492A]. Haman then said to the king: “It is in the king’s interest to preserve peace, but unlikeness is the stepmother of peace. There is a people in your kingdom unlike the rest, using strange laws and moreover despising the king’s decrees. It is expedient for you that they not grow insolent; decree, therefore, that they perish. And lest you suffer loss in taxes, I shall pay ten thousand talents to the treasurers of your treasury.”

The king took the ring which he used and gave it to Haman, saying: “Keep your silver; do with the people what pleases you.” Haman then wrote, in the king’s name and sealed with the king’s ring, letters to all the provinces ordering that the Jews, from child to old man, should be killed and their goods plundered on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month. The edict was immediately posted in Susa.

[Col. 1492B] When the Jews had read this, they wept. Mordecai too clothed himself in sackcloth and sprinkled himself with ashes, wailing loudly before the gates of the palace (Esther IV). For it was not lawful for those clothed in sackcloth to enter the palace. When Esther learned this, she was dismayed; and she sent him clothing, so that, dressed in it, he might come in to her. He refused to accept it, but through a eunuch signified to her the reason for his mourning, and sent her a copy of the decree posted at Susa, urging her to go in to the king and entreat him for her people. She replied: “For thirty days now I have not been summoned to the king; and it has been decreed that whoever approaches without being summoned shall die, unless perhaps the king extends the golden sceptre to that person.” Again Mordecai said to her: “How do you know [Col. 1492C] whether you have come to the throne for this very purpose, that you might be prepared for such a time? If you are silent now, the Lord will deliver his people through another; but you and your father’s house shall perish.” Then Esther instructed Mordecai that all the Jews who were in Susa should fast for three days and pray for her; she herself fasted as well.”

“On the third day, clothed in royal apparel, she stood in the courtyard of the palace opposite the king’s hall, with two maidservants. Leaning on one, she supported herself; the other followed behind, carrying the train of her garment with her fingertips (Esther V). The king was sitting on his throne opposite the entrance to the palace. When he looked at her with a grim expression, she fainted. But when he saw Esther collapse, he was pleased with her and extended the golden sceptre toward her. Rising and drawing near, she kissed the tip [Col. 1492D] of the sceptre. Then the king said: ‘What do you want, Esther? Whatever you ask I shall give you.’ She replied: ‘I beg you to come to a banquet with me today, you and Haman.’ He rose and came to her. Holding her in his embrace, he comforted her, saying: ‘Do not be afraid; the law was made for subjects, but you reign jointly with me.’ Both came to the queen’s banquet. After he had drunk freely, he said: ‘Ask what you wish, Esther, and you shall obtain it.’ She replied: ‘I beg that the king and Haman come to the banquet tomorrow, and I shall reveal my heart to them.’ Haman therefore went out rejoicing. When he saw that Mordecai had not risen for him, he was enraged; and summoning his wife and friends, he recounted to them all his glory, adding that Esther had invited him alone with the king to the banquet. Yet he considered himself to possess nothing [Col. 1493A] so long as Mordecai lived. They said to him: ‘Order a beam fifty cubits high to be prepared, and urge the king to have Mordecai hanged upon it; then go joyfully with the king to the banquet.’ And he ordered the cross to be prepared.”

“That night the king passed without sleep and ordered the Annals to be read to him (Esther VI). They came to the passage where it was written that Mordecai had reported to him the plot of the eunuchs. The king said: ‘What honour has Mordecai received for this loyalty?’ They replied: ‘Nothing.’ The king asked who was in the court, and the servants said: ‘Haman.’ For he himself had entered in order to urge the king concerning Mordecai’s death. When Haman had been summoned and entered, the king said to him: ‘What ought to be done for the man whom the king wishes to honour?’ Thinking [Col. 1493B] that this had been said about himself, he replied: ‘He ought to be clothed in royal robes, crowned with a diadem, seated upon the king’s horse; and the foremost of the princes should hold the horse and, proceeding through the city, proclaim: “Thus shall he be honoured whom the king wishes to honour.”’ The king said to him: ‘Hurry, and do as you have said for Mordecai. Take care not to omit anything of what you have said.’ And Haman did for Mordecai what he had proposed. At first Mordecai resisted, thinking that Haman was mocking him; but once he knew the truth, he consented. Mordecai returned to the gates of the palace. Haman, however, hurried home mourning and with his head covered. His friends said to him: ‘If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish stock, you will not be able to withstand him, but you shall fall.’”

[Col. 1493C] “And behold, the king’s messengers were compelling him to enter, and he entered with the king to the banquet (Esther VII). The king said: ‘Ask what you wish, Esther.’ She replied: ‘Give me my life and my people, lest we perish. Would that we were sold into slavery; then I would groan and be silent.’ The king said: ‘Who is he that dares do this?’ She replied: ‘That Haman is our enemy.’ Hearing this, he was stunned. The king rose in anger and went into the garden; but Haman begged the queen for his life. When the king returned, he found Haman fallen upon the couch on which Esther lay, and said: ‘Does he even mean to assault the queen in my presence?’ Then Arbona the eunuch said: ‘Behold, the gallows which he had prepared for Mordecai stands in Haman’s house.’ [Col. 1493D] The king said: ‘Hang him upon it.’ And Haman was hanged on the gibbet.”

“And the king gave Esther Haman’s house (Esther VIII). Mordecai came in to the king, for Esther had confessed that he was her uncle. The king gave Mordecai the ring which he had ordered taken from Haman. Esther appointed Mordecai over her household. Again she fell weeping at his feet, beseeching him to annul by new letters the former letters which Haman had written against the Jews. The king consented. Mordecai wrote letters, sealed with the king’s ring, to the governors of the provinces: the Jews were not to be killed; rather, the Jews were to kill those prepared to kill them, and the hands of the governors were to be with them. Thus the name [Col. 1494A] of the Jews became famous, so that many among the nations joined their religion.

Mordecai remembered the dream which he had seen and understood its interpretation (Esther X and XI). This was the dream: Voices, thunderings, and earthquakes appeared over the earth. And behold, two dragons were prepared for battle against one another; at their cry the nations were stirred up to fight against the king of the righteous. That day was one of darkness and peril. The distressed nation of the righteous cried to the Lord; and behold, a small spring grew into a great river, a great light arose, the humble were exalted, and they devoured the illustrious.”

Moreover, in the second letter which he wrote on behalf of the Jews, the king excused himself as follows: “Do not suppose that, if we command different things, this arises from fickleness of mind; rather, we render judgement as the necessity of circumstances requires, as the public good demands. Many persons raised to honour by kings have abused it unto pride and plotted against those who gave it. Haman, Macedonian both in disposition and descent, and incidentally contaminating the Persian race, swelled with such arrogance that he attempted to deprive us of our kingdom and life. For by new schemes he sought the death of Mordecai, by whose loyalty we live, and of Esther, our partner in the kingdom, along with all her people; he thought that, once they had been killed, he could plot against our isolation and transfer the Persian kingdom to the Macedonians. But we, by the will of the living God, by whose favour the kingdom was delivered to our fathers and has been [Col. 1494C] preserved until this day, acquit the Jews and command that their enemies be put to death.” Therefore, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the Jews struck their enemies with a great blow throughout the provinces, to the number of seventy-five thousand (Esther IX). On the fourteenth day they held banquets with rejoicing, sending portions to one another. But in Susa they killed five hundred men. On the fourteenth day Esther obtained from the king permission that the enemies of the Jews should still be killed in Susa; Haman’s ten sons were hanged, and about three hundred others perished. Therefore the Jews living in Susa, being occupied with the slaughter for two days, celebrated banquets on the fifteenth day. For this reason Esther and Mordecai commanded that these two days should be included among the feast-days, and that the day [Col. 1494D] of *Purim*, that is, of the lots, should be observed by the Jews, so that no forgetfulness might erase the memory of the event (ibid.). Josephus, however, calls these days “the Days of Reversal,” because the Jews had been turned from mourning to joy. Mordecai also wrote to Judah, the high priest in Jerusalem, who had succeeded his father Elisaphat, that these days should be observed as solemn festivals in Judaea forever.

Incidentals.
