In the days of Ahasuerus, the Athenians began to use twenty-four letters, whereas previously they had used only sixteen. The Senonian Gauls, under Brennus as their leader, invaded Rome and, except for the Capitol, burned and ravaged it for six months; military tribunes began to serve in place of consuls. Anaxagoras the natural philosopher, Heraclitus the Obscure, and Democritus died; Socrates drank poison in prison. Diogenes and Isocrates flourished. Aristotle heard Plato when he was eighteen years old.

## CHAPTER II. On Ochus, or Artaxerxes

[Note: [Col. 1495D] From various sources.] After Ahasuerus, Artaxerxes, called Ochus, reigned. He sent Bagoses as governor over all the regions beyond the Euphrates. Now the high priest in Jerusalem was John, who had succeeded his father Judah. John had a brother, Jesus, who aspired to the high priesthood and therefore secured the friendship of Bagoses. Emboldened by this, Jesus disputed with John in the Temple and so provoked his brother that John killed him. Bagoses, enraged by this, went up to Jerusalem. [Col. 1495B] When they forbade him entrance into the Temple, he replied: “I am cleaner than the corpse by which you have more greatly profaned the Temple.” He entered the Temple and plundered it. He again imposed taxes upon the Temple ministers, as well as the provisions of the seventh year, from which they had been exempted through Ezra’s intervention. Moreover, Artaxerxes, namely Ochus, restored Egypt to his dominion, having driven King Nectanebo into Ethiopia; with him the kingdom of the Egyptians was destroyed. The same Ochus, having captured Apodasmus of the Jews, transferred its inhabitants to Hyrcania and settled them beside the Caspian Sea.

Incidentals.

At that time the Romans defeated the Gauls. Demosthenes and Socrates flourished. Plato died, after whom Speusippus held the Academy.

## CHAPTER III. On Darius, son of Arsames

[Col. 1495C]

[Note: [Col. 1495D] From various histories.] After Ochus, his son Arsames reigned. When John died in Jerusalem, his son Jaddua succeeded him in the priesthood. After Arsames, his son Darius reigned. He appointed Sanballat, of the race of the Cuthaeans, from whom the Samaritans were descended, over the regions beyond the river. Jaddua had a brother, Manasseh, who aspired to the high priesthood; for this reason he took as his wife Nicaso, daughter of Sanballat. While he was serving in the priesthood, the Jerusalemites were angered and ordered him either to leave his wife or not enter the sanctuary. Manasseh therefore went with his wife to his father-in-law. Sanballat promised to build him a temple, modeled upon that of Jerusalem, on [Col. 1495D] Mount Gerizim; but this was to be done with the approval of King Darius. Meanwhile, he founded for him Abisam, or Abiglam—an important and notable Tyrian village on the Mediterranean. Many Jerusalemites went over to Manasseh; Sanballat supplied them with money, allotted them land to cultivate, and provided dwellings.

Incidentals.

At that time Manlius Torquatus, consul of the Romans, had his own son beaten with rods and struck with the axe, because he had fought against the consuls’ command with the enemy, though he had nevertheless won the victory.

## CHAPTER IV. On Alexander

[Col. 1496A]

[Note: [Col. 1496D] From various histories.] At the same time Philip, king of the Macedonians, was treacherously killed by Pausanias, who traced his descent from Orestes. His adopted son Alexander succeeded him, because he is recorded as the son of Nothanabus, at the age of twenty. Wishing to gain Syria, he crossed the Hellespont. Darius’s commanders who were beyond the river assembled against him, and he defeated them on the River Granicus. After traversing Lydia and Iconium, he came to Pamphylia. Then Darius, son of Arsames, gathered a chosen army and crossed the Euphrates and the Cilician Mount Taurus, hoping to defeat the Macedonians in Cilicia. Sanballat rejoiced, thinking that after the victory he would meet Darius and obtain from him the building of the temple which he had promised his son-in-law. He himself, being elderly, took no part in the battles; but events turned out otherwise than he had hoped. Darius was defeated by the Macedonians; his mother, wife, and children were captured, and he fled back to the Persians with a few men. Then Alexander began to aspire to dominion over the East. Entering Syria, he captured Damascus; after subduing Sidon, he besieged Tyre. Sanballat then selected eight thousand of his people and went to Alexandria to assist Alexander, saying that he would more willingly obey Alexander than Darius and would surrender to him the territories placed under his own authority. Alexander received him graciously. Moreover, he told him that he had as his son-in-law Manasseh, brother of the high priest of the Jewish nation, and with him many other powerful men [Col. 1496C] of that nation. He said that they wished to build a temple under Alexander in the appointed place; this, he maintained, would benefit Alexander, because a Jewish power divided in two would not rebel. Alexander consented; Sanballat eagerly built the temple and altar, which remained until the destruction wrought by the Romans, and appointed Manasseh high priest there.

[Note: [Col. 1497D] Addition 1. Behold, this is the third Temple said to have been built: by Solomon in Jerusalem, in Egypt, and here by Sanballat.]

While Alexander was besieging Tyre, he wrote a letter to the high priest in Jerusalem, inviting him to provide help and an army, prepare supplies for sale, and pay him the tribute previously paid to Darius. Jaddua replied that he had sworn an oath to Darius and could not violate the established obligation while Darius lived. Alexander then threatened the Jewish nation that through him they would learn [Col. 1496D] to whom they ought to keep their obligations. He threw up embankments and made Tyre part of the mainland: whereas it had formerly been an island, he made it contiguous with the land. After devastating it, he besieged Gaza. Sanballat died.

After capturing Gaza, Alexander hastened toward Jerusalem. The frightened Jews cried to the Lord, offered sacrifices, and Jaddua prayed for the nation. After he had fallen asleep following the sacrifice, God commanded him to be confident, to adorn the city with silks—that is, hangings—and, clothed in pontifical vestments, to go out to meet Alexander, together with the other priests wearing their prescribed robes [Col. 1497A]. Rising from sleep, he reported the oracle to all. Hearing that Alexander was not far from the city, he went out with the priests and a sacred multitude of citizens to a place called Saphim, which in Latin translation means “the lookout,” from which Jerusalem and the Temple of the Lord could be seen. What happened was contrary to the expectation of all who followed the king. For Alexander, seeing the high priest marked out by his pontifical garment and the golden plate above the turban, on which the name of God was written, dismounted from his horse, approached him alone, worshipped the name of God, and reverenced the high priest. The leaders of the army were astonished and thought the king’s mind deluded. Parmenio alone asked him why he had worshipped the priest of the Jewish nation. [Col. 1497B] He replied: “I did not worship this man, but God, whose high-priestly office he bears. For in a dream, while I was still in the Macedonian city of Lycaea, I saw God in this appearance. While I was considering whether I could gain Asia, he commanded me to be confident, for he himself would lead my army and deliver Persian rule to me. Now, however, in this priest I have for the first time seen his likeness. I am confident that what he promised me will come to pass, and therefore I worshipped God and honoured the man.” Alexander entered the city and sacrificed in the Temple to God, according to the high priest’s direction. They brought him Daniel, in which it was written that a certain Greek would destroy the power of the Persians; thinking that this had been written about him, he rejoiced. On the next day [Col. 1497C], summoning the people, he ordered them to ask whatever they wished. At their request he granted that Jews everywhere should use their ancestral laws and that the seventh year should be free of tribute because of the Sabbath-rest of the land, since in the seventh year the land was not cultivated. He then departed for other cities.

Then the Samaritans, seeing his generosity toward the Jews, said that they were kindred to the Jews, tracing their origin to Ephraim and Manasseh. They asked that he honour their temple on Gerizim; he promised to do so on his return. When they requested remission for the seventh year, he asked who they were. They said that they were Hebrews. When he further asked whether they were Jews, they denied that they were Jews. He answered: “I granted this only to the Jews.” We pass over in silence, however, how Alexander defeated Darius and Porus, how he consulted the [Col. 1497D] trees of the Sun and Moon, and the other marvellous things which he reported in a letter to his teacher Aristotle, hastening on to those events which occurred concerning the people of God.

[Note: [Col. 1497D] Addition 2. The trees of the Sun and Moon. When the sun rose and its brightness touched the tops of the trees, they shook down to their roots; then an answer was given to those who asked questions. There Alexander received answers concerning his wife and [Col. 1498A] his own affairs, and concerning his death if he entered Babylon; and so it came to pass, according to his sister. The priests who used the fruits of the trees of the Sun and Moon lived four hundred years.]

## CHAPTER V. On the confinement of the ten tribes and Alexander’s death

[Col. 1498A]

[Note: [Col. 1497D] From various histories.] When Alexander came to the Caspian Mountains, the children of the captivity of the ten tribes sent to him. They were held under a decree forbidding their departure, and they asked him for permission to leave. When he asked the reason for their captivity, he learned that they had openly departed from the God of Israel by sacrificing to golden calves, and that God’s prophets had foretold that they would not return from captivity. He then replied that they should be confined [Col. 1498B] more closely. As the narrowness of the passes was blocked with ramparts cemented by bitumen, and he saw that human effort was insufficient, he prayed to the God of Israel to complete the work. The mountain precipices came together, making the place impassable. From this it clearly appears that it is not God’s will that they should go out. Yet near the end of the world they will come forth and cause a great slaughter of human beings. As Josephus says: “What will God do for his faithful ones, if he has done so much for an unbeliever?” When Alexander returned to Babylon, he took poison, lost the use of his tongue, and set down his final wishes in writing. He did not wish to transfer his monarchy to anyone, lest anyone equal to him in power should be remembered by posterity; and he appointed as successors to the kingdom the twelve companions whom he had had from his youth. This arrangement did not endure. For only four of them reigned, the others being cast aside, as is set forth in the history of Daniel. He died at the age of thirty-two, having reigned twelve years. Some say that he built twelve Alexandrias, according to the number of years during which he reigned. In Ammon he himself founded Parathonium, that is, a token of his prowess—namely, a triumphal arch.

## CHAPTER VI. On Ptolemy Soter

[Note: [Col. 1498D] From various histories.] After him Ptolemy, surnamed Soter, reigned in Egypt. Having added Syria to his kingdom, he set about adding Judaea also. [Col. 1498D] He went up to Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, knowing that on that day the Jews would not take up arms; under the pretence of sacrificing to God, he entered without opposition. Hence, according to Josephus, as Agatharchides of Cnidus says, he called the Jews ridiculous because they suffered serious loss through needless superstition. Ptolemy took many captives from Judaea and Gerizim back to Egypt. Putting them up for sale, he had them bought and scattered by merchants of the nations. Through this captivity, though it was not general, they were more widely dispersed among the nations. Thus in the Acts of the Apostles we read that Jews from every nation under heaven had assembled in Jerusalem [Col. 1499A] (Acts II). Jaddua was succeeded as high priest by his son Onias; he by his son Simon the Just; and Simon by his brother Eleazar, acting in place of Onias, Simon’s son, who was still a boy.

[Incidentals.]

At that time Appius Claudius the Blind was renowned at Rome; he brought in the Claudian waters [variant: the Hot waters] and paved the Appian Way. The philosopher Theophrastus flourished; as Cicero says, he received his name from the divinity of his speech. When the census was held at Rome—

[Note: [Col. 1499A] Addition. Because by this they ascertain the number of citizens.]

—two hundred and seventy thousand citizens were found. The Romans founded Ariminum and Beneventum.

## CHAPTER VII. On Ptolemy Philadelphus

[Col. 1499B]

After Ptolemy Soter, Philadelphus reigned in Egypt. A learned man and lover of books, he put Demetrius in charge of his library. When he asked him the number of books, Demetrius replied that there were twenty thousand, but said that within a short time the number could reach fifty thousand. He told him that among the Jews there was a law uttered by God’s own mouth and written by his own finger, and said that every effort should be made to have it translated into Greek and kept in the royal archives. For this was the law of the God whom philosophers call Zena, that is, “the Living One.” For *zeni* signifies “to live” or “life”; the common people call him Jupiter. To demonstrate [Col. 1499C] the sanctity of this law, he added that it could be translated only by worshippers of the living God. For when Theopompus wished to insert it into the histories he was writing, he became mad for thirty days. Theodectes too was made blind for the same reason; once they repented, they were healed. Demetrius advised the king to write to the Jewish high priest asking him to send persons skilled in Hebrew and Greek, together with the Law of God, who were sufficient to translate it. He thought that gifts ought to be sent with the letter in order to obtain this.

Aristaeus was present. Having long sympathized with the Jews’ misfortune, he found an opportunity to liberate them and said: “How will you obtain what you ask, while so many Jews serve as slaves in your kingdom? Free them, therefore, and nothing will be more pleasing to the Jewish high priest. Do not suppose that I say this because I am connected with the Jews, but because I know it is in your interest if you honour God, the maker of all things.” The king freed one hundred and twenty thousand Jews, giving their masters one hundred and twenty silver drachmas for each person. When the king said this was a great sum, they said: “It is great indeed, but not for a generous king.” The king then wrote to Eleazar as follows: “I have granted freedom to your nation, which was among us, judging this pleasing to God. Some of them I have assigned to military service; others, whose loyalty I had approved, I have appointed to positions in the palace. I have decided to place your laws in our library. You will therefore do well to send us elderly men able to leave us a careful translation of them. [Col. 1500A] I have now sent one hundred talents of silver for sacrifices to be made, and have set aside fifty talents of gold for making bowls and libation-vessels, as well as gems without number, at the artisans’ discretion. Command us what you wish to be made from these things; we shall receive it most gladly.”

Then Eleazar, sending him what he had requested, wrote back thus: “For translating the Law which you request, I have sent six elderly men from each tribe, carrying the Law.

[Note: [Col. 1501B] Addition 1. Although the ten tribes were taken captive, many nevertheless remained hidden—some having fled to Jerusalem, others even to the Samaritans. Because of this intermixture, the Samaritans said that they were Hebrews, as above, chapter 4, ‘At the same time.’]

It will be an act of your piety, or justice, to send it back to us carefully.” These are the seventy translators, though they were in fact seventy-two. In the manner of sacred Scripture they are called seventy, since it often leaves unmentioned a small number by which a total is exceeded. When they came to [Col. 1500B] the king, he received them kindly, but did not admit them to his presence until the fifth day. For on that day a triumphal festival was impending, namely, in commemoration of a certain triumph which his ancestors had gained on that same day. Accordingly, on that day he received those whom he had decreed to honour before the whole assembly of the princes. After their reception they spent twelve days with the king; he questioned them about matters he had considered in his heart, especially two matters: knowledge of God and the government of a kingdom. After they had instructed him concerning royal administration, they discussed more fully the worship of the one God and the fact that no creature was God. Thus, wherever they encountered a reference to the Trinity, they either passed over it silently or translated it enigmatically, lest they seem to have handed down three gods to be worshipped. [Col. 1500C] They did likewise concerning the incarnation of the Word, as in Isaiah.

[Note: [Col. 1501B] Addition 2. Thus in Isaiah: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isaiah). For all these they translated: “Angel of great counsel.” Gregory, who arranged the ecclesiastical office, used this translation. He uses their translation whenever he adduces the authority of the Fathers or of another source, although in all these matters the Church uses Jerome’s translation, or the Vulgate.]

When Isaiah had said that a child would be born to us and had added his six names, one of which was “God,” they rendered, in place of those six names, “Angel of great counsel,” lest they seem to have handed down a man made divine (Isa. IX). They then showed the king the scroll which they had brought. The king could not sufficiently marvel at the thinness and joining of the sheets, which could not be detected by the eye, although the golden letters appeared so legible against the whiteness of the pages. They were introduced into a secluded house of the king’s beside the sea, intended for deliberation on affairs, and individual cells were assigned to them, together with everything that seemed expedient and convenient for translating. [Col. 1500D] At dawn they went out to wish the king blessings and *polichronitudo*.

[Note: [Col. 1501C] Addition 3. *Polichronitudo* is the prayer offered by the Church for kings, pontiffs, and rulers of the earth, wishing them spiritual, temporal, and eternal blessings, and length of days. For *polis* in Greek means “a multitude”; *chronos*, “time,” in Latin. Such a custom still exists among the Greeks: when they rise in the morning, facing the church, they cry out, “*Polichronitudo basileos*,” that is, “May the king live for a long time.”]

Then they washed themselves in the sea according to Jewish purification; afterward they translated until the ninth hour. From there they went to food and rest, and they completed the work in seventy-two days. Some have therefore thought that at that time they translated only the Pentateuch. Later, either after they had returned, or afterward when some of them came back to the king, they translated the Psalms and Prophets. Nevertheless, if, as Augustine says, it happened miraculously that the same edition of each of them was found without disagreement, it could have happened no less miraculously that in so many days they translated the Law, Psalms, and Prophets. Jerome, however, seems to maintain that [Col. 1501A] they compared their translations of the six days on the Sabbath and fused all of them into one.

He maintains that this is not surprising, since Ezra, having restored the Law through the Spirit, afterward corrected it by means of the old Scripture which was among the Samaritans. When the work was completed, Demetrius, the master in charge of the books, summoned all the Jews in Alexandria and the more learned persons from the province. Their translation was read before all and approved; afterward it was brought to the king and read again before him. When the translators asked the king to give authority for it to remain unalterable, he praised this proposal and said he would do it, provided that they should finally correct it with such care that they would not be compelled to invalidate what had once been judged. He sent them away, honoured with gifts. He also sent gifts to Eleazar [Col. 1501B] the high priest. To the Temple he sent, besides vessels, a golden table adorned with priceless gems; though it was only half a cubit thick, the material surpassed the workmanship.

[Col. 1501C] Incidentals.

[Col. 1501D] At that time Sostratus constructed the lighthouse at Alexandria.

[Note: [Col. 1501D] Addition 1. This was one of the wonders of the world, as Pliny says. The Pharos was a very high tower situated on the seashore, not founded on land but set upon four glass crabs, of such a size that a fire placed at its summit illuminated almost the entire shore at night. The tomb of Aratus in Cilicia is worthy of admiration, for stones thrown against it rebound.]

Aratus flourished; the first silver coin was struck in the City; the Carthaginians defeated the Romans in a naval battle, putting the consul Metellus to flight.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Euergetes

After Philadelphus, his brother Ptolemy Euergetes reigned. The Egyptians called him Euergetes [Col. 1502A], which means “restoration,” because after ravaging Syria, Cilicia, and parts of Asia, he brought back, among the countless spoils which he captured, even their gods, which Cambyses had carried off to Persia. The high priest of the Jews was Onias, son of Simon the Just. He was succeeded by his son Simon, under whom Jesus son of Sirach composed the book of Wisdom called *Ecclesiasticus*, which the Greeks call *panarethon*.

[Note: [Col. 1502B] Addition 1. From *pan*, meaning “all,” and *arethon*, meaning “virtue”: as it were, “wholly virtuous.”]

He makes mention in it of the aforesaid Simon.

[Note: [Col. 1502B] Addition 2. Solomon made three books: *Ecclesiastes*, which begins, “Vanity of vanities”; the Parables, or Proverbs, which in Hebrew are called *Mastot*; and the Song of Songs. There is a fourth, whose author is uncertain, properly called the Book of Wisdom, beginning, “Love righteousness.” There is a fifth, called *Ecclesiasticus*, which Jesus son of Sirach composed. Any one of these may be called a book of Wisdom, as may be observed in passages drawn from these books in epistles. They received this designation either because in each Wisdom is introduced as speaking, or because they form morals, or because Solomon’s salvation is doubted on account of his idolatry.]

But when Onias refused to pay tribute to Euergetes, out of zeal for the Law—or rather, out of greed, as Josephus says, although he testifies that Onias was held in honour—he provoked the king to anger. Even against Onias’s will, Joseph, a noble Jew, son of Tobias and of Onias’s sister, was sent as ambassador to the king. Joseph had a son Hyrcanus. While he was still a boy, his father tested his prudence by giving him three hundred yoke of oxen without reins.

[Note: [Col. 1502C] Addition 3. He killed the oxen and ate their flesh; from their hides he made reins and sowed the land.]

Joseph not only restored peace, but was sent back by the king as governor of Judaea and the neighbouring regions.

[Col. 1502C] Incidentals.

At that time Ennius of Tarentum was brought to Rome by Cato, then quaestor; he was content with modest expenditure and the service of one maidservant. Nearly forty thousand Gauls were killed by the Romans. At Rhodes, the great Colossus fell in an earthquake.

[Note: [Col. 1502C] Addition 1. It was an image of astonishing size: an arrow could not be shot to its summit; [Col. 1502D] its head was so large that it could contain thirty *cori* of grain; and at its lower part, in the feet, there was an opening through which a man could enter and climb to the head.]

## CHAPTER IX. On Ptolemy Philopator

[Col. 1502D]

After Euergetes, his son Ptolemy Philopator reigned; after him, Ptolemy Epiphanes; after him, Ptolemy Philometor, whom Antiochus the Great, king of Syria, defeated and made Judaea subject to himself. The Jewish high priest was the great Onias, son of Simon. Arius, king of the Lacedaemonians, sent ambassadors to him to renew the covenant said to have existed between Abraham and his ancestors. But King Antiochus restored the tribute of the seventh year and of the Temple ministers, which Philadelphus had remitted for the Jews [Col. 1503A] (1 Macc. XII). While he was excessively harassing the neighbouring regions, the matter was reported to the Romans. Scipio Nasica and Scipio Africanus were sent to him, and they removed him from his attacks under the sanction of an oath. Moreover, they took from him as a hostage his firstborn son Seleucus. Wanting to receive him back from them, he gave in his place his younger son Antiochus Epiphanes, on condition that he should be a perpetual hostage—that is, one who would not return—because of the savagery of that Antiochus. Onias went down to Egypt to Ptolemy Epiphanes, as was said above. Antiochus was killed in Persia in the temple of Nanaea and cast out limb by limb by the priests, who had deceitfully promised him treasures and had brought him with only a few men into the inner shrine.

## CHAPTER X. On Seleucus

[Col. 1503B]

After Antiochus the Great, his elder son Seleucus reigned in Syria: a thoroughly wicked but sluggish man. Onias was high priest of the Jews. For when Onias went over into Egypt, his son Simon took his seat in his place; and he was succeeded by his son Onias. Under this Onias, Seleucus sent the messenger Heliodorus to Jerusalem to plunder the common treasury of the Temple. [Note: [Col. 1503C] Addition 1.—Not the vessels, but the votive offerings intended for the Temple’s uses.] When he entered the Temple, two young men rose from hiding-places and killed him. Josephus, however, seems to mean that they were angels in human form. In the Second Book of Maccabees it is read that a terrifying horseman appeared, trampled him down, and that he was crushed and made speechless, though not dead; and that two handsome young men [Col. 1503C] scourged him. Fearing Seleucus’s anger, Onias prayed to the Lord for the dead man, and he rose again (2 Macc. 3). Returning to the king, he said: “If my lord has any persons whose blood he thirsts for, let him send them to Jerusalem to plunder the Temple.”

### Incidental Notice

At that time Aristobulus, a Jew by birth and a Peripatetic philosopher, wrote commentaries of explanation on Moses for Ptolemy Philometor.

## CHAPTER XI. On Antiochus Epiphanes

[Col. 1503D] When Antiochus Epiphanes, who was a hostage at Rome for his father, heard that his father had died and knew his brother’s incapacity, he presumed upon obtaining the kingdom of Syria and secretly left Rome (1 Macc. 1 and elsewhere), although some report that he returned with the Senate’s connivance. Having returned to Syria, he presented himself to all as kindly and generous. He was energetic in action and fierce toward enemies. Thus the people surnamed him Epiphanes, which means “illustrious.” On his brother’s death he reigned in his place.

Then he revealed the wickedness inherent in him, which he had concealed in order to secure the kingdom. Then the sons of Belial arose in Jerusalem, introducing Gentile customs; and they asked Antiochus to establish an ephebia in Jerusalem—that is, [Col. 1504A] a brothel for youths—and that the people of Jerusalem be enrolled as Antiochenes, and gymnasia be established in which instruction was given in Gentile practice (2 Macc. 4). They made themselves foreskins—that is, they did not circumcise their little sons, or they lived according to the custom of the uncircumcised. Some, however, maintain that they made certain coverings for their circumcision, so that, when stripped, they might appear different to the Greeks.

The cause of this disgrace was as follows. Onias, being childless, had two brothers, Jesus, or Onias, and John, who contended for the high priesthood; and, in order to please Antiochus, they turned aside to Gentile customs, so far as even to give themselves Gentile names. Jesus, or Onias, was called Jason; John, however, Menelaus. Since Jason had more supporters, he petitioned Antiochus for the establishment of a gymnasium [Col. 1504B] in Jerusalem. And the wicked men, guilty in matters of food, Sabbath-breaking, and the like, listened to him.

Afterward Antiochus removed Jason and raised Menelaus. [Note: [Col. 1505A] Addition 1.—Augustine says that the sacrificial fire which had survived beneath the waters through the seventy years of the Babylonian captivity was extinguished when Antiochus sold the priesthood to Jason.] Onias followed him to Antioch. For when he had seen his brothers’ crime, he had gone down to the king, in case he might change the king’s mind. Since he could not do this, he remained at Antioch in an asylum. Menelaus then came after him and persuaded Andronicus to kill Onias. [Note: [Col. 1505A] Addition 2.—Yet in the Second Book of Maccabees [Col. 1506A] Jason alone is said to have been Onias’s brother, while Menelaus was the brother of a certain Simon, who, envying Onias, persuaded Seleucus to plunder the common treasury, as has been said above.] Andronicus summoned him out of the asylum and killed him. Angered by the death of the righteous man, the king stripped Andronicus of the purple, had him scourged through the city, and caused him to be killed in the very place where he had killed Onias.

Moreover, when Antiochus had struck Egypt, he deceitfully went up to Jerusalem and, taking advantage of division—that is, civic dissension—did as he pleased [Col. 1504C] there. He struck down many in Jerusalem, and the whole land mourned. When he had returned to Egypt and had been repulsed by Roman envoys, two years later he returned to Jerusalem in fury. [Note: [Col. 1506A] Addition 3.—Within these two years, mounted conflicts were seen in the air over Jerusalem for forty days (2 Macc. 5).] Those favoring him opened the gates to him. He killed those of contrary opinion and plundered the Temple, with Menelaus as his guide, taking the vessels and lamps, the table and sacred vessels, and the golden urn. Nor did he refrain from the curtains. He set up in the Temple an idol of Olympian Jupiter, or Jupiter the Host, or the Stranger. He prohibited Mosaic offerings, removed the bronze altar, and compelled the Jews to eat pork and sacrifice to the idol. He also fortified the citadel in the City of David, placing there a garrison of Macedonians, who were in every respect inhuman toward the Jews. For any whom they found [Col. 1504D] to have circumcised their sons they hanged, together with the little children from their necks (2 Macc. 6).

But when the Samaritans saw the Jews suffering these things, according to their natural habit they declared that they were not related to the Jews. What they had hitherto proclaimed—that the Temple on Gerizim belonged to the Most High God—they denied, writing to Antiochus as follows:

### Report to God Epiphanes from the Sidonians of Shechem

“Our ancestors, because of plagues, followed a certain superstition concerning Sabbaths, building a temple on Gerizim without a deity. Your judges come to us and inflict upon us the same things as upon the Jews, though from the beginning we are known to be Sidonians. Restrain your judges from oppressing us; and we ask that the temple on Gerizim be dedicated in the name of Greek Jupiter, or Anxur—that is, the Hospitable One.”” [Col. 1505A]

Antiochus granted their petition.

# FIRST BOOK OF MACCABEES

[Col. 1505]

## CHAPTER I. On the Maccabees

[Col. 1505B] Then many Jews voluntarily, indeed out of fear of the king, followed his commands; but those who had been proved steadfast clung to their ancestral laws (1 Macc. 1). There was a priest from Modin, a small village of Judaea, named Mattathias, son of John, son of Simon, son of Hasmonaeus, of the course of Joarib—that is, one of those twenty-four courses chosen by David (1 Macc. 2). In the same manner Zechariah is said to have been of the course of Abijah (Luke 1). He had five sons: John, Simon, Judas, Eleazar, and Jonathan; each was known by his own surname. But it is enough to speak of Judas, who was called Maccabaeus.

Seeing these evils, they put on sackcloth and mourned. Envoys sent by the king came to Modin, setting idols in a place in order to compel the Jews to sacrifice to them. They said to Mattathias: “You are a ruler [Col. 1505C] in this city; be the first to carry out the king’s commands.” But he cried: “Even if all obey the king, I and my sons and my brothers shall obey the law of the God of heaven. We shall not sacrifice.”

Then one of the Jews sacrificed in their midst. Mattathias rose up with his men, slaughtered him upon the altar, killed the king’s envoys, and tore down the altar. He cried: “Whoever belongs to God, let him follow me.” With his entire tribe he went into the wilderness, leaving everything behind. Many fled with their sons and wives into the deserts, preferring to live on herbs rather than be defiled. At first the king’s judges tried to bend them by words, that they might choose what was advantageous and not be treated as enemies. But they would not listen. Then the king’s envoys attacked them on [Col. 1505D] Sabbath days, when it was unlawful for them to move weapons, and killed some; others they suffocated in caves with smoke-producing missiles. Three thousand of them perished; others have only one thousand. Many more escaped and joined Mattathias, making him their judge.

He taught them to fight on Sabbaths, saying: “If you keep the law on this point, you will be enemies of the law, giving occasion for the people of God to perish; and the law will perish with the people.” From that time, Josephus says, the custom has remained among us of fighting even if wars arise on such a day. Mattathias gathered armed men, tore down the altars of idols, killed, where he could, those who sacrificed, and ordered uncircumcised boys to be circumcised. He exercised this office for one year.

When he was seriously ill, he summoned his sons and said: “I am setting out upon the appointed [Col. 1506A] way. I commend to you the ancestral [Col. 1506B] laws, that you may die for them with gladness of heart. For bodies are mortal, but memorials of holy men attain the order of immortality. Keep concord, and in counsels regard Simon as a father because of his wisdom. But make Judas your leader in arms because of his courage.” Mattathias died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year and was buried at Modin. Israel mourned him with great mourning. His son Judas Maccabaeus rose in his place and became like a lion, defending Israel with his shield (1 Macc. 3).

## CHAPTER II. On the Battles of Judas Maccabaeus

Then Apollonius, governor of Samaria, marched out in great strength against Judas (1 Macc. 3). Judas met him, struck him down along with many others, and the rest fled. He took abundant spoils and [Col. 1506C] Apollonius’s sword, fighting with it all the days of his life.

Seron, commander of Lower Syria, hearing that Judas had become strong, brought with him those subject to him and Jewish transgressors, and encamped at Bethsura. Judas met him and, seeing his own men dispirited through their small numbers and fasting, urged them to trust not in multitude but in devotion. Fighting with the Syrians, he killed their commander and pursued the fugitives down the slope of Mount Beth-horon as far as the plain. Eight hundred men fell; Josephus says eight thousand. The rest fled to the coastal regions of the Philistines, and fear of Judas fell upon the nations.

When Antiochus heard this, he assembled all his own forces and hired many men from the islands [Col. 1506D] for pay. While distributing wages to the soldiers, he saw that his treasures were failing. For not all tribute was being paid him because of the peoples’ rebellions. He decided to go into Persia and collect the tributes of the regions. He left Lysias, of royal stock, over the affairs of the kingdom, from the Euphrates as far as the borders of Lower Asia, and charged him to rear his son Antiochus until his return. He gave him half the army and the elephants, ordering him to lay waste Judaea, overthrow Jerusalem, and extirpate the Jewish race.

He himself went out from Emath into Persia; having rebuilt Emath, he called it Antioch, and he travelled through the upper regions. Lysias chose Ptolemy, Nicanor, and Gorgias, powerful men among the king’s friends. He sent with them forty thousand [Col. 1507A] infantry and seven thousand cavalry, that they might enter the land of Judah; and they pitched camp at Emmaus on level ground. Syrians came to their aid, together with many Jewish deserters and certain merchants who hoped to purchase Jewish captives.

Judas, however, came with his army to Mizpah and urged his men to put their hope in God. In accordance with the law, he dismissed those recently married and those who had shortly before acquired possessions (1 Macc. 4). Gorgias took five thousand men and three thousand selected horsemen—though others have one thousand cavalry—and went out near sunset to fall upon Judas by night. Judas, anticipating this, determined himself to invade the enemy camp secretly; leaving many fires in the camp, he came to the plain [Col. 1507B] of Emmaus.

Gorgias, finding no one in the Jews’ camp, supposed that they had fled into the mountains and sought them there. At dawn Judas appeared before the enemy in their camp with about three thousand men, more or less, however few they were. Falling upon the enemy unexpectedly, he killed many and pursued the rest as far as Gezer, the plains of Idumaea, and Ashdod; three thousand of them fell. Judas told his men to disregard the plunder while a battle against Gorgias still remained. But when those with Gorgias saw their camp burning—for the smoke told them this from afar—and knew that their own men had been put to flight, they too turned their backs. After the full measure of victory, Judas took much enemy spoil and returned to his own people, praising God.

Many more joined [Col. 1507C] Judas, and he had with him about ten thousand men. The following year Lysias gathered an army of forty thousand men and five thousand cavalry and came into Judaea. Judas met them at Beth-horon with ten thousand men and immediately, laying low those who struck at him, joined battle with them. Five thousand men from Lysias’s army fell. Observing the Jews’ boldness and fearing their desperation unless they were allowed to live in liberty, Lysias returned to Antioch, gathering garrisons of foreigners so that he might return to Judaea with greater equipment.

## CHAPTER III. On the Purification of the Temple

Thus, after Antiochus’s commanders had been defeated so often, Judas persuaded [Col. 1507D] the people to go up to Jerusalem and cleanse the Temple (1 Macc. 4). Finding the Temple deserted and shrubs grown up in it, they mourned with great mourning. Judas chose soldiers to attack those guarding the garrison-citadel, while he cleansed the Temple of its defilement.

Having carefully purified it, he brought in new vessels, the lampstand and table, and also an altar made of gold. [Note: [Col. 1508B] Addition 1.—On the very day on which the Temple had been destroyed, it was rebuilt on that same day after three years had elapsed.] He placed curtains at the entrance and restored the doors. Removing the altar that Antiochus had erected, he built another from new stones; and the Temple was rededicated on the twentieth day of December. This dedication endured thereafter, the other two having fallen into disuse. [Note: [Col. 1508B] Addition 2.—The first was Solomon’s at the building of the Temple; the second, Nehemiah’s at its rebuilding.] “Of this the Gospel says: ‘The Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter’ (John 2).”

[Col. 1508A] They offered burnt offerings on the new altar and burned incense, taking fire from the stones of the old altar. They lit many lamps and called it the Feast of Lights, either because of the multitude of lamps or because God had then enlightened them as they sat in darkness. They appointed Judas high priest. These events occurred after the three years during which the Temple had remained profaned, as Daniel’s preface had predicted four hundred and eight years earlier. They celebrated for eight days beneath booths according to the rite of the Feast of Tabernacles, remembering that shortly before they had lived in caves, and decreeing that their descendants should observe this renewal of the Temple for eight days. [Note: [Col. 1508B] Addition 3.—Observe that here you have a Jewish feast lasting an octave, which is no objection because it was not a feast established by the Law.] Hence Josephus says: “From that time until now we celebrate that festival, calling it Lights, because beyond hope the light of religion appeared to us.” [Col. 1508B]

Then Judas constructed a wall around the city and built towers, assigning guards to them. He also fortified Bethsura, in order to use it as a fortress against enemies; but he had not yet taken the garrison-citadel.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Battles of Judas

[Col. 1508C] The neighboring nations resented the restoration of Jerusalem and the strength of the Jews, and they persecuted them (1 Macc. 5). Judas fought them courageously, struck the Idumaeans with a great blow, fought against Timothy, commander of the Ammonites, put him to flight, devastated Gezer, and returned to Judaea.

The nations in Gilead gathered against the Jews in their territories. The Jews fled to Datheman and sent to Judas for assistance, reporting that Timothy was hastening to capture the place in which they had taken refuge. While the letters were still being read, messengers from Galilee arrived, reporting that the people of Ptolemais, Tyre, and Sidon were gathering against the Jews. Therefore, [Col. 1508D] with enemies reported on both fronts, Judas sent his brother Simon with three thousand picked men to aid the Galileans. He himself went out into Gilead with his brother Jonathan and eight thousand men, leaving Joseph and Azariah as commanders in Judaea to guard it, though they were not to engage any enemy in battle in the meantime.

Simon came into Galilee; the nations were crushed by him, and he pursued them as far as Ptolemais. He took their spoils and the Jews whom they were dragging away captive and returned to Judaea. Judas and Jonathan crossed the Jordan and travelled three days through the wilderness. The Nabataeans met them, received them peaceably, and related what had happened to their brethren in Gilead: how they were held shut up in a fortress [Col. 1509A].

Judas first burned Bosor and plundered it. Rising by night, when at dawn he came to the siege, he saw men bringing ladders and siege-engines to take the stronghold. He came upon them from behind in three divisions, sounded the trumpet, and Timothy’s camp recognized that it was Maccabaeus. They fled before him; nearly eight thousand of them fell; and Judas devastated the cities of the nations in Gilead.

After this Timothy gathered another army and encamped beside a torrent. Judas went to meet them. Timothy said to his commanders: “If Judas crosses over to us, he will be too strong for us. But if he is afraid to cross and camps beyond the stream, let us cross over to him and we shall prevail against him.” Judas crossed the torrent, leaving behind him [Col. 1509B] men to cry that no one should remain. The nations were crushed and fled to a temple at Carnaim. Judas set fire to the temple with all who were in it.

Then Judas gathered all the Israelites in Gilead, together with wives and little children, to come into the land of Judah. When they reached Ephron, they asked the inhabitants for passage, but they would not open to them. Judas uprooted Ephron and passed through it over the slain. Judas gathered up the rearmost all along the way and encouraged them. Having crossed the Jordan, they went up to Mount Zion and offered burnt offerings because none of them had fallen. That same day Judas returned from Gilead and Simon from Galilee.

Meanwhile, while they were absent, Joseph [Col. 1509C] and Azariah, wishing to make a name for themselves, engaged Gorgias, were put to flight, and two thousand of the people fell. Judas, who was regarded almost as a prophet and had foretold to Joseph and Azariah that they were not to go out, was magnified in Israel. Judas devastated the Idumaeans and Philistines. Passing through Samaria, he turned aside to Ashdod, burned their altars and gods, and returned to Judaea with the spoils.

## CHAPTER V. On the Death of Antiochus Eupator in Judaea

While these things were happening in Judaea, Antiochus travelled through the upper regions (1 Macc. 6). He heard that Elymais was a wealthy city in Persia and that it had a rich temple, containing golden curtains, breastplates, and shields which Alexander had left. He sought to plunder it but could not, for the Elymaeans [Col. 1509D] shamefully drove him away. On the journey he received news of how his commanders had been defeated in Judaea.

Enraged, he ordered his chariot to be driven without interruption, arrogantly declaring that he would come to Jerusalem and make it a *polyandrium*—a burial-place—of Jews (2 Macc. 9). Immediately a bitter pain seized his bowels; while rushing along, he fell from the chariot and was severely injured. God showed his power in him, so that he who thought himself able even to command the waves of the sea and weigh the heights of mountains in a balance was carried in a litter. [Note: [Col. 1511A] Addition 1.—God punishes human beings for five reasons: either for correction, as Miriam, Moses’ sister; for greater merit, as Job; for preservation of virtues, as Paul through the angel of Satan; for manifestation of divine glory, as is said of the man born blind [Col. 1511B], “Neither this man nor his parents,” etc.; or to display the beginning here of a punishment that will endure in the future, as with Antiochus.]

Worms swarmed out from his flesh and came forth alive, and the army was burdened by his stench. Since he himself could not endure his own stench, he was brought to acknowledge himself and [Col. 1510A] said: “It is right that a mortal be subject to God.” He vowed that he would free the Jews and make them equal to Athenians. He also promised that he would become a Jew and proclaim God’s power everywhere. Despairing, he wrote all these things to the Jews, asking them faithfully to adhere to his son Antiochus.

When he professed that he suffered this because of the Temple’s violation, Josephus wondered that Polybius, a good man, had said that Antiochus perished because he intended to ravage the temple of Diana in Persia. For one who in no way commits a sin but merely thinks it is held under no guilt. Here, according to Josephus’s opinion, it is clear that the Law restrained the hand, not the mind.

Then Antiochus summoned Philip, [Col. 1510B] his foster-brother, and appointed him guardian of the kingdom, giving him the diadem, robe, and ring, that he might carry them to his son Antiochus and place him upon the royal throne. Antiochus died miserably abroad in the mountains. When Lysias learned this, he made the Antiochus whom he had reared king and called him Eupator. Judas then planned to besiege those in the garrison-citadel. He made ballistae and siege-engines and strengthened the embankment.

Then some of the besieged came out; some of the wicked Israelites joined them; and they came to the king and said: “How long will you not avenge us, who have decreed to serve your father and you? Go up, free your besieged men, and restore to us [Col. 1510C] our inheritances” (1 Macc. 6). The king was greatly angered and gathered an army. Mercenaries also came to him from other kingdoms. There were one hundred thousand infantry, twenty thousand cavalry, and thirty-two elephants.

He approached Bethsura to take it. Judas withdrew from the citadel and placed his camp opposite the king’s camp. At daybreak the king arranged his army. They showed the elephants grape and mulberry blood to sharpen them for battle. One thousand armored infantry and five hundred cavalry stood beside each elephant to guard it; wooden towers were upon every elephant, with thirty-two men fighting from above in each tower, while the beast’s driver was within. Part of the king’s army was spread over the mountains; others moved through low places. [Col. 1510D] The sun shone upon the golden shields; the mountains shone from them. Judas appeared in battle with his men, and six hundred men from the king’s army fell.

Eleazar, Judas’s brother, saw one beast more conspicuous than the rest and, thinking that the king was in it, ran through the enemy, went beneath the elephant, and stabbed it in the belly. The elephant fell and crushed him. Then the Jews withdrew from battle. The king came up after them, captured Bethsura, stationed guards there, besieged Jerusalem, and placed there ballistae, siege-engines, fire-projectiles, scorpions for shooting arrows, and slings.

There was no food in the city because it was the seventh year, and many left. Lysias then heard that Philip had returned from Persia and was seeking to assume [Col. 1511A] the affairs of the kingdom. He advised the king: “We are failing daily; we have little food, the place we are besieging is fortified, and we must attend to the kingdom. Let us therefore give these men pledges of peace, establishing that they may walk in their own laws and serve us.” Peace having been made, the king and his commanders swore. He entered Mount Zion; but seeing the fortifications of the place, he broke the oath and destroyed the wall around it. Returning to Antioch, he found Philip ruling there and took the city by force.

## CHAPTER VI. On Demetrius and Nicanor

At that time Demetrius, son of Seleucus, left the city of Rome, went up to the maritime cities, and reigned there (1 Macc. 7). While still a boy, his uncle Antiochus Epiphanes had deprived him of the kingdom, and he went up to Rome to accuse his uncle. Hearing that his uncle had died, he returned, and many received him. But the army bound Antiochus and Lysias in order to bring them to him. When he learned this, he said: “Do not show me their faces.” [Note: [Col. 1512B] Addition 1.—Because Antiochus is my own brother, it would not be fitting for me to kill him; but you kill him.] The army killed them, [Col. 1511C] and Demetrius sat on his father’s throne.

Then wicked men from Israel came to the king, with Alcimus, an Aaronite, their leader, who wanted to become priest. They accused Judas, saying: “Judas has destroyed all your friends and has driven us from our land. Therefore send a man whom you trust, that he may see the devastation and avenge us.” The king appointed Alcimus prince of the priests and sent Bacchides with an army into Judaea. Bacchides sent messengers deceitfully to Judas and his brothers, speaking about peace. Judas did not heed their words. But many of the people believed them, saying: “A priest from Aaron’s seed has come; he will not deceive us.” They went out to Bacchides, and in one day he killed sixty of them, according to the words: [Col. 1511D] “They poured out the blood of your holy ones around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them” (Ps. 78).

Others fled from him, saying: “There is no truth or justice.” Bacchides withdrew from Jerusalem and encamped at Beth-zecha. He killed many of those who had taken refuge with him and threw them into a well. He entrusted the region to Alcimus, leaving helpers with him; then he himself returned to the king at Antioch.

Alcimus then deceived everyone with words, speaking to each person as he pleased. Suddenly, surrounded by a powerful band of deserters, he did worse things in Jerusalem than all the nations. Noticing this, Judas ceased going out into the regions and took vengeance on the deserters. Seeing that he could not withstand Judas, Alcimus returned to the king, accusing [Col. 1512A] Judas of many things. The king sent Nicanor, who had been with him in Rome, into Judaea, commanding him to destroy the people.

Nicanor came to Jerusalem with an army and deceitfully spoke peaceful words to Judas; they greeted one another. But when Judas understood the ambush, he leapt away and fled back to his own men. Later they fought near the village of Capharsalama. Judas was defeated and fled into the City of David. The priests came out to Nicanor, supplicating and showing him the burnt offerings which they offered for the king. Mocking, he despised them and laid his hand upon his head, swearing: “Unless Judas is delivered to me when I return, I shall burn this place.” Nicanor withdrew from Jerusalem, went to Beth-horon, and received the Syrian army assigned to him.

Judas went out after him [Col. 1512B] with three thousand men. They joined battle on the third day of the month Adar. Nicanor’s camp was crushed; he himself fell first, and his army fled, throwing down its weapons. Men came out from the fortresses throughout Judaea and struck them all down, to the last man. Cutting off Nicanor’s head and the right hand which he had stretched out arrogantly, they hung them opposite Jerusalem; and they cut his tongue into little pieces and gave it to birds to eat. They established that day as an annual feast. “And the land of Judah was quiet from battles for a few days.”

## CHAPTER VII. On the Jews’ Covenant with the Romans

Judas then heard of the name of the Romans and [Col. 1512C] of the deeds they had done throughout the world: how they deprived of kingdoms those whom they wished, or exalted them; how excellently they maintained friendships with their friends; and how in all these matters no one claimed a diadem for himself (1 Macc. 8). They had established a senate, and three hundred and twenty men deliberated. [Note: [Col. 1512D] Addition 1.—The Roman commonwealth was first governed by kings, of whom the first was Romulus and the second Remus; afterward by consuls; thirdly by emperors, of whom Julius Caesar was the first.]

Judas sent Eupolemus son of John and Jason son of Eleazar to Rome. Entering the senate, they said: “Judas Maccabaeus, his brothers, and the Jewish people have sent us to establish an alliance with you and that you may remove from them the Greek yoke.” The speech pleased the Romans. They wrote the terms of the treaty and sent a reply engraved on bronze tablets to Jerusalem, that it might remain there as a memorial, in this manner:

“May it go well with the Romans and the Jewish nation, on sea and land, and may there be peace forever. If war presses upon the Romans, the Jewish nation shall bring them aid without receiving pay from the Romans. The Romans shall do the same for the Jews.”

Then the Romans wrote to Demetrius: “Why have you made your yoke heavy upon our friends and allies, the Jews? Therefore, if they come to us again, we shall render judgment for them against you; we shall fight you by land and sea.”

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Death of Judas

Meanwhile, when Demetrius heard that [Col. 1513A] Nicanor and his men had fallen, he again sent Bacchides and Alcimus into Judaea, together with the right wing. They brought the army to Jerusalem (1 Macc. 9). Rising up, they went to Berea; Judas pitched camp at Laisa with three thousand selected men. Seeing the multitude of the enemy, they were greatly afraid and withdrew from the camp. Only eight hundred men remained with Judas.

Judas too was disheartened, for the battle pressed upon him and he had no time to gather men. Those who remained said to him: “We cannot stand against them; let us now save our lives and return to our brothers; then we shall fight against them.” He replied: “Far be it from us to do such a thing, to flee from them and bring further disgrace upon the glory [Col. 1513B] of our name. Rather, let us die bravely for our brothers.”

They joined battle with the enemy and drove back the right wing. But those in the left wing came upon them from behind. The battle grew heavy; Judas fell, and the rest fled. His brothers Simon and Jonathan redeemed his body from the enemy and carried it to Modin. They buried it in the tomb of their fathers. The people of the land mourned him with great mourning. Wicked men emerged in Israel, a great famine arose, and the entire region surrendered to Bacchides. Bacchides chose wicked men and appointed them masters of the region; they persecuted Judas’s friends. Judas’s friends gathered and chose Jonathan as their leader.

## CHAPTER IX. On Jonathan

[Col. 1513C]

Jonathan rose in the place of his brother Judas, and Bacchides sought to kill him (1 Macc. 9). Jonathan and his men fled into the wilderness of Tekoa. He sent his brother John to the Nabataeans, his friends, that they might lend him their valuable equipment. But the sons of Jambri came out, struck John, and took all that he had.

After this, Jonathan and his brother Simon were told that the sons of Jambri were celebrating a wedding and bringing a bride from Madaba. They rose against them from ambush, killed many in vengeance for their brother’s blood, and returned to the bank of the Jordan. Bacchides heard this and came on a Sabbath day in [Col. 1513D] great force.

Jonathan said to his men: “Behold, battle is before us; the water of the Jordan is on this side and that, with marshes and thickets, and there is no place to turn aside. Therefore cry out to heaven and let us fight.” Battle was joined. A thousand men from Bacchides’s side fell, Bacchides turned to flight, returned to Jerusalem, built fortified cities in Judaea, and placed guards in them. He took the sons of the leading men of the region as hostages and placed them in custody in the citadel at Jerusalem.

Then Alcimus ordered the walls of the inner holy house to be destroyed and the works of the prophets demolished. When he had begun to destroy them, he was struck with paralysis and died in great torment. Bacchides returned to the king, and the land of Judah was quiet for two years.

After these, [Col. 1514A] wicked men in Israel brought Bacchides back into Judaea. He wanted secretly to capture Jonathan but could not, for his plan became known to Jonathan. Jonathan seized fifty of those who were plotting against him and killed them. Jonathan and his men withdrew to Bethbessen, which is in the wilderness, and fortified it. Bacchides went up in great force and besieged Beth-basi.

Jonathan went out, leaving Simon in the city. Jonathan assembled a force and struck many enemies by night in their tents. “Simon, however, went out from the city, set fire to the siege-engines, and they fought against Bacchides and crushed him. Bacchides was angry with the men who had brought him back into Judaea and killed many of them. When Jonathan heard this, he sent envoys to him to arrange peace. Bacchides readily accepted; he swore that he would do Jonathan no harm all the days of his life, restored the captives whom he had formerly taken as spoil in the land of Judah, and returned to his own country. The sword ceased from Israel; Jonathan sat at Michmash, judging the people there and exterminating the wicked in Israel.”

## CHAPTER X.—On Alexander, Who Killed Demetrius
> “At that time Alexander, the son of Antiochus Epiphanes, came up, took possession of Ptolemais, and reigned there” (1 Macc. 10). When Demetrius heard this, he assembled an army and sent to Jonathan, proposing that he make peace with him rather than with Alexander. [Note: [Col. 1515B] Addition 1.—From the time when Antiochus Epiphanes, who had been a hostage at Rome, succeeded to the kingdom after his father’s death—having set aside his brother and Demetrius, his brother’s son—there had been a contest for the kingdom among the successors of those brothers.] Moreover, he gave him authority to raise an army, and ordered that the hostages who were in the citadel [Col. 1514C] be returned to him. Jonathan came to Jerusalem and began to restore the city; he fortified Mount Zion round about, and the guards whom Bacchides had stationed in Judaea fled. Some nevertheless remained in Bethsura, which served as their refuge.

But Alexander heard of the promises that Demetrius had made to Jonathan, and of the battles and exploits performed by Jonathan and his brothers; and he wrote to Jonathan, saying: “We have heard concerning you that you are a mighty man and fit to be our friend. Therefore we now appoint you today high priest of your nation, and order that you be called the king’s friend.” He sent him purple and a golden crown. Jonathan put on the sacred garment on the solemn day of the Feast of Tabernacles, gathered an army, and made abundant weapons [Col. 1514D].

When King Demetrius heard this, he was distressed and sent word to Jonathan in these terms: “Remain in our friendship. I now release all the Jews from tribute; I grant the authority over the citadel in Jerusalem to the high priest; I freely set at liberty every Jewish person captive within my kingdom; and let every feast-day be a day of exemption and remission, and likewise the days appointed around them”—that is, three days before the feast and three after it. “I give Ptolemais and its two bordering cities to the high priest for the necessary expenses of the holy things; and fifteen thousand shekels of silver each year shall be given from the royal accounts, for restoring the works of the holy things, renewing the walls of Jerusalem, and expenses in Judaea.”

But Jonathan and the people did not believe him [Col. 1515A]. They were pleased with Alexander and gave him assistance throughout his days. Then King Alexander assembled an army and moved his camp against Demetrius. Demetrius’s army fled, and Demetrius fell that day.

Then Alexander sent to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, saying: “Give me your daughter as wife.” Ptolemy consented, directing him to meet him at Ptolemais. Ptolemy went out from Egypt with his daughter Cleopatra; and when Alexander met him at Ptolemais, he gave her to him as wife.

Then Alexander summoned Jonathan. When Jonathan came to Ptolemais, he found favor in the sight of the two kings. Certain corrupt men from Israel came after him and accused him. But the king paid them no heed; rather, he exalted Jonathan, clothed him in purple [Col. 1515B], and enrolled him among his chief friends. There are four royal insignia: purple, the golden clasp, the diadem, and the sceptre. Jonathan returned to Jerusalem in glory.

## Chapter XI.—Concerning Demetrius of Crete

After three years Demetrius, son of Demetrius, came from Crete (1 Macc. 10). When his father had been slain in battle, he had fled to the Cretans, his mother’s relatives. Having recovered his strength, he returned to the maritime region of the Philistines and to Coele-Syria. He appointed Apollonius commander of the army [Col. 1515C], and Apollonius challenged Jonathan to battle.

Jonathan set out from Jerusalem with ten thousand men. Coming to Joppa, he drove Apollonius out and took possession of it. Apollonius went to Azotus; Jonathan pursued him, and they joined battle in the plain. Apollonius’s cavalry fled into Azotus and entered the temple of Dagon for protection. Jonathan set fire to the city and the temple, and to those within it. Nearly eight thousand were killed in the field or burned in the temple.

Jonathan then passed on to Ascalon, and the people of Ascalon received him with honor. He returned to Jerusalem. King Alexander heard of his valor and further honored Jonathan, sending him a golden clasp, customarily bestowed upon the kinsmen of kings [Col. 1515D], and giving him Accaron and all its territory. Since Jonathan bore two royal insignia, this was perhaps a sign of the restoration of the Jewish kingdom.

Alexander went up into the upper parts of Cilicia. “And the king of Egypt, his father-in-law, came out with great strength and sought deceitfully to gain Alexander’s kingdom” (1 Macc. 11). The cities were opened to him and came out to meet him, for Alexander had so commanded. As he passed through each city, he left garrisons behind. “As he approached Azotus, they showed him the burned temple of Dagon, the other ruins, and the heaps of those who had been slain; and they said, ‘Jonathan did this,’ in order to make him odious to the king. But the king kept silent.”

Jonathan met Ptolemy at Joppa, and they greeted one another. Jonathan went with the king as far as the River Eleutherus [Col. 1516A], and then returned to Jerusalem. When Ptolemy had gained the cities as far as coastal Seleucia, he sent to Demetrius, saying: “Come, let us make an agreement, and I will give you my daughter. For I regret having given her to Alexander.” Taking his daughter away, he gave her to Demetrius and openly withdrew from Alexander. Ptolemy entered Antioch and placed upon himself the two diadems of Egypt and Asia.

Then Alexander came against him in battle, was defeated by Ptolemy, and fled into Arabia to his mother’s relatives with his son Antiochus. But the king of the Arabs, fearing Ptolemy’s power, killed Alexander, preserved his son, and sent Alexander’s head to Ptolemy, who rejoiced. Yet it happened that Ptolemy died on the third day, and Demetrius reigned [Col. 1516B] upon his fathers’ throne.

In those days Jonathan besieged the citadel in Jerusalem. Certain wicked men from Israel reported this to Demetrius. Angered, he came to Ptolemais and wrote to Jonathan, ordering him not to besiege the citadel but to meet him immediately. Jonathan selected men from the elders of Israel and exposed himself to danger. He took much money and garments, went to the king, and by giving him gifts found favor in his sight. Although many accused him, the king magnified him before all and confirmed for him the high-priestly authority and all that he had possessed before.

Demetrius saw that the land was quiet before him. He dismissed his army to their homes, retaining only a mercenary force; and all his father’s army became his enemy [Col. 1516C]. Tryphon had formerly belonged to Alexander’s party. Seeing that the whole army murmured against Demetrius, he went into Arabia to bring Antiochus, Alexander’s son, back to the land of his father.

At that time, while Demetrius was alienated from his own people, Jonathan sent to him, asking him to expel those in the Jerusalem citadel and the garrisons, because they were attacking Israel. Demetrius replied: “I shall do this and greater things for you when the opportunity arises. But now you will do well if you send men to help me, for my army has deserted me.”

Jonathan sent him three thousand chosen men to Antioch, and the king rejoiced at their arrival. One hundred and twenty thousand Antiochenes rose up and wished to kill the king [Col. 1516D]. The king fled into the palace. He sent the Jews through the city; they killed one hundred thousand people and delivered the king. The remaining citizens gave their right hands to the king and made peace. The Jews were glorified and returned to Jerusalem. “And the land was quiet before Demetrius. Yet he lied in all that he had promised Jonathan, withdrew from him, and grievously oppressed him.”

## Chapter XII.—Concerning the Young Antiochus

At that time Tryphon returned from Arabia, bringing back the young Antiochus and placing the diadem upon him (1 Macc. 11). The armies dispersed by Demetrius gathered to him, fought against Demetrius, and put him to flight. Antiochus and Tryphon gained possession of Antioch.

The young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan [Col. 1517A], saying: “I appoint you to the high priesthood, and I set you over four cities, that you may be among the king’s friends.” He sent him golden vessels, granting him authority to drink from gold, wear purple, and possess a golden clasp. “He appointed Simon, Jonathan’s brother, commander from the borders of Tyre to the frontier of Egypt. Jonathan went out, passed through the cities, came to Ascalon, and its inhabitants received him honorably.”

The people of Azotus, who had at first resisted him, afterward gave him their right hands. He took hostages from them and sent them to Jerusalem. He travelled through the regions as far as Damascus, conducting the affairs of the kingdom. Jonathan heard that the commanders of Demetrius at Cades of Galilee, with a great army, wished to remove him from the affairs of the kingdom. He went to meet them, leaving his brother Simon within the province [Col. 1517B]. All who were with Jonathan fled except two. Jonathan tore his garments and prayed. Then he attacked the enemy, routed them, and those who had withdrawn from him returned to him. He pursued the enemy as far as their camp at Cades; three thousand of them fell, and Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.

He sent to Rome to renew friendship with them (1 Macc. 12). He also wrote to the Spartans, whom we previously called Lacedaemonians, saying: “Long ago Darius, your king, wrote to us in the time of Onias, high priest of the Jews, that you are of Abraham’s race and our brothers; and we entered into brotherhood with you. Since then we have remembered you in our sacrifices and observances [Col. 1517C], as it is fitting for us to remember brothers. And now we have sent to you in order to renew this brotherhood.”

The Spartans replied: “May our cattle and property be yours, and yours ours.” Thus the brotherhood was renewed. Jonathan heard that Demetrius’s commanders had again come out with an army much greater than before, and he went out against them. When they heard of Jonathan’s arrival, they fled by night, leaving their fires in the camp. Jonathan pursued them in the morning but did not catch them, for they had crossed the River Eleutherus.

Jonathan turned aside against the Arabs called Zabadaeans and struck them. Simon, however, turned toward Joppa, having heard that they intended to hand the garrison over to Demetrius’s party [Col. 1517D]. He stationed guards there. Jonathan returned to Jerusalem, renewed its walls, and strongly fortified the space between the citadel and the city, so that the city might stand alone in the land, “and neither buy nor sell”—that is, not be dependent on the goods of others. [Note: [Col. 1518B] Addition 1. In the Book of Maccabees it is thus: “Having summoned the elders of the people, he planned to restore the walls and to raise a great height between the city and the citadel, so as to separate it from the city and leave it standing alone.”]

At that time Tryphon planned to kill the young Antiochus and place the diadem upon himself, but he feared Jonathan, Antiochus’s energetic defender. He therefore chose first to kill Jonathan. He wrote to Jonathan, asking him to meet him at Bethshan. Jonathan came with one hundred and forty thousand men. Seeing that he could not lay hands on him, Tryphon honored him, gave him gifts, and commanded his armies to obey Jonathan as they obeyed himself.

He said to Jonathan: “Why have you troubled the people? Choose a few men and come with me [Col. 1518A] to Ptolemais. I shall deliver it to you, together with the remaining garrisons, the army, and all the officers of the kingdom; then I shall return.” Jonathan believed him. He sent the army back into Judaea and retained only three thousand men, two thousand of whom he dismissed into Galilee. One thousand remained with him.

When he entered Ptolemais, its inhabitants bound him and killed all those with him. All Judaea mourned Jonathan, believing that he had been killed. The nations around Judaea said: “They have no ruler; let us erase their memory from among humankind.” Tryphon assembled an army to come into Judaea and destroy it (1 Macc. 13). In fear, the people went up to Jerusalem and said to Simon: “You are our leader in place of your brothers Judas and Jonathan.”

## Chapter XIII.—Concerning Simon

[Col. 1518B]

Simon hastened to complete the walls of Jerusalem and sent an army to Joppa (1 Macc. 13). When Tryphon learned that Simon had risen in Jonathan’s place, he sent envoys to him, saying: “I have detained Jonathan, your brother, because of the money which he owed in the king’s account. Now send one hundred talents of silver and his two sons as hostages, and we will release him.”

Although Simon knew of his deceit, he nevertheless sent the money and the boys, lest the people complain [Col. 1518C], saying: “He did not ransom his brother because he wished to reign.” But Tryphon lied, entered the region to destroy it, and, when he came near Baschama and saw that he could make no progress, killed Jonathan there and his sons, and returned to his own land.

Simon sent and took Jonathan’s bones and buried him at Modin. He erected seven pyramids for his father and mother, his four brothers, and himself; around them he placed great columns and carved arms and ships upon them for everlasting remembrance.

As Tryphon travelled with the young Antiochus, he treacherously killed him and reigned in his place in Asia. Simon then built fortresses in Judaea and sent to Demetrius to make peace with him. Sending gifts [Col. 1518D], he asked that remission be granted to the region. Demetrius wrote: “We have received the gifts, and we make a great peace with you, remitting errors and offenses down to the present day; and now we release you from every tribute.” Thus the yoke of the nations was removed from Israel.

From that time, the people of Israel began to write the dates in records and public documents in this manner: “In the first year under Simon, high priest, great commander, and ruler of the Jews.” Simon then went down to Gaza and besieged it. He cast out the idolaters and the idols from the city, cleansed its buildings, settled there men who would observe the law, fortified it, and made it his dwelling-place.

He besieged those in the Jerusalem citadel. They cried to Simon that he should receive their right hands [Col. 1519A]. He granted this and expelled them from it, cleansed the citadel from its defilements, and entered it with musical instruments, hymns, and palm branches, decreeing that this day be observed every year with rejoicing. [Note: [Col. 1519B] Addition 1. Thus we read of three feasts in the Book of Maccabees. The first was the feast of the purification of the Temple, discussed above in chapter 3, “Therefore, having been so often defeated.” The second followed the killing of Nicanor, discussed above in chapter 6, “At that time.” The third is found here. Yet none of these was a legal feast.]

Simon saw that his son John was a man of war. He appointed him commander under himself and gave him Gaza as a residence. Then King Demetrius assembled an army and entered Media to gather assistance to attack Tryphon (1 Macc. 14). But Arsaces, king of Persia and Media, sent one of his commanders, who attacked Demetrius’s camp, captured him alive, and placed him in Arsaces’s custody.

“And the land of Judaea was quiet in Simon’s days.” He made Joppa into a harbor and an entrance to the islands of the sea. “He enlarged [Col. 1519B] the borders of his nation, removed uncleanness, and every man sat beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree, with no one to terrify them.” Simon sent to the Spartans to renew the brotherhood. He also sent the Romans a golden shield weighing one thousand minas; the Romans granted him liberty and inscribed the treaty upon bronze tablets, which were placed on monuments on Mount Zion.

## Chapter XIV.—Concerning Antiochus, Son of Demetrius

[Col. 1519C] At that time Antiochus, son of Demetrius, entered the land of his fathers, and the entire army gathered to him, so that few remained with Tryphon (1 Macc. 15). Antiochus wrote to Simon and to the Jewish people: “I confirm for you all that previous kings remitted to you, and permit you to mint your own coinage in your region. When I have obtained the kingdom, I shall greatly honor your nation and the Temple.”

Tryphon, fleeing Antiochus along the coast, withdrew to Dora. Antiochus pursued him and besieged the city by land and sea. At that time Lucius, consul of the Romans, wrote to the kings and regions in the East that they should inflict no harm upon the Jews, their friends, nor assist those who harmed them; but if any corrupt men among the Jews fled to them, they should hand them over to Simon, the ruler of the priests, so that he might punish them according to his law [Col. 1519D].

King Antiochus besieged Dora a second time and confined Tryphon so that he could not leave. Simon sent him two thousand men as assistance, along with silver, gold, and abundant vessels. But Antiochus refused to accept them, broke the treaty he had made with Simon, and sent Athenobius to him, ordering Simon to return the Jerusalem citadel, Joppa, Gaza, and the revenues of the places over which he had ruled; otherwise, he would come and attack him.

Athenobius saw in Jerusalem Simon’s glory [Col. 1520A], his plentiful equipment, and his abundance of gold and silver, and was astonished. Simon replied: “We have not taken another’s land, but the inheritance of our fathers, which our enemies unjustly possessed for a time.” Athenobius returned to the king and reported Simon’s words and glory. The king was greatly enraged.

Tryphon fled by ship to Orthosiada. The king, pursuing Tryphon, appointed Cendebaeus commander of the coastal region and left an army with him to attack Judaea. Cendebaeus built Gedora and stationed soldiers there to ravage the borders of Judaea. When Simon learned this, he summoned his two elder sons, Judas and John, and said: “I and my brothers have fought the enemies of Israel from our youth [Col. 1520B] until this day. But now I am old. You must take my place and fight for your nation. May help from heaven be with you” (1 Macc. 16).

He gave them twenty thousand fighting men and cavalry. They set out against Cendebaeus. A torrent lay between them, and the people feared to cross it. John crossed first, and all followed him. They sounded the sacred trumpets; Cendebaeus and his army turned and fled, and many of them fell wounded. Judas, John’s brother, was also wounded. John pursued the fugitives as far as Cedron. Two thousand men of them fell, and Simon’s sons returned in peace.

## Chapter XV.—Concerning Simon’s Death

[Col. 1520C]

Ptolemy, son of Abubus, had been appointed commander in the plain of Jericho (1 Macc. 16). He was the high priest’s son-in-law and possessed much silver and gold. His heart became proud; he sought to gain the region and devised treachery against Simon and his sons in order to remove them.

Simon travelled through the cities of the region, attending to their needs. He went down to Jericho with his sons Judas and Mattathias. Ptolemy received them into a small fortress which he had deceitfully built, made them a great banquet, and hid men there.
