He entered the banquet with armed men, killed Simon and his two sons, and repaid good with evil. For he also slew [variant: bound] Simon’s wife together with her two younger sons [Col. 1520D].

He wrote to King Antiochus, asking him to send an army in assistance and to hand over to him the region, cities, and revenues. He also sent messengers to the military commanders, asking them to come to him so that he might give them silver, gold, and gifts. Others he sent to seize Jerusalem and the Temple Mount.

He sent still others to Gazara to kill John. But someone hurried ahead to Gazara and reported to John what had happened. John himself hastened to secure Jerusalem and killed those who had come to destroy him. He became ruler of the priests after his father.

# History of the Second Book of Maccabees

[Col. 1521]

## [Col. 1521A] Preface to the History of the Second Book of Maccabees

The Second Book of Maccabees is not a continuation of the history but a recapitulation of the history already narrated. It is a letter written by Judas Maccabaeus and the Jewish senate of Jerusalem to the dispersed Jews, exiled in various regions of the East and especially in Egypt. In it they informed them of two recently instituted festivals and exhorted them to observe and celebrate them annually (2 Macc. 1).

One was the purification of the Temple, performed on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, after three years of pollution caused by Antiochus. The other was instituted on the thirteenth day of Adar, that is, March, and was called in Syriac the day before Mordecai [Note: [Col. 1522B] Addition 1. Under Mordecai’s leadership, the Jews instituted a festival on the thirteenth day of that same month in remembrance of their victory over their enemies on that day. They killed them throughout the provinces, to the number of seventy-five thousand, by permission granted them by Ahasuerus, [Col. 1522C] as is related above in the Book of Esther, near its end.]—namely, the day established because of the extraordinary [Col. 1521B] victory won through the killing of Nicanor, whose head and hand, hung up against the Temple, we mentioned earlier.

They likewise exhorted them to celebrate solemnly the Feast of Tabernacles and the day of the fire that was given from thick water when Nehemiah offered sacrifices. In this part of the letter it is said that Jeremiah hid the ark and the altar of incense in a cave on the mountain which Moses ascended and from which he saw God’s inheritance (2 Macc. 2; Deut. 34). Certain persons who followed Jeremiah came to mark the place for themselves but could not find it. Rebuking them, Jeremiah said:

> “The place shall remain unknown until God gathers the assembly of the people and shows mercy. Then the Lord will reveal these things, and the majesty of the Lord will appear, together with the cloud, as in the days of Moses and [Col. 1521C] as when Solomon acted [3 Kings 8], so that the place might be sanctified to the great God.”

Therefore, what we previously said that Epiphanius had stated differently concerning the manifestation of the ark was perhaps mystical. But lest the Jerusalemites seem to have instituted these festivals without reason, they recapitulated in the letter the wars which they had fought against enemies who had often surged forth from Persia, and how God had delivered them by a mighty hand, signs, and innumerable wonders.

Certain matters are included in this recapitulation that are not found in the history already recounted. Some have already been set forth above; those omitted there will now be supplied. The form of the letter is as follows:

> “The people who are at Jerusalem and in Judaea, the senate and Judas, to Aristobulus, teacher of King Ptolemy, who is of the race of anointed priests, and to the Jews in Egypt: greeting and health. May God do you good and give all of you a heart to worship him and do his will. May he open your hearts to his law and commandments and grant peace. May he hear your prayers, be reconciled to you, and not forsake you in the time of evil. And now we are here praying for you. Since we have been magnificently delivered by God from great dangers [Col. 1522A], let us give abundant thanks to him,”

and the rest which follows (2 Macc. 1).

They began to enumerate their dangers and deliverances wrought by God with the death of Antiochus the Great and of his son Seleucus. Although Seleucus had formerly honored the Temple and supplied from his revenues the expenses for sacrificial ministry, at the instigation of Simon of the tribe of Benjamin—superintendent of the Temple and jealous of Onias—he sent Heliodorus to plunder the common treasury, asserting that it did not belong to the account of sacrifices (2 Macc. 3). These funds had indeed been collected for the sustenance of widows and orphans, and much of it had been deposited by wealthy persons.

They ended the narrative of this letter at the death of Nicanor in this manner:

> “Therefore, after these things done concerning Nicanor, from that time the city has been endured/suffered, or possessed, by the Hebrews. I too shall bring my account to an end here. If it has been well done and as history requires, that is also what I desire; but if it has been done less worthily, allowance must be made for me. For just as it is unpleasant to drink wine always or water always, while their use in alternation is delightful, so a discourse that is continually exact will not be pleasing to its readers. Here, then, shall be the conclusion” (2 Macc. 15).

## Chapter I.—Recapitulation

We shall briefly touch upon certain matters added in this epistolary recapitulation. During Antiochus’s profanation, when Jews were compelled to depart from their ancestral laws, two women were denounced for having circumcised their sons. Their infants were hung at their breasts; after the women had been publicly led through the city, executioners cast them down from the walls (2 Macc. 6).

Eleazar, one of the chief scribes and a man advanced in age, was forced, with his mouth held open, to eat sacrificial swine’s flesh. Some of his former friends secretly brought lawful meat and asked him to pretend that he ate at the king’s command. Refusing, he said: “I may perhaps leave a bad example for the young.” Put to death by scourges, he left behind the memory of his death and an example of virtue.

It also happened that seven brothers were arrested with their mother and compelled to eat pork. When they refused, the king ordered frying-pans and bronze kettles to be heated before them. The firstborn’s tongue was cut out; the skin of his head was stripped off, and the extremities of his hands and feet cut away before his mother and brothers. He was then thrown into a frying-pan and roasted [Col. 1523A].

Each of the brothers was tortured in the same way, according to the order of birth, though each was first urged to obey the king and live. The mother, beyond measure admirable and worthy of honorable remembrance, exhorted each in their ancestral language. Infusing a manly spirit into feminine resolve, she said to them:

> “I do not know how you came to be in my womb; for I did not give you spirit, soul, or life, nor did I myself fashion the limbs of each of you. Rather, he who formed you will in mercy give back to you both spirit and life, since you now despise yourselves for the sake of his law.”

When the youngest still remained [Col. 1523B], the king urged the mother to secure the young man’s safety. She promised that she would advise her son; then, bending toward him, she said in their ancestral language: “My son, have pity on me. Prove worthy of your brothers; accept death, so that in that mercy I may receive you again with your brothers.” The king, indignantly believing himself mocked, treated him more cruelly than all the rest. “Finally, after her sons, the mother also died” (2 Macc. 7).

On account of the great prerogative of their martyrdom, many maintain that the Church celebrates the seven brothers. [Note: [Col. 1524C] Addition 1. The term *martyr* extends to four classes. A martyr is one who dies to preserve God’s law, as the Maccabees did. A martyr is also one who dies for the truth of preaching, as Jeremiah and [Col. 1524D] the other prophets did. Likewise, one is a martyr who dies in Christ’s very place, as the infants did. And one is a martyr who dies for the confession of faith and of Christ’s passion, as Peter and Paul did. The latter are properly called martyrs, that is, witnesses of Christ’s passion. The Church celebrates their feast, while it celebrates no feast of any Old Testament martyr except that of the seven Maccabees. The Church also observes the feast of the infants, although they descended into hell; hence the song of joy is omitted at their feast. If John the Baptist be raised as an objection, we answer that we do not observe the feast of his passion but of his birth, which was a figure of Christ’s birth. The feast of his Beheading, therefore, is not a feast of his passion—especially since he was beheaded around Passover—but marks the time when his head was found. [Col. 1525A] Others relate that there are two observances because his bones were translated at such a time.]

It is also added in the same letter that, when Judas fought against Timothy, five men on horseback appeared from heaven to the adversaries, leading the Jews. Two of them, having the Maccabee [Col. 1523C] between them, surrounded and protected him with their arms, while they hurled darts and lightning bolts against the adversaries (2 Macc. 10).

Not long afterward, as Judas was leaving Jerusalem to fight Lysias, a horseman appeared before them in white clothing, bearing golden armor and brandishing a spear (2 Macc. 11). It is also added that the people of Joppa asked the Jews dwelling among them to embark in boats they had prepared for festive recreation (2 Macc. 12). When they had gone out to sea, they drowned no fewer than two hundred of them. Judas therefore came upon them at night, burned the harbor and the boats, and killed with the sword those fleeing from the fire.

He likewise came by night upon the people of Jamnia and burned the harbor and ships, so that the firelight could be seen from Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia away [Col. 1523D]. It is also added that, after battle had been joined near Jamnia, several Jews were slain. Judas came with his men to take up the bodies of the fallen and lay them in their ancestral tombs. Under the tunics of those killed they found votive offerings to idols from Jamnia. Thus it became clear to all that they had fallen for this reason. They blessed the just judgment of God, who had made hidden things manifest. Turning to prayer, they asked God to blot out their sin.

But Judas, a most valiant man, took up a collection from his men and sent twelve thousand silver drachmas to Jerusalem to be offered there as a sacrifice for the sins or offense of the dead. It is further added that the utterly wicked Nicanor pursued [Col. 1524A] Judas after a treaty had been made with him and afterward [the source reading is incomplete or uncertain], learned that Judas was in the regions of Samaria, and planned to join battle with him on the Sabbath day (2 Macc. 15).

The Jews following Nicanor said to him out of necessity that he should honor the day’s sanctity and God, who beholds all things. He asked them: “Is there a mighty one in heaven who commanded them to keep the Sabbath day?” They replied: “There is one mighty God in heaven who commanded the observance of the seventh day.” He said: “I too am mighty upon earth, and I command that weapons be taken up and the king’s business carried out.”

Since few were with him and they feared Nicanor’s authority and numbers, the Maccabee armed each of those Jews not with the protection of shield and spear but with excellent words [Col. 1524B] and encouragement, especially by telling them a dream he had seen that very night. He had seen Onias, the high priest, who had been trained in virtues from childhood, stretching out his hands and praying for the Jewish people. [Note: [Col. 1525A] Addition 2. Here you have authority for the proposition that we ought to call upon the souls of the saints, that they may pray and intercede for us; by this the Jews are refuted, who deny that the help of any saints is to be sought.]

After this, another man of remarkable age and glory had appeared near him, and Onias had said: “This is the lover of the people of Israel; this is he who prays much for the people and the holy city: Jeremiah, prophet of God.” Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and gave Judas a golden sword, saying: “Receive this holy sword, a gift sent from God, by which you shall overthrow the adversaries of my people Israel.”

Strengthened by this vision, those with Judas attacked the enemy [Col. 1524C] and struck down no fewer than thirty thousand of them, Nicanor being killed with them. They returned to Jerusalem blessing God and hung Nicanor’s head and the hand cut off with its shoulder opposite the Temple. Therefore all, by common counsel, decreed that this day should by no means pass without celebration.

Here ends Judas’s letter to the dispersed Jews. The epistolary recapitulation being complete, let us return to the continuation of the history concerning John, son of Simon.

## Chapter II.—Concerning the Commendation of John Hyrcanus

[Col. 1525A]

After Simon’s death—he had been the last surviving of the five sons of Mattathias the Hasmonaean, leader and priest in Judaea—his son John succeeded him. He was surnamed Hyrcanus after the Hyrcanians whom he had conquered (1 Macc. 16). Josephus commends him in three respects: for his priestly religion, vigor in command, and prophetic gift [Col. 1525B].

He pursued Ptolemy, who had treacherously murdered his father, held his mother and two younger brothers in bonds, and fled to a town beyond Jericho called Agon. John besieged the town and pressed the attack fiercely. Ptolemy, however, beat John’s mother and brothers upon the walls until blood was shed, and John, overcome by filial affection, held back from the assault. Yet his mother cried out that he should not let Ptolemy’s crime against her go unavenged, for she regarded her own death as better in the prospect of immortality.

Because the siege was thus prolonged, the seventh year, observed as a sabbatical year by the Jews, arrived. John withdrew from the siege. Ptolemy killed John’s mother and brothers and fled to Zeno, tyrant of Philadelphia, who was surnamed Cotylas [Col. 1525C].

## Chapter III.—Concerning the Establishment of Hostels and the Death of John
After this Antiochus of Pontus, king of Syria, besieged Jerusalem. Hyrcanus therefore opened two of the eight chambers surrounding David’s tomb, took from them more than three thousand talents, and gave Antiochus three hundred talents to withdraw from the siege. To quiet the people’s murmuring over the opening of the tomb, he used the remaining money to establish, the first to do so, hostels for the poor in Jerusalem. He levelled captured Samaria to the ground; later Herod rebuilt it and called it Sebaste. John died after administering affairs most successfully for thirty-three years, leaving [Col. 1525D] five sons: Aristobulus the first-born, Antigonus, and three younger sons. Since none of them was capable of governing the people, he placed his very eloquent wife over Judaea and over his sons.

## CHAPTER IV. On the restoration of the Jewish kingdom through Aristobulus

Aristobulus, impatient of his mother’s rule, imprisoned his mother and his three younger brothers, and made Antigonus, whom he loved, second after himself. He placed a diadem upon his head, and the kingdom of Judaea was restored. Four hundred and seventy-five years and three months had elapsed from Zedekiah—under whom the kingdom had been interrupted—or from the return from Babylonian captivity. Hence it is often [Col. 1526A] read that the kingdom had been suspended as far as Hyrcanus, and “to Aristobulus” is used intransitively—that is, as far as Aristobulus, son of Hyrcanus. Yet Aristobulus reigned only one year, because he had starved his mother to death in prison.

While Aristobulus lay ill in the tower which Herod afterwards called Antonia, Antigonus was returning from Galilee, where he had performed many distinguished deeds, dressed in new and handsome armour. Entering Jerusalem during the Feast of Tabernacles, out of respect for his brother and to display the splendour of his arms to the people, he entered armed. His enemies, seeing this—especially his brother’s wife, who had cast her eyes upon him but received no encouragement from him—accused him before Aristobulus, saying: “Your brother, hearing that you are ill, has entered in strength [Col. 1526B] and armed, in order to kill you and reign. You may test whether this is so: order him to come to you; if he comes armed, be certain of what we say.”

At his wife’s prompting Aristobulus therefore stationed armed men in an underground passage called the Tower of Straton, through which Antigonus was to pass, so that they might kill him if he came armed. Summoning his brother, Aristobulus instructed the messenger to tell him not to come armed. But the queen bribed the messenger with gifts, so that he told him to come down with his arms: the king wished, he said, to see him in the beauty of his armour.

## CHAPTER V. On the murder of Antigonus

At that time there was in Jerusalem a certain astrologer named Judas, of the sect of the Essenes, who [Col. 1526C] had, from the stars at children’s births, made prognostications, and had predicted to his pupils by his art Antigonus’s death, naming both the day and place. When he saw Antigonus proudly displaying his arms, he cried out: “Wonderful! It is now a fine thing for me to die, since truth has perished before my eyes and one of my predictions has been found false. This Antigonus is alive, though he was to die today at the Tower of Straton. That place, however, is six hundred stadia from here, and the day is four hours old.”

As the old man thus lamented, shortly afterwards Antigonus was killed as he came down armed through the Tower of Straton; the old man recognized that he had been deceived by the ambiguity of the place-names. Hearing of his brother’s death, the king grieved, and his illness grew so severe that, his entrails torn, he vomited [Col. 1526D] blood. A servant assigned to this duty was carrying it outside when, at the place where Antigonus had been killed, he accidentally spilled it upon the still-visible stains of gore. Seeing this, the people cried out, declaring that by God’s will the blood of the murderer had been poured out in vengeance for the slain man.

When the king asked the reason for the cry, no one dared tell him. At last, when he threatened punishment for their silence, they told him the truth. Groaning, he said: “It was not right that the light of God should conceal my crimes, O wicked body, how long will you retain a soul condemned for my mother and brother? Would that I might pour out my blood for them not little by little, but all at once, so that they may receive it!” Having spoken thus, he expired.

## CHAPTER VI. On the tyranny and death of King Alexander

[Col. 1527A]

After his death, his wife—since he had had no children by her—released her husband’s brothers from their chains and made the elder, Alexander, king. He was surnamed Jannaeus and seemed also to excel in moderation. He killed the second brother because he appeared to aspire to the throne, compelled the third to live privately with him, and married a wife named Alexandra, also called Salome.

This man was so utterly wicked that in about seven years he killed fifty-five thousand elders because they detested his crimes. When he had provoked the people, he fortified a palace for himself in the tower called Baris, at which Titus later marvelled [Col. 1527B] because the Jews had abandoned it, although it could have been defended by two men against every living being. He was so hated by the Jews that, when he once asked how he might reconcile them, they answered: “By dying.” For this reason he hanged eight hundred married men in the streets of Jerusalem and killed their wives and children.

When he had rested from warfare and was troubled by quartan fever, thinking that his illness had arisen from idleness, he returned to the untimely exertions of military service. He died in the thirty-eighth year of his reign, leaving two sons, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus. Knowing that his sons were hated by the Jews on account of their father, he left the kingdom to his wife. During her husband’s lifetime she had often gained the people’s goodwill by more than once resisting his tyranny, [Col. 1527C] and she displayed even a feigned piety in her manner of dress.

## CHAPTER VII. On Alexandra’s reign, and her sons Hyrcanus and Aristobulus

While she reigned, she appointed her first-born Hyrcanus high priest, indicating that he was to become king because he was mild in character; but she compelled the younger Aristobulus, because he seemed hot-tempered, to live as a private person. At that time the sect of the Pharisees arose in Judaea; it will later be discussed along with the other sects. Alexandra followed their counsel in all things, so that by their advice she either condemned to exile or put to death every notable man among the Jews. Finally, she killed Diogenes, who had been Alexander’s closest friend. She had indeed raised for herself two armies of foreigners [Col. 1527D] in order to rage more safely against the Jews. Therefore many had fled to Aristobulus to secure his protection.

In the ninth year of her reign Alexandra fell ill, and Aristobulus, having gathered a large body of followers, declared that after his mother he would reign.

> **[Note: Col. 1527D, Addition 1.]** In these times Jugurtha, fighting against the Romans, was captured at Rome by Marius and Sulla. The art of rhetoric began to be taught by Plotius Gallus. Lucretius, driven mad by a love potion, composed several books during intervals of insanity; finally he killed himself.

For this reason, moved by Hyrcanus’s complaints, his mother shut up Aristobulus’s wife and children in custody and took hostages, so that Aristobulus might not seize the kingdom for himself.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the brothers’ manifold discord

[Col. 1528A]

After her death Aristobulus gathered an army and took up arms against his brother. When the brothers met on the plains of Jericho, Hyrcanus was defeated and fled to Jerusalem. At last they returned to concord on the condition that Aristobulus should reign, while Hyrcanus should exercise whatever offices he pleased under him. They even exchanged houses.

Now Antipater the Idumaean was with Hyrcanus. Fearing his prudence and vigour, Aristobulus brought accusations against him. Antipater persuaded Hyrcanus to complain that he had been entrapped by deceit and to flee to Aretas, king of the Arabs, with whose help he might return to the kingdom. They left by night and came to the Arabian king at the town called Petra, where the royal seat was. Thus Aretas gathered an army, [Col. 1528B] came into Judaea, and besieged Jerusalem; and he would have taken it had not Scaurus, commander of the Romans, lifted the siege.

For Syria had by then ceased to have a king and had become tributary to the Romans. Pompey had been sent by the Romans against Tigranes, king of Armenia, and they had sent Scaurus as governor of Syria. Hearing of the brothers’ quarrel in Judaea and judging that the moment had come easily to impose tribute upon Judaea, he entered its borders with a strong force. Envoys came to him from both brothers, each requesting his aid. But Scaurus, corrupted by three hundred talents sent by Aristobulus—as Josephus testifies was characteristic of Romans—sent Roman envoys to the Arabs, threatening them with Pompey’s [Col. 1528C] name unless they withdrew from the siege.

Aretas therefore withdrew and placed Hyrcanus and Antipater at Philadelphia. Frustrated in their hope from the Arabs, they turned their hope against their adversaries. When Pompey arrived at Damascus, they came to him with many gifts, asking him to judge Aristobulus’s violence worthy of hatred and restore Hyrcanus to the kingdom. But Aristobulus too was not without resources, trusting in Scaurus’s corruption. Since Pompey did not show him royal honour, Aristobulus left in anger, without saluting Pompey, and withdrew to Alexandrium because of the town’s impregnable fortification.

Pompey the Great pursued him with an army of Romans and Syrians and ordered him to come down to him from the town. But Aristobulus, being summoned as a subject, had resolved to risk everything rather than obey. Yet, at his advisers’ counsel, he came down from the town, leaving guards there and ordering them to obey only letters written in his own hand; then he went to Jerusalem. Pompey immediately pursued him, made cheerful [Col. 1528D] near Jericho by the report of Mithridates’ death, where lies the richest region of Idumaea, abundant in palms and producing balsam. When its wood is cut with sharp stones, they collect the tear-like liquid that drips from the wounds.

## CHAPTER IX. How Pompey, after Jerusalem was surrendered to him, stormed the Temple

As Pompey hastened to Jerusalem, Aristobulus, frightened, came to meet him, promising the money held at Alexandrium and future obedience to Roman authority; [Col. 1529A] but none of this was carried out. Pompey sent Gabinius to receive the money, but the guards did not even admit him into the town. Angered by this, Pompey placed Aristobulus under guard.

When he besieged Jerusalem, dissension arose within the city. Aristobulus’s supporters insisted upon defending the city; Hyrcanus’s supporters pressed for surrendering it to the Romans. But Aristobulus’s defeated party withdrew into the Temple. Pompey, admitted into the city, stormed the Temple. While he was filling the northern valley with embankments, the work would not have been completed had he not observed the seventh days, on which Jews are not permitted to work, and ordered the embankment to be constructed. Yet in the third month the sanctuary was breached.

Faustus Cornelius, son of Sulla, was the first who dared enter; the Romans who rushed in profaned [Col. 1529B] the Temple and, as is read elsewhere, stabled horses in its porticoes. It is reported that because of this Pompey never afterwards fought without being defeated, though until then he had been extraordinarily fortunate. On the following day Pompey entered the Temple, marvelled at its site, adornment, and religious observances, took nothing away from it, and ordered the temple servants to cleanse the Temple of its defilements. Having imposed tribute upon the people of Jerusalem and appointed Hyrcanus high priest, he took Aristobulus captive together with his two sons, Alexander and Antigonus, and as many daughters. He hastened to Rome through Cilicia, entrusting the administration of Syria and Judaea to Scaurus and leaving two cohorts with him.

## CHAPTER X. On the division of Judaea into pentarchies

[Col. 1529C]

Alexander, Aristobulus’s son, escaped on the journey. Gathering a large force, he ravaged Judaea and threatened Hyrcanus. He held the strongly fortified places of Alexandrium, Hyrcanium, and Machaerus. Gabinius was sent to Syria to succeed Scaurus; Marcus Antonius served under him. When Gabinius had besieged Alexander at Alexandrium, Alexander surrendered himself and his camp on his mother’s advice. On the same woman’s advice Gabinius utterly demolished the fortresses, lest they become refuges for another war. For the woman flattered Gabinius with services, fearing for her husband and the other captives who had been taken to Rome.

After this, having entrusted the care of the Temple to Hyrcanus, Gabinius divided the Jewish people into five councils, [Col. 1529D] as though into pentarchies, thereby breaking Judaea’s pride. At that time Antipater became a close friend of Gabinius and especially of Marcus Antonius, and became so prominent that he was given as wife a granddaughter of the king of the Arabs, named Cypris. By her he had four sons and a daughter. The first-born was Phasael; the second, Herod, later called the Ascalonite; the third, Joseph; the fourth, Pheroras; and the daughter was called Salome.

## CHAPTER XI. On Aristobulus’s escape and renewed captivity

After this Aristobulus escaped from Rome by chance. Having assembled a great force of Jews, he was encircling Alexandrium with a wall; Antony was sent by Gabinius to defeat him. Aristobulus was captured again and taken to Rome with his sons. The Senate held him in custody, but sent his sons back to Judaea, because Gabinius himself had written that he had promised Aristobulus’s wife this in return for the surrender of the fortresses.

Afterwards, while Gabinius was detained in Egypt, Alexander, Aristobulus’s son, again drove the Jews into dissension. But Gabinius returned, made peace, and confirmed Hyrcanus in the high priesthood. After his death Crassus was sent as governor of Syria, to repress also the Parthians, who were now threatening the Romans. To meet the expenses of the Parthian campaign, he took nearly all the gold from the Temple, including the two thousand talents from which Pompey had abstained.

> **[Note: Col. 1530A, Addition 1.]** To him it was said: “You have thirsted for gold; drink gold.”

For this reason he died when gold was poured into his mouth. Cassius succeeded him as governor of Syria and in everything followed Antipater’s advice.

## CHAPTER XII. On Aristobulus’s return to Syria and his murder

[Col. 1530B]

At that time dissension arose among the Romans between the supporters of Pompey and Julius Caesar. After the Senate and Pompey had fled across the Ionian Sea, Caesar gained control of all affairs and of Rome. He released Aristobulus and sent him to Syria with two cohorts, thinking that through him he could easily bring Judaea under his authority. But Caesar’s hope was frustrated: Aristobulus died by poison at the hands of Pompey’s partisans. His body, preserved in honey and denied burial, remained so until, by Antony’s order, it was buried in the royal tombs.

His son Alexander too was killed at Antioch, struck with an axe by Scipio, in accordance with Pompey’s [Col. 1530C] letter, after he had first been formally accused of the acts he had committed against the Romans. Antigonus alone survived; with his two sisters he fled to a certain Ptolemy, son of Mennaeus, who lived below Mount Lebanon. Ptolemy married the younger sister, Alexandra, and by her, as some relate, fathered Lysanias, later tetrarch of Abilene.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Antipater entered Caesar’s favour

Afterwards a battle took place in Emathia, at which Antipater and the Jews fought under Pompey. When he returned to Judaea, fearing Caesar’s attack, he sent his children to their Arab relatives. After Pompey’s death Antipater entered into Caesar’s clientship. Caesar sent Mithridates of Pergamum to storm Pelusium, sending with him Ptolemy, an inhabitant of Lebanon, and Antipater with three thousand Jews. There Antipater’s courage shone most brightly. He was the first to cross the wall; by his prudence he won the people of Memphis to obedience to Caesar; and, after joining battle with the other Egyptians and killing many, he was pierced throughout his body yet, beyond hope, survived the battle. Having won the victory, he had Mithridates as a witness before Caesar to his deeds. Marcus Antonius also commended him on many occasions, and he was made Caesar’s friend. Caesar granted him Roman citizenship and immunity, and, through his favour, confirmed Hyrcanus in the high priesthood.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Antipater was made procurator of Judaea

[Col. 1531A]

At that time Antigonus accused Antipater and Hyrcanus before Caesar, saying that through their counsel his father and brother had perished. Antipater, in reply, cast aside his garment and displayed his multitude of wounds. He said that words were unnecessary when his scars cried out, though he himself was silent, that he had been faithful to the Romans; whereas Antigonus was the son of fugitives, and no one could separate him from Pompey while Pompey lived, nor would anyone now separate him from Caesar.

Caesar then gave Antipater the choice of whatever rank he wished under the high priest in Judaea. Leaving the measure of his rank to Caesar, Antipater was appointed procurator of Judaea, and obtained permission [Col. 1531B] to rebuild his country’s demolished walls. The kingdom too was granted to Hyrcanus, though he was not to be called king. Caesar also placed his kinsman Sextus over Syria.

## CHAPTER XV. How Herod was made governor of Galilee and commander of the Syrian king’s army

After this Antipater appointed his elder son Phasael procurator under himself at Jerusalem and placed Herod over Galilee. Herod, naturally energetic, killed a certain leader of brigands, Hezekiah, with his followers, and made the land so peaceful that Herod was publicly sung of as father of Galilee. Phasael likewise strove, in honourable rivalry, to surpass his brother’s natural ability. For this reason their father was honoured by the people with royal observances; yet [Col. 1531C] he was no less faithful to Hyrcanus.

But no one can escape envy for achievements well performed. Some therefore told Hyrcanus that, after affairs had been entrusted to Antipater and his sons, he sat with the empty name of king. Gradually stirred by this, Hyrcanus ordered Herod to be summoned to answer the charge. After first securing Galilee, Herod hastened to the king, bringing with him a letter from Sextus ordering Hyrcanus to release Herod from every accusation and penalty. Not long afterward Herod became commander of Sextus’s army; and he would then have avenged upon Hyrcanus the injury of the earlier summons, had his father and brother not checked his attack.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Julius Caesar’s death and the signs

[Col. 1531D]

At that time Caesar was killed by the treachery of Brutus and Cassius, having held supreme power for three years and seven months. Rome had been ruled under the seven kings from Romulus for two hundred and forty years. Afterwards the republic was administered under consuls for four hundred and forty-four years. Caesar died in the fifty-sixth year of his life, and his body was burned before the Rostra. The people set up in the forum a solid column of Numidian stone, nearly twenty feet high, above which he was buried; it was also called the Julian Column.

On the hundredth day before his death lightning struck his statue in the forum and tore away the capital letter C from his inscribed name. On the night before the day of his death, the windows of his bedchamber flew open with such a crash that he leapt from his bed, thinking the house was about to collapse. On the same day, as he went to the Capitol, a letter warning him of his imminent death was handed to him. When he was carried back dead, it was found still unopened in his hand.

On the following day three suns appeared in the east; gradually they became one solar body, signifying that the rule of Marcus Lepidus, Marcus Antonius, and Augustus would become a monarchy. Or rather, that knowledge of the Triune God and of the One was soon to come to the whole world. An ox ploughing also spoke, saying: “Before long men will fail more completely than crops.”

## CHAPTER XVII. How Herod attached himself to Cassius

After this Cassius came to Syria, of which he had previously been governor. Raising an army against the young Augustus [Col. 1532B] and Marcus Antonius, he demanded seven hundred talents from the Jews. Herod was first to bring one hundred talents from Galilee and thus gained Cassius’s favour, while Cassius angrily resented the delay of the others. Herod also went with Cassius to battle; Cassius promised him the kingdom of Judaea if he gained the victory.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the avenging of Antipater’s murder by Herod

At that time a certain friend of Hyrcanus named Malichus aspired to the high priesthood. Having decided to attack Hyrcanus by poison, he first resolved to attack Antipater, forgetful of Antipater’s benefits. Antipater received the poison and died through a servant. Malichus, suspected [Col. 1532C] of the murder, repeatedly defended himself before Herod.

Herod complained by letter to Cassius of his father’s death and received a reply instructing him to avenge treachery with treachery. Cassius also wrote to the chiliarchs, ordering them to assist Herod in this affair. Herod therefore invited Hyrcanus and Malichus to dinner; as they went, Malichus was surrounded and killed by the chiliarchs. Hyrcanus collapsed in stupefaction and, scarcely recovering his breath, asked Herod who had killed Malichus. When someone replied, “By Cassius’s command,” he said: “Cassius has kept both me and my country safe, by killing the traitor to us both.”

Not long afterwards, while Herod was ill at Damascus, Phenix, Malichus’s brother, took up arms against Phasael in revenge for his brother, supported by Hyrcanus’s aid. Once he recovered, Herod attempted to attack Hyrcanus; but because of their kinship they returned to agreement.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Herod’s wives and children

Herod had a wife named Doris, but she was of humble birth; by her he had Antipater. He then married Mariamne, Hyrcanus’s granddaughter, and for love of her he circumcised himself and became a proselyte. Herod had nine wives, by seven of whom he had numerous offspring; but it is enough to name a few of them. His first-born was Antipater by Doris; Alexander and Aristobulus were by Mariamne; Archelaus was by Malthace the Samaritan; Herod [Col. 1533A] Antipas, later tetrarch, and Philip were by Cleopatra of Jerusalem. Some, however, think this Herod was Mariamne’s son.

## CHAPTER XX. When Herod and Phasael were made tetrarchs of Judaea by Antony, and concerning their battles, etc.

But when Cassius had been killed at Philippi, Caesar departed for Italy and Antony for Syria. The Jewish nobles accused Phasael and Herod before Antony of holding supreme power by force, while only the name remained to Hyrcanus. Herod, however, appeased Antony with gifts, reminding him of his father’s former friendship with him.

When he was again accused at Antioch by one hundred Jewish men, while Hyrcanus too stood present, Antony asked [Col. 1533B] Hyrcanus who was best fitted to administer affairs. When Hyrcanus preferred Herod and his brothers to the others, Antony rejoiced and promoted them from procurators to tetrarchs of Judaea.

When Antony departed for Rome, Pacorus, king of the Parthians, crossed the Euphrates with a strong force. Lysanias, Antigonus’s nephew, Ptolemy’s son by Alexandra, as stated above, came down to him and promised one thousand talents and five hundred virgins if he would restore Antigonus to the kingdom. Pacorus therefore gave Antigonus many thousands of Parthians. Antigonus was storming Jerusalem; Phasael was guarding part of the walls, while Herod guarded the royal palace. But when Antigonus entered the city during Pentecost, fighting occurred even in the forum.

While peace negotiations were in progress, Antigonus deceitfully requested Pacorus, king of the Parthians, as arbiter of peace. Hyrcanus and Phasael therefore went out, and Antigonus hastened to the Parthian king. Herod would not go down with them, since Mariamne advised him never to trust Parthian good faith. Hyrcanus and Phasael were seized by the Parthians on the journey. Hearing this, Herod fled by night to his fellow-tribesmen, the Idumaeans. He sent ahead his wives, children, and all his baggage, while he himself followed, holding back the attacks of those pursuing him. In flight he found the Jews more troublesome than the Parthians; he fought them sixty stadia from the city and there, because of an incredible victory, later constructed a most strongly fortified castle [Col. 1533D] which he called Herodium.

Having left his wives and children in the town of Masada under the protection of his brother Joseph, he went to Petra, the city of the Arabs. The Parthians not only restored Antigonus to the kingdom, but also handed Hyrcanus and Phasael over to him in chains to be beaten. Antigonus bit off Hyrcanus’s ears so that, if circumstances changed and he were released, he could not recover the high priesthood; for sacred rites must be performed by those who are physically whole.

But Phasael forestalled him by his courage. Since he had neither an iron weapon at hand nor free use of his hands, he dashed his head against a stone and died. On learning that Herod had escaped, he said that he was willing to die calmly, since he left his avenger alive. Some say of Hyrcanus that a physician sent to him by Antigonus poured poison into his ears [Col. 1534A] as though it were medicine, and that he died. Josephus, however, relates that he was sent to the Parthians and held in mockery for a long time.

## CHAPTER XXI. How Herod was made king of Judaea at Rome

On receiving news of his brother’s death, Herod hastened to Rome and was not held back even by winter’s severity. Near Pamphylia his ship was wrecked; after it was repaired at Rhodes, he proceeded to Rome and first explained to Antony the reason for his journey. Antony, astonished and moved by pity at his misfortune, persuaded the Senate to declare Herod king. Crowned, with Augustus and Antony standing on either side, Herod was led to the Capitol, where the Senate’s decree on the matter was deposited.

Herod was accordingly sent back to Judaea, with two commanders, Ventidius and Silo, to place him on the throne. When they came to Galilee, Antigonus bribed Silo, who consequently delayed engaging Antigonus under feigned pretexts. At last the Romans besieged Jerusalem, but because of winter severity and shortage of provisions they withdrew from the siege and wintered in Idumaea and Galilee. Herod nevertheless was not idle: pursuing a multitude of brigands, he suffocated them with fire even in caves.

Among them was an old man, father of seven sons, whom he himself killed in this fashion. Standing at the mouth of the cave, he called them one by one by name and slaughtered each son as he came out. Finally he threw down his wife, after stabbing her, and then himself [Col. 1534C] wounded, upon the dead bodies.

## CHAPTER XXII. How Herod, having expelled Antigonus, was placed upon the royal throne in Jerusalem

At that time Antony was staying near Athens and was already held by his love for Cleopatra. Herod was hurrying to him to complain of Silo’s treachery. Meanwhile Joseph, wishing to perform some notable deed, disregarded Herod’s command and fought Antigonus; he was defeated and beheaded by Pappus, Antigonus’s military commander. Antigonus inhumanely began to beat his headless body with spurs.

When Antony learned of Silo’s treachery, he sent Sosius with Herod in a strong force. Coming into Judaea, Sosius defeated Pappus, who met him, and sent Pappus’s head to Herod’s brother Pheroras as consolation for his slain [Col. 1534D] brother. At last, after Jerusalem had been besieged for five months, when the Romans stormed it in the sixth, they spared no age, though Herod begged them to spare the people.

Antigonus too came down and threw himself at Sosius’s feet. Sosius did not pity him, but mocked him by calling him “Antigona,” and threw him into chains. When the entire mass of soldiers was eager to see the sacred things and plunder the sanctuary, Herod restrained them, saying that victory would be more bitter to him than defeat if, through his fault, they saw what it was unlawful to see. He reproached Sosius, asking whether, after emptying the city of men and wealth, he would leave him king over a wilderness. He assured them that he would give each man a reward from his own resources.

When Sosius had fulfilled his promises, he returned to Antony, taking the defeated Antigonus with him and taking away a golden crown dedicated to God. Antony struck Antigonus with an axe. Herod was thereby confirmed in the kingdom of Judaea, in the fourth year after he had received the diadem at Rome. This is why sometimes more and sometimes fewer years are given for Herod’s reign. Thus the kingdom was transferred from Judah to a foreigner, with Christ’s coming imminent. Hearing that Herod reigned, Hyrcanus returned to Judaea and was restored to his former position, except that he did not perform priestly service.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Mariamne’s death through Salome’s treachery

A quarrel arose between Mariamne and Salome, Herod’s sister. Salome reproached Mariamne with being a courtesan; Mariamne reproached Salome with her low birth. At his sister’s counsel [Col. 1535B] Herod treacherously killed Hyrcanus because Hyrcanus said that the kingdom belonged to him.

To console Mariamne, Herod appointed her brother Jonathan, though he was ten years old, high priest. At Mariamne’s request he expelled Doris and her son Antipater from Jerusalem, allowing them to go up to Jerusalem for prayer only at the three annual festivals. Conversely, at Salome’s prompting Jonathan was killed because he seemed to aspire to the throne.

When Salome accused Mariamne of adultery, she added that Mariamne had explicitly sent her portrait to Antony in order to inflame him with love for her. To discover the truth, Herod hastened to Antony, placing Mariamne under the guard of Salome’s husband and giving him specific sealed instructions: if word should come to him, he was to kill Mariamne. While Herod delayed and learned from Antony that Mariamne had sent the portrait—because Antony so loved Herod that he concealed nothing from him—Salome’s husband revealed to Mariamne what he had been ordered to do.

On Herod’s return, Mariamne, as she slept in his embrace, tearfully told him what he had ordered concerning her death. Leaping from the bed, Herod asked his sister: “Did your husband sleep with Mariamne?” She replied: “He did.” Herod immediately had Mariamne and his sister’s husband killed. But he grieved so intensely at the death of the wife whom he loved beyond measure that, like a madman, he frequently lost his mind. Once recovered, he recalled Antipater with his mother [Col. 1535D] and sent the sons he had had by Mariamne, Alexander and Aristobulus, to Rome to be educated in the liberal arts.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How Augustus added Trachonitis and Ituraea to Herod’s kingdom

After this a battle was fought at Actium between Augustus and Antony. Herod did not take part, having been sent by Antony against the Arabian king at Cleopatra’s request, so that, whichever of them should be defeated, she herself might possess his kingdom. For even then she was plotting the deaths of the eastern kings in order to rule in their place. Although she tried to make Herod unacceptable to Antony and could not succeed, she had already brought under her own authority the territory of Jericho, rich in palms and balsam.

After Antony’s defeat, [Col. 1536A] when Augustus came to Rhodes, Augustus did not regard Antony as defeated while Herod remained alive. Meeting danger face to face, he stood before Caesar in private dress, having laid aside his royal attire, and said:

> “I acknowledge that I was useful and faithful to Antony, as you would have discovered at Actium had I been present. Yet I did not wholly fail him: I sent him aid and grain; nor would I now have failed him if, taking my advice, he had killed Cleopatra, the source of your hostility. Thus I was defeated together with the defeated man, and I laid aside my crown together with my fortune. But I have come to you, resting my hope of safety upon my loyalty.”

Caesar replied:

> “Indeed, be safe, and now reign with greater security. You have deserved to rule many, since you maintain friendship with such fidelity. Antony acted rightly in obeying Cleopatra rather than you. Through his madness we have gained you. I too shall endeavour to benefit you, so that you may not miss Antony.”

As Augustus hastened into Egypt, Herod’s strength was evident not only in battle but also in the desert: for the army going and returning he supplied necessities so fully that there was no lack of water or equipment, and Caesar marvelled. When Cleopatra and Antony were dead, the Romans cried that Herod’s kingdom was too small. Therefore Augustus restored the part of the kingdom which Cleopatra had taken away and added Trachonitis, Ituraea, and the whole coast as far as the Tower of Straton, which Herod later called Caesarea in honour of Augustus Caesar.

He built a royal residence at Ascalon, and thereafter was surnamed the Ascalonite.

> **[Note: Col. 1536C, Addition 1.]** Or, properly, he was called the Ascalonite. For his grandfather, also named Herod, was an Ascalonite by nation and keeper of Apollo’s temple. Idumaean brigands carried off his young son Antipater, who remained with them so long that he later became their leader. Hence he too was called an Idumaean.

For by nationality [Col. 1536C] he was an Idumaean on his father’s side and an Arab on his mother’s. Caesar gave him four hundred Galatian bodyguards, Cleopatra’s attendants, savage men eager for human blood.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Herodians
Those who had previously been called Eleutherians, from the River Eleutherus in Upper Galilee, above which they had originated, were thereafter called Herodians. Since he had previously built at Jerusalem the tower which he called Antonia, and which is now called the Tower of David, he now built another, which he called Agrippina. For he was loved by Caesar after Agrippa, and by Agrippa after Caesar. He also placed a golden eagle of immense weight over the beautiful gate of the Temple in honor of the Romans, a thing the Jews bore with indignation. He also built the Herodium, in which he too was buried. He built Phasaelis in memory of his brother. He restored Samaria, calling it Sebaste as well; there he dedicated a very great temple to Caesar. He also dedicated another temple to Caesar, of white marble, near the source of the Jordan.

> [Note: Col. 1537A, Addition 1. He also built Caesarea of Palestine, where the Tower of Straton stood; there, in anticipation of Augustus’ arrival, he constructed a portico of white marble. There Cornelius the centurion was afterwards made a bishop by Peter.]

In short, there was no place suitable for a kingdom which he would leave without honor to Caesar. In the fifteenth year of his reign he also magnificently adorned the Temple of the Lord; and not only in his own kingdom, but even in neighboring cities, he left memorials of his liberality, as it were works of his industry.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning Herod’s offense against his sons

After this his sons returned from their studies, and Alexander was a most forceful speaker. One of them, Aristobulus, married the daughter of his aunt Salome; the other married the daughter of the king of Cappadocia. They now argued rather freely with their father concerning succession to the kingdom. Offended by this, their father was eager to set Antipater above them. Indeed, in his will he had already openly been declared successor. Therefore the aforesaid brothers secretly discussed their father’s death. Their father, perceiving this, rejected them from his presence. They, however, sailed to Rome to bring their father’s wrong against them before Caesar.

The histories incidentally added to the foregoing books of biblical historiographers, drawn from writers of various times, here come to a happy conclusion.

# EVANGELICAL HISTORY

[Col. 1537]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the conception of the Forerunner of the Lord

“Now in the days of Herod king of Judaea—after thirty years of his reign had elapsed—there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, and his wife, descended from Aaron, was named Elizabeth” (Luke 1).

For David, wishing to enlarge the worship of the Lord, established twenty-four high priests, of whom only one was greater, and he was called the chief of the priests. He appointed sixteen men from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar; and by lot he assigned to each the week of his division. Abijah had the eighth week. Zechariah was of his family; and, while he was offering incense on the Day of Atonement, an angel foretold to him that a son would be born from his wife. Considering his wife’s barrenness and the old age of both, he did not believe, and therefore became mute until the day of the birth. The angel also disclosed to him the boy’s name and greatness, together with his abstinence.

“But Elizabeth conceived, and hid herself for five months.”

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the conception of the Savior

“But in the sixth month Gabriel was sent to Nazareth, to Mary, a virgin betrothed to Joseph” (Luke 1).

When, after greeting her, he had said that she would bear Jesus, the Son of the Most High, she asked how this would occur, since she had resolved in her mind not to know a man unless God should otherwise ordain it. The angel added that she would conceive not by a man, but by the working of the Holy Spirit; and he informed her that her kinswoman Elizabeth had also conceived. For the priestly tribe and the royal tribe had been intermingled. Aaron had a wife from Judah, Elizabeth, sister of Nahshon; and Jehoiada the high priest had Jochebed, daughter of King Joram. And Mary said: “Let it be done to me according to your word.”

And immediately Christ was conceived of the Virgin, complete man in soul and flesh, yet in such a way that the form of his body and limbs could not be distinguished by sight. He is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April [25 March], and, thirty-three years having passed, to have died on the same day.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the birth of the Forerunner

“Mary arose and went into the hill-country of Judah” (Luke 2).

Judah is the name of the kingdom, not of the tribe. Jerusalem was in the tribe of Benjamin; through it she perhaps passed to the town in which they say Zechariah then lived, four miles from Jerusalem, and where John was born. It is read in the Book of the Righteous that the blessed Virgin first lifted him from the ground.

“And when she had greeted Elizabeth, the child leaped in her womb.” When Elizabeth prophesied that she was the mother of her Lord and blessed, Mary uttered a song to the Lord, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord,” and so forth. Mary remained there three months, serving her kinswoman until she gave birth, and then returned to her own home.

On the eighth day, when the child was circumcised and they called him Zechariah after his father, she said: “His name is John.” His father wrote the same thing, taking a writing tablet. A *pugillaris* is a tablet which can be enclosed in the fist, like a writer’s pen. Then Zechariah’s mouth was opened, and, prophesying, he made a song to the Lord: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel.”

These two songs are not sung in the Church in the order in which they were composed. For the one composed second is sung first. Since Zechariah’s canticle reads, “And he has raised up a horn of salvation,” which was accomplished in the Resurrection, it is therefore sung at Lauds; and it speaks to the child who was the dawn of the Sun. And because the Virgin’s canticle reads, “He has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid”—namely, of the Church and of Mary herself—this was accomplished in the sixth age. It also treats there of the Incarnation: “He has received Israel his servant.” Therefore it is sung at Vespers, that is, at the sixth daytime office. Simeon’s third canticle, which follows, is sung at the seventh office, namely Compline, because he asks to be dismissed in peace, which occurs in the seventh age of those at rest. And because these two canticles are evangelical, we sing them standing.

“For the child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was in desert places until the day of his manifestation to Israel.”

When Mary returned to Nazareth, she was found by her betrothed to be pregnant by the Holy Spirit. Not wishing to take her publicly in marriage, he intended secretly to dismiss her. But in a dream he was instructed by an angel to take her in marriage; the angel declared that the child conceived was from the Holy Spirit, so that he should not suspect adultery, and commanded that he call him Jesus, because he would save the people from their sins. Thus Joseph knew that God was to be born, for God alone forgives sins; and, taking his betrothed as wife, he remained a virgin with the Virgin. The Virgin had a husband so that she should not be disgraced as pregnant, that she might enjoy a man’s comfort and service, and that God’s birth might be hidden from the devil.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the census of the world

“In those days an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled” (Luke 2).

Caesar, wishing to know the number of regions in the world subject to Roman rule, the number also of cities in each region, and the names of the persons in each city, commanded that people should converge from suburban towns, villages, and hamlets upon their own city; and that, wherever they lived, they should especially go to the city from which they derived their origin. Each was to give the governor of the province a silver denarius, worth ten ordinary coins—whence it was called a *denarius*—and thus declare himself subject to the Roman Empire. For the coin bore Caesar’s image and the inscription of his name. Since the number of those enrolled by head—or, as others read, those who paid the head-tax—was fixed at a definite total and entered in writing, this declaration was called a *descriptio*, an enrollment.

“This enrollment was first made by Quirinius, governor of Syria.” It is called first with respect to Quirinius, governor of Syria, because Judaea is said to lie at the navel of the inhabited zone; provision was therefore made that the enrollment should begin there, and that other governors should then continue it through the surrounding regions. Or perhaps it was the first universal enrollment, because other, local enrollments had preceded it. Or perhaps the first enrollment, of persons in a city, was performed by the governor; the second, of cities in a region, by Caesar’s legate; and the third, of regions, in the city of Rome before Caesar.

At this point Judaea was first made tributary to the Romans. This enrollment seems to have been made yearly, as is read in the Gospel: “Does not your master pay the tribute this year?” (Matt. 17).

“Joseph went up from Nazareth to Bethlehem, because he was of the house of David, to enroll with Mary his pregnant wife” (Luke 2). If women were enrolled, the sentence should be joined thus: “to enroll with Mary.” If men alone were enrolled, the order is: “Joseph went up with Mary.”

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the birth of the Savior

“And it came to pass, while they were there, that the Virgin bore her firstborn son” (Luke 2)—not one after whom another followed, but one before whom no one came—and, having wrapped him in swaddling clothes, she laid him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the lodging.

It is said that the hay on which Jesus lay was brought to Rome by Helena and is in the church of Saint Mary Major. Within the basilica, not far from the manger, Jerome rests. Paula and Eustochium also rest at Bethlehem. Because of the great number of people who had gathered for the same purpose, it was difficult for poor people to find empty houses. They took refuge in a common passage between two houses, covered over and called a *diversorium* (“lodging-place”), beneath which citizens would gather on days of leisure to converse or visit one another, or to escape inclement weather. Perhaps Joseph had made there a manger for the ox and ass which he had brought with him, and Jesus was placed in it.

Some refer to this the saying of Isaiah: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass the manger of its lord” (Isa. 1); and that of Habakkuk: “You shall be known in the midst of two animals.” This too is represented to us in paintings in churches, which are, as it were, books for the laity.

The Savior was born in the forty-second year of the reign of Caesar Augustus. For we count as part of Augustus’ reign the twelve years which extended from Julius’ death to the battle of Actium.

> [Note: Col. 1540C, Addition 1. At Rome the Temple of Peace collapsed; a fountain of oil burst forth; Caesar had commanded that no one should call him a god.]

He was born in the thirtieth year of Herod’s reign, when the whole world was at peace; in the third year of the one hundred and ninety-third Olympiad; and in the seven hundred and fifty-second year from the founding of the City. The Lord was born during the night preceding Sunday, for if you run backward through the table of computation, you will find for this year the fifth concurrent and the third January regular. Add these together and subtract seven; one remains. Thus you will find that the Kalends of January fell on Sunday. For on the day when he said, “Let there be light,” light was made (Gen. 1), “the Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1).

According to some, the seventh age began with Christ’s Nativity, according to the Apostle, who says, “When the fullness of time had come,” etc. According to others, it began on the day when he was baptized, because regenerative power was given to the waters. According to others, it began with the Passion, because then the gate was opened and, in a certain manner, the seventh rest of those at rest began. From Adam there had passed 5,196 years—according to others, 5,199; from Abraham, 2,012 years according to the Septuagint, but far fewer according to the Hebrews.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the song of the angels and the circumcision of the Lord

“And there were shepherds, two miles from Bethlehem, in the same region, keeping watches by night over their flock” (Luke 2).

It was an ancient custom at both solstices to keep night watches in veneration of the sun. Perhaps this custom had become established among the Jews also through the practice of those dwelling with them.

“And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside them,” announcing that the Savior had been born in Bethlehem and declaring as a sign the child placed in a manger. “And there was with the angel a multitude of angels, saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

> [Note: Col. 1541B, Addition 1. It is read in the Acts of the Pontiffs that Telesphorus added the following evangelical words.]

For through Christ the Father was glorified, and peace was made between God and humanity, between angel and humanity, and between Jew and Gentile. Because of this multitude of angels, or because of the flock of shepherds, some understand that place prophetically called “the tower of the flock”: “And you, misty tower of the flock” (Mic. 4). Yet the place had not only then acquired this name, because Jacob had fed the flock there when Rachel was giving birth.

“The shepherds, passing on as far as Bethlehem, found the thing which had been told to them; and those who heard wondered at the things said to them by the shepherds. Mary also kept all these words, pondering them in her heart, she from whom Jesus was born, who was thought to be Joseph’s son” (Luke 3).

For Christ’s generation was thus: the first formation of humanity was from earth; the second, from the side of a man; the third, from man and woman; and the fourth was that a human being should be born of a woman without a man. Hence Christ was called “Son of Man” by a fitting circumlocution instead of his name. The first and second generation fell; in the third we are generated from the fall; in the fourth we are raised from the fall.

On the eighth day they circumcised the child.

> [Note: Col. 1541B, Addition 2. It is said that the Lord’s foreskin was brought by an angel to Charlemagne at the church of the Lord, and was transported by him to Aachen; later it was placed by Charles the Bald in the church of the Savior at Charroux. Others say it was brought to Antwerp, for there it is held in the highest veneration.]

And they declared his name Jesus, the name given him by the angel before he was conceived (Luke 2).

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the star and the Magi

[Col. 1541C] “But on the thirteenth day, behold, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him’” (Matt. 2).

These men were successors to Balaam’s teaching; they knew of his star through Balaam’s prophecy, and were called *magi* from the greatness of their knowledge. Those whom the Greeks call philosophers, the Persians call Magi. They came from the territories of the Persians and Chaldeans, where there is the river Saba, from which the Sabaean region also takes its name. Some, however, think that they were not Magi learned from the beginning, but became so after they had defeated Herod’s deceit by returning by another route.

Chrysostom says that the star appeared to them a long time before Christ’s birth, and that they therefore came from afar over a long period. Yet it could have happened that, riding dromedaries, they crossed long distances in thirteen days.

“When King Herod heard the Magi, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.” The king feared that someone born from the line of Hyrcanus or Aristobulus would reign, and that he, as a foreigner, would be cast aside. The city, meanwhile, was disturbed, struck by the novelty of the miracle. Having carefully learned from the Magi the rising of the star, so that by it he might know the child’s birthday, the king also asked the priests and scribes where Christ was to be born. They said, according to Micah, that he would be born in Bethlehem Ephrathah (Mic. 5).

Bethlehem was first called Ephrathah after Caleb’s wife, who was buried there; some suppose that she was a daughter of Ur and of Miriam, Moses’ sister. Later, after the famous famine because of which Elimelech went with his household to the Moabites (Ruth 1), when incredible abundance had been restored there, it was called Bethlehem, meaning “house of bread.”

The king told the Magi to report the child to him when they found him, so that he too might come and worship him. For he had already directed his mind toward destroying the child. When they left Jerusalem, the star went before them until it came and stood above the house where the child was.

Fulgentius says that the star was then created, remarkable and distinct from the others: distinct in brightness, because daylight did not obscure it; in location, because it was neither in the firmament with the lesser stars nor in the ether with the planets, but moved through the air along paths near the earth; and in movement, because, first motionless over Judaea, it gave the Magi the sign to come into Judaea. They had, by their own deliberation, gone to Jerusalem as the capital of Judaea. After they left it, the star then first went before them in visible motion; when it had fulfilled its task, it immediately ceased to exist, returning to the underlying matter from which it had been taken.

Some nevertheless report that Bede maintained that it fell into the well of Bethlehem, and that later, in the days of Paula and Eustochium, certain virgins consecrated to God miraculously saw it. Since the brothers with whom he lived the monastic life considered this fabulous, they at one time separated him from their communion.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the offering and names of the Magi

When the Magi entered the house, which Luke calls a *diversorium* (“lodging-place”) (Luke 2), they each offered the child gold, frankincense, and myrrh, according to the customary Sabaean offering (Matt. 2), thereby signifying that he was king, God, and mortal.

These are the names of the three Magi: in Hebrew, Appellus, Amerus, Damasius; in Greek, Galgalat, Magalath, Sarachim; in Latin, Baltassar, Gaspar, Melchior. When they deliberated about returning, they received an answer in a dream not to return to Herod. Going to Tarsus of Cilicia, they hired a ship and returned to their own region.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the Lord’s Hypapante

“And when the days of Mary’s purification had been fulfilled, they brought the child to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord”—that is, to present him by offering him—“and they gave sacrifices for him, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons”; moreover, they redeemed him with five silver shekels (Luke 2).

“And there was in Jerusalem an old man, Simeon, who had received from the Holy Spirit that he should not see death until he had first seen the Lord’s Christ.” Then, by that same Spirit, he came into the Temple; taking the child in his arms and knowing him to be the Christ, he said: “Now you dismiss, Lord,” etc. Prophesying of Christ’s Passion, he said to Mary: “And a sword shall pierce your own soul also,” that is, his Passion. For she could not see her Son crucified without a mother’s grief, even if she hoped that he would rise again. Or the sense is this: the sword will pierce his soul, which is also yours, since you love it as your own.

“At that same hour Anna the prophetess came up and spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Israel.”

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the Lord’s flight into Egypt

[Col. 1543A]

Then Herod saw that he had been mocked by the Magi (Matt. 2). Since the Magi reported nothing to him, Herod thought that they had been deceived by the vision of the star and had been ashamed to return to him; therefore he ceased searching for the child. But when he heard what had been said by the shepherds, and especially the prophecies of Simeon and Anna, he perceived that he had been mocked and began to plan the slaughter of the people of Bethlehem, so that the one whom he did not know might be killed among them.

Therefore, warned by an angel, Joseph fled into Egypt with the child and his mother until Herod’s death. When the Lord entered Egypt, Egypt’s idols fell, according to Isaiah, who says: “The Lord shall ascend upon a swift cloud and enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved” (Isa. 19). They also relate that, just as at the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt there was no Egyptian house in which, by God’s providence, a dead firstborn did not lie (Exod. 2), so now there was no temple in Egypt in which an idol did not fall.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the slaughter of the children, and why it was delayed for a year

> [Note: Col. 1543D. From Josephus.]

When Herod was planning the slaughter of the children, he was summoned by a letter from Caesar Augustus to go to Rome and answer the accusation of his sons. Josephus, however, says that he took his son Alexander with him to Rome and charged him before Caesar with preparing poison for him. As he traveled through Cilicia, hearing that the ships of the Tarsians had transported the Magi, in a violent wind he burned the ships of Tarshish, according to David’s prophecy in the forty-seventh Psalm: “With a violent wind you shall shatter the ships of Tarshish.”

When father and sons had argued before Caesar, reconciliation was achieved on this condition: the young men were to obey their father in all things, but he was to leave the kingdom to whomever he wished. Yet Herod was not freed from his suspicions. Coming to Jerusalem, he summoned the people; with his three sons standing by, he described the reconciliation of the brothers achieved by Caesar and declared himself appointed judge of his successor, lest the Jews think the kingdom would return to their own people.

Then Herod, more securely established in the kingdom than before, “sent and killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its territory, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had carefully learned from the Magi” (Matt. 2). The greater part of them was buried three miles south of Bethlehem.

This is the opinion of the majority and the more common view. Herod had learned that the star arose on the very day on which the Lord was born, and from the star’s rising he knew that the Lord was about one year old and some days more. Therefore, above his age, he raged against boys up to two years old, and below it, down to infants of one night. He feared the child’s *morphoseon*, that is, transformation: lest the child whom the stars served should transform himself beyond his own age or beneath his own appearance.

Chrysostom, however, says that the star appeared a year before the Lord’s birth. Herod believed that the Lord had also then been born, and thus thought that the Lord was two years old with the addition of a few days. He therefore killed boys two years old and thereafter up to five years old, but none younger than two. He explains “from two years old and under” according to numerical reckoning. For just as, in respect of time, those younger than two are lower than them because they were born afterward, so, in respect of number, those older than two are lower than them because they are counted after them. This assertion seems supported by the fact that some bones of the Innocents are so large that they could not have belonged to two-year-olds. Yet it may be said in reply that people then were of far greater bodily size than they are now.

## CHAPTER XII. That Jeremiah’s threat was also prophecy

[Col. 1544B]

“Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremiah” (Jer. 31): “A voice was heard in Ramah,” etc. (Matt. 2).

Ramah is a place near Gibeah, twelve miles from Bethlehem, where, when the tribe of Benjamin had almost been annihilated on account of the Levite’s wife, the few survivors mourned their dead. Jeremiah seems, however, to have introduced this rather as a threat than as a prophecy. He threatened that a ruin as great as that which had occurred among Rachel’s sons was impending over the two tribes, when the voice of mourners was heard at Ramah.

Nevertheless, as Matthew says, he also prophesied the slaughter of the little children; and then Ramah is not the name of a place. Since *Ramah* means “high,” it is as though he had said: “A voice was heard on high.” It also seems that Leah ought to have been said to be weeping for her children, since the Bethlehemites were of the tribe of Judah. But because Benjamin borders Judah, the Evangelist indicates that many Benjaminites were killed because of their proximity, to heighten the enormity of Herod’s crime. Or because Rachel was buried near Bethlehem, by the manner of prophetic speech she is said to have done what was done in that same place.

“And she would not be comforted, because they are not”: that is, she grieved inconsolably because they are not, that is, because they desire to be dead. The Innocents are indeed called martyrs in an extended sense, not because they were witnesses of Christ, but because they were killed for Christ, whom they confessed not by speaking, yet by dying. For them the Church also keeps a feast, although they descended to the underworld. Hence, at their feast, songs of joy are omitted: namely, *Te Deum laudamus* (“We praise you, O God”) and *Gloria in excelsis Deo* (“Glory to God in the highest”); and instead of *Alleluia*, some say *Laus tibi, Christe* (“Praise to you, Christ”), others *Cantemus, eia* (“Let us sing, hey!”), while others say the tract.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the killing of Herod’s two sons

> [Note: Col. 1544D. From Josephus.]

It came about that, because Herod had deprived many people of their sons, he himself was more miserably deprived of his own. For through Antipater’s cunning Alexander and Aristobulus again became suspect to their father. Herod therefore wrote to Augustus, accusing his sons on many counts. Augustus sent Saturninus and Paeanus as legates with a rescript, directing him to judge his sons before them both after summoning a council of nobles, and to do with them whatever he wished if he could convict them.

After hearing the arguments on both sides, they declared those legates to be condemned, though not to death. Then their father put them in chains at Sebaste. Their father also had their accomplices tortured, so that by their confession he might learn more surely whether his sons were plotting against his life. One man confessed that Alexander had promised him much if he would administer poison to his father. A barber also confessed to promised rewards if, while trimming his father’s beard, he would cut his throat. He added that Alexander had said that no hope should be placed in an old man who dyed his gray hair to appear young.

Moved by these things, Herod sent executioners and ordered his sons killed and carried away to Alexandria, there to be buried with their maternal grandfather Alexander.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Herod’s earlier will, his hatred, and Antipater

> [Note: Col. 1545D. From the same source.]

Then Herod drew up a will and appointed Antipater as future king, substituting Herod, surnamed Antipas, in Antipater’s place. But Antipater incurred the people’s unbearable hatred, since everyone knew that he had amassed slanders against his brothers. For this reason even his father no longer regarded him favorably.

Antipater was also angry with his father because he had substituted his brother for him, since he had not wished the kingdom to pass to Antipater’s own sons. Another and greater cause of Antipater’s hostility toward his father arose. The father cherished with paternal affection the orphaned children of the sons whom he had killed, joining them in marriage to his other grandchildren.

According to Josephus, the young children left by Aristobulus were Herod Agrippa, who killed James with the sword, and Herodias, whom Herod Antipas later took from his brother Philip. Antipater therefore feared that Herod might someday restore the kingdom to the orphaned children of his brothers, because they were connected with him on their mother’s side.

He also stirred Pheroras to hatred of Herod, so that Pheroras withdrew from his brother and lived in the land granted him beyond the Jordan. Antipater himself, with his father’s approval, hurried to Rome under certain contrived pretexts. He procured a most potent poison from an Arabian sorceress and stored it with Pheroras’ wife, so that, while he was away, it might be administered to his father by a servant whom he had hired.

## CHAPTER XV. That Herod imprisoned Antipater for plotting against his life

> [Note: Col. 1545D. From the same source.]

While Antipater was in Rome, Pheroras died. Through a maidservant who had angrily left her mistress, Herod learned of the poison stored with Pheroras’ wife. He summoned his brother’s widow and ordered her to bring the poison. As though going to bring it, she went out and threw herself from the roof; but she was brought to the king half alive and said:

> “When your brother, my husband, was dying, he said to me: ‘Bring here, woman, the poison which Antipater left with us, and burn it up before my eyes, lest I carry to the underworld the avenging consciousness of fratricide.’ I burned most of it in the fire, but kept a little for myself because of uncertain contingencies and because I feared you.”

When she had produced the box containing the poison, she died. Having received many further proofs that Antipater was proceeding against his father’s life, Herod promptly recalled him and repudiated his mother. Having publicly accused his son of parricide in the presence of Varus, governor of Syria, who had come to Jerusalem in those days, he placed him in custody at Jericho.
