## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the severity of Herod’s illness

[Col. 1546B]

> [Note: Col. 1546D. From Josephus.]

While the father sought out his son’s accomplices in order to destroy them along with his son by elaborate tortures, he was impeded by a more severe illness. Old age was added to it, for he was already seventy years old, and the disasters involving his sons grievously afflicted his mind.

There were in Jerusalem two sophists, followed by no few young men, who expounded the laws. They judged that, as the king wasted away, it was an opportune time to tear down the golden eagle which the king had placed over the great gate of the Temple contrary to ancestral laws. When it had been torn down, the king, roused, overcame his illness by strength of spirit and appeared before the assembly, endeavoring to press this outrage upon all the people of Jerusalem. But at the people’s entreaties he took vengeance only upon the instigators. Thus he burned alive, together with the two sophists, those who had been lowered on ropes and cut down the eagle.

Afterward he was afflicted by diverse illnesses. He had a considerable fever; an unbearable itching over the whole surface of his body; continual torments of his neck; feet swollen by dropsy; putrefaction of the testicles producing worms; frequent shortness of breath and broken panting—all of which everyone attributed to God’s vengeance. He crossed the Jordan and used hot waters at Callirrhoe. When the physicians judged that his body ought to be warmed with hotter oil, he was lowered into a full bath, and was so weakened that, as though dead, even his eyes rolled and became distorted; nevertheless, at the cries of those standing by, he seemed to look around.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the killing of Jewish nobles at Herod’s death, and Antipater’s death

[Col. 1546D]

> [Note: Col. 1546D. From the same source.]

When he had returned to Jericho and heard that the Jews were joyfully awaiting his death, he ordered the noblest young men gathered from all Judaea to be confined in the hippodrome, that is, the circus prison. He commanded his sister Salome that, when he breathed his last, she should immediately kill them, so that all Judaea might mourn at his death even against its will.

The messengers whom he had sent to Rome returned carrying a letter from Caesar, permitting him to send Antipater into exile or, if he preferred, condemn him to death. Slightly revived by this news, he asked for an apple, which he liked to eat, and then requested a knife for cutting it. Immediately, while he was strained by a violent cough, he looked around to make sure that no bystander would hinder him and raised his right hand to strike himself. But Acciabus, his cousin, restrained his hand. At once the king cried out, and a disturbance arose in the royal house.

When Antipater heard this, rejoicing, he promised the guards much if they would release him. When Herod learned this, he took his son’s rejoicing more grievously than death itself, and immediately sent guards to kill him; he ordered him buried at Hyrcania. Then, at once changing his will, he named Archelaus successor to the kingdom, provided that he should receive the diadem from Augustus.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning Herod’s death and the appointment of Archelaus

> [Note: Col. 1547D. From Josephus.]

Five days after his son’s death, Herod died, in the thirty-seventh year after he had been declared king by the Romans. In other matters he was most fortunate; in domestic affairs most unfortunate. Salome released those whom he had ordered killed. Archelaus buried him at the Herodium, according to his command, omitting no royal splendor from the funeral procession.

After spending seven days mourning his father and lavishly providing funeral feasts for the people—a Jewish custom which impoverished many through funeral expenses—he put on white clothing and went up to the Temple. He was received with varied expressions of popular favor; sitting on the tribunal, he said that he wished even to refrain from the title of king until the succession had been confirmed by Caesar, promising that he would prove better than his father to all. Therefore some cried out for taxes to be reduced, others for customs duties to be abolished, and some for prisoners to be released. Archelaus assented to the requests; after sacrifices had been offered, he was feasting with his friends.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the brothers’ dispute for the kingdom before Augustus
[Note: [Col. 1547D] From the same author.] A disturbance then arose, such as commonly occurs amid political change. For very many mourned the sophists who had been put to death in defence of the Law; and nearly all demanded that the high priest whom Herod had appointed for money be removed. When the day of Unleavened Bread was at hand, the crowd prevented the high priest from performing the sacrifice. Archelaus first attempted to quiet them by words, sending a chiliarch. But when they sent the chiliarch back wounded, Archelaus dispatched a large force of guards and killed about nine thousand; and, warning all by the voice of a herald to return to their homes, he caused everyone to depart, the festival being abandoned. He himself set out for Rome with Nicolaus and Ptolemy, his father's secretaries, and took Salome and her sons with him, so that they might attest his father's final wishes together with the testament, leaving his brother Philip as administrator of the kingdom. Herod Antipas also went to Rome to contend with his brother concerning possession of the kingdom, placing great confidence in the rhetorician Hyrenaeus because of his sharpness in speaking. Caesar likewise, having summoned the leading Romans, gave both parties an opportunity to argue their cases. There too, for the first time, he ordered Gaius, son of Agrippa and [Col. 1548A] his daughter, to sit as his adopted son. Archelaus maintained that the kingdom was owed him both by the claim of age and by the intention of the second testament. Antipas, however, said that the first testament ought to be observed, since his father had written it while in his right mind. The second, he asserted, was invalid, because his father had made it while mentally unsound. For at that time he had even attacked himself with his own hand. He added also that Archelaus had brought Caesar only the shadow of kingship, while he had seized for himself the substance of government; finally, that he had stained the beginning of his authority with the blood of nine thousand slain. Caesar deferred his answer and considered with his advisers, on the basis of what had been learned, whether a single successor to the kingdom ought to be appointed or authority divided among the whole family—especially since he had received various letters [Col. 1548B] from Syria reporting that the Jews had revolted. Meanwhile, the death of Archelaus's mother was also announced.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning four kings in Judaea

[Note: [Col. 1548D] From the same author.] At that very time four kings arose in Judaea. In Idumaea, two thousand veterans who had served under Herod made a king. In Sepphoris of Galilee, Judas, son of Hezekiah, a leader of brigands formerly captured by Herod, placed a diadem upon himself. Beyond the river, too, a certain Simon, one of the royal slaves, relying on his great physical size, was made king by brigands. Shepherds also set up as their king a man of lofty stature, who was a shepherd in the borders of Israel. Philip was sent to Rome by Varus to report these matters to Caesar, but incidentally for two reasons: both to aid Archelaus and, if it should please Caesar for Herod's kingdom to be apportioned among his grandsons, to obtain some share for himself. Fifty distinguished Jews went with him, and drew with them before Caesar eight thousand Jews then living at Rome. For before the final captivity, the Jews had been dispersed and sold everywhere through particular captivities. In order to hear them, Caesar sat with his friends in the palace of Apollo's temple. They set forth the tyranny of Herod and his sons against the Jews and petitioned the Romans to judge the remnants of Judaea worthy of mercy, and either to restore to them their ancient right of kingship, or to join them to the territory of Syria, or to have Judaea administered by Roman judges.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the pretended Alexander

[Col. 1548D] [Note: [Col. 1548D] From the same author.] At that time also, a certain Jew, raised in the towns of the Sidonians, who was remarkably like Alexander, Herod's son—whom his own father had killed—came into Judaea at the instigation of one of Herod's freedmen, who knew all the royal affairs very well. He claimed that the kingdom was owed to him, both because he was Herod's elder son and because he was connected through his mother Mariamne's family. Since many Jews followed him, he also departed for Rome. The Jews then living in Rome crowded around him, eager to see him. When asked how he had survived, he said that the executioners, moved to pity for the brothers, had subjected others resembling them to death. He said that his brother Aristobulus was still alive and concealed [Col. 1549A] in Cyprus or Crete. But Caesar knew Alexander's face very well, having loved him while he was a boy studying at Rome, and having observed him more closely when he afterward disputed with his father. He detected the fraud based on resemblance and sent for Celadus, who also knew Alexander well, to bring the living man before him, promising him his life if he revealed the author of so great a fraud. When the man confessed that he had feigned these things for profit, Caesar laughed, ordered his instigator put to death, and enrolled the false Alexander among the rowers because of his bodily build. This Alexander the poet called the handsome Alexis, that is, “the master's darling” (*Virgil*, *Eclogue* 21).

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the division of the kingdom

[Note: [Col. 1549D] From Josephus.] At length, by the Senate's counsel, Caesar divided Herod's monarchy. He gave one half—namely Judaea and Idumaea—to Archelaus under the title of tetrarch, promising to make him king if he showed himself worthy. He divided the other half into two tetrarchies: the region beyond the river and Galilee fell to the share of Herod the tetrarch; Ituraea, Trachonitis, and Auranitis were assigned to Philip. Archelaus therefore became, as it were, a ruler of two parts, but was never a monarch. Thus, when you read that he was monarch for nine years after his father, understand this according to the common popular opinion and according to his own boast, by which he claimed that he would become king under Caesar's promise. Thus the three brothers were sent back to Judaea after they had sat at Rome [Col. 1549C] for four months awaiting the outcome.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning Jesus' return from Egypt and the death of Glaphyra

Archelaus raged more cruelly than his father, not only against his accusers but even against those subject to him. In the first year of his reign, the angel told Joseph to return with the mother and the child to the land of Israel. Returning from Egypt after seven years, Joseph, hearing that Archelaus was reigning in Judaea in his father's place, did not wish to go there. Warned by an angel, he went into Galilee and lived at Nazareth (Matt. 2). In this place you will find, in the commentary on Matthew, both Archelaus as monarch of the whole kingdom after his father and Herod reigning in Galilee. Now concerning the Saviour's childhood and deeds up to his baptism, the Gospel records nothing except what Luke says: that, at twelve years old, he remained in Jerusalem and, after three days, was found by his parents in the midst of the teachers, listening to and questioning them (Luke 2).

[Note: [Col. 1549D] From Josephus.] Indeed Archelaus, in insult to his own family, repudiated Mariamne, daughter of his brother, whom his father had given him as wife. He married Glaphyra, daughter of the king of Cappadocia, formerly the wife of his brother Alexander; after Alexander's death she had married Juba, king of Libya, and after Juba's death was then living in widowhood with her father. When she returned to Judaea as Archelaus's wife, she dreamed that Alexander stood beside her and said: “Your Libyan marriage had been enough for you; but you have returned again [Note: [Col. 1550A] Addition 1. It is said that there is a small spring there, from which the boy Jesus drew water and served his mother while he was subject to her.] [Col. 1550A] to my household and have shamelessly joined yourself to my brother. Therefore, though unwilling, you shall be mine again.” After relating this dream, she scarcely survived two days.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning Archelaus's exile

At length, after frequent accusations, Archelaus was summoned by Caesar. On the fifth day before he was called, he had dreamed that full and very large ears of grain were being eaten by oxen. When he consulted the magicians whom he had summoned, Simon, an Essaean by origin, interpreted the ears as years and the oxen as changes of circumstances, because oxen turn and alter fields by ploughing them. He therefore said that Archelaus would reign nine years, experience various reversals of fortune, [Col. 1550B] and die. In the ninth year of his rule, however, he came to Rome, was condemned by Caesar, and was driven into exile at Vienne, a city of Gaul.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the first procurator of Judaea

[Note: [Col. 1549D] From the same author.] After the territory of Archelaus had been reduced to a province, Coponius was sent there by Caesar as procurator; he had formerly been Cyrenius's colleague. When Coponius was sent into Judaea as assessor of property, many Jews, and especially a certain Galilean Simon, rebuked the people for accepting mortal masters after God and paying tribute to the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 1550C] Addition 1. A *province* is properly called a land inhabited by those born and reared there. A *colony* is a land inhabited by outsiders, as happened in Samaria.]

While Coponius was governing Judaea on the day of Unleavened Bread, when it was customary for the Temple gates to be opened at midnight, certain Samaritans secretly came to Jerusalem and scattered the bones of dead persons throughout all the porticoes and the whole sanctuary [Col. 1550C]. From then on, stricter guard of the Temple began to be kept, and its gates were not opened before daylight.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the death of Augustus

[Note: [Col. 1550D] From the same author.] At that time Philip, rebuilding Sepphoris, named it Julia in honour of Julia, Caesar's wife; he also called Paneas Caesarea Philippi. When Coponius returned to Rome, Marcus succeeded him; under Marcus Salome, Herod's sister, died. Annius Rufus succeeded him, and under Rufus Augustus died, having reigned fifty-seven years, six months, and ten days; for fourteen, or twelve, of these years Antony had reigned with him. Since the Lord was born in the forty-second year of his reign and was thirty years old in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, Caesar died when the Lord was in his fifteenth year. Some, however, give only fifty-six years for his reign. Others give fifty-eight, reckoning the half-year and the days following it as a full year. He died in the seventy-seventh year of his life at Nola, a city of Campania, boasting that he left a city of marble where he had found one of brick; and he was buried in the Campus Martius [Col. 1551A].

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the emperor Tiberius and Valerius, procurator of Judaea

[Note: [Col. 1551D] From the histories and Josephus.] He was succeeded by the third emperor, Tiberius Nero, son of his wife Julia. He sent Valerius Graccus as procurator into Judaea. Thinking piety a source of profit, Valerius publicly sold the high-priesthood. Having removed Annas, he appointed Ishmael high priest. Not long afterward he expelled him and substituted Eleazar, son of Annas, who held the office for a year. Removing him also, he installed Simon; and after a year he appointed Joseph, also called Caiaphas. After eleven years, however, he left Judaea and returned to Rome. His successor, sent by Tiberius, was Pontius Pilate, [Col. 1551B] under whom Herod built Tiberias in honour of Tiberius.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the Jews' hatred of Pontius Pilate

[Note: [Col. 1552D] From the same sources.] In these times Tiberius summoned many kings to himself and did not send them back. Among them, retaining Archelaus of Cappadocia, he made his kingdom into a province and named Mazaca, the capital of the kingdom, Caesarea. Pilate, coming to Jerusalem and bringing with him images of Caesar which were attached to the military standards, set them up in the city without the Jews' knowledge, and returned to Caesarea. When a great many people from Jerusalem came down to him, begging that the standards be removed—for, because of the Jewish Law, the earlier procurators of Judaea customarily entered the city without standards—Pilate sat on the tribunal and, placing armed soldiers around them, threatened them with death unless they kept quiet. But they chose death rather than profane the ancestral laws. Pilate, admiring the Jews' constancy in their legal institutions, ordered the images removed.

Pilate came again to Jerusalem and, seeing that the city suffered from lack of water, opened the Temple treasuries and began to build an aqueduct from resources dedicated to the Temple, taking its source from a stream two thousand stadia away. The Jews cried out that the work should cease. For this Pilate killed many Jews and wounded most of them. The work was interrupted because the Jews sent Tiberius an embassy accusing Pilate [Col. 1551D].

## CHAPTER XXIX. Josephus's testimony concerning Christ

At this point Josephus gives the following commendation of the Lord Jesus:

> “Now there was at that time Jesus, a wise man—if indeed it is lawful to call him a man. For he was a worker of wonderful deeds and a teacher of those who gladly hear things to come; and he attached to himself many Jews, and also many from among the Gentiles. He was the Christ. When Pilate, upon the accusation of the leading men of our nation, had decreed that he should be crucified, those who had loved him from the beginning did not abandon him. For he appeared to them alive again, as the divinely inspired prophets had foretold that these and other things concerning him would come to pass. And to this day both the name and the race of Christians, who are so called from him, endure.” [Col. 1552A]

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning John's baptism and the beginning of the sixth age

“In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar,” under Valerianus and Asiaticus as consuls, “while Pontius Pilate was procurator of Judaea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, Philip his brother tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zacharias, in the wilderness” (Luke 3), so that by baptizing and preaching he might announce the consolation of redemption: “And he came into all [Col. 1552B] the region of the Jordan, baptizing with a baptism of repentance,” because he urged those to be baptized to repentance and baptized only those whom he saw to be repentant, preaching the baptism to come for the remission of sins, for the accustoming to which he also baptized. For he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3).

Up to this fifteenth year of Tiberius, five thousand two hundred and twenty-five years are reckoned from Adam according to the Septuagint; according to Hebrew truth, four thousand. In the sixteenth year of Tiberius was the eighty-first Jubilee year. Some say that in the same year the sixth millennium began. Their reasoning is that, as circumcision ended in this year and baptism began, so the sixth age begins and the fifth is ended. Some place its beginning at the Lord's Incarnation, reasoning that just as in the fifth age general dating was made by saying “in such-and-such a year from the first Olympiad,” so in the sixth one says “in such-and-such a year from the Lord's Incarnation.” Others maintain that it began with the Lord's passion, saying that the sixth age and the seventh, of those at rest, began together. In the chronicle, however, it is read as beginning from Tiberius's reign.

John wore a garment of camel hair and a leather belt, ate a certain edible kind of locust, and wild honey. “Then all Judaea went out to him and were baptized in the Jordan. But seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees coming for baptism, he said to them: [Col. 1552D] ‘Brood of vipers, who will show you how to flee from the wrath to come? Produce worthy fruits of repentance, and do not say, “We have Abraham for our father,” for the Lord is able from these stones,’” that is, from the Gentiles signified by these stones, “‘to raise up children for Abraham.’” John pointed with his finger to the twelve stones which the twelve leaders of the tribes of Israel took from the middle of the Jordan onto dry ground, and the equal number from dry ground into the Jordan; their heap was to be a testimony that they crossed the Jordan dry-shod (Josh. 4).

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the three sects of the Jews

There were then in Judaea three sects of Jews, differing from the common life and opinion of the rest: Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essaeans.

The Pharisees practised an austere devotion and a very sparing diet. They established their own traditions, by which they defined the traditions of Moses. They wore little sheets of parchment on their foreheads and bound about their left arms, on which the Decalogue was written, because the Lord had said: “You shall have this as something hung before your eyes and upon your hand” (Exod. 3). These were called *phylacteries*, from Greek *phylassein*, “to guard,” and *thorath*, meaning “law.” They also wore larger fringes than others and attached thorns to them, so that, pricked while walking, they might remember God's commandments. They attributed all things to God and to Marmenes, that is, fate. They said that doing what was commanded, or neglecting it, lay largely in human choice, yet that Marmenes aided in each individual matter; they thought that this too arose from the movements of the heavenly bodies. They never answered their superiors and elders in contradiction, saying that God's judgment was to come. They held every soul to be incorruptible, that only the souls of the good pass into other bodies until the resurrection and judgment, but that those of the wicked are shut up in eternal prisons. Because they were separated from the common appearance of humankind, they were called Pharisees.

The Sadducees deny Marmenes, saying that God is inspector of all things and that it lies in human choice whether people do good or evil. In general they denied either punishments or rewards for souls. They also denied that there would be a resurrection of the dead, holding that souls die with bodies, and they said that angels do not exist. [Col. 1553C] They accepted only the five books of Moses and were content with these. They were exceedingly severe, and were not even sociable among themselves. Because of this severity they called themselves Sadducees, that is, “the just.”

The Essaeans in nearly all respects lived a monastic life, despising marriage—not because they thought marriage and the succession of humankind should be abolished, but because they held women's intemperance should be guarded against, believing that none of them kept faith with a husband. They held all things in common; they considered oil disgraceful and regarded uncleanliness as an ornament, provided that they were always clothed in white. They had no fixed city, but had dwellings in various places. Before sunrise they spoke of nothing profane; they prayed to the sun at its rising; then they worked until the fifth hour. Having washed their bodies with water, they ate together and in silence. They regarded an oath as equivalent to perjury. They admitted no one to their sect except after a year's probation. After being received among them, a man had his character tested for two further years. Those caught in sins they expelled from their company, so that, plucking herbs like cattle, they might repent until death. For when ten sat together, no one spoke against the will of the other nine; they avoided spitting into the middle or toward their own right side. They observed the Sabbath so strictly that they did not even relieve themselves on that day. They carried a wooden digging-tool, with which they dug the earth in a most secluded place to relieve themselves, carefully covering themselves with their lowered garment so that they might not insult the daylight [variant: “divine” splendour]; for this reason they immediately filled in the hole again. They lived to a very great age because of the simplicity of their diet; they judged death for justice's sake better than immortality. They held that all souls were created at the beginning and were embodied according to the times. They assigned good souls, once stripped of their bodies, a dwelling beyond Ocean, where enjoyment is laid up for them toward the East; for the evil they assigned stormy and wintry places. There were among them some who foretold the future. Some used wives, but moderately; for if people considered abstinence necessary, or were constrained to abstain from marriage, the human race would fail.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That John confessed that he was not Christ

While John was baptizing, “they sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him to ask him: ‘Who are you?’” (John 1). He confessed that he was [Col. 1554B] neither the Christ, as public opinion supposed, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet. And they said: “Why then do you baptize?” They had asked about Elijah and, under the name of “the Prophet,” about Elisha, because in these two the figure of baptism had previously appeared; and they had read concerning Christ's baptism in Ezekiel's prophecy: “I shall pour clean water upon you” (Ezek. 36). Therefore they thought baptism belonged to no one else. He answered: “I indeed baptize in water, but one stands in the midst of you whom you do not know; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire”—in the Spirit in baptism, in fire in repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1554B] Addition 1. John's baptism can be figured in the washing of heads before baptism. On the Saturday before Palm Sunday, children's heads were anointed with oil and washed, so that no stain might remain there; thus in baptism all sins are wiped away, and this was done as a sign.]

“These things occurred in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning Jesus baptized

[Col. 1554C]

“Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him [Note: [Col. 1555C] Addition 1. Jesus was baptized at the third milestone from Jericho.]” (Matt. 3). There were three principal reasons why Jesus was baptized by John: to approve John's baptism; to fulfil and teach the fulfilment of every humility; and, by the touch of his body, to impart to the waters the power of regeneration, even if perhaps not immediately. For concerning the power and institution of baptism there is a threefold opinion, as is found in the *Sentences*.

Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old—that is, he had entered his thirtieth year, only thirteen days of that year having passed [Col. 1554D] (Luke 3). According to this, Jesus lived only thirty-two and a half years. For on the same day of the following year he changed water into wine; at the next Passover—that is, the Passover of his thirty-first year—John was imprisoned; at the following Passover, that is, in the thirty-second year, John was beheaded; and at the third Passover, that is, in the thirty-third year, the Lord suffered. Thus the Lord lived thirty-two complete years, and as much of his thirty-third as elapsed from Christmas to Passover, which is counted as half a year.

Chrysostom, however, said in the tenth homily on Matthew that he had already completed his thirtieth year, saying: “After thirty years Jesus came [Col. 1555A] to baptism, about to set aside the old Law. Therefore he remained in observance of the Law until this age—which is accustomed to encompass every sin—lest anyone say that he set aside the Law because he had been unable to fulfil it.” And below: “For thirty years he had fulfilled the righteousness of the Law, and then came to baptism, about to teach the Gospel, as though placing a crown upon all observances of the Law.” Chrysostom said this, however, on the occasion of the Lord's words: “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.” According to this opinion, he lived thirty-three complete years and as much of his thirty-fourth as extends from Christmas to Passover.

John, however, tried to prevent Jesus, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” Why did John say that he ought to be baptized, [Col. 1555B] if he had been sanctified in the womb and cleansed from original sin, or at least at circumcision? He understood the human race in himself, as though saying: “Humankind must be cleansed through you.” Or, with respect to the fullness of cleansing, he said that he still had to be cleansed, because even if he had already been cleansed, he was to be cleansed more fully through Christ's blood—as someone who has received an effective medicine is called cured with respect to the cause, yet to be cured with respect to the fullness of its effects.

Jesus said to him: “Allow it for now. For thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness,” that is, superabundant humility. There is due humility: submitting oneself to a greater person for God's sake; abundant humility: submitting oneself to an equal; superabundant humility: submitting oneself to a lesser. As if he said: “Therefore I now submit myself to you, who are lesser, lest greater persons disdain to be baptized and ruled by lesser.” John, understanding this, consented.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning the Holy Spirit and the Father's voice

“And it came to pass, when” nearly “all the people of that land were being baptized, and when Jesus had been baptized and was praying” for those being baptized, that they might receive the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1556A] Addition 1. For this reason there were heretics who said that baptism ought to be administered only on the day of Epiphany, and that the Holy Spirit is not given if anyone is baptized on another day. To uproot this heresy more vigorously, the Fathers decreed that no one should be baptized on that day except in necessity. Where we say, “Do you wish to be baptized?” some say, “What do you seek?” The answer is: “I seek faith,” or “I seek baptism.” Others use both: “What do you seek?” and “Do you wish to be baptized?”], “Jesus immediately came up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened” (Luke 3): that is, an immeasurable brightness appeared around him, as though the aerial and starry heaven had been opened and the splendour of the empyrean heaven poured upon the earth. The Holy Spirit came in the bodily form of a dove and rested upon his head; when it had completed its office, it returned to the material at hand from which it had been taken.

Then the Baptist learned what he had said he did not formerly know: namely, that Christ alone baptizes—that is, retains in himself the power of baptism—though he gives others the power of baptizing. He who had sent John to baptize before him, while John was leading a solitary life, had also told him: “However many you baptize, among them, ‘he upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he alone is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (John 1). And behold, the Father's voice was heard from on high: “You are my beloved Son; in you I have been well pleased” (Luke 3). The brightness is believed to have lasted until after this voice, and the dove to have rested upon his head. What another Evangelist says, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3), has the same sense: namely, “In you and through you I have determined to accomplish my good pleasure.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning Jesus' fast and temptation

“Then Jesus was led by the Holy Spirit,” who had designated him, “into the wilderness; and, when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward [Col. 1556B] he hungered” (Matt. 4). The devil was stirred by the forty days' fast. He knew that for so many days the waters of the flood had been poured out; that the land of promise had been explored by Moses; that the Law had been given by God; and that the children of Israel had lived in the wilderness for so many years on the bread of angels. But when he perceived the Lord to hunger—which is not recorded of Moses or Elijah—he approached in order to tempt him, both to see whether he could cast him down into sin and to discover whether he was the Son of God. For he had heard the words, “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3), and knew that he would come at some time and that through him he would lose his power; but he did not expect him before the judgment.

He tempted him in the same three matters in which he had cast down Adam, though not in the same order: first, in gluttony, so that, seeing bread while hungry, he might be inflamed with an immoderate appetite for food; second, in avarice, when upon the mountain he showed him all the kingdoms of the world—that is, he set before him the world's glory; third, in pride, that he might ostentatiously show himself to be God's Son. Then the Lord cast him off, and Lucifer, having completed every temptation for which he had come, withdrew from the Lord for a time. He returned at the time of the Passion, thinking to cast him down by fear of death. But then, entirely conquered, he was bound in hell, to be released in the days of Antichrist, according to John's Apocalypse (Rev. 20). The devil should be believed to have assumed a human form, in which he could lead the Lord about and speak with him. Whether all the temptations occurred on the last day of the fast alone, or separately over some following days, does not matter for us to know.

The Lord fasted in the wilderness, which lies between Jerusalem and Jericho [Note: [Col. 1556D] Addition 1. At the second milestone from Jericho, called the Quarantana. Below the Quarantana was a little stream from the spring which Elisha healed. At the second mile from the Quarantana, toward Galilee, there is said to be a mountain upon which the devil placed Jesus.]. By his example, moreover, this number of days is penitential in the Church. Therefore the Church does not fast immediately after Epiphany, but about sixty days later, signifying, as it were at the corresponding time, her fast as consecutive with the Lord's fast. This is also so that through repentance we may be shown to ascend to rest, just as the number forty ascends to fifty. For it is a superabundant number, and, when all its aliquot parts are added together, it reaches fifty.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the first calling of the disciples

[Col. 1557A]

One day John was standing with two of his disciples, one of whom was Andrew. Seeing Jesus walking, he said: “Behold, [Note: [Col. 1557D] Addition 1. Why he called him the Lamb is explained by what follows: ‘who takes away,’ that is, comes in order to take away, the sins of the world; for “Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed” for the taking away of sins (1 Cor. 5). Or because “lamb” in Greek is said to derive from *agnon*, meaning “pious,” or in Latin from *agnoscendo*, “recognizing,” because in a large flock a lamb recognizes its mother by her bleating alone. Therefore he is properly called the Lamb in relation to the Passion, because there, being pious and granting us peace, he recognized his Father by obedience and his Mother by care. This is one reason why, in the sacrifice of the altar, “Lamb of God” is said three times, as though: “Lamb, who recognized the Father, have mercy on us; Lamb, who recognized the Mother, have mercy on us; Lamb, who offered yourself for us, grant us peace.”] the Lamb of God, behold, he who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). For this reason those two disciples followed Jesus, to see where he remained, and they remained with him that day.

Andrew then found Simon his brother and said to him: “We have found the Messiah, which is interpreted Christ”—*Christos* in Greek, “anointed” in Latin—and [Andrew] brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said: ‘You are Simon Barjona; you shall be called Cephas,’ which is interpreted Peter.” *Barjona* is Hebrew and means “son of Joanna,” a compound of a whole and a corrupted form. *Cephas* is Hebrew and Syriac; *Petrus* is Greek and Latin. Whether he gave him this name then, or promised that it would be given, is uncertain. It can more safely be said that he then gave the name altogether when he said: “You are Peter” (Matt. 16), or at the choosing of the twelve, where it is said: “And he gave Simon the name Peter” (Matt. 10). But if he gave it now, he confirmed it in what follows.

On the next day, wishing to return to Galilee, Jesus found Philip and said to him: “Follow me.” He was from Bethsaida, a fellow citizen of Andrew and Peter. Philip found Nathanael, his brother, and said to him: “We have found Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth, whom Moses wrote of in the Law and the prophets.” [Col. 1557C] Nathanael said: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” This is read either disparagingly, as though “No,” or permissively. For this expert in the Law had read in prophecy: “He shall be called a Nazarene” (Isa. 11) [Note: [Col. 1558A] Addition 2. “And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and he shall be called a Nazarene,” that is, “flowery,” as another edition says: “And a flower shall rise from his root.”], and perhaps had noted the signs of the Lord's coming. Thus he said: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” as though saying: “Can there at last be something good from Nazareth?”

Philip brought him to Jesus. When he came to him, Jesus said: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.” Nathanael said: “How do you know me?” Jesus answered: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” Nathanael answered him: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel.” For he recognized that the Lord had seen, though absent, what he alone had done, and how and where he had been called by Philip; he confessed him to be Christ and God [Col. 1557D]. Some nevertheless explain this concerning predestination as follows: “When you were in Adam's loins, he being hidden beneath the fig tree, I formerly—and indeed—predestined you.” Jesus then returned to Galilee.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the various opinions of the history

[Col. 1558A]

### Chapter XXXVII. On the Various Opinions Concerning the Gospel History

Thus far the order of the Gospel history is the same in all the writers. Thereafter different arrangements are made, down to John’s imprisonment. Some say that, about the first Passover after the baptism, the Lord changed water into wine, because John, immediately after this miracle, relates that he went up to Jerusalem and cast buyers and sellers out of the Temple [Col. 1558B] (John 2), an act which they say he performed only at Passover. But the Church’s custom opposes them: it holds that this happened at Epiphany and commemorates it solemnly every year.

There were also those who said that he performed this miracle on the very day on which he was baptized. But Matthew says: “Then Jesus was led into the wilderness” (Matt. 4); and Mark: “Immediately the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness” (Mark 1). The Church holds that these three events occurred on the same day, though in successive years: the coming of the Magi on the thirteenth day of the first year; the baptism on that same day of his thirtieth, or thirty-first, year; and the transformation of water on the same day when a year had passed.

> [Note: [Col. 1558D] Addition 1. Bede says that, after a year had elapsed, on the same day he performed the miracle of the five loaves and two fish (John 6).]

Hence Bishop Maximus, in the sermon beginning, “Since many things, brethren, etc.,” says as follows:

[Col. 1558C] “As faithful antiquity handed down to posterity, today the Savior was worshipped by the Chaldeans; today he consecrated the streams of the Jordan by the blessing of his own baptism; today, invited to a wedding, he changed water into wine.”

Thus in older books the day is called the Epiphanies—that is, the multiple manifestations of Christ. For *Epiphany* signifies manifestation. Yet some distinguish these three manifestations by separate names: calling *epiphany* the manifestation effected through the star, as though made from above; *theophany* that at the baptism, as though made by God—that is, by the Father; and *Bethany* that at the wedding, as though made in a house. For *beth* means “house.”

Nevertheless, among the principal and catholic doctors there still remains a twofold opinion concerning the order of the history. Some, [Col. 1558D] writing one Gospel out of the four and following Ammonius of Alexandria, Eusebius of Caesarea, and Theophilus—who sat as the seventh bishop of Antioch after Peter—say that after the fast the Lord preached openly, gathered disciples, and delivered the sermon on the mount before the miracle of the wine, because they read that the Lord and his disciples were invited to the wedding. But the more common and truer opinion is that after that miracle the Lord called disciples secretly and preached secretly until John’s imprisonment, but afterwards did so publicly. We shall follow this order, without prejudice to the other ordering.

### Chapter XXXVIII. On the Transformation of Water into Wine

[Col. 1559A]

“And a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee,” that is, in a village of Galilee so called, “and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding, and his disciples”—that is, certain future disciples, since at John’s word several were already listening to him secretly, and later followed him altogether.

Joseph was not invited, but Mary was. Hence some say that Joseph was dead and that the Virgin had passed into the guardianship of her son, since after this he is not even mentioned in the Gospel. Even if he was not yet dead, it is nevertheless certain that he was dead at the Lord’s Passion, since his wife was entrusted to another.

Some suppose that this wedding was that of John the Evangelist, and that Mary was invited because she was his maternal aunt, and the Lord because he was his cousin. They say that the Lord called him away from this wedding when he wished to marry; but this is not certain.

“And when the wine failed, the mother of Jesus said to him: ‘They have no wine,’” as if to say: Give them wine. “Jesus answered: ‘What is that to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come.’” Although *mulier* (“woman”) is, as it were, an added term denoting weakness, like *molier*, it is sometimes a designation of sex, especially when a virgin is powerful in relation to a man.

The meaning is: You wish a miracle to be performed; but, for performing this, what do I have in common with you? As if he said: I do not do this from the nature which I share with you; but in the hour of my Passion, which has not yet come, I shall suffer from the nature common to you and me.

Nor should it be believed, according to the astrologers, that the Lord said this as those do who suppose that every person has an inevitable hour of death according to the hour of the constellation [Col. 1559C] under which he was born. Rather, he called it his own hour—that is, the hour appointed by himself. For he died voluntarily, not by necessity.

There were six stone water-jars there—that is, vessels for water—set there in accordance with the purification rites of the Jews. The Jews frequently washed their dining vessels; and if by chance they touched anything unclean, they would not eat unless they had washed. They were therefore set there so that, if perhaps any of the guests needed to wash, they might have water ready.

“The servants filled them with water at the Lord’s command, and took the water, made wine, to the master of the feast,” that is, the chief among those reclining at table in the *triclinium*. Some say that a *triclinium* was a house with three rooms, or with three vaults beneath which they reclined. Or perhaps there were three rows of tables there, as is commonly done in refectories. [Col. 1559D] The master of the feast praised the excellence of the wine. Afterwards all together praised the newness of the miracle. “This was the beginning of signs by which Jesus manifested his glory.”

This is not called the beginning because he had done no signs before: he had been born of a Virgin, led the Magi by a guiding star, fasted forty days and forty nights, and done things of that kind. Rather, this was the first performed publicly and intended for public proclamation, or the first performed at Cana of Galilee.

### Chapter XXXIX. On the Instruction of Nicodemus

“There was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night” (John 3), because, being one of the rulers, he feared offending the people. Or because he was a teacher in Israel, he was ashamed to speak openly.

He said to Jesus: “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher; for no one can perform these signs which you perform unless God is with him,” as if to say: Teach me about the kingdom of God.

“Jesus answered: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.’” In the Old Testament, “As the Lord lives” was, as it were, an oath. In the New Testament: “Amen, I say”; and although elsewhere it is said simply, in John alone it is doubled, according to the saying: “Let your speech be, Yes,” as though he said: I speak truth in heart and mouth.

When Nicodemus wondered how a man could be born a second time, knowing only bodily birth, the Lord taught him concerning spiritual birth, [Col. 1560B] which comes from water and the Spirit, neither of which can be repeated. Yet because he was still puffed up with the learning of a teacher, he could not understand; and thus he deserved to hear: “Are you a teacher in Israel, and do not know these things?” So he was invited to humility.

He also instructed him concerning his own human and divine birth, his Passion and Ascension, and many other matters. When he said, “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven,” the sense is: No one ascends except Christ with his body. Or it may be understood figuratively, according to the manner in which we say that the Lord does what we do through him. The sense is: No one ascends except the one whom God causes to ascend.

### Chapter XL. On the First Expulsion of Buyers and Sellers from the Temple

[Col. 1560C]

“At the approaching Passover Jesus went up to Jerusalem and drove out those buying and selling” (John 2); for he is believed to have done this twice. After that Passover John was imprisoned. For John the Evangelist says: “When, after this Passover, Jesus had returned to Judea, John was still baptizing at Aenon” (John 3).

Meanwhile, before going up at Passover, he called certain disciples, taught, and performed miracles, though not so publicly. “Now Jesus was walking by the Sea of Galilee” (Matt. 4). This is a lake formed by the inflow of the Jordan. Though it is fresh water, it is called a sea in Hebrew idiom, because the Hebrew calls every collection of waters *Tharsis*, that is, “sea.” It is called Galilee because it flows past [Col. 1560D] Galilee. At times it is called the Sea of Tiberias, because this famous city stands beside it. When it is called the Lake of Gennesaret, this is from an incidental characteristic: for at times, when its waves are stirred, it produces a breeze from itself.

It extends one hundred and forty stadia in length and forty in width. Josephus, however, says that it received its name from the small district of Gennesar, past which it flows, and which he also calls remarkable. For the whole region is planted with shrubs of very different kinds and denies none of them its fertility and temperateness. There are walnuts there, which especially delight in cold weather; there are also palms, which summer heat nourishes; and figs and olives, for which a gentler air is suited—so that, as though conflicting blessings contended with one another, they flourish through the industry of the soil.

He says that it is watered by a spring which [Col. 1561A] falls into Capernaum, and which some suppose to be a branch of the Nile, because it produces the *coracinus* fish, found nowhere else except in the River Nile.

### Chapter XLI. On the Second Calling of the Disciples

“While the crowds pressed upon him, he saw two boats standing beside the lake. Going aboard one, which was Simon’s, and putting out a little from the land, he taught the crowds from the boat. When he had ceased speaking, he said to Simon: ‘Put out into the deep; and let down the nets for a catch.’ When this was done, they enclosed so great a multitude of fish that the net was almost breaking. Simon and Andrew signaled to the sons of Zebedee, who were in the other boat, to come and help them. They filled both boats, so that they were nearly sinking. When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees and [Col. 1561B] said: ‘Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man.’ The Lord said to him: ‘Do not fear, for henceforth you will catch people.’ And when the boats had been drawn to land”—that is, placed with the intention of returning to them—“they followed him” for a little while, and returned again to their own affairs (Luke 5).

### Chapter XLII. On What the Lord Read at Nazareth

Jesus came to Nazareth and, on the Sabbath day, when more people assembled, entered the synagogue in order to teach more people (Luke 4). Having read in Isaiah, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” etc. (Isa. 61), he said that “today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” As if to say: I am the one of whom this is written. And all fixed their attention on him.

### Chapter XLIII. That the Disciples and John Were Baptizing

[Col. 1561C] After these things Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea—so called specifically from the portion of Judah, or from the kingdom of the two tribes—and remained there with his disciples and baptized, although it was not he himself but his disciples who baptized (John 4). Whether it was John’s baptism or Christ’s is uncertain.

“John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there. For John had not yet been cast into prison” (John 3). Salim is a town situated beyond the Jordan, where Melchizedek once reigned. John also sent many who came to him on to Jesus. Then John’s disciples, troubled, said to him: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—behold, he is baptizing, and all are coming to [Col. 1561D] him.” Rebuking their envy, John said: “I told you that I am not the Christ, but that I have been sent before him. He who comes from above is above all. Therefore I must decrease, but he must increase” (ibid.).

When Jesus recognized their envy, he went up for the feast day of Passover mentioned above. But there also, because he perceived that the Pharisees’ envy had arisen against him—especially when he heard that John had been handed over to prison—he left Judea and again went into Galilee.

### Chapter XLIV. Why John Was Imprisoned

For John rebuked Herod concerning Herodias, because according to the law he had received, it is not permitted for a man to have his brother’s wife while his brother lives (Mark 6).

A commentary on Matthew says that Herodias [Col. 1562A] was the daughter of King Aretas. Herod had taken her from Philip, and after certain hostilities had arisen between them, she had been given to his brother Herod out of hatred for Philip, since the brothers also were enemies of one another.

Josephus relates that Herodias was the daughter of Aristobulus, whom their father Herod had killed together with his brother Alexander. Thus she was the sister of Herod Agrippa, and her grandfather Herod had given her as wife to his own son Herod. For he says that there was another Herod besides the tetrarch, whom his father had begotten by the daughter of Simon the priest; whereas Philip was already dead when Gaius began to reign.

Perhaps this Herod too was called Philip because he bore two names; and thus the Gospel calls Philip the husband whom Josephus calls Herod. Or perhaps she was first married to Herod and afterwards to Philip.

Herod the tetrarch had as his wife the daughter of Aretas, king of the Damascenes. While traveling to Rome, he passed through the place of his brother and secretly agreed with his brother’s wife that, on his return, after repudiating his own wife, he would take her as his wife. This did not escape Herod’s wife; not waiting for her husband’s return, she hastened to her father. When Herod returned, he took Herodias from his brother, and became the enemy of Aretas and Philip. When John rebuked him for this, at Herodias’s instigation he sent John to prison. When Jesus heard this, he came and dwelt at Capernaum, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matt. 4).

### Chapter XLV. On the Third Calling of the Disciples

“Again, as Jesus walked beside the Sea of Galilee, [Col. 1562C] he saw two brothers, Simon and his brother Andrew, casting nets into the sea; and he said to them: ‘Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of people.’ But immediately, leaving their nets and boat, they followed him”—completely. “Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James and John, mending their nets with their father Zebedee; and he called them. Leaving their nets and father, they followed him”—completely (Matt. 4).

“And when Jesus passed on from there, he saw Matthew, also called Levi, son of Alphaeus, sitting at the tax office; and he said to him: ‘Follow me.’ Leaving everything, he followed him” (Matt. 9). *Telos* is Greek; in Latin, *vectigal*, “tax.” Thus he was a publican (Luke 5), that is, one administering public business—business which is administered without sin either scarcely or never.

[Col. 1562D] Note from whom and from what sort of people the Church arose. Had it arisen from the eminent, the power of faith would have been attributed to their learning and power. We have no settled account of the calling of the others.

### Chapter XLVI. On the Lord’s Open Preaching and Miracles

From this point he preached openly, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4). Hence the priests later said to Pilate: “He stirred up all Judea, beginning from Galilee even to this place” (Luke 23). Thus was fulfilled the saying of Isaiah: “In the former time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened” (Isa. [Col. 1563A] 11).

Thus the earliest converts of the Lord, because they were from those regions, were called the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali. Isaiah indeed prophesied concerning the captivity of the ten tribes, which began in those tribes. Nonetheless, he also foretold the future lifting of the burden of sin in those regions through Christ’s preaching.

“Jesus went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and healing every sickness among the people; and his fame spread throughout all Syria” (Matt. 4). Syria is the whole region from the Euphrates to the Great Sea and from Cappadocia to Egypt, containing among other provinces Palestine, where the Jews lived. Hence in the Psalms Tabor and Hermon are called mountains of Syria (Ps. 88 [89]). [Col. 1563B] At times, however, Syria is understood so as to include no part of Judea. Great crowds from different regions followed him. When Jesus saw them, he went up a mountain.

### Chapter XLVII. On the Election of the Twelve Apostles

When he had sat down, he called to himself those whom he himself wished, and made twelve to be with him, whom he also named apostles—that is, “those sent”: Simon, whom he surnamed Peter, and Andrew his brother; James of Zebedee and John his brother. He gave these two the name Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder,” because one of them thundered when he said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). And both often deserved to hear the awe-inspiring voice of the Father: Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew [Col. 1563C] the publican;

> [Note: [Col. 1564A] Addition 1. Before the election of the apostles, some place the healing of the demoniac in the synagogue according to Mark; Peter’s mother-in-law; the healing of many at evening; the scribe who approached on the road; Christ’s sleeping in the boat; the demoniacs of the Gerasenes; the paralytic lowered through the roof; the calling of Matthew and Levi’s feast; Jairus’s daughter and the woman with the flow of blood; the two blind men; and the mute demoniac—of whom Matthew alone speaks.]

James of Alphaeus; Thaddaeus his brother, also surnamed Judas, whom Luke calls Judas of James, and who bore a third name, Lebbaeus; Simon the Canaanite; and Judas Iscariot (Matt. 10).

In this catalogue the apostles’ names are paired, as though of equals, for a reason not well known. But it is rightly asked why James of Alphaeus is counted after James of Zebedee and called the lesser, while the other is called the greater, since by the prerogative of his holiness he was later made archbishop of Jerusalem by the apostles and was older.

To understand this better, we say that Anna—

> [Note: [Col. 1564B] Addition 2. Anna was not from Nazareth, but from Sepphoris, about two miles from Nazareth.]

—after the death of Joachim, by whom she had borne the Virgin Mary, who had been given as wife to Joseph, her son-in-law, married Cleophas, [Col. 1563D] Joseph’s brother. After bearing him a daughter, likewise named Mary, she gave this daughter in marriage to Alphaeus. To Alphaeus were born four cousins of the Lord: James, Simon, and Judas, apostles; and Joseph, also called Barsabas, who was elected with Matthias afterwards in place of Judas.

These four, more than the other relatives, were called the Lord’s brothers, because they were thought to be not only his cognates but also his agnates, as descending from the two brothers Joseph and Cleophas. Yet among them James was called, as it were by antonomasia, the Lord’s brother, because he was extremely like him in face.

Again, when Cleophas died, Anna married a third husband, namely Salome. The daughter she bore by him, as she had done before with the others, she called Mary. Zebedee married this Mary and had by her sons James the Greater and [Col. 1564A] John. Although John was younger by birth, he was called greater because he was called by the Lord first and first adhered to him. The Roman Church observes this, so that in their respective orders those first ordained are the first. Thus Jerome says.

Others, observing that women were commonly designated from their husbands’ names—as Marcia, Cato’s wife—said that, after their first husbands died, these two Marys married Cleophas and Salome; or that their first husbands had two names, and that Zebedee was called Cleophas and Alphaeus Salome.

### Chapter XLVIII. On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount

[Col. 1564B]

“And lifting up his eyes upon the disciples, he taught them, saying: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,’ etc.” (Matt. 5; Luke 6). Matthew and Luke narrate this sermon differently. Therefore some maintain that the Lord first delivered it to the disciples while sitting on the summit of the mountain, and afterwards, standing on its side, delivered it jointly to the disciples and the crowds.

> [Note: [Col. 1564C] Addition 1. But it is said that two miles from Capernaum there is a descent of the mountain where the Lord’s sermon was delivered and the leper was cleansed.]

Others maintain that only one sermon was delivered jointly to the disciples and crowds. Which of these is true is of no great importance for us to know, just as it is of no importance to know whether the mountain where these things happened was Tabor or another mountain in Galilee. We read of this sermon as delivered by the Lord to the disciples only in Matthew and Luke.

### Chapter XLIX. On the Lord’s Prayer

The Lord inserted into this sermon the Lord’s Prayer, which has eight parts (Matt. 6): the first is an appeal for goodwill, followed by seven petitions addressed to God the Father, from whom [Col. 1564D] we ask that our supersubstantial bread—that is, the Son—be given to us. For Christ also taught us to ask the Father in his name.

The first three petitions concern the future life: “Hallowed”—that is, established in us—“be your name.” In this life the name of father in relation to sons is, as it were, mutable, since Judah was sometimes God’s son and sometimes not. Because it could be changed in this way, the Apostle also said: “I fear lest I myself should be found reprobate” (1 Cor. 9). But in the homeland the sons will appear, and God will unchangeably be their Father.

“May your kingdom come”—that is, may your kingdom come to the vision of you—so that there may be a kingdom within the kingdom.

“May your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth”: that is, just as the heavenly Church can will nothing except what it knows you will, so may that Church which still serves on earth renounce its own will for yours.

The following four concern the warfare of this life: “Give us this day our supersubstantial bread,” that is, Christ, who is supersubstantial, that is, above all substances, and is our bread on the altar. Or *super substantialem* consists of two words, and the meaning is: “Give us today,” that is, in the present time, “our bread,” that is, Christ, who belongs especially to the faithful; and this *over and above bread*—that is, besides substantial bread, namely what is necessary for sustenance. As if to say: Give us both breads, for soul and body.

Luke uses “daily” (Luke 10), which is explained only of provision for the journey. The Greek has *epiousion*; the Hebrew, however, *sogolla*, that is, “chief,” “excellent,” or “peculiar.” Perhaps Luke, seeing that Matthew said *sogolla*, which means “peculiar,” said “daily.” But the Greek translator of Matthew, seeing that he had said *sogolla*, which means “excellent,” rendered it *epiousion*. The following three are clear. “Amen.” At the end the Hebrew places one of these three: *amen*, *sela*, *salem*, which means, “truly, always, peace.”

### Chapter L. That the Disciples Were Sent with Power to Heal

“After Jesus had finished these words, he summoned the twelve disciples and gave them power to cast out unclean spirits—

> [Note: [Col. 1565C] Addition 1. Hence the Dragon follows on the third day of the Rogation Days. Here the devil’s power is first destroyed, when a human being is given power over [Col. 1565D] him.]

—and to heal every infirmity. He sent them to preach the kingdom of God and [Col. 1565C] said: ‘Take nothing for the journey; greet no one’”—that is, do not greet people as others do, who are accustomed to greet not from an intention of wishing salvation.

“Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, nor enter the cities of the Samaritans. Freely you have received; freely give. Carry neither money nor bread, nor two tunics”—that is, superfluous ones—“nor shoes nor a staff.”

> [Note: [Col. 1565D] Addition 2. Hence the deacon, having taken the book from the altar, proceeds in silence while bowing, until at the ambo he greets the people, as though entering the house to which he offers peace. He does not carry a cushion—that is, life’s comforts—but another carries it for him. Nor is it an objection that the cushion signifies the light burden of the Gospel. Perhaps this is why the deacon does not say, “The Lord be with you,” except when he reads the Gospel, save rarely. “Rarely” is said because of cardinal deacons or the blessing of the candle.]

According to Mark, however, they were commanded to use sandals or *sandalia*, that is, ankle-boots, and to carry a staff, which is understood as authority to receive necessities (Mark 6). “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves; whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. 10).

### Chapter LI. On the Healing of the Leper

[Col. 1565D]

When Jesus came down from the mountain, he touched the leper, as though now dissolving the figures, and healed him, saying: “I will; be cleansed” (Matt. 8). He added: “See that you tell no one,” as if to say: See [Col. 1566A] how manifestly and completely you have been cleansed. Tell no one—that is, you need tell no one, since the matter is so evident—but “show yourself to the priest” (Luke 5), to whose judgment you must submit.

Behold: others are not yet suited to dissolve the law, yet the healed man preached everywhere.

### Chapter LII. On the Centurion’s Servant

When he entered Capernaum, a centurion, through the intervention of the elders of the Jews, asked him to heal his paralyzed servant (Matt. 8). Jesus said: “I will come and heal him.” The healing power came, however, not his body.

The centurion said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my servant will be healed,” because I too act by a word alone through my servants. Perhaps he had idols in his house, which were unclean to Jews. To those following him Jesus said: “I have not found such great faith in Israel”—understand, Israel of this time. Those who followed him are not included under the name Israel, because he was speaking to them—as in this Gentile. “And the servant was healed in that hour.”

Entering the synagogue on the Sabbath, he taught them and there cast out from a man an unclean spirit that cried: “What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know that you are the Holy One of God” (Luke 4).

### Chapter LIII. On Peter’s Mother-in-Law

“When Jesus came into Peter’s house”—which perhaps he had at Capernaum through his wife, for he himself was from Bethsaida—at the disciples’ request he healed Peter’s mother-in-law of fever (Matt. [Col. 1566C] 8).

### Chapter LIV. On the Widow’s Son

While going to the city of Nain in Galilee, he raised at its gate the son of a widow, touching the bier and saying: “I say to you, arise” (Luke 7). When evening came, they brought him demoniacs and sick persons, and he healed them all. He wished to go across the water (Matt. 8).

One scribe said to him: “Rabbi, I will follow you wherever you go.” He wanted to follow the Lord in order to learn to perform signs for profit, and therefore was not heard by the Lord. But the Lord said to another: “Follow me.” He answered: “Lord, allow me first to bury my father.” Jesus said to him: “Leave the dead”—that is, the dead in sins—[Col. 1566D] “to bury their own dead. But go and proclaim the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). The Lord Jesus would not have forbidden this man the burial had there not been others to bury him.

Another said: “I will follow you, Lord; but first allow me to bid farewell to those at home.” Jesus said to him: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

### Chapter LV. That, When Awakened, He Commanded the Winds and Sea

Then Jesus boarded a boat with his disciples and slept in the stern upon a cushion. When a storm arose, awakened by the disciples, he commanded wind and sea, saying: “Be silent, and be mute” (Mark 4); and the storm ceased.

He did not, as the heretics mistakenly suppose, command them as living beings. On the basis of such expressions, since all things are read to obey God, they have taught that all things are animate. Rather, inanimate things are said to obey him because by his word alone he makes them do what he wishes, according to the manner of speech in which the material cause of sickness is said to be obedient or disobedient to medicine.

### Chapter LVI. On the Two Men Possessed by a Legion

When he had crossed the water into the country of the Gerasenes, which lies opposite Galilee, two violent demoniacs met him. One of them worshipped him and said: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Mark 5).

The demons did not know that he was the Son of God, but conjectured it from his miracles and the Father’s testimony. They said that they were tormented because they were compelled to leave and cease harming people. For Jesus said to him: “Come out, unclean spirit.” [Col. 1567B] They knew that at the judgment they would be tormented in the abyss.

When, in answer to the Lord’s inquiry concerning his name, he said that he was called Legion, it was not that this was his name; rather, it was as though he said: You ask my name in vain, because we are many. They begged him to send them into the herd of swine feeding nearby. Entering the swine, they drove them headlong into the sea.

The inhabitants asked him to depart from their territory. As he entered the boat, he would not take the healed man with him, though he begged. He returned to Capernaum, which Matthew calls his own city (Matt. 9), not by origin but by people, because any city of Galilee may be called a city of Galileans.

### Chapter LVII. On the Paralytic Lowered through the Roof

[Col. 1567C] He healed the paralytic lowered before him through the tiles, first forgiving his sins (Luke 5), which had been the cause of the illness; for what happens because of a cause ought, when the cause ceases, to have its effect cease. Because of the scribes and Pharisees, who thought that he had blasphemed, he told the paralytic to rise and take up his bed. He rose, took it up, and went away.

Since it is evident that a person sometimes falls sick on account of sins, a physician visiting a sick person ought first to urge repentance and confession, lest, while sin remains like iron in a wound, it be futile to apply a poultice.

### Chapter LVIII. On the Well of the Samaritan Woman

As he went up into Judea and returned again to Galilee, he had to pass through Samaria [Col. 1567D]—that is, the region whose capital had been Samaria (John 4). The city had thus lost its old name and was called Sebaste, while the region retained the name.

Coming near Shechem, corruptly called Sychar—

> [Note: [Col. 1568D] Addition 1. Shechem is now called Neapolis, four miles distant from Sebaste. There, near the spring, Jeroboam made the calves which he placed at Bethel and at Dan, which is one mile from Shechem.]

—and there was a well on the estate which Jacob bought from King Hamor and gave to his son Joseph. Tired from the journey, he sat upon Jacob’s well, which had been called this until then. From the event that follows it was afterwards named the Samaritan woman’s well.

Some say that this place is the navel of our inhabited earth, because every year, on a certain day in summer at noon, the sun descends into the well’s water and casts no shadow anywhere—something that philosophers report happens at Syene. They therefore think that Deuteronomy says: “He set him upon [Col. 1568A] the high place of the earth” (Deut. 32).

The disciples went into the town to buy food, and a woman came to draw water. When the Lord asked her for a drink, she remarked upon him, saying that Jews did not associate with Samaritans, recognizing from the fringes of his garment that the Lord was a Jew.

After the ten tribes had been carried away, the king of Assyria sent Persians and Assyrians to inhabit the land for him. Out of fear of wild beasts they had accepted the books of Moses and the laws of the land, but did not cease from idolatry. They were first called Cuthaeans, from a river of Persia; but then they were called Samaritans, as though halfway between Jews and Gentiles. Yet Jews sometimes called them Jacobites—that is, supplanters—because they had supplanted their brothers in the land which belonged to those brothers. Jews did not use their food or vessels.

When, in speaking with Jesus, she learned from him that she had had five husbands and that the sixth man was her concubine, [Col. 1568B] she said: “I see that you are a prophet.” Immediately she asked for a resolution of the question disputed between themselves and the Jews. For the Jews said that Jerusalem and the Temple were the proper place of worship; but the Samaritans said it was Mount Gerizim, where the ancient fathers had worshipped.

Jesus said that the time had come when people would worship neither in Jerusalem nor on that mountain. As if to say: In worship I do not prefer one place to another. Rather, God is to be worshipped everywhere only in spirit and truth—that is, from the love which comes from the Spirit, and for things which are true, that is, eternal.

The woman said to him: “I know that Messiah is coming,” that is, he is near to coming. Perhaps the Samaritans too had noted the signs of the Lord’s advent. *Messiah* in Hebrew, *Christos* in Greek, and *unctus* in Latin mean “anointed.” In Punic also *messe* means “to anoint,” for the Punic and Syrian languages are related to Hebrew.

Jesus said to her: “I am he who speaks with you.” The woman left her water-jar and went into the city, urging the citizens to come out to see the man who had told her everything she had done. She said: “Could this be the Christ?” She feared to affirm what she had heard and believed, lest the men resent being taught by a woman.

When the citizens came out, Jesus called the disciples and said that the fields were ready for harvest—that is, ready to believe—although four months still remained until [Col. 1568D] harvest. From this it is understood that this happened in winter. At their request Jesus entered the town and remained there for several days, and many believed in him.

### Chapter LIX. On the Royal Official’s Son

He came again from Judea, to which he had gone up, into Cana of Galilee (John 4). There was there a certain royal official—that is, one of the more powerful men of the land under the king—whose son was sick, not at Cana but at Capernaum. He begged the Lord to come down and heal his son.

The Lord rebuked him [Col. 1569A] because he did not believe that his son could be healed without bodily presence and touch. Yet as he persisted, he said to him: “Go; your son lives.” Thus, absent in body, he healed him by a word. As the father went down, when he learned that his son had been healed at the hour of the Lord’s word, “he himself believed, and his whole household.”

He is thought to have been a Jew, because the Lord said to him: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” For the Jews seek signs (1 Cor. 1).

### Chapter LX. On Levi’s Feast
“And Levi made him a feast in his own house” (Luke 5). Tax collectors who had been Levi’s associates reclined with him. When the Pharisees reproached him for eating with such persons, he said: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. 9). He also excused the disciples for not fasting: first, because they were inexperienced and could not bear difficult things; and secondly, because he was bodily present with them, whereas, when he should be taken from them, they would fast greatly. From this some say that, after Christ was taken up in the Ascension, the disciples fasted until the sending of the Holy Spirit. For this reason they fast from the Ascension until Pentecost. Nor do they then celebrate weddings, as though they were already beginning the three weeks before the feast of Saint John. But this is not authoritative, nor is anything then said in the Acts of the Apostles about their fasting, but only about prayer.

When the Pharisees sought from him a sign from heaven, he refused them as unworthy, because they were worse than the Ninevites and the queen of the South, who had possessed neither God’s law nor the prophets (Matt. 12). And note that in the more ancient manuscripts one reads *Ninivitae* (“Ninevites”).

## CHAPTER LXI. On the Daughter of the Ruler of the Synagogue, and the Woman with the Issue of Blood

And behold, Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, worshipped him, saying: “My daughter has just died”—that is, she was close to death, as Mark and Luke say (Matt. 5; Luke 9). “Come, lay your hand upon her, and she shall live.” And as he went, a woman suffering from an issue of blood for twelve years came from behind, touched the fringe of his garment, and was healed.

> **[Note: Col. 1569D, Addition 1.]** In the *Ecclesiastical History* it is read that someone made a bronze statue in honour of the Saviour [Col. 1570A] and, beside it, a statue of Martha, where she was healed; a certain herb grew there. At times it grew so much that it touched the fringe of the garment; and it had such power that whoever took some of it was healed of every sickness.

Ambrose, in his sermon *On the Saviour*, says that this woman was Martha. For, in enumerating Christ’s benefits toward humankind, after some preliminary remarks he adds: “While he dries up the languid flow of blood in Martha; while he casts demons out of Mary; while in Lazarus he binds together the body of one restored to life by the warmth of the spirit.”

When he came into Jairus’s house, he took with him only Peter, James, and John his brother, who were as it were his confidential attendants, along with the girl’s father and mother. Having put out those who mocked him because he said, “The girl is asleep,” he took the girl’s hand and said: *Talitha cumi*, which means, “Girl, I say to you, arise.” Yet “I say to you” is not part of the translation. And he ordered food to be given her.

> **[Note: Col. 1570A, Addition 2.]** Some say that this happened in the middle of Jerusalem, beneath Solomon’s palace.

For this is the true proof of a real resurrection. Magicians indeed raise the dead by means of certain characters bound beneath both armpits, and make them speak and walk; but they cannot make them eat.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the Two Blind Men and the Deaf Man

[Col. 1570A]

“And as Jesus passed on from there, two blind men followed him, crying: ‘Son of David, have mercy on us’” (Matt. 9). When he came indoors—that is, to his house at Nazareth—he touched their eyes, and they were opened. Though he told them, “See that no one knows,” they nevertheless spread his fame throughout that whole region.

After they had gone out, they brought him a mute man possessed by a demon; and, when the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke (Luke 11). In Greek, however, “deaf” sounds better than “mute.”

## CHAPTER LXIII. On Beelzebub

When the crowd praised him, the Pharisees said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons” (Luke 11). From Bel, the original name of an idol, different peoples called their idols by different names according to the idiom of their language. The Babylonian said *Bel*, the Moabite *Beel*, the Palestinians *Baal*. Sometimes they added something further, as *Beelphegor*, that is, “god of sexual lust,” who is Priapus. Sometimes they said *Baalim*, the god of the Sidonians, which means “my husband,” that is, “my strength and my head.”

Beelzebub, however, was the name of no idol; rather, the Jews mockingly called a neighbouring idol of the Ekronites [Col. 1570C] by this name. It means “man of flies,” because of the filth of sacrificial blood, which flies pursue. Its final letter is neither *d*, nor *l*, nor *v*, but *b*.
