To them Jesus said: “And by whom do your sons cast them out?” As though to say: If you attribute this casting-out to God in the case of your own sons, why do you not do the same in my case? For among the Jews there were exorcists who cast out demons by Solomon’s exorcisms, especially if the root of a certain herb was placed in the nostrils of the possessed person. Josephus says that he saw an exorcist, seized and brought before Vespasian while he was besieging Jerusalem, who put into the nostrils of a possessed man a ring under whose gem was a root, and adjured the demon; and the demon came out. Then, to prove that the demon had been expelled [Col. 1570D], he placed a basin full of water in the middle and commanded the demon to overturn the basin; and it overturned it.

But the practice by which some enclose an unclean spirit in rings, through which they attack other demons, is not believed to be Solomon’s invention. Augustine says of Cyprian the magician and martyr that, while he was still a magician, he kept three demons enclosed in a certain ivory box; by sending them wherever he wished, he accomplished whatever he desired, and afterward they returned. Yet he could never bring over the girl with whose love he was inflamed, because she always opposed to them the sign of the cross. On learning this, Cyprian was converted to the faith and afterward became a martyr with the virgin Justina.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On Mary Magdalene

[Col. 1571A]

Here some say that the Lord was invited by a certain Pharisee into his house at Nazareth, and that there the sins of Magdalene were forgiven—

> **[Note: Col. 1571A, Addition 1.]** Magdala is a town two miles from Tiberias, which was formerly called Chinnereth.

—and that she followed him (Luke 7). Many say that it happened at Bethany; but neither the place nor the time when it happened can be established from the Gospel.

## CHAPTER LXV. On Martha’s Service

“And it came to pass, as Jesus went up into Judea, that he entered a certain village; and Martha received him into her house and ministered to him” (Luke 10). The sitting of her sister, listening to the Lord, was preferred by the Lord to Martha’s service [Col. 1571B], not because it was of greater merit, but because it would not be taken away from her.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On John’s Question

“Now when John had heard in prison of the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples to him, saying: ‘Are you he who is to come, or do we await another?’” (Matt. 11; Luke 7). John did not doubt, for he had said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). But because his disciples still doubted, he sent them to Jesus. It was as though he said: Go to him and ask him yourselves whether he is the Christ, or whether another is still to come.

Gregory, however, in his commentary on Ezekiel seems to hold that John did not know whether Christ would despoil hell in person or through another. It was as though he said: I am near to descending to my own people [Col. 1571C]. Since I have announced you to those above, do you wish me to announce you to those below?

Jesus removed their doubt by showing certain signs of his coming. When they had departed, he commended John to the crowds, saying: “Among those born of women there has not arisen a greater than John the Baptist.” Here *woman* is not only the name of a sex but also the name of the created being. Whether anyone after him has been, or will be, holier than he is undecided. Nor should this praise lead us to believe the heretics who said that John was an angel made human, since the Lord had also foretold concerning him that it had been said: “Behold, I send my angel,” etc. (Mal. 3).

The Lord added that all the law and the prophets prophesied until John. This must be understood for the most part [Col. 1571D], since afterward Agabus and Philip’s four daughters prophesied (Acts 21). Then he reproached the cities of Galilee in which he had worked very many miracles, and set Tyre and Sidon before them (Matt. 11; Luke 10). Some of the apostles, returning to him, reported what they had taught and done (Mark 6). And he led them into a desert place that they might rest a little, for because of the crowds they did not even have time to eat.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On the Seventy-Two Disciples

“After these things he appointed seventy-two other disciples and sent them two by two before his face—

> **[Note: Col. 1572A, Addition 1.]** In the crowns of churches there are twelve greater towers, as the twelve apostles; twelve lesser ones, as the twelve prophets; and seventy-two lamps, signifying these disciples. Angels are understood as guardians of the church.

—” (Luke 10). These too returned with joy, saying: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us.” Jesus therefore rejoiced and said: “I confess to you [Col. 1572A], Lord, Father of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. And no one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father.”

Let Eunomius be ashamed, who says that he has full knowledge of the Father and the Son. Nor is the mutual relation of the two excluded; for Arius therefore believed the Spirit to be a creature and not equal to them, because he did not know whatever they knew.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the Loosening of the Sabbath and the Rubbing of the Ears of Grain

[Col. 1572B]

And it came to pass on the second-first Sabbath, when Jesus and his disciples were passing through the grainfields, that the disciples ate ears of grain rubbed in their hands (Luke 6). This is explained thus: “On the second-first Sabbath,” adverbially, “when Jesus entered through the fields,” etc. Or it was on the second Sabbath after the first one, concerning which the preceding discussion was given. Or it is one word, which Luke calls *deuteroproton*, and we call *secundoprimum*, “second-first.”

This Sabbath, which the disciples did not observe, was so called because it signified that the spiritual Sabbath was now beginning and that the legal observances were to cease. For the spiritual Sabbath is second-first: that is, superior to the inferior, namely the legal Sabbath, as though made first out of second. What had been first in time became second in the gift of grace [Col. 1572C], as though the head had been turned into the tail. Therefore, if anyone wishes to call Christ the second-first Adam, he will not err.

Or there are two words, and it is called “second” and “first” in respect of time, because the holy Fathers kept Sabbath both before the Law and after it, with the legal Sabbath intervening between. When the Pharisees said, “Why do you do what is not lawful on Sabbaths?” the Lord excused them in many ways: first, because necessity excused them, as it excused David and his servants when he ate the priestly loaves. Nor did the priests sin by circumcising and sacrificing on the Sabbath; secondly, because they did this in the presence of the Lord, the author of the Sabbath. Joshua also did not sin when he went around Jericho for seven [Col. 1572D] days. Nor is a sick person guilty even today if he breaks a fast.

The Pharisees said that this was not lawful on Sabbaths because, according to the Law, it was lawful on another day to eat grain from a neighbour’s crop, but not to reap it with a sickle. Note that the first apostles loosened the Sabbath; yet the Ebionites accept them while rejecting Paul as a transgressor of the Law.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On the Man with the Withered Hand

“And it came to pass on another Sabbath that Jesus entered the synagogue; and there was a man there with a withered hand, and the Pharisees watched him to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath” (Luke 6). When he asked them whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath and they gave no answer, he healed the sick man, refuting the superstitious persons who would draw on the Sabbath an animal that had fallen into a pit. But they discussed among themselves [Col. 1573A] what they should do to Jesus. Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there; many followed him, and he healed them.

## CHAPTER LXX. On the Four Parables Addressed to the Crowds from the Boat

“And it came to pass in those days that Jesus went out onto the mountain to pray, and spent the night there in prayer. And when day came, he called his disciples”—perhaps still asleep—and sat beside the sea (Luke 6). When the crowds gathered, he entered a small boat and taught the crowds standing on the shore from it. Speaking to them in parables, he set before them the parable of the sower: seed cast upon soil bad in three ways and bearing no fruit, and upon one good soil yielding a hundredfold.

> **[Note: Col. 1573C, Addition 1.]** Note that an ancient gloss on this passage says: “The Valentinian heretic is not to be believed when, finding support for his error in this passage, he says that there are lands in the human being and, corresponding to them, three creators: the soul, whose creator is God; the body, whose creator is the devil; and animality, or a certain vital spirit shared by us with brute animals, whose creators are angels. But here he has added not only three but a fourth; nor is the passage understood of these lands. The Catholic man recognizes only two things in the human being, namely soul and flesh. Animality, or the vital spirit, or sensuality—whatever may be shared by us and brute animals—he includes under flesh; and this is what the Catholic man holds.”

Second, he set forth the parable of one sowing good seed, over which an enemy sowed tares. In it, the saying, “Let both grow until the harvest” [Col. 1573B] (Matt. 13), seems contrary to Paul, who says, “Remove the evil one from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5). But before the wheat comes into ear, there is a great resemblance between it and darnel, and they can scarcely be distinguished. Therefore the former saying concerns doubtful cases, while Paul’s concerns evident ones.

Third, he set forth the parable of the mustard seed (Matt. 13). Fourth, he set forth the parable of the leaven which a woman hid in three *sata* of flour (ibid.). A *satum* was a Palestinian measure containing a modius and a half. Privately, moreover, he explained everything to the disciples. Then, having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house, and the disciples said to him: “Explain to us the parable of the tares” (ibid.). For he had explained the first of them [Col. 1573C] in the boat.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On Three Parables Addressed to the Disciples in the House

[Col. 1573D]

Having explained what they asked concerning the parables, he spoke further to them (Matt. 13). He set forth the parable of treasure hidden in a field, to buy which its finder sold all that he possessed. He also set forth another concerning a good pearl found and purchased; and a third concerning a dragnet cast into the sea, in which it is said that in Gehenna there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. This suggests the future resurrection of bodies.

The name *Gehenna* occurs only in the Gospel and is believed to have been coined by the Lord on account of the unquenchable fire consecrated to idols in the valley near Jerusalem, called Topheth; or also *Gehennon*, as though “the land of the sons of Ennon,” that is, of a man so called, through whom idolaters passed their little children, just as we pass them through the water of baptism. The fire too was called Topheth, for a reason not sufficiently known. Or perhaps because, by some natural process, it continually burst forth from the bowels of the earth through porous stones, which we call *tophi* [Col. 1574A].

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the Lord’s Leap

“And coming into his native place, he taught in their synagogue, so that they wondered and said: ‘Whence has this man this wisdom? Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not Mary his mother, and are not his brothers and sisters with us?’” (Matt. 13). This must not be understood according to Helvidius, who taught that the Virgin bore brothers to the Lord by Joseph, or that Joseph [Col. 1574B] had children by another wife. Rather, his cousins were called his brothers, just as Abraham said to Lot: “We are brothers” (Gen. 13).

Mark says that they called the Lord a carpenter (Mark 6). For they thought that he was a carpenter because they called him Joseph the carpenter’s son. “And he healed few there because of their unbelief, saying: ‘No prophet is accepted in his own country’; and they were all filled with anger. Casting him out of the city, they brought him to the brow of the mountain to throw him down; but he, passing through the midst of them, went away” (Luke 4).

The place is still shown there and is called the Lord’s Leap. As the Lord descended through it, he impressed himself upon the rock; and the rock, yielding to him, made a place for him, as though a hiding-place. There, even now, marks said formerly to have been impressions of the folds of his garments [Col. 1574C] may be observed.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On the Beheading of John

At that time Herod the Tetrarch celebrated his birthday before his princes and the leading men of Galilee (Mark 6). The head of John the Baptist was given as a reward to the dancing girl upon a dish. A *discus* is a round vessel, very broad across its upper side; hence a server of food is called a *discoferus*, “dish-bearer.” Sometimes an upper table is called a *discus*. At other times the cloth called a table-cover is termed a *discus*; hence the animals are said to have appeared to Peter in a *discus*, which elsewhere the book of Acts calls a linen sheet.

It is believable that Herod and his wife had previously discussed in secret the killing of John under such a pretext. John’s disciples, however, took his body from prison [Col. 1574D] and buried it. The *Chronicles* and the eleventh book of the *Ecclesiastical History* report that John was bound and beheaded in the fortress of Machaerus in Arabia beyond the Jordan. His body was buried in Sebaste, a city of Palestine, between Elisha and Obadiah; his head was buried at Jerusalem near Herod’s dwelling.

In the time of Julian the Apostate, Gentiles scattered his bones, envying the miracles that occurred at his tomb. The bones, gathered again, were burned by the same persons, and their ashes scattered to the wind. Unwittingly, by doing this to one already dead, they enacted what was as it were a second martyrdom, when on his feast they burn bones gathered from every place. But when the bones were being gathered, certain monks from Jerusalem, secretly mixed among those gathering them, took a large portion, among which there is said to have been the finger with which he pointed out the Lord. Blessed Thecla afterward brought it across the Alps, and it is said to be in the church of Maurienne.

They took the bones to Philip of Jerusalem, the ninth bishop, who sent them through Julian the deacon to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. Theophilus, afterward bishop of that city, placed them in the temple of Serapis, cleansed from its filth, and consecrated a basilica in John’s honour, when, at the command of Theodosius, the shrines of the Gentiles were destroyed.

In the time of the emperor Marcian, John revealed his head to two Eastern monks who had come to Jerusalem to pray. But, not long afterward, it was lost through neglect and carried by others to Edessa—or, according to others, to Emesa, a city of Phoenicia—and for a long time hidden obscurely underground in an urn in a certain cave. Then John once more revealed his head to Marcellus, a devout abbot and priest, while he was living in that same cave. When Marcellus reported this to Julian [otherwise Julioramus], bishop of the same city, it was raised up. From that time the Beheading of John began to be celebrated in that city, on the very day, as we suppose, on which the head was found or revealed. It was afterward taken to Constantinople, and from there to Gaul.

Others maintain that the feast is not of the Beheading, but of the earlier Gathering of his Bones, when they were burned. Josephus gives another cause for the Baptist’s death, saying that he preached righteousness to the people and gathered many together under the pretext of baptism [Col. 1575C]. Herod, fearing the loss of his people as they followed John, killed him. Josephus also relates that the Jews held that, on this account, Herod was miserably defeated soon afterward by the army of King Aretas.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On the Five Loaves and Two Fish

“Herod heard the report of Jesus and said: ‘I beheaded John. But who is this of whom I hear such things?’ And he sought to see him” (Luke 9).—“When Jesus heard this, he went up into a small boat and withdrew privately to a desert place. The crowds followed him on foot from the towns, and he healed them” (Matt. 14).

The feast day called Passover was near. When evening came, the twelve [Col. 1575D] disciples said to him: “Dismiss the crowds, so that they may go and find food for themselves.” And Jesus said: “Give them food, and make them recline upon the green grass,” in groups—that is, in the different companies of people who had come from the villages.

Having received five barley loaves and two fish from a certain boy, who is believed to have been one of the disciples, he gave them through the apostles to the people, about five thousand men, besides women and children; and twelve baskets were filled with the fragments (ibid.). Immediately he compelled the disciples to enter the small boat and go ahead of him across the lake, according to Mark, toward Bethsaida, until he had dismissed the crowds (Mark 6).

Therefore Luke’s statement that this happened in the region of Bethsaida [Col. 1576A] (Luke 9) must be understood not as meaning that it was within its boundaries, but near Tiberias, as John says, and because those places belonged to it (John 6). John’s statement that they crossed the lake to Capernaum (ibid.) must be understood to mean that they passed through Bethsaida on the way to Capernaum.

“When Jesus knew that those men intended to seize him and make him king,” because under such a king they seemed to think that they could not lack anything, “he fled and went up alone onto the mountain to pray” (ibid.). This is the mountain on which he delivered the sermon. The place of this feeding, now called the Table, is a mile from it. Below it is the place where after the resurrection he ate part of a roasted fish (John 21); above it lies that part of the sea upon which the Lord walked (Matt. 14), and which on another occasion he calmed after being awakened (Matt. 8).

## CHAPTER LXXV. That the Lord Walked upon the Sea

[Col. 1576B]

“The boat in which the disciples were was tossed by the waves. Seeing them labouring, Jesus came to them in the fourth watch of the night, walking upon the sea” (Matt. 14). Those keeping watch in military camps divide the night into four watches. The first is called *conticinium*, in which all keep watch together; the second, *intempestum*, in which young men keep watch; the third, *gallicinium*, in which grown men do so; the fourth, *antelucanum*, in which old men do so. The Lord called these by other names: evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning (Mark 13).

When the disciples thought him a phantom and cried out, he said: “It is I; do not be afraid.” He did not say who he was [Col. 1576C], because they could recognize him by his familiar voice. Or he said it in order that they might understand him to be the one who said to Moses: “He Who Is sent me to you” (Exod. 3). Afterward Peter went to him over the waters; when he began to sink, the Lord raised him up. When he entered the boat, the wind ceased, and the boat was immediately brought to the land for which they were heading.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On the Lord’s Words Because of Which Some Went Back

The next day the crowds whom Jesus had fed entered boats arriving from Tiberias and came to Capernaum. Finding Jesus, they wondered how he had come there, since they had seen only the one small boat, which he had not entered (John 6). Although they ate the food he had provided for them, they preferred manna to him [Col. 1576D], saying: “Our fathers ate manna in the desert, as it is written: ‘The Lord gave them bread from heaven.’”

Then Jesus said to them: “I am the bread of life, who came down from heaven.” The Jews murmured, saying: “Is not this the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?” Jesus said: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.” Therefore the Jews disputed with one another, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” Then the Lord added: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.” On hearing this, many of the disciples said: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it? [Col. 1577A]” And they went back and no longer walked with him.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On the Traditions of the Pharisees against the Lord’s Commands

“A certain Pharisee asked Jesus to dine with him” (Luke 11). When he saw him dine with hands not washed by ritual immersion, he murmured within himself. The Lord said to him: You Pharisees cleanse what is outside the cup and dish, but not what is within. It was as though he said: You cleanse bodies but not souls; fools, did not God make both? This is against the Manichees, who say that only souls were created by God, whereas flesh was created by the devil. And he added: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean to you.”

Some scribes and Pharisees, coming from Jerusalem [Col. 1577B], saw his disciples eating with common hands and said: “Why do your disciples transgress the traditions of the elders?” (Matt. 15). Jesus answered: “Why do you transgress the commands of the Lord for the sake of your tradition? For God said: ‘Honour your father and your mother.’” This was said not only of reverence, but also of providing necessary assistance.

These Pharisees taught impiety under the name of piety, saying that children did better if they vowed to God, their true Father, what ought to have been offered to their parents. They instructed them to answer needy parents: “Father, *corban*—that is, what comes from me shall benefit you” (Mark 7). *Corban* is a votive gift. It is as though he said: You want what I have vowed to God to benefit you? Far be it!

“Having called the crowds to him, he said to them: ‘It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person’”—understand, before God—“‘but what proceeds from the mouth’” (Matt. 15). Understand the first of the mouth of the flesh, the second of the mouth of the heart. For vomiting too defiles a person. Hence some books have: “but what proceeds from the heart.” Why then do we not eat things sacrificed to idols, or stolen and plundered things? To avoid scandal. For food is clean in itself.

The disciples said to him: “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” We call a *scalon* or *scandalon* either an obstacle to the foot or the very fall. He answered: “Leave them; they are blind and guides of the blind.” For one must not depart from truth because of scandal.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. That Food Does Not Pass into the Power of Nature

[Col. 1577D]

When Jesus entered the house, Peter said: “Explain this parable to us.” He answered: “Do you not understand that everything entering the mouth goes into the stomach and is sent out into the privy?” (Matt. 15). Nothing from foods passes into the power of nature that shines forth; rather, nature, aided by food, merely grows and remains within itself.

> **[Note: Col. 1578A, Addition 1.]** Heretics say that the Lord was unlearned and ignorant of natural philosophy, because much food is distributed through the limbs, veins, marrow, and sinews. This is proved by those who suffer continual vomiting after taking food and yet are stout. But any evacuation of humours may be called an excretion.

And he added: “But out of the heart come thefts,” etc. Plato held that the ruling part of the soul was in the brain—that is, reason; anger in the gall; and desires in the liver. But according to Christ, the ruling part of the soul is in the heart. Mark uses “makes common” instead of “defiles” (Mark 6), in accordance with Hebrew idiom: they called “common” what was unclean, because they called foods prohibited [Col. 1578A] in the Law “common,” judging them unclean because other nations ate them indiscriminately.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On the Canaanite Woman

Jesus arose from there and went into the region of Tyre—

> **[Note: Col. 1578C, Addition 1.]** Tyre conceals the origin of its name, buried. Before Tyre there was a great marble stone on which Jesus sat. It remained unharmed during the time of the Gentiles, but was later mutilated by the Franks and Venetians. A church was built in honour of the Saviour upon what remained of it.

—and Sidon (Matt. 15). A Gentile Canaanite woman, Syrophoenician by race, begged him on behalf of her daughter, who was grievously troubled by a demon. The Canaanites had once lived among the Jews, but afterward were dispersed. This woman was descended from Syrians and Phoenicians of that dispersion.

Some, however [Col. 1578B], call her Tyrophoenician, because she was as much Phoenician as Tyrian, as Dido also was; by this name they indicate the woman’s region and native land. Jesus did not answer her a word, lest he seem inconsistent with himself, having said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10). When the disciples interceded for her, he answered: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel.” But she came, worshipped, and said: “Lord, help me.” The Lord said to her: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs to eat.”

According to Hebrew custom, he called the Gentiles dogs because they ate blood like dogs. The sense is: I have come to heal Israel, the firstborn, and not yet the Gentiles. She said to him: “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table [Col. 1578C].” As though to say: What you say is true. Therefore do to me what is done to dogs: give me a small portion of bread. Jesus, commending the woman’s faith, said: “Let it be done to you as you wish,” and immediately her daughter was healed.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On the Deaf and Mute Man

“Again he went out of the region of Tyre and came to the Sea of Galilee through the midst of the region of the Decapolis”—that is, he came to that part of the sea opposite which lay [Col. 1578D] the Decapolis, the region of ten cities around Pella and Gadara, across from Galilee (Mark 7). “And they bring to him a deaf and mute man.” He put his fingers into the man’s ears and said: “*Ephpheta*,” that is, “Be opened.” At his command the man’s ears were opened and his tongue was loosed.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the Pool of Bethesda

“After this there was a feast day of the Jews” (John 5). It is not specified which one, but it may be understood as the feast of the New [Year], that is, Pentecost, because the Passover at which John was beheaded has already been mentioned. The account proceeds to the Feast of Tabernacles and afterward to the Dedication. Jesus went up for the feast day.

“Now at Jerusalem there was a sheep pool, called in Hebrew [Col. 1579A] Bethesda, having five porticoes. In these lay a multitude of sick persons waiting for the movement of the water. For an angel descended into it at times and the water was moved; and whoever first entered it after the water’s movement was made sound from whatever infirmity afflicted him.”

*Probaton* is Greek for “sheep” in Latin. Thus it was called because the Nethinim washed sacrifices in it.

> **[Note: Col. 1579C, Addition 1.]** The Nethinim were water-carriers in the Temple. Subdeacons, who supply water to the priest, hold this office.

A reservoir of collected water without fish is usually called a *piscina*, as it were by contrast. When this movement began is uncertain. That it was uncertain when the water would be moved may be inferred from the fact that sick people were always there; they would have gathered only at a fixed hour if it had been known.

Some hand down that the queen of Sheba saw in a vision, in the house of a forest called Nethota, the wood of the Lord’s cross [Col. 1579B]. After she had departed from Solomon, she told him that a man would die upon it, and that through his death the Jews would perish and lose both place and nation (John 11). Fearing this, Solomon buried it in the ground where the pool was afterward made. As the time of Christ’s Passion approached, it floated up, as though foretelling Christ; and from that point the movement described above began. But this is not authoritative.

When Jesus healed there a man who had been afflicted for thirty-eight years, he commanded him to take up his pallet; and the man went, carrying it. A *grabatum* is a poor person’s bed, upon which only something is placed under the head; it is said to derive from the Greek *graba*, “head.” It was the Sabbath. “Therefore the Jews said [Col. 1579C]: ‘It is not lawful for you to carry your pallet.’ He answered: ‘He who healed me told me to go and carry it.’ When they asked who he was, he answered: ‘I do not know.’ Later Jesus found him in the Temple and said: ‘You have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.’ Then the man told the Jews that Jesus had healed him.”

## CHAPTER LXXXII. On the Zeal of the Jews Because Christ Called Himself the Son of God

“When they reproached him because he worked on the Sabbath, he said to them: ‘My Father works until now, and I work’” (John 5). It is as though he said: The Father has not worked only for six days, as you think; God always works, governing and renewing, so that the things created may endure. I work with him; therefore what I do is good. It is thus evident that what is said concerning Sabbath rest is sacramental.

Therefore they sought all the more to kill him because he called God his Father. “Jesus said again: ‘The Father loves the Son; the Son gives life to whom he wills; and the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,’” because the Son alone came in the flesh to judge the world—that is, to convict it—and afterward, at the judgment, the person of the Son alone will appear as judge; and whatever sentence is pronounced by the judge, he will pronounce it. He also foretold to them that another—namely Antichrist—would come not in the Father’s name but in his own, and that they would receive him.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. On the Feeding of the Four Thousand and the Seven Loaves

[Col. 1580A]

“Leaving them, he again went along the Sea of Galilee into a desert place. When a great crowd was there, he said to the disciples: ‘I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat.’ Having received seven loaves and a few little fish from the disciples, he commanded them to recline upon the ground” (Matt. 15; Mark 8).

Perhaps at the other feeding, around Passover, grass still covered the ground; but now, because of the heat of that land, there was no longer grass there, for it was after Pentecost, as we said before. When four thousand men, besides women and children, had been filled, they filled seven baskets with the fragments. A *sporta* is a vessel woven from reeds and palm leaves [Col. 1580B].

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. On a Certain Blind Man
“And Jesus, embarking in a boat with his disciples, came to the district of Magedon” (Matt. 16). Mark calls the same place Dalmanutha (Mark 8), because it bore two names; “and the disciples forgot to take bread, and he taught them: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Herod.” When they thought that they had silently been reproved for forgetting the loaves, he rebuked them for the smallness of their faith, because, with him present, they feared that they might lack necessities. According to Mark, he gave sight here to a blind man. But it is enough for us to set down some of the similar matters. We pass over others because they are canonically parallel to these.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. On the confession of faith which Peter made on behalf of all.

[Col. 1580C] “Now Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi” (Matt. 16; Mark 8). Philip established a city for himself on the northern border of Judaea, and called it Caesarea Philippi, in remembrance of Tiberius and of his own name. It lies in the region of Phoenicia, where, at the foot of Lebanon, two springs rise, Jor and Dan; their streams join beneath Mount Gilboa, below the city of Cedar, beside medicinal baths, and form the Jordan. They also, as it were, compose its name from their own names. Jerome, however, said that this city was formerly called Dan, where Jeroboam set up the golden calf, and that the stream flowing past it was called the Jordan, as though named jointly from the spring and the city. That city is now called Paneas.

Josephus says that, one hundred and twenty stadia beyond Caesarea, there is a small lake called Phiala from its roundness, always full and never overflowing. There the Jordan rises; shortly afterward it enters the ground and bubbles up at the foot of Lebanon, as Philip the tetrarch first discovered. For, having thrown straw into Phiala, he found it emerging at Paneas. Thus Josephus calls the spring beneath Lebanon. He also says that above Seleucia a stream rises from a certain lake, which he calls the Lesser Jordan; and that, when the two streams meet at the place called the Golden Temple of Jupiter, the Jordan is formed.

And Jesus asked his disciples, saying: “Whom do people say the Son of Man is?” (Matt. 16). To be the Son of Man belongs to Christ alone. Adam is the son of earth; others are sons of men; Christ alone is the son of one man. [Col. 1581A] They replied: “Some say John the Baptist; others Elijah; others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets”—that is, Elisha. Because Christ baptized, they thought that the Baptist had risen, or that he was one of the two prophets who, in crossing the Jordan, prefigured baptism, namely Elijah and Elisha. They named Jeremiah because he is read to have been sanctified from the womb (Jer. 1).

Augustine: It may seem troubling that Luke says the Lord questioned the disciples when he was alone praying (Luke 9), whereas Mark says that this occurred on the way (Mark 8). But this troubles him because he never prayed on the road. Perhaps he asked twice.

When he had asked them for his own—or their—opinion, Peter spoke for all: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” [Col. 1581B] (Matt. 16), that is: you are man, insofar as you are anointed above your fellows, and you are God, the Son of the living God. The Hebrews customarily call God “living,” in mockery of idols, which do not live.

And Jesus said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona,” that is, Bar-Joanna, “son of John.” Some say that Jona was corruptly written for Joanna through scribal error. And he added: “You are Peter.” What Latins and Greeks call *petra*, “rock,” Hebrews and Syrians call *cepha*. Thus it is the same: “You are Cephas.” “And upon this rock,” from which you are called Peter, “I will build my Church.” Or: upon this rock which you have confessed, which alone is the foundation. And he promised to give him the keys of the kingdom of heaven—perhaps then to him alone, [Col. 1581C] or after the resurrection together with the others.

“Then Jesus commanded his disciples to tell no one that he himself was the Christ.” Here “then” must be understood as “until, once he had risen, they should preach upon the housetops what they had heard in the ear.”

“Then he began to show them that he had to go to Jerusalem, suffer many things, be killed, and rise on the third day.” Peter took him aside and said: “May this be far from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you!” The Greek has: “May you be merciful to yourself, Lord.” The Lord replied: “Get behind me, Satan; you do not savor the things of God,” that is, follow my judgment and do not oppose me. For *Satan* means “adversary.”

There were some who said that Peter was not rebuked, but Satan, who suggested this to him because of his error—namely, because he believed Satan. They also say that the words addressed to him, “Blessed are you,” are only a future promise: “You will be blessed.” Then, having summoned the crowd with his disciples, he said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” The cross is taken up in three ways: through martyrdom, through mortification of the flesh, and through compassion for one’s neighbour.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. On the Lord’s Transfiguration.

“And after six days he took Peter, James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain, Tabor [Note: [Col. 1582C] Addition 1. Mount Tabor is four miles from Nazareth; on its descent Melchizedek met Abraham. Mount Hermon is two miles from Tabor.], that they might pray” (Matt. 17; Mark 9). Luke calls it the eighth day, counting both the day on which he had foretold that some of them would see the glory of the kingdom before they died and the day on which they saw it (Luke 9). Matthew and Mark count only the six intervening days. [Col. 1582A]

It should be noted that Matthew says James was John’s brother. Augustine, writing on the Epistle to the Galatians, says that James the bishop was present at the Transfiguration, and Ambrose too seems to agree [Note: [Col. 1582C] Addition 2. There appears to be a contradiction among the words of the interpreters Augustine, Ambrose, and Matthew. Matthew says that James, the brother of John, the son of Zebedee, who was called the Greater, though younger by birth, was present at the Transfiguration. Augustine seems [Col. 1582D] to contradict this by saying that James the bishop was present. Yet James the Less, son of Alphaeus—namely, he who was also called the Lord’s brother—is read to have been bishop of Jerusalem. This may be resolved as follows: all were bishops, and so there is no contradiction, especially since he does not say “bishop of Jerusalem,” but simply “bishop.” More troubling is what Ambrose says, that he was the first to ascend the priestly throne; this can in no way be understood of James the Greater. Therefore it must be said that it may be understood of the mystical priestly throne, because he was the first to undergo martyrdom. Hence it is said: “He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword” (Acts XVIII).].

“And it came to pass, while he was praying, that he was transfigured before them: his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow, such as no fuller on earth can make. And Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him about the departure which he was to accomplish at Jerusalem,” that is, about his death. Peter said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make here three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” And a voice came from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.”

When the disciples [Col. 1582B] fell down in fear, Jesus touched them and said: “Rise; do not be afraid.” And when he descended, he commanded them to tell no one until he rose again.

Some say that this glory of Christ was in the air surrounding him, not in the body which was then mortal. Others say that he laid mortality aside for a time. Others say that he always possessed such a body by nature, but made it mortal for a time so that it might be seen and might suffer; and that there he showed himself as he was by nature. They say likewise that he gave himself to the disciples as such at the supper, because a body of that kind can be in a small place. But it is vain in such matters to labour and pursue natural explanations for miracles. Thus, in mortal flesh he showed the glory of immortality, just as after the resurrection he showed scars in immortal flesh, offered himself to be touched, [Col. 1582C] and ate [Note: [Col. 1582D] Addition 3. After the resurrection, bodies will possess four qualities: immortality, impassibility, glorification, [Col. 1583A] and agility. And just as before the Passion, in a mortal body, the Lord showed certain signs of immortality—for example, when he gave his body to the disciples—so also after the resurrection he showed certain signs of a mortal body, for example, when he showed Thomas his scars.].

Thus authors hold diverse views about Moses and Elijah. On Luke you will find a gloss which says that they were there. This could be so concerning Elijah, who is still alive. Another view says that angels assumed their bodies.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. On the lunatic.

[Col. 1583A]

“On the following day, at his father’s prayers, he healed the lunatic son, presented to him, whom the disciples could not heal” (Matt. 17). Lunatics do not suffer from a defect of the moon; rather, demons afflict them at these times in order to defame the moon’s Creator through the moon. Let Julian blush, who says that a child has no sin. For it is read of this man that he had been a lunatic from childhood; if the demon had nothing of his own in him, [Col. 1583B] he would not possess him.

When the disciples asked why they themselves had not cast it out, he said: “Because of your unbelief. For if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move.” This may be understood figuratively of the present devil whom he had cast out, since no one is read to have done it literally, except that at the prayers of Gregory of Neocaesarea a certain mountain is recorded as having withdrawn and made room for the construction of a basilica. At the prayers of a certain Father, a stone too was moved from a garden. Or the saying is an example applied to any impossibility. Hence Luke gives another example: “You will say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be transplanted into the sea,’ and it will obey you” (Luke 17).

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On the Lord’s words by which he indicates the three days of his death.

[Col. 1583C] Some Pharisees came to Jesus and said: “Go away from here,” that is, from Galilee, “because Herod seeks to kill you.” And he said to others: “Go, tell that fox: behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am brought to completion” (Luke 13). This means: He will not kill me; rather, I will lay down my life, so that, entering hell on the first day of my death, I may take from the demon his tyranny. On the next day I shall bring forth the captivity, which I shall restore to health when I show it the opened gate of paradise; or I shall place it in paradise, which is at the farthest eastern edge of the sea, as though restoring humanity to the health it had lost. On the third day I shall rise, brought to completion.

This can nevertheless be referred to the three years of Christ’s working of miracles, [Col. 1583D] in the third of which he was brought to completion. And, as though showing that he would not die within Herod’s jurisdiction, Jesus added: “because it does not permit [the scribe supplied *aliqua*] me, a prophet, to perish outside Jerusalem.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. On the tribute found in a fish’s mouth.

When he came to Capernaum, the collectors of the poll-tax approached him; Peter, sent by the Lord to the sea, caught a fish in whose mouth he found a stater—that is, two didrachmas—and paid for himself and for the Lord (Matt. 17). Although the Lord had a money-box, he did not wish to spend for his own use what had been given him for the needs of the poor.

## CHAPTER XC. That the apostles asked which of them was greater.

“When the disciples had asked on the way which of them [Col. 1584A] was greater, they came to Jesus and said: ‘Who do you think is greater in the kingdom of heaven?’” (Matt. 18; Mark 9; Luke 9). They meant: Tell us who is now greater among us, because that same person will be greater in heaven—a point on which they were mistaken. For in the future all precedence of angels and human beings will cease, as the Apostle teaches.

And Jesus, embracing a little child, taught that those like a little child—that is, humble on the way—will be exalted in the homeland; and that whoever wished to be first among them should become the servant of all. Hence the foremost of all in the Church calls himself “servant of the servants of God.” This little child, as some relate, was Martial, apostle of the Lemovices.

## CHAPTER XCI. On the parable of the sheep, the drachma, and the prodigal son.

After he had said that those who cause the little ones to stumble must, by the metaphor of limbs, be cut off and cast away, [Col. 1584B] and that not one of the little ones is to be despised, he told them the parable of the hundredth sheep brought back after the ninety-nine had been left behind, in order to show how precious the little ones are before the Father (Matt. 18). For although the shepherd loves one hundred sheep more than one, he is more concerned for the lost sheep than for those remaining.

For the same purpose he added the parable of the tenth drachma found. A drachma is a coin of fixed value bearing the image of a king. A drachma is one fourth of a stater [Note: [Col. 1584C] Addition 1. *Dragma, dragmatis* is a kind of poem, of which it is said: “The sweet songs of the *dragmatis*.” *Drama*, without *g*, is a song for performers; the *Song of Love* was written in this form. It is also declined by some as *dramis*, by others as *dramatis*.].

He next adds a third parable on the same subject, that of the prodigal son, in which he shows not only his joy over the return of the little ones but also rebukes the grumbling of the envious. In it he calls the husks the food of swine. According to some, this is the fruit [Col. 1584C] of a tree that makes a sound when eaten. It is a kind of legume with noisy, hollow leaves, which burdens rather than nourishes. Note that what is called *altile* in birds is called *saginatum*, “fattened,” in animals.

## CHAPTER XCII. On forgiving one’s brother seventy times seven.

After the Lord had added instructions concerning rebuking a brother who had sinned against you alone—that is, with you alone knowing: first in private, then before witnesses, then before the Church—and had added, “Whatever you bind upon [Col. 1584D] earth,” etc., Peter asked whether a sinning brother should be forgiven as many as seven times. Jesus answered: rather, “seventy times seven,” that is, four hundred and ninety times—and also “seventy times seven,” that is, every injury (Matt. 18).

“Seventy times seven” is to be read twice: the first exposition refers to time, as though he said, “You will always forgive”; the second to every injury, because seventy-seven [Note: [Col. 1584D] Addition 1. Seven is called the number of universality because the whole course of days runs through the seven days of the week. Eleven is called the number of transgression because it exceeds ten by one and does not reach twelve, which again is a good number with respect [Col. 1585A] to the things signified. Note that everyone is bound to put away inward resentment for an injury, even if the one who harmed him does not ask forgiveness. But if he asks, I am bound to greet him with “hail” and to assist him if he is in need—a thing I am not bound to do unless he asks, unless I am perfect. The Lord indirectly showed through the parable of the servant that one must forgive a petitioner: the servant’s lord recalled his debt because he had refused to have mercy on his fellow servant.] is composed from the number of universality and the number of transgression—that is, from seven and eleven.

## CHAPTER XCIII. That a wife may be dismissed only for fornication.

[Col. 1585A]

After these sayings, Jesus departed from Galilee and came into Judaea beyond the Jordan. Galileans followed him, and he healed them there. Pharisees came to him, testing him, and said: “Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any [Col. 1585B] reason?” (Matt. 19). The Lord told them that God instituted marriage and that therefore a human being may not separate it. For the Lord also willed that a man should cling to his wife, leaving father and mother on her account (Gen. 2), that is, a person should direct his affection more toward the begetting of children than toward care for parents.

For just as moisture rises from the roots into the tree and is transmitted into seed, and does not return to the roots, so affection is transmitted from parents to children and does not turn back: that is, the affection of parents toward children is greater and more ready than that of children toward parents.

When they objected that Moses had permitted a bill of divorce (Deut. 24), and he said that this had been allowed because of hardness of their hearts—that is, it was not punished by any law, for Moses would not place himself above the ordinance [Col. 1585C] of God—he added that, except in the case of fornication, a man may not dismiss his wife. Hearing this, the disciples said that it is not expedient to marry.

Lest they should suppose all continence to be meritorious, the Lord distinguished eunuchs: some are born such, who are properly called castrated—that is, born chaste; others are made so by people, who are properly called *spadones*, from *spata*; others castrate themselves for the kingdom of God, who are properly called eunuchs, that is, “good conquerors,” from *eu*, “good,” and *nuche*, “victory.” This last kind is meritorious.

After he had laid hands upon the children presented to him and blessed them, he departed from there.

## CHAPTER XCIV. On the Galileans whom Pilate killed.

[Col. 1585D] “After these things Jesus was walking in Galilee, because they sought to kill him in Judaea” (John 7). At that time some were present who reported to him about Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. For a certain man, calling himself the Son of God, had led astray many Galileans. When he led them to Gerizim, where he said he would ascend to heaven before them while they sacrificed to him, Pilate came upon them and killed him with all the others, fearing that he might lead the Jews astray as well.

When they thought that these men had perished because they were more wicked than the other Galileans, the Lord said that the Jews were no less criminal and would perish in the same way unless they repented; likewise the Jerusalemites would perish unless they repented, as the eighteen men of Siloam had formerly perished when they were crushed by the tower they were building. Concerning this he gave [Col. 1586A] them the parable of the fig tree bearing no fruit, for which the vine-dresser scarcely obtained a year’s reprieve so that it might not be burned, until he tested it (Luke 13).

## CHAPTER XCV. On the bent woman.

While he was teaching in the synagogue on the Sabbath, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity. A spirit of infirmity—elsewhere called Satan—had bent her over for eighteen years. He laid his hands upon her and she stood upright (Luke 13).

## CHAPTER XCVI. On the Feast of Tabernacles.

“Now the Feast of Tabernacles was near” (John 7), a term meaning “the pitching of booths.” “His brothers said to him: ‘Go over into Judaea, so that your disciples, who gather there from every quarter, may see the works which you do. If you do these things, show yourself to the world’”—as though saying, “If you do them of yourself and not through [Col. 1586B] Beelzebub”; or *if* may mean *because*.

These were Jesus’ kinsmen, who sought his glory in order to share in it. He said to them: “You go up to this feast-day,” that is, to the first day. He himself went up in the middle of the festival, but as though in secret. The Jews, however, sought him, saying: “Where is that man?” “And there was murmuring about him, because some said: ‘He is good’; others, that he was a deceiver.” When he went up, he taught in the Temple; and they murmured, saying: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?” Some said: “Is this not the Christ?” Others said: “We know where this man is from; but when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.” They said this because Isaiah had said: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). “But many from the crowd believed in [Col. 1586C] him, saying: ‘When Christ comes, will he perform more signs than this man does?’” — “And someone from the crowd said to him: ‘Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.’ He answered: ‘Man, who appointed me judge over you?’” (Luke 12).

## CHAPTER XCVII. That those sent to seize Jesus marvelled at his words.

“Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him. And Jesus said: ‘You seek me, and you will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come’” (John 1). As though he said: Such people as you will not come to me; but after the resurrection many will wish to find me bodily, if that were possible, and will not find me—yet they will find me by faith.

“Some said: ‘This is truly the Prophet’; others: ‘This is the Christ.’ [Col. 1586D] When the officers returned to the chief priests and Pharisees, and they said to the officers, ‘Why have you not brought him?’, they answered: ‘No man has ever spoken as this man speaks.’ The Pharisees rebuked them, saying: ‘Have you also been deceived? Which of the rulers or Pharisees has believed in him?’ Nicodemus said: ‘Our law judges no one unless it has first heard from him himself.’” He believed that if they patiently heard him, as he himself had done, they would become like the officers.

“And they said to him: ‘Are you also a Galilean?’” That is, “Are you deceived by a Galilean?” “Search the Scriptures: no prophet rises from Galilee.”

## CHAPTER XCVIII. On the adulteress.

“Jesus again came early in the morning into the Temple, [Col. 1587A] and, sitting, taught the people. The scribes and Pharisees brought to him a woman caught in adultery and asked what he judged ought to be done with her” (John 8). They supposed that in judging the Lord would become either unmerciful or unjust, so that they might mock him as unmerciful or condemn him as acting against Moses.

“But Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground. When they persisted, he raised himself and said: ‘Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her.’ Then he bent down again and wrote.” What did he write? Some say what he answered them. Jerome, in a certain letter to Studius, appears to maintain that he wrote: “Earth, earth, write these men down as rejected”; or, in the letter to Irenaeus: “Earth accuses earth.”

“But when they heard this, they went out [Col. 1587B] one by one, and Jesus was left alone by them, with the woman standing in the midst of the disciples. He dismissed her without condemnation, saying: ‘Go, and sin no more.’” Note that, standing upright, he gave the sentence of justice; likewise, standing upright, the sentence of mercy. For it belongs equally to God both to have mercy and to punish, since every action of Christ is a lesson for the Christian.

## CHAPTER XCIX. On the parable of the rich man wishing to enlarge his barns, and on certain sayings of the Lord.

“Then he said to them: ‘Beware of all greed’” (Luke 12), since human life is short. On this subject he gave them the parable of the rich man who, because of the abundance of his crops, considered enlarging his barns. God said to him: “Fool, this night they will demand [Col. 1587C] your soul from you; and whose will be the things you have prepared?”

“Again Jesus spoke many things to them: ‘I am the light of the world; I bear witness concerning myself,’” etc. (John 8). In the course of these things he plainly declared himself to be the Son of God; said that they would die in their sin; that they would know who he was when they raised him from the earth; that they were neither children of God nor of Abraham; that Abraham would see his day; and he added: “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” He alone truly is, who, before anything came to be, could truly say: “I am.”

The Jews therefore took stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the Temple. Note that the Jews said: “You are not yet fifty years old.” Some have supposed that more years elapsed from the Lord’s incarnation to his passion [Col. 1587D] than we gather from the histories.

## CHAPTER C. On the man blind from birth.

“And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. Having made mud with saliva and anointed his eyes, he sent him to the pool of Siloam [Note: [Col. 1588B] Addition 1. In the valley of Jehoshaphat, according to Syrian tradition; Siloam flows beneath the earth], and he washed and saw” (John 9). Siloam is a spring at the foot of Mount Zion. It does not bubble forth with continual waters but at uncertain times; a kind of reservoir was constructed not far from the spring to receive its waters. Scripture calls this collection sometimes a pool, sometimes a bathing-place.

“Now it was the Sabbath.” Therefore, after the Pharisees heard from the man who had received sight that Jesus had given him sight, they said: “Give glory to God. This man is not from God, since he does not keep the Sabbath.” When he commended Jesus and added, [Col. 1588A] “Do you also wish to become his disciples?”, they cursed him and said: “You may be that man’s disciple; but we are disciples of Moses. We do not know where this man is from”—that is, “we do not approve of him.” For above they had said that they knew him.

They thought Jesus accursed, and all who believed in him accursed. “And when they had cast him out, Jesus found him. When he told him that he was the Son of God, he worshipped him. And Jesus said to him: ‘For judgment I came into the world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.’” That is: By giving you, a blind man, sight, understand that I came to separate the poor in spirit from the proud, who boast that they are learned, so that the former may be enlightened and the latter—that is, the self-styled learned—may incur blindness of mind.

## CHAPTER CI. On the marks of perfection and the impossibility of a rich man’s entering the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 1588B]

“As Jesus was going out on the road, a young man knelt and asked him: ‘What shall I do to have eternal life?’ When he had commanded him to keep the commandments and heard that he had kept them, he taught him concerning perfection and proposed one mark of perfection, saying: ‘Go, sell everything that you have, and come, follow me’” (Matt. 19; Mark 10; Luke 18).

There is the perfection of prelates, whose mark is to leave everything and lay down one’s life for the sheep. There is also the perfection of contemplatives, whose mark is to desire death and to endure life [Col. 1588C] patiently. There is also the perfection of clerics, whose mark is continence.

“Hearing this, the young man went away sorrowful, for he was very wealthy and rich. Then Jesus said to his disciples: ‘It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.’” Here “easier” signifies less by the positive degree of its opposite—that is, it is less difficult because it is less impossible. For God can make a camel pass through the eye of a needle, nothing preventing it. But to place in glory the greedy person, meant here by “rich man,” he cannot do by justice, though he can by power.

Do not be surprised at degrees of comparison among impossibilities. For it is more impossible for a horse to be changed into a stone than into a donkey, which is naturally more akin to it [Col. 1588D] than a stone is. Some said that there was in Jerusalem a small gate called the Needle. When camels came to it by the short route, they could not pass or enter it with their loads; unloaded, they passed through, and, after taking up their burdens again, continued on their way. According to this view, therefore, the comparison signifies not impossibility but analogy. For the greedy person must abandon love of wealth if he wishes to enter life.

That he meant the greedy person under the name “rich man” is evident from the disciples’ addition: “Who, then, can be saved?” For the poor are more numerous than the rich, and thus more can be saved if he had meant possessors of wealth. “Jesus said to them: ‘With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.’” [Col. 1589A] Not that God can save such people as they are, but that he can justify them and then save them.

## CHAPTER CII. That those who leave everything for Christ will judge.

“Then Peter said: ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what therefore will be for us?’” (Matt. 19). Supply: “to leave behind?” For Peter had left all those things of which it was said: “And all is vanity” (Eccl. 1). But he had retained for himself all those things of which it was said: “God is all in all” (1 Cor. 15).

“And Jesus answered: ‘When the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty in the regeneration, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.’” The first regeneration occurs in baptism in the soul; the second will occur at judgment [Col. 1589B] in the body. There those who despise the world will judge with the Lord, not only by cooperation but also by authority. The number twelve is used to signify fullness of power, and the twelve tribes of Israel signify all who are to be judged. For twelve arises from seven, the number of universality—that is, from the parts of seven multiplied into themselves.

Some, however, say that this was said only to the disciples and has already been fulfilled in the world’s subjection, because they sit as though possessing authority over the whole Church. Afterward the discourse was addressed generally to all: “Everyone who leaves house or parents, etc., will receive a hundredfold,” now in this present time, and in the future, “eternal life.” For besides spiritual things, which are as a hundredfold in comparison with carnal things, holy people love other holy people even more than their own relatives.

## CHAPTER CIII. On the rich man and Lazarus.

The Pharisees, hearing him dispute about contempt for the world, mocked him (Luke 16), because the Law promised earthly goods to its observers. But he set before them, against their greed, the example of the rich man, clothed in purple and a feaster, who was tormented in hell because he had received his good things in his lifetime—that is, only those things which he had thought good.

This was not a parable but an actual event, as may be inferred because the beggar is named there, namely Lazarus, who was placed in Abraham’s bosom. For in the upper border of hell there was a place having some light and entirely without material punishment, in which were the souls of the predestined [Col. 1589D] until Christ’s descent into hell. Because of its tranquility this place was called Abraham’s bosom, just as we speak of a mother’s bosom. It was called Abraham’s because he was the first way of faith: he was the first publicly to proclaim that there is only one God.

Job called this place darkness because of the weariness of waiting, saying: “In darkness I have spread my bed” (Job 17). Note that the rich man said that he was tormented in his tongue, that is, for the sin of his tongue, since feasters are usually talkative. Nor is it surprising if the soul is metaphorically said to have limbs, since the Godhead is distinguished by limbs in the same trope. Some nevertheless said that angels and souls have aerial bodies; otherwise souls would not feel burning fire, as you will find in the commentary on Genesis. Others say [Col. 1590A] that bodies are unnecessary for feeling the burning of fire: there is a certain kind of fire such that, if you put your hand upon it, you feel heat without any injury to the hand.

That Abraham said a *chaos* had been fixed between them—or *chaus*, as the old codices have it—perhaps was literally so, or signifies the perpetual dissimilarity of the good and the evil after this life. When the rich man asked that Lazarus be sent to his brothers, he heard: “They have Moses and the prophets.” Hence it is inferred that he was a Jew, for which reason too perhaps Abraham called him son, and he called Abraham father.

## CHAPTER CIV. On the steward of iniquity.

Jesus set before the disciples the parable of the steward of iniquity (Luke 16). A steward is the keeper of a private estate, but here it is taken to mean an administrator. Fearing dismissal and poverty, he secretly showed mercy to his master’s debtors, so that when he was cast out they might remember his benefits and receive him into their houses.

And the Lord praised the steward of iniquity, not because he had acted unjustly, but because he had acted prudently. Prudence is a kind of provision for oneself in the future. From this the Lord drew an argument as from the lesser case, saying: If one who provides for himself in the future, even with deceit, is praised, then “make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal tabernacles.” As though he said: How much more praiseworthy will you be if you provide for yourselves without deceit.

*Mammon* means “riches” in the Syrian language, and *mammos* is Satan, who deceives through wealth. They are called riches “of iniquity” [Col. 1590C] because they are commonly gathered through injustice. Hence the common saying: “Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.” Some, misunderstanding this, seize goods in order to dispense them well. But one who offers sacrifice from the substance of a poor person does the same as if he sacrificed a son in his father’s sight.

Or it may be explained thus: in this saying the Lord provides for us both here and in the future, as though saying: Reserve from your goods what is needed for the comfort of life. From what is superfluous, make friends for yourselves. For whatever is retained beyond life’s necessities and not distributed to the needs of one’s neighbour is money of iniquity—that is, against equity. For in it we do not observe the equity we owe our neighbour, whom we are bound to love as ourselves.

Note [Col. 1590D] that not all poor people can receive us into eternal tabernacles; rather, because we give to them, we shall be received by angels. Nevertheless, it is good, when we can, to choose good poor people.

And the Lord added: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many stripes; but the one who did not know will be beaten with few” (Luke 12). Many therefore turn away their ear lest they hear God’s word, but such people are judged not ignorant, but contemptuous.

## CHAPTER CV. On the daily denarius.

Then the Lord set before them the parable of the householder who hired labourers for his vineyard, at a daily denarius (Matt. 20). Although only five hours of the day are there enumerated, nevertheless all six ages, both of time and of human life, are understood. For in the eleventh hour the fifth and sixth age, or millennium, is understood; likewise old age and decrepitude. For the uniformity of the denarius signifies the same eternity. No one’s life there will be shorter or more abundant than another’s; rather, the same “God [will be] all in all” (1 Cor. 15) is signified in it.

Concerning the murmuring of those who receive it, it may be said that there will not be the murmuring of the envious there, but that of those marvelling at the greatness of the reward. For *murmur* is sometimes taken to mean a confused sound of voices. Or the murmuring may be referred to the present state, while the question why He had made them equal in glory belongs to the future. For they will then at last know the reason for Christ’s delay in glory—a matter on account of which the ancients could murmur—which they never knew: namely, lest they should be glorified without you. But the Lord expressed their amazement, once that same reason had become known, interrogatively: “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will?” Then, concluding the parable, He said: “Thus the last shall be first, and the first last”: that is, Jews and Gentiles will be made equal in entering the kingdom of heaven, because no one entered before the seventh age of those at rest, which begins fully at the Ascension.

> [Note: Col. 1591D, Addition 1. Although it began causally in the Passion, it was nevertheless consummated at the Ascension; just as a sick man, having taken medicine, possesses the cause of health but is not yet wholly well.]

In the resurrection of bodies, too, the elect of whatever age—whether of time or of human life—will be made equal, unless perhaps a few rise beforehand, as though privileged. Yet some say that the words read in this parable, “Is thine eye evil?” and at its end, “Many are called, but few chosen,” refer to those labouring in the vineyard: all the faithful of whatever time or age [Col. 1591C]. Of these, some are good and others evil; and they understand those who receive with murmuring to be the evil, who suppose that they will receive more, and that because they were earlier in the Church, or in time, or in rank, they will also receive more than others. Of these the Prophet says: “A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand” (Ps. 90). And the Lord says in the Gospel that He will say to such persons: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25).

Although the discourse may appear also to concern the same persons, namely those receiving the denarius, nevertheless, according to Tyconius’s rule, different persons are being discussed there: those who receive, and those who do not receive but suppose that they will receive. But now they will neither suppose it nor receive it. Or there may be syneresis: for if the first wished to murmur, their murmuring could reasonably be restrained.

## Chapter CVI. On the Dropsical Man, and the Exhortation to Humility and Mercy

“And it came to pass, when on the Sabbath he ate bread in the house of a certain chief Pharisee, that there was before him a dropsical man” (Luke 14). Dropsy is a watery, subcutaneous humour arising from a disorder of the bladder, accompanied by swelling and foul breath. The Pharisees were watching Jesus to see whether He would heal on the Sabbath. When He asked them whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath and they were silent, He took hold of the sick man and healed him. Afterwards [Col. 1592A] He proved that healing was lawful, because an animal that has fallen into a pit is drawn out on the Sabbath day.

It was strange that they accused Him concerning healings on the Sabbath. For in their traditions they have approximately eighty specified classes of works from which one must abstain on the Sabbath; among them healing is not included, especially healing done by a word alone, as the Lord often healed. He also spoke a parable to those invited: “When thou art invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place.” Against the pride of the Pharisees He taught humility. Note that this is not a parable, but rather an example of one act to be done humbly. Because it is put forward in order that other things may be done after its likeness, it is called a parable: as it were, a likeness in an example.

But He exhorted the man who had invited Him [Col. 1592B] to mercy, saying: “When thou makest a dinner, do not invite thy relatives and the rich, but the poor.” He does not condemn invitations to friends, but the intention of living or eating luxuriously and of inviting one another again in return, from what the Lord says here: “For it shall be repaid thee in the resurrection of the just.” And one of those reclining added: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.” Cerinthus erred in saying that there would also be bodily refreshment there, just as man was created immortal, though not without the nourishment of food.

## Chapter CVII. How at the Feast of Dedication the Jews Wished to Stone Jesus

“Now the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem, and it was winter” (John 10). *Encaenia* is said as though *enchaenea*, from *neos*, “new”; it denotes renewals, and has an intensive sense, because it signifies a transfer upward: namely, when a house, vessel, or garment is transferred from common use to solemn and divine use. In Latin this is called a dedication. The Hebrew, however, calls a dedication the beginning of the use of a new thing—for example, when we first inhabit a new house or put on a new garment.

Here *Encaenia* is the feast of the dedication of the Temple, held annually. This feast did not pertain to the first or second dedication of the Temple, but to the third. The first was in autumn, for Solomon dedicated the Temple on the tenth day of September; and until the destruction of that Temple, two feasts were held each year on the same day: dedication and expiation. But when the Temple was rebuilt by those returning from Babylon, it was dedicated in spring, on 12 March, that is, the twelfth lunar day. When Antiochus Epiphanes had polluted the Temple with the filth of idols and profaned its vessels, Judas Maccabaeus, son of Asamonaeus, of priestly stock, cleansed the Temple, restored the vessels to their places, and as it were dedicated it on 25 December. This dedication was observed in winter in the days of Jesus. Perhaps it is still the Feast of Lights among the Jews, since Josephus also testifies that, even under the Maccabees, this day was called the Day of Lights.

“And Jesus walked in the Temple, in Solomon’s porch.” The porch of the Temple is often called by the name of the Temple, as here; for only ministers of the Temple went up into the Temple itself [Col. 1593A]. That porch was formerly called Solomon’s Temple, in which he was accustomed to stand in prayer, and in which, on the day of dedication, he set up a bronze column above which he prayed with bent knees, although the Jews usually stand when they pray.

“And the Jews said: How long dost thou take away our souls? If thou art the Christ, tell us plainly.” They asked this because, if He called Himself Christ, they might arrest Him as one setting Himself up against Augustus. Therefore Christ moderated His reply, saying: “I speak to you, and ye believe not; the works which I do bear witness of me.” And when He had said, “I and the Father are one,” the Jews took up stones to throw at Him. When they said that they wished to stone Him for blasphemy because, [Col. 1593B] being a man, He made Himself God, He said that Scripture calls men gods, as in: “I said, Ye are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81). Therefore, much more may He whom the Father sent into the world be called God—although “the man God” and “the Word God” are said in different senses. By this ambiguity of the name He softened their anger. “Therefore they sought to seize Him, and He went out of their hands and went beyond the Jordan, where John had first been baptizing.”

## Chapter CVIII. On the Resurrection of Lazarus

“Now there was a certain sick man, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and Martha. And when He received word from the sisters that Lazarus was sick, He said: This sickness is not unto death” (John 11), that is, not to keep him in death; “and He remained two days in the same place,” namely until four days should be completed.

“Then He said to the disciples: Let us go into Judaea again. They said: The Jews wanted to stone thee, and dost thou go there again?” Jesus said that He was as it were the day, and they as the twelve hours; therefore they need not fear to go with Him. Note that if Judas was still good, then he was an hour of the day; but if he was already evil, this was said with Matthias, who replaced him, in his stead. It is also said otherwise, as though He were saying: You think that the Jews persist in their wish to stone Me. As the hours are changeable, so too are human dispositions; indeed, the human heart changes more often in a day than the hours do. And he who walks in the day—that is, in peace, as do I and you—does not strike against anyone; therefore let us go securely.

And He added: “Lazarus is dead, and I rejoice for your sakes that I was not there,” because, when He reports to them things occurring at a distance, their faith is strengthened. Jesus therefore returned to Bethany with His disciples.

> [Note: Col. 1594A, Addition 1. Bethany is only fifteen stadia from Jerusalem.]

Martha met Him outside the village. Having called Mary, and with many Jerusalemites present who had come to console the sisters, they came to the tomb; and at Jesus’ voice Lazarus was not only raised, but came forth, though bound with bands. Many Jews therefore went to the Pharisees and reported what they had seen.

> [Note: Col. 1594A, Addition 2. Behold a double miracle: the dead man was raised, and at Jesus’ voice he walked freely, as though unbound.]

The report of Him was famous among the Jews. For many had already gone up for the feast [Col. 1594A] in order to sanctify themselves. This is believed to have happened on the day read in Lent, namely the preceding Friday. These are the days: namely, the first day of the first month, according to the law.

## Chapter CIX. How the Chief Priests and Jews Conspired against Jesus

“Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council and said: What are we doing? If we let Him go on thus, all will believe in Him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11). [Col. 1594B] As though they said: This place is held venerable and holy among the nations, because Alexander, Pompey, and others revered it, as did the kings of Persia and Egypt. But this man teaches that our sacred rites are to be abolished and are vain. Therefore, knowing the Temple’s wealth and hearing that it may be taken with impunity, the Romans will take it away.

“Then Caiaphas, because he was high priest that year, determined what ought to be done, saying: It is expedient for you that one man should die, and not the whole nation perish.” And he prophesied, though unknowingly, Christ’s death as beneficial to humankind. “Therefore from that day they planned to kill Him.”

> [Note: Col. 1594C, Addition 1. Since He was now destined for death, from the very Sabbath on which they had assembled the council we begin the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, especially in the hymns; and we omit “Glory be to the Father” in the responsories and in the Introit of the Mass, though not yet completely, because the Lord had not yet been handed into the hands of the executioners.]

Indeed, they arranged that He should be brought to Jerusalem when found. “Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among them, but went near the wilderness, to a city [Col. 1594C] called Ephraim.”

## Chapter CX. On the Lord’s Final Coming into Jerusalem

> [Note: Col. 1593. All speak of this ascent except John.]

And it came to pass, when the days of His Assumption were being fulfilled, that He set His face steadfastly to go to Jerusalem. By Jesus’ Assumption Luke means not only the time when He was to be taken from this world to the Father, but also according to the command regarding the Paschal lamb, which was taken from the flock on the tenth day of the first month [Col. 1594D] and kept until the fourteenth day. In this manner Jesus came to the place of the Passion on the tenth day, that is, on Palm Sunday, and remained there until He suffered.

## Chapter CXI. On the Ten Lepers

“And it came to pass, as He went to Jerusalem, that He passed through the midst of Galilee and Samaria. And as He entered a certain village, ten leprous men met Him, saying: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. And He answered: Go, show yourselves to the priests. And as they went, they were cleansed.
