One of them, when he saw that he was cleansed, returned and worshipped Jesus, magnifying God. And he was a Samaritan” (Luke 17).

> [Note: Col. 1595A, Addition 1. The unity of the Church alone falls upon its face in worship. Hence, on non-feast days we conclude the Hours prostrate—if not upon the ground, at least upon the mat—where four things are signified: bodily weakness, because we are taken from dust; weakness of soul, because we cannot raise ourselves; shame, because we dare not lift our eyes to heaven; and prudence, because we see where we fall, that is, we are afflicted in earthly things. And we see why. In private prayers we sometimes pray, like Solomon, with bent knees but uplifted face, as though saying: “Draw me after thee” (Song 1). Sometimes we stand, as though saying: “We shall go rejoicing into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121). Thus in the first posture we express our condition, in the second our desire, in the third our hope.]

Those who did not return were Jews; in this the perfidy of the Jews is indicated.

## Chapter CXII. On the Samaritans’ Refusal of Hospitality to the Lord

[Col. 1595B]

When He had sent messengers ahead of Him into a city of the Samaritans, they did not receive Him in lodging (Luke 9). For the Samaritans envied those going to worship in Jerusalem, because they said that prayer ought to be made on Mount Gerizim on account of the prophets. Angered, James and John said: “Wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” And the Lord rebuked them. Such vengeance as is praised in Elijah is condemned in these men, because he sought it from charity, but they from anger.

## Chapter CXIII. On the Request of the Sons of Zebedee

[Col. 1595C]

Taking the twelve again apart, He said: Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and the prophecies concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled (Matt. 20; Mark 10). For He shall be delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, spat upon, crucified, and shall rise on the third day. Hearing this, the sons of Zebedee, thinking that Jesus’ kingdom in Israel was at hand, prompted their mother to ask Him for an unnamed favour; once it was granted, she was to add: “Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at thy right hand and the other at thy left, in thy kingdom.”

But Jesus did not answer the mother, but those petitioning through their mother: “Ye know not what ye ask.” As though He said: You seek precedence in heaven, where there shall be none. And you seek wrongly: for you wish to reign, though you have not deserved it. [Col. 1595D] “Can ye drink the cup which I am about to drink, or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” They said to Him: “We can.”

> [Note: Cols. 1596B–C, Addition 1. A *calix* is a cup from which we take a hot drink, that is, a beverage which warms: such as wine, beer, mead, and the like, which warm the human body. A *scyphus* is called a vessel from which we take drink that is poured over food merely to soften it, such as plain water, which does not nourish but carries the solid substance of food through the limbs. This is the proper difference between a *scyphus* and a *calix*.]

The cup signifies suffering; baptism signifies death, and is so called from the likeness of wool being dipped. For as wool is dipped and acquires the quality of some colour, so we descend bodily into death and shall rise spiritually. Literally, a cup is a *scyphus* from which we take a hot drink. Macrobius Theodosius says that a *scyphus* is a vessel which the Cilicians invented and called *cilicem*, now called *calix* by changing the letter *i* to *a*.

> [Note: Col. 1596C, Addition 2. Moreover, the Cilicians are a people whose land is exceedingly hot. They invented a certain sort of vessel against the heat, called in Greek *cilicos*; by changing *i* to *a*, it was called *calicos*.]

Cassiodorus, in his exposition of the Psalms, says that a cup is called suffering because it is drunk according to measure: “God is faithful, who does not permit us to be tempted above that which we are able [to bear]” (1 Cor. 10). For a cup is a *scyphus* [Col. 1596A] by which drink is distributed to those drinking in measured portions. According to this distinction between cup and baptism, the Lord rightly added: “Ye shall indeed drink my cup,” and said nothing about baptism. For John endured not martyrdom but many sufferings near death. Others, however, take both cup and baptism in the same sense, namely martyrdom. They say that John was a martyr in intention, because martyrdom did not fail him in intention, and because he was cast into a vat of boiling oil. Jerome says similarly concerning monks: Monks ought to possess the purity of martyrs, for they too are martyrs.

And Jesus added: “But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give to you”—understand, to such men as you are, because you are ambitious. Or, “to you,” as it were, on account of us: that is, because you are my kinsmen. “For God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10): namely, He does not regard someone’s person without merits in granting eternal salvation. When the ten were indignant against the two brothers, the Lord taught both these and those that they would not come to the kingdom except through humility; and He gave Himself as their example, saying: “The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve.” Since man fell through pride, he must return to his own country by another road. To signify this, the lord pope returns in processions by a different way from that by which he went out.

## Chapter CXIV. On Zacchaeus and the Man Previously Given Sight

[Col. 1596C]

Before He entered Jericho, He gave sight to one blind man; and, entering, He passed through Jericho (Luke [Col. 1596D] 18). Zacchaeus, however, chief of the tax collectors, because he was short, climbed a sycamore tree in order to see Jesus passing by (Luke 19). The sycamore is called the wild fig: in its leaves it resembles the mulberry, and in other respects the fig. Hence it is called, as it were, *sycomorus*; but it surpasses in height, whence it is also called *celsa* (“lofty”) by the Latins.

“Jesus said to him: Zacchaeus, come down, because today I must stay in thy house. And he came down and received Him joyfully into his house.” Then Zacchaeus, giving half his goods to the poor, retained half in order to restore from it fourfold to those whom he had defrauded; things were restored twofold or fourfold according to the Law, as was said above. “And Jesus said: Today salvation has come to this house, because Zacchaeus himself has been made a son of Abraham”—not born one, namely, not according to flesh but according to faith.

> [Note: Col. 1597A, Addition 1. Salvation comes to Zacchaeus as he descends. The Jews, still standing on high, pray and hold the chief seats in their synagogues. The Church descends, and its elders become last in the choir and in processions.]

## Chapter CXV. On the Two Blind Men of Jericho

And as He went out from Jericho, a great crowd followed Him (Mark 10). For few dared to enter the wilderness because of robbers. And behold, two blind men were sitting by the way, one of whom was Bartimaeus, that is, son of Timaeus. When they cried, “Son of David, have mercy on us,” and were rebuked to be silent, they cried the more. Jesus stopped, and having called them to Himself [Col. 1597B], touched their eyes; and immediately they saw and followed Him.

## Chapter CXVI. On the Alabaster Vessel of Ointment

Jesus therefore came to Bethany six days before Passover, namely on the Sabbath before Palm Sunday. This was the sixth day before Passover if one counts that day itself and Passover Day, with four intervening days; and He was in the house of Simon the leper (Matt. 26; Mark 14; John 12). Simon had been a leper and was healed by the Lord, but his former name nevertheless remained, just as Matthew is still called the tax collector. Many Jews came there, having assembled for the feast, not only because of Jesus but also to see Lazarus who had been raised. Therefore the chief priests planned to kill Lazarus.

They made Him [Col. 1597C] a supper, and Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining. As Augustine says in *On the Words of the Lord*, when the guests asked about the places of punishments and the seats of hell, Lazarus described them in a detailed account. Thus they at last found a betrayer of hell, which had for long ages been unknown.

Mary had an alabaster of nard ointment: that is, an alabaster box full of nard ointment. As we say a cup of wine, a cup of milk, and the like, so this woman is said to have an alabaster of ointment. Alabaster is a kind of white, translucent marble, varied with intermingled colours, which keeps ointments unspoiled. Nard is an aromatic shrub, with a thick but short, black, brittle root; it has the scent of cypress, very small and dense leaves, and its tops spread out into spikes. Sellers of spices prize the spikes and leaves of nard; hence, in commendation of the ointment, Mark calls it “precious spikenard.” For it was Indian nard; other kinds of nard are cheap. John specified its quality, saying: “A pound of ointment of *nardus pistica*.”

> [Note: Col. 1598C, Addition 1. Or *pistica*, that is, mixed, prepared from spikes and leaves, which is more precious, as Bede says on Mark. Perhaps *pyxis* signifies a mixture, whence *pyxis, pyxidis* (“box”).]

That is, genuine; for *pisteuo* means “I believe” and *pistis* is called “faith,” since it was uncorrupted by any adulterating admixture. Some, however, think that *pisticum* was named from a place. Mary broke, or opened, the alabaster and poured the ointment upon Jesus’ head; she also anointed His feet and wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.

Because Mary anointed the Lord’s feet with ointment on that same day, in memory of this event the lord pope is said to distribute alms to many [Col. 1598A] poor people on the same Sabbath. For the feet of the Lord seated in heaven are still walking on earth. Occupied with this distribution, on that day he does not go out to any church, whereas on the other days of Lent he makes a station in order to celebrate Mass.

> [Note: Cols. 1598C–D, Addition 2. Nevertheless, in certain sacramentaries one reads: “Station at Saint Peter’s.” It may be called vacant because it has no proper antiphon for the Introit, but that of the preceding day is repeated.]

Hence in ancient graduals one reads in the rubric: “The Sabbath is vacant, because the lord pope gives alms.” And in the Roman capitulary of the Gospels, for Friday, leavened bread is given in the Lateran consistory. Do not be troubled if you find Sundays called vacant for another reason.

Judas Iscariot was indignant, as though the ointment had been wasted, although it could have been sold for three hundred denarii and given to the needy. Others also were indignant and said: “Why has this waste of ointment been made?” These, indeed, were indignant for the poor, by whose words Judas perhaps had been persuaded. But Judas was indignant for gain, because he was a thief and, having the Lord’s money-box, carried what was put into it—that is, he not only bore it but carried it away. For he had a wife and children, as is written of him: “Let his children be orphaned and his wife a widow,” etc. (Ps. 108). He gave to his wife and children what he stole.

“And Jesus said to them: Why do ye trouble this woman? She has wrought a good work upon me; she did it for my burial.” As though He said: It is not waste, but the office of burial. John says: “Let her alone, that she may keep it for the day of my burial.” Mark, as though explaining this, says: “What she had”—that is, what she could—“she did; for she has anticipated anointing my body for burial,” understand, to be laid [Col. 1598C] there. As though He said: Let her do while I live, while she can, what she will wish to do when I am dead but will be unable to do. Perhaps, though unknowingly, the woman thus anticipated the anointing for burial by the Holy Spirit. “Then Jesus said: This work shall be remembered wherever this Gospel is preached”; and He aptly said, “this Gospel,” for the Gospels had not yet been written.

## Chapter CXVII. On the Cursing of the Fig Tree and the Riding upon the Ass’s Colt

[Col. 1598D]

When morning came, Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, and His disciples with Him (Matt. 21; Mark 11; Luke 19; John 12). And when He came to Bethphage, a hamlet of priests on the side of the Mount of Olives, He sent two of His disciples into the village opposite them—that is, into Jerusalem—to bring Him an ass and her colt, tied at a crossroads. If anyone objected, they were to say that the Lord had need of them.

This ass is said to have been common property for the poor, who had no beasts of their own. When anyone had worked with her, he gave fodder to her and to the colt, which was likewise being reared for common labour [Col. 1599A]. No one had yet mounted it, and because of this common service some think it was called *subjugalis*, as though exposed to everyone’s ownership. But *subjugalis* is a Greek name. For in Latin it is *asina*, and in Greek it is called *subjugalis*. Both names were instituted for the same reason: this was the first beast that man mounted; and from sitting upon it the Latin called it *asinus*, and the Greek *subjugalis*.

These two are believed to have been Peter and Philip, signifying that they first brought the Gentiles to Jesus: Peter, Cornelius and his household; Philip, Samaria.

> [Note: Col. 1599. This is clear concerning Philip in Acts 8 and concerning Peter in Acts 10.]

On this journey as He went up to Jerusalem, we suppose that He became hungry and came to a fig tree; and when He found on it only leaves and no fruit, He said: “May fruit never again come forth from thee;” and immediately it withered. Jesus did this only as a sign of the synagogue, cursed and dried up in its perverse falsehood. For He was not seeking fruit from it when the season for figs had not yet come. Although Matthew records this as occurring on the following day, and Mark also says that on another day, when He went out from Bethany, He became hungry, we suppose that it is said by recapitulation. Mark narrates that this happened before the expulsion of the sellers from the Temple, which is known to have taken place on Sunday. Yet we follow Mark’s order for no other reason than that he wrote after Matthew. Whether Matthew says that it occurred on Monday by recapitulation, or Mark relates it before the expulsion by anticipation, since the fact itself is not in question, we leave the day to the reader’s judgment.

“And the disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them. And placing their garments upon the colt, they made Him sit upon it.” Mark, Luke, and John say only that He sat upon the colt. Zechariah the prophet likewise said: “Sitting upon an ass’s colt” (Zech. 9). Matthew says that He sat upon the ass and colt. Although the way was short, it may nevertheless have happened that He first mounted the colt and then, perhaps because it was not yet broken and was frisky, dismounted and rode the ass. Even if He rode only the colt, however, Matthew placed Him upon both because either could occur in the mystery. The disciples did not know that this had been prophesied by Zechariah concerning Jesus until Jesus was glorified.

## Chapter CXVIII. How the Lord Was Gloriously Received and Wept over the City

[Col. 1599D]

As Jesus approached the descent of the Mount of Olives, many of those descending with Him spread their garments in the way; others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the way (Matt. 21; Mark 11; Luke 19; John 12). The great crowd gathered for the feast, together with the children and the common people of Jerusalem, took olive branches and went out to meet Him. Those who went before and those who followed cried: “Hosanna to the Son of David.”

*Hosanna* is a Hebrew word composed of a corrupted and an intact element. *Osi* means “save” or “make salvation.” *Anna* is an interjection of entreaty, like *papae* of amazement. Since it does not occur in Latin speech, Jerome rendered it by “I beseech.” Therefore *Hosanna* is as though *osi anna*: “Save, I beseech thee.” It is one word, as we have said, or two by ellipsis—that is, by elision or by the removal of one sounded letter, *i*. Or it is one word, construed thus, they saying: “Hosanna to the Son of David,” that is, “Save, I beseech thee”; or it is two words, and then read thus: “Hosanna, O Son of David.”

Then, turning their speech to one another, they said: “Blessed is He who comes, King, in the name of the Lord”—understand, “may He be” or “He is”—“and blessed is the kingdom of our father David that comes.” As though they said: This is He of whom it was said: [Col. 1600B] “The Lord shall give Him the throne of David His father” (Luke 1). And again, turning their words toward Him, they said: “Hosanna in the highest.” For although perhaps they sought the exaltation of an earthly kingdom, yet unknowingly they prophetically proclaimed Him King of heaven and angels.

Some Pharisees from the crowd told Him to rebuke the disciples. He answered them: “If these are silent, the stones will cry out” (Luke 19), because in the Passion, when these were silent from fear, the rocks rent asunder cried out that He was Lord of the world. “And when He approached Jerusalem, He wept over the city, saying: For if thou hadst known, thou too”—understand, “thou wouldst weep”—“for thine enemies shall surround thee with a rampart and shall not leave one stone upon another in thee.” As though He said: If thou hadst known [Col. 1600C] thy coming ruin and its cause—those things hidden from thee on this day that makes for thy peace—thou wouldst weep.

That the former Jerusalem was utterly destroyed is clear because the place of Calvary, then outside it, and the tomb are now within it. For Aelius Hadrian rebuilt it after its complete destruction, changing both its site and name and calling it Aelia. The Lord rightly said that it would perish, because, though the kite and swallow know their season (Jer. 8), it did not know the time of its visitation. “And when He entered the city, the whole city was stirred, saying: Who is this? But the crowds said that He was Jesus the prophet from Nazareth.”

The Church recalls the memory of this Lord’s procession once every year. The faithful go out [Col. 1600D] with branches, as though to meet the Lord outside the city walls, and proceed to a cross, upon which they strike and lay down the branches they carry, as though the Church said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). They go praying to the cross because thereby it is shown that no hope is to be placed in however great a worldly glory: for mourning overtakes the end of joy (Prov. 14). For the same signification, on that day the Gospel of the Lord’s Passion follows the joy of the procession. Perhaps because the Lord also joined His lament to rejoicing; and we join the Passion to the procession because the Passion was the cause of the destruction for which He wept.

> [Note: Cols. 1602B–C, Addition 1. The Lord’s Temple, whatever it may be, is also called Bethel; who built it is unknown. Some say that Helena built it after finding the Cross; some, Heraclius, when he returned the Cross triumphantly from Persia; some, the Emperor Justinian; and some, a certain king of Egypt named Allachibis, that is, “of the highest God.”]

Those churches [Col. 1601A] which, on the same day, place the Lord’s procession before this observance do more rightly, because that observance ought not to be omitted for the sake of this one. Likewise, those which meet their bishop, standing outside the city at the aforesaid place of the cross, and return to the city with him leading the people, act more orderly.

## Chapter CXIX. On the Second Expulsion of Buyers and Sellers from the Temple

“And Jesus entered into the Temple” (Luke 19). Then He showed that the city’s ruin, for which He had wept, would proceed chiefly from the fault of the priests. For the priests, providing for their avarice, sold sacrificial victims of every kind in the porches of the Temple, lest those coming from afar should offer nothing if they did not find victims ready at hand. And lest the poor, who had brought nothing with them [Col. 1601B], should make the excuse that they had no money, they also set there money-changers who lent money against security.

But because the Law did not allow them to take interest from their brethren, they devised the practice of *collybistae*. For among them *collybia* are called cheap little gifts, such as chickpeas, raisins, and fruits of various kinds, as though what was not permitted in money might be permitted in such things. Ezekiel prohibited this (ch. 22), saying: “You shall not take interest or any excess.” Thus even today some cloak usury under the name of charity.

Having made a scourge of cords, He drove from the Temple the sellers and buyers with their victims.

> [Note: Cols. 1601C–D, Addition 1. All the Evangelists agree concerning the praises, and as it were the prayer, offered on Sunday; but Matthew and Luke state that the expulsion occurred on the same day. Mark, however, states that it occurred the following day. Perhaps it was repeated on those two days. Likewise perhaps the Church’s praises were repeated on the following day, because the Gloss on Exodus says that they were done on the following day, on the passage concerning the lamb to be taken on the tenth day. Thus, it says, according to Bede there is no objection concerning the cursing of the fig tree, which Mark says occurred before the expulsion of the sellers: for the expulsion was also done on the second day, as Mark’s sequence has it. Thus, it says, everything is clear.]

He overturned the tables of the money-changers and said that they should not make His Father’s house, which was a house of prayer (Isa. 56) [Col. 1601C], into a den of robbers. Nor did He allow any vessel not dedicated to God to be carried through the Temple. Some relate that a radiant lightning-flash went out from His eyes; terrified by it, the priests and Levites could not resist Him. According to this, those act rightly who do not permit wax tapers to be sold in churches—unless, perhaps, the Lord did this chiefly for a mystery.

“And the blind and the lame came to Him in the Temple, and He healed them.”

## Chapter CXX. On the Raising of the Temple in Three Days

[Col. 1601D]

“And the chief priests and scribes, astonished, said to him: ‘What sign do you show us, that you do these things?’” (John 2). As though they said: “Do you signify something by this unprecedented act?” Or rather: “We do not believe that you are permitted to do this; therefore show us a sign by which we may believe that you are permitted to do it.” And he answered: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. But they said: ‘This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?’ But he spoke of the temple of his body.”

Solomon’s Temple was completed in seven years. The second Temple, however, was built under Cyrus in thirty years, but not above ground beyond the height to which the priests could lean against it, namely halfway up the back. For the neighboring peoples hindered the construction. Then the work was interrupted by Cambyses’ command for seven years; afterward, for one year under the two Magi, and again for one year under Darius son of Hystaspes. But in the second year of his reign, permission having been received from him, the work was completed in six years.

What is read—that this number of days corresponded to the formation of the Lord’s body—was said with regard to the differentiation of the limbs, not their initial formation. For from the moment of conception all the limbs were formed simultaneously, not at intervals as in a merely human being; though perhaps, even if they were visible, they could not be distinguished so clearly until that period. Jesus did not say this as a command, counsel, or exhortation, but as a prediction: “Destroy,” that is, “you will destroy.”

## CHAPTER CXXI. On the widow’s two small coins.

[Col. 1602C]

And he watched the rich, who were putting their gifts into the treasury (Mark 12; Luke 21). *Phylaxe* in Greek means “to keep” in Latin; *gaza* means “wealth” in Persian. There was a chest with an opening on top, set to the right of those entering near the altar. Into it the money of those making offerings was placed, to restore the Temple buildings, and was kept there.

Yet there was a particular chest there into which only priests put their gifts; it was called the *corban*. There was a third, into which the king or rulers put tribute, called the *musac*. Some, however, distinguish these differently, because one sometimes reads “the *musac* of the Sabbath.” They say that only offerings for feast days were deposited in that chest; and, because *corbam* signifies a vow, they say that votive offerings were deposited in the *corban*. Gifts for other days and voluntary offerings were deposited in the treasury. Yet each of these was called generally a treasury, as was also the place in which they stood. Hence: “Jesus spoke these things in the treasury” (John 8). In Ezekiel also (ch. 44), the priests’ chambers are called treasuries.

“And he saw a certain poor widow putting in two small copper coins,” that is, a quadrans: two little copper coins, worth a fourth part of a shekel, namely five obols. And he said that she had put in more than all the others, because she had put in her whole means of living, while the others gave from their abundance.

## CHAPTER CXXII. On the Pharisee and the tax collector.

He spoke a parable concerning the Pharisee and the tax collector to certain persons who trusted in themselves as righteous because of their outward works and despised others. And he inferred that “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18).

## CHAPTER CXXIII. That the Lord spent the night in Bethany.

When evening had already come, he returned to Bethany and remained there. For by day he taught in the Temple, and by night he went out and stayed in Bethany.

[Note: [Col. 1603B] Addition 1. Because, although the Lord had labored all day preaching to them, he found no one to receive him as a guest at night.]

“And all the people came early,” that is, hurried to him in the morning, “to hear him in the Temple” (Luke 21). [Col. 1603B] And many followed him, and he healed them. Hence John also says (ch. 2): “When he was at Jerusalem at the Passover feast—

[Note: [Col. 1603B] Addition 2. Therefore that whole week is called laborious, because throughout it the Lord labored in renewing all things, just as throughout the first week of the world he labored in creating all things.]

—many believed in his name, seeing the signs which he did.” Matthew records a similar healing in the canonical Gospel, and Mark in his corresponding canonical Gospel.

## CHAPTER CXXIV. On the voice of the Father to Jesus, which some thought was thunder.

[Col. 1603C] “Now certain Gentiles had come up to worship on the feast day, and they said to Philip: ‘Sir, we wish to see Jesus.’ He, taking Andrew with him, told Jesus this. And Jesus answered: ‘The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified’” (John 12).

As though he said: “The fullness of the Gentiles will believe.” Yet he indicated that this would occur after his Passion, saying: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” And because Christ compared himself to a grain of wheat, it is the Church’s custom to make Christ’s body from this grain alone.

And he added: “He who hates his soul,” that is, his life, “in this world preserves it unto eternal life,” that is, he shall live eternally. [Col. 1603D] “If anyone serves me, let him follow me, and he shall be with me forever.”

“Now my soul is troubled; and what shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this hour. Father, glorify your Son.’ And a voice came from heaven: ‘I have glorified [him], and I will glorify [him] again,’” that is, “I begot [him] glorious, and I shall not cease.” Or, with respect to his humanity: “I glorified [him] in baptism and in the Transfiguration; I shall glorify [him] in the Resurrection, Ascension, and Judgment.”

“Some said that thunder had occurred; others, that an angel had spoken to him. And Jesus said: ‘This voice came for your sake. Now the prince of this world will be cast out,’” that is, the prince of the lovers of the world will lose the power of drawing people after himself.

[Note: [Col. 1604A] Addition 1. Since the devil possessed a hand that drew and impelled, he lost the drawing hand but retains the impelling hand. This is signified by the dragon which, during the other three days when it is carried before the procession at the Ascension, follows on the second day.]

“And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself,” that is, from every part of the world. And when they understood [Col. 1604A] this as crucifixion—which perhaps was customarily called by them “being lifted up from the earth”—they objected to him that, if he were lifted up, he would not be the Christ. For they had heard from the Law that Christ remains forever; not defining the point, he said this because only a little light was in them.

## CHAPTER CXXV. On the son who said he would not go into the vineyard, but went.

When evening came, he returned to Bethany. And returning again at dawn on the third Sabbath, he taught the people in the Temple. [Col. 1604B] The chief priests came to him and said: “By what authority do you do these things?” (Matthew 21; Luke 20; Mark 11). As though they said: “Why do you cast people out of the Temple? What do you mean by acting as gatekeeper and teaching without consulting us?”

But Jesus gave them a counter-question rather than an answer: “I too ask you: Was John’s baptism from God or from men?” As though he said: “Since it is certain that you ought to believe John’s testimony about my authority as coming from God.” Because they said they did not know—although they did know—he was unwilling to reveal the truth about himself to them.

That the truth was to be revealed to others and not to them, and why this was so, he indicated by the parable of the two sons. To one the father said: “Go into the vineyard”; and he replied: “I will not,” yet afterward went. The father said to the other: [Col. 1604C] “Go into the vineyard”; he said, “I will go,” but did not go. When Jesus asked which had done the father’s will, they said: “The latter,” evading the issue because they did not wish to speak the truth. The ancient codices have: “The first,” understanding that the saying was directed against them. Hence Jesus adds: “Tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God.”

## CHAPTER CXXVI. On the bloodthirsty tenants of the vineyard.

Again he set before them a parable about a householder who planted a vineyard and leased it to tenant-farmers (Matthew 21; Mark 12; Luke 20). The servants sent to receive the fruits they killed: Isaiah they sawed apart, Ezekiel they dragged over rough places and dashed out his brains, and many they stoned.

And the father, sending his son, said: “Perhaps they will respect my son. Let us say to Arius and Eunomius: behold, the Father is said not to know. Whatever they answer on behalf of the Father, let them understand it of the Son, who says that he does not know the day of the consummation.”

[Note: [Col. 1605A] Addition 1. The Father appears not to know the event’s outcome. Perhaps the Father is said not to know what he causes us not to know, and to do what he causes us to do.]

When the tenants saw him, they said: “This is the heir,” because the priests knew that he had come—the one to whom the Father had said: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2)—and they seized the son and cast him out. What then will the lord of the vineyard do to them? According to Luke they said: “Certainly not!” understanding that they would kill the Messiah. Matthew says that they said: “He will miserably destroy those wicked men and lease his vineyard to other tenants.” Yet they did not say this aloud, but in their conscience. The Lord proved that the Jews would do this because it had been prophesied thus: “The stone which the builders rejected,” etc. [Col. 1605A]

## CHAPTER CXXVII. On the cornerstone.

According to the literal account, a stone had been prepared for the Temple’s construction, yet could not be fittingly set into it until, when the work was completed, it was placed above at the corner. It fitted so aptly that all marveled and understood that it had not happened without significance. This is Christ, who is the foundation in such a way that he rises above the structure.

“When the priests and Pharisees heard this, they wanted to seize him, but they feared the crowds” (Matthew 21).

## CHAPTER CXXVIII. On those invited to the wedding, and the man without a wedding garment.

[Col. 1605B]

“And again he spoke to them in parables: ‘The kingdom of heaven has become like a king who made a wedding feast for his son. When he repeatedly sent for those invited to come, and they excused themselves and would not come, he sent his servants to summon guests from wherever they could. And they brought in the good and the bad, the weak and the lame’” (Matthew 22).

Bodily weakness excludes no one from the kingdom; indeed, it often almost compels one toward it. The king entered to see those reclining at table; this will occur when he comes for judgment. For the whole Trinity will judge, that is, render according to merits. Whoever is found in the Church without a wedding garment, that is, without charity, will be cast into outer darkness, that is, darkness situated locally outside himself, because he had inner darkness within himself.

It may also be said of the darkness of the mind: some have it inwardly, that is, within the Church; others outwardly, outside the Church—namely unbelievers and heretics. Thus evil churchmen will be cast out, so that they may have their portion with unbelievers.

## CHAPTER CXXIX. On the Herodians and paying tribute.

Then the Pharisees took counsel how to trap Jesus in speech, and sent their disciples with the Herodians. For Herod the tetrarch had come for the feast day and had brought Gentile soldiers with him (Matthew 22; Mark 12; Luke 20). Or these may have been survivors of the old soldiers of Herod of Ascalon. Coming to Jesus, they said: “Is it lawful to pay tribute [Col. 1605D] to Caesar, or not?”

For there was already a dispute among the Jews about paying tribute, on account of which the Romans later also rose against them. Jesus said: “Why do you test me, hypocrites? Show me the tribute coin.” A *numisma* is the inscription on a coin, also called its stamp, by which coins are distinguished; but here it is used for the coin itself. That is: “Show me the coin paid for the poll-tax.” When he asked whose image it was and they said, “Caesar’s”—namely Tiberius’s—he inferred: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” namely public taxes, “and to God the things that are God’s,” namely firstfruits, tithes, and offerings.

## CHAPTER CXXX. On the woman with seven husbands.

On that day the Sadducees came, who did not believe in the resurrection [Col. 1606A] and mocked the Pharisees, asking in the Judgment whose wife a woman who had had seven husbands would be (Matthew 22; Mark 12; Luke 20). Either they had invented the case, since it was possible, or perhaps it had actually occurred. When they proposed the same question to Jesus, he answered: “In the resurrection women will not marry, nor will men be married by them,” that is, men will not take wives; for immortal human beings will not need propagation. “Will be married” is a Greek idiom.

He proved the future resurrection from the Lord’s words to Moses in the bush: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3). Because they did not accept the prophets, he could not use their clear testimonies against them. The argument is as follows. They believed that souls perish [Col. 1606B] with bodies. But this authority proves that souls live after the body. Otherwise, if a human being dies and is wholly reduced to nothing, then God said that he was the God of nothing. Therefore, since souls remain after death, it may be inferred that bodies will rise again, so that souls may receive with them what they merited with them. Otherwise they are joined to bodies in vain.

## CHAPTER CXXXI. On the first and second commandments in the Law, and the man wounded by robbers.

“But when the Pharisees saw that he had silenced the Sadducees, they assembled together. And one doctor of the Law came to test him, saying: ‘Master, what is the great commandment in the Law?’ And Jesus said: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one’” (Matthew 22; Mark 12; Deuteronomy 6; Luke 10).

[Col. 1606C] This is not part of the commandment, but introduces the one from whom the following command was given: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” This second commandment concerns one like yourself, who is like God. For man is the image of God.

And the scribe answered: “You have spoken truly, and this is greater than all burnt offerings.” It is clear that there was a dispute between Pharisees and scribes. Some preferred works of the Law to love; others, by contrast, because before the Law many pleased God through love without any sacrifice. The first and second commandments are so called with regard to the matters commanded.

“To him Jesus said: ‘Do this, and you shall live.’ He, wishing to justify himself, said to Jesus: ‘And who is my neighbor?’” Jesus showed him that everyone who performs mercy is a neighbor—and especially the Son of God himself—by setting forth the parable of the wounded man who fell among robbers. This parable was not far removed from reality, because robbers often shed blood in that wilderness. Therefore it was called Adommin, which also signifies “blood.” “And all the people hung upon him, listening to Jesus.”

## CHAPTER CXXXII. On the refutation of the Pharisees by David’s authority.

“When the Pharisees had assembled, Jesus asked them: ‘What do you think of Christ? Whose son is he?’ They said to him: ‘David’s.’ And he said to them: ‘How then does David [Col. 1607A] call him his Lord, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand”?’” (Psalm 102 [Hebrew Psalm 110]). “If David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matthew 22; Mark 12; Luke 20).

As though he said: “You think that Christ will be a merely human being. Therefore, when David existed, Christ did not yet exist, and so he was not David’s Lord. David therefore lied and spoke wrongly.” For fathers are more properly masters of, and are called lords of, their children than children are of their parents.

The Jews imagine that this Psalm was written in the person of Eliezer, who, after the slaughter of the five kings, said: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.” But the subsequent words of the Psalm do not agree.

## CHAPTER CXXXIII. On listening to Pharisaic teachers, but not imitating them.

[Col. 1607B]

“Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to his disciples: ‘The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Do what they say, but do not do what they do’” (Matthew 23). A place does not sanctify a human being, but a human being sanctifies a place. Not every priest is holy, but every holy person is a priest. Let us receive teaching, not conduct: bees need not plants, but flowers.

And he added: “They broaden their phylacteries—

[Note: [Col. 1607C] Addition 1. From *phylaxe*, “to preserve,” and *torac*, “law.” For they had a little scroll hanging from the neck or arm, on which the Ten Commandments of the Law were written. Or *phylacteries* are so called from *phylaxe* and *terion*, “round”; and phylacteries are called the little boxes in which extremities of relics—such as fingers or something else—were kept.]

—and enlarge their fringes,” to which they attached thorns, so that the prick of these might keep the Law continually in mind, as explained above; and they love to be called Rabbi. “But you are not to be called Rabbi, for one is your Master. And do not call anyone your father on earth. [Col. 1607C] For one is your Father, who is in heaven.” The Lord does not forbid teaching from the chair, greetings in the marketplace, or the titles Master and Father, but ambition and vain glory.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV. To whom eternal woe is due.

To show what he teaches must be avoided in the Pharisees, he adds: “Woe to you who love the first seats. Woe to you, hypocritical Pharisees, who bear [Col. 1607D] the key of knowledge and shut the kingdom of heaven before men. Woe to you who devour widows’ houses; woe to you who travel sea and land to make one proselyte—

[Note: [Col. 1608C] Addition 1. A proselyte properly means one who has become a Jew from a Gentile. Although some say that *proselyte* is so called from leaping forth from Gentile life to Judaism, and conversely.]

—that is, to draw some Gentile newcomer to Judaism—“and make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves; for, returning to his vomit, he is worse than before because he is a transgressor. Woe to you who say: ‘Whoever swears by the Temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the Temple is bound. Whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the offering upon it is bound.’”

The priests, in order to invite the people to sacrifice, said that things given and offered to them were holier than the Temple and altar themselves. The Lord said the contrary: the Temple and altar—

[Note: [Col. 1608C] Addition 2. This altar was converted by the Saracens into a clock, and may still be seen.]

—sanctified the offerings made upon them, because they were dedicated to God; but the offerings did not sanctify them at all. Many still suffer from the same fault, thinking it greater to swear by the Gospel than by God.

“Woe to you who tithe every herb and omit mercy and judgment.” The word “you tithe” is ambiguous, for both the person who receives and the person who gives is said to tithe. The Pharisees gave tithes of vegetables in order that people might say: “How can they fail to give other things, when they do not neglect even these?” But the Levites demanded tithes so rigorously that they even exacted vegetable tithes.

Again: “Woe to you, blind guides, who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel.” This is said by comparison with milk, which is strained. It may be related to the preceding words thus: you carefully scrutinize trivial things, like a gnat, such as tithes, but conceal greater things, namely mercy and judgment, as [Col. 1608B] what is swallowed is concealed. Or it may be connected with what was said, “blind guides,” in this way: you diligently reprove the lesser sins of your subjects, cast out the graver ones, and pass over them by dissembling.

Again: “Woe to you who are like whitewashed tombs, which are full of every impurity.” Again: “Woe to you who build the tombs of the prophets and condemn your fathers who killed them. Offspring of vipers, fill up the measure of your fathers. Therefore the Wisdom of God says to you: ‘I will send to you wise men and scribes; some of them you will kill and crucify, and scourge in your synagogues.’” Here it is evident that the heretic lies who says that the God of the prophets is one God and the God of the New Testament another.

“So that upon you”—that is, upon the Church of the wicked—“may come all righteous blood,” that is, vengeance for the righteous, “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar.”

## CHAPTER CXXXV. On Zechariah son of Barachiah.

But it is not recorded, whether the reference is to the eleventh prophet or to the father of John the Baptist, that he was killed in the Temple. It may therefore be said of the son of the priest Jehoiada, whom Joash killed, as is read in the Book of Kings (4 Kings 2). Perhaps his father was surnamed Barachiah, or the name is used for its interpretation. For Barachiah means “blessed of the Lord.” Thus, “son of Barachiah” means “son of the blessed of the Lord.”

In the Gospel of the Nazarenes—

[Note: [Col. 1608D] Addition 1. *Nazaraeus* means “holy,” “flourishing,” or “sprouting”; and those who bound themselves by vow to holiness, either for a fixed period or continually, as Samuel, were called Nazarenes: “And a razor did not [Col. 1609A] pass over their heads” (1 Kings 1). Hence Christ and the apostles are depicted with long hair, not in fact but as a sign of holiness. Yet Christ was called a Nazarene from Nazareth; and a Nazarene was so called not from a place but from holiness. Thus Christ’s first disciples, who wrote the Gospel, were called Nazarenes; but the Church receives only four. And although at first they were called Nazarenes, afterward those following Christ were called disciples, and later, through Peter’s institution, Christians from Christ.]

—it reads “son of Jehoiada.” But Jesus mentioned only a shepherd of sheep and a priest in order to denote the two kinds of human beings: subjects and prelates. For a corrupt generation spares no class.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI. On the threat of Jerusalem’s overthrow.

[Col. 1609A]

Turning his discourse toward Jerusalem, he said: “How often I wished to gather your children and you would not” (Luke 13), that is, how often I gathered your children by my will while you were unwilling, and acted ungratefully. “Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. For I say to you: from now on you will not see me until you say: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’” That is, from the time of the Passion onward, you will not see the Son of Man until the Judgment, when you will see me coming in the glory of one who rules and will extol me as believers do. He also foretold that their blindness would endure until then.

## CHAPTER CXXXVII. On the signs of the overthrow and of his coming.

Having said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. And many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it (John 12; Matthew 24; Mark 13; Luke 19, 21). When he was leaving the Temple, [Col. 1609C] his disciples approached him, pointing out the Temple’s buildings. They had heard him speak of the city’s overthrow; they wanted also to hear of the Temple’s overthrow, because it seemed to them that it could neither be captured nor destroyed. And he said to them: “Days will come in which not one stone will be left here upon another which will not be destroyed.”

When he was sitting on the Mount of Olives—

[Note: [Col. 1609D] Addition 1. From the splendor of the gold that was in the Temple, reflecting the sun, a certain part of the Mount of Olives directly opposite continually shone brightly. There Solomon later built a temple for his women.]

—opposite the Temple—

[Note: [Col. 1609D] Addition 2. On the slope of the Mount of Olives is the Mount of Display, so called because Solomon placed there the idol Moloch.]

—the disciples approached privately and asked him about the signs of Jerusalem’s overthrow and the signs of his coming. He told them some things peculiar to his coming, some peculiar to the overthrow, and some common to both. He forewarned the faithful not to be deceived when they heard many saying that they were Christs. For he will not come unless the signs he foretold come first.

He first gave the common signs: wars and uprisings of nation against nation and kingdom against kingdom; plagues, famines, earthquakes in various places, terrors from heaven, and persecutions of the saints. For before Judaea’s overthrow the elements will avenge their Creator. Then he set forth the special sign of destruction.

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII. The special sign of the overthrow.

[Col. 1610A]

“When you see the abomination of desolation” (Matthew 24), which was spoken of by Daniel (ch. 9), “standing in the holy place”—that is, an abominable image, the sign of desolation, set up in the Temple. Some explain this as the image of Tiberius which Pilate placed in the Temple—

[Note: [Col. 1610B] Addition 1. It is read concerning Pilate that, when he came to Jerusalem, he set up Caesar’s statue in the Temple without the Jews’ knowledge. At last, seeing the steadfastness of the Jews, who all grieved over this, he removed it. The Lord therefore would not have called it a sign of the overthrow, since it had already happened.]

—but this had already occurred. If it is said of the image of Gaius, of which we shall speak below, this was to occur soon, namely within ten years, and thirty-two years before Jerusalem’s overthrow. Therefore it was not suitably described as its sign.

But after Jerusalem was overthrown by Titus, Hadrian placed his statue where the Ark had stood, because some traces of the city still remained, and Jews who had survived in hiding from every quarter sometimes returned to the holy place. Having multiplied again, they removed the statue. For this reason Hadrian applied the final stroke, utterly destroyed the city, and decreed that no Jew should remain in that land. Luke seems to add concerning this final overthrow when he says (ch. 21): “And they will be led captive into all nations.”

## CHAPTER CXXXIX. On the hindrance to flight.

“But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, [Col. 1610C] then let those who are in Judaea flee to the mountains” (Matthew 24; Luke 21; Mark 23). Ecclesiastical History relates that the faithful who were in Judaea fled, at the Romans’ arrival, to the city of Pella by an angel’s warning.

“But pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on the Sabbath.” Taken literally, this does not seem to have been said concerning winter. For that land seems more suitable for flight in winter than in the heat of summer. It may stand concerning the Sabbath, since according to the Law they were not permitted to go more than a thousand paces on the Sabbath. But because Jesus had already ended the observance of the Sabbath, perhaps he said both things mystically—unless we take winter to mean any harshness of weather, since the name winter conveys harshness.

## CHAPTER CXL. The special signs of the Judge’s coming.

[Col. 1610D]

Finally Jesus set forth the signs of his coming, saying: “Then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world; and then there will be signs in sun, moon, and stars, and on earth distress of nations because of the confusion caused by the roar of the sea and waves, with people withering from fear. And unless those days had been shortened” (Matthew 24; Luke 21), “that is, foreknown to be so few, no flesh would be saved—

[Note: [Col. 1610D] Addition 1. For the sea and waves will give such a terrible sound that people will flee from the waters and one person will not hear another.]

—that is, scarcely anyone or no one could endure the afflictions and be saved through patience.” Note briefly that the Lord touched upon certain signs of the Judgment.

## CHAPTER CXLI. On the signs of the fifteen days before Judgment.

[Col. 1611A]

Jerome found in the annals of the Hebrews signs for the fifteen days before the Day of Judgment, but did not state whether these days will be consecutive or intermittent. On the first day the sea will rise forty cubits above the height of the mountains, standing in its place like a wall. On the second it will descend so far that it can scarcely be seen. On the third, sea-monsters appearing above the sea will give roars reaching to heaven. On the fourth, the sea and waters will burn. On the fifth, grasses and trees will give bloody dew. On the sixth, buildings will collapse. On the seventh, rocks will collide with one another. On the eighth, there will be a general earthquake. On the ninth, the earth will be leveled. On the tenth, people will emerge from caves [Col. 1611B] and walk as if insane, unable to speak to one another. On the eleventh, the bones of the dead will rise and stand upon their tombs. On the twelfth, the stars will fall. On the thirteenth, the living will die, so that they may rise with the dead. On the fourteenth, heaven and earth will burn. On the fifteenth, there will be a new heaven and a new earth, and all will rise again.

And Jesus added: “As lightning comes out of the east and appears as far as the west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be” (Matthew 24; Luke 17): sudden, indeed, and flashing. Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, that is, in the air, above the place from which he ascended; and before him will be the instruments of his death, as standards of triumph: the cross, nails, and spear. The scars will be visible in his flesh, so that they may see him whom they pierced (Revelation 1). And every human being will be judged in the Valley [Col. 1611C] of Jehoshaphat, as angels gather them together (Mark 13).

[Note: [Col. 1611C] Addition 1. Note that the Judgment is said to take place in the Valley of Jehoshaphat. But note that there will then be no valley, because on the fourteenth day the earth will be leveled; rather, it will be opposite that place. Or perhaps this is because of the interpretation of the name Jehoshaphat, for it means “judgment.” Thus the Valley of Jehoshaphat signifies the humility of judgment.]

## CHAPTER CXLII. That the Father alone knows the day of Judgment; and on one taken and another left.

Then Jesus adds a general warning: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down by the cares of this age, lest that day come suddenly upon you, [Col. 1611D] as sudden destruction carried away the unaware in the days of Noah and Lot. But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the Son nor the angel, but the Father alone” (Luke 17; Matthew 24; Mark 13).

Here Arius cries out: “Those are not equal, one of whom knows and the other does not know.” Jerome replies in the shorter breviary on the Psalms: the humanity of the Son says that it does not know the end of the world. Gregory, as if explaining this in the *Register*, says: “The only-begotten Son of God knows the hour of Judgment, but not from the nature of his humanity.” Yet it is also explained thus: “He does not know”—supply, “for us,” for whom it is beneficial to remain uncertain, so that we may live as though we were about to be judged shortly. Or “Son” here is said by adoption.

“Then two will be in the field,” that is, in the field of prelates: some good, some evil. “One will be taken,” that is, caught up [Col. 1612A] to meet Christ in the air, “and the other left,” that is, not taken. “Two women grinding at one mill: one will be taken and the other left.” This is said of married persons, who are in the wheel of this world. “Two in one bed: one will be taken and the other left.” This is understood of contemplatives or speculative thinkers. They said to him: “Where, Lord?” namely, will they be taken? And he answered: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered,” that is, where the Lord will be in his body, the eagles—that is, the saints, renewed through resurrection—will be gathered.

## CHAPTER CXLIII. On the watchfulness of the gatekeeper and the ten virgins.

Meanwhile the Son of Man will be like a man who, having gone abroad, left his house and, [Col. 1612B] assigning to each of his servants his work, commanded the gatekeeper to keep watch (Matthew 25; Mark 13; Luke 21). Watchfulness therefore is incumbent on the apostles and apostolic men: watchfulness over themselves and over the flock, and also, in proportion to his capacity, upon every believer.

“Then the kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins,” that is, then the foolish will be separated from the prudent. “But at midnight a cry was made: ‘Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him.’” Jewish tradition holds that Christ will come at midnight, after the pattern of Egypt, when the Passover was celebrated. Some saints likewise hold this opinion: as he was born into the world at night and came from hell at night, so he will also come for Judgment at night. Hence some say it was an apostolic tradition that, on the vigil of Passover, [Col. 1612C] the people should not be dismissed from church before deep night, so that they might, as it were, await the Lord’s coming. They say that this hour of the night is sometimes—indeed, more often—called day because of the brightness of his coming, or typically because of the disclosure of hearts. Others explain, without defining what the Lord calls uncertain: “At midnight,” that is, when no one knows.

## CHAPTER CXLIV. On the entrusting of talents and the ten minas.

He further added the parable of the man departing who gave talents to his servants: five to one, two to another, and one to another (Matthew 25). Having commended those who doubled their talents and rejected the lazy man who hid his own, he said: “To everyone who has, more will be given. But from one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away.” That is, from one who has in the manner in which he ought to have—namely, so as to use it well.

He also added a parable on the same subject, concerning the king who went into a far country to receive a kingdom for himself and return. He gave his servants ten minas—

[Note: [Col. 1612D] Addition 1. The calling of a servant is the canonical election of a bishop. A mina is given to him when the person who laid hands on him gives him the text of the Gospel and says: “Go, [Col. 1613A] preach.” When he first enters his city, he carries the Gospel before his breast, like a merchant displaying his mina. In some Churches, when the archbishop gives him the staff, he says: “Go, preach”; and he immediately blesses the people. This signifies that Moses was sent into Egypt with a staff.]

—and said: “Trade until I come.” According to the Greeks, a mina is reckoned at four thousand drachmas. At his return the first came and said: “Lord, your mina has gained ten minas.” The Lord said to him: “You will have authority over ten cities,” as though he said: “For small merits you will receive things beyond expectation.”

## CHAPTER CXLV. On the winnowing of the threshing floor.

[Col. 1613A]

When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, destined to be witnesses of human deeds, then the good will be separated from the evil, and the good will be placed at the right hand—that is, set in eternity—while the evil will be placed at the left—that is, they will receive what they deserved by choosing the left hand (Matt. 25). Then the Judge will recall, namely, the works of mercy: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, receiving the stranger, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and comforting the imprisoned. A seventh is read in Tobit (chaps. 2, 12): burying the dead. This recollection will be nothing other than that all will know their own merits, for which they will be saved or damned. And these will go into eternal punishment, but those into eternal life.

## CHAPTER CXLVI. Opinions concerning eternal fire

Augustine says concerning eternal fire: “What kind it will be, and in what part of the world it will exist, I think no one knows except by revelation.” That is to say: there is one fire of Gehenna, but it does not torment all in one manner. Just as not all feel the sun’s heat equally, so, although that fire burns equally, it will not be felt equally. Gregory, in Job: In a wonderful manner the fire of Gehenna is bodily; it is fed by no wood, needs no kindling, and is unquenchable, having been created by God from the beginning of the world. The same author: The avenging flame has the burning of vices, but does not have light; it does not shine for consolation, yet, in order to torment more severely, it shines for something. For the reprobate will see themselves in hell, that they may suffer more; for the rich man also saw Lazarus.

Yet in the book *Praenostica*, from the words of Augustine, one reads as follows: “The substance of the lower world, as Augustine says, is incorporeal.” Therefore one rightly asks why the lower regions are said to be beneath the earth if they are not bodily places, and why they are called the lower regions if they are not beneath the earth. But the same doctor says: Therefore they are called the lower regions beneath the earth because, appropriately, likenesses of bodily things are shown in the spirit in such a way that, since the souls of the dead sinned through love of the body, they are presented with those likenesses of bodily things in which those dead in the flesh are customarily buried beneath the earth.

From this statement of Augustine, some conclude that wherever a sinner may be, there the elements will torment him, both in his body and from the places adjoining it. For it is plausible that the soul which of its own will takes from the flesh an incentive to sin should, against its will, receive from that same flesh an incentive to torment. This punishment is rightly called infernal and beneath the earth, because souls incur it through their fall into earthly pleasure. Augustine, *The City of God*: Why should we not say that incorporeal spirits can be afflicted by the punishment of bodily fire? The same: Bodily fire will torment demons and human beings. Jerome, in his Epistle to the Ephesians: No one doubts that hell is beneath the earth.

## CHAPTER CXLVII. On Passover and the different senses of this name

When Jesus had finished these sayings, he said to his disciples: “You know that after two days Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (Matt. 26). He said this to them on Tuesday, and on Thursday evening Passover was imminent, on the fourteenth moon after the vernal equinox. Ambrose says that the name *Pascha* is Greek and means “suffering.” But the Hebrew name *Phase* means “passage” or “crossing.” Augustine, however, says that it is Hebrew, not Greek, and means “passage”; nevertheless, in this name there fittingly coincides a correspondence of both languages. For the Greek for “he suffers” is πάσχειν (*paschein*), whence Passover is thought to mean suffering. But in the Syriac language it means passage. Why that hour is called a passage is explained in Exodus.

*Pascha* is declined either *Pascha, Paschae*, or *Pascha, Paschatis*, and is equivocal in three senses. The evening in which the lamb was sacrificed was called Passover, as here: “After two days Passover will take place.” The whole day preceding that hour was neither called Passover nor was solemn. The lamb too is called Passover, as in: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” And the Apostle says: “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5).

The seven days of Unleavened Bread followed; the first and last of them were solemn, the intervening days less so. Yet these seven days were sometimes called Passover, as in: “They did not enter the praetorium, lest they should be defiled, but might eat the Passover”—that is, that they might eat in purity at Passover; or he calls the unleavened bread Passover because it was used during those days. Nor is it surprising that the days of Unleavened Bread were called Passover, since Passover too is called a day of Unleavened Bread, as in: “The feast day of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover” (Luke 22).

## CHAPTER CLXVIII. On the day and manner in which Judas sold the Lord

Then, namely on Wednesday [Note: [Col. 1614D] Addition 1. That the Lord was sold on the Wednesday before the Passion is shown by the Church’s appointing on that day, before the Epistle, the reading from Isaiah in which one reads: “Behold, his reward is with him” (Isa. 40). In remembrance of this sale, throughout the year this weekday holds second place after Friday among penitential fasts. It often has its own Gospel and its own Epistle, although the Sunday office ought to be repeated throughout the week. For the Mass of the Cross on Friday was devised for this purpose. Likewise the Mass of the Angels on Monday.], the chief priests, seeing that Jesus had gone away and had said, “You will not see me henceforth,” assembled with the elders of the people in the court of Caiaphas. They sought him in order to seize and kill him, though not on the feast day, lest perhaps a disturbance arise among the people (Matt. 26; Luke 22; Mark 14).

When Judas heard that they were assembled, he went and made an agreement with them to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver. Perhaps because he had heard the Lord say that he would die on the third day and thought that death would hold him fast, he wished to make the death impending upon him profitable to himself; and thereafter he sought an opportunity to hand him over without a crowd. Those thirty denarii were worth three hundred ordinary denarii, and thus Judas wished to compensate for the loss of the ointment.

## CHAPTER CLXIX. On the Lord’s Supper

[Col. 1615A]

“Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread” (Matt. 26; Mark 13 [probably OCR for Mark 14]; Luke 22)—that is, on the day in whose evening the lamb was to be sacrificed and eaten with unleavened bread—“the disciples said to Jesus: ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’ And he answered: ‘Go into the city, and you will meet a man carrying a jar of water. Wherever he enters, ask the master of the house [Col. 1615B] for a place to prepare it, and he will show you a large upper room; prepare it there.’”

The Palestinians made dining rooms in the upper part of the house and sleeping rooms below. What Mark calls a *lagena* and Luke an *amphora*, one expressed the kind of vessel and the other its capacity. Therefore, before the feast day of Passover, when evening had come, Jesus came and reclined with his twelve disciples. And he said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.”

John’s words supplied the Greeks with fuel for error. For they say that on the Preparation the moon was the fourteenth [Note: [Col. 1616B] Addition 1. Whereas in truth it was the fifteenth. He gives five reasons for their opinion.], and thus Passover occurred on its evening. But the Lord, knowing that he would suffer on that day, anticipated the eating of the Passover on the preceding evening. And because leavened bread could lawfully be eaten on that night, they make the Lord’s body from leavened bread.

[Col. 1615C] If this is true, it is credible that the Lord ate the lamb, as the Law commanded, and ate unleavened bread. Thus, even if what they say is certain, they err in consecrating leavened bread. That the Lord anticipated Passover is proved from John’s words: he says that the Lord ate before the feast day of Passover (John 13), and that on the Preparation the Jews did not enter the praetorium lest they be defiled, but might eat the Passover. The priests had also arranged not to kill him on the feast day—that is, the first day of Unleavened Bread. Moreover, the Gospel calls the Sabbath after the Lord’s crucifixion “a great Sabbath day,” which is not usually said unless a feast coincides with the Sabbath; and thus the first day of Unleavened Bread fell on the Sabbath.

[Col. 1615D] For the intermediate days between the first and the last were not feast days. Moreover, the women prepared ointments on the Preparation, which would not have been permitted if it had been the first day of Unleavened Bread. To this it can be said that the feast day of Passover was the fifteenth moon, according to: “And on the fifteenth you shall celebrate a solemnity to the Most High Lord.” Therefore, before that day the Lord celebrated Passover according to the Law. Luke too says that the day of Unleavened Bread came on which it was necessary to kill the Passover. It was necessary by the Law on the fourteenth moon of the first or second month. But we do not read of any circumstance in which it was necessary to anticipate the fourteenth moon.

The “great Sabbath day” [Note: [Col. 1616B] Addition 2. From this point he gives their reasons: they take the first from what John says; the second from what Luke says; the third from what others say; the fourth because the Gospel calls the Sabbath after the crucifixion a great Sabbath; and the fifth because the women prepared ointments on the Preparation.] they called so at the three week-long festivals, on whichever of the seven days it occurred. For all seven [Col. 1616A] were solemn, although not as much as the first and the last. To eat unleavened bread, moreover, they had to remain clean for seven days. Hence on any one of those seven days they could not enter the praetorium. As to the statement that the women prepared ointments on a feast day, we say that no days were as strictly festive as the Sabbath; they were permitted to prepare or buy them, as also food, which would not have been permitted on the Sabbath. What if they had prepared them long before, since they had often heard the Lord say that he would die soon? Does not Magdalene seem already to have prepared them and, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, to have anticipated the anointing?

Some, however, say that on the thirteenth moon, namely Wednesday, the Lord supped with his disciples and washed their feet. This is narrated by John alone. On the fourteenth [Col. 1616B] he ate the paschal lamb and gave his body to the disciples, which the others recount. But the practice of the Church is contrary: before the Preparation it washes the feet of the poor. Moreover, if we carefully trace the calendar table backward, we shall find the moon on the twenty-second day before the Kalends of April to have fallen on Friday; therefore on the preceding Friday it was the fifteenth moon. Note that nowhere is the Lord read to have eaten meat except that of the paschal lamb.

## CHAPTER CL. That, rising from supper, he washed the disciples’ feet

[Col. 1616C]

“Jesus, rising from supper, washed the disciples’ feet” (John 13). From his saying, “He who has bathed”—namely in baptism—“does not need except to wash his feet [Note: [Col. 1616D] Addition 1. Note the four layings aside of Christ’s garments. At supper he laid them aside and resumed them; at the pillar he was stripped and reclothed. In the soldiers’ mockery he was stripped and clothed. For he is not read to have been stripped by Herod. At the cross he was stripped and not reclothed. The first pertains to the apostles, whom he resumed shortly afterward; the second to those who were resumed at Pentecost and are gradually resumed; the third to the remnant, who will be resumed at the end; the fourth to the perverse half of our time, which will never be resumed. The second and fourth are represented in the Church when the altars are cleansed. For they are struck with little branches as if with whips [Col. 1617A] and sprinkled with water and wine.]; but you are clean, though not all,” some infer that the apostles were baptized.

When he reclined again, he taught them why he had done this: as an example, namely, of mutually serving one another; as a figure of mutually forgiving injuries; and of mutually helping sinners by praying [Col. 1616D] for them. Therefore the Lord added: “You will be blessed if you do these things.” He would not have said this about foot-washing alone.

## CHAPTER CLI. On the identification of the betrayer and his departure

[Col. 1617A]

“Jesus, troubled in spirit, said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you that one of you will betray me tonight’” (John 13; Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22). Jesus was troubled out of merciful compassion for Judas, whom he was identifying. Thus the saints too are mercifully troubled when concern presses them to separate the tares from the wheat before the harvest. Therefore the philosopher lies who says that disturbance of soul does not befall a wise person.

They said individually: “Is it I, Lord?” To them he said: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me.” The twelve ate with the Lord from the same [Col. 1617B] dish, and others did not; as though he said: One of the twelve will betray me. Perhaps he said “dips” because the juice of wild lettuces was necessary for eating the lamb. A *catinus*, a dish containing liquid, shows that it was an earthenware vessel; a *parapsis* is a vessel in which foods were prepared, because it had equal sides. For *apsis* means an extremity. Or, as some say, the name *parapsis* indicates the squareness of its sides.

Jesus added: “Woe to that man through whom the Son of Man will be betrayed. It would have been good for that man if he had not been born.” “Woe” in Sacred Scripture denotes eternal damnation; that is: “He will perish eternally.” And lest we should understand even the slightest punishment, he added, “Good,” etc.; that is, it would have been better for him had he not been born from the womb but perished in the womb. For then he would have been damned only for original sin. Or it is said in the ordinary manner: it would be better for him not to exist than to exist badly.

Now the disciple whom Jesus loved was reclining in his bosom. Peter signaled to him to ask the Lord privately who would betray him. He is believed to have reclined upon Jesus’ breast only in the sense that, while reclining at table, he leaned before the Lord’s breast. To this disciple asking in a low voice, the Lord in a low voice identified the betrayer: namely, the one to whom he would hand the dipped bread. And he handed the dipped morsel to Judas. Hence the Eucharist is not given dipped; and this is also to remove the heresy which taught that the whole Christ is under both forms together, and under neither form alone.

Then Satan entered Judas, not for the first time then, but so as to possess him as though his own; just as the apostles, after already receiving the Spirit, are again said to receive the Spirit. Then Judas said: “Is it I, Rabbi?” He said to him: “You have said it.” He does not yet identify him before everyone. For it can be understood thus: I do not say it, but you say it. Or it may be explained as an assertion of the heart, as though he said: In speech indeed you ask as though ignorant, but in your heart you hold it certain that you are the betrayer.

“And Judas went out at once; and it was night. Then Jesus said: ‘Now the Son of Man has been glorified’”—that is, once the dark one had been cast out, the clean alone remained with their cleanser. He added: “And God immediately glorified him”—that is, will glorify him. This may be understood of the resurrection, or of the imminent betrayal, through which Christ [Col. 1618A], having died, appeared to those who awaited him in hell.

## CHAPTER CLII. On the Eucharist given to the disciples and not to Judas

“While they were at supper, Jesus blessed bread, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you.’ Likewise, concerning the cup he said: ‘Drink from this, all of you [Note: [Col. 1618D] Addition 1. “Drink from this, all of you”: then, as also in the primitive Church, all who were present at Mass received the sacrament of unity. Now, because not all can receive worthily, they at least receive another sacrament of unity: the kiss of peace. In giving it to the minister, the priest says: “Receive the bond of peace and love,” as though saying, “Drink from this, all of you,” or, “Receive and divide it among yourselves.”], this is my blood of the new covenant,’” supply, “more firmly established,” “which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22).

His saying, “Take and eat,” is perhaps an emphatic repetition. It should not be understood that they themselves administered to themselves the body received from the Lord’s hand; rather, he who consecrated also administered. But it is as though he said: “Eat,” indicating both modes of eating this sacrament. For he did not say of the cup, “Take”; rather, in administering it he said: “Drink.”

Note that in the canon, when the words “This is my body; this is my blood” are uttered, transubstantiation takes place by the power of these words. Hence it is credible that, when the Lord spoke the same words, he changed bread and wine into flesh and blood, and then conferred upon those words that same power for the future. Therefore the text must be construed thus: “He blessed,” supply, saying: “This is my body.” Then he broke it and gave it to his disciples, and said: “Eat.” And he repeated: “This is my body.”

Or perhaps he then blessed it with a blessing not handed down to us; but afterward, for the instruction [Col. 1618C] of the apostles, the power of blessing was handed down by the Lord in these words: “This is my body.” Yet in saying before the handing down of the Eucharist that Judas had gone out, we seem to contradict Luke, who mentions the betrayer after the cup. But perhaps Luke recapitulates the betrayal. Hilary, however, on Matthew proves that Judas was not present: for Jesus said that those drinking the cup would drink with him in the kingdom of the Father, of which Judas was unworthy. Moreover, excluding none of those drinking, he said: “Which will be poured out for you.” But elsewhere he excluded some, saying: “For many.” Nevertheless, it can be said that Judas received the Eucharist, and Hilary’s statement may readily be determined accordingly.

Therefore, when Jesus said, “Do this in remembrance of me,” he instituted this sacrament and tacitly set aside what had preceded it. When he said that he would not drink wine until he drank it new with them, the word is used adverbially: that is, in a new manner, as one made new—namely, not incorporating wine into myself as before.

## CHAPTER CLIII. On the prediction of Peter’s denial

[Col. 1619A]

Then Jesus said to them: “You will all suffer scandal because of me on this night. For it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered’” (Matt. 26; Mark 14). Zechariah the prophet, speaking in the person of the Church, prayed to the Father: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. 13). But the Evangelist, seeing fulfilled what the prophet had prayed, gave the Father’s assenting answer, namely: “I will strike the shepherd.”

When Peter said: “Even if all are scandalized, I shall never be scandalized,” Jesus replied: “Before the cock has crowed twice, you will deny me three times.” Mark expressed this more fully than the others. For after Peter’s first denial the cock immediately crowed; [Col. 1619B] but before the second crowing of the cock he denied again twice, and so Peter’s threefold denial was begun before the first crowing and completed before the second. The other Evangelists, saying, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times,” speak of its beginning; that is: “You will begin the threefold denial.” Mark, however, wrote of its completion.

Peter said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” Peter does not lie, because he believes what he promises to be true [Note: [Col. 1619B] Addition 1. Hence on this Thursday all the hours are mournful, and only the Mass is solemn, in chant and the adornment of its ministries, as though on the day of its institution, almost as on its birthday.
