On the same day chrism is prepared, with which the fonts are anointed [Col. 1619C], because on that same day the doorposts were anointed with the blood of the lamb. Since the eating of the paschal Lamb followed this, the anointing of the baptismal font is deferred until Saturday, so that it may be joined to the eating of the lamb. But the preparation of chrism could not be deferred, because Mass is not celebrated on those days until baptism.].

## CHAPTER CLIV. On the Lord’s discourse after supper

[Col. 1619C]

Then Jesus added, in consolation, the long discourse written by John (chap. 14): “Let not your heart be troubled or afraid. In my Father’s house are many dwelling places; if it were otherwise, I would have told you.” *Minus* is used for “not,” and the meaning is: “If in any respect I had not told you”—not, that is, “if they were not there, I would have told you,” meaning, “I would not have concealed from you; indeed, I would have told you that they are not there.” But supply: you know “that I go to prepare a place for you.”

The dwelling places were already prepared, as he had said, by predestination; yet they still had to be prepared by their opening and by the meritorious actions of those persons themselves. Jerome, however, against Jovinian reads the whole under a single punctuation as follows: “If there were not many dwelling places with the Father, I would have told you that I go to prepare a place for you.” That is, if each person did not prepare a dwelling for himself by his own works, “I would have told you that I go to prepare a place for you.” But to prepare is not my work; it is yours. It is spoken like this: “To sit at my right or left is not mine to give you” (Matt. 20). Yet what each person prepares for himself, God also prepares for him.

[Col. 1620A] For he prepares dwelling places by preparing dwelling places for those dwelling places. When Thomas said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus replied: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” As though he said: By what do you wish to go? I am the way—that is, imitate me. To what do you wish to go? I am the truth—that is, the true and highest end, which alone must be sought. Where do you wish to remain? I am life.

Note that in this discourse he now rebukes them as though they do not know him, now commends them as though they do know; this must be understood according to Ticonius’s rule concerning different persons. There are also certain things in this discourse at which Sabellius applauds, such as, “He who sees me sees the Father”; and others at which Arius exults, such as, “The words which I speak, I do not speak from myself,” “the Father is greater than I,” and the like.

Jesus also added this promise: “He who believes in me will himself do the works which I do, and will do greater than these.” The genitive is used for the ablative in Greek fashion. Peter’s shadow healing was greater than the hem of Christ’s garment, as though he said: He who believes in me will not be greater than I; rather, through him I will do greater things than without him. Augustine says: This is not said of all Christ’s works. I do not dare to deliver a judgment by saying that the salvation of sinners, accomplished by Christ, is greater than angels. Let one who can understand whether creating the righteous is greater than justifying the ungodly, since the latter is of greater mercy and the former of greater power. This discourse concerns the works of righteousness which he then performed, not all his works.

As for his saying, “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete [Col. 1620C],” it must be construed thus: he will give you the Paraclete, who is other than us—that is, another person than us, namely than the Father and the Son. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same advocate or comforter. His saying that the Paraclete is sent in his name means for his recognition and glorification; or because he has the same name as the Son, namely God.

Nor does his saying, “The word which you have heard is not mine,” contradict what he had said: that one who loves him keeps his words. For he said in the singular that the word is the Father’s and is not his—that is, not from himself.

He said to them: “When I sent you without purse, bag, and shoes, did you lack anything?” [Note: [Col. 1621A] Addition 1. As though he said: For a short time you will have persecution; therefore equip yourselves beforehand, with weapons for defense and with bags for storing necessities.] They replied: “Nothing.” And he said to them: “But now, let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let the one who does not have a sword buy one” (Luke 22).

[Col. 1620D] The Lord instructs them concerning discernment among virtues. Some things must always be retained, such as mercy, humility, faith, hope, and charity; others must be changed according to time and place, such as hunger, thirst, vigils, prayers, the labor of working and teaching. Therefore, in a time of persecution he teaches them to take necessities, until the time for evangelizing should return after persecution had subsided.

When they said, “Lord, behold, here are two swords,” he answered, “It is enough” (ibid.). One was to cut off the ear, in whose healing the Lord’s power would be displayed; the other, remaining undrawn, was to show that the apostles were not allowed to do everything they could in defense of the Lord.

Jesus also foretold to them: “Behold, the hour is coming—indeed, it has come—for you to be scattered, each to his own, and to leave me alone” (John 16).—“Afterward, raising his eyes to heaven, he prayed, saying: ‘Father, the hour has come,’” etc. (John 17). He prayed first for himself, then for the disciples, and thirdly for those who would believe through their word.

## CHAPTER CLV. On the Lord’s threefold prayer at the estate of Gethsemane

“Then he came with them to the estate called Gethsemane, which is at the foot of the Mount of Olives across the brook Cedron” (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke [Col. 1621B] 22; John 18). *Cedron* is a Greek plural genitive, which in Latin is said *Cedrorum*, “of cedars.” “Jesus entered the garden with his disciples. Judas also knew that place, because Jesus was accustomed to come there with his disciples. When he had entered, he said to them: ‘Sit here until I go there and pray; and you too pray, that you may not enter into temptation’”—that is, lest you succumb to temptation.

Taking Peter and the sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” This is said in the usual manner: that is, “My soul is very sorrowful,” or “My soul is sorrowful to the point of fearing death and because of the fear of death.” He was giving testimony concerning the apostles’ fall; or *until* may be exclusive. For he was sorrowful until he should free himself and his own by his death. Or it may be inclusive: namely, until after his death the apostles returned to faith in him.

“And having gone forward from them about a stone’s throw, he fell upon his face and prayed: ‘Abba, Father, if possible, let this cup [Note: [Col. 1622B] Addition 1. By the name “cup” the Passion is understood on account of measure, because God’s justice does not permit anyone to suffer beyond what he can bear.] pass from me.’” *Abba* means the same as “Father.” *Abba* is Hebrew and Syriac; *Pater* (“Father”) is Greek and Latin. In this he indicates that God is Father of all nations.

As true man he recoiled from death and wished not to die, if this could be done consistently with justice. For the Father’s justice required that Christ suffer, and from the foundation of the world this mystery had been foreshown by him. This will not to die made the martyrs glorious. For the perception of the flesh desires only what delights it. If dying delighted them, they would not thereby seem to deserve merit; but because they subject this will to die to God, they merit. Hence Christ added: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will.”

Some, however, fastening upon the demonstrative particle, namely “this,” say that he mercifully prayed for the Jews: that, if possible, the Gentiles might enter without the Jews’ blindness, and that he might not drink this cup—namely, the death from the Jews that threatened him.

“When he came to the disciples, he found them sleeping. And he said to Peter: ‘Thus could you not,’” etc. Or he spoke to Peter thus ironically, as though saying: “Was this what ought to be done?” But in common he said to the three: “Why do you sleep? The spirit indeed is willing,” supply, “your spirit”; as though saying, “You had a rather ready spirit when you promised even to die for me, but now the weakness of the flesh is evident.”

“Again he went away and prayed the same words. An angel appeared to him, strengthening him. And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly”—that is, in a struggle against death. He was now, as it were, conquering death in spirit, while he also willed to die; afterward he conquered it in the act itself, namely by rising again. “And [Note: [Col. 1621D] Luke alone records this.] his sweat became like drops of blood [Note: [Col. 1622B] Addition 2. Note that the first shedding of Christ’s blood was at circumcision; the second in sweat; the third in scourging; the fourth in crucifixion; the fifth in the piercing of his dead body by the lance. The first was an example, that we may circumcise our members; the second a sign, because he would water and make fruitful in his blood; the third and fourth a remedy; the fifth a sacrament. Hence the office of the Mass is divided into five parts. Its first part is up to the Epistle, where it begins; the second part extends through the Gospel inclusively; the third to the canon; the fourth to the embolism, which means “an addition,” because it is added at the end, except for “Deliver us,” etc., which in some churches is said aloud; the fifth part extends to the end. But because even on the cross there was a fivefold shedding of blood, the canon alone is also subdivided into five parts: the first to *Qui pridie*; the second to the *Memento*; the third to *Praeceptis*; the fourth and fifth to the embolism, or to the end.] running down upon the ground.” Returning to the disciples, he found them sleeping. A third time he went away and prayed the same words. Then he came to the disciples and said to them: “Sleep now and rest.” After they had slept a little, he said: “Rise; enough. Let us go. Behold, he who betrays me is near.”

## CHAPTER CLVI. On the binding of the Lord and the healing of the servant’s ear

[Col. 1622C]

While he was still speaking, Judas came with a cohort of soldiers received from the governor, and a crowd of attendants received from the chief priests, and with weapons (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18). He had [Col. 1622D] given them the sign that he would indicate Jesus to them by a kiss, and that they should lead him away cautiously. For he thought that Jesus could transform himself by magical arts and escape.

When Jesus received the kiss, he called him friend, either ironically or according to his former state [Note: [Col. 1621D] John alone says this.]. He had first asked them: “Whom do you seek?” They replied: “Jesus.” When Jesus said to those seeking him, “I am he,” they went backward and fell. Afterward they seized Jesus and bound him.

Simon Peter cut off the ear of the servant whose name was Malchus. Jesus healed him [Note: [Col. 1622D] Luke alone records the healing.] and said to Peter: “Everyone who takes the sword will perish by the sword”—namely, the sword that was turned before Paradise [Col. 1623A], or he will perish because he took up the sword. He does not mean the sword given by God, or by the law, or by a judge.

## CHAPTER CLVII. On the flight of the young man

They first brought Jesus to Annas [Note: [Col. 1623D] John alone speaks of Annas], not because he was Caiaphas’s colleague [Note: [Col. 1623B] Addition 1. That is, Caiaphas and Annas had first bought the high priesthood from Pilate; but Caiaphas held it in that year. Rather, because Annas’s house lay on their way, they brought him in there before going to Caiaphas, out of reverence for the priesthood.], but because he was his father-in-law. It would have been disgraceful had they passed by Annas’s house, which stood first.

But a young man [Note: [Col. 1623D] Mark alone speaks of the young man] followed him, wrapped in a linen cloth over his naked—supply, body. For he had no garment other than the linen cloth; leaving it behind, he fled from them. Some hand down that this was John, and his long life indicates that he was then a young man. Jerome, however, on the passage of the Psalm (Ps. 32): “Those who sought my life used violence [Col. 1623B],” says: “The Jews used violence,” either against Peter when they said, “You too are one of them,” or against James, who, when he was dragged away, left his linen cloth behind and escaped from them naked. Yet he seems to have said this by conjecture rather than assertion.

## CHAPTER CLVIII. On Peter’s first denial

“Peter followed at a distance, to see the end. John, however, known to the high priest, brought Peter in. When the maidservant who kept the door saw him, she said: ‘Are you also one of that man’s disciples?’ He [Col. 1623C] said: ‘I do not know him, nor do I know what you are saying’” (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; John 18).

Some, wishing to excuse Peter, say that he rightly said that he did not know him whom no one knows perfectly except the Father. And when he said, “O man, I am not,” he denied himself, not Christ. And when he said, “Man, I do not know what you are saying,” he said that he did not know their false schemes and deceits. But it is foolish to excuse one whom the Lord accused. Peter himself also showed himself guilty by his tears.

Peter was standing with the attendants by the fire. The high priest questioned Jesus concerning his teaching. When Jesus said, “I have spoken openly to the world; ask those who heard,” one of the attendants struck Jesus on the face [Note: [Col. 1624D] John alone records this.]. [Col. 1623D] Jesus said: “If I have spoken well, why do you strike me?” By this Jesus showed that, when someone strikes one cheek, the other is not to be offered by the act itself, but that the mind must be prepared to endure, should need arise. Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas.

## CHAPTER CLIX. On the second and third denials
Peter was standing in the courtyard, warming himself [Note: [Col. 1624D] All speak of this denial, but in different ways.]. When another maidservant said, “This man too was with Jesus,” those standing by said: “Truly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean, and your speech—that is, the dialect of Galilee—makes you known.” Then Peter denied it with an oath; and before this denial he had gone out, and the cock had crowed. And about an hour later a kinsman of Malchus [Col. 1624A] said that he had seen him in the garden with Jesus. Then Peter began to call down curses and to swear that he did not know the man, and immediately the cock crowed. And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Remembering the word which the Lord had spoken, Peter went out and wept bitterly, fleeing to the cave now called Gallicantu; a church has been built on that spot. According to this order of John, Peter’s threefold denial appears to have begun in Annas’s courtyard and to have been completed in Caiaphas’s courtyard. According to others, who make no mention of Annas, it appears to have taken place wholly in Caiaphas’s courtyard. Augustine, in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, maintains that the whole occurred in Annas’s courtyard, and that matters said thereafter, following Jesus’ dispatch to Caiaphas, were stated by recapitulation. Jerome on [Col. 1624B] Matthew, and Bede on Luke, seem to hold that Peter denied him in Caiaphas’s courtyard.

## Chapter CLX. On the sentence of death pronounced upon Jesus

“When morning came, the priests, elders of the people, scribes, and Pharisees assembled before Caiaphas, and they sought false testimony against Jesus (Matt. 26; Mark 14). Two false witnesses said: ‘We heard him say: I can destroy this temple of God made with hands, and after three days rebuild one not made with hands.’ When Jesus did not answer, Caiaphas rose and said to Jesus: ‘I adjure you by the living God: tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the blessed God.’ Jesus answered: ‘You have said it. If I tell you, you do not believe me. Henceforth [Col. 1624C] you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven.’” This may fittingly be understood of his second coming, or of his coming into the world through preachers. “Then the chief priest tore his garments [Note: [Col. 1624C] Addition 1. They did not have this prescribed in the Law, but it ought to have been a sign of grief.] and said: ‘He has blasphemed.’” It was a Jewish custom, upon hearing blasphemy against God, to tear one’s garments. “And he said: ‘What do you think?’ And they said: ‘He is deserving of death.’”

## Chapter CLXI. The first mockery

Then they spat in his face (Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 18); and this too was characteristic of the Jews: to spit in the face of one whom they rejected. They brought him bound to the praetorium [Col. 1624D] and handed him over to Pontius Pilate, the governor; but they did not enter, lest they should be defiled by entering a Gentile’s house.

## Chapter CLXII. On Judas’s hanging

“Then Judas, moved by repentance, brought back the thirty pieces of silver, saying to the chief priests: ‘I have sinned in betraying innocent blood.’ But they said: ‘What is that to us? See to it yourself’ (Matt. 27).” That is, as though they said: “You have seen what you did”; and thus *videris* is a perfect subjunctive. Or: “You will see, when in punishment you perceive that you have sinned”; and thus it is a future subjunctive. Some, however, read it under one punctuation: “What is that to us that you see?”—that is, what does it concern us?

Perhaps Satan, [Col. 1625A] who had possessed Judas, after accomplishing what he wanted, departed from him; and thus Judas was able to grieve over what he had done, so that through grief Satan might enter him again and make him lay hands upon himself. Jerome says on Psalm 108 that Judas offended God more when he hanged himself than when he betrayed him. Having thrown the silver pieces into the Temple, he went away, hanged himself with a noose, and burst open in the middle, his entrails pouring out. In this, in some measure, punishment was brought upon the mouth with which he had kissed the Lord, lest the spirit should depart through his mouth. For when the noose broke, he is thought afterward to have fallen and burst open.

Whether he hanged himself that same day or delayed is uncertain; but that it was before the Lord’s resurrection is found in the commentary on the Psalm. Some nevertheless said that, upon hearing of the resurrection—which he had not expected—[Col. 1625B] he hanged himself; this is not authoritative. The priests said that they were not permitted to put the coins into the *corbona*, because they were the price of blood. “To put” should be understood as “to return,” because they had taken them from there. They bought with them a potter’s field [Note: [Col. 1626A] Addition 1. Above this field, beside the road leading to Ephrathah, is Mount Geon, where Solomon was anointed.] for the burial of strangers, namely, the field of a certain potter. Or *Figuli* (“Potter”) is a proper name. It was called the field of Haceldama, that is, “field of blood.” Since they were the price of death, they gave the coins over for the use of the dead.

Then was fulfilled what is said of Jeremiah: “They received thirty pieces of silver”—whether the priests, or the sellers of the field, or Judas—“and gave them for the potter’s field,” namely, “the price of him who was appraised by the children of Israel”: that is, Christ, whom the children of Israel appraised, that is, bought for a price; or others born from the children [Col. 1625C] of Israel. This is not read in Jeremiah, but in Zechariah (ch. 11) there is almost the same sense in other words. Hence some manuscripts have “through the prophet,” without any name.

Jerome says in the larger Breviary that ancient codices had “Asaph the prophet,” but through copyists’ error it was written “Isaiah,” because they did not know who Asaph was. Therefore Porphyry called Matthew unlearned because he had put Isaiah; but Matthew did not err—rather, the copyist did. Likewise, Jerome says that in Mark it had been written that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour; but unlearned copyists, in place of *episē*, which denotes six and is not a letter but only a numerical sign, wrote the letter gamma, which signifies three. Thus perhaps the gloss in Mark may be read [Col. 1625D] in this way: Mark himself properly said it—understand, he said “sixth”—but the copyist corrupted it; yet he truly said “third” with regard to the mystery.

For although Jerome says that copyists erred in Matthew by writing Jeremiah instead of Zechariah, he also says in his commentary on Matthew that a certain Hebrew showed him an apocryphal book of Jeremiah in which he found these words written verbatim. Origen says on Matthew: “This is found in the secrets of Jeremiah, just as the Apostle brings forward writings of certain secret books, such as: ‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard’ (1 Cor. 2).” For this is found in no canonical book except in the secrets of Isaiah [Note: [Col. 1626A] Addition 2. For each of the prophets had secrets which he did not reveal, namely because he did not know their solution; hence he himself said: “My secret is for myself” (Isa. 24).].

Augustine, in *On the Harmony [Col. 1626A] of the Evangelists*, says that Zechariah alone contains the matter of the thirty pieces of silver, whereas Jeremiah contains the purchase of a field, though not this field. Thus he says that this passage is composed from two sources. Moreover, as Augustine says, some words must be taken as spoken in the person of the Evangelist, and some in the person of the prophet.

## Chapter CLXIII. On Pilate’s words to Jesus and the Jews

While Jesus was in the praetorium, Pilate went out to the Jews [Col. 1626B] and asked what accusation they were bringing against this man (John 18; Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23). First they accused him on two counts: because he forbade tribute to be paid to Caesar, and because he said that he was Christ the king. When Pilate answered that they should take him and judge him according to their own law, they said: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death”—understand, at this time. Or they said this because judicial authority had been transferred to others.

Pilate therefore entered the praetorium. Considering the first charge as if it were nothing, because perhaps he had heard Jesus say, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matt. 22), he said to Jesus concerning the second: “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus answered: “Do you say this of yourself, or did others tell you this about me?” That is: “Did they accuse me of this before you?” [Col. 1626C] Pilate said: “Am I a Jew?”—as though to say: “I am not a Jew, and therefore I do not say this of myself; but your nation, namely the nation which you call yours and from which he was born, handed you over to me” [Note: [Col. 1625D] John alone relates these matters.]. Jesus said: “My kingdom is not of this world.” Pilate said: “Then are you a king?” Jesus answered: “You say that I am a king” [Note: [Col. 1626C] Addition 1. “You say,” that is, what you ask may truly be said—as though he said: Change your manner of utterance; state declaratively what you say interrogatively. The Master says that Pilate would have acted rightly had he waited for Jesus’ answer on this point. Pilate is blamed in this: that he did not wait for truth to be expounded by the Lord, when it could not be expounded by the Pharisees. For the Academics said that truth was in a bottomless well, and they could not expound it.]. “For this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth.” Pilate said to him: “What is truth?” And going out again, he said to the Jews: “I find no case against him.”

“ [Note: [Col. 1626D] Luke alone relates this.] But they cried out: ‘He has stirred up the whole people, beginning from Galilee as far as this place.’”

## Chapter CLXIV. That Herod mocked the Lord

[Col. 1626D]

When Pilate learned that the man was a Galilean (Luke 23), because Herod, who ruled that region, was in Jerusalem at that time, wishing to pay him honour, he sent Jesus to him, so that the lord of Galilee might either acquit or condemn a Galilean man. [Col. 1627A] Thus Herod was reconciled with Pilate over the slaughter of the Galileans which we mentioned earlier. Herod rejoiced, because for a long time he had desired to see Jesus and to see a sign from him. But the priests steadfastly accused Jesus before Herod. When Herod questioned Jesus on many matters and received no answer from him, he despised and mocked him, thinking him foolish or not of sound mind. As a sign of mockery he clothed him in a white garment.

## Chapter CLXV. On the second mockery

Then Pilate told the Jews that neither he nor Herod found any case against Jesus, and that he would therefore punish him with scourges and release him. But the whole crowd cried: “Crucify him” (Luke 23; John 19). When Pilate refused, the Jews accused him on a third count, [Col. 1627B] because he made himself the Son of God.

## Chapter CLXVI. That Pilate sat upon the judgment seat at about the sixth hour

Pilate then feared even more and, entering to Jesus, said to him: “Where are you from?” (John 19). But Jesus gave him no answer. Pilate said to him: “Will you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have power to crucify you and to release you?” Jesus answered: “You would have no power over me at all unless it had been given you from above”—that is, from Caesar; indeed, from God. Since Pilate seemed troubled by fear of superior authority, Jesus said that he sinned less than the Jews.

When Pilate sought to release him, the Jews cried: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.” Hearing [Col. 1627C] this, Pilate brought Jesus out and sat upon the judgment seat in the place called in Greek *lithostrotos*, in Hebrew *Gabbatha*, which means “variegation of pavement.” It was the Preparation, about the sixth hour.

The Jews, mingled with Greeks, frequently used Greek terms. For *parasceve* is Greek and means “preparation” in Latin; thus they called the sixth day, because on it they prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath, just as in the wilderness they gathered manna double. Therefore the sixth hour could have begun, and the things read up to the darkness could have occurred before its completion; and when the sixth hour was completed, darkness came. Mark (ch. 15) says the third hour, preferring to understand the hour at which the Jews crucified him with their tongues. Or John calls the sixth hour the preparation [Col. 1627D] for the Lord’s death. For after they judged him guilty of death during the night, three hours of night and three hours of day passed until the crucifixion. I think that the Lord was crucified in the middle of those hours; therefore now one hour, now the other is given. For the Church celebrates Mass between the third and sixth hours [Note: [Col. 1628A] Addition 1. That on fast days Mass is deferred until after the sixth hour, and in Lent until after the ninth, I think was done more because of our gluttony than for a mystery: lest, after hearing Mass before the sixth hour, we seek an occasion to anticipate the dinner hour. Or perhaps because the sacraments of the Passion, death, burial, and ascension are all present in Mass. In memory of the death and ascension it is celebrated after the sixth hour; in memory of the burial, after the ninth; perhaps in memory of the resurrection it is celebrated [Col. 1628B] in the morning.], and when it is celebrated in the morning, the third hour ought first to be sung.

Though they accused him on many charges, he answered nothing. On the feast day of Passover the governor had customarily, by a recently introduced custom, released one prisoner whomsoever they asked for, in remembrance that on that day they had gone out from Pharaoh’s slavery, the Egyptians themselves compelling them to depart. They killed others—Christ and the two thieves—in remembrance of the firstborn of Egypt; whether they still do the same, I do not know. Since this happened [Col. 1628A] on the fifteenth day of the moon, it is certain that the moon was then at its fifteenth day. When Pilate offered them the choice of innocent Jesus or Barabbas the robber, they chose Barabbas. It is written *Barrabas*, meaning “son of the master”; it is also written *Barabas*, meaning “son of the father.”

## Chapter CLXVII. That Pilate, as though unwillingly, handed Jesus over after scourging, to be crucified

[Col. 1628B]

“Then his wife sent to Pilate, saying: ‘Have nothing to do with that righteous man; for while sleeping I suffered much in a dream because of him’” (Matt. 27). Already from God’s birth, the devil could recognize the mystery of the cross; therefore he laboured to prevent Christ’s death. Perhaps the saints in hell were already rejoicing, and therefore he noticed this. “But Pilate, seeing that he accomplished nothing and that rather a tumult was arising, washed his hands, saying: ‘I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man.’ And all answered: ‘His blood be upon us and upon our children’”—that is, the vengeance for his blood. “Then he handed Jesus, scourged with whips, over to them to be crucified” [Note: [Col. 1628C] Addition 1. Therefore in those days we omit the beginnings and endings of the hours, because he who is Alpha and Omega was taken away from us and handed over to the ungodly.].

[Col. 1628C] It was ordained by the Romans that a person to be crucified should first be scourged, or perhaps this was done so that the Jews, sated with scourging, might desist from death. Even now the column to which Jesus was bound shows traces of blood.

## Chapter CLXVIII. On the mockery [Note: [Col. 1628D] Addition 1. The third mockery. Against these mockeries, by which he was mocked three times, we ourselves, before the revelation of the cross, offer three acts of adoration, saying “Agios,” etc., as though honouring three times him who was three times mocked for us; and we do so in two languages, because the third is still silent. Likewise, against the three accusations we say three vindications in the person of the Saviour: “My people,” etc. There Christ also reproaches them with his three benefits: liberation from Egypt, guidance in the wilderness, and entrance into an excellent land. It is as though Christ said: “You accuse me of denying tribute; rather, you ought to give thanks, because I freed you from tribute. You accuse me because I said that I was king; rather, give thanks, because I royally fed you in the wilderness. You accuse me because I called myself the Son of God; rather, pray that I may lead you into a better and excellent land.”] by the soldiers

The governor’s soldiers took Jesus (Matt. 27; John 19), stripped him, and put around him a scarlet cloak in imitation of the purple worn by kings. Perhaps something purple had been sewn inside that cloak, as is commonly done with a summer cloak, since Mark (ch. 15) also says that he was clothed in purple. Instead of a diadem, they plaited [Col. 1628D] a crown of thorns and placed it on his head. Those who say that they have examined it more closely maintain that the thorns were sea-reeds, whose point pricks no less than a thorn because it is hard and penetrating. Hence the poet:

> …and with the sharp point of a reed.

It is credible that the spikes of the crown drew blood from his head. The scourges likewise drew blood from his back, and his bloody sweat stained other parts of his body, so that we should not say merely that his hands, feet, and side were sprinkled with blood, but that Christ ascended from Bozrah with his whole garment dyed (Isa. 63). Instead of a sceptre they put a reed in his hand, and mocked him as one wishing to reign but unable to do so.

## Chapter CLXIX. The third mockery

[Col. 1629B]

“And, bending the knee, they said: ‘Hail, King of the Jews’” (Matt. 27; Mark 15; John 19). Although Gentiles did this, because it was done at the instigation of the Jews, we do not bend the knee on the Preparation when prayer is offered for the faithless Jews. Yet perhaps the Jews acted thus together with the soldiers. Spitting upon him, they struck his head with the reed; stripping him of the purple, they clothed him again in his own garment and led him out to be crucified, carrying his cross for himself.

## Chapter CLXX. On Simon of Cyrene

As they went out, they found Simon of Cyrene, father of Alexander and Rufus. These two are thought to have been disciples of Jesus. They compelled him to carry the cross behind Jesus (Matt. 27; Mark 15), that is, they pressed him into service [Col. 1629C] for an *angaria*, which is a burden of person and labour; a *perangaria*, however, is of the person alone. “Women followed Jesus, lamenting him [Note: [Col. 1629D] Addition 1. We represent this procession of mourners following the Lord when we make litanies for dangers [Col. 1630A] that threaten; and, according to the Lord’s command, we mourn for ourselves and for our children. Certainly the cross should be placed upon the altar, so that the cross-bearer may take it from the altar; for Simon of Cyrene carried it after it had been taken from Christ’s shoulders.].” He said to them: “Do not weep over me, but over yourselves and your children,” as though he said: “Weep for the impending destruction of your nation.” This may be one reason why we do not celebrate solemnly during Christ’s Passion: the Lord commanded them to weep.

Two evildoers were also led with him to be put to death, and they came to the place of Calvary [Note: [Col. 1629D] All name the place.], which is called Golgotha in Hebrew. Calvary properly means a bare human skull. Because criminals were beheaded there and many skull-bones were scattered there, it was called the Place of Calvary, or Calvary. Ambrose, in his [Col. 1629D] Epistle to the Romans, seems to hold that Adam was buried there, that it was called Calvary from his head, and that the Apostle’s words were addressed to him: “Awake, you who sleep; rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5). Jerome says of this opinion that it is a pleasing interpretation and soothing to the ears, but not true. Therefore we believe that this was inserted into Ambrose by falsifiers, as were many other things. “When they crucified him, he said: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’” [Note: [Col. 1629D] Luke alone gives this first word.].

## Chapter CLXXI. On the division of the garments and the tunic cast for by lot

[Col. 1630A]

Then they made four parts from his garments, except for the tunic, because there were four soldiers who crucified him. The tunic, however, was seamless, made with netted workmanship, and therefore could not be divided; it was woven from the top throughout, having, that is, some piece of cloth laid crosswise over the shoulder, like a strap on fur garments. They cast lots [Note: [Col. 1629D] All relate the casting of lots for the garments [Col. 1630D] above.] for it, to determine whose it should be.

## Chapter CLXXII. On the triumphal title

[Col. 1630B] Pilate wrote the title [Note: [Col. 1630D] Addition 1. There are three kinds of titles: the triumphal, containing the deeds of victors; the proclamatory, written on gates and houses; and the memorial, written above tombs—that is, an epitaph.] of his charge, that is, in the title the cause of his death: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” It is as though he said: “For this reason he was crucified: because he was king of the Jews.” He wrote it in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, so that people of different languages who had assembled for the feast day might read and understand it.

Whether the beginning of the title [Note: [Col. 1630D] Addition 2. Or it was also signified by the three languages that every religion—represented by Hebrew, because religion first flourished among them through the worship of the one God—every wisdom, represented by Greek, and every strength, represented by Latin because of Roman rule, ought to believe him to be God and man.] was written in three languages is uncertain; but the end, namely “King of the Jews,” was written thus: in Hebrew, *Malcus Judaeorum*—“King of the Jews”; in Greek, *Basileos exomosoleon* [as printed]—“King of those who confess”; in Latin, *Rex confitentium*—“King of those who confess.” The cross itself had no addition above its crossbeam, having the shape of a Tau. But Pilate placed above it a peg and an attached board, and the title was on the board. It is said that the Lord’s cross had four different pieces of wood, [Col. 1630C] and perhaps of as many different kinds: the upright timber, the crossbeam, the board placed above, and a certain block into which the cross was fixed [Note: [Col. 1631A] Addition 3. Note that some hold that there were only three nails in the Lord’s cross.], which was buried in the rock. For wood of the Lord’s cross is found to have been palm and cypress, and, as some report, olive and cedar.

The Jews told Pilate to alter the title; he refused and confirmed it, saying: “What I have written, I have written”—that is, I have written it irrevocably. Those passing by blasphemed, saying: “Aha, you who destroy the temple of God,” etc. Likewise the priests mocked him, saying: “He saved others; himself he cannot save.” It is as though they said: “Now it is clear that he healed people not by his own power but in Beelzebub; for he would rather heal himself.” The demons, [Col. 1630D] feeling that their powers had been broken, did this in order that he might come down from the cross. Yet in Tobit, concerning the disembowelling of the fish, the demon is read to have stood upon the arm of the cross and considered whether Christ had any stain of sin.

## Chapter CLXXIII. On the differing merits of the thieves

[Col. 1631A]

One of those hanging with him also blasphemed him; but the other, rebuking the blasphemer, said: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.” And he heard from the Lord: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). Do not understand this of the earthly paradise from which Adam was expelled, nor of the angelic paradise, because before Christ no one ascended to it; rather, it means rest, [Col. 1631B] which is to be with Jesus. Or: “Today you will be with me,” which is to be in paradise. Perhaps his soul was with Christ’s soul in Abraham’s bosom and returned with it.

Because the thief did not then penetrate the heavens, some have erred from this and many other passages of Scripture, thinking that there are many abodes of the blessed apart from heaven: namely Adam’s paradise and places in air and on earth where they will live happily but will nevertheless not see God. Only the perfect, together with the angels, will enjoy the vision of God. For this reason they also suppose that the saying means this: “There are many dwelling places in my Father’s house” (John 14).

## Chapter CLXXIV. That the Virgin was entrusted to a virgin

“Standing by the cross were the Mother of Jesus, Mary of Cleophas, Mary Magdalene, and John. Then Jesus said to his Mother concerning John: ‘Woman, behold your son.’ [Col. 1631C] And to John [Note: [Col. 1631C] Addition 1. Because John stood by at the crucifixion, the Passion according to him is read on that same day, although it is fittingly read last, because he wrote last.] he said: ‘Behold your mother’” (John 19). From that hour the disciple received her as his own, as though he had her for a mother; or “into his own,” that is, under his authority; or into the sharing of his possessions. Yet she is believed to have owned nothing privately; but while the Blessed Virgin was with the apostles, he had special care of her.

## Chapter CLXXV. On the darkness from the sixth hour to the ninth

From the sixth hour darkness came over [Col. 1631D] the whole land until the ninth (Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 24). It was not an eclipse of the sun, as some have lied, because the moon was nearly opposite the sun. An eclipse occurs only at the conjunction of sun and moon. It is read that learning flourished at Athens then; when the philosophers investigated the cause of the darkness and could not discover it, Dionysius the Areopagite said that the God of nature was suffering. They made him an altar and inscribed it “To the unknown God,” concerning which Acts of the Apostles speaks (ch. 16).

Origen, however, seems to hold that this darkness was only over the whole land of Judaea, because if it had spread over the entire world, some pagan histories would record it. And just as darkness was over the Egyptians for three days [Note: [Col. 1632A] Addition 1. Because darkness was spread over three hours, we also celebrate Tenebrae; and, because of the three-day death, we make as it were three-day funeral rites, since even the white monks do not make nine readings except for the dead. Then too the primacy of darkness is indicated, because in those days darkness began to precede daylight. The extinction of the candles signifies the apostles’ flight; or, because it occurs gradually, the killing of the prophets by a wicked generation; and finally understand it as signifying death.], while in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, there was light, so now, as it were conversely, darkness was over the children of Israel while other nations enjoyed light.

## Chapter CLXXVI. On the Lord’s cry to the Father

[Col. 1632B] About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Heli,” or “Heloy, lamma sabacthani” (Matt. 27). *Heli* is one word and means “my God.” *Hel* is the name of God; *oy* means “my.” What that cry of Christ means is interpreted by the Evangelist. Here it is clear that the Psalm which begins with the same words was written about Christ, not, as some suppose, in the person of David, Esther, or Mordecai. “Some said: ‘This man calls Elijah.’” These were Romans who did not understand Hebrew.

Jesus cried out that he had been forsaken by the Father, not because divinity had been separated from humanity, but because he had been so handed over by the Father to calamities that he appeared forsaken. Or he says that he was forsaken by the Father because at that time [Col. 1632C] his Passion appeared almost fruitless: from the whole human race, no one seemed to be redeemed except the thief, who almost alone believed in him. Hence Isaiah says [Note: [Col. 1632C] Addition 1. Isaiah speaks metaphorically: when perhaps at harvest-time the householder proposed to gather the harvest, he found nothing from the ears of grain but straw. So it was with Christ: when, in the time of grace, he ought to have gathered his harvest—that is, the Jews—he found only the one faithful thief.]: “I have become like one gathering straw in harvest” (Isa. 5). And in the Psalm: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140), except for the Blessed Virgin, who, in matters of this kind, is always excepted; for we believe that she too then believed.

## Chapter CLXXVII. On the Lord’s death after tasting vinegar

[Col. 1632D]

Afterward Jesus said: “I thirst.” A vessel full of vinegar had been placed there, and one of the soldiers filled a sponge with vinegar, put it on a reed set upon hyssop and bound around it, and gave it to him to drink (John 19; Matt. 27; Mark 15). Some said that those crucified die sooner if they drink vinegar with gall, and therefore the soldiers carried vinegar with them, so that they could be released sooner from guard duty if those whom they crucified died sooner. It may be that they carried cheap wine to drink, which from the heat had become, as it were, vinegar. Hence, to mark its bitterness, one Evangelist calls it myrrhed wine and another wine mixed with gall.

When Jesus had tasted [Col. 1633A] the vinegar, he said: “It is finished” [Note: [Col. 1633D] John alone gives the sixth word.], namely, everything that had to be done before he died; or he said that the defect of human corruption was finished. Jesus then cried with a loud voice: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” [Note: [Col. 1633D] Luke alone gives the seventh word.]; and bowing his head, he gave up the spirit.

## Chapter CLXXVIII. On the signs at the Lord’s death

“And behold, the veil of the Temple, which was before the Holy of Holies, was torn from top to bottom” [Note: [Col. 1633D] Matthew, Mark, and Luke relate this.]. Remigius said that the veil called the outer veil was torn; this may have been said only mystically. Or perhaps the veil hanging before the Temple doors, placed there to cover the doors, was torn together with the inner veil, as Josephus says. Indeed, the Gospel of the Nazaraeans records that the Temple lintel, of immense [Col. 1633B] size, was broken, and voices were heard in the air: “Let us depart from these dwellings.” The earth too was shaken, rocks were split, tombs were opened, and certain saints rose from the dead, came into Jerusalem, and appeared to many.

Perhaps these were those of whom it is read in the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews that many desired to be buried in the Holy Land, so that they might rise when the Lord rose. Whether some of them remained thus and ascended when the Lord ascended [Note: [Col. 1633C] Addition 1. Bede on Matthew: these are to be believed to have ascended bodily together with him when he ascended.], we do not know. But that some of them died again after they had testified to the Lord’s resurrection, we know, because the bodies of some still rest in Jerusalem; and Saint Iscarioth [Note: [Col. 1633C] Addition 2. Jerome has greater doubts about this person. Saint Iscarioth is said to have been an abbot; when he died, certain monks died in inconsolable grief, and they still appear joined together.], according to some reports, was one of them. “At seeing these things, the centurion [Note: [Col. 1633D] Matthew, Mark, and Luke relate the centurion.] and [Col. 1633C] those who were guarding Jesus with him were afraid and said: ‘Truly this was the Son of God.’” Because, when the Lord died at the ninth hour, the centurion became a herald of our faith, and the faithless withdrew, Joseph and Nicodemus were permitted to arrange the funeral, and the women to come nearer. Therefore at the ninth hour we assemble not for the Mass office but, as it were, for funeral observance.

## Chapter CLXXIX. That, after the thieves’ legs were broken, Christ was pierced with a lance

[Col. 1633D]

The Jews, lest they should remain hanging upon the cross on the great day of the Sabbath, asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken down, lest their feast be defiled by the horror of prolonged suffering [Note: [Col. 1634A] Addition 1. It is thought that the Lord’s cross was fifteen feet high, with an upper board one and a half feet high.] (John 19). After the soldiers had broken the legs of the first thieves and came to Jesus, finding him dead, they did not break any bone of his [Note: [Col. 1634A] Addition 2. Likewise, concerning the place where Christ was crucified, this is written in Greek: *o Theus*, that is, “here [is] God”; *Basileos imon*, that is, “our King”; *Proseruas*, that is, “before the ages”; *Glosae*, that is, “worked”; *Sothias*, that is, “salvation”; *Emesotis*, that is, “in the midst”; *Gis*, that is, “of the earth.”]. “But one of the soldiers pierced his right side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out.” The one who pierced him, [Col. 1634A] as some relate, had almost dim eyes; when Christ’s blood touched his eyes by chance, he saw clearly.

## Chapter CLXXX. On the Lord’s burial

When evening had come, Joseph, a *decurio*—that is, one of the municipal council—from Arimathea, which is Ramathah, the city of Elkanah, Samuel’s father, rich and [Col. 1634B] righteous, of whom some also suppose that the Psalm “Blessed is the man” (Ps. 111) was composed, because he did not consent to the acts and counsels of the others, asked Pilate for the body of Jesus, though secretly (Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19). Nicodemus also came with him [Note: [Col. 1634D] John alone speaks of Nicodemus.], carrying about one hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes. By their bitterness these keep worms away from dead bodies. They took Jesus’ body, wrapped it in the linen shroud which Joseph had bought, and bound it with white linen cloths, which Nicodemus is believed to have brought. Nearby was a new tomb cut out of rock, in which they placed him. Because Jesus’ body was wrapped in a simple linen shroud, Pope Sylvester instituted that the sacrifice of the altar should be celebrated only upon a linen cloth.

## Chapter CLXXXI. On the Lord’s tomb

[Col. 1634C]

Bede says, in his commentary on Mark, that the Lord’s tomb was a round chamber cut from the underlying rock, so high that a man could scarcely touch the roof with outstretched hand. It had an entrance from the east, with a large stone placed as a door. On its northern side was the resting-place for the Lord’s body, made from the same rock, seven feet long and three palms higher than the rest of the floor, projecting like a sarcophagus set upon the pavement; or the resting-place was made in the wall itself, as recesses are made in the walls of houses for storing utensils. Bede also says that the resting-place was open not from above but from the southern side, through which the body was brought in. This nevertheless agrees with the former opinion: it would have been like a sarcophagus [Col. 1634D] slanting over on its side, with an opening above on the side. The colour of the tomb and resting-place is said to have been a mixture of reddish and white.

“Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were there, observing where Jesus’ body had been laid. Returning, they prepared spices while it was permitted them to work; for on the Sabbath they rested” [Note: [Col. 1634D] Matthew, Mark, and Luke relate this.].

## Chapter CLXXXII. On the guards of the tomb
> “But on the next day [Note: [Col. 1634D] On this, Matthew alone, ch. XXVII.], which is after the Preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees came together to Pilate, [Col. 1635A] saying: ‘This deceiver, while still alive, said: After three days I shall rise again. Therefore order the tomb to be guarded, lest his disciples steal him away and say that he has risen.’” According to this wording, it is clear that these things took place on the Sabbath. [Note: [Col. 1635B] Addition 1. Note that, since the Church solemnizes and rejoices in the passions and deaths of the saints, it ought rather to exult and celebrate on the day of the death of its Savior. The holy Fathers assign three reasons, therefore, why it does not solemnize or presume to rejoice. The first is shame for the sin committed in Adam, for which the Lord endured the gibbet of the cross on that day. The second is because of the command by which “it was said to the people through Moses: The Lord will fight for us, and you shall be silent” (Exod. XIV). The third is because of the mystery: through this, as it were, the Church shows that it differs from its enemies by emulation.]

Remigius nevertheless explains *parasceve* here as the preparation for the Lord’s Passion, which began at the first watch of the night, as we said above. He reads it thus: “But on the next day, which is after this Preparation”—that is, after the beginning of this preparation—“this is Friday itself, which dawned after its beginning.” It perhaps seemed to Remigius that the Jews set guards at the tomb and sealed the stone on that day, since they would not have done so on the Sabbath. Hence Pilate says: “You have a guard,” that is, I give you permission to post guards. “Go, guard it.” And this [Col. 1635B] they did.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIII. On the women’s coming to the tomb

[Col. 1635C]

> “Now late on the Sabbath, which was dawning into the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Mary Salome came to the tomb with the spices which they had prepared” (Matt. XXVIII; Mark XVI; Luke XXIV; John XX).

Some say that only two came, because above only two were said to have observed the tomb and, having returned, to have prepared spices. They maintain that “and Salome” is added here as an explanation of the unnamed other Mary. [Note: [Col. 1635D] Addition 1. Chrysostom says that the mother of the sons of Zebedee was called Salome, as though she had two names.] Against them, it is enough to cite the practice of the Church, which represents three women. Luke also says that, besides the Marys, Joanna was present; she is handed down as the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward.

By the word “evening,” Augustine says in *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, the night is signified: the whole by a part. Thus it was “late on the Sabbath,” that is, on the night of the Sabbath. But lest we understand this as the actual evening, which is the beginning of the night, the gender is changed; and, referring to the sense rather than to the noun, it says: “which was dawning into the first day of the week”—that is, the night whose end was the dawn of the first day of the week, namely Sunday. It is as though it said: They came on the night of the Sabbath, but not at just any part of the night: at daybreak.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIV. On another ordering of the days

During this night the former order of natural days ended, in which day preceded night. Thereafter [Col. 1636A] a change of times took place. The Creator made night precede day. This night belonged jointly both to the Sabbath and to Sunday. [Note: [Col. 1636B] Addition 1. By this he brought it about that Christ rose during the night of Sunday, although it was said in Genesis (ch. I) at the beginning: “God said, Let there be light; and there was light.”]

Thus, by synecdoche, the Lord is said to have been in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights: reckoning the final part of the Preparation as the entire day with its night, the whole Sabbath, and the night of Sunday as Sunday itself. Augustine, however, seems to hold that this change occurred on the Preparation, so that the night of Thursday was also the night of the Preparation. And when the sun had already risen—that is, when the sky was already growing pale in the eastern regions—the women said to one another: “Who will roll away for us the stone from the entrance of the tomb? And looking, they saw the stone rolled away, and an angel [Note: [Col. 1636B] Addition 2. Note that the Evangelists appear to disagree concerning the appearance of the angels. Matthew says that the women found one sitting at the entrance to the tomb, upon the rolled-away stone, and does not mention more. Mark says that they found one sitting on the right side of the burial chamber. Luke says that they found two standing. John, who, as the latest writer, speaks as though more accurately, says that they found two sitting, one at the head and the other at the feet. Although these statements differ, they are not contradictory. We believe, however, that three angels appeared: one first sat upon the stone, then moved to the right side of the burial chamber, where the other two had first been standing and later sat.] sitting upon it” (Mark XVI; Matt. XXVIII).

For the earthquake had already occurred when the Lord rose; and Jesus had departed while the tomb remained closed. A voice was heard in the air by a certain monk of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls at Rome, in the year 1111 from the Lord’s Incarnation, as he wondered that the belt with which he was girded had come untied and fallen before him: “Thus could Christ go forth from the closed tomb.” The angel afterward removed the stone in order to indicate that the departure had already occurred. The guards, terrified by fear of him, lay as if dead.

## CHAPTER CLXXXV. Opinions concerning the hour of the Resurrection

[Col. 1636C]

[Col. 1636D] The hour of the Resurrection is commonly asked about, and authors speak of it variously. Jerome, namely in Book XII of the *Questions*, says: “Matthew says, ‘Late on the Sabbath.’ But Mark says: ‘And very early on the first day of the week they come to the tomb, the sun having now risen.’ There is a twofold solution to this question: either we do not accept Mark—for in almost all the Greek books this chapter is absent at the end—or both spoke truly: Matthew when the Lord rose, namely ‘late on the Sabbath’; Mark when Mary Magdalene saw him, namely in the morning.”

Ambrose, at the end of his exposition of Luke, says: “The Lord rose not as the day was drawing toward evening, but at nightfall. Indeed, the Greek expression for evening is *sero*. Thus the Lord [Col. 1637A] rose not in the evening time of day, but late, that is, in the depth of night. Hence the women were able to approach the tomb while the guards rested. And the chief priests said that his disciples came by night. But, that you may know that it occurred at night or in the morning: some of the women know, others do not. Those who keep watch by night know; those who went away do not know.” [Note: [Col. 1637D] Addition. The common opinion is that there was only one Magdalene; nevertheless, what Ambrose calls “the other” may be determined to mean the same woman as another.]

One Mary Magdalene, according to John, does not know; another Mary Magdalene, according to Matthew, does know. For the same woman could not know beforehand and afterward not know; therefore recognize that they are different. One is permitted to hold the Lord’s feet; the other is forbidden. One deserved to see an angel; the other, when she first came, saw no one. One announced to the disciples that the Lord had risen; the other thought that he had been taken away. One rejoices; the other weeps. One meets Christ; the other seeks the dead.

Augustine, as we said above, stated that he rose at dawn. This is supported by the authority which says that the Lord was dead for forty hours and afterward remained on earth for the same number of days before the Ascension: four evening hours of the Preparation and thirty-six hours of two nights and one day. The Church too seems to agree, since it celebrates morning praises for Christ’s Resurrection. Yet in support of Ambrose’s aforesaid opinion, Samson, as a type of the Lord’s Resurrection, rose at midnight and carried away the gates of Gaza. Thus Christ’s soul returned from the underworld and was restored to the body, which was made incapable of suffering. [Note: [Col. 1637D] Addition 2. Perhaps in favor of Jerome’s first opinion is the fact that the Apostles handed down that, on that night, the people were not to be dismissed from the Church until deep night.]

Whether Christ’s soul became incapable of suffering when it left the body, or only when it was restored to the body—lest it be glorified without the body—I do not recall having read. If it is asked where the saints whom he brought out of hell were after the Resurrection, God knows. Or they were, as is said of the Lord, in the furthest regions of the sea—that is, beyond the widest bounds of the world.

The Gloss of Augustine on Matthew fully resolves the apparent differences in the Evangelists concerning the women’s arrivals at the tomb—on account of which Porphyry mocks them—as well as the appearances and number of the angels. Let it suffice to say that ten appearances of Christ after the Resurrection are recorded in the Gospels: five on the day of the Resurrection itself, and five afterward. In the Apostle it is read that he was seen by James (I Cor. [Col. 1637D] XV) and by five hundred brethren at once, but neither the time nor the manner is specified. Some say that when the Lord died James vowed that he would not eat until Christ had risen; thus they say that he appeared to him on that same day of the Resurrection. There were also those who said that Joseph was imprisoned by the Jews on the very evening on which he buried the Lord, that Nicodemus remained hidden and afterward became a disciple, and that therefore Joseph, in prison, was the first among the others to whom Christ appeared, immediately, to comfort him.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVI. That the angels spoke to the women

[Col. 1638A]

And it happened (Luke XXIV), when the women were bewildered in mind by what they had seen, that behold, two men—that is, angels in human bodies—stood beside them. And when they lowered their faces to the ground, the angels said to them: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?”—that is, in the tomb, which is a place of the dead. “He is not here; he has risen, as he told you when he was in Galilee.”

Note that the holy women did not fall down but lowered their faces. Therefore it is ecclesiastical custom, following their example, in memory of the Lord’s Resurrection, and in hope of our own life, that on every Sunday from Easter to Pentecost [Col. 1638B] we do not bend the knee in prayer. “And they added: Go, tell his disciples, and Peter, that he has risen; and behold, he will go before you into Galilee.” “And, remembering the Lord’s words, they went” (Mark XVI).

## CHAPTER CLXXXVII. On the running of John and Peter

> “Mary Magdalene ran and came to Peter and John, and said: ‘They have taken my Lord from the tomb, and I do not know where they have laid him’” (John XX).

The force of love, or the bewilderment of her mind, so acted in her that she did not believe he had not been found unless he had been taken away. Therefore those two ran to the tomb; and, not finding the body, when they saw [Col. 1638C] the cloth from the head and the linen wrappings laid separately, they believed that what the woman had said was true, and returned to their own place, that is, to their lodgings.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVIII. That the Lord appeared to Magdalene

> “But Mary Magdalene, who had returned with them to the tomb, remained outside, weeping. And when she looked inside, she saw the aforesaid angels sitting beside the place of the body, one at the feet and one at the head. They said to her: ‘Woman, why are you weeping?’ She said: ‘Because they have taken my Lord away, and I do not know where they have laid him.’ And turning around, she saw Jesus standing, [Col. 1638D] but did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her: ‘Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?’ She, thinking him to be the gardener, said: ‘Sir, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him up.’ Jesus said to her: ‘Mary!’ And immediately she recognized him and said: ‘Rabboni,’ which is the same as Rabbi; and, falling down, she wished to touch his feet, as she was accustomed to do. And Jesus said: ‘Do not touch me. For I have not yet ascended to my Father’”—supply, “in your heart”—as though he said: You seek one dead; you are not worthy to touch him living. You think he is a stolen corpse, not the Son equal to the Father; “but go and tell my brothers: I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.” That is: it is near at hand that they will see me ascending.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIX. On the command given to the guards

[Col. 1639A]

While these things were happening, the guards returned and reported to the chief priests what had happened. [Note: [Col. 1639D] From the Gospel of Nicodemus and Matthew.] But they, corrupted by abundant money, said: “While we slept, the disciples stole away the body of Jesus.” And this report remained among the Jews to the present day.

## CHAPTER CXC. That the Lord appeared to the women on the way

> “Mary Magdalene then came, now believing; and, having found the other women who had previously been with her, they went together to the disciples, now certain of the Resurrection. And behold, Jesus met them, saying: ‘Hail.’ They came near, held his feet, and worshiped him. Jesus said to them: ‘Go, tell my brothers to go into Galilee; there they will see me’” (Matt. XXVI).

The Lord mentions this [Col. 1639B] appearance of himself in Galilee above the others because we believe that all the disciples were present there. By rebuking some of them for the hardness of their hearts, he is said to have given them fuller assurance.

The women went away and announced all these things to those who mourned and to those who were with them; and these words seemed to them like nonsense. “But Peter, rising, ran to the tomb,” as Luke says. It is then probable that the Lord appeared to him on the way, even though this is not read in the Gospel. Of this it is said: “He appeared also to Peter.” On the first day of the Resurrection he appeared five times.

## CHAPTER CXCI. On the two going to Emmaus

On the same day he was seen by two disciples going to Emmaus. One of them was called Cleophas; the other’s name, [Col. 1639C] Luke was thought to have indicated by keeping it silent, after the manner of writers of sacred Scripture. But Ambrose, in his exposition of Luke, says that he was called Amon.

After the devastation of Judaea under Marcus Aurelius, Emmaus was restored and called Nicopolis. It was sixty stadia from Jerusalem. Greek writers relate that Hercules the giant ran 125 paces in a single breath and stopped; from this stopping they call such a distance a *stadium*. Since eight stadia make a mile, sixty make seven thousand five hundred paces: that is, seven miles and four stadia, or three leagues and three quarters.

Jesus went with them, but their eyes were held so that they did not recognize him; whence it seems that there was something different in [Col. 1639D] their eyes, so that they would not recognize him. Elsewhere it is read that he appeared to them in another form; therefore there was also something different in him, so that they would not recognize him. It could also be that the transformation of the same body from mortal to immortal cannot occur without some alteration, through which it was not immediately recognized—just as, if someone had seen a person as a boy and shortly afterward encountered him as a young man, he would not immediately recognize him.

When they recognized him in the breaking of bread [Note: [Col. 1640A] Addition 1. He broke it and handed it to them. Therefore the host is divided into three parts: one is, as it were, the Lord’s; two are distributed, one to the priest and the other to the minister, or it is reserved for a sick person.] and he vanished from them, they returned to Jerusalem that same hour. They found the Eleven assembled with those who were with them, saying that the Lord had truly risen and had appeared to Simon; and the two related what had occurred on the [Col. 1640A] way and how they recognized him in the breaking of bread.

## CHAPTER CXCII. That the Lord appeared to the others while Thomas was absent

Some of them did not believe, one of whom was Thomas (John XX; Luke XX). After he had gone out, while the others were still discussing what they had heard, and it was already evening, and the doors were shut for fear of the Jews, Jesus stood in their midst and said: “Peace to you. [Note: [Col. 1640D] Addition 1. Hence, when a part of the host is placed in the chalice, where the Resurrection is signified, there is added: “May the peace of the Lord be always with you.” And when the bishop first turns toward the people in the Mass, he says: “Peace to you.” The kiss, however, was introduced much later, for the reason mentioned above.] It is I; do not be afraid.” They were troubled and thought they saw a spirit.

[Col. 1640B] For they did not yet believe either that true flesh could rise on the third day, or that, once raised, it could enter through closed doors. He said to them: “See my hands and my feet; touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.” He showed them the scars of his hands, feet, and side.

The Lord retained the scars in his body, although incorruptible, chiefly for three reasons: to strengthen the Apostles’ faith that he had risen; to show the Father forever the kind of death he endured for us—which is a certain mode of interceding for us; and so that, at the judgment, the faithless may see him whom they pierced (Rev. I). He also did so in order to show to all flesh the signs of his victory. For example: a soldier has acted bravely and has been pierced by many wounds. The [Col. 1640C] physician says to him: “Do you wish to be healed without any scar, or with scars but without any disfigurement?” I think that, as a sign of his glory and to encourage others by his example to do the same, he would preserve the scars.

Note that the Lord showed them two things wondrous according to human reason and opposed to one another: a body both incorruptible and touchable. For what does not decay cannot be touched, and what is touched must decay. Bede nevertheless says that the Lord’s body was subtle through the effect of spiritual power and touchable through the truth of its nature—that is, shown to be touchable in order to prove the reality of his flesh. Or it may be said that the Lord’s body was truly visible and touchable to other incorruptible beings; but to corruptible beings it cannot be seen and touched [Col. 1640D] except miraculously.

## CHAPTER CXCIII. That, after eating with them, he gave the Holy Spirit by breathing upon them

While they were now believing, Jesus said: “Have you anything here to eat?” They offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. He ate and gave them the remains (Luke XXIV; John XX). But it must be known [Col. 1641A] that the foods taken by the Lord after the Resurrection were not merely taken but also consumed, just as water cast into fire is consumed. Before his death, however, he took them for nourishment. For thirsty earth absorbs water differently from the way a sunbeam falling upon it does.

And he said to them: “These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you,” that is, like you, capable of suffering. “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures, and said to them: You will be witnesses to me of these things among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 1641C] Addition 1. Hence, upon hearing the proclamation of the Gospel, we turn toward the east, as though toward Jerusalem, giving thanks because the Gospel came to us from there.]

The disciples therefore rejoiced when they saw the Lord—that is, when they recognized him. He said to them again: “Peace to you”—supply, “be,” or “is.” Yet when the bishop, Christ’s vicar, says to the people, “Peace to you,” only “be” is understood. To show himself Christ’s vicar, [Col. 1641B] he sometimes says “Peace to you,” namely when he first turns toward the people in the Mass, since this was Christ’s first utterance to the disciples after the Resurrection. Later, in the manner of other priests, he says, “The Lord be with you,” in order to show himself to be one of us.

“When he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; whose sins you retain are retained.’” Some adhere to this statement, saying that no one can loose or bind unless he possesses the Holy Spirit, by whose authorization he does this. But they should observe that even before the Resurrection Jesus gave them the same power without breathing upon them, and it is not read there that he gave them the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 1641C] Addition 2. The Apostles are said to have received the Holy Spirit three times: first, for the grace of healings; second, for forgiving sins; third, for speaking various languages.]

Moses foretold both these things there: “They sucked honey from the rock,” that is, the power [Col. 1641C] of binding and loosing and of miracles, from Christ free from sin though still mortal; and afterward, “oil from the hardest rock” (Deut. XXXII), that is, the same power with the Holy Spirit, from Christ incapable of suffering.

## CHAPTER CXCIV. That he appeared to Thomas

> “When he had vanished from them, Thomas returned. And the others [Col. 1641D] said to him: ‘We have seen the Lord.’ He said that he would not believe unless he saw and touched the scars of the wounds. But after eight days, when the disciples were inside and Thomas was with them, Jesus stood in their midst”—the doors being shut—and said to Thomas: “Put your finger here, and see my hands and side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing.” Thomas answered: “My Lord and my God”—that is, “you are.” “And Jesus said: ‘Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed’” (John XX).

Some, however, say that Thomas merely saw and did not dare to touch, because Christ said only: “Because you have seen me.” But since sight is commonly put for any sense, it may be said, “You have seen,” that is, “You have touched,” especially because the Lord had said: “Put your finger here and [Col. 1642A] see.” Jesus did these and other things to strengthen our faith, as well as many things not written in the Gospel.

## CHAPTER CXCV. On the appearance at the Sea of Tiberias

> “After this Jesus manifested himself at the Sea of Tiberias. Seven disciples were fishing one night in order to have food. When they had caught nothing, Jesus stood on the shore in the morning. At his command they cast the net on the right side of the boat and filled it with 153 large fish. John said: ‘It is the Lord.’ Then Peter cast himself into the sea. The others came by boat and found coals on the shore, with a fish laid upon them and bread set beside it. Together they roasted some of the fish which they had caught and ate with Jesus, knowing that it was the Lord” (John XXI).

This was the third manifestation, but after how many days from the eighth day after the Resurrection is not specified. “Then Jesus said to Peter: ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?’” The Lord asked what he knew. But he indicated that we ought both to believe in heart and confess with mouth. Peter said: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.”

One should not punctuate it thus, “Yes, Lord,” as though Peter had said that he loved him more than the others. For he did not know this; but the expression also abounds in Hebrew idiom. Therefore, passing over what he did not know, he answered what he knew. Or it may be read: “Lord, I love you, and moreover you know that I love you,” as though he said: I call you yourself as witness that I love you. Jesus said to him: “Feed my lambs,” as though he said: Let the performance of the work be proof of love.

When he asked the same thing a second time and Peter gave the same answer, he again added: “Feed [Col. 1642C] my lambs.” But after the third answer he added: “Feed my sheep,” as though he said: Feed by teaching; feed by acting; feed by dying. “Then Jesus said to him: ‘When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish,’” signifying that he would be crucified, unwilling according to the sense of the flesh. And he added: “Follow me,” that is, you will follow me in the manner of your death.

## CHAPTER CXCVI. Opinions concerning the death of John the Evangelist

> “Then Jesus began to go away, and Peter began to follow him, thinking that this had been commanded him by the Lord. John also followed him. Peter turned and saw [Col. 1642D] him following, and said to Jesus: ‘But what about this man, Lord?’” (John XXI.)

Supply: “What will he suffer?” For after he had heard that he himself would be crucified, he wished also to know his brother’s end. “Jesus answered: ‘Thus I will that he remain until I come.’” The disciples therefore thought that John would not die until Christ came for judgment. But it would not have been a great gift for the Beloved not to die, since “to be dissolved and to be with Christ is better” (Phil. I). The Lord therefore said that he would finish old age in peace.

Yet some said that he lives in this way: after celebrating Mass, he descended into the tomb which had been dug for him, and a great light shone for several hours; those standing around who were present fell down. When they rose after the light had passed and came to his tomb, they found it empty. Yet [Note: [Col. 1644A] Addition 1. As though he said: What you have heard in the ear, preach upon the housetops. Hence the Gospel is read from an elevated place, as something to be heard everywhere, by everyone, and before everyone. First the sign of the cross is made over the book, as though to say: This is the book of the Crucified One; afterward upon the forehead and breast, as upon both doorposts.] [Col. 1643A] light soil welled up from the bottom, as sand commonly bubbles in springs; and even now the same bubbling is sometimes seen there. Hence many thought that he lived under the earth and that the bubbling was produced by his breath; others think that he has already been translated to heaven. It is better reverently to doubt about such matters than rashly to decide them.

## CHAPTER CXCVII. On the appearance of the Lord in Galilee, where the disciples were commanded to teach and baptize the nations

> “But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them. Seeing him, they worshiped, but some doubted. And he reproached them for the hardness of their hearts. And he said: ‘All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth [Col. 1643B]’” (Matt. XXVIII; Mark XVI),

that is, now my omnipotence is manifest. Or: I had said to you, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles”; but because the Jews rejected me, they have, as it were, given me authority to send people throughout all lands under heaven. Therefore he added: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature,” that is, to humankind, for whose sake every creature was made; or to the one who shares in every creature. Hence man is also called a *microcosm*, that is, a lesser world.

And he added: “Teach all nations”—that is, every kindred of nations—to keep what I have commanded you, “baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” At the beginning of our works, we use the same form of words, but as those invoking God in prayer, that the work we begin may be done for the honor of the Trinity and that the Trinity may cooperate with us. In baptism, however, the words are spoken affirmatively: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” That is, I perform the mystery of baptism, but the authority belongs to the Trinity.

“He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; he who does not believe shall be condemned.” He does not say, “nor is baptized.” For a person is saved without baptism when the condition of necessity excludes it, not contempt for religion. Thus the statement, “Unless one is born again,” etc. (John III), is to be understood as meaning: Whoever has despised being born again.

Heretics of this age adhere to the order of the Lord’s words, saying that one ought not to baptize unless the person believes; therefore they do not accept infant baptism. But they do not understand the time at which this was said. First, because the Gospel was preached to adults, adults were to be baptized, and their faith is required in baptism.
