Their children came afterward; therefore this may be understood as said concerning adults. Or, if it is understood of all, explain it thus: “He who believes and is baptized,” that is, whoever is baptized in faith. For the person to be baptized must believe either personally or through another.

“These signs shall follow those who believe: In my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues [Note: [Col. 1644A] Addition 2. For in the primitive Church it was universal that those who came out of the font immediately spoke [Col. 1644B] in tongues.]; they shall take up serpents,” etc. This too was said for its time. For signs then occurred to convert unbelievers. Because signs are not necessary, they do not now occur as they happened everywhere at that time. When we plant saplings, we pour in water until they become established in the ground.

## CHAPTER CXCVIII. On the Ascension of the Lord

[Col. 1644B]

On the day of the Ascension he came to them in Jerusalem and said: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV; Mark XVI). After he had eaten with them—whence it is understood that the sixth hour had passed—he led them out toward Bethany, to the Mount of Olives. Lifting up his hands, he blessed them. And while they watched, he was raised into heaven, and a bright cloud bore him by the ministry of angels. [Note: [Col. 1644C] Addition 1. The Church represents this final procession after Jesus on Sundays, going out from the church building and returning to it, as though leaving Jerusalem and returning to Jerusalem, and following [Col. 1644D] the cross, just as they followed the Crucified One. Although they returned without Jesus, we return with the cross, because he said: “I am with you until the consummation of the age.” Note also that the primitive Church observed Sunday, as we do now, and Thursday in remembrance of the Ascension; a procession was then held on Thursday. But after the feasts of saints had multiplied, the Thursday observance was abolished and the procession transferred to Sunday. Hence Thursday is said to be akin to Sunday.]

When he had now been taken from the disciples’ sight, they nevertheless continued to look into heaven. Therefore two angels, in the form of men, stood beside them and said: “Men of Galilee, why do you look into heaven?” (Acts I). It is as though they said: Depart; do not wait for Jesus to return now. Yet at the end of time he will come in the same way in which you saw him going into heaven: borne by clouds, he will descend into the air.

They returned to Jerusalem and awaited the promised Holy Spirit. Having received it, when the appropriate times came, they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed. Note the difference: Enoch was translated; Elijah was carried up; Jesus ascended by his own power.

# HISTORY OF THE BOOK OF THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES

[Col. 1645]

## CHAPTER I. How often the Lord appeared to the disciples within forty days

[Col. 1645A]

In the nineteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pilate was still procurator of Judaea and Vitellius governor of Syria, the Lord died and rose again. In rising, he established the truth of the Resurrection by many proofs, displaying many things in his own body contrary to the nature of an immortal body, in order thereby to establish the truth of the Resurrection and to remove from the Apostles and their successors every cause whatsoever of hesitation. For he ate and drank with them, although a spiritual body has no need at all of food for nourishment. In his own body he showed scars, although every deformity of a scar is wholly foreign to the nature of an immortal body.

Besides these proofs, [Col. 1645B] Luke, writing the history of the Acts of the Apostles, supplies others. It was indeed a proof of the true Resurrection that for forty days he appeared to them, speaking about the kingdom of God. This must not be understood to mean that he appeared to the Apostles during each of the forty days. Rather, as may be gathered from the Gospel history, within that number of days he appeared to them ten times.

On the very day of the Resurrection he is recorded as appearing five times: first, to Mary Magdalene; second, to the women returning from the tomb, when they held his feet and worshiped him; third, to Peter, although this is not stated expressly in the Gospel; fourth, to the two going to Emmaus; fifth, to the ten Apostles while Thomas was absent. Sixth, after eight days he appeared to the same men while [Col. 1645C] Thomas was present. Seventh, he appeared to seven disciples while they were fishing at the Sea of Tiberias. Eighth, he appeared on Mount Tabor when they had assembled in Galilee. Thus before the day of the Ascension he appeared eight times. But on the day of the Ascension itself he appeared twice: once to the eleven Apostles while they were eating in the upper room (Acts I).

All of them—the Apostles as well as the other disciples, and also the women—lived in that part of Jerusalem called Mello, namely on Mount Zion, where David had built his palace. There was the great furnished upper room in which the Lord commanded them to prepare the Passover for him. At that time the eleven Apostles lived in that upper room. The other disciples and the women lived round about in various lodgings.

## CHAPTER II. That the Apostles were baptized
[Col. 1645D] And while the eleven were eating in the upper room, the Lord appeared to them, reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, and ate with them. And while eating with them he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father—that is, the promise made by himself, or by the Father through him—and saying that the Father’s authority must be fulfilled: “John baptized with water; but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1). As though he were saying: The Holy Spirit, descending upon you, will cleanse and strengthen you.

There is usually doubt concerning the baptism of the apostles. But on this passage Bede and Augustine say that they were baptized. For Bede says: “You shall be baptized,” which is in the Holy Spirit, does not refer to that time when the apostles and the other faithful of that period were baptized with water for the remission of sins, having received from the Lord the grace of the Holy Spirit; rather, it refers to that which they received more fully when the Lord sent the Holy Spirit. Thus they had not yet been baptized—not, I say, with water, but with the Holy Spirit—though we understand that they had been baptized with the baptism of John, or, more credibly, with the baptism of Christ. For it was fitting that those who baptized others should themselves have been baptized.

Augustine says likewise: It is written [Col. 1646B] when Paul was baptized—he was baptized by Ananias. But it is not written when the other apostles were baptized. Yet we ought to understand that they were baptized, because of that saying of the Lord: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3).

Bede and Augustine wish it to be understood in this way: that they were baptized with Christ’s baptism. And concerning some, it seems sufficiently clear that they were baptized with John’s baptism—for example Andrew, Philip, and Peter, who are known to have been his disciples. Having said this, he commanded them to leave the city, and immediately vanished from their sight.

## CHAPTER III. What the Lord answered to those who questioned indiscreetly

[Col. 1646C] Behold the ninth appearance. Immediately after the meal, the eleven apostles, the other disciples, and the women left the city together, in accordance with the Lord’s command, came to the Mount of Olives, and the Lord immediately appeared to them. How he commanded them to leave the city and vanished from their sight, and how, having left the city, they came to the Mount of Olives and there the Lord appeared to them, is passed over in the History, because it is brief.

Then those who had assembled began to question him, saying: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom of Israel?” (Acts 1). Some of them, being unlearned and carnally minded, meant a temporal kingdom: seeing a foreigner reigning and the Jews subject to a governor, they inquired [Col. 1646D] about the restoration of Israel’s earthly kingdom, supposing that the Lord would then restore it, just as the two disciples said: “We had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

Others, better instructed and knowing that that restoration would come only at the end, namely around the time of judgment, asked about the restoration of Israel’s spiritual kingdom—that is, the enlargement of the Church. As though they said: Will you at this time do what you promised to the Church?

But the Lord did not make them certain about this. Yet, from a certain word placed in his answer, if they had been clever, they could have understood that this restoration was to be delayed for many ages. “It is not for you,” he says, “to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power”: that is, the number of times and seasons up to the end of the age, which lie open to the Father’s knowledge alone. As though he said: It is none of your business to inquire into such secrets, nor are you fit to apprehend them. But be concerned about those things which pertain to you, for you shall indeed “receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you”; strengthened by his power, “you shall be my witnesses” to my resurrection: first “in Jerusalem,” second in Judaea, “then in Samaria,” and finally “to the uttermost [Col. 1647B] part of the earth.” As though he silently said: Before the restoration of that kingdom, the report of the Gospel will range throughout not only Jerusalem, but also all the borders of Judaea and Samaria, and even to the ends of the world.

## CHAPTER IV. On the rise and progress of preaching

The Gospel was first preached in Jerusalem; but because of the stoning of Stephen and the death of James, slain by the sword, they departed from Jerusalem, preaching in the regions of Judaea. Afterwards they crossed to the Samaritans, and then proceeded throughout the whole world.

“And when he had said this” (Acts 1), according to another Evangelist, he “blessed them” with uplifted hands (Luke 24). And after that blessing, “while they watched, he was lifted up; and a cloud received [Col. 1647C] him from their eyes,” because he ascended as though carried in the globe of a cloud. This was not because he needed the cloud’s service to ascend, but in order to show thereby that every creature stands ready to obey its Creator.

## CHAPTER V. What they did when the Lord departed

Sulpicius, bishop of Jerusalem, said of the place of the Ascension that, after a church had later been built there, the place where the footprints of the ascending Christ had stood could never be paved; indeed, the marble slabs sprang back at the edges of those laying them. He says that the dust trodden by the Lord is proof of this, because the imprinted footprints are visible, and the ground still preserves the same appearance, as though pressed by those footprints.

When the Lord had already been snatched from [Col. 1647D] their sight, they nevertheless stood with faces still uplifted, gazing into heaven, though they ought rather to have returned to Jerusalem, since they had been told: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24). And so that they should not stay there any longer, angels were sent to instruct them. Hence it follows: “And while they were looking into heaven as he went”—that is, as he departed, the accusative being used for an absolute ablative, for which the genitive is used in Greek—“or, while they had first looked upon him as he went, and were still looking into heaven, behold, two men,” that is, two angels in the form “of men,” “stood beside them in white garments and said” (Acts 1).

## CHAPTER VI. For what reasons the angels appeared

[Col. 1648A]

“Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?” (Acts 1), as though forgetting what you ought to do. “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven”—that is, in the same substance of flesh in which he was taken up from you into heaven—“will so come as you saw him go into heaven”: that is, just as you saw him ascending into heaven borne by clouds, so you will see him coming in the air upon clouds for judgment.

These two angels appeared for two reasons: namely, to comfort those saddened by the Lord’s absence, and to show that he truly ascended into heaven, namely into the region of angels. He was not like Elijah, who was taken up in a fiery chariot and ascended as far as the sublunary region (4 Kings 2; Ecclesiasticus 8), [Col. 1648B] nor did he pass beyond it; but was merely transferred into the earthly paradise, because it rises so high as to reach the sublunary region, although it does not pass beyond it.

“Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet,” so called because of its abundance of olives, “a Sabbath day’s journey” away—that is, at the distance of a Sabbath-day’s journey from Jerusalem, namely the space of a mile. For Jews were not permitted to go farther from the city, or from the place where they were, on the Sabbath; but they could walk about for a thousand paces.

The old edition has “the mountain of the three lights.” The Mount of Olives was so called because, at night, it was illuminated on its western side by the fire of the Temple—for there was a perpetual fire on the altar—and in the morning, on its eastern side, it first received [Col. 1648C] the sun’s rays before they illumined the city. It also had an abundance of oil, which feeds light.

## CHAPTER VII. In what respect we imitate the apostles

“And when they had returned to Jerusalem, all together they accompanied the apostles as far as their lodgings, and then returned to their own homes [Note: [Col. 1647D] From the Gospel of Nicodemus.].”

The Church represents this procession of disciples, who left the city together and afterward returned together, by holding a procession every Sunday. Thus, just as they went out with the Crucified One going before them, so we go out from the church bearing the cross before us. And although the Crucified One did not return with them, nevertheless we bring the cross back when we return. For although he did not return with them in bodily presence, [Col. 1648D] he did return with them in spiritual presence, according to what he said: “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

Therefore, in going out bearing the Lord’s cross before us, we represent the fact that they went out with the Crucified One going before them. In bringing back the Lord’s cross, though he did not return with them in bodily presence, we represent what he said: “I am with you until the consummation of the age.”

In the primitive Church, however, such a representation was performed in church on Thursday, which at that time was as solemn as Sunday. Thursday was so observed in veneration of the Ascension; Sunday, in reverence for the Resurrection. Hence it became a popular proverb [Col. 1649A] that Thursday is called Sunday’s kinswoman, because it was formerly equally solemn. But because saints’ feasts multiplied, and celebrating so many feasts was somewhat burdensome, it was thereafter established that the procession should take place on Sunday.

## CHAPTER VIII. Where, and with whom, they gathered

“Then the apostles went up into the upper room where they were staying: namely Peter and James, John and Andrew, and the others” (Acts 1). The order of the catalogue is altered here. For the apostles are usually paired in the catalogue as follows: “Peter and Andrew, James and John.” Perhaps elsewhere they are paired thus because of kinship by blood. Here, however, they are paired because of equality in merits, since Luke understood in the Spirit that Peter and John were equal in merit, perhaps because they loved more than the others. [Col. 1649B] Hence they also ran together to the tomb before the others.

“And they all continued together with one accord in prayer with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus,” who is distinguished from the women because she cannot properly be called *mulier*—as though *mollier*, “one who has undergone softening.” Yet sometimes *mulier* denotes sex, not corruption, as there: “What is there between me and you, woman?” (John 2)—“and his brethren,” which must be understood of those of whom it was said before the Passion: “For neither did his brethren believe in him”; but now they believed.

Note that it says, “continuing in prayer,” and nothing is added concerning fasting. Some, nevertheless, fast from the feast of the Ascension until Pentecost, following the example of the apostles, whom [Col. 1649C] they say fasted during that interval, because the Gospel says: “The days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they shall fast” (Matthew 9). It may have been so, but it is not stated here.

## CHAPTER IX. On Peter’s discourse

“In those days” (Acts 1)—that is, in the middle interval between the Ascension and the sending of the Holy Spirit—“Peter rose up in the midst of the brethren and spoke.” For it is certain that Matthias’s election occurred during that period, although the particular day is not determined. Hence it is said, as it were indefinitely, “In those days.”

From this formula of Scripture the Church has adopted its manner of reading. Thus, because in the Acts of the Apostles we frequently find, “In those days,” when a portion of the Epistles is read in church, “In those days” is prefixed. And because the Gospels often say, “At that time,” when portions of the Gospels are read in church each day, “At that time” is prefixed.

“Men and brethren, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold by the mouth of David” (Psalm 113), concerning Judas, “who was guide to those who seized Jesus”—who led the cohort and the king’s officers to the garden in which the Lord was praying. Or because he gave the signal of betrayal with a kiss and so offered them guidance. “He was numbered with us,” that is, he received the lot of this ministry and apostleship, which he obtained, as it were, by lot through the Lord’s election. And “numbered with” is aptly said, because he was reckoned among the apostles in number, not in merit. [Col. 1650A]

Or this refers to what he had said: “who was guide to those who seized Jesus, and received the lot of this ministry,” namely that of leadership—that is, he held this leadership. “And this man indeed acquired a field with the reward of iniquity.” This they expound mystically: that is, with the price received for betrayal he acquired hell, which is called the land of the dying, just as paradise is the land of the living. Others say that Judas was buried there and thus possessed it, but this is not authoritative.

Thus it is said, “he acquired,” meaning, “he caused it to be acquired,” because it was bought from his own possession and possessed by others; and, hanged, he burst open in the middle, “and his entrails were poured out”—but not through his mouth, so that the mouth with which he had kissed the Savior might be spared. For that which had touched so glorious a thing, namely Christ’s mouth, ought not to have been so vilely defiled. [Col. 1650B] It was fitting that the entrails which had conceived betrayal should fall out when ruptured, and that the throat through which the voice of betrayal had gone forth should be constricted by a noose. For the manner of a sin often determines the manner of punishment. Thus a man’s bodily head is cut off because he himself has cut off the head of his mind—that is, reason. Judas likewise died in the air, as one destined to be joined to the powers of the air. For it was fitting that he should be separated from the region of angels and men, since he had offended both. Thus both the manner and the place of his punishment correspond to his guilt.

## CHAPTER X. On the election of Matthias

“And this became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their language Haceldama” (Acts 1). Concerning the words “in their language,” some say that these were not Peter’s words, since he was a Jew speaking to Jews, but Luke’s, who wrote in Greek and expressed the field’s name in Hebrew. Others say that the Latin translator added this. But it is better understood as spoken by Peter and connected with what he had said: “It became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called Haceldama in their language”—that is, in the language of the Jerusalemites. For although Peter was a Galilean and Galileans and Jerusalemites had the same language, their linguistic idioms differed. Hence Peter was told: “Truly you are a Galilean, for your speech makes you known” (Matthew 26), that is, the idiom of the Galilean language. [Col. 1650D]

“For it is written in the book of Psalms”—not “in the books.” Therefore Augustine mocks Jerome for dividing the book of Psalms into five volumes. For then it ought to have been said, “in the fourth book of Psalms”: “Let their habitation become desolate, and let there be none to dwell in it” (Psalm 108), namely the habitation of his people; “and let another receive his episcopate,” that is, another person. For Matthias was chosen from among the seventy-two disciples and substituted for him. Or it is said because Matthias was far other than Judas: a holy man, whereas Judas was wicked. Or, he was the other of the two whose lots were cast.

“Therefore it is necessary that, from among these men who have assembled with us during all the time in which the Lord Jesus came in and went out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from [Col. 1651A] us, one of these should become with us a witness of his resurrection.” As though he said: Since Judas has died, and it was thus prophesied that another would receive his episcopate, we must substitute someone for him who may testify with us to his resurrection, because it was said to us: “You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem,” namely of my resurrection, “and in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the uttermost part of the earth.”

And because a witness ought to testify only concerning matters which he has seen or heard, he must be chosen from among those men who were with us from the baptism of John, after Jesus began to do and teach, until the day of the Ascension, and who saw the Lord’s miracles and heard his teaching. Note that it says, “from among these men,” not from the weaker sex, less suitable for this purpose.

“And they put forward”—preferring them to the others—“the two: Joseph, called Barsabas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias.” Nothing is said of Matthias’s praise, because it is praise enough for him that he was chosen as an apostle. But Joseph is commended so that he might not seem rejected as unworthy. And here we have plainly in the gloss that this Joseph, called Barsabas, was Barnabas, who was later chosen to the apostolate with Paul (Acts 4). But this opinion should not be embraced, because what follows will make it plain that it is unfounded. For this Joseph was the brother of the three apostles, sons of Alphaeus, and was not an apostle.

“And praying, they said: You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen to receive the place of this ministry and apostleship [Col. 1651C] from which Judas fell away, that he might go to his own place. And they gave them lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven.”

Lots are not to be used now, as Jerome teaches on the basis of this passage, because the privileges of a few do not establish a common law. Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit had not yet been sent, and the legal figures had not yet wholly ceased. Therefore lots were still cast, as Scripture often reports was done in the Old Testament. For Saul was chosen by lot; Jonathan and his armor-bearer cast lots; David also cast lots when he chose the twenty-four chief priests (1 Kings 10; 1 Chronicles 24). Yet if anyone is compelled to imitate the apostles by lots, he should first offer prayer to the Lord. Thus Matthias’s election took place between the Ascension and the sending of the Holy Spirit, but on what day is uncertain.

## CHAPTER XI. On the sending of the Holy Spirit

“And when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, all the disciples were together in the same place” (Acts 2), in which Matthias’s election had taken place. But “when the days were fulfilled” seems wrongly said, since this was the first of the seven days over which the festival of Pentecost extended. For there were three feasts extended over seven days: Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles. Therefore it seems that it ought rather to have said, “when the days of Pentecost began.”

But *Pentecost* is equivocal, referring both to the fiftieth day and to the solemnity extended over seven days. For *pentacon* means “fifty”; hence *Pentecost*, meaning a fiftieth, [Col. 1652A] and it is a Greek word, as are *parasceve* and *Scenopegia* [the Feast of Tabernacles]. But the name *Pascha* raises a question. The Hebrews have many Greek words because they were often dispersed through many particular captivities and lived among Greeks, from whom they retained many words.

Thus the sense is: “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled,” that is, of the fifty-day period—for that day was the fiftieth from the Resurrection—and when the days of Pentecost began, that is, of the solemnity to be extended over seven days, all the disciples were in the upper room. “And while they were together in the same place, suddenly there came from heaven,” that is, from the air, “a sound,” because a certain crashing noise resounded in the air, “as of a coming spirit,” that is, a violent sound, so that “as” marks likeness. As though it said: The Holy Spirit came in the likeness of a violent wind, or as a violent Holy Spirit.

And then “as” will express truth, because the Holy Spirit is truly called *vehemens* [vehement], as though *vehens a mente*, “carrying away from the mind,” that is, alienating a person from the mind’s affections. Or, according to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, he is rightly called *vehemens*, as though *vae adimens*, “taking away woe,” that is, eternal condemnation. Therefore what is said, “as of a coming spirit,” can refer both to the sound and to the Holy Spirit, because *spiritus* is equivocal for both, as are Hebrew *Ruha* and Greek *Pneuma*. “And that sound,” or the Holy Spirit, “filled the whole house where they were sitting”—that is, the men and women sitting in the house—fulfilling what had been said to them: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24). [Col. 1652C]

“And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire”: fiery rays in the form of tongues resting upon the head of each one. The very form of the creature in which the Holy Spirit visibly descended upon the apostles then expressed the use for which he descended: the appearance of fire showed that the Holy Spirit was given to them for strength; the form of tongues, for knowledge. For the tongue expounds knowledge; fire strengthens the vessel.

The Holy Spirit was also given to the apostles before the Passion, when they were sent to preach and were told: “Heal the sick, cast out demons, raise the dead” (Mark 6). After the Resurrection he was also given to them for another use, when he breathed upon them and [Col. 1652D] said: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20). There perhaps he gave the other apostles also the keys which he had given Peter (Matthew 16).

“And all were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in diverse tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance”—he who “dividing to each one as he wills, where he wills, when he wills, how much he wills, how he wills, and to whom he wills, breathes” (1 Corinthians 12). Hence either the apostles spoke only one language, namely Hebrew, in such a way that all understood them; or, what is truer, they spoke in all languages, since the Holy Spirit had inspired in them knowledge of all languages, as is read in Wisdom: “The Spirit of the Lord filled the whole world, and that which contains [Col. 1653A] all things”—that is, man, who has affinity with every creature, or for whose sake every creature was made—“has knowledge of speech” (Wisdom 1), that is, of languages. As though it said: “The Spirit of the Lord filled the whole world,” and gave the disciples knowledge of languages.

## CHAPTER XII. On the miracle of tongues

There were in Jerusalem “religious Jewish men,” inhabitants of Judaea; and besides them many others, coming from nearly “every nation under heaven,” because the Jews had been scattered through many captivities, especially under Antiochus Epiphanes, whose captivity was closer in time to this event, and now all had assembled for the feast day.

Having heard the crash that had sounded in the air, they all came [Col. 1653B] to the disciples and were astonished because each one heard them speaking in his own language. And it is rightly said in the singular, “his own language,” because they knew not merely languages but the idioms of languages as well. “But others mocked them, saying: They are full of new wine,” that is, very drunk, because drunkenness from new wine is more powerful than from clarified wine.

## CHAPTER XIII. That Peter convicted the liars by the authority of the prophets

Then Peter rose with the eleven, showing that they were not drunk but filled with the Holy Spirit, saying: “These are not drunk, since it is the third hour of the day” (Acts 25). As though he said: It is not yet the time for eating, and those who are fasting are not accustomed to become drunk.

And because he knew the Law and spoke to those who knew the Law, he showed that Joel had prophesied the coming of the Holy Spirit. And although he introduces Joel’s prophecy only to show that the advent of the Holy Spirit had been foretold, he incidentally joins to it something concerning the day of judgment, because Joel foretold certain signs of judgment—some already fulfilled, others still to be fulfilled.

“It shall be in the last days, says the Lord, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh”—that is, upon both sexes, not upon every individual person—“and your sons shall prophesy,” such as Agabus and Simon Niger, “and your daughters,” such as Philip’s daughters; “and your young men shall see visions,” such as Paul, caught up to the third heaven; “and your old men shall dream dreams,” such as Peter, of whom it is written: “He thought he saw a vision” (Acts 12). Thus far concerns the coming of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1653D]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the wonders in heaven above that have been fulfilled

“And I will give wonders in heaven above” (Acts 2). This was fulfilled when, as a sign of the Lord’s Nativity, a new star appeared in the air; and secondly in the air at the Passion, when the sun was darkened. “And signs on the earth beneath.” This was fulfilled when, as Christ gave up his spirit, the earth trembled, the rocks were split, and the tombs opened.

The blood from the Lord’s wound, or from his sweat—when his sweat became like drops of blood, which was contrary to nature and therefore a sign—and likewise the blood flowing from the side of the dead Lord, contrary to nature, was a sign. “And fire”: that of the vehement Holy Spirit coming upon them. “And vapor of smoke,” [Col. 1654A] that is, the fervor of compunction proceeding from the fire of the Holy Spirit as smoke from fire.

“The sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood.” At the Passion the sun was turned into darkness. But because the moon was then full, whether it was turned to blood could not become known to people, since it was beneath the earth and withdrawn from human sight by the earth’s obstruction. Therefore it is certain of one of these two things that it has already been fulfilled; perhaps the other remains still to be fulfilled.

And all these things shall happen before the great day of the Lord: great in duration, because night will not follow it; in its work, because on it the whole world will be examined; and in brightness, because the sun will shine sevenfold.

## CHAPTER XV. He expounds David’s words concerning Christ

“Men of Israel” (Acts 2), to whom the prophets spoke especially, hear these words: that is, understand that what Joel prophesied (chapter 2) concerning the sending of the Holy Spirit has now been fulfilled, because the Holy Spirit was sent by him whom you killed, who, by the high counsel of the Father’s dispensation, was delivered into your hands, and whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell. Or this may be understood with respect to Christ himself, whom the pains of hell’s punishments did not injure; or with respect to others, who were released by him from the pains of hell. This is clear from the Greek, where it says: “Loosing through him the pains of death.”

That he was raised by God Peter proves through the prophet David, and he cites several verses of the Psalm. But for proving this, the one verse is sufficient: “You will not abandon my soul [Col. 1654C] in hell, nor will you permit your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15). These are Christ’s words to the Father, as though he said: You will not allow, O Father, my soul descending to the lower regions to be held there, nor my sanctified body to decay or be reduced to ashes.

Afterwards he shows that this cannot be understood of David, reproving the Jews for interpreting David wrongly: “Men and brethren, let me speak boldly to you concerning the patriarch David: he died and was buried among us,” and his body was reduced to ashes, and his ashes are still among us. Hence it is clear that he did not say this of himself: “You will not permit your Holy One to see corruption.” Rather, he prophesied “concerning the resurrection of Christ, who was neither abandoned in hell nor did his flesh see corruption. [Col. 1654D] God raised him up, and we are witnesses of this; and, seated at the Father’s right hand, he sent into us the Holy Spirit, who performs in us the things that you see.”

That he was exalted to the right hand of God the Father he again proves by the authority of the prophet David, who says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109). This cannot be understood of David or of any other human being. “Therefore know most certainly that this Jesus, whom you crucified, has thus been exalted and has sent the Holy Spirit.”

## CHAPTER XVI. On Joel’s prophecy fulfilled

“Having heard these things, they were pierced to the heart” (Acts 2), and thus Joel’s prophecy was fulfilled, because after the fire of the Holy Spirit came the vapor of compunction. And they said to Peter and the remaining apostles: [Col. 1655A] “What shall we do, men and brethren?” Peter answered them: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit,” so that you may speak in diverse tongues, as we do.

This was a familiar sign in the primitive Church, because nearly all who came up from the font spoke in every language. Note that Peter says: “Let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.” The apostles long kept unspoken in the primitive Church the form handed down by the Lord, in which the Trinity is expressed, employing this wording: “I baptize you in the name of Jesus Christ,” in order thereby to spread the name of Christ.

“Peter exhorted them with many other words. And those who received his word were baptized. And there were added to the number of the faithful on that day,” namely on Pentecost itself, “about three thousand souls. And they continued in the apostles’ teaching and in the fellowship of the breaking of bread,” and of the Eucharist; for in the primitive Church they frequently gathered together in one accord to receive the Eucharist. Or it means fellowship in the breaking of ordinary bread, which the apostles broke daily for each, for they had nothing of their own. They had even sold their estates and laid the prices at the apostles’ feet. Every morning the apostles went up to the Temple for prayer; returning afterward, they distributed bread to each person, “as anyone had need.”

## CHAPTER XVII. On the paralytic healed by Peter

[Col. 1655C] One day, when Peter and John were going up to the Temple at the ninth hour of prayer, there was a certain man lame from birth, whom the Gloss calls a paralytic, beside the Temple gate called Beautiful, from a particular ornament placed upon it by Alexander Hyrcanus. Herod also placed there a golden eagle, and it was the gate of the court of ritually clean men.

This lame man was carried daily on his pallet to that gate “to ask alms from those entering the Temple.” He asked Peter and John that he might receive alms from them, when they went up to the Temple at the ninth hour of prayer. For the Hebrews had a custom of praying at three hours. Thus Daniel (chapter 6), after the king’s decree had been issued, prayed at each of these three hours, going up to the window of his chamber.

This custom was confirmed by the Church, which observed these same hours, namely the third, sixth, and ninth: because at the third hour the Lord was scourged, at the sixth he mounted the cross, and at the ninth he gave up his spirit. Peter and John looked at the lame man and said: “Look at us.” As though they said: Consider our poverty; we have nothing to offer you. But he looked intently at them, hoping to receive something from them.

Peter said to him: “Silver and gold I do not have.” For what he kept for the use of the poor who had left their patrimonies and cast them at the apostles’ feet was not his own. “But what I have, I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, arise and walk in peace.” And taking his right hand, he lifted [Col. 1656A] him up, and immediately his ankles and soles were strengthened. And he stood and walked and entered the Temple with them, walking and leaping. Luke added this in order to show the fulfillment of: “The lame man shall leap like a stag” (Isaiah 35).

“And all the people saw the lame man walking and praising God. And they were filled with amazement and ecstasy at what had happened to him, knowing that he had been lame from birth. And when they saw Peter and John, they ran to them at the portico called Solomon’s”—that is, in the part where Solomon stood while praying. “And Peter, seeing the people marveling at this miracle, spoke to them.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. That they ascribed nothing to themselves, but everything to God

[Col. 1656B]

“Men of Israel, why do you marvel at us, as though we had performed this miracle by our own power?” (Acts 3). As though he said: We have not done this by our own power, but “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed delivered up and denied before Pilate’s face, when he had judged that he should be released”; and instead you judged Barabbas to be released (Matthew 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 18).

“His name”—that is, the invocation of his name—“and the faith held concerning him, has given this man complete health in the sight of all of you. And now, brethren, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers.” But because this had been foretold by all the prophets, it had to be fulfilled. “Repent therefore, and confess, so that when times of refreshing come from the presence of the Lord”—namely, the time of the Incarnation, which was truly a time of refreshing, or the separation at the universal judgment and the redemption of the righteous—“your sins may be blotted out.”

For sins will then be fully blotted out, when, through the power of the Resurrection, death—the last enemy—is destroyed, “and when he sends him who was preached to you, Jesus Christ, whom heaven must receive,” that is, who must sit at the Father’s right hand, “until the time of the resurrection of us all, of which the Lord spoke from of old through the mouth of all the prophets”: that is, until the common resurrection of all. Then all things foretold by the prophets concerning Christ will truly be fulfilled. And he gives examples of what they foretold concerning Christ, beginning with Moses (Deuteronomy 18).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Sadducees’ envy toward the apostles
As the apostles were speaking to the people, the priests and the magistrates of the Temple came upon them, and all were indignant together because they were extolling him whom they themselves had condemned as guilty (Acts IV). The Sadducees in particular were distressed because they preached the resurrection, which they denied; and they laid hands on them and put them in prison, because it was already evening and they could not judge them. “But many of those who had heard their words believed.” And on that same day five thousand were converted to the faith. This is what is often read: that three thousand were converted to the faith on one day—which happened on the day of Pentecost itself—and five thousand on another day.

## CHAPTER XX. How they answered steadfastly when questioned before the council

“On the following day the chief priests assembled” (Acts IV), that is, those holding precedence among the twenty-four elders of the priests, who are named expressly: “Annas the chief priest,” who surpassed them all, “and Caiaphas, Alexander, and John.” These were the most eminent after Annas; “and all who were of priestly stock,” together with the elders, the Pharisees—devisers of traditions—and the scribes, interpreters of the Law, namely those who expounded the Law to others. We frequently find this distinction in the Gospel.

“And, setting them in the midst of the council, they questioned them: ‘By what power, or in what name, have you done this?’ Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, answered,” first showing that their question was rash. “Are we being judged for a good deed?” That is, are we being dragged into court and accused as criminals? It is as though he said: You accuse us foolishly. “Let it be known to you all that in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom you crucified, this man stands sound before you, whom God raised from the dead. For he is the cornerstone rejected by you builders” (Matt. XXI; Mark XII; Luke XX), that is, crucified by you, who afterwards, having been raised by the Father, “was made the head of the corner”; that is, he was made the ruler of two peoples, who are united in him as in a cornerstone. “And there is salvation in no other. For there is no other name under heaven given to human beings than the name of Christ, in which we must be saved.”

“Now when they saw the steadfastness of Peter and John, observing that they were *idiotae*, unlearned and illiterate men, they marvelled; recognizing them, because they had seen them with Jesus. And because the man whom they had healed was present with them, they could say nothing in reply.”

Observe that here we have a different etymology for the name *idiota* from that given by Isidore. According to Isidore, *idiota* is said as though “separated from ears”: for *idi* means “division,” and *ota* is interpreted “ear”; thus *idiota* means one separated from understanding, that is, a fool. But according to the etymology given here [Col. 1657D], an *idiota* is so called as though from *idioma*, “one’s own language.” Therefore they were called *idiotae* as though content with the single language proper to them, their Hebrew tongue, which they knew sufficiently, and nothing else.

“But they ordered them to withdraw outside the council, and conferred with one another, saying: ‘What shall we do with these men? For it is evident that they have performed a miracle; we cannot deny it. But lest it spread further abroad, let us threaten them that they may no longer speak in this name to any human being.’ And calling them, they commanded them not to speak at all or teach in the name of the Lord Jesus. To them Peter and John said: ‘Judge for yourselves whether it is right to obey God who commands rather than you who forbid.’” It is as though they said: You err in forbidding what God has commanded, and you are not to be obeyed. For where a superior commands [Col. 1658A] and an inferior contradicts, the inferior is not to be obeyed. “We cannot but speak of the things that we have seen and heard.” But they, after threatening them, released them, not daring to lay hands on them because of the people.

When released, “they returned to their own people” in Zion, “and reported all that the chief priests and elders had said to them,” and how they had answered them. “When they heard it, with one accord they raised their voices, saying: ‘Lord, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them; who by the Holy Spirit, through the mouth of David (Ps. I), our father and your servant, said: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ.” For Herod and Pilate, together with the kings and the people of Israel, assembled in this city against your servant Jesus, whom you sent, to do those things which your hand and your counsel had decreed should come to pass. And now, Lord, look upon their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness.’”

Observe that this phrase is often set down: “Herod and Pilate assembled to do what the hand and counsel of God decreed should be done.” But attend to the two words, “to do” and “to be done”: for they indeed assembled to carry out a wicked act. God decreed that that Passion should be undergone, because their action was wicked, while the Passion was good. “And when they had prayed, the place where they were assembled was shaken”; and the Holy Spirit was sent again [Col. 1658C], “and, filled with the Holy Spirit, they spoke the word of God with boldness.”

## CHAPTER XXI. On the mutual charity among the apostles

“And the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). Nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own; rather, all things were held in common among them, and great grace was upon them all. For there was no needy person among them. All who owned houses or fields sold them and laid the proceeds at the apostles’ feet. It was distributed to each as anyone had need.

Then Joseph, who was surnamed Barnabas by the apostles—which is interpreted “son of consolation”—a Levite, a Cypriot by birth, having a field, sold it and laid the price [Col. 1658D] at the apostles’ feet. Therefore, after saying “a Levite,” lest it seem that he could not have possessions because Levites had no inheritance in the land, “a Cypriot by birth” was added, to show that he had been born in the Dispersion and among the Gentiles, and therefore was permitted to have possessions.

But one should adhere to Bede’s statement on this passage and maintain that this was Paul’s companion, not the man who was put forward with Matthias when the lot fell upon Matthias, as some suppose, Bede says, through insufficient attention. For this man is called Barnabas, that is, “son of consolation”; while that Barnabas is interpreted “son of rest.” Hence Luke deliberately added the interpretation of the name, in order to indicate the difference between this one and that one.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the death of Ananias and Sapphira

[Col. 1659A]

“But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife” (Acts V), wished to be in the fellowship of the righteous in order to have the necessities of life without labour; and thus, for gain, he wished to obtain for himself a prebend. Although he had wished to lay the entire price of the field he had sold at the apostles’ feet, he did not fulfil his vow, but “withheld part of the price of the field, his wife knowing of it,” reserving half for himself and laying the remainder at the apostles’ feet. Peter at once foresaw this in the Spirit and said: “Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? Why have you withheld part of the price of the field? You have lied not to human beings but to God,” who searches hearts and destroys all who speak falsehood. “When Ananias heard this, he fell down and expired.”

Here it should be observed that, although in the Gospel the Lord said, “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. V; Luke VI), he nevertheless at times exercised vengeance in the primitive Church. For when laws are first promulgated, severe punishments are customarily inflicted in order to establish them, so that the severity of the punishment may establish the strictness of the law promulgated. Hence, at the beginning of the emerging Law, a man was stoned for gathering wood on the Sabbath (Lev. X). At the beginning of the priesthood, Aaron’s two sons were consumed by fire for offering strange fire. Thus Ananias, withholding part of the price of the field, fell and expired in order to strike terror into others; for such swift vengeance inspired great fear in others. “For great fear came upon all who heard” [Col. 1659C] it. This is an anticipation, since before the wife’s death only a few heard of the man’s death.

“Then the young men rose, carried away the body, and buried it. And after an interval of about three hours, his wife, not knowing, came in. Peter said to her: ‘Tell me, woman, whether you sold the field for so much?’ She said to him: ‘Yes, for so much.’ Peter said to her: ‘Why have you agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who buried your husband stand at the door, and they will carry you out.’” As though summing it up in a brief statement, he said: You will die. For one who is buried is dead. “And immediately she fell at his feet and expired,” because she had been party to the fraud. “And the young men who entered,” those standing at the door, “found her dead and carried her away [Col. 1659D] and buried her by her husband,” that is, beside her husband. For it was the Hebrews’ custom to bury wives beside their husbands, so that the union of dust might follow the union of flesh, and because woman was formed from the man’s rib (Gen. II).

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the signs performed by the apostles

“By the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people, and they were all with one accord in Solomon’s Portico. But no unbeliever dared falsely to join himself to them” (Acts V), because they were terrified by Ananias’s example. “And the multitude of believers in the Lord increased; and they laid the sick in the streets on beds and pallets, so that, when Peter came, they might be overshadowed by the shadow of his body and be delivered from their infirmities.” For Peter was privileged in miracles, and is recorded to have done greater things than Christ.

According to some, *grabbatum* is written with two *b*s, like *Sabbatum*, and they say that the middle syllable should be pronounced short. Others say *grabatum*, as though from *gravatum* (“burdened”), with *v* changed into *b*, and therefore that it should be pronounced long; this is the truer view.

[Note: [Col. 1660A] Addition 1. Observe that *grabatum* properly means a poor person’s pallet, upon which nothing is spread beneath the body; only a support is placed beneath the head.]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the imprisonment of the apostles

“But the chief priest rose up, and the Sadducees were filled with jealousy; and they laid hands on the apostles and put them in public custody” (Acts V), that is, in prison. Observe that above “chief priests” was said in the plural [Col. 1660B], whereas here it is said in the singular, perhaps because one of them had died, namely Annas.

Observe also that the Sadducees are so called as though *Seducaei*, from *sedech*, which means “justice”; hence Melchizedek, as though “king of justice.” For they appropriated the name of justice while being unjust. Or they were called Sadducees from Zadok the priest, to whom Solomon transferred the priesthood from Abiathar, because they boasted that they were of his line. They joined the chief priests in persecuting the apostles because the apostles preached the resurrection, which they denied.

## CHAPTER XXV. How they were brought out of prison by an angel

[Col. 1660C] “But an angel of the Lord, opening the prison doors by night and leading them out, said: ‘Go and speak in the Temple to the people all the words of this life’” (Acts V), namely, of the Christian life. It was unnecessary to add this, since the Christian sect was already widely known.

It is not to be understood that the angel opened the prison doors. Rather, “opening” should be understood as though it said: leading them out as if the doors had been opened. For, according to the teaching of the saints, we should believe that they were led out of prison while the doors remained shut. This was done to confirm them and refute the Jews. For how could Thomas have doubted that Christ, in flesh and bones, entered to the disciples while the doors were shut, when he had seen himself led out of a prison whose doors were shut [Col. 1660D]? And when the Jews said that Christ’s body had been stolen from the tomb, by what theft could they say the apostles had been led out of a closed prison?

In accordance with the angel’s command, the apostles entered the Temple at daybreak and taught the people, because the angel had commanded them to preach in the Temple, namely in the more prominent place, frequented by the priests.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How they were astonished at their removal

“But when the chief priest came, and those who were with him, they summoned the council” (Acts V), to deliberate what should be done with them. For this was why they had been sent to prison: that they might be brought to judgment. “And they sent to the prison to have them brought. But when the officers returned, they reported to them, saying: ‘We found the prison indeed shut [Col. 1661A] with every precaution, and the guards standing at the doors; but when we opened it, we found no one inside.’ When the Temple magistrate and the chief priests heard these words,” that is, the more powerful and wiser men, they wondered how this had happened. “And behold, someone came and said to them: ‘The men whom you put in prison are standing in the Temple and teaching the people.’”

## CHAPTER XXVII. On their reply

“Then the magistrate went with the officers” (Acts V), that is, the chief priest. “Magistrate” is singular, and likewise in the preceding passage according to the Greek. “And he brought them without force,” not daring to use violence against them because of the people, who favoured them. “And they set them before the council, and the chief priest said [Col. 1661B] to them: ‘We strictly commanded you,’ namely with pontifical authority, ‘not to teach any longer in this name,’ namely in the name of Jesus; ‘and behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching. Do you intend to bring upon us this man’s blood?’” That is, the vengeance due for his blood. It is as though he said: Do you accuse us as guilty of innocent blood by preaching him innocent whom we condemned?

All the apostles answered together, out of fervour and zeal, not allowing one person to speak for all: “We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree, and exalted him at his right hand; and we are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom [Col. 1661C] he gave,” not only to us, but “to all who obey him.” In this they urge them to repentance, as though saying: To you too, if you are willing to obey. “When they heard this, they were cut to the heart.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Gamaliel’s counsel

“Then a certain Pharisee rose in the council, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the Law held in honour by all the people, and ordered that the men be put outside for a short time” (Acts V). This Gamaliel, as Clement says in a certain letter, was a disciple of the apostles, like Nicodemus; and they were among the apostles’ counsellors among the Jews, in order often to moderate their anger against them.

Gamaliel therefore spoke in the council as follows: “Men of Israel, take heed to yourselves what you are about to do concerning these men.” It is as though he said: You ought not judge hastily, but wait; for if their work is merely a human work, it will be destroyed of itself, but if it is God’s work, it will endure and cannot be destroyed. He demonstrates this with the example of two men, namely Theudas and Judas the Galilean.

Theudas the Magician, as Josephus relates, called himself a prophet. At his persuasion many sold all that they had and, carrying their goods out of the city, came to the banks of the Jordan. He promised that after three days he would cause the Jordan to divide, and that they would cross on dry ground, as the children of Israel had crossed. While they waited, during those three days the procurator of the governor of Syria came upon them with a multitude of cavalry, killed many of them, and brought Theudas’s head back to Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Another example concerning the same matter

[Col. 1662A]

“After him Judas the Galilean arose in the days of the registration” (Acts V), that is, of the general census made by Augustus, when each person, paying the tax assessed upon him, declared himself subject to the Roman Empire. This Judas the Galilean was an Essene by origin. And, as Josephus relates, he persuaded the Jews to refuse tribute to the Romans, maintaining that those who paid tithes and firstfruits to God ought not to pay taxes to human beings. This teaching prevailed so much that the Pharisees and a great part of the people asked the Lord himself whether tribute ought to be paid to Caesar or not. “Afterwards he himself perished, and all who agreed with him.”

They therefore assented to Gamaliel’s exhortation; and summoning the apostles, they scourged them and, once they had been scourged [Col. 1662B], released them, forbidding them under threat of death to speak any more in Jesus’ name. “And the apostles departed rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus.” See how great was now the strength of faith in them: they could be restrained neither by words nor by lashes; that is, they did not desist when first forbidden by words, and now when beaten with lashes.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the cause of murmuring among Christians

“Now in those days, when the number of disciples was increasing” (Acts VI), that is, Christians, who at that time were called disciples, “there arose a murmur of the Greeks,” that is, of Gentile newcomers residing in the city; or of Jews born in the Dispersion and raised among Greeks, “against [Col. 1662C] the Hebrews, because their widows were being overlooked in the daily ministry.” This was because the widows of the Hebrews were more experienced and therefore were preferred to the others in the distribution of the daily provision.

The cause of the murmuring can be understood in two ways: either because the Greek widows were not admitted to the daily ministry, or because they were excessively burdened in it. Perhaps they made them cooks and assigned them such lowly tasks. But when the apostles saw that this complaint had arisen concerning the administration of the widows—whom it was necessary to provide for because they themselves could not suffice for distributing to each one—they summoned the multitude and said: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God [Col. 1662D] and serve tables. Therefore, brothers, choose from among yourselves seven men of good testimony, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this work,” so that they may serve, or preside over those who serve, “while we devote ourselves to prayer and preaching.”

This proposal pleased the multitude, and they chose seven: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a newcomer from Antioch. He alone was called a newcomer because he was foreign. Or he is called a newcomer because he alone was a newcomer, or because he alone was to become notable, as though foreign. “Those whom they had chosen they set before the apostles; and the apostles, praying, laid hands upon them.” In the Church they correspond to archdeacons, instituted for this reason: to bear [Col. 1663A] the burden of business, so that bishops may more freely devote themselves to teaching and prayer.

But the bishops of our time, finding archdeacons less cautious in such administration, take pains, by a certain provident precaution, to attend to this work—that is, to administration. Observe that because the apostles are recorded to have laid hands on them while praying, prayers are made at ordinations. By this authority, in some churches hands are laid upon deacons at ordination. Those, however, who do not lay hands on them have Bede’s authority on their side. Concerning the statement, “and, praying, they laid hands on them,” Bede says that it should be understood to have happened later, because afterwards they ordained these same men as ministers for the ministry of the sacred altar and of the Lord’s body and blood, and then laid hands upon them. Hence hands are also laid upon priests at their ordination.

“The word of the Lord grew, and the number of disciples in Jerusalem multiplied. A great multitude of priests also obeyed the faith.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the commendation of blessed Stephen

“And Stephen, full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. But some rose up from the synagogue of the Libertines” (Acts VI), so called from a region. Or they were *libertines*, that is, freedmen, who had previously been slaves and afterwards had been granted freedom; thus they were of servile condition, and were the first to oppose Christ’s faith; “and of the Cyrenians,” from Cyrene, a city, “and of those who were [Col. 1663C] from Cilicia and Asia” Minor, which are near one another, “disputing with Stephen. Yet they could not withstand the wisdom and the Holy Spirit speaking in him. Then they brought forward two false witnesses, who testified that he had spoken blasphemy against God and Moses; and they stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes, brought him into the council, and two false witnesses arose and said: ‘This man does not cease to speak against this holy place and Moses.’” That is, they said: He maligns the Temple and the Law. “For we heard him saying that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and alter the traditions which Moses handed down to us. And all who sat in the council, looking at him, saw his face as the face of an angel.”

“And the chief priest said: ‘Are these things so?’” [Col. 1663D] (Acts VII). Then blessed Stephen undertook to make a great speech. Since he was accused of blasphemy against God and Moses, he begins the speech with praise of God, saying that the God who spoke to the fathers and prophets is the God of majesty and glory. He immediately proceeds to commend Moses, beginning from a higher point, namely praise of the fathers from whom Moses descended. He begins, therefore, with Abraham: how, departing from Chaldea, he came into Mesopotamia, then to Haran, and then to Judaea.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On his speech

“Men, brothers and fathers, listen: the God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Haran, and [Col. 1664A] said to him: ‘Leave your land and your kindred’” (Acts VII). A third phrase is added in Genesis (ch. XII), namely, “and your father’s house.” But Stephen omits it because he was speaking to those who knew it. Therefore he touches the history briefly, or passes over it as familiar.

Yet this seems to contradict the book of Genesis, where it appears to state that this was said to Abraham after the death of his father Terah, who certainly died in Haran, where his son also lived with him; and so it was said in Haran. What, then, is meant by the statement here, “before he dwelt in Haran”? It could have been said to him in both places. Or where it says, “and he said to him,” supply: afterwards in Haran. But whether it was said to him in Mesopotamia, in Haran, or in both places, how then was he told [Col. 1664B], “Leave your land”? Had he not already left Chaldea? Certainly; but he was still held there by hope and the desire to return. Therefore he was commanded to leave in mind, having already left in body.

Or it can be said that Mesopotamia and Haran are in Chaldea. Thus, departing from Chaldea—that is, from one part of Chaldea—he came to Mesopotamia, namely another part of Chaldea; from there he came to Haran, which was still Mesopotamia. Then he left the land of the Chaldeans and, in this sense, Mesopotamia; and, in regard to this, it seems to have been said twice. Afterwards he came to Haran, and likewise departed from Haran, “after his father died; the Lord brought him into this land in which you dwell.” Or then he departed from the land of the Chaldeans in mind, and from there—that is, finally, after laying aside that desire—after his father’s death he was transferred into this land.

Or, if the statement “he came to Haran” is understood, this wording is plainly read. Observe that in Hebrew it says “from Ur of the Chaldeans,” that is, “from the fire of the Chaldeans.” For the Chaldeans worshipped fire and passed their little children through fire, just as we pass through the water of baptism. The Hebrews relate that because Terah and his sons, while in Chaldea, refused to worship fire, the Chaldeans cast them into the fire; and Aram, Abraham’s brother, was burned. Abraham, however, was delivered by the Lord. Hence the Lord often said to him: “I am the Lord your God who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans” (Gen. XV).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Continuation of the narrative

[Col. 1664D]

After he was delivered, he came with his father Terah, his brother Nahor, his nephew Lot, and the whole household to Haran. From there, after his father’s death, his brother Nahor remaining there, he came into Judaea. Yet “the Lord gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot’s breadth” (Acts VII), that is, not even the smallest portion, because he possessed nothing there except by title of purchase. For he possessed the cave with its field not as an inheritance, but bought it for a price from Ephron, son of Seor the Hittite. “But God promised to give it as an inheritance to his seed after him,” though he had no son, saying: “Your seed shall be a resident alien,” that is, a sojourner, “in a foreign land” (Gen. XV), for 430 years; and during part of this time, “the Egyptians [Col. 1665A] will subject them to slavery and mistreat them.” For they were in the servitude of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, for one hundred and forty-four years. “And the nation whom they serve I will judge, says the Lord; and afterwards they shall come out and serve me in this place.”

When the wording is arranged in this manner, no difficulty arises from it. Rabanus reckons these 430 years from the day on which this promise was made to Abraham until the departure from Egypt. From the time of the promise made to Abraham until Jacob entered Egypt, 240 years elapsed; and from the entry until the departure, the same number. Thus Rabanus. The Apostle seems to agree with him when he says, “that the Law was given after 430 years” (Gal. III).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How the 430 years are to be reckoned

[Col. 1665B]

Bede and Augustine, because it is said, “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. XXI), adhering to this phrase, reckon the 430 years from Isaac’s birth until the death of the two kings, namely Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan.

Stephen then briefly continues the history: “And he gave him the covenant of circumcision; and he begot Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; and Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob the twelve patriarchs. And the patriarchs, envying Joseph, sold him to merchants into Egypt, who brought him into Egypt” (Acts VII). He passes over this briefly. “And God was with him, delivered him from all his tribulations, and gave him wisdom and favour in the sight of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and appointed him ruler over Egypt and over all his household. Afterwards a great famine arose throughout the whole land. And Jacob, hearing that there was grain in Egypt, first sent his sons; afterwards he himself went down into Egypt with seventy-five persons.”

The truth, according to the book of Genesis (ch. XLII), is that he entered with seventy persons; Jacob himself and Joseph with his two sons are counted, and there are no more than seventy. Luke adds five by anticipation, counting Joseph’s grandsons and following the edition of the Seventy Interpreters, which was regarded as more authoritative. Had he not followed it, perhaps he would have been less believed and his work regarded with suspicion.

“And Jacob himself [Col. 1665D] died in Egypt, and our fathers,” namely the twelve patriarchs, “were transferred to Shechem.” This is read only of Joseph: for the children of Israel, at his request, brought his bones out of Egypt; they are also recorded to have prophesied, and to have been buried at Shechem (Gen. XLVIII). Why, then, is it said in the plural, “they were transferred to Shechem”?

## CHAPTER XXXV. Bede’s opinion on the same question

We must believe Stephen, as Bede says, and Jerome, who in the history of Paula says that she passed through Shechem and found there the tombs of the twelve patriarchs. Therefore, after first being transferred to Shechem, they were afterwards laid in the tomb which Abraham bought for silver from the sons of Hamor, son of Shechem—in the double cave, namely, which he bought for four hundred [Col. 1666A] shekels from Ephron, son of Seor the Hittite; that is, in Abraham’s burial-place, where Adam with Eve, Abraham with Sarah, Isaac with Rebekah, and Jacob with Leah were buried.

But why is it said, “in the tomb which Abraham bought from the sons of Hamor, son of Shechem,” when Abraham is known to have bought the tomb from Ephron the Hittite? Some therefore construe the passage in this way: “They were transferred to Shechem”—Shechem, I say, purchased from the sons of Hamor, son of Shechem. But why does it say “Hamor, son of Shechem,” when Shechem is known to have been Hamor’s son? It could be that there were two Shechems: one whom Luke calls Hamor’s father and another whom Genesis calls his son. Or arrange the construction by joining the beginning and end of the sentence as follows: “from the sons of Shechem, son of Hamor.” Thus this passage agrees with Genesis.

Therefore, to remove all doubt, construe the text thus: “They were transferred to Shechem”—that is, Shechem which Jacob bought from the sons of Shechem, son of Hamor—and afterwards they were placed in the tomb which Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite, namely in Abraham’s burial-place.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Stephen returns to the order of the history

Stephen then returns to the order of the history, since he had in some measure digressed; and the preceding statement is connected with it: “After these things they shall come out and serve me in this place.” “But as the time of the promise drew near, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt, until another king arose in Egypt, who did not know Joseph’s benefits” (Acts VII), [Col. 1666C] that is, who was unmindful of Joseph’s benefits. “He afflicted our fathers, commanding our little children to be killed. And at that time,” when he issued the decree to kill the children, “Moses was born and was pleasing to God.”

See how he descends to the praise of Moses, because he was accused of having blasphemed him. “When he had been nourished for three months in his father’s house, he was cast into the river; and Pharaoh’s daughter took him up” (Exod. II), having come to the river to bathe, “and raised him as her own son. And Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in his words and deeds,” that is, eloquent and strong.

“When he was forty years old, he visited his brothers, the children of Israel,” in [Col. 1666D] the land of Goshen, where he killed an Egyptian who was quarrelling with a Hebrew, thinking that his brothers would understand, as he himself understood in the Spirit, that by his hand the Lord would deliver the children of Israel from the hand of the Egyptians. But they did not understand. And when on the following day he wished to reconcile two Hebrews who were quarrelling, the one who was injuring the other rejected him, saying: “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Do you wish to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” Hearing this, Moses feared for himself and fled to the land of Midian. There, by Zipporah, daughter of the priest of Midian, whom he married, he begot two sons.

“When forty years had been completed, God appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai” (Exod. III), while he was leading his flock into the interior of the wilderness, at the bush; “and the voice of the Lord came [Col. 1667A] to him, saying: ‘I am the God of your fathers.’ And Moses trembled. But God said to him: ‘Take the sandal from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground. I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to deliver them. And now come: I will send you into Egypt.’ This Moses, whom they rejected, saying: ‘Who appointed you ruler over us?’ God sent as their ruler and redeemer from Egyptian slavery, “with the hand,” that is, through the work or aid, “of the angel who appeared to him in the bush. He led them out, performing signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years. This same Moses said to the children of Israel” (Deut. XVIII): “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; [Col. 1667B] you shall listen to him as to me. This is he who was in the Church,” that is, in the assembly of the people of Israel, “in the wilderness of Sinai with the angel who spoke to him on the mountain, and with our fathers; for he received words of life to give to us. But our fathers were unwilling to obey him; rather, they rejected him, and in their hearts turned back to Egypt, saying to Aaron” (Exod. XXXII): “‘Make us gods to go before us.’ And they made a calf and offered sacrifices to it.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. He commends the tabernacle, lest he seem to condemn the holy place

Then, because they said that he disparaged the holy place, he adds praise of the tabernacle. It is called the tabernacle of testimony either because the ark of the testimony was in it, or because cases were decided before witnesses in front of the tabernacle doors. “The tabernacle [Col. 1667C] of testimony,” he says, “was with our fathers in the wilderness, as God, speaking to Moses, ordained that he should make it according to the pattern which he had seen on the mountain.” Our fathers had this until the days of David. In Solomon’s days, however, the Temple succeeded the tabernacle.

Afterwards Stephen begins to accuse them, once he has cleared himself of the charge made against him by the false witnesses. “You stiff-necked people,” he says, “and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” Hearing this, “they were cut to the heart and gnashed their teeth at him.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How they stoned Stephen

[Col. 1667D]

“Now Stephen, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing in human form at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts XII). He appeared to him standing, though crucified, lest he waver when he was to be stoned. By standing, he showed himself ready to aid him; for standing is the posture either of one fighting or of one helping. “Behold,” he said, “I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God.” Then, crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears, “as though horrified to hear blasphemy,” and rushed upon him together; and, casting him out of the city, they stoned him. In this they thought themselves to be acting according to the Law, since by the Law a blasphemer was led outside the camp, [Col. 1668A] and the whole people stoned him.

“And the witnesses”—namely, the two false witnesses, who according to the Law were bound to cast the first stones, since it is said in the Law concerning the blasphemer, “The hand of the witnesses shall be first to stone him”—“laid down their garments,” lest they be defiled by touching him, “at the feet of a young man named Saul.” He was afterwards called Paul. According to Bede, God mercifully provided in this matter that Saul’s hand should not be stained with innocent blood. Yet he merely kept the garments of those who stoned Stephen and consented to them; consequently he would have perished as one deserving death, unless God by grace had inspired him with repentance.

“Therefore they stoned Stephen the Levite, who called upon God and said: ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,’” just as Christ said to the Father, [Col. 1668B] “Into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIV).—“Then, kneeling down, he cried with a loud voice, saying: ‘Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge,’” because “they know not what they do.” For many of them, in killing him, thought that they were fulfilling the Law, as the Lord had foretold: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is rendering service to God” (John XVI).—“And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord. And there arose a great persecution against the Church which was at Jerusalem” (Acts VIII). For when blessed Stephen, one of the leaders of the Church, as it were the chief among the seven deacons, had been killed, they began severely to persecute the others; so greatly that all the disciples, except the apostles—who, as shepherds of the flock, were more steadfast than the rest—“were scattered [Col. 1668C] throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria,” fleeing from the persecutors, as the Lord had commanded: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”

“But devout men attended to Stephen,” that is, according to the custom of that land they diligently cared for his burial, “and made great mourning for him.” Then the apostles, foreseeing that they would later go forth to the Gentiles, made provision for the faithful who would remain at Jerusalem: they ordained James the son of Alphaeus bishop of Jerusalem, and Peter, James, and John laid hands upon him. Therefore today a bishop is not consecrated by fewer than three bishops.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Saul’s first persecution

[Col. 1668D]

“But Saul ravaged the Church, going through the houses, dragging off men and women, and casting them into prison.” Yet he killed no one, the Lord guarding his hands lest they should be polluted with innocent blood. Those who had previously been scattered passed from place to place, nevertheless preaching the word of God; for, though dispersed, they remained steadfast in preaching the Gospel.

“But Philip,” the deacon second after Stephen, “went down into a city of Samaria and preached Christ there.
