And the crowds with one accord gave heed to the things spoken by Philip, seeing the miracles which he performed. For he delivered many demoniacs, healed many paralytics, and made the lame stand upright. Now there was there Simon Magus, deceiving [Col. 1669A] the people; and all, from the least to the greatest, listened to him,” because by magical arts he performed many things. Thus they said that he himself was the great power of God, supposing him to be a prophet, an angel, or the Son of God, because he had driven their minds mad—that is, had overthrown them by magical arts.

And when they believed Philip preaching concerning the kingdom of God, men and women were baptized in the name of Jesus Christ; and Simon pretended to believe and was baptized. For, seeing Philip perform miracles such as he himself could not perform, nor so readily, he thought that they were done by a certain technique. Therefore he was baptized deceitfully, so that he might attach himself more closely to Philip and learn the art by which he could do similar things.

## CHAPTER XL. On Simon Magus’s request

[Col. 1669B]

“Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, they prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit” (Acts VIII) visibly, which perhaps they had not yet done; “for he had not yet come upon any of them,” that is, he had not yet visibly descended. For it is certain that they had received the Holy Spirit invisibly when “they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Then they laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit,” in such a way that it was shown by a visible sign, since they spoke in every language.

It is certain that this Philip was a deacon, not an apostle. This appears from the gloss on Matthew: for the laying on of hands was reserved to the apostles, [Col. 1669C] and for this reason it is now reserved only to their vicars, that is, bishops, who lay hands on and anoint the forehead in confirmation, where the Holy Spirit is given for strengthening. For if this Philip had been an apostle, he would have laid hands upon the baptized immediately, and would not have waited for others to do so.

“Now when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands,” supposing that this was effected by some technique and could be purchased from them for money, “he offered them money, saying: ‘Give me this power, that on whomever I lay hands he may receive the Holy Spirit.’” Thus he wished to buy this power for profit. Peter said to him: “May your money be with you unto destruction.”

This can be construed thus, [Col. 1669D] lest he seem to be cursing the money: “May your money be with you,” supply, “leading you to destruction.” Or he says it as a curse: “May your money be with you in destruction,” that is, keep your money and pay eternal punishment for it. For when saints pronounce a sentence of curse, they do not burst forth into it from a desire for vengeance, but in view of justice.

“You have no part in this word,” namely, that through the laying on of your hands the Holy Spirit should be given. “For your heart is not right before the Lord. Repent therefore of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see you to be in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity.” Peter knew in the Spirit that he would not repent; yet it was [Col. 1670A] his duty to exhort him to do so. But Simon, knowing himself unworthy to be heard by God, did not wish to pray; rather, he said to the apostles: “Pray for me, that none of those things which you have spoken may come upon me.” “But Peter and John returned to Jerusalem, preaching the Gospel in many cities of the Samaritans.”

## CHAPTER XLI. On the eunuch baptized by Philip

“Now an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying: ‘Rise and go southward, to the road which descends from Jerusalem to Gaza’” (Acts VIII), that is, toward Africa. It is as though he said: Go to the road by which one descends from Jerusalem through Gaza into Africa. This Gaza, namely, had been destroyed. For old Gaza, which was formerly the boundary of the Canaanites near Egypt, had been destroyed, and another was built in its place.

[Col. 1670B] “And he rose and went. And behold, an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, powerful in the household of Candace the queen, who was over all her treasures.” It was the custom for eunuchs to guard the treasuries of rulers. He “had come to worship at Jerusalem.” And, as is reported in other histories, Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, had sent many gifts by him to the Temple at Jerusalem. Observe that all queens of the Ethiopians were called Candaces, just as Roman emperors were called Caesars; nor was that country governed except by women.

“And as that Ethiopian returned, sitting in his chariot and reading Isaiah the prophet, the Spirit said to Philip: ‘Go near and join yourself to this chariot.’ And Philip, approaching, heard him reading Isaiah and said: ‘Do you think that you understand what you are reading?’ He replied: ‘And how [Col. 1670C] can I, unless someone shows me?’ And he asked Philip to come up into the chariot and sit with him. Now the passage of Scripture which he was reading—having providentially come before him to be read—was this: ‘Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth’” (Isaiah LIII).

The eunuch, replying to Philip, said: “I beg you, sir, tell me: of whom does the prophet say these things? Of himself, or of someone else?” “Then Philip opened his mouth and, beginning from this Scripture”—that is, the passage about which he was asking—“preached Jesus to him. And as they went along the road, they came to a certain water. And the eunuch said: ‘Behold, water; what prevents me from being baptized?’” Philip answered him: [Col. 1670D] “If you believe with your whole heart, you may be baptized.” He replied: “I believe that Jesus is the Son of God.”

Observe that, although Philip saw the eunuch’s faith in the Spirit, he nevertheless wished to draw from him an explicit confession. He did not wish to baptize him immediately, so that an example might be given to those baptizing and those being baptized: to ask and to confess. Hence today solemn baptism is celebrated on Holy Saturday with a certain delay and prolongation of scrutinies, since the scrutinies begin in the middle of Lent on the day when it is sung, “When I shall have been sanctified” (Ezekiel XXXVI).

“And he ordered the chariot to stop, and they both went down from the chariot, and Philip baptized the eunuch. And when he had come up from the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more; but he went [Col. 1671A] on his way rejoicing. But Philip was found at Azorus, and, passing through, he preached the Gospel to all the cities until he came to Caesarea.” There he is said to have had a house, traces of which are visible even today, as also the chamber of his four virgin daughters, prophetesses.

Now the narrative returns to its proper order by continuing with Paul, and is connected with what was said above: “Saul ravaged the Church.” For what was said concerning Philip and the eunuch’s conversion was incidental.

## CHAPTER XLII. On Saul’s blinding

“Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord” (Acts IX), that is, still threatening and conspiring against them and yearning for their slaughter, “went to the chief priest,” driven by the zeal of rage, [Col. 1671B] and asked him for letters to each synagogue of the Jews that was in Damascus, so that by his authority, “if he found at Damascus any men or women of this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.”

“And as he journeyed, it happened that he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone round about him. Falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’” That is, in my members. “He said: ‘Who are you, Lord?’” Are you God or an angel? “‘I am Jesus,’ he said, ‘whom you persecute. It is hard for you to kick against the goad,’” that is, to rebel against one more powerful. “And trembling and astonished, he said: ‘Lord, what do you wish me to do?’” As though he said: Make your will known to me, [Col. 1671C] for I stand ready to obey you.

The Lord said to him: “Rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you must do.” “Now the men who accompanied him stood astonished, hearing indeed the voice of Paul himself, but not that of the one speaking with him, and seeing no one,” as Paul himself says below: “Those who were with me saw indeed the light, but did not hear the voice of him who spoke with me” (Acts XXII).—“And he rose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened he saw nothing.” He became blind in body, having formerly been blind in mind. “But leading him by the hand”—that is, holding his hands with their own hands and conducting him as a blind man—“they brought him into Damascus. And he was there for three days without sight, and neither ate nor drank.”

During those [Col. 1671D] three days he is believed to have learned the Gospel from the Holy Spirit. Therefore he boasts in the Epistle to the Galatians that he had no human teacher, saying: “Neither did I receive it from man, nor did I learn it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians I). For the false [teachers] charged him with having been taught by Ananias rather than by the Holy Spirit, and therefore called him Ananias’s apostle.

Nor should it trouble anyone if his conversion is sometimes said to have occurred in the first year of the Lord’s Passion and sometimes in the second: one statement uses the ordinary year, the other the commencing year. For if you calculate the first year of the Lord’s Passion from the Kalends of January—that is the ordinary year—Paul was converted in the second year. But if you calculate from the very day of the Passion to the corresponding day of the following year, [Col. 1672A] after the year has come full circle—that is the commencing year—he was converted in the first year of the Lord’s Passion.

## CHAPTER XLIII. How, by the Lord’s command, Ananias visited Paul

“Now there was at Damascus a certain disciple” (Acts IX), that is, a Christian, “named Ananias. And the Lord said to him in a vision,” that is, in a vision of the night: “Ananias.” And he replied: “Behold, Lord, I am ready to obey you.” The Lord said to him: “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and seek in the house of Judas a man named Saul of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying.”

Perhaps Judas was the proper name of his host; or perhaps he was of the tribe of Judah, so that the sense is: “in the house of Judah,” that is, among the Jews who were there from that tribe; or “in the house of Judah,” that is, in the Jews’ quarter. [Col. 1672B] According to Rabanus, a *vicus* (“village” or “quarter”) is so called from the neighbourhood of a city, such that *vici* properly designate the countryside nearest the city. Yet here, and often elsewhere, it is understood differently.

Lest Ananias should fear to come to Saul, whom he knew to be a most fierce persecutor of Christians, the Lord added: “For behold, he is praying,” as though saying: He is not to be feared, for Saul has become Paul and the wolf a lamb. And I have also revealed your coming to him. For already “he has seen in the Spirit that you are coming to him and laying hands upon him, that he may receive his sight.”

Then Ananias said: “Lord, I have heard from many concerning this man how much evil he has done to your saints in Jerusalem; and he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call upon your name.” The [Col. 1672C] Lord said to him: “Go, for this man is a vessel of election to me,” that is, an elect vessel, tested in the furnace of tribulation, “to bear my name before kings, Gentiles, and the children of Israel. You indeed will baptize him, but you will not teach him; for I alone will teach him, and will show him how great things he must suffer for my name,” so that the elect vessel may be tested through many tribulations and may suffer with the saints the evils that he inflicted upon the saints.

“Ananias went,” and, coming to Paul’s lodging, entered to him and, laying his hand upon him, said: “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me to you, that you may see with inward and outward sight, “and be filled with the Holy Spirit,” that is, receive the Holy Spirit more fully afterwards in baptism. “And immediately [Col. 1672D] there fell from his eyes something like scales; and he received his sight, and rising up he was baptized. And when he had taken food, he was strengthened. And he was with the disciples who were at Damascus for some days. And immediately, entering the synagogues, he preached the Lord Jesus, that he is the Son of God. And all who heard were astonished and said: ‘Is this not the man who attacked at Jerusalem those who called upon this name, and who came here for this purpose, to bring them bound to the chief priests?’ But Saul became still stronger in Christ and confounded the Jews who were at Damascus, affirming that this is the Christ.”

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Jews’ envy of Paul

“Now when many days had been fulfilled” after [Col. 1673A] Paul’s baptism, the Jews formed a plan to kill him (Acts IX). From the words, “when many days had been fulfilled,” it may appear that this was not done during his first visit to Damascus but during his second. For perhaps he went into Syria and Cilicia and preached there, converting many. Afterwards, when he came again to Damascus and had more greatly aroused the Jews’ envy during that second visit, they devised a plan to kill him.

But the Jews’ plot was made known to him, and the gates of the city were watched day and night so that he might be killed by treachery—not by the Jews, but by the citizens of Damascus and the governor of the people under King Aretas, at the Jews’ request, as the Apostle himself recounts in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians (chapter XI), saying: “At Damascus [Col. 1673B] the governor of the people under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me.” But his disciples lowered him by night in a basket through the wall.

Observe that in Greek the word “his” is not added; it simply says “the disciples,” because Paul did not have disciples. Rather, all Christians were then called disciples, because the name “Christian” had not yet been devised. Escaping the hands of the Damascenes, Paul came to Jerusalem; wishing to join himself to the disciples of the Lord, namely the apostles, “all were afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.”

Then Barnabas, a Cypriot and a Levite by birth—who, as was said above, had laid at the feet of the apostles of the Lord the price of a sold field—took hold of him and brought him to the apostles. He related how Paul had seen the Lord on the road, that the Lord had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had acted boldly in the name of Jesus. The Epistle to the Galatians shows which apostles he found at Jerusalem: namely Peter and James, bishop of Jerusalem, [Col. 1673C] with whom he stayed fifteen days, as he himself states in the Epistle: “Then, after three years”—namely from my conversion—“I came to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days; but I saw no other of the apostles except James, the brother of the Lord” (Galatians I.18).

“And he was with them,” namely Peter, James, and the other disciples who were at Jerusalem, “coming in and going out” for fifteen days. Then he went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia; there “he spoke with the Gentiles and disputed [Col. 1673D] with the Greeks,” that is, the Jews scattered among the Greeks.

This narrative, because of its excessive brevity, confuses the true sequence of events, as though everything had happened at Jerusalem. For the narrative proceeds thus: “And he was with them, coming in and going out in Jerusalem, acting boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke with the Gentiles and disputed with the Greeks.” “But they,” namely the Jews living among the Greeks with whom he disputed, “sought to kill him. When the brethren learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea”—a city of Palestine—“and from there sent him away to Tarsus,” a city of Cilicia, from which he himself came.

Afterwards the narrative returns to Peter and resumes the Acts of the Apostles, as though by an interposed episode.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the healing of Aeneas

[Col. 1674A]

“Now it came to pass that Peter, as he travelled about preaching, came to Lydda. There he found a certain man named Aeneas, who had lain paralysed on a bed for eight years. And Peter said to him: ‘Aeneas, may my Lord Jesus Christ heal you; rise and make your bed’” (Acts IX). Previously he could not even rise from his bed. And immediately he rose. And all who lived at Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.

Now there was at Joppa a certain female disciple, a Christian, who in Hebrew was called Tabitha, in Greek Dorcas, and in Latin *Damula* (“little doe”) or *Caprea* (“roe-deer”). Yet on Mark we have that Tabitha is interpreted “girl.” Thus *Tabitha cumi* is interpreted “Girl, arise”; and accordingly [Col. 1674B] there are different interpretations of this name.

“Now she was full of good works and almsdeeds which she performed,” and she especially spent much labour sewing clothing for the poor. “And it came to pass in those days,” when Peter had come to Lydda, “that she fell ill and died. And when they had washed the body, they placed it in an upper room. And since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was near at Lydda, sent two men to him, saying: ‘Do not delay to come to us.’” They did not disclose the reason to him.

“Peter arose and went with them. And when they had arrived, they led him into the upper room,” where Tabitha lay dead. “And all the widows stood around him weeping and showing him the garments [Col. 1674C] which Dorcas had made for them,” so that they might show that she had devoted her labour to works of mercy and thus move Peter to compassion.

Then Peter put them all out, not as one about to do something improper that he wished others not to see, like those who contrive something by magical arts or demonic counsel, but because he wished to imitate his Master, who, when about to raise the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, put everyone out of the house except a few. Or perhaps because some were unworthy to behold the miracle. “When all had been put outside, he knelt down and prayed; and, turning to the body, he said: ‘Tabitha, arise.’ And she opened her eyes; and when she saw Peter, she sat up. Giving her his hand, he raised her; and, calling those who had gone out, he restored her to them alive. And the miracle became known [Col. 1674D] throughout all Joppa, and many believed in God. And Peter remained many days in Joppa with Simon the tanner,” or *curiarius*, perhaps from *corium* (“leather”) or *curia* (“court”): perhaps he was an official of a court and was thus called *curiarius*, or because he prepared hides and was therefore called a *coriarius* (“tanner”).

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Cornelius’s conversion

“Now there was a certain man in Caesarea named Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort called the Italian” (Acts X), because it had been sent from the Roman city, which is Italian; for Roman emperors sent their soldiers through the cities to guard the fortifications. He was “devout and God-fearing,” devout above the degree of fear and fearing below the degree of religion—that is, piety—for in the graded ascent of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the degree of piety is above the degree of fear.

[Note: [Col. 1675D] Addition 1. *Pietas* is equivocal: it denotes both the worship of God and compassion for one’s neighbour.]

Therefore, insofar as he was devout, he was above the degree of fear; insofar as he feared God, he was below the degree of religion. By “religion” understand the spirit of piety. He was, I say, devout with all his household, which was devout and God-fearing, “giving many alms to the people,” without respect of persons.

“This man, about the ninth hour of the day, saw clearly in a vision”—that is, in a manifest vision, not in a dream or ecstasy—“an angel of God entering to him and saying: ‘Cornelius.’ And he, looking at him and seized with fear, said: ‘Who are you, Lord?’ The angel said to him: ‘Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. And now send men to Joppa and summon [Col. 1675B] a certain Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the Tyrrhenian Sea.’” For Joppa was a city of the promised land, close to the Tyrrhenian Sea and situated on its eastern shore; Simon the tanner’s house, where Peter lodged, stood by the shore. “He,” said the angel, “will tell you what you ought to do.”

Behold, Cornelius was told by the angel: “Your prayers have been heard.” It is therefore certain that he then had faith, since the saints agree that one comes to works through the merit of faith, and not the reverse. Yet he did not then believe that Christ had been incarnate, because he was uncertain about the time of the Incarnation: he did not know whether Christ had already been incarnate or was yet to be incarnated.

Nevertheless, his faith contained no falsehood; for, since he possessed faith in the Incarnation, he could, without prejudice to faith, be uncertain whether Christ had already come or was still to come in the flesh. For some of the holy Fathers did not know that Christ had been born after he had been born—for example Simeon, until the fortieth day after his birth. Yet it should not be thought that they lacked faith in the Incarnation. For time is not an article of faith; rather, when it had not yet been preached or revealed to them that he had already been born, they could, without prejudice to faith, remain uncertain whether he had already been born or was still to be born.

“When the angel departed from Cornelius, he called two of his household servants and a soldier who feared the Lord.” This is not said of the household servants because it was already evident that his household [Col. 1675D] was devout and God-fearing. “After relating everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.”

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Peter’s vision

“On the following day, as they journeyed and approached the city of Joppa” (Acts X)—or “came into view,” according to another reading, so that they could already be seen from Peter’s lodging, namely from the house of Simon his tanner—“Peter went up to the upper room of his lodging about the sixth hour, to pray in private and eat after prayer,” because it was time to eat, and he was hungry.

“While the servants were preparing the meal and he was at prayer, an ecstasy came upon him.” By the Lord’s action, he experienced an alienation of mind such that he did not use human senses. In an ecstasy of this kind, [Col. 1676A] “he saw heaven opened,” that is, the air; and from the opened air he saw “a certain vessel descending, like a great linen sheet being let down from heaven to earth by four” *linteis* (“linen bands”), or *litiis* (“threads”), or “*initiis*,” which reading is more correct. *Initiae* are soft cords by which children are bound in cradles, made of flaxen material, or of silk for the use of nobles.

Thus the vessel appeared to him like a sheet, suspended in the air by four *initiae* tied to its four corners, and thus “let down to earth; and in it were all kinds of animals, four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth. And when he was hungry, a voice came to him, saying: ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’” It was as though it were said to him in the Spirit: Go over to the Gentiles, kill the vices in them, and thus incorporate them into the Church.

“By no means, Lord,” he said, “for I have never eaten anything common,” that is, unclean. It is an idiom of the Hebrews, who considered foods used commonly by Gentiles to be unclean. Thus they called them “common,” as though unclean. Peter therefore shrank from the command “eat,” because four-footed creatures and creeping things had been shown him which were unclean according to the Law. It seemed grievous to him to use foods forbidden in the Law; and above all he feared the reproach of the Jews if he used Gentile foods.

Therefore, when he recoiled from all these things, a voice came to him a second time, saying: “What God has cleansed, do not call common.” It is certain that this was said to him spiritually [Col. 1676C] concerning the Gentiles, already cleansed through faith in God’s foreknowledge. The first voice addressed to Peter had instructed him concerning their purification, saying: “Kill and eat.” But when creeping things of the earth had been shown to him, it is certain that they had not been purified by God, nor made clean for anyone, Jew or Gentile, to eat.

“This happened to him three times”: namely, the vessel was lowered to the earth once, again, and a third time; and the voice was heard three times, either to confirm the truth of the vision or because of faith in the Trinity. For, as Ambrose says, in the catechism there is a threefold questioning: “Do you believe in God? Do you renounce Satan? Do you wish to be baptized?” Likewise there is a threefold anointing: on the crown or forehead, on the shoulders, and on the breast; and in baptism there is also a threefold immersion.

[Col. 1676D] After the vessel had been shown three times, “the vessel was received into heaven. And while Peter was pondering within himself what this vision might mean, behold, the three men sent by Cornelius, having sought out the house of Simon the tanner, stood at the door, asking whether Simon surnamed Peter lodged there. And while Peter was thinking about the vision, the Spirit said to him: ‘Behold, three men seek you.’” Yet the Spirit did not tell him why they sought him; he learned that afterwards from them. For, in order to preserve humility, the Spirit sometimes touches the mind prophetically in part and does not touch it in part.

“Rise,” he said, “and go down, and go with them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” Peter went down to them and said: “Behold, I am he whom you seek. What is the reason for which you have come?” They answered: “Cornelius, [Col. 1677A] a centurion, a devout and God-fearing man, having testimony from the whole Jewish people, received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he should summon you to his house and hear words from you.” “And he received them into his lodging,” and they stayed with him that night. “On the following day he went forth with them, and with certain brethren who accompanied him from Joppa, that they might be witnesses for him.”

## CHAPTER XLVIII. That Peter, having been summoned, came to Cornelius

“On the next day” (Acts X), the second after leaving Joppa, “he entered Caesarea. And Cornelius was expecting them, having called together his kinsmen and intimate friends.” Intimate friends are those who do not abandon a person in a time of need.

“And when Peter entered, Cornelius came to meet him [Col. 1677B] and, falling at his feet, worshipped him,” outwardly expressing by the gesture of his body the devotion of his mind. “But Peter raised him, saying: ‘Rise, for I too am a man.’” And when many were present, namely the assembled kinsmen and friends, Peter spoke to them, saying: “You know how abominable it is for a Jewish man to associate with a foreigner. But God has shown me that I should call no human being unclean. Therefore I came when summoned without hesitation. I ask, then, for what reason you have summoned me.”

Cornelius answered: “Four days ago I was praying at the ninth hour in my house.” That is, four days from this hour, according to the beginning of days anew. For on the first day he saw the angel and sent the messengers; on the second the messengers came to Joppa; on the third Peter set out with [Col. 1677C] them, and they remained on the road that night; on the fourth they came to Caesarea. “And behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said: ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your alms have been accepted by God. Send to Joppa and summon Simon surnamed Peter.’ And I sent to you at once, and you have done well to come. Now therefore we are all present before you, ready to obey you in all things whatsoever has been commanded you by the Lord.”

Then Peter opened his mouth and said: “Now I have truly learned that God is not a respecter of persons and makes no distinction between Jews and Gentiles; but in every nation the one who fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him. You know” that John preached Jesus of Nazareth; you also know [Col. 1677D] “that the word”—that is, the preaching of the Gospel—“went forth throughout all Judaea,” beginning from the baptism of John by which Jesus was baptized; then continuing with how “God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and power, and he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil. And we are witnesses of all that he did in the region of the Jews, and that they hung him upon a tree,” and that God raised him on the third day. We are witnesses of him, “who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead, and to whom he commanded that we should preach to the people and testify that he is the one appointed by God the Father as Judge of the living and the dead,” because the Father gave all judgment to him. And not we alone, but “all the prophets bear witness to him [Col. 1678A] that everyone who believes in him receives remission of sins through his name.”

## CHAPTER XLIX. That he baptized Cornelius and those who were with him

“While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell and descended suddenly upon all who heard the word” (Acts X). Whether he descended in fiery tongues or in another visible form is uncertain. “And the faithful of the circumcision who were with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even upon the nations,” that is, the Gentiles. “For they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God.”

Then Peter answered: “Can anyone forbid water, that these should not be baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” [Col. 1678B] This is greater than baptism. “And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Christ,” leaving unspoken the form of baptism delivered by the Lord, so as to amplify the name of Christ. In that name are understood he who was anointed, the Father by whom he was anointed, and the Holy Spirit with whom he was anointed.

“Then they asked him.” And, being asked, “he remained with them for some days,” during which he is believed first to have eaten Gentile food, for which he was afterwards reproved. And it was spread everywhere and brought to “the brethren who were in Judaea that the Gentiles had received the word of God” (Acts XI). This was the apostles’ first particular passage to the Gentiles, in which Cornelius and his household were converted.

## CHAPTER L. How Peter was reproved by Christians
[Col. 1678C] “But when Peter had gone up to Jerusalem, the believers of the circumcision disputed with him, saying: ‘Why did you enter the house of uncircumcised men and eat with them?’ (Acts 11).” It was as though they said: You acted against the Law in two respects, because you entered their house and because you shared their food.

Then Peter, “beginning, set the matter before them in order,” explaining the vision shown him by God and how the angel had appeared to Cornelius. Throughout this whole account he added only one phrase to what had been said to Cornelius: “Send and summon Simon, who is surnamed Peter,” where he added, “who will speak words to you by which you and all your household will be saved.” And from his immediately adding, “the Holy Spirit fell upon them, [Col. 1678D] just as upon us at the beginning,” it is inferred that the Holy Spirit descended upon Cornelius and his household in tongues of fire, just as he had descended upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost.

“And then,” he says, “I remembered the word of the Lord which he told us: ‘John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit’ (John 1),” seeing this fulfilled in Cornelius and his household. Having heard Peter’s manifold defense, they ceased reproaching him and gave thanks to the Savior. Thus was fulfilled the prophecy of Job: “From the north shall come gold, and fearful praise unto God” (Job 27). That is, the Gentiles, comparable to the north because of the frozen condition of unbelief and because they were in darkness—that is, in blindness of mind—will receive the light of faith. For their enlightenment [Col. 1679A] fearful praise is directed to God, since, astonished and afraid at the unexpected and sudden conversion of the Gentiles, the believers from Judaea “glorified God.”

## CHAPTER LI. On the Continuation of the History

Now the history returns to its order. For what was inserted concerning Philip, Peter, John, and Paul, after it had previously been said, “Therefore those who had been scattered went about preaching the word of God,” was incidental. The narrative therefore proceeds as follows:

“And those who had been scattered by the persecution which began at the death of Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia” (Acts 11), a province of western Syria, “and Cyprus, speaking the word to no one except Jews alone. But there were some among them from Cyprus and Cyrene. When they entered Antioch, [Col. 1679B] they spoke to the Greeks, proclaiming the Lord Jesus; and the hand of the Lord was with them. And a great number of believers turned to the Lord.”

Bede says concerning this passage that, after the revelation of the sheet, the Church began to grow. Hence it is conjectured that Peter saw in the vision the appearance of a sheet or linen cloth, although elsewhere it is called a vessel and elsewhere a dish. News of the conversion of the Antiochenes was brought “to the ears of the Church which was in Jerusalem”; and, wishing to be fully assured, “they sent Barnabas to Antioch. When he came and saw the grace of the Lord, he rejoiced and exhorted them all to remain in the Lord with steadfastness of heart, because he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.”

Rabanus says concerning this passage that Barnabas is commended in so many ways lest he be thought to have lost the apostleship because of his indignation. Rabanus held the opinion according to which Barnabas was the man upon whom the lot was cast along with Matthias and who was afterward chosen to the apostleship with Paul. We follow another opinion.

But Barnabas, seeing that he was not sufficient to instruct so great a multitude, “went to Tarsus to seek Saul; and, having found him, brought him to Antioch. For a year they lived there and taught a great crowd.” Then, for the first time, the followers of the Christian religion, taking their name from Christ their head, were called Christians; previously they had been called disciples. This was a rather elegant institution among the Gentiles. For it seemed unsuitable [Col. 1679D] and unbecoming that Gentiles converted to the faith should be designated by a common name as followers of the Christian religion. Rather, they were to be named after the Master’s name, just as, in the schools of philosophers, followers were named after their masters—for example, the followers of Epicurus were called Epicureans.

“Now in those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. And one of them, named Agabus, stood up and prophesied through the Holy Spirit that a famine would come over the whole world,” and especially over Judaea, “which occurred under Claudius,” namely in the fourth year of Claudius.

## CHAPTER LII. On the Collection Made for the Poor

Then the disciples resolved to make a collection [Col. 1680A] (Acts 11), so that each person might contribute according to the measure of his means and send something to the poor who were in Jerusalem. These were they who, having sold everything, had laid the proceeds at the apostles’ feet, so that they might be provided for against the famine. And then, for the first time, a collection was made for the needs of the poor and sent to Jerusalem through Barnabas and Paul.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the Death of James the Greater

“At that time King Herod laid hands on some members of the Church to afflict them. And he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword” (Acts 12). To understand this passage—that is, which Herod is meant—it is expedient to set aside for a time the history of the Acts of the Apostles and to pursue the history [Col. 1680B] of the Roman emperors.

This Herod should not be thought to have been Herod the tetrarch surnamed Antipas, but Herod Agrippa. For the former was not a king but a tetrarch: namely, the son of Herod the Great, who agreed with Pilate concerning the Lord’s death, who sent him back to Pilate clothed in a white garment, and who had already been deported into exile at Vienne and died there.

Pilate, then, was already dead. As was stated at the beginning of this history, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar he was procurator of Judaea while Vitellius was governor of Syria; and he was accused before Tiberius on many charges. He was accused by the Jews of the violent slaughter of innocent persons. He was also accused because, despite Jewish protest, he placed images of Gentiles in the Temple.

[Note: [Col. 1679D] From the histories of Josephus and others.]

He was also accused because he had diverted money [Col. 1680C] deposited in the *corbona* to his own use, making from it an aqueduct to his house. For all these reasons he was deported into exile at Lyons, from which he had originated, so that he might die there to the disgrace of his lineage.

Observe that the *musac* was a chest in which the offerings of kings or princes were deposited; the *corbona*, a chest in which priests’ offerings were deposited for repairing the Temple’s roofs and structures; and the treasury (*gazophylacium*), the place in which the offerings of passers-by were deposited.

## CHAPTER LIV. Who Was Appointed Procurator after Pilate’s Death

[Note: [Col. 1680D] These are incidental matters drawn from histories.]

When Pilate died, Vitellius appointed his own brother procurator of Judaea. Wishing to please the Jews, he complied with their wishes in certain matters. [Col. 1680D] Namely, regarding the removal of Caiaphas and the promotion of the son of Annas: at their request he removed Caiaphas from the priesthood and appointed the son of Annas, who was already dead; and he restored to him the robe—namely, that solemn and ancient one which the priest ought to have had in his own custody for use on feast days. But Pilate had transferred it to his own house, and whenever it was needed by the priest on feast days, he could not have it without first paying a price.

In the time of Tiberius, Philip, tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis, died; he was the brother of Herod, tetrarch of Abilene. Thus two tetrarchies were vacant, and Herod Agrippa aspired to one of them.

## CHAPTER LV. On Herod Agrippa’s Intention

[Col. 1681A]

[Note: [Col. 1681D] These are incidental matters, not taken from the biblical text.]

Herod Agrippa was a high-minded and warlike man, but extremely poor; he was the nephew of Herod the tetrarch and the brother of his wife Herodias. For he was the son of Aristobulus, son of Herod the Great, while she was the daughter of that same Herod. He accordingly planned to go to Rome, in case he might obtain from Tiberius one of the vacant tetrarchies.

When he arrived at Rome, Tiberius, seeing him to be a most valiant soldier, kept him with himself and made him attach himself to his son Drusus, for whom he had already established the empire during his own lifetime. This is not the Drusus who lies buried at Mainz.

Herod Agrippa was a man of great generosity; to win the goodwill of the Romans he spent much and incurred many debts. As Josephus relates, there was no man in whom the changeability of fortune could be perceived so clearly. At first misfortune befell him in this: Drusus, the son of Tiberius, died. Tiberius grieved for his death so inconsolably that he removed from his presence all who had been closely attached to Drusus, lest they bring his death back to his mind.

Herod Agrippa was compelled to return to Judaea, and, despairing because of his extreme poverty, entered a tower in order to afflict himself there with hunger and so die. His wife reported this to her sister Herodias, wife of Herod the tetrarch, who begged her husband to call Agrippa back from the tower and provide him with necessities. He agreed, established him at Tiberias, assigned him a house there, and gave him the necessities of life.

One day, when Herod the tetrarch was at Tiberias and feasting, he became [Col. 1681C] more cheerful than usual because he was warmed by wine. He began to reproach Herod Agrippa, who was feasting with him, with the benefits he had bestowed on him—namely, that he had delivered him from the plague of hunger. Agrippa was exceedingly distressed by this and again planned to return to Tiberius, in case he might find his disposition changed.

On his return he encountered Petronius, or Tiberius, and was honorably received by him; he came with him to Rome. Tiberius had two grandsons: one by his son Drusus, namely Tiberius, and the other by his brother Germanicus, namely Gaius. He wished to appoint the son of his son as his successor, because he loved him more.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the Cause of Tiberius’s Enmity toward Herod Agrippa

[Col. 1681D] But Herod Agrippa loved Gaius more and attached himself to him more intimately; therefore he incurred Tiberius’s concealed displeasure. Tiberius did not yet make this known to him, but kept the hidden hatred in his heart.

One day Agrippa was sitting with Gaius in his chariot, and, lifting his hands toward heaven, said: “Would that I might see the death of the troublesome old man, and you lord of the whole world, for you are fit to rule the whole world!” Someone heard this—namely, Agrippa’s charioteer. A few days later the man fled away with damage to Agrippa’s property, was captured, and put in chains. As he was being led to prison, he asked to be brought before the emperor, saying that he would speak in his ear something [Col. 1682A] useful to him.

He was presented to the emperor and deliberately told him that Agrippa had thus wished for Tiberius’s death and Gaius’s sovereignty. But Tiberius did not greatly concern himself with the words of men in chains, and the man was thrown into prison. When Agrippa repeatedly pressed for him to be tried and executed, Tiberius replied: “Brother, it is enough for you that he has been put in chains,” and thus he deferred the matter. For, as Josephus reports, he was dilatory in all his affairs.

Thus, when he appointed procurators in the provinces, he scarcely ever, or never, changed them. When he was repeatedly asked why he did not change procurators, he replied that in this he spared the common people. For procurators who know that they will hold office only briefly squeeze the people even to the blood, and rule more harshly the shorter their tenure; and those who arrive newly in office waste whatever they find.

He illustrated this by the example of a wounded man who lay on the road and did not drive away the multitude of flies from his wound. Another man, coming upon him, thought that he omitted to do so from weakness and drove away the flies that covered the wound. The wounded man said to him: “You have done me harm, for the flies you drove away were already full of blood and troubled me less; but those that come anew will sting me more sharply.” So likewise procurators or officials newly appointed rage more fiercely against their subjects.

## CHAPTER LVII. How Herod Offended Tiberius

One day, as usual, Agrippa urged Tiberius to have his charioteer brought out of prison. Tiberius answered that this would not be advantageous to Agrippa, since the prisoner wished to accuse him while in Agrippa’s own presence and in chains. Since Agrippa was conscious of no guilt, he declared that he wished the man to be brought out and to accuse him.

The man was led out of prison and charged him with treason, because he had prayed for the emperor’s death. Then Tiberius said to the jailer: “Bind this man.” The jailer understood the command as referring to the man who had been brought out and returned him bound to prison.

But one day, while Tiberius was walking in the hippodrome—that is, the horse-racing circus—and holding Agrippa by the hand, he called the jailer and said: “Bind this man.” The jailer and all the rest were amazed that he ordered Agrippa to be bound, since he walked clothed in purple and was of royal stock.

As Agrippa was being led [Col. 1682D] to prison, he suffered intolerable thirst because he had eaten sumptuously. By chance a water-carrier met him and gave him something to drink. After he had been refreshed, Agrippa promised that he would soon reward him in the reign of Gaius, confident that Gaius would shortly reign. He was then put in prison.

One day, while he remained in prison, he stood leaning against a tree in whose branches an owl was perched. One of his fellow captives came to him and said: “Do not suppose that I speak to flatter you because you are my fellow captive. For I wish to tell you what the gods have revealed to me.” He was skilled in augury. “You will soon,” he said, “be freed from prison and raised so high [Col. 1683A] that all your friends and acquaintances will envy you; and in this prosperity you will die, leaving your goods to your sons. But as soon as you see this kind of bird again above you, I know that you will die on the fifth day.”

## CHAPTER LVIII. How Herod Was Freed at the Death of Tiberius

While Herod was in prison, the prison governor treated him with honor, knowing him to be a nobleman and an intimate of Gaius. He tolerated, as though unaware of it, many benefits being conveyed to Agrippa in prison by his friends. He was in prison for six months.

Later, when Tiberius was at Campas, he began to suffer from the illness from which he afterward died. Although elsewhere the Chronicles say that he died in another place, it need not concern us where he died. Seeing that he was about to die, he summoned the nobles of his empire and his two grandsons, Gaius and Tiberius, and resolved that on the following day he would appoint his own successor.

But first he wished to consult the mind of the gods and prayed to his gods that they might indicate which of his grandsons they wished him to appoint to the empire. He determined that he would make emperor whichever of them came to him first on the following day, so as to choose, as it were, by lot; nevertheless, he informed Tiberius that he should arrive first. But in the morning Tiberius would not come until he had eaten.

When Tiberius sent messengers to his grandsons, they found no one but Gaius. Gaius came first to Tiberius. On seeing him, Tiberius wept bitterly, grieved because the other had not come—the one whom he wished to appoint [Col. 1683C] because he loved him more tenderly—though he concealed this. Tiberius said to him:

“Son, you shall succeed me in the empire; though it belonged more properly to Tiberius, as if by hereditary right, as the son of my son. But I see that you are useful to the empire, and I know the purposes of the gods. Take care, therefore, not to oppress him, but always regard him as a brother. Endeavor to administer the affairs of the empire wisely, and perform the rites of my funeral with imperial honor.”

Having summoned the nobles, he announced him as emperor and died. Immediately a report of Tiberius’s death began to spread through the city of Rome. A certain Hebrew, a friend of Herod Agrippa, came to the prison and said to him in Hebrew: “The lion is dead.”

[Col. 1683D] Agrippa began to rejoice wonderfully, so much so that the prison governor asked him what was the cause of such exultation. Agrippa confessed that the Hebrew had announced to him Tiberius’s death in Hebrew. At once the prison governor freed him and seated him beside himself at table.

On the following day other reports spread, namely that Tiberius had recovered and would come to Rome on the third day. The prison governor then reproached Agrippa for deceiving him, fearing that his release of Agrippa might be held against him. He had Agrippa severely beaten and put him back in prison.

Later, certain reports of Tiberius’s death and Gaius’s accession became widespread. Gaius came to Rome [Col. 1684A] and buried Tiberius honorably. On that very day he wished to free Agrippa, but was dissuaded, lest he seem to wish suddenly to undo Tiberius’s acts. A few days later he freed Agrippa, exalted him, gave him two tetrarchies—namely, the tetrarchy of Philip, tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis, and the tetrarchy of Abilene—placed a diadem upon him, and sent him back to Judaea, raised to kingship.

All his relatives envied him, even his sister Herodias. She had pitied him in adversity but now envied him in prosperity, especially because he bore the title of king. Her husband was the elder son of Herod the Great, yet had never deserved to be called king, but only tetrarch.

Day after day she urged her husband to go to Rome and strive by every means to acquire for himself the title of king. But he preferred leisure, because he was wealthy. Therefore his wife, frequently exasperated, said: “May your riches perish, because you love riches more than honors.”

At length, overcome by his wife’s insistence, he went with her to Gaius in great splendor and found Gaius at Baiae. Herod Agrippa, who was present, judging that they had not come for his own benefit, planned to follow after them. But he first sent a messenger, a member of his household and a close friend of Gaius, through whom he sent Gaius a letter. The letter stated that Herod the tetrarch, even while Tiberius was still alive, had made an alliance with the king of the Parthians in order to rebel against the Roman empire. As evidence of this, Agrippa informed him that Herod had in his cities arms sufficient for seventy [Col. 1684C] thousand armed men.

## CHAPTER LIX. That Gaius Ordered His Statue to Be Erected in the Temple

[Note: [Col. 1683D] These are incidental matters and not from the Bible.]

When Herod the tetrarch and his wife Herodias came to Gaius, and Gaius had received them with sufficient honor, Agrippa’s messenger arrived and presented Gaius with Agrippa’s letter. Having read it, Gaius, as though learning it from another source, began to inquire into the circumstances of Herod the tetrarch. Among other questions he asked whether Herod had in his cities as great an abundance of weapons as Gaius had heard; Herod did not deny it.

Then Gaius, believing Agrippa’s report to be true, relegated Herod to exile. But to Herodias, because [Col. 1684D] she was Agrippa’s sister, whom Gaius loved especially, he granted the freedom to return and retain her land. She, however, accompanied her husband into exile, saying that she would not abandon him in adversity, since she had shared in his prosperity. They were deported into exile at Lyons, where they afterward died miserably.

Gaius gave Galilee, which Herod the tetrarch had possessed, to Herod Agrippa; thus Agrippa held three tetrarchies. For the first two years of his reign Gaius was rather mild; afterward his heart was lifted up in pride, and he broke out into such madness that he wished to be worshiped as a god by all the people of his empire. He said that he was Jupiter’s brother.

[Col. 1685A] He even placed his only daughter between Jupiter’s knees, so that after she had come forth from Jupiter’s knees she might appear, as it were, to belong to them both. He therefore sent his image throughout his empire so that all might worship him. All did so except the Jews.

When a riot arose in Alexandria between Jews and Gentiles, and each side came before Gaius for the dispute to be judged, the Gentiles, among the other charges they brought against the Jews, accused them of dishonoring their god, whom all the Gentiles had received in common, because they refused to worship Gaius’s image. Then Gaius first learned that the Jews did not worship his image.

He instructed Petronius, governor of Syria, to set up [Col. 1685B] his statue in the Temple at Jerusalem, so that they might more easily receive it in the surrounding cities. If the Jews should protest, Petronius was to gather the Roman legions, enter Judaea, and spare no one by force of arms.

Petronius therefore gathered an army and entered Judaea. Jews from Jerusalem came to him, together with Herod Agrippa’s friends, who were deeply dear to Gaius, and begged him not to compel them to this. They said that they would sooner allow themselves to be killed; they bared their throats and declared that they would never cultivate the land again, so that they might perish from hunger.

Petronius replied that this had not proceeded from his own counsel, but that he did not dare resist the emperor’s command. Yet, seeing that Gaius would suffer a grave loss if he lost the revenues of all Judaea, he promised that he would intercede with [Col. 1685C] Gaius for them. He sent his letter to Gaius through honorable men, asking him to desist from this command. When they reached Gaius, they did not dare present themselves before him, but went to Herod Agrippa, that he might aid the Jews, because one of Agrippa’s tetrarchies—namely Galilee—lay in Judaea.

## CHAPTER LX. On the Death of the Emperor Gaius

Then Herod invited Gaius to dine with him on the following day. When Gaius was at the banquet the next day, he admired the banquet’s delights. Gaius began to recall how much Herod had endured for his sake—Tiberius’s chains and many other things—and commanded him to ask whatever he wished.

Agrippa replied [Col. 1685D] that Gaius’s favor was sufficient for him. When Gaius persisted in urging him to ask for something, Agrippa asked that he should not place his statue in the Temple at Jerusalem. Gaius was angered; nevertheless, considering Agrippa’s nobility of spirit, because he had not wished to ask for wealth or honors, he granted the request and wrote to Petronius as follows: “If the statue has not yet been placed in the Temple, it need not be placed there.” Thus his statue was not placed in the Temple.

Afterward Gaius changed his mind and wrote back to Petronius as follows: “Because you have despised the emperor’s command and preferred the gifts of the Jews, choose for yourself the manner of death you wish, so that all may learn that it is not safe to oppose the emperor’s command.” But through God’s providence it happened that Petronius heard the report of Gaius’s death before he saw the messengers of this embassy.

[Col. 1686A] For while Gaius was at Rome and returning from the circus games, he was killed by two men at the senators’ instigation. A dissension then arose in the city between the senate-house, the soldiers, and the people. By “senate-house” were meant the senators and consular men—that is, those of consular family or worthy to become consuls.

Because the senators had seen the emperor’s cruelty and the injuries which had thereby come upon the commonwealth, they wished wholly to extirpate the imperial office from the City and restore it to its former state before Julius Caesar, so that the government of the city might be in the discretion of consuls and senators. Conversely, the soldiers and people, fearing the senators’ avarice and loving the emperors’ gifts, made Claudius, Gaius’s uncle, a gentle and pious man, emperor.

## CHAPTER LXI. On the Same Subject

Then Herod Agrippa came to the senators, bringing with him some of the nobler men who were in the senate-house. He pretended to favor their party, though he hated them because of Gaius’s death. He advised them to inform Claudius that he should not stir up a schism in the city, but desist from this undertaking.

The senators asked Herod to go with them to Claudius. He professed himself willing to undertake this embassy and was sent to Claudius with others. In their hearing, he told Claudius what he had said before the senators: that Claudius should desist from the undertaking. But privately he told Claudius not to abandon it, because Agrippa himself would endeavor to make the greater part of the nobles [Col. 1686C] favor Claudius’s party.

He reported to the senators that Claudius refused to desist and began to persuade them not to oppose him, because they could not prevent it. He won over some and finally all; thus Claudius became emperor without opposition. At Herod Agrippa’s persuasion, all who had agreed to Gaius’s death were killed.

Herod Agrippa asked Claudius to annul Gaius’s decree requiring worship of his statue, because it was impious. Claudius granted this and commanded that letters revoking the decree should be posted in a conspicuous place in every city of Judaea, so that all might see them.

## CHAPTER LXII. How, after Killing James, Herod Wished to Seize Peter

[Col. 1686D] Afterward Herod wished to obtain leave from Claudius and return to his own country. Claudius then gave him a fourth tetrarchy, namely Judaea; thus exalted, he returned home. He came first to Judaea and was honorably received by the Jews because he had helped them in many matters.

When the days of Unleavened Bread were near, he came to Jerusalem before the feast day in order to purify himself and attend the feast day in a state of purity (Acts 12). Before the days of Unleavened Bread he killed James, the brother of John. Then, during the days of Unleavened Bread, “seeing that this pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter.”

Clement of Alexandria relates concerning James that, when he had been thrown into prison, he converted his guard to the faith at night. On the next day the guard confessed that he was a Christian. As both were being led to martyrdom, the guard said to James: “Father, grant me forgiveness.” After a brief pause James said: “Peace be with you.” He kissed him, and both were beheaded together.

Herod sent Peter, once seized, to prison, because during the days of Unleavened Bread no one might be killed. Besides the prison guards, “he handed him over to be guarded by four squads of soldiers, intending after Passover to bring him before the people,” so that the people themselves, and not Herod as in James’s case, might kill him. For it seemed more glorious to them if they themselves killed him, because he was the Prince of the Apostles.

## CHAPTER LXIII. How Peter Was Delivered from Herod’s Hand

[Col. 1687B] “But when Herod was about to bring him before the people on the following day, Peter himself was sleeping that night between two soldiers, bound with two chains” (Acts 12), which are said still to be at Rome, “and guards lying before the door were guarding the prison. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood by, and a light shone in the prison chamber.” Miraculously, Peter alone saw the light.

“Striking Peter’s side, he woke him, saying: ‘Rise quickly.’ And immediately the two chains fell from his hands. And the angel said to him: ‘Gird yourself and put on your sandals.’” Peter had removed his belt because of the discomfort of prison, so that his tunic, hanging down about his feet, might temper the cold of the night.

In this an example was given to holy men: in hardships it is permissible to relax something [Col. 1687C] of the strictness of one’s rule. For we read that the apostles and prophets used rough belts for the mortification of the flesh, while Peter temporarily laid aside his belt because of the discomfort of prison.

Peter did as the angel commanded, and the angel added: “Wrap your garment about you and follow me.” “And going out, he followed him and did not know that what was being done through the angel was real”; that is, he did not think it was happening in actual reality, but that it was being shown in an imaginary vision. Hence it follows: “He thought that he was seeing a vision,” and that this was being shown to him in an imaginary vision.

“Passing the first guard,” that is, the prison guards assigned to guard duty, “and the second,” that is, the two squads. Or, by “the first guard” is meant the first [Col. 1687D] squad with its men. “They came to the iron gate that leads into the city,” which is thought to have been in the prison courtyard. For the prison had a courtyard and stood in the outer part of the city, or outside the city. “And it opened to them of its own accord. Going out, they proceeded along one street; and immediately the angel departed from him,” so that Peter might know that he had truly been brought out of prison, though he had thought this was being shown him imaginatively.

“And then, coming to himself,” that is, returning to his senses, for he had been in the greatest amazement, “he said: ‘Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me from Herod’s hand and from all the expectation of the Jewish people.’ And, considering where he was, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was surnamed Mark,” not the Evangelist, “where many [Col. 1688A] were gathered for prayer, that they might pray for Peter.”

When Peter knocked at the gate, a girl named Rhoda came out to see who was there. Recognizing Peter’s voice, she did not open the gate for joy but ran back and announced that Peter was standing at the gate. They said that she was mad, knowing Peter to be imprisoned. But she insisted that it was so. Others among them said: “It is Peter’s angel.”

Jerome says concerning this passage that souls possess such dignity that each one, from the moment of its birth, has an angel assigned to guard it. “But Peter continued knocking. When they opened, they saw him and were astonished. He motioned to them with his hand to be silent,” so that they might see or hear the miracle in silence; or perhaps so that the shouting [Col. 1688B] of those rejoicing might not disclose his arrival in the city.

“He told them how the Lord had brought him out of prison, and said: ‘Report this to James and to the brethren’”—namely, James Alphaeus, bishop of Jerusalem, since the other James had already been beheaded by Herod. “And, going out that same night, he went to another place,” out of fear of Herod and the Jews.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the Death of Herod

On the day after Peter’s deliverance from prison, “there was no small disturbance among the soldiers and guards as to what had happened to Peter” (Acts 12). From this it appears that he had left the prison locked; otherwise there could have been no doubt that he had escaped.

“But when Herod sought for him and did not find him,” carefully questioning the guards whether they knew what [Col. 1688C] had happened to him, “he ordered them to be brought before him,” to punish them. Yet he did not punish them, through the Lord’s providence, so that Peter’s release might harm no one.

A matter being imminent, Herod went down from Judaea to Caesarea of Palestine, near Tyre and Sidon, in order to harm the Tyrians and Sidonians, with whom he was angry. Hearing this, the Tyrians and Sidonians came to Blastus, Herod’s chamberlain and keeper of his treasures. Because he was their friend and patron, they were reconciled to Herod through his mediation. For they could not endure the enmity of so nearby a king.

“On the following day Herod, clothed in royal apparel, sat upon the tribunal before them and addressed them, flattering them. But the people cried out, [Col. 1688D] ‘The voice of a god, and not of a man,’” that is, they gave him praises due to God and not to a human being.

While he was being soothed by flattering favor and did not reject the divine honors offered him, he looked above himself and saw an angel suspended and hovering over his head on a cord—that is, an owl, a messenger of his approaching death. Then, as Josephus relates, he bent toward those applauding him and said: “Behold, I, your god, am dying.” For he knew, according to what the augur had told him when he was being led to prison, that he would die within five days after the appearance of the owl.

“And immediately,” as the history states, “the angel of the Lord struck him”; that is, God’s vengeance came upon him. For for five days he was tortured by pain in his belly, and worms gnawed his entrails [Col. 1689A]; and thus, gradually “consumed by worms, he expired.”

## CHAPTER LXV. On Agrippa

He left a son called Agrippa, not surnamed Herod, who was still at Rome and did not possess his father’s whole kingdom, but only a part. He possessed the land of two and a half tribes beyond the Jordan. Hence we read that, when the destruction of Jerusalem was imminent, the believers in Judaea, at an angel’s warning, withdrew into the kingdom of this Agrippa, the son of Herod Agrippa.

## CHAPTER LXVI. The Return of the History to Its Order
Then the narrative returns to its proper order and is connected with what was said above: that a collection had been made by the faithful at Antioch and sent to the poor in Jerusalem [Col. 1689B] through Barnabas and Saul (Acts 11). For what was inserted about Herod—the death of James, the imprisonment and release of Peter—was incidental. The narrative therefore proceeds concerning the return of Barnabas from Jerusalem as follows: “The word of the Lord was growing and multiplying. And Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem, taking with them John, who was surnamed Mark” (Acts 12), after they had completed their ministry.

“Now in the Church which was at Antioch,” besides those who had come from Jerusalem, there were “prophets and teachers, among whom were Simon, who was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen, who was the foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch” (Acts 13), that is, nourished on the same milk as he. The same persons [Col. 1689C] may be understood to have been prophets and teachers. Or the distinction may be made thus: prophets concerning future matters, and teachers concerning past matters. Observe that this Simon was called Niger, “Black,” from his complexion, if it is a Latin word; or, if it is Hebrew, he was called Niger as though “ascending from strength to strength.” *Niger* is Hebrew and is interpreted “ascending.”

“While they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said to them: Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work to which I have called them.” Having heard the counsel of the Holy Spirit, they sent Saul and Barnabas to Jerusalem, to Peter, James, and John, who were there. These, rejoicing at the command of the Lord or of the Holy Spirit, “fasting and praying, laid hands upon them” [Col. 1689D], as upon men being ordained. Whether, besides the laying on of hands, they performed any other solemnity of ordination for them is uncertain. Nor do we read anything concerning the ordination of the apostles, or that the Lord laid hands upon them. Yet it is certainly held concerning Peter that he celebrated Mass at Antioch. But for the apostles it may have sufficed for ordination that the Lord said to them: “Do this in remembrance of me.” And although Barnabas and Paul had not been present, yet because they were later chosen to the apostleship by the counsel of the Holy Spirit, perhaps in this respect they were privileged along with the others, and no other solemnity of ordination was celebrated for them.

Many in the primitive Church were promoted to the priesthood without this solemnity of ordination, and many laymen were made priests without first receiving the diaconate and the preceding orders. “And having laid hands upon them, they dismissed them. And they, indeed, sent by the Holy Spirit,” with the same guide of their journey who had separated them from the others, “went down to Seleucia, and from there sailed to Cyprus. And when they came to Salamis, they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews,” because of their reverence, or their hardness; and they “had John,” surnamed Mark, with them “in the ministry” of preaching [Col. 1690A].

## CHAPTER LXVII. How Paul and Barnabas converted the proconsul Sergius

“And when they had passed through the whole island of Cyprus, as far as Paphos, they found a certain man, a magician, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus [Col. 1690B], who was with Sergius Paulus, a prudent man” (Acts 13), a man of great rank. For he was a proconsul, that is, second after a consul. “This man, having summoned Barnabas and Paul, desired to hear the word of God; but Elymas the magician resisted them.” Observe that one name is the interpretation of the other: *Elymas* means “magician”; thus the common name for workers of magic was made this man’s proper name.

“But Saul, who is also Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looking intently at him, said: O man full of every deceit and all fraud, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness, do you not cease to subvert the straight ways of the Lord?” Notice the words, “Saul, who is also Paul.” The saints relate that, after Sergius Paulus had been converted to the faith, he was called Paul. Hence this is the first mention of the name Paul. [Col. 1690C] Origen alone says that he always had two names, namely Saul and Paul. Or, when he received the apostleship, he first received this name: he who had first been called Saul after Saul the persecutor, having been made humble from proud, was called Paul instead of Saul, as though “small” and “humble.” Hence, as if interpreting his own name, he calls himself the least of the apostles.

He seems to have been promoted to the apostleship with Barnabas in the thirteenth year after the Lord’s Passion, and to have received the name Paul; and in the fourteenth he set out for his ministry among the Gentiles. This agrees sufficiently with Ecclesiastical History, where it is read that the apostles were commanded, after the Passion, to preach in Judaea for twelve years. But in the thirteenth year they began gradually to pass to the Gentiles, though not yet completely; afterwards they left the borders of Judaea entirely.

[Col. 1690D] “And now,” he says, “behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you,” that is, God’s vengeance will be exercised upon you. “For you shall be blind” in the light of your head, just as you are blind in the light of your mind, “not seeing the sun for a time,” the material sun, because through faith you do not see the Sun of righteousness. “And immediately there fell upon him a mist and darkness; and, becoming blind,” that is, turning himself about as a blind man does, “he sought someone to give him a hand,” in order to lead him. “Then the proconsul, seeing the miracle, immediately believed, marvelling at the teaching of the Lord.”

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On John’s departure from them

“But when Paul and Barnabas with him [Col. 1691A] had sailed from Paphos, they came to Perga, a city of Pamphylia; and then John, departing from them, returned to Jerusalem” (Acts 13), whence he had come with them. Perhaps the reason why he departed from them was blameworthy; and this was the cause of the dissension between Paul and Barnabas, concerning which you will hear below.

But Paul and Barnabas “came to Antioch of Pisidia,” the qualification being added to distinguish it from the other Antioch, called Antioch of Syria, which was formerly called Reblatha and which we still call Antioch. “And entering the synagogue on the Sabbath day, they sat down,” as though intending to hear the Law, not to preach. “But after the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue said to them: Brothers, if there is among you any word of exhortation, speak.”

## CHAPTER LXIX. On the preaching of Paul and Barnabas in the synagogue

[Col. 1691B]

“But Paul, rising and making a sign for silence with his hand” (Acts 13), began to deliver a great discourse, beginning from a higher point. “Men of Israel,” he said, “and you Gentiles who fear God, listen. The God of the people Israel chose our fathers and exalted the people when they were sojourners in Egypt,” serving in mud and brick, whence he brought them out with a strong hand. “And for forty years he endured their ways in the wilderness”; afterwards, bringing them into the promised land, “destroying seven nations” which inhabited the land, “he distributed their land to them by lot, after about four hundred and fifty years.”

This is to be understood thus: from Isaac’s birth until Israel’s departure from Egypt [Col. 1691C] there elapsed four hundred [and fifty] five years. Afterwards, forty years having been completed in the wilderness, they came into the land of Canaan and the land was divided. Therefore from Isaac’s birth until the division of the land there elapsed four hundred and fifty years. And after four hundred and fifty years the Lord gave judges to his people; and from then the people of God were under judges until Samuel’s time. “And thereafter they asked for a king, and he gave them Saul,” who reigned over them forty years, the years of Samuel being counted together with his. Thus it is found in the Chronicles of the Hebrews. “And when he had been removed, he raised up David as their king” (1 Samuel 16), concerning whom he bore witness, saying: “I have found a man after my own heart.” From David’s seed God would raise up Jesus, the Saviour of Israel [Col. 1691D], whose coming John heralded.

## CHAPTER LXX. Still on the same subject

“Men and brothers,” he says, “sons of the race of Abraham” (Acts 13), “and those among you from the Gentiles who fear God, to you in particular the word of this salvation has been sent. For those who dwelt in Jerusalem and their rulers, not knowing that this was Jesus, and also not knowing the voices of the prophets which are read every Sabbath,” in condemning him to death fulfilled them unknowingly. “But God raised him from the dead on the third day, and he was seen for forty days by those who came up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people. And we announce to you that promise which was made to our fathers [Col. 1692A], because God has fulfilled it to your children by raising Jesus.”

“Therefore let it be known to you, brothers, that through him remission of sins is proclaimed to you from all,” namely from all sins, “from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses. He who believes in him is justified. Take care that you are not despisers, lest there come upon you” the vengeance of God that threatens despisers in this manner: “See, you despisers, and wonder, and perish,” that is, seeing, you shall wonder and perish, “because I work a work in your days which you do not believe” (Habakkuk 1), that is, because you do not believe the work “which I shall work in your days,” namely the Incarnation.

## CHAPTER LXXI. Why they passed to the Gentiles

[Col. 1692B]

“And as they were going out, they begged that he might speak on the following Sabbath” (Acts 13), still in the synagogue. And when they left the synagogue, “many Jews and proselytes,” that is, Gentiles, or Jews coming from the Dispersion, “followed Paul and Barnabas. But on the following Sabbath almost the whole city assembled to hear the word of God. Seeing this, the Jews were filled with zeal,” namely the zeal of envy; stirred by it, they began to contradict “the things said by Paul, blaspheming.” For a blasphemer is one who, from envy, speaks against the truth.

Then Paul and Barnabas, filled with zeal for God, said boldly: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you,” according to the Lord’s words: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” [Col. 1692C] (Matthew 15:24). “But because you reject it and make yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.” Note that, although this is read as said here by Paul and Barnabas in Antioch of Pisidia, which is not in Judaea but in Greece, in many places it is read as said by the apostles in Judaea, namely when they wished to pass to the Gentiles after preaching in Judaea for twelve years. This need not trouble you, for it could have been said in both places.

“For thus God commanded us: I have placed you as a light of the Gentiles, that you may be their salvation to the uttermost part of the earth.” These are, in Isaiah, chapter 49, the words of the Father to the Son. It is as if the Father said to the Son: I sent you so that, after the darkness of unbelief, you might scatter the light of truth among the Gentiles to the ends of the earth. But although this was spoken particularly [Col. 1692D] to Christ, it is not contrary that it is here read as spoken to Paul, for the union of head and members is so great that what was said to the head the members reckon as said to themselves; just as Christ the head reckons persecution of his members as inflicted on himself, saying: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9), that is, in my members.

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the Gentiles’ reception of the preaching

“But when the Gentiles heard” mention of their salvation, “they rejoiced and glorified God. And many of them believed” (Acts 13). The Jews, however, inflamed with zeal and envious spite, “stirred up devout women and the leading men of the city, and aroused persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and expelled them from their territory.” But they, “shaking off the dust from their feet” [Col. 1693A], as the Lord had commanded, as a testimony against them, “came to Iconium.”

Entering the city, they spoke in the synagogue (Acts 14), and “a great multitude of Jews and Greeks believed. And they remained there a long time, speaking boldly,” while the Lord confirmed their preaching with miracles. Yet some Jews, persisting in unbelief, “stirred up and provoked the minds of the Gentiles to anger against” the believers. The city was divided: some favoured the Jews and others the apostles. “And when an attempt was made by Gentiles and Jews together with their rulers to mistreat the apostles and stone them,” that is, to drive them away with stones, “they fled to the cities of Lycaonia, namely Lystra and Derbe.” [Col. 1693B]

Although it is said here, “they came to Lystra,” according to the course of the narrative, in what follows, where it says, “There was a certain infirm man at Lystra,” it would more properly have been said, “at Lystrae.” But the name of the city can have several declensions, so that it may be said *Lystra, Lystrae*, or *Lystrae, Lystrarum*, or *Lystris*, indeclinably. Hence it follows: “And there was a certain man at Lystris,” which agrees with the Greek, where it is written: “Paul and Barnabas stayed at Lystris.”

This man was “infirm in his feet, lame from his mother’s womb,” and he sat because he could neither walk nor stand; “nor had he ever walked. This man heard Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing,” by revelation of the Holy Spirit, “that he had faith to be healed,” namely such faith as was sufficient for salvation [Col. 1693C]—or seeing that he believed that he would be healed—“said with a loud voice: In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, rise,” and stand “upright on your feet. And immediately he leaped up and walked.”

But when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they thought that he and his companion Barnabas were gods appearing to them in human form, “and they raised their voices, saying: Gods, made like men, have come down to us.
