And they called Barnabas Jupiter,” because he seemed to be the greater; “but Paul Mercury,” who, according to their opinion, always accompanied Jupiter, and who is said to have been eloquent and learned and to have seemed to grant eloquence to men. Hence *Mercurius* is so called by the Latins as though “running in the middle between ears and tongues”; but by the Greeks he is called *Hermes*, that is, “interpreter” [Col. 1693D].

“The priest also of Jupiter, who was in the city, wished to sacrifice to Barnabas and Jupiter, bringing bulls to be sacrificed and garlands”—either to adorn the front of the temple, according to the Gentile rite, or to place on their heads as adornment, or for some other reason or religious observance unknown to us. But when Paul and Barnabas heard that they wished to offer them divine honours, they tore their garments, as Jews always did on hearing blasphemy against God, and forbade such things to be offered to them, saying that they were mortal human beings who had come rather to call them back from idolatry; and “with difficulty they restrained the crowds from sacrificing to them.”

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On the persecution which they suffered

[Col. 1694A]

While they remained and taught at Lystra, Jews arrived from Iconium and Antioch; having stirred the crowds to persecute Paul, they stoned him and cast him out as though he were a worthless corpse (Acts 14), “thinking him to be dead.” Speaking to the Corinthians concerning this stoning, he says: “Once I was stoned” (2 Corinthians 11). Afterwards his disciples stood around him; he revived, and, without the Jews knowing, they brought him back into the city, where he recovered.

“On the next day he departed with Barnabas to Derbe,” and preached there as he had done at Lystra. Finally they returned through the same cities through which they had come, strengthening the brethren in the faith and appointing presbyters, that is bishops, in the large cities [Col. 1694B], because at that time bishops and presbyters were designated by the same name. They therefore appointed bishops in their place because they were about to depart and were uncertain whether they would ever return to them. As they returned through Lystra and Iconium, they came to Antioch of Pisidia. “And passing through Pisidia, they came into Pamphylia,” the region in which is the city of Perga, where they spoke the word of God; they went down to the city of Attalia [Col. 1694D], “and from there sailed to Antioch,” whence they had first set out, having been separated by the Holy Spirit for preaching the Gospel.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On the decision of the question of circumcision

When they came to Antioch and had gathered the faithful of Antioch [Col. 1694C], they reported to them how great things God had done through them among the Gentiles; and they remained there no small time with the disciples (Acts 14). While they were staying there, certain Christians came down from Judaea, yet still Judaizing, and they belonged to the sect of the Pharisees. “Therefore there arose no small dissension between them and Paul and Barnabas,” because they preached that faith without the observances of the Law was not sufficient for salvation. Many agreed with them, being steeped in old custom.

They determined that, in order to settle this dispute, they should go up to Jerusalem to the chief apostles, namely Peter and James, bishop of Jerusalem. Paul went up with Barnabas, taking Titus also, as he himself relates in the Epistle to the Galatians (chapter 5). Those who had come down from Judaea went up against them, namely “certain persons from the heresy of the Pharisees” who had been converted to the faith. When they came to Jerusalem and were in the presence of the apostles Peter and James and of the elders, they rose up against Paul and Barnabas, saying: “It is necessary for believers to be circumcised and to keep the law of Moses.”

Having heard the opinion of each party, “the apostles and elders came together to decide concerning this.” After much discussion and inquiry among the apostles and elders, Peter rose and reasonably showed that the yoke of the Law should not be imposed upon believers, because he himself, by God’s counsel, had baptized Cornelius and preached the word of the Gospel to the Gentiles; and God had confirmed his preaching [Col. 1695A], cleansing their hearts by faith and sending the Holy Spirit upon them before they were visibly baptized, without commanding them to observe the legal ordinances. “Why then,” he says, “do you now test God by placing a yoke upon the necks of the disciples which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?”

Then Paul and Barnabas began to relate “how many signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them,” and the multitude was silent, listening to them.

## CHAPTER LXXV. On the address of James, the Lord’s brother

When silence had been made, James spoke, adhering to Peter’s statement: “Men and brothers, listen to me. Simon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, calling them to the faith and to the testimonies of the prophets” (Acts 15). Having introduced testimonies from various prophets [Col. 1695B], he pronounced a definitive decision by pontifical authority, saying: “Therefore I judge that those who are converted to God from among the Gentiles should not be troubled; but I advise that we direct a letter to them, that they abstain from idolatry, fornication, things strangled, and blood.”

For idolatry had especially flourished among the Gentiles; fornication was regarded among them as something almost natural and involving no guilt. Therefore the apostles specifically decreed that these things should be forbidden to Gentiles. They were also inclined to shed blood. They were accustomed also to drink blood sacrificed to their gods. Therefore they were specifically forbidden to shed and to drink blood. But why they literally prohibited a strangled animal to them is not sufficiently clear. [Col. 1695C]

This counsel of James pleased the apostles and elders. By common agreement they chose men through whom they might send the letter with Paul and Barnabas, namely Judas and Silas; and the salutation was prefixed in this manner.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On the letter sent to converts from the Gent-[lacuna]

“The apostles and elders, brothers, to the brothers converted from the Gentiles: greeting” (Acts 15). After the salutation, the text of the letter was as follows: “We have heard that certain persons who came down from Judaea have troubled you, overturning your souls, wishing to impose upon your necks the yoke of the Law. Therefore, by common consent, we have decided to choose men and send them to [Col. 1695D] you with our most beloved men Paul and Barnabas. For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose upon you no further burden than that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication. If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well. Farewell.”

## CHAPTER LXXVII. How they consoled those converted from the Gentiles

Therefore Paul and Barnabas went down to Antioch (Acts 15), and those two men were sent with them. When they had come down, they gathered the multitude and delivered the letter to them. Having heard the consolation that the yoke of the Law was not being imposed upon them, the Gentile brethren rejoiced. Judas and Silas, being prophets, consoled them and greatly strengthened them [Col. 1696A] in the faith.

This should not be passed over: concerning his aforesaid ascent to Jerusalem to settle the dispute just mentioned, the Apostle writes to the Galatians as follows: “Then, after fourteen years from my conversion, I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also, and I conferred with them concerning the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles” (Galatians 2). From this number of years it is inferred that, in the same year in which Paul went up to Jerusalem—namely, the fourteenth after his conversion—Peter went up to Rome and in the same year sat in the episcopal chair, in which he sat twenty-five years. Fourteen and twenty-five make thirty-nine. But in the twenty-fifth year after the promotion of blessed Peter to the Roman see, namely the last year of Nero, Peter and Paul suffered; and [Col. 1696B] thus it was the thirty-ninth year after Paul’s conversion.

Hence it is inferred that Paul was converted to the faith in the same year in which the Lord suffered, since it is established that Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom in the thirty-eighth year after the Lord’s Passion, which was Nero’s last year. But if it is sometimes read that Paul was converted to the faith in the second year after the Lord’s Passion, this must be understood as the second year then beginning, but not yet completed in the ordinary reckoning, as has been determined elsewhere. Therefore in the fourteenth year after the Lord’s Passion, namely the fourth year of Claudius, Peter went up to Rome and sat in the episcopal chair for ten years under Claudius, who reigned fourteen years, and Nero after him for the same number of years.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. He determines when blessed Peter sat at Antioch and when at Rome

[Col. 1696C]

It may be asked at what time Peter sat in the see of Antioch. For it is certain that he sat at Antioch in the episcopal see for seven years; this must necessarily be understood as seven of the fourteen years which elapsed from the Lord’s Passion until his promotion to the Roman see. After the seven years in which he sat in the see of Antioch, by the Lord’s counsel he went from Jerusalem to Rome; but on his journey he passed through Antioch in order to strengthen his subjects in the faith. And, as is found in the Chronicles, he appointed Eudochius in the see of Antioch.

During this passage through Antioch he was rebuked by Paul because, while eating with certain brethren from Judaea and fearing to offend them, he distinguished [Col. 1696D] foods and thus compelled the Gentiles to Judaize. Hence Paul says: “When Cephas came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face” (Galatians 2).

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On the cause of the dissension between Paul and Barnabas

In the year in which Peter went up from Antioch to Rome, while Paul and Barnabas remained at Antioch, there was a certain procurator in Judaea who by force wished to usurp for himself the authority to appoint the high priest and to change him at his pleasure, so that he might appoint one or two high priests in the same year. When the Jews saw that they could not resist him, they asked him for permission to consult Claudius, emperor of the Romans, so that by his will he might obtain this power, or else desist [Col. 1697A]; and he granted it.

When they had sent messengers to Rome, Agrippa was there, the son of Herod Agrippa, whom his father, when dying, had left in the hands of Claudius. Claudius delayed sending him to Judaea as ruler, both because of the Jews’ savagery and because of his youth. Hearing that his people’s cause was being conducted, Agrippa intervened for them and obtained their request. Claudius wrote back to the procurator that he should desist from such extortion, and he desisted. He also wrote back to the Jews that they should give thanks to Agrippa, through whose intercession they had obtained this; and the Jews informed him that he should send Agrippa to them and make him, as it were, king and lord, though he still delayed.

Later, when it seemed fitting to him [Col. 1697B], he sent Agrippa to Judaea; yet he did not restore to him the whole of his father’s territory—for his father had held the whole kingdom in its entirety—but gave him the region of Galaaditis, namely beyond the Jordan, the land of two tribes and half a tribe. He also gave him the authority to appoint the high priest in Jerusalem at his pleasure, an authority which he had denied to the procurator. This was Agrippa, into whose kingdom the faithful departed from Judaea when Jerusalem’s destruction was imminent, having been forewarned by an angel, as you have above on Matthew.

But let us now continue concerning Paul and Barnabas, who were still remaining in Antioch, preaching the word of God; Judas had gone away, while Silas remained with them (Acts 15). After some days it seemed expedient to them to return through the cities in which they had preached the word of God, to visit the brethren and [Col. 1697C] strengthen them in the faith. “But Barnabas wished to have in his company John, who was surnamed Mark.” Paul, however, did not wish this, saying that he ought not to be taken because, stationed in the front line of battle, he had stood too fearfully, and because through fear of death he had abandoned preaching when, that is, departing from Pamphylia, he returned to Jerusalem. Therefore he ought not to be taken for preaching, lest he harm others by a bad example.

“And there arose a dissension, so that they departed from one another.” The saints excuse them, because they did not depart from one another moved by hatred, but were stirred to this by the Holy Spirit, so that, divided, they might preach in more places and gain more people. “But Barnabas, having taken Mark, sailed to Cyprus.” From his unwillingness [Col. 1697D] to leave Mark, it is inferred that Mark was his kinsman. They are read to have been cousins. “But Paul departed, taking Silas,” whom the Lord had caused to remain for this purpose, that he might cooperate with him, and “he travelled through Syria and Cilicia.”

“Afterwards he came to Derbe and Lystra” (Acts 16), “where there was a certain Christian named Timothy, son of a widowed woman, or of a Jewish woman, born of a Gentile father; all the faithful who were at Lystra bore witness to his religious character.” Paul made him their bishop, but circumcised him in order to remove scandal among the Jews, lest they be scandalized by having an uncircumcised bishop—not because legal observances were necessary after the truth of the Gospel, but because they were to be taken away from the Jews gradually, not suddenly, and the mother was, as it were, to be buried with honour [Col. 1698A]. Afterwards Paul took Timothy with him, and “passing through the cities, he commanded the decrees of the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem to be observed; and the Churches were strengthened and multiplied.”

## CHAPTER LXXX. That the apostles were forbidden to go where they wished

“But passing through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, wishing to go into Asia Minor, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit” (Acts 16), who knew human hearts, because at that time they would not have believed. Therefore the Holy Spirit did not wish holy things to be given to dogs, nor the impious to be condemned more severely for despising the preaching. He also wished these provinces to be reserved for other apostles. For Philip and John preached in Asia [Col. 1698B] Minor; Luke in Bithynia, from which likewise they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit. Thus two reasons are given why they were forbidden those provinces: either lest holy things be given to dogs, or because the Holy Spirit had assigned them to other apostles—Asia Minor to John, Bithynia to Luke.

Origen, where he treats of first-fruits and tithes to be given to priests, gives a third reason. He says that God, providing bodily sustenance for his servants, forbade the disciples to enter such provinces because of famine: namely, that very great famine during which Helena supported the poor brethren who were in Jerusalem, which occurred in the fourth year of Claudius. This Helena was not Constantine’s mother [*sic*], but queen of the Abigeni. The king of the Abigeni [Col. 1698C] was captivated by love for her, took her as his wife, and she conceived by him. When he slept with her one night and placed his hand upon the womb of the pregnant woman, a voice was heard by him saying: “Take care not to harm the child, for he will be great in the world.” Astonished by such a voice, he told this to his wife.

Afterwards they reared the child born to them with the utmost care. When his father died, the child became king and is commended in many respects. The cause of this commendation was that, hearing that one God was worshipped by the Jews, he worshipped that same God and accepted circumcision and Jewish rites. His mother Helena, coming to Jerusalem, found the faithful there suffering from hunger, because it was a time of famine; and, having brought an abundance of silver to buy with, she purchased grain from every quarter [Col. 1698D] and supported the brethren who were in Jerusalem.

While she was still in Judaea, word was brought to her that her son had died. Immediately she returned, had his corpse taken from the grave, and brought it back to Judaea. Not far from Jerusalem she caused two mausoleums to be built; in one she placed her son’s body, and she commanded that, when she died, her own body should be placed in the other. Thus it was done; traces of the mausoleums are still visible, and many are deceived into thinking that it is the mausoleum of Helena, Constantine’s mother.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the vision that appeared to Paul by night

“When Paul and his companions had passed through Mysia, they came to Troas; and a vision was shown to Paul by night” (Acts 16). “A Macedonian man appeared [Col. 1699A] to him,” that is, an angel of that people, made like a Macedonian man in the character of his language or in a particular appearance, “standing and beseeching him and saying: Cross over into Macedonia and help us.” From these words he appears to have been a man, not an angel; for angels do not need help except God’s. But the angel spoke this while assuming the person of the Macedonians.

“When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to depart for Macedonia, being assured that God had called us to preach the Gospel to them.” Observe the phrase, “we sought.” Here Luke first shows that he was Paul’s companion; perhaps he first attached himself to him at this point. Thus nowhere earlier does he say “we came”; everywhere he says “they came,” and the like. But here for the first time he joins himself to Paul’s companions. Observe also that where it says, “there was a Macedonian man standing,” [Col. 1699B] the gloss on the word “standing” is brief: angels are always said to stand. Many following this gloss emend the Easter antiphon, “The angel sat,” to “The angel stood”; but they are mistaken. It must always be understood in this book that angels are read in the Gospel to have sat at the tomb.

“Sailing from Troas, we came with a straight course to Samothrace, and on the following day to Philippi, which is the first city of Macedonia,” that is, the first encountered by those arriving from the sea, “and it was a colony.” That city is called a colony which is filled with settlers by us because of a lack of native inhabitants. Hence *colonia* is so called, as it were, from new cultivators. “And we stayed there for some days; and on the Sabbath days we went out beyond the gate beside a river, where there seemed to be a place suitable for prayer,” that is, for speech or supplication [Col. 1699C]. For *orare*, “to pray,” is also understood as “to plead” and as “to make supplication.”

## CHAPTER LXXXII. That they were received by a woman dealing in purple

“And sitting down, we spoke to the women who had assembled” (Acts 16). “And a certain woman named Lydia, a dealer in purple from the city of the Thyatirans, heard us speaking.” She may be understood as a dealer in purple in the sense of one who wore purple, perhaps because she was of royal descent. Or, more probably, as a worker in purple cloth or as one who sold purple cloth. “When she had been baptized, with all her household, she begged us, saying: If you judge me faithful, enter my house and stay with me. And we entered, compelled.” For they still shrank from entering Gentile houses [Col. 1699D] in order to avoid giving offence to the Jews.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. On the pythonic spirit cast out of the girl
“Now it happened, as we were going out to prayer, that a certain girl having a pythonic spirit met us” (Acts 16). This may be understood either as a pythoness, or as one operating through a pythonic spirit by magical art, or as one afflicted by a pythonic spirit. For in Sacred Scripture this name is used in these two senses: either a *pythoness* is a woman who, through a pythonic spirit, performs the raising of the dead by magical art—as did she who, at Saul’s request, summoned from the lower world the soul of Samuel, or rather an unclean spirit in his place. [Col. 1700A] This kind of magical art was invented by Apollo Python and is named from his surname. A pythoness, then, is said to be one possessed by a pythonic spirit and using it as her instrument for divination; and this seems the more likely sense here. She was profitable to her masters, because they received much gain from her divination.

“This girl, following Paul and his companions, cried out, saying: ‘These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us the way of salvation.’” And she cried thus for many days, perhaps through a natural good disposition, or rather because the Holy Spirit constrained the pythonic spirit so that it might speak truth through her. “But Paul, turning around while she was crying behind him, said to the” unclean “spirit: ‘I command you in the name of Jesus Christ: come out of her.’ And it came out of [Col. 1700B] her,” because it was unworthy that the lying spirit should announce the word of the Gospel through her.

“But when her masters saw this, knowing that they would thereby suffer a very great loss, they seized Silas and Paul, led them to the forum before the rulers, and, bringing them before the magistrates, said: ‘These men, being Jews, are disturbing our city and preaching some new religion which it is not lawful for us to accept, since we are Romans.’” For it had already been decreed by the Romans that no new god should be worshipped unless the senate approved. “And the crowd rushed against them, and the magistrates, having torn their tunics, ordered them to be beaten with rods [Note: [Col. 1699D] On this, see 2 Corinthians 11.], and, after they had been scourged, sent them to prison, commanding the jailer to guard them carefully. Having received the command, he put [Col. 1700C] them into the inner prison, fastening their feet in the stocks.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. On the earthquake by which the prison doors were opened.

“But at midnight Paul and Silas were singing hymns and, praying, praising God” (Acts 16). And while they were praying at midnight, “suddenly there was an earthquake”—that is, by that earthquake all the foundations of the prison were shaken, the doors opened, and the bonds “of all” who were in prison “were broken”: not only those of Paul and Silas, but of the others also.

“But the jailer awoke, and, seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, thinking that all the prisoners had escaped.” Although Paul was in the midst of the dark [Col. 1700D] prison, he saw this in the spirit and cried out: “Do yourself no harm. For all whom you were guarding are here.” He knew that the jailer then wished to lay hands upon himself because he thought all had escaped. “And, having asked the attendants for a light, the jailer entered; and, trembling”—both because of what had happened in the earthquake and because he understood that Paul knew he intended to kill himself—“he fell at the feet of Paul and Silas. Leading them out of the prison, he said: ‘What must I do, sirs, to be saved?’ They answered him: ‘Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you and your whole household shall be saved.’ And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house [Col. 1701A]; and, taking them in that hour, he washed their wounds and was baptized.” Thus he washed, and was washed.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. How they were released by the magistrates.

“And when he had brought them into his house” (Acts 16), “he set a table before them, and rejoiced with his whole household, having believed in God. And when day came, the magistrates sent officers to the jailer, saying: ‘Release those men.’” Treating them as contemptible persons, they released them, however, lest more people should believe, since the miracle had already become known to them.

“And the jailer reported these words to Paul: ‘The magistrates have sent orders that you be released. Now therefore go out in peace.’ Paul replied: ‘They sent us, Roman men, into prison after scourging us, though uncondemned’”—that is, persons registered under Roman [Col. 1701B] rule by professing subjection and endowed with Roman freedom—“‘and now they cast us out secretly [Note: [Col. 1701C] Addition 1. So that, just as the laying of hands upon them was public, so their expulsion might also be public.]. Not so: let them come themselves and put us out.’” When this was reported “to the magistrates, they were afraid upon hearing that they were Romans. They came and brought them out, and begged them to leave the city. Going out, they passed through Lydia; and after seeing the brethren, they comforted them. And” from there “they departed and came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews” (Acts 17).

Paul, as was his custom, entered the synagogue and for three Sabbaths reasoned with them from the Scriptures, preaching Christ as having died and risen again. Some of them believed and joined Paul and Silas; also not a few women, and a great multitude from among proselytes and Gentiles. But the Jews, moved by jealousy and [Col. 1701C] taking some wicked men from the rabble, stirred up the city against them.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. That Jason was accused through the envy of the Jews.

“And coming to Jason’s house”—where they had been lodging—(Acts 17), “they sought to bring them out before the people.” Not finding them, and thinking that Jason had concealed them, “they dragged Jason and some brethren before the city rulers, saying: ‘These are the men who stir up the city; Jason has received them, and those who receive them act against Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king besides Caesar.’” And [Col. 1701D] they stirred up the rulers against them. “After receiving satisfaction from Jason and the others, they released them.”

Perhaps Jason and the other brethren denied that they had received them; or, if they admitted it, they made satisfaction. “By night they sent Paul and Silas away to Beroea. They entered the synagogue of the Jews and preached there; and many Beroeans believed, including not a few honorable women.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. What Paul did at Athens.

“The Jews who were at Thessalonica heard that the word of God was being preached by Paul in Beroea; they came there also, stirring up the multitude. And immediately the brethren sent Paul away, that he might go as far as the sea [Col. 1702A]” (Acts 17), because the Jews persecuted him more fiercely, since he was the leader in preaching the word. “But Silas and Timothy remained there. Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens.” Seeing the city devoted to idolatry, he quickly sent word to Timothy and Silas to come to him, and they came.

The Epicureans, who placed human happiness in bodily pleasure alone, and the Stoics, who placed it in virtue of mind alone, disputed with Paul. Though they disagreed among themselves, they unanimously agreed in attacking the Apostle, saying: “What does this word-sower want to say?” Paul truly was a sower of words, but a reaper of morals, expecting an abundant fruit from such a harvest. Others said: “He seems to be a proclaimer [Col. 1702B] of new demons.” “And they seized him and brought him to the Areopagus,” that is, to the district of Mars, in which there was a temple of Mars. For the Athenians named individual districts after the gods whom they worshipped: the district in which Mars was worshipped they called Areopagus, because *Arioth* means Mars. The district in which they worshipped Pan they called Panapagum; and thus they named the individual districts after the individual gods. The Areopagus was, however, a more eminent district, because the council chamber of the magistrates and the schools of liberal arts were there.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On the altar of the Unknown God.

When Paul stood before the philosophers, they said: “You bring certain new things to our ears. Can we know what this new teaching is?” (Acts [Col. 1702C] 17). As though they said: Can you give a reason for what you are saying?

“Therefore Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: ‘Men of Athens, in every respect I judge you to be superstitious. For as I was passing by, I saw your images; and among them I found an altar with this inscription: To an Unknown God,’” or “Of an Unknown God.” That is to say: This altar is dedicated to an Unknown God. For each altar bore an inscription indicating to whom it was dedicated. “‘This Unknown God,’ he says, ‘to whom you have consecrated this altar, I proclaim to you. He is the God who made the world and all things in it, in whom we live and move and are.’”

How this altar was consecrated to that Unknown God is not related by the history of the Acts of the Apostles; therefore it belongs to us to supply this, namely, to say it.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. That the Athenian philosophers said that the God of nature was suffering.

[Col. 1702D]

[Note: [Col. 1701D] This is an excursus drawn from historical accounts.] For on the day of the Lord’s Passion, the philosophers who were at Athens, seeing darkness come over the whole surface of the earth, could not discover its cause among natural causes. At last they were led to say that the God of nature was suffering. The Athenians said: “Let us set up an altar to that God.” The altar was dedicated, and the inscription was placed upon it: “To an Unknown God.”

When they wished to offer burnt offerings and sacrifices to that Unknown God, the philosophers said: “He has no need of our goods; rather, make genuflections before his altar and offer supplication to him [Col. 1703A], because he seeks not an offering of cattle but the devotion of souls.” Paul proclaimed to them this Unknown God, affirming that he had died, risen, and ascended into heaven, and would judge the world at its end (Acts 17).

“When he preached the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others,” neither rejecting nor accepting, said: “We shall hear you about this again.” Paul departed from their midst; and some, attaching themselves to him, believed. Among them was Dionysius the Areopagite, whom the Apostle later ordained bishop of Corinth. Since the history of the Acts of the Apostles omits the manner of his conversion, it belongs to us to supply it.

## CHAPTER XC. On Dionysius the Areopagite.

[Note: [Col. 1703] An excursus taken from the history of Saint Dionysius.] This Dionysius was a teacher in the Areopagus, and although he readily believed at Paul’s exhortation, nevertheless he did not confess that he believed until after a long disputation with Paul. But after much debate, while he was still disputing with Paul, perhaps a blind man passed before them on the road. Dionysius immediately said to Paul: “If you say to this blind man, ‘See, in the name of your God,’ and he sees, I shall believe at once. But lest you use magical words, because perhaps you know words having such efficacy, I shall prescribe to you the form of words. You shall say to him,” he said, “in this form: ‘In the name of Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin, crucified, dead, who rose and ascended into heaven—see!’”

And that every suspicion might be removed, Paul instructed Dionysius himself to utter the same words. [Col. 1703C] Dionysius spoke to the blind man in that form of words, commanding him to see; immediately he saw, and Dionysius confessed that he believed.

When Paul preached at Athens and had converted many, he came to Corinth. There he found “a certain Jew named Aquila with his wife Priscilla” (Acts 18), whom the Apostle often mentions when he greets his friends. They “had recently come from Italy, all Jews having been compelled by an edict of the Emperor Claudius to leave his kingdom,” because, through the excessive familiarity she had with them, they had so drawn his wife Agrippina toward their rites that she was already Judaizing.

“Paul lodged with Aquila and Priscilla because they practiced the same trade” that he himself was accustomed to practice, obtaining his livelihood [Col. 1703D] by the labor of his own hands, “namely, the trade of tent-making.” For they made tents or pavilions, necessary both for inhabitants of the land on account of excessive heat and for travelers. The word *scenofactoria*, “tent-making,” may be said to derive from *scenos*, interpreted as “shade,” or, according to others, from *scenos*, interpreted as “rope.” For they were rope-makers.

“When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia,” where he had left them, “Paul preached the word of the Gospel earnestly,” with their assistance. When the Jews held his preaching in contempt, he shook the dust from his feet in testimony against them, as the Lord had commanded, saying: “I am clean from your blood,” because, so far as lay in me, I wished [Col. 1704A] to call you back from your impiety. But because you are stubborn, “I turn to the Gentiles. Departing from there, he went to the house of a certain Gentile named Titus, whose house adjoined the synagogue.”

This must not be understood of Titus to whom the Apostle wrote epistles, who was his disciple and whom he also ordained bishop of Crete. “And Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, was converted with his entire household”—that Crispus, namely, of whom the Apostle says in writing to the Corinthians: “I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius” (1 Corinthians 1). “And many Corinthians, hearing of his conversion, believed and were baptized. The Lord appeared to Paul in a vision, saying: ‘Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent; for I am with you, and no one shall lay a hand [Col. 1704B] upon you to harm you.’ And he remained there for a year and six months.”

## CHAPTER XCI. That the Jews stirred up Gallio against Paul.

“The Jews therefore rose up unanimously against Paul and dragged him” before Gallio, who was procurator of Achaia and of the region in which Corinth was located (Acts 18). They accused him of preaching contrary to the law. Gallio said to them: “If you charged this man with some manifest crime, I would judge him; but since this is a dispute about your law, I do not care to judge it.”

Seeing that the procurator did not favor the Jewish party, the Gentiles “seized Sosthenes, ruler of the synagogue, before him and beat him; and none of these things [Col. 1704C] concerned the procurator.” Paul, after remaining still for many days, was at Cenchreae, the port of Corinth. About to embark and sail to Syria, he cut his hair, which he had allowed to grow because he had been a Nazirite by vow. Nazirites for a time let their hair grow by vow; when the term of the vow was completed, they shaved it and put it into the sacrificial fire.

Some manuscripts read “they cut their hair.” Hence some refer this to Aquila and Priscilla. But Augustine and Jerome refer it to Paul.

## CHAPTER XCII. That Paul disputed against the Jews at Ephesus.

Paul came to Syria, bringing Aquila and Priscilla with him (Acts 18). “When he came [Col. 1704D] to Ephesus, he entered the synagogue and disputed with the Jews. Though they asked him to remain longer with them, he did not consent; but, taking leave of the brethren, he departed from Ephesus,” leaving Aquila and Priscilla there. He himself traveled through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening the brethren.

While Aquila and Priscilla were at Ephesus, a certain Jew named Apollos came to Ephesus, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man and skilled in the Scriptures. He had been baptized with John’s baptism and already believed that Christ was the Messiah promised in the Law. He held right views about the Father and the Son, but had as yet heard nothing concerning the Holy Spirit. Seeing him preach boldly, [Col. 1705A] Aquila and Priscilla took him aside and explained to him more carefully the one God. Whether they baptized him with Christ’s baptism is not recorded.

When Apollos wished to return to Corinth, Aquila, Priscilla, and the other faithful at Ephesus wrote to the faithful at Corinth to receive him and not to reject him as a Jew. When he came to Corinth, he greatly aided the brethren there. For he vigorously refuted the Jews, and the brethren were greatly strengthened thereby.

## CHAPTER XCIII. How those who had received John’s baptism were baptized.

“Now it happened” (Acts 19), “when Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul, having traveled through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples [Col. 1705B] baptized by John but not yet confirmed, because after baptism they had not received the laying on of hands. He asked them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’”—that is, the laying on of hands through which the Holy Spirit is given. They replied: “But we have not even heard mention of the Holy Spirit.” He said to them: “John’s baptism is not sufficient.” They were immediately baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. When he had laid hands upon them after baptism, they received the Holy Spirit and spoke in various tongues. Some of them prophesied, declaring future things.

They were nearly twelve in all—perhaps eleven or ten; “nearly” is added as a qualification. The Apostle Paul preached there boldly for three months, disputing [Col. 1705C] and persuading concerning the kingdom of God. He who had previously been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to preach in Asia Minor was now, by inspiration of the same Holy Spirit, preaching at Ephesus. From this it is evident that the judgments of God are wonderful.

When he preached at Ephesus, some hardened and stubbornly unbelieving people spoke evil of his teaching before the multitude. Departing from them, he separated the disciples with himself, disputing in the school of a certain Tyrannus—that is, a nobleman; or perhaps it is the proper name of the man from whom he rented the house in which he taught his disciples, acting as a schoolmaster. He did this for two years. In the same two-year period he wrote the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

God worked great and many miracles through his hands, so that sick persons were healed when *semicinctia* were laid upon them [Col. 1705D]. *Semicinctia* are garments hanging from one side only, or certain belts, or a kind of cloth used by the Hebrews to wipe away the sweat of laborers.

## CHAPTER XCIV. On the power of the name of Jesus.

Certain exorcists, seeing that Paul cast out demons at the invocation of Jesus’ name (Acts 19), devised the use of the same verbal formula for casting out demons. For although they cast out demons through Solomon’s exorcisms, as Josephus relates, they did not do so without much labor and without employing certain herbs and gems. Therefore, to cast out demons more easily, they adjured them [Col. 1706A] in this manner: “I adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.” Thus demons came out from those possessed.

There were seven sons of Sceva, a chief priest, who especially adjured demons in this manner. One day, while they were adjuring a demon to come out of a possessed body, the demon answered: “Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?” Then it leapt upon them and beat them. The report spread throughout the whole region, and fear was instilled into all the exorcists—indeed, all the more so that they might not dare henceforth to adjure demons in this way.

All the magicians who ruled demons by magical art gathered together and burned their books before Paul’s feet. Afterwards Paul resolved to go to Jerusalem and thence to Rome. He sent Timothy [Col. 1706B] and Erastus beforehand to Macedonia to prepare the collections which he was to carry to Jerusalem for the needs of the poor who were in Jerusalem. He himself remained for a time in Asia Minor.

## CHAPTER XCV. On the disturbance stirred up by Demetrius.

At that time there arose a great disturbance at Ephesus (Acts 19). Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines and images of Diana, summoned the craftsmen of the same trade and addressed them thus: “You know that we acquire much profit from this craft. But Paul preaches that things made by hands are not gods. Therefore, if his teaching prevails, we shall no longer make any profit; moreover, the temple of great Diana will be accounted as nothing, and her majesty, which the whole world worships, will be destroyed.”

Immediately filled with anger, they cried out unanimously, running through the city: “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!” Seizing Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul’s companions, they dragged them into the theatre—that is, the public spectacle-place in which offenders were punished. When Paul heard this and wished to enter the theatre, not fearing to expose himself to death, some friends dissuaded him because of the assembled people.

After the disturbance had ceased (Acts 20), Paul summoned the disciples, exhorted them, bade them farewell, and departed for Macedonia, and thence for Athens. After he had remained there three months, the Jews laid snares for him as he was about to sail for Syria, knowing that he was carrying collections. Formerly, when he had been [Col. 1706D] an empty-handed traveler, they had not laid snares for him. He therefore decided to return through Macedonia in order to avoid the ambush.

Some of his companions went by a direct route. “Going ahead, Luke says, they awaited us at Troas, while we came around by a circuitous route. But after the days of unleavened bread, we sailed from Philippi, the first city of Macedonia, and in five days came to Troas, where we remained seven days. On the first day of the week, while we were staying over, Paul discoursed with them, intending to depart the next day; and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were assembled.”

## CHAPTER XCVI. On the dead man raised by Paul.

As a certain young man sat upon a window [Col. 1707A] (Acts 20), overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third storey. Lifted from the ground, he was brought to Paul dead; his name was Eutychus. Paul went down to him, lay upon him, embraced him, and said: “Do not be troubled, for his soul is still in him.” He said this in order to remove their despair. The Lord used a similar expression when he said: “The girl is not dead, but sleeping” (Matthew 9).

The young man was raised, ate food, and was strengthened. Thus, amid the words of preaching, an occasion for healing occurred, so that Paul’s teaching might be confirmed by the display of a miracle, and that the memory of the teacher who was about to depart from them might be impressed more firmly upon their minds.

“But we, Luke says, having boarded ship, sailed to Assos, intending to await Paul there; for he himself had arranged to travel overland in the meantime. When he came back to us, we took him aboard and came to Miletus. Paul had intended to sail past Ephesus without delaying there, for he was hurrying, if possible, to be at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.

But from Miletus he did not sail onward; rather, he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Church. They came to Miletus, and he exhorted them, saying that he was going up to Jerusalem. ‘Behold,’ he said, ‘bound in the Spirit’”—that is, constrained to this by the Holy Spirit—“‘I go to Jerusalem, not knowing what shall happen to me there,’ though the Holy Spirit testifies to me through others that chains and tribulations await me there. For the Holy Spirit had revealed [Col. 1707C] concerning him to others, though not to him. ‘But I fear none of these things, nor do I make my soul’”—that is, temporal life—“‘more precious than myself’”—that is, than my soul—“‘provided that I may finish my course and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the Gospel of God’s grace. And now, behold, I know that you shall see my face no more.’”

After much exhortation, he knelt down with them all and prayed. Falling upon Paul’s neck, weeping, they kissed him, grieving most of all because he had said that they would see his face no longer. They accompanied him as far as the ship.

Having been torn away from them and passing through many cities and regions, “we came [Col. 1707D] to Tyre” (Acts 21), where we remained seven days. There we found certain disciples who, through the prophetic spirit, told Paul what would happen to him at Jerusalem and urged him not to go up. Afterwards we departed, all of them with their wives and children accompanying us outside the city. Having taken leave of them, we boarded the ship; they returned to their homes. We came to Ptolemais, greeted the brethren, and stayed with them one day.

## CHAPTER XCVII. On Agabus’ prediction to Paul.

The next day we came to Caesarea (Acts 21) and entered the house of Philip the deacon. He had four virgin daughters, prophetesses, who foretold to Paul what would happen to him at Jerusalem. After we had stayed there some days, a prophet from Judea named Agabus came [Col. 1708A] down. Coming to us, he took Paul’s belt, bound his own hands and feet with it, and said: “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘The Jews at Jerusalem shall bind in this manner the man to whom this belt belongs, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’”

On hearing this, both we and those of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem. He replied: “Why do you weep and afflict my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.” Since we could not dissuade him, we ceased, saying: “Lord, let your will be done.”

Afterward, having made ready, we went up to Jerusalem, and some of the disciples who were with us in Caesarea brought Jason, our host. When we came to Jerusalem, [Col. 1708B] the brethren gladly received us. The next day Paul went in with us to James, bishop of Jerusalem. Bede says on this passage that James governed the Church of the Jerusalemites for thirty years, namely until Nero’s seventh year, and that, according to Josephus, he was struck in the head with a fuller’s club. Bede says that he was thrown down from the Temple. Elsewhere it is read that he was stoned. Both may have occurred: after they threw him down, they stoned him as though he were a worthless corpse.

But since Bede says that Bishop James died in Nero’s seventh year, it is plainly unauthentic what is read in the epistle of Clement. According to the tenor of that epistle, Clement says that he was commanded by Peter, whom he succeeded in the apostleship, to send letters after Peter’s death to Bishop James, so that he might be instructed by him. But James the bishop died in Nero’s seventh year, while Peter lived until the fourteenth; therefore it is clear that this account is worthless.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. On his making an offering, by advice, according to the Law.

When Paul entered to James, the elders assembled (Acts 21). After greeting them, he related in detail what great things God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. Hearing this, they magnified God and said to Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed. Yet all are still zealous for the Law,” wishing, together with the faith they had received, to observe the legal rites; and [Col. 1708D] they have heard concerning you that you preach the abolition of the Law. You have become odious, as though a destroyer of Moses’ Law. The multitude will therefore assemble when they hear that you have come. We advise you, then, to purify yourself according to the Law along with four men who have a vow upon them, so that the false report which has spread about you may appear false.

With his consent, it was decreed that Jewish converts to the faith should not be forbidden to observe the legal rites, provided only that they did not place their hope in them.

Distinguish four synods held at Jerusalem in the primitive Church. The first concerned the appointment of Matthias in Judas’s place. The second concerned the election of the seven deacons. The third concerned legal observances, when it was decreed that no burden should be imposed upon Gentiles converted to the faith, at the time when Paul and Barnabas went up from Antioch [Col. 1709A] to Jerusalem. The fourth is that which is discussed here, when it was decreed that Jews should not be prohibited from legal observances, provided they did not place their hope in them.

## CHAPTER XCIX. That Paul was bound by the governor at the outcry of the Jews.

The next day Paul, purified with the four men, entered the Temple with them and offered his offering, as did the others (Acts 21). When the seven days were completed, Jews who had come from Asia, persecuting Paul, saw him in the Temple. Having seen Trophimus the Ephesian walking through the city with him, they thought that he had brought him—a Gentile—into the Temple. They stirred up the whole people against him and laid hands on him, crying: “Men of Israel, [Col. 1709B] help! This is the man who everywhere teaches against the people, the Law, and this place; moreover, he has brought Gentiles into the Temple and defiled the holy place.”

The whole city was stirred, and a disturbance of the people occurred. Seizing Paul, they dragged him out of the Temple and closed the doors, lest he flee into the Temple. While they were seeking to kill him, word was brought to the tribune of the cohort, namely Claudius Lysias, who had been sent by the governor Felix. Taking soldiers and centurions, he ran to them; when they saw him, they stopped beating Paul. He seized Paul and ordered him bound with two chains, until he should learn the cause of his arrest. Since he could not hear because of the tumult, he ordered him to be taken into the barracks, namely the royal tower.

When Paul came to the steps—perhaps the steps of the Temple, or the steps of the house itself—he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd. For all the people followed, crying: “Take him away,” that is, to death. As Paul was being brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune: “May I say something to you?” The tribune replied: “Do you know Greek?” He said: “I do.” The tribune spoke Greek so that the Jews would not understand. “Are you not that Egyptian who some days ago stirred up a revolt and led four thousand Sicarii into the wilderness?” Josephus says that he had several thousand more; it may be that he first came with fewer and afterwards had more.

## CHAPTER C. On the Egyptian who had deceived the people.

[Col. 1709D]

This Egyptian had acquired for himself the reputation of a prophet through magical art. Having gathered thirty thousand Jews, he led them through the wilderness as far as the Mount of Olives, intending to rush upon Jerusalem and capture it. But Felix the governor met him with many thousands of armed men, put him to flight with a few companions, and killed the others.

Paul answered the tribune: “I am a Jew, not an Egyptian, a citizen of Tarsus in Cilicia, a city not unknown” (Acts 21). He was not, however, born at Tarsus but in a town of Galilee named Giscala. When that town was captured by the Romans, he was transferred with his parents to Tarsus and educated there. Hence he calls himself a Tarsian because of his upbringing, though born at Giscala—just as Christ is called a Nazarene [Col. 1710A] though he was born at Bethlehem.

He was not educated in Tarsus itself, but in the municipalities adjacent to the city. Therefore he does not call himself a *civis*, “citizen,” but a *municeps*, one belonging to the municipality and territory of the city in which he was brought up. *Municipia* are rural districts neighboring a city which render to it the obligations or taxes due.

## CHAPTER CI. That, recognized by the people, Paul was permitted to speak to the governor.

In what follows it is explained more fully why Paul called himself a Roman citizen. The sum is that his father, through diligent services, had acquired the favor of the Romans and had been granted Roman liberty by them, so that he himself and his heirs were regarded as Roman citizens. Thus, by hereditary right, [Col. 1710B] Paul possessed the status of Roman citizenship.

“I ask you, therefore, permit me to speak to the people.” Being permitted, he began to speak in Hebrew. Hearing this, they gave him even greater silence. “Men, brethren” (Acts 21), “I am a Hebrew man, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed by him; and I was a zealot for the Law, as you also are, and I persecuted Christians. The high priest is my witness to this, from whom I received letters to Damascus, so that, if I found any Christians there, I might bring them bound to Jerusalem.”

He afterwards related how the Lord struck him with blindness on the road; how he was converted and baptized by Ananias; and how, after much travel, he returned from Damascus to Jerusalem. While praying in the Temple, [Col. 1710C] he fell into an ecstasy, saw, and heard Christ saying to him: “Hurry, and leave Jerusalem quickly, because they will not receive your testimony concerning me.” He answered: “Lord, they themselves know that I persecuted the followers of the Christian name and was present at Stephen’s stoning, guarding the garments of those who stoned him.” As though to say: This example of my conversion ought to suffice for them.

The Lord said to him: “Go, for I shall send you far away to the nations.” As though he said: The Jews will not believe you even on that account; therefore I shall send you to the Gentiles, who are far from the Jews both in place and in disposition.

## CHAPTER CII. That Paul made himself a Roman citizen.

When the Jews had listened to him in silence as far as this word, [Col. 1710D] on hearing (Acts 22) that he had been appointed to the Gentiles, they unanimously cried out, casting off their garments and throwing dust into the air in the greatness of their grief, as though expressing frenzy, saying to the tribune: “Take such a man from the earth; for it is not lawful that he should be heard.” And the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, namely, into that tower which was called Antonia and Agrippina, and to be beaten with scourges and tortured—but not so as to kill him—until they had satisfied themselves with his torments. And when they had bound him with thongs, Paul said to the centurion standing by: “Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman citizen who has not been condemned?”—that is, one not convicted of any charge through judicial procedure. “On hearing this, the centurion went to the tribune, saying: What are you about to do? This man is a Roman citizen.” [Col. 1711A] And the tribune came to Paul and asked him whether he was a Roman. And he acknowledged it. The tribune said: “I bought this citizenship for a great sum of money.” “But I,” Paul said, “was born into it,” because his father, as has been stated above, before begetting him, having secured for himself the favour of the Romans, had been granted Roman citizenship by them, both for himself and for his heirs. And immediately those who were to torture him withdrew, because the tribune was afraid when he heard that he was a Roman citizen.

## CHAPTER CIII. On the schism brought about among the Jews by Paul’s contrivance.

On the following day, wishing to learn more carefully the ground of the accusation against Paul (Acts 22), he released him and ordered the priests to assemble for a council. And bringing [Col. 1711B] Paul forward, he set him among them. And Paul began openly to address the council (Acts 23): “Men and brethren,” he said, “I have lived before God with every good conscience unto this day.” And immediately Ananias, the high priest, commanded those standing near to strike him on the mouth, as though he were boasting shamelessly. Paul said to him: “God will strike you, you whitewashed wall.” As though he said: God will take vengeance on you, hypocrite, because, although you sit in Moses’ seat and seem to judge according to the Law, you judge contrary to the Law. For although you count me a blasphemer, you do not judge me according to the procedure of the Law, which commands that a blasphemer be led outside the camp and, once led out, stoned by all the people.

Or perhaps Paul prophesied the abolition of the Jewish priesthood when he said: “God will strike [Col. 1711C] you,” as though he said: God will destroy you and your priesthood—that is, the priesthood of the Jews. Then those standing by said: “Do you revile God’s high priest?” Then Paul said: “I did not know, brethren, that he was the high priest; indeed, had I known this, I should be guilty. For it is written: ‘You shall not revile the ruler of your people’” (Exod. 22). Or he said, as it were mystically, that he did not know—that is, that the Jewish priesthood had been rejected—because, although he knew that this man was not truly high priest, he nevertheless answered moderately, instructing others to conduct themselves more modestly towards their prelates.

Then Paul, fearing the violence of the Jews, devised a way to stir up a schism among them. And since Pharisees and Sadducees were present, he professed before all that he belonged to the sect [Col. 1711D] of the Pharisees (Phil. 3), so as thereby to win their favour and, by their assistance, escape the hands of the others. And when he had made this profession, a great dissension arose between the Pharisees and Sadducees.

## CHAPTER CIV. That the Lord strengthened Paul.

“And certain Pharisees arose and contended for Paul against the Sadducees, saying: ‘We find nothing evil in this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?’” (Acts 23). They said this against the Sadducees, who denied the existence of angel, spirit, or soul. And when so great a dissension had arisen, the tribune, fearing that Paul might be torn apart by the Sadducees, who wished to seize him, ordered the soldiers to go down and take him from [Col. 1712A] their midst and bring him into the barracks; and so it was done. On the following night the Lord appeared to Paul, saying: “Be steadfast; for as you have borne witness concerning me in Jerusalem, so you must bear witness also at Rome.”

## CHAPTER CV. How a conspiracy was formed for Paul’s death.

When day came, certain Jews gathered together (Acts 23) and bound themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul; the Greek has *they anathematized*. There were more than forty men who had made this conspiracy, and they came to the chief priests and elders, saying: “We have bound ourselves by a vow to taste nothing until we kill [Col. 1712B] Paul. Therefore persuade the tribune to bring him again before you, as though you intended to ascertain something more certain concerning him. But we shall be ready to kill him.”

Perhaps Paul’s nephew, his sister’s son, heard this and entered the barracks and reported it to Paul. Paul summoned one of the centurions and said: “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to report to him.” And when the young man came to the tribune, he explained the Jews’ treachery and plot against Paul. Then the tribune dismissed the young man, ordering him to reveal this to no one. And having summoned two centurions, he said to them: “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go on foot as far as Caesarea, and seventy horsemen—that is, men who are not to go on foot—and two hundred spearmen, from the third [Col. 1712C] hour of the night; prepare ten beasts of burden for Paul and his companions, and bring him safe and unharmed to Felix the governor.”

## CHAPTER CVI. That he contended before the governor against Tertullus the orator.

The tribune also wrote a letter to the governor in this form (Acts 23): “CLAUDIUS Lysias sends greetings to the most excellent governor FELIX.” He did not observe the practice which we observe in our letters; for he did not put first the name of the more eminent person, but his own name, though he was of lower rank than the governor. Afterwards he set forth in the letter the cause of Paul’s accusation and the manner and order of the proceedings.

When the messengers arrived at Caesarea with Paul, they delivered the letter to the governor and set Paul before him. After reading the letter and learning [Col. 1712D] that he was from Cilicia, the governor said: “I will hear you when your accusers have come,” and he ordered him to be kept in Herod’s praetorium. But after five days Ananias, the high priest, came down (Acts 24) with the elders and with a certain orator, Tertullus, who was their advocate. Tertullus pleaded before Felix and accused Paul on many counts. Then, with the governor’s permission, Paul answered, showing that he had committed nothing worthy of death, and that the Jews persecuted him on account of the truth—namely, because he preached the resurrection.

And when Felix heard that the dispute concerned their law, he made light of it and said: “I shall hear you when the tribune Lysias comes down.” He ordered Paul to be kept in free custody, so that he could freely [Col. 1713A] come and go and walk about, and that none of his people should be forbidden to minister to him. Some days later Felix came with his wife Drusilla and summoned Paul. This Drusilla was a most beautiful Jewish woman, whom Lazitus, king of the Amazons, had once desired. When he wished to marry her, she refused, saying that she would by no means marry an uncircumcised man. Afterwards he circumcised himself and married her.

## CHAPTER CVII. That Felix wished to extort money from Paul.

When Felix had been sent by Claudius as governor of Judaea, he courted her through the Jews, asking her to marry him. At length she was persuaded by the example of her kinswoman Berenice, who had formerly left her husband and married a wealthier man, namely King Agrippa, son of Herod Agrippa, [Col. 1713B] who possessed the land beyond the Jordan. Therefore Drusilla left her former husband, Lazitus king of the Amazons, and married Felix. Since this Drusilla was a Jewess, she gladly listened to Paul speaking about the faith which is in Jesus Christ. And when Paul disputed about righteousness, chastity, and the future judgment, the governor trembled on hearing that he himself would be judged. And he said to Paul: “Go away; when I have a convenient opportunity, I shall summon you” (Acts 24). He said this, however, hoping to receive something from him. For he thought Paul had money; therefore, summoning him more frequently, he spoke with him.

When two years had been completed, Festus, sent by Nero, succeeded Felix. But if the two years are understood to run from Felix’s governorship, this cannot stand, since he had long before been appointed governor by Claudius. Festus, however, was sent by [Col. 1713C] Nero, who succeeded Claudius. And if the two years are understood to run from Paul’s accusation, neither can this stand; for two years had not yet elapsed since he had come to Jerusalem. Therefore they must be understood as two years from the accusation against Felix—that is, from the time when he was accused by the Jews.

## CHAPTER CVIII. On the sedition between Jews and Gentiles.

For a dissension arose between Jews and Gentiles at Caesarea concerning the honour of civic status. The Jews preferred themselves to the Gentiles because Herod of Ascalon, who had received circumcision, had been the founder of the city and had called it Caesarea in honour of Caesar. The Gentiles preferred themselves to the Jews, saying that the city’s original construction had been performed by Gentiles, and that before Herod rebuilt it, it was called [Col. 1713D] Strato’s Tower.

At first Felix favoured the Jewish party until he had emptied their purses; afterwards he favoured the Gentile party so far as to grant the Gentile soldiers permission to enter Jewish houses and plunder their goods. Therefore he was accused by the Jews before Nero, and two years after the accusation he was removed from the governorship and Festus was appointed in his place. But wishing, at the end of his governorship, to please the Jews, he left Paul in bonds (Acts 24).

When Festus came into the province (Acts 25), after three days he went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem. The chief priests and leading Jews asked him to order Paul brought to Jerusalem, laying an ambush for him in order to kill him on the way. But Festus replied that he would soon [Col. 1714A] return to Caesarea and would hear their accusation there, if they came down together with him.

## CHAPTER CIX. On Paul’s appeal.

After Festus had remained in Jerusalem a few days, he went down to Caesarea (Acts 25), sat on the judgment-seat, and Paul was brought forward. He was accused on many counts by those who had come down from Jerusalem, but they could not prove the charges brought against him, Paul answering every charge. Festus, however, wishing to please the Jews, said to Paul: “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there concerning these matters before me?” Paul replied: “I stand before Caesar’s tribunal; there I ought to be judged.”

There was at Caesarea a seat beside which Paul stood, prepared by Herod for Caesar, so that he might sit upon it if he should at any time [Col. 1714B] come to Caesarea, or for those whom he might send as judges. Paul excused himself, saying: “I have done the Jews no wrong, as you know. If I have committed anything worthy of death, I am willing to die; but if I have committed nothing, no one has the right to hand me over to them, because I appeal to Caesar.” Then Festus, having consulted with his council, replied: “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go.”

## CHAPTER CX. On Agrippa’s request to Festus.

After some days had passed (Acts 25), Agrippa came down to Caesarea with his wife Berenice. Josephus says concerning Berenice: it should not be understood that she was his wife, but as though she were his wife. For she was his sister—that is, his kinswoman according to Hebrew usage—and he loved her very tenderly; and he was accused of abusing her. [Col. 1714C]

King Agrippa came down to Caesarea when he heard that Festus was there, in order to accuse the Jews before him. For this Agrippa was hostile to the Jews, because, having received authority from the Roman emperor to appoint the high priest in Jerusalem, he appointed as priests men who were not Aaronites. He had made in his palace a lofty window from which he could see all the sacrifices being performed in the Temple. Since the Jews took this ill, they erected a wall before the window, higher than the window itself. Agrippa therefore came especially to ask Festus to throw down that wall. Yet the reason for Agrippa’s coming down to Caesarea is not found in the history of Acts; Josephus supplies it.

## CHAPTER CXI. How Paul pleaded before Festus and Agrippa.

[Col. 1714D]

When Agrippa had come down, Festus received him honourably. After he had stayed with him for several days, Festus consulted him about what he should do concerning Paul. Having set forth the Jews’ accusation against Paul, Agrippa replied that he wished to see Paul (Acts 25). On the following day Agrippa and Berenice came with great pomp—that is, with a great crowd surrounding them; or “with great pomp,” that is, with elaborate display; or “with great eagerness,” that is, with a strong desire to hear Paul. And when they had entered the audience hall with the tribunes and leading men of the city, Paul was brought in at Festus’s command. Festus said: “King Agrippa and all of you who are here together, behold [Col. 1715A] this man, concerning whom the whole multitude of the Jews has petitioned me at Jerusalem, declaring him worthy of death. Yet I have found nothing in him worthy of death. Therefore, because he has appealed to Augustus, I have decided to send him to Rome. But it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner without stating his charge. Therefore, King Agrippa, I consult you concerning this, because I have nothing certain to write about him.”

“Then Agrippa said to Paul: ‘You are permitted to speak for yourself.’” Then Paul, stretching out his hand in the manner of public speakers, or to make silence, began to give an account of all the matters concerning which the Jews accused him. “I count myself fortunate, King Agrippa,” he said, “that I am to make my defense before you, since you are skilled in the Law of Moses and know the customs of the Jews. [Col. 1715B] Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently.” And he continued by relating the manner of his conversion and the point on which the Jews accused him.

After Paul’s many words, Festus replied in a loud voice: “You are mad, Paul; much learning drives you mad.” Paul said: “I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but I speak words of sobriety and truth. For King Agrippa knows these things, in whose presence I speak. I think none of these things is unknown to him; for none of them has been done in a corner. Do you believe the prophets, Agrippa? I know that you believe.” Agrippa said to him: “In a short time you persuade me to become a Christian.” Paul said to him: “I pray to God that not only you, but also all who hear me today, may become such as I am—except for these bonds. For I do not wish them to be bound.”

## CHAPTER CXII. That Paul was sent to Rome.

[Col. 1715C]

Then the king, the governor, Berenice (Acts 26), and those sitting with them rose. And when they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying: “This man has done nothing worthy of death or bonds.” Agrippa said to Festus: “This man could have been released, if he had not appealed to Caesar.” And Agrippa decided that, since he had appealed, he should be sent to Caesar. Paul was handed over to Julius, a centurion of the Augustan cohort (Acts 27), that is, of soldiers sent by Augustus.

At the same time the Jews sent messengers to Rome against Agrippa, against whom they had many complaints, because, as we stated above, he had appointed Ishmael high priest, although he was not [Col. 1715D] of Aaron’s lineage. Here Josephus gives a catalogue of the priests who had served from the institution of the priesthood to its end, divided into three periods. From Aaron to David’s time there were thirteen, one after another, in 612 years; sons succeeded fathers. Aaron’s firstborn son, Eleazar, succeeded him as high priest; Eleazar’s son succeeded him, and so thereafter. For none of Ithamar’s line were high priests, but only lesser priests, except for a few around David’s time. For in Eli the priesthood passed to Ithamar’s sons. Abiathar also was of Ithamar, whom Solomon deposed and in whose place he appointed Zadok, who was of Eleazar.

## CHAPTER CXIII. An incidental account of the Jewish priests.

[Col. 1716A]

David, wishing to enlarge the worship of God, saw that one high priest was insufficient for the ministry, because, if he fell ill, there was no one meanwhile to place the incense, which had necessarily to be offered every day. He therefore appointed twenty-four high priests, sixteen of whom were of Eleazar’s lineage and eight of Ithamar’s. Yet one of those twenty-four was supreme, and was called the chief of the priests. They served by weeks, which descended by hereditary right to their descendants. Each of the twenty-four high priests, when he was serving, had with him twenty-four lesser priests, and the same number [Col. 1716B] of Levites, and the same number of gatekeepers, together with twice as many Nethinim.

There were eighteen chiefs of the priests from David’s time to the Babylonian deportation, over 466 years. From the deportation the priesthood ceased until the return from captivity under Zerubbabel and Jesus the high priest. From that point until the time of the Maccabees was the period of the priests. But the time of the Maccabees is not reckoned as belonging to the priesthood, because they were at once leaders and priests; and this continued until Herod, who caused all whom he could find of priestly descent to be killed, lest the kingdom return to them. He sold the high priesthood, sometimes to one person, sometimes likewise to several. In all, there were twenty-nine high priests until the destruction [Col. 1716C] of Jerusalem.

Josephus gives no total of the years from Herod’s time to Jerusalem’s destruction, but they are known to have been 105: for Herod reigned thirty years before the Lord’s birth; the Lord lived thirty-three years; and forty-two years elapsed from the Lord’s death to Jerusalem’s destruction. But enough on these matters.

## CHAPTER CXIV. On the storm at sea which Paul foretold.

Paul was handed over to Julius the centurion (Acts 27), as has been stated. The Lord gave Paul favour in his eyes, so that he treated him humanely and did not prevent his friends in the cities through which he passed from ministering to him. Luke continues, therefore, the account of the journey: “Having embarked,” he says, “on an Adramyttian ship, we began to sail along the coasts of Asia.” Some, dividing it by syllables, wish to read *ad Rumentinam*, so that, according to them, it means “a ship bound for Rumentina,” namely Rome; but it is better called Adramyttian from the name of the city. For Adramyttium is a city of Africa. Afterwards Luke lists the cities through which they passed, which need not be enumerated except where events occurred that must not be omitted. Among other places they came to Lystra, where Paul had many friends who ministered to him.

There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and transferred us to it, as Luke says; that is, he transferred us from the ship upon which we had first embarked [Col. 1717A] to that one. When we had sailed slowly for many days, because the wind prevented freer progress, we at last sailed to Crete; and from there we scarcely reached the place called Fair Havens. There we remained for a long time, not daring to put out to sea, since navigation was unsuitable because the fast had passed—that is, because there was great hunger on the ship, rendering the sailors weaker for sailing.

Or this may be understood of the fast of the seventh month, which falls between the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles, namely between the tenth and fifteenth days of September; and thus it proves that navigation was unsafe, because it was already the seventh month, which, according to the Hebrews, is winter, since they count April as the first month. It is not safe to sail in winter. Or it may be understood of the fast instituted in memory of the death of Gedaliah, which is held at the end of September. Or of the fast of the tenth month, held in January, which they instituted upon hearing reports concerning the building of the Temple in Babylon.

Since the centurion and the others were troubled that they could not sail, Paul comforted them, saying: “Men, I perceive”—perhaps from signs of the storm, or in a prophetic spirit—“that you can sail only with [Col. 1717B] much damage, not only to the cargo and ship but also to your lives.” But the centurion believed the helmsman or shipmaster more than Paul—that is, the master of the ship. For a *nauclerus* is one to whose lot the ownership of a ship falls; for *cleros* means “lot.” What compelled the centurion to trust the shipmaster rather than Paul was that the harbour in which they were was not suitable for wintering. Therefore all advised sailing away from there, if somehow they could reach another harbour more suitable for wintering.

Against Paul’s advice, with the south wind blowing favourably and eagerly seeking the intended harbour, they put out to sea. When they had proceeded a little way, a typhonic wind rose and rushed against the ship; it was called *Euro-aquilo*. A typhonic wind is so called because it seems to inflate the sea and make it swell; for *typhos* is interpreted “inflation.” When the ship was caught and could not strive against the wind, rowing having ceased, we were carried aimlessly, drifting towards a certain island [Col. 1717D] called Cauda. We could scarcely secure the boat, which had been put from the ship into the sea to assist the vessel, because it was nearly broken by the violence of the waves.

A *scapha* is called a light little vessel hollowed out of a single tree. Or it is called a small wicker boat covered with raw hide, of the kind used by pirates. It is called from *scaphon*, interpreted “mirror,” because pirates use boats of this kind to observe and reconnoitre. Such little boats are carried on ships, and when shipwreck threatens, are put into the sea to aid the ship; for by these the ship is girded about and armed in preparation for a storm. Since they were thus violently tossed by the tempest, on the next day they made a jettison—that is, they threw the ship’s equipment overboard.

## CHAPTER CXV. That Paul encouraged those placed in danger.

[Col. 1718A]

When neither sun appeared by day, nor moon and stars by night, all hope of safety was removed (Acts 27). And after they had kept a prolonged fast—perhaps voluntarily, to remove the storm, or necessarily, because they may have been pressed by scarcity of provisions, all being thrown into the water—Paul stood in their midst and said: “It would have been sound counsel to obey me and avoid this injury and loss. Yet now I urge you to be of good courage. Be assured that none of you will perish or suffer loss, except the ship. For this night an angel of God, whose servant I am, stood by me, saying: ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, [Col. 1718B] God has granted you all who sail with you’”—that is, through your merit he will preserve them, so that none of them may perish. “Therefore,” he says, “be of good courage. For I believe my God that it will be as it was told me; and we must come upon a certain island.”

He foretells this truth to them so that, when they see it fulfilled, they may hope more confidently for safety. “But when the fourteenth night came, about midnight the sailors suspected that some land was appearing to them. Letting down a lead weight, by which the depth of the sea is sounded, they found twenty fathoms. And having gone a little farther, they found fifteen fathoms; and, fearing lest they should fall upon rough places, they cast four anchors from the stern and wished for day.”

## CHAPTER CXVI. On Paul’s steadfastness.

[Col. 1718C]

When the sailors wished to flee by lowering the boat into the sea (Acts 27), Paul, seeing this in the spirit, said to the centurion and the soldiers: “Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved.” Immediately the soldiers cut the boat’s ropes, and it went away over the sea. As day was dawning, Paul urged them all to take food so that they might be stronger to endure the labour. “Today,” he says, “is the fourteenth day since we awaited clear weather and have remained fasting, taking nothing.” Perhaps on that day they had eaten nothing, or perhaps several days had passed without food. “Take courage,” he says, “and eat; for not even a hair from [Col. 1718D] your head will perish.”

Having said this, he took bread in the sight of all, with thanksgiving according to his usual custom; and after breaking it, he began to eat. The others also, becoming more cheerful, took food; and there were 276 souls in the ship.

## CHAPTER CXVII. Continuation of the history.

Then, strengthened by food, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea (Acts 27). When day came, they did not recognize the land.
