But they noticed a certain bay with a shore, upon which they planned, if they could, to run the ship. Having raised the anchors, they committed themselves to the sea without attempting to row. Raising the *artemon*, they headed for the shore in the direction the wind carried them. An *artemon* is a small sail adapted more to steering the ship [Col. 1719A] than to speed.

When they struck a *bithalassus*, they ran the ship aground. A *bithalassus*, properly speaking, is a tongue of land projecting into the sea, surrounded by sea on either side. It is called *bithalassum*, as though “a divided sea,” parted by intervening land. When the ship struck the *bithalassus*, the bow remained immovable, but the stern was broken by the force of the incoming sea. All the soldiers advised that the prisoners should be killed, lest any perhaps escape by swimming.

## CHAPTER CXVII. On Paul’s word to the centurion.

But the centurion (Acts 27), wishing to save Paul, forbade this to be done and permitted all who could escape, by whatever means, to do so. As Paul had foretold, they all escaped and came ashore on an island called Mitylene. When they had landed, [Col. 1719B] the barbarian inhabitants of the island carefully showed them the offices of humanity. Having kindled a fire, they revived them.

While Paul was gathering sticks (Acts 28) and putting them on the fire, a viper, hidden among the sticks, fastened itself to his hand. When the barbarians saw the viper hanging from his hand, they said to one another: “Certainly this man is a murderer; for though he has escaped shipwreck, divine vengeance does not allow him to live any longer.” But Paul shook the viper into the fire and suffered no harm. They expected his hand to swell, because swelling usually follows poison. When they had waited a long time and found no injury in his hand, they turned their attention to one another and said: “This man is a god.”

## CHAPTER CXIX. That he healed the ruler’s father and others.

[Col. 1719C]

It happened that the father of Publius, the ruler of the island, was suffering from fevers and dysentery (Acts 28), that is, from diarrhoea. When Paul entered to him and, praying, laid hands upon him, he healed him. After this was done, all the sick people on the island came to him and were healed.

After some months they found an Alexandrian ship which had wintered at the island of Mitylene, whose name was *Castrum Insigne*—either of the island, because traces of certain fortifications that had anciently been built there were still visible, or of the ship, because emblems resembling fortifications were woven into its sails. Another translation has, “whose figurehead was the Dioscuri,” the twin Castors, namely Castor and Pollux, whom the Gentiles [Col. 1719D] especially invoke in danger at sea, and therefore they had built a temple for them on the seashore. This is clearer in another translation, where it reads, “whose figurehead was the sons of Jupiter.” For the Gentiles invent tales that Castor and Pollux were sons of Jupiter.

When they boarded the ship, the inhabitants honoured us with many honours and put aboard what was necessary. When they came to Syracuse, they stayed there three days; then they came to Rhegium; and from there, after one day, the south wind blowing, they came to Puteoli. Some books instead have *Puteolosum*, the name of an island where they found brethren and, at their request, remained seven days. When the brethren in Rome heard of their arrival, they came to meet them as far as [Col. 1720A] the Forum of Appius—that is, a place established by Appius on the seashore. Arriving there at night, they found provisions for sale, where three taverns had been set up, namely three houses on the shore in which foodstuffs were displayed for sale.

## CHAPTER CXX. That he was received by the Christian brethren.

When Paul saw the brethren coming to him (Acts 28), he gave thanks to God and took courage—that is, he feared less. Since Christians were already at Rome before Paul’s arrival, it is clear from this passage that Peter and Paul were not the first to preach to the Romans. If one sometimes reads of the establishment or confirmation of the faith, this should be understood as establishment or confirmation, not as primary instruction.

When they came to Rome, [Col. 1720B] Nero had not yet been confirmed in his rule, nor had his wickedness gained strength. Hearing that there was a controversy concerning the law of the Jews and Christians, he despised it. Paul was permitted to go freely about the city, with only one soldier guarding him. Yet he feared that the Jews who had persecuted him in Judaea might have sent letters to the Jews at Rome, so that they might kill him by deceit. Therefore, after the third day, he summoned the leading Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them: “Brethren, I have not come to accuse my people; but I was compelled to appeal to Caesar because I was unjustly handed over by the Jews into Roman hands. Therefore, brethren, I want you to know that there is no cause for my death except that I preach the resurrection of the dead.”

They said [Col. 1720C] to him: “We have received no letters concerning you from Judaea, nor has any brother who has come here spoken evil concerning you. But we wish to hear from you what you think of the sect of Christians, to which you adhere; for we have heard that it is everywhere opposed.” On an appointed day many came to him in his lodging. He explained to them the Law and the prophets, preaching concerning Jesus from morning until evening. Some believed what was said; others did not believe. As they departed in disagreement, Paul began to rebuke them in this way: “Well did the Holy Spirit speak of you through Isaiah (ch. 6; Matt. 13), saying: ‘Go to this people and say to them: You will hear with your ears and not understand; and seeing you will see and not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown fat, [Col. 1720D] and they have heard heavily with their ears and have closed their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, be converted, and I heal them.’ Since this saving work of God has been sent to the Gentiles, they too will hear.”

## CHAPTER CXXI. During what time he preached freely.

Paul remained for two whole years in the lodging that he had rented (Acts 28), in free custody; and he received all who came in to him, preaching the word of God and teaching concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance. Observe that Nero had already reigned two years before Paul came to Rome. Having come to Rome, Paul was in free custody for two years, and afterwards for ten years in still freer circumstances, because Nero had not yet [Col. 1721A] been confirmed in his rule and granted him free permission to walk about, travel through the regions of the West, and preach.

## CHAPTER CXXII. In what year of Nero’s reign he suffered.

But in the fourteenth year of Nero’s reign, when his wickedness had now become strong and he had already conspired against the Jews, Paul was placed in prison at Rome. There he converted many of Nero’s household and gained the friendship of Seneca, Nero’s teacher. In that same fourteenth year, namely the final year of Nero’s reign, both he and Peter were crowned with martyrdom. Hence those err who say that they were not killed on the same day, unless this means the same day after the year had come round; but this cannot stand, since it is certain that they were killed in the same year, namely the fourteenth, and on the same day.

## CHAPTER CXXIII. In what places Peter and Paul were executed.

[Col. 1722A]

Some seem to understand too little concerning the place, thinking that they were killed in the same location because it is read: “The glorious princes of the earth, as they loved one another in their life, so in death they were not separated.” Yet it seems rather that Paul, as a citizen, was killed by a more honourable death, because he was beheaded by the sword, and was in the catacombs toward the west. Peter, however, was crucified in the Vatican, that is, in the district outside the city where casks were made. Thus Paul died by the more honourable death, because he was beheaded. For nobles were put to death by the sword, and in a more honourable place, namely in the catacombs.

[Col. 1721]

# SERMONS OF PETER COMESTOR.

(*Bibliotheca Patrum Lugdunensis*, vol. XXIV, p. 1386, at the end of the Works of Peter of Blois.)

## [INTRODUCTION.]

Concerning these sermons, Peter de Goussainville writes as follows in the Prolegomena to Peter of Blois [Note: [Col. 1721] See *Patrologia*, vol. CCVII. Among those also published by Buseus, several—namely sermons 7, 15, 17, 21, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28, 34, 35, 40, and 51—are printed among the works of Hildebert of Le Mans. PATROLOGIA EDITORS.]:

> “That the sermons published by Buseus under the name of Peter of Blois are those of Peter Comestor, or Manducator, is clearer than daylight. Buseus, otherwise a most learned man, is nevertheless to be excused. Knowing that certain sermons had been composed by Peter of Blois, but having no copy of any of them available to him, he finally obtained a single manuscript sent to him from Louvain, bearing the title: ‘Sermons of Master Peter’; and he conjectured that they were sermons of Peter of Blois. Yet very many manuscripts found in various libraries state with the greatest clarity that they are not his but Peter Manducator’s. We shall produce five or six manuscript codices which we have seen and collated. The first is the Mentelian manuscript, that is, the copy of Jacques Mentel, doctor of medicine at Paris. This ancient codex restores these sermons to their rightful author, Peter Manducator, and is entitled: ‘Order of the Sermons of Master Peter Manducator through the cycle of the year.’ At the end of the codex occur these words: ‘Here end the Sermons of Master Peter Manducator.’  
>
> “The second codex belongs to Marmoutier; it is of excellent and ancient authority, since it was copied about Comestor’s own time, as is apparent from these words at the end of the codex, written in precisely the same hand as the rest of the work: ‘This book belongs to St Martin,’ etc. ‘The book was made in the time of William the Almoner, in the eighth year of Abbot Hervé.’ This Hervé, as appears from the list of abbots of Marmoutier found in the notes on Guibert of Nogent, held the pastoral office from the year of Christ 1178 until 1186. The beginning of the codex is as follows: ‘Here begin the chapters of the Sermons of Master Peter Manducator contained in this volume,’ etc.  
>
> “The third is a Corbie manuscript codex, of no slight authority, in which there is no title. The sermons, however, are the same as in the preceding manuscript. The fourth is Carthusian, from the monastery of Val-Dieu in the district of Perche. This codex, written nearly five hundred years ago, bears on its first page: ‘Order of the Sermons of Master Peter Manducator through the yearly cycle in synod,’ etc. Finally, we saw three distinguished codices of these sermons in the library of the monastery of St Victor at Paris, in whose church Peter Comestor is buried. They likewise bear the title, ‘Sermons of Master Peter Manducator’; and besides those published by Buseus, they contain several other sermons by the same Peter Manducator which have not yet come to light.” [Note: [Col. 1721] Peter Comestor, ch. 81 of the *Historia evangelica*.]

[**SERMONS OF PETER COMESTOR**]

## FIRST SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

[Col. 1721B]

“There was at Jerusalem a sheep-pool, whose water was moved at the descent of an angel; and whoever first went down into it was healed of whatever sickness or infirmity held him” (John 5). In Greek, *probaton* (πρόβατον) is called in Latin “a sheep” or “livestock”; the pool was therefore called *probatica* because the Nethinim washed in it the flesh of sacrificial victims before it was burned upon the altar of burnt offerings. Our annals say nothing about either the cause or the time of this miraculous movement. Yet it is credible that it occurred when the Saviour’s advent was imminent; otherwise the chronicle of earlier times would not have passed it over in silence.

There are two traditions concerning its cause. The first is that, from Solomon’s days, the wood of the Lord’s cross had lain hidden there in the depths of the earth; at the Saviour’s advent it floated up and was found. Therefore, upon the discovery of the saving cross, a saving draught was made there.

The second tradition is more plausible. Christ Jesus, the man who is the mediator of God and humankind (1 Tim. 2), displayed to the peoples of East and West visible signs of his coming in the flesh. It is credible that he supplied the Jews, placed at the navel of the nations and especially because he was being sent to them, with a manifest and visible sign—particularly since the Jews sought a sign. To the eastern peoples a new star indicated the rising of the new King. [Note: [Col. 1723D] Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*; Peter Comestor, *History of Genesis*, ch. 37.] This was fitting, for in Nimrod’s days they worshipped fire and the host of heaven, and they attributed even events affecting us to motions of the stars. Thus a new star announced to them that a king had risen on earth who would bring to an end in the heights the superstition attached to the stars.

He also gave the western peoples a sign at Rome: not merely that a spring of oil burst forth and flowed as far as the Tiber, but also that, on the very night on which a virgin gave birth, the Temple of Peace utterly collapsed. The Romans, flourishing in their world monarchy, had built the Temple of Peace with much labour, great expense, and great ambition; it was marvellous in the eyes of its beholders. When they consulted Apollo about its duration, they received the answer that it would remain until a virgin gave birth. Rejoicing over this, they inscribed over its doors the title: “THE ETERNAL TEMPLE OF PEACE.” Accordingly, on the same night on which the virgin gave birth, it collapsed wonderfully and disastrously, as though it were openly being said to them: “The Saviour has been born, the living and true God; before his face the deaf and dumb idols shall fall. For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1).

The Jews, however, received their sign in water consecrated to the use of sacrificial victims, as though it were said to them: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Ps. 84 [85]), and the sacrifices that were figures shall cease. Yet, since all things happened to them in figure (1 Cor. 10), while these things were done and written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, let us investigate the spiritual meaning of that movement.

The sheep-pool signified the Blessed Virgin. She could be called not only sheep-like because of her simplicity and innocence, but also a ewe; for she bore the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1). If she bore a lamb, it was indeed probable that she was a ewe. The Angel of Great Counsel descended into her (Luke 1), and she was moved by a threefold movement: in the separation of flesh, the removal of the fuel of sin, and the power of blessing.

When the power of the Most High overshadowed her [Col. 1723C] (ibid.), it separated from her the little piece of flesh from which the Saviour’s flesh was formed. In her, too, was extinguished that natural *fomes*, the infirmity of nature from which arise in us illicit impulses that are not within our power. The angel also brought her blessing, saying: “Hail, blessed among women” (ibid.), that is, “the only strong woman among the weak.” [Note: [Col. 1724D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, XI.2.] For *mulier* (“woman”) is derived from softness, as though *mollier* (“softer”).

This is the strong woman of whom it is written: “Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31); and concerning whose strength it was said to the devil: “She shall crush your head” (Gen. 3). For that ancient horned serpent attacks us principally with two horns: pride of spirit and impurity of flesh. That strong woman crushed these two horns in herself, healing contraries by contraries: she cast down pride of spirit by humility, and the impurity of flesh by her vow of virginity. She is the strong woman who put her hand to mighty things. For she pursued together two things that are difficult, or impossible, to fulfil at once: she vowed virginity and at the same time consented to marriage.

There was also in her a fourth movement, which it is not lawful to pass over in silence and which may be understood from a slight alteration of a name. For *virgo* (“virgin”), with *o* changed to *a*, becomes *virga* (“rod”). In this way she became a rod, according to the saying: “The Virgin Mother of God is a rod.” For the Saviour when born had three rods: the rod of support, used by old men; the rod of instruction, used by teachers in their schools; and the rod of dominion, used by kings. In this manner the Saviour had three rods: the Virgin’s flesh, the cry of preaching, and the chalice of suffering. The first was the rod of the root, the second of the wilderness, the third of the kingdom. Of the first it is written: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 2 [11]); of the second: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of the Lord” (Isa. 40); of the third: “The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Heb. 1). Through the first, being made in the likeness of men, he was found in outward appearance as one of us (Phil. 2). Through the second he instructed us; through the third he delivered us.

Thus the Virgin was a rod of support. That old man, the Ancient of Days, whose going forth is from the days of eternity (Mic. 5), whom Daniel saw (ch. 7) with a white head and feet of metal, could not speak in his own tongue, could not walk, could neither thirst nor hunger, nor could he undergo the other evidences of our weakness. But, leaning upon this rod, he underwent our weaknesses, as was necessary and fitting.

After this movement of the water, one person was healed in it. This is the unity of the Church, which attained salvation from the Lord through faith in the Lord’s incarnation. Yet it may move us that, after the Lord’s incarnation had taken place, those who believe in him are said to be saved from sins, since it is certain that even the ancient fathers could not have been saved without faith in the incarnation. Those who went before and those who followed all cried: “Hosanna in the highest” (Matt. 21).

We must therefore attend carefully to the difference between us and them. This, indeed, is the difference: after the incarnation those who go down are healed; before it, those who went up were healed. For expectation of a future thing, toward which we strive, is like ascent; recollection of a past thing, to which we return, resembles descent.

Moreover, there were other pools in which the Saviour worked during the days of his flesh; by comparing them with the sheep-pool, the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his desires (Ps. 110 [111]), will shine forth more clearly. There was the pool of Siloam, to which the blind man, anointed with mud, went and saw (John 9). There was also, outside Jerusalem, a pool in the Fullers’ Field, for washing garments (2 Kings [4 Kings] 18). There was likewise a pool in Samaria, in which dogs licked Ahab’s blood after he had been struck by an arrow of his own men at Ramoth-gilead (3 Kings [1 Kings] 22).

The pool of Siloam therefore fittingly signifies evangelical teaching, in which the Gentile people, blind from birth, received sight, according to the words: “The people of the Gentiles who walked in darkness saw a great light; upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has risen” (Matt. 4). The fullers’ pool, in which garments rather than persons were washed, signifies the Mosaic law; its purification, according to the Apostle (Heb. 9), availed for the cleansing of the flesh, not the spirit. Whoever was unclean by touching a corpse, leprous, suffering a discharge of seed, a woman after childbirth or during menstruation, and persons of this kind, were excluded from entering the Temple (Lev. 12). They could not share in ordinary human society until they were cleansed by legal purification; but such purifications had no power to turn them away from sin.

The pool of Samaria signifies the traditions of philosophers, who judge nothing true unless human reason affords them proof. In it the dogs—that is, the demons of the Gentiles—licked blood: that is, they turned every force of natural gifts and all human ingenuity toward their own worship. These are the physicians upon whom the woman with the issue of blood spent all her substance, and who did her no good (Luke 8). Of them it is written: “The sea-monsters laid bare their breasts; they gave their teats to their young” (Lam. 4).

Let us now see what the Lord worked in each of these pools. To make this clear, let us designate them by names suited to them. The first, as we said, was called *probatica*; let the second be called the Lord’s pool, the third the eclipsing pool, and the fourth the sophistical pool. We call the law of Moses “eclipsing,” because, like the Syrtis, it possessed water interwoven with sand. It had certain commandments that cleansed unto justification, but others that cleansed no one unto salvation.

The first pool was one of solitude; the second, of satisfaction, according to: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7); the third, of promise; the fourth, of deception. The Saviour made the first fruitful and channelled forth the second—for “his sound went forth into all the earth” (Ps. 18 [19]); he fulfilled the third, himself testifying when he said: “I came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5); and he dried up the fourth, according to: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1), and elsewhere: “I will strike Egypt into seven streams, so that they may cross it shod” (Isa. 11).

He descended into the first, and it was moved; he established the second, and it was unmoved; he filled the third, and it was thoroughly moved; he struck the fourth, and it was removed. He performed these four acts in four regions of his embassy. Sent by the Father as envoy to the lost sheep of Israel, five regions were given to him, that in each he might discharge the proper office of his mission. We may define these regions as follows: the Virgin’s womb, the middle of the world, the gibbet of the cross, the house of the strong man, and the ends of the sea.

In the first region he shod himself: he bound upon himself the fastening of his sandals, the explanation of which John the Baptist confessed himself unworthy to give (Mark 1), wishing visibly to come forth to us as a bridegroom from his chamber (Ps. 18 [19]). In this region he made the sheep-pool fruitful. Going out into the second, namely the middle of the world, he worked salvation in the midst of the earth (Ps. 73 [74]). He rejoiced as a giant to run his course (Ps. 18 [19]): beginning from Galilee, passing through the middle districts of Decapolis, and traversing all Judaea (Matt. 4), he preached the Gospel of the kingdom, gathered disciples, performed wonders in human sight, and thus channelled forth the Lord’s pool.

Ascending into the third region, he trod the winepress alone (Isa. 63); his garment became red; he offered the true victim to God the Father; and thus he fulfilled the promises of the legal figures. Descending into the fourth region, he bound the strong man and plundered his goods; he beat with a staff the one who held the dominion of death; he restrained the rage of the dogs, lest they violently lick human blood (Matt. 12).

In the fifth region, indeed, he did not work so openly before human eyes; rather, he placed the captivity that he had led captive at the ends of the sea—that is, over the broadest bounds of the world—so that at last, at the Ascension, the members together with the head might penetrate the heavens. In this region he walked from those whom he had stationed at the ends of the sea to those whom he had gathered in the upper room of death; “the heart and soul of the multitude were one” (Acts 4). He was about to leave them on earth so that they might bear witness to him throughout all Judaea and Samaria and even to the uttermost part of the earth. Coming therefore to these, he said: “I leave my peace to you”; but to those: “I give my peace to you” (John 14), as though saying to both: “Peace be with you.”

Hereafter the Saviour will come once more, but not as rain upon the fleece (Ps. 76 [77]); rather, like a collapse drawing an inevitable weight behind it. He will come, I say, “as a mighty man overcome with wine” (Ps. 77 [78]), and will spare no one. To those at his right hand he will bring joy; but upon those at his left he will thunder terribly, bringing an evil report and a harsh word. May Jesus Christ our Lord, our judge—who will come to judge the living and the dead—deliver us from that evil report and harsh word (Ps. 11 [12]).

## SERMON II. FOR ADVENT II  
Delivered in the Schools

“I turned back toward the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which faces east; and it was shut. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord’” (Ezek. 44).

Here Ezekiel represents the human race desiring to escape from the pit of misery and the mire of filth (Ps. 39 [40]). It is as though he said: “Banished from the homeland of blessedness and cast down into this vale of weeping, I cast my eyes through all former ages, seeking the way of salvation, and I did not find it. Heaven could not free me; nor earth, nor the world with all its furnishings, nor man. For we are all afflicted and sick together. Nor could an angel free me, since he rather despises than reveres my defect.”

“At last I turned back to the way of the gate of the sanctuary,” that is, to the Virgin’s childbirth. Now no one of sound understanding is ignorant that the Lord Jesus Christ exists from two natures and in two natures. The divine nature is the inner sanctuary, because it gives to drink from the torrent of its delight those who are within—I mean the angels and the spirits of the blessed, who already rest in their homeland, in their palace, indeed in their chamber. The human nature is the outer sanctuary, because it refreshes the Church Militant, which still has its tent beneath the sun, by participation in his body and blood. Or rather, the former is called the inner sanctuary because it is hidden, and the latter the outer because it is manifest.

For no human being shall see the Trinity of persons in unity of essence and live; but the Trinity of substances in unity of person we know, speak of, and expound. When the Lord came to us to renew us, he made a new thing upon the earth: namely, a temporal trinity answering, as it were by contrast, to the eternal Trinity. The inner sanctuary, therefore, is the Word in the beginning with the Father, sustaining all things by the word of his power (Heb. 1). The outer sanctuary is the Word made flesh in time, making purification for the sins of our inner weakness (ibid.).

The gate is God the Father, according to the Son’s saying: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16). Hence also the Psalmist: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven” (Ps. 18 [19]); and: “He went out from the Father; his return is to the Father.” The gate of the outer sanctuary was the Blessed Virgin, through whom God, made human, entered our city—not, I say, that city concerning which the Lord says through the prophet, “I am the Lord, and I do not enter the city” (Isa. 37); but that city of which he himself says, “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5), whose foundations are in the holy mountains (Ps. 86 [87]), and which the rush of the river—that is, the Spirit of the Son—has made glad.

This is the Church, the city of the great King, and it faces east. For all who conceive from intercourse that is not without concupiscence, although they bring their offspring into the light of birth, nevertheless, because they themselves carry along the sack and the desert of a sack, are darkened by the soot of sin and sit in darkness and in the region of the shadow of death. The Virgin’s Son alone was so brought forth into the light that he is not only light himself, but enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1).

“And it was shut.” Although no one doubts the Virgin’s virginity, yet so that certainty may be made still more certain by the Lord’s authority, the prophet adds this affirmation: “And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened; a man shall not pass through it.’” The same point is stressed three times. Here, however, “man” is understood not as denoting sex but husband, so that a more explicit point may be made: it is as though he said, “Not even her husband, that is, Joseph, shall know her.” It is fitting that it is mentioned as shut behind, because she is undoubtedly virgin both before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth.

It follows: “And it shall be shut to the prince”—that prince, undoubtedly, of whom the Lord said: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12); and again: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 14). Yet just as, in the words “A man shall not pass through it,” bodily integrity is indicated, so in the words “It shall not be opened to the prince” integrity of mind is indicated, since she removed from her mind every consent to evil suggestion.

But the following words, “The prince shall sit in it,” must not be understood of the aforesaid prince. For how could one who is not permitted to enter be said to sit in it? This prince is he of whom it is said: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9). Sitting is indeed used for humility, as in: “You have known my sitting down and my rising up” (Ps. 138 [139]); and again: “Rise after you have sat down” (Ps. 126 [127]), that is, after humility hope for exaltation. The assumption of the form of a servant was no small humiliation of the Word.

It follows: “That he may eat bread before the Lord.” For he himself said: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4). Therefore, obedient to the Father even unto death (Phil. 2), reconciling us to God, and doing the other things of this kind, he ate bread before the Lord, restoring freedom to us by his will.

You have heard these things expounded concerning the Virgin’s childbirth, her integrity, and the fruit of our salvation. Yet the same matters may also be fittingly applied to us who devote ourselves to reading and sacred Scripture. For the most part we have left behind the fictions of poets, who are compared to talkative frogs; we have sailed past the pallid arguments of the sophists, who are called hateful to God (Ecclus. 37). We have bid farewell to the pompous opinions of philosophers, who, while they still lived among us, attempted to raise their eyes above heaven. Their more learned members—I mean the Academics—confessed that truth lies hidden as it were in the well of the abyss.

We have abandoned, I say, the boastful tongue in order to possess a humbled tongue that speaks; we follow the truth-speaking tongue instead of the empty-speaking tongue. For we sought wisdom, but behold, it was not in the land of those who speak pleasantly. We heard of it in Ephrathah—that is, in a mirror—or in a cave—that is, in an image and in concealment—but behold, we found it in the fields of the forest (Ps. 131 [132]), that is, in the manifestation and obscurity of the New and Old Testaments.

Each of us, I say, can now truly say: “I turned back toward the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which faces east.” Just as the Church has two parts, militant and triumphant—the one on the way, the other in the homeland—so their holiness is different. The outer sanctuary, therefore, namely the holiness of the present Church which is still outside, is justification through faith and good works. Its gate is sacred Scripture, which teaches us to live rightly in the midst of this crooked generation; through it, whoever enters and goes out shall find pasture (John 10). The way of this gate is charity.

A human being, placed at the crossroads of this world and standing, as it were, at the earth’s navel, may turn east, west, south, or north. For there are four human ways: the way of frailty, the way of necessity, the way of vanity, and the way of truth. The way of frailty is the Jericho road, by which a human being passes in God’s image like flowing water, passing through the succession of times until he returns to his dust. This slopes southward, which is warm; for we live by a certain natural heat, and when that is extinguished, it is necessary to enter another way, namely the way of necessity.

This is the way of all flesh, by which the spirit passes, going and not returning. Of it the poet says:

> Yet I must go where Numa and Ancus have gone.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.6

This slopes westward. The way of vanity is life in sins; it can more fittingly be called a precipice, by which we fall from blood to blood, dragging a long garment behind us. This is the broad way leading to death, when we revel through the plains of licence. Of it it is said: “Their ways are darkness and slipperiness” (Ps. 34 [35]); and again: “Their way is a stumbling-block to them” (Ps. 48 [49]). This slopes northward, toward him who said: “I shall set my throne in the north” (Isa. 14). Of this Solomon says: “The north wind is cold and hard in name, as though the right hand binding waters” (Ecclus. 43), that is, freezing the streams of grace.

The way of truth is charity, concerning which the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12). This slopes eastward, because it is the way that leads to life, and therefore we must strive to enter through it. By this way we must go to sacred Scripture. Yet we cannot conceal that many of us approach it by another way: some in order to surpass others through much knowledge, others for profit, others for praise, others to build themselves up, and others to build up their neighbours also.

But hear what one man said on these matters [Note: [Col. 1727D] St Bernard, Sermon 36 on the *Song of Songs*.]: “To wish to know in order that we may know is pride; to wish to know in order that we may be known is vain glory; to wish to know in order that we may gain is simony; to wish to know in order that we may be built up is prudence; to wish to know in order that we may build others up is charity.”

Moreover, this gate faces east, that is, toward God. “Whoever gives any of his seed to the idol Moloch shall die the death, and the people of the land shall stone him” (Lev. 20). The seed is the word of God (Luke 8). “Idol” means “form,” as a diminutive derived from Greek *eidos* (εἶδος), “form.” Moloch is interpreted “ruler”; the idol Moloch is the devil, who rules in the world not truly but only as it were. Therefore whoever learns or teaches the word of God for some worldly advantage gives his seed to the idol Moloch, and such a person shall die the death of the soul. As the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul; when he departs, the soul dies. For God has no fellowship with an idol: “The bed is narrow and the covering short; both cannot cover it” (Isa. 28).

> Nor do the majesty of God and the love of the world agree well, nor do they remain in one dwelling.  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I

For the friend of the world becomes the enemy of God (Jas. 4). What we say is hard and difficult to fulfil. But consider that it has been said to us: “Issachar, a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries” (Gen. 49), namely the teaching of both Testaments, “saw that rest was good, and that the land was excellent, and put his shoulder to the burden” (Matt. 7 [an incongruous citation in the source]). Therefore you, since you are already on the way, seek and you shall find; since you have already approached the gate, knock and it shall be opened to you. May he who opened the eyes of the man blind from birth (John 9)—Jesus Christ our Lord, our teacher, our judge, who shall judge the living and the dead and the world by fire—open your understanding to comprehend the Scriptures.

## SERMON III. ON THE FEAST OF ST NICHOLAS  
Delivered in the Schools

“Whoever does not humble himself like this little child shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18; Mark 10). These are the Saviour’s words which you heard through my mouth. A question had arisen among the apostles as to which of them was greater. But because this proceeded from the arrogance of the Pharisees, who loved the chief seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men (Matt. 23), the humble master and teacher of humility, calling them back to humility, set in their midst a little child—Martial, as tradition relates, the apostle of Limoges [Note: [Col. 1727] Peter Comestor, ch. 90 of the *Historia evangelica*; see Baronius, *Annals*, vol. 1, year 73.]—and said: “Whoever does not humble himself like this little child shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” It is as though he said: “Whoever is not humble by the benefit of virtue, as this child is by the benefit of age, shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Yet, with all due respect to the Saviour, these words may belong to the present age and to today’s solemnity. The Church of God is “as an army set in array” (Song 6). In a battle-line the stronger soldiers are sent forward, the strongest are arranged at the rear, and the fearful and weak are in the middle. In this manner there were strong men in the primitive Church, who endured the first assaults of this age and founded God’s Church with their blood. At the end there will be the strongest, whose tribulation will be so great that, if possible, even the elect will be shaken (Matt. 24). But in our times there is a certain tender, emasculated middle rank, scarcely sufficient even for believing, much less for battle.

Let Mother Church therefore employ the aforesaid words for these weak people; and let us begin her admonition more deeply, letting mother and little children speak as it were in a dialogue.

The mother speaks to them:

> “Little children, my husband, your father, has returned to him who sent him and has left me pregnant. Yet he put his words in my mouth, so that I might exhort those whom I should thereafter bring into the light to follow him without delay; for he has gone ahead to prepare a place for us. For I heard him say: ‘If it were not so, I would have told you: I go to prepare a place for you’ (John 14). Go therefore, little children; set out after your father, for he has also left you provisions for the journey.”

One replies for them all:

> “Mother, the way is narrow and difficult, and I cannot manage it. Moreover, the robber sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, to kill those passing by. The robber must be feared, for he said: ‘I shall not be moved from generation to generation, without evil’ (Ps. 10 [11]). The rich must be feared, concerning whom that great traveller—the Psalmist, I mean—said while stumbling: ‘But as for me, my feet were almost moved,’ etc. (Ps. 72 [73]).”

The mother replies:

> “My son, take with you the seal of your father, which he himself left me, saying: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me’ (Mark 8). I have set it up high in churches made by hands, so that all who enter may see and reflect that deliverance from death belongs to the Lord alone; and whoever wishes may take it up. Many children have already gone ahead, including delicate virgins, following their father directly in his footsteps; follow the path they have marked. You will be so safe with this seal that even a physical representation of it affords consolation amid whatever dangers one may encounter. Thus even a demon said of a Jew: ‘A vessel empty, but sealed.’” [Note: [Col. 1729D] Gregory, *Dialogues*, III.7.]

The son replies:

> “What are you saying, mother? No one has hated his own flesh (Eph. 5); even Christ shrank from dying. Peter was led unwillingly to the cross (John 21). The Apostle wished, if it were possible, to be clothed over, not to be unclothed (1 Cor. 5 [2 Cor. 5]). What then shall the little cedar-shoot do where the cedar of Lebanon is shaken? You know my tenderness, mother. At appointed hours I can scarcely pray; on prescribed days I do not fast without reserving my stomach for a luxurious supper. Though my storehouses are full, overflowing from one kind of abundance into another, I can scarcely set apart two mites to offer to the poor. I have garments stretched out on poles, folded in sleeves, merely fodder for moths; I can scarcely bring myself to take old rags, fit for no use, to warm the sides of the poor. And you say, mother, that I should dip my foot in blood. Change your speech, mother; change the way. This is the way of the strong; bearded men walk upon it.”

The mother replies:

> “Do not be afraid, my son; there is another way,”

…has the name “milky”; (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.) If you cannot follow your father by the red way, follow him by the white one [Col. 1729D]. For my Beloved himself is “white and red” (Song 5). I indeed saw him going by the red way: bound in the garden, that is; struck on the cheeks with open hands; smeared with spittle; scourged with whips; crowned with thorns; sated with reproaches; nailed to the gibbet; and pierced with a lance after death. Yet before this he travelled by the white way, namely the way of humility. I saw him humbled in the manger, humbly hanging upon the Virgin’s breasts, placed beneath the hands of the priests when they invoked over him the name of the Lord, and borne in the trembling hands of Simeon. I saw him with his parents at Nazareth, “and he was subject to them” (Luke 2); indeed, as is reported, he daily brought water to his mother from the spring that is there. [Note: [Col. 1730D] P. Com., ch. 23, *History of the Gospel*.] I saw his head—revered by angels and feared by kings—bow beneath the hands of the Baptist (Matt. 3). The Baptist trembled and did not dare touch him, until the Lord said [Col. 1730A]: “Allow it for now; thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all humility.” If, therefore, my son, the way of suffering terrifies you, walk by the way of humility.

Yet, my son, observe carefully which path you tread. Humility has a fourfold way. Some are humble while everything goes well for them; but if the hand of the Lord touches them, they blaze with anger and immediately set their mouth against heaven. Some humble themselves in order to rise; some humble themselves in order to escape. For the oak is broken by the violence of the wind, whereas the reed escapes it. The first humility, therefore, is domestic; the second, wandering; the third, sophistical; the fourth, the Lord’s. The first is natural, the second fleeting, the third two-faced, the fourth admirable. By the first walk the faint-hearted; by the second, murmurers; by the third, sad hypocrites; by the fourth, simple doves. Of the first it is written: “From faintness of spirit and from the tempest” (Ps. 54); of the second: “He will praise you when you have done well for him” (Ps. 48); of the third: “A glorious thing is humility which desires [Col. 1730B] to be cloaked, lest pride prevail”; of the fourth: “Unless he humble himself as this little child, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18).

This little child, my son, of whom Isaiah foretold: “The calf, the lion, and the sheep feed together, and a little child shall lead them” (Isa. 11), is called little not because of smallness of stature—for he is “beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Ps. 44)—but because he bore a lesser share of human penal suffering. For he had punishment, not guilt.

Moreover, the Lord’s humility is subdivided. It is due, abundant, and superabundant. Due humility is to submit oneself to one greater for the Lord’s sake. Your father taught the first and the second; he both possessed and taught the third. Consider, my son, what you have in abundance, and serve your lesser brethren as one subject to them. Have you material means? Distribute them to one who lacks them. Have you learning? Put it out at interest, that you may receive it back with increase. Have you exhortation? “Let your fountains be dispersed abroad” (Prov. 5), so that people and beasts may drink. [Col. 1730C] Have you “the labour of your hands” (Ps. 127)? Render a tenth to the Lord your God. Since you shall eat what remains, “you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (ibid.). Have you repose—have you “fled afar and remained in solitude” (Ps. 54)? Pray for the people; intercede for the remaining multitude of the lesser brethren; cry to the Lord and say: “Either forgive them, or blot me out of the book of life” (Exod. 32). Hear your brother and master Paul saying: “Though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all” (1 Cor. 9). Therefore, in accordance with his teaching, honour those of your own conduct with double honour; take the lead in showing honour to your equals; receive those weak in faith. “Do this, and you shall live” (Luke 10). This is your father’s way; the humble walk by it.

The aforesaid exhortation of the Saviour may also be directed to the memory of the blessed confessor for whom the Church today celebrates solemnly on earth and rejoices on high; and it is especially fitting for men of learning. For our Nicholas too was a scholar when he was called by the Lord to sit “with the princes of the earth.” Nor shall we depart [Col. 1730D] from the tenor of the dialogue: let the teacher speak to his disciple as a father to a son. By the kingdom of heaven is understood Sacred Scripture, in accordance with: “The kingdom of heaven shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruit” (Matt. 21).

Therefore the father, opening his mouth, says: “My son, the first of all things to be desired is wisdom, but it is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job 28). “He who does not humble himself as this little child shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Behold, my son, humility is the first entrance to it. You hear also the philosopher: when he was asked what is necessary for the discipline of study, he replied: “A humble mind, eagerness in inquiry, a quiet life, silent investigation, poverty, a foreign land.” Observe that he put humility first, and defined it in three particulars: namely, that you should despise no writing, since not everything is found in Cato; that you should not blush to learn from anyone, because

[Col. 1731A] “What you do not know, perhaps Ofellus knows”; and that, puffed up with pride, you should not look down on those who know less. Yet, my son, a fuller humility is necessary for you. Unless your humility exceeds the humility of philosophers, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven—that is, you shall not attain the hidden meaning of Sacred Scripture—unless, I say, you possess the humility of Nicholas.”

To him the son said: “Explain, father, what it is, so that I may enter by it.” The father replied: “While he still hung upon his mother’s breasts, on Wednesday and Friday he sucked at the nipples once a day.” The son, almost smiling, answered: “Father, shall I enter again into my mother’s womb, and, born anew, lie upon my mother’s breasts?” The father said to him: “It is not so, my son. What is said is mystical: break the mouth of the letter, and you shall find the marrow of understanding.”

For the six breasts signify the six kinds of knowledge, and the six weekdays the times at which they were discovered. They are rightly called weekdays (*feriae*), because knowledge is learned in leisure-time. In the beginning of the newborn world [Col. 1731B] the ancient enemy handed down to the first parents the knowledge of a harmful freedom: not to be under the Lord; and the proud attribution of guilt, so that they might covertly turn aside their own blame upon their maker. Second, wretched man found against his many deficiencies the solace of the mechanical arts, which he later extended to the abuse of superfluity. Third, not content with these, he dared to investigate the natural causes which God had concealed in things themselves, so that, as though he had been present among the stars, he imagined that he had discovered their motions, risings and settings, combustions and aspects; and he taught that occurring events are bound by fatal necessity.

Fourth, the Father of mercies, seeing man labouring to no purpose, published in the canon of each Testament the knowledge of life. Fifth, some went after the vanities of their own inventions and, mocking ecclesiastical simplicity, stained Sacred Scripture with the blotches of heresies, as though with a variegated leprosy. [Col. 1731C] Sixth, men arose who had zeal for God; in their first disputations they repelled, as it were by a powerful antidote, the poison that had been introduced. Afterwards, setting hand to pages, they left us a vast multitude of expositions.

You see, my son, that the six words of traditions emerged in their respective times, as though on six weekdays. Only the Sabbath remains, where no one will say to another: “Teach me” (Ps. 118). “For all shall be taught by God” (John 6). Listen further, my son, and be silent. Consider the distinctive character of each breast, that you may know to which you should bring your mouth and from which you should withdraw it. The first breast was the serpent’s; the second, Egypt’s; the third, the philosopher’s; the fourth, God’s; the fifth, the heretic’s; the sixth, the Catholic man’s.

From the first flowed poisonous milk; from the second, sour milk, because the sweetness of human prosperity is sprinkled with many bitternesses; from the third, inflated milk; from the fourth, curdled milk; from the fifth, milk mixed with water—for the worst tavern-keepers mixed wine with water [Col. 1731D]; from the sixth, pure milk. The first, therefore, is to be rejected, according to: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 16). The second is to be moderated, according to: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6). The third is to be cultivated, so that whatever is fluid in the philosophers may be stored up and what is dreggy cast away. The fourth is to be drawn from: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour” (Isa. 12). The fifth is to be avoided, according to: “After a first and second admonition, avoid a heretical person” (Titus 3). The sixth is to be drunk, according to: “Drink and be made drunk, my children” (Jer. 25).

Of the first it is written: “The asp warmed eggs; it gave breasts to its young.” Of the second: “My son, if sinners have nursed you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1). Of the third: “Even the lamias bared their breasts and nursed their young” (Lam. 4). These are the physicians on whom the woman with the issue of blood uselessly spent all her substance (Luke 8). Of the fourth: “We shall remember your breasts [Col. 1732A] above wine; the upright love you” (Song 1). Of the fifth: “Give them, O Lord, a childless womb and dry breasts” (Hos. 9). Of the sixth: “Your stature is likened to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters” (Song 7).

Persist still, my son, and grasp their character from their proper names. The first is called *paralogia* (“false reasoning”); the second, *scenologia* (“worldly learning”); the third, *physiologia* (“natural philosophy”); the fourth, *theologia* (“theology”); the fifth, *cacologia* (“evil teaching”); the sixth, *pantologia* (“universal learning”). For this last, pertaining to all things, returns to each as to its head: it overthrew *cacologia*, explained theology, stripped natural philosophy, moderated worldly learning, and trampled false reasoning underfoot.

There remains, my son, the Sabbath, where only *alleluia* will be heard. You know, my son, that the breasts of the sixth weekday are set before you, yet are not to be sucked—not in the day, that is, in matters that can be understood. Let the remainder be burned with fire, and only once. For there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4); there ought to be one Catholic doctrine.

Hear, my son, how glorious is humility, the salt and seasoning of the other [Col. 1732B] virtues. Let us therefore humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that in the time of tribulation Jesus Christ our Lord, our judge, may exalt us when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON IV. ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD, AND ON BLESSED LUCY. Delivered to Religious.

“King David had grown old, and was not warmed although he was covered with skins. Abishag the Shunammite was found, and she slept with the king and warmed him. But the king did not know her” (3 Kings 1).

In this we are instructed according to the literal sense: when illnesses and the defects of nature are accompanied by further hardships, we must oppose them as far as possible by human counsel, lest, by committing everything to God, we seem rather to tempt him than to implore him.

We read of another Shunammite that, as Elisha was going on his way, the great Shunammite constrained him, and in a more distinguished place of her dwelling prepared for him a chair, [Col. 1732C] a table, a lampstand, and a bed (4 Kings 4). In its literal sense this instructs us in three matters. First, the virtue of hospitality is commended to us when it says, “She constrained him.” For the affection of hospitality ought to be so great that guests must even be compelled. Thus Lot forcibly pressed the reluctant angels to enter beneath the roof of his house (Gen. 19); and the disciples travelling to Emmaus compelled the Lord to remain with them (Luke 24). Second, the work of virtue is shown here, when we read that she honourably received him and prepared the necessities of human use. For guests should be honoured according to place, time, and person. Third, the reward of the deed is shown when we read that the prophet gave the hostess a son and afterwards raised him from the dead.

We also read in Solomon of a third Shunammite, whom he called back four times as she fled: “Return, return, Shunammite; return, return, that we may look upon you” (Song 6). But she is set down only as a figure. We do not read of a fourth Shunammite; [Col. 1732D] but Luke (ch. 30) speaks of a widow who offered two small coins and thereby deserved God’s commendation. In the mystical sense she is not inappropriately added to those mentioned above; and by reason of their kinship we may call her a Shunammite.

These four came beforehand as figures. The young Shunammite prefigured the Blessed Virgin; Solomon’s Shunammite, the Gentile world; the great Shunammite, a virgin martyr—namely Lucy; and the Gospel Shunammite, the venerable college of watchers, who, despising all things for Christ, follow him more safely and swiftly insofar as they are less encumbered. Let us therefore treat these four also in the order of time.

The first is the lowly Shunammite; the second, the wretched Shunammite; the third, the great Shunammite; the fourth, the widow Shunammite. The first is the singular Virgin; the second, the general virgin, of whom the Apostle says: “I have betrothed you to one husband as a chaste virgin” (2 Cor. 11); the third, the particular virgin; the fourth, the special virgin. The first [Col. 1733A] was God’s mother and daughter; the second, a harlot and bride; the third, strong and delicate; the fourth, poor and fettered. The first warmed ancient David; the second returned to Solomon; the prophet raised the third’s son; the Lord preferred the fourth over all who made offerings. The Lord dwelt in the first clothed in purple and sackcloth—that is, in two natures. To the second he came with fire and sword, according to: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12; Matt. 10); and again: “I came not to cast peace upon the earth, but a sword.” But he received the third with rose and lily, and humbled the fourth in ashes and haircloth.

Of the first it is written: “King David had grown old.” He who is before times and through whom times were made—did he grow old through time? Far from it. Rather, he had grown old in this sense: he had deferred the restoration of humankind—and, to speak more fully, of the universe—until the old age of time. For the Church of the first-created human beings was half-ruined; human nature was ruined in the first-created human beings; the earth was cursed in [Col. 1733B] their work; the lights of heaven were punished through a diminution of light and unremitting labour. Finally, “every creature was groaning and in travail until now” (Rom. 8). The Almighty seemed to pass over this confusion of the universe by dissimulation: he “was not warmed,” that is, he showed us scarcely any effect of warmth.

For the Lord is fire (Deut. 4); there is the fire of the Lord; and there is fire for the Lord: that is, the Holy Spirit, the movement which arises from him through the cooperation of free will, and the outward work done for God, so that God may thereby be glorified. The Spirit dwelt in no one; no movement arose in anyone; no one’s work appeared, although he was covered with a countless and immeasurable multitude of sacrifices.

Therefore the young Shunammite was sought. All who foretold the Virgin’s childbirth were, as it were, sent to seek her. David was sent, who speaks to her, as though present though hidden seminally in his loins: “Hear, daughter, and see,” etc. (Ps. 44). [Col. 1733C] Isaiah sought her, saying: “Send forth, O Lord, the lamb, the ruler of the earth,” etc. (Isa. 16). Jeremiah, as one certain, said: “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31). Ezekiel, as though dreaming images from his excessive solitude, saw the eastern gate of the sun always shut (Ezek. 44). Since none of them had found her, at last the angel Gabriel was sent, carrying the document of greeting in his hand; he found the Virgin at Nazareth, and, when he had greeted her, she was found with child in her womb (Luke 1).

“And she slept with David”: that is, flesh from the Virgin’s flesh was united to the Word of God in unity of person, and David was warmed for us. For “the kindness and humanity of God our Saviour appeared” (Titus 3). Therefore the Creator of human beings came to the dung-heap of human beings for the salvation of human beings, in the likeness of human beings; but he did not know her—that is, he left her closed. And he burned so greatly with love for us that he tasted death for us, even death on a cross (Phil. 2); and there David appeared—that is, “strong of hand.” For the hand, [Col. 1733D] not armed but fastened with nails, overthrew the aerial powers, the Jews, and death itself.

But Solomon was made dead, because by his blood he made earthly things at peace with heavenly: humankind with God, humankind with angel, humankind with humankind, Jew with Gentile. Seeing the people of the Gentiles fleeing like a harlot pursuing her lovers, who promised her grain, wine, oil, wool, and flax, he cried after her once, twice, three times, and four times: “Return” (Song 6). For four things are to be loved with charity: a person is bound to love God, himself, his neighbour, and his own body.

The Gentiles had withdrawn from the love of God, for though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God; departing into their vanities, they “served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. 1). That they did not love themselves is clear, because “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10). Nor did they love their neighbours, because they even initiated their sons to demons, passing them through fire consecrated to idols. They likewise subjected their own bodies to dishonour, even so far as to emasculate male strength into femininity. Therefore our Solomon cried: “Return, Shunammite, to the love of God; return to love of yourself; return to love of your neighbour; return” (Song 6) [Col. 1734A] “to love of your own body.”

When she was received as his bride, Solomon became Elisha—that is, “bald.” Elisha’s baldness was so great that boys mocked him, crying: “Go up, bald man! Go up, bald man!” (2 Kings 2). By hair earthly goods are often understood, as is signified by the ecclesiastical tonsure. Hence the Levites, at the time of their offering, shaved all the hair of their flesh (Num. 8). [Note: [Col. 1733D] Gregory Nazianzen, Oration I against Julian; Chrysostom, *Against the Gentiles*.] Thus Christ in the nursing Church was, as it were, bald, because the Church had neither estates nor possessions until [Col. 1734B] the time of Constantine. Indeed, the faithful suffered such hunger that Julian the Apostate, taunting them with the reproach of poverty, was accustomed to call them “ragged Galileans.”

This Christ was received by the great Shunammite: Lucy, the virgin and heroine of great virtue, a strong woman found far away, in the region of Syracuse. In the virginity which she dedicated to God, she made a bed for Christ; in the miracles which she performed, a lampstand—concerning which blessed Agatha bore testimony to her; and in her teaching, a table. For she taught her mother, whom she had healed, that alms given at the end of life are suspect, since then riches are more likely to abandon a person than to be abandoned by that person. [Note: [Col. 1734D] See Surius, vol. VI.] Her mother is said to have persisted for three years in selling her property for the use of the poor. She prepared a chair in steadfastness of mind, which God also signified in her very body, when she could not be drawn to a brothel by any strength of men or oxen.

But Elisha, her guest, raised her son: that is, he placed her spirit in her own hands, so that, as Christ’s attendant, she might retain her life when she wished and for as long [Col. 1734C] as she wished, and lay it down when she wished. For, in the midst of a fire kindled with pitch and oil, and even pierced through with a sword, she stood preaching and foretelling that peace would be restored to the Church after the death of Maximian. She did not cease until all the priests had been gathered; then, bidding them farewell, she died.

But, thanks be to God, the water of contradiction has now dried up in the Church. The Church passed through intolerable water in the martyrs and through the snares of hunters in the heretics. Our Jesus introduced another kind of martyrdom, for “idleness is the enemy of the soul” (Ecclus. 33). Monasteries were founded while the trumpet of the Holy Spirit sounded throughout the world: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132).

The widow Shunammite offered two small coins: humility of spirit and moderation of dress. Yet when we introduced the martyrdom of cenobites after the martyrs, it must be understood as more enduring with respect to beginning and development, not with respect to inception. For in the growth of religion, as with a tree, three things are considered. When a seed germinates in the depths of the earth, the tree has an inception (*initium*), from *initianum*, meaning “cast inward,” from *iacio*, “to throw.” When the earth’s surface is broken and a single, slender shoot emerges, it has a beginning (*principium*), that is, its first head. When, through the favour of a milder breeze, it spreads out into little branches, it has a development (*exordium*), since many things arise from one. [Col. 1734D]

In this way the regular common life of brethren had its inception in Zion in the time of the apostles; and it was initiated in three things: brotherly charity, common property, and common obedience. Of the first it was said: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). Of the second: “No one said that anything which he possessed was his own” (ibid.). Of the third: “They laid all things at the feet of the apostles” [Col. 1735A] (Acts 4), as those professing their due subjection to them. For these three things it is said to them: “Be prudent as serpents” (Matt. 10), that is, preserve the head. In these there may under no circumstances be a dispensation.

The beginning, however, it received in some respects from Lord Benedict and in others from Doctor Augustine. [Note: [Col. 1735D] St Benedict and St Augustine added certain things to the rule of religious.] As though adding colours to a rough image, they added rules about the plainness of food, modest quantity of clothing, austerity of beds, restraint of the lips, the times of fasts, the forms and distinctions of prayers, and relief in labours. In these latter matters a dispensation may be allowed, but with simplicity of heart. Hence it is added: “And simple as doves” (ibid.). For some hunt for an occasion to obtain a dispensation rather than wait for one.

Its development, however, occurred in our own days, though under uncertain authors; for many offshoots have sprung up. Some delight in white, some in black, some in grey garments, as though these were their distinctive languages. Some are maintained by the revenues of possessions and the services of retainers; [Col. 1735B] others seek a meagre livelihood from the labour of their hands and the produce of livestock. Others are fed by the gifts of alms, entrusting their lives to God. Others, bearing the cross before them for the defence of the Church, expose their blood. Doing all things in the Lord’s name, they seem to say to one another: “Magnify the Lord with me” (Ps. 33).

We have called this Shunammite fettered. For she had heard that the Lord hears “the groans of the fettered,” and she put her feet into the fetter of wisdom and her neck into its chain. When she was permitted to feast, she afflicted herself by fasting; when she was permitted to sleep, she imposed upon herself vigils in the untimely night; when she was permitted to speak, she set a guard upon her mouth; when she was permitted to walk about, she enclosed even her feet within material walls. Finally, she deprived her eyes, as it were, of sight; her ears, of hearing; her nostrils, of smell; her tongue, of speech; her hands, of touch; her feet, of motion.

This fettering produces mortification of the flesh [Col. 1735C] and a ready defence against enemies of every kind, so that even the adversary cannot utter a word against it. For someone approaches the fettered person and, wishing to draw him into forbidden things, says: “Let us go out. Let us see theatrical spectacles, maidens’ dances, young men’s athletic contests, circles of horsemen, and the like.” The fettered person replies: “Why do you provoke me to see? I have no eyes.” The other says: “Do I not see two lights flashing in your head and casting sight as far as bodies placed before them?” The fettered person answers: “The eyes you see are not mine. I have given them to another; they are lights of truth. Far be it that my eyes should see works of vanity.”

In this way there is a sufficiently apt and elegant answer in excuse of the members. Indeed, this fettered Shunammite and the wretched Shunammite still fight upon earth; the other two triumph in heaven. By their prayers and merits may Jesus Christ our Lord, our judge, draw you from wickedness to triumph, from the world to God, [Col. 1735D] when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON V. ON THE SAME ADVENT OF THE LORD

“The Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved” (Isa. 19).

Isaiah, speaking in the Spirit, foretold the Lord’s advent in the flesh. Though in many places he was the herald of the Lord’s advent—as there: “Then shall the lame man leap as a stag, and the eyes of the blind shall be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped” (Isa. 35)—yet in the foregoing words he foretold in particular the Saviour’s advent, that is, the incarnation.

Those who write chronicles report [Note: [Col. 1735D] P. Com., *History of the Gospel*, ch. 10; Athanasius, *On the Incarnation of the Word*; Origen, Homily 3, “Diverse …”] that, when the Lord fled into Egypt, there was no temple in Egypt in which an idol did not fall. It is also read in the annals [Note: [Col. 1736D] Baronius, vol. I of the *Annals*.] composed by the Jews that, when the children of Israel departed from Egypt, Egypt’s idols fell. But it is not recorded that the idols of Egypt fell at anyone’s entrance, except when the mother arrived with the child.

This chapter of Isaiah foretold in particular the Lord’s first advent. That light cloud is the Redeemer’s flesh, all the more free from sins because it was less subject to original guilt. The cloud’s lightness is freedom from sin; for sin is accustomed to drag us down to the depths, and therefore is rightly understood under the name of a weighty thing. In Zechariah it is written: “Wickedness sits upon a talent of lead” (Zech. 5), and elsewhere: “Like lead in mighty waters.” Therefore the Lord, ascending upon the light cloud, entered Egypt in order to remove from it the cloud by which it was covered (Exod. 15).

For it was enveloped in a fourfold cloud: a cloud of darkness, a cloud of dew, a cloud of hail, and a cloud of the shadow of death. But, that these matters may be seen more fully, we must begin more deeply, so that what has been set forth beforehand may become clearer [Col. 1736B] when it has been explained more fully. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as though deliberating together at the first creation of humanity, said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1), and like to us.

Four likewise, the king’s firstborn daughters—virgins—co-operated with God in the creation of man: truth, mercy, justice, and peace. Truth, because, as the Lord had promised that he would do, he brought the matter to fulfilment by carrying it out; mercy, because man was created to make good the deficiency among the angels; justice, because rational man was set over the other creatures, so that he who excelled the others by the benefit of creation might be raised above them by a just dominion. Peace co-operated because, although the human person is composed of such diverse elements—namely flesh and soul—and although he gathered all the elements here into one, there should be none to disagree, but each should rejoice in union with the other, and they should be one through a single composition [Col. 1736C], until those natural bonds are broken and, with the greatest pain, what had been joined is separated. Hence it is said: “There is no pain like the pain of those who are dying.”

These daughters, as they co-operated with God in man’s creation, so also did they co-operate in his just casting down. For man, “when he was in honour, did not understand” (Ps. 48), and therefore, expelled from paradise, he was subjected to the miseries of this world on account of the merit of his sin. And because in man’s fall the serpent, Adam, and Eve sinned in different ways, they were punished differently, so that whoever had transgressed more than another in guilt might be found to suffer more than another in punishment. Hence divine vengeance brought it about that Adam was punished by one curse, Eve by two, and the serpent by three. To Adam it was said: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 2). But to the woman he said: “You shall be subject to your husband, and in pain you shall give birth” (ibid.). To the serpent thus: “You shall eat the earth, and you shall go upon your breast; I shall place enmities between you and the woman, and you shall lie in wait for her heel, and she shall crush your head” (ibid.).

[Col. 1736D] The aforementioned daughters of the king, as they were not absent when God created man, were not absent when he punished the sinner. For him whom the Lord punished after the fall, before the fall he had threatened that he would punish in this manner if he sinned, as it is said: “On whatever day you eat, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2). Mercy co-operated, because the one who by sinning had made himself miserable was made mortal as a remedy for misery; for although it is misery to be miserable, it would be a most grievous burden for misery to be without end. The shortness of life is a remedy for the miserable, who are tormented more tolerably precisely because they die quickly. Justice was not absent there: for the one more deserving of punishment is punished more. Peace was present. For from the reason implanted in human nature man knew that he could be reconciled to God if, by worthily repenting, he recovered the peace which he had lost through sinning.

Hence the first parents had tunics of skin to cover their nakedness (Gen. 3), so that, through repentance, the ways of the human condition might return to peace with the Creator. The Lord had removed these daughters of the king far from the ways of men. These virtues had abandoned mankind; darkness succeeding them had covered the human race with clouds. Hence Hosea cried: “Nowhere truth, nowhere mercy; everywhere murder, everywhere theft” (Hos. 4:2).

There are four clouds, as we have said, and they are opposed to the aforesaid daughters of the king—that is, to the virtues. The first cloud is of darkness, the second of dew, the third of hail, the fourth of the shadow of death. The first was promising; the second deceiving; the third punishing; the fourth killing. The first was from the east; the second from the south, because it possessed a sufficient shadow; the third from the west, because it covered the light; the fourth from the north, because it had no light.

By the cloud of darkness are rightly understood those things which concealed truth. For Abel’s being killed (Gen. 4), and the ram being sacrificed in Isaac’s place—what else did all this signify, not openly but beneath a certain darkness, except the future incarnation of the Lord? By the cloud of dew may rightly be understood the learning of the philosophers, who, with a subtle kind of knowledge, disputed concerning the invisible and unknown things above as though they were things subject to the senses. But because such men attributed to themselves, and not to God, what wisdom they possessed, what was more just than that they should be deprived of the gift of him to whom, through the swelling of pride, they showed themselves ungrateful?

By the cloud of hail are understood the punishments which, according to the different kinds of sins, pressed upon the necks of the Jews under the state of the old law. Hence some, observing the harshness of the law, the burden of servile obligation, fell into this madness: to say that the giver of the law was not God but the prince of darkness. By the cloud of the shadow of death are understood sins, by whose demand all things tended toward death.

The first cloud was opposed to truth [Col. 1737C], the second to justice; for the philosophers forgot justice, or attributed to their own nature what they possessed by God’s gift. The third was opposed to mercy, the fourth to peace, because through the multitude of sins peace had departed from the hearts of sinners. Of the first cloud it is said: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17). Of the second it is said: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One” (Isa. 45); of the third we read: “Before him the clouds passed, hail and coals of fire” (Ps. 17); of the fourth it is written: “You have set a cloud before you, lest prayer pass through” (Lam. 3).

The world was wrapped in these clouds as in the darkness of errors. But the Lord, clothed in flesh, entered Egypt and illumined our darkness by the light of his presence. Therefore, when the aforesaid clouds had been removed as certain obstacles, the king’s four firstborn daughters came forth rejoicing: “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84).

The Church recalls this prophecy only in the fourth week of the Advent of the Lord, because in the preceding three she commemorates the longing of the ancient Fathers who desired Christ’s coming. Hence in the first is read the untying of the she-ass, by which the liberation of the synagogue was signified. In the second and third is expressed how greatly the Lord’s coming was awaited; and therefore in the second the Church sings, “People of Zion,” etc.; in the third, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” etc.

The same is signified by the seven vowel antiphons, each of which begins with O and closes with a word in the imperative—indeed, the supplicatory—mood; by these the desire and fervour of those awaiting him are openly revealed. And just as the idols of Egypt literally fell at the Lord’s coming, so spiritually the idols of souls fell when “the Dayspring from on high visited our weakness” (Luke 2). Hence the first antiphon says: “Come to teach us”; the second: “Come to free us”; the third: “Come to redeem”; the fourth: “Come and bring forth the captive”; the fifth: “Come [Col. 1738A] to enlighten”; the sixth and seventh: “Come to save.”

In the first, teaching is requested, by which the ignorance that was threefold may be put to flight. For man was ignorant of God, ignorant of himself, and ignorant of the virtues. But this ignorance, like an idol of Egypt, fell when the light shone in the darkness. In the second, it is requested that he free us from slavery, which was likewise threefold: slavery to the devil, to sin, and to debt—that is, to the punishment owed for sin. In the third, redemption is sought, and this in three ways: from the literal law, from toil, and from the enemy. In the fourth, that we may be brought forth from prison—that is, from hell, in whose mouth, middle, and lowest part certain persons were then held. In the fifth, we ask that he enlighten us, so that, enlightened by him, we may deserve the three graces of heavenly things through the eye of faith, and so that, when at last received into their fellowship, we may enjoy them fully. In the sixth and seventh salvation is doubled, signifying that through him both the mortality of the flesh and the flesh’s capacity for suffering will be removed from us. And as the Lord, clothed in the cloud of flesh, entered Egypt, and as, borne by clouds, he rose from Egypt into heaven, so he will come for judgment, separating grain from chaff, lambs from goats, good from evil, setting you at his right hand—Jesus Christ our Lord, who will come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON VI. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

“While all things held the middle of silence, and night in its course,” etc. (Wisdom 18). The aforesaid Scripture announced that time when the almighty Word of God came to us, speaking to us concerning our salvation: descending from the bosom and heart of the Father into the womb of the mother. For God, “who had spoken to the Fathers in many ways and by many means through the prophets, has in our days spoken to us in his Son” (Heb. 1), of whom he says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 3; 17). Hear him, I say—that is, obey him—you who wish to ascend from the valley of tears to the mountain of joys.

Therefore the Word of God came to us—the Word of God, the Son of God—from royal seats, humbling himself that he might exalt us, becoming poor that he might enrich us, becoming human that he might make us divine.
