He came to us, I say—but when? While all things held the middle of silence, in the night, after the cockcrow.

When the cocks first begin to crow—those which have crowed and are still to crow—there is, between the preceding cries and the cries that follow, a certain silence called *conticinium*. This *conticinium*, or silence, is intermediate between the earlier and later cries; and if anything happened then, while all things held the middle of silence, it would not improperly be said to happen.

In the night of this world, in its unseasonable and deep night, the prophets were like certain cocks, rousing the human race, deeply asleep, with their cries, and proclaiming also the sunrise. The Mass said in the most holy night at cockcrow represents this as well. Moses, like a cock, broke the silence of the unseasonable night and cried out: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren like myself; you shall hear him” (Deut. 18). “And every soul that does not hear that prophet shall be exterminated from his people.”

Another loud-crying cock cried again and said: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49). Isaiah cried out like the Lord’s cock; he cries, I say, and declares: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc. (Isa. 7). Jeremiah cried: “Behold, the Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31). Truly a man—the one who alone “did not walk in the counsel of the wicked” (Ps. 1), whom a woman encompassed in her womb, brought forth, and yet did not lose her integrity.

Daniel cried: “When the Holy of Holies comes, transgression shall cease,” etc. (Dan. 9). I pass over the other prophets, whom it would take long even to enumerate [Col. 1739A]. To them, as to cocks, the Lord gave understanding (Job 38), so that, knowing beforehand, they might proclaim the advent of the true light long before its rising. Therefore the cocks cried out, as if singing together and saying: “For those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, and for the people walking in darkness, a light shall rise” (Isa. 9).

These fell silent. The apostles also, who were like cocks destined to crow at the very twilight of the light, were still silent. Yet they were to cry out, and so greatly that “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18). Does he not seem to you a cock who says: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin”? (1 Cor. 15). And again: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13). All things held the middle silence: the prophets who had cried out, and the apostles who were to cry out. This silence was intermediate and mediating between the cries of both—that is, those who had cried and those who were to cry out for Christ.

[Col. 1739B] Therefore, while all things held the middle of silence, the almighty Word—that is, the Word of the Father—came from royal seats. And fittingly, in the midst of silence, the mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2), man coming to men, the immortal one coming to save mortals dead through death, arrived. Mindful also of his mediation, he “worked salvation in the midst of the earth,” in the midst between heaven and earth; reconciling, as it were, heaven and earth, raised up from the earth, he died on the cross.

Consider, then, the dispensation: in the middle he rises, in the middle he dies, in the middle he works salvation. The mystery of this matter also appears in the words: “while night in its course was making its middle journey, he came from royal seats.” What is this night? Perhaps it is the time in which, from the origin of the world until the end of the last age, the children of Adam live in this dark Egypt, enduring the heavy darkness of their ignorance and scarcely seeing one another. Do they not fail to see themselves when they do not see one another’s hearts in turn? Because of the darkness of hearts unseen, there is room for lying and deception, while those who lie and deceive conceal themselves in this night.

In the midst of this night came, to those sitting in darkness, that light which “enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1), destined truly to drive away every darkness when it “will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4). He had seen the middle course of this night who said: “Lord, I have heard,” etc., “you will revive your work in the midst of the years” (Hab. 3).

Moreover, if this interpretation displeases anyone, I do not argue contentiously; I gladly assent to a better opinion. Therefore, while all things held the middle of silence, while night in its course had reached the middle of its journey, your almighty Word came from royal seats. The Word came in silence; the Word came to those who were silent. Among men it is an urbane and courtly custom that, when a more honourable and powerful person wishes to speak, those standing around should keep silence. Thus, while Job was speaking, the leaders restrained their tongues and put their finger upon their mouths (Job 29).

Therefore, when the God of gods spoke, calling his land to faith from the rising of the sun to its setting (Ps. 49), the prophets are silent and fall quiet. Let the Word of God now come to those who are silent. Let us hear what the Lord God says to us: “Hear, Israel, the commandments of life, and write them in your heart as in a book, and he will give you a land flowing with milk and honey” (Deut. 4).

These words of the Lord show us three things: by what name we ought to be called; what we ought to do; and what reward we ought to expect. Our name is great: nothing is greater or more excellent than this name. For we are called Christians from Christ. What more could be conferred upon the creature than to be called by the name of its Creator? If, then, we agree in name, let us agree also in reality. For it is said: “He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2).

Great is that by which we are named here; and not slight is this. Here we are called Israel, which means “a man seeing God,” according to the manner of seeing God. But how can anyone see God? Is it not written: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1)? And: “Shall a man live and not see me?” (Exod. 33). Yet it must be known that, although a man has two bodily eyes, by which he cannot see God, since God is spirit—nor even angels or souls—he has two inner eyes, faith and love. By these he sees God “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13), so that afterwards he may see him in the reality itself, which is eternal life. For “this is eternal life: that they may know you” (John 17).

Since that vision is, as it were, the merit, and the other the reward—when we shall see face to face (1 Cor. 13)—behold, from the name is shown what we ought to do. It is said: “Hear the commandments,” and not only hear, but “write them in your heart.” But perhaps some among us say: “How can one write who does not know letters or how to compose books?” It is not commanded that you write on parchment, but in your heart. So that it may first become clear how you can write in your heart [Col. 1740B], listen to the preparation of a book, in order that you too may strive to prepare all things in your heart.

First, parchment is given to the scraper, so that with a scraper he may remove every superfluity, grease, roughness, and stain. Then pumice is applied, so that what scraping could not remove—namely hairs and other minute things—may be erased by pumice. In addition, before writing, a rule is needed so that the line may not be drawn crookedly.

So you too, as with a scraper, cut your flesh with the bitterness of repentance; cut down the thickets of sins, so that whatever sins you incurred through pleasure of the flesh you may erase through punishment of that same flesh. Remove greed, lust, envy, and such things from your heart. Mortify your flesh; undertake discipline. But how few do these things! When fasting is prescribed, one excuses himself: “How could I fast while others eat?” And if he is commanded to undertake discipline, he replies: “My nature cannot endure it; I should die at once.” If he is commanded to give a coin, he replies that he will have none until the month is over.

Behold, the parchment has been scraped; all criminal things have been removed. In this way Job, Christ’s athlete, acted when he scraped his sores with a potsherd (Job 2). But because there still remain other things without which this life is not lived—things called venial, because they readily obtain pardon—pumice is still needed: that is, almsgiving and prayer. For these extinguish such venial matters as laughing excessively and occasionally drinking more than is sufficient; for continual excess would be criminal.

But before you write in this book, take up a rule: the examples of the holy Fathers Peter, Paul, and Stephen the martyr. Direct your heart by these rules, that it may be straight and not crooked. The heart is crooked in those who murmur against the Lord: praising in one respect and blaspheming in another; blaspheming in adversity and praising in prosperity. “For he will praise you when you do him good” (Ps. 48). Do not murmur in this way, having a crooked heart. Consider whether it pleases God your Creator for you to contradict his own disposition. See that “a father chastises the son whom he receives” (Heb. 12).

Have a straight heart, blessing God in all things, knowing that if he sends you adversity, it is for correction on account of sin; if prosperity, it is so that you may give to others, etc. Therefore always bless him, saying with the Prophet: “I will bless the Lord at every time,” etc. (Ps. 33); “Rejoice in the Lord,” etc. (Ps. 96), so that the Lord too may bless you. “How good the God of Israel is to those who are upright of heart,” not perverse (Ps. 27). “With the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverted” (Ps. 17).

Now the heart is prepared. Nothing remains except that I teach you what to write. On the first leaf write: “Your God is one” (Deut. 6), that is: believe in and love the almighty Father. On the second part of the same leaf write: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. 20). Believe that the Son, sent as less than the Father according to his humanity, is equal to him according to divinity. For one dishonours the Father who does not believe that he has a Son proper to him and equal to himself, as though he were powerless or envious. Third, believe in the Holy Spirit, in whom rest is given—here, in tranquillity of mind, and in the future, in blessedness. Write these things on the first leaf, which pertain to the worship of God.

On the second, write the things that follow, which pertain to one’s neighbour. The first of these: “Honour your father and mother” (ibid.), not only by defending them with words, but by supplying what they need. But we not only fail to show them the reverence due, or to provide necessities, but we despoil them of their own possessions.

> “The son, before the day, inquires into his father’s years.”  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I

Yet the reward is overturned when it is said: “That you may be long-lived upon the earth” (ibid.). We see this fulfilled in the land of the dying, yet it is promised “upon the earth.” This is the land of the dying, where no one descends unless he is dying or dead. How will one love strangers if he does not love his own?

Write fifth: “You shall not kill” (ibid.), so that you kill neither in body nor in mind. For you can be a murderer in will, so that you kill neither body nor soul. You kill your neighbour’s soul when you make yourself an example of evil and lead him into error: you kill his soul. Write sixth: “You shall not commit theft” (ibid.), that is, cease not only to be a violent extortioner, but also a more fraudulent usurer. Who can more cunningly steal his neighbour’s goods than one who, having lent forty, and with the debtor making no protest, demands fortyfold repayment for the forty?

Write seventh: “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid.): do not know a woman unless she is joined to you in marriage. Whatever is done in any other way is criminal. And even in lawful intercourse you can exceed the bounds. Eighth: “You shall not bear false witness” (ibid.). Here swearing is forbidden, since it leads to perjury.

The ninth verse is: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s property—neither ox, nor ass, nor field, nor vineyard” (ibid.). Was this not prohibited above? No: there it was the act; here it is the will. “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife”—indeed, this too was there: “You shall not commit adultery.” For there it was the act; here it is the will, which is indeed criminal if it grows so great that you can say: “Nothing remains in me, if I had the opportunity.” Why do you burn so fiercely with lust? Can the one woman you have not suffice you?

Behold, the book has been prepared and inscribed. The writing is good, the writing of God; but the devil lies in wait like an ape. “Turn your eyes away” (Song 6); immediately he approaches, puts on his hand, erases what you wrote, and adds his own letters. Thus the devil, unless you are on guard, lays the contrary things over them. Therefore “keep your heart with all vigilance,” as Solomon says (Prov. 4), lest the ancient enemy be able to uproot what you have planted.

Therefore add to the book, as a strengthening agent, the grace of God, which is at hand for all if they consent. You can carry this book with you, and will need no bearer. This book is small enough; with closed eyes it can be examined by both cleric and layperson. If you write this book, hear what and how greatly Truth itself, which neither lies nor can lie, promises you.

[Col. 1741D] “I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey.” Milk is a liquid proceeding from flesh; honey, from heaven—that is, from the temperate air. Thus in us are two natures: flesh and soul. By “flowing,” understand full and perfect abundance. That is: “I will give you the fullness of blessedness,” with respect both to body and soul. May Jesus Christ, our Lord and our judge, make us inhabitants of this land when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON VII. ON THE APPEARANCE OF THE LORD, OR EPIPHANY

(It appears among the sermons of Hildebert of Le Mans. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI, col. 409, sermon 14.)

## SERMON VIII. ON SAINT VINCENT. To Those in the Cloister

“To the victor I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise [Col. 1742A] of my God” (Rev. 2). You have heard the promise, and the person to whom the promise was made. For eating from the tree is promised to the victor. But from whom it is promised, and at what time it was made, is not evident from the sequence of the words. The one who promises is a prince, for such is the promise of princes. By their exhortations they encourage the heart, or hearts, of those fighting, saying: “Fight, act manfully, and strengthen your hearts” (Deut. 31).

Thus the Father says: “To the victor I will give to eat,” etc. This prince himself is not the prince of this world, nor is it his promise or his sharing in it, because he was cast from paradise by the Lord. Hence: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10); and Isaiah: “How you have fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning!” (Isa. 14). Who, then, is the one who promises? It is the Lord—the Father, namely. For the promise concerns the Son, who is the tree of life in the midst of paradise. The Son is life.

But he who formerly was life only with the Father—hence “in him was life”—became a tree planted beside streams of water [Col. 1742B] (Ps. 1), that is, beside the failings of men, so that he who had formerly been invisible might become visible to us in human flesh, as the sun becomes visible in a wheel. Hence he is now not merely tree, nor merely life, but tree and life—that is, God and man. God the Father promises this tree to the victor, saying: “I will give you to eat from the tree of life.” He says to the conqueror, “I give you.” This word, “I will give,” is deferred; but “I give” is favourable: the conqueror and fighter can say it. For it is given in the homeland, but promised to the victor on the way.

But if we consider the sense of the words more subtly, he both gives to the victor and promises to the victor: now sacramentally, and in the future without satiety. Hence: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). He gave this tree as a price; he also gave it to us as provision for the journey, which he promises as reward. Thus we have seen who promises, to whom, and what is promised.

At what time this promise was made may be understood from the surface of the history. For John the Evangelist, still a young man, fled at the time of the Passion after casting aside the linen cloth (Mark 14); but later, when he had grown old and had been exiled to the island of Patmos (Rev. 1), there he saw his Apocalypse, in which this is contained:

“And write to the angel of Ephesus: ‘To the victor I will give to eat,’” etc. And this occurred in the time of grace. This can also be proved by reasoning. For there are three times: before the law, under the law, and under grace. Before the law no one fought; under the law no one resisted; therefore in those times no one conquered. Before the law, indeed, everyone believed whatever pleased him to be lawful. Therefore no one fought against the devil; rather, each willingly followed him, and thus no one was a conqueror. The promise was not therefore made then.

Nor was it made under the time of the law. For the law only revealed sins (Rom. 3), but brought no one to perfection (Heb. 7); rather, the devil dragged every person unwillingly with him. Therefore no one resisted, no one was consequently victorious, and the promise was not then made. It was therefore made in the time of grace. And because we have been bound by him so long, how shall we be able to be freed from his [Col. 1742D] dominion and resist him? By a threefold confidence: the Father’s promise, the Son’s exhortation, and the Holy Spirit’s consolation.

“While all things held the middle of silence, your Word came from royal seats” (Wisdom 18). There are only three things that can be silent: God, angel, and man. God was silent when he seemed, as it were, to dissemble, as though not caring about humanity’s liberation. Or, since he was an enemy to man, did he not provide for man? Man, as though affected by long weariness, ceased to cry out. And so, while all things held the middle of silence, your almighty Word came from royal seats to redeem those who are in the world.

For he was life and light: unfading life and incomprehensible light. Therefore life and light came: life came to give life by removing death; light came to give light by putting darkness to flight. Thus he freed us from sin and the yoke of demons. Therefore your Word came, etc. The Father speaks, the Son speaks, the Holy Spirit speaks. The Father speaks words of promise; the Son, words of exhortation; the Holy Spirit, words of consolation. Thus the Son speaks in exhortation, the Father in promise, the Holy Spirit in consolation.

Do you wish to hear words of exhortation? “As I live, says the Lord, I do not will the death of the sinner, but life, that he may be converted and live” (Ezek. 33). “As I live,” as though the mystery of the living God were in the law. This is not the Lord’s oath, but sarcasm—that is, hostile mockery—as though he said: “The Jews thought they held me in death when they killed me; but I rose again. Therefore, as though in mockery, he said: ‘As I live’; and therefore I do not will the death of the sinner,” etc. Great is the exhortation.

Do you wish to hear the Holy Spirit’s consolation? “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). Trusting in this threefold confidence, we must fight so that we may conquer. For we have three enemies: the flesh, the world, and the devil. The flesh is a domestic enemy and therefore more to be feared; the world is a sophistical enemy and therefore to be guarded against; the devil is an ancient enemy [Col. 1743B] and therefore more to be hated. The flesh suggests pleasures; the world, vanities; the devil, wicked things. The flesh binds us; the world bruises us; the devil kills us. The flesh suggests lust; the world, greed; the devil, pride. The flesh lowers us below ourselves through lust; the world draws us outside ourselves through greed; the devil raises us above ourselves through pride.

The flesh’s suggestion must be greatly feared, for it binds us. We do not dare to kill it, but are bound to supply it with necessary nourishment. Of this the Apostle says: “Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). And that strong soldier of Christ, Job (ch. 7), said: “O guardian of men, why have you set me as your adversary, and why have I become burdensome to myself?” For he had experienced the inward warfare between flesh and spirit. This is Samson’s Delilah, concerning whom Solomon says: “From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth” (Mic. 7).

Of the second enemy it is said: “Whoever loves the world is an enemy of God” (Jas. 4). This is that Nebuzaradan who, besieging Jerusalem, set guards at the gate so that none of the citizens might be permitted to leave (Jer. 52). This is the world, which besieges the gates of the soul: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. When the soul sometimes goes out through the gates of the eyes, it sees a woman to desire her; it sees alluring variety of vain furnishings and limitless wealth, etc. Why go through each one? It cannot go out without finding the soldiers of the world.

But if it goes out through the gates of the ears, the world offers it empty tales, dressed-up lies, and endless perjuries. If it goes out through the gate of the nostrils, the world displays before it scented preparations coloured with musk; it finds the air corrupted with various fragrances, perfume compounded from costly spices. But if it goes out through the gate of taste, the world offers it bread made with every art of baking, wine excellent in fragrance, flavour, and colour, and whatever dainty thing earth, air, or sea possesses, proportionately prepared with salted foods. But if it goes out through the gates of the hands [Col. 1743D], it finds the softness of costly clothing. One cushion on which to lean does not suffice; several are heaped together, that it may immerse itself wholly among them. At the touch of another’s little flesh, it is delighted. Behold: through whatever gate it goes out, the enemy deals sophistically with it.

There remains the ancient enemy, and therefore he is more to be feared: the hammer of the whole earth. He suggests wicked things to us. But how shall we be able to resist this wicked trinity—namely, flesh, world, and devil? Not by ourselves at all. What then must be done? We have the ineffable Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—by whose help we can conquer. Through the Father we conquer the devil; through the Son, the world; through the Holy Spirit, the flesh. Will not one of these suffice to resist? Certainly not. The whole Trinity is necessary; otherwise we cannot resist it except by faith and help.

But what do we have from the Father against the devil, from the Son against the world, and from the Holy Spirit against the flesh? Listen: by the Father’s benefit and counsel we resist the devil; by the Son’s word and example, the world; by the overshadowing and burning of the Holy Spirit, the flesh. Do you wish to hear the Father’s benefit? “He sent his Son,” who bound the strong devil (Matt. 12). He gave us counsel when he said: “This is my beloved Son; hear him” (Matt. 17), and no other.

The Son taught us by word: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. 19); and elsewhere: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc. (Matt. 5). He taught by example when, born from a poor little Virgin, laid in a manger, wrapped in humble cloths, he had nowhere to lay his head (Matt. 8). Poor women also, who followed him, supplied him with necessities out of their own substance. By the Spirit’s overshadowing: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). By the burning [Col. 1744B] of charity he repels the incentives of the flesh, just as the poetic woman repelled summer heat with heat.

> “[Another] supplied thyme and fragrant herbs to the reapers.”  
> —[Note: Col. 1743D; Virgil, *Eclogues* II.]

This faith—namely, in the Holy Trinity—is required in baptism, so that each person may be able to resist the wicked trinity. Therefore God will give all these things to the victor to eat from the tree of life, etc.; thus also to blessed Vincent as conqueror, for he conquered all these things. No testimony is stronger than that borne by enemies: his very torturers openly confessed, “We are conquered.” Therefore he gives him to eat from the tree of life, which is in the midst of paradise.

He rightly says “in the midst,” because there are other trees which eat this tree. Hence: “The trees of the field and the cedars of Lebanon shall be filled” (Ps. 103), and shall eat. For the root of the tree, the vine of Sorek and its branches, the shrubs covering the mountains, the trees of the field bearing every fruit in the house of God, and the pomegranates likened to the cheeks of the bride (Song 4)—of these it is not necessary to speak individually.

Therefore to you, who keep watch in attendance upon this martyr [Col. 1744C], the eating of this tree is promised. For he left you heirs in his contest; and lest you think I speak flatteringly, you are martyrs. For the martyrdom you endure in the cloister is graver than that accomplished by the sword. The latter is material and momentary; yours spiritual and lasting, and therefore more dangerous. For the rigor of your order, unless it is softened, is martyrdom to you. The remembrance of past sins and love are like a sword passing through your souls. Understand the temptations which you endure. Of this sword it is said: “And a sword shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2).

Therefore to you, who are already conquerors of two enemies—the flesh and the world—the eating of this tree is promised.

Yet there remains combat with the third enemy, namely the devil. You have renounced the world; in accordance with the tenor of the Rule, you have withheld much from your flesh. Only the ancient enemy remains, whose food is delicate. He does not eat [Col. 1744D] coarse hay, but the subtlest and finest, like an ox. This hay is the religious monk, or anyone made lean by fasts and pale by afflictions and nightly vigils. He must therefore be resisted vigorously; but he cannot be conquered without prayer. God must therefore be entreated to grant us victory over these enemies, so that we may be found worthy to eat of the tree of life—may he deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns now and for ever. Amen.

## SERMON IX. ON THE HYPOAPANTE OF THE LORD, OR ON THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN. To Those in the Cloister.

“He was offered, because he willed it” (Isa. 53). How often was the Lord offered because he himself willed it? First he was offered in the Temple; afterwards, on the wood. First, as a child, he was offered by his parents (Luke 2); afterwards, as one of perfect age, he offered himself for his parents. The first offering was for purification; the last, for sacrifice. Yet in both cases he was offered because he himself willed it. For just as “he did whatever he willed” (Ps. 134), so he did everything that he did because he willed it.

Yet the prophet, speaking of the offering of sacrifice, after saying beforehand, “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter,” etc. (Isa. 53), as though expressing the chief cause of the whole Passion, concluded the foregoing words thus: “He was offered, because he willed it.” With all due respect to the prophet, however, this seems more expressly said of the offering for purification, precisely because it adds, “because he himself willed it.” For although he was born, circumcised, offered, baptized, and suffered because he willed it, each of these may nevertheless be more expressly distinguished by its own qualification, in this manner: he was circumcised because he ought to have been; offered because he willed it; baptized because it was beneficial; and suffered because it was necessary.

Certainly, as a little child he was born of a woman, made [Col. 1745B] under the Law. So that he might not abolish but fulfil the Law, he was, as it were, bound to be circumcised, since the Law compelled the circumcision of the little children among the children of Israel, threatening the uncircumcised with the penalty of death when it said: “The soul that has not circumcised the flesh of its foreskin shall perish from the people of Israel” (Gen. 17). Nor was there anything in the letter of the Law by which Christ could be excused if he had remained uncircumcised. If he said, “I have no sin; I have no need of the remedy of circumcision,” he would not thereby be excused according to the Law, because it had not added this exception.

But according to the Law he ought not to have been offered on the day of purification; indeed, the Law itself seems to exclude him from purification and from the offering made for it. For it is written in the Law: “A woman who, having received seed, gives birth to a male,” etc. (ibid.), as though it openly said: “Do not approach purification, Lord Jesus: you are free from sin, cleansing the hearts of your own by faith; you were conceived without seed and born of the Holy Spirit. Wait until you offer yourself for the world. Do not approach, most holy Virgin, [Col. 1745C] for you are neither properly a woman nor did you give birth after receiving seed.”

[Note: [Col. 1745D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XI, ch. 7.]

For a woman is properly called, as it were, *mollier* [“softer”], one who experiences softness, who has already undergone the female conditions of her body. Thus, although the Law seemed positively to forbid it, he was offered not from obligation but because he willed it. Why did he will it? Because in this way he taught us; for every action of Christ is a lesson for the Christian. He taught us to add voluntary works beyond those owed; for the less obligatory they are, the more welcome they are.

He was baptized because it was beneficial: by the touch of his body he imparted regenerative power to the waters. He suffered because it was necessary—that is, it was more fitting to redeem us in this way.

[Note: [Col. 1745D] Bede on Luke, ch. 10; Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XIII, ch. 10.]

Another means by which God could redeem us was indeed possible, but none was more fitting. For nothing could equally move us to know God as the fact that he laid down his life for us. This love alone moves the foot of those returning from Babylon.

These things, expounded simply in this manner, nourish us, but do not yet build us up. Understood morally, however, the things done today concerning the Lord both nourish and build up, especially contemplatives. They do not, divided in two, serve God in part and the world in part; nor, occupied with saving sacrifices, do they offer themselves as a whole burnt offering, “a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. 12). For what was done today concerning the Lord is read as having been done by his parents. But contemplatives are his parents. Hence he himself, stretching out his hand toward the disciples, said: “These are my brothers,” etc. (Matt. 12).

But although many things were done, we select four to investigate. First, that he was offered because he willed it (Luke 8 [an erroneous citation as printed]); second, that they offered for him “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Luke 2); third, that Simeon received him in his arms; fourth, the devotion of the faithful, which devised the carrying of lights. These build up the contemplative man: [Col. 1746A] thus one must pass to Rachel’s embraces, and thus remain there. For by these four things four stages of religious life are indicated: beginning, manner, progress, and end. The voluntary offering indicates the beginning of religious life; the birds offered, its manner; Simeon’s carrying, its progress; and the lights carried, its end.

Certainly, the vow of religious life and continence is imposed upon no one. Moses clothed his brother Aaron, on the day his hands were consecrated, in holy garments—except for the linen breeches, which Aaron put on himself (Lev. 8). Of the same matter Truth himself says: “Not all receive this saying. Let him who can receive it, receive it” (Matt. 19). Therefore the beginning of religious life and continence is voluntary: it is said, “Make vows”—this belongs to the will—“and fulfil them” (Ps. 75)—this, after the vow, belongs to necessity. Elsewhere Christ also declares that this beginning is voluntary, saying: “If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have,” etc. (Matt. 19). And elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow [Col. 1746B] me” (Matt. 16), locating the beginning of his perfection and renewal in the human will. As Christ was offered because he willed it, so anyone entering the strictness of an Order offers himself because he wills it.

The birds, however, express the manner of religious life that follows upon the offering. Under the Law the Lord willed that only these birds should be offered to him: the turtledove and the dove. Behold, there are two birds here—and two are enough: there are two parts of a human being, soul and flesh. Let the soul be simple and innocent; let the flesh be unspotted and continent. Behold, there are two sacrifices here, and they are enough. We shall pass over the application of the turtledove to the flesh and of the dove to the spirit, because it is more frequently heard and more often read.

[Note: [Col. 1746D] St Bernard, sermon 59 on the *Song of Songs*.]

We state only this concerning the turtledove: once it has lost its mate, it never thereafter perches except on a dry branch. What an exquisite seat continence has, if it perches upon dry poverty. The book of experience has taught each of us how friendly the dryness of food is to continence, and how opposed to it are softness and gluttonous excess. Review the whole [Col. 1746C] life of the Saviour, from the Virgin’s womb to the cross’s gallows: you will find in him nothing but the marks of poverty. Not without reason did the Lord’s discourse on the mountain, which is the teaching of all religious life, begin from poverty: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5). Nothing is freer, nothing safer, than poverty. Whoever gathers riches carries fire in his bosom; whoever seeks riches sleeps with a serpent. Riches, as someone says, are acquired with labour, possessed with fear, and never lost without pain.

How elegantly the philosopher mocked riches:

[Note: [Col. 1746D] Crates of Thebes; Jerome, book II against Jovinianus.]

He had sold his possessions, reduced their price to a weight of gold, and cast it into the sea, saying: “Go to ruin, most ruinous riches! I shall drown you, lest I be drowned by you.” “Who is this man, that we may praise him?” How sweet a vehicle the dry branch of poverty is to the righteous man was known to him who said: “I chose to be cast down in the house of God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83). And elsewhere: “Better is a little for the righteous than the many riches of sinners” (Ps. 36).

[Note: [Col. 1746D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XII, ch. 7.]

Nor have we thought it right to pass over this concerning the dove: some doves, with a change in the position of their neck, change their colour as well. One colour appears on the neck when it is turned to the left, another when it is turned to the right. Hence some think that the dove (*columba*) is named from the neck (*collum*). So too the contemplative becomes all things to all persons according to place and time, in order to gain all. The Apostle possessed this vicarious variety of colours when he said: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5). He spoke wisdom among the perfect; but among the lesser he judged that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2). He seemed to be of one colour in one direction and another in the other. This is the ladder on which Jacob saw angels [Col. 1747A] ascending and descending (Gen. 28): men are lifted above themselves in contemplation, and place themselves beneath themselves by condescending to the lesser.

Nor is it without significance that two young birds of each kind were offered. In these are figured two classes of contemplatives. Certainly, just as there are two branches of contemplation—reading and prayer—in which the whole meditation of the contemplative is occupied, so there are some who devote more effort to prayer and apply themselves less to reading; these are the cloistered. There are others who keep watch over reading and pray less often; these are the scholars.

After this follows the matter of progress, which is marked by Simeon’s carrying. Three persons are recorded as carrying the Lord: the Virgin in her womb, Simeon in his arms, and finally Joseph on his shoulders when he fled into Egypt. This is the progress of religious life: that first a man should be a righteous hearer, then a teacher, and finally, if the Lord calls him, a pastor. For nine months the Virgin carried the Lord in her womb; nor was this all when he came forth into the light, since [Col. 1747B] he was not carried by Simeon until the fortieth day.

Consider this, good man, you who strive to imitate Christ. If a suggestion arises in your heart such as this: “I have lived religiously a long time; I am noble, well-known, and skilled in outward matters. My knowledge is sufficient to instruct subjects. I ought to have been superior and abbot rather than that man, and to honour the dignity of the episcopal chair”—say to your soul: “Soul, my hour has not yet come; Christ is not yet fully strengthened so as to be carried in the hands of an old man.” Simeon was old: grow old in religious life before you are brought into public view. Moreover, the name Simeon means “hearing sorrow.” And you too, if you are drawn into public affairs, if you are called, hear what ought to make you sorrowful, and say: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5).

Therefore, cloistered men, we must not rise except after long sitting. “It is vain for you to rise before light; rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126): thus it is not done without God’s command. For Simeon too came in the Spirit into the Temple. Why should you go out from light into darkness, from bed into the mire’s wallowing-place, from paradise into the field of Damascus, where righteous Abel perished? Why do you wish, instead of saffron, to embrace dung? Far be this from you; may it never happen to you. Therefore you ought to be drawn to the chair with much greater difficulty. If teaching alone among inward things is so perilous, it is grievous to carry upon one’s shoulders a child now somewhat grown.

It is a perilous thing to descend into Egypt, to the manifold monster of gods. Yet the Egyptians are men of great flesh: seated over pots of meat, they think gain is godliness. From Egypt the Lord called his Son (Matt. 2), who served in mud and brick (Exod. 1). Do not return there, son of God, unless, after the likeness of Christ, Egypt’s idols fall before your face. And do so only when God specially calls you; for an angel warned Joseph in a dream to go into Egypt (Matt. 2).

[Col. 1747D] There remains the end. The end of holy conduct is the same as that of life: holiness is useless unless it ends with life. Hence: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). For the end, not the battle, crowns. Thus the Lord judges “the ends of the earth” (1 Sam. 2). As a figure of this, he commanded the tail of the sacrifice to be offered to himself, and Aaron wore a hyacinth-blue *hypodyte* [undergarment] (Lev. 8). The carrying of lights impresses this perseverance upon the minds of those who carry them. For no one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, or extinguishes it; rather, once lit, he sets it on a lampstand, so that, shining without cease, it may illumine darkness with its brightness (Matt. 5).

Or, because Christ is signified in the wax taper, the faithful are today instructed by the very lights in the example of Christ’s perseverance, as though we were told: “See what you carry in your hands: you carry a type of Christ. Carry his faith in your mind, confession of his name in your mouth, and imitation in your work.” Indeed, three substances in the one person of Christ are signified by the burning light. [Col. 1748A] By the wax Christ’s flesh is signified; for the bee, which is not dissolved into lust and is not corrupted by sexual union, produces wax. Thus Christ’s flesh was made neither “of bloods” nor of the will of the flesh, but from the inviolate Virgin, from God. The wick hidden in the wax is the soul, sheltered in the dwelling-place of flesh. The fire consuming both is his divinity, because “our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12). Hence Simeon also called Christ “a light made for revelation to the Gentiles and glory of the people Israel” (Luke 2).

Therefore this is carried in the hands today. An example is set before those who carry it, but especially before the contemplative: an example of patience even unto death, and death upon a cross (Phil. 2). Jesus was sent only “to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 10). Therefore, when Jesus was raised upon the cross, while the children of Israel stood before him and said, “Let him now come down from the cross, and we shall believe him” (Matt. 15 [as printed]), why, hearing that he could readily accomplish the purpose for which he had come, did he not come down? Why, Lord Jesus, by an easy descent from the cross, did the fullness of the Jews not enter, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter without their blindness? (Rom. 11.) There is some reason, though it is hidden from us. Why did you not heed them? Something is enclosed; but, Lord, open it to us, so that you also may do likewise.

You, I say, men of contemplation, are fastened to the cross with the Lord. Because you wish to go after him, you take up your cross—namely, the cross of obedience and penitence—so that each may say: “Behold, I am gathering two pieces of wood” (1 Kings 17), by which our cross is joined together. I dare to say that the contemplative man hangs upon a stricter cross than Christ, because it endures longer and restrains him in more respects. Let us compare Christ’s cross with the contemplative’s cross, and what we say will become clear. Christ’s limbs were nailed fast so that they could not perform their functions; yet his tongue, free from crucifixion, spoke, for there he prayed for his crucifiers. Into the hands [Col. 1748C] of the Father he commended his spirit (Luke 23). But the contemplative man has bound all his limbs so tightly with the nails of obedience that not even his tongue may speak; even in necessities, he assists his mute sister by a gesture of the hand.

What, then, must we do upon this cross? Certainly what Christ did upon his: we must die upon it, because Christ died upon his. If the world makes an uproar, if demons and one’s own flesh do so, and say: “Come down from the cross; you are young, and you can climb upon it in old age,” say to it: “Nothing is more certain than death; nothing more uncertain than the hour of death. I shall keep watch and stand upon the cross until, bowing my head, I yield up my spirit.” Nor should any one of you lose heart if the flesh, as though unwillingly, suffers such great things, lest what it does as though unwillingly be done to no purpose. For the time will come when our flesh will rejoice over these things, when it will delight to remember them.

Nature once consulted its spirit, as a father, concerning a remedy for its wounds, and heard from the Spirit: “Son, you cannot be healed unless you allow yourself to be bound, cut, and [Col. 1748D] burned.” And it said: “I consent, Father.” It was therefore bound with the cords of the Rule which it had undertaken. It is cut and burned while it lives in many vigils, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness. It necessarily cries to the spirit: “Father, release me; release me, Father.” The compassionate spirit stands by and says: “A little while, son, and you will be released. Remember that this was done with your consent.” The Father does not release it until the healing hand has omitted nothing required by the circumstances. So too our flesh now cries out in certain matters, until, through long habit of living in this way, what had been harsh becomes light. Then it will rejoice that it was bound and will say: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in my God” (Ps. 83).

Therefore act manfully and be strengthened (Deut. 31), carrying the lesser light in your hands and the greater light in your minds, until Jesus Christ—our Lord, our judge, who will come to judge the living and the dead and the world through fire—leads you to the inaccessible light.

## SERMON X. AT THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST, OR ON ASH WEDNESDAY.

[Col. 1749A]

“When you fast, wash your face, anoint your head with oil, lest you appear to men to be fasting” (Matt. 7 [as printed]). If the words you have heard from my mouth were thought to be ours, I should seem ridiculous. For it is absurd and detestable that one who is fasting should have a washed face and be smeared with ointment. Rather, it belongs to one fasting to seek filth, sit in ashes and haircloth, wear dirty garments, mortify the flesh, reduce one’s food, have a sad and pallid countenance, not wash one’s face, and not sit at luxurious tables, one’s head anointed, with the wealthy.

Thus that farmer in the Gospel (Luke 18 [as printed]), when he was commanded to cut down the tree, said: “Leave it this year, until I dig about it and put on manure, so that it may bear fruit.” He does not say, “I shall put on ointment,” but “manure and filth.” Let us hear a similar saying from that supreme wise man, Solomon, whose wisdom all admired. He says: “The eyes of the wise man [Col. 1749B] are always in his head” (Eccl. 2). What is more foolish? What more astonishing? For the fool has eyes in his head just as the wise man does. Both Solomon’s words and those proposed by us seem words of vanity. Yet they are words of truth and wisdom, and contrary to vanity. Why, then, does Truth speak so childishly? Why does that Wise Man, whose wisdom was admired by all, speak so foolishly?

John Scotus says: Scripture customarily speaks to the “God-seeing” kind of humanity, not to the foot-following kind. For, as he himself says, there is a twofold kind of humanity: the foot-following kind and a certain God-seeing kind. The foot-following kind consists of those who cannot know God through an understanding of the Scriptures, but somehow track his footsteps through the visible things of this world. For through the visible things of this world they behold God’s invisible things (Rom. 1). The aforementioned sayings are not set before this kind of humanity, but before the God-seeing kind: those who see God through understanding of Scripture, such as scholars [Col. 1749C] and learned cloistered persons. They are set before them so that they may labour over the proper meaning of these words, passing beyond their surface, and thus know that beneath the childlike surface of the words something else lies within and something else sounds outwardly.

Therefore, as we sit at the rich man’s sumptuous table, already, as it were, filled with varied and precious dishes, the master of the household sets before us a small and lowly dish to relieve our disgust—namely, a nut. But a nut has an inedible shell and within it an edible, sweet, and pleasant kernel. Let us therefore crack the nut in order to obtain the kernel; let us cast away the leaves in order to find the fruit. We say, then, that beneath this surface of words we should dig a well in order to draw living water. Let us do as the prophet did, to whom it was said: “Man of God, there is death in the pot”; he added a little flour, so that the pot might be sweetened (2 Kings 4). Let us also add the little flour of mystical understanding, so that the bark and surface of the letter may be sweetened.

We say, [Col. 1749D] therefore, that three things are set before us on this surface of words: to fast, to wash the face, and to anoint the head. These are the three things in which the perfection of human religious life consists. What are they? To turn away from evil, to do good, to refer both to God, and to attribute to God all that we have. Behold all that human religious life contains. To fast, then, is to turn away from evil, for abstinence from vices is customarily denoted by the word “fasting”; to wash the face is to do good; and to anoint the head is to attribute both to God, attributing to oneself nothing but evil.

But perhaps you may say: “This exposition is brief; it is not enough for us. You could dig the well more deeply and draw living water; you have offered us only gravel.” Let us see, then, whether it can be expounded more aptly, more usefully, and more keenly. As we said, three things are proposed there; yet they are set forth antithetically—that is, as opposites—to those things which the ancient enemy first persuaded the first human being to do, his threefold persuasion. First, he persuaded him to show God; second, to hide his face from the face of God walking in Paradise at midday; third, to eat from the tree of life. Here, conversely, it is said: there, that he should pierce his head; here, that he should anoint it; there, that he should veil his face; here, that he should wash it; there, that he should eat; here, that he should fast. We must believe him who commands fasting, etc., and not him who urged the contrary. Hear the Father: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Matt. 3); reject that other one. Observe also that the manner of fasting, and the manner in which one ought not to fast, are here set forth threefold.

The manner of fasting is to wash the face and anoint the head. The manner in which one ought not to fast is shown when it says: “Lest you appear to men to be fasting.” Thus there is a praiseworthy fast and a condemnable fast. The condemnable fast is that which people see; but there are four fasts which people see. For the sick person fasts; the disgusted person fasts; the miser fasts; and the hypocrite fasts. The sick person fasts in order to recover health; the disgusted person, in order to regain appetite; the miser, in order to save money; the hypocrite, in order to appear holy. Medicine causes the sick person’s fast; gluttony, the disgusted person’s; stinginess, the miser’s; vainglory, the hypocrite’s. The physician sees and approves the sick person’s fast; Epicurus, the disgusted person’s; the heir who has been instituted, the miser’s; the public, the hypocrite’s. The sick person’s fast is health; the disgusted person’s fast is gluttony; the miser’s is stinginess; the hypocrite’s is feigned religion. These fasts, even if not all are dangerous, as is the sick person’s, are nevertheless fruitful.

Therefore, when you fast, do not appear to people to be fasting; but when you fast, wash your face and anoint your head. These words are as though the Father spoke directly to the Son, as though the Son had proposed and said: “Father, you have blotted out my iniquity and washed me. But I still ask: ‘Wash me yet more from my iniquity’” (Ps. 50). The Father answers: “I have washed you, son, in the washing of regeneration; therefore now wash your own face.” But the son may say: “How shall I wash my face? I have no water. If, however, you wish me to wash my face, act with me for good; for I am not sufficient for myself. All the good things I possess I attribute to you, and to myself only evils.” But the Lord commands: “When you have done good things, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke 17). Hence Paul says: “It is not of the human being who wills or runs, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. 9).

Therefore, hearing his son say, “I have no water and thirst for it, like a stag that longs for springs of water” (Ps. 41), the Father calls and invites him thus: “You who thirst, come to the waters, and draw with joy from the fountains of the Saviour” (Isa. 12). There is a threefold water here from the fountains of the Saviour: the water of tears, with which he wept over Lazarus and over the holy city, saying, “For if you too had known,” etc. (Luke 19); the water which he put into the basin when he washed the disciples’ feet (John 13); and the water which poured from his side with blood. There is, therefore, inward water, upper water, and outward water. The inward water is the water of tears; the upper water, the water of the sacraments; the outward water, that of the disciples. The first is contrition; the second, confession; the third, satisfaction in deed. The first washes the mind; the second refreshes it; the third makes it fruitful.

Therefore the water of contrition, or washing, washes the bed of conscience. Hence the Prophet says: “Every night I shall wash my bed,” etc. (Ps. 6). The second, which is confession, washes the face from vices. Hence it is said:

[Note: [Col. 1749D] St Bernard, sermon 2 *On the Resurrection*.]

“In confession all things are washed.” The third, which is satisfaction in deed, washes the hands. Hence it is said: “I shall wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. 25). The first, therefore, is owed to God; the second, to the prelate; the third, to one’s neighbour. We ought to be contrite before God, confess to the prelate, and perform good works for our neighbour.

The first water is for healing, of which it is said: “You have shaken your land, Lord, and troubled it; [Col. 1751A] heal its breaches, for it has been shaken” (Ps. 59). The second is for justification—not because it makes one righteous, but because the righteous person performs it. Hence it is said: “That you may be justified in your words” (Ps. 50). The third is for the crown, of which the Apostle says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course; there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4).

But this confession of sins must be pure, sincere, humble, and faithful. Unless it is pure, it is empty.

[Note: [Col. 1751D] St Ambrose, book X on Luke, ch. 96.]

For there are some who divide their sins in half, confessing some and keeping silent about others. Such a person is not covered by God’s cloak, because the cloak is not his own but the devil’s. Yet, to confirm their error, they cite authorities of the New and Old Testament, saying: “I am not bound to confess, because tears wash away the offence which it is shameful to confess with the mouth.” And elsewhere: “The Lord rained upon one city and did not rain upon another; one part was drenched from another, while another part remained dry” (Amos [Col. 1751B] 4). And: “At whatever hour the sinner groans,” etc. They also say:

[Note: [Col. 1751D] St Ambrose, in the work cited.]

“I have read of Peter’s tears; I have not read of his confession” (Ezek. 33, according to the Septuagint). And: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3). Certainly it is not so: individual sins must be confessed.

Confession ought to be humble, not arrogant. Humble confession is that which begins confessing with the beginning of the fast; otherwise the fast makes no progress. Hence this is customarily read on this Beginning of the Fast, to signify that the beginning of confession ought to accompany the beginning of fasting. Thus the saying must be read with this addition, so that it reads: “When you fast, also wash your face,” etc. It is as though it said: “Confess at once when you begin to fast.”

But because we cannot live without incurring venial sins, confession of venial sins is not removed at the end, but prescribed. Hence at the end of Lent the washing of the disciples’ feet is read, or the saying is read: “He who has bathed does not need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John 13). He did not say “he who is to be washed,” but “he who has bathed”; nor did he say “except that he wash his face and feet,” but only “his feet.” It is as though he said: At the beginning of the fast one ought to wash away mortal sins, confessing them purely and humbly; at the end, the venial sins which one has incurred.

There are also some who diminish their sins and cover them with a certain cloak of words, so that they confess themselves to have sinned less than they have sinned. This is contrary to humility and must not be done. To the point: do you wish to hear how useful humility in confession is, and how far it differs from arrogance? Hear King David, rebuked by Nathan over the sin involving Uriah, immediately confess: “I have sinned” (2 Sam. 12). He sat in ashes and haircloth; and the Lord, seeing his humility, immediately remitted him, Nathan saying to him: “God has taken away your sin from you” (ibid.). Behold the usefulness and example of humble confession.

Do you wish to hear of arrogant confession? Saul is rebuked by Samuel and says, “I have sinned.” But because he said it arrogantly, he immediately deserved to hear: “God has taken away your kingdom from you” (1 Sam. 15). Behold how great is the difference between humble and arrogant confession. Confession must be faithful, not despairing, unlike Judas’s confession: he said, “I have sinned” (Matt. 27), and immediately ran to the noose and hanged himself. So Cain said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve to be forgiven” (Gen. 4). Let confession, therefore, be true, so that nothing remains unconfessed; humble, so that one confesses without a cloak of words and does not despair; faithful, so that one hopes well and does not presume.

Therefore, when you fast, wash your face—that is, confess immediately.

But this is not sufficient. Hence he adds: “Anoint your head with oil.” “The head of a woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ; the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). Therefore God is our head, because the mediator of God and human beings (1 Tim. 2) is the head of the Church. Anoint, therefore, your head—that is, God. But what does this mean? How [Col. 1752A] can I anoint my head, since he himself is at the right hand of the Father? It is wonderful. Who anointed him? How can he be anointed?

God’s anointing is threefold, and he ought to have a threefold anointing. Under the time of the Law only three persons were anointed: king, priest, and prophet. But the anointing of prophets is rarely found. He himself was king; hence he says through the prophet: “But I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. 2). He himself was priest, offering himself as the true sacrifice for us. To him the Father says: “You are a priest for ever,” etc. (Ps. 109). He himself was prophet; hence Moses says: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as me” (Deut. 18). But by whom was he anointed? By the Father, as it is said: “God, your God, has anointed you,” etc. (Ps. 44). And by the Holy Spirit, as is read in Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord has rested upon me, because he anointed me; he sent me to evangelize the nations” (Isa. 61). Therefore in this anointing the whole Trinity is understood: the Son anointed; the Holy Spirit, by whom he was anointed; [Col. 1752B] and the Father, who anointed him.

Mary Magdalene anointed him; it is read of her (Luke 7) that she anointed both his feet and his head. Those three women prepared the third anointing, but did not anoint him because they did not find him in the tomb (Mark 16). The first anointing, then, is that of fullness, and we do not possess it; the second, that of devotion, which we can possess here; the third, that of thanksgiving, which we shall complete in the future. For, compared with future thanksgiving, how small—or even nonexistent—is the thanksgiving we perform here! This is signified by the third anointing, which could not be completed.

Therefore let us fast, wash our faces, and anoint our head with oil—that is, let us turn away from evil and do good. Let us bless the Lord, so that at last we may hear that blessing of the children: “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matt. 25). Let us hear it, I say, from the Lord Jesus Christ, our judge, who will come to judge the living and the dead and the world through fire.

## SERMON XI. IN LENT

[Col. 1752C]

Cast the stones out of the streets (Jer. 50). The Lord Jesus, our saving physician, has prepared remedies for our souls in the likeness of bodily medicine. For as long as harmful humours remain in the body, it is useless to add medicines; when iron remains in a wound, it is no use applying a poultice. Therefore, in order to expel vices from us during Lent, the Catholic Church customarily performs certain visible acts as well, by which she not only drives away vices but also shows the faithful that they are especially to be repelled in these days. Since the tongue of man cannot suffice to enumerate the whole multitude of crimes, let it suffice to disclose the flight from the seven principal ones, which are these: pride, avarice, lust, gluttony, envy, anger, and sloth.

These are the stones to be cast out of the streets; these are the enemies of whom it is said in Deuteronomy (ch. 28): “Your enemies shall come against you by one way, and shall flee before you by seven,” because all vices come upon us through self-will alone. Hence Truth says: “From the heart proceed thefts, murders, adulteries,” and so forth (Matt. 15).

> [Note: Col. 1752D. St Bernard, Sermon 3 on the Resurrection.]

Take away a person’s own will, and there will no longer be sin, nor hell. Christ showed in himself that this will must be rejected for the common good, when he set aside his own will, though good, in favour of the common will. His own will was that he should not die; for neither the Father, nor the angel who was to be restored, nor humankind which was to be redeemed, willed this. Yet there was another will in him, a common one: namely, that he should die. This the Holy Trinity willed; this rational creation willed; this he himself also willed. The former was good; but this was better. Therefore he preferred that it should become common, and said: “Not as I will, but as you will, let it be done” (Matt. 26).

Through this self-will alone we sin. It is so bold and shameless that it arms itself against its own Creator. For the wicked person would wish to have impunity for his crimes; therefore he would wish God to be unjust and like himself; therefore he would wish God not to exist. When, then, the aforesaid vices come upon us, they are exceedingly grievous enemies to us. Pride takes God away from a person; lust takes away the person himself; avarice takes away his neighbour; gluttony deceives him; envy bruises him; anger scourges him; sloth binds him.

Mother Church, however, as we have said, visibly expels these enemies from her children in seven ways, as though by seven paths during the days of fasting. On the first day, called the Head of the Fast, and almost on the last, namely at the Lord’s Supper, she sets before us a draught that expels pride. This is fittingly done first and last, because this vice is first and last. It was first among those who departed from God—that is, the devil and the first man—and it is last among those returning to God; for it rages after all the virtues, as Prudentius makes clear in the *Psychomachia*. The application of ashes is a most salutary remedy against it, as though at the outset of the contest one said to humankind: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10). What is flesh but flesh? Let flesh be clothed in purple and silk: it is nevertheless nothing but flesh. Behold humility, a most celebrated work, as though a draught excluding pride.

Likewise, at the Supper we bend down to wash the feet of the poor, as though it were said to us: “Thus it befits us to fulfil all humility.” At that time we also take medicine against avarice. It has been instituted that each day, before eating, the brethren wash the feet of the poor and provide them with food.

> [Note: Col. 1753D. Alcuin Flaccus, book *On the Divine Offices*.]

At the head of the Church, the lord pope also gives alms on Palm Saturday as a sign of this matter; and concerning him it is even read: “Saturday is free, because the lord pope gives alms.” For just as on that day Martha is read to have prepared a banquet for the Lord, at which Mary anointed his head and Lazarus, who had been raised, was present (Luke 10), so the Church on that same day refreshes Christ’s body—that is, his members still upon earth. This refreshment indeed pleases God more than that in which refreshment is given to his own bodily self. For he loved this his body, which is the Church, more than even that body which he drew from the Virgin: he exposed that one to blows and wounds, indeed to death, in order to provide safety for this one. Behold how effective a medicine against avarice: the distribution of our goods.

A greater remedy is also applied against gluttony: abstinence greater than usual. The Church customarily celebrates the office of Mass between the third and sixth hours on days when she does not fast, so that at the hour when Christ is believed to have been sacrificed, that same sacrifice may be represented. Since one Evangelist says that he was crucified at the third hour (Mark 15), and another at the sixth hour (Matt. 27), we infer that he was crucified during the interval between those hours. Thus, in recounting things that we have seen, we variously designate intermediate intervals of time by the names of their limits. When, therefore, we are not fasting, we customarily take refreshment after the offices of Mass and the sixth hour. But in seasons of fasting the office of Mass is postponed until after the sixth hour, so that abstinence from food may be prolonged until after the ninth.

> [Note: Col. 1753D. Chapter *Solent*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1; St Bernard, Sermon 3 on Lent; *Micrologus*.]

In Lent, however, the office of Mass is postponed even until after the ninth hour, so that refreshment may also be deferred until after Vespers. Abstinence greater than usual therefore removes the poison of gluttony. Although this may suffice to repress lust—

> [Note: Col. 1754D. Terence, *Eunuchus*.]

—for without Ceres and Bacchus Venus grows cold—yet at the same time a special medicine against lust has been introduced. A veil is placed between those chanting the psalms and the people, indeed for another and greater symbolic reason, but also to remove the wantonness and licence of the eyes, through whose windows the death of lust more frequently enters. In the earliest churches, and almost down to modern times, psalmody in choir was so conducted that those chanting could be seen by the people from the shoulders upward, as also in the court of the priests before the Temple; but during Lent, curtains being interposed, mutual sight was denied.

Moreover, against anger, as against the other vices, a remedy is applied to us: namely, genuflection. Nothing more readily breaks anger, because genuflection moves the one who has suffered injury to forgiveness, and naturally brings the one who inflicted it to tears.

> [Note: Col. 1754D. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 11, ch. 1.]

For there is a certain natural affinity between the eyes and knees. Those who treat of natural things assert that a child in its mother’s womb has its eyes placed over its knees; whence they say that *genua* (“knees”) received their name from the cheeks, *genae*, placed above them. Therefore, when the knees are bent, the eyes naturally burst into tears, responding in natural affection to their foster-siblings.

A fitting remedy has also been prepared against envy: namely, the bowing of the head at the end of Mass, as though we were told: “The envious person wastes away at the sight of another’s abundant possessions; but you, faithful one, lower your eyes, lest you see that from which you suffer—or rather, from which you perish.” Likewise against sloth. Sloth is worldly sadness: when we are so affected by losses of possessions or bodily discomfort that we become weary even of praying, reading, or doing anything of this kind. Because it is close to the precipice of despair, it is called *acedia*, as if “situated toward a fall,” that is, beside a fall. To dispel this torpor, the Church has also instituted bodily movement in action: that processions should be made from church to church. The Roman pontiff observes this almost every day of Lent, though other churches customarily go out on more or fewer days.

In this manner we represent, at this season, the expulsion of sins from ourselves; but the figure is empty without the reality. Let us therefore truly be cleansed in the sight of the Lord, so that he may transfer us, cleansed, from the world to himself—he who cleansed us by his blood, Jesus Christ our Lord, our judge when he shall come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON XII. FIRST SUNDAY IN LENT

“He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven” (Ps. 90 [91]). The Most High inclined the heavens and came down (Ps. 17 [18]); and he came down so far that he was made in the likeness of men and found in outward appearance as a man (Phil. 2). He came down so far that he humbled himself beneath the hand of a servant in order to be baptized. Thus the Baptist trembled when he saw the head, terrible to kings and to be worshipped by powers, bowed beneath his hands (Matt. 3). He humbled himself so far that, when he had fasted and was hungry, the tempter dared approach him (Matt. 4), in order to pierce him with the same darts by which he had left the first man wounded and half-dead.

But the tempter was defeated, and the Most High defeated him. Yet by what help did the Most High overcome him? Did he employ the help of his power? By no means. For he could immediately have crushed Satan beneath his feet, which he did not do, although it is written even concerning his members: “You shall walk upon the asp and basilisk, and shall trample the lion and dragon” (Ps. 90 [91]). Did he employ the help of his justice? By no means. For he could rightly have said: “Depart now, Satan, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). Did he employ the help of angels? By no means, for it is read that the angels stood at a distance, watching the contest of their Lord. What, then, was the help of the Most High? He defeated the devil with the authorities of sacred Scripture.

Let us too employ this help of the Most High, especially in this fixed and short span of forty days, because the enemy now presses more fiercely and now undertakes more grievous contests. But you will say: “Blessed, then, are the learned, for whom sacred Scripture is ready at hand, who have prepared authorities from both Testaments by which they may extinguish the fiery darts of the enemy.” If this is so, certainly they are blessed; but certainly it is not so. For not all learned persons dwell in the help of the Most High. Some fear sacred Scripture; others even mock it; others destroy it; others despise it; others pass through it; others dwell in it.

Those who fear it are slothful; those who mock it are proud; those who destroy it are heretics; those who despise it are false brethren; those who pass through it are guests; those who dwell in it are citizens. For there are some whose god is their belly (Phil. 3). When they hear, “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccles. 1), observing and considering toil and pain, they prefer to rest and remain ignorant rather than learn with labour, saying that knowledge is nothing but labour and affliction of spirit (ibid.). It is as though they said: “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, drink, eat” (Luke 12). For wise person and fool alike shall perish. They even seek consolation for their ignorance from the help of the Most High; for it is written: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes; but he who does not know it and does not do it was beaten with few” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “It is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. 2).

But I fear for these fearful ones, lest, when he who is full of days comes, and all the books are opened and the door shut, they say, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” and he says to them, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25)—as though he said: “Because you did not know me, I do not know you.”

There are others who magnify their tongues, saying that sacred Scripture is not knowledge and is not learning. For they call nothing knowledge except certain niceties of words: as though, by examining the hairs of one’s head, we might learn to argue in proof or disproof; or discover the causes of things by philosophical reasoning; or deliver rhetorical declamations before a judge. “What knowledge,” they say, “is it to know that Abraham had two sons, or that Noah was preserved in the ark with seven souls?” And other things of this kind: this is the skill of storytellers, not learning. Or, “What knowledge is it to know the number of Abraham’s oxen, or Sebeon’s asses, or Job’s camels? This is the knowledge of bankers, not learning.”

But let them hear what our harpist says: “Because I did not know learning, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. 70 [71]). That is, the learning which is knowledge that puffs up, possessed by those who wish to be “as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). But I fear for these people, lest, when the Lawgiver comes—the one who first wrote the law with his finger in human hearts, repeated it written on tablets of stone, and delivered the law of grace with his own mouth—he say to them: “Because you were ashamed of me and of my words before people, I also shall be ashamed of you before my Father and the holy angels” (Luke 9).

There are others who destroy Scripture. These are those who “became vain in their thoughts,” who paint the images of their own hearts upon the pages of sacred Scripture; who adapt the letter, resistant though it be, to their own inventions; and squeeze the meaning out of Scripture until blood flows. Like a brood of vipers, they strike the sides of their mother so that, when she dies, bloodthirsty young may emerge, feeding on flesh and plunder. But I fear for these, lest, when he comes from whose mouth proceeds a two-edged sword, whose head is white as wool and whose feet are like bronze (Dan. 10), he say to each of them: “Friend, you have grown broad, fat, and sleek, and have kicked; and because you ensnared the simple by your evasions, and sought outward things in the letter rather than the marrow, you shall be cast, bound hand and foot, into outer darkness” (Matt. 8).

There are also those who despise Scripture. Here I fear for our own party: these are the clergy of the churches. We certainly read sacred Scripture, expound it, and approve it, because it clothes and feeds us; but we fulfil in deed none of the things that it commands or prepares. We are like crosses at crossroads which point out the way to passers-by, as though we said: “The yoke of Scripture that you speak of is good, but we cannot bear it now.” To touch briefly upon a few things out of many: we consume in superfluous uses the goods granted for food and clothing—the goods, I say, of Christ’s poor.

For who are they who feast splendidly every day? The clergy. Who are they who eat foods sought out from air, sea, and land? The clergy. Who are they who, having peace and security at all times, are not in human toil and are not scourged with humankind? The clergy. We, therefore, are Christ’s false brethren: we possess his patrimony as though by right of brotherhood. Yet how false we are is plain to the bleary-eyed and the barbers. The patrimony which he acquired for himself so gloriously, we consume gluttonously. He purchased it by blows and scourges; we consume it in cups and dishes. He acquired it amid reproaches and persecutions; we consume it in banquets and drunkenness. He acquired it by the death of the cross; we consume it in the luxury of the flesh. See how falsehood answers truth by its opposite.

I fear lest, when that brother of ours returns, who has now gone away as if on a journey, he settle accounts with us concerning the patrimony entrusted to us. What shall we be able to say? Surely this: “Brother, we possessed all that was yours; nor were we content with it, nor did we follow you. What then shall become of us?” And he may truly answer: “Remember, brethren, that you received good things in your lifetime; now you shall receive evil things.” Or rather, I fear that he may fall upon us without mercy, according to the prophet who represents the Lord as speaking to the angels concerning mitigation of punishments and saying: “Now have pity on the wicked man, for he has acted unjustly in the land of the saints” (Isa. 26). It is as though he said: “Other wicked people must be spared, but not these, because they committed abominable acts in the land of the saints which they possessed.”

There are those who pass through Scripture: these are scholars, who continually devote themselves to the study of sacred Scripture. But I fear that they pass through it toward transient things, desiring to be enlarged in honours, enriched in possessions, and extended in favour. I fear, I say, lest, like the Ishmaelites, they pass by and buy Joseph in order afterward to sell him to Potiphar, the chief cook of the king of Egypt (Gen. 39). They must fear lest, when the king of Gerar comes with the commander of his army to Isaac beside the well of Satiety, he say: “Friend, behold, you have become exceedingly rich and powerful; depart from us” (Gen. 26). But where will they go if they depart from him? There is no middle place: whoever is not in the kingdom shall be in hell.

There are those who dwell in Scripture: those who carry out in deed what they affirm with their mouths; those, namely, who possess it and stand in it. For “to dwell” is said from *habitus*, a settled state, and from standing. They twist the neck of the dove toward the armpits (Lev. 1), and carry the straps of the high priest’s mitre over both shoulders, lest they be like the sluggish, who are unable even to raise a hand to their mouths.

Observe next what is promised to one dwelling thus: “He shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven”; that is, he shall remain in God’s twofold protection and in both parts of himself. For “to abide” has two references. God’s protection is twofold, bodily and spiritual: the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come. Hence in what follows it is compared to a shield: “His truth shall surround you with a shield.” A shield is broad above and narrow below. So also the Lord gives a narrow protection in the present life, because this is expedient: providing, namely, food and clothing, and we are content with these. Yet we should not fear insufficiency.
