No food is cheaper than bread and water; yet in the strength of that food Elijah walked forty days and forty nights (3 Kings 19).

Future protection has breadth. For it is said to us: “They shall put into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing” (Luke 6); and one shall be protected in both soul and body. “For the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtle-dove a nest in which to lay her young” (Ps. 83 [84]). The soul builds herself a house out of foundation, wall, and roof. But one soul builds herself Beth-aven, that is, “the house of an idol”; another Bethel, that is, “the house of God.” The former lays the concupiscence of the flesh as a foundation, the concupiscence of the eyes as a wall, and places pride above as a roof. Pride is that which rages after all virtues; and since it is heavenly by origin, it inhabits the minds of the exalted and claims height for the house of the idol. But the soul which, contrariwise, lays down sobriety, requires justice for its wall, and places humility above, builds its house upon firm rock, living soberly, justly, and piously, according to the Apostle’s counsel (Tit. 2).

Likewise the turtle-dove—that is, the flesh or animal nature—prepares itself a nest. A nest is made from dry and worthless straw. But flesh also, if it attends to its own fragility and worthlessness, lays up its works in a nest. Hence it is said: “Son, remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7). The last things of our flesh are five: base material, lowly activity, mournful entrance, difficult continuance, and dreadful departure. Concerning the baseness of its material, hear the philosopher, who, when a tyrant asked what he had been, what he was, and what he would be, answered each question sufficiently: “Worthless semen, a vessel of excrement, food for worms.” Consider how lowly activity from such material is: Saint Zechariah, when he was to beget Saint John from Saint Elizabeth, did not wish to be seen. The mournfulness of entrance is plain, because all who are born of Eve cry either “E” or “A,” as though made prophets of their impending misery. Concerning the difficulty of continuance, consult Boethius, who says:

> [Note: Col. 1757D. Book 2 of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, prose 4.]

> “There is no one who does not quarrel with some part of his condition; for who does not judge another’s condition better?”

Concerning the terror of departure, hear Blessed Martin:

> [Note: Col. 1757D. Sulpicius, *Life*.]

Seeing the devil standing by as he was about to depart, he said: “Why do you stand here, bloodthirsty beast?”

> [Note: Col. 1757D. Augustine, Sermon 4 on Peter and Paul; Prosper, *On the Promises*, part 2, ch. 19; Ordinary Gloss on Tobit.]

In Tobit (ch. 6), in connection with the gutting of the fish, it is read that the devil stood by Christ as he died on the cross, to see whether any stain of sin might be found in him. What, then, can we expect concerning ourselves? In remembrance of these things, the turtle-dove which has a nest abides under the protection of the God of heaven. Therefore the one whom the God of heaven protects will fear none of the things beneath heaven.

Let us therefore dwell in the help of the Most High. Let us not pass through Egypt itself, but go on as far as Bethlehem, and see this word which has come to pass there. Indeed, follow him who goes before. For as he was a Bethlehemite in his birth, a Nazarene in his course, and a Jerusalemite in his death, so let us be filled in the Scriptures as in the house of bread; afterward let us be Nazarenes—that is, those who put forth shoots—so that we may bear fruit from the things we have heard; and at our departure let us be those seeing peace, which surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4). May he draw us to it, he who drew captivity captive with himself (Eph. 4), Jesus Christ our Lord, our judge, when he shall come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON XIII. SECOND SUNDAY IN LENT

“The Spirit drove Jesus into the desert, and he was tempted by Satan, and fasted forty days and forty nights; and he was with the beasts, and angels ministered to him” (Mark 1; Matt. 4). Every action of Christ is instruction for the Christian. As he taught in order to teach humanity, and died in order that humanity might live, so he fasted in order to instruct humanity. Therefore the God-man fasted among us; he fasted, but for us; he fasted, yet above us. For during the forty days he did not taste food even once. “This has been done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes”; we cannot attain to it.

Nevertheless, the Church suitably fasts according to her measure, or, more truly, afterward.

> [Note: Col. 1757D. Baronius, *Annals*, vol. 1, p. 117.]

On the day of the Epiphanies Jesus went up from the Jordan into the desert in order to fast. But the Church fasts in the following season, as though following in the footsteps of her head. For she reads that it was said to her in Peter: “Follow me” (John 21). And elsewhere: “Go behind me” (Matt. 16). There is, however, a special reason why the Church does not fast at the same time as Christ: namely, to avoid the heresy of certain people. There were heretics—

> [Note: Col. 1758D. See Bellarmine, book 1, *On Good Works*, ch. 16, at the end of vol. 3.]

—who said, concerning the passage “And Jesus, having been baptized and praying” (Luke 3), that Jesus prayed in order that those who were baptized on the same day as Christ might then receive the Holy Spirit, and might fast at the same time. But far be this from the Father of mercies: that his mercy should be bound to any fixed time in showing mercy to the children of adoption. To refute this, the Church instituted fasting in the following season; and, in order to root out that heresy more forcefully, she forbade under anathema anyone to baptize on the day of the Epiphanies unless necessity requires it.

Moreover, it should not be passed over in silence that the word *Quadragesima* (“Lent”) has a threefold meaning. Sometimes *Quadragesima* means the Sunday now being observed; sometimes the period of time extending until Easter; sometimes the forty fast-days, of which four have now been observed and thirty-six remain. Jerome indicates the first meaning of this name in his letter to Marcella.

> [Note: Col. 1758D. In Letter 15, *In Praise of Asella*; and in Letter 54 he takes it in the second sense. Leo I, Letter 4, ch. *Si quis*; *On Consecration*, distinction 4.]

For the Church has two Septuagesimas: one of days, the other of weeks. Although both begin together with “They surrounded me,” they do not end together. The Septuagesima of days ends on the Saturday after Easter; the Septuagesima of weeks, at “All you who thirst, come to the waters.” In observing them, we recall two seventies: one of ages, the other of years.

That captivity in which the people of God suffered under the Chaldeans for seventy years is well known, according to that saying of Jeremiah (ch. 25): “You shall be delivered into a hostile hand, and shall serve King Nebuchadnezzar for seventy years.” The Church represents this in the Septuagesima of days, taking a day for a year. Therefore she suppresses songs of gladness during these days, according to the saying, “I shall take away from you the voice of joy and gladness, the voice of bridegroom and bride” (Baruch 2), and especially the songs of angels, *Alleluia* and “Glory to God in the highest,” because it is written: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?” (Ps. 136 [137]).

By the Septuagesima of ages, moreover, we mean six ages of those dying and a seventh of those rising again. In these the miserable human being eats bread in the sweat of his brow (Gen. 3), drawing from the stock of sin and death a calamity as though hereditary. The Church laments this general misery of the human race in the Septuagesima of weeks, taking a week for an age. Yet because, in the sixth age of those at rest, although many are afflicted in purgatory, some rest in it, concerning whom it is said: “From henceforth the Spirit says that they may rest from their labours” (Apoc. 14), the Church says in the seventh week: “Rejoice, Jerusalem.” In accordance with this Septuagesima of weeks, this Sunday is called Quadragesima: the first is called Septuagesima, the second Sexagesima, the third Quinquagesima, and the fourth Quadragesima. This could in no way hold according to the Septuagesima of days.

These four Sundays are designated by their own particular names, but the next three are not, because the Lenten fast begins at different times among different groups in these four. Regular cenobitic monks begin at Septuagesima; the Greeks at Sexagesima; our clergy, on the authority of Pope Telesphorus—

> [Note: Col. 1759. Telesphorus, in the letter to all bishops, distinction 5, ch. *Statuimus*.]

—at Quinquagesima; and the whole army of Christian warfare, young men and virgins, old together with young, at this Quadragesima.

Why the period until Easter, though extending over forty-two days, is called Quadragesima, Augustine answered in his book *On Christian Doctrine*. The Church represents the affliction which the people of God endured for forty years in the wilderness, in a land without way and without water, according to the saying: “For forty years I was offended with that generation,” and so forth (Ps. 94 [95]). For the stiff-necked people, often provoking God to anger, fell in the wilderness through unfamiliar labours and unprecedented deaths, so that a desirable land might be given to their new generation. And because in those forty years they reached forty-two stations, forty-two days are found in this Lent. Just as they, after the years and stations had elapsed, crossed the Jordan and ate the grain of that year and the fruits of palm trees, so at the end of this Lent our catechumens, passing through the waters of baptism, approach the food of salvation.

The forty fast-days called Quadragesima were instituted at different times. It was an apostolic tradition to fast for thirty-six days before Easter. Having heard in the Law that the Lord claimed for himself the first fruits and tithes of crops, they likewise decreed to sanctify to God the first fruits of days and the tithes of days. They established the fasts of the four seasons as first fruits, in which twelve days are observed as the first fruits of the twelve months. Since the tenth part of 366 days is thirty-six days, they consecrated these days also as a tithe of days by fasting. Later the apostolic Fathers added four, so that the number of the Lord’s fast might be completed.

There was, however, another reason for adding these four days, which we have thought worthy to explain: namely, that four fasts performed before people might be emptied of their force. There is the fast of the sick person, the fast of the disgusted person, the fast of the miser, and the fast of the Pharisee. The sick person fasts in order to recover health; the miser fasts in order to save money; the disgusted person fasts in order to acquire appetite; the Pharisee fasts in order to be seen. Hence it is read at the beginning of the fast: “Do not become gloomy like the hypocrites” (Matt. 6). And since it has been said by what number of days one ought to fast, in imitation of Christ, it must also be said in what manner.

Mark briefly indicates the manner in the chapter already cited, determining six points concerning Christ, the leader of those who fast: namely, himself, the place of the fast, his suffering and activity, his dwelling with the beasts, and the ministry of the angels. Let the Christian fast in this manner; nor should he be troubled if some of these things are frightening, for some also are soothing. The leader of those who fast is trustworthy; the place, however, terrible; the suffering unavoidable; the activity difficult; the companionship mournful; the end desirable. Yet the leader strengthens, the place unsettles, the suffering bruises, the activity gladdens, the companionship troubles, and the end gives life. Therefore let us follow the leader, enter the place, not fail in suffering, persevere in activity, suffer with our fellow-dwellers, and attain the end.

The arranger of the ecclesiastical office has set these matters forth quite carefully through the antiphons at the Introit with which he has furnished the Sundays of this season. On the first Sunday, which is now being observed, the leader of those who fast, as though stirred by their cries, said: “He shall call upon me, and I will hear him” (Ps. 90). On the second, wretched man, observing the place of terror and vast solitude—the straits, that is, which he suffers in this body of death—cries to his leader: “Remember thy mercies, O Lord” (Ps. 24). And shortly afterward: “Deliver us, O Israel, from all our straits” (ibid.). On the third, observing Satan’s temptations as intolerable water [Col. 1760A] and inextricable snares, he cries: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord, and he shall pluck my feet out of the snare” (ibid.). On the fourth, observing the works of mercy and justice which God performs in him—as though breathing again and walking in exultation—and as though saying, “I have delighted in the way of thy testimonies, as in all riches” (Ps. 118), he bursts into joy and says: “Rejoice, Jerusalem”; and shortly afterward: “Rejoice with gladness, you who were in sorrow.” On the fifth, he considers that he dwells in the midst of a perverse nation, a brother of dragons and companion of ostriches; and, seeing dregs with oil, chaff with grain, vinegar with wine, and wishing to be separated, he not without reason cries out: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42), etc. On the sixth, seeing now the ministry of angels drawing near, seeing a measure prepared before him, he hastens in desire and says: “O Lord, do not put thy help far from me,” etc. (Ps. 21).

[Col. 1760B] Let us, moreover, pursue each point more clearly. The leader of those who fast is spirit; but not every spirit is to be believed, and therefore discernment of spirits must be exercised. There is a spirit of wickedness, a spirit of the world, a spirit of the flesh, a spirit of man, and a Spirit of truth. Of the spirit of wickedness the Apostle says: “Our struggle is against spiritual wickedness” (Eph. 6). He rejoices concerning the spirit of the world because certain people to whom he had preached were not subject to it; but he grieves concerning others because they were puffed up by the spirit of the flesh. He testifies of the spirit of man that it alone knows the things that belong to the spirit of man (1 Cor. 2). But the Spirit of truth has filled the whole world (Wis. 1), and there is none who can hide himself from his heat (Ps. 18).

Do you wish to distinguish among these spirits? You shall know them by their suggestions. The spirit of wickedness suggests deadly things; the spirit of the world, vain things; the spirit of the flesh, pleasant things; the spirit of man, reasonable things; the Spirit of truth, impossible things. For he asserts that [Col. 1760C] he will make man God, and that, though reduced to ashes, he will raise the body up conformed to Christ’s body of glory.

Secure in such a leader, let the one who fasts choose the desert; that is, let his members abandon the accustomed workshops of fleshly desires. Let the eyes cease to see vanity; let the ears cease to attend to foolish trifles or empty tales, and to irrelevant matters; let the tongue cease to speak deceits and lies; let the throat cease to gorge itself with food and be drunk with wine, wherein is excess; let the hands cease to shed innocent blood; let the feet cease to run after strange children, “who have grown old and limped from their paths” (Ps. 17).

In such a desert the faster will not fear Satan’s fourfold temptation. For if his foot slips, his leader will put a hand beneath him, according to that saying: “His truth shall surround thee with a shield; thou shalt not fear the terror of the night, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks in darkness, the assault and the noonday demon” (Ps. 90); these we pass over as familiar.

[Col. 1760D] The activity of one who fasts is threefold: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer. In these he is comparable to a goat. Though a goat has three qualities we detest, it nevertheless has three that are commendable. It is a foul-smelling animal, wanton, and shaggy—qualities to be rejected. It is commended because it feeds standing upright, feeds on bitter things, and seeks high places. In this manner let the faster in the desert feed on bitter things: namely, fasting, weeping, and mourning. Let him “eat ashes like bread and mingle his drink with weeping” (Ps. 101). If he sees his brother suffering need, let him not draw his hand back, but raise it, so that in helping the poor he may be wholly raised toward God. In prayer let him ask for sublime things. Prayer is that subtle little bird which penetrates the heavens and reaches the Lord’s feet, nor ceases until it has made its plea.

What the faster owes to his fellow-dwellers, the father of the nations teaches: “Bear one another’s burdens” [Col. 1761A] (Gal. 6), that you may be members one of another. With these five, then, let him safely approach the ministry of angels. For angels are priests, according to Malachi: “The lips of the priest keep knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, for he is an angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). The Apostle also commanded a woman to pray veiled in church, because of subjection and because of the angels (1 Cor. 11). Their ministry is to dispense the Lord’s body and blood to those who approach after fasting. For the bread that descended from heaven, formed in the Virgin’s womb and baked in the oven of the cross, is dispensed by them upon the table of the altar.

Therefore let us pray, each and all, that, cleansed through the abstinence of fasting, we may worthily approach the ministry of angels; so that at last Jesus Christ our Lord, our judge, when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire, may draw us into the fellowship of the firstborn.

## SERMON XIV. FOR MIDWEEK, OR THE SUNDAY *Laetare*

[Col. 1761B]

“Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her; rejoice with gladness, you who were in sorrow, that you may exult and be filled from the breasts of your consolation” (Isa. 66).

Why does the Church today so solemnly exhort us to rejoice? It is not enough to say that we should rejoice; she repeats the command that we should be glad, indeed adds that we should exult in consolation. What is the meaning of this threefold exhortation to joy? Certainly it seems rather unsuitable, for it does not answer to the season or accord with the observance. This is a time of affliction and sorrow for the redemption of sins; tears wash away offenses, not catechumens. For at the beginning of this Lenten season the Church has prescribed for us a manner of life in fasting, weeping, and mourning, and songs of gladness have been suppressed. The observance of this season consists in mortification of the flesh, frequent prayer, vigils in the untimely night, the receiving of ashes, bending of knees, and the like; all these are signs not of joy but of sorrow.

[Col. 1761C] What moves us still more is that this week is adjacent to Passion Sunday. But who, except a Jew or one who judaizes, could exult at its remembrance? We must therefore not doubt that, under a mystery of deeper meaning, the Church so solemnly makes today’s exhortation to rejoicing, not once but three times. For this threefold exhortation represents three exultations: one past, one daily, and one consequent. It is a recollection of the past, an urging of the daily, and a commendation of the consequent.

The past exultation occurred when the children of Israel, carried away into exile, first sat and wept beside the rivers of Babylon (Ps. 136), but afterward, upon receiving permission to depart, exulted. The daily exultation occurs when the wretched spirit, still laboring in this body of death, breathes again into its own freedom through God’s grace—temptations having for a time been lulled, or at least somewhat mitigated—so that, even for a short time, it may give itself to God alone. The consequent exultation occurs when the spirit, now free from the body’s burden, flies forth as from a prison and rests from its labors, joyfully awaiting the glorious resurrection of its body.

This threefold exhortation to joy, therefore, recalls the past joy, urges the daily joy, and commends the consequent joy. But let us consider why it occurs on this Sunday rather than on others. Israel’s captivity lasted seventy years. In seventy there are seven decades; when six decades of years had ended, in the seventh decade, in its seventh year, a decree went forth from Cyrus the king, that Israel, having cast off the yoke of slavery, might freely return to the land of its birth. At receiving this decree, the Hebrews exulted so greatly that they are said to have celebrated a Jubilee in that same year.

[Col. 1762A] To signify this seventy-year period, the Church has instituted two seventies in this season: one of days and another of weeks. Both indeed begin on the same day—namely, the Sunday “They surrounded me”—but they end at different times. The seventy of days ends on the Saturday in albs, while the seventy of weeks has this week as its final week. Thus, to represent Israel’s exultation in the seventh decade after six decades, the Church bursts into a song of joy in the seventh week after six weeks.

Likewise, after six general temptations the breathing spirit of the wretched man exults; hence: “In six tribulations he shall deliver thee, and in the seventh evil shall not touch thee” (Job 5). In the same way, after the six ages of man, in the seventh the free spirit exults with joy. The six general temptations that oppress, and almost crush, the wretched spirit are considered according to the six local positions of bodies: before and behind, above and below, right and left. Thus the wretched spirit is tempted from below [Col. 1762B] and from above, from before and behind, from the right and from the left. The lower temptation is contemptible; the upper, astonishing; the frontward, terrible; the backward, ugly; the right-hand, volatile; the left-hand, heavy.

The lower temptation comes from one’s own flesh, which whispers to us in flattering speech that we should follow its desires. The wretched spirit is addressed as though the flesh said: “Why do you labor so greatly in watchfulness, and why are you worn away by foolish toil? Why do you always pursue fleeting wisdom amid hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, many vigils and labors? The learned and unlearned alike die; the same destruction awaits men and beasts. Feast, eat, sleep, and rest; thus you will receive your share from your labor.”

Yet, because this admonition is gross and craven, it attacks the educated spirit under the appearance of right. “There are four things which you, dear spirit, are bound to love out of charity: God, yourself, your neighbor, and me, your vehicle. Remember: if you neglect me, you despise charity; unless you supply my deficiencies, you will not fulfill the rule of charity. Yet, though you ought to provide me with life’s comforts, you impose labors upon me. These are not provisions, but deprivations.”

What the flesh proposes concerning necessary provision for itself is true. But we, appointed judges between the necessities and superfluities of the flesh, do not weigh them equally; we are more inclined to introduce superfluities. This temptation of the flesh, however, is contemptible. Who would not cast aside a man pursuing the desires of the flesh, like a pig in a mire, frogs in mud, worms in dung? Even the pagan philosophers expelled Epicurus, who preferred the pleasure of the flesh to virtue, from the church of philosophers as a heretic. Indeed, in contempt for the flesh, a philosopher replied to a man asking, “What was I, what am I, what shall I be?” and said: “Vile seed, a vessel of dung, food for worms.”

[Col. 1762D] The second temptation is from above, that is, from reason, the higher part of the soul, when reason consents to the flesh, takes pleasure in it, and is drawn as though captive into service to the handmaid over whom it ought to rule. This is astonishing. For example, how greatly would you marvel if you saw a little ass riding its rider, driving the man by reins and spurring him with its heels? The miracle here is no different. It is likely that if Achsah, daughter of Caleb, had carried on her shoulders before her father the ass which she rode (Judg. 1), she would sooner have been cast out by him than heard.

The third is from without: this is the fearsome suggestion of demons, who hide snares for us on the path by which we walk. The prophet boasts that he escaped them, saying: “He delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word” (Ps. 90). But when I hear of a snare and hunters, I tremble entirely with horror and groan as I recall our misery. Are we, then, beasts? We certainly are: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” [Col. 1763A] (Ps. 48). But how many, and how great, are the snares of these hunters? They have not entered into the heart of man, nor is the tongue sufficient to explain them. Yet blessed Anthony saw them in the spirit and was terrified.

> [Note: Col. 1763D. St Athanasius, in his *Life* of Anthony.]

Still, to set forth one of these snares, let us hear the Apostle, for he too has the Spirit of God: “Those who desire to become rich in this world,” he says, “fall into a snare and into the temptation of the devil” (1 Tim. 6). Riches, therefore, are the devil’s snare. But hear Truth in the Gospel concerning how inextricable this snare is: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). For no one easily triumphs over avarice when it has once triumphed over him. Alas! We seek rather to be entangled in these snares than released from them. If hunters pursued us sounding horns, this temptation would be less dreadful because it could more easily be avoided. But they lie in ambush in secret, that they may shoot at the upright in darkness.

[Col. 1763B] The fourth is from behind: this is the recollection of past sins for pleasure, when someone exults in the most evil deeds he has done and is often inflamed by the recollection to return to the same thing. Such recollection must not be regarded as a light offense. It is not enough for a man to have despised God; rather, he as it were reproaches him to his face for what he despised.

Remember that the children of Israel worshiped the molten calf. In vengeance for this crime, the Levites passing through the midst of the camp are recorded to have slain three thousand men (Exod. 32). Recall the graves of lust: when the people remembered the pots of meat, the garlic, and the melons with which they had abounded in Egypt, and murmured, fourteen thousand of them perished (Num. 11). Why was the recollection of foods, together with murmuring, punished more severely than idolatry? The judgment is dreadful and not to be investigated. This is the ugly temptation, for it is like a hump disfiguring a man’s back, which has hardened from humors gathered together.

[Col. 1763C] The fifth is from the right, that is, from prosperity, when fortune smiles upon a man and his prosperity is not interrupted by misery: “Their sheep are fruitful, abundant in their offspring; their storehouses are full, pouring forth from one thing into another. They call blessed the people that has these things.” But you, prophet, what do you say? “It is not so; but blessed is the people whose God is the Lord” (Ps. 143). You also, Solomon, tell us what you think of it: “The prosperity of the simple,” he says, “will destroy them” (Prov. 1). And you, poet, who have read the disadvantage of prosperity in the book of experience, say:

> … O gifts of the gods, not yet understood …  
> … Poverty, fruitful in men, flees …  
> (Lucan, book V.)

[Col. 1763D] Prosperity enfeebles the virtues of the mind, makes men effeminate, blinds the eyes of the mind, and suffocates the vital spirit. This temptation is called volatile, for it resembles a flying ant, which is so cheerful that, forgetting food, it wastes away in flight and dies. Haughty riches make a man such that he can truly say: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21), “because I forgot to eat my bread.”

The sixth is from the left: this is pressing adversity, which so bruises the wretched spirit that it makes it either murmur or blaspheme. It often acts so that the pit of despair closes its mouth over him, especially when he sees some utterly depraved person prospering in his evil way.

[Col. 1764A] This burden would have crushed Boethius to death,

> [Note: Col. 1763D. Boethius, book V of *The Consolation of Philosophy*.]

unless he had received from God the consolation of consoling philosophy. Our psalmist recalls that he almost failed beneath it, saying: “My feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped, because I envied the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72). With these six temptations, like storms thundering all around, the wretched spirit is enclosed, ever placed as it were between hammer and anvil—except that, lest it fail altogether, it is sometimes withdrawn from them for a little breathing-space in this manner.

The third exultation is after this life, when the courses of the six ages have passed. Each age indeed has its own innate and natural trouble, by which the wretched spirit is carried along through each age as by torrents, paying back to nature, which exacts them, the tribute of miseries. These troubles can readily be perceived by comparing the six ages of the world.

The first age was from Adam to Noah. It had its own trouble, because Cain killed his brother at its beginning (Gen. 4). The second was from Noah to Abraham; its noted trouble was that the flood of waters covered the face of the earth (Gen. 7). The third was from Abraham to David.

> [Note: Col. 1763D. Jerome, in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, says this is a fable; Peter Comestor, ch. 41 of the *History of Genesis*. Col. 1764D.]

In this age Abraham and his brother Haran were cast by the Chaldeans into the fire through which they themselves passed. Abraham indeed was brought out by the Lord, but Haran died. The fourth was from David to the deportation. In it, we believe that few are unaware how grievously David suffered from Saul, from enemies, and from his son. The fifth was from the deportation to Christ. In it the people of God were captured, the holy city overthrown, the temple destroyed, and the Law burned. The sixth, which is now in progress: in it Christ was scourged, mocked, spat upon, filled with reproaches, and condemned to a most shameful death.

[Col. 1764B] Corresponding to these are assigned the troubles of the ages of man: in infancy the elder brother kills the younger; in childhood man suffers the flood; and so forth. But we have judged it fitting to make this assignment elsewhere, lest an overlong sermon burden rather than edify the hearer.

## SERMON XV. FOR PALM SUNDAY

(It appears among the Works of Hildebert of Le Mans. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI, col. 476, Sermon 29.)

## SERMON XVI. FOR PASSION WEEK

“Set thy house in order, for thou shalt die and not live” (Isa. 38).

This admonition was familiar and was once given by the Holy Spirit to Hezekiah, who reigned over Judah and Jerusalem. It is general and daily for every faithful soul; but it is particular and annual in this Lenten season, in which a fixed and brief number of days has been appointed for us to correct the negligences of other times. For when Hezekiah, after innumerable triumphs, had been lifted up in pride and had not given God fitting thanks, he fell mortally ill; Isaiah came in the Spirit and said: “Set thy house in order”—that is, provide who shall succeed you as king; unless you repent of your pride, you shall die.

[Col. 1764D] More generally, the Holy Spirit cries day by day to each of us: “Set thy house in order,” for unless you set it in order, you shall die the death of the soul, and afterward eternal death.

> [Note: Col. 1764D. Jerome, vol. II, to Avitus.]

And do not believe Origen, who teaches as doctrine that the Lord will not be angry forever and will one day even have mercy upon demons. For “thou shalt not live,” that is, you will never afterward be recalled to life.

More particularly, in this season each of us is told: “Set thy house in order,” like a glass flask: if a stone falls upon it, or it falls upon a stone, it will be broken. Easter day is near; prepare yourself to communicate in the Eucharist, for this season is like Easter’s preparation day. If you approach with your house not set in order, you shall die, for you will eat and drink judgment to yourself. But if you wish to approach with a house not set in order, you shall die, because you will sin unto death.

[Col. 1765A] In the early Church, all who were present at the consecration of the Eucharist communicated in it. Hence the Collects which we say after Communion are expressed in the plural, for example: “Refreshed with spiritual food and drink,” etc.; and again: “The sacraments which we have received,” etc. But after the number of believers increased, and it seemed not appropriate that all should approach the Eucharist, it was decreed that the faithful should communicate at least on Sundays. When, however, the chaff that grew in abundance began to cover the grain, the charity of many grew cold, iniquity increased, and very few were found worthy to receive the cup of salvation, it was decreed that the faithful should communicate at least at three solemnities each year: Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas. For in this manner the Lord commanded the ancient fathers that every male in Israel should appear before him three times a year, but not empty-handed.

[Col. 1765B] Now, however, because the days are evil and nearly all “have turned aside and become unprofitable” (Ps. 13), I do not dare to say by the Church’s command, but through her silent permission, it has been introduced that they gather in church to communicate once a year; and it is not lawful to omit this. Thus, as on that day the children of Israel perpetually ate the figurative lamb (Exod. 12), and on that same day the Lord gave his disciples his flesh and blood and commanded them to do this in remembrance of him (Matt. 26), so we too may eat on that day the flesh of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1).

But we must consider to which householder the Holy Spirit speaks, and concerning which house he commands that it be set in order. Four houses are certainly spoken of in theology: the house of the devil, the house of man, the house of the soul, and the house of the Lord.

[Col. 1765C] The devil’s house is the children of unbelief, vessels of iniquity, concerning whom he himself says: “I will return to my house from which I came out” (Matt. 12). But because that householder is hardened like a stone, this admonition is not addressed to him. We must therefore consider the other three.

The house of man is made by hands and visible; the house of the soul is created and rational; the house of the Lord is regenerated and spiritual. Man inhabits his house, the soul administers it, and the Lord illumines it: man by necessity, the soul by nature, and the Lord by grace. Of man’s house the unjust steward said: “When I am removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses” (Luke 16). This present admonition is not believed to concern the ordering of that house, since it is commanded to be despised rather than loved. For Abraham was told: “Go out from thy land and from thy kindred” (Gen. 12); and the bride was commanded: “Forget thy people [Col. 1765D] and thy father’s house” (Ps. 44).

The house of the soul is man himself. By “soul,” however, I mean reason, to which, like a householder, has been entrusted the guardianship and appointed ordering of our flesh and soul. Of this house it is said: “Three things drive a man from his house: smoke, dripping water, and a bad wife”—that is, the sin of ignorance, the sin of suggestion, and the sin of first concupiscence. This last not only does not allow reason to rule in its own house, but even compels it to serve as a handmaid.

But the house of the Lord is the soul itself. Thus, in a wonderful manner, the soul is both the house of man and the house of God; hence the Apostle: “The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man, Christ; the head of Christ, God” (1 Cor. 11). Of this house it is said: “Wisdom has built herself a house,” etc. (Prov. 9). To remove so great a householder from the administration of his house would be foolish and vain. “For who has helped the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11). It is clear, then, that it was said to the soul: “Set thy house in order.”

This ordering is exceedingly difficult and requires much diligence. Those through whom it is done themselves need ordering. For just as it is difficult to find guardians if the guardians themselves must be guarded, so it is difficult to find ordering if those who do the ordering must themselves be ordered. The virtues are the means by which the soul orders its house, and they too must be ordered, lest they grow wild beyond measure. For one must beware both of too little and of too much.

[Col. 1766A] A brief example makes this clear. There are two grounds for bloodletting: quality and quantity. Excess is no less harmful than corruption. What is more friendly to human nature than blood? What is more delightful to man than virtue? Virtue, therefore, must sometimes be diminished. Hear the physician most skilled under the Law, who says: “Do not be too just; there is a just man who perishes in his justice” (Ecclus. 7). Hear another, more skilled under grace, who said: “Do not be wise beyond what you ought to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. 12). Which vein of the virtues, do you think, ought to be spared, if justice and wisdom require bloodletting?

Therefore, if the wretched spirit is wise, let it answer the Holy Spirit and say: “Lord, what dost thou command me to order in my house? This labor lies before me. ‘To will is present with me, but I do not find the power to accomplish’” (Rom. 6). Teach my ignorance; help my incapacity. For as without thee I know nothing, so without thee I can do nothing.

The Holy Spirit will surely say to it: “Search the Scriptures” (John 5), which the Son wrote through me, “for I am the tongue and pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44), and you will find the ordering of your house fully laid out. Let our soul therefore read the Scriptures, and it will find what it sought.

This householder is powerful and has a very large retinue. He has servants who are external and run about among outward things; he also has inward servants who always stand before his face. The external servants are the five bodily senses—that is, the members assigned to the senses. Their ordering is frequently and easily found in Scripture. For it is written: “Turn away thine eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118); “Restrain thy tongue [Col. 1766C] from evil and thy lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. 33). Stop up your ears, lest they receive reproach against their neighbor. Restrain your nostrils, lest they seek pleasure in strange odors. Close your hand, lest it receive gifts against the innocent. Put your feet into the fetters of wisdom, lest they run to shed blood. And there are many similar sayings concerning their ordering.

The inward servants are especially the four affections of the soul, which the poet mentions when he says:

> Hence they desire, fear, rejoice, and grieve.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI.)

These, I say, are joy and sorrow, hope and fear. For just as a wealthy householder cannot do without a doorkeeper, steward, cupbearer, and chamberlain, so these stand by us, ministering after the fashion of these offices. Fear is the doorkeeper; sorrow, the steward; joy, the cupbearer; hope, the chamberlain.

Of fear it is said: “Fear of punishment is the gate of the kingdom.” And elsewhere: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). This doorkeeper has two gates and a little door between the leaves of the gates. He must set these in the way and close them if perverse thoughts should seek to rush into the soul. These thoughts must be cast out like dead flies lest they spoil the sweetness of the ointment (Ecclus. 10), like the birds which Abraham drove away (Gen. 15).

[Col. 1766D] One gate is deprivation of the vision of God; the other is the fire that shall not be extinguished; the little door is the worm of conscience that shall not die (Isa. 66). Therefore, when enemies rush in, fear should oppose these barriers and say: “You shall by no means enter, lest because of you my master be deprived of the vision of God, tortured with eternal fire, and perish with his own conscience as witness and accuser.”

Zephaniah mentions the two gates: “From the first gate,” he says, “there shall be a cry, and from the second a howl” (Zeph. 1). For the wicked shall cry when their conscience accuses them; they shall howl when they hear the harsh word: “Go, ye cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

Therefore let the soul tell its doorkeeper to watch, lest, like Ish-bosheth, while the maidservant doorkeeper slept, it be struck in the groin by thieves (3 Kings 4). With the doorkeeper watchful, the soul sits more securely and calls the steward more calmly, saying: “Set the table, gird thyself, and serve me” (Luke 17).

[Col. 1767A] Let sorrow hasten and first set before it the bread of tears for sins. This is the daily bread which we ought to eat for our daily transgressions. He fed on this bread who said: “My tears were my bread day and night” (Ps. 41); and again: “Thou shalt feed us with the bread of tears” (Ps. 79).

But let the soul say to sorrow: “Child, hast thou any relish?” (John 21). “Man does not live by bread alone” (Matt. 4). “Set before me a cooked dish, otherwise my soul will sit dry.” Let sorrow therefore set before it dishes of cooked food: first, remembrance of our miseries; second, remembrance of exile and the delay of our homeland; third, the difficulty of returning.

As it sets forth the first, let it say: “Remember that thou art ashes, and unto ashes thou shalt return” (Gen. 3); and: “Son, remember thy last things, and thou shalt never sin” (Ecclus. 7). As it sets forth the second, let it say: “Woe to thee, because thy sojourn has been prolonged; thou dwellest with the inhabitants of Kedar; thy soul shall be a long-time sojourner” (Ps. 119); and again: “You sit beside the rivers of Babylon and ought to weep when you remember Zion” (Ps. 136). As it sets forth the third, let it say: “The just man shall scarcely be saved; and where shall you, wretched man, appear?” (1 Pet. 4). “What will you do, little shrub of the desert, when the cedar of Lebanon is shaken?”

This steward is hard and severe, but faithful. His food is harsh, but health-giving; it is bitter to taste, but once swallowed it will become sweet. Its seasoning is humility, for humility is the firstborn daughter of the highest King, the salt and seasoning of all the other virtues.

[Col. 1767B] Refreshed by such food, let the soul call the cupbearer and say: “I thirst” (John 19); “mix a drink that may gladden my face, for the food has strengthened my heart.” For as it is written: “Blessed are you who weep now” (Matt. 5); likewise it is written: “Rejoice, you just, in the Lord” (Ps. 32).

Let joy hasten and offer three kinds of drink. The first is the infusion of the first grace that works; the second, cooperation with subsequent grace; the third, final perseverance. As it offers the first, let it say: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us, and therefore thou hast given joy to my heart” (Ps. 47). As it offers the second, let it say: “Thy ordinances are songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118). As it offers the third, let it say: “Have charity, and do whatever you will: all difficult things are easy to one who loves.”

> “A drop hollows out a stone.”  
> (Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book IV, elegy 10.)

“Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and thy heart shall be strengthened” (Ps. 26). This cupbearer is cheerful and to be embraced; this drunkenness, which makes men sober, is blessed.

[Col. 1767D] The golden cup of Babylon is suspect; I would rather thirst. Let the fourth servant approach—namely, hope—which has spread the bed, and say: “You have eaten enough and drunk; rise, come, lie down, rest. I have also prepared three beds for you: the resurrection of the flesh, the communion of saints, and eternal life. Hope without doubt, for this mortal body shall put on immortality, and this corruptible body incorruption” (1 Cor. 15). Besides this, the joy of all shall be the joy of each; you shall rejoice no less in another’s good than in your own. Beyond these things, you shall live a blessed and unending life.

This chamberlain must be heard, because he restores to due order the bed which man had disturbed in his infirmity. Blessed is the soul if it orders its house in this way. Therefore let us strive, each and all, that we may worthily pass from the table of sorrow to the table of communion, and afterward from both be transferred to the table of the Father, made heirs of God and fellow heirs of Christ our judge, who is to come [Col. 1768A] to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON XVII. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER
When Jesus had loved his own who were in the world, he loved them even to the end (John 13). It may be questioned whom Jesus calls “his own,” since the earth is his, and all who dwell in it. What we have said may suitably be understood either of all the elect, or of those specially chosen among the elect, or of all Christians.

Of the elect: “When he had loved his own,” etc. Here we must consider who loved, how, whom, and how greatly. Who? The Lord Jesus. How? Freely. Whom? His enemies. How greatly? Until the end of the world, and especially at the end—that is, in the sixth age—when, humbled for us, he exalted us by his Passion. From eternity God chose us to be saved, according to the saying: “God knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2). And again: “The Lord knows the number of his beasts” (Prov. 12). That it is God who loved is shown by the Prophet saying: “You are my God” (Ps. 15). That he loved us freely is then disclosed to us when it is added: “You have no need of my goods” (ibid.). The Apostle teaches whom he loved (Rom. 5), when he says: “While we were enemies, he himself first loved us.” How greatly he loved us is evident from the Passion which he endured for us.

It may also be understood of those specially chosen, whom he chose in the flesh under the Father. For he deigned to mark them with the distinctive language of his own character and to unite them to himself by a certain intimacy of love, sending them into the whole world, that they might be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judaea, and Samaria (Acts 1). Here again we must consider who loved, how, whom, and how greatly. Who? The Master and Lord. How? With familiar affection. Whom? The weak things of the world—indeed, the least: fishermen, poor and unlearned men, persons of no rank. They were in the world, but not of the world; for the world had withered in their hearts. [Col. 1768C] How greatly he loved them, and with what intimate affection, is declared by the Supper celebrated today. The Maker of heaven, the Creator and re-creator of humankind, rose from supper, girded with a linen cloth, and washed the disciples’ feet (John 13). The hands of the Saviour were humbled to the feet of servants, so that, by this example of humility, the swelling of pride might be wiped from human hearts.

For three particular reasons the Lord humbled himself in the ministry of washing feet: as an example of humility, as a proof of love, and because of its sacramental meaning. Concerning the example of humility he says: “I have given you an example, that you also may do likewise” (ibid.). And again: “This I command you, that you love one another” (John 15). Indicating the sacramental meaning of that washing, the Lord said to Peter: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me.” This is not to be understood of outward washing, but of what is signified through it: namely, the remission of venial sins.

Finally, at supper he gave his body to the disciples, under the form of bread and wine, to eat and henceforth to consecrate, saying: “Take and [Col. 1768D] eat: this is my body” (Matt. 26). And again: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). Christ was for us a price on the cross, provision for the journey on the way, and in the homeland he will be a reward, being the food of the great—that is, of the perfect. Elijah received this food and, in its strength, walked forty days until he came to Horeb, the mountain of God (3 Kings 19). This is the mountain of which the Prophet says: “Who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Ps. 14).

By the forty days is understood the entire time in which one lives in the present world; throughout it the faithful soul is refreshed by the provision of Christ’s body. The passage may also be understood of Christians, with a slight alteration of the words: thus the Lord loved his own so that he loves them unto the end. “His own,” that is, both good and bad people—bad people, at least through participation in the sacraments, even if not through final conduct. Upon all these the Saviour’s grace freely bestows many benefits: it grants small things and great; small things through the blessing of the left hand, great things through the blessing of the right; small things in temporal matters, great things in spiritual matters. Of the blessing of the left hand it is said: “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 35).

God grants Christians great things by repelling adversities, granting prosperity, and preserving what has been granted: he repels adversity, lest we succumb to troubles; he bestows prosperity, that we may love the giver; he preserves his gifts, lest by ingratitude we fall away from the giver’s grace. And we should observe that there is a great mercy of God, a greater, and a greatest: great in patience, greater in correction, greatest in justification. In patience he waits for amendment; in correction he rebukes for righteousness; in justification he raises up for the crown.

Each of these consists in three things: patience in the repulsion of evils, the granting of goods, and the preservation of gifts granted; correction in words of threatening, in acts of delight—for “God scourges the son whom he loves” (Heb. 12)—and in [Col. 1769B] examples for imitation. Therefore let us love God without presumption, fear him without despair, and imitate him without pretence. Justification too consists in, or is marked by, three things: the infusion of grace, the cooperation of free choice, and finally consummation. The first belongs to beginners, the second to those making progress, the third to those who arrive.

There is also this greatest good: continuance in good, advancement from good to better, and being caught up in the best. God catches up the saints into the best; for even if it were possible that they should live longer after the foreknown day of their death, they would not thereby merit more. So too concerning the condemned: even if they lived longer than God foresaw that they would live, if that were possible, they would not thereafter become less evil. Therefore, brothers, let us pray the Lord to love us to the end and, by his most gracious mercy, direct us in the way of life.

Let us not, with that younger brother, ask for a kid to eat with our friends (Luke 15). A kid is a foul-smelling and wanton animal, customarily offered for sins, and by it sins are understood. He seeks and eats kid’s flesh who, although he restrains his hands from the deed, yet inwardly burns with perverse thought. If one who, by a purpose of stricter life, has subjected his neck to the yoke of obedience thereafter dislikes the mortifications of vigils and disdains to endure the small discomfort of a less soft bed, he eats kid’s flesh with friends if, abandoning his purpose, he returns to things he had renounced.

Others, though they do not eat the kid with friends, nevertheless eat it in them or for them. They eat it in them when they consent to their sins and, instead of reproving them, by consenting to their perversity teach them to pour themselves out over the precipices of vices. They eat it for them when they distribute the common goods of the Church, as though they were their own, to nourish those persons’ excess. Such people either do not know, or pretend not to know, that a little is enough for nature, while nothing is enough for excess. Hence: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, but grant me only what is necessary for my sustenance” (Prov. 30); and: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6).

Therefore let us pray together, let us pray each individually, that the Lord Jesus, our king and our judge, who was humbled on earth for us, may raise us to heaven through examples of humility, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XVIII. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER, II

“You know that after two days the Passover will take place” (Matt. 26). Jesus Christ, the mediator of God and humankind (1 Tim. 2), after foretelling to the disciples who questioned him the signs of Jerusalem’s overthrow and of his coming for judgment, added: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place.” He did not deal thus with the Israelite nation, nor did he reveal his secrets to them in this way when he spoke through Moses. To servants, who do not know their master’s will concerning the future truth of the Paschal lamb, he multiplied speech and concealed truth beneath figures. But to these, as to friends, [Col. 1770A] who know what their Lord wills—and therefore he first said, “You know”—he handed down the truth in brief, not merely in the brevity of speech but in the brevity of time. For after two days Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed before their eyes (1 Cor. 5); he was offered for them because he himself willed it (Isa. 53).

Yet these same words may fittingly be understood as spoken by Mother Church. For as Christ and the Church are two in one flesh (Eph. 5), so they can often be two in one voice. Mother Church therefore exhorts the children of her womb to prepare themselves to eat the food of salvation, saying: “Little children, you know that after two days the Passover will take place. The feast-day of unleavened bread called Passover is near. You must approach the food of unity, as far as the horn of the altar. But let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (1 Cor. 11). If you are still in Egypt, or if you have advanced only after completing the journey of one day, it is not yet granted you to eat the Lord’s Supper: you must first travel the journey of two days.

David, king and prophet, when he was present in spirit in the heavenly court, brought back to us from heaven’s lofty dwelling the equipment for this two-day journey, saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36). Therefore, children, proceed through day and day: turn away from evil and do good; root out what is harmful and sow what is useful; and be ready on the third day, lest the table of salvation become for you “a snare and a recompense and a stumbling-block” (Ps. 68). More than usual, or beyond your usual practice, cultivate devotion; show moderation, pursue humility, put on seriousness, so that you may in some measure appear to suffer with Christ as he suffers, who in his life wrought a passive passion; in his death, an active Passion, through which he wrought our salvation in the midst of the earth.

Such an admonition of Mother Church is surely useful, but it is still thin: water refreshing, but not yet satisfying. Therefore let us dig with Isaac a well of abundance until most plentiful waters flow forth, [Col. 1770C] so that people and beasts may drink (Gen. 26), that is, the two kinds of people in the Church. Certainly, according to Dionysius’s hierarchy:

> [Note: [Col. 1769D] Dionysius, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.]

there are two kinds of faithful persons in the Church of God. The first is called *Deividum*; the other is called the following class, or attendants (*pedissequum*). By *Deividos* we mean ministers of the Church, to whom the utterances of God have been entrusted, to whom it was said: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Matt. 13); to whom Christ says: “All things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). By attendants we mean the multitude of the people, who sit beside the feet of the *Deividus*, that they may hear the law from his mouth and receive from his hand in due season. The former are oxen ploughing; the latter asses feeding beside them. The former are Aaronites, to whom it has been granted to see the ark of testimony and the Cherubim of glory with unveiled face; the latter are Kohathites, who carry holy things on their shoulders, but only when wrapped. These are the twin offspring of the Church.

To these two Mother Church speaks, but with a proper and distinct admonition for each. For the *Deividi* must be admonished differently from the attendants. She exhorts the *Deividi*, as those running more swiftly after the giant who “rejoiced to run his course” (Ps. 18), saying: “Children, you know that after two days the Passover will take place.”

We shall first pursue this admonition concerning the three days. Its meaning is: “Little children, remember that after three days you will sit at the rich man’s table. Look carefully at what is set before you; know that you ought to prepare like things for him. Christ has prepared a table before you, saying: ‘Do this in remembrance of me’” (Luke 22). You must understand this not merely as remembrance in memory, but rather as imitation. For Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps (2 Pet. 2).

To this one speaks for all: [Col. 1771A] “Tell us, Mother, what did Christ leave for us to imitate?” Mother replies: “I saw him bound in the garden, struck on the face in the high priest’s courtyard, smeared with spittle, mocked in the judge’s praetorium, scourged with rods, crowned with thorns, stretched over his whole body upon the cross’s gibbet, nailed fast, pierced with a lance, shut up in the tomb of a councillor, surrounded by guards. These are the steps of my God; this is Christ’s way. The Christian walks upon it.”

The child replies: “This saying is hard, Mother; and who can hear it?” (John 12). “This imitation is difficult, and I cannot attain it.” Mother replies: “Do not be afraid, child, but hear and be silent: behold, now is the acceptable time” (2 Cor. 6) for following Christ. That water of contradiction has dried up; the torrent from which Christ drank on the way has dried up. The Father of mercies and God of all consolation has moderated the original way of the martyrs, who dyed their foot in blood. If you cannot pour out blood, at least pour out water; in this you have no excuse.”

The child replies: “Whence shall I get this water, Mother?” She replies: “You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour” (Isa. 12), who cried out, saying: “All who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55). These are the three kinds of water which I saw Christ pour out. I saw him pour out tears over the holy city (Luke 19), and while he stood at Lazarus’s tomb (John 11). I saw him pour water into a basin when God, the Creator of all things, bent himself down to wash human feet (John 13). I saw, when one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, that blood and water immediately flowed out separately (John 19).

“In this manner you need a threefold washing with water, just as a threefold stain defiles you: of heart, mouth, and deed. Therefore pour out the first, second, and third waters. The first is inward, the second above, the third outward; the first is contrition, the second confession, the third satisfaction. The first washes the bed, according to the saying: [Col. 1771C] ‘Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will soak my couch’ (Ps. 6). The second washes the face, according to: ‘Anoint your head and wash your face’ (Matt. 6). The third washes the hands; hence: ‘I will wash my hands among the innocent’ (Ps. 25). The first washes unto cleanness: ‘Wash yourselves; be clean’ (Isa. 16). The second washes unto righteousness: ‘Speak your iniquities, that you may be justified’ (Isa. 43). The third washes unto the crown; hence the Apostle: ‘I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course; there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness’ (2 Tim. 4).

“This threefold outpouring of water is sufficient for you, child, that you may enter without stain into the sight of your God. This is the three-day period that I set before you: having completed this journey of three days, you will keep Passover in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5).

It remains for us to continue concerning the admonition to the *Deividus*. Mother says to him: “My son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours: firstfruits, tithes, offerings, vowed gifts, and freewill offerings I have given you. Therefore patiently incline [Col. 1771D] your ear to the words of my mouth” (Ps. 77). Christ has exalted you as one chosen from his people and has said: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me” (John 12). Therefore you must follow him wherever he goes. Know that after two days you will keep Passover: that is, not in water only, as your brother does, but in water and blood. Set your brother’s three days before yourself as the first day. There remains for you a second day, longer than the first, in the fivefold shedding of blood. For Christ also, whom you follow, shed blood five times. “Go, and do likewise” (Luke 10), lest his blood, which was shed for you, be required of you.

At his circumcision iron passed through his flesh. On this night, when he had prayed at greater length, his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground (Luke 22). On the following day he was bound to a pillar and scourged with rods, so severely that traces of blood are marked upon the pillar to this very day. Afterwards, when they suspended him upon the wood, they pierced [Col. 1772A] his hands and feet (Ps. 21), and his flesh was sprinkled with blood. Finally, blood and water came forth from the side of the sleeper. Christ shed his blood so many times not only to redeem you, but also to instruct you.

The first shedding was thus made for you as instruction, the second as an example, the third as testimony, the fourth as a price, the fifth as a sacrament. In these Christ teaches you what you owe to yourself, to your brother, and to me: circumcision to yourself, sweat to your brother, scourging to me. I pass over circumcision because I have often impressed it upon you, and more fully in the sermon:

> [Note: [Col. 1771D] Sermon 39, which begins: “Be instructed.”]

And this may be inserted here: you ought to water your brother, who is like the earth and the footstool of your feet, so that he may germinate amid the labour and sweat of your brow. Do not cease, even if a sword should pass through your own soul (Luke 1). But toward me, because I am the pillar and foundation of truth, you must be bound inseparably, so that neither hunger nor nakedness nor peril nor sword may separate you from the confession of faith; rather, you should choose to die than to be separated, even in a time of peace. Do not entangle yourselves in secular affairs or look back.

Further, if you are raised from the earth so that they place you in the chair of the elders and you judge with the senators of the earth, nail your hands fast—that is, shake them free of every gift. Do not pursue rewards, lest they make you an old blind man; lest Jacob’s voice sound forth while Esau’s hands are present (Gen. 27). Crucify your feet: stand at the gate of the house of the Lord, cry out in season and out of season (2 Tim. 4), and let not your footsteps be moved (Ps. 16). Let your bones be countable—that is, let good works shine before human beings, that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5).

Finally, if you have died to the world, if you have fled far away in order to rest in solitude (Ps. 54), forbid all your senses their use in outward things: you will have ears and not hear, eyes and not see, hands and not touch, feet and not walk (Ps. 113). You will cry to your God [Col. 1772C] in your throat. Then only water of humility and blood of obedience will flow from the side of the sleeper. Whoever does these things shall not be moved for ever (Ps. 14). With these things you will not appear empty before your God, and you will keep Passover securely—which is necessary even for one however perfect. For though the ulcer of sin has been healed in baptism and penance, the itching of the ulcer remains, and the Eucharist relieves it.

Moreover, as the apostles knew that the Passover would occur after two days, so we also know that after two days the Passover will occur. We know that whoever approaches unworthily, whoever that person may be, will bear judgment. Let us therefore prepare ourselves for the table of communion, who sit in Scripture at the table of refreshment, that Jesus Christ our Lord, our judge, may finally call us to the table of the Father, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XIX. ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN

*Delivered in the schools.*

[Col. 1772D]

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him today” (Song 3). Glorious things have often been said of the glorious Mother of God. And I perhaps, even if I speak with the tongues of human beings and angels (2 Cor. 13), shall still labour in vain, because the well is deep (John 4), and I have nothing with which to draw. Yet I cannot be silent where every creature speaks. Let my speech only be pleasing, and it will not be fruitless.

What among us is judged more glorious than to see a king in his splendour, walking clothed in purple and crowned with his diadem? Far more gloriously was our King crowned today in the bridal chamber of his mother. Today indeed was fulfilled that saying of Jeremiah (ch. 31): “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man.” For after the angelic annunciation—“You shall conceive and [Col. 1773A] bear a son”—and the modest assent of the Virgin, “Let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1), the Son of God was conceived—or, to speak more truly, begun. For he was not conceived from different seeds joined together, but formed from the Virgin’s flesh alone; not through intervals of time like other human beings, but immediately a man in all his members, immediately endowed with the same power and strength that he possessed when, at thirty years of age, he preached. Therefore in the Prophet he is designated by the name “man.”

How he was crowned there today Scripture urges us to see: “Daughters of Zion, go forth,” etc. This discourse is indeed directed especially to us, I mean to the learned, to whom it is given to know mysteries, but to the rest in parables (Luke 8), and especially to those who devote themselves to ecclesiastical studies, who, setting aside the eloquent but fruitless verbosity of philosophers, come to draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour (Isa. 12). These are not without reason understood by the daughters of Zion.

For by Jerusalem [Col. 1773B] and Zion the Church is understood. Thus the daughter of Zion and the daughters of Jerusalem are children of the Church. Israel, in the literal sense, lies beside Zion; and its fortified district, called Mello, was situated in Zion (3 Kings 9). Therefore by the daughters of Jerusalem we understand lay people, as less skilled and in need of a fortified town’s guardianship; by the daughters of Zion, the learned, both because of their excellence in knowledge, because of their guardianship and instruction of others, and because Zion is interpreted “watching” or “observation.” For it was said to the Prophet—and to us in the Prophet: “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3).

To these, I say, it is said: “Daughters of Zion,” to whom the Lord opened the understanding that you might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24), “go forth.” The same was said to Abraham, the man of God: “Go forth from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. 12). There are three things which compel us to sin: the prompting of our own flesh, the prompting of our neighbour, and the prompting of the devil, or of the world. Let us therefore go forth [Col. 1773C] from our land—that is, restrain our Eve; from our kindred—that is, close our ears to a neighbour giving evil counsel, like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth (Ps. 37); and from our father’s house—that is, let us flee the world and its prince, the devil, who deceives us by his pleasures—fleeing to the Most High, that he may overshadow us with his shoulders and that we may hope beneath his wings (Ps. 90).

Even if Scripture did not admonish us to go forth, the unbearable character of the place itself would compel us to leave. Which of us, if lying in mud, would not prefer to get out rather than remain? What is this world and all its desire but mud and filth? Hear what is said of lovers of the world: “They have rotted like beasts in dung” (Joel 1). Hear the Apostle, who counts such things as dung (Phil. 3). How much filth is piled upon this dung-heap is evident. Adam, the first and greatest giant of all, vomited upon us the filth of disobedience; and its stain was so great that it wretchedly defiled his entire posterity. The second, Cain, cast in the dung of fratricide; Lamech poured over it the stench of second marriage (Gen. 4). Even before the flood, women mounting men and men submitting their bodies to womanly acts heaped filth upon filth (Gen. 6). Let whoever can reckon how many pollutions have filled this valley down to the present day, to an intolerable stench.

Therefore go forth swiftly, daughters of Zion. Why embrace dung instead of saffron-coloured things? You are human beings, not swine. And you who have come to study have indeed gone forth from your land and your kindred, coming with the queen of Sheba to hear Solomon’s wisdom (3 Kings 10). Yet you must go forth more by the disposition of your mind than by the movement of your body. It is especially profitable for you also to go out, because whoever eats a sour grape has his teeth set on edge and cannot break bread (Jer. 31). But what is the cause? Have teeth, losing their former strength, become softened? Has bread been deprived of the delight that makes it sweeter than other foods? Not at all: numbness is the cause.

So too, one engaged in study, if he entangles himself in secular affairs, becomes numb through habit. Nature is sufficient for our study; learning is pleasant; the numbness of habit dreads to break bread. Therefore go forth and behold King Solomon. Solomon bore three names: Jedidiah, Solomon, and Ecclesiastes. Jedidiah means “beloved of the Lord” or “by the Lord.” This is Christ insofar as he is from the beginning with the Father. It is as though Scripture said: I do not say, “Behold Jedidiah,” because, as he is with the Father, one beside another, no human being will see him with the Father in Zion and live. You may believe; you cannot yet see. Nor do I say, “Behold Ecclesiastes,” that is, the preacher. For this is still to come, when all flesh shall see the salvation of God, and amid so great an assembly he shall thunder harshly to some, saying: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25), while to others he will smile with gentle speech, saying: “Come, you blessed” (ibid.).

Understand, therefore, Jedidiah, because he is beyond reproach. Await Ecclesiastes, when he shall be terrible. Now behold Solomon, because he is now gracious and desirable to behold. For Solomon means “peaceful.” This is Christ the man, who is our peace, who made both one, dissolving the wall of enmities between us and God (Eph. 2). Behold him: he was seen by all. “Our eyes have seen the salvation of God” (Luke 2). And though rejected and filled with reproaches, behold the king, because he is at once rich and poor.

But today behold him in his diadem. A crown is one thing, a diadem another. A crown is a simple golden circle, which kings use on lesser solemnities. A diadem is, as it were, a double crown, when another circle, set with gems, is added above the crown itself. Indeed, the interpretation of the Greek name itself expresses doubleness. The crown, therefore, is the soul’s natural goods; the gems placed above it to make a diadem are gratuitous goods. For when the soul’s natural affections are ordered within it, they crown and adorn it; when disordered, they are its mockery. Hence Solomon: “A beautiful but foolish woman is a golden ring in her nostrils” (Prov. 11).

There are, indeed, four natural affections: fear, hope, joy, and sorrow. Hence the poet:

> “They desire, fear, rejoice, and grieve.”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.)

These ought to be ordered so as to crown the head of the soul. Fear is on the forehead; for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1). Hope is upon the head, because it concerns only future things and things not seen. Joy is on the right, so that all joy may be in the Lord, who will place us on the right; sorrow is on [Col. 1774D] the left, for we ought to grieve over transgressions, which cause the placing of the goats on the left.

But if the four principal virtues are placed in order upon these, they make a diadem for the soul. These are justice, prudence, temperance, and fortitude. Justice must be placed upon fear, because “he who fears God will do good” (Ecclus. 15) and renders to God and neighbour what belongs to each.

> [Note: [Col. 1773D] Ulpian, law “Justice,” *Digest*, On Justice and Law.]

For justice is the constant and perpetual will rendering to each person his or her own right. Prudence must be placed upon hope, for hope has two accompanying things greatly to be feared: the abyss of despair and the thunderbolts of presumption. Therefore one must hope prudently, lest anyone, considering God’s justice too greatly, say with Cain: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. 4); or, considering God’s mercy too greatly, presumptuously say: “Even if a mother forgets her son, God nevertheless will not forget us” (Isa. 49).

Temperance must be placed upon joy; for one must always rejoice with trembling. The Apostle clearly indicates this, for after saying, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” he immediately adds: “Let your moderation be known to all” (Phil. 4). Fortitude must be placed upon sorrow, lest the depth of sorrow swallow us and the pit press its mouth down over us. Thus the soul is adorned with the weapons of righteousness on the right and the left (2 Cor. 6).

Therefore on this day of the Lord’s conception Christ the man was crowned with this diadem in his mother’s womb, because both natural and gratuitous goods were in him, and these most perfectly ordered. But by saying that his mother crowned him, it is understood that both one person and another also crowned him. His stepmother crowned him, his father crowned him, and his household crowned him.

His stepmother—that is, the Synagogue—crowned that head terrible to angels with a crown of thorns in ignominy. But on the day of resurrection his Father crowned him with the crown of immortality [Col. 1775B] and glory. On the day of the final winnowing his household will crown him. For he will come with the senators of the earth (Prov. 31), because the Lord will come and all his saints with him; and in their midst he will judge all.

His mother’s crown was a crown of mercy, for solely by the merciful act of his will he was made human. His stepmother’s crown was a crown of misery; his Father’s was a crown of glory. Hence the Apostle: “There is laid up for me a crown of glory” (2 Tim. 4). The last will be a crown of power, for he will come “like a mighty man exhilarated by wine” (Ps. 77). In his mother’s crown he is imitable; in his stepmother’s crown, contemptible; in his Father’s crown, admirable; in his household’s crown, terrible. The wicked will see him in the crown of power and perish; the righteous will see him in the crown of glory and rejoice.

Act, therefore, lest we too perish with those who perish; let us prepare ourselves for the coming of the Judge who sees all things. For if he finds us unprepared, what can excuse us? Will penitence excuse us? Yet we despise it while in the flesh. Will good works excuse us? Yet when it is the time to act, we do not act. Will the frailty of flesh excuse us? But virgins will stand against us, who in the flesh conquered the frailty of flesh. Rightly will he say to us: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25), where the fire is not quenched and the worm does not die (Isa. 66), where there is continual groaning, utmost pain, and penal sensation.

Let us therefore set before our eyes how evil it is to become exiles from the heavenly homeland, to be deprived of the communion of saints, to die to blessed life, and to live for everlasting death. From this may Jesus Christ our Lord, our judge, deliver us, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XX. ON THE GREATER LITANY
Still their food was in their mouth, and the wrath of God rose up against them (Ps. 77). In the literal sense, the Prophet reproaches the Jews—a stiff-necked people, an evil seed [Col. 1775D], wicked children—for the benefits bestowed on them by God and for their ingratitude. For in the wilderness, disdaining bread from heaven, they desired the flesh of Egypt; and the Lord gave them flesh according to their desire: flesh in such abundance, for he gave them winged birds like the sand of the sea (ibid.). But while their food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose up against them, because they were struck down by an unexpected death, and their corpses rotted in the wilderness.

Yet this prophetic utterance is not merely a reproach addressed to the Jews, as has been said, but is also prophecy and threat. It is therefore reproach with respect to those who went before, prophecy with respect to those to come, and threat with respect to those present. But when it is reproach, this is its meaning: “Still their food was in their mouths”; but let them grieve, because the wrath of God rose up against them. When [Col. 1776A] it is prophecy, this is its meaning: “Still their food was in their mouths”; but let them fear, because the wrath of God will rise up against them.
