But when it is threat, this is its meaning: “Still their food,” etc.; but let them beware lest the wrath of God rise up against them.

The reproach, therefore, is fourfold in reference—that is, it can be drawn toward four things, and is suitably referred to the four preceding cases; the prophecy likewise is fourfold in reference, whereas the threat is annual. For four cases preceded the prophecy, to which this reproach may not inappropriately be applied: the first parents; the human race in Noah’s time; the Sodomites; and the children of Israel in the wilderness. The first parents had received the command not to taste of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; but they “would not understand, that they might do good” (Ps. 35), and became vain in their hearts, imagining that they would become like gods, knowing good and evil; and, transgressing the command, they ate the forbidden food (Gen. 3). And still their food was in their mouths, and the wrath of God rose up against them.

Punishment [Col. 1776B] was inflicted on them for sin, because they were cast down into the pit of misery and the mire of filth. Job lays open this misery when he says: “Man born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries,” etc. (Job 14); and the Psalmist: “The groans of death surrounded me” (Ps. 17); and the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). Yet the wrath of God rose up, standing, as it were, over them; it did not fall upon them so as utterly to crush and destroy them with its whole weight, without hope, namely, of rising again, as it crushed the devil. For he punished them moderately when he added mortality to their misery.

What I am eager to say is remarkable, yet plainly true. Mortality, although it is a punishment to humankind, is nevertheless mercy to one who considers more truly. For if immortality had been preserved for them together with the misery inflicted, then their misery would have been immortal and thus eternal; and so it would not have differed from the misery of demons. But, just as misery was tempered through mortality and made passing, [Col. 1776C] and a turning sword was set before Paradise (Gen. 3)—that is, a sword suited to turning, plainly to removing—so the human being, fallen from the blessedness in which he was with God, nevertheless did not descend with the devil into the abyss of endless misery, but received an intermediate place: miserable, yet with an end.

The foregoing reproach can also be applied to the people of Noah’s days, because, as Truth says in the Gospel (Matt. 24): “In Noah’s days they ate and drank, and sudden destruction came upon them.” Thus, while their food was in their mouths, the wrath of God rose up against them.

It can likewise suitably be applied to the Sodomites. For we read (Ezek. 16) that the sin of Sodom was the pride of life and abundance of bread and fullness. Therefore, amid their very banquets and drunkenness, while food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose up against them. It may no less be applied to the children of Israel in the wilderness, as first expounded; and against them too the wrath of God rose up, for he crushed them. For, as [Col. 1776D] Jerome says:

> [Note: [Col. 1775] On Nahum, chapter 1.]

God should not be reckoned unjust because he drowned the human race by the Flood, consumed the Sodomites with fire and sulphur, and struck down the children of Israel in the wilderness, since they were punished thus lest he punish them eternally.

Moreover, the prophecy, as we have said, is fourfold in reference.

> [Note: [Col. 1775] Gregory of Tours, *History*, book 10; Paul the Deacon, book 3, chapter 11.]

For David prophetically foretold the destruction of the city of Jerusalem wrought by the Romans, the punishment of the wicked at the Judgment, and also a groin plague among the Romans, for whose removal the present Litany was instituted at Rome. For concerning the day of judgment Truth says: “For just as it happened in Noah’s days, when people ate and drank and said, ‘Peace, peace and security,’ an hour came upon them which they did not expect” (Matt. 24). Woe, therefore, is foretold for them: “Still their food was in their mouths,” etc.

We also read concerning the Jews [Col. 1777A]:

> [Note: [Col. 1777D] Micrologus, chapter 57; Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 5, chapter 14.]

that when they had come to Jerusalem for the feast-day of Passover, at which according to the Law they ate the paschal lamb and unleavened bread, in the very days of unleavened bread the Roman army unexpectedly arrived and shut up within the city walls an innumerable multitude of Jews in want of food and drink. Thus David, truly foreseeing the desolation of his city wrought in vengeance for the Lord’s blood, prophesied: “Still their food was in their mouths,” etc.

Likewise, the Romans, during the paschal days, without discerning the body and blood of the Lord which they had received, devoted themselves especially to feasting, games, and luxury. Yet during the days of fasting they had lived continuously in self-restraint, as though the end of the Lord’s resurrection had put an end to their restraint; and as though, while awaiting the reception of their Lord, they had prepared a clean lodging for him, only to loosen the reins of their self-indulgence once he had been received. Therefore, while the food of the Lord’s body and the feasting [Col. 1777B] by which they wished, as it were, to compensate for the preceding fasts—while, I say, this food was still in their mouths—the wrath of God rose up against them: namely, the bubonic plague.

For a swelling appeared in the groin, and some redness in the face; and almost without a sensation of pain people died everywhere—at table, on the road, in conversation, and in games. This plague spread so widely that Pelagius, the pope of that time, also died of the same plague. Blessed Gregory succeeded him, while still a deacon.

> [Note: [Col. 1777D] John the Deacon, *Life of Blessed Gregory*, book 1, chapter 36. [Col. 1778D] Gregory, book 11 of the *Letters*, chapter 2. Baronius, vol. 8, p. 6.]

So that perhaps the Lord might turn and forgive, Gregory ordained that on this day the entire Roman people should afflict themselves with fasting and, in the deepest humility, approach the basilica of Blessed Peter, there to implore God’s mercy with tearful litanies. Having prostrated himself in prayer with the whole multitude before the steps of the basilica, when he rose from prayer he saw an angel above the Castle of Crescentius, wiping a bloody sword and returning it to its sheath. He understood that the devastation would cease. Yet about eighty persons who had prostrated themselves together for prayer were found dead; and thereafter, its name having been changed, it was called the Castle of the Angel.

The threat, as we have said, is annual. For when every year the Apostle is read, saying: “Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord; therefore among you are many weak and sick, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11)—what else is this than as if he said: “Beware lest the saving food be so in your mouths that for this reason the wrath of God rises against you; lest the food given to you for resurrection become for you a downfall”?

But I do not think it should be passed over that we say in the plural: “Their foods.” For there is food for beasts, food for the faithful, and also food for the great. The food of beasts is substantial and necessary, concerning which it is said: “He gives the beasts their food” (Ps. 146). This is sustenance from the fruits of the earth and from animals [Col. 1777D] granted us to repair the natural losses of the belly.

But the food of the faithful is saving and mystical: I mean the Eucharist. For only the faithful person says to the Lord: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. 22). And Solomon directs these words only to a son: “My son, you have sat at a rich man’s table. Put a knife to your throat, and observe what is set before you” (Prov. 23). Know that you ought to prepare like things for him. For “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2).

Concerning this food the prophet says: “The Lord will make on this mountain a feast of fat things full of marrow, a feast of clarified vintage” (Isa. 25), as if he said: In the valley of Tophet—that is, in the synagogue—there was made a feast of fat things and sweet wine, where the cup in the Lord’s hand is full of mixed wine. But on this mountain—that is, in the Church—there is food full of marrow and clarified drink.

That this food belongs only to the faithful is disclosed by the Church in the scrutinies of the catechumens, who remain present until the *Secreta* of the Mass office and are thereafter dismissed; as if she said to them: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs” (Matt. 15).

But the food of the great is spiritual and intellectual. This is Sacred Scripture, which offers as many dishes to the learned as it contains teachings. For in the Church we call the learned “the great”; concerning them the Apostle says: “You who are greater, instruct such persons” (Gal. 6). For they have been appointed watchers for the house of Israel; hence we call our prelates bishops.

> [Note: [Col. 1778D] Augustine, *Confessions*, chapter 10, cites this passage.]

Wisdom says of them: “I am a special food for the great.” Certainly, the food is there assigned by the Lord’s grace: “You shall eat the very oldest of the old; and when new things arrive, you shall cast out the old” (Lev. 26). The “very oldest” before the old are the moral precepts of Sacred Scripture, which under nature’s guidance were written by God’s finger in our hearts. [Col. 1778B] The “old,” however, which came after them, are the figurative precepts of the Mosaic Law, which had to be observed until the thing signified arrived. The new things that arrive are evangelical perfection.

“Unless your righteousness exceeds,” Christ says, “the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 5)—as though the prophet were saying to us: You who are to become great in the Church, who understand more than the aged, who, the veil of the letter having been removed, will behold the horned face of Moses with unblinking eyes: keep the moral and evangelical precepts, but cast away the ceremonial ones.

Therefore, after so many examples of those who perish, we must take the utmost care lest, while spiritual foods are still in our mouths, the wrath of God come upon us and we perish. Rather, let us implore him whom we receive, that after the sacramental foods of this present time Jesus Christ our Lord, our Judge, may draw us to the table of the Father, when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON XXIV. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JAMES THE APOSTLE, SAINT CHRISTOPHER THE MARTYR, AND GERMANUS THE CONFESSOR  
For regular clergy.

“By the mouth of two or three, every word shall stand” (Deut. 17; Matt. 18). Moses, in Deuteronomy—or rather, the Lord through Moses—having given the children of Israel a form for judgments, also specified a sufficient number of witnesses for decisions in cases. But since “all these things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10), the number of witnesses necessary for us on the day of the final winnowing may fittingly be declared here, when we shall all stand before the tribunal of the eternal Judge to render an account of the things we do in the body.

For our God, who “was led as a sheep to slaughter and did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53), will come openly and will not keep silence, when he sits—namely, the Ancient of Days, whose hair is white as snow, whose feet are like bronze, about whom thrones are set, and before whom the books of all shall be opened (Dan. 10). He will have the winnowing-fan in his hand and will separate the grain from the chaff; [Col. 1779A] he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire, but gather the grain into his granary (Matt. 3). In this winnowing, under the aforesaid number of witnesses, each person will either be acquitted or condemned.

But because there are other witnesses as well, let us discuss them too, so that the meaning of these may be clearer. There are indeed three orders of witnesses: the first, middle, and last. The first is in heaven, the second in the Church, the last on earth. Of the first it may be said: “By the mouth of three witnesses every word has stood”; of the second: “By the mouth of three witnesses every word stands”; of the third: “By the mouth of three witnesses every word will stand.”

John explains the first in his catholic Epistle, saying: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit” (John 5). Concerning the last he adds: “And there are three who bear witness on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood” (ibid.). The middle order consists of apostles, martyrs, and confessors. That the apostles are witnesses, hear Christ saying: “You shall be my [Col. 1779B] witnesses in all Judaea and Samaria, and to the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1). Concerning them it is also written: “With great power the Apostles gave testimony to Christ’s resurrection” (Acts 4).

The martyrs themselves are indicated as witnesses by their name: by antonomasia they have claimed the general name as their special one, because they confessed not only by speaking but also by dying. The Lord shows that confessors are witnesses when he speaks to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear the word from my mouth, and you shall testify—or announce—to them from me” (Ezek. 3). And elsewhere: “Son of man, testify, and say: The end comes; the end has come” (Ezek. 7). These three bear witness in the Church concerning what ought to be believed and what ought to be avoided.

The first order of witnesses, therefore, is principal; the second, doctrinal; the third, judicial. The first is to be adored, the second imitated, the third awaited with fear. The first creates and gives increase; the second plants and waters; the third acquits and condemns. The first [Col. 1779C] makes sheep together with goats; the second makes sheep out of goats; the third separates sheep from goats.

Of the first it is therefore said: “By the mouth of three witnesses let every word stand.” By “word” a work is understood, according to the saying: “The Lord will not do a word which he has not revealed to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3). Now there is no work in the body of the universe that does not proceed from the court of the supreme Emperor, whether by his doing it or permitting it to be done. Moreover, if “there is no evil in a city which God does not do” (ibid.), it is certainly clear that there is no good which is not done by him—or, in another way: every work in the universe is of three kinds. There is the work of creation, the work of reconciliation, and the work of glorification.

For the world is like a garden, because from it and in it all things arise; or rather, because from knowledge of things arises knowledge of the Creator. Therefore, just as in a garden there are three times—planting, ripening, and gathering—so also in the world there are the three things just named. These three are distinctively attributed to the three Persons, not because we teach that the works of the Trinity are divided, but because Scripture and doctrine are accustomed to distinguish the works through the Persons in order to indicate the distinction of the Persons. Thus the Father created, the Son reconciled, and the Holy Spirit glorified. Hence the Father is called author, the Son mediator, and the Holy Spirit comforter. Therefore the Father is praiseworthy, the Son lovable, and the Holy Spirit desirable.

Hear Scripture attribute creation to the Father: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), that is, the Father in the Son. Hear the Apostle concerning the reconciliation of the Son: “He himself is our peace, who made both one”; and elsewhere, “In his body he broke down the middle wall of hostility” (Eph. 3). The Spirit, however, grants rest after labor; hence it is written: “From now on the Spirit says that they may rest from their labors” (Rev. 14). For then works will be spiritual, since our bodies too will become spiritual: the body will cling [Col. 1780A] to the spirit, and the Spirit to God, so that it may become one spirit with him.

Concerning the Father’s creation the Son said: “My Father has worked until now”; and concerning his own reconciliation he added: “But I now work” (John 5). Concerning glorification the Spirit will be able to say: “The Father and the Son have worked until now; henceforth I shall work, and I shall make a new heaven and a new earth” (Isa. 65).

There follows the second order of witnesses, in whose mouth every word stands. All their teaching is contained in three matters: spiritual generation, a particular love for the incarnate Word, and the form of Christian religion. The noble philosophers of the nations have indeed handed down to us quite diligently and cautiously the causes and principles of bodily generation. Moses too dealt with the generation of heaven and earth and of everything in them. He also narrated the bodily generations of the Fathers from whose loins Christ was to be born; but he passed over spiritual generations in silence.

The Old Testament likewise instructed us concerning the love of God in the words: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc. (Deut. 6; Matt. 22); but it nowhere expressly set forth the manner in which one should love God made man. It is indeed frequently said, but not frequently explained, that Christ according to his humanity is to be loved less than God and more than one’s neighbour. The religious form of the ancients was in figures and in marriage, because cursed was he who did not produce seed in Israel (Exod. 23); Christian religion has been figured in a far different pattern. Therefore the aforesaid witnesses of the Church necessarily bore witness concerning these three matters: spiritual generation, the love of the God-man, and the form of Christian religion.

> [Note: [Col. 1779D] Jerome, book 1 against Jovinian, and on Isaiah, chapter 56.]

Moreover, each of these three has three parts. Spiritual generation is the renewal of the spirit, of which it was said: “Putting off the old man, put on the new, who was created according to God” (Eph. 4). This occurs in baptism, in penance, and in martyrdom. The first is necessary [Col. 1780C] for every living person, the second for every sinner, the third fitting for every preacher. Christ commanded the first under penalty: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). He established the third, saying: “Whoever loses his life for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel shall save it in the future” (Matt. 10). Of these Peter says: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized” (Acts 2); and elsewhere: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2).

There are therefore in this life four generations: one bodily and three spiritual. Of these four, the first is natural, the second sacramental, the third penitential, the fourth triumphal. The first occurs through transmission, the second through immersion, the third through contrition, the fourth through struggle. A fifth will be the one we await, when “this mortal puts on immortality and this corruptible puts on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15). Of these five generations the Prophet says: “You shall endure with the sun and before the moon, from generation unto generation” (Ps. 61). By the moon he meant the Church, which has attained generation after generation. For in these four the Church does not have an abiding city, but seeks the fifth that is to come. Hence Sacred Scripture quite often signifies the present life by the number forty and the future life by the number fifty. For forty signifies “born four times,” fitting the way in which we are generated four times; fifty, “born five times,” fitting the homeland in which we shall be generated a fifth time.

There follows the love of the Word made man, which likewise is threefold: Christ is to be loved sweetly, wisely, and strongly. Sweet is the remembrance of what he accomplished for us in the flesh. Let us consider that the King of glory endured the troubles of an infant crying, was wrapped in lowly cloths, sat down weary from travel; that the teacher of truth had opponents in his words, observers in his deeds [Col. 1781A], mockers in his torments. Let us attend to the Virgin’s Son smeared with spittle, struck with blows, bruised with lashes, nailed fast with nails; the Creator of heaven and earth hanging on the cross, pale in death, disfigured in body.

The memory of these things is so sweet that it draws tears, fills the eyes, and moistens the face. This sweet love of Christ is especially necessary for us in prayer, so that when we lie prostrate before him, we may, as it were, alternately kiss and embrace the feet of the Crucified with our hands, water them with tears, and wipe the blood away with our hair. Peter loved him only in this manner when he heard: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not understand the things of God” (Matt. 16)—you who seek to hinder God’s wise dispensation. For it is not enough that you love how to hold him, since you do not yet know how to love him.

Christ, therefore, must be loved wisely, so that we understand that this man is also the power [Col. 1781B] and wisdom of God; that we hold this man as making all things with the Father, creating angels, joining the elements, separating the boundaries of the world, governing all things with the Father, and in nothing unlike the Father. To hold this is perfected understanding. This is the wisdom for which the wisdom of the wise has been destroyed and the prudence of the prudent rejected (1 Cor. 1). This is the rod of Moses that swallowed the rods of the magicians (Exod. 7), concerning which it was said: “Their judges, joined to the rock, were swallowed up” (Ps. 140).

This wisdom is especially necessary for us under the pressures of adversities. For if we consider that all things are done by God’s just judgment, though hidden, we shall not murmur in adversities; rather, with blessed Job (ch. 1), we shall cry: “Blessed be God.” For because we love wisely the Wise One, we rejoice in his wise ordering. Peter loved him in this way when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of God” (Matt. 16). Paul loved him sweetly when he said: “Far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6); wisely when he said: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus” (2 Cor. 5).

[Col. 1781C]

Moreover, because Christ suffered for us, he must be loved strongly by us, so that we should rather lay down our life for him than lay aside the confession of his name. Since Peter did not possess this manner of loving when he denied him at a servant-girl’s voice, he lost both kinds of love which he had possessed. He had indeed pretended to love strongly when he said: “I lay down my life for you” (John 13); but strong love does not tolerate eclipse, does not know how to bend, admits no fear. Yet, in the end, one who loves strongly restores what was lost.

This love is especially powerful at life’s last moments, so that we may thus love him who looses the proportionate bonds of soul and body: we may find it pleasing that he looses them, and say: “You have broken my bonds, O Lord; I shall sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise, and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115).

There follows the form of Christian religion, which is certainly [Col. 1781D] threefold and which the Apostle briefly defines when he says: “Let us live soberly, godly, and justly in this world” (Titus 2): soberly in relation to ourselves, justly toward our neighbour, and godly toward God. By these steps one goes from virtue to virtue, until the God of gods is seen in Zion (Ps. 83). This is the ladder by which Jacob saw angels ascending and descending (Gen. 28). Thus one goes to the stars: the ladder is short, not laborious, distinguished by only three steps.

Each step likewise is three palms in height, and has three parts. Sobriety is in things taken, things put on, and things added. By things taken, let us mean food and drink, by which we naturally repair the losses of the belly. Things put on are garments, which we place upon ourselves so that we may not feel the harshness of the air. Things added are houses and their furnishings, with every necessary household item, which are added around us for human use.

Justice toward one’s neighbour likewise has three parts, which the Lord handed down when he said: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5). Thus [Col. 1782A] we render our neighbour his due by loving, doing good, and praying. Piety toward God similarly has three parts: believing, fearing, and loving. For since God is God, he is also Lord and Father. Let the Christian therefore say: “I believe in God; I fear the Lord; I love the Father.” For this distinction is made in the prophet: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? If Father, where is my love?” (Mal. 16).

Concerning the third order of witnesses, the words are “of two or three,” which was left unsaid in the preceding cases. These are, as was said, the spirit, water, and blood (1 John 5). It will indeed suffice if the Holy Spirit dwelling within gives someone the testimony of faith, together with baptism; or if there are spirit and martyrdom; or even the Spirit alone, where a condition of necessity has excluded water, not contempt for religion. But where the three have come together, the testimony will be complete.

Indeed, today a feast is celebrated concerning the second order of witnesses, in honor of three witnesses: James the apostle, Christopher the martyr, and Germanus the confessor. [Col. 1782B] Let us therefore strive to celebrate it so that it may serve the glory of the Prince of witnesses, the veneration of the glorified witnesses, and the salvation of us who venerate them.

These witnesses are to be feared, but especially by you to whom we speak, who continually keep watch at the feet of Saint Germanus. Such a great witness is to be feared. He has indeed been appointed a watchman for this house and its inhabitants. He is your guardian: he does not doze or sleep, and he preserves all things in his heart, comparing the things you do.

Do you suppose that, when in the hour of silence you talk with someone, you can say: “No one hears me. There is only one person, and a friend, to whom I speak; walls have no ears and do not hear”? Do not err: Saint Germanus is not mocked. Your guardian hears what you say, to whom you say it, where and when you say it, and often with what intention you say it.

If perhaps you disdain the common food prescribed by the Rule and, beyond bodily necessity and the appropriateness of place and time, care for yourself more luxuriously than is proper behind barred doors and closed windows, saying, “No one sees me; every judge is far away,” [Col. 1782C] do not err: Germanus sees you. Do you think he does not notice hands anointed by the touch of meats, belchings after salted foods, the sparkling of eyes among cups? He certainly notices—and takes notice—until he who overturns the strictness of his order turns away from the one who overturns himself.

But you will say: “I shall flee from Germanus’s face. We have more remote and private cells where we may live as we please.” There too the eye of Germanus will follow you. Rather, you ought to live more honorably there: let your speech be so circumspect that it comes first to the file before it comes even once to the tongue; let your gait be modest, your diet spare, your dress moderate, so that people may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven and your Germanus, your patron, who is on earth.

Moreover [Col. 1782D], these witnesses of the second order are greatly to be feared by us in proportion as we commit more detestable acts publicly—which is the graver matter. They are to be feared lest they act against us; they are to be invoked that they may act for us. But the Judge is more to be feared, lest he punish; more to be invoked, that he may spare. Therefore let each of us invoke him; let all of us invoke him, that Jesus Christ our Lord, our Judge, may deliver us from evil report and harsh speech (Ps. 111) on that dreadful day when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON XXV. ON THE FEAST OF THE SAME SAINTS

(Printed among the sermons of Hildebert of Le Mans. See *Patrologia*, vol. 171, col. 644, sermon 63.)

## SERMON XXVI. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT PETER IN CHAINS

(See the same place, col. 627, sermon 59.)

## SERMON XXVII. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT PETER IN CHAINS
“Thou hast burst my bonds, O Lord; to thee will I sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. CXV). Peter, bound by [Col. 1783A] Herod, could say, “Thou hast burst my bonds,” when he was led out of Herod’s prison by the angel; when he himself said: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and has rescued me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jews” (Acts XII). Likewise, when the prophecy of crucifixion was laid upon him, he could pour forth a sacrifice of praise, namely this: “I give thee thanks, O Lord, because I have deserved to become a sacrifice for thee.” Thus he himself could say: “To thee will I sacrifice a sacrifice of praise”; and so, although David had prophesied this in his own time, Peter too could, in the prophetic spirit, have foretold it concerning the manner of his death and passion, and afterwards also concerning thanksgiving, when he said: “To thee will I sacrifice a sacrifice of praise.”

For in Peter’s death his bonds were loosed—the natural bonds, that is, or, if you prefer, the proportionate bonds—by which body and soul are so amicably joined that, even when the soul departs from them, it would not depart if that were possible, but would be further clothed, as the Apostle says (I Cor. V). Thus this [Col. 1783B] verse of the psalm may be expounded concerning Peter’s bonds, and perhaps even better still. But since we have perhaps perceived these matters as plain enough for everyone, let us seek other, more hidden bonds. For the more hidden a teaching is, the more pleasant it is; the more lingering, the more welcome.

Accordingly, some bonds belong to vanity and some to truth. Of the bonds of truth, some are of necessity and some of will. Let us subdivide them thus. The bonds of vanity are, generally, sins—especially the seven principal vices, such as avarice, pride, and so forth. But since their teaching does not belong to the present occasion, and is perhaps too extensive, since I cannot undertake it, I shall follow custom as best I can. Since seven is the number of universality, I shall comprehend under seven all the bonds of vanity. The first is negligence; the second, curiosity; the third, covetousness; the fourth, experience; the fifth, habit; the sixth, contempt; the seventh, malice.

By these seven the victorious devil binds a man. Consider, therefore, what and how the conqueror does to the conquered: first he casts him down; secondly, he distracts him; having distracted him, he takes him captive; having taken him captive, [Col. 1783C] he binds him; having bound him, he imprisons him; having imprisoned him, he torments him; having tormented him, he oppresses him and suffocates him. But sometimes the conquered man rises up, casts down his conqueror, distracts him when cast down, takes him captive when distracted, binds him when captured, imprisons him when bound, torments him when imprisoned, oppresses him when tormented, and suffocates him. Thus he who was first held in bonds is now released from bonds.

Released, therefore, from the bonds of negligence, what praise, what sacrifice, ought he to offer to the Lord? “Lord, thou hast brought my feet out of the pit of misery and from the mire of filth” (Ps. XXXIX). And again: “Thou hast brought my eyes from tears and my feet from falling” (Ps. LV). What shall one brought out of the snare of curiosity say? “Turn away my eyes, lest they behold vanity; give me life in thy way” (Ps. CXVIII). What shall one brought out of the snare of covetousness say? “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess thy name” (Ps. CXLI). And when he has been brought out of the snare of experience, what shall he say? “The world is crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI). What shall one brought out of the snare of contempt say? [Col. 1783D] “I was humbled, and he delivered me” (Ps. CXIV). What shall one brought out of the snare of habit say? “I will render my vows in the sight of all his people, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. XXI). What shall one brought out of the snare of malice say—malice being placed last, just as wisdom is seventh among the gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom being so called from *sapor*, “taste,” just as malice makes a man altogether tasteless? “Lord, thou hast brought my soul up from hell; thou hast saved me from those who go down into the pit” (Ps. XXIX).

By these snares a man ensnares himself, or the devil ensnares a man. Peter looses men from these snares; to him was given the power of binding and loosing, because “whatever he shall bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVI). These are the bonds of vanity.

There are two bonds of necessity, by which a man binds himself in baptism: by confession, when he is asked, “Dost thou wish to be baptized?” and answers, “I do”; and when he is asked, “Dost thou believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth?” and answers, “I believe”; or by renunciation, when he is asked: “Dost thou renounce the devil and [Col. 1784A] all his pomps?” and answers, “I renounce.” These are necessary for every Christian. Peter—that is, the Church—binds these. Here are hope, faith, and so forth. A person departing at the last is loosed from these, because from that point faith and hope shall be brought to an end. And what praise does one thus released offer? A general praise necessary for all Christians: to know what God is in himself, what in the angel, what in the world, what in the elect, and what in the reprobate. Let him say: In himself God is beginning and end (Apoc. XXII); in the angel, sweetness and savour; in the world, wonder and beauty; in the elect, sustenance and help; in the reprobate, terror and horror. This is the sacrifice pleasing to God and universal.

The bonds of will are obedience and religious profession. A man binds himself to these willingly—I speak of the religious. For it is a grave thing to leave customary ways. He imposes a great bond upon himself who was accustomed to be free to himself and now gives himself over to another’s will. He places a great bond upon himself who used to walk through the fields of licence, conversing with companions, and now submits himself to regular silence. He imposes a great [Col. 1784B] bond upon himself who used to take part in feasts and drinking whenever he pleased, and now cannot eat or drink except at the appointed hours. These are the aforesaid hidden bonds of which we have spoken: bonds by which a man both binds himself and is bound.

It remains, therefore, that because to Peter was given the power of binding and loosing, we too should pray: “O God, who didst cause the blessed apostle Peter, released from bonds, to depart unharmed, we beseech thee, loose the bonds of our sins”—our Lord, our Judge, Jesus Christ, who shall come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XXVIII. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

(It is read among the works of Hildebert of Le Mans. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI, col. 627, sermon 59.)

## SERMON XXIX. ON THE FEAST OF THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 1784C]

“I will go for myself to the mountain of myrrh and to the hills of Lebanon, and I will speak to my bride” (Song IV). A certain bridegroom speaks here, who has a bride and promises that he will visit her. Observe, therefore, that this bridegroom is not always at home. Perhaps he takes care lest his love become cheap; and because it would more quickly become wearisome if he were always present, he sometimes withdraws himself and sometimes departs for a time, so that, while he is sought in his absence, he may be held more tightly in his presence.

Perhaps he was away when he spoke these words. But lest an overly long delay should somehow produce forgetfulness, he was arranging to return and said: “I will go for myself.” He tells himself what he is about to do, because what is sweet to do is sweet to say; and, in some manner I do not know, we are never weary of speaking of what we greatly desire. “I will go,” he says, “for myself.” He goes to himself because exclusive love admits no sharer in its secret; he goes to himself because he desires no companion on the journey and permits no partner in love.

But you ask who this [Col. 1784D] bridegroom is and who his bride is. The bridegroom is God; the bride is the soul. The bridegroom is at home when he fills the mind with inward joy. He departs when he withdraws the sweetness of contemplation. But in what likeness is the soul called a bride? It is a bride because it has received the pledge of gifts of grace; a bride because it is joined to him by chaste love; a bride because it is made fruitful with the offspring of virtues.

There is no soul that has not received a pledge from this bridegroom. But one pledge is common and another special. The common pledge is that we have been born, that we have received charisms of virtues, that we feel, understand, and discern. The special pledge is that we have been regenerated, that we have obtained remission of sins, that we have received charisms of virtues. Whatever each person has, that is a pledge to that person. To the rich, his riches are a pledge, by which he is sustained lest the hardship of poverty break him. To the poor, his poverty is a pledge, by which he is chastened lest abundance cause him to run to excess through incontinence. [Col. 1785A] To the strong, his strength is a pledge, by which he is strengthened for vigorous good work. To the weak, his weakness is a pledge, by which he is restrained lest he accomplish evil. To the wise, his wisdom is a pledge, by which he is enlightened so as to advance. To the unwise, his simplicity is a pledge, by which he is humbled lest he become proud. In short, whatever human frailty endures in this life, the merciful Creator, insofar as his goodness permits, dispenses either for the correction of wickedness or for the perfection of virtue. Therefore we ought to give thanks in all things, so that, while we acknowledge his mercy everywhere, we may always advance in his love.

“I will go,” he says, “for myself to the mountain of myrrh,” and so forth. Myrrh, bitter to taste and preserving dead bodies from decay, signifies the mortification of the flesh. Lebanon, which is interpreted “whitening,” signifies purity of heart. This, then, is the way by which the bridegroom comes to the bride: the mountain of myrrh and the hills of Lebanon. First, through abstinence, he kills the lust of the [Col. 1785B] flesh; then, through purity of heart, he wipes away the mind’s ignorance; finally, as if on the third day, coming to converse with the bride, he slays the soul with his desire.

Therefore he fittingly said, “the mountain of myrrh,” not “the hill of myrrh”; and “the hills of Lebanon,” not “the mountains of Lebanon,” because we ought to be steadfast in affliction and humble in the successes of virtue. For the height of a mountain signifies the eminence of magnanimity and moderation; a hill, the restraint of humility. Again, in using “mountain” in the singular and “hills” in the plural, he signifies that in mortifying outward pleasure, what we lose is little, whereas in the inward illumination of the mind, the good we find is manifold.

On the mountain of myrrh we receive fortitude against fleshly lust; on the hills of Lebanon we receive illumination of mind against ignorance; in the bridegroom’s conversations we receive charity against ill will and hardness of heart. Power belongs to the Father, wisdom to the Son, [Col. 1785C] and charity to the Holy Spirit. This is what is meant by sinning against the Father, sinning against the Son, and sinning against the Holy Spirit. When we sin through frailty, we sin against the Father, as if against power; when we sin through ignorance, we sin against the Son, as if against wisdom; when we sin through ill will, we sin against the Holy Spirit, as if against love.

Therefore, to sin against the Father or against the Son is forgiven either here or in the world to come (Matt. XII), because one who sins through frailty or ignorance has, just as he has some excuse in guilt, so also some remission due to him in punishment: either in this age, if he repents, so that he may obtain pardon more easily; or in the age to come, if he persevered in evil, so that he may suffer a more tolerable punishment. But those who sin from malice have no excuse for their offence; therefore their punishment ought to have no remission. If they repent in this age, they must be punished by full [Col. 1785D] satisfaction; but if they do not repent, they must be punished by full condemnation in the age to come. Such persons therefore receive remission neither here nor in the age to come—not because pardon is denied to the penitent, but because full recompense is owed to complete sin.

“I will speak,” he says, “to my bride.” God speaks to the soul in two ways: differently to the harlot and differently to the bride; differently to the ugly and differently to the beautiful; differently to the sinful woman and differently to the justified woman. He rebukes the ugliness of the former and praises the beauty of the latter. By rebuking, he shakes the former with fear; by praising, he kindles the latter toward love. He speaks to the former when he shows her her stains; he speaks to the latter when he recalls to her memory the gifts he has bestowed. He illuminates the former’s darkness, so that she may know what she is and mourn what she has done; he touches the latter with the affection of inward sweetness, so that she may recall what she has received and not forget him who gave it.

“I will speak to my bride.” [Col. 1786A] If, therefore, I am a bridegroom and have spoken to my bride, know that apart from death I can speak of nothing. After the bridegroom had said these things to himself, he immediately set out; and, coming and seeing the bride, at once, as though struck with wonder at her appearance, he burst forth in these words: “Thou art wholly beautiful, my nearest one,” and so forth (Song IV). Or this may be joined with the preceding words: “I will speak to my bride,” namely: “Thou art wholly beautiful, my nearest one.” But this is received more pleasantly: “Thou art wholly beautiful, my nearest one.”

Every soul is either turned away from God or turned toward God. Of those turned away, some are far off and some very far off. Of those turned toward God, some are near and some nearest. She who is far off is already ugly; likewise, she who is near is beautiful, but not yet wholly so. She who is nearest is wholly beautiful. “Thou art wholly beautiful, my nearest one, and there is no stain [Col. 1786B] in thee” (ibid.). He is wholly beautiful in whom nothing of beauty is lacking; he is wholly beautiful in whom no ugliness is present. “I am wholly beautiful, because everything beautiful is in me. Thou art wholly beautiful, because nothing ugly is in thee. There is no stain in thee.”

“Come to Lebanon, bride.” Thus far we have heard by what way the bridegroom came to the bride, and what he said upon coming to her. Henceforth let us hear by what way the bride ought to come to the bridegroom: “Come,” he says, “to Lebanon.” He invites and calls her, because he did not come to her in order to remain with her, but in order to draw her to himself. “Come to Lebanon; come, thou shalt come to Lebanon.” He says “Come” twice in invitation; the third time, affirming, he adds: “Thou shalt come.”

But what is this affirmation except congratulation, by which he rejoices in our good purpose? It is as if he said: “I praise obedience, I see the intention, I do not fail to recognize devotion. I call and thou answerest; I invite and thou hast acted; therefore thou shalt come.” But why does he say “Come” twice? So that one who is outside oneself may first return to oneself, and one who is within oneself may ascend above oneself. First he is in us and warns transgressors to return to their heart. Then he is above us, so that he may invite the justified to himself. “Come,” he says, “come: come from outside into thyself; come from within, inwardly above thyself, to me.”

“Come to Lebanon, [Col. 1786C] bride; come to Lebanon; come from Lebanon, come to Lebanon, come from Lebanon” (ibid.): from the whitening, to Lebanon—not whitened, but white. Come from a purified heart to the purifier of hearts, not purified but pure. Thou dost not reach me if thou remainest in thyself; ascend above thyself and thou shalt find me. Thou shalt come to me and pass to Mount Seir, or Sanir. Seir is interpreted “rough” or “hairy”; Sanir, “night bird” or “stench.” Seir is the same as Edom, that is, Esau. Esau and Jacob were two brothers (Gen. XXV). Esau was born first, but was supplanted by Jacob, who was born afterwards. Esau was a hunter and had devoted himself to rustic pursuits; Jacob, a simple man, dwelt at home.

What do these two brothers signify except the two movements that are in a human being—that is, the lust of the flesh and the lust of the spirit? We know, moreover, what the Apostle says: “Not first that which is spiritual” (I Cor. XV), but that which is carnal is first. That is, Esau is born first. But when the desire of the spirit is strengthened, the desire of the [Col. 1786D] flesh withers: that is, Esau is supplanted by Jacob, born afterwards. Again, the lust of the flesh, like Esau the hunter, feeds outside; but the lust of the spirit, like Jacob the simple man, delights within.

Seir, therefore, “hairy,” is the ugly and unbecoming movement of the flesh; and it is well called hairy, because just as a hair fixes its root in the flesh but, as it grows, extends beyond the flesh, so the movement of the flesh arises from necessity but, as it grows beyond measure, flows out even into the will. And just as hair can be cut without pain, so the appetite of the flesh, insofar as excess is concerned, may be cut away, as though outside the sensation of the flesh, without harm; but insofar as it concerns necessity, it may be uprooted only as though within the flesh, and not without harm.

We have said what Seir is; now let us see what Mount Seir is. For this Seir has a mountain and a valley; indeed, to say more, it has a mountain, a plain, and a valley. In the valley it is weak; on the plain it is strong; on the mountain it is unconquerable. Seir on the mountain is the appetite of the flesh in necessity. Seir in the [Col. 1787A] valley is the appetite of the flesh in pleasure. When the flesh receives sustenance merely in order to live, Seir is on the mountain; but when it seeks nourishment for strength, Seir is on the plain. When it asks for luxuries in order to indulge in wantonness, Seir is in the valley.

Why, then, is it unconquerable on the mountain? Because bodily sustenance is necessary to those who still dwell in this flesh. Why is it strong on the plain? Because bodily strength is sometimes useful for the soul’s progress. Why is it weak in the valley? Because fleshly pleasure is always superfluous. In the valley it is forbidden; on the plain it is permitted; on the mountain it is rewarded. In the valley it serves; on the plain it fights; on the mountain it reigns. In the valley is luxury; on the plain, temperance; on the mountain, frugality. In the valley, with grace aiding, it is easily trampled down; on the plain it is conquered with difficulty; on the mountain, lest it be conquered, our daily weakness itself continually supplies it with strength.

He who cuts away superfluities tramples Seir in the valley. He who even diminishes something of [Col. 1787B] necessities conquers Seir on the plain. But he who gives nature only what is necessary for sustenance renders, as it were, the service due to Seir as a collector on the mountain. Nevertheless, it must be known that this Seir is conquered without difficulty where it rules most dangerously; whereas it is utterly unconquerable where it may be endured without danger. If, however, Sanir is read, which is interpreted “night bird” or “stench,” it may fittingly be referred to the same fleshly movement. It is called nocturnal either because it comes secretly, when the enticement of pleasure creeps in under the appearance of necessity, or because blindness of mind is born from fleshly delight. A night bird, therefore, is a hidden and unforeseen movement of the flesh. Why the lust of the flesh is called a stench requires no exposition.

“And Hermon” (Song IV). Hermon is interpreted “his anathema.” Whose “his,” except that of anathema itself? Therefore one must first ask what anathema is; then add what “the anathema of anathema” is. [Col. 1787C] Anathema is separation; the anathema of anathema is separation from separation. And perhaps, if being separated is evil, yet being separated from one who is separated will be good.

Who can better be called an anathema than the apostate angel, who first separated himself through pride from the fellowship of that heavenly city and, by the merit of his transgression, because he refused to remain a member of the Head, was cut off from the unity of that body and became the head of all the wicked? It is clear, moreover, that every human being, according to the first generation by which one is conceived in sin, is born with sin, is a member of this head, and belongs to that fellowship. But whoever is regenerated through the sacraments of faith and becomes a member of Christ is separated from the unity of this body. Who, then, is anathema except the devil and his members? And who are the anathema of anathema except those who, separated from the devil’s body, have become members of Christ?

We have now said what Hermon signifies; let us see what Mount Hermon signifies. [Col. 1787D] For, just as was said above concerning Seir, so it may now be said concerning Hermon: some are Mount Hermon and others Valley Hermon. Those may be called Valley Hermon who, although already separated from the devil by faith, nevertheless still lie cast down in the lowest desires through a carnal life. Plain Hermon are those faithful people who hold a sort of middle condition: neither depressed to the depths through fleshly pleasure, nor able to rise to higher things through spiritual conduct. But Mount Hermon are those who are separated from the devil not only by faith but also stand raised against the devil through eminence of virtue and steadfastness of mind. These indeed are those whom the ancient enemy envies more; he sees them not only divided from himself but also raised against himself. These, therefore, are those whom he strives incessantly to crush by persecution; he sees that they have both withdrawn from him and stand against him. They often suffer tribulations all the more grievous because they have the common [Col. 1788A] enemy of all as uniquely hostile to themselves. Therefore we understand nothing better by Mount Seir than frugality, and nothing better by Mount Hermon than the patience of the saints.

There follows: “From the dens of lions” (ibid.). What is meant by the dens of lions except, so to speak, sleeping cruelty? And what is sleeping cruelty except fleshly pleasure? It first delights unwary people in experience, but afterwards torments them in conscience and then in punishment. Consider how, in the delight of fleshly pleasure, the cruelty of future damnation now sleeps. Solomon says: “The lips of a harlot are a dripping honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her latter end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword” (Prov. V). And again: “Whoso is simple, let him turn aside to me.” And she said to the foolish: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant.” “And he knew not that giants are there, and her guests [Col. 1788B] in the depths of hell” (Prov. IX).

And the Lord, speaking to blessed Job concerning the ancient enemy, says: “He sleeps under the shadow, in the concealment of reeds, in moist places” (Job XL). For the devil rests in those minds which are cold within from want of the warmth of divine love, which now rejoice outwardly in the pleasure poured in by fleshly delights, and which do not foresee what bitterness will follow. The dens of lions, therefore, are the blandishments of fleshly pleasures: they now seem soft in experience, but will afterwards be felt cruel in punishment. For now the lion lies down and sleeps, because the devil, pretending himself pleasing to the minds of carnal people through the delight of sin, does not yet show what he will be. But he will begin to awake when those whom he now holds willingly in guilt by seducing them with unlawful pleasures he afterwards, raging openly, drags unwillingly to torments.

There follows: “From the mountains of leopards” (Song IV). A leopard is produced from a lion and a pard. The lion is [Col. 1788C] cruel; the leopard is spotted. Therefore, just as lions fittingly signify demons because of cruelty, so pards fittingly signify heretics because of variety: since they rend the unity of faith with diverse and perverse doctrines, they bear a body infected, as it were, with certain spots. Who, then, are leopards except proud lovers of this age, whom the devil first begets into unbelief through the teaching of heretics and then inflames into vices through love of this world? The mountains of leopards are the riches and pomps of this age, in which the perverse exalt themselves and pursue the path of the elect all the more fiercely because they see the elect lowly and humble in this world.

Therefore it is well said to the bride: “Thou shalt come and pass to Mount Seir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” It is as though it were said: Thou shalt pass to Mount Seir from the dens of lions; thou shalt pass to Mount Hermon from the mountains of leopards. But what is it to pass from the dens of lions to Mount Seir except to pass from incontinence to chastity, from pleasure to frugality? And what is it to pass from the mountains of [Col. 1788D] leopards to Mount Hermon except to pass from pride to humility, from cruelty to patience? Observe that he said “from dens,” not “from a den”; “from mountains,” not “from a mountain”; and “to a mountain,” not “to mountains.” Thus we advance from dens to a mountain, from many things to one, because the more we begin, by fleeing the world, to draw near to God, the more we are gathered into one, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who shall come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XXX. ON THE FEAST OF ST AUGUSTINE. TO RELIGIOUS

“A living dog is better than a dead lion” (Eccl. IX). The surface of the letter seems dry and bloodless indeed, but “the well is deep” (John IV). Let us dig it out, and perhaps we shall find living water, sweet to drink. Ecclesiastes, the wisest [Col. 1789A] of men, has prepared for us a great dish in a small vessel, something precious in earthenware, great food and food for the aged. For, under the metaphor of the living dog and the dead lion, he compared and preferred the simple, humble, and despised Christian in the house of his God to the Jew who glories in the righteousness of the Law and to the philosopher of the Gentiles who is proud of worldly wisdom.

For the former lives by his faith (Hab. II); the latter sleep as dead men in graves, “of whom the Lord has not yet had remembrance” (Ps. LXXXVII). Yet we ought not despair of them, because one who sleeps may go on to rise, and rise in order to live. Hence the Apostle says: “Awake, thou that sleepest; arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten thee” (Eph. V). For as the just person presently lives a mortal life and will afterwards live a living life, so the wicked person presently exists in a mortal death and will hereafter die a living death. Solomon therefore used the aforesaid metaphor in commendation of the faithful.

Yet we [Col. 1789B] too can use the same words figuratively, make a familiar expression new, make Solomon’s words our own, and form from them our own new sense in praise of Father Augustine. Perhaps someone, in commending Father Augustine, says that he was a philosopher, named among the greatest; he praises in him a Ciceronian torrent of eloquence, marvels that Augustine knew how to marry his words to things with the breathless language of Demosthenes, and declares that every kind of philosophical learning was in him. To such a person we can reply: “Brother, what you commend in Father Augustine is but little. Certainly, while he was a philosopher, he was eloquent but an unfruitful teacher; an unlearned lion, and dead. But by God’s mercy, he became from a dead lion a living dog; from a teacher of error, a teacher of truth; a guardian of the Lord’s flock. From one who had been an enemy and assailant of the faith, he became a defender of Christ, according to the saying: ‘O Lord, the tongue of thy dogs [Col. 1789C] from enemies’” (Ps. LXVII). Thus it shines forth that a living dog is better than a dead lion. For from the dead—as though they did not exist—confession perishes, according to the saying: “The dead shall not praise thee, O Lord” (Ps. CXIII). And lest we should not know of what kind of lion Augustine had been, it is defined by the qualifying word when he is called “dead.”

Four kinds of lions are indeed read of in Holy Scripture: there is the lion who is God, and the lion of God, who in Hebrew is called *Ariel*; there is the lion who is the Devil, and the lion of the Devil. The first lion is life; the second, a living lion; the third, death; the fourth, a dead lion. The first stands upon a watchtower; the second walks along the road; the third lies in a den; the fourth roars in the street.

Of the first it is read: “The lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V). He stands upon the watchtower, seated at the right hand of the Father, and looks down upon the children of men to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God. Of him Isaiah writes that, when the watchman had seen a rider upon a camel, it is added: “[Col. 1789D] And the lion cried: I stand continually upon the watchtower of the Lord, by day and by night” (Isa. XXI).

The living lion properly signifies the martyr, who does not fear what man may do to him. Of him Solomon says: “There are three things which walk well, and a fourth which proceeds happily: the lion, strongest of beasts, which will not fear the encounter of any” (Prov. XXX). This is the martyr, who dips his foot in blood, that at last he may fly upon the wings of the winds.

The lion who is the Devil lurks in a den; he lies in wait in order to seize those who walk well and divide the prey among his cubs. Of him Peter says: “The roaring lion goes about, seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith” (I Pet. V).

The dead lion roars in the street; he terrifies and crushes those who tread the broad road which leads to death. Of him Solomon says: “The sluggard says: ‘There is a fierce lion; I shall be killed in the midst of the streets’” (Prov. XXVIII). This may be understood of an ungodly ruler, according to: “A roaring lion, an ungodly ruler over a poor people” (Prov. [Col. 1790A] XXVIII). But it is more truly understood of the philosopher, who is compared with the king of animals because he went before the merely animal people in instruction: teaching them not only what was useless and harmful, but also what the highest good in life was—yet in a varying and untrue manner.

For Epicurus declared bodily pleasure to be the highest good in life; the Stoic, contempt of death; the Peripatetic, virtue of mind. This is otherwise than the truth. For the highest good in life is the grace of God through Jesus Christ. Thus the Apostle says: “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. VII). Such a lion was Father Augustine, puffed up by the wisdom of the world and distracted by the wisdom of the flesh, both of which are hostile to God. For he was a dead lion: to be wise by the wisdom of the world is to be foolish; to be wise by the wisdom of the flesh is to be mad. Hence the Lord says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” (I Cor. I).

Afterwards, as we have said, from a dead lion he became a living dog. How useful the watchful guarding of dogs is is read in the *Philippic* of Demosthenes.

> [Note: [Col. 1789D] Plutarch, *Life of Demosthenes*:] “Philip of Macedon had besieged Athens. While they were discussing peace, he said to the Athenian envoys: ‘Give me ten orators from among yourselves, whom I shall choose, and I shall withdraw and be your ally forever.’ Demosthenes answered: ‘We shall not give them.’ For wolves and shepherds had a dispute, and, as they conferred, the wolves said: ‘The sole cause and seedbed of hatred between us is your dogs. Give us the dogs.’ And the deceived simplicity of the shepherds gave them the dogs. Then the wolves boldly attacked the unguarded flocks and raged against them at their pleasure.”

Moreover, in Holy Scripture “dog” is written both in grim and in golden letters—that is, it is understood both in a good and in an evil sense. Indeed, even in the Law the dog is so detestable that one who redeems the firstborn of a dog is commanded to be killed.

Yet four qualities are commended in the dog: useful barking; a healing tongue; marvellous keenness of scent—for by the mere trace of the air it detects game far away [Col. 1790C]—and praiseworthy faithfulness, because it follows its master through paths and pathless places even to death, and serves him unto death. Whoever has carefully examined Father Augustine’s books will undoubtedly recognize all these things in him.

Like a barking dog, he disputed against heretics and false brethren. Like a healer, he possessed words of eternal life, a wholesome antidote against the troubles of the age and the languors of the soul; and experience of it is not deceptive. For he has also shown us in writing, as far as human frailty can comprehend, what God is: teaching what God is in himself, in the world, in the angel, in the elect, and in the reprobate. In himself he is Alpha and Omega; in the world, Creator and Ruler; in the angel, beauty and savour; in the elect, Liberator and Helper; in the reprobate, terror and horror.

Like one keen of scent, he carefully considered what he should say, to whom, when, and how. Like one faithful in his speech, he inserted nothing of adulterated opinion: everything was pure and faithful, “tried in the earth, purified sevenfold” [Col. 1790D]; so that of him it may be said not only truly but admiringly: “Who, do you suppose, is the faithful and wise servant whom the Lord has set over his household, to give them food in due season?” (Matt. XXIV). Behold, then, how great is the usefulness of the dog raised from the dead lion.

But this usefulness belongs generally to all; there was also another, special usefulness in his instruction of the Canons Regular. For he restored, rather than instituted, the canonical life. It is the life of the apostles and of the poor who, after the Saviour’s death, lived together in Jerusalem: “the multitude of them had one heart and one soul”; they laid the prices of their possessions at the apostles’ feet, keeping nothing as their own (Acts IV).

The apostles established the head of this canonical life in three things: common property, common obedience, and common heavenly love. Father Augustine revived this life, which had lain dormant through intervals [Col. 1791A] of time, not only by word but also set it down in writing. He added certain matters for the beauty of the order—or rather, for manuring the barren fig tree, lest it be cut down and cast into the fire—namely, concerning sobriety in food, moderation in clothing, custody of the lips, times of fasting, distinctions among prayers, and other matters of this kind.

This particular usefulness, moreover, was found in the dead lion—but dead in another manner than before, that is, slain so that he might live. According to this sense the Lord says: “I will thus kill, and thus make alive” (Deut. XXXIII). And Peter was told: “Kill and eat” (Acts X). This is the lion slain by Samson, in whose mouth a honeycomb was found (Judg. XIV). For our Samson, the bridegroom of the Timnite woman, broke him as one breaks a kid of the goats—that is, as a sinner and son of sinners.

Certainly a sinner is likened to a kid in three respects. A kid is a foul-smelling, wanton, shaggy animal. The foulness of the sinner is in habitual practice, wantonness, and instability; his roughness is in the gnawing of the worm. Of the foulness it is written: “They go up to the heavens and go down to the abyss; they staggered like drunken men” (Ps. CVI). Of the roughness: “Your land shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III).

In the mouth of this slain lion a honeycomb was found (Judg. XIV), that is, the sweet-sounding ordering of regular discipline. For as, in one body of a honeycomb, many cells flowing with honey are enclosed, so in one place are many men serving God canonically: in one place of prayer, one place of refreshment, one place of sleep, one place of correction. The Prophet marvels at the sweetness of this life, saying: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII).

Yet it pleases me to examine the honeycomb more closely. Three things are commended in honey. It is sweet—and no sweetness is like the sweetness of honey; it cleanses; and it descends. For, contrary to the nature [Col. 1791C] of other liquids, that which is thick and dreggy in it floats above, while that which is more liquid descends to the bottom.

In this manner there are three things which Father Augustine bestowed upon Canons Regular: moderation, chastity, and humility. Moderation corresponds to sweetness, chastity to cleansing, humility to descent. The philosopher, observing the sweetness of moderation, called it the golden mean. For

> It is right to be taught even by an enemy.  
> [HORACE, *Odes*, II.10.]

Martial also, writing to his son Martial concerning the sweetness of a moderate life, says:

> The things which make life happier,  
> most delightful Martial, are these:  
>   
> [lacuna] a seldom-worn toga [lacuna]  
>   
> Easy companionship, a table without artifice.  
> Desire to be what you are.  
> [MARTIAL, *Epigrams*, X.47.]

[Col. 1791D] But we can express the sweetness of moderation more deeply. Three things accompany moderation: sufficiency, tranquillity, and security. It is sufficient because it does not hunger after things to be sought, does not brood over things acquired, and does not torment itself over things lost. It is tranquil because it is not drained by cares, distracted by business, or torn by reproaches. It is secure because it does not fear the slanders of neighbours, the ambushes of robbers, or the assaults of enemies.

Next comes the cleanliness of the body, of which it is written: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I). The Lord calls this sanctification, saying to Moses: “Go down and sanctify the people today and tomorrow” (Exod. XIX). David likewise said that the vessels of the young men were clean, because they had abstained since yesterday and the day before yesterday (I Kings XXI).

Moreover, three things strengthen and preserve the purity of chastity: if one continually recalls the dissolution of the body, the tribunal of the Judge, [Col. 1792A] and the torment of Gehenna’s punishment. Of the first it is written: “My son, remember your last things, and you shall not sin for ever” (I Kings XXI). For the second the Prophet prays: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. CXVIII). The third is indicated here: “You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from before the bow” (Ps. LIX).

Third remains humility, most necessary for the Regular man who has chosen to follow poor Christ as a poor man. “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. X). Satan was proud in heaven; the cloistered person is proud on the dungheap. Pride is more tolerable in a rich person than in a poor one. True humility is to be unable to commit an injury and able to endure one when committed. And when we have done all things, let us say: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke XVII).

> [Note: [Col. 1791D] Basil, *On the Hexaemeron*.] The praise of humility is read in this manner: It is the firstborn daughter of the highest King, the salt and seasoning of the other virtues, the sweet vehicle for those in bonds who have put their feet into the fetters [Col. 1792B] of wisdom.

Moreover, three things nourish deeply rooted humility: constancy in submission—“Blessed is he who has borne the yoke from his youth” (Lam. III); consideration of one’s own frailty; and comparison with a better man, so that a person may always consider what he himself lacks and what others possess.

See how wealthy a householder Father Augustine is, who set before the guests at his table two most abundant courses: one of saving doctrine, the other of Regular discipline; one for theologians, the other for canons; one like a portion of roasted fish, that is, the following of Christ who suffered; the other like a honeycomb, by which he marked out the Canons from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head.

Yet those who eat here will still hunger, and those who drink here will still thirst. Blessed are they who hunger, because they shall be filled (Matt. V), when the Lord shall satisfy them with the torrent of his delight. Therefore let us pray, each and all together, that from the table of our father Augustine Jesus Christ our Lord, our Judge, may draw us to the table of his Father [Col. 1792C] when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XXXI. ON THE SAME FEAST OF ST AUGUSTINE

“My son, you have found honey: eat what is sufficient, lest perhaps, filled with it, you vomit it up” (Prov. XXV).

Solomon in the Proverbs has handed down to us moral instruction sufficiently careful and sufficient. That it is careful is evident because he proposes to instruct his hearer as a son; and a father instructs a son carefully, because an instructed son is a father’s glory. Hence: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you” (Deut. XXXII).

That it is sufficient is evident because he instructed the son in many ways: at one time while ignorant, at another when already competent to instruct others. The ignorant son: “Go, sluggard, to the ant; consider her ways, and learn wisdom” (Prov. VI); and elsewhere: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and in whom prudence abounds” [Col. 1792D] (Prov. III). The son already knowing: “My son, you have found honey: eat what is sufficient,” etc. The son knowing how to instruct others: “Let your fountains be dispersed abroad, and divide your waters in the streets” (Prov. V). And in the vision of Samuel: “My son, open your mouth for the dumb and for the causes of all who pass by” (Prov. XXXI).

In the aforesaid parable, concerning the moderate eating of honey that has been found, he morally instructs us toward moderate inquiries into Holy Scripture, so that something may remain in it to be burned by fire, lest, attempting lofty matters beyond our strength, we fail while searching in our investigation.

Yet besides the moral sense, a mystical meaning lies under the same parable, like two kernels dwelling beneath one rind. For King Solomon made us a great and precious dish in a small vessel: placing in an earthen vessel not only the moral meaning, like a small food and the food of little ones, but also the mystical meaning, like a great food and the food [Col. 1793A] of the mature.

Certainly the moral sense is simple, but the mystical is manifold. For there is a threefold exhortation in it: the first general, the second individual, the third special. The first is addressed to the general righteous person, the second to Father Augustine, the third to the Regular canon.

First, then, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation exhorts the universal Church, as the only Son whom his soul loves, in this manner: “You have found honey,” speaking to him as it were by antithesis: “My son, when through the things that were made you knew God from the creation of the world, and did not glorify him as God, but rather served the creature instead of the Creator (Rom. I), and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of men, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents, you found gall—the incurable gall of dragons (Job XX)—and ate the grape of gall and the most bitter cluster.

“But, when a strong and wholesome antidote had been applied through the hand of the Mediator, you vomited out the gall. And when you knew me, and Jesus Christ whom I sent, and the Spirit consubstantial with us, to be one, sole, and true God, you found honey: that is, faith in and worship of the one and triune God. Nor improperly, my son, do I call the Catholic faith honey, on account of likeness. For honey cleanses; and of faith it is written: ‘Cleansing their hearts by faith’ (Acts XV), and elsewhere, ‘Cleansed by faith in the Holy Spirit.’

“But attend, my son, to what follows: ‘Eat what is sufficient for you’; that is, eat only, and do not drink. For there are people who adulterate sincerity by mixing it with other liquids: they do not eat honey but drink a honeyed liquid.

> [Note: [Col. 1793D] Tertullian, *On Prescription*, ch. 48; Augustine, *On Heresies*.]

“Some mix water with honey to make the drink hydromel; others, vinegar, to make oxymel. The Ebionites, teaching that faith is not sufficient for salvation, mixed legal observances with faith as with honey. Do not err, my son. The water of Marah, which the children of Israel could not drink because of its bitterness, has been dried up (Exod. XV). The water of the six jars, which were set there according to [Col. 1793C] the purification of the Jews, was changed into wine (John II).

“Those, however, mix vinegar with honey who, together with faith, observe Gentile rites and superstitions. There are those who follow omens, interpretations of dreams, and divinations by lots. There are those who observe days, months, and years, seeking in them omens for actions to be undertaken. They avoid the fifth moon as ill-omened for beginning works, and follow the seventh or the tenth as lucky. Others place their hope of safety more superstitiously than religiously in washings at certain springs, incisions in trees, and the fastening on of little labels.

“Detest, my son, these harmful drinks of honey, and eat the pure honey which is sufficient for your salvation, lest perhaps you vomit it up—that is, lest what you received for cleansing turn to your defilement. For vomit defiles the one who vomits. But if you vomit it up, I too shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. III).

The second exhortation follows, in which mother Church speaks to one of her sons who, though he once gloried in worldly wisdom, became foolish in her so that he might be wise with God: namely, blessed Augustine. I pass over the exhortation of his mother according to the flesh, Monica, who, on account of her incomparable and almost unique love for her son, was not improperly so called. She laboured day and night to make a Catholic out of a philosopher. With womanly courage she did not fear the long stretches of air, land, and sea, but followed her son everywhere, pursued him with living exhortations, until she attained what she intended.

I pass over, I say, the exhortation of the mother from whom he was born by nature as a son of wrath; I come to the exhortation of her from whom he was reborn by grace as a son of life, which began thus: “My son, you have found honey.” But since Augustine, among the august doctors, was more *augustus* in inquiry, [Col. 1794A] let us patiently hear his inquiry as well.

He therefore replies to his mother in this manner: “What is this, mother, that you are dealing with me concerning the praise of honey? In Holy Scripture I have read and reread more disgrace for honey than praise of it. Through Moses the Lord forbade honey and leaven to be offered to himself (Lev. II). They were sometimes offered to the priest, but never to the Lord. Jonathan almost incurred sentence of death for eating honey (I Kings XIV). Solomon also says: ‘The lips of a harlot drip honey’ (Prov. V). ‘The Jews also, surrounding Jesus like bees, are said to have had a honeycomb in their mouth and a sting upon their back.’”

His mother answers: “My son, you have spoken shrewdly. There is honey that is detestable and honey worthy of praise. For the name ‘honey’ is written in sacred speech in both grim and golden letters. Yet there is one honey which I proposed to commend to you: namely, honey from the rock, which is read to have been given to God’s people as a supreme benefit: ‘That he might suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone’ (Deut. XXXII).

“But in order that you may know how to distinguish honey from honey, consider the different kinds of honey in nature. Besides wild honey, which is gathered from reeds and which perhaps the Forerunner of the Saviour used (Matt. III), there are four kinds of honey.

> [Note: [Col. 1794D] Justin, book III; Virgil, *Georgics*, book IV.]

“Honey is found upon the surface of the field, in leaves or herbs. Honey is found in the trunks of trees: this was sought as a scanty food by primitive people who ate acorns and beech mast. Honey is gathered from fashioned little houses, called hives, which the shepherd Aristaeus devised for collecting a swarm of bees, after he had restored bees from the decaying corpse of a young bull. Honey is also found in a hollow of the rock.

“Corresponding to these four kinds of honey, recognize four kinds of knowledge. The first is philology, which the philosopher calls theoretical; the second, which he calls practical; the third, which he calls sophistical; and the fourth, which the philosopher did not know, but which [Col. 1794C] we call evangelical.

“The first is like honey upon the surface of the field, because philosophers placed in prominence the natural causes which God had hidden in created things, in order that they too might be prominent, according to: ‘We have magnified our tongue’ (Ps. XI). The practical is like honey in trunks, because it is recognized as necessary for human needs. The sophistical is like honey hidden in little houses: for it is desirous but not existent.
