To it the bold and foolish woman invites, declaring stolen waters sweeter and hidden bread more pleasant (Prov. IX). The evangelical is like honey from the rock, for it treats of the rock upon which the Church is founded (Matt. XVI).

“The philosopher is occupied with the first, the statesman with the second, the heretic with the third, and the Catholic with the fourth. The first treats the secrets of nature; the second, the management of affairs; the third, the death of the soul; the fourth, eternal blessedness. Therefore the first is like honey that puffs up; the second, honey that stings; the third, honey that destroys; the fourth, honey that nourishes. For the first puffs up, according to: ‘Knowledge without charity puffs up’ (I Cor. VIII); the second torments, according to: ‘The sweetness of human happiness is sprinkled with many bitternesses’; the third kills, whence it is written: ‘A living dog is better than a dead lion’ (Eccl. IX); the fourth gives life, like a spring of living water leaping into eternal life. Hence Peter says: ‘Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life’ (John VI).

“You see, therefore, my son, that the three aforementioned kinds possess the surface of knowledge, not its marrow; the image, not the truth. The fourth, however, is true wisdom. For the name of wisdom is derived from two things, namely tasting (*sapere*) and knowing (*scire*). This alone is truly wisdom which makes you taste and possess the savour of eternal life. Of it it is said: ‘Wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul’ [Col. 1795A] (Wis. I), that is, savoury knowledge.

“You erred, my son. You thought yourself learned when you divided the theoretical into the intellectual, the intelligible, and the rational: that is, into theology, philology, and physiology—namely, that which treats of God, that which treats of spirits, and that which treats of bodies. You thought yourself prudent when you divided the practical into private, domestic, and political. You admired the torrent of Cicero’s eloquence, the polished exhortations of Isocrates, and the breathless words of Demosthenes, which gave life to matters to be done by living speech. You laboured over the hurried condensations of Aristotle, which he published so briefly that it was as though he had not published them.

“In all these things wisdom is indeed eloquent, but barren. For they are not spirit and life, concerning which the Lord said through the prophet: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent’ (Isa. XXIX; I Cor. I). Now at last, my son, you have found honey: that is, knowledge of both natures of Christ. You know the mystery of our redemption hidden from the ages; you hold the sacraments of the Church as healing ointments and bandages for our wounds; you rejoice in the sure hope of blessedness.”

Augustine answers: “What is this, mother, that you have departed from your customary comparison, comparing the Gospel with honey rather than silver? For it is written of it: ‘The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire,’ etc. (Ps. XI).”

His mother replies: “The comparison, my son, is indeed new, but apt. For in honey, contrary to the nature of other liquids, what is dreggy and thick floats on top, while what is more liquid descends to the bottom. Consider this very thing in Christ’s works, which Gospel history narrates. God worked great wonders and signs among the people. He wrought some luminous and beautiful things before men, but they were inferior to his final and, as it were, dreggy work. His final work—and I call it as it were dreggy—was spittle, scourges, slaps, [Col. 1795C] a most shameful death, the death of robbers. Yet this was higher than the rest. For it was greater to free us from death through death than to raise the dead. By this work he triumphed over death and the Devil. Because of this, the name which is above every name was given to him; authority was given to him in heaven, on earth, and in the sea (Phil. II).

“But attend, my son, to what follows: ‘Eat what is sufficient for you.’ For I do not exclude drinking by silence; rather, the sense is: at times drink it, at times eat it. Christ himself also invited us to drink, saying: ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink’ (John VII); and in the prophet: ‘You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour’ (Isa. XII).

“Therefore, where evangelical doctrine is easy, it is like drink; but if you find something difficult, as it were more substantial, eat it, chew it, divide it: that is, consider piously and diligently what you say, concerning what you say it, for what reason, and in what respect, lest perhaps you vomit it up, but rather bring it forth in a belch. Those vomit, my son, who think wrongly; those belch who divide food among their fellow-servants at the proper time. But observe that a belch carries with it the taste of the thing eaten. And you, my son, when you dispute concerning faith, avoid profane novelties of words, and assign to the matters you treat words that are cognate and authoritative.”

The third exhortation follows, according to which Father Augustine speaks to the Regular canon, to whom he handed down the institutions of regular life and set them down in little documents. He did not, however, hand down the beginning of common life—for that was the tradition of the apostles and of that multitude whose heart and soul were one in God (Acts III)—but Father Augustine added certain supererogatory observances concerning moderation of life and purity.

Augustine therefore says to the canon: “My son, you have found honey. When you were in the world, you were tormented by the stings of cares, because, according to Ecclesiastes, [Col. 1796A] in all affairs done under the sun there is nothing but labour and affliction of spirit. But you have fled afar off and remain in solitude” (Ps. LIV), in the leisure of contemplation and the paradise of the cloister. “You have found honey”: that is, moderation in life, which the philosopher called golden.

> [Note: [Col. 1795D] Horace, *Odes*, II.10.]

“For the characteristic of your order is moderation in food, clothing, bearing, gait, tonsure, psalmody, and such things. Excess in such matters often produces intemperance; excessive austerity sometimes produces impatience, sometimes hidden pride. But attend to the sweetness of moderation in three things: it is sufficient, tranquil, and secure. It is sufficient because it does not hunger after things to be sought, brood over things acquired, or torment itself over things lost; tranquil because it is not drained by cares, distracted by business, or worn away by reproaches; secure because it does not fear the slanders of neighbours, the ambushes of robbers, or the assaults of enemies.

“Eat this sweetness of moderation and do not drink it—that is, do not thin [Col. 1796B] its solidity or soften the rigour of the order, wishing, as though privileged, to eat more luxuriously, drink more deliciously, sleep more softly, speak more freely, keep watch less, or pray more feebly. But eat the honey you have found in this manner: obey without dispute; live in common without singularity; read with modesty and simplicity; pray with confidence and devotion. Finally, make no dispensation from the order without compensation or compelling necessity.

“You have received the eating of threefold honey. Let each eat the honey allotted to him. Let the Christian eat the honey of faith: let him believe God to be three and one, and he will eat. Let the learned person eat the honey of evangelical instruction: let him piously and diligently attend to what he says concerning what, what for what reason, and what in what respect. Let the Regular canon eat the honey of moderation, lest, climbing too high, he burst and fall, or, seeking the depths, be dissolved and perish.

“Let us therefore eat, each one and all together, until Jesus Christ our Lord, our Judge, draws us to meet him in the air to eat bread at the table of God, when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.”

## SERMON XXXII. ON THE SAME FEAST OF ST AUGUSTINE. TO THOSE IN THE CLOISTER

“Take your son Isaac, whom you love, and offer him to me upon one of the mountains which I shall tell you” (Gen. XXII).

The sequence of the history, understood simply, greatly edifies the children of obedience and virtue. For just as one must obey willingly, so also cheerfully and swiftly. Obedience without delay pleases God; but slow and disputatious obedience does not please God—obedience which, when something is commanded, asks by arguing why and for what reason it is commanded.

Our father Abraham is set before us as an exquisite example of this obedience. For just as he is truly called an old man, faithful, the first path of believing, so he can no less truly be called an old man, faithful, the first path of obeying. For the Lord commanded him to sacrifice his son. But what son? Listen, and be astonished: the son of great promise. For it had been said to him: “In Isaac your seed shall be called” (Gen. XXII); “and your seed shall be as the stars of heaven and as the sand which is on the shore of the sea”—the son of his extreme old age (Gen. XXII). For at a hundred years old he had begotten him by an aged barren woman, the son of his own wife. From Hagar the handmaid he had received Ishmael, an archer: but Isaac was the son promised marvellously, received yet more marvellously, and reared religiously.

Yet amid all this Abraham neither contradicted, nor murmured, nor hesitated, nor displayed the face of a grieving man. Rather, as though putting off the father, he armed himself against his son with pious cruelty in order to obey. Let the child of obedience attend here—you who have made the vow and profession of obedience: go and do likewise; do this and you shall live [Col. 1797A] (Luke X). For you shall be Abraham’s seed. “Now promises were made to Abraham and to his seed” (Gal. III).

Yet I know not what greater thing this voice murmurs, what more tender thing it whispers in our ears. For though these things happened so long before us, they were nevertheless written for our sake, things spoken allegorically. Let us therefore strip away the leaves of the vine, that we may find the fruit of supernatural understanding: like the kernel beneath the shell, the grain beneath the straw, the treasure beneath the earth.

But that we may fulfil the purpose of today’s solemnity, let us consider whether we can apply the things said of our father Abraham to our father Augustine. Let us attempt to say something on this by God’s gift, which may redound to God’s glory, to Father Augustine’s veneration, and to the salvation of us who venerate him.

According to the Hebrews, Abraham received three names at three periods. First he was called Ram, according to: “Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram” [Col. 1797B] (Job XXXII). This means “high,” while he was still in Chaldea, in his land and kindred, in his father’s house (Gen. XII). Afterwards, when he ascended to the land of Canaan at God’s call, he was called Abram, which is interpreted “high father.” Finally, on the day of his circumcision, when the Lord marked him out, he was called Abraham (Gen. XVII), that is, “father of many”—with “nations” understood.

Observe these same things in Father Augustine. At first he was high: he was a philosopher numbered among the great, a most acute investigator of the liberal arts. He was high, I say, in the height of swelling pride, not charity; in the height of knowledge that puffs up, not that edifies. He was a fragrant cedar, abundant in leaves but without edible fruit. He was high according to: “I saw the ungodly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. XXXVI).

But the preaching of the Saviour came to him: the voice of the Lord breaking cedars. “The Lord broke in pieces the cedar of Lebanon, and he became beloved like a calf of Lebanon” (Ps. XXVIII): that is, a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God. For he became a Christian and at last bishop of Hippo; and thus was finally called Abram, that is, “high father.” For just as sacred bishops are called shepherds of the flock, so they are also fathers of the people because of paternal care and concern. Then, from the shattered cedar, he became a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord.

For prelates are compared with olive trees because of the threefold power of oil: oil gives light, nourishes, and warms weary limbs. So too prelates enlighten us by word, nourish us by example, and comfort the needy with temporal assistance. But Father Augustine, forgetting the things behind, stretched himself toward those before. He applied not only his mind but also his hand to the exposition of Holy Scripture, so that he might fortify—or rather reveal as fortified—the tower of David with a thousand volumes, like a thousand shields hanging from it. He also ordered a Rule for clerics living canonically, extending the line of canonical moderation like a wise architect, [Col. 1797D] so that they might live in common, practising the apostolic life: having one heart and one soul in the clergy, and no one possessing anything as his own among them (Acts IV).

In these two things he became Abraham, that is, father of many nations. For from east and west, north and south, his exposition flourishes and his regular institution flourishes; and then at last he became like a vine abundant on the sides of God’s house. The two sides are those who read and those who pray: that is, scholastic theologians and Canons Regular. To theologians he gave abundant doctrine; to canons, discipline. To the former he poured pungent wine, the wine of fervour; for the latter he mixed soporific wine, the wine of repose.

We pass over his doctrine in silence, since to multiply words about a manifest matter would be superfluous. But let us briefly pursue something concerning regular discipline. Let us return, however, to the aforementioned history, [Col. 1798A] which indicates to us, concerning Regular discipline, its origin, progress, and end. For it was said by the lord Father Augustine to one wishing to live regularly, and indeed to anyone wishing to become a canon:

“Take your son,” etc. The Lord seems to say to him: “My son, do you wish to become a canon? Then take your son Isaac, whom you love.” Isaac means “laughter”: this is a person’s own will, in whose fulfilment one greatly rejoices and delights. This must first be offered to God, so that a person may not live for himself or will anything for himself; rather, it must be offered to the Lord upon one of the mountains which the Lord shall show. “By the word of the Lord the heavens,” that is, the books, “were established” (Ps. 32). In them the Lord has shown us many kinds of mountains; but it is enough to speak only of four.

Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2), is called a mountain, according to: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be above the summit of the mountains” (Isa. 2); concerning whom the Psalmist says: “The mountain of God is a curdled mountain, a rich mountain” (Ps. 67). This kind of mountain may also be called by us the Church, which likewise is called Mount Sion, according to: “But I have been appointed king by him over Sion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2). Moreover, dew descends from Mount Hermon upon Mount Sion, as ointment from the head onto the beard, the beard of Aaron, and down to the hem of his garment (Ps. 132). “For of his fullness we have all received” (John 1).

The apostles too are called mountains, as in: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86). And these are called curdled, according to: “Why do you look suspiciously upon curdled mountains?” (Ps. 67). The virtues too are called mountains, but lofty ones, as in: “The high mountains are for the deer” (Ps. 103). Moreover, according to Matthew, Christ, seated upon Mount Tabor, addressed his disciples, enumerating eight virtues, which he named beatitudes (Matt. 5). Hear, therefore, a remarkable thing. Mount Hermon sat upon Mount Tabor in order to fortify Mount Sion. He spoke to curdled mountains, treating of lofty mountains.

Upon one of these lofty mountains—that is, the first, namely poverty of spirit—the will of one wishing to become a canon must be offered. For “one” is often used for “first,” as in: “One of the Sabbath” (John 20), that is, the first of the Sabbath. And when the moon is spoken of, it is “one of the lights,” that is, the first. This is poverty of will, upon which the discipline of religion is firmly rooted. This is the dry branch upon which the turtle-dove of chosen chastity has settled. [Note: Col. 1797D. Varro, book IV, *On the Latin Language*.] For how great an obstacle, how grave a loss, superfluity and abundance of riches bring upon religious life we read more readily in the book of experience than we can declare in words. For the sin of Sodom is also said to have been abundance of bread and pride of life (Ezek. 16). The worm of riches is pride, and its inseparable companion is luxury; through these religion is avoided, its finest colour is changed, and the stones of the sanctuary are scattered.

Indeed, the excellence of voluntary poverty shines forth more fully when compared with other forms of poverty. There are five kinds of poverty: the poverty of misfortune, the poverty of greed, the poverty of extravagance, the poverty of cunning, and the poverty of will. The beggar has the first, the miser the second, the prodigal the third, the whitewashed wall the fourth, the man in fetters the fifth. The first is a scourge; the second, poison; the third, a winnowing-fan; the fourth, a covering; the fifth, a building. The first is miserable, because it torments; the second harmful, because it kills; the third windy, because it puffs up; the fourth deceitful, because it dissembles; the fifth glorious, because it crowns. [Note: Col. 1798D. Seneca, *Letters*, 2.] Nor is it surprising if a Christian lover of moderation commends poverty of spirit, since Epicurus, teacher of pleasure, commended it, saying: “Happy is cheerful poverty.” Yet it is not poverty if it is cheerful.

Upon this, therefore—his own will—the devout man offers what is especially contained in the vow and profession of obedience. And this is enough concerning the origin of regular discipline.

There follows its progress. Abraham saddled the ass, taking two servants with him. Isaac carried the wood, while Abraham carried fire and a sword. Isaac was bound, but was released when the ram was sacrificed in his stead (Gen. 22). The ass is our flesh, to which rod, burden, and fodder are due. It must be governed and chastised on the journey, lest, having grown fat, thick, and swollen, it kick back and become disobedient, as the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9).

The two servants obedient to Abraham’s command are the five bodily senses. Yet we called them two because to each sense, for carrying out its proper function, two instruments of bodily members have been assigned. Thus Abraham acts in the regular canon, lest the flesh become wanton and lest death enter through the windows of the senses into the soul [Col. 1799B]. Isaac carries dry wood: these are superfluous thoughts, which recall former good things to the mind and set impending evils before the face of the thinker. Again and again there returns to mind affection for relatives, the rejoicing of contemporaries, the varied furnishings of utensils. He remembers the time when he said to his soul: “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” (Luke 12). He recalls the time when he was allowed to do whatever pleased him, when he was his own master. He also thinks of the evils at hand: for he must leave familiar things, contend with nature, undertake hardships, and await greater hardships. These are biting cares, which do not cease to arise and to sift the holy purpose of the man. Amid them the holy man is cooked, until he is thoroughly cooked. These are the dying flies that spoil the sweetness of ointment (Eccl. 10). These are the birds which Abraham drives away while carrying fire and the sword (Gen. 15).

The sword, moreover, is some regular occupation—reading, prayer, meditation, or some regular work. Abraham seems to say: “My son, always be doing something, lest biting cares find you idle.”

> If you take away idleness, the dry wood  
> which you carry with you perishes.

Yet the sword is not enough unless the fire of the Holy Spirit is added. For “our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4). He burns wood, hay, and stubble to ashes, and purifies virtues. One of the Fathers gave us an elegant illustration of the burning of such things. [Note: Col. 1799D. Cassian, *Institutes*, book V, ch. 32.] Having received many letters from those dear to him, he read none of them; instead, gathering them together, he threw them into the fire, as though saying: “Go into the fire, trifling little papers, deceptive letters, so powerful for overthrowing a resolution. I shall burn you lest I be burned by you.”

Furthermore Isaac is bound. There are seven bonds of obedience, which the blessed Father set out more fully; the length of the discourse has imposed silence upon us concerning them [Col. 1799D]. Isaac is bound in other ways as well. He was permitted to speak, but set the guard of silence over his mouth; he was permitted to walk about, but put his feet in the fetters of wisdom; he was permitted to feast, but restrained the jaws of his mouth with bit and bridle; he was permitted to sleep, but rises at midnight to confess to the Lord. And, to conclude briefly: what he formerly was permitted to do because it pleased him is now not permitted, nor even what pleases others.

Yet Isaac is released, and, when released, he walks freely—provided that the ram is sacrificed. The ram is the sticky and rebellious habit of one’s former and perverse manner of life. It attempts to shake the stable wall of the mind with battering blows, and it renders newness of life unpleasant. For example, if you eat a sour grape, your teeth are set on edge; while the numbness remains, bread is unpleasant to you, but once the numbness is removed, you perceive the pleasantness of food. In the same way, if the habit of secular life is sacrificed within you [Col. 1800A], you perceive the sweetness of regular discipline. Do you find pleasing the moderation that brings salvation? the tranquillity of mind? the purity of body? the security of death and the certain expectation of salvation? Thus our Isaac is released and walks freely. For the Lord has set his feet in a spacious place. If by chance he is occasionally drawn outward, the yoke seems to him heavy and unbearable.

This is enough concerning progress. The end of regular discipline is the same as that of life. For Christ too was taken down from the cross only when dead. One goes out when the human spirit is released from the prison of its body, when the bonds and physical knots are loosed by which, from the beginning, flesh is joined to spirit. And Isaac returns to his mother Bersabee. “The Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother” (Gal. 4). Bersabee is interpreted “well of satiety,” or “seventh well,” or “well of the oath”; these meanings converge. For this is the satiety of eternal blessedness, concerning which it is written: “I shall be satisfied when thy glory appears” (Ps. 16); and, “Thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy delight” (Ps. 35). In it, through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, Christ will conform those who love him to the body of his glory, which the Lord has sworn—and he shall not repent of it (Ps. 109)—to give us [Col. 1800B]. There Isaac shall judge nations and reign for ever.

Therefore, having these promises, beloved, act manfully; let your heart be strengthened (Ps. 30), and wait for the Lord. When he gives us the seat of judgment, may he also give us, together with you, the seat of refreshment, the blessedness of rest, and the brightness of light—Jesus Christ our Lord, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XXXIII. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS. To those in the cloister.

Do not consider who I am that speak to you, nor who you are to whom I speak. I am like contemptible dust “which the wind shall cast forth from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1), and so my discourse is to be despised. You are fellow-citizens of the saints and members of God’s household (Eph. 2), who savour the things of God, not the things upon earth (Matt. 16). Do not, I say, lest perhaps any one of you silently answer me: “Those who are well have no need of a physician. Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4). But remember that both I who speak and you who hear are human beings, and that what you hear through my mouth is the word of the Lord. Attend, therefore, not to who I am, but rather to whose words I speak. They are the words of a noble man of urbane eloquence, namely Isaiah, who says: “On that day the Lord shall make on this mountain a feast of rich things, a feast of vintage, of rich things full of marrow, of wine clarified” (Isa. 25).

In the literal sense, this prophecy concerns the gathering of the saints which will take place on the day of judgment, on the day of final winnowing: when he who is full of days, holding the winnowing-fan in his hand, will winnow his threshing-floor, so as to gather the grain into the barns but burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (Matt. 3); when the sheep will be separated from the goats, not only in merit but also in place. That hour, however, is customarily called “day” in Holy Scripture, in contrast to the days now passing. For, if we wish to speak precisely, these present days can no less be called nights than days, because they revolve in the alternating succession of days and nights. But then the sun and moon will stand motionless, one in the east and the other in the west; and there shall be continual day in the kingdom, just as there are endless darknesses in hell.

On that day, I say, the Lord will make this feast: that is, through the angels as reapers the saints will be gathered from east and west, to recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of the Father, and as it were to eat at his table (Matt. 8). For there, as the dwelling-place of all who rejoice shall be, there shall be the sound of confession like the sound of one feasting [Col. 1801A] (Ps. 41); and in this sense its fulfilment is still awaited.

Yet it is expounded otherwise, as already fulfilled in the table of the Lord’s body, in the bread of blessing, which was made for us the price on the cross, provision for the journey in pilgrimage, and will be reward in the homeland. Thus the Lord made for us a feast of rich things full of marrow. The plural is used for the singular: namely, the feast of the fattened calf, which the father killed for the salvation of the son who had been dead and revived, whom he received back safe and sound (Luke 15). This is the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, but offered at the end of the ages, slain in the milk of his mother (Rev. 13). And because he is received at the altar under two species, it is added: “of wine clarified,” so that we refer “rich things” to the eating of the flesh and “vintage” to the drinking of the blood. This saving food is called clarified; for all other human flesh is conceived in iniquity, whereas Christ’s flesh neither contracted sin nor did he himself sin in it.

It may also be expounded in a third way. For that prophetic expression may be triple in application, since it can not incongruously be applied to the solemnity of the present day. On this day, indeed, the Lord makes a feast. Here, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, “day” means the time of fullness, the time of grace and truth. Before the coming of the Saviour, the human race was enveloped in a double darkness: the darkness of ignorance and the darkness of sin. A person did not know his Creator, did not know himself, did not know his native land. What is more obscure than this darkness? Moreover, people did not know that many things, though they existed, were sins; they thought few were grave or worthy of punishment; they believed none would be punished by God. What is more harmful than this night?

But the Son of God came and revealed hidden things. The true light came and enlightened every person (John 1); the sun of righteousness came (Mal. 4), and shone upon us. “The people of the Gentiles, who walked in darkness, saw a great light” (Isa. 9; Matt. 4). Rightly, therefore, this time is called day because of illumination. For *dies*, “day,” is named from *dian*, “brightness.” Of this time the Prophet said: “This is the day which the Lord has made,” etc. (Ps. 117). When the Apostle had called this time acceptable, he added by way of explanation: “Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6). On this day, therefore, the Lord made a feast on this mountain, that is, in this Church. For “this” refers demonstratively to the present Church, in which we still groan, subject to vanity.

There are two parts of the Church: the militant and the triumphant, and each is called a mountain in Holy Scripture. The militant is called a mountain because of the height of its life; the triumphant because of the eminence of its glory. Of the former the Prophet says: “Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle?” (Ps. 14), that is, in the militant Church; and after this—indeed, because of this—“who shall rest in thy holy mountain?” (ibid.), that is, in the triumphant Church. The militant Church is called a mountain in: “But I have been appointed king by him over Sion, his holy mountain, preaching his commandment” (Ps. 2). Certainly he speaks of this mountain, upon which he also preached; and thus he speaks only of the militant Church, because I preached only in it.

On this mountain, therefore, on this day the Lord made a feast of rich things—that is, the commemoration of All Saints. Although Boniface IV, pope, is recorded to have instituted it [Note: Col. 1801D. Bede, *On the Deeds of the English*, book II, ch. 4; Paul the Deacon, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, book IV, ch. 11; Anastasius, *Chronicle*], after obtaining from the Emperor Phocas the grant of the Pantheon, nevertheless this was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our days. For do both good and evil proceed from the mouth of the Most High? If there is no evil in a city which the Lord has not done (Amos 3), it is clear that there is no good which the Lord does not do.

Indeed, saints are not called by the name of “rich things”; rather, “full of marrow” is added. For there is a fatness to be detested, and a fatness to be commended: external and internal fatness. It is external when, multiplied by the fruit of his grain, wine, and oil (Ps. 4), a person trusts in the multitude of his riches (Ps. 11); when his storehouses, full and pouring forth from one into another (Ps. 6), do not allow him to make God his helper, but make their belly their god; when he places his hope in his own arm, leaning upon flesh as a reed-staff, which not only throws down the one who leans upon it but also pierces the hand of the one holding it. Of these it is said: “Their iniquity has come forth from their fatness” (Ps. 72). The Lord cursed this fatness in the fat cows of Samaria (Amos 4); because of it the beloved, grown fat, swollen, and thick, kicked back (Deut. 32). Christ complains of such people, saying: “Fat bulls have surrounded me” (Ps. 21).

But internal fatness is desirable when charity is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5), and the head of our mind is made fat with oil. This fatness was desired by him who said: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62). The lawgiver understood this spiritually when he said: “All fat shall belong to the Lord by a perpetual ordinance throughout all your generations” (Lev. 3). In this sense the evangelical householder said, “My fattened beasts are killed” (Matt. 22): “fattened beasts,” that is, animals which grow fat by being fed. Therefore the saints are rich and full of marrow, that is, filled with inward fatness, because the Spirit distributes to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12). But because saints still fight beneath the sun, though the Church does not yet celebrate their memory in a solemnity, “vintage” is added.

[Note: Col. 1802D. Varro, book IV, *On the Latin Language*.] *Vindemia* means grapes not only when they are on the vine, but when they are gathered from it; for *vindemia* is as though *uva a vite dempta*, “a grape removed from the vine.” Thus the memory is celebrated today of those saints who have already flown from their bodies as from a prison, removed from the state of the present Church as grapes taken from a vine.

Yet what we say may perhaps seem incongruous. For Christ is the vine, as he himself testifies: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15). When saints depart, therefore, when they pass from death to life and from the world to the Father, are they then removed from Christ? Far be it! Rather, then they are with Christ all the more truly because more blessedly. In one respect, however, they cease to be with Christ. For Christ is called both vine and life: vine on the way through faith, as it were the way of life; life in the homeland through sight. They therefore cease to be in Christ-the-vine and are more truly in Christ-the-life: that is, they no longer possess faith and hope, but sight and reality; they cease to believe and begin to live.

Nevertheless, some elect persons are still in purgatory: some perhaps must be purified until judgment, some for a shorter and others for a longer time. But the present solemnity is not for such persons; and therefore “clarified” is added. Those, then, who have been gathered from the present Church have contracted nothing of hay, wood, or stubble (1 Cor. 3), that is, nothing combustible. These, I say, are honoured by the faithful in today’s solemnity.

Nor, I think, should we pass over hastily why Holy Scripture so often calls the fullness of eternal blessedness a feast, breakfast, supper, or wedding. I think it is said not merely because of the pleasantness and fullness of joy, but because Scripture wished figuratively to suggest the distinctions among those who rejoice. For just as guests are separated through dining-rooms and recline in different banqueting-halls, so in the house of the great householder there are many dwelling-places of the blessed (John 14). His Son indicated this not only in words but also in deed, when, in the miraculous feeding from seven loaves, he caused people to sit down, some in hundreds and others in fifties (Mark 6); for “star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15).

In commemorating these distinctions among the blessed today, the Church has included them within a sevenfold division, having been instructed by the sevenfold Spirit. First, both in reading and in singing psalms, it commemorates the Blessed Virgin; second, the angels; third, the Fathers of the Old Testament; fourth, the apostles; fifth, the martyrs; sixth, the confessors; seventh, the virgins. In the same way, in that weekday prayer in which it asks for the intercession of all saints, it uses the same distinction, saying: “Grant, we beseech thee, almighty God, that the intercession of the holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary,” etc. This is the order of the feast of rich things.

[Note: Col. 1803D. Cicero, *On Old Age*.] Note, however, that “feast” here is properly called *convivium*, not from *convivando*, “feasting together,” but from *convivendo*, “living together.” Thus this order of those living together is arranged by analogy with the order of those feasting together. For in the kingdom of God they shall neither marry nor be given in marriage (Matt. 22), nor shall they eat or drink, having spiritual bodies and therefore not needing food; but they shall truly live because they shall live blessedly.

It may perhaps seem presumptuous that the Church, while still on earth, dares to distinguish in this way the modes of blessedness which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2). But Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and men, founder and ruler of the Church, both taught these distinctions in words and left them written through Levi, whom he had called from the tax-office (Luke 5). For at the beginning of the sermon delivered on the mountain, when he arranged the seven beatitudes with their rewards, he gave us the order of the aforesaid distinction, unless we refuse to acknowledge it. He assigned first place to the humble, second to the meek, third to mourners, fourth to those hungering for righteousness, fifth—to permit a change of order here—to the pure in heart (yet these too are said to be ordered thus in Greek), sixth to the merciful, seventh to peacemakers (Matt. 5). It is the same order as before, but marked with different words.

The humble, placed first, are Christ in his humanity and the Blessed Virgin, who above all others and before all others enjoy the enjoyment of the Godhead. So great, indeed, was the Saviour’s humility that it seemed almost to correspond to his majesty: as the majesty of the Son of God was incomprehensible, so the humility in the Son of Man was beyond estimation. For, though he was in the bosom of the Father, he bowed down the heavens and descended, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 1); born poorer still from a poor virgin, filled with reproaches, condemned to the death of robbers, and, after dying, pierced with a lance. He himself testifies to his poverty: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8). Thus, as he taught, reclining in the last place, he deserved to hear from the Father: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 11).

Because of her outstanding humility, the Blessed Virgin is also said to recline in the same banquet-hall. Though she was of royal seed and heard from the angel, “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1), and knew herself to be the Mother of the Son of God, she was not lifted up in womanly pride. Rather, expressing the humility of her heart through the speech of her flesh, she said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (ibid.), professing herself a handmaid, though queen of angels and human beings. In the canticle too which she sang to the Lord, considering nothing in herself worthy of commendation, she mentions humility alone: “For he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (ibid.).

The second banquet-hall is that of the meek, that is, the angels. Meekness is considered in three respects: if a person is sociable, so as to live with anyone and be gracious toward them; if one does not injure one who injures him; and lastly, if one does good even to one who injures him. These qualities are pre-eminent especially in the angels. When that foolish and shameless Lucifer separated himself from God and from his fellow angels, they remained in fellowship, strengthened in their meekness. They also patiently bear the injuries which we daily inflict upon them when we resist their guardianship; being injured, they do not injure us. Indeed, they compassionately deal more gently with us and, as is likely, like physicians devote greater care to the sick than to the healthy; and they rejoice more over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance (Luke 15).

The third dwelling is that of mourners, that is, the Fathers of the Old Testament. Attending to their captivity and seeing redemption delayed, they lamented tearfully: “How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget us utterly?” (Ps. 12). Thus our harpist wept, though he was king in Israel, saying: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with those dwelling in Cedar” (Ps. 119). Jeremiah bewailed this captivity in the *Lamentations* with a fourfold alphabet, saying: “See whether there is sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1). With how many tears, with how many sobs interrupting his speech, do we believe that he spoke who said: “Do you think I shall endure? Do you think I shall see? O that that birth might find me!” [Note: Col. 1803D; Col. 1804D. He seems to speak of St Augustine, *Confessions*, book VIII, ch. 11.] In this manner others too sat and wept beside the rivers of Babylon (Ps. 136); yet, as they went on their way weeping, they sent their seed ahead [Col. 1804B] (Ps. 130), that is, the seed meriting salvation.

The fourth dwelling is that of those hungering for righteousness, that is, the apostles. Although individual believers, and all believers together, desire the righteousness of each person and of all people, the apostles above others longed for our righteousness, laying down their lives in order to win us (1 Cor. 9). See how greatly he thirsted for the righteousness of his brethren, who said: “I wished to be anathema from Jesus for my brethren” (Rom. 9). These were wild asses awaiting the fullness of the Gentiles in their thirst (Ps. 103). Those who write on the natures of things report that, on the days of the equinoxes, wild asses distinguish the hours of day and night by their braying, and, as natural timekeepers, at the first hour of day, wherever in the world they are, utter a bray. [Note: Col. 1804D. Isidore; Conrad Gesner, book I, *History of Animals*.] Likewise at the second and third hours and thereafter; they do the same for the hours of night, so that by nature’s benefit they have, as it were, their own clock-indicator, almost in their dens.

In this way the apostles, through their preaching, distinguished to all the ends of the earth works of light from works of darkness, separating works of the flesh from works of the spirit. They themselves were called by the Lord the twelve hours of the day (John 11), so that they might be known to distinguish day and darkness not only by word but also by number. For they are the calves that filled the whole world with their lowing, because “their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18; Rom. 10).

The fifth dwelling is that of the pure in heart, that is, the martyrs. It is said by analogy. Just as someone sweeping his threshing-floor with brooms cannot clean it completely without some chaff remaining hidden either in corners or hollow places; but if a strong gust of wind comes upon it, the whole floor is cleared of every little piece of chaff: so it is credible that the hearts of martyrs before the hour of martyrdom were humanly occupied by some slight thoughts, but when that hour came, a mighty spirit came upon them and God wiped away from their hearts every movement of the flesh [Col. 1804D], so that even life itself did not feel itself naturally loved.

For when they were led to martyrdom, they looked with a stern countenance and dry eyes upon their parents, wives, and children, who, disfiguring their faces with their nails, cried piteously after them—as though nature now had no claim upon them. Who had so nearly cleansed the threshing-floor of their hearts of these things except the Spirit, cleansing their hearts by faith?

The sixth place is that of the merciful, that is, the confessors. These are men of oil, who first, having mercy upon their own souls, crucified their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5). Second, merciful toward their neighbour, they put their hand to works of mercy; and their mercy had no end except the end of their lives. They are called *confessores*, “confessors,” not *confitentes*, “those confessing.” Properly speaking, *confitens* refers to confession of sin, whereas *confessor* refers to confession of praise.

Those confessing depart who, while the foundation remains sound, do not pass without wood, hay, and stubble (1 Cor. 3); after their confession, they shall thereafter pass through fire and be saved, as it were. Confessors are those who, conscious of nothing against themselves, rise full from the table of this present life and, as it were, pour forth a hymn to God: “We give thee thanks for all thy benefits.”

The seventh place is that of peacemakers, that is, virgins and holy women. This is not because all women reigning with the Lord have possessed bodily integrity; for that blessed woman who was a sinner in the city had known a man (Luke 7). But the whole assembly received its name from its more worthy part. Or all may be called virgins because of integrity of mind. Indeed, I think Lucretia can more truly be called a virgin than the untouched woman whom no one has known.

These are named from peace, in order to show by the very name that what is, as it were, the natural reproach of woman has been taken away from them. For woman is a restless creature, suited to quarrels and strife, fitted for sowing discord. She was also the first author of discord between man and God. Naturally, too, there is a greater struggle between a woman’s flesh and spirit than in a man; for the weaker her flesh and the less ready her spirit, the more difficult the conflict and the nearer to despair, the more praiseworthy are victory and peace. Therefore adoption as children of God is promised to her: on the surface of the wording, a reward greater than the preceding rewards, but in the marrow of meaning the same as theirs—perhaps lest they might seem able to complain even from the lower banquet-hall, as though the consolation of a greater reward were added.

Nevertheless, the rewards set before the preceding orders are also fittingly applied. The kingdom of heaven belongs to the humble, because Christ not only shares them in it but, as Lord, distributes it to whom he wills. To the angels belongs possession of the land of the living, as an unbroken attainment of inheritance. For human beings were exiles from it [Col. 1805C] until the gate was opened, whereas angels, as soon as they were made, were immediately confirmed after a short time and possessed it. Consolation was given to the Fathers of the Old Testament when they saw captivity led captive by the Lord (Eph. 4), when, death having now been conquered, souls knew that bodily death would be swallowed up in victory. Fullness is given to the apostles when they see the Church crying to the Lord from the ends of the earth. It belongs to the martyrs to see God; thus Stephen, their chief deacon, saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God’s power (Acts 7). The same is believed to have happened to many of them amid their very torments. Because confessors showed mercy, judgment with mercy shall be theirs (Jas. 2).

Today the Church has appointed that this order of the feast of rich things full of marrow should be venerated in solemn memory. For whoever does not venerate the saints with whatever devotion he can is proved not to love the Lord; one who is ungrateful to the members is undevoted to the head. Yet it especially concerns you to venerate the saints, since you have resolved to imitate their feast even on earth. For you have chosen to dwell as men of one manner of life in the house of God, having the same food, no unequal clothing, the same place of eating, of sleeping, of discipline, and of prayer.

Yet your assembly differs in name from their congregation. Your gathering is called a *conventus*, as though from a way; for you come together as companions on the road, so that the labour of the journey may be less through the pleasantness of fellowship. Their congregation, however, is called a *convivium*, “feast,” from life, as was said.

Stand therefore in your ways; hold fast the resolve of the holy convent, so that at last you may deserve to arrive at their feast, where Jesus Christ, our Lord and our Judge, “will gird himself, and pass among you and minister to you” (Luke 12)—he who is to come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XXXIV. ON THE SAME FEAST.

[Col. 1806A]

(See sermon 73 of Hildebert of Le Mans, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI, col. 695.)

## SERMON XXXV. ON THE SAME FEAST.

(See ibid., col. 739, sermon 85, entitled: “ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH.”)

## SERMON XXXVI. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH.

“Holiness becomes thy house, O Lord, unto length of days” (Ps. 92). The Lord of the house is holy; holy is the house of the Lord. And what becomes what is holy except holy things? For, as has been said both poetically and truly:

Small things suit small things; [Col. 1806B] so it may be said reverently and truly: holy things suit what is holy. Therefore holiness befits the holy house of the Lord—not any kind of holiness, not perfunctory or momentary holiness, but everlasting holiness. Hence the Lord says: “Be holy, as I too am holy” (Lev. XIX). As my holiness is unceasing, so yours too must endure unto length of days. The present life is called “days,” in which many days succeed one another through the interposition of nights. But the length of days that is to follow is the life to come, which will stretch without end in the continuous course of one day. Therefore the holiness of the Lord’s house will not end within these days; rather, it will be perfected in length of days. Nor does holiness befit only one house of the Lord, but every one; for he has several houses.

We may judge the number of his houses from the number of houses which cenobites build for themselves. For instruction about such matters should be taken from those who have resolved, insofar as they can, to imitate the Lord in all things. For they have left everything behind, just as Christ had nowhere [Col. 1806C] to lay his head (Luke IX). Obediently they bear the cross after Christ, just as Christ bore it—not as Simon was compelled to carry it (Matt. XVII). Poor and naked, they run after the giant who rejoiced to run his course: the freer they are from burdens, the more unencumbered are they on the journey. It is therefore likely that they had the Lord as their instructor even in their dwellings.

Now we see that the common dwelling of such persons is enclosed by four houses; whence it is rightly called a cloister. There is a house of God, a house of refreshment, a house of rest, and a house of provision—I mean the storehouse in which necessities for use are kept. In this manner the Lord has four houses: the house of prayer, the same as theirs, of which he himself says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer, says the Lord” (Isa. LIII); the house of the whole universe, that is, the world, whence: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. XXIII); and he himself says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII); and elsewhere: [Col. 1806D] “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI). He also has a house of rest, namely the soul of the righteous; whence: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI). He also has a house of refreshment, namely the undefiled body; whence the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” (I Cor. VI). It is called a house of refreshment because, as many services of the members devoted to righteousness serve sanctification, so many dishes, as it were, are set before God for refreshment.

On account of these four houses, he is customarily called by four names: God in the temple, Lord in the world, Bridegroom in the soul, and Master of the household in the holy body. Each of these houses has its own holiness. But we pass over the holiness of the world in silence; the present solemnity compels us to speak of the holiness of the others.

[Col. 1807A]

The dedication of a temple, the sanctification of the body, the religion of the soul, and the adoption of children are spoken of. For the church has been dedicated—that is, once and for all confirmed for divine uses, so that thereafter we do not employ it for common uses; for to dedicate is to confirm, as it were to consecrate to God. Religion, properly speaking, belongs to the members. Through the sin of the first parent the members broke out into disordered movements; unless these are bound again under the fear of God, they will be carried into the ruin of disgrace. The Prophet desired his members to be bound in this way, saying: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. CXXVIII).

But the soul alone is sanctified by adoption, that is, by prevenient grace. Nor should you wonder if we say that the present solemnity pertains not only to the holiness of the temple but also to that of human beings. For the dedication of human beings is more celebrated than that of temples. Human beings solemnize the dedication of a temple on earth; angels rejoice over the dedication of a human being in heaven. The former is visible, accomplished once, and completed in a short time; the latter is invisible and everlasting, begun here and to be completed in length of days. [Col. 1807B] Here is building; there, dedication. The former was celebrated by a pontiff who was a human being, subject to suffering like us; the latter is performed by Christ, the high priest standing over the good things to come. The former is an image of the latter; the latter is the truth of its image.

Let us see in what the sanctification of a temple consists, so that from these things we may mystically gather the holiness of human beings. As I suppose, the dedication of a temple is fulfilled in five things: sprinkling, inscription, anointing, illumination, and blessing. It is sprinkled with water, to which three things are added: salt, ashes, and wine; and the sprinkler should be made from hyssop. Then the pavement is inscribed with the Greek and Latin alphabet, with lines drawn from corner to corner and intersecting in the middle in the form of a cross. Next, it is anointed with holy chrism in twelve places, and afterward twelve candles are lit over the same places. Finally, the dedication is concluded by the bishop’s blessing. The institution and meaning of these things belong to another inquiry; but how [Col. 1807C] in this manner, the sanctification of human beings is accomplished is the subject of the present discussion.

First, indeed, the holy person is sprinkled with the water of repentance and mourning. Peter was sprinkled with this water when he wept bitterly, to wash away the stain of his threefold denial (Matt. XXVI). Of this same water the Prophet says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall soak my couch” (Ps. VI). And elsewhere: “My tears were my bread by day and by night” (Ps. XLI). Let us see how necessary this water is.

Solomon says: “My son, when you sit at a rich man’s table, consider what is set before you; remember that you ought to prepare the like for him” (Prov. XXIII). Christ is rich, and we sit at his table, sharing in his flesh and blood. He set water and wine before us; for he came not in water only, but in water and blood (John V). Perhaps the time is unsuitable, or your poverty does not suffice, for you to set wine before him. The chief martyr, Lord Stephen, set wine before him, all the sweeter because it was newer. [Col. 1807D] The holy martyrs set wine before him, who founded the Church of God with their blood. The time of vintage has indeed passed; perhaps weakness of spirit prevents human hands now from finding wine. Therefore it is necessary at least to set water before him. Yet this water is not simple: it must have with it three things—salt, ashes, and wine.

Salt is the fear of the Lord; hence in Leviticus: “In every sacrifice you shall put the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God” (Lev. I). For the fear of the Lord accompanies every degree: every Christian who offers sacrifices of works must have the fear of God before his eyes in all things. Ashes are the remembrance of the human circuit. For our life is like a line drawn in a circle, returning to the same point: beginning from dust, advancing, as it were, in a circular course through natural failings, and returning to dust. The hand of the Lord who drives us onward made this inevitable course for us when he said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III). [Col. 1808A] Wine is the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion. These three make the water of repentance holy and pleasing to God. For who, possessing the fear of the Lord, remembering the last things, and recalling that the Lord was condemned to a most shameful death for his sake, would not dissolve into tears? Who is so stony that he is not wholly shaken and trembles, saying: “You have moved my earth, O Lord, and troubled it; heal its breaches, for it has been shaken” (Ps. LIX)?

There follows the inscription. This is the rigor of your order, handed down to you by the holy Fathers and committed to writing. These are the elements of your religious life, with which the novice canon must be imbued. The inscription is twofold, because it must be written indelibly both on the tablets of the heart and on the pavement of our body—not as upon ice before the face of the sun. In each case it is written from corner to corner. But is not a heart with corners called deceitful and customarily detested? Here, however, we call the two corners of the heart the humble heart and the lofty [Col. 1808B] heart.

The humble heart is when someone, reckoning himself to be nothing, says, even after doing everything, that he is an unprofitable servant (Luke XVII). Of this heart it is said: “You transgressors, return to the heart” (Isa. XLVI). The lofty heart is when someone is borne upward in mind, saying: “But for me it is good to cleave to God” (Ps. LXXII); concerning it it is said: “A person shall come to a lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. LXIII). Therefore, from the humble heart to the lofty heart—that is, whether you think humbly of yourselves or transcend yourselves in mind—hold firmly in steadfast heart the boundaries inscribed upon you, lest perhaps it be said of you: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke XIV).

This inscription has also been made upon our bodies. For you bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in your body; the distinguishing mark has been impressed upon you, by which the distinction of your order is readily apparent even to the eye. The shaving of the head, the lowliness and cleanliness of garments, the dry sobriety of food, composed movement, gait, gesture, and bearing, and the other things of this kind, are inscriptions impressed upon you and signs of your God, [Col. 1808C] so that you may say: “He has placed a sign upon my face, that I may admit no lover except him.” [Note: Saying of St. Agnes; Col. 1807D.] These signs extend from one corner of the body to the other, that is, from head to feet, so that no deformity from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head may seem to find a place in you; or from the beginning of your profession until life’s end, because it falls short of the truth of sacrifice not to offer the tail of the victim (Lev. III).

There follows the anointing. We may understand your twelvefold anointing as the apostolic imitation which you have set before yourselves. For other cenobites, whom we call monks, chose each one the individual care of himself, lest one be burdened by another’s weight; hence they are not permitted either to baptize, to preach to others, or to impose penances. But you, imitators of the apostolic multitude “whose heart was one and whose soul was one” (Acts IV), can and ought to provide both for yourselves and for others.

Yet since anointing [Col. 1808D] is customarily called an infusion of spiritual grace, we may not incongruously refer this twelvefold infusion to the bestowal of twelve virtues—a matter that can be dealt with briefly. There are four virtues which we call cardinal: justice, which renders to each what is its own, namely to God, oneself, and one’s neighbor; prudence, which concerns guarding against sins and troubles; temperance in prosperity; and fortitude in adversity. Each of these has two associated virtues. Mercy and truth stand beside justice; for unless mercy encounters truth, it is no longer mercy but misery; and unless truth encounters mercy, it is no longer truth but severity. Mortification of the flesh and obedience stand beside prudence; for by the chastening of the flesh we provide beforehand against many excesses. For, to omit other examples:

> “Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold.”
>
> [Note: Terence, *Eunuchus*; Col. 1808D.]

[Col. 1809A] What more powerfully restrains us from unlawful things than the vow of obedience, by which you have bound yourselves wholly? Humility and kindness stand beside temperance. For riches are customarily *hyperiphanae*, that is, proud, and in prosperity they bring covetousness along with them. Therefore one must be humble and kind, dispensing one’s goods to one’s neighbors.

Hope of life and contempt for the world stand beside fortitude. Why do you think Lawrence was so strong in adversity that he even seemed to joke amid the flames, saying, “It is roasted; turn it and eat”? Was it not because he possessed an unfading hope of unfading life? Why do you think holy Job, amid so many sores of the body and sudden losses of possessions, so often and steadfastly blessed God? Was it not because he regarded all these things as dung?

There follows illumination, though it is already evident: charity cannot be hidden. This lamp has been set upon a lampstand; your works shine before human beings, so that they may glorify [Col. 1810A] your Father who is in heaven (Matt. V). For after your loins have been girded, burning lamps are in your hands (Luke XII). Of the final blessing we say that it will then take place, when your glory appears, when this mortal puts on immortality, when the Holy Spirit tells the afflicted spirit to rest from its labors (I Cor. XV). For at the placing of the stones, no sound of hammer or axe will be heard in Jerusalem. Therefore, now made rough through repentance, inscribed through discipline, anointed through grace, illuminated through action, you await the final hand of the one who blesses. For you know in whom you have believed, and you are certain that the just Judge will set before you the blessing for which you wait. May Jesus Christ our Lord, our Judge, bless us together with you with that blessing when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

The sermons delivered at synods follow.

[Col. 1809]

## SERMON XXXVII

[Col. 1809B]

“If Pharaoh says to you, ‘What is your occupation?’ answer: ‘We are shepherds’” (Gen. XLII).

Here salutary and weighty counsel is given. It is important to know who gave it, to whom, and where. Joseph gave it; to whom? To his brothers; where? In Egypt. While Joseph was in the land of his birth, he is not recorded as having given counsel to his brothers; rather, his brothers mocked him, stripped him of his coat, formed a wicked plan against him, sold him to the Ishmaelites, and the Ishmaelites to the Egyptians. But after he was exalted in Egypt, he gave his brothers salutary counsel: “If Pharaoh says to you,” and so forth.

Brothers, since all these things happened to them in a figure (I Cor. X), this may be understood of the supreme Joseph, in whose figure Joseph went beforehand into Egypt. Joseph, indeed, means “increase.” This is Christ, who increases his own here according to the measure of the journey, and will finally magnify them in glory. While he was in the land of his birth, namely Judea, like Joseph he was mocked by his brothers, stripped of his coat, sold, and crucified. For in crucifying him they dyed his coat—that is, his flesh—in his own blood.

This true Joseph gave true and salutary counsel to his brothers, saying: “If Pharaoh says to you,” and so forth. But to which brothers? For all Christians who do his will are his brothers, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my father and brother and sister and mother” (Matt. XII). Yet he does not give this counsel to all his brothers, but to his particular and privileged brothers, the prelates, to whom the Lord entrusted the care of his flock. He forewarns them on earth, knowing that Pharaoh—that is, the devil—will always trouble his own and never cease from evil thoughts, saying: “If Pharaoh,” that is, the devil, “says to you, ‘What is your occupation?’ Why do you stand idle? You are far too poor in possessions and unable to satisfy your pleasures. You know the old and true proverb: ‘As much as you have, so much are you worth.’ Provide for tomorrow; gather money; you can abound in gold and silver and precious and abundant household goods. Gather into your granaries, so that your storehouses may be full, pouring forth from one into another.”

If he wishes or attempts to deceive you by this false suggestion, answer: “We are shepherds.” These names, “men” and “shepherds,” fit one another, indeed are fittingly joined. One is a name of age and also of dignity; the other, of labor. Hence the Apostle says: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child” [Col. 1810B] (I Cor. XIII). Therefore this name “man” indicates both age and priestly dignity; but “shepherd” indicates the care of the Lord’s flock. Priests, then, are both men and shepherds; but they must beware of being detestable men. For there are detestable men, and there are good men.

Detestable men are like the elders of Israel, of whom Ezekiel records that they had their backs toward the temple of the Lord, despising the Creator, because their faces were toward the east and they worshiped the rising sun (Ezek. VIII)—not the Creator, but the sun. Again, detestable men are those who wish to establish their own righteousness, seeking what is their own and not what is Jesus Christ’s (Phil. II). Priests ought not to be such, but like the six men described in Ezekiel, who came by way of the upper gate facing north, held swords in their hands, and sought to avenge the Creator’s injury (Ezek. IX). Or, to state it more plainly, they ought to be such as Peter addresses when he says: “Men of Israel, and you who fear the Lord, hear” (Acts II).

And, to put it more explicitly, I shall tell you not only what sort of persons priests ought to be, but whom they ought to be. They ought to be the three men mentioned in Ezekiel: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. XIV)—that is, rulers, continent persons, and married persons. By Noah, who guided the ark amid the waves, the prudent are understood; by Daniel, the pure; by Job, the merciful. Every priest ought to be these three men: prudent, pure, and merciful; and thus he will be both man and shepherd. Thus he will also beware lest, when he is one of the two in the field, he himself be left and the other taken (Matt. XXIV).

Therefore we are all, as the Gospel has it, in the Lord’s field; indeed, more fittingly, in the Lord’s fields. For there are four kinds of fields in the house of the Lord, as those who treat natural matters have also taught. The first is a flower-filled field, the second pasture, the third a field for sowing, and the fourth a planted field. You are the first; sacred Scripture is the second, which feeds and refreshes you; the subject flock is the third, in which seed is sown; and the fourth is every penitent lying at your feet. The first is among you; the second before you; the third beneath you; the fourth beside you.

The first [Col. 1810D] has flowers, which the Apostle enumerates in the Epistle to Titus, saying: “A bishop must be without accusation, as God’s steward—not proud, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not a striker, not greedy for shameful gain; but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, continent, holding fast the faithful word which is according to doctrine” (Titus I). The second has two pastures, the Old and New Testaments, in which the spiritual person ought to exercise himself, giving time to prayer [Col. 1811A] and reading. Thus at last he will be able to sow the word of God in the subject flock, namely in the third, the field for sowing. [Col. 1811A]

The fourth has a vineyard to be cultivated with manifold labor. Great labor is expended in cultivating a vineyard: it must first be pruned, secondly dug, thirdly staked, and finally manured. This manifold labor is required in cultivating the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth. First it must be pruned: that is, the sinner standing at your feet must confess sins, and you must inquire not only what he did, but with what intention he acted and how long he remained in it, because according to this you ought to impose a greater or lesser burden. Nor should you rest with the sins he confesses, but also cautiously draw from his mouth whether he has committed such and such acts. For if he says one thing and conceals another, he cannot be healed—just as a wound is incurable so long as it hides iron within itself, even though remedies are applied.

Second, it remains to dig the vineyard—that is, to frighten the sinner, lest he return like a dog [Col. 1811B] to his vomit, lest he easily commit a similar deed. Third, it remains to stake the vineyard—that is, to fasten to the penitent, lest he fall into despair, a stake by which he may be supported: an example of a sinner to whom the Lord showed mercy, such as David, who was a murderer and also committed adultery; Paul, the persecutor of the Church; and blessed Mary the sinner. Fourth, it remains to manure the vineyard—that is, to impose upon the sinner a penance, according to your judgment and discretion, great or small according to the nature of the sin, the penitent’s contrition and means, and the sufficiency of bodily strength.

Thus you ought to keep watch in the vineyard of the Lord. But if he finds such watchfulness, you will encounter him as a perfect man, “unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV), our Lord and our Judge, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XXXVIII

[Col. 1811C]

“I was made like unto them in the hands of the prophets,” says the Lord (Hos. XII). [Col. 1811D] Who is the Lord who says this? Certainly, the Lord of the prophets; as though he said: “I was made like unto them in the hands of my prophets.” They are prophets of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit: of the Father, because they are sent by him; of the Son, because they speak of him; of the Holy Spirit, because they are filled by him.

That they belong to the Father is clear from the authority which says: “God, who at many times and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets” (Heb. I). That they belong to the Son, as those of whom they spoke, is evident from the saying: “That all things might be fulfilled which were said of him in the law, the psalms, and the prophets” (Luke XXIV). They are the instrument of the Holy Spirit, for through them the Holy Spirit speaks certain hidden things by which human weakness is instructed. And it should be noted that the word stated by us above is *diasyrtic*—that is, mocking or derisive. For it may suitably be interpreted in two ways: with reference to the Levitical prophets and to the evangelical ones.

With reference to the Levitical prophets: “I was made like unto them in the hands of the prophets,” and so forth. The prophets foretold the Lord in speech and deed, and they were his as a creature belongs to its Creator. David, who lay hidden, was the herald of him whom he foretold and bore the type of God hidden among the Jews. When he beat the drum at the gates of the city (II Kings VI), he prefigured Christ’s suffering on the cross; hence it is said: “They numbered all my bones” (Ps. XXI). For, stretched out on the cross like the skin on a drum, he washed us from our sins because of our sins. David hid himself in a cave (I Kings XXII); and the Lord lay in the tomb, of which the cave in which David lay was a type. After the second anointing David reigned in peace; and Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more: death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. VI). Rightly, therefore, is it said: “I was made like unto them in the hands of the prophets.”

What we have said may also be referred to the evangelical prophets, that is, to priests. In their hands—that is, their deeds—the Lord was made like unto them, that is, shown by certain likenesses. [Col. 1812A] The priests of God possess this likeness in many respects. God is a foundation, and they are foundations; God is a mountain, and they are mountains; God is a shepherd, and they are shepherds. But God alone is the door.

Priests contemplate the depths of wisdom. They dig out a well so that they may drink most limpid water from the depth: that is, so that they may find spiritual understanding in the letter. These are those who find fruit beneath the leaf, grain in the chaff, and the kernel within the shell. To signify this, the Gospel book, closed to others, is presented to them opened, so that they may kiss it, as though it were said to them: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Matt. XIII).

Although priests have the Lord’s type in many ways, they do so especially in four things that were supremely present in the head and descended from the head to the members: preaching; intercession, or prayer, for enemies; the dispensation of Christ’s body; and exemplary conduct. For the Lord Jesus preached, prayed, distributed his body, [Col. 1812B] and left an example of life. That he preached, I have from what is said: “I cried out; my throat became hoarse” (Ps. LXVIII). And elsewhere: “I have been established by him as king over Sion, his holy mountain, preaching his command” (Ps. II).

The Lord prayed, as at the supper, when he said: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you gave me from the world, and also those who shall believe in me through their word” (John XVII); and at his Passion: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII). He gave his body to the disciples in the form, or under the form, of bread and wine; he gave himself to us as an example, according to the saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI); and again: “If anyone wishes to remain in Christ, he ought himself also to walk as he walked” (John II).

The Lord requires these things in priests; they ought to be found in them, so that they may worthily be heard for themselves and for others. They are obliged to preach, the Lord saying: [Col. 1812C] “Son of man, I have appointed you a preacher to the house of Israel” (Ezek. XXXIII); and: “Cry out; do not cease; raise your voice mightily” (Isa. XL). A priest ought to pray for others, for they “eat the sins of the people” (Hos. IV), that is, the offerings for sins. They ought to be such that they intercede with the Lord for sinners and, by kindly mediation, cause the people to flee from the angry one to the appeased one. Hence the saying: “When you have sinned, offer a sacrifice for sin, and the priest shall pray for you” (Lev. IV).

In external affairs, great care is taken lest one chosen to intercede be found offensive to the judge. For one who did not fear to offend the judge in his own person poorly sets himself up as an intercessor for others. Rash is the person who acts as an advocate in a matter in which he himself needs an advocate. They consecrate the Lord’s body, receive it, and give it to others to receive. Through their ministry bread and wine are transubstantiated into Christ’s flesh. Great ought to be the holiness of those whose dignity has efficacy in things so holy. [Col. 1812D]

By exemplary conduct they ought to devote themselves to the salvation of others, so that others, seeing their good works, may glorify their Father who is in heaven. Hence one of the saints says: “Be imitators of me, dearest brethren, as I am of God” (I Cor. XI). On account of this ministry a priest is called *sacerdos*, as though *sacrum dans*, “one giving what is sacred.” [Note: Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, ch. 12; Col. 1811D.] For he gives the sacred from God—that is, preaching; sacred prayer to God; the sacred thing of God—that is, flesh and blood; and sacred exemplary living on behalf of God.

A priest ought to offer these things to the Lord, and with accompanying offerings: preaching with wine and oil; intercession with rose and lily; the body and blood with fire and sword; exemplary conduct in measure, number, and weight. In preaching he ought to terrify through punishments and soothe through rewards. Preaching tastes of wine when it instills fear of punishments; it pours in oil when it impresses love of heavenly things. The priest offers intercession with rose and [Col. 1813A] lily. In the rose martyrdom is signified; in the lily, innocence of life.

There are three kinds of martyrdom: in the shedding of blood, in the mortification of the flesh, and in compassion for one’s neighbor. Therefore, when the priest compassionately stoops to his neighbor through the zeal of compassion, and preserves innocence in himself, he offers prayer to the Lord with rose and lily. The Lord’s body must be offered with fire and sword. By the sword, the circumcision of the members is understood. One circumcises the eyes who turns them away lest they see vanity; one circumcises the hands who restrains them from harmful work; one circumcises the feet who directs them onto the way of truth; and one circumcises the lips together with the feet who fulfills in life what he teaches in speech.

As the sword pertains to the flesh, so fire pertains to the soul. God is fire; hence: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV). The ministry of a priest is the fire of God; hence: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Ps. CIII). [Col. 1813B] A contrite spirit is fire for God, according to the saying: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. L). Therefore, lest he retain anything unclean, the priest should circumcise his members, have a contrite spirit, and so offer a sacrifice pleasing to the Lord.

In exemplary conduct the priest must maintain measure; in administration, number; in considering his own capacity, weight. In every kind of discernment such ought to be the priest who bears the vessels of the Lord, offers sacrifice to the Lord, and brings the vows of those subject to him before God in devout meditation. But some priest will say: “Why are such great things demanded of us, when few things were demanded of the ancients?” Let him hear what was forbidden to priests in the time of the law. In their appointed turns, when each was about to perform service, he was forbidden sexual embraces with women, *sicera*—intoxicating drink—and wine; indeed, everything that can intoxicate; and ordinary conversation. Evangelical priests ought all the more to abstain from these things, lest impurity of life creep in amid duties of purity.

Antiochus Epiphanes, [Col. 1813C] in the time of the Maccabees, forcibly entered the temple of the Lord and placed in it, beside the ark of the covenant, an idol of Olympian Jupiter. When the Maccabees afterward prevailed, they found the place polluted; and, after casting out the filth, they cleansed it by many purifications (I Macc. I). Therefore whoever approaches the altar of the Lord defiled by lust sets the idol of Venus beside the Son of the Virgin. Whoever utters the sacred words of that sacrament with an unclean mouth spits in the Savior’s face; and when he puts the most holy cross into an unclean mouth, he casts it down, as it were, into the mud of the streets (I Cor.
