XI). The person who still rejoices in the touch of another’s skin, who burns with the heats of vices, approaches this sacrament for his own judgment.

May he who made us, our Judge, our Lord Jesus Christ, help us to approach this sacrament worthily—he who is to come to judge the living and the dead.

## SERMON XXXIX
Be instructed, you who judge the earth (Ps. 2). Do not suppose that I have taken an opening foreign to yourselves. For, if you do not wish to conceal it, you are those who judge the earth. Now the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5); and the Son, having gone abroad and seated in the glory of God the Father, has appointed beneath himself two judges in the lower realm: the judge of heaven and the judge of the forum, assigning to each definite limits of judgment. The judge of the forum judges the men of earth; the judge of heaven judges the earthliness of men—that is, the earthliness of sinners, as though contracted from the earth. The judge of the forum judges between man and man, between cause and cause; the judge of heaven judges between holy and profane, between guilt and punishment. Therefore the Prophet cries to you: “Be instructed, you who judge the earth.”

But do not congratulate yourselves over the word “instruction,” as though you were now permitted to be instructed: properly speaking, to be instructed is to learn; but one who is already bound by office to teach is not permitted to be learning. He who already sits in Moses’ chair ought not to put his hand beneath the master’s rod. The sense, therefore, is: “Be instructed,” [Col. 1814A] that is, be learned, set beyond all uncouthness. For there is a twofold uncouthness: that of the mind and that of the body. Uncouthness of mind is ignorance; uncouthness of body is impurity. It is therefore yours to possess both wisdom and purity. For as it was said to you, “Be prudent” (Matt. 10), so it was said, “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). As it was said to you, “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5), on account of wisdom, so it was said to you, “You are the light of the world,” on account of purity, “that your clean works may shine before men” (ibid.).

Of your wisdom it is written: “The lips of the priest preserve wisdom, and they seek the law from his mouth; for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). But of purity it is written: “A clean man shall expiate the unclean” (Num. 19). Nor is it enough for a priest to employ one without the other, any more than one foot without the other is enough for walking. A priest’s wisdom without purity is like a grape-cluster that shrinks into a berry, or like fire that vanishes into smoke. Purity [Col. 1814B] without wisdom, however, is like a lamp without light, or food without salt.

Moreover, the addition, “You who judge the earth,” is to be understood not only substantively but also temporally, as though it said: Then above all be learned, when you judge the earth. For there greater caution and diligence are required, where no teaching comes to one’s aid. For nowhere in the decisions of the Fathers or in the authoritative writings of the ancients is judgment concerning penitents expressly set down. In other matters that concern us, however, you have the sufficiency of Scripture, to which you attend as to a lamp in a dark place (2 Pet. 1), which does not permit you to go astray.

For three things especially concern you: a manner of life, the order of your ministry, and a method of judging. Concerning the manner of life, it has been handed down that a priest’s life ought to be circumcised. A priest’s life must not be merely shaved close, so that he acts evil deeds together with good ones; nor intermittent, so that he sometimes turns from good and does evil; rather, “let his garments always be white” [Col. 1814C].

This manner of life has been handed down by example and by word. For old Abraham was circumcised, and the child Jesus. Certainly you are both elders and little children: elders, I say, as guardians of the daughter of Zion; elders, I say, in whom wisdom flourishes. Yet unless you become as little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 18): possessing, through the benefit of virtue, what little children possess through the benefit of age. For “the Lord gives understanding to little children” (Ps. 118).

Moreover, in many places Sacred Scripture sets before us this manner of life. Therefore you who know letters and have entered into the powers of the Lord, hear briefly the circumcision of your life. If a perverse thought rises into your heart, crush it under your feet and dash it against the rock. Turn away your eyes lest they see vanity; stop your ears lest they hear the voice of the enchanter who charms vehemently (Ps. 57). “Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. 33). Bind your jaws [Col. 1814D] with bit and bridle (Ps. 31), lest gluttony and lust reign in you. Let your loins be girded with strength (Luke 12); put your feet into the fetters of wisdom. If you see a thief, do not run with him, and do not make your portion with adulterers.

Yet a more-than-abundant circumcision is necessary for your hands, with which you physically handle the Word of Life. But perhaps you will boast of the cleanliness of your hands and say: “I have not shed blood; I have not touched another’s property against the Lord’s will; I have shaken my hands free from every gift.” Nor is it enough for you, priest of God Most High, that your wretched spirit should not exult at the touch of another’s skin and that the hand should not be made unclean.

Now concerning the order of your ministry it is written: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5), “lest you enter into temptation” (Luke 22)—that is, without omitting the canonical hours. There are indeed eight canonical hours, the number of which took its origin from Ezra (2 Esdr. 9). But the manner of psalmody was handed down by the Psalmist. For it is read [Col. 1815A] that Ezra, during the days of Tabernacles at Jerusalem, read from a platform the law of the Lord, which he had restored, while the whole assembly of Israel listened: four times by night and four times by day. The Levites gave a signal among the people and silence was kept; and after each reading the priests prayed over the prostrate people.

We nevertheless, although we sing psalms eight times, do so only once at night, according to the words, “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Ps. 118). Nor does “midnight” mean the exact middle of the night, but whatever time lies between twilight and dawn. Seven times, however, we sing psalms by day, as it is written: “Seven times a day I have uttered praise to you, Lord” (ibid.).

The reasons for psalmody at these times are chiefly drawn from the Gospel. At midnight the Church sings psalms, because Christ was born at night, when shepherds were keeping the watches of the night over their flock (Luke 2). Christ also rose at midnight, as Samson prefigured when, rising at midnight, he carried the gates of Gaza to the summit of the mountain [Col. 1815B] (Judg. 16). Concerning the judgment also to come at night it is written: “At midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matt. 25). This was prefigured when the destroying angel struck Egypt’s firstborn, from man to beast (Exod. 12).

At dawn the Church celebrates morning praises, because then, when the Resurrection had been announced through angels, joy was restored to the disciples in the morning, and those who had wavered were raised up. Thus it is said in the morning canticle: “He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant” (Luke 1).

At the first hour the Church sings psalms because then the Lord Jesus was handed over, bound by Pilate. At that same hour after the Resurrection he appeared to seven disciples who were fishing, standing on the shore and saying, “Children, have you any relish?” (John 21).

At the third hour we sing psalms because then the Lord was crucified by the tongues of the Jews, according to the words: “Their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56). [Col. 1815C] At the same hour, on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended in tongues of fire upon the one hundred and twenty men in Zion’s upper room (Acts 2).

At the sixth hour we sing psalms because then the Lord was stretched out upon the wood, given vinegar to drink, and darkness came over all the earth.

At the ninth hour we sing psalms because then the Lord Jesus, bowing his head, yielded up the spirit; and, pierced by a lance, he supplied us with the two sacraments of our salvation (Matt. 27). The veil of the temple was torn, the earth shook, the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened (ibid.).

At evening we sing psalms because then, at supper, the Lord gave his body and blood to his disciples under the form of bread and wine, and established that it should henceforth be done in remembrance of him (Luke 22). At the same hour he was buried, and at the same hour he was recognized by the disciples in the breaking of bread.

At twilight we sing psalms because then the Lord prayed at length in his agony, and his sweat became as drops of blood falling to the earth [Col. 1815D] (Luke 22; John 20). At the same hour he was surrounded by guards; and at the same hour, when the doors were shut, he stood in the midst of the disciples and said, “Peace be with you” (Luke 24).

It is sufficiently clear how, concerning your manner of life and the order of your ministry, you possess ample instruction in Scripture. It is yours, however, carefully to consider the method of judging; for penitential judgment is discretionary, and the period of satisfaction is not specified, because with God the measure of sorrow has greater weight than the measure of time.

Behold: the Lord’s little sheep sits at your feet, confessing at the confessor’s feet, weeping and groaning as one conscious of his error, in order to open his mouth before the Lord, awaiting the Lord’s judgment through your mouth. What is incumbent upon you to do, priest of God Most High? First, two things present themselves to you: encouragement and exhortation. Observe the skilled physician: upon entering, he encourages the sick person. “Go, and do likewise” (Luke 10), lest the penitent despair because of the greatness of the sin, the enormity of the deed committed, [Col. 1816A] or the multitude of crimes. Set before him examples: Peter, who denied the Lord while the Lord was present, but, converted through repentance, strengthened his brethren. Tell him of Paul, who from a persecutor of the Church became a vessel of election (Acts 9). Tell him of the woman who had been a sinner in the city, and how she became the apostle of the apostles.

After this add a brief exhortation, saying: “Pour out your heart like water, child, before the Lord.” Other liquids, when poured out, emerge as if with delay and difficulty, leaving behind in their vessels something turbid of themselves. Water, however, when poured out, goes forth easily and altogether at once. There are some who confess with difficulty and delay, as though seeking excuses by evasions or diminishing their sin. This outpouring is not like water. Some do not pour out everything: they retain certain things, either terrified by fear, entangled by shame, or held back by distrust of their ability to refrain. To such people it must be said: “He does not seek healing who conceals what must be healed”; no poultice is to be applied while iron remains in the wound.

Nevertheless, if, because of the brevity of time and the multitude of penitents, you are unable to give encouragement and exhortation individually, set these matters forth publicly and generally by preaching at the beginning of Lent. Finally, hear the penitent’s confession patiently. Having heard it, “pass from gate to gate through the midst of the camp,” as Moses did, girded with a sword, consecrating his hands even in the blood of his kinsmen (Exod. 32). To pass from gate to gate is to inquire diligently into the causes of sins, namely their beginnings and their ends: whether he did this by chance or by deliberate choice; whether at another’s suggestion or from the malice of his own mind; whether sin was sown in him or inborn. If it was inborn, judge it more gravely than what was sown. Thus the Lord judged the devil’s crime to be inborn, and therefore irremediable; but humanity’s crime to be sown, and therefore [Col. 1816C] remediable.

Nature itself likewise teaches you this. The mud of a cesspool smells more foully and corrupts the air more powerfully than street mud. The former has its defect inborn; the latter arises merely from dripping rain and dust laid upon the ground. You must also inquire diligently into the final cause: whether his iniquity proceeded from fatness or from leanness. For some steal or seize things under compulsion of necessity. Others commit the same acts through the abyss of covetousness, which nothing satisfies. Judge the latter worse than the former.

Pass through the midst of the camp, sparing no one from affection and harming no one from hatred. To flatterers it has been said: “Woe to you, deceitful plasterers, who coat a wall without tempering” (Ezek. 13). But to those who burden beyond what is due it has been said: “Woe to you, lawyers, who lay unbearable burdens upon men’s shoulders, while you yourselves are unwilling to move them with your finger” (Matt. 23).

Now, in judging evil works, hear the Apostle saying: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity,” [Col. 1816D] and so forth; and he concludes thus: “Those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5). Read therefore carefully in the Apostle the catalogue of grave sins; do not diminish any of them, for “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6).

Concerning judgment on perverse speech, authority is not so explicit; yet we may select a few examples from many. There is an idle word, a vain word, and an indecent word. Of the first it is read: “For every idle word that men have spoken, they shall render an account” (Matt. 12). Of the second it is written: “Each has spoken vain things to his neighbour” (Ps. 11). Of the third the Apostle says: “Let no foul speech proceed from your mouth” (Eph. 4).

The first commonly occurs in private conversations through a certain pleasure in talking; the second occurs at crossroads and in public conversations, when people neglect their own affairs and discuss others’ business—matters concerning princes, the leisure of clerics, and the privileges of monks. The third occurs in the comic inventions [Col. 1817A] of actors. These and similar things, if they happen rarely and are not done from malice of mind, you will judge venial.

There is besides a false word, a deceitful word, and an iniquitous word. Of the first it is read: “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5), namely when it is spoken as testimony against one’s neighbour (Ps. 2). Of the second it is read: “They spoke with heart and heart” (ibid.). Of the third: “They have devised an iniquitous word against me” (Ps. 40)—that is, by thinking evil things about God. These and similar things, even if spoken only once, you will judge grave sins.

But take care, when you judge these matters, that you are not found liable to judgment in them, lest it be said to you: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam in your own eye?” (Matt. 7). For what is commonly venial for the flock is grave for the priest; what is error in a sheep is ruinous in a shepherd. Judge therefore with discernment, you who judge the earth, lest at last the Lord Jesus Christ, our Lord and our judge, judge you strictly when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XL

*(Found among the Works of Hildebert; Patrologia, vol. CLXXI, col. 761, sermon 90.)*

## SERMON XLI

“And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Ps. 2). Kings are feared by all, while they themselves fear no one. Who, then, speaks so imperiously and commands kings to understand and be instructed? It is he who is in heaven, who commands wind and sea, through whom kings reign and princes hold the earth (Prov. 8). He is that Terrible One who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible in the sight of the kings of the earth (Ps. 75). The supreme King commands the kings beneath him what he has ordained, saying: “Behold now, O kings, understand.”

There are four kinds of kings: [Col. 1817C] kings of nations, kings of souls, kings of darkness, and kings of bodies. Kings of nations are the earthly rulers of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kings of the nations exercise lordship over them” (Luke 22). Kings of darkness are demons, of whom the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of this darkness” (Eph. 6). Kings of souls are priests, of whom it is written: “When the Heavenly One makes distinctions over her, kings shall be made white in Selmon” (Ps. 67). Kings of bodies are souls; hence Solomon says: “The heart of kings is in the hand of God” (Prov. 21), meaning the souls that rule their bodies.

The first are called benefactors, the second poisoners, the third truth-speaking, and the fourth peace-making. The first are beneficent because they know:

> To spare the subjected and to subdue the proud.  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid I.)*

Thus the Lord also added: “Those who have authority over them are called benefactors” (Luke 22). The second are maleficent [Col. 1817D] because they sit secretly with the rich in order to kill the innocent. The third are truth-speaking because they sit upon Moses’ chairs as teachers of truth, possessing the words of eternal life (Matt. 23). The fourth are peace-making because, when “the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5), the mind which presides establishes peace between the two—though a thin peace, such as can be had in a body of death, especially among those born under original sin. For the spirit, corrupted from the beginning, corrupted the flesh; and the flesh, corrupted after the beginning, corrupted the spirit.

The first rule over us; the second oppose us; the third serve us—whence the Apostle says, “Though free from all, I made myself the servant of all” (1 Cor. 9); the fourth work within us. But to which kings does the Lord speak here? Certainly the Lord does not speak to the kings of darkness, since they are neither worthy nor deserve to be heard, nor could the Lord’s word be received in them. For their heart has been hardened like stone. Therefore the Lord’s word is addressed to the other three kinds of kings, [Col. 1818A] each of whom has his own earth to judge.

For a fourfold earth is spoken of, besides the earth of those who perish, which has been given into the hand of the wicked. There is the earth that we tread; the earth that we seek; the earth that we bear; and the earth that we make. The earth that we tread is this visible and common earth, of which the Psalm says: “The earth is the Lord’s” (Ps. 23). The earth that we seek is the heavenly homeland; hence the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26). The earth that we bear is our body; hence Isaiah says: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Ps. 84), that is, from the Virgin’s flesh. The earth that we make is sin; hence the Lord says: “Heaven is my throne, but earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66).

The first is called the earth of those dying; the second, of those living; the third, of mortals—that is, of human beings; the fourth, of those sleeping—that is, of sinners. The first is called an element, the second an elevation, the third a creature fashioned, and the fourth a ruin. The first [Col. 1818B] carries us; the second calls us; the third weighs us down—for “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9); the fourth refines us. This is the furnace beside which the Lord sits, refining and cleansing the sons of Levi (Mal. 3).

It remains to consider which kings judge which earth. Kings of nations judge the earth of those dying; kings of bodies, the earth of mortals; kings of souls, the earth of those sleeping. God alone judges and rules the earth of the living. Therefore the blessed Trinity speaks here to this threefold class of kings: the Father to kings of nations, the Son to kings of bodies, and the Holy Spirit to kings of souls.

At the birth of the incarnate Word, the Father, as it were, spoke to kings, saying: “And now, O kings, understand.” For when Christ was born and magi came from the East saying, “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?”, King Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (Matt. 2). Against this agitation the Father says: “And now,” that is, in the time of grace, you kings of the earth, do not be disturbed; rather understand how great is the king who has been born.

First, understand through the signs that occurred in Judaea before the Lord’s birth: such as the water of the sheep-pool, at whose stirring by an angel a sick person was healed; and at his birth, such as the multitude of the heavenly host which sang, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2). Second, understand through the signs that occurred among the nations at the birth itself: for a remarkable star appeared, according to Balaam’s prophecy, “A star shall arise from Jacob” (Num. 24). Third, understand also from signs that occurred in the West. For at Rome a fountain of oil burst from the ground and flowed as far as the Tiber. There too, on that same night, the Temple of Peace fell utterly, in accordance with the oracle of the idols which had foretold that it would not fall until a Virgin gave birth.

Having understood this, be instructed by the teachers of truth and the heralds of the newborn king, you who judge the earth, concerning how you should serve him. But I shall instruct you briefly: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2).

With the same words the Son, raised from the dead, speaks to kings of bodies. For noble philosophers understood God’s invisible things through the things that were made (Rom. 1). Through the ineffable governance of the world they also understood the Almighty. From the motions of the planets and the firmament they understood that unlawful impulses must be restrained by the movement of reason. Yet they did not understand the future resurrection of bodies. Therefore Christ, raised from the dead, showing his disciples the true resurrection of the flesh for forty days—going in and out, eating and drinking, appearing to them and speaking of the heavenly kingdom—seems to have burst forth in these words: “And now,” that is, at least after so many proofs of the Resurrection, you kings of bodies who judge the earth—that is, you souls who rule your bodies—understand and be instructed what you must henceforth think: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3), since, when this earthly house is destroyed, it is rebuilt in heaven, not made with hands. This [Col. 1819A] mortal shall put on immortality; this corruptible shall put on incorruption (1 Cor. 15).

It remains to see how the Spirit speaks the aforesaid words to the kings of souls. Let us therefore change the plural number into the singular, so that what is said to one may be understood as said to the rest. The Holy Spirit speaks, then, as the Father to the Son, to the priest celebrating divine things when, with arms outstretched as though crucified, he stands before the truly Crucified One; indeed, when he visibly beholds the image of the Crucified One in the cross set before him.

The Spirit says to him: “Son, though you are detained with other occupations, now—that is, at least in the sight of the Lord your God—understand.”

The priest replies: “What should I understand, Father?”

The Spirit says: “Understand, I say, the Christ before whom you stand: he who truly died, who is truly alive, who will be your judge. You will not stand before him securely, as you do now, but will render an account of yourself and of your brother. Therefore prepare here [Col. 1819B] the words which you will speak in judgment” (Ps. 111).

He replies: “Father, this understanding is wonderful, and I shall not attain it through myself. Teach me, therefore, what I owe to myself and what to my brother, especially since, as Christ testifies, you ought to teach us all truth” (John 14).

The Spirit says: “My son, do not seek far away for instruction from the things around you. Understand from these things what you owe to yourself; from the things set before you, what you owe to your brother. You have bound your throat with the garment cast around you, whose ends, brought round before the breast, you have gently tied. You are clothed in a linen tunic commonly called an *alb*, which, because of its fullness around the loins, you have tightly girded; its sleeves are so narrow and fitted to the hands that they have no crease there. But observe that the Levitical priest used this same garment; it was then so tight and fitted to the body that it never had a crease, prefiguring the narrowness of that time. For they received the spirit of servitude in fear.

But around you it has breadth because of the liberty of the adoption of sons, by which the Son has set you free. Understand, son, that four things are bound in you: throat, breast, loins, and hands—as though it were said to you: Let no perverse thoughts rise into your heart; “keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Ps. 33); “let your loins be girded,” and so forth (Luke 12).

Certainly he desired the binding of the breast who said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 50); and likewise the binding of the throat, saying: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth” (Ps. 140). He also wished the loins and hands to be disciplined when he said: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118). But observe, son, that the binding about the throat and breast is light and almost loose; that about the loins and hands, however, is exceedingly tight. For a movement of the mind is not in your power, and therefore you may sin venially in these matters.

Elijah shut heaven before he shut his mind, thinking that he alone remained of the prophets of the Lord, when seven thousand men still remained who [Col. 1819D] had not bent their knees before Baal (3 Kings 19). Likewise the tongue slips easily, because it sits in moisture. For even the Prince of the Apostles denied at the voice of a serving-girl. Since you cannot easily restrain the tongue, you may sin venially in it.

But in the loins, son, do not err by calling a lapse of the flesh venial, as though it were a natural motion or nature’s due tribute: “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6). You have taken upon yourself drawers; you have opened your mouth in a vow of continence. Be clean, that you may cleanly handle the Cleanser of the world.

Restrain your hands, therefore, son—not, I say, merely from theft, robbery, and such acts, which are lawful for no one—but “shake your hands free from every gift.” Do not love gifts; do not pursue payment. Freely you received the sacraments; freely give them (Matt. 10). Eat in order that you may preach the Gospel; do not preach the Gospel in order that you may eat. If you become an extorter of gifts, when you approach the Lord Jesus Christ he may say to you: “Do not touch me” (John 20). Your voice sounds like Jacob’s, [Col. 1820A] but your hands are Esau’s (Gen. 27): they are the hands of Briareus, not of a presbyter.

Behold, son, from these bindings you may understand how you ought to turn away from evil. But how you ought to do good, understand from the remaining vestments: namely, the handkerchief, the stole, and the chasuble. For the handkerchief, also called the *maniple*, you wear on the left. In former times reapers carried a handkerchief tied to their belt in order to wipe away sweat; therefore understand that you are a reaper. “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the workers are few” (Matt. 9); and therefore the Lord of the harvest sent you to reap—that is, to gather faithful persons into the Church from every place, by word and example and by participation in the sacraments. This harvest is now one of human beings; the harvest close at hand will be one of angels, when they gather all stumbling-blocks out of the kingdom of God (Matt. 13).

The ancient Fathers carried a handkerchief to wipe away the flow of tears—those to whom it was said, “Blessed are you who now weep,” and so forth (Matt. 5). Bede says in his *Martyrology* that Father Arsenius always carried a handkerchief, either in his bosom or in his [Col. 1820B] hand, because of the flow of tears. Accordingly understand, son, from the handkerchief how many streams of water your eyes ought to pour forth. You ought to weep for your own transgressions, for those of your flock, for the prolongation of your sojourn, and for longing for your homeland.

The *orarium*, also called the stole, you wear over your neck. Its two ends extend at least to the knees and should cross at the middle of the breast in the shape of a cross, as though saying: “The burden of the Crucified One is light, and his yoke sweet.” It is called an *orarium* because, on account of the offences of your people, you ought to supplicate the Lord with humble bending of the knee and to appease indignation by your prayers.

The *planeta*, also called the *casula* or chasuble, surrounds and protects your whole person and surpasses the other vestments. This is charity, of which the Apostle says (1 Cor. 12): “I show you a still more excellent way.” Without it the other things, though they may be present, cannot profit, as the same Apostle testifies: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and angels; though I have faith so as to remove mountains; though I give up my body so that I may burn—if I do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13).

Therefore without charity, son, you are nothing; indeed, without the foregoing things you may be called a priest, but you cannot be one. Perhaps you are a shepherd in the sight of men, but a ravager in the sight of angels; a wolf, not a ram; a thief, not a minister. Could not Christ, standing there, say to you: “Son, how did you enter here without a priestly garment?” And again: “Who are you here? Behold, you will be carried away like a cock of the poultry-yard” (Isa. 22). I fear lest he bind you hand and foot and cast you into the outer darkness (Matt. 12).

It remains, son, that from the things before you, you understand what you owe to your brother. You see before you God and man hanging on the cross, bruised by wounds, raised upon the cross, bloodied by his own blood, dead with bowed head, pierced in the right side by a lance, and, while he lived, praying for his crucifiers. You too, son, carry the cross, following your forerunner, in compassion for your neighbour [Col. 1820D] and mortification of the flesh. In this also do not cease to pray for persecutors.

If your people speak ill of you, if they deny you due reverence, if they muzzle the ox that treads out the grain by withholding your due support, do not render evil for evil (Rom. 12); rather conquer evil with good; rather pray for them, saying: “Lord, forgive them this sin, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23).

Perhaps a wolf attacks your flock, and you place yourself as a wall for the house of Israel. The wolf, however, in order to remove you from its defence, will pierce your feet—that is, will attack your servants and household members who run about your business—and will impoverish some of them, imprison others in chains, and afflict some with death. He will also pierce your hands, depriving you of the fruit of grain, wine, and oil (Ps. 4). He will waste the necessities of life that arise from the work of your hands. Perhaps he will attack your side—that is, your relatives, who are your bone and your flesh—labouring to make you offend [Col. 1821A] God so that you may not lose your kinsman. Perhaps he will lie in wait for your life and thirst for your blood. But amid these things do not be moved: crucified with Christ, do not descend from the cross. Say to the tyrant: “I shall not be moved from this defence for ever.” Say to the Lord: “Lord, for your sake we are put to death all day long; we are made like sheep for slaughter.”

Therefore, you, son, and all kings of souls, understand and be instructed in these things aforesaid, you who judge the earth. “For with the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Matt. 7). May Jesus Christ our Lord, our judge, when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire, render into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing.

Amen.

## SERMON XLII
They sat upon the ground; the elders of the daughter of Zion were silent (Lam. II). The saying of the weeping Jeremiah which you have heard through my mouth [Col. 1821B] lamented the desolation of the city and the filth of the dust in which the elders sat before the face of the God of Israel—those who, when they ought to sit in the chair of Moses, sat in the stench of a dungheap. Under the tenor of these words may also be set forth the lamentation of the Saviour, mourning the negligence and silence of the elders of the daughter of Zion. The prophet’s mourning lamentation was indeed brief and temporary; the Mediator’s complaint, however, is continual and unceasing.

Surely the bridegroom complains of the negligence of his bride’s guardians. For [uncertain: Nois, son of Turgaten] took as his virgin wife the daughter of Zion—that is, the Word of God. God, the Son of God, joined the Church to himself through faith and incorruptible love, without the stain of sin, without the wrinkle of duplicity. At the time of his marriage he was bodily present with her: he was seen on earth and lived among human beings for the time appointed by the Father. When that time was completed, he returned to the Father. For his going forth was from the Father, and his return [Col. 1821C] was to the Father. Hence he himself says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; and again I leave the world, that I may return to the Father” (John XVI).

But when he returned to the Father, he entrusted his bride to the keeping of elders; that is, he left presbyters as her guardians and vicars. For πρεσβύτης (*presbytēs*) in Greek is *senex*, “elder,” in Latin. Presbyters are called elders not so much because of age as because of gravity of character. “For the grey hairs of a human being are his understanding” (Wis. IV). They are called elders by this analogy: what old people possess through the benefit of age, these possess through the practice of virtue. For through long experience of time wisdom flourishes in the old; and, through the diminution of natural heat, continence flourishes in them as well.

We have the prophet Malachi’s testimony concerning wisdom: “The lips of the priest preserve wisdom, and from his mouth they seek knowledge” (Mal. II). Elsewhere the Lord says concerning continence: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII). Nor does this commendation made by the hand of the Saviour differ from ordinary human custom. [Col. 1821D] The rulers of lands customarily entrust their wives to eunuchs for safekeeping; so too the Lord entrusted his bride to eunuchs for guarding.

[Note: [Col. 1821D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book X.]

Here we do not mean eunuchs by violence, whom we call *spadones*, from the sword; nor eunuchs by nature, whom we call *castrati*, that is, “born chaste”; but we mean eunuchs by grace and virtue, those who “made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX). The Saviour deplores their negligence and slothful guardianship, saying: “They sat upon the ground; the elders, guardians of the daughter of Zion, were silent.”

The office of priests is to walk about and to sit in Simon’s boat while the crowd sits on the ground, just as Christ walked upon the sea while gathering his disciples. He sat in the boat and taught the crowds who were on the shore from the boat. Truth says in the Gospel concerning walking: “Behold, I send you, that you may go and bear fruit” [Col. 1822A] (John XV). And elsewhere: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XVIII). Ezekiel too saw in the Spirit the walking of priests.

They ought to walk from sheep to sheep: from the sick to the broken, from the broken to the straying, from the straying to the strong. They ought to strengthen the sick, bind up the broken, call back the straying, and preserve the strong, lest they incur that prophetic rebuke: “What was sick you did not strengthen; what was broken you did not bind up; what was straying you did not bring back; what was fat and strong you devoured” (Ezek. XXXIV).

Moreover, they ought to sit in Simon’s boat. Nor should it seem a small thing to you to sit in Simon’s boat; for, on the journey, sitting in Simon’s boat is the highest and supreme rank of sitting. There is indeed another rank of sitting, higher and greater than this: at the Father’s table, or on the judge’s throne, concerning which it was said: “You too shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). But this latter is supreme [Col. 1822B] in the homeland; the former is supreme on the journey.

For there are three ranks of sitting on the journey: the first lesser, the second greater, the third supreme. The first is general, the second particular, the third spiritual. The first is to sit upon the rivers of Babylon (Ps. CXXXVI); the second is to sit at the rich man’s table; the third is to sit in Simon’s boat. In the first sit the faithful, in the second young men, in the third elders. In the first sit those reborn, in the second the learned, in the third prelates. The first justifies, the second enlightens, the third perfects.

One must sit upon the rivers of Babylon: that is, above the flow of this world’s water—not despising water, without which we do not live, but rejecting the instability, greed, and excess with which we live badly. One must sit not upon the axle, but upon Fortune’s wheel.

The rich man’s table is Holy Scripture, in which our Saviour sets before us many delicate dishes; the depth of whose riches has no end. He is abundant [Col. 1822C] beyond the children of men, for his storehouses are full, overflowing from one thing into another (Ps. CXLIII). To sit in Simon’s boat is what the Lord says: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

But by antithesis we make sittings contrary to these. For when we ought to sit beside Babylon’s rivers, we sit by the flesh-pots of Egypt. Those who ought to sit at the rich man’s table are such as those of whom it is said: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (I Cor. X)—that is, to mock. Prelates, however, whose task it is to sit in Simon’s boat, sit upon the ground; and the Lord laments this, saying: “The elders sat upon the ground,” etc. When they ought to walk, they sat; and they did not sit in Simon’s boat in order to teach the crowds upon the ground, but, grievous to say, they sat on the ground—that is, they turned the whole priestly office toward earthly profit, “seeking what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s” (Phil. III).

Of those who sit upon the ground, some sit in another’s land and others in their own. Those sit in another’s land who join field to field, house to house, and heap wealth upon wealth—not for themselves, but for the nephews whom they have reared, or, worse still, for the *manzerim* [Col. 1822D] whom they have had by their concubines.

[Note: [Col. 1822D] *Manzer*, a Hebrew word: that is, born of a prostitute.]

Those sit in their own land who labour for their own advantage, serving pleasure or devoting themselves to bodily health. Our Saviour did not teach thus. Such a person is not of his school. Those devoted to pleasure are not in Christ’s school, but Epicurus’s. Those who study bodily health are not in the Saviour’s school, but Hippocrates’. “All things have their time” (Eccles. III), but these men alter the times: they pursue health when they ought rather to pursue salvation. For salvation is the health of the soul; bodily health is bodily soundness. Now is the time of salvation; hence the Apostle: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI). In the future will be the time of bodily health, when “this mortal [Col. 1823A] shall put on immortality.” Hence the Apostle: “We await Jesus Christ, our Saviour, who will reform the body of our lowliness, made conformable to the body of his glory” (Phil. III).

It has been said how the elders sat upon the ground; now it must be said how they were silent. He could have said, “They were silent,” but the fuller expression is “They all became silent”: that is, they were silent together, because they omitted both parts of speaking. There are two parts of speaking, life and teaching, in which priests ought to shine forth, just as they excel in honour; for both are necessary. For as much as good conduct benefits by example, so much does silence harm. Yet they do not imitate the Saviour, of whom it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I). They neither instruct by example nor teach by word.

Further, “they all became silent”: that is, they suppressed every mode of speaking. There are three modes of speaking: teaching, exhorting, and praying—teaching truth, exhorting to right conduct, and praying in intercession. They are to teach [Col. 1823B] the truth concerning faith and its articles; exhort concerning morals; and pray in intercession for their own ignorance and that of the people. Of the first the Lord says: “Go, teach” (Mark XVI). Of the second we read in Jeremiah: “Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, that you may pluck up and destroy, and build and plant” (Jer. I). Of the third the Apostle says: “First of all I urge that supplications, petitions, prayers,” and so forth, “be made among you” (I Tim. II).

“They all became silent” also means that they had every cause for silence. There are three causes of silence: ignorance, incapacity, and negligence. Ignorance is shameful; incapacity difficult; negligence gross. What, indeed, is more shameful than to begin to learn when we ought to teach? An elderly beginner in the alphabet is a ridiculous thing, as the philosopher testifies.

[Note: [Col. 1823D] Seneca, *Letters*, 36; Gesner, book II, *On Quadrupeds*; Ovid; Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XII.]

Incapacity is difficult, since a prelate sometimes knows how to teach but cannot, because conscience presents an obstacle and shuts his mouth. It is like a pebble placed in the mouth; it is that little frog which stops the mouths of dogs.

[Note: [Col. 1824D] Pliny, book XXXII, chapter 10.]

For there is a kind of frog [Col. 1823C] which is mute, without a voice, green, and small, called *calamita* because it lives among reeds; when cast into the mouths of dogs, it prevents their barking. In the same way, a biting conscience prevents a guilty person from teaching; and again, what is most difficult, does not permit him to remain silent. Woe, then, to the inflated bladder! If he wishes to speak, conscience answers him that God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my justices and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. XLIX). But if, fearing to teach, he resolves to keep silent, conscience then rises and says: “Why are you silent? Are you not bound to preach? Have you not heard Scripture threatening: ‘Woe to you, dumb dogs’?” (Isa. LVI).

Negligence is gross. Some, considering the labour and pain, prefer to surrender themselves to idleness rather than labour in the Lord’s vineyard. Of them it is written: “Woe to you, dumb dogs, lazy and sleepy, unable to bark.” And elsewhere: “Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently” (Jer. XLVIII).

You have heard the Saviour’s lamentation; but we should fear still more lest we incur his rebuke, proceeding from the greatest indignation [Col. 1823D]. For rebuke is graver than lamentation. We cloak the poison of malice; we conceal a wolfish disposition beneath sheep’s clothing; we hide our crimes under the regular tonsure, cheap dress, humble gait, and other such things. At last, solemnly dressed, we approach the altar and begin the prayer: “Take away from us, O Lord, our iniquities”; and we press a kiss upon the altar. Might not Christ, on the contrary, stand and say: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke XXII).

Therefore, lest the Saviour may rightly complain of you, more rightly rebuke you, and most rightly condemn you: go, teach the crowds from the boat, so that, when the Son sits upon the seat of his majesty, Jesus Christ, our Lord and our judge, may draw you from your sitting in the boat, through the judge’s seat, to the Father’s table, when he comes [Col. 1824A] to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON XLIII

“Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me” (John XII). The Lord uttered this short saying upon the earth, speaking to his ministers concerning the manner of ministering. But what Lord, and to what ministers? Concerning the Lord there is no uncertainty: just as there is one Teacher and one Father for us upon earth, so too there is one Lord. Of him it is said: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV). He alone owns “the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. XXIII).

But concerning the ministers there may be doubt, because the same Lord has ministers in different places; in the same place, ministers of different times; and in the same place and time, ministers of different orders. Therefore we must see to the ministers of what place, time, and order he speaks.

Hear concerning places: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Ps. XIV). He therefore has a tabernacle; he has a holy mountain; he has the Church militant; he has the Church triumphant. The ministers of the mountain are all “ministering spirits sent for his sake” (Heb. I). Hence: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire” (Ps. CIII); and elsewhere: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII). To these ministers of that place it is said: “Whoever ministers to me, let him enjoy me.” It remains, therefore, that it was said to the ministers of the tabernacle: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me.”

But in this tabernacle too there are ministers of different times. We distinguish the Church militant according to three times. It had a time before the incarnation of the Word; it had a time when the Lord was made in the likeness of human beings and found in outward form as a man [Col. 1824C] (Phil. II); and it has had a time when the man departed from us into a far country, leaving his goods to his servants, to each according to his own ability (Mark XIII). In the first time Christ was arranging to come to us; in the middle time he stood among us as mediator; in the third he departed from us, but for our sake, as he himself says: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John XIV). In the first he was awaited; in the middle he was manifested; in the third he is hidden.

To the ministers of the first time he said: “Whoever ministers to me, let him await me”; to those of the second: “Whoever ministers to me, let him walk with me”; to those of the third: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me.” Yet in the present time too there are ministers of different orders. There are doorkeepers, Nethinim, Levites, and priests. Ministers properly so called are also stewards: those who distribute food at the proper time to sons, servants, and hired workers; who break bread for the little ones; who prepare wholesome food and distribute it once prepared. The Lord’s saying is addressed to these—to you, therefore, O Fathers.

But perhaps you will answer the Lord: “Lord, where are you going?” (John XVI)—where?—“that we may follow you.” But if you do not wish to dissemble, you know both the way and where and by what route he walked; and whoever wishes to minister to Christ ought himself to walk as he walked. Indeed, Lord Jesus, we are without excuse. “We have seen your goings, O God, the goings of our God”; we have seen his walking and your following, yet we do not call them to mind, nor are we reluctant to hear of them.

Hear of his walking: “I will be their God, and I will walk among them” (Lev. XXVI; II Cor. VI). Hear of the minister’s following: “Moses, my most faithful minister, in all my house” (Heb. III; Num. XII). Therefore Christ walked in his own house, and the minister followed him in the same house. But note that he says, “in all.” There is only one house, of which it is said: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek,” etc. (Ps. XXVI). And elsewhere: “Who makes those of one manner to dwell in a house” (Ps. LXVII). For one is the dove, one the beloved [Col. 1825A] (Song VI), the only one of the Only-Begotten. Thus he says “in all the house,” that is, in every part of the house. We must therefore see what the parts of the house are; how the Lord walked in them; how the minister ought to follow; and by what paths.

It belongs to imperial majesty to have three parts in its palace: a dining hall, in which it refreshes its own; a court, in which it decides lawsuits; and a bedchamber, in which it rests in sleep. In this manner our Emperor, who commands winds and sea, was in the dining hall, instructing us; in the court, judging us; and in the bedchamber, dying for us: instructing by deeds and words; judging according to each person’s merits; dying in order to give us life.

Moreover, observe how he walked in each of these parts. In the dining hall he refreshed now the greater, now the lesser, with loaves. For as he taught the crowds in parables, so also, opening his mouth and lifting his eyes to his disciples, he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc. (Matt. V). In the court he at times rebuked the wicked and at times commended the good. For as he said: “Woe to you, hypocritical Pharisees” (Matt. XXIII), and many things of this sort, so too he said to the disciples: “You are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth” (Matt. V). “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

He himself testifies concerning the bedchamber: “I slept and took my rest, and arose, because the Lord upheld me” (Ps. III). Therefore he walked in the bedchamber from the bed of pain to the bed of rest, from the wood of the cross to the tomb of the councillor. Because he himself bore all our pains and sicknesses (Isa. LIII), he turned the bed of pain for himself in his infirmity.

You have seen your forerunner walking, minister of the Lord: you must follow him wherever he goes; otherwise you will not be most faithful in all the Lord’s house, as Moses was (Num. XII). I think he is called “most faithful” in order to indicate the three parts of the house. For “most faithful” is said in relation to “faithful” and “more faithful.” For this reason too, I think, the Lord applied three adjectives to his servant, calling him [Col. 1825C] good, faithful, and prudent: “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matt. XXV); and elsewhere: “A faithful and prudent servant” (Matt. XXIV).

Therefore, it is necessary for the minister walking through the parts of the house to be faithful, more faithful, and most faithful: prudent in the dining hall, faithful in the court, good in the bedchamber. In the dining hall, that he may instruct soberly; in the court, that he may decide justly; in the bedchamber, that he may intercede devoutly. He is to instruct because he is a sower of the word; decide because he is a prelate; intercede because he is an advocate: a sower of the word in the chair, a prelate in court, an advocate in the Mass.

It remains for you to see how you are to walk in these places. Enter the bedchamber mindful of youth, so that you may fittingly say: “I will enter unto the altar of God, unto God who gives joy to my youth” (Ps. XLII). Enter the court knowing no commerce, so that you may say: “Because I have not known commerce, I will enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. LXX). Enter the dining hall mindful of going about, so that you may say: “I went about and offered to the Lord a sacrifice of joyful cry” (Ps. XXVI).

Standing at the altar, be the man of whom it is said: “There was a man in Ramathaim-sophim” [Col. 1825D] (I Sam. I). Hence Wisdom says: “O men, to you I cry” (Prov. VIII). Have neither the old age of corruption nor the childishness of folly. Do you think that, when I stand before my God, who is bodily though invisibly present on the altar, if he smells in me the rancour of old corruption, he will say to me: “Ancient in evil days” (Dan. XIII), “today evils shall come upon your head which you formerly practised”? If he perceives in me the childishness of folly—when I ought to sing wisely, yet do not understand what I say or do, or why—will he not curse me with the children crying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (IV Kings II)? Truly I say to you: it would be better for me to eat live coal than Jesus, who died for us.

Sitting in the court, know no commerce; shake your hand free of every gift, lest you spare the poor, lest gifts blind you and make you an *abocellus*—“without eyes”—lest, loving gifts and pursuing recompense, you become drunk and forget the judgments of God. Reclining in the dining hall, remember your circuit: I went around three things—many people, many things, and much.

Many people: namely, many sick, straying, and strong sheep—curing the first, calling back the second, strengthening the third. Hear the teacher Paul making the circuit: “I am debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish” (Rom. I). Many things: because “a good man brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matt. XII). Hear the same Paul: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (I Cor. II). And elsewhere: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (ibid.).

One must also run much, lest tribulation, distress, famine, or nakedness separate you from the word of God; but, according to the Apostle: “Carry out your ministry, do the work of an evangelist, press on in season and out of season” (II Tim. IV).

It remains to see by what paths we ought to walk—that is, by what names the three aforementioned paths are designated. The path of the dining hall is called the way of commandments; the path of the court, the way of truth; the path of the bedchamber, the way of testimonies. Of the first the Prophet says: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” [Col. 1826B] (Ps. CXVIII); of the second: “I chose the way of truth” (ibid.); of the third: “I delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches” (ibid.). The teacher of God’s commandments must be swift—that is, ready—and broad of heart. Hence Peter: “Concerning the faith and hope which are in us, we are ready to give an answer to everyone who asks” (I Pet. III). And the Apostle: “My heart is enlarged toward you, O Corinthians” (II Cor. VI).

That the way of truth must be maintained in the court, no one doubts. This is the royal road along which one must proceed, turning neither to the right nor to the left. The first path, therefore,

> Has the name Milky,  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book II),

that is, doctrinal. The second has the name, the way of the bedchamber, that is, judicial; for this reason it is called the way of testimonies, because whatever is done or said in the Mass is testimony to the things the Lord did or said concerning death and in death. Hence he himself says: “As often as you do these things, do them in remembrance of me” [Col. 1826C] (Luke XXII). And Paul: “As often as you do these things, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death” (I Cor. XI).

To draw out a few of the many things visibly done, it is worthwhile that you attend. The priest, renewed in mind and dress, stands at the altar and directs a prayer to the Father, called the *collect* because, as advocate for all, he gathers their prayers and brings them before the Lord. This is the way of testimonies. For it testifies to and recalls that Christ, at supper, brought the prayers of all to the Father. For after he had prayed for those present whom the Father had given him out of the world, he added: “I pray not for these only, but for those who will believe through their word” (John XVII).

He prays for what he asks to be done through our Lord—that is, Christ—recalling: “If you ask anything of the Father in my name, he will give it to you” (John XIV). The number of prayers also belongs to the way of testimonies. Nevertheless, according to the primary institution and Roman order, one prayer is to be said first, just as there is one gradual, one alleluia, one epistle, and one Gospel; but by the institution of the Fathers three are sometimes said, sometimes five, and seven. A number other than these is, I do not say blameworthy, but exceptional.

When three are said, it recalls that the Lord prayed the same words three times, saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI). When five are said, it recalls the Lord’s passion divided into five parts, summed up in the five wounds. When seven are said, it recalls the comprehensiveness of the Lord’s Prayer, contained in seven petitions; perhaps it should be called presumptuous to exceed their number.

When he crosses from the right horn of the altar to the left, in order sometimes to read the Gospel there, and at the end returns to the right, he bears witness to the passage of Gospel preaching from the Jews to the Gentiles, and to its eventual return to the Jews. When he passes through the canon with hands outstretched, he expresses the form [Col. 1827A] of the cross, upon which the Lord stretched out his hands toward an unbelieving people. When, bowed down, he says, “Humbly we beseech you,” etc., he represents Christ, who, bowing his head, gave up the spirit (John IX). When he rises again and says, with his voice somewhat raised, “To us also sinners,” etc., striking his breast, he recalls the centurion and certain others returning, striking their breasts and saying: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Luke XXIV).

Before saying, “Let us pray: instructed by saving precepts,” etc., he uncovers the chalice, which until then had been covered more out of reverence than mystery, and lifts it once uncovered. Then he sets it down and covers it. This is the way of testimonies. For he recalls that Joseph took the Lord’s body from the cross, placed it in a tomb wrapped in linen, and rolled a stone to the entrance of the tomb (Matt. XXVII). And because the Lord was shut in the tomb for three days, he first continues through three settings-down in the canon before again removing the veil.

First, he says the preface to the Lord’s Prayer, extending from “Instructed by saving precepts” to “we dare to say.” Secondly, he says the prayer itself, first introduced there by blessed Gregory. Thirdly, he says the embolism of the same prayer: “Deliver us, we beseech you,” etc. Once these are completed, as though the three days were accomplished, he uncovers the chalice; and, breaking the host over the right side, he places the particle which he breaks into the chalice, mingling it with the blood. He recalls the soul and body which had been separated from one another during those three days and, in the resurrection—which is indicated by the removal of the veil—returned to their former union.

Finally, he offers peace to those standing around, because after the resurrection Christ too, standing in the midst of his disciples, said: “Peace be to you” (John XX). He also instructs us that, if anyone approaches the Eucharist without peace and unity with the Church, that person eats and drinks judgment upon himself. This is why peace is not offered in Masses for the dead: those who have died in Christ have been transferred from the significant kiss of peace [Col. 1827C] to true peace—that is, from the figure of peace to the reality of peace.

At Mass, indeed, on feast days the final dismissal is, “Go, it is the dismissal”; on weekdays, “Let us bless the Lord.” This too is a way of testimonies, not of Christ’s deeds like the matters previously mentioned, but of a certain tradition of the Church. For in the days of the Church’s birth, only on Sundays and feast days did believers who were customarily occupied with secular business come together to hear the solemnities of Mass. When these had been duly completed, permission was announced for them to return to their own affairs, lest they seem to withdraw improperly, or presume at some time to return before the rite was completed. On weekdays, however, those committed solely to divine offices attended Mass; they neither had nor have to be granted leave to depart back again. “For one who serves as a soldier of God does not entangle himself in secular affairs” (II Tim. II).

Indeed, if you minister to Christ in the manner described, you will fulfill what was said at the beginning: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me.” We minister to him; therefore let us follow [Col. 1827D] him. Let us follow so that at last we may attain him; let us attain him so that finally we may comprehend him; and let us comprehend him so that we may reign with Jesus Christ, our Lord and our judge, eternally, when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON XLIV

“The little ones asked for bread, and there was no one to break it for them” (Lam. IV). In the *Lamentations*, Jeremiah wept over the destruction of the city, recounting the cruelty of mothers who, laying aside motherhood, cooked their children to a palm’s measure and devoured them. The Lord also says of the shepherds of Israel who did not care for the flock: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel” (Ezek. XXXIV). Turning his speech toward them, he says: “You ate what was fat; you did not bind up what was broken [Col. 1828A]; you did not call back what was straying; you did not heal what was weak. Nor did you merely cover yourselves with wool, but you became butchers” (ibid.).

You likewise, brothers, take heed lest the Lord say to any one of you, as if for all: “I appointed you steward over my household, and you did not minister bread to them; indeed, from a steward you became a dissipater, from a watchman a spearman. Wicked servant, I shall cast you into the outer darkness until you pay the last farthing” (Matt. XVI). Therefore, brothers, the Lord’s bread must be distributed to hungry children. But note that there is clean bread to be distributed to children, and unclean bread to be distributed or given to servants. These breads are still joined together in God’s house, as chaff with grain on the threshing floor.

We read of three kinds of bread in Holy Scripture: Pharaoh’s loaves, loaves of offering, and loaves of presentation. The first are the loaves of laypeople; the second, the loaves of Levites; the third, loaves of presentation or salvation. In the first you are judges; in [Col. 1828B] the second, priests; in the third, shepherds.

Pharaoh’s loaves are divided in the Catholic Epistle into three parts: “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (I John II). The first is lust, the second avarice, the third pride. Lust enfeebles, avarice torments, pride inflates. Lust produces impurity, avarice generates envy, pride gives birth to injustice. Lust presses a person beneath himself; avarice draws him outside himself; pride snatches him above himself: beneath himself through defilement, outside himself through wandering, above himself through arrogance.

Lust depresses a person beneath himself because, although made in God’s image, he lives as a pig. Avarice draws a person outside himself because it makes him embrace dung as though it were saffron. Pride raises him above himself, so that he sets his mouth in heaven. Thus by lust he goes to delight in vices, by avarice to find comfort in transient things, and by pride to glory in power.

You judge lust by the authority of Phinehas, who struck the Hebrew coupling with the Midianite woman (Num. XXV); the second by the authority of the Lord, who drove buyers and sellers out of the Temple (John XV); and the third by the authority of Elijah, who, sending fire from heaven, burned two captains of fifty with their men (IV Kings I). Therefore lust must be pierced through, avarice cast out, and pride burned.

The bread of offering is like incense and fragrant incense which the priest offered to the Lord: that is, prayer, of which it is said, “Let my prayer enter into your sight as incense,” etc. (Ps. CXL). This bread is threefold. Prayer ought to be ample, devout, and pure. Ample, so that you pray for enemies, according to: “Pray for those persecuting and slandering you” (Matt. V). Devout, so that you do not ask half-heartedly; for whatever you ask piously and perseveringly for yourselves will be given to you, immediately or later. Purity consists in three things. We must consider what sort of person asks, what he asks, and from whom he asks. What sort of person? One worthy to obtain. What? Life, or the merit of life, or what pertains to life. From whom? From the Father, [Col. 1828D] because one who is Father wishes to give. By doing this, you are priests.

[Note: [Col. 1827D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVII, chapter 12.]

For *sacerdos*, “priest,” is as it were *sacrum dans*, “one giving sacred things.” The person who offers prayer to God in the manner described gives sacred things to God.

The bread of propitiation, or salvation, is threefold: the bread of angels—that is, the Eucharist, of which it is said, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII); the bread of children—that is, the word of teaching, of which it is said, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs” (Matt. XV); and the bread of friends—that is, the example of life, of which it is said, “Friend, lend me three loaves” (John XXI).

On account of this threefold bread, Peter was told three times: “Feed my sheep” (Luke XI [probably John XXI]); as though the Lord were saying to him: Feed them with the Eucharist; feed them with teaching; feed them with a good life. What was said to Peter was said to all the apostles, and to you, their vicars and successors. Therefore feed with angelic bread; feed with the word; feed with example, so that the Lord may draw you from the pastures of anxious care to the pastures of fullness, [Col. 1829A] Jesus Christ, our Lord and our judge, when he comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

## SERMON XLV. TO PRIESTS
Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor man; in the evil day the Lord will deliver him (Ps. 40). My brothers and lords, great is the eminence of your dignity, order, and office—unless you choose freely to disguise or deny what is true. You know how great is the necessity imposed upon you of preserving continence and living piously and religiously among those over whom divine mercy has set you in spiritual matters. Let me say a brief and true word to you in peace. The higher we are than others in dignity, order, and office, the more despised we are in God’s sight if conduct unworthy of dignity contradicts that dignity; if a disordered life speaks against our order; if the uncleanness of an incontinent life assails the purity of our office. Sacred order and continence agree together and harmonize fittingly. [Col. 1829B] If we are found in sacred order without continence, by as much as we are raised by our order, by so much are we cast down by incontinence.

Works of piety must always be practised by us, especially at this time, when divine mercy has granted us pious tears and repentance, so that we may return through repentance, confession, and mortification of the flesh to him from whom we withdrew by sinning. The flesh, when joyful, drew us into guilt; let it, when afflicted, draw us back to pardon. At another time he had little religion who, at this time, has not proved more religious. What constitutes a work of piety, and what reward belongs to the work, the Prophet discloses when he says: “Blessed is he who understands,” etc. These words are so plain and so evident that whatever may be said in expounding them is more likely to entangle than to unfold the matter, to introduce darkness rather than light. Yet, through God’s mercy, there is something more subtle to investigate.

The Prophet calls Jesus “needy and poor,” who, out of great compassion for us, [Col. 1829C] clothed himself in flesh and lived among us as poor and needy, possessing, in so far as he was man, not even a place where to lay his head, according to the saying: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8). Yet he laid that head upon the altar of the cross, dying as true man so that other human beings might not die an eternal death. Understand concerning this needy and poor man: he believes Jesus Christ to be God and the Son of God, though seized, though scourged, though stretched upon the cross, though pierced by a lance, though smeared with spittle. Whoever beholds these things with pious faith, whoever embraces them in faith and virtue, although he may sometimes fall through the weakness of the flesh, nevertheless divine mercy does not finally depart from him, because “the Lord will deliver him in the evil day.”

He calls the day of judgment “evil,” not because it is evil in itself, but because it is bitter to many on account of the bitterness of what will occur in it. For what is more bitter than to be thrust into punishments that will never fail, to suffer misery without [Col. 1829D] end, to endure darkness without any alternation of light? To live amid such punishments is continually to die and never to come to an end, according to the saying of St Gregory. [Note: [Col. 1829D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XV, ch. 9.] “He whose life dies in sin, his death shall live in punishment.” What greater shame could there be than for the consciences of each person to be opened in the sight of the holy angels and all the saints? Hence it is said: “The Ancient of Days sat, and behold, the books were opened” (Dan. 7). The books of consciences will then be opened, which are now kept sealed by wicked obstinacy. If all the secrets of any one of us now came forth to the knowledge of us all, he could scarcely remain standing for shame when he saw himself thus exposed. None of us has lived so rightly, none of our works are so upright, that he would not be covered with extraordinary blushes if he saw the hiding places of his conscience laid open to all. Rightly, therefore, is the day of judgment called bitter, when [Col. 1830A] nothing is covered that will not be revealed.

The prophet Hosea indicates the distinction, or pre-eminence, of our estate over others—of clerics over laypeople—when he says: “If Israel has committed fornication, at least do not you, Judah, offend; do not enter into Gilgal, and do not go up to Beth-aven” (Hos. 4). These are the words of the prophet Hosea, who by both name and deed prefigured the Saviour. For *Hosea* means “saviour,” signifying that Saviour who “saved his people from their sins” (Matt. 1). Of him it is elsewhere said: “He himself will come and save us” (Isa. 35); for he came to seek and save what had perished. Hosea, at the Lord’s command, took a harlot as his wife; and the Son of God, obeying the Father, joined the Church to himself on the altar of the cross. The woman who had committed fornication was taken by Hosea; and the Gentile world, defiled with the filth of idolatry, was washed in Christ’s blood and thus given to him as a bride—among those who triumph, having neither wrinkle nor blemish (Eph. 5). See how great is the correspondence of sign to thing signified, herald to proclamation, shadow to reality, promise [Col. 1830B] to truth.

“If Israel has committed fornication,” etc. It is the custom of Holy Scripture to signify the ten tribes by the name Israel, and the two tribes by the name Judah. The two tribes held the citadel of the kingdom and the dignity of the priesthood. For the Levitical tribe, which interceded for others by prayer and offering, did not depart from the tribe of Judah and Benjamin. Before the division of the kingdom, all the tribes were called Israel; but after the division had taken place, the name that had been common to all became special to the larger part, that is, to the ten tribes. Therefore laypeople are rightly signified by Israel, and clerics by Judah; although the latter are fewer in number, they are more eminent in dignity.

If, therefore, Israel—that is, laypeople—commit fornication, at least do not you, Judah, offend. Clerics, ministers of the altar, and prelates ought not to be drawn into sin by the example of sinners, but by word and example ought to draw others to live purely. If luxury defiles laypeople, at least let purity of life not desert the prelates of the churches, so that, by as much as they are preferred to others in dignity, by so much [Col. 1830C] they may be considered more conspicuous in purity. Blessed is the person who excels in character as well as in honours. Let pure conduct, my brothers, be the companion of our dignity, lest a perverse manner of life contradict the reverence which our dignity demands.

*Israel* is interpreted “a man seeing God.” Let the people remember that they were created to see God; let them live cautiously, lest they fall away from him to whom the interpretation of their name summons them (Hos. 1). *Judah* means “confessing.” Clerics are bound to a twofold confession: confession of their own sin and confession of divine praise. Let us be diligent, lest, mute in either respect, we lose him for whom devout confession longs. It should be noted that, speaking of Judah, he says, “do not offend.” He offends who leaves undone what he ought to do. For prelates it is not only a mortal matter to commit mortal sins, but also not to rebuke those who commit them, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Insist in season and out of season; rebuke, reprove, exhort, with all patience” (2 Tim. 4). He who is bound to rebuke others and does not rebuke them subjects himself to a more grievous punishment. [Col. 1830D] [Note: [Col. 1830D] Chapter *Facientis*, Distinction 86.] Hence the saying: “Cursed is the man who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48). He is not free of the guilt of wicked association who ceases to oppose a manifest crime.

“Do not enter into Gilgal, and do not go up to Beth-aven.” Gilgal was a place in the wilderness where the people were circumcised a second time (Josh. 5), not in the same persons, but in others of the same multitude. For some time circumcision had been deferred in the wilderness; but when Gilgal was reached, it was repeated—not in those previously circumcised, but in those to be circumcised anew. Similar to this manner of speaking is the saying: “When he slew them, they sought him and returned” (Ps. 77): not those slain, but others frightened by the slaughtered.

Beth-aven is the place where Jacob saw that glorious vision—the angels ascending and descending—and said: “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” [Col. 1831A] (Gen. 28). Hence the place was called Bethel, that is, “house of God.” Afterwards the people, led astray by foolish error, worshipped idols in the same place; and the place was called Beth-aven, that is, “house of an idol.”

Gilgal and Beth-aven signify two vices, luxury and avarice, from which we are freed with greater difficulty in proportion as we are more grievously assailed by them. *Gilgal* is interpreted “rolling-place” and signifies luxury, in which one who loves the impurities of the flesh wallows, according to the saying: “A washed sow returns to wallowing in the mire, and a dog returns to its vomit” (2 Pet. 2). Hence it is elsewhere said: “A lustful man is useless for everything.” Beth-aven means “house of an idol” and signifies avarice. For avarice is the service of an idol (Gal. 5). Let us not enter Gilgal, my brothers, defiling ourselves through luxury; nor let us go up to Beth-aven, serving idols through avarice.

In the manner of his command the Prophet indicated how much caution is needed in avoiding vice. “Do not enter Gilgal”: he does not advise departure but forbids entry. For luxury is never more easily [Col. 1831B] conquered than by flight, nowhere more cautiously avoided than by turning aside from it, never more perfectly overcome than by restraining oneself from encountering it. Hence the Apostle: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6); and David: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136); and again:

> Neglected fires are accustomed to gather strength.

Hence Jerome: [Note: [Col. 1831D] Jerome, Epistle 4, to Demetrias.] “Destroy the enemy—that is, luxury—while it is still small; let wickedness be crushed in its first seed.” And this:

> Resist beginnings: medicine is prepared too late,  
> when evils have grown strong through long delay.  
> (Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, book I.)

Therefore, cutting off every occasion of falling through luxury, let us not enter Gilgal. Let us not merely detest luxury, but flee every occasion drawing us toward it: namely places and persons—places suitable for lust and persons well fitted to deceive. [Col. 1831C] For all these are full of the devil’s snares.

At Gilgal the people were circumcised a second time; and a twofold circumcision is required for luxury to be fully conquered: circumcision of heart and circumcision of body. We are circumcised in heart and body when the body is guarded from unclean action and the heart is restrained from shameful thought. Hence it is said: “Burn my reins and my heart, O God” (Ps. 25). And again: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12). He said “loins,” not “loin”; for it is not enough to gird the bodily loin unless we also gird the loin of the heart. Ezekiel saw a man girded with a long garment down to the loins (Ezek. 23); John in the Apocalypse saw a man girded up to the breasts (Rev. 1). Let us therefore be girded not only down to the loins, by guarding the body, but up to the breasts, by restraining the heart from unclean thoughts.

“Do not go up to Beth-aven.” Where the Prophet—or rather, the Lord through the prophet—forbade avarice, he fittingly mentions ascent, thereby showing that avarice entangles not only the lowly but also the great: “They all love gifts and pursue rewards” (Isa. 1). And not infrequently, when the flesh has been subdued by abstinence, avarice creeps in, polluting and staining the whole conscience with blood. Few are found whom the scent of gifts does not incline and bend; but blessed is he “who shakes his hand free from every gift” [Col. 1831D] (Isa. 33). This pest draws many along with it, is conquered with difficulty, inflames the mind to seize, but continually relaxes it into tenacious keeping. Warning against both, the Prophet says: “Do not desire robberies. If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61).

These two vices are daughters of the leech of whom Solomon speaks (Prov. 30). A leech is a worm so called from sucking blood. The nature of this worm is that, when applied to suck blood, it does not cease sucking before it ceases to live; when it stops sucking, it begins to die.
