Such is the devil, who, for as long as and as much as he can, never ceases to deceive us; and the more wickedly he deceives us, the more grievous a punishment he brings upon himself. His daughters are luxury and avarice, which become more and more inflamed in the person whom they begin to suck. How many thousands of people has this father led to hell through these daughters? I think that a third part of humankind perishes through the occasion of these daughters. Luxury is sometimes moderated for a little while, but afterwards returns more strongly in proportion as it has been resisted more weakly. Nothing is enough for avarice. While the avaricious mind burns for what it does not possess, it thinks little of whatever it has:

> The love of money grows in proportion as money itself grows.  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*.)

Yielding to the Apostle’s command, as we have presented our members to uncleanness for iniquity, so let us present them to righteousness for sanctification (Rom. 6). [Col. 1832B] Let us flee luxury, detest avarice, neither entering Gilgal nor ascending Beth-aven.

We, brothers, who are called men, who are strong, who ought to have manly spirits—what shall we say before our judge, now gentle but terrible in the future? Young maidens, weak in age and frail in sex—namely Agnes and Cecilia—will judge us. One of them attained the glory of martyrdom in her thirteenth year. These women, preserving virginity, suffered gloriously for Christ. But we wretches, strong in body yet weak in spirit, have already reached mature age: and what have we ever endured for the Lord? We have left none of the world’s delights untouched; the desires of our wantonness range through every meadow. I fear that this terrible saying may resound in our ears, though unwillingly: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6). And because we cannot resist vices by ourselves, let us all pray, let each one pray, to our merciful fellow-brother Jesus Christ, that he may deign to help us—[Col. 1832C] he who now refreshes us with the food of his flesh and will hereafter satisfy us with the vision of the Trinity, our gracious master Jesus Christ, who will come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XLVI

“An angel stood beside the altar of the temple, having a golden censer in his hand, and much incense was given to him” (Rev. 8). The passage you have heard is one statement, and the Lord revealed two mysteries through it to his servant John in the Apocalypse: one concerning Christ, the other concerning Christ’s minister, that is, the priest.

Concerning Christ, thus. *Angel* is the name of an office, for angels are also messengers (Heb. 1). All the orders of blessed spirits are sent for the ministry of human salvation. Therefore all are angels, according to the saying: “He makes his angels spirits”; but they are often specified in Holy Scripture by the authority entrusted to them. Some preside over regions, of whom Daniel speaks [Col. 1832D] (ch. 10): “the prince of the Greeks,” “the prince of the Persians”; others preside over churches, of whom the Apocalypse speaks (ch. 2): “Say to the angel of Ephesus,” “to the angel of Laodicea”; others preside over persons, whence in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. 12): “Peter’s angel stands at the door.” But in the chapter cited above no qualifying designation is added, so that we may understand not “the angel of the Lord,” but “the angel, the Lord”: Christ Jesus, the Angel of Great Counsel, who, when he rose, stood beside the altar.

An altar is so called as though *arida*, “dry”; for whatever is burned dries into ashes. On the altar of the cross Christ’s flesh was dried like a potsherd in a furnace. Hence: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21). Because in dying he lay upon the altar, in rising he stood beside the altar: that is, he was raised from the flux of mortality into the state of everlasting immortality. “For now he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

Immediately much incense was given to him. Incense is sometimes a type of prayer: “Let my prayer enter before you like incense, O Lord” (Ps. 140). Sometimes it is a type of exaltation, as in: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness like a column of smoke, from spices?” (Song 3). Christ, rising again, was greatly exalted in majesty, power, and renown. Of majesty it is written: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2). Concerning power he himself testified: “All power has been given to me in heaven, on earth, and in the sea” (Matt. 28). Concerning renown he likewise foretold: “You shall be my witnesses in all Judaea and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1).

When Christ rose, moreover, he had a golden censer in his hand. Gold signifies wisdom. Therefore Christ’s flesh is the golden censer in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. 2). This is the golden urn full of manna (Heb. 9), which, while he suffered, was in the hands of executioners, according to the saying: “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked” (Job [Col. 1833B] 9). But when it blossomed again, it was placed in the hand of the Mediator.

It remains to apply what we have said to the priest; and then it may be said precisely: “The angel of the Lord stood beside the altar of the temple.” For the priest too is an angel. Hence in Malachi: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and from his mouth they seek wisdom; for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2).

Now in this passage three matters are considered: the priest’s office, namely to enter unto the altar of God; and the twofold reason for entering. The first is that he may bear a golden censer in his hand—that is, handle with his hands the Lord’s body consecrated by the word, and dispense it by his ministry. The second is that by the manifold intercession of prayers he may assuage the divine indignation toward the people. In order that this may become clear, we must begin higher up with the threefold office of priests, and explain each in separate chapters. For he is a pastor, a judge, and an intercessor: pastor in the Church, [Col. 1833C] judge in the chair, intercessor in the Mass; pastor that he may instruct soundly, judge that he may decide justly, intercessor that he may give help piously.

Let us treat each point more fully. Of the first: “The angel of the Lord walked about the courts of the temple, having rods in his hand, and much pasture was given to him.” Of the second: “The angel of the Lord sat upon the chair of the temple, having a golden cup in his hand, and many draughts were given to him.” Of the third: “The angel stood beside the altar of the temple, having a golden censer in his hand, and much incense was given to him.”

It belongs to a pastor to walk about, according to the saying: “I have chosen you, that you may go and bear fruit” (John 15). There were four courts of the temple: the first of priests, the second of men, the third of women, the fourth of the unclean. Correspondingly there are four kinds of sheep under a pastor: weak sheep, broken sheep, wandering sheep, and strong sheep, according to Ezekiel: “What was weak you did not heal; what was broken you did not bind up; what had wandered you did not bring back; what was strong you strengthened” [Col. 1833D] (Ezek. 34).

A weak sheep is one that believes for a time and withdraws in time of temptation, like Peter, who confessed the Son of God but afterwards denied him at the voice of a servant-girl. Lest such a sheep fail, let the pastor encourage it in this manner: “My son, if you come to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. 10). “The Father chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12), that he may grant an inheritance to the chastened.

A broken sheep is one “that has rotted in its dung” (Joel 1), that rejoices in most evil things and glories when it has done evil (Prov. 2). Let the pastor rouse such a sheep, that it may arise, in this manner: “Awake, you who sleep; arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5). But if it does not awake at the touching hand, let him employ the pricks of threats, saying: “Your fire shall not be extinguished and your worm shall not die” (Isa. 66); “you shall pass from snowy waters to heat,” where there will be weeping [Col. 1834A] and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 8).

A wandering sheep is one that follows a strange flock. If it follows Arius, let the pastor tell it what Truth said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). If, in accordance with Nestorius, it asserts two persons in Christ, let it hear from the pastor: “Yet there are not two, but one Christ.” A strong sheep is one which, with the Apostle, forgetting what is behind, stretches itself toward what lies ahead. Such a sheep must be strengthened in this manner: “Stand in your ways and consider which is the eternal way. Wait for the Lord; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened; and endure the Lord” (Ps. 26).

Thus, walking about, the pastor has five rods in his hand. The first is the rod of power; the second, of discipline; the third, of teaching; the fourth, of mercy; the fifth, of guardianship. By the first he punishes; by the second he corrects; by the third he instructs; by the fourth he commands; by the fifth he protects. The first is terrible; the second favourable; the third useful; the fourth sweet; the fifth praiseworthy. He has the first for the proud, the second [Col. 1834B] for the restless, the third for little ones, the fourth for the devout, the fifth for all. Such a man is indeed given abundant pastures, for such a pastor brings forth new things and old from his treasury. God-man gave their sum to Peter when he said three times: “Feed my sheep” (John 21): he designated three pastures, as though saying, “Feed them by teaching, feed them by life, feed them by your death.”

It remains for us to discuss judgment. The angel of the Lord sits upon the chair of the temple when he judges between cause and cause, when he separates the clean from the unclean; but let him attend to what cup he has in his hand. There is a golden cup of Babylon (Jer. 51), from which Jeremiah gave the kings of the earth to drink, and in which are mixed wine of error and wine of dizziness. This is the wisdom of the world, which is foolishness with God (1 Cor. 3), and the wisdom of the flesh [perhaps read *carnis*, “of the flesh”], which is hostile to God. The first counsels empty things, the second pleasant things; to be wise through the first is to be foolish, through the second to be mad.

There is also a cup in the Lord’s hand, full of pure wine mixed with wine (Ps. 74). [Col. 1834C] Let the priest have this in his hand, so that he does not regard the face of the powerful, nor show mercy to a poor person in a bad cause; so that, not blinded by gifts and not made drunk by hatred or love, he does not forget God’s judgments. Above all, when he sits [sic] as a confessor, he has a cup in his hand, in which many draughts are given to him: namely, three kinds of wine. The first is purgative, the second cheering, the third sleep-inducing. The first is of severity, the second of pleasantness, the third of rest. The first is the threat of eternal punishment; the second, assurance of pardon together with the promise of life; the third, the injunction to cease from sin—as though he said: “Go, now sin no more” (John 5).

It remains to explain intercession. The angel stands beside the altar of the temple while the antiphon at the entrance is sung. For thus we read in the Apocalypse, when the seven angels were sounding their trumpets: “The angel stood beside the altar of the temple,” etc. Celestine instituted forty-five antiphons to be sung at the entrance, with a triple celebration, [Col. 1834D] that is, with threefold repetition. The priest’s entrance to the altar represents Christ’s coming in the flesh: he was foretold by the prophets, at last testified to by the apostles, and manifested in Christ himself. Therefore the antiphon is sung first to represent the prophecy of the prophets; it is sung a second time to signify the testimony of the apostles; it is sung a third time because of the manifestation of the Lord Jesus. Hence the priest, in the type of Christ, turns toward the singers while the *Glory be to the Father* is sung, as though Christ were saying: “Behold, I am present.”

Yet in the original institution there was another reason for turning. The antiphon was sung until the priest, having turned and raised his hand, signalled to the singer to say: “Glory be to the Father.” Thus the priest, standing as though in the midst of young women beating timbrels, approaches to kiss the altar, as though Christ said: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14). Thereupon much incense is given to him, that is, the support of manifold prayers.

I do not think this is said with reference to the number of prayers, which some multiply to the point of weariness. Properly, just as there is one Gospel, one Epistle, one gradual, one alleluia, so there ought to be one collect, one secret, and one post-communion prayer. Yet, lest we seem to evade the traditions of the Fathers, multiplication is tolerable if it does not exceed seven. For the petitions of the Lord’s Prayer are contained under this number. Thus “much incense” is said because there are properly ten prayers in the Mass. [Col. 1835A] The first is called the collect; the second, the secret; the last, the post-communion. There are seven in the canon besides the Lord’s Prayer.

In the first the priest prays either for good things, that they may be present, or for evil things, that they may be absent. It is called the collect because, gathering the petitions of all into one, he alone presents them to the Lord. Yet he first greets those for whom he prays in this manner: “The Lord be with you.” Although this form of greeting may seem to have been taken from the angel who said to Gideon, “The Lord is with you, most valiant of men” (Judg. 6), or from Boaz, who said to the reapers, “The Lord be with you” (Ruth 2), it is nevertheless better taken from Chronicles. There the priest said to King Asa and the people gathered with him for battle: “Hear, King Asa, and all the people of Judah and Benjamin: the Lord be with you” (2 Chron. 15), who have gathered to do his will. The people’s response, moreover, is found in the Second Epistle to Timothy (ch. 4), where it is written: “The Lord Jesus be with your spirit.”

In every greeting he turns toward the people, except in the greeting preceding the preface. For he is now approaching the consecration of the Lord’s body; he has, as it were, put his hand to the plough; he may no longer look back.

The collect is used before the offering, where he prays for the blessing of the offering. Because it is said by the priest alone, it is called the Secret, as are the following prayers, which are likewise said by him alone. Yet there is a special reason why it is called secret. It is handed down that one of the Fathers, while saying the Secret aloud, was mocked by shepherds singing after his manner. [Col. 1835C] When he cursed them, they were struck by lightning. Therefore it was introduced that it should not be heard by the people.

Among the seven prayers in the canon, the first is for the holy catholic Church: that God may deign to protect and govern it throughout the whole world together with its shepherd, our pope. What some add concerning their king and bishop is a new tradition. In the second he prays for those standing around, whose faith is known to God. Hence catechumens, because they have not yet received the sacraments of faith, are excluded beneath the canon at the beginning of the canon. [Note: [Col. 1835D] William Durand, *Rationale*, book XIV, ch. 36.] In the third he prays for himself, that the Lord, being appeased, may accept the offering of his service. At last he comes to the consecration of the divine body. When this has been completed, in the fourth he humbly prays for acceptance of the offering, that it may be carried by the hands of an angel into the sight of the divine majesty. In the fifth he prays for the dead who rest in Christ. In the sixth, for sinners, that the Lord, giver of pardon, may admit them. Finally, raising his voice, he pronounces the preface together with the Lord’s Prayer; seventh, he says its embolism, a word meaning “an addition”: namely, “Deliver us.” In the embolism he prays secretly for peace to be given.

In the last prayer, which is called the post-communion, he prays spiritually for those who have approached the Lord’s communion. These, indeed, are the priest’s many incenses. Great care must be taken that he does not offer them upon strange fire. In the canonical epistle, strange fire is described in three divisions: “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2), that is, luxury, avarice, and pride. The first defiles, the second torments, the third inflates.

Nadab and Abihu, on the day of their consecration, offered upon the fire of luxury; for it is related that on the preceding night they had known their wives, and thus fire devoured them (Num. 26). Korah, and with him two hundred men—that is, men seeking the priesthood—offered upon the fire of avarice, [Col. 1836A] and fire devoured them (Num. 16). Uzziah, usurping the priesthood together with the kingdom, was struck with leprosy on his forehead (2 Chron. 26). In this way, the priest who offers upon strange fire will not escape the eternal fire. May Jesus Christ, our Lord and judge, deliver us from it, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XLVII. TO PRIESTS AND PRELATES
“Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48 [49]). The God of vengeance, the Lord, repeatedly recalls through these prophetic servants both the benefit that he bestowed upon man, the sin that man introduced, and the punishment that the Judge inflicted, so that he may thus give those who fear him a sign, that they may flee from before the bow.

Moreover, that great Potter, who formed the dawn and the sun, laments in these words the first-born man, his noble creature, whom he had formed for honour, but who through his own fault was transformed into disgrace. For, when he wished to exist through himself, he ruined himself and transmitted ruin as an inheritance to all posterity. Yet, lest posterity be able to complain as though it were paying what it had not taken, the Potter assigns the whole cause of human ruin to the thing formed—God to man. For, having been made in the image of God, man, filled with the winnowing breath, begot us in his own image, since by the law of nature, as the father is, so are the children.

Nevertheless, these words may significantly be addressed to the ministers of the Church, the shepherds of the Lord’s flock, in order to shake them out of negligence and impress caution upon them. Above all and more than all others, they must beware of falling: the higher their rank, the heavier their fall. The argument is made to them as from the lesser, as though one said: “Consider, O lords, you who are a royal priesthood, a holy nation, set in the superlative degree [Col. 1836C] of humankind: if the fall from the positive degree is so great, how much more grievous is it from the superlative? If it is so great from the lowest, how great from the highest?”

Indeed, to omit others, there are four degrees by which the priest of the Most High God ascends, so that he may stand upon the watchtower and keep the watches of the night over his flock. The first is that of nature; the second, of grace; the third, of excellence; the fourth, of power. In the first we are born; in the second we are born again; in the third we are advanced; in the fourth we are placed in authority. By the first we are human beings; by the second, believers; by the third, priests; by the fourth, shepherds—that is, born, reborn, sealed, and set over others.

Each of these degrees has its own proper character. The first is in honour, the second in beauty, the third in dignity, the fourth in power. Surely no one, we believe, is ignorant of humanity’s honour in the first degree. Man was made in his soul according to the image and likeness of his God (Gen. 1); in an upright body, bearing the likeness of that soul; with a face lifted high, so that he might contemplate [Col. 1836D] heaven and the lights of heaven. For his sake the visible world was made with all its furnishings: lord of the living creatures of the earth, inhabitant of Paradise, fellow-citizen of angels, member of the household of the Lord of Hosts, destined from man to become, as it were, God.

Yet though he was in honour, he did not understand that he should be subject to his Maker; but, wishing to be coexistent with him, he fell, compared with senseless beasts and made like them. He is like them not only in his needs, since he shares the earth’s food with beasts, but also in the affections of his heart: he crawls in breast and belly; he lives crafty like a fox, unstable like a bird, lustful like a sow, wrathful like a bear, proud like a horse, foolish like an ass. And, what is more detestable, he retains his soul’s likeness in an upright body; but in his soul, bent down, he has exchanged the likeness of God for a beastly likeness.

The philosophers did not know the remaining three degrees—namely, those of believer, priest, and shepherd—and unbelievers do not know them. Therefore we confess to you: “Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11). Let us, then, to whom it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom (Matt. 13), consider the degrees of one ascending. For the believer, ascending from the washing, is clothed in beauty, ascending from the honour of the image to the beauty of adoption.

This is the beauty which the Prophet compares with and prefers to snow, saying: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50 [51]). This is the beauty for which the bridegroom addresses the bride: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4). This is the beauty to which our Psalmist, the king in Israel, exhorts his daughter: “Hear, daughter, forget your people and your father’s house; and the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44 [45]). This is Christ’s snow-white garment, such as no fuller can make on earth. This is the white garment put upon the baptized person.

Nevertheless, when the man of God was in this beauty, he did not understand; indeed, insulting the Holy Spirit [Col. 1837B], he changed the garment of believers into the likeness of an Ethiopian skin. He was compared to lusting beasts and made like them—beasts which kick against the goad, throw off the yoke laid upon them, turn aside from the path, and therefore are beaten until they become quiet; or, if they grow more insolent under the lashes, are cast out. And does a father spare the rod because he hates his son?

But the greatest misery is where correction is not applied, because amendment is despaired of. Hence the Lord says to Jerusalem: “I will no longer be angry with you” (Ezek. 16).

It remains—indeed, it concerns us—to consider the dignity of the third degree: how great the rank of priesthood is. Here one must first observe that the ascent to this degree is now longer than it was in the primitive Church. There, one who was merely a believer became a deacon or a priest. Later certain ranks of the minor orders were introduced, through which one ascends to the priesthood as by Songs of Ascents.

This is the ivory throne whose backrest [Col. 1837C] is golden, to which one ascends by six purple steps, strewn in the middle with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem; there the priest of the Most High God ascends to the dignity of intimate service. In the work of creation there was no one to assist the Spirit of the Lord or to be his counsellor. But in the mystery of our redemption he chose to have fellow-workers, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22).

Therefore the priest is the Redeemer’s fellow-worker, the counsellor of the Lord of Hosts; through his counsel those who have offended return to the grace of their God. He is the steward of Christ’s table, offering food to the Father together with the servants. His word is joined to the element, and it becomes a sacrament; by his hand the wisely prepared healing medicine is made, through which those wounded by the serpent are restored to health.

The dignity of the priest also shines forth in outward matters. How great a thing it is that, at the lifting of his hand, the heads of the people bow so that he may invoke over them the name of their God! How great a thing it is that kings of nations and princes of peoples, with bent [Col. 1837D] knees, offer him gifts and kiss his hand, that they may be sanctified through its touch!

Nevertheless, when the man entrusted with the sacred mysteries was in this dignity, he did not understand. Rather, seeking his own interests and sitting in ambush against his Lord, he is compared with raging beasts and becomes more insane than they. Such beasts either tear their own limbs with their teeth, dash themselves brainless against every obstacle, or, rushing headlong, plunge into destruction. In the same manner his prayer becomes sin to him; the Lord’s table becomes for him a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block.

Whether he teaches or is silent, woe to the vessel: for God says to the teacher, “Why do you recount my just ordinances and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49 [50]). But the silent man incurs the woe of the sleepy and dumb dog, unable to bark, and shall go down alive into hell (Isa. 56).

Finally, we must consider the fourth and last degree: when a man ascends from the dignity of priest to the power of judge, to the care of shepherd, so that, called by the Lord like Aaron, he may hear from him: “Feed my sheep” (John 21). To say it briefly, he is appointed Christ’s vicar among those below, a prelate of the Church, possessing primacy in judgment and access to the heavenly court: fisher of men, shepherd of souls, avenger of wrongs, avenger of penitents, guarantor of rewards, walking upon asp and basilisk, trampling lion and dragon.

Nevertheless, when the exalted man was in this power, he did not understand; but, grown fat, thick, and swollen, he magnified rebellion against the Lord. Therefore he was compared with dying beasts and became more rotten than they. His error is drawn into an example; his stench spreads from sea to sea: malicious like Lucifer, who drew a third part of the stars after himself; idle like Adam, who did not correct his companion (Gen. 3); greedy like Saul, who kept every fat thing (1 Sam. 15); deceitful like Antichrist, and therefore the Lord slew him with the breath of his mouth (2 Thess. 2).

Therefore let him who stands in an exalted place take heed lest he fall [Col. 1838B] (1 Cor. 10). You, then, to whom the Lord has given the nations as his inheritance to cultivate and the ends of the earth as his possession, labour during this present day and do not fear: for tomorrow you shall go forth, and the Lord shall be with you—Jesus Christ our Lord, our Judge, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XLVIII. TO PRELATES

“Jonah went down into the inner part of the ship and slept a deep sleep” (Jonah 1). These things happened before our time in ancient days, but they were written for our sake, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. The word of the Lord came to Jonah, son of Amittai, that he should go and preach repentance to the Ninevites and announce their crimes to them. But he who was sent despised the command; despising it, he fled; fleeing, he fell asleep. When he was by chance discovered and cast into the sea, a great fish swallowed him; but, penitent and praying, he was restored to dry land.

The history of Jonah especially instructs one sent by the Lord to preach, to whom it is said: “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up your voice, announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. 58)—that is, the fisher of men, shepherd of souls, announcer of crimes, intercessor for penitents, guarantor of rewards. Through it he can understand his rank, fear his fall, avoid danger, and hope for consolation: his rank in the commission entrusted to him; his fall in rashness; danger to be fled in being swallowed; consolation in restoration.

That we may know the rank, let us see who is sent, by whom he is sent, and to where he is sent by the Lord. For “he does not enter through the door,” etc. (John 10). If he has forced himself in by violence, introduced himself by simony, or been brought in through a false representation, he is far from the truth of a shepherd. Such were Uzziah, Simon Magus, and the two hundred and fifty adherents of Korah.

Jonah, son of Amittai, is sent—that is, the dove, son of truth [Col. 1838D]. For the teacher of the dove, that is, of the Church, and fellow-minister of the dove, that is, of the Holy Spirit, must not depart from conformity to the dove: if he harms no one; if he builds in the clefts of the rock; if he has groaning instead of song. He is also a dove if, at the changes of its neck—that is, in preaching—he changes colour. For the aged must be admonished differently, etc. Let him preach consolation to weak sheep, healing to the broken, recall to the wandering, exhortation to the strong.

Doves also contend with one another by a certain spreading of their wings. This is the sole contention of priests: the good contention, namely the emulation of virtues. Of this it is said: “Covet the better gifts” (1 Cor. 12), that is: “Be imitators of me, beloved, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11). Let them strive to imitate the good, to equal them, or to surpass them.

Behold the rank. For Christ’s vicar is a dovelike man, a son of truth, and a prelate of the Church. If it is something to be a human being, it is great to be a believer; greater to be a priest; greatest [Col. 1839A] to be a shepherd. Let him also be truthful in mind, word, and deed. For just as it is truly said, “The words of a priest are either true or sacrilegious,” so no less truly may it be said that a priest’s words and deeds are either true or sacrilegious.

He is sent to Nineveh, that is, to the Church, of which it is said: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved,” etc. (Song 4); and one enters it by a journey of three days when it is said: “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Concerning the fall: he flees from the face of the Lord, not from that of the people. For we are like whitewashed tombs, etc.: in ecclesiastical tonsure, in a white garment, in solemn chanting, in unceasing intercession, and in consuming the sins of the people in manifold ways. He goes down into the inner part of the ship: bilge-water cannot remain in the middle; it sinks lower than the rest because it goes before those who fall.

Noah’s ark has five dwelling-places (Gen. 7). In the highest are people and birds—prelates and contemplatives—because they ought to be free for God alone. In the second are wild animals, that is, active persons, who are divided. After the wild animals are those who bear the name only, not the spiritual reality; in the bilge are dung and water gradually entering, whose weight drags down the upper things.

For he is greedy like Saul, idle like Adam, malicious like Satan; and malice is an evil that draws evil toward itself. He sleeps a deep sleep. There is a sleep of weakness, necessity, truth, and vanity: brief, great, light, heavy; to be allowed, awaited, embraced, or rejected, because it is useful, unavoidable, lovable, or detestable. And provide an authority for each danger.

Leviathan, the dragon made in the sea to play with it (Ps. 103 [104]), swallows him: desolation. But let not the fugitive servant despair: if he repents, if he cries out from the depths, the Lord will rescue him from the belly of the fish, from the jaws of hell, and set him at his right hand among the sheep. May our Lord Jesus Christ set us among them when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON XLIX. TO MONKS

“My son, guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it proceeds life” (Prov. 4). On the surface of the letter it appears that a father speaks to his son; but it is not sufficiently clear what father speaks to what son. For there is a carnal father and a spiritual father. From the first we are born according to the flesh for labour, by nature children of wrath (Eph. 2); from the second, through water and Spirit, we are reborn for righteousness, children of grace by adoption.

Yet if a carnal father were speaking, it is probable that he would have used a human and ancient proverb concerning the guarding of the body, saying: “My son, guard your body with all vigilance.” For he guards a good fortress who guards his body. It remains, therefore, that a spiritual father speaks about the righteousness of the spirit.

But this father too is divided into two. The first spiritual father is he who begets us by the word of truth, or regenerates us by the power of baptism. In this sense Mark is called Peter’s son (1 Pet. 5), and Paul said to the Galatians: “My little children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4). The second spiritual Father [Col. 1839D] is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 1), the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation. The first is our father who is on earth; the second is our Father who is in heaven. Therefore, since the first is still one of us, like us capable of suffering, he would more suitably have said: “My son, let us guard our heart with all vigilance.”

It remains, then, that God the Father speaks to the Son—or, more truly, that God the Father speaks to sons. He has three sons: Job, Daniel, and Noah: namely, the active man, the contemplative man, and the prelate of both. The first is the son of grace; the second, the son of obedience; the third, the son of the right hand, who, grasping the oar in his right hand, guided Peter’s little ship like a strong helmsman. The first is born in baptism; the second in the profession of an order; the third in canonical promotion.

Let us therefore set these three sons before the face of their Father. For he himself said: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18). Raising his eyes to his sons, let him open his mouth and say: “Little sons, hear your Father; incline your ear to the words of my mouth in order to keep them, for in keeping them there is great reward.”

The sons reply: “Speak, Father, and we shall hear you. Grant us to keep what you say, because we are not sufficient of ourselves even to think anything good as from ourselves” (2 Cor. 3).

The Father says to them: “The guarding of the heart rests upon all three of you in common as a necessity. For life and death are in the hands of the heart. You have read in the Gospel concerning death: ‘From the heart proceed thefts, murders, blasphemies’ (Matt. 15), whose wage is eternal death. But that life comes from the heart, hear my disciple Solomon of one night, who says: ‘Life proceeds from the heart’ (Prov. 4). And another disciple of mine, Paul of three days, says: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness’ (Rom. 10).

“But beyond this common guardianship, son of grace, the guardianship of your body also rests upon you [Col. 1840B]. For you still dwell in the midst of a crooked nation, brother of dragons and companion of ostriches; you still groan like a lily among thorns, like grain among chaff. Therefore it concerns you to guard the workshops of the five senses, lest death enter your soul through their windows. Every day you see desirable things, hear entertainments, smell fragrances, taste pleasant things, and touch soft things.

“And you likewise, son of the right hand, must guard your flesh. For you two shine amid a crooked nation like a fixed light in the firmament. Moreover, the guardianship of the brethren has been entrusted to you: ‘I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel’ (Ezek. 3). Therefore, son of the right hand, guard with all vigilance your heart, your flesh, and your flock. But you, son of grace, guard with all vigilance your heart and your flesh, so that you may say with the Psalmist: ‘My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in my God’ (Ps. 83 [84]).

“But you, son of obedience, have withdrawn by flight [Col. 1840C], and by remaining in solitude have placed your flesh in safety, as though in a lofty fortress, that it may not be shaken from afar by the assaults of waves barking around it. You hear the sound of shores but do not dread shipwreck. Therefore, my son, guard your heart with all vigilance; for you are guardian of this one thing alone, and for this reason you are called a monk.

“Further, little sons, carefully observe why I said that the heart must be guarded with all vigilance. The phrase is figurative, expressed by way of a comparison. You see someone walking in the open air carrying in his hands a lighted wax taper; he shields it with both hands lest the force of the winds extinguish it, and if at times he is burned, he patiently endures the burning. In this manner you carry your illumined heart as a burning lamp in your hands, so that you may say: ‘My soul is always in my hands’ (Ps. 118 [119]).

“The heart is illumined when it knows God; and to know him is to keep his commandments, according to the saying: ‘He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar’ (1 John 2). It is illumined in three ways: by repentance it is kindled, by correction it burns, by watchful care it shines. Unless guarded, this light is extinguished by three winds. The flesh comes from the east: for the body, corrupted originally, weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things (Wis. 9). The world comes from the west: for the world and all its glory pass into setting. The devil comes from the north. But the south wind feeds the flame of the lamp.

“The two hands guarding the lamp are, in the active person, almsgiving and fasting; in the prelate, teaching and life; in the contemplative, reading and prayer.”

You have heard the Father speaking with his sons concerning the guarding of the heart against the violence of the winds. Yet we may treat more fully of the number and force of the winds. For there are six general temptations that oppress and almost crush the wretched spirit; they may be considered according to the six local positions of bodies: namely, before, behind, above, below, on the right, and on the left [Col. 1841A]. Thus the spirit is tempted from below, from above, from before, from behind, from the right, and from the left.

The lower temptation is contemptible; the upper, wonderful; the front, terrible; the rear, ugly; the right, fleeting; the left, heavy. The lower temptation is the pleasure of the flesh; the upper, the consent of reason; the front, the attack of the demon; the rear, the recollection that calls past things back; the right, prosperity that raises up; the left, adversity that breaks down.

May he who created you, recreated you, and gathered you together so that you might be of one disposition in the house (Ps. 67 [68]) deliver you from these temptations; and may Jesus Christ, our Lord and Judge, raise you from the dust when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

## SERMON L. TO MONKS

[Col. 1841B]

“The Lord is my portion; I have said that I will keep your law” (Ps. 118 [119]). The Prophet has expressed for us with sufficient precision, and without wearisome prolixity, the form of sacred religion: namely, by saying what, under God’s inspiration, he chose and what he promised by vow. “The Lord is my portion”: behold the choice. “I have said that I will keep your law”: behold the profession. Concerning this there is also: “I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness” (ibid.).

By the first a person is initiated into religion; by the second, if it is observed, he ascends to perfection. The first is chosen voluntarily, according to the saying: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. 53 [54]); by the second, in the face of the Church, with angels present and Christ’s vicar standing by, the monk is bound. In these two consists the whole sum of monastic religion and regular discipline, like a great dish in a small vessel.

Let us first consider the choice. Therefore let the cloistered man, the fettered man who has put his feet into the fetters of wisdom, choose the Lord as his own portion—not with other things, not before other things, but him alone without other things—and say: “Others choose other things. Some, pursuing bodily pleasure, live like swine; another stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it. These glory in chariots and those in horses, and are raised up until a pit is dug for the sinner. But you alone are my portion, Lord.”

It is a most wisely ordered exchange to leave all things for him who is above all things. Yet the person who intends to leave all things must remember also to number himself among those things to be left; indeed, he must principally deny himself for the sake of him who emptied himself for our sake (Phil. 2), so that he may safely say with Peter: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19).

He uses sound counsel who chooses to glory in the Lord rather than to delight in the flesh and be tossed about in the world. I suppose he heard and trembled at the voice of him who said: “If you live according to the flesh, you shall die” (Rom. 8). He heard also another saying: “A friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4). Most dangerous indeed is the friendship in which and through which divine offence is incurred.

Considering this, the cloistered man has laid aside the poisonous venom of carnal pleasures and rejected the heavy burden and the ass's millstone of secular affairs. Choosing as his portion God, who is truly good and uniquely sweet, he keeps hard paths for the sake of the words of his lips (Ps. 16 [17]), and enlists in the Lord’s service under the bond of profession.

To conclude briefly, consider in a few words the benefit of your choice.

> [Note: Col. 1841D. St Bernard, *On Counsel*, book I, chapter 4.]

Your choice is prudent, necessary, and secure. It is prudent for choosing what is better: “Cursed is he who has made his portion worse.” But the cloistered man has chosen for himself the best portion, which shall not be taken from him (Luke 10). It is necessary for catching up: for a swift and unencumbered runner is needed by one who would match in running him who “rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18 [19]). You cannot follow one who runs while burdened. It is also secure for living in peace: for if you choose the Lord alone, you do not long after things to be acquired, labour over things acquired, or torment yourself over things lost.

Moreover, you may judge by a brief example how salutary the obligation of profession is. A father has a sick son, who cannot be cured without cutting and cautery. The father asks his son whether he wishes to be bound. Desiring health, the son asks to be bound, cut, and burned. But once bound, when he begins to feel the iron and fire, he cries out, rages, and demands to be released; yet his father does not release him until he is cured.

In this manner the monk has willingly and knowingly bound himself to regular discipline. If he feels any trouble or affliction, he will bear it patiently—things which, after enduring the trial, he will rejoice to have endured. For patience is like Elisha’s meal (2 Kings 4), which knows how to sweeten the bitterness of the whole food, so that there may be no death in the pot.

Moreover, two things are necessary for acquiring patience: comparing the punishment that you endure with the reward that you expect, and remembering the Lord’s Passion. Consider in your heart that the sufferings which you endure are not comparable (Rom. 8), either with past guilt, which is forgiven you, or with future glory, which is promised you. Attending to this, you will endure patiently.

Recall how much your God endured for you. Though he was the Father’s only Son, he died for us lest he remain alone. He purchased brothers for himself with his own blood: he was struck with blows, smeared with spittle, filled with reproaches, crowned with thorns, carrying his cross, counted among criminals, stretched out upon the wood, pierced with nails, and after death wounded by a lance. What monk, considering these things, would not marvel and say: “What shall I repay to the Lord for all that he has repaid to me?” (Ps. 115 [116]). It is shameful for a member to be delicate beneath a thorn-crowned head, to have shining skin beneath the bloodied flesh of Christ.

It remains to speak of the law which you said was to be kept. If you understand this to mean the law of God’s commandments, which is undefiled and converts souls (Ps. 18 [19]), concerning which it is written: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, from your law” (Ps. 93 [94]), then keeping it is necessary for every believer, for everyone who loves life and desires to see good days.

But you have chosen another law for yourself: the apostolic law which the apostles established under the Lord’s inspiration, namely the law of common life. This consists especially in three things: common brotherly love, common property, and common obedience. Of the first it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul in God” (Acts 4).

Of the second: “No one said that anything which he possessed was his own” (ibid.). Of the third: “They laid all things at the apostles’ feet and obeyed them” (ibid.). These three are the head of monastic religion [Col. 1842D]. “Be therefore wise as serpents” (Matt. 10). Guard this head carefully. In these matters no dispensation is possible, nor may a person be obeyed against this principle (Acts 4).

Judas did not preserve brotherly charity, and, hanging himself, burst open in the middle. Ananias and Sapphira sinned against common property, and expired at Peter’s feet (Acts 5).

> [Note: Col. 1842D. Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 36.]

Simon Magus withdrew from the obedience he had undertaken, became a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth, and finally perished with his whole body broken (Acts 8).

In additional observances, however, you may make dispensations by changing, subtracting, or adding; for Lord Benedict added certain ornaments to this head—or, more truly, dug around the barren fig tree that it might bear fruit and put dung upon it that it might bear more fruit. These concern the sparseness of food, the cheapness of clothing, the humility of beds, the times of fasts, the guarding of the lips, the exercise of labours, and the ordering [Col. 1843A] of prayers.

Yet, before this aforesaid foundation and these additional observances, the Rechabites, before Christ’s coming in the flesh, chose desert dwelling and a more austere frugality of life (Jer. 35), drinking the tradition of their father Rechab’s fervour.

> [Note: Col. 1843B. Perhaps: “from the mouth of their father.”]

John the Baptist also left you a pattern of secluded life and an example of more austere living (Matt. 3). Nevertheless, certain vices secretly soften this strictness of the order, as though ratified by the oath of profession, especially if the vice of curiosity boils up—a vice which, worse still, cannot exist alone.

Curiosity openly displayed in the village is shameful; therefore it wishes to cover its head, lest it become cheapened. At times a monk goes out to his relatives under the pretext of health; he returns to his native soil so that for some days he may breathe there the free and familiar air, or perhaps bring back some refreshment from friends for the brethren. At other times, under the pretext of the brethren’s advantage, a monk goes out to the princes of the earth, an importunate petitioner, and calls gain, however acquired, “piety.”

When he returns, he carefully watches the hour of his entrance lest he be obliged to enter at the common table of the brethren or at common prayer. Although he proposes to do this under a pretext of good, the truer reason is that he dislikes the half-cooked and oiled vegetables of the cloister, wine mixed with water, silence, and sitting in the cloister, which he considers a prison. For he desires to eat more elegantly, drink more tastily, speak more freely, lie more softly, keep watch less, and pray more scantily.

But the monk who does not remain in the cloister escapes the vice of curiosity.

> [Note: Col. 1844B. “Escapes” (*evadit*) should read “incurs” (*incurrit*).]

For he suffers a certain itching of the mind and seeks furtive byways for his own will: every day new and elaborate occupations; new tastes in actions or labours; varied readings, not for edification but to deceive [Col. 1844A] the passing day. He goes out more often to guests and, as if sympathizing with the miseries of the poor, inquires about the peace of the princes of the earth. He speaks about the harshness of soldiers and the excesses of clerics, interspersing his discourse with sighs, as though moved with pity for them.

At the sound of the bell he intends to leave because he must; nevertheless, he does not fail to instil into their ears that, should the abbot or prior come, they should remember to commend him to them. This kind of vice is very dangerous; and one must fear lest the man who is such finally become “like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1).

More detestable than this, however, is the vice of singularity. The singular person despises the others and declares that he alone lives religiously. By whispering among the brethren, he supplies kindling for hatred and seedbeds of discord; he secretly disparages some and openly tarnishes the good deeds of others. His hand is against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him. One must fear lest the boar from the wood destroy him [Col. 1844B], and the solitary wild beast devour the solitary man (Ps. 79 [80]).

Against these and similar things, look up to heaven, lifting pure hands in prayer; be diligent guardians of conscience and followers of good works. Follow the royal road of your fathers who went before you, until Jesus Christ, our Lord and Judge, transfers you from the road to the homeland, from contest to palm, and from labour to rest, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

# SOLILOQUIES ON THE INSTRUCTION OF THE SOUL

## BOOK ONE

Prologue. 843  

CHAPTER I.—The religious life is not free from temptations. Nor is this greatly to be wondered at or worried over; rather, all care should be directed to ensuring that the soul is not overcome by temptations. 843  

CHAPTER II.—By meditation on what things, and by what methods and remedies, the violent temptations of the flesh ought to be conquered and subdued by a religious person. 845  

CHAPTER III.—A chapter in which the faults of the brethren are openly declared is hostile only to those deceived by pride and anger; nor should it be called a prison or workhouse, but a gate of paradise and a door of heaven. 847  

CHAPTER IV.—The multitude and severity of commands issued by superiors ought not to disturb a religious person, since the voice of the commanding superior is the voice of God. Finally, it is not a fault to fall short in any commands of superiors, but to despise them, etc. 851  

CHAPTER V.—The greatness and weight of obligation in commands are also to be inferred from the authority of the one commanding. Nothing commanded, whether small or great, is to be despised in these matters. 852  

CHAPTER VI.—The rule of the cloister, which bears heavily upon some who are eager to wander, is holy, useful, beneficial to the soul, and suited to bodily health. 854  

CHAPTER VII.—Divine psalmody ought to be a burden to no one. Rather, effort should be directed toward meditating in the heart upon what we utter with the mouth. 855  

CHAPTER VIII.—It greatly benefits and befits religious men to be engaged from time to time in bodily work, as occasion and necessity require. 855  

CHAPTER IX.—Nothing is more disgraceful or more unworthy of a religious person than pampering the skin, craving refined foods, and finally making the belly one’s god. 856  

CHAPTER X.—Vigils should be highly valued, because they make the soul more fit for the contemplation of divine things. Conversely, a religious person ought to avoid offices that are seedbeds of cares, unless obedience commands otherwise. 857  

CHAPTER XI.—The silence of religious life is like a wall and bulwark, without which the pursuit of true piety cannot long endure. [Col. 1871] 858  

## BOOK TWO

CHAPTER I.—The end for which a religious person entered religious life should be kept continually before his eyes; and he should carefully weigh what he vowed to God in profession. 859  

CHAPTER II.—The form of profession customary in the Premonstratensian Order is set forth, and it is explained what those vow who vow conversion of their manner of life and stability of place. 860  

CHAPTER III.—The remaining matters contained in the same formula of profession are explained, and it is shown how dangerous and serious is the sin of private ownership in religious persons who have professed renunciation of what is their own. Further, it teaches what obedience is owed to superiors and what constitutes the sounder party when electing a prelate. 863  

CHAPTER IV.—How the manifold transgressions of vows and of the divine law ought to be expiated; to whom sins are to be confessed, etc. 865  

CHAPTER V.—It is shown at length that the sins of religious persons ought to be confessed only to their own prelates, and that no one should easily be deterred from this by fear of disclosure and disgrace. 866  

CHAPTER VI.—Nothing is more necessary in religious life than mutual love between prelates and subjects. What should be thought about private works of piety? 869  

CHAPTER VII.—Conclusion of the work, in which every religious person is commanded to be fervent, constant in every good work, humble, and holy, etc. 870
